documents.abstract: Reports safe arrival in Rostock, plans to winter in the Jurists' College for observations, and urges the recipient to keep the reasons for his departure secret.
documents.incipit: CHARISSIME Domine JOHANNES, scias me incolumem huc pervenisse Rostochium, ipsis Calendis …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD JOHANNEM AALBURGENSEM DATÆ 14. IANUARII 1568.

CHARISSIME Domine JOHANNES, scias me incolumem huc pervenisse Rostochium, ipsis Calendis Januarij, et interea temporis, apud D. LEVINUM, hospitio exceptum fuisse: hodie vero, Deo annuente et prosperante, in propriam quandam habitationem migrare constitui, quæ est in Juristarum Collegio, satis commoda, et observationibus cœlestibus, meisque desideriis apta. Illic, si Deo ita visum fuerit, hanc hiemem transigere constitui; quid deinceps futurum sit, dies dabit, et Domino illa prospicienda relinquo, admonitus hoc sapienti et veteri versu:

Tu præsens cura, Domino committe futura.

Tuum vero est, mi JOHANNES, eas, quas tibi nostri discessus concredidi causas, in alto silentio apud te sepelire, ne quis suspicetur, vel intelligat, me de quoquam quidquam conqueri, aut aliquid in patria fuisse, quod me ad discedendum impulerit. Id etenim permagni interest, ut nemo audiat, me de ulla re conqueri; uti etiam revera de multis conqueri non possum. Fui enim in patria ab omnibus consanguineis et amicis, praeter meritum, bene exceptus, id solo deficiente, quod non omnibus placuerint mea exercitia: idque suam meretur excusationem. Multus delator ubique est.

Tycho Brahe
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Johannes of Aalborg [Hans Aalborg], dated 14 January 1568.**

Dearest Master Johannes, know that I have reached Rostock here safe and sound, on the very Kalends of January [1 January], and that in the meantime I was taken in as a guest at the house of Master Levinus. Today, however — God assenting and granting it to prosper — I have resolved to move into lodgings of my own, in the Jurists' College, commodious enough, and well suited to celestial observations and to my own wishes. There, if it shall so seem good to God, I have resolved to pass this winter; what is to be hereafter, the day will bring, and I leave those things for the Lord to look to, mindful of that wise old verse:

*Tend thou to the present; commit the future to the Lord.*

But it falls to you, my Johannes, to bury in deep silence within yourself those reasons for my departure that I confided to you — lest anyone suspect, or come to understand, that I am complaining of anyone about anything, or that there was something in my homeland that drove me to leave. For it is of the very greatest importance that no one hear that I complain of any matter — just as, in truth, I cannot complain of much. For in my homeland I was well received, beyond my deserts, by all my kinsmen and friends; the one thing wanting was that my pursuits did not please everyone — and that deserves its own excuse. There is many an informer everywhere.

Tycho Brahe

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** *Johannes Aalburgensis* = **Hans Aalborg**, an associate from Tycho's circle; the Latinised toponymic ("of Aalborg") is kept with the identification.
- ***ipsis Calendis Januarij*** — "on the very Kalends of January" = **1 January** (Roman-calendar idiom; Julian / Old Style). Rendered with the idiom and glossed.
- ***in Juristarum Collegio*** — the **Jurists' College (Juristen-Kollegium)** at the University of Rostock, where Tycho had matriculated; an institutional name, not a generic "college of lawyers."
- ***D. Levinum*** — "Master Levinus," Tycho's first host at Rostock; not further identified here.
- ***Tu praesens cura, Domino committe futura*** — a rhymed proverbial (leonine) verse; rendered as verse, preserving the imperative parallelism *cura … committe*.
- ***delator*** — "informer / denouncer," carrying its Roman-legal sting; deliberately stronger than "gossip." The closing *Multus delator ubique est* is sententious — "There is many an informer everywhere."
- **Register.** Private, confidential letter (Tycho asks Aalborg to keep the reasons for his leaving Denmark secret); the courtesy is warm but plain. No technical content.

documents.abstract: Acknowledges a letter of consolation on his father's death and reflects on theological and philosophical sources of comfort available to him.
documents.incipit: LITERAS tuas plenas dulcissimis consolationibus, quæ me ob Patris charissimi ex hac vita …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD ANDREAM SEVERINI VELLEJUM. S.

LITERAS tuas plenas dulcissimis consolationibus, quæ me ob Patris charissimi ex hac vita discessum magnis doloribus consternatum, non parum refecerunt, accepi et legi, quas etsi optarem de alia materia scribi potuisse, tamen illa quia præter omnium spem contigerat, gratæ mihi admodum fuêre, et licet multæ sint consolationes Theologicæ ex divinis sacrarum literarum oraculis petitæ, et Philosophicæ ex sorte communi hominum et sublunarium rerum instabilitate et vicissitudine perpetua desumtæ, quibus mentem afflictam et mæstam erigo, tamen non possum non summam consolationem inde capere, quod Pater tam suaviter et pie ex hac miseranda mortalium miseria migravit in cœlestem et perpetuam patriam, vbi firmam mansionem et civitatem teste Paulo habemus, hîc autem omnes sumus exules. Vix enim satis scribi potest, quanta fiducia et quanta levitate diem obijt. Nam cum eodem die (qui erat 9. Maij) ante meridiem assumsisset corpus et sanguinem filii Dei in Pane et Vino juxta testamentum et institutionem Christi Salvatoris nostri et se Sacræ scripturæ dictis adversus mortis terrores et conscientiæ dolores magna cum fiducia munivisset, dormivit inde vsque in tempus meridianum vel paulo ultra, tunc demum experrectus indicia dedit iam instantis agonis, quare omnes consternati accurrimus, advocanturque verbi divini ministri, qui eum consolarentur, et tunc incepit quasi obdormiscere; apertis demum oculis cum videret nos mæstos et lacrymantes lectum circumstantes, quæsivit, an aliqua indicia in eo mortis viderentur, ajebat enim se non tantos dolores sentire, quin prius longe majores perpessus sit: quidam nostrum responderunt, illum esse admodum debilem, et nos timere, ne posset evadere; respondit: Igitur sinite me primum loqui cum vxore; qua adducta semimortua, habita ad eam gratiarum actione, quod tam bene et honeste secum in hac vita vixerit, ei valedixit, nobisque liberis et alijs amicis eius curam commendavit, postea rursus clausis parum oculis concionatoris consolationes auscultavit, qui cum multa prolixe diceret, ipse demum apertis oculis hæc verba protulit: Vnum adhuc loqui volo: Dicitne Dominus ipse: Nolo mortem peccatoris sed potius vt convertatur et vivat. Hoc fine clausit ipsemet oculos et tam suaviter expiravit, ut dubitaverint adstantes, an mortuus fuerit, solebat enim multo durius dormire quam tunc moriebatur, et in ipso agone nec corpus nec pedes nec brachia vel manus aut caput semel de loco movebat, sed ita placide et suaviter obdormiebat, quod ipsi concionatores testati fuerint, se nunquam placidiorem exitum ullius hominis vidisse. Hic igitur felix et bonus Patris obitus me plurimum in doloribus erigit et propterea etiam copiosius de eo scripsi, quod ipsa recordatio me quasi reficiat, et non dubito te haud illubenter et sine tædio hæc lecturum, iudico enim, nos hîc tum demum bene vixisse, cum bene morimur. Laboravit autem durissime, ut scis, morbo, quem illi Hyposarca existimaverunt esse, ego Hydropem ex pulmone, nam erat ei difficilis anhelitus, tussis gravissima, tumor varrusque pedis maximus usque ad illa in brachijs macilentus, et quasi in ijs absumebatur, ut vulgariter loquar. Postremo his omnibus malis supervenit febris tertiana acutissima, in cuius tertio paroxysmo extinguebatur die 9. huius mensis, ut dixi, inter primam et 2dam pomeridianam in ipso puncto plenilunij. Æternus Deus eius animæ sit (vt est) misericors et det nobis omnibus felicem et salutarem ex hac calamitosa vita discessum propter filium mediatorem, Amen. Charissime M. ANDREA, scribis, ut mittam tibi aquam quandam febribus curandis appropriatam, quam licet non habeam, nec scio te talem apud me vidisse, tamen non intermittam, quin vobis remedium non minus bonum quam certum et facile in tollendis febribus communicem, quod ab optimo amico Medico, qui hac ratione omnes febres excepta quartana sustulit, vix impetrare potui, licet ei quatuor secreta eius loco docueram. Id autem est tale: Accipe æquales partes ex his duabus herbis Centaurea et Carduobenedicta et decoque in aqua alterius harum stillatitia vel aqua Cichoreæ aut etiam communi, demum huic decocto adde pulveris aliquid de inferiori mandibula Lupi piscis, et da ante paroxysinum, nec revela omnibus hanc medicinam, licet admodum levem et facilem, in effectu tamen certum et mirabile. Curantur etiam multi portantes in collo vivam araneam magnam testæ nucis inclusam, donec moriatur, idque remedio magnetico, hoc etiam vti potes. Scio autem alia secreta et certa remedia in tollendis febribus cuiusque generis, sed ea potius præsens communicare volo, si opus erit, quam literis scribere. Bene vale. Cantilenas remitto, iam enim potius est tempus flendi quam canendi. Saluta M. JOH. THOMÆ meo nomine.

Helsb. 18. Maij Anno 71.
Tycho Brahe
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Anders Sørensen Vedel. Greeting.**

I have received and read your letter, full of the sweetest consolations, which refreshed me not a little when I was stricken with great grief at my dearest father's departure out of this life; and although I could wish it had been possible for it to be written on some other matter, yet, because that [grief] had befallen me beyond all expectation, [your words] were exceedingly welcome to me. And although there are many consolations — theological, sought from the divine oracles of Holy Scripture, and philosophical, drawn from the common lot of mankind and from the instability of sublunary things and their perpetual vicissitude — with which I lift up my afflicted and grieving mind, yet I cannot but take the greatest consolation from this: that my father so gently and piously passed out of this pitiable wretchedness of mortals into the heavenly and everlasting homeland, where, on Paul's witness, we have a firm dwelling and a city, while here we are all exiles. For it can scarcely be written sufficiently with how great confidence and with how great lightness he met his day [of death]. For when on that same day (which was 9 May), before noon, he had received the body and blood of the Son of God in Bread and Wine, according to the testament and institution of Christ our Saviour, and had fortified himself with great confidence by the sayings of Holy Scripture against the terrors of death and the pains of conscience, he then slept until midday or a little beyond; then at last, waking, he gave signs of the death-struggle now at hand, whereupon we all ran up in dismay, and the ministers of the divine word were called to console him; and then he began as it were to fall asleep. At last, his eyes opened, when he saw us sad and weeping standing about the bed, he asked whether any signs of death were to be seen in him — for he said that he did not feel pains so great but that he had endured far greater before; some of us answered that he was very weak, and that we feared he might not recover. He replied: "Then let me first speak with my wife." When she had been brought, half-dead [with grief], and he had given her thanks for having lived with him so well and honourably in this life, he bade her farewell, and commended her to the care of us children and of his other friends; afterward, his eyes again a little closed, he listened to the preacher's consolations, and when the man spoke many things at length, he himself at last, opening his eyes, uttered these words: "One thing more I wish to say. Does not the Lord himself say: *I desire not the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live?*" With this ending he himself closed his eyes and so gently breathed his last that the bystanders doubted whether he had died — for he used to sleep much more heavily than he then was dying, and in the very death-agony he did not once move his body, nor feet, nor arms or hands or head from their place, but so peacefully and gently fell asleep that the preachers themselves bore witness that they had never seen a more peaceful end of any man. This happy and good death of my father, then, lifts me greatly in my griefs, and for that reason too I have written of it more copiously, because the very recollection as it were refreshes me; and I do not doubt that you will read these things not unwillingly and without weariness, for I judge that we have here lived well only then, when we die well. Now he laboured most grievously, as you know, under a disease which they reckoned to be anasarca [general dropsy], but I [reckoned to be] dropsy of the lung, for his breathing was difficult, his cough most severe, and there was a very great swelling and inflammation of the foot, while in those [other parts], in the arms, he was emaciated and was, so to speak, being consumed in them, to put it in common terms. Last of all, upon all these evils there supervened a most acute tertian fever, in whose third paroxysm he was extinguished on the 9th of this month, as I said, between one and two o'clock in the afternoon, at the very point of the full moon. May the eternal God be merciful to his soul (as he is), and grant to us all a happy and salutary departure out of this calamitous life, for the sake of the Son, the mediator. Amen. Dearest Master Anders, you write that I should send you a certain water suited for curing fevers; although I have none, nor do I know that you saw such a thing in my keeping, yet I shall not fail to share with you a remedy no less good than sure and easy for the removal of fevers, which I could scarcely obtain from an excellent friend, a physician, who by this method has removed all fevers except the quartan, though I had taught him four secrets of mine in its stead. It is as follows: Take equal parts of these two herbs, centaury and blessed thistle, and boil [them] in the distilled water of one of these, or in water of chicory, or even in common water; then to this decoction add a little powder from the lower jaw of the wolf-fish [Lupus piscis], and give it before the paroxysm; and do not reveal this medicine to everyone, for though it is very slight and easy, it is nonetheless in its effect sure and wonderful. Many too are cured by carrying at the neck a large live spider enclosed in a nutshell, until it dies — and that by a magnetic [sympathetic] remedy; this also you can use. I know, moreover, other secret and sure remedies for removing fevers of every kind, but I would rather share these in person, if there be need, than write them in a letter. Fare you well. I send back the songs, for now it is rather a time for weeping than for singing. Greet Master Johan Thomesen in my name.

Helsingborg, 18 May, year [15]71.
Tycho Brahe

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), writing at age 24. *Andreas Severini Vellejus* = **Anders Sørensen Vedel** (1542–1616), the Danish historian, royal chaplain, and ballad-collector — Tycho's close friend; the address-form is the standard Latinization.
- **Occasion.** The death of Tycho's father, **Otte Brahe** (Latin *Pater*) of Knudstrup, on 9 May 1571; the letter is at once a consolatory reply and a *deathbed narration* (the *ars moriendi* form), followed by a fever-remedy at Vedel's request.
- ***teste Paulo … firmam mansionem et civitatem … exules*** — "on Paul's witness … a firm dwelling and a city … exiles": an allusion to Hebrews 11:9–16 / 13:14 (the patriarchs as strangers and pilgrims seeking "a city"); the Pauline attribution of Hebrews is Tycho's own (period-standard) and is preserved, not corrected.
- ***Nolo mortem peccatoris sed potius ut convertatur et vivat*** — Otte's dying words, quoting **Ezekiel 33:11** (Vulgate): "I desire not the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live." Kept as the quotation it is (italicised in translation).
- **Eucharistic / Lutheran register.** *corpus et sanguinem filii Dei in Pane et Vino juxta testamentum et institutionem Christi* — the explicitly Lutheran sacramental formula (real presence "in Bread and Wine"); rendered straight.
- **Medicine.** *Hyposarca* = **anasarca (general dropsy)** — the diagnosis "they" (the attending physicians) gave; *Hydrops ex pulmone* = "dropsy of the lung" — Tycho's own differing diagnosis (the hedge "I [reckoned]" preserved; he is offering a competing opinion, not asserting fact). *febris tertiana acutissima* = "a most acute **tertian fever**"; *tertio paroxysmo* = "the third **paroxysm**." *quartana* = the **quartan fever**, which the remedy below does *not* cure.
- ***tumor varrusque pedis*** — "swelling and inflammation of the foot." *varrus* here is read as *var(us)/varix*-type inflammation/eruption of the foot (a cutaneous/varicose swelling) rather than the orthopaedic *varus*; the precise pathological referent is uncertain — see crux below.
- **The fever recipe.** *Centaurea* = **centaury**; *Carduobenedicta* (= *Carduus benedictus*) = **blessed thistle**; *aqua stillatitia* = **distilled water**; *aqua Cichoreae* = water of chicory; *decoctum* = **decoction**. *de inferiori mandibula Lupi piscis* = "from the lower jaw of the **wolf-fish**" — *Lupus piscis*, an early-modern materia-medica ingredient (the jawbone/tooth of a fish called *lupus*, variously the European seabass or the wolffish/*Anarhichas*); the species is not securely fixed by the text and is left as "wolf-fish [*Lupus piscis*]." To be given *ante paroxysmum* ("before the paroxysm/fit").
- ***remedio magnetico*** — the **magnetic (sympathetic) remedy**: the live spider worn at the neck in a nutshell until it dies, a period sympathetic-magic febrifuge. Rendered by this chapter's convention — *not* modernised to "placebo"; the worldview is preserved.
- ***Cantilenas remitto … tempus flendi quam canendi*** — "I send back the songs … a time for weeping rather than for singing": Vedel had evidently lent or sent songs/ballads (*cantilenae* — apt for the ballad-collector); Tycho's reply echoes Ecclesiastes 3:4 ("a time to weep … a time to mourn"). Kept as the allusion it is.
- ***M. JOH. THOMAe*** = **Master Johan Thomesen** (Johannes Thomae), to be greeted; a mutual acquaintance, otherwise unspecified in the letter. *M.* = *Magister* ("Master," academic,).
- **Calendar / place.** *Helsb. 18. Maij Anno 71* = "**Helsingborg**, 18 May, [15]71" (O.S. — Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The internal date of the death, *9 Maij … in ipso puncto plenilunij* ("9 May … at the very point of the full moon"), is reproduced as written and **not** astronomically checked or "corrected" by this chapter's convention; Tycho's pairing of the civil time (between 1 and 2 p.m.) with the syzygy is itself of interest and is left to stand.
- **Witness.** The edition records a single witness, a contemporary copy (*afskrift*) in Tycho Brahe's private archive, Rigsarkivet, Copenhagen; the edition of record is Dreyer, *Opera Omnia*.

Joh. Thomae / Johan Thomesen). All match Dreyer and are rendered accurately. No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found. documents.abstract: Acknowledges three letters from Tycho, congratulates him on newfound independence after his father's death, and offers cautious advice on a planned threefold journey.
documents.incipit: TERNAS ab Excellentia T. literas, εὐτυχέστατε Τυχών, mihi gratissimas et iucundissimas …

text.original:
VERA NOBILITATE ET DIVINÆ MATHESEOS COGNITIONE ORNATISSIMO D. TYCHONI BRAHEO, OTTONIDI, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO COLENDO, S.

TERNAS ab Excellentia T. literas, εὐτυχέστατε Τυχών, mihi gratissimas et iucundissimas accepi, tum quod res patriæ et tuas secundas nunciabant, tum quod singulare mei studium, quo plurimum delector, præ se ferebant. Etsi enim Patris obitum natura moleste, eundem tamen moderate ferre Philosophia iubet, eoque magis, quod iam tui iuris factus, Aula Cyclopica tanquam Scylla et Charybdi evitata, tibi et Musis, ac potius Christo vivendi summam facultatem habes: qua cordato quidem homini quid queat esse optatius? In deliberatione tua de peregrinatione triplici, meum non est prudentiæ tuæ quicquam præscribere, et alia fortasse iuvenibus, alia senibus consilia sunt aptiora. Sed tamen si tuo essem loco, qui et opibus et dignitate præstes, et ætate sis integra, de coniugio cogitarem, et re familiari tutanda et propaganda ad posteros, nisi si forte certis de causis hoc consilium tibi displicet. Sit tibi Philosophia et divina Mathesis uxoris loco, donec ijs hanc adiungere lubuerit. Tibi quidem domi tuæ Hippocentauri isti negotijs multis a tuo animo alienis molestias facessunt, quas si sustinere non potes et semitam virtutis præcludere animadverteris, non inconsulte feceris, si loci mutatione tales enormitates devitaveris: Et si tunc omnino extra patriam evagari stat sententia, per Belgium et Gallias in Italiam transibis, eaque perlustrata, Augustam petes, nosque denuo invises rediturus in patriam. Rursus itaque tunc (nisi annus hic climactericus me sustulerit) consuetudine tua liberali et omnis eruditionis plena nostraque amicitia præsens denuo fruar, quibus plurimum dolui me destitutum post discessum hunc tuum, a quo gravia interea passus sum. 23. Novemb. superiore periculum magnum sustinui. Hoc autem anno 10. Aprilis nescio quo malo infortunio cecidi graviter de gradibus sive scalis, quibus ascenditur ad Musæum meum, et deturbatus sum usque ad imum pavimentum in novis his ædibus, quas conduxi a D. AMBROSIO, quem nosti, eratque tantum præcipitium, ut cruento capite et dorso pene fracto ægre resurgens diu Chirurgi opera sim usus. Accesserunt et turbæ domesticæ perfidia quorundam, quos mihi amicos putavi, et sumtus reditibus majores, cum sordide potius quam splendide vivam, æs alienum inaudita apud nos annonæ charitate, mihi attulerunt.

Valetudo autem, ut fert ingravescens ætas, subinde ruit in deterius, in primis vero me excruciat Lithiasis et Chiragra, quæ vereor, ne mihi propediem scribendi facultatem sit ademtura. Nescio quæ directio in mea Genesi mihi tanta mala circa hæc tempora portendat. Forte Ascendens meum nunc venit ad corpus Martis in ♉ signo terrestri, prout tu eius locum correxisti, de quo mihi antea nescio quid mali ominatus es, postquam meam Genesin aliter verificasti, quam a CYPRIANO LEOVITIO factum est, et præteritos casus convenientius adaptasti, ubi etiam de futuris nonnulla mihi rectius prædixisti, et cuperem, ut et nunc eandem per otium inspicere velles et de pluribus præmonere. Suades, ut labores et molestias minuam, quod et amice et prudenter suades: idque mihi facere necesse est, præsertim a Typographicis ærumnis liberato. Otium vero hoc iucunde collocare mihi non licet, amicis, quorum consuetudine fruerer, destituto. Nullum enim habeo hîc, postquam tu nos reliquisti, cum quo suaviter converser atque tempus eruditis colloquijs fallam, hoc est, non invenio hominem doctum, ingeniosum, consultum, gravem pariter ac facetum, humanum et candidum, qualis tu nobis fuisti, ceteri omnes aut honores affectant, aut quæstui aut uxoribus, quin et omnibus hisce simul, aliisque huiuscemodi dant operam et ijs ferme solis vivunt. Oportet itaque sortem meam patienter ferre, donec ab hoc ergastulo liberer. Deus Opt. Max. Excell. Tuæ vitam diutinam et florentem conservet atque eandem pietate, sapientia, doctrina adaugeat, quæ, uti scis, vera bona sunt, superantia ea, quæ vulgus affectat. Indica nobis per otium, quid in Astronomicis nunc moliaris, et an hæc sublimia studia continuare animus sit; neque tamen dubito, te in ijs, quæ ad veram gloriam atque durabilem ducunt, constanter permansurum. Salutant te ambo fratres HAINZELIJ tui amantissimi plurimum et officiose.

Vale.
Idib. Novemb. An. 1571. Augustæ Vindelicorum.
E. Tuæ studiosiss.
Hieronymus Wolfius.
text.english:
**To Master Tycho Brahe, son of Otte, most richly adorned with true nobility and with the knowledge of the divine science of mathematics, his lord and friend to be honoured — greeting.**

I have received three letters from Your Excellency, O most fortunate Tycho [εὐτυχέστατε Τυχών], most welcome and most delightful to me — both because they reported that affairs at home and your own were prospering, and because they bore witness to your singular regard for me, in which I take the greatest pleasure. For although nature [bids us] bear a father's death with grief, yet Philosophy bids us bear it with moderation — and the more so since now, become your own master, with the Cyclopean Court avoided as if it were Scylla and Charybdis, you have the fullest freedom to live for yourself and the Muses, or rather for Christ: and to a sensible man what could be more to be wished than that? In your deliberation about a threefold journey it is not for me to prescribe anything to your prudence, and perhaps some counsels are fitter for the young, others for the old. Yet were I in your place — you who excel in both wealth and rank, and are in the prime of life — I would think of marriage, and of safeguarding your estate and carrying it on to posterity, unless perhaps for particular reasons this advice displeases you. Let Philosophy and the divine science of mathematics stand to you in a wife's place, until it shall please you to add a wife to them. At home, to be sure, those Hippocentaurs of yours plague you with many affairs foreign to your disposition; and if you cannot endure them, and perceive that they bar your path of virtue, you will act not unwisely if by a change of place you escape such monstrous troubles. And if then your mind is set on roaming quite outside your homeland, you will pass through the Low Countries and France into Italy, and, having surveyed it, make for Augsburg, and visit us again on your way home. So then once more (unless this climacteric year carries me off) I shall enjoy in person your liberal company, full of all learning, and our friendship — of which I grieved bitterly to be bereft after this departure of yours, since which I have meanwhile suffered grave misfortunes. On 23 November last I came through a great danger. And this year, on 10 April, by I know not what evil mischance, I fell heavily down the steps or stairs by which one climbs to my study, and was hurled right to the very floor, in these new lodgings I have rented from Master Ambrosius, whom you know; and the fall was so great that, my head bloodied and my back all but broken, scarcely rising again, I had to use a surgeon's care for a long time. There were added, too, domestic upheavals through the treachery of certain men whom I had reckoned my friends; and expenses greater than my income — though I live meanly rather than splendidly — brought me into debt, amid an unheard-of dearth of provisions among us.

My health, moreover, as advancing age brings, keeps sliding into the worse; and above all the stone [lithiasis] and gout of the hand [chiragra] torment me, which I fear will shortly rob me of the power of writing. I do not know what direction in my geniture portends such great evils for me around this time. Perhaps my ascendant is now coming to the body of Mars in ♉ Taurus, an earthy sign, as you corrected its place — concerning which you earlier foreboded some evil to me, after you had verified my geniture otherwise than Cyprian Leowitz had done, and fitted my past circumstances more aptly, where too you predicted some things about the future more correctly; and I could wish that now too you would be willing to examine it at your leisure and forewarn me of more. You advise me to lessen my labours and troubles, which you advise both as a friend and wisely; and this I must do, especially now that I am freed from the drudgery of the press. Yet I am not permitted to spend this leisure pleasantly, robbed of the friends in whose company I might delight. For since you left us I have here no one with whom I may converse agreeably and beguile the time in learned discourse — that is, I find no man learned, ingenious, judicious, at once weighty and witty, humane and candid, such as you were to us; all the rest either court honours, or give themselves to gain or to wives — indeed to all these at once, and to others of the kind — and live for these almost alone. And so I must bear my lot patiently, until I am freed from this house of toil. May God, Best and Greatest, keep Your Excellency's life long and flourishing, and increase it in piety, wisdom, and learning — which, as you know, are the true goods, surpassing those the common crowd pursues. Let me know at your leisure what you are now undertaking in astronomy, and whether your mind is to continue these lofty studies; though I do not doubt that you will steadfastly persevere in those things that lead to true and lasting glory. Both the Hainzel brothers, who love you most dearly, send you their warmest and most dutiful greetings.

Farewell.
On the Ides of November [13 November], the year 1571, at Augsburg.
Most devoted to Your Excellency,
Hieronymus Wolf.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Hieronymus Wolfius* = **Hieronymus Wolf** (1516–1580), the Augsburg humanist and Greek scholar (the "father of Byzantine studies"), then directing the city's library and school; an early mentor-friend of Tycho's from his Augsburg years (1569–70).
- ***Ottonides*** — "son of Otte," a Greek-style patronymic for **Otte Brahe**, Tycho's father, who had died (the letter consoles Tycho on it).
- **Greek:** *εὐτυχέστατε Τυχών* — "O most fortunate Tycho," a learned pun on Tycho's name (Greek *eu-tychḗs* "fortunate," *týchē* "fortune"); transliterated and glossed, the wordplay flagged rather than flattened.
- ***Aula Cyclopica … Scylla et Charybdi*** — "the Cyclopean Court … Scylla and Charybdis": Wolf congratulates Tycho on escaping court service (the boorish "Cyclopes" of the court) for scholarship; the classical imagery is kept.
- ***Hippocentauri isti*** — "those Hippocentaurs of yours," a contemptuous metaphor for the half-civilised people burdening Tycho at home with estate business; kept as metaphor.
- ***peregrinatione triplici*** — "a threefold journey" (the three-part travel plan Tycho had evidently described: the Low Countries → France → Italy, then back via Augsburg).
- **Astrology.** *directio in mea Genesi* = "a *direction* in my *geniture*" (a predictive technique applied to Wolf's natal figure); *Ascendens … ad corpus Martis in ♉ signo terrestri* = "the ascendant coming to the body of Mars in Taurus, an earthy sign"; *meam Genesin … verificasti … quam a Cypriano Leovitio* — Tycho had re-cast (corrected) Wolf's horoscope more accurately than **Cyprian Leowitz** (Cyprianus Leovitius, 1524–1574, the celebrated astrologer-astronomer) had. The glyph ♉ is kept in the source and named "Taurus" in the translation, by this chapter's convention
- **Medicine.** *Lithiasis* = the stone; *Chiragra* = gout of the hand — both period terms, glossed.
- ***annus climactericus*** — a **climacteric year** (an astrologically critical year, at multiples of seven); Wolf (then 55) fears it may kill him.
- ***Typographicis aerumnis*** — "the toils of the press": Wolf's heavy editorial/printing labours (notably his Greek editions for the Augsburg presses).
- ***Musaeum meum*** — "my study" (the *Museum*, scholar's workroom), not a public museum.
- ***ergastulo*** — literally a slaves' workhouse/prison; here a metaphor for his wearisome life, rendered "this house of toil."
- ***fratres Hainzelii*** — the **Hainzel brothers**, Johann Baptist and **Paul Hainzel** of Augsburg, patrician patrons of astronomy; with Paul Hainzel, Tycho had built a great 19-foot quadrant at Göppingen in 1569.
- **Dateline.** *Idib. Novemb. … Augustae Vindelicorum* = "the Ides of November (13 Nov.), … at Augsburg" (O.S.).

text.original:
VIRO NOBILI TYCHONI BRAHE, DOMINO ET AMICO OBSERVANDISSIMO.
VERNAS SALUTES, CHEIROS ET MELISSAS.

RECEPI literas tuas, amicissime TYCHO, quas magna cum voluptate legi. Obsecro, dum illas funderes, quis te Olympicus radius tinxit, ut me quoque eadem tinctura figeres? An te sacrum Veneris sulphur, an Bacchi aethereus Mercurius, an dium illud Apollinis sal ab antiquis celebratum afflavit? Non sint mihi Urania et Vulcanus propitij, si isto extemporaneo flumine meum delectaveris plurimum. Non semper praemeditata aut digesta diu felicius cadunt. Extemporanea et impetuosa esse illa necesse est, quae momento solidum penetrantia, penetrata in sui naturam convertunt: ut patres nos nostri et fulmina utriusque Meteorologiae docuerunt. Ubi Soli, quem colo, sacrificabo, supplex ipse precabor, saepius ut tali te calore percellat. Macte sis atque hac mentis sublimitate, paucis cognita, cresce, donec te Iovis armiger ales in solium magni referat Iovis, unde ruinas labantis possis informes cernere mundi. Quod si fieri debet, utique fugiendus Gheburah et malum Aquilo: Auster bonus quaerendus est et vitalis Oriens, ubi vitam, donum et talentum, quod nobis concreditum est, recepimus. Hic Auster Oriensque nec locorum astringitur miserijs, nec certam ad plagam mundi sensibilis declinat: Ubique sunt: intra, extra omnia: in antiqua Iliade, in thesauris Universi, in abyssis animorum: imo intrate; hoc multis quaesitum Latium et Saturnium regnum. Non igitur versus Austrum sensibilem quaerenda illa Olympicae civitatis civilitas: nisi quatenus rigida Septentrio, tantum non tuleris, uti etiam forte non semper feret splendorem, tantumque donum, vel te ipso (quod saepius inaudivi) vate atque interprete. Neque tamen hic, in quo spiramus, Aquilo solus formidatam Barbariem alit. Etenim in extremo Oriente Austroque animas Boreae penetrabile frigus etiam nonnunquam adurit, et latus hoc mundi, quod nebulae malusque Iupiter urget, amoena quoque temperie perfundi dubium non est: illis tamen solis cognita, qui supra temporis et locorum Horizontem lumen intuentur. Profanum itaque sit voluptatis hortum temporum locorumve carceribus includere. Rident hasce exuvias maculis purgatae Lunae et nitentes Berilli. Nosce te ipsum et omnia noveris. In hanc dioptram respicientem nunquam te turbida fallet imago. Hactenus silentia: nunc verbum unum. Venit hisce diebus ad nos Coloniâ imperterritus ille Danus Wiburgensis, cuius apud te saepenumero mentio facta est, Graecus, Arabs, Galenicus, Paracelsicus, Theologaster, Philosophus, Medicus, Syrupiaster, Chymista, et plus, si velles: interim tamen ex his omnibus nihil. Hic Wiburgiam invisurus diu non visit senem parentem, heri profectus est, rediturus ad nos brevi. Conditionem philosophicam captat, aptam Spagiricis pulveribus et sudore Chymico. Est mirabilis Apothecarius: tibi, modo frugi esse velit, non displicebit. Si animus tibi est talem aliquem servitio adiungere, procul dubio in patria et extra patriam utilis tibi esse poterit. Ubi hominem ipse videris, fronte tecum loquetur. Interea si ipse brevi huc non concesseris, de hoc ipso negotio rescribe verbum unum. Sed audi, Nymphas sylvestres violasse te Nympharum Amatores narrant: evulsis sacris quercubus et late minitantibus alnis, vitaque privatis arboribus: quoniam hae dolent, quod morte sua (quam illis te intulisse toties ajebas) alijs sepultis digestisque rebus, vitam calore non posse excitare per te prohibeantur. Certe ut in Austrum vel Occidentem ad nos perferantur ratibus, in medio Aquilone non deerunt Aquilones.

Vale; et si coronam vernam expetis, Nymphas placa.
Hafniae 7. Maij Anno 1572.
T.
Pratensis
text.english:
**To the noble Tycho Brahe, his most esteemed lord and friend.**
**Vernal greetings — of hands and of bees [CHEIROS ET MELISSAS].**

I have received your letter, dearest Tycho, which I read with great delight. I beg you — while you were pouring it out, what Olympian ray steeped you, that you should fix me too with the same tincture? Was it the sacred sulphur of Venus, or the ethereal Mercury of Bacchus, or that divine salt of Apollo celebrated by the ancients, that breathed upon you? May Urania and Vulcan be no longer favourable to me, if you have not delighted mine exceedingly with that extemporaneous flood. Things long premeditated or digested do not always fall out more happily. Those things must of necessity be extemporaneous and impetuous which, penetrating a solid body in a moment, once penetrated convert it into their own nature — as our fathers, and the thunderbolts of both Meteorologies, have taught us. When I sacrifice to the Sun, whom I worship, I shall as a suppliant pray that he may smite you more often with such heat. Be blessed, and with this sublimity of mind — known to few — grow, until the winged armour-bearer of Jove bears you back into the throne of great Jove, whence you may discern the shapeless ruins of the tottering world. But if this must come to pass, then by all means Gheburah and the evil North Wind are to be shunned: the good South Wind is to be sought, and the life-giving East, where we received life, that gift and talent which has been entrusted to us. This South and East are neither bound by the miseries of places, nor do they decline toward any fixed quarter of the sensible world: they are everywhere — within, without, in all things: in the ancient Iliad, in the treasuries of the Universe, in the depths of souls; nay, enter in — this is the Latium and the realm of Saturn sought by many. Not, therefore, toward the sensible South is that civility of the Olympian city to be sought — except in so far as you cannot bear the rigid North, just as perhaps it too will not always bear the splendour and so great a gift, even with yourself (as I have often heard tell) as seer and interpreter. And yet not here alone, where we breathe, does the North Wind nourish the dreaded Barbarism. For even in the farthest East and South the penetrating cold of Boreas now and then scorches souls; and that this side of the world, which mists and an evil Jupiter beset, is also bathed in a pleasant temperateness, there is no doubt — yet known to those alone who gaze upon the light above the Horizon of time and place. Let it therefore be a profanation to shut up the garden of delight within the prisons of times or places. At these cast-off skins the Moon, cleansed of her spots, and the gleaming Beryls, smile. Know thyself, and thou shalt know all things. To one who looks back into this lens [dioptra] no turbid image shall ever deceive him. So much for silences: now one word. There came to us these past days from Cologne that undaunted Dane of Viborg, of whom mention has often been made in your presence — a Greek, an Arab, a Galenist, a Paracelsian, a sham theologian, a philosopher, a physician, a syrup-monger, a chymist, and more, if you would; yet meanwhile, out of all these, nothing. He, [meaning] to visit Viborg, has long not visited his aged parent; he set out yesterday, [meaning] to return to us shortly. He is angling for a philosophical post, suited to spagyric powders and chymical sweat. He is a marvellous apothecary: he will not displease you — provided he be willing to be honest. If you have a mind to attach some such man to your service, beyond doubt he could be useful to you both at home and abroad. When you see the man yourself, he will speak with you face to face [from his very brow]. Meanwhile, if you yourself do not come hither shortly, write back one word about this very matter. But hear this: the Lovers of the Nymphs relate that you have done violence to the woodland Nymphs — the sacred oaks torn up, and the alders that threaten far and wide, and the trees robbed of life; for these grieve that by their own death (which you so often used to say you had inflicted on them) they are hindered, by you, from being able to rouse life by heat, once other things have been buried and digested. Certainly, that they may be carried over to us by rafts into the South or the West, in the very midst of the North there will be no lack of North Winds.

Farewell; and if you long for a vernal crown, appease the Nymphs.
At Copenhagen, 7 May, the year 1572.
Thine,
Pratensis.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Pratensis* = **Johannes Pratensis** (Hans Philipsen, 1543–1576), Tycho's physician-friend and intimate, then rising at the University of Copenhagen (professor of medicine from 1571). The May 1572 exchange between the two introduced the subject of Tycho's *De nova stella* (1573): the new star of November 1572 was found later that year, and the published volume carried Latin poems by friends including Pratensis. This is the affectionate, ostentatiously learned reply to a lost letter of Tycho's that Pratensis judges blazing with inspiration.
- **Salutation.** *VERNAS SALUTES, CHEIROS ET MELISSAS* — "Vernal greetings, *cheiros* and *melissas*." The two nouns are transliterated Greek: **χείρ / χεῖρας** ("hand[s]") and **μέλισσα / μελίσσας** ("bee[s]"). The phrase is a precious humanist conceit — "greetings of hands and of bees," i.e. greetings as busy/sweet as bees in spring — kept in Greek-derived form and glossed rather than smoothed. **Flagged crux:** the exact construction (*salutes* governing two Greek accusatives) is deliberately mannered; the gloss preserves the playfulness without over-determining it.
- **Hermetic-alchemical imagery (sustained).** The letter is saturated with the language of the *prima materia* and the alchemical *tria prima*: *sulphur — Mercurius — sal* ("sulphur, Mercury, salt," the three principles, here divinised as "of Venus / of Bacchus / of Apollo"); *tinxit … tinctura* ("steeped … tincture," the alchemical *tinctura* that transmutes); *Vulcanus* (fire/the alchemist's furnace) paired with *Urania* (astronomy); *Spagiricis pulveribus et sudore Chymico* ("spagyric powders and chymical sweat" — *spagyric*, the Paracelsian art of separation-and-recombination, kept as period term). The conceit of the extemporaneous as that which "penetrates a solid body in a moment and converts it into its own nature" is alchemical-transmutational imagery applied to literary inspiration; rendered literally and flagged, not paraphrased away.
- ***fulmina utriusque Meteorologiae*** — "the thunderbolts of both Meteorologies," i.e. the doctrine of lightning in both the natural-philosophical (Aristotelian *Meteorologica*) and a second (likely Scriptural/divine, or Paracelsian) sense; the precise pairing is left open and flagged.
- ***Gheburah*** — **Geburah** (Hebrew גְּבוּרָה, "Severity / Might"), the fifth Sephirah of the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, associated with judgment, Mars, and the harsh north. **Flagged crux:** Pratensis pairs *Gheburah* with *malum Aquilo* ("the evil North Wind") against *Auster bonus / vitalis Oriens* ("the good South / life-giving East") — a Christian-Kabbalistic cosmography in which the rigorous North is to be fled for the merciful South/East. The Hebrew term is kept untranslated in the body and identified here; its force is allusive and not fully recoverable, hence the Possible grade below.
- **Cardinal-direction allegory.** *Aquilo / Boreas / Septentrio* (North Wind / north) stand for harshness, "Barbarism," and the unwelcoming Danish climate (literal and figurative); *Auster* (South Wind) and *Oriens* (East) for life, warmth, and grace. Pratensis insists these are *not* fixed geographical quarters but inward and everywhere ("within, without, in all things … in the depths of souls") — a Neoplatonic-Hermetic interiorising of the compass, kept literal.
- ***Iovis armiger ales … in solium magni Iovis*** — "the winged armour-bearer of Jove [the eagle] … into the throne of great Jove": the eagle of Jupiter bearing the soul aloft (Ganymede / apotheosis imagery), from which Tycho might "discern the shapeless ruins of the tottering world" — a contemplative ascent above the sublunary realm.
- ***Latium et Saturnium regnum*** — "the Latium and realm of Saturn," i.e. the Golden Age (Saturn's reign in Latium, *Aeneid* VIII), here the inward paradise "sought by many."
- ***maculis purgatae Lunae et nitentes Berilli*** — "the Moon cleansed of her spots, and the gleaming Beryls": the purified Moon and beryl (a scrying-stone) as emblems of the cleansed, all-reflecting soul. *Beryllus* as a speculum/scrying medium is a Hermetic commonplace; kept literal.
- ***Nosce te ipsum*** — "Know thyself" (the Delphic γνῶθι σεαυτόν, in Latin); ***dioptram*** = *dioptra* (a sighting-tube / lens), here a metaphorical optical glass of self-knowledge in which "no turbid image shall deceive." Kept as *dioptra* and glossed "lens"; cf. the optical sense, not Tycho's later instruments.
- ***imperterritus ille Danus Wiburgensis*** — "that undaunted Dane of Viborg": an unnamed itinerant physician-alchemist from **Viborg** (Jutland), arrived via **Cologne** (*Colonia*), whom Pratensis recommends to Tycho with heavily ironic praise — *Graecus, Arabs, Galenicus, Paracelsicus, Theologaster, Philosophus, Medicus, Syrupiaster, Chymista* ("a Greek, an Arab, a Galenist, a Paracelsian, a sham theologian, a philosopher, a physician, a syrup-monger, a chymist") — "yet out of all these, nothing." *Theologaster* and *Syrupiaster* are pejorative coinages (sham-theologian, syrup-quack), preserved. The man "is angling for a philosophical post" suited to alchemical work; Pratensis sounds Tycho on hiring him. **The figure is unidentified;** flagged.
- ***fronte tecum loquetur*** — "he will speak with you from his [own] brow / face to face," i.e. you will read the man in his very countenance; idiom kept and glossed.
- **The Nymphs / felling-of-trees passage.** *Nymphas sylvestres violasse te … evulsis sacris quercubus et late minitantibus alnis* — "you have done violence to the woodland Nymphs, the sacred oaks torn up and the wide-threatening alders [felled]." A playful, semi-mythological reproach: Tycho is charged (by the "Lovers of the Nymphs") with clearing timber — *and* the conceit is alchemical, for the felled trees "grieve" that, killed by Tycho (*morte sua, quam illis te intulisse toties ajebas*), they cannot now "rouse life by heat" (i.e. serve as fuel/fire for his furnace) "once other things have been buried and digested." **Flagged crux:** the passage fuses a literal estate-clearing (Tycho cutting wood, on Knudstrup land or for fuel) with an alchemical pun on death/putrefaction/heat (*sepultis digestisque rebus … vitam calore … excitare*) and an *Aquilones*-wordplay (*"in the midst of the North there will be no lack of North Winds [Aquilones]"*, the wind that drives the rafts). The double sense — sylvan complaint and chymical allegory — is rendered as literally as the syntax allows and not resolved into one reading; this is the principal driver of the overall grade.
- ***coronam vernam … Nymphas placa*** — "if you long for a vernal crown, appease the Nymphs": a closing flourish returning to the spring/Nymph conceit of the salutation.
- **Calendar / place.** *Hafniae 7. Maij Anno 1572* = "At **Copenhagen** (*Hafnia*), 7 May 1572" (O.S.; Denmark was on the Julian calendar). The subscription *T.* abbreviates *Tuus* ("Thine"). No in-letter date discrepancy.
- Correction. Latin corrected 'Olympiae' to 'Olympicae' (Dreyer VII p.7) and removed the duplicated pronoun in 'profectus is est' to 'profectus est' (Dreyer VII p.8); English unaffected in both cases.

Dreyer TBOO VII pp.6-9 read as page images; the letter (Johannes Pratensis to Tycho, 7 May 1572) runs pp.7(bottom)-8, between the Wolfius letter and Tycho's reply of 17 May. documents.abstract: Replies in hendecasyllabic verse cast as prose, expressing delight at Pratensis's letter and lamenting the displacement of true learning by scholastic barbarism.

documents.editorial_note: **Editorial note.** The hendecasyllabic poem that the rubric announces — **absent from the working transcription** when this file was first made — has now been **recovered and supplied from Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VII pp. 9–10**, taken from the digitised text. Long-s misreadings are silently normalised (*suêre→fuêre*, *srugum→frugum*); a stray footnote-anchor caret after *Monstrabit* is dropped; one genuinely uncertain word is flagged in the Apparatus (the subject *is* in *"quas nunc is … intulêre Musis"*, where the plural verb wants a plural subject — *ii*/*hi*). The poem is a warm verse-letter answering Pratensis's of 7 May 1572: a humanist exhortation to scorn scholastic "Barbarism" and climb to the study of Earth and Heaven, then practical business — a prospective alchemical assistant ("that undaunted Dane"), the playfully mythologised delay in delivering felled timber ("despoiling the Nymphs," forbidden by Ceres until the harvest rites are done), and a request for distilling **cucurbits** from the potter Andreas.

text.original:
Sequitur mea responsio, quae carmine constat hendecasyllabico instar prosae consignato.

DOCTORI MEDICO JOHANNI PRATENSI, INPRIMISQUE SUO COLENDO AMICO. VULCANUM, URANIAM, JOVEM FAVENTES.

Servus noster, ut est domum reversus, asportavit epistolam remissam a te, care Pratensis, qua relecta, dici vix ego credo posse, quanta nobis hinc animi fuit voluptas. Namque haec abditiore visa vere est rerum cognitione plena, plusque antiquae sophiae tenere, quam nunc suetum est (proh dolor) in scholis doceri. Sed nemo tamen invidebit illis, spero, Barbariem merasque nugas, quas nunc dulcibus intulêre Musis. Namque hunc quis revocabit? quis reducet? Monstrabitne viam, suapte si quis mavult sponte via carere vera. Sed tu, docte Pratensis, nil moratus illos (ut facis) altiora scande, et Terrae simul et Poli supernos perlustrans aditus labore suavi, vulgo subtrahe te caduca temnens. Major gloria namque rebus altis debetur, nec habent pusilla laudem. Quid cessas? remoras habere nullas mens prognata polo potest, sed illa sublimis penetrat domos Deorum, libans Ambrosiam et suave nectar, quod dijs Jupiter ipse miscet, et dijs (si qui sunt) genitis simul ministrat etc. Sed cur digredior, mororve multis? Praestat nunc, ut epistolae tuae remittam responsum, brevibus quod his habeto.

Imperterritus ille Danus ad me quamprimum fuerit reversus illinc, mox se conferat huc iubeto, huncque praesentem cupio videre praesens, et cognoscere num sit aptus ille nostris moribus, et quid ipse sese facturum statuat, velitne furnis inservire meis fovens labores Vulcani et studijs vacare nostris, mecumque perque aliquod manere tempus. Tum demum statuam, quid inde fiet.

De Nymphis etiam scias, Pratensis, illas me spoliasse sat revera Alnis quercubus et suis capillis. Verum quod spolia illa non fuêre ad vos hactenus, ut decet, relata, in causa est Dea quae vocatur Alma, et frugum genetrix Ceres, quod illa cernens prae foribus suos labores instare, agricolas iuvare causam Nympharum vetuit, simul minata, se non propitiam futuram in illud tempus, quando solet venire messis, si Nymphas colerent diebus illis, quos sacros Cereri dedit vetustas. Coguntur miseri parere Divae, quae fructus tribuit Soli quotannis. Silvestres potius volunt vocare Nymphas, quam Cereris carere donis. Ast quando fuerint peracta sacra, quae nunc frugiferae Deae celebrant, Nymphas agricolae iuvare debent, vel si forte alicui interesse sacris (ut fit) displicet, otiosus ille Nympharum spolijs onustus ad vos mittetur, faciam ut ferat ferenda. Sed nunc scribere plura vix vacabit. Ergo care Pratensis, valeto. Et cum sis medicus, valere semper ut possis, facile est: saluta amicos. Fac me posse cucurbitas habere, quas vestrum figulum parare nobis (ut spero) impiger Andreas procurat. Dicas huic etiam precor salutem. Herrevadi, 17. Maij Anno 1572.

Tycho Brahe tibi dicatus.
text.english:
There follows my reply, which consists of a hendecasyllabic poem set down in the manner of prose.

**To the Doctor of Medicine Johannes Pratensis, and most especially to his cherished friend. May Vulcan, Urania, and Jove be favorable.**

Our servant, as soon as he had got home, brought the letter sent back by you, dear Pratensis; and when I had read it over, I scarcely think it can be told how great a delight of mind it gave us. For it seemed truly full of a more hidden knowledge of things, and to hold more of the ancient wisdom than it is now the custom (alas!) to teach in the schools. Yet no one, I hope, will envy those [schools] the Barbarism and the mere trifles which [they] have now brought in upon the sweet Muses. For who will call it back? who will lead it back again? Does he [only] point out the road [to ruin] who, of his own will, prefers to do without the true way? But you, learned Pratensis — heeding them not at all (as is your wont) — climb to higher things, and, surveying with sweet toil the upper approaches alike of Earth and of Heaven, withdraw yourself from the crowd, scorning the things that perish. For greater glory is owed to lofty matters, and little things win no praise. Why do you hold back? A mind born of heaven can brook no hindrance, but, sublime, it pierces to the homes of the Gods, sipping Ambrosia and sweet nectar — which Jupiter himself mixes for the gods, and serves at the same time to the gods (if any there be) [that are] begotten — and so on. But why do I digress and delay with many words? Better now that I send back the answer to your letter, which take in these few [lines].

As soon as that undaunted Dane has come back to me from there, bid him betake himself hither at once; and I desire, myself present, to see him in person, and to learn whether he is suited to our ways, and what he resolves to do — whether he is willing to tend my furnaces, fostering the labors of Vulcan, and to give himself to our studies, and to stay with me for some space of time. Then at last I shall decide what is to come of it.

About the Nymphs, too, you should know, Pratensis, that I have indeed despoiled them well enough of their alders and oaks and their tresses [their leafage]. But that those spoils have not yet been delivered to you, as is fitting, the cause is the Goddess called Alma, and Ceres, mother of the crops: for she, seeing her own labors pressing at the door [the harvest near], forbade the farmers to assist the Nymphs' cause, threatening at the same time that she would not be favorable at that season when the harvest is wont to come, if they should court the Nymphs on the days antiquity made sacred to Ceres. The poor wretches are forced to obey the Goddess, who grants the soil its fruits each year; they would sooner summon the woodland Nymphs [later] than go without Ceres' gifts. But once the rites are accomplished that they now celebrate for the fruit-bearing Goddess, the farmers must aid the Nymphs; or if it happens to displease anyone to take part in the rites (as happens), that idle fellow, laden with the Nymphs' spoils, shall be sent to you — I will see that he carries what is to be carried. But now there will scarcely be leisure to write more. So, dear Pratensis, farewell. And since you are a physician, it is easy for you to be able to be always well: greet our friends. See that I can get the **cucurbits** [gourd-shaped distilling vessels] which your potter — the tireless Andreas, I hope — is seeing to make for us. Bid him too, I pray, good health. Herrevad, 17 May, in the year 1572.

Tycho Brahe, devoted to you.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), writing from Herrevad in May 1572, before *De nova stella* and his establishment on Hven; in this period resident at Herrevad Abbey with his maternal uncle Steen Bille, already deep in alchemy (the "labors of Vulcan," the furnaces and cucurbits below).
- **Recipient.** *Johannes Pratensis* = **Hans Philipsen / Johannes Pratensis** (1543–1576), Tycho's physician-friend at Copenhagen (later professor of medicine there), one of his closest correspondents in 1572 and, per *Tycho Brahe and Prague* (2002), "the first to hear Tycho's ideas on the nova of 1572".
- **Place.** *Herrevad* — Herrevad Abbey (Herrevadskloster) in Scania, where Tycho was then living and working with Steen Bille; kept as is by this chapter's convention (Dreyer's page prints the dateline place as the garbled *"Herizuad"* = Herrevad.)
- **Occasion.** Tycho's reply to a letter of **Johannes Pratensis dated 7 May 1572** (Copenhagen, = idx brahe-t_15720507001). The two were actively exchanging Latin verse as letter-content in these weeks, months before the *Carmen ad fratrem* was printed.
- ***carmen hendecasyllabicum … instar prosae consignato*** — "a hendecasyllabic poem set down in the manner of prose": the reply is in eleven-syllable (Phalaecian) verse, but **written out continuously, not laid out line-by-line as verse**. This is a **distinct** poem from the *Carmen ad fratrem ejus gemellum* of 1572 (which is in dactylic distichs); the rubric is Dreyer's, from cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66 fol. 40r. The translation follows the as-prose layout.
- **The superscription.** *VULCANUM, URANIAM, JOVEM FAVENTES* — "(invoking) Vulcan, Urania, and Jove favorable": the three patrons frame the letter's three strands — **Vulcan** (the alchemical furnace-work), **Urania** (astronomy), **Jove** (good fortune/friendship). A characteristic Tychonic sign-off flourish in embryo.
- **The humanist exhortation.** The opening movement praises Pratensis's letter as full of "more hidden knowledge" and "ancient wisdom," and contrasts it with the "Barbarism and strange trifles" of the contemporary "schools" — Tycho urging his friend to "climb to higher things" and survey "Earth and Heaven," scorning the perishable crowd. The Neoplatonic image of the heaven-born mind "piercing to the homes of the Gods, sipping Ambrosia and nectar" is the period commonplace, rendered without sharpening.
- **The "undaunted Dane."** A prospective **alchemical assistant** — Tycho asks that the young man, once back, come to Herrevad so Tycho can judge whether he is "willing to tend my furnaces, fostering the labors of Vulcan, and give himself to our studies." Concrete evidence of Tycho's 1572 alchemical establishment and his recruiting for it.
- **The Nymphs / Ceres allegory (the literary centrepiece).** A practical matter — the delivery of **felled timber** (alders and oaks, "the Nymphs' tresses") — is dressed as myth: the spoils cannot yet be sent because **Ceres** (the harvest-goddess, here also *Alma*) has forbidden the farmers to work for the woodland **Nymphs** during the days "antiquity made sacred to Ceres," on pain of a poor harvest; once the harvest rites are done, the timber will come. A deliberate superimposition of literal timber-clearing on a mythological-religious conceit, rendered faithfully rather than flattened to its prose sense.
- ***cucurbitas*** — **cucurbits**: gourd-shaped earthenware **distilling vessels** (the lower vessel of an alembic), to be made by the potter **Andreas**. Another alchemical-apparatus detail, consistent with the furnace-work above. *figulum* = potter.
- **Textual note (poem now supplied).** The hendecasyllabic poem, absent from the working transcription, is **supplied from Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VII pp. 9–10** (cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.7, apograph; with corrections from 10686.66) and taken from the digitised text. One genuine reading-crux remains: in *"Barbariem mirasque nugas, quas nunc **is** … intulêre Musis"* the plural verb *intulêre* wants a plural subject, so the transmitted *is* is probably *ii*/*hi* ("they," i.e. the schools/barbarians); flagged *[ii?]*, not silently emended. Long-s misreadings (*suêre→fuêre*, *srugum→frugum*) are normalised and declared.
- **Calendar.** *17 May 1572*, Old Style (Julian); Denmark kept O.S. until 1700. The dateline is internal to the poem (*Herrevad, 17 May 1572*) and matches the edition label.
- **Correction.** Four Latin corruptions in the hendecasyllabic poem corrected per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII pp.9-10: a corrupted "mirasque" plus a phantom bracketed "is [ii?]" restored to "merasque" (with the phantom word removed); "Monstrabit" restored to the interrogative "Monstrabitne"; "siet" restored to "fiet"; and "(ut sit)" restored to "(ut fit)". English corrected to match at three of the four places where sense was affected: "strange" to "mere" trifles, the flat statement recast as a rhetorical question, and "(as may be)" to "(as happens)"; the fiet/siet correction needed no English change since the existing rendering already carried the future sense.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VII pp.9-10 read as page images, with particular attention to the hendecasyllabic poem per the audit's note that it was restored by an earlier pass. The restoration does NOT hold up clean: four word-level corruptions cluster inside the poem itself (merasque->mirasque plus a phantom 'is [ii?]' insertion; the dropped -ne on Monstrabitne; fiet->siet; ut fit->ut sit), while the prose second half of the letter (the Danish assistant, the Nymphs passage, the cucurbits, the closing 'Herrevadi/Herizuad. 17. Maij Anno 1572. TYCHO BRAHE tibi dicatus.') matches Dreyer exactly. Individually each defect is low/medium severity and none invents a fact wholesale, but their concentration in precisely the passage flagged for verification means the 'restored' poem cannot be certified clean — hence *serious* and grade C rather than a pass.

**4 defects found:**
- **text error** (medium). Dreyer's poem reads 'merasque' (mere/sheer trifles) with no 'is'/'ii' present at all; our transcribed original corrupts the word to 'mirasque' (strange/wondrous) and inserts a phantom, editorially-flagged 'is [ii?]' that is simply not in Dreyer. The English follows the corrupted Latin ('strange' rather than 'mere'). Dreyer prints: *Barbariem merasque nugas, quas nunc dulcibus intulêre Musis*.
- **text error** (medium). Dreyer's poem has the interrogative enclitic -ne (Will he show the way...?); our transcribed original drops it, turning a rhetorical question into a flat statement. Dreyer prints: *Monstrabitne viam*.
- **text error** (low). Dreyer prints 'fiet' (it will become/happen, future indicative of fio); the transcribed original has 'siet' (an archaic subjunctive of esse), a different word. Dreyer prints: *quid inde fiet*.
- **text error** (low). Dreyer prints 'ut fit' (as happens/is the case); the transcribed original has 'ut sit' (subjunctive of esse), changing the parenthetical's grammatical mood and licensing the looser English 'as may be' rather than 'as happens'. Dreyer prints: *(ut fit)*.

**Repaired.** All four defects verified directly against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.9-10 page images (not the digitised text layer): merafque (l.14), Monftrabitne (l.16), fiet (l.30 p.9), and (ut fit) (p.10 l.3) all read exactly as Dreyer's claim states. No other part of the letter was touched; every changed word is accounted for in outcomes above.

text.original:
VIRO VERE NOBILI ET GENEROSO TYCHONI BRAHE DE KNUDSTRUP, DOMINO OPTIMO ET AMICO SYNCERO. SALUTEM ET VER MELISSEUM.

RECEPI literas tuas, TYCHO optime, quibus negotia tua promovenda apud Artifices tuos mechanicos committis. Quod tardius ad te redeat hic tuus Tabellarius, in causa fuit, quod nundinæ Roschildenses me ultra propositum detinuerint: ubi mihi tantisper commorandum fuit, donec de vase meo et bonis Francofurto per Flensburgenses mercatores missis, fieri poteram certior.

Negotia tua sic se habent. Absolutæ sunt imagines omnes in Globo tuo. Divisus Meridianus et Horizon, paratum pedestale, sed hîc difficultas est non parva, de inauratione videlicet, de coloratione, seu pictura, ut scribis. Primum quidem Aurifaber non confidit se super argenteam totius Globi faciem, aureas stellas, cum debita imaginum repræsentatione, inducere posse. Etenim multis rationibus apud me nunc, tum apud te antea id explicavit. Quod ad Pictorem attinet, ille nunquam circulos illos et divisiones tam exacte, ut nunc insculptæ, exprimet, sed incrustabit quidem colorum crusta superficiem tersam et levem, quæ obtenebrabunt ea, quæ Aurifaber subtiliter delineavit. Ut interim sileam, quomodocunque hoc fuerit, non fore tandem diuturnum (etenim multis illa via incommodis obnoxia est) quam cito poterit vel læsione aliqua vel fortuito attactu pars crustæ coloratæ enucleari?

Sed audi meum consilium, quod ex Aurifabri quoque sententia tibi denuncio. Opus est nobile et regium imo aureum. Et quia Horizon et Meridianus et pedes deaurari debent, agedum deauremus prius totam superficiem Globi, hac tamen ratione, ut imagines ipsæ una cum stellis appareant minus tersæ: *das ist matt*, ut illi loquuntur. Partes autem intermediæ, seu superficies ipsa Globi polienda erit, et ad micationem et splendorem rutilantem deducenda, qui quoque splendor in ipsis stellis (si voluerimus) indui possit, ut iubar illud aureum, tanquam scintillans ex sublustri imaginis lumine, emicet.

Ita et forma illa stellarum insculpta exacte repræsentabit, quarum cuspidum subtilitatem coloribus æmulari, difficile est. Illi enim tenues illas cuspides et cavitates, quæ toti figuræ decus adijciant, oblinient, et replebunt venustate istorum angulorum deformata. Ita tandem aureus erit Globus, simplicitate cœli materiam et faciem æmulans, sic pedes capiti respondebunt, longe ablegatis versicoloribus et muliebribus illis oblectamentis oculorum: quæ quosdam delectant, ut monstra in picturis. Cedant variegationes instabiles, color unicus esto: color aureus esto. Sic non, si cervix equina humano capiti adiuncta fuerit, in piscem desinet atrum.

Sed mi TYCHO, hoc meum consilium est, tuo illæso et salvo iudicio. Ad pedem, Meridianum et Horizontem deaurandum significat se opus habere ad minimum 4 roseis nobel: si nostrum consilium amplexus fueris, addantur 3 vel 4 ad summum, et totum sese oculis nostris Silenus ille aperiet aureus. Tu imprimis sententiam tuam super hac re significa, et Aurifaber dicit se aurum hîc habere non posse: tuum erit ad pedes et Meridianum et Horizontem 4 nobiles rosatos, ut dixi, inprimis mittere. STEPHANUS hodie vel cras imponet rotulas, et experietur processum, urgebo quantum potero et promovebo. Instrumentum ferreum bene procedit, hac septimana, imo vesperi absolvetur, ut promisit Artifex.

Quod ad Typographum attinet, post prandium intelliges, tunc plura addam, iam enim animus est in patinis. Figuræ nunc excinduntur, instigo quantum possum. De papyro difficultas magna est: sed tamen corrademus. De epistola mea et carmine, quia nondum propter occupationes confecta sunt, ne sis solicitus, quoniam tota posterior pars operis primum absolvenda est, tuque interea nobis aderis. Sed ante 4 dies certum nuntium habebis, cum quo omnia mittam necessaria.

Titulum quoque una mitto, quem præfigemus operi; consulimus, ut ita relinquas. Etenim singula verba perlustravimus diligenter, sed si quid mutari voles, fiet id ubi veneris satis mature, quoniam titulus postremo cudetur. De reliquis iubeo te non esse sollicitum: curabimus ea diligenter. Verbum illud, quod titulo assuisti LVCVBRATIONES, nescio, an hîc locum habere possit. Nocturnæ quidem sunt, sed an lucubrationibus Atticis respondeant, etiamsi non dubitem: tamen ne magno aliquid hiatu promittamus et speciosis titulis et vastis fores exornemus, author sum. Non, quod etiam augustiore inscriptione dignum hoc opus tuum non iudicem: sed ut moderata illa submissiore in ipso limine adhibita, in ipso operis incalescentis progressu, potentius in animum lectorum, tantorum mysteriorum non præscium illabamur. Summa, titulum hunc immutare quoties libuerit, et Genialis tulerit impetus, dabitur occasio. Si pro contemplatione mathematica considerationem mathematicam poni voles, unum erit.

Lucubrationibus operam dant nigra lolligine ad lucernam chartas imbuentes, lucubrationibus pallescunt ad oleum legentes. Lucubrantur quoque qui ad mediam noctem vel Auroram ipsam madidi sunt. Et aurigis nautisque, si quibus alijs, suæ sunt lucubrationes. Nos exemti prostituta illa æquivocatione vocabuli, rerumque Domini facti, homonymias in eas terras relegabimus, in quibus vivos homines mortui incursant boves. Sed hæc post prandium. Nos sacra inebriet ambitio, non e vulgi fornicationibus petita, sed e castis Uraniæ et sororum Vestalium adytis etc.

Pro lignis mihi transmissis et dono datis gratias ago quam possum maximas, relaturus si potero. Ita hominum bonorum res comparata est, ut alij aliorum beneficis egeant. Vos tanto culmine mundi positi nobis inferioribus Dij esse potestis aut lupi, si exteriorem Anatomiam consideremus. Si abditam illam et interiorem, tu quoque et par et superior esse et potes, et, si cunabula vestra spectetis, debetis merito. Tu non exutus exteriori vinculo, etiam interiore nobiscum libertate triumphas, qua civitate donatus et eiusdem Reipublicæ civis et Augustus semper. Reliqua occupat fornicaria et infidum vulgus pellicibus satiatur suis. Illa pulchritudo te cæcum habet, oculis orbate sensilibus lucem ne respice.

Vale. Hafniæ raptissime 16. Aprilis Anni 1573.

Pratensis
text.english:
**To the truly noble and high-born Tycho Brahe of Knudstrup, best of patrons and unfeigned friend. Greeting, and a spring of honey.**

I have received your letter, excellent Tycho, in which you commit to me the furthering of your business with your mechanical craftsmen. That this courier of yours comes back to you later than expected was owing to the Roskilde fair, which held me beyond what I had intended: I had to wait there until I could get certain word of my cask and of the goods sent from Frankfurt by the Flensburg merchants.

Your affairs stand thus. All the figures on your globe are finished. The meridian and the horizon are divided, the pedestal is ready — but here the difficulty is not small: namely the gilding, and the colouring or painting, as you write. First, the goldsmith has no confidence that he can lay golden stars, with the figures duly represented, over the silvered face of the whole globe; he has explained this to me now at length, as he did to you before. As for the painter: he will never render those circles and divisions as exactly as they now stand engraved. He will merely crust over the clean, smooth surface with a crust of colours, and these will darken what the goldsmith has finely drawn. And let me say nothing, meanwhile, of the fact that however it turns out it will not last — for that method is exposed to many mishaps: how quickly might a piece of the coloured crust be picked away by some knock or a chance touch?

But hear my counsel, which I give you with the goldsmith's judgement behind it. The work is noble and royal — nay, golden. And since the horizon, the meridian and the feet must be gilded, come then: let us gild the whole surface of the globe first, but on this principle — that the figures themselves, together with the stars, should appear *less* burnished: *das ist matt*, as they say. The parts between, that is the surface of the globe itself, must be polished and brought to a glittering, ruddy brilliance; and that brilliance could be laid on the stars themselves too (if we wish), so that the golden radiance may flash out as if sparkling from the faint light of the figure.

In that way the engraved form of the stars will also represent them exactly — stars whose fineness of point it is hard to rival in colours. For the painters will smear over those slender points and hollows that give the whole figure its beauty, and will fill them in, the grace of those angles being spoilt. So at last the globe will be golden, rivalling in its simplicity the substance and the face of heaven; so the feet will answer to the head, once those particoloured, womanish delights of the eye are sent packing — the things that please certain people, as monsters do in paintings. Let unstable variegation give way; let there be one colour only: let the colour be gold. Then it will not happen that, a horse's neck having been joined to a human head, the thing tails off into a black fish.

But, my Tycho, this is my counsel — your own judgement untouched and intact. For gilding the foot, the meridian and the horizon he indicates that he needs at least 4 rose nobles; if you adopt our plan, let 3 or 4 more be added at the most, and that golden Silenus will open himself whole to our eyes. Signify your view on this above all — and the goldsmith says he cannot get gold here: it will be for you to send, first of all, the 4 rose nobles for the feet, the meridian and the horizon, as I have said. Stephanus will fit the little wheels today or tomorrow and will test the working of it; I shall press and further it as much as I can. The iron instrument is coming on well: it will be finished this week — indeed this evening, as the craftsman has promised.

As for the printer, you shall hear after lunch; then I shall add more, for at this moment my mind is on the dishes. The figures are being cut now; I urge it on as much as I can. About the paper there is great difficulty — but we shall scrape some together. As for my letter and my poem: do not be anxious that they are not yet finished, my occupations being what they are, since the whole latter part of the work has to be completed first, and you will be with us in the meantime. But within four days you will have a sure messenger, by whom I shall send everything needful.

I send the title as well, which we shall prefix to the work; we advise you to leave it as it stands, for we have gone over every single word with care. But if you should want anything altered, it can be done when you come, in good time, since the title is struck off last. About the rest I bid you not to worry: we shall see to it diligently. That word which you have stitched onto the title — LUCUBRATIONES — I do not know whether it can have a place here. Nocturnal these studies certainly are; but whether they answer to the *Attic* lucubrations — though I do not doubt it — still I am of the opinion that we should not promise something with a great gaping mouth, nor dress out the doorway with showy and cavernous titles. Not that I judge this work of yours unworthy even of a more august inscription; but that, a modest and more subdued one being used on the very threshold, we may steal the more powerfully into the minds of readers — who are not forewarned of such great mysteries — as the work warms to its progress. In sum, there will be occasion to change this title as often as you please, and as the genial impulse takes you. If you should want *mathematical consideration* put in place of *mathematical contemplation*, it will be all one.

They give their labour to "lucubrations" who steep their paper in black cuttlefish-ink by lamplight; readers grow pale over the oil at their "lucubrations". They "lucubrate" too who are soused till midnight or till dawn itself. And carters and sailors, if anyone, have lucubrations of their own. Let us, freed from that prostituted equivocation of the word, and made masters of the matter, banish such homonymies to those lands where dead oxen charge at living men. But of this after lunch. Let a sacred ambition intoxicate us — one sought not from the fornications of the crowd, but from the chaste sanctuaries of Urania and her Vestal sisters, etc.

For the timber sent me and given as a gift I give the greatest thanks I can, and shall repay it if I am able. Such is the condition of good men, that some have need of the kindnesses of others. You who are set at so great a height of the world can be to us below either gods or wolves, if we consider the outward anatomy; if that hidden and inward one, then you too can be both our equal and our superior — and, if you look to your cradle, you deservedly ought to be. You, not stripped of the outward bond, yet triumph with us in an inward liberty; endowed with that citizenship, a citizen of that same commonwealth, and always Augustus. The rest is taken up by the harlot, and the faithless crowd is sated with its concubines. That beauty holds you blind; you who are bereft of the eyes of sense, do not look back at the light.

Farewell. Copenhagen, in the greatest haste, 16 April 1573.

Pratensis
