documents.apparatus:
- **Correction of record — this letter is *not* lost.** This chapter previously published the letter as *"(lost; editorial note only)"*, graded Possible, on the ground that the only surviving text was Dreyer's six-word note *Responsio ad has interijt…* ("the reply to these has perished"). That was an artefact of a **defective transcription**, not of the tradition. The harvested tekstnet text captured only the first block of the page — the editorial loss-note that stands *before* the letter — and dropped the letter itself. The letter survives complete: tekstnet prints it in full, and its own source-line cites **TBOO VII pp. 10–13**, four printed pages. The loss-note refers to a *different*, genuinely lost reply, and is retained above the letter as apparatus, where it belongs. The Latin and translation above are new.
- **Correspondent.** *Johannes Pratensis* = **Hans Philipsen Pratensis** (1543–1576), professor of medicine at Copenhagen from 1571, Paracelsian, and Tycho's closest friend of these years; Tycho would write his epitaph in 1576. He is here acting as Tycho's agent in Copenhagen, managing both craftsmen and printer while Tycho is away (at Herrevad).
- **The globe.** The object is a metal celestial globe with **engraved constellation figures on a silvered surface**, with a divided meridian and horizon ring and a pedestal — not the great wooden Augsburg globe. The crux of the letter is a **finishing dispute**: the goldsmith (*Aurifaber*) cannot lay gold stars over silver; the painter (*Pictor*) would smother the engraving under a crust of pigment. Pratensis's solution — gild the whole globe, leave the figures and stars **matt** and burnish the ground between them to a ruddy lustre, so the figures read as matt gold against bright gold — is argued on grounds at once technical and aesthetic. The German gloss ***das ist matt***, quoted as the craftsmen's own word, is the vocabulary of the Copenhagen workshop breaking into the Latin.
- **Cost.** The gilding of foot, meridian and horizon needs **at least 4 rose nobles**, with 3 or 4 more if the whole-globe scheme is adopted; and *"the goldsmith says he cannot get gold here"* — Tycho must send the coin itself. A rare, concrete costing of a Tychonic instrument at the point of manufacture.
- **The printing of *De nova stella* — the letter's principal historical value.** The "work" whose figures are being cut, whose paper is scarce, and whose title is under negotiation is **Tycho's first book**, *De nova stella* (Copenhagen: Lorentz Benedicht, 1573). Three things follow:
 - Pratensis promises *"my letter and my poem"* (*de epistola mea et carmine*) for the volume. Both are in the printed book: the prefatory **letter of Johannes Pratensis** (*"TYCHONI BRAHE OTTHONIDI… IOHANNES PRATENSIS, MEDICUS, S. D."*) stands among its preliminaries.
 - **Tycho had wanted *LUCUBRATIONES* ("Nocturnal Studies") on the title-page**, and Pratensis talks him out of it — objecting that the word is debased by equivocation (scribblers, drinkers, carters and sailors all "lucubrate") and that a title should not "dress out the doorway with showy and cavernous titles." *Lucubrationes* does **not** appear on the printed title-page.
 - Pratensis offers Tycho a straight choice: *"if you should want mathematical **consideration** put in place of mathematical **contemplation**, it will be all one."* The printed title reads **…*Contemplatio Mathematica***. The letter therefore catches the title of Tycho's first book at the moment it was settled, and shows which counsel prevailed.
- **Classical texture.** The Latin is dense with allusion, and the translation preserves rather than flattens it: *"a horse's neck joined to a human head… tails off into an ugly fish"* and *"monsters in paintings"* are **Horace, *Ars Poetica* 1–5**, turned into an argument against polychromy; the **golden Silenus** that "will open himself whole to our eyes" is the *Sileni Alcibiadis* of Erasmus's *Adagia* (the coarse figurine that opens to disclose a god), here inverted — the outside is to be gold as well; *"my mind is on the dishes"* (*animus est in patinis*) is proverbial (Terence, *Eunuchus* 816). The closing turn — a sacred ambition drawn *"from the chaste sanctuaries of Urania and her Vestal sisters"* — names the muse Tycho would take for his own.
- **Calendar.** Dated *Hafniæ … 16. Aprilis Anni 1573*. Denmark was on the Julian calendar; the date is **Old Style**, reproduced as written and not converted.
- **Flagged crux.** The final clause, *"oculis orbate sensilibus lucem ne respice"*, is syntactically strained (*orbate* taken as a vocative of *orbatus*) and its sense is compressed; it is rendered close to the Latin rather than smoothed, and should be checked against Dreyer's text before it is quoted.
- **Correction.** "tails off into an ugly fish" corrected to "tails off into a black fish", restoring the colour-term atrum that Pratensis's Latin carries (Dreyer, TBOO VII, p.11) and that echoes Horace's Ars Poetica.

documents.incipit: AFFINEM meum, Generose Domine TYCHO, in patriam suam discedentem, absque meis literis ad …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO DOCTRINAQUE ET VIRTUTIBUS PRÆSTANTISSIMO D. TYCHONI BRAHE OTTONIDI DANO, IN CURIA KNUDSTRUP, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO PLURIMUM COLENDO. S.

AFFINEM meum, Generose Domine TYCHO, in patriam suam discedentem, absque meis literis ad te venire nolui: cum quod scirem, amicorum plurimi te facientium literas tibi non ingratas fore: tum quod vehementer ex te scire desiderem, quid de novo illo ante aliquot menses exorto sidere sentias. Mirum est, quanta sit doctissimorum et in hac arte exercitatissimorum virorum discrepans sententia. Nam alij (ut de materia non dicam) Cometam appellare volunt, alij stellam propter speciem apparentem: alij mediam quandam naturam habere asserunt. Italus quidam (nomen eius excidit) hoc sidus non novum, sed unum esse ex numero Cassiopeae, lumine miraculose illustrat© et accenso, acerrime contendit, scripto in publicum edito, et senatui Veneto dedicato. Praeterea de distantia eius a Terra magna est controversia. Alij enim id in elementarem regionem collocant, ex quorum numero noster D. PAULUS HAINZELIUS est. Alij in aetheream regionem, quorum opinioni astipulatur D. PEUCERUS, APIANUS, Landgravius Hassiae, et alij, qui tamen et in hoc dissentiunt, ut alij supra Lunam, alij supra Venerem, imo alij in primum Mobile collocare non dubitent, freti observationibus instrumentorum, doctrinae parallaxeos, et Triangulorum. Sed quomodo una eademque doctrina ex firmis demonstrationibus extructa, potest artifices adeo incertos reddere, ut ita dissentiant? Haec velim explices, et quid de hac re statuas, per occasionem, etiam propter communia studia literis significare ne graveris, te etiam atque etiam rogo. Id si feceris, erit mihi tam gratum, quam quod gratissimum, quod etiam tanquam testem studij et amoris tui erga me in perpetuum conservabo. Utinam hisce temporibus una vixissemus, ut observationis modum ex te cognoscere potuissem: qua in re nihil mihi gratius contigisset. Sed optando quid consequi possim, non video. Amissa bona plerunque desiderantur, id quod non mea, sed temporis culpa factum video fato quodam. Praesens ergo status boni consulendus erit.

Tu interim feliciter in Domino vale.
Datae Augustae Rheticae Calendis Iulij 1573
T. E.
Deditiss. et studiosiss.
IOHANNES MAIOR
text.english:
**To the most noble Master Tycho Brahe, son of Otte, the Dane, at the manor of Knudstrup, most outstanding in learning and in the virtues, his lord and friend to be greatly honoured — greeting.**

I was unwilling, noble Master Tycho, that my kinsman, as he departed for his homeland, should come to you without a letter from me — both because I knew that letters from friends who esteem you highly would not be unwelcome to you, and because I ardently desire to learn from you what you think about that new star which arose some months ago. It is wonderful how greatly the most learned men, and those most practised in this art, differ in opinion. For some (to say nothing of its substance) wish to call it a comet, others a star on account of its apparent form; others assert that it has a certain intermediate nature. A certain Italian (his name escapes me) most fiercely contends — in a work issued to the public and dedicated to the Venetian Senate — that this heavenly body is not new, but is one of the number of [the stars of] Cassiopeia, [its] light having miraculously been made bright and kindled. Moreover there is great controversy about its distance from the Earth. For some place it in the elementary region — of whose number is our Master Paul Hainzel; others in the aethereal region, with whose opinion Master Peucer, Apian, the Landgrave of Hesse, and others side — who nevertheless also disagree in this, that some place it above the Moon, others above Venus, indeed others do not hesitate to place it in the *primum mobile*, relying on the observations of instruments, on the doctrine of parallax, and on [the doctrine] of triangles. But how can one and the same doctrine, built up out of firm demonstrations, render its practitioners so uncertain that they thus disagree? I beg you again and again to explain these things, and not to find it burdensome — as occasion offers, and for the sake of our common studies — to signify by letter what you determine on this matter. If you do this, it will be as pleasing to me as what is most pleasing; and I shall preserve it forever as a witness of your zeal and affection toward me. Would that we lived together in these times, so that I might have learned the manner of observation from you — in which matter nothing more welcome could have befallen me! But I do not see what I can attain by wishing. Good things, once lost, are for the most part longed for — which I see came about by a certain fate, through no fault of mine, but of the time. The present state of things, then, must be made the best of.

Meanwhile, fare you happily well in the Lord.
Given at Augsburg in Raetia, on the Kalends of July [1 July] 1573.
Yours,
most devoted and most zealous,
Johannes Major.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Iohannes Maior* = **Johannes Major** (the Latin sender-form). Writing from Augsburg in 1573, in the circle of the Augsburg patrician-patron **Paul Hainzel** (whom he calls "our Master Paul Hainzel"). He is otherwise a minor figure of the Augsburg learned circle through which Tycho had passed in 1569–70; the letter is preserved among the same Vienna *Epistolae* volume (cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66) as the Wolf and Hainzel letters of the period. The edition's heuristic language tag (la) is correct: the letter is wholly Neo-Latin, with no code-switching.
- ***Ottonides*** — "son of Otte," a Greek-style patronymic for Tycho's father **Otte Brahe**; *in Curia Knudstrup* = "at the manor of **Knudstrup**" (the Brahe family seat in Scania; kept as is by this chapter's convention).
- ***affinem meum … discedentem*** — "my kinsman, as he departed": the unnamed kinsman of Major's was the bearer carrying this letter back to Denmark; not further identified.
- **The "new star" (the 1572 nova).** *novo illo … exorto sidere* = "that new star which arose some months ago" — the **nova/supernova of November 1572 in Cassiopeia (SN 1572, "Tycho's star")**, the central event of Tycho's early career and the subject of his *De nova stella* (1573). The whole substance of the letter is the contemporary debate over its nature and distance. Note Major's hedge *(ut de materia non dicam)* "(to say nothing of its substance)" — preserved, not sharpened.
- ***Cometam … stellam … mediam quandam naturam*** — the three contemporary positions on what the object *was*: a comet, a (fixed) star, or something of intermediate nature. Rendered literally.
- ***Italus quidam (nomen eius excidit) … senatui Veneto dedicato*** — "a certain Italian (his name escapes me) … dedicated to the Venetian Senate." Major reports the view that the object is **not new** but a pre-existing star of Cassiopeia whose light was miraculously kindled. The Italian author is left unnamed by Major himself (*nomen eius excidit*, "his name has slipped [my memory]"); the work dedicated to the Venetian Senate plausibly points to one of the several Venetian nova-tracts of 1573, but Major's own uncertainty is preserved and the identification left open rather than asserted.
- **Textual crux — *lumine … illustrat© et accenso*.** The working transcription prints *illustrat©*, a corrupt token (a transcription/digitised text layer artifact, not a Latin word). The grammar requires an ablative agreeing with the ablative-absolute construction *lumine … accenso* ("the light having been kindled"); the intended reading is therefore **_illustrato_** ("[its light] having been made bright"), here adopted in the translation as *"[its] light having miraculously been made bright and kindled."* The printed corrupt form is retained verbatim in the Source block by this chapter's convention; the reading was not confirmable against a clean page image of Dreyer, hence flagged.
- **The distance debate.** *elementarem regionem* = "the **elementary region**" (the sublunary realm of the four elements); *aetheream regionem* = "the **aethereal region**" (the celestial realm above the Moon). The dispute over whether the new star lay below or above the Moon is precisely the parallax question Tycho's own observations settled in favour of the supralunary placement.
 - *D. Paulus Hainzelius* = **Paul Hainzel** of Augsburg (with whom Tycho had built the great Göppingen quadrant in 1569), here placing the object in the elementary (sublunary) region.
 - *D. Peucerus* = **Caspar Peucer** (Wittenberg); *Apianus* = **Philipp Apian** (the Ingolstadt/Tübingen mathematician, son of Peter Apian); *Landgravius Hassiae* = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** — named as siding with the aethereal (supralunary) placement.
- ***primum Mobile*** — the *primum mobile*, the outermost moving sphere of the Ptolemaic-Aristotelian cosmos; kept in Latin and italicised.
- **Technical terms.** *doctrina parallaxeos* → "the doctrine of **parallax**"; *observationibus instrumentorum* → "the observations of **instruments**"; *doctrina … Triangulorum* → "the doctrine of triangles" (i.e. trigonometry, the computational basis for deriving distance from parallax).
- ***artifices*** — here "practitioners" (of the mathematical art), i.e. the astronomers themselves; Major's rhetorical point is that a single rigorous *doctrina* nonetheless yields contradictory results in their hands.
- **Closing formulae.** *feliciter in Domino vale* → "fare you happily well in the Lord"; *Datae … Calendis Iulij 1573* → "Given … on the Kalends of July (1 July) 1573" (Roman-calendar idiom kept and glossed, this chapter's convention); *T. E. / Deditiss. et studiosiss.* = *Tuae Excellentiae deditissimus et studiosissimus*, "most devoted and most zealous to Your Excellency".
- **Place.** *Augustae Rheticae* = **Augsburg** (here qualified *Rhetica*, "of Raetia," the antiquarian regional epithet; cf. the more usual *Augusta Vindelicorum*), this chapter's convention
- **Calendar.** *Calendis Iulij 1573* = the Kalends of July, i.e. **1 July 1573** (O.S.; Denmark and the Empire were pre-Gregorian). The as-written dateline agrees with the edition label (*1573. 1. juli. Augsburg*); no discrepancy.
- **Correction.** Latin: 'astipulator' corrected to 'astipulatur' per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 13.

text.original:
NOBILITATE ET ERUDITIONE PRÆSTANTI IUVENI, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE.
S. P. D.

DICERE non possum, Nobilissime et amantissime mi TYCHO, quanta voluptate me affeceris, non saltem eruditissimis literis, ad me nuper datis, sed et contemplatione tua vere Mathematica, de miraculosa illa ad Cassiopeiam stella, quæ ante paucas hebdomadas plane conspici desijt, quam ego quidem Cometam appellare solitus sum, secundum receptam ex ARISTOTELIS schola opinionem, licet ut fatear id, quod res postulat, propriæ meæ observationes, Quadrante illo maximo, ex tuo præscripto hîc fabrefacto, obtente convincant, id, quicquid erat iubaris, non infra Lunam fuisse, sed in altissimo æthere, siquidem nullæ proveniant parallaxes ex meis diligenter institutis observationibus, et tamen non ausus fui dicere, supra Lunam extitisse, ne contra Philosophum, cuius præcipua est autoritas, quippiam affirmarem, qui Cœlum nova non admittere corpora indubitanter statuit. Sed prævaleat autoritati experientia, præsertim cum tu accuratissimis tuis Instrumentis et Observationibus idem, quod ego, deprehenderis: nimirum nullam prorsus adfuisse huic φαινομένῳ parallaxin, veluti etiam satis evidenter in hoc tuo eruditissimo scripto demonstrasti, quod sane longe antecellit omnium aliorum hactenus de eadem stella in publicum editas conceptiones, ita ut vix cum hac conferri mereantur: et optarem quam maxime, me id prius obtinuisse, ut descriptum eius cum doctis hinc Mathematicis, cum duraret adhuc ea stella, præsertim MÆSTHLINO, qui idem tecum sentire videtur, licet non tam evidenter atque dilucide, sed per ambages quasdam demonstret, communicare potuissem. Sed spero, me plura exemplaria a te obtenturum, eademque, uti polliceri videris, auctiora reddita, tum demum alijs ea impertiar. Interea hoc meum, uti rem pretiosam, reservabo, et fratri meo atque WOLFIO nostro ostendam. Quamprimum igitur plura eiuscemodi publicaveris, me eorum facere participem ne supersedeas quæso. Adiunxi hisce observationes meas in hac ipsa stella, et quibusdam alijs, factas eodem Quadrante permagno, tuo instinctu hîc elaborato, quas examinare poteris, et tuam postea mihi de ijs indicare censuram. Plura nunc scribere non vacat, ob negotiorum molem in hoc officio, quod sustineo, publico. Tu itaque vale, optime mi TYCHO, et sæpius me tuis eruditis literis invisere ne omittas.

Iterumque etiam atque etiam vale.
Datæ Augustæ Vindelicorum, Anno 1574 die 10. Martij.
T.
Paulus Haintzel.
text.english:
**To the young man pre-eminent in nobility and learning, Master Tycho Brahe — sends heartiest greeting.**

I cannot tell you, my most noble and most loving Tycho, with what delight you have filled me — not only by the most learned letter lately sent to me, but also by your truly mathematical reflection on that miraculous star by Cassiopeia, which a few weeks ago entirely ceased to be seen, [the star] which I, for my part, have been accustomed to call a comet, in accordance with the opinion received from the school of Aristotle — although, to confess what the matter requires, my own observations, obtained with that great quadrant built here after your prescription, prove that the brightness, whatever it was, was not below the Moon, but in the highest aether, seeing that no parallaxes whatever arise from the observations I diligently set up; and yet I did not dare to say that it had stood above the Moon, lest I affirm anything against the Philosopher, whose authority is paramount, who lays it down beyond doubt that the heaven admits no new bodies. But let experience prevail over authority, especially since you, with your most accurate instruments and observations, have found the same as I — namely, that there was present to this phenomenon [φαινομένῳ] no parallax at all, just as you have also demonstrated quite evidently in this most learned writing of yours, which indeed far surpasses the conceptions about the same star hitherto published by all others, so that they scarcely deserve to be compared with this one. And I would wish as much as possible that I had obtained it earlier, so that I might have been able to share a description of it with the learned mathematicians hereabouts, while that star yet lasted — especially with Maestlin, who seems to hold the same view as you, although he demonstrates it not so evidently and clearly, but by certain roundabout ways. But I hope that I shall obtain more copies from you, and these — as you seem to promise — rendered fuller; and only then shall I impart them to others. Meanwhile I shall keep this [copy] of mine as a precious thing, and show it to my brother and to our Wolf. As soon, therefore, as you publish more of this kind, do not, I beg, forbear to make me a sharer of them. I have attached to this [letter] my observations made upon this very star, and upon certain others, with the same very great quadrant elaborated here at your prompting, which you will be able to examine, and afterwards to convey to me your judgement upon them. There is no leisure to write more now, on account of the mass of business in this public office which I sustain. So farewell, my excellent Tycho, and do not omit to visit me more often with your learned letters.

And again, again and again, farewell.
Given at Augsburg, in the year 1574, on the 10th day of March.
Yours,
Paul Hainzel.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** *Paulus Haintzel* = **Paul Hainzel** (1527/8–1581), patrician of Augsburg, town councillor (Stadtpfleger / magistrate — hence *hoc officio … publico*, "this public office which I sustain") and patron of astronomy. With Tycho during the latter's Augsburg years (1569–70) he built a great quadrant at his suburban estate at Göggingen, the *Quadrans maximus* repeatedly invoked here. One of the **Hainzel brothers** of the editorial glossary; the *frater meus* of this letter is his brother **Johann Baptist Hainzel**.
- **Recipient / superscription.** *Domino Tychoni Brahe* — Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), then 27 and freshly the author of *De nova stella*. The salutation *S. P. D.* = *salutem plurimam dicit*, "sends heartiest greeting"; the subscription *T.* (here likely *Tuus*, "Yours") + signature.
- **Occasion — the writing in hand.** *hoc tuo eruditissimo scripto* / *descriptum eius* is **Tycho's *De nova stella*** (Copenhagen, 1573), his account of the new star (SN 1572) that appeared in Cassiopeia in November 1572. Hainzel acknowledges receiving a copy, praises it above all rival accounts, and asks for further, *auctiora* ("fuller") copies — Tycho apparently having promised an enlarged treatment.
- **The phenomenon.** *miraculosa illa ad Cassiopeiam stella … quae ante paucas hebdomadas plane conspici desijt* — the nova faded from naked-eye visibility in early 1574, consistent with "ceased to be seen a few weeks ago." Hainzel records that he had habitually called it a **comet** (*Cometam appellare solitus sum*), per the Aristotelian doctrine that placed all change in the sublunary realm; his own parallax measurements, however, forced the contrary conclusion.
- **Astronomy — technical terms**. *parallaxes / parallaxin* → **parallax**; *Quadrante illo maximo … permagno* → "that great / very great **quadrant**" (Tycho's instrument-type, here the Göggingen quadrant built *ex tuo praescripto* / *tuo instinctu*, "after your prescription / at your prompting"); *Instrumenta et Observationes* → **instruments and observations**; *infra / supra Lunam … in altissimo aethere* → "below / above the Moon … in the highest aether" (the crux of the cosmological dispute: a body with no measurable parallax must lie beyond the Moon, in the supposedly immutable heavens). *censura* rendered "judgement" (a scholar's verdict on submitted work).
- **Greek.** *φαινομένῳ* (dative sing. of *φαινόμενον*, *phainómenon*) = "to this **phenomenon**." Transcribed as printed and translated; the iota-subscript spelling of the dative is retained. Hainzel uses the technical Greek noun for the celestial appearance rather than committing to "comet" or "star."
- ***Philosophus*** — "the Philosopher," i.e. **Aristotle** (*ARISTOTELIS schola* named earlier in the sentence), whose dictum that the heavens admit no new bodies (*Coelum nova non admittere corpora*) Hainzel is reluctant to contradict openly: *praevaleat autoritati experientia*, "let experience prevail over authority" — a notable methodological declaration.
- **Persons named.** *MAeSTHLINO* = **Michael Maestlin** (1550–1631), then a young Tübingen mathematician, whose own 1573 tract on the nova likewise argued for its supralunary, parallax-free position — Hainzel notes Maestlin reaches the same view *per ambages quasdam* ("by certain roundabout ways"). *WOLFIO nostro* = **Hieronymus Wolf** (1516–1580), the Augsburg humanist, "our Wolf." *frater meus* = Hainzel's brother (Johann Baptist Hainzel).
- **Place / dateline.** *Datae Augustae Vindelicorum, Anno 1574 die 10. Martij* = "Given at **Augsburg** (*Augusta Vindelicorum*,), in the year 1574, on the 10th day of March" (O.S.; Denmark and the Empire were on the Julian calendar in 1574, the Gregorian reform being still eight years off). The as-written dateline agrees with the catalogue label (1574.10.marts.Augsburg); no discrepancy.
- **Closing formula.** *Iterumque etiam atque etiam vale* = "And again, again and again, farewell" — an intensified *Iterum vale* (: *Again, farewell*), the doubled *etiam atque etiam* kept as the affectionate redundancy it is, not smoothed.
- **Reading note.** *id quicquid erat iubaris* — *iubar* (poetic, "radiance, brightness, a heavenly light") is read as a partitive genitive after *quicquid*: "the brightness, whatever it was." The hedge (*quicquid erat*, "whatever it was") is preserved rather than resolved to "the star" / "the comet," matching Hainzel's deliberate refusal to pre-judge the object's nature.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VII pp.14-16 read as page images. Letter ("NOBILITATE ET ERUDITIONE PRAESTANTI IUVENI, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE") runs p.14-15, ending with signature "Paulus Haintzel." Collated the technical vocabulary (Quadrante illo maximo, the Greek phainomeno), proper names (Aristotelis, Maesthlino, Wolfio), and closing date (Anno 1574 die 10 Martij) against Dreyer — exact match. Published English faithfully renders the nova/comet argument, the parallax claim, and the closing greetings with no defects.

text.original:
HIERONYMUS WOLFIUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.
S. P. D.

PRÆRIPUISTI, TYCHO Nobilissime, tu meas mihi partes gratias agendi singulari humanitati tuae, me senem, qui iam nihil sum, nisi telluris inutile et miserum pondus, amicum non aspernanti. Sed hic verae doctrinae fructus nimirum est: ut quo sis sublimior, eo summissius te geras. Ego certe tui doctissimi colloquij desiderio (in hac solitudine, quam valetudo mihi offert) saepissime afficior. Et si quid absens, quod tibi gratum iucundumque esset, praestare possem, facerem profecto et fideliter et libenter. Sed perfidia Tabellarij fecit, ut et Bibliotheca D. AMBROSIJ nostri excideris et armillam SCHRECKENFUCHSIJ, amissa pecunia, non acceperis. Quibus de rebus et a MAIORE et Consule nostro certior utique fies: qui mihi mandavit, ut e SCHRECKENFUCHSIO cognoscerem, an eiusmodi armilla esset? et an et quanti vellet vendere? id quod ego prima occatione facturus sum. Raro est enim occasio hinc literas Friburgum mittendi. Unde praevideo, longiusculam esse moram intercessuram, antequam ista ad te perferantur. Sed ut quimus, quando, ut volumus, non licet.

Quae de magnitudinibus stellarum respondes, grata sunt: nec ignoro, quosdam casum stellarum allegorice de praecipuorum doctorum lapsu interpretari. Sed magnitudo ista omnem humani animi cogitationem excedens, corporum coelestium, me saepe quasi attonitum facit et extra me ipsum cum summo stupore rapit cum axiomatibus religionis nostrae conferentem tam angustis et temporum et locorum finibus circumscriptae, et vilissimos nos homunciones et foedissima miserrimaque animalcula omni coelorum ornatui non aequanti modo, sed infinito intervallo praeferenti. Neque IULIANO CÆSARI scribunt quicquam fuisse visum absurdius, quam statuere Solis interitum et terrenorum corpusculorum resurrectionem. D. certe Petrus Epistolae 2, cap. usi. diserte scribit: οἱ νῦν οὐρανοὶ και ἡ γῆ θεοῦ λόγῳ τεθησαυρισμένοι εἰσί, πυρὶ τηρούμενοι εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως καὶ ἀπωλειας τῶν ασεβῶν ανθρώπων. Nec dissimilia sunt apud EZECHIELEM, ESAIAM et alios prophetas: quae non videntur posse ἀλληγορεῖσθαι. Philo autem in libello περὶ αφθαρσίας κόσμου tot tamque invictis rationibus mundi aeternitatem probare mihi quidem videtur: ut nihil illis praeter autoritatem sacrarum Literarum opponi possit. Quos tamen ut recte intelligamus, etiam atque etiam videndum est. Itaque tibi autor sum et loca illa diligenter expendendi, et cum eruditis non modo Philosophis, sed etiam Theologis conferendi, inprimisque cum D. HEMMINGIO, qui Philosophiam cum Theologia et eloquentiam cum utraque coniunxit. Oppugnant et Philosophastri nonnulli (in quibus THOMAS ERASTUS, Heidelbergensis Medicus, maxime triumphat) et Theologastri divinatricem Astrologiam ut et religioni adversantem et divinitus interdictam. Mihi vero videtur nihil Christianismum magis oppugnare, quam infinita coelorum et altitudo et magnitudo. Quibus de rebus in Astrologia mentionem abs te fieri, ac potius accurate illas quaestiones tractari oportere censeo. Praedictionum fidem autem maxime labefactare videntur haec, quae tibi refutanda relinquo. Nam me et ingenium et doctrina in hoc genere destituit.

1. Controversia de numero et motu coelorum.
2. De motu planetarum.
3. De ratione constituendi Thematis Natalitii.
4. Diversa et dissidentia pronunciata de effectibus siderum. Nec enim Arabes cum Ptolemaica doctrina, nec Indi (ut ex ABRAHAMO conicio) cum utrorumque dogmatibus consentiunt.
5. Incerta regnorum et urbium initia et magnarum coniunctionum et trigonorum.
6. Gemellorum summa dissimilitudo rebus plerumque omnibus.
7. Incertum momentum infantis editi, et incertae corrigendi rationes.

Nam quotus quisque stellae alicuius altitudinem observat? Ptolemaicas autem ☌ et ☍ et HERMETIS trutinam magnorum errorum et absurditatum convincit ANTONIUS MONCULMIUS. Iam casus alios alij ad alios significatores referunt, et diversi eventus diversum Horoscopum in mea Genesi plurimis insignibus infortunijs, nonnullis etiam successibus nobilitata, ostendunt: Et in progressionibus vel adhibita vel omissa latitudo quantum discrimen facit? Quid vero de CAMERARIO dicas, viro eruditissimo, mihique, dum viveret, amicissimo, qui et de Horoscopo et de motu singulorum planetarum 27 partes detrahit? Ita mihi pro ♒ horoscopat ♑ : ♄ in ♏, ♃ in ♋, ☉, ☿ in ♌, ♀in ♍, ☾ in ♎ versatur. Ingens utique discrimen. Haec et alia plura tuae industriae erit ita declarare, ut et rudiores (quo in numero et ego senex nomen meum profiteor) edoceantur, et impudentibus calumniatoribus ora obturentur. Philosophicum istud otium ita comparatum, ut fructus eius latissime pateant, et multorum ardua in speciem negotia longe superent ex animo tibi gratulor. Teque hortor (etsi minime quidem id opus est) ne vel ullo splendoris aulici fuco, vel ignobilis nobilitatis ludibrijs et ludicris exercitijs ab honestissimo isto instituto te unquam depelli patiaris. Macte tua virtute TYCHO: sic itur ad astra. Quod me tu ad aequani[mi]tatem adhortaris: agnosco benevolentiam erga me tuam, parebo fidelissimis tuis monitis quantum potero, etsi natura parum fortis. Equidem pro virili

Conor, sed cedit patientia victa dolori.
Verba levant animos, sed dolor aure caret
Expugnata malis sapientia nostra labascit
Dum gravis excruciat, dum diuturna lues.

Equidem legi et Theologorum et Philosophorum omnia solatia: eaque dum mihi bene est, aequi bonique facio: et animi perturbationes moderari, σὺν θεῷ δ' εἰπεῖν, possum mediocriter, sed dolores corporis non verbis, sed aut lapidibus et herbis, aut morte levantur. Nam naturae necessitas aeque mihi atque CARNEADI dolorem auget: neque me CLEANTHES in morbo vociferantem et eiulantem, magnificis suis versibus, quos citat EPICTETUS et eleganter vertit SENECA, quicquam iuvat:

Duc me parens celsique dominator poli,
Quocunque placuit. Nulla parendi mora est.
Assum impiger. Fac nolle? comitabor gemens,
Malasque patiar, quod pati licuit bono.
Ducunt volentem fata, nolentem trahunt.

Sed haec hactenus; unum restat, ut gratias humanitati tuae et Avun­ culi STENONIS BILDIJ liberalitati agam: qui MARCUM HARTLIEBIUM, discipulum meum, malis edoctum, quid sit parentum et praeceptorum monita contemnere, benigne suscepistis. Spero vos beneficia bene posituros.

Novarum rerum nihil scribo, quia paucas scio, easque malas; sed quae hic feruntur, e PETRO cognosces. Septentrionalia vobis notiora utique sunt: sed quae hîc de Megalopyrgio, de Sueco, de Polonis, adeoque ipsa Saxonia nunciantur, parum spem bonam faciunt. AMURATHES SELYMI successor omnes fratres natu minores interfectos, cum patre sepeliendos curasse fertur, Caesari octo annorum dedisse indueras, totam belli molem in Persas conversurus. Sed vereor, ne haec beatorum somnia sint, et nos inopinantes a perfidissimo et potentissimo hoste opprimamur. Vale et ignosce, meque tui memoriam sacrosanctam conservaturum persuasum habeto, ὦ εὐτυχέστατε Τυχών, dum memor ipse mei, dum spiritus hos reget artus.

Consul armillas mittit, negatque tibi meas nugas fore usui: nec ijs onerandum esse Petrum, cum tu his longe meliora habeas instrumenta. Ego Astrolabium (nescius idem esse cum armilla) a SCHRECKENFUXIO mihi donatum, dono tibi mitto: una cum annulo Astronomico a IOACHIMO RINGELBERGIO quondam confecto; quae si tibi (id quod vereor) usui futura non sunt, μνημόσυνον tamen WOLFIJ tui esse patieris. De ceteris plura scribent Cos. HAINZELIUS et M. MAIOR. Literas a SCHRECKENFUXIO ad me datas tibi mitto, imperitus aestimator huius machinae. Iussi ipsum petere quid amplius exigat.

Iterum vale.
Nonis Martii 1575.
HIERON. WOLFIUS tuus.

S. P. Charissime WOLFI, literas 22.
Februarii a te ad me scriptas una cum 16 Coronatis in auro 27. eiusdem accepi.
Petis autem in illis, ut tibi instrumentum aliquod transmittam, quod quidem
recusare nolebam, eo quod alias libenter tibi gratificer. Ad pretium porro
splendidius quod attinet, te iudicem in hac re libenter patior. Quod propria
manu non scribam, in causa est adversa valetudo, ut fortasse ex nuncio melius
percipies, quam ut paucis scribi possit. Ceterum TYCHONIS BRAHE persona, quam
literis tuis depingis, notissima mihi est. Ad erectionem porro huius sphæræ
materialis quod attinet, opus erit solertia quadam, ne colores et numeri in ea
defricentur. Si præterea quid desiderares, postes me certiorem reddere. Habebis
enim semper a me responsum. Tabellarius iste occasionem rescribendi
monstrabit.

Hisce bene vale.

Datæ Friburgi 1.
Martii anno 75.

T.
OSWALDUS
SCHRECKENFUXIUS.
text.english:
**Hieronymus Wolf to Tycho Brahe. He sends heartiest greeting.**

You have forestalled me, most noble Tycho — robbing me of my own part, which was to give thanks to your singular kindness, in that you do not disdain as a friend an old man who is now nothing but an useless and wretched burden upon the earth. But this, to be sure, is the fruit of true learning: that the loftier you are, the more humbly you bear yourself. For my own part I am most often seized with longing for your most learned conversation, in this solitude that my ill-health affords me. And if from afar I could render any service that would be welcome and agreeable to you, I would do it indeed, both faithfully and gladly. But the treachery of the carrier brought it about that you both lost Master Ambrosius's library [Bibliotheca], and — your money gone — did not receive Schreckenfuchs's armilla. Of these matters you will in any case be informed more fully both by the Magistrate [Maior] and by our Consul — who charged me to learn from Schreckenfuchs whether there were such an armilla, and whether, and at what price, he was willing to sell it; which I shall do at the first opportunity. For there is rarely a chance of sending letters from here to Freiburg. Whence I foresee that a fairish delay will intervene before these things are conveyed to you. But [we do] as we can, since we may not [do] as we would.

What you reply concerning the magnitudes of the stars is welcome; nor am I ignorant that certain men interpret the falling of the stars allegorically, of the lapse of the foremost learned men. But that magnitude of the heavenly bodies, exceeding all the thought of the human mind, often makes me as it were thunderstruck and snatches me out of myself with the utmost amazement — when I compare it with the axioms of our religion, hemmed in within such narrow bounds of both time and place; [a religion] that sets us most vile manikins, foulest and most wretched little animals, not merely on a level with all the adornment of the heavens, but ahead of it by an infinite interval. Indeed, [men] write that nothing seemed more absurd to Julian Caesar than to maintain the destruction of the Sun and the resurrection of earthly little bodies. Master Peter, certainly, in his 2nd Epistle, last chapter, writes expressly: "the heavens that now are, and the earth, are stored up by the word of God, kept for fire against the day of judgement and of the destruction of impious men" [οἱ νῦν οὐρανοὶ καὶ ἡ γῆ θεοῦ λόγῳ τεθησαυρισμένοι εἰσί, πυρὶ τηρούμενοι εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως καὶ ἀπωλείας τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἀνθρώπων]. And [things] not unlike are in Ezekiel, Isaiah, and the other prophets — which do not seem able to be allegorized [ἀλληγορεῖσθαι]. Philo, however, in his little book On the Incorruptibility of the Cosmos [περὶ ἀφθαρσίας κόσμου], seems to me at least to prove the eternity of the world by reasonings so many and so unconquerable that nothing can be set against them save the authority of the sacred Writings. Yet, in order that we may rightly understand these [authorities], the matter must be looked into again and again. And so I am your advocate both for weighing those passages diligently, and for conferring about them with learned men — not only Philosophers but also Theologians — and above all with Master Hemmingsen, who has joined Philosophy to Theology, and eloquence to both. Certain petty-philosophers too (among whom Thomas Erastus, the Heidelberg physician, triumphs most of all) and petty-theologians assail divinatory Astrology as both opposed to religion and divinely forbidden. To me, however, it seems that nothing assails Christianity more than the infinite height and magnitude of the heavens. I judge that you ought to make mention of these matters in [your work on] Astrology — or rather that those questions ought to be treated with precision. But the things that seem most of all to shake the credit of [astrological] predictions are these, which I leave to you to refute; for both wit and learning fail me in this kind.

1. The controversy concerning the number and motion of the heavens.
2. The motion of the planets.
3. The method of establishing the nativity figure [Thema Natalitii].
4. The diverse and disagreeing pronouncements concerning the effects of the stars. For neither do the Arabs agree with the Ptolemaic doctrine, nor the Indians (as I conjecture from Abraham) with the dogmas of either.
5. The uncertain foundings of kingdoms and cities, and of the great conjunctions and trigons.
6. The utmost dissimilarity of twins in nearly all matters.
7. The uncertain moment of the infant's birth, and the uncertain methods of correcting it.

For how few there are who observe the altitude of any star! And as for the Ptolemaic conjunctions [☌] and oppositions [☍] and the *trutina* of Hermes, Antonius Montculmius convicts them of great errors and absurdities. Now some men refer one set of events to one set of significators, others to another; and divers outcomes show a divers Horoscope [ascendant] in my geniture, which is ennobled by very many notable misfortunes and by some successes too. And in the progressions, how great a difference does the latitude, whether applied or omitted, make? But what would you say of Camerarius — a most learned man, and, while he lived, most friendly to me — who subtracts 27 degrees both from the Horoscope and from the motion of each several planet? Thus for me he casts ♑ Capricorn as horoscope [ascendant] instead of ♒ Aquarius: ♄ Saturn is set in ♏ Scorpio, ♃ Jupiter in ♋ Cancer, ☉ the Sun [and] ☿ Mercury in ♌ Leo, ♀ Venus in ♍ Virgo, ☾ the Moon in ♎ Libra. A vast difference, surely. It will be for your industry to set forth these and many other matters in such a way that both the more untaught (in whose number I, an old man, enrol my name) may be instructed, and the mouths of shameless slanderers stopped. That philosophic leisure of yours, so contrived that its fruits lie open most widely and far surpass the business of many men [though] arduous in appearance — I congratulate you on it from my heart. And I exhort you (though indeed there is no need of it) never to suffer yourself to be driven from that most honourable resolve, either by any rouge of courtly splendour or by the mockeries and idle exercises of an ignoble nobility. Go on and prosper in your virtue, Tycho: thus is the way to the stars. As for your exhorting me to equanimity — I acknowledge your goodwill toward me, and I shall obey your most faithful admonitions as far as I can, although by nature little stout. Indeed, with all my manhood I

Strive, but my patience, vanquished, gives way to the pain.
Words lighten the spirit, but pain has no ear;
Stormed by ills, our wisdom totters and slips
While the grievous, the long-drawn sickness racks [me].

Indeed I have read all the consolations both of the Theologians and of the Philosophers; and, while it is well with me, I make light of them [reckon them fair and good]; and the perturbations of the mind, to speak with God's help [σὺν θεῷ δ' εἰπεῖν], I can moderate moderately well — but the pains of the body are relieved not by words, but either by stones and herbs, or by death. For the necessity of nature increases the pain for me as much as for Carneades; nor does Cleanthes, with those magnificent verses of his (which Epictetus cites and Seneca elegantly turns) at all help me as I cry out and wail in my sickness:

Lead me, Father and ruler of the lofty pole,
Whithersoever it has pleased thee. There is no delay in obeying.
Here I am, unflagging. Suppose I will not? I shall follow, groaning,
And suffer in wickedness what I might have suffered as a good man.
The Fates lead the willing; the unwilling they drag.

But enough of this. One thing remains: that I give thanks to your kindness and to the generosity of [your] uncle Steno Bille, in that you have graciously taken in Marcus Hartlieb, my pupil — taught by hardships what it is to despise the admonitions of parents and preceptors. I hope you will lay out your benefactions well [to good effect].

Of news I write nothing, since I know little, and that bad; but what is reported here you will learn from Peter. Northern affairs are surely better known to you; but what is told here of Megalopyrgium [Megalopyrgio], of the Swede, of the Poles, and indeed of Saxony itself, gives little good hope. Amurath [Murad III], the successor of Selim, is said to have had all his younger brothers killed and buried together with their father, [and] to have granted the Emperor a truce of eight years, meaning to turn the whole weight of war against the Persians. But I fear these are the dreams of the blessed, and that we, off our guard, may be overwhelmed by a most treacherous and most powerful enemy. Farewell, and forgive [me]; and hold it for assured that I shall keep the memory of you inviolate, O most fortunate Tycho [ὦ εὐτυχέστατε Τυχών], so long as I am mindful of myself, so long as breath shall rule these limbs.

The Consul sends the armillae, and denies that these trifles of mine will be of use to you, nor that Peter should be burdened with them, since you have instruments far better than these. I, for my part, send you as a gift an Astrolabe (not knowing it to be the same as an armilla) given to me by Schreckenfuchs, together with an astronomical ring once made by Joachim Ringelberg; and if these are not going to be of use to you (which I fear), you will yet allow them to be a keepsake [μνημόσυνον] of your Wolf. Of the rest, Consul Hainzel and Master Maior will write more. I send you the letter given to me by Schreckenfuchs, [I being] an unskilled appraiser of this machine. I have bidden him ask what more he requires.

Again, farewell.
On the Nones of March [7 March], 1575.
Your Hieronymus Wolf.

**Greeting. Dearest Wolf** — I received the letter written by you to me on 22 February, together with sixteen gold crowns, on the 27th of the same [month]. In it you ask that I send you some instrument, which indeed I was unwilling to refuse, since on other occasions too I gladly oblige you. As for the finer price, moreover, I am glad to let you be the judge in this matter. That I do not write in my own hand, the cause is ill health, as perhaps you will learn better from the messenger than can be written in a few words. For the rest, the person of Tycho Brahe, whom you depict in your letter, is very well known to me. As for the setting-up of this material sphere, moreover, there will be need of a certain skill, lest the colours and numbers on it be rubbed away. If besides you should want anything further, [you] will be able to make me aware of it — for you will always have an answer from me. This messenger will show the occasion for writing back.

With this, farewell.

Given at Freiburg, 1 March, in the year [15]75.

Yours, Oswald Schreckenfuchs.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Hieronymus Wolfius* = **Hieronymus Wolf** (1516–1580), the Augsburg humanist and Greek scholar (the "father of Byzantine studies"), director of the city's library and school; an early mentor-friend from Tycho's Augsburg years (1569–70). This is the companion to his letter of 13 November 1571 (identifier brahe-t_15711113001): the same illness (the stone and gout), the same landlord (Ambrosius), the same Hainzel circle, the same name-pun sign-off recur.
- **Salutation.** *S. P. D.* = *salutem plurimam dicit*, "sends heartiest greeting".
- ***Bibliotheca D. Ambrosij*** — "Master Ambrosius's library"; *Ambrosius* is the landlord named in the 1571 letter (the lodgings Wolf had rented from him). The phrase is most likely the *book-collection* lost in transit through the carrier's bad faith, alongside the armilla; "library" is kept literal.
- **The instrument.** *armilla Schreckenfuchsij* / *Astrolabium … a Schreckenfuxio* — an **armillary** (zodiacal sphere) constructed at **Freiburg** by **Oswald Schreckenfuchs** (Oswaldus Schreckenfuchsius, 1511–1579), mathematician and astronomer. The biographers confirm the episode: in March 1575 Wolf and Paul Hainzel wrote to Tycho about procuring from Schreckenfuchs "a zodiacal sphere constructed according to the description of Ptolemy" (Dreyer, *Tycho Brahe*; Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, calls it a "Ptolemaic Armillary," noting Schreckenfuchs's own term *sphaera materialis*). Wolf's parenthesis *"nescius idem esse cum armilla"* ("not knowing it to be the same as an armilla") shows he did not realise his own gift-astrolabe and the armilla under discussion were the same class of instrument — hence "armilla" and "Astrolabium" are both kept as written, the confusion preserved.
- ***annulus Astronomicus a Ioachimo Ringelbergio*** — an "astronomical ring" (annular sundial/computing ring) once made by **Joachim Sterck van Ringelberg** (Ioachimus Fortius Ringelbergius, c. 1499 – c. 1536), the Antwerp polymath.
- **Officials.** *Maior / M. Maior* — a magistrate (Lat. *maior*, civic official) of Augsburg, distinct from the Consul; *Consul noster / Cos. Hainzelius* — the **Hainzel** consul of Augsburg (Johann Baptist Hainzel, of the patrician family met in the 1571 letter), here acting as the broker forwarding the instruments. *Petrus* (Peter) is the carrier/intermediary through whom news and parcels pass.
- **The cosmological debate.** Wolf engages Tycho on the *magnitudines stellarum* (sizes of the stars) and the tension between the apparent infinity of the heavens and Christian doctrine — citing **Julian "the Apostate"** (*Iulianus Caesar*), **2 Peter 3:7** (the *D. Petrus … cap. usi.* = *capite ultimo*, the last chapter), Ezekiel, Isaiah, and **Philo of Alexandria's** *De aeternitate mundi* (*περὶ ἀφθαρσίας κόσμου*, "On the Incorruptibility of the Cosmos"). The hedges are preserved ("seems to me at least," "do not seem able to be allegorized").
- **Greek.** *οἱ νῦν οὐρανοὶ καὶ ἡ γῆ θεοῦ λόγῳ τεθησαυρισμένοι εἰσί, πυρὶ τηρούμενοι εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως καὶ ἀπωλείας τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἀνθρώπων* = 2 Peter 3:7, "the heavens that now are, and the earth, are stored up by the word of God, kept for fire against the day of judgement and of the destruction of impious men." · *ἀλληγορεῖσθαι* = "to be allegorized." · *σὺν θεῷ δ' εἰπεῖν* = "to speak with God's help" (a stock qualifier). · *μνημόσυνον* = "memorial, keepsake." · *ὦ εὐτυχέστατε Τυχών* = "O most fortunate Tycho," the learned pun on Tycho's name (Greek *eu-tychḗs* "fortunate"), as in the 1571 letter. The source preserves several scribal/print accent and breathing irregularities (e.g. *ασεβῶν ανθρώπων*, *αφθαρσίας*); reproduced as printed in the Source block, normalised in the translation gloss only.
- **Astrology — the critics.** *divinatricem Astrologiam* = "divinatory Astrology." *Thomas Erastus* (1524–1583), Heidelberg physician, a noted opponent of judicial astrology. *Philosophastri / Theologastri* — coinages of contempt, "petty-philosophers / petty-theologians." *Antonius Montculmius* (also *Moncalmius*) — a 16th-c. critic who, Wolf says, refuted the Ptolemaic conjunctions/oppositions and the *trutina Hermetis*.
- **Astrology — technical terms.** *☌* / *☍* = **conjunction / opposition** (glyphs kept in source, named in translation, this chapter's convention). *trutina Hermetis* = the "balance (scales) of Hermes," the *Trutina Hermetis*, the classic rule for rectifying a nativity from the Moon's place at conception (kept as a technical term). *significatores* = **significators**; *Horoscopum / horoscopat* = the **horoscope** in its original sense of the **ascendant**/ascending degree (translated "horoscope [ascendant]" to avoid the modern "natal chart" sense); *progressiones* = **progressions**; *latitudo* = (celestial) **latitude**. *partes* (geometric/zodiacal) = **degrees**.
- **The Camerarius rectification.** *Camerarius … qui … de Horoscopo et de motu singulorum planetarum 27 partes detrahit* — **Joachim Camerarius** ("a most learned man, while he lived most friendly to me"; the elder, 1500–1574, or his son Joachim the Younger, the physician-astrologer), who subtracts **27 degrees** from Wolf's ascendant and from each planet's place. The resulting placement, as printed: ascendant **♑ Capricorn** (in place of **♒ Aquarius**); **♄ Saturn in ♏ Scorpio**, **♃ Jupiter in ♋ Cancer**, **☉ Sun and ☿ Mercury in ♌ Leo**, **♀ Venus in ♍ Virgo**, **☾ Moon in ♎ Libra**. All glyphs kept in the Source block and named in English.
- ***sic itur ad astra*** — "thus is the way to the stars," Virgil, *Aeneid* 9.641; here a deliberate astronomical double-entendre (kept as the proverbial tag).
- **Verse 1** (*Conor, sed cedit patientia victa dolori …*) — an elegiac quatrain on the limits of patience under chronic pain; kept as verse. The first line adapts the topos of Ovid (cf. *patientia victa* / pain-overcomes-resolve), but the quatrain is given without a named source in the letter; the attribution is therefore not asserted.
- **Verse 2** (*Duc me parens celsique dominator poli …*) — **Seneca's** Latin version of the prayer of **Cleanthes** the Stoic, *Epistulae morales* 107.11 (the Greek original cited by **Epictetus**, *Enchiridion* 53). Wolf names both sources in the prose. Kept as verse; the last line is the famous *Ducunt volentem fata, nolentem trahunt* ("The Fates lead the willing; the unwilling they drag").
- ***Carneades*** — the Academic philosopher, here the type of the man whose physical pain no philosophy can argue away. *Cleanthes … in morbo vociferantem* — Wolf, ill, casts himself as a Cleanthes who cries out despite the Stoic hymn.
- **Persons (closing).** *Avunculus Steno Bildij* = **Steen (Steno) Bille**, Tycho's maternal uncle (at whose Scanian manor of Herrisvad Tycho observed the 1572 nova); *vos … suscepistis* is plural — Wolf thanks Tycho *and* Bille jointly for taking in his pupil. *Marcus Hartlieb* (Hartliebius), Wolf's wayward pupil, placed in their household. *D. Hemmingius* = **Niels Hemmingsen** (Nicolaus Hemmingius, 1513–1600), the eminent Copenhagen theologian, recommended as the man who joined philosophy, theology, and eloquence (Dreyer's note records that Hemmingsen, drawing on Calvin's *Admonitio adversus astrologiam*, was himself hostile to astrology — an irony Wolf does not flag).
- **News / political.** *Megalopyrgio* — literally "great-tower" (Gk. *megas* + *pyrgos*); a Graecized name whose referent is **not securely identifiable** — possibly a Latinized German toponym/personal name (e.g. a "Großturm"-type place) or a coded designation in Wolf's news-passage. *Sueco* = "the Swede" (the Swedish king, John III); *Poloni* = the Poles (the contested 1574–76 royal succession after Henry of Valois's flight); *Saxonia* = Saxony. *Amurathes Selymi successor* = **Murad III** (r. 1574–95), successor of **Selim II**, who on his accession (December 1574) had his five younger brothers strangled and buried with their father — the event Wolf reports. *Caesar* = the Holy Roman Emperor (Maximilian II). **Reading crux:** *"Caesari octo annorum dedisse indueras"* — *indueras* is corrupt; the sense plainly requires *indutias* ("a truce/armistice of eight years"), and is so translated, but the printed form is kept in the Source block and flagged here. The 1568 Adrianople truce between the Ottomans and the Habsburgs was indeed renewed under Murad.
- **Calendar / place.** *Nonis Martii 1575* = "on the **Nones of March** (7 March), 1575" (Old Style; Denmark and the Empire were pre-Gregorian). The edition's catalogue label "1575. 7. marts. Augsburg?" agrees with the dateline on the day; the place is supplied by the catalogue with a query (the dateline names no place), and is given as **Augsburg** on the strength of Wolf's residence and the companion 1571 letter (*Augustae Vindelicorum*), but the letter text itself does not name it — hence "Augsburg" in the header is editorial. *Iterum vale* = "Again, farewell".
- **What the recovered text is.** The published tail of this letter (Hieronymus Wolf to Tycho, 7 March 1575) says Wolf is sending Tycho, as a gift, an astrolabe and an astronomical ring, and adds "I send you the letter given to me by Schreckenfuchs" (*Literas a Schreckenfuxio ad me datas tibi mitto*). The recovered segment is that very enclosure: a letter from Erasmus Oswald Schreckenfuchs to Wolf, dated four days earlier (1 March 1575) from Freiburg, which Wolf then forwarded on to Tycho.
- **Confirms Tycho's 1569 visit to Schreckenfuchs.** Schreckenfuchs writes that "the person of Tycho Brahe, whom you depict in your letter, is very well known to me" (*notissima mihi est*) — direct first-hand corroboration of the personal acquaintance recorded in Mosley (*Bearing the Heavens*), where Tycho is said to have visited Erasmus Oswald Schreckenfuchs (1511–1579), professor at Freiburg, and admired his instrument collection during his 1569 travels.
- **Erasmus Oswald Schreckenfuchs** (1511–1579) was a mathematics and Hebrew professor successively at Tübingen, Freiburg and Basel, known for folio commentaries on Peurbach, Sacrobosco and the *Tabulae directionum* (Gingerich, *Annotated Census of Copernicus' De revolutionibus*).
- **Commercial/practical detail.** The letter records a payment of sixteen gold crowns received from Wolf on 27 February for an instrument (evidently the "material sphere" — an armillary instrument — that Wolf then re-gifted to Tycho "not knowing it to be the same as an armilla," per the published tail), with Schreckenfuchs leaving the final price to Wolf's judgement and warning that assembling it will require care so its painted graduations ("colours and numbers") are not rubbed off in handling.
- **Crux: *postes* in "Si praeterea quid desiderares, postes me certiorem reddere."** "Postes" (nominative/accusative plural of *postis*, "doorpost") does not construe grammatically in this clause. The translation above renders the evident intended sense — "[you] will be able to make me aware of it" — on the assumption that this is a corrupted or miscopied form of *poteris* ("you will be able"), which also fits the following clause ("for you will always have an answer from me"). The source reading has not been altered; this is flagged as an unresolved transcription crux, not silently corrected.
- **Correction.** Restored Wolf's numbered seven-item list of astrological controversies (Dreyer, TBOO VII p.16), missing in full from both the Latin source text and the translation, between 'Nam me et ingenium et doctrina in hoc genere destituit.' and 'Nam quotus quisque stellae alicuius altitudinem observat?'

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. All 5 Dreyer pages read as page images (TBOO VII pp. 15-19, the full letter Wolf-to-Tycho 7 March 1575 plus the enclosed Schreckenfuchs postscript). Collated opening (PRAeRIPUISTI, TYCHO Nobilissime...), closing (Nonis Martij 1575 / HIERON. WOLFIUS tuus, and the appended Schreckenfuchs note dated Friburgi 1. Martii anno 75), the Greek 2 Peter quotation, the Camerarius horoscope-degree table, the sums (16 gold crowns, 22/27 February dates), and named persons (Ambrosius, Schreckenfuchs, Consul, Maior, Hemmingsen, Erastus, Montculmius, Camerarius, Cleanthes/Epictetus/Seneca, Steno Bille, Marcus Hartlieb, Petrus, Amurath/Murad III) against the page images. One serious defect found: an entire Dreyer-printed numbered list (the seven astrological controversies Wolf poses) is missing from our transcribed original and consequently from the translation. Aside from that dropped list, the remaining text (including the verse quotations and the enclosed Schreckenfuchs letter) matches Dreyer exactly.

**1 defect found:**
- **text error** (**high**). Dreyer (TBOO VII p.16) prints a full numbered seven-item list of the specific astrological controversies Wolf is asking Tycho to refute (heavens' motion, planetary motion, nativity-casting method, Arab/Indian doctrinal disagreement, uncertain civic foundings, twins' dissimilarity, uncertain birth-moment) between 'destituit.' and 'Nam quotus quisque'; our transcribed original drops the whole list, so the translation never had it to render. This is exactly the itemised agenda the rest of Wolf's paragraph (star altitudes, Ptolemaic aspects, horoscope discrepancies, Camerarius) is answering point-by-point, so its loss removes the structuring frame a scholar needs. Dreyer prints: *1. Controversia de numero et motu coelorum. 2. De motu planetarum. 3. De ratione constituendi Thematis Natalitii. 4. Diversa et dissidentia pronunciata de effectibus siderum. Nec enim Arabes cum Ptolemaica doctrina, nec Indi (ut ex Abrahamo conijcio) cum utrorumque dogmatibus consentiunt. 5. Incerta regnorum et urbium initia et magnarum conjunctionum et trigonorum. 6. Gemellorum summa dissimilitudo rebus plerumque omnibus. 7. Incertum momentum infantis editi, et incertae corrigendi rationes.*.

**Repaired.** Collated against the Dreyer page images for this letter (TBOO VII pp.15-19; read as page images, not the digitised text layer): p.16 prints the numbered list 1-7 exactly as the audit cites, in the exact location claimed. Restored both the Latin (normalising long-s and ss-ligature to the edition's spelling already used throughout this document, e.g. 'ae' not the ligature, no lowercase 'j' in common words) and a matching English translation of the seven items. No other cruces surfaced on the pages read (pp.15-18); p.19, the Schreckenfuchs exchange, was outside the defect's location and was not needed.
