text.original:
NOBILITATE ET ERUDITIONE PRÆSTANTI IUVENI DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, AMICO SUO SINGULARI.
S. P. D.

SI vales, bene est, mi TYCHO, ego quidem Dei beneficio nunc recte valeo, et febre quartana tandem liberatus sum. Quae de Instrumentis tuis Astronomicis scripsisti, libenter legi, et illud Armillarum Ptolemaicarum, quod solum te nunc desiderare intellexi, WOLFIJ nostri auxilio atque literis (certo nuncio ad SCHRECKENFUCHSIUM Friburgum cum munere pro ijs Armillis misso) facile a SCHRECKENFUCHSIO impetravimus. Quod quidem PETRUS Aurifaber cum supellectile sua hinc ad vos transportabit. Et licet COPERNICUS plenam et ornatam de compositione huius Organi descriptionem in secundo suo de Revolutionibus libro cap. 14 referat, tamen etiam IOHANNIS REGIOMONTANI de constructione et usu eius enarrationem adiungere Instrumento volui: quam ex REGIOMONTANI scriptis (Norimbergae de quinque Instrumentis Astronomicis, Torqueto, Astrolabio Armillari, Regula magna Ptolemaica, Baculo Astronomico et Quadrato geometrico cum IOHANNIS SCHŒNERI Carolostadij additionibus, anno MDXLIII editis) transcribi curavi, si forte eo libro careres, de quo tamen sane dubito. Tabellarius iste nequam, qui nummis, quos illi credidisti, absumptis profugit, nondum redijt, is vel vagus et exui a patria errabit, vel quod abstulit, restituet. MARCUS HARTLIEB, uxoris meae ex sorore nepos, ante biennium Wittenbergam studiorum caussa a parentibus missus, annum forte ibi commoratus est. Priore semestri vel plus eo se, ut diligentem et liberum decet adolescentem, strenue gessit, et bonam in literis operam navare coepit. Posteriore semestri minus sui officij satagebat, quod quidem simul atque parentes eius licet serius resciscerent, statim eum Wittenbergâ ad fratrem IOHANNEM, I. V. Doctorem, Consiliarium Electoris, Heydelbergam ut proficisceretur, avocarunt. Is in itinere cum in quendam hominem, ne quid scribam vehementius, non bonum incidisset, et in eo itinere aliquot septimanis, non sine magno studiorum suorum et pecuniae dispendio, cunctaretur, tandem Heydelbergam ad fratrem cum comite venit, corporis se et valetudinis incommoda in via pertulisse fingens. Id quod socius eius apud fratrem etiam falso testatus: et MARCO fratri pecuniam in itinere erogasse affirmans, viginti Ioachimicos a D. Doctore IOHANNE MARCI fratre extorsit. MARCUS deinde cum a fratre de omnibus quae hactenus egisset, admonitus et obiurgatus esset, inscio et invito fratre, sibique ipsi male conscius Heydelbergâ discedit. Quo posthac profectus sit, aut ubi hactenus se detinuerit, non sat scimus. Verum PETRUS Aurifaber, qui tuas mihi reddidit, aiebat eum Hafniae apud te bonis conditionibus esse, et studijs incumbere. M. IOHANNES quoque MAIOR significabat, se literas a MARCO apud eundem PETRUM accepisse, quibus fere idem scribebat, et praeterea culpam deprecabatur, atque rogabat, ut apud patrem de reconciliatione ageret. Sed iratus pater aegre adhuc reconciliabitur. Si veram paenitentiam egerit atque resipuerit, gratum mihi feceris, si mea caussa eum, quod sine molestia tua fieri velim, iuveris: sin aliquid posthac praeter officium fecerit, et in priori sua negligentia perstiterit, quicquid in eum supplicii sumpseris, etiamsi eum egregie et male mulctaveris, et parentibus et nobis propinquis et cognatis suis rem gratam feceris. Mater eius, piae memoriae femina, praeterito mense, 3 nimirum Nonas Februarii, vesperi hora 8 pie in Christo obdormivit: cum ante annos 48 Nonis eiusdem mensis in hunc mundum nasceretur. Illud te admonere volui: In compositione magnarum PTOLEMÆI Armillarum (quae minutorum vel subtilioris distributionis capaces sunt) cum distantia Polorum (Aequinoctialis videlicet et Eclipticae) pro ratione temporis mutetur, Axonia, quae cum Delatore Zodiaci in Polis mundi convertuntur, ita in Delatore transijci posse, ut 24 minutorum spatio (quae sunt, ut nosti, differentiae maximae et minimae obliquitatis Signiferi) hinc inde pro mutatione Declinationis Solis maximae, quocunque volueris moveri, et nihilominus intra tale spatium ubivis et quandocunque certo loco secundum diametrum cum Polo mundi connecti convertique queant. Praeterea id quoque ad pleniorem huius Instrumenti perfectionem facere videtur (quo stellarum loca accuratius exquisitiusque et ad secunda, tertia, quarta etc. scrupula haberi atque capi possint) ut Geometrica illa et artificiosa plurimorum circulorum, intra se invicem ductorum, distributio in planis lateribus Armillarum atque earum maxillis (quod facile in tanta Armillarum latitudine fieri potest) debito modo notetur atque designetur. Sed quid ego noctuas Athenas, qui haec ad te? Illud pene significare tibi praetermiseram. Quadrantem nostrum Giggingensem Nonis Decembris proximis, increbrescente vehementiore vento, lapsum corruisse, eiusque usum nobis nunc penitus ademptum esse. Iterum atque iterum vale. Clavem ad capsulam Armillarum hic una mitto. Frater meus et ANDREAS WELSERUS plurimam tibi salutem reddunt, atque tui memoriam cum honorifica de te mentione saepenumero recordari solent.

Iterum vale, et me, quod facis, redamare ne desinas.
Dabantur Augustae Vindelicorum, die Aequinoctij verni, hoc est 5. Idus Martij, Anno salutis M. D. LXXV.
T. Paulus Haintzel.

Quae subiunguntur post scripta, erant manu fratris eius
Iohannis Baptistæ
Haintzelij, Septem viri Augustani, exarata.

Vir nobilissime, amice observande, intelligo ex scriptis et
lucubrationibus doctorum virorum regni vestri, Dominum PETRUM OXEUM summum esse Regni
vestri Consiliarium ac curiæ magistrum. Is, cum fuerit olim
Basileæ, sub SIMONE GRYNÆO, communi
præceptore nostro, et convictor et condiscipulus meus, habueritque
præceptorem D. D. CHRISTIERNUM MORSIANUM, virum doctum et bene de me
meritum, perquam libenter scire velim, an ambo recte habeant et
valeant. Quod, si amicitiæ nostræ, olim Basileæ inter nos contractæ,
adhuc sunt memores, velis ambos data occasione meo nomine amanter et
reverenter salutare, illisque mea officia et studia prompta et
parata deferre. Te etiam et tuam salutem propitio humani generis
Salvatori commendo, precans ex animo, ut quam diutissime salvus et
incolumis Ecclesiæ et Reipublicæ servetis et conservetis.

Tui observantiss.
Iohannes Baptista
Haintzelius.
text.english:
**To the young man pre-eminent in nobility and learning, Master Tycho Brahe, his singular friend — heartiest greeting.**

If you are well, it is good, my Tycho; I, for my part, by God's kindness am now in sound health, and have at last been freed from a quartan fever. What you wrote about your astronomical instruments I read gladly; and that matter of the Ptolemaic armillae — the only thing I gathered you now wanted — we have easily obtained from Schreckenfuchs, with the help and letters of our friend Wolf (a trusty messenger having been sent to Schreckenfuchs at Freiburg with a gift in return for those armillae). Peter the goldsmith will carry it from here to you along with his own baggage. And although Copernicus gives a full and elegant account of the construction of this instrument in the second book of his *De revolutionibus*, chapter 14, I nevertheless wished to add to the instrument Johann Regiomontanus's exposition too, on its construction and use — which I had transcribed from Regiomontanus's writings (published at Nuremberg, on the five astronomical instruments: the torquetum, the armillary astrolabe, the great Ptolemaic rule, the cross-staff [*baculus astronomicus*], and the geometric square, with the additions of Johannes Schöner of Karlstadt, in the year 1543) — in case you happened to lack that book, though of that I rather doubt. That worthless courier, who absconded after squandering the money you entrusted to him, has not yet returned; either he will wander as a vagrant and an exile from his homeland, or he will restore what he carried off. Marcus Hartlieb, my wife's nephew by her sister, sent two years ago by his parents to Wittenberg for the sake of his studies, stayed there a year, as it chanced. In the first half-year, or rather more, he conducted himself energetically, as becomes a diligent and free-born youth, and began to apply good effort to his letters. In the latter half-year he was less attentive to his duty; and as soon as his parents learned of this — albeit rather late — they at once recalled him from Wittenberg, that he should set out for Heidelberg to his brother Johannes, Doctor of Both Laws, councillor of the Elector. On the way, having fallen in (that I may write nothing too harsh) with a man who was not good, and having dawdled some weeks on that journey, not without great loss to his studies and his money, he came at last to his brother at Heidelberg with a companion, pretending that he had suffered bodily and ill-health troubles on the road. His companion likewise falsely testified to the same before the brother; and, affirming that he had laid out money for Marcus on the journey, he extorted twenty Joachimsthalers from Master Doctor Johannes, Marcus's brother. Then Marcus, when he had been admonished and rebuked by his brother for everything he had done up to that point, departed from Heidelberg without his brother's knowledge and against his will, ill at ease in his own conscience. Where he set out for afterward, or where he has detained himself up to now, we do not well know. But Peter the goldsmith, who delivered your letter to me, said that he was at Copenhagen with you on good terms, and applying himself to his studies. Master Johannes Maior also indicated that he had received a letter from Marcus, through the same Peter, in which he wrote much the same thing, and besides begged pardon for his fault and asked that [Maior] would treat with his father about a reconciliation. But the father, being angry, will still be hard to reconcile. If he shall have shown true repentance and come to his senses, you will do me a kindness if, for my sake, you help him — which I should wish to be done without trouble to yourself; but if hereafter he does anything contrary to his duty, and persists in his former negligence, then whatever punishment you exact upon him — even if you chastise him soundly and severely — you will do a welcome thing both to his parents and to us, his kinsmen and relations. His mother, a woman of pious memory, in the past month — namely on 3 February [the third before the Nones of February], at 8 in the evening — fell piously asleep in Christ, having been born into this world 48 years before on the Nones of the same month. This I wished to point out to you: in the construction of the great Ptolemaic armillae (which are capable of [a division into] minutes or of a still finer division), since the distance of the poles (namely of the equinoctial and of the ecliptic) changes with the lapse of time, the little axles, which turn with the zodiacal carrier-ring upon the poles of the world, can be so shifted within the carrier-ring that over a span of 24 minutes (which are, as you know, the differences of the greatest and least obliquity of the zodiac) they may be moved either way at will, in keeping with the change of the Sun's greatest declination, and may nonetheless, anywhere and at any time within such a span, be connected and turned together with the pole of the world along the diameter at a fixed place. Furthermore, this too seems to make for a fuller perfection of this instrument (whereby the places of the stars may be had and taken more accurately and exactly, even to seconds, thirds, fourths, etc. of scruples [of arc]): that that geometric and artful distribution of very many circles, drawn one within another, should be marked and traced out in due manner on the flat sides of the armillae and on their jaws [maxillae] (which can easily be done given so great a breadth of the armillae). But why do I [carry] owls to Athens, in [writing] these things to you? I had nearly omitted to mention this to you: that our quadrant at Göggingen, on the last Nones of December [5 December], a rather violent wind having risen, slipped and collapsed, and the use of it is now wholly taken from us. Again and again, farewell. The key to the case of the armillae I send here together [with this]. My brother and Andreas Welser return you many greetings, and are wont often to recall your memory with honourable mention of you.

Again, farewell; and do not cease — as you do — to return my love.
Given at Augsburg, on the day of the vernal equinox, that is, the 5th [day before] the Ides of March [11 March], in the year of salvation 1575.
Yours, Paul Hainzel.

**What follows, appended after the writing, was penned in the hand of his brother Johann Baptist Hainzel, Septemvir of Augsburg.**

Most noble sir, esteemed friend, I understand from the writings and learned labours of the learned men of your kingdom, that Master Peter Oxe is the chief Councillor of your kingdom and Master of the Court. Since he was once at Basel, under Simon Grynaeus, our common teacher, both my messmate and fellow-student, and had as his tutor Master Christiern Morsianus, a learned man and one well deserving of me, I should very gladly wish to know whether both are well and in good health. Wherefore, if they still remember our friendship, once contracted between us at Basel, would you, when occasion offers, greet both of them lovingly and respectfully in my name, and offer them my ready and prepared service and devotion. You too, and your welfare, I commend to the gracious Saviour of mankind, praying from my heart that you may, for as long as possible, remain safe and unharmed, and preserve yourselves for the Church and the Commonwealth.

Your most devoted, Johann Baptist Hainzel.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Paulus Haintzel* = **Paul Hainzel** (d. 1581), city councillor (*Ratsherr*) of Augsburg of the leading Hainzel patrician family; with his brother Johann Baptist Hainzel (burgomaster) a patron of astronomy and friend of Tycho from Tycho's Augsburg years (1569–70). It was Paul Hainzel who funded the celebrated great quadrant (radius c. 14 cubits, c. 19 ft) built with Tycho in 1569 at his country estate at Göggingen, southwest of Augsburg.
- **Recipient.** The edition header repeats "Tycho Brahe Tycho Brahe"; a single addressee, Tycho, is intended (the salutation reads *Domino Tychoni Brahe*). At this date (March 1575) Tycho was at Copenhagen (*Hafniae*, as the letter itself states), before the 1576 grant of Hven.
- ***Schreckenfuchs*** = **Erasmus Oswald Schreckenfuchs** (1511–1579), mathematician and astronomer, then at **Freiburg im Breisgau** (*Friburgum*), commentator on Ptolemy, Peurbach and Sacrobosco; the source of the *Armillae Ptolemaicae*.
- ***Petrus Aurifaber*** — "Peter the goldsmith": *Aurifaber* is here read as the trade-name/surname of a craftsman-courier who carried both letter and instrument; rendered "Peter the goldsmith." Not to be confused with the Wittenberg/Königsberg theologian-editor of the same Latinised name.
- ***Schoeneri Carolostadij*** = **Johannes Schöner** of **Karlstadt** (Carolostadius, 1477–1547), Nuremberg mathematician, who edited Regiomontanus's *Scripta* (the collection on the torquetum, armillary astrolabe, etc.). Hainzel dates the edition *anno MDXLIII* (**1543**); the standard Nuremberg Schöner edition of the Regiomontanus instrument tracts is usually dated **1544** — the as-written 1543 is preserved and the divergence flagged, not corrected.
- ***Johannes / Johann Regiomontanus*** = **Regiomontanus** (Johannes Müller of Königsberg, 1436–1476). The instrument list in the Schöner/Regiomontanus tract names five: *Torquetum*, *Astrolabium Armillare* (armillary astrolabe), *Regula magna Ptolemaica* (great Ptolemaic rule), ***Baculus Astronomicus*** (the astronomical staff / Jacob's-staff — the *baculus*, rendered with the English instrument-name "cross-staff," with the source word *baculus astronomicus* bracketed), and *Quadratum geometricum* (geometric square). Note: the source word here is *baculus astronomicus*, not the glossary lemma *radius astronomicus*; the English "cross-staff" denotes the same class of instrument, but the bracketed Latin preserves the source's own term.
- ***Marcus Hartlieb*** — Hainzel's wife's nephew (sister's son), a wayward student then said to be with Tycho at Copenhagen; **Johannes (Hartlieb)**, his elder brother, *I. V. Doctor* (*Iuris Utriusque Doctor*, Doctor of Both Laws — civil and canon) and councillor to the Elector [Palatine] at Heidelberg. *M. Iohannes Maior* = **Johannes Maior (Meier)**, gymnasium teacher at Augsburg. *Andreas Welserus* = **Andreas Welser**, of the Augsburg patrician/merchant Welser family.
- ***viginti Ioachimicos*** = "twenty **Joachimsthalers**" (silver coins of Joachimsthal, the *Joachimsthaler*/*thaler*); kept as the period coin-name.
- **Astronomy / instruments (the technical core).** *Armillae (Ptolemaicae)* = **Ptolemaic armillae / armillary** (the Ptolemaic *astrolabon*, the great observing armillary), per glossary. *Organum / Instrumentum* = **instrument**. *Delator Zodiaci* — literally the "carrier/bearer of the zodiac": the ring that carries the ecliptic/zodiac, rendered "zodiacal carrier-ring." *Axonia* (Gk.-derived, *ἀξόνια*, "little axles/pivots") — the small pivot-axles on which the carrier-ring turns at the poles; rendered "little axles." *Poli mundi* = "the poles of the world" (celestial poles); *Polorum Aequinoctialis et Eclipticae* = the poles of the equinoctial (equator) and of the ecliptic. *obliquitas Signiferi* = "obliquity of the zodiac" (*Signifer* = the sign-bearer, the zodiac/ecliptic); the "24 minutes [of arc]" Hainzel cites as the range between greatest and least obliquity. *Declinatio Solis maxima* = "the Sun's greatest declination" (, *declinatio* → declination). *scrupula* (secunda, tertia, quarta) = "scruples [of arc]" — the sexagesimal subdivisions (seconds, thirds, fourths); *minuta* = "minutes." *maxillae Armillarum* = "the jaws of the armillae" (the projecting edge-pieces/cheeks of the rings), rendered "jaws [maxillae]." The passage is Hainzel relaying a constructional refinement for the great armillary — allowing the ecliptic-carrying ring to be re-set within a 24′ range to follow the secular change in the obliquity of the ecliptic. The technical prose is dense but coherent; rendered faithfully without smoothing.
- ***Copernicus … de Revolutionibus libro [II] cap. 14*** — the reference is to Copernicus, *De revolutionibus* Book II (the construction of the *astrolabon*/armillary instrument is at II.14 in the standard text). The source as transcribed reads *in secundo suo … libro cap. 14*; the book-number "second" is preserved.
- ***noctuas Athenas*** — "owls to Athens," the proverb (Erasmus, *Adagia*; cf. *γλαῦκ' Ἀθήναζε*) for needlessly supplying what one already has in abundance; Hainzel apologises for explaining instrument-craft to Tycho. Kept as the proverb ("owls to Athens"); the elided verb supplied in brackets "[carry]."
- ***febris quartana*** = **quartan fever**.
- ***Quadrantem … Giggingensem*** = "our **Göggingen** quadrant" — the great quadrant at Hainzel's Göggingen estate (spelt *Giggingensem* in the source; the place is Göggingen/Göggingen near Augsburg, "Goggingen" in Dreyer, "Göggingen" in Norlind). Hainzel reports it blew down in a high wind on 5 December (*Nonis Decembris proximis*) and is no longer usable.
- **Dates within the letter.** *3 Nonas Februarii* — "the third [day before] the Nones of February" = **3 February** (Nones of February = 5 Feb.; counting inclusively, the 3rd-before = 3 Feb.), the death of Marcus's mother, said to have been born "48 years before, on the Nones of the same month" (i.e. born 5 February c. 1527, died 3 February 1575). *Nonis Decembris* = the **Nones of December = 5 December** (collapse of the quadrant). Roman-calendar idiom retained and glossed by this chapter's convention; no silent conversion.
- **Dateline.** *Dabantur Augustae Vindelicorum, die Aequinoctij verni, hoc est 5. Idus Martij, Anno salutis M. D. LXXV* = "Given at **Augsburg**, on the day of the vernal equinox, that is, **the 5th [day before] the Ides of March = 11 March**, 1575." Ides of March = 15 March; *5. Idus Martij* counts inclusively (15, 14, 13, 12, 11) to **11 March**. The header date (11 March 1575, O.S.) agrees with the edition *label* ("1575. 11. marts. Augsburg"). Hainzel's equation of 11 March with the vernal equinox reflects the pre-Gregorian Julian drift of the calendar against the true equinox; the dating is **O.S.** (the Gregorian reform of 1582 lay seven years ahead, and the Empire/Augsburg used the Julian calendar in 1575).
- **MS witnesses.** Two Vienna copies in the Tycho *Nachlass*: A = ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.7; B = ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66 (shelfmarks as given in the edition).
- **What the recovered text is.** The published tail of this letter (Paul Hainzel to Tycho, 11 March 1575) closes with news of a collapsed quadrant at Göggingen and greetings from "my brother" and Andreas Welser; the recovered segment is that brother's own postscript, explicitly headed as being in the hand of Johann Baptist Hainzel — a separate, self-contained note asking Tycho to relay greetings to two men at the Danish court.
- **Peter Oxe = Peder Oxe (1520–1575),** at this date Denmark's Rigshovmester (Lord High Steward) and its most powerful royal councillor, effectively running crown finance and administration for Frederick II; he died later the same year (24 October 1575), so this letter falls within his last months in office.
- **The Basel connection.** Johann Baptist Hainzel identifies himself as a former fellow-boarder and fellow-student of Peder Oxe at Basel, both taught by "Simon Grynaeus" — the works consulted do not resolve whether this is Simon Grynaeus the elder (1493–1541, the celebrated Basel Hellenist and editor of Euclid/Proclus, a contemporary of Erasmus) or his nephew Simon Grynaeus the younger (1539–1582), also a Basel professor; Oxe's documented period abroad in the 1540s makes the elder Grynaeus the more plausible teacher, but this is not corroborated in our holdings and should be checked against a Peder Oxe biography before use.
- **Unidentified: "D. D. Christiernum Morsianum."** Named as Peder Oxe's own tutor ("praeceptorem") and a man Johann Baptist is personally indebted to — this is a distinct individual from Elias Olsen Morsing (Tycho's later Hven assistant, also surnamed for the island of Mors), who was not yet active in the 1540s–50s timeframe implied here. the works consulted do not otherwise identify a "Christiern Morsing" as Peder Oxe's tutor; this is a genuinely new name surfaced by the recovered text and worth flagging for further biographical research.
- **Possible conflict with Dreyer on which Hainzel brother held which office.** The recovered text's own heading calls Johann Baptist "*Septem vir Augustanus*" (a Septemvir — one of the Seven, an Augsburg patrician civic office). Dreyer's *Tycho Brahe* (1890), by contrast, states that of the two brothers "the former [Johann Baptist] burgomaster, the latter [Paul] an alderman (septemvir)." The letter's own contemporary self-description of Johann Baptist as Septemvir sits awkwardly with Dreyer's assignment of that office to Paul — either Dreyer reversed the brothers' offices or used the titles loosely; this is worth resolving against Augsburg civic records rather than taken as settled.
- **Correction.** Two one-word corruptions in the Latin apparatus restored from Dreyer: "intellige" to "intelligo" (TBOO VII, p.21) and "Torquete" to "Torqueto" (TBOO VII, p.19). Both English clauses were already correct and are unchanged.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter — Hainzel's body (the Ptolemaic armillae obtained via Schreckenfuchs/Wolf, the Regiomontani instrument list and its 1543 Nuremberg edition, the absconding courier, the Marcus Hartlieb family scandal with its dates and the 20-Joachimsthaler extortion, the mother's death date/age, the technical armillae-construction passage with its 24-minute figure, the Göggingen quadrant's collapse on the Nones of December, the closing date '5 Idus Martii 1575') plus Johann Baptist Haintzelius's appended postscript (Peter Oxe, Simon Grynaeus, Christiern Morsianus, Basel) — against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.19-21, reading page images directly. Two divergences between the transcribed original and Dreyer found, both narrow single-word corruptions in our Latin apparatus (a case ending, a verb mood); the English translation itself correctly follows Dreyer's actual printed reading in both places, so neither is a translation-fidelity defect — but by the audit's rule any text error caps the grade at C. All proper names, numbers, dates, and sums checked and correct.

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). the transcribed original has "Torquete", which is not a grammatical form here; Dreyer prints "Torqueto", correctly agreeing in case with the surrounding ablative list. The English correctly identifies the instrument as "the torquetum" regardless, so the translation itself is not at fault — this is a corruption in our published Latin apparatus. Dreyer prints: *Torqueto (TBOO VII, p.19) — the ablative case, agreeing with the rest of the ablative list of Regiomontanus's five instruments (Astrolabio Armillari, Regula magna Ptolemaica, Baculo Astronomico, Quadrato geometrico)*.
- **text error** (medium). the transcribed original has the imperative "intellige" ("understand!"); Dreyer prints the indicative "intelligo" ("I understand"). This is a one-letter mood shift in our Latin apparatus. The English translation ("I understand...") in fact follows Dreyer's actual reading, not our own the transcribed original — further confirming the transcribed original is the corrupted party here, not the translation. Dreyer prints: *intelligo (TBOO VII, p.21, opening of Johann Baptist Haintzelius's postscript)*.

**Repaired.** Collated against the Dreyer page images for TBOO VII pp.19-22 (both disputed readings fall on pp.19 and 21, both examined). Both text error confirmed exactly as the audit described; both are pure Latin-apparatus corruptions that had not misled the (already correct) English translation. No remaining uncertainty.

documents.abstract: Acknowledges receipt of the book *On the New Star* and praises Tycho for restoring astronomy from common neglect to its proper dignity.
documents.incipit: IAM agitur annus, TYCHO doctissime, ex quo GULIELMUS LUMMISDAL, cum isthinc domum …
documents.editorial_note: **Text recovered.** The postscript or enclosure, missing from the first transcription, has been restored from the text of record and translated. The Source and English columns below are now complete.

text.original:
GENEROSISSIMO AC DOCTISSIMO VIRO TYCHONI BRAHE OTTHONIDI.
S. P. D.

IAM agitur annus, TYCHO doctissime, ex quo GULIELMUS LUMMISDAL, cum isthinc domum rediret, librum tuum de Nova Stella reddidit, quod munus multis nominibus mihi fuit gratissimum, vel quod abs te esset, id est, ab homine claritate generis illustri, eximia ingenij felicitate, et literis perinde expolito, qui illam Philosophiae partem, quae est, ut cecinit vester MANILIUS,

Regales animos primum dignata movere,
Proxima tangent es rerum fastigia coelo,
iacentem erexisti, et e vulgi manibus in suam sedem, hoc est, regiam reduxisti. Cumulat etiam rari muneris gratiam tua humanitas, qui e tam excelso et dignitatis et doctrinae culmine nos humiles, penitus penitusque iacentes non solum favens spectas, sed prope manu attollis, et hortaris exemplo, ut et nos velle cupiamus nube vehi, validique humeris insistere Atlantis: illamque etsi falsam, plurimis nationibus tamen pro vera receptam opinionem tuis monumentis, labore et industria refutas, ingenia scilicet hominum sub hac languenti et frigida coeli plaga inertiae a natura damnata esse. Igitur cum omnes populi septentrionales publice, et nos privatim tibi debeamus plurimum, non existimabis, arrogantius a me factum, quod ad hunc usque diem non rescripserim. Procul enim a meae vitae instituto et moribus hoc crimen abesse, omnes norunt, qui me non ignorant. Neque etiam eos clam est, quam proximo biennio morbis assiduis gravissime afflictus fuerim, ac nullam pene horam ad scribendum vacuam habuerim, adeo ut cum alia multa leviora sim coactus intermittere, tamen quinque libros de Sphaera iam dimidiatos emittere, ac spem scribendi carminis penitus abijcere. Quamobrem tibi gratulor, qui istam generis claritatem a maioribus, ingenij felicitatem nactus, aetatem adhuc integram doctrina sic excolueris, ut familiae a natura splendidissimae tua virtute splendorem adieceris. Nos in hac aetatis effetae ignavia certe currenti libenter applaudemus, et si quid officij praeterea exigi a nobis poterit, tibi, quoad potero, gratificabor. Hunc autem GULIELMUM LUMMISDAL, qui has tibi tradet, rogavimus, ut de statu rerum et studiorum tuorum diligenter me certiorem faceret: quem etiam tibi commendamus, ut pro claritate tua ipsum in quacunque re iuves.

Vale.
Sterlini postridie Nonas Aprilis, Anno 1575.
GEORGIUS BUCHANANUS.

Interea autem, dum hæ Buchanani literæ forte sunt in itinere, ego cum quodam
nobili, eius Conterraneo, miseram illi libellum meum de Nova Stella, ea adhuc
durante, editum. Cum vero exemplum nullum earum literarum mihi supersit,
Epigramma solum modo apponam, eidem libro manu scriptum præfixeram .

AD CLARISSIMUM VIRUM ET POETAM EXCELLENTEM GEORGIUM BUCHANANUM
SCOTUM.

Hunc tibi non magnum mittit, Buchanane, libellum

    Ignotus Boreis Tycho remotus aquis:

Sit licet ignotus, tamen is te novit, amatque,

    Carminibus toto notus es orbe tuis.

Nec Boreas animos poterit disiungere nostros,

    Nam te etiam Boreæ frigidus Axis habet

Qualis enim cœlum convolvi Dania spectat,

    Talis et hoc ipsum Scotia vestra videt.

Exigua hæc igitur nostri monumenta laboris

    A Borea in Boream consule missa boni.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most learned gentleman Tycho Brahe, son of Otte. He sends heartiest greeting.**

A year is now going by, most learned Tycho, since William Lumisden, on his way home from your parts, delivered your book *On the New Star* — a gift most welcome to me on many counts: both because it came from you, that is, from a man illustrious in the renown of his lineage, of outstanding felicity of intellect, and likewise polished in letters, who has raised up that part of Philosophy which (as your Manilius sang)

first deigned to stir the minds of kings,
[and which,] touching the topmost summits of things, lies next to heaven,
[—that part of Philosophy] which lay prostrate, and have led it back out of the hands of the common crowd into its own seat, that is, into a royal one. Your kindness, too, heaps grace upon a rare gift: you who, from so lofty a peak both of rank and of learning, not only look favourably upon us lowly men, lying utterly and altogether prostrate, but well-nigh raise [us] up with your hand, and exhort [us] by your example, so that we too may long to wish to be borne upon a cloud and to stand upon the shoulders of mighty Atlas; and you refute, by your works, by labour and industry, that opinion — false, yet received as true among very many nations — namely, that the intellects of men under this faint and cold tract of sky are by nature condemned to sluggishness. Therefore, since all the peoples of the north owe you most greatly in public, and we in private, you will not reckon it done too presumptuously by me that to this very day I have not written back. For all who are not unacquainted with me know that this fault is far from the rule and habit of my life. Nor is it hidden from them how grievously I have been afflicted, throughout the last two years, by relentless illnesses, and how I have had scarcely an hour free for writing — so much so that, while I have been compelled to set aside many other lighter [tasks], [I have been forced] nonetheless to let go of my five books *On the Sphere*, now [only] half-done, and to cast away utterly the hope of writing the poem. Wherefore I congratulate you, who, having got that renown of lineage from your ancestors, [and] felicity of intellect, have so cultivated with learning an age still in its prime that by your own merit you have added splendour to a family by nature most splendid. We, in the sluggishness of this worn-out age of ours, will gladly applaud one [who is] surely running [his course]; and if any further service can be required of us, I shall oblige you so far as I shall be able. This William Lumisden, moreover, who will hand this [letter] to you, we have asked to inform me diligently of the state of your affairs and of your studies; him too we commend to you, that, in keeping with your renown, you may help him in whatever matter [there may be].

Farewell.
At Stirling, the day after the Nones of April [6 April], the year 1575.
George Buchanan.

Meanwhile, however, while this letter of Buchanan's happened to be on its way [to me], I had, through a certain nobleman, his countryman, sent him my little book on the New Star, published while it [the star] was still lasting. But since no copy remains to me of that letter [which accompanied the gift], I shall set down only the epigram which I had prefixed, written in my own hand, to that same book.

**To the Most Renowned Man and Excellent Poet, George Buchanan the Scot.**

This not-great little book, Buchanan, Tycho sends to you —
    unknown, removed by northern waters:
Though he be unknown, yet he knows you, and loves you;
    by your songs you are known through the whole world.
Nor will the North Wind be able to part our two spirits,
    for the cold Axis of the North holds you too;
For such as Denmark sees the heavens wheeling,
    such likewise does your own Scotland see this very thing.
These slight memorials, then, of my labour,
    sent from one North to another North, take in good part.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent / sender.** *Georgius Buchananus* = **George Buchanan** (1506–1582), the Scottish humanist, Latin poet, and historian — at this date tutor to the young James VI and a senior figure at the Scottish court — writing from Stirling. His own *De Sphaera*, the five-book Latin didactic poem on the cosmos mentioned here, was never completed and was published posthumously (1586). The source cites his collected *Opera omnia* as edition of record.
- **Recipient.** *Tychoni Brahe Otthonidi* — Tycho Brahe; *Otthonidi* "son of Otte" is the Greek-style patronymic for **Otte Brahe**, Tycho's father (cf. *Ottonides* in the 1571 Wolf letter, this chapter's convention).
- ***S. P. D.*** = *salutem plurimam dicit*, "sends heartiest greeting".
- ***Gulielmus Lummisdal*** = **William Lumisden** (Lumsden), the Scot who carried Tycho's book to Buchanan a year earlier and now carries this reply back; spelled *Lummisdal* in the source on both occurrences. He is commended to Tycho in the closing sentence.
- ***librum tuum de Nova Stella*** — Tycho's *De nova stella* (Copenhagen, 1573), his account of the 1572 supernova in Cassiopeia. The phrase is descriptive ("your book on the new star"), not necessarily the exact title-page wording.
- **The Manilius quotation.** *ut cecinit vester Manilius* — "as your Manilius sang," from the *Astronomica* (Book I, opening), the work Buchanan treats as Tycho's poetic patrimony (*vester*, "your [people's]," addressing the astronomer-poet). The two verses concern *Philosophia* / astronomy: the science that "first deigned to stir the minds of kings" and, "touching the topmost summits of things, lies next to heaven." **Textual crux:** the source's second line reads *"Proxima tangent es rerum fastigia coelo"* — a garbled setting of the standard *proxima tangentis rerum fastigia caelo* (the participle *tangentis* split across a line-end into *tangent | es*). The printed form is kept verbatim in the Source block; the translation follows the intelligible reading *tangentis* ("touching"), construing it with the science that lies *proxima … caelo* ("next to heaven"). The grammatical hinge (whether *tangentis* qualifies the science or stands in another case) is the one genuinely soft point and is flagged here, not smoothed.
- ***nube vehi, validique humeris insistere Atlantis*** — "to be borne upon a cloud and to stand upon the shoulders of mighty Atlas": a poetic image of being lifted to the heavens (Atlas the sky-bearer); kept as metaphor.
- **The "northern sluggishness" topos.** *ingenia … hominum sub hac languenti et frigida coeli plaga inertiae a natura damnata esse* — the (classical, Ptolemaic-climatic) commonplace that minds bred under the cold northern sky are doomed to dullness; Buchanan's compliment is that Tycho's work *refutes* it. Rendered straight, with the hedge *etsi falsam … pro vera receptam* ("though false, yet received as true") preserved.
- ***quinque libros de Sphaera … dimidiatos emittere*** — Buchanan's own poem *De Sphaera* in five books, here described as *dimidiatos*, "[only] half-done." The infinitive *emittere* is governed by *sim coactus* ("I have been compelled") and stands in parallel with *intermittere* ("set aside") and *abijcere* ("cast away utterly") — a list of works illness *forced him to give up*, not works he published. *emittere* is therefore rendered "let go of," not "put out/publish": Buchanan is enumerating renunciations, and the *De Sphaera* was in fact never finished by him (it was completed and published posthumously, 1586). *spem scribendi carminis … abijcere* registers the same loss — his fear of never finishing it (illness, *morbis assiduis*). His epistemic framing — that illness *forced* (*coactus*) these renunciations — is kept; no claim is sharpened.
- ***istam generis claritatem a maribus … nactus*** — "having got that renown of lineage from the men of your line." *a maribus* is specifically "from the males / the male line" (descent through the male line), not the neutral "from your forebears"; the specificity is preserved in the translation and noted here.
- **Calendar / place.** *Sterlini postridie Nonas Aprilis, Anno 1575* = "at **Stirling**, the day after the Nones of April, the year 1575." The Nones of April fall on the 5th; *postridie Nonas* is therefore **6 April** (O.S.; Scotland used the Julian calendar). This matches the edition *label* ("1575. 6. april. Stirling"); no discrepancy. The Roman-calendar idiom is rendered with both idiom and civil date by this chapter's convention
- **Orthography.** Source spellings *ingenij, abijcere, Otthonidi, coelo, vehi* and the capitalised proper names are humanist-Latin conventions, left as printed in the Source block.
- **What the recovered text is.** This is not part of Buchanan's letter (the sender of record) at all, but Tycho's own explanatory note, in the first person, inserted to account for how the correspondence began: while Buchanan's letter of 6 April 1575 (the published tail) was crossing in transit, Tycho had already sent Buchanan a presentation copy of his *De Nova Stella* (1573) via an unnamed Scottish nobleman, "his countryman." Since Tycho no longer had a copy of his own covering letter, he preserves only the Latin epigram he had inscribed by hand in the gift book itself.
- **The epigram is Tycho's own autograph dedicatory verse to George Buchanan** (1506–1582), the Scottish humanist, poet and historian — at this date tutor to the young James VI and one of the most celebrated Latin poets in Europe. The poem plays on the North/"Boreas" conceit throughout: Tycho, "unknown" in Scotland, sends greetings from one cold northern land (Denmark) to another (Scotland), arguing that the shared northern sky under which both men live unites them despite personal unacquaintance.
- **Confirms the gift-exchange context of the Buchanan correspondence.** The published tail of Buchanan's own reply names William Lumisden ("Gulielmus Lummisdal") as the bearer entrusted to bring news of Tycho's affairs back to Buchanan; the recovered note shows this was already the second leg of an exchange that began with Tycho's own unsolicited gift of *De Nova Stella*, carried by a different, unnamed Scottish nobleman — evidence of Tycho using his 1572 nova publication as an instrument of international humanist self-introduction within a year of its printing.
- **William Lumisden / "Gulielmus Lummisdal"** (the courier named in Buchanan's own letter) is not further identifiable in the works consulted at this date; the only Lumisden the works consulted yield is the unrelated eighteenth-century Jacobite antiquary Andrew Lumisden (1720–1801), too late to be relevant here.
- **Correction.** Latin corrected from the corrupted 'a maribus' to 'a maioribus' ('from your ancestors'), restoring the word split across the Dreyer page break; English corrected to match, and the bracketed gloss explaining the corrupted reading removed. Per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII pp.21-22.

text.original:
IOHANNES PRATENSIS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.
SALUTEM ET OMNIA FAUSTA.

RECEPI literas tuas, TYCHO optime, et pyxidem obsignatam cum pecunia, quam postera statim die Rostochium misi; qui tulit, chirographum quitantiarium referet: cui quoque negotium dedi de vase tuo huc perferendo. Ubi venerit, diligenter curabo. Quam vellem te apud nos hîc esse: desiderio enim tui tangimur non parvo. Avet animus cognoscere ex te, quid rei in mundo agatur, quem nuper aliqua ex parte perlustrasti. Sumus hîc extra cœli Solisque vias, scenam mundanæ fabulæ vix audimus quidem, tantum abest ut spectatores simus. Sed fuerit hoc fatum Aquiloni debitum. Tu nuper reversus a fœcundo illo Austro, postquam nobis cœli aperuisses penetralia, prius inaccessa ignotaque, moxque nobis inscijs et inopinantibus in Austrum dilapsum sub mediam brumam, totam deinde perlustrasti Teutoniam, atque Italiæ vicinas oras, cumque viris doctis atque ingentibus ingentes et doctos miscuisti sermones: quæ tua semper fuit voluptas. Sed vereor, ne hi una cum iucundo placidoque Austro te istuc alliciant, ut tacite eo mediteris iter. Sic enim Genius mihi in somnis dictavit, susurrans, te Basilæam præ alijs Germaniæ urbibus exoptare vicinam Italis atque Gallis, ubi magnus ille ERASMUS olim floruit, et multi etiamnum eximij viri clarent. At mallem te, modo amplus ille tuus sic restringi posset Genius, nobiscum in hac manere patria, et rigidos Boreæ flatus una persentiscere, ac quantum in te est emollire, fi non prorsus avertere: aut saltem ut huius intemperiei socium patientem in te habeamus. Sed si omnino nos relinquere stat sententia, uti etiam forte meretur hæc tuo Genio atque ingenio minus apta intemperataque aura, et importuna conversatio: da saltem adhuc insigne aliquod tuarum doctrinarum specimen: quale id fuit, cum te ultimo a nobis inexpectantibus subducens reliquisti. Fecisti autem hoc (quod laudo, bonique omnes prædicant) in Regis, qui sic expetebat, gratiam, quod nemo ex illustri nobilitate Danica ante te præstitit unquam, nec, uti existimo, quispiam in posterum facturus, adeo ut tute primus et postremus sis, qui hanc laudis adoream tibi vendicaris, quibus istæ, quas tui ordinis homines affectant, gloriolæ comparari nequeunt. Si itaque hoc meritum priori adjunxeris, ut antequam te carituri simus (vereor enim ne id fiat, licet tu propositum nos celes) nobis plura adhuc explanare non degravatus fueris, nos beatiores quam antea reddideris, tibique adhuc plus devinxeris. Et si id commodum tibi non fuerit, saltem de Hypothesibus PTOLEMÆI et COPERNICI nos summatim instrue, quænam harum verior sit, et utrum ulli earum acquiescendum, an vero potius Ptolemaica assumptio sit castiganda, prout a te factum est, et Copernicea ad stabilitatem Terræ convertenda, uti etiam insinuasti tuoque sic nobis præluxisti ingenio: aut si quid aliud in his secretioris cognitionis, quod nos fugiat, animo volvis, impertiaris quæso. Quin et hoc ex te scire aveo, idque ego solus, utpote qui in prælectione publica II libri PLINIJ de mundo circa hunc nodum resolvendum non parum hæserim: quomodo videlicet intelligendum sit, quod dictus autor in fine XVI cap. ea, quæ in Stationibus et Regressibus Planetarum videmus per inhibitionem et repercussionem radiorum Solarium fieri, ubi epicyclos omnes tollere videtur, ac si veteribus in usu non fuissent, mirabili sane invento, a se, uti tandem insinuare videtur, primum comperto, si modo res hæc ipsi cœlo congrua sit, et suis numeris constare possit, quod tibi per otium dispiciendum relinquo. Locus, quem indicavi, te de pluribus admonebit. Haberem et plura eius generis, de quibus avide tecum conferre cuperem, et nisi hyems et invalitudo ob continuas in pulmonem defluxiones mihi obstaret, ad vos in Scaniam transirem, atque ibi tecum, quæ nostra est voluptas, aliquandiu suaviter philosopharer. Sed, o spes hominum fluxæ et irritæ. Cogimur sæpe esse ubi nolumus, et rapimur eo, quo non ire deliberavimus. Verum optime mi TYCHO, amplius detinere te nolo. Tu fac nos hîc Haffniæ brevi tua præsentia exhilares, atque ingeniorum nostrorum radios, iam lumen remittentes, et in crepusculum tendentes vespertinum, illustres ac vegetiores reddas, animisque nostris sacer, uti soles, illabaris.

Iamque vale, et fratrem tuum, aliosque qui tecum sunt, sanguine iunctos ex me officiose saluta.
Dabantur Haffniæ ult. die Ianuarij Anno 1576.
T.
IOH. PRATENSIS.
text.english:
**Johannes Pratensis to Tycho Brahe. Greeting, and all good fortune.**

I have received your letter, excellent Tycho, and the sealed box with the money, which I sent on to Rostock the very next day; the man who carried it will bring back a receipt for the quittance — to him I also gave the charge of conveying your vessel here. When it arrives, I shall see to it carefully. How I wish you were here with us: for we are touched by no small longing for you. My mind is eager to learn from you what is going on in the world [in mundo], which you have lately surveyed in some part. We are here outside the paths of the heaven and the Sun; we scarcely so much as hear the scene of the world's play — so far are we from being its spectators. But let this be the fate owed to the North. You, lately returned from that fruitful South, after you had opened to us the inner recesses of the heaven, before inaccessible and unknown — and then, while we were unaware and unsuspecting, having slipped away into the South in mid-winter — went on to traverse all Germany [Teutonia] and the neighbouring shores of Italy, and with men learned and great mingled great and learned discourse: which was ever your delight. But I fear lest these, together with the pleasant and mild South, lure you thither, so that you secretly plan a journey there. For thus a Genius dictated to me in my dreams, whispering that you long, before other cities of Germany, for Basel — close to the Italians and the Gauls — where that great Erasmus once flourished, and where many distinguished men are still illustrious today. Yet I would rather — if only that ample Genius of yours could be so reined in — that you remain with us in this homeland, and feel together with us the harsh blasts of Boreas, and, so far as in you lies, soften them, if not turn them away entirely; or at least that we may have in you a patient companion in this inclemency. But if it is your fixed resolve to leave us altogether — as perhaps this air, ill-suited and intemperate for your Genius and disposition, and this troublesome society, deserves — then give us at least some further notable specimen of your learning, such as that was when, withdrawing yourself from us last time when we did not expect it, you took your leave. This you did (a thing I praise, and which all good men proclaim) for the sake of the King, who so desired it — a thing no one of the illustrious Danish nobility ever rendered before you, nor, as I judge, will any do hereafter, so that you are at once the first and the last to claim this glory of praise for yourself, with which those little glories that men of your order pursue cannot be compared. If, therefore, you will add this service to the former — that, before we must do without you (for I fear that this will come to pass, though you conceal your intention from us), you will not think it a burden to expound still more to us — you will render us happier than before, and bind us yet more to yourself. And if that be not convenient to you, then at least instruct us in summary on the Hypotheses of Ptolemy and of Copernicus: which of these is the truer, and whether one ought to rest in either of them, or whether rather the Ptolemaic assumption is to be corrected — as has been done by you — and the Copernican turned back to the stability of the Earth, as you have also intimated and have by your genius thus lighted the way for us; or, if you turn over in your mind anything else of more secret knowledge in these matters that escapes us, share it, I beg. Moreover, this too I am eager to learn from you — and I alone — inasmuch as in my public lecture on the second Book of Pliny on the world I have stuck not a little over untying this knot: how, namely, it is to be understood that the said author, at the end of chapter XVI, [says] that those things which we see in the Stations and Retrogradations of the planets come about through the inhibition and repercussion of the Sun's rays — where he seems to do away with all epicycles, as though they had not been in use among the ancients — by a truly marvellous discovery first found out by himself, as he at length seems to intimate (if only this matter be congruous with the heaven itself, and can be made to agree with its own numbers): which I leave to you to examine at your leisure. The passage I have indicated will admonish you of further matters. I should have many more things of this kind too, about which I would eagerly desire to confer with you; and were not the winter and my ill-health — owing to continual catarrhs flowing down upon the lung — in my way, I would cross over to you into Scania, and there with you, which is our delight, philosophize agreeably for a while. But — O the fleeting and idle hopes of men! We are often compelled to be where we would not, and are dragged off whither we had resolved not to go. But, my excellent Tycho, I do not wish to detain you longer. Do you make us here at Copenhagen glad before long by your presence, and the rays of our wits — now sending back their light and tending toward the evening twilight — render bright and more vigorous, and glide, hallowed, into our spirits, as you are wont to do.

And now farewell, and dutifully greet from me your brother and the others who are with you, joined to you by blood.
Given at Copenhagen, the last day of January, the year 1576.
Yours,
Joh. Pratensis.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Iohannes Pratensis* = **Johannes Pratensis** (Hans Philipsen, 1543–1576), professor of medicine at Copenhagen and one of Tycho's closest friends; a Paracelsian physician in the circle of Petrus Severinus. He would die suddenly later in 1576. The letter's anxiety that Tycho may leave Denmark is poignant against that backdrop.
- **Recipient/dating context.** Written 31 January 1576, shortly before Frederik II's grant of Hven (gift made 18 February 1576 N.S. / O.S. discussion aside) — Pratensis still fears Tycho will emigrate; the worry is real, not formulaic.
- ***pyxidem obsignatam … vase tuo*** — "the sealed box … your vessel": Pratensis is forwarding money to Rostock on Tycho's behalf and arranging carriage of a *vas* (an alchemical/chemical vessel, given Tycho's and Pratensis's shared Paracelsian chemistry). *chirographum quitantiarium* = a written quittance/receipt; kept literal.
- **Geography of the metaphor.** *Aquilo / Boreas* = the North (Denmark) and its cold winds; *Auster* = the South (Germany/Italy), figured as "fruitful" and "mild." *Teutonia* = Germany; *Scania* = Skåne/Scania (where Tycho's family seat Knudstrup lay). The whole passage casts Denmark as offstage, "outside the paths of the heaven and the Sun" — the rhetorical conceit of provincial darkness.
- ***Genius*** — rendered "Genius" (the tutelary/inner spirit, twice: the dream-Genius that whispers, and Tycho's own "ample Genius"); kept as a period term, not flattened to "genius" in the modern sense.
- ***Basilaeam … magnus ille ERASMUS*** — **Basel** (where Erasmus of Rotterdam had lived and where his press flourished); Pratensis imagines Tycho drawn there for its nearness to Italy and France and its humanist lustre.
- **Astronomy — the Ptolemy/Copernicus request.** *de Hypothesibus PTOLEMAeI et COPERNICI … Ptolemaica assumptio sit castiganda … et Copernicea ad stabilitatem Terrae convertenda* — Pratensis asks Tycho to adjudicate the two **hypotheses** (geometric world-models): whether to **correct** ("castigate") the Ptolemaic *assumptio* and to **turn the Copernican system back to the stability of the Earth.** This is an early external witness — pre-dating the Hven instruments and the *De mundi* (1588) — that Tycho was already intimating a reformed, geo-stable model: "as has been done by you … as you have also intimated." Read with care: Pratensis reports Tycho's *insinuation*, not a finished system; the hedges (*insinuasti*, *praeluxisti*) are preserved.
- **The Pliny crux.** *in praelectione publica II libri PLINIJ de mundo … in fine XVI cap. … Stationibus et Regressibus Planetarum … per inhibitionem et repercussionem radiorum Solarium … ubi epicyclos omnes tollere videtur* — Pratensis, lecturing publicly on **Pliny, *Natural History* Book II** (the cosmological book, "de mundo"), is stuck on a passage he places "at the end of chapter XVI," where Pliny explains the planets' **stations and retrogradations** as caused by the **inhibition and repercussion of the Sun's rays**, seeming thereby to dispense with epicycles entirely and to claim the explanation as his own discovery. (The relevant Plinian matter is in the chapters on planetary motion, *NH* II §§69–77 in modern numbering; Pratensis's "chapter XVI" follows the chapter-division of his 16th-century edition and is **not** silently renumbered here — see calendar/citation note.) *nodum resolvendum* = "untying this knot," the interpretive difficulty; *suis numeris constare* = "agree with its own numbers" (be quantitatively consistent). Rendered with Pliny's own causal language ("inhibition and repercussion of the Sun's rays") kept intact.
- ***radios … in crepusculum tendentes vespertinum*** — "the rays [of our wits] tending toward the evening twilight": the closing conceit that without Tycho the Copenhagen scholars' intellects are guttering toward dusk; *crepusculum* = **twilight** (glossary). *animis nostris sacer … illabaris* — "glide, hallowed, into our spirits," a near-sacral compliment.
- **Orthography.** Humanist Latin of c. 1576: *coeli, foecundo, Ptolemaeī* with the *ae*-ligature; *ij* for *ii* (*alijs, eximij, inscijs, PLINIJ*); *fi non prorsus avertere* — the printed *fi* is a long-s misreading for *si* ("if not"), kept as printed in the Source block and read *si* in the translation (it parses only as *si*, parallel to the later *si … non fuerit*). No negation is added or dropped by this reading.
- **Dateline.** *Dabantur Haffniae ult. die Ianuarij Anno 1576* = "Given at Copenhagen, the last day of January, the year 1576" — i.e. **31 January 1576** (O.S.; Denmark was on the Julian calendar). The catalogue label ("1576. 31. januar. København") agrees with the dateline. *Haffnia* = Copenhagen (glossary). The subscription *T.* before the name is the writer's flourish (cf. exemplar usage), left as "Yours,".
