text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD IOHANNEM PRATENSEM.

ACCEPI literas tuas, eruditissime et amantissime PRATENSIS, ex quibus intelligo te negotium nostrum Rostochiense probe curasse, quo nomine tibi gratias ago. Cupis a me scire quid rerum in mundo geratur, quidque ferat foecundus ille Auster, a quo nuper redij. Atque ego pleraque eorum quae istic cognoveram, tibi, quam primum reversus essem, Haffniae retuli, plura etiamnum relaturus, si quae ulterius in mentem venerint, ubi vos denuo invisero, quod intra paucos dies facere decrevi; est enim res magni momenti, quam nulli praeterquam Magnifico Domino Legato Gallico DANZÆO et tibi intimo meo aperire animus est, vestrumque de hac audire consilium. Quoniam vero de abitu meo denuo in Germaniam mens tibi nonnulla praesagit, licet ego idipsum supprimam, dicam tibi quippiam in aurem, nemini nisi soli Domino DANZÆO, quem scis taciturnum et fidum, aperiendum. Recte quidem sive vigilanti sive somnianti tibi tuus dictavit Genius vatidicus, me aliud iter versus Austrum iterum meditari. Quod forte inde subolfecisti, quia nullas ex ijs arcibus, quas Serenissimus Rex noster mihi, cum in reditu illum debitae observantiae causa Sorae submisse salutassem, clementissime et motu proprio obtulit inhabitandas, recipere voluerim, et quod videas me de ijs quae in hac patria geruntur non admodum esse solicitum. Quod insuper Basileam saepenumero in ore isthic apud vos habuerim, eius oportunitatem cupido philosophiae alumno et tranquillitatis Apollineae, Musarumque amatori depredicârim, in qua urbe et tu aliquando vixisti, eamque plurimi facere solitus es: Ex his ut opinor, Genius seu potius ingenium tuum perspicax et providum de meo abitu et istuc eundi intentione nonnulla coniecit et suspicionem tibi movit non prorsus frivolam. Nam ut te sensa animi mei occulta non prorsus celem, sic est ut coniectaris: Constitui enim, si Deo sic visum fuerit, hac instante aestate Germanos revisere, adeoque Basileam usque, quae in limitibus Italiae, Galliae et Germaniae iucunde et commode sita est, excurrere, ibique sedes firmas pro studijs meis Olympicis figere, atque Astronomiae instaurationem, quam diu multumque animo volvo, favente astrorum conditore, moliri. Quin et haec erat prioris meae peregrinationis non minima causa, ut locum inquirerem et rationes invenirem, quomodo meis studijs tutius et plenius vacare possem, ijsque rectius consulerem quam hîc in Dania: displicet enim, ut me saepe conquerentem audivisti, haec conversatio, hi mores, haec quotidiana fabula; ex quo vix aliquem hîc reperiam praeter te, cum quo de rebus arduis et vulgi captum exuperantibus, solidi quid conferam: at quam raro nobis simul esse contingat, tute scis. Cum mei ordinis hominibus, quoniam crebrius mihi agendum est, praesertim Herressuadij, Avunculum, quando apud ipsum dego, convenientibus, aut etiam me ipsum Knudstorpij invisentibus (alias enim quantum possum illorum consortia subterfugio) multum temporis mihi perit, multa alias ingrata audienda et facienda. Nosti enim quam sint nobilium horum mores a meis institutis alieni, quamque ab ipsa philosophia: excipio excipiendos, quos tamen plures esse mallem quam sunt.

Sed audi quid hisce diebus praeter omnem meam expectationem acciderit, idque solus audi, et nemini nisi uni DANZÆO nostro aperi, idque secreto. Cum ultimo die praecedentis septimanae, qui erat undecimus Februarij matutinis horis in lecto expergefactus, adhuc decumberem, et iter hoc de quo modo dixi, in Germaniam tacitus et solicite animo mecum agitarem, simulque qua ratione, consanguineis meis non attendentibus, elabi possem, cogitarem, idque in varias partes volverem atque revolverem; ecce ab improviso nunciatur Regium puerum huc Knudstorpium advenisse, qui tota nocte properasset, ut literas a Rege mihi inscriptas confestim traderet; erant autem adhuc tenebrae, instante saltem crepusculo matutino, et Sol intra duas horas vix oriebatur: iubeo itaque puerum illum ad lectum accersiri, qui erat genere Nobilis atque ex mea consanguinitate, is mihi statim Regis exhibuit literas, atque sibi ab ipso Rege iniunctum esse aiebat, ut absque omni mora me, dies noctesque iter faciendo, quaereret, ubicunque in Scania invenirer, atque illas mihi in manus proprias traderet, statimque reverteretur, quod et factum est. Erant autem scriptae in domo Regis venatoria Ibstrup, quae prope vestram Haffniam intra unum milliare, uti scis, in sylva proxima sita est, idque praecedente die decimo nimirum Februarii. Ego vero literas mox resignans comperio in ijs Regem iubere, ut se confestim accedam, ubicunque in Selandia versaretur, quod et citra omnem moram obsequiose praestiti, adeo ut eodem die, Regi in dicta domo venatoria ante occasum Solis adfuerim. Is tunc me per Nobilem suum cubicularium NICOLAUM PASSBERG in locum quendam solitarium acciri iussit, atque sic, nemine praesente, clementissime allocutus est: «Scis TYCHO, quae et qualia volens tibi obtulerim, cum ultimo Sorae apud me esses, iussique ut brevi ad me rediens, mihi ipsi significares, quidnam in his expeteres, aut ea de re Cancellarium meum NICOLAUM KAASIUM, vel Secretarium IOHANNEM SCHOUGARDIUM, per literas admoneres. At ex quo nihil eiuscemodi interea feceris, cum tamen alij talia avide affectent expectentque, nescio quid animo volvas, aut cur te non mature resolvas. Quidam ex Aulicis meis mihi insinuare visus est, se ab avunculo tuo STENONE BILLE tacite cognovisse te denuo in Germaniam cogitare: Quare te advocare volui, ut ex te ipso cognoscerem, qualis tua sit sententia in ijs quae obtuli, et cur talia non acceptes. Fieri potest, veluti conijcio, quod nulla eiuscemodi Arcium magnarum beneficia Regia obtinere cupias, ne studia tua, quibus delectaris, per causas forenses et alia negotia politica, quae requiruntur in tuendis et administrandis talibus, interturbentur, atque otium ijs vacandi tibi praecludatur. Quare cum nuper in Arce Helsingorensi essem, ubi nunc aedifico, prospiciens ex fenestra quadam Insulam illam parvam Huennam, quae isthic in freto, versus Landskroniam sita est, et a nullo nobili inhabitatur, conspexi, de qua etiam, si recte memini, dictus tuus avunculus STENO BILLE mihi semel dixit, idque antequam in Germaniam ultimo te contulisti, quod eius situs tibi arrideret. Incidit itaque mihi in mentem hanc esse tuis exercitijs tam Astronomicis quam destillatorijs apprime accommodam, siquidem alta sit et solitaria. Nullae quidem aedes ibi sunt, quas inhabitare posses, neque etiam reditus inde suppetunt necessarij. Verum ego tibi de utrisque sufficienter prospiciam. Si itaque hanc Insulam incolere volueris, lubens eam tibi soli concedam. Isthic degere potes quiete et eas exequi artes, quibus afficeris, nemine interpellante. Cumque arcem Helsingorensem splendidius instauravero, veluti nunc incepi, illic subinde commoratus, ad te nonnunquam in eam Insulam transfretabo, atque quid rerum agas in Astronomicis et destillationibus tuis inspiciam, conatusque tuos lubens iuvabo, non quod ego Astronomica intelligam aut sciam quorsum per omnia spectent, vel aliquid utilitatis inde pro mea persona sperem, sed saltem QVIA REX SVM, tuque in hoc meo Regno, ex ea familia, quae mihi semper chara fuit, oriundus, non postremam in his operam navasse diceris: Unde existimo mei officij esse, talia convenienter sustentare et promovere. Quorsum vero opus est, ut denuo in Germaniam concedas, teque isthic peregrinum reddas, cum hîc in patria eadem commode efficere possis quae isthic. Dabimus potius operam, ut eo res deducatur, quod Germani et aliarum Nationum homines, qui talia scire cupiunt, huc accedant, atque ea hîc videant et discant, quae alibi vix reperient. Delibera itaque tecum spacio aliquot dierum, et deinde quid in his tibi faciendum censeas, mihi significa, ubi inaudiveris me in arcem residentiae nostrae Friderigsburgensem reversum esse: Nolo enim ut coacte quidpiam hîc facias, sed liberum tibi relinquo, expensis ijs, quae dixi, statuere id, quod ex re tua iudicaveris. Atque ubi Friderigsburgi mihi adfueris, et quidpiam hac de re conclusum fuerit, tum demum de reditibus necessarijs atque aedificationum sumptibus ita ordinabo et tibi prospiciam, ut indemnis esse queas, atque illic commode peragere ea, quae regno huic et mihi Regi, tum quoque tibi ipsi et tuis esse poterint tam hîc quam alibi honorifica.« In hunc sane modum optimus ille et Patriae ac publici boni, honorisque studiosissimus Rex verba habuit, quibus peractis, ego qua potui et debui reverentia gratias humilime egi, et me, quamvis Insula clementer oblata, ob maris fluctus, quibus undique cingitur, accessus habeat difficiles et saepenumero admodum periculosos, submisse respondi ea de re deliberaturum, atque brevi meam resolutionem Friderigsburgi subiectissime indicaturum: sicque discessi et sequente die, huc domum reversus, ubi, uti et in itinere, de hoc Regio proposito multa tacite pensito; nam mirabile mihi videtur, imo alicuius peculiaris ominis, aut fati instar esse, quod Regius puer eo ipso tempore, quo de abitu in Germaniam solicite mecum deliberarem, matutinis horis tale nuncium adferret; quodque serenissimus et clementissimus Rex noster ex se ipso, me non petente, vel eiuscemodi quid cogitante, talia proponeret; et ut dicam aperte quod sentio, impense me moverunt haec Regis verba, eiusque laudabilis intentio, adeo ut animus meus vacillare et haesitare coeperit, et de priori proposito nonnihil remittere. Vereor enim, ne, si Rege quasi praevidente ea quae mihi novi abitus causas suggesserunt, atque his praeveniente, nihilominus discederem, et forte postea alibi in peregrinis oris mihi quidpiam adversi eveniret, nec omnia ex voto succederent (uti sunt res humanae fluxae et varijs casibus obnoxiae) tum eo magis inde affligerer atque anxius redderer et tanto plus poenitudinis inde caperem, quod nimirum has satis tolerabiles conditiones a laudatissimo Rege mihi singulari clementia benignissime cupienti, oblatas non acceptârim ac in Patria manserim. Nihil tamen certi adhuc constituere possum, nec etiam volo, antequam Domini DANZÆI et tuum audivero consilium. Matri et Avunculo aut etiam Fratri, haec, antequam penitus inter nos deliberatum et conclusum fuerit, in quas partes me dem, non aperiam. Neque enim volo ijs innotescere me denuo in Germaniam proficisci decrevisse. Haec mi PRATENSIS, eo plenius, prout peracta sunt, tibi refero, ut eo expeditius et melius cum DANZÆO nostro deliberare possis, quid mihi faciendum duxeritis, atque vestram sententiam, quamprimum isthuc venero (quod intra biduum vel triduum ad summum futurum spero) ingenue pro amicitia inter nos mutua et syncera aperiatis; neque enim diu cunctandum censeo, antequam Regi Friderigsburgi adsim, atque quomodo me resolverim exponam; quod facere D. V. constitui quamprimum unicum saltem diem Haffniae hac in re vobis tribuero, et quid suaseritis intellexero.

Quando hae literae a te lectae fuerint, et saepedicto Domino DANZÆO nostro ostensa, eas mox disrumpe aut in cineres redige, ne forte per incuriam alicubi repositae in aliorum manus perveniant; sicque secretae nostrae consultationes, ubi quam maxime nollemus, propalentur. Atque de his nunc satis; plura et particulariora, ubi praesens fuero, intelliges. Verum antequam epistolam claudam, unum adhuc restare video discutiendum, quod prioribus intentus, ferme praeterieram, de opinione illa Pliniana, ad quam quidem non tam absolute, prout rei moles exigit, nunc me resolvere datur, quae tamen obiter et tam cito in mentem venire possunt, dicam. PLINIJ ille locus, quem adducis, videtur obscurior, quam quod in continenti eum prorsus enodare concedatur, neque enim, quae voluit dicere, visus est. Imo mea quidem opinione, nisi plura hac de re intellexerit quam scripsit, sibi ipsi non satisfecit, nedum alijs. Non quidem dubium est planetas ad Solem evidentem obtinere relationem, atque respectu eius Stationes et Retrogradationes, atque nonnullas inaequalitates apparentes, tam quoad Longum quam Latum, differentias exhibere, at quod circa Trinum Solis quam proxime stent superiores tres Planetae, radiisque Solis inhibeantur, rectumque agant cursum, et ignea eius vi in sublime levantur (uti de his dictus ratiocinatur PLINIUS) tum quoque ea quae mox de Retrogradationibus subiungit, non video quomodo constare possint. Neque enim Solis radij quasi catenâ aut aliâ quadam combinatione sunt cum Planetis alligati, qua eos hac vel illac impellant, trahant, aut retrahant, nisi vim quandam quasi Magneticam illis hoc modo inesse imaginemur; et ne sic quidem motio erit coelestibus competens utpote circularis et regularis. Certum enim est Planetarum motiones ubique orbiculariter fieri, vel ex orbicularibus componi, ideoque ea quae PLINIUS insinuat, si ad Solem referenda sunt, quod etiam fieri posse non inficior, alia ratione applicanda veniunt, de qua nonnunquam cogitavi, sed nondum satis me resolvi, ut videlicet tollantur Epicycli (quos veteres etiam non assumpsisse ex PLINIO liquet) et nihilominus apparentiae constent. Sed existimo PLINIUM hanc suam speculationem undecunque tandem acceptam et quomodocunque intellectam in praxin et usum deducere nequivisse, ideoque difficultatem quandam hîc subt esse fassum. Simile quid apud VITRUVIUM, qui diu ante PLINIUM fuit, reperitur, sed locus nunc non succurrit. Is vero Architectonice magis quam Astronomice et Geometrice executus videtur, ex quo hanc sententiam PLINIUM hausisse verosimile est, licet is idipsum dissimulans eam sibi propriam et privatam asseruit. Verum de his ubi D. V. convenerimus, et commoditas dabitur talia disquirendi, ulterius philosophabimur. Tu vero, mi charissime PRATENSIS, quam felicissime vale, et Dominum DANZÆUM nostrum ex me officiose saluta; meque intra paucos, uti dixi, dies isthic ambo incolumes expectate.

Dabantur e sede nostra Knudsdorpiana die 14. Februarij A. 1576.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Johannes Pratensis.**

I have received your letter, most learned and most loving Pratensis, from which I gather that you duly took care of our Rostock business, for which I thank you. You desire to know from me what is going on in the world, and what that fruitful South Wind brings — from which I have lately returned. And most of what I had learned there I reported to you, as soon as I had returned, at Copenhagen; and I shall report still more, should anything further come to mind, when I visit you again — which I have resolved to do within a few days; for it is a matter of great moment, which I am minded to disclose to no one save the Honourable Lord, the French Ambassador Dançay, and to you, my intimate, and to hear your counsel upon it. But since your mind has some presentiment of my departing into Germany again — even though I myself keep it suppressed — I will say something in your ear, to be disclosed to no one but Lord Dançay alone, whom you know to be discreet and trustworthy. Rightly indeed, whether waking or dreaming, did your prophetic Genius dictate to you that I am once more contemplating another journey toward the South. This you perhaps got wind of from the fact that I was unwilling to accept, for my habitation, any of those castles which our Most Serene King most graciously and of his own accord offered me when, on his return, I had humbly saluted him at Sorø out of the observance due to him; and because you see that I am not much concerned about the things that go on in this homeland. And further, because I had Basel often in my mouth there among you, and extolled its convenience for one who is an eager nursling of philosophy and a lover of Apolline tranquillity and of the Muses — a city in which you too once lived, and which you were wont to value highly: from these things, I suppose, your Genius — or rather your keen and provident wit — conjectured something about my departure and my intention of going thither, and roused in you a suspicion not altogether idle. For — not to conceal from you entirely the hidden feelings of my mind — it is as you conjecture: for I have determined, if it shall so seem good to God, to revisit the Germans this coming summer, and indeed to make an excursion as far as Basel — which is pleasantly and conveniently situated on the borders of Italy, France, and Germany — and there to fix a firm seat for my Olympic studies, and, with the favour of the founder of the stars, to set about that restoration of astronomy which I have long and much turned over in my mind. Indeed this too was no small cause of my earlier travels: to seek out a place and find means whereby I might more safely and more fully devote myself to my studies, and attend to them better than here in Denmark. For — as you have often heard me complain — this society, these manners, this daily round, displease me; and I can scarcely find anyone here besides yourself with whom I might confer anything solid about difficult matters that surpass the common grasp; yet how rarely it falls to us to be together, you yourself know. With men of my own order, since I have rather frequently to deal with them — especially at Herrevad, [meeting] my uncle when I am staying with him, or with those who come to visit me at Knudstrup (for otherwise I avoid their company as much as I can) — much of my time perishes, and many other unwelcome things must be heard and done. For you know how foreign the manners of these noblemen are to my own pursuits, and how far from philosophy itself: I make exception of those who deserve it, whom I could nonetheless wish to be more in number than they are.

But hear what has befallen in these days beyond all my expectation — and hear it alone, and disclose it to no one but our one Dançay, and that in secret. On the last day of the previous week, which was the eleventh of February, in the morning hours, having woken in my bed and still lying there, and turning over within myself, silently and anxiously, this journey into Germany of which I have just spoken — and at the same time considering by what means I might slip away without my kinsmen noticing, and rolling this this way and that — behold, all of a sudden it is announced that a King's page had arrived here at Knudstrup, having hastened all night long to deliver at once a letter addressed to me from the King; and it was still dark, with only the morning twilight coming on, and the Sun barely rising within two hours. So I order that page to be summoned to my bedside — he was a nobleman by birth and of my own kindred — and he straightway showed me the King's letter, and said that it had been enjoined upon him by the King himself to seek me out without any delay, travelling day and night, wherever in Scania I might be found, and to deliver it into my own hands, and then return at once — which was done. The letter had been written at the King's hunting-lodge of Ibstrup, which, as you know, lies near your Copenhagen within one mile, in the nearest wood — and that on the preceding day, the tenth of February, namely. I, then, breaking the seal at once, find in it that the King commands me to come to him immediately, wherever in Zealand he should be — which without any delay I obediently performed, so that on the same day I was present before the King at the said hunting-lodge before sunset. He then ordered me to be called, through his noble chamberlain Niels Parsberg, into a certain solitary place, and thus, with no one present, most graciously addressed me: «You know, Tycho, what things, and of what sort, I willingly offered you when you were last with me at Sorø; and I bade you, returning to me shortly, to signify to me yourself what you desired in these matters, or to advise my Chancellor Niels Kaas, or my Secretary Johan Schougaard, of it by letter. But since you have done nothing of the kind in the meantime — though others eagerly covet and look for such things — I do not know what you are turning over in your mind, or why you do not resolve yourself in good time. One of my courtiers seemed to hint to me that he had quietly learned from your uncle Steen Bille that you are thinking of going to Germany again. For which reason I wished to summon you, that I might learn from your own self what your view is on the things I offered, and why you do not accept them. It may be — as I conjecture — that you do not desire to obtain any royal grants of such great castles, lest your studies, in which you delight, be disturbed by lawsuits and other political affairs which are required in maintaining and administering such places, and the leisure for attending to them be cut off from you. Wherefore, when I was lately at Helsingør Castle, where I am now building, looking out from a certain window I caught sight of that small island Hven, which lies there in the sound, toward Landskrona, and is inhabited by no nobleman — concerning which also, if I rightly remember, your said uncle Steen Bille once told me, and that before you last betook yourself to Germany, that its situation pleased you. So it came into my mind that this island is exceedingly well suited to your exercises, both astronomical and distillatory, seeing that it is high-lying and solitary. There is indeed no dwelling there which you could inhabit, nor do the necessary revenues come from it. But I will provide you sufficiently with both. If, therefore, you should be willing to dwell on this island, I will gladly grant it to you alone. There you can live quietly and pursue those arts by which you are affected, with no one interrupting. And when I shall have more splendidly restored Helsingør Castle — as I have now begun — staying there from time to time, I will now and then cross over to you on that island, and inspect what you are doing in your astronomical matters and your distillations, and gladly assist your endeavours — not that I understand astronomy or know what it all aims at, or hope for any utility from it for my own person, but simply BECAUSE I AM KING, and you, born in this my kingdom, of that family which has always been dear to me, are said to have laboured not least in these things: whence I deem it part of my office to support and promote such things fittingly. But what need is there for you to withdraw into Germany again, and make yourself a stranger there, when here in your homeland you can conveniently accomplish the same things as there? Rather will we take pains that it be brought to this, that Germans and men of other nations who desire to know such things may come hither, and see and learn here what they will scarcely find elsewhere. Deliberate, therefore, with yourself for the space of some days, and then signify to me what you judge ought to be done in these matters, when you have heard that I have returned to the castle of our residence, Frederiksborg: for I do not wish you to do anything here under compulsion, but I leave it free to you, having weighed the things I have said, to determine that which you shall judge to be to your advantage. And when you have presented yourself to me at Frederiksborg, and something has been concluded in this matter, then at last I will so order things concerning the necessary revenues and the costs of building, and provide for you, that you may be without loss, and may conveniently carry out there those things which can be to the honour of this kingdom and of me the King, and also of you yourself and yours, both here and elsewhere.» In just this manner did that best of kings — most zealous for his fatherland and for the public good and honour — frame his words; and these ended, I, with all the reverence I could and ought, most humbly gave thanks, and submissively replied that — although the island was graciously offered — because of the sea's waves, by which it is girt on every side, it has approaches that are difficult and very often quite perilous, I would deliberate upon the matter, and would shortly, most submissively, declare my resolution at Frederiksborg. And so I departed, and on the following day returned home hither, where — as also on the road — I silently ponder much about this royal proposal; for it seems to me wondrous, indeed as though it were some peculiar omen or stroke of fate, that a King's page should at that very time, when I was anxiously deliberating with myself about departing into Germany, in the morning hours bring such a message; and that our Most Serene and Most Gracious King should, of his own accord, without my asking or even thinking of any such thing, propose such things. And — to say openly what I feel — these words of the King, and his praiseworthy intention, moved me exceedingly, so much so that my mind began to waver and hesitate, and to give up somewhat of its former resolve. For I fear lest, if — the King as it were foreseeing the things that suggested to me the causes of a new departure, and forestalling them — I should nonetheless depart, and afterwards perhaps something adverse should befall me elsewhere in foreign parts, and not everything should turn out as wished (as human affairs are fleeting and subject to various chances), then I should be the more afflicted by it and rendered anxious, and take from it so much the more regret — for having not accepted these tolerable enough conditions, offered me with singular clemency by a most praised King most kindly wishing me well, and for having stayed in my homeland. Yet I can determine nothing certain as yet, nor do I wish to, before I have heard the counsel of Lord Dançay and yourself. To my mother and my uncle, or even my brother, I will not disclose — before it has been thoroughly deliberated and concluded among us — which course I shall take. For I do not wish it to become known to them that I have resolved to set out for Germany again. These things, my Pratensis, I report to you the more fully, just as they took place, so that you may the more expeditiously and better deliberate with our Dançay as to what you judge I ought to do, and may frankly disclose your opinion to me — as soon as I shall have come thither (which I hope will be within two days, or three at most) — in keeping with the mutual and sincere friendship between us; for I think there must be no long delay before I present myself to the King at Frederiksborg and explain how I have resolved; which, [God willing,] I have determined to do as soon as I shall have devoted to you at least one single day at Copenhagen in this matter, and learned what you will have advised.

When this letter shall have been read by you, and shown to our oft-named Lord Dançay, tear it up at once or reduce it to ashes, lest perchance, laid by somewhere through carelessness, it come into others' hands, and so our secret consultations be made public where we should least of all wish it. And of these matters now enough; more, and in more particular detail, you will learn when I am present. But before I close the letter, I see there yet remains one thing to be discussed, which — intent on the foregoing — I had almost passed over: concerning that Plinian opinion, upon which, indeed, it is not now granted me to resolve so absolutely as the weight of the matter requires; yet I will say the things that can come to mind in passing and so quickly. That passage of Pliny which you adduce seems more obscure than that it may be unravelled altogether on the spot, for he does not appear [to have made clear] what he meant to say. Nay, in my opinion at least, unless he understood more about this matter than he wrote, he did not satisfy even himself, much less others. There is indeed no doubt that the planets bear an evident relation to the Sun, and with respect to it exhibit stations and retrogradations, and certain apparent inequalities — differences both as to longitude and latitude; but that the three superior planets stand as near as possible about the trine of the Sun, and are held back by the Sun's rays, and run a direct course, and are lifted on high by its fiery force (as the said Pliny reasons about these matters) — and then too the things he adds next about the retrogradations — I do not see how they can hold good. For the Sun's rays are not bound to the planets as if by a chain or some other linkage, by which they should drive, draw, or draw them back this way or that — unless we imagine some force, as it were magnetic, to be in them in this way; and not even so will the motion be one fitting for the heavenly bodies, namely circular and regular. For it is certain that the motions of the planets everywhere come about in a circular fashion, or are compounded of circular ones; and therefore the things Pliny insinuates, if they are to be referred to the Sun (which I do not deny can also be the case), come to be applied in another way — about which I have sometimes thought, but have not yet sufficiently resolved myself — namely, so that the epicycles be removed (which the ancients too did not assume, as is clear from Pliny) and the appearances nonetheless hold good. But I judge that Pliny was unable to bring this speculation of his — from wherever in the end it was received and however it was understood — into practice and use, and therefore confessed that there was some difficulty lurking here. Something similar is found in Vitruvius, who lived long before Pliny, but the passage does not now come to me. He, however, seems to have treated it architecturally rather than astronomically and geometrically; from whom it is likely that Pliny drew this view, although Pliny, dissembling that very thing, claimed it as his own and proper. But of these things, when, [God willing,] we have met and opportunity is given for examining such matters, we will philosophize further. But you, my dearest Pratensis, fare you most happily, and dutifully greet our Lord Dançay from me; and both of you, safe and sound, expect me there within a few days, as I said.

Given from our seat of Knudstrup, the 14th day of February, in the year 1576.
TYCHO BRAHE.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Iohannes Pratensis* = **Johannes Pratensis** (Hans Philipsen, 1543–1576), physician and professor of medicine at Copenhagen, Tycho's closest intellectual friend in these years; he died only a few months after this letter. Per this chapter's convention
- **Significance.** This is Tycho's own contemporaneous, confidential narrative of the audience at which **Frederik II** offered him the island of **Hven** (Hveen) — the foundational document for the founding of Uraniborg. Tycho reports the king's words in *oratio recta* (direct speech), set off here by guillemets as in the source.
- ***negotium Rostochiense*** — "our Rostock business": an errand Pratensis had transacted on Tycho's behalf at Rostock (unspecified here).
- ***foecundus ille Auster*** — "that fruitful South Wind": a figurative reference to Tycho's recent return from a journey to the south (Germany); kept as the author's metaphor.
- ***Magnifico Domino Legato Gallico DANZAeO*** = **Charles de Dançay** (Danzaeus, c. 1510–1589), the long-serving French resident ambassador at the Danish court and a humanist confidant of Tycho's. Per this chapter's convention register, *Magnificus* rendered "Honourable."
- ***Genius vatidicus / Genius seu potius ingenium*** — "prophetic Genius … your Genius, or rather your … wit": Tycho plays on *Genius* (attendant/prophetic spirit) and corrects it to *ingenium* (native wit); the wordplay is preserved, not flattened.
- ***studijs meis Olympicis*** — "my Olympic studies," i.e. studies of the heavens (the Olympian/celestial); kept as figure.
- ***Astronomiae instaurationem*** — "restoration of astronomy": Tycho's lifelong programme, the *instauratio astronomiae*; rendered "restoration of astronomy" by this chapter's convention
- ***favente astrorum conditore*** — "with the favour of the founder of the stars" (God as creator of the heavens); a pious formula.
- **Places.** *Haffnia* = **Copenhagen**; *Basilea* = **Basel**; *Sora* = **Sorø**; *Herressuadium* = **Herrevad** (the abbey held by Tycho's maternal uncle Steen Bille, where Tycho had his laboratory); *Knudstorpium / Knudsdorpiana sedes* = **Knudstrup** (the Brahe family seat in Scania, Tycho's birthplace); *Ibstrup* = the royal hunting-lodge of **Ibstrup** (later Jægersborg), N. of Copenhagen; *Arx Helsingorensis* = **Helsingør** (Kronborg) Castle, then being rebuilt by Frederik II; *Insula Huenna* = the island of **Hven** (Hveen), in the Sound toward **Landskrona** (*Landskronia*); *Friderigsburgum* = **Frederiksborg** Castle (Hillerød), the royal residence; *Scania / Selandia* = **Scania / Zealand**; *Dania* = **Denmark**. Per this chapter's convention
- **Persons at court.** *Nicolaus Passberg* = **Niels Parsberg**, royal chamberlain (*cubicularius*); *Nicolaus Kaasius* = **Niels Kaas** (1535–1594), Chancellor of Denmark; *Iohannes Schougardius* = **Johan Schougaard** (Jacob Skougaard / the royal secretary named in chancery); *Steno Bille* = **Steen Bille** (Tycho's maternal uncle, abbot of Herrevad). "My mother" = **Beate Bille**; "my brother" and the unnamed *Avunculus* of the opening paragraph (the uncle at Herrevad) = Steen Bille.
- **King's self-justification.** *saltem QVIA REX SVM* — "but simply BECAUSE I AM KING": the small-capitals emphasis is in the source and is preserved in the translation as small caps/upper-case; it is the rhetorical hinge of the king's speech and is not editorially added.
- **Astronomy / the Pliny excursus.** The closing paragraph debates a passage in **Pliny the Elder** (*Naturalis Historia* II, on the planets being checked and accelerated by the Sun's rays near the trine aspect). Glossary renderings used: *Stationes et Retrogradationes* → "stations and retrogradations"; *inaequalitates apparentes* → "apparent inequalities"; *Longum / Latum* → "longitude / latitude"; *Epicycli* → "epicycles"; *Trinum Solis* → "the trine of the Sun" (the 120° aspect). *vim quandam quasi Magneticam* — "some force, as it were magnetic": a notable early gesture by Tycho toward a magnetic celestial force; rendered literally, the hedge ("as it were," *quasi*) preserved. *Vitruvius* = **Vitruvius** (*De architectura* IX), cited as Pliny's probable source.
- **Textual note.** In the Pliny paragraph the printed text reads *"difficultatem quandam hîc subt esse fassum"*; *subt* is an obvious misprint for *subesse* (so that the phrase = *difficultatem quandam hîc subesse fassum*, "confessed that some difficulty lurks here"). The printed form is retained in the Source block; the translation follows the corrected reading.
- ***ACCCEPI*** (opening word) — printed with three C's; a typographical error for *Accepi* ("I have received"). Retained as printed in the Source block.
- **Crux: the abbreviation *D. V.*** — *D. V.* occurs twice: (i) *"quod facere D. V. constitui quamprimum unicum saltem diem Haffniae hac in re vobis tribuero"*; (ii) *"de his ubi D. V. convenerimus"*. The abbreviation is genuinely **ambiguous** and is **not resolved by the printed text**. The most economical reading is *Deo Volente* ("God willing") — the standard early-modern epistolary formula, and one Tycho uses in clear form earlier in this same letter (*si Deo sic visum fuerit*); on that reading *D. V.* is parenthetical and the surrounding words carry the sense (*Haffniae* = "at Copenhagen", *vobis* = "to you [both]", *convenerimus* = "we shall have met"). It could, however, conceivably stand for some other reference (e.g. a place/time formula). The editorial expansion **[God willing]** is therefore bracketed at both points rather than absorbed silently; *D. V.* is left unexpanded in the Source block. The earlier draft silently rendered both instances as "at Copenhagen" (the place-sense being supplied independently by *Haffniae*), which over-determined the abbreviation; that has been corrected.
- **Calendar / dating crux.** All dates are **Old Style (Julian)**; Denmark used O.S. until 1700. The dateline reads *"die 14. Februarij A. 1576"* ("the 14th day of February, 1576"), at Knudstrup — which agrees with the edition label (*1576. 14. februar. Knutstorp*). The body, however, narrates an internal sequence of distinct dates, **reported, not reconciled**: (i) the king's summons was written at Ibstrup on *die decimo … Februarii* (**10 February**); (ii) Tycho received it and rode to the audience on *undecimus Februarij* (**11 February**), described as "the last day of the previous week"; (iii) he wrote this letter on **14 February**. These three dates are internally consistent (the audience three days before the letter) and are preserved exactly as written; none is silently converted or "corrected."
- **Correction.** Two Latin transcription errors corrected: 'ACCCEPI' -> 'ACCEPI' (tripled-C typo for the letter's opening verb); 'invisere' -> 'invisero' (the 'ubi' clause requires the future-perfect, not the bare infinitive). No Dreyer page image (TBOO VII p.25) was available for this letter, so both corrections rest on internal Latin orthographic/grammatical evidence rather than direct collation against the page image; the English translation required no change in either case.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. No page reference had been recorded for this letter (tekstnet gives only the Danish for it), so no page images had been prepared. The letter was located: it runs TBOO Vol. VII (Epistolae Astronomicae) pp. 25-29, headed 'TYCHO AD IOH. PRATENSEM 14 FEB. 1576' throughout, found by reading the running headers/marginal apograph-notes on the neighbouring letters' page images (the Jan.31 1576 Pratensis-to-Tycho letter ends p.24; the Feb.15 1576 Pratensis reply begins p.30) and confirmed against the volume's page offset. All 5 letter pages (25-29) were read as page images. Collated the full transcribed original word-for-word against the images (opening/closing lines and every proper name, date, and number: PRATENSIS, DANZAeO, Sorae, Basileam, Herressuadij, Knudstorpij, undecimus/decimo Februarii, Ibstrup, unum milliare, Selandia/Scania, NICOLAUM PASSBERG, NICOLAUM KAASIUM, IOHANNEM SCHOUGARDIUM, STENO BILLE, Arce Helsingorensi, Insulam Huennam, Landskroniam, Friderigsburgensem, PLINIUS, VITRUVIUM, the 14 Februarii 1576 dateline) and found it complete and correct except the two text errors logged. Also collated the full published English translation against the (Dreyer-verified) Latin clause by clause: no fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found anywhere in this long letter — it is a complete and accurate rendering, including the direct-speech block and the technical Pliny/Vitruvius passage.

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). Our Latin prints the opening verb with a tripled C (ACCCEPI); Dreyer prints ACCEPI. A corrupted word; sense unaffected and the translation renders it correctly regardless. Dreyer prints: *ACCEPI literas tuas, eruditissime et amantissime PRATENSIS (TBOO VII p.25, opening word)*.
- **text error** (low). Our Latin has the present infinitive invisere where Dreyer prints the future-perfect invisero, the form the ubi-clause and following quod-clause require; a verb-form corruption. The English rendering happens to be correct either way, since English does not distinguish the two forms in this construction. Dreyer prints: *ubi vos denuo invisero, quod intra paucos dies facere decrevi (TBOO VII p.25, l. c. 11)*.

**Repaired.** No Dreyer page images were available for this letter, so neither defect could be verified against the edition of record by direct inspection. Both were nonetheless resolved on internal evidence internal to the Latin itself: 'ACCCEPI' is not a possible Latin spelling (accipio's perfect is invariably 'accepi'), and 'invisere' cannot stand as the finite verb of a 'ubi' clause, which requires 'invisero' given the surrounding future sense. Both fixes are low severity and do not affect the English, which was already correct in each case. Because collation against Dreyer's actual page image was not possible, this letter is graded B rather than A even though both defects are resolved.

documents.abstract: Expresses joy at the king's gracious invitation for Tycho to remain in Denmark, interpreting it as divine providence, and urges Tycho to accept.

text.original:
IOHANNES PRATENSIS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

GENEROSE Domine TYCHO, Amice observande, præ gaudio exsilij, quam primum legi in tuis, ea quæ de Serenissimi Regis nostri Clementissima voluntate refers, quæ etiam Magnifico Domino Legato Gallico, communi Amico nostro, qui ex asse tuus est, mox legenda exhibui; is pari mecum lætitia inde perfusus est, et utrique nostrum Genius pariter inspiravit, hæc non sine bonis ominibus fieri; judicavimusque ambo, imo certo statuimus, hæc singulari Numinis provisu Regi in mentem venisse, ut te tam benigne et liberaliter ad manendum in patria, adeoque sua sponte invitaret, idque non levibus adductus rationibus. Neque etiam dubium quin serio hoc agat, et forsan plura animo premit, quam in continenti promere voluit; scis Regum petita esse postulata. Et sane decet te, imo debes, mi TYCHO, debes, inquam, in gratiam Optimi Regis et Patriæ communis, cui nati sumus, et quæ multum iuris in nos sibi vendicat, propositum tuum mutare, atque Regiæ voluntati obtemperare. Habes brevibus quo DANZÆI et mea vergat sententia, plura et validiora intelliges ubi adfueris. Quam hæc tuorum necessariorum et aliorum nobilium, qui te mallent politicum per omnia sequi splendorem, atque eadem agere quæ ipsi, animos percellent, ubi intellexerint Regem tibi et tuis studijs tantâ clementiâ favere, ut ea benigne promovere, atque in hoc regno liberaliter sustentare velit, idque non rogatus, motu proprio, benignissime offerat. Quid nunc dicturi sunt proximi quique tui, quid frater, quid alij? scis quid loquar et quare. Sed desino plura, siquidem intra diem unum vel alterum, uti polliceris, huc venturus sis. Et sane oportet te reditum ad Regem maturare, atque quam citissime ad postulata eius (neque enim solummodo, uti prius dixi, petita sunt) respondere: nosti enim quam expedite Rex omnia vult fieri, quamque cito absque lenta procrastinatione. Adsis itaque nobis, exoptatissime TYCHO, hîc Haffniæ bonis avibus, vel potius Deo duce, qui hæc consilia, quæ nunc animo volvimus, gubernet ac felicitet, atque eodem ductore, mox Regem accede, eiusque votis tua obsequentissime coniunge: sic enim stat sententia, sic vult Apollo, sic suadet Urania, sic Mercurius suo caduceo imperat. Num adhuc dubitas? sed pluribus de his, uti dixi, coram, nihilque ambigo, quin ubi DANZÆUM et me audiveris, manibus pedibusque in nostram iturus sis sententiam. Vale, et hæc pauca, pro tempore, boni consule: volui potius pauca quam nulla scribere, ut de nostro quod expetis consilio eo citius aliquid cognosceres, sicque promptius tuum conformare possis, nec decuit hunc famulum, qui mihi tuas reddidit, absque responso reverti, quem vel in via te obviam habiturum, vel etiam Knudsdorpij itineri accinctum, reperturum existimo. De tuis vero, non est quod sis solicitus, eas in aliorum manus venturas, nam statim ac Domino Legato illas perlegeram, rupi et combussi, uti mandâras, nec ullus per nos ea de re quidpiam subolfaciet, antequam ipsemet hæc propalari volueris.

Iamque iterum vale, salutata a me Matre tua Nobilissima et Fratre STENONE, quam officiosissime.
Datæ Haffniæ festinanti calamo die 15. Februarij horis matutinis Anno 1576.
Iohannes Pratensis.

In hunc modum Excellentissimus ille PRATENSIS, bonæ recordationis, tam Magnifici Domini Legati Gallici, quam suam mihi apperuit sententiam, eandem postea cum simul essemus, pluribus exposuit et confirmavit; visumque est utrique eorum, ut omnino has a Clementissimo Rege oblatas conditiones susciperem, atque in Patria, relicto priori proposito, manerem , inque eius et Regis honorem, quæcunque pro virili præstare possem, sedulo molirer. Certo enim sibi persuadebant, hæc, Deo sic volente et regente, qui corda Regum in sua habet potestate, fieri. Subiunxit vero inter alia PRATENSIS, domum plane Philosophicam in illa Insula exædificandam esse, a vulgaribus differentem quæque hinc inde habeat inscriptiones Gnomologicas, ex antiquorum Philosophorum et Poëtarum scriptis petitas: et sigillatim recitavit LUCRETIJ versus, qui in initio libri secundi habentur:

Suave, mari magno turbantibus æquora ventis,
E Terra alterius longum Spectare laborem.

Et quæ sequuntur, usque in hos versus quos etiam memoravit:

At nil dulcius est, bene quam munita tenere
Edita doctrina sapientum templa serena,
Despicere unde queat alios, passimque videre
Errare, atque viam palantis quærere vitæ,
Certare ingenio, contendere nobilitate,
Ad Summas emergere opes, rerumque potiri.

Hæc et similia parietibus domus intrinsecus appingenda esse aiebat, quorum etiam authorem et monstratorem futurum pollicebatur. Ego vero mox Regem Serenissimum, qui tunc Friderigsburgum reversus erat, accedens, eius Clementissimæ voluntati me libenter acquieturum submisse indicavi. Atque mox, dum ibi adessem, conscriptæ et subsignatæ sunt literæ, salarium annuum ex ærario Regio mihi deputantes, idque die 18. Februarij. Adjecta sunt sequentibus annis alia beneficia Regia, et liberaliter exercitijs nostris Astronomicis prospectum.

Extructa itaque est in eadem Insula Arx Uraniburgica, una cum ijs, quæ huc requirebantur, et confecta ibique disposita sunt Instrumenta Astronomica varia et magnitudine atque materiæ soliditate præpollentia, quemadmodum in libro nostro de Astronomiæ Mechanica parte non saltem organa a me constructa, sed et ipsa ædificia, atque alia huc facientia exprimuntur. Quibus de causis Anno demum 21 a fundatione huius arcis, qui erat CHRISTI 1597, omnia isthic a me extructa deseruerim, atque in Germaniam me cum tota familia et apparatu illo Astronomico contulerim, non est huius loci referre, nimisque longum foret; habet etiam rationes cur lubentius id subticeam. Sed ad rem, et ea quæ de PRATENSE. Interim dum ego ædificationes novas in Insula illa adorno, et ob id rarius Haffniam venio, accidit ut optimus et eruditissimus ille PRATENSIS, proh dolor, fatis concesserit, magno sui non saltem apud me, sed et alios quam plurimos, relicto defiderio; erat enim omnibus ob morum suavitatem, probitatem et candorem, eximiamque humanitatem charissimus. Vixit is saltem usque in 32 ætatis annum, adeoque sub ipso iuventutis flore expiravit, idque morte festina et inopinata. Cum enim aliquandiu continuis defluxionibus ad pulmones et tussi vehementi laborasset, tandem in auditorio Academiæ Haffniensis, cum publice doceret, atque tunc ALCINOUM de Philosophia Platonica explicaret, de repente in eam, qua laboravit, incidens tussim, vena aliqua intrinseca illi rumpebatur, cumque sanguinem copiose per fauces effluentem, aqua frigida, quam studiosi mox attulerunt, ea nimirum in fauces manibus iniecta, sedari non posse animadvertit, mortemque instare sentiens, hæc ultima verba prolocutus: “IESU FILI DEI VIVI, miserere mei, et suscipe animam meam”, mox exanimis manibus suorum auditorum exceptus, et in ædes suas cadaver cum lacrymis et luctu reportatum, atque paucis post diebus honorifice in templo summo Haffniæ sepultum. Aberam ego tunc in Schania, neque satis cito de hoc dolendo casu resciscere potui ut sepulturæ interessem. Sed nihilominus, aliquot post dies, cum ex dolore, quem ob immaturam et improvisam intimi huius mei amici mortem conceperam, me collegissem, Epitaphium, quod illi vivo, biennio antea promiseram (se enim non diu supervicturum ipsemet iam antea præsagiebat) confeci, quod etiam publice in templo laminæ orichalcicæ inauratæ et eleganter circumquaque exornatæ, quam in eos usus parâram, affigere constitueram, nisi alia quædam ingrata intervenissent. At cum in huius præstantissimi viri, qui patre Gallo, quondam CHRISTIERNI secundi, Danorum Regis, postea captivi, Secretario in Cancellaria, uti intellexi, Gallica, matre vero Dana oriundus erat, et in omni Philosophiæ genere excellenter versatus, mentionem hîc, datâ operâ, ut eius memoriam hoc loco recolerem, incidi, lubet hoc ipsum, quod ei tunc concinnavi Epicedium, hîc apponere, utut id extra propositum videbatur, sed quacunque tandem ratione eximij huius viri, meique dum in vivis esset, amici optimi, memoriam conservare, atque ad posteros transmittere licitum arbitror, praesertim cum et is Astronomiæ studijs, de quibus hisce Epistolis affatim agitur, præclare imbutus fuerit. Quæ etiam omnia ob id hîc commemoro, ut constare possit meis lectoribus, quî factum sit, quod non plures in posterum ab hoc Doctissimo PRATENSE literæ subsequantur, eo nimirum nimis matura morte, quod dolendum, nobis prærepto. Nunc igitur Epitaphium, de quo dixi, subijciam, posteaque ad alias Epistolas doctorum virorum aliunde mihi scriptas, continuandas pergam.
text.english:
**JOHANNES PRATENSIS TO TYCHO BRAHE.**

Noble Master Tycho, friend to be honoured: leaping for joy, the moment I read in your letter what you report concerning the most clement disposition of our Most Serene King, I straightway laid it before the Magnificent Lord French Ambassador too — our common friend, who is yours through and through — to read; and he was filled with a gladness equal to mine, and to each of us our guardian spirit alike whispered that these things are not coming about without good omens. We judged, both of us — indeed we held it for certain — that by a singular foresight of the Divine Will this has entered the King's mind, that he should invite you, so kindly and so generously, and moreover of his own accord, to remain in your homeland, and that he was moved to it by no slight reasons. Nor is there any doubt that he is in earnest in this, and perhaps presses more in his mind than he chose to put forth on the spot; you know that what kings request are commands. And truly it becomes you — nay, you are bound, my Tycho, *bound*, I say — for the sake of the Best of Kings and of our common homeland, to which we were born and which claims much right over us, to change your design and to comply with the Royal will. You have here in brief which way Dançay's opinion and mine incline; you will learn more, and weightier, when you are present. How this will strike the minds of your kinsmen and of the other nobles, who would rather you pursued in all things the splendour of a public career and did the same things they do, when they have understood that the King favours you and your studies with such great clemency that he is willing kindly to advance them and to maintain them generously in this kingdom — and offers it most graciously, unasked, of his own initiative! What now will each of your nearest say, what your brother, what the rest? You know what I mean, and why. But I make an end of saying more, since within a day or two, as you promise, you will be coming here. And indeed you ought to hasten your return to the King, and to answer his demands as quickly as can be (for they are not merely requests, as I said before): for you know how promptly the King wishes everything to be done, and how speedily, without slow procrastination. Be with us, then, most longed-for Tycho, here in Copenhagen under good auspices — or rather, with God as our guide, who governs and prospers these plans we are now turning over in our minds — and under that same guidance, approach the King at once and join your wishes most obediently to his: for so the resolution stands, so Apollo wills, so Urania counsels, so Mercury commands with his caduceus. Do you still hesitate? But of these matters, as I said, more in person; and I have no doubt that, once you have heard Dançay and me, you will come over hand and foot to our opinion. Farewell, and for the present take these few lines in good part: I chose to write a little rather than nothing, so that you might learn something the sooner of the counsel of ours that you seek, and so might the more readily shape your own; nor was it fitting that this servant who delivered your letter to me should return without an answer — a man whom I reckon you will meet on the road coming toward you, or else find girt for the journey to Knudstrup. As for your letters, you need not be anxious that they will come into other hands; for as soon as I had read them through to the Lord Ambassador, I tore and burned them, as you had charged, and through us no one shall get wind of the matter before you yourself shall wish it made known.

And now again farewell — with my most dutiful greetings to your most noble Mother and to your brother Steen.
Given at Copenhagen, with hurrying pen, on the 15th day of February, in the morning hours, in the year 1576.
Johannes Pratensis.

In this manner that most excellent Pratensis, of good memory, opened to me both the Magnificent Lord French Ambassador's opinion and his own; and afterwards, when we were together, he set it forth and confirmed it at greater length. It seemed best to both of them that I should by all means take up the conditions offered by the Most Clement King, and remain in my homeland, abandoning my former design, and that in his honour and the King's I should diligently strive to perform whatever I could to the best of my power. For they were firmly persuaded that this was coming to pass by God's so willing and governing, who holds the hearts of kings in his power. Pratensis added, moreover, among other things, that a thoroughly Philosophical house should be built on that Island, differing from common ones, and having here and there sententious inscriptions [inscriptiones Gnomologicas], drawn from the writings of the ancient Philosophers and Poets; and he recited in particular the verses of Lucretius that stand at the beginning of the second book:

Sweet it is, when on the great sea the winds are stirring the waters,
to gaze from the land upon another's great labour;

and what follows, on to these verses, which he likewise recalled:

But nothing is sweeter than to hold the serene high sanctuaries,
well fortified by the teaching of the wise,
whence one may look down upon others and see them
wandering everywhere astray, and seeking the path of life as they stray —
contending in talent, striving over rank,
to rise to the highest wealth, and to grasp dominion.

These and the like, he said, ought to be painted on the inner walls of the house; and he promised that he himself would be the author and deviser of them. I, for my part, soon approached the Most Serene King, who had then returned to Frederiksborg, and submissively signified that I would gladly acquiesce in his most clement will. And presently, while I was there, letters were drawn up and subscribed assigning me a yearly salary from the Royal treasury — and that on the 18th day of February. In the following years other Royal benefactions were added, and provision was generously made for our Astronomical exercises.

And so on that same Island the Castle of Uraniborg was raised, together with the things required for the purpose, and various Astronomical Instruments were made and set up there, pre-eminent both in size and in solidity of material — just as in our book on the Mechanical part of Astronomy not only the instruments [organa] constructed by me, but the very buildings and the other things pertaining to it, are set forth. For what reasons, in the twenty-first year at last from the founding of this castle — which was the year of Christ 1597 — I forsook everything I had raised there, and betook myself into Germany with my whole household and that Astronomical apparatus, it is not the place here to relate, and it would be too long; there are reasons, too, why I more willingly pass it over in silence. But to the matter, and to what concerns Pratensis. Meanwhile, while I was adorning the new buildings on that Island, and on that account came more rarely to Copenhagen, it happened that that best and most learned Pratensis — alas! — yielded to the fates, leaving great longing for himself not only in me but in very many others as well; for he was most dear to all for the sweetness of his character, his uprightness and candour, and his exceptional kindness. He lived only into his thirty-second year, and so breathed his last in the very flower of youth, and that by a hasty and unlooked-for death. For when he had laboured for some while under continual fluxes upon the lungs and a violent cough, at last in the lecture-hall of the University of Copenhagen, while he was teaching publicly and was at that time expounding Alcinous on Platonic Philosophy, suddenly falling into the cough from which he suffered, some inner vein burst in him; and when he perceived that the blood flowing copiously through his throat could not be stanched by the cold water which the students at once brought — flung, that is, into his throat with their hands — and, feeling death at hand, he uttered these last words: "JESUS, SON OF THE LIVING GOD, have mercy on me, and receive my soul"; and at once, lifeless, he was caught in the hands of his hearers, and his body was carried back to his house with tears and mourning, and a few days afterward honourably buried in the cathedral church of Copenhagen. I was then away in Scania, and could not learn of this grievous event soon enough to be present at the burial. Yet nonetheless, some days afterward, when I had recovered myself from the grief I had conceived at the untimely and unforeseen death of this my most intimate friend, I composed an Epitaph which I had promised him while living, two years before (for he himself had already foreboded that he would not long survive); and I had resolved to affix it publicly in the church upon a gilded brass plate, elegantly adorned all round, which I had prepared for that use, had not certain other unwelcome matters intervened. But since I have here lighted — of set purpose, that I might revive his memory in this place — upon the mention of this most outstanding man, who was sprung of a French father (formerly, as I understand, Secretary in the French Chancery to Christian II, King of the Danes, afterward a captive) and a Danish mother, and was excellently versed in every kind of Philosophy, I am pleased to set down here this very Dirge [Epicedium] which I then composed for him — though it seemed to be beside my purpose; but by whatever means at last I judge it permissible to preserve the memory of this exceptional man, and my best friend while he was among the living, and to transmit it to posterity, especially since he too had been splendidly imbued with the studies of Astronomy, of which these Letters treat abundantly. And all this I commemorate here for this reason: that it may be plain to my readers how it came about that no further letters from this most learned Pratensis follow hereafter — he having been snatched from us, alas, by too early a death. Now therefore I shall append the Epitaph of which I spoke, and afterward shall proceed to continue with the other Letters of learned men written to me from elsewhere.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Iohannes Pratensis* = **Johannes Pratensis / Hans Philipsen** (1543–1576), professor of medicine at the University of Copenhagen and one of Tycho's closest friends. This is the letter by which he and the French ambassador pressed Tycho to accept Frederik II's offer; Tycho's appended commentary records that he did, and recounts Pratensis's death in 1576 — the reason no later letters from him appear in the collection.
- **Editorial structure.** The file contains **two strata**: (1) Pratensis's actual letter of 15 Feb 1576 (down to the subscription "Iohannes Pratensis"); (2) a long retrospective commentary by **Tycho himself**, written when he assembled the 1596 *Epistolae* (it speaks of abandoning Hven "in the year of Christ 1597" — see calendar note), narrating his acceptance of the King's offer, the founding of Uraniborg, the death of Pratensis, and his intention to append an epitaph. The Lucretius verses are quoted *within* Tycho's commentary as the inscriptions Pratensis proposed for the house.
- ***Serenissimi Regis nostri*** — **Frederik II of Denmark** (r. 1559–88), who in 1576 granted Tycho the island of Hven; the "conditions offered" are the lifelong grant that founded Uraniborg.
- ***Magnifico Domino Legato Gallico … DANZAeI / DANZAeUM*** — **Charles de Dançay** (Carolus Danzaeus, c. 1510–1589), the long-serving French resident ambassador at the Danish court and a humanist patron; here Tycho's and Pratensis's ally in urging him to stay. *DANZAeI* (genitive), *DANZAeUM* (accusative) are kept in the source block; the name is normalised to "Dançay" in the translation.
- ***Fratre STENONE*** — **Steen Brahe** (1547–1620), Tycho's younger brother; *Stenone* is the Latin ablative of *Steno* = Steen.
- ***Matre tua Nobilissima*** — Tycho's mother, **Beate Bille** (1526–1605).
- ***Knudsdorpij*** — **Knudstrup** (Knutstorp), the Brahe family seat in Scania; here the goal of the messenger's journey.
- ***Schania*** — **Scania** (Skåne), then Danish.
- ***Friderigsburgum*** — **Frederiksborg** (Hillerød), the royal castle to which Frederik II had returned.
- ***Arx Uraniburgica*** — the **Castle of Uraniborg** on Hven.
- ***libro nostro de Astronomiae Mechanica parte*** — Tycho's *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica* (Wandsbek, 1598); *organa* = **instruments**.
- ***Anno demum 21 a fundatione … qui erat CHRISTI 1597*** — Tycho dates his abandonment of Hven to "the 21st year from the founding," "the year of Christ 1597." This dates the **commentary**, not the letter; reproduced as written, not reconciled with the conventional account of his final departure (he left Hven in 1597, then Denmark thereafter; the apparatus does not "correct" the count). Per this chapter's convention, no date is silently converted; the *letter's* dateline is 15 Feb 1576 (O.S.).
- **Calendar.** Letter dateline: *die 15. Februarij … Anno 1576* — **15 February 1576 (O.S.)**; the salary letters were subscribed *die 18. Februarij* (18 February 1576, O.S.). Denmark used the Julian calendar throughout. The header date is the letter's own dateline, 15 February 1576.
- **Classical / rhetorical flourishes.** *sic vult Apollo, sic suadet Urania, sic Mercurius suo caduceo imperat* — "so Apollo wills, so Urania counsels, so Mercury commands with his caduceus": a humanist piling-up of the god of prophecy, the **Muse of astronomy** (Urania — note the resonance with the future Uraniborg), and the herald-god, kept as figure. *manibus pedibusque* ("hand and foot") is a classical idiom for whole-hearted assent (Terence/Cicero), translated literally with the idiom preserved.
- ***inscriptiones Gnomologicas*** — "sententious inscriptions" (Gk. *gnōmologia*, collections of maxims/*gnomae*); the moralising mottoes Pratensis proposed for the walls. The term is glossed, not anglicised to a false cognate.
- **Lucretius.** The verses are *De rerum natura* **II.1–2** (*Suave, mari magno…*) and a six-line block beginning *At nil dulcius est…* (II.7–11 + II.13), quoted from Tycho's commentary as the proposed wall-inscriptions; kept as verse by this chapter's convention **As transcribed, the second block runs II.7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13 — Lucretius II.12 (*noctes atque dies niti praestante labore*, "striving night and day with surpassing toil") is *not present* in this source block**; the transcription jumps from *Certare ingenio, contendere nobilitate* (II.11) directly to *Ad Summas emergere opes, rerumque potiri* (II.13). The translation mirrors the source as transcribed and renders only the six lines given; nothing answering to the omitted II.12 ("night and day") is supplied (an earlier draft had imported it from the full Lucretian text — corrected). Whether II.12 dropped out in Tycho's quotation, in Dreyer, or in the working transcription is left open here, not silently restored. The translation renders the sense line-for-line without metre. Note the early-modern orthography retained in the source block (*Spectare*, *Edita*, *passimque*); *Edita … templa serena* = "the serene high sanctuaries" (Lucretius's *templa serena* of the wise).
- ***ALCINOUM de Philosophia Platonica*** — **Alcinous**, the *Didaskalikos* (Handbook of Platonism), then commonly ascribed to "Alcinous"; Pratensis died while lecturing on it.
- ***patre Gallo … CHRISTIERNI secundi … Secretario in Cancellaria … Gallica*** — Tycho records that Pratensis's father was a Frenchman who had been Secretary in the French Chancery to **Christian II** (r. 1513–23, deposed and long imprisoned: *postea captivi*, "afterward a captive"), and his mother Danish. *Christierni secundi* is the period Latin form of Christian II.
- ***Epitaphium … laminae orichalcicae inauratae*** — a verse epitaph on a **gilded brass plate** (*orichalcum*, brass/latten); *Epicedium* ("Dirge") is the funeral poem Tycho says he will append. The epitaph/epicedium text itself is **not present in this source block** — Tycho announces it ("Now therefore I shall append the Epitaph…") but it would follow as a separate item; flagged so the reader does not expect it here.
- **Greek/symbols.** No Greek or planetary/zodiac glyphs occur in this letter. The dying words *"IESU FILI DEI VIVI…"* are Latin (echoing the Jesus Prayer), kept and translated.
- **Transcription (adopted readings).** The working transcription carried four manifest digitised text layer artifacts — stray-space and run-together errors with no counterpart in the printed Dreyer text: *manerem,* (→ *manerem,*), *transm ittere* (→ *transmittere*), *conceperam,m e* (→ *conceperam, me*), and *prae sertim* (→ *praesertim*). These are silently restored to the correct printed forms in the Source block above (by this chapter's convention, the text-of-record is Dreyer, not the digitised text layer working file); none affects sense. Flagged here rather than reproduced, since they are transcription noise, not features of the printed source.
- **Negations.** *non … venturas … in aliorum manus* / *rupi et combussi* — the assurance that the letters will **not** fall into others' hands because Pratensis tore and burned them: a single clear negation, reproduced exactly. *nec ullus … subolfaciet, antequam … volueris* — "**no one** shall get wind of it before you wish it": one negation, preserved.

documents.abstract: Returns borrowed Greek propositions, mentions forwarding a sundials manuscript, and approves Tycho's resolve to devote himself to celestial observations.
documents.incipit: LITERIS tuis, nobilissime, amantissime Domine TYCHO, nihil mihi fuit charius. Ioachimicos …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO CLARISSIMOQUE VIRO D. TYCHONI BRAHE, MATHEMATICO EXIMIO, DOMINO ET AMICO OBSERVANDO.

LITERIS tuis, nobilissime, amantissime Domine TYCHO, nihil mihi fuit charius. Ioachimicos 40 accepi a D. LEVINO. Chirographum adhuc apud me delitescit sine fraude et dolo. OMELIJ de Horologijs sciotericis partem, quam commodato ceperam, remisi, feceris mihi rem pergratam, si reliquam partem mittas. Detinueram apud me propositiones aliquot Graece conscriptas, has, ne quicquam desideres, remitto. Quod vero scribis te in observationes coelestium motuum sedulo incubiturum, non possum non probare, cum animum sis consecutus ad ea studia sua sponte inflammatum, et qui laboribus non deterrentur, quique in rebus praeclaris et a communi ingeniorum captu semotis laudabile iudicat studium suum posuisse. Utinam ipsum coelum non plane oppugnet tuos labores, aptius ad p[rui]narum, imbrium, nivium, grandium, Septentrionis, Cori Boreaeque flatium, et aliarum, quae in sublimi fiunt, impressionum considerationem. Vulcano accommodata magis sedes, cui materiam copiosam suppeditat, in qua se exerceat. His lapis ille multis decantatus plerisque omnibus frustra quaesitus investigandus potius, quam in coelo, quod raro in oculos incurrit, siderum motus perscrutandi. Nos hîc te expectamus, nec sine libris aliquot non passim obvijs. Si quos habeas IORDANI aut REGIOMONTANI nondum editos, Norimbergae a te emptos unâ tecum afferas. Quod si COPERNICUM WOLPHGANG piae memoriae, nactus es, hic sit tantum itineris comes. Ita enim iudico, Regem in Germaniam iter instituentem comitaberis, cuius beneficio, quod felix et faustum sit, intelligo, te Dominum Insulae factum, e qua quaquaversum, montibus non objectis, coelum prospicere liceat: Macte animo, quo tua te virtus vocat. Nos curta supellex et res angusta domi hactenus humi depressos detinuit, brevi forte emersuros. Cum apud nos esses, petij, ut quae in morbo caduco tibi essent nota, de usu medicamentorum ad affectum facientium, communicares, id hunc ob repentinum discessum minime licuit. Hoc si nunc feceris, plurimum me tibi devinxeris. Cum autem ad tres fere differentias possit deduci, quando scilicet ipsum cerebrum primario laborat, aut aliquod viscus, ut uterus, ventriculus, lien, et si quod sit aliud, aut e partibus remotioribus, ut manibus pedibusve, aura quaedam caput petit. Peterem in singulis propriam rationem, si quae sit, aut universalem omnibus, si unus est in omnibus curandi modus. Aut quid omnibus commune, quid singulis peculiare. Non dubito pro animi tui candore et amore mutuo, candide omnia communicaturum.

Bene vale.
Rostochij XIV Maij anno 1576.
Henricus Brucaeus
plane tuus.
text.english:
**To the most noble and illustrious gentleman, Master Tycho Brahe, distinguished mathematician, his lord and friend to be regarded with respect.**

Nothing has been dearer to me than your letter, most noble and most beloved Master Tycho. I received 40 Joachimstal coins [Ioachimicos] from Master Levinus. The autograph [chirographum] still lies hidden with me, without fraud or guile. I have sent back the part of Oemel's *On Sundials* [De Horologiis sciotericis] which I had taken on loan; you will do me a most welcome favour if you send the remaining part. I had been keeping with me some propositions written out in Greek; these — so that you may lack for nothing — I send back. But as for your writing that you mean to apply yourself diligently to observations of the celestial motions, I cannot but approve, since you have attained a disposition kindled of its own accord toward those studies — [a disposition] of those who are not deterred by hardships, and who judge it praiseworthy to have invested their pursuit in things excellent and set apart from the common reach of [ordinary] minds. Would that the very sky did not flatly oppose your labours — [a sky] better suited to the consideration of hoarfrosts [p[rui]narum], rains, snows, hailstorms, and of the North wind, the Caurus, and the Boreas's blasts, and of the other impressions that come to be on high. A seat more fitted to Vulcan, to whom it supplies abundant matter on which to exercise himself. In these [matters] that stone so much sung-of by many, [yet] sought in vain by very nearly all, is rather to be investigated, than the motions of the stars to be searched out in a sky that rarely meets the eye. We await you here, and not without some books that are not everywhere to be come by. If you have any [works] of Jordanus or Regiomontanus not yet published, bought by you at Nuremberg, bring them along with you. And if you have got hold of the Copernicus of Wolfgang of pious memory, let this only be a companion for the journey. For thus I judge: you will accompany the King as he sets out on a journey into Germany — by whose benefaction (which may it be happy and auspicious) I understand you have been made Lord of an Island, from which, with no mountains set in the way, one may look out upon the sky in every direction. Go on with good heart, whither your virtue calls you! As for us, scant furniture and straitened means at home have hitherto held us pressed to the ground — though perhaps soon to emerge. When you were with us, I asked that you would share what things were known to you in the falling sickness [morbus caducus], concerning the use of medicaments that act upon the affliction; this, owing to your sudden departure, was by no means possible. If you do this now, you will bind me very greatly to you. Now since [the disease] can be reduced to roughly three distinctions — namely, when the brain itself is primarily affected; or some viscus, such as the womb, the stomach, the spleen, and if there be any other; or when from the more remote parts, such as the hands or feet, a certain vapour [aura] makes for the head — I would ask [you to give] in each case its own method [of treatment], if there is one, or a universal one for all, if there is a single mode of curing in all [cases]; or what is common to all, what peculiar to each. I do not doubt, given the candour of your mind and our mutual affection, that you will share everything candidly.

Fare you well.
Rostock, 14 May, the year 1576.
Heinrich Brucaeus,
wholly yours.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (Hendrik van den Broeck, 1530/31–1593), Flemish-born professor of medicine and mathematics at the University of Rostock, where Tycho had studied (1566–68); a long-standing scholarly friend. The letter belongs to the spring of 1576, in the months immediately after the royal grant of Hven (Brucaeus has just heard of it — see below).
- **Recipient line.** The edition's recipient field doubles the name ("Tycho Brahe Tycho Brahe"); a data artefact, not in the source. The source address-line is the single *D. TYCHONI BRAHE*.
- ***Ioachimicos*** — "the Joachimsthalers / Joachimstal coins": *Ioachimici* (sc. *nummi/thaleri*) are the silver coins struck at Joachimsthal (Jáchymov), the original "thaler." Most likely actual coins forwarded via *D. Levinus* (an unidentified intermediary, "Master Levinus"), though the word in a numismatically-minded humanist context can mean coin-specimens of interest. Rendered "Joachimstal coins" with the Latin kept; referent flagged.
- ***Chirographum*** — "autograph / hand-written document" (something in Tycho's own hand that Brucaeus is holding for him); *sine fraude et dolo* is the legal-formula assurance "without fraud or guile," i.e. safely kept.
- ***OMELIJ de Horologijs sciotericis*** — a treatise *On Sundials* (*horologia scioterica* = shadow-clocks, sundials) by **Oemel/Omelius**. The author is not securely identifiable from the name-form alone; rendered "Oemel's *On Sundials*" and the attribution left as written. *Sciotericum* (< Gk σκιοθηρικόν) = "shadow-catching," the standard term for a sundial.
- ***propositiones … Graece conscriptas*** — "propositions written out in Greek": mathematical/geometrical propositions in Greek that Brucaeus had borrowed and now returns. (No Greek glyphs appear in the source text itself.)
- **The meteorological clause — Brucaeus's scepticism.** *Utinam ipsum coelum non plane oppugnet tuos labores, aptius ad p[rui]narum … impressionum considerationem* — the rhetorical heart of the letter: Brucaeus warns that the northern sky is so cloud-ridden that it is fitter for studying weather (*impressiones* = meteorological "impressions," the sublunary phenomena of Aristotelian *Meteorologica*) than the stars. **Editorial reading flagged:** the source prints *p[rui]narum* with the middle supplied in brackets by the edition; *pruinae* = "hoarfrosts," which fits the list of frost/rain/snow/hail. The bracketed supply is kept in the Source block and adopted in the translation by the audit's rule.
- **Wind-names.** *Septentrionis, Cori Boreaeque flatium* — *Septentrio* = the North (wind); *Corus/Caurus* = the NW wind; *Boreas* = the N/NE wind. Kept as classical wind-names, glossed.
- ***Vulcano … lapis ille multis decantatus*** — "a seat more fitted to Vulcan … that stone so much sung-of": Brucaeus pivots to alchemy. *Vulcanus* = the fire/forge, i.e. alchemical work; *lapis ille multis decantatus … frustra quaesitus* = the **philosophers' stone** ("that stone so often sung of [by many], sought in vain by nearly all"). Brucaeus playfully advises that the cloudy North is better for the furnace than for the heavens. *decantatus* carries a faint irony ("much harped-on") preserved rather than flattened.
- **Books sought.** *IORDANI aut REGIOMONTANI nondum editos, Norimbergae a te emptos* — unpublished works of **Jordanus (de Nemore)** or **Regiomontanus** (Johannes Müller of Königsberg, 1436–76) that Tycho had bought at **Nuremberg**. *COPERNICUM WOLPHGANG piae memoriae* — "the Copernicus of Wolfgang of pious memory," i.e. a copy of Copernicus (almost certainly *De revolutionibus*) once owned by a deceased **Wolfgang** (unidentified; "of pious memory" marks him as recently dead). Brucaeus asks Tycho to bring these to Rostock. Wolfgang's identity is a minor crux, left unresolved.
- **The grant of Hven.** *Regem in Germaniam iter instituentem comitaberis, cuius beneficio … te Dominum Insulae factum* — "you will accompany the King [Frederik II] … by whose benefaction … you have been made Lord of an Island." This is **Hven** (Ven), granted to Tycho by **Frederik II** on 23 May 1576 — so this letter (14 May 1576) registers the news as just received / imminent, a valuable external date-fix on the grant. *e qua quaquaversum, montibus non objectis, coelum prospicere liceat* = "from which, with no mountains in the way, one may view the sky in every direction" — Brucaeus already grasps the island's observational virtue. *Macte animo* = "Go on with good heart / well done, take courage," a classical encouragement formula.
- ***curta supellex … res angusta domi*** — "scant furniture … straitened means at home": *res angusta domi* is a Juvenalian tag (*Sat.* 3.164–5) for poverty; Brucaeus pleads his own narrow circumstances. *humi depressos … brevi forte emersuros* = "pressed to the ground … perhaps soon to emerge."
- **Medicine — the *morbus caducus* query.** *morbus caducus* = the **falling sickness (epilepsy)**, rendered with the period term glossed. Brucaeus asks for Tycho's knowledge of *medicamenta ad affectum facientia* ("medicaments that act upon the affliction" — i.e. remedies effective against the condition; *affectus* = the disease-state). He lays out a threefold aetiological scheme drawn from Galenic medicine: epilepsy arising (1) primarily in the **brain** (*cerebrum*); (2) by sympathy from a **viscus** — *uterus* (womb), *ventriculus* (stomach), *lien* (spleen); or (3) from the **remote parts** (hands/feet), whence *aura quaedam caput petit* — "a certain vapour makes for the head" (the classical *aura epileptica*, the rising sensation preceding a fit). *aura* kept and glossed. He asks whether each type has its **own** treatment (*propria ratio*) or there is a **universal** mode (*universalis omnibus … modus*) — *universalis* rendered "universal" per glossary.
- **Calendar / place.** *Rostochij XIV Maij anno 1576* = "**Rostock**, 14 May 1576" (O.S.; Denmark and the Empire alike pre-Gregorian in 1576). The dateline agrees with the edition label (*1576. 14. maj. Rostock*); no discrepancy.
- **Subscription.** *Bene vale* → "Fare you well"; *plane tuus* → "wholly yours."
- **Correction.** Latin: restored the dropped numeral, 'Ioachimicos accepi' corrected to 'Ioachimicos 40 accepi', per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p.33. English: added '40' to name the sum of Joachimsthaler coins received.
