documents.incipit: GENEROSE et clarissime vir, Domine et amice perpetuo colende, recordari mei PRATENSIS …

text.original:
NOBILI ET GENEROSO VIRO TYCHONI BRAHE A KNUDSTORP, AMICO SUO PLURIMUM COLENDO.

GENEROSE et clarissime vir, Domine et amice perpetuo colende, recordari mei PRATENSIS sine lacrymis non possum, cum animæ plus quam dimidium perdiderim meæ. At cum dolor iste nobis communis sit, ego frustra me affligendo tibi molestus esse desinam, et tuis literis respondebo. Quæ certe mihi fuerunt gratissimæ, et plurimum profuerunt. Nam illæ me veterno quodam oppressum excitarunt, et quasi in tenebris lumine privatum errantem in rectam reduxerunt viam, ut ea, quæ me decent, præstarem. Scias igitur, mi amantissime TYCHO, lapidem angularem paratum esse, sed cum inscriptionem seu dedicationem, et quædam alia mystica sacraque ille optimæ recordationis PRATENSIS sibi reservasset, iurareque voluisset, ego mihi (quod tantus vir facile conficere potuisset) tribuere non ausus sum, ut quicquam in ijs, nisi te mandante, vel potius præscribente, tentare voluerim. Te igitur oro, si Mercurium tibi caducei usuram negare non velis (illius enim verbis lubenter utor) ut, quod tui studiosissimus in se receperat, et mihi iure quodam debebat, tute perficias et persolvas, vel ego cogar (etsi invitus) nescio quid in te desiderare. Ut autem hac in re facilior promptiorque sis et mihi citius respondeas, ne magnum illud opus nostra mora et tua culpa remoretur, oro ut ijs, quæ in schedula scripsi, addas, immutes, subtrahas, vel ut uno verbo omnia complectar, una litura deleas, et statuas, quid sit faciendum, quid scribendum, cum id facile efficere queas, et ego tibi obsequar lubentissime. Quod si me tui amantissimum esse et observantissimum credideris, non falleris.

Vale, Vir præstantissime, et cito rescribe.
Haffniæ 26. die Iunij Anno 1576.
Tibi deditissimus amicus
Carolus Danzeus.
text.english:
**To the noble and high-born gentleman Tycho Brahe of Knudstrup, his most esteemed friend.**

High-born and most renowned Sir, my Lord and ever-to-be-esteemed friend: I cannot call to mind my dear Pratensis without tears, since I have lost more than the half of my own soul. But since that grief is shared between us, I shall cease to be troublesome to you by afflicting myself in vain, and I shall reply to your letter — which was assuredly most welcome to me, and profited me greatly. For it roused me, oppressed as I was by a kind of lethargy, and, as one wandering in darkness deprived of light, led me back into the right road, that I might perform the things which befit me. Know then, my most beloved Tycho, that the cornerstone is ready; but since that Pratensis of most excellent memory had reserved to himself the inscription, or dedication, and certain other secret and sacred matters, and had wished to take an oath upon it, I have not dared to take upon myself (a thing which so great a man could easily have accomplished) the attempting of anything in these matters, except at your bidding, or rather your prescription. I beg you, therefore — if you will not refuse Mercury the loan of his herald's-staff for your use (for I gladly use his words) — that what one most devoted to you had taken upon himself, and by a certain right owed to me, you yourself may carry through and discharge; or else I shall be compelled (though unwilling) to find some lack in you, I know not what. And so that you may be the more accommodating and ready in this matter and reply to me the sooner — lest that great work be delayed by our procrastination and your fault — I beg that to the things I have written on the slip you add, alter, take away, or (to embrace all in one word) blot out with a single stroke of the pen, and determine what is to be done, what is to be written, since you can easily bring it about, and I shall comply with you most gladly. And if you will believe me to be most loving and most respectful of you, you will not be deceived.

Farewell, most excellent Sir, and write back quickly.
At Copenhagen, the 26th day of June, the year 1576.
Your most devoted friend,
Charles de Dançay.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Carolus Danzeus* = **Charles de Dançay** (c. 1510–1589), the long-serving French resident ambassador at the Danish court of Frederik II, a humanist and patron of learning and one of Tycho's older friends and protectors during the Uraniborg years. He signs *Tibi deditissimus amicus* ("Your most devoted friend").
- **Addressee superscription.** *TYCHONI BRAHE A KNUDSTORP* — "Tycho Brahe of Knudstrup," naming the family seat (Knutstorp in Scania); kept by this chapter's convention
- ***Pratensis*** = **Johannes Pratensis** (Hans Philipsen, 1543–1576), professor of medicine at Copenhagen and Tycho's intimate physician-friend. Dançay's opening lament — *animae plus quam dimidium perdiderim meae* ("I have lost more than the half of my own soul") — and the phrase *ille optimae recordationis Pratensis* ("that Pratensis of most excellent memory") place the letter shortly after Pratensis's death (he died in May 1576); the *dolor … nobis communis* ("grief shared between us") is the bereavement Dançay and Tycho hold in common. The Horatian echo (*animae dimidium meae*, Horace, *Odes* I.3.8) is preserved in the literal rendering.
- ***lapis angularis* ("the cornerstone").** The foundation/cornerstone of **Uraniborg**, Tycho's observatory-castle on Hven, whose building was begun in 1576; the cornerstone was laid on 8 August 1576. *paratum esse* = "is ready / prepared." The letter shows Dançay overseeing the preparation of the stone in Copenhagen and awaiting from Tycho the wording of its dedicatory inscription. **Crux flagged:** the Latin says only *lapidem angularem paratum esse* — that the stone is *ready/prepared*, not that it is laid; no completed-construction sense is read in. Nothing beyond the as-printed claim is asserted.
- ***inscriptionem seu dedicationem, et quaedam alia mystica sacraque*** — "the inscription, or dedication, and certain other secret and sacred matters." Pratensis had reserved to himself (*sibi reservasset*) the composing of the cornerstone's dedicatory inscription and certain undisclosed "mystic and sacred" elements, and had wished to bind it by oath (*iurareque voluisset*); with his death, Dançay asks Tycho himself to supply the wording. *mystica sacraque* is left as "secret and sacred," not narrowed to a specific rite, since the text does not specify.
- ***Mercurium … caducei usuram* ("Mercury … the loan of his herald's-staff").** A learned conceit: Dançay asks Tycho to lend the eloquence of **Mercury** (god of messengers and of letters) — i.e. to compose the inscription's words. *caduceus* = Mercury's herald's-staff (caduceus); *usuram … negare* = "to refuse the use/loan of." The parenthesis *illius enim verbis lubenter utor* ("for I gladly use his words") signals that the conceit is Dançay's playful borrowing of Mercurial idiom; kept as figure, not flattened.
- ***quod … in se receperat, et mihi iure quodam debebat*** — "what [Pratensis], most devoted to you, had taken upon himself, and by a certain right owed to me." The subject of *receperat* / *debebat* is the late Pratensis, who had undertaken the task; Dançay now presses Tycho to "carry it through and discharge" (*perficias et persolvas*) the obligation in his stead. Read with care: the hedged *nescio quid in te desiderare* ("to find some lack in you, I know not what") is a courteous, deliberately vague half-threat, preserved with its qualifier (*etsi invitus*, "though unwilling").
- ***schedula*** — "the slip / note": a small sheet (the draft text Dançay enclosed) that he invites Tycho to amend; *una litura deleas* = "blot [it] out with a single stroke of the pen," the standard idiom for editorial deletion.
- ***magnum illud opus*** — "that great work": the building of Uraniborg, of which the cornerstone is the present concern.
- **Negation check.** The letter contains the conditional courtesy *si … negare non velis* ("if you will not refuse"), the modesty topos *tribuere non ausus sum* ("I have not dared to take upon myself"), and the closing *non falleris* ("you will not be deceived"); each negation is reproduced, none added or dropped. The *nisi te mandante, vel potius praescribente* ("except at your bidding, or rather your prescription") is an exceptive, not a negation, and is rendered as such.
- **Calendar / place.** *Haffniae 26. die Iunij Anno 1576* = "At **Copenhagen** (Hafnia), the 26th day of June, the year 1576" (O.S.; Denmark used the Julian calendar). The dateline agrees with the edition label.
- **MS witnesses.** Two copies in Vienna, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686 (item.7 = A; item.66 = B), as given in the source header; shelfmarks reproduced as supplied.

documents.incipit: GENEROSE et clarissime vir, amice perpetuo colende, cum hîc Holbecæ apud Dominum PACKIUM …

text.original:
GENEROSO ET VERE NOBILI VIRO TYCHONI BRAHE A KNUDSTORP, AMICO SUO SEMPER OBSERVANDO.

GENEROSE et clarissime vir, amice perpetuo colende, cum hîc Holbecæ apud Dominum PACKIUM essem, redditæ mihi sunt tuæ literæ. Tristia obmittam, cum corrigi non possint: lapis promissus paratus est, inscriptio addita, ut voluisti, cum me vocabis, mature adero, gratissimumque mihi feceris, si plures invitaveris! Ego idem quoque facturus sum, ne vulgaris hæc sit dedicatio. Utinam ille PRATENSIS viveret et nobis unâ adesse posset. Ego D. IOHANNI FRANCISCO nisi adfuerit, ominatus sum aliquid mali. Ille igitur volens (ut spero) vel metu aderit. Literas tuas hîc expecto, ubi iam iucundissime et suavissime vivo. Vale, Vir præstantissime, et DANZEUM tuum, ut incepisti, ama, credeque illum tibi esse deditissimum.

Vale et vale felicissime.
Holbecæ 14. Iulij A. 1576.
Tibi deditissimus Carolus Danzeus.
text.english:
**To the high-born and truly noble man Tycho Brahe of Knudstrup, his ever-to-be-honoured friend.**

High-born and most illustrious man, friend forever to be cherished: while I was here at Holbæk with Master Pack, your letter was delivered to me. The sad matters I shall pass over, since they cannot be put right. The promised stone is ready, the inscription added as you wished; when you summon me, I shall be there in good time, and you will do me a most welcome favour if you invite more people! I too shall do the same, so that this dedication may not be a common one. Would that the late Pratensis were living and could be present with us together. As for Master Iohannes Franciscus, unless he is present, I have foreboded some ill. He therefore — willingly (as I hope), or else out of fear — will attend. I await your letter here, where I am now living most agreeably and most pleasantly. Farewell, most excellent man, and love your Dançay, as you have begun [to do], and believe him to be most devoted to you.

Farewell, and most happily farewell.
At Holbæk, 14 July, the year 1576.
Most devoted to you,
Charles de Dançay.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Carolus Danzeus* = **Charles de Dançay** (c. 1510–1589), the long-serving French ambassador (resident) at the Danish court of Frederik II. A humanist and a steady patron-friend of Tycho's from the early 1570s; he was among the small circle invited to the ceremonies attending the founding of Uraniborg. The address-form *Tychoni Brahe a Knudstorp* ("Tycho Brahe of Knudstrup," the family seat in Scania) is the standard noble style; *Danzeum tuum* ("your Dançay") is the writer's affectionate self-reference, rendered in the third person as in the Latin.
- **Place / occasion.** *Holbecae apud Dominum Packium* — at **Holbæk** (the Zealand market town), staying *apud Dominum Packium*, "with Master Pack" — i.e. as the guest of a host surnamed **Pack/Packe** (the Latin genitive *Packii* gives a nominative *Packius*; the man is otherwise unidentified here and is left as named). The *lapis … inscriptio addita … dedicatio* ("the stone … the inscription added … this dedication") almost certainly concerns the **foundation/dedication stone of Uraniborg**, whose cornerstone was laid on Hven on 8 August 1576 (O.S.); Dançay reports the inscribed stone ready and pledges to attend the ceremony and to bring guests so that it "not be a common dedication." This reading is consistent with the date (mid-July 1576, weeks before the laying) but rests on the historical context rather than on any word in the letter; flagged accordingly. *(Tycho's own commemorative verses for the Uraniborg cornerstone survive; whether the *inscriptio* here is that text or a separate dedicatory inscription the letter does not say — left open.)*
- **Persons named.**
 - *Pratensis* = **Johannes Pratensis** (Hans Philipsen, 1543–1576), professor of medicine at Copenhagen and Tycho's close physician-friend. *Utinam ille Pratensis viveret* ("would that the late Pratensis were living") shows him already dead at the time of writing — Pratensis died in 1576 — so the wish is for a departed friend; *ille* + the past-counterfactual subjunctive carry the sense "the late," made explicit in brackets-free idiom here ("the late Pratensis") and noted.
 - *D. Iohannes Franciscus* = "Master Iohannes Franciscus" — an associate (Italian first-name form *Giovanni Francesco*) expected at the same gathering; not further identified in the letter and left as named. The clause *nisi adfuerit, ominatus sum aliquid mali … vel metu aderit* is playful: "unless he attends I have foreboded some ill [for him]; so he will attend, willingly or out of fear." The threat is jocular, not literal.
- **Negations (checked).** Two negative constructions: (1) *cum corrigi non possint* — "since they cannot be put right" (one *non*); (2) *ne vulgaris haec sit dedicatio* — the purpose-negative *ne*, "so that this dedication may not be a common one"; and the conditional *nisi adfuerit* — "unless he is present." Each is reproduced once; none added or dropped.
- **Epistolary formulae.** Heading *GENEROSO ET VERE NOBILI VIRO … AMICO SUO SEMPER OBSERVANDO* — the honorific superscription, rendered in full. Closing *Vale et vale felicissime* ("Farewell, and most happily farewell") and *Tibi deditissimus* ("Most devoted to you," parallel to Wolf's *E. Tuae studiosiss.*) by this chapter's convention
- **Calendar.** *Holbecae 14. Iulij A. 1576* = "At Holbæk, 14 July, the year 1576" (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The dateline agrees with the edition label (*1576. 14. juli. Holbaek*); no discrepancy. (The edition's note that MS witness B is also the witness for the 1571 Wolf letter, cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66, reflects shared-codex foliation, not a dating issue.)

documents.abstract: Thanks Tycho for the gift of his book on the New Star, congratulates him on safe return to his homeland, and expresses continued regard.
documents.incipit: BENEVOLENTIÆ tuæ erga me singularis, generose Domine, testimonium sunt non solum tui …

text.original:
NOBILITATE GENERIS, DOCTRINA ET VIRTUTE PRÆSTANTISSIMO DN. TYCHONI BRAHE OTTONIDI, DOMINO DE KNUDSTRUP, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO SUMMA OBSERVANTIA COLENDO. S.

BENEVOLENTIÆ tuæ erga me singularis, generose Domine, testimonium sunt non solum tui sermones suavissimi, quibus hîc liberaliter sum institutus, sed etiam liber tuus de Stella Nova editus, quem mihi dono mittere non dubitasti. Quare quamprimum eum a D. WOLFIO, Compatre meo charissimo, accepi, prima quacunque occasione oblata ad te gratitudinis ergo scribendum duxi, præsertim cum id meus in te amor et singularis observantia, qua te semper sum prosecutus, flagitaret, ne aut spacio temporis aut locorum intervallis diminuta esse videretur. Dominationi igitur tuæ primum de salvo atque incolumi in patriam reditu gratulor, eamque incolumitatem tibi perpetuam esse precor. Deinde pro libro tibi gratias, quas possum, maximas ago. Etsi autem ea non est mei ingenij facultas, ut parem gratiam referre possim, tamen affirmo, me omne meum studium, omnem meam observantiam cultum honorem denique tibi dicasse, meque tuarum maximarum virtutum, quas semper sum admiratus, memoriam perpetuo conservaturum esse. Porro te ignorare nolo, mi Domine TYCHO, SCHISLERUM γνωμονοποιὸν nostrum confecisse Globum ex cupro fabrefactum secundum omnes dimensiones perfectæ, veluti tuum Automaton, rotunditatis, cuius diameter quinquepedalis. Globus autem tali arte est fabrefactus, ut in 8 partes dissolvi et rursus in integrum restitui possit, necessitate exigente, quem in Hispaniam unâ cum Astrolabio quantitatis eiusdem per MARCUM FUGGERUM est misurus. Cum itaque viderem Globum, de tuis commodis cogitans quærebam, num etiam maiorem conficere posset? qui respondit ita, seque ad tale corpus conficiendum motum esse ex eo, quod audivisset D. tuam hîc artificem quæsivisse, qui id præstaret, seque posse æque conficere eiusmodi corpus, cuius diameter esset 8 vel 10 pedum, et ea arte, ut in 40 circiter partes resolutus facilime vasique inclusus, commodissime vel per mare vel per terras transportari possit. Cum autem ulterius quærerem, quantum cuperet pro tali corpore conficiendo, me ad D. tuam hac de re scripturum, respondit, non minus quam 1000 aureos, circulis exceptis et pede. Quare cum hîc Globum viderim ligneum, qui tamen propter ligni naturam suis ex æquo partibus non respondere videretur, hac de re certiorem facere volui, ut si forte eiusmodi corpus globosum D. tua habere cuperet, quod et ad durationem et perfectionem magis accederet, sciret, hîc esse Artificem, qui hoc se præstare posse diceret. Proinde si qua in re mea opera uti volueris, efficiam ut te nec sumptuum pœnitere queat, nec ego cura, opera et studio tibi defuisse videar, modo cum aliquo agas, qui artifici dimidium sumptuum tuo nomine exponat. In ceteris neque diligentia neque fide unquam deero.

Novi quod ad te scriberem non habebam, nisi forte scire velis, hoc ipso die post obitum PEUTINGERI in Duumvirum, quem nos vulgo Stadtpfleger nominamus, MARCUM FUGGERUM electum esse cum omnium civium admiratione.

Hisce vale feliciter, et me, quod facis, amare perge.
Augustæ Rheticæ postridie Cal. Augusti 1576.
D. T. deditissimus Iohan. Maior.
text.english:
**To the most excellent in nobility of birth, in learning, and in virtue, Master Tycho Brahe, son of Otte, Lord of Knudstrup, his lord and friend to be honoured with the utmost regard. Greeting.**

Tokens of your singular goodwill toward me, noble Lord, are not only your most delightful conversations, in which I was here generously instructed, but also your published book on the New Star, which you did not hesitate to send me as a gift. And so, as soon as I received it from Master Wolf, my dearest co-godfather, I judged that I should write to you to express my gratitude at whatever first occasion offered itself — especially since my love for you and the singular regard with which I have always attended you demanded it, lest [that regard] should seem to have been lessened either by length of time or by the distances of place. I therefore congratulate Your Lordship first of all on your safe and unharmed return to your homeland, and I pray that that safety may be perpetual for you. Next, for the book I give you the greatest thanks I can. And although it is not within the power of my talent to render an equal thanks, yet I affirm that I have dedicated to you all my zeal, all my regard, my devotion, and in short my honour, and that I shall preserve forever the memory of your very great virtues, which I have always admired. Furthermore, I would not have you ignorant, my Lord Tycho, that Schissler, our gnomon-maker [γνωμονοποιός], has completed a Globe fashioned out of copper, perfect in all its dimensions of roundness — like your own Automaton — whose diameter is five feet. And the Globe has been fashioned with such art that it can be taken apart into 8 pieces and again restored to a whole, as need requires; this he is about to send into Spain, together with an Astrolabe of the same size, by way of Marcus Fugger. And so, when I saw the Globe, thinking of your advantage, I asked whether he could also make a larger one. He answered yes, and [said] that he had been moved to make such a body from the fact that he had heard Your Lordship had sought here for a craftsman who might furnish it, and that he could equally make a body of the kind whose diameter would be 8 or 10 feet, and [made] with such art that, taken apart into about 40 pieces and easily packed in a chest, it might most conveniently be transported either by sea or by land. But when I asked further how much he would want for making such a body — [saying] that I would write to Your Lordship about this matter — he answered, not less than 1000 gold pieces, the circles and the foot [stand] excepted. And so, since I have seen here a wooden Globe which nevertheless, owing to the nature of wood, did not seem to correspond evenly in its parts, I wished to inform you of this matter, so that, if perhaps Your Lordship should wish to have a spherical body of this kind — one which would come nearer both to durability and to perfection — you might know that there is here a Craftsman who said he could furnish this. Accordingly, if in any matter you should wish to use my service, I shall see to it that you can neither regret the expense, nor [that] I shall seem to have failed you in care, effort, and zeal — provided you deal with someone who, in your name, lays out half the expense to the craftsman. In all else I shall never be wanting either in diligence or in fidelity.

News that I might write to you I had none, unless perhaps you should wish to know that on this very day, after the death of Peutinger, Marcus Fugger has been elected as Duumvir — whom we commonly call *Stadtpfleger* — to the admiration of all the citizens.

With these things, fare happily, and continue, as you do, to love me.
At Augsburg of the Rhaetians, the day after the Kalends of August [2 August] 1576.
Most devoted to Your Lordship, Johan Maior.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Iohan. Maior* = **Johannes Major** (Johann Mair), an Augsburg friend and regular correspondent of Tycho's from his Augsburg years; named alongside Hieronymus Wolf and the Hainzel brothers among Tycho's Augsburg circle (Christianson, *On Tycho's Island*). He signs himself *D. T. deditissimus* ("most devoted to Your Lordship").
- ***Ottonidi … Domino de Knudstrup*** — "son of Otte, Lord of Knudstrup": the Greek-style patronymic for **Otte Brahe** (Tycho's father) plus Tycho's principal Scanian seat, Knudstrup, kept as in.
- ***liber tuus de Stella Nova*** — Tycho's *De nova stella* (Copenhagen, 1573), his book on the 1572 supernova in Cassiopeia, here acknowledged as a presentation gift.
- ***D. Wolfio, Compatre meo*** — **Hieronymus Wolf** (1516–1580), the Augsburg humanist (cf. the 1571 Wolf→Brahe letter, same circle); *compater* is the spiritual-kinship tie "co-godfather" (godparent to the same child / fellow sponsor), rendered literally rather than reduced to "friend."
- **Greek.** *γνωμονοποιὸν* (gnōmonopoión, accusative of *γνωμονοποιός*) = "maker of gnomons / dials," here a learned epithet for the instrument-maker; transcribed as printed (final-sigma not normalised in the inflected form) and translated "gnomon-maker." *gnomon* is kept by this chapter's convention
- **Instrument-maker.** *Schislerum* = **Christoph(er) Schissler the elder** (active in Augsburg from 1546), the celebrated maker of fine astronomical and geometrical instruments. Scholarship notes that this very letter is the principal evidence on the question of who built the shell of Tycho's *Globus Magnus Orichalcicus*: Major reports Schissler *offering* to make Tycho a globe, which Mosley (*Bearing the Heavens*, citing TBOO VII, 36.5–26) reads as evidence that Schissler was *not* in fact the maker of Tycho's existing instrument. The letter is reported, not adjudicated, here.
- ***veluti tuum Automaton*** — "like your own Automaton": rendered literally. The referent is uncertain — most plausibly Tycho's own great globe / a mechanical celestial device of his — and is left unglossed rather than guessed.
- ***Globum … in 8 partes dissolvi … in 40 circiter partes resolutus … vasique inclusus*** — the demountable copper globe (5-foot diameter) dismantles into 8 parts; the proposed larger one (8–10-foot diameter) into about 40 parts, packable in a chest for transport by sea or land.
- ***Marcum Fuggerum*** — **Marcus Fugger** (1529–1597), of the Augsburg banking dynasty; the shipping agent for the Spain consignment and, per the closing news, newly elected *Duumvir* / *Stadtpfleger* (city magistrate) of Augsburg.
- ***Peutingeri*** — the **Peutinger** whose death created the vacancy Fugger filled; of the prominent Augsburg Peutinger family (the antiquary Konrad Peutinger's descendants). *Stadtpfleger* (the German civic title) is kept and glossed by Major's own Latin equivalent *Duumvir*.
- ***1000 aureos, circulis exceptis et pede*** — "1000 gold pieces, the circles and the foot excepted": the price quoted excludes the mounted graduated circles (*circuli*) and the stand/base (*pes*). *aurei* rendered "gold pieces" (gold coins, likely gulden/florins) rather than over-specified.
- ***Astrolabio quantitatis eiusdem*** — "an Astrolabe of the same size," i.e. matching the 5-foot globe, the pair destined for Spain.
- ***modo cum aliquo agas, qui artifici dimidium sumptuum tuo nomine exponat*** — the one conditional clause: Major's offer of service is conditioned on Tycho's dealing through an agent who will advance the craftsman half the cost in Tycho's name. Rendered as a single positive proviso (one *modo*-clause, no negation).
- **Dateline / calendar.** *Augustae Rheticae postridie Cal. Augusti 1576* = "at **Augsburg** [*Augusta Rhaetica*], the day after the Kalends of August, 1576" (O.S.). *postridie Kalendas Augusti* = the day after 1 August = **2 August**; this agrees with the edition label ("2. august"). **Dating crux flagged:** Mosley cites the letter as "**1 August 1576**" (*Bearing the Heavens*), i.e. the Kalends itself; the discrepancy is the standard ambiguity over whether *postridie Cal.* is reckoned as 1 or 2 August. The Roman idiom is reproduced and glossed to 2 August per the literal reading; the date is **not** silently reconciled to Mosley's 1 August.
- **MS witness.** The edition gives the witness as Vienna, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66 — the identical shelfmark recorded for the 1571 Wolf→Brahe letter; this may be a edition carry-over rather than a verified folio for this letter. Recorded as given, not relied on.

documents.abstract: Recalls their meeting at Regensburg and expresses grief at their swift parting, explaining the long delay in writing by lawsuits and pressing occupations.
documents.incipit: CUM disiungerer a te Ratisbonae hyeme praeterita, nobilissime D. TYCHO, non minus …

text.original:
THADDÆUS HAGECIUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE. S.

CUM disiungerer a te Ratisbonae hyeme praeterita, nobilissime D. TYCHO, non minus moeroris reliquit ea disiunctio nostri quam tuus laetitiae adventus attulerat. Nam postquam te ex primo congressu mutuoque nostro colloquio cognovi, ita eram studio tui propter tuas eximias ingenij dotes et maximas virtutes incensus, ut tum demum conquiescerem animo, cum tecum essem. Itaque tam citam a nobis disiunctionem, quae me dulcissimo fructu iucundissimae conversationis nostrae privavit, non potui non dolere et conturbatiore animo ferre, neque illi ullum aliud levamen afferre potui, quam amorem et cogitationem tui, ut cum corpore tecum esse non liceret, saltem animo amantissimo tecum essem. Ac talem meum animum erga te iamdudum declarassem mea epistola, nisi toto hoc praeterito tempore multis hisque maximis fuissem districtus occupationibus, praesertim vero forensi quadam lite, cuius causa etiamnunc hîc me commorari diutius quam vellem oportet. Illa negotia, mi TYCHO, adeo me perturbarunt, ut hactenus neque in studijs nobis communibus, neque in his quae mecum liberalissimo animo communicasti, quicquam facere potuerim. Sed dabit Deus his molestijs quoque finem. Noster PIRCKMANNUS Ratisponâ domum reversus, re communicata cum fratre suo de opere TRAPEZUNTIJ imprimendo, quod Basiliensibus Typographis ipsomet consultore, ut scis, daturus eram, studiose a me fratris nomine binis literis petijt, ut sibi imprimendum concederem. Ego qui prae ceteris ipsi gratificari cupiebam, proxima Quadragesima misi opus illud. Nunc tantopere expetitum plane negligere videtur. Nuper enim scripsit ad me fratrem suum cum PLANTINO de impressione agere velle, putare etiam quosdam, antea in Italia fuisse evulgatum hunc librum. Hinc videtur extinctum esse desiderium excudendi operis. Ego vero impressum antea fuisse non existimo. Nusquam enim exstant exempla etiam in Bibliothecis clarorum virorum. GESNERUS quoque in sua Bibliotheca mentionem faciens operum TRAPEZUNTIJ et pro more suo loca, ubi singula impressa sunt indicans, huius nostri operis meminit quidem, sed non ait aliquando fuisse impressum. Utut sit, ego doleo quod librum non habeam in meis manibus et quod vagetur incertis sedibus. Utinam saltem integer redeat ad me, non facile deinceps exibit et custodietur arctius. De nostra stella an aliquid annotaveris, scire aveo. Ego meam responsionem contra RAYMUNDUM hyeme praeterita miseram imprimendam Francofurtum WECHELO, ut prodiret ad ferias Paschatis. Is vero cum primo spem fecisset, tandem nimis sero se excusavit imprimere non posse. Quoniam autem ea responsio iam antea fuit in multorum manibus, quibus legendam et iudicandam dederam, omnesque evulgationem eius expectabant exoptabantque, maturare editionem oportuit. Itaque curavi illam Pragae excudi. Eius exemplum tibi mitto, rogoque ut eam legas, et quae tibi in ea displicuerint, in ijs me libere moneas et coarguas. Si quid praeterea habueris ex tuis observatis distantijs stellarum, aut quidpiam aliud, mecum communicare ne graveris rogo. De HEMMINGIO vestro et statu Ecclesiarum vestrarum aliquid etiam adijcies. Tuo Achati quem tecum adduxeras Augustâ, si adhuc tecum est, adscribo salutem.

Bene vale.
Pragae 23. Augusti 1576.
T. ex animo THADDÆUS.
text.english:
**Thaddaeus Hagecius to Tycho Brahe — greeting.**

When I was parted from you at Regensburg last winter, most noble Master Tycho, that parting left no less of grief in me than your coming had brought of joy. For after I came to know you from our first meeting and mutual conversation, I was so kindled with devotion to you, on account of your outstanding gifts of mind and your very great virtues, that I found rest in my spirit only then, when I was with you. And so I could not but grieve at so swift a parting from us — one that robbed me of the sweetest fruit of our most delightful conversation — and bear it with a more troubled mind; nor could I bring to it any other relief than my love and the thought of you, so that, since I was not permitted to be with you in body, I might at least be with you in a most loving mind. And I would long since have declared such a disposition of mine toward you by a letter of mine, had I not, throughout all this past time, been distracted by many and very great occupations, and especially by a certain lawsuit, on whose account I am even now obliged to linger here longer than I would wish. Those affairs, my Tycho, have so disturbed me that until now I have been able to accomplish nothing, neither in the studies common to us, nor in those matters which you shared with me in your most generous spirit. But God will grant an end to these troubles too. Our friend Pirckmann, having returned home from Regensburg, after the matter had been discussed with his brother concerning the printing of the work of Trapezuntius — which, as you know, I was myself, as adviser, going to give over to the printers of Basel — earnestly asked of me by two letters, in his brother's name, that I would grant it to him to be printed. I, who desired to oblige him before others, sent that work this past Lent. Now, though it was so greatly sought after, he seems plainly to neglect it. For he recently wrote to me that his brother wishes to treat with Plantin about the printing; and that some men even think this book was previously published in Italy. Hence the desire to print the work seems to have been extinguished. I, for my part, do not judge it to have been printed before. For nowhere do copies survive, even in the libraries of famous men. Gesner too, in his *Bibliotheca*, when making mention of the works of Trapezuntius and indicating, after his custom, the places where each was printed, does indeed recall this work of ours, but does not say that it was ever printed. However that may be, I grieve that I do not have the book in my own hands and that it wanders about in uncertain abodes. Would that it might at least return to me whole; thereafter it will not easily go out, and will be guarded more closely. I am eager to know whether you have noted down anything about our star. As for me, I had sent my reply against Raymundus last winter to be printed at Frankfurt by Wechel, so that it might come out at the Easter fair. But he, although at first he gave me hope, at last — far too late — excused himself, [saying] that he could not print it. But since that reply had already before been in the hands of many, to whom I had given it to be read and judged, and all were awaiting and longing for its publication, it was necessary to hasten the edition. And so I had it printed at Prague. I send you a copy of it, and I ask that you read it and, in whatever in it has displeased you, freely admonish and correct me. If besides this you have anything from your observed distances of the stars, or anything else, I ask you not to find it burdensome to share it with me. About your friend Hemmingius and the state of your churches you will add something too. To your Achates, whom you had brought with you from Augsburg, if he is still with you, I add my greeting.

Fare you well.
Prague, 23 August 1576.
Yours from the heart, Thaddaeus.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus Hagecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayek, 1525–1600), the imperial physician and astronomer at Prague, author of the *Dialexis de novae … stellae … apparitione* (Frankfurt, 1574) on the 1572 nova. He and Tycho had met at the Imperial Diet of **Regensburg** in the winter of 1575 (here *hyeme praeterita*, "last winter"), where the imperial coronation of Rudolf II took place; the meeting began their long correspondence and friendship.
- **Recipient.** *Tycho Brahe* — addressed as *nobilissime D. TYCHO*, "most noble Master Tycho." The edition header repeats "Tycho Brahe Tycho Brahe"; only one recipient is meant.
- ***Ratisbona*** = **Regensburg** (where the two had met); *Ratisponâ* (ablative) "from Regensburg." *Augusta* = **Augsburg**. *Francofurtum* = **Frankfurt** (am Main), site of the great book fair (*ferias Paschatis*, "the Easter fair").
- ***opus TRAPEZUNTIJ*** — a work of **George of Trebizond** (Georgius Trapezuntius, 1395–1486), the Byzantine-Italian humanist. Hagecius held a manuscript of an unpublished Trapezuntius work which he was trying to see into print; the whole middle passage concerns the frustrated negotiations over it (Basel printers → the Pirckmann brothers → Plantin).
- ***PIRCKMANNUS*** — **Pirckmann** (Pirckheimer/Pirckmann), the agent at Regensburg acting with his brother over the printing; not securely identified beyond the letter. Left in the period form. *fratre suo* = "his brother."
- ***PLANTINUS*** = **Christophe Plantin** (c. 1520–1589), the great Antwerp printer.
- ***GESNERUS … in sua Bibliotheca*** = **Conrad Gessner** (1516–1565) and his *Bibliotheca universalis* (Zurich, 1545), the standard bibliographical reference; Hagecius cites it as evidence that the Trapezuntius work was never printed. *Bibliotheca* here = the *bibliography/catalogue of authors*, not a physical library; rendered as the title *Bibliotheca*.
- ***nostra stella*** — "our star," i.e. the **new star (nova) of 1572** in Cassiopeia, the shared subject of Hagecius's and Tycho's work; *De nostra stella an aliquid annotaveris* asks whether Tycho has recorded fresh observations of it.
- ***responsionem contra RAYMUNDUM*** — Hagecius's **reply against "Raymundus"** = **Annibale Raimondo of Verona**, who had argued the 1572 nova was a sublunary (atmospheric) phenomenon; Hagecius's rebuttal is the *Responsio ad virulentum … scriptum … Hannibalis Raymundi* (Prague, 1576), which he here says he has just had printed at Prague (after Wechel at Frankfurt declined) and encloses for Tycho. Tycho too criticized Raimondo on the nova. Period form *RAYMUNDUM* kept in translation as "Raymundus."
- ***WECHELO*** = the Frankfurt printing house of **Wechel** (André/Andreas Wechel, d. 1581); dative *Wechelo* "to Wechel."
- ***HEMMINGIO vestro … Ecclesiarum vestrarum*** — *Hemmingius* = **Niels Hemmingsen** (1513–1600), the leading Danish Lutheran theologian at Copenhagen, then under suspicion of crypto-Calvinism; *vestro / vestrarum* ("your," plural) marks him and the Danish churches as belonging to Tycho's national sphere. Period form kept as "Hemmingius."
- ***Tuo Achati*** — "your **Achates**": a classical allusion (*fidus Achates*, the faithful companion of Aeneas, *Aeneid*) for the trusted assistant/companion whom Tycho had brought from Augsburg; Hagecius does not name him and neither does the translation. Kept as the allusive "Achates."
- ***forensi … lite*** — "a certain lawsuit / forensic suit" detaining Hagecius at Prague. *commorari … diutius quam vellem*: "to linger longer than I would wish" — the hedge ("than I would wish") preserved.
- ***incertis sedibus*** — "in uncertain abodes," of the wandering Trapezuntius manuscript; the personifying metaphor (*vagetur*, "wanders") kept.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S.* = *salutem* (dicit), "greeting". *Bene vale* = "Fare you well." *T. ex animo* (subscription) = "Yours from the heart" (*Tuus ex animo*).
- **Calendar / place.** *Pragae 23. Augusti 1576* = "Prague, 23 August 1576." A Catholic correspondent in Imperial service, but the dateline is given plainly without a style mark; in 1576 (pre-1582) Old and New Style coincide, so no O.S./N.S. divergence arises. Marked [O.S.] in the header by project convention for a pre-Gregorian Julian date; not silently converted.
- ***Quadragesima*** = **Lent** ("this past Lent," *proxima Quadragesima*), here a season-dating of when he sent the work.
- **Catalogue note.** The edition label ("1576. 23. august") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy.
- **Correction.** Latin corrected from 'ipsemet' to 'ipsomet' (ablative, agreeing with 'consultore'), per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII p.37.

T. ex animo THADDAEUS.') is fully present on printed pages 37-38, immediately followed on page 38 by the next letter's heading (Petrus Severini to Tycho) and page 39 belongs entirely to a different letter (Tycho to Petrus Severini, 3 Sept 1576) — confirming the letter is complete and not truncated, so reading beyond page 4 was unnecessary. documents.abstract: Responds to two long-unanswered letters, mourning the death of Pratensis and acknowledging Severinus's account of his personal difficulties.
documents.incipit: BINAS a te charissime D. D. PETRE recepi literas, quibus interea nihil a me responsum …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET DOCTISSIMO VIRO DOCTORI PETRO SEVERINI, MEDICO REGIO, PHILOSOPHO EXIMIO, SUO AMICO. S.

BINAS a te charissime D. D. PETRE recepi literas, quibus interea nihil a me responsum est, non quod amicitiæ et officii immemor essem, sed quod multis negotiis et amicorum visitationibus interea (ut fit) distractus fuerim. In prioribus communis nostri fratris et amici immortali memoria dignissimi PRATENSIS casum et immaturum inexpectatumque a nobis discessum merito deploras. In posterioribus vero proprias, quibus conflictaris in vitæ cursu, difficultates doles.

Etsi vero PRATENSIS nostri abitus potius, quam obitus ab omnibus merito doleatur, utpote qui ob multarum scientiarum excellentem peritiam, vitæque et morum incomparabilem suavitatem, in omnium animis perpetuum sui desiderium reliquerit; tamen cum nos divinis oraculis et philosophia aliquatenus imbuti, statuamus eos, qui corpoream et visibilem hanc mundi formam, urgentibus fatis, reliquerunt, ad beatioris mundi incolas migrare et tanto beatius deinde vivere, quanto infinita felicitas finitam miseriam exsuperat; o Horizontum temporis et æternitatis imperscrutabile discrimen; cumque is, qui hinc discessit, non decessit PRATENSIS, fuerit et divina et humana Philosophia ita edoctus, ut in eius, per quem omnes misericordiam meremur, pia invocatione et officij sui in hac mortali vita fideli vocatione, in æternitatem migraverit, et dum fata sinebant, vitam hanc mortalem bene et laudabiliter transegerit; idcirco non dubitamus cum eo longe melius nunc actum esse, quam nobiscum, qui inter tot errorum et fluctuationum procellas misera spe, quod reliquum est in corpore vitæ, fovemus. Unde non est quod tam ipsius casum doleamus, quam proprium, quod tanto viro, tam præclaris animi dotibus ornato, tamque sincero et fido amico orbati simus. Verum cum et nos frustra hoc faciamus, utpote qui nullo luctu nullis lacrymis exoptatissimum amicum in hanc vitam revocare possimus, nostroque desiderio nulla ratione succurri possit, patienter feramus id, quod inexorabile fatum nulla impatientia mutari permittit. Unum restat, quo amici defuncti exuvias ornare possumus, nempe ut Epitaphium illi dignum confici curemus, quo eius memoria, alias quidem immortalis, sed pro civili et politica consuetudine ad posteros et eos, qui ipsum in vivis non norunt, conservari possit; huius, quantum ad sumtus attinet, ego eorum particeps ero, tu de inscriptione cogita. Id autem imprimis fieri oportet, ne, si diu differatur, in perpetuam (ut fit) oblivionem abeat. Dies enim diei memoriam delet.

Quantum vero ad posteriores tuas literas attinet, magis est quod nostram in hac vita sortem deploremus; quod tot assidue, dum hîc peregrinamur, itinerum difficultatibus et asperitatibus impediamur. Tu, dum necessaria Philosophiæ adminicula sectaris, libertatem Philosophicam in Aula aliquamdiu si non plane amittis, saltem in exilium abigis, unde eam revocare, ingentis, ut experiris, est difficultatis. Aula enim quosvis blando et benevolo vultu recipit, sed protervo et invito dimittit. Verum patientia, taciturnitate et consilio multæ difficultates tandem exsuperantur, tempore etiam aliam atque aliam fortunæ mutationem inducente. Sed danda est opera, ne, dum ab his fluctibus et tempestatibus evadere conamur, in novos impingamus et Charybdin evitantes in Scyllam devolvamur. Invia enim est inter tot scopulos, procellas et voragines ad Philosophiam via. Verum si cui auxilio Supremi portum attingere datur, is poterit magnum alterius spectare laborem, non quia vexari quenquam est iucunda voluptas, sed quibus ipse malis careas quia cernere suave est.

Petis insuper a me, charissime D. D. PETRE, ut hypotheseos COPERNICI in triplici motu Terræ explicationem tecum communicem; qua is solerti ingenio per solam Terram, tum primi mobilis rapidissimum motum, tum octavæ sphæræ inæqualem tarditatem, ipsius denique Solis annuum cursum salvari posse demonstravit. Primus est, quo Terra circa axem sui Æquatoris versus ortum spatio 24 horarum convolvi imaginatur, eaque ratione rapidissima illa primi mobilis circumgyratio, qua omnes secum inferiores sphæras in occasum convolvere a veteribus statuebatur, penitus excluditur. Alter motus est, quo centrum Terræ interea annuum cursum, quem veteres Soli attribuebant, absolvit, eaque via Eclipticæ ductum ijs in locis, ubi hi Solem locabant, designat. Tertius vero est, quo axem Æquatoris Terræ ad planum Eclipticæ, quod centrum ipsius (ut dixi) describit, variabilem et annuo hinc motu revertentem inclinationem habere oportet; alias enim apparentes Solis ab Æquatore declinationes, dierumque incrementa et decrementa cum umbrarum discriminibus hypothesi huic non congruerent. Sed et in hoc tertio motu mirabili industria per binos circellos circa axem Æquatoris Terræ descriptos, salvat inæqualitatem motus fixarum ideo nobis apparentem, quod Æquator Terræ inæqualiter in antecedentia promoveatur, alteramque Æquatoris mobilitatem, qua ad Eclipticam accedit et recedit, eodem artificio excusat. Verum hæc omnia, ut sunt ingeniose a solertissimo illo Artifice excogitata; ita, nisi machina talis extruatur, in qua oculariter demonstrentur, difficulter intelligi possunt. Id vero et plura alia, Deo conatus nostros adiuvante, aliquando facturus sum, ubi vulgi strepitu semoto mihi Philosophica quiete frui licuerit, et in ijs, quæ in motibus adhuc desiderantur, tunc diligentiorem trutinam adhibebo. Tu interim da operam, ut libertatem pristinam recuperare possis et tandem animum ad continuandum Philosophiæ studium componere, ni mavis sequi viam universæ carnis, cumque alijs reliquos frustrare inglorius annos. Vale et saluta magnificum Dominum Decanum meo nomine officiosissime.

Iterum terque quaterque vale.
Datæ Knudsdorp die 3. Septembris Anno 1576.
Spero me brevi vobis Haffniæ affuturum.
Tuus
Tycho Brahe.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and most learned man, Doctor Peter Severinus, royal physician, distinguished philosopher, his friend — greeting.**

I have received two letters from you, dearest Master Doctor Peter, to which meanwhile nothing has been answered by me — not because I was forgetful of friendship and duty, but because in the interval I was (as happens) drawn off by many affairs and by the visits of friends. In the earlier one you rightly lament the fall of Pratensis, our common brother and friend, most worthy of undying remembrance, and his untimely and unexpected departure from us. In the later one, however, you grieve over the difficulties of your own, with which you struggle in the course of your life.

But although the going-away rather than the death of our Pratensis is rightly mourned by all — inasmuch as, by reason of his excellent skill in many sciences and the incomparable sweetness of his life and character, he has left in the hearts of all a perpetual longing for himself — yet since we, imbued to some degree with the divine oracles and with philosophy, hold that those who, the fates pressing, have left this bodily and visible form of the world pass over to the inhabitants of a more blessed world and thereafter live the more blessedly, by as much as infinite felicity surpasses finite misery — O the inscrutable boundary of the horizons of time and of eternity! — and since he who departed hence, [yet] did not pass away, Pratensis, was so instructed in both divine and human philosophy that he passed into eternity in the devout invocation of Him through whom we all merit mercy, and in the faithful calling of his office in this mortal life, and, while the fates allowed, conducted this mortal life well and laudably: therefore we do not doubt that it now goes far better with him than with us, who amid so many storms of error and wavering cherish, with wretched hope, what remains of life in the body. Hence it is not so much his fall that we should grieve over as our own — that we have been bereft of so great a man, adorned with such illustrious gifts of mind, and so sincere and faithful a friend. But since we too do this in vain — inasmuch as by no mourning, by no tears, can we call back into this life a most longed-for friend, and our longing can be relieved by no means — let us patiently bear that which inexorable fate permits to be changed by no impatience. One thing remains, by which we can adorn the remains of our deceased friend: namely, that we see to it that a worthy epitaph be made for him, by which his memory — undying indeed in other respects, but, in accordance with civil and political custom, [to be preserved] for posterity and for those who did not know him among the living — may be preserved. Of this, so far as concerns the expense, I shall be a sharer in their part; do you give thought to the inscription. And this above all must be done, lest, if it be long deferred, it pass (as happens) into perpetual oblivion. For day deletes the memory of day.

As for your later letter, there is the more reason for us to deplore our lot in this life: that, while we sojourn here, we are so constantly hindered by the difficulties and harshnesses of [so many] journeys. You, while you pursue the necessary supports of philosophy, lose your philosophical liberty at Court for a time — if not wholly lose it, at least drive it into exile, whence to recall it is, as you find, of immense difficulty. For the Court receives anyone with a bland and benevolent face, but dismisses him insolent and unwilling. Yet by patience, silence, and counsel many difficulties are at length overcome, time too bringing on one change of fortune after another. But care must be taken lest, while we try to escape from these waves and tempests, we strike upon new ones, and, avoiding Charybdis, we tumble into Scylla. For the way to philosophy, amid so many rocks, storms, and gulfs, is hard to travel. Yet if it be granted to anyone, by the help of the Most High, to reach harbour, he will be able to look upon another's great toil — not because to see anyone harassed is a pleasant delight, but because it is sweet to discern from what ills you yourself are free.

You ask of me besides, dearest Master Doctor Peter, that I share with you the explanation of Copernicus's hypothesis in the threefold motion of the Earth, by which he, with skilful ingenuity, demonstrated that through the Earth alone could be saved both the most rapid motion of the *primum mobile*, and the unequal slowness of the eighth sphere, and finally the annual course of the Sun itself. The first is that by which the Earth is imagined to be revolved about the axis of its equator toward the east in the space of 24 hours; and by this means that most rapid whirling of the *primum mobile* — by which the ancients held that it carried all the lower spheres with it round to the west — is wholly excluded. The second motion is that by which the centre of the Earth meanwhile completes the annual course which the ancients attributed to the Sun, and by this path marks out the tracing of the ecliptic in those places where they located the Sun. The third, however, is that by which the axis of the Earth's equator must have, with respect to the plane of the ecliptic which its centre (as I said) describes, a variable inclination, returning by an annual motion from this [variation]; for otherwise the apparent declinations of the Sun from the equator, and the increases and decreases of the days together with the differences of the shadows, would not agree with this hypothesis. And in this third motion too, by marvellous industry, by means of two little circles described about the axis of the Earth's equator, he saves the inequality of the motion of the fixed stars that appears to us for this reason — that the Earth's equator is advanced unequally into the preceding [signs] — and by the same artifice he accounts for the other mobility of the equator, by which it approaches and recedes from the ecliptic. But all these things, ingeniously as they have been devised by that most skilful Artificer, can nevertheless hardly be understood unless such a machine be built up in which they may be demonstrated to the eye. This indeed, and many other things, I shall, with God aiding our endeavours, do at some time, when, the din of the crowd set aside, it shall be permitted me to enjoy philosophical quiet; and then I shall apply a more diligent scrutiny to those things which are still wanting in the motions. Do you meanwhile take pains that you may recover your former liberty, and at length settle your mind to continuing the study of philosophy — unless you prefer to follow the way of all flesh, and, along with others, to waste your remaining years inglorious. Farewell, and greet the magnificent Lord Dean in my name most dutifully.

Again, and a third and a fourth time, farewell.
Given at Knudstrup, 3 September, the year 1576.
I hope to be with you shortly at Copenhagen.
Yours,
Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), writing from **Knudstrup** (*Knudsdorp* in the source; Knutstorp, the Brahe family seat in Scania) in September 1576 — months after Frederik II's 23 May 1576 grant of Hven, and just before Tycho settled there. The closing "I hope to be with you shortly at Copenhagen" reflects this transitional moment.
- **Recipient.** *Petrus Severinus / Petro Severini* = **Peder Sørensen** (Petrus Severinus, 1540/42–1602), the Danish Paracelsian physician and author of *Idea medicinae philosophicae* (1571), at this date **royal physician** (*medicus regius*) to Frederik II. The salutation's *philosopho eximio* marks his standing as a natural philosopher, not merely a court doctor.
- **Person — Pratensis.** *Pratensis* = **Johannes Pratensis** (Hans Philipsen, 1543–1576), professor of medicine at Copenhagen and the intimate friend of both Tycho and Severinus, who had died suddenly (his death is dated to 1576; the works consulted confirm Tycho's *Epitaphium D. Joh. Pratensi* was printed at Uraniborg, 1584). The whole consolatory first half turns on him. **Wordplay flagged:** *abitus potius, quam obitus* ("a going-away rather than a death") and *qui hinc discessit, non decessit* ("who departed hence, [yet] did not pass away") are deliberate sound-figures contrasting *abitus/obitus* and *discessit/decessit*; the English keeps the antithesis but cannot reproduce the Latin assonance.
- **Person — *magnificum Dominum Decanum*.** "the magnificent Lord Dean" — an unnamed dean (likely the dean of the Copenhagen medical faculty or a cathedral dignitary) whom Severinus is asked to greet; not further identifiable from the text, so left unidentified rather than guessed.
- **Place.** *Haffnia* = **Copenhagen**; *Knudsdorp* = **Knudstrup / Knutstorp** (kept as in).
- **The Copernican passage (technical core).** Tycho gives a careful exposition of the **threefold motion of the Earth** in Copernicus's hypothesis: (1) the **diurnal rotation** about the axis of the equator, eastward, in 24 hours, which removes (*penitus excluditur*) the *primum mobile*'s westward whirl; (2) the **annual revolution** of the Earth's centre, reproducing the Sun's apparent annual course along the **ecliptic** (*Ecliptica*); (3) the **third (declination/precession) motion**, the conical motion of the equatorial axis relative to the ecliptic plane, which Copernicus modelled with *binos circellos* ("two little circles") to save both the unequal precession of the fixed stars (*motus fixarum … in antecedentia*, motion into the preceding signs) and the variation in the obliquity (*qua ad Eclipticam accedit et recedit*). Controlled-glossary renderings used: *declinatio* → **declination**, *primum mobile* kept as a technical term, *Ecliptica* → **ecliptic**, *sphaera* → **sphere**, *motus* → **motion**. **Note on Tycho's stance:** this is an expository, admiring account of Copernicus ("that most skilful Artificer") written *before* Tycho's own geo-heliocentric system; he calls for a physical *machina* (a model/orrery built up so the motions can be "demonstrated to the eye") and reserves judgement on "those things which are still wanting in the motions" (*quae in motibus adhuc desiderantur*) — his hedge is preserved, not sharpened into a critique he does not yet make.
- **Classical allusions.** *Charybdin evitantes in Scyllam devolvamur* — the Scylla-and-Charybdis topos (cf. the same image in Wolf's 1571 letter). The closing sententia *quibus ipse malis careas quia cernere suave est* renders **Lucretius**, *De rerum natura* II.1–4 (*Suave, mari magno … alterius spectare laborem*); Tycho adapts the Epicurean lines, and the rendering keeps them as the moral aphorism Tycho intends, with the source flagged here rather than smoothed away. *Viam universae carnis* ("the way of all flesh") is a Scriptural turn (cf. Joshua 23:14 / 1 Kings 2:2).
- **Sententiae kept.** *Dies enim diei memoriam delet* — "For day deletes the memory of day," kept as the free-standing maxim it is. *Iterum terque quaterque vale* — "Again, and a third and a fourth time, farewell" (the *terque quaterque* echoes Virgil, *Aeneid* I.94); rendered as the intensified valediction, distinct from a plain *Vale*.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S.* = *salutem* → "greeting"; *D. D. PETRE* = *Domine Doctor Petre* → "Master Doctor Peter"; *Vale … Iterum … vale* → "Farewell … Again … farewell". The doubled subscription (*Tuus / Tycho Brahe*) and the postscript-style line about Copenhagen are kept in their source order.
- **Calendar.** *Datae Knudsdorp die 3. Septembris Anno 1576* = "Given at Knudstrup, 3 September 1576" (**O.S.**; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The dateline matches the catalogue label (*1576. 3. september. Knutstorp*); no date discrepancy.
- **Edition note.** The source's edition field gives the **Dänische Bibliothek** (the 18th-century Copenhagen/Leipzig periodical of Danish-historical documents), the early printing recorded for this letter; it is also edited in **Dreyer**, *Opera Omnia* VII (*Epistolae*). The sole MS witness given is **A = Odense, Karen Brahes bibliotek, 298 (857 b)**.

documents.abstract: Asks Tycho to intercede with the King or court friends on behalf of a Scottish soldier owed outstanding pay from the Danish-Swedish war.
documents.incipit: GENEROSE et clarissime vir, Scotus hîc quidam in hoc postremo bello Danico et Suetico …

text.original:
NOBILI ET GENEROSO VIRO, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE OTTONIDI A KNUDSTORP, AMICO SUO SEMPER OBSERVANDO.

GENEROSE et clarissime vir, Scotus hîc quidam in hoc postremo bello Danico et Suetico stipendia sub Capitaneo IOHANNE CLARICO Scoto meruit, et parum, uti opinor, illi restat, ipsi etiam serenissimo Regi aut quaestoribus eius incognitum et memoria elapsum. Quod si tu hunc afflictum tua gratia et favore apud Regem aut per aulicos amicos iuvare possis, obnixe te oro, ut id facias. Et hoc etiam tibi persuadeas, quod tibi hac de re nec scripsissem, nec molestus fuissem, si literae, quas tibi BUCHANANUS, serenissimi Scotorum regis Praeceptor, nunc scribit, ad id me non impulissent; cuius preces magnum apud te pondus habituras esse spero, cum ille Poëta sit doctissimus, et Theologus minime seditiosus, nec Reipublicae perturbator, nec etiam ARISTOTELI nimium addictus, quo etiam quidam Theologiam profitentes abutuntur. Scotus ille responsum hîc a te expectabit, et literas ad aulicos amicos, ut negotia isthic tutius et facilius expedire possit. Postea si voles, BUCHANANO rescribas. De Astronomicis quibusdam libenter te audiam disserentem, ubi simul affuerimus. Nam Theorias Planetarum revolvere, et faciliori a te excogitata Methodo discere plurimum aveo. Astrologica, quibus tu moderate uteris, nec nimium (quod laudo) ijs tribuis, non valde vitupero quidem, sed neque admodum suspicio, ut multi alias solent, siquidem a Domino CALVINO olim in his absterritus sum, cum Argentinae simul essemus, quando istis vaticinijs admodum addictus fuissem. Habent enim nescio quid, quod hominem trahit ad se, ut ijs nimium adhaereat et fidat. Is enim, cum vidisset, me eo credulitatis in hisce praedictionibus pervenisse, ut de adulterijs etiam mulierum hinc nonnulla, quae, ut fatear quod verum est, raro falsos habuerint eventus, praedicere me posse iactarem, pro sua autoritate et gravi iudicio me increpavit, et male mihi minatus est, si ista non relinquerem. Quare cum eum suspicerem, atque in pretio haberem, mecumque STURMIUS plurimum illis tribueret, non ausus sum talia ulterius serio attingere. Astronomica tamen semper plurimi aestimavi, atque uti merentur, magnifeci, et etiamnum magnifacio. Quare in ijs aliqua etiam hac invalescente aetate de praeceptore discere plurimum desidero, quod et te mihi non denegaturum spero.

Vale, Vir integerrime, et me, quod plura non scribam, excusatum habe, Uraniamque tuam meis verbis reverenter saluta.
Haffniae 17. die Novembris Anno 1576.
Tibi deditissimus
Carolus Danzeus.
text.english:
**To the noble and well-born gentleman, Master Tycho Brahe, son of Otte, of Knudstrup, his friend ever to be esteemed.**

Well-born and most distinguished sir, a certain Scot here served for pay, in this last Danish and Swedish war, under Captain John Clark, a Scot, and there remains owing to him, as I think, but little, [a matter] unknown even to his most serene Majesty himself or to his treasurers, and slipped from memory. If you can help this afflicted man by your goodwill and favour with the King, or through friends at court, I earnestly beg you to do so. And let yourself be persuaded of this too: that I should neither have written to you on this matter nor have troubled you, had not the letter which Buchanan, the tutor of the most serene King of the Scots, is now writing to you, driven me to it; whose entreaties I hope will carry great weight with you, since he is a most learned poet, and a theologian by no means seditious, no disturber of the commonwealth, nor yet too much addicted to Aristotle — whom certain professors of theology also abuse. That Scot will await here a reply from you, and letters to friends at court, so that he may dispatch his affairs there more safely and easily. Afterwards, if you wish, you may write back to Buchanan. On certain matters astronomical I shall gladly hear you discourse, when we are together. For I greatly long to turn over the theories of the planets, and to learn [them] by an easier method devised by you. As for astrological matters — which you use in moderation, and to which you do not (a thing I praise) attribute too much — I do not greatly disparage them, to be sure, but neither do I altogether look up to them, as many on other occasions are wont to do; since I was once frightened off these things by Master Calvin, when we were together at Strasbourg, at a time when I had been quite addicted to those prognostications. For they have some I-know-not-what that draws a man to them, so that he clings to them and trusts them too much. For he [Calvin], when he had seen that I had come to such a pitch of credulity in these predictions that I would even boast that I could foretell from them some things, indeed, concerning the adulteries of women — which, to confess what is true, had rarely had false outcomes — by his authority and grave judgement rebuked me, and threatened me harshly if I did not give those things up. Wherefore, since I looked up to him and held him in esteem, and since Sturm too with me attributed much to those [prognostications], I did not dare to take up such things seriously any further. Yet astronomical matters I have always valued most highly, and have, as they deserve, esteemed greatly, and still esteem greatly. Wherefore I greatly desire to learn something even in these, in this my advancing age, from a teacher — which I hope you too will not refuse me.

Farewell, most upright sir, and hold me excused that I write no more; and reverently greet your Urania in my words.
At Copenhagen, the 17th day of November, the year 1576.
Most devoted to you,
Charles de Dançay.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Carolus Danzeus* = **Charles de Dançay** (c. 1510–1589), the long-serving French (royal) ambassador (resident) at the Danish court, a Huguenot humanist and a close friend and supporter of Tycho. The biographical literature confirms the letter's own testimony that Dançay "had been a Protestant since youth, when he had studied with Johann Sturm and John Calvin" (J. R. Christianson, *On Tycho's Island*, p. 54) — directly corroborating the references to *Calvinus*, *Sturmius*, and *Argentina* (Strasbourg) below.
- ***Ottonidi a Knudstorp*** — "son of Otte, of Knudstrup": *Ottonides*, a Greek-style patronymic for **Otte Brahe**, Tycho's father; **Knudstrup** (Knutstorp), the Brahe family seat in Scania.
- ***hoc postremo bello Danico et Suetico*** — "this last Danish and Swedish war": the **Northern Seven Years' War** (1563–1570) between Denmark–Norway and Sweden, in which Scottish (and other) mercenaries served the Danish crown.
- ***Capitaneo Iohanne Clarico Scoto*** — "Captain John Clark, a Scot" (Latin *Ioannes Claricus*): a Scottish mercenary officer in Danish service; the *Scotus quidam* of the opening is an unnamed soldier of his company seeking arrears of pay. The individual is not further identifiable from the letter; **crux flagged** (see Confidence).
- ***serenissimo Regi … quaestoribus eius*** — "his most serene Majesty … his treasurers": **Frederik II of Denmark** and the crown's fiscal officers, who have overlooked the soldier's outstanding pay.
- ***Buchananus, serenissimi Scotorum regis Praeceptor*** = **George Buchanan** (1506–1582), the Scottish humanist, poet, and historian, then **tutor (*Praeceptor*) to the young James VI of Scotland** (the *serenissimus Scotorum rex*). The characterisation — "a most learned poet, a theologian by no means seditious … nor too much addicted to Aristotle" — is Dançay's vouching for Buchanan's standing as he forwards Buchanan's (separate, enclosed/forthcoming) letter of recommendation to Tycho.
- ***nec etiam Aristoteli nimium addictus, quo … quidam Theologiam profitentes abutuntur*** — "nor too much addicted to Aristotle, whom certain professors of theology also abuse": a humanist's jab at the scholastic over-reliance on Aristotle; *abutuntur* in its period sense "make wrong/excessive use of."
- ***Theorias Planetarum revolvere … faciliori … Methodo*** — "to turn over the theories of the planets … by an easier method": *Theoricae planetarum* is the planetary-theory genre; Dançay wishes to learn the planetary theories by some simpler method of Tycho's own devising. *revolvere* "to turn over (in study), peruse."
- **Astrology.** *Astrologica … directio*-type technical vocabulary is absent here; the passage is about astrology *as a practice* (*vaticinia*, *praedictiones* — "prognostications, predictions"). Dançay's confession that he had grown so credulous as to predict *adulteria mulierum* ("the adulteries of women") is rendered literally; the hedge *raro falsos habuerint eventus* ("had rarely had false outcomes") is preserved, not sharpened.
- ***a Domino Calvino olim … absterritus sum, cum Argentinae simul essemus*** = "frightened off … by Master **[John] Calvin**, when we were together at **Strasbourg**": *Argentina* (Argentoratum) is the Latin name of **Strasbourg**, where Calvin resided 1538–1541 and where the young Dançay studied. The episode dates Dançay's renunciation of judicial astrology to that period.
- ***Sturmius*** = **Johann Sturm** (1507–1589), the humanist educator and rector of the Strasbourg gymnasium; here named as one who, with Dançay, had once "attributed much" to astrological prognostications.
- ***hac invalescente aetate*** — "in this my failing age": *invalescens* here in the sense of *growing weak / declining* (not the commoner classical "growing strong"); Dançay, then in his mid-sixties, contrasts his advanced years with his wish still to learn astronomy. The reading is contextually secure but the word is Janus-faced; noted.
- ***de praeceptore discere*** — "to learn … from a teacher": *de praeceptore* "from a teacher," i.e. with Tycho as his instructor.
- ***Uraniam tuam … reverenter saluta*** — "reverently greet your Urania": **Urania**, the Muse of astronomy, here standing figuratively for Tycho's astronomical pursuit (and, by extension, his observatory programme); a learned flourish, not a person. Cf. the *Sacris Uraniae* sign-off idiom.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S.* (in the heading sense) — the address-formula closes *Amico suo semper observando* ("his friend ever to be esteemed"); *Vale, Vir integerrime* → "Farewell, most upright sir"; *Tibi deditissimus* → "Most devoted to you".
- **Place / calendar.** *Haffniae 17. die Novembris Anno 1576* = "at **Copenhagen** (Hafnia), the 17th day of November, 1576" (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The dateline as written agrees with the edition's catalogue label (*1576. 17. november. København*); **no date discrepancy.**
- **Edition / witnesses.** Edition of record: *Tychonis Brahei … epistolae … 1568–1587* (= Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VII). MS witnesses: A = Vienna, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.7; B = Vienna, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66.
- **Correction.** Corrected the English rendering of "hac invalescente aetate" from "this my failing age" to "this my advancing age" — the Latin participle denotes age gaining ground, not declining.

Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter word-for-word against Dreyer TBOO VII pp. 40-41; the transcribed original matches Dreyer exactly with no text error. Verified names and references (Captain John Clark/Iohanne Clarico, Buchanan the Scottish king's tutor, Calvin at Strasbourg/Argentinae, Johann Sturm/Sturmius). The single defect found is a low-severity nuance shift ("invalescente" rendered as "failing" rather than "advancing/increasing") that does not change the letter's overall sense. No fabrication, omission, or sense-altering mistranslation found, matching the translator's own grade Probable.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (low). "Invalescente" (from invalesco, to grow strong/increase) means an age that is advancing or gaining on him, not one that is weakening. "Failing age" imports a connotation of decline that the Latin participle does not literally carry; a more neutral rendering would be "this advancing age of mine" or "as age grows upon me". At: “Wherefore I greatly desire to learn something even in these, in this my failing age, from a teacher”.

**Repaired.** Verified against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.40-42; the phrase appears on p.41 line 25, matching the transcribed original exactly ("hac invalefcente ætate"). Only the English translation required correction; the Latin was already sound. No other defects found on these three pages.

documents.incipit: EX litteris tuis, clarissime Domine Doctor CAMERARI, intellexi, maximam partem librorum …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO VIRO D. IOACHIMO CAMERARIO IUNIORI, PHILOSOPHO ET MEDICO EXIMIO, AMICO SUO COLENDO. DOCTOR CAMERARIUS MEDICUS ZU NÜRRENBERG.

EX litteris tuis, clarissime Domine Doctor CAMERARI, intellexi, maximam partem librorum Mathematicorum BRECHTALII esse distractam; nihilominus peto, ut eos, qui residui adhuc sunt, velis mihi, iuxta catalogum tibi missum, curare colligi, eosque huic artifici Mechanico GEORGIO LAUBIMVOLFI ad me transmittendos tradere. Et insuper, si quos alias in Mathematicis et Chymicis inveneris seu novos seu veteres, quos mihi usui fore existimas, unâ adiungas velim. Precium horum omnium ex tuo decreto artifex hic persolvet; pecunia meo nomine interea ab alio artifice IOHANNE von der SCHACK nomine, mutuo accepta, donec ego eam hîc in Dania (est enim is huc venturus) vel etiam Noribergæ restituero. Ignoscas autem mihi, quod ita audacter toties his meis negotijs molestus tibi sim; id facio fretus singulari tua humanitate, qua te eximie præditum, cum Noribergæ ultimo essem, non obscure cognovi. Peto autem, ut per occasionem me de tuis studiis et laboribus certiorem reddas, utrum in Spagyrica Medicina profectum aliquem feceris. Ego hac æstate nihil fere eximii in ea arte elaboravi, impeditus architectura, quam nunc præ manibus habeo. In Insula enim hîc quadam, quæ sita est in medio famosissimi et celeberrimi freti, ubi omnes naves ab Oriente in Occidentem transeunt, et e contra, ædes Philosophicas non exiguis sumptibus extruo. Hac enim Insula eo nomine a Rege donatus sum, ut eo, cum fert animus, secedere possim, et a vulgi strepitu semotus altioribus vacare exercitiis. Ubi vero ædificium hoc absolvero, divina ope conatus nostros auxiliante, spero me commoditatem non exiguam adepturum philosophandi tum in superiori et cœlesti Astronomia, tum etiam in hac inferiori Spagyrica rerum præparatione. Et si quid mea opera et sumptibus inveniri queat, quod tibi aliisve amicis id expetentibus usui esse possit, lubens communicabo. Vale, vir doctissime et humanissime, et amicitiam inter nos brevi tempore Noribergæ contractam longa tempora ne sinamus obliterare.

Iterum vale.
Datæ in Insula nostra Huena, d. 21. Novemb. An. 1576.
T.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the most distinguished man, Master Joachim Camerarius the Younger, eminent philosopher and physician, his friend to be honoured. Doctor Camerarius, physician, at Nuremberg.**

From your letter, most distinguished Master Doctor Camerarius, I understood that the greater part of Brechtel's mathematical books has been dispersed; nonetheless I ask that you be willing, on my behalf, to see to it that those which still remain are collected, according to the catalogue sent to you, and that you hand them over to this mechanical craftsman Georg Labenwolf to be sent on to me. And besides, if you should anywhere else come upon any [books], whether new or old, in mathematics and in chemical matters [chymicis], which you judge will be of use to me, I would wish you to add them in the same [consignment]. The price of all these the craftsman here will pay out according to your decision; the money [being] meanwhile borrowed in my name from another craftsman, one named Johann von der Schack, until I shall have repaid it either here in Denmark (for he is going to come hither) or else at Nuremberg. But forgive me that I should so boldly, and so often, be a nuisance to you with these affairs of mine; I do this relying on that singular kindness with which I plainly recognised you to be eminently endowed, when I was last at Nuremberg. I ask, moreover, that as occasion offers you make me more certain of your studies and labours, [namely] whether you have made any progress in spagyric medicine. I myself this summer have worked out almost nothing of note in that art, being hindered by the building-work [architectura] which I now have in hand. For on a certain island here, which is set in the midst of a most famous and most celebrated strait, where all ships pass from the East into the West and contrariwise, I am erecting a philosophical dwelling at no small expense. For I have been granted this island by the King on this account, that I may withdraw thither when the spirit moves me, and, removed from the din of the crowd, give myself to loftier pursuits. But when I shall have completed this edifice — the divine power aiding our endeavours — I hope to attain no small convenience for philosophising, both in the higher and celestial astronomy, and also in this lower spagyric preparation of things. And if anything can be discovered by my labour and expense that may be of use to you, or to other friends seeking it, I shall gladly share it. Farewell, most learned and most humane man, and let us not allow a long span of time to blot out the friendship contracted between us in a short space at Nuremberg.

Again, farewell.
Given on our island of Hven, the 21st day of November, the year 1576.
T[ycho].
Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** *Ioachimus Camerarius Iunior* = **Joachim Camerarius the Younger** (1534–1598), the Nuremberg physician, botanist, and bibliophile, son of the humanist Joachim Camerarius the Elder; a noted collector of scientific books and a hub of the Nuremberg learned network. The German address-line *"DOCTOR CAMERARIUS MEDICUS ZU NÜRRENBERG"* ("Doctor Camerarius, physician, at Nuremberg") is preserved as a code-switch into German by this chapter's convention
- **Dateline crux (flagged, not reconciled).** The source dateline reads *"d. 21. Novemb. An. 1576"* ("the 21st day of November, year 1576"), and the header follows it. The edition label catalogues the letter as *"1576. 8. november"*; the as-written date is led with and the catalogue date appended by this chapter's convention. The 8 November label is not substantiated by the letter's own subscription and is recorded here, not silently adopted. (The letter is the one printed at Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VII, p. 42; Thoren, *Lord of Uraniborg*, also dates it 21 November 1576.)
- ***librorum Mathematicorum BRECHTALII*** — "Brechtel's mathematical books": the dispersed library (or stock) of one **Brechtel** at Nuremberg, identified in the source only by the genitive *Brechtalii*. The owner is not further specified in the letter; left as "Brechtel" without assertion of which Nuremberg Brechtel is meant.
- ***artifici Mechanico GEORGIO LAUBIMVOLFI*** — "the mechanical craftsman Georg Labenwolf": **Georg Labenwolf** (the Nuremberg art-bronze founder, builder of fountains and waterworks), here the agent forwarding the books to Hven. Tycho had met Labenwolf at Nuremberg in 1575; Labenwolf came to Hven c. 1577 and built the Uraniborg fountain (Hannaway / Christianson, *On Tycho's Island*; Thoren, *Lord of Uraniborg*, p. 114, citing this letter, VII, 42). The Latinised genitive *Laubimvolfi* is kept in the source and the standard form "Labenwolf" used in the translation.
- ***alio artifice IOHANNE von der SCHACK*** — "another craftsman, one named Johann von der Schack": a second artisan from whom Camerarius is to borrow the purchase-money in Tycho's name. The name is given in German (*von der Schack*) within the Latin sentence; kept as written.
- **Technical / glossary terms.** *Spagyrica Medicina / Spagyrica rerum praeparatione* — **spagyric medicine / spagyric preparation**, the Paracelsian-alchemical (distillation/separation) branch of medicine and chemistry; kept as the period term, not modernised. *Chymicis* — "chemical [matters]," the early-modern *chymia* embracing both chemistry and alchemy; rendered "chemical" with the bracketed Latin retained. *architectura* — here in the concrete sense of "building-work / construction" (the Uraniborg fabric then under way), not the abstract discipline; rendered "building-work [architectura]." The contrast *superiori et coelesti Astronomia … hac inferiori Spagyrica* ("the higher and celestial astronomy … this lower spagyric [art]") is Tycho's stock pairing of the science of the heavens above with the alchemy of the elements below; rendered literally.
- ***aedes Philosophicas*** — "a philosophical dwelling": Uraniborg, described here while still under construction (1576), before it bore that name in print. *altioribus … exercitiis* = "loftier pursuits."
- **Place.** *Insula nostra Huena* = **Hven** (the island in the Øresund granted to Tycho by Frederik II in 1576); *famosissimi et celeberrimi freti* = the Øresund, "a most famous and most celebrated strait." *Noribergae / Noribergam* = **Nuremberg**.
- **Epistolary formulae.** Heading *S.* is not present; the salutation is the honorific address only. *Vale … Iterum vale* → "Farewell … Again, farewell." Subscription *Datae* "Given," *T. / TYCHO BRAHE* — the abbreviated initial expanded as *T[ycho]*.
- **No MS witnesses** are recorded for this letter (the edition witnesses field is empty); the text descends through its print in Camerarius's *Animadversiones* (pars VII), the edition of record, and is reprinted in Dreyer VII.
- **Calendar.** O.S. (Julian); Denmark kept Old Style. No conversion applied by this chapter's convention
