text.original:
HENRICUS BRUCÆUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

SERIUS quam velim, nobilissime amicissimeque D. TYCHO, tuis literis respondeo. Nunc nactus idonei Tabellarij potestatem, alijs sepositis, ad scribendum me dedi. Et recte tu quidem inobservata currere sidera, nec tam serenitatem deesse quam perdi scribis. Quae quamvis vere dicantur, quod magna pars plerisque nihil agendo effluat, tamen hisce studijs arctoa Urania occinere videtur. Hoc latus mundi nebulae dirusque Iuppiter urget. Nisi forte Academici in media luce caecutiunt, qui umbras sectantur, vel ut tuis verbis utar, formalitates verborum inanium. Id quomodo in hoc doctrinae genere fieri queat, in quo ornari res ipsa negat, contenta doceri, non perspicio. Sed hoc forte intelligis, auditorum oculos in coelum esse deducendos, aut ipsum docentem non debere scholastico pulvere contentum in illo consenescere. Ego hoc vere affirmare possum, quicquid solidi in eo doctrinae genere hisce temporibus in lucem proditum est, hoc ab Academicis profectum esse. Nam et PURBACHIUS Academicus. Idem REGIOMONTANUS, STOFLERUS. Quid de COPERNICO dicam, quem Bononiae cum DOMINICO MARIA observasse, scripta sua testantur, et Romae docuisse scio. Ut interim REINHOLDUM et RHETICUM taceam. De me nihil habeo quod dicam, quo forte respicis, nisi, non omnes sibi hunc studiorum scopum proponere, et multos destitui necessarijs, aliisque causis impediri. Et tamen hic Academicus fortasse tuis aliorumque observationibus adiutus, facta cum veterum observationibus collatione, accommodatas aliquas hypotheses extruere, et his, Geometria duce, rationem tabulas condendi demonstrare. Et inani sua pompa verborum (sic enim labores nostros vocare videris) deducere suos auditores ad recludenda veri penetralia. Verum ego suum cuique ut sit pulchrum, remitto. Imo gaudeo et laudo aliquos esse, quibus mentem et animum Dij dederunt, ut in nobili et arduo studio incumbendum sibi persuadeant. Utinam mihi ipsorum laboribus et sumptibus frui liceret, velim me dare unâ observatorem. Progredere, mi TYCHO, quo virtus tua te vocat, Dij tibi ingenium, Dij fortunam et indefessum studium dedere, da operam, ut agnoscat posteritas, te non frustra vixisse, et crassum aërem naturae beneficio et studio vince.

Venio nunc ad ea, quae de medicamentis obiter inter nos mota sunt, ubi ignorantiam decoctionum, infusionum et aliorum operum seplasiariorum minime tibi obieci. Sed hoc tum temporis me existimare memini, te necdum satis perspexisse vim et facultatem eorum, quid possint in obstructionibus tollendis, in crassis et viscidis humoribus incidendis, quantum ad intemperies corrigendas, et alia quae quotidie usu veniunt, siquidem praxin Medicam publice non exerceas, uti nos, neque etiam opus habeas. Neque, mi TYCHO, aut spiritu vitrioli aut lapidum pretiosorum viribus omnia absolvi possunt. Quod si tamen quis purius et defecatius vires eliciat separatione puri ab impuro, eum ego seplasiariujs praetulerim, uti et tu facis, et illius laboribus fruar. Non enim ars consistit in illa separatione, uti neque in dococtionibus et alijs praeparationibus, sed morborum causarumque dignotione, in naturae aegrotantis, in medicamentorum recta applicatione. Quamvis illam purificationem ego non privaverim, ut neque medicamentorum praeparationem et longe minus medicamentorum veteribus ignotorum usum utilem. Quae duo priora eius generis sunt, ut existimem, a stupidissimo quoque, sed laborioso, si praeeuntem habeat, percipi posse, tantum abest, ut subtilem ARISTOTELIS naturae interpretis discipulum requirant. Sunt enim haec (loquor de praeparationibus, non de commodo usu) mechanici operis et nullius ingenij et mentis, ubi Doctor peritus et fidelis adsit. Verum illud fuit subtilis verborum indagatoris et sententiae, autorem per scapham ligonem intelligentem et verborum portentis secretiora quaedam medicamenta describentem assequi. Ego autem arbitror, rerum cognitionem satis per se difficultatis afferre, etiamsi verborum tenebris non involvatur. Ob id tibi gratias ago, quod pro nostra amicitia confectionem vitrioli aperueris, quamvis adhuc sola tua descriptione fruamur, quod vitris recipientibus destituamur. Sumtibus enim minime deterreor. Partem alteram de Horologijs velim, si commode fieri queat, ad me mitti cum libello illius nobilis Angli de Radio, si eo carere queas, aut saltem titulum primis literis ad me mittito, quamvis libellum malim. Cum enim in Anglia sit excusus et nunc miserabilis sit Belgicus status, vix alibi consequar. Utrum aliquid librorum Lipsiae sis nactus, scire velim, et quos.

Est hic Magister LUCAS Hamburgensis non ineruditus, et harum artium, quas uterque nostrum summe colit, non imperitus, Musices non ignarus. Hic cuperet tuo beneficio iuvari, et si vel Haffniae conditio offerretur docendi, aut etiam nobilis alicuius liberi forent instituendi, operam suam offert. Uxorem habet, curta est illi supellex, ut laborandum sit illi omnino de auxilio. Itaque hunc habeas de meliore nota commendatum; nam et moribus est integerrimis et eruditus. Non dubito te, cum de omnibus optime mereri studeas, etiam nostro nomine facturum omnia, quae ab optimo nostrique amicissimo expectari possunt. Quod si existimes necessarium, ut illum coram videas, dabo operam, ut ad te transcurrat, cum aut in Insula, aut Haffniae te esse intellexero.

Bene vale, et me, ut soles, ama.
Rostochij VIII. Decembris 1576.
HENRICUS BRUCÆUS, plane tuus.
text.english:
**Heinrich Brucaeus to Tycho Brahe.**

I reply to your letter later than I would wish, most noble and most beloved Master Tycho. Now, having got the use of a suitable courier, I have set everything else aside and given myself to writing. And rightly indeed do you write that the stars run by unobserved, and that it is not so much that clear skies are lacking as that they are wasted. Although this is truly said — that for most men a great part [of the clear skies] runs off in doing nothing — yet the northern Urania seems to sing a warning against these studies. This side of the world is pressed by fogs and by a baleful Jupiter [i.e. foul weather]. Unless perhaps it is the Academics who are blind in broad daylight, men who chase after shadows, or — to use your own words — the formalities of empty words. How that can come about in this kind of learning, in which the subject itself refuses to be dressed up, being content to be taught, I do not perceive. But perhaps you mean this: that the listeners' eyes are to be led up to the heavens, or that the teacher himself ought not, content with scholastic dust, to grow old in it. For my part I can truly affirm that whatever solid work in that kind of learning has been brought to light in these times has proceeded from the Academics. For Peurbach too was an Academic. So was Regiomontanus; so Stoeffler. What shall I say of Copernicus, whom — as his own writings attest — observed at Bologna together with Domenico Maria, and who, I know, taught at Rome? To say nothing meanwhile of Reinhold and Rheticus. About myself I have nothing to say — at which you perhaps glance — except that not all men set themselves this goal of study, and that many are deprived of the necessary means and hindered by other causes. And yet this Academic, perhaps aided by your observations and those of others, might — once a comparison has been made with the ancients' observations — build up some fitting hypotheses, and from these, with Geometry as guide, demonstrate the method of constructing tables; and with his "empty pomp of words" (for so you seem to call our labours) lead his listeners on to unlock the inner sanctuaries of truth. But I leave it to each man that his own should seem fair to him. Indeed I rejoice and praise that there are some to whom the gods have given the mind and spirit to persuade themselves that they must apply themselves to a noble and arduous study. Would that it were granted me to enjoy the fruit of their labours and expenses; I should be willing to give myself [to it] as an observer alongside [them]. Press on, my Tycho, whither your virtue calls you; the gods have given you genius, the gods have given you fortune and tireless zeal: take pains that posterity may acknowledge that you did not live in vain, and conquer the thick air by nature's favour and by [your] zeal.

I come now to those matters concerning medicines that were raised between us in passing, where I by no means charged you with ignorance of decoctions, infusions, and the other operations of the apothecaries. But I remember that I thought at that time that you had not yet sufficiently perceived their power and capacity — what they can do in removing obstructions, in cutting through thick and viscid humours, how far [they avail] toward correcting distempers, and in other matters that come up daily in practice — seeing that you do not practise medicine publicly, as we do, nor indeed have need to. Nor, my Tycho, can all things be accomplished either by spirit of vitriol or by the powers of precious stones. But if nevertheless someone elicits the powers more purely and more cleanly by the separation of the pure from the impure, him I would prefer to the apothecaries — as you also do — and I would enjoy the fruit of his labours. For the art does not consist in that separation, just as it does not in decoctions and other preparations, but in the diagnosis of diseases and their causes, in [the constitution] of the ailing nature, in the right application of the medicines. Although I would not have stripped that purification [of its value], nor likewise the preparation of medicines, and far less the useful employment of medicines unknown to the ancients. The first two of these are of such a kind, I think, that they can be grasped by even the most stupid man — provided he is industrious and has someone to lead the way — so far are they from requiring the subtle disciple of Aristotle, the interpreter of nature. For these things (I speak of the preparations, not of their proper use) are of mechanical workmanship and call for no genius or mind, where a skilled and faithful Doctor is at hand. But that other thing was [the work] of a subtle searcher-out of words and meaning: to make out an author who understands a *ligo* [mattock] by *scapha* [skiff], and who describes certain more secret medicines by monstrous [coinages of] words. I, however, judge that the knowledge of things brings difficulty enough of itself, even if it be not wrapped up in the darkness of words. For this I thank you, that for our friendship's sake you have disclosed the confection of vitriol — although as yet we enjoy only your description of it, since we lack the receiving glasses [retort-receivers]. For by the expense I am by no means deterred. The second part, concerning Horologes [clocks/timekeeping], I should like, if it can conveniently be done, to be sent to me, together with that little book of the noble Englishman on the *Radius* [cross-staff] — if you can do without it — or at least send me the title in the first letter [you write], though I should prefer the book itself. For since it was printed in England, and the state of the Low Countries is now wretched, I shall hardly come by it elsewhere. I should like to know whether you have got hold of any books at Leipzig, and which.

There is here one Master Lucas of Hamburg, not unlearned, and not unskilled in these arts which both of us cultivate to the highest degree, nor ignorant of Music. He would wish to be helped by your kindness; and if a teaching position should be offered, whether at Copenhagen, or even if the children of some nobleman were to be instructed, he offers his services. He has a wife, his furnishings are scant, so that he must by all means labour for [some] support. So have him commended to you under the better mark; for he is both of the most upright character and learned. I do not doubt that you, since you strive to deserve best of all men, will also do on our account all that can be expected from the best of men and our most loving friend. But if you think it necessary that you see him in person, I shall take pains that he run over to you, once I learn that you are either on the Island [Hven] or at Copenhagen.

Fare you well, and love me, as you are wont.
At Rostock, 8 December 1576.
Heinrich Brucaeus, wholly yours.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (Henry Brucaeus, c. 1530/31–1593), Flemish-born professor of mathematics and then of medicine at the University of **Rostock**, where the young Tycho had studied; one of Tycho's standing scholarly advisers, repeatedly consulted on instruments, books, and the publication of his work on the comet and the new star. The closing *plane tuus* ("wholly yours") matches the warm, collegial register throughout.
- **Place / dateline.** *Rostochij VIII. Decembris 1576* = "At **Rostock**, 8 December 1576" (O.S.; Denmark and the Empire were still on the Julian calendar). The dateline agrees with the catalogue label (*1576. 8. december. Rostock*); no discrepancy.
- **MS witness.** Recorded as given in the source header: Vienna, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66. *(Note: the same shelfmark string is carried in the edition header for the 1571 Wolf letter; this looks like a edition-level collation artifact rather than a genuine shared folio, and is flagged here without being silently corrected.)*
- **Opening sense.** *inobservata currere sidera, nec tam serenitatem deesse quam perdi* — Brucaeus quotes back Tycho's own complaint: the stars "run by unobserved," and clear skies are not so much *lacking* as *wasted* (let slip). The whole opening paragraph answers a lost Tycho letter point by point, quoting Tycho's phrases (*formalitates verborum inanium*, *inani … pompa verborum*) back at him.
- ***arctoa Urania*** — "the northern Urania": Urania (Muse of astronomy) in her *arctoa* (Arctic / far-northern) aspect, i.e. astronomy as practised in the cloudy north; rendered literally, the personification kept.
- ***dirus Iuppiter*** — "a baleful Jupiter," a learned periphrasis for bad weather (Jupiter as sky-god / the air), glossed "[i.e. foul weather]"; the astronomical-mythological double sense is preserved rather than flattened to "the weather."
- **The "Academics."** Brucaeus defends university men (*Academici*) against Tycho's evident jibe that they "chase shadows" and the "formalities of empty words." The roll he cites — *Purbachius* (**Georg Peurbach**), *Regiomontanus* (**Johannes Regiomontanus**), *Stoflerus* (**Johannes Stöffler**), *Copernicus* (with *Dominico Maria* = **Domenico Maria Novara**, Copernicus's Bologna teacher), *Reinholdus* (**Erasmus Reinhold**), *Rheticus* (**Georg Joachim Rheticus**) — are all academically-placed astronomers, marshalled as proof that solid work came from within the universities.
- ***accommodatas aliquas hypotheses … rationem tabulas condendi*** — "some fitting *hypotheses* … the method of constructing *tables*": *hypotheses* in the period sense of geometrical models/parameters, not "conjectures"; *tabulae* = astronomical tables. *Geometria duce* = "with Geometry as guide."
- ***crassum aërem … vince*** — "conquer the thick air": the heavy, foggy northern atmosphere of the opening; a closing exhortation that ties back to *Hoc latus mundi nebulae … urget*.
- **Medicine / alchemy.** The second paragraph answers an exchange on *medicamenta*. Glossary-fixed and period renderings: *decoctiones* = **decoctions**; *seplasiarii* = **apothecaries** (period sense of the dealers in unguents/drugs); *obstructiones* = "obstructions"; *crassis et viscidis humoribus incidendis* = "cutting through thick and viscid **humours**"; *intemperies* = "**distempers**" (humoral imbalances); *spiritus vitrioli* = "**spirit of vitriol**" (the distillate of vitriol/sulphuric acid); *confectio vitrioli* = "the **confection of vitriol**" (its preparation, which Tycho had disclosed); *separatio puri ab impuro* = "the separation of the pure from the impure," the alchemical/spagyric refining Brucaeus subordinates to clinical judgement (*morborum causarumque dignotio* = "diagnosis of diseases and their causes"). The period framing is kept and not modernised to chemistry.
- ***vitris recipientibus*** — "the **receiving glasses**," i.e. the glass receivers/receiver-vessels of a distillation train (rendered "[retort-receivers]"); Brucaeus lacks the apparatus, not the will or the funds (*sumtibus … minime deterreor*).
- **The *scapha / ligo* crux.** *autorem per scapham ligonem intelligentem et verborum portentis secretiora quaedam medicamenta describentem assequi* — Brucaeus jabs at an obscurantist author who hides plain things behind "monstrous words": one who "understands a *ligo* [mattock/hoe] by *scapha* [skiff/boat]," i.e. wilfully misnames the commonplace. The phrase is proverbial in tenor (cf. the Greek tag "to call a spade a spade," here inverted — *not* calling a spade a spade); the exact target author is not named in the text. Rendered with both Latin nouns glossed and the polemical sense kept; **flagged** rather than resolved to a named work.
- **The *Horologia* / English *Radius* book.** *Partem alteram de Horologijs* — "the **second part, concerning Horologes**": a treatise/section on clocks or timekeeping that Tycho had (or was preparing), of which Brucaeus wants the second part. *libello illius nobilis Angli de Radio* — "that little book of the **noble Englishman on the *Radius***": a printed English book on the *radius astronomicus* (**cross-staff**). Brucaeus notes it "was printed in England" and is now hard to obtain because the Low Countries (*Belgicus status*) are in upheaval (the Dutch Revolt). The most likely referent is **Thomas Digges**, who made a noted study of the cross-staff fitted with transversal divisions (Dreyer, *Tycho Brahe*; cf. J. J. Roche, "The Radius Astronomicus in England," *Annals of Science* 38 [1981]); a reference to his father **Leonard Digges** (*A geometrical practise, named Pantometria*, London 1571) is also possible. The identification is **probable, not certain**, and is flagged.
- ***Magister Lucas Hamburgensis*** — "**Master Lucas of Hamburg**," an otherwise here-unidentified learned man (musician and mathematician) whom Brucaeus commends to Tycho for a teaching or tutoring post; *de meliore nota commendatum* = "commended under the better mark" (i.e. warmly, in the higher class of recommendation).
- ***in Insula, aut Haffniae*** — "on the **Island** [= **Hven**] or at **Copenhagen** (*Haffnia*)": by Dec. 1576 Tycho was establishing himself on Hven, granted to him by Frederik II that year; Brucaeus already locates him there.
- **Formulae.** *D. TYCHO* = "Master Tycho"; *Bene vale, et me … ama* = "Fare you well, and love me [as you are wont]"; *plane tuus* = "wholly yours."
- **Negation check.** The dense medical paragraph turns on several negations, all reproduced one-for-one: *ignorantiam … minime tibi obieci* ("I by **no means** charged you with ignorance"); *te **necdum** satis perspexisse* ("you had **not yet** sufficiently perceived"); ***Neque** … aut spiritu vitrioli aut … omnia absolvi possunt* ("**Nor** can all things be accomplished either … or …"); *non … ars consistit in illa separatione, uti **neque** in decoctionibus* ("the art does **not** consist in that separation, just as it does **not** in decoctions"); *illam purificationem ego **non** privaverim, ut **neque** … et longe minus …* ("I would **not** have stripped that purification [of value], **nor** likewise … and far **less** …"); *etiamsi verborum tenebris **non** involvatur* ("even if it be **not** wrapped up in the darkness of words"). No negation added or dropped.
- **Correction.** "eximere" corrected to "extruere" (Dreyer, TBOO VII, p.43); English "draw out some fitting hypotheses" corrected to "build up some fitting hypotheses" to match.

documents.abstract: Reports that the Ptolemaic armillae have been entrusted to the mill craftsman to be fitted according to Tycho's specification, despite others' objections about water use.
documents.incipit: TYCHONI BRAHE EX SORORE NEPOTI CHARISSIMO. Is, quo vita, salus, via, statque redemptio …

text.original:
TYCHONI BRAHE EX SORORE NEPOTI CHARISSIMO.
Is, quo vita, salus, via, statque redemptio nostra,
Corporis atque animæ det tibi fausta, precor.

IAM iam literas tuas, Nepos e sorore charissime, de negotijs tuis expediendis apud fabrum ferrarium meum, per famulum tuum accepi, petitionibus tuis quam libentissime satisfacturus, nec officium ullum erga te, quem semper intime dilexi, pollicitationis in me claudier sinam. Armillas, quas, si recte memini, Ptolemaicas appellas, et pro quibus ornandis mihi cupreos circulos misisti, artifici hîc in moletrina ex tuo præscripto ornandos commisi, etiam frementibus et reluctantibus alijs, qui aquam pro conficienda farina nimium exhauriri prætendunt. Sed vereor, ne is iuxta tuam mentem Armillas istas rite parare et levigare norit. Verum, ubi ipsemet me accesseris, rectius de his dispicies. Has scribens, literas Regias accepi, ut ad suam Maiestatem sine mora veniam. Ubi autem a Regia Maiestate liberabor, Lares Huenenses seu potius Uraniburgicos, adeoque te ipsum invisam, tuis Musis thura libando.

His paucis quam feliciter vale.
Datæ Herrisuadi 5 Nonis Maij Anno 1577.

STENO BILDE.
text.english:
**To Tycho Brahe, his most beloved nephew through a sister.**
May He in whom are our life, our salvation, our way, and our redemption
grant you what is favourable for body and soul — this I pray.

Just now, my most beloved nephew through a sister, I have received your letter, by the hand of your servant, about getting your business dispatched at my blacksmith's; and I shall meet your requests most willingly, nor shall I let any duty of my promise toward you — whom I have always loved most dearly — be closed off within me. The armillae which, if I remember rightly, you call Ptolemaic, and for the fitting-out of which you sent me copper circles, I have entrusted to the craftsman here at the mill to be fitted out according to your specification — even though others grumble and resist, alleging that too much water is drawn off [thereby], [water] needed for making the flour. But I fear he may not know how to prepare and burnish those armillae duly, in keeping with your intention. Yet when you come to me in person, you will look into these matters more rightly. As I write this, I have received a letter from the King [literae Regiae], [bidding me] come to His Majesty without delay. But when I am freed from the Royal Majesty, I shall visit my household gods of Hven — or rather of Uraniborg — and indeed you yourself, offering incense to your Muses.

With these few words, may you fare most happily.
Given at Herrevad, the 5th [day, reckoned to] the Nones of May, the year 1577.

Steen Bille.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** *Steno Bilde* = **Steen (Sten) Bille** (1527–1586), Tycho's maternal uncle and the lord of **Herrevad Abbey** (Herrevadskloster) in Scania. The salutation *ex sorore nepoti* ("nephew through a sister") fixes the relationship: Steen's sister **Beate Bille** was Tycho's mother. Steen Bille was the figure who drew the young Tycho into alchemy and metallurgy, on whose Herrevad estate Tycho kept his first observatory and observed the 1572 nova; here, a year after the grant of Hven (1576) and during the building of Uraniborg, he is acting as Tycho's local agent for instrument-fitting.
- **Recipient / place.** *Tychoni Brahe* = **Tycho Brahe**; *Herrisuadi* = **Herrevad** (Herrevadskloster), the former Cistercian abbey in Scania held by Steen Bille. *Lares Huenenses seu … Uraniburgicos* = "my household gods of **Hven** — or rather of **Uraniborg**": *Lares* (the Roman household deities) stands metonymically for "home/household"; Bille corrects himself to name the rising house, Uraniborg, on the island of Hven.
- **Opening couplet.** The two verse lines are an elegiac distich (hexameter + pentameter) of pious well-wishing; kept as verse by this chapter's convention *Is, quo … statque redemptio nostra* paraphrases Christ as "life, salvation, way, redemption" (cf. John 14:6, *via, veritas, vita*).
- **Instruments.** *Armillas … Ptolemaicas* = **armillae**, here specified as **"Ptolemaic"** — i.e. armillary rings of the Ptolemaic (astrolabon / *organon parallacticum*) type Tycho was then constructing; rendered "armillae" by this chapter's convention *cupreos circulos* = "copper circles," the raw graduated rings sent for finishing; *ornandos … parare et levigare* = "to be fitted out … to prepare and burnish," the dressing and polishing of the metal rings.
- ***faber ferrarius / artifex … in moletrina*** — Bille's "blacksmith" and the "craftsman … at the mill" (*moletrina* = a water-mill / grinding-mill). The complaint that fitting the instruments "draws off too much water needed for making the flour" indicates the metalwork was being done at the abbey's water-mill, in competition with the milling of grain — a vivid material detail of where early Tychonic instruments were physically made.
- ***literae Regiae … ad suam Maiestatem*** — "a royal letter … to His Majesty": **Frederik II of Denmark** (r. 1559–88), summoning Bille to court. *a Regia Maiestate liberabor* = "when I am freed from the Royal Majesty [i.e. from this royal summons / duty]."
- ***tuis Musis thura libando*** — "offering incense to your Muses," a humanist flourish for "paying devout respects to your studies (at Uraniborg)"; cf. the Tychonic sign-off idiom *sacris Uraniae lita*. Kept as metaphor.
- **Latinity.** *claudier* — archaic/poetic passive infinitive (= *claudi*), "to be closed off"; rendered without flattening the deliberate archaism. *dispicies* (from *dispicio*) = "you will look into / discern," not *despicies* "you will despise."
- **Dateline crux (date as written vs. catalogue label).** The dateline reads *"5 Nonis Maij Anno 1577"* — literally "5 [to the] Nones of May." The **Nones of May fall on 7 May**; reckoned in the Roman inclusive manner, *a. d. V Nonas Maias* (7, 6, 5, 4, **3**) = **3 May**. The edition label *"1577. 3. maj"* is therefore **consistent** with the dateline once the Roman count is resolved, and the header gives 3 May (O.S.). The printed form *"5 Nonis"* (Arabic numeral + ablative *Nonis* rather than the regular *V Nonas*) is a non-classical chancery/transcription rendering of *a. d. V Nonas Maias*; it is preserved verbatim in the Source block and not normalised. No date is asserted in the header beyond what this reckoning substantiates. (Denmark used the Julian calendar [O.S.] throughout, by this chapter's convention)
- **MS witnesses.** A = Vienna, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.7; B = Vienna, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66 (shelfmarks as given in the source header).

documents.abstract: Thanks the university for his election as rector and declines the office, citing personal unfitness and pressing obligations that prevent him from discharging its duties.
documents.incipit: MAGNIFICE Domine Rector, clarissimique viri, Hafniensis Academiæ venerandi professores! …

text.original:
MAGNIFICO DOMINO RECTORI ET CLARISS. VIRIS, REGIÆ ACADEMIÆ HAFNIENSIS PROFESSORIBUS VENERANDIS, DOMINIS ET AMICIS PERPETUO OBSERVANDIS.
S.

MAGNIFICE Domine Rector, clarissimique viri, Hafniensis Academiæ venerandi professores! Quod unanimi consensu, singulari vestro favore impellente, me nihil tale a vobis expectantem Rectoratus honoribus insignire et in Reipublicæ vestræ litterariæ per subsequens Annuum tempus Administratorem eligere non dubitaveritis, vobis omnibus et singulis reverenter habeo gratias. Ego vero præterquam quod me tanto officio digne sustinendo minime idoneum agnoscam, ideoque electionis huius rationem vestræ potius benevolentiæ et favori adscribendam censeam, quam quod revera tale aliquid a me præstari possit, gravibus insuper ijsque non paucis, hoc præsertim tempore, distrahor curis et negotijs, quo minus vestræ voluntati satisfacere et tam præclaro officio rite obeundo vacare possim. Inprimis vero ob Architecturæ in ædificiis constituendis occupationes, quibus in hac Insula, a veteri desolatione in habitabilem oram, Deo conatui nostro favente, revocanda, implicor. Quapropter reverenter et obnixe vestras Excellentias rogatas volo, ut, consideratis his negotijs, quibus hoc ipso tempore, quo vobis adesse oporteret, impedior, me a tanto munere obeundo, quod alias etiam nostris viribus impar est, excusatum habere velint. Imposterum vero, Dei nutu, liberato mihi ab hoc occupationum onere, si quid erit, quo mea tenuitas vestræ Academiæ et vobis in quocunque officij genere usui esse possit, lubens omnique conatu pro virium mensura præstare et volo et debeo. Omnemque meam operam, quacunque in re litterariæ Reipublicæ vestræque utilitati inservire possit, vobis perpetuo defero. Deus optimus et æternus, autor omnis scientiæ et veritatis, vos vestraque studia in suum honorem et publici boni utilitatem diu clementer conservet.

Valete.
Datæ in Insula Huena Maij die 21. Anno Christi 1577.
Mag. et Exc. V. amantiss.
Tycho Brahe.
text.english:
**To the Magnificent Lord Rector and the most distinguished men, the venerable professors of the Royal University of Copenhagen, my lords and friends ever to be regarded — greeting.**

Magnificent Lord Rector, and most distinguished men, venerable professors of the University of Copenhagen! Inasmuch as by unanimous consent, prompted by your singular favour, you did not hesitate to distinguish me — who expected no such thing from you — with the honours of the rectorship, and to elect me as Administrator of your literary commonwealth for the year following, I reverently give thanks to you, all and each. But I, for my part — besides that I acknowledge myself by no means fit to sustain so great an office worthily, and therefore judge that the reason for this election ought rather to be ascribed to your goodwill and favour than to any such thing being in truth performable by me — am moreover distracted, at this time especially, by grave cares and affairs, and those not few, so that I am the less able to satisfy your wish and to be free to discharge so illustrious an office duly. Above all [I am so distracted] on account of the occupations of architecture, in setting up buildings, in which I am entangled here on this Island — [the Island] to be recalled, from its old desolation, into a habitable shore, with God favouring our endeavour. Wherefore I would reverently and earnestly have Your Excellencies asked that, these affairs being considered — by which, at the very time when I ought to be present with you, I am hindered — they may be willing to hold me excused from discharging so great a charge, which besides is unequal to our powers. But hereafter, at God's nod, when I am freed from this burden of occupations, if there shall be anything wherein my slender means may be of use to your University and to you in any kind of service whatsoever, I both will and ought to perform it gladly and with every effort according to the measure of my strength. And I offer you in perpetuity all my labour, in whatever matter it may serve the advantage of the literary commonwealth and your own. May God, best and eternal, the author of all knowledge and truth, long and graciously preserve you and your studies, to His own honour and to the advantage of the public good.

Farewell.
Given on the Island of Hven, the 21st day of May, in the year of Christ 1577.
Most loving toward Your Magnificences and Excellencies,
Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / occasion.** Tycho Brahe, writing from **Hven** (Lat. *Huena*), declines the **rectorship of the University of Copenhagen** to which the rector and professors had elected him for the coming academic year. He pleads unfitness (a courtesy topos) and, more concretely, that he is consumed by the building works on Hven — Frederik II had granted him the island in 1576, and in 1577 the construction of **Uraniborg** was under way. The letter is the formal *recusatio* of an honour.
- **Recipients.** The collegium of the *Regia Academia Hafniensis* — the University of Copenhagen (founded 1479) — addressed through its sitting **Rector** (*Magnificus Dominus Rector*, the standard university style) and the body of professors.
- **Salutation / subscription formulae.** *S.* = *salutem (dicit)*, "(sends) greeting". *Valete* → "Farewell" (plural). *Mag. et Exc. V. amantiss.* = *Magnificentiae et Excellentiae Vestrae amantissimus*, "Most loving toward Your Magnificences and Excellencies" — the closing courtesy keyed to the collective addressees (*Magnificentia* the rector's style, *Excellentia* the professors'); rendered in the plural to match the body's *vobis*.
- ***Reipublicae … litterariae … Administratorem*** — "Administrator of your literary commonwealth": the rectorship cast in the humanist trope of the university as a *res publica litteraria* (republic of letters); the rector being its annual *Administrator*. *per subsequens Annuum tempus* = "for the year following" (the one-year rectorial term).
- ***Architecturae in aedificiis constituendis occupationes*** — "the occupations of architecture, in setting up buildings": Tycho's Hven construction works (Uraniborg, begun 1576–77). Rendered literally; *Architectura* kept as "architecture" (building-craft).
- ***a veteri desolatione in habitabilem oram … revocanda*** — "to be recalled, from its old desolation, into a habitable shore": the island is the implied object (*Insula … revocanda*, gerundive of purpose/destiny). *ora* "shore, edge, region"; here the once-derelict island made habitable. The slight strain of *oram* ("shore/region") used of an island is the author's, kept rather than smoothed.
- ***Deo conatui nostro favente*** — "with God favouring our endeavour": ablative absolute; *conatui* dative governed by *favente*. One of three pious framings (*Deo … favente*; *Dei nutu*; the closing *Deus optimus et aeternus*).
- ***quod alias etiam nostris viribus impar est*** — "which besides is unequal to our powers": i.e. the office exceeds his strength even apart from the building works. *impar … viribus*, "unequal to [his] strength."
- ***mea tenuitas*** — "my slender means": a self-deprecating abstract ("my slenderness/lowliness"), the conventional modesty formula; rendered "my slender means."
- ***Dei nutu*** — "at God's nod / by God's will"; *nutus* the divine assent. Kept as "at God's nod."
- **Calendar / place.** *Maij die 21. Anno Christi 1577 … in Insula Huena* = "21 May 1577, on the Island of Hven" (**Old Style**; Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). The dateline agrees with the edition label (*1577. 21. maj. Hven*); no discrepancy. *Huena* = **Hven** (the island in the Øresund granted to Tycho in 1576; site of Uraniborg).
- **Orthography.** Humanist *-ij-* for *-ii-* (*negotijs, ijsque, officij*) and *Maij*; *autor* for *auctor*; capitalised honorific abstracts (*Rectoratus, Administratorem, Annuum*). No Greek, no symbols, no astrological or technical-instrument vocabulary in this letter.

documents.abstract: Reports a prior letter of thanks for Tycho's treatise on the 1572 star, and describes discussions with Schissler and Gemperlin regarding the construction of a globe.
documents.incipit: POST tuum Augusta discessum, generose Domine TYCHO, ad te semel litteras dedi, in quibus …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO DOCTRINAQUE ET VIRTUTIBUS PRÆSTANTISSIMO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE OTTONIDI DANO, DOMINO DE KNUDSTRUP, DOMINO SUO OBSERVANTER COLENDO.

POST tuum Augusta discessum, generose Domine TYCHO, ad te semel litteras dedi, in quibus T. D. pro scripto de stella anno 1572 visa edito, mihique dono misso gratias egi. Deinde aliquid de voluntate SCHISLERI et Globi conficiendi ratione cuiuscunque magnitudinis subiunxi. Spero autem easdem litteras tibi esse redditas. De voluntate vero tua cum nihil adhuc certi cognoverim, pauca eadem de re tum cum affine meo PETRO tum cum N. GEMPERLIN pictore egi coram, ut de mea erga te benevolentia tibi quid certi constaret. Meretur enim virtus tua, ut tibi omnibus modis gratificetur. Quare cum singulari Dei beneficio ad excolendas artes Mathematicas, quas ipse impense amo, excitatus esse videaris, Deum Opt. Max. precor, ut tibi vitam largiatur diuturnam, quo laudatissimis artibus iam quidem nutantibus brevique casuris tuo ingenio quam felicissime succurrat. Quadrans, quem hîc in horto Domino Consuli magna industria extruxisti, adhuc constat et usui observationum cœlestium inservit. Machina certe ingens, vixque ullibi nostro ævo similis reperitur, quam etiam magnus ille PETRUS RAMUS summopere, cum hîc et tecum esset, admiratus est. D. WOLFIUS tibi plurimam salutem ex me dicere voluit: ipse scripsisset, nisi publica negotia illi impedimento fuissent et affinis meus non cum summa festinatione abitum parasset.

Vale feliciter.
Augustæ Rheticæ pridie Matthæi Apostoli 1577.
T. D. deditiss.
M. Iohan. Maior.
text.english:
**To the most noble and, in learning and in virtues, most excellent Master Tycho Brahe, son of Otte, the Dane, Lord of Knudstrup, his lord to be honoured with respect.**

After your departure from Augsburg, noble Master Tycho, I once sent you a letter, in which I gave thanks to Your Lordship for the writing on the star seen in the year 1572, published and sent to me as a gift. Then I added something concerning Schisler's intention and the method of constructing a globe of any size whatever. I hope, moreover, that that same letter has been delivered to you. But since I have as yet learned nothing certain about your wishes, I have dealt face to face a little on the same matter, both with my kinsman Peter and with N. Gemperlin the painter, so that something certain about my goodwill toward you might be established for you. For your virtue deserves that one should oblige you in every way. Therefore, since by God's singular favour you seem to have been roused to the cultivation of the mathematical arts, which I myself ardently love, I pray to God, Best and Greatest, that He grant you a long life, whereby He may most happily succour, through your genius, those most praiseworthy arts that are now indeed faltering and soon to fall. The quadrant which you built here in the garden for the Lord Consul, with great industry, still stands and serves the use of celestial observations. A mighty machine, to be sure, and scarcely anywhere is its like to be found in our age — which that great Peter Ramus, too, when he was here and with you, exceedingly admired. Master Wolf wished me to convey his heartiest greeting to you: he would have written himself, had public affairs not been a hindrance to him, and had my kinsman not prepared his departure in the greatest haste.

Fare you happily well.
At Augsburg in Rhaetia, the day before [the feast of] Matthew the Apostle, 1577.
Most devoted to Your Lordship,
Master Johann Major.

- **Correspondent.** *M. Iohan. Maior* = **Johann Major** (Magister), a mathematics-minded Augsburg correspondent within Tycho's circle from his 1569–70 Augsburg sojourn. The *M.* is the academic *Magister* ("Master,"); *T. D.* = *Tua Dominatio* ("Your Lordship") and *T. D. deditiss.* = *Tuae Dominationi deditissimus* ("most devoted to Your Lordship"), expanded in the translation.
- **Recipient address.** *TYCHONI BRAHE OTTONIDI DANO, DOMINO DE KNUDSTRUP* — "Tycho Brahe, son of Otte, the Dane, Lord of Knudstrup." *Ottonides* is the Greek-style patronymic for **Otte Brahe**, Tycho's father (cf. brahe-t_15711113001); **Knudstrup** (Knutstorp, Scania) is the Brahe family seat.
- ***scriptum de stella anno 1572 visa*** — "the writing on the star seen in the year 1572": **Tycho's** *De nova stella* **(Copenhagen, 1573)**, his account of the 1572 supernova in Cassiopeia, which he had sent Major as a gift.
- ***Schisler***. **Christoph Schissler (Schissler the Elder, c. 1531–1608)**, the celebrated Augsburg maker of mathematical and astronomical instruments; the letter relays his "intention" (*voluntas*) and a scheme for constructing a **globe** (*globus*,) of arbitrary size. The reading of the proper name follows the source; identification is editorial.
- ***affinis meus Petrus*** — "my kinsman Peter": *affinis* denotes a relative by marriage (an in-law); the man is named only as Peter and is not further identified here.
- ***N. Gemperlin pictor*** — "N. Gemperlin the painter": **Georg Gemperle(in)** (or a relative), an Augsburg painter; the initial *N.* stands for an unsupplied forename (Latin *Nomen*/*nescio quis* convention), left as "N." rather than expanded.
- ***Quadrans … in horto Domino Consuli … extruxisti*** — "the quadrant which you built in the garden for the Lord Consul": the **great quadrant** Tycho erected at Augsburg in 1569–70 in the garden of **Paul Hainzel** (the *Consul*, i.e. a burgomaster of Augsburg), the c. 19-foot (5–6 m) instrument described in Tycho's *Mechanica*. *Consul* is the Latin term for the city's chief magistrate (Bürgermeister); rendered "Consul" with the office flagged here. *Quadrans* → **quadrant**.
- ***Machina … ingens*** — "a mighty machine": *machina* here = the large instrument (the quadrant), in the period sense of a great engineered structure; rendered "machine" with the sense noted.
- ***Petrus Ramus*** — **Petrus Ramus (Pierre de la Ramée, 1515–1572)**, the French humanist and logician, who visited Augsburg and met Tycho there (c. 1570) and admired the Hainzel quadrant; he was killed in the St Bartholomew's Day massacre, August 1572, hence "that great Peter Ramus" is spoken of as deceased.
- ***D. Wolfius*** — **Hieronymus Wolf** (1516–1580), the Augsburg humanist and Greek scholar (cf. brahe-t_15711113001), here sending greetings via Major.
- **Astronomy / instruments.** *artes Mathematicae* → "the mathematical arts"; *observationum coelestium* → "celestial observations" (cf. *motus*, *altitudo*,); *quadrans* and *globus* by this chapter's convention
- ***laudatissimis artibus iam quidem nutantibus brevique casuris … succurrat*** — the hope that Tycho's genius may "succour those most praiseworthy arts, now faltering and soon to fall": the author's own hedged, elegiac framing of the state of the mathematical sciences is preserved, not sharpened.
- **Calendar / place.** *Augustae Rheticae pridie Matthaei Apostoli 1577* = "at **Augsburg in Rhaetia**, the day before [the feast of] **Matthew the Apostle**, 1577." The feast of St Matthew the Apostle is **21 September**; *pridie* ("the day before") therefore = **20 September** (O.S.; Denmark and the Empire alike were still on the Julian calendar in 1577). The Roman-style ecclesiastical dateline is kept and glossed by this chapter's convention; the as-written date (20 September) agrees with the edition label ("1577. 20. september. Augsburg"). *Augusta Rhaetica* is a variant of *Augusta Vindelicorum* = **Augsburg**.
- **MS / edition.** MS witness as given: Vienna, ÖNB, cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66 (the same Vienna codex of Tycho's incoming correspondence as the Wolf letter). Edition of record per the source's edition field: Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia* VII (*Epistolae*).

documents.abstract: Urges Severinus to observe the current comet and to intercede with the King to prevent Tycho being called away before he completes his instrumental observations.
documents.incipit: ...... hæc ego ad te perscribere volui, ut et tu huius Cometæ si non instrumentalem …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD D. PETRUM SEVERINI.

...... hæc ego ad te perscribere volui, ut et tu huius Cometæ si non instrumentalem saltem ocularem et physicam observationem instituere possis, et apud Regem efficere, ne forte ego hinc avocer interim, dum Cometa fulget, ut plenam eius observationem per instrumenta, quæ hîc solum in promtu habeo, perficere possim. Si vero, antequam servus meus has tibi reddiderit, id quod caveri vellem, factum est, da operam, ut Regis consensu per alias literas infectum fieri possit.

Vale et saluta amicos.
Datæ Haffniæ 14. Nov. 1577.
T.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Master Peder Sørensen [Petrus Severinus].**

...... this I wished to write out to you, so that you too may set up an observation of this comet — if not an instrumental one, then at least a visual and physical one — and may bring it about with the King that I not perchance be called away from here in the meantime, while the comet shines, so that I may carry through a full observation of it by means of the instruments which I have ready to hand only here. But if, before my servant shall have delivered this [letter] to you, the very thing I should wish to be guarded against has [already] been done, then take pains that, with the King's consent, it may be undone by another letter.

Farewell, and greet our friends.
Given at Copenhagen, 14 November 1577.
T.
TYCHO BRAHE.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / dateline.** Tycho Brahe, writing from **Copenhagen** (*Haffnia*) on 14 November 1577 (O.S.). The edition label and the dateline agree; the header date is the as-written date. Tycho subscribes first with the initial "T." and then his full name, both reproduced.
- **Recipient.** *D. Petrum Severini* = **Peder Sørensen**, Latinized **Petrus Severinus** (1542–1602), the Danish Paracelsian physician and theorist (*Idea medicinae philosophicae*, Basel 1571), at this date a royal physician (*medicus regius*) close to **Frederik II** — which is precisely why Tycho asks him to intercede *apud Regem* ("with the King"). *D.* = *Dominus*, rendered "Master" by this chapter's convention
- **Fragment.** The source is a **fragment**: it begins mid-sentence after a row of points (*"...... haec ego"*), so the lost antecedent of *haec* ("these things / this") — evidently Tycho's preceding report of his own observations of the comet — is not in the text of record. The leading ellipsis is preserved; no opening salutation survives. No MS witness is recorded in the source; the *Nye Samlinger* printing is the text of record (later reprinted by Dreyer).
- **Occasion — the comet of 1577.** *huius Cometae* = "this comet" is the **Great Comet of 1577** (C/1577 V1), Tycho's observations of which (showing it to lie beyond the Moon, i.e. in the celestial, supralunary region) became the foundation of his 1588 *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis*. The letter is thus contemporaneous with the comet's apparition (it was conspicuous in November 1577).
- **Technical terms.** *instrumentalem … observationem* / *per instrumenta* → "an instrumental observation" / "by means of the instruments" (*instrumenta* → **instruments**,); *ocularem et physicam observationem* → "a visual and physical observation," i.e. a naked-eye observation of the comet's appearance and physical character (tail, colour, motion) as opposed to a measured *instrumental* one. *physica* is rendered "physical" (its period sense: of the body's nature/appearance), not "in physics"; flagged so the contrast with *instrumentalem* is not flattened.
- **Negations / legal force (checked).** Two negations in the source, both reproduced exactly: (1) *si non instrumentalem saltem …* = "if not an instrumental one, then at least …" (the *non … saltem* concessive pair); (2) *ne forte ego hinc avocer* = "that I not perchance be called away from here" — a negative purpose clause (*ne*) governing Tycho's request, **not** an assertion that he will be called away. No negation added or dropped.
- **Conditional close.** *Si vero … id quod caveri vellem, factum est, da operam, ut … infectum fieri possit* — a real (indicative) condition: "But if … the very thing I should wish to be guarded against has [already] been done, then take pains that … it may be undone." *caveri vellem* keeps Tycho's own hedged optative ("the thing I should wish guarded against") rather than naming the feared event, which the fragment leaves implicit (apparently an order summoning him away from Copenhagen/Hven while the comet was visible). *infectum fieri* = "to be made undone / annulled" (legal-administrative idiom: to rescind by a further letter, *per alias literas*, with the King's consent). The referent of the feared "thing" is not stated in the surviving text; it is left implicit rather than supplied.
- **Closing formula.** *Vale et saluta amicos* = "Farewell, and greet our friends". *Datae Haffniae* = "Given at Copenhagen."

documents.abstract: Notes Tycho's failure to write after Gemperlinus's return from Denmark, and reflects on the astrological prediction of danger to life Tycho had made for him.
documents.incipit: REDIERUNT e Dania vestra, Nobilissime Domine TYCHO, superiore anno GEMPERLINUS, nuper …

text.original:
ET NATALIUM SPLENDORE ET INGENIJ PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO DN. TYCHONI BRAHÆO OTTONIDI, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO COLENDO.
S.

REDIERUNT e Dania vestra, Nobilissime Domine TYCHO, superiore anno GEMPERLINUS, nuper Aurifaber, quorum neuter me accessit, uterque tamen per alios salutem mihi tuo nomine dixit. Etsi autem speraveram te pro necessitudine nostra ne absentis quidem mei memoriam abiecturum, tamen cum astra non quidem exitium (id enim a religione nostra et saniore Philosophia esset alienum) sed vitæ saltem periculum superiore anno, te autore, mihi portenderint, minus miror, me utcunque viventem in mortuis abs te numerari, si forte prædictio illa apud te mollior fuit, quam mihi tunc indicare voluisti, ideoque supervacaneis litteris supersedisse. Memineris tamen, Ascendens meum necdum Saturni Anaretæ oppositum attigisse, quod ex tua quoque supputatione circa annum ætatis meæ 65 demum eveniet, quem etiam ob id ex Astrologicis ratiocinijs fatalem mihi esse insinuasti, a quo, ut conscius sis, si forte mea ætas et nostra colloquia tibi memoria exciderunt, adhuc triennio absum. Aiebas etiam fieri posse, ut directionem Horoscopi ad Trinum suum proprium circa annum 68 incidentem assequerer, plerumque id concedi ijs, qui Aquarium ascendentem obtinent, mihi revelasti, quando de his et similibus familiariter et iucunde sermones miscuimus, atque e thesauris tuis Astrologicis, quos alias in abscondito habes, mihi quædam impartiri voluisti, quorum etiamnum magna animi voluptate recordor. Quare cum adhuc et vivam et qualitercunque valeam, quod te non ignorare arbitror, qui tam probe meam Genesin et hinc pendentia fata nosti, quatenus humanæ subiacent industriæ, nullatenus eam tibi inhumanitatem tribuo, ut me, quamvis pauperem et genere ignobilem, sed a Musis ditatum et nobilitatum asperneris, vel superbiam, ut secundis rebus elatus, neminem tenuioris fortunæ hominem amicitia tua dignum existimes, vel calliditatem, ut benevolentiam pro tempore ex loco simules. Sed facessant hæc omnia, indigna generosa natura, qualem esse tuam e diutina nostra conversatione expertus sum, pleneque persuasum habeo. De me autem sic existimes velim, me tibi et viventem et mortuum fore amicum.

Vale.
Augustæ Vindelicorum. 9. Maij Anno 1578.
Hieronymus Wolfius.
text.english:
**To a man most pre-eminent both in the splendour of his birth and in the excellence of his genius, Master Tycho Brahe, son of Otte, his lord and friend to be honoured.**
**Greeting.**

There returned from your Denmark last year Gemperlinus, lately a goldsmith — neither of whom came to me, yet each, through others, conveyed a greeting to me in your name. And although I had hoped that, given the bond between us, you would not cast off the memory even of me in my absence, yet since the stars portended to me last year — on your authority — not indeed destruction (for that would be foreign to our religion and to a sounder philosophy), but at least a danger to life, I wonder the less that I, living however I may, am reckoned among the dead by you, if perhaps that prediction was milder with you than you then chose to disclose to me, and that you therefore forbore from a superfluous letter. Yet you should recall that my ascendant has not yet reached the opposition of Saturn the Anareta, which by your reckoning too will come about only around my sixty-fifth year of age — which year, for that very reason, you intimated from astrological reasonings to be fatal to me; and from that year, so that you may be aware (in case perhaps my age and our conversations have slipped your memory), I am still three years distant. You also said it could come to pass that I should attain the direction of the horoscope to its own proper trine, falling around the sixty-eighth year; you revealed to me that this is for the most part granted to those who have Aquarius as the ascendant — when we mingled discourse about these and like matters in a familiar and pleasant way, and you were willing to impart to me certain things out of your astrological treasures, which otherwise you keep hidden, things which even now I recall with great delight of mind. Wherefore, since I both still live and am, however that may be, in health — which I judge you do not fail to know, you who so thoroughly know my geniture and the fates that hang from it, in so far as they lie subject to human industry — I in no way ascribe to you that inhumanity, that you should spurn me, poor though I am and of ignoble birth but enriched and ennobled by the Muses; nor that arrogance, that, exalted by good fortune, you should judge no man of slenderer means worthy of your friendship; nor that craftiness, that you should feign goodwill for the time, as the place requires. But away with all these things, unworthy of a generous nature such as I have found yours to be from our long converse, and of which I am fully persuaded. As for me, I would have you so judge: that I shall be your friend both living and dead.

Farewell.
At Augsburg, 9 May, the year 1578.
Hieronymus Wolf.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Hieronymus Wolfius* = **Hieronymus Wolf** (1516–1580), the Augsburg humanist and Greek scholar (the "father of Byzantine studies"), then directing the city's library and school; an early mentor-friend of Tycho's from his Augsburg years (1569–70). The same correspondent as the 13 Nov. 1571 letter (brahe-t_15711113001), and continuing its themes — Wolf's own horoscope as cast by Tycho, and his astrologically-feared old age.
- ***Ottonides*** — "son of Otte," a Greek-style patronymic for **Otte Brahe**, Tycho's father (kept, as in the 1571 letter).
- ***Gemperlinus, nuper Aurifaber*** — "Gemperlinus, lately a goldsmith": **personal crux, flagged.** The Latin reads as one or two travellers returned from Denmark. *Gemperlinus* is most plausibly the Augsburg painter **Abdon (or Tobias) Gemperle / Gämperlin**, of the Augsburg artist family; *nuper Aurifaber* ("lately/recently a goldsmith") is left as a literal apposition rather than resolved into a named second man — the syntax (*quorum neuter … uterque*, "neither of whom … each") requires **two** persons, but the text names only the one and characterises the other only by trade. The pairing is recorded, not invented; do not assert a single identity for "Aurifaber."
- ***necessitudine nostra*** — "the bond/tie between us" (a close personal connection), rendered "the bond between us."
- **Astrology.** The letter is built on the natal figure Tycho had cast for Wolf (cf. the 1571 letter):
 - *Ascendens meum necdum Saturni Anaretae oppositum attigisse* — "my ascendant has not yet reached the opposition of Saturn the **Anareta**." *Anareta* (ἀναιρέτης, "the destroyer/killer") is the technical astrological term for the planet that, by direction, marks the native's death; here Saturn is identified as Wolf's anaretic planet. The term is kept (Latinised *Anareta*) and glossed; *oppositum* rendered "opposition" by this chapter's convention
 - *directionem Horoscopi ad Trinum suum proprium* — "the **direction** of the horoscope to its own proper **trine**" (a predictive *direction*,; *Trinum* = the trine aspect, *aspectus*; *Horoscopi* here = the ascendant/natal degree). Kept as a directional technique.
 - *Aquarium ascendentem* — "Aquarius as the **ascendant**"; zodiac sign named, no glyph in source.
 - *Genesin … et hinc pendentia fata* — "my **geniture** and the fates that hang from it" (*genesis* → geniture,).
 - *e thesauris tuis Astrologicis, quos alias in abscondito habes* — "out of your astrological treasures, which otherwise you keep hidden": Wolf alludes to Tycho's reticence in sharing his astrological methods.
- **Theological hedge — preserved.** *astra non quidem exitium (id enim a religione nostra et saniore Philosophia esset alienum) sed vitae saltem periculum … portenderint* — Wolf is careful to deny that the stars portend outright *destruction* (which would offend "our religion and a sounder philosophy"), only a *danger to life*. The qualifier is rendered intact, not sharpened into a flat prediction of death.
- **Age arithmetic (consistent, recorded not corrected).** Wolf (b. 1516) writes in 1578 at age 62; he says the anaretic year is his 65th and that he is *"still three years distant"* (*adhuc triennio absum*) from it — 62 + 3 = 65. Internally consistent. The further *directio* to the trine he places "around the sixty-eighth year." No date discrepancy.
- **Sub-text.** The letter's occasion is Wolf's gentle reproach that Tycho had fallen silent — Wolf surmising that Tycho, believing his own death-prediction, had written him off "among the dead" (*in mortuis … numerari*) and so spared a "superfluous letter." The closing protestation (*me tibi et viventem et mortuum fore amicum*, "I shall be your friend both living and dead") answers that surmise.
- **Dateline.** *Augustae Vindelicorum. 9. Maij Anno 1578* = "at **Augsburg**, 9 May 1578" (O.S.). The edition label ("1578. 9. maj. Augsburg") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy.

documents.abstract: Reports finding Maestlin's book on the 1577 comet in the Frankfurt catalogue and offers to forward it, discussing whether Tycho's own demonstration should supersede refutation of others.
documents.incipit: PRODIJT catalogus librorum Francfurti ad Mœnum venalium, inter ceteros hunc invenio: …

text.original:
HENRICUS BRUCÆUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.
S. P.

PRODIJT catalogus librorum Francfurti ad Mœnum venalium, inter ceteros hunc invenio: Observatio et demonstratio Cometæ ætherei, qui anno 1577 et 1578 constitutus in sphæra ♀ apparuit, autore M. MICHAËLE MÆSTLINO, Tubingæ apud GEORGIUM GROPENBACHIUM. Hunc nondum videre contigit, quod si ad manus meas pervenerit, curabo, ut ad te mittatur, vel eo potissimum nomine, ut si forte eam methodum, easque rationes et observandi et demonstrandi sequeretur, quas tu approbas, ut tibi constet, in quibus, et quantum eis tribuendum iudices et in quibus dissentias. Porro cum multi in eodem genere laborârint, ut hinc inde edita scripta testantur, sumeret sibi forte quis laborem aliorum sententiam refellendi, id quod mihi minime probatur, cum rei propositæ vera demonstratione ex Geometricis fundamentis eruta, et observationum certitudinis confirmatione, abunde secus sentientes confutentur. Tu interim in tuis observationibus elabora et profer in lucem, quod pluteum cædat et demorsos sapiat ungues.

Nostras observationes non mitto. Cum enim eas ad Geometriam, tanquam ad Lydium lapidem revocarem, et animadverterem, aliquid in ijs desiderari, abieci aliquo, ut ipse nesciam ubi lateant. Hoc tamen satis recordor me nullam sensibilem parallaxin hinc colligere potuisse, sed calculum potius in contrarium abijsse, id, quod miratus sum, reluctante nostro ARISTOTELE.

Tu interim bene vale, et me mutuo ama.
Rostochij IV. Decem.
text.english:
**Heinrich Brucaeus to Tycho Brahe.**
Heartiest greeting.

A catalogue of the books for sale at Frankfurt am Main has come out, and among the rest I find this one: *Observation and Demonstration of the Aetherial Comet, which, established in the sphere of ♀ Venus, appeared in the year 1577 and 1578*, by the author Master Michael Maestlin, at Tübingen at the press of Georg Gruppenbach. It has not yet fallen to me to see it; but if it comes into my hands, I will see to it that it is sent on to you — chiefly for this reason, that if perhaps he were to follow that method, and those principles both of observing and of demonstrating, which you approve, it may be clear to you in which points, and how much you judge is to be allowed to them, and in which you disagree. Furthermore, since many have laboured in the same kind, as the writings published here and there bear witness, someone might perhaps take upon himself the labour of refuting the opinion of others — a thing of which I by no means approve, since, once the true demonstration of the matter proposed has been drawn out from geometrical foundations, and confirmed by the certainty of observations, those who think otherwise are abundantly confuted [thereby]. You, meanwhile, work away at your own observations, and bring forth into the light something that may be carved on the bookcase and savour of nails bitten [to the quick].

Our own observations I do not send. For when I called them back to Geometry, as to a touchstone, and noticed that something was wanting in them, I threw them aside somewhere — so that I myself do not know where they lie hidden. Yet this much I well recall: that I was unable to gather any perceptible parallax from them, but rather the calculation went off to the contrary — at which I marvelled, our Aristotle resisting [it].

You, meanwhile, fare you well, and love me in return.
At Rostock, 4 December.

- **Salutation.** *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam (dicit)*, "(sends) heartiest greeting".
- **The book.** *Observatio et demonstratio Cometae aetherei … autore M. Michaële Maestlino, Tubingae apud Georgium Gropenbachium* = Michael Maestlin's *Observatio et demonstratio cometae aetherei, qui anno 1577 et 1578 … apparuit* (Tübingen: **Georg Gruppenbach** [Latin *Gropenbachius*], 1578). *M.* before the name = *Magister* ("Master," academic; this chapter's convention). The title is given as a quotation of the fair-catalogue entry; rendered in English with the Latin work-title-sense preserved. **Maestlin** = Michael Maestlin (1550–1631), the Tübingen astronomer (later Kepler's teacher), who like Tycho treated the 1577 comet as supralunary, but did so within a Copernican frame, associating the comet with the **sphere of Venus** — exactly the point of the *in sphaera ♀* phrase.
- **Symbol.** *in sphaera **♀*** — the planetary glyph for **Venus**; named in the translation, glyph kept in the source block.
- ***catalogus librorum Francfurti ad Moenum venalium*** — the printed catalogue of books offered for sale at the **Frankfurt am Main** book fair (the *Messkatalog*), Brucaeus's source for the new title.
- **Astronomy / technical.** *parallaxin* = **parallax**: Brucaeus reports that his own reduction of his comet observations yielded **no perceptible parallax** — i.e. pointed to a supralunary (aetherial), not a sublunary, comet. *ad Geometriam, tanquam ad Lydium lapidem revocarem* — "I called them back to Geometry, as to a **touchstone**" (the *Lydius lapis*, the Lydian stone used to assay gold; a stock metaphor for a decisive test); kept and glossed. *vera demonstratione ex Geometricis fundamentis eruta* — "the true demonstration drawn out from geometrical foundations," Brucaeus's (and Tycho's) methodological creed: a sound geometrical-observational demonstration confutes opponents without polemic.
- ***reluctante nostro Aristotele*** — "our Aristotle resisting [it]": the no-parallax result contradicted Aristotelian physics, in which comets are sublunary meteorological phenomena (and would therefore show parallax). "Our Aristotle" marks Brucaeus's own Aristotelian allegiance; he registers surprise (*miratus sum*) that his calculation ran against the doctrine. The participle is left as an ablative absolute ("Aristotle resisting") rather than smoothed.
- **Allusion.** *profer in lucem, quod pluteum caedat et demorsos sapiat ungues* — a learned **Horatian** allusion (cf. *Satires* I.10.70–71, on painstaking composition: the poet who "scratches his head and bites his nails to the quick"; *pluteus* = the writing-desk/bookrest, also the board scored in revision). The sense: produce something so finely worked that it bears the marks of laborious, polished craftsmanship. Rendered close to the Latin ("that may be carved on the bookcase and savour of nails bitten [to the quick]") with the figure preserved rather than paraphrased away; *[to the quick]* bracketed as an interpretive completion of *demorsos*.
- **Subscription.** *Tu interim bene vale, et me mutuo ama* = "You, meanwhile, fare you well [*bene vale*, this chapter's convention], and love me in return" — a standard humanist epistolary close.
- **Place.** *Rostochij* = **Rostock**, the seat of the university and of Brucaeus.
- **Calendar.** *IV. Decem.* = **4 December**, given without year in the dateline; the edition label supplies **1578**, consistent with the Frankfurt-fair / Maestlin-1578 content. Denmark and the Empire were on the **Julian calendar (Old Style)** in 1578 (the Gregorian reform came in 1582); dated O.S. accordingly. No year is asserted in the header beyond what the catalogue date and internal content (the 1578 Maestlin imprint) substantiate.
- **MS witness — flag.** The edition records witness A as *cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66* — **the same shelfmark/folio carried for the 1571 Wolf letter** in this corpus. This is very likely a edition propagation artifact rather than a true codicological fact (two distinct letters cannot occupy the identical leaf). The shelfmark is reported here exactly **as given**, but should be verified against Dreyer's apparatus before citation; not silently corrected.

documents.abstract: Reports receiving German comet writings via Paul Hainzel, praises Maestlin's observations and demonstration above the rest, and discusses solar apogee, eccentricity, and the eighth sphere.
documents.incipit: S. REDDITAe mihi sunt literae tuae, doctissime et amantissime Domine WOLFI, quas circa …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD HIERONYMUM WOLFIUM.

S. REDDITAe mihi sunt literae tuae, doctissime et amantissime Domine WOLFI, quas circa finem Martij huius anni ad me dedisti, quae non minimum mihi attulerunt voluptatem, quod ex ijs te pro ea aetatis et consuetae valetudinis invalida ratione salvum et incolumem esse intelligerem. Scripta vero eorum, qui de Cometa aliquid in Germania publicârunt, quae tunc temporis a WILLERO tam cito habere non potuisti, a Domino PAULO HAINZELIO recepi, in quibus prae caeteris placet MÆSTLINI diligentia et proxime ad veritatem accedens observatio eique innixa Mathematica demonstratio. Nec dubito, quin is, si sumtibus ad instrumenta metallica magna et exquisita conficienda instructus esset, aliquid egregij ex observationibus in restituendis et corrigendis motibus coelestium corporum moliretur. In Apogei certe anticipatione et Excentricitatis Solis augmento, tum etiam octavae Sphaerae celeriori, quam existimat COPERNICUS, promotione, quantum ex ijs, quae HAINZELIUS communicavit, percipio, a nostris inventis proximeque elapsis, aliquot annis sedulo factis observationibus non multum discrepat, ut latius ad Dominum HAINZELIUM perscripsi. Ephemerides eius, vel si quae alia ab ipso publicata sunt, ad me transmittas velim. Et, si is aliqua familiaritate tibi coniunctus est, ipsum etsi mihi ignotum meo nomine salutes quaeso et ab ipso impetres, ut per occasionem mihi scribat, suasque observationes, si quas habet exactiores, mecum (si ita libuerit) communicet; ego vicissim idem ipsi praestiturus sum et ipsius conatus, quacunque ratione licuerit, promovere studebo. Si vero interea aliquot Scripta de Cometa illo adeptus es praeter ea, quae ad me misit Dn. HAINZELIUS, peto ut mihi illa, qualiacunque sint, transmittere non graveris. Ego propter varias occupationes tam Regis, quam amicorum nomine incidentes, inprimis vero propter aedificationem et oeconomiae novae instituendae molestias, quibus implicor, ea quae de hoc Cometa concepi, et quae ex observationibus certis demonstrare satago, nondum absolvere potui. Spero tamen per otium hybernum, Deo volente, me id effecturum, ubi et alia quaedam, quae Astronomiae erratis corrigendis opportuna sunt, elaborare animus est. Huic enim studio vacare inter plurimas alias occupationes non intermittam, et instrumenta huic negotio idonea partim parata habeo, partim indies parari curo, quae et magnitudine et habilitate et diligenti elaboratione mechanicae veterum et recentiorum Astronomiae tractationi, sumtu magno, labore diuturno, confectione exquisita minime cessura confido. Aedificationis vero nostrae structuram ita adornavi, ut his utendis sideribusque commode in ea observandis quam maxime competat. Eam enim ob causam in hanc Insulam secessi, ut Philosophiae et Astronomicis exercitijs libere operam navare possim; et quanquam praeteritis proxime annis ob aedificationum molestias nonnihil in his strenue exequendis impeditus fuerim, tamen spero, me in posterum (si Deus vitam et vires suppeditaverit) maiori commoditate, quam interea paro, id recompensaturum. Haec ad te perscribere hoc tempore placuit, ne hic doctissimus vir Μ. ANDREAS SEVERINI mihi familiaritate iunctus ad te pari ratione mihi devinctum sine nostris literis veniret. Is enim, cum se causa lustrandi quasdam in Germania Bibliothecas per aliquod tempus discurrere velle proposuisset, Augustam etiam ad vos se abiturum aiebat. Peto itaque, ut si qua in re ipsius desideria promovere possis, efficias, ut sentiat, te non solum TYCHONIS, sed eius insuper amici amicum esse. Bene vale carissime WOLFI, et quavis data occasione mihi scribere et quod saltem licet, calamo et charta gratam amicitiae nostrae memoriam conservare ne intermittas; ego vicissim nullam occasionem frustra praeterlabi sinam, quin intellifas, me tui perpetuo amantissimum permanere.

Iterum quam felicissime et diutissime vale, mi carissime WOLFI.
Datae in Insula nostra Huaena 1579.
T.
Tycho Brahe.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Hieronymus Wolf.**

Greeting. Your letter has been delivered to me, most learned and most loving Master Wolf, which you sent me around the end of March of this year; and it brought me no small pleasure, in that from it I understood you to be safe and unharmed — so far as the frailty of your age and habitual health allows. The writings of those who have published something on the Comet in Germany, which at that time you could not get so quickly from Willer, I have received from Master Paul Hainzel; among which, above the rest, what pleases me is Maestlin's diligence, and his observation that comes nearest to the truth, and the mathematical demonstration grounded upon it. Nor do I doubt that he, if he were furnished with the means to make large and exquisite metal instruments, would attempt something outstanding, from observations, toward restoring and correcting the motions of the heavenly bodies. In the anticipation of the apogee, certainly, and in the augmentation of the Sun's eccentricity, and then too in the swifter advancement of the eighth sphere than Copernicus reckons — so far as I perceive from what Hainzel communicated — he does not differ much from my own findings, made by careful observations diligently carried out over the last several years just past, as I have written more fully to Master Hainzel. His ephemerides, or any other things published by him, I should wish you to forward to me. And if he is joined to you by any familiarity, I beg you to greet him in my name, though he is unknown to me, and to obtain from him that he write to me as occasion serves, and share with me (if it so please him) his own observations, if he has any more exact; I in turn shall render him the same, and shall strive to advance his endeavours by whatever means is allowed. But if in the meantime you have obtained any writings about that Comet besides those that Master Hainzel sent me, I ask that you not find it a burden to forward them to me, whatever they may be. I, on account of various occupations falling to me both in the King's name and in that of friends — but above all on account of the building, and the troubles of setting up a new household, in which I am entangled — have not yet been able to finish those things which I have conceived about this Comet, and which I am busy to demonstrate from sure observations. Yet I hope, God willing, to accomplish it during the winter leisure, when I have a mind to work out certain other things too that are fit for correcting the errors of astronomy. For I shall not leave off devoting myself to this study amid very many other occupations; and the instruments suited to this business I have partly ready to hand, and partly am seeing made from day to day — instruments which, in magnitude, in handiness, and in careful workmanship, I am confident will yield in no way (at great cost, by long labour, with exquisite manufacture) to the mechanical and astronomical treatment of the ancients and the moderns. Indeed I have so arranged the structure of our building that it may be as fully suited as possible to using these and to observing the stars conveniently within it. For it was for this very reason that I withdrew to this Island, so that I might freely give my effort to Philosophy and to astronomical exercises; and although in the years just past I have been somewhat hindered, on account of the troubles of the building-works, in pursuing these vigorously, yet I hope that hereafter (if God supplies life and strength) I shall make it good with greater convenience than I am [now] preparing in the meantime. I have thought fit to write these things to you at this time, lest this most learned man, Master Andreas Severini, joined to me by familiarity, should come to you — who are bound to me on equal terms — without a letter from me. For he, having proposed that he wished to travel about for some time in order to survey certain Libraries in Germany, said that he would also go off to you at Augsburg. I therefore ask that, if in any matter you can advance his wishes, you bring it about that he may perceive you to be the friend not only of Tycho, but moreover of Tycho's friend. Fare you well, dearest Wolf, and at every occasion given do not leave off writing to me and — what at least is permitted — preserving with pen and paper the pleasing memory of our friendship; I in turn shall let no occasion slip by in vain, but that you may understand me to remain forever most loving of you.

Again, as happily and as long-livedly as may be, farewell, my dearest Wolf.
Given on our Island of Hven, 1579.
T.
Tycho Brahe.
