documents.abstract: Accompanies two Danish students with a letter of introduction and notes that local astrologers erred in observing a recent eclipse, expecting more exact results from Tycho.
documents.incipit: DUO Dani studiosi hâc transeuntes, qui se tua familiaritate aliquando usuros sperant, …

text.original:
HIERONYMUS WOLFIUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

DUO Dani studiosi hâc transeuntes, qui se tua familiaritate aliquando usuros sperant, petierunt a me, ut sibi literulas ad Excellentiam tuam darem, quo se mecum fuisse probare possent. Etsi autem nuper nescio quid scripseram, neque nunc quicquam scriptione magnopere dignum habebam, tamen quia, mi nobilissime et doctissime D. TYCHO, libenter etiam absens tecum colloquor, morem illis gessi. In observatione proximæ eclipseos nostrates Astrologi omnes, alij plus, alij minus, a vero initio aberrarunt. Exquisitiora abs te expectamus. Nova quæ passim feruntur, e popularibus tuis cognosces. Augustana plæraque antiquum obtinent. Consul HAINZELIUS tibi familiarissimus superiori anno elocavit filiam, eius frater duobus filijs locupletes puellas uxores dedit. Nos Scholastici etsi rerum nostrarum satagentes, asininam fortunam æqui bonique facimus; tuæque Excellentiæ cœleste illud et beatum insulæ Uraniæ, vel potius fortunatæ, otium gratulamur.

Vale.
Augustæ Vind. pridie Idus Martias Anno 1580.
T. Excellentiæ studiosiss.
Hieron. Wolfius.
text.english:
**Hieronymus Wolf to Tycho Brahe.**

Two Danish students passing this way, who hope to enjoy your acquaintance one day, asked me to give them a little letter to Your Excellency, by which they might prove that they had been with me. And although I had lately written something or other [to you], and had nothing now much worth the writing, yet — since, my most noble and most learned Master Tycho, I gladly converse with you even when absent — I obliged them. In the observation of the recent eclipse all our astrologers, some more, some less, strayed from the true beginning [of it]. From you we expect more exact things. The news that is bandied about everywhere you will learn from your own countrymen. Most things at Augsburg keep to their old course. Consul Hainzel, your most intimate friend, married off a daughter last year; his brother gave wealthy girls in marriage to two sons. We scholastics, though busied about our own affairs, take our asinine fortune in good part; and we congratulate Your Excellency on that heavenly and blessed leisure of the isle of Urania — or rather, of the fortunate isle.

Farewell.
At Augsburg, the day before the Ides of March [14 March], in the year 1580.
Most devoted to Your Excellency,
Hieronymus Wolf.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Hieronymus Wolfius* = **Hieronymus Wolf** (1516–1580), the Augsburg humanist and Greek scholar (the "father of Byzantine studies"), then directing the city's library and school, and an early mentor-friend of Tycho's from his Augsburg years (1569–70). This is among the last of his letters to Tycho; Wolf died on 8 October 1580, some months after writing it.
- **Recipient/place.** *Tycho Brahe*, by 1580 established on **Hven** at **Uraniborg**; *Augusta Vindelicorum* = **Augsburg**.
- ***Duo Dani studiosi*** — "two Danish students": travelling Danes carrying the letter as a token of introduction (a commonplace of the humanist letter of recommendation). They are not named.
- ***Consul Hainzelius … eius frater*** — "Consul Hainzel … his brother": the **Hainzel brothers** of Augsburg, patrician patrons of astronomy with whom Tycho had collaborated (with Paul Hainzel he built the great 19-foot Göppingen quadrant in 1569). The title *Consul* denotes the Augsburg burgomaster's office; the source names neither brother individually, so which of the two (Johann Baptist or Paul) is the *Consul* and which the *frater* is left as the text leaves it, rather than assigned. The brother is said to have married off **two sons** to wealthy girls.
- **Astronomy.** *in observatione proximae eclipseos … a vero initio aberrarunt* — "in the observation of the recent eclipse … they strayed from the true beginning": the Augsburg astrologers misjudged the moment of first contact; Wolf defers to Tycho for *exquisitiora*, "more exact" determinations. The eclipse is not named in the letter; a total lunar eclipse fell on 31 January 1580 (O.S.), which a mid-March letter could naturally call "recent," but the identification is inferential and is not asserted by the text.
- ***Astrologi*** — rendered "astrologers" in the period's undifferentiated sense (astronomer-astrologers); no separate technical term is used.
- ***insulae Uraniae, vel potius fortunatae*** — "the isle of Urania, or rather the fortunate isle": a learned pun. *Insula Uraniae* names Hven after Urania, muse of astronomy (the conceit behind *Uraniborg*); Wolf glosses it as the *insula fortunata* — the "Fortunate Isle" of classical geography — playing on Tycho's blessed *otium* (leisure) there. The wordplay is kept rather than flattened.
- ***Nos Scholastici … asininam fortunam aequi bonique facimus*** — "We scholastics … take our asinine fortune in good part": *aequi bonique facere* is the idiom "to take in good part, put up with"; *asinina fortuna* ("an ass's lot") is Wolf's self-deprecating figure for the scholar's drudgery (cf. the *ergastulum* of his 1571 letter). Kept as metaphor.
- ***Augustana plaeraque antiquum obtinent*** — "most things at Augsburg keep to their old course," i.e. little has changed; *plaeraque* = *pleraque*.
- **Orthography.** Humanist Latin: *hâc* (with circumflex, "this way"); *literulas* (diminutive, "a little letter"); consonantal *j* in *alij, filijs, popularibus tuis*; *plaeraque* for *pleraque*. Reproduced as printed in the Source block.
- **Salutation/subscription.** *T. Excellentiae studiosiss.* = *Tuae Excellentiae studiosissimus*, "Most devoted to Your Excellency".
- **Calendar / dating crux.** Dateline: *pridie Idus Martias Anno 1580* = **the day before the Ides of March = 14 March 1580** (the Ides of March falling on the 15th), O.S. The edition **catalogues** the letter as *"1580. 14. januar"* (14 January). The two disagree on the **month** (March vs January) while sharing the day (14th) and year (1580); the disagreement is plausibly a *Martias*/*Januarias* transcription or cataloguing slip. Per this chapter's convention the as-written dateline governs the header — hence **14 March 1580**, with the catalogue date appended and the discrepancy flagged here rather than reconciled. No date is asserted that the source text does not substantiate.

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET DOCTISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO THADÆO HAGECIO, MEDICINÆ ET PHILOSOPHIÆ DOCTORI CELEBERRIMO, AMICO SUO PLURIMUM COLENDO.

CLARISSIME et charissime D. D. THADDÆE. Binas a te recepi literas, ex quo Ratisbonæ simul fuimus, et quamdiu licuit, illic familiaritatem contraximus. Quod autem prioribus nihil interea a me responsum sit, scias propterea minime factum esse, quod amicitiæ nostræ immemor essem, et tui ob locorum et temporis intervalla oblitus. Nam nulla Horizontis vel locorum quantumvis magna intercapedo, vel temporis diuturnitas tui memoriam et amorem mihi adimet, sed inopia tabellariorum et commoditatum ad te ferendi meas literas effecit, ut hactenus nihil rescripserim, donec nunc tandem PAULUS WITTICHIUS alteras a te mihi attulerit, in quibus eum mihi multis commendas, iuvenem sane qui in Mathematicis exercitijs adeo sedulam hactenus operam navavit, ut non saltem dignus sit, qui ab omnibus bonis et doctis commendetur et ametur, sed etiam, qui ipsa commendatione maior sit. Fuit is mecum aliquandiu hîc in mea Astronomica Insula, et in triangulorum compendijs plura quam antea, communicatâ operâ, extricabimus. Nam et ego talibus insudavi atque in posterum ulterius, volente Numine, insudabo, quo hæc ratio, quæ per προσθαφαίρεσιν procedit absque tædiosa multiplicatione et divisione, plenius excolatur et locupletetur, in quibus tamen ille necdum satis est versatus, sed assuescet successive. Visus est enim is, quod et sponte fatetur, saltem initia quædam hîc iecisse admonitus ijs verbis, quæ se a me audivisse, dum semel Wittebergam ipso illic studente transirem et me horum studiorum causa convenisset, licet ego eorum recordari non potuerim. Verum is nunc ne aliquid damni in re familiari capiat, patriam et suos revisere constituit, brevi huc ad me, veluti sponte dixit, reversurus, ut simul observationes instrumentis meis, quæ varia et insigni magnitudine atque diligenti elaboratione nec parvis sumtibus et laboribus adorno, iucunde et utiliter exerceamus. Exstruo etiam insignem domum, quæ instrumentorum varij generis commodam dispositionem admittet, unâ cum laboratorio peculiari pro chymicis exercitijs, præsertim quantum ad Medicinam Spagiricam spectat, continuandis. Perduxi autem non sine magno sumtu et constanti labore, multis exantlatis molestijs et difficultatibus, eo usque opus totum, ut Deo feliciter auspicante futura proxime septimana sim migraturus in novas illas Ædes Uraniæ perpetuo, modo astra Borealia sic tulerint, dicatas, et illic nactus maiorem commoditatem tranquillitatemque, Deo volente, per otium hybernum observationes et demonstrationes nostras, quas habui varias et certas tam in ultimo maiori Cometa quam hoc minori, qui nunc conspicitur, absolvam, easque tibi et alijs eruditis communicabo; ubi inter alia certo ex diversis observationibus et rationibus demonstraturus sum, neutrum horum Cometarum exstitisse in Elementari regione, sed longe super Lunam in ipso æthere sedes et motum suum obtinuisse. Nam prior etiam Horizonti vicinissimus nunquam admisit parallaxin maiorem tertia parte unius gradus, sed semper minorem, uti multis rationibus infallibiliter demonstraturus sum. Huius, qui nunc durat, Cometæ parallaxes adeo sunt exiguæ, ut sint insensibiles pene, ut plane non dubitem eum esse æthereum. Tuæ observationes in ultimo Cometa ob instrumentorum penuriam non fuerunt exactæ neque intervallo 18 minutorum temporis per REGIOMONTANI rationem parallaxes ita variabantur, ut discerni et indagari poterant, etiamsi cætera, quæ ad observationem requirebantur, quæ sane non levia erant nec facile dabilia, recte se habuerunt. Neque Cometa unquam cum Aquila visus est culminare, nec si factum esset, parallaxis inde dari potuit, ut in Dialexi tua præ occupationibus minus considerate docuisti et in illo libro de Cometa exercuisti. Distantiæ vero a stellis diversis horis factæ et insensibiliter mutatæ, ut ipsemet asseris, convincunt minime tantam fuisse parallaxin, quantam asseris, imo ne sensibilem quidem; sed de his alibi latius. SCULTETI demonstrationes falsis nituntur fundamentis et erroneis observationibus, ut ipse WITTICHIUS, a quo eas desumsit, nunc fatetur; ideo nihil probat, quod eandem fere tecum posuerit parallaxin. Sed brevi, Deo volente, habebis meas observationes et demonstrationes in utroque Cometa a rei veritate, quatenus in sensus cadit, non aberrantes. Addam etiam instrumentorum meorum formam et constructionem et Solaris cursus exquisitam restitutionem, quam præcedentibus annis inquisivi, adeo ut cum observationibus indies conveniat, veluti WITTICHIUS mecum sæpe expertus est, a quibus calculus tam ALPHONSI quam COPERNICI nonnunquam semisse unius gradus, interdum paulo plus, aberrat. Longe enim alius est motus centri eccentrici Solis in suo circello, quam antecessores nostri deprehenderunt, vel ipse etiam COPERNICUS constituit, adeo ut eccentricitas Solis nunc sit 2p 5m scrupulis tredecim maior opinione COPERNICI. Apogæum vero Solis iuxta 5p ♑ hæret longe anterius quam habent COPERNICI Hypotheses. Aliter enim apparentiæ Solares non respondent, ut ex multis observationibus demonstravi, et brevi, Deo volente, communicabo eruditis. Deprehendi etiam celeriorem longe nunc esse motum octavæ sphæræ, quam COPERNICUS constituit, adeo quod æquinoctia ferme quarta parte unius gradus celerius anticipârit, quod per Spicam facta observatione eadem via qua COPERNICUS multoties observavi et demonstravi. Sed de his et alijs data maiori commoditate et otio ad te latius perscribam.

Nunc unum addam, quod tua interesse et in tuum commodum ac rei familiaris incrementum spectare confido. Rettulit mihi PAULUS noster, quomodo a Machiavellicis istis invidis et osoribus stipendio in aula Cæsaris privatus sis, neque interea certam et commodam vivendi rationem denuo assecutus es. Suaserim itaque, ut si res tuæ ita ferant, huc in Daniam ad nos conferas, visurus quales hîc commodidates adipisci queas; certo enim tibi polliceor me effecturum apud Regiam Maiestatem, et apud primarios Regni nostri nobiles, ut si hîc Medicinam exercere velis, liberale et sufficiens salarium a Rege et a cetera nobilitate pro opera medica amplam remunerationem obtineas, et in honore et existimatione, uti par est, apud nostrates magno cum rei familiaris emolumento degas, modo hisce meis consilijs morem gesseris, qua in re, si ipsemet tam cito venire nequeas, mihi tuam voluntatem significes rogo; ego interea procurabo ut omnia, quæ in tuum commodum spectare possint, apud nos copiosius et melius adipiscaris, quam in patria tua vel usquam alibi in reliqua Germania hactenus contigerunt. Tute igitur quid faciendum tibi sit, tecum delibera, et mihi, ut dixi, mature significa. De meis pollicitationibus non est quod quicquam dubites; efficiam enim ut experiaris in ipso effectu maiora his et omnia tibi Deo felicitante ex voto cessura. Deus Optimus Maximus te conservet, et in omni bono et utili proposito consilio et auxilio sit.

Vale.
Datæ in Insula nostra Huena 4. Novembris Anno 1580.
T. TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and most learned man, Master Thaddaeus Hagecius, most celebrated Doctor of Medicine and of Philosophy, his friend much to be honoured.**

Most renowned and most dear Master Doctor Thaddaeus. I have received two letters from you since we were together at Regensburg, and there, for as long as we were allowed, struck up a close acquaintance. But that nothing has meanwhile been answered by me to the earlier of them — know that this came about by no means because I was unmindful of our friendship and had forgotten you through the intervals of place and time. For no gap of horizon or of places, however great, nor any length of time, shall take from me the memory and the love of you; rather it was the lack of letter-carriers and of opportunities of conveying my letters to you that brought it about that hitherto I have written nothing in reply — until now at last Paul Wittich has brought me a further letter from you, in which you commend him to me at length: a young man indeed who has up to now devoted such diligent effort to mathematical exercises that he is not merely worthy to be commended and loved by all good and learned men, but is even greater than the commendation itself. He was with me here for some while on my astronomical island, and in the shortcuts of triangles we shall, by shared labour, work out more than before. For I too have toiled at such things, and shall in future toil at them yet further, God willing, so that this method, which proceeds by *prosthaphaeresis* [προσθαφαίρεσιν], without tedious multiplication and division, may be more fully cultivated and enriched — in which, however, he is not yet sufficiently versed, but will grow accustomed to it by degrees. For he seems — as he himself freely admits — to have laid at least certain beginnings here, prompted by those words which [he says] he had heard from me, when once I was passing through Wittenberg while he was studying there and he had met me on account of these studies, although I myself could not recall them. But now, lest he take some loss in his domestic affairs, he has resolved to revisit his homeland and his own people, intending — as he said of his own accord — soon to return here to me, so that together we may pleasantly and usefully carry out observations with my instruments, which I am furnishing of various and remarkable size and with careful workmanship and at no small expense and labour. I am also building a notable house, which will allow a convenient arrangement of instruments of various kinds, together with a special laboratory for the pursuit of chemical exercises, especially so far as they concern Spagyric Medicine. And I have, not without great expense and constant labour, and after many troubles and difficulties endured, brought the whole work so far forward that — God prospering the venture — next week I am to move into those new lodgings dedicated to Urania forever (provided the Northern stars so allow), and there, having gained greater convenience and tranquillity, I shall, God willing, complete during the winter's leisure our observations and demonstrations — which I have had, various and sure, both on the last, greater Comet and on this lesser one now in view — and shall communicate them to you and to other learned men; where, among other things, I am going to demonstrate with certainty, from diverse observations and reasonings, that neither of these Comets existed in the Elementary region, but obtained its seat and motion far above the Moon, in the aether itself. For the earlier one, even when nearest the horizon, never admitted a parallax greater than a third part of one degree, but always less, as I shall demonstrate infallibly by many arguments. The parallaxes of this Comet now lasting are so small as to be almost imperceptible, so that I quite do not doubt it to be aethereal. Your observations on the last Comet were, owing to the scarcity of instruments, not exact; nor, over an interval of 18 minutes of time, did the parallaxes by Regiomontanus's method vary in such a way that they could be discerned and traced out — even granting that the rest of what was required for the observation (things by no means slight, nor easily supplied) were rightly disposed. Nor was the Comet ever seen to culminate with Aquila; and even if it had been, no parallax could be derived from that — as in your *Dialexis* you taught, less considerately, on account of your other occupations, and as you argued in that book on the Comet. But the distances from stars, taken at different hours and changed imperceptibly (as you yourself assert), prove that the parallax was by no means so great as you assert — nay, not even perceptible; but of these things more fully elsewhere. Scultetus's demonstrations rest on false foundations and erroneous observations, as Wittich himself — from whom he took them — now admits; therefore it proves nothing that he posited nearly the same parallax as you. But shortly, God willing, you shall have my observations and demonstrations on both Comets, not erring from the truth of the matter, so far as it falls within the senses. I shall add too the form and construction of my instruments, and an exquisite restoration of the Sun's course, which I have investigated in the preceding years, so that it agrees with the observations from day to day — as Wittich has often found with me — from which the calculation both of the Alphonsine [Tables] and of Copernicus sometimes errs by half of one degree, occasionally by a little more. For the motion of the centre of the Sun's eccentric in its little circle is far other than our predecessors detected, or than Copernicus himself laid down, so that the eccentricity of the Sun is now greater than Copernicus's estimate by 2 parts [degrees], 5 minutes, [and] thirteen seconds. And the Sun's apogee stands fixed near 5 degrees of ♑ Capricorn, far earlier than Copernicus's Hypotheses have it. For otherwise the solar appearances do not answer, as I have demonstrated from many observations, and shall shortly, God willing, communicate to the learned. I have also detected that the motion of the eighth sphere is now far swifter than Copernicus laid down, so that it anticipates the equinoxes by nearly a fourth part of one degree more swiftly — which, by an observation made through Spica, in the same way as Copernicus, I have many times observed and demonstrated. But of these and other matters I shall write to you more fully when greater convenience and leisure are given.

Now I shall add one thing, which I am confident concerns your interest and looks to your advantage and the increase of your estate. Our Paul has reported to me how you have been deprived of your stipend at the Emperor's court by those Machiavellian enviers and haters, and that you have not meanwhile secured anew any sure and convenient means of living. I would therefore advise that, if your affairs so allow, you betake yourself hither into Denmark to us, to see what advantages you may obtain here; for I promise you with certainty that I shall bring it about, with His Royal Majesty and with the foremost nobles of our Kingdom, that — if you are willing to practise Medicine here — you may obtain a liberal and sufficient salary from the King, and ample remuneration for your medical service from the rest of the nobility, and may live in honour and esteem, as is fitting, among our countrymen, with great profit to your estate — provided you comply with these counsels of mine; in which matter, if you yourself cannot come so quickly, I ask that you signify your will to me; I meanwhile will see to it that you obtain among us, more abundantly and better, everything that can look to your advantage, than has hitherto fallen to you in your homeland or anywhere else in the rest of Germany. Deliberate, then, with yourself what you ought to do, and signify it to me, as I have said, in good time. There is no reason for you to doubt anything of my promises; for I shall see to it that you experience, in the very effect, greater things than these, and that all things — God prospering it — fall out for you according to your wish. May God, Best and Greatest, preserve you, and be your counsel and aid in every good and useful purpose.

Farewell.
Given on our Island of Hven, 4 November, in the year 1580.
Yours, Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** Tycho Brahe writing from Hven; the recipient *Thaddaeus Hagecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayek, 1525–1600), Bohemian physician, astronomer and personal physician at the Imperial court in Prague. This is **Tycho's first letter to Hagecius** (corroborated by Solc, in *Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science*), opening a correspondence that ran to Tycho's Bohemian years. The two had met in person at Regensburg (*Ratisbonae*) — the 1575 Imperial Diet, where Maximilian II was crowned.
- **Place.** *Insula nostra Huena* = the island of **Hven** (Ven); *mea Astronomica Insula* ("my astronomical island"). The *novae Aedes Uraniae … dicatae* ("new lodgings dedicated to Urania") = **Uraniborg**, into which Tycho says he will move "next week."
- **Paul Wittich.** *Paulus Wittichius* = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586) of Wrocław (Breslau / "the Wroclavian"), the mathematician who visited Hven in 1580 and carried Hagecius's letter of recommendation. The passage is the locus classicus of the **prosthaphaeresis priority dispute**: Tycho claims Wittich "freely admits" he had merely "laid certain beginnings here," *prompted by words Wittich said he had heard from Tycho* at Wittenberg — a claim Tycho hedges carefully (*licet ego eorum recordari non potuerim*, "although I myself could not recall them"; *veluti sponte dixit*, "as he said of his own accord"). The hedges are preserved, not sharpened; cf. Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, on Tycho's self-positioning as "originator" of the method.
- **Technical — *prosthaphaeresis*.** *haec ratio, quae per προσθαφαίρεσιν procedit absque taediosa multiplicatione et divisione* — the additive-subtractive computing method (using trigonometric product-to-sum relations) that replaces laborious multiplication and division in spherical-triangle reduction (*triangulorum compendia*, "the shortcuts of triangles"). The Greek **προσθαφαίρεσιν** (accusative of προσθαφαίρεσις, *prosthaphaíresis*, lit. "addition-and-subtraction") is kept in the Source block and rendered *prosthaphaeresis* per glossary — never reduced to "trig identity."
- **Comets.** *ultimus maior Cometa* = the **great comet of 1577**; *hoc minori, qui nunc conspicitur* = the **comet of 1580**, in view as Tycho wrote. Tycho's central claim: *neutrum horum Cometarum exstitisse in Elementari regione, sed longe super Lunam in ipso aethere* — neither comet lay in the sublunary **Elementary region** but far above the Moon, in the aether — established by the smallness of their **parallax** (1577: never more than ⅓ of a degree; 1580: "almost imperceptible," *insensibiles pene*).
- **Critique of Hagecius's *Dialexis*.** *in Dialexi tua … et in illo libro de Cometa* = Hagecius's *Dialexis de novae et prius incognitae stellae … apparitione* (Frankfurt 1574, on the 1572 nova) and his tract on the comet (*Descriptio cometae … anni 1577*, Prague 1578). Tycho faults the parallax method as too crude given instrument scarcity (*instrumentorum penuria*) and an 18-minute observing interval, faults the *culminating with Aquila* derivation, and notes the distances "changed imperceptibly" between hours — flagging Hagecius's claimed parallax as *not even perceptible*. The criticism is professional, softened by *prae occupationibus minus considerate* ("less considerately, on account of your other occupations").
- ***Scultetus*.** *Sculteti demonstrationes* = **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (Schultz, 1540–1614) of Görlitz, mathematician; Tycho says Scultetus's cometary demonstrations rest on Wittich's erroneous data, which Wittich "now admits."
- **Solar theory (technical figures — verbatim).** *eccentricitas Solis nunc sit 2p 5m scrupulis tredecim maior opinione COPERNICI* = the solar eccentricity is greater than Copernicus's value by **2 parts, 5 minutes, thirteen seconds** (i.e. 2°5′13″); here *p* (*partes*) = degrees, *m* (*minuta*) = arc-minutes, *scrupula* = arc-seconds. *Apogaeum … iuxta 5p ♑* = the solar **apogee (apse)** near **5° of Capricorn** (♑ kept in Source, named in translation by this chapter's convention). The Alphonsine and Copernican calculation is said to err by up to ~½° (*semisse unius gradus, interdum paulo plus*). *motus centri eccentrici Solis in suo circello* = the motion of the centre of the solar eccentric on its "little circle" (the Copernican small-circle device for the variable eccentricity). **Note:** the figures are reproduced exactly as written; "2°5′13″ greater than Copernicus" is Tycho's stated *difference*, not an absolute value — not silently reconciled to any modern figure.
- **Precession.** *celeriorem … motum octavae sphaerae … aequinoctia ferme quarta parte unius gradus celerius anticipârit* = the **motion of the eighth sphere** (precession) is now swifter, the equinoxes anticipated by nearly ¼° faster than Copernicus laid down; verified *per Spicam* (by observation of the star **Spica**, α Virginis, Copernicus's own precession reference star), *eadem via qua Copernicus* ("in the same way as Copernicus").
- **Medicine / alchemy.** *laboratorio … pro chymicis exercitijs … quantum ad Medicinam Spagiricam spectat* = the laboratory for chemical work, "especially as concerns **Spagyric Medicine**" (the Paracelsian alchemical pharmacy) — the period term kept, not modernised.
- **The invitation to Denmark.** *a Machiavellicis istis invidis et osoribus stipendio in aula Caesaris privatus sis* = Hagecius had lost his court stipend to "those Machiavellian enviers and haters" — Tycho offers to secure him a salaried medical post under *Regia Maiestas* (**Frederik II**) and the Danish nobility. Solc notes the invitation concerned Hagecius **as a physician**, not as an astronomer.
- **Authorities named.** *Regiomontani ratio* = the parallax method of **Regiomontanus** (Johannes Müller, 1436–76); *calculus … Alphonsi* = the **Alphonsine Tables**; *Copernicus* / *Copernici Hypotheses* = Copernicus and the planetary models of *De revolutionibus* (1543).
- **Epistolary formulae.** Salutation *Clarissimo et doctissimo viro … amico suo plurimum colendo* and *Clarissime et charissime D. D. (= Domine Doctor) Thaddaee* rendered by this chapter's convention; subscription *Vale* → "Farewell"; *Datae … 4. Novembris Anno 1580* in the dateline.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *4. Novembris Anno 1580* — Denmark was on the **Julian calendar (Old Style)** throughout Tycho's career; the date is O.S. The edition label ("1580. 4. november. Hven") agrees with the as-written dateline; **no date discrepancy**.
- **Editorial marks.** The superscript sigla in the working transcription (printed as raised letters keyed to the apparatus of the edition of record) have been silently dropped from both the Source block and the translation, as they are editorial reference marks, not part of the letter text. *DD*, *D.* expanded as *Dominus/Domine* by this chapter's convention

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ORNATISSIMOQUE VIRO, MAGISTRO BARTHOLOMÆO SCULTETO, GORLICENSI, MATHEMATICO EXIMIO, AMICO VETERI PLURIMUM COLENDO.
S.

GRATUM mihi fuit, charissime SCULTETE, vir doctissime, quod nostri, et veteris amicitiae, Lipsiae olim inter nos initae, memoriam conserves. Id enim ex libellis, mihi a te dono missis (qui pergrati erunt) liquido perspexi. Pro qua tua benevolentia gratias tibi habeo maximas; daboque operam, ut intelligas, me tui etiam memoriam, quamvis multorum annorum locorumque intervallo disiuncti simus, ex animo minime obliterasse. Legi, et diligenter perspexi scriptum tuum de Cometa anni 77. magna diligentia a te elaboratum; sed ut ingenue et amice de ijs, quae sentio, te moneam, videris partim impossibilibus, partim datis minus exquisite observatis parallaxeos mensuram superstruere. Nam neque Calendis Ianuarij Cometa cum illis duabus stellis, quas assumis, supra Horizontem in eodem circulo Verticali esse poterat, neque stellarum intercapedo rite sumpta est, cum sit illa re vera plus ¾ unius gradus minor tua assignatione; ut de altitudinibus nihil dicam. Nec enim fieri poterat, ut spacio 12 minutorum temporis mutaretur parallaxis uno gradu 7 minutis, etiamsi adhuc longe propior Terrae statueretur Cometa; et ipsemet vides, ex tota inductione absurdum sequi. Nam quod capite octavo longitudinem Cometae 4 gradibus cum ½ fere discrepantem a priore positione calculus admittat, per angulorum angustiam minime excusare poterat. Sed existimo te destitutum exquisitis instrumentis et medijs, quibus observationes perficeres; alias demonstrationem tam accuratam et ingeniosam firmiori fundamento superstruxisses, reique veritatem propius attigisses. Ego sane varijs et exquisitis instrumentis, quae in promptu habeo, e solido metallo, tanta magnitudine ad amussim elaborata, ut singulorum minutorum sint capacia, eius Cometae apparentias observavi, et parallaxes multis modis geometrice demonstratas in numeros redegi. At nusquam invenire potui, Cometam illum parallaxin admittere tantam, quae unius gradus partem tertiam attingeret, ut suo loco sufficienter demonstrabimus. Ultimo vero Cometae apparentiae die, eodem usus observationis et demonstrationum adminiculo, sensibilem esse parallaxin certissimis rationibus deprehendi. Hinc omnibus huius rei amatoribus quam primum per otium licuerit, copiosiorem et sufficientem descriptionem, certis observationibus et demonstrationibus innixam, Deo volente proponam. Instrumenta, quibus in observationibus coelestibus utor, sunt eiusmodi, ut nihil in his, quod ad perfectionem faciat, desiderare possis. Quadrantes e solido metallo fabricatos, Azimutha scrupulose unâ indicantes, tantae magnitudinis habeo, ut singula minuta, quaedam etiam cuiuslibet minuti quartam partem discernant. Armillas HYPARCHI et PTOLOMÆI metallicas, singulorum minutorum capaces, quae novis quibusdam compendijs ad amussim elaboratae sunt, habeo. Sextantem Astronomicum, pro capiendis stellarum distantijs, exquisitius et facilius quam per Radium, quo unâ tamen utor, mira tractandi commoditate pridem parari feci. Globum apprime rotundum, sex pedes in diametro exuperantem, construi curavi, qui singulorum pene minutorum capax, stellarum loca, e coelo per veras distantias desumpta, continebit, et in numeros facili compendio resolvet. Torquetum Armillare magnum e metallo solido, tum etiam regulas HYPARCHI, Azimutha unâ cum altitudinibus monstrantes, longitudine sufficienti nunc confici curo, pluraque alia, Astronomicis exercitijs inservientia, organa, magna et exquisita, partim perfecta habeo, partim indies perfici elaboro. Aedificium etiam, quod Uraniae nomine insignivi, in medio huius Insulae his Astronomiae exercitijs et Spagyricis laboribus apprime opportunum, nec minus secundum architectonicae artis decoram symmetriam extructum, magno sumptu nunc tandem absolvi. Impendi autem tum in hoc, tum in instrumentorum constructionem, intra quinquennium proxime elapsum, plus * ib millibus Ioachimicorum. Serio enim, et pro rei dignitate Astronomica hîc tractanda, commoditatesque aptas iudicavi constituendas, minime ignorans, non esse cuiusque, sumtus tanto negotio rite instruendo sustinere, et eos, qui possint, id in alijs rebus ludicris potius praestare, quam ut tantae scientiae facultates impendant. Quam cupide optarem, ut hic mihi simul adesses! Videres sane ea, quae te non mediocriter oblectarent. Sed quia id fieri vix potest (uxorem enim, uti audio, duxisti) et Reipublicae insuper das operam, effice, ut per literas saltem crebrius confabulemur. Invenies me in conservanda vel per has amicitia minime negligentem. Mitto tibi fasciculum literarum, et te obnixe rogatum volo, ut per certum hominem ad Dominum D. THADEUM HAGECIUM Pragam illas transferri procurare velis. Dedi PAULO WITICHIO a nobis discedenti quasdam ipsi etiam mittendas, quas tamen minus fideliter procuravit, et multis alijs minus sincere mecum egisse (cum tamen benevole fuerit exceptus) deprehendi. Cum enim mea, quae nancisci poterat, clam abstulisset, observandique sidera nostris instrumentis compendia et rationes perspexisset (quibus tamen tractandis minime idoneus erat, nam ne unam quidem observationem aut Cometae aut alicuius stellae, vel Radio saltem capere illi possibile erat, nedum ut Cometae parallaxes deprehenderet, prout DUDITIO frustra persuasit) tandem sub praetextu, quod avunculus eius mortuus esset, haereditatem sibi deberi professus, hinc domum reversus est, et, quo mirabar maxime, finxit se intra paucas hebdomadas reversurum, cum tamen ego eius opera minime indigerem, eoque potius carerem, quam ut multo labore mihi comparata clam a me subduceret, sibique alibi arrogaret, quod, uti in Cometa fecit, sic etiam in Solaris cursus restitutione, et octavae Sphaerae emendatione, quam a nobis nactus est, facturum non dubito. Sed reddidit is me prudentiorem, effecitque, ne cuivis posthac mea committam. At, quia Solaris cursus a nobis restituti mentio facta est, mitto tibi anni proxime futuri Ephemerim Solarem, ex nostra motuum ratione, quam annis aliquot praeteritis, praesertim 78, de coelo instrumentis et Geometricis demonstrationibus in numeros redegi. Hanc si cum ipso coelo, beneficio alicuius instrumenti, contuleris, invenies eam motui Solis, quantum sensus discernere possunt, apprime congruere, a quo tamen uterque calculus Astronomicus hactenus usurpatus longe interdum aberrat, ecclipsibus etiam id ipsum non obscure ostendentibus. Tu itaque per instrumenta nostros motus examina, ita tamen, ut Poli altitudo in ipso scrupulo nota sit, et parallaxeos Solaris habeatur ratio, instrumentique tanta fuerit magnitudo, ut singula minuta commode discernat. Sed, ne videar epistolae metas transcendere, tecum amplius colloqui ipsa charta nos prohibet. Tuum erit per occasionem mihi rescribere. Si quae praeterea fuerint edita, quae a me expeti posse iudicaveris, ut DUDITIJ de Cometis et Astrologia libellum, et si quae sunt alia huiusmodi, peto ut ea ad me transmittere velis. Ego, ubi per otium (ut spero) hybernum, mea, quae proposui de Cometis, absolvero, tecum ea, et si quae habuero alia, tibi grata, lubens communicabo, daboque operam, ut me perpetuo tui memorem experiaris.

Vale, mi SCULTETE, et mei memoriam, uti facis, conserva.
Datae Uranienburgi in Insula nostra Huaena 12. Octobr. An. 1581.
TYCHO BRAHE, Danus.
text.english:
**To the most distinguished and accomplished man, Master Bartholomäus Scultetus of Görlitz, an outstanding mathematician, an old friend much to be honoured.**
Greeting.

It was welcome to me, dearest Scultetus, most learned man, that you keep alive the memory of our old friendship, formed between us long ago at Leipzig. For I clearly perceived this from the little books sent to me by you as a gift (which will be most welcome). For this kindness of yours I give you the greatest thanks; and I shall take care that you understand that I too, although we are sundered by an interval of many years and places, have by no means erased the memory of you from my heart. I have read, and diligently examined, your treatise on the comet of [the year] '77, worked out by you with great diligence; but — to advise you frankly and in friendship of what I think — you seem to build the measure of your parallax partly upon impossibilities, partly upon data less than exactly observed. For neither could the comet, on the Kalends of January [1 January], have been above the horizon on the same vertical circle as those two stars which you assume, nor is the interval between the stars rightly taken, since it is in truth more than ¾ of one degree less than your assignment — to say nothing of the altitudes. For it could not happen that in the space of 12 minutes of time the parallax should change by one degree and 7 minutes, even were the comet placed far closer still to the Earth; and you yourself see that an absurdity follows from the whole induction. For as to the fact that in the eighth chapter your calculation admits a longitude of the comet differing by nearly 4½ degrees from the earlier position, this could by no means be excused by the narrowness of the angles. But I judge that you were lacking the exact instruments and means by which you might perfect your observations; otherwise you would have built a demonstration so accurate and ingenious upon a firmer foundation, and would have come nearer to the truth of the matter. I, for my part, with the various and exact instruments which I have ready to hand — [made] of solid metal, of so great a size, [and] wrought to the line so that they are capable of [reading] single minutes — observed the appearances of that comet, and reduced to numbers the parallaxes demonstrated geometrically in many ways. But nowhere could I find that that comet admitted a parallax so great as to reach a third part of one degree, as I shall sufficiently demonstrate in its place. But on the last day of the comet's appearance, using the same aid of observation and of demonstrations, I detected by most certain reasonings that the parallax was perceptible. Hence, as soon as leisure shall allow, I shall — God willing — set forth for all lovers of this matter a fuller and sufficient account, resting upon sure observations and demonstrations. The instruments which I use in celestial observations are of such a kind that you could desire nothing in them that would conduce to perfection. I have quadrants fashioned of solid metal, indicating the azimuths together [with the altitudes] scrupulously, of so great a size that they distinguish single minutes, and some even a quarter part of any minute. I have metal armillae of Hipparchus and Ptolemy, capable of [reading] single minutes, which have been wrought to the line by certain new contrivances. I had an astronomical sextant prepared some while ago, for taking the distances of the stars more exactly and more easily than by the cross-staff (which nevertheless I use as well), with a remarkable convenience of handling. I had a globe constructed, exceedingly round, exceeding six feet in diameter, which — capable of [reading] almost single minutes — will contain the places of the stars, taken from the heavens by their true distances, and will resolve them into numbers by an easy method. I am now having made a great armillary torquetum of solid metal, and also the rules of Hipparchus, showing the azimuths together with the altitudes, of sufficient length; and many other instruments serving for astronomical exercises, great and exact, I have partly finished, partly am labouring to have finished day by day. The building too, which I have marked out with the name of Urania, in the middle of this island — exceedingly suited to these exercises of astronomy and to the spagyric labours, and built no less according to the comely symmetry of the architectural art — I have now at last completed at great expense. And I have spent, both on this and on the construction of the instruments, within the five-year period most lately elapsed, more than [* ib] thousand thaler. For I judged that, in earnest and according to the dignity of the astronomical matter to be handled here, suitable conveniences must be established, being by no means ignorant that it is not [in the power] of everyone to bear the expenses of duly equipping so great an undertaking, and that those who can [bear them] would rather lay them out on other frivolous things than expend their means on so great a science. How eagerly I could wish that you were here with me at the same time! You would assuredly see things that would delight you not a little. But because that can scarcely come about (for you have taken a wife, as I hear) and you moreover give your service to the commonwealth, bring it about that we may at least converse more often by letter. You will find me by no means negligent in keeping up our friendship even by these [letters]. I send you a packet of letters, and I earnestly wish to ask you to be willing to see to it that they be conveyed by a trusty man to Master Doctor Thaddaeus Hagecius at Prague. To Paul Wittich, on his departing from us, I gave certain [letters] to be sent by him as well, which however he saw to less than faithfully; and I have found that he dealt with me less than sincerely in many other matters too (although he had been kindly received). For when he had secretly carried off my [materials] which he could lay hold of, and had inspected the methods and procedures of observing the heavenly bodies with our instruments (for handling which, however, he was by no means fit, for it was not possible for him to take even a single observation, of a comet or of any star, even with the cross-staff at least, far less to detect the parallaxes of a comet, as he falsely persuaded Dudith) — at last, under the pretext that his uncle had died, professing that an inheritance was owed him, he returned home from here, and — at which I marvelled most — pretended that he would return within a few weeks; whereas I had no need at all of his service, and would rather be without it than have him secretly withdraw from me things gained by me with much labour, and arrogate them to himself elsewhere — which, as he did in the matter of the comet, so too in the restoration of the solar course, and in the emendation of the eighth sphere which he obtained from us, I doubt not he will do. But he has made me more prudent, and has brought it about that I shall not hereafter entrust my [work] to anyone whatever. But, since mention has been made of the solar course restored by us, I send you a solar ephemeris for the year next to come, [drawn] from our theory of the motions, which in some years past — especially '78 — I reduced to numbers from the heavens by instruments and geometrical demonstrations. If you compare this with the heaven itself, by the help of some instrument, you will find it to agree exceedingly well with the motion of the Sun, as far as the senses can discern — from which, however, both kinds of astronomical calculation hitherto in use sometimes stray far, the eclipses too showing this very thing not obscurely. You therefore examine our motions by instruments, yet in such a way that the altitude of the pole be known to the very scruple [minute], and that account be taken of the solar parallax, and that the instrument be of so great a size that it conveniently distinguish single minutes. But, lest I seem to overstep the bounds of a letter, the paper itself forbids me to converse with you further. It will be for you to write back to me when occasion offers. If, besides, there have been anything published which you shall judge could be sought by me — such as Dudith's little book on comets and astrology, and if there are any others of this kind — I ask that you be willing to transmit them to me. I, when I shall have finished — at the winter leisure (as I hope) — the things I have proposed concerning comets, will gladly share them with you, and any others I may have that are agreeable to you, and will take care that you find me ever mindful of you.

Farewell, my Scultetus, and keep up the memory of me, as you do.
Given at Uraniborg, on our island of Hven, 12 October, the year 1581.
Tycho Brahe, the Dane.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** **Tycho Brahe** writing from his newly-completed Uraniborg. The addressee, *Bartholomaeus Scultetus, Gorlicensis* = **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (Bartholomäus Schultz, 1540–1614), mathematician, cartographer and astronomer of **Görlitz** (Lusatia), later its mayor; he and Tycho had known one another from their **Leipzig** student years (1562–65), as the letter recalls. The source is one of four Tycho-to-Scultetus letters printed in the *Singularia historico-literaria Lusatica* (27th collection, 1743), noted by Dreyer (*Tycho Brahe*, p. 133, app. p. 177ff).
- **The comet of '77.** *Cometa anni 77* = the **great comet of 1577**, the central object of Tycho's cometary work (and of Scultetus's own tract, which Tycho here critiques). *Calendis Ianuarij* = "on the Kalends of January," i.e. **1 January** [1578, O.S.] — the Roman-calendar idiom kept and glossed. Tycho's critique is technical: the comet and Scultetus's two reference stars could not have shared one *vertical circle* (azimuth circle) at that moment; the stellar interval is overstated by > ¾°; and a parallax change of 1°7′ in 12 minutes of time is impossible. He reports his own finding that the comet's parallax never reached ⅓° — i.e. it lay far beyond the Moon (the supralunary-comet thesis).
- **Technical terms** (editorial glossary–5.2): *parallaxis* → parallax; *altitudo* → altitude; *circulus Verticalis* → vertical circle; *longitudo* → (celestial) longitude; *azimuth* kept; *organa* → instruments; *quadrantes* → quadrants; *armillae* → armillae; *sextans Astronomicus* → astronomical sextant; *Radius* → cross-staff (*radius astronomicus*); *globus* → globe; *Torquetum Armillare* → armillary torquetum; *regulae* → rules (parallactic rules). *ad amussim* ("to the line/by rule") rendered "wrought to the line." *Spagyricis laboribus* = **spagyric (alchemical) labours** — the laboratory work at Uraniborg; the period term is kept.
- ***Armillas Hyparchi et Ptolomaei*** / ***regulas Hyparchi*** — "the armillae of **Hipparchus** and **Ptolemy**" and "the rules of Hipparchus": Tycho names his instrument types by their ancient prototypes (Ptolemaic armillary rings; the Hipparchan/Ptolemaic *regulae*). Names retained in the Greco-Latin form used.
- ***Aedificium … quod Uraniae nomine insignivi*** — "the building which I have marked out with the name of Urania": **Uraniborg** ("Urania's castle"), named for the muse of astronomy, declared "now at last completed."
- **The expenditure crux.** *plus \* ib millibus Ioachimicorum* — **flagged crux.** *Ioachimici* = **Joachimsthaler / thalers** (silver coins of Joachimsthal), rendered "thaler." The numeral preceding *millibus* is corrupt in the printed source: it appears as an editorial mark (*\**) followed by *ib*, not a legible figure. The sense is secure ("more than [N] thousand thaler [spent] within the last five years on Uraniborg and the instruments"), but the **quantity itself is not recoverable from this text** and is left bracketed [* ib] rather than silently emended to any specific number. (Tycho elsewhere gives figures on the order of a "tonne of gold"; that comparandum is *not* imported here.)
- ***Thadeus Hagecius*** = **Tadeáš Hájek (Thaddaeus Hagecius)** of **Prague**, imperial physician and astronomer, Tycho's principal Bohemian correspondent; Tycho asks Scultetus to forward an enclosed packet to him.
- ***Paulus Witichius*** = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586) of Breslau (Wratislaviensis), the mathematician who had stayed with Tycho on Hven in 1580. Tycho's bitter charge — that Wittich secretly carried off Tycho's methods (instrument designs, the *prosthaphaeretic*/observational procedures, the work on the **solar course** [*Solaris cursus restitutio*] and the **emendation of the eighth sphere** [the fixed-star catalogue / precession]) and would "arrogate them to himself elsewhere" — is preserved at full force, including the parenthetical claim that Wittich was incompetent at the instruments ("could not take even a single observation … even with the cross-staff"). *prout Duditio frustra persuasit* = "as he vainly persuaded **Dudith**." The hedges and Tycho's own qualifiers (*non dubito* "I doubt not"; *cum tamen benevole fuerit exceptus* "although he had been kindly received") are kept unsharpened.
- ***Duditius*** = **Andreas Dudith** (András Dudith, 1533–1589), the humanist who had published on the comet of 1577 (his *De cometarum significatione*); Tycho both reports Wittich's failed attempt to persuade Dudith of cometary parallax and asks Scultetus to procure "**Dudith's little book on comets and astrology**" for him.
- ***Solaris cursus restitutio*** → "the restoration of the solar course"; *octavae Sphaerae emendatio* → "the emendation of the eighth sphere" (the sphere of the fixed stars) — both rendered per the *restitutio/instauratio* glossary entry. *Ephemeris Solaris* → "solar ephemeris," derived from Tycho's solar theory worked out "especially [in] '78."
- ***in ipso scrupulo*** — *scrupulus* here = the **minute of arc** ("known to the very scruple"); the gloss "[minute]" is bracketed.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datae Uranienburgi in Insula nostra Huaena 12. Octobr. An. 1581* = "Given at **Uraniborg**, on our island of **Hven**, 12 October 1581" (**O.S.**; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The dateline (12 October) agrees with the edition label (12 October 1581); no discrepancy. *Datae* ("Given") kept.
- **Greek / symbols.** No Greek and no astronomical/zodiac glyphs occur in this letter. The only non-alphabetic mark is the corrupt numeral sign (*\**) in the expenditure clause, treated above.
- **Orthography.** Source-printed forms retained in the Source block (*ijs, medijs, Genesi-style -ij-, intercapedo, ecclipsibus, Uranienburgi, Huaena, PTOLOMAeI, BARTHOLOMAeO*); the *ae*-ligature spellings (*-MAeO, -MAeI*) reproduced as printed by this chapter's convention(2).
- **Correction.** English clause corrected from 'as he vainly persuaded Dudith' to 'as he falsely persuaded Dudith' — Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, pp.62-63, confirms the Latin 'frustra persuasit' as printed (perfect tense = successful persuasion, but groundless); the prior English wording reversed the sense to imply a failed attempt. The Latin text itself needed no correction.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Full sentence-by-sentence collation of the transcribed original and the published English against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.61-63 (complete letter text; p.64 confirmed to begin a different letter). Every name (Scultetus, Wittich, Hagecius, Dudith), number (12 minutes; 1 degree 7 minutes; 4.5 degrees; a third of a degree; a six-foot globe; a five-year span; the uncertain '* ib' thousand-thaler sum) and the closing date (12 October 1581) match Dreyer exactly; the transcribed original is verbatim Dreyer apart from long-s normalization. One ambiguous rendering of 'frustra persuasit' flagged above; otherwise no fabrication, omission, or hedge-loss found. Self-assigned grade was C; independent collation finds the letter substantially sound, downgraded only for the one nuance-flip.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (low). Latin 'frustra persuasit' most naturally means Wittich DID succeed in persuading Dudith, but groundlessly/falsely (frustra = without real basis); the English 'vainly persuaded' reads to a modern eye as 'tried but failed to persuade', which reverses whether Dudith was actually taken in by Wittich's false claim to have detected the comet's parallax. At: “as he vainly persuaded Dudith”.

**Repaired.** Verified the single mistranslation against the Dreyer page images (TBOO VII pp.62-63, where the phrase 'prout DUDITIO fruftra perfuafit' spans the page break). The Latin as stored already matches Dreyer exactly, so only the English clause was corrected, per the grammar of 'persuasit' (successful persuasion) plus 'frustra' (groundlessly/falsely) rather than 'vainly' (implying failure). Nothing else in the letter was altered.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD THADDÆUM
HAGECIUM.
S.
ANNUS integer iam fere est elapsus, charissime Domine Doctor THADDÆE, vir
clarissime, ex quo tibi ultimo scripsi, idque per PAULUM WITICHIUM Wratislaviensem hinc in patriam revertentem. At
quia interea temporis nihil literarum a te receperim, mutua illa benevolentia,
qua nos invicem in Comitijs Ratisbonensibus olim complexi sumus, et innata illa tibi atque
constanti erga amicos affectione, tam diuturnam in rescribendo dilationem minime
admittente, non potui non suspicari, literas illas per
eum cui traditae erant, ad manus tuas non pervenisse. Utque idipsum nunc potius
crederem, effecit libellus tuus de ultimo Cometa, quem BARTHOLOMÆUS SCULTETUS veteri
amicitia Lipsiae mihi coniunctus ante biduum
per quendam hominem vasa Spagyrica illinc nobis ex conductoA afferentem mihi transmitti curavit. Cum enim in hoc scripto videaris meam
ex observationibus certis de utriusque Cometae parallaxibus derivatam sententiam
desiderare, quam tamen tunc temporis dilucide, nec minus vere, uti spero, brevibus tibiA aperui, fieri non potuisse arbitror, ut literae illae tibi, veluti
sperabam, redditae sint. Nec enim eorum, quae in his significaveram (etiamsi nulla
interea rescribendiA occasio oblata fuisset) tam subito oblitum fuisse, vel ea penitus
neglexisse te, virum harum rerum et cupidum et intelligentem, mihi persuadere
possum. Quae autem in ijs literis tibi tunc temporis de ultimis duobus Cometis,
ex observationibus nostris reseravi et nunc denuo iudicanda indicoA, ea fere sunt huiusmodi: In Cometa, qui Anno 77 fulgere coepit, ex
omnibus nostris observationibus (quae per diversa e solido metallo exquisite
elaborata, singulorumque minutorum adamussim capacia instrumenta magnâ
diligentia inquisitae sunt, diversaque demonstrationis methodo in numeros
redactae) nunquam deprehendi parallaxin eamA, quae fit in Horizonte, maximam tertiam unius gradus partem attigisse, sed
saepenumero hac multo minorem extitisse, ut suo loco intelligentibus, varijs
rationibus sufficienter demonstrabimus. Cumque in libello tum temporis de eodem
Cometa edito, parallaxin 5 partium admisisses, et ob id sublunarem illum
extitisse Cometam opinatus esses, amice te in ijsdem literis admonui, rationem
REGIOMONTANI in investigandis parallaxibus, quate usum esse asseris, utquamvis satis
demonstrabilem, tamen tam subtili negocio minus sufficientem et accommodam esse.
Multo enim speculative vere demonstrantur, quae fi in praxin et sensuum Mechanicam tractationem deducantur, plurimum a scopo
petito aberrabunt, praesertim ubi ex minimis, uti hoc loco fit, ea quae maxima
sunt investigantur. Imo etiamsi REGIOMONTANI illaA speculatio hîc locum aliquem habuisset, et intervallum temporis exquisite
satis sumptum altitudinibus et azimuthis rite datis congrueret (in quibus tamen
singulis, etiamsi adsint instrumenta magna et exquisita, quae raro tamen in
promtu sunt, ea quae par est praecisione adamussim capiendis, quanta opus sit
diligentia, quantaque non bene exercitatis eveniat difficultas, nemo nisi diu in
hac Mechanica Astronomiae palaestra sedulo versatus, sibi persuadere poterit)
nihilominus tamen ex tam angusto temporis intervallo, quod 18 saltem scrupulorum
assumebas, parallaxes quae tantillo tempore insensibiliter variantur,
sensibiliter discernere impossibile erat. Ideoque dum motus proprij impedimenta
temporis brevitate declinare visum fuit, tota res ad impossibilitatem quandam
redacta est. Nos sane ultra vicesies eam REGIOMONTANI in discernendis
parallaxibus rationem, ex diversis et satis certis observationibus, non mediocri
(uti scis) labore, in numeros resolvimus. At nusquam parallaxin invenimus
tantam, quantam Luna etiam a terris remotissima admittit, saepenumero etiam
nullam. Ideoque tuis placitis, etiam cum eadem methodo (utquamvis subtilissimoA negocio minus sufficienti), qua tu, usus essem, subscribere non potui.
Nec etiam idipsum, quod ad confirmationem huius subiungis, ex coeli videlicet
mediatione cum Vulturis lucida, parallaxin comprobare
possibile erat. Nam etiamsi eorum simul per meridianum transitus, qui interdiu
tunc fiebat, aspectabilis fuisset, parallaxin, nisi plura adessent data, hinc
nemo ulla ratione colliget, ut per incuriam in tua Dialexi inter occupationes
alias minus considerate docuisti. Quod vero parallaxis istius Cometae non solumA tanta non fuerit, sed ne quidem multum perceptibilis, testantur propriae
tuae observationes, quas in distantijs Cometae ab ore Pegasi pluribus interiectis
horis, minimum tamen variari deprehendisti, ut revera ob id parallaxinA, si qua fuit, exiguam esse, orbemque Lunae plurimum exuperasse Cometam,
vel tuis observatis, quibus tamen contraria admittebas, convinci possit. Haec,
inquam, tum temporis de priori Cometa ad te perscripsi. Video autem in hoc
ultimo scripto te nobiscum sentire, et consideratis ijs, quas tuncA temporis non animadvertebas, contrarietatibus sententiam revocasse,
reique vestigandaeA nucleum penitius invenisse, qua in re tibi et veritatis amatoribus (qui
tua autoritate abuti, et observationibus ac demonstratis minus exquisitis adduci
poterant, ut falsae Peripateticorum de Cometis opinioni subscriberent) plurimum
gratulor. Quod ad SCULTETI demonstrationes, quae eandem fere tecum parallaxin
inferebant, attinet, cum incerto fulciantur fundamento, falsisque datis
superstruantur (nam, ut alia taceam, impossibile erat Cometam eo die cum ijs fixis, quas assumit, supra Horizontem in eodem extitisse
circulo verticali, et stellarum etiam, quam praesupponit,
distantia plus ¾ unius gradus erronea sit, ut de caeteris hinc quis facile, quid
sentiendum sit, colligat) minime eas pro veritate indaganda recipiendas, suo
loco dilucide ostendemus. Quantum vero ad hunc ultimum Cometam, qui anno 80
fulsit, attinet, videris mihi scopum ipsum longe exactius attigisse, et
certioribus observationibus rei veritatem probabilius demonstrasse. In quibus id
saltem ad exquisitam praecisionem penitius investigandam desiderarem, ut motus
proprij Cometae inter binas observationes mutationem non neglexisses. Cum enim
Cometa intervallo duarum horarum eo die in suo circulo 27' (motus siquidemA diurnus a nobis inventus est 5p 23m) locum mutaverit, hanc differentiam, si res praecise tractanda foret,
non praetereundam iudico, quoniamA ex minimis hoc loco de longe maioribus ratiocinamur. Instrumentum etiam
ob id, quo altitudines capis, cum dena aut quina minuta saltem admittat, in tam
subtili indagine minime sufficiens esse poterit. Sunt tamen tuae observationes et
his innixaeA demonstrationes eiusmodi, ut si hinc non exquisite, quot minutorum fuerit
parallaxis, et in quo praecise orbium coelestium versaretur Cometa ille, ad
amussim constare possit, tantam tamen fuisse, ut Lunae inferiora non permearet,
cuivis harum rerum perito non aegre persuadere poterint. Quantum ad nostras in
hoc Cometa observationes attinet, meam sententiam tum temporis non minus quam
iam per literas tibi indicavi, videlicet me toto apparitionis tempore, ex
omnibus et diversimodis exquisitissimis instrumentis, diligenter habitis et
examinatis observationibus, huius Cometae notabilem aliquam fuisse parallaxin, nusquam percipereA potuisse. Nam ut caetera (commodiore loco commemoranda) taceam, certo
deprehendi Cometam illum, tam in Meridiano, cum altissimus esset, quam iuxta
Horizontem in ipso puncto occidentalis Azimuthi, eandem exquisite ab Aequatore
declinationem obtinuisse, nisi quantum motus proprius interea, diurno motui
proportionalis, eam variaverit, quod fieri minime potuit in tanta altitudinum
differentia, si sensibilis aliqua parallaxeωs adfuisset quantitas. Id ipsum
etiam tum omnibus rationibus a REGIOMONTANO in suo libello propositis, quae usum
hîc haberent, tum alijs quibusdam exactioribus et minus errori obnoxijs a nobis
circa parallaxium dimensiones excogitatis, plane se eodem modo habere certo
deprehendimus, ut per ocium copiose firmis rationibus, Mathemata intelligentibus
demonstrabimus. Contuli etiam acceptoA tuo libello nonnulla cum nostris observationibusA et in ijs miram deprehendi convenientiam, quae ad parallaxium certitudinem
confirmandam facere poterat. Nam die 13. Octobris cum Cometa esset iuxta
Meridianum, eius distantiam a lucidiore capitis Pegasi tam Radio quam Sextante
Astronomico (instrumento peculiari a nobis tali
machinatione invento, ut per hoc longe facilius, commodius et exactius, quam per
Radium stellarum capiantur intercapedines) deprehendi partis 1 min. 16 uno
saltem scrupulo pene insensibili tua distantia maiorem, quae tamen differentia
pro hac terreni orbis distantia ad quintum usque scrupulum, si in ipsa
convexitate orbis Lunae fuisset Cometa, excrevisset, longeque plus, si vel in
regione ignea (modo aliqua foret) vel supremitate aëris, ut diu falso opinati sunt omnes Aristotelici, exarsisset. Sic die etiam 21.
Octobris cum Cometa esset proximus lucidae Aquilae, ei stellae
a vertice imminens, eandem plane tecum deprehendi distantiam. Nam licet haec hora
8 uno scrupulo nobis minor visa fuerit, tamen usque ad decimam hanc
observationem continuandoA exquisite p. 6 m. 22 apparebat, quod cum tua annotatione adprime
consentit. Et quemadmodum fieri minime potuit, ut intervallo duarum horarum
saltem uno scrupulo variaret a fixa Cometae illa distantia, si sensibilis admodum
adfuisset parallaxis, sic etiam intervallo 6 graduum orbis terrestris, quod est
inter tui et nostri loci observationem, eandem eodem tempore praecise obtinere posseA a fixisA distantiam corpus aliquod Luna inferius, MathemataA intelligenti non persuadebitur. Obtulit autem se eo die optata comae
moditas ad Vulturis stellam parallaxes examinandi, eo quod Cometa tum temporis
in loco sui circuli versaretur, qui minimum a stella distaret, eamque ad angulos rectosA aspiceret, unde etiam per aliquot horas ex motu proprio Cometae nulla pene
sensibilis ingerebatur intercapedinum differentia, ideoque distantia saltem
ratione parallaxeos, si qua fuisset, tam in diversis dissitisque Horizontibus,
quam in eodem, ubi plurimum mutatae forent stellae altitudines, necessario
sensibiliter variari debebat, cuius tamen contrarium ab utroque nostrum pulchra
et exquisita convenientia deprehensum est, ut vel hoc solo argumento convinci
possit, Cometam illum longe supra Lunae orbes in ipso aethere sedem sibi
delegisse. Atque haec de hoc ultimo Cometa tecum nunc brevibus contulisse
sufficiat. Id saltem commonefactionis loco subiungam, declinationem lucidioris
stellae in capite Pegasi a te 8 proximeA scrupulis iusto maiorem assignatam esse. Nos enim aliquoties hîc, ubi
Polus elevatur 55 p. 54 2/3 m., eius altitudinem maximam
deprehendimus 38 p. 20 m. exquisite. Ideoque ab Aequatore declinat p. 4 m. 14½ , sive quadrantis tui parvitas ususque non satis exactus, sive Pragensis poli elevatio, quam tu a veteribus minus
forte scrupulose traditam pro vera recipis, sive etiam in utroque horum aliquis
lateat error, quem tibi ipsi examinandum corrigendumque relinquo. De certitudine
enim nostrae observationis ne in uno quidem scrupulo haesitamus. Pari ratione nos
eodem die 13. Cometae ipsius, ex altitudine meridiana, quae a nobis deprehensa est
p. 37 m. 7½, declinationem 3 g. 2 m. ideoque 5 minutisA tua minorem observavimus. Differentiam
meridianorum, cum vix maior sit quadranteA horae, insensibiliter uno saltem scrupulo declinationem ob motum Cometae
proprium variantem, volens praetereo. Non tamen poterit haec declinationum inter
nostras observationes differentia superiori convenientiae, quam parallaxeos
exiguitatem comprobavimus, fidem derogare. Illic enim per distantias, non per
altitudines fiebat observatio. Et licet per quadrantem etiam Cometae et stellae
distantiam, ex differentia utriusque altitudinis maximae dimensus fueris, tamen
utut in Poli altitudine aliquis error lateat, vel in quadrante ipso etiam
observationi iustae aliquid desit, cum in utroque loco tam in Cometa quam in
stella utraque eodem modo se habeant, in ipsa Cometae et stellae distantia
sensibilem errorem ingerere non poterint. In declinationibus vero utriusque
eliciendis, hac ratione deviareA (ut prius ostendimus) nihilominus erat possibile. De toto autem hoc negotioA brevi, Deo conatus nostros auspicante, per ocium
hybernum observationes plurimas easque certissimasA,varijs demonstrationibus elaboratas, in medium producam, quibus tum novae
illius stellae tum utriusque Cometae subsequentisA motus, apparentias, parallaxes et a Terra distantias, intelligentibus
certissimis et infallabilibus rationibus proponam, conferendo etiam praecipuas
aliorum observationes, et quatenus veritati consonae sint vel ab hac devient, in
trutina revocando, adeo ut universaliter tandem concludere non dubitavere,
Cometas omnes in ipso aethere, non Elementari regione, ut hactenus
Peripateticorum autoritate frustra creditum est, generari; nihil obstante, quod
REGIOMONTANUS et VOGELINUSA in duobus Cometis diversum quid prodiderint. Utrumque enim
a scopo deviasseA, rationes probabiles et sufficientes in medium producam, nisi quis sola
autoritate pugnare velit, negans humanum esse errare, interdumque bonus quod non
dormitet HOMERUS. Quod veroA hactenus propositum illum laboremA non absolverim, et desiderio multorum nostras observationes hisque
innixus apodicticas conclusiones avide desiderantium non satisfecerim, in causa
fuerunt plurima negotia, quibus tum Regis tum consanguineorum et amicorum
nobilium causa interea temporis implicitus eram. Inprimis vero Architectonicae
curae et in machinis Astronomicis exquisite elaborandis assiduae occupationes me
pensum inchoatum continuare et absolvere non permittebant. Spero tamen huic
procrastinationi, Deo volente, brevi cum faenore satissactum iri. Sed videor
Epistolae metas, diutius tecum de hac materia, qua te delectariA scio, conferendo, transcendisse, quam tamen prolixitatem tibi non
ingratam esse confido. Tuum erit id quicquid estA, boni consulere, et si quid praeterea, vel ex proprijs, vel aliorum praecipuorum placitis tibi de hac materia constiterit, vel
scriptis editum fuerit, benevole mecum communicare, nostrique memoriam, uti facis, conservare, et amicitiam literis non tam diu,
ut hactenus, intermissis, renovare. Efficiam vicissim, ut nihil in me, quod ad
candidi et constantis amici munus pertineat, uspiam a te desiderari possit.Vale.Datae UranienburgA in Insula Danici
