text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Thaddaeus Hagecius.**

Greeting.

A whole year is now nearly elapsed, dearest Master Doctor Thaddaeus, most distinguished man, since I last wrote to you — and that by way of **Paulus Wittich** of Wrocław, as he was returning home from here. But because in the meantime I have received no letter from you — when that mutual goodwill with which we once embraced one another at the **Diet of Regensburg**, and that affection toward your friends which is inborn in you and constant, by no means admits so long a delay in writing back — I could not but suspect that those letters had not reached your hands through the man to whom they had been entrusted. And what makes me now incline rather to believe just that is your little book on the latest comet, which **Bartholomaeus Scultetus** — bound to me by an old friendship from Leipzig — saw to it, two days ago, that it should be conveyed to me by way of a certain man who was bringing us from there [Leipzig] some spagyric [chemical] vessels we had hired [or: ordered]. For since in this writing you seem to want my opinion concerning the parallaxes of both comets, derived from sure observations — an opinion which nevertheless at that earlier time I disclosed to you plainly, and (as I hope) no less truly, in brief — I judge that it cannot have happened that those letters were delivered to you, as I had hoped. For I cannot persuade myself that you — a man both eager for these matters and understanding of them — so suddenly forgot the things I had signified in that letter (even if no occasion for writing back had meanwhile presented itself), or that you wholly neglected them.

Now the things which at that time I unlocked to you in that letter about the last two comets, from our observations, and which I now again set forth for your judgement, are roughly of this kind: In the comet which began to shine in the year [15]77, from all our observations — which were sought out with great diligence by means of various instruments exquisitely wrought from solid metal and exactly capable of [reading] single minutes [of arc], and were reduced to numbers by a varied method of demonstration — I never found that parallax, the one that occurs at the horizon, to have reached at most a third part of one degree, but very often it proved much less than this, as I shall sufficiently demonstrate to the understanding, in its proper place, by various arguments. And whereas in the little book then published about the same comet you had granted a parallax of 5 degrees [partium], and on that account had judged that comet to be sublunar, I warned you as a friend in those same letters that the method of **Regiomontanus** for investigating parallaxes — which you assert you used — although demonstrable enough, is nonetheless less adequate and suited to so subtle a business. For many things which are truly demonstrated speculatively, if they be carried over into practice and the mechanical handling of the senses, will stray very far from the mark aimed at — especially where, as happens in this case, the things that are greatest are investigated from the least. Nay, even if that speculation of Regiomontanus had had some place here, and an interval of time taken exactly enough had agreed with altitudes and azimuths duly given (in each of which, however — even though great and exquisite instruments be at hand, which yet are seldom ready — to be captured exactly with the precision that is fitting, how much diligence is needed, and how much difficulty befalls those not well practised, no one can persuade himself save one who has long and assiduously laboured in this mechanical wrestling-school of astronomy) — nonetheless, from so narrow an interval of time, which you assumed to be only 18 minutes [scrupulorum], it was impossible sensibly to discern parallaxes that in so little time vary imperceptibly. And so, while it seemed [good] to evade the hindrances of the proper motion by the brevity of time, the whole matter was reduced to a kind of impossibility. We, to be sure, have more than twenty times resolved into numbers that method of Regiomontanus for discerning parallaxes, from various and sufficiently sure observations, with no slight labour (as you know). But nowhere did we find a parallax as great as the Moon admits even when most remote from the earth — and very often none at all. And therefore I could not subscribe to your verdicts, even when I had used the same method (although less adequate to so very subtle a business) as you did.

Nor was it even possible to confirm the parallax by that very thing which you add for its corroboration — namely from the [comet's] culmination [coeli mediatione] together with the bright star of the Vulture [Altair]. For even if their simultaneous transit across the meridian, which then took place in the daytime, had been observable, no one will by any reasoning gather a parallax from this, unless more data were present — as through carelessness you taught, less considerately, amid your other occupations, in your *Dialexis*. But that the parallax of that comet not only was not so great, but was not even much perceptible, is attested by your own observations, in which you found that, over the distances of the comet from the mouth of Pegasus, with several hours intervening, [the distance] nevertheless varied very little — so that in truth on that account it can be proved, even by your own observations (to which, however, you were admitting contrary [conclusions]), that the parallax, if there was any, was tiny, and that the comet far exceeded [was far beyond] the orb of the Moon. These things, I say, I wrote out to you at that time about the earlier comet.

But I see that in this latest writing you agree with us, and that — having considered the contradictions which at that time you were not noticing — you have recalled your opinion and have found more inwardly the kernel of the matter to be investigated; on which I heartily congratulate you and the lovers of truth (who could be drawn by an abuse of your authority, and by less exquisite observations and demonstrations, to subscribe to the false opinion of the Peripatetics about comets). As for **Scultetus's** demonstrations, which inferred nearly the same parallax as you, since they rest on an uncertain foundation and are built upon false data (for, to say nothing of other matters, it was impossible that the comet should have stood that day, above the horizon, in the same vertical circle with those fixed stars which he assumes; and the distance of the stars too, which he presupposes, is in error by more than ¾ of one degree — so that from this one may easily gather what is to be thought of the rest) — we shall plainly show, in its proper place, that they are by no means to be accepted for the investigation of the truth.

But as far as concerns this latest comet, which shone in the year [15]80, you seem to me to have struck the mark itself far more exactly, and to have demonstrated the truth of the matter more plausibly with surer observations. In which I would wish at least this much, for a more inward investigation toward exquisite precision: that you had not neglected the change of the comet's proper motion between two observations. For since the comet, in the interval of two hours that day, shifted its place by 27′ in its own circle (the daily motion having indeed been found by us [to be] 5°23′), I judge this difference not to be passed over, if the matter is to be treated precisely, since in this case we reason about far greater things from the least. The instrument too, on this account, with which you take the altitudes — since it admits of at least ten or five minutes [of error] — can by no means be adequate in so subtle an inquiry. Yet your observations, and the demonstrations resting on them, are of such a kind that, even if from these it cannot be made out exactly to a hair how many minutes the parallax was, and in which of the celestial orbs precisely that comet moved, nevertheless that it was so great that it did not pass beneath the regions below the Moon [Lunae inferiora] — this they will be able to persuade, without difficulty, anyone skilled in these matters.

As far as concerns our observations of this comet, I indicated my opinion at that time no less than I now [indicate it] to you by letter — namely, that throughout the whole time of [its] apparition, from observations diligently made and examined with all our most exquisite instruments of various kinds, I was nowhere able to perceive any notable parallax of this comet. For, to be silent about the rest (to be recalled in a more convenient place), I certainly found that comet to have held exactly the same declination from the Equator both on the Meridian, when it was highest, and near the Horizon, at the very point of the western Azimuth — except insofar as the proper motion, proportional to the daily motion, varied it in the meantime, which could by no means have happened, given so great a difference of altitudes, if any sensible quantity of parallax had been present. This very thing too we certainly found to behave plainly in the same way, both by all the reasonings set forth by Regiomontanus in his little book that would have application here, and by certain others, more exact and less liable to error, devised by us concerning the measurement of parallaxes — as I shall demonstrate at leisure, copiously and with firm reasonings, to those who understand the mathematical sciences.

I have also, on receiving your little book, compared several things with our observations, and in them I found a marvellous agreement, which could serve to confirm the certainty of the parallaxes. For on 13 October, when the comet was near the Meridian, I found its distance from the brighter [star] of the head of Pegasus — both by the cross-staff [radius] and by the **Astronomical Sextant** (a particular instrument invented by us with such a contrivance that by it the intervals of stars are taken far more easily, conveniently, and exactly than by the cross-staff) — to be 1° 16′, greater than your distance by only one minute [scrupulo], almost imperceptible; which difference, however, for this distance of the terrestrial orb, would have grown to as much as the fifth minute [scrupulum] if the comet had been at the very convexity of the orb of the Moon — and far more, if it had blazed either in the fiery region (supposing there were any) or in the uppermost part of the air, as all the Aristotelians long falsely supposed. So too on 21 October, when the comet was nearest the bright star of the Eagle [Altair], standing over that star from the zenith [a vertice imminens], I found exactly the same distance as you. For although at the 8th hour this seemed to us one minute less, yet, continuing this observation up to the tenth [hour], it appeared exactly 6° 22′ — which agrees admirably with your annotation. And just as it could by no means have happened that, in the interval of at least two hours, that distance of the comet from the fixed star should vary by one minute, if a quite sensible parallax had been present, so too no one understanding the mathematical sciences will be persuaded that some body lower than the Moon could, in the interval of 6 degrees of the terrestrial orb — which lies between your observation-place and ours — at the same time precisely hold the same distance from the fixed stars.

Moreover, on that day the wished-for convenience of the [comet's] coma presented itself for examining the parallaxes against the star of the Vulture [Altair], because the comet was then situated at the place of its own circle which was least distant from the star, and looked toward it at right angles; whence too, for some hours, scarcely any sensible difference of intervals was introduced by the proper motion of the comet — and therefore the distance ought necessarily to have varied sensibly by reason of parallax at least (if there had been any), both in different and far-apart Horizons, and in the same [Horizon], where the altitudes of the stars would have changed very much. Yet the contrary of this was found by both of us, with a fine and exquisite agreement — so that even by this single argument it can be proved that that comet chose its seat for itself far above the orbs of the Moon, in the aether itself. And let it suffice to have now conferred with you briefly thus much about this latest comet.

This much at least I will add by way of admonition: that the declination of the brighter star in the head of Pegasus has been assigned by you nearly 8 minutes [scrupulis] greater than is right. For we, several times here — where the Pole is elevated 55° 54⅔′ — have found its maximum altitude to be exactly 38° 20′. And therefore it declines from the Equator 4° 14½′ — whether [the cause be] the smallness of your quadrant and a use not exact enough, or the elevation of the Prague pole, which you, perhaps less scrupulously handed down by the ancients, receive as true, or whether also some error lurk in both of these — which I leave to you yourself to examine and correct. For concerning the certainty of our observation we do not hesitate even by a single minute. By the like reasoning, we on the same 13th observed the declination of the comet itself, from the meridian altitude — which was found by us [to be] 37° 7½′ — [to be] 3° 2′, and therefore 5 minutes less than yours. The difference of the meridians, since it is scarcely greater than a quarter of an hour, [and] the declination varying imperceptibly by at least one minute on account of the comet's proper motion, I willingly pass over. Yet this difference of declinations between our observations cannot detract from the credibility of the agreement above, by which we proved the smallness of the parallax. For there the observation was made by distances, not by altitudes. And although by the quadrant too you measured the distance of the comet and the star from the difference of each one's maximum altitude, nevertheless — whatever error may lurk in the altitude of the Pole, or whatever may be lacking to a correct observation in the quadrant itself — since in both places, both in the comet and in each star, they behave in the same way, they cannot introduce a sensible error into the distance of the comet and the star itself. But in eliciting the declinations of each, to deviate in this way (as we showed before) was nonetheless possible.

Now concerning this whole business I shall shortly — God favouring our endeavours — bring forth into the open, during the winter leisure, very many observations, and those most certain, elaborated with various demonstrations; in which I shall set forth, to the understanding, by most certain and infallible reasonings, the motions, appearances, parallaxes, and distances from the Earth both of that new star and of each of the two subsequent comets — comparing also the principal observations of others, and, insofar as they are consonant with the truth or deviate from it, calling them back into the balance [weighing them]; so that I shall not have hesitated at last to conclude universally that all comets are generated in the aether itself, not in the Elementary region, as has hitherto been believed in vain on the authority of the Peripatetics — notwithstanding that **Regiomontanus** and **Vögelin** put forth something different concerning two comets. For I shall bring forth into the open probable and sufficient reasons that each of them deviated from the mark — unless someone wish to fight by authority alone, denying that to err is human, and [denying] that sometimes even good **Homer** nods.

But that I have not hitherto finished that work I proposed, and have not satisfied the desire of the many who eagerly long for our observations and the apodictic conclusions resting on them — the cause of this has been very many affairs in which I was meanwhile entangled, on account both of the King and of my noble kinsmen and friends. But above all, architectural cares and continual occupations in exquisitely elaborating astronomical machines [instruments] did not allow me to continue and finish the task begun. Yet I hope that this procrastination, God willing, will shortly be made good with interest. But I seem to have overstepped the bounds of a letter, by conferring with you so long about this material, in which I know you take delight — a prolixity which nonetheless I trust is not unwelcome to you. It will be for you to take in good part this, whatever it is; and if anything besides has become established for you about this material — whether from your own [findings] or from the verdicts of other eminent men — or has been published in writing, to share it with me kindly, and to preserve, as you do, the memory of us, and to renew our friendship by letters not interrupted so long as hitherto. I, for my part, will bring it about that nothing pertaining to the office of a candid and constant friend can anywhere be found wanting in me by you.

Farewell.

Given at Uraniborg, on the Island of the Danish Hellespont, Hven, on 12 October, the year 1581.

T[uus]. Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus Hagecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayck, 1525–1600), Prague physician, astronomer, and imperial counsellor to Rudolf II; the leading Bohemian observer of the 1572 nova and the comets of 1577 and 1580, and Tycho's principal Prague correspondent. His *Dialexis de nova et prius incognita stella* (1574) and his comet tract are both referenced below.
- **Sender's self-naming.** The letter opens with the heading "TYCHO BRAHE AD THADDAeUM HAGECIUM" run together with the first word "ANNUS" in the transcription; reproduced as printed. The subscription "T.TYCHO BRAHE" is read **T[uus] Tycho Brahe** ("Your Tycho Brahe").
- **Persons named.**
 - *Paulus Witichius Wratislaviensis* = **Paul Wittich** of Wrocław (Vratislavia), the mathematician who had visited Hven in 1580 and carried Tycho's earlier (now-apparently-lost) letter homeward. (Tycho's later coolness toward Wittich postdates this letter.)
 - *Bartholomaeus Scultetus* = **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (Barthel Schultz, 1540–1614) of Görlitz, mathematician and cartographer, Tycho's friend "from Leipzig"; he forwarded Hagecius's tract. His own cometary demonstrations are criticised below.
 - *Regiomontanus* = **Johannes Müller of Königsberg** (1436–1476), whose method of determining cometary parallax (in *De cometae magnitudine longitudineque*) Hagecius had used.
 - *Vogelinus* = **Johannes Vögelin** (Vogelin, d. 1549), Vienna mathematician, author of a tract on the comet of 1532 (*Significatio cometae … 1532*), here paired with Regiomontanus as a predecessor who reached a non-aethereal result.
 - *Homerus* = **Homer**; the closing tag *bonus … dormitet Homerus* echoes Horace, *Ars Poetica* 359 (*indignor quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus*), "I am vexed whenever good Homer nods" — i.e. even the greatest authorities sometimes err.
- **Works referred to.**
 - *libellus tuus de ultimo Cometa* — Hagecius's tract on the comet of 1580, identified in the literature consulted (Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*; Norlind) as his *Apodixis physica et mathematica de cometis* (1581), forwarded by Scultetus.
 - *libello … de eodem Cometa edito* (with the 5° parallax) — Hagecius's earlier tract on the comet of 1577, his *Descriptio cometae … 1577* (Prague, 1578).
 - *tua Dialexi* — Hagecius's *Dialexis de nova et prius incognita stella* (Frankfurt, 1574), here cited for a careless inference about parallax from culmination.
- **The astronomical substance (the central crux of the Tychonic comet programme).** Tycho rebuts Hagecius's 1578 finding of a **5° parallax** for the 1577 comet (which would place it *sublunar*, in the Aristotelian "elementary region"). Tycho's own instruments give a horizontal parallax of *at most ⅓ of a degree, often much less, sometimes none* — proving the comet was **supralunar, in the aether**. The argument is the same anti-Peripatetic one Tycho would publish in his comet book (*De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis*, 1588).
- **Technical terms (editorial glossary–5.2).** *parallaxis* → parallax; *altitudo* → altitude; *azimuthus* → azimuth (kept); *declinatio* → declination; *Aequator* → Equator; *meridianus* → meridian; *coeli mediatio* → culmination (the star's transit of the meridian); *orbis Lunae* → orb of the Moon; *aether / aethere* → aether; *Elementaris regio / regio ignea* → Elementary region / fiery region (Aristotelian sublunary physics); *motus proprius* → proper motion; *motus diurnus* → daily motion; *circulus verticalis* → vertical circle; *a vertice* → from the zenith. **Instruments:** *Radius* → cross-staff (radius astronomicus); *Sextans Astronomicus* → Astronomical Sextant (Tycho's own bipartite-arc sextant, here advertised as his invention); *quadrans* → quadrant; *instrumenta e solido metallo … singulorum minutorum adamussim capacia* → instruments of solid metal capable of single arc-minutes.
- **Units of arc.** *gradus / partes* (here "degrees"); *scrupulum / minutum / scrupulorum* are arc-minutes (or, with "18 scrupulorum," minutes **of time** for the observation-interval — note the ambiguity at the *18 saltem scrupulorum* passage: in context "an interval of time … of only 18 minutes" it is **time**-minutes; elsewhere *scrupulum* is **arc**-minutes). Figures are reproduced exactly as written: parallax "5 partium" (5°); proper motion "27′" in two hours; daily motion "5° 23′"; Pegasus-distance "1° 16′"; Altair-distance "6° 22′"; pole-elevation of Hven "55° 54⅔′"; star max-altitude "38° 20′"; star declination "4° 14½′"; comet meridian altitude "37° 7½′"; comet declination "3° 2′."
- **Greek.** *parallaxeωs* (line: "si sensibilis aliqua parallaxeωs adfuisset quantitas") — the genitive of *parallaxis* written with a Greek-letter ending (-εως) embedded in the Latin word; reproduced as printed, translated "of parallax."
- **Stars (period star-names → modern identification).** *lucida Vulturis / Vulturis stella* = "the bright star of the Vulture" = **Altair** (α Aquilae; "Vultur volans" was the classical name); *lucida Aquilae* = "the bright star of the Eagle" = likewise **Altair**; *os Pegasi / lucidior capitis Pegasi* = "the mouth / brighter [star] of the head of Pegasus" = **Enif** (ε Pegasi). The comet's position is fixed by its distances from these.
- **Place-formula.** *Uranienburg in Insula Danici Hellesponti Huaena* = "Uraniborg, on the island of the Danish Hellespont, Hven" — Tycho's standard conceit, the Øresund as the "Danish Hellespont." *Comitia Ratisbonensia* = the **Diet of Regensburg** (1575), where Tycho and Hagecius had met in person.
- **Editorial apparatus markers in the source.** The transcription carries scattered superscript "A" sigla attached to words (e.g. *ex conductoA, tibiA, indicoA, eamA, illaA, parallaxinA, … BRAHE.A*). These are **lemma-anchors of the critical edition's variant apparatus** (recording readings of MSS A and B), **not** part of Tycho's text. Per this chapter's convention(2) they are reproduced **as printed** in the Source block, but are **not** rendered in the translation. Likewise the source's *fi* (for *si*) and *satissactum* (for *satisfactum*) are retained as printed; *satissactum* is an evident typographic doubling for *satisfactum* ("made good/satisfied"), translated accordingly.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 12. Octobris Anno 1581* — Old Style (Julian; Denmark kept O.S. until 1700). This **agrees** with the catalogue label (1581.12.oktober). The in-text observation dates "13. Octobris," "21. Octobris" are likewise O.S. and refer to October 1580 (the apparition of the comet "which shone in the year [15]80"), not 1581; no silent correction made. No in-letter date discrepancy.
- **Correction.** Restored the epistolary salutation formula S. (Greeting), printed by Dreyer between the heading and the letter's opening word (TBOO VII p.64) but absent from our source Latin and English; added to both texts.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Full visual collation against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.64-69 . Checked opening and closing lines and every proper name, number, date, and place-name: Paulus Wittich of Wrocław, Diet of Regensburg (Comitiis Ratisbonensibus), Bartholomaeus Scultetus of Leipzig, Regiomontanus, Vogelinus/Vögelin, Homerus; the parallax figures (1/3 degree max, 5 partium, 18 scrupulorum, >20-fold [vicesies] recomputation, 27' motion / 5°23' daily rate, 10-or-5-minute instrument tolerance, 1°16' and 1' and 5' differentials, hour 8 vs hour 10, 6°22', 6-degree terrestrial baseline, nearly-8'-declination error, pole elevation 55°54⅔', max altitude 38°20', declination 4°141⁄2', comet altitude 37°71⁄2', declination 3°2', 5' difference, quarter-hour meridian gap, plus-3/4-degree Scultetus error); the dates 12/13/21 October 1581 and the closing date-line "12 October 1581". All of these render Dreyer's printed text accurately with no fabricated, dropped, or flipped content, and the bracketed editorial glosses (e.g. [Altair]) are clearly marked supplements per the audit's own exclusion rule, so not counted. The single defect found is the dropped opening "S." salutation-formula word, present in Dreyer but absent from our transcribed original and consequently untranslated — a genuine text error by the letter's strict definition, though of no substantive consequence. This is an unusually clean letter; the published grade Probable undersold rather than oversold it on substance, but the letter-of-the-rule text error caps the grade at C.

**1 defect found:**
- **text error** (low). Dreyer prints a standalone "S." (the epistolary salutation formula, "greeting") between the heading and the letter's opening word; our transcribed original omits this word entirely, so the published English also carries no trace of it. Trivial and formulaic — it adds no propositional content — but it is a verified, word-level discrepancy between our Latin and Dreyer's print. Dreyer prints: *TYCHO BRAHE AD THADDAEUM HAGECIUM. S. [then decorative initial] ANNUS integer...*.

**Repaired.** Verified the single defect directly against the Dreyer page image (TBOO VII p.64, line 4), which shows HAGECIUM. followed by a standalone S. on its own line before the decorative initial A(NNUS). The rest of the letter (pp.64-70, 7 pages) was and carried no other listed defects, so no other changes were made per the prime rule.

documents.abstract: Reports receiving Tycho's letter, regrets his own was not delivered, and defends Wittich, who conveyed Tycho's letter faithfully and invited Hagecius to join him on Hven.

text.original:
NOBILITATE GENERIS, VIRTUTE ET DOCTRINA PRÆSTANTI AC MATHEMATUM ILLUSTRATORI EXIMIO D. TYCHONI BRAHE DANO, INSULÆ HUÆNÆDANICI HELLESPONTI PRÆSIDI, DOMINO ET AMICO OBSERVANDO.
S.

ACCEPI literas tuas, Vir Nobilissime et amice observande, quæ fuerunt et gratissimæ et exoptatissimæ. Sed cum ex eis intellexissem meas tibi non fuisse redditas, vehementer conturbatus sum, cœpique quiritari de iniqua sorte, quod ea utrique nostrum invidit illam iucunditatem, quam percepturi eramus, tu quidem legendo mea, ego sciendo, mea tibi reddita esse. Fuisset etiam liberatus sinistra suspicione apud te WITTICHIUS noster, quod tuas mihi non reddidisset, qui certe non solum primo quoque tempore fidelissime tuas mihi per certos homines reddidit, verum etiam literis suis mihi persuadere annisus est, ut me transferrem isthuc, invitabatque ut comes esse vellem sui ad te reditus. Addebat ad persuadendum te ex certa scientia et voluntate Regis ea ad me perscribere ac daturum fuisse ipsummet Regem literas invitatorias ad me, si prius ipsi per te de mea certa voluntate constitisset, quam nunc solum per tuas literas explorare voluit. Hæc vero etsi in tuis ad me non ita diserte perscripta et expilata essent, tamen persuasiones illas ab optimo et propensissimo eius erga utrumque nostrum animo proficisci accipiebam. Tuas quoque rationes, quod ab eodem animo proficiscerentur, admittebam omniaque illa interpretabar, ut verum amicum decuit. Quare carere debes hac in parte omni sinistra suspicione de WITTICHIO nostro. Præstitit enim officium boni viri et amici fidelissimi. Me vero respondisse ad tuas mense Februario anni præteriti, testis esse potest D. CHYTRÆUS. Ad ipsum enim meas ad te misi, et ut eas ad te perferendas curaret, rogavi. Respondit mense Aprili anni superioris se meas accepisse et ad te primo quoque tempore et commoditate missurum esse. Intercidisse igitur meas inter Rostochium et Hafniam oportuit, si alicui perferendæ datæ sunt. Hæc tu ipse, si ita lubet, ex ipsomet D. CHYTRÆO cognoscere poteris. Quod ad invitationem attinet, ut me transferam isthuc, ardua et difficilis est quæstio. Ac primum quæso te, mi TYCHO, expende ipsemet accuratius et verte omnes rationes, quam mihi ea difficilia sint factu. Sum ingravescente ætate; ago enim annum 56. Sum pater multorum liberorum. Commigrare igitur in alienas terras et quasi spontaneum exilium eligere, ubi et mores gentis et lingua peregrina est, profecto difficile, durum et miseriâ plenum est. Addo neque honorificum mihi et meis futurum esse absque honesta et decenti vocatione in alienas terras migrare. Quid enim aliud vestrates dicturos aut saltem suspicaturos esse cogitare possum, quando me non vocatum venisse ad vos conspicerent, quam me hinc vel eiectum vel egestate compulsum alienas quæsivisse sedes? Quid nostrates? Levem et inconstantem parumque prudentem, quod me unius hominis amica invitatione tam facile permoveri passus sim, incerta pro certis elegerim, verba honoris pro amplissimis rebus acceperim. Dicent etiam haud dubie temerarium et inconsideratum, et qui conditionis et existimationis suæ nullam scirem habere rationem, quod qui olim Cæsaris Medicus fuerim, honeste et decenter accitus; qui ante quinquennium a Rege Sueciæ, deinde ab ordinibus Stiriæ expetitus, cui etiam, si voluissem aut vellem, locus fuerit, et esse possit adhuc apud Regem Poloniæ, denique qui huius Regni nobilis civis sum, nunc sponte et temere extra patriam ultro sedes quæram et servitium expetam. Ac ut tandem finiam, migrare ad vos honorifice non vocatus, non propositis mihi certis conditionibus, plane non videtur consultum, non meæ ætatis est, non conditionis, non dignitatis. Excurrere vero ad te, ut præclara illa tua studia Chymica et Mathematica meis oculis conspicerem, teque præsentem complecterer, et in tuo amore totus conquiescerem, percuperem sane, nisi in eo quoque non paucæ essent difficultates et quidem graves: iter longum et difficile, sumptus non exigui, denique excursio illa nimis magna esse videretur. Sed si aliqua commoditas veniendi isthuc et redeundi se offerret, prætermittere eam nulla ratione vellem. Nunc quoque impedior cura uxoris meæ, quæ partui vicina est. Vides, mi TYCHO, meas iustas et honestas rationes, quibus impediar et detinear, ut neque tuæ benevolentiæ, quam ego summam et optimam esse erga me agnosco, neque meo desiderio satisfacere queam. Itaque pro tuo isto erga me optimo et benignissimo animo, cura et solicitudine mei, quod mihi optima cupias, omniaque officia amoris et benevolentiæ sponte deferas, tibi maximas, quas verbis exprimere licet, ago et habeo gratias, vicissimque tibi persuasissimum esse cupio, me ita amore tui incensum esse, ut si liceret tecum esse, reliquum meæ vitæ iucundissimum putarem, tuaque causa nihil non facturum esse.

Hæc fere in prioribus meis ad te scripseram, quæ quoniam alicubi perijsse intelligo, denuo repetere hisce oportuit. Venio ad alteram Epistolæ tuæ partem. Gratulor tibi vehementer istud otium Mathematicum, in quo te versari intelligo. Macte virtute, mi TYCHO, et in hoc cursu, ut cœpisti, studium illud Astronomicum illustrare perge. Ephemeridem Solarem huius anni ex tuis observationibus exstructam accepi, et pro ea maximas tibi ago gratias. Mihi tantæ magnitudinis instrumentum nullum est, ut singula scrupula capere possit, neque in meis ædibus ea mihi est commoditas, ut etiamsi tale quid habeam, collocare queam. Quadrante hactenus meo usus sum in meis stellarum et Cometarum observationibus. In eo dena et quina habentur scrupula. Radium satis magnum habeo, de quo hauddubie WITTICHIUS noster tibi significavit. Ad Solem igitur nullæ mihi fuerunt observationes.Placet quod in Sole habeas rationem parallaxeos, quam huc usque omnes neglexerunt. WITTICHIUS noster eam quoque minime prætermittendam esse censuit. In Apogeo Solis video te tribus circiter gradibus anteriorem esse Copernico. Sed variatio Apogei etiam plurium graduum non mutat notabiliter motum Solis, in cuius Apogei constitutione laborarunt summi Artifices. De Cometarum parallaxibus quæ perscripsisti, ea quoque plurimum grata et iucunda fuerunt. In parallaxi Cometæ anni 77 meum lapsum iam ante agnovi et memet correxi. Nam non ita instructus fui instrumentis idoneis, quam olim Viennæ in observatione novi sideris. Defuerunt mihi etiam multæ aliæ commoditates. Ac tu optime admones ex meo ipsius scripto longe minorem parallaxin fieri oportuisse, quemadmodum huius erroris in Epistola ad MYLIUM et in scripto de proximo Cometa Gœrlitij impresso mentionem feci. Quod culminaverit cum Aquila, non ita a me scriptum est, quasi id a me fuisset observatum (nam culminatio illa Sole supra Horizontem exstante fuerat) sed quod saltem crassiori quadam indagine, collata cum alijs observationibus, de parallaxi aliquo modo iudicium fieri posse existimaverim. Scripsit autem alius quidam ineptus et meus plagiarius, culminasse Aquilam cum Cometa die 6 Decemb. h. 5. Ceterum quæ ego in mea Dialexi olim cap. 9 de invenienda parallaxi ex culminatione Phænomeni cum aliqua stella fixa scripseram, ea iamdudum correxi, ac caput 7,9 et 1O plane mutavi. Illustravi etiam aliquot problemata DIGGSEI et alia adieci tum mea, tum a WITTICHIO accepta. Et certe hæc doctrina parallaxium mediocriter per nos illustrata est, de quo tamen tuum et aliorum intelligentium erit iudicium. Librarius solum nunc nos moratur, qui nostra illa imprimere vetat. Et ut admirandi illius novi sideris Historia ad posteros transmitteretur, non tantum nostra illa de parallaxibus adiungentur meæ Dialexi, sed omnium aliorum scripta nostræ sententiæ consentientia. Titulus libri erit talis, ut hic in charta descriptum vides. Vellem tuas quoque observationes Cometarum prodire, fuitque hæc causa, cur eas in meo proximi Cometæ scripto desideraverim. Nam quod æthereus fuerit uterque Cometa, id iam ante ex tuis ad me intellexeram, ideoque iam ante, ipso adhuc lucente Cometa, ad multos perscripseram. Proxima quadragesima fui Vratislaviæ apud meam filiam et commoratus sum illic ultra mensem. Mea de parallaxibus cum WITTICHIO contuli, qui mecum communicavit vestras observationes proximi Cometæ, quas habuistis diebus XI, XII, XIII et XVII Octob. Ex his ego experiri volui, in deductione calculi aberraverim, an momenta observationum non recte abs te aut a WITTICHIO consignata sint. Nam ex vestris illis datis ne verisimile quidem in parallaxibus omnibus illis diebus quicquam invenire potui. In altitudinibus Cometæ inter nos alias satis recte convenit. Relinquitur igitur, ut momenta temporum minus recte assignata fuerint. Et certi temporis consideratio hac in parte valde est difficilis. Subduc quæso tuum calculum et omnia accuratius considera meque admone. Ego ipse quoque, modo aliquid otij nactus fuero, denuo repetam calculum et vestra examinabo. Nam eorum in meo opere facere cupio mentionem, ut nostra sententia de Cometis in animis eruditorum eo magis confirmetur. Quod si post discessum isthinc WITTICHIJ aliquot dierum alias quoque habes illius Cometæ observationes, eas mecum communicato.

B. V.
Pragæ ex ædibus nostris die 1. Maij Anno 1582.
T. ex animo
THADDÆUS HAGECIUS
ab Hayck.
text.english:
**To Master Tycho Brahe the Dane, eminent in nobility of birth, in virtue, and in learning, and an outstanding adorner of the mathematical sciences, governor of the island of Hven in the Danish Hellespont, his lord and friend to be honoured — greeting.**

I have received your letter, most noble Sir and friend to be honoured, and it was both most welcome and most longed-for. But when I gathered from it that mine had not been delivered to you, I was greatly distressed, and began to lament my unjust fortune, in that it had begrudged both of us the pleasure we were to have had — you in reading what I wrote, I in knowing that my letter had been delivered to you. Our friend Wittich, too, would have been freed from any sinister suspicion in your eyes of not having delivered your letter to me — he who assuredly not only delivered yours to me most faithfully at the first opportunity, by trustworthy men, but also strove by his own letters to persuade me to remove myself thither, and invited me to be willing to be a companion of his return to you. He added, by way of persuasion, that you were writing this to me from sure knowledge and at the King's wish, and that the King himself would have given letters of invitation to me, had it first been established for him through you concerning my settled willingness — which he now wished only to ascertain through your letter. And although these things had not been set out and unpacked so explicitly in your letter to me, nevertheless I took those persuasions to proceed from his most excellent disposition, most kindly inclined toward us both. Your own reasons too I admitted, as proceeding from the same disposition, and I interpreted all those things as became a true friend. Wherefore on this point you ought to be free of any sinister suspicion regarding our Wittich; for he discharged the office of a good man and a most faithful friend. That I did indeed answer your letter in February of last year, Master Chytraeus can be a witness. For I sent my letter to you by his hand, and asked him to see to its being carried on to you. He replied in April of last year that he had received my letter and would send it on to you at the first opportunity and convenience. It must therefore be that my letter went astray between Rostock and Copenhagen, if it was indeed given to someone to carry on. These things you yourself, if you so please, will be able to learn from Master Chytraeus himself. As regards the invitation, that I should remove myself thither — it is a hard and difficult question. And first I beg you, my Tycho, weigh it yourself more carefully and turn over all the considerations of how difficult these things are for me to do. I am of advancing years, for I am in my 56th year. I am the father of many children. To migrate, then, into foreign lands and as it were to choose a voluntary exile, where both the customs of the people and the language are strange — that is assuredly difficult, harsh, and full of misery. I add that it would be neither honourable for me and mine to migrate into foreign lands without an honourable and fitting summons. For what else can I think your people would say, or at least suspect, when they saw that I had come to you uninvited, than that I had either been cast out from here or driven by want to seek a dwelling abroad? And what would my own people say? — That [I am] fickle and inconstant and little prudent, in that I let myself be so easily moved by one man's friendly invitation, that I chose uncertainties for certainties, that I took words of honour for the most ample rewards. They will say too, without doubt, that [I am] rash and inconsiderate, and one who knew to take no account of his own station and reputation — that I, who was once the Emperor's physician, honourably and fittingly summoned; who five years ago was sought after by the King of Sweden, then by the Estates of Styria; for whom too, had I wished or were I to wish it, there was a place, and could yet be one, with the King of Poland; and finally I, who am a noble citizen of this Kingdom — that I should now, of my own accord and rashly, go out beyond my homeland unbidden to seek a dwelling and beg for service. And to make an end at last: to migrate to you, not honourably summoned, with no fixed conditions set before me, plainly does not seem advisable; it is not suited to my age, nor to my station, nor to my dignity. But to make an excursion to you — that I might behold with my own eyes those splendid Chymical and Mathematical studies of yours, and embrace you in person, and rest wholly in your love — that I should indeed greatly desire, were there not in this too difficulties, and grave ones: a long and difficult journey, no slight expense, and finally that excursion would seem too great an undertaking. But if some convenient opportunity of coming thither and returning should present itself, I would by no means wish to let it pass. Now too I am hindered by concern for my wife, who is near her delivery. You see, my Tycho, my just and honourable reasons, by which I am hindered and held back, so that I can satisfy neither your kindness — which I acknowledge to be the greatest and best toward me — nor my own longing. And so, in return for that most excellent and most kindly disposition of yours toward me, your care and solicitude for me, in that you wish me the best and unprompted offer me every office of love and goodwill, I give and hold the greatest thanks that words can express; and in turn I wish you to be most fully persuaded that I am so kindled with love of you that, were I permitted to be with you, I would deem the rest of my life most delightful, and that there is nothing I would not do for your sake.

These things, more or less, I had written in my earlier letter to you, which, since I understand it perished somewhere, it has been needful to repeat anew herewith. I come to the other part of your letter. I congratulate you heartily on that Mathematical leisure in which I understand you to be engaged. Go on and prosper in virtue, my Tycho, and in this course, as you have begun, press on to illustrate that Astronomical study. I have received the Solar Ephemeris of this year, constructed from your observations, and for it I give you the greatest thanks. I have no instrument of such size that it can take in the single minutes [of arc], nor in my house is there the convenience that, even if I had some such thing, I could set it up. Hitherto I have used my quadrant in my observations of the stars and comets. On it are reckoned tens and fives of minutes. I have a fairly large cross-staff (*radius astronomicus*), of which our Wittich has doubtless informed you. To the Sun, therefore, I have had no observations. I am pleased that for the Sun you take account of parallax, which up to now everyone has neglected. Our Wittich too judged that it should by no means be passed over. In the apogee of the Sun I see that you are about three degrees in advance of Copernicus. But a variation of the apogee, even of several degrees, does not notably change the motion of the Sun, on the establishing of whose apogee the greatest craftsmen have laboured. What you have written about the parallaxes of the comets was also most welcome and delightful. As to the parallax of the comet of [15]77, I already acknowledged my slip before this and corrected myself. For I was not so furnished with suitable instruments as I once was at Vienna in observing the new star. Many other conveniences too were lacking to me. And you rightly point out that, from my own writing, a far smaller parallax ought to have resulted — just as I made mention of this error in the *Letter to Mylius* and in the tract on the recent comet printed at Görlitz. That [the comet] culminated together with Aquila was not so written by me as though it had been observed by me (for that culmination occurred while the Sun stood above the horizon), but [I wrote it] because I reckoned that at least by some rougher line of inquiry, compared with other observations, some judgment about the parallax could in some way be made. But a certain inept fellow, and my plagiarist, wrote that Aquila culminated together with the comet on 6 December, at the 5th hour. As for the rest — what I once wrote in my *Dialexis*, chapter 9, on finding parallax from the culmination of a phenomenon together with some fixed star — that I corrected long ago, and I have wholly changed chapters 7, 9, and 10. I have also elucidated several of Digges's problems, and added others, both my own and ones received from Wittich. And indeed this doctrine of parallaxes has been moderately well elucidated by us — though on that the judgment will rest with you and with others who understand. The printer alone now delays us, who forbids those things of ours to be printed. And so that the History of that admirable new star may be transmitted to posterity, there will be joined to my *Dialexis* not only those writings of ours on parallaxes, but the writings of all others that agree with our view. The title of the book will be such as you here see written out on the [enclosed] sheet. I should wish your observations of the comets too to come out, and this was the reason why I missed them in my tract on the recent comet. For that each comet was ethereal, that I had already understood beforehand from your letters to me, and therefore had already, while the comet was still shining, written to many. This past Lent I was at Wrocław with my daughter, and I stayed there above a month. I compared my [findings] on parallaxes with Wittich, who shared with me your observations of the recent comet, which you took on the 11th, 12th, 13th, and 17th of October. From these I wished to test whether I had gone astray in working out the calculation, or whether the moments of the observations had not been correctly recorded by you or by Wittich. For from those data of yours I could not find anything even plausible in the parallaxes on all those days. In the altitudes of the comet we otherwise agree well enough between ourselves. It remains, therefore, that the moments of time were less correctly assigned. And the consideration of exact time is in this respect very difficult. Work out your calculation, I beg, and consider everything more carefully, and advise me. I too, as soon as I have got some leisure, will repeat the calculation anew and examine your [observations]. For I desire to make mention of them in my work, so that our view about comets may be the more confirmed in the minds of the learned. But if, after Wittich's departure from there, you have other observations of that comet for some days, share them with me.

Fare you well.
At Prague, from our house, the 1st day of May, the year 1582.
Yours from the heart,
Thaddaeus Hagecius
ab Hayck.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayck* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (1525–1600), physician, astronomer, and astrologer; personal physician to Emperor Maximilian II and then Rudolf II at the Prague court. He and Tycho had met in 1575 at Rudolf's coronation as King of the Romans; he was Tycho's chief Bohemian correspondent. It was Hagecius who in July 1580 sent **Paul Wittich** to Hven with a letter of recommendation. The letter answers an invitation (conveyed via Wittich, allegedly with royal — i.e. Imperial — backing) to settle near Tycho, which Hagecius here declines.
- ***INSULAe HUAeNAe DANICI HELLESPONTI PRAeSIDI*** — "governor of the island of Hven in the Danish Hellespont": a learned flourish for Tycho as lord of **Hven** in the Øresund (cast as the "Danish Hellespont," the strait); *praeses* rendered "governor." The capitalised salutation reproduces the manuscript's display capitals; *D.* = *Dominus* ("Master/Lord,").
- ***WITTICHIUS noster*** = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586), the Silesian mathematician from Wrocław who spent some months on Hven in 1580 and later carried Tychonic methods to Kassel. "Our Wittich" (*noster*) marks him as the friend common to both. The whole opening turns on a lost-letter misunderstanding: Tycho suspected Wittich of not delivering a letter; Hagecius exonerates him.
- ***Regis … literas invitatorias*** — "the King('s) … letters of invitation." The "King" (*Rex*) is **Rudolf II** (Holy Roman Emperor, also styled King of Bohemia / of the Romans); the proposal was that Tycho settle, or be invited, under Imperial auspices. Rendered "King" literally, as the source has *Rex* (not *Caesar* / *Imperator*) here; that Hagecius styles himself *Caesaris Medicus* below ("the Emperor's physician") confirms the same sovereign is meant.
- ***D. CHYTRAeUS*** = **David Chytraeus** (1530–1600), the Rostock theologian and professor, here the intended forwarding intermediary for Hagecius's earlier (lost) letter, which therefore "went astray between Rostock and Copenhagen" (*inter Rostochium et Hafniam*; Rostock → Copenhagen,).
- **Hagecius's refusal — career résumé.** *olim Caesaris Medicus* = "once the Emperor's physician"; *a Rege Sueciae … ab ordinibus Stiriae expetitus* = sought "by the King of Sweden" (**John III of Sweden**) and "by the Estates of Styria"; *apud Regem Poloniae* = a place possible "with the King of Poland" (**Stephen Báthory**); *huius Regni nobilis civis* = "a noble citizen of this Kingdom" (Bohemia). He pleads age (*ago annum 56* — "in my 56th year"), many children, and his wife "near her delivery" (*partui vicina*).
- **Astronomy — solar theory.** *Ephemeridem Solarem … ex tuis observationibus exstructam* = "the Solar Ephemeris … constructed from your observations." *rationem parallaxeos … in Sole* = Tycho's reckoning of **solar parallax** "which up to now everyone has neglected." *In Apogeo Solis … tribus circiter gradibus anteriorem … Copernico* = Tycho's value for the **apogee of the Sun** ("apse,") is "about three degrees in advance of Copernicus." Glossary renderings (parallax, apogee, motion) used throughout.
- **Instruments.** *Quadrante … meo* = "my quadrant," reading "tens and fives of minutes" (*dena et quina … scrupula*) — i.e. graduated only to 5′; *scrupulum* (arc-minute) rendered "minute [of arc]." *Radium satis magnum* = "a fairly large **cross-staff** (*radius astronomicus*),". *singula scrupula capere* = an instrument fine enough "to take in the single minutes."
- **The comet-parallax controversy (the technical core).** *Cometae anni 77* = the great **comet of 1577**. Hagecius concedes his earlier *lapsus*: his published parallax ( c. 5°, which would place the comet sub-lunar) was too large; he had already corrected himself, having lacked good instruments — "not so furnished … as once at Vienna in observing the new star" (*novum sidus* = the **nova of 1572**, the subject of his *Dialexis*). *Epistola ad MYLIUM* = his published *Letter to Mylius*; *scripto … Goerlitij impresso* = his comet tract printed at **Görlitz** (*Goerlitium*). *culminaverit cum Aquila* = the comet's culmination "together with [the constellation/star] Aquila" — Hagecius stresses this was a computed/inferred datum (the culmination fell while the Sun was up, so it was not directly observed), a "rougher line of inquiry" (*crassiori … indagine*). *alius quidam ineptus et meus plagiarius* = "a certain inept fellow, and my plagiarist," who misreported the culmination on 6 December at the 5th hour — left unnamed in the source and so here.
- ***Dialexi … cap. 9 … caput 7,9 et 1O*** — his *Dialexis* (1574, on the 1572 nova); he has revised chapter 9 (and recast chapters 7, 9, 10) on deriving parallax from a phenomenon's culmination with a fixed star. *1O* is printed with a capital-O for the zero/numeral; read "10." *problemata DIGGSEI* = problems of **Thomas Digges** (*Diggseus*, c. 1546–1595), the English mathematician, from his *Alae seu scalae mathematicae* (1573) on the 1572 nova.
- ***Librarius … imprimere vetat*** — "the printer (*librarius*) … forbids those things of ours to be printed": publication of his enlarged collection (his *Dialexis* + others' parallax writings agreeing with his view, prefaced by a *Historia* of the new star) is being held up by the bookseller-printer. *Titulus … ut hic in charta descriptum vides* = the proposed title was written out on a sheet enclosed with the letter (not preserved in the text).
- **The 1582 comet collation.** *proximi Cometae* = "the recent comet" (the comet of **1580**, the most recent before this letter). *aethereus … uterque Cometa* = "each comet was ethereal" (super-lunary) — Hagecius had already accepted this from Tycho's letters. *Proxima quadragesima … Vratislaviae* = "this past Lent … at **Wrocław**" (*Vratislavia*), with his daughter. There Wittich shared **Tycho's observations of the comet on 11, 12, 13, and 17 October**. Collating them, Hagecius could find "nothing even plausible" in the parallaxes; since the altitudes agreed, he infers the recorded **times** (*momenta temporum*) were imprecisely assigned — "the consideration of exact time is in this respect very difficult." He asks Tycho to recompute and to send any further observations made after Wittich left Hven.
- **Subscription.** *B. V.* = *Bene vale*, "Fare you well". *T. ex animo* = "Yours from the heart" (*T.* = *Tuus*). *ab Hayck* = the family name *z Hájku*, kept as written.
- **Calendar / place.** *Pragae … die 1. Maij Anno 1582* = "at **Prague** … the 1st day of May 1582." Denmark and Bohemia were both still on the **Julian calendar** in May 1582 (the Gregorian reform took effect only that October), so the date is **O.S.** with no Julian–Gregorian gap at issue. The header date matches the dateline; the edition label ("1582. 1. maj. Prag") agrees — no discrepancy.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VII pp.69-72 read as page images. Collated the full Latin the transcribed original against the printed text sentence by sentence: salutation heading, every proper name (Wittichius/Wittich, Chytraeus, Mylius, Digges/Diggsei, Vienna, Görlitz/Goerlitium, Wrocław/Vratislavia, Rostock, Copenhagen/Hafnia, Sweden/Suecia, Styria/Stiria, Poland/Polonia, Aquila), every number and date (age 56, five years/quinquennium, three degrees apogee, comet of [15]77, 6 December hour 5, Dialexis chapters 7/9/10, the four October observation dates XI/XII/XIII/XVII, 1 May 1582 dateline), and the opening and closing lines all match Dreyer exactly (allowing for long-s/ligature typography only). Then checked the published English against the Latin clause by clause: no invented facts, no dropped sentences, no flipped pronouns/antecedents, no hardened hedges, all bracketed English supplements are clearly marked. One trivial artifact noted but not counted as a defect: our stored the transcribed original renders 'caput 7,9 et 1O' with a capital letter O in place of the digit 0 (Dreyer prints '10'); this is a typographic glyph slip with no semantic effect and the English translation correctly reads 'chapters 7, 9, and 10', so it does not rise to a reportable text error.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE THADDÆO AB HAYCK S.

REDDIDIT mihi ante aliquot septimanas Gœrlicius quidam Mercator literas tuas, clarissime Domine D. THADDÆE, amice carissime, ex quibus præter singularem tuam et constantem erga nos benevolentiam intellexi etiam priores meas ad tuas manus secus ac suspicabar pervenisse. Unde WITTICHIUM satis ea in re nunc excusatum habeo. Saltem id admiror, quod nihil literarum a discessu suo elapso tempore ad me dederit. Sed habet is forte sua impedimenta, neque occasio facile in promptu est. Quare et hac in parte nihil ipsi imputo. Cum vero is qui tuas mihi attulerat, nunc ad me reversus sit, ut responsum, prout ipsi etiam iniunxeram, tibi reportaret, ego quamvis eo tempore id evenerit, quo maxime ad scribendum ob negociorum multitudinem impeditus sim, et a Serenissimo Rege nostro insuper avocer, non potui tamen intermittere, quin aliquid literarum tibi perferendum ipsi traderem, ne tui oblitus tibique rescribere data opera neglexisse apud te excusari possem. Quæ itaque tuis literis pro hac brevi occasione temporis respondenda habui, sic brevibus accipe.

Quod adventum tuum ad nos prolixe excusas, tibi ea in re non plurimum contrarior, neque ego aliam ob causam nomine Regis te huc invitavi, quam quod a WITTICHIO intelligerem officio in Aula Imperatoris destitutum cogitare de alia eligendæ vitæ et sustinendæ familiæ ineunda ratione, adeo ut iam quoque a Rege Sueciæ te vocatum esse dixerit. Cum vero ex proprijs tuis literis intelligam, res tuas non esse eo loco, ut patriam mutare alienoque Domino servire velis, nihilque tibi ad commodam vivendi rationem deesse in patria, tibi plurimum congratulor, et meam voluntatem, quod tibi, si opus fuisset, non deesse voluerim, ut boni consulas oro.

Quod de Apogeo ☉ scribis restitutionem nostram accedere propius Alphonsinorum rationibus, quam COPERNICI, ego sane ea in parte nullum habui respectum neque ALPHONSI neque COPERNICI; sed ex plurimis exquisitis observationibus Geometrice ad invicem collatis iuxta quartam partem ♋ hærere Apogeum (quam interdum una parte minus, interdum una plus) reperi, ut quamvis ex minimis hîc inquirantur maxima. Eccentricitatem vero multoties in eodem, quo assignavi, scrupulo reperi, novem minutis Coperniana maiorem. Et licet eccentricitas maxima ex parte prosthaphæreses variet, præsertim iuxta medias elongationes, tamen circa Apogeum et Perigeum intolerabilis est duarum vel trium partium loci, sub quo hæret Apogeum, error.

Quod lapsum in Cometa anni 77 et quosdam alios in Dialexi emendaveris, libenter audio. Id vero quod de culminatione Cometæ cum Aquila in excusationem adducis, mihi non satis facit. Impossibilia enim non erant ad probandum tentanda neque excusationem ullam merentur; sed emendanda potius et revocanda, partim propter imperitos, partim propter invidos et malevolos. Scribis te editurum copiosius scriptum de Nova Stella et Cometis præteritis, ubi intelligo, te etiam mea quædam velle adiungere, a quo tamen, si impressum non est, quantum ad mea attinet, ut supersedeas, te rogatum velim. Ipse enim decrevi, quam primum licuerit, quædam enucleatius et de Nova Stella (ubi pleraque festinanter scripta restitui, multa copiosius in demonstrationum certitudinem adduxi) et de subsequentibus præcipuis duobus Cometis, tum etiam de tertio illo non adeo illustri, qui hoc anno mense Maio in Septentrione sub Heniochi sidere per IO dies nobis apparuit, in lucem emittere observationefque certas in medium adducere et infallibilibus demonstrationibus rem omnem tum in motu et situ eorum, tum in parallaxibus comprobare. Nam quod quasdam observationes hîc habitas in Cometa anni 80 a WITTICHIO acceperis, et inde parallaxes indagare conatus fueris, oleum et operam perdidisti. Tempora enim ex diversis horologijs et ijsdem nondum satis correctis annotata erant, nec illam discretionem adhibueras, quænam certiora alijs essent, et quæ sibi invicem in quolibet horologio corresponderent, multo minus ut per transitus stellarum sive per Meridianum sive per certum Azimuth, prout necessarium erat, et a nobis postea factitatum est, ea corrigeres, adeo ut ob id pluribus minutis ubique fere aberratum sit, ut mirum esse non debeat, quod tantam in parallaxibus constituendis inconvenientiam, ob temporum incertitudinem inveneris. Ego vero etsi tempora omnia aliter correcta habeam, quam prima fronte præbebant ipsa horologia, tamen in parallaxibus indagandis longe certiori nitor ratione, quam ubi temporis opus sit intervallo. Ibi enim ex minimo peneque insensibili errore maximus et intolerabilis augmentatur. Ideoque alijs quibusdam rationibus, ubi exquisita temporis cognitio non requiritur, inquisivi, tam hunc quam antecedentem Cometam (in tertio enim nondum feci periculum, nec adeo facile erit possibile) pene insensibilem habuisse parallaxin, quemadmodum hæc et alia quædam sufficienter ex certis observationibus demonstrari intelliges, ubi libellus noster de tota hac materia in lucem prodierit, quem spero me per hybernum otium, Deo conatus nostros adiuvante, absoluturum. Velim itaque nihil mearum observationum in publicum edas, priusquam hinc certior factus fueris, quænam sit mea de his sententia, a qua te plurimum abesse et temporibus incertis minimeque correctis inniti video, et mirari satis non possum WITTICHIUM tibi tempora observationum transposita et per transitus stellarum minime verificata obtulisse, cum tamen ipsimet præsenti dixerim horologijs non esse fidendum, sed longe accuratiore emendatione opus esse. Quantum ad distantias fixarum indagandas attinet, ego non amplius fidem adhibeo Radio multas ob causas, quas longa foret mora hîc recensere. Sed post discessum WITTICHIJ duo exquisita instrumenta in hunc usum adinveni, quæ semper eandem distantiam in scrupulo præbent, adeo ut nec in defectu nec excessu aberrare possint. Oportet autem in utroque instrumento duos esse, qui observent. Et quamvis utrumque instrumentum ipsa fabricatione longe differat, tamen in quolibet eadem et sibi correspondens exquisite fit observatio. Sic nos per hæc invenimus distantiam polaris ab undecima Cassiopeæ p. 26 m. 25 exquisite (nisi quod aliquando dimidio scrupulo minor apparuit), quam tu 9 minutis maiorem collocas. Sic etiam in alijs discrimen inveni, de quo alio tempore tecum latius conferam. In declinatione Spicæ nullam differentiam inter tuas et meas observationes reperio. Nam et ego multoties hîc eius altitudinem maximam p. 25 m. 10¼ præcise observavi, ubi Æquator attollitur p. 34 m. 7, adeoque declinatio p. 8 m. 57 plane ut tua, quod errorem quartæ partis in æquinoctij præcessione Copernico hucusque irrepsisse convincit, posita eadem cum ipso latitudine, quam etiam exquisite duarum esse partium per alia instrumenta deprehendi, ut alibi hæc et plæraque alia copiose demonstrabo. Sed interim dum scribo, tempus me alio vocat, prohibetque, quantum velim, tecum colloqui. Dabo tamen operam, ut alia occasione oblata, copiosius de his atque alijs tecum agam. Vale, et mihi, cum licuerit, rescribere non intermitte. Verumtamen addam hoc unum, quod pæne neglexeram. Hisce diebus Comes quidam Anglus primarius Reginæ ad Regem nostrum Legatus, ut ipsum in ordinem Equitum Divi GEORGIJ honorifice consuetis ceremonijs reciperet, cum perfunctus esset sua apud Regiam Maiestatem legatione, me hic invisit, unâque inter cæteros Comites Medicum Doctorem THOMAM MUFETUM secum habuit. Is cum tui inter nos honorifica incidisset mentio, petijt ut tibi per occasionem datam suo nomine plurimam salutem dicerem tuumque filium, qui in Anglia est, recte habere indicarem.

Iterum feliciter vale.
Datæ Uranienburgi in Insula Huæna 23. Septemb. 1582.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Thaddaeus ab Hayck — greeting.**

A few weeks ago a certain merchant of Görlitz delivered to me your letter, most distinguished Master Thaddaeus, dearest friend, from which — besides your singular and constant goodwill toward us — I also understood that my earlier letter had reached your hands otherwise than I had supposed. So now in that matter I hold Wittich sufficiently excused. The only thing I wonder at is that he has sent me no letter at all in the time elapsed since his departure. But perhaps he has his own impediments, and an opportunity is not readily at hand. So in this respect too I impute nothing to him. And since the man who had brought me your letter has now returned to me, in order to carry back a reply to you, as I had also enjoined upon him — although it has fallen out at a time when I am most of all hindered from writing by a multitude of affairs, and am moreover called away by our most Serene King — I could not, even so, refrain from handing him at least some few lines to convey to you, lest I might be excused in your eyes as having forgotten you and deliberately neglected to write back. And so what I have had to answer to your letter, given this brief occasion of time, receive thus, in brief.

As to your excusing your coming to us at such length, in that matter I do not greatly contend against you; nor did I invite you here in the King's name for any other reason than that I understood from Wittich that, deprived of your office at the Emperor's court, you were thinking of entering upon some other plan of choosing a way of life and supporting your family — so much so that he said you had by now even been summoned by the King of Sweden. But since from your own letter I understand that your affairs are not in such a state that you would wish to change your homeland and serve another lord, and that nothing is wanting to you in your homeland for a comfortable manner of living, I congratulate you most heartily; and I beg you to take in good part my goodwill, in that I wished not to fail you, had there been need.

As to your writing that our restoration of the apogee of the Sun [☉] comes nearer to the reckonings of the Alphonsines than to those of Copernicus: I, for my part, in that matter had no regard either for Alphonso or for Copernicus; rather, from very many exquisite observations geometrically collated with one another, I found the apogee to lodge at about the quarter-point of Cancer [♋] (sometimes one degree less, sometimes one more) — so that here, indeed, the greatest matters are inquired into from the least. As for the eccentricity, I many times found it, at the very minute I had assigned it, greater than the Copernican by nine minutes. And although the eccentricity varies the prosthaphaereses in great part, especially about the mean elongations, yet around the apogee and perigee an error of two or three degrees in the place at which the apogee lodges is intolerable.

That you have corrected the slip concerning the comet of [15]77, and certain others, in the *Dialexis*, I gladly hear. But what you bring forward in excuse, concerning the culmination of the comet together with [the constellation] Aquila, does not satisfy me. For impossibilities ought not to have been attempted as if to be proved, nor do they merit any excuse; rather they are to be corrected and recanted — partly for the sake of the unskilled, partly for the sake of the envious and ill-disposed. You write that you are going to publish a fuller work on the New Star and on the comets past, where I understand that you also wish to append certain things of mine; from which, however — if it is not yet printed — so far as my own [matter] is concerned, I should wish you asked to forbear. For I myself have resolved, as soon as it shall be permitted, to bring into the light certain things more fully worked out, both concerning the New Star (where I have restored most of what was written in haste, and have carried much, more copiously, into the certainty of demonstrations) and concerning the two chief comets that followed, and then also concerning that third, not so conspicuous one, which this year in the month of May appeared to us in the North under the constellation of Auriga [Heniochus] for 10 days — and to bring forward sure observations into the open, and to prove the whole matter by infallible demonstrations, both as to their motion and place, and as to their parallaxes. For as to your having received from Wittich certain observations made here on the comet of [15]80, and having tried thereby to investigate the parallaxes — you have wasted oil and labour. For the times had been noted down from various clocks, and those not yet sufficiently corrected; nor had you applied that discrimination as to which were more reliable than others, and which corresponded with one another in any given clock — much less so as to correct them by the transits of stars, whether through the meridian or through a fixed azimuth, as was necessary, and as has since been done by us — so that on this account there has been error of several minutes almost everywhere; so that it ought to be no wonder that you found so great an inconsistency in establishing the parallaxes, on account of the uncertainty of the times. But I, although I have all the times corrected otherwise than the clocks themselves presented them at first appearance, nevertheless in investigating parallaxes rely upon a far more reliable method than where there is need of an interval of time. For there, from the least and almost imperceptible error, the greatest and intolerable one is magnified. And therefore by certain other methods, where exquisite knowledge of the time is not required, I have found that both this comet and the preceding one (for on the third I have not yet made the test, nor will it easily be possible) had an almost imperceptible parallax — just as you will understand these and certain other things to be sufficiently demonstrated from sure observations, once our little book on this whole matter shall have come into the light, which I hope, God assisting our endeavours, to complete during the winter's leisure. I should wish, therefore, that you publish nothing of my observations before you have been made more certain from here what my own opinion on these matters is — from which I see you are very far removed, and that you rely on times that are uncertain and by no means corrected; and I cannot wonder enough that Wittich offered you observation-times that were transposed and by no means verified by the transits of stars, since I had nevertheless told him myself, in person, that the clocks were not to be trusted, but that there was need of a far more accurate correction. As regards investigating the distances of the fixed stars, I no longer place faith in the cross-staff [*Radius*], for many reasons that it would be a long delay to recount here. But after Wittich's departure I devised two exquisite instruments for this use, which always yield the same distance to the [arc-]minute, so that they cannot err either in deficiency or in excess. It is necessary, however, that on each instrument there be two persons observing. And although each instrument differs greatly in its very construction, yet on either one the same and mutually corresponding observation is exquisitely made. Thus by these we have found the distance of the pole star from the eleventh star of Cassiopeia to be exquisitely 26 degrees 25 minutes (except that sometimes it appeared less by half a minute), which you place greater by 9 minutes. So too in other cases I have found a discrepancy, of which I shall confer with you more fully at another time. In the declination of Spica I find no difference between your observations and mine. For I too have many times here precisely observed its greatest altitude to be 25 degrees 10¼ minutes, where the equator is raised 34 degrees 7 minutes, and so the declination [is] 8 degrees 57 minutes, plainly as yours — which proves that an error of a quarter[-degree] in the precession of the equinox has hitherto crept in upon Copernicus, the same latitude being posited with him as I have also exquisitely ascertained, by other instruments, to be of two degrees — as I shall demonstrate copiously, these and most other things, elsewhere. But meanwhile, while I write, the time calls me elsewhere, and forbids me to converse with you as much as I would wish. I shall nonetheless take pains, when another occasion is offered, to treat with you more fully of these and other matters. Farewell, and do not, when it shall be allowed, neglect to write back to me. Yet I will add this one thing, which I had almost overlooked. In these recent days a certain English Count, the Queen's chief ambassador to our King — sent to receive him honourably, with the customary ceremonies, into the Order of the Knights of Saint George — when he had discharged his embassy before His Royal Majesty, visited me here, and had with him, among the other companions, the physician Doctor Thomas Muffet. When honourable mention of you fell among us, he asked that, given the occasion, I should convey to you in his name his very warm greeting, and indicate that your son, who is in England, is doing well.

Again, fare you happily well.
Given at Uraniborg, on the island of Hven, 23 September 1582.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus ab Hayck* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayck, 1525–1600), Bohemian court physician and astronomer at Prague, the leading astronomical figure of Rudolf II's circle and Tycho's chief Bohemian correspondent. His *Dialexis de novae et prius incognitae stellae … apparitione* (Frankfurt, 1574) treated the 1572 nova, and he also published a *Descriptio* of the comet of 1577. (No structured person-profile is yet held for him; identification from the literature consulted — Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, and Dreyer, *Tycho Brahe*.)
- **Sender's address-formula.** *S.* = *salutem (dicit)*, "(sends) greeting".
- ***Goerlicius … Mercator*** — "a merchant of **Görlitz**" (the Lusatian town), the unnamed carrier who both delivered Hagecius' letter and was to bring back this reply.
- ***Wittichius*** = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586), the Wrocław/Breslau mathematician who had stayed several months on Hven in 1580 and who connected Hagecius and Tycho; Tycho here repeatedly faults the observation-*times* Wittich passed to Hagecius (see the parallax discussion). Tycho's irritation that the comet-of-1580 timings were "transposed and by no means verified by the transits of stars" is part of the larger Wittich-priority friction.
- ***Serenissimo Rege nostro*** — **Frederik II of Denmark** (r. 1559–88), Tycho's patron, in whose name Tycho had (per this letter) invited Hagecius to Denmark; *a Rege Sueciae … vocatum* refers to a reported competing summons from the King of Sweden (John III).
- ***Aula Imperatoris*** — the court of **Emperor Rudolf II** in Prague, the office from which Hagecius had reportedly been "deprived" (*destitutum*).
- **Astronomy — solar apogee.** *Apogeo ☉ … iuxta quartam partem ♋* — the apogee of the Sun lodging "at about the quarter-point of **Cancer**" (i.e. near Cancer 6¼°, *quarta pars* = the fourth part/quarter of the 30° sign). The glyph ☉ is named "Sun" and ♋ "Cancer" in the translation, the glyph kept in the source. *Alphonsinorum rationibus … Copernici* — the **Alphonsine** tables vs. **Copernicus**; Tycho insists he followed neither authority but his own observations. *quamvis ex minimis hîc inquirantur maxima* — rendered literally ("the greatest matters are inquired into from the least"), a sententious turn kept; *maxima/minima* not interpreted away.
- **Astronomy — eccentricity & prosthaphaeresis.** *eccentricitatem … novem minutis Coperniana maiorem* = "the eccentricity … greater than the Copernican by nine minutes." *prosthaphaereses* kept untranslated (Tycho's additive-subtractive correction; this chapter's convention); *medias elongationes* = "the mean elongations"; *circa Apogeum et Perigeum* = "around the apogee and perigee." *partium* and *minutis/scrupulo*: in this technical register *pars/partes* = **degree(s)** and *scrupulum/minutum* = **(arc-)minute** — rendered accordingly and noted here.
- **Comets.** *Cometa anni 77* = the great **comet of 1577**; *duobus … praecipuis Cometis* = the two chief comets (1577 and 1580); *tertio illo … qui hoc anno mense Maio … sub Heniochi sidere per IO dies* = a fainter third comet of **May 1582** seen "under the constellation of Auriga" for **10 days**. *Heniochi sidere*: *Heniochus* (Greek *Ἡνίοχος*, "the Charioteer") = the constellation **Auriga**; named in English, the Latinised Greek noted. ***IO dies***: the printed/transcribed form *IO* is the Roman numeral **10** (= *decem*); reproduced as printed in the Source block and read "10 days." *culminatione Cometae cum Aquila* — Hagecius' claim about the 1577 comet culminating together with **Aquila** (the Eagle), which Tycho rejects as an impossibility to be recanted, not excused.
- **Parallax method.** *oleum et operam perdidisti* = "you have wasted oil and labour" — the proverbial *oleum et operam perdere* (to waste lamp-oil and toil), kept as the idiom it is. *per transitus stellarum sive per Meridianum sive per certum Azimuth* = correcting clock-times "by the transits of stars, whether through the meridian or through a fixed azimuth"; *Azimuth* kept. *pene insensibilem … parallaxin* = "an almost imperceptible parallax" — Tycho's supralunary conclusion for the comets; the hedge *pene* ("almost") preserved.
- **Instruments.** *Radio* = the **cross-staff** (*radius astronomicus*), which Tycho says he no longer trusts for stellar distances. *duo exquisita instrumenta … duos esse, qui observent* — two newly devised instruments each requiring two observers; rendered descriptively (Tycho does not name them here).
- **Stellar measurements.** *distantiam polaris ab undecima Cassiopeae p. 26 m. 25* = "the distance of the **pole star** [*polaris*] from the **eleventh star of Cassiopeia**, 26°25′"; *quam tu 9 minutis maiorem collocas* = "which you place greater by 9 minutes." *declinatione Spicae … p. 8 m. 57* = the declination of **Spica** (α Virginis), 8°57′; *altitudinem maximam p. 25 m. 10¼ … Aequator attollitur p. 34 m. 7* = greatest altitude 25°10¼′, equator-altitude (co-latitude complement) 34°7′ at Hven. *errorem quartae partis in aequinoctij praecessione Copernico … irrepsisse* = Tycho's charge that "an error of a quarter[-degree] in the precession of the equinox has crept in upon Copernicus." *latitudine … duarum … partium* = the (ecliptic) latitude of Spica "of two degrees."
- **The English embassy.** *Comes quidam Anglus … in ordinem Equitum Divi Georgij* — the English embassy to install Frederik II in the **Order of the Garter** (the Order "of the Knights of Saint George"); the chief ambassador was **Peregrine Bertie, Lord Willoughby de Eresby** (the 1582 Garter mission). *Thomam Mufetum* = **Thomas Muffet** (Moffet/Moufet, 1553–1604), the English physician and entomologist, who accompanied the mission and visited Hven. *tuum filium, qui in Anglia est* — Hagecius' son then in England, whom Muffet reports to be well.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datae Uranienburgi in Insula Huaena 23. Septemb. 1582* = "Given at **Uraniborg**, on the island of **Hven**, 23 September 1582" (O.S. — Denmark kept the Julian calendar; this chapter's convention). The dateline date agrees with the edition label (1582-09-23); no discrepancy. The header carries the as-written date.
- **Orthography.** *THADDAeO / THADDAeE / Uranienburgi*: the source prints the *ae*-ligature form (*Ae*), reproduced as in the transcription. *observationefque*: the transcription's long-s reading of *observationesque* ("and … observations"), kept as printed in the Source block and read *-sque*. *negociorum, ijsdem, ijs, alijs, horologijs, parallaxin* are period spellings, normalised in sense only.
