documents.abstract: Acknowledges Dançay's letter, urges him to endure court intrigues with composure, and conveys greetings from Erik Lange.
documents.incipit: MAGNIFICE Domine DANZÆE, Amice summa observantia colende, reddidit Architectus meus mihi …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD CAROLUM DANZÆUM.

MAGNIFICE Domine DANZÆE, Amice summa observantia colende, reddidit Architectus meus mihi literas a te missas, quibus percepi te, licet inter politica negotia iam multum temporis apud Cimbros consumseris, nondum tamen Huenensium memoriam obliterasse, pro qua benevola erga nos affectione tibi magnas habeo gratias. Nos licet absentes tui memoriam indies recolimus, optamusque ut brevi incolumis ad nos revertaris. Quod Sycophantæ quidam aulici te vexent, oportet te magno animo ferre, et finem expectare, quo videbis omnia in ipsorum retundi caput. Hoc genus hominum delectatur aliorum afflictione, quam indies astute machinatur, ut sibi tandem perniciem (debitam mercedem) vel Deo ultore parent. Sed tute hoc nosti melius. Salutem quam ERICUS LANGIUS mihi per te dixit, velim ut ipsi referas, quamvis nunc eo felicitatis pervenerit (uti ab architecto meo intelligo) ut vix indigeat auspicatiore voto. Multiplicationem enim farinæ adinvenisse ferunt ab unitate in ternarium novo Alchymiæ mysterio, quo lapidis illius auriferi omnem fermentationem et multiplicationem (quibus tot annis insudatum est) excellentiore invento illudit; quis enim ignorat panis perpetuo sufficientem copiam, quæ ex ista multiplicatione promanat, auro et argento præstantiorem esse, cum his carere possint homines, illo autem nequaquam. Caveat itaque sibi ab Alchymistarum invidia et prospiciat, ne arti struant insidias, fermentumque peregrinum admisceant. Diu multumque mecum cogitavi, in quem usum panis potius quam auri et argenti augmentationem investigaverit; tandem incidit mihi in mentem Draconis illius Iutici, qui olim bellum civile ipsorum Patriæ movit, feruntque ob penuriam alimentorum in tanta militantium copia bellum illud Troiæ decennium excessisse, quod alias citius finiri potuisset magno illorum commodo; veritus itaque ne vetus ille Draco reviviscat vel novus aliquando ex improviso exoriatur, Patriæ suæ hoc utilissimo invento providere voluit. Laudo ipsius prudentiam et Patriæ eius congratulor, quod talem sibi genuerit protectorem et in commeatus penuria provisorem incomparabilem. Is rectissime mihi exequutus videtur Philosophorum mentem, qui nos non nobis sed Patriæ nasci asseverabant. Ego per occasionem congratulatorium carmen in laudem tanti mysterij ipsi compingam, siquidem Draconis illius memoriam tantæque victoriæ celebrationem amplius referre non liceat, cum in profundum maris tota ipsius recordatio sit submersa. Sed forsan te a serijs detineo, dum tecum de his diutius iocor. Da operam ut ad nos ante hyemem revertaris, magno enim tui desiderio detinentur, ut multi alij, sic vel ego maxime, qui te tanto temporis locorumque intervallo tuaque exoptatissima conversatione admodum illibenter careo. Deus opti. max. te nobis incolumem quam citissime restituat, tuaque omnia negotia optato successu secundet.

Vale.
Datæ in ædibus Uraniæ 21. Augusti 1583.
T. T.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Charles de Dançay.**

Magnificent Master Dançay, friend to be cherished with the utmost regard: my architect has delivered to me the letter you sent, from which I gathered that, although you have by now spent much time on political affairs among the Cimbri [Danes], you have nonetheless not yet blotted out the memory of the people of Hven — for which kindly affection towards us I owe you great thanks. We, though far off, daily call your memory to mind anew, and wish that you may soon return to us safe and sound. As for the fact that certain court flatterers vex you, you must bear it with a great spirit and await the end, in which you will see all of it beaten back upon their own heads. This kind of men delights in the affliction of others, which day by day they cunningly contrive, only that at last they may prepare destruction for themselves (their deserved wages) — or with God as avenger. But you yourself know this better [than I]. The greeting that Erik Lange sent me by your hand, I would have you carry back to him — although he has now reached such a pitch of good fortune (as I understand from my architect) that he scarcely needs any more auspicious wish. For they report that he has discovered the multiplication of flour, from unity into a threefold quantity, by a new mystery of alchemy, whereby, with this more excellent discovery, he makes a mockery of all the fermentation and multiplication of that gold-bearing stone [the philosophers' stone] over which men have sweated so many years; for who does not know that a perpetually sufficient supply of bread, such as flows from this multiplication, is more excellent than gold and silver, since men can do without these, but by no means without that? Let him therefore beware of the alchemists' envy, and take care that they lay no snares against the art, and mix in no foreign leaven. Long and hard did I ponder with myself to what use he should have investigated the augmentation of bread rather than of gold and silver; at length there came into my mind that Jutish Dragon, who once stirred up a civil war in their fatherland — and they say that, owing to a scarcity of provisions amid so great a host of fighting men, that war outran the ten-year war of Troy, though otherwise it might have been ended sooner, to their great advantage; and so, fearing lest that old Dragon should come back to life, or a new one some day arise unforeseen, he wished to provide for his fatherland by this most useful invention. I praise his prudence and congratulate his fatherland, that it has begotten for itself such a protector and, in a dearth of supplies, an incomparable provisioner. He seems to me to have carried out most rightly the mind of the Philosophers, who used to affirm that we are born not for ourselves but for our fatherland. As occasion serves, I shall compose for him a congratulatory poem in praise of so great a mystery — if indeed it be no longer permitted to recall the memory of that Dragon and the celebration of so great a victory, since the whole remembrance of it has been sunk into the deep of the sea. But perhaps I am keeping you from serious matters, while I jest with you too long about these things. See to it that you return to us before winter, for many others are held by a great longing for you, and so above all am even I, who most unwillingly do without you across so great an interval of time and place, and without your most-longed-for conversation. May God, Best and Greatest, restore you to us safe and sound as swiftly as may be, and prosper all your affairs with the success you wish.

Farewell.
Given in the House of Urania [Uraniborg], 21 August 1583.
Yours truly [Tuus Totus],
Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / place.** Tycho Brahe, writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven; *in aedibus Uraniae* ("in the House / dwelling of Urania") is Tycho's own learned name for the residence-observatory, rendered with the gloss.
- **Recipient.** *Carolus Danzaeus* = **Charles de Dançay** (c. 1510–1589), the long-serving French resident ambassador to the Danish court, a humanist and friend of Tycho; here evidently absent from Hven on diplomatic business "among the Cimbri."
- ***apud Cimbros*** — "among the Cimbri," a learned classicising name for the **Danes / the Danish (Jutland) realm**; kept and glossed, not modernised to "in Denmark."
- ***Architectus meus*** — "my architect": the builder/master-craftsman in Tycho's service at Uraniborg, who carried the correspondence; rendered "my architect" and treated as the recurring bearer of news.
- ***Sycophantae quidam aulici*** — "certain court flatterers / sycophants": *sycophanta* in this register = informer/flatterer/slanderer, not the modern narrow sense; rendered "court flatterers."
- ***Ericus Langius*** = **Erik Lange** (1553–1613), Danish nobleman and devoted alchemist, Tycho's friend (and later, through Sophie Brahe, his prospective brother-in-law), whose lifelong and ruinous pursuit of the philosophers' stone is the target of the whole satirical passage.
- **The alchemical satire.** The letter's core is sustained irony. *lapis ille aurifer* = the **gold-bearing stone**, i.e. the philosophers' stone; *fermentatio* and *multiplicatio* are technical alchemical operations (the "multiplication" or augmentation of the stone's power). Tycho's joke inverts the goal: Lange, he says, has discovered the *multiplicatio farinae* — the "multiplication of flour/bread" *ab unitate in ternarium* ("from unity into a threefold quantity," i.e. one part yielding three) — a feat better than gold-making, since men can live without gold but not without bread. The praise is mock-encomiastic throughout; *fermentum peregrinum* ("a foreign leaven") puns on alchemical *ferment* and the leaven of bread.
- ***lapidis illius auriferi … fermentationem et multiplicationem (quibus tot annis insudatum est)*** — the parenthesis ("over which men have sweated so many years") is Tycho's own aside on the futility of the long alchemical labour; preserved as a parenthesis, the hedge not sharpened into a flat verdict.
- ***Draco ille Iuticus*** — "that Jutish Dragon": an allusion (mock-heroic) to a legendary/historical episode of civil war in the Danish/Jutish past in which famine among the troops protracted the conflict beyond even the ten-year siege of Troy. The exact saga-referent is not specified in the letter; the comparison is rhetorical, and is left as Tycho frames it (see crux below). *in profundum maris … submersa* ("sunk into the deep of the sea") continues the mock-epic register: the memory of the dragon/victory is now lost.
- ***congratulatorium carmen*** — Tycho proposes, *per occasionem* ("as occasion serves"), to write a congratulatory **poem** for Lange in praise of the supposed discovery — itself part of the joke; rendered as prose intention (no verse is given in the letter).
- ***Philosophorum mentem, qui nos non nobis sed Patriae nasci asseverabant*** — "the mind of the Philosophers, who used to affirm that we are born not for ourselves but for our fatherland": a commonplace (ultimately Ciceronian/Platonic, *non nobis solum nati sumus*); kept as the sententious tag it is.
- **Subscription.** *T. T.* = ***Tuus Totus*** ("Yours wholly / entirely truly"); expanded in brackets in the rendering. *Vale* = "Farewell".
- **Calendar / dating crux.** The dateline reads ***21. Augusti 1583*** = **21 August 1583** (Old Style; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The edition label field, however, catalogues the letter as **"1583. 21. maj"** (21 May 1583). These disagree by three months. The header follows the **as-written dateline (21 August)** by this chapter's convention, with the catalogue date appended in parentheses; the identifier (…15830821001) likewise encodes August, corroborating the dateline against the label. The discrepancy is recorded, **not** silently reconciled — the source text substantiates only 21 August.
- **MS witness.** The witness is given only as a copy (*Afskrift*) in Tycho Brahe's private archive, Rigsarkivet, Copenhagen — i.e. a scribal copy, not an autograph original.

documents.abstract: Disapproves of Brucaeus's neglect of mathematical studies, praises his plan to expound Proclus's Hypotheses, and requests a copy, while noting those Hypotheses rest on imperfect Ptolemaic foundations.
documents.incipit: EX literis tuis nuper ad me datis, charissime D. D. BRUCÆE, intellexi te recte valere, id …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO D. D. HENRICO BRUCÆO.
S. P.

EX literis tuis nuper ad me datis, charissime D. D. BRUCÆE, intellexi te recte valere, id quod pergratum cognitu fuit. Quod vero studia Mathematica paulatim negligas, non probo. Nec enim tanta tibi est aetas, ut ea iucundissimam horum tractationem avertere possit, sed quaestuosior est vestra Medicina iuxta vetus dictum: Dat GALENUS opes etc. Et plerumque mortales quo plus senescunt, eo redduntur avariores, ac terrestribus plus proni inhiant, coelestibus posthabitis. Quod tamen nonnihil ad neglecta haec studia redire, et PROCLI Hypotheses explicare decreveris, laudo plurimum, velimque mihi exemplar Hypothesium illarum PROCLI mittas. Nondum enim Latinum habere potui, quamvis satis mihi constet, eas, siquidem Ptolemaicis nituntur fundamentis, coelo minime esse ad amussim consonas. Nos enim aliquot annorum praecedentium exquisitissimis in motu Solis observationibus deprehendimus, nec Ptolemaicam, nec Copernianam Hypothesin ipsius apparentijs satisfacere, longeque aliam esse Apogei et Eccentricitatis rationem, quam uterque horum artificum praesupposuit: ut brevi, Deo volente, ex quamplurimis ijsdemque minime fallacibus observationibus Astronomiae cultoribus palam reddemus. Motus enim Solis adeo exacte nobis constat, ut singulis diebus cum serenitas observationem ratam largitur, nostrae calculationi ex proprijs Tabulis in ipso scrupulo ad amussim correspondeat, differenti tam Alphonsina quam Coperniana ratione saepenumero quamplurimum, adeo ut hoc anno, Sole aequinoctium vernum ingrediente, defecerit in ipsius motu COPERNICI ratio semisse partis, abundaverit vero Alphonsinorum ratio partis quadrante. Paulo enim propiores nunc sunt Alphonsini vero, quam ipse COPERNICUS, quantum ad Solis motum attinet, quamvis ambo intolerabiliter devient. In motu vero Lunae verior est exactiorque Hypothesis COPERNICI. Idque tum crebrae observationes Lunaris cursus circa 90 gradum ab ortu, tum parallaxes ipsius diligentius a nobis examinatae nos saepenumero docuerunt; utut et hae non parum devient. Desideratur enim aliquid in medijs motibus. Et proportio semidiametrorum Epicycli utriusque ad semidiametrum Concentrici paulo aliter limitanda venit, et forte alia adhuc minus perspecta inaequalitas. COPERNICUS enim rudiori Minerva suas observationes perfecit destitutus magnis, exquisiteque e solido metallo elaboratis instrumentis, qualia nos quamplurima, tum varietate structurae, tum magnitudinis et elaborationis affabre et perfecte, ingenti sumtu, industriaque assidua parata habemus, adeo ut neminem etiam priscorum Mathematicorum, utut regijs sumtibus adiutorum (quatenus ex scriptis eorum colligere est) unquam ad coelestes motus perscrutandos tanta magnitudine diligentiaque elaborata organa in usu habuisse, si haec aspiceres, facile nobis concederes. Neoterici vero nec nostra nec superiori aetate necessariam in his elaborandis constructionis formam diligentiamque adhibuerunt, ut ob id mirum non sit, paulatim collabascere Astrorum scientiam, adeo ut ipsius motus nondum exacte constet, nec anni quantitas rata sit, ut nihil nunc dicam de ceteris. Verum in his omnibus alio tempore, Deo volente, tibi alijsque Eruditis nostras observationes et his innixas demonstrationes communicabo, instrumentorumque, quibus in motu coelestium corporum ad amussim perscrutando utor, structuram exactamque elaborationem indicabo, ut constare possit, observationes a nobis habitas, quibus fundantur demonstrationes, exactas esse, nullique fallaciae obnoxias. Nec enim unico, sed pluribus instrumentis, ijsdemque diversimode fabrefactis eandem veritatis metam attingere solemus, modo observationi fides rata habebitur. Si tibi commodum esset hac aestate nos invisere, forte hîc videres, quae frustra remotius quaereres, nec te poeniteret eius itineris, pergratumque mihi advenires hospes, omni officiorum genere excipiendus; tunc coram de quamplurimis colloqui conferreque possemus, afpiceresque ea praesens, quae calamus chartaque non capiunt. Petis, ut Instrumentum aliquod Hypothesium Copernicearum tibi mittam, quale olim apud SCHRECKENFUXIUM vidi, id quod lubens facerem, si tale paratum haberem, neque enim unquam animum adieci ad eiusmodi organa conficienda, quae saltem inventa aliorum explicarent, cum ex nuda delineatione ea facile percipi possint, et adhuc sub iudice lis est, an res ita se habeat, nec ne. Quapropter omnem potius operam impendi in extruendis organis, quibus motus coelestes exacte constarent, ut antecessorum inventa per haec in trutinam vocari possint et ad veritatis metas examinari. Quorsum enim opus erat in nondum satis perspecta re illustranda aliquid laboris et temporis impendere, cum praesertim haec alias leviori negotio facile intelligi possit? Vidi equidem apud SCHRECKENFUXIUM parvulam machinam, qua se Hypotheses COPERNICI effinxisse existimabat. Sed dum rem postea penitius perpenderem, deprehendi, eam structuram minime menti COPERNICI sufficere. Putabat enim is eadem machina, prout inveheretur diversimode, tam Ptolemaicas quam Copernianas Hypotheses exprimi posse, id quod plane est impossibile. Nec facile dabitur, omnes motus Copernianae inventionis unica machina mechanice exprimere, quae sibi ipsi omnibus in partibus correspondeat, praesertim ob incomparabilem Octavae Sphaerae ad orbem Terrae distantiam, utquamvis longe cincinnior sit, paucioribusque indigeat circulis COPERNICI speculatio circa mundi symmetriam quam Ptolemaica. Et per triplicem illum motum unius Terrae plurima in coelo apparentia concinne salvari possunt, quibus plurimi alias excogitati orbes, circulique vix sufficerent, dummodo res se re vera ita haberet, et tales ipsi Terrae congruerent revolutiones, quod nos in duobus motibus, quos huic attribuit COPERNICUS, diversimode se habere, exquisitis observationibus deprehendimus. Motum enim annuum in circulo magno circa Solem Terrae nequaquam adesse, expertus sum in fine anni elapsi 82 et principio 83 ex parallaxibus Martis tum temporis acronychij, et ob id Terrae in minori distantia vicini, quam Sol a Terra removetur, idque iuxta COPERNICI placita ad 1/3 quasi partem, unde maiores parallaxes, quam Sol ipse inducere debuisset, cum tamen longe minores fuisse, creberrimis exquisitissimisque et sibi invicem correspondentibus observationibus eas deprehendimus; ut ob id tota Martis sphaera ulterius removeatur a nobis, quam ipse Sol. Quapropter tollitur illa Hypothesis in totum, qua COPERNICUS Solis motum et Epicyclos omnes reliquorum Planetarum ex Terrae annuo circuitu ingeniose quidem et satis concinne ex ARISTARCHI Samij fundamentis in lucem productis excusare nititur. Alterum vero declinationis motum cum suis librationibus, per quem aequinoctiorum inaequalem anticipationem et obliquitatis Eclipticae mutationem excusat Copernicus, neque ipsi Terrae adesse, diversa, longeque celerior, aequinoctiorum mutatio, quam tantillo etiam tempore admittit COPERNICI ratio, nos certiores reddet, et anni quantitas a REGIOMONTANI observationibus huc usque Copernianae rationi nequaquam consentiens. Ut taceam obliquationem Signiferi etiam nunc esse trinis scrupulis maiorem quam COPERNICUS et antecessores nostri superiori aetate annotârunt. Causam erroris ex Opticis fundamentis alibi declarabo. Et de his omnibus alijsque quamplurimis ad artem ipsam restituendam, motusque coelestes ad amussim in numeros revocandos pleniorem commemorationem, Deo adiuvante, instituam. An vero tertius ille motus, quo quotidiana revolutio salvatur, Terrae et vicinis elementis insit, non facile quis dixerit: Cum eadem ratione in hac atque in primo mobili apparentiae tantae concitationis excusari possint, et minori quidem circuitu, ideoque commodiore cornpendio omnium sphaerarum secundi mobilis repentina ab ortu in occasum restitutio salvari, prout etiam Pythagoreis et Platonicis placuisse video. Verisimile tamen est, Terrae, tamquam gravissimo et densissimo opacoque corpori nequaquam hunc celerrimum inesse motum, sed potius ipsi coelo, cuius forma et materiae subtilitas constantiaque motui perpetuo et quamvis celerrimo aptior est. Frustra itaque expetis, charissime BRUCÆE, eorum in organo ob oculos planiorem repraesentationem, quorum in ipso coelo realis non existit forma. Sed tantum ingeniose ad salvandas aliqua ratione motuum apparentias a COPERNICO excogitata sunt. Si tamen Studiosos ipsius inventis imbuere voles, id per delineationem planam, quantum quidem opus est, facile perfeceris.

Sed est aliud, quod mea plurimum interest, de quo tecum agam. Conscripsi iamdudum quaedam de trium Cometarum intra proximum septennium visorum, et de Novae Stellae Phaenomenis, quibus motus omnes distantiasque et cetera, quae in considerationem veniunt, ex certis observationibus demonstro, et plurima alia tum ad hanc contemplationem tum ad totam artem facientia in medium profero, eaque tandem tum amicorum hîc in patria, tum plurimorum in Germania Angliaque solicitationibus persuasus in lucem edere constitui. Cum autem ob luem Epidemicam, multo iam tempore grassantem, non tutum fuerit, Hafniae apud Typographos nostrates quippiam eiusmodi expedire et nunc alijs quibusdam occupentur impressionibus, ut mature editionem hanc per eos absolvere non liceat, decrevi itaque ipsemet Typographiam quandam, quatenus proprijs meis lucubrationibus excudendis sufficiat, hîc Uraniburgi constituere, ut tam haec, quam alia, quae Deo volente in posterum absolvere conabor, Astronomiaeque cultoribus communicare, hîc penes meipsum Typis nostris mandari possint, eoque pacto figurae demonstrationum numerique et characteres, quibus, uti scis, in hac materia opus est, correctas certiusque adornari, et omnia a meipso ut emendate prodeant cognosci; siquidem pauci reperiantur, qui in his studijs exercitentur, et errores incidentes inter imprimendum rite discernere emendareque possint. Conduxi itaque hunc Typographicum servum, IOACHIMUM nomine, ut mihi hoc in negotio exsequendo inserviat, ablegavique illum nunc Witebergam, ut illinc mihi praelos, omniaque necessaria, quae hîc haberi nequeunt, comparet, cumque ipsi soli, nec mihi satis noto non adeo tutum sit pecuniam concredere, ad Scribam Arcis Witebergensis, cui nomen est VALENTINUS (cuius vitricus filias Regis nostri instituit, quique olim Witebergae familiaris mihi est) 50 Ioachimicos transscripsi, ut is illic exponat pro Typis alijsque ad opus pertinentibus, prout hic noster necessarium esse significaverit. Mitto itaque, charissime BRUCÆE, tibi 50 illos Ioachimicos, quos velim aurigae Witebergensi, quam primum ad vos venerit, tradas, ut is dicto Arcis Scribae VALENTINO eos unâ cum literis meo nomine perferat. Debet autem hic meus Typographus unâ Witebergam ire, vel potius praecedere, si auriga illic non adfuerit, illicque tam diu commorari, donec omnia necessaria ad Typographiam instituendam parata, huc per aurigam eundem abducere possit; si vero quid interea ad te literarum dederit, exigente forte id ipsum rei exsequendae conditione, rogo, ut confestim Hafniam ad Doctorem IOHANNEM FRANCISCUM transmittas, ut inde absque omni mora eas habere possim. Addidi etiam praeter illos 50 Witebergam mittendos, duos Thaleros, partim ut aurigae pro sua opera debitam mercedem hinc numerare possis, partim ut pro superfluo libellos quosdam Mathematicos mihi compares, quales nosti me expetere, ut Astronomica MÆSTLINI, si quae postea ad vos pervenere. Desidero etiam scriptum illud Germanicum MÆSTLINI, quod significasti ipsum edidisse contra restitutionem Calendarij Gregorianam. Cupio enim illud videre, si forte ipsius rationes in anni metis constituendis inde perspicere licuerit. Non usque adeo mihi displicet illa temporis reformatio a GREGORIO Pontifice noviter instituta: quamvis plurimi plus odio Pontificum quam veritatis amore huic contradicunt. Qua in re affectibus veritatis lumen offuscantibus nimium indulgent. Certum est scrupula illa, quae ad 6 horarum completionem deficiunt, super integros dies anni longo jam tempore Solstitia aequinoctiaque per plurimos dies anticipasse, ut non coincidant dies festi amplius cum constitutionibus primitivae Ecclesiae. Quam si rem penitius perspiciamus in Christiana Republica, nulla revera fit dierum differentia. Neque rerum externarum usus necessarius, ubi divinitus non mandantur. Vult enim vulgus contineri in officio, ordine et distributione temporum atque ceremonijs. Praestabat itaque vero propius in his accedere et cum veterum constitutionibus potius concordare, quam longius inde deviare, quamvis hac in ipsa restitutione Gregoriana non habeatur ratio exactae annuae quantitatis. Nam et haec vulgaribus Astronomicis adhuc penitus incognita est. Rogo itaque ut omnium eorum scripta in Germania, qui aliquid hoc in negotio publicârunt, sive pro sive contra, mihi transmittas, ut quomodo invicem et cum veritate consentiant, cognoscere possim. Libellum etiam Sphaericum MÆSTLINI mihi mittas, et SCALIGERUM de emendatione temporum, Gratiopolitanum etiam de Triangulis, operaque Abbatis Messanensis Siculi. Nulla enim eorum habeo. Et oro, ut mihi quam primum haec et quaecunque alia, quibus scis me delectari, illic adipisci poteris, quanticunque constent, compares, Hafniamque ad D. IOHANNEM FRANCISCUM mittas; quicquid exposueris, statim remittam, tibique quacunque in re usus postulaverit, vicissim gratificari non intermittam. Sed video chartam amplius vix sufficere, meque, dum tecum avidius loquor, epistolae metas currenti calamo transscendere. Quare nunc illi frenum inijciam: teque Deo Opt. Max. commendo. Vale et saluta meo nomine clarissimum virum D. DAVIDEM CHYTREUM et D. LEVINUM BATTUM Doctoremque PETRUM MENIUM, ceterosque amicos. De toto negotio mihi rescribe.

T.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the most distinguished Master Heinrich Brucaeus. Heartiest greeting.**

From your letter lately sent to me, dearest Master Brucaeus, I learned that you are in good health, which was most welcome to know. But that you are gradually neglecting the mathematical studies, I do not approve. For your age is not so great that it might turn you from the most delightful pursuit of these things; rather your Medicine is more profitable, according to the old saying: "Galen gives wealth," and so on. And for the most part mortals, the older they grow, the more grasping they become, and the more eagerly they gape after earthly things, with the heavenly set aside. Yet that you have resolved to return somewhat to these neglected studies, and to expound the *Hypotheses* of Proclus, I praise most highly, and I would wish you to send me a copy of those *Hypotheses* of Proclus. For I have not yet been able to obtain a Latin one — although I am sufficiently sure that they, inasmuch as they rest upon Ptolemaic foundations, are by no means exactly consonant with the heaven. For we, by the most exquisite observations of the Sun's motion over several preceding years, have found that neither the Ptolemaic nor the Copernican hypothesis satisfies its appearances, and that the reckoning of the apogee and of the eccentricity is far other than either of these craftsmen presupposed: as shortly, God willing, we shall make plain to the cultivators of astronomy from very many and by no means deceptive observations. For the motion of the Sun is so exactly established for us that on every single day, when clear weather grants a sound observation, it corresponds to our calculation from our own Tables to the very arc-second, exactly — often differing very greatly from both the Alphonsine and the Copernican reckoning, so much so that this year, as the Sun entered the vernal equinox, Copernicus's reckoning fell short in its motion by half a degree, while the Alphonsine reckoning ran over by a quarter of a degree. For the Alphonsines are now a little nearer the truth than Copernicus himself, so far as the Sun's motion is concerned, although both deviate intolerably. But in the motion of the Moon the hypothesis of Copernicus is truer and more exact. And this both the frequent observations of the Moon's course around the 90th degree from rising, and its parallaxes more diligently examined by us, have many times taught us — even though these too deviate not a little. For something is wanting in the mean motions. And the proportion of the radii of each epicycle to the radius of the concentric must be set a little otherwise, and perhaps there is yet another, less perceived, inequality. For Copernicus completed his observations with too rough a craft [*rudiori Minerva*], being without great instruments wrought exquisitely out of solid metal, of which we have very many ready — both in the variety of their construction and in their magnitude and workmanship, skilfully and perfectly [made], at enormous cost and with unremitting industry — so much so that, if you were to look upon these, you would readily grant us that not even any of the ancient mathematicians, though aided by royal expense (so far as one can gather from their writings), ever had in use instruments wrought to such magnitude and accuracy for scrutinising the celestial motions. But the moderns, neither in our own age nor in the one before, applied the form and the diligence of construction needful for working these things out, so that it is no wonder the science of the stars has gradually crumbled, to such a degree that not even its [the Sun's] motion is yet exactly established, nor is the quantity of the year sure — to say nothing now of the rest. But concerning all these matters, at another time, God willing, I will communicate to you and to other learned men our observations and the demonstrations resting upon them, and I will set forth the structure and exact workmanship of the instruments which I use in scrutinising the motion of the celestial bodies to the very mark, so that it may be established that the observations made by us, on which the demonstrations are founded, are exact and liable to no deception. For it is our custom to reach the same goal of truth not with a single instrument but with several, and those fashioned in diverse ways, provided sound trust be placed in the observation. If it were convenient for you to visit us this summer, perhaps you would see here what you would seek in vain further afield, nor would you regret that journey, and you would come to me as a most welcome guest, to be received with every kind of courtesy; then we might converse and confer face to face about very many matters, and you would behold in person those things which pen and paper do not contain. You ask that I send you some instrument of the Copernican hypotheses, such as I once saw at Schreckenfuchs's, which I would gladly do if I had such a one ready — for I have never set my mind upon constructing instruments of that kind, which would only display the inventions of others, since they can easily be grasped from a bare drawing, and the case is as yet before the judge [*sub iudice lis est*] whether the matter stands so or not. Wherefore I have rather spent all my effort on building instruments by which the celestial motions might be exactly established, so that through these the inventions of our predecessors may be called to the balance and tested against the marks of truth. For to what purpose was it to spend any labour and time in illustrating a matter not yet sufficiently understood, especially when this can otherwise easily be grasped with lighter trouble? I did indeed see at Schreckenfuchs's a little machine, by which he supposed he had figured forth the hypotheses of Copernicus. But when afterwards I weighed the matter more deeply, I found that this construction is by no means adequate to the mind of Copernicus. For he supposed that by the same machine, according as it was driven in diverse ways, both the Ptolemaic and the Copernican hypotheses could be expressed — which is plainly impossible. Nor will it readily be granted that all the motions of the Copernican invention can be mechanically expressed by a single machine that corresponds to itself in all its parts, especially because of the incomparable distance of the Eighth Sphere from the orb of the Earth; even though, as regards the symmetry of the world, the Copernican speculation is far more elegant and needs fewer circles than the Ptolemaic. And through that threefold motion of the single Earth very many of the appearances in the heaven can be neatly saved, for which the many orbs and circles otherwise devised would scarcely suffice — provided the matter truly stood so, and such revolutions agreed with the Earth itself: which we, by exquisite observations, have found to stand otherwise in the two [of the] motions that Copernicus attributed to it. For that the annual motion in the great circle about the Sun is by no means present in the Earth, I have proved at the end of the past year [15]82 and the beginning of [15]83 from the parallaxes of Mars, at that time acronychal [rising at sunset], and on that account nearer the Earth, at a lesser distance than the Sun is removed from the Earth — and indeed, according to the tenets of Copernicus, nearer by about a third part — whence [there should have arisen] greater parallaxes than the Sun itself ought to have induced; whereas in fact we found them [to be] far smaller, by the most frequent and exquisite observations corresponding mutually to one another; so that on that account the whole sphere of Mars is removed further from us than the Sun itself. Wherefore that whole hypothesis is overthrown by which Copernicus strives — ingeniously indeed and neatly enough — to account for the Sun's motion and all the epicycles of the remaining planets out of the Earth's annual circuit, the foundations of Aristarchus of Samos being brought back into the light. And as for the other motion, of declination with its librations, by which Copernicus accounts for the unequal anticipation of the equinoxes and the change in the obliquity of the Ecliptic — that this too is not present in the Earth, a different and far swifter change of the equinoxes, than the reckoning of Copernicus admits even in so little a time, will assure us; and the quantity of the year, [as derived] from the observations of Regiomontanus, in no way agreeing thus far with the Copernican reckoning. To say nothing of the fact that the obliquity of the Zodiac [Signifer] is even now three arc-minutes greater than Copernicus and our predecessors in the former age noted. The cause of the error I will explain elsewhere from optical foundations. And concerning all these matters, and very many others bearing upon the restoration of the art itself and upon recalling the celestial motions exactly into numbers, I will, with God's help, set forth a fuller account. But whether that third motion, by which the daily revolution is saved, is present in the Earth and the neighbouring elements, no one would readily say: since by the same reckoning the appearances of so great a rushing can be accounted for in this [hypothesis] as in the *primum mobile*, and indeed with a lesser circuit, and therefore with a more convenient economy the sudden restoration of all the spheres of the second movable [heaven] from east to west may be saved — as I see was the opinion of the Pythagoreans and Platonists too. Yet it is likely that this swiftest motion is by no means present in the Earth, as a most heavy and most dense and opaque body, but rather in the heaven itself, whose form and the subtlety and constancy of whose matter is fitter for a perpetual and ever so swift a motion. In vain, therefore, do you ask, dearest Brucaeus, for a plainer representation before the eyes, in an instrument, of those things of which there exists in the heaven itself no real form. But they were only ingeniously devised by Copernicus to save by some reckoning the appearances of the motions. If, however, you wish to ground students in his inventions, you will easily accomplish this — so far as need be — by a flat drawing.

But there is another matter, in which I am most concerned, that I shall take up with you. I composed, some while ago, certain things about the phenomena of the three comets seen within the last seven years, and about the New Star, by which I demonstrate, from sure observations, all the motions and distances and the rest of the matters that come into consideration; and I bring forward very many other things bearing both on this contemplation and on the whole art; and at length, persuaded by the solicitations both of friends here in my homeland and of very many in Germany and England, I have resolved to publish them. But since, on account of the epidemic pestilence now long raging, it has not been safe to dispatch anything of the kind at Copenhagen among our local printers — and they are now occupied with certain other printings, so that it is not possible to complete this edition through them in good time — I have therefore resolved to set up myself, here at Uraniborg, a certain printing-house, so far as suffices for printing my own lucubrations, so that both these and other things which, God willing, I shall hereafter strive to complete and to communicate to the cultivators of astronomy, may be committed to type here with myself, by our own press; and in that way the figures of the demonstrations and the numbers and the characters, of which, as you know, there is need in this subject-matter, may be set out corrected and more surely, and that all things may be known to come forth from me correctly — since few are to be found who are practised in these studies and can duly discern and amend the errors that occur in the course of printing. I have therefore hired this typographic servant, Joachim by name, to serve me in carrying out this business, and I have now sent him off to Wittenberg, to procure for me thence the presses and all the necessaries that cannot be had here; and since it is not very safe to entrust money to him alone, who is not sufficiently known to me, I have transferred 50 joachimsthalers to the secretary of the Castle of Wittenberg, whose name is Valentinus (whose stepfather instructs the daughters of our King, and who was formerly a familiar of mine at Wittenberg), that he may lay them out there for the type and the other things pertaining to the work, as this man of ours shall have signified to be necessary. I therefore send to you, dearest Brucaeus, those 50 joachimsthalers, which I would wish you to hand over to the Wittenberg carrier as soon as he comes to you, that he may carry them, together with a letter in my name, to the said Castle-secretary Valentinus. Now this printer of mine ought to go to Wittenberg together [with the carrier], or rather to go ahead, if the carrier should not be there, and to tarry there so long until, all the necessaries for setting up the printing-house being ready, he may bring them hither by the same carrier; but if meanwhile he should send any letter to you — the very condition of carrying out the business perhaps requiring it — I ask that you forward it at once to Copenhagen, to Doctor Johannes Franciscus, so that I may have it thence without any delay. I have added too, besides those 50 to be sent to Wittenberg, two thalers, partly that you may pay out from here to the carrier the wage due for his labour, partly that with the surplus you may procure for me certain mathematical booklets, such as you know I seek — like the astronomical [works] of Maestlin, if any have lately reached you. I also want that German writing of Maestlin which you indicated he had published against the Gregorian restoration of the Calendar. For I desire to see it, in case I might perceive from it his reckonings in fixing the marks of the year. That reform of time newly instituted by Pope Gregory does not displease me so very much — although very many contradict it more out of hatred of the Popes than out of love of truth. In which matter they indulge too much in passions that darken the light of truth. It is certain that those scruples [fractions] which fall short of the completion of the 6 hours, over the whole days of the year, have for a long time now made the solstices and equinoxes fall earlier by very many days, so that the feast-days no longer coincide with the constitutions of the primitive Church. But if we look into this matter more deeply, in the Christian Commonwealth no real difference of days arises. Nor is the observance of external things necessary, where they are not divinely commanded. For the common crowd wishes to be kept to duty, order, and the distribution of times, and to ceremonies. It was therefore preferable in these matters to come nearer to the truth and rather to concord with the constitutions of the ancients than to deviate further from them — although in this very Gregorian restoration no account is taken of the exact quantity of the year. For this too is as yet utterly unknown to the common run of astronomers. I therefore ask that you forward to me the writings of all those in Germany who have published anything in this business, whether for or against, so that I may learn how they agree with one another and with the truth. Send me also the *Spherical* booklet of Maestlin, and Scaliger *On the Emendation of Times*, the Grenoble man [Gratiopolitanus] too *On Triangles*, and the works of the Sicilian Abbot of Messina. For I have none of them. And I beg that, as soon as you can obtain them there, you procure for me these and whatever else you know delights me, at whatever they cost, and send them to Copenhagen to Master Johannes Franciscus; whatever you lay out, I will at once repay, nor will I fail to gratify you in return in whatever matter your need shall require. But I see that the paper now scarcely suffices any longer, and that I, while I talk with you too eagerly, am overstepping the bounds of a letter with a running pen. Wherefore I will now put a bridle on it: and I commend you to God, Best and Greatest. Farewell, and greet in my name the most distinguished man Master David Chytraeus and Master Levinus Battus and Doctor Petrus Menius, and the rest of my friends. Write back to me about the whole business.

T.
Tycho Brahe.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (Hendrik van den Broeck, 1530/31–1593), professor of medicine and mathematics at the University of Rostock, where Tycho had studied; a senior scholarly friend. This chapter's person register lists him among Tycho's German-academic correspondents (Rostock).
- **Date / place.** The source carries **no dateline and no place** — it ends simply "T. TYCHO BRAHE." The edition label is *s.l.* (*sine loco*, "without place"), and the identifier encodes only the year, 1584 (the day-component is 0000). The header therefore asserts only "[1584]" with the bracketed note that the source supplies no day-date, rather than manufacturing one. The standard scholarly dating is **spring 1584** (Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VII, p. 80; cf. Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*; Thoren, *Lord of Uraniborg*, who place it in spring 1584). That secondary date is not in the source text and so is kept out of the header, recorded here instead. No O.S./N.S. tag is given because the source supplies no day to qualify; Tycho in Denmark wrote Old Style.
- **Significance.** This is the much-cited letter in which Tycho first reports to a colleague that the **Mars parallax** measured at the 1582/83 opposition was far smaller than the Copernican annual orbit requires, which he takes to overthrow the Earth's annual motion. The passage is the documentary anchor for the genesis of the Tychonic system; the translation preserves the empirical, still-tentative register (he is reporting a result and its inference, not yet announcing a finished world-system).
- **Salutation.** *S. P.* = *Salutem plurimam* (dicit), "(sends) heartiest greeting". *Clarissimo D. D. Henrico Brucaeo*: *D. D.* = *Domino Doctori*, "to Master Doctor"; rendered "to the most distinguished Master Heinrich Brucaeus."
- **Astronomy — technical terms**: *parallaxis* → parallax; *apogaeum*/*eccentricitas* → apogee/eccentricity; *motus* → motion; *hypothesis* → hypothesis (kept); *epicyclus* → epicycle; *concentricus* → concentric; *medii motus* → mean motions; *octava sphaera* → Eighth Sphere (the fixed stars); *primum mobile* / *secundum mobile* → kept Latin (the prime mover / second movable heaven of the scholastic cosmos); *obliquitas Eclipticae* / *obliquatio Signiferi* → obliquity of the Ecliptic / of the Zodiac (*Signifer*, "the sign-bearer," = the zodiac); *aequinoctiorum anticipatio* → anticipation (precession) of the equinoxes; *anni quantitas* → the quantity (length) of the year; *acronychius* → acronychal (rising at sunset, i.e. at opposition) — glossed in brackets.
- **Measurement idiom.** *in ipso scrupulo ad amussim* — "to the very arc-second, exactly"; *scrupulum* here = arc-second / minute fraction (the period term for a sexagesimal fraction of a degree); *ad amussim* ("to the carpenter's line") = "to the very mark / exactly," a recurring Tychonic tag for instrumental precision, kept consistent. *semisse partis* = half a degree (*pars* = degree); *partis quadrante* = a quarter of a degree; *trinis scrupulis* = three arc-minutes. *scrupula illa, quae ad 6 horarum completionem deficiunt* (in the calendar passage) = the fractional residue short of the full 6 hours (the ¼-day surplus of the tropical year over 365 days) — "scruples/fractions," kept as the period term.
- ***rudiori Minerva*** — proverbial ("with rougher Minerva," i.e. with cruder skill/equipment); kept and glossed "with too rough a craft."
- ***sub iudice lis est*** — Horace, *Ars Poetica* 78: "the case is [still] before the judge," i.e. the matter is unsettled; retained as the embedded tag with a gloss.
- **Copernican motions.** Tycho counts the three Copernican terrestrial motions: (1) the **annual** motion in the *circulus magnus* about the Sun; (2) the **motion of declination** with its *librations* (Copernicus's mechanism for variable precession and changing obliquity); (3) the **daily** rotation. The translation keeps his careful gradation: he holds (1) **disproved** by the Mars parallax, (2) contradicted by the equinox/year evidence, and (3) merely **undecided** ("no one would readily say") — leaning to a moving heaven on physical grounds. No hedge is sharpened: *non facile quis dixerit*, *verisimile tamen est* are rendered "no one would readily say," "yet it is likely."
- ***Aristarchus of Samos*** — *Aristarchi Samii*: the ancient heliocentrist whose "foundations" Tycho says Copernicus revived.
- **Persons named in the business section.**
 - *Proclus* — the Neoplatonist; his *Hypotyposis astronomicarum positionum* ("Hypotheses [of the astronomers]"), which Brucaeus meant to expound; Tycho wants a Latin copy.
 - *Schreckenfuxius* = **Erasmus Oswald Schreckenfuchs** (1511–1579), mathematician (Freiburg/Tübingen); Tycho recalls a planetary model-machine he saw at his house.
 - *Maestlinus* = **Michael Maestlin** (1550–1631), the Tübingen astronomer (later Kepler's teacher); Tycho asks for his astronomical works, his *Sphaera* booklet, and his German tract against the Gregorian calendar.
 - *Scaliger de emendatione temporum* = **Joseph Justus Scaliger**, *De emendatione temporum* (1583).
 - *Gratiopolitanus de Triangulis* = "the Grenoble man on Triangles" — most likely **Bartholomaeus Pitiscus** is anachronistic here (1595); the period reference is to a trigonometric work by a writer styled *Gratiopolitanus* (of Grenoble, *Gratianopolis*). Identity not certain from the text; **flagged** rather than asserted.
 - *Abbas Messanensis Siculus* = "the Sicilian Abbot of Messina" — Tycho wants his works; the precise figure is not specified in the letter and is **left unidentified** rather than guessed.
 - *Ioachimus* — the hired **printer ("typographic servant")** sent to Wittenberg to procure the press; the Uraniborg printing-office Tycho is here founding (1584) would produce *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* and the *Epistolae*.
 - *Valentinus* — the **secretary (scriba) of Wittenberg Castle**, a former Wittenberg acquaintance, whose stepfather tutored the Danish king's daughters; entrusted with the 50 joachimsthalers.
 - *Iohannes Franciscus* — **Johannes Franciscus** (Hans Frandsen / Johannes Franciscus Ripensis), Tycho's Copenhagen forwarding contact.
 - *David Chytraeus* (1530–1600), Rostock theologian-historian; *Levinus Battus* (Levinus Battus, Rostock physician); *Petrus Menius* — Rostock friends to be greeted.
- **Coinage.** *Ioachimici* → **joachimsthalers** (the Joachimsthal silver coin, the "thaler"); *Thaleri* → **thalers** (kept distinct as the source distinguishes the 50 *Ioachimici* from the additional 2 *Thaleri*).
- **Calendar passage.** Tycho's measured approval of the **Gregorian calendar reform** (1582) is notable for a Lutheran: he separates the astronomical correctness of dropping the accumulated surplus from confessional opposition ("more out of hatred of the Popes than love of truth"), while noting the reform still does not embody the *exact* length of the year. No date is converted; the discussion is doctrinal-astronomical, not a dateline.
- **Negation check.** The pivotal scientific clauses turn on negations, rendered count-for-count without addition or removal: *Motum … annuum … Terrae **nequaquam** adesse* ("the annual motion is **by no means** present in the Earth"); *cum tamen longe minores fuisse* — the observed parallaxes were *far smaller*, **not** greater, than required; *neque ipsi Terrae adesse* (the declination-motion likewise **not** present in the Earth); *non facile quis dixerit* (of the daily motion, "**no one would readily say**" — left open, not denied). These are the clauses whose sense the whole letter rests on, and the polarity is preserved exactly.
- **Orthography.** As-printed early-modern forms retained in the Source block: *BRUCAeO/BRUCAeE* (ae-ligature), *ijs/alijs/proprijs* (ij for ii), *afpiceres* and *cornpendio* (printer's *f*-for-*s* and *rn*-for-*m* misreadings in the source transcription) — these last two are left **as printed** in the Source block; read *aspiceres* ("you would behold") and *compendio* ("economy") respectively, which the translation follows.
- **Correction.** Five word-level corrections collated against Dreyer, TBOO VII pp.78-80: struehirae emended to structurae (p.78); the inserted first name Henrico removed from two body addresses to Brucaeus where Dreyer prints the surname alone (p.78, p.80/81), with the corresponding Heinrich removed from the English; exacto corrected to exacte (p.79); and the inserted pronoun ea removed before videres (p.79), with the English clause those things which collapsed to what accordingly.
- **Correction.** Restored Dreyer's reading in the sentence sending the joachimsthalers to Brucaeus a second time: removed the duplicated first name 'Henrico'/'Heinrich' (not present in Dreyer's mid-letter apostrophe, which repeats only 'BRUCAEE') and restored the omitted sum '50' before 'illos Ioachimicos' / 'those... joachimsthalers' (Dreyer, TBOO VII, p. 81).

documents.incipit: BINAS a te Clarissime M. ANDREA, ex quo e Cymbria vestra domum reversus sum, accepi …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO DOCTISSIMOQUE VIRO MAGISTRO ANDREÆ SEVERINI VELLEIO AMICO SUO PLURIMUM DILECTO.
SALUTEM.

BINAS a te Clarissime M. ANDREA, ex quo e Cymbria vestra domum reversus sum, accepi literas, utrisque negotium Typographi illius tractas; respondissem dudum tuæ petitioni, si hyemis importunitas non obstitisset, literasque ad te transmittendi prius fuisset oblata occasio. Scias itaque me illum Holsaticum Typographum, de quo scribis, non multopere expetere. Quod si sponte huc transmigrare velit, eius conatus, quantum in me est, promovebo. Conduxi autem alium iuvenem non uxoratum, qui mihi in impressoria arte exsequenda inserviet, et Francofurtum ad Nundinas pecuniam pro stylo impressorio diversi generis mihi coëmendo nunc transmitto; propriamque officinulam hîc instruere conabor, quæ quotannis mihi usui emolumentoque erit. Si quid tu postmodo prelo destinatum absolveris hucque transmiseris, meis impensis excudetur, si tibi ita visum fuerit. Est autem Typographicus servus, quem conduxi, admodum bene in arte peritus et laborator diligens. Nec ex re mea fuit uxoratum illum cum tota sua familia maiore dispendio quam compendio sustentare. Si post festum Paschatis nos denuo hîc inviseris, veluti discedens ultimo te singulis annis facturum promisisti (testante idipsum graphica tua parietis nostræ inscriptione REVORTAR 83/84/85 oculis nostris quotidie obvia) rem feceris mihi longe gratissimam, habeo enim quædam, de quibus tecum coram agere plurimum exoptarem. Ego enim vix ob negotiorum impendentium multitudinem Cymbriam hac instante æstate revisere potuero. Tu itaque, si cum coniuge itineris socia (modo id possibile erit) mihi adfueris, hospes advenies exoptatissimus. Tuaque causa illud quicquid est itineris viceversa suscipiam, si quando opus fuerit. Vale et saluta METTAM tuam eiusque Patrem et Matrem, Magistrum IACOBUM et amicos omnes ceteros.

Iterum feliciter vale.
Datæ Uraniburgi die 16. Februarij Anno 1584.
T.
TYCHO BRAHE manu propria.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 77; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Negotium illud de historia CHRISTIANI III, cum ad ABSADONEM GYLDENSTIERN venero, facile, quasi nobis id minime factitantibus, expediam, tibique postmodo librum vel eius copiam transmittam. Litteras et pixidem ALBERTO FRISIO destinatam tradi procura.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and most learned man, Master Anders Sørensen Vedel, his most dearly beloved friend. Greeting.**

Two letters from you, most renowned Master Anders, I have received since I returned home from your Cimbria, and in both you treat of the business of that typographer; I should have answered your request long ago, had the harshness of winter not stood in the way, and had an opportunity of conveying a letter to you been offered sooner. Know, then, that I do not greatly want that Holstein typographer of whom you write. But should he be willing of his own accord to remove hither, I shall further his endeavours so far as lies in me. I have, however, engaged another young man, unmarried, who will serve me in carrying out the printer's art; and I am now sending money to Frankfurt to the Fair, to buy up for myself printing-type [*stylus impressorius*] of various kinds; and I shall try to set up here a little workshop of my own, which will be of use and profit to me year by year. If hereafter you finish anything intended for the press and send it hither, it shall be printed at my expense, if so it seem good to you. The printer's servant whom I have engaged is, moreover, very well skilled in the art and a diligent workman. Nor was it to my advantage to maintain that married man with his whole household at greater cost than profit. If, after the feast of Easter, you visit us again here — as at your last departure you promised you would do every year (the very thing being witnessed by your own inscription drawn on our wall, REVORTAR 83/84/85, daily before our eyes) — you will do me a thing by far most welcome, for I have certain matters which I should most greatly desire to deal with in your presence. For I shall scarcely be able, on account of the multitude of pressing affairs, to revisit Cimbria this coming summer. You, therefore, if (provided it be possible) you are with me together with your wife as companion of the journey, will come as a guest most longed-for. And for your sake I shall undertake that journey, whatever it amounts to, in turn, should there ever be need. Farewell, and greet your Mette and her father and mother, Master Jacob, and all your other friends.

Again, happily, farewell.
Given at Uraniborg, the 16th day of February, in the year 1584.
T[ycho].
TYCHO BRAHE, in his own hand.


*[Postscript:]* That business of the history of Christian III, when I shall have come to Absalon Gyldenstierne, I shall easily dispatch — as though we were by no means busying ourselves with it — and shall afterwards convey to you the book, or a copy of it. See that the letter and the little box [pyxis] destined for Albert Friis be delivered.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Magister Andreas Severini Vellejus* = **Anders Sørensen Vedel** (1542–1616), Tycho's former preceptor and lifelong friend, the Danish historian and balladeer; appointed Royal Historiographer in 1584. He lived at Ribe in Jutland, where his residence Liljebjerg ("Lily Hill") — with its book and manuscript collections, gardens, and (from 1585) its own printing press — became known as a "Little Uraniborg." The letter shows the two men setting up their presses in the same period.
- **Place.** *Uraniburgum* → **Uraniborg**, Tycho's observatory-mansion on the island of Hven. Tycho established his own printing press at Uraniborg in 1584, the very year of this letter (Dreyer, *Tycho Brahe*); the letter documents its provisioning.
- ***Cymbria / Cymbriam*** — **Cimbria**, the humanist Latin name for **Jutland** (the Cimbric peninsula); "your Cimbria" = Vedel's home region, where he resided at Ribe. Kept and glossed.
- ***Typographus / Typographicus servus*** — "typographer / printer's servant," i.e. the pressman or compositor Tycho needed to operate his press. The *Holsaticus Typographus* is an (unnamed) **printer from Holstein** whom Vedel had recommended; Tycho declines to seek him out, having already hired an unmarried young man.
- ***stylus impressorius*** — literally "printing stylus," here the standard period term for **printing-type (founts of type)**; Tycho is buying type "of various kinds" (*diversi generis*, i.e. several founts/sizes) at the Frankfurt book fair. Rendered "printing-type"; the Latin flagged.
- ***Francofurtum ad Nundinas*** — "to **Frankfurt** to the Fair," i.e. the **Frankfurt book fair** (the *Frankfurter Messe*), the great European entrepôt for type, books, and printing materials. *Nundinae* = the (market-)fair.
- ***officinulam*** — diminutive of *officina*, "a little workshop"; here the small printing-office Tycho means to establish. Rendered "a little workshop of my own."
- ***prelo destinatum … excudetur*** — "intended for the press … shall be printed": *prelum* = the press; *excudere* = to print/strike off. Tycho offers to print at his own expense any work Vedel prepares — an offer reflecting the patronage economics of owning a press.
- ***maiore dispendio quam compendio*** — "at greater cost than profit," a rhetorical jingle (*dispendium* / *compendium*) explaining why a married pressman with a whole household was uneconomic; the antithesis is preserved.
- ***graphica … parietis nostrae inscriptione REVORTAR 83/84/85*** — "your own inscription drawn on our wall, REVORTAR 83/84/85": at his departures Vedel had written on a wall at Uraniborg the Latin *REVORTAR* ("I shall return," variant of *revertar*) with the successive years 1583 / 1584 / 1585, as a standing pledge to return yearly. *graphica … inscriptio* = a drawn/written inscription; rendered literally. The years are reproduced exactly as transcribed (83/84/85); the form *REVORTAR* (for *revertar*) is kept as written, not corrected.
- ***festum Paschatis*** — "the feast of **Easter**"; the proposed time for Vedel's visit.
- **Persons greeted.** *METTA tua* = **Mette Hansdatter**, Vedel's wife (married 1581), daughter of **Hans Laugesen**, Bishop of Ribe; "her father and mother" are the bishop and his wife. *Magister Iacobus* = a "Master Jacob" of Vedel's Ribe circle (not further specified in the text). Names kept in their source forms with identification.
- **Subscription.** *T. … TYCHO BRAHE manu propria* — "T[ycho]. … Tycho Brahe, in his own hand," the autograph subscription formula (*manu propria* = with his own hand); preserved.
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Datae Uraniburgi die 16. Februarij Anno 1584* = "Given at Uraniborg, the 16th day of February, in the year 1584" (Old Style; Denmark held the Julian calendar until 1700). The dateline as written agrees with the catalogue label (16 February 1584); no discrepancy. No date is silently converted.
- **Edition / witness note.** Text of record is Dreyer's *Opera Omnia*; the MS witness recorded in the edition is a copy (*Afskrift*) in Tycho Brahe's private archive at the Rigsarkivet, Copenhagen — i.e. an apograph, not the autograph dispatched to Vedel.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript, restored from Dreyer VII p.77 (dropped by the working transcription).

text.original:
PRISCÆ AC VERÆ NOBILITATIS INSIGNISQUE ERUDITIONIS AC VIRTUTIS VIRO DN. TYCHONI BRAHE OTTONIDI, DOMINO INSULÆ HUENÆ, DN. ET AMICO SUO PLURIMUM OBSERVANDO.
S.

LITERÆ tuæ, generose Dn. TYCHO, mihi duabus de causis fuerunt gratissimæ, cum quod familiaritatem inter nos hîc Augustæ conflatam, literarum beneficio fulcire non dedignatus es, tum quod scirem, eum qui dicebatur obijsse anno 82, adhuc in vivis esse et hac aura inter superstites felicissime frui. Qua felicitate ut quam diutissime vel propter Rempubl. literariam ad artes Mathematicas restaurandas temporum iniuria collapsas, fruaris, Deum Opt. Max. toto pectore oro. Porro ad petitionem tuam quod attinet de emendis libris, feci quod potui. Inprimis autem mihi curæ fuit SCALIGERI de emendatione temporum, qui in fine appendicem habet complectentem iudicium, quo Gregorianum seu Lilianum, ut ipse vocat, Calendarium in universum improbat, uti videbis. Huic adiunxi aliorum in Germania editorum scripta quotquot habere potui, quæ in unum volumen sunt coniecta et Heidelbergæ edita post. Edidit et IACOBUS HEERBRANDUS Theologus Tubingensis Theses contra Calendarium, quibus nostrorum Theologorum sententiam de non recipiendo Calendario comprobavit, sed a Senatu sunt prohibitæ et explosæ, ut sic loquar. Superioribus scriptis adiunxi HAGECIJ Responsionem ad HANNIBALEM et GRAMINÆUM de Stella Nova, quæ ante triennium per me ad te non missa esse recordor. Proinde tibi non ingrata futura auguror. Librum de Triangulis, quem inprimis desiderare videris, venalem non reperi. Precium singulorum, quorum undecim in peculiari scheda his literis inclusa notatum invenies, pro quibus affinis meus mihi, ut voluisti, satisfecit. WERNERI libros cum de motu octavæ Sphæræ, tum de Observationibus stellarum fixarum, si aliquando in vetere quadam Bibliotheca invenero, faciam, ut me tui non immemorem fuisse intelligas. Reperi et alios libros Astronomicos in Catalogis WILLERIANIS, partim de Horologijs, partim de Astrologia, h. e. illa divinatrice arte tractantes, qui etsi plerique in promptu non erant, et a tuis studijs mihi quodammodo alieni videantur esse, singulorum tamen titulos consignare volui, precio plerisque adiecto. Si igitur ex his quidam tibi arridens tuum erit semestre spacium vel circiter ante me certiorem facere, ut si WILLERUS eius generis libros in promtu non habeat, eos tamen interea temporis huc transferendos curare possit. Qua in parte tibi meum studium et operam polliceor. Doctoris AMBROSIJ libri ante triennium WELSERO mortuo ab hæredibus sunt distracti et venditi.

Novarum rerum fere nihil habeo, nisi quod inter Senatores civitatis nostræ propter Calendarium Gregorianum magna animorum distractio fuerit. Maior enim pars non tam Pontifici] quam nostri contenderunt, Calendarium propter vicinos Bavaros et Episcopum Augustanum recipiendum esse tanquam politicam causam, ut correspondentia cum vicinis in commercijs, iudicijs et contractibus servari possit. Pauci ex nostris, tres præsertim Ædiles Curules asserentes Theologorum nomine, Calendarium non esse mere politicum negotium, sed etiam Theologicum, eo quod a Pontifice sit ortum et sub pœna excommunicationis recipiendum mandetur, minime igitur nostris Civibus et Ecclesijs obtrudendum esse, provocantes ad Cameram Imperialem mense Martio 1583. Tandem mense Maio An. 84 est lata sententia contra Ædiles et adhærentes, quapropter die 18. publicatur sententia, et ijdem 4 Domini iubentur domi suæ se continere, donec aliud quid de illis statuatur. Die 25. Maij, circa meridiem Præfectus Urbis, der Stadtvogt, iussu Senatus Doctorem MYLIUM Augustanum, nostrum primarium Theologum ex urbe in pilento educere conatur. Sed quid fit? Populus hoc audito accurrit et aurigam, quo minus progrediatur, strictis gladijs adoritur, MYLIUMQUE e pilento vi extractum in ædibus Pistoris prope portam Geggingensem habitantis abscondit, neglectis militibus custodiam in porta agentibus. Mox confluunt Cives armati vociferantes: nostrum Theologum cupimus. Dum hæc aguntur, Senatus ceteros Theologos in Curiam convocat, tractaturus cum illis de Calendario recipiendo; quod tum constanter denegârunt. Altero die post eliguntur ex singulis ordinibus, Patricio, Mercatorio et Plebeio 6 viri, qui de pace et tumultu sedando cogitent. Mox ultimo Maij advolant legati cum Wirtenbergici, tum Ulmenses, qui litem ita composuerunt, ut ex scripto vel publicatione in fasciculum tuum coniecta videre est. Non dubito, quin diversorum diversa sint futura iudicia de Theologis nostris. Sed non solum Legati, Iurisconsulti etc. verum etiam Tubingenses ipsi recipiendi Calendarij authores fuerunt, respicientes præsens periculum, et desertionem Ecclesiæ, salvo verbo et libertate Ecclesiæ retenta. Sed de statu huius urbis nostræ fortasse prolixius, quam par est. Id saltem a te, si non nimis audax viderer, expeterem, ut tuo nos iudicio de hoc Calendario neoterico informares ac firmares, an videlicet id priori præstet ac cœlo rectius congruat, nec ne. Id enim te unicum efficere posse, utpote qui luminarium motibus sedulo invigiles, persuasum habemus. Et sunt vota non nostra saltem, sed plurium. Quod superest, mi TYCHO, Deum Opt. Max. precor, ut tibi largiatur et vires animi et corporis, qui organa et opera in gratiam Matheseos studiosis inchoata absolvere, feliciterque ad finem perducere queas, quo sane nihil neque cognitu iucundius neque gratius accidere poterit.

Vale feliciter.
Datæ Augustæ Rheticæ vulgo Vindelicorum postridie Pentecostes CIↃ IↃ LXXXIV.
IOHAN. MAIOR.
text.english:
**To a man of ancient and true nobility and of distinguished learning and virtue, Master Tycho Brahe, son of Otte, lord of the island of Hven, his lord and friend much to be respected.**
Greeting.

Your letter, noble Master Tycho, was most welcome to me for two reasons: both because you did not disdain to shore up, by the kindness of a letter, the friendship struck up between us here at Augsburg, and because I [thereby] learned that the man who was said to have died in the year [15]82 is yet among the living and most happily enjoys this air among those who survive. That you may enjoy that happiness as long as possible — if only for the sake of the republic of letters, toward restoring the mathematical arts that have collapsed through the injury of the times — I beg God, Best and Greatest, with my whole heart. Further, as concerns your request about the books to be bought, I have done what I could. First of all my care was for Scaliger's *On the Emendation of Times*, which at the end has an appendix containing a judgement whereby he wholly condemns the Gregorian, or as he himself calls it the Lilian, Calendar, as you will see. To this I have added the writings of others published in Germany, as many as I could obtain, which have been thrown together into a single volume and afterwards published at Heidelberg. Jacob Heerbrand, the Tübingen theologian, also published *Theses against the Calendar*, in which he confirmed our theologians' opinion about not accepting the Calendar; but they were banned by the Senate and hooted down, so to speak. To the foregoing writings I have added Hájek's *Reply to Hannibal and Graminaeus concerning the New Star*, which, I recall, was not sent to you by me three years ago. Accordingly I forecast it will not be unwelcome to you. The book *On Triangles*, which you seem especially to want, I have not found for sale. The price of each item — of which you will find eleven noted on a separate slip enclosed with this letter — [is set out], for which my kinsman has, as you wished, made satisfaction to me. As for Werner's books, both *On the Motion of the Eighth Sphere* and *On the Observations of the Fixed Stars*, if at some time I find them in some old library, I will see to it, so that you may understand I have not been unmindful of you. I have found also other astronomical books in the Willer catalogues, treating partly of timepieces, partly of astrology — that is, of that divinatory art — which, although most were not readily at hand, and may seem to me somewhat foreign to your studies, I nevertheless wished to record the titles of each, with the price added in most cases. If, therefore, some one of these takes your fancy, it will be for you to inform me about a half-year, or thereabouts, in advance, so that, should Willer not have books of that kind ready to hand, he may yet be able in the meantime to arrange for them to be brought here. In that matter I promise you my zeal and effort. Doctor Ambrosius's books were, three years ago, on Welser's death, dispersed and sold off by the heirs.

Of new matters I have almost nothing, except that among the senators of our city there has been a great clash of minds over the Gregorian Calendar. For the greater part — not so much [out of regard for] the Pope as our own [men] — contended that the Calendar was to be accepted, on account of the neighbouring Bavarians and the Bishop of Augsburg, as a political matter, so that correspondence with the neighbours in commerce, lawsuits, and contracts could be maintained. A few of our own — three Aediles Curule especially, asserting in the theologians' name that the Calendar was not a merely political business but also a theological one, in that it had arisen from the Pope and was being ordered to be accepted under pain of excommunication, and therefore by no means to be forced upon our citizens and churches — appealed to the Imperial [Chamber of Justice] in the month of March 1583. At length in the month of May, in the year [15]84, sentence was passed against the Aediles and their adherents; wherefore on the 18th day the sentence is published, and those same 4 gentlemen are ordered to confine themselves to their houses until something else be decided about them. On the 25th day of May, about noon, the Prefect of the City — *der Stadtvogt* — by order of the Senate attempts to lead Doctor Mylius of Augsburg, our chief theologian, out of the city in a carriage. But what happens? The people, on hearing this, run up and, that he may go no further, set upon the driver with drawn swords, and, Mylius having been dragged out of the carriage by force, hide him in the house of a baker living near the Göggingen gate, the soldiers keeping guard at the gate being disregarded. Soon the citizens flock together in arms, crying out: "We want our theologian." While these things are going on, the Senate summons the rest of the theologians to the Town Hall, intending to treat with them about accepting the Calendar; which they then steadfastly refused. The day after, there are chosen from each of the orders — Patrician, Mercantile, and Plebeian — 6 men, to consider the settling of the peace and the tumult. Soon, on the last [day] of May, envoys hasten in, both from Württemberg and from Ulm, who composed the dispute in such a way as may be seen from the written notice, or publication, thrown into your packet. I do not doubt that different men's judgements of our theologians will be different. But not only the envoys, jurists, etc., but even the Tübingen men themselves were authors of accepting the Calendar, looking to the present danger and the desertion of the Church — the Word and the liberty of the Church being kept safe. But [I write] of the state of this our city at greater length, perhaps, than is fitting. This at least I would ask of you, if I should not seem too bold: that you inform and confirm us, by your judgement, about this newfangled Calendar — namely whether it is better than the former one and agrees more rightly with the heaven, or not. For we are persuaded that you alone can settle this, inasmuch as you watch diligently over the motions of the luminaries. And these are the wishes not of us alone, but of many. For what remains, my Tycho, I pray God, Best and Greatest, to bestow on you strength both of mind and of body, that you may be able to complete the instruments and works begun for the benefit of those devoted to mathematics, and bring them happily to their end — than which, in truth, nothing more delightful or more welcome to know could befall.

Fare you happily well.
Given at Augsburg of Raetia, commonly [Augsburg] of the Vindelici, the day after Pentecost, 1584.
Johannes Major.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Iohan. Maior* = **Johannes Major** (Hans Mair), an Augsburg correspondent and book-agent for Tycho in the early 1580s; he procures and prices books from the Augsburg trade (notably the Willer catalogues) on Tycho's commission. (Not to be confused with the Wittenberg poet Georg Major or the earlier theologian.) The MS is an Afskrift (copy) in the same Vienna codex (cod. Vindob. lat. 10686) that preserves Tycho's incoming Augsburg correspondence.
- **Address & opening.** *Ottonides* — "son of Otte," the Greek-style patronymic for **Otte Brahe**, Tycho's father (cf. the Wolf letter, 1571). *Dominus insulae Huenae* = "lord of the island of **Hven**," Tycho's seat (Uraniborg). *S.* = *Salutem (dicit)*, "(sends) greeting".
- **"the man said to have died in [15]82."** A rumour of Tycho's death had reached Augsburg; Major expresses relief at finding him alive. Reported, not glossed away.
- **Books named.**
 - *Scaliger,* De emendatione temporum *(Paris, 1583)* — Joseph Justus Scaliger's chronological work; Major flags its closing appendix condemning the Gregorian ("Lilian") calendar. *Lilianum* after **Luigi Lilio (Aloysius Lilius)**, the calendar's designer.
 - *Jacob Heerbrand,* Theses contra Calendarium — the Tübingen Lutheran theologian's anti-Gregorian theses.
 - *Hájek,* Responsio ad Hannibalem et Graminaeum de Stella Nova — **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku (Thaddaeus Hagecius)**, the Bohemian astronomer, replying to **Annibale Raimondo** ("Hannibal") and **Theodor Graminaeus** on the new star of 1572. *ante triennium* = "three years ago."
 - *Liber de Triangulis* — a "book *On Triangles*," unfound for sale; most likely **Regiomontanus,** De triangulis omnimodis, though the bare title is not decisive (so kept untranslated-in-title and not pinned to an author).
 - *Werner,* De motu octavae sphaerae *and* De observationibus stellarum fixarum — **Johann Werner** of Nuremberg.
 - *Catalogi Willeriani / Willerus* — the famous Augsburg book-trade catalogues of **Georg Willer**, issued for the Frankfurt fairs; *Willerus* is the bookseller himself. *Horologia* rendered "timepieces."
 - *Doctoris Ambrosii libri … Welsero mortuo* — the library of a "Doctor Ambrosius," dispersed by the heirs on the death of a **Welser** (the great Augsburg patrician house); the identity of "Doctor Ambrosius" is not fixed by the text and is left as the name stands.
- **The 1584 Augsburg Calendar dispute (the *Kalenderstreit*).** The letter's chief news is the Augsburg confessional riot over the Gregorian reform of 1582, a contemporaneous event of which Major is an eyewitness reporter. *Aediles Curules* = the city's senior magistrates (rendered "Aediles Curule," the antique title Major uses for them); *Camera Imperialis* = the **Reichskammergericht** (Imperial Chamber of Justice), rendered "Imperial [Chamber of Justice]" with the bracketed noun supplied. *Praefectus Urbis, der Stadtvogt* — Major glosses his own Latin with the German civic title; the code-switch *der Stadtvogt* is kept verbatim and italicised. *Doctor Mylius Augustanus* = **Georg Mylius** (Müller), the leading Lutheran preacher of Augsburg, whose attempted expulsion (25 May) triggered the popular tumult. *porta Geggingensis* = the **Göggingen gate** (Gögginger Tor). The settling envoys come from **Württemberg** and **Ulm**; the Tübingen theologians ultimately favoured accepting the calendar *salvo verbo et libertate Ecclesiae* ("the Word and the liberty of the Church kept safe").
 - *non tam Pontifici] quam nostri* — the printed/transcribed text carries an editorial bracket after *Pontifici*, marking a defective construction (an expected verb/participle governing the dative, e.g. *obsequentes*, is wanting). Rendered "not so much [out of regard for] the Pope as our own [men]," with the supplement bracketed; the crux is flagged, not smoothed (see Confidence).
- **The question put to Tycho.** Major asks Tycho's astronomical verdict on whether the *Calendarium neotericum* ("newfangled / new-fashioned Calendar," the Gregorian) *coelo rectius congruat* — "agrees more rightly with the heaven" — appealing to him as one who *luminarium motibus sedulo invigiles* ("watches diligently over the motions of the luminaries"). *luminaria* = the two luminaries (Sun and Moon).
- **Technical / glossary terms.** *artes Mathematicas restaurandas … collapsas* — the **restoration of the mathematical arts** that have "collapsed" (Tycho's *instauratio* programme,), rendered "restoring the mathematical arts." *organa et opera* — *organa* = **instruments**, here paired with *opera* ("works"); rendered "the instruments and works." *Matheseos* (gen. of *Mathesis*) — "of mathematics" (the divine science of mathematics, as in the Wolf letter). *Astrologia, h. e. illa divinatrix ars* — astrology glossed by Major himself as "that divinatory art."
- **Numerals & money.** *undecim … in peculiari scheda* — eleven priced items on an enclosed slip (the *scheda*); *affinis meus … satisfecit* — Major's kinsman has paid him on Tycho's behalf. *die 18.*, *die 25. Maii*, *ultimo Maii*, *mense Martio 1583*, *mense Maio An. 84* — dates kept as written.
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Datae Augustae Rheticae vulgo Vindelicorum postridie Pentecostes CIↃ IↃ LXXXIV* = "Given at Augsburg of Raetia, commonly [Augsburg] of the Vindelici, **the day after Pentecost, 1584**." The Roman-numeral year **CIↃ IↃ LXXXIV** = MDLXXXIV = **1584** (the apostrophus form CIↃ = 1000, IↃ = 500). Augsburg in 1584 was a Protestant correspondent writing **Old Style (Julian)** — indeed the whole letter is *about* Augsburg's refusal of the Gregorian reform — so the dateline is O.S.: Pentecost (Whitsunday) fell on **7 June 1584 O.S.** (Julian Easter 19 April + 49 days), and the day after = **8 June 1584 O.S.**, which agrees with the edition's catalogue date "1584. 8. juni." Header date follows the as-written dateline; no silent conversion. *Augusta Rhaetica vulgo Vindelicorum* — Major's learned double name for Augsburg (Roman *Augusta Vindelicorum*; here also styled "of Raetia"),.
- **Subscription.** *Vale feliciter* = "Fare you happily well".
