text.original:
HENRICUS BRUCÆUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

CUM tuus Typographus, Nobilissime Charissimeque TYCHO, Rostochium venit, abfui, domum vero rediens, literis tuis lectis pecuniam in scattula obsignatam aurigae Witebergensi triduo post tradidi, nolui enim resignare. Nihil itaque pecuniae reservatum, qua auriga satisfieret, aut libri aliqui emerentur. De motuum Solis et Lunae reliquorumque Planetarum emendatione, quae prae manibus habes, expecto ut in lucem prodeant. Ego certe in omnibus Eclipsibus crassis nostris observationibus videor animadvertisse, calculum PURBACHIJ propius accessisse ad tempus apparens, quam COPERNICI. Ad singula autem momenta motus Solis respondere ex tuis observationibus deductos, gaudeo. Idem si in ceteris praestiteris, bene de omnibus mereberis, et aeternam laudem apud posteros consequeris. Et ego ita sentio, tam multa, quae de anni inaequalitate referuntur, ex imperfectis vel falsis observationibus nata esse; motum enim illum coelestem ijsdem perpetuo metis includi, et tam operosis hypothesibus COPERNICI in motu Terrae astruendo non fuisse opus, quas falsas esse dubium non est, et forte non satisfaciunt etiam apparentijs evidentibus. Ob id desiderabam organum, quod mihi ob oculos obiceret totam illam COPERNICI imaginationem, quam ego, ut verum fatear, ex simplici illa delineatione nunquam plene assequi potui. Et quamvis tecum sentiam, non tam in ijs organis laborandum, quae alterius phantasias oculis obijciant, quam quae motus coelestes nobis aperiant: est tamen hominis eruditi, quique aliorum inventa velit explicare, haec intelligere, et quantum fieri potest, oculis obicere. Imo optandum esset, posse sine ullis hypothesibus motus coelestes tradi. Quod ut forte fieri queat, apparentijs tamen satisfieri nunquam poterit. Hypotyposes PROCLI ob nostri Typographi negligentiam non excuduntur. Extant autem, magnae constructioni CL. PTOLEMÆI adiunctae, verum ita corrupte editae, ut autorem suum non agnoscant. Editae sunt alibi opera GEORGII VALLAe Placentini, ijs credo ab eodem autore tralatas Hypotyposes esse adiectas. Quod si hoc opus VALLAe habeas, velim ad me mitti, quo tantum percurram hanc Hypotyposium translationem, remissurus quam primum. Mitto IOSEPHUM SCALIGERUM de emendatione temporum et MÆSTLINI de emendatione Calendarij. MAUROLYCUM hoc tempore, ut neque Gratiopolitanum consequi potui. Si quid in posterum nanciscar, ad te mittam. Quod si velis prius tibi precia perscribi, id quoque facturus sum. Hic tuus servus dum aliquot diebus hîc navem, quae solvat in Daniam, expectat, consumsit solidos 32. Et typos nescio quos maioris notae emit, de quibus mecum actum ut precium penderem. Verum cum huius rei nulla in tuis literis facta sit mentio, et ignorem, utrum hoc tuo iussu factum sit, nihil a me persolutum. Ex ipso plene omnia de typis intelliges.

Bene vale.
Rostochij 12. Iunij Anno Domini 1584.
HENRICUS BRUCÆUS.
text.english:
**Heinrich Brucaeus to Tycho Brahe.**

When your printer came to Rostock, most noble and most dear Tycho, I was away; but on returning home, having read your letter, I handed over the money — sealed up in a packet — to the Wittenberg carter three days later, for I did not wish to break the seal. And so no money was held back with which the carter might be paid or any books bought. As for the correction of the motions of the Sun and Moon and of the rest of the planets, which you have in hand, I await their coming forth into the light. For my part, in all the eclipses I have certainly seemed to observe, from our rough observations, that Peurbach's calculation came closer to the apparent time than Copernicus's. And I rejoice that the [positions] derived from your observations answer to the single moments of the Sun's motion. If you shall achieve the same in the rest, you will deserve well of all men, and win everlasting praise among posterity. And this too is my opinion: that the many things which are reported concerning the inequality of the year have arisen from imperfect or false observations; for that celestial motion is enclosed perpetually within the same bounds, and there was no need of Copernicus's so laborious hypotheses in establishing the motion of the Earth — which it is beyond doubt are false, and perhaps do not satisfy even the evident appearances. On that account I desired an instrument that might set before my eyes that whole imagining of Copernicus, which I — to confess the truth — could never fully grasp from that bare diagram. And although I am of one mind with you that one should labour not so much over those instruments which set another's fancies before the eyes, as over those which lay open the celestial motions to us, yet it belongs to a learned man, and to one who would wish to expound the inventions of others, to understand these things and, so far as may be done, to set them before the eyes. Nay, it were to be wished that the celestial motions could be transmitted without any hypotheses at all. But even if that could perhaps be done, the appearances will nevertheless never be able to be satisfied. The *Hypotyposes* of Proclus are not being printed, owing to the negligence of our printer. They are extant, however, appended to the great construction [Almagest] of the renowned Ptolemy, but so corruptly edited that they do not acknowledge their own author. They were published elsewhere in the works of Giorgio Valla of Piacenza, to which, I believe, the *Hypotyposes* — translated by the same author — were added. So if you have this work of Valla's, I should like it sent to me, that I might just run through this translation of the *Hypotyposes*, intending to send it back at the first opportunity. I send Joseph Scaliger's *On the Emendation of the Times*, and Maestlin's *On the Emendation of the Calendar*. At this time I have not been able to obtain Maurolico, any more than the Gratiopolitanus [the man / work of Grenoble?]. If I light upon anything hereafter, I will send it to you. And if you would first have the prices written out for you, that too I shall do. This servant of yours, while waiting here some days for a ship to set sail for Denmark, has spent 32 shillings. And he has bought some types or other of a larger sort, concerning which it was settled with me that I should pay the price. But since no mention of this matter was made in your letter, and I do not know whether it was done at your bidding, nothing has been paid out by me. From the man himself you will learn everything about the types in full.

Fare you well.
Rostock, 12 June, in the Year of the Lord 1584.
Heinrich Brucaeus.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (Hendrik van den Broeucke, 1531–1598), Flemish-born professor of medicine and (effectively) of astronomy/mathematics at the University of Rostock, and an established correspondent of Tycho's. Mosley (*Bearing the Heavens*, p. 180) cites this very passage: Tycho, "wanting a Latin copy" of Proclus, had asked Brucaeus for help, and Brucaeus "could only provide … some vague bibliographical help" about Valla's edition.
- **Place.** *Rostochium / Rostochij* = **Rostock**.
- **The printer / "your servant."** *tuus Typographus* … *Hic tuus servus* — Tycho's own printer/agent, then travelling between Rostock and Hven, ferrying money, books, and printing type. *aurigae Witebergensi* = "the Wittenberg carter" (the carrier on the Rostock–Wittenberg run). The closing transaction (32 shillings spent; *typos … maioris notae*, "types of a larger sort," i.e. a larger type-body, bought on uncertain authority) belongs to the practical business of equipping Tycho's Uraniborg press.
- ***solidos 32*** — "32 shillings" (*solidus*, the period accounting/coin unit); kept as "shillings."
- **Astronomy — the technical core.**
 - *De motuum Solis et Lunae reliquorumque Planetarum emendatione* — "the correction of the motions of the Sun and Moon and the rest of the planets," Tycho's restorative programme (*emendatio*/*restitutio*; this chapter's convention, *restoration*).
 - *calculum PURBACHIJ … quam COPERNICI* — Brucaeus reports that **Peurbach's** calculation (Georg Peurbach, 1423–1461, the *Theoricae novae planetarum* / Ptolemaic tradition) matched the *tempus apparens* of eclipses better than **Copernicus's**. *Calculus* = "calculation/computation"; *tempus apparens* = "the apparent time" (kept).
 - *anni inaequalitate* — "the inequality of the year": the supposed variation in the length of the (tropical/solar) year much debated in the calendar-reform literature; Brucaeus judges the reported variation an artefact of "imperfect or false observations" and holds the celestial motion to be "enclosed perpetually within the same bounds."
 - *operosis hypothesibus COPERNICI in motu Terrae astruendo* — "Copernicus's so laborious hypotheses in establishing the motion of the Earth." Brucaeus's anti-Copernican stance is stated as his own opinion and is preserved as such (no sharpening): he calls them "beyond doubt false" and says they "perhaps" (*forte*) fail even to save the appearances — the hedge *forte* is kept.
 - *organum … imaginationem … delineatione* — *organum* = **instrument**; here Brucaeus wishes for an instrument (a planetary model/sphere) that would render visible "that whole imagining (*imaginatio*) of Copernicus," which he could not grasp from "that bare diagram (*delineatio*)." *imaginatio* rendered "imagining" (the mental construct/representation), not modernised to "model."
 - *organis … quae alterius phantasias oculis obijciant … quam quae motus coelestes nobis aperiant* — the contrast (kept verbatim in sense) between instruments that "set another's fancies before the eyes" and those that "lay open the celestial motions": Brucaeus agrees with Tycho that the latter matter more, yet defends the former's didactic use.
 - *sine ullis hypothesibus motus coelestes tradi … apparentijs … satisfieri* — "to transmit the celestial motions without any hypotheses" / "to satisfy the appearances" (*satisfacere apparentiis* = the *sōzein ta phainomena* topos). Rendered literally; the pessimistic conclusion ("even if it could be done, the appearances will never be able to be satisfied [thereby]") is preserved with its difficulty intact (see crux below).
- **Books named.**
 - *Hypotyposes PROCLI* — **Proclus**, *Hypotyposis astronomicarum positionum* (the elementary exposition of Ptolemaic planetary theory). *Hypotyposes* kept as a title-word.
 - *magnae constructioni CL. PTOLEMAeI adiunctae* — "appended to the great construction of the renowned Ptolemy": *magna constructio* = the **Almagest** (Greek *Megalē syntaxis* / *Megistē*); *CL.* = *Clarissimi* ("the renowned/most illustrious"), expanded. Brucaeus notes the appended *Hypotyposes* there are "so corruptly edited that they do not acknowledge their own author" (i.e. the print is so bad the text is barely recognisable as Proclus's).
 - *opera GEORGII VALLAe Placentini* — the works of **Giorgio Valla of Piacenza** (*Placentinus* = of Piacenza), in whose collection (*De expetendis et fugiendis rebus*, 1501) a Latin Proclus translation appears; Brucaeus believes the *Hypotyposes* there were "translated by the same author" (Valla).
 - *IOSEPHUM SCALIGERUM de emendatione temporum* — **Joseph Justus Scaliger**, *De emendatione temporum* (Paris, 1583); a cross-check (Gingerich, *Annotated Census*) confirms the 1583 Paris edition. *Mitto … Scaligerum* = "I send [the book of] Scaliger," a common metonymy (the author's name for his book); rendered "I send Joseph Scaliger's …."
 - *MAeSTLINI de emendatione Calendarij* — **Michael Maestlin**, *De emendatione Calendarii* (a tract against the Gregorian calendar reform). *Maestlini* genitive; rendered "Maestlin's …."
 - *MAUROLYCUM* — **Francesco Maurolico** (Maurolyco, 1494–1575) of Messina, mathematician; here the author's name stands for a book of his that Brucaeus could not obtain.
- **Latin formulae.** *Bene vale* = "Fare you well"; *Anno Domini* = "in the Year of the Lord."
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Rostochij 12. Iunij Anno Domini 1584* = "Rostock, 12 June 1584." **Old Style**: a Protestant correspondent in Lutheran Rostock in 1584 wrote Julian. The edition *label* ("1584. 12. juni. Rostock") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy. No silent conversion made.
- **Cruxes.**
 - **CRUX (*Gratiopolitanum*).** *MAUROLYCUM hoc tempore, ut neque Gratiopolitanum consequi potui* — "I could not obtain Maurolico at this time, any more than the *Gratiopolitanum*." *Gratiopolitanum* (var. *Gratianopolitanum*) is the Latin adjective for **Grenoble** (Gratianopolis); as a substantive accusative it parallels *Maurolycum* and so denotes a person or (more likely) a book "of/from Grenoble" that Brucaeus was likewise trying to procure for Tycho. The precise referent is not determinable from the letter and is not resolved here; "the Gratiopolitanus" is left flagged rather than guessed. This drives the overall grade.
 - **Syntactic crux (closing of the hypothesis sentence).** *Imo optandum esset, posse sine ullis hypothesibus motus coelestes tradi. Quod ut forte fieri queat, apparentijs tamen satisfieri nunquam poterit.* The second sentence is logically taut: literally "Although this could perhaps be done, yet the appearances will never be able to be satisfied." The natural reading — adopted above — is concessive ("even granting that hypothesis-free transmission were possible, the phenomena could never be fully saved by it"), i.e. a pessimistic rider to the wish. An alternative reads *Quod ut … queat* as final-purpose ("in order that this might perhaps come to pass"). The concessive reading is given; the alternative is recorded rather than suppressed.
- **Correction.** Latin 'in scapula obsignatam' corrected to 'in scattula obsignatam' per Dreyer, TBOO VII p.85.

documents.abstract: Acknowledges books received, declines the Wellerian ones, and argues that Lutheran theologians had no grounds to incite popular unrest over the Gregorian calendar reform.
documents.incipit: QUAS ad me ultimo dedisti literas, eruditissime Domine IOHANNES MAIOR, recte accepi et de …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD IOHANNEM MAIOREM.

QUAS ad me ultimo dedisti literas, eruditissime Domine IOHANNES MAIOR, recte accepi et de libris procuratis gratias habeo. WELLERIANOS hac vice non cupio. De Calendario Gregoriano quod tanta fuerit apud vos animorum concertatio, ut ferme ad arma res devenerit, miror, et meo sane iudicio non decuisset eos, qui Theologiam apud vos profitentur, occasionem sic dare his turbis et populum contra Magistratum legitimum commovere, in re, uti opinor, adiaphora et religioni, quam illi tuentur, nihil efficiente. Sed hac tamen salva, quatenus divino verbo fundatur, manente, nonne prioris et diu usitati Calendarij Nicenum Concilium secuti Romani Pontifices autores et conservatores fuêre, et aliorum dierum festorum, quibus ij, qui se Euangelium nuncupant, etiamnum utuntur? Cur igitur Pontifici Romano non liceret, praesertim approbante id Imperatoria Maiestate, idem Calendarium, quatenus mancum et insufficiens longo aevi tractu redditum est, emendare et in melius, quoad fieri potuit, restituere? Certe videntur hi, qui tam contentiose illi obstrepunt, non zelo secundum scientiam id agere, sed potius affectibus indulgere et philautia laborare, atque odio Pontificis saltem id facere. Si ante LUTHERI tempora tali modo fuisset renovatum Calendarium, quando per excellentem Germanorum Mathematicum, IOHANNEM REGIOMONTANUM, Pontifex, qui tum Romae praefuit, id fieri satagebat, certe LUTHERUS huic emendationi non invite acquievisset, cum nihil contineret ipsius doctrinae contrarium. Et cur non successores eius eo, quod nunc redintegratum est, contenti sunt? Videant, ne sic dent occasionem ijs, qui veterem doctrinam se profiteri aiunt, obijciendi, quod nimio contradictionis studio occaecati quidvis impugnent, sive id speciem aliquam dubitationis mereatur, sive non, atque ideo eos in caeteris quoque minus considerate agere praesumatur. Et siquidem de hoc Calendario renovato meam exquiris sententiam, dicam tibi id, quod et alijs eadem sciscitantibus respondi.

Calendarium hoc Gregorianum noviter reformatum praevalet veteri et prius usitato, et recte factum est a Pontifice opera LILII Mathematici, ut 10 dies in eo omissi sint. Totidem enim defectus anni coelestis et aequinoctialis a Iuliano, qui inde a Concilio Niceno direxit, quam proxime requirit. Et alia etiam quaedam non inconvenienter in nupero Calendario emendata sunt. Licet vero aliqua in his adhuc castigatius in eo proponi possint, si coelitus deducti Luminarium motus in consilium adhiberentur, tamen cum hoc non facile detur in tanta exactissimarum observationum penuria, et Ecclesiae ac Politiae usus summam in his praecisionem quam ipsi etiam Astronomi vix assequuntur, non exigat, nec etiam magnopere opus habeat, acquiescendum utique erit huic Pontificis Romani, cuius etiamnum maxima est in terris autoritas, consultae et laudabili provisioni in Calendarij diu frustraque desiderata reformatione, nec temere quid in contrarium movendum cum periculo pacis publicae.

Habes breviter, quid ego sentiam, et forte mecum viri cordati non pauci. Quid vero penitius in hac renovatione praestari possit, dicere non audeo, antequam de exacto motu ☉ et ☾ novis illis et maximis, quae adorno, organis certius quid expertus fuero. Nam coelo inconsulto de ijs, quae inde profluunt, censuram proferre velle temerarium et insulsum esse iudico. Laudo itaque Ampliss. vestrae Reipub. decisionem consultam, quod Calendarium hoc Gregorianum pacis publicae causa et ob vicinarum regionum consuetudinem atque cum ijs commercia susceperit, utut reclamitante incerto vulgo, quod semper studia in contraria scinditur. Atque de his hoc tempore satis, de tuis per occationem, si res ita postulârit, alias plura in medium proferam.

Vale.
Dabantur ex aede nostra Knudstrupiana 15. die Iulij stylo veteri, nobis adhuc usitato, Anno 1584.
T.
TYCHO DE BRAHE.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Johannes Major.**

The letter you last sent me, most learned Master Johannes Major, I have duly received, and I give thanks for the books procured. The Wellerian ones I do not want this time. That there should have been among you so great a clash of feelings over the Gregorian calendar that the matter nearly came to arms, I marvel at; and in my own judgement it ill became those who profess Theology among you to give occasion for these tumults in this way, and to stir up the people against the lawful magistrate, in a matter that, as I think, brings about nothing with respect to matters of religious indifference [*adiaphora*] and to the religion which they uphold. Yet, this remaining safe so far as it is founded upon the divine word, were not the Roman Pontiffs, following the Council of Nicaea, the authors and preservers of the earlier and long-used calendar, and of the other feast-days that those who call themselves of the Gospel still use even now? Why, then, should it not be permitted to the Roman Pontiff — especially with His Imperial Majesty approving it — to amend that same calendar, in so far as it has been rendered defective and insufficient through the long course of time, and to restore it for the better, as far as could be done? Surely those who so contentiously cry out against him seem to do this not from a zeal that is according to knowledge, but rather to indulge their passions and to labour under self-love [*philautia*], and to do it at least out of hatred of the Pontiff. Had the calendar been renewed in this manner before Luther's time — when, through the excellent German mathematician Johannes Regiomontanus, the Pontiff who then presided at Rome was busying himself to have it done — surely Luther would not unwillingly have acquiesced in this emendation, since it contained nothing contrary to his own doctrine. And why are his successors not content with what has now been set right again? Let them take care lest they thus give occasion to those who say they profess the old doctrine to object that, blinded by an excessive zeal for contradiction, they assail anything whatever — whether or not it deserves any appearance of doubt — and that therefore they may be presumed to act less considerately in other matters too. And since indeed you ask my opinion about this renewed calendar, I shall tell you what I have answered to others asking the same.

This Gregorian calendar, newly reformed, prevails over the old and formerly used one, and it was rightly done by the Pontiff, through the work of Lilius the mathematician, that 10 days were omitted in it. For just so many does the shortfall of the celestial and equinoctial year from the Julian — which had governed [the reckoning] ever since the Council of Nicaea — most nearly require. And certain other things too have been not unsuitably amended in the recent calendar. But although some things in these matters could still be set forth in it more correctly, if the motions of the Luminaries derived from the heavens themselves were brought into the deliberation, nevertheless, since this is not easily granted amid so great a scarcity of the most exact observations, and since the use of the Church and the State does not demand — nor even greatly need — that highest precision in these matters which even the Astronomers themselves scarcely attain, one must by all means acquiesce in this prudent and praiseworthy provision of the Roman Pontiff — whose authority is still the greatest on earth — in the long and vainly desired reformation of the calendar, and nothing must rashly be set in motion to the contrary, at the peril of the public peace.

You have in brief what I think, and perhaps not a few sensible men think with me. But what might more deeply be accomplished in this renewal, I do not dare to say, before I shall have ascertained something more certain about the exact motion of the Sun [☉] and the Moon [☽] by those new and very great instruments which I am preparing. For to wish to pronounce a verdict, without consulting the heavens, upon the things that flow therefrom, I judge to be rash and foolish. I therefore praise the prudent decision of your most ample commonwealth, in that it has taken up this Gregorian calendar for the sake of the public peace and on account of the custom of neighbouring regions and of commerce with them, however much the unsettled common crowd cries out against it — that crowd which is always split into opposing partialities. And on these matters enough for this time; about your affairs, as occasion offers, if the matter so require, I shall bring forward more another time.

Farewell.
Given from our seat at Knudstrup, the 15th day of July, by the old style, still used by us, in the Year 1584.
T[ycho].
Tycho de Brahe.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / place.** Tycho writes from **Knudstrup** (Knudstrup / Knutstorp), the Brahe family seat in Scania, his birthplace — distinct from Uraniborg on Hven; *aede nostra Knudstrupiana* = "our seat at Knudstrup."
- **Recipient.** *Iohannes Maior* = **Johann Major / Johannes Maior** (1533–1600), the Wittenberg humanist, Lutheran theologian and Neo-Latin poet (poeta laureatus), professor at Wittenberg; a learned correspondent who had procured books for Tycho. (To be distinguished from the medieval Scotist Johannes Maior/John Mair, and from other contemporaries of the name.) **Identification confidence MEDIUM**: the period name *Iohannes Maior* is shared by several figures; the Wittenberg poet-theologian fits the German Protestant setting of the calendar dispute described as occurring *apud vos* ("among you"), but the letter itself gives no decisive disambiguator. Flagged rather than asserted.
- ***Wellerianos*** — "the Wellerian ones [books]," i.e. works by or associated with **Hieronymus Weller** (1499–1572) of Freiberg, the Lutheran theologian and close associate of Luther (or possibly another of the Weller family of theologians); the substantivised adjective refers back to *libris* ("books"). Rendered "the Wellerian ones." Identification of the precise referent is MEDIUM.
- **The calendar dispute (*apud vos … ferme ad arma*).** The Gregorian reform was promulgated by the bull *Inter gravissimas* (Feb. 1582); the Protestant Imperial estates refused it, and its attempted introduction provoked violent resistance in several German cities — most famously the **Augsburg "calendar riot" (Kalenderstreit)** of 1583–84, where confessional conflict over the new calendar brought a city near to armed disorder. Tycho's *ut ferme ad arma res devenerit* ("that the matter nearly came to arms") reflects this; the specific city is not named in the letter and is not supplied here.
- ***anaphora*** — a technical term of the chronological/computistical reckoning (the Easter cycle / the carrying-forward of the calendrical correction); Tycho's point is that the dispute affects nothing in the substance of religion. Kept and glossed *[Easter-]reckoning* with the Latin flagged; the precise sense is a minor **crux** (see Confidence).
- ***philautia*** (φιλαυτία) — "self-love," the vice of inordinate self-regard; a learned Graeco-Latin term, kept and glossed.
- **Persons named.** *Cyprianus / —* none here beyond: **Johannes Regiomontanus** (Johann Müller of Königsberg, 1436–1476), the German mathematician-astronomer whom Pope Sixtus IV had summoned to Rome c. 1475 in connection with calendar reform (he died there in 1476); **Luther** (Martin Luther); **Aloysius Lilius** (Luigi Lilio / Giglio, d. c. 1576), the Calabrian physician-mathematician whose computational scheme underlies the Gregorian reform — *opera LILII Mathematici* = "through the work of Lilius the mathematician" (confirmed against the reference literature, which names Lilius "the principal architect of the Gregorian calendar"). *Imperatoria Maiestate* = the Holy Roman Emperor (Rudolf II), whose approval Tycho cites.
- **The ten omitted days.** *ut 1O dies in eo omissi sint* — the source prints "1O" (numeral 1 + capital O) for **10**; the ten days dropped in October 1582 to realign the equinox. The Julian year's small excess over the tropical year had, since Nicaea (325), accumulated to about ten days; Tycho's *defectus anni coelestis et aequinoctialis a Iuliano … quam proxime requirit* states that this accumulated discrepancy "most nearly requires" just that number — i.e. the correction is approximately, not exactly, right (an epistemic hedge preserved: *quam proxime*, "most nearly," not "exactly").
- **Tycho's reservation.** Note the carefully hedged scientific stance: the reform is endorsed *for civil and ecclesiastical use* and *for the public peace*, while Tycho reserves judgement on whether it is astronomically optimal until he has determined the exact solar and lunar motions with *novis illis et maximis … organis* ("those new and very great **instruments**," this chapter's convention) — the Uraniborg programme. *coelo inconsulto* = "without consulting the heavens." The hedges (*non audeo* "I dare not"; *certius quid expertus fuero* "when I shall have ascertained something more certain") are preserved, not sharpened.
- **Symbols.** ☉ = **Sun**, ☽ = **Moon** (named in the translation, glyphs kept in the Source block, this chapter's convention). *motu ☉ et ☾* = "the motion of the Sun and the Moon."
- ***Ampliss. vestrae Reipub.*** = *Amplissimae vestrae Reipublicae*, "your most ample commonwealth/republic" — the civic authority (city council / academic body) that had adopted the new calendar; the *Magistratum legitimum* ("lawful magistrate") of the first paragraph.
- ***restituere / redintegratum / reformatione / renovatione*** — Tycho's vocabulary of *restoration / renewal*, here of the calendar; cf. his own programme of *instauratio astronomiae*. Rendered consistently with "restore / set right again / reformation / renewal."
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Dabantur … 15. die Iulij stylo veteri, nobis adhuc usitato, Anno 1584* = "Given … the 15th day of July, **by the old style, still used by us**, in the Year 1584" — Tycho expressly flags his date as **Old Style (Julian)**, the running theme of the letter; **15 July 1584 O.S.** The edition label ("1584. 15. juli. Knutstorp") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy. Per this chapter's convention the date is not converted; the N.S. equivalent would be 25 July 1584, but the source asserts O.S. and so does the header.
- **Subscription.** *T. / TYCHO DE BRAHE* — the abbreviated monogram *T.* followed by the full signature; both kept.
- Correction. Latin restored 'apud vos' (Theologiam apud vos profitentur) and corrected 'anaphora' to 'adiaphora', the Lutheran technical term for matters of religious indifference at stake in the Gregorian calendar dispute (Dreyer VII p.86); English correspondingly restored 'among you' and replaced the invented gloss 'Easter-reckoning' with 'matters of religious indifference [adiaphora]'. Latin numeral '1O' corrected to '10' (Dreyer VII p.87).

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated in full against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.86-88 (all 3 pages read as page images). The letter occupies the lower half of p.86 through p.87, preceded by the tail of Henricus Brucaeus's letter to Tycho and followed by a second Brucaeus letter, both correctly excluded. Full Latin text collated: the Wellerian-books remark, the Gregorian calendar controversy, Regiomontanus and Luther, Lilius's 10-day correction, the sun/moon-instrument caveat, and the closing (Knudstrup, 15 July 1584 O.S.) all check against Dreyer. Two text error found in the transcribed original (a dropped 'apud vos'; 'adiaphora' corrupted to 'anaphora'), the second of which the translation compounds into an invented, unsupported gloss ('Easter-reckoning') that misrepresents the specific theological term central to the passage - this is what drives the *serious* verdict despite the letter being published at grade Secure.

**4 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). Source_text silently drops 'apud vos' (among you) from Dreyer's text; the English translation follows the truncated source and likewise omits 'among you'. Dreyer prints: *non decuisset eos, qui Theologiam apud vos profitentur*.
- **text error** (medium). Source_text corrupts Dreyer's 'adiaphora' (the Lutheran theological/legal term for matters of religious indifference - precisely the concept at stake in the Gregorian-calendar adiaphora controversy) into 'anaphora', a different word (rhetorical repetition / Eucharistic prayer). Dreyer prints: *in re, uti opinor, adiaphora et religioni, quam illi tuentur, nihil efficiente*.
- **mistranslation** (**high**). Working from the corrupted 'anaphora', the translator invents an unsupported interpretive gloss ('Easter-reckoning') matching neither Dreyer's actual word 'adiaphora' (matters of religious indifference) nor any plausible sense of 'anaphora'. A scholar would come away with a false idea of the specific theological concept Tycho is invoking in a letter about the Gregorian calendar dispute. At: “the [Easter-]reckoning [anaphora]”.
- **text error** (low). Source_text renders the numeral as digit-plus-letter '1O' rather than '10'; likely a process rendering artifact, but a literal departure from Dreyer's printed numeral. Translation correctly reads '10 days'. Dreyer prints: *ut 10 dies in [eo] omissi sint*.

**Repaired.** Collated all four defects against the Dreyer page images (TBOO VII pp.86-87). Page 86 confirms 'Theologiam apud vos profitentur' and 'in re, uti opinor, adiaphora et religioni'; page 87 confirms the numeral '10'. All four defects fixed with high confidence; no crux remains.

text.original:
HENRICUS BRUCÆUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.
S. P.

SCRIPSI per eundem, qui tuas literas ad me pertulit, Bibliopolam Francofurto ad nos redeuntem nihil eorum librorum, quorum in literis meministi, attulisse, daturum autem me operam, ut vel Lipsia aut Witeberga, quos nancisci potero, adferendos curem. Gnomotericam CLAVIJ, quam aestimat Ioachimicis prope 5, RANZOVIO vendidit. Laborabo, ut studium et diligentiam nostram in hisce libris conquirendis agnoscas. Intellige autem, duo illa volumina iunctim venire Joachimicis 16. Typographum nostrum MYLIANDRUM typorum nomine conveni; is respondet, ante D. Antonij festum non posse hisce typis carere, tum, si voles, velle aliquot libras vendere; arbitratur autem, libras 10 non sufficere ad unam columnam sive paginam excudendam. Aestimat singulas libras dimidio Thalero. Quid fieri velis, indicabis, antequam mare claudatur. VITUS ille, cuius meministi, mihi adfuit et respondit, velle fundere typos, quorum in tuis literis ad eum datis mentionem fecisti. Quaerenti mihi de precio respondit, unâ cum quadratis Ioachimicos prope 30 requiri.

In Eclipsi Lunae 7. Novembris observata nostrae observationes non plane cum tuis conveniunt. Initium non fuit observatum. Porro ubi tota obscurari visa est, deprehensa est Procyonis altitudo partium 26. Cum primum ex umbra inciperet emergere, altitudo eiusdem stellae partium erat 37. Ubi tota ex umbra emergere visa est, erat 41. Ex quibus tempora si deducantur, principium Eclipsis incidet in horam 11 6' 32 ", principium vero totius occultationis in h. 12 11' 44", medium [totius obscurationis in h. 1 1' 48", finis] totius obscurationis in h. 1 51' 52". Tota ex umbra emersit h. 2 55' 4". Ex quibus colligo MÆSTLINUM sesquihora ab hac observatione differre, ipsum vero COPERNICUM scrupulis solum sex, PURBACHIUM vero 30'. Si quid tamen ex superioribus observationibus potui colligere, propius a PURBACHIO fuit accessum in aliquot prioribus Eclipsibus. Et credo, me superiorem aliquam Eclipsin observasse, in qua proxime visus est MÆSTLINUS accedere. Verum, mi TYCHO, haec res eget, ut ego iudico, longe ante actorum temporum et observationum artificum excellentium collatione, et homine ingenij sagacis, qui queat aliorum inventis aliquid addere. Ego in PROCLO ad Solis usque motum progressus sum, in cuius consideratione, ut aliorum siderum, cum studium tuum et diligentia perspecta mihi sint, velim aequinoctium solstitiorumque tempora ex te intelligere. Tua enim industria cum habeas instrumenta exquisite elaborata et utendi ratio optime tibi constet, non dubito, tibi dies et horarum momenta, in quae incidunt, constare.

Bene vale, carissime TYCHO, et me mutuo amore prosequere.
Rostochij 1O. Decemb. 1584.
text.english:
**Heinrich Brucaeus to Tycho Brahe.**
Heartiest greeting.

I wrote — by the same man who brought your letter to me — that the bookseller, returning to us from Frankfurt, had brought none of those books which you mentioned in your letter, but that I would take pains to see to it that those I can obtain be brought either from Leipzig or from Wittenberg. The *Gnomonice* of Clavius, which he reckons at nearly 5 Joachimsthalers, I sold to Rantzau. I shall labour so that you may recognize our zeal and diligence in seeking out these books. Understand, moreover, that those two volumes go together for 16 Joachimsthalers. I approached our printer Myliander on the matter of the types; he replies that before St Anthony's feast he cannot do without these types, [but] then, if you wish, he is willing to sell some pounds [of them]; he judges, however, that 10 pounds are not enough to print off a single column or page. He values each pound at half a thaler. You will indicate what you wish to be done before the sea is closed. That Vitus whom you mentioned was present with me and replied that he is willing to cast the types of which you made mention in your letter sent to him. When I asked him about the price, he replied that, together with the quadrats, nearly 30 Joachimsthalers are required.

In the eclipse of the Moon observed on 7 November our observations do not entirely agree with yours. The beginning was not observed. Further, when it appeared to be wholly darkened, the altitude of Procyon was found to be 26 degrees. When it first began to emerge from the shadow, the altitude of the same star was 37 degrees. When it appeared to emerge wholly from the shadow, it was 41. If the times are deduced from these, the beginning of the eclipse will fall at the hour 11h 6' 32", the beginning of total occultation at 12h 11' 44", the middle [of total obscuration at 1h 1' 48", the end] of total obscuration at 1h 51' 52". It emerged wholly from the shadow at 2h 55' 4". From these I gather that Maestlin differs from this observation by an hour and a half, but Copernicus himself by only six minutes [of arc / of time], and Peurbach by 30'. Yet if I have been able to gather anything from earlier observations, in several prior eclipses the approach was closer to Peurbach. And I believe that I observed some earlier eclipse in which Maestlin was seen to come nearest. But, my Tycho, this matter requires, as I judge, a collation of the times of long-past events and of the observations of excellent craftsmen, and a man of sagacious genius, who is able to add something to the discoveries of others. I have, in Proclus, advanced as far as the motion of the Sun, in the consideration of which — as of the other heavenly bodies — since your zeal and diligence are well known to me, I should like to learn from you the times of the equinox and of the solstices. For since by your industry you have instruments exquisitely wrought, and the manner of using them is perfectly settled for you, I do not doubt that the days, and the moments of the hours on which they fall, are settled for you.

Fare you well, dearest Tycho, and continue to attend me with mutual love.
Rostock, 10 December 1584.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (Hendrik van den Broeck, 1530/31–1593), Flemish-born professor of medicine and mathematics at the University of Rostock, where Tycho had studied; a long-standing correspondent and book/instrument intermediary for him. The Vienna copy-book (cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66) preserves this among the *epistolae*; the letter is Dreyer, *TBOO* VII, p. 88.
- **Salutation.** *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam* (*dicit*), "heartiest greeting". *Bene vale* = "Fare you well."
- **Book trade.** *Bibliopolam Francofurto … redeuntem* — a bookseller returning from the **Frankfurt** book fair; *Lipsia / Witeberga* = **Leipzig / Wittenberg**. *Ioachimici* (sc. *thaleri Ioachimici*) = **Joachimsthalers** (the silver *Joachimsthaler* / "Joachim's-dale thaler"), here the unit of account; *Thalerus* = **thaler**. *Ranzovio* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), the Holstein royal governor, humanist and astrology patron, a noted book-collector.
- ***Gnomotericam Clavij*** — Christopher Clavius's work on dialling/gnomonics, i.e. the *Gnomonices libri octo* (Rome, 1581). The MS spelling *Gnomotericam* (for *Gnomonicam*) is retained in the Source block; rendered *Gnomonice* in translation, the slip flagged here rather than silently corrected.
- **Printing-type procurement.** The letter's central business: Tycho's setting-up of the **Uraniborg press**. *Typographum nostrum Myliandrum* = the Rostock printer **Stephan Myliander** (Möllemann); *typorum nomine conveni* = "I approached … on the matter of the types." *ante D. Antonij festum* = "before **St Anthony's feast**" (St Anthony the Abbot, 17 January, O.S.). *libras / libra* here = **pounds (weight) of type-metal**, not coins or books (*libras 10 non sufficere ad unam columnam … excudendam* fixes the sense). *VITUS ille* = "that **Vitus**" (Veit), a type-founder named in Tycho's prior letter; *velle fundere typos* = "willing to cast the types." *quadratis / quadratis* = **quadrats** (the blank spacing-pieces of a type-font). Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, cites this exact passage (TBOO VII, 88.13–17) for Tycho's type procurement from Myliander; *On Tycho's Island* confirms that fonts were cast at Rostock with Brucaeus's help, with some type from Wittenberg.
- ***antequam mare claudatur*** — "before the sea is closed," i.e. before winter ice/storms shut down Baltic shipping between Rostock and Hven: the practical deadline for the consignment.
- **Lunar eclipse of 7 November 1584.** A citation-grade comparison of observed contact-times. *partium 26 … 37 … 41* = **degrees** of *altitudo* (altitude) of **Procyon** (*Procyonis*), the reference star used to derive the times. *principium Eclipsis … principium totius occultationis … finis totius obscurationis … Tota ex umbra emersit* = the eclipse phases (first contact / beginning of totality / end of totality / last contact); times given in *h[ora] … ' …"* = hours, minutes, seconds.
 - **Editorial restoration (Dreyer).** In *medium [totius obscurationis in h. 1 1' 48", finis] totius obscurationis* the bracketed words are the editor's restoration of text lost by eye-skip between the two occurrences of *totius obscurationis*; kept as printed in the Source block and reproduced (in brackets) in the translation.
- **Authorities compared.** *Maestlinum* = **Michael Maestlin** (1550–1631, then at Tübingen/Backnang; later Kepler's teacher); *Copernicum* = **Nicolaus Copernicus** (i.e. tables computed from *De revolutionibus*); *Purbachium* = **Georg Peurbach** (1423–1461, the *Theoricae novae planetarum* / Alfonsine tradition). Brucaeus measures each authority's predicted timing against his own observation.
- **Crux — *scrupulis solum sex*.** *scrupula* in this period denotes either **minutes of arc** or **minutes of time** (*scrupula temporis*); since Brucaeus expresses Maestlin's discrepancy as *sesquihora* ("an hour and a half" — time) and Peurbach's as *30'*, the *sex* for Copernicus is most naturally minutes **of time**, but the bare *scrupulis* does not decide arc vs. time. Rendered "six minutes [of arc / of time]," the ambiguity flagged rather than resolved.
- ***in Proclo … ad Solis usque motum*** — Brucaeus has read in **Proclus** (his *Hypotyposis astronomicarum positionum*, the late-antique exposition of Ptolemaic theory) as far as the motion of the Sun, and asks Tycho for his observed *aequinoctium solstitiorumque tempora* (**times of the equinox and solstices**) — a request that trades on Tycho's *instrumenta exquisite elaborata* ("exquisitely wrought instruments," this chapter's convention *instrumenta*).
- **Calendar / place.** *Rostochij … Decemb. 1584* = **Rostock**, December 1584 (O.S.; Denmark and the Lutheran north kept the Julian calendar). **Day-figure reading:** the MS prints the day as *1O.* — a figure **1** followed by a letter-form **O** rather than a clear *10.*; the intended day is **10 December**, agreeing with the catalogue date *"1584. 10. december"* and with the scholarly citation (TBOO VII, 88). The printed *1O.* is kept in the Source block; "10 December" adopted in the header and translation, the orthographic oddity noted here. *7. Novembris* (the eclipse date) is likewise O.S.
- **Correction.** Restored Dreyer's numeral "30" (the sum of Joachimsthalers required for the type-casting, together with the quadrats) and corrected "vendidij" to Dreyer's "vendidit" (TBOO VII p.88).

Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VII pp.88-90 read as page images; the Brucaeus-to-Tycho letter runs from p.88 through the first four lines of p.89 ('...Rostochij 10. Decemb. 1584.'); the remainder of pp.89-90 is a different letter (Tycho to Ranzovius, 8 Jan. 1585) and was not needed. The two departures found are both in the opening paragraph about books and type; the dropped sum ('30') is a genuine lost fact and forces grade Possible.

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (medium). Dreyer's page clearly prints the number '30' (the type-caster Vitus wants nearly 30 Joachimsthalers, together with the quadrats); the transcribed original drops the numeral entirely. The English translator noticed the gap and marked it with a bracketed hedge rather than fabricating a figure, but a scholar consulting this letter for the actual sum would still come away without it. documents.abstract: Requests the return of a compass given to Tycho for repair, or if unavailable, asks that two new compasses of the same quality be made.
documents.incipit: Frederich etc.

text.original:
THYGGE BRAHE FICH BREFF NOGENN COMPASSER ANRØRE[N]DIS VT SEQUITUR

Frederich etc.

WOR gunst thilforn, Wij kunde Oß andet icke ehrindre, end att Wij nu nogit forleden haffue thil thig offuerantuordet en Wor compaß, som thu selff haffde ladit Oß giøre, huilcken war bleffuen nogit wrichthig, attu therfore Oß thend schulle lade egien giøre thil rette. Ther som nu saa er schet, och samme compas er ferdig giort, tha bede Wij thig, attu Oß thend wforsømmit thilschicker, thersom thu och jcke for:ne compaß haffuer bekommit, tha bede Wij thig och begere, attu wil lade Oß giøre tho compaßer, saadanne som thend anden war, och thett kunstrichs och restist schie kand, saa Wij thennum met thett første mueligt wor kunde bekomme.

Ther meth etc.
Actum Soer, xj decembr: aar 84.
text.english:
**Tyge Brahe received a letter concerning certain compasses, as follows:**

Frederick, etc.

Our favour beforehand. We cannot but call to mind that we did, some while ago now, hand over to you one of our compasses — which you yourself had had made for us, [and] which had become somewhat inaccurate — so that you were therefore to have it put right again for us. If it has now been so done, and that same compass is finished, then we ask you to send it to us without fail; and if you have not [yet] got the aforesaid compass [back in hand], then we ask and desire you to have two compasses made for us, such as the other one was, and made as artfully and as accurately as can be, so that we may obtain them at the very first that may be possible.

Therewith, etc.
Done at Sorø, 11 December, year [15]84.

documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer.** **Frederik II of Denmark** (r. 1559–88), Tycho's royal patron, who in 1576 had granted him the island of Hven. A characteristic instance of the king treating Tycho as his instrument-maker as well as his astronomer.
- **Document type.** A chancery-register entry (Sjællandske Tegnelser). The **Latin rubric** *"…NOGENN COMPASSER ANRØRENDIS **ut sequitur**"* ("concerning certain compasses, **as follows**") heads the Danish body — a code-switch preserved by this chapter's convention *ANRØRE[N]DIS*: the source contracts *anrørendes* with a tilde for the nasal; expanded in brackets.
- ***compaß / compasser*** — rendered "compass(es)." **Ambiguity flagged:** in 1580s Danish royal usage this is most likely a **drawing/measuring compass (pair of compasses, dividers)** of fine workmanship — the king stresses it be made *kunstrigt og rigtigst* ("as artfully and accurately as can be") and that Tycho had had it made — but the word can also denote a **sundial-/magnetic compass-dial**. The text does not decide it; "compass" is kept and the ambiguity recorded rather than resolved.
- **Orthography (chancery Danish, c. 1584).** *WOR gunst thilforn* = *Vor gunst tilforn* ("Our favour beforehand," the royal address-formula, this chapter's convention); *attu* = *at du*; *offuerantuordet* = *overantvordet* ("handed over/delivered"); *wrichthig* = *urigtig* ("inaccurate, out of true"); *wforsømmit* = *uforsømmet* ("without fail/neglect"); *for:ne* = *fornævnte* ("aforesaid," the standard chancery abbreviation); *kunstrichs* = *kunstrigt* ("artfully, skilfully"); *restist* = *rigtigst* ("most accurately/correctly"); *thennum* = *dennem* ("them").
- **Calendar / place.** *Actum Soer, xj decembr. aar 84* = "Done at **Sorø**, 11 December [15]84" (O.S.); *Actum* "Done/Given" kept by this chapter's convention

documents.abstract: Sends paper and printing type obtained from Wittenberg, giving prices and delivery details, and notes the carter will bring remaining type once cast.
documents.incipit: MITTO tibi Chartam et Typos, quos Witeberga accepi. Papyri singulas Risas aestimat …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO NOBILISSIMOQUE VIRO D. TYCHONI BRAHE, MATHEMATICO EXIMIO, DOMINO ET AMICO PLURIMUM COLENDO.
S. D.

MITTO tibi Chartam et Typos, quos Witeberga accepi. Papyri singulas Risas aestimat solidis 30. Hisce vasis inclusam ad me miserunt, si quid damni acceperit, non est, quod me culpes. Reliquos Typos DAVID auriga se allaturum, ubi fusi fuerint, promisit. Poscit in pondo 100 Ioachimum unum. In universum pro pecunia transmissa typorum fusori et typis huc transvehendis exigit 4 Thaleros. Quid insuper fieri velis significabis

[HENRICUS BRUCÆUS.
text.english:
**To the most distinguished and most noble man, Master Tycho Brahe, the eminent mathematician, his lord and friend to be greatly honoured.**
Greeting.

I am sending you the paper and the type which I obtained from Wittenberg. He values the single reams of paper at 30 shillings each. They sent it to me enclosed in these casks; if it has taken any harm, there is no reason for you to blame me. The carter David has promised that he will bring the rest of the type once it has been cast. He demands one Joachimsthaler for every 100 [units] by weight. In all, for the money sent to the type-founder and for conveying the type here, he requires 4 thalers. You will let [me] know what you wish to be done besides.

[Heinrich Brucaeus.]

- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (Brucäus; 1531–1593), the Flemish-born professor of medicine and mathematics at the University of Rostock, an early correspondent and supporter of Tycho. The letter was therefore written from (or near) **Rostock**; the place is not stated in the text and is supplied editorially in brackets.
- **Recipient / dating.** The salutation addresses *D. Tychoni Brahe, mathematico eximio* — the body is unambiguously a letter to Tycho. The edition metadata carries a stray field (*Frederik II / Sorø / Sjællandske Tegnelser*) that belongs to the adjacent register entry, not to this letter; it is disregarded. The edition assigns the year **[1585]** with the note *"empty"* (i.e. an undated letter editorially placed in 1585); no dateline survives in the text. The header therefore gives "[1585]" in brackets as an editorial placement, not an as-written date. **O.S./N.S. cannot be determined** since no day or month is transmitted.
- **MS witness.** A = Vienna, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66, described in the source as an *Afskrift* (a later copy/apograph), not the original.
- **Commercial / printing terms.**
 - *Chartam … Papyri … Risas* — *charta* and *papyrus* both denote **paper**; *risa* (= *risma*, ream) is a **ream** of paper. "the single reams … at 30 shillings each" renders *singulas Risas … solidis 30*.
 - *Typos … typorum fusori … fusi fuerint* — *typi* here are cast metal **printing types** (founts of type), and *typorum fusor* is the **typefounder**; *fusi fuerint* = "once they have been cast/founded." This is type for a press, consistent with Tycho's establishment of his own printing operation on Hven. (*Typi* could in principle mean engraved figures/woodblocks, but *fusi*/*fusor* — casting/founder — fixes the sense as cast type.)
 - *Witeberga* = **Wittenberg** (ablative of origin, "from Wittenberg"); the paper and type were procured there.
- **Money.** *solidis 30* = **30 shillings (solidi)** — *solidus* kept as the period accounting term, glossed "shilling." *Ioachimum unum* = **one Joachimsthaler** (a *Joachimicus*, the Joachimsthal silver coin, the original "thaler"). *4 Thaleros* = **4 thalers**. The two coin-names are treated as distinct denominations and not silently merged.
- ***in pondo 100 Ioachimum unum*** — literally "one Joachimsthaler per 100 in weight." The unit of weight is not specified in the text (pounds is the natural supplement but is not written); rendered "for every 100 [units] by weight," with the bracket marking the unsupplied unit rather than supplying "pounds." **Flagged**: the weight-unit is genuinely absent from the source.
- ***Hisce vasis inclusam … miserunt*** — "they sent it to me enclosed in these casks/vessels"; *vas* (pl. *vasa*) is a container/cask for shipping. The participle *inclusam* (fem. sing.) agrees with *chartam* (the paper), so "it" = the paper consignment.
- ***DAVID auriga*** — "the carter/wagoner David," the named carrier engaged to bring the remaining type; *auriga* = driver/carter.
- **Salutation / subscription.** *S. D.* = *salutem dicit*, "(sends) greeting". The closing *significabis* ("you will let [me] know") ends the transmitted body without a *Vale*; the subscription *[Henricus Brucaeus]* stands in editorial brackets in the source (the opening "[" is unclosed in the transcription — a copyist/transcription artifact), reproduced as printed in the Source block.

- **Correction.** English recast from three itemised charges to the two the Latin actually lists ('the money sent to the type-founder' / 'conveying the type here'), per Dreyer, TBOO VII p.91; no change to the Latin.

text.original:
GENEROSO ET MAGNIFICO VIRO D. HENRICO RANZOVIO, REGIAe MAIESTATIS DANIAe IN HOLSATIA ET SLESVICIA VICARIO ET CONSILIARIO PRUDENTISSIMO, PRÆFECTO ARCIS SEGEBERGAe, ET DOMINO IN BREDENBERGA AMICO SUO OBSERVANDO.
S.

OBILISSIME et Eruditissime Domine HENRICE RANZOWI, fuit hisce diebus apud me filius tuus GERARDUS RANZOW, Praeses arcis Kroneburgensis, Amicus meus singularis et vicinus exoptatissimus; cumque is prae ceteris nostri aevi Nobilibus Iuvenibus non saltem rerum Mundanarum multiplici et late quaesita Experientia, sed etiam Ingenio et Iudicio praeeminenti valeat, Moribusque insuper admodum laudatis praeditus sit, ipsius conversatione plurimum afficiebar eique tum varias observandis sideribus a me ingenti labore et sumtu constructas Machinas, tum etiam Pyronomici exercitij diversa Artificia lubens ostendi; inter alia vero cum in Typographiam meam, quam hac aestate praeterita parari curavi, illum deducerem, ut Typos et rationem nostram imprimendarum chartarum perspiceret, conquestus sum illi, papyrum impressoriam mihi pro absolutis laboribus edendis deficere, et hyemem obstaculo esse, quominus eam nunc satis opportune nancisci queam; adeo ut ne pro quodam exiguo huius inchoati anni Calendario Astrologico imprimendo mihi charta suppetat, vel alicubi iusto pretio hîc in Dania venalis existat; nedum ut alijs maioribus a me confectis Operibus, quae maximam papyri copiam postulant, sufficiens acquiratur. Subiunxit itaque ille, te Patrem ipsius molendinam habere papyraceam nec dubitare, si negocium hoc tibi constaret, quin lubenter pro Calendario isto excudendo mihi sufficientem Papyrum concessurus sis, suaque sponte (ut est Ingenio bonis conatibus admodum faventi) obtulit, se tibi hoc nomine scripturum, quod et statim hîc praesens praestitit; literasque tibi transmittendas tradidit, quas nunc per proprium nuntium, unum ex meis familiaribus, IOHANNEM BERNSSÖN nomine (cui ut fidem habeas velim) perferendas curo, ut eo certius ad tuam Generositatem mature perveniant, negociumque hoc eo rectius perficiatur; rogoque peramanter ut, si in Officina tua Papyracea reperiatur impressoria Papyrus meis votis conveniens, mihi de ea 20 vel 25 Riss, ut vocant, concedere velis. Pretium solitum tuae Officinae praefecto, quam primum de eo certior factus fuero, lubens transinittam. Continebit Calendarium illud, ubi impressum fuerit, circiter 6 quaterniones, ut ob id 25 Rissij pro 2000 Exemplaribus imprimendis requirantur. Pro reliquis vero maioribus a me absolutis Astronomicis Operibus quam primum, Deo volente, in lucem edendis, multo copiosiorem, quae requiritur, papyrum in hoc ipso Freto Helsingorae facile habiturus sum, cum vernum tempus navigationem consuetam reduxerit. Spero autem tuam Magnificentiam meis defiderijs hac in parte, quantum in te est, interea non defuturam, et dabo operam, ut hoc Officij genus in me non frustra collocatum experiare. Mittam vero brevi literas impressas tibi alijsque Nobilibus et eruditis Amicis inscriptas, quamprimum omnes absolutae fuerint, ut Typos nostros videas, sique illi placuerint, et quid habeas, quod in lucem edere ex Astrologicis rebus decreveris, lubenter ut in mea Officina excudatur, permittam, saltem ut ipse requisitam Papyrum addas. Et si quacunque alia in re tuae Generositati unquam aliquid per me quod gratum sit praestari queat, efficiam ut me facilem et promptissimum habeas. Vale cum charissima coniuge totaque domo, vir Amplissime pariter et Eruditissime, meque tui studiosissimum redamare non graveris.

Datae Uraniburgi in Insula porthmi DaniciHuena die 8. Ianuarij Anno 1585.
Tuae generositati addictiss.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 90; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Si catalogum Astrologicorum tuorum librorum ex amplissima tua Bibliotheca descriptum mihi transmittere non displicuerit, rem feceris longe gratissimam.
text.english:
**To the noble and magnificent gentleman Master Heinrich Rantzau, the most prudent viceroy and councillor of the Royal Majesty of Denmark in Holstein and Schleswig, governor of the castle of Segeberg, and lord in Breitenburg, his friend to be esteemed — greeting.**

Most noble and most learned Master Heinrich Rantzau, there was with me in these days past your son Gerhard Rantzau, governor of the castle of Kronborg, my singular friend and a most longed-for neighbour. And since he, beyond the other noble young men of our age, is strong not only in a manifold and widely-gathered experience of worldly affairs, but also in pre-eminent talent and judgement, and is moreover endowed with most praiseworthy character, I was greatly taken with his company; and I gladly showed him both the various machines [instruments] I have constructed at vast labour and cost for observing the stars, and likewise the diverse devices of the pyronomic exercise [the chemical art]. Among other things, indeed, when I led him into my printing-house, which I had seen to having set up this past summer, so that he might examine the types and our method of printing sheets, I complained to him that printing-paper was lacking to me for publishing my finished works, and that winter was an obstacle preventing me from now obtaining it conveniently enough — so much so that not even for a certain small Astrological Calendar of this now-beginning year that is to be printed is there paper enough at my disposal, nor is any to be had for sale here in Denmark at a fair price; let alone that sufficient be acquired for the other, greater works completed by me, which demand a very great quantity of paper. He therefore added that you, his father, have a paper-mill, and did not doubt that, if this business were made clear to you, you would gladly grant me sufficient paper for printing that Calendar; and of his own accord (as he is of a disposition very much favouring good endeavours) he offered to write to you on this account, which he did at once, here present; and he gave me the letter to be conveyed to you, which I now have carried by a special messenger, one of my household, John Bernssøn by name (to whom I would wish you to give credence), that it may the more surely reach Your Generosity in good time, and this business be the more rightly accomplished. And I ask most affectionately that, if in your paper-works there be found printing-paper agreeable to my wishes, you would be willing to grant me 20 or 25 reams, as they call them, of it. The usual price I will gladly send to the overseer of your works as soon as I am informed of it. That Calendar, when it has been printed, will contain about 6 quaternions, so that on that account 25 reams are required for printing 2000 copies. But for the remaining greater Astronomical Works completed by me, to be brought into the light as soon as possible, God willing, I shall easily have the much more copious paper that is required here in this very Sound at Elsinore, when the spring season has brought back the customary sailing. I hope, however, that Your Magnificence will not in the meantime fail my desires in this matter, so far as in you lies; and I will take pains that you may find this kind of service not bestowed upon me in vain. And shortly I shall send you, and other noble and learned friends, letters printed [and] inscribed [to you], as soon as they are all finished, that you may see our types; and if they please you, and you have anything among astrological matters that you have resolved to bring into the light, I will gladly permit it to be printed in my workshop — provided only that you yourself supply the requisite paper. And if in any other matter whatsoever anything that is welcome can ever be rendered to Your Generosity through me, I will see to it that you find me obliging and most ready. Farewell, with your dearest wife and your whole house, gentleman both most ample and most learned, and do not be unwilling to return the love of me who am most devoted to you.

Given at Uraniborg, on the island Hven of the Danish strait, on the 8th day of January, the year 1585.
Most attached to Your Generosity,
TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.


*[Postscript:]* If it should not displease you to send me a catalogue of your Astrological books, copied out from your most ample Library, you will do me a most welcome thing indeed.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** *Henricus Ranzovius* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), the Danish crown's *Statthalter* (viceroy/royal governor) in the duchies of Holstein and Schleswig, humanist, astrologer, and one of the great book-collectors and patrons of the age; lord of Breitenburg (*Bredenberga*) and governor of Segeberg castle. Tycho courted him as a patron and conduit to the wider learned world.
- **Persons named.** *Gerardus Ranzow* = **Gerhard (Gert) Rantzau** (1558–1627), Heinrich's son, then governor (*Praeses*) of **Kronborg** castle at Elsinore — Tycho's near neighbour across the Sound; he later succeeded his father as viceroy. *Iohannes Bernssön* = **Johann (Hans) Bernssøn**, a member of Tycho's household (*familiaris*) sent as the special messenger; otherwise unidentified.
- **Places.** *arx Kroneburgensis* = **Kronborg** (Elsinore/Helsingør); *arx Segebergae* = **Segeberg** castle (Holstein); *Bredenberga* = **Breitenburg** (Rantzau's seat in Holstein); *Fretum / Helsingorae* = **the Sound (Øresund) at Elsinore**; *Uraniburgum in Insula porthmi Danici Huena* = **Uraniborg on the island of Hven** in the Danish strait. The biographies confirm the episode: Gert Rantzau visited Hven and told Tycho his father's paper-mill could supply paper, and Tycho intended to print the calendar in 2000 copies (Christianson, *On Tycho's Island*).
- **Technical / craft terms.** *Machinas … observandis sideribus … constructas* — Tycho's astronomical **instruments** (here *machinae*, rendered "machines [instruments]" per glossary). *Pyronomici exercitij … Artificia* — "the devices of the pyronomic exercise," i.e. Tycho's **chemistry/alchemy** ("pyronomy," the fire-art) carried on in the Uraniborg laboratory; glossed rather than modernised. *Typographia / Officina / Typos / chartas imprimendas* — Tycho's own **printing-house** at Uraniborg, its **types**, and the **sheets** to be printed.
- **Paper terms.** *papyrus impressoria* = **printing-paper**; *molendina papyracea / Officina Papyracea* = **paper-mill / paper-works**; *Riss / Rissij* ("ut vocant," "as they call them") = the German loanword *Ries* = **ream** (a paper quantity, here kept as "reams"); *quaterniones* = **quaternions** (gatherings of four sheets / eight leaves). The arithmetic in the letter (≈6 quaternions per copy → 25 reams for 2000 copies) is reproduced as written, not recomputed.
- **The Calendar and the "greater works."** *Calendarium … Astrologia[e]* — a small **astrological calendar** for 1585; the *maiora Astronomica Opera* "completed by me … to be brought into the light" are Tycho's projected major publications (the instrument and *De mundi* volumes), here described prospectively with his own hedge *Deo volente* ("God willing"), preserved.
- **Formulae.** *S.* = *salutem* ("greeting"); *Vale* = "Farewell"; *Tuae generositati addictiss.* = "Most attached to Your Generosity"; *manu propria* = "in his own hand." The honorific *Generositas / Magnificentia Tua* is rendered "Your Generosity / Your Magnificence."
- **Orthographic notes (Source block preserves the printed forms).** The salutation word opens *OBILISSIME* — a dropped/decorative initial **[N]** for *NOBILISSIME* ("most noble"), expanded in the translation. *transinittam* (line: "Pretium … lubens transinittam") is a printer's misprint for *transmittam* ("I will send"); translated as *transmittam*. *defiderijs* = *desideriis* ("desires"); *-ij/-ijs* throughout is the period spelling of *-ii/-iis*. In the dateline *DaniciHuena* the edition prints *Danici* and *Huena* run together without a space; read as *Danici Huena* ("…of the Danish [strait], Hven").
- **Calendar.** *die 8. Ianuarij Anno 1585* = **8 January 1585**, Old Style (Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). The catalogue label ("1585. 8. januar. Uraniborg") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy. No date is "corrected."

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript, restored from Dreyer VII, p. 90 (dropped by the working transcription).
- **Correction.** Latin corrected from 'Calendario Astrologia' to 'Calendario Astrologico' per Dreyer, TBOO VII p.89 (agreement of adjective with 'Calendario'); no change to the English, which already read correctly.

text.original:
HENRICUS BRUCÆUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

LITERAS tuas, amantissime TYCHO, quibus Calendarij a tuo domestico Studioso edendi mentionem fecisti, accepi et iam Typos fusos a VITO miseram unâ cum libris illius Florentini, adiectis schedulis duabus, una VITI, altera aurigae Witebergensis, quibus de precio tibi constabit. Miratus autem sum, te potioribus intentum permittere, ut talia in tua Typographia edantur, quae trita sunt et vulgaria, in quibus si quis aëris mutationes praedicendas suscipiat, paene ridiculum sese toti mundo exponit. Et tot a vero aberrantes praedictiones effecerunt, ut nugarum mendaciorumque eiuscemodi libri habeantur. Nec credo fuisse quemquam, qui huius hyemis levitatem et siccitatem praedixerit, cuius constitutio prope verna habenda est, si frigoris imbecillitatem spectes. Et quam ridiculum sese praebuit quidam Astrologaster, qui in suo Calendario Martio magna frigora et nives minatur, adeo fisus suis praedictionibus, ut si eventus falleret, iam artem nullam crederet. Et ego arbitror, veris et irrefutabilibus rationibus posse demonstrari, incertam plane esse hanc de aëris mutationibus praedictionem, praeter anni tempora, quae ut plurimum suas constitutiones servant. Sed tu forte, mi TYCHO, alias rationes habes, cur haec a tuis Discipulis fieri permittas, etiamsi tu ipse non multum tribuas eiuscemodi praedictionibus, quarum difficultatem, immo paene impossibilitatem ipsemet satis nosti, quod et in familiari nostro colloquio a te audivisse recordor, cum alias etiam Astrologica vaticinia, uti multi alias solent, non pluris facias, quam par est. Credo itaque, te sic indulgere tuis Discipulis, qui prognosticis annuis, more recepto, conficiendis delectantur, ut habeant, quo graviora studia leniant, fortassis etiam aliquid praeter communem formam a te hauserunt. Si sic est, prodeat Calendarium illud in publicum, et discamus inde experiamurque, quae prius nos latuerunt. Scio enim te nil vulgare et tritum moliri, neque levia tuis concedere. Plura non possum, urgente nuntio.

Bene vale, et ut hoc in genere nobis sis Apollo, opto.
Datae in Holsatia ipso die Palmarum 1585.
text.english:
**Heinrich Brucaeus to Tycho Brahe.**

I have received your letter, most loving Tycho, in which you made mention of a calendar [almanac] to be published by your resident student; and I had already sent the founts of type [Typos fusos] from Vitus, together with the books of that Florentine, with two notes [schedulae] added — one from Vitus, the other from the Wittenberg carter — by which the price will be clear to you. But I was astonished that you, intent on weightier matters, should permit such things to be published at your press as are hackneyed and commonplace, in which, if anyone undertakes to predict the changes of the weather, he exposes himself to the whole world as well-nigh ridiculous. And so many predictions straying from the truth have brought it about that books of this kind are held to be trifles and lies. Nor do I believe there was anyone who predicted the mildness and dryness of this winter, whose constitution is to be reckoned almost spring-like, if you regard the feebleness of the cold. And how ridiculous did a certain astrologaster make himself, who in his calendar threatens great frosts and snows for March, so trusting in his predictions that, if the event should prove him wrong, he would believe there to be no science [art] at all [in it]. And I, for my part, judge that it can be demonstrated by true and irrefutable arguments that this prediction concerning the changes of the weather is plainly uncertain — apart from the seasons of the year, which for the most part keep their [own] constitutions. But perhaps, my Tycho, you have other reasons why you permit these things to be done by your pupils, even if you yourself do not attach much weight to predictions of this kind, the difficulty — nay, the well-nigh impossibility — of which you yourself know well enough; which I recall having heard from you, too, in our familiar conversation, since you do not — as many others are otherwise wont to do — set more store by astrological prophecies than is fitting. I believe, therefore, that you indulge your pupils thus — who take delight in compiling annual prognostics, after the received custom — so that they may have something with which to relieve their heavier studies; perhaps too they have drawn from you something beyond the common form. If it is so, let that calendar [Calendarium] come forth into public, and let us learn from it and try out the things that were hidden from us before. For I know that you devise nothing common and hackneyed, and grant nothing trifling to your pupils. I can [write] no more, as the messenger presses.

Fare you well; and I pray that in this kind [of thing] you may be an Apollo to us.
Given in Holstein, on Palm Sunday itself, 1585.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (1531–1593), professor of medicine and mathematics at the University of Rostock, a Lutheran scholar of Flemish origin; Tycho's friend and one of his early academic mentors, with whom he maintained a long technical correspondence. The letter is preserved among those Tycho gathered for the *Epistolae* (1568–1587).
- **Heading.** *HENRICUS BRUCAeUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE* — "Heinrich Brucaeus to Tycho Brahe," the editorial/archival rubric of the copy; kept as the salutation line.
- **Subject — the *Calendarium* / annual prognostic.** The letter concerns an almanac (*Calendarium*; *prognostica annua*) that one of Tycho's resident students (*domesticus Studiosus … Discipuli*) was to print at the Uraniborg press (*tua Typographia*). Brucaeus's whole drift is a friendly remonstrance: weather-prediction almanacs are *trita et vulgaria* ("hackneyed and commonplace"), beneath Tycho's press; he is surprised Tycho permits them, while granting that Tycho himself sets little store by such forecasting. Tycho's press did issue student prognostications in this period (e.g. those of his *famuli*), so the reference is to a real publishing activity, not a hypothetical.
- **Persons named in the consignment.** *VITO / VITI* = **Vitus** (Veit), evidently an agent/founder at or near Wittenberg who supplied **type** (*Typos fusos*, "cast/founded types"); *aurigae Witebergensis* = "the Wittenberg carter/wagoner," the carrier who conveyed the consignment. *libris illius Florentini* = "the books of that Florentine" — an unidentified Florentine (bookseller or author) whose books accompanied the type; left unidentified rather than guessed. *schedulis duabus* = "two notes/slips" (here invoices or price-memoranda), *una VITI, altera aurigae* "one from Vitus, the other from the carter," *quibus de precio tibi constabit* "by which the price will be clear to you."
- **Astrology / meteorology (technical sense).** *aëris mutationes praedicere* = "to predict the changes of the weather/air" — the standard early-modern term for almanac weather-forecasting (astro-meteorology), not astronomy proper. *anni tempora … suas constitutiones servant* = "the seasons of the year keep their own constitutions" (*constitutio* in the medical-meteorological sense of the prevailing temperament of a season); rendered "constitution" consistently. *Astrologica vaticinia* = "astrological prophecies."
- ***Astrologaster*** — a contemptuous coinage, "petty/quack astrologer" (the *-aster* suffix = a poor imitation, as *grammaticaster*, *philosophaster*); kept as **"astrologaster"** with the pejorative force flagged rather than smoothed to a neutral "astrologer."
- ***Calendario Martio*** — "in his calendar for March" (i.e. the March entry/forecast of the offending astrologer's almanac), not a calendar *of* Mars; rendered "in his calendar … for March."
- ***artem nullam crederet*** — *ars* here = "science / art [of prediction]"; "he would believe there to be no science at all [in it]," i.e. would abandon faith in the whole art if his forecast failed.
- **Crux: *Calcearium illud*.** *prodeat **Calcearium** illud in publicum* — literally "let that shoe-leather / cobbler's-stuff (*calcearium*) come forth into public." *Calcearium* (from *calceus*, "shoe") is not a standard word; the most natural reading is a deliberately dismissive/jocular tag for the almanac just described ("that cobblery," i.e. that pieced-together job of work), parallel to *nugae* "trifles" above. It is **not** securely established, however, that this is the intended sense; the word may conceal a proper name, a title, or a copyist's corruption in the Vienna copy (*Afskrift*). The dismissive sense is given in the translation with the Latin retained in brackets, and the reading is flagged here rather than silently normalised. **This is the named crux that holds the grade to Possible.**
- ***ut … nobis sis Apollo*** — "that you may be an Apollo to us": a closing compliment, Apollo as god of both medicine and the [astral] arts; Brucaeus wishes Tycho to be their authority "in this kind [of thing]" (*hoc in genere*), i.e. in setting astrology/almanac-making on a sound footing.
- **Epistolary formula.** *Bene vale* = "Fare you well". *Plura non possum, urgente nuntio* = "I can [write] no more, as the messenger presses" — a stock close signalling haste.
- **Dateline & calendar.** *Datae in Holsatia ipso die Palmarum 1585* = "Given in **Holstein**, on **Palm Sunday** itself, 1585." Brucaeus, of Rostock, wrote while in Holstein (the duchy south of Denmark). *Die Palmarum* = Palm Sunday, the Sunday before Easter; the dateline gives the moveable feast, **not** a civil day-of-month. In the Julian (Old Style) calendar that Brucaeus, as a Rostock/Holstein Lutheran, used in 1585, Easter fell on 18 April O.S., placing **Palm Sunday on 11 April 1585 O.S.** The edition label ("1585. 4. april. Holsten") assigns **4 April**, which matches *neither* the Old-Style nor the New-Style Palm Sunday for 1585 (N.S. Palm Sunday = 14 April); 4 April 1585 O.S. was a Sunday but the *fifth* Sunday in Lent (Judica/Passion Sunday), not Palm Sunday. **The discrepancy is flagged, not reconciled:** the header leads with the as-written feast-date ("Palm Sunday 1585 [O.S.]") and appends the catalogued "(catalogued 4 April 1585)"; the basis of the catalogue's "4 April" is not recoverable from the letter text and is left unresolved. No date is silently converted.
- **Correction.** Latin: 'Calcearium' corrected to 'Calendarium' throughout its single occurrence, per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 92 — the letter's subject is an almanac, not shoe-leather. English: the corresponding clause corrected from 'that shoe-leather' to 'that calendar', and the earlier clause on astrological prophecies corrected to restore the sense that Tycho is the exception to what 'many others' customarily do (overvalue such prophecies), not a fellow example of restraint.

Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter (the type-founts/Vitus passage, the astrologaster-and-weather-prediction critique, the pupils'-prognostics defense) against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.91-92 as page images. Confirmed a source-text word corruption (Calcearium for Calendarium) that directly produces nonsensical English, and a contrast-flip mistranslation in the 'many others' clause. Both defects change what a scholar would take away from the letter.

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (**high**). Dreyer clearly prints 'Calendarium' (the calendar/almanac that is the letter's entire subject — set up in the opening line 'Calendarij... edendi mentionem fecisti'). The transcribed original has the nonword 'Calcearium', which the translator then rendered literally as 'shoe-leather', producing a baffling non sequitur in a letter that is otherwise coherently about an almanac. Dreyer prints: *prodeat Calendarium illud in publicum*.
- **mistranslation** (medium). The Latin's 'uti multi alias solent' borrows its verb from the main clause and means 'as many others are otherwise accustomed [to value them more than is fitting]' — i.e. Brucaeus is praising Tycho as an exception to a common failing. The English reads as though the 'many others' also show the same restraint, inverting the compliment into a banal generalization. At: “since you also set no more store than is fitting by astrological prophecies, as many otherwise are wont to do”.

**Repaired.** Verified both defects by direct visual inspection of the Dreyer TBOO VII pp.91-93 page images. 'Calendarium' is unambiguous on p.92 and directly continuous with the letter's opening subject (a student's almanac). The mistranslation defect concerns English phrasing only (the Latin the transcribed original itself was already correct and unchanged); the corrected clause follows the Latin's word order and the elliptical-verb reading given in the audit's own diagnosis, staying close to the source without adding interpretive colour beyond restoring the correct logical direction of the compliment.
