documents.incipit: PERFUNCTUS Legatione apud Cæsaream Maiestatem, a Serenissimo Rege nostro sibi adiuncta, …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET VIRTUTE ERUDITIONEQUE PRÆEMINENTI VIRO D. DOCTORI THADDÆO AB HAYCK, MEDICO ET MATHEMATICO INPRIMIS EXCELLENTI, INCOLÆ PRAGENSI, AMICO SUO PERPETUO COLENDO.
HERRN DOCTOR THADÆUS ZU PRAG ZUERFRAGEN.
S.

PERFUNCTUS Legatione apud Cæsaream Maiestatem, a Serenissimo Rege nostro sibi adiuncta, reversusque huc in patriam frater meus STENO BRAHE, non saltem literas mihi a te attulit, Eruditissime et longe charissime Domine D. THADDÆE, sed insuper narravit, quanta humanitate ipsum exceperis, quamque liberaliter et iucunde tractâris. Quod sane magna cum voluptate percepi, tibique gratias habeo plurimas, quod mei absentis memoriam hac ratione in fratre præsente recolueris. Nam ex benevolentia ipsi præstita, me quoque ob veterem quæ nobis intercedit necessitudinem a te complexum esse, satis evidenter persuasum habeo, relaturus sane gratiam, si de te vel ullo tuorum bene merendi unquam offeratur occasio. Rescripsissem vero tuis literis maturius, si per nuncij commoditatem id licuisset. Interea vero dum hinc inde perquiri curo, qua ratione ad te nostræ mittantur, ecce forte fortuna accessit quidam, qui se in istis Bohemiæ oris habitare aiebat, cupereque cum quodam ex mihi inservientibus Artificibus natione Bohemo (qui aliquot annis in quibusdam ad Instrumentorum fabricam facientibus diligentem mihi navavit operam) sermonem miscere, illiusque in patria, si quæ velit, negotia procurare. Hac oblata scribendi commoditate, cum is meas etiam ad te perferri literas, sedulo se curaturum addiceret, non potui non, utut alijs maxime occupatus negocijs, sepositis omnibus, has illi ad te perferendas committere.

Quantum ad Dialexin tuam a te denuo locupletatam attinet, cum editionem eius differri ob Typographorum avaritiam intelligam, et mihi eius copiam offeras, si de mea voluntate certior factus fueris, rogo ut eam ad me prima quaque occasione transmittas. Dabo operam ut vel hîc meis typis edatur, vel tibi quamprimum citra ullam libri iacturam remittatur. Eorum etiam quæ de Nova Stella et aliquot Cometis præcedentibus annis conspectis a diversis hinc inde in medium allata sunt, si singulorum exemplaria unâ miseris, rem feceris longe gratissimam. Conscripsi enim et ego quædam de hoc toto negotio, quæ proprijs typis propediem, Deo conatus nostros felicitante, edere constitui, id quod hactenus, ex quo omnia ad Typographiam pertinentia in promptu parata haberem, ob Papyri inopiam, quam peculiarem requiro, procrastinatum est. Cum enim Mercenariæ naves partim ob earum arrestationem in Hispania, partim ob Antwerpiæ diuturnam obsidionem hac æstate fretum hoc, in solita copia, non transnavigaverint, factum est, ut Papyro, quæ hac ratione inter alias merces e Gallijs et Belgicis civitatibus copiosa et varia apportari solet, præter spem destitutus sim. Verumtamen per naves Hollandicas, papyrum nostro negotio, in sufficienti copia et forma, aptam, a Telonij Regij, quod Helsingoræ est, præfecto, mihi certo procuratam, indies expecto; quamprimum vero hæc allata fuerit, editionem non diutius differam. Interim percuperem variorum in hac materia opiniones perspicere, ut constare queat, quinam veritatis metam, ad quam tendimus, collimatius attingant, vel si quæ devia inciderint, quorsum ea deflectantur, explorem. Te itaque nostris desiderijs nequaquam defuturum tum propria (quæ exactissima fore persuasum habeo) tum etiam aliorum placita mittendo, nullum mihi movetur dubium. Ubi nostra de his commentatio excusa fuerit, per primam quamque oblatam occasionem hanc tecum vicissim communicabo, tuæque censuræ lubens subijciam. Percepi insuper ex literis tuis, duos illos Nobiles Gallos, qui me hîc inter peregrinandum salutârant, tecum aliquandiu suaviter vixisse, vosque interea Chymica quædam medicamenta confecisse; ego vero, cum hi mecum essent, ignorabam eos vulgaris Medicinæ nedum Spagyricarum præparationum fuisse studiosos, alias et ego de hac re cum illis non iniucunde contulissem. Ostendi quidem ipsis meum, quod subterraneum est, Laboratorium, idque licet in ijs quæ ad Pyronomicam artem faciunt, non vulgariter sit instructum, tamen illi dissimulabant se quicquam horum intelligere. Quo consilio id fecerint, ignoro. Nec interim dum hic adsunt, quicquam intellexeram eos tam cito Pragam venturos, alias nequaquam sine meis te accessissent literis. Petis ut quempiam Chymicarum præparationum peritum ad te mittam, si forte peregrinando huc appulerit, id quod lubenter facturus sum, sed vereor ne votis tuis hac in parte minime eventus respondeat. Rarissimi enim sunt apud nos his exercitijs addicti, ideoque rariores eo nomine huc confluunt. Alchymistis vulgaribus, qui se multa scire vaniloque profitentur, quantum sit fidendum, ipsemet facile ex tot illorum imposturis perspectum habes. Meum itaque erit consilium, ut fidelem aliquem iuvenem harum rerum studiosum tibi adiungas, ipsumque successive instruas, quoad in his laboribus per diuturnam exercitationem reddatur expeditior; fabricando enim, ut dici solet, fabri fimus. Si quid egregij hactenus a vobis in hac Arte inventum fuerit, velim mecum communices, ego vicissim eorum, quæ in mea Officina Hermetica nata sunt et tibi placitura intellexero, te reddam participem. Cum unâ Ratisbonæ essemus, libellum quendam a me accepisti, nescio cuius authoris, de Chymicis medicamentis præparandis, sed et titulum libri neque exacte teneo, in octava forma fuisse satis recordor. Eum librum nusquam postea venalem habere licuit, utut sæpius Bibliopolas eo nomine in Germania sollicitari curaverim, quod forte ideo minus fieri poterat, quia nomen authoris et titulus libri mihi exciderant. Peto itaque ut vel eius libelli exemplar, si forte uspiam apud vos venale exstat, vel saltem titulum libri cum authoris nomine ad me transmitti curare velis. Et si quæ præterea de hac materia noviter prodierunt, quæ artem et ingenium sapiant, unâ per te obtineam, rem pergratam feceris. IOHANNIS WERNERI opusculum de motu octavæ sphæræ Norimbergæ olim, ut existimo, impressum multo tempore late conquisivi, sed nondum uspiam adeptus sum. Si itaque librum hunc istic nactus fueris, et me eius participem reddideris, tum etiam, si tractatum illum manuscriptum ignoti authoris de Directionum significationibus, quem Ratisbonæ apud te vidi, per aliquem descriptum, adiunxeris, multum meis desiderijs gratificaveris. Sumtus omnes lubens remittam, tuisque votis vicissim, ubicunque licuerit, me præbebo officiosissimum. Commentaria TRAPEZUNTIJ in PTOLOMÆUM si adhuc penes te habes, necdum impressa prodierunt, sique eis carere potes, mihi perscribe, qua ratione transigendum tecum fuerit, ut ea (si alias Typis mandari nequeant) abs te impetrem. Fieri enim potest, ut proprijs impensis editionem eorum instituam, ne tanti viri excellens labor penitus intercidat, et usum destinatum Astronomiæ studiosis omnino præcludat. Unum etiam adhuc restat, quod te magnopere, ni tibi nimium sim molestus, rogatum velim. Cum non mediocri sumtu propriam hîc Uraniburgi Typographiam adornârim, in qua non solum ea quæ de Nova Stella et succedentibus aliquot Cometis a me cœlitus animadversa diligenter exponuntur demonstranturque, sed etiam ea quæ ad æterna illa et Mundo coæva sidera spectant, quæque multis et exquisitis a cœlo ipso (per Organa maxima, solide et ad amussim, ingenti labore et sumtu præcedentibus aliquot annis constructa) petitis observationibus, Astronomiam totam, tum quo ad Luminarium, tum etiam reliquarum tam errantium quam inerrantium Stellarum, exactam motus rationem, veritati apparentiarum (quatenus ea in sensus nostros vel subtilissime indaganti cadit) consentientem, pristino vigori restituunt; ea inquam et quam plurima alia ad Mathematicam inprimis scientiam pertinentia, quæ vel hactenus a nobis absoluta sunt, vel in posterum, Deo vires et ingenium suppeditante, elaboranda veniunt, constitui (eodem favente) proprijs typis excudere, et Reipub. literariæ non sine singulari, uti spero, emolumento communicare. Cumque præter eas, quas tum in ipsam Typographiam omnibus necessarijs adminiculis rite instruendam insumserim impensas, tum etiam non minores in Operum, quæ excudenda veniunt, apparatum requirantur, præsertim in his Mathematicis rebus, quæ sine figurarum multiplici delineatione sumtuosos labores requirente, nequaquam dextre institui queunt (prout hæc omnia tibi ipsi adeo perspecta sunt, ut longa non indigeant probatione): Idcirco ne tot sumtus et labores cum dispendio mearum rerum in rei literariæ gratiam incassum faciam, si forte quæ hîc meis Typis impressa fuerint, in Germania vel alibi confestim recudantur, per Amicitiam nostram te rogatum velim, ut a Cæsarea Maiestate mihi vel per temetipsum vel per alios, Privilegium ratum impetres, ut intra decennium libros in Astronomia et reliqua Mathematica scientia a me elaboratos turpisque proprijs in hac mea Officina Uraniburgica excusos, in ullis Imperij locis Cæsareæ Maiestati subiectis, denuo imprimere vel publicare et divendere, sub certa mulcta et amissione exemplarium, nequaquam liceat. Cavebo vicissim, ne libri a me publicandi quidpiam, quod vel Relligionis controversijs, vel Reipublicæ constitutioni offensioni siet, ullo in loco contineant. Et si quid ipsa Cæsarea Maiestas vicissim hoc nomine a me præstandum postulaverit, ipsius Maiestati meam Operam et obsequium humiliter defero. Præterea si qui sumtus in eos, qui hæc ex Cæsaris decreto exsequuntur, conscribendoque Privilegio occupantur, erogandi veniunt, quamprimum per te de his certior factus fuero, lubens omnia quæ requiruntur mittam. Tuum itaque erit, charissime THADÆE, omnem movere lapidem, ut Privilegium hoc a Cæsarea Maiestate primo quoque tempore obtineam. Cuperem enim idipsum operi meo, quod de novis æthereæ Regionis Generationibus nostro ævo conspectis inscripsi, et omnium primo typis edere decrevi, præfigere, ut eo tutius per Autoritatem Cæsarianum nostris laboribus et limitibus consulatur. Qua autem forma et quibus verbis Privilegium hoc optime comprehendi queat, tuæ sagacitati latius indicandum disponendumque relinquo. Nec dubito quin meæ de te expectationi hac in parte sedulo sis satisfacturus. Ut vero Typorum nostrorum, quos hactenus conquisivi, characterem perspicias, mitto tibi quædam carmina, præterita hyeme recreandi a serioribus studijs animi gratia ad quosdam Nobiles et eruditos amicos exarata, et ne Typi et Typographus ob Papyri inopiam prorsus feriarent, in nostra Officina excusa. Addidi etiam ædificij nostri in hac insula Astronomiæ honori et restaurationi sumtuose extructi designationes aliquot, ut tibi absenti aliquo modo ædes hasce Uraniæ (cui et tu ab ineunte ætate sacra litasti) dicatas, intueri liceat. Omnium quoque in hisce contentorum Organorum Astronomicorum delineationem unâ misissem, sed nondum ob sculptoris mei in Germaniam abitum, eorum figuræ penitus absolutæ sunt. Binorum saltem Instrumentorum picturam mitto, quorum fabricam et usum ex ipsa inspectione facile assequeris. Ubi sculptor reversus fuerit, cæterasque machinas suis lineamentis expresserit, faciam te eorum participem. Curo enim has omnes figuris convenientibus excidi, eo quod peculiari volumine harum omnium structuram et multiplicem infallibilemque usum, Astronomiæ alumnis patefacere decreverim. Sed video me copiosius tecum agendo epistolæ modum excedere, quare ne te ulterius, quam par est, detineam, finem scribendi faciam, teque cum tota domo Divinæ tutelæ commendabo. Vale, et nostris desiderijs prima quaque opportunitate responde. Si nulla offeratur commodior ratio, literas unâ cum ijs de quibus mentionem feci, Rostochium ad Doctorem HENRICUM BRUCÆUM perferri cura. Is enim confestim per crebra quæ inde huc appellunt navigia me eorum compotem reddet.

Iterum mi charissime THADÆE vale quam felicissime.
Datæ Uraniburgi 25. Augusti Anno 1585.
Tui amantissimus
TYCHO BRAHE
manu propria.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 97; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Si ante instantem hyemem responsum a te accepero, rem feceris mihi longe gratissimam.
text.english:
**To the most renowned man, pre-eminent in virtue and erudition, Master Doctor Thaddaeus ab Hayck, physician and mathematician of the first excellence, citizen of Prague, his friend to be honoured perpetually.**
**Doctor Thaddaeus at Prague, to be enquired for.**
Greeting.

Having discharged the embassy to His Imperial Majesty entrusted to him by our Most Serene King, and having returned hither to his homeland, my brother Steno Brahe not only brought me a letter from you, most learned and far dearest Lord, Master Thaddaeus, but moreover related with what great kindness you received him, and how generously and pleasantly you entertained him. This indeed I learned with great pleasure, and I owe you the warmest thanks that in this way, in my brother's presence, you kept in mind one who was absent. For from the goodwill shown to him I am quite plainly persuaded that I too — on account of the old bond that subsists between us — have been embraced by you; and I shall surely repay the favour, if ever an occasion offers of deserving well of you or any of yours. I would indeed have replied to your letter sooner, had the convenience of a messenger allowed it. But while I was seeing to enquiries, this way and that, by what means my letters might be sent to you, behold, by sheer good fortune there came a certain man who said that he dwelt in those parts of Bohemia, and that he wished to fall into conversation with one of the craftsmen in my service, a Bohemian by nation (who for some years did diligent work for me on certain matters pertaining to the making of instruments), and to attend to that man's affairs in his homeland, if he should want anything. This opportunity of writing being offered — since he undertook that he would also see to it carefully that my letters were conveyed to you — I could not but, however much I was busied with other matters, set everything aside and entrust these [letters] to him to convey to you.

As for your *Dialexis*, now enlarged anew by you: since I understand that its publication is being delayed through the greed of the printers, and you offer me a copy of it if you shall have been made more certain of my wish, I ask that you send it to me at the very first occasion. I shall take pains either that it be published here with my own types, or that it be returned to you as soon as possible without any loss of the book. Of those things too which, concerning the New Star and several Comets observed in the preceding years, have been brought forward into public by various men here and there — if you send copies of each together [with it], you will do a most welcome thing. For I too have composed certain things about this whole matter, which I have determined to publish shortly with my own types, God prospering our endeavours — something which up to now, although I had everything pertaining to the press ready at hand, has been put off for want of paper, of which I require a particular kind. For since the merchant ships, partly because of their seizure in Spain, partly because of the long siege of Antwerp, did not this summer sail through this Sound in the usual quantity, it came about that I have been, beyond expectation, left without paper — which, by this route, among other merchandise, is wont to be brought in abundant and varied supply from the cities of France and the Low Countries. Nevertheless, through Dutch ships, I daily expect paper fit for our business, in sufficient quantity and format, certainly procured for me by the warden of the Royal Toll which is at Helsingør; and as soon as this has been brought, I shall delay the edition no longer. Meanwhile I should much like to inspect the opinions of various men on this subject, so that it may be established who reach more nearly on the mark [collimatius] the goal of truth toward which we strive, or, if any have fallen into byways, that I may explore in what direction they have swerved. And so I move no doubt that you will by no means fail our desires, by sending both your own views (which I am persuaded will be most exact) and also those of others. When our commentary on these matters has been printed, I shall in turn communicate it to you by the very first occasion offered, and gladly submit it to your judgement. I learned moreover from your letter that those two noble Frenchmen who had greeted me here during their travels lived for some while pleasantly with you, and that you meanwhile prepared together certain chemical medicines; but I, when they were with me, did not know that they were students of ordinary medicine, much less of spagyric preparations, otherwise I too would have conferred with them on this matter not unpleasantly. I did indeed show them my Laboratory, which is underground, and although it is fitted out for the things that pertain to the pyronomic art [the art of fire] in no common way, yet they dissembled that they understood any of these things. With what design they did this, I do not know. Nor meanwhile, while they were here, had I understood that they would come to Prague so soon, otherwise they would by no means have approached you without a letter from me. You ask that I send to you someone skilled in chemical preparations, should one perhaps put in here while travelling — which I shall gladly do; but I fear that in this part the outcome may scarcely answer to your wishes. For very rare among us are those given to these exercises, and therefore the rarer do they flock hither on that account. As for how far one is to trust the common alchemists, who profess vaingloriously to know much, you yourself easily have it perceived from so many of their impostures. My counsel therefore will be that you attach to yourself some faithful young man, a student of these matters, and instruct him by degrees, until by long practice he be rendered more expert in these labours; for, as the saying goes, by making [things] we become makers [smiths]. If anything excellent has so far been discovered by you in this Art, I should wish you to share it with me; I in turn will make you a sharer of those things which have been born in my Hermetic Workshop and which I shall have understood will please you. When we were together at Regensburg, you received from me a certain little book, of I know not what author, on the preparing of chemical medicines; but neither do I exactly hold the title of the book — that it was in octavo format I well enough recall. That book I have nowhere since been able to have for sale, although I have often had booksellers in Germany solicited for it by name — which perhaps could the less be done for that reason, because the author's name and the book's title had slipped from me. I ask therefore that you see to it that there be sent to me either a copy of that little book, if perhaps it is anywhere for sale among you, or at least the title of the book together with the author's name. And if besides anything has lately come out on this subject that savours of skill and ingenuity, [and] I obtain it through you at the same time, you will do a most agreeable thing. The little work of **Johannes Werner** *On the Motion of the Eighth Sphere*, printed long ago at Nuremberg, as I think, I have widely sought after for a long time, but have not yet anywhere obtained. If therefore you have come upon this book there, and make me a sharer of it, and then too, if you add — copied out by someone — that manuscript treatise of an unknown author *On the Significations of Directions*, which I saw at Regensburg in your keeping, you will much gratify my desires. All the costs I shall gladly remit, and in turn, wherever it shall be allowed, I will show myself most dutiful to your wishes. **Trapezuntius's** Commentaries on **Ptolemy**, if you still have them in your possession, [and] they have not yet come out in print, and if you can do without them, write to me by what arrangement the matter is to be settled with you, so that I may obtain them from you (if otherwise they cannot be committed to the press). For it may be that I will undertake their edition at my own expense, lest the excellent labour of so great a man perish utterly, and altogether shut off the use intended for students of astronomy. One thing still remains, on which I should greatly wish to ask you — unless I be too troublesome to you. Since at no slight cost I have here at Uraniborg furnished a press of my own, in which are diligently set forth and demonstrated not only those things which, concerning the New Star and several succeeding Comets, I have observed from the heavens, but also those things which regard those eternal stars coeval with the World, and which — by many and exquisite observations sought from the heaven itself (through the greatest **instruments**, soundly and to a nicety, with vast labour and cost constructed in some preceding years) — restore to its former vigour the whole of Astronomy, both as to the exact reckoning of the motion of the Luminaries and also of the rest of the Stars, both wandering and fixed, [a reckoning] consonant with the truth of the appearances (so far as that falls to our senses, even to one investigating most subtly): these things, I say, and very many others pertaining especially to Mathematical science, which either have so far been completed by me, or in future, God supplying strength and ingenuity, come to be worked out — I have determined (with His favour) to print with my own types, and to communicate to the Republic of Letters, not without singular profit, as I hope. And since, beyond the expenses which I have laid out both upon duly furnishing the press itself with all necessary apparatus, and also no smaller ones [are] required for the apparatus of the Works which come to be printed — especially in these Mathematical matters, which without the manifold drawing of figures, requiring costly labours, can by no means be aptly set up (all of which is so thoroughly evident to you yourself that it needs no long proof): therefore, lest I make so many costs and labours, with loss of my own means, in vain for the sake of letters, should perhaps the things printed here with my types be at once reprinted in Germany or elsewhere — by our Friendship I should wish to ask you that you obtain for me from His Imperial Majesty, either through yourself or through others, a confirmed **Privilege**, [providing] that within ten years it be by no means permitted, in any places of the Empire subject to His Imperial Majesty, to reprint anew, or publish and sell, the books in Astronomy and the rest of Mathematical science worked out by me and printed with my own types in this my Uraniborg Workshop — under a fixed fine and forfeiture of the copies. I shall take care, in turn, that the books to be published by me contain in no place anything which may give offence either to the controversies of Religion or to the constitution of the Commonwealth. And if His Imperial Majesty in turn shall demand anything to be performed by me on this account, I humbly offer my service and obedience to His Majesty. Moreover, if any costs come to be expended upon those who execute these things by the Emperor's decree, and who are occupied in drawing up the Privilege, as soon as I have been made more certain of these through you, I will gladly send all that is required. It will be yours therefore, dearest Thaddaeus, to move every stone, that I may obtain this Privilege from His Imperial Majesty at the very first time. For I should wish to prefix it to that work of mine which I have entitled *On the new Generations of the ethereal Region beheld in our age*, and which I have resolved to publish first of all — so that the more safely, through Imperial Authority, provision may be made for our labours and bounds. But in what form and in what words this Privilege may best be framed, I leave to your sagacity to indicate and dispose more fully. Nor do I doubt that in this part you will diligently satisfy my expectation of you. And that you may perceive the character of our types, which I have so far procured, I send you certain poems, written last winter to certain noble and learned friends for the sake of refreshing the mind from more serious studies, and printed in our Workshop so that the types and the typographer should not be wholly idle for want of paper. I have added also some delineations of our building, raised at great cost on this island for the honour and restoration of Astronomy, so that you, [though] absent, may in some way look upon this house dedicated to Urania (to whom you too, from your earliest years, have offered sacred rites). I would have sent together a drawing of all the Astronomical **instruments** contained in these [buildings], but their figures are not yet entirely completed, owing to my engraver's departure into Germany. I send at least a picture of two Instruments, whose construction and use you will easily grasp from the very inspection. When the engraver has returned, and has rendered the rest of the machines in their outlines, I shall make you a sharer of them. For I am having all of these cut in suitable figures, because I have resolved to lay open, in a separate volume, the structure and the manifold and infallible use of all of them, to the nurslings of Astronomy. But I see that, in dealing with you more copiously, I exceed the measure of a letter; wherefore, that I may not detain you further than is fitting, I shall make an end of writing, and commend you, with your whole house, to the Divine protection. Farewell, and answer our desires at the very first opportunity. If no more convenient means offer, see that the letters, together with those things of which I have made mention, are conveyed to Rostock to Doctor **Heinrich Brucaeus**. For he, by the frequent vessels which put in here from there, will at once make me possessed of them.

Again, my dearest Thaddaeus, fare you most happily.
Given at Uraniborg, 25 August, the year 1585.
Your most loving
TYCHO BRAHE
with his own hand.


*[Postscript:]* If I shall have received a reply from you before the coming winter, you will do me a thing most welcome indeed.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** *Thaddaeus ab Hayck / Thaddaeus Pragensis* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayck)** (1525–1600), the leading Bohemian physician, astronomer and astrologer, personal physician at the Imperial court at Prague, and Tycho's long-standing friend and correspondent. The pair had met at the Imperial Diet of Regensburg (*Ratisbona*) in 1575, twice referenced here. Hagecius was Tycho's principal channel to the Imperial chancery; this letter sets in motion the application that yielded the printing **Privilege** Rudolf II granted Tycho.
- **Salutation rubric (German).** *HERRN DOCTOR THADAeUS ZU PRAG ZUERFRAGEN* — "Doctor Thaddaeus at Prague, to be enquired for" — a German address/direction line over the Latin honorific superscription; a delivery instruction (the bearer is to ask after the addressee at Prague). The code-switch is preserved by this chapter's convention
- ***Steno Brahe.*** **Steen Brahe** (1547–1620), Tycho's brother, here returning from a royal embassy to the Imperial court; he had carried Hagecius's letter back to Hven.
- ***Serenissimo Rege nostro*** — **Frederik II of Denmark** (r. 1559–88), "our Most Serene King."
- ***Dialexis*** — Hagecius's *Dialexis de novae et prius incognitae stellae … apparitione* (Frankfurt, 1574), his tract on the 1572 New Star, here described as "enlarged anew" (a revised/expanded version Hagecius was preparing). Kept as the title; not translated.
- ***Nova Stella … aliquot Cometis*** — the **New Star** (the 1572 nova, *stella nova* in Cassiopeia) and the comets of the intervening years (notably the comet of 1577); Tycho is gathering the published responses for his own work in progress. *De novis aethereae Regionis Generationibus* (below) is the project — eventually the *Astronomiae instauratae Progymnasmata* and the comet volume.
- ***collimatius*** — "more nearly on the mark"; *collimare* (the period orthography of *collineare*, to aim/sight along a line) is Tycho's habitual metaphor of taking aim at the "goal (mark) of truth" (*veritatis metam*). Rendered with the aiming sense; the Latin flagged.
- **Paper-supply passage.** The shortage is tied to two datable events of 1585: the Spanish seizure (*arrestatio*) of foreign (esp. Dutch) merchant ships in Spanish ports (May 1585) and the long **siege of Antwerp** (taken by Parma, 17 August 1585). *Telonium Regium … Helsingorae* = the **Sound Toll** at **Helsingør** (Elsinore); its *praefectus* (warden/customs-master) is procuring Dutch paper for Tycho.
- **Alchemy / chemistry.** *Spagyricae praeparationes* = **spagyric preparations** (Paracelsian chemical pharmacy); *Pyronomica ars* = "the **pyronomic art**," the art of regulated fire (furnace-work), rendered with a gloss; *Officina Hermetica* = "**Hermetic Workshop**" (Tycho's alchemical laboratory at Uraniborg); *Laboratorium … subterraneum* = the underground laboratory. *fabricando … fabri fimus* — "by making we become makers," a proverb (a variant of *fabricando fit faber* / *fabricando fabri fimus*); kept as the maxim it is. *vaniloque* (for *vaniloquae* / vaingloriously) describes the boasting of common alchemists.
- **Books sought.** *Iohannis Werneri opusculum de motu octavae sphaerae* = **Johann Werner**, *De motu octavae sphaerae* (Nuremberg, 1522), on the motion of the eighth (fixed-star) sphere — i.e. precession/trepidation. *Commentaria Trapezuntij in Ptolomaeum* = the commentary of **Georgius Trapezuntius** (George of Trebizond, 1395–1472/3) on **Ptolemy's** *Almagest*; Tycho offers to print it at his own expense if Hagecius will release the manuscript. *tractatus … de Directionum significationibus* — an anonymous manuscript treatise "On the Significations of **Directions**" (*directio* = a predictive astrological technique, per glossary), which Tycho had seen in Hagecius's keeping at Regensburg.
- **Instruments / observatory.** *Organa maxima* = "the greatest **instruments**" (per glossary; the great Uraniborg instruments); *Typographia … Uraniburgi* = Tycho's own **press at Uraniborg**; *aedes Uraniae* = the house "dedicated to **Urania**" (Uraniborg, lit. "castle of Urania," the Muse of astronomy); *sacra litasti* echoes the Tychonic flourish "devote yourself to the rites of Urania". The "two Instruments" whose pictures he encloses, and the *peculiare volumen* on the structure and use of all his instruments, anticipate the *Astronomiae instauratae Mechanica* (1598).
- ***Astronomiam … pristino vigori restituunt*** — "restore the whole of Astronomy to its former vigour": Tycho's programme of *instauratio / restitutio astronomiae* (glossary), rendered with "restore … to its former vigour" / "restoration of Astronomy."
- **The Privilege request (legal core).** The operative clause is a single negative prohibition: Tycho asks that *nequaquam liceat … denuo imprimere vel publicare et divendere* — "that it be **by no means permitted** … to reprint anew, or to publish and sell" — his works, within ten years (*intra decennium*), anywhere in the Empire, *sub certa mulcta et amissione exemplarium* ("under a fixed fine and forfeiture of the copies"). One prohibition, governing the triad reprint / publish / sell; reproduced as one negation. His reciprocal undertaking is itself negative — *Cavebo … ne libri … quidpiam … contineant* ("I shall take care that the books contain nothing …") — a second, distinct negation, kept as such. No conditional is reversed or merged.
- ***turpisque proprijs*** **(textual crux).** The witness reads *"a me elaboratos **turpisque proprijs** in hac mea Officina Uraniburgica excusos."* As transcribed, *turpisque* ("and base/shameful") is unconstruable here and is almost certainly a copyist's corruption of ***typisque propriis*** ("and **[printed] with my own types**") — exactly the phrase Tycho uses twice elsewhere in this same letter (*proprijs typis … edere; proprijs typis excudere*). The translation follows the evident reading **"printed with my own types"**; the corrupt printed form is retained in the Source block by this chapter's convention(2). The MS is a copy (*Afskrift*), consistent with a scribal slip.
- ***Heinrich Brucaeus.*** *Doctor Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (1530/31–1593), professor of medicine and mathematics at **Rostock** (*Rostochium*); Tycho proposes him as the postal relay, since ships ply frequently between Rostock and Hven.
- **Dateline / calendar.** *Datae Uraniburgi 25. Augusti Anno 1585* = "Given at **Uraniborg**, 25 August 1585" (**O.S.** — Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). The dateline matches the catalogue *label* (1585.25.august.Uraniborg); no discrepancy. *manu propria* — "with his own hand," the autograph subscription.
- **Greek / symbols.** None present (no Greek interpolation, no planetary or zodiac glyphs in this letter).

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (after "manu propria"), restored from Dreyer VII, p. 97 (dropped by the working transcription).

Full collation: read all 6 Dreyer page images (TBOO VII pp.93-98), covering the entire Hagecius letter from opening salutation to closing signature and the postscript at the foot of p.97. Checked every proper name (Steno Brahe, Thaddaeus Hagecius, Henricus Brucaeus, Johannes Werner, Trapezuntius/Ptolemaeus), place name (Uraniborg, Helsingoer, Nuremberg, Regensburg, Rostock), number (decennium/ten years, Binorum/two instruments) and the date (25 August 1585) against the page images; all match the transcribed original and the published English exactly. The postscript, flagged in the transcribed original as previously dropped by the working transcription and restored, is confirmed genuinely printed at the foot of Dreyer p.97 (immediately before the next letter, to Andreas Severini, begins) and is present and correctly translated in the published English. text.original:
EXEMPLAR LITERARVM ILLVSTRISSIMI PRINCIPIS WILHELMI HASSIÆ LANDTGRAVII AD NOBILISSIMVM DOMINVM HENRICVM RANTZOVIVM, DE COMETA ANNI 85, QUÆ EX PARTE OCCASIONEM PRÆBUERUNT ALIQUOT SUBSEQUENTIBUS.
WILHELM VON GOTTES GNADEN LANDTGRAUE ZU HESSEN/ GRAUE ZU CATZENELNBOGEN/ DIETZ/ ZIGENHAYN VND NIDDA.

VNSERN gnedigen gruß zuuor/ Vester lieber besonder/ wir haben ewer schreiben de dato Segenberg/ den 22 verschienes Monats Septemb. neben dem vns zugeschickten Buch empfangen/ Thun vns deßwegen gegen euch gnediglich bedancken/ vnd wollen dasselbige zu seiner zeit mit lust verlesen. Darneben wollen wir euch auch nicht verhalten/ das vff angeben Pauli Wittichij/ wir vnsere Instrumenta Mathematica dermassen verbessert/ das/ da wir zuuor kaum 2 Min. scharff/ wir jetzo ½ ja ¼ einer min. obseruiren können/ Haben vns derhalben vff die Art Quadrantem Horizontalem, deßgleichen ein Sextantem, ad obseruandas distantias Stellarum inter se, lassen zurichten/ jedes von gutem Messing vnd bicubital. Halten auch drey Gesellen Astronomiæ et Obseruationum peritos ad iustificanda loca Stellarum Fixarum, Wiewol vnsere vorige Obseruationes, die wir selbst in otio vor angehung vnser Regierung nostris oculis genommen/ vnd dauon jhr als wir nicht anders wissen/ Copey gehabt/ nit vber 4 oder minut. vffs meiste ab hisce discrepiren werden/ hoffen auch bald damit zu endt zukommen/ wann wir nur klar Wetter circa nouilunium hetten/ welches vns diß gantze Jahr vber gemangelt. Nuhn has vns vnser Mathematicus CHRISTOPHORVS ROTHMANNVS zugeschrieben/ dz er einen kleinen Cometen vff den 8 huius, Abends vmb 9 vhr in 23 grad. 15 minut. piscium, cum Latitudine merid. 14 grad. 0 min. Vnd vff den 9 eiusdem in 25 grad. 50 min. piscium cum Latitud. merid. 13 grad. et 6 min. obseruiret, Denselbigen haben wir gestern den 19 zu Abend allhier doch mit keinen Instrumenten, sondern allein per lineas rectas vff vnserm Globo obseruiret, vnd jhn im 21 gr. Arietis, cum Declinatione latitud. 4 gr. merid. gefunden. Er ist klein/ vnd vmb vnd vmb hero voller Haer/ das wir achten/ er sey ex genere Cometarum, so man vnsers versehens Circæos nennet/ vnd tempore maximarum coniunctionum zuerscheinen pflegen/ Was er nun bedeuten wird/ sonderlich dieweil er gar Saturninus, vnd Saturno coniunctus, gibt die zeit/ vnd möchten wol wissen/ ob er auch bey euch gesehen werde/ Mögen auch wol leiden/ das jhr TYCHONEM BRAHEN mit vormeldung vnsers gnedigen grusses/ Apparitionem et Obseruationem huius Cometæ, zuwissen thut/ mit begeren/ das er vns zuwissen thue/ wie er jhn Obseruiret habe/ Denn weil er so klein/ halten wirs dafür/ er werde von weinigen obseruirt werden/ Das wollen wir vns vorsehen/ vnd seind euch mit Gnaden geneigt/

Datum Rottenburgk am 20 Octobris, Anno 85.
text.english:
**A copy of a letter of the Most Illustrious Prince Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, to the Most Noble Lord Heinrich Rantzau, concerning the comet of the year [15]85, which letters in part gave occasion to several of those that follow.**
**Wilhelm by the grace of God Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Catzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain and Nidda.**

Our gracious greeting beforehand. Our trusty and well-beloved: we have received your letter dated Segeberg, the 22nd of the past month of September, together with the book sent to us, and we therefore thank you graciously for it, and intend to read it through with pleasure in due time. Besides this we will also not conceal from you that, upon the instruction of Paul Wittich, we have so improved our mathematical instruments [Instrumenta Mathematica] that, whereas before we could scarcely observe [to] 2 minutes precisely, we can now observe [to] half — indeed a quarter — of a minute. We have therefore had set up after that fashion a horizontal quadrant [Quadrantem Horizontalem], likewise a sextant [Sextantem], for observing the distances of the stars from one another [ad observandas distantias Stellarum inter se], each of good brass and two cubits [in size]. We also keep three journeymen skilled in astronomy and in observations [Astronomiae et Observationum peritos] for verifying the places of the fixed stars [ad iustificanda loca Stellarum Fixarum] — although our earlier observations, which we ourselves took at leisure with our own eyes [nostris oculis] before the commencement of our reign, and of which, so far as we know, you have had a copy, will at most differ from these by no more than 4 minutes [or so]; and we hope soon to come to an end with it, if only we had clear weather around the new moon [circa novilunium], which has been lacking to us this whole year through. Now our mathematician Christoph Rothmann has written to us that he observed a small comet on the 8th of this month, in the evening at about 9 o'clock, in 23 degrees 15 minutes of Pisces, with southern latitude [cum Latitudine merid.] 14 degrees 0 minutes; and on the 9th of the same [month] in 25 degrees 50 minutes of Pisces, with southern latitude 13 degrees and 6 minutes. This same [comet] we observed here yesterday, the 19th, in the evening — yet with no instruments, but only by straight lines [per lineas rectas] upon our globe [Globo] — and found it in 21 degrees of Aries, with a southern declination of latitude [cum Declinatione latitud.] of 4 degrees. It is small, and all about it full of hair [hairy], so that we judge it to be of the kind of comets [ex genere Cometarum] that, as we suppose, are called *Circaei*, and that are wont to appear at the time of the great conjunctions [tempore maximarum coniunctionum]. What it will now signify — especially since it is wholly Saturnine [Saturninus], and conjoined with Saturn [Saturno coniunctus] — time will tell; and we should well like to know whether it has been seen with you also. We can also well allow that you make known to Tycho Brahe, with the conveyance of our gracious greeting, the appearance and observation of this comet [Apparitionem et Observationem huius Cometae], with the desire that he make known to us how he has observed it; for, since it is so small, we hold it [likely] that it will be observed by few. This we shall await, and we are inclined to you with [our] grace.

Given at Rotenburg, the 20th of October, in the year [15]85.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), the observing prince of Kassel, builder of one of the two great pre-telescopic observatories (with Tycho's on Hven). The titulature names his subsidiary fiefs: *Catzenelnbogen* (Katzenelnbogen), *Dietz* (Diez), *Ziegenhain*, *Nidda*.
- **Recipient.** *Henricus Rantzovius* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), royal governor (*Statthalter*) of the Danish duchies of Schleswig-Holstein, humanist patron and astrological writer, and a hub of scientific correspondence linking Tycho, Kassel, and the German learned world. His seat at **Segeberg** (*Segenberg*) is the place of his own letter here acknowledged.
- **Document type and frame.** The piece is not a letter to or from Tycho but a **copy (*Exemplar*) of Wilhelm's letter to Rantzau**, which Tycho printed as a prefatory document in his *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Uraniborg, 1596) because, as the Latin rubric says, it "in part gave occasion" to the correspondence that follows. The rubric and the full titulature are in **Latin**, the body in **chancery German** with constant code-switching into Latin for technical nouns — preserved by this chapter's convention
- **Language note.** The body is **German** (Early New High German / chancery: *vff* = *auf*, *dz* = *daß*, *jhn* = *ihn*, *zuuor* = *zuvor*, *vmb* = *um*, *weinigen* = *wenigen*), not Danish despite the *de* heuristic tag — verified by reading. The opening *VNSERN gnedigen gruß zuuor / Vester lieber besonder* is the standard princely address formula, rendered by this chapter's convention ("Our gracious greeting beforehand … Our trusty and well-beloved").
- **Paul Wittich.** *Pauli Wittichij* = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586), the Wrocław mathematician whose visit to Kassel in 1584 transmitted the instrument-improvement techniques (sights, transversal/diagonal graduation) he had learned at Hven — the reciprocal-influence figure between Tycho and Rothmann. The claim that Wittich's "instruction" raised Kassel's precision from c. 2′ to ¼′ is Wilhelm's own (not silently sharpened).
- **Instruments.** *Quadrantem Horizontalem* → **horizontal quadrant**; *Sextantem … ad observandas distantias Stellarum inter se* → **sextant, for observing the distances of the stars from one another**; *bicubital* → **two cubits [in size]** (about 1 metre on a side). *Globo* → **globe** (a celestial globe, on which Wilhelm read off the comet's place graphically, *per lineas rectas*, "by straight lines," lacking instruments that evening).
- **Astronomical terms.** *loca Stellarum Fixarum* → **places of the fixed stars**; *iustificanda* → **verifying** (here in the sense of correcting/confirming the catalogue places); *circa novilunium* → **around the new moon**; *Declinatione* → **declination** (but note the source's own redundant phrase *Declinatione latitud.*, lit. "declination of latitude," flagged below). Positions are given in zodiacal longitude (degrees within a sign) with latitude; *merid.* = *meridionalis*, **southern**.
- **Astrology.** *Saturninus … Saturno coniunctus* → **Saturnine … conjoined with Saturn**: the comet is read as Saturn-natured and in conjunction with Saturn, hence ominous; *tempore maximarum coniunctionum* → **at the time of the great(est) conjunctions** (the Saturn–Jupiter great-conjunction doctrine). Pisces and Aries are named in English by this chapter's convention (the source writes the sign-names in Latin, *piscium / Arietis*; no glyphs appear).
- ***Circaeos*** — *Circaei*, a comet-class name. Wilhelm flags his own uncertainty (*vnsers versehens*, "as we suppose"), preserved as a hedge. The term is not in the standard Aristotelian/Ptolemaic comet taxonomies in this spelling; it appears to render a category of "hairy"/bearded comets (cf. the description *vmb vnd vmb hero voller Haer*, "all about full of hair"). Left untranslated and flagged as a lexical crux rather than forced to a modern class.
- **Comet of 1585.** The object is the comet of October 1585, independently observed at Kassel (by Rothmann, 8–9 Oct.) and noted here by Wilhelm (19 Oct., by globe). The request that Rantzau forward the appearance and observation to **Tycho Brahe** — and ask how Tycho observed it — is the occasion of the ensuing Tycho–Kassel exchange.
- **Calendar.** Both dates — Rantzau's letter of *22 September* (Segeberg) and Wilhelm's of *20 October* (Rotenburg) — are **Old Style**; Hesse, like Denmark, retained the Julian calendar until 1700. *Datum Rottenburgk am 20 Octobris, Anno 85* = "Given at **Rotenburg** (Rotenburg an der Fulda), 20 October [15]85" (O.S.). The internal dates (comet seen "on the 8th … and on the 9th," and "yesterday, the 19th") are consistent with the 20 October dateline and with the catalogue label; no discrepancy. Per this chapter's convention no date is converted.
- **Negation check.** The source carries two consequential negations, both reproduced and neither added: (1) *wir … wollen euch auch **nicht** verhalten* → "we will **also not** conceal from you" (a courtesy litotes = "we wish you to know"); (2) *werden … **nit** vber 4 … minut. … discrepiren* → "will differ by **no more** than 4 minutes" — the precision boast, where the negation governs the magnitude and must not be dropped or doubled.

documents.incipit: PERIUCUNDUM mihi auditu fuerat, amantissime D. Magister ANDREA, quod nuper Hafniæ ex …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD ANDREAM SEVERINI VELLEIUM.
S.

PERIUCUNDUM mihi auditu fuerat, amantissime D. Magister ANDREA, quod nuper Hafniæ ex epistola tua Magnifico Domino DANZÆO inscripta intellexeram te brevi nos invisurum, modo hyems iter tuum non impediverit, vel potius gentis in retractandis pollicitis consuetudo. Cur vero nunc has ad te mittam, fraudulenta discessio cuiusdam servi me impulit, quod se in hunc modum habet: ob turpiter et inhoneste commissa facinora cum ancilla mea, quæ claves ad penu meum conservabat, cum qua ipse et libidinem et furta exercuit, unâ cum hoc altero, quem nunc secum abduxit, quæ etiam eo nomine cum infamia a me dimissa est. Hæc tamen omnia hactenus dissimulavi, parcens ipsius famæ, ob ætatem, artem et Ripenses amicos, adeo ut nemo me ea rescivisse de ipso intellexerit, sed saltem in alios corrivales ipsius tota culpa redundârit, nulla ipsius facta mentione, prout nostra postulat amicitia, quia est res malo exemplari propter alios meos opifices et servos, impune citra omnem causam et necessitatem se subducere. Ubi ipsum recepero, si resipuerit et culpam deprecatus fuerit, lenius cum illo agam quam promeritus est, præsertim te pro illo per literas intercedente. Omnem itaque move lapidem, charissime M. ANDREA, ut certo mihi restituatur, quod sane non difficulter efficere poteris, et da operam ne intelligam te minus sincere meas partes in hoc negocio agere, ne labefactetur amicitia nostra, quæ propemodum vacillare nonnihil mihi videtur ex literis Domino DANZÆO a te perscriptis, ubi vehementiæ et acerbitatis ob nescio quos versus me insimulas. Callide quidem satis pro teipso, ut apud æmulos per tralationem a suspicione consensus te liberes, sed pro tuo TYCHONE minus candide et fortasse etiam pro intimo tuo proprio sensu et iudicio minus vere. Vale et da operam, ut in hoc negocio tuam erga me fidem experiar. Saluta METTAM cum utroque parente ceterisque amicis nostris. Iterum vale et admonitionem hanc meam ut libere prolatam patienter et sincere accipe.

Iterum terque quaterque vale et ante hyemem, si per tempestates licuerit, nos invise.
Datæ Uraniburgi die 11. Nov. Anno 1585.
TYCHO BRAHE
mea manu.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 98; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
De alijs rebus et privatis negotijs forsan alias commodius vel etiam coram tutius agam.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Anders Sørensen Vedel.**
Greeting.

It had been most delightful for me to hear, most loving Master Anders, what I lately learned at Copenhagen from your letter addressed to the Magnificent Master Dançay — that you would shortly visit us, provided the winter does not hinder your journey, or rather the nation's habit of going back on what it has promised. But the reason why I now send these [lines] to you is that the fraudulent departure of a certain servant has driven me [to it], the matter standing thus: on account of deeds shamefully and dishonourably committed with a maidservant of mine — she who kept the keys to my storeroom, with whom he practised both lust and thefts, together with this other [man] whom he has now carried off with him — she too has on that account been dismissed by me in disgrace. Yet all this I have hitherto dissembled, sparing his reputation on account of his age, his trade, and his Ribe friends, so that no one has perceived that I had found this out about him, but rather the whole blame has overflowed onto certain other rivals of his, with no mention made of his deed — as our friendship requires — because it is a matter of bad example, on account of my other workmen and servants, that he should withdraw himself with impunity, without any cause or necessity. When I have got him back, if he comes to his senses and begs pardon for his fault, I will deal more leniently with him than he has deserved, especially with you interceding for him by letter. So move every stone, dearest Master Anders, that he may surely be restored to me — which indeed you will be able to bring about without difficulty — and take care that I do not perceive you to be playing my part in this affair less than sincerely, lest our friendship be undermined, which seems to me to be on the point of wavering somewhat, from the letter written out by you to Master Dançay, where you charge me with vehemence and harshness on account of some verses or other. Cunningly enough, to be sure, on your own behalf — so that among [our] rivals you might, by shifting [it onto me], free yourself from the suspicion of complicity — but on behalf of your own Tycho less candidly, and perhaps also, as regards your own innermost feeling and judgement, less truthfully. Farewell, and take care that in this affair I may put your good faith toward me to the test. Greet Mette, with both her parents and the rest of our friends. Again farewell, and receive this admonition of mine, as freely uttered, patiently and sincerely.

Again, and thrice and four times, farewell; and before winter, if the storms allow, visit us.
Given at Uraniborg, the 11th day of November, in the year 1585.
TYCHO BRAHE,
in my own hand.


*[Postscript:]* Of other matters and private affairs I shall perhaps treat more conveniently on another occasion, or even more safely face to face.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Andreas Severini Vellejus* = **Anders Sørensen Vedel** (1542–1616), royal historiographer, translator of Saxo Grammaticus (1575), and Tycho's old friend; based at **Ribe** (hence the *Ripenses amici*, "Ribe friends," below). Addressed throughout as *Magister* / *M. Andrea* (academic "Master," this chapter's convention).
- **Salutation.** *S.* = *salutem (dicit)*, "(sends) greeting". Subscription *mea manu* = "in my own hand."
- **Dançay.** *Magnifico Domino Danzaeo* / *Domino Danzaeo* = **Charles de Dançay** (Carolus Danzaeus, d. 1589), French royal ambassador (*legatus regis Galliarum*) resident at the Danish court, a friend and patron of Tycho; the *Opera Omnia* index lists him under *Leg. Gal.* (legatus Galliae) and records his role at Uraniborg's foundation-stone laying. Vedel's letters reached and were copied at Copenhagen, where Tycho read of his intended visit.
- **Mette.** *Mettam* = **Mette**, Vedel's wife (Mette Hansdatter), greeted "with both her parents." Kept as the Danish given name.
- **Place / calendar.** *Datae Uraniburgi die 11. Nov. Anno 1585* = "Given at **Uraniborg** (on Hven), the 11th day of November, 1585" (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The dateline agrees with the catalogue label; header date as written.
- **The runaway-servant matter.** *fraudulenta discessio cuiusdam servi* = "the fraudulent departure of a certain servant." Tycho writes that this *servus* had carried off with him "this other [man]" (*hoc altero, quem nunc secum abduxit*) and had been entangled with a *ancilla* ("maidservant") who held the storeroom keys; she has been dismissed *cum infamia* ("in disgrace"). Tycho asks Vedel to *omnem move lapidem* ("move every stone," = leave no stone unturned, the proverbial *omnem movere lapidem*) to have the man *restored* to him (*restituatur*) — i.e. returned, as an absconding servant under early-modern master-servant obligation.
- **Negation control.** The source carries the principal negations *non impediverit* ("does not hinder"), *nulla ipsius facta mentione* ("no mention made of his deed"), *ne intelligam te minus sincere … agere* ("that I do not perceive you to be acting less than sincerely"), and *ne labefactetur amicitia* ("lest our friendship be undermined"). The doubled litotes *minus candide … minus vere* ("less candidly … less truthfully") is preserved as understatement, not flattened to "dishonestly/falsely."
- **The quarrel over verses.** *ob nescio quos versus me insimulas … vehementiae et acerbitatis* = Vedel had, in his letter to Dançay, accused Tycho of "vehemence and harshness" *on account of some verses or other* (Tycho's dismissive *nescio quos*, "I know not what / some … or other," is kept as a hedge). *per tralationem … a suspicione consensus te liberes* — *tralatio* (= *translatio*) here in its rhetorical/figurative sense of *transferring* or *shifting* [the blame] onto Tycho so as to clear himself of "the suspicion of complicity" (*consensus*) before their *aemuli* ("rivals"). Rendered "by shifting [it onto me]"; the bracketed object is editorial.
- **Idioms / register.** *iter tuum non impediverit, vel potius gentis in retractandis pollicitis consuetudo* — a barbed aside, "or rather the nation's habit of going back on what it has promised" (*gens* = the [Danish] people/nation; *retractare pollicita* = to withdraw promises); kept as written. *Iterum terque quaterque vale* echoes the Virgilian *terque quaterque beati* ("thrice and four times"), an intensifying farewell-flourish; rendered literally.
- **Editorial insertions.** Bracketed words — "[lines]," "[man]," "[other man]," "[it onto me]," "[our]," "[to it]," "[yet]" — supply grammatically implied objects/subjects with no separate word in the Latin, by this chapter's convention

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (after "mea manu"), restored from Dreyer VII, p. 98 (dropped by the working transcription).

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VII pp.97-99 read as page images. The letter runs from the bottom of p.97 through p.98, including the postscript 'De alijs rebus et privatis negotijs forsan alias commodius vel etiam coram tutius agam' printed at the foot of p.98 immediately before the source citation line - confirming the record's apparatus note that this postscript is genuinely in Dreyer and was correctly restored. Collated the servant/maidservant narrative (three-person structure: fleeing servant, ancilla, 'hoc altero'), all proper names (Danzaeus, Mette), the Ripe/Ribe reference, and the closing date/signature (11 Nov 1585) word-for-word. the transcribed original matches Dreyer exactly; the published English renders the syntax (including the correct antecedents for 'cum qua'/'quem'/'quae') accurately throughout.

text.original:
NOBILITATE GENERIS, VIRTUTE ET ERUDITIONE PRÆSTANTI DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE DANO DOMINO ET AMICO OBSERVANDO.
S.

NOBILISSIME Domine TYCHO et amice observandissime, longa intercapedo locorum facit, ut rarissime per literas colloqui possimus, alioqui non intermitterem, quin te saepius meis literis salutarem, aut si iter esset saltem dierum sex aut 8, in hac mea ingravescente aetate, ipsoque senio (nam a die 1. Octob. 60 ingressus sum aetatis annum) ipsemet te convenirem. Cum autem praeter omnem meam spem et opinionem incidissem in HENRICUM meum popularem servum Magnif. D. IACOBI SEGURII Legati Sereniss. Regis Navarrae ad quosdam Germaniae principes, ac is servus Dresdâ salutandi amicos suos gratia Pragam excurrisset, diceretque se in Daniam rectâ cum Domino suo profecturum esse, nolui eum vacuum meis literis dimittere istuc neque hanc occasionem scribendi ad te praetermittere. Scias igitur me unâ cum meis omnibus integra adhuc ex Dei beneficio frui valetudine, praeterquam quod senum morbi crebrius iam me invadunt, vires animi et corporis languescunt, ut etiamsi quam maxime velim oblectare studijs Astronomicis, non possim. Taceo alia multa. Meam Dialexin auxeram iam olim aliquot problematis partim novis, partim ex DIGGSEI Alis et Scalis derivatis de invenienda parallaxi quorumcunque Phaenomenûm; in multis memet correxi a priore editione. Et ut esset veluti Synopsis quaedam scriptorum de Nova Stella, volui omnium Authorum scripta nostris consona uno volumine edere, quibus adiunxi aliquot Cometarum historias. Qua de re iam ante ad te perscripseram, ac tu rogaveras, ne tuum scriptum adiungerem, quod illud ipse elimaturus pluraque ei additurus esses. Hoc meum opus nondum quidem prodijt, quod sane non mea culpa, sed Typographorum accidit, quod Astronomica non libenter edant. Cum autem intellexissem te domi in tua Urania etiam Typographiam instituisse pro edendis tuis lucubrationibus, tractaverisque idem, quod ego, argumentum de inventione parallaxium, nactus hanc occasionem, volui mittere ad te meam illam Synopsin, ut vel ordine a me designato eam (siquidem tibi probabitur) tuis typis ederes vel excerperes inde, quae tibi utilia viderentur, tuoque operi adiungeres. Ego certe gratum nostrum studium et operam posteritati fore iudico, si plenam historiam a pluribus conscriptam novi istius sideris proposuerimus. Nihil dico de doctrina parallaxeos omnium phaenomenωn, quae hucusque a nemine fuit tradita. Tu ea omnia multo rectius intelligis, quam ut a me explicari possint. Nihil dicam de his amplius. Sed librum meum quaeso accipe et evolve, et si placet dignumque editione censes, volesque illum tuis typis edere aut tuo operi adiungere, retineto apud te. Sin displicuerit, aut aliquid intercesserit, quod tuis typis imprimi non possit, rogo ut meum librum per eundem mihi remittas. Nullum enim aliud exemplum habeo, nollemque quantulumcunque hunc meum laborem perire. Quicquid statueris de libro, ratum et firmum erit apud me. Omnem tibi in illum potestatem trado, adeoque in me, ut libere moneas et reprehendas, fidemque amicitiae in hac re mihi potissimum praestes.

B. V.
Pragae ad lucernam, quod servus ille D. SEGURIJ summo mane abitum pararet, die 13 Decemb. veteris Calendarij, nos 23 numeramus, Anno 1585
T. studiosiss.
THADD.
text.english:
**To the Lord Tycho Brahe, the Dane, outstanding in nobility of birth, in virtue, and in learning, my lord and friend to be respected.**
Greeting.

Most noble Lord Tycho and most esteemed friend, the long distance between our places makes it that we can converse by letter only very seldom; otherwise I would not fail to greet you more often by my letters — or, if the journey were of only six or eight days, in this my advancing age and very old age (for on 1 October I entered my sixtieth year) I would meet with you in person. But since, beyond all my hope and expectation, I had come upon Henricus, my fellow-countryman, a servant of the Magnificent Master Jacobus Segurius, envoy of the Most Serene King of Navarre to certain princes of Germany — and since that servant had made an excursion from Dresden to Prague for the sake of greeting his friends, and said that he would set out directly into Denmark with his master — I was unwilling to send him off thither empty of any letter of mine, nor to let slip this occasion of writing to you. Know, then, that I, together with all my household, still by God's kindness enjoy unbroken health, except that the ailments of old men now assail me more frequently, and the powers of my mind and body grow faint, so that even though I should most greatly wish to take delight in astronomical studies, I cannot. Of much else I say nothing. My *Dialexis* I had, some while ago now, enlarged by several problems, partly new, partly derived from Digges's *Wings and Ladders*, on finding the parallax of any phenomena whatsoever; in many places I corrected myself from the earlier edition. And so that there might be, as it were, a kind of *Synopsis* of the writings on the New Star, I wished to publish in one volume the writings of all the authors that agree with our own, to which I have added some histories of comets. Concerning this matter I had already written to you before, and you had asked that I not add your own writing, since you were going to polish it yourself and to add more to it. This work of mine has not, indeed, yet come forth — which truly has happened not through my fault, but through the printers', because they do not willingly publish astronomical [works]. But since I had learned that you too had set up a printing-house at home in your Urania, for the publishing of your lucubrations, and that you had treated the same subject as I — on the finding of parallaxes — having got this occasion, I wished to send you that *Synopsis* of mine, so that either you might publish it in your types in the order I have laid out (if indeed it shall meet your approval), or might excerpt from it whatever should seem useful to you and add it to your own work. I, for my part, judge that our zeal and labour will be welcome to posterity, if we shall set forth a full history of that new star, compiled by many [hands]. I say nothing of the doctrine of the parallax of all phenomena, which up to now has been handed down by no one. You understand all those things much more correctly than they can be explained by me. I shall say nothing further about these matters. But take, I pray, my book and unroll it, and if it please you and you judge it worthy of publication, and you shall wish to publish it in your types or to add it to your own work, keep it by you. But if it shall displease you, or anything shall stand in the way so that it cannot be printed in your types, I ask that you send my book back to me by the same man. For I have no other copy, and I would not wish this labour of mine, however slight, to perish. Whatever you shall determine concerning the book will be settled and firm with me. I hand over to you all power over it, and indeed over myself, so that you may freely admonish and reprove [me], and may show to me, above all in this matter, the faith of friendship.

Fare you well.
At Prague, by lamplight — because that servant of Master Segurius was making ready to depart at break of day — on 13 December of the Old Calendar, which we reckon the 23rd, in the year 1585.
Most devoted to you,
THADD[aeus].

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus Hagecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayek, 1525–1600), Prague physician, mathematician, and astronomer to the Imperial court of Rudolf II; Tycho's chief Bohemian correspondent and later instrumental in bringing him to Prague. He signs himself in the shortened form *THADD.*
- **Self-dating / age.** *a die 1. Octob. 60 ingressus sum aetatis annum* — "on 1 October I entered my sixtieth year." Taken with the birth year usually given as 1525 (1 October 1525), this is internally consistent. Reproduced as written; no correction made.
- ***Iacobi Segurii … Legati … Regis Navarrae*** — **Jacques de Ségur-Pardaillan**, diplomatic envoy of **Henri of Navarre** (the future Henri IV of France) sent in 1585 on a mission to the German Protestant princes (and onward, per this letter, toward Denmark) to build an anti-Catholic-League coalition. *Sereniss. Regis Navarrae* = "the Most Serene King of Navarre." *HENRICUM meum popularem* = "Henricus, my fellow-countryman" (i.e. a fellow Bohemian/Czech in Ségur's service) — the courier of this letter.
- ***Dialexis*** — Hagecius's *Dialexis de novae et prius incognitae stellae … apparitione* (Frankfurt am Main, 1574), his treatise on the new star (nova) of 1572. He reports having enlarged it with new *problemata*. Title kept in Latin.
- ***DIGGSEI Alis et Scalis*** — Thomas **Digges**, *Alae seu scalae mathematicae* ("Wings, or Mathematical Ladders," London, Thomas Marsh, 1573), the English work on determining the parallax/distance of the 1572 nova. *DIGGSEI* is the as-printed (metathesised) genitive of *Diggeseus*; *Alis et Scalis* = ablative of *Alae … scalae* ("the *Wings and Ladders*"). The title is rendered descriptively and the Latin form noted.
- **Astronomy.** *parallaxi … parallaxeos … parallaxium* → **parallax** throughout. *invenienda parallaxi quorumcunque Phaenomenûm* = "finding the parallax of any phenomena whatsoever"; *doctrina parallaxeos omnium phaenomenωn* = "the doctrine of the parallax of all phenomena." Here *phaenomena* denotes celestial appearances (novae, comets, and the like) whose distance is at issue — not "phenomena" in the modern generic sense.
- **Mixed-script spelling.** *Phaenomenûm* (gen. pl., printed with circumflex) and especially *phaenomenωn* — the latter written with a **Greek omega (ω)** embedded in an otherwise Latin word, a learned grapho-play on the word's Greek origin (*φαινόμενα*). The omega is preserved in the Source block by this chapter's convention; the word is read as the Latin genitive plural *phaenomenon* and rendered "phenomena."
- ***Nova Stella / novi … sideris*** → "the New Star" / "that new star" — the supernova of 1572 (B Cassiopeiae), the common subject of Hagecius's, Digges's, and Tycho's works. *Synopsis* — Hagecius's planned collected volume of concordant authors on the nova, with appended *Cometarum historias* ("histories of comets"); title-word kept.
- ***in tua Urania … Typographiam instituisse*** — "you had set up a printing-house … in your Urania," i.e. at **Uraniborg** on Hven, where Tycho had established his own press for his *lucubrationes* (learned night-works/writings). The substance dovetails with Tycho's contemporaneous parallax work on the nova and comets.
- **Epistolary formulae.** Opening *S.* = *salutem* ("greeting,"). *B. V.* = *Bene vale* ("Fare you well,"). *T. studiosiss.* = *Tui studiosissimus* ("Most devoted to you").
- **Calendar (in-letter double date — not converted by the editor).** The dateline reads *die 13 Decemb. veteris Calendarij, nos 23 numeramus* = "13 December of the Old Calendar [Julian/Old Style], which we reckon the 23rd [Gregorian/New Style]." Writing from Imperial Prague, which had adopted the Gregorian reform, Hagecius gives **both** styles, accommodating Tycho's Danish Old-Style usage while noting his own New-Style count — the 10-day gap stated explicitly in the source. The header leads with the as-written O.S. date (13 December, matching the catalogue label) and appends the source's own N.S. equivalent (23 December). No silent conversion or correction has been made.
- ***Pragae ad lucernam*** — "at Prague, by lamplight": written in haste before dawn because the courier was leaving at *summo mane* ("at break of day"). Place: *Pragae* = **Prague** (Hagecius's residence).
- **Minor textual point.** *nllem* (in *nllemque … hunc meum laborem perire*) is an evident misprint/contraction for *nollem* ("I would not wish"); read as *nollem* and so translated. *intercapedo* for classical *intercapedo/intercapedinem* and *amicitae* for *amicitiae* are as-printed orthographic forms, silently read to sense.

documents.abstract: Describes Uraniborg and its facilities, reports progress on astronomical and chemical works, and petitions the Emperor for an imperial printing privilege to protect publication.
documents.incipit: CUM ex liberalitate et optimo erga me studiaque astronomica animo serinissimus rex Daniæ, …

text.original:
POTENTISSIME IMPERATOR D. D. CLEMENTISSIME.

CUM ex liberalitate et optimo erga me studiaque astronomica animo serinissimus rex Daniæ, dominus meus clementissimus, astronomiæ instaurandæ gratia insulam Huenam mihi addixerit, in qua meis sumptibus extruxi arcem in varia domicilia ad literarum studia, exercitia astronomica, chymica, opificia, oblectamenta et ad alios usus distinctam et distributam; cui arci Uranieburgo a studio astronomico nomen indidi. Ut igitur et voluntati regis nostri et multorum de me expectationi satisfacerem, ab annis pluribus omne meum studium et operam in instauranda astronomia posui, iamque nonnulla in ea arte elaborata habeo, cætera sub incude, ut dicitur, versantur, adornantur et expoliuntur. Quæ omnia in reipub: literariæ commodum omnibus communia facere vellem, nostris prælis in eadem arce excusa. Verum plurimum vereor ne maximis meis impensis, quas tum in typographiam, tum in opifices feci, et in excudendis operibus mathematicis adhuc facturus sum, defrauder, si labores mei maximis sumptibus comparati ab alijs typographis in Germania et sub ditione Maiestatis Vestræ recudantur et divenduntur. Quare Maiestatem Vestram cum omni submissione rogo, quæcumque ex mea officina in mathematicis studijs proditura sint, sive à me elaborata, sive illustrata, ne ea a quoquam typographo recudantur, clementer privilegio ad decennium cavere dignetur, idque sub mulcta transgressoribus irrogari solita. Cavebo vicissim, ne libri a me publicandi quidpiam, quod vel religionis controversiis vel reipubl: constitutioni offensioni siet, ullo in loco contineant. Et si quid Cæs: Ma: V: in hisce mathematicis studijs quidpiam à me postulaverit, aut ego intellexero qua in re gratum servitium eidem præstare possem, me semper promptum et paratum habebit, cui omne meum studium, operam, officium et obsequium humiliter defero. Et ut Cæs: Ma: V: rectius intelligat et ædificium nostræ arcis et totum animi nostri propositum mitto eidem eiusdem arcis totiusque nostræ insulæ designationem.

Cum his me Cæs: Ma: V: commendo.
S: Cæs: Ma: V: addictissimus
Tycho Brahe Danus Dom: de Knudstrup.
text.english:
**MOST POWERFUL EMPEROR, MOST MERCIFUL LORD AND MASTER.**

Whereas, out of his generosity and his most excellent disposition toward me and toward astronomical studies, the most serene King of Denmark, my most merciful lord, has assigned to me the island of Hven for the sake of the renewal of astronomy [*astronomia instauranda*] — on which, at my own expense, I have raised a castle laid out and divided into various dwellings for literary studies, for astronomical and chemical exercises, for workshops, for recreations, and for other uses; to which castle I gave the name Uraniborg, from the astronomical study [pursued there] — therefore, that I might satisfy both the will of our King and the expectation many have of me, for several years now I have set all my zeal and labour upon the renewal of astronomy [*instauranda astronomia*], and I now have a number of things in that art worked out, while the rest are, as the saying goes, [still] on the anvil, being furnished and polished. All of which I should wish to make common to all, for the benefit of the republic of letters, printed off at my presses in that same castle. But I greatly fear that I may be defrauded of the very great expenses which I have incurred, both on the printing-house and on the workmen, and which I am still going to incur in printing off mathematical works, if my labours, procured at very great cost, should be reprinted and sold off by other printers in Germany and under the dominion of Your Majesty. Wherefore I ask Your Majesty, with all submission, that whatever shall issue from my workshop in mathematical studies, whether worked out by me or illustrated [by me], may not be reprinted by any printer; [and that] you would mercifully deign to provide for this by a privilege for ten years, and [that] this [be enforced] under the penalty customarily imposed upon transgressors. I, for my part, will take care that the books to be published by me contain nothing, in any place, that may give offence either to the controversies of religion or to the constitution of the commonwealth. And if Your Imperial Majesty should require anything of me in these mathematical studies, or if I should understand in what matter I might render some welcome service to the same, you will always have me ready and prepared, to whom I humbly offer all my zeal, labour, duty, and obedience. And that Your Imperial Majesty may the more rightly understand both the structure of our castle and the whole purpose of our mind, I send to the same a drawing [*designatio*] of that same castle and of our whole island.

With these [words] I commend myself to Your Imperial Majesty.
Most devoted to Your Imperial Majesty,
Tycho Brahe, the Dane, Lord of Knudstrup.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender and recipient.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), then resident on Hven, writing to **Rudolf II** (1552–1612), Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1576–1612), seeking the imperial printing privilege that would protect his self-published works against unauthorized reprinting in the Empire. The literature confirms this is Tycho's first printing privilege, "a ten-year Imperial charter awarded in 1586" (Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, 2007); "by May 1586 Tycho had his ten-year copyright" (Christianson, *On Tycho's Island* / *Lord of Uraniborg*). The privilege is the same one later cited (alongside *regum quorundam*) in the apparatus of the 1602 *Mechanica*.
- **Document type / no dateline.** The letter is preserved as the enclosure (*Beilage*) to the Imperial Registry (*Reichsregistratur*) at Vienna, filed under **28 March 1586**. The body carries **no dateline**: it ends with the subscription only. The edition label ("1586. empty") records exactly this — a 1586 letter with an empty (absent) in-text date. Per this chapter's convention, the header therefore does not assert a date the source substantiates; it gives the year the text supports (1586) and appends the archival/registry date "(catalogued 28 March 1586)", flagged here rather than presented as an authorial dateline. **The "28 March" is the registry filing date, not necessarily the date of composition or dispatch.**
- **Calendar.** Denmark and the Imperial chancery were both on the **Julian calendar (Old Style)** in 1586; the filing date 28 March is O.S. No conversion is performed.
- ***astronomia instauranda / instauranda astronomia*** — "the renewal of astronomy," Tycho's programmatic phrase (*astronomia instaurata*, "astronomy restored/renewed"), kept consistent per glossary. The verb recurs twice in the source and is rendered identically both times.
- ***arx / Uranieburgum*** — "castle"; the name **Uraniborg** ("citadel of Urania," the Muse of astronomy), Tycho's observatory-house on Hven, here spelled *Uranieburgo* in the source. *insula Huena* = the island of **Hven**.
- ***Dom: de Knudstrup*** — "Lord of **Knudstrup**," Tycho's ancestral seat in Scania (kept as is,).
- ***sub incude … versantur*** — "are on the anvil," a proverbial idiom (*incudi reddere*, Horace) for work still being hammered into final form; the metaphor is kept.
- ***reipublica literaria*** — "the republic of letters," the commonwealth of learning; rendered literally.
- ***designatio*** — here a **drawing / plan** (a depiction of Uraniborg and the island enclosed with the letter); rendered "a drawing," with the Latin flagged, since the term can also mean "design/layout."
- **Editorial / orthographic notes.** *serinissimus* (for *serenissimus*) and *reipubl: constitutioni offensioni siet* are reproduced as transmitted; *siet* is the archaic subjunctive *sit* ("may be"). The chancery contractions are expanded silently only in translation: *Caes: Ma: V:* = *Caesarea Maiestas Vestra* ("Your Imperial Majesty"); *D. D.* in the address = *Domine ac Domine* ("Lord and Master"); *S:* before the subscription = *servus* / *subditus* ("servant/subject," here taken with *addictissimus*). The penalty clause *sub mulcta transgressoribus irrogari solita* ("under the penalty customarily imposed upon transgressors") supplies no figure; "[be enforced]" is bracketed as an editorial supplement to the elliptical Latin.
- **Negation check.** The source contains the negations *ne … recudantur*, *ne … defrauder* (governed by *vereor ne*, "I fear that"), *ne ea a quoquam typographo recudantur*, and *ne libri … quidpiam … contineant*. Each is reproduced once in the translation; none added or dropped. Note that *vereor ne defrauder* is the standard Latin *verb-of-fearing* construction — "I fear **that** I may be defrauded" (not "I fear that I may **not** be"); the *ne* is the fearing-clause marker, not a negation of the verb, and is rendered accordingly.
