documents.incipit: MIN gandske wenlig helsen etther nu och althidt forsendt medt Gudt vor herre. Kierre fru …

text.original:
ERLIG OCH WELBYRDIG FRUE BERITTE BØLLE THIL GUNDERSLØFFHOLM, MIN KIERRE FADERSØSTER GANDTSKE WENLIGEN THILSCHREFFUIT.

MIN gandske wenlig helsen etther nu och althidt forsendt medt Gudt vor herre. Kierre fru Beritte och kierre fadersøster, betacker jeg etther saa gandske gierne for aldt ehre och gott, y mig althidt giortt och beuist haffuer, huilckett att forschylde jeg alle min dage will findes willig och redebon thil medt altt hues vdi min ringe formu kandt werre. Giffuendis etther wenligen thilkiende, att then byggemestere, som y schriffuer mig thil om, wedt naffn mester Hans, handt icke nu er her hoeß mig, men jeg wenntter hannom hidt att skulde komme om en dag tre eller fire. Och tror jeg icke andett, indt handt io well skulde kunde giørre samme arbedt, att thett schulle werre vstraffeligt, thersom handt icke haffuer tagett naagett andett arbedt ahn att bygge vdi sommer, men bliffuer medt etther om etthers arbedt forehnett. Huorfor jeg gierne will, naar handt hidt kommer thil mig, giffue hannom etthers arbedt ahn, och sige hannom ther om hues leylighedt y haffuer schreffuett mig thil, att handt fanger etthers wille her vdi att wide, och hues beschen handt giffuer fran sich, will jeg entten schrifftlich lade etther wide, eller handt och selff skall komme thil etther, och giffue etther nerwerendis thilkiende. Kierre fru Beritte och kierre fadersøster, will jeg icke lenger oppeholde etther medt thenne min schriffuelfe, men giør althidt gierne, hues jeg wedt etther thil ehre och tieniste kandt werre, och will her medt nu och althidt haffue etther then alsommechtigste Gudt thil siel och liiff befalendis.

DatumVraniborg then 30. januarii anno 1586.
Tyge Brahe
Egen hand.
text.english:
**Written most kindly to the honourable and well-born lady Birgitte Bølle of Gunderslevholm, my dear father's sister.**

My wholly friendly greeting sent to you now and always with God our Lord. Dear Lady Birgitte and dear father's sister, I thank you so very gladly for all the honour and kindness you have always done and shown me, which to repay I shall all my days be found willing and ready, with all that may be within my poor means. Making known to you in friendly wise that the builder you write to me about, by name Master Hans, is not now here with me, but I expect him to come hither in a day or three or four. And I do not doubt but that he should indeed be able to do the same work, so that it would be beyond reproach, provided he has not taken on some other work to build this summer, but comes to an agreement with you about your work. Wherefore I am glad, when he comes hither to me, to put your work to him, and to tell him concerning it whatever circumstances you have written to me of, so that he may learn your wishes herein; and whatever answer he gives, I will either let you know in writing, or he shall himself come to you and make it known to you in person. Dear Lady Birgitte and dear father's sister, I will not detain you longer with this my writing, but [will] always gladly do whatever I know may be to your honour and service, and herewith will now and always have you commended to the most Almighty God in soul and body.

Given at Uraniborg, the 30th of January in the year 1586.
Tyge Brahe
[in his] own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), writing from his seat on Hven; the closing *Egen hand* ("[in his] own hand") marks the letter as an autograph — consistent with the witness being the surviving original (not a register copy).
- **Recipient.** *Frue Beritte Bølle thil Gundersløffholm* = **Birgitte Bølle** (Berthe/Berete Bølle, d. 1592), of **Gunderslevholm** in Zealand, widow of the councillor Christoffer Gøye. Tycho addresses her as *min kierre fadersøster* — "my dear father's sister" (paternal aunt). The address-leaf style *Erlig och welbyrdig frue … thil Gundersløffholm* ("honourable and well-born lady … of Gunderslevholm") is the standard noble titulature; the seat-name *thil Gunderslevholm* denotes her as holder of that estate.
- **Place.** *Vraniborg* = **Uraniborg**, Tycho's house on the island of Hven.
- **Master Hans, the builder.** *then byggemestere … wedt naffn mester Hans* = "the builder … by name Master Hans." On the testimony of Friis (*Bidrag til dansk Kunsthistorie*), the "Bygmester Hans" recommended in this very letter is most probably **Hans van Steenwinckel the Elder** (c. 1545–1601), the Netherlandish-Danish architect-builder then active in Denmark (engaged in 1585 on the restoration of St. Petri church in Copenhagen, and afterwards on the architectural work of Tycho's mural-quadrant decoration at Uraniborg). The identification is Friis's, offered as a probability; the letter itself names him only as *mester Hans*, so the surname is supplied in the apparatus and not inserted in the body.
- ***byggemestere / arbedt*** — "builder" / "work" (i.e. a building commission); Birgitte Bølle had evidently written to ask Tycho to engage Master Hans for building work on her estate, and Tycho here acts as intermediary.
- **Register.** A private kinship-and-patronage letter in the polite-familial Danish epistolary register, not chancery: the doubled courtesy formulae (*gandske wenlig helsen*, *kierre fru Beritte och kierre fadersøster*), the service-and-honour protestations, and the pious commendation-formula (*haffue etther … Gudt thil siel och liiff befalendis*, "have you commended to God in soul and body") are the conventional opening and closing topoi of the genre, rendered in matching English period courtesy rather than modernised.
- **Epistemic register preserved.** Tycho hedges throughout and these hedges are kept: *jeg wenntter hannom … att skulde komme* ("I expect him … to come"); *tror jeg icke andett, indt handt io well skulde kunde giørre* ("I do not doubt but that he should indeed be able to do"); and the conditional *thersom handt icke haffuer tagett naagett andett arbedt ahn … men bliffuer … forehnett* ("provided he has not taken on some other work … but comes to an agreement"). The single negation in that conditional (*icke haffuer tagett … ahn*, "has not taken on") is reproduced exactly once; the clause is a genuine condition on Hans's availability, not a statement that he has so taken on other work.
- **Orthography (early-modern Danish, c. 1586).** *thilschreffuit* = *tilskrevet* ("written to"); *etther* = *eder* ("you," dat./acc.); *althidt* = *altid* ("always"); *betacker* = *betakker* ("thank"); *forschylde* = *forskylde* ("repay, requite"); *redebon* = *redebon* ("ready"); *ringe formu* = *ringe formue* ("poor means/ability"); *thilkiende* … *giffuendis* = *give til kende* ("make known"); *hannom* = *hannem* ("him"); *vstraffeligt* = *ustraffeligt* ("beyond reproach, blameless"); *forehnett* = *forenet* ("agreed, united"); *beschen* = *besked* ("answer, information"); *nerwerendis* = *nærværende(s)* ("in person, present"); *oppeholde* = *opholde* ("detain"); *alsommechtigste* = *allermægtigste* ("most almighty"); *siel och liiff* = *sjæl og liv* ("soul and body/life").
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Datum Vraniborg then 30. januarii anno 1586* = "Given at Uraniborg, 30 January 1586" (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The dateline date agrees with the catalogue label, so no discrepancy arises. *Datum* ("Given") kept by this chapter's convention (cf. *Actum*); in the source it is run together with the place (*DatumVraniborg*) — printed thus and not re-spaced in the source block.
- **Language note.** The edition heuristic tags this *da*, which reading confirms: it is early-modern Danish throughout (no German body, no Latin code-switch beyond *Datum* and the title-style *thil [Gundersløffholm]*). This is the German-orthography-Danish risk-class only insofar as forms like *schriffuer*, *schulle*, *wforsømmit*-type *w-/sch-* spellings appear — but the morphology and lexicon are Danish.

Literarum ad Tuam Celsit. reuerenter mitteremA, fretus hac Cels. Tuæ clementi inuitatione, quæ meam audaciam excusabitA. De Cometa itaque cuius Obseruationem T. Celsitud. a me diligenterA desiderat, notum facio Cels. TuaeA, eum 18 Die Octobris proxime elapsi Anni, mihi Sidera more solito

mihi delineatam vna miserit, rem etiam fecerit longe acceptissimam. Nam
plurimum scire aueo, anne (veluti ex probabili coniectura assequor)
Celsitudinis Tuæ noua hæc Instrumenta plurimum similitudinis cum quibusdam

PAVLVS ille WITTICHIVS, ex
cuius præscripto Tua Celsitudo sua Organa innouataA esse asserit, et Instrumentorum quorundam, quæ partim tunc parata
habebam, partim in posterum elaborare decreui, elaborationemA et vsum, diuisionisque et Pinnacidiorum, quibusA in omnibus similiter ferme vtor, rationem explorauit, seque mox in
Germaniam, quædam alia prætendens,
recepit. Ex ipsa vero Sextantis sola appellatione conijcere licet Witichiumnon multum a nostris aliena Tuæ
Celsitudini proposuisse. Nam Sextantis Instrumentum, cuius et fabrica
adeoque ipsum nomen recens a me excogitatum erat, tuncA in vsu paratum habebam, cum Witichius mihi adesset. Verum cum ipsa experientia me
multoties commonefaceret eam Sextantis Fabricam, quam tunc adinueneram, ob
certa quædam impedimenta Stellarum intercapedinibus praeciseA indagandis non sufficere, eius vsus iam dudum a nobis antiquatus est.
Quare si Sextans ille quo T. Celsitud. Siderum interualla obseruari curat,
eadem ratione confectus est, qua is quem Wittichius hic conspexit, vix admodumA ratas nullique fallaciæ obnoxias eius beneficio
licebit obtinere distantias. Impossibile enim est ex vnico oculo, circa
Centrum InstrumentiA quiescente, binarum Stellarum, præsertim si remotiores inuicem
fuerint, diuersa simul præcise contueri loca. Nec enim Centrum visus Centro
Instrumenti apte vniri potest, aut per vllas Parallaxes hæc differentia satisA conuenienter excusari; Nec pupilla Oculi in maioribus interstitijs
binas Stellas intuendo immota manet, vnde Centrum visus etiam aliquantulum variareA, necessarium euadit. Imo vero, quod in hoc subtili negotio magni
momenti est, cum non vtrinque quælibet Stella circa Pinnacidium per rimulas
Parallelas æquabiliter et bifariam secta conspiciatur, vtrum accepta
distantia iusto maior minorue fuerit, nequaquam certo constabit. Excogitaui
itaque posteaA alium Sextantis conficiendi modum, eumque bifurcatum, ita vt per
binos Obseruatores quælibet Stella seorsim conspiceretur, vtrinqueA per duoA diuersa Pinnacidia. Quam etiam constructionis rationem WittichioA dum hîc præsens esset, aperui, postque ipsius
discessum eiuscemodi Sextantem parari curaui, qui sane satis exactus erat,
et Stellarum interuallis citra omnem sensibilem errorem capiendis
sufficiebat. Verum cum sua tractatione paulo difficilior et laboriosior
esset, nec satis cito negotium expediret, hic etiam Sextans apud me in vsu
esse desijt. Quod si Tuæ Celsitudinis Instrumentum ad eius similitudinem
confectum estA (nam Ideam huius Wittichio
hic monstraui, quæ ipsi perplacuit) non dubito quin distantiæ per eum
acceptæ recte se habeant, licet paulo difficilius et tardius (vt dixi)
obtineantur. Vt itaque tum errorem omnem, tum etiam difficultatem in hoc
negotio dextre absoluendo euitarem, aliam et
diuersam a prioribus eamque expeditissimam, ante quadriennium inueni
Sextantis conficiendi rationem plane simplicem et naturalem, quo per binos
etiam Obseruatores in circumferentia Instrumenti motis Pinnacidijs, quæ
rimulas habent Parallelas, distantiæ Stellarum circa Cylindrum in Centro

discernuntur. Tales autem binos affabre elaboratos huic vsui destinatos
habeo, quorum quilibet 4 cubitos sua capacitate adæquat. Vt vero Celsitud.
Tua huius Sextantis compositionem facilius compræhendat, mitto tum ædificij
in Astronomiæ honorem proximis Annis in hac Insula Huenna, non mediocri sumtu a me extructi, picturam, tum
etiam Sextantis (de quo loquor) aliquo modoA repræsentatam delineationem, vna cum designatione fulcri, cuius
beneficio in omnem Stellarum situm, ac inclinationem commode conuoluitur.
Addita est ab altera parte pictura Armillarum Æquatoriarum; Sic enim hoc
Instrumentum iam pridem a me excogitatum, eo quod Ascensiones Rectas et
Declinationes Siderum respectu Æquatoris metiatur, appellare libuit. Talium
autem Armillarum duo OrganaA tantæ quantitatis, vt singula scrupula discriminatim exhibeant,
confici curaui. Sed et in his ipsis, quæ Ptolemaicis
Armillis longe sunt expeditiores et minus erroribus obnoxiæ (velut nos ipsa
docuit experientia, cum Ptolemaicas etiam Armillas e solido Metallo eiusdem
pene quantitatisA in promptu habeamus) ante biennium nouam quandam et multo
expeditiorem structuram excogitaui, quæ saltem sesquialtero Circulo et Axe
rotundo, totum negotium mira facilitate et certitudine absoluit. Huius
Organi Machinam in Colle quodam extra ædes hasce Vraniæ dicatas constitutam,
et ad vsus commoditatem gradibus subterraneis vndique successiue
ascendentibus, circumdatam, summa cumA diligentia construxi, cuius Diameter 10 pedes continet. Huic plurimum
tribuo, quo ad Siderum Ascensiones Rectas et Declinationes, in quouis eorum
apparente situ adamussim indagandas, cuius etiam adminiculo vtplurimum
Cometæ apparentias, quas T. Celsitud. mitto, peruestigaui. Non autem
difficile esse exA datis Ascensionibus Rectis et Declinationibus respectu Æquatoris, eas
in Longitudines et Latitudines, quantum ad Eclipticam, redigere T. Celsit.
satis perspectum habet, siue id fiat per Triangulorum Sphæricorum rationes,
aut peculiarem aliquam Tabulam ex his deriuatam (qualem nos ad singulos
Ascensionis Rectæ gradus, et DeclinationisA vtrinque ab Æquatore 32 grad. scrupuloseA supputatam huic negotio destinauimus) siue etiamA Mechanice per Globum magnum, qualem etiam 6 pedum in Diametro vndique
Orichalco aptissime obductum et omni sui parte rotundissimum, paratum habeoA. Sed nimis longum foret hoc loco omnia mea Instrumenta Astronomice eorundemque vsum
commemorareA: quæ numero sedecim, structuræ Magnitudine,
Formæ varietate, et vsus multiplicis aptitudine, exacteA elaborata, præclari Thesauri loco (nec enim mediocri diligentia,
labore et sumtu parata sunt) possideo; quorum pleraque e solido Metallo
existunt, quædam vero, licet e certa et durabili lignea materia, vt pote
leuiori, necA nimio pondere ob quantitatis molem se ipsa inepte aggrauanteA, peculiari quadam ratione multipliciter componunturA, ita vt ne per se quidem mutationi facile subijciantur: nihilominus
tamen exterius Orichalcicis laminis, partim vt diuisionis subtilitati
accommoda euadant, partim vt eo firmius persistant, affabre muniuntur.
Magnitudinem vero distinctioni scrupulosæ sufficientem habentA, adeo vt nonnulla senos et quinos, quædam quaternos et ternos cubitos
adæquent. Quibus vsurpandis, tum etiam ijs, quæ ex Obseruationibus
demonstrari possunt, e Triangulis in numeros reducendis, vtplurimum octonos,
interdum etiam plures Arti Astronomicæ operam nauantes Studiosos, hic mecum
alo et instruo, nec vllius Serenitatis commoditatem siue Diurnam, siue
Nocturnam, in Solis, Lunæ, reliquorumque qui conspici queunt Planetarum et
Affixarum etiam Stellarum Phænomenis cælitus inquirendis, incassum abire
permittimus. De Instrumentorum vero singulorum Fabrica et Vsu, quia peculiarem LibrumA conscribere decreui, quiA Mechanicam Astronomiæ partem complectetur (quo
etiam nomine nunc illa omnia delineari, et figuras eorum Æneis aut BuxeisA laminis insculpi curo) Idcirco longiore de his commemoratione
supersedeo. Vbi autem laborem hunc (DEO successum largiente) absoluero, vel
saltem Figuræ omnes excisæ fuerint, Tuæ Cels. id quicquid erit perspiciendum
expendendumque transmittam. Tum enim Celsit. T. solo intuitu omnia facilius
cognoscet, quam ex longa et tædiosa de his relatione. Quod veroA hæc ipsa Instrumenta, quibus in Sideribus obseruandis assidue vtor,
admodum exacta sint, et ne quidemA tenuiter sensibilem errorem admittant, vel ex hoc solo comprobatur,
quod eiusdem Sideris locus per plura et diuersimode fabricata Organa varia
ratione depræhensus, in idem prorsus scrupulum sedulo attendentibus recidat.
Vt autem Celsitudo Tua specimen aliquod eorum, quas ex meis Obseruationibus
hactenus parta sunt, habeatA, adiunxi vna Solaris cursus huius Anni ex propria restitutione
deriuatam Ephemeridem, eamque ad Longitudinem 30 part. cui Celsitudinis Tuæ
ditio HASSIA congruit, directamA. Scrupula Secunda, prout Tabulæ nostræ in motu Solis, Obseruationibus
certis Geometrice fundatæ exhibent, annotaui, non quod ista subtilitas sit
vllo Instrumento in ipso Cœlo comprehensibilisA, vt Tua Celsit. optime nouit, sed ne neglectis secundis de scrupulis
primis aliqua ambiguitas oriretur. Peto itaque a Tua Celsitudine obnixeA, vt hanc nostram in cursus Solaris numeratione instaurationem per sua
Instrumenta expeririA, mihique de hac suam Sententiam clementer significari curare velitA. Oportet autem in his rite pensitandis Declinationem Eclipticæ
maximam præsupponere P. 23. Min. 31½. qualem nos peculiari quadam ratione, non ex altitudine Solis maxima
in vtroque Solstitio (hæc enim praxis ob Refractionem radiorum, quæ sit SoleA circa Brumam decliui, in nostro Horizonte deficit a vero plus
quaternis scrupulis) aliquoties pluribus Organis depræhendimus. Parallaxin quoqueA Solarem vbique Altitudinibus obseruatis addendam esseA, non dubium est, quin Celsitud. T. satis compertum habeat.
Refractiones insuper Radiorum Solarium, quæ decliuioresA Altitudines maiores sensibus ingerunt, quam reuera existunt (idque ob
Diaphanum Aëris pauloA minus perspicuum Diaphano AetherisA, vt in Opticis hæc demonstrantur) euitandæ sunt; præsertim si
Altitudines obseruatæ minores tertia aut ad summum dimidiaA Quadrantis parte fuerint. Nam vsque in hunc fere terminum
Refractionem aliquam perceptibilem fieri, peculiari quadam industria
expertus sum. Quo vero adhuc propiores Horizonti euadunt, eo etiam maiorem
Refractionem causantur, adeo vt Sol in ipso Ortu et OccasuA, etiam in Aëre purissimo, dimidio ad minimum gradu altior appareat,
quam rei veritas admittat. Sic etiam in Luna, cæterisque Planetis, et
affixis Sideribus per Refractionem cum decliuiores sunt, eorum Altitudines
et Declinationes veraque loca aliquantulum variantur. Quare in humilioribus
Altitudinibus, si scrupulose res tractanda sit, non
nimium erit Obseruationibus fidendum. Præterea multum interest, quibus modis
Æquatoris ad Horizontem inclinatio in loco Obseruationis depræhensa sit. Nam
per Solis Altitudines Meridianas, licet in vtroque Solstitio, adhibita etiam
Parallaxi accipiantur, ob Refractionem (de qua dixi) in Brumali decliuitate
sese insinuantem, nequaquam negotium hoc ea qua par est præcisione
absoluitur. Consultissimum itaque fuerit Poli sublimitatem ex ipsa Polari
Stella, cum est in Altitudine maxima et minima, studiose perquirere. Ea enim
cum mediocris in magnitudine satisque perspicua sit, et paruum circa Polum
describat Circulum, nec ob id Horizonti tantum appropinquet, vt Refractio
aliqua veram Altitudinem immutet, in hac Pragmatia citra omnem errorem
absoluenda, quam commodissima est. Si itaque Tua Celsitudo, et huius Polaris
(inquam) Stellæ Altitudinem maximam vel minimam, reliquis Obseruationibus
adiungi, meque de ea certiorem reddi curaueritA, fecerit rem mihi admodum exoptatam. Sic enim adhibita ipsius a Polo
distantia (quæ hoc Anno ex nostris Obseruationibus est part. 2. mint. 55.
secund. 50) ad exactissimam Poli et Æquatoris, eius loci in quo Tua
Celsitudo Obseruationes suas fieri procurat Eleuationem, indubitanter
perueniemus, et de Declinationibus Solis, StellarumqueA certitudinem ratam, modo Instrumenta recte se habeant, constituemus.
Quapropter si Celsitud. Tua ea (de quibus iam dixi) omnia, videlicet
Parallaxin Solis, assignatam Declinationem maximam, et prædicta ratione inuentam Æquatoris Eleuationem in consilium
adhibuerit, Refractionisque quæ fit infra tricesimum gradum Altitudinis
implicationem præcauerit, experietur vtiqueA Solaris cursus numerationem a nobis adinuentam Apparentijs Cœlestibus exacteA consentire. Quam vero ante omnia necessarium fuerit Solis motum
scrupulose exploratum habere, si ea quæ in Astrorum cognitione desiderantur
certius instauranda sint, Tua Celsitudo nequaquam ignorat: cum sine hoc, nec
Anni exacta quantitas, quæ motuum mensura est, nec inerrantium quidem
Stellarum, multo minus erraticarum qui ex his patet, situs indagari queat.
Siquidem Solis reuolutioA omnium cæterarum reuolutionum Cœlestium norma regularis existit. QuidA vero in Lunari etiam cursu non minori diligentia a nobis cælitus
peruestigato, inque cæterorum Planetarum motu examinando, et rectificandis
Affixarum Stellarum locis, hactenus non mediocri Labore et Diligentia
præstiterimus, Celsitud. T. suo
tempore, vbi omnia in ordinem redacta, et pluribus ObseruationibusA adaucta fuerint, cognoscet acA
dijudicabitA. In primis enim T. Cels. iudicioA hosce meos labores subiectos velim, eo quod sciam Celsitud. Tuam in
hac Scientia eximium Artificem, solide de his rebus iudicare
posseA. Sed video me dum auidius cum Tua Cels. de Astronomicis negotijs
colloquor, Epistolæ leges nimia prolixitate transcendere, et diutius, quam
par est, Celsitudinem Tuam hisce legendis occupatam detinere. Itaque calamum inhibeboA, Tuamque CelsitudinemA DEO tam Cœlestium, quam Terrestrium Creaturarum Authori commendaboA. Is Tuam Cels. et in suæ Ecclesiæ, cuius curam, quod nunc rarissimum est, agisA, et Reipub. Tutelam, ac bonarum Artium, inprimisque Diuinæ illius
Astronomiæ propagationemA, quam diutissime incolumem et florentem conseruet. Valeat T. Cels. et
si quæ mihi ad hæc respondere dignetur, exhibitori harum committat, cui
nomen est PETRVS IACOBI, qui mihi per
aliquot Annos domesticus fuit, et tum in Astronomicis, tum PyronomicisA exercitijs fidelem nauauit operam. Ideôque non per alios mearum rerum
ignaros, sed potius huncA mihi charum et fidelem, qui plura etiamA, quam calamo libet compraehendereA, vbi opus fuerit,
referre possetA, negotium perferendi ad T. Cels. has Literas expedireA, certius et conuenientiusA esse duxi. Huic itaque T. Celsitud. fidem in omnibus adhibeat, et quæ
ad me referenda fuerint tuto concredat. Iterum Tua Celsitudo quam
felicissime et diutissime valeat.Datæ Vraniburgi in Insula
Porthmi Danici Huenna, Calendis Martij, Anno
1586.T. C. addictiss.TYCHO

text.english:
**To the Most Illustrious Prince and Lord, Lord Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda; the most clement Prince and Lord. [He sends] greeting.**

When recently I was at the court of our Most Serene King, Most Illustrious Prince, the noble youth Gerhard Rantzau — governor of the castle of Kronborg, which the same renowned King has now for the first time caused to be magnificently built up on the nearby shore of Zealand — delivered to me certain letters sent me by his most noble and most learned father, a man most devoted to astronomical matters, Master Heinrich Rantzau, Royal Vicegerent in Holstein. On opening them I found among them a copy of a letter of Your Highness written to Master Heinrich Rantzau himself, which, received most eagerly, I read over again and again with great pleasure. For it wonderfully refreshed me to perceive from it, not obscurely, that Your Highness has not, even at this riper age, amid such various occupations and cares of governing the commonwealth, laid down from the heart the affection and zeal long since begun toward the deeper investigation of that divine Science of the Stars; but rather, with renewed strength and applied diligence, has furnished certain new instruments, more exact than the earlier ones, by which the very places of the stars may be restored far more scrupulously than before. On which account indeed I most heartily congratulate both Your Highness's heroic virtue and your fame, never to die among grateful posterity, and likewise the increase of astronomical knowledge.

Now in the same letter Your Highness makes mention of a certain small and altogether round comet, observed in the preceding year about 8 October by Your Highness's mathematician Christoph Rothmann in the last decan of Pisces [♓] and in southern latitude, which Your Highness yourself detected on 19 October in 21° of Aries [♈] with a latitude still 4 degrees southerly; and Your Highness asks of Master Rantzau that he signify whether that comet was seen in our regions. But by name Your Highness desires to learn from me whether I too, and by what method especially, observed the same comet in the heavens. And although I had several times resolved in my mind to write to Your Highness — both on account of that lofty, never sufficiently praised, divinely-bestowed industry and untiring assiduity with which you inquire so consummately into matters of the aether (on which account you far surpass all princely men both of the earlier age and of our own), and also because Your Highness, nearly eleven years ago now, embraced me most clemently and benevolently when I was present at Kassel, and most willingly and variously conferred with me about astronomical matters, which are our delight — yet, since I feared lest I should bring some annoyance to Your Highness by my untimely letters (especially since, over the interval of so many years and amid such great affairs of governing the commonwealth, the memory of me might easily have slipped from Your Highness's heart), it came about that I have deferred my long-standing purpose of writing up to this very day. But since Your Highness, by the said letter transmitted to Master Rantzau, has not disdained clemently to greet me, and of your own accord, taking occasion from the recently seen comet, has invited me to write to you, I took up courage more boldly, and, congratulating myself greatly that this opportunity of fulfilling a desire of many years was being offered me so very conveniently, I judged it must by no means be deferred any longer, but that I should reverently send some letter to Your Highness — relying on this clement invitation of Your Highness, which will excuse my boldness.

Concerning the comet, then, the observation of which Your Highness diligently desires of me, I make known to Your Highness that it first of all appeared to me on the 18th day of October of the year just past, as I was contemplating the stars in my usual manner; and that from this very day, up to the middle of November — that is, for as long as it could be seen — whenever convenient clear weather was granted, it was most diligently observed with exquisite instruments liable to no error. But that this comet became known to us a whole ten days later than to Your Highness's mathematician — the cause of that was the continual obscurities of clouds, mixed with very frequent and tempestuous damps, which had so overcast our hemisphere almost from the beginning of October that they entirely shut off the sight of the heaven and the stars throughout all that time, up to the aforesaid day on which the comet was seen. Of those things, however, which from this time, when it first began to be seen by us, throughout its whole duration, whenever the longed-for clear weather shone forth, were variously and diligently detected here in the heavens, I send certain of the more principal ones, written on a separate sheet (lest, by inserting them here, the letter should grow too much), for Your Highness to peruse at leisure. But a fuller and more complete declaration, established by more observations and by sure demonstrations resting on these — not only about this lately-seen comet, but also about three others seen in some of the years just past, and likewise about that new and admirable star that arose near the constellation of Cassiopeia — Your Highness will obtain when our Work *On the New Phenomena of the Aethereal World* seen in this age comes into the light. For as soon as everything in it has been brought to its colophon and printed here in my own printing-house (the Deity favouring), I shall transmit it to Your Highness to inspect and judge.

But because, in proving all these things more clearly against the standard of Truth as against a touchstone [a Lydian stone], I have resolved to bring forward also the observations and opinions of others, as many as I have been able to have, and to weigh them both among themselves and against the appearances themselves — without any prejudice and without immodest censure of others, only that Truth itself might thereby shine forth the more manifestly — I wish Your Highness humbly and earnestly entreated not to disdain to communicate with me your observations both of that star near Cassiopeia and of the other subsequent comets, which you have made exact. For I do not doubt that, just as Your Highness, in the said new star, entered the inner sanctuaries of truth more rightly than many others (in that, namely, you assert it to have had no perceptible *parallax*, and therefore to have stood in the supreme aether — while very many of the astronomers who set it among the elementary [sublunary] things erred intolerably), so also in the observations of comets you have attained the appointed goal far more accurately than the rest. But above all I desire to obtain from Your Highness, with what entreaties I can, that you not be loath clemently to share with me also those things which, in the other stars coeval with the World, you have hitherto discovered — especially by those new instruments — both as to distances and as to declinations or meridian altitudes. I in turn shall see to it that like observations both of the same and of other stars, as they have been detected by our instruments in the heavens, are written out and sent back to Your Highness, so that, a comparison being made mutually, the certainty of the instruments and observations may be the better judged. Moreover, you would do me a thing far most acceptable if Your Highness should send me, drawn out, the form and structural plan of your new instruments — especially as regards the *sextant*. For I greatly long to know whether (as I gather from probable conjecture) these new instruments of Your Highness have much resemblance to certain of mine; and that especially as concerns the subdivisions of the degrees by transversal *points*, and a peculiar manner of construction of the *pinnules* by parallel slits, exceedingly suited to nocturnal observations of stars.

For that famous Paul Wittich was here with me five years ago — from whose prescription Your Highness asserts your instruments were renewed — and he explored the construction and use of certain instruments which I partly then had ready, partly resolved to elaborate in future, and the plan of the division and of the pinnules, which in all of these I use in nearly the same way; and he soon betook himself into Germany, alleging certain other matters. And from the sole name of "sextant" one may conjecture that Wittich proposed to Your Highness things not much different from ours. For the instrument of the sextant — of which both the fabric and indeed the name itself had recently been devised by me — I then had ready in use when Wittich was with me. But since experience itself many times admonished me that that fabric of the sextant which I had then devised did not suffice for precisely investigating the intervals of the stars, on account of certain impediments, its use was long ago abolished by us. Wherefore, if that sextant by which Your Highness has the intervals of the stars observed is constructed on the same plan as the one which Wittich saw here, it will scarcely be possible by its means to obtain distances that are fixed and liable to no fallacy. For it is impossible, from a single eye resting at the centre of the instrument, to behold precisely at the same time the differing places of two stars, especially if they are rather remote from one another. For the centre of vision cannot fittingly be united with the centre of the instrument, nor can this difference be excused sufficiently conveniently by any *parallaxes*; nor does the pupil of the eye, in viewing two stars at greater intervals, remain unmoved, whence it becomes necessary that the centre of vision too vary somewhat. Nay rather — and this is of great moment in this subtle business — since each star is not seen on both sides equally and bisected at the pinnule by the parallel slits, it will by no means be certainly established whether the distance taken is greater or less than the just one.

I therefore afterward devised another way of constructing the sextant, and that a bifurcated one, so that by two observers each star might be seen separately, on both sides through two different pinnules. This plan of construction too I disclosed to Wittich while he was present here; and after his departure I had a sextant of this kind prepared, which was indeed exact enough and sufficed for taking the intervals of the stars without any sensible error. But since in its handling it was somewhat more difficult and laborious, and did not despatch the business quickly enough, this sextant too ceased to be in use with me. And if Your Highness's instrument is constructed in its likeness (for I showed Wittich the idea of this here, and it greatly pleased him), I do not doubt that the distances taken by it are correct, although obtained a little more difficultly and slowly (as I said). Therefore, in order to avoid both all error and also the difficulty in despatching this business dexterously, four years ago I found another plan of constructing the sextant, different from the earlier ones and most expeditious, plainly simple and natural, by which, also by two observers, with the pinnules (which have parallel slits) moved on the circumference of the instrument, the distances of the stars are discerned most expeditiously on both sides, about a cylinder resting at the centre, without any suspicion of error. And I have two such, skilfully wrought and destined for this use, each of which equals four cubits in its span.

But that Your Highness may the more easily comprehend the composition of this sextant, I send both a picture of the building erected by me in recent years on this island of Hven, at no slight cost, in honour of Astronomy, and also a drawing in some fashion representing the sextant (of which I speak), together with a delineation of its support [fulcrum], by whose benefit it is conveniently turned about to every position and inclination of the stars. There is added on the other side a picture of the Equatorial Armillae; for it has pleased me thus to call this instrument, long since devised by me, because it measures the right ascensions and declinations of the stars with respect to the equator. And I have had two such armillae made, of so great a size that they exhibit single minutes distinctly. But even in these very ones — which are far more expeditious than the Ptolemaic armillae and less liable to errors (as experience itself has taught us, since we have Ptolemaic armillae too, of solid metal, of nearly the same size, ready to hand) — two years ago I devised a certain new and much more expeditious structure, which, with but one and a half circles and a round axle, despatches the whole business with marvellous ease and certainty. The machine of this instrument I constructed with the utmost diligence, set on a certain hill outside these houses dedicated to Urania, and surrounded, for convenience of use, by subterranean steps ascending successively on all sides; its diameter contains ten feet. To this I attribute very much, for investigating exactly the right ascensions and declinations of the stars in whatever apparent position of them; by whose aid also I have for the most part investigated the appearances of the comet which I send Your Highness.

But that it is not difficult, from given right ascensions and declinations with respect to the equator, to reduce them into longitudes and latitudes, as far as concerns the ecliptic, Your Highness has sufficiently perceived — whether it be done by the methods of spherical triangles, or by some special table derived from these (such as we have, for each degree of right ascension and of declination, scrupulously computed to 32 degrees on each side of the equator, destined for this business), or also mechanically by a great globe, such as I have ready, six feet in diameter, most aptly covered on all sides with brass and most perfectly round in every part. But it would be too long in this place to recount all my astronomical instruments and their use: which, sixteen in number, exactly elaborated in magnitude of structure, variety of form, and aptness of manifold use, I possess in place of a splendid treasure (for they have been prepared with no slight diligence, labour, and cost); of which most are of solid metal, but some, although of sure and durable wooden material — being lighter, and not, by excessive weight on account of the mass of their size, unfittingly burdening themselves — are composed in manifold fashion by a certain peculiar method, so that they are not even of themselves easily subject to change; nevertheless they are skilfully fortified on the outside with brass laminae, partly that they may turn out suited to the fineness of the division, partly that they may stand the more firmly. And they have a magnitude sufficient for scrupulous distinction, so that some equal six and five cubits, some four and three. For the using of which, and also for reducing into numbers, from triangles, those things which can be demonstrated from observations, I maintain and instruct here with me for the most part eight, sometimes even more, students devoting their effort to the Art of Astronomy; nor do we suffer the convenience of any clear weather, whether by day or by night, to pass in vain, in inquiring into the heavenly phenomena of the Sun, the Moon, the rest of the planets that can be seen, and the fixed stars also.

But concerning the fabric and use of each single instrument, because I have resolved to write a special Book which shall embrace the Mechanical part of Astronomy (on which account also I am now having them all delineated, and their figures engraved on plates of copper or boxwood), I therefore forbear a longer recounting of these things. But when I shall have completed this labour (God granting success), or at least when all the figures shall have been cut, I shall transmit to Your Highness whatever it will be, to be perused and weighed. For then Your Highness will, by a single glance, more easily learn everything than from a long and tedious account of these things. But that these very instruments, which I assiduously use in observing the stars, are very exact, and do not admit even a faintly sensible error — that is proved from this alone, that the place of the same star, detected by several and diversely-fabricated instruments by various methods, falls, for those attending diligently, to exactly the same minute.

But that Your Highness may have some specimen of those things which have hitherto been gained from my observations, I have adjoined an Ephemeris of the Sun's course for this year, derived from my own restitution, and directed to the longitude of 30 degrees, to which Your Highness's dominion of Hesse corresponds. I have noted the seconds, as our Tables in the motion of the Sun (founded geometrically on sure observations) exhibit them — not because that fineness is comprehensible by any instrument in the heaven itself, as Your Highness very well knows, but lest, the seconds being neglected, some ambiguity should arise concerning the minutes. I therefore earnestly ask of Your Highness that you be willing to have this restoration of ours in the numeration of the Sun's course tested by your instruments, and your opinion of it clemently signified to me. But in rightly weighing these things one must presuppose the maximum declination of the ecliptic [the obliquity] to be 23 degrees, 31½ minutes — which we have several times detected with several instruments by a certain peculiar method, *not* from the maximum altitude of the Sun at either solstice (for this practice, on account of the refraction of the rays, which occurs when the Sun is low near the winter solstice, falls short of the true by more than four minutes in our horizon). That the solar *parallax* too is everywhere to be added to the observed altitudes, there is no doubt that Your Highness has sufficiently ascertained. The refractions of the solar rays besides — which, when [the Sun is] low, force upon the senses altitudes greater than they really are (and that on account of the diaphanous medium of the Air being a little less transparent than the diaphanous medium of the Aether, as these things are demonstrated in Optics) — are to be avoided, especially if the observed altitudes be less than a third, or at most a half, of the quadrant. For I have, by a certain peculiar industry, found by experience that some perceptible refraction occurs up to nearly this limit. But the closer [the bodies] come to the horizon, the greater refraction they cause, so that the Sun, at its very rising and setting, even in the purest air, appears at least half a degree higher than the truth of the matter allows. So too in the Moon, and the other planets, and the fixed stars, when they are low, their altitudes and declinations and true places are somewhat varied by refraction. Wherefore, at lower altitudes, if the matter is to be handled scrupulously, the observations are not to be trusted too much.

Besides, it makes much difference by what methods the inclination of the equator to the horizon at the place of observation has been detected. For by the meridian altitudes of the Sun — even if they be taken at either solstice, with the parallax also applied — on account of the refraction (of which I have spoken) insinuating itself in the winter-solstitial lowness, this business is by no means despatched with the precision that is fitting. It will therefore be most advisable to seek out studiously the height of the pole from the Pole Star itself, when it is at its maximum and minimum altitude. For since it is of moderate magnitude and sufficiently perspicuous, and describes a small circle about the pole, and on that account does not approach the horizon so much that any refraction alters its true altitude, it is most convenient for despatching this practical operation without any error. If therefore Your Highness should have the maximum or minimum altitude of this Pole Star (I say) adjoined to the rest of your observations, and should make me more certain of it, you will have done a thing much to be wished by me. For thus, applying its distance from the pole (which this year, from our observations, is 2 degrees, 55 minutes, 50 seconds), we shall arrive indubitably at the most exact elevation of the pole and equator of that place in which Your Highness has your observations made, and shall establish a fixed certainty concerning the declinations of the Sun and of the stars, provided the instruments are in good order. Wherefore, if Your Highness shall take into counsel all those things (of which I have already spoken) — namely the parallax of the Sun, the assigned maximum declination, and the elevation of the equator found by the aforesaid method — and shall guard against the complication of the refraction which occurs below the thirtieth degree of altitude, you will assuredly find by experience that the numeration of the Sun's course discovered by us agrees exactly with the celestial appearances.

But how necessary it is, before all else, to have the Sun's motion scrupulously explored, if those things which are sought in the knowledge of the stars are to be restored more surely, Your Highness by no means is ignorant: since without this neither the exact quantity of the year, which is the measure of the motions, nor even the positions of the fixed stars, much less those of the wandering ones (which is evident from these), can be investigated. Inasmuch as the revolution of the Sun stands as the regular norm of all the other celestial revolutions. But what we have hitherto accomplished, with no slight labour and diligence, in the lunar course also (investigated by us in the heavens with no less diligence), and in examining the motion of the rest of the planets, and in rectifying the places of the fixed stars — Your Highness will learn and judge in due time, when everything has been reduced to order and augmented with more observations. For above all I would wish these labours of mine subjected to Your Highness's judgement, because I know Your Highness to be an outstanding artist in this Science, able to judge solidly of these matters.

But I see that, while I converse rather greedily with Your Highness about astronomical affairs, I am overstepping the laws of a letter by excessive prolixity, and detaining Your Highness, occupied in reading these things, longer than is fitting. And so I shall check my pen, and commend Your Highness to God, the Author of celestial as of terrestrial creatures. May He preserve Your Highness, as long as possible, safe and flourishing, both for the protection of his Church — whose care you take, which is now most rare — and of the commonwealth, and for the propagation of the good Arts, and especially of that divine Astronomy. May Your Highness fare well; and if you should deign to answer me anything to these things, entrust it to the bearer of this letter, whose name is Peter Jacobsen [Petrus Jacobi], who was my domestic for some years, and rendered faithful service both in astronomical and in pyronomic [chemical] exercises. And therefore I have judged it surer and more fitting to despatch the business of carrying this letter to Your Highness not through others ignorant of my affairs, but rather through this man, dear and faithful to me, who, where there shall be need, could also relate more than it pleases [me] to comprehend with the pen. To him therefore let Your Highness lend credence in all things, and safely entrust whatever is to be reported back to me. Again may Your Highness fare most happily and most long.

Given at Uraniborg, on the island of Hven in the Danish Sound, on the Kalends of March, in the year 1586. Most devoted to Your Highness, Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** **Wilhelm IV "the Wise," Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), founder of the Kassel observatory and Tycho's chief astronomical peer-patron; his court mathematician **Christoph Rothmann** (here named) handled the technical exchange. This is the **opening letter of Tycho's printed *Epistolae astronomicae* (Liber I, Uraniborg 1596)** and one of the most important documents of his instrument-making programme: it sets out the Hven establishment, the sextant's evolution, the Wittich episode, and Tycho's solar and refraction theory.
- **Occasion.** The exchange was rekindled by a letter Wilhelm IV had written to **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), the great Holstein humanist and Danish *Statholder* (royal vicegerent), a copy of which reached Tycho through Rantzau's son **Gerhard Rantzau** (1558–1627), then governor (*Praefectus*) of the newly rebuilt **Kronborg** castle at Elsinore. Tycho recalls being received by the Landgrave at Kassel "nearly eleven years ago" — i.e. on his 1575 tour.
- **The comet of 1585.** Observed by Rothmann from c. 8 October 1585 in the last decan (last 10°) of **Pisces (♓)**, southern latitude; by the Landgrave himself on 19 October in **21° Aries (♈)**, 4° south latitude. Tycho first saw it 18 October (ten days late, owing to October cloud) and observed it to mid-November. The full treatment is promised in his *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (the "Work *On the New Phenomena of the Aethereal World*"), then in press at Uraniborg, which would also treat the **1572 new star in Cassiopeia** and three further comets.
- **Paul Wittich.** **Paul Wittich** (Wittichius, c. 1546–1586) of Breslau, the mathematician whose visit to Hven (here "five years ago," i.e. 1580) and subsequent journey to Kassel transmitted Tycho's instrument designs to the Landgrave — the point Tycho is delicately reclaiming here ("from whose prescription Your Highness asserts your instruments were renewed"). The whole sextant discussion is Tycho asserting his own priority for the transversal-point divisions, the parallel-slit pinnules, and the *name and fabric* of the sextant. (See Thoren, *The Lord of Uraniborg*, and the Wittich/priority discussion among the works consulted.)
- **The instruments.** The letter is the earliest connected description of the Uraniborg instrumentarium later figured in the *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica* (1598): the three successive **sextant** designs (single-observer → bifurcated two-observer → the final two-observer cylinder sextant, "four cubits"); the **equatorial armillae** (*armillae aequatoriae* — Tycho's own coinage for the instrument measuring right ascension and declination); the simplified armillary of "one and a half circles and a round axle," ten feet in diameter, set on a mound with subterranean steps (the great equatorial armillary in the southern observatory crypt); and the six-foot brass-covered **globe**. The "sixteen instruments … a precious treasure" and "eight or more students" describe the working establishment c. 1586. The promised "special Book … the Mechanical part of Astronomy" is the *Mechanica* itself.
- **Technical glossary.** *Ascensiones Rectas* → right ascensions; *Declinationes* → declinations; *Longitudines et Latitudines (ad Eclipticam)* → (ecliptic) longitudes and latitudes; *Parallaxis* → parallax; *Refractio* → refraction; *Armillae aequatoriae* → equatorial armillae; *Sextans* → sextant; *Pinnacidia* → pinnules (sights); *organa/Instrumenta* → instruments; *restitutio / instauratio* → restitution / restoration; *Apparentiae* → appearances. The **obliquity of the ecliptic** ("maximum declination of the ecliptic") Tycho gives as **23° 31½′**, and the **Pole Star's distance from the pole** as **2° 55′ 50″** for 1586 — both reproduced as written. *Pyronomicis exercitijs* = "pyronomic exercises," i.e. chemical/alchemical furnace-work (Paracelsian *pyronomia*); the bearer **Petrus Jacobi = Peter Jacobsen Flemløse**, Tycho's chief assistant, served in both astronomy and alchemy.
- **Latin idiom.** *ad Veritatis normam tanquam Lydium lapidem* — "to the standard of Truth as to a Lydian stone [touchstone]," the proverbial assayer's touchstone. *calamum inhibebo* — "I shall check my pen" (apology for prolixity). *Sacris Uraniae* register: the building "in honour of Astronomy" is Uraniborg, the "houses dedicated to Urania."
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Calendis Martij, Anno 1586* = **1 March 1586**, Old Style (Lutheran Denmark kept the Julian calendar); rendered with the Roman idiom glossed. Header date agrees with the edition label.
- **Text note.** The scattered superscript "A" markers (*curasA, depraehenditA, animumA, sibiA, prorogârimA*, etc.) are editorial/footnote sigla in the working transcription, not part of the Latin; they are left in the Source block as printed and read through in translation. One word-join in the witness, "*Witichiumnon*" (= *Witichium … non*), is likewise a transcription artefact.

Audited against the transcribed original alone: full sentence-by-sentence collation of the Latin against the published English, checking every proper name, date, number, and technical claim — Gerhard/Heinrich Rantzau and their titles, Kronborg, the recipient's four county titles, Rothmann's comet sighting c. 8 Oct in the last decan of Pisces with southern latitude, Wilhelm's own sighting 19 Oct at 21 deg Aries / 4 deg S, Tycho's first sighting 18 Oct (consistent with the stated 10-day lag behind Rothmann), the Kassel visit ' c. 11 years ago', the Wittich visit '5 years ago', the two later sextant redesigns '4 years ago' and '2 years ago', the 16 instruments, the 6-foot globe, the 10-foot armillary, the obliquity 23 deg 31.5', the pole-star distance 2 deg 55' 50", the refraction figures (>4', >=0.5 deg, below 1/3-1/2 quadrant, below 30 deg), the 8 resident students, and the closing date/place/signature (Uraniborg, Hven, Kalends of March 1586, bearer Petrus Iacobi). No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found; the nova-parallax sentence correctly keeps 'Tua Celsitudo' (Wilhelm) as the subject praised, not flipped onto Tycho. text.original:
HENRICUS BRUCÆUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

NOBILISSIME, charissimeque D. TYCHO, si vivis et vales, gaudeo. Superioribus enim mensibus spargebatur fama mihi acerba, quam avertant Superi, te nostri amantissimum e vivis excessisse. Cum tamen dubius essem, emi tibi Gnomonicen CLAVIJ Bambergensis, et MAGINI Tabulas novas et Ephemeridas ad Calendarij emendationem a GREGORIO XIII Pontifice Maximo institutam, compositas. Æstimat autem Bambergensis Gnomonicen Ioachimicis<sup></sup> 7, Ephemeridas vero, in quibus in motuum supputatione errores a STADIO commissos adiunxit, unâ cum Tabulis æstimat Ioachimicis XI vel XII, ut<sup></sup> tota summa Ioachimicorum sit 18. Emi autem hac conditione, ut si tibi forte non placerent, aut forte eosdem iam esses nactus, Bibliopola ad se recipiat. Quid igitur hac in parte fieri velis, quam primum significes cupio. Ego, quod mare esset clausum, citius procurare non potui. Nam ad Paschatis festum aut libri sunt restituendi aut pecunia numeranda. Iam enim libros ineunte hyeme apud me deposuit. Tu ut valeas et quid agas, fac intelligam, an aliquid sub prælo sit, et quid premas. Tuos Cometas expecto, post tot aliorum labores aliquid præstanti tuo ingenio dignum, quod miretur posteritas. Calendarij enim editioni<sup></sup> cum indicijs mutationum aëris non credo, quod aliquem ex tuis ridendum populo velis cum alijs præbere. Quod enim CATO de Aruspicibus, id ego de hisce prædictionibus cogitare soleo. Mirari se aiebat, si cum sibi mutuo occurrunt, non rideant. Nunc venio ad postremas tuas literas, in quibus (quantum memini) tu decoctiones, infusiones, et nescio quæ alia in Galenicis rides, nec quicquam videris probare, nisi quod summo labore extractum ex metallis aut quintas essentias aut tincturas aut spiritus sapiat. Patere nos obvijs uti paratuque facilibus; feras etiam in amico non moleste, plures ab eo restitui decoctis, infusis, et sola ptisana, quam maxima eorum turba, quise solos sapere arbitrantur, quintis essentijs, tincturis, spiritibus, alijsque occultis, ut ipsi iudicant, naturis, quæ tamen omnes a primis qualitatibus dependent. Decoctione certe facultates rerum coctibilium in liquorem transferri, nullus negaverit. At ex auro et lapidibus pretiosis, corallis nihil decoctione deciditur? Fateor id; nos hæc ijs relinquimus, quibus licet ex unico vitrioli spiritu multas tincturas parare, addito colore alterius rei mixtione. Scis quem notem. Neque hæc a me referuntur, ut si quid a posteris bene ad humani generis salutem sit inventum, id damnem; absit, immo laudem magis et sequar alijsque communicem. Insanientis enim hominis fuerit, ac animi plane maligni, calumniari, quæ bene sunt dicta, et aliorum inventa deprimere. Quid igitur, inquies, in hoc genere Chymico non laboras, et hoc quicquid est cognitioni humorali elementari primarum qualitatum, alijsque verbosis GALENI nugis non adiungis? Sic enim ex sulphure, sale et hydrargyro compositum genus hominum eructare solet. Dicam quod verum est; magistris destituor, mutos non intelligo. Tu itaque, qui iam aliquot annis in hoc genere laboras et sedulo versatus es, si quid habes, quod in gravissimis morbis Apoplexia, Epilepsia, Paralysi contractis Melancholia, divina manu succurrat, communica, et componendi rationem utendique modum et mensuram demonstra. Memini de te audivisse, Epilepticos non paucos a te curatos, verum an id per spiritum vitrioli facias ignoro. Si sic, aperi quæso quomodo pares, quæ admisceas, quomodo exhibeas, quoties et quo tempore. Age noli invidere amico, quæ habes, qui tui semper fuit et erit studiosissimus amantissimusque. Bene vale integerrimeque amantissimeque mi TYCHO, et me, quod facis, mutuo ama. Rostochij XV Martij An. Domini 1586.
text.english:
**Heinrich Brucaeus to Tycho Brahe.**

Most noble and dearest Master Tycho, if you are alive and well, I rejoice. For in the months past a report bitter to me was being spread abroad — which may the Powers above avert — that you, most loving of us, had departed from among the living. Yet, since I was in doubt, I bought for you the *Gnomonice* of Clavius of Bamberg, and Magini's new *Tables* and *Ephemerides*, composed [to accord] with the reform of the calendar instituted by Pope Gregory XIII. Now the man of Bamberg values the *Gnomonice* at 7 *Joachimsthalers*<sup>[A]</sup>; the *Ephemerides*, however — in which he has appended the errors committed by Stadius in the computation of the motions — together with the *Tables* he values at 11 or 12 *Joachimsthalers*, so that<sup>[A]</sup> the whole sum comes to 18 *Joachimsthalers*. But I bought them on this condition: that if perhaps they should not please you, or perhaps you should already have got hold of the same, the bookseller take them back to himself. What, then, you would have done in this matter, I desire that you signify as soon as possible. I, because the sea was closed, could not procure them sooner; for at the feast of Easter either the books are to be returned or the money to be paid out — since he deposited the books with me at the beginning of winter. Make me understand how you are and what you are doing — whether anything is under the press, and what you are printing. I await your *Comets*: after the labours of so many others, something worthy of your outstanding genius, that posterity may marvel at. For as to an edition of a calendar<sup>[A]</sup> with forecasts of changes of the weather, I do not believe that you would wish to set forth any of your [men] to be laughed at by the people along with the others. For what Cato [said] of the soothsayers, that I am wont to think of these predictions: he used to say he wondered that, when they meet one another, they do not laugh. Now I come to your last letter, in which (as far as I recall) you laugh at decoctions, infusions, and I know not what else among the Galenicals, and seem to approve of nothing unless it taste of what is extracted with the utmost labour from metals — either quintessences or tinctures or spirits. Allow us to use the things that come to hand and are easily prepared; and do not take it amiss in a friend, [to hear] that more people are restored by him with decoctions, infusions, and barley-water alone than by the very great crowd of those who reckon that they alone are wise, with quintessences, tinctures, spirits, and other occult natures (as they themselves judge them) — which all nonetheless depend upon the first qualities. That by decoction the powers of decoctible things are transferred into a liquid, no one would deny. But from gold and precious stones, from corals, is nothing brought down by decoction? I grant it; we leave these things to those who are permitted, out of a single spirit of vitriol, to prepare many tinctures, the colour being added by the mixture of some other thing. You know whom I mark. Nor are these things recounted by me so that, if anything has been well discovered by later men for the welfare of the human race, I should condemn it — far from it; rather I would the more praise and follow it and share it with others. For it would be the part of a man out of his senses, and of a downright malicious mind, to slander things that are well said, and to disparage the inventions of others. What then, you will say, do you not labour in this Chymical kind, and not join this — whatever it is — to the humoral, elemental knowledge of the first qualities, and to Galen's other wordy trifles? For thus the breed of men compounded out of sulphur, salt, and quicksilver is wont to belch forth. I shall say what is true: I am bereft of masters; the dumb I do not understand. You, therefore, who now for some years labour in this kind and are diligently versed in it — if you have anything that, in the gravest diseases, in apoplexy, epilepsy, paralysis of contracted [limbs], melancholy, may by a divine hand bring relief, share it, and show the manner of compounding and the mode and measure of using it. I remember having heard of you that not a few epileptics were cured by you; but whether you do it by spirit of vitriol I do not know. If so, open up, I pray, how you prepare it, what you mix in, how you administer it, how often and at what time. Come, do not begrudge a friend the things you have — [a friend] who always has been and will be most devoted and most loving toward you. Fare you very well, most upright and most loving my Tycho, and love me, as you do, in return. At Rostock, 15 March, in the year of the Lord 1586.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (Hendrik van den Broeck, 1530/31–1593), Flemish-born physician and professor of mathematics, then of medicine, at the University of Rostock; one of Tycho's older academic correspondents and an early teacher-figure. The letter answers a lost (or earlier) letter of Tycho's on remedies and engages him as a bibliographical agent.
- **Place.** *Rostochium* → **Rostock**; the Hanseatic port and university town. *quod mare esset clausum* ("the sea was closed") refers to the winter closure of Baltic shipping, delaying delivery — not a political blockade.
- **Books purchased for Tycho.**
 - *Gnomonicen CLAVIJ Bambergensis* = the *Gnomonices libri octo* (Rome, 1581) of **Christophorus Clavius** ("of Bamberg," Clavius's birthplace), the Jesuit mathematician and chief architect of the Gregorian reform. *Gnomonice* (the art of sundials/shadow-instruments) is kept as the work-title, not glossed to "dialling."
 - *MAGINI Tabulas novas et Ephemeridas* = the *Ephemerides* and *Novae coelestium orbium theoricae*/tables of **Giovanni Antonio Magini** of Bologna, here described as *compositas … ad Calendarij emendationem … a GREGORIO XIII … institutam* — computed to agree with the Gregorian calendar reform of 1582.
 - *errores a STADIO commissos* — the computational errors of **Johannes Stadius** (1527–1579), whose own widely-used *Ephemerides* Magini's apparatus corrected.
- **Currency.** *Ioachimici* = **Joachimsthalers** (silver thalers struck at Joachimsthal/Jáchymov); the prices (7 + 11–12 = 18) are given in this coin. Rendered "Joachimsthalers," the Latin retained on first use.
- **Apparatus markers in the source.** The superscript **A** appearing three times in the Dreyer text (*Ioachimicis<sup>A</sup> 7*, *ut<sup>A</sup> tota summa*, *editioni<sup>A</sup> cum indicijs*) is **not part of the letter**: it is Dreyer's witness/variant siglum (A = the Vienna MS, cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66) keyed to footnotes in *Opera Omnia* VII. It is reproduced in the Source block as printed and bracketed Secure in the translation, where it carries no semantic content.
- **Allusion: Cato on the soothsayers.** *Quod enim CATO de Aruspicibus … Mirari se aiebat, si cum sibi mutuo occurrunt, non rideant* — the proverbial *risus haruspicum*: the elder Cato's remark (reported by Cicero, *De divinatione* 2.24.51) that he wondered how one *haruspex* could meet another without laughing. Brucaeus applies it to weather-prognostication; the **soothsayer (haruspex)** rendering is kept literal.
- **Astrology / publishing.** *Calendarij … editioni cum indicijs mutationum aëris* = an edition of a (prognosticating) calendar "with forecasts of changes of the weather" — i.e. an astro-meteorological almanac; Brucaeus presumes Tycho would not lend one of his own people to such a popularly-derided genre. *Cometas* = Tycho's projected work on comets (the *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis*, on the 1577 comet, then in preparation/press); kept as the work-reference *Comets*.
- **Medicine / alchemy (the core of the letter).** A Galenist's defence against Tycho's Paracelsian (chymical) leanings.
 - *decoctiones, infusiones … sola ptisana* → **decoctions, infusions … barley-water alone** (*ptisana*, the classic Galenic barley-tisane). *decoctio* by this chapter's convention → **decoction**.
 - *quintas essentias / tincturas / spiritus* → **quintessences / tinctures / spirits** — the Paracelsian preparations Brucaeus distrusts.
 - *primae qualitates* → **the first qualities** (hot/cold/wet/dry of Galenic-Aristotelian medicine); *cognitio humoralis elementaris* → **humoral, elemental knowledge**.
 - *spiritus vitrioli* → **spirit of vitriol** (the distillate of vitriol, ≈ sulphuric acid / its preparations); kept as the period term, not modernised.
 - *ex sulphure, sale et hydrargyro compositum genus hominum* → "the breed of men compounded out of **sulphur, salt, and quicksilver**" — a barbed reference to the Paracelsian *tria prima* (the three principles), turned against the Paracelsians themselves; *hydrargyrus* = quicksilver/mercury.
 - Diseases: *Apoplexia, Epilepsia, Paralysi contractis [membris], Melancholia* → **apoplexy, epilepsy, paralysis of contracted [limbs], melancholy**. *contractis* is read as agreeing with an understood *membris* ("contracted/cramped limbs"); the elision is flagged, the supplied word bracketed.
 - *remedium*-register: Brucaeus's claim that ordinary remedies *restore* (*restitui*) more patients is preserved as a comparative boast, not sharpened into a universal.
- **"You know whom I mark."** *Scis quem notem* — Brucaeus pointedly declines to name the alchemist he is criticising (one *ex unico vitrioli spiritu multas tincturas parare … addito colore* — counterfeiting many tinctures from a single spirit of vitriol by adding colour); the studied reticence is kept, the target left unnamed as in the source.
- **Epistolary formulae.** Opening *si vivis et vales, gaudeo* — the old "if you are alive and well, I rejoice" formula. Close *Bene vale … mi TYCHO, et me … mutuo ama* → **"Fare you very well … my Tycho, and love me … in return."** *studiosissimus amantissimusque* → in the affective superlative register.
- **Dateline / calendar.** *Rostochij XV Martij An. Domini 1586* = "At **Rostock**, 15 March, in the year of the Lord 1586" (**O.S.**; Denmark and Lutheran Mecklenburg both still on the Julian calendar in 1586). The edition *label* gives the place only ("Rostock"); the as-written date 15 March 1586 is carried into the header. No in-letter date discrepancy.

documents.incipit: QUOD prioribus tuis litteris, Nobilissime et Eruditissime Domine RANZOVI, nunc quam vel …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD HENRICUM RANZOVIUM.

QUOD prioribus tuis litteris, Nobilissime et Eruditissime Domine RANZOVI, nunc quam vel tu expectâras vel ipse proposueram, serius respondeam, effecit Hyemis asperitas, quæ insulam hanc undique glacie circumsæptam, quo minus hinc multo tempore solveretur, præpedivit, dumque interea alijs rebus occupor, facile fit, ut per incuriam mora hæc mihi vel invito obrepuerit, quam ut candide interpreteris etiam atque etiam te rogatum volo. Quantum ad Landgravij petitionem attinet de observationibus Cometæ præterito anno visi, quas a me ipsius Celsitudo desiderat (velut ab exemplari litterarum tibi inscriptarum mihi transmisso cognovi) existimo me ipsius desiderijs pro virili satisfecisse. Dedi enim hoc nomine circa initium huius mensis ad ipsius Celsitudinem litteras et unâ adiunxi compendiosam quandam eius Cometæ ex observationibus nostris descriptionem. Habebam autem primum in animo hæc tibi mittere, ut per commodam opportunitatem tuo iussu D. Landgravio adferrentur. Verum cum interea negotium quoddam in nundinis Francfordensibus expediendum mihi occurreret, quod certum aliquem et proprium nuntium requirebat, non ignarus Cassellas, ubi Principis Landgravij aula est, in ipso itinere versus Francofurtum constitui, uni ex meis domesticis, qui ad nundinas illas meo nomine profecturus erat, ea etiam, quæ D. Landgravio erant perferenda, commisi; verum ut tu etiam conscius reddaris eorum, quæ Principi illi a me communicata sunt, curavi tum epistolam, tum etiam ea, quæ de Cometa illo conscripseram, denuo exarari eorumque singulorum exemplar tibi inspiciendum cognoscendumque mitto. Addidi etiam Diarium quoddam Astrologicum et Metheorologicum huius anni, a quodam meo studiosorum elaboratum et sex alia exemplaria. Motuum ... Solis a nobis restitutum, cuius in litteris ad D. Landgravium datis fit mentio, siquidem is in hoc Diario continetur, non ... iudicium opus esse peculiari carta denotare.

Quantum vero ad posteriores tuas litteras attinet, quas ante triduum accepi, unâ cum D. Decani Coloniensis litteris et quibusdam picturis urbium et aliarum rerum per cupri cælaturam expressis, cuperem equidem ipsius D. Decani votis in mittendis plurium urbium, quas expetit, delineationibus, adiectis etiam rerum illic gestarum annalibus, satisfacere, sed neminem hîc habere possum, qui eas apprime delineare novit. Nec mihi circa rerum Astronomicarum penitiorem inquisitionem gnaviter occupato otium conceditur ad diversa negotia evagandi. Rescribam autem ipsemet Domino Decano, quam primum per otium licuerit, nunc enim præpeditus sum quodam libello Regi nostro conscribendo, quem intra Paschatis festum me absoluturum promisi. Quod si quid interea ad ipsum litterarum dederis, rogo ut moram hanc meam in rescribendo apud ipsum excusare velis; dabo operam, ut prima quaque occasione ipsius expectationi satisfiat. Vale. Datæ Uraniburgi 23. Martij Anno 1586.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO HEINRICH RANTZAU.**

That I reply to your earlier letter, most noble and most learned Master Rantzau, later now than either you had expected or I myself had proposed, the harshness of the winter has brought about, which — hemming this island in on every side with ice — hindered any passing from here for a long time; and while in the meantime I am taken up with other matters, it easily comes about that through inattention this delay crept up on me even against my will. I ask you again and again to interpret it charitably. As far as concerns the Landgrave's request about the observations of the comet seen this past year, which His Highness desires of me (as I learned from a copy, sent to me, of the letter addressed to you), I judge that I have, to the best of my ability, satisfied his wishes. For on this account, about the beginning of this month, I sent a letter to His Highness, and along with it I added a certain compendious description of that comet drawn from our observations. Now I had at first in mind to send these to you, so that, at a convenient opportunity and at your bidding, they might be conveyed to the Lord Landgrave. But since in the meantime a certain piece of business to be dispatched at the Frankfurt fair came up for me, which required some sure and particular messenger, [and] knowing that Kassel, where the court of the Prince Landgrave is, lies right on the route toward Frankfurt, I entrusted to one of my household, who was about to set out to that fair in my name, those things too that were to be delivered to the Lord Landgrave; but, so that you also may be made privy to the things that have been communicated by me to that Prince, I had both the letter and also the things I had written about that comet copied out anew, and I am sending you a copy of each of them to inspect and learn. I have added too a certain astrological and meteorological diary [almanac] of this year, worked up by one of my students, and six other copies. [...] of the motions of the Sun restored by us, of which mention is made in the letter sent to the Lord Landgrave — since it is contained in this diary — [it is] not [...] there be need to note [it] [judgement?] on a separate sheet.

But as far as concerns your later letter, which I received three days ago, together with the letter of the Lord Dean of Cologne and certain pictures of cities and of other things rendered by copper engraving: I should indeed wish to satisfy the wishes of the Lord Dean himself in sending the drawings of the several cities which he seeks, with the annals of the things done there added as well; but I can have no one here who knows how to draw them aptly. Nor, busily occupied as I am about the deeper investigation of astronomical matters, is leisure granted me to range off into diverse affairs. But I shall myself write back to the Lord Dean as soon as leisure permits; for now I am held up by a certain little book to be written for our King, which I have promised to finish within the feast of Easter. But if in the meantime you should send him any letter, I ask that you be willing to excuse this delay of mine in writing back to him; I shall take pains that at the very first occasion his expectation be satisfied. Farewell. Given at Uraniborg, 23 March, the year 1586.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), writing from **Uraniborg** on the island of **Hven**.
- **Recipient.** *Henricus Ranzovius* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), royal governor (*Statthalter*) of the Danish king in the duchies of Schleswig-Holstein, seated at Breitenburg/Wandsbek; humanist, astrologer, and prolific patron and middleman of learned correspondence. He routinely served as an intermediary between Tycho and the Hesse-Kassel court, which this letter exemplifies.
- ***Landgravius / Princeps Landgravius / Celsitudo*** — **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), the astronomer-prince of Kassel; *Celsitudo* = "His Highness". His *aula* (court) is at **Kassel** (*Cassellae*;).
- ***Cometae praeterito anno visi*** — "the comet seen this past year": the **comet of 1585** (observed at Kassel by Rothmann and at Uraniborg by Tycho). Tycho's "compendious description … from our observations" is the report he had just sent to the Landgrave at the start of March 1586.
- ***D. Decanus Coloniensis*** — "the Lord Dean of Cologne," not further specified in the letter; left as given. He had sent, via Rantzau, copper-engraved city views (*picturae urbium … per cupri caelaturam expressae*) and sought reciprocal city-drawings with local annals — a topographical-antiquarian exchange of the kind Rantzau brokered. **Identification left open** (no internal evidence names him).
- ***nundinae Francfordenses*** — the **Frankfurt (book) fair**, the great clearing-house through which Tycho's household agent travelled, conveniently by way of Kassel.
- ***Diarium … Astrologicum et Metheorologicum … a quodam meo studiosorum elaboratum*** — "an astrological and meteorological diary [almanac] of this year, worked up by one of my students": a calendar/almanac produced under Tycho's roof; *studiosus* = a student/assistant of Tycho's. *Metheorologicum* is the source spelling (for *meteorologicum*), retained.
- ***Motuum … Solis a nobis restitutum*** — "the [...] of the motions of the Sun restored by us": Tycho's **restored solar theory** (*motus Solis restitutus*; cf. *restitutio / instauratio astronomiae*, this chapter's convention), to which his own almanac's solar positions were computed. **Textual crux:** the working transcription carries two ellipses ("Motuum... Solis" and "non... iudicium opus esse peculiari carta denotare") that are not resolvable from the local material — no Dreyer *Opera Omnia* vol. VII page image was available to collate against. The clause is left lacunose in the translation, with the gaps marked "[...]"; the closing sense is, with low confidence, "[it is] not [necessary] … that there be need to note [it] on a separate sheet" — i.e. the solar tables need not be set out separately because they are already contained in the diary. The reading of *iudicium* ("judgement," but here perhaps "computation/forecast") within the gap is uncertain. Not smoothed; see Confidence.
- ***libellus Regi nostro conscribendus*** — "a little book to be written for our King" (**Frederik II of Denmark**, this chapter's convention), promised within Easter. A short presentation work, unspecified here.
- **Allusion.** *Hyemis asperitas … glacie circumsaeptam* — the winter ice-bound isolation of Hven, given as the literal cause of the postal delay; not a topos but a recurrent material fact of correspondence from Uraniborg.
- **Calendar.** *Datae Uraniburgi 23. Martij Anno 1586* = "Given at Uraniborg, 23 March 1586." Denmark was on the **Julian calendar (Old Style)**; dated O.S. The edition label gives only the place (*Uraniborg*); the as-written dateline **23 March 1586** governs the header. No in-letter date discrepancy.
- **Formula.** *Vale* = "Farewell".

Collated the full letter word for word against Dreyer, including the genuinely lacunose sentence ('Motuum....
