documents.incipit: RUDOLPHUS etc. Notum facimus tenore præsentium universis, quod cum nobis humiliter …

text.original:
IMPRESSORIUM AD DECENNIUM PRO TYCHONE BRAHE DANO.

RUDOLPHUS etc. Notum facimus tenore præsentium universis, quod cum nobis humiliter exposuerit syncere nobis dilectus Tycho Brahe Danus, dominus de Knudstrup, se pro singulari instaurandae astronomiæ studio nonnulla mathematica concinnasse opera ac pluribus etiam nunc incumbere, quæ pro communi usu bonoque publico typis in lucem ædere decreverit, vereri autem, ne forte æmuli aliqui ipsum sperato laborum ac sumptuum suorum fructu atque emolumento privare conaturi sint, demisse proinde supplicando, ut privilegio Nostro Cæsareo huiusmodi imposturas avertere clementer dignaremur. Nos sane indemnitati hac in parte suæ benigne consultum cupientes, humilibus eiusdem precibus deesse noluimus.

Ideoque omnibus ac singulis calcographis, bibliopolis ac alijs quamcumque librariam negociationem exercentibus, firmiter inhibemus ac vetamus, ne quis opera illa astronomica seu mathematica, quæ dicti Tychonis Brahe studio et elucubratione in lucem prodierint, per decem annorum spacium a prima cuiuslibet æditionis die computandum intra Sacri Romani Imperij, Regnorumque et Dominiorum Nostrorum hereditariorum fines, in toto vel in parte simili aut alia quapiam figura vel charactere imitari, recudere aliove recudenda dare vel alibi impressa adducere, vendere aut distrahere clam vel occulte præter expressam ipsius voluntatem et consensum ausit. Si quis autem secus faciendo privilegium hoc Nostrum Cæsareum transgredi conatus fuerit, eum non solum libris illis omnibus perperam sic excusis et adductis (quos quidem prædictus Brahe tamquam author eorum vel mandatarius ipsius, ubicunque deprehensos propria authoritate vel magistratus loci illius auxilio sibi vendicare poterit) de facto privandum sed pœna insuper x marcharum auri puri, fisco Nostro Imperiali fraudis vindici et sæpedicti Tychonis Brahe usibus ex æquo pendenda irremissibiliter decernimus mulctandum. Dummodo tamen, pro eo ac pollicetur, huiusmodi libri nihil in se scandalosum vel Sacri Romani Imperij constitutionibus de re litteraria æditis aut orthodoxæ religioni catholice adversum sive in textu sive in præfatione aut alias quoque modo contineant, ideoque idem Brahe terna ad minus cuiuslibet operis exemplaria quamprimum proprijs suis sumptibus ad Cancellariam Nostram Imperialem transmittere teneatur, quatenus privilegio hoc Nostro Cæsareo uti voluerit. Quod si neglexerit, eo ipso privatus et exutus plane censeatur. Mandamus ergo universis et singulis Nostris ac Sacri Romani Imperij Regnorumque et ditionum nostrarum hæreditariarum subditis ac fidelibus dilectis cuiuscunque status, gradus, ordinis, conditionis aut dignitatis exstiterint, tam ecclesiasticis quam sæcularibus, ijs præsertim qui in magistratu constituti vel proprio vel superiorum suorum nomine et loco iuris ac iustitiæ administrationem exercent, ne quenquam privilegium ac interdictum hoc Nostrum Cæsareum impune transgredi, spernere, negligere aut violare patiantur, sed contumaces, si quos compererint, prescripta pœna plecti alijsque idoneis ac opportunis rationibus coerceri curent, quatenus et ipsi eandem mulctam incurrere noluerint. Harum testimonio litterarum, manu Nostra subscriptarum ac sigilli Nostri Cæsarei impressione munitarum.

Datum Pragæ, die 28. martij anno etc. 1586.
text.english:
**PRINTING PRIVILEGE FOR TEN YEARS IN FAVOUR OF TYCHO BRAHE THE DANE.**

Rudolf, etc. By the tenor of these presents we make known to all: that whereas Tycho Brahe the Dane, lord of Knudstrup, sincerely beloved of us, has humbly set forth to us that out of his singular zeal for the restoration of astronomy he has composed certain mathematical works, and is even now engaged upon several more, which he has resolved to issue into the light through the press for the common use and the public good — but that he fears lest perhaps certain rivals may seek to deprive him of the hoped-for fruit and profit of his labours and his expenses — humbly petitioning, accordingly, that we would graciously deign by our Imperial privilege to avert impostures of this kind: we, indeed, benignly desiring that provision be made for his protection from loss in this matter, have been unwilling to fail his humble prayers.

And therefore we firmly inhibit and forbid all and each of the printers [calcographers], booksellers, and others carrying on any sort of book-trade whatsoever, that no one dare — for the space of ten years, to be reckoned from the day of the first edition of each [work], within the bounds of the Holy Roman Empire and of our hereditary kingdoms and dominions — to imitate, reprint, or give to be reprinted those astronomical or mathematical works which shall have come into the light through the said Tycho Brahe's study and lucubration, in whole or in part, in a like or in any other form or type, or to bring in [copies] printed elsewhere, or to sell or to dispose of them, secretly or covertly, against his express will and consent. But if anyone, by acting otherwise, shall have attempted to transgress this our Imperial privilege, we irremissibly decree that he is in fact to be deprived not only of all those books thus wrongly printed and brought in (which indeed the aforesaid Brahe, as their author, or his agent, wherever they are caught, shall be able to claim for himself by his own authority or with the help of the magistrate of that place) — but is moreover to be fined a penalty of ten marks of pure gold, to be paid out without remission in equal parts to our Imperial treasury, the avenger of the fraud, and to the uses of the oft-named Tycho Brahe. Provided always, however — in accordance with what he promises — that books of this kind contain nothing scandalous in themselves, nor anything contrary either to the constitutions of the Holy Roman Empire issued concerning literary matters or to the orthodox Catholic religion, whether in the text or in the preface or in any other manner whatsoever; and that therefore the same Brahe be bound, as soon as possible at his own expense, to transmit at least three copies of each work to our Imperial Chancery, in so far as he shall wish to make use of this our Imperial privilege. But if he shall have neglected this, by that very fact let him be deemed plainly deprived and stripped of it. We command, therefore, all and each of our subjects and faithful beloved of the Holy Roman Empire and of our hereditary kingdoms and dominions, of whatever estate, rank, order, condition, or dignity they may be, ecclesiastical as well as secular — and those especially who, set in a magistracy, exercise the administration of law and justice, whether in their own name or in the name and stead of their superiors — that they suffer no one to transgress, spurn, neglect, or violate with impunity this our Imperial privilege and interdict, but that they see to it that the contumacious, if they find any, be punished with the prescribed penalty and constrained by other fitting and opportune means — in so far as they too would not wish to incur the same fine. In testimony of which [we have issued] this letter, subscribed by our hand and fortified with the impress of our Imperial seal.

Given at Prague, the 28th day of March, in the year etc. 1586.

documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer.** **Rudolf II** (1552–1612), Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1576–1612), King of Bohemia and of Hungary, residing at Prague. The edition records the sender as "Rudolf 2." and leaves the recipient field "empty," which is correct: this is not a personal letter but an **Imperial *privilegium impressorium*** — a printing-monopoly grant issued *in favour of* Tycho, the operative parties being the Empire's printers and booksellers, not a named addressee. The header therefore renders the recipient slot as the bracketed function of the instrument.
- **Beneficiary.** *Tycho Brahe Danus, dominus de Knudstrup* = **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), styled by his patrimonial seat **Knudstrup** (Knutstorp, Scania); *syncere nobis dilectus* ("sincerely beloved of us") is the standard chancery courtesy-formula for a favoured suppliant, not evidence of personal acquaintance (Rudolf would not become Tycho's patron until 1599).
- **Document type & rubric.** *IMPRESSORIUM AD DECENNIUM* = "a printing-privilege for a ten-year term" (*impressorium*, the chancery noun for a printing licence/privilege). The grant is registered in the Imperial *Reichsregistratur* (witness A), hence the formulaic *RUDOLPHUS etc.* opening and *anno etc. 1586* closing, where *etc.* abbreviates the full Imperial titulature and regnal-year formula of the register.
- **Term of the privilege.** *per decem annorum spacium a prima cuiuslibet aeditionis die computandum* — ten years, counted **from the first day of publication of each individual work** (not from the date of the grant); a per-title term, characteristic of these privileges.
- ***instaurandae astronomiae studio*** — "zeal for the restoration of astronomy": *instauratio astronomiae*, Tycho's own programmatic phrase (*astronomia instaurata*), rendered "restoration" by this chapter's convention
- ***calcographis*** — "printers" (chalcographers/typographers); paired with *bibliopolis* (booksellers) and the catch-all *alijs quamcumque librariam negociationem exercentibus* (any others in the book-trade).
- **The prohibited acts.** *imitari, recudere aliove recudenda dare … adducere, vendere aut distrahere* — to imitate, reprint, give out to be reprinted, import (copies printed elsewhere), sell, or dispose of; *in toto vel in parte … simili aut alia quapiam figura vel charactere* = "in whole or in part, in a like or any other form or type [character]." *praeter expressam ipsius voluntatem et consensum* = "against [i.e. without] his express will and consent."
- **Penalty (negation/legal force verified).** The sanction is cumulative, not alternative: *non solum … privandum sed poena insuper … mulctandum* = "not only to be deprived … but moreover to be fined." The confiscated stock the offender forfeits; the fine is *x marcharum auri puri* = **ten marks of pure gold**, *ex aequo pendenda* = "to be paid in equal parts" between the Imperial fisc (*fraudis vindex*, "avenger of the fraud") and Tycho's own use. *irremissibiliter* = "without remission." The author's recovery right — *quos … propria authoritate vel magistratus loci illius auxilio sibi vendicare poterit* — lets Brahe or his agent seize offending copies *by his own authority or with the local magistrate's help*.
- **The conditions on Tycho (proviso clause).** *Dummodo tamen … nihil in se scandalosum … contineant* = "provided, however, that [the books] contain nothing scandalous," nothing against the Empire's press-laws (*Sacri Romani Imperij constitutionibus de re litteraria*) or *orthodoxae religioni catholice* ("the orthodox Catholic religion") — a notable confessional clause binding the Lutheran Tycho's output, *sive in textu sive in praefatione* ("in text or preface"). The deposit requirement: *terna ad minus cuiuslibet operis exemplaria … ad Cancellariam Nostram Imperialem transmittere* = "transmit **at least three copies** of each work to our Imperial Chancery," at Tycho's own expense — a condition precedent: *quatenus privilegio … uti voluerit. Quod si neglexerit, eo ipso privatus … censeatur* = "in so far as he shall wish to use the privilege; but if he neglects [it], by that very fact let him be deemed deprived." (Negation count in this clause confirmed: *nihil … vel … aut … adversum*, one governing negation distributed over the enumerated objects; rendered as a single "nothing … nor … or.")
- **The mandate to officials.** *ne quenquam … impune transgredi … patiantur, sed … plecti … coerceri curent, quatenus et ipsi eandem mulctam incurrere noluerint* — magistrates are not to allow violation and are to see the contumacious punished, *"in so far as they too would not wish to incur the same fine"* (i.e. on pain of incurring the penalty themselves; the conditional *quatenus … noluerint* is a veiled threat to negligent officials — its mood is consistent across the parallel clause at the proviso's end and is rendered, not smoothed).
- **Attestation.** *manu Nostra subscriptarum ac sigilli Nostri Caesarei impressione munitarum* = "subscribed by our hand and fortified with the impress of our Imperial seal" — the register's note of the original's authentication.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datum Pragae, die 28. martij … 1586* = "Given at **Prague**, 28 March 1586." Denmark and the Empire's chancery practice here are not in tension on the figure as transcribed; the edition label ("1586-03-28 Prag") agrees with the dateline. Treated as **Old Style** by this chapter's convention (the date is given without an *n.s.* marker; the equivalent N.S. date would be 7 April 1586, but the source does not flag a style and none is asserted here beyond the as-written figure).

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO XIV pp.32-35 read as page images (letter no. 52, IMPRESSORIUM AD DECENNIUM PRO TYCHONE BRAHE DANO, spanning pp.33-34). Collated the Latin privilege text against the printed page in full: the ten-year term (per decem annorum spacium), the ten-mark-of-pure-gold penalty (x marcharum auri puri), the at-least-three-copies deposit requirement (terna ad minus... exemplaria), and the closing Datum Pragae, die 28. martij anno etc. 1586 all match exactly, essentially word for word. BRAHE, HERRN ZU KNUDSTRUP.AWILHELM VON
GOTTES GNADEN LANDTGRAUE ZU HESSEN/ GRAUE ZU CATZENELNBOGEN/ DIETZ/ ZIEGENHAIN VND NIDDA/ ETC.AVNSERN günstigen Gruß zuuor/ Vester Lieber Besonder/ Wir haben ewer schreiben
de dato den 1 Martij empfangen/
gelesen/ vnd daraus neben andern verstanden/ das der Kön. W. zu Denmarck/ StadthalterA in Holstein
Henrich Rantzow Euch vnser
schreiben/ so wir an jhnen des letzt erschienen Cometens halben gethan/
zugeschickt/ Das jr vns nun darauff ewre Obseruationes
desselbigen Cometen so gutwillig zugeschickt/ dzA thun wir vns gnediglichen bedancken/ vnd wöllenA euch nicht verhalten/ das so bald wir ewere Obseruationes gesehen/ haben wir vnsern Mathematicum gefordert/ vnd seine Obseruationes eiusdem Cometæ mit den ewern conferirt, vnd befunden/ das nach gebüerender æquation
temporis et Longitudinum beyderley Obseruationes

Ewren/ sondern seind nur quadrupedalia, lassen vns auch
bedüncken/ wo sie grösser weren/ sie würden desto vnbreuchlicher/ et propter molem desto vbler zu tractiren sein/
doch möchten wir Ewere Instrumenta/ sonderlich den Globum auch gern sehen vnd examiniren,
auch Euch gönnen/ das jhr in loco
Meridionalis vaporibus minus obnoxio ewere Wohnung hettet/ damit jhr

sie jetzo durch angeben des WITTICHII, et diligentia et industria vnsers Vhrmachers
M. Just Burrjj, qui quasi indagine alter ArchimedesA ist/ seind angerichtet/ Wie aber dem/ so haben wir Ewerm zu vns abgefertigtenA vergünstiget/ dieselben abzuschreiben/ vnnd Euch zuzubringen. Was aber
prædictam nouam Stellam antrifft/ haben wir an demselsten
gar keine Parallaxin, auch gar keinen motum weder in Longitudinem noch Latitudinem, sed tantum in recta Linea in Altitudinem aut
profunditatem mercken können/ aber in dem grossen Cometen, so Anno 77 erschienen/ da haben wir
deßmals keinen aulicum Mathematicum gehabt/ darumb haben wir auchA seine Parallaxin nicht eigentlich obseruiren können/ aber wie jhr aus jetzigen vnsers Mathematici
Obseruation zusehen/ so wil der auch nicht/ das der jetzo
letzt erschienenA
Comet einige Parallaxin gehabt habe/ Ergo
ist das fundamentum Philosophicum nichtig/ das die Cometen in summa Regione Aëris infra circulos Lunæ solten generirt werden/ Also auch finden wir nicht allein aus
vorigen vnsern sondern auch jetzigen vnsers Mathematici gar fleißigen Obseruationibus, das warlich Stellæ fixæ viel in
einem andern stande seind/ dann sie in Tabulis annotirt, Dann
jhrer viel vmst etzliche gradus anders befunden/ tam in Longitudine, quam in Latitudine, accedit quod Latitudo, quæ
tamen consensu omnium Astronomorum debebat esse inuariabilis, in vielen
vnd fast allen sich valde sensibiliter, ja schier vff ein
halben grad vnd mehr verruckt. Ob nun solches geschehen sey vitio
Typographorum, oder ob die Stellæ fixæ in se proprium
aliquem motum haben/ geben wir euch als dem vornemststen dieser zeit
Mathematico, der die sach auch selbst angreifft vnd
verstehet/ vnd nicht ein Mathematicus vnderm Dach ist/ wie
die meisten seind/ zu iudiciren anheim. Was vnsere Instrumenta betrifft/ haben wir sie ewern abgefertigten alleA sehen lassen/ der euch daruon wird bericht thun können/ Dann den Sextanten lassen wir warlich nicht verachten/ Sintemal wir zu
etzlichen mahlen vnserm Mathematico zween Stern dardurch abzusehen befohlen/ Da wir

Quæ omnia videbantur miraculosa nisi Vitellio in suis Opticis harum rationem præbuisset. Wir

per calculum reformiren, dann den Instrumenten/ sie werden so fleißig gemacht als sie wöllenA/ adamussim nicht zu trawen. Welches wir euch vff ewer
schreiben hinwider nicht wolten verhalten/ mit gnedigen gesinnen/ jhr wollet vns
ewere Obseruationes, dergleichen loca vera
nostrarum Obseruationum, wie jhr vnsere gegen den ewrenA
per calculum findet/ hinwider zuschicken/ Damit wir es mit
den vnsern zu collationiren. Cætera ex adiuncta Mathematici Epistola intelliges. Vnd wir seind euch mit gnedigen willen jederzeit wollgeneigt/ADatum in vnser FestungACassel am 14 Aprilis, Anno
86.WILHELM LANDTGRAFF ZU HESSEN.WILHELM LANDTGRAFF ZU HESSEN.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VI, pp. 50–51; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
POSTSCRIPTA. OB wir wol in der Epistola melden, das wir die Obseruationes ewerm abgefertigten abzuschreiben zugestelt, Dieweil sie aber fast mühesamb zu discernieren, So haben wir durch ein andern gedachte Obseruationes beyd Cometarum, vnd auch Solis, so viel wir dero noch beyhanden haben, abschreiben lassen, vnd thun sie euch hiermit vbersenden. Was aber Obseruationem Fixarum betrifft, haben wir loca Longitudinum & Latitudinum, wie sie vnser Globus gibt, hinein verzeichnet. Es soll sie aber vnser Mathematicus, wenn er die vbrigen, so er propter vaporosum Caelum bißhero nicht obseruiren können, auch darzu bekümpt, alle rechnen, glauben doch, es werde nicht ein grosser differentz zwischen beyderley Obseruation sein. Oculum [Tauri], dextrum hum. Orionis, Canem minorem & maiorem, die haben wir nicht allein per distantiam inter se, & Latitudinem Meridianam lassen obseruiren, Sondern durch vnser minuten vnd Secunden Vhrlein: welches gar gewisse stunden geben, vnd a Meridie in Meridiem offtmals nicht ein minuten varijren, jhr tempus der culmination in Meridiano gar [accurate] zu etlich viel mahlen, vnd daraus jhr Longitudinem vel potius Caeli metationem genommen, das vnsers bedünckens wir dero gewiß sein. WILHELM LANDTGRAFF ZU HESSEN.
text.english:
**To the steadfast, Our trusty and well-beloved Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup. — Wilhelm, by the grace of God Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda, etc.**

Our gracious greeting beforehand, Our trusty and well-beloved. We have received your letter, dated the 1st of March, and read it, and understood from it, among other things, that the King's Majesty of Denmark's governor [*Statthalter*] in Holstein, Heinrich Rantzau, forwarded to you our letter — the one we had addressed to him concerning the comet last seen [*des letzt erschienen Cometens*]. That you have now, in response, so willingly sent us your *observations* of that same comet — for that we graciously give you our thanks; and we will not conceal from you that, as soon as we had seen your *observations*, we summoned our *mathematician*, and compared his *observations of the same comet* [*Obseruationes eiusdem Cometae*] with yours, and found that, after the due *equation* of *times and longitudes* [*aequation temporis et Longitudinum*], the two sets of *observations* throughout scarcely differ from one another by more than one minute — which is truly a great thing, and a sign that both our and also your *instruments* are exact and good, and that the *observers*, too, were diligent and had good eyesight. Our *instruments*, namely the *quadrant* and *sextant* that our *mathematician* uses, are not so large as yours, but are only *four feet [in size]* [*quadrupedalia*]; and it seems to us, too, that were they larger, they would be the less serviceable, and *on account of their bulk* [*propter molem*] the harder to handle. Yet we should be glad to see and *examine* your *instruments* too, especially the *globe*; and we wish you, too, that you had your dwelling *in a place less exposed to the vapours of the south* [*in loco Meridionalis vaporibus minus obnoxio*], so that you might *observe* these things the better. Now as for our sending you our *observations of the new star toward Cassiopeia* [*Obseruationes nouae Stellae ad Cassipeiam*], and likewise of the other comets and of *the Sun* [*Solis*] — the case is that at the time, when those *observations* were made, our *instruments* had not yet been so carefully calibrated as they are now set in order [*angerichtet*] through the indications of *Wittich* [*WITTICHII*] and the *diligence and industry* of our clockmaker Master Just Bürgi, who is, as it were, *another Archimedes in his ingenuity* [*qui quasi indagine alter Archimedes ist*]. Be that as it may, we have granted your messenger sent to us [leave] to copy those out and to bring them to you. But as concerns *the aforesaid new star* [*praedictam nouam Stellam*], we have been able to detect in it *no parallax at all* [*gar keine Parallaxin*], and also *no motion at all, neither in longitude nor in latitude, but only along a straight line, in altitude or in depth* [*gar keinen motum weder in Longitudinem noch Latitudinem, sed tantum in recta Linea in Altitudinem aut profunditatem*]; whereas in the great comet that appeared in the year [15]77, we had at that time no *court mathematician* [*aulicum Mathematicum*], and therefore we could not properly *observe* its *parallax*. But as you may see from our present *mathematician's observation*, he too will not have it that the comet last now appeared had any *parallax* whatever. *Therefore* [*Ergo*] the *philosophical foundation* [*fundamentum Philosophicum*] is void — the one that the comets ought to be *generated in the highest region of the air, below the circles of the Moon* [*in summa Regione Aëris infra circulos Lunae*]. Likewise, too, we find, not only from our former but also from our present *mathematician's* most diligent *observations*, that in truth *the fixed stars* [*Stellae fixae*] stand much in another position than they are noted in the *Tables* [*Tabulis*]; for many of them we have found to be by several *degrees* otherwise, *both in longitude and in latitude* [*tam in Longitudine, quam in Latitudine*]; *added to which the latitude — which nevertheless, by the consensus of all astronomers, ought to be invariable* [*accedit quod Latitudo, quae tamen consensu omnium Astronomorum debebat esse inuariabilis*] — has shifted in many, indeed in almost all of them *very sensibly* [*valde sensibiliter*], nay by nearly half a degree and more. Now whether this has come about *through a fault of the printers* [*vitio Typographorum*], or whether *the fixed stars* have *some proper motion of their own* [*in se proprium aliquem motum*], we leave to you to *judge* — as the foremost *mathematician* of this age, who himself also takes the matter in hand and understands it, and is not a *mathematician under the roof* [a closet astronomer], as most are. As concerns our *instruments*, we let your messenger see them all, who will be able to report to you about them; for the *sextant* we truly do not let be despised, inasmuch as several times we ordered our *mathematician* to sight two stars through it — whereupon, after we ourselves had taken the *distance of the two* [*distantiam vtriusque*], shifted the *instrument*, and let him sight anew, he sighted them so sharply that *within the first, second, and third observation* [*intra primam, secundam et tertiam Obseruationem*] not a quarter of one minute of difference was to be felt. Therefore, when there is an error, one must, in our opinion, not seek it so subtly *in the centre of vision* [*in centro visus*], but much rather *in the craftsman* [*beym artifice*]. Further, we have very gladly heard your *judgement concerning the inquiry into the true altitude of the pole or of the equator* [*iudicium de inquirenda vera Altitudine Poli vel Aequatoris*]; for we too have found that if one will seek these things *from the greatest altitude of the Sun in either tropic* [*ex Altitudine Solis maxima in vtroque tropico*], it does not at all agree with the *observation* of the *circumpolar stars*. On that account we have, through our *mathematician*, had several stars *that do not set* [*quae non occidunt*] *observed in the meridian on this side of and beyond the pole* [*in Meridiano cis et vltra Polum*], as you may see herewith; from which we have taken our *polar elevation of this place, and the things that pertain thereto* [*Eleuationem Polarem huius loci et quae his accidunt*]. Likewise, too, for some years past we have found *a very sensible refraction* [*Refractionem valde sensibilem*], both *in the Sun and in the stars near the horizon* [*in Sole et Stellis circa Horizontem*]; and once, too, we found *setting Venus* [*Venerem occidentem*] (which we *observed* most diligently) to remain *stationary* [*stationariam*] for very nearly a quarter of an hour, *so much so that at that time nothing was moved by the sweep of the primum mobile, and it still appeared elevated by two degrees and more above the horizon, when in reality it was just as far below the horizon, and then it vanished as if in an instant* [*adeo vt eo tempore nihil raptu primi mobilis moueretur, et adhuc appareret Eleuata duobus et amplius gradibus supra Horizontem, cum totidem reuera esset sub Horizonte, deinde autem quasi ad momentum euanuit*]. *All of which would have seemed miraculous, had not Witelo, in his Optics, supplied the explanation of them* [*Quae omnia videbantur miraculosa nisi Vitellio in suis Opticis harum rationem praebuisset*]. We also send you herewith — yet *in good confidence*, in which you are also to keep it and *not yet* for the present *divulge* it [*noch zur zeit nicht spargiren*], but only *compare* it with your own *observations* [*nur mit Ewren Obseruationibus conferiren wöllet*] — the *observations* of several notable stars, as our *mathematician observed* them both *in the meridian* [*in Meridiano*] and also *by the sextant* [*per Sextantem*]. If you now have a mind to compute, you may readily find from them the *true places, both of longitude and of latitude* [*loca vera tam Longitudinis, quam Latitudinis*]; in our *globe* they match well. But our *mathematician* is yet to *reform all these by calculation* [*per calculum reformiren*], for the *instruments* — be they made as carefully as they will — are not to be trusted *to a hair's exactness* [*adamussim*]. All of which we would not, in turn, withhold from you in reply to your letter; with the gracious intention that you should, in turn, send us your *observations*, and likewise the *true places of our observations* [*loca vera nostrarum Obseruationum*], as you find ours against yours *by calculation* [*per calculum*], so that we may *collate* it with our own. *The rest you will gather from the enclosed letter of [our] mathematician* [*Caetera ex adiuncta Mathematici Epistola intelliges*]. And we are at all times well disposed toward you with gracious goodwill.

Given in our fortress [of] Kassel, the 14th of April, in the year [15]86.

Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse.
Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse.


*[Postscript:]* Postscript. Although We say in the letter that We had handed Our messenger sent to us the observations to copy, yet since they were rather laborious to discern, We have therefore had the said observations — both of the comets and of the Sun, so many of them as We still have to hand — copied out by another, and We herewith send them over to you. But as concerns the observation of the fixed stars, We have noted into it the places of longitude and latitude, as Our globe gives them. But Our mathematician is yet to compute them all, when he obtains besides the rest, which he has hitherto been unable to observe on account of the vaporous sky; We believe, however, that there will be no great difference between the two sets of observation. The eye [of the Bull, i.e. Aldebaran], the right shoulder of Orion [Betelgeuse], the Lesser and Greater Dog [Procyon and Sirius] — these We have had observed not only by their distance from one another and their meridian latitude, but also by Our minute- and second-clocks, which give quite exact hours and from meridian to meridian often do not vary by even one minute; their time of culmination in the meridian We have observed quite [accurately] several times over, and from it taken their longitude, or rather their mensuration of the heaven, so that in Our opinion We are sure of them. Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), "the Wise," the founder of the Kassel court observatory and Tycho's chief astronomical correspondent among the German princes. The full titulature (Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, Nidda) is the standard Hessian chancery style; preserved by this chapter's convention
- **Recipient address.** *Dem Vesten … Vester Lieber Besonder* — the princely chancery address-formula; *vest* ("steadfast, firm") is the honorific for an untitled nobleman, and *Vester Lieber Besonder* is rendered "Our trusty and well-beloved" by this chapter's convention *Herrn zu Knudstrup* — Tycho's hereditary seat at **Knudstrup** in Scania.
- **The "A" markers in the source.** The base text (the 1596 *Epistolae astronomicae* print, as transmitted in the working transcription) carries scattered capital **A** glyphs at certain word- and line-junctions (e.g. *KNUDSTRUP.A*, *StadthalterA*, *abgefertigtenA*). These are structural/transcription artefacts (line- or column-break markers), not part of the German text; reproduced verbatim in the Source block by this chapter's convention(2), and silently ignored in the translation.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Henrich Rantzow* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), the royal *Statthalter* (governor) of the Danish king in Holstein, humanist and astrological patron, who acted as the intermediary relaying Wilhelm's letter to Tycho. *Kön. W. zu Denmarck* = "the King's Majesty of Denmark" (Frederik II).
 - *WITTICHII* = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586), the Silesian mathematician who had worked at Uraniborg in 1580 and then at Kassel (1584), carrying Tycho's instrument-design principles to Bürgi; *durch angeben des Wittichii* = "through the indications/instructions of Wittich."
 - *M. Just Burrjj* = **Jost Bürgi** (1552–1632), Wilhelm's clockmaker and instrument-maker (also "Joost/Jobst Bürgi"); *Vhrmacher* = "clockmaker." *qui quasi indagine alter Archimedes* — *indagine* (ablative of *indago*, "investigation, ingenuity") gives "another Archimedes, as it were, in his ingenuity," Wilhelm's famous compliment.
 - *vnser Mathematicus / aulicus Mathematicus* — the **court mathematician**, i.e. **Christoph Rothmann** (named only by office here, not by name); the *adiuncta Mathematici Epistola* ("enclosed letter of the mathematician") is Rothmann's accompanying letter.
 - *Vitellio* = **Witelo** (fl. 1270s), author of the *Perspectiva* (here called *Optica*), the standard medieval optical authority; Wilhelm invokes him for the theory of atmospheric *refraction* that explains the anomalous setting of Venus.
- **Latin code-switching.** The letter constantly switches into Latin for technical nouns and whole clauses; retained italics on first use by this chapter's convention The longest fully-Latin stretch (the setting-Venus / *primum mobile* / Witelo passage) is translated in full and the Latin flagged inline.
- **Technical terms (editorial glossary).** *Obseruationes* → observations; *Quadrant / Sextant* → quadrant / sextant; *Globus* → globe; *Instrumenta* → instruments; *Parallaxin* (acc. of *parallaxis*) → parallax; *motum … in Longitudinem / Latitudinem* → motion in longitude / latitude; *Stellae fixae* → fixed stars; *Refractionem* → refraction; *Eleuatio Polaris* → polar elevation (altitude of the pole); *aequatio temporis* → equation of time(s); *loca vera* → true places; *primum mobile* → kept (the outermost sphere driving the daily rotation). *adamussim* = "to the line, exactly to a hair's breadth" — rendered "to a hair's exactness."
- ***quadrupedalia*** — "four-foot [instruments]," i.e. of about four feet in dimension; Wilhelm contrasts the modest size of the Kassel quadrant and sextant with Tycho's larger instruments.
- ***Mathematicus vnderm Dach*** — literally "a mathematician under the roof," i.e. a purely theoretical/closet astronomer who does not observe; the bracketed gloss "[a closet astronomer]" is editorial.
- **Symbols / glyphs.** None present (no planet or zodiac glyphs); celestial bodies are named in words (*Solis*, *Venerem*, *Cassipeiam*).
- **Scientific substance (for the apparatus record, not interpolated into the translation).** This is the celebrated letter in which Wilhelm reports two of the Kassel programme's headline findings: (1) the comet of 1585 (and the 1572 *nova ad Cassiopeiam*) showed **no parallax**, refuting the Aristotelian *fundamentum philosophicum* that comets are sublunary atmospheric exhalations; and (2) the **fixed-star latitudes** have shifted by up to half a degree from the received *Tables* — Wilhelm leaves open whether this is *vitio Typographorum* (printers' error) or a real *proper motion*, and refers the question to Tycho. (Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, identifies this as the origin of the fixed-star-latitude question in the printed correspondence.) These points are rendered faithfully from the text; the contextual gloss is not added to the body.
- **Negation check.** The clauses carrying legal/scientific force are preserved one-for-one: *wöllen euch nicht verhalten* ("we will **not** conceal"); *gar keine Parallaxin … gar keinen motum* (**no** parallax … **no** motion at all); *wil der auch nicht, das … Parallaxin gehabt habe* ("he too will **not** have it that [the comet] had any parallax"); *lassen wir warlich nicht verachten* ("we truly do **not** let [the sextant] be despised"); *so subtil nicht suchen* ("**not** seek it so subtly"); *gar nicht … eintreffen* ("does **not** at all agree"); *noch zur zeit nicht spargiren* ("**not** yet … divulge"); *adamussim nicht zu trawen* ("**not** to be trusted to a hair's exactness"); *nicht wolten verhalten* ("we would **not** … withhold"). No negation added or dropped.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datum … Cassel am 14 Aprilis, Anno 86* = "Given at **Kassel**, 14 April [15]86." Wilhelm and the Kassel court used the **Julian calendar (Old Style)**, as did Tycho; so 14 April 1586 is O.S. The incoming letter it answers is dated *den 1 Martij* (1 March), likewise O.S. The edition *label* records only the place ("Kassel"); the header date is taken from the dateline by this chapter's convention(1). The double subscription line (*WILHELM LANDTGRAFF ZU HESSEN* twice) is as transmitted; reproduced.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** German closing postscript, restored from Dreyer VI, pp. 50–51 (dropped by the working transcription); star-names and one adverb disambiguated against Dreyer's facing Latin (VI, p. 53).

text.original:
THADDÆUS HAGECIUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.
S.

SERO admodum redditæ sunt mihi literæ tuæ, amicorum optime, nihilo minus fuerunt gratissimæ. Sors iniqua fecit, ut neque tuæ ad me tempestive afferri, neque meæ ad te perferri potuerint. Tuæ enim 25. Augusti scriptæ mihi demum 18. Martij redditæ sunt. Aiebat ille, qui eas attulit, tempestate aëris in itinere fuisse remoratum. Ego vero longe ante, quam tuas accepissem, in ipsis ferijs Nativitatis D. nactus quandam oportunitatem et spem perveniendi isthuc D. SEGURIUM, eius servo et meo populari dederam meas ad te unâ cum meis illis lucubrationibus, quæ si habuissent cursum felicem, tuo desiderio tempestive aliqva ex parte satisfactum fuisset. Pervenerant autem meæ hinc Francofurtum usque. Et ecce, accidit quidpiam, quod D. SEGURIUS consilium eundi in Daniam mutare coactus fuerit, et meæ literæ cum lucubrationibus meis illinc sunt ad me remissæ, quemadmodum hæc omnia intelliges ex meis literis hisce nunc adiunctis, quas illo tempore scripseram. Vides, mi TYCHO, quomodo nostri sensus in unum conspiraverint, modo fortuna favere voluisset optatis nostris, cui iam iam, ne amplius nos eluderet, occurrere ac proprium nuncium ad te mittere volui. Mitto igitur ad te bonum et fidelem iuvenem, qui stipendio a me conductus aliquando in mea domo servivit arte sartoria, cuius est peritus. Is me deliberante de Tabellario ad te ablegando et quærendo, num aliqui Rostochienses hîc essent, cum nullum invenirem, et tempus laberetur, suam mihi hic iuvenis obtulit operam, iturum se ad te, si modo sufficiens viaticum essem ei daturus. Accepi conditionem, et eius voluntatem sum amplexus libentissime. Dedi viaticum perveniendi isthuc, tu vicissim eidem ut redeat ad me, prospicies et laborem eius compensabis. Affert autem tibi primum Privilegium impressorium, quale petebas, non absque difficultate impetratum, eo quod non soleant eiusmodi Privilegia ulli concedi, nisi prius manuscripto exemplo in Cancellariam deposito. Nonnullos enim impetrasse eiusmodi Privilegia pro certis quibusdam libris, qui nec inchoati quidem fuerunt et prodierunt nunquam. Evici tamen meo studio, ut tibi in genere tale daretur Privilegium, quale alius habet nemo. Tu eo fruere ad commodum Reipublicæ literariæ. Taxam pro eo dedi in Cancellariam 12½ Fl., quemadmodum ex schedula Taxatoris Privilegio adiuncta cognosces. Affert item tibi meum exemplum TRAPEZUNTIJ PIRCKMANNUS enim Coloniæ cum a me librum magno studio impetrasset, spe facta illum suis typis edendi multis diagrammatis deterritus, quod magnos sumtus requirerent, mutavit sententiam, ac tandem librum ad me remisit; qui mihi profecto semper admodum charus fuit. Ac certe voluissem ex animo illum facere communem omnibus studiosis, nec dubitabam omnibus scholis futurum admodum gratum; imo isthoc interprete Studiosi introducti fuissent ad lectionem operum PTOLEMÆI, inque eo potius quam in SACROBUSTI libello ieiuno versati fuissent. Ac si saltem primi duo libri aut tres ederentur, sufficerent scholis. Primus liber, scis, olim fuit a REINHOLDO editus et scholijs lllustratus; is posset TRAPEZUNTIJ commentarijs inseri. Sed tu de editione statues, quod tibi optimum videbitur. Interea utere et fruere meo libro, et, si tibi placuerit, describi cura. Sin displicuerit, remitte per eundem hominem. Mitto etiam tibi libellum de Directionum Significationibus. CARIONIS esse dicitur; quanquam existimabam, te Ratisponæ illum descripsisse. Libellus WERNERI de motu Octavæ Sphæræ non invenitur amplius venalis. Fuit adiunctus alijs quibusdam WERNERI opusculis, quæ iam nusquam apparent. Hisce diebus accepi literas Francofurto a Nobilibus illis Gallis una cum Diario a tuo ELIA in tua Officina edito. Hoc mihi fuit admodum gratum, non tantum quod ab illis esset mihi donatum, sed quod tuum nomen asscriptum conspicerem, ad cuius conspectum statim verberavit animum cogitatio, tuum hunc genuinum esse partum; quem legens ordine videbar teipsum loquentem audire. In quo, si non fallor, dico prudenter factum esse, quod nomen tuum non sis professus, illudque maioribus tuis operibus reserves. Licet, ut ingenue fatear, non est vulgare illud Diarium, neque conferri ullo modo potest vulgatis illis Diarijs, quæ isti Diarifices annuatim edere consueverunt. Nam et Cometæ proximi, de quo mihi plane constabat nihil, accuratam habet descriptionem; et motus ☉ et ☾ ex tua observatione habet constitutos. Sed vulgus hominum nescit discernere inter aurum et orichalcum. Itaque prudenter eos facere existimo, qui in levioribus istis vulgi iudicio aut nomen suum non profitentur aut suis discipulis illum honorem relinquunt.

Designatione tuæ insulæ admodum sum delectatus. Unum eius exemplum reliqui in Cancellaria Cæsari monstrandum. Armillæ et Sextantis tui picturam sum contemplatus; quam vellem ipsam machinam videre, et si paulo essem iunior, accurrerem ad te.

Quod tam liberaliter de omnibus mecum communicas, magnas tibi ago gratias. Meas lucubrationes de Nova Stella et Cometis duobus mitto ad te. Quæ illis sunt adiuncta, videbis in ipso opere. Si iudicaveris precium operæ fore, ut uno volumine cum tuis, quæ habes, edantur, omnia tuo iudicio relinquo. Sin putaveris commode edi non posse, aut mea aliena esse a tuis, mea rursum ad me remitte. Nam nuper ad me scripsit magnus quidam et doctus vir, in editionem impensas se facere velle. Sed ego cum tuis mea prodire mallem, quæ, ut spero, non sunt futura dissona. Alios scriptores de Cometis proxime præteritis, præter illos, quos meæ Dialexi seu meis opusculis adiunxi, non habeo. MÆSTLINI de Cometa anni 77 scriptum te vidisse existimo. B. V. et Dom. fratrem tuum meis verbis saluta officiosissime, ac etiam eius collegam, quem hîc secum habuit. Pragæ 19. Maij iuxta novum, aut 9 iuxta vetus Calendarium, Anno 1586.
text.english:
**Thaddaeus Hagecius to Tycho Brahe. Greeting.**

Your letter was delivered to me very late, best of friends; none the less it was most welcome. Unkind fortune brought it about that neither could yours be conveyed to me in good time, nor mine carried through to you. For yours, written on 25 August, were delivered to me only on 18 March. The man who brought them said he had been held up on the road by foul weather. I, however — long before I had received yours — at the very feast of the Lord's Nativity [Christmas], having got a certain opportunity and a hope that Master Ségur would reach you over there, had given to his servant, a countryman of mine, my letters to you together with those lucubrations of mine; and if these had had a fortunate passage, your wish would have been satisfied in good time, at least in part. My [parcel] had got as far as Frankfurt from here. And lo, something happened whereby Master Ségur was forced to change his plan of going into Denmark, and my letters along with my lucubrations were sent back to me from there — all of which you will understand from this letter of mine, now enclosed, which I had written at that time. You see, my Tycho, how our minds have conspired into one — if only fortune had been willing to favour our wishes; and so now, at once, that she might trick us no longer, I resolved to meet her and to send a messenger of my own to you. I am sending you, then, a good and faithful young man, who, hired by me for wages, served for a time in my house in the tailor's craft, in which he is skilled. While I was deliberating about despatching a courier to you, and was asking whether there were any men of Rostock here — and, finding none, while the time was slipping away — this young man offered me his service, [saying] he would go to you, if only I would give him sufficient travelling-money. I accepted the terms, and embraced his willingness most gladly. I have given him travelling-money to reach you over there; you in turn will see to it that he returns to me, and will recompense his labour. He brings you, first, the printing privilege, such as you were asking for, obtained not without difficulty, in that privileges of this kind are not usually granted to anyone unless a manuscript copy has first been deposited in the Chancery. For some men have obtained privileges of this kind for certain books which were not even begun and never appeared. Yet I prevailed by my efforts that such a privilege be given you in general terms, such as no one else has. Enjoy it for the good of the Republic of Letters. I paid the fee for it into the Chancery, 12½ florins, as you will learn from the assessor's slip attached to the privilege. He brings you likewise my copy of Trapezuntius. For Pirckmann at Cologne, when he had with great eagerness obtained the book from me — a hope being held out that he would publish it in his own type — was frightened off by the many diagrams, because they would require great expense, changed his mind, and at last sent the book back to me; and it has, in truth, always been very dear to me. And assuredly I would from my heart have wished to make it common to all students, nor did I doubt it would be most welcome to all the schools; indeed, with this man as their guide [interpreter], students would have been led on to the reading of the works of Ptolemy, and would have been engaged in that rather than in Sacrobosco's meagre little book. And if at least the first two or three books were published, they would suffice for the schools. The first book, you know, was once published and illustrated with scholia by Reinhold; it could be inserted into Trapezuntius's commentaries. But you will decide about the edition as shall seem best to you. Meanwhile use and enjoy my book, and, if it please you, have it copied. But if it does not please you, send it back by the same man. I am also sending you a little book on the Significations of Directions. It is said to be Carion's — though I had supposed that you had copied it out at Regensburg. Werner's little book on the motion of the eighth sphere is no longer to be found for sale. It was attached to certain other of Werner's small works, which now appear nowhere. In these days I received a letter from Frankfurt from those French noblemen, together with the Diary published by your Elias at your workshop. This was most welcome to me, not only because it had been given to me by them, but because I caught sight of your name appended to it; and at the sight of it the thought at once struck my mind that this was your own genuine offspring; and reading it through in order, I seemed to hear you yourself speaking. In which — if I am not mistaken — I say it was prudently done that you did not declare your name, but reserve it for your greater works. Although, to confess frankly, that Diary is no common one, nor can it in any way be compared with those common Diaries which those diary-mongers are wont to publish year by year. For it has an accurate description of the recent comet, of which I knew plainly nothing; and it has the motions of the ☉ Sun and ☾ Moon established from your observation. But the common run of men knows not how to tell gold from brass. And so I judge that those men act prudently who, in those lighter matters [left] to the judgement of the crowd, either do not declare their own name or leave that honour to their pupils.

I was greatly delighted with the map of your island. I have left one copy of it in the Chancery, to be shown to the Emperor. I have studied the picture of your armillary and sextant; how I wish I might see the machine itself, and were I a little younger, I would hasten to you.

For sharing everything with me so generously, I render you great thanks. I am sending you my lucubrations on the New Star and on the two comets. What is attached to them you will see in the work itself. If you shall judge it worth the trouble that they be published in one volume with your own [writings] which you have, I leave it all to your judgement. But if you shall think they cannot conveniently be published, or that mine are foreign to yours, send mine back to me again. For lately a certain great and learned man wrote to me that he was willing to bear the expenses for the edition. But I would rather that mine came out together with yours, which, I hope, will not prove discordant. Of other writers on the comets just past, besides those whom I have appended to my Dialexis, that is, to my small works, I have none. I suppose you have seen Maestlin's writing on the comet of the year [15]77. Greet B. V. and your lord brother in my words most dutifully, and also his colleague, whom he had here with him. At Prague, 19 May by the new, or 9 [May] by the old Calendar, in the year 1586.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus Hagecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayck, 1525–1600), Prague physician, astronomer, and mathematician; personal physician at the imperial court (Maximilian II, then Rudolf II) and Tycho's most important Bohemian correspondent and conduit to the Imperial Chancery. His 1574 *Dialexis* on the 1572 nova is the work referred to below.
- ***D. SEGURIUS*** — **Master Ségur**: Jacques de Ségur-Pardaillan, diplomat of Henri de Navarre (the future Henri IV), engaged in a Protestant-alliance legation through northern Europe in 1585–86. Hagecius had entrusted an earlier packet to his servant in the hope it would reach Tycho via Ségur's planned journey "into Denmark," which was then abandoned.
- ***Privilegium impressorium*** — a **printing privilege** (imperial copyright), here granted *in genere* ("in general terms," covering Tycho's works as a class rather than a single named book), which Hagecius stresses is exceptional; the Chancery fee was **12½ florins** (*Fl.*). *Taxator* = the fee-assessor; *schedula* = the assessment slip.
- ***TRAPEZUNTIJ … exemplum*** — **George of Trebizond** (Georgius Trapezuntius, 1395–1486) and his Latin commentary/translation of Ptolemy's *Almagest*; Hagecius is lending Tycho his own copy. *PIRCKMANNUS Coloniae* = a printer/publisher **Pirckmann at Cologne** who had considered printing it but balked at the cost of the many diagrams (*diagrammata*). *Interpres* is rendered "guide/interpreter" — the printed Trapezuntius would introduce students to Ptolemy.
- ***SACROBUSTI libello ieiuno*** — the "meagre little book" of **Sacrobosco** (Johannes de Sacrobosco, *De sphaera*), the standard elementary university text Hagecius hopes a printed Ptolemy would displace.
- ***REINHOLDO … editus*** — **Erasmus Reinhold** (1511–1553), Wittenberg astronomer, who had edited and annotated the first book [of the *Almagest*]; Hagecius proposes it could be combined with Trapezuntius's commentaries.
- ***libellum de Directionum Significationibus … CARIONIS*** — a little book on **the significations of [astrological] directions** (*directio* = a predictive astrological technique, glossary), attributed to **Johann Carion** (1499–1537), court astrologer at Brandenburg; Hagecius notes Tycho may instead have transcribed it himself at **Regensburg** (*Ratisbona*).
- ***WERNERI de motu Octavae Sphaerae*** — **Johann Werner** of Nuremberg (1468–1522), *De motu octavae sphaerae* (1522), the tract on the motion of the eighth (fixed-star) sphere — i.e. on precession (Copernicus had criticised it); Hagecius reports it can no longer be bought.
- ***Diario … a tuo ELIA in tua Officina edito*** — the **Diary** (almanac/ephemeris-calendar) issued at Tycho's own Uraniborg workshop (*Officina*) under the name of **Elias Olsen Morsing** (*Elias*), Tycho's assistant; published anonymously of Tycho. The "recent comet" with an accurate description and the ☉/☾ positions "established from your observation" is the **comet of 1585**, treated in Morsing's *Diarium astrologicum et meteorologicum* (Uraniborg, 1586).
- ***Nobiles Galli*** — "those French noblemen," the same French (Navarrese) party connected to the Ségur legation, from whom Hagecius received both the letter and the Diary.
- **Symbols.** ☉ = **Sun**, ☾ = **Moon** (glyphs kept in the Source block, named in the translation by this chapter's convention).
- ***Designatio tuae insulae*** — the **map/plan of your island** (Hven), one copy of which Hagecius left in the Chancery to be shown to the **Emperor** (Rudolf II). *Armillae et Sextantis tui pictura* — the engraved **picture of your armillary and sextant** (glossary: *armillae* = armillary, *sextans* = sextant); *machina* = the instrument itself, rendered "machine."
- ***Meas lucubrationes de Nova Stella et Cometis duobus*** — Hagecius's own studies on the **New Star** (the 1572 nova; his *Dialexis*, named below) and on **two comets**, which he offers for joint publication with Tycho's works.
- ***MAeSTLINI de Cometa anni 77*** — **Michael Maestlin**'s tract on the **comet of 1577** (*Observatio et demonstratio cometae aetherei*, 1578).
- ***B. V. et Dom. fratrem tuum*** — the greeting to "**B. V.**" (initials unexpanded in the text — a person Tycho and Hagecius both know; left as given, not guessed) and to "your lord brother and his colleague whom he had here with him." **Crux flagged:** the referent of *B. V.* is not determinable from the letter; the brother is unnamed. Rendered literally, not resolved.
- **Calendar / dateline.** *"Pragae 19. Maij iuxta novum, aut 9 iuxta vetus Calendarium, Anno 1586"* = "At Prague, 19 May by the new, or 9 [May] by the old Calendar, 1586." Hagecius, in Catholic Imperial Prague, gives **both styles explicitly**: **19 May New Style = 9 May Old Style** (the 10-day Gregorian gap, this chapter's convention). The identifier and the edition's catalogue date use the O.S. **9 May**; the header leads with the as-written date and records both. No silent conversion is made — both are present in the source.
- **In-letter date data.** The two transit dates inside the letter (*"Tuae enim 25. Augusti scriptae mihi demum 18. Martij redditae sunt"* — written 25 Aug., delivered 18 Mar.) are reproduced as written; no style is assigned to them in the source and none is imposed here.
- **MS witness.** Recorded as given in the edition: *A = Vienna, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66*. **Note:** this shelfmark is identical to the witness cited for the 1571 Wolf letter (brahe-t_15711113001), which is suspect — the edition may carry a duplicated/erroneous folio reference. Flagged, not corrected.
