text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE D. D. THADDÆO HAGECIO.
S.

BINAS a te uno eodemque tempore per hunc, quem ad me ablegasti, Tabellarium recepi literas, clariss. D. D. THADDÆE, amice perpetuo colende, quae quam mihi fuerint acceptae, vix dici potest, tum quod a te, tanto viro tamque amico sincero constantique, missae forent, tum etiam quod rerum, quarum desiderio magnopere flagrabam me compotem ubertim reddiderint. Ex prioribus circa Solstitium hybernum praeteriti anni ad me datis intelligo, te tunc temporis Dialexin tuam locupletius auctam et recognitam unâ cum aliorum quorundam de eadem materia scriptis ad me misisse, idque per Serenissimi Regis Navarrae Legati servum, tuum conterraneum, qui ob remoratum Domini sui ad nos adventum et librum et literas tibi remiserat. Cum posterioribus vero praeter Privilegium Caesareanum mihi in Typographicis concessum et librum eundem unâ cum TRAPEZUNTIJ Commentarijs in PTOLEMÆI Almagestum libellumque CARIONIS de Directionum Significationibus, additis quibusdam alijs a te elaboratis opusculis, perlibenter accepi. Pro Privilegio autem Caesareo, quod tanta fide et diligentia impetrasti, summas tibi habeo gratias. Praestitisti sane ea in re officium amici minime fucati; daboque operam, quae in Privilegio continentur, a me sartâ tectâ fide praestentur. Taxam 12½ flor. a te in Cancellaria pro eo expositam Tabellario tibi restituendam tradidi, et viaticum, quo ad te revertatur, adiunxi, proque labore suo ipsum remuneravi. TRAPEZUNTIJ in PTOLEMÆUM commentarios, quos adeo benevole mecum communicas, interea reservabo, donec apud PLANTINUM, celebrem illum Antverpiensem Typographum, periculum fecero, an is velit eos Typis suis exprimere. Si annuerit, illi mittam, fietque id cum tui nominis, prout decet, mentione honorifica, quod Astronomiae Studiosis tam insignem Thesaurum non invideris. Interea aliud exemplar describi curabo, ne, si forte Archetypum aliquo casu interciderit, tantis TRAPEZUNTIJ laboribus penitus privemur. Quam primum vero responsum a PLANTINO accepero, te de his certiorem reddam. Si vero negocium non successerit, commentarios illos tibi citra omne dispendium restitui curabo. Quantum ad tuas lucubrationes attinet, de Nova Stella et duobus Cometis unâ cum materijs similibus hisce annexis, nondum ea omnia plene, quamvis id avide percuperem, mihi perlegere licuit, eo quod Tabellarius hic ad me accesserit ijs ipsis diebus, quibus Comitia Regni nostri in vicina Haffnia celebrarentur, unde factum est, ut circa id tempus vel mihi eo ad consanguineos et amicos nobiles, qui e toto Regno confertim illuc confluxerant, excurrendum fuerit, vel etiam ex illis nonnulli me hîc, finitis ijsdem Comitijs, inviserint. Cumque nuntius nunc reditum ad te urgeat nec ulterius a me detinendus sit, eo quod ob causas antedictas, tum etiam ob Sereniss. Reginae nostrae, me in hac Uranoburgi Insula clementer invisentis, accessum supervenientem praeter opinionem diutius hîc substiterit, ideo ut per otium commodum librum tuum perlegam, mecum pauculo tempore eum retinebo, id quod bona tua venia fieri posse, vel ex proprijs tuis literis mihi persuadeo. Remittam illum vel per proprium quendam servum natione Bohemum, Mechanicum meum Opificem, qui in patriam reditum intra paucas hebdomadas a me, ut suos revisat, impetravit, postmodum denuo huc reversurus. Quod si haec ratio minus commode successerit, in Nundinis Autumnalibus Francofurtum ad Bibliopolam et Typographum illum Gallum, de quo mihi significas, tibi restituendum transferri curabo. Interim vero apud modo dictum PLANTINUM Antverpiensem de tuo etiam hoc libro per literas expiscabor, an eum suis sumtibus edere non gravetur, tibique ipsius voluntatem postea significabo. Haud sane illibenter ipsemet per propriam nostram Typographiam tuum hunc foetum publicum redderem vel seorsim per se vel nostris in simili materia adiungendo, veluti a me expetis, sed obstat, quod meum opus de Novis mundi Aetherei generationibus nostro aevo conspectis in iustam per se excrescit magnitudinem, ita ut non patiatur ipsa libri quantitas, tam prolixas lucubrationes adiungi, nisi in monstrosum et immodicam dilataretur formam. Nam et ipsemet hanc ob causam cogor in quibusdam brevior esse, quam alias vellem. Verendum enim alioquin, ne non saltem liber sua crassitudine modum excedat, sed et papyrus, quam in his ultimis Nundinis Francofurtensibus huic negotio comparavi, nequaquam operi sufficiat. Ad haec ante hyemem otium mihi vix editioni operam dandi suppetit, eo quod aestivo tempore alijs negotijs per amicorum et nobilium conversationem utplurimum distrahar, idque praesertim nunc ob Illustrissimi Ducis Mechelburgensis ULDARICI soceri Regij ad arcem Cronenburgam recens in propinquo Selandiae littore magnifice extructam indies expectatum adventum, qui etiam, quantum ex Regina filia intellexi, et nostras aedes accedere ante suum e Dania discessum non [de]dignabitur. Cumque non paucas hebdomadas apud Sereniss. Regem nostrum unâ cum alijs quibusdam Germaniae Principibus commorabitur, haud dubie ob nobilium et eruditorum virorum, qui eos comitabuntur, crebrum interea, uti fieri solet, ad me confluxum, liberiore otio citra diuturni temporis iacturam vix perfruar, adeo ut ante hybernum tempus impressioni rerum nostrarum (ut dixi) vacare minime liceat. Et quia non parum deinde temporis requiritur ad absolvendam nostri operis editionem, nimis tarde fortassis tuis votis satisfecero, si postea demum tuos labores seorsim hic excudi curavero. Qua in re papyrus etiam impressoria, quae difficillime hisce temporibus ob tumultus in Regnis et locis a nobis occidentalibus obortis, unde in copia alias adferri solet, non minimum obstaculi ingeret. Consultius itaque mihi videtur, si PLANTINUS editionem detrectaverit, librum ad te remittere, ut eius viri, de quo scribis, impensis publicae utilitati communicetur. Nam quantum ego hactenus eum obiter saltem ob otij importunitatem percurrendo cognoscere potui, dignus sane videtur, qui cum nominis tui memoria posteritati consecretur. Et licet a meis vix diversa contineat, vellem tamen, ut parcius de nostris, quo ad Novam Stellam attinet, ageres. Erant enim ea, quae olim de hac re a me conscripta sunt, admodum ieiuna et immatura, quae, Deo volente, absolutiora et castigatiora in hoc alio opere invenies. Id etiam monere volui, quod percurrendo ea, quae ex mea Novae illius Stellae contemplatione summatim excerpsisti, reperiam, te in quodam loco modeste satis insinuare, quod declinationem illius stellae diversimode in differentia 4 scrupulorum intra paucas lineas admiserim. Etsi vero hunc lapsum pro tuo candore, eo quod differentia tantilla pro nullo reputari debeat, excuses, nolui tamen me in numerationem Astronomicam vel in minimis impingere. Quare admirabundus libellum meum protinus revidebam, invenique te per festinationem procul dubio nimiam incuria quadam legisse in posteriori loco 62 gr. 2 m., cum libellus noster habeat 62 g. minus 2 min., id quod indicat, desiderari duo minuta ad completionem 62 grad., idque, uti scis, idem plane est, quod prius dixeram, declinationem eius stellae fuisse 61° 58'; nolebam enim ijsdem verbis eadem repetere. Tuum itaque erit in hoc loco nostri scripti animadversionem, si id publicaveris, quo ad hanc brevem ac incuriam a teipso facile commissam revocare; ubi totum librum diligentius perlegero, si quid mihi occurrerit admonitione dignum, sincere et amice te de singulis commonefaciam. Id saltem generaliter nunc indicabo, praeterquam quod rationes inveniendi parallaxes Cometarum, quas tum ex alijs, tum a teipso inventas in medium proponis, talia data utplurimum requirant, quae inter observandum Cometas rarissime et difficulter offerantur, ut ipsemet multoties expertus sum. Accedit et hoc (quod maioris momenti est), omnes illas parallaxium investigationes, quas liber tuus continet, ne ijs quidem exceptis, quas e REGIOMONTANI tractatulo explicas, Cometam omni motu proprio destitui, et non nisi raptu primi mobilis convolvi, praesupponant, id quod in nullo hactenus Cometarum locum meruit, in sola illa Nova ad Cassiopaeam Stella competebat. Cumque motus proprius Cometarum saepenumero maior sit ea diversitate, quae per parallaxes, si quam habeant, insinuatur, nullatenus, non considerato motu hoc proprio, parallaxium differentiae per ullum eorum problematum, quae adducis, (quantum hactenus perspexi) manifestantur. Haec vero ea de causa neutiquam indico, quod putem, teipsum ista non considerasse, sed ut operam des, quo ea potissimum discentibus proponantur, quae in ipsa ... quam commodissime citra omne obstaculum administrari queant. Porro cum ex literis tuis intelligam, Diarium illud huius Anni a Studioso meo ELIA editum ad tuas manus pervenisse, et inter alia non displicuisse, quae in eo de Cometa proxime viso referuntur, mitto tibi paulo exactiorem et copiosiorem eiusdem Cometae descriptionem, qualem cum Illustriss. Principe Domino GUILIELMO Landtgravio Hassiae nuper communicavi, veluti ipsius Celsit. per literas ad Dn. HENRICUM RANZOVIUM, Vicarium Regium in Holsatia horum studiorum amantiss. a me fieri expetierat. Sed ut eo rectius occasionem omnem huius negotij intelligas, adiunxi exemplar Epistolae eiusdem Illustrissimi Principis Landgravij ad praedictum RANZOVIUM, mihi ab hoc transmissum, tum etiam exemplar mearum ad ipsius Illustriss. Celsitudinem de hoc negotio et alijs Astronomicis rebus, tibi lectu non ingratis futuris, perscriptarum literarum unâ cum ipsius Celsitud. ad me dato responso, adiunctis insuper literis CHRISTOPHORI ROTHMANNI, ipsius Celsit. Mathematici, et scripto eiusdem de eodem Cometa, quod tibi eo nomine exarari curavi. Percipies ex his omnibus proculdubio plurima, quae tuis desiderijs arridebunt. Instrumentorum speciem meorum et quorundam, quae ad observationes exactius, quam hactenus factitatum est, caelitus pervestigandas attinent, ex meis ad principem Landgravium literis non sine voluptate cognosces. Consensum vero inter observationes Cometae Landgravianas et nostras ex literis ipsius Domini Landgravij et Mathematici scripto non citra admirationem intelliges. Peperit autem hanc convenientiam Instrumentorum ad quorundam ex meis similitudinem a Landgravio instituta restauratio, prout WITTICHIUS illi formam, divisionem et pinnacidia hîc apud me explorata non aliter, ac si ipsemet eorum inventor esset, mei nulla facta mentione propalavit, quo nomine etiam aurea catena ab ipso Principe donatus est. Accidit tamen illi, quod plerunque dolose agentibus evenire solet, ut pinnacidiorum quadruplicium undique parallelorum exactam rationem non indicaverit, sive quod ipsi exciderit, sive quod paucioribus rem absolvere praesumserit, unde Landgravij observatores in diuturni temporis et laboris iacturam implicuit, donec ipsa experientia, quae desiderabantur, ipsimet animadvertissent, velut ex Mathematici illius Epistola copiosius intelliges. Agit sane minus sincere mecum WITTICHIUS (quem ego hîc tum ob tuam commendationem, tum ob proprium ipsius ingenium in precio habui, pluraque, quam forte opus fuisset, concredidi) quod mea sine meo consensu sub suo nomine publica faciat, non quod alijs mea inventa invideam, sed quia ipsemet de Mechanica Astronomiae parte peculiari opere tractare et multorum diversorumque organorum structuram posteris communicare decrevi. Quam itaque ab alijs gratiam pro tot arduis laboribus et sumtibus incredibilibus non immerito, vel te iudice, reportare debebam, iste, quantum in ipso est, praeripere sibique, alienis plumis se instar corniculae AeSOPICAe exornando, attribuere conatur. Sed valeant haec cum caeteris, quae a perverso ingratoque mundo enormiter astuteque fieri consueverunt. Commode tamen hoc accidit, ut ea, quae tunc temporis WITTICHIUS apud me vidit alijsque pro suis postea venditavit, nullam obtineant comparationem ad haec, quae postmodum in hoc genere a me elaborata sunt, adeo ut priora nunc ipsemet parvifaciam et pro antiquatis seponam, quemadmodum haec latius cognosces, ubi opus illud nostrum, cuius antea memini, quod Mechanicam Astronomiae partem luculenter tractabit, in publicum prodierit. In quem etiam usum instrumenta mea omnia artificiose delineata aeneis laminis insculpi procuro. Ubi vero non saltem haec, sed et alias nostras pro Astronomia instauranda lucubrationes illumque de Aetherei mundi novis Generationibus librum, quem nunc prae manibus habeo, typis nostris, Deo conatus fortunante, publicavero, te eorum, quem etiam arbitrum praecipuum (utpote harum rerum inter paucos apprime intelligentem) in his eligo, compotem reddere non intermittam. Sed iam demum animadverto, me, dum non sine voluptate diutius tecum colloquor, Epistolij limites transgredi. Quapropter nunc pedem retraho, manumque e tabula tollens te Deo Opt. Max. cum tota familia commendo. Is te quam diutissime conservet incolumem et felicem. Vale nostramque amicitiam, siquidem praesens corpore (velut olim Ratisbonae) non licet, animo saltem (quod facis) absens conserva, eamque per Literas data quacunque opportunitate continua, quod et ipse vicissim praestare nequaquam intermittam. Resalutat te frater meus STENO BRAHE officiosissime. Iterum quam felicissime vale et plura a me, ubi librum tuum remisero, expecta. Datae Uraniburgi Calendis Iulij stylo veteri Anno 1586.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe sends greeting to Master Thaddaeus Hagecius.**

I have received two letters from you at one and the same time, by the courier whom you despatched to me, most renowned Master Thaddaeus, friend ever to be honoured; and how welcome they were to me can scarcely be said — both because they were sent by you, so great a man and so sincere and constant a friend, and also because they have abundantly put me in possession of things for which I was greatly burning with desire. From the earlier letter, sent to me about the winter solstice of last year, I understand that you had then sent me your *Dialexis*, more fully augmented and revised, together with certain writings of others on the same subject, and that [you sent it] by the servant of the Ambassador of the Most Serene King of Navarre, your fellow-countryman, who, on account of his master's delayed arrival here among us, had sent both the book and the letter back to you. But with the later letter I most gladly received, besides the Imperial Privilege granted to me in matters of printing, that same book together with the *Commentaries* of Trapezuntius on Ptolemy's *Almagest*, and Carion's little book *On the Significations of Directions*, with certain other small works wrought by you added. For the Imperial Privilege, which you obtained with such fidelity and diligence, I owe you the greatest thanks. You have truly performed in that matter the office of a friend in no way feigned; and I shall take care that what is contained in the Privilege be discharged by me with faith kept whole and entire. The fee of 12½ florins which you laid out for it in the Chancery I handed over to the courier to be repaid to you, and I added travel-money for his return journey to you, and rewarded him for his labour. The commentaries of Trapezuntius on Ptolemy, which you so kindly share with me, I shall keep meanwhile, until I have made trial with Plantin, that celebrated printer of Antwerp, whether he be willing to set them in his type. If he assents, I shall send them to him, and it shall be done — as is fitting — with honourable mention of your name, in that you did not begrudge so notable a Treasure to the students of Astronomy. Meanwhile I shall have another copy transcribed, lest, if by chance the archetype should be lost by some mishap, we be utterly deprived of Trapezuntius's so great labours. And as soon as I have a reply from Plantin, I shall inform you of these matters. But if the business does not succeed, I shall see that those commentaries are returned to you without any expense to you.

As regards your own lucubrations, on the New Star and the two Comets together with similar matters annexed here, it has not yet been permitted me to read through all of it fully — much though I eagerly longed to do so — because this courier reached me in those very days when the Diet of our Kingdom was being held in neighbouring Copenhagen; whence it came about that around that time I had either to make an excursion thither to my kinsmen and noble friends, who had thronged together there in a crowd from the whole Kingdom, or else some of them, the Diet being ended, visited me here. And since the messenger now presses for his return to you and is not to be detained by me any longer — because, for the aforesaid reasons, and also on account of the imminent visit of our Most Serene Queen, who graciously visits me on this Island of Uraniborg, he has stayed here longer than expected — therefore, that I may read your book through at convenient leisure, I shall keep it with me for a little while, which I persuade myself may be done with your good leave, even from your own letter. I shall send it back either by a certain servant of mine, a Bohemian by nation, my mechanic-craftsman, who has obtained from me leave to return to his homeland within a few weeks, to see his own people, intending afterwards to return here once more. But if this means should succeed less conveniently, I shall see that it is conveyed back to you at the Autumn Fair at Frankfurt, to the bookseller and that French printer of whom you write to me. Meanwhile, however, I shall fish out by letter from the same Plantin of Antwerp, regarding this book of yours too, whether he would not object to publishing it at his own expense, and afterwards make his will known to you. I would by no means unwillingly make this offspring of yours public myself through our own printing-house — either separately on its own, or by adjoining it to my own [works] on a similar subject, as you ask of me — but it stands in the way that my work *On the New Generations in the Aethereal World seen in our age* swells by itself to a just magnitude, so that the very size of the book does not allow such lengthy lucubrations to be adjoined, unless it were dilated into a monstrous and immoderate form. For I myself am compelled for this reason to be briefer on certain points than I should otherwise wish. For otherwise it is to be feared not only that the book may exceed due measure by its thickness, but also that the paper which I procured for this business at the last Frankfurt Fair may by no means suffice for the work. Besides this, before winter I have scarcely leisure to devote to the edition, because in summertime I am for the most part distracted by other business through the company of friends and noblemen, and especially now on account of the daily-expected arrival of the Most Illustrious Duke of Mecklenburg, Ulrich, the King's father-in-law, at the castle of Kronborg, lately built in magnificent fashion on the nearby shore of Zealand — who also, as far as I have understood from the Queen his daughter, will not disdain to come to my house too before his departure from Denmark. And since he will stay not a few weeks with our Most Serene King, together with certain other Princes of Germany, doubtless on account of the frequent concourse to me meanwhile (as is wont to happen) of noble and learned men who will accompany them, I shall scarcely enjoy freer leisure without the loss of long time, so that before wintertime it is by no means permitted me (as I said) to be at leisure for the printing of our matters. And since no little time is then required to complete the edition of our work, I shall perhaps satisfy your wishes too late, if only afterwards I see to your labours being printed here separately. In which matter the printing-paper too — which is most difficult [to obtain] in these times, on account of the tumults that have arisen in the Kingdoms and places to the west of us, whence it is usually brought in abundance — will throw up no small obstacle. It therefore seems to me more advisable, if Plantin should decline the edition, to return the book to you, that it may be communicated to the public benefit at the expense of that man of whom you write. For so far as I have hitherto been able to know it, by running through it only cursorily on account of the importunity of [scant] leisure, it truly seems worthy to be consecrated to posterity together with the memory of your name. And although it contains scarcely anything different from my own [findings], yet I could wish that you would deal more sparingly with my matters, as regards the New Star. For those things which were once written by me on this subject were exceedingly meagre and immature, which — God willing — you will find more complete and more corrected in this other work [of mine]. This too I wished to point out: that, in running through the things which you have summarily excerpted from my contemplation of that New Star, I find that you in a certain place modestly enough hint that I admitted the declination of that star differently, with a discrepancy of 4 minutes, within a few lines. But although you excuse this slip, out of your candour, on the ground that so tiny a difference ought to be reckoned as nothing, yet I was unwilling to stumble in Astronomical reckoning even in the smallest matters. Wherefore, in astonishment, I straightway re-examined my little book, and found that you — through doubtless excessive haste, by a certain carelessness — had read in the latter place 62 degrees 2 minutes, whereas our little book has 62 degrees *minus* 2 minutes, which indicates that two minutes are wanting to the completion of 62 degrees; and this, as you know, is exactly the same as what I had said before, that the declination of that star was 61° 58′; for I did not wish to repeat the same things in the same words. It will therefore be for you, in this place of our writing, to recall [correct] this brief carelessness, easily committed by yourself, if you publish it; and when I have read the whole book more diligently, if anything occurs to me worthy of remark, I shall sincerely and as a friend remind you of each point. This at least I shall now indicate in general: besides the fact that the methods of finding the parallaxes of Comets, which you set forth — both as found by others and by yourself — for the most part require such data as, in observing Comets, are very rarely and with difficulty available, as I myself have many times found by experience. There is added this too (which is of greater moment): that all those investigations of parallax which your book contains — not even excepting those which you explain from Regiomontanus's treatise — presuppose the Comet to be devoid of all proper motion, and to be wheeled around only by the rapture of the *primum mobile*; which has hitherto held good in no Comet, [and] applied to that New Star near Cassiopeia alone. And since the proper motion of Comets is very often greater than that diversity which is suggested by parallaxes (if they have any), in no way — the proper motion not being taken into account — are the differences of parallax made manifest by any of those problems which you adduce (so far as I have hitherto perceived). But I by no means indicate these things for the reason that I think you yourself did not consider them, but that you may take care that those things especially be set before learners which … can be carried out in [it] as conveniently as possible without any obstacle.

Further, since I understand from your letters that the *Diary* of this Year, published by my student Elias, has come into your hands, and that, among other things, the matters which are reported in it concerning the lately-seen Comet have not displeased you, I send you a somewhat more exact and fuller description of the same Comet, such as I lately shared with the Most Illustrious Prince and Lord Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse — as His Highness had requested be done by me, by letter to Master Heinrich Rantzau, Royal Vicegerent in Holstein, a most ardent lover of these studies. But that you may the more rightly understand the whole occasion of this business, I have adjoined a copy of the Letter of the same Most Illustrious Prince the Landgrave to the aforesaid Rantzau, transmitted to me by the latter; then also a copy of my own letter, written out to His Most Illustrious Highness concerning this business and other Astronomical matters that will not be unwelcome for you to read, together with His Highness's reply given to me; with the letters of Christoph Rothmann, His Highness's Mathematician, added besides, and a writing of the same on the same Comet, which I had drawn up for you under that title. From all these you will doubtless gather very much that will smile upon your desires. You will learn, not without pleasure, the appearance of my instruments, and of certain ones which pertain to investigating observations from the heavens more exactly than has hitherto been done, from my letters to the Prince Landgrave. And the agreement between the Landgravian observations of the Comet and our own you will learn, not without admiration, from the letters of the Lord Landgrave himself and the writing of his Mathematician. Now this agreement was brought about by the restoration of Instruments undertaken by the Landgrave after the likeness of certain of mine — inasmuch as Wittich divulged to him the form, the division, and the sights [*pinnacidia*] explored here at my house, no otherwise than as if he himself were their inventor, with no mention made of me; for which reason he was even presented with a golden chain by the Prince himself. Yet it befell him — as is wont to happen to those who act deceitfully — that he did not indicate the exact principle of the fourfold sights parallel on every side, whether because it slipped his memory, or because he presumed to accomplish the matter with fewer [than were needed]; whence he involved the Landgrave's observers in a loss of long time and labour, until they themselves should perceive by experience itself the things that were wanting, as you will learn more fully from that Mathematician's Letter. Wittich indeed acts less than sincerely with me (whom I here held in esteem, both on account of your recommendation and on account of his own talent, and to whom I entrusted more, perhaps, than there was need) in that he makes my [inventions] public under his own name without my consent — not because I begrudge my inventions to others, but because I myself have resolved to treat the Mechanical part of Astronomy in a special work, and to communicate to posterity the construction of many and diverse instruments. The thanks, therefore, which I ought deservedly to have carried off from others for so many arduous labours and incredible expenses — even by your judgement — that man, so far as in him lies, tries to snatch beforehand and to attribute to himself, adorning himself with others' feathers like the little crow of Aesop. But farewell to these things, together with the rest that the perverse and ungrateful world is wont to do outrageously and craftily. Yet this falls out conveniently, that the things which Wittich at that time saw at my house and afterwards peddled to others as his own bear no comparison to these which I have since wrought in this kind, so that I now myself set little store by the former and lay them aside as outdated — as you will learn more amply when that work of ours, which I mentioned before, which will treat the Mechanical part of Astronomy lucidly, comes forth into public. For which use also I am having all my instruments, artfully delineated, engraved on copper plates. But when I shall have published — by our own type, God prospering the endeavour — not only these, but also our other lucubrations for the restoration of Astronomy, and that book *On the new Generations of the Aethereal world* which I now have in hand, I shall not fail to put you in possession of them — you whom I also choose, in these matters, as chief arbiter (being, among the few, one most thoroughly understanding of these things). But now at last I notice that, while I converse with you at greater length, not without pleasure, I am overstepping the bounds of a brief letter. Wherefore I now draw back my foot, and, lifting my hand from the tablet, commend you, with your whole household, to God, Best and Greatest. May He keep you safe and happy as long as possible. Farewell, and preserve our friendship — since [we may] not [enjoy it] present in body (as once at Regensburg), yet at least in mind, absent (as you do) — and continue it by Letters at whatever opportunity is given, which I in turn shall by no means fail to do. My brother Sten Brahe returns your greeting most dutifully. Again, fare you most happily, and expect more from me when I shall have sent your book back. Given at Uraniborg on the Kalends of July, Old Style, the year 1586.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus Hagecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayck, 1525–1600), Bohemian physician, astronomer, and personal physician to Emperor Rudolf II — Tycho's most important Central-European scientific correspondent, who later (1599) helped bring Tycho to the Imperial court. The two had met in person at the Imperial Diet of **Regensburg** in 1575 (alluded to: *velut olim Ratisbonae*).
- ***Dialexis*** — Hagecius's *Dialexis de novae et prius incognitae stellae … apparitione* (Frankfurt, 1574), his treatise on the 1572 New Star; here the revised/augmented version sent to Tycho.
- **Persons named.** *Trapezuntius* = **George of Trebizond** (Georgius Trapezuntius, 1396–1486/72), whose Latin commentary on Ptolemy's *Almagest* Hagecius lent in manuscript; Tycho hoped Plantin would print it. *Carion* = **Johann Carion** (1499–1537), astrologer; *De Directionum Significationibus* his astrological tract on directions. *Plantinus* = **Christophe Plantin** (c. 1520–1589), the great Antwerp printer. *Wittichius* = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586) of Wrocław, who stayed with Tycho on Hven in 1580 and afterward, the letter charges, passed off Tycho's instrument-designs as his own at Kassel. *Guilielmus Landtgravius Hassiae* = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), the observing prince. *Christophorus Rothmannus* = **Christoph Rothmann**, the Landgrave's mathematician. *Henricus Ranzovius* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), royal *Statthalter* (Vicegerent) in Holstein and patron of learning, the intermediary of the Tycho–Kassel correspondence. *Dux Mechelburgensis Uldaricus* = **Ulrich III, Duke of Mecklenburg** (1527–1603), father of Queen Sophie. *Steno Brahe* = **Sten Brahe** (1547–1620), Tycho's brother. *Studiosus meus Elias* = **Elias Olsen Morsing** (d. 1590), Tycho's assistant, who published the *Diarium astrologicum et meteorologicum* for 1586 with the description of the 1585 comet. The *Regina nostra* / *Regina filia* is **Sophie of Mecklenburg**, queen of Denmark.
- **Places / institutions.** *Uraniburgum* → **Uraniborg** (on Hven); *Haffnia* → **Copenhagen**; *Cronenburga* → **Kronborg** castle, then newly rebuilt; *Antverpia* → Antwerp; *Francofurtum* / *Nundinae Autumnales* → the Frankfurt Autumn book-fair; *Ratisbona* → Regensburg.
- **Privilege & fee.** *Privilegium Caesareanum … in Typographicis* = the **Imperial printing privilege** Hagecius secured for Tycho from Rudolf II's chancery; the *Taxa 12½ flor.* is the chancery fee (12½ florins/guilders) Hagecius advanced and Tycho repaid via the courier.
- ***opus de Novis mundi Aetherei generationibus*** — Tycho's planned *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (the comet volume, eventually 1588); here still in preparation, with paper bought at Frankfurt and copperplates of the instruments being engraved.
- **Astronomy / cometary parallax.** *parallaxes Cometarum* → **parallaxes of comets**; *motus proprius* → **proper motion**; *raptu primi mobilis convolvi* → "wheeled around by the rapture of the *primum mobile*" (the daily diurnal carrying-motion of the outermost sphere). Tycho's substantive objection: Hagecius's parallax methods (including those drawn from **Regiomontanus**, *De cometae … problemata*) assume a comet has *no* proper motion and moves only with the *primum mobile* — true only of the fixed New Star of 1572 in Cassiopeia, not of comets, whose proper motion swamps any parallactic shift. The hedges (*quantum hactenus perspexi*, *si quam habeant*) are preserved.
- **The declination crux (62° *minus* 2′).** Tycho corrects Hagecius's reading of his New-Star declination: Hagecius read **"62 gr. 2 m."** (62°02′), but Tycho's *libellus* (the 1573 *De nova stella*) reads **"62 g. minus 2 min."** = 62° − 2′ = **61° 58′**. The "discrepancy of 4 minutes" (*differentia 4 scrupulorum*) Hagecius noted is thus a misreading of *minus*, not a genuine inconsistency. *Scrupulum* = minute of arc; rendered "minute." Numerals reproduced exactly as printed (62 gr. 2 m. / 62 g. minus 2 min. / 61° 58′).
- ***pinnacidia*** → **sights** (the slit-sight devices on Tycho's instruments), per glossary (*pinnacidium, pinnula* → sight, pinnule). *pinnacidiorum quadruplicium undique parallelorum* → "the fourfold sights parallel on every side" — Tycho's improved four-edged parallel-slit sights, the detail Wittich failed to convey to the Kassel observers. The Wittich/golden-chain episode is corroborated at Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, citing TBOO VI, 89.29–34 and VII, 68.21–25.
- ***corniculae Aesopicae*** — "the little crow of Aesop," the jackdaw/crow that decked itself in others' (the peacock's) feathers (Aesop, *Phaedrus* I.3); the proverbial figure for plagiarism. Kept as the fable-allusion.
- ***organorum structuram … Mechanicam Astronomiae partem*** — the projected *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica* (instrument-book, eventually 1598); *Astronomia instauranda* = "the restoration of Astronomy," Tycho's programme (glossary).
- ***arbiter praecipuus*** — "chief arbiter": Tycho names Hagecius the principal judge of his forthcoming work, *utpote harum rerum inter paucos apprime intelligentem* ("one, among the few, most thoroughly understanding of these things").
- **Textual notes.** *non [de]dignabitur* — the printed text reads *non dedignabitur* ("will not disdain"); the *de-* is bracketed following the edition (the litotes "will not disdain" = "will deign," intended sense). At *quae in ipsa... quam commodissime* the edition marks a **lacuna** (the noun governed by *in ipsa* is wanting); rendered "in [it]" with the gap flagged, not smoothed. *Epistolij* (diminutive of *epistola*) = "a brief letter / note." *manum e tabula tollere* — proverbial ("to lift the hand from the tablet," i.e. to know when to stop), here translated literally with the idiom signalled.
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Datae Uraniburgi Calendis Iulij stylo veteri Anno 1586* = "Given at Uraniborg on the **Kalends of July** (= 1 July), **Old Style**, 1586." Tycho explicitly marks *stylo veteri* (Julian/O.S.) — apt, since Hagecius in Imperial service used the New Style. The catalogue label gives only the place (Uraniborg); the as-written dateline date (1 July 1586 O.S.) governs the header, consistent with it. No in-letter date discrepancy. The earlier *Solstitium hybernum praeteriti anni* ("the winter solstice of last year") dates Hagecius's first letter to ~December 1585.
- **Witness.** A single MS witness is given (Vienna, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66); the printed text-of-record is the 1596 *Epistolae* volume (= Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VII).
- **Correction.** Collated against Dreyer, TBOO VII p.107. Corrected the ungrammatical 'tractatio' to Dreyer's printed ablative 'tractatulo' ('quas e REGIOMONTANI tractatulo explicas'); no change to the English, which already rendered the correct sense.

documents.abstract: Reminds Young of his promise to visit Uraniborg and invites him to come the following day, noting that Erik Lange and Falk Gøye also await his arrival.
documents.incipit: EX quo Magnificentia tua, nuper mihi Helsingoræ præsenti, se ante reditum in patriam me …

text.original:
PETRO IUNIO TYCHO BRAHE.

EX quo Magnificentia tua, nuper mihi Helsingoræ præsenti, se ante reditum in patriam me in hac tenella insula certo certius invisuram, promittere non gravabatur, cumque omne promissum (veluti communiter fertur) in debitum abeat, idcirco non saltem obnixe petere, sed confidentius etiam exorare non dubito, ut T. M. me crastina luce (quam ipsa etiam commodam auram allaturam non obscure clara pollicentur astra) in hisce Uraniæ dicatis ædibus invisere dedignari nolit; erit sane T. M. non saltem Serenissimi et potentissimi Regis sui nomine, sed etiam proprio, cum Musis sit addictissima, Uraniæ Musarum sorori non postremæ longe acceptissima, cuius etiam præsentiam tum ERICUS LANGIUS, tum etiam FALCHO GOIE, viri nobiles et T. M. studiosissimi ambo, mecum sic avide præstolantur. Da itaque operam, ut votis nostris exoptatus respondeat eventus. Vale. Datæ Uraniburgi 18 Augusti 1586.

Tuæ Magnificentiæ studiosissimus
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Peter Young.**

Since Your Magnificence, lately when present with me at Helsingør, did not hesitate to promise that, before returning to your homeland, you would visit me more surely than surely upon this tender little island — and since every promise (as the common saying goes) passes into a debt — I do not, therefore, hesitate not merely to entreat you most earnestly, but even more confidently to beg, that Your Magnificence may not disdain to visit me tomorrow by daylight (which the stars too, clear and unobscured, promise will bring fair weather of its own) in this dwelling consecrated to Urania; and Your Magnificence will assuredly be most welcome by far — not only in the name of your own most serene and most mighty King, but in your own right as well, since you are most devoted to the Muses — to Urania, not the least of the Muses' sisters; and your presence too is so eagerly awaited, together with me, by both Erik Lange and Falk Gøye, noblemen and both most devoted to Your Magnificence. Take pains, then, that the longed-for outcome may answer to our wishes. Farewell. Given at Uraniborg, 18 August 1586.

Most devoted to Your Magnificence,
Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), writing from his observatory at Uraniborg on Hven.
- **Recipient.** *Petro Iunio* = **Peter Young** (Petrus Junius, 1544–1628), the Scottish humanist and diplomat, former tutor (with George Buchanan) to **James VI of Scotland**, and the king's almoner and librarian. In the summer of 1586 he was in Denmark on a diplomatic mission; the *Serenissimus et potentissimus Rex suus* ("his own most serene and most mighty King") of the letter is James VI. Tycho's *Magnificentia tua / T. M. (Tua Magnificentia)* honorific — "Your Magnificence" — suits an ambassadorial visitor.
- **Persons named.** *ERICUS LANGIUS* = **Erik Lange** (1553–1613), the Danish nobleman and alchemist, Tycho's friend (later betrothed to Tycho's sister Sophie); *FALCHO GOIE* = **Falk Gøye** (1545–1594), Danish nobleman of Tycho's circle. Both are present at Uraniborg and join in awaiting Young; *viri nobiles … studiosissimi ambo* = "noblemen and both most devoted [to you]."
- **Place.** *Uraniburgi / Uraniae dicatis aedibus* = **Uraniborg** ("dwelling consecrated to Urania,"); *Helsingorae* = **Helsingør** (Elsinore), where the prior meeting occurred. *hac tenella insula* = "this tender little island," i.e. Hven — a self-deprecating diminutive (*tenella*, "delicate, dainty").
- **Allusion / idiom.** *omne promissum … in debitum abeat* — "every promise passes into a debt": a proverbial commonplace (cf. *promissum cadit in debitum*) by which Tycho courteously presses Young to make good his pledge; rendered as a saying, with *veluti communiter fertur* ("as the common saying goes") preserved.
- ***certo certius*** — "more surely than surely," an emphatic figura etymologica; kept as the redundant superlative rather than flattened to "quite certainly."
- ***Uraniae Musarum sorori non postremae*** — "to Urania, not the least of the Muses' sisters": Urania, Muse of astronomy, here personifies Tycho's science; the litotes *non postremae* ("not the least") is preserved as understatement.
- **Astrology / meteorology.** *commodam auram allaturam non obscure clara pollicentur astra* — "the stars, clear and unobscured, promise [the day] will bring fair weather": a light astrometeorological flourish (Tycho kept a meteorological diary at Uraniborg); *aura* here = "weather/breeze," not "air" in the abstract. No technical term from the editorial glossary occurs; the prediction is a courteous forecast, not a formal *iudicium*.
- ***crastina luce*** — "tomorrow by daylight": fixes the invitation to the following day, 19 August 1586 (O.S.); the visit is daytime ("by the light").
- **Salutation / subscription.** Heading *PETRO IUNIO TYCHO BRAHE* = "Tycho Brahe to Peter Young" (dative addressee + nominative sender, standard for the *Opera Omnia* register). *Tuae Magnificentiae studiosissimus* = "Most devoted to Your Magnificence".
- **Dateline.** *Datae Uraniburgi 18 Augusti 1586* = "Given at Uraniborg, 18 August 1586" (Old Style; Denmark used the Julian calendar). The catalogue date (label: Uraniborg) and the as-written dateline agree.

documents.incipit: UNSERN günstigen Gruß zuuor/ Vester Lieber Besonder/ Wir machen vns keinen zweiffel/ jhr …

text.original:
DEM VESTEN VNSERM LIEBEN BESONDERN TYCHONI BRAHE, HERRN ZU KNUDSTRUP.
WILHELM VON GOTTES GNADEN LANDTGRAUE ZU HESSEN/ GRAUE ZU CATZENELNBOGEN/ DIETZ/ ZIEGENHAIN VND NIDDA/ ETC.

UNSERN günstigen Gruß zuuor/ Vester Lieber Besonder/ Wir machen vns keinen zweiffel/ jhr werdet vnser Antwortlich schreiben/ so wir den 14 verschienes Monats Aprilis, aus vnserer Vestung allhier an Euch gethan/ numehr beneben den vberschickten Obseruationibus vor lengst empfangen/ vnd vnsere meinung darab vernohmen haben. Dieweil vns aber biß noch vnserm gnedigen begeren nach/ darauff kein antwort zukommen/ Vnd vns dann diese gelegene Bottschafft zu euch vorgestossen/ So haben wir nicht vmbgehen können/ Euch hiermit voriges vnsers schreibens gnediglich zu erinnern/ Vnd ist demnach an Euch vnser gnediges begeren/ weil Vnsere vnd Ewere Obseruationes, so viel den negst erschienen Cometam, auch Stellam nouam ad Cassiopeiam antrifft/ gar nahe zusammen treffen/ Ihr wollet vns nicht allein Ewer Iudicium vber vnsere Obseruationes Stellarum fixarum hinwider zuschicken/ Sondern auch Ewere Obseruationes, was jhr so woll dabeuor/ als auch darsieder von Stellis fixis obseruit, communiciren, darmit wir sie gegen den vnsern zu conferiren, Sonderlich aber wollet vns Altitudinem vestri Poli/ wie jhr die bey Euch habt/ zuschicken/ Vnd werdet jhr aus beygefügten vnsers Mathematici schreiben/ vnsere meinung weiter vernehmen. Wolten wir Euch also gnediglich nicht verhalten/ vnnd seind Euch mit gnedigen guten Willen wollgeneigt/

Datum in vnser Stadt vnd Vestung Cassell am 26 Augusti, Anno 1586.
WILHELM LANDTGRAFF ZU HESSEN.
text.english:
**To our trusty and well-beloved Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup.**
**Wilhelm, by the grace of God Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda, etc.**

Our gracious greeting beforehand. Trusty and well-beloved: we make no doubt that you have by now long since received our letter in reply, which we sent to you from our fortress here on the 14th of the past month of April, together with the *observations* [*Observationibus*] forwarded [with it], and have learned our opinion thereon. But since, in accordance with our gracious desire, no answer to it has as yet come to us, and since this convenient messenger to you now presents itself, we could not forbear graciously to remind you herewith of our previous letter. And it is accordingly our gracious desire of you that — since our and your *observations*, so far as concerns the lately-appeared *comet* [*Cometam*], and also the *new star toward Cassiopeia* [*Stellam novam ad Cassiopeiam*], agree very closely together — you would not only send us back your *judgment* [*Iudicium*] upon our *observations of the fixed stars* [*Observationes Stellarum fixarum*], but also communicate to us your *observations* [*Observationes*] — whatever you have observed of the *fixed stars* [*Stellis fixis*] both before and since — so that we [may compare them] [*conferiren*] against our own; but above all, that you would send us the *altitude of your pole* [*Altitudinem vestri Poli*] as you have it with you. And you will learn our opinion further from the enclosed letter of our *mathematician* [*Mathematici*]. This we would graciously not withhold from you, and are well disposed toward you with gracious good will.

Given in our city and fortress of Kassel, the 26th of August, in the year 1586.
WILHELM, LANDGRAVE OF HESSE.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Wilhelm* = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), "Wilhelm the Wise," a practising astronomer who maintained an observatory at Kassel staffed by the mathematician Christoph Rothmann and the instrument-maker Jost Bürgi. This is an early item in the Hven–Kassel correspondence that Tycho printed himself as the *Epistolarum astronomicarum liber primus* (Uraniborg, 1596). The princely *Wir/Euch* register and the full titulature are preserved by this chapter's convention
- **Recipient address.** *DEM VESTEN VNSERM LIEBEN BESONDERN … HERRN ZU KNUDSTRUP* — "to our trusty and well-beloved … Lord of Knudstrup." *Vester* (= *fester*) is the chancery honorific for a nobleman ("steadfast, trusty"); *Lieber Besonder* is rendered per the glossary formula "trusty and well-beloved." Knudstrup = the Brahe family seat in Scania.
- **Salutation.** *Unsern günstigen Gruß zuvor* — a variant of the princely address-formula; rendered "Our gracious greeting beforehand" (cf. *Unsern gnedigen Gruß zuvor*). *günstig* ("favourable, gracious") is here treated as equivalent to *gnedig*.
- **The April letter.** Wilhelm refers to his own reply of **14 April 1586**, sent with a set of observations, to which Tycho had not yet responded. The date is reproduced as written ("the 14th of the past month of April"); not converted (O.S.).
- **Latin code-switch (technical nouns).** The German body switches into Latin for the scientific lexicon, a feature kept visible by this chapter's convention: *Observationibus* / *Observationes* → "observations"; *Cometam* → "comet" (the comet of 1585); *Stellam novam ad Cassiopeiam* → "new star toward Cassiopeia" (the supernova of 1572, SN 1572 — *stella nova*, here rendered literally "new star," not modernised); *Iudicium* → "judgment" (an opinion/assessment); *Observationes Stellarum fixarum* / *Stellis fixis* → "observations of the fixed stars" / "fixed stars"; *Altitudinem vestri Poli* → "the altitude of your pole" (the elevation of the celestial pole at Hven = its geographical latitude; *altitudo* → "altitude" by this chapter's convention); *Mathematici* → "mathematician" (Wilhelm's court mathematician, **Christoph Rothmann**,, whose own accompanying letter is the "enclosed letter"). These Latin forms are italicised and the source word given in brackets on first occurrence by this chapter's convention.
- **Verbs of comparison.** *conferiren* (Latinate German infinitive, from *conferre*) → "compare"; rendered in brackets "[may compare them]" because the German clause *darmit wir sie gegen den vnsern zu conferiren* lacks an explicit finite verb of obtaining (literally "so that we, to compare them against ours"). The supplied "[may compare]" is bracketed as an editorial completion of the elliptical purpose-clause; cf. Mosley's reading ("so that we may compare them with ours," *Bearing the Heavens*, p. citing Wilhelm to Tycho, 26 August 1586). *communiciren* → "communicate."
- ***dabevor … darsieder*** — "before … since" (*dabevor* = *zuvor/davor*; *darsieder* = *seither/seitdem*), i.e. observations made both prior to and subsequent to some prior reference point.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datum … am 26 Augusti, Anno 1586* = "Given … the 26th of August, in the year 1586." Hesse-Kassel, Protestant, kept the **Julian calendar** in 1586 (the Protestant German states did not adopt the Gregorian reform until 1700); the dateline is therefore Old Style. The edition *label* "Kassel" is the place, not a date; the as-written dateline 26 August 1586 governs the header, with no discrepancy to flag. *Datum* ("Given") corresponds to the Danish *Actum* formula.

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO VIRO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE DANO, DOMINO ET AMICO OBSERVANDO.
URANIBURGI SEU IN HYENA INSULA.
S.

NOBILISS. D. TYCHO, Domine et amice observande. Post discessum nobilis illius viri vestratis, qui falcones Imperatori nostro a Rege vestro attulerat, measque ad te literas perferre debuerat, binas ad te dedi literas, easque opera mei amici per Dresdam curavi ad te perferendas; eas an acceperis, vehementer scire desidero, non quod magni alicuius momenti essent, sed ut cognosceres non mea culpa, sed iniqua sorte quadam accidere, quod meæ tibi vel tardius reddantur, vel penitus non perveniant ad te, quam fortunam, profecto, valde defleo. An igitur omnes meas huc usque adeoque librum VERNERI acceperis, magnopere rogo me edoceas. Tuum librum primum avide expecto, alij etiam, præsertim nobiliss. D. IACOBUS CURTIUS, Vicecancell. Imperij, eadem cupiditate expetunt. Etsi autem mihi in ista mea senili ætate (nam ad 1. Octob. si ita Deus volet, magnum climacterem complebo) ob studia medica et alias curas, in Astronomicis studijs versari non conceditur, tamen vehementer oblector, quoties facultas datur saltem inspiciendi aliorum lucubrationes. De Commentarijs TRAPEZUNTIJ quid nunc iudices, scire velim, num putes ex re scholarum fore, si initio saltem duo priores libri ederentur, postea reliqui.

De rebus Gallicis vos istic melius. En quam nullum est scelus quantumvis horrendum, quod Monachus aggredi non audeat. Dixerim ego Monachos istos et Papistas Catholicos, non a fide sed verius, ut ita dicam, a Catholicitate omnium scelerum nominandos esse. Archid. MAX. hodie Polonicos limites transcensurus esse dicitur. Expectabimus igitur illum huc intra dies non usque adeo multos; Deus faxit, ut sanus redeat ad nos. B. V. Pragæ die 7. Septembris novo stylo Anno 1589.

T. studiosiss.
THAD.
text.english:
**To the most noble man, Master Tycho Brahe the Dane, his lord and friend to be esteemed. At Uraniborg, or on the island of Hven. Greeting.**

Most noble Master Tycho, my lord and friend to be esteemed. After the departure of that noble man, your countryman, who had brought falcons to our Emperor from your King and was to have carried my letters on to you, I sent you two letters, and arranged through a friend of mine, by way of Dresden, for them to be conveyed to you; whether you have received them I am most eager to know — not because they were of any great moment, but so that you might understand that it is through no fault of mine, but through some unkind fate, that mine [my letters] are delivered to you either too late, or do not reach you at all — a fortune which I do indeed bitterly lament. I therefore greatly beg you to inform me whether you have received all of mine up to now, and so too **Werner's** book. Your first book I await eagerly; others too, and especially the most noble Master **Jacobus Curtius**, Vice-Chancellor of the Empire, seek it out with the same longing. But although in this my old age (for on 1 October, if God so wills, I shall complete my great climacteric) it is not granted me, on account of my medical studies and other cares, to be engaged in astronomical studies, yet I take vehement delight, as often as the chance is given me, in at least examining the lucubrations of others. On the *Commentaries* of **Trapezuntius**, I should like to know what you now judge — whether you think it would be to the schools' advantage if at the outset at least the two former books were published, and afterwards the rest.

Concerning French affairs, you there [know] better. See how there is no crime, however dreadful, that a Monk does not dare to attempt! For my part, I would say that those Monks and Papist Catholics ought to be named, not from the faith, but more truly — so to speak — from the *catholicity* [universality] of all crimes. Archduke **Maximilian** is said to be about to cross the Polish borders today. We shall therefore look for him here within days not so very many; God grant that he return to us safe and sound. Fare you well. At Prague, on the 7th day of September, New Style, in the year 1589.

Most devoted to you,
Thaddaeus [Hagecius].

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thad[daeus]* = **Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayek** (Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku, c. 1525–1600), Bohemian physician, astronomer, and personal physician to Emperors Maximilian II and Rudolf II at Prague; Tycho's chief scientific correspondent in the Empire and the man who in 1600 brokered Tycho's introduction to Kepler. His *Dialexis de nova stella* (1574) had independently argued the 1572 nova was supralunary, aligning him with Tycho.
- **Addressee / place.** *Tychoni Brahe Dano … Uraniburgi seu in Hyena insula* = **Tycho Brahe**, at **Uraniborg** on the island of **Hven** (*Hyena* is a Latinised spelling of Hven/Hveen; kept as written and identified here, by this chapter's convention).
- ***nobilis illius viri vestratis, qui falcones Imperatori nostro a Rege vestro attulerat*** — "that noble countryman of yours who had brought falcons to our Emperor from your King": a Danish envoy bearing a gift of falcons (a recurring Danish-crown diplomatic present) from **Frederik II** (or, if late 1588 onward, the regency for the boy **Christian IV**) to **Rudolf II**. Used here as a now-failed letter-carrier; the detail is kept literal and the identification flagged as inferential.
- ***librum Verneri*** — "Werner's book": the treatise of **Johann Werner** of Nuremberg (1468–1522), almost certainly his *De motu octavae sphaerae* / the 1522 *In hoc opere haec continentur* containing the method of *prosthaphaeresis* and the eighth-sphere motion — a text Tycho is known to have circulated and criticised. Identification of the exact title flagged as probable, not certain.
- ***Iacobus Curtius, Vicecancell. Imperii*** — **Jacob Kurtz von Senftenau** (Jacobus Curtius, d. 1594), Imperial Vice-Chancellor and a mathematically-minded official at the Prague court; a real intermediary between Tycho and the Imperial circle.
- ***magnum climacterem*** — "[my] great climacteric," the **grand climacteric**, the 63rd year (9 × 7), held astrologically the most perilous of life's climacteric years (this chapter's convention, cf. *annus climactericus*). Hagecius states he will complete it on 1 October [1589]. The translation keeps his own conditional hedge *si ita Deus volet* ("if God so wills") and does not adjust it to any externally-reckoned birth-year.
- ***studia medica*** — "medical studies": Hagecius was an active court physician, hence his apology that medicine and "other cares" keep him from astronomy.
- ***lucubrationes*** — "lucubrations," works composed by lamplight / studious nocturnal labours; kept in the period sense.
- ***Commentariis Trapezuntii*** — "the *Commentaries* of **Trapezuntius**": **George of Trebizond** (Georgius Trapezuntius, 1395–1486), whose commentary on Ptolemy's *Almagest* was a standard but contested humanist text; Hagecius asks Tycho's editorial judgement on a staged publication ("the two former books first, the rest afterwards"). *ex re scholarum* rendered "to the schools' advantage."
- ***De rebus Gallicis … Monachus … scelus … horrendum*** — "concerning French affairs … a Monk … a dreadful crime": the assassination of **King Henri III of France** by the Dominican friar **Jacques Clément** on 1 August 1589 (Henri died 2 August). The literature (Strauss, *Brahe Iconography*; Weber cat. 177) confirms the 1 August 1589 regicide-by-monk. Hagecius's bitter pun — that "Monks and Papist Catholics" should be named not *a fide* (from the faith) but *a Catholicitate omnium scelerum* (from the *catholicity* — universality — of all crimes) — turns *Catholicus* against itself; the wordplay is kept and glossed rather than flattened.
- ***Archid. Max. … Polonicos limites transcensurus … sanus redeat*** — "Archduke **Maximilian** … about to cross the Polish borders … may he return safe": **Archduke Maximilian III of Austria** (the "Deutschmeister"), defeated claimant to the Polish throne, taken prisoner at Byczyna (Pitschen) in January 1588 and held by the Poles. His release under the Treaty of Bytom-Będzin (negotiated 1589) is the "return" Hagecius anticipates — a further internal anchor to **1589**, not 1586.
- ***B. V.*** — *Bene vale* = "Fare you well".
- ***T. studiosiss.*** — *Tui studiosissimus* = "Most devoted to you".
- **Greek.** None present in this letter.
- **Symbols.** None present in this letter.
- **DATING CRUX (named).** The dateline reads **"Pragae die 7. Septembris novo stylo Anno 1589"** — Prague, 7 September 1589, **New Style** (Bohemia, under Imperial/Catholic rule, had adopted the Gregorian calendar; Hagecius marks the style explicitly, *novo stylo*). The edition identifier (15860907001) and label imply **1586**. **The internal evidence is decisive for 1589, not 1586:** (i) the Henri III assassination-by-monk (1 Aug 1589); (ii) Archduke Maximilian's anticipated release/return from Polish captivity (1589, post-Byczyna 1588); (iii) the explicit dateline "Anno 1589." The header therefore leads with the as-written **7 September 1589 [N.S.]** and appends "(catalogued 1586)" by this chapter's convention; the catalogue year is treated as an error, **not** silently reconciled, and the discrepancy is recorded here. No calendar conversion of the day itself is performed; only the style (N.S.) is flagged.

documents.incipit: NON dubito, Nobilissime Domine, Mathematicorum præstantissime, quin in recenti adhuc …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, EQVITI DANO, DOMINO A KNVDSTRVP, MATHEMATICO NOSTRO SECVLO PRÆSTANTISSIMO, ETC. DOMINO AC FAUTORI SUO VNICE COLENDO, ETC. S. P.

NON dubito, Nobilissime Domine, Mathematicorum præstantissime, quin in recenti adhuc habeas memoria, quæ in proximis nundinis Francofordiensibus mandato Illustrissimi Principis nostri transmittendo aliquot Obseruationes ad T. Excell. perscripserim, et vt a T. Excell., etiam atque etiam petierim, vt his nostris Literis respondere dignaretur. At cum nullum adhuc a T. Excell. viderimus responsum, valde dubitat Illustriss. Princeps noster, num eæ ad manus tuas peruenerint. Mandauerat enim Illustriss. ipsius Celsitudo, vt non tantum suæ Celsitudinis clementem salutationem, verumetiam ingens tuæ responsionis videndæ desiderium per ministrum tuum tibi significarem. Quapropter cum nullus Dies intercedat, quin de T. Excell. responsione ab Illustrissimo principe nostro interroger, eiusque intermissionem semper a disiunctione locorum excusare cogar, peto a T. Excell. adhuc maiorem in modum, ne responsionem in Salutem et promotionem Astronomiæ diutius intermittat. Ipse quidem, quibuscunque possum rationibus, Astronomiam Illustrissimo Principi nostro etiam atque etiam commendare non desino: dummodo T. Excell. mihi in subsidium veniat, atque currentem et bene admonitum acrioribus calcaribus instiget. Acer et ad palmæ per se cursurus honores: Si tamen horteris, fortius ibit equus. De Altitudinibus Stellarum Meridianis a me per Quadrantem obseruatis, inuenio Quadranti non iuste secundum Horizontis planum a Wittichio et Horologiario nostro perpendicula esse applicata, sed ostendi ab eo Altitudines Stellarum iusto et quidem integro minuto maiores, quam reuera sint: Quod licet toties Illustriss. Principi nostro ab eo tempore, quo hîc Mathematicum ago, dixerim, credere tamen noluit, donec nuper defectionem tam Horologiario, quam Illustriss. ipsius Cels. ad oculum ostenderem. Nec dubito, quin tu quoque eundem errorem in nostris Obseruationibus iamdudum animaduerteris. Iteratis igitur Obseruationibus inuenio correctis perpendiculis Eleuationem Poli huius loci ex Stella Polari 51 grad. 19 min. vno scilicet minuto minorem. Ad summam, non dubito, quin pro tuo erga Astronomiam singulari Amore Nobilissimam hanc Scientiam etiam atque etiam apud Illustrissimum Principem nostrum sis commendaturus. Scis hanc Artem omnino Regiam esse, ac Regum ac Principum fauorem desiderare. Plura scriberem, præsertim de impuro illo nebulone Nicolao Raymaro Vrso Dithmarso, qui superiori Hyeme apud T. Excell. Typographicam Literarum collectionem et ordinationem, vt opinor, exercuit, quomodo scilicet hic te conuicijs proscindere non desierit, et quomodo te defenderim: nisi angustia temporis me impediret. Cum nuper in præsentia Illustrissimi Principis JOANNIS CASIMIRI Ducis Palatini, etc. Itemque, Inclyti Domini a Donaw, tui honorificam, vt par erat, facerem mentionem: dici vix potest, quomodo Dominus a Donaw te commendârit, adeo vt me iam pridem tui amore flagrantem iam totum inflammârit.

His igitur bene et feliciter vale, optime TYCHO, et de Astronomia bene mereri ne desine.

Cassellis 7 Calend. Septembris, Anno 86.

T. T.
CHRISTOPHORVS ROTHMANNVS Bernburgensis.
text.english:
**To the most noble man, Master Tycho Brahe, Danish knight, Lord of Knudstrup, the most outstanding mathematician of our age, etc., his lord and patron singularly to be honoured, etc. — heartiest greeting.**

I do not doubt, most noble Lord, most outstanding of mathematicians, that you still hold in fresh memory how, at the last Frankfurt fair, by the command of our Most Illustrious Prince, I wrote out to Your Excellency several observations to be conveyed [to you], and how again and again I begged of Your Excellency that he would deign to answer this letter of ours. But since we have as yet seen no reply from Your Excellency, our Most Illustrious Prince greatly doubts whether they reached your hands. For his Most Illustrious Highness had charged me to signify to you, through your servant, not only his Highness's gracious greeting, but also a vast desire to see your reply. Wherefore, since not a day passes but I am questioned by our Most Illustrious Prince concerning Your Excellency's reply, and am always forced to excuse the delay of it by the separation of our places, I ask of Your Excellency yet more earnestly that he not put off any longer a reply for the welfare and advancement of astronomy. For my own part, by whatever arguments I can, I do not cease to commend astronomy again and again to our Most Illustrious Prince — provided that Your Excellency come to my aid, and goad on with sharper spurs one who is already running and well-admonished. The keen [horse] will of itself run on to the honours of the palm; yet if you urge him, the horse will go the more strongly. As to the meridian altitudes of the stars observed by me with the quadrant, I find that the plumb-lines were not rightly applied to the quadrant along the plane of the horizon by Wittich and our clock-maker, but that it [the quadrant] showed the altitudes of the stars greater by a full minute, indeed an entire minute, than they truly are: which, although I told our Most Illustrious Prince so many times from the time when I have been acting as mathematician here, he was nevertheless unwilling to believe, until lately I showed the fault to the clock-maker and to his Most Illustrious Highness before their very eyes. Nor do I doubt that you too have long since noticed the same error in our observations. Therefore, with the observations repeated and the plumb-lines corrected, I find the elevation of the pole of this place, from the Pole Star, to be 51 degrees 19 minutes — that is, less by one minute. In sum, I do not doubt that, out of your singular love toward astronomy, you will commend this most noble science again and again to our Most Illustrious Prince. You know that this art is altogether a royal one, and craves the favour of kings and princes. I would write more — especially about that foul scoundrel Nicolaus Raymarus Ursus Dithmarsus, who last winter, as I suppose, practised the typographical collection and arrangement of letters [i.e. typesetting] at Your Excellency's [house], [and about] how indeed he has not ceased to slash at you here with insults, and how I defended you — were not the shortness of time hindering me. When lately, in the presence of the Most Illustrious Prince Johann Casimir, Duke Palatine, etc., and likewise of the renowned Lord von Dohna, I made honourable mention of you, as was fitting, it can scarcely be told how the Lord von Dohna commended you, so that he wholly inflamed me, already long since burning with love of you.

With this, then, farewell — well and happily — best Tycho, and do not cease to deserve well of astronomy.

Kassel, the 7th [day before] the Kalends of September [26 August], in the year [15]86.

Yours truly,
Christoph Rothmann of Bernburg.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Christophorus Rothmannus Bernburgensis* = **Christoph Rothmann** (c. 1550/60 – c. 1600), of Bernburg in Anhalt; mathematician and astronomer to **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel**. This is one of the Rothmann–Tycho letters Tycho himself published in the 1596 *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Liber I) printed at Uraniborg — the edition of record for this letter.
- **Recipient titulature.** *Equiti Dano, Domino a Knudstrup* = "Danish knight, Lord of Knudstrup" (Tycho's family seat in Scania). *Mathematico nostro seculo praestantissimo* = "the most outstanding mathematician of our age." *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam* ("heartiest greeting," this chapter's convention).
- **"Illustrissimus Princeps noster."** Throughout, "our Most Illustrious Prince" / "his Highness" = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (Rothmann's employer), not named in the body. *Celsitudo* = "Highness" by this chapter's convention
- **"the last Frankfurt fair."** *proximis nundinis Francofordiensibus* — the Frankfurt book fair (spring or autumn), the standard conduit for scholarly correspondence and observations between the Kassel and Hven circles.
- **Equestrian proverb.** *currentem … acrioribus calcaribus instiget … Si tamen horteris, fortius ibit equus* — "spur on one already running … yet if you urge [him], the horse will go the more strongly": a classical commonplace (cf. *currentem incitare*, "to spur the willing horse"; Ovid, *Ex Ponto* II.6.38 *fortius ut moveant, calcar habere volunt*). Rothmann casts himself as the eager horse needing only Tycho's encouragement. Kept as the running metaphor; *ad palmae … honores* = "to the honours of the palm [of victory]."
- **Instrument / observation.** *Altitudines Stellarum Meridianae … per Quadrantem* = "meridian altitudes of the stars … with the quadrant". *perpendicula* = the **plumb-lines** by which the quadrant's vertical was set; mis-set "along the plane of the horizon," they introduced a systematic error of a full arc-minute. *Eleuatio Poli … ex Stella Polari* = "elevation of the pole … from the Pole Star," i.e. the observed latitude of Kassel, corrected to **51° 19′** (one minute less than before). *ad oculum* = "before their very eyes / demonstrably." *Horologiarius* rendered "clock-maker" (the court instrument-mechanic).
- **"Wittich."** *a Wittichio* = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586), the Silesian mathematician who had visited both Hven (1580) and Kassel; here blamed (with the clock-maker) for the faulty plumb-line setting. Tycho's later quarrel over priority for the geo-heliocentric arrangement involved Wittich and Ursus; Rothmann names him neutrally as the prior installer.
- **"Ursus."** *Nicolaus Raymarus Ursus Dithmarsus* = **Nicolaus Reimers Bär (Ursus)**, of Dithmarschen — the future Imperial mathematician and Tycho's bitterest priority-rival. *impuro illo nebulone* = "that foul scoundrel": Rothmann's invective. The clause *Typographicam Literarum collectionem et ordinationem … exercuit* literally "practised the typographical collection and arrangement of letters" = **worked as a typesetter/compositor** during his stay at Hven the previous winter (1584/85) — a pointed status-jab. *te conuicijs proscindere* = "to slash at you with insults." This passage is an early datable trace of the Tycho–Ursus feud, from Rothmann's pro-Tycho side.
- **Other persons.** *Joannes Casimirus Dux Palatinus* = **Johann Casimir of the Palatinate-Simmern** (1543–1592), Count Palatine, administrator of the Electoral Palatinate. *Dominus a Donaw / a Donaw* = a **Lord (Burgrave) von Dohna**, of the prominent Prussian-Silesian noble house (the precise individual is not specified in the letter; likely one of the Burgraves von Dohna active at the Reformed German courts). Both are reported praising Tycho.
- **Royal-art topos.** *hanc Artem omnino Regiam esse, ac Regum ac Principum fauorem desiderare* = "this art is altogether a royal one, and craves the favour of kings and princes" — the standard plea that astronomy needs princely patronage, here urging Tycho to keep the Landgrave engaged.
- **Sign-off formula.** *His igitur bene et feliciter vale* — *vale* is rendered with the controlled formula **"farewell"**; the adverbial pair *bene et feliciter* ("well and happily") qualifying it is retained alongside, set off with dashes, so that the fixed *vale* gloss is preserved without dropping Rothmann's doubled adverb.
- **Subscription.** *T. T.* = *Tui tibi* / *Tuus totus* ("Yours truly / wholly yours"); expanded conventionally.
- **Printed-edition markers.** The working transcription carries scattered superscript letter-anchors (rendered as a stray "A" in several places, including a spurious "A" splitting the opening *S. P.* | *NON dubito*) — these are footnote/marginal-note sigla of the 1596 printed *Epistolae*, **not** part of Rothmann's prose; they are silently removed from both the cleaned source block and the translation.
- **Dateline — calendar crux (flagged, not reconciled).** The letter is subscribed *Cassellis 7 Calend. Septembris, Anno 86*. By the Roman idiom (inclusive counting, with 1 September = *Kalendis Septembris*), **"7 Kalends of September" = 26 August 1586** (this chapter's convention, Roman-calendar idiom glossed to civil date). The edition's metadata and identifier, however, label the letter **"7 September 1586"** (whence identifier …090700). The two do not agree; by the audit's rule the dateline is reproduced as written and the discrepancy recorded, not silently corrected. The header gives the literal Roman reading with its civil equivalent; the identifier-date (7 Sept.) is noted as the editorial/catalogue date. All O.S. (Hesse-Kassel and Denmark kept the Julian calendar).
- **Place.** *Cassellis* = **Kassel**.

text.original:
DEM VESTEN VNSERM LIEBEN BESONDERN TYCHONI BRAHE, HERRN ZU KNUDSTRUP.
WILHELM VON GOTTES GNADEN LANDTGRAUE ZU HESSEN/ GRAUE ZU CATZENELNBOGEN/ DIETZ/ ZIEGENHAIN VND NIDDA/ ETC.

UNSERN gnedigen Gruß zuuor/ Vester lieber besonder/ Wir haben euch nun zu zweyen vnderschiedenen mahlen/ wol bey ewrem Diener/ den 14 Aprilis, als auch hernacher den 26 Augusti geschrieben/ vnd vnsere Obseruationes Stellarum fixarum vberschickt/ vnd darneben in gnaden begeret/ nicht allein ewer Iudicium darauff vns zuzuschreiben/ sondern auch ewre Obseruationes dargegen zuuberschicken. Wann vns aber biß noch von euch kein antwort einkommen/ welches vns gleichwol verwundert/ Als haben wir nicht vnderlassen wollen/ bey dieser gelegenen Botschafft/ euch nachmahls zuerinnern/ Vnd ist an euch vnser gnediges begeren/ Ihr wollet vns nicht allein auff solche vnsere schreiben hinwieder beantworten/ Sondern auch ewre Obseruationes vbersenden/ damit wir sie mit den vnsern zu conferiren haben. Das versehen wir vns/ vnd seind Euch mit gnaden geneigt/

Datum in vnser Stadt vnd Vestung Cassell am 14 Octob. Anno 86.
WILHELM LANDTGRAFF ZU HESSEN.
text.english:
**To the trusty, our dear and especial [friend] Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup.**
**Wilhelm, by the grace of God Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda, etc.**

Our gracious greeting beforehand. Trusty, dear, and especial [friend]: we have now written to you on two separate occasions — duly by your servant, on 14 April, and again afterward on 26 August — and have sent over our *observations of the fixed stars*, and therewith graciously requested that you not only write us your *judgement* upon them, but also send over your own *observations* in return. But since to this hour no answer has come to us from you — at which we are, indeed, not a little surprised — we would not omit, by this convenient messenger, to remind you once more. And it is our gracious desire of you that you would not only reply again to these our letters, but also transmit your observations, so that we may have them to *compare* with our own. This we look for of you, and we remain graciously inclined toward you.

Given in our city and fortress of Kassel, on 14 October, in the year [15]86.
Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** **Wilhelm IV "the Wise," Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), the princely founder of the Kassel observatory and Tycho's chief astronomical peer-patron; his mathematician Christoph Rothmann (see brahe-t_15870812001) handled the technical detail.
- **Titulature.** The full style — *Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda* — is reproduced; these are the constituent lordships of the Hessian title and are kept in their German forms.
- **Register.** Chancery letter in the princely first-person plural (*Wir … euch … unser gnädiges Begehren*); the deferential-yet-commanding tone of a prince to a foreign noble savant is preserved ("it is our gracious desire of you…"). *Vester* (= *fest/getreu*) "trusty"; *lieber besonder* "dear and especial," the standard chancery address.
- **Code-switching (kept and italicised).** The Latin technical and bureaucratic nouns embedded in the German — *Observationes Stellarum fixarum* ("observations of the fixed stars"), *Iudicium* ("judgement / expert opinion"), *Observationes*, and the verb *conferiren* ("to compare/collate") — are rendered into English but flagged as the Landgrave's own Latin within the German, by this chapter's convention
- **Substance.** A reminder that the Landgrave's two earlier letters (14 April, 26 August 1586) enclosing Kassel's fixed-star observations have gone unanswered; he presses again for Tycho's *Iudicium* and a reciprocal set of Hven observations to collate — the data-exchange that underlies the printed correspondence.
- **Calendar.** O.S. (Lutheran Hesse kept Julian).

Checked the published English against the transcribed original clause-by-clause: the two prior-letter dates (14 April, 26 August), the place and date of this letter (Kassel, 14 October [15]86), the full title string (Hesse / Katzenelnbogen / Dietz / Ziegenhain / Nidda), and every substantive clause are rendered accurately. No fabrication, omission, or mistranslation found.
