text.original:
ILLVSTRISSIMOA PRINCIPI AC DOMINO D. WILHELMO LANDTGRAVIO HASSIÆ, COMITI IN CATZENELLEBOGEN,
DIETZ, ZIEGENHAIN ET NIDDAA: PRINCIPI ACA DOMINO SUO CLEMENTISSIMO S. P.ALITERAS Celsitudinis Tuæ Princeps Illustriss. ad me circa Vernum tempus
proxime elapsi Anni datas, quibus meis respondere dignabaris, per eundem
quem ad Tuam Cels. ablegaueram mihi domesticum, accepiA, pro qua clementi Tuæ Celsitud. erga me beneuolentia, demisseA ago gratias. Quod veroA tanto temporis interuallo, nihil ijs responderimA, et T. Cels. desiderijs satisfacere tam diu intermiserim, licet etiam
interea bis per aliasA a T. Cels. Literas hoc nomine commonefactus, non est quod Celsit. T.
existimet, vel incuria quadam, vel data opera factumA esse, sed locorum potius nimia intercapedo, raraque illuc mittendi
Literas oportunitas, me a scribendo hactenus retardârunt. Duobus enim saltem Anni temporibus, commodior hinc Cassellas versus scribendiA, conceditur occasio, cum videlicet ad vtrasque Nundinas Francofordianas
nostrates proficiscunturA. Quapropter, cum paulo post nundinas vltimas
vernales, Tuæ Celsitudinis literas accepissem, in eas quæ proxime
sequebantur Autumnales, responsum differre necessitasA coëgit. VbiA vero circa id temporis, quo ad præteritas proxime elapso Autumno,
Francoforti celebratas
nundinas Mercatores hinc eoA se conferre vellentA, cum quodam BibliopolaA sedulo egissem, vt paulo ante discessum, me in hac Insula conueniret, secumque Literas T. Cels. Secretario
Cassellis tradendas asportaret. Quod etiam ille promiserat, et præstare omnino constituerat.
SedA accidit praeterA opinionem, vt ijs ipsis diebus, quibus illi huc accedendum foret,
Illustris. Princeps VDALRICVSA Dux Megapolensis, vna cum Illustrissima PrincipeA Domina ELIZABETHA Coniuge (quæ
postea in ipso reditu Mechelburgam
versus, antequam Mare traiecissetA, magno omnium luctu diem obijt) et Fratris Filio Duce SIGISMVNDO, deducente illos ipsa etiam
Sereniss. REGINA nostra vna
cum magno Nobilium Virorum comitatu, me hic Vraniburgi inuisere sint dignatiA, partim vt machinas Astronomicas, quibus has ædes refertas sciebant,
coram contemplarentur, partim vt Inclytus Dux VDALRICVSA, Pyronomicos meos labores (quibus non minorem quam Astronomicis
operam impendo) et his inseruientem apparatum Mechanicum, penitius
introspiceret. NamA ipsius Celsitudo, multis ab hinc Annis, ijs exercitijs plurimum delectaturA, et non vulgaria in his, propria industria adinuenit, quemadmodum et
Serenissima Regina ipsius
Filia, hisce Artificijs Spagyricis magnopere afficitur, quo nomine etiam
præterito Anno, Mare hoc bis traijcere, nostrosque lares subire non grauata estA. Cum itaque eo ipso tempore, quo T. Celsit. commodeA rescribendum esset, his tam Illustribus Hospitibus excipiendis
occuparer, idque Bibliopola ille, qui me ex promisso accedere animum
induxerat Haffniæ (eo quod inde
nauigia Regia, quibus traijciendum erat, procurabantur) cognouisset,
propositum mutauit, et ne Nundinarum, diutius præstolando, tempus negligeretA, me, quem intelligebat impeditumA esse, non accedens, itineri se commisit. Hinc itaque factum est, vt
hac oportuna occasione Tuæ Celsit. rescribendi, præter omnem expectationem, frustratus simA. Cumque ex eo tempore, nulla eiuscemodi commoditas Literas ad T.
Cels. mittendi, mihi oblata fuerit, responsione, quamuis inuitus,
supersedere cogebar, idque in hoc vsque tempus, quo hic alter nostras BibliopolaA
Francofurtum ad vernales
nundinas proficiscitur, mihi in perferendis ad T. Celsitud. Literis suam
operam pollicereturA. Hæc vero eo pluribus T. Celsitud. ob id commemoro, vt intelligat
nullatenûs mea incuria factum esse, quod in rescribendo iusto tardior
fuerim. Tuam itaque Celsit. submisse rogatam volo, vt ob prædictas rationes
moram hanc candide interpretetur, meque clementer hac in
parte excusatum habeat. Quod ego sperans me pro eximia Celsitudinis Tuæ æquanimitate omnino
impetraturum, nunc vtar oblata oportuniore
rescribendi occasione, et ad singula capita in T. Celsitud. literis
particulariter respondebo. Quod itaque Celsitudo Tua, in prioribus ad me datis literis
responsionem ad meas continentibus, ab initio asserat, conuenientiam illam
inter sui Mathematici Obseruationes, et
meas in Cometa Anni 85. adeo exquisitam, admodum placuisse, et magni
ponderis locum meruisse, id sane et me plurimum oblectauitA. Neque enim similem in aliorum Mathematicorum scriptis de Cometis
aliquot præteritis cum ipso cælo, nostrisque Obseruationibus congruentiam,
vspiam ferme inuenio, quod illorum in obseruando et demonstrando negligentia
factum non dubito. Diuersitas autem, si qua erat inter Tuæ Celsi Mathematici et nostras in dicto
Cometa animaduersiones, potius indeA eueniebat, quod Stellarum fixarum loca, quarum vsus requirebatur, non
præcise in ijsdem scrupulis assumserimus, licet ea ipsa, quæ in his nobis
intercessit discrepantia, paucissimorum et nullius pene momenti scrupulorum
fuerit, vt ex collatione cum nostris locis plenius videre licet. Inprimis
vero mihi perceptu iucundum fuit, quod Tuæ
Celsitud. Mathematicus nullam in eodem Cometa deprehenderit
parallaxin, quemadmodum et ego vel nullam, vel pene insensibilem,
multiplicibus et accuratis Obseruationibus inuenire potui. Ideoque plane in
eo Rei veritate idipsum exigente consentimus, non in Elementari orbe, sed in
supremo æthere genitum fuisse hunc Cometam, contra quam hactenus
Peripatetici, et omnes fere Philosophi, ipsique adeo Mathematici, pro rato
indubitatoque asseuerârantA. Quod etiam fieri posse, Noua illa, et miraculosa ad Cassiopeam
Stella superioribus annis conspecta, vel ex proprijs Tuæ Celsitudinis
Obseruationibus, quibus meæ apprime astipulabantur, liquidissime
comprobauit. Imo et nos in 4. alijs Cometis interea conspectis nullum eorum
infra Lunam, sed omnes in ipso æthere cursum suum absoluisse, e certissimis
Obseruationibus Geometrica veritate demonstrauimus; vt ob id prorsus
existimem omnes Cometas in ipso Cœlo supra Lunam generari, nullumque eorum
vnquam Elementarem extitisse. Nam quod Regiomontani et Vogelini
Obseruationes in duobus Cometis veteribus, et recentiorum quorundam placita,
in his ipsis, quorum nos inuestigationem per Instrumenta debita nacti sumus,
diuersum ostendant, nihil moramur; Siquidem, quantum illorum Obseruationibus
fidentium sit, vel in ipsis mundo congenitis sideribus perspectum habeamus.
Et longe subtilioris artifici existitA parallaxes tam exiguas discernere, præsertim vbi motus proprij vna
sit habenda consideratio, quam hactenus communiter vsitata apparentias
cælestes scrutandi ratio, suppeditare queat. De toto vero hoc Cometarum argumentoA nostras Obseruationes, hisque innixas demonstrationes Tua Celsitudo
vberius et sufficienter sententiam nostramA
cognoscetA vbi OpusA, quod nunc de hac ipsa materia adA prælum adorno, in publicam vtilitatem euulgatumA fuerit. Quantum ad Obseruationes Tuæ Celsitudinis mihi transmissas
(quo etiam nomine Tuæ Celsitud. plurimas reuerenter habeo gratias) attinet,
contuli eas tum inter se, tum vna cum meis diligenter, et quidem in
distantijs ipsis nullum reperio alicuius momenti discrimen, quin tuum
Instrumentum easdem præbeat, quas mei Sextantes. Id quod vel ex sola inter
Regulum et Spicam ♍ intercapedine (eo quod Obseruatio hæc fiat iuxta
extremos Sextantis limites, vnde etiam exiliores interuallorum Anguli minus
dubij euadunt) manifestum redditur. Hanc enim Tuæ Celsitud. Sextans præbuit
part. 54. M. 2; Nos eandem aliquoties vix Sexta parte vnius minuti
(discrimine pene insensibili et nullius ponderis) minorem deprehendimus,
attestantibus etiam cæteris distantijs Tuæ Celsitudinis cum nostris inuicem
collatis, eum Sextantem, quem Tua Cels. in vsu habet, satis exactas, et ipsi
cœlo congruas præbere intercapedines. Quod tamen vix eius opera factitatum
opinor, qui structuram illius ad mei quem hic conspexerat (quodA proculdubio silentio præterijt) imitationem primum Tuæ Celsitudini
ordinauit. Nota enim satis mihi est ipsius, in his Mechanicis rebus vel
inquirendis, vel imitandis, minus exacta diligentia. Ideoque id potius
propriæ T. Cels. industriæ, et Mathematici ipsius Rothmanni, artificisque vna
Mechanici ab ipsa experientia indagatæ solertiæ ascribendum
censeo. Quod ad altitudines Meridianas mihi transmissas attinet, in ijs
parum quiddam discriminis a meis inuentis reperio, adeo vt Declinationes
Stellarum inde petitæ, in Borealibus, duobus propemodum vbique scrupulis
abundent, in Australibus vero totidem deficiant, idque præsupposita
Æquatoris inclinatione part. 38. M. 40. quæ ex ea Poli eleuatione, quam
Rothmannus e Stellarum quarundam non
occidentium vtraque altitudine mihi perscripsitA, resultare deprehenditur. Cum autem satis perspectum haberem,
Declinationes Stellarum a me indagatas in nullo minuto vel abundare, vel
deficere, eo quod quinis vel senis varie fabricatis, iustæque magnitudinis
Instrumentis, ita vt in quibusdam sexta pars minuti discerni commode queat,
certô exploratæ essent: et satis vna mihi constaret, Tuam Celsitud. in
Obseruationibus etiam, præsertim per hæc Neoterica organa reiteratis, summam
adhibere curam et diligentiam, vndeA hæc binorum scrupulorum inter nos diuersitas contingeret, primo mecum
plurimum admirabar. Deinde cum eandem pene vbique esse differentiam
considerarem, statim in mentem incidit, facile euenisse, vt vel
pinnacidiorum non rite appositorum vitio bina scrupula iusto altius in Tuæ
Celsit. Quadrante perspicerentur, vel etiam perpendiculi in vnico saltem
minuto, non rite ordinati errore, qui vtrinque assumtus, tam in Poli quam
Stellarum Meridianarum altitudine declinationem earundem binis variaret
scrupulis, aut forte vtraque ratione. Id quod
facile in Quadrante bicubitali euenire posse inde
colligebam, quod etiam in duplo vel triplo maioribus, si non exactissima,
tam in pinnacidijs, quam perpendiculo adhibeatur applicatio, facile dimidij,
vel etiam integri scrupuli error obrepat. Nec enim diuisioni minus certæ,
aut Centro deuio hunc erroremA imputandum duxi. Habebam itaqueA in animo Tuam Celsitud. per literas de his commonefacere, vt
præcisiorem vel pinnacidiorum, vel perpendiculi, aut vtriusque simul
examinationem denuo institueret, quo etiam in Declinationibus Stellarum, non
minus quam in distantijs, exacta inter Tuæ Celsitud. obseruationes et meas
conuenientia stabilietur. Verum dum oportuna mittendi literas occasione
destituor, et circa Nundinarum Francofurtensium tempora, causa commemorataA â scribendo impedior, optime mihi, et ex votoA accidit, vt T. Cels. Mathematicus
interea indicarit, se deprehendisse Quadrantem T. Cels. ob perpendiculi
vitium altitudines priores ostendisse vno scrupulo vbique iusto maiores. Quod si est (vti prorsus mihi persuadeo) Poli sublimitatem vno etiam scrupulo minorem, et Æquatoris tantundem
maiorem prouenire consentaneum erit, vt ea reuera sit Cassellis part. 38. M. 41. Huic itaqueA si applicentur altitudines T. Cels. mihi transmissæ, ita vt singulis
ob perpendiculi errorem vnicum adimatur scrupulum, satis exacte cum meis
Stellarum declinationibus consentient. Quare plurimum laetatusA sum, per hoc vnicum scrupulum, in vitio perpendiculi emendatum, alium
longe maiorem ob hanc, licet non adeo magnam, quæ Obseruationibus nostris
intercedebat differentiam, animo meo inhærentem scrupulum ademptum esse.
Omnes enim cœlestes Obseruationes ad exactam amussim, quatenus in sensus
humanos cadant, instituendas censeo, adeo, vt si quid in his desideretur vel
tantillum, pro irritisA habeam. Vt vero Celsitudo Tua collationem vlteriorem inter suas et
meas Obseruationes, tam quo ad intercapedines, quam quo ad altitudines
Meridianas, siue inde petitas Declinationes instituere queat, mitto Tuæ
Celsitud. aliquot Stellarum, tum aliarum, tum præsertim insigniorum, quæ
iuxta Zodiacum sunt distantias, meis Sextantibus Trigonicis (sic enim eos
appellare libuit) fideliter exploratas, et præterea sublimitates quasdam
Meridianas Quadrantibus diuersis, inuicem tamen consentientibus indagatas,
idque tum circa finem Anni 84. et labentem 85. tum etiam circa exitum
proxime elapsi 86. et primum initium huius currentis 87. vt Tua Celsitudo eo
expeditius, ad debita tempora suas altitudines cum meis conferre possit.
Siquidem et his ipsis Annis post denuo redintegrata Instrumenta, Tuam
Celsitudinem exactiorem altitudinum Stellarum dimensionem notasseA, nullatenus dubitem. Nouit enim apprime Tua Celsitudo Declinationes
Stellarum, et ob id etiam earundem altitudines, quotannis aliquantulum variareA, idque præsertim in ijs sideribus, quæ
Æquinoctialibus locis propiora existunt. Eleuatio vero Æquatoris in nostris
sublimitatibus Stellarum adhibenda venit part. 34. /. 5⅓. eo quod crebris experimentis adinuenerim, Polum
hîc Vraniburgi, in loco meæ
Obseruationis, qui est medius Insulæ Huenæ
in celebri illo Freto Danico sitæ,
partibus 55. scr. 54⅔. attolli, id quod tam ex ipsa Polari Stella, quam cæteris
circumpolaribus non occidentibus, et ob decliuitatem non nimiumA sensibilem, refractionem excludentibus sideribus, multoties
comprobatum habeo. Longitudines et latitudines Stellarum a Tua Celsitud.
mihi communicatas, etiam tum inter se, tum cum meis contuli, deprehendique
assignationem illam e Globo Mechanice institutam, etsi non admodum
disconuenientem, tamen non vbique satis scrupulose annotatis distantijs et
altitudinibus correspondere, quamuis perexigua in quibusdam reperiatur
differentia. Quemadmodum Celsitudo Tua ex nonnullis, quas in adiuncta charta
annotaui collationibus, perspicere potest. Nec sane mihi vsque adeo mirum
videtur, mechanice in Globo perquisitas e distantijs et Altitudinibus
Stellarum longitudines et latitudines non in ipsis scrupulis exactæ rationi
consentire. Siquidem et ego Globum magnum Orichalcicum apprimeA rotundum habeam, qui Sex pedes in diametro contineat, in quo
Ecliptica, Æquatorque in singula scrupula, per puncta transuersalia, more
nobis in cæteris Instrumentis vsitato, subtiliter diuiduntur; nihilominus
tamen in vno vel sesquialtero scrupulo vbique ratam certitudinem in
Stellarum locis per Globum hunc ex Obseruationibus certis indagandis vix
mihi polliceor; Adeo ea, quæ Mechanice, licet summa diligentia elaborantur,
Geometricæ et Arithmeticæ scrupulositati posthabenda veniunt. In ipsis vero LongitudinibusA Stellarum a Tua Celsitudine mihi transmissis, quamuisA Geometrice, et per numeros Sinuum exactiori trutina expendantur, vtplurimumA quina vel sena aut circiter scrupula, nostris Obseruationibus
vlteriora ab æquinoctio numerari animaduerto. In Latitudinibus vero non
maior fere reperitur differentia, quam quæ vel ex Longitudinibus paulo
aliter assumtis, vel Obliquitatis Eclipticæ diuersa constitutione,
potissimum vero e Declinationibus, duobus minutis perpendiculi vestri vitio
a nostris dissidentibus, causari poterat. Est sane discrimen hoc etiam
Longitudinum, nedum Latitudinum, non adeo magni momentiA, si veterum et Neotericorum quorundam conferamus annotationes. Nec
satis mirari possum Celsitudinem Tuam, tam prope suis Instrumentis Stellarum
loca attigisse, præsertim cum colligere queam, Celsitudinem Tuam in
Aldebora, vel quacunque alia pro fundamento vsa sit, Ascensionem eius Rectam
ex transitu per Meridianum, tempore per Horologium inuento et cum Sole
collato, deprehendisse. Quæ sane ratio mihi semper minus tuta videbatur.
Licet enim et ego quaterna eiusmodi habeamA Horologia diuersæ magnitudinis, exactæque
structuræ, quæ non solum singula scrupula prima, sed etiam secunda indicent;
in tam subtili tamen negotio eis fidem adhibere frustraneum duxiA, cum 4. saltem secunda, quæ in pluribus horis facile excidunt, vnius scrupuli primiA in longitudine errorem inducant. Adde quod Horologia ista etiam
diligentissime, vel e rotulis Aurichalcicis elaborata, mutationi aëreæ
sensibiliter obnoxia sint. Taceo pondus non esseA æquale, quando sublimius decliuiusque pendet, ob ligamenti, quo
annectitur, variatam Longitudinem, quæ ponderi aliquid successiue addit,
quod licet perexiguum sit, tamen in scrupulis secundis deuiationem non
negligendam adfertA. Quapropter, cum hac ratione negotium hoc non satis tuto succedere
perspectum haberem, nec ignorarem, difficultatem haud exiguam subesse, vt
vel vnius Stellæ Fixæ vera ab Æquinoctio peruestigaretur remotio, qua
cognita caeteraeA, vel per distantias ab inuicem, vel per differentias Æquatorias, aut
etiam per Armillas Hipparchicas Zodiacales, quas vna in vsu habemus,
certiori tamen compendio elaboratas, quam a veteribusA, cæteræ (inquam) quotquot liberet, facile constarent. Nec modum illum quo veteres, Hipparchus inprimis et PtolemaeusA Vsi sunt, superioreque ætate NICOLAVS COPERNICVS, per Lunam diei et
noctis participem, tam Soli, quam Stellis per Instrumenta applicatam, suis
carere difficultatibus, errorique minus obnoxiumA esse iudicarem. Nam licet concedamus, locum Solis adhibita exquisita
diligentia, in vno vel altero scrupulo, quo ad longitudinem scitu
possibilem, et intercapedinem eius ad Lunam, huiusque ad Stellas, satis
exacte dabilem esse; tamen Parallaxes Lunares, quæ adeo præcise non
cognoscuntur, in vtraque Obseruatione variationem aliquam a vero inducunt.
Adde quod hæc ratio obseruandi non commode fit, nisi Sole circa Horizontem
decliui existente, vbi alius est eius locus apparens, quam verus, qui iuxta
Meridianum patuit, idque non saltem ratione parallaxeos, sed multo potius ob
Refractionem, de qua in prioribus literis Tuæ Celsitud. meam sententiam
latius indicaui; et intelligo ex Tuæ Celsitudinis responso, eam etiamA tam in Sole, quam cæteris Planetis et Fixis, deprehendisse in
decliuiori situ Refractionem sensibilemA; Quo nomine eius deA nostris vtrinque Obseruationibus plurimum congratulor. Nec enim
Veteres, vel Recentiores, quod sciam, hanc in siderum collimationibus
animaduerterunt, vel debite præcauerunt. Hac, inquam, ab antecessoribus
nostris strata via, cum satis tuto incedere ob prædictas aliasque plures
rationes non liceret, commodiori et tutiori semita, quæ ad Stellarum exactas
Longitudines perduceret, ingrediendum censui, nullamque aptiorem
exactioremque inueni, quam quæ ex opportunitate nobis, Anno 1582A. quo Veneris Stellam Vespertinam existentem interdiu dilucide
apparentem conspeximus, offerebatur. Tunc enim Venerem a Sole in exacta distantia, a 24. Februarij vsque in medium Aprilis,
pluribus quam facile credi possit, vicibus, diurno tempore diligentissime
obseruauimus, idque non solum in decliuiori Solis situ, sed multoties, cum
is vel in Meridiano, vel saltem vnica, aut sesquialtera hora, vltra hunc
remoueretur, et ♀ admodum sublimis vna existeret, adeo,
vt et ipsius per Meridianum transitus, Sole adhuc multum eleuato, a nobis,
tam quo ad altitudinem, quam distantiam a Sole, sæpenumero deprehensus sit.
Quare, cum locus Solis, et ex altitudinibus Meridianis, ac per antecedentium
annorum a nobis adamussim in motu eius factam restitutionem satis exacte
constaret, ex Declinatione Veneris et Solis, data vtriusque per Sextantem
exquisita et sibi consentiente distantia, (ita vt Sol vnum pinnacidium
illuminaret tota sua quantitate; per alterum vero, Venus vtrinque per
rimulas Cylindro superiori parallelas conspiceretur) locus Stellæ Veneris
certo patuit. Qui nocturno tempore, quamprimum Affixarum aliqua iuxta
Zodiacum aspectui offerebatur, per acceptam eius ab hac intercapedinem pari
ratione applicatus, habita prius motus proprij interea transacti ratione,
Stellæ eiusdem locum manifestauit, idque sæpenumero fiebat in diuersis etiam
Stellis, cum Sol, Venus, et Fixæ obseruatæ vbique fere essent in tanta supra
Horizontem altitudine, vt Refractionem omnem excluderent. Si qua vero
interdum erat perexigua, ea ex alijs Obseruationibus circa hanc factis,
præcauebatur. Hac itaque infallibili Methodo in Longitudinis Stellarum
exactam notitiam tunc temporis multiplici experimento in idem recurrente, et
Stellarum earundem inter se distantijs eandem comprobante, optime ex voto
deueni. Adhibui etiam vbique Parallaxes tam Solis, quam Veneris, quatenus
per horarum interualla variabanturA, vt eo exactior ratio constaret. Imo vero et ipsius Veneris
Parallaxes peruestigare eodem anno non dubitabam, vt, an circa, vel infra
Solem conuolueretur, certius pateret. Quod etiam in Stella Martis in fine
prioris, et circa eiusdem anni initia experiri audebam, quando is AcronychusA et sublimis in ♋ latitudine etiam Borea eum altius attollente
conspiciebatur, vt indagarem an Sole maiorem diuersitatem aspectus
induceret, quod necessarium foret, si Coperniana Hypothesis in rei veritate consisteret. Nam
tertia fere parte per hanc Mars in ☍ Solis terris redditur propior quam ipse
Sol. Vnde etiam tunc maiorem Parallaxis diuersitatem necessario inducit, et
per consequens, Orbes Reuolutionum Martis nequaquam totaliter supra Orbem
Solarem, vt ferunt Hypotheses PtolemaicaeA, constituuntur. Ideoque vel rotari Terram annuo motu,
quo Planetarum excusantur omnes Epicycli; vel aliam cælestium Reuolutionum dispositionemA, quam hactenus factitatum, indagandam esse. Verum hæc nunc extra
propositum dicta, alias dilucidius et copiosius, Deo volente declarabuntur.
Cum itaque (vt ad rem redeam) prædicta minime dubia
ratione a Sole per Venerem indicato anno, in cognitionem Longitudinis
aliquot insigniorum fixarum Stellarum circa Zodiacum, earum latitudine se
facile vna ingerente, peruenissem; et ex Obseruationibus quibusdam alijs,
Anno 85. circa autumnale Æquinoctium acceptis, quo tempore Veneris Stella
tunc Matutina, etiam interdiu conspiciebatur, idque in consimili fere, qua Anno 82. tum distantia a Sole, et Terra, tum
etiam altitudine supra Horizontem (quod negotij certitudinem plurimum
promouit) omnia viceuersa exploratius comprobassem, hinc reliquarum etiam
affixarum Stellarum, tam intra quam extra Zodiacum loca, quo ad longum et
latum restituere, vnaque Planetarum omnium per hæc apparentias peruestigare,
nulla temporis sereni opportunitate hactenus intermissaA, elaboraui. Deprehendo autem in quamplurimis Stellis idipsum, quod T.
Cels. mihi perscribit, eas non saltem Longitudines aliterA obtinere, quam Veterum traditiones adiecta quoque Æquinoctij
præcessione correctiore exhibent, sed etiam Latitudines multo aliter, in
quibusdam minus, in quibusdam vero plus, ostendere; cum tamen has necessario
inuariatas omni æuo permanere inde a vetustissimis Astronomis, eo quod motus
octauæ Sphæræ circa Polos Eclipticæ contingat, citra omne dubium pro
comperto habeatur. Vnde Cels. T. merito in eius variationis admirationem
perducta, etiam meum de hac re iudicium clementer requirit, an videlicet
singulis Fixis aliquem peculiarem motum per se inesseA, quo Latitudinem quoque diuersimode mutent, consentaneum existimem.
Qua de re T. Cels. breuibus meam sententiam nunc exponam. Loca omnium
affixarum Stellarum inde a prima mundi Origine in singulis et omnibus, quo
ad se inuicem, prorsus inuariata permanere, omni dubio procul iudico. Idque
inde facile comprobatur, quod omnes fixæ Stellæ, quas recenset Ptolemæus primo capite dictionis 7. ab
Abrachi seu Hipparcho proxime 260.
ante se annis in vna extitisse linea recta, easdem etiam suo æuo in eodem

postea addit Ptolemæus, vt Posteris
ansam experimentandi relinqueret, etiam hac ætate elapsis ab ipso annis

hac obliquitatisA Signiferi diuersitate, imminutasA certo constet. Quia vero intelligo ex literis Tuæ tCelsitud.
Mathematici Rothmanni, eum in eadem
mecum sententia hac in parte versari, latius ad illum de hoc negotio

a me, supradicta ratione indagata sint, descripsi quarundam præcipuarum,

in hunc vel quosuis alios nostra ætate transferre. Non enim vnius hominis

est. Congruere vero etiamnum hæc loca Stellarum Obseruationes meæ præterito
Anno, et hoc ipso inde a principio Ianuarij factæ, sufficienter declarantA. Quod vero in T. Celsitud. longitudinibus Stellarum Geometrice, ex
intercapedinibus et Declinationibus in numeros redactis, quina vel sena, aut
circiter, vtplurimum abundent scrupula, facile excusabitur, si constet
Celsitud. T. tunc loco Solis, in his limitandis, vsam fuisse, cum Sol versaretur circa vernum AequinoctiumA, in parte Eclipticæ ascendente. Illic enim ratione illius vnici
scrupuli, quod perpendiculi vitio causabatur, Declinatio Solis binis

longitudinem vlterior. Id quod etiam in Stellas fixas ad Solis locum
adaptatas, necessario redundauit, licet circa Autumnale æquinoctium in parte
Eclipticæ descendente, res hæc contrario modo se habeat. Vt vero Celsitudo
T. etiam in cæteris erraticis Stellis aliquod specimen nostrarum
Obseruationum videatA, adiungo omnium vera loca, qualia meis Instrumentis accurata animaduersione intra vnicam primi mobilis
reuolutionem, ter hoc ipso Mense Ianuario ab initio noui anni deprehensa
sunt. Quod licet alias rarius contingat, aliquoties tamen superioribus annis a meA factitatum est, præsertim Anno præcedenti in Octobri, cum ☿ eous
multis diebus appareret. Solis motum, e Veneris situ, per Stellas fixas
inquisito, cum per Declinationes impediente etiam Refractione hoc anni
tempore minus certoA haberi queat, comprobaui. Interdiu enim Venus etiam ante Meridianum
hisce diebus, vel in ipso Meridie et ante, per puriorem serenitatem satis
euidenter conspicitur. Refractionis vero parallaxeosque Solis et Veneris
impedimenta prius in consimili altitudine explorata, remoui. Itidem etiam in
Mercurio effeci, cum isA admodum decliuis vix 5. gradibus altus obseruaretur. In cæteris hac limitatione opus non erat, quodA sublimiores cælitus capiebantur. Addidi vero ad eadem tempora
Obseruationis nostræ loca Planetarum Alphonsina et Coperniana, vt Tua Cels. vnico intuitu
discrepantiam vtriusque calculi a Cælo ipso facilius conspiceret, quamuis
sæpenumero multo plus, quam nunc exorbitent. Peto autem a T. Celsitud.
quibus possum precibus, vt Obseruationes has nostras nemini communicare
velit, cauereque, ne publicæ fiant, præsertim quantum ad Fixarum
longitudines latitudinesque attinet, quas ob id etiam, peculiari charta,
seorsim notari curaui. Nouit enim Tua Celsitudo quamA optime, quantum temporis, laboris, diligentiæ, et sumtuum requiratur,
antequam adA huius rei exactam cognitionem peruenire liceat. Et sane nulli alteri
in tota Germania, vel alibi, cuiuscunque esset conditionis, hæc mea inuenta
communicarem, suppressique ea hactenus, quamuis a multis hoc nomine
solicitatus. Plerique enim cum nihil per se egregij in his præstare velint,
aliorum inuentis et laboribus sese ornare, eaque pro suis venditare, non
sine graui autoris iniuria haud erubescunt. Verum non dubito Celsitud. Tuam
hæc sibi soli reseruaturam, quemadmodum etiam Obseruationum T. Celsit. mihi
communicatarum neminem facio participem. In tota vero hac Astronomica tractationeAmultoA plura essent, de quibus copiosius cum Tua Celsit. perlibenter agerem,
sed nec charta, nec commoditas id nunc patitur. Habeo multorum praetereaA annorum accuratas et multiplices Obseruationes, non saltem in affixis
Sideribus, sed etiam in omnibus erraticis, quotiescunque nobis aspectabiles
illuxerunt, quas præclaræ possessionis loco (nec enim paucis Vigilijs, et
exiguo labore ac diligentia comparatæ sunt) conseruo. Eas vero cum aliorum
inuentis conferre, et tandemA, in vsum publicum producereA, vt tota Astrorum scientia exacte apparentijs cælestibus satisfaciat,
elaboro. Dedi autem in mandatis huic viroA, vt Celsit. T. vel ipsius
Mathematico plura, quam nunc scribere commodum erat, meo
nomine exponeretA. Hæc vero eo prolixius ad Cels. Tuam nunc perscripsi, partim quod sciam Celsitud. T. his Astronomicis rebus
impense delectari, partim vt moram in respondendo hactenus admissam ipsa in
rescribendo copiâ recompensaremA. Ne vero modum in vtroque excedere videar, Tuamque Celsitud. nimia
prolixitate molestem, nunc finem faciam, et cætera, si quæ hîc desiderantur,
Tuæ Celsitud. Mathematico per literas
indicabo. Id saltem Tuam Celsitud. Colophonis loco humiliter et obnixe obtestorA, vt omnibus neruis hanc diuinam Astrorum scientiam a mendis, quibus
scatet, vindicare, excultioremque reddere, quod etiam suapte sponte hactenus
egregie factitauit, in posterum magis magisque conari non intermittat. Hac
enim ratione T. Celsit. apud omnem Posteritatem tam sublimem et diuinam
scientiam veneraturamA, gratissimam diutissimamque sui memoriam conseruabit, quæ eo magis
perpetua præstantiorque erit, quôd non e terrenis, et interitui obnoxijs
rebus, quas vulgus suspicit, comparata sit. Nouit Celsit.
Tua hoc studium non esse tenuioris fortunæ hominum, neque ab illis, etiamsi
quam maxime cuperent, intelligerentque, debito modo excoli posse. Cumque
nullus sit præter T. Celsit. inter omnes Europæ Principes Viros, quem Deus
hoc Heroico ingenio ornârit, vt tam arduam scientiam penitius intelligat,
eamque ab erroribus vindicare, et omnibus modis redintegrare nôrit, decet
sane Tuam Celsit. huius Principalis et Principis cognitione dignissimæ scientiæ præ
cæteris viris Principibus praecipuamA etiam curam gerere, eiusque instaurationem, et ad Posteritatem
conseruationem, omni conatuA moliri. Hoc etiam nomine Tua Celsit. suum Mathematicum CHRISTOPHORVM ROTHMANNVM, sibi præ alijs
commendatum habeat, eo quod ipsum hisce exercitijs admodum solertem et
fidelem nauare operam, ac exactæ veritatis percupidum esse indagatorem
multis indicijs cognoscam. Verum superuacanee hæc Tuæ Cels. suggero, cum sua
sponte animo sit ad res Astronomicas amplificandas propensissimo. In quo
proposito Deus admirandæ et pulcherrimæ huius machinæ cælestis author, Tuam
Celsit. quam diutissime, cum felici omnium animi et corporis bonorum
successu confirmet. Valeat Tua Cels. et mecum de hoc ipso Æthereo et sublimi
negotio vlterius conferre, suisque literis reuisere non dedignetur.Datæ Vraniburgi18. die IanuarijA, Anno 87.Tuæ Celsitudini addictissimusTYCHO BRAHE.
text.english: **To the Most Illustrious Prince and Lord, the Lord Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, Count in Catzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda: his most clement Prince and Lord — heartiest greeting.** The letter of Your Highness, Most Illustrious Prince, written to me about the spring of the year last past — in which you deigned to reply to mine — I received through the same servant of my household whom I had despatched to Your Highness; and for that clement benevolence of Your Highness toward me I humbly give thanks. As for the fact that over so great an interval of time I have answered them nothing, and have so long delayed to satisfy Your Highness's wishes — although meanwhile twice reminded on this score by other letters from Your Highness — there is no reason for Your Highness to suppose it done either through any negligence or of set purpose; rather, it was the too-great distance between our places, and the rare opportunity of sending letters thither, that have hitherto held me back from writing. For at two seasons of the year only is the more convenient occasion of writing hence toward Kassel granted — namely when our countrymen set out for the two Frankfurt fairs. Wherefore, since I had received Your Highness's letter a little after the last spring fairs, necessity compelled me to defer my answer to the autumn fairs that next followed. But when, about the time at which the merchants from here were minded to betake themselves thither for the past fairs held at Frankfurt this last autumn, I had busily arranged with a certain bookseller that a little before his departure he should meet me on this island and carry off with him the letter to be delivered to Your Highness's secretary at Kassel — which indeed he had promised, and had fully resolved to perform — it happened beyond expectation that, in those very days on which he was to come hither, the Illustrious Prince Ulrich, Duke of Mecklenburg, together with the Most Illustrious Princess the Lady Elizabeth his consort (who afterward, on the very return journey toward Mecklenburg, before she had crossed the sea, died to the great grief of all), and with his brother's son Duke Sigismund — our Most Serene Queen herself escorting them, together with a great retinue of noblemen — deigned to visit me here at Uraniborg: partly to behold at first hand the astronomical engines with which they knew this house to be filled, partly that the renowned Duke Ulrich might inspect more closely my pyronomic labours (on which I expend no less effort than on the astronomical) and the mechanical apparatus that serves them. For His Highness has these many years past taken the greatest delight in those exercises, and has by his own industry discovered things not commonplace therein, just as the Most Serene Queen his daughter is greatly devoted to these Spagyric arts — on which account too, in the past year, she did not grudge to cross this sea twice and to enter our dwelling. Since therefore at that very time, at which Your Highness should fittingly have been written back to, I was occupied in receiving these so illustrious guests; and since that bookseller, who from his promise had brought me to resolve to come to him at Copenhagen (because the royal vessels by which the crossing had to be made were procured from there), had learned of it, he changed his plan, and lest by waiting longer he should lose the time of the fairs, he — understanding me to be hindered — without coming, committed himself to his journey. Hence it came about that, beyond all expectation, I was balked of this opportune occasion of writing back to Your Highness. And since from that time no such convenience of sending a letter to Your Highness was offered me, I was forced, however unwillingly, to forbear my reply — and that right up to this present time, in which this other bookseller of ours sets out for Frankfurt to the spring fairs and has promised me his service in conveying a letter to Your Highness. These things I recount to Your Highness at the greater length on this account, that you may understand it was in no way through my negligence that I have been slower than was right in replying. I would therefore submissively ask Your Highness, for the aforesaid reasons, to interpret this delay candidly, and to hold me clemently excused in this part. And hoping that I shall, by Your Highness's singular even-temper, altogether obtain this, I shall now make use of the more opportune occasion of replying that is offered, and shall answer particularly to each head [of matter] in Your Highness's letter. As to the fact, then, that Your Highness, in the earlier letter sent me containing a reply to mine, asserts at the outset that that agreement between your mathematician's observations and mine on the comet of the year [15]85 — so exact — was greatly pleasing to you and earned a place of great weight: this indeed delighted me too in the highest degree. For nowhere do I find in the writings of other mathematicians, concerning several past comets, a like congruence with the heavens themselves and with our observations — which I do not doubt has come about through their negligence in observing and demonstrating. But the difference, if any there was between Your Highness's mathematician's remarks and ours on the said comet, arose rather from this, that we had not assumed the places of the fixed stars, whose use was required, precisely in the same scruples [minutes] — although that very discrepancy which fell between us in these matters was of the very fewest scruples, and of almost no moment, as may be seen more fully from the comparison with our places. And it was especially pleasant for me to perceive that Your Highness's mathematician detected no parallax in that same comet — just as I too was able to find either none, or scarcely any sensible one, by manifold and accurate observations. And so we plainly agree on this point, the truth of the matter itself requiring it, that this comet was generated not in the elementary orb, but in the highest ether — contrary to what hitherto the Peripatetics, and almost all philosophers, and indeed the mathematicians themselves, have asserted as settled and beyond doubt. That this too can be so, the new and miraculous star observed by Cassiopeia in earlier years has most clearly proved — even from Your Highness's own observations, with which mine fully concurred. Nay, in 4 other comets meanwhile observed we too have demonstrated, with geometrical truth from most certain observations, that none of them ran its course beneath the Moon, but that all ran it in the ether itself — so that on that account I altogether judge that all comets are generated in the heaven itself above the Moon, and that none of them was ever elementary. For as to the fact that the observations of Regiomontanus and Vögelin on two ancient comets, and the opinions of certain more recent men, show something different in these very [comets] of which we have obtained the investigation by the due instruments — we make no account of it; since [we may see] how much credit is to be placed in their observations, even in the very stars congenital with the world that we hold in view. And it is the work of a far subtler craftsman to discern parallaxes so minute — especially where the proper motion must at the same time be taken into consideration — than the manner of scrutinising the celestial appearances commonly used hitherto can supply. But of this whole argument of the comets Your Highness will more fully and sufficiently learn our opinion, grounded on our observations and on the demonstrations resting upon them, when the work which I am now preparing for the press on this very matter shall have been published for the public benefit. As to the observations transmitted to me by Your Highness (on which account too I most reverently render Your Highness many thanks): I compared them diligently, both among themselves and together with mine, and indeed in the distances themselves I find no discrepancy of any moment, but that your instrument yields the same as my sextants. Which is made manifest even from the single interval between Regulus and Spica of ♍ Virgo alone (because this observation is made near the extreme limits of the sextant, whence too the slighter angles of the intervals come out less doubtful). For this Your Highness's sextant yielded as 54 degrees 2 minutes; we found the same several times scarcely smaller by a sixth part of one minute (a difference all but imperceptible and of no weight) — the other distances of Your Highness too, when compared with ours in turn, attesting that the sextant which Your Highness has in use yields intervals sufficiently exact and congruent with the heaven itself. Yet I think this was scarcely the doing of him who first arranged its structure for Your Highness in imitation of mine, which he had seen here (a thing which he doubtless passed over in silence). For well enough known to me is his less-than-exact diligence in these mechanical matters, whether in investigating or in imitating them. And so I judge it rather to be ascribed to Your Highness's own industry, and to that of your mathematician Rothmann, and to the skill of the mechanical craftsman as well, searched out by experience itself. As to the meridian altitudes transmitted to me: in them I find some little discrepancy from my own findings, so much so that the declinations of the stars derived from them, in the northern [stars], are nearly everywhere in excess by two scruples, and in the southern fall short by as many — and this on the presupposition of an inclination of the equator of 38 degrees 40 minutes, which is found to result from that elevation of the pole which Rothmann wrote me from the double altitude of certain non-setting stars. But since I held it sufficiently established that the declinations of the stars investigated by me are neither in excess nor deficient by any minute (because they had been surely explored by five or six instruments variously constructed and of due size, such that in some a sixth part of a minute may conveniently be discerned), and since it was at the same time sufficiently certain to me that Your Highness too employs the greatest care and diligence in observations — especially those repeated by these newer instruments — at first I greatly wondered with myself whence this difference of two scruples between us should arise. Then, when I considered that the difference was almost everywhere the same, it at once came into my mind that it had easily come about that, either by the fault of sights not rightly fitted, two scruples were perceived too high in Your Highness's quadrant, or else by the error of a plumb-line not rightly set even in a single minute — which, assumed on both sides, would in the altitude both of the pole and of the meridian stars vary their declination by two scruples — or perhaps by both reasons. Which I gathered could easily come about in a two-cubit quadrant, from this: that even in ones double or triple the size, if not the most exact application be made both in the sights and in the plumb-line, an error of half, or even of a whole scruple, easily creeps in. For I did not judge this error to be imputed to a less-certain division, or to a deviant centre. I had it therefore in mind to warn Your Highness of these things by letter, that you might once more institute a more precise examination either of the sights, or of the plumb-line, or of both at once, whereby in the declinations of the stars, no less than in the distances, an exact agreement between Your Highness's observations and mine might be established. But while I am deprived of a fit occasion of sending a letter, and about the time of the Frankfurt fairs am hindered from writing for the reason mentioned, it has fallen out for me most happily and as I could wish that Your Highness's mathematician has meanwhile indicated that he detected that Your Highness's quadrant, on account of a fault in the plumb-line, showed the earlier altitudes everywhere greater by one scruple than was right. And if this is so (as I am wholly persuaded), it will follow that the elevation of the pole comes out smaller by one scruple, and that of the equator greater by as much — so that it is in truth at Kassel 38 degrees 41 minutes. If, then, the altitudes transmitted to me by Your Highness be applied to this, so that from each a single scruple be taken away on account of the plumb-line's error, they will agree quite exactly with my declinations of the stars. Wherefore I rejoiced greatly that, by this single scruple corrected in the fault of the plumb-line, another scruple far greater — clinging to my mind on account of this difference (though not so great a one) that intervened between our observations — has been taken away. For I judge that all celestial observations are to be instituted to an exact rule, so far as they fall within the human senses — so much so that if anything be wanting in them even by the least amount, I count it for null. But that Your Highness may institute a further comparison between your observations and mine, both as regards the intervals and as regards the meridian altitudes, or the declinations derived from them, I send Your Highness the distances of some stars — both others, and especially the more notable ones that lie along the zodiac — faithfully explored with my trigonic sextants (for so it has pleased to call them); and besides, certain meridian altitudes investigated with diverse quadrants, agreeing nevertheless among themselves — and that both about the end of the year [15]84 and the running [15]85, and also about the close of the lately-past [15]86 and the very beginning of this current [15]87 — that Your Highness may the more readily compare your altitudes with mine at the due times. Since indeed I in no way doubt that in these very years, after the instruments were again renewed, Your Highness has noted a more exact measurement of the altitudes of the stars. For Your Highness very well knows that the declinations of the stars, and on that account their altitudes too, vary somewhat from year to year — and that especially in those stars which are nearer to the equinoctial places. But the elevation of the equator to be employed in our altitudes of the stars comes to 34 degrees 5⅓ [minutes], because by frequent experiments I have found that the pole here at Uraniborg, in the place of my observation — which is the middle of the island of Hven, situated in that famous Danish Sound — is raised by 55 degrees 54⅔ scruples; which I have many times verified, both from the pole-star itself and from the other circumpolar non-setting stars, and from the stars that, by reason of a slope not too perceptible, exclude refraction. The longitudes and latitudes of the stars communicated to me by Your Highness I likewise compared, both among themselves and with mine, and found that that assignment, made mechanically from a globe, though not greatly disagreeing, yet does not everywhere correspond to the distances and altitudes scrupulously noted — though in some a very slight difference is found, as Your Highness can perceive from several comparisons which I have noted in the appended sheet. Nor indeed does it seem to me so very wonderful that longitudes and latitudes sought out mechanically on a globe from the distances and altitudes of the stars should not agree to the exact reckoning in the very scruples. Since I too have a great brass globe, perfectly round, which contains six feet in diameter, on which the ecliptic and the equator are finely divided into single scruples by transversal points, after the manner usual with us in the other instruments; nevertheless I scarcely promise myself everywhere a fixed certainty within one or one-and-a-half scruples in the places of the stars to be investigated by this globe from sure observations — so much do the things that are worked out mechanically, albeit with the greatest diligence, come to be set after geometrical and arithmetical exactitude. But in the very longitudes of the stars transmitted to me by Your Highness — although they be weighed by a more exact balance, geometrically and through the numbers of the sines — I observe that for the most part they are reckoned five or six scruples, or thereabouts, further from the equinox than [in] our observations. In the latitudes, however, there is found hardly a greater difference than what could be caused either from the longitudes assumed a little otherwise, or from a different determination of the obliquity of the ecliptic, but chiefly from the declinations, which differ from ours by two minutes through the fault of your plumb-line. To be sure, this difference, even of the longitudes, much less of the latitudes, is of no very great moment, if we compare the notations of certain ancients and moderns. And I cannot sufficiently wonder that Your Highness has come so close with your instruments to the places of the stars — especially since I can gather that Your Highness, in Aldebaran, or whatever other [star] you used for a foundation, detected its right ascension from its transit across the meridian, the time found by a clock and compared with the Sun. Which method always seemed to me less safe. For although I too have four such clocks of diverse size and exact structure, which indicate not only the single first scruples [minutes] but also the seconds, yet in so subtle a business I have judged it vain to place trust in them, since 4 seconds at least — which in many hours easily slip away — bring in an error of one first scruple in longitude. Add that those clocks, even though most diligently wrought from little brass wheels, are sensibly liable to the change of the air. I say nothing of the weight not being equal when it hangs higher or lower, by reason of the altered length of the cord by which it is attached, which little by little adds something to the weight — which, though very slight, yet brings in, in the seconds, a deviation not to be neglected. Wherefore, since I had perceived that this business does not succeed safely enough by this method, and was not ignorant that no slight difficulty underlies it — that even the true distance of one fixed star from the equinox might be investigated, which once known, the rest [might] either by their distances from one another, or by the equatorial differences, or even by the Hipparchan zodiacal armillae which we have in use (worked out, however, by a surer compendium than by the ancients), the rest (I say), as many as one pleased, might easily be established — and since I judged that the method which the ancients, Hipparchus above all and Ptolemy, used, and in a later age Nicolaus Copernicus, by the Moon (the partner of day and night, applied by instruments both to the Sun and to the stars), is not without its difficulties and is less exempt from error: for although we grant that the place of the Sun, with exquisite diligence applied, is, as to longitude, knowable within one or another scruple, and its interval to the Moon, and the Moon's to the stars, can be given sufficiently exactly — yet the lunar parallaxes, which are not so precisely known, in either observation bring in some variation from the truth. Add that this manner of observing is not conveniently done unless the Sun be low about the horizon, where its apparent place is other than its true place which appeared at the meridian — and that not merely by reason of parallax, but much more on account of refraction, of which I more fully indicated my opinion in my earlier letter to Your Highness; and I understand from Your Highness's reply that you too have detected, both in the Sun and in the other planets and fixed stars, a sensible refraction in the lower situation — on which account I much congratulate you over our mutual observations on both sides. For neither the ancients nor the more recent men, so far as I know, have noted this in the sightings of the stars, or duly guarded against it. This way, I say, having been laid out by our predecessors — since it was not permitted to walk safely enough along it for the aforesaid and several other reasons — I judged that I must enter upon a more convenient and safer path, which should lead to the exact longitudes of the stars; and I found none fitter and more exact than that which, from the opportunity offered us, was presented in the year 1582, when we beheld the star of Venus, being the Evening Star, clearly appearing by day. For then we observed Venus at her exact distance from the Sun, from 24 February right up to the middle of April, on more occasions than can easily be believed, in the daytime most diligently — and that not only in the Sun's lower situation, but many times when it was either at the meridian, or at least removed beyond it by one, or one-and-a-half, hours, and ♀ Venus stood very high along with it — so much so that her very transit across the meridian, with the Sun still much elevated, was many times detected by us, both as to altitude and as to distance from the Sun. Wherefore, since the place of the Sun was established sufficiently exactly both from the meridian altitudes and through the restoration of its motion made by us to the rule from the preceding years, then from the declination of Venus and of the Sun — the exquisite and mutually-agreeing distance of both being given through the sextant (so that the Sun illuminated one sight with its whole magnitude, while through the other Venus was seen on both sides through the little slits parallel to the upper cylinder) — the place of the star Venus was surely disclosed. Which place, at night-time, as soon as some one of the fixed stars near the zodiac was offered to view, applied by like reasoning through the interval taken of it from this [Venus] — account being first had of the proper motion meanwhile transacted — disclosed the place of that same star; and this was often done in diverse stars as well, since the Sun, Venus, and the fixed stars observed were almost everywhere at so great an altitude above the horizon that they excluded all refraction. And if there was sometimes any very slight one, it was guarded against from other observations made about this matter. By this infallible method, then, I attained most happily, as I wished, to an exact knowledge of the longitude of the stars at that time — manifold experiment recurring to the same result, and the distances of those same stars from one another confirming the same. I also everywhere employed the parallaxes both of the Sun and of Venus, in so far as they were varied through the intervals of the hours, that the reckoning might stand the more exact. Nay, I did not hesitate that same year to investigate the parallaxes of Venus herself, that it might more surely be clear whether she revolved about the Sun, or below it. Which thing I also dared to try in the star of Mars at the end of the previous [year] and about the beginnings of the same year, when it was seen acronychal and high in ♋ Cancer, a northern latitude too lifting it higher — that I might search out whether it produced a greater diversity of aspect [parallax] than the Sun; which would be necessary, if the Copernican hypothesis consisted in the truth of the matter. For by it Mars in opposition (☍) is rendered nearer to the Earth by almost a third part than the Sun himself. Whence too it then necessarily induces a greater diversity of parallax; and consequently the orbs of the revolutions of Mars are by no means constituted wholly above the solar orb, as the Ptolemaic hypotheses hold. And therefore either the Earth must be turned by an annual motion, by which all the epicycles of the planets are excused [done away with]; or another disposition of the celestial revolutions, than has been practised hitherto, must be sought out. But these things, now said outside my purpose, will another time, God willing, be set forth more clearly and copiously. Since therefore (to return to the matter) by the aforesaid, in no way doubtful, reckoning I had come, from the Sun through Venus in the year indicated, to a knowledge of the longitude of several of the more notable fixed stars about the zodiac (their latitude easily thrusting itself in along with it); and since from certain other observations, taken in the year [15]85 about the autumnal equinox — at which time the star of Venus, being then the Morning Star, was likewise seen by day, and that at almost a like distance from the Sun and the Earth, and likewise at a like altitude above the horizon as in the year [15]82 (which greatly furthered the certainty of the business) — I had proved all things over again the more exactly in reverse; hence I have worked to restore, as to length and breadth, the places of the remaining fixed stars too, both within and without the zodiac, and at the same time to investigate through these the appearances of all the planets, no opportunity of clear weather being hitherto let slip. Now I find in very many stars the very thing which Your Highness writes me — that they have not only longitudes other than the ancients' traditions exhibit (even with the more correct precession of the equinox added), but also latitudes much otherwise, in some less, in some indeed more — whereas it is held for ascertained, beyond all doubt, that these necessarily remain unaltered in every age from the most ancient astronomers, because the motion of the eighth sphere takes place about the poles of the ecliptic. Whence Your Highness, rightly led into wonder at that variation, clemently asks also my judgement on this matter — namely whether I deem it consonant that there is in the several fixed stars some peculiar motion of their own, by which they change their latitude too in diverse ways. On which matter I shall now set forth my opinion to Your Highness in brief. The places of all the fixed stars, from the first origin of the world, in each and all, as regards one another, I judge to remain wholly unaltered, far beyond all doubt. And this is easily proved from this: that all the fixed stars which Ptolemy enumerates in the first chapter of the seventh book — [stated] by Abrachis or Hipparchus, some 260 years before him, to have stood in one straight line — these same [stars] also in his own age remained in the same situation as regards one another. And since these same, and also those which Ptolemy afterward adds (that he might leave to posterity a handle for experimenting), are observed even in this age — 1400 years having elapsed since him — to retain exactly the very same position which the same Ptolemy enumerates (which could by no means be the case if one star changed its longitude or latitude, with respect to its own sphere, otherwise than another), it will be easy to reason that all the fixed stars subsist in the same situation, as regards themselves, in every age, without any diverse and disorderly change of latitude or longitude. But as to the fact that certain fixed stars, even among the more notable, are found which obtain a latitude much other than Hipparchus and Ptolemy noted — it is likely that this was committed partly through their less-exact observation, partly through the negligence of so many copyists who perhaps were ignorant of the subtlety of the business. For the printing art was scarcely devised before 150 years ago, and previously, over so great an interval of time, by copying so often, many things could be assigned faultily, especially in the characters of numbers — since even in this very printing art, unless diligent correction be applied, an easy slip is admitted, especially in this matter. There is added this too, that by certain proofs it is confirmed from the heavens, in very many fixed stars (especially those about the zodiac), through that change of the inclination of the ecliptic to the equator which has been made from the times of Timocharis, Hipparchus, and Ptolemy down to now, that the latitudes of all the fixed stars have likewise been successively varied, in proportion as their longitudes draw nearer or further from the tropical places. Which indeed seems wonderful, since it is otherwise surely established that the motion of the eighth sphere takes place about the poles of the ecliptic, [and] that the latitudes of the stars are not diminished otherwise than by this minute difference of the obliquity of the Zodiac-bearer [the signifer/ecliptic]. But since I understand from the letters of Your Highness's mathematician Rothmann that he is engaged in the same opinion with me in this part, I have written to him more fully about this business, and have confirmed [him] in the opinion conceived, through more certain observations of very many stars, the intervening doubts being removed. Hence Your Highness will understand some occasion of variation in the latitudes of certain stars. But if any greater one coincides, this must needs come about, as I said before, either from the ancients' less-certain notation, or from the copyists' slip. For the rest, that Your Highness may more clearly know in what situation the places of the fixed stars have been investigated by me, in the aforesaid manner, I have described the longitudes and latitudes of certain principal ones, especially those along the zodiac, which I have reduced to the beginning of this passing year, just as these have been detected by our more exact observations, that Your Highness may the more readily compare those places with your own. I have not judged it worth the trouble to add the assignment of more stars, since even from fewer — nay, from a single one rightly determined — all the rest easily become known to anyone who has convenient and sure instruments to hand. But the interval of motion from the year [15]82 (in which I obtained, as I indicated above, the fittest observations in these matters) I have borrowed neither from the Copernican change of the equinoxes (which he derived from Spica of ♍ Virgo observed, into the first star of ♈ Aries, retaining the Ptolemaic interval of longitude and without consulting the heaven), nor from the Alphonsine reckoning, but I have completed this business from the very observation of Copernicus made on the said Spica of ♍ Virgo in the year 1525, and compared with our more recent one. For since Copernicus asserts that in that year the meridian altitude of Spica was 27 degrees 0 minutes, and the pole of Frauenburg is elevated 54 degrees 22¼ minutes — as, three years ago, I had a trial made by my own exquisite instrument, through a certain student sent thither by me with the instrument [organum] — the declination of Spica was then 8 degrees 37¾ minutes; and therefore, her latitude being assumed at 1 degree 59½ minutes, such as we found (smaller only by half a scruple than Copernicus's position, which alters this business not at all, since I presuppose the same in both cases), the longitude of Spica for that time comes out at 17 degrees 14 minutes of ♎ Libra — although Copernicus himself sets it 7 scruples further on, and that doubtless by the fault of an elevation of the pole less exquisitely known, which it is credible that he investigated through the Sun, from the greatest and least altitude, by a reckoning fallacious on account of refraction in the lower situation. And since at this time Spica declines, by our observations, 8 degrees 57 minutes precisely, and, the former latitude being assumed, her longitude falls at 18 degrees 4 minutes of ♎ Libra, the eighth sphere has, from Copernicus's observation down to now, over an interval of 61 years, advanced 50 minutes. Wherefore in 73 years (provided not fewer) it accomplishes one degree in our age — whereas, nevertheless, the Copernican anticipation of the equinoxes now demands an almost slowest advance of the fixed stars, such that they accomplish a single degree in nearly a hundred years. Hence, then, it appears how much one is to adhere to the Copernican findings about the precession of the equinoxes, whereby the motion of the eighth sphere is excused (to say nothing now of the Sun and the rest) — however subtly devised by that incomparable astronomer. But the exact knowledge of the apparent motion of the eighth sphere I judge scarcely thoroughly searchable by any mortal absolutely. Since [the sphere] has as yet completed no whole revolution, and the little portions of the circuit handed down to us from Timocharis through Hipparchus, Ptolemy, Albategnius [al-Battānī], and Copernicus do not suffice — nor, if they did furnish it, do they stand scrupulously enough [consistent]. Since therefore by experience, in the aforesaid manner, the anticipation of the equinoxes about these times has become known, it was easy to transfer the proportional motion from the year [15]82 into this or any other [years] of our age. For it is not consonant that any sensible inequality in this part should occur in the lifetime of one man. But that these places of the stars still agree, my observations, made in the past year and in this very [year] from the beginning of January, sufficiently declare. As to the fact that in Your Highness's longitudes of the stars — [computed] geometrically from the intervals and declinations reduced to numbers — for the most part five or six scruples, or thereabouts, are in excess, this will easily be excused, if it be established that Your Highness then, in delimiting these, used a place of the Sun [computed] when the Sun was about the vernal equinox, in the ascending part of the ecliptic. For there, by reason of that single scruple which was caused by the plumb-line's fault, the declination of the Sun was rendered higher by two scruples than it ought to have been, and therefore its place [was] further on by five [scruples] in longitude. Which necessarily redounded also onto the fixed stars adapted to the Sun's place — although about the autumnal equinox, in the descending part of the ecliptic, this matter holds in the contrary way. But that Your Highness may see some specimen of our observations in the other wandering stars too, I add the true places of all, such as have been detected by my instruments by accurate remark within a single revolution of the primum mobile, three times in this very month of January from the beginning of the new year. Which, though it otherwise rather rarely happens, has nevertheless been done by me several times in earlier years, especially in the preceding year in October, when ☿ Mercury appeared in the east for many days. The Sun's motion, sought out from the situation of Venus through the fixed stars — since at this time of year it can less surely be had through the declinations, refraction also hindering — I have verified. For in the daytime Venus is, even before noon in these days, or at noon itself and before, seen clearly enough through the purer serenity [of the sky]. But the impediments of refraction and of the parallax of the Sun and of Venus, explored beforehand at a like altitude, I have removed. Likewise I did in Mercury too, since it was observed very low, scarcely 5 degrees high. In the rest there was no need of this delimitation, because they were taken higher up from the heavens. But I have added, for the same times of our observation, the Alphonsine and Copernican places of the planets, that Your Highness might at a single glance the more easily perceive the discrepancy of each calculation from the heaven itself — although they often go astray much more than now. But I ask Your Highness, with what prayers I can, that you be willing to communicate these our observations to no one, and to take care that they do not become public — especially as regards the longitudes and latitudes of the fixed stars, which on that account too I had noted separately, on a sheet of their own. For Your Highness knows full well how much time, labour, diligence, and expense is required before one may attain an exact knowledge of this matter. And indeed to no other in all Germany, or elsewhere, of whatever condition he might be, would I communicate these my findings; and I have suppressed them hitherto, although solicited by many on this score. For most men, since they will themselves perform nothing excellent in these matters, do not blush to adorn themselves with the findings and labours of others, and to vend them as their own, not without grave injury to the author. But I doubt not that Your Highness will reserve these for yourself alone — just as I too make no one a sharer of the observations communicated to me by Your Highness. But in all this astronomical treatment there would be much more, on which I would most gladly treat more copiously with Your Highness — but neither the paper nor the convenience now permits it. I have besides accurate and manifold observations of many years, not only in the fixed stars, but also in all the wandering ones, as often as they shone visible to us, which I preserve in the place of a glorious possession (for they have been procured by no few vigils, and by no small labour and diligence). And I am working to compare these with the findings of others, and at length to bring them forth for the public use, that the whole science of the stars may exactly satisfy the celestial appearances. And I have given it in charge to this man, that he should set forth to Your Highness, or to your mathematician, in my name, more things than it was convenient now to write. These things I have now written to Your Highness the more at length, partly because I know that Your Highness takes intense delight in these astronomical matters, partly that I might recompense the delay hitherto admitted in replying by the very copiousness in writing back. But lest I seem to exceed measure in both, and burden Your Highness with too great prolixity, I shall now make an end, and shall indicate the rest — if anything here be wanting — to Your Highness's mathematician by letter. This one thing at least, in the place of a colophon, I humbly and earnestly beseech of Your Highness: that with all your sinews you not cease to strive, more and more hereafter, to vindicate this divine science of the stars from the faults with which it teems, and to render it more cultivated — which indeed you have hitherto, of your own accord, done excellently. For in this way Your Highness will preserve, among all posterity that shall venerate so sublime and divine a science, a most welcome and most lasting memory of yourself — which will be the more perpetual and excellent because it is procured not from earthly things, liable to perishing, which the common crowd looks up to. Your Highness knows that this study is not for men of slenderer fortune, nor can it be cultivated by them in the due manner, even if they should most greatly desire it and understand it. And since there is none besides Your Highness, among all the princely men of Europe, whom God has adorned with this heroic genius, so as to understand so arduous a science more deeply, and to know how to vindicate it from errors and to restore it by every means — it surely becomes Your Highness, before other princely men, to bear an especial care of this science (most worthy of a princely and of a prince's knowledge), and to strive with all effort at its restoration and its preservation to posterity. On this account too let Your Highness hold your mathematician Christoph Rothmann commended before others, because I recognise by many tokens that he bestows in these exercises a most skilful and faithful labour, and is a most eager investigator of the exact truth. But I suggest these things to Your Highness superfluously, since of your own accord you are of a mind most inclined to the enlarging of astronomical matters. In which purpose may God, the author of this admirable and most beautiful celestial machine, confirm Your Highness as long as possible, with a happy issue of all the goods of mind and body. May Your Highness fare well, and not disdain to confer further with me about this very ethereal and sublime business, and to revisit me with your letters. Given at Uraniborg, the 18th day of January, in the year [15]87. Most devoted to Your Highness, Tycho Brahe.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** Tycho Brahe at **Uraniborg** (on Hven) → **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), the astronomer-prince whose Kassel observatory was Tycho's principal scientific correspondent. The opening titulature lists his comital styles — *Catzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, Nidda* — kept as in the source.
- **Edition of record.** Printed by Tycho himself as Letter [I] in the *Epistolarum astronomicarum liber primus* (Uraniborg 1596); reprinted in Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VI. MS witness given in the edition: Vienna, ÖNB Cod. Vindob. lat. 10689.10.
- **DATELINE CRUX (header date).** The body subscription reads **"Datae Vraniburgi 18. die Ianuarij, Anno 87"** = **18 January 1587 (O.S.)**. The edition's label/catalogue field reads "1587. 1. januar." (1 January). Per this chapter's convention, the header follows the **as-written dateline (18 January)** and appends the catalogued date. The body text independently corroborates a mid-/late-January writing: Tycho says the new observations were "detected... three times in this very month of January from the beginning of the new year" and reduced "to the beginning of this passing year [15]87" — consistent with the 18th, not the 1st. The "1 January" label is most likely a catalogue normalisation to the year-start, not a substantiated dateline; the discrepancy is flagged, not reconciled. **Calendar:** O.S. (Julian); Denmark and Hesse both kept Old Style in 1587.
- **Textual note — the stray capital "A".** Throughout the source block, isolated uppercase **A** characters appear attached to or following words (e.g. *S. P.A*, *accepiA*, *responderimA*, *Anno 1582A*). These are **apparatus/footnote anchor artifacts** carried over from the digitised critical-edition base (Dreyer's variant-note sigla), not part of Tycho's Latin. They are reproduced **as printed** in the Source block by this chapter's convention(2) and silently disregarded in the Translation. Likewise *tCelsitud.* (for *Celsitud.*) and the run-together final lines (*Datae Vraniburgi18. die...*) are transcription artifacts of the base file; word-spacing is restored only in the translation.
- **Persons.** *Ulrich, Duke of Mecklenburg* (Udalricus Dux Megapolensis, 1527–1603) and his consort *Elizabeth* (Elizabeth of Denmark, 1524–1586, sister of Frederik II — her recently-reported death "to the great grief of all" dates the visit to 1586); *Duke Sigismund* (Sigismund August of Mecklenburg, the brother's son). *"Our Most Serene Queen"* = **Sophie of Mecklenburg**, queen of Denmark, daughter of Duke Ulrich (hence Tycho's "the Most Serene Queen his daughter"). *Christoph Rothmann* (Christophorus Rothmannus) = Wilhelm IV's mathematician at Kassel, repeatedly named. *Regiomontanus* and *Vögelin* (Johannes Vogelin) — 15th–16th-c. cometary observers. *Copernicus*, *Ptolemy*, *Hipparchus* (*Abrachis* = Arabic-derived form of Hipparchus), *Timocharis*, *Albategnius* (al-Battānī) — the chain of authorities for the eighth-sphere motion.
- **Places.** *Cassellae* → **Kassel**; *Haffnia* → **Copenhagen**; *Francofurtum / Nundinae Francofordianae* → **Frankfurt / the Frankfurt (book-)fairs**; *Fruenburgum* → **Frauenburg/Frombork** (Copernicus's observing site); *Fretum Danicum* → **the Danish Sound** (Øresund); *Insula Huena* → **the island of Hven**.
- **Astronomical technical terms** (per glossary–5.2): *parallaxis* → **parallax**; *refractio* → **refraction**; *declinatio* → **declination**; *ascensio recta* → **right ascension**; *longitudo/latitudo* → **(celestial) longitude/latitude**; *eleuatio Poli / Aequatoris* → **elevation of the pole / of the equator**; *altitudo Meridiana* → **meridian altitude**; *praecessio aequinoctiorum / anticipatio aequinoctiorum* → **precession / anticipation of the equinoxes**; *octaua Sphaera* → **the eighth sphere**; *primi mobilis reuolutio* → **a revolution of the primum mobile**; *aspectus diuersitas* (here = parallax in the older idiom) → **diversity of aspect [parallax]**, flagged; *acronychus* → **acronychal** (rising at sunset, opposite the Sun); *restitutio (motus)* → **restoration (of the motion)**; *instauratio* → **restoration** (Tycho's programme,). Instruments: *Sextans (Trigonicus)* → **(trigonic) sextant**; *Quadrans bicubitalis* → **two-cubit quadrant**; *pinnacidia / pinnulae* → **sights**; *perpendiculum* → **plumb-line**; *Armillae Hipparchicae Zodiacales* → **Hipparchan zodiacal armillae**; *Globus Orichalcicus* → **brass globe**; *Organum* → **instrument**; *Horologia* → **clocks**.
- **Units.** *partes / gradus* → **degrees**; *scrupula prima* → **(first) scruples** = arcminutes; *scrupula secunda* → **seconds (of arc/time)**. Tycho uses *scrupulum* for both arcminute and, of clocks, second; rendered "scruple(s)" with a bracketed gloss "[minutes]" at first occurrence, per the source's own usage, not silently modernised.
- **Astrology / hypothesis.** *Coperniana Hypothesis / Hypotheses Ptolemaicae* → **the Copernican hypothesis / the Ptolemaic hypotheses**. The Mars-parallax passage is the celebrated test that led Tycho away from both pure systems toward his own; *"vel rotari Terram annuo motu… vel aliam… dispositionem"* preserves his open, hedged disjunction ("either… or…") — not silently resolved to the geo-heliocentric system he had not yet here announced.
- **Symbols (named in translation, glyph kept in Source):** **♍** Virgo, **♎** Libra, **♈** Aries, **♋** Cancer, **♀** Venus, **☿** Mercury, **☍** opposition. Per.
- **"Pyronomic / Spagyric" passage.** *Pyronomici labores* → **pyronomic labours** (fire-/furnace-craft, i.e. distillation/alchemy at Uraniborg); *Artificia Spagyrica* → **Spagyric arts** (Paracelsian chemistry) — period terms kept, not modernised to "chemistry."
- **Numeric readings carried verbatim** (not "corrected"): Regulus–Spica interval 54° 2′; Kassel equator-inclination 38° 40′, corrected in-letter to 38° 41′ after the one-scruple plumb-line fault; Uraniborg pole-height 55° 54⅔′ and equator-elevation 34° 5⅓′; Frauenburg pole 54° 22¼′; Copernicus's Spica meridian altitude 27° 0′ and declination 8° 37¾′, latitude 1° 59½′, longitude ♎ 17° 14′ (Tycho) vs. 7′ further (Copernicus); Tycho's own Spica declination 8° 57′, longitude ♎ 18° 4′; eighth-sphere advance 50′ over 61 years → 1° per 73 years. The fractions (⅓, ⅔, ¼, ¾, ½) are reproduced as in the base text.
- **No negations added or dropped.** The courtesy-laden excuse-clauses (*"non est quod… existimet, vel incuria… vel data opera factum esse"*; *"nullatenus dubitem"*; *"nemini communicare velit, cauereque ne publicae fiant"*) were each counted and reproduced with the same polarity; the secrecy request and the "to no one… would I communicate" pledge are rendered without weakening.
