text.original:
CLARISSIMO VIRTUTE ET ERUDITIONE PRÆEMINENTI VIRO D. DOCTORI THADDÆO HAGECIO AB HAYK, MATHEMATICO ET MEDICO INPRIMIS EXCELLENTI, AMICO SUO PERPETUO COLENDISSIMO.
ZU PRAG.
S.

REMITTO tibi nunc tandem, eruditiss. amantissimeque D. THADÆE, doctas et ingeniosas illas tuas de Nova Stella et Cometis aliquot lucubrationes, quas Francofurtum ad hasce proxime instantes vernales Nundinas (ut illinc per eundem Bibliopolam Gallum, de quo mihi significasti, ad te procurentur, vel, si is officium hac in re detrectârit, ut per hunc ipsum, cui eas tradidi, negotium hoc apud aliquem certum hominem expediatur) perferendas curavi. Quod vero eas nunc tua expectatione proprioque meo proposito tardius hunc tuum foetum recipias, nuntiorum penuria in causa fuit; rarissime enim aliquis hinc ad vos proficiscitur, et, cum nulla commodior daretur occasio, volebam praeteritis autumnalibus nundinis Francofordensibus idem praestitisse, et ob id cum quodam nostratium Bibliopolarum illuc ad dictas nundinas quotannis proficiscentium egeram, ut is hîc ante suum discessum me conveniret secumque librum tuum unâ cum meis literis Francofurto ad te mittendum asportaret; nam et ipsi etiam literas ad Illustriss. Principem Landgravium Hassiae ipsiusque Cels. Mathematicum ROTHMANNUM, ubi Cassellas pertransiret, expediendas unâ committere volebam; ille vero, mihi suam operam hac in re non gravatim promittens, omnino me ante discessum suum accedere constituerat. Verum accidit ijs ipsis diebus, quibus illi huc veniendum erat, ut Illustribus hospitibus, utpote Regina ipsa denuo me invisente et secum utrumque parentem adducente unâ cum duce SIGISMUNDO, patrui filio, magnoque nobilium virorum comitatu, excipiendis occuparer, quod ille ubi cognoverat, et iam iam dies illi instarent, quibus sine mora abeundum erat, me non accedens itineri se unâ cum socijs commisit. Hinc itaque eveniebat, ut, hac commoditate librum tuum remittendi mihi tunc praerepta, usque in hoc tempus illum mecum retinere coactus fuerim, quemadmodum etiam Illustrissimo Principi Landtgravio hanc meam iustam excusationem, quod etiam ipsius Celsitudinis votis in rescribendo tardius satisfaciam, proxime elapsis diebus per literas indicavi. Perlegi autem hunc tuum librum non sine voluptate et diligentia, tuumque in hac materia indefessum studium pari labore et industria coniunctum commendatione dignissimum censeo. Essent quidem nonnulla, quae paulo enucleatius forent constituenda, si observationes exactae unâ cum otio tibi suppeterent, sed sunt ea utplurimum eiuscemodi, quae non facile cuivis obvia occurrant, nec usque adeo magni momenti exsistunt. Quod nullae ex omnibus illis eruditis et ingeniosis alias satis, quibus Parallaxes indagare doces, rationibus motui proprio Cometarum (quo rarissime carent) satisfaciant, existimo, me in ultimis ad te datis literis admonuisse; quare alia erit Parallaxium a motu Cometarum proprio separatarum instituenda ratiocinatio, si non solum speculative, sed etiam in ipsa praxi veritatis scopum collimatius attingere intendamus; quod tibiipsi ulterius expendendum considerandumque relinquo. Stellarum Cassiopeae tum a se invicem, tum etiam a Nova illa Stella remotiones paulo aliter se habent, quam tui etiam correctiores et reiterati numeri exhibent; sic etiam distantia polaris stellae ab 11a Cassiopeae, pro qua tantum laborasti, 9 scrupulis in tua annotatione abundat. Nequaquam omnino per Radium Astronomicum exquisitae et ipsi coelo congruae stellarum distantiae ulla adhibita diligentia capi possunt, quacunque tandem longitudine et divisionum subtilitate Radius ille praeditus sit, ut alio loco certis rationibus confirmabo, ubi, favente Numine, opus nostrum de prima et Mechanica Astronomiae parte absolutum fuerit et publicae utilitati communicatum. Ut enim ipsissima stellarum intercapedo obtineatur, necesse est utramque stellam bifariam per rimulas, quae lineas visuales a superiori pinnacidio ubique paralelas efficiunt, centraliter intueri. Quod nequaquam Radio praestari potest, ideoque nova quaedam organa, quae huic incertitudini praeveniant et stellarum exactas infallibilesque remotiones exhibeant, iam dudum excogitavi, quorum fabricam et usum in praenominato opere aliquando (Deo conatus nostros secundante) perspicies. Declinatio Novi Sideris a te constituta 4 ad minus scrupulis iusto maior est, et ratio inquirendi eius longitudinem e tempore transitus per Meridianum non caret evidentibus obstaculis; difficillime enim exactissima illa temporis momenta cognita veniunt, et licet hoc magna adhibita industria possibile concedamus, nihilominus Solis locus vel ex ipso COPERNIANO calculo depromtus huic negotio non sufficit, siquidem Solari in coelo cursui nequaquam congruus existit, ut ex ea, quae in Diario isto, quod a nobilibus Gallis accepisti, reperitur, restitutione colligere potes. Oportuit etiam affixarum stellarum loca, quorum usus in Stella illa Nova et Cometis requirebatur, prius per certas observationes emendata habere, ut ea, quae superstruerentur, rectius constarent; quod dum non solum a te omnibusque fere alijs hactenus neglectum est, sed etiam a me in tractatulo nostro de Stella illa Nova dudum edito praetermissum, factum est, ut scopum ipsum in certis et exactis longitudinibus latitudinibusque et ijs, quae hinc derivari possunt, cognoscendis non satis praecise in Stella illa Nova attigerimus. Horum verum a me emendationem in opere, quod nunc de tota hac materia impressioni adorno, brevi, Deo volente, invenies. Si itaque tua omnino edere decrevisti (in quo proposito ut perseveres, potius autor quam dissuasor esse velim), percuperem, ne quid ex meo illo libello adiungeres, cum omnia correctiora et elimatiora sim propediem in lucem emissurus. In Cometa anni 1577 videris non eandem quam in Nova Stella adhibuisse diligentiam, licet teipsum postea in alio quodam scripto oportune correxeris. Nam plane exigua et fere insensibilis illi Cometae aderat Parallaxis, et rectissime omnium de eo scripsit MÆSTLINUS, ut ob id immerito illum in quibusdam taxes. Ratio illa observandi per filum in directum ad stellas extensum non quidem exactae certitudini satisfacit, nihilominus si exquisita et nulli fallaciae obnoxia organa in promtu non sunt, dubijs et incertis imo ipsi Radio quamoptime elaborato hanc filarem observandi rationem anteferrem. Sed de his suo loco et tempore copiosius. TRAPEZUNTIJ in PTOLOMÆUM introductionem an quispiam sit Typographorum Francofurtum venientium, qui eam typis edere velit, expiscari curo. Interea librum illum mecum conservo, quod bona tua venia fieri non diffido. Et quia constitui (Deo favente) proxima instante aestate in Germaniam excurrere (modo veniam a Sereniss. Rege nostro, uti spero, impetravero), cumque tunc quamprimum Cassellis (ubi Principem Landtgravium ob commune hoc studium convenire decrevi) discessero, Francofurtum me conferre in votis habeo idque circa tempus autumnalium Nundinarum. Ideo, si TRAPEZUNTINA illa editio prius non successerit, inter alia librum illum mecum accipiam eiusque publicationem omni conatu tunc procurabo, quod eam etiam ob causam tibi nunc indicare volui, ut, si forte res tuae ita ferrent, quod in illa mea excursione alicubi in vobis vicina Germania vel Lipsiae aut Dresdae simul convenire possimus, interea tecum de hoc deliberare possis; nihil enim mihi gratius eveniret, quam si facultas daretur, ut quemadmodum Ratisbonae olim nunc iterum alicubi vel pauculis diebus nos invicem gratis sermonibus coram complecti possemus. Tuum itaque erit mature aliquid certi hac in re statuere et mihi tuam voluntatem prima quaque occasione significare. Pragam in illo itinere accedere vix mihi commodum erit; etiamsi enim omnia votis meis successerint, non tamen ante initia Iulij hinc discedere statui, et ante hyemem in patriam mihi necessario ad mea revertendum erit. Tu itaque da operam, ut medium aliquod inveniatur, quo votis nostris utrinque (nam et te idipsum exoptare non dubito) satisfiat, mecumque tuam mentem in his quam primum (ut prius etiam rogavi) communica. Existimo, me tibi ultimo misisse exemplar quoddam Literarum Illustriss. Principis WILHELMI, Landtgravij Hassiae, quibus meis respondebat, unâ etiam cum Mathematici ipsius Celsitudinis CHRISTOPHORI ROTHMANNI literis. Et quia semel atque iterum ab eodem Principe de responsione sollicitatus sum, eo quod easdem ob causas, quibus tibi etiam hactenus scribere non licuit, hanc multo tempore differre coactus fuerim, proxime idcirco elapsis diebus, nactus iam tandem commodam occasionem, ipsius Celsitudini rescripsi; quare, ut meum etiam hoc responsum cum prioribus Principis huius literis conferre possis, adiunxi hîc illius exemplar, praesertim cum eam inprimis materiam contineat, qua te plurimum affici compertum habeo. Addidissem quoque exemplar meae ad ROTHMANNI literas responsionis, verum, cum is, per quem nunc hasce mitto, abitum festinet, eo quod Cimbriam, patriam suam, ante Nundinarum illarum Francofordensium accessum invisere constituerit, non relinquebatur nobis tantum temporis, ut descriptionem eius fieri curare concederetur, ipsa etiam prolixitate, qua Landtgravianas literas fere in duplo excedunt, pro hac tanta otij penuria idipsum non admittente; sed haec et alia suo tempore commodius fortassis obtinebis. Cumque nunc charta deficiens scribendi finem facere admoneat, pluribus supersedeo, teque, charissime THADÆE, cum tota familia Deo omnium rerum autori commendo. Is te quam diutissime conservet animo corporeque incolumem. Vale et prima quaque oblata occasione rescribe. Iterum quam felicissime vale. Datae Uraniburgi die 25. Ianuarij Anno 1587.

Tuus
TYCHO BRAHE.

Boni consule has raptim exaratas et incertas literas, quas recognoscere, nedum rescribere nuncij festinatio non admittebat.
text.english:
**To the most distinguished man, pre-eminent in virtue and learning, Master Doctor Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayk, mathematician and physician especially excellent, his perpetual and most honoured friend.**
**At Prague.**
**Greeting.**

I now at last send back to you, most learned and most beloved Master Thaddaeus, those learned and ingenious lucubrations of yours on the New Star and on several comets, which I have arranged to have conveyed to Frankfurt for this spring fair now next at hand (so that from there they may be procured for you by the same French bookseller of whom you informed me; or, should he decline the office in this matter, so that this business may be dispatched through this very man to whom I have handed them, by way of some trustworthy person). That you now receive back this offspring of yours later than your own expectation and my own intention, the scarcity of messengers was the cause; for very rarely does anyone set out from here to your parts, and, since no more convenient occasion offered, I had wished to have done the same at the past autumn fair at Frankfurt, and on that account I had dealt with a certain one of our [Danish] booksellers who travel there to the said fair every year, that he should call on me here before his departure and carry off with him your book together with my letters, to be sent from Frankfurt to you; for I wished at the same time to entrust to him also letters to be dispatched to the Most Illustrious Prince, the Landgrave of Hesse, and to his Highness's mathematician Rothmann, when he should pass through Kassel; and he indeed, promising me his service in this matter not grudgingly, had quite resolved to come to me before his departure. But it happened in those very days on which he was to come here that I was occupied in receiving illustrious guests — namely, the Queen herself visiting me again and bringing both her parents with her, along with Duke Sigismund, her uncle's son, and a great retinue of noblemen — and when he learned this, and the days were now pressing upon him on which he had to leave without delay, he, not calling on me, committed himself to the journey along with his companions. Hence, then, it came about that, this convenience of sending your book back having then been snatched from me, I was forced to keep it with me right up to this present time — just as also I made known this just excuse of mine to the Most Illustrious Prince the Landgrave, in letters a few days ago now, [namely] that I am satisfying his Highness's wishes too somewhat tardily in replying. I have, however, read this book of yours through, not without pleasure and diligence, and I judge your tireless zeal in this subject, joined with equal labour and industry, most worthy of commendation. There would indeed be some points which would need to be established a little more clearly, if exact observations together with leisure were available to you; but these are for the most part of such a kind as do not easily come to anyone's notice, nor are they of such great moment. That none of all those learned and ingenious methods otherwise sufficient, by which you teach how to track down parallaxes, satisfy the proper motion of comets (which they very rarely lack), I think I pointed out in my last letter sent to you; wherefore another reckoning of parallaxes separated from the proper motion of comets will have to be instituted, if we mean to attain the mark of truth more pointedly not only speculatively but also in the very practice [of it] — which I leave to you yourself for further weighing and consideration. The distances of the stars of Cassiopeia, both from one another and also from that New Star, stand somewhat otherwise than even your corrected and repeated figures present them; so too the distance of the pole star from the 11th [star] of Cassiopeia, over which you laboured so much, is in your annotation in excess by 9 minutes [scruples]. By no means at all can the exact distances of stars, congruent with the heaven itself, be taken by the cross-staff (radius astronomicus) with any diligence applied, with whatever length and fineness of divisions that staff be at last endowed — as I shall confirm in another place with sure reasons, when, by the favour of the Deity, our work on the first and Mechanical part of astronomy shall have been completed and communicated to the public good. For in order that the very interval of the stars be obtained, it is necessary to look at each star centrally, in two parts, through little slits which everywhere make the lines of sight parallel from the upper sight (pinnule); and this can by no means be furnished by the cross-staff. And therefore I devised long ago certain new instruments, which forestall this uncertainty and exhibit the exact and infallible distances of the stars — whose construction and use you will at some time perceive in the aforesaid work (God seconding our efforts). The declination of the New Star, as established by you, is greater than is right by at least 4 minutes [scruples], and the method of inquiring after its longitude from the time of its transit across the meridian is not free of evident obstacles; for those most exact moments of time become known only with the greatest difficulty, and although we grant this possible with great industry applied, nonetheless the Sun's place, even when drawn from the Copernican calculation itself, does not suffice for this business, since it is by no means congruent with the Sun's course in the heaven — as you can gather from that restoration which is found in that Diary which you received from the noble Frenchmen. It was also necessary to have the places of the fixed stars — whose use was required in that New Star and in the comets — first emended through sure observations, so that the things to be built upon them might stand more correctly; and while this has hitherto been neglected not only by you and by almost all others, but was also passed over by me in our little treatise on that New Star published long ago, it came about that we did not attain the mark itself precisely enough, in the case of that New Star, in coming to know the sure and exact longitudes and latitudes and the things that can be derived from them. But you will shortly find, God willing, the emendation of these things by me, in the work which I am now dressing for the press concerning this whole subject. If therefore you have quite resolved to publish your [writings] (and in that purpose I would rather be your encourager than your dissuader, that you persevere in it), I would greatly wish that you add nothing from that little book of mine, since I am about very soon to send into the light everything in more corrected and more polished form. In the comet of the year 1577 you seem not to have applied the same diligence as in the New Star, although you afterwards opportunely corrected yourself in some other writing. For that comet had a plainly minute and almost imperceptible parallax, and of all men Maestlin wrote about it most correctly, so that on that account you undeservedly censure him in certain points. That method of observing by a thread stretched straight out toward the stars does not indeed satisfy exact certainty; nonetheless, if exquisite instruments not liable to any deception are not at hand, I would prefer this thread-method of observing to dubious and uncertain ones — indeed even to the cross-staff however excellently wrought. But of these things more copiously in their place and time. Whether there be any of the printers coming to Frankfurt who may be willing to publish it in type, I am taking care to fish out — [I mean] Trebizond's introduction to Ptolemy. Meanwhile I keep that book with me, which I do not doubt may be done by your good leave. And since I have resolved (God favouring) to make an excursion into Germany this coming summer (provided I obtain leave, as I hope, from our Most Serene King), and since then, as soon as I shall have departed from Kassel (where I have determined to meet the Prince Landgrave on account of this common study), it is among my wishes to betake myself to Frankfurt, and that around the time of the autumn fair: therefore, if that Trebizond edition shall not have succeeded beforehand, I shall among other things take that book with me and then procure its publication with every effort — which I wished to indicate to you now for this reason too, that, if perhaps your affairs should so bear it, [namely] that in that excursion of mine we might be able to meet together somewhere in the Germany neighbouring you, or at Leipzig or Dresden, you might in the meantime be able to deliberate with me about this; for nothing more welcome could befall me than if the opportunity were given that, just as once at Regensburg, so now again we might somewhere, even for a very few days, embrace one another in person with pleasing discourse. It will therefore be for you to settle something certain in this matter in good time, and to signify your will to me at the very first occasion. To approach Prague on that journey will scarcely be convenient for me; for even though everything succeed according to my wishes, I have nonetheless resolved not to depart from here before the beginning of July, and before winter I shall necessarily have to return home to my affairs. Do you therefore see to it that some middle way be found by which our wishes on both sides may be satisfied (for I do not doubt that you yourself long for the very same thing), and communicate your mind to me on these matters as soon as possible (as I asked before too). I think I sent you last time a certain copy of the letter of the Most Illustrious Prince Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, by which he was replying to mine, together also with the letter of his Highness's mathematician Christoph Rothmann. And because I have been solicited once and again by the same Prince concerning a reply — since, for the same reasons by which I have been hitherto unable to write to you also, I was compelled to defer this for a long time — therefore a few days ago now, having at last got a convenient occasion, I wrote back to his Highness; wherefore, so that you may be able to compare this reply of mine too with the earlier letters of this Prince, I have here appended a copy of it, especially since it contains in particular that subject by which I have found that you are very much affected. I would have added too a copy of my reply to Rothmann's letter; but, since the man through whom I now send these things hastens his departure — because he has resolved to visit Cimbria, his homeland, before the approach of that Frankfurt fair — there was not left to us so much time that the making of a transcription of it could be allowed, the very length too (by which they exceed the Landgrave's letters by nearly double) not admitting of this, given so great a scarcity of leisure; but these and other things you will perhaps obtain more conveniently in their time. And since now the failing paper warns [me] to make an end of writing, I forbear from more, and commend you, dearest Thaddaeus, with your whole household, to God the author of all things. May He keep you as long as possible unharmed in mind and body. Farewell, and write back at the very first occasion offered. Again, most happily, farewell. Given at Uraniborg, the 25th day of January, the year 1587.

Yours,
Tycho Brahe.

Take in good part this letter, hastily scrawled and uncertain, which the messenger's haste did not permit me to revise, let alone to rewrite.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** *Tycho Brahe*, writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven. The addressee, *Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayk* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius, 1525–1600), the Bohemian physician, astronomer, and personal physician at the imperial court in **Prague**; like Tycho he had observed and written on the 1572 New Star and on comets, and the two had met at the Regensburg imperial diet of 1575 (the *Ratisbonae olim* of the letter). The superscription's *ZU PRAG* ("at Prague") is a German code-switch within an otherwise Latin address; preserved by this chapter's convention
- **Salutation.** *S.* = *salutem* ("greeting"), this chapter's convention
- **Persons named.** *Illustriss. Princeps Wilhelmus, Landgravius Hassiae* = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel**; his court *Mathematicus Christophorus Rothmannus* = **Christoph Rothmann**. *Maestlinus* = **Michael Maestlin** (1550–1631), the Tübingen astronomer (later Kepler's teacher), whose treatment of the 1577 comet Tycho here defends against Hagecius's criticism. *Trapezuntius* = **George of Trebizond** (Giorgio da Trebisonda, 1396–1486), whose Latin commentary/"introduction" to Ptolemy's *Almagest* Hagecius wished to see printed at Frankfurt. *Dux Sigismundus, patrui filius* = a **Duke Sigismund**, named as the cousin ("son of [the Queen's] paternal uncle") in the royal visiting party; *Regina ipsa … utrumque parentem adducente* refers to **Queen Sophie of Denmark** (of Mecklenburg) bringing both her parents (Duke Ulrich III of Mecklenburg and Duchess Elisabeth) — the Mecklenburg ducal house, to which Sigismund belonged.
- **Places.** *Francofurtum / Francofordenses Nundinae* = **Frankfurt** and its **book fair** (*Nundinae*, "the fair," held spring and autumn). *Cassellae* = **Kassel**. *Lipsia* = **Leipzig**; *Dresda* = **Dresden**; *Ratisbona* = **Regensburg**. *Cimbria* = **Cimbria**, the Jutland/Holstein region of the messenger's homeland (rendered as the Latin name).
- **Technical terms (per glossary–5.2).** *Parallaxis* → **parallax**; *motus proprius (Cometarum)* → **proper motion (of comets)**; *Declinatio* → **declination**; *longitudo / latitudo* → **longitude / latitude**; *transitus per Meridianum* → **transit across the meridian**; *affixae stellae* → **fixed stars**; *organa / nova organa* → **instruments / new instruments**; *Radius Astronomicus* → **cross-staff (radius astronomicus)**; *pinnacidium* → **sight (pinnule)**. *Stella Nova* / *Novum Sidus* → **the New Star** (the supernova of 1572 in Cassiopeia). *Cometa anni 1577* → **the comet of 1577**.
- ***scrupulis*** — *scrupulum* here = **minute of arc**; "9 scruples / 4 scruples" rendered "9 minutes / at least 4 minutes [scruples]," keeping the period term in brackets. The discrepancies Tycho cites (the pole-star/11th-Cassiopeiae distance "in excess by 9 minutes"; the New Star's declination "greater than is right by at least 4 minutes") are his own corrections to Hagecius's figures and are reported, not adjudicated.
- ***opus nostrum de prima et Mechanica Astronomiae parte*** — Tycho's projected great work on the "first and Mechanical part of astronomy"; *Mechanica* here is the planned instrument-and-method volume (cf. the later *Astronomiae instauratae Mechanica*, 1598). *opere, quod nunc … impressioni adorno* = the work "now dressing for the press" on the New Star — the *Astronomiae instauratae Progymnasmata*, then in preparation. *tractatulus noster de Stella illa Nova dudum editus* = Tycho's "little treatise on that New Star published long ago," i.e. *De nova stella* (1573). Per this chapter's convention, *restitutio* (of the Sun's place) → **restoration**.
- ***Diario isto, quod a nobilibus Gallis accepisti*** — "that Diary which you received from the noble Frenchmen": an ephemeris/diary containing a solar restoration; the "noble Frenchmen" are not further identified in the letter and are left unidentified here (no silent expansion).
- ***ratio observandi per filum*** — Hagecius's "thread-method" of observation (sighting along a thread stretched toward the stars); kept as described. Tycho's qualified judgment — that he would prefer it to a poorly made cross-staff *if* better instruments are unavailable — is preserved with its conditional intact.
- **Epistemic hedges preserved.** Tycho's recurrent qualifiers are kept verbatim in force: *Deo favente / Deo volente / favente Numine / Deo conatus nostros secundante* ("God favouring / God willing / by the favour of the Deity / God seconding our efforts"); *uti spero* ("as I hope"); *fortassis* ("perhaps"); *vix mihi commodum erit* ("will scarcely be convenient"). None is flattened to plain assertion.
- **Closing formulae.** *Vale … Iterum quam felicissime vale* → **"Farewell … Again, most happily, farewell"**. *Datae Uraniburgi* → **"Given at Uraniborg."** The postscript *Boni consule …* is a self-deprecating apology for a "hastily scrawled" (*raptim exaratas*) letter the messenger's haste left unrevised.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 25. Ianuarij Anno 1587* — **25 January 1587**, Old Style (Denmark used the Julian calendar until 1700; this chapter's convention). The catalogue label ("1587. 25. januar. Uraniborg") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy. No date is converted.
- **Language.** Latin throughout (the heuristic tag *la* is correct on reading), with two non-Latin tokens: the German address *ZU PRAG* and the place-name *Cimbria*. No Greek occurs in this letter.
- **Correction.** Latin text-error fixed: 'nuntiorum penuriam causa fuit' restored to Dreyer's 'nuntiorum penuria in causa fuit' (TBOO VII, p.111); the English translation was already correct and unaffected.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter (TBOO VII pp. 110-115) against Dreyer's page images. Checked the opening and closing formulas and every proper name, number, date and place-name: SIGISMUNDO, 9 scrupulis (pole-star/Cassiopeia distance), 4 scrupulis (New Star declination), ROTHMANNUM, WILHELMI Landtgravii Hassiae, Lipsiae/Dresdae/Ratisbonae, Cimbriam, TRAPEZUNTIJ/PTOLOMAEUM, 25 Ianuarii 1587 — all match Dreyer exactly, and the closing farewell and postscript ("Boni consule...") match verbatim. The translation is faithful and complete throughout. The sole defect is a the transcribed original/Dreyer divergence (text error) in the messenger-scarcity clause on p.110-111; it does not change what a scholar would take from the English, but per the grading rule any text error caps the grade at C.

**1 defect found:**
- **text error** (low). Our Latin drops the word "in" and turns "penuria" into "penuriam", corrupting Dreyer's idiomatic "in causa fuit" ("was the cause") into an ungrammatical phrase; the English translation itself renders the intended sense correctly and is unaffected. Dreyer prints: *nuntiorum penuria in causa fuit*.

**Repaired.** Verified TBOO VII p.111 directly from the Dreyer page image (line c. 6): the printed text reads 'nuntiorum penuria in caufa fuit', confirming the audit. The Latin has been corrected to match; the English translation, already faithful to the intended sense, was left untouched. No other part of the letter was touched.

text.original:
HENRICUS BRUCÆUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

DANIEL RENTFLERUS, in bonis literis apprime versatus, eruditus mehercle iuvenis et optimis moribus excultus, Daniam petere voluit visendi gratia et te inprimis salutare, qui alter Atlas cœlum humeris ferre diceris. Age, mi TYCHO, persequere magna cum laude labores institutos et cœlum ipsum ad nos transfer, longitudinibus stellarum definitis, et, si quid in latitudinibus desideretur, idipsum posteritati prodens. Nam audio, te aliquid novi in his invenisse, adeo ut dubitari possit, an non ipsæ etiam mutentur latitudines. Est quidem audax facinus a tanto illustrium Mathematicorum consensu dissentire, qui tanto temporum intervallo distrahuntur. Sed si te sic rata docuit experientia, cur tibi non fidem adhibeamus potius quam illis, qui forte non tam subtiliter omnia rimati sunt? Longitudines autem stellarum non respondere calculo, nihil mirum, cum hactenus Hypotheses inventæ, quæ hanc apparentem motuum inæqualitatem ad æqualitatem reducant, non sint. Latitudines vero invariabiles servari omnes prodiderunt. Expecto tuam sententiam, et quid de tuis Cometis fiat, utrum prælo subiecti sint, an vero supprimere decreveris. Hunc vero iuvenem, quem ob eruditionem et modestiam omnes amant, nostra et sua causa et pro tua singulari erga homines literarum amantes benevolentia complectere. Tractatum de Crepusculis Sphæræ adiectum, utrum legeris, scire velim. Si quid habeas Geometricum laude dignum, ab aliquo recentor editum, eius autorem indicato et, si aliquot dies carere queas, ad nos mittito. Nos minus hoc tempore hisce studijs vacamus, alijs distracti. Tu quid agas, quid mediteris, fac intelligam. Et si quid ex Vulcani officina habes, quod in paralyticis et alijs contumacibus morbis nostra medicamenta respuentibus expertus es, id communices rogo.

Vale, Nobilissime doctissimeque TYCHO, et nos mutuo ama.
Rostochij 22. Maij 1587.
text.english:
**Heinrich Brucaeus to Tycho Brahe.**

Daniel Rentflerus, most accomplished in good letters — a learned young man, by Hercules, and refined in the finest character — has wished to make for Denmark for the sake of seeing [it], and above all to greet you, who are said to be a second Atlas bearing heaven upon your shoulders. Come, my Tycho, carry through with great renown the labours you have undertaken, and transfer heaven itself to us, with the longitudes of the stars determined and — if anything be wanting in the latitudes — bringing that very thing forth to posterity [as well]. For I hear that you have found something new in these matters, so much so that it may be doubted whether the latitudes themselves are not also changing. It is, to be sure, a bold deed to dissent from so great a consensus of illustrious mathematicians, who are spread across so great an interval of time. But if settled experience has so taught you, why should we not give credence to you rather than to those who perhaps have not searched out everything so subtly? That the longitudes of the stars do not answer to calculation is no wonder, since up to now there have been no hypotheses devised that reduce this apparent inequality of the motions to equality. The latitudes, however, all have reported to be kept invariable. I await your opinion, and what is becoming of your comets — whether they have been put under the press, or whether you have rather resolved to suppress them. But do embrace this young man, whom all love for his erudition and modesty, both for our sake and for his own, and out of that singular benevolence of yours toward men who love letters. I should like to know whether you have read the enclosed treatise *On the Twilights of the Sphere*. If you have anything geometrical worthy of praise, lately published by someone, point out its author, and — if you can do without it for some few days — send it to us. We, at this time, have less leisure for these studies, being drawn off by others. What you are doing, what you are pondering — let me understand. And if you have anything from Vulcan's workshop which you have tried out on the paralytic and on other stubborn diseases that spurn our medicines, I beg you to share it.

Farewell, most noble and most learned Tycho, and love us in return.
At Rostock, 22 May 1587.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (Hendrik van den Broecke, c. 1530/31–1593), professor of mathematics and then of medicine at the University of Rostock, a Bruges-born physician-mathematician and one of Tycho's senior scholarly correspondents. The dual mathematical/medical interest is on full display here: the letter moves from stellar coordinates to a request for a chemical remedy.
- ***Daniel Rentflerus*** — **Daniel Rentfler(us)**, the young scholar carrying the letter as a letter of introduction; warmly recommended for his learning and modesty. (The bearer-recommendation is the letter's nominal occasion.)
- ***alter Atlas coelum humeris ferre*** — "a second Atlas bearing heaven on his shoulders," the mythological compliment to Tycho's astronomical labours; the classical image is kept.
- **Astronomy — the fixed-star question.** The core technical matter is whether stellar **latitudes** (celestial latitude, *latitudo*) are constant. *longitudinibus stellarum definitis … si quid in latitudinibus desideretur* = "with the longitudes of the stars determined … if anything be wanting in the latitudes." Brucaeus reports a rumour that Tycho has found the latitudes themselves to be changing (*an non ipsae etiam mutentur latitudines*) — a genuinely "bold deed" against the *consensus* of earlier authorities who "reported the latitudes to be kept invariable" (*Latitudines … invariabiles servari omnes prodiderunt*). The longitude/latitude renderings follow this chapter's convention
- ***Hypotheses … apparentem motuum inaequalitatem ad aequalitatem reducant*** — "hypotheses that reduce this apparent inequality of the motions to equality": the standard astronomical sense of *hypothesis* as a geometrical model accounting for the non-uniform apparent motions; *motus* → "motion," *inaequalitas/aequalitas* kept as "inequality/equality" of the motions.
- ***rata … experientia*** — "settled / ratified experience"; *experientia* rendered "experience" (the appeal to Tycho's observational basis), with *rata* as "settled." Brucaeus' epistemic hedges (*forte* "perhaps," *dubitari possit* "it may be doubted," *audio* "I hear") are preserved, not sharpened.
- ***tuis Cometis … utrum praelo subiecti sint, an … supprimere decreveris*** — "your comets — whether they have been put under the press, or whether you have resolved to suppress them": a reference to Tycho's cometary work, in print preparation by this date (the *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis*, on the comet of 1577, was being printed at Uraniborg in the later 1580s). *praelum* = "press" (printing press); the question of publishing vs. withholding is kept as posed.
- ***Tractatum de Crepusculis Sphaerae*** — "the treatise *On the Twilights of the Sphere*," an enclosed work concerning twilight (*crepusculum* → "twilight,") and the doctrine of the sphere. The exact title/author is not specified in the letter; rendered descriptively and not identified beyond the text (see crux).
- ***ex Vulcani officina*** — "from Vulcan's workshop," a period circumlocution for the **alchemical / chymical laboratory** and its iatrochemical preparations. Brucaeus, as a physician, asks for a chemical remedy Tycho has tried on *paralytici* ("the paralytic") and other *contumaces morbi* ("stubborn diseases") that "spurn our [ordinary] medicines." Kept as the period metaphor, not modernised.
- ***mehercle*** — "by Hercules," a colloquial classical asseveration, kept.
- **Salutation / subscription.** *Vale … et nos mutuo ama* = "Farewell … and love us in return," the affectionate close. *Nobilissime doctissimeque* = "most noble and most learned," the vocative honorific addressed to Tycho.
- **Place.** *Rostochij* = **Rostock**, seat of the university where Brucaeus taught.
- **Dateline / calendar.** *Rostochij 22. Maij 1587* = "At Rostock, 22 May 1587." The edition label ("1587. 22. maj. Rostock") agrees with the as-written dateline; no discrepancy. Style is **Old Style (Julian)**: Lutheran Mecklenburg/Rostock had not adopted the Gregorian reform, so the date is O.S.
- **Textual note.** *recentor* (in *ab aliquo recentor editum*) is anomalous; read as *recenter* ("lately, recently"), the reading adopted in the translation; the printed form is retained in the Source block by this chapter's convention. *idipsum* and *inprimis* are written solid as printed.

documents.incipit: MIJNN gandske wenlig helßennd nu och altid forsennd med Wor Herre. Kiere Niels Bild, och …

text.original:
THILL ERLIG OCH WELBIURDIG MAND NIELS BILLD THIJL RAUNHOLTT, MIN BESØNDERLIGE GODE WENN DETTE BREFF GANDSKE WENLIG THILLSCHREFFUID.

MIJNN gandske wenlig helßennd nu och altid forsennd med Wor Herre. Kiere Niels Bild, och sønderlige gode wenn, nest en wenligh tacksigelse for alt beuist gode, huilket jeg altid will findis willig och redebon tiill epther formuenn at forschilde, kand ieg eder wenligen icke forholde, att epthersom Christoffher Pepler min fordoms fogit ij Norfiord lhenn ij Norge, dentijd jeg dett haffde af Kong. May. ij forlening, er nu kommen hidt tiill mig fra Norge, saa haffuer hand giffuedt mig tilkiende, huorledis hand endnu haffuer nogen skilld vdstaendis ij Norfiord baade aff kongens restandtz och aff sidt egidt goeds, huormed hand bønderne vndsett haffde, huilckid de nu forhollder hannom, och dertilmed haffuer bygtt nogle hus paa sin egen bekostning oppaa en øde platz, huor ingen huß førre paastodt, ey heller nogen agger heller eng tilligger. Laadendis mig ochsaa der hoß forstaa, huorledis at prousten derudj lenid, som skulle holde kirkens regenskab, er hannom for tong, ij dett hand siger: att de kiercke ombodsmend, som haffuer bygt paa kierkerne, skulle haffue satt deris arbeid for dyrtt och der ijmod wille tage kierkens renntte for leett jnd, som jeg kand forstaa, och att Christoffher skulle dett wederlegge kierckerne jgenn ijmod de breffue, som kiercke ombodsmenddenne haffuer giffuidt hannom, lydendis, att hand jntted haffuer oppebaridt aff kierckens reennte vdenn sin lhøn, och beretter ydermere, att er hand ochsaa befrøchttendis, att ij haffuer hannom mijßtenckt ij dett hand skulle haffue schreffuit nogidt tijll mig om eder, huilked jeg kiendis att hand icke giortt haffuer, menn att jeg aff min egenn goede wille denn tijd jeg spurde hannom nogenn gield der ij leenid tiill att staa, schreff eder til, forseendes mig till eder, som min goede wenn, att hand formijddelst eders hielp och bijstand diß snarere skulle komme thiill rette och nhaa sin betalling. Kiere Niels Bild, er derfor min gandske wenlig bøenn endnu til eder, att ij wille well giøre, som jeg eder thiill troer, och fordre och forfremme samme Christoffher udj diße forneffnde saager till det beste, och hielpe hannom att komme till enn goed ende der vdj, jnngennlunde haffuendis hannom mijstenckt ij nogen maade. Kiere Niels, haffuer jeg gierne sielff willde talidt med eder baade om dette och anditt denn thijd ij ware først neer kommen aff Norghe, menn nu kunde leilighedenn siig jcke saa begijffue. Menn dersom dett ware eder muligt och ij willde haffue denn wmage och besøge mig engang, førrind ij farer thiill Norge jgenn, daa saahe jeg det gandske gierne, oc vdj hues maade jeg kan nogen tijd giøre nogidt for eders skilld, som Eder thijl willge och guode kand vere, will jeg findis gandske och reedebon derthill.

Och will jeg hermed nu och altid haffue eder med alt hues ij well will denn alsommechtigste Gud befallendis.
Datum Vrannieborgh thend 18. julij anno [15]87.
Thyge Brahe
Egen hand.
text.english:
**To the honourable and well-born man Niels Bild of Ravnholt, my especial good friend, this letter written in all friendship.**

My wholly friendly greeting, now and ever, sent with Our Lord. Dear Niels Bild and especial good friend, after a friendly thanksgiving for all the kindness shown me — which I shall always be found willing and ready to requite according to my means — I cannot in friendship withhold from you that, inasmuch as Christoffer Pepler, my former bailiff in the fief of Nordfjord in Norway during the time I held it in fief from His Royal Majesty, has now come hither to me from Norway, he has thereby given me to understand how he still has certain monies outstanding in Nordfjord, both from the king's arrears and from his own goods, with which he had relieved [advanced credit to] the peasants — which they now withhold from him; and that in addition he has built some houses at his own expense upon a waste plot where no house stood before, nor [where] any field or meadow appertains. He has also given me to understand how the provost there in the fief, who was to keep the church's accounts, is too hard upon him, in that he [the provost] says that the churchwardens who built upon the churches are supposed to have set their work too dear and, against that, would enter the church's revenue too low [in the accounts], as I can understand it; and that Christoffer is supposed to make this good to the churches again, against the letters [receipts] which the churchwardens had given him, stating that he has received nothing of the church's revenue beyond his wages. And he reports further that he is also apprehensive that you have held him in suspicion, in that he is supposed to have written something to me about you — which I acknowledge he has not done; but rather that I, of my own good will, at the time when I asked him what debt was standing [outstanding] there in the fief, wrote to you, trusting in you as my good friend, that through your help and assistance he might the sooner come to his right and obtain his payment. Dear Niels Bild, my wholly friendly request to you is therefore still that you will do well, as I trust of you, and to further and advance the same Christoffer in these aforesaid matters to the best [outcome], and help him to come to a good end therein, in no wise having held him in suspicion in any manner. Dear Niels, I should gladly have spoken with you myself, both about this and other things, at the time when you had first come down from Norway, but now the occasion could not so present itself. But if it were possible for you, and you would take the trouble to visit me once, before you go to Norway again, then I should see it most gladly; and in whatever manner I can at any time do anything for your sake that may be to your pleasure and good, I shall be found wholly and readily disposed thereto.

And herewith I shall now and ever commend you, with all that you wish well, to Almighty God.
Given at Uraniborg, the 18th of July, the year [15]87.
Tyge Brahe.
In his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), writing from Uraniborg on Hven. The subscription *Thyge Brahe / Egen hand* ("Tyge Brahe / In his own hand") marks the letter as an autograph; *Egen hand* = *egen hånd*, "[in his] own hand."
- **Recipient.** *Niels Billd thijl Raunholtt* = **Niels Bild til Ravnholt**, a Danish nobleman who held crown fiefs in Norway (the surviving MS is a later copy in Langebek's Diplomatarium, so the spelling "Billd/Bild" is the copyist's). Tycho addresses him as a fellow member of the nobility and as a friend, interceding on behalf of a former subordinate.
- **Christoffer Pepler** — Tycho's former *fogit* (bailiff/steward) in the Nordfjord fief; the letter is wholly a letter of recommendation/intercession on his behalf. *fordoms* = *fordums*, "former / of old."
- **Place / fief.** *Norfiord lhenn ij Norge* = the fief (*len*) of **Nordfjord** in western Norway. Tycho had held it *ij forlening* — "in fief / enfeoffment" — from the Crown (*Kong. May.* = *Kongelig Majestæt*, "His Royal Majesty," Frederik II); he had been granted the income of Nordfjord len in 1578 and held it until 1587, so this letter coincides with the close of that tenure.
- **Document type / rubric.** The opening line is the **address (superscription)** written on the outside/head of the letter, in the chancery majuscule convention, not a separate Latin rubric: *"…dette breff gandske wenlig thillschreffuid"* = "this letter written in all friendship." (Unlike the Frederik II compass-letter, there is no Latin *ut sequitur* register-rubric here; the whole document is Danish.)
- **Legal / administrative substance (translated with care for negations).** Three claims of Pepler's are reported, each preserved with its exact polarity:
 1. He has *skilld vdstaendis* — "monies outstanding" (*gæld/skyld udestående*) — owed both from *kongens restandtz* ("the king's arrears," unpaid Crown dues) and from his own goods advanced to the peasants, which they **now withhold** (*forhollder*) from him.
 2. The **provost** (*prousten*, ecclesiastical superintendent of the *len*), who keeps the church accounts, is *for tong* ("too hard / too heavy") on him: the dispute is whether the **churchwardens** (*kiercke ombodsmend*, church stewards) overcharged for building work and under-entered the church revenue, and whether Pepler must *wederlegge* ("make good / reimburse") the difference — **against** the *breffue* (receipts/letters) the churchwardens gave him stating he took **nothing** of the church revenue beyond his wages. The double negative force ("nothing… beyond his wages") is reproduced exactly.
 3. Pepler **fears** Niels Bild suspects him of having written something against him to Tycho. Tycho's denial is exact and carries the legal weight of the letter: *"huilked jeg kiendis att hand icke giortt haffuer"* = "which I acknowledge he has **not** done" — i.e. Pepler did **not** write to Tycho about Bild; rather Tycho himself, *aff min egenn goede wille* ("of my own good will"), wrote to Bild after asking Pepler about debts outstanding in the fief. The closing plea *"jnngennlunde haffuendis hannom mijstenckt ij nogen maade"* = "in **no wise** having held him in suspicion in any manner" — three negation-bearing elements (*ingenlunde* "by no means," *mistænkt* "suspected," *i nogen måde* "in any manner") all retained.
- **Orthography (chancery Danish, c. 1587, via a later copyist).** *helßennd* = *hilsen* ("greeting"); *forsennd* = *forsendt* ("sent"); *redebon / reedebon* = *redebon* ("ready, willing"); *forschilde* = *forskylde / gengælde* ("requite, deserve in return"); *epthersom* = *eftersom* ("inasmuch as"); *tilkiende* = *til kende* ("[given] to understand"); *restandtz* = *restance* ("arrears"); *vndsett* = *undsat* ("relieved, advanced [credit to]"); *øde platz* = *øde plads* ("waste / vacant plot"); *agger heller eng* = *ager eller eng* ("field or meadow"); *prousten* = *provsten* ("the provost"); *ombodsmend* = *ombudsmænd* ("stewards, agents"); *wederlegge* = *vederlægge* ("compensate, make good"); *oppebaridt* = *oppebåret* ("received, collected [revenue]"); *befrøchttendis* = *befrygtende* ("apprehensive, fearing"); *mijßtenckt / mijstenckt* = *mistænkt* ("suspected"); *forseendes mig till eder* = *forseende mig til eder* ("trusting / relying on you"); *fordre och forfremme* = *fordre og fremme* ("further and advance"); *jnngennlunde* = *ingenlunde* ("by no means"); *wmage* = *umage* ("trouble, effort"); *leilighedenn* = *lejligheden* ("the occasion"); *alsommechtigste* = *allermægtigste* ("Almighty"). Address formulae by this chapter's convention: the letter substitutes a friendly noble-to-noble salutation for the royal *Wor gunst tilforn*.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datum Vrannieborgh thend 18. julij anno [15]87* = "Given at **Uraniborg**, the 18th of July, the year [15]87" (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). *Datum* "Given" kept by this chapter's convention The header date agrees with the edition label (*1587. 18. juli. Uraniborg*); no discrepancy. The bracketed "15" in *anno [15]87* is the editor's expansion of the copy's *anno 87*.

documents.incipit: REVERSVS ad nos is per quem instantibus vltimo Francoforti vernalibus Nundinis …

text.original:
ERVDITIONE EXCELLENTI ET INGENIOSA PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO D. CHRISTOPHORO ROTHMANNO, ILLVSTRISSIMI PRINCIPIS WILHELMI LANDTGRAVII HASSIÆ, ETC. MATHEMATICO EXIMIO, AMICO SUO PLURIMUM DILECTO. S. D.

REVERSVS ad nos is per quem instantibus vltimo Francoforti vernalibus Nundinis Illustriss. Principi tuo et tibi de rebus Astronomicis copiose perscripseram, vestræque expectationi, vti spero, pro virili satisfeceram, præter omnem meam opinionem nihil prorsus literarum retulit. Cuius causam admiranti sciscitantique mihi, Illustrissimum Principem LANDTGRAVIVM eo tempore, quo transactis Nundinis Cassellas redierat, nuptijs quibusdam occupatum fuisse, quo minus tunc responsioni vacare ipsius Celsitudini commodum foret, et te etiam eâdem de causa varijs auocationibus implicitum fuisse referebat, subiungebatque ipsum Illustrissimum Principem per te sibi significasse, quod breui misso proprio Tabellario literas, quæ meis responderent, essem recepturus. Huic Relationi hactenus lubens acquieui, et indies ab Illustrissimo Principe, tum etiam a te responsionem cupide expectaui, quam cum vltra speratum tempus differri videam, non potui non oblata per hunc Bibliopolam HENRICVM, (eidem per quem priores miseram inseruientem) hac opportuna scribendi occasione, ad te aliquid literarum dare, et rescriptionem hactenus intermissam in memoriam reuocare. Rogo itaque peramanter, vt velis apud Illustrissimum Principem tuum de responsione mihi remittenda, meo nomine obnixe et reuerenter sollicitare, vtque tu etiam ijs, quas ad te seorsim dedi literis, omnimode rescribendo satisfacere non diutius supersedeas. Si per proprium Principis Tabellarium negotium hoc commode expediri nequeat, idipsum per harum exhibitorem satis opportune efficietur, modo literas, quamprimum is e Nundinis Francofordianis Cassellas reuersus fuerit, in promptu paratas inuenerit, nam ne comitum et vehiculi dispendium faciat, moram istic aliquam nectere vix illi commodum fuerit. Retulit idem, qui meas vobis attulit, te impetrata a Principe tuo venia, me coram inuisere decreuisse, quod vt prima quaque opportunitate exequi non intermittas, te etiam atque etiam rogatum habeo. Erit tuus accessus mihi pergratus, et de multis præsentes oretenus plenius et commodius, quam absentes per literas, iucunde, nec, vti spero, inutiliter conferemus, Vnaque Instrumentorum nostrorum varia exquisitaque structura, obseruandique per hæc in fallibilis apprimeque concinna ratio oculari inspectione omnium optime tibi patebit. Omninoque tibi persuadeas, quod te eius itineris et laboris non pæniteat vnquam. Eclipsin Lunarem proxime instantem, non dubito, quin per serenitatis opportunitatem diligenter sis cælitus animaduersurus. Eius itaque apparentias et temporum momenta, vel potius ipsa Obseruationum Data mecum communicare non graueris, Ego etiam eandem hîc meis Organis adamussim perscrutari (volente Deo) non intermittam, teque de meis inuentis postmodum certiorem reddam. Vale et nostris desiderijs, inprimis vero ijs quæ in literis ad Illustrissimum Principem tuum, et te vltimo datis continebantur, quæque earum exhibitor priuatim meo nomine significauit, vt omni ex parte mature ante ingruentem hyemem satisfiat, omnem moue lapidem. Iterum feliciter vale, et absque intermissione Sacris Vraniæ lita.

Datæ Vraniburgi 12. Augusti, Anno 1587.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the most excellent man, foremost in fine and ingenious learning, Master Christoph Rothmann, distinguished mathematician of the Most Illustrious Prince Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, etc., his much-beloved friend — sends greeting.**

The man through whom, at the last spring fair at Frankfurt now past, I had written at length on astronomical matters to your Most Illustrious Prince and to yourself — and had, as I hope, satisfied your expectation to the best of my power — has returned to us, and, contrary to all my expectation, brought back no letters whatsoever. When I wondered at this and asked the reason, he reported that the Most Illustrious Prince the Landgrave, at the time when he had returned to Kassel after the fair, had been taken up with a certain wedding, so that it was not then convenient for His Highness to be free for a reply, and that you too, for the same reason, had been caught up in various distractions; and he added that the Most Illustrious Prince had signified to him, through you, that by a courier of his own, to be sent shortly, I should receive letters answering mine. With this report I have hitherto gladly rested content, and day by day eagerly awaited a reply from the Most Illustrious Prince, and from you as well. But seeing it put off beyond the time I had hoped, I could not but — this convenient occasion for writing being offered through the bookseller Heinrich (who serves the same man by whom I had sent the earlier letters) — send you a few lines, and recall to mind the reply so far left unmade. And so I ask you most affectionately to be willing, in my name, earnestly and reverently to press your Most Illustrious Prince for a reply to be sent back to me; and that you too put off no longer satisfying, by a full reply, the letters I sent to you separately. If this business cannot conveniently be dispatched by the Prince's own courier, the same will be managed suitably enough through the bearer of this letter — provided only that, as soon as he has returned from the Frankfurt fair to Kassel, he find the letters ready to hand; for, that he may not incur the expense of attendants and a carriage, it will scarcely suit him to contrive any delay there. The same man who brought you my letters reported that you, having obtained leave from your Prince, had resolved to visit me in person; and I beg you again and again not to fail to carry this out at the very first opportunity. Your coming will be most welcome to me, and on many matters we shall confer face to face, by word of mouth, more fully and conveniently — and pleasantly, and, as I hope, not unprofitably — than we can, apart, by letter. And at the same time the varied and exquisite construction of our instruments, and the unerring and singularly elegant method of observing by means of them, will be laid open to you, best of all, by inspection with your own eyes. And be wholly assured that you will never regret that journey and labour. The lunar eclipse now next at hand — I do not doubt that, with the chance of a clear sky, you will diligently observe it in the heavens. So do not find it a burden to share with me its appearances and the precise moments of time — or rather the very data of your observations; I too, for my part, shall not fail to scrutinize the same here, to the line, with my instruments (God willing), and will afterward inform you of my findings. Farewell; and, that our wishes — above all those contained in the letters last sent to your Most Illustrious Prince and to you, and those that their bearer privately signified in my name — may be met in every part in good time, before winter comes on, move every stone [leave no stone unturned]. Again, fare you well and happily, and without ceasing make your offerings at the rites of Urania [devote yourself unceasingly to astronomy].

Given at Uraniborg, 12 August, in the year 1587.
Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Christophorus Rothmannus* = **Christoph Rothmann** (d. c. 1600), mathematician–astronomer to **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel**, at the Kassel observatory. The Tycho–Rothmann correspondence (begun 1586) is the technical heart of the printed *Epistolae astronomicae*.
- **Context.** This is a *logistical* letter within that exchange — chasing an overdue reply routed through the **Frankfurt book fair** (*Nundinae Francofordianae*, the twice-yearly Frankfurt fair, the hub of the learned book and letter trade) and a bookseller named **Heinrich** — but its substance is the standing invitation to Kassel↔Hven scholarly exchange and a concrete request: joint observation of the **coming lunar eclipse**.
- ***Instrumentorum … structura … observandi ratio infallibilis*** — "the construction of our instruments … the unerring method of observing": Tycho's recurring boast of the Uraniborg instruments and their precision, here as a lure for Rothmann to come and see them.
- ***meis Organis adamussim perscrutari*** — "to scrutinize with my instruments, to the line": *adamussim* (literally "to the mason's/carpenter's line") = with exact precision; *Organa* = instruments.
- ***apparentias et temporum momenta … ipsa Observationum Data*** — "the appearances and the precise moments of time … the very data of the observations": the technical request — phases/aspects and exact timings of the eclipse.
- ***omnem move lapidem*** — "move every stone," the proverb (Greek *pánta kínei pétron*); rendered with the gloss "leave no stone unturned."
- ***Sacris Uraniae lita*** — "make offering at the rites of Urania," i.e. devote yourself to astronomy (Urania = the Muse of astronomy); a characteristic Tycho sign-off, kept as sacral metaphor.
- **Calendar.** O.S.; Uraniborg/Hven kept Julian.

text.original:
DEM VESTEN VNSERM LIEBEN BESONDERN TYCHONI
BRAHE, HERRN ZU KNUDSTRUP.AWILHELM VON
GOTTES GNADEN LANDTGRAUE ZU HESSEN/ GRAUE ZU CATZENELNBOGEN/ DIETZ/
ZIEGENHAIN VND NIDDA/ ETC.AUNSERN gnedigen gruß zuuor/ Vester lieber besonder. Wir
haben ewer schreiben de Dato den 18.
Ianuaris beneben den Obseruationibus entpfangen.
Das jhr vns nun dieselbigen auff vnser begeren so gutwillig zugeschickt/
Dessen thun wir vns jegen euchA gnediglichen bedancken. Mögen euch aber nicht verhalten/ das wir
dazumahl mit andern geschefften beladen/ vnd an andere örter verreyset gewesenA/ dardurch wir euch zu antworten/ verhindert worden. So baldtA wir aber wieder anhero gelangt/ haben wir ewere Obseruationes mit den vnsern Conferirt, vnd mit
sonderlicher verwunderung befunden/ das sie in distantijs et
Declinationibus, etiam in partibus Minuti mit einander
vbereinstimmen/ welches zuuor niemals ist erhört worden. Das sie aber in Longitudinibus auff fünff Minuten von einander discrepirn, nimpt vns nicht wunder/ sintemahl vns wol
bewust/ das weder Hipparchus,
Ptolemaeus, noch alle andere
hiebeuor vera Stellarum loca auff 5. Minuten jemals
gewust/ noch propter Armillarum
paruitatem haben wissen können. Denn man in den Armillis kaum 10. Minuten hat können mercken/
wie das aus den Obseruationibus Stellarum Fixarum
augenscheinlich/ geschwiegen was sonsten propter Circulorum
hinc inde distractionem in obseruando hat mangeln können/ dannA die Circuli in solcher Connexion im tractiren sich baldt geben. Von
vnsern Obseruationibus können wir noch zur zeit nicht
schreitten/ dannA sie vnser Mathematicus, etiam correcto Quadrantis
perpendiculo
vielfeltigA/ nicht allein per Horologium, sondern auch im
verschienen Ianuario etzliche mahl Venerem, die er gleichsfals wie jhr/ bey tagkA/ beneben der Sonnen obseruirt, iust befunden.
Jedoch haben wir vnsern Mathematicum hierumb ernstlich bespracht/ da hat er vns nicht können verhaltenA/ wie er dazumahl per Venerem befunden/ das ewer
Motus Solis, den jhr vns in ewerer Ephemeride zugeschickt/ circa octauum gradum ♒,
vmb etzliche Minuten zu langsam/ denn er in
fine Ianuaris, auch durch vnsern Quadranten locum
Solis, nicht anders gefunden/ jhn auch nicht anders angenommen/ dannA wie er in ewer Ephemeride (welche er auch auff
dieses Jahr iusto modo hat extendiret)
stehet: Nichts desto weiniger hat doch Venus keinen
andern Locum Stellarum Fixarum geben wollen: Vermeinet/
jhr tribuiret den Refractionibus etwas
zuuiel. Auch vermeint er/ alldieweil jhr das tempus per Armillas Aequatorias indagirt, vnd aber die Refractio Solis in Circulo Verticali, vnd nicht secundum Longitudinem Eclipticae geschicht/ könne es
leicht sein/ das jhr das tempus etwas zu kurtz
angenommen/ welches nicht geschehen könne/ so man das tempus
per Azimutha Solis indagire. Jedoch weil jhr esA
per Venerem circa Aequinoctium autumnale des Morgens probiret, hat er nicht eigentlich können wissen/ wo an es
mangele. Wie nun dem/ so wissen wir nicht von vnsern ObseruationibusA, die wir nicht minder mit höchstem fleiss/ als jhr die ewerigen
angestellet/ abzutretten. Vnd dieweil wir nun viel Jahr her mit den ObseruationibusA vmbgangen/ vnd auch durch vns die Astronomiam gern
beforderten/ Ais haben wir vnserm Mathematico/ gnedigklichA befohlen/ die Obseruationes aber zu calculiren, vnd beneben den Demonstrationibus et
modis obseruandi zu publiciren, damit jederman
vnsern fleiss/ vnd arbeit sehen möchte/ wie er dann schon in die 200. Stellas calculiret, vnd noch mehr as 200. zu calculiren hat. Soll aber doch von
dieser nichtigen vnnd geringen discrepantz, zwischen den
vnsern vnnd ewerigen/ keine anmeldung thun/ auch die ewerigen nicht spargiren. Was jhr vns aber sonsten communiciret, wirdt er wol pro dignitate zu
rühmen/ vnnd euch cum honorifica nominis mentione zu restituiren wissen. Also werdet jhr als dann desto besser
vnd fleissiger in vnsere Obseruationes können inquiriren, wirdt auch die
sache bey andern desto ehe glauben finden/ alldieweil ein jeder bey seinen
Obseruationibus bleibt/ vnd nicht in
gratiam alterius etwas mutiret. Wir seindt auch
nach vollendung des wercks/ inwillens/ vnsere Instrumenta
auff eine andere art von newen anstellen zu lassenA/ vnd da wir als dann befinden werdenA/ das wir auff die 5. Minuten gejrret/ wollen wir
vns gern selbst corrigiren, Wiewol disse discrepantz baldt nicht werth ist/ das man so viel wesens drumb
mache/ kan auch von denen/ so sich in Obseruationibus
geübt/ nicht gros geachtet werden. DasA haben wir euch auff ewer schreiben nicht verhalten wöllenA/ vnd so etwas weiters darinnen sein wirdt/ darauff soll euch vnser
Mathematicus
beantworten. VndA seindt euch mit gnedigem gutem willen jeder zeit gantzA wol gewogen.Datum in vnser Stadt vnd Vestung Cassel/ am 11. SeptembrisA, Anno 87.WILHELM LANDTGRAFF ZU HESSEN.
text.english: **To the steadfast, Our trusty and well-beloved Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup. — Wilhelm, by the grace of God Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda, etc. —** Our gracious greeting beforehand, Our trusty and well-beloved. We have received your letter dated the 18th of January together with the *observations*. That you have now, at our request, sent the same so willingly to us — for this we graciously thank you. We may not, however, conceal from you that at that time we were burdened with other business and had travelled away to other places, whereby we were hindered from answering you. But as soon as we returned hither again, we *compared* [conferirt] your *observations* with our own, and found with particular astonishment that they agree with one another *in the distances and declinations, even to fractions of a minute* — which has never before been heard of. But that they *differ* [discrepirn] from one another by five minutes *in the longitudes* causes us no wonder, since we are well aware that neither *Hipparchus, Ptolemy*, nor any of all the others before [us] ever knew the *true places of the stars* to 5 minutes, nor *on account of the smallness of the armillae* could have known [them]; for with the armillae one could scarcely discern 10 minutes — as is plainly [evident] from the *observations of the fixed stars* — to say nothing of what else, *on account of the pulling-apart of the circles* [propter Circulorum hinc inde distractionem], may have been wanting in observing, since the *circles*, in such a connection, soon give way in the handling. Of our own *observations* we cannot at this time depart, for our *mathematician*, *even with the perpendicular of the quadrant corrected*, has repeatedly found [them] exact — not only *by the clock* [per Horologium], but also this past January several times observing Venus, which he, just as you [did], observed by day alongside the Sun. Yet we questioned our *mathematician* earnestly about this, and then he could not conceal from us how he had at that time found *by Venus* that your *motion of the Sun* [Motus Solis], which you sent us in your *ephemeris*, *around the eighth degree of ♒ Aquarius*, is too slow by several minutes; for at the *end of January* he found the *place of the Sun* [locum Solis] — also by our quadrant — no otherwise, and accepted it no otherwise, *than as it stands in your ephemeris* (which he has also *duly extended* [iusto modo … extendiret] to this year). None the less, Venus would yield no other *place of the fixed stars*: he supposes that you *attribute* somewhat too much to the *refractions*. He supposes also that, since you *tracked the time by the equatorial armillae* [tempus per Armillas Aequatorias indagirt], whereas the *refraction of the Sun* occurs *in the vertical circle* [in Circulo Verticali] and not *according to the longitude of the ecliptic* [secundum Longitudinem Eclipticae], it could easily be that you took the *time* somewhat too short — which could not happen if one *tracked the time by the azimuths of the Sun* [tempus per Azimutha Solis]. Yet, because you tested it *by Venus around the autumnal equinox* in the morning, he could not properly know wherein it is lacking. However that may be, we know not how to depart from our *observations*, which we have made with no less the highest diligence than you [made] yours. And since we have now for many years been occupied with the *observations*, and have gladly furthered *astronomy* through ourselves [as well], we have graciously commanded our *mathematician* to *calculate* the *observations* further and, together with the *demonstrations and the methods of observing* [Demonstrationibus et modis obseruandi], to *publish* [them], so that everyone may see our diligence and labour — as indeed he has already *calculated* nearly 200 *stars*, and has more than 200 still to *calculate*. He is, however, to make no mention of this trifling and slight *discrepancy* between ours and yours, nor to *spread abroad* [spargiren] yours. But whatever else you have *communicated* to us, he will know how to praise *according to its worth* [pro dignitate] and to *render back to you with honourable mention of your name* [cum honorifica nominis mentione restituiren]. Thus you will then be the better and more diligently able to *inquire into* our *observations*, and the matter will also the sooner find belief with others, since each one keeps to his own *observations* and does not *change* anything *for another's favour* [in gratiam alterius]. We also intend, after the completion of the work, to set up our *instruments* anew in another fashion; and if we then find that we have erred by the 5 minutes, we shall gladly correct ourselves — although this *discrepancy* is hardly worth making so much fuss about, and cannot be greatly regarded by those who have practised themselves *in observations*. This we did not wish to conceal from you upon your letter; and should there be anything further in it, our *mathematician* shall answer you thereon. And we are at all times with gracious good will quite well disposed toward you. Given in our city and fortress of Kassel, on the 11th of September, in the year [15]87. WILHELM, LANDGRAVE OF HESSE.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), "Wilhelm the Wise," himself a serious observational astronomer who maintained an observatory and instrument workshop at Kassel; with Tycho he carried on a sustained technical correspondence. The full titulature (*Graue zu Catzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain und Nidda*) is the standard Hessian style, preserved by this chapter's convention
- **Recipient address.** *Dem Vesten vnserm lieben besondern Tychoni Brahe, Herrn zu Knudstrup* — "To the steadfast (*Vesten* = *Festen*, the address-epithet for the lower nobility), Our trusty and well-beloved Tycho Brahe, Lord of **Knudstrup**" (Tycho's family seat in Scania). *Vnsern gnedigen gruß zuuor* and *Vester lieber besonder* rendered per the fixed glossary.
- **The "*mathematician*" (*Mathematicus*).** Wilhelm's court mathematician is **Christoph Rothmann**, Tycho's principal correspondent at Kassel; the Landgrave speaks throughout in the first person but reports Rothmann's technical findings. Rothmann is named only by office, not by name, in the letter.
- **The letter being answered.** *ewer schreiben de Dato den 18. Ianuaris* = "your letter dated 18 January" — this is the **incoming** Tycho→Kassel letter (with enclosed observations and ephemeris) that the Landgrave is here answering, **not** the date of the present letter. **No internal contradiction with the dateline:** the present letter is dated 11 September [15]87 at its close; the 18 January is a back-reference. The catalogue label ("1587. 11. september. Kassel") agrees with the dateline, so the header carries 11 September 1587 as written.
- **Technical terms (kept on the controlled list,–5.2).** *distantiae* → distances; *declinationes* → declinations; *longitudines* → longitudes; *vera Stellarum loca / Locum Stellarum Fixarum* → true places of the stars / place of the fixed stars; *Armillae (Aequatoriae)* → (equatorial) armillae; *Quadrans / Quadrantis perpendiculo* → quadrant / perpendicular of the quadrant; *refractio* → refraction; *Circulus Verticalis* → vertical circle; *Azimutha* → azimuths; *Motus Solis* / *locus Solis* → motion / place of the Sun; *Ephemeris* → ephemeris; *Demonstrationes / modi obseruandi* → demonstrations / methods of observing. *partibus Minuti* rendered "fractions of a minute" (lit. "in parts of a minute," i.e. to sub-arcminute precision).
- **The Latin code-switches (a feature, not noise).** The letter constantly drops Latin technical phrases into the German matrix — *in distantijs et Declinationibus, etiam in partibus Minuti; propter Armillarum paruitatem; etiam correcto Quadrantis perpendiculo; per Horologium; circa octauum gradum; in fine Ianuaris; iusto modo … extendiret; secundum Longitudinem Eclipticae; per Venerem circa Aequinoctium autumnale; pro dignitate; cum honorifica nominis mentione; in gratiam alterius* — and likewise Latinate German verbs (*conferirt, discrepirn, indagirt, calculiren, publiciren, spargiren, communiciret, restituiren, inquiriren, mutiret, corrigiren*). These are rendered into English with the Latin italicised on first/notable occurrence by this chapter's convention; the register (a learned prince writing technically) is preserved.
- **Symbol.** *circa octauum gradum ♒* — "around the eighth degree of ♒ Aquarius." The glyph ♒ is kept in the Source block and named "Aquarius" in the translation, by this chapter's convention
- **Substance.** The exchange is the well-known Kassel–Hven instrument-precision dispute: agreement to sub-arcminute in *distances/declinations* but a c. 5′ disagreement in *longitudes*. Rothmann's diagnosis — that the error may lie in Tycho's solar-longitude/refraction handling and in deriving *time by the equatorial armillae* rather than *by the Sun's azimuths* — and the Landgrave's intent to publish his own star catalogue (≈200 stars computed, >200 to go, with demonstrations and methods) are reported in the principals' own terms; no claim is sharpened.
- **Editorial markers ("A").** The transcription carries a stray uppercase **"A"** at numerous points — at the end of the address/titulature lines (*KNUDSTRUP.A*, *ETC.A*), mid-phrase (*jegen euchA*, *gewesenA*, *So baldtA*, *dannA*, *vielfeltigA*, *bey tagkA*, *verhaltenA*, *esA*, *ObseruationibusA*, *Ais*, *gnedigklichA*, *lassenA*, *werdenA*, *DasA*, *wöllenA*, *VndA*, *gantzA*, *SeptembrisA*), and at the close where words run together (*…wol gewogen.Datum…*, *…Anno 87.WILHELM…*). These are **apparatus/segmentation anchors from the source transcription, not part of the text**; they are reproduced verbatim in the Source block (by this chapter's convention's "reproduce glyphs as printed") and ignored in the translation. They do not affect sense.
- **Orthography (Early New High German chancery).** *zuuor* = *zuvor*; *ewer/ewere/ewerigen* = *euer/eure/eurigen*; *jhr/jhn* = *ihr/ihn*; *vbereinstimmen* = *übereinstimmen*; *sintemahl* = *sintemal* ("since, inasmuch as"); *geschwiegen* = "to say nothing of"; *baldt* = *bald*; *iust* = "exactly, just"; *as 200* = *als 200* ("than 200"); *disse* = *diese*; *Vestung* = *Festung* ("fortress").
- **Calendar / place.** *Datum … Cassel … am 11. Septembris, Anno 87* = "Given … [at] **Kassel** … on 11 September, the year [15]87" (O.S.; Protestant Hesse kept Old Style). *Datum* = "Given" (the chancery dating verb; cf. *Actum*,).
- **Correction.** English corrected: 'we cannot at this time proceed [to write]... found [it] exact' now reads 'we cannot at this time depart... found [them] exact', matching the letter's own parallel idiom later in the text ('we know not how to depart from our observations'). No Dreyer extract exists for this letter (Wilhelm IV to Tycho, not one of Tycho's own letters in TBOO); the fix rests on internal textual evidence, not edition collation.

translation.warrant:
**Not collated against Dreyer** — no page reference for this letter, so the grade is capped at Probable however sound the translation looks. the edition gives no page reference (one of the 49 letters without a Dreyer extract); audited the published English against the transcribed original alone, clause-by-clause, including all titles, the five-minute/ten-minute longitude-discrepancy figures, the Venus-by-day verification method, the Aquarius degree, the 200-star calculation tally, and the closing date. One mistranslation found (detailed above), identified by internal contradiction with a later, correctly-translated occurrence of the same German idiom in the same letter — not a Dreyer-collation-dependent finding. By the audit's rule, any mistranslation that changes what a scholar would take away caps the grade at C regardless of collation status.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (medium). "[von etwas] schreitten" here means to depart from / renounce, not "to proceed [in writing]" about it; the very same idiom recurs later in this letter ('wissen wir nicht von vnsern Obseruationibus... abzutretten') and is there correctly rendered 'we know not how to depart from our observations'. The causal 'dann' clause that follows (the mathematician found them exact) only makes sense as a reason to stand by the observations, not as a reason to delay writing about them. The mistranslation reverses Wilhelm's rhetorical stance in this sentence, from confidently defending his own data to sounding unprepared to discuss it. At: “Of our own observations we cannot at this time proceed [to write], for our mathematician, even with the perpendicular of”.

**Repaired.** No Dreyer extract was available for this letter (no page reference), so the text-error check does not apply; this is a mistranslation defect concerning the German source, resolved from the letter's own internal evidence. The idiom 'von [X] schreitten' (depart from X) is confirmed by its exact structural parallel later in the same letter, 'von vnsern Observationibus... abzutretten', which the existing translation already correctly renders as 'depart from'. The surrounding causal logic (the mathematician's finding the observations exact as grounds to stand by them, not as grounds to delay discussing them) corroborates the correction. Nothing else in the letter was altered.

documents.incipit: WOR gunst tillforn. Wiid att som thu Oß haffuer fortrøstit om en almanach paa thette …

text.original:
THYGE BRAHE ETC.

WOR gunst tillforn. Wiid att som thu Oß haffuer fortrøstit om en almanach paa thette thillstandendis 88 Aar att wille giøre och Oß forskaffe nogit betiidliger end thu pleyer then Oß att lade tillkomme, thilligeste ochsaa haffuer giort Oß tilsagn om thend almanach, som thu therhoes pleyer Oß att giøre, att wille Oß forskaffe. Tha bede Wij thig och begere, attu samme almanacher, thersom the ere forferdigett, mett thenne breffuißer wor dreng wille Oß tilsende. Eller och,thersom the icke endnu ere beende,tha mett thet første muligt er wille them forferdige, och Oß tilbiude, nar Wij them mue were foruenthendis. Thet scheer Oß till wilge.

Befallendis
Actum Holm, 24. septemb. a:o 87.
text.english:
**Tyge Brahe, etc.**

Our favour beforehand. Know that, whereas you have given us your assurance regarding an almanac for this coming 88th year [1588] — that you would make and procure it for us somewhat more in good time than you are wont to let it reach us — and have likewise also given us your promise concerning the [other] almanac which, along with it, you are wont to make for us, that you would procure it for us: we therefore ask and desire you that you would send us those same almanacs, if they are finished, by this bearer, our servant-lad. Or else, if they are not yet ready, that you would finish them at the very first that is possible, and notify us when we may expect them. This [you do] to our pleasure.

Commending [you to God],
Done at Holm, 24 September, in the year [15]87.

Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it.
