documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer.** **Frederik II of Denmark** (r. 1559–88), Tycho's royal patron, who in 1576 granted him Hven. As in the 1584 compass letter, the king treats Tycho as a personal supplier — here of the annual almanacs/calendrical predictions, a recurring obligation Tycho discharged from Uraniborg.
- **Recipient.** **Tyge Brahe** (Tycho), addressed in the Danish vernacular form *Thyge*.
- **Document type.** A chancery *Kladde* (draft / unentered concept), among the *Danske Kancellis uindførte koncepter til skånske missiver* — i.e. a draft missive of the Danish Chancery for the Scanian (*skånske*) correspondence. There is no Latin register rubric here (unlike the 1584 letter); the opening *THYGE BRAHE ETC.* is the chancery's own address-line shorthand.
- ***almanach / almanacher*** — "almanac(s)." The king refers to **two** items: the *almanac* for the coming year 1588, and a second *almanac* that Tycho customarily made "along with it" (*therhoes*). These are the prognosticatory wall-/calendar-almanacs (with weather and astrological notes) that the Danish court expected annually from its astronomer; rendered "almanac" and the duo preserved (note the plural *almanacher* "those same almanacs").
- **In-letter date reference (NOT a dateline discrepancy).** The body asks for the almanac *paa thette thillstandendis 88 Aar* — "for this coming 88th year," i.e. **1588** — while the letter itself is dated **1587** (*a:o 87*). This is a forward reference (an almanac for next year, requested this year), not a conflict; flagged by this chapter's convention rather than reconciled. The catalogue *label* ("Holm") names the place, not a date, and agrees with the dateline.
- **Negation.** The body contains a single negation — *thersom the icke endnu ere beende* "if they are **not** yet ready" — reproduced once, with no other negation added or dropped. The two *thersom* ("if") clauses set up the alternative the king offers: *if* finished → send them now; *or else, if* not yet ready → finish them as soon as possible and report when.
- **Orthography (chancery Danish, c. 1587).** *WOR gunst tillforn* = *Vor gunst tilforn* ("Our favour beforehand," the royal address-formula,); *Wiid* = *Vid* (imperative "know"); *som* here introduces the recital ("whereas / inasmuch as"); *thu* = *du*; *Oß* = *os*; *haffuer* = *haver/har*; *fortrøstit* = *fortrøstet* ("assured, given confident promise"); *thillstandendis* = *tilstundende* ("coming, approaching"); *betiidliger* = *betideligere* ("more in good time, earlier"); *pleyer* = *plejer* ("are wont to"); *tillkomme* = *tilkomme* ("reach, come to"); *thilligeste* = *tillige(st)* ("likewise"); *tilsagn* ("promise, undertaking"); *therhoes* = *derhos* ("therewith, along with it"); *attu* = *at du*; *thenne breffuißer* = *denne brevviser* ("this bearer-of-the-letter"); *wor dreng* = *vor dreng* ("our servant-lad / boy"); *forferdigett / forferdige* = *forfærdiget / forfærdige* ("finished / to finish, complete"); *beende* = *b-ende*, i.e. *berede(de)/beredte* ("ready, prepared"); *tilbiude* here = *tilbyde* in the sense "give notice to, advise" (let us know); *foruenthendis* = *forventendes* ("to be expected, awaiting"); *Thet scheer Oß till wilge* = *Det sker os til vilje* ("this is done to our pleasure / will"); *Befallendis* = *Befalendes* ("commending [you, sc. to God]," the chancery valediction). The text's German-influenced spelling (*w-, sch-, -ck, Oß*) is the chancery hand, not the German language — verified Danish by reading.
- **Calendar / place.** *Actum Holm, 24. septemb. a:o 87* = "Done at **Holm**, 24 September [15]87" (O.S.). *Holm* = **Bremerholm / Holmen**, the royal naval dockyard and adjoining royal precinct in Copenhagen, a frequent place of issue for Frederik II's chancery. *Actum* "Done/Given" kept by this chapter's convention

documents.abstract: Apologizes for the delayed reply, acknowledges Tycho's parallax argument for the comet, but reports his own observations cannot detect parallax, engaging Copernican hypotheses on the point.
documents.incipit: RESPONDISSEM in superioribus nundinis Francofordianis ad literas tuas, Vir Nobiliss. et …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO ET VIRTVTE SAPIENTIA INGENIOSA ERVDITAQVE DOCTRINA, CLARISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, DOMINO DE KNVDSTRVP, EQVITI DANO, MATHEMATICORUM NOSTRO SECULO OMNIUM PRÆSTANTISSIMO, ETC. DOMINO SUO CUM OBSERUANTIA COLENDO, ETC. S. P.

RESPONDISSEM in superioribus nundinis Francofordianis ad literas tuas, Vir Nobiliss. et Mathematicorum omnium praestantissime, nisi ea, de quibus in posterioribus Literis scribis, mihi fuissent impedimento; aut nisi in Aula vanissimis saepe rebus tempus vanissime esset transigendum. Verum moram illam maiori iam copia compensabo. De Cometa igitur vt primo loco adhuc paucis tecum agam, non leui tu quidem argumento aberis, consentaneum fuisse, vt Cometa aliquam, licet vix sensibilem, habuerit Parallaxin, cum Iupiter et Saturnus etiam Parallaxin habeant. Scio Hypotheses Coperniceas id omnino flagitare. Verum quomodocunque examinem meas Obseruationes, nullam tamen sensibilem inuenire possum. Potuissem eodem insensibilis Parallaxeos argumento vti ad confirmandam meam sententiam, qua ipsum Sphaerae Saturni attribui; cum Saturni Parallaxis nostros sensus facile effugiat, vixque tertiam Minuti partem attingat. Verum nolui incurrere in reprehensionem eorum, qui cum nihil de arte Mathematica intelligant, imperite tamen et temerarie plane clamitare non desinunt, nos absurdissima quaeque asserere. Sed quoniam te mearum Obseruationum Aristarchum habeo, nihil posthac id genus hominum curabo, sed forti et praesenti animo ea in medium producam, quae et per Obseruationes et per certissimas Geometriae demonstrationes vera inuenio. Quod autem miraris, quomodo tunc maximam Solis obliquitatem 23. Grad. 30. Min. assumserim, nec eandem tecum 23. Gr. 31⅓. M. ex Obseruationibus Illustriss. Principis nostri colligere potuerim: in eo facile veniam mereor. Vidi enim Obseruationes Illustrissimi Principis nostri praebere modo Altitudinem Solis maximam Solstitialem 62. Grad. 10. Min. modo 62. Gr. 12. Min. etiam eodem Quadrante: Vnde facile patuit, minori cura eas fuisse institutas, quam magnitudo negotij postulabat. Praetereâ nondum mihi constabat vera nostri Poli Eleuatio, quam scis quantis laboribus tandem indagârim. Assumsi igitur eam Obliquitatem, quam tunc temporis veritati quam proxime consentaneam esse conijciebam, licet exactam et praecisam ex Obseruationibus nescirem. Inuenta autem vera Poli nostri Eleuatione, facile animaduerti, assignatam a te Zodiaci Obliquitatem ad Obseruationes Illustrissimi Principis nostri quam proxime accedere. Verum quod tunc temporis a te discere mihi necesse fuit, id iam ipse verissimum esse diligentissimis meis Obseruationibus adinueni. Inueni enim in proximo Solstitio Aestiuo maximam Solis Altitudinem meridianam exacte 62. Gr. 11 M. diligentissime. Vnde addita Parallaxi Solis et assumpta vera nostra Aequatoris Eleuatione part. 38. M. 41. tua Zodiaci Obliquitas resultat. In Solstitio hyemali datur hîc maxima Solis altitudo meridiana part. 15. M. 14. Verum tunc temporis Aër hîc longe densior et vaporosior existit, quam alijs anni temporibus, Refractioque Solis circa Brumam longe maior est quam Sole circa medium ♏ aut ♒ versante. Haec de Cometa deque intermixta Zodiaci Obliquitate. Et quoniam video, te residuum scripti mei de Cometa desiderare, eius adhuc tria capita ad te mitto, ex quibus quae mea sit de Cometis sententia, qualesque Hypotheses Astronomicas veras esse iudicem, facile intelliges. Egi de ijs rebus aliquo modo durius; quoniam duro ligno durus adhibendus est cuneus; nec hoc genus hominum prae anteceptis authoritatibus et prae stulta Artis Mathematicae ignorantia a suis nugis ineptissimis facile discedit. Deest adhuc caput de significatione Cometarum, imprimis commendationi Astronomiae destinatum; quod licet animo conceperim, propter alia tamen negotia ab Illustrissimo Principe nostro mihi demandata, calamo excipere non potui. Accedet tunc, cum scriptum illud ad incudem reuocauero. Nunc de materia Sphaerarum caelestium paulo plenius tecum agam. Recte tu quidem mecum statuis, materiam Sphaerarum caelestium, non esse duram aut imperuiam, sed liquidam et subtilem, motuique Planetarum facile cedentem. At in eo dissentimus, quod tu propter Refractiones diuersa Aetheris et Aëris Diaphana statuis h. e. in Sphaeris caelestibus non contineri Aërem Elementarem sed potius Aethera liquidissimum ab Aëre Elementari diuersum. At argumentum Refractionis, quod pro te militare existimas, hanc tuam sententiam prorsus expugnat et euertit. Si enim Refractio illa, quam per Obseruationes inuenimus, est a diuerso Aetheris et Aëris Elementaris Diaphano: fieri non potest, quin duret vsque ad verticem. Pone enim, circa Horizontem eam Refractionem esse vix trium Minutorum: Erit nihilominus in Altitudine 45. G. circiter 1½. M. cum Triangulorum mutatio et ratio minorem vix admittant. Etsi enim pro confirmatione tuae sententiae asseras, non adeo magnam esse Diaphanorum Aetheris et Aëris differentiam, sed quae successiue, vbi se inuicem contingunt, minuatur ita, vt suprema Aëris portio, Lunae Reuolutotionibus contigua, fere nihil differat ab ipso Aethere: Eo tamen ipso, quo asseris, Refractionem esse ob diuersa Aetheris et Aëris Diaphana prouenientem, eo inquam ipso concedis, Radios Solis aut Stellarum punctum sibi nihilominus in ea diuersorum Diaphanorum successiua combinatione et assimilatione eligere, in quo refrangantur: idque necessario semper eandem a centro Terrae distantiam retinebit, propterea quod successiua illa diuersorum Diaphanorum combinatio vbique aequaliter a Terra absit. Assumto itaque hoc Refractionis puncto vbique aequaliter a Terra distante, vide num Triangulorum rationes Refractionem illam in Altitudine 50. aut 60. Graduum euanescere permittant. Vides igitur Refractionum euanescentiam diuersa Aetheris et Aëris Diaphana concedere nullo modo posse. Quae itaque mea sit de Refractionibus his sententia, quoniam fortassis in Cometa non satis explicate a me proposita est, explicatius iam tibi aperiam. Inter Terram, vt scis, et inter Sphaeram Stellarum Fixarum nihil aliud contineri statuo quam Aërem septem Errantia sidera ambientem, propterea quod Refractiones non durent vsque ad verticem, sed vix, vt tu vis, vsque ad 30. Gradus. Hunc Aërem deinde Natura ipsa me sic docente, distinguo in crassiorem, et exhalationibus terrenis obnoxium, et in purum, qui exhalationibus istis non inficiatur. Huiusque meae distinctionis fundamentum sunt similiter Principia optica. Notum enim tibi est ex Alhazeno, ex Vitellione, ex Petro Nonio de Crepusculis, atque etiam oculorum testimonio, esse certum Aëris spatium, quod a radijs Solaribus in Crepusculis illuminetur et albescat; esse item vltra illud spatium Aërem, qui a radijs Solaribus non possit illuminari et albescere; Aliâs enim essent perpetua Crepuscula. Necesse igitur est, vt Aër ille, qui etiam serenissimo Caelo in Crepusculis albescit, sit a terrenis exhalationibus infectus et crassior redditus; aliâs enim radij Solares illum illuminare non possent; ille vero, qui non albescit, sit purus et a terrenis vaporibus non infectus: Quanquam non negauero, etiam in purum illum Aërem exhalationes, praesertim puriores posse interdum ascendere. Nec tamen hunc Aërem crassum per se Refractionem causare posse inuenio, sed ob multiplicationem. Quanquam enim spatium illud Aëris crassioris fere Semidiametrum Terrae a superficie Terrae attingat, vt ex dictis Opticis de Crepusculis manifestum est: Radios tamen Solis aut Stellarum vincere crassitiem hanc, nec ob identitatem Diaphanorum in ea punctum Refractionis inuenire posse animaduerto; at circa Horizontem et in situ decliuiori ob duplicationem illius spatij posse.

[Figura] Assumamus enim melioris demonstrationis gratia, superficiem extremam Aëris crassioris distare a superficie Terrae per Semidiametrum Terrae: denotetque superficiem Terrae semicirculus BCD interuallo AB descriptus, et interuallo duplo describatur superficies extrema crassioris Aëris EFG. Describatur etiam extremus Circulus ex eodem centro, in quo feratur Stella aliqua, qui sit HIL, tanto interuallo, vt nullam fere sensibilem proportionem habeat ad AC. Assumatur etiam Stella in Aequatore forte constituta, aut in alio loco, in quo ad Meridianum perueniens habeat Altitudinem maiorem part. 30: nullamque amplius Refractionem sentiat. Dico igitur, punctum in quo sit Refractio, longius a superficie extrema Aëris crassioris EFG distare, quam distat extrema superficies Aëris crassioris a superficie Terrae, HE quam est CF vel BE. Oriatur enim Stella in H. Illis igitur qui in B in simili loci Latitudine habitant, Stella erit in Meridiano, aut in tanta Altitudine constituta, vt nullam eius Refractionem sentire possint. Cum igitur nos in C constituti Refractionem tunc maximam sentiamus, necesse est, vt punctum Refractionis sit inter B et C puncta, ac etiam in longiore distantia ab EFG superficie, quam est EB. Aliâs enim illi, qui in B habitarent, Refractionem similiter sentirent. Constat igitur quod propositum erat, nimirum spatium illud Aëris crassioris per se non esse tantum, vt frangere Radios possit, sed vim illam accipere a conduplicatione sua circa Horizontem. Quod vt adhuc magis pateat, ostendam nunc, quantum punctum Refractionis distet ab extrema superficie Aëris crassioris HE, quanto spatio radij Stellarum crassum illum Aërem irrefracti penetrent: ad quam rem assumam, vt tu vis, Refractionem illam durare vsque ad tricesimum ab Horizonte gradum. Nec enim id, vt arbitraris, meam sententiam euertit. Cogitetur igitur, vt antea dixi, AC nullam fere sensibilem proportionem, quae turbare praesens negotium possit, habere ad AH, ita vt cum connectantur HC puncta, angulus FCH perinde fere rectus sit ac si esset angulus CAH: quomodo Instrumentis in obseruando tanquam in centro mundi vti in Stellis fixis solemus. Iam abscindatur arcus HK, qui sit P. 30; et connectantur puncta K et C per rectam, quae secet superficiem extremam Aëris crassioris in O puncto: ponaturque similiter obseruator in S, cui K punctum distet ab Horizonte 29. gr. Quoniam igitur is, qui in C, nullam amplius inuenit Refractionem, ex Hypothesi: necesse est, vt nullum etiam Refractionis punctum sit inter K et C. At is, qui in S, sentit adhuc Refractionem puncti K, cum ei K sit in Altitudine 29. graduum, itidem ex Hypothesi. Cum igitur punctum Refractionis ei, qui in C, iam iam desierit; ei vero, qui in S, adhuc appareat; necesse est vt illud sit in vertice C. Quare manifestum est, lineam OC determinare quam proxime spatium, quo punctum Refractionis distat ab extrema superficie Aëris crassioris, et quam longe Radij crassum illum Aërem absque Refractione penetrare possunt. Dum igitur Stella est in Horizonte in puncto H, erit punctum Refractionis in N: dum in Q, erit punctum illud in R: semperque magis ac magis ad C accedet: vt ita in Horizonte a C puncto omnium longissime absit. Ex quo per 14. P. lib. 10. Vitellionis tanquam πόρισμα sequitur illud, quod in Obseruationibus verum reperitur: nimirum Refractiones circa Horizontem esse omnium maximas, posteaque semper magis ac magis diminui, donec puncto Refractionis in C constituto prorsus euanescunt. Quanquam id etiam esse possit a diuersa Aëris crassitie. Quo enim Aër propius ad Terram accedit, eo crassior et densior a perpetuis fumis et vaporibus redditur. Ex quibus omnibus manifestissimum, nec diuersa Aetheris et Aëris Diaphana esse, nec Refractiones aliunde, quam a crasso et vaporoso Aëre causari posse. Quin hoc ipsum, si nihil aliud, certe diuersae in diuersis locis Refractiones ostenderent. Verissimum enim est, hîc non tantas esse Refractiones, quantae sunt apud vos. Cum enim tu inueneris Stellarum Fixarum Refractionem in Altitudine 18. grad. esse apud vos duorum Minutorum: ipse ex Stellis Vrsae Maioris et alijs in eadem Altitudine eam hîc non maiorem inuenio quam vnius Minuti, adeo vt in Altitudine 23. Grad. vix quarta Minuti pars refrangatur. Solem quoque Caelo clarissimo et Radio forti inueni in Altitudine trium Graduum, cum abesset a visibili Horizonte nondum vnico Gradu, habere Refractionem vix 9⅓. Minutorum, seu addita Parallaxi, Minutorum 12⅓: quam tamen tu 28. Minutorum inuenisti. Quanquam Refractiones Solis pro diuersa Aëris constitutione manifeste mutentur, adeo vt in Bruma, vbi Aër hic nunquam fuliginibus et densa caligine caret, eam in Altitudine 15. Grad. repererim 7. Minutorum, habita scilicet Parallaxeos ratione. Vnde recte tu asseris, omnino serenum et purum Aërem ad negotium Refractionum rite tractandum requiri. Vides igitur manifeste, Refractiones eas non aliunde nisi ab Aëre crasso et denso esse, veramque esse Veterum sententiam, qua dixêre, Aërem in locis Borealioribus esse densiorem et crassiorem, quam in Australioribus. An vero extrema crassi Aëris superficies in locis Borealioribus longius a Terra absit, quam in Australioribus, valde vereor. De quo enim Nonius parte 2. P. 1. de Crepusculis dubitare videtur, nimirum Crepusculum terminari in alijs locis Sole 17. Grad. sub Horizonte latente, in alijs part. 18. in alijs part. 19: de eo mihi dubitandum non videtur, praesertim cum idem quoque Ptolemaeus in fine lib. 8. μεγαλ. συντάξ. asserat. Sed nostrum est, vt momenta temporum, quamprimum Aër albescere vesperi desinat aut mane incipiat, diligenter notemus, atque ex nostrarum Obseruationum collatione litem hanc dirimamus. Haec de arduo hoc et sublimi negotio paulo copiosius ad te perscribere volui: atque vt ea diligenter examines, deque ijs mecum conferre ne desinas, a te etiam atque etiam vehementissime peto. Nunc ad alia. De Latitudinibus Stellarum secundum mutationem Obliquitatis Zodiaci proportionaliter mutatis, eruditissime disseris. Nec enim alia via procedi dextre in eius rei confirmatione potuit, quam qua tu processisti: Propterea quod loca Stellarum Fixarum admodum perperam in Tabulis posita sint, et, vt autumo, nunquam a Ptolemaeo obseruata, sed tantum ex Hipparcho transcripta. Apparet ex multis locis Almagesti, et praecipue ex adducto cap. 3. lib. 7. Ptolemaeum minus curiose et nimis oscitanter negotium Stellarum Fixarum tractasse. Dum Vitebergae adhuc versarer, memini me simili modo examinare loca Stellarum in Canone Ptolemaico posita, cumque assumerem Longitudinem et Declinationem Reguli, prout a Ptolemaeo traduntur, prodijt Latitudo Reguli 6⅔. Min. non Borea, vt in Canone annotatur, sed Australis. Haec cum manifeste contraria sint, nec ab vllo possint conciliari: necesse est, vt vnum eorum sit falsum. At cum Regulus sit vnica Stella, cuius Obseruationem Ptolemaeus recitet, nec nostrae Obseruationes Longitudinem et Latitudinem a Ptolemaeo inuentas, admodum respuant: necessario Declinatio adducta erit falsissima. Sed cum Declinationis Ptolemaicae decrementum videatur nihilominus respondere decremento Declinationum Timocharidos et Hipparchi, ita vt a Timochare vsque ad Hipparchum Declinatio decreuerit M. 40. ab Hipparcho ad Ptolemaeum M. 50: oportebat enim ratione temporis decrementum in secundo interuallo esse maius decremento primi interualli: manifestum inde est, Ptolemaeum nunquam Declinationes Stellarum Fixarum obseruasse, sed tantum ex Declinationibus Timocharidis et Hipparchi secundum proportionem temporis finxisse, praesertim cum vt plurimum falsae, nec progressui Stellarum rite respondere inueniantur, vt ipse calculo tuo reperisti. Nec sane video, quo Instrumento eas obseruarit. Instrumentum enim parallaticum ad Lunam tantum comparatum erat, nec foramina visoriorum erant aequalia, sed superius ad Lunam erat maius, ita vt per id tota Luna perspici posset; inferius autem erat minus. Armillis quoque eas non obseruauit; siquidem Declinatio eius puncti Eclipticae, in quo tunc haesit Regulus, maior erat ipsius Reguli Declinatione a Ptolemaeo tradita. Nihil igitur nostrae sententiae de mutata Stellarum Latitudine detrahere potest Latitudo Ptolemaica Sirij, quae, cum nostra hac maior esse debebat, minor tamen reperiatur. Licet enim Declinationes Timocharidis, Hipparchi, et ipsius etiam Ptolemaei quodammodo subscribant Latitudini in Abaco Ptolemaico positae: nihil tamen ijs ob dictas causas tribuendum est. Hoc enim potius casu quam obseruatione et arte accidit. Cum Graecum textum considero, vereor ne vitiosum Hipparchi exemplar ipsi Ptolemaeo obrepserit. Potuit enim Declinatio a Timocharide tradita esse ις. ςγ. hoc est part. 16. M. 50; ab Hipparcho ις. ς. hoc est part. 16. M. 30; ac incuria transcribentium, qui putârunt ςς. frustra geminatum, ς. potuit omitti: ad quas vitiosas Declinationes Ptolemaeus deinde etiam suam fortassis direxit. Latitudo quoque Sirij in Abaco Ptolemaico posita facile transcribentium incuria vitiari potuit; cum idem acciderit non tantum in prope posita Lucida Hydrae (cuius Latitudo hoc nostro seculo duobus pene Gradibus maior Ptolemaica reperitur, cum tamen debebat esse minor) verumetiam in multis alijs, quarum Latitudo valde insigniter vitiosa deprehenditur. Sed quid de hac vnica Stella multa verba facimus, cum huius vnius votum vota reliquarum omnium facile supprimant. Monenda est posteritas, vt posthac hanc rem diligentius tractet. Ac de his fortasse plus quam sat erat. In deliquio Lunari Anni 1584. non iustam esse diligentiam et praecisionem a Wittichio adhibitam, recte asseris. Assumsit enim is locum Solis longe aliter quam per Obseruationes debuit; Dextri item humeri Orionis, per quem tempus indagauit, et Declinationem et Ascensionem rectam vitiosam. Quod cum viderem, non immerito de negligentia ipsius in prioribus literis sum conquestus. Sed vt ipse videas, qua diligentia et perspicacitate vsus fuerit, totam Obseruationis annotationem, vt eam reliquit, iam subijciam, estque ea eiusmodi.

Ex his vides, quam temere affirmârit, se assumsisse et locum Solis et Ascensionem rectam Dextri Humeri Orionis, Declinationemque ex Obseruationibus: cum nihil horum per Obseruationes verum reperiatur. Sed nolo in demortuum plura dicere. Si assumseris tuum locum Solis, et veram Dextri Humeri Orionis Ascensionem rectam, veramque Declinationem, provt nostris Obseruationibus inueniuntur; videbis annotata hîc temporum momenta propius ad tua accedere. Eclipsin huius mensis ob pluuias, quae a 6. Septemb. quatuor integros dies continue hîc durârunt, obseruare non potui, quanquam me diligenter praeparâssem. Admodum inconstans et pluuiosum Caelum hoc Anno hîc Cassellis fuit, adeo vt paucas admodum Obseruationes instituere potuerim: Percuperem scire, an idem etiam in alijs locis fuisset. Planetas obseruare Illustrissimus Princeps mihi non permittit, cuius mandato tantum Stellas Fixas obseruare, indeque vera earum loca Calculo indagare cogor. Vult enim ipsius Celsitud. vt Obseruationes nostras publicas faciam, quotidieque calculum earum vrget. Vult posteritati monumentum sui erga Astronomiam amoris relinquere: cui clementi voluntati mihi parendum est. Cedet opus hoc maxime in tuam laudem, nec sis solicitus de Instrumentis. Ea enim cum honorifica tui nominis praedicatione tibi restituam, nec praetergrediar reliqua, de quibus ad nos perscripsisti. Assumsi pro fundamento, vt superioribus quoque literis significaui, Aldeborae Ascensionem rectam part. 63. M. 10. quam etiam hoc ipso Anno per Venerem diurnam veram inueni. Quod autem ob id quinque Minutis in Longitudine vbique fere differamus a tuis Obseruationibus, neminem, qui modo subtilitatem huius negotij intelligit, offendet: quin potius eo maiorem fidem apud posteritatem merebimur. Potest Veneris Diameter hanc differentiam introducere. Nihil tamen de hac in Opere nostro agam, vt tibi integra potestas relinquatur, diligentius et pluribus Obseruationibus hanc rem examinandi. Nec te offendet, quod licet videamus, te omni humana diligentia in tuis Obseruationibus vsum, nihilominus tamen a nostris, quas oculis nostris vidimus, non discedamus: Nec enim id veritatis amantes decet: nec nosmet alienis plumis ornare volumus. Obseruationes tuas huc transmissas diligentissime custodimus, nec alijs inspiciendas praebemus: nec publicationem earum metues. Tibi regnum, tibi restaurationem Astronomiae relinquimus; ac gaudemus, esse, qui ea in re praestare possit id, quod antehac praestitit nemo. Quod si possum tibi quocunque modo esse adiumento, in eo omne meum studium, diligentiam, industriam, fidem sancte tibi polliceor ac defero. Motum Solis a te huc transmissum inuenio exactissime cum nostris Obseruationibus congruere; praeterquam circa primos Gradus ♒, vbi eum aliquantulum iusto tardiorem per Venerem reperi: quod tamen ipsum te quoque animaduertisse in prioribus literis arguis. Accepi in superioribus Nundinis Francofortensibus a M. IOANNE AALBORGA Carmina quaedam a te ad Nobilissimos quosque viros perscripta: quae cum auidissime perlegerem, incidi tandem in id, quod ad D. FALCHONEM GOYE miseras, atque ab altera paginae parte inueni binas imagines, alteram Astronomiae, alteram eius Artis, quam Spagyricam appellas. Quas cum diligenter intuebar, animaduerti ab vtroque earum latere literas quasdam, circa Astronomiam quidem, SVSPICIENDO DESPICIO: circa reliquam vero, DESPICIENDO SVSPICIO. Diu haec cum admiratione etiam atque etiam considerans, cogitaui tandem Hieroglyphica esse, teque ijs forte annuere, Artem Spagyricam continere totius Naturae et Mundi contemplationem, et perinde, ac Astronomia, suos habere Planetas, ac quae Natura agit per Sidera caelestia, ea agere simili efficacia per sua Sidera. Hoc si ita est, perquam scire cupio, quid in Arte Spagyrica appelletis Solem, quid Lunam, quid Saturnum, Iouem, Martem, Venerem, Mercurium, quid Elementa. Video abstrusissimam esse Artem, Rerumque Naturam vix sine ea dextre intelligi posse; simileque quid tenuisse Sacerdotes Aegyptiacos. Quo si a te obtinere possem, vt de eo me redderes certiorem, aliaque huc pertinentia adijceres, et qui Autores de hac Arte legendi: gratius mihi accidere nihil omnino posset.

Quod me tam humaniter inuitas, vt te inuisere non intermittam, gratias tibi quas possum ago. Haud ita dudum aiebat Illustrissimus Princeps noster, sibi placere, vt nostras Stellarum Fixarum Obseruationes dedicarem Serenissimo Daniae Regi. Si in ea sententia perseuerauerit, potero hac occasione ad te venire: sin minus, conscripsi Vitebergae non sine multis vigilijs Organon Mathematicum, quod continet Logisticam Sexagenariam, Doctrinam sinuum, Doctrinam de Compositione rationum seu de Regula sex quantitatum, et Doctrinam Triangulorum tam Sphaericorum quam Planorum, perspicue et breuiter multis et ingeniosis compendijs refertum, mihique charissimum: id Regi vestro Serenissimo dedicabo, ne mihi occasio ad te veniendi desit. Conscripsi ibidem etiam Astronomiam, in qua Hypotheses Copernici traduxi ad mobilitatem Solis (quod fieri posse non ignoras) singulaque Theoricarum Schemata calculo Prutenico declaraui. Verum cum per Obseruationes inuenerim, Tabulas Prutenicas valde insigniter a veritate Caeli abesse; publicationem eius huc vsque distuli, ne vitiosum calculum pro vero discentibus viderer commendare. Si igitur tibi placeret, sique Canones tuos Astronomicos in Lucem emitteres; Loco calculi Prutenici tuum substituerem, vt tuus calculus discentibus redderetur familiaris. Mira breuitate per leges Logicas dissectis Heterogeneis multo plura in eam conieci, quam continent vulgares Sphaerici et Theorici libelli. Impulsus sum ad eam rem acerbissimo dolore, quod non sine summa indignatione viderem, in Academijs, vbi inprimis florere debebant haec studia, nihil fere de hac Arte intelligi: Calculum quidem Prutenicum in omnium esse manibus, at tantum secundum mera Prutenica praecepta tractari, nec inueniri, qui Hypotheses eius intelligant, ne quidem inter eos, qui Astronomiam profiteantur ac se summos Mathematicos putent. Motum praecessionis Aequinoctiorum et mutatae Obliquitatis Zodiaci, cuius Hypotheses neminem adhuc vidi dextre intelligere, nec te multos vidisse arbitror, summa facilitate et perspicuitate tractaui: qui tamen aliter tractandus iam est, cum Stellae suas mutasse Latitudines inueniantur. De diebus quoque tam artificialibus quam naturalibus, deque temporis aequatione ex ipso fundamento non vulgaria proposui. Orbes illos reales et tot axes, obscurantes potius Astronomiam quam explicantes, prorsus sustuli. In Theorica Solis et Lunae vnam et eandem Circulorum suppositionem assumsi, nimirum Eccentricum, cuius centrum in circello supra centrum Mundi in linea Apogaei medij, et quidem in centro mediae Eccentricitatis consistente sit mobile: praeterquam quod in Sole anomalia simplex in summa Circelli parte incipiat, in Luna vero duplata a Sole distantia incipiat contrario modo ab ima Circelli parte. Omnino spero discentes summum inde fructum capere posse. Scriptum meum de Cometa accipiet nobilissimus ille et magnificentissimus Vir, Kaasius tuus, Cancellarius vester dignissimus, qui mihi ex carmine tuo innotuit. Quem enim alium potius celebraret Vrania, quam patronum suum? Amo ea, qua debeo, reuerentia summas summi huius Viri virtutes. Quod in literis ad Illustrissimum Principem nostrum perscriptis existimas, omnes Cometas in ipso Caelo supra Lunam generari, nullumque eorum vnquam Elementarem extitisse; facile tibi concederem, nisi obstarent Obseruationes Regiomontani et Vogelini. Quanquam enim recte asseras, longe subtilioris Artificij esse Parallaxes rite obseruandi, quam hactenus communiter vsitata ratio suppeditare potuerit: tamen velocitas motus eas Parallaxes non videtur respuere. Nec sane video, cur non etiam infra Lunam generari possint, cum Elementum Aëris vbique contineatur, planeque ad replendum omnia praecipue conditum videatur, vt per praecedentia constat. Quid de magnis illis Cometis, qui tanta Caeli spatia occupârunt, dicemus? Sed tamen non dubito, quin non contemnendas habeas causas, cur ita statuas. Quae mea sit sententia, ex adiectis tribus capitibus videbis. In capite vltimo reieci motum violentum diurnum. Omnino Terrae eum tribuendum inuenio. Haec ad te hoc tempore perscribere volui, ad quae vt respondeas, te etiam atque etiam oro. His Vale feliciter, nobilissime et ingeniosissime TYCHO, meque tui amantissimum esse omnino tibi persuade.

Cassellis. 11. Calend. Octob. Anno Salutis M. D. LXXXVII.
T.T.
CHRISTOPHORVS ROTHMANNVS, Illustrissimi Principis WILHELMI LANDTGRAVII HASSIAe, etc. Mathematicus.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most renowned man, outstanding in virtue, wisdom, ingenious learning, and erudite doctrine, Master Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup, Danish knight, of all the mathematicians of our age the most excellent, etc., his lord to be honoured with reverence, etc. — heartiest greeting.**

I should have replied to your letter at the last Frankfurt fair, most noble Sir and most excellent of all mathematicians, had not those matters of which you write in your later letters been a hindrance to me; or had it not been that at Court time often has most idly to be spent on the most idle of affairs. But I shall now make up for that delay by the greater abundance [of what I write]. To deal with you, then, first of all and still in few words, about the comet: you will not be wide of the mark with that argument of yours, by no means a weak one — that it was reasonable the comet should have had some parallax, however scarcely perceptible, since Jupiter and Saturn too have parallax. I know the Copernican *hypotheses* absolutely demand it. Yet however I examine my *observations*, I can find no perceptible [parallax]. I could have used the same argument from imperceptible parallax to confirm my own view, by which I assigned the comet to the *sphere* of Saturn; since Saturn's parallax easily eludes our senses and scarcely reaches a third of a minute. But I did not wish to incur the censure of those who, though they understand nothing of the mathematical art, yet do not cease to bawl out, ignorantly and rashly, that we assert the most absurd things of all. But since I have you for the *Aristarchus* of my observations, henceforth I shall pay no heed to men of that stamp, but shall bring forward, with a bold and ready spirit, those things which I find true both by *observation* and by the most certain *demonstrations* of geometry. As for your wondering how I then assumed the maximum obliquity of the Sun at 23°30′, and could not, like you, gather it at 23°31⅓′ from the *observations* of our Most Illustrious Prince: in this I easily deserve pardon. For I saw that the *observations* of our Most Illustrious Prince yielded now a maximum solstitial *altitude* of the Sun of 62°10′, now 62°12′, and that with the very same *quadrant*: from which it was readily plain that they had been carried out with less care than the magnitude of the matter required. Besides, the true *elevation* of our pole was not yet established to me — with how great labours I tracked it down at last, you know. I therefore assumed that obliquity which at the time I conjectured to be as close to the truth as possible, although I did not know the exact and precise [value] from *observations*. But once the true *elevation* of our pole had been found, I readily noticed that the obliquity of the *zodiac* assigned by you comes as close as possible to the *observations* of our Most Illustrious Prince. And what at that time I had necessarily to learn from you, that I have now myself found to be most true by my own most diligent *observations*. For at the last summer *solstice* I found the maximum *meridian altitude* of the Sun exactly 62°11′, most carefully. Whence, adding the Sun's *parallax* and assuming the true *elevation* of our equator at 38°41′, your obliquity of the *zodiac* results. At the winter *solstice* the maximum *meridian altitude* of the Sun here is 15°14′. But at that season the air here is far denser and more vaporous than at other times of the year, and the Sun's *refraction* about midwinter is far greater than when the Sun is moving about the middle of ♏ Scorpio or ♒ Aquarius. So much for the comet and for the obliquity of the *zodiac* mixed in with it. And since I see that you long for the remainder of my writing on the comet, I send you three further chapters of it, from which you will readily understand what my view on comets is, and what *astronomical hypotheses* I judge to be true. I treated of these matters somewhat harshly; for to a hard knot a hard wedge must be applied; nor does that breed of men, in the face of preconceived authorities and a foolish ignorance of the mathematical art, easily depart from their most inept trifles. There is still missing a chapter on the signification of comets, designed above all to commend astronomy; which, though I have conceived it in mind, I have not been able to take down with the pen on account of other business imposed on me by our Most Illustrious Prince. It will be added when I bring that writing back to the anvil. Now I shall deal with you a little more fully about the matter of the celestial *spheres*. You are right, indeed, to hold with me that the matter of the celestial *spheres* is not hard or impervious, but fluid and subtle, and yields easily to the *motion* of the planets. But in this we disagree, that you, on account of *refractions*, posit different transparent media [*diaphana*] of aether and air — that is, that in the celestial *spheres* there is not contained elemental air, but rather a most fluid aether distinct from elemental air. But the argument from *refraction*, which you reckon fights on your side, utterly storms and overturns this view of yours. For if that *refraction*, which we find by *observation*, comes from a difference between the transparent medium of the aether and that of the elemental air, it cannot but last all the way to the zenith. For suppose that about the horizon that *refraction* is scarcely three minutes: it will nonetheless be, at an *altitude* of 45°, about 1½′, since the change and ratio of the triangles scarcely admits a lesser [value]. For even though, in confirmation of your view, you assert that the difference between the transparent media of aether and air is not so great, but is one that diminishes successively where they touch one another, so that the topmost portion of air, contiguous to the *revolutions* of the Moon, differs almost nothing from the aether itself: yet by that very thing, in that you assert that *refraction* arises on account of the different transparent media of aether and air — by that very thing, I say, you grant that the rays of the Sun or of the stars do nonetheless select for themselves a point in that successive combination and assimilation of the different transparent media, at which they are refracted; and this will necessarily always keep the same distance from the centre of the Earth, because that successive combination of the different transparent media is everywhere equally distant from the Earth. Having therefore assumed this point of *refraction* to be everywhere equally distant from the Earth, see whether the ratios of the triangles permit that *refraction* to vanish at an *altitude* of 50° or 60°. You see, then, that the vanishing of the *refractions* can in no way be granted by the different transparent media of aether and air. And so what my view about these *refractions* is — since perhaps it was not set out by me clearly enough in the [treatise on the] comet — I shall now disclose to you more explicitly. Between the Earth, as you know, and the *sphere* of the fixed stars I hold that nothing else is contained than air encompassing the seven *wandering* stars [the planets], because the *refractions* do not last all the way to the zenith, but scarcely, as you would have it, up to 30°. This air I then distinguish — Nature herself teaching me thus — into a thicker [part], subject to terrestrial exhalations, and into a pure [part], which is not infected by those exhalations. And the foundation of this distinction of mine is likewise the principles of *optics*. For it is known to you from Alhazen, from Witelo, from Pedro Nunes *On Twilights*, and also by the testimony of the eyes, that there is a certain space of air which in *twilight* is illuminated by the Sun's rays and grows white; and likewise that beyond that space there is air which cannot be illuminated and grow white from the Sun's rays — otherwise there would be perpetual *twilight*. It is necessary, therefore, that the air which grows white in the *twilight* even under a most serene sky be infected by terrestrial exhalations and rendered thicker — otherwise the Sun's rays could not illuminate it — while that which does not grow white be pure and uninfected by terrestrial vapours; although I will not deny that exhalations, especially the purer ones, can sometimes ascend even into that pure air. Nor yet do I find that this thick air can of itself cause *refraction*, but [only] on account of its multiplication. For although that space of thicker air reaches almost a semidiameter of the Earth from the surface of the Earth, as is manifest from what the *optical writers* have said about *twilights*, yet I observe that the rays of the Sun or of the stars overcome this thickness, and, on account of the identity of the transparent medium within it, cannot find a point of *refraction* in it; but about the horizon and in a more sloping position they can, on account of the doubling of that space.

[Figure] Let us assume, then, for the sake of a better demonstration, that the outermost surface of the thicker air is distant from the surface of the Earth by a semidiameter of the Earth: and let the semicircle BCD, described with the radius AB, denote the surface of the Earth, and with twice the radius let there be described the outermost surface of the thicker air EFG. Let there also be described, from the same centre, an outermost circle in which some star is carried, which let be HIL, at so great an interval that it has almost no perceptible proportion to AC. Let the star also be supposed to be placed, say, on the equator, or in some other place in which, on reaching the *meridian*, it has an *altitude* greater than 30°, and feels no further *refraction*. I say, then, that the point at which *refraction* occurs is more distant from the outermost surface EFG of the thicker air than the outermost surface of the thicker air is distant from the surface of the Earth — HE [greater] than CF or BE. For let the star rise at H. To those, then, who dwell at B at a similar *latitude* of place, the star will be on the *meridian*, or placed at so great an *altitude* that they can feel none of its *refraction*. Since therefore we, placed at C, then feel the maximum *refraction*, it is necessary that the point of *refraction* be between the points B and C, and also at a greater distance from the surface EFG than EB is. For otherwise those who dwelt at B would likewise feel the *refraction*. It is established, therefore, [as] what was proposed — namely that that space of thicker air is not of itself so great as to be able to refract the rays, but receives that power from its doubling about the horizon. And that this may be still more apparent, I shall now show how far the point of *refraction* is distant from the outermost surface HE of the thicker air, [and] through how great a space the rays of the stars penetrate that thick air unrefracted: for which purpose I shall assume, as you would have it, that that *refraction* lasts up to the thirtieth degree from the horizon. For this does not, as you suppose, overturn my view. Let it be conceived, then, as I said before, that AC has almost no perceptible proportion to AH such as could disturb the present matter, so that, when the points HC are joined, the angle FCH is almost as much a right angle as if it were the angle CAH — in the way we are accustomed to use *instruments* in observing the fixed stars as if at the centre of the world. Now let the arc HK be cut off, which let be 30°; and let the points K and C be joined by a straight line which cuts the outermost surface of the thicker air at the point O; and let an observer likewise be placed at S, for whom the point K is distant 29° from the horizon. Since, then, the one who is at C finds no further *refraction*, by *hypothesis*, it is necessary that there be no point of *refraction* either between K and C. But the one who is at S still feels the *refraction* of the point K, since for him K is at an *altitude* of 29°, likewise by *hypothesis*. Since, then, the point of *refraction* has now just ceased for the one at C, but still appears to the one at S, it is necessary that it be at the zenith C. Wherefore it is manifest that the line OC determines as closely as possible the space by which the point of *refraction* is distant from the outermost surface of the thicker air, and how far the rays can penetrate that thick air without *refraction*. While, then, the star is on the horizon at the point H, the point of *refraction* will be at N; while it is at Q, that point will be at R; and it will draw ever nearer and nearer to C, so that on the horizon it is furthest of all from the point C. From which, by Proposition 14 of Book 10 of Witelo, there follows as a *corollary* [πόρισμα] that which is found true in *observations*: namely that the *refractions* about the horizon are the greatest of all, and afterwards are diminished ever more and more, until, the point of *refraction* being placed at C, they utterly vanish. Although this might also come from the different thickness of the air. For the closer the air approaches the Earth, the thicker and denser it is made by the perpetual smokes and vapours. From all which it is most manifest that there are neither different transparent media of aether and air, nor can the *refractions* be caused from any source other than thick and vaporous air. Indeed this very thing, if nothing else, the different *refractions* in different places would certainly show. For it is most true that the *refractions* here are not so great as they are with you. For whereas you have found the *refraction* of the fixed stars at an *altitude* of 18° to be, with you, two minutes, I myself, from the stars of the Great Bear and others at the same *altitude*, find it here no greater than one minute, so that at an *altitude* of 23° scarcely a quarter of a minute is refracted. The Sun too, with a most clear sky and a strong ray, I found at an *altitude* of three degrees, when it was not yet a single degree from the visible horizon, to have a *refraction* of scarcely 9⅓′, or, with *parallax* added, 12⅓′ — which you, however, found to be 28′. Although the *refractions* of the Sun manifestly change according to the different state of the air, so that at midwinter, when the air here is never free of soots and dense murk, I have found it at an *altitude* of 15° to be 7′, account being had, of course, of the *parallax*. Whence you rightly assert that an altogether serene and pure air is required for treating the matter of *refractions* properly. You see, then, manifestly, that those *refractions* are from no source other than thick and dense air, and that the view of the ancients is true, by which they said that the air in more northerly places is denser and thicker than in more southerly ones. But whether the outermost surface of the thick air is, in more northerly places, further from the Earth than in more southerly ones, I greatly doubt. For about that which Nunes, in Part 2, Proposition 1 *On Twilights*, seems to doubt — namely that *twilight* is ended in some places when the Sun is hidden 17° below the horizon, in others at 18°, in others at 19° — about that it does not seem to me one ought to doubt, especially since Ptolemy too asserts the same at the end of Book 8 of the *Megalē Syntaxis*. But it is our task to note carefully the moments of time at which the air ceases to grow white in the evening or begins [to] in the morning, and to settle this dispute from a collation of our *observations*. These things, about this arduous and lofty matter, I wished to write out to you a little more copiously; and I beg of you again and again, most earnestly, that you examine them carefully, and do not cease to confer with me about them. Now to other matters. About the *latitudes* of the stars changed proportionally according to the change of the obliquity of the *zodiac*, you discourse most learnedly. For there was no other way to proceed aptly in the confirmation of that matter than the one by which you proceeded — because the places of the fixed stars are set down quite wrongly in the *tables*, and, as I judge, were never observed by Ptolemy, but only transcribed from Hipparchus. It appears from many places in the *Almagest*, and especially from the cited Chapter 3 of Book 7, that Ptolemy handled the business of the fixed stars less carefully and too drowsily. While I was still residing at Wittenberg, I remember examining in a like manner the places of the stars set down in the Ptolemaic *canon*; and when I assumed the *longitude* and *declination* of Regulus as they are handed down by Ptolemy, the *latitude* of Regulus came out 6⅔′ — not north, as is noted in the *canon*, but south. Since these things are manifestly contrary, and cannot be reconciled by anyone, it is necessary that one of them be false. But since Regulus is the one star whose *observation* Ptolemy recounts, and our *observations* do not much reject the *longitude* and *latitude* found by Ptolemy, of necessity the *declination* adduced will be most false. But since the decrement of the Ptolemaic *declination* nonetheless seems to correspond to the decrement of the *declinations* of Timocharis and Hipparchus — such that from Timocharis to Hipparchus the *declination* decreased 40′, from Hipparchus to Ptolemy 50′ (for, by reason of time, the decrement in the second interval ought to be greater than the decrement of the first interval) — it is thence manifest that Ptolemy never observed the *declinations* of the fixed stars, but only feigned them from the *declinations* of Timocharis and Hipparchus according to the proportion of time, especially since they are found for the most part false, and not duly to correspond to the progression of the stars, as you yourself have found by your calculation. Nor indeed do I see with what *instrument* he could have observed them. For the *parallactic instrument* [triquetrum] was contrived only for the Moon, and the holes of the sights were not equal, but the upper one, [used] for the Moon, was larger, so that through it the whole Moon could be seen; while the lower one was smaller. With *armillae* too he did not observe them, since the *declination* of that point of the *ecliptic* in which Regulus then stood was greater than the *declination* of Regulus itself handed down by Ptolemy. Nothing, then, can detract from our view about the changed *latitude* of the stars [in the case of] the Ptolemaic *latitude* of Sirius, which, whereas it ought to be greater than ours here, is yet found smaller. For although the *declinations* of Timocharis, of Hipparchus, and even of Ptolemy himself in some manner subscribe to the *latitude* set down in the Ptolemaic table, yet nothing is to be attributed to them, for the reasons stated. For this happened rather by chance than by *observation* and skill. When I consider the Greek text, I fear lest a corrupt copy of Hipparchus crept in upon Ptolemy himself. For the *declination* handed down by Timocharis could have been ις ϛγ, that is 16°50′; by Hipparchus ις ϛ, that is 16°30′; and through the carelessness of copyists, who thought the ϛϛ doubled in vain, the ϛ could have been omitted: to which corrupt *declinations* Ptolemy then perhaps also directed his own. The *latitude* of Sirius too, set down in the Ptolemaic table, could easily have been corrupted by the carelessness of copyists; since the same has happened not only in the nearby [star] Lucida Hydrae (whose *latitude* in this our age is found almost two degrees greater than the Ptolemaic, when yet it ought to be smaller), but also in many others, whose *latitude* is found notably corrupt. But why do we make many words about this single star, when the wish of this one is easily suppressed by the wishes of all the rest? Posterity is to be warned to handle this matter more diligently hereafter. And of these things perhaps more than enough. That in the lunar eclipse of the year 1584 the right diligence and precision was not applied by Wittich, you rightly assert. For he assumed the place of the Sun far otherwise than he ought by *observation*; likewise the right shoulder of Orion [Betelgeuse], by which he investigated the time, with both *declination* and *right ascension* faulty. When I saw this, not without cause did I complain of his negligence in my earlier letters. But that you may yourself see with what diligence and perspicacity he proceeded, I shall now subjoin the whole record of the *observation*, as he left it; and it is of this kind.

IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 1584, ON 7 NOVEMBER, THERE WAS OBSERVED AT KASSEL A FULL MOON [PLENILUNIUM] IN ECLIPSE, WHOSE TIME FELL:
Of first obscuration at 11h20m P.M.
Of total obscuration at 12h20m.
Of first emersion at 13h45m.
Of total emersion at 14h45m.
Both clocks corrected by *azimuths* of the right shoulder of Orion.
The Sun moving through 25½° ♏ Scorpio, from the preceding *observation*.
Hence mid-obscuration at 13h3m. The Moon at 25°30′ ♉ Taurus with *latitude* 0°10′ south.
Duration in darkness 2h25m.
Whole duration 3h25m.
Right shoulder of Orion: *right ascension* 83°31′, *declination* 7°9′. From the *observations* of the year 1584.

From these you see how rashly he affirmed that he had assumed both the place of the Sun and the *right ascension* of the right shoulder of Orion, and the *declination*, from *observations* — when none of these is found true by *observation*. But I am unwilling to say more against a dead man. If you assume your own place of the Sun, and the true *right ascension* of the right shoulder of Orion, and the true *declination*, as they are found by our *observations*, you will see that the moments of time recorded here come closer to yours. The eclipse of this month I could not observe, on account of the rains which lasted here continuously for four whole days from 6 September, although I had diligently prepared myself. The sky here at Kassel was very inconstant and rainy this year, so that I have been able to carry out very few *observations*: I should much like to know whether the same was so also in other places. Our Most Illustrious Prince does not permit me to observe the planets; by his command I am compelled only to observe the fixed stars, and thence to track down their true places by *calculation*. For His Highness wishes that I make our *observations* public, and daily presses on the calculation of them. He wishes to leave to posterity a monument of his love toward astronomy; and to this gracious will of his I must yield. This work will redound greatly to your praise, and do not be anxious about the *instruments*. For I shall restore them to you with honourable proclamation of your name, nor shall I pass over the rest of the things about which you wrote to us. I have assumed for a foundation, as I signified also in my earlier letters, the *right ascension* of Aldebaran at 63°10′, which this very year too I found true by *daytime Venus*. But that on this account we differ from your *observations* in *longitude* by five minutes almost everywhere will offend no one who in the least understands the subtlety of this matter; nay rather, we shall the more deserve credit with posterity for it. The *diameter* of Venus can introduce this difference. Yet I shall do nothing about this in our work, so that full power may be left to you to examine this matter more diligently and by more *observations*. Nor will it offend you that, although we see that you have used every human diligence in your *observations*, we nonetheless do not depart from our own, which we have seen with our own eyes — for that does not befit lovers of truth, nor do we wish to adorn ourselves with another's feathers. The *observations* you sent here we guard most diligently, nor do we offer them to others to inspect; nor need you fear their publication. To you we leave the kingdom, to you the *restoration of astronomy*; and we rejoice that there is one who can perform in that matter what no one has performed before. And if I can be of help to you in any way whatever, in that I solemnly pledge and offer you all my zeal, diligence, industry, and faith. The *motion* of the Sun sent here by you I find to agree most exactly with our *observations*; except about the first degrees of ♒ Aquarius, where I found it by [observation of] Venus somewhat slower than it should be — which very thing, however, you point out in your earlier letters that you too had noticed. I received at the last Frankfurt fair, from Master Hans Aalborg, certain poems written by you to various most noble men; and as I read them through most avidly, I came at last upon the one you had sent to Master Falk Gøye, and on the other side of the page I found a pair of images, one of Astronomy, the other of that Art which you call *Spagyric* [alchemy]. As I gazed at them attentively, I noticed on either side of each of them certain words — concerning Astronomy, indeed, "BY LOOKING UP I LOOK DOWN" [SVSPICIENDO DESPICIO]; but concerning the other, "BY LOOKING DOWN I LOOK UP" [DESPICIENDO SVSPICIO]. Long pondering these with wonder, again and again, I thought at last that they were *hieroglyphs*, and that you perhaps signified by them that the *Spagyric* Art contains the contemplation of all Nature and of the World, and that it has, just as Astronomy does, its own Planets, and that what Nature does through the heavenly Stars, it [the Art] does with like efficacy through its own Stars. If this is so, I greatly desire to know what in the *Spagyric* Art you call the Sun, what the Moon, what Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, what the Elements. I see that the Art is most abstruse, and that the Nature of Things can scarcely be aptly understood without it; and that the Egyptian Priests held something similar. So that if I could obtain from you that you should inform me about it, and add the other things pertaining to this, and which Authors are to be read on this Art: nothing at all could happen to me more welcome.

That you so kindly invite me not to refrain from visiting you, I give you what thanks I can. Not long ago our Most Illustrious Prince was saying that it would please him for me to dedicate our *observations* of the fixed stars to the Most Serene King of Denmark. If he persists in that resolve, I shall be able on this occasion to come to you; but if not, I have composed at Wittenberg, not without many vigils, a *Mathematical Organon* [Organon Mathematicum], which contains the *sexagesimal logistic*, the *doctrine of sines*, the doctrine of the composition of ratios, or of the *rule of six quantities*, and the doctrine of *triangles*, both *spherical* and *plane*, set out clearly and briefly, packed with many ingenious shortcuts, and most dear to me: this I shall dedicate to your Most Serene King, that I may not lack occasion for coming to you. I have likewise composed there an *Astronomy*, in which I have transferred the *hypotheses* of Copernicus to the mobility of the Sun (which you are not unaware can be done), and have set out the several diagrams of the *Theorica* by the *Prutenic* calculation. But since I have found by *observation* that the *Prutenic Tables* depart notably far from the truth of the heavens, I have hitherto deferred its publication, lest I should seem to commend a faulty calculation to learners as true. If, then, it should please you, and if you would bring your *astronomical canons* into the light, I would substitute yours in place of the *Prutenic* calculation, so that your calculation might be made familiar to learners. With wonderful brevity, the heterogeneous [matters] having been dissected by the laws of Logic, I have cast into it far more than the common little books of *Spherics* and *Theorica* contain. I was driven to that work by a most bitter grief, that I saw, not without the greatest indignation, that in the Universities, where above all these studies ought to flourish, almost nothing is understood of this Art: that the *Prutenic* calculation is indeed in everyone's hands, but is handled only according to the bare *Prutenic* precepts, and that none are found who understand its *hypotheses*, not even among those who profess Astronomy and think themselves the highest mathematicians. The *motion* of the precession of the equinoxes and of the changed obliquity of the *zodiac* — whose *hypotheses* I have so far seen no one aptly understand, nor do I think you have seen many [understand them] — I have treated with the greatest ease and perspicuity; though it must now be treated otherwise, since the stars are found to have changed their *latitudes*. About the *artificial* days as well as the *natural* ones, and about the *equation of time*, I have proposed, from the very foundation, things not commonplace. Those real *orbs* and so many axes, obscuring astronomy rather than explaining it, I have wholly done away with. In the *Theorica* of the Sun and Moon I have assumed one and the same supposition of circles, namely an *eccentric* whose centre is movable on a little circle [*circellus*] above the centre of the World, on the line of the mean apogee, and indeed placed at the centre of the mean *eccentricity*: except that in the Sun the *simple anomaly* begins at the highest part of the little circle, while in the Moon the doubled distance from the Sun begins, in the contrary way, from the lowest part of the little circle. I altogether hope that learners can derive the greatest profit from it. My writing on the comet will be received by that most noble and most magnificent Man, your friend Kaas, your most worthy Chancellor, who became known to me from your poem. For whom else should *Urania* rather celebrate than her patron? I love, with the reverence I owe, the highest virtues of this highest Man. As for your thinking, in the letter written to our Most Illustrious Prince, that all comets are generated in the heaven itself above the Moon, and that none of them was ever Elemental — I would readily concede it to you, were not the *observations* of Regiomontanus and Vögelin in the way. For although you rightly assert that observing *parallaxes* properly is of a far subtler skill than the manner hitherto commonly in use could supply, yet the velocity of the *motion* does not seem to reject those *parallaxes*. Nor indeed do I see why they cannot also be generated below the Moon, since the Element of Air is contained everywhere, and seems to have been established chiefly to fill all things, as is established by what precedes. What shall we say about those great comets which occupied such vast spaces of the heaven? But yet I do not doubt that you have not-to-be-despised reasons why you so determine. What my own view is, you will see from the three chapters appended. In the last chapter I have rejected the violent diurnal *motion*. I find that it is altogether to be attributed to the Earth. These things I wished to write out to you at this time, to which I beg you again and again to reply. Herewith fare you happily well, most noble and most ingenious TYCHO, and persuade yourself altogether that I am most loving of you.

At Kassel, the 11th [day before] the Kalends of October [21 September], in the Year of Salvation 1587.
Yours, yours,
CHRISTOPH ROTHMANN, Mathematician of the Most Illustrious Prince Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, etc.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Christophorus Rothmannus* = **Christoph Rothmann** (c. 1550/60 – c. 1600), mathematician and astronomer to **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592). The Kassel court observatory was, with Hven, the leading observational establishment in northern Europe; the Tycho–Rothmann exchange (1585–90) is among the most substantive scientific correspondences of the century. This is Rothmann's reply within that exchange.
- **Recipient titulature.** *Domino de Knudstrup, Equiti Dano* — "Lord of Knudstrup, Danish knight": Tycho's noble seat (Knudstrup, Scania) and rank, kept by this chapter's convention
- **"the comet."** The comet of 1585, the subject of Rothmann's treatise (*Descriptio accurata cometae anni 1585*), three chapters of which he encloses. The debate over whether it showed *parallax* (and so lay below or above the Moon) is the live question.
- ***Hypotheses Coperniceae / Hypotheses Copernici*** — "Copernican hypotheses": rendered *hypotheses* throughout (the period sense = geometrical model/supposition), per glossary; never "theory."
- ***Aristarchum*** — "the *Aristarchus* of my observations": Aristarchus of Samos as the type of the sound, ancient judge/authority; Rothmann makes Tycho the arbiter of his observations. Kept as the classical name with gloss.
- **Obliquity figures.** Rothmann's 23°30′ vs. Tycho's 23°31⅓′ for the maximum obliquity of the ecliptic; solstitial altitudes 62°10′/62°11′/62°12′; pole elevation (equator elevation) 38°41′. All reproduced exactly; no value silently normalised.
- **Refraction theory (the core of the letter).** *Refractio* → **refraction**; *Diaphanum* → **transparent medium** (the period optical term for a refracting/transmitting medium); *Aether liquidissimus* vs. *Aër Elementaris* → "most fluid aether" vs. "elemental air." The dispute: Tycho attributes astronomical refraction to a difference of *diaphana* between aether and air; Rothmann argues refraction arises only from the thick, vapour-laden lower air ("by its doubling about the horizon"), so that there is no aether at all between Earth and the fixed stars — only air encompassing the planets. This is a landmark statement against celestial spheres / for a unitary air-filled cosmos. Rendered fully and faithfully; the geometric demonstration (points A–S, semicircle BCD, surfaces EFG/HIL) is translated literally with the lettering preserved.
- ***[Figura] / Figur 9*** — the source carries a figure reference (the diagram of the refraction demonstration); marked **[Figure 9]** as an editorial insertion since the diagram is not in the text stream.
- **Optical authorities.** *Alhazenus* = **Alhazen** (Ibn al-Haytham); *Vitellio* = **Witelo** (the 13th-c. *Perspectiva*; "Prop. 14, Bk 10" cited); *Petrus Nonius de Crepusculis* = **Pedro Nunes**, *De crepusculis* (Lisbon, 1542). *Crepusculum* → **twilight** by this chapter's convention
- **Greek.** (1) *μεγαλ. συντάξ.* = *Megalē Syntaxis*, the Greek title of Ptolemy's *Almagest* (here "the *Megalē Syntaxis*"). (2) *πόρισμα* = *pórisma*, "corollary" (a geometer's term, kept and glossed). (3) The numeral-letters **ις ϛγ / ις ϛ** are Greek alphabetic numerals: ις = 16, ϛ (stigma) = 6, γ = 3; Rothmann's textual-criticism argument is that a *declination* of 16°50′ (ις ϛγ — reading the second cluster as minutes) was miscopied to 16°30′ (ις ϛ) when a doubled stigma ϛϛ was taken for dittography. The numeral forms are transcribed in the source block and the arithmetic is explained here; **see crux below** — the exact letter-forms and Rothmann's intended minute-values are a genuine textual difficulty.
- **Star catalogue critique.** *Regulus* (α Leonis), *Sirius* (α Canis Maioris), *Lucida Hydrae* (α Hydrae, Alphard), *Aldebaran* (*Aldebora*, α Tauri), *Dexter humerus Orionis* = the **right shoulder of Orion** (Betelgeuse, α Orionis). *Timocharis* and *Hipparchus* are the ancient observers whose *declinations* Rothmann argues Ptolemy merely interpolated ("feigned … according to the proportion of time") rather than observed — an early, pointed charge of fabrication against the *Almagest* star places. *Canon / Tabula / Abacus* → tables/canon. *Almagest* cited "Bk 7, ch. 3."
- **Instruments.** *Instrumentum parallaticum* = the **parallactic instrument / triquetrum** (Ptolemy's, for the Moon); *Armillae* → **armillae / armillary** by this chapter's convention; *Quadrans* → **quadrant**. *Venus diurna* → **daytime Venus** (Venus observed by day, used to carry the reference longitude — Tycho's and Rothmann's technique).
- **Wittich.** *Wittichius* = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586), the Silesian mathematician who had worked both at Hven and at Kassel; here recently dead ("*demortuus* … I am unwilling to say more against a dead man"). Rothmann reproduces and faults Wittich's 7 November 1584 lunar-eclipse record. The eclipse record block is set as its own paragraph, mirroring the source's tabular list; *Plenilunium eclipticum* → "full moon in eclipse"; *Mora in tenebris* → "duration in darkness." Times are given in the source's hour-count from noon (P.M.); reproduced as written (11h20m … 14h45m), **not** converted.
- **Symbols.** Zodiac glyphs kept in the source block and named in English by this chapter's convention: **♏ = Scorpio, ♒ = Aquarius, ♉ = Taurus.**
- **Tycho's emblem.** *Suspiciendo despicio / Despiciendo suspicio* — Tycho's twin mottoes ("By looking up I look down" / "By looking down I look up"), here flanking the personifications of **Astronomia** and the *Ars Spagyrica* (Tycho's term for **alchemy/spagyric art**) on the verso of a poem Tycho had sent to **Falk Gøye** (Danish nobleman). Rothmann reads the device as *hieroglyphica* and asks Tycho for his alchemical planet-metal correspondences. *Spagyrica* kept (period term for Paracelsian chemistry), glossed "alchemy."
- **Persons named.** *M. Ioannes Aalborga* = **Hans Aalborg**; *Kaasius … Cancellarius vester* = **Niels Kaas**, Chancellor of Denmark (Tycho's patron at court), known to Rothmann from a poem of Tycho's; *Regiomontanus* (Johannes Müller of Königsberg) and *Vogelinus* = **Johannes Vögelin** (Vienna, d. 1549, author on comet parallax) — the two authorities whose comet *observations* keep Rothmann from fully conceding Tycho's supralunary-only thesis.
- **Rothmann's own works.** *Organon Mathematicum* — his unpublished mathematical handbook (sexagesimal logistic, *doctrine of sines*, *regula sex quantitatum* = the rule of six quantities / compound proportion, plane and spherical *trigonometry*); kept in Latin and glossed. *Astronomia* — his treatise transposing Copernicus's *hypotheses* to "the mobility of the Sun" and computing the *Theorica* schemes by the *Prutenic* (Reinhold's *Tabulae Prutenicae*) calculation, which he reports departs notably from the heavens. *Logistica Sexagenaria* → **sexagesimal logistic** (computation in base-60). *restitutio/restauratio Astronomiae* → **restoration of astronomy** by this chapter's convention (Tycho's programme: "to you we leave the *restoration of astronomy*").
- **Cosmology — abolition of solid orbs.** *Orbes illos reales et tot axes … prorsus sustuli* — "those real orbs and so many axes … I have wholly done away with": Rothmann, like Tycho, rejects solid celestial spheres. The lunar/solar *Theorica* description (*Eccentricus … circellus … in linea Apogaei medij … centrum mediae Eccentricitatis*; *anomalia simplex*) is rendered with glossary terms (*eccentric, apogee, eccentricity, anomaly*) and the diminutive *circellus* as "little circle."
- ***motum violentum diurnum … Terrae tribuendum*** — "the violent diurnal motion … to be attributed to the Earth": Rothmann states he has rejected the violent daily rotation of the heavens and assigns the diurnal motion to the Earth — an openly Copernican (or at least diurnally-rotating-Earth) commitment. Rendered without softening.
- **Dateline (calendar crux flagged, not converted).** *Cassellis. 11. Calend. Octob. Anno … M.D.LXXXVII* = "At Kassel, the 11th [day before] the Kalends of October, 1587." By the Roman inclusive count, *ante diem XI Kalendas Octobris* = **21 September** — i.e. the Roman-calendar idiom denotes a September date, not 1 October. The edition/edition label "11. oktober. Kassel" reflects a **different reckoning of the dateline** (and/or an O.S.→N.S. consideration: Hesse-Kassel was Protestant and still on the Julian calendar in 1587, so no Gregorian gap is expected for an internal German Protestant date). Per this chapter's convention the dateline is reproduced as written, the Roman idiom is glossed to its civil date (21 Sept., O.S.), and the discrepancy with the "11 October" label is **flagged, not reconciled.** *Anno Salutis* → "in the Year of Salvation." *T.T.* = *Tui Tuus* / *Tuus Totus*, "Yours, [yours]" — an affectionate subscription.
- ***S. P.*** (heading) = *Salutem Plurimam* (dicit), "heartiest greeting," by this chapter's convention
- **Correction.** fabrication removed: the English diagram marker '[Figure 9]' invented a sequence number absent from the Latin's unnumbered '[Figura]'; corrected to '[Figure]'.

text.original:
HENRICO RANZOVIO PRODUCI CIMBRICO TYCHO BRAHE.
S. D.

QUOD nihil hac tota æstate ad te literarum dederim, nobilissime eruditissimeque Domine HENRICE RANZOVI, amice inprimis colende, neque oblivione ulla tui, cuius memoriam cum filio GERHARDO, amico et vicino meo dilecto, sæpius recolo, neque negligentia voluntaria factum existimes. Verum cum in dies expectarem ab illustrissimo Domino GULIELMO Landgravio Hassiæ litteras, quibus meis secundo ad ipsum datis per proprium tabellarium respondere pollicitus est, ut earum exemplar tibi unâ cum prioribus, quibus invicem de rebus Astronomicis ex voto egimus, inspiciendum mitterem, accidit ut diutius quam sperabam rescriptio illa procrastinata sit adeo, ut iam primum circa medium Octobris responsum a prædicto illustrissimo Principe ad Literas in Ianuario ipsi perscriptas acceperim. Contigit vero commodum, quod his ipsis diebus quendam ex meis domesticis Lubecam ablegaverim, ut papyrum impressoriam, quam operi cuidam, quod nunc typis meis elaboratur, sufficientem desidero, illic mature procuret, et quædam alia negotia, quæ in mandatis habet, unâ meo nomine expediat. Idcirco non inscius, Segebergam unius saltem diei itinere illinc abesse, nolui ipsum tam prope sedes, in quibus moraris, accedere, quin aliquid a me tibi literarum adferret meoque nomine officiose salutem diceret. Dedi itaque huic in mandatis, ut te Segebergæ conveniret hasque literas cum adiunctis tibi tradere non intermitteret. Invenies in his illustrissimi Domini Landgravij et ipsius Mathematici ROTHMANNI responsionem ad priores meas, quarum (ni fallor) tibi exemplar prius misi. Adiunxi etiam ea, quæ eidem illustrissimo Principi et dicto ipsius Mathematico postea de rebus Astronomicis luculenter rescripsi, et ab ipso Principe denuo remissum responsum, quod modo accepi, unâ addidi. Literæ Mathematici, quæ adiunctæ erant, non tam cito ob prolixitatem et copiam transcribi poterant, eo quod nuncius meus ob venti oportunitatem abitum festinaret. Sed alio tempore, si ita tibi placuerit, eas facile obtinebis. Addidi etiam festinanter quædam, quæ ex tempore mihi in mentem venerunt, ad hasce ultimas Landgravianas literas per nuncij et otij oportunitatem respondenda, et literarum notis certos paragraphos designavi, quibus responsiones eisdem literis adaptatæ quadrant. Hinc quid de affixarum restitutionibus utrinque sentiamus, facile percipies et non sine voluptate magnam congruentiam animadvertes. Non enim me latet, quanto desiderio rerum Astronomicarum afficiaris, et quam egregie de his meritus sis. Tuum erit, mecum, si quid vel ab antedicto Principe vel ex propria Bibliotheca aut aliunde habes, quod ad Astronomicam, qua utrinque delectamur, materiam illustrandam facit, vicissim communicare. Vale, et huic nuncio meo in ijs, quæ illi expedienda iniunxi, tuo consilio authoritateque, ubi opus fuerit, ne deesse velis.

Iterum feliciter cum nobilissima uxore et sobole non degenere totaque domo vale.
Datæ Uraniburgi 19. Octobris Anno 1587.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Heinrich Rantzau, Governor of the Cimbrian land.**
Sends greeting.

That I have sent you no letter this whole summer, most noble and most learned Master Heinrich Rantzau, my friend especially to be honoured, you must not suppose to have come about either from any forgetfulness of you — whose memory I often recall together with your son Gerhard, my dear friend and neighbour — or from any wilful negligence. Rather, since I was daily awaiting letters from the most illustrious Lord Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse — to which, after I had written to him a second time, he had promised to reply by his own courier — so that I might send you a copy of them, along with the earlier ones in which we dealt with one another on astronomical matters to our mutual wish, it came about that that reply was put off longer than I had hoped, so much so that it was only now, around the middle of October, that I received the answer of the aforesaid most illustrious Prince to the letter written out to him in January. But it has fallen out conveniently that in these very days I have dispatched one of my household to Lübeck, that he might procure there in good time printing paper — which I find sufficient for a certain work that is now being produced at my press — and might at the same time, in my name, settle certain other affairs which he has in charge. Therefore, not unaware that Segeberg is at least one day's journey distant from there, I was unwilling that he should pass so near the seat where you reside without his bringing you some letter from me and dutifully conveying a greeting in my name. And so I gave him charge to meet with you at Segeberg and not to fail to deliver to you this letter together with its enclosures. In them you will find the reply of the most illustrious Lord Landgrave and of his own Mathematician Rothmann to my earlier ones, of which (unless I am mistaken) I sent you a copy before. I have added also those things which I afterwards wrote back at length on astronomical matters to that same most illustrious Prince and to his said Mathematician, and I have added together with them the answer sent back again by the Prince himself, which I have just received. The Mathematician's letters, which were enclosed, could not be transcribed so quickly on account of their prolixity and abundance, since my messenger was hastening his departure because of the favourable wind. But at another time, if it so please you, you will easily obtain them. I have also hastily added certain things which occurred to me on the spur of the moment, to be answered to these last letters of the Landgrave as the opportunity of messenger and leisure allowed; and I have marked off particular paragraphs with letters of the alphabet, by which the replies fitted to those same letters correspond. From this you will easily perceive what each of us holds concerning the restorations of the fixed [stars], and you will note, not without pleasure, the great agreement. For it is not hidden from me with how great a longing you are moved toward astronomical matters, and how excellently you have deserved well of them. It will be for you in turn to share with me, if you have anything either from the aforesaid Prince, or from your own library, or from elsewhere, which serves to illuminate the astronomical subject in which we both delight. Farewell; and to this my messenger, in the matters which I have enjoined upon him to settle, do not be unwilling to lend your counsel and authority, where there shall be need.

Again, happily, farewell — with your most noble wife and your offspring that does not fall short of its stock, and your whole house.
Given at Uraniborg, 19 October, the year 1587.
