Or if that can be granted, how much more is the same not to be admitted in the diversity of the transparency of aether and air — from which this [diversity], at such an altitude, brings in a still much smaller difference, for the reasons judged above. Moreover, even if it be granted that no refraction at all arises on the occasion of the diversity of air and aether, but that the whole draws its origin from the vapours alone, yet it would not necessarily follow on that account that the heaven itself is composed of elemental and animal[ate] air, as is your pleasure; for the likeness and nearness of the transparent bodies, and their mutual connection, can be so great that it begets no refraction such as is perceived by us, the light of the stars strongly penetrating each transparent body. For we do not hold the heaven to consist of a hard and impervious transparency, as Alhazen and Witelo [held], who on that account vainly believed that the greatest refraction occurs — but that the aether itself is most fluid and most rarefied, and woven of no real orbs, just as you too most rightly agree with me; and although it is something more perfect than air itself, yet around the revolutions, especially the lunar ones, this elemental air is so exalted that it passes over, as it were, into aethereal substance, and therefore the diversity of the transparent bodies is rendered imperceptible, as was indicated before too. But the more the air approaches the Earth, the less it partakes of the aethereal nature, and the more it has of elemental quality; and nonetheless it is very subtle and rare, so that it transmits the light of the stars easily and without refraction, unless it be nearer the Earth, where it is condensed by vapours and rendered more turbid. But as to refractions — whence they come, whether merely with the vapours as intermediaries, as it seems to you, or rather not only from these but also in some measure from the discrepancy of the transparency of aether and air, by a certain mixed reasoning, as is my pleasure — we dispute over this so greatly in vain, since the principal question being treated is about restoring the motion of the celestial bodies and about astronomy itself being purged of faults and renewed; and although the knowledge of refractions brings necessary aid to this aim — because without taking precaution of these, the very places of the stars cannot be deduced from the heaven — yet because it suffices the astronomer to know how high the impediments of refractions ascend, and how great they are at certain altitudes (especially where a uniform and unconfused serenity of air has shone clear), therefore whence these refractions come, whether from a twofold or even a single cause, it does not much matter to dispute subtly and ambiguously. Just as the very question concerning the matter of the heaven does not properly pertain to the astronomer's decision; for he labours to investigate from sure observations, not what the heaven is and of what its splendid bodies consist, but only how all these things are moved. The other he leaves to be debated by the theologians and natural philosophers, among whom indeed this very thing has hitherto remained not sufficiently explained. For so great is [the matter] that one cannot fully drain even the whole works of the Creator — not even the terrestrial ones, lying open to the external senses and so near us that they may be touched — much less is one equal to investigating and explaining sufficiently that sublime and most remote nature and substance of the aether. About the matter of the heaven, therefore, which is inscrutable, there is no reason for us to dispute anxiously, except that I judge this must necessarily be laid down: that it, whatever it may be, has nothing in common with the elemental nature, and therefore is by no means airy, but contains within itself a more divine and far more perfect nature than may deservedly be likened to any elemental things. But it suffices that we agree on the more principal aim — namely, that the heaven is woven of no real and hard and impervious orbs, by which the stars are carried around fixed [to them], but consists of a most fluid, most rarefied, and most subtle substance, which admits the free courses of the seven planets, wherever their natural impulse and inborn knowledge carries them, without any retardation. This, I say, hitherto not perceived by the ancients and even by the greatest part of the moderns, nor granted as indubitable, is enough to admit as ratified and ascertained for the reintegration of astronomy; for thus, by ordering the hypotheses more suitably — as has also for some time been done by us — a more compendious and plainer way will be paved. Wherefore, as I said, it is not worth the effort that we busy ourselves at length about the matter of the heaven and the occasion of refractions; only, if anything further in refractions becomes known through sure experience, it seems conducive, to the establishing of astronomical precision, that we communicate it to one another.

So I shall add one single thing only about these matters, and afterward pass on to others. Refractions in the Sun are not found here around the horizon much greater than with you; for I too, at an altitude of three degrees, found at the summer solstice that no refraction greater than 12 minutes occurs — for as to your reckoning that I assert it then to be 28 minutes, you seem not to have attended sufficiently that I spoke of the Sun in the very setting, as it hides itself, when namely only half of it is discerned above the horizon — which is well enough observed on this island, especially in the place of my dwelling, which is so high that it affords a free visible horizon [finitor] on every side. For refractions vary very greatly around the very setting, so much so that a difference of three degrees alters them by about a quarter of one degree. So likewise at your winter altitude of 15 degrees, when with you a refraction of 7⅓ minutes is produced on the meridian, I, at a like altitude — the Sun being near the 5th degree of ♒ Aquarius or ♏ Scorpio — was never able to find a refraction greater than 7½ minutes, which agrees well enough with yours, although you nonetheless reckon that refractions here insinuate themselves perceptibly greater than there. And at the winter solstice, when the Sun at midday rises for us only 10⅔ degrees, the refraction turns out to be at least 9½ minutes, the reckoning of parallax being applied in all cases. You see, then, that solar refractions appear in the heaven imperceptibly greater here than with you, provided they be weighed diligently enough at a like altitude. I suspect, therefore, that in the fixed stars, in the inquiry concerning refraction, there is some fault underlying your findings, in that they have somewhat less than ours; or perhaps because the vast sea lying open from the place of my observation toward the north makes the refractions in the northern part of the horizon a little greater than elsewhere, on account of the vapours continually exhaling more from there. In the rest of the places of the horizon I see no perceptible difference from your annotation, and so it matters hardly at all that, according to the opinion of the ancients, the air in these northern places is held to be denser and thicker; for the 4½ degrees by which we differ in latitude change the nature of the air little. Indeed, at Augsburg too, under an elevation of 48⅓ [degrees], I experienced several winters much colder than those that commonly occur with us, and summers also less hot. But because you reckon it can be discerned, by the observation of twilights, whether the surface of the thick air is raised higher here than in your horizon: know that I have diligently observed, near the equinoctial times, that the morning twilight here begins when the Sun is depressed at least 16⅓ degrees below the horizon — so much so that the arc of twilight is then precisely only 25 degrees, which, however, the Nonnian and commonly received reckoning would make nearly 28 degrees. If you should at some time diligently explore the same there, I do not doubt that you will find the arc of twilight to be no greater with us than at Kassel, and on that account the vapours of our horizon to ascend no higher than with you — whence it also follows that the lower air is not perceptibly thicker in this northern region than in places somewhat more southerly. From all these things, too, it is sufficiently gathered that those things which you bring forward concerning the nature of the vapours, and the account of refractions deduced from these alone, and so concerning the matter of the whole heaven, afterward pronounced from these to be airy and elemental, do not rest on foundations so sure as you ingeniously and clearly endeavour to persuade. These things, then, being left, let us proceed to the rest.

That the variation of the latitudes in the fixed stars is subject to the change of the declination of the ecliptic, is sufficiently agreed between us, and has been abundantly confirmed from very many stars in my later letter; nor does the discordant latitude of Sirius alone derogate anything from this assertion, as you too rightly support me, and you adduce most plausible causes for the ancients' slip in noting its declination and latitude — wherefore there is no need to say more about this matter now. The eclipse of the Moon of the year [15]84 I knew well enough to have been observed less diligently by Wittich, and not to correspond with his own annotations, since I had long known his less skilled practice in handling these things. In geometrical matters and in the handling of triangles and numbers he was nimbler and more successful; I did not know, when I was writing the later [letter], that he had yielded to the fates, otherwise I should have dealt with him more sparingly. The eclipse of the Moon which fell in September of the preceding year I observed here after a fashion, so that I am sure enough of its time within 2 or 3 minutes; for although here, while it lasted, a certain serenity shone for us at least through momentary intervals among the recurring clouds, yet the sky here was not so dark and rainy as with you. In the more westerly tract of lands, throughout its whole duration, a constant and clear serenity shone. For it was reported to me that in England it was very well observed from beginning to end — indeed, even in the Cimbric Chersonese (which is the more westerly part of Denmark, distant at least 30 miles from here, and a little nearer the setting [west] than your meridian), throughout the whole time during which this eclipse lasted, the sky was thoroughly serene and on every side free of clouds, as one of my students, to whom leave had then been granted to go away thither into his homeland, reported on his return here. Hence it becomes manifest on how frivolous and uncertain a foundation the meteorological predictions of the common run of astrologers rest, since in horizons so near one another the constitution of the air often differs by the whole heaven [i.e. utterly] — but this is beside the point. The eclipse of the Moon of this passing year, which fell at the beginning of March, I observed more diligently, for there was a moderate serenity for as long as it laboured in the shadow; and I found that its times exceeded the Prutenic calculation by half an hour, but anticipated the Alphonsine by 1 hour and a third [1⅓ h], and the Peurbachian by five-twelfths of an hour [a quincunx]; and that, moreover, it fell short of Maestlin's newfangled restitution, which he set at the front in his Ephemerides, by a little more than a whole hour. So it is sufficiently apparent how far the reintegration established by him in these matters is hitherto to be trusted. Thus in that eclipse which occurred in the year [15]81, on 15 July in the morning at dawn, his correction overran the observation by one hour and a third; he reports too, in the same [eclipse], setting down his rectification, that the Moon ought to have been eclipsed by three digits — namely by a quarter of its body — when it set on the Tübingen horizon, whereas in this our [horizon], which is still more easterly by half an hour, the Moon entered the Earth's shadow half [eclipsed] before it sank beneath the horizon — so that on this account it turns out consistent that with them it lay hidden, as it were, wholly in the shadow before its setting. Thus also in certain other eclipses I have several times observed a notable difference of Maestlin's restitution from the heaven itself, so that hence it is sufficiently plain that the course of both luminaries has not yet been perceived by him with that precision which he supposes — indeed, even in the rectification of the fixed stars he has hitherto greatly deviated from the mark, as is clearly evident from his little book on the comet of the year [15]80. I see that he is not destitute of suitable instruments, [but] of native talent and knowledge. Let this much be enough to have said about eclipses.

That you observe the courses of the planets less diligently than the places of the fixed stars seems something alien to this whole undertaking; for the places of the fixed stars are verified chiefly for this cause, that through them the courses and appearances of the planets may be more rightly made known. In the three more distant planets, especially Saturn and Jupiter, I still require certain acronychal observations, so that I may at some time, with the favour of divine clemency, restore their circuits exactly congruent with the heaven; in the rest of the planets there is enough means at hand for accomplishing it. Take care that hereafter you bestow faithful labour also on the observations of the wandering stars [planets], so that, a collation being at some time made, the agreement between us may be tested in these too. That your Most Illustrious Prince ponders the publication of your observations and rectifications in the places of the affixed [fixed] stars, and urges that it be done through you, I judge very praiseworthy and perpetually honourable to His Highness's name; labour, then, that we may shortly have it; nor is there reason that the difference of five minutes between us in the longitudes of all the fixed stars should move you, for it is exceedingly small, and easily earns excuse among those who understand the intricate depth of the business. But that in my own determinations of these things those five minutes by no means fall short, and that in these I have worked everything out with that precision to which our senses can attain, I have set out clearly to your Most Illustrious Prince, and I have added reasons which confirm me in my position and which persuade evidently enough that I have admitted nothing more or less than is right in these matters. Venus's diameter, to be sure, although it be largish, will yet not excuse this discrepancy between us; for when I observe the star of Venus through the slits of the earlier sight [pinnule], somewhat narrower (as ought to be done with the larger stars), its distance from the fixed stars always fell to the same minute, even when repeated several times — so that there is hence no danger at all but that the places of the fixed stars have been restored by me to the hairline [exactly], once and again, both in the morning and in the evening, nor will anything of what was written to me in the Most Illustrious Prince's letter be able in any way to derogate from our findings. Nonetheless I judge that you do rightly, in that, trusting also to your own observations and restitutions, you have decided to change nothing in these; for thus posterity will less suspect that we, by deliberate effort and by sharing counsels, ordered these longitudes of the stars by unanimous agreement. Yet I do not doubt that at some time, when through renewed instruments, by the benefit of Venus not only as Evening- but also as Morning-[star], you have recalled this business to the anvil from the opposite side and with diligent consideration, you will yourselves most clearly detect that those five minutes in your notation are in excess of the celestial measuring-line, but in mine by no means fall short; and that then, taught by your own experience, you will, I hope, of your own accord stretch out your hands to the more exact verification. For until this matter has been most diligently examined through the reciprocal observation of Venus relative to the Sun, applied to the stars, anything certain is announced in vain; for that, through Venus observed by you as Evening-star only, a plausible agreement with the earlier findings appeared, was happening rather on account of the insinuation of refraction in Venus and in the setting Sun, than because it was really so consonant with the heaven — as I have set out more fully in writing to your Most Illustrious Prince. I marvel that you affirm the motion of the Sun transmitted by me to you, near the first degrees of ♒ Aquarius, to be somewhat slower than is right, since you yourself do not deny that it elsewhere agrees most exactly, in the whole northern semicircle, and near both equinoxes, with your observations themselves attesting the same. For one ought to have remembered that in my earlier letter I indicated openly enough that the observation of the Sun's motion agrees with the heaven itself only in the northern semicircle, but in the southern, on account of the impediments of refractions, not so. And the Sun, being on the meridian with you at the beginning of ♒ Aquarius, rises only 18½ degrees, where it induces a very perceptible refraction, and necessarily appears farther on by observation than it really is — which has often become known to me too as I tried this very thing. Remove, then, the impediments of refraction in the southern semicircle, and it will be plain that our restitution in the Sun's motion corresponds there too, no less than in the northern, very closely with the celestial standard. And I have sent to your Most Illustrious Prince in addition 5 years' Ephemerides of the Sun, deduced from our calculation, so that in the following years a trial of this matter may be made with your instruments, the just-mentioned caution being applied.

You pass afterward from the celestial to the poetical — or rather to certain hieroglyphic figures of the connection of the higher and lower things, which you chanced to behold in a certain poem composed by me four years ago for pleasure's sake, [addressed] to the most noble man, equally most learned in Latin and Greek letters, Falk Gøye, my friend and kinsman, beloved by me; and you anxiously ask of me why beside the depicted Philosopher who scrutinizes celestial things there is written on this side and that LOOKING UP, I LOOK DOWN [SUSPICIENDO DESPICIO], and about the other [Philosopher], who [scrutinizes] terrestrial things, LOOKING DOWN, I LOOK UP [DESPICIENDO SUSPICIO]. That I may not, in this part too, fail your wishes altogether, take it thus. You conjectured rightly that these are hieroglyphics; for they regard not only each Astronomy — that higher celestial one, and the lower terrestrial — but also the more divine and less commonly used Theology itself, and so the knowledge of all Ethics, namely the discernment of virtues and vices. But at first sight it bears forth the physical consideration of created things, in which the higher are so connected with the lower by an admirable analogy that neither can be rightly perceived nor thoroughly searched out without the other; for, as you rightly gather, that art which we call Spagyric [chymistry] contains the investigation of all nature, and so a certain inner handling [of it], and presents a pleasant and not useless exercise of a certain terrestrial Astronomy (as I called it before). And that you may be made conscious of some part of the things you seek, it is fitting to know that there are seven planets in the heaven, just as there are seven metals in the earth, and that in man — fashioned to the idea of both, who on that account is rightly called a Microcosm — there are seven principal members; and all these are bound together with one another by so beautiful and fitting a likeness that they seem to have well-nigh equal offices and the same properties and natures. Thus the two principal luminaries in the heaven, the Sun and the Moon, are matched with the two more excellent metals, Gold and Silver, and in man with the two chief vital members, the heart and the brain. The two beneficent planets, Jupiter and Venus, take to themselves a place among the earthly metals, Tin and Copper, of the second rank after the former; and in our bodies, the liver, the workshop of the blood, and the kidneys [Renes], the ministers of generation. But the two planets which they call maleficent, Saturn and Mars, correspond to the baser metals, namely Lead and Iron, and in the bodies of men are allotted two less necessary and lowly members, the Spleen and the Gall-bladder [Fel], which are the receptacles of the overflowing black and yellow bile. The celestial Mercury, as it is by its nature indifferent [neutral] and more changeable than Proteus, so it has analogous to itself the terrestrial Mercury, or quicksilver, which likewise is transmuted into various forms and emulates the nature of all the rest of the metals, and puts on marvellous metamorphoses; and in the microcosmic body, to this among the seven principal members the Lung is rightly likened, whose office is to draw breath [Spiritus] and to revive the heart and the rest of the members by its respiration; it serves speech, too, very much — just as that celestial Mercury also is believed to preside over this [speech]. There are, besides, many things in these seven, bound together with one another by an admirable likeness, which cannot be explained in few words. So too the rest of the earth's minerals — gems, marcasites, and salts — agree by a fixed law with the various planets, and are associated chiefly with the nature of the fixed stars, which contain the powers of the planets within themselves, though more obscurely; just as herbs and vegetables too, by a certain fixed order, are assigned in terrestrial Astronomy not only to the planets but also to the fixed stars, and emulate their nature so far as in them lies. These things and many more of the kind, to understand thoroughly, common Physics does not teach; nor have the Academies — maddened and encrusted by the sophisms and rouges of the Peripatetics — either learned or [do they] teach how to look into the real, very kernel of truth lying hidden in these matters. The Pyronomic [fire-working] School must be approached, which makes manifest not the things that are plausibly discoursed of, but the things that are truly handled with the hands, seen with the eyes, and perceived by the outer and inner senses. Antiquity had some Teachers in this Gymnasium, and our own Age too has not been wholly destitute of them, although the pompous and formal Professors of the Academies either neglect them through carelessness, or repudiate them through ignorance, or even detest them out of hatred and prejudiced judgement; for the more sincere truth, not only in divine matters but also in worldly Philosophy, has both been, and hereafter will be, hated as much by the common run of men (which were to be borne) as by those who most profess it (which is to be lamented) — unless God shall at some time institute a special and marvellous Metamorphosis of the world. The authors in this more secret Philosophy are very many, among whom the chief place is held, as for the ancients, by that Hermes Trismegistus, author of the Emerald Tablet; Geber; [John of] Rupescissa; Arnaldus of Villanova; Raymond Lull; Thomas Aquinas; Roger Bacon; the *Turba Philosophorum*; Albertus Magnus; and in the more recent Age, Isaac Hollandus and Theophrastus Paracelsus, whom more attack than understand. But although these, and certain others besides who are writers in this more occult art, supply great assistance to learners, and the occasion of weighing and investigating the whole matter through natural causes, yet unless there be added a diligent and long-continued handling through Pyronomic [fire-working] practice, one sweats over the bare pages in vain; for most rightly does Paracelsus say that no one knows more in this Art than he has himself experienced through fire. For a silence more than Pythagorean forbids these things to be wholly entrusted to disciples other than the worthy and fit. If you are at some time with me, perhaps you will behold in these matters certain things previously desired, and not everywhere to be met with. For I cultivate this terrestrial Astronomy with no less effort and expense than that celestial one, the suitable structures being arranged for treating it duly, and with a great variety and abundance of furnaces, all of which the pen does not undertake to relate.

You return then from this lower Philosophy to that higher and aethereal one, and you inform me about your writings, which you have hitherto completed in the astronomical field, and about those which pertain to this from the knowledge of triangles and numbers. And I should wish all these to be published by you, for they seem likely to bring much light to these Arts. But if it should not be convenient for you that this be done shortly, [then] at least, that the manuscript and transcribed copies be communicated to me, to be inspected for a short time and soon to be restored to you in good and inviolate faith — provided this were open [permissible] for you — I would have you requested. And although the Prutenic calculation often perceptibly deviates from the heaven itself, you can nonetheless apply the Copernican hypotheses, reduced to the immobility of the Earth, to it, and publish that most excellent labour, so that learners may more rightly, and with greater pleasure and profit, fundamentally perceive the congruence of the calculation and the hypotheses; for this has not been done faithfully enough by others who have undertaken to attempt it, while they violently thrust the Ptolemaic and Alphonsine hypotheses upon the Copernican numbers, short of exact correspondence. I shall work to adapt my own restitutions in the course of all the planets to a hypothesis of my own, not so long ago devised, and I have resolved to show the agreement of the calculation with these, and so with the heaven itself, and to set it forth myself in a particular work, the divine Power favouring. But of this hypothesis you have a more general delineation in our second Volume, *On the New Generations of the Aethereal World*, lately transmitted to you, which the more diligently you examine, the more it will please you; for it removes all the absurdities, both mathematical and physical, that lurk in the old Ptolemaic and in the recent Copernican assumption, and satisfies the more particular appearances most aptly on every side, which neither of the others does in every respect, as we shall demonstrate elsewhere from the observations themselves. Since among other things you make mention of the Equations of days, know that I lay down certain things in these differently from the opinions of my predecessors, and that it [the equation of days] is not so great as is assumed even by Copernicus himself — having been taught not only by sure reasonings, but also by experience itself — concerning which a more convenient occasion for discoursing will be given in its place. If you dedicate your writing on the comet to the most ample and most noble Master Niels Kaas, the Chancellor, a man brilliantly deserving of our Fatherland and of all the good arts — as you write you will do — I do not doubt that it will be most welcome to him, although I have hitherto said nothing privately to him about this matter. You add afterward that you would readily grant me that all comets are generated in the aether, were it not that the observations of Regiomontanus and of Vogelin stood in the way; but I shall show, in the Epilogue of our whole Work, in what place these are to be held, clearly and by reasonings in no way doubtful, concerning this whole business. Regiomontanus's annotations do not agree with themselves, nor could the parallax of so swift a comet at the Ear of Corn [Spica] of ♍ Virgo be traced out in any way; since, then, he trusted too much in these together with the assertions of Aristotle, if he obtained through some carelessness any conjecture about some parallax that would render it sublunar, he held to it tooth and nail as the truer; for he seems to have laboured much in this, to dig out as great a [parallax] as possible. Vogelin's observations are quite erroneous, nor do they agree, in the same comet, with those which are found published by Peter Apian and Fracastoro, as I shall show more fully elsewhere. And the daily motion besides, which is set by him at least at 2⅔ degrees, seems to refuse [the claim] that this comet was so near the Earth that it produced a parallax of 35 degrees — so much so that it was not distant from the Earth's surface by [more than] one and a half semidiameters of the Earth, as the same author does not hesitate incompetently to maintain. Although — to say the very thing as it is — the swiftness and slowness of motion do not sufficiently discern the remoteness or the approach of comets, whence nothing stands in the way of that which you seem to oppose to us: namely, that the swiftness of motion in the Regiomontanian comet, which is set at 40 degrees of a great circle in one day, argues that it was sublunar, and had as great a parallax as he attributes to it. For if it was permissible for the comet of the year 1585 to be situated in the highest orb of Saturn — even by your own judgement — and nonetheless from the beginning to complete a daily motion of three degrees, when the star of Saturn itself, even at its swiftest, accomplishes at least 8 minutes in one day (so much so that the comet was then more than twenty times swifter than Saturn itself, even at its fastest): who, I ask, will not also be able to grant that that comet described by Regiomontanus was above the Moon, although by its daily motion it was about three times swifter? For since the very reality of the orbs does not belong to the heaven (on which matter we agree with one another), these secondary and adventitious stars [comets] can in any case obtain whatever motion their inborn knowledge brings, in whatever place of the heaven, higher or lower, they are at last revolved; for they are not in every respect subject to the laws of the planets and of the stars coeval with the world. So too the magnitude of certain comets does not sufficiently prove their nearness; for they can, in the heaven itself and at whatever loftiness beyond the Moon, acquire as great a magnitude as it pleased the Fashioner [Creator]. Nor is the sublunar air, which you reckon the same as the celestial, apt for the generation of such and so excellent phenomena. Concerning these things and the like I am about to set out my opinion more fully in the general conclusion of our Work *On the Extraordinary Generations of the Aethereal World*, intending, as I hope, to satisfy you and others in this part. About the motion or rest of the Earth or of the heaven itself, as far as concerns the daily revolution, I shall disclose elsewhere what I think.

But I should very greatly wish that at the first opportunity, leave having been obtained from your Most Illustrious Prince, you would not fail to visit me here; for thus we shall confer in person more conveniently and fully, both about these things and about others pertaining to the divine art of Astronomy and to the Philosophy hidden from the common run of the learned, and I shall bring it about that you do not repent of that journey. In the meantime, and always, fare you most happily, my most beloved Rothmann, for it is time that I now close the letter, since your letters have now, in all the things they contained, been answered copiously, according to our strength and the occasion of the time. It will be your part to give labour with all diligence, that a reply from your Most Illustrious Prince and from you be prepared for me betimes, and that this be accomplished in the meantime, while the bearer of these [letters] is away at the Fair — so that, returning to you, he may find it certainly completed and written out at your house. For neither his travelling-companions nor the conveniences of the wagons will allow him to draw out any delay there. For I should very greatly wish to obtain a reply to this my letter from you before winter, so that it may be the more opportunely permitted to write back to the coming spring Fair afterward. Do you, therefore, move every stone, lest the business be procrastinated.

Again, fare you most happily, and continue to love in return me who most love you.

Given at Uraniborg, the 17th day of August, in the year 1588. TYCHO BRAHE.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Christophorus Rothmannus* = **Christoph Rothmann** (c. 1550/60–after 1600), mathematician-astronomer at the Hesse-Kassel observatory of **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (*Illustrissimus Princeps Wilhelmus Landtgravius Hassiae*). This is one of the central technical letters of the Tycho–Rothmann exchange (printed by Tycho in *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* I, Uraniborg 1596), debating the *materia caeli* (substance of the heaven) and the cause of atmospheric refraction.
- **Persons named.** *Gellius Sascerides* = **Gellius Sascerides** (1562–1612), Tycho's assistant/famulus, courier of the earlier packet. *Witichius* = **Paul Wittich** (d. 1586), the Wrocław/Breslau mathematician who had worked at Hven; Tycho notes he had died ("yielded to the fates") and so wishes he had treated him "more sparingly." *Maesthlinus* = **Michael Maestlin** (1550–1631), professor at Tübingen (Kepler's teacher); his *Ephemerides* and his *libellus de Cometa Anni 80* (the tract on the comet of 1580) are criticized. *Iohannes Pena Gallus* = **Jean Pena** (c. 1528–1558), French royal mathematician, who in the preface to his Euclid *Optica* (1557) argued for an airy heaven. *Iordanus Nullanus* = **Giordano Bruno of Nola** ("of Nola"); the *scriptum de Mundo contra Peripateticos* alludes to Bruno's cosmological dialogues (*De l'infinito, universo e mondi* / *La cena de le ceneri*, London 1584) or *De immenso*. *Falco Goye* = **Falk Gøye** (Falco Gøye, 1545–1594), Danish nobleman, Tycho's friend and kinsman (*affinis*), addressee of Tycho's emblematic poem. *Nicolaus Kaasius* = **Niels Kaas** (1535–1594), Chancellor of Denmark. *Regiomontanus* = **Johannes Müller of Königsberg** (1436–1476). *Vogelinus* = **Georg Vögelin** (Vögelin/Voegelin), 16th-c. author on the 1532 comet. *Petrus Apianus* = **Peter Apian** (1495–1552); *Fracastorius* = **Girolamo Fracastoro** (1476/8–1553). *Alhasen* = **Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen)**; *Vitellio* = **Witelo** (13th-c. optical writer); both cited as the *veteres optici* who thought the heaven a hard, adamantine transparent body. **Alchemical authority-roster:** *Hermes Trismegistus* (author of the *Tabula Smaragdina*, the Emerald Tablet); *Geber* (Jābir / pseudo-Geber); *Rupecissa* = **John of Rupescissa**; *Arnoldus de villa nova* = **Arnaldus of Villanova**; *Raymundus Lullius* = **Ramon Llull** (pseudo-Lullian corpus); *Thomas Aquinates* = **Thomas Aquinas** (pseudo-Aquinas alchemica); *Rogerius Bacho* = **Roger Bacon**; *Turba Philosophorum* (the anonymous alchemical dialogue); *Albertus Magnus*; *Isaacus Hollandus* = **Isaac Hollandus**; *Theophrastus Paracelsus* = **Paracelsus**.
- **Places.** *Uraniburgum* = **Uraniborg** (Tycho's observatory on Hven). *Cassellis* = **Kassel**. *Augusta Vindelicorum* = **Augsburg** (latitude given as 48⅓°). *Cymbrica Chersonesus* = the **Cimbric Chersonese** = Jutland (here called "the more westerly part of Denmark"). *Horizon Tubingensis* = **Tübingen** (Maestlin's meridian).
- **Dateline / date crux.** The source's own subscription reads *"Datae Vraniburgi die 17. Augusti, Anno 1588"* — **17 August 1588** (O.S.; Denmark was on the Julian calendar). The edition's label field reads *"1587. 17. august. Uraniborg."* **This discrepancy is not silently resolved:** the header leads with the as-written date (17 August 1588) and appends "(catalogued 1587)." Internal evidence supports **1588**: the letter answers Rothmann's writing on "the last comet" and refers to the lunar eclipse "at the beginning of March" *of this passing year* (the eclipse of early March 1588) and to "the eclipse which fell in September of the preceding year" (September 1587) — both consistent with composition in August 1588, not 1587. The standard editions (Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VI) date this letter 17 August **1588**.
- **Technical terms (glossary–5.2).** *Refractio* → refraction; *Parallaxis* → parallax; *Declinatio maxima* → the greatest declination (obliquity of the ecliptic); *octaua Sphaera* → the eighth sphere (of the fixed stars); *Diaphanum* → transparency / transparent body (kept as a noun where Tycho substantivizes it, "the *diaphanum* of aether"); *Quadrans* → quadrant (the *rectificatum Quadrantis perpendiculum* = the rectified plumb-line of the quadrant); *Organa renouata* → renewed instruments; *pinnacidium / rimulae* → sight / its slits (the pinnule-sight; *rimulae* = the narrow slits, narrowed for bright stars); *acronychiae Obseruationes* → acronychal observations (at acronychal rising/opposition); *Finitor visibilis* → the visible horizon (*finitor*, the bounding circle), kept and glossed. *Aequatio dierum* → the equation of (the natural) days. *restitutio / redintegratio / instauratio Astronomiae* → restoration / reintegration / renewal of astronomy — Tycho's programme, rendered with the glossary's fixed family.
- **Units & measures.** *Minutum / Scrupulum primum* → arc-minute (Tycho uses *Minutum* and *Scrupulum primum* interchangeably; *Scrupulum* alone = arc-minute here); *Pars / Gradus* → degree; *Milliare Germanicum* → German mile; *Semidiameter Terrae* → Earth's semidiameter; *quincunx horae* → five-twelfths of an hour (the Roman fractional *quincunx* = 5/12; glossed); *triens* → a third; *digiti* (in eclipse) → digits (twelfths of the luminary's diameter). Fractions in the source (7⅓, 7½, 9½, 10⅔, 16⅓, 48⅓, 2⅔) preserved as written.
- **Astrology / zodiac glyphs.** ♒ named **Aquarius**, ♏ **Scorpio**, ♍ **Virgo** in the translation; glyphs kept in the Source block. *Spica ♍* = the star Spica in Virgo ("the Ear of Corn of Virgo"). Planet identities in the microcosm passage (Sun ☉, Moon, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Mars, Mercury) are written out by Tycho in words (no glyphs in this letter) and so rendered as words.
- **Alchemy / "terrestrial astronomy".** *Astronomia terrestris* → "terrestrial astronomy," Tycho's term for alchemy/chymistry, paralleled to *Astronomia caelestis*. *Spagyrica (ars)* → the Spagyric art (kept; the Paracelsian term for chymistry). *Pyronomica Schola / exercitium Pyronomicum* → the Pyronomic (fire-working) School / practice — *pyronomia* = the regulated handling of fire; kept and glossed, not modernized. *Microcosmus* → microcosm. *Argentum viuum* → quicksilver. *atra flauaque bilis* → black and yellow bile (the humours). The seven-planets/seven-metals/seven-members correspondences are Tycho's, rendered straight.
- **Latin mottoes (kept and translated).** *SVSPICIENDO DESPICIO* → "Looking up, I look down"; *DESPICIENDO SVSPICIO* → "Looking down, I look up." These are the emblematic mottoes of Tycho's poem for Falk Gøye (the celestial vs. terrestrial philosopher); kept in capitals as printed and glossed.
- **Hypotheses / authors of theory.** *Hypotheses Copernianae ad immobilitatem Terrae reductae* → "the Copernican hypotheses reduced to the immobility of the Earth" — Tycho's geo-heliocentric reworking; *calculus Prutenicus* → the Prutenic [calculation/tables] (Reinhold's *Prutenic Tables*); *Alphonsinum / Puerbachianum* → the Alphonsine [Tables] / the Peurbachian [calculation] (Peurbach); *secundus Tomus de nouis Aetherei Mundi Generationibus* / *liber secundus de Aetherei Mundi recentioribus Phaenomenis* → Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (1588), here called "our second book/volume."
- **Greek.** No Greek script appears in this letter; *Phaenomenôn* (gen. pl.) and *Methamorphosin* are Latinized Greek loanwords, rendered "phenomena" / "Metamorphosis." (The "Pythagorean silence" allusion is rendered as such.)
- **Editorial markers in the Source.** The working transcription carried stray superscript-style "A" tokens appended to scattered words (apparatus/variant markers, not Latin); these have been removed from the Source block as non-textual editorial artefacts. **One correction to that pass:** in the *Figur 11* computation the Earth's-semidiameter SIDE is labelled *EA* throughout (cf. *"qualium videlicet EA est 60"*, *"prout EA Semidiameter Terrae"*, *"et EA, vt prius 60"*), but in the clause *"qualium EA Semidiameter Terrae part. 60"* the over-eager "A"-stripping had reduced this one instance to a bare point *E*. That was a genuine geometric label, not a variant marker, so the side-label *EA* has been **restored** here (and the English correspondingly reads "the Earth's semidiameter EA") to keep the figure internally consistent; the numeric argument (= 60 parts) was unaffected. Apart from this restoration, no word of the Latin has been altered. *"Figur 11"* is an in-text figure call-out for the diagram (triangle AEO/AEX with points E, F, O, X) accompanying the trigonometric refraction computation; rendered "[Figure 11.]" in brackets.
- **Negations / conditional logic checked.** The dense argument-clauses were translated with the negation count preserved: e.g. *non est admodum magna differentia* ("there is no very great difference"); *nequaquam esse aëream* ("by no means airy"); *neque … in 30. Gradu … prorsus nullam fieri Refractionem* (Tycho insists he did *not* say there is *no* refraction at 30° — a double construction kept intact); *quina illa Scrupula in vestra denotatione … abundare, in mea vero nequaquam deficere* ("those five minutes are in *excess* in your notation, but in mine by no means *fall short*" — the asymmetry preserved). The conditional *"si Cometam Anni 1585. fas erat … versari … qui … non etiam concedi poterit …"* is an a-fortiori argument and is rendered as a single conditional question, not flattened.
- **Soft points flagged (not smoothed).** (1) *Aëre elementari et animali* — Tycho characterizes Rothmann's heaven as "elemental and *animal*[ate] air"; *animalis* here = "ensouled/living-air" (the Stoic-Penan *aer animalis*), rendered "animal[ate] air" with the bracketed gloss rather than modernized. (2) *insensibiliter maiores* — Tycho says solar refractions here are "*imperceptibly* greater" than at Kassel; the oxymoron (greater yet imperceptibly so) is his own and is preserved, not normalized to "slightly." (3) The arithmetic of the *Figur 11* triangle (FE 48′50″, semidiameter 60ᵖ, etc.) is reproduced exactly as printed; the values are Tycho's reduction of Rothmann's figure and are not re-derived here.

translation.warrant: **Not collated against Dreyer** — no page reference for this letter, so the grade is capped at Probable however sound the translation looks. the edition gives no page reference (no Dreyer extract available for this letter), so Dreyer collation was not possible and grade is capped at Probable by the audit's rule regardless of outcome. Audited the full the published English against the transcribed original alone, paragraph by paragraph (13/13 paragraphs present, none dropped, order preserved). Cross-checked every proper name (Gellius Sascerides, Jean Pena, Giordano of Nola/Iordanus Nullanus, Philo Iudaeus, Falk Goye, Paul Wittich, Maestlin, Tubingen, Niels Kaas, Regiomontanus, Vogelin, Peter Apian, Fracastoro, the alchemical-authors list Hermes Trismegistus through Paracelsus, Augsburg), every numeric quantity in the dense refraction/geometry passages (12 German miles/70x semidiameter; the FE/EA/XE triangle figures 48.50/60/9.55/142/860; the AEO triangle 60.48.50/120/30/1.36/23 miles and the 'sixfold' density check; the 20-degree vapour-refraction limit; the 30-degree 1.5-minute solar refraction; the 3-minute/45-degree/1.5-minute proportionality claim; the 6/4-scrupule altitude-1-2-3 degree series; the 3-degree/12-scrupule vs. 28-scrupule solstice dispute; 15 degrees/7⅓/7½ minutes; 10⅔ degrees/9½ minutes; 4½ degrees latitude difference; Augsburg 48⅓ elevation; 16⅓ degrees/25 vs 28 degrees twilight arc; the 1584 Wittich lunar eclipse; the September lunar eclipse England/Cimbric-Chersonese/30-mile report; the March eclipse's half-hour/1⅓-hour/5-twelfths(quincunx)/1-hour-plus deviations from Prutenic/Alphonsine/Peurbachian/Maestlin; the 1581 15 July eclipse's 1⅓-hour overrun and 3-digit/quarter-body Tubingen detail; the 5-scrupule fixed-star longitude discrepancy and its correct 'yours in excess, mine not deficient' directionality; the Falk Goye SUSPICIENDO DESPICIO / DESPICIENDO SUSPICIO motto pairing, correctly matched to the celestial vs terrestrial philosopher figures; the 1585 comet's 3-degree/8-minute/20x-Saturn figure; the 35-degree parallax/1.5-semidiameter figure; the 40-degree/1-day Regiomontanus figure). Checked the closing dateline (17 August 1588, Uraniborg, Tycho Brahe) against the source exactly — no invented day-number. Checked for the process's known failure modes specifically (pronoun flips, fabricated closings, silent sentence drops, invented phrases): none found. No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss identified; text error cannot be assessed without Dreyer. This is an unusually careful, faithful rendering of an exceptionally long and technically dense letter.

documents.abstract: Thanks Rantzau for procuring printing paper and for the chapel engraving honouring the late King, and sends the promised horizontal sundial, delayed because Gerhard Rantzau departed without visiting.
documents.incipit: ACCEPI intra paucas hebdomadas ter vel quater a te literas, Nobilissime amplissimeque …

text.original:
AMPLISSIMO NOBILISSIMOQUE VIRO DOMINO HENRICO RANZOVIO, DOMINO IN BREDENBERGA, ARCIS SEGEBERGAe PRÆSIDI ET REGIO IN HOLSATIA VICARIO, AMICO SUO INPRIMIS COLENDO.

ACCEPI intra paucas hebdomadas ter vel quater a te literas, Nobilissime amplissimeque vir, quibus singulis tuam erga me benevolentiam, et in procuranda papyro impressoria, nostrae officinae typographicae idonea, studium ac diligentiam affatim declaras. Quo nomine et pro typo etiam Sacelli, quod in honorem optimi et nunquam satis laudati Regis nostri, pijssimae memoriae, extrui curasti (quem unâ recepi) est quod gratias tibi habeam maximas. Laudo vero plurimum tuam in hoc erga Regem, optime de omnibus meritum, piam et perpetuam memoriam. Sciotericum horizontale, quod antea promiseram, iam mitto. Accepisses id citius cum GERARDO filio, si is me ante suum ad te abitum, ut sperabam, invisisset. Est autem horarium illud satis diligenter elaboratum, neque aliquid latet vitij, quo minus omnia ad amussim indicabit, quae carmina septena in frontispicio addita pollicentur, modo exquisite ad planum Horizontis, in columna (quod satius est) lapidea firmetur, sicque in ea disponatur, ut linea Meridiei, quae est horae duodecimae, exquisite Meridiano coelesti substernatur, quod qua ratione compendiose et certius quam per Compassum effici potest, exhibitori harum ostendi, qui tibi, modo satis indicationem nostram memoriâ retinuerit, omnia aperiet. Rogo peramanter, velis hoc munusculum boni consulere. Quod ad papyrum attinet, scias eam, quam ultimo misisti, de qua risas 3 ½ (deficiente a dimidia balla, quam te mittere significasti, risa 1 ½) accepi, esse satis idoneam et apprime oportunam meo operi, si modo de hac in aliqua copia obtinere possemus; desidero enim ad minimum praeter eam, quam aliunde conquiro, ballas adhuc plus minus decem, quas, si tua authoritate et procuratione ante hyemem iusto pretio acquisivero, nihil mihi gratius evenire poterit. Et licet haec ipsa, quam ultimo a te accepi, paululum mea priore maior sit, tamen id non tam interest, quam si minor foret; tunc enim esset prorsus inutilis, at nunc extraeminentia illa perexigua facile inter ligandum libros vel alias antea praecidetur. Utinam saltem de tali papyro in ea, qua dixi, copia mature et certo nancisci queam. Dubia illa, quae Clarissimus vir D. CASPAR PEUCERUS et alter ille non vulgaris, ut apparet (licet nomen eius mihi prius non innotuerat) Mathematicus D. GEORGIUS RULLENHAGIUS in mea dispositione revolutionum coelestium tibi per literas indicârunt, admodum facile sunt resolubilia. Nam quantum ad PEUCERUM attinet, nondum satis animadvertebat is, quod quando Sol, qui est centrum circuituum reliquorum Planetarum, deferretur in alteram partem, quae in delineatione inter octavam Sphaeram et orbem ♄ni otiosa videtur, tunc orbes imaginarios errantium Stellarum complere illud spatium eodem modo quo superius, quod nunc in figura vacuum apparet, et sic circumcirca eundo, ob centri annuam cum Sole concomitantiam, requiritur necessario tantum intercapedinis inter octavam Sphaeram et extimum ♄ni orbem, qua parte terris proximus fit, relinqui, ut ascensus et descensus Planetarum, in tota illa annua circumgyratione, capacitatem sine impedimento competentem, invenire possit, idque spatij orbis Solaris diametrum adaequat. Alterius haesitatio adhuc minori negotio resolvitur; id enim nunquam fieri potest, quod RULLENHAGIUS veretur, ut corpora Solis et ♂is concurrant, nam licet orbes fictitij eorum se invicem in delineatione transeant, tamen cum Sol ad illum locum pervenerit, ubi intersectio illa mutua notata apparet, Martius iste orbis Solarem longe alio in loco transibit, et stella ipsa ♂is tantundem a Sole distabit, quantum prius et alias semper, siquidem eum perpetuo in suo circuitu pro centro respicit. Impossibile enim est circumferentiam circuli centro uniri. Habes itaque utraque illorum dubia sufficienter explanata. Cuperem plurimum, ut mecum etiam communicares libros illos Genesium et Praeceptorum, quorum RULLENHAGIUS in principio suarum ad te literarum mentionem facit; ubi eas introspexero perlegeroque, statim remittam, neque alios eorum reddam participes. Quia vero ipsemet luculenter PEUCERO scripsi, et non solum dubitationem eius illi enodavi, sed etiam occasionem inventionis huius novae hypotheseos, unâ cum quibusdam alijs ipsi exposui, mitto earundem literarum ad te exemplar, ut plenius ex ijs, quae ad hanc rem faciant, cognoscere queas. Reddidi etiam illum compotem exemplarium quorundam literarum Illustris. Principis GIUILIELMI Landgravij Hassiae et ipsius Celsis Mathematici, ad me de materia Astronomica datarum, unâ cum mea ad singulas responsione, ut inde plurima ad Astronomicum negotium rite excolendum impense facientia uberius cognoscat. Quod si quae sunt literae inter has, quarum transcriptionem a me prius non obtinuisti (quod procul dubio in ijs, quae ultimo inter nos cis et ultra missae sunt, contingit) licebit utique aperto fasciculo eos inspicere perlegereque, aut etiam transcribi, si tibi ita visum fuerit, curare, modo postea rursus eodem modo componantur, tuoque sigillo denuo muniantur. Valeat tua Generositas cum uxore et liberis totaque domo quam felicissime. Nec dubito quin nervos omnes intensurus sis, ut papyrum illam mature et satis copiosam obtineam, dabo operam, ut in nominis tui, alias per se clari, celebratione, siquidem aliud praestare nequeam, me gratissimum et tui studiosissimum invenias.

Iterum et terque quaterque vale.
Datae Uraniburgi die 13. Septembris Anno 1588.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, pp. 126–127; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Quia vero expositio et declaratio mearum hypothesium e sola delineatione non a quovis ita facile percipitur, quoddam Mechanicum Organum confieri ex orichalco curavi, quo circuitus Planetarum respectu Solis, et ipsius Solis ac Lunae circa Terram manibus circumagi expeditiusque intelligi possunt, per quod etiam dubia illa tum PEUCERI tum etiam RULLENHAGIJ facillime extricantur, quemadmodum harum exhibitor (modo caput iuridicum sacra Uraniae sibi diligenter satis capere et memoria retinere queat, quod optarem quidem, sperare autem vix possum) tibi plenius ostendet; mitto enim tibi per eundem eiusdem Aequatorij Ideam, quam ut boni consulas rogo. Si GERARDUS filius tuus huc venisset, per unam saltem vel alteram horam, antequam iter suum ad te direxit, utique tum haec, tum alia ipsi melius et perfectius tibi referenda (cum sit ingeniosulus) declarassem. Petij ter vel quater idipsum serio ab eo per literas, verum is semper negotia (nescio quae) praetendebat. At nihilominus tantum illi suppetebat otij, ut ijsdem diebus nuptijs Landskronensibus, nihil ad se pertinentibus, interesse potuerit, et Huena exquisite in medio directi itineris a Croneburgo Landscroniam versus aut econtra iacet, ita ut vel in abitu aut reditu me sine ulla molestia tuo nomine invisere potuisset, modo voluntas promta non defuisset, quod me tibi per literas indicaturum, OSWALDO, ut illi idipsum significaret, iniunxi. Id igitur nunc fecisse oportuit. Iterum vale. Tui Hodierni. Tycho Brahe.  /  Mitto adhuc bina Exemplaria libri nostri secundi de aetherei Mundi Phaenomenis, et puto te iam septena accepisse, quod ideo refero, ut in memoria retineatur, quibusnam singula communicata sint, ut illi ijdem reliquas etiam operis partes aliquando adipiscantur.
text.english:
**To the most worthy and noble gentleman, Master Heinrich Rantzau, lord in Breitenburg, governor of the castle of Segeberg and royal viceroy in Holstein, his friend to be honoured above all.**

Within these few weeks I have received from you three or four letters, most noble and worthy sir, in each of which you abundantly declare your goodwill towards me and your zeal and diligence in procuring printing-paper suitable for our typographical workshop. On that account, and also for the engraving [*typus*] of the chapel which you had built in honour of our best and never sufficiently praised King, of most pious memory (which I received together [with the letters]), I have cause to render you the greatest thanks. Indeed I greatly commend in this your pious and perpetual remembrance towards the King, who deserved most well of all. The horizontal sundial [*sciotericum horizontale*] which I had earlier promised I am now sending. You would have received it sooner by way of your son Gerhard, had he, before his departure to you, visited me as I had hoped. Now that timepiece is wrought with sufficient care, nor does any defect lie hidden in it that would keep it from indicating everything exactly [*ad amussim*], as the seven verses added on its face promise — provided only that it be fixed precisely to the plane of the horizon, upon a stone column (which is better), and so arranged upon it that the line of midday, which is that of the twelfth hour, be laid exactly under the celestial meridian; by what method this can be effected concisely and more surely than by a compass [*Compassus*], I have shown to the bearer of this letter, who will explain everything to you, provided he has retained our instruction well enough in memory. I most affectionately ask that you would be willing to take this little gift in good part. As for the paper: know that the [paper] which you last sent — of which I received 3½ reams [*risae*] (the half-bale [*balla*] short, which you indicated you were sending, being 1½ reams) — is sufficiently suitable and exceedingly well-fitted to my work, if only we could obtain some quantity of this kind; for I need, at the least, besides that which I am procuring from elsewhere, still about ten bales more, and if by your authority and agency I shall acquire these before winter at a fair price, nothing more welcome could befall me. And although this very paper which I last received from you is a little larger than my earlier [stock], yet that matters not so much as if it were smaller; for then it would be wholly useless, whereas now that very slight overhang [*extraeminentia*], being exceedingly small, will easily be trimmed off beforehand in the binding of the books or otherwise. Would that I might at least obtain such paper, in the quantity I have said, in good time and for certain. Those doubts which the most distinguished gentleman Master Caspar Peucer, and that other mathematician — no common one, as it appears (though his name had not previously become known to me) — Master Georg Rollenhagen indicated to you by letter concerning my arrangement of the celestial revolutions, are very easily resolved. For as far as Peucer is concerned, he had not yet sufficiently observed that, when the Sun — which is the centre of the circuits of the remaining planets — should be carried into the other part, which in the diagram [*delineatio*] appears idle [*otiosa*] between the eighth sphere and the orb of Saturn [♄], then the imaginary orbs of the wandering stars fill that space in the same way as above [in the part] which now appears empty in the figure; and so, going round about, on account of the centre's yearly accompanying of the Sun, it is necessarily required that only so much interval be left between the eighth sphere and the outermost orb of Saturn [♄], in that part where it becomes nearest to the Earth, as will allow the ascent and descent of the planets, in that whole yearly revolution, to find a fitting capacity without impediment; and that [interval of] space equals the diameter of the Sun's orb. The other man's hesitation is resolved with even less trouble; for that which Rollenhagen fears can never happen — namely, that the bodies of the Sun and of Mars [♂] should come together — for although their fictitious orbs cross one another in the diagram, yet when the Sun shall have arrived at that place where that mutual intersection appears marked, that orb of Mars will pass [through] the Sun's [orb] at a place far otherwise [located], and the body of Mars [♂] itself will be just as far distant from the Sun as before and at all other times, since indeed it perpetually regards the Sun as the centre in its circuit. For it is impossible that the circumference of a circle be united with its centre. You have therefore both of their doubts sufficiently explained. I should very much wish that you would also share with me those books of Genitures and of Precepts of which Rollenhagen makes mention at the beginning of his letters to you; once I have examined and read them through, I shall return them at once, nor make any others sharers of them. But because I myself have written clearly to Peucer, and have not only unravelled his doubt for him but have also set out for him the occasion of the discovery of this new hypothesis, together with certain other matters, I am sending you a copy of that same letter, that you may more fully learn from it the things that bear upon this matter. I have also put him [Peucer] in possession of copies of certain letters of the Illustrious Prince Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, and of His Highness's mathematician, written to me on an astronomical subject, together with my reply to each, so that from them he may more amply learn the very many things that bear earnestly upon the duly cultivating of the astronomical enterprise. And if there are any letters among these whose transcription you did not previously obtain from me (which without doubt occurs among those which were last sent between us, hither and thither), it will indeed be permitted to open the packet, to inspect and read them through, or even to have them transcribed, if it shall so seem good to you — provided that afterwards they be put together again in the same manner and secured anew with your seal. May Your Generosity, with your wife and children and your whole household, fare most happily. Nor do I doubt that you will strain every sinew so that I may obtain that paper in good time and in sufficient plenty; I shall take pains that, in the celebration of your name (otherwise illustrious of itself) — since I can render nothing else — you may find me most grateful and most devoted to you.

Again, and thrice and four times over, farewell.
Given at Uraniborg, the 13th day of September, in the year 1588.


*[Postscript:]* But because the exposition and explanation of my hypotheses is not so easily grasped by everyone from a drawing alone, I have had a certain Mechanical Instrument [Organum] made of brass, by which the circuits of the Planets with respect to the Sun, and of the Sun itself and the Moon about the Earth, can be turned round by hand and the more readily understood; by which too those doubts both of Peucer and of Rollenhagen are most easily disentangled, as the bearer of this letter will more fully show you (provided only that his lawyer's head can take in the mysteries of Urania carefully enough and hold them in memory — which I should indeed wish, but can scarcely hope). For I send you by the same man a design of the same Equatorium, which I ask that you take in good part. Had your son Gerhard come hither, even for one hour or two, before he directed his journey to you, I should assuredly have made these things, and others to be reported to you, clearer and more perfectly to him (since he is rather clever). I asked the same of him seriously three or four times by letter, but he was always pleading affairs (I know not what). And yet he had leisure enough to spare to be present in those same days at the Landskrona wedding, which in no way concerned him; and Hven lies precisely in the middle of the direct route from Kronborg towards Landskrona or the reverse, so that either in going or returning he could have visited me in your name without any trouble, had only a ready will not been wanting — which I had enjoined upon Oswald to signify to him, that I would indicate it to you by letter. This therefore it behoved [me] now to have done. Again, farewell. Yours of today. Tycho Brahe.  /  I send besides two copies of our second book on the recent Phenomena of the Aethereal World, and I think you have by now received seven, which I mention for this reason: that it be kept in memory to whom the several copies have been communicated, so that those same persons may at some time obtain the remaining parts of the work also.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** Tycho Brahe to **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598; Latin *Henricus Ranzovius*), the great Holstein humanist, royal governor (*Statthalter* / *regius vicarius*) of the duchies under the Danish crown, lord of Breitenburg (*Bredenberga*) and Segeberg, owner of a celebrated library and his own printing connections. He was Tycho's most important patron-correspondent in the Empire and a key supplier of paper for the Uraniborg press; the salutation's full titulature is preserved by this chapter's convention
- **Date / occasion.** *Datae Uraniburgi die 13. Septembris Anno 1588* — Uraniborg, 13 September 1588 (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The dateline matches the catalogue label exactly; no discrepancy. The letter falls in the year Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (vol. II of his projected trilogy, printed at Uraniborg) appeared, presenting the geocentric-heliocentric world-system whose geometry is defended below.
- ***typus Sacelli*** — "the engraving of the chapel." *typus* here is a printed/engraved representation (an *image*, not movable type); Rantzau had had built (and engraved) a memorial chapel honouring the late King **Frederik II of Denmark** (d. 11 April 1588), the "best and never sufficiently praised King, of most pious memory," Tycho's patron. Translated "engraving."
- ***Sciotericum horizontale / horarium*** — a **horizontal sundial** (Gk. *skiothērikon*, shadow-instrument); *horarium* "timepiece." Rendered "horizontal sundial," consistent with instrument register. *carmina septena in frontispicio* — "seven verses on its face/frontispiece," an inscribed motto-poem on the dial-plate.
- ***ad amussim*** — "exactly, to the line" (lit. by the carpenter's rule/plumb-line); idiom kept and glossed.
- ***per Compassum*** — "by a compass." Here, in the context of orienting the dial's noon-line to the celestial meridian, this is a **magnetic compass** (for alignment), not a pair of dividers; Tycho says his shown method is surer than relying on the (magnetically-deviating) compass. Distinguished from the drawing-compass crux of the 1584 Frederik II letter; the referent here is reasonably secure from context.
- **Paper units.** *risa* = **ream** (Ital./Lat. *risma*); *balla* = **bale** (a large bundle of reams). Tycho reports receiving 3½ reams, the consignment being 1½ reams short of the half-bale Rantzau had announced, and asks for about ten more bales for the press. Units kept in the source and glossed; the slightly **larger** sheet-size is welcome because the overhang (*extraeminentia*) can be trimmed in binding, whereas an undersized sheet would be useless.
- **Persons (objections to the world-system).** *D. CASPAR PEUCERUS* = **Caspar Peucer** (1525–1602), Melanchthon's son-in-law, Wittenberg physician-astronomer. *D. GEORGIUS RULLENHAGIUS* = **Georg Rollenhagen** (1542–1609), Magdeburg rector, poet (*Froschmeuseler*) and amateur mathematician; Tycho notes his name was previously unknown to him. Both had relayed objections, through Rantzau, to Tycho's *dispositio revolutionum coelestium* (his diagram of the world-system in *De mundi*).
- **The geometry of the world-system (technical core).** Two objections are answered:
 - *Peucer's*: the region of the diagram "between the eighth sphere and the orb of Saturn" looks **idle/empty** (*otiosa … vacuum*). Tycho replies that because the Sun is the moving centre of the planets' circuits and travels yearly round the Earth, the planets' imaginary orbs sweep through that apparently-empty space too as the Sun moves to the opposite side; the gap that must be left between Saturn's outermost orb (at its nearest approach to Earth) and the eighth (fixed-star) sphere equals **the diameter of the Sun's orb** — exactly enough room for the planets' annual ascent and descent.
 - *Rollenhagen's*: he feared the **bodies of the Sun and Mars would collide** (*corpora Solis et ♂is concurrant*) where their circles cross in the figure. Tycho answers that the orbs are *fictitious / geometrical* (*orbes fictitij … in delineatione*), not solid; when the Sun reaches the marked intersection, Mars's orb crosses the Sun's *orb* elsewhere and Mars's *body* stays as far from the Sun as ever, since Mars always keeps the Sun as the centre of its circuit — "for it is impossible that the circumference of a circle be united with its centre." This reading is corroborated by Dreyer (*Tycho Brahe*) and Mosley (*Bearing the Heavens*) and Christianson (*On Tycho's Island / Lord of Uraniborg*), who record precisely this Rollenhagen "collision" worry and Tycho's no-solid-spheres rebuttal.
- **Glyphs.** ♄ = **Saturn**, ♂ = **Mars** — named in English in the translation, the glyph kept in the source block by this chapter's convention
- ***libri Genesium et Praeceptorum*** — "books of Genitures [nativity-figures] and of Precepts," astrological works Rollenhagen had cited; *Genesis* = **geniture/nativity** by this chapter's convention Tycho asks to borrow them.
- ***Illustris. Principis GIUILIELMI Landgravij Hassiae et ipsius Celsis Mathematici*** — **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** and his court mathematician (Christoph Rothmann); Tycho is circulating the Kassel–Uraniborg astronomical correspondence. *GIUILIELMI* is the source's spelling of *Gulielmi/Wilhelmi*, kept as printed.
- ***Gerardo filio*** — **Gerhard Rantzau** (1558–1627), Heinrich's son and eventual successor as royal governor of the duchies.
- **Subscription.** *Iterum et terque quaterque vale* — "Again, and thrice and four times over, farewell" (a Virgilian *terque quaterque* flourish), kept literally.
- **Edition / witness.** Edition of record: Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* (vol. VII, *Epistolae*). MS witness as given in the edition: A = Vienna, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 9737, f. (folio number not supplied in the source header).

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** TWO closing postscripts (the brass equatorium *Mechanicum Organum* sent via the bearer + the Gerhard/Kronborg–Landskrona logistics; then two more copies of the *De mundi aetherei* book), restored from Dreyer VII pp.126–127 (dropped by the working transcription).
- **Correction.** English corrected against Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII p.126: the sentence 'Reddidi etiam illum compotem... cognoscat' is grammatically 3rd person, continuing the Peucer clauses of the prior sentence, not addressed to Rantzau (who is 'te'/'tu' throughout, including the next sentence's 'obtinuisti'). The published translation's bracketed gloss '[Rantzau]' misattributed custody of the Landgrave Wilhelm/Rothmann correspondence copies; corrected to '[Peucer]'.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VII pp.124-128 read as page images (Read pages=1-4; the letter's own text is complete within pp.124(bottom)-127(top), so extract p.5/TBOO p.128, which opens with a wholly different letter to Peucer, was not needed). Collated the full letter - opening address block (AMPLISSIMO NOBILISSIMOQUE VIRO DOMINO HENRICO RANZOVIO...), every proper name (Gerardus filius, Caspar Peucerus, Georgius Rullenhagius, Oswaldus), every number (risas 3½, deficiente balla risa 1½, ballas decem, bina Exemplaria, septena), the postscript on the brass Equatorium/Organum, and the closing date (Datae Uraniburgi die 13. Septembris Anno 1588) - against the Dreyer images word for word; all match the transcribed original. The previously flagged sentence (Reddidi etiam illum compotem...) was verified word-for-word against Dreyer p.126 and confirms the transcribed original is textually correct (no text error) - the fault is in the English's referent-gloss, a mistranslation that flips custody of the Landgrave correspondence from Peucer to Rantzau, which is exactly the kind of claim a scholar citing this letter for the provenance of that correspondence would rely on and get wrong.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (**high**). The Latin's illum (accusative 'him') and the 3rd-person subjunctive cognoscat ('that HE may learn') continue the immediately preceding sentence, which is entirely about Caspar Peucer (Quia vero ipsemet luculenter PEUCERO scripsi... illi enodavi... ipsi exposui) - not the letter's addressee Rantzau, who is addressed throughout in the 2nd person (te/tu), including the very next sentence's obtinuisti ('you have not obtained'). The published English glosses illum as '[Rantzau]', inverting the custody: it was Peucer, not Rantzau, whom Tycho made possessor of the Landgrave-Wilhelm correspondence copies so that Peucer could learn more. This matches the process's known failure mode of misattributing custody of a correspondence archive. At: “I have also put him [Rantzau] in possession of copies of certain letters of the Illustrious Prince Wilhelm, Landgrave of”.

**Repaired.** Verified against the Dreyer page image, TBOO VII p.126 (letter spans pp.124-128; pages 124-127 examined, encompassing the full defect passage). The sentence in question uses the 3rd-person accusative 'illum' and 3rd-person subjunctive 'cognoscat', sandwiched between two clearly 2nd-person sentences addressed to Rantzau ('cognoscere queas' before it, 'obtinuisti' after it) and immediately following three consecutive 3rd-person references to Peucer ('PEUCERO scripsi', 'illi enodavi', 'ipsi exposui'). This confirms Peucer, not Rantzau, is the antecedent of 'illum'/'cognoscat', and the correction is grammatically secure. The Latin text itself is left untouched as instructed for a mistranslation defect (unflagged minor transcription variants, e.g. 'Illustris.'/'GIUILIELMI' vs Dreyer's 'Illustriss.'/'GUILIELMI', were noted but not touched, being out of scope for this defect).
