But yet it would follow thence that no Star, except those which pass the zenith and are at the zenith, is seen with true light, but [with light] confused and weakened. For every Refraction weakens the light and colour of the thing seen, as **Alhazen book 7, chapter 7** and **Witelo book 10, prop. 10** demonstrate. Since therefore that diversity is not detected from the comparison of a zenith-Star to the rest free from vapours, neither will Refraction be able to be granted. But you here [go] rather into all things diverse [self-contradiction]. For you say that these Refractions of aether and air are sensible below 30°, but in a higher position insensible; and yet afterward you add that the **Refraction of the Sun, which you found at an Altitude of 30° [to be] 1½ minutes**, can scarcely be excused by vapours alone. Would that you said it is wholly from the diverse Transparency of aether and air — I should certainly demonstrate that at an Altitude of **45°** it ought still to be nearly **one minute**. For it is truer than truth itself that, if some sensible Refraction of aether and air be granted below 30°, it cannot become insensible so suddenly in a higher position. For, the same media remaining, the Refractions themselves cannot be changed so suddenly, since their Angles do not decrease so suddenly — nay, whether they occur from Air to Water, or from Air to glass, or from Water to glass, or contrariwise, they retain nearly the same proportion in increasing and decreasing, as may be seen from the Table set in **Witelo book 10, prop. 8**. Looking to which too I wrote in [my] earlier letter that, if about the Horizon there be given a Solar Refraction of **3 minutes** arising from the diverse Transparency of aether and air, it is given at an Altitude of 45° [as] **1½ minutes**. For although the Refractions themselves and the Angles of Refraction will decrease by some — yet not very dissimilar — proportion; which, if time did not fail me, I would easily examine by Calculation. But that the Refractions decrease so suddenly about the Horizon, that is from the mere **vapours**, which about the Earth are both grosser and (as I demonstrated) multiplied, and are also sought [reached] by rays from the side. Otherwise, if the same media remained, disposed in the same quantity and the same manner, so sudden a change of Refractions could not happen, as can be demonstrated. But there still remains a **demonstration which no one will ever be able to break**. For if there is a Refraction arising from the diverse Transparency of aether and air, it will necessarily be **greater in the Fixed Stars, which are farther distant, than in the Sun, which is nearer** (to say nothing meanwhile of the Moon). For in a Triangle, one Angle and one Side remaining, the other sides being produced, the remaining Angle at the remaining side is made greater, by **Euclid I.21**. For necessarily the same Angle of Refraction will remain at the same Altitude, since the same media remain; nor can the Angle of Refraction in the Sun or Moon be other than in the Fixed [stars]. From which it is most manifest that, if you posit the Refraction in the Sun to become insensible at some certain Altitude, it ought still to be sensible in the Fixed Stars at the same Altitude. Since, therefore, through Observations not this but rather the contrary is found, you yourself being witness — Refraction cannot be generated by a diverse Transparency of aether and air; and therefore, as I have several times now proved from Optics, the Transparencies of aether and air cannot be diverse, but [are] the same. If therefore you wish to call that pure Air "Heaven," I do not fight at all — only let not pure Air be determined to differ from the celestial, and so let not diverse Transparencies be introduced, since the defect of Refraction does not permit that one be subtler than the other. But as to what you bring from the **Chymists** — that there lurks in earthly things a certain **fifth essence**, which you call celestial — that I both believe and most pleasantly contemplate. Nevertheless it does not follow thence that this fifth essence is the same as that matter which is poured around the Planets; but rather that it is **generated by the Sun**. For just as the **Sun of the Microcosm** (as you most pleasantly teach), from blood and attracted Air (from which, on account of respiration, its inborn nature seems to retain the subtler part and reject the rest) — just as, I say, the Sun of the Microcosm, from Air and blood prepared in the right chamber [of the heart], generates the **vital spirit** in the left chamber — so too the **Sun of the whole universe**, from Earth, Water, and Air, seems to generate that fifth essence in natural things. Or, if this essence is the same as that matter poured around the Planets, it will be the same also as the pure Air, on account of the demonstrations adduced. These [things], a little more fully than I had proposed at the beginning, I wished to write out to you about this matter still — not indeed from a zeal for contradicting, but from mere **love of truth** [φιλαληθέια]. Nor can anything certain about the generation and matter of Comets be brought forward, unless this question be decided. But about this I will deal at more length, God granting, in our **Observations of the Fixed Stars** — omitting, however, mention of this our dissension, lest it perchance detract something from the truth of the matter. Nor do I make mention even of you, unless I can [do so] without reproach; but then rather, the name omitted, I treat the things themselves.

Now to those **Philosophical** [matters]. But first one [thing] still. I cannot sufficiently wonder that you have found the **beginning of morning Twilight**, about the equinoxes, [with] the Sun scarcely **16½°** below the Horizon, depressed in the vertical circle — whereas I have found the **end of evening Twilight** about the vernal equinox here [with] the Sun depressed **24°** below the Horizon, in such a way, however, that no further trace of whiteness appeared. You, therefore, attempt the same too in the **evening Twilights**, where I judge these Observations to be more exact, because it can more easily be noticed when the trace of whitening Air ceases than when it begins — the Observer always doubting whether that trace of whiteness pertains to the morning Twilight. I too will try the same in the morning [twilights]. To those sweetest [things], then, drawn from the inmost and profound **Philosophy**, I now come. For the rest do not seem to need a reply; nor could I observe anything here about **Eclipses**, on account of the rainy Sky. I give you, therefore, the greatest thanks I can, that you have deigned to instruct me so amply in those more secret [matters]; and I ask you again and again, in greater measure, that you do this in the future too. When I read them, I almost cried out for joy. How far truer and more beautiful they are than what is handed down in Aristotle! But do you make me understand more. You wrote in [your] earlier letter, when you made mention of **Ramus**, that **all things consist of number, weight, and measure**. What this is, then, I would wish you to explain to me again and again; and add, if it please, about the **spirits — Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury** — how these agree not only with other natural things but also with human bodies; which of these vegetates, nourishes, and increases our body, which makes [it] feel, which moves [it]; or, as they commonly speak, which is the **natural**, which the **vital**, which the **animal** [spirit]. For your **Medicine** pleases me greatly. Likewise about the **Fixation of spirits**: how spirit can fix spirit, and one be the soul of the other, and why by you the **soul** is said [to be] the medium that unites spirit and body, whereas in our body the soul is not the bond of the spirits, but rather the spirits are the bond of the soul. Likewise whence the **stone** [calculus] is generated in man, and whence **Gout** [Podagra] arises. For if you inform me about these, nothing more pleasant or welcome could befall me. But perhaps I burden you too impudently, and am too long in [my] reply to the later letter. Wherefore I now proceed to the earlier.

As to your requiring, then, in both letters — the later as well as the earlier — my **judgment about those [things] contained in the second Tome of the Comet[s]** sent to me: I indeed acknowledge it to be of such a kind that it can easily be neglected. For through yourself, as a supreme artificer, you understand what can be, what cannot. But yet, that you may have what you seek: you have so carried out the matter, and so demonstrated that that **Comet completed its course in the aether**, that no man not ignorant of the Mathematical art at least can contradict you — and that so amply and clearly that none [could do so] more amply or more unfoldedly. Wherefore see that we have the remaining Tomes too as soon as possible. For thus you will most greatly promote not only the business of Comets but also our **Art**. In the **third Chapter** you make mention of the **maximum Latitude of the Moon**, which I too found nearly the same as you; but the **Head of the Dragon** [the ascending node] is distant from the **Tables** by more than four degrees, as I found by distances and the Globe, nor do I think the calculation will produce a smaller difference — which I would easily examine if time did not fail me. About the **matter of Comets** and how they are generated, I could find nothing in it, except in **chapter 9, on the generation of the tail** — about which, however, whether it is generated **from the Sun or from Venus** (into whose opposite parts exactly, as you teach in chapter 7, it was stretched out through the whole time of the apparition), you doubt; but yet you at last incline to the Sun's side, and think this can happen by a still-latent and undiscovered Optical reasoning. But you are not ignorant, from chapter 7 of my writing sent to you, that I doubt about the whole generation of the tail — whether it occurs through transmitted rays. For when I had recited the opinion of **Cardano, Scaliger, and Apian** about the generation of the tail, I at last subjoined that I, to confess frankly, in this opinion about the generation of the tail follow the judgment of others rather than my own. For there always stuck then in my mind that the **tail must be of the same matter — though rarer — as the body of the Comet itself**, because the Sun's rays, even if they pass through the Comet's body, yet after the passage cannot appear, without matter in which they may similarly be reflected, in that pure Air — since not even after **Crystal** or bodies of that kind does the condensed light of the Sun appear, unless a material thing be set [under it] against which that **Pyramid** [cone of rays] strikes; likewise because that tail is dispersed, nor are its rays continuous, but sometimes begin to appear abruptly far behind the head, and for other causes. Since, however, I had never observed such tailed Stars, nor had yet diligently considered the form and habit of the tail in any [comet], and saw that opinion reprehended by no one, I yielded to such and so supreme Men — which, however, as you know, I could not do without protestation. But that that judgment of mine about the tail, against those supreme men, was true, I learned last winter. For when by chance I happened upon those **Ephemerides of Cyprian** [Leovitius], which, gilded, together with the sacred Bible and a self-moving Globe and a small Quadrant, our most Illustrious Prince is wont always to carry with him, I found written at the beginning of them thus: *"In the year 1558 after the salvation shown to the whole globe of lands, there appeared a **Comet**, which on the 13th [day before the] Kalends of September [20 Aug] was observed by the most Illustrious Prince and Lord, Lord **Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse**, by a **Torquetum**, about the ninth hour, at 21° of Virgo [♍], distant in Latitude 31° from the Ecliptic, stretching its coma toward the extremity of the tail of Ursa Major, while it itself was in the Asterism of **Coma Berenices**, where there are stars Venereal and Lunar. Thence on the 12th [before the] Kalends [21 Aug] it advanced to 23° of Virgo, [but] in Latitude it advanced either little or nothing. Lastly, on the 10th [before the] Kalends [23 Aug], advanced to 28° of Virgo, into 35½° of Latitude. And since it was quite obscure, it ceased to be observed by the most Illustrious Prince. The Length of the tail could not easily be attained by sight. It is established that the **Pole of the Comet's motion** was not far from **Alrucaba** [the pole-star region] toward the head of Ursa Major."* Such was the whole note. From which it is most manifest that the **tail of that Comet regarded neither the Sun nor any other Planet, but appeared by itself, by its own course**. Wherefore I now establish that the **tails are of the same matter as the head, and appear in the same way as the head, by illumination** — which is also manifest from this: that the head of the Comet, in its disappearance, appears dispersed in the same way as the tail. Nor is that **curvature of the tail**, as I think, rightly excused by you, since nothing such appears in the Stars and Planets similarly existing in a straight line, especially in so small an interval as that tail was. Do you see whether this my opinion can be true. For thus those **great Comets in Seneca and Pontanus** — of which the one equalled the whole **Milky Way**, the other occupied **fifty degrees** — will be easily explained, and the curvatures of the tails will need no excuse. But although you do not assert what kind of matter of Comets you posit, yet at the end of the Work, dealing with **Graminaeus**, you seem to reject my opinion and to build up that the opinion is Aristotle's. But [mine] differs much from Aristotle's opinion. For he posits it [the matter] tenacious, slow, gross, and viscous; I [posit it] tenuous, light, and thoroughly purged and concocted by the rays. He wills it to be burned and to appear on account of the burning; I [will] it not to be burned but to be consumed and dispersed by the rays of the Stars, and to appear by illumination. He [places it] below the Moon; I [place it] not only below the Moon but also in the Spheres of the Planets. What your opinion is, I do not know. For I am a **Davus, not an Oedipus** [no riddle-solver]. From the Title, however — *On the new generations of the aethereal World* — which you wished [it] to be thus, in the letters both to our most Illustrious Prince and also in the recent [ones] sent to me, I conjecture that you, according to your opinion, make it celestial, and introduce **generation into the Heaven**. Whether, then, you think it is exhaled from the bodies of the Planets, or otherwise generated by them, I cannot know. This, I think, is certain: that, since you introduce **generation into the Heaven, you also introduce corruption**. For according to your Art, generation does not exist except from corruption. But I cannot deal more with this matter, since I am ignorant of your opinion.

About your **new Hypotheses** too, of which you make mention in the 8th chapter, I do not follow you in all [respects]. I myself indeed, when I was writing my **Astronomical Elements**, in the same way placed the Moon, then the Sun, about the Earth — but in **homocentric-epicycle-upon-epicycle [constructions]** [*Homocentrepicyclepicyclis*]; and at the centre of the greater and first Epicycle of the Sun, again [I placed] the homocentric-epicycle-upon-epicycles of the remaining Planets, so that the centre of the homocentrics in the remaining Planets was always the same as the centre of the greater Epicycle of the Sun, and was carried around together, through the mean motion of the Sun, in the homocentric of the Sun. But I did this by no new reasoning, but entirely **according to Copernicus**; nor could I do otherwise, so as to transfer conversely, through all [points], the Hypotheses of Copernicus to the mobility of the Sun; and I saw that both **Rheticus** and **Reinhold** had understood that reasoning. And according to this manner our most Illustrious Prince too had, last year, an **automaton** [ἀυτόματον] constructed — of wondrous smallness indeed, but yet exhibiting the motions of all the Planets. For it is a little orb, flat on both sides, containing scarcely 6 inches in diameter, on one plane face of which is contained the Theoric of the Moon with its Epicycles and the Head of the Dragon; but on the other, the Theorics of the Sun and of all the remaining Planets; and all the motions are exhibited, not only of the Anomalies and of the centres, and the true [motion] in Longitude, but also, in the three superior [planets], in Latitude. But whether your Hypotheses are the same with these and agree, I cannot know for certain. For although I see clearly enough that the general **sketch** [*Hypotyposis*] and order of the Spheres, and the very circles of the Planets — whether homocentric or eccentric — are the same, yet, since you call yours **new**, and write in [your] recent letter that they satisfy the particular appearances most aptly on every side (which, however, neither of the others does in every way), they seem to be **diverse from the inverted Copernican [hypotheses]**. For if they were the same, they would not satisfy the appearances more than the Copernican [hypotheses] themselves, since whatever appearances arise from the Copernican [hypotheses] themselves, those too arise entirely, through all [points], from the inverted [ones] without any difference. Then you seem to carry the centres of the homocentrics of the remaining Planets around **not in the homocentric or centre of the greater Epicycle, but in the very Eccentric of the Sun** — since you do the same too in the Comet. And if it were so, they would deservedly be **new and diverse**, since by this reasoning the **Eccentricity of the Sun would necessarily mix itself into all the Planets**, and would introduce other appearances. But that the Observations answer to this supposition, I should scarcely believe. I know indeed that **Copernicus** demonstrates that the change of the Sun's Eccentricity is noticed in the remaining Planets too, which, however, he neglected in the Tables as less sensible. (Whence I too transposed that little Epicycle of the Sun into the greater Epicycle, which otherwise would have had to be placed back at the Earth, in such a way that it would have passed through the centre of the Earth by its lowest part.) Nevertheless, that is altogether necessary from his Hypothesis, since by the **Eccentric of the Sun he understands the Eccentric of the Earth**, whose centre, if it be changed, will necessarily change the Eccentricities of the remaining Planets, since they all regard this centre and their magnitudes are numbered from this centre. Whether, then, as I said, yours are entirely the same with the inverted Copernican [hypotheses], I cannot know for certain. But as to what you think — that the more diligently I shall have surveyed that general disposition of the Spheres, the more it will please me — know that the entirely contrary has long since happened to me (about which [I have spoken] also with the most Erudite man **Gellius Sascerides**). For the longer I consider it, the less it pleases me. For although it shows how, according to the mean motion of the Sun, the superior Planets are rendered direct, stationary, or retrograde, yet (which the Ptolemaic [system] also does) it only shows **that** they so come about, not **why** they so come about, and sprinkles the Planets with the **stain of retrogression**. But the **Copernican** [system] shows not only **that** those retrogressions and stations occur, but also **why** they so occur — not that there is so great an inconstancy of motion in the Planets themselves, which always regard their own proper motion, but that those retrogressions so **appear to us on account of the motion of the Earth**, and are thought to be in the Planets, whereas in reality they are in the Earth. Thus most beautifully **no motion is left except the proper [one]**: the first in the diurnal Revolution of the Earth, the second in its annual motion, the third in the Moon, the fourth in Venus, the fifth in Mercury, the sixth in Mars, the seventh in Jupiter, and the eighth at last in Saturn — without any stain of violence or retrogression. Then, who will ever believe that the **Centre of the greater Epicycle of the Sun is endowed with such efficacy** that it can drag all the Planets after itself — nay, drag [them] from their Spheres and lift [them] up again — when they are connected by no corporeal and tenacious matter? For which cause too, when I showed our most Illustrious Prince that Hypothesis of yours in your second Tome of the Comet[s], which he soon, as he beheld it, recognized (being sufficiently known to him from the Automaton): *"Good gods,"* he said in jest, *"that circle of the Sun must be far stronger than bronze, since it can drag so many Planets with it."* For there stuck in his mind what I had so often sung into his most Illustrious Highness's ear — that the **motion of Traction must be removed from the Heaven**. Nor, as I think, will it easily be able to be granted to the Sun that it disturb the proper motions of the remaining Planets by this its **traction**. Besides, this inverted Copernican reasoning introduces **confusion into the Spheres of the Planets**. For although no collision of celestial bodies can follow thence (as you strive to excuse), yet no true or determined distinction of the Spheres remains, but all are confused among themselves. But the Copernican Hypothesis attributes to each Planet its own and determined space, from which it cannot go out by its motion. But you know that **God is the author not of confusion but of order**, and so founded nature that it abhors confusion — much less would he have wished to look upon this most beautiful edifice of inexhaustible wisdom with so great a stain. There is added this too: that **Nature does not act through more [means] when it can [act] through fewer**. Likewise that the change of the Sun's Eccentricity is felt in the remaining Planets too — which, although it can in some way be excused by the transposition of the Sun's lesser Epicycle to the Earth (as I said), yet nonetheless all things are by this reasoning feigned to come about **through traction**. These, then, and many other [things] considering again and again, I can find nothing other than that **no Hypothesis except the single one of Copernicus is true**. Nor does it sin against Physical principles; nor, because the Earth is a gross body, will it on that account be unfit for moving. For what do you think the other Stars are? For I think Copernicus does not err when he says that **gravity is nothing other than a certain natural appetite implanted in the parts by the divine providence of the Maker of the universe, that they may bring themselves into their unity and integrity, coming together into the form of a globe**; and that this affection is also in the Sun, the Moon, and the other lights of the Wanderers, so that by its efficacy they remain in that roundness in which they present themselves — which nonetheless effect their circuits in many ways. And surely, since the Earth, like the other Planets, is endowed with a round figure, and likewise hangs free in the Air, why do we say it is unfit for moving? We see that if we erect or suspend a globe most exactly and subtly on [its] Poles and Axis, and so, hanging freely, impel it into a gyre, it retains this motion long enough, nor can it suddenly be checked. If, therefore, an **artificial** motion, even impeded, can do this, how much more a **natural** [one], unimpeded? But the Physical absurdities **Copernicus** has more than sufficiently refuted. Nor does the **authority of the sacred writings** stand in the way either. For these are written not for me and you alone, but for absolutely all men, to whose grasp they also speak — as all the Theologians too confess in the explication of **Genesis chapter 1**. Otherwise the **Moon** would, against the Geometrical demonstrations, be greater than the rest of the Stars. But this too is manifest from the following. The **Hebrews** thought that the clouds could not hang on high unless there underlay some hard and impervious matter which sustained the Water. Accommodating himself, therefore, to their grasp, God says, *"I will make the Heaven iron, lest it rain,"* etc.; likewise, *"he opened the windows of Heaven"* in the Flood, etc.; likewise **Moses**, when he says that on the first day the **Firmament** was founded, to separate the Waters above us from the Waters below us. By which I think nothing else can be understood than that **that force, by which the clouds so hang on high, was founded on the first day**. So too, since we for Optical reasons think the Heaven to be as it were a stretched-out **tent**, therefore the sacred writings, following this opinion of the common [people], call the Heaven "stretched-out" [*expansum*], and the Prophets say that God stretches out the Heaven like a tent. For neither did these understand more about this matter than other common men, or even than **Lactantius**; nor did the Holy Spirit wish to reveal to them the wisdom which God poured into Nature, but that which is contained in that stupendous and supernatural mystery of the Redemption of the human race. And why was **Solomon** held wise even to a miracle, except that he had a far more excellent knowledge of the whole of Nature than anyone else before him? **Paul** too, when he says (Romans 1) that God is recognized from these visible [things], argues not obscurely that a far greater wisdom of God lies hidden **in Nature** than is revealed in the sacred writings. **In Nature**, I say: for of the mystery of Redemption, which the sacred writings properly treat, and of the recognition of the true God, I now do not speak. Thus the authority of the sacred writings, although it be brought forward quite plausibly, yet in reality in this matter will be able to stand in the way not at all; but we shall know only so much as we find out through **Mathematical Demonstrations**. But although Gellius Sascerides said that you have **Geometrical Demonstrations of your assertion**, yet this I, for a certain cause, should scarcely believe. Yet I do not on that account judge that the **Copernican Hypotheses are to be proposed to learners**, since they are scarcely perceived by the Artificers [skilled] — as not even **Maestlin** rightly understands the motion of **libration** in the Latitudes and the obliquity of the Zodiac; but [I judge] that those [hypotheses] which are easiest of all [should be proposed], so that step by step the access to Copernicus may be opened. Wherefore I too, in my Astronomical Elements, expunged that foregoing inversion, and substituted **Eccentrics on a mobile centre**, so that the learners might the more easily understand the motions and places of the Apogees, and, an Epicycle being added in the Planets, the directions, stations, and retrogressions might become the more manifest, nor the reckoning of the Latitudes be so obscure and intricate. Yet, lest I should fail the ingenious and those who already understand the common forms of the single motions, or wish to build **Automata**, I subjoined at the end, as a Corollary, that **Inversion of Copernicus** of which I spoke above, so that thus I might prepare the learners for the reading and easier understanding of Copernicus. But perhaps [I have said] more about this matter than was enough: to other [things], then.

As to what you think, toward the end of the **refutation of Roeslin**, that the **minimum Eccentricity of the Sun** has passed [occurred] — the same I too establish. For I refer the minimum Eccentricity and obliquity of the Sun to **Peurbach**. Nor is **Rheticus** to be heard either, who, while he writes that **al-Battānī** [Albategnius] too freely abuses the mysteries of **Astrology**, here falls into the same fault himself. For how can the change of the Sun's Eccentricity effect a change of empires? Nor do you unjustly reprehend that which **Philip Melanchthon** first introduced — namely, that the Sun has now been made nearer to the Earth — although **Cardano** too, in book 3 of the *Subtleties*, erroneously establishes the same. For they did not attain Copernicus's mind in this matter. I do not doubt that you too could find a far more exact **Hypothesis of the Comet's motion**, since the proportional decrement of its motion sufficiently argues that it was composed of circular [motions]. Nevertheless I judge it altogether superfluous to constitute **Hypotheses of Comets**, since none completes a Period, nor can any utility redound thence. Wherefore in my writing too I omitted the constitution of a Hypothesis. I myself beheld that Comet [of 1585] of which you deal in that Tome at **Bernburg, 10 November**, together with **Johann Troldenirer**, then prefect of the castle of Bernburg, by whom I had been invited to the **Martinmas feast**; it appeared to all dwelling at Bernburg on that day. For the Sky there was serene. When I showed that your second Tome to our most Illustrious Prince, he was occupied more than three whole hours in diligently unrolling it, and it pleased his Highness wondrously, so much so that he did not cease to praise it even to the bystanders; and he contended there with me that that book had been sent to him by you, but I argued from the inscription that it was mine, and subjoined that you would send the whole Work, if it were completed, to his most Illustrious Highness. See, therefore, that you **redeem my pledge**. And if [you should send] the same also to [his] **Son Maurice** — though not in this doctrine, yet in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew splendidly instructed and erudite beyond his Age — and likewise to **Bernhard, Prince of Anhalt**, dwelling here in our Court with Maurice, whom his parent **Joachim Ernst** of most happy memory had, together with [his] brothers, instructed in these Arts too, through **Caspar Gottschalk**, a man not unskilled in Mathematics: if, I say, you send that completed Work of yours hither to these two also, I do not doubt that you will do them a most welcome thing, by this reasoning **tacitly inciting them** to the love and cultivation of these most pleasant Arts, according to the grasp of [their] age. Those **Mathematical works** of which I wrote in [my] earlier letter I am about to publish shortly, the divine clemency favouring, when I will transmit them to you. But it would now be time that I at last close this too-prolix Letter, had not our most Illustrious Prince given me another [thing] in [his] commands. For since his most Illustrious Highness is so occupied in the **marrying-off of [his] Daughter** that he cannot reply, he commanded me to reply myself to those [things] which your Letter contains. But I find nothing in it which much needs a reply, or which has not been more than sufficiently set forth in his most Illustrious Highness's earlier letters sent to you — except that, in the **Observations instituted through Venus**, you seem to accuse us of error, and to confer the fault on the **Refractions**. But the Refractions could not stand in my way, since I instituted the Observations through Azimuths too, and, the distance of Venus from the **Third [star] of Aries [♈]** and others taken after the Sun's setting, on account of the Refractions (which, however, I separated [out]), it would necessarily have been found smaller than just, and so the places of the Stars would have been drawn back into the preceding [direction], against the order of the signs. But I do not wish to deal more about these. For you will see the reckoning of our Observations in our **Work** shortly to be published, God willing. I see, therefore, that nothing further now remains than that I at last finish this Letter. Wherefore fare best and most happily, most Noble and most Excellent Lord Tycho, and to me far dearest; and receive my candour in the best part, and write me back as soon as possible. Again, farewell.

Kassel, the 13th [day before the] Kalends of October [literally; = 13 October per the catalogue], in the Year of salvation 1588. Yours truly, **Christoph Rothmann.**

documents.apparatus:
- **Edition of record.** Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia* vol. VI (*Epistolae astronomicae*); the edition's source_edition is Tycho's own 1596 print, in which Rothmann's letter appears; no MS witness recorded. **Cross-check:** page-collated at **vol. VI pp. 151–161**; the **Alhazen book 7 ch. 2/4/[7]** and **Witelo book 10 props. 3/8/10** citations, Euclid I.21, the 52-radii / 1:100000 / 1:140608 figures, the twilight depressions (16½° / 24°), the 1558-comet positions, and the dateline are all confirmed against Dreyer (page anchors in the Editorial note). The one item not confirmable from the digitised text: the *chapter* digit of the second Alhazen citation (book 7, ch. 7) is digitised text layer-illegible in the page image; book 7 is legible and ch. 7 is secure from the surrounding series.
- **Sender / recipient.** **Christoph Rothmann** (c. 1555 – c. 1600), mathematician to **Landgrave Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel**, working at the Kassel observatory alongside the clockmaker **Jost Bürgi**. Tycho (Uraniborg). This is Rothmann's substantive reply in the great **Tycho–Rothmann correspondence**, answering Tycho's two letters (the comet-book *Tomus II* sent via **Gellius Sascerides**, received 11 July, and a later one) — the natural-philosophical heart of the exchange.
- **Thesis 1 — fluid air-heavens (optics).** Rothmann holds the "surrounding matter" of the heavens is **pure air, identical in transparency to sublunary pure air** (against a distinct aether). His proofs are optical: (a) **diverse transparencies must produce refraction** (Alhazen 7.2/7.4, Witelo 10.3); so if there were an aether/air boundary, there would be a refraction-"point," contradicting observation; (b) refraction **weakens light** (Alhazen 7.7, Witelo 10.10), yet zenith-stars are not brighter than others; (c) the **decisive demonstration** (Euclid I.21): a real aether/air refraction would be **greater for the fixed stars (farther) than for the Sun (nearer)** at the same altitude — but observation shows the opposite, so the refraction is from **vapours near the Earth**, not an aether/air boundary. He turns Tycho's own "refraction to the zenith" against him, and notes the **warm-window/cold-air** experiment. Subsidiary: no **sound** from stellar motion in pure air (the gross-air wind analogy; the *Superi* would be deafened); Melanchthon's *Physics* on the elements' proportion; the 52-Earth-radii lunar distance implying air 1:140,608 the Earth-globe. On the **fifth essence** (Tycho's chymical point): Rothmann grants it lurks in earthly things but holds it **generated by the Sun** (the **Sol Microcosmi** / heart-chambers / vital-spirit analogy), not identical with the planetary "surrounding matter."
- **Thesis 2 — comet tails self-luminous.** Reversing his earlier deference to **Cardano/Scaliger/Apian**, Rothmann now holds the **tail is of the head's own (rarer) matter, shining by illumination, not pointing at the Sun** — proved by the **Landgrave's 1558-comet record** (quoted from **Cyprian Leovitius's** gilded *Ephemerides* that Wilhelm IV carried with his Bible, self-moving globe, and small quadrant): the comet's tail pointed toward **Ursa Major**, not the Sun. The tail's **curvature** (inexplicable on Tycho's straight-ray view) and the **great comets of Seneca and Pontanus** (one equalling the Milky Way, one of 50°) confirm it. On comet *matter*, Rothmann's view differs from Aristotle's (tenuous/ray-purged, not gross/burning; in the planetary spheres, not just sublunary); he notes that Tycho, by introducing **generation into the heaven**, must introduce **corruption** too.
- **Thesis 3 — the Copernican defence (the historic core).** Rothmann reads Tycho's "new hypotheses" as **"inverted Copernicus"** (geo-heliocentric), and may be **diverse** only in carrying the planets' homocentric centres on the **Sun's eccentric** (mixing the solar eccentricity into all planets — which observations would not support). He had himself built such constructions (*Homocentrepicyclepicycli*) "entirely according to Copernicus" (as did **Rheticus** and **Reinhold**); the Landgrave had a 6-inch **automaton** showing all planetary motions. But Rothmann rejects the geo-heliocentric arrangement: it shows only **that**, not **why**, retrogressions occur (the "stain of retrogression"), whereas **Copernicus shows why** — the retrogressions are the Earth's motion reflected; only **proper motions** remain (Earth's diurnal + annual, then Moon/Venus/Mercury/Mars/Jupiter/Saturn). The **traction objection**: the Sun's epicycle-centre cannot "drag" the planets with no connecting matter (the Landgrave's joke that "the Sun's circle must be stronger than bronze"); the system "**confuses the spheres**," and "God is the author of order, not confusion," and "Nature does not act through more when fewer suffice." He affirms **gravity as Copernicus defined it** (a natural appetite of parts toward their whole, in all the globes — *De rev.* I.9), the Earth's fitness to move (the spun-globe analogy), and that **Scripture accommodates the vulgar** (Genesis 1; the "iron heaven," "windows of heaven," the firmament = "that force by which clouds hang"; the "stretched tent"; Lactantius; Solomon's natural wisdom; Paul, Rom. 1: greater wisdom lies in Nature than is revealed in Scripture). He doubts Tycho really has "geometrical demonstrations" for his system. Yet for **teaching** he keeps non-Copernican forms (even **Maestlin** misunderstands the libration), reserving the "Copernican inversion" as a corollary to ease students toward Copernicus.
- **Other matters.** The **twilight** discrepancy (Tycho's morning 16½° vs Rothmann's evening 24° depression); the request for Tycho's chymical-medical teaching (Ramus's "number, weight, measure"; the **Sulphur/Salt/Mercury** spirits; natural/vital/animal spirits; soul-spirit-body union; the **stone** and **gout**); praise of the comet *Tomus II* (the aethereal course "irrefutably demonstrated"); the **lunar max-latitude** agreement but the **ascending node** ("Head of the Dragon") off the Tables by >4°; the **minimum solar eccentricity/obliquity** referred to **Peurbach**; **Rheticus** and **Melanchthon/Cardano** faulted on solar-eccentricity-and-empires and "the Sun now nearer"; comet-hypotheses "superfluous" (no period); the **1585 comet** seen at **Bernburg** (10 Nov, with **Johann Troldenirer**, at a Martinmas feast); the Landgrave's 3-hour absorption in the *Tomus II* and the dispute over whose copy; the request for completed copies for **Maurice** (the future Moritz the Learned) and **Bernhard of Anhalt** (tutored by **Caspar Gottschalk**); and the closing defence of the **Venus observations** (refraction "separated out," azimuths used) — Rothmann answering for the Landgrave, busy "marrying off his daughter."
- **Persons & places.** **Gellius Sascerides**; **Wilhelm IV** (*Illustrissimus Princeps*); **Maurice of Hesse**; **Bernhard of Anhalt**, **Joachim Ernst of Anhalt**, **Caspar Gottschalk**; **Johann Troldenirer** (Bernburg); **Alhazen** (Ibn al-Haytham), **Witelo** (*Vitellio*); **Aristotle, Plato, Pliny, Lactantius, Solomon, Paul, Moses, Christ/Nicodemus**; **Copernicus, Rheticus, Reinhold, Maestlin, Peurbach, al-Battānī, Cardano, Scaliger, Apian, Ramus, Roeslin, Graminaeus**; **Philip Melanchthon**; **Seneca, Pontanus**; **Cyprian Leovitius**. Places: **Kassel** (*Cassellis*), **Bernburg**, **Knudstrup** (Tycho's title).
- **Greek / Latin / technical tags.** *φιλαληθέια* = love of truth; *ἀυτόματον* = automaton (the Kassel planetary clock-model); *Homocentrepicyclepicycli* = Rothmann's coinage for homocentric-epicycle-upon-epicycle constructions; *Diaphana* = transparencies/media; *Crepuscula* = twilights; *Pyramis* (of rays) = the optical cone; *Davus sum, non Oedipus* = "I am a Davus, not an Oedipus" (Terence — no riddle-solver); *Superi* = the gods above. *Sol Microcosmi* = the heart as the body's sun. The Copernican **gravity** definition quotes *De revolutionibus* I.9; the planet-order recital echoes I.10. Glyphs: ♍ Virgo, ♈ Aries. *Torquetum* = the medieval observing instrument (used for the 1558 comet). *Alrucaba* = the pole-star/Ursa-Minor region (Arabic).
- **Dateline crux (named).** The source reads *"Cassellis 13. Calendas Octobris … M.D.LXXXIIX [1588]."* Strict Roman dating (*a.d. XIII Kal. Oct.*) = **19 September**; the catalogue/edition reads **13 October** (taking "13" + "Octobris"). The form is anomalous (no "ante diem"; "Calendas" loosely). The header follows the catalogue's **13 October**, shows the literal dateline, and flags the discrepancy here rather than silently resolving it. **Old Style** (Lutheran Hesse). Within the 1558-comet quote, the Roman dates resolve as: *13 Kal. Sept.* = 20 Aug, *12 Kal.* = 21 Aug, *10 Kal.* = 23 Aug 1558.
- **Editorial interventions in the source block (declared).** c. 30 digitised text layer-intruded **apparatus "A" sigla** removed as non-textual (as in the letters to Scaliger of 23 Aug 1598, to Peucer of 1590, to the Landgrave of 16 Aug 1588, and to Herwart of 16 Nov 1599); *obseruamus est* in the 1558-comet quote — **confirmed to be Dreyer's own printed reading**, which he flags with a dagger († sic); it is therefore the edition's reading, not a downstream transcription slip — left in the source block and rendered as *observatus* in translation; *Illustridimus* (for *Illustrissimus*), *praefertim* (for *praesertim*), *aspexere* (for *aspergere*?) left as printed; v/u orthography retained.

No fabricated facts, no dropped clauses, no hardened hedges, no misattributions found. documents.incipit: NOBILISS. vir, domine et amice observande. Binas ab eo tempore, quo meus famulus abs te …

text.original:
NOBILITATE GENERIS, VIRTUTE ET DOCTRINA PRÆSTANTI AC MATHEMATUM ILLUSTRATORI EXIMIO D. TYCHONI BRAHE DANO, INSULAe HUENAe DANICI HELLESPONTI DOMINO, D. ET AMICO OBSERVANDO.
S.

NOBILISS. vir, domine et amice observande. Binas ab eo tempore, quo meus famulus abs te redijt, dedi ad te literas. Alteras Gallus quidam Mathematicus praestans, cuius nomen nunc non succurrit, reddere debuerat, alteras Rostochiensi tabellario tradideram. Cum neutrarum facias mentionem, utrasque intercidisse conicio. Tuae literae cum libro abs te edito sub finem mensis Iulij sunt mihi redditae. Et, profecto, fuerunt gratissimae, quibus perlectis ad librum avidissime accessi et percurri, initio celeriter, ut generalem totius operis cognitionem haurirem. Vehementer, ita me Deus amet, eo sum oblectatus. Doleo autem, quod tum ob aetatem iam ingravescentem, tum ob curas domesticas ac professionem Medicam, quae alimenta affert, illi studio amplius navare non possum; nihilominus aliorum in hoc studij genere laboribus mirifice delector.

De tuo libro quod dicam habeo nihil, ita accurate omnia sunt abs te excussa et examinata, ut mea lima non egeant. Novam illam orbium coelestium dispositionem nondum accuratius considerare potui. D. CURTIUS Caesaris Consiliarius et Procancellarius Imperij, Mathematicus excellens et iudicio acri, fuit quoque vehementer tuo scripto delectatus. Cum eius iudicium de tuo libro requirerem, respondit non temere de hypothesibus iudicandum esse. Rem attentius considerandam esse. Te officiose salvere iussit, cohortarique, ut coeptum cursum non interrumpas. Inter alia dixit quoque te nimis multam fecisse mentionem et praedicasse nimium VINCKLERUM illum hominem Astronomiae rudissimum. Ex mea Dialexi integras pagellas descripsit, et pessime suo Cometae Anni 77 accommodavit. In mea epistola ad MYLIUM impressa adiunxeram in chartula, quid insuper nugatus fuisset de Cometa Anni 80. Adscribebat eidem parallaxin maximam 15 fere grad. et tamen supra Lunam illum collocabat. Te hanc annotatiunculam meam non animadvertisse existimo, alioquin dedolasses eum asperiori dolabro et pectine acriori depexuisses, aut plane praeterijsses silentio, tanquam omnium indignissimum qui caeterorum, quorum abs te honorificentissima facta est mentio, latus clauderet. Sed valeat iste nugator et ardelio. Satis ipsemet propinavit se deridendum omnibus. Porro quod a me in plerisque dissentias, non fero moleste, mi TYCHO, neque tibi propterea succenseo, imo gratias ago maximas, quod tuo beneficio factus sim eruditior, et veritas abs te asserta est, iamque triumphat. Non mihi mea ita placent, nec meos partus ita diligo, ut in illis et errata et nevos aliquos non agnoscam, et cum possint abstergi, venustiorque forma induci, admittere nolim. SCULTETICUM ingenium mihi non est, qui quod aliquando candide meam de eius Cometa Anni 77 et de Calendarij sui editione sententiam tulerim, et quod nimium Papissare et cum Iesuitis colludere videretur, odium erga me concepit, et tum in literis ad amicos perscriptis, tum in suis istis nugacissimis Calendarijs suggillare non destitit, donec illi significari mandassem, desinat me lacessere, alioquin clausurum me ipsi os. Sic mea amica commonefactio in odium et simultatem erupit. Iam vero sibi temperat et sapit. Nuper enim per meum filium me salvere iussit. Ego vicissim dabo operam, ut et benevolum meum erga se animum, et redintegrandae cum ipso amicitiae cupidissimum esse liquido agnoscat. Haec ideo commemoro, ut meum animum plane cognoscas.

Meis lapsibus omnino patrocinari nec possum, nec debeo. Ac etsi contra tuas defensiones pro MÆSTLINO aliquid dici possit, tamen tuo iudicio repugnare nolo, tum etiam quod MÆSTLINUM ob insignem peritiam Mathematum mirifice diligo, tantumque tribuo, ut dicere ausim, sed absque aliorum invidia, scholas Germanicas, PRÆTORIO unico excepto, parem ipsi habere neminem. Hoc tantum adijcio, bona tua et MÆSTLINI pace, de ratione motuum Cometarum, quod Planetarum ideo certae hypotheses sunt constitutae, quia eorum motus integri poterant animadverti, quomodo item accederent ad Solem aut ab eo regrederentur. At Cometae non absolvunt suas periodos, neque certa lege accedunt ad Solem, et recedunt ab eodem. Itaque non videtur possibile motus eorum rationem explicare et veluti vincire certis legibus. Pulchram quidem et ingenuosam fuisse speculationem MÆSTLINI praedicas, et ego assentior. Sed pulchritudo et subtilitas veritati, virtuti in hac universitate omnium pulcherrimae, anteferenda non est, quam veritatem nec MÆSTLINUM nec quemquam alium in Theoria Cometarum plane, quomodo aliorum Planetarum, video esse assequutum. Tendimus quidem eo omnes, maxime vero tu, qui ex professo iam tractas hoc argumentum, et iam ex hisce, quae veluti fundamenta futuri aedificij posita esse video, multa profecto mihi de te polliceor, et Deum oro ut ad haec Dei opera mirabilia illustranda longum satis curriculum vitae concedere dignetur. Porro in calculo MÆSTLINI, quem tu sequeris, te commonefacere volui, ut inspicias, an ille in numeris alicubi lapsus sit, an vero nos fallamur, item an ea differentia notabilem in sequentibus errorem pariat. Inspexi meas chartas, in quibus olim MÆSTLINI calculum a me examinatum reperi. Primum Epocham Commutationis mediae ad diem 24 Novembris cum MÆSTLINO statuis 206 gr. 33'. Meus calculus habet tantum 206 gr. 18'. Aequationem Commutationis Cometae habet MÆSTLINUS 5, 48', tu vero 5, 1 2/3. Item Aequationem Eccentri habet MÆSTLINUS O, 5. Sic et ego; tu vero 1, 18 1/3. Haec fortassis levicula sunt. Videnda tamen, an in scopo ad quem tendimus, notabilem aliquam differentiam afferant. Mihi repetere et prosequi calculationem ob meas occupationes non licuit.

De nova Stella nullos alios scriptores, praeter illos quos in mea Dialexi vidisti adductos, cognovi.

APIANI Astronomicum aliquando habui, et diligenter inquisivi an ex ipsius Datis in parallaxium cognitionem pervenire potuissem, verum insufficientia fuerunt eius Data. Alicubi diserte scribit parallaxim Cometae inveniri non posse, nisi prius distantia eius a Terra cognita fuerit, quod falsissimum esse nemo est qui ignoret. Ab APIANO igitur nihil est quod expectes. Hunc eruditum pulverem, in quo nos versamur, ille ne somniavit quidem. Eius artem saepe RHETICUS, bonae memoriae, vocare solitus erat faden Dunst.

IOANNIS PENAe Galli scriptum de Cometa nunquam vidi. Librum illum, quem olim tibi Ratisbonae donaveram, ab eo tempore nunquam vidi, neque etiam authoris recordari possum. Lustrabam, Bibliothecas nostrates, invenire non potui. Eius loco mitto ad te olim expetitum librum VERNERI de Elementis Conicis, ubi etiam tractatulus de motu 8 Sphaerae et alia habentur. A FABRICIO Vienna illum accepi, te salvere iubet. His quod addam habeo nihil, nisi ut feliciter valeas. Datae Pragae die 1. Novemb. veteri stylo Anno 88.

Literas quas scripsisti 17 Augusti ex mercatu Francofordensi accepi, una cum alijs ad SCULTETUM, quas illi Gorlicium misi.

T. studiosiss.
THAD.
text.english:
**To Master Tycho Brahe the Dane, outstanding in nobility of birth, in virtue and in learning, and an eminent illuminator of the mathematical sciences, lord of the island of Hven in the Danish Hellespont, my lord and friend to be esteemed — greeting.**

Most noble sir, my lord and friend to be esteemed. Since the time when my servant returned from you I have sent you two letters. The one a certain distinguished French mathematician — whose name does not now come to me — was to have delivered; the other I had handed to the Rostock courier. Since you make mention of neither, I conjecture that both have gone astray. Your letter, together with the book published by you, was delivered to me toward the end of the month of July. And indeed they were most welcome; once they had been read through I turned most eagerly to the book and ran through it, at first quickly, so as to drink in a general acquaintance with the whole work. Vehemently, so help me God, was I delighted by it. Yet I grieve that, both on account of my now advancing age and on account of my domestic cares and my profession of medicine, which supplies my livelihood, I am no longer able to devote myself further to that study; nonetheless I take wonderful delight in the labours of others in this kind of study.

Concerning your book I have nothing to say, so accurately has everything been sifted and examined by you, that it does not need my file. That new arrangement of the celestial orbs I have not yet been able to consider more closely. Master Curtius, the Emperor's Councillor and Vice-Chancellor of the Empire, an excellent mathematician and of keen judgement, was likewise vehemently delighted by your writing. When I sought his judgement of your book, he replied that one must not judge rashly concerning hypotheses, [and] that the matter must be considered more attentively. He bade me greet you dutifully, and exhort you not to interrupt the course you have begun. Among other things he also said that you had made too much mention of, and praised too highly, that Vinckler, a man most ignorant of astronomy. From my *Dialexis* he copied out whole little pages, and most wretchedly fitted them to his comet of the year [15]77. In my letter to Mylius, [now] in print, I had added on a slip what he had moreover trifled about concerning the comet of the year [15]80. He assigned to it a parallax of nearly 15 degrees at the maximum, and yet placed it above the Moon. I think you did not notice this little note of mine; otherwise you would have hewn him with a rougher axe and combed him down with a sharper comb, or else passed him over altogether in silence, as the least worthy of all to close the file of the others, of whom most honourable mention has been made by you. But let that trifler and busybody fare [as he may]. He has himself given all men enough to mock at. Furthermore, that you dissent from me in very many points I do not take amiss, my Tycho, nor am I angry with you on that account; rather I give the greatest thanks, that by your kindness I have been made more learned, and the truth has been asserted by you, and now triumphs. I am not so pleased with my own things, nor do I so cherish my own offspring, that I do not acknowledge in them both errors and certain blemishes, and — when they can be wiped away and a more comely form put on — am not unwilling to admit it. I have not a Scultetus's temper, who, because I once frankly delivered my opinion of his comet of the year [15]77 and of the edition of his calendar, and because he seemed to play the papist too much and to collude with the Jesuits, conceived a hatred toward me, and ceased not to taunt me, both in letters written to friends and in those most trifling calendars of his, until I had ordered it to be signified to him that he should stop provoking me, or else I would shut his mouth for him. Thus my friendly admonition burst out into hatred and feud. But now indeed he restrains himself and is wise. For lately, through my son, he sent me his greeting. I in turn shall take pains that he may plainly recognise both my goodwill toward him and that I am most desirous of renewing my friendship with him. These things I therefore recall, that you may know my mind clearly.

My own lapses I can in no way defend, nor ought I. And although something might be said against your defences on Maestlin's behalf, yet I am unwilling to oppose your judgement — and also because I wonderfully cherish Maestlin for his remarkable skill in the mathematical sciences, and rate him so highly that I would venture to say (but without envy toward others) that the German schools, with the single exception of Praetorius, have no one equal to him. This much only I add — by your leave and Maestlin's — concerning the account of the motions of comets: that the hypotheses of the planets have been established as certain for this reason, that their motions could be observed entire, and likewise how they approached the Sun or receded from it. But comets do not complete their periods, nor do they approach the Sun and recede from it by a fixed law. And so it does not seem possible to explain the account of their motions and, as it were, to bind them with fixed laws. You proclaim that Maestlin's speculation was indeed beautiful and ingenious, and I agree. But beauty and subtlety are not to be set before truth — that virtue most beautiful of all in this universe — which truth I do not see that either Maestlin or anyone else has fully attained in the theory of comets, in the manner [achieved] for the other planets. We all do indeed strive toward that, but most of all you, who now treat this subject professedly; and already, from these things which I see laid down as it were the foundations of a future edifice, I truly promise myself much concerning you, and I pray God that he may deign to grant a course of life long enough for the illustrating of these wonderful works of God. Furthermore, in Maestlin's calculation, which you follow, I wished to put you on notice, that you may examine whether he has somewhere erred in the numbers, or whether instead we are deceived, and likewise whether that difference begets a notable error in what follows. I have looked over my papers, in which I once found Maestlin's calculation examined by me. First, the epoch of the mean commutation for the 24th day of November you set with Maestlin at 206 deg. 33′. My calculation has only 206 deg. 18′. The equation of the commutation of the comet Maestlin has at 5°, 48′, but you at 5°, 1 2/3′. Likewise the equation of the eccentric Maestlin has at 0°, 5′. So have I too; but you at 1°, 18 1/3′. These things perhaps are trifling. They must be looked into, nonetheless, [to see] whether in the goal toward which we strive they bring some notable difference. To repeat and pursue the calculation has not been permitted me, on account of my occupations.

Of the new star I have come to know no other writers besides those whom you saw adduced in my *Dialexis*.

Apian's *Astronomicum* I once had, and I diligently inquired whether from his own data I might have arrived at a knowledge of the parallaxes; but his data were insufficient. Somewhere he expressly writes that the parallax of a comet cannot be found unless its distance from the Earth has first been known — which there is no one who does not know to be utterly false. From Apian, therefore, there is nothing for you to expect. This learned dust in which we are engaged he did not so much as dream of. His art Rheticus, of good memory, used often to call *faden Dunst* [insipid vapour].

The writing of Jean Pena the Frenchman on the comet I have never seen. That book which I once gave you at Regensburg I have never seen since that time, nor can I even recall the author. I scoured our local libraries [but] could not find it. In its place I send you the book of Werner *On the Conic Elements*, long sought by you, in which there is also a little treatise on the motion of the eighth sphere and other matters. I received it from Fabricius at Vienna; he bids you greeting. To these I have nothing to add, save that you fare happily. Given at Prague, the 1st day of November, Old Style, the year [15]88.

The letter you wrote on 17 August I received from the Frankfurt fair, together with others addressed to Scultetus, which I sent on to him at Görlitz.

Most devoted to you,
Thad[daeus].

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus Hagecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayek, 1525–1600), Bohemian physician, astronomer and personal physician at the imperial court in Prague; a leading European authority on the nova of 1572 and the comet of 1577, and Tycho's chief correspondent and ally in Bohemia. He signs *THAD.* (abbreviated).
- **Recipient address.** *INSULAe HUENAe DANICI HELLESPONTI DOMINO* — "lord of the island of **Hven** in the Danish Hellespont": the Hellespont = the Øresund (the Sound), in whose narrows Hven (Uraniborg) lies; an honorific conceit for Tycho's seat.
- **The book published by you.** *libro abs te edito … Novam illam orbium coelestium dispositionem* — Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (Uraniborg, 1588), which presents the comet of 1577 and, in cap. VIII, the **new arrangement of the celestial orbs** (the geo-heliocentric / Tychonic world-system). Hagecius received it in late July 1588.
- ***D. Curtius*** = **Jacob Kurtz (Curtius) von Senftenau** (d. 1594), Imperial Councillor and Vice-Chancellor (*Procancellarius Imperii*) under Rudolf II, a capable mathematician; his cautious verdict — *non temere de hypothesibus iudicandum* ("one must not judge rashly concerning hypotheses") — is preserved verbatim and unsmoothed.
- ***Vincklerus*** — **Nicolaus Winckler** (Vincklerus, d. 1613), physician and astrological writer of Hall in Swabia; Hagecius (reporting Curtius) dismisses him as *Astronomiae rudissimum* ("most ignorant of astronomy") and a plagiarist of the *Dialexis*. The vituperative imagery — *dedolasses … asperiori dolabro et pectine acriori depexuisses* ("you would have hewn him with a rougher axe and combed him down with a sharper comb") and *nugator et ardelio* ("trifler and busybody") — is kept as metaphor.
- ***Dialexis*** — Hagecius's *Dialexis de novae et prius incognitae stellae … apparitione* (Frankfurt, 1574), his treatise on the 1572 nova; *integras pagellas descripsit* = "copied out whole little pages."
- ***Mylius*** — Hagecius refers to his own printed *epistola ad Mylium* (the letter to Mylius), almost certainly addressed to the Görlitz physician-astronomer of that name; the precise identification is not fixed by the text and is left as given.
- ***Scultetus*** — **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (Bartoloměj Scultetus, 1540–1614), mathematician, cartographer and calendar-maker of **Görlitz** (*Gorlicium*); the *Cometa Anni 77* is his tract on the 1577 comet, the *Calendaria* his almanacs. *Papissare* (a coinage, "to play the papist") and *cum Iesuitis colludere* ("collude with the Jesuits") are confessional jibes, kept literal. The closing postscript routes Tycho's letters to Scultetus via Görlitz.
- ***Maestlin*** = **Michael Maestlin** (1550–1631), mathematician at Tübingen, Kepler's teacher; his *De Cometa anni 1577* attempted to bind the comet's motion to a circular path about the Sun. Hagecius rejects this in principle: comets *non absolvunt suas periodos* ("do not complete their periods") and so cannot be reduced to *certae hypotheses* like the planets. *PRAeTORIO unico excepto* — **Johannes Praetorius** (1537–1616), mathematician at Altdorf, named as the only German mathematician Hagecius rates Maestlin's equal.
- **Cometary calculation (technical).** The numerical comparison concerns Maestlin's reduction of the 1577 comet, which Tycho follows. *Epocha Commutationis mediae* = "epoch of the mean **commutation**" (the heliocentric–geocentric elongation angle) for 24 November: Tycho/Maestlin 206° 33′ vs. Hagecius 206° 18′. *Aequatio Commutationis* (the **equation of commutation**): Maestlin 5° 48′, Tycho 5° 1 2/3′. *Aequatio Eccentri* (**equation of the eccentric**): Maestlin and Hagecius 0° 5′, Tycho 1° 18 1/3′. The minutes-values are transcribed exactly as printed (e.g. *5, 1 2/3*, *1, 18 1/3*); fractional minutes are kept, not rounded. *Aequatio* in its astronomical sense is rendered **equation** per glossary. *parallaxin maximam 15 fere grad.* = "a parallax of nearly 15 degrees at the maximum" — *maximam* is the source's own word (not an editorial insertion); the gloss "[the] maximum" stands on Hagecius's text. The internal contradiction Hagecius flags in Winckler (a c. 15° parallax would place a body well *below* the Moon, yet Winckler set it *above* the Moon) is preserved, not corrected.
- ***Apiani Astronomicum*** — **Peter Apian**'s *Astronomicum Caesareum* (Ingolstadt, 1540); Hagecius judges its cometary data insufficient for parallax and singles out Apian's claim that a comet's parallax cannot be found without first knowing its distance — which he calls *falsissimum* ("utterly false"). *Hunc eruditum pulverem* ("this learned dust") is his self-deprecating figure for the technical drudgery of the discipline.
- **German interpolation.** *faden Dunst* — Early New High German, "insipid/stale vapour" (*fad* "insipid" + *Dunst* "vapour, haze"); reported as **Rheticus**'s habitual put-down of Apian's art. Transcribed verbatim in the source and glossed; **Rheticus** = **Georg Joachim Rheticus** (1514–1574), Copernicus's disciple, *bonae memoriae* ("of good memory," i.e. now deceased).
- ***Ioannes Pena*** — **Jean Pena** (c. 1528–1558), French royal mathematician; his views on comets appeared in the preface to his edition of Euclid's *Optica/Catoptrica* (Paris, 1557). *Verneri de Elementis Conicis* — **Johannes Werner** (1468–1522) of Nuremberg, whose works include *De motu octavae sphaerae* (on the motion of the eighth sphere = precession/trepidation) and treatises on conics; sent in Pena's place. *Fabricius* (at Vienna) — most plausibly **Paul Fabricius** (c. 1519–1589), imperial mathematician and physician at Vienna; identification offered, not asserted, as the text gives only the surname.
- **Places.** *Pragae* = **Prague**; *Ratisbona* = **Regensburg**; *Vienna*; *Gorlicium* = **Görlitz**; *mercatus Francofordensis* = the **Frankfurt** (book) fair.
- **Calendar.** The dateline reads *Datae Pragae die 1. Novemb. **veteri stylo** Anno 88* — "Given at Prague, the 1st day of November, **Old Style**, the year [15]88." Hagecius, writing from Catholic Prague (on the Gregorian/New Style calendar since 1584), here deliberately gives the date in **Old Style** for his Danish correspondent, who kept the Julian calendar; the explicit *veteri stylo* is the period's own gap-bridging convention. No conversion is supplied or implied beyond what the text states. The catalogue *label* ("1588. 1. november") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy.
- **Correction.** Two mistranslations corrected against Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p.146 (Latin unaltered, confirmed correct as stored): 'am unwilling to admit it' restored to 'am not unwilling to admit it' (the negative result clause 'non...ita...ut...nolim' had lost its outer negation, reversing Hagecius's stated openness to correction); and 'he bade me greet [him in turn]' corrected to 'he sent me his greeting' (the idiom 'me salvere iussit' had been reversed in direction, making Hagecius the greeter rather than the greeted).

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full the published English against the transcribed original and against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.145-147 (Hagecius to Tycho, 1 Nov 1588), read as page images. our transcribed original matches Dreyer's printed Latin essentially verbatim throughout — no text error found. Checked opening address/header, closing subscription, and every proper name (Curtius, Vinckler, Scultetus, Maestlin, Praetorius, Apian, Rheticus, Ioannes Pena, Werner, Fabricius, Mylius) and every number/date (24 November, 206gr33'/206gr18', 5,48'/5,1⅔, 0,5/1,18⅓, c. 15 degrees parallax, comet years 77 and 80, 17 August, 1 November 1588, Frankfurt fair, Görlitz, Regensburg/Ratisbona) — all render correctly with no fabricated or dropped facts, names, or figures, and no whole sentence or clause is silently omitted. Found two localized but genuine sense-reversing mistranslation (both negation/direction flips, not fabrications): (1) Hagecius's stated willingness to have his own errors corrected is rendered as an unwillingness; (2) the direction of a reconciliatory greeting with Scultetus (Scultetus greets Hagecius first) is reversed into Hagecius being told to greet Scultetus. Both are confined to single clauses and do not corrupt any name, date, or number — the translation is otherwise careful and largely faithful across a long, dense letter — but per the grading rule any sense-changing mistranslation caps the grade at C.

**2 defects found:**
- **mistranslation** (medium). The Latin is a negative result clause ("Non mihi mea ita placent... ut... non agnoscam, et... admittere nolim" = 'I am not so pleased with my own things that I fail to acknowledge errors, or refuse to let them be corrected'). Both verbs sit inside the same 'not so X that...' negation, so the sense is that Hagecius DOES acknowledge his errors and IS willing to have them corrected. The English drops the negation on the second verb and reads as a flat, un-negated assertion ('am unwilling to admit it'), inverting Hagecius's stated position from openness-to-correction to refusal — exactly backward, and it undercuts the humility topos that sets up his forbearance toward Tycho's disagreements in the very next sentence. At: “and — when they can be wiped away and a more comely form put on — am unwilling to admit it.”.
- **mistranslation** (medium). "[Scultetus] me salvere iussit" is the standard Latin epistolary greeting idiom (literally 'he bade me be well/greeted' = 'he sent his greeting to me') — Scultetus is the one extending the greeting to Hagecius, via the son as go-between. The English reverses the direction, making it read as Scultetus ordering Hagecius to send greetings to him — the opposite of who initiated the conciliatory gesture. This also breaks the logic of the immediately following sentence ('Ego vicissim dabo operam...' = 'I IN TURN will take pains...'), which presupposes Scultetus acted first. At: “For lately, through my son, he bade me greet [him in turn].”.

**Repaired.** Verified both mistranslation defects against the Dreyer page image (TBOO VII p.146, lines 5 and 14-15 respectively), read visually in the extract PDF. Both Latin phrases match the stored the transcribed original exactly, so only the English clauses were corrected — one restoring a dropped negation in a 'non...ita...ut' construction, the other restoring the correct direction of a standard epistolary greeting idiom. Nothing else in the letter was altered.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD HENRICUM BRUCÆUM.

RUPISTI tandem altum illud silentium, quo per totam aestatem aliquid ad me literarum dare supersedisti, amantissime BRUCÆE, quod autem nunc demum quasi e profundo somno expergefactus me tuis eruditis literis reviseris, est quod moram hanc hactenus commissam condonem, teque excusatum habeam. Agis autem in his mecum veluti ex professo de ijs, quae continentur in libro meo secundo Aethereorum Phaenomenωn, tibi praeterito vere per quendam e meis domesticis hinc in Germaniam proficiscentem transmisso, quaeque in priore eius parte inveniuntur, te sedulo perlegisse ostendis, posteriore leviter attacta. Visum itaque est tibi ad ea, quae de his ad me perscripsisti, in hunc modum respondere. Quod in priore eius voluminis portione contenta ex observationum et demonstrationum certitudine accomodationeque approbas et commendas, inprimis vero neotericae meae Hypotheseos circa dispositionem revolutionum coelestium inventionem tibi admodum placere asseveras, mihi pergratum est. Equidem quantum ad Hypotheseos eius constitutionem attinet, suspicabar eam tuo Genio non arrisuram, siquidem alias tam vehemens et constans sis autoritatis antiquorum conservator et propugnator, adeo ut nonnunquam nimium his tribuere et certioribus rationibus ipsique experientiae non parum derogare videaris; sed aliter tamen hîc accidit quam putabam: Hanc enim nostram mundani systematis Hypotyposin a veteribus nunquam perspectam, nec etiam a recentioribus ullis prius excogitatam non solum tuo suffragio comprobas, sed etiam ceteris, quod eiuscemodi, quae illae a PTOLEMÆO et COPERNICO propositae, non admittat absurda, anteferendam censes. Ut autem eo rectius intelliges, qua ratione in huius Hypotheseos inventionem ante aliquot annos pervenerim, mitto tibi exemplum literarum, nuper ad clarissimum et doctissimum virum D. CASPAREM PEUCERUM a me datarum, quibus eius quibusdam dubijs (quae ad nobilissimum virum Dominum HENRICUM RANZOVIUM, qui illi eius Hypotheseos nudam delineationem e libro meo excerptam communicârat, perscripsit, cuius etiam verborum unâ cum alterius cuiusdam Mathematici de eadem re ambigua sententia copiam facio) respondendum duxi, ut hac occasione plenius de hoc toto Astronomico negotio cum tanto Philosopho et Mathematico conferrem. Ex his plurima non saltem [ad] Hypotheseos huius rationes et uberiorem declarationem, sed etiam ad totam rem Astronomicam peculiariter facientia percipies tuo Genio, uti opinor, non displicitura. Ubi vero has ipsas literas perlegeris, vel etiam, si lubet, transcribi curâris, velim eas mihi remitti, siquidem exemplar hoc reservare cupiam, neque otium nunc suppetat, ut id denuo exarari faciam. Quae circa Astronomiae instaurationem desideras, ut omnia huic Hypothesi fundata eque certis observationibus Geometricis in numeros redacta Phaenomenis exacte correspondeant, etiam in his literis ad Dominum PEUCERUM datis, quo ordine et quanto conamine rem tantam aggredi molirique, favente Coeli ipsius et Universi Opifice, proposuerim, invenies. Nec est, ut pertimescas, quod laboris immensitas, rei tam arduae difficultas, temporis requisiti diuturnitas aut sumtuum magnitudo ullave alia molestia, eodem supremo Numine conatibus nostris aspirante, me absterrebunt, quo minus gratae, uti spero, posteritati tam divinae et sublimis artis restitutionem ea praecisione (absit invidia dicto) qua hactenus a nemine exantlata est, consecrem, omnibusque suis numeris, quantum quidem ab uno homine praestari potest, absolutam relinquam.

Sed de his hoc loco satis. Est tamen, quod tibi hac in re conquerar. Quidam nimis perfrictae frontis, quem indignum censeo, ut hîc nominetur, qui etiam, ubicunque fuit aut est, seipsum, qualis sit, prodit, hanc meam Hypothesium inventionem sibi arrogare, idque publico scripto, Argentinae hoc anno edito, asserere non erubuit. An et hanc cum reliquis, quae apud me clam descripsit, dum nobilissimo viro ERICO LANGE inserviens, in eius comitatu per aliquot dies fuit, subtraxit, aut qua alias ratione eius dispositionem hîc hauserit, noverit ipse; et Studiosi mei similem quandam inter segestria tunc iacentem, quae minus apposite delineata erat, monstrârunt. Certe quam fraudulenter et subdole hic egerit, reliqua, quae hîc, me inscio, ex meis descripsit, quorum aliquam partem recepi, ipsius manu exarata, satis convincunt, utut Hypothesin illam inter eas schedas non reperio; sed poterat hanc alibi abscondisse aut in memoria retinuisse, cum forte non suppeteret delineandi commoditas. Norunt domestici mei Studiosi illam Hypothesin iam aliquot annis a me fuisse constitutam atque illis ostensam: quin et liber hic de Cometa Anni 77, etsi prae se ferat editionem hoc Anno 88 factam, tamen norunt omnes, qui mecum sunt, eundem Anno 87 in mea Typographia excusam esse, data opera autem uno anno tardiorem notatam, quo esset ob novitatem acceptior. In hoc autem libro eandem mecum Hypothesin generaliter explicari, te non ignorare, ex iam dictis liquet. Sed egregie prodidit iste, qui sibi eam nuper vendicaret, se illam non probe intelligere, nedum ut eius autor sit, dum Martium orbem Solarem totaliter ambientem pingit et fingit, quod impossibile esse vel ex solo Copernico saltem obiter introspecto discere potuisset. Et quî, quaeso, is novas unquam condet Hypotheses, coelestibus revolutionibus analogas, qui multorum annorum exquisitis observationibus non est instructus, ut inde, quid in hactenus usitatis Hypothesibus desideretur, et quomodo idipsum restitui possit, solerter pervestiget? Sine his adminiculis novam aliquam inventionem iactare frivolum est planeque ridiculum, cum non habeat, unde probet per ipsas apparentias, cur prioribus relictis sic innovare [oporteat] et quomodo per multiplices observationes hanc apparentijs coelestibus rectius congruere confirmet. Sed facessant istae ineptiae, quibus nemo, nisi rem non intelligens, fidem adhibuerit.

Ad epistolam tuam redeo, ea, quae postmodum continet, ordine, ut constitui, disquisiturus. Emendationem locorum affixarum stellarum cap. 2 a me propositam ex declinatione stellae et transitu per meridianum aliquantulum in dubium vocare videris, eo quod exquisita temporis notitia Solisque locus praecise vix constare possint; id licet aliquo modo non abs re dicatur, et a me etiam circa finem eiusdem capitis in Additione fol. 31 incipiente idem fere asseveretur, nihilominus tamen adhibita competenti diligentia, et medijs quibusdam temporis minimas particulas aequali ductu, quoad fieri potest, exhibentibus, qualia nobis non pauca in promtu sunt, etiam haec ratio absque admodum sensibili errore locum meretur, praesertim si crebra reiteratione examinetur, donec obtenta non admodum sensibiliter differant, ut patet ex observationibus prioribus eo modo institutis, quae pag. 30 oculis subijciuntur, si conferantur cum alijs reiteratis et diverso modo per Solem intermediante Veneris stella ad fixa sidera diductis, quae pag. 33 exhibentur. Differentia enim est perexigua, utpote quae decimam unius gradus partem, ubi maxima est, non excedat, et in sex vel septem stellis tria minuta vix attingat; quae sane praecisio a veteribus non est extricata, ut mirari satis non possim, quod in ea, quibus tunc usus sum, instrumentorum parvitate et penuria vel per hanc ipsam tam lubricam ad deflectendum viam adeo prope tamen ad scopum collimârim. Verum exactiorem et nulli ambiguitati obnoxiam stellarum fixarum loca verificandi rationem in eadem Additione breviter indicavi, per distantias videlicet a Sole ad Venerem interdiu apparentem factas et noctu ab hac ad stellas relatas. Qua de re in antecedenti libro plenius ago, et per aliquot eo modo accurate factas animadversiones, easque tam Eoas quam vespertinas, stellarum inerrantium loca in veram et praecisam ab Aequinoctio vernali distantiam repono; idque ex ipsis observationibus ita et non aliter se habere posse demonstro, annotatis etiam earum veris latitudinibus, in quibus non minus quam longitudinibus nimium hactenus aberratum est. Solaris etiam cursus ad nostra tempora exactissima restitutio ibidem praemittitur, siquidem ex eo cetera omnia dependeant. Ubi Apogei locus eccentricitatisque vera quantitas e certis aliquot praecedentium annorum observationibus pluribus et non fallacibus instrumentis coelitus diligenter habitis Geometrice demonstrantur, adiecta aequalium motuum etiam correctorum et prostaphaereseωn e reperta eccentricitate extracta Tabula, ut de Solis motu apparentijs praecise congruente nullum amplius restet apud me dubium. Subiungam forsan de Lunari curriculo etiam subtiliter restituto nonnulla, quando per plurium annorum observationes eius perplexam semitam tam quoad longum quam latum plenius extricabo. Video te adhuc ruminare ea, quae doctissimus GEMMA FRISIUS in libello de Radio Astronomico quoad fixarum in Globum aliquem denotationem et postea Aequatoris Eclipticaeque in eodem designationem molitus est. Verum ego convenientius certis de causis fieri iudico, ut Aequator et Ecliptica prius in Globo ordinentur et in minimas particulas distribuantur, postea secundum harum exigentiam impositis affixarum locis et varia ratione hinc inde comprobatis, ita ut in unum et idem punctum recidant. Per distantias tamen beneficio Radij Astronomici factas, prout GEMMA tradidit et postea a multis tentatum est, negotium hoc nunquam dextre absolvetur. Impossibile enim est, per Radium, quantacunque longitudine praeditus sit, et qualicunque subtilitate divisus, etiam saepissime reiterando observationem exactas in ipso scrupulo stellarum rimari intercapedines, ut alibi per suas causas ostendemus. Ideoque ego primus Sextantes huic officio apprime idoneos et ubique veras stellarum remotiones in eodem minuto aut etiam huius aliquota parte, quotiescunque repetatur observatio, praebentes excogitavi, quibus etiam aliquot iam annis praecisa subtilitate distantias siderum inquirendo feliciter usus sum. Quin et frustra in Globum reponuntur stellae, quocunque tandem instrumento coelitus deriventur, nisi is admodum magnus sit, qualem ego sex pedum in diametro possideo, qui undiquaque orichalcicus est et divisionem graduum in singula sexagena minuta per ductum transversalem, more nobis usitato, discriminatim exhibet, absolutaque insuper rotunditate praeditus est. In hoc omnium affixarum loca instrumentis varijs ex ipso coelo deducta contignare decrevi, quorum etiam magna et praecipua pars iam antea a me in promtu habetur. Quare non est, quod dubites, me sponte mea ea, quae ad fixarum stellarum praecisam restitutionem faciunt, omni possibili diligentia moliri, ut nulla admonitione, vel eorum quae cap. 2 a me proponuntur, recapitulatione, opus fuisset.

Praeterea latitudinem Lunae PTOLEMÆI placitis quarta parte gradus unius maiorem a me adinventam, suspectam habes, eamque per eclipsium Lunarium magnitudinem et calculum illi correspondentem impugnas. Autoritatem insuper REGIOMONTANI, COPERNICI, WERNERI et aliorum insignium Mathematicorum convocas, quod illi Ptolemaicam Lunae latitudinem maximam praecise 5 partium perpetuo retinuerint, quos non dubitas magna diligentia eam coelitus ita se habere deprehendisse. Ptolemaicam insuper latitudinem omni carere vitio existimas ob loci suae observationis opportunitatem, quae Lunam iuxta Tropicum aestivum in maxima latitudine borea exigentem vertici quam proxime adunivit, semotis ob id parallaxium et refractionum impedimentis etc. De his ut tecum plenius agam, veritas ipsa postulat. Scias itaque, Lunae latitudinem maximam non temere aut sine crebra exactaque observatione a me Ptolemaica 15 scrupulis maiorem constitutam.
