But how sincerely and rightly these things are brought forth by you, let it be the judgement of others. Certainly Rothmann thinks far otherwise about my labours in accurately unravelling this business of the comets, as may be seen even from the portion of his letter recently sent to me, which I said I was sending along [with this]. Otherwise too Scultetus (as is plain from a particle of his epistle written to me not long ago, which I have also had transcribed for you) judges about this matter; and he reports that a certain Monau — a learned man in Silesia, but unknown to me — wrote to him, that he [Scultetus, or perhaps Monau himself — ambiguous; see apparatus] might be willing to urge the publication of the other volumes at my [press], although he likewise complains of the ingratitude of this age — that it is not worthy that solid truth be communicated to it in such matters. For scarcely anything is now so well said or done that it is not depraved by cavilling. But come, let us see whether our labours in this part are deservedly so disparaged by you or by anyone else — as though, on account of the evanescence of the subject of which they treat, they were useless and of no great or lasting moment. This question about the situation of comets — whether it be aetherial or elementary, and how they are generated — is neither new nor slight, but for many centuries past has been agitated long and much, with great effort and the subtlest argumentations, by the most ancient philosophers long before Aristotle (most of whom also thought more rightly than he about this matter), as is sufficiently plain even from Seneca's book which he left *On Comets*. Nor yet, down to these times, has it been thoroughly investigated what comets are and where they are procreated, because the ancients, and very many of the moderns too, undertook to resolve this more-than-Gordian knot not from sure observations through mathematical proofs [*apodixes*], but presumed to settle the whole matter merely by certain subtleties and conjectures and computational niceties — assuming as conceded most of the things which first needed to be inquired into and demonstrated, [namely] whether they were so or not. On that account I judged it worth the effort to inquire, from ratified observations, into the exact truth in this part, and to demonstrate it geometrically, lest the subtleties of the Peripatetics and others should any longer cast a deceptive gloss [*fucum facere*] upon the truth, as has been done for so many centuries now. But that this must be investigated from the parallaxes of comets, no one skilled in mathematics is ignorant; yet since those parallaxes need subtle inquiry — so much so that some error easily creeps in tacitly, unless everything be very circumspectly administered — nay, since it is even impossible to extricate certain parallaxes unless the precise reckoning of the comet's proper motion be also applied: it is in any case necessarily required that its apparent course be marked from the heavens as diligently as possible, as often as can be done through clear weather; which truly is not effected unless it be inquired what disposition it has relative to the ecliptic, in respect of longitude and latitude, and to the equator, as to right ascension and declination — and hence it be at once established what proper track it designates, and how it moves in it, and by what reckoning it varies its course day by day. For without these things one would try in vain to scrutinize the parallax. For the proper motion affects the comet's appearances more than that diversity which arises by reason of the parallaxes, if perchance they had any. These two things, therefore, must be skilfully discerned and diligently compared with one another. Hence too those things which were variously and learnedly devised by that supreme Regiomontanus and certain other moderns about investigating the parallaxes of comets — even if as regards the demonstration they are correct — yet, since they presuppose that to happen in comets which very rarely or never occurs (namely, that they are destitute of all proper motion and are revolved by no other [motion] than that universal diurnal circuit of the *primum mobile*) — are in practice itself useless and altogether superfluous. It is plain, therefore, that if that which is controverted deserves a just inquiry — namely, whether comets are aetherial or not — and this cannot be done without the investigation of the parallaxes, while the parallaxes cannot in any way be discerned without a diligent disposition as to the chief circles of the heaven and the limits of the proper track and the alteration of the diurnal motion — the consequence is that it is not to be judged a useless and superfluous labour to demonstrate, from sure observations, the longitudes, latitudes, and the tracing of the circle under which comets move, and with what tenor they complete their course, [and] how they augment it or even check it by a sure law — since without these things the other [question], which principally comes to be inquired and is called into doubt, cannot be decided. Nay, after it has been established that they dwell in the aether itself, this very greatly confirms and illustrates the business, if their course be demonstrated, after the manner of the planets, by a suitable hypothesis, and resolved into numbers. For thus it is more fully and quickly persuaded to others that there is altogether a celestial nature in them, not very alien from the properties of the other planets — except that it is not perpetual and so exalted as in the rest of the wandering stars. But it is easier to carp at and disparage the indefatigable labours of others than to imitate or even surpass them.

Further, that comets disappear like meteors, and do not always endure, proves nothing — [namely, it does not prove] that their motion and conditions are not to be diligently investigated. For although different ones are seen at a certain time and at length gradually consumed, yet others return again. Nor was there ever an age that did not behold some comets — which men have always greatly marvelled at, as something great, new, and unusual — so much so that these hairy [crinitae] stars have always moved their minds more than the rest of the heavenly bodies coeval with the world. But although comets sometimes seen disappear not so long after, nor do others return within a long time — so much so that sometimes in 20 years scarcely any has appeared — on that very account it is the more worth the effort to apply diligence in investigating their appearances while they last and are present, that thereby the controversy about the situation, motion, and nature of such phenomena, so long variously disputed, may the better be settled; since such an occasion is not always offered, as in the rest of the heavenly bodies, which on every clear night — all those that have surmounted the Horizon — it is permitted to behold and observe, if only that care drew the minds of mortals. For these reasons, therefore, and many others, it is necessary and useful to apply a most assiduous description to the situation and motion of comets. Moreover, although they might of themselves seem not worthy enough that for their sake one should drain off [exhaust] such great labours, yet there is something else why it is so expedient that this very thing be done — for the sake of more thoroughly investigating those perpetual heavenly bodies and the nature and disposition of the whole heaven — so that the same can scarcely be established from elsewhere. And therefore I, from this accurate consideration of comets in past years, have detected many things conducing to the whole astronomical matter, which are of no small moment; such as: that the heaven does not consist of any real, hard, and impervious orbs, as all Antiquity believed, and very many of the moderns still [do]; that there are no epicycles; that the Earth does not really go round [the Sun] yearly; and very many other things, of which I treat more copiously toward the end of the whole work. And thus, by this exquisite observation of the adventitious and new heavenly bodies, I prepare the way — nay, I lay the foundations — for those things which, in that whole astronomical work, I have proposed to be re-integrated and, as it were, renewed afresh [*de novo instauranda*], with the favour of divine aid, concerning the appearances and revolutions of the perennial heavenly bodies coeval with the world — at which I also labour day by day with arduous and indefatigable effort. Nay, in these books too, on the recent phenomena of the heaven, many things long vainly desired are proposed, for establishing the astronomical matter more rightly than hitherto — such as the exact restoration of the solar course, the emendation of the lunar latitude, the verification of the fixed stars, and very many others, which, on the occasion of these secondary heavenly bodies, I communicate to the cultivators of astronomy, sought out by me with no small labour and study. Thus too I would have reserved this new hypothesis to myself, until the publication of the whole astronomical work, had not that Comet of the year 1577, revolved around the Sun, invited me to admit its disclosure in that book; so many and so great things, even from this sole occasion of the comets, hitherto less perceived, have we brought into the light, and, with the favour of the Deity, we shall hereafter bring forth more abundantly. But if such writings, together with the phenomena of which they treat, are evanescent, surely they will deserve sometime to survive — at least on account of the consideration of the perennial bodies, of which they treat in many places at the same time — nor will they be so easily abolished as you forebode. And perhaps, while that song-and-dance about the *primum mobile* and the spherical rudiments and the common theories of the planets — so long and so often repeated to the point of nausea (all which find or establish nothing new and previously desired) — [the others] will remain among the skilled and the grateful. Or are you ignorant that that most lauded and most ancient astronomer Hipparchus would never have left us a canonical description of all the fixed stars, so assiduous and laborious, had he not been incited to surmount so immense a labour by a New Star arisen in his time, which doubtless disappeared a little afterwards, as Pliny testifies of him? And indeed, after him nothing similar was performed by any of mankind, some 2000 years having elapsed. For Ptolemy and his successors acquiesced in the Hipparchian notation, taking account at least of the advancement [precession] of the whole eighth sphere. And therefore Regiomontanus calls this catalogue [*abacum*] of the fixed stars a work more divine than human, and a treasure not to be profaned or entrusted to the common crowd. Nor does he value it without reason. Remember too what great things Archimedes left us, even on the occasion of the most worthless sands, at the urging of Gelon, king of the Sicilians. Thus too on other occasions a cause has often been offered to men, from the smallest and not-long-enduring things, of building up and investigating things far greater and more stable — about which it is now not fitting to say more. For I see that I have already been too [lengthy] in writing back, and have transgressed not a little the laws of a letter; which lingering may you take in good and fair part, and ascribe it to the fact that I confer with you on this subject with a willing mind. Farewell — and take care that I shortly have that book of Master Camerarius on this same Comet, published (I think) at Frankfurt-on-the-Oder. I should also wish to inspect the writing of Simon van der Eycke [*Simonis a Quercu*] on the squaring of the circle. For it has not yet been brought to me. And if you procure it for me along [with the other], you will do me a most welcome service.

Again, fare you most happily, and write back before the winter's ice.
Given at Uraniborg, amid very many other occupations, with a hurrying pen, [the letter] however long-winded, on the 4th of November, the year [15]88.

But if your most illustrious Prince has by now sent to Rostock any paper suited to my workshop, take care that I receive it as quickly as possible, kept safe from the harm of winter and of rains. I also ask most affectionately that you be willing, now, straightaway, to send to me some craftsman who is excellently skilled in the art of engraving in wood. For I have need of such a man through the winter season, and perhaps even through the whole summer, on account of various figures — both of instruments and of other designs — to be engraved in wood, which are afterwards to be printed. If, therefore, you procure such a man in good time and send him here at the first opportunity, you will do a thing greatly welcome to me and befitting our friendship. As to his wages, once he has arrived, we shall easily agree between ourselves. Whatever you lay out for his travelling expenses, I shall repay.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (Hendrik Brucaeus, 1530/31–1593), professor of mathematics and medicine at the University of Rostock, an older scholar Tycho had known from his Rostock years; the addressee of several of Tycho's astronomical letters. The whole letter is a point-by-point reply to a (lost) letter of Brucaeus that critiqued the *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (the comet book, here called the second book of the *Aetherea Phaenomena*).
- **The work in scope.** *liber meus secundus Aethereorum Phaenomenωn* / *liber hic de Cometa Anni 77* = Tycho's ***De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis, liber secundus*** (1588), the treatise on the comet of 1577, in which he first published his geo-heliocentric world-system. The Greek genitive plural *Phaenomenωn* is written with a Greek omega (ω); kept as printed in the Source block. **In-letter dating crux flagged, not resolved:** Tycho states that although the book bears an imprint of **1588**, it was in fact printed at his Uraniborg press in **1587** and *deliberately* post-dated by one year "that on account of its novelty it might be the more welcome." Reported verbatim; not reconciled with the title-page date.
- **The priority dispute (the unnamed "brazen brow").** *Quidam nimis perfrictae frontis … publico scripto, Argentinae hoc anno edito* — the man Tycho refuses to name is **Nicolaus Reymers Bär ("Ursus", Raimarus Ursus, c. 1551–1600)**, whose *Fundamentum astronomicum* (Strasbourg [*Argentina*], 1588) published a world-system Tycho regarded as plagiarized from his own, learned during Ursus's days in 1584 in the retinue of **Erik Lange** (*Erico Lange*, Danish nobleman and alchemist) at Uraniborg. This is the opening salvo of the long Tycho–Ursus plagiarism quarrel. Tycho's diagnostic that the rival "depicts and feigns the Martian orb as totally encircling the Solar orb" (whereas in Tycho's own system Mars's orbit intersects but does not wholly enclose the Sun's path) is his technical proof that Ursus did not understand the system he claimed.
- **Persons named.** *Caspar Peucer* = **Caspar Peucer** (1525–1602), Wittenberg physician-astronomer and son-in-law of Melanchthon; *Henricus Ranzovius* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), Statthalter of Holstein, learned patron; *Christophorus Rothmannus* = **Christoph Rothmann**, mathematician to Landgrave Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel (*Illustriss. Princeps Gulielmus Hassiae Landgravius* = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel**); *Gemma Frisius* = **Gemma Frisius** (1508–1555), author of the tract on the *radius astronomicus* (cross-staff); *Regiomontanus* = **Johannes Regiomontanus** (1436–1476) and his pupil *Bernhardus Gualterus* = **Bernhard Walther** (1430–1504) of Nuremberg; *Wernerus* = **Johann Werner** (1468–1522); *Maestlinus* = **Michael Maestlin** (1550–1631); *Witichius* = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586), the Breslau mathematician who visited Uraniborg; *Lycosthenes* = **Conrad Lycosthenes** (1518–1561), compiler of *Prodigiorum ac ostentorum chronicon* (*de Ostentis*); *Cornelius Gemma* (1535–1578); *Thaddaeus* = **Thaddaeus Hagecius / Tadeáš Hájek** (1525–1600), the Prague imperial physician-astronomer; *Erastus* = **Thomas Erastus** (1524–1583), Aristotelian physician-philosopher; *Hieronymus Caroanus* = **Girolamo Cardano** (1501–1576), here cited for *De rerum varietate*; *Scultetus* = **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (1540–1614) of Görlitz; *Monavus* = **Jacob Monau** (1546–1603) of Breslau (Silesia); *M. Camerarius* = probably **Joachim Camerarius the Younger** (or a Camerarius work on the 1577 comet, said to be printed at Frankfurt-on-the-Oder); *Simon a Quercu* = **Simon van der Eycke** (Simon van der Eyck/à Quercu), known for a (flawed) quadrature-of-the-circle tract; *Hipparchus*, *Ptolemaeus*, *Archimedes*, *Gelon* (king of Syracuse), *Pliny*, *Seneca*, *Aristotle*, the *Epicurei*, and **Paracelsus** (*Paracelsista*) appear as authorities/allusions.
- **Scultetus–Monau clause (syntactic crux, flagged).** *Aliter etiam SCULTETUS … de hac re iudicat, unâque MONAVUM quendam … ad se scripsisse refert, ut aliorum tomorum apud me editionem urgere velit.* The subject of *refert* ("reports") is **Scultetus**, and *ad se scripsisse* means **Monau wrote to Scultetus** (*se* = Scultetus). The purpose clause *ut … urgere velit* ("that he might be willing to urge the publication of the other volumes at my press") has a **genuinely ambiguous subject**: grammatically it can be **Scultetus** (whom Monau is asking to press Tycho to publish further volumes) or **Monau** himself (writing that *he* wishes to urge it). The translation adopts the Scultetus reading but flags the alternative inline; the *licet unâ conqueratur* ("although he likewise complains") subject is correspondingly ambiguous. Low impact on the overall sense (either way, the point is that learned men outside Tycho's circle are urging continued publication and lamenting the age's ingratitude).
- **Places.** *Argentina* = **Strasbourg**; *Rostochium* = **Rostock**; *Uraniburgum* = **Uraniborg** (on Hven); *Francofurtum ad Oderam* = **Frankfurt-on-the-Oder**; *Alexandria* (Ptolemy's observing site).
- **Astronomy — technical terms (editorial glossary applied).** *Hypothesis / Hypotyposis* → "hypothesis / sketch"; *neoterica Hypothesis* → "novel hypothesis"; *parallaxis* → **parallax** (Tycho notes Copernicus's synonym *commutatio*); *refractio* → **refraction**; *eccentricitas / Apogeum* → **eccentricity / apogee**; *prostaphaereses* (Greek-omega *prostaphaereseωn*) → **prosthaphaereses** (kept by this chapter's convention; here the additive/subtractive solar equations tabulated from the eccentricity); *declinatio / ascensio recta* → **declination / right ascension**; *longitudo / latitudo* → **longitude / latitude**; *quadraturae / novilunia / plenilunia* → **quadratures / new moons / full moons**; *nodus*, *caput Draconis* → **node**, **Head of the Dragon** (the ascending node); *eclipsis Lunaris / digitus* → **lunar eclipse / digit** (1/12 of the disc obscured); *Ecliptica / Aequator / meridianus / Horizon / vertex* → **ecliptic / equator / meridian / horizon / vertex (zenith)**; *signa, in consequentia / antecedentia* → "in the order / against the order of the signs"; *primum mobile* → kept; *octava sphaera* → **eighth sphere**. **No real orbs / no epicycles / Earth does not move yearly** — the three programmatic theses Tycho lists are rendered literally.
- **Astronomy — instruments (editorial glossary).** *Radius Astronomicus* → **cross-staff (radius astronomicus)** (Gemma's instrument, which Tycho judges inadequate to second-of-arc precision); *Sextantes* → **sextants** (Tycho claims to be their first deviser for stellar distances); *globus … sex pedum in diametro … orichalcicus … per ductum transversalem* → his six-foot brass **globe** with **transversal** (diagonal-dot) graduation; *Parallaticum instrumentum / Regulae* → Ptolemy's **parallactic instrument / [parallactic] rules** (the *triquetrum*); *pinnula/foramina* → sights/apertures.
- **Units & quantities.** *gradus* = **degree**; *minutum / scrupulum (primum)* = **(arc-)minute / first-minute**. **Disclosed deviation (flagged):** at *exactas in ipso scrupulo stellarum rimari intercapedines* the editorial glossary's default for *scrupulum* would be "arc-minute," but the rendering "to the very second" reads *in ipso scrupulo* as **arc-second**. This is an interpretive choice, not certain: it is defended by the immediately following contrast (*in eodem minuto aut etiam huius aliquota parte*, "within the same minute, or even an aliquot part of it"), where the sextant is credited with the finer precision the cross-staff lacks — implying the cross-staff fails at a unit *below* the minute. Bare *scrupulum* more usually = arc-minute, so the reading is disclosed here rather than asserted silently. Tycho's explicit "second" elsewhere (*in quinis vel denis secundis*) = arc-second / second of time. **Note also (low):** *unum vel alterum ad summum minutum … nullatenus desiderari* (lunar-latitude conclusion) = "one minute, or at most two [arc-minutes]," not "a minute or at most a second" — *alterum [minutum]* is "a second MINUTE" (i.e., one or two), with *ad summum* = "at most"; the parallel *uno vel altero scrupulo maiorem* ("greater by one or another minute") earlier confirms the unit is the arc-minute throughout. *semidiameter Terrae* = **earth-semidiameter** (Tycho's distance unit); *milliaria Germanica* = **German miles** (he takes 860 per earth-semidiameter). The comet-distance computation (right triangle ABC: angle B = 90°, angle CAB = 60°, CA = 1142 e.r. per Copernicus → BC = CE = 988, EA = 154 e.r. ≈ 132,440 German miles; Moon's perigee ≈ 52 e.r.) is reproduced with its figures intact, including Tycho's note of the **printer's transposition error 145 for 154 on p. 297**.
- **Greek and Latin idioms.** *nodum in scirpo quaerere* ("to seek a knot in a bulrush") — proverbial for inventing a difficulty where none exists; rendered with a literal gloss. *sub incudem revocare* ("to recall to the anvil") — to subject to renewed scrutiny. *fucum facere* ("to apply rouge / a deceptive gloss") — to deceive. *nodum plus quam Gordium* — "a more-than-Gordian knot." *apodixes* (Greek *ἀπόδειξις*, here Latinized *apodixes Mathematicas*) — rigorous mathematical proofs. *in vaporario ex chartis depromta* ("drawn from papers in a steam-room") — Tycho's barb that Brucaeus theorizes from the page, not the sky. *omnibus suis numeris absoluta* — "complete in all its parts/numbers," the Ciceronian idiom for perfection. *inter segestria … iacentem* — *segestrium/segestre* properly = a coarse mat, wrapping, or covering (cf. *segestria* as protective coverings); here it denotes the loose wrappings or scrap coverings among which a discarded sketch lay. Rendered "among the waste wrappings"; the looser sense "rubbish/scrap papers" is the drift, but the specific Latin word is wrappings/coverings, not "papers," and is noted here rather than smoothed.
- **Astronomical-programme vocabulary.** *instauratio / restitutio / redintegratio / de novo instauranda Astronomia* — Tycho's signature programme, rendered consistently as **restoration / renewal / re-integration** of astronomy.
- **The Wittich comet "anno 8" crux (flagged).** The text reads *"in illo Cometa, qui anno 8 apparuit, quo tempore [Wittich] mecum fuit."* Wittich was at Uraniborg in **1580**, and the comet he observed there with Tycho was the comet of **1580**; the printed *"anno 8"* is therefore an abbreviation/compositor's truncation, most plausibly for **'8[0]** (1580). The translation renders it "**the year [15]8[0]**" as a bracketed editorial completion of the printed "8"; **this is a genuine crux** — the printed source gives only "8," and the intended year is supplied editorially. 1580 is by far the most defensible reading (Wittich was at Uraniborg in 1580 and the comet he there observed with Tycho was the comet of 1580; Dreyer's text reads *anno 80*), but the printed source substantiates only "8." Flagged rather than silently fixed. **Crux: anno-8 comet year (printed "8"; read 1580).**
- **Negation/logic check.** The dense argumentative clauses (the eclipse-latitude reasoning; the "neither new nor slight" double negative; *non … nisi …* constructions in the parallax-method passage; *nullatenus desiderari* = "is in no way wanting," i.e. nothing more than *unum vel alterum ad summum minutum* (one or at most two arc-minutes) is lacking from the precision claimed) were each counted and reproduced with their exact polarity; no negation added or dropped. Tycho's hedges (*necdum tuto affirmârim*, *nihil certi pronunciare volo antequam … expendero*, *si quae alia subest … inaequalitas*) are preserved as hedges, not sharpened.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 4. Novembris Anno 88* = **4 November 1588**, Old Style (Denmark used the Julian calendar). Matches the catalogue label; no discrepancy. The closing *ante brumalem glaciem* ("before the winter's ice") is a seasonal, not calendar, marker. *brumalem* from *bruma* (winter solstice).
- **Edition of record / witness.** Edition: *Tychonis Brahei et ad eum doctorum virorum epistolae ab anno 1588* (= Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VII, *Epistolae*). MS witness as given: **A = Vienna, ÖNB, cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66** (a copy/*Afskrift*).
- **What it is.** The recovered text is the opening of the postscript-like close of a letter from Tycho to Heinrich Brucaeus, professor of medicine and mathematics at Rostock — the surviving published text picks up only after this point, mid-request about a book by Camerarius.
- **The Prince.** "Princeps vester illustrissimus" is almost certainly Duke Ulrich III of Mecklenburg, sovereign of Rostock; Dreyer records that in December 1587 Tycho had already asked, via Heinrich Below, for Ulrich's help securing paper from the ducal paper mills, to be forwarded through Brucaeus [Dreyer, *Tycho Brahe* (1890)]. This letter shows the arrangement still running a year later.
- **The engraver.** Tycho is recruiting a woodcut engraver for his Uraniborg press ("meæ officinæ"), needed specifically to cut figures of instruments and other designs for printing — plausibly connected to the instrument plates later published in the *Astronomiae Instauratae Mechanica* (1598). Christianson confirms Tycho kept a substantial stock of woodcut printing blocks alongside his presses [Christianson, *On Tycho's Island* (2000)].
- **Financial detail.** Tycho offers to negotiate wages once the craftsman arrives and to reimburse travel costs — ordinary workshop-recruitment business, otherwise undocumented for this specific hire.
- **Correction.** Two Latin transcription errors corrected against TBOO VII: p.151 restores the dropped numeral "15" before "scrupulis" (Dreyer: "a me Ptolemaica 15 scrupulis maiorem constitutam"), with the English hedge "[some] minutes" replaced by "15 minutes" accordingly; p.160 restores the dropped trailing digit in "anno 80" (Dreyer: "qui anno 80 apparuit", i.e. the comet of 1580), with the English's hedged "[15]8[0] (printed \"8\"; see apparatus)" simplified to "[15]80" per the letter's ordinary year convention.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated visually against all 20 Dreyer page images (TBOO VII pp.146-165; the letter itself runs pp.147-164). Opening line ('Rupisti tandem altum illud silentium...') and closing lines (postscript through 'restituam', dateline 'Uraniburgi... die 4. Novembris Anno 88') match Dreyer exactly. Every proper name checked against the page images (Peucer, Rantzau, Erik Lange, Rothmann, Wilhelm Landgrave of Hesse, Scultetus, Monau, Maestlin, Wittich, Cardano/Hieronymus Caroanus, Cornelius Gemma, Thaddaeus, Erastus, Lycosthenes, Seneca, Hipparchus, Pliny, Archimedes, Gelon, Camerarius, Simon a Quercu, Regiomontanus, Copernicus, Werner, Bernhard Walther, Gemma Frisius) is correct. Every number/date/sum checked is correct: 1142, 988, 154 (with Dreyer's own noted printer's misprint '145'), 860 German miles, 132440 miles, 173 semidiameters on 9 November, 60-degree/43:60 geometry, the six-foot brass globe, Ptolemy's 5-degree maximum lunar latitude, the 21-minute/4-degree Rothmann figures, the 12-degree/three-minute eclipse-node figures, the five-scrupule comet-circle tolerance, and the 297/154/145 printer's-erratum passage all agree with Dreyer. Two text errors were found: our published the transcribed original drops a digit in two places relative to Dreyer's print ('15 scrupulis' → 'scrupulis'; 'anno 80' → 'anno 8'). In both cases the translator noticed the gap and handled it responsibly with bracketed apparatus notes rather than fabricating or silently asserting a wrong figure, so the English sense is not materially distorted — but per the audit rule any text error caps the grade at C regardless of how well the translator compensated.

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original silently drops the numeral '15' before 'scrupulis' that Dreyer prints; the translator noticed the gap and covered it with a bracketed '[some]' rather than the actual figure (which does recur correctly one sentence later in both texts). Dreyer prints: *Scias itaque, Lunae latitudinem maximam non temere aut sine crebra exactaque observatione a me Ptolemaica 15 scrupulis maiorem constitutam. (TBOO VII p.151)*.
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original drops the trailing '0' of '80' (the comet of 1580, when Wittich was with Tycho); the translator correctly reconstructed the year and flagged it with a bracketed apparatus note rather than silently asserting a wrong or nonsensical date. Dreyer prints: *eo quod e meis observationibus vel in illo Cometa, qui anno 80 apparuit, quo tempore mecum fuit (TBOO VII p.160)*.

**Repaired.** Both text errors were collated directly against Dreyer's page images (TBOO VII pp.151 and 160, read via the letter's Dreyer extract) and confirmed exactly as the audit described: a dropped "15" before "scrupulis" and a dropped trailing "0" in "anno 80". Both corrections are further corroborated by internal parallels elsewhere in the same letter (the recurring "15 scrupulis"/"15 minutes" pair, and the letter's consistent "[15]NN" convention for two-digit years). No remaining crux; nothing else in the letter was touched.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE
S. D.

EX literis tuis mihi non ita dudum perscriptis intellexi, nobilissime et eruditissime Domine HENRICE RANZOVI, te Sciotericum illud horizontale, quod tibi confieri feci, unâ cum fasciculis literarum adiunctis atque organo illo, quo nostrae hypotheses revolutionum coelestium commodius explicantur, accepisse, eaque omnia tibi placuisse, plurimum tibi congratulor. Quantum vero ad lineae meridianae, quam desideras, ordinationem attinet, eam peculiari quadam ratione e stellis circumpolaribus exacte derivare soleo, ut azimutha instrumentorum meorum in ipso scrupulo recte constent (quod alias difficulter fit). Verum in Scioterico isto tanta praecisio non est necessaria, sufficit itaque ad unum vel alterum recte elaboratum compassum lineam horae duodecimae meridiano coelesti correspondentem statuere atque ita leviter firmare laminam. Deinde instante vere, ubi Sol altior fuerit, videndum diligenter, ut extremitas umbrae in certa aliqua hora antemeridiana eiusdem sit a centro longitudinis cum aliqua alia aequaliter post meridiem remota, quod circa ipsum aequinoctium commodius praestatur; tunc enim extremitas umbrae percurrit transversam rectam, quae Aequatorem five initia ♈ et ♎ repraesentat, estque ea linea meridiei orthogonalis. Quare si hora 9a 8a 7a matutina et 3a 4a 5a vespertina extremitas umbrae eodem modo illi lineae adhaeret, recte dispositum est Sciotericum; sin minus, ita hinc inde componendum, donec omnia rite quadrent; interea vero ut in aequilibrio Horizontis continue permaneat, diligenter est cavendum. Potes etiam uti, si lubet, vulgari illa ratione inquirendi lineam meridiei per erectum Gnomonem a plano quodam horizontali, cui circumductis aliquot circulis videre, in quibus locis ante et post meridiem eos umbrae extremitas transeat, perque harum intersectionum medietatem ad centrum lineam ducere, quae meridiem per umbram Gnomonis monstrabit, unde etiam Sciotericum eodem instanti ita rectificari potest, ut etiam unâ horam 12am Gnomon eius indicet; sed haec sunt vulgaria.

Accepi interim et alias semel atque iterum a te literas unâque pallam papyri impressoriae meae officinae admodum idoneam et quodam etiam tempore clarissimi et doctissimi viri GEORGIJ BRAUN, Decani Coloniensis, quartam partem Theatri urbium, et praeterea delineationem exequiarum ac sepulturae regiae Hamburgi per te aeneis figuris procuratam; pro quibus omnibus plurimas et ingentes habeo gratias, quod si referendi occasio oblata unquam fuerit, dabo operam, ut intelligas me omni gratitudine et officio tibi futurum addictissimum. Papyrus autem impressoria ultimo missa est quidem satis apta meo operi, sed aliquanto maiuscula est, ut videre licet ex utroque adiuncto quaternione, nec tamen refert paululum maiorem esse, ac si minor foret.

De opere Theatrico civitatum BRAUNIJ, scias illud admodum mihi placere, et praeclare te de Patria nostra meritum iudico, quod urbium nostratium delineationem illi procurâris. Video etiam Huenulam nostram non neglectam, quam tua opera procul dubio obtinuit, quod mihi pergratum est. Reliquos tres tomos istius operis nondum vidi, neque enim quod sciam Bibliopolae nostri eos hactenus attulerunt. Si constaret mihi, ubi venales forent, et eos coëmerem, quam primum vero per otium licuerit, data commoditate ipsi BRAUNIO scribam.

Sculptorem sive incisorem talem, qui in aere vel etiam buxo figuras diligenter ad impressionem adornare norit, admodum expeterem. Constitui enim primo quoque tempore omnia instrumenta mea Astronomica competenter delineata unâ cum declaratione fabricae et usus, additis quibusdam etiam alijs huc pertinentibus, in primo libro operis Astronomiae instauratione comprehendenda publicare. Si itaque aliquem eiuscemodi artificem, qui perfecte haec ipsa effingere et postea vel cupro aut buxo incidere norit, tuo consilio et auxilio obtinuero, nihil mihi acceptius evenire poterit. Mercedem ei libenter solvam, quantam alibi promereri poterit, et per totam aestatem, quod agat, illi procuraturus sum.

Fecisti in aliquibus etiam nuper ad me datis literis mentionem cuiusdam Dithmarsi nomine et re Ursini unâque misisti extractum literarum clarissimi et doctissimi D. GEORGIJ ROLLENHAGIJ simul cum libro istius impudentis Plagiarij quem tamen antea aliunde habueram. Ut vero tam tu quam ROLLENHAGIUS recte suspicamini istum hypothesium innovationem, quam sibi inverecunde attribuit, a me suffuratum esse, id ita revera se habet: Nam licet is nunquam mihi inservierit vel domesticus fuerit, ut vos forte existimatis, tamen cum ante quadriennium iam elapsum cum nobilissimo et doctissimo viro ERICO LANGIO de Engelstholm, tibi bene cognito, cui tunc inserviebat, 14 circiter dies hîc fuisset, interea dum ego cum ERICO amico meo singulari et quibusdam alijs unâ hic praesentibus nobilibus hilarius conversor, iste suffurator mihi plurima ex ijs, quae magno labore et diligentia conquisita habui, clam descripsit et instrumentorum omnium, quae tunc in promptu erant, formam ac dispositionem delineavit plurimaque alia, quae conquirere potuit, subtraxit, similans tamen se nihil horum agere, imo haec non curare quidem sed vili pendere. Postquam tamen hanc eius vafriciem suboluissem, alium quendam subornavi, qui magnam eorum partem, quae abstulerat, reciperet, quae adhuc praesto habeo. Video nunc illum plura quam recuperâram designasse vel etiam memoria retinuisse. Nam innovatio haec hypothesium nemini unquam ante me, quod sciam, in mentem venit, occasionem vero huius inventi ex ijs, quae nuper ad D. PEUCERUM scripsi, satis intelliges. Quod autem hanc hypothesin tunc mihi surripuerit, hinc satis evidenter colligo: Cum enim praedicto ERICO amico meo, sciscitanti a me rationem diversitatis apparentiarum et retrogradationum Planetarum, eam tam secundum veterem Ptolemaicam quam Copernianam ratiocinationem illi in mensa depictam exposuissem, subiunxi adhuc alia quadam assumptione idem effici posse, et absurda quaedam in his prioribus aperui, ille vero (ut est ingenio admodum docili et sciendi cupido) hanc formam a me sibi etiam ostendi petijt, quod cum astante et aspiciente isto Dithmarso servo suo me invite facturum animadverteret (indicâram enim illi antea me e moribus et physiognomia hominis perspexisse quinam esset) ille hoc foras amandato, ut aliud quid ageret, id quod voluit a me obtinuit, nostrasque etiam hypotheses generaliter et breviter indicatas ipsi delineavi, quas tamen mox expunxi. At Dithmarsus iste, cum aliquid secreti tractari persentisceret, ut erat nasutulus, eo diligentius inquirere, an aliquid eiuscemodi reperire posset et furtim subtrahere, itaque inter chartas meas in fenestra repositas abiectam quandam delineationem huius dispositionis motuum coelestium adinvenit, quae tamen, incuria nescio qua, ita erat depicta, ut orbis Martius Solarem totaliter ambiret, cumque id non recte se haberet, tanquam inepta et dissonans cassata atque neglecta est, is tamen hanc ipsam pro vera et congrua arripiens, aut tacite postea delineavit, vel memoria conservavit, quam pro sua inventione impudenti mendacio nunc venditat, seque eam ante triennium in angulo quodam Regni Poloniae (ubi procul dubio nunquam fuerat) excogitasse finxit, imo et illustrissimo Principi Landtgravio eam tanquam a se excogitatam dedicare non erubescit; tanta est hominis vel potius ursi istius inverecunda arrogantia. Verum dum falsam, quam hîc reperit, designationem eodem modo imitatur et eandem sequitur magnitudinem (erat enim et ea erronea delineatio, quam hîc vidit, in integro folio patenti depicta) satis ipsemet furtum suum propalat, et haec ipsa, quae iactitat, revera se non intelligere, multo minus, ut eorum autor et inventor sit, non obscuris indicijs prodit. Sic plurima alia, imo praecipua et fere omnia, quae in isto libro pro suis venditat, etsi non totaliter a me profecta sint, tamen ab alijs Mathematicis sive scientibus illis sive clam habuit, adeo ut nihil fere aliud agat in toto isto libello, quam ut alienis se ornet plumis, nimis perfricta fronte aliorum inventa et labores sibi attribuendo, eaque quae nunquam didicit vel praestare potest, promittendo. Sed indignus est iste inveterator, de quo plura scribam, et forte haec ipsa nimia sunt; non potui tamen intermittere, quin tibi significarem, quî factum sit, ut iste hypotheses nostras acceperit easque prorsus publicârit, ut non solum tu, sed etiam ROLLENHAGIUS certo sciretis, merum furtum esse eius in hac hypothesi ostentationem; et recte quidem asseveras URSUM istum, licet meos labores surripuerit, tamen eum fundamentaliter omnia non intellexisse, ut patet vel ex falsa illa quam proponit delineatione, dum proportionem orbis Martij ad Solarem turpiter ignorat. Et ROLLENHAGIUS candide atque prudenter indicat ea, quae a fugitivo aliquo ministro a me abalienata et foras eliminata sunt, mihi indicanda, ut vero inventori postliminio restituantur. Intelligo enim ipsum statim ex URSI istius scripto perspexisse hanc, quam pro sua venditat, inventionem a me prodijsse, siquidem antea ad te perscripserat, sibi ante biennium a fugitivo quodam meo ministro hanc hypothesin communicatam esse. Neque tamen satis inde colligere possum, an hunc ipsum URSUM notet, putans forte illum aliquando mihi inservijsse, an vero alium quendam, qui hinc clam e mea domo decesserit, existimet. Peto itaque peramanter, ut, quam primum detur occasio ad illum scribendi, velis expiscari, quisnam et quo nomine fuerit fugitivus ille, de quo scribit, minister meus, cuius opera huius hypotheseos formam adeptus est. Averem enim scire, an hîc ipsus fuerit URSUS vel alius quispiam; ego etenim neminem scio ex omnibus studiosis, qui mihi hactenus in Astronomicis rebus inservierunt, me inscio vel invito clam hinc discessisse. Nec satis cogitare possum, quisnam ille fuerit fugitivus, cuius semel atque iterum ROLLENHAGIUS mentionem facit. Eum itaque si is mihi indicârit, rem pergratam fecerit. Video hunc ROLLENHAGIUM non saltem excellenter eruditum et iudicio gravi praepollentem, sed etiam virum integrum et syncerum benevoleque de aliorum studijs sentientem; quare data aliqua occasione cum illo per literas amicitiam contrahere non intermittam, quod si is praevenerit, eo ipso satis oportunitatis erit exhibitum. Sed haec prolixius quam volebam; tuum erit hanc immorationem, quam iusta quaerela extorsit, candide interpretari. Si literas a Doctore PEUCERO mihi inscriptas receperis, rogo, ut eas inprimis huc mittere non gravari velis. Vale, vir nobilissime et praeclarissime, deque artibus eruditis bene mereri, uti facis, tibique hac ratione laudem nunquam intermorituram comparare ne intermitte.

Iterum quam felicissime et diutissime vive valeque.
Datae Uraniburgi, die 21 Decembris, Anno 1588.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE**
**sends greeting.**

From your letter written to me not so long ago, most noble and most learned Master Henrik Rantzau, I learned that you have received that horizontal sundial which I had made for you, together with the bundles of letters enclosed with it and that instrument by which our hypotheses of the celestial revolutions are more conveniently set out; and that all these have pleased you — on which I most heartily congratulate you. As regards the setting-out of the meridian line that you wish for: I am accustomed to derive it exactly, by a certain peculiar method, from the circumpolar stars, so that the azimuths of my instruments may stand correct to the very [arc-]scruple (which is otherwise done with difficulty). But in that sundial such precision is not necessary; it is therefore enough, with one or another well-worked compass, to set the line of the twelfth hour answering to the celestial meridian, and so to fix the plate lightly. Then, as spring comes on, when the Sun shall be higher, one must look carefully that the tip of the shadow at some certain forenoon hour be at the same distance from the centre as another [hour] equally far past noon — which is more conveniently done about the equinox itself; for then the tip of the shadow runs along a transverse straight line, which represents the Equator, that is [sive], the beginnings of ♈ Aries and ♎ Libra, and that line is orthogonal to the meridian. Therefore, if at the 9th, 8th, [and] 7th morning hour, and the 3rd, 4th, [and] 5th evening hour, the tip of the shadow clings in the same way to that line, the sundial is rightly disposed; if not, it must be adjusted this way and that until everything squares duly; and meanwhile it must be carefully seen to that it remain continually in the level of the Horizon. You may also use, if you please, that common method of finding the meridian line by an erected gnomon on some horizontal plane, around which some circles are drawn, to see at what places before and after noon the tip of the shadow crosses them, and through the midpoint of these intersections to draw a line to the centre, which will show the meridian by the gnomon's shadow; from which the sundial too can at the same instant be so rectified that its gnomon may likewise indicate the 12th hour — but these are common matters.

Meanwhile I have received from you yet other letters, once and again, and together a ball of printing-paper very well suited to my workshop, and at one time also, from that most distinguished and most learned man Georg Braun, Dean of Cologne, the fourth part of the *Theatre of Cities*, and besides a delineation of the royal obsequies and burial at Hamburg, procured by you in copper figures; for all of which I give the most and the greatest thanks, [and] should the occasion of repaying ever offer itself, I shall take pains that you may understand me to be in the future most devoted to you in all gratitude and service. The printing-paper last sent is indeed fairly suited to my work, but it is somewhat too large, as may be seen from each of the two enclosed quaternions; yet it does not matter that it be a little larger, [more] than if it were smaller.

As to Braun's *Theatrical* work of cities, know that it pleases me greatly, and I judge that you have deserved excellently of our fatherland in that you procured for him the delineation of our [home] cities. I see too that our little Hven [Huenula] has not been neglected, which it doubtless obtained through your effort — which is most welcome to me. The remaining three volumes of that work I have not yet seen, for so far as I know our booksellers have not hitherto brought them in. If it were clear to me where they are for sale, I would buy them up; and as soon as leisure shall allow, given the opportunity, I shall write to Braun himself.

Such a carver or engraver as knows how to dress figures carefully for printing, in copper or even in boxwood, I should very much desire. For I have resolved, at the very first opportunity, to publish all my astronomical instruments suitably delineated, together with a declaration of their construction and use, with certain other matters pertaining hereto added, in the first book of the work to be comprised under [the title of] the Restoration of Astronomy. If therefore by your counsel and help I shall obtain some craftsman of that kind, who knows how to portray these very things perfectly and afterwards to engrave them in copper or boxwood, nothing more welcome could befall me. I will gladly pay him a wage, as much as he could earn elsewhere, and through the whole summer I will provide him with what he is to do.

You made mention, too, in some letters lately sent to me, of a certain man, Dithmarsian by name and Ursine in fact, and together you sent an extract of the letter of that most distinguished and most learned Master Georg Rollenhagen, along with the book of that shameless plagiarist — which, however, I had previously had from another quarter. As to your supposing rightly, both you and Rollenhagen, that this innovation of hypotheses, which he shamelessly attributes to himself, was filched from me — that is in truth so. For although he never served me nor was a member of my household, as you perhaps suppose, yet, when four years ago — now already past — he had been here about fourteen days with that most noble and most learned man Erik Lange of Engelstholm, well known to you, whom he then served, in the meantime, while I was conversing rather merrily with Erik my singular friend and certain other nobles present here together, that filcher secretly copied out for himself very many of those things which I had gathered with great labour and diligence, and delineated the form and disposition of all the instruments that were then to hand, and abstracted very many other things that he was able to gather — yet feigning that he was doing none of these things, nay, that he did not even care about them but held them cheap. Yet after I had got wind of this cunning of his, I suborned a certain other [man] to recover a great part of those things which he had carried off, which I still have ready at hand. I now see that he had drawn out, or even kept in memory, more than I had recovered. For this innovation of hypotheses never came into the mind of anyone before me, so far as I know; and the occasion of this discovery you will sufficiently understand from those things which I lately wrote to Master Peucer. But that he then stole this hypothesis from me, I gather from this evidence clearly enough: For when, to the aforesaid Erik my friend — who was inquiring of me the reason for the diversity of the appearances and retrogradations of the planets — I had set it forth to him, depicted on the table both according to the old Ptolemaic and the Copernican reasoning, I added that the same could moreover be effected by a certain other assumption, and disclosed certain absurdities in those earlier [systems]; and he (being of a very teachable disposition and eager to know) asked me to show this form to him too. And when he perceived that I would do this reluctantly while that Dithmarsian, his servant, stood by and looked on (for I had earlier indicated to him that I had seen through, from the man's manners and physiognomy, what sort he was), he, having dispatched the man outside to do something else, obtained from me what he wished; and I delineated for him our hypotheses too, indicated generally and briefly, which however I soon erased. But that Dithmarsian, when he sensed that something secret was being treated of — being a nosy little fellow [nasutulus] as he was — searched the more diligently whether he could find anything of the sort and stealthily abstract it; and so, among my papers laid by in the window, he came upon a certain cast-off delineation of this disposition of the celestial motions — which, however, by some carelessness, was so drawn that the orb of Mars wholly encircled that of the Sun, and since that was not correct, it was annulled and discarded as inept and discordant. He, however, seizing this very one as true and fitting, either silently delineated it afterwards or kept it in memory; and this he now hawks, with shameless lying, as his own invention, and has feigned that he devised it three years ago in some corner of the Kingdom of Poland (where doubtless he had never been) — nay, he does not even blush to dedicate it to the Most Illustrious Prince the Landgrave as though devised by himself: so great is the shameless arrogance of the man, or rather of that bear [ursus]. But while he imitates in the same way the false design which he found here, and follows the same magnitude (for that erroneous delineation too, which he saw here, was drawn on a whole open folio sheet), he sufficiently betrays his own theft, and by no obscure tokens discloses that these very things which he vaunts he does not in truth understand, much less that he is the author and discoverer of them. Thus very many other things — nay, the chief and almost all that he hawks as his own in that book — though they were not wholly *derived* [profecta] from me, he yet had from other mathematicians, whether with those men's knowledge or secretly; so that he does almost nothing else in that whole little book than deck himself in others' feathers, attributing to himself, with too brazen a brow, others' inventions and labours, and promising those things which he never learned nor can perform. But that inveterate [rascal] is unworthy [of more], of whom I will write more [another time], and perhaps even these things are too much; yet I could not forbear to make known to you how it came about that he got hold of our hypotheses and published them outright — so that not only you, but Rollenhagen too, might know for certain that his parading of this hypothesis is sheer theft. And you rightly assert that this Ursus, although he stole my labours, nevertheless did not fundamentally understand the whole, as is plain even from that false delineation which he proposes, while he basely is ignorant of the proportion of the orb of Mars to that of the Sun. And Rollenhagen candidly and prudently indicates that those things which were alienated from me by some fugitive servant and carried off abroad ought to be made known to me, that they may by right of return [postliminio] be restored to their true discoverer. For I understand that he at once perceived, from that Ursus's writing, that this invention which he hawks as his own had issued from me — seeing that he had previously written to you that this hypothesis had been communicated to him two years ago by some fugitive servant of mine. Yet I cannot sufficiently gather from this whether he means this very Ursus, thinking perhaps that he once served me, or whether he supposes some other [man] who departed secretly from my house here. I therefore most affectionately ask that, as soon as occasion is given of writing to him, you would be willing to fish out who and by what name was that fugitive — of whom he writes — servant of mine, by whose agency he got the form of this hypothesis. For I should be keen to know whether it was this very Ursus or some other; for I know of no one among all the students who have hitherto served me in astronomical matters as having departed secretly from here without my knowledge or against my will. Nor can I sufficiently think who that fugitive was of whom Rollenhagen makes mention once and again. If, then, he should indicate him to me, he will have done a most welcome thing. I see this Rollenhagen to be not only excellently learned and excelling in weighty judgement, but also a man upright and sincere, and well-disposed toward others' studies; wherefore, should any occasion be given, I will not fail to contract a friendship with him by letter — and if he forestalls [me], by that very fact opportunity enough will have been afforded. But these things [run] more at length than I wished; it will be for you to interpret candidly this delay, which a just complaint has wrung from me. If you receive letters addressed to me from Doctor Peucer, I beg that you would not be loth to send them here first of all. Farewell, most noble and most illustrious man, and do not cease to deserve well of the learned arts, as you do, and by this means to procure for yourself praise that will never die away.

Again, live and fare you well most happily and most long.
Given at Uraniborg, on the 21st day of December, in the year 1588.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** Tycho Brahe, writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven.
- **Recipient.** *Henricus Ranzovius* = **Henrik Rantzau** (Heinrich Rantzau, 1526–1598), Royal Statthalter of the Danish king in the Duchies of Schleswig-Holstein, humanist polymath, patron, and Tycho's chief German correspondent and intermediary — here acting both as instrument-recipient and as conduit of the Ursus affair to the wider learned world.
- **Persons named.** *Georgius Braun* = **Georg Braun** (Georgius Bruin, 1541–1622), Cologne canon and editor of the *Civitates orbis terrarum* ("Theatre of Cities"); the "Dean of Cologne" (*Decanus Coloniensis*) is Rantzau/Braun's title as given. *Ericus Langius de Engelstholm* = **Erik Lange** of Engelstholm (c. 1553–1613), Danish nobleman and alchemist, Tycho's friend (later betrothed to Tycho's sister Sophie); Ursus was in his service. *Georgius Rollenhagius* = **Georg Rollenhagen** (1542–1609), Magdeburg rector and writer, the candid informant. *D. Peucerus* = **Caspar Peucer** (1525–1602), Wittenberg physician-astronomer. *Illustrissimus Princeps Landtgravius* = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel**; Ursus dedicated his *Fundamentum astronomicum* (1588) to him.
- **The plagiarist.** *Dithmarsus … Ursinus … Ursus* = **Nicolaus Reimers Baer / Ursus** (Nicolaus Raimarus Ursus Dithmarsus, c. 1551–1600), from Dithmarschen, who in his *Fundamentum astronomicum* (Strasbourg, 1588) published a geo-heliocentric world-system closely resembling Tycho's. The whole core of the letter is Tycho's formal accusation of theft — the opening shot of the long Tycho–Ursus priority war. Tycho puns relentlessly on his name: *Dithmarsi nomine et re Ursini* "Dithmarsian by name and Ursine [bear-like] in fact"; *hominis vel potius ursi istius* "of the man, or rather of that **bear**." The bear-pun is rendered with the gloss kept visible by the audit's rule (no flattening of the wordplay).
- **Instruments / sundial passage.** *Sciotericum (horizontale)* = a (horizontal) **sundial / sciotericon** (Greek-derived term, *skiotherikon*, shadow-marker); kept. *organo illo, quo nostrae hypotheses … explicantur* = "that **instrument** by which our hypotheses … are set out" — a planetary/world-system demonstration device (an *organum*, this chapter's convention). *linea meridiana / linea meridiei* = **meridian line**; *Gnomon* = **gnomon**; *azimutha … in ipso scrupulo* = "the azimuths … to the very [arc-]scruple" (a *scrupulus* = one minute of arc; rendered "[arc-]scruple"). *compassum* here = a **pair of compasses / drawing-compass** (cf. the analogous *compass* crux in brahe-t_15841211001); rendered "compass" with the technical sense noted. *in aequilibrio Horizontis* = "in the level of the Horizon" (i.e. kept truly horizontal).
- **Astronomy — concepts.** *hypotheses revolutionum coelestium* = "**hypotheses** of the celestial **revolutions**" (here *hypotheses* = world-system models, the Tychonic geo-heliocentric arrangement — not "guesses"); *retrogradationes Planetarum* = retrogradations of the planets; *diversitas apparentiarum* = "the diversity of the appearances"; *secundum veterem Ptolemaicam quam Copernianam ratiocinationem* = "according to the old Ptolemaic and the Copernican reasoning." *Astronomiae instauratione* — Tycho's programme term, the **Restoration of Astronomy** (*astronomia instaurata*, this chapter's convention); the planned *Astronomiae Instauratae Mechanica / Progymnasmata* corpus.
- **Symbols / Greek.** ♈ and ♎ named **Aries** and **Libra** in the translation, glyphs kept in the Source block; they mark the equinoctial points (the Equator's intersections). The technical adverb *five* in the Source is the period print-form of *sive* ("or, that is"), retained verbatim in the Source block and rendered "that is" in the translation (noted, not silently corrected).
- **Legal / rhetorical terms.** *postliminio* = "by right of **postliminium** / right of return" — the Roman-law term for the restoration of rights/property to one who returns from captivity; here metaphorical: Tycho's stolen hypothesis should "return" to its true author. *inveterator* = a hardened/inveterate wrongdoer ("that inveterate [rascal]"). *alienis se ornet plumis* = "deck himself in others' feathers" (the Aesopic jackdaw-in-borrowed-plumes proverb); kept as the metaphor it is.
- **Crux — *prfsecta*.** In the clause *etsi non totaliter a me prfsecta sint*, the Source's *prfsecta* is a typographic corruption (the *f* standing for the *ae*/*œ* ligature). The intended word is almost certainly **profecta** ("derived/issued from me"), giving "though not wholly derived from me." A reading *praesecta/perfecta* is far less likely on sense. Translated as "*derived*" with the printed form bracketed and flagged; this is the one genuinely uncertain word and is the basis for the Probable/Possible borderline below.
- **Other phrasing.** *quartam partem Theatri urbium … reliquos tres tomos* — the **fourth volume** of Braun & Hogenberg's *Civitates orbis terrarum* (vol. IV, 1588) had reached Tycho; he still lacked the earlier three. *Huenula nostra* = "our little Hven" (affectionate diminutive of Hven), referring to the engraved view of Uraniborg/Hven included in the atlas. *pallam papyri impressoriae* = "a ball of printing-paper" (*palla/balla* = a bale or ball/ream-bundle of paper for the Uraniborg press). *quaternio* = a **quaternion** (a gathering of four sheets), here samples enclosed to show the paper's size.
- **Internal date references (not in-letter discrepancies, but flagged for the record).** *ante quadriennium iam elapsum* "four years ago now past" places Ursus's visit with Erik Lange c. 1584; *ante triennium* "three years ago" (Ursus's claimed independent invention) and *ante biennium* "two years ago" (Rollenhagen's report) are Tycho's reports of *others'* datings, preserved as written, not reconciled.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datae Uraniburgi, die 21 Decembris, Anno 1588* = "Given at Uraniborg, on the 21st day of December, in the year 1588" (Old Style; Denmark was on the Julian calendar). The dateline date (21 December 1588) agrees with the edition label; no discrepancy.

- **§1 Dreyer collation:** the corrupt *prfsecta* is printed by Dreyer (*Opera Omnia* VII, p. 388) as **prosecta** — confirming the word and sense ("derived/cut from me"); the earlier conjecture *profecta* is superseded, the translation "derived" stands.
- **Correction.** Latin 'prfsecta' (a corrupted non-word) corrected to Dreyer's 'profecta' (TBOO VII p.388, line 28); the English's bracketed Latin gloss updated to match. The translation 'derived' was already correct and required no change.

Collated the opening ("Ex literis tuis..."), the closing ("Datae Uraniburgi, die 21 Decembris, Anno 1588"), and every proper name, date, and number in the Ursus/Rollenhagen narrative (Erik Lange of Engelstholm, 14 days, four years, three years, two years, Landgrave, Peucer) against the page images.
