For he, in the very scruples [minutes], by means of the cross-staff [radius astronomicus] (an instrument diligently perfected by his father), subtly measured the distances of the comet from two more conspicuous fixed stars, which with it constituted a nearly equilateral triangle (which makes not a little toward inquiring after the certainty of the place from this). And although the cross-staff of itself does not everywhere afford sufficiently precise distances within a few minutes, especially in the larger intervals, yet its aberration is not so great as to dispose the comet here otherwise than it ought by more than a quarter of a degree — which variation in no way disproves what we intend. But the matter stands far otherwise with the torquetum, by which instrument the observations of the Most Illustrious Prince were taken. For even if it were of just size, yet it is intricately composed of too many and diverse parts, and many things are required for the disposition of the several ones, which during observation are with difficulty managed at once, so much so that while one is guarded against, another is easily neglected; and any one of them by itself can suggest some sensible error. I say nothing of the fact that the instrument itself too too much burdens itself by its own mass, since its dispositions are not adapted to its turning according to equilibrium. So that there is none among all the astronomical instruments devised by the ancients which exhibits to the observer a less ready and assured certainty — however ingeniously its structure [be devised], by which the Arabs, the first inventors (as I think) of this, tried to reduce the armillae used by Hipparchus and Ptolemy into a certain flat framework of circles, more compendiously and at less cost. I now say nothing of the fact that the Most Illustrious Prince's torquetum, by which those observations were performed — although it was made of solid brass — was nonetheless too small, as I saw, when fifteen years ago I tarried in person for some days with the Most Illustrious Prince at Kassel. For he then had two such torqueta, neither of which presented a sufficiently capacious size, and both indeed had long since been antiquated by His Highness, because they by no means exhibited sure markings of the heavenly bodies, the Prince himself even hinting as much. It therefore easily happened, observing through a torquetum not so large, that a deviation of several degrees from the mark was committed — which by the benefit of the cross-staff, with the investigation sought from the distances of the stars, could safely enough be guarded against; and the tail, which of itself appeared thin, as one may gather from the very observations of the Most Illustrious Prince, in its extension not with difficulty, as to its long interval, suggested some frustration to the sight. Wherefore, if from observations of comets you labor to prove that their tail is of the very substance of the body, and is borne of itself, and does not always regard the Sun, it will be necessary that you implore aid from elsewhere; for this comet, which you allege, makes much rather against you than for you, as has now been shown enough and more.

Now to other matters. The things you object to our reasonings concerning the curvature of the tail make little to the point. If you can find a fitter occasion for the bending of the hairs than [one] from optics, bring it forward. That the tail is, however, the comet's own portion, existing of the same matter, so that for this reason it can of itself exhibit various forms — this I shall by no means have conceded to you. Not otherwise do you less aptly apply the things I wrote about Graminaeus at the end of the work. For I did not say that he, as to the situation of comets, adheres to the Aristotelian opinion, but only that, as to matter, [it] consists of terrestrial fumes, as he [Aristotle] will have it, and [is] drawn up into the lofty ether. But since you yourself confess this to be your opinion too, you assuredly slip into the same absurdities which I shall amply show elsewhere; for it makes no difference whether you call those vapors slow and tenacious, or thin and light, or burning or illuminated, provided you admit them to be terrestrial and sublunary, and raised in whatever manner into the highest heaven. Moreover, since from certain words written to the Most Illustrious Prince — by which I named my work to be published *On the new generations of the ethereal world* — you gather that I introduce generation into the heaven, and consequently corruption too: you seem here to catch at my words too strictly. For I there took the word "generation" in a broader sense, for that which newly exists or appears, not seen before, nor did I sustain the part of the grammarian in the propriety of that expression. But why did you not rather seize on the printed title of the book itself, which I inscribed more circumspectly than is required in any letter, *On the new phenomena of the ethereal world*, deliberately avoiding the word "generation," that there might be no place for cavil? Elsewhere you will see yourself to be still far from my opinion.

Concerning the constitution of the celestial hypotheses devised by me, I do not wish at present to bring much forward by way of defense and confirmation; for that would be too prolix, nor would it be sufficiently accomplished without a manifold demonstration sought from sure observations. I shall rather give my effort, that on another occasion, when I am about to treat expressly of the restitution of the celestial motions — the Author of the heaven favoring [me] — it may be known in fact that these our hypotheses satisfy the celestial appearances to a nicety, and far excel both the Ptolemaic and the Copernican, and correspond better to truth itself. But if those [hypotheses] so displease you that you prefer, with Copernicus, to revolve the earth and seas in the heaven yearly together with the neighboring Moon, and so to exalt [the earth] with a threefold motion — though it be one and simple body — beyond the lot of the stars (than which it is nonetheless far inferior and more unfit for moving): for my part that too will be open and entire to you. Nor is the way now difficult, since you have mingled elemental air with the heaven and the revolutions of the stars; why not the earth and seas too? Is this not to confound the lower regions with the upper, and to invert the whole order of the nature of things? Yet, lest you be deceived: there is no [reason] that you should persuade yourself that the physical absurdities which accompany the Copernican hypothesis have been sufficiently refuted by him; nor do the things adduced by you hither confirm the whole matter beyond doubt, as I shall show elsewhere, discussing these and many more of the kind. Much less will the things put forward by you in excusing those passages in which Sacred Scripture asserts the contrary be able to merit a place. For the authority and reverence of the divine letters both is and ought to be greater than that it should be seemly for them to be dragged this way, after the manner of a buskin [cothurnus]. For although they themselves, in physical matters and certain others, for the most part accommodate themselves to the grasp of the common crowd, yet far be it that on that account we should hold them to speak so vulgarly [that we should not] also believe them to put forward true things. Thus Moses, although in the first chapter of Genesis, treating of the creation of the world, he does not unlock the inner shrines of astronomy — writing as he was for an uncultivated people — nonetheless brings forward nothing that could not be conceded even by the astronomers themselves. For what you think follows from him — that the Moon, contrary to geometrical demonstrations, would be larger than the rest of the stars — the Text itself does not admit. For it has it thus: "And God made two great lights, the greater for the ruling of the day, the lesser for [that] of the night, and the stars too, and he placed them in the fluid heaven to illuminate the lands." Here Moses speaks at least about the magnitude of the light by which the Sun and Moon illuminate the lands beyond the other stars, not about the quantity of bodies. And therefore he calls the Moon the lesser light, because it does not illuminate the earth in the nocturnal time so much as the Sun in the diurnal. For if he had understood these things of the magnitude of the body, and had accommodated himself at least to the common crowd's view, he would not have called the Moon less than the Sun; inasmuch as its visible diameter is certainly discerned scarcely less than the Sun's, if not rather, for the most part, somewhat larger. But no astronomer would deny that the Moon, after the Sun, is the great luminary before the other heavenly bodies, and that it illuminates the earth by night far more than the rest, and dispels the darkness. Thus the astrologers themselves call the Sun and Moon — the latter the luminary of the night, the former of the day — which agrees exceedingly well with Moses. About the other stars I do not now dispute, whether round about, near their boundaries, they pour out more brightness than the Moon itself, although on account of the excessive distance that light does not strike the earth. For Moses too in that place was treating at least of this light which touches the lands and serves the use of living creatures. So too you detract too much from the Prophets, when you say that they understood no more of the nature of things than other common men. For although they did not treat physics expressly — for that was not [part] of their office — yet they mingle into their oracles many things drawn from physics, which no one, however much imbued with natural philosophy, will be able to gainsay. Nor does it follow from this that they were ignorant of astronomy and physics, which flowed down to them even from the first patriarchs, because they treat of these things more sparingly. For it was not seemly to mingle philosophical and worldly things too much with the theological mysteries which they chiefly treated. The authority of the sacred letters therefore still stands unmoved, as we shall see more fully in its place. Nor will the position of Copernicus be vindicated from this by any effort of yours.

But as to what you object to my invention of the hypotheses — a certain violent dragging, and a confusion of order, and a blemish of retrogradation in the five planets — we do not delay over it. For it is consonant [with reason] that it is not a certain involuntary dragging, but a natural and divinely implanted concomitance and observance, by which the five planets always regard the Sun, wherever it go, in the middle [meditullium] of their revolutions. And by what corporeal and tenacious matter, I ask, are the magnet and iron coupled, so that the one seeks the other, even with another body interposed? If this can happen naturally, without violence, in terrestrial inanimate things, what [shall we say] of celestial things, which the Platonists and the wiser of the philosophizers would not deny to be animate and to have a divinely innate knowledge, wonderful and more excellent than is thought? Weigh more diligently those things which are adduced by Pliny at the end of the 16th chapter of book 2, concerning the reason of the stations and regressions of the three superior planets — which, although they seem ambiguous and obscure or altogether absurd, yet are not all plainly about nothing. And it is sufficiently gathered hence that the most ancient mathematicians, who also set the earth resting in the middle of the world, were wholly ignorant of epicycles, and by some other more occult reasoning referred those appearances, which are thence saved, to the Sun; nor did they judge it inconvenient that the planets be so subject to the Sun, although no material connection intervened. But the Text itself will admonish you of more. Nor is any confusion committed in my hypotheses; for the heaven is single and like to itself from the Moon to the eighth sphere, in which the planets freely ascend and descend, as they go around the Sun walking in the middle in a most beautiful harmony. For I do not believe that you wish again to introduce some real distinction of the celestial orbs, contrary to what was long ago agreed between us. The retrogradation of the planets, which is discerned with respect to us and to the eighth sphere, afflicts them with no fault, inasmuch as, with respect to themselves, they always regard the Sun in the same manner, uniformly intent on their destined course. But these things, and many others which can perhaps be plausibly inferred by some against our reckoning of the motions, I shall in their time, God breathing upon our endeavors, discuss sufficiently.

But I did not take the occasion of constructing these hypotheses from the Copernican [ones] inverted; and if you ever thought any such thing, that, as you well enough know, was not made known to me, nor was anything similar ever to be gathered from Rheticus or Reinhold. But when I had observed, by subtle and accurate observation — especially that had in the year [15]82 — that Mars at acronychal [rising, in opposition to the Sun] becomes nearer to the earth than the Sun itself, and that on that account the long-received Ptolemaic hypotheses cannot stand; and moreover that comets seen in the heaven and dwelling opposite the Sun are not rendered subject to the earth's annual motion (although they are not so far distant that it [the motion] plainly vanishes, as happens in the fixed stars), [and] that the Copernican assumption too in the earth's motion totters: there remained no other way of saving the celestial appearances than this very one which has lately been put forward by me with a general indication. If, therefore, I shall have demonstrated those two [points] to hold thus, then assuredly it will be sufficiently confirmed that neither the Ptolemaic nor the Copernican hypothesis agrees with the truth of the matter, but this our [hypothesis] alone — [to say] nothing now of many other things which make not a little hither. For it does not seem convenient to report particular and individual matters in this place.

I greatly wondered, at first, when I read in your letters that these my hypotheses had been previously known to the Most Illustrious Prince — inasmuch as he had them expressed in a certain automaton [model]. Nor could I sufficiently think how this could come about, since I was perfectly conscious to myself that I had learned these from no mortal before I myself was led thither from observations, and that meanwhile they had lain hidden with me, not previously published. But after the little book of that Ursus of Dithmarschen — whom you once, in certain letters given to me, adorned with a worthy eulogy, [now] calling [him] an impure scoundrel — had been sent to me (and that by the most learned man Master Georg Rollenhagen, dwelling at Magdeburg, who also had indicated long before that these our hypotheses had been communicated to him two years earlier by a certain fugitive servant of mine; and therefore, knowing them to have been first invented by me, and grieving that that Ursus undeservedly attributed them to himself, he wished that book to become known to me, so that I might recognize that theft and again claim for myself what had been cast out abroad by others): from that I sufficiently perceived whence this ordering of the celestial revolutions had reached you. Inasmuch as that plagiarist reports that, about three years ago, after he had devised this in a certain corner of the kingdom of Poland (understand rather on the island Hven of the kingdom of Denmark, when in the year [15]84, in September, he was present here with the most noble and learned man Master Erik Lange, my singular friend, whom he was then serving, [these things] secretly snatched from me, like certain others too), he offered [them] to the Most Illustrious Prince of Hesse, and they were reduced into a brazen automaton by His Highness's craftsman Jost Bürgi. But that impostor sufficiently betrays his theft, and along with it his ignorance of the matter which he peddles. For while he keeps the orb of Mars wholly encompassing [the orbit around] the Sun, he imitates a certain false delineation, which, by I know not what carelessness, was here so depicted, and on that account, as inept, thrown away somewhere among my papers — which I still have at hand, sought out under the same name, that the very thing might plainly appear. And since he could not amend that fault committed in depicting the diagram, he sufficiently makes known to the intelligent that he does not understand that invention, much less is its author — however he has not blushed to arrogate to himself what was got together here, impudently, and to dedicate it to the Most Illustrious Prince Wilhelm as his own contrivance. Besides, he has many other things in that little book, which, although he has not carried them all off from here, yet he has partly scraped together from you, partly from other mathematicians in Germany, whether secretly or openly; so much so that, if the things belonging to others be taken away, almost nothing remains that will be his. But let that fellow be off with his plagiarism — to you and other learned men, among whom he once was, [it is] sufficiently clear who he is, and how brazen-faced and arrogant a trifler. These things I wished to answer briefly concerning my hypotheses; more you will understand in a more convenient place and time, which without doubt (unless you have sworn too obstinately to the words and opinion of Copernicus) will satisfy you.

That I could have prefixed in every respect a more fitting hypothesis for the comet of the year [15]77 — namely, out of several composite circular motions — I myself had it well enough known, and this is sufficiently indicated in the book itself, and the reason added why I forbore to furnish it; whence there was no need of that replication. But to have proposed this very hypothesis which I indicated there is not without a certain utility, as you suppose; for thus it is the more confirmed that comets are really celestial, and that their motions are not stirred up tumultuously. You rightly excused yourself to the Most Illustrious Prince [in saying] that that second volume was not transmitted to His Highness but to you, and as it were in my name you promised that, when the whole work has been finished, I would communicate it entire to His Highness. For this I determined beforehand with myself, and there is no [reason] for you to doubt that your faith [pledge] in this part is to be redeemed. The remaining two princes too will have copies, as you advise. The Most Illustrious Maurice, the Landgrave's son — whom I rejoice to have advanced so much in letters and languages — would that he had also tasted astronomical matters, that he might thus also succeed his father, laudably practiced in these. Likewise the Most Illustrious Bernhard of Anhalt will not be to be passed over, since he is imbued with the sacred [things] of mathematics. But that the first volume did not come out at this fair — the impediment was that lately I did not obtain the printing-paper for which I had sent, the excessive abundance of waters delaying the messenger, and on account of certain other obstacles which it is not pertinent to relate. But as for those things which you judge to make for you concerning your observation in ♀ Venus and ☉ the Sun, made for the verification of the fixed stars, and what I think about this matter, I have answered briefly in a letter given to the Most Illustrious Prince; wherefore it is not worth the trouble to repeat them here. Nor is the opportunity granted me of writing more now — nay, I have scratched out these very things in haste, not only [jotting them down] among many other occupations as they came to mind in passing, but moreover laboring under a heavy pain of the forehead and of the half-head [hemicrania], on account of a head-cold which a few days before I had contracted from the nocturnal chill while observing, [and which was] prematurely stopped up [congested] — so that I have conceived these very things with the greatest difficulty. For there is not so much leisure left over that it is free [to me] to attend to medication. It will therefore be yours, in these difficulties, candidly to interpret things heaped together less neatly, and, if leisure and health did not allow [me] to reply now to everything point by point, to take in good part these things written back in a general way, and not to cease loving me, as you do, and more often, as opportunity is offered, to revisit [me] with letters. Farewell. Given at Uraniborg, 21 February, the year 1589. Tycho Brahe.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Christophorus Rothmannus* = **Christoph Rothmann**, mathematician/astronomer at the Hesse-Kassel court of **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse** (*Illustrissimus Princeps Wilhelmus Landtgravius Hassiae*). This is one of Tycho's most substantial polemical letters in the famous Tycho–Rothmann exchange (printed by Tycho himself in the 1596 *Epistolae astronomicae*, Liber I). It joins issue on (1) the substance of the heavens, (2) twilight/refraction, (3) lunar latitude and the nodes, (4) the nature of comet tails, (5) the geoheliocentric ("Tychonic") hypotheses, (6) Scripture vs. Copernicanism, and (7) the Ursus plagiarism.
- **Edition of record.** The source's edition field gives *Tychonis Brahe Dani epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Uraniborg, 1596) = Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VI; no MS witness is listed in the edition.
- **Salutation/subscription.** *S. D.* = *salutem dicit*, "(sends) greeting" — here rendered "heartiest greeting" in the courtesy register; *Vale* = "Farewell"; *Datae* = "Given." Per glossary.
- **Calendar.** The dateline *Datae Vraniburgi 21. Feb. Anno 1589* matches the catalogue label ("1589. 21. februar. Uraniborg"); no discrepancy — Old Style, the Danish norm. **In-text Roman-calendar idiom:** *13. Calendarum Septembris* = the 13th day before the Kalends of September = **20 August** (inclusive Roman counting); glossed in the translation, not silently converted. Tycho himself confirms the equivalence in the next sentence ("*die 20. Augusti, qui plane idem est…*"), so the gloss is internally substantiated.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Franciscus Vallesius* = **Francisco Valles** (1524–1592), Spanish physician-philosopher ("el Divino"), author of *De sacra philosophia*.
 - *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (Rostock; glossary).
 - *Regiomontanus, Copernicus, Wernerus* (**Johannes Werner**), *Rheticus, Reinholdus* (**Erasmus Reinhold**) — the mathematical-astronomical authorities Tycho weighs.
 - *Ioannes Baptista Benedictus* = **Giovanni Battista Benedetti** (1530–1590), Venetian patrician, mathematician at the Savoy court; the cited work is his *Diversarum speculationum mathematicarum et physicarum liber* (Turin, 1585); the *Baron Sabaudus Philibertus* is the Savoyard addressee of the closing letter cited.
 - *Regiomontanus, Fracastorius* (**Girolamo Fracastoro**), *Apianus* (**Peter Apian**), *Gemma Frisius* — earlier comet observers cited for the anti-solar tail.
 - *Cornelius Gemma* = **Cornelius Gemma** (1535–1578), son of Gemma Frisius (hence *Instrumentum a Patre suo diligenter excultum*, "an instrument diligently perfected by his father"); cited work *De naturae divinis characterismis* (Antwerp, 1575).
 - *Maesthlinianum scriptum* = the writing of **Michael Maestlin** on the 1577 comet (*Observatio et demonstratio cometae*, 1578); Kepler's teacher.
 - *Graminaeus* = **Theodor Graminaeus** (Dietrich Graminäus), Cologne mathematician who wrote on the 1577 comet.
 - *Ursus Dithmarsicus* = **Nicolaus Reimers Ursus ("Bär")** of Dithmarschen; *Georgius Rollenhagius* = **Georg Rollenhagen**, Magdeburg schoolman/poet; *Ericus Lange* = **Erik Lange**, Danish nobleman-alchemist (Tycho's friend, in whose service Ursus visited Hven in Sept. 1584); *Iustus Byrgius* = **Jost Bürgi**, the Kassel court clockmaker/instrument-maker. *Mauritius, Landtgravii Filius* = **Moritz of Hesse-Kassel** (later Landgrave Moritz "the Learned"); *Bernhardus Anhaltinus* = **Bernhard of Anhalt**.
 - *Moses* / *Prophetae* — Scriptural authority; the quotation conflates **Genesis 1:16–17** (the "two great lights"); *liquidum Caelum*, "fluid heaven," reflects Tycho's own fluid-heavens reading rather than the firmament of the received text — flagged as Tycho's paraphrase, not a verbatim Vulgate citation.
- **Technical terms (glossary-consistent).** *Refractio* → refraction; *Crepusculum* → twilight; *Nadir / Zenith (vertex)* → kept; *Quadrans Altitudinis* → altitude-quadrant; *Caput Draconis* → "Head of the Dragon," glossed [the ascending node]; *Nodi* → nodes; *Latitudo Lunae* → latitude of the Moon; *Zyzigiae* → syzygies; *Acronychus* → acronychal (rising in opposition to the Sun); *Retrogradatio* → retrogradation; *Hypotheses* → hypotheses; *Aequinoctium vernum* → vernal equinox; *Meridianus / Finitor / Horizon* → meridian / horizon (*Finitor* is the bounding horizon-circle); *Circulus verticalis* → vertical circle. *Radius Astronomicus* → **cross-staff (radius astronomicus)**; *Torquetum* → torquetum (kept; the medieval instrument Tycho disparages); *Armillae* → armillae; *Organa Astronomica* → astronomical instruments; *Globus* → globe. *Restitutio / redintegratio (Astronomiae)* → "restitution / restoration (of astronomy)" — Tycho's *instauratio* programme. *Diaphanum / Diaphanitas* → "transparent medium / transparency."
- **Star/coordinate names rendered, glyphs kept in Source.** *Baltheus Orionis* = the Belt of Orion; *Humerus dexter Orionis* = Betelgeuse (right Shoulder of Orion); *Spica ♍* = Spica; *Arcturus*; *cauda Vrsae Maioris* = the tail of Ursa Major (Alkaid, the last star); *sinister lacertus Bootis* = the left arm of Boötes; *Booten* (Greek acc.) = Boötes; *Canicula* = the Lesser Dog / Procyon region (Aristotle's example). Zodiac glyphs ♓ ♍ ♎ ♏ named Pisces / Virgo / Libra / Scorpio; planet glyphs ♀ ☉ named Venus / Sun, glyphs retained in the Source block. *Part. / Min. / Grad.* rendered "degrees / minutes"; fractional degrees (2¼, 3⅔, 6⅗, 9⅔, 16⅚) reproduced as printed.
- **Natural-philosophy / alchemical idiom.** *Quinta Essentia* → "fifth essence" (quintessence). *Tria principia Paracelsi* → "the three principles" (Paracelsus's *tria prima*: salt, sulphur, mercury), which Tycho reads as an image of the Trinity. *Mumia* (Terrae / Aëria / Aquea) → kept as *mumia* (the Paracelsian vital-matter term — not "mummy"); flagged below. *Iliad / in Iliado suae naturae* → "an Iliad analogous to its own nature" — *Ilias* here used in the sense of a "world / abundance proper to" a thing; an unusual usage, kept literally and flagged. *Phlegma* → "phlegm" (alchemical: the watery, inert fraction). *eleuatio / per saepius reiteratam eleuationem* → "elevation" (i.e. repeated distillation), glossed. *Orichalcum* → brass.
- **Rhetorical / classical idiom.** *in modum Cothurni* → "after the manner of a buskin [*cothurnus*]" — i.e. stretched to fit like the cothurnus that fits either foot; a proverbial figure for twisting a text to suit any meaning; kept as image. *sub incudem veritatis reuocare* → "call back to the anvil of truth." *ad amussim / ad vnguem* → "to a nicety / exactly." *Colophon / ad Colophonem* → "to the colophon" (= to completion). *perfrictae frontis* → "brazen-faced" (lit. of a rubbed/hardened brow). *Nebulo* → "scoundrel."
- **Substantive cruxes / hedges preserved.**
 - *meditullium* — the planets regard the Sun "in the **meditullium** of their revolutions": the central point/midst of their orbits; rendered "the middle" with the technical sense flagged. This is the core statement of the Tychonic geoheliocentric arrangement.
 - The magnet–iron analogy (*Magnes et Ferrum … vnum alterum appetat*) is Tycho's physical defence of sun-tethered planetary motion *without* material orbs; rendered straight, the period sense ("appetite/seeking") kept.
 - Tycho's hedges are preserved throughout and **not sharpened**: *aliquatenus persentiscere queam* ("I can to some extent perceive"); *vix credi possit* ("it can scarcely be believed"); *vt verum fatear, neque haec ratiocinatio mihi ita satisfacit* ("to confess the truth, neither does this reasoning so satisfy me"); *quod tamen nondum satis obtentum est* ("which however has not yet been sufficiently attained"); *non omnia sunt plane de nihilo* ("are not all plainly about nothing"). The parenthetical correction *(intellige potius in Insula … Huena)* — "understand rather on the island Hven" — is Tycho's own bracket-style interjection inside the Source; rendered as his parenthesis, not an editorial one.
 - *libellus … ollus istius Vrsi* (l. 449 of source): the printed form reads *lib ollus*, evidently *libellus* ("little book") broken across a line; the intended word *libellus* is adopted in translation and the printed split kept in the Source block.
- **Correction.** Restored Tycho's chapter-3 self-citation and active verb ('as I indicate there in chapter 3', for 'capit. 3. indico') where the published English had recast it as a passive 'indication [section] 3'. Corrected the constellation gloss 'the Lesser Dog [Canicula]' to 'the Dog-star [Canicula]' (Canicula = Sirius in Canis Major, not Canis Minor). No change to the Latin.

translation.warrant:
**Not collated against Dreyer** — no page reference for this letter, so the grade is capped at Probable however sound the translation looks. the edition gives no page reference for this letter, so no collation against Dreyer was possible; by the audit's rule, graded at most B on that basis alone. Audited the full letter (the transcribed original c. 42,000 characters Latin / the published English c. 50,000 characters) paragraph by paragraph against the transcribed original: checked every date (10, 12, 15 Feb; 1558; 1577/80/82/85; 1582; 1584 Sept.), every degree/minute value in the twilight-observation and 1558-comet/Cornelius-Gemma passages (over 30 numeric values, all exact), every proper name (Rothmann, Vallesius, Paracelsus, Brucaeus, Regiomontanus, Copernicus, Werner, Maestlin, Benedetti/Philibert, Fracastoro, Apian, Gemma Frisius, Cornelius Gemma, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, Rheticus, Reinhold, Erik Lange, Georg Rollenhagen, Ursus, Jost Bürgi, Landgrave Wilhelm, Maurice, Bernhard of Anhalt), page/chapter citations (Pag. 254 cap. 4 Maestlin; Pliny lib. 2 cap. 16; Aristotle Meteor. lib.1 cap.6), and the opening/closing formulae and dateline (Uraniborg, 21 Feb. 1589). No fabrication, omission, or sense-altering mistranslation found; two low-severity mistranslations noted above (a garbled book-chapter citation, and a constellation-identification slip in an Aristotle quotation).

**2 defects found:**
- **mistranslation** (low). "capit. 3." is almost certainly an abbreviated chapter citation ("capite 3" = chapter 3) to Tycho's own printed book, and "indico" is Tycho's own verb ("I indicate"); the English recasts the citation as an unexplained "indication [section] 3" and shifts the verb to a passive "it is taken", losing the citation form and Tycho's agency without changing the substantive claim. At: “the maximum latitude of the Moon was found by you nearly the same as it is taken there, indication [section] 3”.
- **mistranslation** (low). "Canicula" is the standard Latin name for Sirius/the Dog-star in Canis Major (the star Aristotle references, Meteorologica I.6); "the Lesser Dog" specifically denotes the separate constellation Canis Minor (Procyon), so the gloss misidentifies which star/constellation is meant, though it does not affect Tycho's substantive point about faint comae being visible only in very clear air. At: “he himself saw a certain star in the thigh of the Lesser Dog [Canicula] to have had a coma”.

**Repaired.** No Dreyer page images were available for this letter (no page reference), so the base Latin transcription could not be collated against the edition of record and is reproduced unchanged. Both mistranslation defects were verified from internal evidence by locating the exact Latin clauses (capit. 3. indico; Caniculae femore) against the published English and confirming the mismatch described in the audit: a citation-plus-active-verb recast as a passive noun phrase, and Canicula (Canis Major/Sirius) mislabeled as the Lesser Dog (Canis Minor). Both clauses have been corrected minimally; nothing else in the letter was touched.

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET VARIA ERUDITIONE EXCULTISSIMO DN. THADDÆO HAGECIO AB HAICK, MEDICO ET MATHEMATICO PERITISSIMO, AMICO SUO PERPETUO COLENDO.
AHM HERN DOCTOR THADDEO HAGETIO ZU PRAG WONHAFFTIG.
S.

CUM hodie primum a nobili iuvene TAGONE KRABIO nostrate hinc in Cæsariam aulam iamiam abituro cognovissem illum Pragam transiturum, non intermittendum duxi, quin aliquid literarum ad te darem, optime et eruditissime mi THADDÆE, præsertim quia nihil adhuc responsi ad ultimas meas receperim, quod tamen indies avide expecto; dilationem vero hanc internunciorum inopiæ et hyemis importunitati imputandam censeo, absit enim ut de tua ergo me promta voluntate quicquam addubitem. Nunc itaque cum per hunc nobilem Danum rescribendi occasio percommodum offeratur, ne responsione ulterius supersedeas, te etiam atque etiam rogatum habeo, imprimis vero ut de ijs, quæ liber noster secundus Cometæ anni 77 tibi dudum transmissus continet, mecum ingenue et aperte conferre non gravatim duxeris. Eum enim te iam evolvisse satis mihi persuadeo. Primus liber, qui de Stella Nova affatim tractat, nunc typis meis excuditur; procrastinationi, quæ interiecta est, non saltem remoratio Privilegij Gallici Cæsariano adiungendi, sed etiam papyri impressoriæ defectus præter expectationem meam ansam dederunt. Nunc vero cum utrisque his remoris satis provisum sit, spero hunc quoque tomum brevi publici iuris futurum. Et quantum per impedimenta ac distractiones (quibus utplurimum æstivo tempore implicor) licebit, operis istius maturationem urgebo. In hoc non solum ea, quæ ad Novam Stellam proprie faciunt, accurate et luculenter declarata demonstrataque invenies, sed multa insuper alia ad totius Artis Astronomicæ redintegrationem plurimum facientia; quæque hactenus diu frustraque desiderata fuêre, qualia sunt: Solaris curriculi e multorum annorum exquisitissimis observationibus Geometrice ostensa et in numeros hisce proximis sæculis satisfacientes reducta restitutio, item affixarum Stellarum, præsertim vero earum, quæ circa Zodiacum versantur, præcisa et ipsi cœlo adamussim consona verificatio, et pleraque alia nunc non attinet singillatim referre. Id saltem te oratum cuperem, ut MUNOSI Hispani et Italorum istorum tum etiam aliorum, qui de hac stella aliquid publicârunt, scripta mecum communicare non intermittas, si quæ forte tibi innotuerunt ad nos non perlata. Idem etiam circa rem Cometicam expeterem. peterem. Constitui enim in singulis iuxta librorum finem, aliorum placita et animadversiones sub incudem veritatis revocare, ubi in primo atque ultimo tomo, quibus de Nova hac Stella et Cometa anni 80 agitur, tuarum lucubrationum honorificam, ut par est, introducere mentionem commodius erat, quam in illo intermedio libro de Cometa anni 77. Circa hunc enim nimium ab ipso cœlo (vel teipso iudice) deflexisse deprehenderis. Plura hoc tempore scribere festinus Nobilis huius abitus non patitur, verum ubi per hunc ad nos redeuntem, vel quacunque alia oblata oportunitate responsum a te recepero, uberius et pluribus de toto hoc negotio tecum agam. Intereaque et semper quam diutissime et felicissime vale, et Amplissimos Generosissimosque Barones D. IOHANNEM SEPTIMIUM a Lichtenstein et D. FELICIANUM ab Herberstein , quorum uterque Daniam superioribus annis pertransiens, me Uraniburgi invisere non gravatus est, meo nomine officiose saluta. Receperunt vero ambo in se WITICHIANORUM scriptorum et librorum, quos post fata reliquit, meo nomine procurationem, de qua ut eos per commoditatem oblatam admonere velis, peramanter peto.

Iterum et sæpius vale.
Raptim Hafniæ die 22. Martij Anno Domini 89.
Tui amantiss.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the most distinguished and, in varied erudition, most accomplished Master Thaddaeus Hagecius of Hájek, most skilled physician and mathematician, his perpetual friend to be honoured.**
**To Herr Doctor Thaddeus Hagetius, resident at Prague.**
Greeting.

Since only today I learned from the noble young man Tage Krabbe, our countryman — now on the very point of departing hence for the Imperial court — that he will be passing through Prague, I judged that I must not let it slip without giving you some letter, my most excellent and most learned Thaddaeus, especially because I have as yet received no reply to my last [letter], which nevertheless I daily await eagerly; this delay, however, I reckon must be charged to the scarcity of go-betweens and the inclemency of winter, for far be it from me to doubt anything of your ready good will towards me. Now therefore, since through this noble Dane a most convenient occasion of writing back is offered, I have you asked again and again that you put off your reply no further — and above all that you do not find it irksome to confer with me frankly and openly about the things contained in our second book, on the comet of [the year] '77, sent to you long ago. For I am sufficiently persuaded that you have already perused it. The first book, which treats fully of the New Star, is now being printed on my own press; the delay that has intervened was occasioned, not only by the holding-back of the French privilege that is to be joined to the Imperial one, but also, beyond my expectation, by a shortage of printing-paper. But now that both these hindrances have been sufficiently provided against, I hope that this volume too will shortly come into the public domain. And so far as my obstructions and distractions allow (in which I am for the most part entangled in the summer season), I shall press on the ripening of that work. In it you will find not only those matters that pertain properly to the New Star accurately and lucidly set forth and demonstrated, but, besides, many other things conducing greatly to the renewal of the whole Art of Astronomy; and such things as have hitherto long and vainly been longed for, namely: a restoration of the Sun's course, shown geometrically from the most exquisite observations of many years and reduced into numbers satisfactory for these latest centuries; likewise a precise verification of the fixed stars — and especially of those that move about the Zodiac — exactly consonant with the heaven itself; and many other things which it is now not fitting to recount one by one. This at least I would wish you entreated: that you not omit to share with me the writings of Muñoz the Spaniard and of those Italians, and also of others, who have published something about this star, if any perchance have come to your knowledge that have not been conveyed to us. The same I would also request concerning the matter of the comet[s]. For I have determined, in each [volume], near the end of the books, to recall the opinions and observations of others to the anvil of truth, where, in the first and last volume — in which this New Star and the comet of [the year] '80 are treated — it was more convenient to introduce honourable mention of your lucubrations, as is fitting, than in that intermediate book on the comet of '77. For concerning this [comet] you will be found to have strayed too far from the heaven itself (even by your own judgement). The haste of this nobleman's departure does not allow me to write more at this time; but when I have received a reply from you — through this same man returning to us, or by whatever other opportunity offered — I shall deal with you more fully and at greater length about this whole affair. And in the meanwhile, and always, fare you as long and as happily as can be; and greet in my name, with all courtesy, the most ample and most noble Barons, Lord Johann Septimius von Lichtenstein and Lord Felician von Herberstein, each of whom, passing through Denmark in earlier years, did not find it irksome to visit me at Uraniborg. Both of them have, moreover, taken upon themselves the charge, in my name, of Wittich's writings and books, which he left behind after his death; concerning which I most lovingly ask that you be willing to remind them when the convenience is offered.

Again and oftentimes, farewell.
In haste, at Copenhagen, the 22nd day of March, in the Year of the Lord '89.
Most loving of you,
TYCHO BRAHE,
by my own hand.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Haick* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius, 1525–1600), Prague physician, astronomer and imperial counsellor at the court of Rudolf II; a leading observer of the 1572 nova and the comets of the 1570s–80s, and Tycho's principal scientific correspondent in the Empire. The two had exchanged cometary observations since the mid-1570s. The honorific styles him "most skilled physician and mathematician."
- **The two address lines.** The first (Latin) is the formal superscription; the second is a **German address/docketing line** — *"Ahm Herrn Doctor Thaddeo Hagetio zu Prag wohnhaftig"* = "To Herr Doctor Thaddeus Hagetius, resident at Prague" — a routing direction (the code-switch is preserved by this chapter's convention). *AHM* = *am/an dem*; *WONHAFFTIG* = *wohnhaftig*, "resident, dwelling."
- ***S.*** = *salutem (dicit)*, "(sends) greeting".
- **Bearer.** *nobilis iuvenis Tago Krabius nostras* = the noble young **Tage Krabbe** ("our countryman," i.e. a Dane), here serving as letter-carrier on his way to the Imperial court (*Caesarea aula*) by way of Prague.
- **The works in progress.** Tycho describes his *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* in its planned three-volume form: *liber primus* "de Stella Nova" (Book I, on the new star of 1572), *liber secundus … Cometae anni 77* (Book II, on the comet of 1577 — i.e. the 1588 *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis*, already sent to Hagecius), and the *ultimus tomus* on the *Cometa anni 80* (the comet of 1580). *redintegratio totius Artis Astronomicae* = "the renewal of the whole Art of Astronomy" — Tycho's *instauratio/restitutio* programme; *restitutio Solaris curriculi* = "restoration of the Sun's course"; *verificatio affixarum Stellarum* = "verification of the fixed stars."
- ***typis meis excuditur*** — "is being printed on my own press": Tycho's Uraniborg printing-house. *papyri impressoriae defectus* = "a shortage of printing-paper"; *Privilegium Gallicum Caesariano adiungendum* = the **French privilege** (printing licence) to be joined to the **Imperial** one.
- ***publici iuris futurum*** — "will come into the public domain / be made public," the standard idiom for publication.
- ***sub incudem veritatis revocare*** — "to recall … to the anvil of truth," a metaphor (the anvil on which others' opinions are hammered/tested) kept as metaphor; *lucubrationes* = "lucubrations" (works of night-study/learned labours), kept.
- **Muñoz.** *Munosi Hispani … scripta* = the writings of **Jerónimo Muñoz** (Hieronymus Munyos/Munosius, c. 1520–1591), the Valencia mathematician whose *Libro del nuevo cometa* (1573) reported the 1572 nova; Tycho asks Hagecius to forward Muñoz's and the Italians' tracts on the new star.
- ***rem Cometicam*** — "the matter of the comet[s]," i.e. the cometary controversy/literature generally.
- **The named barons.** *Iohannes Septimius a Lichtenstein* = **Johann Septimius von Liechtenstein**; *Felicianus ab Herberstein* = **Felician von Herberstein** — Austrian/Imperial noblemen who had visited Tycho at Uraniborg on earlier passages through Denmark. *Daniam … pertransiens* "passing through Denmark"; *me Uraniburgi invisere* "to visit me at Uraniborg."
- **Wittich's books.** *Witichianorum scriptorum et librorum … quos post fata reliquit … procuratio* = the charge (custody/administration) of the writings and books **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586) left at his death; the two barons had undertaken to manage them, and Tycho asks Hagecius to remind them — a matter bearing on the books and papers Tycho hoped to recover from Wittich's estate. *post fata reliquit* = "left behind after his death" (*fata*, lit. "the fates" = death), rendered straight.
- **Dateline / place.** *Raptim Hafniae die 22. Martij Anno Domini 89* = "In haste, at **Copenhagen** (Hafnia), the 22nd day of March, in the Year of the Lord [15]89" (**O.S.** — Denmark kept the Julian calendar; this chapter's convention). The catalogue label ("1589. 22. marts. Copenhagen") agrees with the dateline. *manu propria* = "by my own hand," marking an autograph subscription.
- **Textual crux (flagged, not smoothed).** After *Idem etiam circa rem Cometicam* the source reads **"expeterem. peterem."** — a duplicated/dittographic verb (the compound *expeterem* "I would request" followed by an isolated *peterem* "I would ask," with an intervening full stop). This is almost certainly a printing/transmission slip; the sense ("the same I would also request concerning the matter of the comet[s]") is not in doubt, but the doubled reading is preserved verbatim in the Source block by this chapter's convention rather than silently emended. Likewise *Tagone Krabio* (ablative): the bearer's forename appears as *Tago*; rendered "Tage Krabbe."
- **No date discrepancy and no negation reversal.** The dateline matches the label; the letter's several negations are reproduced exactly (*non intermittendum*, *absit … ut … addubitem*, *ne … supersedeas*, *non gravatim*, *non intermittas*, *non gravatus est*, *non patitur*), with no count altered.

Collated every proper name (Tago Krabbe, Munoz the Spaniard/MUNOSI Hispani, Johann Septimius von Lichtenstein, Felician von Herberstein, Paul Wittich/WITICHIANORUM), every year cited (comet of '77, comet of '80), and the closing date '22. text.original:
HENRICUS BRUCÆUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.
S. D.

LEGI responsionem tuam ad meas literas de Cometa, in qua non eo candore usus videris, quem expectabam, nec eo animo nostra accepisse, quo scripta sunt. Miraris, me tuam Hypothesin probare, cum veterum autorum errores mordicus tueri soleam. Quid ita? An quia infinitis tenebrionum erroneis sententijs non assentiar, miraris? Ego vero levitatis magnae, ingenij parvi, imbecillis iudicij arbitror, non recte expensis adversariorum opinionibus, quibus calumniandi quam recte sentiendi maior est cura, subito assentiri. Soleo ego diu multumque premere, quae contradicuntur, et quomodo refelli queant, cogitare, tum vel in priore sententia persistere, aut etiam aliter sentientibus adhaerere. Non me movent convitia, quibus tenebriones veteres tam Medicos quam Philosophos obruunt, et hac ratione turbae indoctae fucum faciunt. Mihi veritatis semper magnum fuit studium, dissentiendi levitas semper invisa. Quod vero Dithmarsus iste tuam Hypothesin surripuerit, non est, quod hoc te admodum moveat. Cum enim observationibus destituatur, e quibus Hypothesis confirmatur et motuum ratio construitur, nihil profecerit, alienis plumis se ornasse, neque intelligentibus persuaserit, suum esse inventum. Perge in opere inchoato, et macte animo prosequere institutum. Haec ad immortalitatem via.

Quod vero de Lunae maxima latitudine scribis, quam 15 scrupulis statuis Ptolemaica maiorem, non facere magnum in eclipsibus discrimen, quae circa nodos incidunt, verum est; attamen in maxima distantia a nodis, in qua eclipses incidere possunt, aliquid, credo, dabit. Sed quare me in tenebrionis sententiam trahis, qui sidera humore vesci credidit, cum alio nostra spectet oratio? Videbimus, quam solide a te eorum sententia refellatur, qui sentiunt, hunc aërem undiquaque permeabilem coelestem regionem implere. Quantum enim ex literis ad PEUCERUM datis colligere possum, statuisti omnium sententias secus sentientium refellere. Hypothesin quoque tuam explicas. Verum ego prius de ea cum quodam, qui apud te fuit, contuli, et videor assecutus. Quod autem scripsi totam tractationem de Cometis circa individua versari, quorum cognitio unâ cum ipso Cometa intercidit, verum est, cum nec motus idem, nec corporis forma eadem unquam sit reditura. Non ivero tamen infitias, multa cum his tradi posse, ut non pauca tuo operi sunt inserta, quae ingeniose inventa et cum iudicio accommodata ad alia plura transferri commode possint. Quare non est, quod sphaericorum libellorum aetatem superatura scribas, quorum plerique non Bosphorum visent, ut de suis poëmatis prodidit HORATIUS, sed pharmacopolia et cauponas, ut habeant, in quod piper, thus, lardum et alia eius generis reponant. Atque utinam Sphaericis id tantum libellis usuveniret, et non maximae parti scriptorum, quae hisce temporibus in lucem eduntur, nisi forte in Bibliothecis aliquandiu delitescant blattis et tineis exposita. Quid itaque de meis mihi pollicear, ipse intelligis; spem magnam immortalitatis suorum scriptorum alijs relinquo. Non est autem, quod graviter feras, quod de Cometae distantia scripsi. Sic enim acceperam: post enim animadverti, de apparente te loqui.

Quod ad postremas tuas literas attinet, quibus nostri sat Boreaae datum meministi, quid aliud tibi respondeam, quam quod summis tam Medicis quam Philosophis visum est, non habeo, quorum ea fuit sententia, coelum sequi hominum naturas. Durum et asperum dura et aspera ingenia ferre, moderata temperatum. Id naturalibus rationibus posset confirmari, sed supersedeo. Quod si aliqui studijs liberalibus exculti, aut bonorum consuetudine humaniores et civiliores evaserint, hoc veterum sententiam minime evertit. Ipse si progrediare versus Boream, sic re ipsa deprehendes. Nec volo comparationem, quae semper est odiosa, instituere. Sufficit, utplurimum ita se habere. Possent enim incidere causae, quae coeli sive aëris constitutionem nihil morentur. Nam et Scythae non pauci temperata satis loca incolunt, barbari tamen et inhumani permanent, sic a puero educati. Et alij Regum aut Magistratus studio ad humanius vitae genus transferuntur. At Philosophi hasce causas restringunt, et quid aër per se efficiat, referunt, Boeotoque aëre natum scribunt.

Sculptorem conveni, is se adfore aperto mari pollicebatur et in Insulam tuam traiecturum; verum non apparuit. Ex hisce literis et chartulis adiunctis, intelliges, quid actum sit; quid fieri insuper velis, perscribes.

Bene vale, amantiss. TYCHO.
Rostochij 23. Martij An. 1589.
Henricus Brucaeus,
plane tuus.
text.english:
**Heinrich Brucaeus to Tycho Brahe.**
Sends greeting.

I have read your reply to my letter on the comet, in which you do not seem to me to have shown the candour I expected, nor to have taken my words in the spirit in which they were written. You wonder that I approve your hypothesis, when I am wont to defend the errors of the ancient authors tooth and nail. Why so? Is it because I do not assent to the countless erroneous opinions of the obscurantists that you wonder? For my part, I judge it a mark of great fickleness, of small wit, of feeble judgement, to assent suddenly without having rightly weighed the opinions of one's opponents — opinions in which the care to slander is greater than the care to think rightly. I am wont to press long and hard upon things that are disputed, and to consider how they may be refuted, and then either to persist in my earlier opinion, or even to side with those who think otherwise. I am not moved by the abuse with which the obscurantists overwhelm the ancients, both physicians and philosophers, and by this means throw dust in the eyes of the unlearned crowd. The pursuit of truth has always been a great thing with me; the fickleness of dissent always hateful. But that that fellow from Dithmarschen has filched your hypothesis — there is no reason this should much trouble you. For since he is destitute of the observations from which the hypothesis is confirmed and the account of the motions is constructed, he will have gained nothing by decking himself in others' feathers, nor will he have persuaded men of understanding that the invention is his own. Press on in the work begun, and with good heart pursue what you have set in hand. This is the road to immortality.

As for what you write about the Moon's greatest latitude — which you set at 15 minutes greater than the Ptolemaic value, [saying] that it makes no great difference in the eclipses that fall near the nodes — that is true; yet at the greatest distance from the nodes at which eclipses can fall, it will, I believe, yield something. But why do you drag me into the opinion of that obscurantist who believed the stars feed on moisture, when my discourse looks to something else? We shall see how solidly you refute the opinion of those who hold that this everywhere-permeable air fills the celestial region. For as far as I can gather from the letter you sent to Peucer, you have resolved to refute the opinions of all who think otherwise. You also set out your hypothesis. But I had previously conferred about it with a certain man who had been with you, and I think I have grasped it. As for my having written that the whole treatment of comets turns upon individual things, the knowledge of which perishes together with the comet itself — that is true, since neither the same motion nor the same bodily form will ever return. Yet I do not deny that much can be handed down along with these things; so that not a few matters are inserted into your work which, ingeniously discovered and judiciously adapted, can conveniently be carried over to many other matters. Wherefore there is no reason for you to write that [your work] will outlast the age of the little books on the sphere — most of which will not visit the Bosphorus, as Horace declared of his own poems, but the apothecaries' shops and the taverns, to serve as wrapping in which to store away pepper, frankincense, lard, and other things of that kind. And would that this befell the little books on the sphere alone, and not the greatest part of the writings that are brought to light in these times — unless perhaps they lie hidden for a while in libraries, exposed to bookworms and moths. What, then, I may promise myself of my own [writings], you yourself understand; I leave the great hope of the immortality of their writings to others. There is, moreover, no reason for you to take ill what I wrote about the comet's distance. For so I had understood it; but afterwards I noticed that you were speaking of the apparent [distance].

As for your last letter, in which you recall that enough was conceded by me to the North, what other answer am I to give you than what has seemed [right] to the greatest of physicians as well as philosophers — whose opinion was that the heaven follows the natures of men[?] [It is] harsh and rough natures that bear the harsh and rough [climate], temperate natures the temperate. This could be confirmed by natural arguments, but I forbear. But if some, refined by the liberal studies, or grown more humane and civil by the company of good men, have turned out so, this in no way overturns the opinion of the ancients. If you yourself should travel northward, you will discover it so in the very fact. Nor do I wish to set up a comparison, which is always odious. It is enough that for the most part it is so. For causes might intervene that pay no heed to the constitution of the heaven or of the air. For not a few Scythians too inhabit lands temperate enough, and yet remain barbarous and uncivil, having been so reared from boyhood. And others are brought over to a more humane way of life by the zeal of their kings or magistrates. But the philosophers limit these causes, and report what the air of itself effects, and write that [such a one] was born under a Boeotian air.

I have met with the sculptor; he was promising that he would come, once the sea was open, and cross over to your island; but he has not appeared. From this letter and the little papers enclosed you will understand what has been done; what you wish to have done besides, you will write [to me].

Fare you well, most loving Tycho.
At Rostock, 23 March, the year 1589.
Heinrich Brucaeus,
wholly yours.

Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (Hendrik van den Broucke, 1530/31–1593), Flemish-born professor of mathematics and then of medicine at the University of Rostock, and an elder correspondent and early supporter of Tycho. The letter is his reply in the running 1588–89 exchange occasioned by Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (Uraniborg, 1588), the comet treatise.
- **Recipient / salutation.** *S. D.* = *salutem dicit*, "sends greeting". The closing apostrophe *Bene vale, amantiss. Tycho* ("Fare you well, most loving Tycho") addresses Tycho in the vocative; *plane tuus* = "wholly yours."
- ***Dithmarsus iste … tuam Hypothesin surripuerit*** — "that fellow from Dithmarschen has filched your hypothesis": **Nicolaus Reimarus Ursus** (Nicolai Reymers Bär, "Ursus," c. 1551–1600), born in Dithmarschen, whom Tycho accused of stealing his geo-heliocentric world-system after a visit to Uraniborg; Ursus had published a like system in his *Fundamentum astronomicum* (Strasbourg, 1588). The literature (Gingerich, *Annotated Census of De revolutionibus*) confirms the identification "Nicolaus Raimarus Ursus Dithmarsus." Brucaeus's point — that without observations the borrowed scheme is worthless — is rendered without softening Tycho's own charge of theft.
- ***Hypothesis*** — kept as "hypothesis" throughout (the world-system / geometric model); *motuum ratio* = "the account of the motions."
- **Astronomy (Moon's latitude).** *de Lunae maxima latitudine … quam 15 scrupulis statuis Ptolemaica maiorem* = "the Moon's greatest latitude, which you set at 15 minutes [of arc] greater than the Ptolemaic [value]"; *scrupulus* = arc-minute, here "minute(s)." *quae circa nodos incidunt* = "[eclipses] that fall near the nodes"; *nodus* → **node**, *eclipsis* → **eclipse**. *maxima latitudine* / *maxima distantia*: the qualifier "greatest" is the source's own (*maxima*), not an editorial insertion.
- ***qui sidera humore vesci credidit*** — "[the obscurantist] who believed the stars feed on moisture": the old doctrine (Stoic / Aristotelian-meteorological) that the heavenly bodies are nourished by exhalations drawn up from below; Brucaeus protests that this is not the doctrine Tycho should impute to him.
- ***hunc aërem undiquaque permeabilem coelestem regionem implere*** — "this everywhere-permeable air fills the celestial region": the fluid-heavens question (whether one continuous, permeable air-like medium extends through the heavens, as against solid celestial spheres) which Tycho's comet work pressed; Brucaeus expects Tycho to refute the solid-orb party.
- ***literis ad Peucerum datis*** — "the letter sent to **Peucer**": **Caspar Peucer** (1525–1602), Wittenberg physician-astronomer and Melanchthon's son-in-law, another node of this correspondence-network.
- ***individua … quorum cognitio unâ cum ipso Cometa intercidit*** — "individual things, the knowledge of which perishes together with the comet itself": *individua* in the logical sense of unrepeatable particulars; a comet, being a transient singular, leaves no recurring motion or form, so (Brucaeus had argued) the science of it dies with it — qualified, as Brucaeus does, by his concession that transferable method survives.
- ***sphaericorum libellorum*** — "the little books on the sphere": the elementary *Sphaera* textbooks (in the tradition of Sacrobosco), here disparaged as ephemeral.
- **Allusion (Horace).** *non Bosphorum visent, ut de suis poëmatis prodidit Horatius, sed pharmacopolia et cauponas … in quod piper, thus … reponant* — Horace's conceit (*Epistles* I.20; cf. *Ars Poetica*) of the worthless book ending as wrapping-paper for grocers' pepper and incense. The grim list (*piper, thus, largum*) is kept; *largum* is read as "bulk/ample goods" of the same shop-stock kind, paralleling *alia eius generis*. *blattis et tineis* = "bookworms and moths."
- ***nostri sat Boreaae datum*** — "enough was conceded by me to the North": refers back to Tycho's previous letter on the old climate-theory of national character (the *Boreas*, the north wind / the North). *Boreaae* is the manuscript form (with doubled vowel) for *Boreae*. The whole third paragraph debates the classical-medical doctrine — *coelum sequi hominum naturas*, "the heaven follows the natures of men" — that climate shapes temperament: northern peoples harsh because their climate is harsh.
- ***Scythae … barbari … Boeotoque aëre natum*** — the Scythians as the type of the cold-dwelling barbarian; *Boeoto aëre natum* = "born under a Boeotian air," the proverbial dull/stupid air of Boeotia (cf. *Boeotum in crasso … aëre*, Horace, *Epistles* II.1.244). Kept as allusion; the philosophers' position (that air *of itself* dulls or sharpens wit) is distinguished from the king-and-magistrate counter-causes Brucaeus allows.
- ***summis tam Medicis quam Philosophis*** — "the greatest of physicians as well as philosophers": the Hippocratic–Galenic and Aristotelian authorities behind the climate doctrine. Punctuation: the source runs the rhetorical question *quid aliud tibi respondeam … non habeo* together; an editorial *[?]* and *[It is]* are bracketed to carry the sense without recasting.
- ***Sculptorem … in Insulam tuam traiecturum*** — "the sculptor … would cross over to your island": a craftsman (engraver/carver) Brucaeus had engaged on Tycho's behalf, to come to **Hven** once the sea was open (i.e. ice-free) in spring; *aperto mari* = "the sea being open." *chartulis adiunctis* = "the little papers enclosed."
- **Dateline.** *Rostochij 23. Martij An. 1589* = "at **Rostock** [Rostochium], 23 March 1589" (Old Style; Denmark and the Lutheran north kept the Julian calendar). The header date matches the dateline; the edition label ("1589. 23. marts. Rostock") agrees, so no discrepancy arises.
- **Editorial insertions.** Bracketed words (*[saying]*, *[other]*, *[value]*, *[such a one]*, *[right]*, *[It is]*, *[?]*, *[your work]*, *[yet]*, *[to me]*, *[distance]*) supply syntax implied but not lexically present in the source; the source's own hedges (*credo* "I believe," *videor assecutus* "I think I have grasped," *Non ivero infitias* "I do not deny") are preserved unsharpened.
- **Correction.** Latin corrected against Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia VII, page 167: "largum" corrected to "lardum" (lard/bacon). The English's bracketed guess "[other] bulk goods" replaced with "lard".

Collated the full letter: the Dithmarschen/hypothesis dispute, the Peucer reference, the Moon's-latitude figure (15 scrupulis), the Horace/spherical-booklets passage, the Scythian/Boeotian-air passage, the sculptor paragraph, and the closing date (Rostochij 23. Martij An. 1589) all match Dreyer. One word-level text error found (largum/lardum, low severity, does not change the passage's overall sense) forces the grade to C per the rubric even though the verdict is *minor*.

**1 defect found:**
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original misprints 'lardum' (lard/bacon, a stock item merchants wrapped in waste paper, per the Horace/spice-shop trope Brucaeus is invoking) as 'largum', an adjective that cannot function as a listed noun; the English's odd bracketed '[other] bulk goods' is a downstream guess at the corrupted word rather than a rendering of 'lardum'. Dreyer prints: *in quod piper, thus, lardum et alia eius generis reponant*.

**Repaired.** The single defect site was collated against Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia volume VII, page 167 (page image, not the digitised text layer). Confirmed: "ut habeant, in quod piper, thus, lardum et alia eius generis reponant." No other cruxes were found on the sampled pages.
