documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Ioannes Craigus* = **John Craig** (d. c.1620), Scottish physician and mathematician, educated on the Continent (Frankfurt an der Oder, where Duncan Liddel studied under him; later Königsberg), and from the 1580s royal physician at the court of James VI in Edinburgh. He entered a protracted epistolary dispute with Tycho over the geo-heliocentric world-system (treated in Adam Mosley, "Tycho Brahe and John Craig: The Dynamic of a Dispute," 2002); this letter is an early, still-courteous instalment of that exchange. The subscription *Doctor* marks his medical doctorate.
- **The astronomical objection (the substance of the letter).** Craig grants the structure of Tycho's *Hypothesis* — *Terra luminarium et Sol caeterorum Planetarum centrum*, "the Earth the centre of the luminaries [Sun and Moon], the Sun the centre of the remaining planets," i.e. the geo-heliocentric arrangement. His objection is that *Mars acronychus terris propior fiat Sole*: that Mars at opposition (**acronychal** — rising at sunset, hence diametrically opposite the Sun) is brought nearer the Earth than the Sun is. This is the celebrated consequence of Tycho's system that the Martian orb must intersect the solar orb — the very point that made Tycho abandon the solid celestial spheres. Craig reads it as an *absurdum*; the hedge *non alienum … sed tamen absurdum implicat* is preserved (he concedes the merit, then flags the flaw).
- **Craig's proposed remedies.** (1) *si punctum Terrae vicinius quam Sol statuatur centrum* — set the planets' centre at a point **nearer the Earth than the Sun**; (2) failing that, *duplici epicyclo augeatur orbis Planetae superioris* — augment a superior planet's orb with a **double epicycle** (here = a second, additional epicycle), so that solid orbs (*orbes*) can still be assigned to the planets without intersection. Craig's programme — *ut Physicis et Mathematicis pariter satisfiat*, "that satisfaction be given to the *Physicists* and the *Mathematicians* alike" — is to save both the physical reality of solid spheres and the geometry; this is the crux of his disagreement with Tycho, who held the spheres to be fluid/non-existent.
- **Duncan Liddel.** *M. Duncanus Liddelius* = **Duncan Liddel** (1561–1613), Scottish mathematician and physician, then teaching at Frankfurt an der Oder / Rostock (later Helmstedt; he endowed a mathematics chair at Aberdeen in 1613). *M.* = *Magister*, "Master" (academic). *cantationem … scripsit* — literally "wrote his *song/chant*"; here a faintly belittling figure for Liddel's set-piece on the double-epicycle device. Kept as the metaphor "little tune," with the diminutive force flagged rather than smoothed to a neutral "account."
- **Chymica / alchemy.** *Chymicis … versatum* — Craig solicits Tycho's chemical (Paracelsian-iatrochemical) secrets. *Rollandus … in suis Centurijs curarum* = the *Centuriae curationum* / *Centuries of cures*, a medical-recipe collection (most plausibly the *Curationum … centuriae* genre associated with the period's iatrochemists; the precise "Rolland" is not securely fixed — see crux). The named preparations: *aqua benedicta* "blessed water" (a period purgative/emetic compound — *not* holy water in the devotional sense); *balsamum sulphuris* "balsam of sulphur" (sulphur dissolved in oil, an iatrochemical remedy); *spiritus vitae* "spirit of life"; *extractum esulae* "extract of **spurge**" (*esula* = *Euphorbia esula*, a drastic purgative), which Craig says he prepares *communi modo per spiritum vini*, "in the common way, by spirit of wine," but suspects a *singularis ratio*, a special method. *distillatae aquae purgantes* = "distilled purging waters." Period terms retained and glossed by this chapter's convention; none modernised.
- **Peter Paysen.** *Petrus Paysen Danus* — **Peter Paysen** (Peder Paysen), a Dane, here described as a learned traveller skilled in languages and mathematics, carrying this letter as a letter of introduction to Tycho. Not otherwise identified here; the name is given as written.
- **Dateline.** *Datae Edenburgi 9. Iulij* = "Given at **Edinburgh**, 9 July." The source dateline carries **no year**; the edition label supplies *1589*, consistent with the Tycho–Craig exchange and with the Berlin-copy witness. The header therefore reads "9 July 1589," but note that the year is editorial/catalogue-supplied, not present in the dateline. **O.S.**: a Scottish correspondent in 1589 wrote Old Style (Scotland did not adopt the Gregorian calendar until 1600/1752); the 9 July is Julian.
- **Edition / witness.** Printed in the *Commercium litterarium clarorum virorum* (the edition of record per the source); MS witness A = a handwritten copy bound in a copy of Tycho's astronomical writings, now in Berlin (shelfmark not specified in the source).
- **Formulae.** *Bene et feliciter vale* → "Fare you well and happily". *Tuus … Doctor* subscription rendered in full.

text.original:
VNSERM MATHEMATICO VND LIEBEN GETREWEN CHRISTOPHORO ROTHMANNO.
WILHELM VON GOTTES GNADEN LANDTGRAUE ZU HESSEN/ GRAUE ZU CATZENELNBOGEN/ DIETZ/ ZIEGENHAIN VND NIDDA/ ETC.

LIEBER Getrewer/ Wir mögen dir in gnaden nicht verhalten/ das Zeiger dieses D. Nicodemus Frischlinus vorhabens ist/ eine Reyse in Daniam zuthun. Dieweil er dann sonder zweiffel zu dem TYCHONI de BRAHE kommen wirdet/ Als ist an dich vnser befelich in gnaden/ das du etwa ein sein schreiben an jhnen thuest/ vnd von jhme zuwissen begerest/ was er jtzo gutes vorhabe/ vnd wann er seine vorgehabte Arbeit dermahls eins werde außgehen lassen/ Dann vns verlange sehr darnach solchs zusehen. Das thun wir vns zu dir mit gnaden versehen.

DatumHombergk am 26. Iulij, Anno 89.
WILHELM LANDTGRAFF ZU HESSEN.
text.english:
**To Our Mathematician and trusty well-beloved Christoph Rothmann.**
**Wilhelm, by the grace of God Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda, etc.**

Trusty well-beloved. We would not graciously withhold from you that the bearer of this [letter], Master Nicodemus Frischlin, has it in mind to undertake a journey into Denmark [*Daniam*]. Since, then, he will without doubt come to Tycho de Brahe [*TYCHONI de BRAHE*], it is therefore Our gracious charge upon you that you write him some letter of yours to him, and desire to learn from him what good thing he now has in hand, and when he will at length let his earlier-undertaken work go forth; for We greatly long to see such [a thing]. This We graciously look for from you.

Given at Homberg, the 26th of July, in the year [15]89.
Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), the astronomer-prince of Kassel and Tycho's principal German correspondent. The titulature — *Landgraf zu Hessen, Graf zu Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain und Nidda* — is the standard Hessian style; preserved in full by this chapter's convention
- **Recipient.** **Christoph Rothmann** (c. 1550 – c. 1600), the Landgrave's resident mathematician/astronomer at Kassel from late 1584. Here addressed as the prince's subordinate — *Vnserm Mathematico vnd lieben getrewen* ("Our Mathematician and trusty well-beloved") — in the princely *Wir/du* register.
- **The bearer.** *D. Nicodemus Frischlinus* = **Nicodemus Frischlin** (1547–1590), the Neo-Latin poet, dramatist, and philologist (here *poeta laureatus* of the Count Palatine). Mosley (*Bearing the Heavens*) confirms the occasion exactly: Wilhelm, hunting at Homburg in July 1589 and lacking recent news of Tycho's work, learned that Frischlin intended to travel to Denmark and induced him to go via Kassel carrying these instructions for Rothmann. *Zeiger dieses* ("the bearer of this [letter]") is the chancery formula for the courier carrying the document.
- **Code-switches (German → Latin).** The letter switches into Latin for the proper-name material the chancery treats as fixed: *in Daniam* ("into Denmark," accusative of motion); *zu dem TYCHONI de BRAHE* (dative *Tychoni*, the Latin name retained whole inside the German clause); the heading *Christophoro Rothmanno* and *Datum* ("Given"). The code-switch is preserved by this chapter's convention; *Datum* rendered "Given."
- **Negations / legal force.** Two negation-bearing constructions, both reproduced exactly. (1) *Wir mögen dir … nicht verhalten* is a courtly litotes — literally "We may not withhold from you," i.e. "We would not keep from you / We are pleased to inform you"; rendered "We would not … withhold," keeping the single negation rather than flattening it to a plain positive. (2) *sonder zweiffel* = "without doubt," rendered as such. The operative clause *ist … vnser befelich … das du …* is a gracious command ("it is Our charge upon you that you …"), not a request; the three governed verbs — *ein schreiben … thuest* (write a letter), *zuwissen begerest* (seek to learn), and the indirect questions *was er … vorhabe / wann er … außgehen lassen [werde]* — are kept in their subordinate, reported-question mood.
- ***was er jtzo gutes vorhabe / seine vorgehabte Arbeit … außgehen lassen.*** "What good thing he now has in hand" and "let his earlier-undertaken work go forth [= publish it]": the Landgrave is asking Rothmann to draw from Tycho, through Frischlin, news of Tycho's current projects and especially when he will at last *publish* the work already undertaken — *außgehen lassen* in the period sense "issue, bring out (in print)." The phrasing is kept neutral; no specific Tychonic title is named in the source, so none is supplied.
- **Place / dateline crux.** The dateline reads *DatumHombergk am 26. Iulij, Anno 89* (the 1596 print runs *Datum* and *Hombergk* together without a space; transcribed verbatim). The **place is Homberg**, a Hessian landgravial seat where Wilhelm was hunting — **not Kassel**, which the edition label field gives. Mosley's "hunting at Homburg in July of that same year" corroborates the dateline against the catalogue label; the header therefore leads with the as-written "Homberg" and appends "(catalogued Kassel)." Homberg (Efze), north of the Schwalm hunting grounds, is the most probable referent for a Hessian *Hombergk* hunting dateline, though the source does not disambiguate it from other Hessian Hombergs; flagged rather than asserted. Date *26. Iulij Anno 89* = 26 July 1589, Old Style (Hesse keeping the Julian calendar; this chapter's convention); not silently converted.
- **Edition of record.** The letter is printed in Tycho's own *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Liber I, Uraniborg 1596) — the volume Tycho printed at Hven — whence Dreyer's *Opera Omnia* VI. No manuscript witness is recorded in the edition.

text.original:
LITERÆ CHRISTOPHORI ROTHMANNI AD TYCHONEM BRAHE, AD ANNVM OCTUAGESIMUM NONUM POTIUS PERTINENTES. S. P.

QVID superioribus tibi literis scripserim, et qua ratione syncere voluntati tuæ morem gesserim, tibique meum qualecunque, nec fortassis vsque adeo magni momenti iudicium candide explicarim, Nobilissime Excellentissimeque Dn. TYCHO, mihique longe charissime, tibi est notissimum. Etsi autem in proxime præteritis Nundinis Francofurdensibus responsum non sine desiderio expectaremus, tamen nihil prorsus, quod a te esset, nobis exhibitum est. Cuius rei causam, cum a me impense requireret Illustrissimus Princeps noster, nihil aliud respondere potui, quam aut te non habuisse cui recte literas ad nos committere posses, aut alijs negotijs impeditum fuissent. Hoc vero tempore, de nouo, ab Illustrissimo Principe meo, iam extra munitionem Cassellanam, in Comitatu Hombergico, venationibus vacante, literas mihi attulit Dn. D. NICODEMVS FRISCHLINVS, vir ex eruditis suis scriptis tibi forte notissimus, et Com. Palat, ac Poët. Laure, quibus iubeor, vt a te simul et responsum flagitem, ac te insuper admoneam, ne Opus tuum de Recentioribus mundi ætherei Phænomenis absolutum, Illustriss. ipsius Celsitudini mittere, vlterius differas. Se enim maximo eius videndi desiderio teneri, vt ipsa verba, quæ in dictis Illustriss. ipsius Celsitudinis literis continentur, referam. Scis me superioribus tibi literis significasse, quod spem fecerim Illustriss. ipsius Celsit. de Opere illo tuo â te huc mittendo. Id itaque iam Illustrissimus Heros adeo vrget. Quod igitur superioribus feci literis, illud adhuc a te vehementer etiam atque etiam maiorem in modum peto contendoque, vt fidem meam redimas. Deinde etsi Illustriss. Princeps noster superiori Autumno nihil literarum ad te dedit, varijs modis impeditus, tamen nihilominus aliquas iam a te expectat, præsertim de statu tuo quid agas, et quid iam tibi sit de Astronomicis laboribus præ manibus: Nec ipsi gratior vlla est, quam sibi quæ BRAHÆ præscripsit pagina nomen. Sed non dubito, quin in his omnibus Illustriss. ipsius Celsit. sis cumulatissime satisfacturus. Cum item Illustriss. et Clementiss. Princeps meus mihi mandarit, vt per hunc doctissimum sane virum tibi scriberem, facile per te intelligere poteris, Illustriss. ipsius Celsit. hoc suo ad me mandato hunc tibi eo commendatiorem reddere voluisse. Sed tamen id per te propter studia Philosophica facturus es, vt non ignoro. Cognoui etiam ex literis fratris mei Iohannis, quod disputationes nostras ad Dn. D. PEVCERVM miseris, quodque Dn. PEVCERVS alia consilia proferat, nec mihi aut tibi suffragari velit. Sed hæc quo sint habenda loco tu intelligis. Nihil consilium hîc, nihil humana valet authoritas. Doctrinam Triangulorum qui intelligit, sua sponte in veram pedibus ibit sententiam. Tu fac responsione tua, vt ad dulcissimas nostras Philosophicas disputationes redeamus. Sed fortasse plus quam sat erat.

Tu igitur Nobiliss. et Excellentiss. Dn. TYCHO quam optime vale, quæque scripsi in optimam partem accipe.
Cassellis, 6. Calendas Augusti, Anno 1589.
T. T.
CHRISTOPHORVS ROTHMANNVS.
text.english:
**A LETTER OF CHRISTOPH ROTHMANN TO TYCHO BRAHE, BELONGING RATHER TO THE YEAR EIGHTY-NINE. Heartiest greeting.**

What I wrote to you in my last letter, and in what spirit I sincerely complied with your wish, and frankly set out for you my own judgement — such as it was, and perhaps not of any very great moment — is very well known to you, most noble and most excellent Master Tycho, and to me by far the dearest of men. But although at the Frankfurt fair just past we were awaiting a reply not without longing, yet nothing at all that came from you was delivered to us. When our Most Illustrious Prince pressed me earnestly for the cause of this, I could answer nothing else but that either you had had no one to whom you could properly entrust a letter to us, or that you had been hindered by other business. But at this time, anew, from my Most Illustrious Prince — who is now outside the fortifications of Kassel, in the County of Homberg, taking his leisure at the hunt — a letter has been brought to me by Master Doctor Nicodemus Frischlin, a man perhaps very well known to you from his learned writings, Count Palatine and Poet Laureate, by which I am ordered both to demand a reply of you and, moreover, to admonish you not to defer any longer the sending of your completed Work on the recent phenomena of the aethereal world to His Most Illustrious Highness himself. For he is held by the greatest desire to see it — to report the very words contained in the said letter of His Most Illustrious Highness. You know that in my last letter I indicated to you that I had raised His Most Illustrious Highness's hope of that Work of yours being sent here by you. This, therefore, the Most Illustrious Hero now presses so much. What I did, then, in my last letter, that same I still ask and strive for from you vehemently, again and again, in even greater measure: that you redeem my pledge. Next, although our Most Illustrious Prince sent no letters to you last autumn, hindered in various ways, yet he nonetheless now awaits some from you, especially concerning your situation — what you are doing, and what you now have in hand of your astronomical labours; nor is any page more welcome to him than one that has set the name of BRAHE at its head. But I do not doubt that in all these matters you will give His Most Illustrious Highness the most abundant satisfaction. Since my Most Illustrious and Most Clement Prince has likewise charged me to write to you through this man — most learned indeed — you will easily understand for yourself that His Most Illustrious Highness, by this command of his to me, wished to render this man the more commended to you on that account. Yet you will do this on your own account, for the sake of philosophical studies, as I am well aware. I have learned, too, from the letters of my brother Johannes, that you sent our disputations to Master Doctor Peucer, and that Master Peucer puts forward other opinions, and is unwilling to side with either me or you. But in what regard these things are to be held, you understand. Here counsel avails nothing, human authority avails nothing. Whoever understands the Doctrine of Triangles will, of his own accord, go on foot into the true opinion. Do you, by your reply, bring it about that we return to our most delightful philosophical disputations. But perhaps [I have said] more than was enough.

Do you therefore, most noble and most excellent Master Tycho, fare as well as may be, and take in the best part the things I have written.
At Kassel, the sixth day before the Kalends of August [27 July], in the year 1589.
Yours wholly,
Christoph Rothmann.

- **Recipient / addressee titulature.** *Nobilissime Excellentissimeque Dn. TYCHO* — "most noble and most excellent Master Tycho" (*Dn.* = *Dominus*, this chapter's convention).
- **The Prince.** *Illustrissimus Princeps noster / Illustriss. ipsius Celsit. / Illustrissimus Heros* — **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592). *Celsitudo* → "Highness" and *Princeps* → "Prince" by this chapter's convention; *Heros* ("Hero") is kept as Rothmann's honorific flourish. *munitio Cassellana … in Comitatu Hombergico* = "the fortifications of Kassel … the County of Homberg" (Homberg an der Efze, in Hesse).
- ***Nicodemus Frischlinus*** = **Nicodemus Frischlin** (1547–1590), the Württemberg humanist poet and dramatist, *Comes Palatinus* (Count Palatine) and *Poeta Laureatus* (Poet Laureate) — here the bearer of the Landgrave's letter, whom Rothmann commends to Tycho. *Com. Palat, ac Poët. Laure.* expanded accordingly.
- ***Opus tuum de Recentioribus mundi aetherei Phaenomenis*** — Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (the second volume of his projected trilogy, the comet/world-system book printed at Uraniborg), here named as the work the Landgrave is impatient to receive. Rendered "[your] Work on the recent phenomena of the aethereal world."
- ***Nundinae Francofurdenses*** — "the Frankfurt fair" (the Frankfurt book fair), the standard early-modern channel for transmitting scholarly letters and books.
- ***disputationes nostras … ad Dn. D. Peucerum miseris*** — "you sent our disputations to Master Doctor Peucer." **Caspar Peucer** (1525–1602), Wittenberg physician-astronomer, whom Tycho was using as an arbiter; Rothmann learned, via his brother **Johannes Rothmann**, that Tycho had circulated their private debate to Peucer, who would side with neither. Mosley (*Bearing the Heavens*) quotes this very sentence and dates the letter 27 July 1589, corroborating the dateline below.
- ***Doctrina Triangulorum*** — the **Doctrine of Triangles** (trigonometry); Rothmann's point that the dispute will be settled by mathematics, not authority. *sua sponte … pedibus ibit sententiam* renders an idiom of formally "going over" to an opinion (as a senator crosses the floor *pedibus in sententiam*); kept as "will … go on foot into the true opinion."
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam* → "heartiest greeting". *quam optime vale* → "fare as well as may be" (, *Vale*). *T. T.* = *Tuus Totus* → "Yours wholly," the subscription.
- **Heading.** *AD ANNVM OCTUAGESIMUM NONUM POTIUS PERTINENTES* — "belonging rather to the year eighty-nine": **this is the editor's (Tycho's own 1596) note correcting the letter's placement to 1589**, printed as part of the running head. It is translated, not dropped, because it is itself the textual evidence resolving the date.
- **Dateline / calendar.** *Cassellis, 6. Calendas Augusti, Anno 1589* = "At Kassel, *ante diem VI Kalendas Augusti*, 1589." Counting inclusively from the Kalends of August (1 Aug.): pridie = 31 July, III Kal. = 30, IV = 29, V = 28, **VI Kal. Aug. = 27 July**. The date is **27 July 1589 (O.S.** — Hesse-Kassel kept the Julian calendar at this period; the Protestant German states did not adopt the Gregorian reform until 1700). Roman-calendar idiom is given with the civil gloss by this chapter's convention.
- **Date crux — catalogue vs. source (RESOLVED, flagged).** The edition label reads *"1587. 17. januar. Kassel."* This is contradicted by **two** internal witnesses: (1) the letter's own running head, *ad annum octuagesimum nonum … pertinentes* ("belonging rather to the year eighty-nine"), and (2) the dateline, *Anno 1589*. The internal content also fixes 1589: the reference to *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* as a completed work the Landgrave is awaiting, the prior-autumn silence, and the circulation of the disputations to Peucer all belong to mid-1589. Mosley independently dates the letter **27 July 1589**. The header therefore leads with the as-written date (27 July 1589) and notes the catalogue date; the "17 January 1587" label is a catalogue error and is **not** adopted. Per this chapter's convention, the discrepancy is recorded and not silently reconciled in the body.
- **Edition of record.** The edition field cites *Tychonis Brahe Dani epistolarum astronomicarum libri … primus* (Uraniborg, 1596), the volume Tycho printed himself; this corresponds to Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VI (the *Epistolae* of the Hesse-Kassel exchange). No manuscript witness is listed in the source.

translation.warrant: **Not collated against Dreyer** — no page reference for this letter, so the grade is capped at Probable however sound the translation looks. No Dreyer page images were available for this letter (no page reference; one of the letters for which no page images were available). Audited the published English against the transcribed original alone: proper names (Nicodemus Frischlin, Peucer, the unnamed Illustrissimus Princeps = Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel), the Frankfurt fair reference, and the date '6 Calendas Augusti, Anno 1589' (= 27 July, rendered correctly as '[27 July]') all check out, and every clause is translated faithfully with no fabrication, omission, or hedge-loss detected. Grade capped at Probable by the audit's rule because Dreyer collation was not possible.

text.original:
LITERASA tuas, Nobilissime Excellentissimeque D. TYCHO, quas tu 21. Februarij
dederas, vix 17. Augusti accepimus, hoc est, sex diebus post, cum alteras ad me
datas scripseras. Quanquam autem varijs iam distrahar occupationibus, tamen
paucis tibi respondendum duxi: Praesertim cum videam, te literas meas superiores,
forte ob varias occupationes etA etiam morbumA , longe aliter intellexisse, quamA ego scripseram. Obijcis enim ea mihi, quae nec vnquam ex verbis illius
Epistolae colligi poterunt, nec etiam mihi vnquam in mentem venerunt. Vbi enim
quicquam detraxi authoritati sacrarum literarum? An ea, quae dixi, non etiam tu
ipse et TheologiA omnes sacras literas interpretantes dicunt? Nisi forte existimas, duo cum
dicant idem, non esse idem: Ideoque in me id reprehendendum esse, quod alijs
facile possit concedi. Si Augustinum
legeris, multo liberius de sacris literis loquentem inuenies. Eandem nuper
sententiam cum exhibuissem Illustrissimo Principi nostro et nostris
Theologis viris summis, ne litem hanc facerem meamA (Nam in nostris Obseruationibus ei peculiare caput attribui, vbi ostendi,
sacras literas non obstare nostrae de liquiditate materiae caelestis sententiae) nec
Princeps nec Theologi eam improbârunt, aut quid reprehendendum in ea inuenerunt.
Et tibi idem faciendum erit, si modo quintam tuam Essentiam defendere volueris.
Mihi solius DEI gloria in omnibus meis actionibus proposita est: ne quid impium
de me cogites. De Crepusculis quoque ne me prorsus caecum effice. Nec enim tam temerarius sum, vt in his rebus quicquam scribam,
quod expertus non sim. Scio desinere Crepusculum Sole 17. Gradibus sub
Horizontem depresso, si vulgariter Crepusculum pro luce dubia accipias. At ego definiuiA Crepusculum eôusque, donec nullum amplius vestigium albicantis Aëris
appareat, quod omnino necessarium est, si extremam superficiem Aëris crassi, qui
illuminari potest, determinare exactius volueris. Considera igitur Aërem circa
locum occubitus Solis, desinente vulgari Crepusculo, eumque cum alijs locis
Horizontis circumcirca, vt ad Ortum, ad Septentrionem, ad MeridiemA confer, diuersitatem coloris et vestigia illa albicantis Aëris omnino
reperies. Sed et Refractionibus meis nescio cur detrahas. Quomodo enim alias
inuenire possum aut etiam eruere, quam ipsa Instrumenta praebent? An in tuam
gratiam hoc faciam? Iniqua certe a me postulas, si hocA postulas. Sed nec titulum Tomorum tuorum de nouis Mundi Aetherei
generationibus repraehendi, nec etiam repraehendendus est, nec tua excusatione
indiget: Siquidem quae fiunt, etiam generari dicuntur; et reuera Cometae in Caelo
generantur. Proposui ea non assertiue, sed dubitanter et interrogatiue potius,
praecipue vt explicares mihi sententiam de vestra generatione et corruptione. Quae
etiam de Cometarum cauda scripsi, eaA potius tuo iudicio subieci, quam vt vera vrserim. Et Illustrissimus
Princeps noster
facile excusationem meretur, quoniam tunc temporis vix incipiebat tractare
Obseruationes, necdum Stellarum Fixarum loca correxerat, nec erat in
Obseruationibus exercitatus, nec velim Obseruationem illam publices. Sed et nec
meam de Cometarum generatione sententiam scriptis tuis immisce. Si enim
publicandam censuissem, ipse iamdudum publicassem. Pugnares ea rationeA cum muto, siquidem nemo meam istam sententiam adhuc nouit. Postquam mea
scripta publica facta fuerint, poteris ea in tuis scriptis pro libito examinareA, siquidem tunc publici iuris erunt: At de nondum editis non est
praeiudicium introducendum. Superiore aestate cum de materia StellarumA cogitaui, in aliam sententiam incidi: Inueni etiam, quae de trabibus
discurrentibus cap. 7. proposueram, prorsus falsa esse. Quapropter totum illud
caput de materia Cometarum eorumque illuminatione sum mutaturus, longeque alia
ratione tractaturus, si alium adhuc insuperA Cometam obseruauero, omnique diligentia inspexero et considerauero. De
eo, quod Planetae in subtilissimo et purissimo Aëre pendeant, vlterius tecum non
agam. Tractaui hanc meam sententiam in opere nostro Stellarum Fixarum, nec te
immiscui, sed rem ipsam tractaui. Idem et tibi faciendum erit, vt quibuscunque
possis modis sententiam tuam defendas. Iudicabunt postea Doctissimi Mathematici,
cuius sententia vera sit. Nec enim nos ipsi in hac materia et Actoris et Rei et
Iudicis personam sustinere possumus, sed requiritur ad
sententiam pronuntiandam persona tertia, φιλαληθὴς et nullo prorsus praeiudicio et affectuA fascinata. Reuera Mysterium Trinitatis a Deo creaturis inditum est, et
reperiuntur in hoc inferiore mundo omnia terrenaA ex Terra, Aqua et Aëre, vt superioribus quoque literis significauiA, seu potius ex Terrena materia, Aqueo glutine et Aëreo spiritu constare;
Quam materiam sic dispositam deinde Calor caelestis vel Sol accedens specifica et
ingenita sua virtute, luce perfundit, excitat et viuificat. De hominis anima nihil dico, quae est diuinae particula aurae. Sed haec alibi tractaui. Video me tandem apud te obtinuisse, quod
Diaphanitas Aëris puri nihil differat a Diaphanitate materiae Planetis
circumfusae: Reliquam etiam sententiam sine dubio veram, te docebit veritas
temporis filia. De Hypothesibus Ptolemaei
et Copernici, vtra vera sit, peculiari
olim scripto discutiemus, nec vlteriorem hîc disputationem instituemus. Nec enim Cometa ille Anni 85 in
Solis opposito conspectus, quicquam certi hic nos docere poterit, licet
motui terrae non sit redditus obnoxius. Si enim motus eius tot gradibus
motum reliquorum Planetarum superare potuit, potuit etiam excludere
motum terrae annuum. Huc accedit, quod natura motus ex circularibus
compositi sit, ut omnia sint πρὸς ἄλληλα, et quomodocunque transponas
eccentricos et epicyclos, idem tamen motus eademque a terra distantia
suo modo seruato proueniat, quemadmodum ex Copernico lib. 3 Reuol. cap. 20, lib. 4 cap. 3, et lib.
5 cap. 4, 22 et alijs locis patet, ut nos alibi tradidimus. Ad
hypotheses tuas quod attinet, recte conijcis, generalem illam mundi
delineationem Illustrissimo Principi nostro a Thersite illo fuisse exhibitam. Ita
enim is cum horologiopaeo nostro hac sua
futilitate Celsitud.
ipsius in mea absentia (aberam enim peregre) occupauerat,
ut cum ego redirem haecque ab Illustrissimo Principe perciperem,
satis negotij haberem, ut falsitatem eius Illustrissimo Principi offenderem.
Erat enim uera Copernici inuersio mihi satis nota ex meis Astronomicis
Elementis, quae nec tunc nec etiam nunc uidit Illustriss. Princeps noster. Ac
dixi palam, hominem illum haec ex suo cerebro
non habere, siquidem Doctrinam Triangulorum prorsus ignorabat: et cum
latitaret se apud te collectorem literarum in tua typographia egisse,
dixi haec eum ex nemine alio cognouisse praeterquam ex te. Non tamen
persuadere poteram prorsus Illustrissimo Principi nostro haec falsa esse,
quanquam omnia et ex Ptolemaeo et
ex Copernico adducebam; adeo
Illustriss. ipsius Celsit. ab horologiopaeo erat occupata. Constructo tamen tandem eo
Instrumento, quod homuncio ille in eo scripto delineauit, ad oculum et
Illustriss. Princeps et Horologiopaeus uidit, eas hypotheses ueras esse non
posse, praesertim ex Marte. Assumebant enim tantum eccentriculum Solis,
inque eo eccentricos reliquorum Planetarum circumducebant, omissa
aequantium ratione, seu, si secundum Copernicum loquendum est, omissis
prorsus illis circellis. Nec homo ille sciebat rationes et quantitates
diametrorum et eccentricitatum, sed haec ex Copernico desumebat Horologiopaeus noster, qui satis coram Illustrissimo
Principe ex
me audiebat, quomodo res tractanda esset. Nec ego quicquam de ijs
dixissem, nisi mei officij fuisset, Illustrissimum Principem meum ab
approbatione (petebat enim ab Illustrissima ipsius Cels.
testimonium approbationis impudentissimus ille) ab approbatione inquam
falsae rei retrahere. Et quotiescunque colloquebar cum Illustriss.
ipius
Celsit., semper aderat etiam Horologiopaeus, qui hominis partes agebat. Tantum enim in
mea absentia homo ille ad Illustrissimum Principem erat admissus: postea
uero nunquam amplius admittebatur, ob quam causam etiam in praefatione
tecte in me inuehitur. Et quomodo poteram illum commendare Illustrissimo
Principi
nostro, cum nec eam ipsam delineationem nec quicquam admodum de hac re
intelligerit. Nec tamen rite Horologiopaeus noster ex me perceperat, quomodo res
tractanda esset: uerum post hominis illius discessum explicaui
Illustrissimo Principi, quomodo omnia data et rationes diametrorum in
circulis ex Copernico essent
assumenda transponendaque, quae tunc facile arripiebat Horologiopaeus, cui Copernicum in germanicum sermonem transtulerat utcunque
Vrsus ille. Ita postea curabat sibi
Illustrissimus Princeps noster per Horologiopaeum confici automaton
perfectissimum, omnium Planetarum motum secundum calculum Copernici
perfecte exhibens, de quo etiam superioribus literis scripsi. Nam illud,
quod delineauit homo ille in scripto suo, nullius est momenti, nec hic
reliquit sed secum abstulit, pro eius fabrica interpretans HorologiopaeoCopernicum, a quo etiam mea
compendiaA quoquo modo
cognouit, et in illo scripto manifestissima maleuolentia Horologiopaeo homini illiterato et idiotae
tribuit, quem tamen ego primus demonstrationem 47 p. 1 Eucl. docui, iam
mercedem anguinam reportans. Obliquitatem illam Zodiaci horologiopaeus
noster ex meis obseruationibus transcriptam etiam in secundis scrupulis
ipsi transmisit: ut et alia ex meis obseruationibus collutione Horologiopaei surrepta sunt. Sed nolo cum
impuro illo et Horologiopaeo nostro rem
habere: Doctissimi uiri facile iudicabunt, unde fluxerint pleraque, et
quid cuique tribuendum sit. Quod nomen meum
omisit, rem mihi pergratam fecit. Si tibi uidebitur, poteris ab ipso
hypotheses tuas uindicare. Vix credere potes, quomodo et te et me et
miserum illum Ptolemaeum miserumque Copernicum et omnes doctos conuituiis
peterent stupidosque et nihil intelligentes asinos appellarent illi
homines duo: soles se mundi lumina iactantes: adeo homine illiterato et
uix prima initia intelligente nihil quicquam est intolerabilius aut
iniustius. Sed haec nobis sunt pro nihilo habenda et contemnenda.
Perscripsi tamen hac de re superiore Mense Maio ad amicum meum singularem
uirum in quocunque doctrinarum genere et excellentissimum et
uersatissimum D. Ioannem Dee, ipsique significaui, quod non solum mea
Horologiopaeo illiterato et idiotae
tribuerit, uerumetiam tibi systema illud mundi surripuerit: iam astute
doctorum aucupia quaerens, quos tamen antea Vatiniano prorsus odio cum
Horologiopaeo prosecutus esset.
Omnis Aristippum decuit color et status et res. Scripsi etiam eum reuera
talem esse, qualem se in praefatione descripsit. Sed nolo cum isto
homine, ut dixi, rem habere, nec dignus est, ut nomen ipsius scriptis
nostris inferatur. Facile uidebunt docti, ex te eum illud systema
habere, siquidem ipse fatetur, se doctrinam Triangulorum ex Horologiopaeo nostro didicisse. Quomodo autem
sine doctrina Triangulorum de systemate illo et de ordinatione circulorum caelestium
deque eorum quantitate quicquam scire potuit? Ipse
quoque in Elementis meis Astronomicis tibi illud systema tribuam, ut et
Instrumentorum nostrorum rationem tibi in opere nostro stellarum fixarum
restitui. Sed de hoc satis. 
Habebat in animo Illustriss. Princeps noster tibi ad
literas tuas respondere; Verum subita festinatione iter ingrediens Smalcaldiam petijt, vt hac ratione responsio
sit impedita. Quemadmodum et eo circa hoc tempus maxime impeditur, quod iam
operam det ceruis, qui rem Veneream sectantur, figendis. Nihilominus tamen
Illustriss. ipsius Celsitudinem a te literas expectare et de te saepe cogitare,
ex iniecta literarum copia poteris intelligere, quas praeterito mense Iulio ex
comitatu Hombergico Illustriss. ipsius
Celsitud. ad me dedit: Secundum quarum tenorem et Mandatum Frischlino quoque literas ad te perferendas
tradidi. Quae proximis literis ad me scripsisti de structuris et occupationibus
tuis aestiualibus, quod nimirum Molendinam ad conficiendam chartam construxeris,
Illustrissimo Principi
meo indicaui, cui res perplacebat. Literas illas, quas ad Gellium Sasceridem scripseras, nuper tradidi
Praeceptori Nobiliss. ROSENCRANTZII,
qui me et ex te et ex Nobiliss. D. DEEA, amico meo singulari, perquam humaniter salutabat, seque
cum alijs ad eundem Gellium literis has quoque missurum aut laturum spondebat.
Nuper D. VICTORINVS SCHONFELDT, mathematum apud Marpurgenses professorA, per CHRISTOPHORVM HARSACHIVM,
Illustrissimi Principis
nostri Consiliarium a me petijt, vt Filium suum tibi commendarem, atque ex te
cognoscas rem, num posses illum inter studiosos tuos aliquamdiu recipere et in
his artibus erudire; Sique hoc tibi videretur, se eum sequente aestate ad te missurum. Si igitur tibi hoc commodum est, poteris voluntatem tuam ad proximas
Nundinas mihi declarare, vt sciat quid sibi agendum sit. Haec iam summa
festinatione varijs distractus occupationibus breuiter respondere volui, quae vt
in optimam partem accipias etiam atque etiam oro. Plura scribam, cum occasionem
et otium nactus fuero.Vale igitur Nobilissime Excellentissimeque D.
TYCHO, meque quod facis ama.Cassellis 22. Septemb., Anno 89.T. T.CHRISTOPHORVS ROTHMANNVS.
text.english: Your letter, Most Noble and Most Excellent Master Tycho, which you had despatched on 21 February, we received scarcely on 17 August — that is, six days after you had written and sent to me the other one. But although I am now pulled this way and that by various occupations, I judged that I should answer you in a few words: especially since I see that you have understood my earlier letter — perhaps on account of your various occupations and also your illness — far otherwise than I had written it. For you charge me with things that can never be gathered from the words of that letter, and that never even entered my mind. For where did I detract anything from the authority of the sacred Scriptures? Are not the things I said said also by you yourself, and by all the theologians who interpret the sacred Scriptures? Unless perhaps you reckon that, when two say the same thing, it is not the same thing — and that therefore that is to be censured in me which could readily be granted to others. If you read Augustine, you will find him speaking far more freely about the sacred Scriptures. When I lately set out the same opinion before our Most Illustrious Prince and our theologians, men of the highest rank — lest I make this quarrel my own (for in our [book on the] Observations I assigned it a chapter of its own, where I showed that the sacred Scriptures do not stand in the way of our opinion concerning the fluidity of the celestial matter) — neither the Prince nor the theologians disapproved it, nor did they find anything in it to be censured. And you too will have to do the same, if only you wish to defend that quintessence of yours. The glory of God alone is set before me in all my actions: do not think anything impious of me. About the twilights, too, do not make me out to be quite blind. For I am not so rash as to write anything in these matters that I have not tested by experience. I know that twilight ends when the Sun is sunk 17 degrees below the horizon, if you take "twilight" in the common sense for the doubtful light. But I defined twilight [as lasting] up to the point where no further trace of whitening air appears — which is altogether necessary, if you wish to determine more exactly the outermost surface of the dense air that can be illuminated. Consider, then, the air around the place of the Sun's setting, once the common twilight has ended, and compare it with the other places of the horizon round about — as toward the East, toward the North, toward the South — and you will quite certainly find a difference of colour and those traces of whitening air. But I do not know why you also detract from my refractions. For how else can I find them, or even extract them, than as the instruments themselves furnish? Am I to do this to please you? You demand of me what is surely unjust, if you demand this. But I have not faulted the title of your volumes "On the new generations of the aetherial world," nor is it to be faulted, nor does it need your excuse: since the things that come into being are also said to be generated; and comets are indeed generated in the heavens. I put those things forward not assertively, but rather doubtfully and by way of question, chiefly so that you might explain to me your opinion concerning your generation and corruption. The things I also wrote about the comet's tail, those too I rather submitted to your judgement than urged as true. And our Most Illustrious Prince readily deserves to be excused, since at that time he was scarcely beginning to deal with the observations, had not yet corrected the places of the fixed stars, nor was he practised in observations — and I should not wish you to publish that observation. But neither should you mix my opinion concerning the generation of comets into your writings. For if I had judged it should be published, I should myself have published it long ago. You would be fighting by that argument with one who is dumb, since no one yet knows that opinion of mine. After my writings have been made public, you will be able to examine them in your writings at your pleasure, since they will then be common property; but concerning things not yet published no prejudgement is to be brought in. Last summer, when I reflected on the matter of the stars, I fell into a different opinion: I found, too, that the things I had put forward in chapter 7 about the running beams are utterly false. Wherefore I am going to alter that whole chapter on the matter of comets and their illumination, and to treat it on a far different principle, if I shall yet observe still another comet besides, and inspect and consider it with all diligence. As for that the planets hang in the most subtle and purest air, I will not deal with you any further. I have treated this opinion of mine in our work on the Fixed Stars, and have not mixed you in, but have treated the matter itself. The same you too will have to do, namely to defend your opinion by whatever means you can. The most learned mathematicians will judge afterwards whose opinion is the true one. For we ourselves cannot in this matter sustain at once the part of plaintiff and of defendant and of judge; rather, for pronouncing sentence a third person is required, a lover of truth [φιλαληθὴς] and bewitched by no prejudice and affection whatever. The Mystery of the Trinity has truly been imparted by God to created things, and in this lower world all earthly things are found to consist of Earth, Water, and Air — as I signified also in my earlier letters — or rather of an earthy matter, a watery glue, and an airy spirit; and this matter, thus disposed, the celestial Heat or the Sun, approaching, then floods with light by its own specific and inborn virtue, rouses and quickens. Of the soul of man I say nothing, which is a particle of the divine breath. But these things I have treated elsewhere. I see that I have at last won this point with you, that the transparency of the pure air differs in nothing from the transparency of the matter poured around the planets: as for the remaining opinion, also without doubt true, truth, the daughter of time, will teach it you. Concerning the hypotheses of Ptolemy and of Copernicus, which of the two is true, we shall one day discuss in a writing of its own, nor will we set up any further disputation here. For neither will that comet of the year [15]85, seen in opposition to the Sun, be able to teach us anything certain here, even though it was not rendered subject to the motion of the earth. For if its motion could surpass the motion of the other planets by so many degrees, it could also exclude the annual motion of the earth. To this is added that the nature of motion is compounded of circular motions, so that all are in relation to one another [πρὸς ἄλληλα], and however you transpose the eccentrics and epicycles, yet the same motion and the same distance from the earth comes out, its own manner being kept — as is clear from Copernicus, Book 3 of the Revolutions, chapter 20, Book 4 chapter 3, and Book 5 chapters 4, 22, and in other places, as we have set forth elsewhere. As regards your hypotheses, you rightly conjecture that that general delineation of the world was displayed to our Most Illustrious Prince by that Thersites. For so had he, together with our clockmaker, by this triviality of his occupied His Highness in my absence (for I was away abroad on travels), that when I returned and learned these things from the Most Illustrious Prince, I had business enough to expose its falsity to the Most Illustrious Prince. For the true inversion of Copernicus was well enough known to me from my Astronomical Elements, which neither then nor even now has our Most Illustrious Prince seen. And I said openly that that man did not have these things out of his own brain, since he was utterly ignorant of the Doctrine of Triangles [trigonometry]; and since it lay hidden that he had acted as a collector of letters [a typesetter] in your printing-house with you, I said he had learned these things from no one else but you. Yet I could not altogether persuade our Most Illustrious Prince that these things were false, although I adduced everything both from Ptolemy and from Copernicus — so much had His own Highness been occupied by the clockmaker. Yet at last, when that instrument had been constructed which that little man had delineated in that writing, both the Most Illustrious Prince and the clockmaker saw with their own eyes that those hypotheses could not be true, especially from Mars. For they assumed only a little eccentric of the Sun, and within it carried round the eccentrics of the remaining planets, the reckoning of the equants being omitted — or, if one is to speak according to Copernicus, those little circles being utterly omitted. Nor did that man know the ratios and quantities of the diameters and eccentricities, but our clockmaker took these from Copernicus, who heard well enough from me, in the presence of the Most Illustrious Prince, how the matter was to be handled. Nor should I have said anything about these things, had it not been my duty to draw back my Most Illustrious Prince from approval (for that most shameless man was seeking from His own Highness a testimonial of approval) — from approval, I say, of a false thing. And as often as I conferred with His own Highness, the clockmaker too was always present, who played the man's part. For only in my absence had that man been admitted to the Most Illustrious Prince; but afterwards he was never admitted again, for which cause he also covertly inveighs against me in his preface. And how could I commend him to our Most Illustrious Prince, when he understood neither that delineation itself nor anything much about this matter? Nor yet had our clockmaker rightly grasped from me how the matter was to be handled; but after that man's departure I explained to the Most Illustrious Prince how all the data and the ratios of the diameters in the circles were to be assumed and transposed from Copernicus — which the clockmaker then readily seized upon, to whom that Ursus had translated Copernicus into the German tongue after a fashion. So afterwards our Most Illustrious Prince had made for himself, through the clockmaker, a most perfect automaton, perfectly exhibiting the motion of all the planets according to the calculation of Copernicus, about which I also wrote in my earlier letters. For that which that man delineated in his writing is of no moment, and he did not leave it here but carried it off with him, interpreting Copernicus for the clockmaker for his construction — from whom too [the clockmaker] he learned my compendious methods in some way or other; and in that writing, with the most manifest malevolence, he attributes [them] to the clockmaker, an unlettered man and an idiot, whom nevertheless I was the first to teach the demonstration of Euclid I.47, now reaping a serpent's wage [for it]. That obliquity of the Zodiac, transcribed from my observations, our clockmaker transmitted to him even down to the seconds; just as other things too were filched from my observations through the clockmaker's collusion. But I will have nothing to do with that impure fellow and our clockmaker: learned men will easily judge whence most things flowed, and what is to be attributed to each. That he omitted my name, he did me a most welcome service. If it shall seem good to you, you will be able to vindicate your hypotheses from him. You can scarcely believe how those two men would assail with insults both you and me and that wretched Ptolemy and wretched Copernicus and all the learned, and call [them] stupid asses understanding nothing — vaunting themselves as the suns and lights of the world: so that nothing whatever is more intolerable or more unjust than an unlettered man who scarcely understands the first rudiments. But these things are to be reckoned by us as nothing and to be despised. I have nevertheless written fully about this matter, last May, to my singular friend, a man in every kind of learning both most excellent and most versed, Master John Dee, and signified to him that he [Ursus] not only attributed my [work] to an unlettered clockmaker and idiot, but had even filched from you that system of the world: now craftily seeking to snare the learned, whom nevertheless he had before pursued, together with the clockmaker, with a thoroughly Vatinian hatred. "Every complexion and condition and circumstance became Aristippus." I wrote also that he really is such as he described himself in his preface. But I will have nothing to do, as I said, with that man, nor is he worthy that his name be brought into our writings. The learned will easily see that he has that system from you, since he himself confesses that he learned the Doctrine of Triangles from our clockmaker. But how, without the Doctrine of Triangles, could he have known anything about that system and the ordering of the celestial circles and their quantity? I too shall attribute that system to you in my Astronomical Elements, just as I have also restored to you the design of our instruments in our work on the fixed stars. But enough of this. Our Most Illustrious Prince had it in mind to reply to your letter; but, setting out on a journey in sudden haste, he made for Schmalkalden, so that by this circumstance the reply has been hindered. Just as he is also greatly hindered around this time by the fact that he is now devoting his pains to spearing the harts that pursue the work of Venus [are in rut]. Nevertheless, that His own Highness awaits a letter from you and often thinks of you, you will be able to gather from the enclosed bundle of letters which His own Highness gave to me last July from the county of Homberg; according to the tenor and command of which I also handed to Frischlin letters to be conveyed to you. What you wrote to me in your latest letter about your buildings and your summer occupations — namely that you have built a mill for making paper — I reported to my Most Illustrious Prince, to whom the matter was very pleasing. Those letters which you had written to Gellius Sascerides I lately handed to the tutor of the most noble Rosenkrantz, who greeted me most kindly both on your behalf and on behalf of the most noble Master Dee, my singular friend, and undertook that he would send or carry these too, along with other letters, to the same Gellius. Lately Master Victorinus Schönfeld, professor of mathematics among the Marburgers, asked of me, through Christoph Harsach, a councillor of our Most Illustrious Prince, that I commend his son to you, and [asked] that you learn the matter from him — whether you could receive him for some time among your students and instruct him in these arts; and if this seemed good to you, that he would send him to you next summer. If, therefore, this is convenient to you, you will be able to declare your will to me by the next Fair, so that he may know what he is to do. These things, now in greatest haste, distracted by various occupations, I wished to answer briefly; and I pray you again and again that you take them in the best part. I shall write more, when I have got the occasion and the leisure. Farewell, then, Most Noble and Most Excellent Master Tycho, and love me as you do. At Kassel, 22 September, the year [15]89. Yours wholly, Christoph Rothmann.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Christophorus Rothmannus* = **Christoph Rothmann** (c. 1550/60 – c. 1600), mathematician-astronomer at the court of Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel; Tycho's chief correspondent on observational and cosmological method. This is one of the more pointed letters in the exchange: Rothmann defends himself against Tycho's charges (on Scripture and the fluidity of the heavens, on twilight, on refractions) and then narrates the **Ursus affair** at length.
- **Recipient / persons.**
 - ***Illustrissimus Princeps noster*** = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), Rothmann's patron.
 - ***Thersites … Ursus … horologiopaeus … homo ille / homuncio*** — the central polemic. **Ursus** is **Nicolaus Reimers Baer** (Nicolaus Raimarus Ursus, c. 1551–1600), whom Rothmann brands "that Thersites" (Homer's lowborn railer, *Iliad* 2) and the "little man / fellow." The ***horologiopaeus*** ("clockmaker," from Greek *hōrológion* + *-poios*) is Wilhelm IV's instrument-/clock-maker **Jost Bürgi**, here Ursus's collaborator in presenting a "world-system" delineation to the Landgrave. Rothmann's allegation — that Ursus had worked as a typesetter (*collectorem literarum*) in Tycho's Uraniborg printing-house and there pilfered Tycho's geo-heliocentric system — is the documentary seed of the Tycho–Ursus priority quarrel that culminated in Tycho's *Apologia* and Kepler's *Apologia Tychonis contra Ursum*. **Identification flagged:** the letter never names Ursus except as "Thersites"/"Ursus"; "Bürgi" is supplied editorially and is not in the Latin.
 - ***D. Ioannem Dee / D. DEE*** = **John Dee** (1527–1608/9), to whom Rothmann says he wrote in May denouncing Ursus — a notable datum for Dee's continental network in the late 1580s.
 - ***Gellius Sascerides*** = **Gellius Sascerides** (1562–1612), Danish physician-astronomer, Tycho's former assistant on Hven.
 - ***Praeceptori … ROSENCRANTZII*** = the tutor of a young **Rosenkrantz** (Danish noble family) then travelling; not further specified in the text.
 - ***Victorinus Schonfeldt*** = **Victorinus Schönfeld** (1525–1591), professor of mathematics at Marburg; he seeks a place for his son among Tycho's students. ***Christophorus Harsachius*** = **Christoph Harsach (Harssach)**, a councillor of the Landgrave. ***Frischlino*** = (likely) **Nicodemus Frischlin** or a courier of that name; identification not secured by the text.
- **Places.** *Cassellis* = **Kassel**. *Smalcaldia* = **Schmalkalden**. *comitatu Hombergico* = the **county/district of Homberg** (Hesse). *Marpurgenses* = **Marburg**. *Uraniborg / typographia tua* implied — Tycho's printing-house on Hven.
- **Technical terms (per editorial glossary–5.2).** *Crepusculum* → **twilight**; *Refractiones* → **refractions**; *eccentricos / epicyclos / eccentriculum / aequantium ratione / circellos* → **eccentrics / epicycles / little eccentric / the reckoning of the equants / little circles**; *Obliquitas Zodiaci* → **obliquity of the Zodiac**; *in secundis scrupulis* → **down to the seconds** (of arc); *Stellarum Fixarum loca* → **the places of the fixed stars**; *Instrumenta* → **instruments**; *Doctrina Triangulorum* → **the Doctrine of Triangles** (= trigonometry; kept literal with gloss). *liquiditate materiae caelestis* → **the fluidity of the celestial matter** (Rothmann's fluid-heavens doctrine). *quinta Essentia* → **quintessence** (Tycho's retained Aristotelian fifth element, which Rothmann challenges). *Cometa Anni 85* = the **comet of 1585**.
- **Astronomical-source citations.** *Copernico lib. 3 Reuol. cap. 20, lib. 4 cap. 3, et lib. 5 cap. 4, 22* = Copernicus, *De revolutionibus*, Book 3 ch. 20, Book 4 ch. 3, Book 5 chs. 4 and 22 — given as Rothmann wrote them, untranslated as references.
- **Works named.** *Tomorum tuorum de nouis Mundi Aetherei generationibus* = Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (1588), here paraphrased by Rothmann as "your volumes on the new generations of the aetherial world." *nostris Obseruationibus / opere nostro Stellarum Fixarum / Elementa mea Astronomica* = Rothmann's own (largely unpublished) works on observations, the fixed stars, and astronomical elements. *demonstrationem 47 p. 1 Eucl.* = **Euclid, Elements I.47** (the Pythagorean theorem).
- **Greek (transcribed and translated).**
 - *φιλαληθὴς* (philalēthḗs) = "lover of truth," qualifying the disinterested third-party judge required to settle a scientific dispute.
 - *πρὸς ἄλληλα* (pròs állēla) = "in relation to one another" / "mutually" — that the circular components of planetary motion are interrelated, so eccentric/epicycle transpositions preserve the same motion and distance.
- **Allusions.**
 - *diuinae particula aurae* = **Horace, Satires II.2.79** ("a particle of the divine breath"), of the human soul.
 - *Omnis Aristippum decuit color et status et res* = **Horace, Epistles I.17.23** ("Every complexion, condition, and circumstance became Aristippus") — kept as the quoted sententia, applied ironically to Ursus's chameleon adaptability.
 - *Vatiniano … odio* = "Vatinian hatred," proverbial extreme hatred (after Catullus / Cicero on P. Vatinius).
 - *mercedem anguinam* = "a serpent's wage" — the proverbial ingratitude (a snake biting its benefactor) Rothmann says he got for teaching the clockmaker.
 - *ceruis … qui rem Veneream sectantur, figendis* — a courtly euphemism: the Landgrave is busy "staking out" (hunting) the harts in rut; rendered with the period decorum kept.
- **Epistolary formulae.** Opening *LITERAS tuas … accepimus* (no salutation rubric in this printed text). Closing *Vale … Cassellis 22. Septemb., Anno 89. T.T.* — *Vale* → **Farewell**; **T.T.** = *Tuus Totus* ("Yours wholly"), expanded in translation.
- **Calendar / DATING CRUX (flagged, not reconciled).** The dateline as printed reads **"Cassellis 22. Septemb., Anno 89"** = **22 September 1589 (O.S.;** Hesse-Kassel kept the Julian calendar at this date**)**. The edition's catalogue **label field reads "1589. 22. august. Kassel"** — i.e. **22 August**, one month earlier, contradicting the letter's own dateline. Per this chapter's convention the header leads with the **as-written September date** and appends the catalogued August date; the discrepancy is recorded, not resolved. The August reading is unsupported by the source text and is most plausibly a catalogue slip (or a confusion with the "17. Augusti" receipt-date that opens the letter). Internal date data are consistent with September: Rothmann says he received Tycho's 21 February letter "scarcely on 17 August," reports writing to Dee "last May," and refers to letters the Landgrave gave him "last July" — all anterior to a September composition.
- **Source-text artefacts (working transcription).** The verbatim Source block reproduces the local working transcription (harvested from the modern critical edition, normalising the 1596 *Epistolae*). Stray superscript-**A** tokens appended to words (*LITERASA, etA, morbumA, quamA, TheologiA, meamA, definiuiA, MeridiemA, hocA, eaA, rationeA, examinareA, StellarumA, insuperA, affectuA, terrenaA, significauiA, aurae.A, compendiaA, satis. A, DEEA, professorA, missurum. A, Septemb.A*) are **editorial footnote/variant anchors** carried over from the source apparatus, **not** part of Rothmann's Latin; they are left in the Source block (this chapter's convention forbids silent alteration of the transcription) and are ignored in the translation. Likewise the run-together *HorologiopaeoCopernicum*, the variant spelling *ipius* for *ipsius*, and the compressed closing *…ama.Cassellis…Anno 89.T. T.CHRISTOPHORVS ROTHMANNVS.* are transcription artefacts; word-division is restored only in the translation.
- **Negation check.** The dense polemical clauses were checked for negation count: e.g. *Vbi enim quicquam detraxi…?* (rhetorical "where did I detract anything…?"); *ne quid impium de me cogites* ("do not think anything impious of me"); *ne me prorsus caecum effice* ("do not make me out quite blind"); *nec velim Obseruationem illam publices* / *nec … sententiam scriptis tuis immisce* (two distinct prohibitions: "I should not wish you to publish that observation" and "do not mix my opinion into your writings"); *nec dignus est, ut nomen ipsius scriptis nostris inferatur* ("nor is he worthy that his name be brought into our writings"). Each negation in the source is reproduced once in the translation.
- **Correction.** Two low-severity translation fixes: 'de vestra generatione et corruptione' restored to 'your generation and corruption' (2nd-person 'vestra', not 3rd-person 'their [the comets']'); 'ceruis...figendis' restored to 'spearing' (the gerundive of figere, active spearing/shooting) in place of 'staking out'.

translation.warrant:
**Not collated against Dreyer** — no page reference for this letter, so the grade is capped at Probable however sound the translation looks. the edition gives no page reference for this letter, so by the audit's rule this is capped at grade Probable and audited against the transcribed original alone (no Dreyer collation performed). Full clause-by-clause collation of the published English against the transcribed original: every proper name (Augustine, Ptolemy, Copernicus, Ursus, the unnamed clockmaker/Horologiopaeus, Gellius Sascerides, Rosenkrantz, John Dee, Frischlin, Victorinus Schonfeldt, Christoph Harsach), place-name (Kassel/Cassellis, Schmalkalden/Smalcaldiam, Homberg/Hombergico, Marburg/Marpurgenses), date (21 February, 17 August, 22 September anno 89, last May, last July), and number (six days, 17 degrees, chapter 7, comet of [15]85, Copernicus lib.3 cap.20/lib.4 cap.3/lib.5 cap.4,22, Euclid I.47) checks out against the Latin with no fabrication, omission, or hardened hedge found. No sentence found silently dropped; the closing valediction and signature match exactly with no fabricated addition. Two low-severity pronoun/verb-sense mistranslations found (listed above); neither changes what a scholar would take away from the letter's substance.

**2 defects found:**
- **mistranslation** (low). "vestra" is a 2nd-person possessive ("your") consistent with Rothmann's tu/tuus address of Tycho throughout the letter; the translation silently recasts it as 3rd-person "their [the comets']", shifting whose opinion is being solicited. At: “chiefly so that you might explain to me your opinion concerning their [the comets'] generation and corruption”.
- **mistranslation** (low). "figendis" (gerundive of figere, to pierce/transfix/shoot) denotes active spearing or shooting of the rutting stags, i.e. hunting them; "staking out" implies passive surveillance rather than the kill, softening the verb's sense. At: “he is now devoting his pains to staking out the harts that pursue the work of Venus [are in rut]”.

**Repaired.** No Dreyer extract was available for this letter (no page reference), so no text error-type claim could be checked against the edition of record; there were none to check. Both defects are mistranslation-type and were verified from the letter's own the transcribed original, which is internal evidence independent of Dreyer: 'vestra' is unambiguously a 2nd-person possessive (contrasts with 3rd-person eorum/sua) and 'figendis' is the gerundive of figere (to spear/transfix), not a verb of passive watching. Both fixes are grammatically certain from the source text as published. Nothing else in the letter was touched.

text.original:
TYGE BRAHE FICK BREFF,

at hand her epter schulde holde thend løckte paa Kulden bedre wed mackt end til theß scheed er, saa der ingen klagemaall aff søefarende folck der offuer kommer.

Actum Haffniæ 20. 7bris a:o 1589.
text.english:
**Tyge Brahe received a letter,**

that he should hereafter keep the beacon on Kullen better maintained than has been done hitherto, so that no complaint from seafaring folk arises over it.

Done at Copenhagen, 20 September, in the year 1589.

documents.apparatus:
- **Document type.** Not a letter *text* but a **chancery-register entry** (Sjællandske Tegnelser — the "Zealand registers" of outgoing crown letters): the register records, in the third person, that "Tyge Brahe received a letter [to the effect] that…". The translation keeps that register form rather than recasting it as direct address.
- **Issuer.** Entered as from **Christian IV**, but in 1588–89 the king was a child (b. 1577); the realm was governed by the **Regency Council (rigsråd)** until 1596. The letter therefore issues *in the young king's name* through the chancery — hence the impersonal register form. Rendered "[In the name of] King Christian IV" in the header.
- ***thend løckte paa Kulden*** — "the beacon [lantern] on **Kullen**": the light on the Kullen headland (Skåne), whose upkeep was a duty attached to Tycho's crown holdings. *løckte* = *lygte* (lantern/light); *paa Kulden* = "on Kullen." This is the documentary basis for the well-known friction over Tycho's neglect of the Kullen light.
- **Orthography / language note.** The text is **Danish**, in late-16th-c. chancery spelling whose German-style features (*sch-, w-, -ck-, theß*) caused the edition's language tagging to mis-tag it "German." Verified by reading: *hand* = *han* (he), *her epter* = *herefter*, *schulde* = *skulle*, *wed mackt* = *ved magt* ("in repair/maintained"), *klagemaall* = *klagemål* (complaint), *aff søefarende folck* = *af søfarende folk* (by seafaring folk). Recorded as a Phase-C correction.
- **Date crux — RESOLVED.** Collated against Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* XIV p. 50 (item 77; *Sjællandske Tegnelser* XVII, 208), who dates and datelines the letter **1589**; the chancery register sequence (items 77–79, all 1589) confirms it. The working transcription's *a:o 1588* was a misreading of the register's **1589**, corrected here in the Source block and translation. (*7bris* = September, the seventh month counting from March.)

documents.abstract: Directs Tycho to account before the Council of the Regency for wax salvaged from a 1587 English shipwreck off Anholt, which the crown claims as wreck.
documents.incipit: Christian 4. etc.

text.original:
TILL TYGE BRAHE NOGEN WOX ANRØRENDIS VT SEQUITUR

Christian 4. etc.

WOR gunst tilfornn. Wiid, att thenne breffuißer Thomes Loeding haffuer wnderdanigst tilkiende giiffuit, huorledis for nogen tiid siiden wdj a:o 87 er st[r]andit ett schiib paa Anholt, som haffuer tilhørt nogen kiøbmend aff Engelland, huor wdj haffuer werrit eblant andit guodtz noget wox, aff huilcket en part schal werre strandit och bierget wed Wardbierg, en part wed Laugholm, och ett støcke ther for Hueen schal werre indkommen, huilcket du til thig schal haffue anammit, och fornemme Thometz Loeding paa for:ne engelsche kiøbmends wegne haffuer wnderdanigst werrit begierendis, hannom samme wox motte betalis och fornøyes. Tha epterdj att alt huis wrag, som saaledis her vdj riigit nogen stedts kand strande och indkomme for Wor och cronens grund, tilkommer Oß och cronen allenne, bede Wij thig och wille, attu thig ther om emoed Wor elsk:e tilforornede regierings raad erklerer, epter att Wij slige høighet wille Oß allenne forbeholdit haffue, hannom ochsaa samme wox, som du wdj saa maade haffuer ladet anamme, betaler och fornøyer, att hand sig wiidere for Oß icke schal haffue sig at beklage.

Ther met etc.
Actum Haffniæ 25 septem: a:o 1589.
text.english:
**To Tyge Brahe, concerning certain wax, as follows:**

Christian IV, etc.

Our favour beforehand. Know that this bearer-of-the-letter, Thomes Loeding, has most humbly made known how, some time since, in the year [15]87, a ship was wrecked off Anholt which had belonged to certain merchants of England, in which there was, among other goods, some wax — of which one part is said to have been wrecked and salvaged near Varberg, one part near Laholm, and a piece [of which] is said to have come in there off Hven, which you are said to have taken in to yourself; and, as we understand, Thomes Loeding, on behalf of the aforesaid English merchants, has most humbly been requesting that the same wax be paid for and made good to him. Then, inasmuch as all such wreck as may in this manner be stranded and come in anywhere here within the realm upon our and the crown's ground pertains to us and the crown alone, we ask and will of you that you make declaration of yourself concerning this before our beloved appointed Council of the Regency — since we will have reserved such prerogative to ourselves alone — [and] that you also pay and make good to him the same wax, which you have in such manner caused to be taken in, so that he shall not have [cause] to complain of you to us any further.

Therewith, etc.
Done at Copenhagen, 25 September, in the year 1589.

documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer.** **Christian IV of Denmark** (1577–1648), at this date eleven years old and still a minor; he had been elected king-designate in 1580 and acclaimed in 1584, but did not assume personal rule until 1596. Letters issued in his name during 1588–96 are acts of the **regency government** (the *regeringsråd*), which the letter itself names — hence the king's command to Tycho to "declare himself" *before* the Council of the Regency. The young king succeeded Frederik II (Tycho's patron, d. 4 April 1588), whose own chancery dealings with Tycho over instruments are the subject of the sibling pilot letter (brahe-t_15841211001).
- **Recipient.** **Tyge (Tycho) Brahe**, then resident on **Hven (Hveen)**, where he held the island in fief from the crown; the wreck-and-salvage jurisdiction at issue turns on that tenancy.
- **Bearer / claimant.** *Thomes Loeding* (also *Thometz Loeding* in the genitive) — the bearer of the letter, acting *paa … engelsche kiøbmends wegne* ("on behalf of the English merchants") who owned the wrecked cargo. Identity otherwise undetermined; the spelling suggests an agent or factor rather than one of the principals (named only collectively as "certain merchants of England").
- **Document type.** A chancery-register entry (**Sjællandske Tegnelser**), as in the 1584 Frederik II letter. The **Latin rubric** *"TILL TYGE BRAHE NOGEN WOX ANRØRENDIS **VT SEQUITUR**"* ("To Tyge Brahe, concerning certain wax, **as follows**") heads the Danish body — a code-switch preserved by this chapter's convention The closing *Actum Haffniae* ("Done at Copenhagen") is likewise the standard Latin chancery formula.
- **Places.** *Anholt* — the island in the Kattegat (notorious for wrecks). *Wardbierg* = **Varberg** and *Laugholm* = **Laholm**, both on the then-Danish coast of Halland (now Sweden). *Hueen* = **Hven**, Tycho's island. *Haffniae* = **Copenhagen** (Latin *Hafnia*,).
- **Legal substance (*wrag* / regalian salvage right).** *alt huis wrag … tilkommer Oß och cronen allenne* = "all such wreck … pertains to us and the crown alone": the king asserts the crown's **regalian right of wreck** (*ius naufragii* / strandret) over goods cast up on crown ground. *slige høighet … Oß allenne forbeholdit haffue* — *høighet* here is the sovereign **prerogative / regalian right** ("such prerogative … reserved to ourselves alone"), not "highness" as a style of address. The command's force is twofold and is read as conjoined (the two infinitive clauses *erklerer … betaler och fornøyer* both governed by *bede Wij thig och wille, attu …*): Tycho is (1) to render account of the matter before the Regency Council, and (2) to pay and satisfy the claimant for the wax — i.e. the crown takes the salvage right but directs Tycho to compensate the owner so the claim is closed.
- **Negation.** The source carries **exactly one** negation in the operative clause: *att hand sig wiidere for Oß icke schal haffue sig at beklage* = "so that he shall not have [cause] to complain of you to us any further." Reproduced as a single negation; the purpose-clause is the consequence of Tycho's compliance, not a prohibition laid on the claimant.
- **Orthography (chancery Danish, c. 1589).** *WOR gunst tilfornn* = *Vor gunst tilforn* ("Our favour beforehand," the royal address-formula,); *Wiid* = *Vid* ("know," imperative); *breffuißer* = *brevviser* ("bearer of the letter"); *wnderdanigst* = *underdanigst* ("most humbly"); *tilkiende giiffuit* = *tilkendegivet* ("made known"); *st[r]andit* — the register copy reads *standit*; Dreyer prints *st[r]andit*, restoring the elided *r* (so too in the source block, where the bracketed *r* is editorial); *eblant* = *iblandt* ("among"); *guodtz* = *gods* ("goods"); *bierget* = *bjerget* ("salvaged"); *anammit / anamme* = *annammet / annamme* ("taken in, received"); *for:ne* = *fornævnte* ("aforesaid," the standard chancery abbreviation); *begierendis* = *begærendes* ("requesting"); *motte* = *måtte* ("might"); *fornøyes / fornøyer* = *fornøjes / fornøjer* ("be satisfied / make good, satisfy"); *epterdj* = *efterdi* ("inasmuch as"); *wrag* = *vrag* ("wreck, flotsam"); *riigit* = *riget* ("the realm"); *tilkommer* = *tilkommer* ("pertains/belongs to"); *Wor elsk:e tilforornede regierings raad* = *Vor elskelige tilforordnede regerings råd* ("our beloved appointed Council of the Regency"); *erklerer* = *erklærer* ("declare/explain [yourself]"); *slige* = *slige* ("such"); *forbeholdit* = *forbeholdt* ("reserved"); *wiidere* = *videre* ("further"); *beklage* = *beklage* ("complain").
- **Calendar.** *Actum Haffniae 25 septem: a:o 1589* = "Done at Copenhagen, 25 September, in the year 1589" (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700,). The in-letter date *a:o 87* ("in the year [15]87") refers to the wreck, two years before the letter; it is not a dating discrepancy with the dateline. The edition label ("1589. 25. september. København") agrees with the dateline.
