Moreover that most renowned man, excellently deserving of public learning, Master Caspar Peucer, in a letter sent to me especially on this account, gathered very many sayings of Holy Scripture making toward this, and learnedly and excellently subscribed to my opinion concerning the most tenuous, most limpid, and nonetheless super-elemental matter of the heaven. And this chiefly, so that he might thereby also prove that the invention of my hypotheses is by no means absurd. When I shall have published, more fully than has hitherto been done, my uncontaminated reasonings about the matter of the heaven — that it is everywhere passable and packed with no solid orbs (as has hitherto been believed to gratify the ancients), and yet not [made] of an elemental and animate air, as you, and a certain John Pena the Frenchman, and certain others dare to proclaim — and when I shall have handed them over to others to judge, I shall by no means refrain — even without your prompting — from citing the authority of Holy Scripture, which deserves to hold the first place in establishing all wisdom and in founding all science. For I have always held that the glory of God alone is to be regarded in all things — which you too rightly approve — since truth cannot be inspected without His revelation and gift; for every perfect gift is from God. You seem to reproach me wittily [*salse*, with a pun on *sal*, "salt"] for assigning my "quintessence" to the aether — a manner of speaking not unknown among the chemists, nor disapproved by the ancient philosophers either, nor even by Aristotle himself (although in these matters he was not everywhere sufficiently perspicacious). But the salt is sweet, limpid, purged of all earthiness, exalted, in no part insipid or rank-smelling, but analogous to circular perpetuity — and not yet tasted [by you]. When you have smelled it, or perceived its savour, then for the first time pronounce judgement on these things; meanwhile it is better to refrain from premature prejudice. You ask that I not make you blind concerning twilights, nor accuse you of rashness, as though you write things you have not yourself experienced. But I have never presumed either to blind you or to pronounce you rash. Would that it were permitted both to me and to you and to others to be freed from that fog of the mind by which we are obscured more than we believe, and from worldly rashness — just as the external weakness of the eyes can be mended, especially by chemical means, with no great difficulty; truly, in that, so far as it could be done, I should think the very greatest labour ought to be spent. For that labour would not be uselessly bestowed. You say you know that twilight ends when the Sun is depressed 17 degrees below the horizon, taking "twilight" in the common sense for doubtful light. You suppose, then, that I am peddling an opinion at least approved by the crowd and hitherto contained in the astronomers' books, and have contributed nothing to it from my own observations. But what an accusation is this! Have I dealt with you by letter so long that you should still hold it unascertained that I am a devotee of the truth, that I seek it from no source other than either just reasoning and experience, or — what is chief — divine revelation, and that I do not of set purpose set up the false as true? You could sufficiently have gathered that I do not wish to see blindly even in greater matters that bear more on astronomy, far less that in the case of twilights — most easily observable things — I should pronounce anything idle, colluding merely with the common opinion of the Ancients, without observation of my own. I knew well enough that twilight is to be determined when no part of the air anywhere around the horizon grows even the least bit white — which was done most diligently several times, both by myself and by at least seven or eight students serving me in astronomical matters, so that no trace, not even the least, of air illuminated by the Sun could be discerned on any nearest surface of the horizon when the times of the twilights were noted; the stars' equatorial distances from the meridian being applied, and the Sun's exact place, and all things diligently weighed by a geometrical balance — and freely communicated to you, for this same reason, that, if you were willing to open your eyes, you might perceive [these times] not to have been fixed at pleasure or by common opinion. If, then, you with two eyes, and with at least a pair of instruments, can discern these things more keenly than all of us with sixteen eyes at the least, and with as many instruments and more wherever it was needed — I do not, to be sure, envy you this lynx-sightedness [*lincaeitas*] and modest requirement of means; rather I marvel. Indeed, I should congratulate you on a yet greater acuity and fuller sufficiency. So then, about twilights, persuade yourself of whatever you please, abounding in your own sense; I do not in the least hesitate that the things I have set forth are sufficiently confirmed, by many experiments too, and liable to no true refutation. Only see to it that, in disparaging the not-doubtful observations of others — so as to defend your own assertions about the like existence of air and aether (which you try in great part to prove from the discrepancy of vapours in different horizons, and more thickened and sublimated in the more northerly than in the southerly regions) — you do not enwrap the very truth, toward which we ought to tend, in more vapours, obscurities, and mists than all the dense and dusky vaporosities around the terrestrial horizon, in any place whatever, whether southern or northern. Accordingly, you wish not to know why I do not subscribe to the *refractions* exactly, since you could not otherwise extract them by instruments, and you assert that therefore nothing here is to be done to gratify me, and that in demanding this I demand unfair things. But when did I ever ask of you that, with the truth set aside, you should bring forward anything to gratify me, or press for things so unfair? For that would indeed be unfair, had I done so. On the contrary, I have always admonished, much rather, that the truth itself be more deeply unfolded, since this is well-nigh the fairest and most excellent of all the virtues. Why I cannot in every part approve the refractions asserted by you, my instruments too teach me. If, with one and another — and those at least two-cubit ones, sprung though they were from my own invention and disclosed to you through Wittich, and not even then sufficiently matured — you alone can collimate these and other things more accurately than I with more than twenty instruments, most of them four-cubit and five-cubit, and with several observers employed too, sufficiently strong in keenness of sight: well, there is reason why I should not envy you this prerogative either. Indeed it will even be so that you should give me thanks, because through the instruments devised by me (for you are not now ignorant of that) I have made you so perspicacious. Persuade yourself of this much at least: just as it is wont to happen in the art of wrestling, that no athlete forthwith discloses to his trainers those things which might at any time, through some lack, work against himself in that exercise — so neither has Wittich nor any others published all my matters that are exactly necessary for tracking down the truth, but they still, for the greater part, remain safe and whole [*sarta tecta*] with their author. In vain, therefore, do you boast too much of your instruments and observations. Perhaps, were you here and saw all things yourself, through far more and least-doubtful instruments, or with your own eyes alone, in my presence, you would say otherwise. But also your refractions being too small and your twilights too wide do not sufficiently agree with each other. It is necessary, therefore, that no slight error lurk in one or the other, or in both — or else that the air in this place a little more to the north, as concerns twilights, be somewhat more purged than it is there, but as concerns refractions more turbid — which, even with you yourself as judge, cannot stand together. Attend, therefore, more diligently to these matters; or, if it pleases you less, or it is not in readiness, at least acquiesce in the not-at-all-doubtful decision of others, and presume to decide nothing here prematurely for yourself. The title of my book, which you elsewhere called into doubt, or even assailed, you now approve, and no longer reckon worthy of reproach — although I did not publish that [title] which you alleged, nor prefix it to any book, but only noted it in passing in certain letters sent to your Most Illustrious Prince. I congratulate, therefore, both you and myself that you have so handsomely come to your senses; for before you objected that I introduce corruption into the heaven, since I used the word "generation" there concerning the comet, pressing my words too rigidly. But take care rather, lest now, in asserting deliberately that comets are generated in the heaven, you somewhere sin against [accepted] opinion — not so much grammatically as physically — provided it be fitting to retain the proper sense of the word. That you proposed those things not assertively but doubtfully and interrogatively, so that I might more fully explain my opinion — that is nothing new to me; for Wittich too and most others have dealt with me thus, objecting things that merited no doubt, in order to fish out certain others. But after I had carefully tested this in that case, and in others too, I became more cautious — although not a few things acquired here and there in Germany at my expense and labour, and that by the grace of God alone, are still peddled and proclaimed by others as their own; which I make little of. Nor do I take it ill that some rivulets are diverted to foreigners, while the very fountain still gushes, by God's bounty, in the keeping of its lord. Yet false things are not to be put forward in order that true things be known; for true and false are at odds — unless someone, as is done among the geometers, when nothing can be proved assertively, reduces the matter to absurdity by negation. Likewise, the things you proposed about the comet's tail — both in that writing of yours on the Comet of the year [15]85 and in the letters sent to me — you now retract, and assert that you did not press them as true, but only so as to submit them to my judgement. But although both that writing and your letters bear another aspect, nonetheless it pleases me well that here too you have returned to the road. For it pleases me that you now see well enough how little force your reasonings have, and the things you adduced by way of confirmation from the Most Illustrious Prince's Observation of the Comet of the year [15]58 (since I set those before your eyes in my earlier letter) — so much so that, as appears, you yourself would prefer not to have written them. The things you bring forward, beyond what I produced, to excuse that observation, find easy place with me — I who would impute [the discrepancy] not so much to an observation a little astray, but rather to the fact that you pressed this one too incautiously, and tried thereby to evade the findings of all others in very many comets. You ask that I not publish these things, and that I not mix your opinion about the generation of comets into my writings. But I cannot conceal this from you here: that I have been asked by letter, by the most noble man Master Heinrich Rantzau, the King's vicar [governor] in Holstein, and also by the most renowned and learned Master Caspar Peucer, an outstanding philosopher, and by certain other not unlearned men, who request and approve it, to publish in a special volume or two the astronomical letters written to me from various quarters here and there, together with my reply to each. Which I judged ought not to be denied them. And since the said Rantzau had requested that chiefly your Most Illustrious Prince's letters, and yours, be set in type — and since they deserve of themselves to occupy the earlier and more principal part of the volume — and since that book is now under the press, I cannot, for your sake, retract what I have assigned to others and make done things undone. Nor do I see why this should have been demanded of me, or why I should grant it, since nothing in this matter is admitted that would be harmful to your Most Illustrious Prince, or that derogates from him in any part, but rather only such things as redound, as is fitting, to His Highness's commendation. Nor is any danger or detriment created for you from this, since I always speak and think of you honourably. But if you change certain things proposed in your earlier writings and letters, and correct them on better deliberation, nothing departs from your reputation thereby, even if the earlier things be published. Indeed it is better that others learn how difficult it is, even for ingenious and industrious men, to disentangle the hiding-places of truth, and that not all things which at first sight are thought to be right hold good in every respect. And that day teaches day, and that later thoughts, for the most part — though not always — surpass earlier ones. Other quite outstanding men have retracted many things previously held by them, less considerately, as true — even in those matters where the tracking-down of truth was not so difficult as here. Since, in the Epilogue of the whole Work, which I have in hand concerning the Adscititious Phenomena of the Heaven [*Ascititia Caeli Phaenomena*], I inquire professedly into the nature and procreation of comets, according to the opinions of all, however many have come to my knowledge, I cannot but indicate this opinion of yours too — shared with certain others — and how incongruous it is, as I wrote to you elsewhere. Nevertheless, since I see you correcting yourself in these matters and superseding your earlier conceptions, I shall make mention of it there too, and shall fittingly excuse it. I shall not make your writing on the comet public; nonetheless to cite and weigh some things from it will redound rather to your laudable mention than be a reproach. You say indeed that I shall be fighting with a mute man, if I do so. But you were not mute when you wrote these things and consigned them in letters sent to me; for written marks, especially those penned in your own hand, stand for the words and speech themselves — nay, they deserve even more weight. So too, as regards my own letters — which I had never resolved to make public, unless asked by friends, as I said, since they were penned only in passing, as it came to my mouth, amid very many affairs — know that I do not so repent of them but that I leave you free, whether privately or publicly, in whatever manner you please, to discuss, approve, or disapprove what is contained in them. If, by just reasons, either you or anyone else shall sufficiently demonstrate that something in these or others of my [writings] does not hold rightly, I do not blush to correct them. Nor shall I, with any prejudice, set about inquiring into yours. See that you use the same candour about mine too, and do not, with a certain youthful ardour, pronounce a premature opinion. I congratulate you that, from considering the matter of the stars and the Milky Way, you have turned to a different opinion about the conformation of comets than that with which you were before imbued — one little physical, and far less mathematical. For here you are on the good road, if you have learned how to enter it and know all its lodging-places. For I could not sufficiently marvel by what fog of judgement you dared to assert such great absurdities — that the body of comets, by your own admission distant from the Earth nearly as far as Saturn's revolutions (as you recorded of the one that appeared in the year [15]85), and therefore necessarily greater by many *parasangs* than the Earth and Sea and all the surrounding vapours, as the geometrical demonstrations bear — should nonetheless have ascended thence into the highest aether, by I know not what unknown snatching-away, and should be a part much greater than its own whole; and that quite against the mathematical principles. If the physicists like to think so, let them join these doleful ditties [*naeniae*] to the rest. Rightly, therefore, do you draw the further conclusion that the things about *running beams* [*Trabes discurrentes*] — by occasion of which you perhaps slipped into so discordant a view — since they really contribute nothing here, and these are as far apart from one another as heaven and earth, you have caught out to be wholly false. I had it in mind to admonish you of these things too in my last letter; how I neglected it, I do not recall. For in your writing on the Comet of the year [15]85, where you try to assert such things, I had noted these matters in the margin for memory's sake, which I judged ought to be brought to mind either then or otherwise as occasion offered. Those exhalations [*halitus*] or chasms [*chasmata*] are far nearer to us than that they could be illuminated, in winter time, by a Sun depressed too far below the horizon, as geometrical and optical reasoning teaches. Moreover in the year 1588 I made an evident trial of this on 6 December, about the eighth hour of the evening. For I observed then, by careful inspection, very many chasms flying and whitening here and there toward the North — so that they bore a certain light that even illumined the Earth's shadow — to be far nearer to us than certain denser clouds dispersed separately around the northern horizon; so much so that those chasms evidently appeared to run between us and the clouds, so that others of my people too, to whom I showed it, discerned it clearly enough. Therefore, with the Sun submerged toward the Antipodes, that illumination of the vapours could not take place; since not even the clouds, more remote from the Earth, could have been struck by its light — which will easily be plain by measuring these things geometrically. Now those clouds of which I speak were not continuous, but disposed sparsely around the horizon, to an altitude — as regards the visible horizon — of about 10 degrees. Since, therefore, the Sun's rays do not, in that submersion of it below the horizon, touch the part of the Earth's shadow so near to us, it is asserted in vain that anything of this kind happens through illumination from it. I have considered something similar rather often, especially in this very year on 2 January, likewise about the eighth hour of the evening, when very many chasms were seen here toward the North, which were perceived to be far nearer than the clouds. Wherefore in vain did you seek some support from this for establishing that unnatural generation of comets. And if you wish to know what I think about these chasms: I judge it to be a certain terrestrial sulphurousness, burning and running in the nearby air, and sometimes filling the whole heaven by ascending to the zenith — yet at a modest distance from our sight — forerunners of winds, or of dryness and cold soon to follow; sometimes too, if they happen often and last too long, indications of air inclined to the contagion of an epidemic pestilence. For that disease has not a little in common with the sulphurous nature; whence too it is more readily dissolved by terrestrial sulphur excellently purified and exalted — especially if it be reduced into an agreeable liquor — as like by its like. For that maxim of the Galenists is not always true: that contraries are cured by contraries. These things about these matters I have thought it good now to bring to your mind. Most rightly, therefore, will you have done, if you change, as you promise, that whole chapter on the matter of comets and their illumination, and treat it more considerately. Nor is there need that yet another comet be awaited. For those which have passed most recently, even in our own age, abundantly convince [us] that your earlier opinion can in no way stand; which our observations in these matters will easily teach you, provided they can merit some credence. But if you judge that our decisions — though sought with what diligence could be, and not, as I hope, brought forward beside the point — are not such that you think one should safely rely on them: come then, await yet another comet, if any should occur meanwhile, and scrutinize it more diligently by measuring it, provided that be granted you. If you then find something different from our conclusions, there will be time enough to bring it forth, whatever it shall be; meanwhile, if you suspend judgement — provided it displease you to acquiesce in ours — it will not be ill-advised. That the planets hang [*pendere*] in the most subtle and purest air (though that is said quite improperly, since in truth they do not hang) — that you no longer wish to dispute this further with me, I gladly accept; and you do well in no longer calling the matter of the heaven animate and elemental. For here you will never obtain anything from me. If my reasons — partly already brought forward, partly to be further declared elsewhere, and adduced from lower and palpable things, yet analogous to the higher — do not suffice for you, [then] as far as I am concerned you are free to think whatever you wish. Treat this question wherever you please, and whether you involve me or not, it will be the same. I shall not, when occasion to treat of this matter is given, forbear to defend my opinion with sufficient probability. I in no way shun the judgement of most learned men who understand the matter itself; for I do not arrogate so much to myself as to presume to settle this dispute alone. I have always held the love of truth [*philalithia*] in esteem — perhaps to my greater inconvenience (which, however, I bear not ill) than to my profit. Nor have I ever permitted myself to be obscured, of set purpose, by the bewitchment of prejudice, as you seem to impute; for, as far as it has been divinely granted me to discern true from false, I have continually striven to do so. If you appeal to some third person (for I see you dealing with me juridically in a mathematical matter — for your brother too reported that you incline toward jurisprudence, perhaps because it is more lucrative and more conspicuous to the world) — I too accept the condition, and willingly challenge any philosophers in Germany or elsewhere capable of these matters. And, that someone be named: to the most renowned and excellent man Master Caspar Peucer, if you so please, I leave the whole matter — since he is in the first rank versed in both philosophy and the mathematical disciplines, and not slothfully devoted to the study of theology (whence this question can in great part be decided), and at the same time prevails by grave judgement and age. Nor need it occur to you to suspect that he will be a judge too favourable to my side (for you know, if you wish to be a jurist, that the favour of the judge avails more than ten laws written in the Code) — for he has never been known to me; but with your Most Illustrious Prince — whom, in a letter sent to me, he calls his best benefactor, and not undeservedly — and with you too, when present, he contracted a not ungrateful friendship. If there are others among your countrymen, or even elsewhere, to whom you wish to lodge an appeal, I too appeal to the same — provided they have inspected the matter under discussion more deeply, and have learned to understand both the higher and the lower things, and to reconcile these with one another, knowing the one from the other. For whatever is above, that also is below, as that Hermes truly Thrice-Greatest [*Trismegistus*] among mortals used to say. That the hidden mystery of the Trinity lurks in all created things, you rightly grant to me — although your philosophy concerning these matters, which you adduce, is more outward than inward, and too obvious to the senses; since that which is chief, and in which the kernel of the matter resides, does not appear at first sight. For it is not enough to say that all lower things consist of Earth, Water, and Air, since these very mothers too have certain other threefold principles, not yet sufficiently perceived by the common philosophers, of which there is now no place to dispute. You add then that you see — that you have now at last obtained — that I have conceded to you that the diaphaneity of pure air differs in nothing from the diaphaneity of the matter poured around the planets; and you do not on that account doubt that truth, the daughter of time, will in its own time teach me your remaining opinion too. But with what eyeglasses [*perspicilla*] did you ever see this so keenly? Or by what means could you ever gather it from my writings? I marvelled, reading these things, why you should wish to allege that I propose things contrary to myself in this part. So I inspected again the copy of the letter last addressed to you, from which you doubtless wished to gather this. But I find nothing of the kind in it — rather, the plain contrary of your assertion. I there first gave an example, from lower things, which by the benefit of the spagyric art [*ars spagyrica*] can be exalted into such subtlety that they represent a like diaphaneity, so far as it is discerned by the senses; and nonetheless I showed them to be of a different substance — and therefore that what you intended does not follow, even were it conceded, on account of refractions not tending to the zenith, that there is an imperceptible discrepancy between the heaven and purer air as regards diaphaneity, [it would] therefore [not follow that they] consist of one and the same matter. In this way I reasoned with you, nor on that account did I concede the diaphaneity of air and aether to be entirely the same; nay, I added these words, indicating otherwise: "So too the diaphaneity of heaven and air, even if they were quite the same — which however has not yet been sufficiently established — nothing nonetheless prevents [them] from having a different substance and matter." Why, then, I ask, do you boast that you have obtained from me that which I said in open words has not yet been sufficiently established? Why do you so injuriously invert my meaning? And why do you so inconsiderately precipitate judgement about these tenets [*placita*]? If truth, the daughter of time, shall ever inform me better, I shall surely not shrink from accepting the truth; and that on whatever occasion it shall at last be granted. Yet I do not yet see why I should assent to any of your opinions about which there is controversy between us. Nor will you evidently demonstrate that I have retracted anything of those things which I have hitherto written to you, even in passing, or otherwise issued, that is of any moment — whereas you not a few things, even in this very letter, formerly keenly defended, not merely call into doubt but wish to be wholly void: As that you did not assert the Prophets to have understood no more in physics than the sluggish crowd; and that Moses, speaking of the two great luminaries, did [something] against the geometrical demonstrations, as if this were not to detract from Holy Scripture; that you entangle the question raised about the Copernican motion of the Earth with the matter of the heaven, and strive to prove this from Augustine and other modern theologians by confounding heaven and earth; that you do not reproach the title of my volumes on the celestial generation of comets, though before you objected that I introduce corruption into the heaven if I assert generation; that you asserted the comets' tails, in so many words, and also from some observation, formerly as though they were parts of the body, consisting of the same matter, and now no longer hold them as true — nay, wish the very observation, [though] written out, to be undone; that the whole opinion about the generation of comets, formerly thrust upon me on account of a certain "Graminaeus," you now so set aside that you judge a whole chapter must on that account be changed in your writing and treated otherwise; that the running beams, formerly illumined by the Sun, you now deprive of its light — and whatever other corollaries there are. For I do not wish to dig out everything too scrupulously. Yet I do not review these things in order to reproach you with acknowledging and amending your deviations. For that I praise, and would that you had done so more often, and had permitted yourself to be instructed by truth the daughter of time, as you rightly said. Thus you would have touched the centre of the circle, which is unique, more on a straight line. If you ever show that I have written anything that needs retraction, I shall be grateful; that I have as yet retracted anything of mine I am not conscious — not that it cannot happen, as we are human, but because what you say you see in my writings has not yet been open to my eyes, nor do I yet acknowledge it. That comparison which I proposed, and somewhat explained to you, between the liquor of Water and of Wine, both purified, with respect to the matter of Air and of Heaven, perhaps deserved a greater reception than that it should be so taken. For in truth the heaven is related to elemental air just as some spirit of Wine or of another generous liquor is to purged water. And although they be almost the same in diaphaneity, yet far different in substance. Nor do I know whether a better comparison can be drawn from terrestrial things. Hence it is that certain of those who philosophize have not hesitated to call the Spirit of Wine especially — moderately exalted and purified several times, and at length freed by continual and long-lasting circulation from elemental intemperance — "Aether," or "Philosophical Heaven"; although whether it can be done in the manner they propose, [and] that certain other things be not wanting, I do not now wish to say. This much at least I would dare openly to affirm: that in each terrestrial substance there lurks something analogous to the celestial nature — in some more, in some less — which savours properly neither of Air, nor Water, nor Earth, nor even the Element of Fire (if such there were in the nature of things), although these elemental qualities too are present in each, in a certain grosser composition. Nor must it be thought that this super-elemental power is in the elemental things only from the Sun or the rest of the stars, although I would not deny this in some part. For some things are more conformed to these, some to other stars; meanwhile, however, the universal essence of the heaven too, in which these astral virtues dwell, [is such that] all lower things — according as they more or less emulate it — [are governed] not otherwise than as the stars themselves are revolved in the heaven, befitting their own nature. But let this much now suffice to have discoursed about these matters, since they do not pertain to the commonly received philosophy, and would perhaps scarcely be accepted there. The Ptolemaic or the Copernican hypotheses, whichever of these you approve, will, as far as I am concerned, be free to you. I would only advise that you form your judgement about the heaven from the heaven itself, not from papers and ingenious demonstrations, perhaps not everywhere consonant with the heaven itself. Let it therefore be permitted me too to pronounce freely what the heaven has taught me in these matters. About the Filcher of my System [*Surreptor mei Systematis*] I will add no word here, for he is not worth it. I replied to you briefly in my last [letter] to the things you objected to this innovation of hypotheses of ours; a fuller resolution of this kind, and of other doubts, you will obtain when I shall have treated professedly of the motion of the Secondary Movables [*Secunda Mobilia*], and shall have laboured to render it, as regards the reckoning, exactly conformable to the heaven itself, and shall (the Maker of the heavens favouring) have, as I trust, brought the whole matter to the wished-for end. If you think out anything more meanwhile that you suppose can be brought to the contrary, you will do a not ungrateful thing by freely producing it. For sometimes by contradiction the Truth is rendered more illustrious. The occasions which impelled me to such an ordering of the Celestial Revolutions I have also briefly indicated to you. For I was brought to this neither rashly nor for a light cause, but the heaven itself taught me to think thus of it, with no other Teacher, nor any books, nor jumbles of Tables [*Tabularum Farragines*] contributing anything here. I conferred too with certain other learned mathematicians in Germany about this our modern invention, which, although it does not much please certain Aristotelians, especially those too addicted to the realities of the orbs, is nonetheless reckoned quite elegant by the more judicious, who weigh the matter without preconceived opinion and inspect it more rightly. Although, to say what the case is, even though I do not despise the judgements of others, yet whether they make for or against, I care not much, provided experience itself, drawn down from heaven, evidently convince [me] that the matter is so. I know how abstruse the inner recesses of Nature have always been, and how far, very often, those things we think we rightly perceive in physics stray from the mark. Therefore I think one should rest not so much in the authority and applause of others, but rather that it befits us ourselves to make trial whether the matter be so or otherwise, and to weigh all things in the balance of Observations and Demonstrations, and to prove them. But there is now no place to discourse more on these things. But since I see that the Copernican opinion about the threefold motion of the Earth much pleases you, I shall propose, in each of these [motions], at least a single doubt — though far more could be given — and one not so laborious. First, as regards the diurnal motion about its own axis, by which the Earth is feigned to be wheeled round in 24 hours, and thus the universal course from east to west is explained away: tell me how it can come about that a leaden globe, let down in due fashion from a very high tower, should touch perpendicularly and exactly the point of the Earth placed beneath it; for that this can by no means happen, the Earth being carried round meanwhile, since its course is most swift, a geometrical computation will teach you: seeing that in one second-scruple of time the Earth must be revolved, even in these more northerly regions, nearly 150 of the larger paces [*passus maiores* — the greater Roman pace as a unit of distance]. From this reason out the rest. For the fall of the lead does not accompany the air, but violently passes through it. Concerning the second motion of the Earth, the annual — which would remove the eighth Sphere so far that the orb which this [annual motion] would describe vanishes with respect to it — explain whether it seems probable to you here that the space which is from the Sun, then the centre of the universe, to Saturn, is contained more than 700 times within [the space between] this [Saturn] and the Sphere of the Fixed [stars], and that the whole [space] filled with no stars. And yet it is necessary that this be so, if only the annual orb of the Earth is to appear of the size of one minute. Nay, then too the Fixed Stars of the third magnitude, which have one minute in diameter, will necessarily be equal to this whole Annual Orb — that is, they will comprehend in diameter 2284 Semidiameters of the Earth. For they will be distant nearly 7,850,000 of those same Semidiameters. What shall we say of the Stars of the first magnitude, of which some occupy two, certain ones nearly three minutes in visible diameter? And what if the eighth Sphere be removed yet higher, so that the Earth's annual motion vanishes there altogether? Deduce these things, if you please, geometrically, and you will see how great absurdities — even by inferring thus (to say nothing of others) — accompany this assumption. The third [motion], the annual being taken away, falls of itself; or if it seems to you able to hold together with it, how, I ask, can it come about that the Axis of the Earth is gyrated yearly in the contrary direction to the motion of the centre, so correspondingly that it nonetheless appears to be at rest? How too is it granted that the Axis and the Centre are agitated by a double and different motion, in a single and simple body? — to say nothing in reply about that third, diurnal [motion] supervening about the Axis. I am silent too about the entanglements of the librations, [and that they are], not everywhere corresponding to the advancement of the Fixed [stars] to which they are assigned, very discordant. Weigh these and like things carefully with yourself, and, if it be granted, resolve them at leisure. You will have more elsewhere. If, therefore, the Copernican reasoning cannot hold — as indeed it cannot — the Ptolemaic [reasoning], which Copernicus (to say nothing of others) has sufficiently refuted, nothing will hinder our invention from deserving a place. You set forth, finally, the causes why your Most Illustrious Prince has not replied to mine, which I gladly accept. I would now write to His Highness, but nothing occurs [to me] besides what I consigned in my last. And at the same time I fear lest I trouble Him — occupied with the administration of the commonwealth and other cares — with my meagre letters. Frischlin, of whom you write, has not come hither, nor sent any letter from you, though otherwise he would not be received by me unkindly; for I have heard that the man is of varied learning and eloquent. You make mention besides of the Mill suitable for making paper, which I indicated I would build, lest I be so often and so long frustrated for printing-paper to be brought from Germany for striking off my lucubrations; and you say this pleased your Prince, which I readily believe. For in these things too we have a certain mutual confluence. For just as His Highness delights in making architecture, ramparts, ditches, aqueducts, fishponds, gardens and mills and like mechanical structures, so I too, after my own measure, especially in summer time, when it is not permitted to be free for higher matters, and these are more conveniently handled. For these too smack of something geometrical, provided they are to be made with due symmetry. That mill is now ready, with a very high and very broad rampart holding back sufficient water both in summer and in winter time, and a wheel 12 ells in diameter driven by the least water, and performing a double work besides the paper-work. With very many fishponds too disposed in order here and there, so that when it shall be necessary, these mill-pools too may supply waters. And all these things were dry a few years ago. Moreover I am building here another mill for my peasants and workmen dwelling round about in the neighbourhood, where too almost no water is now thought to be at hand. For I do not wish that others should survey the paper-works and the things pertaining to my own domestic affairs, and untimely disturb them. If Victorinus Schönfeldt sends his son hither to visit me, by me it is permitted him; as soon as it shall seem [good] to him or to me that he return to his own, it will be free enough to both. Whether he be promoted to Master of the Liberal Arts or not is all one to me; yet I should prefer him to be such, rather than to be [merely] so called. But this is not displayed at so light a price; it would suffice to be a disciple of these [arts]. But I see, my dear Rothmann, that in replying to your letter — written more tersely and, as appears, with a hurrying pen — I have been too copious; which I admitted the more readily, lest I should seem to wish to avenge your brevity (as if indulging too much in retaliation) by no reply at all, or even a shorter one. For although I am now entangled in more affairs than you were in writing yours, or perhaps ever otherwise, yet I wished to be hindered by no other occupations from replying to yours, and that so amply; which in my last [letter] too, besides the illness I signified, was really so — so that, with so much time elapsed, leisure for replying to you doubtless was at hand, more conveniently and less adversely. If, however, anything of freer admonition is written in these, take it in the better part and ascribe it to the love of our common studies. Farewell, and if you have leisure, write back now at once, so that, God willing, you may obtain a reply again by the next coming Fair. Meanwhile take in good part these things, penned likewise with a hurrying pen.
Again, happily farewell.
Given at Uraniborg, 24 November, in the year 1589.
Tycho Brahe.


*[Postscript:]* POSTSCRIPT. Since I have learned, both from your letter and from elsewhere, that the most illustrious Prince Landgrave has resolved to make public his observations of the fixed stars over several years, and to employ your labour in carrying out this undertaking: I ask, for the honour and the benefit of Astronomy, that you do not grudge to hasten these labours — perhaps no less than the labours of Hercules — lest, by too much procrastinating, they either perish altogether, or scarcely at last see the light of publication for the common advancement of this Art. For from this both those who are now living and posterity, whom the care of such lofty matters touches, will easily judge how erroneous the places of the "fixed" stars have been, and how little congruent with the heaven, of which (whether through the want or the carelessness of the craftsmen) we have hitherto made use in so many ways, since nothing surer was at hand; and at the same time it may become plain how great a task it was to track down the boundary-markers [*Hermas*] of the Stars; and, by comparing your observations with mine — which I have resolved shortly (the Maker of the Stars favouring) to publish — you may discern how much more accurate, and with what constancy of labour, this matter has been carried through on both sides. For the fact that your restitutions differ from mine, in almost all the Stars, by abounding as it were by a twelfth of one degree, will easily find its excuse with those who understand the intricate difficulty of the matter. Nor indeed could it be otherwise than that the limits of the Stars fixed by you should somewhat exceed their genuine distance from the equinoctial point, since you carried it out only by means of the evening star Venus (and not likewise the morning star), and not often enough at that, the refraction then insinuating Venus to the eyes a little further in longitude than is right. Whence it follows that the Stars derived from her across that interval grow, in their longitudes too, more than was needful — to say nothing of that slippery way of observing by Azimuths and Altitudes, together with the markings of the times obtained less surely from clocks, in all of which you, as I not without reason suspect, place too secure a trust. But since in our first Volume of the Astronomical Progymnasmata, in the second chapter, where I treat expressly of the exact verification of the fixed stars, I shall set forth abundantly how the limits of the Stars — falling back at last precisely into one and the same place, and most aptly analogous to one another — have been determined by us not only from Venus western of the Sun but also from the same Venus eastern; and likewise, after about eight hundred [stars], in their canonical distribution into fixed places as to longitude and latitude, I shall insert some mention of the Landgravian rectification in these matters too, and why it almost everywhere exceeds ours by some 5 minutes, as I shall show: I am unwilling now to dwell upon this very point further here. Do you only take pains that those who desire them may shortly enjoy your Atlantean labours in this part as well. And so once again, farewell.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** **Tycho Brahe**, writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven, to **Christoph Rothmann** (*Christophorus Rothmannus*, c. 1555–c. 1600), mathematician at the Hesse-Kassel court of **Landgrave Wilhelm IV** (*Illustrissimus Princeps Wilhelmus Landtgravius Hassiae*;). This is one of the principal letters of the Tycho–Rothmann correspondence, in which the two debate the materiality of the heavens, the truth of the Copernican system, the nature of comets, atmospheric refraction, and twilight. It was printed by Tycho himself in the *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Uraniborg, 1596), the volume named in the source's edition field; that printed text is reproduced (with the *Opera Omnia* VI critical text as edition of record).
- **Dateline.** *Datae Vraniburgi 24. Nouemb. Anno 1589* = "Given at **Uraniborg**, 24 November, in the year 1589" (Old Style; Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). The catalogue label ("1589. 24. november. Uraniborg") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy.
- **Greek.** This letter contains **no Greek-script interpolations** (the heuristic and several technical terms — *philalithia*, *parasanga*, *chasma*, *trismegistus* — are Greek loanwords written in Latin letters; see below). They are transliterations, not Greek script, and are kept as printed.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Franciscus Vallesius* = **Francisco Valles** (de Covarrubias, 1524–1592), Spanish physician-philosopher; his *De iis quae scripta sunt physice in libris sacris* ("Sacra Philosophia," 1587) is the work meant.
 - *Lambertus Danaeus* = **Lambert Daneau** (c. 1530–1595), French Reformed theologian; *Physica christiana / Physice Theologica* is meant. "Codex" here = the two Testaments ("the Old and the New Codex"), kept literal with a gloss.
 - *Stagyrita iste Graecus* = **Aristotle** (of Stagira); the dismissive demonstrative *iste* ("that Greek of Stagira") is preserved.
 - *Caspar Peucer* = **Caspar Peucer** (1525–1602), Wittenberg physician-philosopher and Melanchthon's son-in-law; Tycho repeatedly invokes him as an ally on the fluidity of the heavens and proposes him as arbiter.
 - *Ioannes Pena Gallus* = **Jean Pena** (c. 1528–1558), French mathematician; in the preface to his Euclid *Optica* (1557) he argued the heavens are filled with ordinary (elemental) air — the view Tycho rejects ("not of an elemental and animate air").
 - *Wittichius* = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586), the Wrocław mathematician who visited Hven in 1580 and (Tycho complains) carried instrument-designs and methods to Kassel and elsewhere; he is the unnamed *Surreptor mei Systematis* ("Filcher of my System") of the later passage — Tycho's standing grievance over priority for the geo-heliocentric system. Flagged: the identification of the "Filcher" with Wittich (vs. Ursus / Nicolaus Reimers Baer) is contextual; the letter does not name him, so "Filcher of my System" is kept and the candidate noted, not asserted.
 - *Henricus Ranzovius* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), royal *Statthalter* (governor; *Vicarius Regius*) of Holstein, humanist patron; one of those urging Tycho to publish the correspondence.
 - *Hermes … Trismegistus* = **Hermes Trismegistus**; the maxim *Quicquid est supra, id etiam infra* ("whatever is above, that also is below") paraphrases the Hermetic/Emerald-Tablet *correspondence* doctrine; kept with the Latin.
 - *Graminaeus quidam* — "a certain Graminaeus": **Theodor Graminaeus** (Gravius), a 16th-c. writer on comets whose theory Rothmann had (Tycho says) earlier pressed; treated as a proper name, flagged below.
 - *Frischlinus* = **Nicodemus Frischlin** (1547–1590), the wandering humanist poet-scholar; Tycho notes he never arrived.
 - *Victorinus Schonfeldt* = **Victorinus Schönfeld** (1525–1591), Marburg professor of mathematics/medicine, whose son might visit Hven.
- **Astronomical / physical terms (editorial glossary,–5.2).** *parallax*-free here, but: *refractiones* → **refractions**; *Crepusculum* → **twilight**; *Horizon, Meridianus, Altitudo, Azimuth* per glossary; *octava Sphaera / Affixarum Sphaera* → **eighth Sphere / Sphere of the Fixed [stars]**; *Orbis Annuus* → **annual orb**; *Stellae Fixae, magnitudo* → **Fixed Stars, magnitude**; *Semidiameter Terrae* → **Earth-semidiameter** (Tycho's unit of cosmic distance); *Secunda Mobilia* → **Secondary Movables** (the planetary orbs/motions below the *primum mobile*). *Organa / Instrumenta* → **instruments**; *bicubitalia / quadricubitalia / quincubitalia* → "two-/four-/five-cubit" (instrument sizes); *collimare* → **collimate** (sight along). *minutum* = arc-minute; *Scrupulum secundum temporis* = "second-scruple of time" = one **second of time** (kept literal with gloss).
- **The threefold Copernican motion.** *mobilitas … triplex a Copernico asserta* = the **diurnal** (axial), **annual** (orbital), and the **third** motion (Copernicus's annual conical motion of the axis, the *motus declinationis*, here *librationum intricationes*). Tycho's three objections — the falling-lead/tower argument, the immense empty gap to the fixed stars (and the resulting monstrous physical size of stars), and the incoherence of a third axial motion — are his standard anti-Copernican physical arguments; rendered faithfully, with his hedges ("to say nothing of others," "though far more could be given") preserved.
- **Numbers (verified against the source, not normalised).** Sun depressed *P. 17* below the horizon = **17 degrees** (Rothmann's value for the end of twilight). *Rota 12 ulnarum* = a mill-wheel **12 ells** in diameter. *plusquam 700 vicibus* = the Sun–Saturn space contained **more than 700 times** in the gap to the fixed stars. *2284 Semidiametros Terrae* and *7850000 … Semidiametris* = **2284** and **≈7,850,000** Earth-semidiameters — reproduced exactly as printed. *sesquicentum passus maiores proxime* = **nearly 150 of the larger paces** (*passus maiores* = the greater Roman pace taken as a unit of distance; *maiores* qualifies *passus*, not "and more"; *proxime* = "nearly"). Dates within the letter: trials of **6 December 1588** and **2 January 1589** ("this very year"), both *circa octauam vespertinam* ("about the eighth hour of the evening"); the Comet of **1585** (Rothmann's tract) and the Landgrave's observation of the Comet of **1558**. None silently converted.
- **Alchemical / chemical terms.** *quinta Essentia* → **quintessence**; *Ars Spagyrica* → **spagyric art** (Paracelsian chemistry); *Spiritus Vini* → **Spirit of Wine** (distilled alcohol); *circulatio* → **circulation** (repeated distillation); *defaecatus / exaltatus / depuratus* → **purged / exalted / purified** (alchemical operations); *Sulphureitas Terrestris* → **terrestrial sulphurousness**; *Caelum Philosophicum* → **Philosophical Heaven**. The *salse / Sal* wordplay (Rothmann mocking Tycho's "quintessence," Tycho retorting that "the salt is sweet … not yet tasted") is a pun on *sal* "salt" / *salse* "wittily, with salt"; flagged in the translation, not flattened.
- **Medical note.** *Contraria contrarijs curari* — "that contraries are cured by contraries," the **Galenic** allopathic maxim, which Tycho disputes in favour of a *simile suo simili* ("like by its like") logic for treating a sulphur-natured pestilence; the period sense is kept, not modernised.
- **Latinate / rhetorical terms kept and glossed.** *rhapsodice* → "in a disjointed/patchwork fashion"; *Dedomena* (Greek *δεδομένα*, "the givens/data") → "the *data*"; *sarta tecta* → "safe and whole" (legal idiom, "in good repair"); *naeniae* → "doleful ditties"; *parasangae* → "parasangs" (Persian leagues, a learned distance-word); *lincaeitas* → "lynx-sightedness" (from Lynceus); *perspicilla* → "eyeglasses"; *philalithia* → "love of truth"; *Tabularum Farragines* → "jumbles of Tables." All retained-Latin technical/rhetorical terms italicised on first use.
- ***Ascititia Caeli Phaenomena*** — the planned **Epilogue** "On the Adscititious [adventitious / supervenient] Phenomena of the Heaven," i.e. Tycho's projected treatment of comets etc. within his larger work; kept as a title.
- **Titulus libri / Tomi de Cometarum caelesti generatione** — the disputed title asserting the *celestial generation* of comets; the *generatio / corruptio* quarrel (Rothmann earlier charging that "generation in the heaven" imports Aristotelian *corruption* into the incorruptible heavens) is the running terminological dispute, rendered with the technical Aristotelian senses intact.
- **Textual note (*deduxere* / *deduxero*).** Near the end (*…ad optatum finem rem omnem deduxere*), the 1596 printed text / *Opera Omnia* base read here gives the syncopated archaic form ***deduxere*** (= *deduxerō*, future perfect, 1st sing., "I shall have brought"); the source block reproduces the printed *deduxere* as required by §2/. The unsyncopated *deduxero* is the equivalent classical-regular spelling; both readings carry the identical sense, so the English ("shall … have brought the whole matter to the wished-for end") is unaffected. Recorded here, not silently normalised.
- **Negation check.** Several pivotal negated clauses were counted and reproduced one-for-one, e.g.: *Neque enim ego te vspiam in illis impietatis accusaui* ("for nowhere did I accuse you of impiety" — one negation, on the accusation); *nec … te caecum efficiam, neque temeritatis accusem* (Rothmann's two requests, both kept); *nec te occaecare, nec temerarium pronuntiare vnquam praesumsi* ("I have never presumed either to blind you or to pronounce you rash" — double negative correlatives preserved); *me … non amplius ea pro veris habere, imo ipsam Obseruationem … infectam cupere* (Rothmann no longer holds them true, *and* wishes the observation undone — both polarities kept). No negation added or dropped.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Substantial closing POSTSCRIPTA (Rothmann's fixed-star observations, the per-star c. 1/12° longitude excess, the Venus-vespertine refraction error, the "Quantae molis erat Stellarum inquirere Hermas" tag), restored from Dreyer VI, pp. 199–200 (dropped by the working transcription).
- **Correction.** "to investigate the Stars, like a Hermes" corrected to "to track down the boundary-markers [*Hermas*] of the Stars": "Hermas" is the accusative object of "inquirere" (with genitive "Stellarum"), not a mistaken reference to the god Hermes.

translation.warrant:
**Not collated against Dreyer** — no page reference for this letter, so the grade is capped at Probable however sound the translation looks. the edition gives no page reference for this letter, so by the audit's rule this is audited against the transcribed original alone and capped at grade Probable; no Dreyer page images exist to collate. Checked systematically against the Latin: opening/closing formulae, the 1589-11-24 Uraniborg date and signature, every proper name (Vallesius, Daneau, Peucer x3, Pena, Rantzau, Frischlin, Schonfeldt, Wittich, 'Graminaeus', Hermes Trismegistus), every number and date (17 degrees twilight, 7/8 students, 16 eyes, 2-cubit/4-cubit/5-cubit/20+ instruments, 6 Dec 1588, 2 Jan 1589, c. 10 degrees, comet years '85/'58, 150 paces, 700x, 2284 semidiameters, 7,850,000, 12-ell wheel, 800 stars, 5 minutes), the custody of the Epistolae Astronomicae correspondence (correctly kept with Tycho, who received the letters and is publishing them with his own replies — not misattributed), and several sarcastic self-boast passages (the sixteen-eyes/twenty-instruments taunt, 'primus forte omnium... probare elaboraui', the Peucer-as-judge passage) where subject/object assignment is correctly preserved in each case, not flipped. The restored postscript (Dreyer VI, 199-200) is present in both the transcribed original and the published English and matches closely. One low-severity mistranslation found in the postscript (the 'Hermas'/boundary-markers allusion rendered as an invented Hermes-simile); no fabrication, no omission, no dropped closing, no misattributed custody, no invented day-number found elsewhere in this very long letter.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (low). "Hermas" is the accusative object of "inquirere" ("to track down the boundary-markers [hermae] of the Stars", i.e. to fix their true positions, echoing Virgil's 'tantae molis erat'), not a simile subject; the English invents a comparison ('like a Hermes') that has no counterpart and drops the actual object of the verb. At: “it may become plain how great a task it was to investigate the Stars, like a Hermes”.

**Repaired.** No Dreyer page images were available for this letter (no page reference), so the underlying Latin ("viaque simul constare queat, Quantae molis erat Stellarum inquirere Hermas") could not be collated against the printed edition and is left untouched. The mistranslation is nonetheless demonstrable from internal grammatical evidence alone: "Hermas" is unambiguously the accusative-plural direct object of "inquirere" governed by the genitive "Stellarum", not a simile subject, and the letter's own later genuine allusion to "Hermes Thrice-Greatest [*Trismegistus*]" plausibly explains how the translator's eye was drawn to the wrong word. Graded B per the audit's rule (sound but uncollated), matching the incoming audited_grade.

documents.incipit: NOBILISS. Domine et amice observande. Cum intellexissem Legatum Regis vestri D. …

text.original:
ANTIQUA NOBILITATE VIRO CLARISS. ET ERUDITIONE PRÆSTANTI D. TYCHONI BRAHE DANO, URANIEBURGI DOMINO, D. ET AMICO OBSERVANDO.
S.

NOBILISS. Domine et amice observande. Cum intellexissem Legatum Regis vestri D. VINSHEMIUM ad nostrum Imp. venisse, quam primum mihi per valetudinem licuit, statim eum adij et percontatus sum, an aliquid literarum abs te mihi attulisset. Iam enim diu exoptabam tuas, quibus saltem edocerer de meis ad te, num omnes, quas scripsi, aut aliquæ illarum tibi essent redditæ. Cum autem ille negaret se quicquam habere abs te, vellicare animum meum cœpit cogitatio, num mihi succenseres putaresque me data opera ad tuas respondere noluisse. Hoc si ita est, obsecro te, mi TYCHO, depone hanc suspicionem ex animo tuo. Non induo nunc in hoc meo senio, crede mihi, illam barbariem, ut ad amici literas non respondeam. Absit illud longe a me, ita me Deus amet, mi TYCHO, respondi ad singulas tuas semper. Quod si tibi redditæ non sunt, non mihi, quæso, imputa, sed iniquæ sorti, quæ nobis invidet illam voluptatem, quam uterque capturi eramus ex literarum lectione, et hominum infidelitati. Annus est integer, cum per civem quendam Gorliciensem, opera MYLIJ, dedi ad te literas unâ cum opusculo VERNERI, quod aliquando a me expetebas. Hæc cum literis SCULTETI ad te perferri debebant. Quid cum illis factum sit, nescio, postea cum hoc vere missus esset nobilis vestras a Rege ad Imp. cum falconibus, ac ille quoque tuas ad me attulisset literas, ipse eum alloquutus dixi me ipsi literas ad te daturum esse. Sed cum biduo abessem urbe medicinæ faciendæ gratia, ille interea præter spem et nostræ aulæ consuetudinem citius expeditus hinc discessit, quod quam ægre tulerim, dici non potest. Nactus autem mox altero aut tertio die amicum, apud quem deplorabam elapsam mihi occasionem mittendi literas ad te, statim ille suam mihi detulit operam, dixitque se Dresdæ habere amicum, cuius opera fidelissime perferrentur ad te. Dedi itaque illi meas, quibus adhuc alias adiunxi. Si non sunt tibi redditæ, ne mihi culpam adscribas rogo, imo vero hanc meam iustam salva conscientia excusationem eo animo, quo amicum decet, accipias, meque primo quoque tempore de his omnibus edoceas, animumque meum nimis solicitum hanc ob rem tranquillum reddas. Hæc repeto hisce meis, cum ignorem, qualem cursum habuerint priores meæ.

Quid impediverit, quod huc usque primus liber tuus non prodierit, quidve nunc præ manibus habeas, ut me certiorem reddas magnopere peto. Mea Mathemata iam diu quiescunt et quasi in DEMOCRITI puteo abdita latent. Si mihi Deus longius vitæ curriculum concesserit, cogito in meis ædibus extruere aliquam speculam, unde aliquando astra contemplari possem.

Æstate præterita partem meæ domus reparare cœpi. Aliud, quod scribam, non habeo. De rebus Gallicis veriora vos istic habere existimo. Ad nos varia et incerta afferuntur iuxta hominum affectiones varias. Illud certissimum habetur, Regi huc usque feliciter successisse. Genevæ obsidionem solutam narrant, relicta tamen fuisse quædam præsidia in obsidione, quæ Genevenses effusi ex urbe dispulerunt et novum commeatum in urbem invexerunt. Deus suam Ecclesiam contra tyrannos potenti sua manu tueatur et defendat.

B. V. mi amantiss. TYCHO.
Datæ Pragæ die ultima Novemb. veteri stylo Anno 1589.
T. studiosiss.
THAD.
text.english:
**To a man of ancient nobility, most renowned and outstanding in learning, Master Tycho Brahe the Dane, Lord of Uraniborg, his lord, and friend to be esteemed.**
Greeting.

Most noble lord and friend to be esteemed. When I had learned that your King's legate, Master Vinshemius, had come to our Emperor, as soon as my health allowed me I went to him at once and inquired whether he had brought me any letter from you. For I had long been most eager for word from you, by which I might at least be informed about my own [letters] to you — whether all those I wrote, or any of them, had been delivered to you. But when he denied having anything from you, a thought began to gnaw at my mind: whether you might be angry with me and think that I had deliberately refused to answer your letters. If this is so, I beseech you, my Tycho, put this suspicion out of your mind. I am not now, believe me, in this my old age, taking on that barbarousness of not answering a friend's letters. Far be that from me — so help me God, my Tycho — I have always answered each of yours. And if they have not been delivered to you, do not, I pray, charge it to me, but to unkind fortune, which begrudges us that pleasure which we were each to take from the reading of letters, and to the faithlessness of men. It is a full year since, through a certain citizen of Görlitz, by the agency of Mylius, I dispatched a letter to you together with the little work of Werner which you had once been asking of me. These were to be conveyed to you with Scultetus's letter. What became of them I do not know. Afterwards, when this spring a nobleman of yours had been sent by the King to the Emperor with falcons, and he too had brought me your letter, I myself spoke with him and said that I would give him a letter for you. But since I was away from the city for two days for the practice of medicine, he meanwhile — beyond my expectation and contrary to the custom of our court — was dispatched more quickly and departed hence, at which I cannot say how grieved I was. But having soon, on the second or third day, come upon a friend, to whom I was lamenting the lost opportunity of sending a letter to you, he straightway offered me his service, and said that he had a friend at Dresden, by whose agency they would be conveyed to you most faithfully. And so I gave him mine, to which I added yet others. If they have not been delivered to you, I beg you not to ascribe the fault to me, but rather to accept this just excuse of mine — [made] with a clear conscience — in the spirit that befits a friend, and to inform me about all these matters at the very first opportunity, and to render my mind, too anxious on this account, tranquil. I repeat these things in this present letter of mine, since I do not know what course my earlier ones have taken.

What has hindered your first book from coming out hitherto, or what you now have in hand — I greatly ask that you make me more certain of it. My own mathematical studies have long lain at rest and lie hidden, as it were, in Democritus's well. If God grants me a longer course of life, I am thinking of building some little observatory at my house, whence I might one day contemplate the stars.

This past summer I began to repair part of my house. I have nothing else to write. Of French affairs I judge that you there have truer [reports]. To us things are brought various and uncertain, according to men's various dispositions. This is held most certain: that the King has hitherto succeeded happily. They report that the siege of Geneva has been raised — yet that certain garrisons had been left behind in the siege, which the Genevans, pouring out from the city, drove off, and brought a fresh supply of provisions into the city. May God watch over and defend His Church against the tyrants with His mighty hand.

Fare you well, my most loving Tycho.
Given at Prague, on the last day of November, Old Style, in the year 1589.
Most devoted to you,
Thad[deus].

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *THAD.* / *Thaddaeus Hagecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayek, 1525–1600), Bohemian physician, astronomer, and personal physician to the Emperor at Prague; one of Tycho's most important Central-European correspondents, and later instrumental in bringing Tycho into Imperial service. The closing subscription contracts his name to *THAD.*; *T. studiosiss.* = *Tui studiosissimus*, "Most devoted to you". Dreyer prints the letter in *Opera Omnia* VII among Tycho's incoming correspondence.
- **Recipient address.** *D. TYCHONI BRAHE DANO, URANIEBURGI DOMINO* — "Master Tycho Brahe the Dane, Lord of Uraniborg." *Uranieburgi* = **Uraniborg** on Hven.
- **Salutation.** *S.* = *Salutem* ("Greeting,").
- ***Legatum Regis vestri D. VINSHEMIUM*** — "your King's legate, Master Vinshemius": an envoy of **Frederik II's** son and successor **Christian IV** (a minor; the regency government) to the Imperial court of **Rudolf II**. The name *Vinshemius* (Winsheim / Veit Ortel von Winsheim and family) recurs in this same Hagecius–Tycho correspondence (the correspondence preserves a *VITUS VINSHEMIUS* returning from Wittenberg with Lutheran tracts for Tycho), so the reading is secure as a surname even though the legate's full identity is not fixed by this letter alone.
- ***nostrum Imp.*** = *nostrum Imperatorem*, "our Emperor" — **Rudolf II**, Holy Roman Emperor, resident at Prague, whose physician Hagecius was ("our court," *nostrae aulae*, below).
- ***opusculo VERNERI*** — "the little work of Werner": **Johann Werner** of Nuremberg, almost certainly his *De motu octavae sphaerae* (Nuremberg, 1522). Tycho avidly pursued this tract in the years of his prosthaphaeresis-priority quarrel with Ursus (Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, on Tycho's "avid pursuit … of the *De motu octavae sphaerae* of the Nuremberg astronomer Johannes Werner"); the present letter documents Hagecius procuring a copy for him.
- ***per civem quendam Gorliciensem … cum literis SCULTETI*** — "through a certain citizen of Görlitz … with Scultetus's letter": **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (Bartholomäus Schultz, 1540–1614), the Görlitz mathematician, surveyor, and burgomaster, a mutual friend and a regular relay-point in Tycho's correspondence (Dreyer lists "Scultetus at Leipzig" among Tycho's foreign correspondents). The Görlitz citizen is the carrier; Scultetus's own letter was to travel in the same packet.
- ***opera MYLIJ*** — "by the agency of Mylius": an intermediary, *Mylius* (the latinised form of *Mühl/Müller/Möller*); not further specified in the letter and left unidentified rather than guessed.
- ***nobilis vestras … cum falconibus*** — "a nobleman of yours … with falcons": a Danish nobleman sent by the crown to the Emperor bearing falcons — Danish (and especially Icelandic/Norwegian) falcons were a standing diplomatic gift to the Habsburg court. *vestras* (for *vester*) is a chancery/period spelling, "of yours" (Danish).
- ***in DEMOCRITI puteo abdita latent*** — "lie hidden, as it were, in Democritus's well": the proverbial *Democritus's well* (cf. *veritas in puteo* — truth lies hidden in a well), the saying attributed to Democritus that truth lies sunk in the depths; Hagecius means his mathematical work lies buried out of sight. The classical allusion is kept.
- ***speculam … unde astra contemplari possem*** — "some little observatory … whence I might contemplate the stars": *specula* in its astronomical sense, a watch-tower / observatory. A poignant aspiration from a man of 64, set against Tycho's Uraniborg.
- ***primus liber tuus*** — "your first book": **Tycho's *Epistolarum astronomicarum liber primus*** (the first volume of the *Astronomical Letters*), which Tycho was then printing at his own Uraniborg press; it appeared in 1596. Hagecius asks why it has not yet come out — a securely datable reference to the work's protracted production.
- **French affairs / the King.** *De rebus Gallicis … Regi huc usque feliciter successisse* — the French Wars of Religion: "the King" is **Henri IV of Navarre**, who had succeeded to the French throne on the assassination of Henri III (1 August 1589) and was campaigning against the Catholic League; Hagecius reports (from a Protestant standpoint) that he has so far prospered.
- ***Genevae obsidionem solutam*** — "the siege of Geneva raised": Protestant Geneva was under pressure from **Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy** in 1589 (the opening of the Savoy–Geneva war). Hagecius relays a report — explicitly marked as *varia et incerta*, "various and uncertain" — that the siege had been lifted and the Genevans had driven off the besieging garrisons and revictualled the city. The epistemic hedge is preserved, not sharpened into a flat statement of fact.
- ***Deus suam Ecclesiam contra tyrannos … tueatur*** — "May God … defend His Church against the tyrants": the optative subjunctive *tueatur … et defendat* is rendered as a prayer ("May God …"), matching the Protestant-confessional register of the war news.
- **Subscription.** *B. V.* = *Bene vale*, "Fare you well"; *Datae Pragae … T. studiosiss. THAD.* = "Given at Prague … Most devoted to you, Thad[deus]."
- **Calendar.** *die ultima Novemb. veteri stylo Anno 1589* = "on the last day of November, Old Style, in the year 1589" = **30 November 1589 (O.S.)**. Hagecius, writing at the Catholic Imperial court (which had adopted the Gregorian calendar), expressly flags *veteri stylo* ("Old Style") to align his date with Tycho's Danish reckoning — itself a small monument to the calendar gap discussed in this chapter's convention The as-written date agrees with the catalogue label (30 November 1589); no discrepancy. No silent conversion made.
