text.original:
CLARISSIMO VARIOQUE DOCTRINARUM GENERE ERUDITISSIMO EXCELLENTISSIMOQUE VIRO D. THADDÆO HAGGECIO AB HAYCK, PHILOSOPHIAe ET MEDICINAe DOCTORI EXIMIO, AMICO SUO IN PRIMIS COLENDO.
ZU PRAG IM LANDT ZU BEHMEN AN HERN DOCTOR THADDÆUM HAGGECIUM.

SCRIPSI tibi non ita dudum, mi amantissime et doctissime D. D. THADDÆE, atque ad ultimas a te acceptas respondi, solicitudinemque omnem de prioribus tuis, quas suspicabaris non redditas mihi, uti spero, ademi. Nunc et alteras addo, ne semper a te praeveniar aut scriptionem tamdiu, ut antea, procrastinem. Licet enim non magnopere occurrat, quod nunc scribam, tamen idipsum potius indicabo, quam quod nihil mittam, praesertim cum instantibus Francofurtianis iam Nundinis occasionem has ad te mittendi prae foribus esse videam; ut si non recta, saltem inde per ambages meae ad te perferantur. Quas antea circa Novembris initia ad te paulo luculentius exaravi, iamdudum redditas confido. Nam bina exemplaria transscribi curavi seorsimque per diversos internuntios mitti, ne ambae interciderint. Quid te illic voluerim, iam procul dubio cognovisti. Nec dubito, quin in Privilegio Caesareano ampliore procurando, tuam mihi praestiturus sis fidelem operam; quod si impetraveris, fac ut mature habeam; primus enim Tomus Operis nostri, cui illud praefigendum destinavi, iam indies ad Colophonem deducitur. Nam eius tertia et ultima pars, quae aliorum placita, inter quae etiam tua, expendit, iam sub praelo est. Misi etiam tum temporis Apologeticum quoddam Scriptum, quo praestanti cuidam in Scotia Mathematico, Aristotelea tutanti et nostra convellere aggresso, occurri. Hoc si perlegisti, velut te fecisse non dubito, tuum mihi de eo iudicium communica, et si quid desiderari aut minus absolute tractatum censueris, ingenue admone. Fieri enim potest, ut Apologiam hanc secundo Tomo, qui de eodem Cometa, circa quem potissimum movetur controversia, agit, subiungam, quo locupletior reddatur. Si quae igitur inter revidendum atque recognoscendum castigatione aut suppletitione indigere perspexero, eis providebo. Literas meas, quas tibi inde a prima familiaritate Ratisponae contracta inscripsi, si quas forte reservasti, rogavi, ut singularum exemplum transscriptum mihi mitteres, quod et nunc peto, praesertim quantum ad eas attinet, quae aliquid ad Astronomicam vel Cometometricam materiam faciunt. Cur id cupiam, tunc indicavi. Et ut scias, rem ita se habere, mitto aliquam partem libri I Epistolarum Astronomicarum, quae hactenus typis absoluta est; in qua saltem eae, quae ab Illustriss. Principe WILHELMO, Hassiae Landgravio, et eius Celsit. Mathematico, unâ cum mea ad singulas responsione, ultro citroque hactenus missae sunt, continentur. Addam et illas, quas me redeuntibus ab hisce Nundinis mercatoribus (Cassellas enim pertranseunt) recepturum existimo, unâ cum mea responsione, sicque primam Tomi illius Epistolarum partem claudam. In secunda et tertia (nam et hunc trifariam subdividere lubet) aliorum de re Astronomica mecum per literas conferentium Apographa unâ cum mea rescriptione exhibebo. Illic tua quoque, quotquot in meis Archivis reperio, addam. Atque id erat caussae (ut denuo inculcem) cur mearum ad te, quas in promptu omnes non habeo, copiam desiderârim. Habeo alias non paucas Eruditorum de hac materia collationes, quas Astronomiae cupidis lectu non ingratas fore confido. Continent enim multa peculiaria et non ubique obvia ad artis penitiorem illustrationem plurimum conducentia atque rem insuper Cometicam affatim et enucleate excutientia. Licebitque primum Tomum ad tria vel quatuor Alphabeta, prout libuerit, hac ipsa Typorum forma deducere ita, ut iustae reddatur quantitatis, et Neotericorum coeli Phaenomenωn libros singulos magnitudine adaequet. Reliquas literas, quae hoc comprehendi commode non poterint, in alium sequentem digeram, sicque ordine et successive Eruditorum mecum collocutiones Astronomicas certis voluminibus, etiam alia interim agens, complectar, ne prorsus intercidant, cum multa cognitu haud indigna contineant. Has igitur primitias boni consule, tuamque de ijs sententiam mihi perscribe. Invenies vel in his plurima disquisitionem accuratam merentia; nam praeterquam quod de observationibus atque instrumentis aliter quam antea factitatum instituendis quaedam agant, de coeli essentia, stellarum refractionibus, hypothesibus coelestium motuum, tum etiam Cometis atque plerisque eiuscemodi varie inter nos disputatur. Quae omnia tuo solerti iudicio discernenda relinquo. Rogoque peramanter, velis cum Nobilissimo et amplissimo viro D. IACOBO CURTIO de his omnibus vel saltem eorum praecipuis per otij commoditatem conferre mecumque vestram eruditam censuram communicare. Nam et ROTHMANNUS, cum quo de plerisque non ingrata mihi est controversia, ad arbitros provocat, quod et ego non detrecto. Inspicite, legite, dijudicate. Nolim tamen, ut pluribus hos quaterniones communices, antequam totus liber consummatus prodierit. Primus quaternio deest, in quo titulus atque praefatiuncula quaedam extabunt, qui in totius absolutionem, uti fieri solet, differtur. Quamprimum Tomus anterior Ascititiorum coeli Phaenomenon, qui nunc sub praelo est, extremam manum calcographicam senserit, te eius reddam participem. Ne vero te, quem talibus affici scio, nimis diu sine meis detinerem, volui has qualescunque Epistolarum pagellas, etsi non ad destinatam maturitatem perductas, tecum impertiri, ut haberes quo aliquantulum, donec caetera absolvantur, animum per otium, nostra etiam qualiacunque legendo, pasceres. Tuum itaque erit omnia in meliorem partem interpretari et errata typographica, si quae, uti non dubito (necdum enim mihi ipsi ista relegere vacabat) commissa sint, propria industria, qua res ipsas satis intelligis, emendare.

Quin et aliud quiddam nunc occurrit, quod a te hisce expetam. Incidi proximis diebus, dum tuas literas evolvo, in chartam, qua observationes nonnullas a te coelitus habitas mihi denotasti, inter quas ab initio Martis stella mense Septembri et sequent. anni 1578 (licet in tua scheda per incuriam aliquam annus 1579 ponebatur), quando acronychius erat, in distantia a 1a ♈ aliquoties denotata. Quoniam vero ob raras serenitates eius observationem meis organis tunc instituere, uti cupiebam, non licuit, hancque acronychiam eius dispositionem cum pluribus alijs postmodum aliquot sequentibus annis diligenter desuper acquisitis conferre aveam, ipsius motus expendendi restituendique gratia, rogo amanter, ut si quas plures habeas in ♂ tunc praesertim temporis factas animadversiones, quoad distantiam tum ab ea ipsa, tum alijs etiam stellis, et quoad altitudinem meridianam, si eam nactus es, id quicquid erit, in meum usum describi curare velis; et praeterea quotcunque alias observationes Astronomicas in promptu habes. Licet enim sciam, eas ob Radij atque aliorum instrumentorum, quibus usus es, minus exactam perfectionem non satis praecise se habere, tamen qualescunque tandem fuerint, eas cognoscere non inutile duxerim. Nam et nonnunquam has limitare atque, sicubi opus fuerit, ex circumstantijs ipsis corrigere non difficile erit.

Qui de Nova Stella atque Cometis scripserunt, modo plures ad manus habueris, quam me obtinuisse putas, et eorum copiam facias velim. Si mittenda Rostochium ad D. D. HENRICUM BRUCÆUM, aut Lubecam Mercatori meo IACOBO BUCK, ut is nobili viro HENRICO RANZOVIO, Regis nostri in Holsatia Vicario, amico meo singulari, illa transmittat, procurâris, utique ea cito et certo accepturus sum.

Vide, quot nunc scripserim, licet ab initio vix, quae exararem, me habiturum putârim. Talis est inter nos animorum confluentia, ut unum pariat alterum. Da operam, ut brevi luculenter respondeas. Ego posthac in rescribendo maturior ero. Vale et magnificum Dominum CURTIUM meis verbis officiose saluta, a quo etiam responsionem, modo per publica otium illi supererit, indies expecto.

Iterum quam felicissime atque diutissime vale.
Uraniburgi die 23. Februarij 1590.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE.
POST SCRIPTA

CUM eo ipso die, quo has literas meo Amanuensi ad mundum describendas tradidissem, circa vesperas Veneris a Sole digressioni maximae observandae intenderem, ecce Cometes quidam ad eandem coeli occiduam plagam ex improviso apparuit, ideoque hasce literas interea mecum reservandas duxi, donec omnes istius ascititij sideris apparentias coelitus per totam eius durationem accurate deductas scrutatus essem, ut mea etiam inventa, ex quo sciam te talibus plurimum affici, unâ transmitterem. Addidi itaque brevem eiusdem Cometae descriptionem, qualem illustrissimo quoque Principi WILHELMO, Hassiae Landgravio, nuper hac de re scribens communicavi. Plenius de eodem tertio nostro Tomo agam. Illic enim hunc prioribus adiungere omnesque eius apparentias, quodque omnino Parallaxi destituebatur, e multiplicibus et certis observationibus Geometrice demonstrare constitui; interim has pauculas de eodem crinito sidere conceptiones, e ratis tamen animadversionibus derivatas, boni consule. Quod autem tamdiu a prima scriptione negotium hucusque distulerim, praeter opinionem meam factum est. Licet enim expectandum erat, donec Cometes ille prorsus evanesceret, quod post sextum diem Martij accidit, et aliquantulum temporis ad eius habitudines ex observationibus rimandas requireretur, accidit insuper, ut statim post Martij medium Sereniss. Scotorum Rex cum splendido suo comitatu me hic inviseret, atque ex eo tempore per aliquot continuos dies pluribus peregrinis hospitibus excipiendis occuparer, quo minus inceptam telam pertexere licuerit. Hincque factum est, quod literas hasce usque in sextam septimanam mecum retinuerim, quod indicandum duxi, ne cur tam diverso tempore haec scribantur, mirareris, sed moram hanc eo citius excusatam haberes. Iterum vale. Haec scribebantur quarto Aprilis.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and, in every varied kind of learning, most erudite and most excellent man, Master Thaddaeus Hagecius of Hájek, distinguished Doctor of Philosophy and of Medicine, his friend to be honoured above all.**
**At Prague, in the land of Bohemia, to Master Doctor Thaddaeus Hagecius.**

I wrote to you not so long ago, my most loving and most learned Master Doctor Thaddaeus, and answered the last [letter] received from you, and — as I hope — I removed all your anxiety about your earlier ones, which you suspected had not been delivered to me. Now I add yet another, lest I be always forestalled by you, or, as before, put off writing for so long. For although nothing much comes to mind that I might now write, I shall sooner report this very fact than send nothing — especially since, with the Frankfurt fair now at hand, I see the chance of sending this to you to be right at the door; so that, if not directly, then at least from there, by roundabout ways, my [letters] may be carried to you. Those which earlier, around the beginning of November, I penned to you somewhat more fully, I trust have long since been delivered. For I had two copies transcribed and sent separately by different messengers, lest both should be lost. What I wanted of you over there you have now doubtless learned. Nor do I doubt that, in procuring a more ample Imperial privilege [for me], you will render me your faithful service; and if you obtain it, see that I have it in good time, for the first Volume of our Work, before which I have determined that it be set, is now day by day being brought to its colophon. For its third and last part, which weighs the opinions of others — among which yours too — is now under the press. I also sent at that time a certain apologetic writing, by which I countered a certain distinguished Mathematician in Scotland who, defending Aristotelian doctrines, had set out to demolish ours. If you have read this through — as I do not doubt you have done — share with me your judgement of it, and if you think anything is wanting or treated less than fully, frankly advise me. For it may be that I shall append this Apology to the second Volume, which treats of the same Comet about which the controversy chiefly turns, so that it may be rendered the fuller. If, then, in revising and re-examining, I perceive that any [parts] need correction or supplementation, I shall provide for them. My own letters, which I wrote to you ever since our first acquaintance was formed at Regensburg — if perhaps you have kept any — I asked that you send me a transcribed copy of each, which I ask again now, especially as regards those which bear in any way on Astronomical or Cometometric matter. Why I desire it, I indicated then. And that you may know the matter to be so, I send some part of Book I of the Astronomical Letters, which has so far been completed in print; in which there are contained at least those which, [exchanged] between the Most Illustrious Prince Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, and His Highness's Mathematician, together with my reply to each, have so far been sent back and forth. I shall add also those which I expect to receive from the merchants returning from this fair (for they pass through Kassel), together with my reply, and so I shall close the first part of that Volume of Letters. In the second and third (for I am pleased to subdivide this too into three) I shall set forth the transcripts of others who confer with me by letter on Astronomical matters, together with my reply. There I shall add yours too, as many as I find in my archives. And this was the reason (to drive it home again) why I desired a supply of my [letters] to you, all of which I do not have ready at hand. I have not a few other collations of the Learned on this subject, which I trust will be not unwelcome reading to those eager for Astronomy. For they contain many things peculiar and not everywhere to be met with, conducing greatly to a deeper illustration of the art, and besides sifting the matter of Comets fully and clearly. And it will be possible to bring out the first Volume, as I please, to three or four Alphabets [of signatures], in this very form of type, so that it be rendered of a just size and match in bulk the individual books of the Moderns on the phenomena of the heaven. The remaining letters, which cannot conveniently be comprised in this [Volume], I shall arrange into another following one; and so, in order and successively, I shall embrace in fixed volumes the Astronomical conversations of the Learned with me — doing other things meanwhile — lest they perish utterly, since they contain much not unworthy to be known. Take these first-fruits, then, in good part, and write me your opinion of them. You will find even in these very many things deserving careful inquiry; for, besides that they treat of certain matters concerning observations and instruments to be established otherwise than was done before, there is varied disputation among us concerning the essence of the heaven, the refractions of the stars, the hypotheses of the celestial motions, and then also Comets and very many things of that kind. All of which I leave to be discerned by your skilful judgement. And I ask you most lovingly: be willing, at your leisure's convenience, to confer with the most noble and most ample man Master Jacob Curtius about all these, or at least the chief of them, and to share with me your learned assessment. For Rothmann too, with whom I have a controversy on very many points that is not unwelcome to me, appeals to arbiters — which I too do not decline. Inspect, read, judge between [us]. I would not, however, have you communicate these quires to more [people] before the whole book has come out complete. The first quire is lacking, in which the title and a certain little preface will stand, which is deferred until the completion of the whole, as is wont to be done. As soon as the earlier Volume on the adventitious phenomena of the heaven, which is now under the press, shall have felt the final engraver's hand, I shall make you a partaker of it. But, lest I detain you — whom I know to be affected by such things — too long without anything of mine, I wished to share with you these few pages of Letters, of whatever sort, though not brought to their intended maturity, so that you might have something on which, for a little while, until the rest are finished, you might feed your mind at leisure, by reading even these such-as-they-are [works] of mine. It will therefore be for you to interpret everything in the better part, and the typographical errors — if any have been committed, as I do not doubt (for I had not yet had leisure to read these over myself) — to amend by your own industry, with which you understand the matters themselves well enough.

But yet another thing now comes to mind, which I would ask of you by this [letter]. In recent days, while unrolling your letters, I came upon a paper on which you noted down for me some observations taken by you from the heaven, among them — from the beginning — the star of Mars, in the month of September and following of the year 1578 (although in your sheet, by some carelessness, the year 1579 was put), when it was acronychal, [its distance] noted several times from the 1st [degree] of ♈ Aries. But since, owing to the rare clear spells, I was not then able, as I wished, to set up an observation of it with my instruments, and I long to compare this acronychal disposition of it with several others diligently acquired thereafter in some following years, for the sake of weighing and restoring its motion, I ask lovingly that, if you have several more observations of ♂ Mars made especially at that time — as to distance both from that same [star] and from other stars too, and as to meridian altitude, if you have obtained it — whatever it may be, you would be willing to have it written out for my use; and besides, as many other Astronomical observations as you have ready at hand. For although I know that, on account of the less than exact perfection of the cross-staff and the other instruments you used, they are not held with sufficient precision, yet whatever sort they may finally have been, I should reckon it not useless to know them. For it will sometimes be no hard matter to bound these and, wherever there be need, to correct them from the circumstances themselves.

Those who have written on the New Star and on Comets — if only you have more at hand than you think I have obtained — I would wish that you make a supply of them too. If you arrange for them to be sent to Rostock to Master Doctor Heinrich Brucaeus, or to Lübeck to my merchant Jacob Buck, that he may transmit them to the noble man Heinrich Rantzau, my King's Vicar in Holstein, my especial friend, I shall in any case receive them quickly and surely.

See how much I have now written, though at the outset I scarcely thought I should have anything to set down. Such is the confluence of minds between us, that one [thing] begets another. Take pains to answer clearly soon. I, hereafter, shall be more prompt in writing back. Farewell, and greet the magnificent Master Curtius dutifully in my words, from whom too I daily await a reply, if only leisure from public affairs be left to him.

Again, fare you well most happily and most long.
At Uraniborg, the 23rd day of February 1590.
Yours, Tycho Brahe.
POSTSCRIPT

On the very day on which I had handed these letters to my amanuensis to be copied out fair, towards evening I was intent on observing the maximum elongation of Venus from the Sun, when behold! a certain Comet appeared unexpectedly in that same western quarter of the heaven; and so I judged that this letter should meanwhile be kept back with me, until I had scrutinized all the appearances of that adventitious star, accurately derived from the heaven throughout its whole duration, so that I might transmit my own findings too along with it — since I know you to be much affected by such things. I have therefore added a brief description of the same Comet, such as I lately communicated to the most illustrious Prince Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, when writing to him on this matter. I shall treat of it more fully in our third Volume. For there I have determined to join this [comet] to the earlier ones, and to demonstrate geometrically, from manifold and sure observations, all its appearances, and that it was altogether without parallax; meanwhile take in good part these few conceptions about the same hairy star, derived nevertheless from sound observations. But that I have put off the business so long, until now, from the first writing, has happened beyond my intention. For although it had to be waited until that Comet vanished entirely — which happened after the sixth day of March — and some little time was required for tracing out its conditions from the observations, it happened besides that, straight after the middle of March, the Most Serene King of the Scots, with his splendid retinue, visited me here, and from that time, for several continuous days, I was occupied in receiving many foreign guests, so that I was the less able to finish weaving the web I had begun. And hence it came about that I have kept this letter with me right up to the sixth week — which I judged should be indicated, lest you wonder why these things are written at such different dates, but might rather hold this delay the more readily excused. Again, farewell. These [last lines] were written on the fourth of April.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** **Tycho Brahe**, at Uraniborg on Hven, to **Thaddaeus Hagecius** (*Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku*, Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayck, 1525–1600), the Bohemian court physician, astronomer and humanist at Prague — a long-standing correspondent of Tycho's since the *De nova stella* exchanges of the 1570s. The acquaintance "first formed at Regensburg" (*Ratisponae*) refers to their meeting at the 1575 Imperial Diet.
- **Address line (German).** *ZU PRAG IM LANDT ZU BEHMEN AN HERN DOCTOR THADDAeUM HAGGECIUM* = "At Prague, in the land of Bohemia, to Master Doctor Thaddaeus Hagecius" — the cover/direction in chancery German over the Latin salutation and body; the code-switch is preserved by this chapter's convention *Behmen* = Böhmen (Bohemia).
- **Other persons.** *D. Iacobus Curtius* / *Dominus Curtius* = **Jacob Curtius (Jakob Kurtz von Senftenau)**, Imperial Vice-Chancellor at the court of Rudolf II, an astronomically literate patron whom Tycho cultivated (and through whom the imperial privilege was sought). *Rothmannus* = **Christoph Rothmann**, the Hesse-Kassel mathematician, with whom Tycho carried on his great cosmological controversy; *Illustriss. Princeps Wilhelmus, Hassiae Landgravius* = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel**; *D. D. Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** of Rostock; *Iacobus Buck* = **Jacob Buck**, Tycho's merchant-agent at Lübeck; *Henricus Ranzovius* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), royal *Statthalter* (Vicar) of Holstein, the great Schleswig-Holstein humanist and Tycho's friend and conduit. *Sereniss. Scotorum Rex* = **James VI of Scotland** (later James I of England), who visited Hven in March 1590 during his stay in Denmark for his marriage to Anne of Denmark.
- **The "Scottish Mathematician."** *praestanti cuidam in Scotia Mathematico, Aristotelea tutanti et nostra convellere aggresso* — the unnamed Scot defending Aristotle is **John Craig (Craig of Edinburgh)**, with whom Tycho conducted the comet-parallax dispute; the *Apologeticum Scriptum* is Tycho's reply to him.
- **The Work in press.** *primus Tomus Operis nostri* … *Tomus anterior Ascititiorum coeli Phaenomenon* refers to Tycho's *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* / *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* programme: the volume "on the adventitious (*ascititia*) phenomena of the heaven" = the comet volume (*De mundi … recentioribus phaenomenis*, 1588, of which the third part on others' opinions was still under the press); *liber I Epistolarum Astronomicarum* = the **Epistolarum astronomicarum liber primus** (Uraniborg, 1596), here being printed in instalments, opening with the Wilhelm/Rothmann correspondence.
- **Technical / printing terms.** *Privilegium Caesareanum* = an **Imperial privilege** (copyright/printing protection). *Colophon* kept as printed. *Alphabeta* (*ad tria vel quatuor Alphabeta … deducere*) = "Alphabets" of printer's signatures (gathering-sequences A–Z); rendered "[of signatures]". *quaterniones / quaternio* = **quires** (gatherings of four sheets); *primus quaternio deest* = "the first quire is lacking" (title-leaf + preface deferred to last, normal practice). *sub praelo* = "under the press"; *extremam manum calcographicam* = "the final engraver's/printer's hand." *Apographa* = transcript-copies. *Nundinae Francofurtianae* = the **Frankfurt [book] fair**.
- **Astronomy.** *acronychius / acronychia dispositio* = **acronychal** (rising at sunset / in opposition to the Sun) — kept as the technical term. *digressio maxima* (a Sole) = **maximum elongation** (here of Venus from the Sun); by the audit's rule the interpretive sense is the glossary's *elongatio* → elongation, and "maximum" renders *maxima* without bracketing since it stands in the source. *altitudo meridiana* = **meridian altitude**. *refractiones stellarum* = **refractions of the stars**. *hypotheses coelestium motuum* = **hypotheses of the celestial motions**. *Parallaxis* = **parallax** — Tycho's point that the comet "was altogether without parallax," i.e. supralunary. *organa* = **instruments**; *Radius* = the **cross-staff (radius astronomicus)**. *Cometometrica materia* = "Cometometric matter" (cometary measurement) — a coinage kept and glossed. *Nova Stella* = the **New Star** (the 1572 nova). *crinitum sidus / Cometes* = "hairy star / Comet"; the 1590 comet was observed at Uraniborg from late February to 6 March.
- **Symbols.** **♈** = the zodiac sign **Aries** (*a 1a ♈* = "from the 1st [degree] of Aries"); **♂** = the planet **Mars**. Per this chapter's convention the glyphs are kept in the Source block and named in English in the translation.
- **In-letter date discrepancy (flagged, not reconciled).** Within the Mars-observation request, Tycho records that Hagecius's own sheet was dated *anni 1579* but that the observations in fact belong to *September 1578* — "*licet in tua scheda per incuriam aliquam annus 1579 ponebatur*." This is Tycho's own note of an error in his correspondent's document; reproduced as written, not resolved.
- **Calendar / dating.** Datelined *Uraniburgi die 23. Februarij 1590* (Old Style; Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700), with the postscript expressly dated *quarto Aprilis* ("the fourth of April") — Tycho explaining that he held the letter back roughly six weeks to append his observations of the comet (vanished "after the sixth day of March") and because of James VI's mid-March visit. The catalogue *label* dates the letter "1590. 23. februar." (the body date); the header leads with that as-written dateline and notes the postscript date. **No conversion is performed**; both internal dates (23 February; 4 April) are O.S. as the body gives them.
- **Greek lettering.** *Phaenomenωn* — the genitive plural is written with a Greek omega (ω) embedded in the otherwise Latin word (*Phaenomen-ων*), a learned typographic affectation; the glyph is preserved in the Source block.
- **Formulae.** *S.* in the address = *salutem* ("greeting"); *Vale / Iterum … vale / Iterum vale* = "Farewell / Again … fare you well / Again, farewell"; *D. D.* = *Domine Doctor* ("Master Doctor"); *Tuus* = "Yours."
- **Correction.** English 'Take pains to answer briefly and clearly soon' corrected to 'Take pains to answer clearly soon', removing a redundant double-rendering of 'brevi' ('soon'); Latin confirmed unchanged against Dreyer, TBOO VII p.227.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Full letter (the transcribed original and the published English) collated line by line against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.224-229 page images (letter proper on pp.225-228; p.224 is the tail of the preceding letter, p.229 the head of the next). Verified verbatim: the heading/salutation, all proper names (Hagecius, Wilhelm Landgrave of Hesse, Jacob Curtius, Rothmann, Heinrich Brucaeus, Jacob Buck, Heinrich Rantzau), the Scottish-King visit sentence (historically correct: James VI's March 1590 visit to Uraniborg), the Mars/Aries observation passage (years 1578/1579, 1a Aries, Mars symbol), and both closing dates (23 February 1590 main letter, 4 April postscript). Latin the transcribed original matches Dreyer's print exactly throughout the checked passages — no text error. One low-severity mistranslation found (the doubled 'brevi'). No fabrication, omission, or hedge-loss found.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (low). 'brevi' is the standard temporal adverb ('soon, shortly'), already rendered correctly as 'soon' at the end of the clause; the translator also renders it a second time as 'briefly' (a manner sense 'brevi' does not carry here), adding an unsupported descriptor that sits oddly against 'luculenter' ('fully/clearly'), which if anything implies the opposite of brevity. At: “Take pains to answer briefly and clearly soon.”.

**Repaired.** Verified visually against Dreyer page images, TBOO VII pp.224-227 (the relevant portion of the extract). The Latin clause is confirmed verbatim, isolating this as a pure translation defect; the English is corrected to drop the unsupported extra 'briefly and'. Nothing else on these pages was checked as no other defect was declared for this letter.

text.original:
ALIA TYCHONIS BRAHE AD CHRISTOPHORVM ROTHMANNVM. S. P.

SVPERIORIBVS meis literis, Doctissime ROTHMANNE, tuis vltimis luculenter respondi, idque quamprimum eas accepissem, atque te, vt denuo rescriberes mature, quo iterum hisce instantibus Nundinis Francofurdianis responsionem vicissim adornarem, rogabam. Sed video te in respondendo segniorem, tardumque nimis, semperque occupationes alias praetendere. Licet vero ego non paucioribus forte detinear; nihilominus tamen scriptionem non intermitto. Cum itaque nostrates, Nundinas Francofurdenses petituri, iter accelerent, breues hasce, ne omnino sine meis isthac transeant, mittere volui, quibus te de responso admonerem, vtut, quae scribam, multa nunc non occurrant. Hoc tamen te scire volui, Tomum meum primum iam pene Typographica opera absolutum; Nam in tertia, eaque vltima parte labor nunc vrgetur. Distinctione autem prima, non saltem curriculum Solis et Lunae, nostris seculis adamussim correspondens, denotatur, atque demonstratiue in numeros resoluitur: Sed et postea plurimarum Affixarum, praesertim Zodiaco obuersantium, accurate loca verificantur, rationesque, cur sic et non aliter constituenda veniant, adduntur. Vbi haec cum vestris contuleritis, facile ipsimet de discrepantiola nobis intercedente, vtri nostrum potius sit assentiendum, censuram proferetis. Neque etiam dubito vestros circa Fixarum loca corrigenda vtiles labores, propediem publicam lucem visuros. Quin et aliud quippiam occurrit hîc addendum. Postquam literae eaedem, quas ad te vltimo dedi, emittebantur, reperit Amanuensis meus integram pagellam, nescio, quâ incuriâ prius omissam et alicubi sepositam, nonnulla continentem, quae inter transscribendum neglexerat. Quod etiam nuper reuidendo exemplar, cognoui. Iussi itaque, vt quae tunc praetermissa erant, seorsim in charta describerentur, atque hisce adiungerentur, loco vna denotato, vbi interferenda forent. Tuum igitur erit, hanc praeteritionem candide accipere, et ad has quoque quaestiunculas, vbi rescripseris, respondere.

Vale.
Vraniburgo, die 23. Februarij, Anno 1590.
T. TYCHO BRAHE.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VI, pp. 203–204; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
POSTSCRIPTA. INTERIM dum hae exurantur, Cometes quidam hoc ipso die 23. Februarij vesperi, inter obseruandum Venerem, prope maximam suam a Sole digreßionem, circa occasuram caeli plagam nobis conspiciebatur, ad Piscis Borei Asterismum situs. Longitudo eius erat hora 8. M. 5. in 26. P. 18. M. 5. ♓ lat. P. 18. M. 20. Borea. Caudam tenuem, sed decem circiter gradus longam adamußim in Solis oppositum, atque versus Zenit dirigit; tunc temporis eam in lucidiorem pedis Andromedae, licet non tam alte, sed saltem ad stellulam in capite Piscis Borei, eiaculando. Motum habet concitatiorem, quam priores a me obseruati; videtur enim intra vnam reuolutionem diurnam, octo pene gradus, in suo ductu absoluere. Tendit in signorum consequentia, sed latitudinem versus Boream vna sensibiliter adauget. Tu quoque, si vobis conspectus fuerit, hunc diligenter obserua, & Paralaxes solerter enuclea, quod & ego, fauente Numine, praestare non intermittam. Ecce tibi occasio oblata, tua dubia in Cometis, quo ad caudam, & alia resoluenda videbis vtique, quae a nobis in his tradita sunt, non incongrua eße, & caudas nequaquam partem corporis, sed defluuium quoddam radiorum solarium, illud penetrantium, reuera existere. Si Mercatores duas vel tres dies Hasmae adhuc moram traxerint, antequam ad Nundinas abeant, & serenum interea fuerit, ego huius crinitae apparentias plenius denotabo, & Illustrißimo Principi tuo, quae interea deprehendero, statim per literas significabo.
text.english:
**Another from Tycho Brahe to Christoph Rothmann. Heartiest greeting.**

In my earlier letter, most learned Rothmann, I replied fully to your last, and that as soon as I had received it; and I was asking you to write back again promptly, so that I might in turn prepare a reply once more for these approaching Frankfurt fairs. But I see that you are rather sluggish in answering, and far too slow, and that you are always pleading other occupations. Yet although I too am perhaps detained by no fewer, nonetheless I do not break off my writing. And so, since our people who are bound for the Frankfurt fairs are hastening their journey, I wished to send this short letter — lest they pass that way altogether without something from me — by which I might remind you about a reply, even though there are not many things that occur to me to write now. This much, however, I wished you to know: that my first volume is now nearly finished, so far as the printing work goes; for the labour is now being pressed on in the third and last part. In the first division, not only is the course of the Sun and Moon, corresponding to a hair's breadth with our own age, set out and resolved demonstratively into numbers; but afterwards too the places of very many of the fixed [stars], especially those lying along the Zodiac, are accurately verified, and the reasons are added why they are to be established thus and not otherwise. When you [pl.] have compared these with your own [results], you will easily yourselves deliver judgement, concerning the little discrepancy that comes between us, as to which of us is rather to be assented to. Nor indeed do I doubt that your useful labours toward correcting the places of the fixed [stars] will shortly see the public light. Moreover, something else also occurs to be added here. After that same letter which I last sent you had been dispatched, my amanuensis found a whole little page — omitted earlier by I know not what carelessness, and set aside somewhere — containing some matters which he had neglected in the course of transcribing. This too I came to know lately, when reviewing the copy. I therefore gave orders that the things which had then been passed over should be written out separately on a sheet, and joined to this present [letter], with the place marked at the same time where they were to be inserted. It will therefore be for you to take this omission in good part, and, when you write back, to answer these little questions also.

Farewell.
From Uraniborg, the 23rd day of February, in the year 1590.
T[ycho]. Tycho Brahe.


*[Postscript:]* POSTSCRIPT. Meanwhile, as these [pages] are being printed off, a certain Comet was seen by us this very day, the 23rd of February, in the evening, while we were observing Venus near her greatest elongation from the Sun, in the quarter of the sky about to set, placed at the asterism of the Northern Fish. Its longitude at the 8th hour, 5 minutes, was 26°18′5″ in Pisces [♓], latitude 18°20′ North. It directs a thin tail, but about ten degrees long, exactly opposite the Sun and toward the Zenith, at that time darting it toward the brighter [star] of Andromeda's foot, though not so high, but only as far as the little star in the head of the Northern Fish. It has a motion more rapid than the earlier ones observed by me; for it seems to accomplish, within one diurnal revolution, almost eight degrees in its course. It tends in the order of the signs, but at the same time perceptibly increases its latitude toward the North. You too, if it shall come into your view, observe it diligently and skilfully tease out its parallaxes, which I also, with the favour of the Deity, shall not fail to do. Behold, an occasion is offered you: you will assuredly see your doubts about Comets — as regards the tail, and the other matters to be resolved — that what we have set down on these points is not incongruous, and that the tails are by no means a part of the body, but are in truth a certain effluence of the Sun's rays penetrating it. If the merchants tarry yet two or three days at Hasmae before they depart to the fairs, and it shall be clear in the meantime, I shall more fully note this comet's appearances, and shall at once signify by letter to your most illustrious Prince whatever I shall have meanwhile observed.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), writing from Uraniborg on Hven. The heading *ALIA … S. P.* ("Another … heartiest greeting") is the running rubric of the 1596 *Epistolae* volume, which prints a connected series of the Tycho–Rothmann exchange; *ALIA* ("another [letter]") marks this as a further item in that sequence. *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam* ("heartiest greeting"), by this chapter's convention
- **Recipient.** *Christophorus Rothmannus* = **Christoph Rothmann**, mathematician and astronomer at the court of Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel. The two carried on a substantial technical correspondence in the later 1580s; by early 1590 Rothmann's replies had fallen off (Tycho's complaint here), and Rothmann would soon visit Hven in person (Aug.–Sep. 1590).
- **Place.** *Vraniburgum* = **Uraniborg**, Tycho's observatory-house on the island of Hven.
- ***Nundinae Francofurdianae / Francofurdenses*** — "the **Frankfurt fairs**," the twice-yearly Frankfurt book fair (here the spring fair), the standard conduit by which learned correspondence and books travelled north. The two spellings appear as printed and are kept.
- ***Tomum meum primum … Distinctione … prima … tertia, eaque vltima parte*** — Tycho's "**first volume**" is the *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* (the work on the renewal of astronomy: solar/lunar theory and the fixed-star catalogue), then in the press; *Distinctio* is rendered "division" (a major part of the work) and *pars* "part." The volume was in fact not completed in Tycho's lifetime; the optimistic "nearly finished" is his own forecast and is preserved, not corrected.
- **Astronomy.** *curriculum Solis et Lunae* → "the course of the Sun and Moon" (the solar and lunar theory/motions); *demonstratiue in numeros resoluitur* → "resolved demonstratively into numbers" (worked out into computed tables); *Affixae / Fixae* → "the **fixed [stars]**" (*stellae affixae / fixae*); *Zodiaco obuersantium* → "lying along [facing toward] the Zodiac" (the zodiacal stars whose places matter for the ecliptic frame); *loca verificantur* → "the places are verified" (*verificare*, to establish/confirm a position, here kept as "verify"); *Fixarum loca corrigenda* → "correcting the places of the fixed [stars]."
- ***adamussim*** — "to a hair's breadth, exactly" (literally "to the mason's line/rule"); rendered "corresponding to a hair's breadth with our own age," i.e. agreeing exactly with present-day observation.
- ***discrepantiola*** — a diminutive, "the **little discrepancy**" between Tycho's and the Kassel results; the diminutive (a courteous minimising) is kept rather than flattened to "discrepancy."
- ***censuram proferetis … cum vestris … ipsimet*** — the second-person **plural** here ("you [pl.] have compared … you will deliver judgement … with your own [results]") embraces the Kassel team (Rothmann together with the Landgrave's instrument-maker Jost Bürgi and the wider Kassel programme), as against the singular *te / tibi* addressed to Rothmann himself elsewhere in the letter. The number-shift is preserved.
- ***Amanuensis*** — "**amanuensis**" (Tycho's copying-secretary at Uraniborg); *pagella* → "little page," *charta* → "sheet," *exemplar* → "the copy" (the fair copy/exemplar of the letter being transcribed). The episode: a page of the previous letter had been left out in transcription, found afterwards, and is now being sent as a separate insert with its insertion-point marked.
- ***quaestiunculas*** — a diminutive, "**little questions**" (the minor queries on the recovered page); diminutive kept.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S. P.* → "heartiest greeting"; *Vale* → "Farewell"; *candide accipere* → "take in good part" (*candide*, frankly/kindly). Per this chapter's convention
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 23. Februarij, Anno 1590* = 23 February 1590, **Old Style** (Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700; this chapter's convention). The edition label ("1590. 23. februar. Uraniborg") agrees with the as-written dateline; no discrepancy. Catholic-territory correspondents of these years would have dated this day 4 March N.S., but Tycho writes O.S. and no conversion is made.
- **Orthography.** Printed *u/v* conventions of the 1596 Uraniborg edition are reproduced as set (*SVPERIORIBVS, vltimis, vt, breues, Affixarum, reuidendo*); the circumflex on *hîc, quâ, incuriâ* is the edition's. No editorial normalisation applied.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing comet postscript (23 Feb observation among Venus-observations; tail anti-solar, per-accidens-optical), restored from Dreyer VI pp.203–204 (dropped by the working transcription); 1596-edition u/v + ß orthography kept.
- **Correction.** 'at Hven' corrected to the transliterated 'at Hasmae' — the source's place-name does not match Tycho's usual Latin for Hven and could not be identified with confidence (no Dreyer page available for this letter). Restored the dropped 'M. 5.' arcsecond figure to the comet's longitude, now '26°18′5″ in Pisces'.

translation.warrant:
**Not collated against Dreyer** — no page reference for this letter, so the grade is capped at Probable however sound the translation looks. the edition gives no page reference for this letter (one of the 49 without a Dreyer extract), so audited against the transcribed original alone by the audit's rule and capped at grade Probable regardless of findings. Two numeral/place-name anomalies were noted in the postscript, which the packet itself flags as editorially restored/spliced text (from Dreyer VI pp.203-204, not supplied here as page images) — neither could be adjudicated without that extract.

**2 defects found:**
- **mistranslation** (medium). The transcribed original reads "Hasmae" for the place where merchants are tarrying before the fair; this matches neither Tycho's usual Latin for Hven (Huenna) nor any recognisable place-name, so "Hven" is asserted with no clear counterpart. No page images were available to check whether Dreyer's actual reading is e.g. Hafniae (Copenhagen), which would fit the merchant context better. At: “at Hven”.
- **omission** (low). The source's garbled numeral string carries an extra "M. 5." element after the degree/minute pair for the comet's longitude that the English silently drops rather than rendering. At: “26°18′ in Pisces”.

**Repaired.** No Dreyer extract exists for this letter (no page reference), so neither fix could be checked against the edition of record; both rest on internal evidence within the packet itself. The Hasmae/Hven mismatch is demonstrable by comparison with Tycho's consistent 'Huenna'/'Huena' usage elsewhere in this corpus, so the unsupported 'Hven' gloss was removed in favour of a literal transliteration rather than a new guess. The dropped 'M. 5.' longitude figure is restored as arcseconds by analogy with the parallel, already-correct latitude clause's degree/minute structure, but the exact place-name behind 'Hasmae' and the precise unit of the restored figure remain unverified cruces. Grade C.

text.original:
NOBILISS. ET CLARISS. VIRO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, HWENAe INSULAe DOMINO, REGIS DANIAe CONSILIARIO ET MATHEMATICO DOCTISSIMO, AMICO SUO HVENAM DANIAe MITTANTUR.
NOBILISS. ET CLARISS. VIR, AMICE COLENDE, S. P.

ANTE biduum nobis D. FULLERUS noster obviam factus inter alia retulit, quam honorifice abs te fuerit acceptus, quam admiranda viderit, et quod legerit, quae ad primas meas responderis, ubi ego: iamdudum mihi constat, in illa Uraniae arce cum summa humanitate eximiam scientiam habitare; sed sciscitatus sum, an meminerit, quae de mota quaestione scripseris? Non, inquit, nam pleraque captum meum superabant; hoc tantum percepi, plures sententiae suae demonstrationes afferri. Demonstrationes ego libenter intelligam, et si constiterint, facile ijs cedam, quique hoc ὅτι sic docuerit, maioris apud me authoritatis hac ex parte, quam ARISTOTELES erit, quod authoritas ex veritate aestimanda sit, non haec ex illa, nisi in Divinis, ubi ipsa Veritas ἔφα. Verum si coniecturis agatur, plus habeant probabilitatis oportet quam contrariae, ut maiorem fidem mereantur. Ego, clariss. vir, si quas petij longitudines accepissem, iamdudum quid veri hîc esset, demonstratione explorassem; alioqui in hac quaestione versari non libet. Nam nunc etiam peto, ut quos in Numeris Canonis Sinuum errores longo usu tuo cognoveris, prima occasione mecum communices; nam nobis singulare quiddam prae manibus est, in quo perficiendo ingentem opem hic Canon praestat, sique error suberit, nobis cum fenore suppeditabitur. Vel ijs essem contentus, qui sunt infra 60 (quamvis et reliquos ascribas) nam qui supra sunt, singulari compendio exhibere potero, quod hîc amicitiae nostrae causa ascribam.* [Footnote 1 — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 240; dropped by the working transcription: "Canon, quo ipse utor, Rheinoldi est excusus Tubingae anno 1554 apud heredes Morhardi, tabulis directionum insertus."]

Figur

Duorum arcuum trientem complentium sinus semidifferentiae est differentia sinuum (eorundem arcuum). Sint duo arcus ab, ad complentes trientem, quia ac est 60, et quanto minor ab deficit ab ac, tanto maior ad superat. Differentia est bd, sinus dimidij differentiae est ed, quem demonstro esse aequalem lineae dg, quae differentia est duorum sinuum dk et bm seu gk. Cum ilk sit 60, erit kil 30 et uterque gfi et bfe erit 60, quare totus efg erit 120. In duobus orthogonijs latera be et ed sunt aequalia et ef commune, quare reliqua reliquis erunt aequalia, et angulus bfe aequalis efd angulo, qui erit 60, et tertius angulus dfg erit 60; in duobus orthogonijs efd et dfg anguli efd et dfg sunt aequales et latus df commune, quare reliqua reliquis aequantur, et latus ed aequale erit lateri dg, quod propositum fuit. Itaque dabitur quilibet sinus supra 60, si sinui arcus tanto minoris 60 addatur sinus dimidij differentiae duorum arcuum, ut ed ad bm facit dk; sic Canon Sinuum tertia parte minuetur.

Canonem fecundum dimidio abbreviabo alio compendio, quod etiam hîc annotabo. Duorum arcuum quadrantem complentium semidifferentia fecundorum est fecundus differentiae eorundem. Sint duo arcus cb, bf quadrantem aequantes, quia caf rectus est, fecundus cb est db, fecundus bf est bh, differentia duorum arcuum est be, cuius fecundus est bg, quem dico esse dimidium bm differentiae inter duos fecundos. Diametris sc. ai et dh se secantibus, erit hi aequalis ad, et ob id erit aequalis dk arcui, cum ad et dk sint aequales; ergo angulus dak aequalis erit iah, et ablato igitur cb seu eius aequali ef ex bf, relinquitur be differentia duorum arcuum. Rursum db, cui sit aequalis mh, aufero a bh, remanebit bm, cuius dimidium est bg; nam ab aequalibus semidiametris dg et gh, aequalibus db et mh ablatis, remanent bg et gm aequalia. Si igitur detur fecundus db et quaeritur fecundus bh, aufero arcum cb a bf et differentiae be fecundum in canone quaero bg, hunc duplico, erit bm, et addo fecundum minoris mh, proveniet fecundus totius. Si differentia be fuerit maior 45 gradibus, duplici operatione opus erit, priori reperietur fecundus differentiae, posteriori fecundus totius.

Figur

Quia in has speculationes incidi et figura servit, tertium ascribam, quo omnem RHETICI Canonem, de quo tantopere gloriatur, eximio fecundi usu tollam, ut dabo hypothenusam ad in partibus, qualium db sinus est sinus totus, db sinu in fecundo reperto, ut sit 3420201, arcus 20 erit angulo 18° 52½ , ut db fecundus 3420201 ad ab S. T. sic ab S. T. ad bh fecundum supplementi anguli 18° 52½ , qui ex Canone dabitur; est enim ab medium proportionale inter duo fecundos. Ut ergo ab S. T. ad bh fecundum, sic erit db sinus 3420201 ad S. T. db fecundus 3420201 est ad ad S. T. ut ab S. T. ad fecundum bh; sed db sinus 3420201 est ad ad S. T. ut db fecundus 3420201 ad ab S. T. Ergo db sinus 3420201 est ad ad S. T. ut S. T. ab ad fecundum bh; dabitur igitur in Canone fecundus bh et erit ad in eo numero partium qualium db est S.T. ad ad, quia termini non mutantur. Et idem numerus qui in priori fecundus, inde sinus est; abiectis igitur his terminis, si db ponatur sinus totus, erit ad fecundus supplementi anguli 18 52½ . Simili modo si detur sinus ab, dabitur ad in partibus qualium ab est S. T. Non vulgaris hic usus est fecundi Canonis, quo maxima reperiuntur, de quibus alias pluribus conferemus, nam nihil apud me horum secretorum erit, quin libenter ut ea suggeret memoria communicabo: tu haec tanquam amicitiae nostrae μνημόσυνοv boni consule.

Discessit hinc Sereniss. Rex noster praeter omnium opinionem et expectationem; nam mihi proficiscendum unâ fuit, sed hyeme valetudinem terrente, locus fuit excusationi, sed si de abitu eius constitisset, nihil inde deterruisset, nunc vero discussa prope hyeme cum redeundi occasio redeat, faxit omnipotens Deus, ut incolumis cum Sereniss. Regina nostra quam primum revertatur, hoc communibus et privatis votis assidue petitur. In Illustriss. Reginae comitatu ferunt Medicum esse D. ANDREAM KRAGIUM, qui tamen hîc non sit moraturus, sed ex nostratibus quispiam sufficiendus; id si ita fuerit, cuperem mei haberi rationem, siquidem eo loco dignus esse potero, non deerit nostratium D. D. consiliariorum promotio, quibus notus sum, et cum quibus sanguinis necessitudo intercedit. Vestratium tu conciliare mihi poteris, quod quasi ex te profectum sit, facias amanter peto, Domino fratre tuo et D. KRAGIO literis tuis in mei favorem et commendationem salutatis. Ideo hic locus acceptus esset, quod praxis nostra cum summa corporis nostri molestia coniuncta sit, nam maxima in equis itinera quacunque coeli tempestate nobis saepe conficienda sunt, quibus corpus meum minus nunc idoneum esse experior, ut multo acceptior sit futura, quae cum minore corporis labore est, quare rogo, ut tuo beneficio, si fieri id posset, melius valetudini meae consulere queam. Sed ita velim ad eos scribas, ut si quaeratur Illustriss. Reginae nostrae Medicus, tuo amico ipsi omnibus modis faveant, idque quasi ex teipso; vides, quantum mihi ex amicitia nostra pollicear, quam non pudeat res meas ei credere, quod certe minime facerem, nisi singularem de tua erga me benevolentia spem haberem. Huius anni Eclipses quam accurate observaturus sis, facile intelligo; nobis id non datur, nam nec sunt organa, quibus fidere possumus, nec artifices, qui nobis parent. Momenta initij et finis ac medij (praeter visualem Diametrum) definienda existimo datis fixarum altitudinibus, nam altitudo, ut principium, sensu per instrumentum notum dari, non ex alijs demonstrari debet. Sed finem faciam, ne sim molestior. Coeli et Terrae Dominus tibi adsit, tuisque faveat conatibus et incolumem conservet, tui amantissimum tuis literis revise.

Datae Edinburgi pridie Calend. Martij.
Tuus IOAN. CRAIGUS, philosophiae et medicinae doctor.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 242; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Si quid singulare in chymicis habueris, quod putes amico communicandum, facias velim.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most distinguished man, Master Tycho Brahe, Lord of the island of Hven, Counsellor to the King of Denmark and most learned mathematician, his friend — to be conveyed to Hven in Denmark.**
**Most noble and most distinguished sir, friend to be honoured, heartiest greeting.**

Two days ago our [friend] Master Fuller, having met me, reported among other things how honourably he had been received by you, what marvellous things he had seen, and that he had read what you had replied to my first [letter] — whereupon I [said]: it has long been settled in my mind that in that citadel of Urania a singular learning dwells together with the utmost courtesy; but I asked whether he remembered what you had written about the question that was raised. "No," he said, "for most of it was beyond my grasp; I gathered only this much, that several demonstrations of his own view are brought forward." Demonstrations I shall gladly understand, and if they hold good I shall readily yield to them; and whoever shall have taught me this *that* [ὅτι] in such a way will be, in this matter, of greater authority with me than Aristotle — for authority is to be assessed from truth, not truth from authority, except in things divine, where Truth itself has spoken [ἔφα]. But if the matter is conducted by conjectures, they must have more probability than the contrary ones, that they may earn greater credit. I, most distinguished sir, had I received the longitudes I sought, would long since have explored by demonstration what truth there is here; otherwise I have no wish to busy myself with this question. For now too I ask that, at the first occasion, you communicate to me whatever errors in the Numbers of the Canon of Sines you have come to know by your long use [of it]; for we have a certain singular [undertaking] in hand, in the perfecting of which this Canon affords mighty help, and if an error lurk [in it], it will be repaid to us with interest. I should be content even with those [sines] which are below 60 (although you might write out the rest as well), for those that are above I shall be able to exhibit by a singular compendium, which I here append for our friendship's sake.\* [Footnote 1: "The Canon which I myself use is Rheinhold's, printed at Tübingen in the year 1554 by the heirs of Morhard, inserted in the Tables of Directions."]

[Figure]

The sine of the half-difference of two arcs filling out a third [of the quadrant, i.e. summing to 60°] is the difference of the sines (of those same arcs). Let there be two arcs *ab*, *ad* filling out a third [of the quadrant], since *ac* is 60; and by however much the lesser, *ab*, falls short of *ac*, by so much the greater, *ad*, exceeds [it]. The difference is *bd*; the sine of half the difference is *ed*, which I demonstrate to be equal to the line *dg*, which is the difference of the two sines *dk* and *bm* (that is, *gk*). Since *ilk* is 60, *kil* will be 30, and each [angle] *gfi* and *bfe* will be 60; wherefore the whole [angle] *efg* will be 120. In the two right [triangles] the sides *be* and *ed* are equal, and *ef* [is] common; wherefore the remaining [parts] will be equal to the remaining, and the angle *bfe* equal to the angle *efd*, which will be 60, and the third angle *dfg* will be 60. In the two right [triangles] *efd* and *dfg* the angles *efd* and *dfg* are equal and the side *df* [is] common; wherefore the remaining [parts] are equal to the remaining, and the side *ed* will be equal to the side *dg* — which was [the thing] proposed. And so any sine above 60 will be given, if to the sine of an arc as much below 60 there be added the sine of half the difference of the two arcs, as *ed* added to *bm* makes *dk*; thus the Canon of Sines will be lessened by a third part.

I shall abbreviate the *secundus* [versed-sine] Canon by a half, by another compendium, which I shall also note here. The half-difference of the *secundi* [versed sines] of two arcs filling out a quadrant is the *secundus* [versed sine] of the difference of those same [arcs]. Let there be two arcs *cb*, *bf* equalling a quadrant, since *caf* is a right [angle]; the *secundus* of *cb* is *db*, the *secundus* of *bf* is *bh*, the difference of the two arcs is *be*, whose *secundus* is *bg*, which I say to be half of *bm*, the difference between the two *secundi*. The diameters, namely *ai* and *dh*, cutting one another, *hi* will be equal to *ad*, and on that account [the arc *hi*] will be equal to the arc *dk*, since *ad* and *dk* are equal; therefore the angle *dak* will be equal to *iah*; and so, *cb* (or its equal *ef*) being taken from *bf*, there is left *be*, the difference of the two arcs. Again, *db* — to which let *mh* be equal — I take from *bh*; there will remain *bm*, whose half is *bg*; for from the equal semidiameters *dg* and *gh*, the equals *db* and *mh* being taken away, there remain *bg* and *gm* equal. If therefore the *secundus db* be given and the *secundus bh* is sought, I take the arc *cb* from *bf*, and seek in the canon *bg*, the *secundus* of the difference *be*; this I double — it will be *bm* — and I add the *secundus* of the lesser, *mh*: the *secundus* of the whole will result. If the difference *be* be greater than 45 degrees, there will be need of a double operation: by the former the *secundus* of the difference will be found, by the latter the *secundus* of the whole.

[Figure]

Since I have fallen upon these speculations and the figure serves [the purpose], I shall append a third, by which I may do away with the whole Canon of Rheticus — in which he glories so greatly — by an outstanding use of the *secundus* [versed sine]: so that I shall give the hypotenuse *ad* in [such] parts as those of which *db*, the sine, is the whole sine [the radius]; *db* having been found in the *secundus*, so that it be 3420201, the arc 20[°] will [correspond] to an angle of 18° 52½′; as *db* the *secundus* 3420201 is to *ab* the whole sine [radius], so is *ab* the whole sine to *bh* the *secundus* of the supplement of the angle 18° 52½′, which will be given from the Canon — for *ab* is the mean proportional between the two *secundi*. As therefore *ab* the whole sine is to *bh* the *secundus*, so will *db* the sine 3420201 be to the whole sine. *db* the *secundus* 3420201 is to *ad* the whole sine as *ab* the whole sine to the *secundus bh*; but *db* the sine 3420201 is to *ad* the whole sine as *db* the *secundus* 3420201 to *ab* the whole sine. Therefore *db* the sine 3420201 is to *ad* the whole sine as the whole sine *ab* to the *secundus bh*; therefore the *secundus bh* will be given in the Canon, and *ad* will be in that number of parts of which *db* is the whole sine — [the ratio] *ad* to *ad* [being unity], since the terms are not changed. And the same number which [stands] as *secundus* in the former [case] is thence the sine; with these terms cast off, therefore, if *db* be set as the whole sine, *ad* will be the *secundus* of the supplement of the angle 18° 52½′. In like manner, if the sine *ab* be given, *ad* will be given in parts of which *ab* is the whole sine. This use of the *secundus* Canon is no common one, by which the greatest [things] are found, about which we shall confer more at another time; for none of these secrets will be [withheld] by me, but I shall gladly communicate them as memory shall suggest them: take these things in good part, as a memorial [μνημόσυνον], as it were, of our friendship.

Our most serene King departed hence beyond everyone's opinion and expectation; for I too had to set out with [him], but, the winter making one fear for [his] health, there was room for an excuse — though, had his departure been [firmly] settled, nothing would have deterred [me] from it. But now, the winter being nearly dispelled, since the occasion for returning comes round [again], may almighty God grant that he return safe, together with our most serene Queen, as soon as possible — this is sought unceasingly by public and private prayers. In the most illustrious Queen's retinue they say the physician is Master Andrew Krag, who, however, is not to remain here, but someone from among our own [countrymen] is to be supplied [in his place]; and if that be so, I could wish that account be taken of me — since I shall be able to be worthy of that post, the recommendation of our own lordly counsellors, to whom I am known and with whom there is a tie of blood, will not be lacking. Those of your [side] you can win over for me — which I lovingly ask you to do, as though it had proceeded from yourself — your lord brother and Master Krag being saluted in your letters in my favour and commendation. This post would be welcome for this reason, that our practice is bound up with the utmost trouble to our body; for we often have to accomplish very great journeys on horseback in whatever weather of the sky, for which I now find my body less fit, so that one will be much more welcome that is [attended] with less labour of the body; wherefore I ask that, by your good offices, if it could be done, I may be able to provide better for my health. But I should wish you to write to them in such a way that, if a physician for our most illustrious Queen be sought, they may by all means favour your friend himself — and that as though [it came] from your own self. You see how much I promise myself from our friendship, that I am not ashamed to entrust my affairs to it — which assuredly I should by no means do, had I not a singular hope of your goodwill towards me. How accurately you will observe this year's eclipses, I readily understand; to us that is not granted, for we have neither instruments in which we can trust, nor craftsmen who will obey us. The moments of the beginning and the end and the middle (apart from the visual diameter) I judge must be determined from given altitudes of the fixed [stars]; for altitude, as a first principle, ought to be given by sense through a known instrument, not demonstrated from other [things]. But I shall make an end, lest I be too troublesome. May the Lord of Heaven and Earth be with you, and favour your endeavours and keep you safe; revisit him who most dearly loves you with your letters.

Given at Edinburgh, the day before the Kalends of March.
Yours, John Craig, doctor of philosophy and of medicine.


*[Postscript:]* If you should have anything remarkable in chemical matters that you think ought to be shared with a friend, I should wish you to do so.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Ioan. Craigus* = **John Craig** (d. 1620), the Scottish physician and mathematician, an Aristotelian who from c. 1588 disputed Tycho's astronomical and trigonometrical positions; he later became chief physician to James VI/I. Tycho gave Craig an inscribed copy of *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (Uraniborg, 1588), now in Edinburgh University Library, and "wrote out a long defence of his ideas against a challenge by Craig, for which Craig later apologized" (Gingerich, *Census*; cf. A. Mosley, "Tycho Brahe and John Craig: The Dynamic of a Dispute," in *Tycho Brahe and Prague*). The signature *philosophiae et medicinae doctor* fits this John Craig.
- **Recipient address.** *Tychoni Brahe, Hwenae insulae domino, Regis Daniae consiliario et mathematico* — Tycho on Hven, the king's counsellor and mathematician; the cover instruction *Hvenam Daniae mittantur* ("let it be sent to Hven in Denmark") is the postal direction, kept.
- ***D. Fullerus noster*** — "our Master Fuller," a Scottish intermediary (evidently recently a visitor to Uraniborg) who carried news between Craig and Tycho; not further identified here.
- ***mota quaestione*** — "the question that was raised": the standing Tycho–Craig controversy (over cometary parallax / the structure of the heavens and the trigonometric methods bound up with it).
- **Greek.** (1) *ὅτι* ("the *that*"): the **fact** (*to hoti*), as opposed to the reasoned cause (*to dioti*) — a scholastic/Aristotelian distinction; rendered "this *that*" with gloss. (2) *ἔφα* (Doric for *ἔφη*, "[he] has spoken"): an echo of the Pythagorean *αὐτὸς ἔφα* ("he himself said it") transferred to divine Truth — "where Truth itself has spoken." (3) *μνημόσυνοv*: "memorial, keepsake" (*mnēmosynon*); printed with a final *v* for ν in the source, kept verbatim, named in the translation. All three transcribed and glossed by this chapter's convention
- **Subject of the letter — trigonometric compendia.** Craig sends three geometric demonstrations for **abbreviating the standard tables**, the prosthaphaeresis-adjacent computing economies that lay at the heart of the dispute and of Tycho's manual of trigonometry (on which see Dreyer, "On Tycho Brahe's Manual of Trigonometry," *The Observatory* 39 (1916): 127–131; Thoren, "Prosthaphaeresis Revisited," *Historia Mathematica* 1988):
 - **(i)** the table of **sines** can be shortened by a third, because the sine of any arc above 60° equals the sine of an arc as far below 60° plus the sine of half their difference;
 - **(ii)** the table of *secundi* can be halved by an analogous relation across the quadrant;
 - **(iii)** Rheticus's whole canon (the *Opus palatinum*/great canon of **Rheticus**, Georg Joachim Rheticus, 1514–74) can be dispensed with by exploiting the *secundus*.
- ***fecundus*** **(printed form; the editorial crux of the technical sections).** Dreyer's text and the working transcription read *fecundus / fecundorum / fecundi* throughout the second and third demonstrations. This is read here as the *sinus **secundus*** — i.e. the **versed sine** (*sinus versus*, the "second sine" of period usage: radius minus cosine) — the *f* standing for long-*s* / Craig's own spelling. The mathematics is internally consistent only on this reading (the *secundus* of an arc and of its supplement, the mean-proportional relation *ab² = secundus(arc) · secundus(supplement)·R*, and the value **3420201** for the radius-scaled versed sine of 20°). The printed *fecundus* is retained verbatim in the Source block; the translation renders it "*secundus* (versed sine)" and the reading is flagged here. **Crux named: *fecundus* = *secundus*/versed sine.**
- **Diagram letters and numbers.** The lettered points (*ab, ad, ac, bd, ed, dg, dk, bm, gk; cb, bf, db, bh, be, bg, mh, gm; ai, dh, hi, ad*) are the figure labels; left untranslated as labels. *S. T.* = *sinus totus*, the **whole sine** (the radius, the tabular maximum), rendered "whole sine [radius]." **3420201** is the radius-scaled value Craig computes. *18° 52½′* and the arc "20" are kept as printed. **"IΛ7":** a garbled numeral in the first demonstration (the context — *kil* = 30, the angles summing to 120° in triangle *efg* — requires the angle *gfi* = 30°); the printed *IΛ7* (apparently a corrupted "30") is kept verbatim in the Source block and not silently corrected. **Crux named: the figure value *IΛ7*.**
- ***tanquam amias tiliae nostrae μνημόσυνον*** — **textual crux.** *amias tiliae* yields no Latin sense and is read as a corruption of ***amicitiae nostrae*** ("of our friendship"), giving "as a memorial, as it were, of our friendship" — coherent with the immediately preceding pledge to share his "secrets" with Tycho. The printed *amias tiliae* is kept verbatim in the Source block; the emendation is signalled in the translation. **Crux named: *amias tiliae* → *amicitiae*.**
- **Court news.** *Sereniss. Rex noster … cum Sereniss. Regina nostra* — **James VI of Scotland** and his queen, **Anne of Denmark**: James sailed to Norway/Denmark in late 1589 to fetch Anne (whose autumn crossing had been storm-driven back), wintering at Kronborg/Copenhagen and returning in spring 1590 — exactly the "departure beyond expectation" and hoped-for spring return Craig describes. The Danish sojourn is the occasion of the whole letter (Craig angling, via Tycho, for the post of queen's physician).
- ***D. Andream Kragium / D. Kragio*** — **Andreas Krag (Anders Krag)**, a Danish physician then attending Queen Anne's retinue; Craig (using the near-homonym to his own name without comment) hopes to succeed him if Krag does not stay on, and asks Tycho to commend him to Krag and to Tycho's "lord brother" (*Domino fratre tuo*, presumably **Steen Brahe** or another of Tycho's brothers).
- **Eclipse method.** *organa … artifices* = **instruments … craftsmen**: Craig laments having neither trustworthy instruments nor instrument-makers, unlike Tycho. He holds that the *momenta* (moments) of an eclipse's beginning, middle, and end should be fixed from observed **altitudes of fixed stars** through a known instrument — altitude being a sensory first principle (*principium*), not a quantity to be demonstrated from others — *praeter visualem Diametrum* ("apart from the visual [apparent] diameter").
- **Calendar / place.** *Datae Edinburgi pridie Calend. Martij* = "Given at **Edinburgh**, on the day before the Kalends of March" = **28 February** (1590 being a common year). Scotland reckoned by the **Julian calendar (Old Style)**; the date is O.S. The edition label ("1590. 28. februar. Edinburgh") agrees with the dateline; the year 1590 is not in the dateline itself but is supplied by the catalogue and by the James-VI/Anne-of-Denmark context. Roman-calendar idiom kept and glossed by this chapter's convention.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (before the signature), restored from Dreyer VII, p. 242 (dropped by the working transcription).
- **Correction.** Four defects corrected per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII pp.240-241: a garbled marginal line-number 'IΛ7' fused into the geometric proof text removed (both angles read simply '60'); the corrupted present-plural 'suppeditantur' restored to the future-singular 'suppeditabitur' (a promise of recompense, not a claim about compounding errors); a dropped footnote (Dreyer's footnote 1, p.240, naming Rheinhold's Canon printed at Tübingen 1554 by the heirs of Morhard) restored in place in both Latin and English; and the line-break-hyphenated 'ami-citiae' (mangled to 'amias tiliae') restored to 'amicitiae'. English corrected at the three places where sense was affected; the English for the amicitiae fix needed no change as it already carried the right sense.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter visually against Dreyer TBOO VII pp. 239-242 (the extract's nominal p.243 was also read and confirmed to belong to the following Tycho-Ranzau letter, not this one). Checked opening/closing lines, all proper names (Fuller, Aristoteles, Rheticus, Krag), numbers (60, 30, 120, 3420201, 18 52 1/2, arcus 20), and the postscript. Found four text error-class departures of the transcribed original from Dreyer, two of which (the fabricated 'IΛ7' value and the mis-redirected Rheinhold-canon footnote) materially change what a scholar would take away.

**4 defects found:**
- **text error** (medium). Our Latin corrupts Dreyer's future-singular 'suppeditabitur' (it will be repaid to us with interest, i.e. Craig promising to reward Tycho generously for corrections) into a present-plural 'suppeditantur'; the English then compounds this by inventing a bracketed gloss ('the errors are passed on, compounded') with no counterpart in Dreyer, reversing the sense from a friendly promise of recompense into a nonsense claim about errors accumulating. Dreyer prints: *fique error fuberit, nobis cum fenore fuppeditabitur (p.240, line 5)*.
- **text error** (**high**). Dreyer's sentence states both angles gfi and bfe equal 60 ('uterque... et... erit 60'). The transcribed original fused the printed marginal line-number '15' into the sentence as garbled 'IΛ7', and the English then literally translates this artifact as if it were a real geometric value ('gfi will be IΛ7'), fabricating a nonsensical quantity a mathematically literate reader would immediately flag. Dreyer prints: *erit kil 30 et uterque gfi et bfe erit 60 (p.240, line c. 13, the '15' after 'gfi' is Dreyer's marginal line-count marker, not text)*.
- **text error** (medium). Dreyer prints a genuine footnote here naming the sine canon Craig uses (Rheinhold's, printed at Tubingen in 1554 by the heirs of Morhard, inserted in the Tables of Directions) - a proper name, place, and date. The transcribed original drops this footnote's content entirely and instead attaches its asterisk marker to a differently-located, unrelated postscript ('Si quid singulare in chymicis...', actually printed beside the signature on p.242), misleading the reader about what was recovered versus what remains missing. Dreyer prints: *footnote 1, p.240: 'Canon, quo ipse utor, Rheinoldi est excusus Tubingae anno 1554 apud heredes Morhardi, tabulis directionum insertus.'*.
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original mangles the line-break-hyphenated word 'ami-citiae' (amicitiae, friendship) into 'amias tiliae', a text error versus Dreyer. The English translator correctly guessed the intended sense ('of our friendship') despite the corrupted source, so no defect propagates into the translation itself. Dreyer prints: *tu haec tanquam ami-citiae nostrae μνημόσυνον boni consule (p.241, word split across a line-break hyphen)*.

**Repaired.** All four defects verified directly against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.239-241 page images (not the digitised text layer): the geometric proof (p.240 l.14), suppeditabitur (p.240 l.5), footnote 1 (p.240, bottom), and the ami-citiae line break (p.241 ll.23-24) all read exactly as the audit's Dreyer claim states. No other part of the letter was touched; every changed word is accounted for in outcomes above.
