text.original:
TYGE BRAHE FICK BREFF ETT AFF HANS BØRNN ANRØRENNDIS VT SEQUITUR

Sophia etc.

WOR gunst thilfornn. Wider, att ßom j wnderdannigst lader giffue thilkiennde, att ßom j epther thennd sthormegthigste hogbornne første och herris her Fr[e]drich thend annden, Danmarckis, Norgis etc. konning, Wor kierre sallig affganngnne here och gemhals begierre, epther thennd naade och begaffuede forstanndtt, ßom j mett synderlig flid och sthuderinng, jcke wden stor omkostning, haffuer forhuerffuitt wdj thennd lofflige astronomiæ konnst, haffuer paa thennd jnßel Huen anretthitt och fulddreffuitt enn ahnßehelig bygning, och ther wdinnden ßynnderlig ny och fornemme jnstrumennther thill ßamme lofflig astro[no]miæ konnstis jnstauration och forbedrinng haffuer forhuerffuitt och ther thill forordnnitt, saa att hogbemelte Wor kierre ßalig herre haffuer haffdt tthill ßlig ethers flitthig forneme och lofflig konnst en synderlig gefallenn och welbehag, och epther att ßamme lofflige konnst er aff ether ther paa lannditt anretthitt och fuldkommitt, haffuer j althiid [ønsket], att epther ethers dødtt och affganng enn aff ethers egnne wdj synderlighed, ßom wdj samme lofflig konnst kunnde findis schickelig och dueligh, motthe ther thill forordnnis, och ßamme jnnßell mett hues ther paa anretthett, stiffthett och fuldkommitt er, niude och beholde, och therforre haffuer haffd wdj achtt och forßett, hoes hogbemelte Wor kierre sallige herre att wille paa thett wnnderdannigst forhuerffuitt Hanns Kierlighetz thilladellße, att therßom nogen aff ethers egne børnn kunde kiendis ther thill duelig och skickeligh, thennd tha for andre ßamme jnßell Huenn mett hues ther anretthitt er att schulle werre nest att bekomme, och therfor er aff Oß wnnderdannigst begierrendis, att Wij naadigst wille bekiennde och ßige hueß Wij haffue hørtt aff hogbemelte Wor kierre sallige herre om ßamme ethers forßett och menning. Tha wille Wij paa ßlige ethers wnnderdannigste begierre naadigst jcke forholde, att Wij weed Oß naadigst att erindre och er aldellis wittherlig, att Wij haffue hørtt aff hogbemelte Wor kierre sallige herre, nogenn thiid for Hans Kierlighedtz dødelig affganng, attj Hannß Kierlighet thett schall haffue forgiffuitt att wille jnstituere enn aff ethers egnne børnn, ßom schulle findis schichelig och duelig wdj ßamme lofflig astronomie konnst, huilke Wij well jnndnu kannd thilßinde føre och erachthe, och haffue hørtt aff hogbemelte Wor kierre sallige herre, och wille ßligtt paa ethers wnnderdannigst anlangende ether naadigst jcke forennttholde, och althiid ellers mett ald gunst och naade ether werre beuogenn.

Befallendis etc.
Actum Haffniæ thend 6. martij anno 1590.
text.english:
**Tyge Brahe received a letter, one concerning his children, as follows:**

Sophie, etc.

Our favour beforehand. Know that, as you most humbly cause it to be made known — that, in accordance with the desire of the most mighty, high-born prince and lord, lord Frederik the Second, King of Denmark, Norway, etc., our dear departed lord and consort of blessed memory; and in accordance with the grace and the gifted understanding that you, with singular diligence and study, [and] not without great cost, have acquired in the laudable art of astronomy — you have set up and carried through, upon that island Hven, a considerable building, and have therein acquired and appointed singular new and excellent instruments for the renewal [instauration] and improvement of that same laudable art of astronomy, so that our aforementioned dear lord of blessed memory had toward such diligent, excellent, and laudable art of yours a singular liking and good pleasure; and inasmuch as that same laudable art has been set up and brought to completion by you there on the land [i.e. on Hven], you have always [wished] that, after your death and decease, one of your own [children] in particular — such as might be found fit and able in that same laudable art — might be appointed thereto, and might enjoy and keep that same island, together with whatever has been established, founded, and completed upon it; and you have therefore had it in mind and intent to wish to obtain, in the most humble manner, from our aforementioned dear lord of blessed memory His Love's permission, that if any of your own children might be found able and fit thereto, that one should then, before [i.e. in preference to] others, be the next to obtain that same island Hven with whatever has been set up [there]; and it is therefore most humbly desired of us that we would graciously acknowledge and declare what we have heard from our aforementioned dear lord of blessed memory concerning that same intent and meaning of yours. Then upon such most humble desire of yours we would graciously not withhold [the reply] that we graciously call to mind, and it is entirely known to us, that we have heard from our aforementioned dear lord of blessed memory, some while before His Love's mortal decease, that His Love is said to have declared that he would institute one of your own children, such as might be found fit and able in that same laudable art of astronomy — which [matter] we can indeed still recall to mind and bear in remembrance, and have heard from our aforementioned dear lord of blessed memory; and we would, upon your most humble petition, graciously not withhold the same from you, and would in all else always be inclined toward you with all favour and grace.

Commending [you to God], etc.
Done at Copenhagen, the 6th of March, the year 1590.

documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer.** **Sophie of Mecklenburg** (1557–1631), queen dowager of Denmark, widow of **Frederik II** (d. 4 April 1588). The letter is a chancery-register entry from her own register (*Dronning Sophies tegnelser*), written during the minority of her son **Christian IV** (b. 1577; crowned 1596), when she was active in royal business. She had a personal interest in astronomy and astrology and had visited Tycho on Hven.
- ***Wor kierre sallig affganngnne here och gemhals*** — "our dear departed lord and consort of blessed memory," i.e. **Frederik II**, who in 1576 had granted Tycho the island of **Hven** (*Huen / jnßel Huen*, Latin *Hvenna / Venusia*). The whole letter is Sophie's response to a petition (*supplication*) from Tycho, asking her to confirm, from her own memory, a verbal undertaking of the late king.
- **Document type & rubric.** A chancery-register copy; the **Latin rubric** *"…HANS BØRNN ANRØRENNDIS **ut sequitur**"* ("concerning his children, **as follows**") heads the Danish body — a code-switch preserved by this chapter's convention, exactly as in the Frederik II compass-letter of 1584. *ANRØRENNDIS* = *anrørendes* ("concerning, touching"). *Sophia etc.* abbreviates the full royal style.
- **Substance.** The petition concerns the **hereditary succession to Hven and Uraniborg**: Tycho asks the dowager to attest that Frederik II had verbally promised that, after Tycho's death, one of Tycho's own children — if found *schickelig och dueligh* ("fit and able") in astronomy — should have first claim to the island and its establishment (the buildings and instruments). Sophie confirms she distinctly remembers hearing the late king say so, "some while before his mortal decease." The undertaking was never honoured: after Tycho left Denmark (1597) Hven reverted to the crown.
- ***astronomiae konnst … jnstauration och forbedrinng*** — "the art of astronomy … its renewal [*instauration*] and improvement." *jnstauration* is a direct Latin loan (*instauratio*) and is Tycho's own programmatic term (this chapter's convention: *instauratio astronomiae* = "the renewal of astronomy," *astronomia instaurata*); kept as **renewal [instauration]**. *konnst* here = "art / science / skill," the period sense, not modern "art."
- ***jnstrumennther*** — "instruments," the Uraniborg astronomical instruments. The Danish uses the Latin loan directly.
- ***Hanns Kierlighet / Hans Kierlighedtz*** — "His Love / His Love's": the chancery honorific *Hans Kærlighed* (German *Seine Liebden*, Latin *Dilectio Sua*), a formal third-person style used between and of high princes. Rendered literally as **His Love** and flagged here; it denotes the late king, not affection in the ordinary sense.
- ***begaffuede forstanndtt*** — "gifted understanding" (*begavet forstand*), i.e. natural talent / endowed intelligence.
- **Honorifics & register.** Throughout, the queen writes of herself in the royal plural (*Wij* "We," *Oß* "us") and addresses Tycho with the deferential second-person plural (*j / ether / ethers* "you / you / your"), while Tycho's own act is repeatedly marked *wnderdannigst / wnnderdannigste* ("most humbly / most humble"), the subject-to-sovereign register; preserved. *WOR gunst thilfornn* = *Vor gunst tilforn*, "Our favour beforehand" (the royal address-formula, this chapter's convention).
- **Orthography (chancery Danish, c. 1590).** Heavy German-influenced spelling (*sch-, w-, -tt, ß, doubled n/l*) that can fool automatic language detection — reading-verified as **Danish**, not German. Selected forms: *Wider* = *Vider* ("Know ye"); *j* = *I* ("you," pl.); *epther* = *efter* ("according to / after"); *sthormegthigste* = *stormægtigste* ("most mighty"); *hogbornne* = *højbårne* ("high-born"); *gemhals* = *gemal(s)* ("consort"); *forhuerffuitt* = *forhvervet* ("acquired / obtained"); *anretthitt* = *anrettet* ("set up / established"); *fulddreffuitt / fuldkommitt* = *fuldrevet / fuldkommet* ("carried through / completed"); *ahnßehelig* = *anselig* ("considerable, imposing"); *gefallenn och welbehag* = *gefallen og velbehag* (German-loan doublet, "liking and good pleasure"); *schickelig och dueligh* = *skikkelig og dygtig* ("fit and able"); *forordnnis* = *forordnes* ("be appointed"); *niude och beholde* = *nyde og beholde* ("enjoy and keep"); *forßett och menning* = *forsæt og mening* ("intent and meaning"); *erachthe* = *agte / erakte* ("bear in mind, deem"); *forennttholde / forholde* = *forholde* ("withhold"); *beuogenn* = *bevågen* ("favourably inclined").
- ***[ønsket]*** — at *haffuer j althiid [ønsket]* the source/edition supplies the verb "[wished]" in brackets, the construction otherwise lacking its main verb; the bracketed editorial supplement is carried into the translation as **[wished]**.
- **Calendar / place.** *Actum Haffniae thend 6. martij anno 1590* = "Done at **Copenhagen** (*Hafnia*), the 6th of March, the year 1590" (**O.S.** — Denmark kept the Julian calendar; this chapter's convention). *Actum* "Done/Given" kept by this chapter's convention *Befallendis etc.* (= *befalendes*, "commending [you to God / to God's protection]") is the closing-formula head, abbreviated in the register.

documents.incipit: QVÆ ad T. Celsit. hoc tempore perscriberem, Princeps Illustrissime, etsi non multa …

text.original:
ILLVSTRISSIMO PRINCIPI AC DOMINO, DOMINO WILHELMO, HASSIÆ LANDGRAVIO, COMITI IN CATZENELNBOGEN, DIETZ, ZIEGENHAIN ET NIDDA: PRINCIPI AC DOMINO SUO CLEMENTISSIMO S. P.

QVÆ ad T. Celsit. hoc tempore perscriberem, Princeps Illustrissime, etsi non multa occurrerent, simulque vererer, ne meis importunis literis T. Celsit. Reipub. negotijs occupatiorem molestarem (nam et semel atque iterum iamdudum literas, quibus nihil responsum est, transmisi, vnde T. Celsit. alijs curis auocari, neque his vacare collegi.) Attamen, quoniam nouum quoddam Phœnomenon sese proxime antecedentibus diebus, cœlitus conspiciendum exhibuit: Cometes videlicet aspectu non adeo magnus, sed pallido et subobscuro vultu lucens: Sciens T. Celsit. huius apparentias cognoscendi cupidam esse (ex quo in vltimo, ante quinquennium viso, simile quid a me expetitum sit) non supersedendum duxi, quin aliquid literarum, vel hoc saltem nomine ad T. Celsit. mitterem, veluti paulo ante T. Celsit. Mathematico scribens, quando nonnullas in eodem Cometa obseruationes continuassem, me facturum spopondi. Circa illudipsum enim tempus Cometa apparere cœpit, et expectandam erat, donec ratas aliquot in eo animaduersiones nancisci licuit. Ne igitur res diutius differatur, quæ hactenus sedulâ denotatione explorata habeo, T. Celsit. communicanda duxi, vt cum sui Mathematici in eodem Cometa obseruatis (nec enim dubito eundem etiam a vobis animaduersum esse) conferre queat. Occasio autem qua illum primum conspeximus, erat huiusmodi. Die 23. Februarij, cum Veneris Stella terris descendendo appropinquans, circa maximam a Sole remotionem versaretur, nactus post quatriduanas aëris obscuritates, exoptatam aliquam serenitatem, illius obseruationi sedulo attendendum censui. Siquidem ex dato ipsius loco, in remotissima, respectu Solis, tam Vespertina, quam Eoa dispositione, ad Apogæi atque Eccentricitatis cognitionem perueniri posse, prout quoque a Ptolemæo et Copernico factitatum est, T. Celsit. non ignorat. Non paucas igitur eiuscemodi a Sole digressiones maximas, matutinas atque vespertinas, iam antea aliquoties exploraui, quibus et hanc adiungere satagebam; vixque bis vel ter Venus iam Instrumentis denotata erat, vbi ex improuiso Stellam quandam subobscuram, inter Andromedæ atque Arietis Asterismos, iuxta Piscem Borealem sese præter solitum ostendentem, cum nullam eiuscemodi illic esse oportere satis perspectum haberem, animaduerteremus, quæ etiam subinde radiolos quosdam ad verticem exerere cernebatur. Neque enim Crepusculum vespertinum iam satis præterierat, vt Stellæ minus conspicuæ euidenter discernerentur. Cœpi itaque statim cum meis Studiosis hoc insolitum Phœnomenon per Instrumenta demetiri, et vix elapso horæ quadrante, deprehendi ex motu eius, quem vel tantillo tempore sensibiliter alterabat, tam Declinatione, quam Distantia a Fixis nonnihil variata, non genuinum, sed ascititium quoddam e Cometarum numero Sidus existere, vtut cauda illa tenuior, quam post Crepusculi finem promptius monstrabat, tunc vix oculis perciperetur. Mitto autem T. Celsit. seorsim in adiecta charta breuem quandam eiusdem Cometæ descriptionem, e meis obseruationibus, quas adeptus sum, ex tempore et festinanter concinnatam, quam cum vestris aduersionibus conferre licebit. Rogoque, vt T. Celsit. hanc nostram voluntatem boni consulat. Veneris Stella toto Februario et Martio interdiu, etiam in ipso Meridie apparuit, quod in posterum quoque pro maiori Aprilis parte futurum iudico. Si itaque T. Celsit. Mathematicus illi obseruandæ, tam interdiu, quam noctu operam sedulam nauauit, admodum oportunam, de quinis illis Minutis, quibus in Longitudinibus Stellarum differimus, decernendi arripuit ansam. Ex quo tam Venus quam Sol adeo sublimes obseruationi patuerint, vt Refractionum impedimentis vix implicarentur. Nec dubito, quin vel inde, adhibita solerti circumspectione colligere detur, me Longitudinem Fixarum nequaquam iusto plus anticipâsse. Constitueram T. Celsit. de his omnibus prius scribere, per Mercatores nostrates Francofurdum euntes, sed accidit, vt circa eosdem dies, quibus illi itineri se committebant, Serenissimus Scotorum Rex, cum suis Consiliarijs reliquoque Nobilium Comitatu, me in hac Insula inuisere dignatus sit, et exinde quasi quotidianos hospites habuerim. Hincque factum est, quod tardius atque constitueram, hasce mittere cogar. Quæ tamen mora non sine fænore accidit, nam eo plus temporis concedebatur, per interualla, ea, quæ in dicto Cometa prius subito exararam, plenius, et enucleatius recognoscendi, vt non dubitem, hæc ipsa, quæ mitto, vtut paucula et breuia, omnimode recte sibi constare, atque apparentijs istius Cometæ apprime esse analoga. Sed cum non ignorem T. Celsit. pro sua clementi et candida erga nos affectione, hanc dilatiunculam equi bonique accipere, nolo in eâ excusandâ plus occupari, quam forte opus sit, sed me meaque omnia T. Celsit. commendata cupio.

Vale.
Vraniburgo, Calendis Aprilis, Anno 1590.
T. Celsit.
Addictissimus
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the Most Illustrious Prince and Lord, Lord Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, Count in Catzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain and Nidda: his most gracious Prince and Lord — heartiest greeting.**

As to what I might write at length to Your Highness at this time, Most Illustrious Prince — although not much offered itself, and at the same time I feared that with my importunate letters I might trouble Your Highness, who are rather much occupied with the business of the commonwealth (for once and again, some while ago now, I sent letters to which no reply has come, from which I gathered that Your Highness is called away by other cares and has no leisure for these things) — nevertheless, since a certain new phenomenon has shown itself in these last few days to be seen in the heavens, namely a comet not so very large to the sight, but shining with a pale and somewhat dim face, and knowing that Your Highness is desirous to learn of its appearances (from the fact that with the last one, seen five years ago, something similar was sought of me), I judged that I ought not to forbear from sending Your Highness at least some letter, if only on this account — just as, writing a little while ago to Your Highness's Mathematician, I gave my pledge that I would do so, once I had carried on some observations on this same comet. For it was about that very time that the comet began to appear, and it had to be waited out until it was possible to obtain a few settled observations upon it. So then, lest the matter be put off any longer, I judged that what I have thus far explored by careful recording was to be communicated to Your Highness, that you may be able to compare it with the observations made by your Mathematician on the same comet (for I do not doubt that it was noticed by you also). Now the occasion on which we first caught sight of it was of this kind. On the 23rd of February, when the star Venus, drawing near the earth as it descended, was about its greatest distance from the Sun, having obtained — after a four-day obscurity of the air — some longed-for clear weather, I judged that careful attention should be given to observing it. For from its given place, when at its greatest distance with respect to the Sun, in both an evening and a morning disposition, one can arrive at the knowledge of the apogee and of the eccentricity, just as was done by Ptolemy and Copernicus too, as Your Highness is not unaware. Not a few greatest elongations of this kind from the Sun, both morning and evening, I had therefore already explored several times before, and I was busy to add this one too to them; and Venus had hardly yet been recorded by the instruments two or three times when, unexpectedly, we noticed a certain somewhat dim star showing itself contrary to custom between the asterisms of Andromeda and Aries, near the Northern Fish — since I held it well enough ascertained that no such star ought to be there — which was also seen from time to time to put forth certain little rays toward the zenith. For the evening twilight had not yet sufficiently passed for the less conspicuous stars to be clearly distinguished. I therefore began at once, with my students, to measure out this unusual phenomenon by the instruments, and scarcely had a quarter of an hour elapsed when I perceived, from its motion — which it appreciably altered even in so brief a time, with both its declination and its distance from the fixed stars somewhat varied — that it was no genuine star, but a certain adventitious one, of the number of comets, even though that thinner tail, which it showed more readily after the end of twilight, was then scarcely perceived by the eyes. But I send to Your Highness separately, on an enclosed sheet, a certain brief description of this same comet, drawn up offhand and in haste from the observations I have obtained, which it will be possible to compare with your own notes. And I ask that Your Highness take this our goodwill in good part. The star Venus appeared all through February and March in the daytime, even at midday itself, which I judge will be so in time to come too, for the greater part of April. If, therefore, Your Highness's Mathematician has devoted careful labour to observing it, both by day and by night, he has seized a most opportune handle for deciding about those five minutes by which we differ in the longitudes of the stars. Since both Venus and the Sun lay open to observation so high up that they would scarcely be entangled in the impediments of refractions. And I do not doubt that even from this, with diligent circumspection applied, it may be possible to gather that I have by no means anticipated the longitude of the fixed stars more than is right. I had resolved to write to Your Highness about all these things sooner, by way of our merchants going to Frankfurt; but it happened that, about the same days on which they were committing themselves to that journey, the Most Serene King of the Scots, with his Councillors and the rest of his retinue of nobles, deigned to visit me on this island, and that thereafter I had, as it were, daily guests. And hence it came about that I am compelled to send this present letter later than I had resolved. Yet that delay did not occur without interest [returned], for so much the more time was granted, in the intervals, for recognizing more fully and more thoroughly the things which I had earlier scratched down hurriedly on the said comet — so that I do not doubt that these very things which I send, though few and brief, are altogether rightly consistent in themselves, and exceedingly well matched to the appearances of that comet. But since I am not unaware that Your Highness, in keeping with your gracious and candid affection toward us, takes this little delay as fair and good, I do not wish to occupy myself in excusing it more than perhaps need be, but I desire myself and all my affairs to be commended to Your Highness.

Farewell.
From Uraniborg, on the Kalends of April [1 April], the year 1590.
Your Highness's
Most devoted,
TYCHO BRAHE.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Wilhelmus, Hassiae Landgravius* = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), the "astronomer prince," with whose Kassel observatory Tycho maintained his most important scientific correspondence. The titulature *Comiti in Catzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain et Nidda* names the subsidiary Hessian comital domains (Katzenelnbogen, Diez, Ziegenhain, Nidda); the place-names are left in their as-printed forms.
- **Sender / place.** *Tycho Brahe*, writing from **Uraniborg** (*Vraniburgum*) on the island of Hven.
- **Salutation.** *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam (dicit)*, "(sends) heartiest greeting". *T. Celsit.* = *Tua Celsitudo*, **Your Highness**; rendered consistently throughout. The subscription *Addictissimus* = "Most devoted."
- **The phenomenon.** *nouum quoddam Phoenomenon … Cometes* — **a comet**, that of late February 1590, first detected by Tycho on the night of the Venus observation. *non genuinum, sed ascititium … Sidus … e Cometarum numero* — "no genuine star, but a certain adventitious one, of the number of comets": the diagnosis turns on the body's measurable proper motion in a quarter-hour. *radiolos … ad verticem exerere* = "to put forth little rays toward the zenith"; *cauda … tenuior* = "a thinner tail."
- ***in vltimo, ante quinquennium viso*** — "the last one, seen five years ago": the **comet of 1585**, on which the Landgrave had earlier sought Tycho's observations. ("Five years" is loose for late 1585 → early 1590.)
- ***T. Celsit. Mathematico*** — Your Highness's Mathematician: **Christoph Rothmann**, the Kassel mathematician and Tycho's chief observational interlocutor in this period.
- **Venus / greatest elongation.** *circa maximam a Sole remotionem* = "about its greatest distance from the Sun" = **greatest elongation**; *in remotissima … tam Vespertina, quam Eoa dispositione* = "at its greatest distance … in both an evening and a morning disposition" (*Eous* = of the dawn, the morning star). Tycho states the standard method — that from Venus's place at greatest elongation one derives the **apogee** (*Apogaeum*) and **eccentricity** (*Eccentricitas*) of its orbit, "as was done by Ptolemy and Copernicus too." *digressiones maximas* = "greatest elongations" (here digression in the technical sense). The daytime visibility of Venus near midday is noted as an observational opportunity.
- **Star positions.** *inter Andromedae atque Arietis Asterismos, iuxta Piscem Borealem* = "between the asterisms of Andromeda and Aries, near the Northern Fish" (*Piscis Borealis*, the northern fish of Pisces). *Asterismus* = "asterism" (constellation-figure).
- **Technical terms.** *Instrumenta* → **instruments**; *Declinatio* → **declination**; *Distantia a Fixis* → "distance from the fixed stars"; *Fixae* → **the fixed stars**; *Refractiones* → **refractions**; *Crepusculum (vespertinum)* → **(evening) twilight**; *Meridies* → "midday / meridian"; *zenith* (*verticem*) kept/named by this chapter's convention *Studiosi* rendered "students" (Tycho's resident assistants at Uraniborg).
- **The five-minute discrepancy.** *de quinis illis Minutis, quibus in Longitudinibus Stellarum differimus* = "those five minutes by which we differ in the longitudes of the stars": the standing **5-arcminute disagreement** between Tycho's and Kassel's stellar **longitudes**. Tycho argues that the high-altitude daytime observations of Venus and the Sun — being "scarcely entangled in the impediments of refractions" — afford a test that, he expects, will confirm "that I have by no means anticipated [overstated] the longitude of the fixed stars more than is right." His epistemic hedge (*Nec dubito, quin … colligere detur* "I do not doubt that … it may be possible to gather") is preserved, not sharpened into a claim of proof.
- **The royal visit.** *Serenissimus Scotorum Rex … me in hac Insula inuisere dignatus sit* = "the Most Serene King of the Scots … deigned to visit me on this island": **James VI of Scotland** (later James I of England), who visited Hven on 20 March 1590 while in Denmark for his marriage to Anne of Denmark — the cause of the letter's delay. *per Mercatores nostrates Francofurdum euntes* = "by our merchants going to Frankfurt" (the Frankfurt fair as the postal channel to Hesse).
- ***non sine faenore*** — literally "not without interest" (financial metaphor): the delay paid a dividend, in extra time to perfect the comet observations. Rendered with the metaphor kept ("without interest [returned]").
- ***adiecta charta*** — "an enclosed sheet": the separate comet-observation summary accompanying the letter, now lost from / not part of this text.
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Vraniburgo, Calendis Aprilis, Anno 1590* = "From Uraniborg, on the **Kalends of April (1 April)**, the year 1590" (Old Style; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The Roman-calendar idiom *Calendis Aprilis* is the 1st of April; this agrees with the catalogue label (*1590. 1. april. Uraniborg*), so no date discrepancy arises. The Roman idiom is glossed by this chapter's convention

documents.incipit: SERIUS ego quidem, Nobilissime mi RANZOVI, tuis iam respondeo literis, non tam mea culpa, …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO ET AMPLISSIMO VIRO, VIRTUTE ET ERUDITIONE IMPRIMIS CONSPICUO, DOMINO HENRICO RANZOVIO, DOMINO DE BREITENBERGA ET REGIO IN HOLSATIA AC DITHMARSIA GUBERNATORI ETC. AMICO SUO PLURIMUM COLENDO.

SERIUS ego quidem, Nobilissime mi RANZOVI, tuis iam respondeo literis, non tam mea culpa, quam quod de Insignibus Sturorum certior interea temporis fieri nequiverim. Licet enim diligentissime hincinde per sororem quoque meam SOPHIAM a Domina GURUILDA, relicta D. LAGONIS BRAHE vidua, id expiscari attentârim, votis tamen nostris nondum est satisfactum, ut et adiunctæ indicabunt literæ. Accessit et hoc, quod septimanis præteritis hospitum, qui me invisebant, multitudine sim præpeditus, quo minus, uti volebam, tuæ petitioni satisfacere vacârit. Ne vero adhuc te sine responso diutius detineam, non amplius rescriptione abstinendum duxi, licet nihil, quod ad Insignia illa attinet, adhuc compertum habeam. Ubi tamen aut ex Svecia vel aliunde rem ipsam cognovero, curabo, ut resciscas. Quod ad figuras libris præfigendas attinet, eas Buxo solummodo insculptas expeto, neque enim Typographus meus cupreus aptare novit. Typi WOLFFIANI meis non correspondent, præterea eos carius æstimat atque Vitebergenses, ubi aptiores veneunt 20 floren. in centenar. ut de ijs iam plura agere non sit necessum. Et ut rem ipsam dicam, non admodum mihi stylo nunc est opus, donec Chartopæum denuo acquisivero. Is enim, quem ad me misisti, Rostochium pro socio et veteramentis conquirendis ablegatus, acceptis præter voluntatem meam a D. BRUCÆO sex Ioachimicis, Wismariam, illic se veteramenta collecturum simulans, abijt, posteaque veterator iste se subduxit. Idem quoque mihi accidit cum priore, qui a IOACHIMO BUCK Lubecensi pecuniam nactus nusquam deinceps comparuit. Scripsi lamdudum tibi de ijs, quæ a me tum temporis, cum Calendarium Ranzovianum misisti, expetebas, sed colligo ex literis tuis, meas ad manus tuas non pervenisse. Ubi interea deliteant, ignoro. Plura per commodum otium scribam et conabor, quantum in me est, ut Insignium istorum Sturianorum delineatione potiaris. Vale, meaque, uti facis, promovere stude. Dabo vicissim operam, ut quæ tibi accepta cognovero, ubi potuero, fiant.

Iterum vale.
Datæ Uraniburgo 2. Aprilis Anno 90.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 243; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Literas quas adiunxi ad Illustriss. Principem Landgravium, si Casselas mitti procurâris, et alteram Pragam versus, rem feceris pergratam. Tunc etiam quæ Lubecam et Hamburgum dirigendæ veniunt.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most distinguished man, conspicuous above all for virtue and erudition, Master Henrik Rantzau, lord of Breitenburg and royal governor in Holstein and Dithmarschen, etc., his friend much to be honoured.**

Rather late, indeed, my most noble Rantzau, do I now reply to your letter — not so much through my own fault as because in the meantime I have been unable to gain surer knowledge concerning the arms of the Stures. For although I have most diligently attempted to fish that out from here and there — through my sister Sophia too, from the Lady Gørvel, the widow left by Master Lage Brahe — our wishes have nonetheless not yet been satisfied, as the enclosed letter[s] will also show. There was added this too, that in the past weeks I have been hindered by the multitude of guests who were visiting me, so that I had less leisure than I wished to satisfy your request. But lest I keep you still longer without a reply, I judged that I ought not to abstain from writing any further, although as yet I have learned nothing that bears upon those arms. Whenever, however, I shall have learned the matter itself, whether from Sweden or from elsewhere, I shall see to it that you are informed. As regards the figures to be set at the front of the books, I want them engraved in boxwood only, for my typographer does not know how to fit copper [plates]. The Wolffian types do not match mine; besides, he prices them more dearly than the Wittenberg ones, where more suitable ones are sold at 20 florins the hundredweight — so that there is no need to deal further with these matters now. And to speak the matter plainly, I have no great need of a graving-tool [stylus] at present, until I shall have acquired a paper-maker again. For the one whom you sent to me, having been dispatched to Rostock to seek out a partner and old materials, and having received — against my will — six Joachim-dollars from Master Brucaeus, went off to Wismar, pretending that he would collect old materials there, and afterwards that old rogue stole away. The same thing also befell me with the earlier one, who, having got money from Joachim Buck of Lübeck, never afterwards appeared anywhere. I wrote to you long ago about those things which you were requesting from me at the time when you sent the Rantzovian Calendar, but I gather from your letter that mine did not reach your hands. Where they lie hidden meanwhile, I do not know. I shall write more at convenient leisure, and shall endeavour, so far as in me lies, that you may obtain a drawing of those arms of the Stures. Farewell, and continue, as you do, to advance my interests. I in turn shall give my effort that whatever I learn is welcome to you may, when I can, be brought about.

Again, farewell.
Given at Uraniborg, 2 April, the year [15]90.
TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.


*[Postscript:]* The letters which I have enclosed for the most illustrious Prince the Landgrave — if you would see to it that they are sent to Kassel, and the other one toward Prague — you will do a most welcome thing. And then likewise those that are to be directed to Lübeck and Hamburg.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** *Tycho Brahe* at Uraniborg → *Henricus Ranzovius* = **Heinrich (Henrik) Rantzau** (1526–1598), lord of **Breitenburg** and royal *Statthalter* (governor / viceroy) of Schleswig-Holstein and Dithmarschen on behalf of the Danish crown — the great humanist patron, book-collector and astrological enthusiast with whom Tycho corresponded extensively. The address-formula's full titulature (*Domino de Breitenberga et regio … gubernatori*) is reproduced in full by this chapter's convention/.
- ***Insignia Sturorum / Sturianorum*** — "the arms of the **Stures**," the heraldic coat of arms of the Swedish noble Sture family, on which Rantzau (an avid genealogist and armorial collector) had asked Tycho to procure information. Rendered "arms"; the heraldic, not military, sense. Tycho's answer is throughout a hedged non-result: he has *nihil … adhuc compertum* ("learned nothing as yet"), preserved as such — no sharpening to a positive finding.
- ***soror mea Sophia*** = **Sophie (Sophia) Brahe** (1559–1643), Tycho's learned younger sister, here acting as his intermediary in the genealogical inquiry.
- ***Domina Guruilda, relicta D. Lagonis Brahe vidua*** = the **Lady Gørvel** — Gørvel Faddersdatter Sparre — described as the widow left by **Master Lage Brahe**. *Relicta … vidua* is pleonastic in the Latin ("the widow left behind by"); rendered "the widow left by Master Lage Brahe" without trimming the doubling.
- ***expiscari*** — literally "to fish out," kept as the live metaphor ("fish that out").
- ***adiunctae … literae*** — "the enclosed letter[s]." Latin *literae* is formally plural but regularly denotes a single letter; number left as the Latin gives it, with the alternative flagged here rather than silently singularised.
- **Printing matter.** *figuras libris praefigendas … Buxo … insculptas* = woodcut **figures** (illustrations/plates) to be set at the front of books, "engraved in **boxwood** only" — i.e. woodblocks, *buxus* being the standard fine engraving-wood. *Typographus meus cupreus aptare novit*: Tycho's own printer at Uraniborg "does not know how to fit copper [plates]" — i.e. cannot execute copperplate (intaglio) engraving. *aptare* = "to fit/mount," kept literal.
- ***Typi Wolffiani*** — "the **Wolffian** types," i.e. printing type from a founder/supplier named Wolff (most plausibly the Hamburg/Lübeck-area trade Rantzau had access to); identification not secured, so the epithet is kept as an adjective and flagged. *eos carius aestimat atque Vitebergenses* = "he prices them more dearly than the **Wittenberg** ones." *20 floren. in centenar.* = "20 florins the hundredweight (per *centenarius*)," a price-by-weight for cast type; kept literal.
- ***stylo … non est opus … donec Chartopaeum … acquisivero*** — *stylus* here is the engraver's/graving tool (the means of producing the *figurae*), not handwriting style; rendered "graving-tool [stylus]" with the Latin flagged, since the bracketing of cause (no engraver) and effect (no paper-maker) shows Tycho means the physical apparatus of book-production. *Chartopaeus* (Gk. χαρτοποιός) = **paper-maker**; the Uraniborg paper-mill's workman.
- **The two absconding paper-makers.** *Is … Rostochium pro socio et veteramentis conquirendis ablegatus … sex Ioachimicis … Wismariam … abijt … veterator iste se subduxit*: the paper-maker Rantzau had sent, dispatched to **Rostock** to recruit a partner and gather *veteramenta* (**old materials** — i.e. rags/old paper-stock for pulp), pocketed **six Joachim-dollars** (*Ioachimici* = Joachimsthaler) from Brucaeus against Tycho's will, decamped to **Wismar**, and absconded. *veterator iste* ("that old rogue") puns on *veteramenta*; the wordplay (old-stock / old-hand-at-trickery) is noted, the insult rendered "that old rogue." *D. Brucaeo* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (1531–1593), professor of medicine and mathematics at Rostock, Tycho's correspondent there. *Idem … cum priore, qui a Ioachimo Buck Lubecensi pecuniam nactus*: the same had happened with an earlier paper-maker, who took money from **Joachim Buck of Lübeck** and vanished.
- ***Calendarium Ranzovianum*** — the **Rantzovian Calendar**, Rantzau's own *Calendarium* (an astrological-computational almanac he compiled and sent to Tycho). Kept as a title.
- ***manu propria*** — "in his own hand," Tycho's autograph subscription; the witness is a chancery/archival register copy at Vienna (ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.25; see the collation note below — the *9737* siglum belongs to the preceding Craig letter), so the *manu propria* describes the original, not the surviving copy.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datae Uraniburgo 2. Aprilis Anno 90* = "Given at **Uraniborg**, 2 April [15]90" (O.S.; Denmark kept Old Style until 1700). The dateline (2 April 1590) agrees with the edition label; no discrepancy.
- **Greeting / closing formulae.** No opening *salutem*; the letter opens directly after the address. *Vale … Iterum vale* = "Farewell … Again, farewell". *meaque … promovere stude* = "continue … to advance my interests," the reciprocal-patronage register kept.

- **§1 Dreyer collation:** MS-witness corrected to **cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.25** (Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VII, p. 243, assigns this letter to 10686²⁵; the *9737* siglum belongs to the preceding Craig letter).

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (after "manu propria"), restored from Dreyer VII, p. 243 (dropped by the working transcription).

Collated the full letter word-for-word against Dreyer TBOO VII pp. 242-243, including the restored postscript on letters for the Landgrave/Kassel/Prague/Lübeck/Hamburg, which Dreyer does print immediately after the signature "Tycho Brahe, manu propria" — confirming the working transcription's restoration is accurate. Verified all names (Gørvel/Guruilda, Lage Brahe, Brucaeus, Joachim Buck) and figures (six Joachim-dollars, 20 florins per hundredweight). text.original:
NOBILISSIMO, ET VIRTVTE, SAPIENTIA, INGENIOSA ERVDITAQVE DOCTRINA
CLARISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, DOMINO DE KNUDSTRUP, EQUITI
DANO, MATHEMATICORUM NOSTRO SECULO OMNIUM PRÆSTANTISSIMO, ETC.
DOMINO SUO CUM OBSERUANTIA COLENDO. S. P.

ASI, vt OVIDIVS canit, Carmina proueniunt animo deducta sereno, Nobilissime Excellentissimeque Domine TYCHO, multo magis profundissimæ et subtilissimæ Mathematicæ Disputationes, quæ cum Carminum exaratione non sunt comparandæ, animum a perturbationibus liberrimum requirent. Non igitur rem aut a nostra amicitia alienam, aut excusatione omni, vt tu arguere videris, indignam commisissem, si responsione supersedissem. Qui enim maiores cruciatus aut dolores excogitari possunt, quam ego in Podagra iam vltra biennium, et in Calculo, hâc Hyeme, grauissimis omnium morbis, sustineo? Qui morbi hâc Hyeme alternatim me inuadentes, corpus meum tam debilitarunt, mentemque pene de statu suo præcipitarunt, vt ne literam quidem potuerim fereA exarare. Superiore autem æstate, quanquam præter Podagram, languores continuos, et ab omni labore horrores in me depræhenderem, nesciebam tamen, qualem morbum mihi essent apportaturæ et inflicturæ insolitæ illæ lassitudines: Quod mihi iam acerbissimis doloribus et cruciatibus satis innotuit. Spiritus enim Podagricus (ita enim iam libet eum appellare) in tantam malitiam in me excreuit, vt non tantum vias vrinarias, et renes, verum etiam venas mesaraicasA arenâ rubeâ, et tartaro arctissime constiparit, adeo vt quamprimum comederim aut biberim, propter nutrimenti a naturâ attracti inhibitionem, et vrinæ expulsionem, vehementissimos cruciatus et in mesaraicis, et in vijs vrinarijs, instar dolorum cholicorum sentiam, cibumque assumtum retinere in ventriculo propter nauseam et vomitum nequeamA. Et extant in me non obscura signa, quæ eundem Spiritum in alijs quoque membris idem tentare non obscure arguunt. Tentaui Medicinam Galenicam, me curante eruditissimo Dn. Doct. BVTTERO, Medico Illustrissimi Principis nostri; verum sine omni successu. Cum ea vrinam pellere voluit, obstante tartaro, in vijs vrinarijs ante vesicam, vehementissimos cruciatus sustinui. Quid balnea quoque et insessiones possint, facile intelligis, cum propter Podagram pedes ipsis immittere prohibear; extremis autem membris non calefactis, intermedia vix debito modo calefiant. Quanquam herbarum virtutes licet tartarum fortassisA frangere possint, in aquam tamen eumA dissoluere non possuntA; quod hîc omnino necessarium est, si aut in intestina regurgitare, aut per vesicam abire transudando debeat, morbusque radicitus curari. Num etiam hæc tanta spiritus Podagrici malitia possit ex fecibus Salem Petræ in me generare, eumque ad extremum gradum subtilitatis continuâ sublimatione perducere, adeoque mihi in momento vitam eripere, tibi expendendum relinquo, qui facile intelligis, quid notem. Hic enim Spiritus, cum fixæ, vt scis, sit Naturæ; reliqui autem Spiritus meliores, qui huius malitiam retundere possunt, sint volatiles, et per cogitationum intentiones, quibus me exuere nequeo, quotidie absumantur, an non in immensum virtutem suam augere, et tandem sibi solum totum imperiumA assumere, a nullo impeditus, poterit? Proinde ad sola Diuina merito me totum conuerterem, omissis Philosophicis, quanquam et hæc Diuina sint. Attamen cum iam qualemqualem cruciatuum remissionem quodammodo sentiam, pro Amore in te meo, qui certe vulgaris non est, et pro nostra Amicitia intermittere non potui, quin aliquid saltem, quod mihi in his meis ærumnis in mentem venire possit, ad tuas Disputationes iam seorsim in Charta ad me missas, responderem.

Quod igitur COPERNICVM de triplici motu Terræ impugnando, priore loco de diurno motu affers; si Terra 24. horis circumuolui fingatur, fieri non posse, vt globus plumbeus ex altissima turri demissus, punctum Terræ infra se positum, perpendiculariter ad amussim contingat; cum illud propter velocissimum Terræ motum, sese necessario interea subducatA, globumque plumbeum post se relinquat: Hoc satis a COPERNICO enodatum et dissolutum est. Cadentium enim, et ascendentium, vt ipse ait, duplicem fateamur esse motum oportet Mundi comparatione, et omnino compositum ex recto, et circulari: Quandoquidem quæ pondere suo deprimuntur, cum sint maxime terrea, non dubium, quin eandem seruent partes Naturam, quam suum totum. Id quod tibi multo minus dubium esse debet, cum tu ex meliore Philosophia scias, quod Natura Naturâ delectetur, Naturaque Naturam retineat. Si corporibus illis sui motus scientia est naturalis, vt tu vis, erit ea etiam partibus. Quemadmodum enim in alijs rebus naturalibus, verbi causa, partes Auri retinent Naturam totius, nec eo modo separatæ a toto id, quod a Natura ipsis peculiariter et specifice insitumA erat, abijciunt: Ita et in his corporibus, quæ motum, vt tu non inepteA vis, naturalem habent, partes primariam hanc insitam sibi prærogatiuam, et præcipuam ac specificam dignitatem non abijcient. Sed quid de casu rerum grauium solicitus esA, cum omnia, quæ in superficie Terræ libera et a toto separata iacent, quinimo ipsa Turris, ex qua Globus plumbeus dimitteretur, ipsaque ædificia ruerent, atque a Terræ motu relinquerentur necesse esset, si partes non retinerent motum totius: quod quam sit contra Naturæ Sapientiam, nemo non videt. Quod autem de Supputationibus affers, Terram ea ratione in vno secundo temporis scrupuloA reuolui debere in borealioribus ibi plagis sesquicentum passus maiores proxime: Quæso vtrum censebitur credibilius et sapientiæ NaturaeA, quæ semper per pauciora agit, conuenientius: an vt sesquicentum passus, an vero vt tot millia non passuum, sed milliarium Germanicorum in vno secundo temporis scrupulo conficiat? et quidem sub eodem effectu et fine? An non id vehementissime cum dicta Naturæ sapientia, qua semper pauciora et breuiora eligit, pugnabit, si assumto cœli motu per omnium Stellarum et Planetarum diuersos, vehementissimos, menteque humana incomprehensibiles atque etiam innumerabiles cursus efficere cogetur, quod poterat in vno facilime præstare? An non et hoc, quod ea ratione Planetis duplex et Ubi ipsi contrarius inesset centri motus? Nescio etiam, an fixa Sidera in tanta motus pernicitate, tam constanter suas ab inuicem distantias custodire possent. Sed sexcenta eiuscemodi proferriA possent, quæ satis conuincunt, motum diurnum in nullo alio corpore quam in terra quærendum esseA.

Ad annuum autem motum quod attinet, cur mihi non verisimile videatur, spatium a Sole ad Saturnum tot vicibus contineri intra Saturnum et affixarum Stellarum remotionem? aut quid absurdi sequitur, si Stella tertiæ Magnitudinis æquat totum orbem annuum? An id aut cum voluntate diuina pugnat, aut diuinæ Naturæ impossibile est, aut infinitæ Naturæ non competit? Hæc demonstranda omnino tibi sunt, si absurdi quid hinc colligere volueris. Non tam facile absurditatis argui possunt, quæ vulgo absurda primâ fronte videntur, sed longe maior est diuina Sapientia et Maiestas. Et quantumcunque etiam Mundi Vastitatem, et Magnitudinem concedas, nullam tamen proportionem ad infinitum Creatorem habebit. Quo maior Rex, eo maius et amplius palatium decere putat suam MaiestatemA. Quid cogitabis de DEO?

In tertio vero terræ motu, cur axis terræ non annuatim reflecteretur, vt quiescere nihilominus appareret? aut cur non axem et centrum duplici diuersoque motu agitari detur? Si terra impacta esset duro aliquo orbi et ab eo circumferretur, hæc fortassis locum habere possent. At cum terra liberrime in aëre pendeat, cur non, si centrum promoueatur, axis nihilominus super eodem centro possit nutare eo, quo Natura velit? Centrum enim semper in axe est, et est quasi Polus, vt ita dicam, reflexionis axis, nec vna reflectitur, sed respectu reflexionis est immotum. At hæc axis reflexio facilius intelligitur, si per idem terræ centrum etiam ducatur axis Zodiaci, vero Zodiaci axi parallelus, qui in immensitateA Sphæræ cum vero axe idem videbitur, circa quem videbitur axis terræ reflecti, non quidem ad Angulos rectos, sed ad tantum Angulum, quanta est Zodiaci obliquitas. Scio hoc in loco COPERNICVM esse admodum obscurum, nec facile perceptibilem. Sed hæc alio modo longe facilius possunt explicari, nec opus est triplici terræ motu, sed sufficiunt diurnus, et annuus. Nec axis terræ reuera reflectitur, siquidem manet semperA idem Angulus intersectionis planorum Eclipticæ et Æquatoris, axisque terræ motu annuo ita circumducitur, vt semper paralleliter versus eandem mundi partem spectet, adeoque propter euanescentiam orbis annui in immensitate Sphæræ ad vnum et idem punctum videatur semper collimare: Ex quibus, superueniente motu diurno, reflexio, tanquam effectus resultare videtur. Sed hæc fusius et enucleatius DEO dante, inuenies in secundo libro nostrarum Obseruationum, vbi de præcessione æquinoctiorum agemus. Librationem quoque licet in cursu Mercurij non probem, tamen eiusmodi esse video, vt in planis circulorum sese variantibus, naturalior motus excogitari non possit. Sed horum omnium explicatio nimis obscure a COPERNICO proposita est, et effectus cum causa sine distinctione ita confusus, vt quid velit, non facile a quoquam intelligatur. Sed plus intendo mentem, quam valetudo mea patitur. Alibi hæc fusius habebis.

Cometam eadem die, quâ tu, vidi, et Illustrissimo Principi nostro ostendi, qui apud me commorabatur, donec Horizontem subiret. Obseruaui eum, quantum in hac mea valetudine potui: quarum qualiumcunque obseruationum copiam seu exemplar ad te mitto, vt ipse inde motum et congruentiam cum tuis eruas.

Hæc igitur hac vice tibi sufficiant in his meis ærumnis, quæ quantæ sint, facili potes assequi coniectura ex eo, quod iam in flore ætatis constitutus, eiusmodi morbos sustineam. Desidero Oleum Vitrioli rubicundissimum illud et fragrantissimum, itemque Oleum Tartari, non quidem communis, sed singulariter per singulare mysterium indagati, vt te sine dubio non fugit, aliasque insuper extractiones et solutiones. Pro quibus si fortassis nuncium ad te ablegauero (Hîc enim, vt et vix in alijs Germaniæ locis, iustam eorum præparationem, nancisci nequeo) non dubito, quin pro nostrâ Amicitiâ mihi ea sis communicaturus, salutique meæ pro virili consulturus: Aut occasione oblatâ, ipse in posterum, pro Disputationibus Medicamenta mitte, quorum ratio iam merito potior est. Sed de tua in me beneuolentia non dubito.

Vale mi Nobiliss. Dn. TYCHO.
Cassellis ex lecto meo, 18. Aprilis, Anno 1590.
T. T. CHRISTOPHORVS ROTHMANNVS.
text.english:
**To the most noble man, most renowned for virtue, wisdom, and ingenious and erudite learning, Master Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup, Danish knight, of all the mathematicians of our age the most pre-eminent, etc., his lord to be honoured with all observance — heartiest greeting.**

If, as Ovid sings, "songs come forth drawn from a serene mind," most noble and most excellent Master Tycho, then much more do the most profound and most subtle mathematical disputations — which are not to be compared with the composing of verses — require a mind utterly free from disturbances. I should not, therefore, have committed an act either alien to our friendship, or undeserving of any excuse (as you seem to charge), had I forgone a reply. For what greater torments or pains can be conceived than those I endure in gout [podagra], now for over two years, and in the stone [calculus], this winter — the gravest of all diseases? These diseases, assailing me by turns this winter, so weakened my body and all but cast my mind from its seat, that I could scarcely [barely] even trace a letter. Last summer, moreover, although besides the gout I detected in myself continual languors and a horror of all labour, yet I did not know what disease those unwonted weaknesses would bring upon me and inflict; which has now become known to me well enough through the bitterest pains and torments. For the gouty spirit [spiritus podagricus] (for so I now please to call it) has grown to such malignancy in me that it has most tightly clogged not only the urinary passages and the kidneys, but also the mesaraic [mesenteric] veins, with red gravel and with tartar — so that, as soon as I have eaten or drunk, owing to the inhibition of the nourishment drawn in by nature and to the expulsion of urine, I feel the most violent torments both in the mesaraic [veins] and in the urinary passages, after the manner of colic pains, and I cannot retain the food I have taken in my stomach, on account of nausea and vomiting. And there are in me not obscure signs which argue, not obscurely, that the same spirit is attempting the same thing in my other members too. I tried Galenic medicine, being treated by the most learned Doctor Butterus, physician to our Most Illustrious Prince — but without any success. When it sought to drive out the urine, with the tartar blocking [the way], I endured the most violent torments in the urinary passages before the bladder. What baths too and sitz-baths can do, you easily understand, since on account of the gout I am forbidden to put my feet into them; and the outer members not being warmed, the parts between are scarcely warmed in due measure. And although the virtues of herbs may perhaps be able to break up the tartar, yet they cannot dissolve it into water — which is here altogether necessary, if it must either flow back into the intestines, or pass off through the bladder by sweating out, and the disease be cured from the roots. Whether this so great malignancy of the gouty spirit can also generate saltpetre [salt of stone, *sal petrae*] in me out of the dregs, and bring it by continual sublimation to the extreme degree of subtlety, and so snatch away my life in a moment, I leave to you to weigh — you who easily understand what I mean. For since this spirit, as you know, is of a fixed nature, while the other and better spirits, which can blunt its malignancy, are volatile, and are daily consumed through the strainings of thought, of which I cannot rid myself — will it not be able to increase its power immeasurably, and at last to assume to itself alone the whole dominion, hindered by none? Therefore I should rightly turn myself wholly to divine matters alone, setting aside philosophical ones — though these too are divine. Nevertheless, since I now in some manner feel some remission, such as it is, of the torments, for my love toward you, which is surely no common love, and for our friendship, I could not refrain from at least replying — with whatever might be able to come into my mind amid these afflictions of mine — to your disputations, now sent to me separately on a sheet.

As, then, to what you bring forward in assailing Copernicus on the threefold motion of the Earth: in the first place, concerning the diurnal motion — that, if the Earth be supposed to revolve in 24 hours, it cannot be that a leaden ball let down from a very high tower should strike exactly perpendicular upon the point of the Earth set beneath it, since that point, on account of the Earth's most rapid motion, must necessarily withdraw itself meanwhile and leave the leaden ball behind it: this has been sufficiently unravelled and resolved by Copernicus. For of things falling and rising, as he himself says, we must confess the motion to be twofold in relation to the World, and altogether compounded of the rectilinear and the circular — seeing that the things which are pressed down by their own weight, being most earthy, [leave] no doubt that the parts preserve the same nature as their whole. Which ought to be far less doubtful to you, since you know from a better philosophy that Nature delights in Nature, and Nature retains Nature. If to those bodies the knowledge of their own motion is natural, as you will have it, it will belong to the parts also. For just as in other natural things — for example, the parts of gold retain the nature of the whole, nor when thus separated from the whole do they cast off that which had been peculiarly and specifically implanted in them by Nature — so too in these bodies, which have motion natural [to them], as you not ineptly will have it, the parts will not cast off this primary prerogative implanted in them, and their chief and specific dignity. But why are you anxious about the fall of heavy things, when all things which lie on the surface of the Earth free and separated from the whole — nay, the very tower from which the leaden ball would be released, and the buildings themselves — would necessarily collapse and be left behind by the Earth's motion, if the parts did not retain the motion of the whole: which, how contrary it is to the Wisdom of Nature, no one fails to see. But as to what you bring forward concerning the computations — that on that reckoning the Earth must in one second of time revolve, in the more northerly regions there, about a hundred and fifty paces or more: I ask, which will be reckoned the more credible, and the more conformable to the wisdom of Nature (which always acts through fewer means) — that it should accomplish a hundred and fifty paces, or that it should accomplish so many thousands, not of paces, but of German miles, in one second of time? and that to the same effect and end? Will it not most vehemently clash with the said wisdom of Nature, which always chooses fewer and shorter [ways], if, the motion of the heaven being assumed, it must produce, through the diverse courses of all the stars and planets — most violent, incomprehensible to the human mind, and indeed innumerable — what it could most easily have effected in one [body]? And is there not also this: that on that reckoning there would be in the planets a twofold motion of the centre, and one contrary to it [in its place / *Ubi*]? I do not know, either, whether the fixed stars, in so great a swiftness of motion, could so constantly keep their distances from one another. But six hundred things of the kind could be brought forward, which sufficiently prove that the diurnal motion is to be sought in no other body than in the Earth.

But as concerns the annual motion: why should it not seem probable to me that the space from the Sun to Saturn is contained so many times over within [the interval] between Saturn and the remoteness of the fixed stars? Or what absurdity follows, if a star of the third magnitude equals the whole annual orb? Does this either clash with the divine will, or is it impossible to the divine Nature, or does it not befit the infinite Nature? These things you must by all means demonstrate, if you would gather any absurdity from this. Those things are not so easily to be convicted of absurdity which to the common run seem absurd at first sight; rather, far greater is the divine Wisdom and Majesty. And however great a vastness and magnitude of the World you grant, yet it will have no proportion to the infinite Creator. The greater the King, the greater and more ample a palace he thinks befits his Majesty. What will you think of GOD?

But in the third motion of the Earth: why should not the axis of the Earth be turned back [reflected] annually, so that it should nonetheless appear to be at rest? Or why should it not be granted that the axis and the centre are agitated by a twofold and diverse motion? If the Earth were fixed into some hard orb and carried round by it, these [objections] perhaps might have place. But since the Earth hangs most freely in the air, why not — if the centre be advanced — should the axis nonetheless be able to nod upon the same centre, in whatever way Nature wills? For the centre is always in the axis, and is, so to speak, the Pole of the reflection of the axis; nor is it reflected together [with it], but in respect of the reflection is unmoved. But this reflection of the axis is more easily understood if through the same centre of the Earth there be also drawn an axis of the Zodiac, parallel to the true axis of the Zodiac, which in the immensity of the Sphere will appear the same as the true axis, about which the axis of the Earth will appear to be reflected — not indeed at right angles, but at as great an angle as is the obliquity of the Zodiac. I know that in this place Copernicus is exceedingly obscure, and not easily intelligible. But these things can be explained far more easily in another way, nor is there need of a threefold motion of the Earth, but the diurnal and the annual suffice. Nor is the axis of the Earth really reflected, since there remains always the same angle of intersection of the planes of the Ecliptic and the Equator, and the axis of the Earth is so carried round by the annual motion that it always looks parallel-wise toward the same part of the World, and so, on account of the vanishing of the annual orb in the immensity of the Sphere, it appears always to aim at one and the same point: from which, the diurnal motion supervening, the reflection seems to result, as it were an effect. But these things, God granting, you will find more fully and more clearly set out in the second book of our Observations, where we shall treat of the precession of the equinoxes. The libration too, although in the course of Mercury I do not approve it, yet I see it to be of such a kind that, in the planes of the circles varying themselves, a more natural motion cannot be devised. But the explanation of all these things has been propounded by Copernicus too obscurely, and the effect so confounded with the cause without distinction, that what he means is not easily understood by anyone. But I am straining my mind more than my health allows. You shall have these things more fully elsewhere.

The comet I saw on the same day as you, and showed it to our Most Illustrious Prince, who was staying with me, until it sank below the Horizon. I observed it, as far as in this state of health I could: of which observations, such as they are, I send you a copy or specimen, that you may yourself draw out from it the motion and the agreement with your own.

Let these things, then, suffice you for this time, amid these afflictions of mine — how great they are, you can easily reach by conjecture from this, that, set as I now am in the flower of my age, I endure diseases of this kind. I long for that most ruddy and most fragrant Oil of Vitriol, and likewise Oil of Tartar — not indeed of the common sort, but of that singularly sought out through a singular mystery, as without doubt does not escape you — and besides other extractions and solutions. For which, if perhaps I shall dispatch a messenger to you (for here, as also scarcely in other places of Germany, I cannot obtain a proper preparation of them), I do not doubt that, for our Friendship's sake, you will impart them to me, and will look to my health to the best of your power. Or, when occasion offers, do you yourself in future send Medicaments in return for the Disputations, the consideration of which now deservedly weighs more with me. But of your goodwill toward me I do not doubt.

Farewell, my most noble Master Tycho.
At Kassel, from my bed, 18 April, the year 1590.
Most devoted to you,
Christoph Rothmann.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Christophorus Rothmannus* = **Christoph Rothmann** (c. 1550 – c. 1600), mathematician and astronomer at the court of **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel**. His correspondence with Tycho on cosmology, instruments, and the comet of 1585 is among the most substantial of the period; this letter is one of those Tycho selected for his printed *Epistolae astronomicae* (1596). Rothmann here defends the Copernican explanations against Tycho's objections — though he is no doctrinaire Copernican — while pleading grave illness.
- **Edition of record.** *Tychonis Brahe Dani epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Uraniborg, 1596), Liber I — the volume Tycho printed himself; reprinted in Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VI. No manuscript witness is recorded in the source header.
- **Salutation / titulature.** *DOMINO DE KNUDSTRUP, EQUITI DANO* = "Lord of Knudstrup, Danish knight" — Tycho's ancestral seat and his noble rank; *MATHEMATICORUM NOSTRO SECULO OMNIUM PRAeSTANTISSIMO* = "of all the mathematicians of our age the most pre-eminent." *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam (dicit)*, "heartiest greeting". Subscription *T. T.* = *Tuus Totus* / *Tibi Toto*, "Wholly yours / Most devoted to you."
- **Ovid allusion.** The opening *vt OVIDIVS canit, Carmina proueniunt animo deducta sereno* paraphrases **Ovid**, *Tristia* I.1.39 (*carmina proveniunt animo deducta sereno*) — verses come from a serene mind; rendered as a quotation. The printed text begins "ASI, vt…" where the engrossed initial capital **S** of *Si* has dropped from the extraction (the decorative initial letter); the sense is *Si … Carmina proueniunt …, multo magis … Disputationes … requirent* ("If … songs come forth …, much more do … disputations … require [a serene mind]"). Reading adopted: *[S]i*; flagged.
- **Medicine / alchemy.** *Podagra* = gout (here gout of the feet); *Calculus* = the stone (, *lithiasis*); *venae mesaraicae* = the mesaraic (mesenteric) veins; *tartarum* = tartar (Paracelsian morbid concretion); *dolores cholici* = colic pains; *Medicina Galenica* = Galenic medicine; *Salem Petrae / Sal Petrae* = saltpetre (here imagined generated in the body by sublimation). The *Spiritus Podagricus* ("gouty spirit") of "fixed" vs. "volatile" nature is Rothmann's own Paracelsian-iatrochemical coinage — kept literal and flagged, not modernised. *Oleum Vitrioli* = Oil of Vitriol (concentrated sulphuric acid); *Oleum Tartari* = Oil of Tartar (deliquesced potassium carbonate) — alchemical preparations Rothmann requests of Tycho, who ran a laboratory at Uraniborg.
- **Physician.** *Dn. Doct. Butterus, Medico Illustrissimi Principis nostri* = Doctor **Butterus** (Butter), physician to the Landgrave Wilhelm IV ("our Most Illustrious Prince").
- **Astronomy / cosmology.** The body is a point-by-point reply to Tycho's objections against the **threefold motion of the Earth** attributed to Copernicus (diurnal rotation, annual revolution, and the "third motion" of the axis — the conical motion Copernicus posited to keep the axis fixed in direction). Technical renderings by this chapter's convention: *motus diurnus / annuus* = diurnal / annual motion; *praecessio aequinoctiorum* = precession of the equinoxes; *obliquitas Zodiaci* = obliquity of the Zodiac (ecliptic); *libratio* (in *cursu Mercurij*) = libration (of Mercury's course); *orbis annuus* = the annual orb (Earth's orbit); *Stella tertiae Magnitudinis* = a star of the third magnitude. *axis … reflecti / reflexio* is Copernicus's term for the conical sweep of the axis — rendered "reflected / reflection" (Rothmann argues the apparent "reflection" is a derived effect, not a third real motion).
- **The falling-ball argument.** *globus plumbeus ex altissima turri demissus* = the leaden ball dropped from a high tower (the standard anti-rotation objection); Rothmann answers with the doctrine that the parts share the nature and motion of the whole (*partes retinent Naturam / motum totius*).
- **Measures.** *sesquicentum passus* = "a hundred and fifty paces" (one and a half hundred); *milliaria Germanica* = German miles. *secundum temporis scrupulum* = "a second of time" (the *scrupulum* being the sixtieth subdivision) — rendered "one second of time."
- ***Ubi ipsi contrarius*** — *An non et hoc, quod ea ratione Planetis duplex et Ubi ipsi contrarius inesset centri motus?* The clause is compressed; *Ubi* (the scholastic category "Where / place") is here used substantively, so "a twofold motion of the centre, and one contrary to it [in its place]." The exact construction is elliptical in the printed text; rendered closely and flagged.
- **Theology.** *Quo maior Rex, eo maius et amplius palatium decere putat suam Maiestatem. Quid cogitabis de DEO?* — the analogy that a greater King requires a greater palace, applied to God and the immensity of the heavens, is Rothmann's signature defence of a vast (Copernican) cosmos; kept as written.
- **The comet.** *Cometam eadem die, quâ tu, vidi* — Rothmann reports observing a comet the same day Tycho did, shown to the Landgrave, and encloses his observations. (The comet of early 1590; the reference is to the body Tycho had asked about.)
- **Source-text artifacts.** The source as extracted carries stray capital **"A"** characters fused to the end of certain words at edition line-breaks and at the very end of the letter (e.g. *fereA*, *mesaraicasA*, *nequeamA*, *fortassisA*, *eumA*, *possuntA*, *subducatA*, *insitumA*, *inepteA*, *esA*, *scrupuloA*, *NaturaeA*, *proferriA*, *esseA*, *imperiumA*, *MaiestatemA*, *immensitateA*, *semperA*, *ROTHMANNVS.A*). These are **apparatus/footnote anchor markers of the printed edition** (variant-note sigla), not part of Rothmann's Latin; they are reproduced verbatim in the Source block by this chapter's convention but carry no lexical value and are disregarded in the translation. The decorative dropped initial *[S]i* (see Ovid note) is the only place an editorial reading was adopted.
- **Negation check.** The dense conditional/negative argumentation was verified clause by clause: *fieri non posse* ("it cannot be"), *non dubium quin* ("no doubt that"), *nec … abijciunt* ("nor do they cast off"), *non abijcient* ("will not cast off"), *nemo non videt* ("no one fails to see" = everyone sees), *An non … pugnabit?* ("Will it not clash?"), *Nec axis … reuera reflectitur* ("Nor is the axis really reflected"), *nancisci nequeo* ("I cannot obtain"), *non dubito* ("I do not doubt"). Each negation in the source is reproduced; none added or dropped.
- **Calendar / place.** *Cassellis … 18. Aprilis, Anno 1590* = at **Kassel**, 18 April 1590. The Hesse-Kassel court used the **Julian calendar (Old Style)** at this date; so dated **[O.S.]**. The edition label ("1590. 18. april. Kassel") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy. *ex lecto meo* = "from my bed," consistent with the body's account of illness.

documents.abstract: Acknowledges receipt of three letters including the Apologia, promises a full reply via courier Curtius, and requests specimen models of the sextant and armillae.
documents.incipit: NOBILISS. Domine TYCHO et amice plurimum observande. Accepi binas abs te literas, eodem …

text.original:
NOBILISS. ET DOCTISS. D. TYCHONI BRAHE DANO, DOMINO URANIBURGI, DOMINO ET AMICO PLURIMUM OBSERVANDO.

NOBILISS. Domine TYCHO et amice plurimum observande. Accepi binas abs te literas, eodem tenore verborum, alteris adiuncta Apologia. Deinde die 24. Aprilis novo stylo accepi alias a studioso quodam Rostochiensi, scriptas abs te 25. Ianuarij. Ad eas omnes a me et a Domino CURTIO propediem accipies responsum plenissime, unâ cum Privilegio luculentiori, quae omnia noster tabellarius, quem ipsemet D. CURTIUS ad te ablegabit. Sic enim inter nos iam est constitutum. Haec brevibus per eundem studiosum, qui Rostochium revertitur, tibi significanda esse duxi.

B. V.
Datae
Pragae die 1. Maij novo stylo Anno 1590.
T. studiosiss.
THAD.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 244; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Si fieri posset, ut mihi modellam, ut vocant, seu exemplum tuorum instrumentorum observatoriorum (puta Sextantis et Armillarum; in Quadrante enim non erit ulla difficultas) ex charta conglutinata aut asserculis mitteres, ad quorum exemplum similia iustae magnitudinis mihi construi curarem, faceres mihi rem gratissimam, et posset ea noster tabellarius, qui ad te cum nostris literis veniet, mihi afferre. Non puto enim tibi deesse manuarios artifices, qui modellas illas construere possunt. Indicabis etiam mihi, quantae magnitudinis a me sint omnia illa construenda.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most learned Master Tycho Brahe the Dane, Lord of Uraniborg, his lord and friend much to be honoured.**

Most noble Master Tycho and friend much to be honoured. I have received two letters from you, in the same wording, with the Apologia enclosed with one of them. Then, on 24 April New Style, I received others from a certain student of Rostock, written by you on 25 January. To all of these you will shortly receive a most full reply from me and from Master Curtius, together with a more splendid Privilege — all of which our courier — whom Master Curtius himself will send to you — will bring. For so it has now been settled between us. These few things I thought ought to be made known to you by the same student, who is returning to Rostock.

Fare you well.
Given
at Prague, the 1st day of May New Style, in the year 1590.
Most devoted to you,
Thad[deus].


*[Postscript:]* If it could be done that you would send me a model, as they call it, or a specimen of your observatory instruments (the Sextant, say, and the Armillae; for in the case of the Quadrant there will be no difficulty), made of glued paper or of little boards, so that on their pattern I might have similar ones built for me of the proper size, you would do me a most welcome thing; and our courier, who will come to you with our letters, could bring them to me. For I do not suppose that you lack handicraftsmen who can construct those models. You will also indicate to me of what size all those things are to be built by me.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus Hagecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayek, 1525–1600), Bohemian physician, astronomer and personal physician to Emperor Rudolf II at Prague; Tycho's foremost correspondent in the Empire and the conduit through whom Tycho cultivated his standing at the imperial court. He signs himself only *THAD.* (an abbreviated forename).
- **Recipient / place.** *D. Tychoni Brahe Dano, Domino Uraniburgi* = "Master Tycho Brahe the Dane, Lord of **Uraniborg**" (Tycho's seat on the island of Hven; this chapter's convention). The dateline place *Pragae* = **Prague**.
- ***Curtius / D. Curtius / Domino Curtio*** — **Jacob Kurz von Senftenau** (Iacobus Curtius, d. 1594), **Imperial Vice-Chancellor** (*Imperii Vicecancellarius*) under Rudolf II, learned in letters and mathematics, who of his own accord procured, drafted and dispatched at his own expense the imperial printing privilege for Tycho. (His role is stated explicitly in a companion letter of the same correspondence: *"Iacobus enim Curtius, Imperii Vicecancellarius … hoc Caesaris privilegium mihi sponte propria procuravit, conscripsit, suisque sumptibus conducto tabellario transmisit."*) Here he is named both as co-author of the forthcoming reply and as the *tabellarius* (courier) who will convey it.
- ***Privilegio luculentiori*** — "a more splendid Privilege": the **imperial printing privilege**. Tycho had been dissatisfied with the first imperial privilege as too weak; Hagecius arranged a stronger one, dated **13 June 1590** and drafted by Vice-Chancellor Curtius, printed in the *Mechanica* (Norlind, *Tycho Brahe*, 1970). The comparative *luculentiori* ("more splendid / more substantial") is Hagecius's own hedge, signalling the improvement over the earlier grant; preserved, not flattened to a bare "privilege".
- ***Apologia*** — a defensive/explanatory tract by Tycho enclosed with one of the two letters; left in Latin as a title-word. Tycho repeatedly used *Apologia* for self-vindicating pieces (cf. the lost Danish Apologia and the apologetic prefatory matter of this period); the referent here is not further specified in the letter and is not pressed.
- ***eodem tenore verborum*** — "in the same wording": the two letters Hagecius received from Tycho were duplicates of one another (a common safeguard against loss in transit), not two distinct messages.
- ***studioso quodam Rostochiensi … qui Rostochium revertitur*** — "a certain student of **Rostock** … who is returning to Rostock": an unnamed student serving as carrier in both directions; the present note is sent back by his hand. Rostock was Tycho's old university town and a node in his northern correspondence relay.
- ***B. V.*** — *Bene Vale*, "Fare you well"; expanded silently in the source as the standard valediction.
- ***T. studiosiss.*** — *Tui studiosissimus*, "Most devoted to you" (this chapter's convention, on the model of *E. Tuae studiosiss.*).
- **Calendar.** The dateline reads *"die 1. Maij **novo stylo** Anno 1590"* — explicitly **New Style (Gregorian)**, consistent with the edition label (1 May 1590, Prague). As a correspondent in Catholic Imperial service, Hagecius writes N.S.. The two **in-letter** dates are reported as found and not converted: the receipt *"die 24. Aprilis novo stylo"* (24 April N.S.) is marked N.S. in the text; Tycho's own letter *"scriptas abs te 25. Ianuarij"* (written 25 January) carries no style marker — Tycho on Hven kept **Old Style** (Denmark retained the Julian calendar until 1700), so this date is presumably O.S. as written by Tycho, but the letter does not say so and the point is flagged rather than silently resolved.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (after the subscription "T. studiosiss. THAD."), restored from Dreyer VII, p. 244 (dropped by the working transcription) — Hájek's request for paper/board models of Tycho's sextant + armillae, which closes the cross-reference to the 1 Aug Tycho→Kurz reply. (Dreyer prints "medellam"; the incipit elsewhere "modellam".)
- **Correction.** Three Latin corruptions corrected per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII pp.243-244: 'D. CURTIUS' restored to 'quem ipsemet D. CURTIUS' (the dropped relative clause that distinguishes the courier from Curtius, who dispatches him); 'modestas illas' restored to 'modellas illas' (those instrument-models, not 'those modest ones'); and 'medellam' restored to 'modellam' (model, not remedy). English corrected to match at the first two places, where sense was genuinely affected; the third needed no English change since the translator had already rendered the intended sense despite the corrupted Latin.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter (address, body, date, and the restored postscript) against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.243-244, reading the page images directly. Found three places where the published the transcribed original departs from Dreyer's printed text, one of which (the dropped 'quem ipsemet') changes who is said to act as courier, and one of which (modestas/modellas) changes the sense actually delivered in the English.

**3 defects found:**
- **text error** (**high**). the transcribed original silently drops 'quem ipsemet' (whom... himself); Dreyer distinguishes an unnamed courier from Curtius, who sends him, whereas the published text and its translation collapse the two into one person, misidentifying Curtius as the courier who will personally deliver the documents. Dreyer prints: *quae omnia nofter tabellarius, quem ipfemet D. CURTIUS ad te ablegabit.*.
- **text error** (low). the transcribed original reads 'medellam' (remedy) where Dreyer prints 'modellam' (model); the translator evidently recognised the intended sense and rendered 'model' anyway, masking the corruption already present in the published the transcribed original. Dreyer prints: *modellam*.
- **text error** (medium). the transcribed original reads 'modestas illas' (those modest [ones]) where Dreyer prints 'modellas illas' (those models, referring back to the requested instrument-models); here the English follows the corrupted the transcribed original, so the sense delivered to the reader is genuinely altered. Dreyer prints: *manuarios artifices, qui modellas illas construere poffunt*.

**Repaired.** All three defects verified directly against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.243-244 page images (not the digitised text layer): 'quem ipfemet D. CURTIUS' (p.243), 'modellas illas' (p.244 l.11), and 'modellam' (p.244 l.6) all read exactly as the audit's Dreyer claim states. No other part of the letter was touched; every changed word is accounted for in outcomes above.
