documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Johannes Antonius Maginus Patavinus* = **Giovanni Antonio Magini** (1555–1617), the Paduan-born mathematician and astronomer who held the chair of mathematics at **Bologna** (from 1588, having beaten Galileo for the post). A prolific ephemerides-maker and cartographer; the *Patavinus* ("of Padua") marks his birthplace, not his then-residence.
- **Edition of record.** The letter survives because **Tycho himself printed it** in his *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica* (1598), under a chancery-style Latin rubric (*DESCRIPTUM LITERARUM … = "A copy of a letter …"*); reprinted by Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VII. No manuscript witness is recorded in the edition.
- ***studioso quodam Dano … domesticus*** — "a certain Danish student … a member of your household": an unnamed former Uraniborg famulus then in Italy who served as Magini's intermediary, carrying both the *Mechanica*-precursor gift-book to Magini and Werner's volume back toward Tycho. Identity not given in the letter; left unidentified rather than guessed.
- ***librum tuum eruditissimum*** — "your most learned book": the work Tycho had sent. Most plausibly the *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (1588, the comet book), to which Magini refers again below as *primum tuum de mundi Aetherei phaenomenis librum*; not named outright here, so rendered generically.
- ***nuper a me elucubratum Opus*** — "a Work lately worked out by me": Magini's forthcoming volume, almost certainly his *Novae coelestium orbium theoricae* (Venice, 1589), the planetary-theory work he describes lecturing on below.
- **Astronomy — technical terms** (editorial glossary): *compendiosam descriptionem stellarum fixarum* → "a compendious description of the fixed stars" (Tycho's emended star catalogue); *Ephaemerides* → **Ephemerides**; *Eccentricitates Planetarum* → "eccentricities of the planets"; *commensurationum … orbis* → "proportions of the orb"; *aequatio Eccentricitatis* → "equation of the eccentricity" (*aequatio* in the astronomical sense by this chapter's convention); *tabulae Prutenicae* → **Prutenic Tables** (Reinhold's 1551 Copernican tables); *resolutae tabulae* → "resolved tables."
- **The Mars eccentricity figures.** Magini cites Copernicus's Mars eccentricity as *partium 5.51'.30''* and Ptolemy's as *partium 6* — rendered **5°51′30″** and **6 degrees**. The figures are reproduced exactly as printed; *partium* ("of parts/degrees") is the period idiom for degrees. This is the crux of Magini's "heresy": that the Martian eccentricity is *not* constant but varies with its own period, so that one table cannot serve both maximum and minimum — the very problem Kepler would later resolve. Magini's claim is preserved as his own hedged conjecture (*in eâ sum haeresi, ut putem* = "I am of this heresy, that I think"); no silent sharpening. **[maximum] — editorial insertion (flagged).** In the clause *Martis aequationes supputatae ad Eccentricitatem a Copernico observatam partium 5.51'.30''* the Latin says only "the eccentricity observed by Copernicus," not *maximam*; *maxima* appears earlier in the letter (*si tabula efficiatur pro maxima Eccentricitate*) but not here. Magini's argument — that one table fitted to the maximum value cannot serve the minimum — implies that the 5°51′30″ figure he attributes to Copernicus functions as the maximum, so "[maximum]" is a defensible reading; but because the word is not in this clause it is bracketed as an editorial insertion rather than presented as translation.
- ***Systema Universi a te excogitatum*** — "the System of the Universe devised by you": Tycho's **geo-heliocentric (Tychonic) system**. Magini approves it but objects to the intersection of the orbs of the Sun and Mars — *cuperem Solis Orbem ac Martis nequaquam sese intersecare* ("I could wish the Orb of the Sun and of Mars by no means cut across each other"). This is a real point of resistance: solid celestial orbs cannot interpenetrate, yet the Tychonic geometry forces the Mars-orb to cross the Sun's.
- ***Martem acronycum*** — "acronychal Mars," i.e. Mars at **opposition** (rising as the Sun sets; Greek *akrónychos*, "at nightfall"). The observation that Mars at opposition comes nearer the earth than the Sun is precisely what compels the orb-intersection Magini dislikes; rendered "Mars at opposition [acronychal Mars]" to keep the technical term and gloss it.
- ***Cometa anno 1577*** — the **Great Comet of 1577**, the subject of Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis*; Tycho's parallax work on it placed it above the Moon, the same supralunary result that bears on the orb question.
- ***Verneri librum de motu octavae Sphaerae*** — **Johannes Werner's** *De motu octavae sphaerae* (Nuremberg, 1522), on the motion of the eighth (fixed-star) sphere — trepidation theory. The literature (Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*) confirms Tycho's avid, frustrated pursuit of this rare book; Magini's gift of a copy via the Danish student is the concrete favour returned for the *Mechanica*-precursor.
- ***Coelestium Orbium hypotheses / theoricae*** — Magini's own planetary "hypotheses of the Celestial Orbs" (the *Novae coelestium orbium theoricae*), which he says he will expound publicly this year with geometrical demonstrations.
- ***saepe dictus studiosus*** — "the often-mentioned student": *saepe dictus* is a fixed idiom ("the oft-mentioned / aforesaid"), referring to the Danish intermediary already named repeatedly in the letter (*studioso quodam Dano … eodem studioso … studioso isto*). The adverb *saepe* qualifies *dictus* (the student has been "often mentioned"), not the main verb *significavit*; rendered "the often-mentioned student signified to me," not "the student often signified to me."
- **Latin idiom.** *in eâ sum haeresi* — literally "I am in that heresy/school of thought"; the word *haeresis* here carries its neutral Greek sense ("a chosen tenet, sect-opinion"), with a self-deprecating wink, not the theological charge — rendered "I am of this heresy" to keep the flavour. *ne latum quidem unguem deflexi* — "I have not deviated even a finger's breadth," a Ciceronian idiom (*latum unguem*, "a nail's breadth"), kept literal. *lucubrationes tuas* — "your lucubrations" (works composed by lamplight; scholarly labours), kept as the period term.
- **Epistolary formulae**. Opening *ILLUSTRIS VIR* → "Illustrious Sir"; subscription *Illustri dominationi tuae Addictissimus* → "Most devoted to Your Illustrious Lordship" (*dominatio tua*, "Your Lordship," the courteous Italian-chancery form).
- **Calendar / dateline crux.** *Bononiae Idib. Septemb. 1590* = "At Bologna, on the Ides of September, 1590." Magini, in Catholic Italy, wrote on the **Gregorian (New Style)** calendar, ten days ahead of the Julian reckoning Tycho kept on Hven; the Roman idiom is kept and glossed, and *not* converted to Tycho's Old-Style equivalent (which would be 3 September O.S.). Per this chapter's convention the style is flagged, the date not "corrected." **Label-vs-dateline discrepancy (flagged, not reconciled):** the edition label catalogues the letter "1590. 11. september n.s.," **two days earlier than the dateline the text itself bears** (the Ides = 13 September). Per this chapter's convention the header therefore leads with the as-written date — 13 September [N.S.] — and appends the catalogued date (11 September); nothing in the source substantiates the 11th, which may reflect a separate cataloguing tradition or a slip. The discrepancy is recorded here and not silently resolved.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD GELLIUM SASCERIDEM.

... Quod librum meum IO. ANTONIUS MAGINUS perlegerit, eumque sibi et alijs eruditis eiusdem professionis viris placuisse testatus sit, grata mente accipio. Pollicitationem autem nostram emendandorum motuum perturbasse illum, equidem non miror, ex quo tam ipse, quam nonnulli alij, hactenus tot tantosque labores (ubi nemo illo maiores, excepto COPERNICO et Reinholdino fundamento, quod tamen multimode locupletavit) in calculandis Tabulis coelestium motuum et Ephemeridibus, exantlârunt; cum nihilominus coelum ipsum non modo in minutijs, sed etiam in gradibus aliquot deviationem a Tabulis saepenumero ostendat. Hac in Sole quidem ipso caeterorum Planetarum chorago, circa Aequinoctium vernum, paulo plus dimidio gradu anticipando aberrant; ut nihil nunc dicam de caeteris Planetis, in quorum nullo non admodum evidens Coeli et Tabularum disconvenientia invenitur, ut suo tempore ex Observationum mearum acervo ob oculos ponam. Quid in aethereorum corporum Revolutionibus, quo ad numerorum denotationem ipsi coelo correspondentem, favente ipso coelestium Opifice, praestiterim, perspiciet doctissimus ille vir, quando opus nostrum Astronomiae instaurationis, quod multo iam tempore molimur, publici iuris factum fuerit. Illic etiam in secunda videlicet eius voluminis parte, Planetarum quinque gyrationes, cum eorum trium qui Solem ambientes Terram simul includunt, tum etiam reliquorum duorum, qui circa eumdem revoluti hanc non includunt, quo ad omnes singulorum proportiones, et particulares etiam inaequalitatum apparentium excusationes atque demonstrationes, luculenter cognoscet; et unâ circa Eccentricitates atque Apogaea, prout communiter appellantur (quae tamen ego secundum propriam Hypothesin aliter ordino atque tueor) unâ cum Orbium omnium symmetria atque commensuratione, voti compos reddetur. Sed ipse in suis recentioribus Theoricis, quas numeris Coperniceis rectius et competentius, quam antea in tabulis a se editis Astronomicis, applicuit, dum realitatem et soliditatem ipsorum Orbium, Aristotelea et veterum quorumdam imitatione, approbat (quae tamen revera nulla est) id pluribus conatur exequi, quod alias paucioribus requisitis possit praestari. Quin et alia quaedam inaequalitatis particularis insinuatio, quo ad quinque errantium siderum apparentias, adhuc in occulto subest, quam nec veteres Ptolemaicae, nec recentiores Coperniceae quocumque modo usurpatae excusant Hypotheses. Hanc tamen non minus quam caeteras (quae ab Epicyclis vel motu annuo Terrae cum commixtis Eccentricis et Aequantibus proveniunt) favente Numine, nostrae concinniore, uti spero, ratiocinatione expedient Hypotheses. Quantum ad obliquitatis Ecclipticae (de qua etiam certior fieri avet) mutationem attinet, ego eam hisce temporibus esse partium 23. M. 31½ exacte, pluribus et maximis, ijsdemque affabre e solido metallo elaboratis Instrumentis aliquot annorum reiteratis Observationibus, sedulo adinveni, nec sensibiliter minorem hactenus umquam fuisse existimo. Nam quod COPERNICUS et quidam eius Synchroni eam 3½ scrupulis angustiorem reddiderunt, id evenit, quod Refractionem ☉lis circa Brumale Solstitium, non uti oportuit, praecaverint; ut de Instrumentorum, quibus confisi sunt, in tam subtili rimatione, insufsicientia nihil dicam. Quin neque Poli altitudinem ex Sole per utrumque Solstitium, eandem ob causam, rite scrutati sunt; adeo ut cum ipsemet Fruenburgi, in loco habitationis Coperniceae, per proprium Instrumentum periculum de altitudine Polari accurate (uti scis) fieri curassem, deprehensum sit, ipsum 3¼ Minutis eamdem iusto minorem consignasse; quod non parum illi erroris in Apogaeo et Eccentricitate Solari, unâ cum toto eius curriculo competenter denotando invexit, coincidentibus et alijs quibusdam deviationum occasionibus, quas alibi a me reseratas nunc praetereo. An autem summa Eclipticae obliquitas in posterum aliquatenus accrescet vel coarctabitur, non adeo promptum est decernere. Nec enim Hypothesis Copernicea (utut admodum ingeniosa) circa Aequinoctium et huius obliquitatis mutationem, locum meretur. Verisimilius tamen duco, hanc Eclipticae ab Aequatore digressionem, subsequentibus saeculis paululum dilatatum iri. Quemadmodum Eccentricitatem Solis nunc etiam pedetentim augeri, non autem circa citimum decrementum, ut fert Copernicea ratiocinatio, versari, haud dubijs inditijs compertum habeo. Nec adeo mirum est, COPERNICUM hac in parte deceptum fuisse, cum ipsam quoque sui temporis Solis Eccentricitatem, unâ cum Apogaeo, minus dextre scrutatus sit, ob causas alio loco (ut dixi) a me manifestatas. Est enim circa haec tempora Eccentricitas Solis vera et indubia part. 2. Min. 9, de 60 totius Semidiametri Eccentrici 13 proxime scrupulis maior COPERNICI opinione; et Apogaeum versatur hoc anno paulo post medietatem sexti gradus ♋ ipsius numeratione 3½ Gradibus anterius (velut etiam in reliquorum Planetarum Apogaeis disponendis non paucis gradibus ab eo peccatum est, ut Eccentricitates horum nunc praeteream) quemadmodum idipsum exquisitis observationibus et certis demonstrationibus a me esse adinventum, ipsemet satis perspectum habes; prout etiam caput primum anterioris nostri Tomi recentiorum Coeli Phaenomenωn, haec et alia ad Solaris cursus accuratam restitutionem facientia, affatim patefacit atque demonstrat. Illic brevi MAGINUS ea quae in Solaris tramitis restitutione hactenus desiderantur extricata reperiet, quibus etiam postmodum in suarum Ephemeridum recognitione tuto, absque iniuria coelestium apparentiarum, uti poterit. De declinatione Zodiaci maxima, an unquam maior fuerit, quam a PTOLEMÆO et eius aliquot antecessoribus assignata est, etsi nonnihil certis de causis ambigam, malo tamen eorum denotationi acquiescere, nec sensibiliter maiorem antea fuisse statuere. An tamen in ipsis Minutijs illorum observatio rite constet, tam Instrumentorum, quibus usi sunt, in minimis animadversionibus fallacia, quam Parallaxeos atque refractionis Solaris neglectus, me non parum ancipitem reddunt. Affixarum Stellarum iuxta nostras diuturnas et sedulas observationes restitutarum Catalogum, quem unâ expetit MAGINUS, ex secundo capite eiusdem primi libri obtinebit. Illic enim circiter 500 Stellae in ipso minuto, et quo ad latitudinem et longitudinem proprijs Instrumentis desuper acceptae rectificantur, praemissa fundamentali restitutionis earumdem ratione ac Geometrica demonstratione. Consultius itaque erit, ut suarum Ephemeridum ad praelum revocationem eousque differat, donec hunc nostrum primum tomum nactus fuerit, quod spero instanti aestate futurum. Est enim iam ad finem Typographico labore ferme perductus, deficiente saltem decimo et ultimo capite, idque ob papyri impressoriae penuriam, quam tamen sufficienti copia brevi me habiturum arbitror, ex propria mea, quam in hac insula eius conficiendae gratia magnis impensis iam nuper construi curavi, moletrina, quae iam prorsus parata Chartopaeum idoneum, pro quo conquirendo meum in Germaniam amandavi Typographum, solummodo expectat. Rationem Trianguli non rectanguli, ex cognitis duobus lateribus cum angulo comprehenso, reliqua absque perpendiculari compendiosius quam communiter sit, venandi, ex quarto meo Dogmate Triangulorum planorum illi aperire poteris, uti ei satisfiat. Nec mihi displicet, quod illi Dogmatis sexti et noni Compendiorum nostrorum operationem patefeceris; siquidem, uti video, demonstrationes horum et similium ab alijs, qui se alienis ornant plumis, nunc divulgentur. Res enim ita se habet, prout refers, quod Plagiarius iste Ursinus (qui etiam mearum hypothesium inventionem pro sua inverecunde publicavit, utut eam fundamentaliter non intelligat, quod satis liquet ex Martis orbe falso ab eo ordinato, ut de caeteris nunc taceam) eas, quas pro suis venditavit, Triangulorum demonstrationes et compendiosas in numeros resolutiones, apud IUSTUM BYRGIUM Landgravianum Automatopaeum, qui eas a WITICHIO impetravit, nactus sit. Cum WITICHIO autem, quando hîc ante tuum ad me adventum aliquandiu commoratus est, de his et alijs ad rem Mathematicam facilius excolendam, liberaliter contuleram, qui hinc discedens postea apud Illustrissimum Principem Landgravium Hassiae pleraque eorum unâ cum quorundam Instrumentorum ex meis concinna fabrica, propalavit, quae nunc alij perfrictae frontis homines pro suis inventionibus sibi vendicare non erubescunt, adeo ut nulla fere ad primos inventores redundet gratia. Verumenimvero quaecumque de Triangulorum tam planorum quam sphaericorum, quatenus ad rem Astronomicam extruendam stabiliendamque conducunt, compendiosa tractatione hactenus comperta habeo, ea omnia in primam partem Astronomiae redintegrandae, tam secundum demonstrationes Geometricas, quam numerorum praxim, sufficienter digeram. Illinc MAGINUS atque alij varias easdemque faciles et abbreviatas Triangulorum explanandorum et in numeros resolvendorum inventiones percipient. Quae hactenus dicta sunt Clarissimi et doctissimi MAGINI ad te perscriptam Epistolam eiusque in ea ad me directas petitiones spectantia, poteris ad ipsum prima quaque occasione, responsionis loco per literas referre, aut etiam, si lubet, hanc Epistolae partem descriptam transmittere. Si ipsemet ad me aliquid literarum dederit, aut lucubrationum suarum miserit, ulterius cum illo lubens conferam, et de pluribus, sicubi opus fuerit, commonefaciam, atque ipsius desiderijs non gravatim obviabo ...
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO GELLIUS SASCERIDES.**

… That Giovanni Antonio Magini has read my book through, and has testified that it pleased him and other learned men of the same profession, I receive with a grateful mind. That my promise to amend the [planetary] motions has unsettled him, for my part I do not wonder, since both he himself and several others have hitherto drained off so many and so great labours (in which no one [accomplished] more than he, save Copernicus and the Reinholdian foundation, which he nonetheless enriched in manifold ways) in computing Tables of the celestial motions and Ephemerides — and yet the heaven itself often shows a deviation from the Tables not only in minutes but even in several degrees. In the Sun itself, indeed — the choragus [leader of the dance] of the other planets — they err about the vernal equinox by anticipating [running ahead] a little more than half a degree; to say nothing now of the other planets, in none of which is there not found a very evident disagreement of Heaven and the Tables, as in due time I shall set before [men's] eyes from the heap of my observations. What I have achieved, by the favour of the celestial Maker himself, in the Revolutions of the ethereal bodies — as regards a numerical reckoning corresponding to the heaven itself — that most learned man will discern when our work of the *restoration of astronomy* [*Astronomiae instauratio*], which we have long been labouring at, shall have been made public. There too, namely in the second part of that volume, he will clearly come to know the gyrations of the five planets — both of those three which, encircling the Sun, at the same time enclose the Earth, and of the remaining two which, revolved about the same [Sun], do not enclose it — as to all the proportions of each, and the particular accountings and demonstrations also of the apparent inequalities; and, together with the symmetry and commensuration of all the orbs, he will, in one [exposition], regarding the eccentricities and apogees as they are commonly called (which, however, I arrange and maintain otherwise, according to my own hypothesis), be granted his wish. But he himself, in his more recent *Theorics*, which he has fitted to the Copernican numbers more rightly and aptly than before in the astronomical tables he had published, while he approves — in imitation of Aristotle and certain of the ancients — the reality and solidity of the orbs themselves (which in truth is none), attempts to carry out with more [machinery] what could otherwise be accomplished with fewer requisites. Moreover, a certain other intimation of particular inequality, as regards the appearances of the five wandering stars, still lies hidden in concealment, which neither the old Ptolemaic nor the more recent Copernican hypotheses, employed in any manner whatever, account for. Yet this one, no less than the others (which arise from epicycles, or from the annual motion of the Earth combined with eccentrics and equants), our hypotheses will, by the favour of the Deity, dispatch by a neater reasoning, as I hope. As regards the change of the obliquity of the ecliptic (about which too he is eager to be made more certain), I have for my part found out diligently — by repeated observations of several years, with many and very large instruments, skilfully wrought of solid metal — that in these times it is exactly 23 [degrees], 31½ minutes, and I judge that it has never hitherto been perceptibly smaller. For as to the fact that Copernicus and certain of his contemporaries made it narrower by 3½ scruples [minutes], that came about because they did not, as they ought, guard against the refraction of the ☉ Sun about the winter solstice; to say nothing of the insufficiency of the instruments they relied on in so subtle a probing. Nor, for the same reason, did they duly investigate the altitude of the Pole from the Sun through both solstices; so that, when I myself had had a careful trial of the polar altitude made at Frauenburg, in the place of Copernicus's dwelling, by my own instrument (as you know), it was discovered that he had set the same down 3¼ minutes smaller than is right — which brought upon him no small error in determining the [solar] apogee and the solar eccentricity, together with its whole course, properly, other occasions of deviation coinciding too, which, disclosed by me elsewhere, I now pass over. But whether the maximum obliquity of the ecliptic will in time hereafter increase or be contracted to some extent, is not so easy to decide. For the Copernican hypothesis (however highly ingenious) concerning the equinox and the change of this obliquity does not deserve [its] place. Yet I judge it more probable that this departure of the ecliptic from the equator will, in succeeding centuries, be widened a little. Just as I hold it ascertained by no doubtful tokens that the eccentricity of the Sun is now likewise being gradually increased, and is not engaged about a nearest decrement, as the Copernican reasoning would have it. Nor is it so much to be wondered at that Copernicus was deceived in this part, since he also investigated less skilfully the eccentricity of the Sun of his own time, together with the apogee, for the reasons disclosed by me (as I said) in another place. For about these times the true and undoubted eccentricity of the Sun is 2 parts, 9 minutes — of the 60 of the whole semidiameter of the eccentric — about 13 scruples greater than Copernicus's opinion; and the apogee this year stands a little past the middle of the sixth degree of ♋ Cancer, 3½ degrees earlier than his reckoning (just as in disposing the apogees of the other planets too he erred from [the truth] by not a few degrees, to pass over for now the eccentricities of these) — exactly as you yourself have well enough perceived that this very thing was found out by me through exquisite observations and sure demonstrations; just as the first chapter of the earlier Tome of our recent *Phenomena of the Heaven* [*Coeli Phaenomena*] also abundantly sets forth and demonstrates these and other matters bearing on the accurate restoration of the Sun's course. There Magini will shortly find disentangled those things which have hitherto been wanting in the restoration of the solar track, which afterwards he will be able to use safely, without injury to the celestial appearances, in the revision of his Ephemerides. As to the maximum declination of the zodiac — whether it was ever greater than was assigned by Ptolemy and several of his predecessors — although for certain reasons I am somewhat in doubt, I yet prefer to acquiesce in their determination, and to hold that it was not perceptibly greater before. Whether, however, their observation rightly holds good in the very minutes [of arc], both the fallibility of the instruments they used in the smallest discernments, and their neglect of parallax and of solar refraction, render me not a little of two minds. The Catalogue of the fixed stars, restored according to our long and diligent observations — which Magini desires together [with the rest] — he will obtain from the second chapter of the same first book. For there about 500 stars, taken from above with proper instruments as to both latitude and longitude, are rectified to the very minute, the fundamental method of their restoration and the geometrical demonstration being set out beforehand. It will therefore be more advisable that he defer the recalling of his Ephemerides to the press until he shall have obtained this first tome of ours, which I hope will be in the coming summer. For it has now been almost carried through to its end by the labour of the press, only the tenth and last chapter being wanting, and that on account of a scarcity of printing-paper — which, however, I think I shall shortly have in sufficient supply from my own paper-mill, which I lately had built at great expense on this island for the making of it, and which, now wholly ready, awaits only a suitable papermaker, to procure whom I have sent off my printer into Germany. The method of hunting out, for a non-right-angled triangle, from two known sides with the included angle, the remaining [parts] without [dropping] a perpendicular, more concisely than is commonly done, you will be able to disclose to him from my fourth Theorem of plane triangles, so that he may be satisfied. Nor does it displease me that you have disclosed to him the working of the sixth and ninth Theorems of our Compendia; since, as I see, the demonstrations of these and the like are now being divulged by others, who deck themselves in another's feathers. For the matter stands thus, just as you report — that that plagiarist Ursinus (who has also shamelessly published the invention of my hypotheses as his own, although he does not fundamentally understand it, which is clear enough from the orb of Mars falsely arranged by him, to say nothing now of the rest) obtained those demonstrations of triangles, and concise resolutions into numbers, which he peddled as his own, from Justus Byrgius [Jost Bürgi], the Landgrave's automaton-maker [clockmaker], who got them from Wittich. Now with Wittich, when he stayed here for some while before your coming to me, I had liberally conferred about these and other matters tending to the easier cultivation of the mathematical art; and he, departing hence, afterwards made most of them public at the court of the Most Illustrious Prince, the Landgrave of Hesse, together with the neat construction of certain instruments [taken] from mine — which now other men of brazen brow [shameless men] do not blush to claim for themselves as their own inventions, so that scarcely any thanks redound to the first discoverers. But truly, whatever I have hitherto found out, by concise treatment, concerning triangles both plane and spherical — in so far as they conduce to building up and establishing the science of astronomy — all of it I shall set out sufficiently in the first part of [my] *Astronomy Restored*, both according to geometrical demonstrations and to the practice of numbers. Thence Magini and others will gather various, and those easy and abbreviated, methods of explaining triangles and resolving them into numbers. The things that have been said thus far, bearing on the letter written out to you by the most renowned and learned Magini and his requests directed in it to me, you will be able to relate back to him by letter at the very first occasion, in the place of a reply; or also, if you please, to transmit this part of the letter copied out. If he himself shall have sent me any letter, or any of his lucubrations [scholarly works], I shall gladly confer with him further, and shall advise him about more matters wherever there shall be need, and shall not grudgingly meet his desires …

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** **Tycho Brahe** writing from Uraniborg (no place is named in the excerpt) to **Gellius Sascerides** (Gellius Sascerides / Gjellis Saksesen, 1562–1612), the Danish physician-astronomer who had studied on Hven, travelled to Italy in 1589–90, and acted there as Tycho's intermediary with the Italian astronomical community — chiefly **Giovanni Antonio Magini** of Bologna. (His later betrothal to Tycho's daughter Magdalene and its collapse is the famous "Gellius affair," not at issue here.)
- **Excerpt status.** The text opens and closes with ellipses (*…*) in the edition: this is an extract, not the whole letter. No salutation, dateline, or subscription is transmitted in this portion.
- **Person identifications (first occurrence).** *Io. Antonius Maginus* = **Giovanni Antonio Magini** (1555–1617), professor of mathematics at Bologna, author of widely-used planetary tables and ephemerides; *Copernicus* = Nicolaus Copernicus; *Reinholdino fundamento* = the work of **Erasmus Reinhold**, i.e. the *Prutenic Tables* (1551), the Copernican-numbered tables on which Magini's own were founded; *Ptolemaeus* = Ptolemy; *Ursinus / Plagiarius iste Ursinus* = **Nicolaus Reimers Ursus** (Nicolai Reimers Bär, "Ursus," d. 1600), the Dithmarschen autodidact and imperial mathematician whom Tycho accused of stealing his geoheliocentric world-system (the priority dispute that runs through the late letters); *Witichio* = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586) of Wrocław, who visited Hven in 1580 and later Kassel; *Iustus Byrgius Landgravianus Automatopaeus* = **Jost Bürgi** (1552–1632), the Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel's celebrated clockmaker and instrument-/mechanism-maker; *Illustrissimus Princeps Landgravius Hassiae* = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel**.
- **Place identifications.** *Fruenburgi* = **Frauenburg** (Frombork, Ermland/Warmia), Copernicus's residence, where Tycho had a measurement of the polar altitude taken (referring to the 1584 mission of his assistant Elias Olsen Morsing); *hac insula* = the island of **Hven**; *in Germaniam* = Germany.
- **The world-system passage.** *Planetarum quinque … trium qui Solem ambientes Terram simul includunt … reliquorum duorum, qui circa eumdem revoluti hanc non includunt* — a precise statement of Tycho's geoheliocentric model: the three superior planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars), whose solar orbits enclose the Earth, and the two inferior (Venus, Mercury), whose solar orbits do not. *Hypothesis* / *Hypotheses* kept (rendered "hypothesis/hypotheses"); Tycho's emphatic *secundum propriam Hypothesin* underlies the priority claim against Ursus. *realitatem et soliditatem ipsorum Orbium … quae tamen revera nulla est* — Tycho's rejection of solid celestial orbs (the comet-derived doctrine), set against Magini's Aristotelian retention of them; the hedge "in truth is none" is Tycho's and is preserved.
- **Technical terms (editorial glossary).** *motus* → motion; *Tabulae / Ephemerides* → Tables / Ephemerides; *Revolutiones* → Revolutions; *Eccentricitas / Eccentricus* → eccentricity / eccentric; *Apogaeum* → apogee; *Aequans* → equant; *Epicyclus* → epicycle; *Orbis / Sphaera* → orb / sphere; *Aequinoctium vernum* → vernal equinox; *Brumale Solstitium* → winter solstice; *Parallaxis* → parallax; *Refractio* → refraction; *obliquitas Eclipticae* / *declinatio Zodiaci maxima* → obliquity of the ecliptic / maximum declination of the zodiac; *Poli altitudo* → altitude of the pole; *restitutio / instauratio Astronomiae* → restoration / renewal of astronomy. *Astronomiae instaurationis opus* / *Astronomiae redintegrandae* refer to Tycho's projected magnum opus (the *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata*, then in press on Hven, which the letter describes as nearly finished but lacking its tenth chapter for want of paper).
- **Greek.** One Greek-derived term, *Phaenomenωn*, is printed with a Greek omega (ω) for the genitive ending in the edition — i.e. *Coeli Phaenomenōn*, "of the Phenomena of the Heaven"; the printed mixed-script form is retained in the Source block. *Chorago* (*choragus*, χορηγός) "leader of the chorus/dance," used metaphorically of the Sun as ruler of the planetary dance, is glossed in brackets.
- **Symbols.** *☉lis* = a contraction of *Solis* (genitive of *Sol*) using the Sun glyph ☉ + the ending *-lis*; rendered "of the ☉ Sun," glyph kept in the Source block. *♋* = the sign Cancer (named "Cancer," glyph kept), by this chapter's convention
- **Numerical values (verbatim, not modernised).** Obliquity given as *partium 23. M. 31½* = "23 [degrees], 31½ minutes"; Copernicus's value *3½ scrupulis angustiorem* = "narrower by 3½ scruples [minutes of arc]" (*scrupulum* = minute of arc here); Frauenburg polar-altitude error *3¼ Minutis … iusto minorem*; solar eccentricity *part. 2. Min. 9, de 60 totius Semidiametri Eccentrici* = "2 parts 9 minutes, of the 60 of the whole semidiameter of the eccentric" (i.e. eccentricity expressed in sixtieths of the eccentric's radius), *13 proxime scrupulis maior Copernici opinione*; apogee *paulo post medietatem sexti gradus ♋ … 3½ Gradibus anterius*. These figures are reproduced exactly; no recomputation or correction is offered.
- **The plagiarism transmission-chain.** Tycho's account: his triangle-theorems and *prosthaphaeresis*-style "concise resolutions into numbers" (compendious computational devices) passed Hven → Wittich → Bürgi at Kassel → Ursus, who published them (and Tycho's world-system) as his own. *qui se alienis ornant plumis* ("who deck themselves in another's feathers") and *perfrictae frontis homines* ("men of brazen brow") are Tycho's invective and are kept as such. The literature (Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*; Thoren, *Lord of Uraniborg*) corroborates this transmission and the Wittich/Bürgi link, and records that Ursus, when accused, named Wittich and Bürgi as his source. Tycho's *Dogmata* (*Dogma quartum / sextum / nonum*) of plane triangles are rendered "Theorem(s)"; *Compendia* "Compendia."
- **Negation check.** The passage turns on several load-bearing negatives, reproduced one-for-one: *non miror* ("I do not wonder"); *non modo … sed etiam* ("not only … but even"); *in quorum nullo non … invenitur* (double negative, "in none of which is there not found" = in every one there is found); *quae tamen revera nulla est* ("which in truth is none"); *non autem circa citimum decrementum* ("and is not engaged about a nearest decrement"); *non erubescunt* ("do not blush"); *non gravatim* ("not grudgingly"). The double negative *nullo non* is intentional litotes and is kept as such rather than flattened.
- **Calendar / dating.** No dateline survives in the excerpt. The catalogue date is **1 October 1590** (label *"1590 1. oktober"*; Dreyer dates it October 1590, O.S.). Because the source text carries no dateline of its own, the header gives the catalogued date marked "[O.S., catalogued]" rather than asserting an as-written date the text does not substantiate. The witness is a **copy** Gellius Sascerides incorporated into his own letter to Magini of **1 February 1591** (Bologna, Archivio Malvezzi de' Medici) — consistent with an autumn-1590 original that Gellius forwarded onward, as the closing instruction ("transmit this part of the letter copied out") anticipates. Denmark used Old Style throughout; Magini in Bologna used New Style — a gap relevant to the courier chronology but not to any in-text date here.
- **Correction.** 'Plagiarius iste Ursinus' (Dreyer, TBOO VII p.281): the epithet 'Ursinus' restored in the English (was flattened to the bare name 'Ursus'), preserving Tycho's derisive pun on Ursus's bear-name.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Read the full letter's Dreyer page images visually. Checked the opening and closing lines and every proper name, number, date and sum: obliquity 23 deg 31.5 min, Copernicus's error 3.5 scrupuli and 3.25 minutes at Frauenburg, solar eccentricity 2 part. 9 min. of 60 (13 scrupuli greater than Copernicus), apogee 3.5 degrees, c. 500 stars, triangle theorems 4/6/9, and the names Magini, Reinhold, Byrgius/Bürgi, Witichio/Wittich all confirmed exact against the page images. Only defect found is the low-severity Ursinus/Ursus epithet softening noted above; nothing rises to fabrication, omission, or a sense-changing mistranslation.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (low). Dreyer prints the adjectival epithet 'Ursinus' (a derisive pun on Nicolaus Reimers Bär/Ursus's bear-name), which the English flattens into the bare proper name 'Ursus' — the correct historical referent is preserved but the wordplay/exact printed form is not. At: “that plagiarist Ursus”.

**Repaired.** Verified directly against the Dreyer page images for this letter (TBOO VII pp.278-281, read as page images, not the digitised text layer): p.281 confirms 'Plagiarius ifte Urfinus' exactly as the audit cites. Only this clause was touched; the Latin was already correct ('Ursinus'), so only the English required correction. No other cruces surfaced on the pages read.

documents.incipit: AVENIT iam nuper huc in Daniam ad me T. Celsit. Mathematicus CHRISTOPHORVS ROTHMANNVS, …

text.original:
ILLVSTRISSIMO PRINCIPI AC DOMINO, DOMINO WILHELMO, LANDGRAVIO HASSIÆ, COMITI IN CATZENELLEBOGEN, DIETZ, ZIEGENHAIN ET NIDDA: PRINCIPI AC DOMINO CLEMENTISSIMO. S. D.

AVENIT iam nuper huc in Daniam ad me T. Celsit. Mathematicus CHRISTOPHORVS ROTHMANNVS, Princeps Illustrissime, tuæque Celsit. literas attulit, quibus adeo diutinam in scribendo ad me intermissionem tum ob curarum molem, tum etiam Mathematici aduersam valetudinem, benigne exponit. Quod vero studium Mathematicum T. Celsit. ob tot tantaque administrationis publicæ, senij etiam successiue obrepentis impedimenta, non prorsus repudiet, sed quantum per ocium licuerit, etiamnum continuet, mihi quam iucundum auditu est. Attamen, quod pari alacritate, quâ antea, priora inuena nunc recognoscere, tractareque vix promtum sit, mirum esse non debet; cum anni, curæ et morbi, vna cum corporeæ sanitatis molestatione, ipsum quoque animum atque ingenij vires, potiorem nostrî partem, non parum aggrauent atque obnubilent. Verum enimuero quicquid in hoc genere T. Celsit. propriâ operâ adeo sufficienter atque copiose, vt prius, ob causas antedictas, in posterum præstare vix suffecerit, id per alios idoneos artifices sua autoritate atque hortatu, tum etiam sumtibus et liberalitate, compensare facile sustinebit.

Intelligo ROTHMANNVM valetudinis causâ aërem mutasse, quod licet T. Celsit. atque alijs minus tutum atque consultum ab initio videbatur, tamen quantum ex ipsiusmet relatione cognosco, illi non infeliciter cessit. Nam statim ab itineris ingressu successiue vires recuperauit, et interea dum hîc moraretur, non admodum infirmo vsus est habitu. Quamuis resolutiones et coagulationes istæ Tartareæ, quibus intrinsecus infestatur, adeo alte etiam in hac iuuenili ætate radices egerint, vt non tam facile per solam loci mutationem, atque victus rationem, prorsus exstirpari queant, cum et Galenistarum, vtut satis verbose et affectate de his et similibus disserentium medicationes quasi ex alto despiciant. Neque enim citra rem aiebat incomparabilis ille Germanorum Philosophus et Medicus, a quamplurimis citius improbatus quam intellectus, Aureolus Theophrastus, Tartaream Roades nequeunt curare Podagram, per Roades (suo more ludens in vocabulis) rudes et inexpertos Medicos intelligens. Excellentiora sane et præsentiora hîc requiruntur Medicamenta, quam Syrupi, atque Decocta, Pillulæque aut similes Seplasiariorum impuræ et confusæ mixtiones suppeditare queant. Sed de his, cum alterius sint negotij, plura non addam.

Fuit autem ipsius ROTHMANNI accessus mihi inprimis gratus, tam quod a T. Celsit. mihi commendabatur, quam quod ipsum ob egregiam et penitiorem Artis Astronomicæ et rerum Mathematicarum cognitionem plurimi semper fecerim. Inspexit ille omnia mea Instrumenta Astronomica, de quibus ipsemet ad T. Celsit. referet. De Globo quoque Orichalcico quadrupedali, vel potius ampliori in diametro, quem Automatopæus T. Cel. iam præ manibus habet, me certiorem fecit. At vereor, vt sola tornatione eum ad exactam rotunditatem vndiquaque perducat. Id quod meus, qui maior adhuc est, vtpote sexpedalis, me satis superque docuit. Sed ipsa experientia in his et similibus optima erit Magistra.

Quantum ad Statum Regni nostri attinet, omnia adhuc, diuino fauore, tuta et pacata sunt. Serenissimus Rex noster electus prospere degit, et cum Regni Primatibus nunc in Cymbria comitia peragit, quæ tamen hisce diebus finiuntur. Ego meo more studijs indulgeo Philosophicis, quantum per alias occupationes atque auocamenta licet. Liber noster primus recentiorum cœli Phænomenon fere extremam Typographi manum subijt, sed Papyri impressoriæ defectus remoram aliquam, quo minus prorsus absolutus sit, iniecit. Licet enim ipsemet in hac Insula Moletrinam pro Papyro conficienda non paruis sumtibus extrui curârim, tamen cum Chartopæo idoneo destituam nihil adhuc subsidij, quantum ad Papyri præparationem, hinc obtinere licuit. Spero tamen me breui e vicina Germania eiuscemodi artificem obtenturum, qui per instantem Hyemem, ea quæ desiderantur, confecturus sit; sicque in libro illo deficientia supplere commodum erit.

Scripsi circa initium præteriti Aprilis tuæ Celsitudini, de Cometâ huius Anni, qui paulo ante illuxerat, vnaque eius succinctam descriptionem e nostris Obseruationibus deriuatam transmisi, prout per literas ad ROTHMANNVM antea datas me facturum pollicitus eram. Verum, cum ab eodem nunc intelligam, id quicquid erat, T. Celsit. interea non esse redditum, in itinere intercidisse suspicor. Curaui itaque denuo eiusdem Cometæ expositionem transscribi, et his literis adiungi, quam vt T. Celsit. expendat, dijudicet, bonique consulat, rogo.

Plura non addam, ne Celsit. T. alijs forte occupationibus præpeditam nimium detineam. Vale.

Datæ Vraniburgi, Calendis Octob. Anno 1590.
T. Celsit. Addictiss.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the Most Illustrious Prince and Lord, Lord Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, Count in Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain and Nidda: the most clement Prince and Lord. Greeting.**

Your Highness's mathematician Christoph Rothmann has just now come hither to me into Denmark, Most Illustrious Prince, and has brought Your Highness's letter, in which you kindly set forth the cause of so long an intermission in writing to me — both the burden of cares, and likewise the mathematician's ill health. But that Your Highness's mathematical pursuit — amid so many and so great impediments of public administration, and of old age too creeping on by degrees — is not utterly given up, but still continued so far as leisure has allowed, is most pleasant for me to hear. And yet that it should now be scarcely ready to review and handle your earlier findings [*priora inuena*] with the same eagerness as before ought to be no wonder, since the years, the cares and the maladies, together with the affliction of bodily health, weigh down and overcloud not a little the mind itself too and the powers of the intellect, the better part of us. But truly, whatever in this kind Your Highness, by reason of the aforesaid causes, shall hereafter scarcely have been able to perform by your own labour as fully and copiously as before, that you will easily manage to make good through other suitable craftsmen, by your authority and encouragement, and likewise by your outlays and liberality.

I understand that Rothmann changed air for his health's sake; and although this seemed at the outset less safe and less advisable to Your Highness and to others, yet, so far as I learn from his own report, it has turned out for him not unhappily. For straightway from the start of the journey he recovered his strength by degrees, and meanwhile, while he tarried here, he was of no very infirm condition — although those tartareous dissolutions and coagulations by which he is inwardly beset have driven their roots so deep, even at this youthful age, that they cannot so easily be wholly rooted out by mere change of place and regimen of diet, since they as it were look down from on high upon the medications of the Galenists too, however verbosely and affectedly these discourse of such matters and the like. For not without reason did that incomparable Philosopher and Physician of the Germans — sooner condemned than understood by very many — Aureolus Theophrastus, say: ["]The *Roades* cannot cure tartareous Gout["], meaning by *Roades* (playing on words after his manner) crude and inexperienced physicians. More excellent and more efficacious medicines are surely required here than the syrups, and decoctions, and pills, or like impure and muddled mixtures of the drug-sellers, can supply. But of these, since they belong to another business, I shall add no more.

Now Rothmann's coming was especially welcome to me, both because he was commended to me by Your Highness, and because I have always set great store by him for his outstanding and more inward knowledge of the astronomical art and of mathematical matters. He inspected all my astronomical instruments, of which he will himself report to Your Highness. He also informed me concerning that four-foot brass globe — or rather, somewhat larger in diameter — which Your Highness's automaton-maker [*Automatopaeus*] now has in hand. But I fear whether he will bring it to exact roundness on every side by turning alone. The which my own, which is still larger, being six feet, has taught me well enough and more. But experience itself, in these matters and the like, will be the best mistress.

As to the state of our realm, all is still, by divine favour, safe and at peace. Our Most Serene elected King is faring prosperously, and is now holding an assembly with the chief men of the realm in Cymbria [Jutland], which however is ending in these very days. I, after my manner, give myself to philosophical studies, so far as other occupations and distractions permit. Our first book of the more recent phenomena of the heavens has all but received the printer's final hand, but a shortage of printing-paper has thrown in some delay, whereby it is the less quite finished. For although I myself have, at no small cost, had a mill for making paper built on this island, yet, being without a suitable papermaker, I have as yet been able to obtain no help from it as regards the preparation of the paper. I hope nevertheless that I shall shortly obtain such a craftsman from nearby Germany, who through the coming winter will make what is wanting; and so it will be convenient to supply what is deficient in that book.

I wrote to Your Highness about the beginning of last April concerning the comet of this year, which had shone forth a little before, and along with it I sent a brief description of it derived from our observations, as I had promised in an earlier letter to Rothmann that I would do. But since I now learn from him that whatever it was has not in the meantime been delivered to Your Highness, I suspect it was lost on the way. I have therefore had the account of the same comet transcribed afresh, and joined to this letter, which I beg Your Highness to weigh, judge, and take in good part.

I shall add no more, lest I detain Your Highness too long, hindered as you perhaps are by other occupations. Farewell.

Given at Uraniborg, on the Kalends of October [1 October], the year 1590.
Most devoted to Your Highness,
Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** Tycho Brahe → **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), the astronomer-prince of Kassel and Tycho's chief observational peer; their decade-long correspondence is the backbone of the 1596 *Epistolarum astronomicarum liber I*, in which this letter was printed.
- **DATING CRUX (resolved).** The source dateline reads *"Calendis Octob. Anno 1590"* = 1 October 1590 (O.S.). The edition label gives "1587. 1. oktober." — a **catalogue error**, contradicted by the letter's own internal evidence: it is written just after **Christoph Rothmann's stay on Hven** (*interea dum hîc moraretur* — "while he tarried here"), which the biographies date to **August 1590** (Rothmann sailed to Hven on the evening of 1 Aug. 1590 and stayed the month; Christianson, *On Tycho's Island*; Thoren, *Lord of Uraniborg*). It also mentions the elected King Christian IV's assembly *in Cymbria* and the comet *huius anni* (the comet of 1590). The header therefore leads with the as-written **1590** date and appends the catalogued 1587 in parentheses; by this chapter's convention the dateline is not silently altered, and the discrepancy is recorded here, not reconciled in the body. The year-as-written ("Anno 1590") is unambiguous in the source.
- **Salutation / subscription formulae.** *S. D.* = *salutem dicit*, "sends greeting". *T. Celsit. Addictiss.* = *Tuae Celsitudini Addictissimus*, "Most devoted to Your Highness." *Celsit. / Celsitudo* throughout rendered "Your Highness". The recipient's full titulature (Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, Nidda) is preserved.
- ***Christophorus Rothmannus*** = **Christoph Rothmann**, mathematician at the Kassel court; the carrier of this letter's enclosed comet-account and Tycho's interlocutor of the preceding years.
- **Paracelsus passage (medical / alchemical).** *resolutiones et coagulationes istae Tartareae* — "those **tartareous** dissolutions and coagulations," the Paracelsian *tartarus* doctrine of mineral concretions (here Rothmann's chronic ailment); kept as the period term, not modernised. *incomparabilis ille Germanorum Philosophus et Medicus … Aureolus Theophrastus* = **Paracelsus** (Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, "Aureolus"), named with conspicuous praise — Tycho's own Paracelsian sympathy. *Galenistarum … medicationes* — the rival **Galenist** physicians, whom Tycho has the *tartarus* "look down on from on high." *Seplasiariorum … mixtiones* — the *seplasiarii*, retail drug-/ointment-sellers (after the Seplasia, the perfumers' street in Capua); rendered "drug-sellers." See this chapter's convention (period medical terms glossed, not modernised).
- **The Paracelsus tag — CRUX.** *"Tartaream Roades nequeunt curare Podagram"* is given as a saying of Paracelsus and is rendered literally ["The *Roades* cannot cure tartareous Gout"], with *Roades* kept untranslated because Tycho **immediately glosses it himself**: *per Roades (suo more ludens in vocabulis) rudes et inexpertos Medicos intelligens* — "by *Roades* (playing on words after his manner) meaning crude and inexperienced physicians." *Roades* is thus a deliberate Paracelsian word-coinage / pun (on *rudes*, "crude"); it is not smoothed into ordinary Latin. *Podagra* (lit. gout of the foot) is here the genus "gout"; rendered "Gout." The maxim's exact wording may be corrupt or a paraphrase of a Paracelsian dictum — flagged, not silently corrected.
- ***priora inuena*** — rendered "your earlier findings." *inuena* is unusual (apparently for *inventa*, "things found/discovered"); the reading is kept as printed in the Source block and the sense flagged here rather than emended.
- **Instruments.** *Instrumenta Astronomica* → "astronomical instruments." *Globo … Orichalcico quadrupedali* → a four-foot **brass globe** (*orichalcum* = brass/latten); Tycho contrasts it with his own *sexpedalis* (six-foot) globe — the celebrated great brass globe of Uraniborg. *Automatopaeus* (Greek-formed, "maker of self-moving devices / automaton-maker") → the Landgrave's instrument-/automaton-maker at Kassel, i.e. **Jost Bürgi**; rendered "automaton-maker" with the Greek-derived term flagged. *sola tornatione … ad exactam rotunditatem* — "to exact roundness by turning [on the lathe] alone," a technical worry about globe-truing.
- ***Liber noster primus recentiorum coeli Phaenomenon*** — "our first book of the more recent phenomena of the heavens": the volume in press, i.e. the *Epistolarum astronomicarum liber I* (eventually 1596), here described as *fere extremam Typographi manum subijt* ("has all but received the printer's final hand") but delayed by a paper shortage.
- **Paper-mill / papermaker.** *Moletrinam pro Papyro* → the **paper-mill** Tycho built on Hven; *Chartopaeo idoneo destituam* — "being without a suitable **papermaker**" (*chartopoeus*, Greek-formed, "paper-maker"); he hopes to fetch one *e vicina Germania* ("from nearby Germany"). Tycho's epistemic hedge *Spero … obtenturum* ("I hope … I shall obtain") is preserved as a hope, not an accomplished fact.
- ***Serenissimus Rex noster electus … in Cymbria comitia*** — the "elected King" is **Christian IV** (elected 1580 as a child, crowned 1596); *in Cymbria* = in **Cimbria / Jutland** (the Cimbrian peninsula), where a *comitia* (assembly / *herredag*) of the realm's *Primates* (great men) was being held. Calendar context O.S.
- **The comet of 1590.** *Cometâ huius Anni, qui paulo ante illuxerat* — the comet of 1590, on which Tycho had sent Rothmann a *succincta descriptio … e nostris Obseruationibus deriuata* ("a brief description derived from our observations") *circa initium praeteriti Aprilis* (about the beginning of last April); the original being lost in transit (*in itinere intercidisse suspicor* — "I suspect it was lost on the way"), Tycho re-encloses a fresh transcript. Tycho's suspicion is kept as a suspicion (*suspicor*), not asserted.
- **Source-text reconstruction note.** The working transcription had collapsed the original print's paragraph breaks (line/paragraph boundaries survived only as stray inserted capitals — *.AVENIT*, *senijA*, *adeoA*, *suffeceritA*, *morareturA*, *requirunturA*, *mihiA*, *amplioriA*, *meA*, *tutaA*, *rogo.A*, *.A Plura*, *Calendis Octob.A*). The Source block above restores the paragraphing on these markers and on the letter's clear logical movements (salutation; Rothmann's arrival + the Landgrave's studies; the Paracelsian medical digression; the instruments / globes; the realm + book-in-press; the comet; close + dateline); the stray capitals have been removed and the word-joins they marked separated. No word of the source has been added or dropped. Greek-derived coinages (*Automatopaeus*, *Chartopaeus*, *Seplasiarii*) are Latin-script in the source and so kept; there is no Greek-alphabet text in this letter.
- **Calendar.** *Calendis Octob. Anno 1590* = "on the Kalends of October (1 October), the year 1590," Old Style (Denmark and the Hessen court both kept O.S.). Roman-calendar idiom rendered with the idiom and glossed to the civil date by this chapter's convention.

documents.abstract: Chides Vedel for long silence, reports the press stands idle for lack of paper, and asks help finding a skilled papermaker for the new Uraniborg mill.
documents.incipit: MIROR [te] dilecte M. ANDREA, in tanto tempore mihi nihil scribere: existimo vos …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD ANDREAM SEVERINI VELLEJUM. S.

MIROR [te] dilecte M. ANDREA, in tanto tempore mihi nihil scribere: existimo vos Lillebergenses de Lillehuenensibus nihil amplius cogitare, ac si essent remoti extra Solis cœlique vias; fac ut per hunc ministrum meum cognoscam quid rerum agas et quomodo cum tuis vivas et valeas. Typographia mea iam feriatur ob papyri impressoriæ defectum. Misi hisce diebus Typographum meum in Germaniam pro conquirendo papyro et conducendo idoneo Cartopæo, nam moletrina mea, papyro conficiendæ destinata, iam parata est. Si tibi de tali artifice alicubi quicquam constiterit, da operam ut eum mature habeam, et tuos etiam labores urge, nec nimium procrastina.

Vale. Saluta uxorem unâ cum Parentibus et liberis.
Datæ Uraniburgi 5. Octob. 1590.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Anders Sørensen Vedel. Greeting.**

I am astonished, dear Master Anders, that in so long a time you write nothing to me: I suppose that you people of Liljeberg [vos Lillebergenses] give no further thought to us people of little-Hven [Lillehuenensibus], as if we were set apart, beyond the paths of the Sun and the heavens. See to it that, through this servant of mine, I may learn what you are about, and how you live and fare with your household. My printing-press now stands idle for want of printing-paper. I have these last days sent my printer into Germany to procure paper and to engage a suitable papermaker [Cartopaeus], for my mill, intended for the making of paper, is now ready. If anything has come to your knowledge anywhere about such a craftsman, take pains that I may have him in good time; and press on your own labours too, and do not put them off too long.

Farewell. Greet your wife together with your parents and children.
Given at Uraniborg, 5 October 1590.
Yours, TYCHO BRAHE.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** *Tycho Brahe* writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven to *Andreas Severini Vellejus* = **Anders Sørensen Vedel** (1542–1616), the Danish historian and royal historiographer, then resident at **Ribe**; an old friend of Tycho's (the addressee, too, of the 1571 letter on his father's death). The edition's recipient field confirms the identification.
- **Salutation / address.** *S.* = *salutem [dicit]*, "[sends] greeting". *M. ANDREA* — *M.* = *Magister* (academic "Master"), rendered "Master Anders."
- **The wordplay *Lillebergenses … Lillehuenensibus*.** The letter's one rhetorical flourish: Tycho coins two mock-ethnic demonyms. *Lillebergenses* — "the people of *Lilleberg*/Liljeberg," i.e. Vedel and his circle (Liljeberg was Vedel's house/printing establishment at Ribe). *Lillehuenenses* — "the people of *Lille-Hven*," i.e. "little Hven," Tycho and his household on the island of Hven. The jest plays the two place-names against each other ("you Liljeberg-folk" vs. "us little-Hven-folk"); the coinages are kept transliterated in the translation and the sense glossed, rather than flattened into plain "you" and "us." *[te]* in the opening clause (*MIROR [te] … nihil scribere*) is an editorial supplement in the source, retained in brackets.
- **Hyperbole.** *ac si essent remoti extra Solis coelique vias* — "as if we [lit. they] were set apart, beyond the paths of the Sun and the heavens": a playful astronomer's hyperbole for being forgotten, not a literal claim; kept as figure.
- **The Uraniborg press and paper-mill.** *Typographia mea … feriatur ob papyri impressoriae defectum* — Tycho's own printing-house (the press he set up on Hven) "stands idle for want of printing-paper." *moletrina mea, papyro conficiendae destinata, iam parata est* — "my mill, intended for the making of paper, is now ready": the **paper-mill Tycho built on Hven**, here reported newly completed. *Cartopaeus* (Greek-derived coinage, *χάρτης* "paper" + *-ποιός* "maker") = a **papermaker / paper-craftsman**; rendered "papermaker," the term flagged. *Typographus meus* = "my printer," sent to Germany to buy paper and recruit such a craftsman. This passage is a documentary datum for the Hven press/paper-mill chronology (cf. *Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen*).
- **Closing.** *Vale* = "Farewell". *Saluta uxorem unâ cum Parentibus et liberis* — "Greet your wife together with your parents and children." *Tuus* = "Yours."
- **Calendar.** *Datae Uraniburgi 5. Octob. 1590* = "Given at Uraniborg, 5 October 1590," **Old Style** (Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700; this chapter's convention). The as-written dateline (5 October 1590) agrees with the edition label ("1590. 5. oktober. Uraniborg") — no discrepancy. The header carries the as-written date; no conversion is made.
- **MS witness.** A = Copenhagen, Rigsarkivet, *Tycho Brahes privatarkiv*, a copy (*Afskrift*), per the source header.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VII pp.275-276 read as page images. Collated the Lillebergenses/Lillehuenensibus wordplay opening, the printing-press-idle-for-paper clause, the printer-sent-to-Germany-for-a-papermaker sentence, the mill-ready clause, the request to find a suitable papermaker, the closing greetings, and the Uraniborg/5 October 1590 date against the transcribed original and the published English; every clause, name, and date matches word for word (VELLEIUM/VELLEJUM is a mere I/J spelling variant). No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, hedge-loss, or text-error found; the translator's own grade Secure is upheld.

documents.incipit: CLARISSIME et eruditissime vir, amice summopere dilecte. Quas ad me circa Æquinoctium …

text.original:
EXCELLENTISSIMO ET CLARISSIMO VIRO DOMINO IOACHIMO CAMERARIO, PHILOSOPHIÆ ET MEDICINÆ DOCTORI EXIMIO, EARUNDEMQUE IN INCLYTA NORIBERGENSIUM REPUBLICA EXCULTORI, ET CIVI, AMICO SUO INPRIMIS COLENDO.

CLARISSIME et eruditissime vir, amice summopere dilecte. Quas ad me circa Æquinoctium vernum huius anni dedisti, literulas accepi, et quod tardius atque brevius, quam expectabam, meis iam dudum ad te datis respondebas, te ob occupationum molem, qua distineris, amicitia etiam nostra candidius omnia interpretante, lubens excusatum habeo. Librum meum secundum recentiorum cœli Phaenomenωn tibi allatum, nec displicuisse, mihi auditu gratum est; quodque illum ad Illustrem et excellentiss. virum Dominum VINCENTIUM PINELLUM Patavium miseris, adhuc multo acceptius habeo. Si is, ut est Mathematum insigniter peritus, suum gravissimum atque eruditissimum de ijs, quæ inibi continentur, per literas communicârit iudicium, adhuc longe gratissimam rem tam ille quam tu mihi præstiteritis. Idque, ut mature fieret, exoptarem. Intellexi iam nuper ex literis cuiusdam Studiosi Dani, qui Patavij studijs incumbit, GELLII SASCERIDIS nomine, qui octennium mihi in studijs Astronomicis et Pyronomicis diligenter inservivit, prædicto Domino PINELLO tractatulum etiam quendam meum de huius anni Cometa forte tua quoque opera redditum esse, utpote ab Illustrissimo Principe Hassiæ Landgravio (ad quem ista breviter perscripseram) tibi transmissum. Quem adeo secretum et charum habeat, ut ne GELLIO quidem meo nedum alijs eum describere, nomini nostro (uti ait) favens, concedat. Quæ viri illius sincera et benevola erga me de facie illi ignotum voluntas inprimis omnem gratitudinem meretur. Si et de hac Cometæ illius descriptiuncula suam eruditam subiunxerit censuram, benefecerit. Tomum nostrum primum, qui iam typis meis pene absolutus est, restante saltem ultimo et decimo capite ob papyri impressoriæ defectum (cui tamen propria moletrina illi usui destinata et non parvis impensis in hac Insula iam nuper a me extructa sufficienter mox subveniam) futura æstate favente divino auxilio obtinebitis, unâque tertium de quatuor alijs minoribus Cometis postmodum conspectis, inter quos hic, de quo dixi, paulo ante vernum tempus huius anni prodiens, quartus et ultimus est. Habebitis etiam unâ (modo tam cito Typographico labore ad colophonem deduci poterit) Epistolarum Astronomicarum volumen, in quo plurimæ et variæ eruditissimorum virorum literæ mecum de re Astronomica et Cometometrica affatim conferentium unâ cum nostra ad singulas responsione continebuntur. Has ternorum librorum evulgationes Operi illi magno de perennium et Mundo coævorum syderum revolutionibus ad normam cœlestem ad amussim restituendis, quod longo iam tempore molior, quasi prodromi sive præludij loco præmittere animus est. Plæraque enim continebunt, quæ ingenti illi molimini atque structuræ viam sternent et nonnulla ponent fundamina. Quæ cum (vires atque industriam suppeditante Cœlestium Opifice) magnis laboribus exantlata fuerint, vos eorundem quoque reddam participes.

Sed est, mi CAMERARI, quod te nunc obnixe rogatum cuperem nomine eius, cuius antea mentionem feci, Studiosi, cui ob ingenium, diligentiam et morum integritatem, quodque multis (uti dixi) annis fidelem mihi præstitit operam, quam optime cupio. Scripsi itaque Domino IOACHIMO POMERIO vestræ civitatis Senatori primario, ut illi meo nomine 50 Coronatos confestim per Mercatores Venetijs negotiantes collybo sive literis cambij (ut vocant) transmitti procuret. Ego nulla intercedente mora, Lubecæ vel ubicunque in propinquo voluerit, renumerari unâ cum interesse non invite curabo. Sin vero Dominus POMERIUS se hac in parte (quod tamen non spero) difficilem præbuerit, da tu operam, amantissime CAMERARI, ut GELLIUS meus mature et quam citissime fieri poterit, 50 illos Coronatos Patavij, vel ubicunque in Italia agat, obtineat. Fiet illud absque omni tuo damno, egoque ad recompensandum et promptus et gratus inveniar. Admonui etiam eundem GELLIUM per literas, ut quotiescunque aliquid illi ad studiorum suorum sublevamen necessarium fuerit (tum etiam in sumptus Instrumenti cuiusdam Astronomici, quod illic ob quædam in Italia commodius quam hîc observationi patentia meis impensis fieri iniunxi) statim ad Dominum POMERIUM et te de eo audacter scribat, atque a vobis meo nomine expetat. Præbete igitur vos faciles obsecro in exponendo et subministrando illi, quicquid a vobis petierit. Scio enim satis, illum superflua non desideraturum. Ego vicissim bona et integra fide spondeo, id quicquid erit, quod in eius usum a vobis erogatum fuerit, primo quoque tempore citra omne dispendium, etiam cum lucro in vicinia, ubicunque vobis placuerit, persolutum iri. Da operam, charissime CAMERARI, ut omnia votis meis hac in parte quam optime respondeant. Feceris mihi officium ea in re multis nominibus acceptum.

Quin et aliud quiddam est, quo te molestare, amicitia nostra sic suadente, non intermittam. Si eximius ille Poëta MELISSUS adhuc vobiscum est, vel etiam alibi, per literas illum roga, ut carmen quoddam egregium in effigiem meam, unâ cum circumscriptis Insignibus, atque in Operis commendationem ex sua illa melliflua poëtica vena concinnare non gravetur, ita ut unum latus paginæ in 4to typis impressum adimplere possit. Et si quos excellentes in Italia et Gallia, tum etiam alibi in Germania vestra nosti Poëtas, illos eodem nomine in mei gratiam rogatos habe. Inveniar vicissim erga ipsos gratus. Poterit quilibet inventionem extruere, prout libuerit et spiritus feret poëticus, ut consideratis et expensis singulis, quæ maxime placuerint, seligam. Icona autem meam brevi (volente Deo) obtinebis per peculiarem quendam hominem, quem Noribergam cum Instrumento quodam e nostris, ut illic nonnulla cœlitus mihi denotet, mittere decrevi. Qua de re antea quoque, si recte memini, te per literas me aliquando facturum certiorem reddidi; et cum Domino POMERIO, quando hîc præsens aderat, oretenus collocutus sum, qui mihi operam suam, quo nuntius ille meus commodum observationi cœlesti atque a turba separatum locum, dum illic est, nanciscatur, non invite addixit. Qua in parte ut tuum quoque subministres unâ cum consilio auxilium, te etiam atque etiam rogatum habeo. Verum nolo te a tuis multiplicibus occupationibus ulterius avocare, unicum saltem amanter insuper petens, ut adiuncturum literarum fasciculum absque omni mora ad antenominatum Studiosum GELLIUM SASCERIDEM in Italiam Patavium tuto et certo perferri procurare non molestum ducas. Ego ad tibi vicissim, quacunque occasione dabitur, gratificandum perpetuo me polliceor quam paratissimum.

Vale cum uxore et tota familia quam diutissime felicissimeque.
Datæ Uraniburgi die 21. Octobris Anno 1590.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the most excellent and most renowned man, Master Joachim Camerarius, distinguished Doctor of Philosophy and of Medicine, and a cultivator of those same disciplines in the illustrious commonwealth of the Nurembergers, and a citizen [of it], his friend to be honoured above all.**

Most renowned and most learned man, friend most exceedingly beloved. I have received the little letter you sent me around the spring equinox of this year; and that you were replying later and more briefly than I expected to those [letters] of mine long since sent to you, I gladly hold you excused on account of the mass of business by which you are kept occupied — our friendship, too, interpreting everything in the kinder light. That my second book of the more recent phenomena of the heavens [Phaenomenωn], having been brought to you, did not displease you, is welcome news to me to hear; and that you sent it on to the illustrious and most excellent man Master Vincenzo Pinelli at Padua, I take as much more welcome still. If he — being as he is signally skilled in the mathematical sciences — should communicate by letter his most weighty and most learned judgement concerning the things contained therein, both he and you will have rendered me a thing far more welcome yet. And I could wish that this be done in good time. I have lately understood from the letter of a certain Danish student who is engaged in his studies at Padua, by name Gellius Sascerides — who for eight years diligently served me in astronomical and pyronomic studies — that a certain little treatise of mine too, on this year's comet, was delivered to the aforesaid Master Pinelli, perhaps by your agency as well, having been transmitted to you by the Most Illustrious Prince the Landgrave of Hesse (to whom I had briefly written these things out). [Pinelli] holds it so secret and dear that he will not allow even my Gellius, let alone others, to copy it out — favouring our name (as he says). That man's sincere and benevolent disposition towards me — towards one unknown to him by face — deserves above all every gratitude. If he should append his learned assessment of that little description of the comet too, he will have done well. My first volume, which is now almost completed at my press — only the last and tenth chapter remaining, on account of a shortage of printing-paper (which, however, I shall presently relieve sufficiently by my own paper-mill destined for that use, and built at no small expense here on this island just lately by me) — you shall obtain next summer, God's help favouring it; and together with it the third [volume], concerning four other lesser comets observed thereafter, among which this one of which I have spoken, appearing a little before the spring season of this year, is the fourth and last. You will have together with these also (provided it can be brought so quickly to its colophon by the labour of the press) a volume of Astronomical Letters, in which will be contained very many and various letters of most learned men conferring with me fully on astronomical and comet-measuring matters, together with my own reply to each. It is my intention to send these publications of three books ahead, as it were in the place of a forerunner or prelude, before that great Work on the revolutions of the everlasting stars coeval with the World, to be restored exactly to the celestial standard — which I have now for a long time been labouring at. For they will contain most things which will pave the way for that vast undertaking and structure, and will lay down some foundations. And when these (the Maker of the Heavenly Things supplying strength and industry) shall have been drained dry through great labours, I shall make you sharers in them as well.

But there is something, my Camerarius, in which I should earnestly wish you now to be asked [for help], in the name of that student of whom I made mention before, for whom — on account of his talent, diligence, and integrity of character, and because (as I have said) for many years he rendered me faithful service — I wish as well as possible. I have therefore written to Master Joachim Pomarius, the foremost Senator of your city, that he procure 50 crowns to be transmitted to him at once in my name, through the merchants trading at Venice, by exchange or by letters of exchange (as they call them). I, with no delay intervening, shall not unwillingly see to its being repaid, together with the interest, at Lübeck or wherever nearby he may wish. But if Master Pomarius should in this part show himself difficult (which, however, I do not expect), do you take pains, most loving Camerarius, that my Gellius may in good time and as quickly as possible obtain those 50 crowns at Padua, or wherever he may be in Italy. It will be done without any loss to you, and I shall be found both ready and grateful to make recompense. I have also admonished this same Gellius by letter that, as often as anything be necessary to him for the relief of his studies (and also for the costs of a certain astronomical instrument which, on account of certain things being more conveniently open to observation in Italy than here, I have charged to be made there at my expense), he should at once write boldly about it to Master Pomarius and to you, and request it from you in my name. Show yourselves therefore accommodating, I beseech you, in laying out and supplying to him whatever he shall have requested of you. For I know well enough that he will not desire superfluous things. I in turn pledge in good and entire faith that whatever it shall be that is disbursed by you for his use will, at the very first opportunity, be paid back without any loss — indeed with profit — in your neighbourhood, wherever it shall please you. Take pains, dearest Camerarius, that everything may answer as well as possible to my wishes in this matter. You will have done me a service welcome on many counts therein.

Indeed there is yet another thing, with which — our friendship so urging — I shall not refrain from troubling you. If that distinguished poet Melissus is still with you, or even elsewhere, ask him by letter that he not think it a burden to compose, out of that mellifluous poetic vein of his, some excellent poem upon my portrait — together with the arms inscribed around it — and to the commendation of the Work, such that it may fill one side of a page printed in quarto. And if you know any excellent poets in Italy and France, and also elsewhere in your Germany, have them asked on the same account for my sake. I shall in turn be found grateful towards them. Anyone may construct his conceit just as he pleases and as the poetic spirit shall carry him, so that, the several pieces being considered and weighed, I may select those which shall most have pleased. My likeness, moreover, you shall shortly obtain (God willing) through a certain particular man whom I have resolved to send to Nuremberg with one of our instruments, that he may there note down for me some [phenomena] from the heavens. Of which matter also I earlier, if I rightly remember, gave you notice by letter that I would at some time do so; and with Master Pomarius, when he was here present, I spoke by word of mouth, who not unwillingly assigned me his assistance, so that that messenger of mine, while he is there, may obtain a place convenient for celestial observation and set apart from the crowd. In which part, that you too may supply your aid together with your counsel, I have you asked again and again. But I do not wish to call you away further from your manifold occupations, asking lovingly besides only this one thing: that you not think it a trouble to procure that the attached bundle of letters be conveyed without any delay, safely and surely, to the aforenamed student Gellius Sascerides into Italy, to Padua. I in turn promise myself ever most ready to gratify you, on whatever occasion shall be given.

Farewell, with your wife and your whole household, as long and as happily as may be.
Given at Uraniborg, on the 21st day of October, in the year 1590.
TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.
