documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven. *manu propria* = "in his own hand" — the autograph subscription.
- **Recipient.** *Ioachimus Camerarius* = **Joachim Camerarius the Younger** (1534–1598), physician, botanist and humanist of **Nuremberg** (*Noribergensium Republica* = "the commonwealth of the Nurembergers," i.e. the Free Imperial City of Nuremberg); son of the elder Joachim Camerarius. *Philosophiae et Medicinae Doctori* = "Doctor of Philosophy and of Medicine."
- **Persons named.**
 - *Vincentius Pinellus* = **Gian Vincenzo Pinelli** (1535–1601), the great Paduan bibliophile and patron of learning whose house was a centre of scientific exchange; *Mathematum insigniter peritus* = "signally skilled in the mathematical sciences."
 - *Gellius Sascerides* = **Gellius Sascerides** (1562–1612), Tycho's former assistant on Hven, then a Danish student at **Padua**; later (1594) the broken betrothal to Tycho's daughter Magdalene soured the relationship. *octennium … inservivit* = "served me for eight years." Mosley (*Bearing the Heavens*) and Dreyer both treat this letter as the key evidence that Tycho was financing Sascerides' instrument-building and use in Italy.
 - *Illustrissimus Princeps Hassiae Landgravius* = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592).
 - *Ioachimus Pomerius* = **Joachim Pomarius** (latinised; the Nuremberg patrician/senator), here *Senatori primario* "the foremost Senator of your city."
 - *Melissus* = **Paul Melissus Schede** (1539–1602), the celebrated German Neo-Latin poet and *Comes Palatinus*. (He did in fact later address verses to Tycho; cf. his letter of 5 March 1600 from Heidelberg.)
- **Tycho's publishing programme (the works named).**
 - *Liber meus secundus recentiorum coeli Phaenomenωn* = "my second book of the more recent phenomena of the heavens" = the *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (1588), Tycho's "second book" treating the comet of 1577. The word *Phaenomenωn* is written with a **Greek omega (ω)** in the genitive-plural ending — a learned graphic flourish on a Greek loan-word; kept as printed in the Source block and rendered "phenomena."
 - *Tomus primus* = "the first volume" = the planned *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* (the long-gestating work on the new star of 1572 and the restored solar/stellar theory); here reported as all-but-printed at Tycho's own Uraniborg press, with only the tenth and last chapter held up by a paper shortage — hence the new **paper-mill** (*moletrina*) on Hven. The phrasing *de … syderum revolutionibus … ad normam coelestem ad amussim restituendis* ("the stars … to be restored exactly to the celestial standard") is Tycho's *instauratio* programme (this chapter's convention: *restitutio/instauratio* → **restoration/renewal**).
 - *tertium [volumen] de quatuor alijs minoribus Cometis* = "the third [volume], on four other lesser comets" — the never-completed third cometary volume; *hic … Cometa* (this year's comet, *paulo ante vernum tempus huius anni*, "a little before the spring of this year") = the **comet of 1590**, the fourth and last of the four lesser comets.
 - *Epistolarum Astronomicarum volumen* = "a volume of Astronomical Letters" = the *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Liber I, printed at Uraniborg 1596). *Cometometrica* = "comet-measuring [matters]" — Tycho's coinage; rendered literally and flagged.
 - *Opus illud magnum … prodromi sive praeludij loco praemittere* = "to send [these three works] ahead in the place of a forerunner or prelude before that great Work": Tycho casts the three publications as a *prodromus* to his comprehensive astronomy.
- **Technical / lexical notes.**
 - *studijs Astronomicis et Pyronomicis* = "astronomical and **pyronomic** studies": *pyronomia* = the art/management of fire, i.e. the **alchemical/distillatory (laboratory) work** Tycho ran on Hven alongside astronomy. Rendered "pyronomic" and glossed; not modernised to "chemistry."
 - *50 Coronatos* = "50 **crowns**" (gold *scudi/coronati*); *collybo sive literis cambij (ut vocant)* = "by exchange or by letters of exchange (as they call them)" — *collybus* (Greek κόλλυβος, money-changing) and the bill-of-exchange mechanism for remitting funds via Venice merchants; Tycho's own *ut vocant* hedge preserved. *unâ cum interesse* = "together with the interest."
 - *Instrumentum … Astronomicum* (this chapter's convention: *organum/instrumentum* → **instrument**); *ob quaedam in Italia commodius quam hîc observationi patentia* = "on account of certain things being more conveniently open to observation in Italy than here" (lower latitude / southern stars).
 - *Icona / effigiem meam … unâ cum circumscriptis Insignibus* = "my likeness / my portrait … together with the arms [coat of arms] inscribed around it"; *in 4to* = "in quarto." Tycho is soliciting laudatory verse for an engraved author-portrait to accompany the *Work*. *melliflua poëtica vena* = "mellifluous poetic vein."
 - *coelitus … denotet* = "may note down [phenomena] from the heavens": the instrument is sent to Nuremberg so the messenger can make observations there; *commodum … atque a turba separatum locum* = "a place convenient [for observation] and set apart from the crowd."
- **Epistolary formulae.** Superscription closes *Amico suo inprimis colendo* = "his friend to be honoured above all"; *S.* (in the address) = *salutem*, "greeting". Subscription *Vale … quam diutissime felicissimeque* = "Farewell … as long and as happily as may be"; *Datae … die 21. Octobris* = "Given … on the 21st day of October."
- **Calendar.** Denmark was on the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar in 1590; the dateline *die 21. Octobris Anno 1590* is therefore O.S. (= 31 October N.S.). The edition label ("1590. 21. oktober. Uraniborg") agrees with the source's own dateline; **no discrepancy.** No date is internally conflicting; the year-references *huius anni* are all 1590.

documents.abstract: Asks Young to convey thanks for the royal visit to Uraniborg and to solicit a privilege for the typographical labors, while chiding him for long silence.

text.original:
PETRO IUNIO TYCHO BRAHE

ETSI nihil ad me tanto tempore dederis literarum, nobilissime et eruditissime D. PETRE IUNI, utut præsens te id sæpius facturum addixeris: ego nihilominus oblata hac oportuna per hunc eruditum iuvenem occasione, intermittere nolui, quin aliquid saltem ad te chartis exararem, teque iamdudum inter nos contractæ amicitiæ atque tuarum promissionum commonefacerem. Cupio autem quam maxime ex te cognoscere, quomodo serenissimus et laudatissimus Rex vester cum suavissima Regina nostrate vivat et valeat, rogoque peramanter, ut ipsius Maiestati meo nomine submisse gratias agere velis, quod meas Uraniæ dicatas ædes in hac insula invisere non sit dedignata, omniaque prospera et ex voto ipsius Maiestati ex me preceris atque exoptes. Si ab ipsius Maiestate privilegium quoddam pro meis typographicis laboribus, quos et præsens spectavit, ne videlicet in Scotia recudantur aut divendantur, absque meo concessu, tua authoritate atque intercessione impetrâris, feceris mihi rem pluribus nominibus gratam. Mitto autem tibi exemplar privilegij Cæsarei mihi nuper procurante amplissimo viro D. IACOBO CURTIO, Imperij Pro-Cancellario, clementer concessi et in membrana conscripti. Addam etiam unâ, si nuntij festinatio feret, ipsius Procancellarij literarum ad me unâ datarum descriptum: quo hac ratione promptius concipies, quomodo privilegium illud, quod expeto, ordinandum veniat. Quamvis Cæsareum illud imitari non sit admodum necesse, tua eloquendi et res ipsas scitis verbis complectendi eximia facultas, facile quid scribendum sit, suggeret. Optarem vero privilegium illud, si non ante hiemem, saltem circa veris primordia, quamprimum huc naves e Scotia solvant, obtinere, ut operibus meis unâ cum Cæsareano atque aliorum quorundam Regum diplomatis præfigatur. Quin et aliud quiddam est, mi IUNI, de quo te commonefacere non supersedendum duxi. Addixisti, cum mecum esses, te non solum BUCHANANI effigiem, sed etiam ipsius vitam a te ipso conscriptam, mihi e Scotia missurum. Effigiem quidem accepi, quam et Serenissimus Rex vester, quamprimum in musæo meo conspexit, hilari vultu agnovit. Vitæ descriptionem adhuc desidero: fac in utroque stes promissis. Rogo insuper, ut D. Doctorem IOHANNEM CRAGIUM, medicinam Edinburgi facientem et præstantissimum, si quis alius in Scotia, Mathematicum, Regi vestro de meliore (ut aiunt) nota commendatum habeas. Est enim dignus, ut ametur et promoveatur. Neque enim ægre fero, quod libro nostro secundo de recentioribus ætherei mundi phænomenis quædam contraria opposuerit eademque ad me perscripserit, quibus etiam apologetice satis luculenter obviavi. Sed hominem eo plus diligo, quod eiuscemodi attentare ausus sit, omnibus in Germania eruditis Mathematicis, suas priores conceptiones, quas dilui, retractantibus, silentibus et quasi obmutescentibus; quemadmodum ipse suo tempore plenius cognosces. Plura nunc non addo, cum et hæc ipsa forte nimia sint, ex quo tu tam diutino silentio distineris. Sin tandem aliqua scripseris, ego crebrius et copiosius; nec sinam me ullo officij genere a te superari.

Vale.
Datæ Uraniburgi die 27. Oct. An. 1590.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Peter Young**

Although you have sent me no letter in so long a time, most noble and most learned Master Peter Young — for all that, when you were here, you pledged you would do so more often — I nonetheless, with this opportune occasion offered through this learned young man, was unwilling to let it pass without at least scratching something out to you on paper, and reminding you of the friendship contracted between us this while since, and of your promises. I greatly desire to learn from you how your most serene and most praised King fares and prospers, together with our most charming Queen; and I most affectionately ask that you be willing, in my name, humbly to render thanks to His Majesty, that he did not disdain to visit my house dedicated to Urania on this island, and that on my behalf you pray and wish His Majesty all things prosperous and according to his desire. If from His Majesty you should obtain, by your authority and intercession, a certain privilege for my typographical labours — those which he also viewed while present — to the effect, namely, that they not be reprinted or sold off in Scotland without my consent, you will do me a thing welcome on several counts. I am sending you, moreover, a copy of the Imperial privilege graciously granted to me lately, through the procurement of the most distinguished man Master Jakob Kurtz, Vice-Chancellor of the Empire, and written out on parchment. I shall add as well, if the messenger's haste allow, a transcript of the Vice-Chancellor's own letter sent to me along with it: so that by this means you may the more readily grasp how that privilege which I seek ought to be drawn up. Although it is not at all necessary to imitate that Imperial one, your outstanding faculty of expression — of embracing the matters themselves in apt words — will easily suggest what should be written. I should wish, indeed, to obtain that privilege, if not before winter, then at least about the first beginnings of spring, as soon as ships set sail hither from Scotland, so that it may be set at the front of my works together with the Imperial diploma and those of certain other Kings. But there is also another matter, my dear Young, of which I have judged that I ought not to forbear reminding you. You pledged, when you were with me, that you would send me from Scotland not only Buchanan's portrait, but also his life, written by yourself. The portrait, to be sure, I have received — which your most serene King too, as soon as he beheld it in my study, recognized with a cheerful countenance. The account of his life I still want: see that in both you stand by your promises. I ask besides that you should hold Master Doctor John Craig — who practises medicine at Edinburgh and is a most excellent mathematician, if any other in Scotland is — commended to your King on the better footing (as they say). For he is worthy to be loved and advanced. Nor indeed do I take it ill that in our second book on the more recent phenomena of the ethereal world he set certain contrary things in opposition, and wrote the same out to me, which I also met, apologetically, clearly enough; but I esteem the man the more for this, that he dared to attempt something of this kind, while all the learned mathematicians in Germany are retracting their earlier conceptions, which I refuted, falling silent and as it were struck dumb — as you yourself will learn more fully in your own time. I add no more now, since even these very things are perhaps too much, given that you are held back by so long a silence. But if at length you write something, I [shall write] more often and more copiously; nor shall I allow myself to be outdone by you in any kind of courtesy.

Farewell.
Given at Uraniborg, the 27th day of October, the year 1590.
TYCHO BRAHE.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), writing from **Uraniborg** on the island of Hven (*Uraniburgum*, "house dedicated to Urania," the muse of astronomy — the phrase *meas Uraniae dicatas aedes* puns on the name of the residence).
- **Recipient.** *Petrus Iunius* = **Peter Young** (1544–1628), Scottish humanist, former tutor to **James VI** of Scotland and a royal envoy. He had accompanied (or been part of the circle of) the king's visit to Hven. The Latinized surname *Iunius/Iuni* (vocative *Iuni*) renders "Young."
- **The King and Queen.** *serenissimus … Rex vester* = **James VI of Scotland** (later James I of England), who visited Uraniborg in spring 1590 while in Denmark for his marriage; *suavissima Regina nostrate* = his queen, **Anne of Denmark** ("our [own countrywoman]," daughter of Frederik II). Confirmed in the literature consulted (Dreyer, *Tycho Brahe*; *Tycho Brahe and Prague*).
- **The royal visit.** *meas … aedes in hac insula invisere non sit dedignata* — the visit of James VI to Hven; Tycho asks Young to convey humble thanks. The deferential third-person *ipsius Maiestati* / *non sit dedignata* (singular Majesty) is kept.
- **Scottish privilege.** *privilegium … pro meis typographicis laboribus … ne … in Scotia recudantur aut divendantur, absque meo concessu* — Tycho seeks a royal Scottish printing-privilege forbidding the unauthorized reprinting or sale of his works (printed at his own Uraniborg press) in Scotland, parallel to privileges he held elsewhere.
- **Imperial privilege.** *privilegium Caesareum … procurante … D. IACOBO CURTIO, Imperij Pro-Cancellario* = **Jakob Kurtz von Senftenau** (Jacobus Curtius), Imperial Vice-Chancellor (*Pro-Cancellarius / Procancellarius*), through whom Tycho had obtained an Imperial printing-privilege, granted *in membrana* (on parchment). *Caesareum diploma* / *Caesareano … diplomati* rendered "Imperial diploma."
- **Buchanan.** *BUCHANANI effigiem … ipsius vitam a te ipso conscriptam* = a portrait of **George Buchanan** (1506–1582), the great Scottish humanist and historian (and James VI's tutor), together with a life of Buchanan written by Young himself. Tycho acknowledges receiving the portrait but is still awaiting the *vita*.
- **John Craig.** *D. Doctorem IOHANNEM CRAGIUM, medicinam Edinburgi facientem … Mathematicum* = **John Craig** (d. 1620), the Scots Aristotelian physician and mathematician at Edinburgh with whom Tycho conducted an epistolary dispute over whether the comet of 1577 was supralunary; Craig had objected to claims in Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (Uraniborg, 1588). Tycho here speaks warmly of him and asks Young to commend him to the king *de meliore nota* ("on the better footing," a Ciceronian idiom, flagged with *ut aiunt* "as they say").
- ***libro nostro secundo de recentioribus aetherei mundi phaenomenis*** — "our second book on the more recent phenomena of the ethereal world" = the second part of Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (1588), treating the comet of 1577. *contraria opposuerit … apologetice … obviavi*: Craig raised objections, which Tycho says he answered apologetically (i.e. in defence/refutation), *satis luculenter* "clearly enough." The author's own hedge is preserved.
- ***hunc eruditum iuvenem*** — "this learned young man," the unnamed bearer of the letter, the *occasio* prompting it.
- ***musaeo meo*** — "my study" (the *Museum*, a scholar's workroom), as in the Wolf letter, not a public museum.
- **Epistolary formulae.** Heading *PETRO IUNIO TYCHO BRAHE* (dative addressee + nominative sender), with no salutation verb; *Vale* → "Farewell"; *nec sinam me ullo officij genere a te superari* keeps the courtesy-competition topos ("nor shall I allow myself to be outdone … in any kind of courtesy").
- **Calendar / place.** *Datae Uraniburgi die 27. Oct. An. 1590* = "Given at Uraniborg, 27 October 1590" (**O.S.** — Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The dateline agrees with the catalogue label; no discrepancy.
- **Conditional logic (checked).** Two future-more-vivid conditions govern the requests: *Si … impetrâris, feceris mihi rem … gratam* (Scottish privilege) and *Sin tandem aliqua scripseris, ego crebrius* (the closing reciprocity). Both are positive (no negation reversed); the single negation in *ne … recudantur aut divendantur* (the privilege is to *forbid* reprinting/selling) is preserved as a prohibitive clause.

documents.incipit: LITERAS tuas circa initia Septembris ad me Hamburgo perscriptas, vir praestantissime …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO INPRIMISQUE ERUDITO VIRO D. THOMAe SAVELLO, ANGLO, AMICO SUO DILECTO. ENGELANDTT. S.

LITERAS tuas circa initia Septembris ad me Hamburgo perscriptas, vir praestantissime eruditissimeque, misit huc clarissimus vir D. Doctor WINSHEMIUS, easque dum peregre in Seelandia absum, die 22. Novembris recepi, quae mihi admodum gratae erant. Nec enim insolitum quid accidit, si viri eruditi in varijs Europae locis, utut de facie mihi ignoti, ad me subinde dent literas. Quod et ego vicissim per occasionem facere non supersedeo. Non tamen ita mihi ipsi placeo, nec tanto me dignor honore, quo tu candore et benevolentia singulari erga me potius allectus, quam quod eiuscemodi quid agnoscam, me afficis. Si praesens praesentem aliquando allocutus fuisses, ex quo sic aliquoties animum induxeras, equidem tuus huc accessus mihi percarus evenisset. Solent praeter alias nationes diversas tui quoque Conterranei Angli me quotannis, aestatis praesertim tempore, crebro invisere, quos et, uti par est, in pretio habeo, et prout cuiusque fert ingenium atque desiderium, libenter cum illis de re qualibet proposita confero, quod et tecum non gravatim facerem, cum ex literis tuis perspiciam, tanquam ex ungue leonem, te ingenij acumine iudicio et eloquentia praepollere, modo Aeolus atque Neptunus tam averso animo mihi tuum huc adventum non invidissent. Reddentur forte alias placatiores, nam et eos, qui ventis atque undis praesunt, instar eorum mutabiles esse condecet. Nec fera tempestas toto perdurat in anno. Dabitur forsan aliquando occasio, qua, his faventibus et benignius aspirantibus, id quod hactenus non successit, commodius expedies. Eris mihi, ubi id evenerit, hospes apprime acceptus. Interim quod licet et decet, quodque a me tam obnixe expetis, praestare non intermittam. Mitto siquidem bina Exemplaria libri nostri secundi de recentioribus coeli Phaenomenis. Licet enim non libenter haec a caeteris tomis nondum typis integre absolutis, avello, tamen tuae sincerae et amicae petitioni morem gerere volui. Habebis et reliquos, sine quibus hic pene mutilus est, quando typis nostris ad Colophonem fuerint deducti. Interea temporis per otium hunc, quo nunc te dono, evolve, disquire, dijudica. Et si quid in hoc dubij, aut minus apodictice prolatum adinveneris, ingenue admone, tuamque et aliorum praestantium in Anglia Philosophorum de singulis eruditam censuram, sive pro sive contra nos faciat, conquire, audacter profer, meque per literas, cum libera restituetur navigatio, de his certiorem redde. Vale et magnificum spectatissimumque virum Dominum DANIELEM ROGERSIUM, Regineae Maiestatis Consiliarium atque Secretarium dignissimum (qui etiam Legationis huc in Daniam munere functus, me cum suo comitatu aliquando invisere non est gravatus) meo nomine saluta, unâque illum de mihi promisso serenissimae Reginae Privilegio librario, pro quo iam aliquoties frustra ad ipsum scripsi, admone ut mature stet promissis, quo Diploma illud primo vere, si antea ob hyemis asperitatem fieri nequeat, certo obtineam, cum caeteris quibusdam, ab Imperatore atque alijs Regibus impetratis, Operibus nostris praefigendum. Aut si Privilegium illud non est missurus, indicet saltem, quod et cur id non concedatur, sicque fidem datam apud me sufficienter redemerit, eritque excusatus. Saluta quoque meo nomine officiose Nobilissimum et excellentissimum Dominum IOHANNEM DEE, quem in patriam feliciter reversum audivi, ipsique hoc nomine congratulor, omniaque prospera opto. Nobilissimum quoque et pariter eruditissimum Mathematicum THOMAM DIGGESSÆUM ex meo ore non insalutatum relinque, cui etiam ex animo faveo et bene cupio. Utrique autem horum librum nostrum transmissum ostende, ut et illi in eum disquirant atque suam de eius contentis sententiam libere pronuntient. Quod si literis ad me datis praestiterint, ego et respondere et amicitiam in posterum cum illis colere atque de rebus Philosophicis et Mathematicis iucunde conferre nequaquam detrectabo.

Iterum atque iterum diu et bene vale.
Dabantur Uraniburgi, Calendis Decembris, Anno 1590.
TYCHO BRAHE
manu propria.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 285; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Addidi quaterna Exemplaria meae Effigiei nuper Amsterodami cupro insculptae. Si qui sunt apud vos excellentes poëtae, quales in fecunda et facunda vestra et terra et venâ plurimos inveniri non dubito, cuperem, ut argutum aliquod Epigramma in Iconam hanc atque operum meorum commendationem delectationis ergo luderent. Quâ in re eruditißimus Dominus DANIEL ROGERSIUS suam quoque erga me probare poßet benevolentiam, modo a Reipublicae serioribus negotijs tantillulum vacaret.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and especially learned gentleman, Master Thomas Savile, Englishman, his beloved friend. England. Greeting.**

Your letter, written out to me from Hamburg about the beginning of September, most excellent and most learned Sir, the renowned gentleman Doctor Winsheim sent on hither, and I received it on 22 November while I was away from home in Zealand — and it was most welcome to me. For it is no unusual thing that learned men in various parts of Europe, however unknown to me by face, send me letters from time to time; which I too, in turn, do not refrain from doing when occasion offers. Yet I am not so well-pleased with myself, nor do I deem myself worthy of so great an honour, as that with which you regard me — drawn rather by your singular candour and goodwill toward me than because I recognize anything of the kind [in myself]. Had you at some time addressed me in person, face to face — since you had so often turned your mind that way — your coming here would assuredly have proved most dear to me. Besides other various nations, your own countrymen the English are wont to visit me often every year, especially in the summer season; and these, as is fitting, I hold in esteem, and, according as each one's bent and wish carries him, I gladly confer with them on whatever matter is put forward — which I would do with you too, and not grudgingly, since from your letter I perceive, as the lion from its claw, that you excel in keenness of intellect, in judgement, and in eloquence: if only Aeolus and Neptune had not, with so adverse a temper, begrudged me your coming hither. They will perhaps be rendered more placable another time, for it befits even those who preside over the winds and the waves to be, like them, changeable. Nor does a fierce tempest endure throughout the whole year. Perhaps occasion will some day be given whereby — with these favouring and breathing more kindly — you will more conveniently accomplish what has not hitherto succeeded. When that comes to pass, you will be to me a guest most welcome. Meanwhile what is permitted and seemly, and what you so earnestly seek of me, I shall not fail to perform. For I am sending two copies of our second book, *On the More Recent Phenomena of the Heavens*. Although indeed it is not willingly that I tear these away from the other volumes, not yet wholly finished at the press, nevertheless I wished to comply with your sincere and friendly request. You shall have the rest also — without which this one is well-nigh mutilated — when they shall have been brought to the colophon by our press. In the meantime, at your leisure unroll, examine, and judge this [book] with which I now present you. And if you find anything in it doubtful, or set forth less than apodictically, frankly admonish me; and seek out your own learned verdict, and that of other eminent philosophers in England, on the several points — whether it make for us or against us — boldly bring it forward, and by letter inform me of these things, when free navigation shall be restored. Farewell; and greet in my name the magnificent and most distinguished gentleman Master Daniel Rogers, Her Majesty the Queen's Councillor and most worthy Secretary (who, when discharging here in Denmark the office of an embassy, did not grudge to visit me at one time with his retinue), and at the same time admonish him concerning the printing-privilege promised me by the most serene Queen — for which I have already several times written to him in vain — that he stand maturely by his promises, so that I may certainly obtain that diploma in the first spring, if it cannot be done before on account of the harshness of winter, to be prefixed to our works together with certain others obtained from the Emperor and from other Kings. Or, if he does not intend to send that privilege, let him at least indicate that, and why, it is not granted, and so he will have sufficiently redeemed in my eyes the pledge he gave, and will stand excused. Greet also dutifully in my name the most noble and most excellent gentleman Master John Dee, whom I have heard has happily returned to his homeland, and on this account I congratulate him and wish him all prosperity. The most noble and equally most learned mathematician Thomas Digges, too, do not leave ungreeted from my lips, to whom likewise I am heartily favourable and wish well. To both of these show our book, sent on [to them], that they too may examine into it and freely pronounce their opinion on its contents. And if they perform this by letters sent to me, I shall by no means decline both to reply and henceforth to cultivate friendship with them, and to confer pleasantly on philosophical and mathematical matters.

Again and again, long and well, farewell.
Given at Uraniborg, on the Kalends of December, the year 1590.
TYCHO BRAHE
in his own hand.


*[Postscript:]* I have added four copies of my likeness, lately engraved on copper at Amsterdam. If there are among you any excellent poets — such as I do not doubt are to be found in great number in your fertile and eloquent land and vein — I should wish that, for delight's sake, they might play [i.e. compose] some witty Epigram upon this Image and in commendation of my works. In which matter the most learned Daniel Rogers could also prove his goodwill toward me, if only he had a little leisure from the graver affairs of the Commonwealth.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / place.** Tycho Brahe writing from **Uraniborg** on the island of Hven, at the height of his Hven period.
- **Recipient.** *Thomas Savellus, Anglus* = **Thomas Savile** (c. 1561–1593), Oxford scholar, younger brother of Sir Henry Savile (Warden of Merton, Provost of Eton). He had corresponded with Tycho from Hamburg in September 1590. He died in 1593; the *De recentioribus phaenomenis* copy Tycho here despatches survives in the **Bodleian Library, Oxford** (Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, App. I, citing TBOO VII, 284.15–16, 285.1–3; Norlind 1970, 123). The address "*Savello*" is the Latinised form; the modern surname is Savile, not (as sometimes conflated) the elder brother Sir Henry.
- **Address-line *ENGELANDTT*.** A vernacular geographic tag — German/Danish *Engeland* ("England") — appended after the Latin salutation, marking the letter's destination. It is a chancery/postal direction, not Latin; kept verbatim in the source block and rendered "England." in the translation. *ANCLO* in the address is a copyist's form of *ANGLO* ("Englishman"); printed *C* for *G* is retained in the source block.
- **Intermediary.** *D. Doctor Winshemius* — "Doctor Winsheim," the learned go-between at Hamburg who forwarded Savile's September letter to Hven. The exact identity (the Latin toponymic surname *Winshemius* = "of Windsheim") is not firmly fixed by the present sources; identified only as the Hamburg forwarder named in the letter. **Flagged**, not asserted.
- **Persons greeted.**
 - *Daniel Rogersius* = **Daniel Rogers** (c. 1538–1591), the English diplomat and humanist, "Her Majesty's Councillor and Secretary," who had served on an embassy to Denmark and had visited Tycho on Hven. Tycho presses him about the English printing-privilege promised by Queen **Elizabeth I** (*serenissima Regina*).
 - *Iohannes Dee* = **John Dee** (1527–1608/9), the English mathematician and magus, whom Tycho has heard "has happily returned to his homeland" (Dee returned to England from the Continent in late 1589). Tycho's request that Dee see a copy is the documentary basis for the long-discussed Dee↔Tycho contact.
 - *Thomas Diggessaeus* = **Thomas Digges** (c. 1546–1595), Dee's pupil, the English Copernican mathematician.
- **Work sent.** *liber noster secundus de recentioribus coeli Phaenomenis* = Tycho's **second book, *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis*** (Uraniborg [C. Weida], 1588), treating the comet of 1577. The two copies are to be shown to Dee and Digges; Tycho explicitly invites criticism ("whether it make for us or against us"). *reliqui … tomi … ad Colophonem* — the remaining volumes of the projected set (the *Progymnasmata* etc.) "not yet wholly finished at the press," to follow when carried "to the colophon."
- **Classical figures / sententiae.**
 - *tanquam ex ungue leonem* — "as the lion from its claw," the proverb (*ex ungue leonem*): to judge the whole from a small part; here, Savile's quality inferred from his letter. Kept as the proverb.
 - *Aeolus atque Neptunus* — Aeolus (god of the winds) and Neptune (god of the sea): a periphrasis for the storms that prevented Savile's intended crossing to Hven. The conceit is sustained ("those who preside over the winds and the waves … changeable"; "a fierce tempest [does not] endure throughout the whole year").
 - *cum libera restituetur navigatio* — "when free navigation shall be restored": the same maritime obstacle that frustrated the visit also delays the post.
- **Technical / institutional terms.** *Privilegium librarium / Diploma* — a **printing-privilege** (book-privilege), the legal monopoly Tycho sought to prefix to his works, "together with certain others obtained from the Emperor and from other Kings"; rendered "printing-privilege / diploma," not modernised to "copyright." *apodictice* — "apodictically," i.e. demonstratively/with certainty (the Aristotelian sense); retained as a technical adverb.
- **Negations (verified count).** The letter's force turns on several negations, each reproduced one-for-one: (1) *Non tamen ita mihi ipsi placeo, nec … dignor* — a double negative of modesty ("I am **not** so well-pleased … **nor** do I deem myself worthy"), Tycho deflecting Savile's praise; (2) *non gravatim facerem* — "I would [confer] … and **not** grudgingly"; (3) *modo … non invidissent* — counterfactual, "**if only** … had **not** begrudged"; (4) *non est gravatus* — Rogers "did **not** grudge to visit me"; (5) *Aut si Privilegium illud **non** est missurus … quod et cur id **non** concedatur* — "Or if he does **not** intend to send … why it is **not** granted"; (6) *nequaquam detrectabo* — "I shall **by no means** decline." None added or dropped.
- **Calendar.** *Calendis Decembris, Anno 1590* = "on the Kalends of December (1 December), 1590," Roman-calendar idiom glossed to the civil date by this chapter's convention (Tycho, on Hven, used Old Style). The reception date *die 22. Novembris* (22 November) is likewise O.S. The edition *label* ("1590. 1. december. Uraniborg") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy.
- **Subscription.** *manu propria* — "in his own hand," the autograph attestation.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript, restored from Dreyer VII, p. 285 (dropped by the working transcription); the four Amsterdam-engraved portrait copies and the epigram request naming Daniel Rogers (parallels the 7 Dec 1590 Rantzau portrait passage).
- **Correction.** Latin address heading 'ANCLO' corrected to 'ANGLO' and 'praeponere' corrected to 'praepollere' (Dreyer TBOO VII pp.283-284); the English translation already read correctly in both places and required no change.

translation.warrant:

Collated the full letter body and the restored postscript against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.283-286 (page images, read visually). The translation is faithful throughout, including the restored postscript (quaterna Exemplaria / Epigramma request), and every checked name/number/date (Winshemius, 22 Novembris, Rogersius, Dee, Diggessaeus, Calendis Decembris Anno 1590) matches. Two low-severity text error corruptions were found in the stored Latin the transcribed original itself (ANCLO/ANGLO; praeponere/praepollere); by the audit's rule any text error mandates grade Possible regardless of its severity, even though neither reached the English.

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original reads 'ANCLO' in the address where Dreyer prints 'ANGLO' (i.e. Anglo/Englishman); the English translation renders 'Englishman' correctly regardless, so the corruption did not propagate downstream. Dreyer prints: *D. THOMÆ SAVELLO, ANGLO,*.
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original has 'praeponere' where Dreyer prints 'praepollere'; the published English actually tracks the correct Dreyer verb ('excel'), so the corruption is confined to the stored the transcribed original and did not mislead the translator. Dreyer prints: *te ingenij acumine iudicio et eloquentia praepollere*.

**Repaired.** Verified against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.283-286 (page images, not the digitised text layer). Both text error are confirmed: p.283 heading reads 'D. THOMÆ SAVELLO, ANGLO,' and p.284 reads 'te ingenij acumine iudicio et eloquentia praepollere'. No other discrepancies found on collation of the full letter and postscript against the printed pages.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD IACOBUM CURTIUM.

RESCRIPSI tuis humanissimis pariterque eruditissimis hac praeterlapsa aestate ad me datis literis, vir amplissime et nobilissime, amice in primis honorande, idque per eundem quem tunc temporis ad me ablegâras Tabellarium, nec dubito, quin literae meae tibi satis certo redditae sint; quare de ijs, quae tunc ultro citroque inter nos agebantur, nunc ulterius quidpiam movere, minus duco operaepretium. Unum saltem vel alterum est, de quo te denuo hisce compellandum censui. Cum Geographiae exacta cognitio Astronomiae penitius excolendae non parum (uti scis) subsidij adferat, haec vero ab antecessoribus nostris non minus quam altera nequaquam satis accurate et solide exculta est: decrevi itaque proprijs Instrumentis missis hincinde per Europam idoneis observatoribus quorundam praecipuorum locorum latitudines atque longitudines indagari curare, et primo quoque tempore cum portatili quodam Sextante, cochleis ad dissolutionem et compositionem hincinde dispositis, compagniatum quendam ex meis in Germaniam amandabo, qui Rostochij, Vitebergae, Dresdae elevationes polares exactius, quam antea factum est, scrutetur, indeque Pragam et ad vos transiens idem illic scrutabitur. Tum instrumenti huius fabricam concinnam atque usum apprime expeditum coram perspicies, atque si ita lubuerit, imitari facies. Postea Noribergam translato Organo, ibi etiam poli sublimitatem exactissime observari in votis habeo, idque eam potissimum ob caussam, ut ex observationibus quibusdam BERNHARDI GUALTERI discipuli REGIOMONTANI, illic ante unum proxime seculum habitis, ijsdemque inter se invicem collatis atque expensis, de Apogaeo atque Eccentricitate Solari, augeanturne an vero minuantur, aliquid certi et indubitati concludere queam, quod absque eius loci polari elevatione scrupulosissime cognita fieri haud posse tute non ignoras. At hanc e Solaribus altitudinibus etiam in utroque Solstitio diligenter exploratis, rimari non satis tutum est, ut diutina nos docuit experientia, caussaeque, cur id fiat, alibi a nobis exponuntur. Peractis autem ijs, quae Noribergae intermediante hoc instrumento denotanda habeo, optarem quidem illud in Italiam, ut et illic polares quaedam designarentur altitudines, transportari. Verum cum Alpium longinquae et praeruptae salebrae non parum impedimento sint, quo minus Organum hoc in Ausoniam sartum tectum absque ulla laesione perferatur, suo etiam pondere itineris difficultates respuente, vix id praestari posse mihi persuadeo. De alia igitur ratione, qua nihilominus in praecipuis quibusdam Italiae civitatibus nostris desiderijs satisfiat, mecum constitui. Degit enim nunc Patavij iuvenis quidam nostras GELLIUS SASCERIDES nomine, qui mihi paulo antea octennium domesticus fuit, atque tam in exercitijs Astronomicis quam Pyronomicis fidelem navavit operam; huic per literas iam nuper significavi, ut illic Sextantem quendam ad instar cuiusdam meorum, quos hîc vidit atque tractavit, meis sumptibus confieri procuret atque eius beneficio quorundam Italiae locorum latitudines ratas inquirat, meque de his postea certiorem reddat. At cum ne hîc quidem consistere animus sit, sed usque in Aegiptum ad septemplicis Nili ostia observationes extendere, Alexandriam videlicet in locum vetustissimae habitationis Ptolemaicae, partim ut Poli altitudo mihi usitato more illic accuratissime explorata cum Ptolemaica consignatione conferri queat, et an rite satisque exacte, de quo etiam certis de caussis non parum dubito, ab eo constituta sit, aut etiam, ut nonnulli, sed frustra, uti opinor, suspicantur, mutationem aliquam tot interlapsis seculis senserit, indubitate dignoscatur, partim ut per ☾am, cum circa 90am ab horizonte Eclipticae partem versatur, si modo per eclipsationes non liceat, longitudo eius loci, qua Geographi autoritati Ptolemaicae confisi praecipue utuntur, et de Meridianorum respectu huius atque aliorum Europae locorum differentijs aliquid rati et ambiguitati non obnoxium decernere liceat. Verumenimvero, cum instrumentum, quod in Italia parari iussi, non commode in Aegiptum, ob itineris nimiam intercapedinem aliasque difficultates transvehi operâ unius alicuius hominis possit, nec etiam unicum tanto labori atque indubiae pervestigationi sufficiat, et is etiam, de quo dixi, GELLIUS meus ex his Arctois locis oriundus, Maris Adriatici atque Mediterranei aestuationes, tum etiam aëris Aegiptiaci subtilitatem atque fervorem absque valetudinis iactura aut vitae periculo vix sustinuerit, et res haec per se alias sit magni momenti, plurimumque ad Geographiae adeoque ipsius Astronomiae plenariam instaurationem conducat, omnem idcirco movendum esse duco lapidem, ut etiam hîc votis nostris respondeat successus. Hîc vero tuum quam maxime desidero expetoque unâ cum consilio auxilium. Si enim ad Magnificentiss. Coesareae Maiestatis Legatum, qui Venetijs moratur, interposita etiam, si opus fuerit, eiusdem Caes. Maiestatis auctoritate, literas dare non gravatus fueris, quibus is rogetur admoneaturque, ut ab Illustrissimo Venetorum Principe atque Senatu amplissimo impetret, ut duo vel tria eiuscemodi Instrumenta per idoneos artifices adamussim fabrefieri mandent, et duos vel tres harum rerum capaces et industrios iuvenes locorum insuper et viarum non ignaros deputent sumtusque et necessaria, quod illis perfacile est, largiantur, quo Alexandriae non unico saltem, [sed] si id forte in tanto itinere laesionem aliquam admiserit, duobus vel tribus loci eius tam longitudo quam latitudo diligentissime indagetur: si inquam tua intercessione atque ope hoc ipsum Venetijs mature procuratum fuerit, equidem non dubiam concipio spem, omnia exoptatationi nostrae feliciter et commode satisfactura. Instrumenta autem eiuscemodi affabre et absque vitio elaborandi rationem artificibus Venetis praescribet antedictus GELLIUS, tum etiam eos, qui observandi gratia Alexandriam amandandi venient, de eorum usu atque tractatione, caeterisque ad coelestem denotationem rite et citra errorem perficiendis sufficienter instruet, stellarumque quarundam declinationes atque distantias meis hîc organis antea conquisitas, quibus uti et instrumentorum certitudinem examinare comprobareque poterint, suppeditabit. De quibus etiam omnibus illum ante paucas septimanas affatim per literas admonui. Nec dubito, quin is in diligenter exequendis ijs, quae illi a me iniuncta sunt, suo officio non sit defuturus, cum ipsius fidem et solertiam pari integritate coniunctam iamdudum diu multumque exploratam habeam. Quapropter te praestantissime et spectatissime vir non solum per eam, quae nobis intercedit, amicitiam, sed ulterius quoque per divinae illius Astronomiae incrementa atque restaurationem, quam te prae multis alijs summis votis exoptare expectareque non ignoro, et quibus insuper possum precibus, obnixe rogatum habeo, ut nostris desiderijs hac in parte subvenire, illisque tua autoritate atque suasu adeoque manuductione et auxilio praesto esse non molestum ducas.

Cedit illud, ut spero, non solum in antiquissimae et praestantissimae syderalis scientiae atque Cosmographiae promotionem et commodum, verum etiam in inclytissimae Caesareae Maiestatis atque amplissimae Reipub. Venetae, tuique ipsius, qui haec procuras atque promoves, laudem atque apud posteros, si qua restabit benemeritorum gratia, memoriam et perpetuam celebrationem. Cumque nihil diffidam te sponte tua ad rem Astronomicam sublevandam locupletandamque et meis in his conatibus adiutandis (cuius et iam antea eximium specimen in procurando illo honorifico atque illustri Diplomate Caesareano exhibuisti) propensum esse, nolo te pluribus rogando diutius hac de re interpellare, cum ultro currenti equo calcaria (ut est in proverbio) addere non deceat. Alterum adhuc saltem superest, de quo tuum consilium capere satago. Cuperem Caesareae Maiestati ipsemet scribere, et tum ob Diploma illud ab eius Maiestate mihi gratiose et clementer concessum submisse gratias agere, tum etiam quaedam alia, quae ipsius Maiestati forte non ingrata atque incommoda sint futura, humiliter atque secreto indicare. Vereor autem ne ipsius Maiestatem serenissimam atque augustissimam meis tenuioribus literis interpellando eius Maiestati aut etiam alijs dignitate atque auctoritate in aula praepollentibus offensioni sim futurus, ita ut in minus dextram partem mihi res haec vertatur. Te itaque iterum atque iterum peramanter rogatum habeo, ut quid a me hac in parte fieri liceat et deceat, ingenue commonefacere velis, et per primam quamque opportunitatem, etiam, si fieri possit ante Maris Balthici navigationes impedientem congelationem, mihi de singulis rescribere, atque quid sperandum faciendumque sit, significare non graveris. Vale vir amplissime, meque tui studiosissimum et perpetua amicitia tibi devinctum retinere (quod et ultro per me fiet) non intermitte. Communi amico nostro THADDÆO seorsim scripsi, cui etiam quam optime cupio omniaque ex animi sententia opto.

Iterum quam diutissime felicissimeque vale.
Datae Calendis Decembris Anni veteris Iuliani 1590.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Jacob Curtius.**

I wrote back, most ample and most noble sir, friend above all to be honoured, to the most courteous and likewise most learned letter you sent me this past summer, and that by the very courier you had then dispatched to me; nor do I doubt that my letter was delivered to you securely enough. Therefore I judge it less worth the trouble now to raise anything further about those matters that were then debated back and forth between us. There is, at least, one thing or another about which I have thought you should be addressed anew on these matters. Since an exact knowledge of geography brings no small aid (as you know) to the deeper cultivation of astronomy, but this [geography] has been by our predecessors no less than the other [astronomy] in no way cultivated accurately and soundly enough, I have therefore resolved to have the latitudes and longitudes of certain principal places investigated, by sending my own instruments here and there through Europe to suitable observers; and at the very first opportunity I shall send off one of my men, in company [*compagniatum*], into Germany, with a certain portable sextant [*Sextante*], [fitted] with screws set here and there for taking apart and putting together, that he may scrutinize at Rostock, Wittenberg, and Dresden the polar elevations more exactly than has been done before, and thence, passing to Prague and to you, will scrutinize the same there. Then you will see in person the neat construction of this instrument and its altogether ready use, and, if it so please you, you will have it imitated. Afterwards, the instrument [*Organo*] having been carried to Nuremberg, I have it among my wishes that the height of the pole be there too observed most exactly, and that chiefly for this reason: that from certain observations of Bernhard Walther, the pupil of Regiomontanus, made there nearly a century ago, and these compared with one another and weighed, I may be able to conclude something certain and indubitable concerning the solar apogee and eccentricity — whether they are increasing or in fact decreasing — which you are well aware cannot be done without that place's polar elevation being most scrupulously known. But to search this out from solar altitudes, even though diligently observed at both solstices, is not safe enough, as long experience has taught us, and the reasons why this is so are set out by us elsewhere. And when those things are accomplished which I have to mark down at Nuremberg by means of this instrument, I should indeed wish it to be transported into Italy, so that there too certain polar altitudes might be determined. But since the far-off and sheer ruggedness of the Alps is no small hindrance to this instrument's being carried into Ausonia [Italy] sound and whole without any damage — its very weight, too, refusing the difficulties of the road — I can scarcely persuade myself that this can be brought off. I have therefore settled with myself on another plan, by which our desires may nonetheless be satisfied in certain principal cities of Italy. For there is now living at Padua a certain young countryman of ours, Gellius Sascerides by name, who a little while ago was for eight years a member of my household, and bestowed faithful service both in astronomical and in pyronomic [chemical] exercises. To him I have lately signified by letter that he should there see to it that a certain sextant be made at my expense, after the pattern of one of mine which he saw and handled here, and that by its use he investigate the fixed latitudes of certain places of Italy, and afterwards make me more certain of these. But since my mind is not to halt even here, but to extend the observations as far as Egypt, to the mouths of the sevenfold Nile — namely to Alexandria, the site of Ptolemy's most ancient dwelling — partly so that the height of the pole, most accurately explored there in my usual manner, may be compared with Ptolemy's record, and that it may be discerned beyond doubt whether it was duly and exactly enough established by him (whereof I also, for certain reasons, no little doubt), or whether even, as some — but in vain, as I think — suspect, it has undergone some change in so many intervening centuries; and partly so that, by the Moon [☾], when it is situated about the 90th part of the ecliptic from the horizon, if only it not be permitted by eclipses [*eclipsationes*], the longitude of that place — which geographers, trusting in Ptolemy's authority, chiefly use — and the differences in respect of the meridians of this and of other places of Europe, may be settled in something fixed and not liable to ambiguity. But in truth, since the instrument which I have ordered to be prepared in Italy cannot conveniently be conveyed into Egypt by the effort of any single man, on account of the journey's excessive length and other difficulties — nor would a single one suffice for so great a labour and an indubitable investigation — and since that Gellius of mine of whom I spoke, born in these arctic regions, could scarcely endure the swells of the Adriatic and Mediterranean seas, and then too the thinness and heat of the Egyptian air, without harm to his health or peril of his life; and since this matter is otherwise in itself of great moment, and contributes very much to the full restoration [*instaurationem*] of geography and indeed of astronomy itself: I therefore judge that every stone must be moved, so that here too success may answer to our wishes. And here I most especially long for and seek your help together with your counsel. For if you would not find it burdensome to give a letter to the most magnificent Legate of His Imperial Majesty who resides at Venice — with the authority of the same Imperial Majesty interposed too, if there be need — by which he may be asked and admonished to obtain from the Most Illustrious Prince of the Venetians and the most ample Senate that they command two or three instruments of this kind to be skilfully made to the line by suitable craftsmen, and that they appoint two or three young men capable of these matters and industrious, and moreover not ignorant of the regions and the routes, and bestow the expenses and necessaries (which is very easy for them), so that at Alexandria — not by one instrument only, [but,] should that perchance suffer some damage on so great a journey, by two or three — both the longitude and the latitude of that place may be most diligently investigated: if, I say, this very thing be procured in good time at Venice by your intercession and aid, then for my part I conceive no doubtful hope that all will turn out happily and conveniently to our longing. The aforesaid Gellius will prescribe to the Venetian craftsmen the method of working instruments of this kind skilfully and without fault, and will also sufficiently instruct those who shall come to be sent off to Alexandria for the sake of observing in their use and handling, and in the other things to be carried out duly and without error for celestial measurement; and he will supply the declinations and distances of certain stars previously ascertained here with my instruments [*organis*], by which they will be able both to make use of them and to examine and verify the trustworthiness of the instruments. Of all which things, too, I have fully admonished him by letter a few weeks ago. Nor do I doubt that he will not fall short of his duty in diligently carrying out those things which have been enjoined upon him by me, since I have long ago thoroughly and at length tested his fidelity and skill joined with equal integrity. Wherefore, most excellent and most esteemed sir, I hold you earnestly entreated — not only by that friendship which subsists between us, but further also by the advancement and restoration [*restaurationem*] of that divine astronomy, which I am well aware that you, beyond many others, long for and await with the highest wishes, and by whatever prayers I can besides — that you would not deem it troublesome to come to the aid of our desires in this part, and to be ready for them by your authority and persuasion, and indeed by your guidance and help.

This will redound, as I hope, not only to the promotion and advantage of that most ancient and most excellent sidereal science and of cosmography, but also to the praise of the most renowned Imperial Majesty and of the most ample Venetian Republic, and of yourself, who procure and promote these things, and — among posterity, if any gratitude for those who have deserved well shall remain — to your memory and perpetual celebration. And since I in no way distrust that you are of your own accord inclined to relieve and enrich the astronomical enterprise and to assist me in these endeavours of mine (of which you have already before now displayed a signal token in procuring that honourable and illustrious Imperial Diploma), I do not wish to importune you longer about this matter by asking more, since (as the proverb has it) it does not become one to add spurs to a horse already running of its own accord. There remains still at least one other thing, about which I am eager to take your counsel. I should wish to write to His Imperial Majesty myself, and both to give humble thanks for that Diploma graciously and clemently granted me by His Majesty, and also to indicate humbly and in secret certain other things which will perhaps be neither unwelcome nor disadvantageous to His Majesty. But I fear lest, by importuning His most serene and most august Majesty with my too-slight letter, I should give offence to His Majesty or even to others prevailing in dignity and authority at court, so that this matter should turn out to my less favourable side. I therefore hold you, again and again, most lovingly entreated, that you would be willing frankly to advise me what may be lawful and fitting for me to do in this part, and that you would not find it grievous, at the very first opportunity — even, if it can be done, before the freezing-over that impedes the navigations of the Baltic Sea — to write me back about each point, and to signify what is to be hoped and to be done. Farewell, most ample sir, and do not cease to keep me as most devoted to you and bound to you by perpetual friendship (which will also be done by me of my own accord). To our common friend Thaddaeus I have written separately, for whom too I wish all that is best and desire all things according to the mind's intent.

Again, farewell as long and as happily as may be.
Given on the Kalends of December [1 December] of the old Julian year 1590.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** Tycho Brahe, writing from Uraniborg on Hven (place not named in the dateline; supplied in brackets), to **Jacob Kurz von Senftenau** (*Iacobus Curtius*, d. 1594), **Imperial Pro-Chancellor** (*Reichsvizekanzler*) at the court of Emperor Rudolf II in Prague. Kurz was the patron who in 1590 procured for Tycho the imperial privilege ("Diploma") protecting his publications in the Habsburg lands — the *Diploma Caesareum* referred to twice below — and a correspondent of Tycho's through the intermediacy of Thaddaeus Hagecius.
- **MS witness.** A = Vienna, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.5, the *Kladde* (Tycho's retained draft); hence the sole authority is a draft, not the dispatched original.
- ***Tabellarium*** — "courier" (the letter-carrier Kurz had sent).
- **The portable sextant project.** *portatili quodam Sextante, cochleis ad dissolutionem et compositionem … dispositis* — a **sextant** (per glossary) made demountable by screws for transport; Tycho's plan to fix the latitudes/longitudes of principal European cities by circulating his own instruments. *compagniatum quendam ex meis* — "one of my men, in company"; *compagniatum* is a non-classical (Italianate/mercantile) coinage for an associate or travelling companion, kept literal.
- **Itinerary of the instrument.** *Rostochij, Vitebergae, Dresdae* = Rostock, Wittenberg, Dresden; thence *Pragam et ad vos* = Prague and "to you" (i.e. to Kurz at the Imperial court); then *Noribergam* = **Nuremberg**. *elationes polares / poli sublimitatem / polari elevatione* — all rendered consistently "polar elevation / height of the pole" (= geographic latitude).
- **Bernhard Walther.** *BERNHARDI GUALTERI discipuli REGIOMONTANI* = **Bernhard Walther** (c. 1430–1504), the wealthy Nuremberg patrician and observer, pupil and collaborator of **Regiomontanus** (Johannes Müller, 1436–76); his late-15th-century Nuremberg solar observations are Tycho's reason for re-determining Nuremberg's latitude. *ante unum proxime seculum* rendered "nearly a century ago."
- **Astronomy — concepts.** *Apogaeo atque Eccentricitate Solari* = "the solar **apogee** and **eccentricity**"; *augeanturne an vero minuantur* — Tycho's open question whether they are increasing or decreasing, the disjunction preserved. *in utroque Solstitio* = "at both solstices"; *Eclipticae … 90am … partem … ab horizonte* — the Moon at the point of the ecliptic 90° from the horizon (the nonagesimal), used for a longitude determination by lunar method *if eclipses are not available* (*si modo per eclipsationes non liceat*); the conditional hedge is kept. *Meridianorum … differentijs* = differences of meridians (= longitude differences).
- ***instauratio / restauratio*** — rendered "restoration" throughout (*plenariam instaurationem … Geographiae adeoque ipsius Astronomiae*; *divinae illius Astronomiae … restaurationem*), Tycho's programmatic term by this chapter's convention (*astronomia instaurata*).
- **Gellius Sascerides.** *GELLIUS SASCERIDES* (1562–1612), Danish scholar, eight years a member of Tycho's Uraniborg household, then (from 1589) at **Padua** (*Patavij*); later briefly engaged to Tycho's daughter Magdalene. *in exercitijs Astronomicis quam Pyronomicis* — "astronomical and **pyronomic** exercises"; *pyronomic* = chemical/alchemical (the art of fire), kept as the period term and glossed.
- **The Alexandria / Egypt scheme.** *septemplicis Nili ostia … Alexandriam … in locum vetustissimae habitationis Ptolemaicae* — the sevenfold mouths of the Nile, and Alexandria as **Ptolemy's** observing-site; Tycho proposes to re-measure Alexandria's latitude against *Ptolemaica consignatio* (Ptolemy's record) and to fix its longitude by lunar observation, testing whether Ptolemy's value was exact or has changed over the centuries. *Ausoniam* = poetic for **Italy** (Ausonia), glossed in the translation.
- **The Venetian request.** *Magnificentiss. Coesareae Maiestatis Legatum, qui Venetijs moratur* = the Imperial Legate (ambassador) resident at **Venice**; *Illustrissimo Venetorum Principe atque Senatu* = the Doge ("Prince of the Venetians") and Senate of the **Venetian Republic** (*Reipub. Venetae*). *adamussim* = "to the line, exactly" (kept). The bracketed *[sed]* at "non unico saltem, [sed] si id forte…" follows Dreyer's supplement; the printed draft omits the conjunction, recorded here rather than silently absorbed.
- **The Imperial Diploma.** *Diplomate Caesareano / Diploma illud* — the imperial privilege (printing privilege/copyright for the Habsburg realms) Kurz had procured, later printed at the front of Tycho's *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata*. *Caesareae Maiestati* = His Imperial Majesty (**Rudolf II**); Tycho's wish to write to the Emperor directly, and his fear of giving offence to courtiers, are stated as his own hedged apprehension and kept hedged.
- **Proverb.** *ultro currenti equo calcaria … addere* — "to add spurs to a horse already running of its own accord," kept as the proverb Tycho flags (*ut est in proverbio*).
- **Thaddaeus.** *THADDAeO* = **Thaddaeus Hagecius** (Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku, 1525–1600), Imperial physician at Prague and Tycho's chief Bohemian correspondent and intermediary with Kurz; here the *communis amicus*.
- **Symbol.** *per ☾am* = *per Lunam*, "by the Moon" — the Moon glyph ☾ kept in the Source block and named in the translation by this chapter's convention
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Datae Calendis Decembris Anni veteris Iuliani 1590* = "Given on the **Kalends of December** (1 December) of the **old Julian year** 1590" — Old Style, and explicitly so labelled by Tycho (*Anni veteris Iuliani*), a deliberate flag of the O.S./N.S. distinction toward an Imperial (Gregorian-calendar) correspondent. The header date agrees with both the dateline and the catalogue label (1 December 1590). *Maris Balthici … congelationem* — the freezing of the **Baltic Sea** that would halt shipping, Tycho's seasonal deadline for a reply.

- **Back-translation fix.** *non ingrata atque incommoda* — the single *non* governs both adjectives; rendered "neither unwelcome nor disadvantageous" (the earlier "not … and disadvantageous" risked leaving *incommoda* un-negated).
- **Correction.** Latin corrected against Dreyer, TBOO VII p.285: restored the dropped syllable in 'elevationes polares' (the working transcription read 'elationes'); the English translation already read 'elevations' correctly and needed no change.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. All 5 pages (TBOO VII pp. 285-289) read as page images and collated the full letter clause-by-clause against the transcribed original and the published English. Confirmed page 289 is NOT part of this letter: it is the opening of a separate letter, Tycho to Giovanni Antonio Magini, dated 1 Dec 1590 (header 'TYCHO AD IOAN. ANT. MAGINUM 1 DEC. 1590') — the Curtius letter itself runs only pp. 285(partial)-288 and ends complete with 'Datae Calendis Decembris Anni veteris Iuliani 1590.' on p.288; the printed_pages metadata range is one letter too wide. Within the actual letter, checked every proper name (Curtius, Bernhard Walther/Gualterus, Regiomontanus, Gellius Sascerides, Thaddaeus), every place-name (Rostock, Wittenberg, Dresden, Prague, Nuremberg, Ausonia/Italy, Padua, Egypt, Alexandria, Venice, Baltic Sea), and every number (octennium/8 years, duo vel tria and duos vel tres = 'two or three' x2, 90am/90th, the closing date 1 Dec 1590) against Dreyer's printed Latin: all match. Found one text error (see defects) where our transcribed original departs from Dreyer's print; translation itself is otherwise an unusually faithful, near clause-by-clause rendering with no fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss detected.

**1 defect found:**
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original prints "elationes polares" where Dreyer prints "elevationes polares"; the same letter's own later phrase "eius loci polari elevatione" (p.286) confirms "elevationes" is the intended/correct word, so this is a dropped-syllable corruption in our Latin transcription, not a variant reading. The translation renders it correctly as "elevations" regardless, so no reader-facing meaning is lost. Dreyer prints: *qui Rostochij, Vitebergae, Dresdae elevationes polares exactius, quam antea factum est, scrutetur (TBOO VII p.285, line 36)*.

**Repaired.** Collated against Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII pp.285-289 (page images), specifically p.285 line 36, confirming 'elevationes polares' against the working transcription's 'elationes polares'. The letter's own later use of 'polari elevatione' (p.286) independently corroborates the reading. No crux remains outstanding for this letter's single audited defect.
