text.original:
NOBILISSIMO ET AMPLISSIMO VIRO, VIRTUTE ET ERUDITIONE INPRIMIS CONSPICUO, DOMINO HENRICO RANZOVIO, DOMINO DE BREITENBERGA ET REGIO IN HOLSATIA AC DITHMARSIA GUBERNATORI, AMICO SUO PLURIMUM COLENDO. BREDENBERG. S

NON desinam, Nobilissime et praeclarissime vir, te crebrioribus literis compellare, vel potius inter graviores tuas, cum publicas tum privatas, occupationes interpellare, donec aliquid tandem responsi a te receperim. Ternas enim aut etiam quaternas per aestatem et non ita dudum ad te dedi literas, quibus nihil rescriptum est. Cuperem autem quam maxime, te operum nostrorum Mathematicorum maturationem et publicationem tuo auxilio atque consilio, quod et te lubenter facturum non diffido, promovere, idque ea potissimum ratione, ut de Chartopaeo idoneo mihi primo quoque tempore, cum omnia, quae ad opificium illud requiruntur, iam hîc in procinctu sint, prospiciatur. Si itaque CASPARUS ille, quem ab ERICO LANGIO accepi, in tua, uti mihi relatum est, laborat Moletrina, peroptarem illum ad me remitti, si modo absque tuo dispendio eius opera carere poteris. Neque enim illi amplius imputabitur, quod sex Ioachimicis a Procuratore meo Lubecensi, IOACHIMO BUCKIO, praeter voluntatem meam abreptis, clam se subduxerit. Id illi, te etiam uno vel altero verbo pro ipso, ut tutius huc accedat, intercedente, lubens condonabo atque in posterum tum salario tum alijs necessarijs illi sufficienter prospiciam. Persuade saltem, ut audacter et certo citoque huc veniat. Erit illud absque illius damno nec sine emolumento.

STURORUM in Svecia olim celebrium gentilitia insignia necdum depicta conquirere licuit, utut multos, tam Danos quam Svecos, hoc nomine solicitârim. Inter quos etiam fuit Doctorculus quidam Italus, apud Ducem CAROLUM in Svecia medicinam faciens. Qui cum praeterito vere me hîc invisisset, insignium illorum procurationem non invite in se recepit. At cum postea aestate elapsa semel ad me scripserit, nullam eorum mentionem fecit, sed saltem πάρεργα nonnulla, de quibus non tam curiose cum illo egeram, adducebat. Interim tamen cognovi a quibusdam Danis Nobilibus, STURORUM arma prae se ferre piscem quendam, eodem nomine Stör appellatum, fluvio cuidam incumbentem. Verum incerti erant, an veterum in Svecia STURORUM haec ipsa fuerint arma, anque aliud praeterea additum vel ademptum habuerint. Si quid certius posthac de his cognovero, te de ijs commonefaciam.

Adiunxi hîc terna Exemplaria meae effigiei nuper Amsterodami cupro expressae, sed citra voluntatem meam et praemonitionem nimijs monilibus onustae, nec omnia decenter, prout praedelineatum erat, imitantis; ut ob id aliam illic confieri curem. Vellem autem te obnixe rogatum, ut, si per alias tuas seriores curas licuerit, Epigramma quoddam argutum et acutum in hanc atque Operum meorum Astronomicorum, quibus praefigetur, celebrationem concinnare non graveris; idemque, ut ab alijs in Holsatia atque vicinis locis excellentibus Poëtis, quales illic nonnullos reperiri non dubito, praestetur, procurare. Si quid nostra Venula Pegasea in hac Hvenula Uraniburgica vicissim tibi et caeteris recinere sustinuerit, equidem id Musis caeteris Uraniae primaevae, imprimisque sorore Calliopea obsecundantibus efficere non supersedebo.

Scripsi etiam semel atque iterum filio tuo GERARDO de Privilegio Hispanico, pro Operum meorum indemnitate, intercedente Secretario Proregis Portugaliae, MATTHIA ab Otten, Holsato, Ulissiponae agente, obtinendo, ut literis hac hyeme illuc mittendis ipsum denuo ea de re adiunctis etiam meis admoneret. Verum multo iam interlapso tempore, nihil ab eo responsi recipio, planeque aures obturare atque oculos nostris claudere videtur. Forte iam aliquanto plus dissitus, ut Hvenam amplius intueri nequeat, tam minutulae Insulae nullam curam habet. At vastum est coelum, quod spectat et scrutatur. Nec me eius inhabitatorem, ex quo, cum vicini essemus, fraterno animo nos invicem complectebamur, adeo cito ob tam modicam disiunctionem animo et memoria prorsus eliminare decuit. Anne sic Quam procul ex oculis tam procul ibit amor? Spero tamen ipsum brevi tam ad se, quam mei recordationem rediturum, atque amici officio benevole functurum. Quod ut citius fiat, te monitore adeoque instigatore opus esse video, quod et ut facias atque caeteris meis desiderijs subvenire non detrectes, etiam atque etiam te per amicitiam nostram diu multumque sartam tectam perduraturam, rogatum habeo. Vale et felici atque diutina fruere senecta.

Iterum cum tota domo suaviter dege et vale.
Datae Uraniburgi 7. Xbris Anno 1590.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most distinguished man, conspicuous above all for virtue and erudition, Master Henrik Rantzau, Lord of Breitenberg and royal Governor in Holstein and Dithmarschen, his much-to-be-honoured friend. At Breitenberg. Greeting.**

I shall not cease, most noble and most renowned man, to accost you with more frequent letters — or rather to interrupt you amid your weightier occupations, both public and private — until I have at length received some answer from you. For three or even four times over the summer, and not so long ago, I have sent you letters, to which nothing has been written back. Yet I should wish most greatly to advance, by your aid and counsel — which I do not doubt you will gladly give — the hastening and publication of our mathematical works; and this chiefly for this reason, that a suitable papermaker [Chartopaeus] be provided for me at the very earliest time, now that all the things required for that craft are already in readiness here. If, therefore, that Caspar whom I took on from Erik Lange is working, as has been reported to me, in your mill [Moletrina], I should most earnestly wish him to be sent back to me — provided only that you can do without his service without loss to yourself. For it shall no longer be charged against him that he slipped away secretly when six joachimsthalers had been snatched from him, against my will, by my agent at Lübeck, Joachim Bucke. This I shall gladly forgive him — you too interceding for him with a word or two, so that he may come hither the more safely — and hereafter I shall provide for him sufficiently, both in salary and in other necessaries. Only persuade him to come hither boldly and surely and quickly. It will be without loss to him, and not without profit.

The hereditary armorial bearings of the Sture, once famous in Sweden, I have not yet been able to obtain depicted, although I have solicited many on this account, both Danes and Swedes. Among them was also a certain little Italian doctor [Doctorculus], practising medicine in Sweden at the court of Duke Charles. When he had visited me here last spring, he took upon himself, not unwillingly, the procuring of those arms. But when afterwards, the summer being past, he wrote to me once, he made no mention of them, but only adduced a few side-matters [πάρεργα], about which I had not dealt with him so attentively. Meanwhile, however, I learned from certain Danish noblemen that the arms of the Sture display a certain fish, called by the same name *Stör* [sturgeon], lying upon a river. But they were uncertain whether these very arms were those of the ancient Sture in Sweden, and whether they had besides anything else added or taken away. If hereafter I learn anything more certain about these matters, I shall apprise you of it.

I have here enclosed three copies of my portrait lately engraved in copper at Amsterdam — but, against my will and without my forewarning, loaded with excessive ornaments [necklaces], and not imitating everything fittingly as had been pre-drawn; so that on this account I am seeing to having another made there. And I should wish to ask you earnestly that, if your more serious other cares permit, you would not find it burdensome to compose some witty and pointed epigram in celebration of this [portrait] and of my astronomical works, before which it is to be set; and that you procure that the same be furnished by other excellent poets in Holstein and neighbouring places, of whom I do not doubt that not a few are to be found there. If our little Pegasean vein [Venula Pegasea] in this little Hven of Uraniborg [Hvenula Uraniburgica] shall in turn undertake to sing back something to you and the rest, I for my part shall not refrain from doing so, with the other Muses of primeval Urania complying, and above all her sister Calliope.

I have also written once and again to your son Gerhard about obtaining a Spanish privilege, for the protection of my works, through the intercession of the Secretary of the Viceroy of Portugal, Matthias von Otten, a Holsteiner, acting at Lisbon — that, by letters to be sent thither this winter, he should again remind him of that matter, with mine too enclosed. But, much time having now elapsed, I receive no answer from him, and he seems quite to stop his ears and to close his eyes to my affairs. Perhaps, being now somewhat more far removed, so that he can no longer behold Hven, he has no care for so very tiny an island. But vast is the heaven, which he beholds and scrutinizes. Nor was it fitting that he should so quickly cast me — its inhabitant, with whom, when we were neighbours, he embraced and was embraced in a brotherly spirit — so utterly out of mind and memory, on account of so slight a separation. Is it thus: *the further from the eyes, the further love will go?* Yet I hope that he will shortly return both to himself and to remembrance of me, and will kindly perform the office of a friend. That this may be done the sooner, I see there is need of you as monitor and indeed as instigator; and that you do this, and not refuse to come to the aid of my other desires, I ask you again and again, by our friendship — long since established, and to endure long and much, kept whole and sound. Farewell, and enjoy a happy and long old age.

Again, live pleasantly with your whole household, and farewell.
Given at Uraniborg, 7 December, in the year 1590.
TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), writing from Uraniborg on Hven. The subscription *manu propria* ("in his own hand") marks the letter as an autograph subscription.
- **Recipient.** *Henricus Ranzovius* = **Henrik Rantzau / Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), the great Holstein humanist, statesman, and *Statthalter* (royal Governor) of the Danish king in the duchies of Holstein and Dithmarschen, seated at **Breitenberg** (Lat. *Breitenberga*; the subscript address *BREDENBERG*). A leading patron of letters and of Tycho; the two corresponded extensively. *Dominus de Breitenberga* = "Lord of Breitenberg."
- **Place / address.** *Bredenberg* (Breitenberg, Rantzau's seat in Holstein) names the destination; the letter is **dated from Uraniborg** (by this chapter's convention, *Uraniburgum* → Uraniborg, on Hven). *Holsatia* = Holstein; *Dithmarsia* = Dithmarschen.
- **The papermaker and the printing project.** *operum nostrorum Mathematicorum maturationem et publicationem* — Tycho's drive to print his own works at Uraniborg (he had set up his own press and was establishing a paper-mill on Hven). *Chartopaeus* (Gk.-Lat. coinage, *χάρτης* + *-ποιός*) = **papermaker**; *opificium illud* = "that craft" (paper-making). *Moletrina* = "mill" (here Rantzau's paper-/grinding-mill). *Caspar* (taken on *ab Erico Langio*, from **Erik Lange**, the alchemist nobleman and Tycho's friend and brother-in-law-to-be) is the sought paper-worker. *sex Ioachimicis* = **six joachimsthalers** (silver *Joachimsthaler* coins). *Procurator … Lubecensis* = Tycho's agent/factor at **Lübeck**, **Joachim Bucke**.
- **The Sture arms.** *STURORUM … gentilitia insignia* — the hereditary armorial bearings of the **Sture**, the great Swedish noble family. *Doctorculus quidam Italus … apud Ducem Carolum* — a "certain little Italian doctor" (diminutive, mildly contemptuous) at the court of **Duke Charles** of Södermanland (later **Charles IX of Sweden**). The pun: the Sture arms show a fish — German *Stör*, "sturgeon" — echoing the family name; *fluvio … incumbentem* = "lying upon a river." Tycho preserves the uncertainty (*incerti erant, an …*) over whether these are the authentic ancient arms; the hedge is kept (no silent sharpening).
- **Greek.** *πάρεργα* — "side-matters, by-works, incidental trifles" (sing. *πάρεργον*); transcribed as printed and glossed. Here = matters incidental to (and distracting from) the business of the arms.
- **The portrait.** *meae effigiei nuper Amsterodami cupro expressae* — Tycho's **portrait engraved in copper at Amsterdam** (*cupro expressae* = "struck/expressed in copper," a copper-plate engraving), to be prefixed to his astronomical works. *nimijs monilibus onustae* = "loaded with excessive necklaces/ornaments" — Tycho's complaint that the engraver over-ornamented him against the *praedelineatum* ("the pre-drawn [design]"). He asks Rantzau for a celebratory *Epigramma* and to procure others from Holstein poets.
- **The poetic flourish.** *Venula Pegasea … Hvenula Uraniburgica* — "our little Pegasean vein [of poetry] in this little Hven of Uraniborg": *Venula* and *Hvenula* are playful diminutives (a small poetic "vein"; a "little Hven"), with a sound-play *Venula / Hvenula*. *Musis … Uraniae primaevae … sorore Calliopea* — the Muses of "primeval Urania" (Urania, Muse of astronomy) and her sister **Calliope** (Muse of epic/heroic poetry). The diminutives and wordplay are kept as wordplay, not flattened.
- **The Spanish privilege.** *filio tuo Gerardo* = Rantzau's son **Gerhard Rantzau** (1558–1627). *Privilegium Hispanicum … pro Operum meorum indemnitate* — a **Spanish printing-privilege** (copyright protection, "for the indemnity of my works"). *Secretario Proregis Portugaliae, Matthia ab Osten, Holsato, Ulissiponae agente* = the Secretary of the **Viceroy of Portugal** (then under the Spanish crown), **Matthias von der Osten**, a Holsteiner, *agente Ulissiponae* = "acting at **Lisbon**" (*Ulissipo / Olisipo*, Lisbon).
- **The "vast heaven" passage.** The conceit turns on Hven's smallness against the heaven the addressee "beholds and scrutinizes" (*spectat et scrutatur*) — i.e. astronomy itself dwarfs the island; Tycho reproaches the (unnamed) far-off correspondent for forgetting him. The referent of *ipsum / eius inhabitatorem* in this paragraph is the same person to whom Tycho complains of silence; he is the one now "more far removed" and unable to "behold Hven." (Read by Dreyer as continuing the matter of the unanswered letters; Tycho keeps the figure deliberately allusive.)
- **Sententia / verse.** *Anne sic Quam procul ex oculis tam procul ibit amor?* — kept as a proverbial sententia and set off in the translation ("*the further from the eyes, the further love will go?*"); a variation on the *quantum oculis, animo tam procul ibit amor* topos (Propertius III.21.10), framed as a question. Rendered as a quoted maxim, not absorbed into the prose.
- **Formulae.** *S* (after the address) = *salutem [dicit]*, "(sends) greeting". *Vale … Iterum … vale* = "Farewell … Again … farewell". *manu propria* = "in his own hand."
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Datae Uraniburgi 7. Xbris Anno 1590* = "Given at Uraniborg, 7 December 1590." *Xbris* = *Decembris* (the *X-* = Roman numeral ten / *decem-* abbreviation for December); expanded to "December." Old Style (Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). The as-written dateline (7 December 1590) agrees with the catalogue label; no discrepancy.
- **Correction.** Secretary's surname corrected from 'Osten' to 'Otten' in the Latin (Dreyer TBOO VII p.301); the English correspondingly corrected from 'Matthias von der Osten' to 'Matthias von Otten', removing an unsourced 'der' not present in either Latin form of the name.

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ERUDITISSIMOQUE VIRO BARTHOLOMÆO SCULTETO, RERUM MATHEMATICARUM EXCELLENTER PERITO, CIVI GORLICENSI, VETERI AMICO SUO PLURIMUM DILECTO.

TOTA hac præterlapsa æstate nihil a te literarum accepi, dilecte mi SCULTETE, sive quod nihil scripseris, ob tabellariorum penuriam, aut Bacho, cui † proces, id non admittente, sive quod literæ istæ interciderint. Quicquid id est, ego nihilo minus has ad te dare, ut[ut] pluribus alijs implicitus occupationibus, non gravabor. Expectas forte Tomum nostrum primum recentiorum cœli Phænomenorum, quem etiam iam dudum obtinuisses, si papyri impressoriæ defectus nostros conatus non retardasset. Licet enim proprium molendinum eius conficiendæ gratia hîc magnis impensis extrui curaverim, omniaque huc requisita iam parata sint, attamen chartopæo, quem in Germaniam pro coëmendis veteramentis amandâram, se subducente, feriatur opus, cum eiusmodi artificem denuo conquirere non in promptu sit. Scripsi tamen in diversa loca pro chartopæo idoneo; quo accepto, spero me hac hyeme de sufficiente papyro typographiæ meæ prospecturum, sicque tomi nostri ascititiorum cœli corporum propediem maturabuntur, ut ad perennium illorum considerationem atque in demonstrationes et numeros resolutionem propius accedere liceat. Memini, te mihi aliquando scripsisse, quod magnam farraginem observationum cœlestium, Lipsiæ aliquando compositarum, reserves; cupio igitur, ut quicquid eiusmodi in archivis tuis habes, illud depromptum atque descriptum mecum communices. Qua de re puto me tibi antea scripsisse. Nam licet non ignorem, observationes istas minime ratas esse, utpote instrumentis vel nullis vel fallacibus acceptas: tamen cum sæpenumero per lineas rectas vel alias dispositiones ad stellas fixas solo oculari intuitu facta sit collimatio, ego, qui loca fixarum stellarum ad amussim emendata habeo, aliqualem Planetarum positum hinc ratiocinabor, et multa alias in his limitabo atque concinnabo, diligenti in singulis adhibita circumspectione; quo, si non exacto, haud nimium tamen aberranti usui, sicubi opus fuerit, destinentur. Eclipses quoque amborum luminarium, inprimis vero Lunæ, sive Gorlicij sive alibi a te vel alijs fideliter observatas, aut aliunde conquisitas, nancisci desidero, quo Meridianorum præsertim differentiam hinc discernam. Si quid superesset scriptorum atque observationum RHÆTICI, id totum mihi prece et pretio comparari averem, quemadmodum et Witichiana, si quæ adhuc residua sunt. Tu in his atque alijs eiusmodi, fac, quod potes, et amici desiderijs gratificari non grave duxeris. Ego sumptus libenter rependam inveniarque vicissim gratus. Addidi his terna meæ effigiei exemplaria, iam nuper in Belgio cupro expressa, rogans, ut, si qui apud vos, aut in vi[ci]nia reperiantur excellentes Poëtæ, quales illic dari nullum est dubium, ut nervosa aliquot et arguta epigrammata in iconem hanc atque operum meorum Astronomicorum celebrationem, delectationis gratia, concinnent, efficere velis, et prima quaque opportunitate cum ceteris, de quibus dixi, huc in Daniam ad me transmittere. Præstiteris hac in parte rem gratam omnique officio vicissim compensandam. Curo id ipsum in alijs quoque regionibus fieri, ut, collatis omnibus, quæ maxime placuerint, seligam. Nam et ego canora Poësi non parum afficior, soleoque interdum a severioribus occupationibus hac me recreare. Plura nunc non addo, cum tu nihil ad ultimas meas rescripseris. Fac igitur, ut propediem aliquid a te responsi habeam, moxque copiosiora a me expectabis.

Vale!
Datæ Uraniburgi die 8. Dec. Anno 1590.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and most learned man Bartholomaeus Scultetus, excellently skilled in mathematical matters, citizen of Görlitz, his old and most beloved friend.**

All this past summer I received no letters from you, my beloved Scultetus — whether because you wrote nothing, on account of the scarcity of couriers, or because Bacchus, to whom †*proces*[?], would not allow it, or because those letters of yours went astray. Whatever the cause, I for my part shall nonetheless not find it a burden to send you these lines, however entangled I am in many other occupations. Perhaps you are expecting our first volume of the more recent phenomena of the heavens, which you would indeed have obtained long since, had a shortage of printing-paper not held back our efforts. For although I have, for the sake of producing it, had a mill of my own built here at great expense, and all the requisites for it are now ready, nevertheless — since the paper-maker, whom I had sent off into Germany to buy up rags, has slipped away — the work stands idle, because to seek out a craftsman of that kind anew is not a thing ready to hand. I have, however, written to various places for a suitable paper-maker; and once one is obtained, I hope this winter to make provision of sufficient paper for my printing-house, and so the volumes of ours on the adscititious bodies of the heavens will soon be brought to maturity, so that one may approach more nearly to the consideration of those perennial bodies and to their resolution into demonstrations and numbers. I recall that you once wrote to me that you keep in reserve a great medley of celestial observations, made at one time at Leipzig; I desire therefore that whatever of that kind you have in your archives, you would bring it forth, write it out, and share it with me. About this matter I think I have written to you before. For although I am well aware that those observations are by no means to be relied upon, taken as they were with instruments either non-existent or deceptive, nevertheless — since the sighting was very often made toward the fixed stars by straight lines or other arrangements, by the bare gaze of the eye alone — I, who have the places of the fixed stars corrected to the exact line, shall from this reason out some approximate position of the planets, and shall in many cases set bounds to these and bring them into order, with diligent circumspection applied to each particular; so that they may be destined for a use which, if not exact, yet is not too greatly erring, wherever there shall be need. The eclipses too of both luminaries — and especially of the Moon — whether observed faithfully by you or by others at Görlitz or elsewhere, or gathered from some other quarter, I long to come by, so that from these I may discern in particular the difference of meridians. If any of the writings and observations of Rhaeticus should survive, I should be eager to procure the whole of it for myself by entreaty and by price — and likewise the Wittich materials, if any are still left over. In these and other matters of the kind, do what you can, and may you not reckon it a burden to gratify a friend's desires. I shall gladly repay the expense and shall be found grateful in my turn. I have added to these [letters] three copies of my likeness, lately engraved in copper in the Low Countries, asking that — if any excellent poets are to be found among you, or in the neighbourhood (and there is no doubt that such are to be had there) — you would arrange for them to compose, for the sake of pleasure, some sinewy and pointed epigrams upon this image and in celebration of my astronomical works, and to send them here to me into Denmark at the very first opportunity, together with the other things of which I have spoken. In this you will have rendered a welcome service, to be repaid in turn by every good office. I am seeing to it that this same thing is done in other regions also, so that, all being brought together, I may select those that please most. For I too am affected not a little by tuneful poetry, and am wont at times to refresh myself with it from my more serious occupations. I add no more now, since you have written nothing in reply to my last. See to it, therefore, that I soon have some answer from you, and presently you will expect more copious matter from me.

Farewell!
Given at Uraniborg on the 8th day of December, in the year 1590.
TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** *Bartholomaeus Scultetus* = **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (Bartholomäus Schultz, 1540–1614), the Görlitz mathematician, cartographer and astronomer, later (from 1592) burgomaster of the city. He had been Tycho's fellow-student at Leipzig in the 1560s and remained a lifelong correspondent; the two had exchanged observations of the comet of 1577. The edition gives no MS witness; the text-of-record is the **Singularia historico-literaria Lusatica** (the Lusatian historical-literary miscellany in which the letter was printed), per the source's edition field. Dreyer (*Opera Omnia* VII, p. 93 et seq.) prints letters of this correspondence.
- **Place.** *Gorlicensis / Gorlicij* = **Görlitz** (Lusatia); *Uraniburgum* = **Uraniborg**, Tycho's observatory-house on the island of Hven; *in Daniam* = "into Denmark"; *Belgium* = the **Low Countries** (here the place of the portrait engraving).
- ***Tomum nostrum primum recentiorum coeli Phaenomenorum*** — "our first volume of the more recent phenomena of the heavens": Tycho's planned **first volume on the recent celestial phenomena**, i.e. the comet/new-star series eventually realised as the *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* and *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (the latter printed 1588, still being completed/distributed). *Tomi nostri ascititiorum coeli corporum* — "the volumes of ours on the **adscititious** (i.e. newly-arisen, non-permanent) bodies of the heavens": comets and new stars, contrasted with the *perennia* (the fixed, perennial bodies). *ascititiorum* rendered "adscititious" to keep Tycho's own distinction between transient and permanent celestial bodies; not smoothed to "additional."
- **Paper-mill passage.** *proprium molendinum … extrui curaverim* — Tycho's own **paper-mill** built at great expense at Hven to supply his press; *chartopaeus* = **paper-maker** (Greek-derived; both occurrences); *veteramenta* = "rags/old materials" (the rag stock from which paper was made), here "rags"; *typographiae meae* = "my printing-house." The whole is the documented Hven paper-mill / press supply crisis of c. 1590.
- ***farraginem observationum … Lipsiae … compositarum*** — "a medley of observations made at **Leipzig**": Scultetus's early Leipzig-era observations, which Tycho wishes copied out of his archives.
- **Technical / observational.** *loca fixarum stellarum ad amussim emendata* — "the places of the fixed stars corrected **to the exact line** (*ad amussim*)," i.e. precisely; *collimatio … solo oculari intuitu* — "sighting by the bare gaze of the eye alone," contrasted with proper instruments; *aliqualem Planetarum positum … ratiocinabor* — "I shall reason out some **approximate** position of the planets." The hedges (*aliqualem*, "minime ratas," *si non exacto haud nimium tamen aberranti*) are preserved, not sharpened: Tycho explicitly judges Scultetus's old data unreliable yet usable within bounds.
- ***Eclipses … amborum luminarium … quo Meridianorum … differentiam hinc discernam*** — "eclipses of both luminaries [Sun and Moon] … so that I may discern the **difference of meridians**": lunar (and solar) eclipses used as simultaneous events to determine the **difference in longitude (meridian difference)** between observing stations. *eclipses (Lunae)* per glossary.
- ***RHAeTICI*** — **Rheticus** (Georg Joachim Rheticus, 1514–1574), Copernicus's only disciple; Tycho is eager to acquire any surviving writings and observations of his "by entreaty and by price." Spelled *RHAeTICI* with the *ae*-ligature in the source.
- ***Witichiana*** — "the **Wittich** materials": the papers and books of **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586), the Wrocław (Breslau) mathematician whose work on prosthaphaeresis and on the geo-heliocentric arrangement bore on Tycho's own system and his quarrel with Ursus. Tycho actively pursued Wittich's *Nachlass* after his death; the request here ("if any are still left over") fits that well-documented hunt. The neuter plural adjective *Witichiana* = "the things pertaining to Wittich."
- ***terna meae effigiei exemplaria … in Belgio cupro expressa*** — "three copies of my likeness, lately engraved in copper in the Low Countries": copies of the **engraved portrait of Tycho**, sent with a request for celebratory **epigrams** (*nervosa et arguta epigrammata*, "sinewy and pointed epigrams") to adorn the image and praise his astronomical works — Tycho's habitual cultivation of a learned poetic apparatus around his self-presentation.
- **Salutation / subscription.** Opening superscription translated in full by this chapter's convention; *Vale!* = "Farewell!"; *manu propria* = "in his own hand."
- **Calendar.** *Datae Uraniburgi die 8. Dec. Anno 1590* = "Given at Uraniborg, the 8th day of December, the year 1590" (**Old Style**; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The dateline agrees with the catalogue label (1590. 8. december. Uraniborg); no discrepancy. The header date is the as-written dateline date.

- **Crux (graded below).** *"aut Bacho, cui † proces, id non admittente"* — the printed source carries a **dagger (†)** marking a corruption, and the word *proces* is not construable Latin in context. The sense of the surrounding clause is secure — Tycho jokingly lists, among the reasons Scultetus may not have written, that **Bacchus** (i.e. wine / good-fellowship / the season's drinking) "would not allow it." But the exact words governed by *cui* ("to whom …") cannot be recovered from the corrupt text: plausible underlying readings (e.g. *cui [tu] preces [debes]* "to whom you owe your prayers," or a verb such as *operam das* "to whom you devote yourself") are conjecture only. The corrupt form *† proces* is **kept verbatim in the Source block and in the translation**, flagged with the dagger and a bracketed query, and **not** smoothed into a fluent reading.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD GELLIUM SASCERIDEM.

.... Dici non potest quam mihi gratum fuerit, quod intellexerim Excellentissimum et præstantissimum MAGINUM Patavium venisse, illicque æstivum semestre consumere decrevisse, quodque Instrumentum illud Sextantis Astronomici, de quo ad te scripsi, per vos elaboretur. Spero enim vos aliquot Stellarum Observationes hac æstate illo intermediante illic obtenturos. An Organum omni ex parte rite constet, distantiæ et declinationes stellarum transmissæ patefacient. Cuperem Altitudines Meridianas Solis, tum etiam Affixarum Stellarum, præsertim quæ hîc decliviores sunt, eodem diligentius observari, ut Refractionum ratio certius pateat. Eclipses quoque Lunares per Altitudines Fixarum illustrium sedulo notari, ut differentia meridianorum nostrorum innotescat, apprime consultum duxerim. Atque hæc et similia ipsemet MAGINUS, etiam te absente, facile expediet. Si Planetarum quoque loca per distantias a fixis sideribus, ijs præsertim quæ a nobis restituta Catalogus transmissus exhibet, subinde rimatus fuerit, utique quanta sit Cœli et Canonum Astronomicorum differentia experietur. Mars in ultimo Acronycho situ eundem ferme locum (digrediente ad ternos gradus Alphonsinorum calculo) cœlitus designavit, quem rationes Coperniceæ postulant, nisi quantum in simplici motu Solis atque Æquinoctiorum præcessione ab eo aberratum est, cum alias ♂ pernox factus, intra unum vel alterum gradum, nonnunquam etiam plures, calculum Coperniceum eludat. Quod vero nunc tam prope consenserit, id causæ fuit, quod circa Perigæum Solis illi opponebatur; idque nostram Hypothesium cœlestium restitutionem evidenter confirmat; præsertim cum iuxta medias inter Apogæum et Perigæum Solare elongationes ♂ Acronychius factus, plurimum a Coperniceis numeris dissentire deprehendatur, idque in diversas partes, prout Eccentricitatis insinuatio postulat. Idem in reliquis duobus superioribus Planetis usu venit, licet in his ob orbium magnitudinem minus sentiatur. Concurrunt tamen et aliæ quædam causæ, ex commensuratione veterum, adeoque ipsius COPERNICI, non satis accurate instituta; quæ omnia non est huius loci extricare.

In operibus meis perficiendis excudendisque nihil hac æstate laboratum est, ob varia impedimenta et avocamenta minus grata; si hiems tranquillius et exoptabilius otium præbuerit, favente cœlesti Numine, inchoatam telam pertexam, posteaquam cum præstantissimo MAGINO alijsque in Italia eruditis Philosophis id, quicquid erit, lubens communicari curabo. Si interea ipsius opera Privilegia a Pontifice et Duce Mantuæ alijsque Italiæ proceribus, quotquot impetrare licuerit, prout benevole pollicetur, obtinuero, rem præstiterit mihi summopere acceptam omnique gratitudinis significatione compensandam.

Canonem Radicum Quadratarum, quem molitur, avide desidero. Scio equidem tali ratione Tangentium ac Secantium Tabulas excusari posse, an vero promtiori compendio, nondum dixerim. Scripsissem ipsemet nunc MAGINO, sed ad matrem Aulæ magistram (quæ apud Reginam Fridrichsburgi diutius quam sperassem hærens, et proprijs commoditatibus destituta minus prospera fruitur valetudine) avocor, et pleraque alia, quæ me a scriptione retardant, nunc incidunt obstacula. Interim eximium hunc et magni nominis Virum, qui mei, ut non obscure, tum ex ipsius tum etiam tuis litteris perspexi, est amantissimus, meo nomine diligenter resalutare, omniaque grati et benevoli erga ipsum animi officia sincere offerre ne supersedeas. Quamprimum otium et oportunitatem commodiorem nactus fuero, illi scribere et de rebus Astronomicis cum eo ulterius conferre (ex quo videam eum earum tam gnaviter cupidum, quam excellenter peritum) non intermittam.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Gellius Sascerides.**

.... It cannot be told how welcome it was to me to have learned that the most excellent and most distinguished Magini has come to Padua, and has resolved to spend the summer half-year there, and that the instrument of that astronomical sextant, about which I wrote to you, is being worked up by you [pl.]. For I hope that this summer, with him as intermediary, you will obtain there observations of several of the stars. Whether the instrument is correctly set up in every part, the distances and declinations of the stars sent over [to me] will reveal. I could wish that the meridian altitudes of the Sun, and also of the fixed stars — especially those that are rather low here — be observed more carefully in the same place, so that the principle of the refractions may be more surely laid open. I should think it especially advisable, too, that lunar eclipses be diligently noted by the altitudes of conspicuous fixed stars, so that the difference of our meridians may become known. And these things and the like Magini himself, even in your absence, will easily dispatch. If he shall also from time to time have investigated the places of the planets by their distances from the fixed stars — especially those that the catalogue sent over presents as restored by us — he will assuredly find by trial how great is the difference between the heavens and the astronomical tables. Mars, in its last acronychal position, marked out from the heavens nearly the same place (the Alphonsine calculation diverging by three degrees) which the Copernican principles require — except in so far as it has erred therefrom in the simple motion of the Sun and in the precession of the equinoxes — whereas at other times Mars, become an all-night star [pernox], by one degree or another, sometimes even more, eludes the Copernican calculation. But that it now agreed so closely, the cause of this was that it stood in opposition to it [the Sun] near the perigee of the Sun; and this evidently confirms our restoration of the celestial hypotheses, especially since, when Mars becomes acronychal near the mean elongations between the solar apogee and perigee, it is found to disagree very greatly from the Copernican numbers — and that on opposite sides, as the working-in [insinuatio] of the eccentricity requires. The same comes about in the case of the remaining two superior planets, although in these, on account of the magnitude of the orbs, it is less perceived. Yet certain other causes also concur, arising from the commensuration of the ancients, and indeed of Copernicus himself, established not accurately enough; all of which it is not the place here to disentangle.

Toward the completing and the printing of my works nothing has been laboured this summer, on account of various hindrances and distractions less than welcome; if the winter affords a calmer and more desirable leisure, then, by the favour of the heavenly Deity, I shall weave through the web I have begun — after which I shall gladly see to it that whatever it may be is communicated to the most distinguished Magini and to the other learned philosophers in Italy. If meanwhile, through his good offices, I shall have obtained privileges from the Pontiff and from the Duke of Mantua and from the other magnates of Italy — as many as it may be allowed to procure, as he kindly promises — he will have rendered me a service most highly acceptable, and to be repaid with every token of gratitude.

The table of square roots, which he is working on, I eagerly long for. I know indeed that by such a method the tables of tangents and secants can be struck off, but whether by a readier shortcut, I would not yet say. I should myself have written now to Magini, but I am called away to my mother, the mistress of the [Queen's] court (who, lingering with the Queen at Frederiksborg longer than I had hoped, and deprived of her own comforts, enjoys less than prosperous health), and very many other obstacles that hinder me from writing now arise. Meanwhile, do not forbear to greet again diligently, in my name, this exceptional man of great renown — who, as I have perceived not obscurely, both from his own and from your letters, is most loving toward me — and to offer him sincerely all the offices of a grateful and well-disposed mind toward him. As soon as I have obtained more convenient leisure and opportunity, I shall not fail to write to him and to confer further with him on astronomical matters (since I see that he is as zealously desirous of them as he is excellently skilled in them).

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** **Tycho Brahe** to **Gellius Sascerides** (Gellius Sascerides Hafnianus, c. 1562–1612), the Danish scholar who had studied and worked at Uraniborg and was then travelling in Italy. Gellius is the intermediary between Tycho and Magini; in 1594 he would become entangled in the notorious broken-betrothal affair with Tycho's daughter Magdalene.
- **Person named.** *MAGINUS* = **Giovanni Antonio Magini** (1555–1617), professor of astronomy at Bologna; the third party in this exchange. Tycho asks Gellius to use Magini, then summering at **Padua** (*Patavium*), to procure Italian printing privileges and to make trial observations.
- **Transmission / dating crux.** The letter survives **only** as an excerpt that Gellius Sascerides copied into his own letter to Magini, written at **Padua, 14 March 1592** (the date the edition's witness field records). That is the date of the *covering* letter, **not** of Tycho's letter. Within that covering letter Gellius states the source explicitly: *"Habes, doctissime Magine, quae ad me Tycho suis in litteris, **elapso autumno**, de te scripsit"* — "you have what Tycho wrote to me about you in his letter, **last autumn**." Tycho's letter is therefore datable to **autumn 1591** (O.S.; Denmark used the Julian calendar). Dreyer (*Opera Omnia* VII, pp. 305–307) accordingly catalogues it under **1591**, with no month or day; the edition label "1591. empty" reflects this. The header gives the substantiated **autumn 1591** and appends the catalogue year. The leading *"...."* in the source marks that Dreyer prints only the portion Gellius transcribed, not a complete letter.
- **Place.** No place is named in the excerpt; Tycho was resident at **Uraniborg** on Hven throughout 1591, and the reference to his mother's attendance on the Queen at Frederiksborg fixes the Danish setting. The bracketed *[Uraniborg]* is editorial.
- **Instruments / observation programme.** *Instrumentum illud Sextantis Astronomici* → the **astronomical sextant** Tycho had described to Gellius for building in Italy; *Organum* → the **instrument**. The verbs *patefacient / obtenturos / observari* are second-person plural (*per vos … vos … obtenturos*): Tycho addresses Gellius and his Italian collaborators together. *Altitudines Meridianas* → **meridian altitudes**; *Affixarum / Fixarum Stellarum* → **fixed stars**; *declinationes* → **declinations**; *Refractionum ratio* → "the principle/account of **refractions**". The lunar-eclipse-by-fixed-star-altitudes method is for determining the **difference of meridians** (longitude difference between observing sites).
- **Catalogue of restored stars.** *ijs … quae a nobis restituta Catalogus transmissus exhibet* — the star catalogue Tycho had sent, whose positions he describes as **restored** (*restituta*; cf. his programme of *astronomia instaurata*,). *Canonum Astronomicorum* → the **astronomical tables** (Alphonsine and Copernican), tested against the sky.
- **The Mars passage (technical).** *Mars in ultimo Acronycho situ* → "Mars in its last **acronychal** position" (*acronychus / pernox* = rising at sunset, i.e. at opposition; rendered "all-night star" where Tycho varies to *pernox*). *digrediente ad ternos gradus Alphonsinorum calculo* → "the **Alphonsine** calculation diverging by three degrees." *rationes Coperniceae / calculum Coperniceum / Coperniceis numeris* → the **Copernican** principles / calculation / numbers. *simplici motu Solis atque Aequinoctiorum praecessione* → "the simple motion of the Sun and the **precession** of the equinoxes." *circa Perigaeum Solis illi opponebatur* → Mars "stood in **opposition** to it [the Sun] near the **perigee** of the Sun." *Apogaeum et Perigaeum Solare* → solar **apogee and perigee**; *elongationes* → **elongations**; *Eccentricitatis insinuatio* → "the working-in [*insinuatio*] of the **eccentricity**" — *insinuatio* is here rendered literally and flagged (see crux). *Hypothesium coelestium restitutionem* → "the **restoration** of the celestial **hypotheses**," Tycho's claim that the close Mars opposition confirms his own (geo-heliocentric) world-system. *reliquis duobus superioribus Planetis* → "the remaining two superior planets" (Jupiter and Saturn); *orbium magnitudinem* → "the magnitude of the **orbs**". *commensuratione veterum* → "the **commensuration** of the ancients."
- **Symbol.** The Mars glyph **♂** appears twice in the source for *Mars*; named "Mars" in the translation, glyph retained in the Source block. (Favaro's edition renders the same glyph as the garbled *cT / </*.)
- **"My works … the web I have begun."** *In operibus meis perficiendis excudendisque* → "completing and **printing** my works"; *inchoatam telam pertexam* → "I shall weave through the web I have begun," the loom metaphor for finishing the *Astronomiae instauratae* programme (the press at Uraniborg). *favente coelesti Numine* → "by the favour of the heavenly Deity," a piety formula, kept.
- **Privileges.** *Privilegia a Pontifice et Duce Mantuae* → printing **privileges** (copyright grants) from **the Pope** and the **Duke of Mantua** (Vincenzo I Gonzaga), to be sought through Magini's good offices.
- **Mathematics.** *Canonem Radicum Quadratarum* → "the **table of square roots**" Magini was preparing; *Tangentium ac Secantium Tabulas* → "tables of **tangents and secants**"; *promtiori compendio* → "a readier shortcut." Tycho's hedge is preserved verbatim: *an vero promtiori compendio, **nondum dixerim*** → "but whether by a readier shortcut, **I would not yet say**."
- **"My mother, the mistress of the court."** *matrem Aulae magistram* → **Beate Bille** (c. 1526–1605), Tycho's mother, who served as *hofmesterinde* (mistress of the court / chief lady-in-waiting) to the queen dowager **Sophie of Mecklenburg**. *apud Reginam Fridrichsburgi* → "with the Queen at **Frederiksborg**" (the royal castle at Hillerød). *minus prospera fruitur valetudine* → "enjoys less than prosperous health"; the litotes is kept.
- **Closing courtesies.** *resalutare … omniaque … officia sincere offerre ne supersedeas* → the request that Gellius return Tycho's greetings to Magini and offer every courtesy; *de rebus Astronomicis cum eo ulterius conferre* → "to confer further with him on **astronomical matters**." The excerpt breaks off without a subscription, since Gellius transcribed only the substantive body.
- **Calendar.** No dateline survives in the excerpt. Tycho's letter = autumn 1591 (O.S.); the covering letter that preserves it = Padua, 14 March 1592 (Gellius writing from Catholic Italy would have used New Style, but no style is internally specified — recorded, not converted). No in-letter date discrepancy beyond the covering-letter/source-letter distinction set out above.
