text.original:
ILLVSTRISSIMO PRINCIPI AC DOMINO, DOMINO WILHELMO, LANDGRAVIO HASSIÆ, COMITI IN CATZENELLEBOGEN, DIETZ, ZIEGENHAIN ET NIDDA: PRINCIPI AC DOMINO CLEMENTISSIMO. S. D.

REDDIDIT mihi, Illustrissime Princeps, a Celsit. T. amandatus hoc nomine Tabellarius, die 23. Martij, literas Celsit. T. 3. Februarij labentis Anni ad me scriptas: in quibus Celsit. T. statim ab initio, de tarditate et raritate mearum literarum, quodque ex Obseruationibus meis Mathematicis nihil adipiscatur, mecum expostulat. At ego superiori æstate Celsit. T. scripsi, atque in Cometa proxime elapsi Anni meas Obseruationes communicaui, et simul, quæ de illo Mathematice breuiter dicenda habui, exposui: Ad quæ omnia nihil adhuc responsi accepi, adeo vt addubitem, an ea ad Celsit. T. manus sarta tecta peruenerint, nec ne: præsertim, cum ROTHMANNO a Celsit. T. huc ablegato, qui ante Hyemem præteritam, circa Septembris finem, hinc decessit, nihil de his constiterit. Scripsi etiam denuo per eundem ROTHMANNVM, sed meas Celsit. T. non fuisse allatas, cum ipse ROTHMANNVS nondum sese in Aula Celsit. T. stiterit, haud obscure conijcio. Mansit ille hîc mecum quinque circiter septimanas, intereaque cum illo de rebus Astronomicis non inuite contuli, vnaque Instrumentorum meorum formam, Magnitudinem, Diuisionem et Pinnacidiorum rationem ipsum designare, vti ipsi libuit, libenter permisi: quorum aliqua, dum hîc moraretur, ad T. Celsit. literis consignata, se missurum aiebat, nonnulla vero plenius perlustrata et accuratius descripta secum Cassellas allaturum indicabat. Non tamen omnia ad T. Celsit. quæ in Machinis Astronomicis peruiderat se referre audere tacite insinuabat: neque enim Celsit. T. in omnibus illi fidem habituram existimabat, siquidem pleraque in illis omnem fidem excedere, nec vestra his conferri posse, sponte fateretur, ne, si forte horum magnitudinem, exquisitam structuram, et inter obseruandum tractandi stabilitatem, prout res erat, luculenter exponeret, in gratiam mei id loqui, et vestris hac in parte fabricis, quippiam minus decore derogare videretur: At ego illi liberum reliqui, ea, quæ hic viderat, siue dicere, siue tacere, prout ipsemet consultius id esse arbitraretur. Sed cum intra semestre iam elapsum ad T. Celsit. nondum reuersus sit, satis se Pythagoreum in meis non omnimode istic propalandis, exhibuit. Ego sane, cum Brumam instare viderem, vtpote tum Michaëlis Festo præ foribus existente, a quo tempore, ob appropinquantem Hyemem, nauigationes maris Baltici magis magisque importunæ euadunt, ipsum adhortatus sum, imo quantum licuit vrsi, vt quam citissime fieri posset, se Cassellas reciperet. Neque enim dubitabam, Celsi!. T. desiderio cognoscendi ea, quæ hîc viderat, quæque mecum egerat, impense teneri. Is quidem propediem se istuc rediturum spondebat, at interim per patriam suam sibi transeundum, negotiorum quorundam expediendorum gratia, referebat. Fieri itaque potest, vt istic valetudinarius delitescat, erat enim cum hinc decederet, minus adhuc confirmatâ sanitate, quod color faciei admodum plalescens, satis innuebat. At quod per literas idipsum, vel si quas alias habuerit diuturnæ istius moræ causas, non significarit, miror: neque enim facile crediderim, humanitus ipsi quippiam accidisse. Videbatur alias T. Celsit. vti par erat, obsequentissimus: Et Stellarum descriptionem atque ex obseruationibus vestris demonstrationem, prout illi iniunctum erat, breui se animo lubenti absoluturum satis promisit: quod vt mature etiam efficeret, ipsum sedulo et sæpius instigaui, quo collatio tandem inter nostras vtrinque Obseruationes institui queat, et qua de causa Quina illa Scrupula, in quibus differimus, desiderentur, euidenti aliqua comprobatione enodari possit. Cum autem ex eo tempore, quo hinc decessit, omnino nihil de eo, vbi locorum hæreat, constiterit (in Daniâ enim eum esse non est quod T. Celsit. suspicetur) remitto literas, quas T. Celsit. mihi per hunc eundem Tabellarium ad illum dirigendas transmisit: cum Celsit. T. multo commodius possit, in quâ Germaniæ parte nunc commoretur, explicari (si modo nondum Cassellas reuersus sit) atque eo literas, siue has siue alias propria autoritate dirigere. Quantum ad Mathematicas Obseruationes et Stellarum Fixarum designationes, quas Cel. T. sibi communicari clementer cupit, sciat me Octingentarum circiter Fixarum canonicam descriptionem nunc moliri, eamque Tomi nostri primi Progymnasmatum Astronomicorum (qui adhuc sub Prælo est) Capiti 2. inserere decreuisse, vnaque earum Obseruationes quas habui accuratiores, et his innixas demonstrationes Geometricas. Quin et alia de Sole et Luna cælitus deducta Obseruata, atque in Numeros per Triangulorum rationem digesta, idem Tomus cap. 1. complectitur; vt nihil dicam de ijs, quæ nouam illam et supra modum mirandam Anni 1572. Stellam, alias luculenter tractata concernunt. Quibus subinde nonnulla ad reliquos quoque Planetas pertinentia, oportunitate sic exigente, intermiscentur. Ostendi autem ROTHMANNO hîc præsenti Volumen illud Progymnasmatum, quoad hactenus absolutum est, in quo etiam pauculi desiderantur quaterniones, cum per se alias magnum sit, et vsque in quintum Alphabetum excreuerit. Is T. C. de contentis in eo, quatenus in memoria habet, vbi reuersus fuerit, certiorem facile reddet. Quam primum vero Opus illud, totaliter labore Typographico absolutum fuerit, nullatenus intermittam quin C. T. eius reddam participem. Sunt quædam ingrata obstacula, quibus quo minus non solum hoc, sed et alia quæ meditor, Astronomiæ instaurandæ sustentacula ad optatum finem, eâ quâ maxime cuperem maturatione perducere queam, nolens volens impediar, sed spero et ab his atque alijs felicem et exoptatam liberationem, quacunque tandem id ratione fieri queat. Omne solum forti Patria, et cœlum vndique supra est. Interim C. T. non ægre ferat, quod plura ex meis Obseruationibus et inuentis Astronomicis non mittam, id enim minus consultum, nec etiam, ob tot viarum mari terrâque anfractus, atque hominum, in quorum forte manus interea peruenire possent, non omnino perspectam sinceritatem, satis tutum arbitror. Mora hæc qualiscunque fuerit, fenore, vti spero, compensabitur. Daniæ Patriæ nostræ status, quem scire iam denuo expetis, est in hoc quasi interregno, adhuc (quod diuinæ bonitati acceptum ferimus) satis tranquillus et fortunatus. Serenissimus Princeps noster in Regem electus, indies proficit non saltem ætate et corporis vigore atque robore, sed et, quod pluris faciendum duco, virtute atque bonis artibus; ita vt non dubiam conceperimus spem, illum optimi et laudatissimæ memoriæ Patris heroica vestigia non segniter suo tempore ingressurum; atque ad Rempub. laudabiliter et decenter administrandam eximie idoneum futurum, tanquam ad hoc natum, et diuinitus nobis in locum præstantissimi Parentis regno huic præmature adempti, restitutum. Interim autem dum iunior hic Princeps adhuc sub Curatoribus, viris præcipuis, ob ætatem versatur, Quatuor Seniores e regni Consiliarijs Reipu. gubernacula administrant: Inter quos Primarius est Dn. NICOLAVS CAASIVS, Cancellarius, vir vsu rerum, iudicio et consultâ prudentiâ, insigniter, præter Generis antiquam Nobilitatem, clarus. In literis etiam humanioribus, præsertim vero Historijs, et quæ ad Politiarum gubernationem conducunt, apprime versatus. Si quid vero arduum et solito grauius inciderit, in Comitia Regni, quæ quotannis semel circa Solstitium æstiuum celebrantur, ad vniuersum Regni Senatum, vel etiam ante statutum tempus, si opus fuerit, conuocatum, defertur. Ita vt Aristocratia quædam, quæ etiam reipub. forma non admodum improbata est, apud nos, donec Serenissimus Rex Electus ad maturiorem ætatem peruenerit, existat. Intereaque omnia moderate et consulte administrantur, vna cum Principis nostri, vti par est, summa obseruantia. DEVS in posterum etiam benedictionem clementer largiatur, vt omnia pacate et feliciter succedant et conseruentur, exoptatissimumque nostrum Principem benigne protegat, et in suscepto virtutis tramite confirmet. Quantum ad me meaque attinet, ea pristinam ferme retinent conditionem. Ego in hac Insula priuatus dego nec me rebus immisceo politicis, quod etiam nunquam libens feci, nisi necessitate aliqua compulsus. Sunt alias satis multi qui ista affectant, quique talibus Officijs, me forte multo melius præesse queant, quibus ego hanc, vbi eam assequuntur, fortunam nullatenus inuideo, sed multo potius gaudeo, quod in copia reperiantur, qui me talibus verius oneribus quam honoribus liberent, vt eo commodius et tranquillius, ocio frui Philosophico liceat, atque rebus cœlestibus potius quam terrenis vacare; quamuis ne sic quidem ab impedimentis et tumultuationibus, quas vita suggerit ciuilis, plane exemtus, etiam cum maxime cupiam, esse queam; siue id sic quodam fato meo, siue quorundam sinistrâ intelligentiâ eueniat. Verum ego animi magnitudine, integritate, et veri iustique obseruantiâ id, quicquid erit, fauente nobis diuino, quod omnia æquis introspicit oculis, numine, exsuperare adnitar; et altiores curas cœlesti Philosophiæ, cui me hactenus totum deuoui, aspirante etiam nostro conatui cœlestium opifice, porro impendere pergam. De Animali isto, cuius etiam Celsit. T. in literis suis meminit, sic habeat: Nullum eiuscemodi hîc in Dania reperitur, neque Hafniæ, neque prope Friderisburgum. Fui enim aliquoties cum Sereniss. Rege nostro, laudatissimæ memoriæ, in ferarum horto Friderifburgensi, neque tamen huiusmodi animal vnquam conspexi, nec a quoquam relatione audiui illud istic nutriri. Hafniæ autem cognoui ante Annum vnum vel alterum animal fuisse e Noruegia oriundum, quod Rangiferum Latini vocant, Noruegi autem Rinsdüer/ quod an adhuc ibi sit valde dubito, non enim possunt istæ bestiæ calorem, qui vel apud nos est, sustinere. Scripsi nihilominus ad præfectum Arcis Hafniacæ, qui itidem affirmabat Ceruum istum Rangiferum in æstate præterita præ calore expirasse, alias eum facile ab ipso pro T. Celsit. impetrassem. Existimo autem hanc ipsam esse feram de qua Celsit. T. scribit, et aberratum ab eo saltem esse in nomine, tunc quoque proceritate, ob cornuum longitudinem et multifariam intricationem, quisquis ille tandem fuerit, qui apud Celsit. T. hac de re mentionem fecerit. Adiunxi vero huius Animalis genuinam designationem, non tam ex Icone Gesneriana, quæ tamen non multum aberrauit, quam indicatione cuiusdam ex Studiosis meis, qui Bergis in Noruegia natus est, atque se aliquoties huiuscemodi feras vidisse refert. Tunc quoque de natura earum, quæ illi comperta erant, nonnulla significauit, quæ etiam annotanda duxi, vt T. Celsit. desiderijs etiam hac in parte, quantum in me est, satisfieret. Si in posterum aliquid certius vel de hoc, vel alijs, quibus Celsit. T. delectari cognouero, intelligere licuerit, haud intermittam, quin Celsit. T. de ijs certiorem reddam. Habeo ipsemet Alcem quandam iuniorem, mihi nuper dono datam, quam si Celsit. T. expetit, non grauatim eam per occasionem mittam, et si in alijs longe potioribus quippiam per me fieri poterit, quod Celsit. T. acceptum siet, inueniar in exsequendo quam paratissimus.

Valeat T. Celsit. quam diutissime et felicissime.
Datum Vraniburgi, Cal. Aprilis, Anno 91.
T. Celsit. Addictiss. TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the Most Illustrious Prince and Lord, Lord Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, Count in Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain and Nidda: most clement Prince and Lord — greeting.**

The courier dispatched for this purpose by Your Highness delivered to me, Most Illustrious Prince, on 23 March, the letter Your Highness had written to me on 3 February of the current year: in which Your Highness, right from the outset, complains to me of the tardiness and rarity of my letters, and that from my mathematical observations [you] gain nothing. But I wrote to Your Highness last summer, and communicated my observations of the comet of the year just past, and at the same time set out what I had briefly to say about it mathematically: to all of which I have as yet received no reply, so that I begin to doubt whether or not these reached Your Highness's hands sound and entire — especially since, of these matters, nothing was known to Rothmann, who was sent here by Your Highness and who departed hence before this past winter, around the end of September. I also wrote again by the same Rothmann, but I conjecture, not obscurely, that mine were not brought to Your Highness, since Rothmann himself has not yet presented himself at Your Highness's court. He stayed here with me about five weeks, and in the meantime I conferred with him about astronomical matters not unwillingly, and gladly permitted him, as it pleased him, to sketch the form, magnitude, division and arrangement of the sights [*pinnacidia*] of my instruments — some of which, while he tarried here, he said he would send to Your Highness committed to writing, while others, more fully surveyed and more accurately described, he indicated he would bring with him to Kassel. Yet he tacitly hinted that he did not dare to report to Your Highness everything he had observed in the astronomical machines: for he reckoned that Your Highness would not give him credence in all things, since he would freely confess that most things in them surpass all belief, and that yours cannot be compared with these — lest, if perchance he were to set out plainly, as the matter stood, their magnitude, their exquisite construction, and their steadiness in handling while observing, he should seem to be saying it to gratify me, and on that head to detract somewhat unbecomingly from your own apparatus. But I left him free either to tell or to keep silent about what he had seen here, as he himself judged the more advisable. Yet since within the half-year now elapsed he has not yet returned to Your Highness, he has shown himself Pythagorean enough in not making my affairs known there in every particular. I, for my part, when I saw mid-winter at hand — Michaelmas being then before the door, from which season, owing to the approaching winter, voyages on the Baltic Sea become more and more troublesome — urged him, indeed pressed him as far as I could, to betake himself to Kassel as soon as ever might be. For I did not doubt that Your Highness was held by an eager desire to learn the things he had seen here and had transacted with me. He for his part pledged that he would return thither shortly, but said that in the meantime he had to pass through his own homeland, for the sake of dispatching certain business. It may therefore be that he lies hidden there in poor health, for when he departed hence his health was as yet not fully restored, as the rather pallid colour of his face sufficiently intimated. But that he has not signified this very thing by letter, or whatever other causes he may have had for that long delay, I marvel at; for I should not easily believe that anything has befallen him in the way of mortality. He seemed otherwise, as was fitting, most obedient to Your Highness; and he promised fully that he would shortly, with a willing mind, complete the description of the stars and the demonstration from your observations, as had been enjoined upon him: and that he might accomplish this in good time, I diligently and repeatedly urged him on, so that a collation might at length be set up between our observations on both sides, and that the reason why those five minutes [*scrupula*], in which we differ, are wanting might be unravelled by some evident proof. But since, from the time when he departed hence, absolutely nothing has been known of him — where in the world he is lodged (for there is no reason for Your Highness to suspect that he is in Denmark) — I send back the letter which Your Highness transmitted to me by this same courier to be directed to him: since Your Highness can much more conveniently find out in what part of Germany he now resides (if only he has not yet returned to Kassel), and direct thither, on your own authority, the letter, whether this one or others. As for the mathematical observations and the designations of the fixed stars which Your Highness clemently desires to be communicated to him, let it be known that I am now at work on a canonical description of about eight hundred fixed stars, and have determined to insert it into Chapter 2 of the first volume of our *Astronomical Preliminary Exercises* [*Progymnasmata*] (which is still under the press), together with the more accurate observations of them which I have had, and the geometrical demonstrations resting upon these. Indeed the same volume, in Chapter 1, also embraces other observed data concerning the Sun and Moon, derived from the heavens and reduced into numbers by the method of triangles; to say nothing of those things that concern that new and beyond-measure marvellous Star of the year 1572, elsewhere fully treated. With these are interspersed, from time to time, as occasion so requires, some things pertaining also to the remaining planets. Now I showed Rothmann, while he was present here, that volume of the *Progymnasmata*, so far as it has hitherto been completed, in which even a few quaternions are still wanting, although it is otherwise great in itself and has grown right up to the fifth alphabet. He, when he has returned, will easily inform Your Highness of its contents, so far as he holds them in memory. But as soon as that work has been wholly completed by the labour of the press, I shall by no means fail to make Your Highness a sharer in it. There are certain unwelcome obstacles by which, willy-nilly, I am hindered from bringing not only this, but also the other supports of the astronomy to be restored which I am planning, to their wished-for end with that swiftness which I should most greatly desire; but I hope for a happy and longed-for deliverance from these and others, by whatever means it may at last come to pass. To the brave man every soil is a fatherland, and the heaven is overhead on every side. Meanwhile let Your Highness not take it ill that I do not send more of my observations and astronomical findings, for I judge that less advisable, nor indeed sufficiently safe, on account of so many windings of the roads by sea and land, and the not entirely well-ascertained good faith of the men into whose hands they might perchance fall in the meantime. This delay, of whatever sort it shall have been, will, as I hope, be compensated with interest. The state of our fatherland Denmark, which you now ask again to know, is in this quasi-interregnum still (a thing we set down to the divine goodness) tranquil and fortunate enough. Our Most Serene Prince, elected as King, advances day by day not only in age and in the vigour and strength of body, but also — what I reckon should be valued more highly — in virtue and in good accomplishments; so that we have conceived no doubtful hope that he will in his own time tread, not slothfully, in the heroic footsteps of his Father of best and most praiseworthy memory, and will be exceedingly fit to administer the commonwealth laudably and becomingly, as one born for this and divinely restored to us in the place of that most excellent Parent prematurely taken from this kingdom. In the meantime, however, while this younger Prince still abides, on account of his age, under Guardians, men of the foremost rank, Four Elders from the Councillors of the realm administer the helm of the commonwealth: among whom the chief is Master Niels Kaas, the Chancellor, a man notably distinguished — besides the ancient nobility of his line — by experience of affairs, by judgment and by considered prudence. He is also exceedingly well-versed in the more humane letters, but especially in history and in the things that conduce to the government of polities. But if anything arduous and weightier than usual arises, it is referred to the Diet of the realm — which is held once each year about the summer solstice — to the whole Senate of the realm, convened even before the appointed time, if there be need. So that a certain Aristocracy — which is also a form of commonwealth not altogether disapproved — exists among us, until the Most Serene Elected King shall have reached a riper age. And in the meantime all things are administered with moderation and counsel, together with the highest deference, as is fitting, toward our Prince. May GOD also for the future clemently bestow His blessing, that all things may turn out and be preserved peacefully and happily, and may He kindly protect our most longed-for Prince and confirm him in the path of virtue he has taken up. As for what concerns me and mine, they keep almost their former condition. I live as a private man on this island and do not mix myself in political affairs, which indeed I never did willingly, unless compelled by some necessity. There are otherwise quite enough who court such things, and who could preside over such offices perhaps far better than I — to whom I in no way envy this fortune, when they attain it, but rather rejoice much more that there are found in abundance those who may free me from such burdens (more truly so than honours), so that I may the more conveniently and tranquilly enjoy philosophical leisure, and be free for heavenly rather than earthly matters; although not even thus can I be wholly exempt from the impediments and tumults that civil life supplies, even when I most desire it — whether this comes about by some fate of mine, or by the sinister contrivance of certain persons. But I shall strive to surmount it, whatever it shall be, by greatness of spirit, by integrity, and by observance of the true and the just, the divine power favouring us — which looks into all things with impartial eyes; and I shall go on henceforth to devote my higher cares to that heavenly Philosophy to which I have hitherto wholly given myself, the Maker of the heavens likewise breathing favour upon our endeavour. Concerning that Animal, of which Your Highness also makes mention in your letter, let the matter stand thus: no creature of that kind is to be found here in Denmark, neither at Copenhagen nor near Frederiksborg. For I have several times been with our Most Serene King, of most praiseworthy memory, in the game-park at Frederiksborg, and yet never beheld any animal of this sort, nor heard from anyone by report that it is kept there. At Copenhagen, however, I learned that a year or two ago there had been an animal originating from Norway, which the Latins call *Rangifer* [reindeer], but the Norwegians *Rinsdüer* [*Rensdyr*]; whether it is still there I greatly doubt, for these beasts cannot endure the heat that there is even among us. I wrote nonetheless to the governor of the Castle of Copenhagen, who likewise affirmed that that *Rangifer* deer had expired this past summer from the heat — otherwise I should easily have obtained it from him for Your Highness. I judge, however, that this very beast is the one of which Your Highness writes, and that he at least went astray in the name — and also in the stature, on account of the length and the manifold tangling of the horns — whoever in the end it was who made mention of this matter to Your Highness. I have, moreover, appended a true depiction of this Animal, not so much from the figure in Gesner, which nevertheless did not greatly err, as from the information of one of my students who was born at Bergen in Norway, and who relates that he has several times seen beasts of this kind. Then too he signified some things, which were known to him, about their nature, which I have thought worth noting down, so that Your Highness's wishes might be satisfied in this part also, so far as is in me. If hereafter I shall have come to learn or to understand anything more certain, whether about this or about other things in which I shall have learned that Your Highness takes delight, I shall by no means fail to inform Your Highness of them. I have myself a certain young Elk [*Alces*], lately given to me as a gift, which, if Your Highness desires it, I shall not grudgingly send as occasion offers; and if in other and far weightier matters anything can be done by me that may be acceptable to Your Highness, I shall be found most ready in the carrying-out.

May it fare with Your Highness as long and as happily as may be.
Given at Uraniborg, the Kalends of April, the year [15]91.
Your Highness's most devoted, TYCHO BRAHE.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient (edition-tag discrepancy — flagged).** The edition records the recipient as **Christoph Rothmann**, but the letter is addressed and written *to* **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592): the salutation names him with full titulature, and the body addresses *Celsitudo Tua* / *Cels. T.* ("Your Highness") throughout. Rothmann is the *subject* of the letter, discussed in the third person — Tycho reports on Rothmann's visit and unexplained failure to return to Kassel. The header therefore follows the source's own salutation; the edition's recipient:Christopher Rothmann is an indexing error.
- **Sender / place / date.** **Tycho Brahe**, writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven. Dateline *Datum Vraniburgi, Cal. Aprilis, Anno 91* = "Given at Uraniborg, the Kalends of April [1 April], 1591" (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The Roman-calendar idiom *Cal. Aprilis* is the 1st of the month; rendered with idiom and civil gloss by this chapter's convention The catalogue label ("1591. 1. april. Uraniborg") agrees with the dateline.
- **Edition of record.** Tycho's own *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Liber I), printed at Uraniborg/Wandsbek, 1596 — reprinted in Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VI. The 1596 volume is the publication in which Tycho assembled his exchange with the Hesse-Kassel court (the Landgrave and Rothmann). No manuscript witness is recorded in the edition.
- ***Wilhelm, Landgravius Hassiae*** — Landgrave Wilhelm IV "the Wise" of Hesse-Kassel, the leading princely patron of observational astronomy of the day, with his own observatory at Kassel; *Catzenellebogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain et Nidda* are the subsidiary Hessian comital titles, retained as in the source.
- ***Rothmannus*** — **Christoph Rothmann**, the Landgrave's mathematician at Kassel. He had travelled to Hven and stayed with Tycho "about five weeks" in 1590, and at the date of this letter had still not returned to Kassel; Tycho's report of his pallor and disappearance is historically the last clear contemporary trace of Rothmann's movements. *"satis se Pythagoreum … exhibuit"* — "he has shown himself Pythagorean enough," i.e. as discreetly silent (about Tycho's instruments) as the secrecy-bound Pythagoreans; kept as the allusion.
- **Instruments.** *Instrumentorum … formam, Magnitudinem, Diuisionem et Pinnacidiorum rationem* = "the form, magnitude, division and arrangement of the sights of [my] instruments." *Pinnacidium* → **sight (pinnule)** per the controlled instrument glossary. *Machinis Astronomicis* rendered "astronomical machines" (Tycho's large instruments). *vestra … fabricis* / *vestris … fabricis* — the Landgrave's *own* apparatus at Kassel, with which Rothmann diplomatically declined to compare Tycho's.
- **Technical: the five minutes.** *Quina illa Scrupula, in quibus differimus* = "those five minutes [of arc] in which we differ." *Scrupulum* here is the astronomical minute (the c. 5′ standing discrepancy between the Hven and Kassel stellar positions that the planned *collatio* — collation — was to resolve). Rendered "minutes," with the Latin retained in brackets.
- **The *Progymnasmata*.** *Tomi nostri primi Progymnasmatum Astronomicorum … adhuc sub Praelo* = the first volume of the *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata* ("Preliminary Exercises for the Restoration of Astronomy"), then in press (it appeared posthumously, 1602). *Octingentarum circiter Fixarum canonicam descriptionem* = "a canonical description of about eight hundred fixed stars" (Tycho's star catalogue). *demonstrationes Geometricas … per Triangulorum rationem* = "geometrical demonstrations … by the method of triangles" (trigonometric reduction). *nouam illam … Anni 1572. Stellam* = the new star (nova) of 1572, the subject of the volume's later parts.
- **Printing units.** *pauculi … quaterniones* = "a few quaternions" (gatherings of four sheets); *vsque in quintum Alphabetum excreuerit* = "has grown right up to the fifth alphabet" — signature-alphabets (each c. 23 gatherings), i.e. the book had already run to a very large extent. Kept as period printing-house idiom.
- **Astronomy programme.** *Astronomiae instaurandae sustentacula* = "the supports of the astronomy to be restored" — Tycho's *instauratio astronomiae* programme. *Omne solum forti Patria, et coelum vndique supra est* — a sententia ("To the brave man every soil is a fatherland, and the heaven is everywhere overhead"), echoing the Ovid/proverbial *omne solum forti patria est*; kept as the maxim it is, foreshadowing Tycho's own later exile.
- **Danish politics (the regency).** Written during the minority of **Christian IV** (b. 1577; elected king 1580, crowned only 1596): *Serenissimus Princeps noster in Regem electus* = "our Most Serene Prince, elected as King." *Patris … laudatissimae memoriae* = **Frederik II** (d. 4 April 1588), the "Father of most praiseworthy memory." *Quatuor Seniores e regni Consiliarijs* = the **four regents** of the Rigsråd governing during the minority; *Dn. NICOLAVS CAASIVS, Cancellarius* = **Niels Kaas** (1535–1594), Chancellor of Denmark and chief of the regency. *Comitia Regni … circa Solstitium aestiuum* = the Diet (assembly of the Rigsråd) meeting about midsummer. *Aristocratia … reipub. forma* = "an Aristocracy … a form of commonwealth," the regency described in classical constitutional terms.
- **The animals (reindeer and elk).** *Animal … quod Rangiferum Latini vocant, Noruegi autem Rinsdüer* = "the animal which the Latins call *Rangifer* [reindeer], but the Norwegians *Rinsdüer*" (Danish/Norwegian *rensdyr*); the vernacular word is set off by the source's own virgule (*Rinsdüer/*), preserved in the Source block. The Copenhagen specimen had died of heat (*prae calore expirasse*). *Icone Gesneriana* = the woodcut in **Conrad Gessner**'s *Historia animalium* (1551–58). *Studiosis meis, qui Bergis in Noruegia natus est* = one of Tycho's students born at **Bergen**, Norway. *Alcem quandam iuniorem* = "a certain young Elk" (*Alces*, the European elk/moose), which Tycho offers to send — the very animal that (per the later tradition) is said to have died at Landskrona; here only the offer is made. *praefectum Arcis Hafniacae* = the governor (lensmand) of Copenhagen Castle.
- **Places.** *Hafnia* → **Copenhagen**; *Friderisburgum / Friderifburgensi* → **Frederiksborg** (the long-s misprint *Friderifburgensi* kept in Source); *Cassellae* → **Kassel**; *Bergae* → **Bergen**; *Vraniburgum* → **Uraniborg**.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S. D.* = *salutem dicit*, "sends greeting". *Valeat T. Celsit. quam diutissime et felicissime* = "May it fare with Your Highness as long and as happily as may be." *T. Celsit. Addictiss.* = *Tuae Celsitudini Addictissimus*, "Your Highness's most devoted."
- **Source orthography / printer's slips (kept in Source block).** *Celsi!. T.* (a printer's exclamation-point for *Celsit.*), *plalescens* (for *pallescens*, "growing pale"), *Friderifburgensi* (long-s/f confusion), *Rinsdüer/* (with virgule): all reproduced verbatim by this chapter's convention and read in the translation as the obvious intended forms, noted here rather than emended in place.

translation.warrant: **Not collated against Dreyer** — no page reference for this letter, so the grade is capped at Probable however sound the translation looks. the edition gives no page reference for this letter, so by the audit's rule this was audited against the transcribed original alone and capped at grade Probable regardless of quality. Read the full Latin (Tycho to Wilhelm IV) against the full English line by line, checking every proper name (Wilhelm IV's titles Catzenellebogen/Dietz/Ziegenhain/Nidda, Rothmann, Niels Kaas), place (Uraniborg, Copenhagen, Frederiksborg, Bergen, Kassel, Norway), number (23 March, 3 February, 1 April/Cal. Aprilis, anno 91, c. 800 fixed stars, five 'scrupula' of arc, five weeks, half-year, Four Elders, fifth alphabet, Chapters 1-2) and clause-level sense (the Rothmann-delay narrative, the Progymnasmata description, the Danish-regency passage, the reindeer/elk digression). No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found; the translation renders even the difficult indirect-discourse and subjunctive passages (e.g. the Rothmann-reticence sentence) with the correct subject/antecedent throughout.

documents.abstract: Welcomes news that the first volume of De recentioribus coeli Phaenomenis is in press, noting particular interest in the fixed-star content, and inquires about Rothmann's welfare.

text.original:
DEM VESTEN/ VNSERM LIEBEN BESONDERN TYCHONI
BRAHE, HERRN ZU KNUDSTRUP.WILHELM VON GOTTES
GNADEN/ LANDTGRAUE ZU HESSEN/ GRAUE ZU CATZENELNBOGEN/
ETC.AVESTER lieber Besonder/ Daß jhr vns vnderm dato Vraniburg. am 2. Aprilis zu verstehen geben/ daß jhr jetzo den ersten
Tomum de Recentioribus coeli Phaenomenis in Druck zu
verfertigen fürhabt/ vnd vns denselbigen zu communiciren
erbotten/ das ist vns vmb so viel desto lieber gewesen zu vernemen/ dieweyl
jhr in gedachtem Tomo quasi ex professo Stellarum Fixarum
(darnach wir so lange zeit besonders verlangen gehabt) nicht allein tractieret, fsondert auch etliche hundert Stern auß ewern
Obseruationibus emendiret erzehlen thut. Wollen
demnach desselben Operis gewertig seyn/ mit Gnaden zu
verschulden. Anlangendt vnsern Mathematicum, hat er sich
zwar vor etlichen Monaten bey vns seiner Leibs Kranckheit halben beklagt/
Ist aber/ vnangesehen er vns schrifftlich zu verstehen geben/ vnd wir jhm
solchs gnediglichen befohlen haben/ gleichwol nicht angelangt. Daß er aber
nicht wider kömpt/ können wir vns nicht gnugsam verwundern/ vnd machen vns
schier die gedancken/ oder Suspition, daß er etwan ein schwere vnd schedliche KranckheitA habe/ Je lenger er nu denselben bey sich hat/ je erger es mit jhm
wirdt werden. Was das Riens betrifft/ ist ein DenischerA Jung bey vns deß GeschlechtsA ein Bilde/ der hat vns davon gesagt/ daß dero im Thiergarten zu
Friderichsburg/ Jtem/ zu
Koppenhagen/ etliche seyn sollen.
Wir haben jhn auch gefragt/ obs der Reiner seyen/ hat er nein gesagt/
sondern seye gar ein hoch Thier. Alß haben wir in libro GermanicoA Gesneri de Animalibus
Anno 1563. zu Zürich gedrucktA
folio LXXXV. Iconem et descriptionem desselben gefunden/ Aber bey denen/
so mit der Königin hieraussen zu Wolffenbüttel gewesen/ keinenA bericht davon haben können. Der Rhenen Böck oder Thier haben wir auß SchwedenA auff zwey mal fast in die hundert stück lassen abholen/ die sich auch
in Winterzeit gantz wol gehalten/ vnd auffm Eiß den Schlitten/ jhrem brauch
nach/ gezogen/ So baldt aber die Werme eingetreten/ alle gestorben/ daß wir
also sehen/ daß sie sich im Sommer/ vnd wennA die Werme antrit/ hier zu Landt nicht halten können. Was aber die
Elendt betrifft/ haben wir einesA in vnserm Thiergarten zur Zapffenburg/ helt sich von Martini biß
auff dato noch wol/ leufft vnd springt/ vnd ist guter
ding/ vnd sonderlich wennA wir in vnserm Thiergarten auff vnserm
grünen Wäglein herumb fahren/ leufft er den nechsten zu vns zu/ vnd wartet
auff vns alß wennsA ein Hund were/ Aber die Gehörn wollen jhm nicht sehr wachsen/ vnd
seyndt biß auff dato nicht vber eins Fingers lang. Ob nu das etwan ein Signum seye/ daß sie
sich nicht wol wöllen in diesem Landt arten/ das wirdt man sehen. Wir haben
wider in Schweden geschickt/ ob wir dero
mehr bekommen köndten/ Wo aber jhr vns eins oder zwey/ sonderlich die da
zahm weren/ zuschicken kündet/ daran thet jhr vns zu sonderm angenemen
gefallen/ Wir wollens auch in Gnaden hinwider erkennen/ vnd euch die
auffgewendte Vnkosten vnd Zehrung gnediglich erstatten. Was denn anlangt die
begerte Papiermacher/ mögen wir euch gnediglich nicht verhalten/ daß wir
vnder vns einen eintzigen haben/ derselb richtets allererst an/ vnd macht
sehr schro Werck/ wie auß gegenwertigen Papier/ vnd euch zugefertigtem
Brieff zu sehen/ Wir wollen vns aber zu Franckfurt vmbhören lassen/ ob wir nicht ein oder zween
darzu bewegen köndten/ daß sie sich zu euch begeben wolten/ Doch müssen wir
zuuor wissen/ welcher gestalt jhr sie halten vnd vnderhalten wollet: Wollen
wir alßdan jhre Abfertigung auffs ehest befördern helffen. Wolten wir euch/
dem wir mit Gnaden sonders wol gewogen/ alsoA gnediglich nicht verhalten.Datumin vnser Stadt vnd VestungACassel/ am 22. Maij, Anno 1591.WILHELM LANDTGRAFF ZU HESSEN.
text.english:
**To the worshipful, our trusty and well-beloved Tycho Brahe, lord of Knudstrup. Wilhelm, by the grace of God Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, etc.**

Our trusty and well-beloved: That you gave us to understand, under date of Uraniborg, 2 April, that you now have it in hand to bring out in print the first volume *On the More Recent Phenomena of the Heavens* [*de Recentioribus coeli Phaenomenis*], and have offered to communicate the same to us — this has been so much the more welcome to us to learn, inasmuch as in the said volume you treat, as it were professedly [*quasi ex professo*], of the *Fixed Stars* (for which we have so long had a particular longing), and not only that, but also recount several hundred stars amended out of your *observations* [*Obseruationibus*]. We shall accordingly look forward to that *work* [*Operis*], to requite it with [our] grace. As concerns our *mathematician* [*Mathematicum*], he did indeed, some months ago, complain to us of his bodily sickness; but, notwithstanding that he gave us to understand [the same] in writing, and that we graciously commanded him thereto, he has nonetheless not arrived. That he does not come back, we cannot sufficiently wonder at, and we almost form the thought, or *suspicion* [*Suspition*], that he may have some grave and harmful sickness; [and] the longer he now keeps it by him, the worse it will become with him. As concerns the *reindeer* [*Riens*], there is a Danish lad with us, of the **Bilde** [Bille] family, who has told us of it, that there ought to be some of them in the menagerie at Frederiksborg, likewise at Copenhagen. We also asked him whether they be the reindeer; he said no, but [that] it is quite a tall beast. So we have, in Gessner's German *book on animals* [*libro Germanico … de Animalibus*], printed at Zürich in the year 1563, on folio 85, found the *image and description* [*Iconem et descriptionem*] of the same; but from those who were out here at Wolfenbüttel with the Queen we could get no account of it. The reindeer-bucks, or beasts, we have had fetched out of Sweden, on two occasions, to nearly a hundred head, which also held up quite well in the winter season and drew the sledge upon the ice after their custom; but as soon as the warmth set in, they all died, so that we thus see that in summer, and when the warmth comes on, they cannot keep [alive] here in [this] land. But as concerns the elk, we have one in our menagerie at Zapfenburg; it has held up well from Martinmas until now, runs and leaps and is of good cheer, and especially when we drive about in our menagerie in our little green cart, it runs straight up to us and waits for us as if it were a dog; but its antlers will not grow much for it, and to this day are not above a finger's length. Whether this be perhaps a *sign* [*Signum*] that they will not well take to breeding in this land — that one will see. We have sent again into Sweden [to ask] whether we might get more of them; but if you could send us one or two, especially such as were tame, you would thereby do us a particularly agreeable favour. We shall also acknowledge it again in grace, and graciously reimburse you the costs and expenses laid out. As, then, concerns the requested *papermakers*, we may not graciously conceal from you that we have among us a single one; the same is only just now setting up, and makes very coarse work, as is to be seen from the present paper and from the letter dispatched to you. But we will have inquiry made for us at Frankfurt, [to see] whether we might not move one or two thereto, that they should be willing to betake themselves to you; yet we must first know in what manner you would keep and maintain them: we will then help to further their dispatch as soon as possible. This we would not graciously conceal from you, to whom we are by [our] grace especially well disposed. Given in our city and fortress of Kassel, on 22 May, in the year 1591. Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), "the Wise," the observing prince of Kassel whose astronomers Christoph Rothmann and Joost Bürgi corresponded with Tycho; the long Tycho–Hesse exchange (vols VI–VII of Dreyer) is the documentary core of late-16th-c. observational astronomy. The titulature *Graue zu Catzenelnbogen* (Count of Katzenelnbogen) is the standard Hessian style.
- **Recipient address.** *Dem Vesten* — "to the worshipful/steadfast," the chancery honorific for an untitled nobleman (*vest/fest* "firm, steadfast"); *vnserm lieben Besondern* = "our trusty and well-beloved" (this chapter's convention, *Vester lieber besonder*). *Herrn zu Knudstrup* — lord of **Knudstrup** (Knutstorp), the Brahe family seat.
- **Date crux (catalogue vs. dateline).** The edition label reads **"1587. 22. maj."**; the letter's own dateline reads **"am 22. Maij, Anno 1591."** The header follows the dateline by this chapter's convention The internal evidence corroborates **1591**, not 1587: the Landgrave is replying to Tycho's letter of "2 April" announcing that he now has the *first volume* "de Recentioribus coeli Phaenomenis" *in Druck* (in press) — i.e. the volume on the new-star/comet phenomena and the fixed-star catalogue (the work issued from Uraniborg as the *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* / *De mundi … recentioribus phaenomenis*), whose printing was under way in the early 1590s, not 1587. The "1587" label is treated as a catalogue mis-dating and recorded, **not** silently corrected. The letter is printed in Tycho's own *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Uraniborg, 1596), the edition of record. Date is **Old Style** (Hesse, like Denmark, kept the Julian calendar).
- ***vnsern Mathematicum*** — "our mathematician," **Christoph Rothmann**, the Landgrave's astronomer, who had travelled to Hven in 1590 and, pleading illness, never returned to Kassel; the Landgrave's puzzlement ("we cannot sufficiently wonder … that he does not come back") fixes the situation in 1590–91. Identification of *Mathematicum* with Rothmann is secure on context; named here on first occurrence.
- **The natural-history matter (reindeer / elk).** The bulk of the letter answers a request from Tycho for live northern animals. *Riens / Rhenen* = **reindeer** (*Rentier*); *Reiner* likewise the reindeer; *Elendt* = the **elk / European moose** (*Elch*). *Thiergarten* = menagerie / animal park. Places: *Friderichsburg* = **Frederiksborg**; *Koppenhagen* = **Copenhagen**; *Zapffenburg* = **Zapfenburg** (the Landgrave's game park near Kassel); *Wolffenbüttel* = **Wolfenbüttel**. *die Königin* — "the Queen": almost certainly **Sophie**, the Hessian-born consort/dowager moving between the Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel and Hessian courts (her exact identity not made explicit in the letter; left as "the Queen").
- ***Gessner's German book on animals … Zürich 1563, folio 85.*** = Conrad **Gessner**, *Thierbuch* (the German *Historiae animalium*), Zürich 1563; the Landgrave cites *Iconem et descriptionem* ("the image and description") on fol. 85 — a code-switch into Latin for the bibliographic reference.
- ***deß Geschlechts ein Bilde.*** **Resolved:** Dreyer's facing 1596 Latin (*Opera Omnia* VI p. 247) renders it *ex familia BILDORVM*, 'of the family of the Bildes' — *Bilde* is the surname of the Danish noble **Bille/Bilde** family (here a young Bille in Hessian service), not 'image-maker'. Rendered 'of the Bilde [Bille] family.'
- **The papermakers.** *Papiermacher* — Tycho was equipping his own paper mill on Hven; the Landgrave reports that his single papermaker "makes very coarse work" (*sehr schro[ff] Werck*), evidenced by "the present paper," and offers to recruit one or two from **Frankfurt** for Tycho — conditional on first knowing *welcher gestalt jhr sie halten … wollet* ("in what manner you would keep and maintain them"). The conditional is preserved (the dispatch is promised only *alßdan*, "then," after that condition is met); no royal-style command here, a princely offer with a stated precondition.
- **Latin code-switching (chancery German over a learned-Latin technical lexicon, this chapter's convention).** Technical and bibliographic nouns are kept in Latin in the source and italicised on first use in the translation: *den ersten Tomum de Recentioribus coeli Phaenomenis*, *quasi ex professo*, *Stellarum Fixarum*, *Obseruationibus*, *Operis*, *Mathematicum*, *Suspition*, *Iconem et descriptionem*, *Signum*. The closing *Datum … Anno 1591* is the Latin dating formula.
- **The superscript "A" markers** scattered through the source (*ETC.A*, *KranckheitA*, *DenischerA*, *GeschlechtsA*, *gedrucktA*, *LXXXV.A*, *keinenA*, *SchwedenA*, *wennA*, *einesA*, *alsoA*, *am 22.A*, *VestungA*, final *…HESSEN.A*) are not part of the text: they are the anchor-marks of the 1596 printed edition's **marginal sidenotes/apparatus**, carried over as artefacts of extraction. They are reproduced as-printed in the Source block by this chapter's convention(2) and carry no lexical content; the translation ignores them. Likewise *fsondert* (for *sondern*) and *Datumin* / *.WILHELM* (lost word-spacing) are extraction run-ons, read as *sondern* and *Datum in* / *. Wilhelm*.
- **Princely register.** The plural-of-majesty *Wir/vns/euch–jhr* and the recurring *gnediglich(en)* ("graciously") are preserved throughout; *Wolten wir euch … gnediglich nicht verhalten* = "this we would not graciously conceal from you" (a standard chancery close). Two negations occur in that clause-pair (*nicht … nicht verhalten* across the final two sentences); both are the idiomatic litotes "we would not conceal" and are reproduced exactly, not collapsed.
- **Correction.** 'befohlen' (from 'befehlen', to command) had been rendered as 'graciously granted him this'; corrected to 'graciously commanded him thereto', consistent with the sense of the following sentence expressing surprise at his non-return.

translation.warrant:
**Not collated against Dreyer** — no page reference for this letter, so the grade is capped at Probable however sound the translation looks. the edition gives no page reference for this letter, so by the audit's rule this is audited against the transcribed original alone and capped at grade Probable. Checked the full German letter clause by clause against the published English: the reindeer/elk menagerie passage (Frederiksborg, Copenhagen, Gessner's De Animalibus Zurich 1563 folio 85, the c. 100 reindeer from Sweden, the elk at Zapfenburg since Martinmas with antlers 'not above a finger's length'), the papermaker request (one papermaker at Kassel, inquiry to be made at Frankfurt for one or two more), and the closing date '22. Maij, Anno 1591'. All numbers, names, and place-names match with no fabrication or omission. One mistranslation found in the passage about 'our mathematician' (almost certainly Rothmann): 'befohlen' (commanded) is rendered as 'granted', inverting the agency of that clause. No Dreyer collation performed.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (medium). German 'befohlen' (from 'befehlen') means 'commanded/ordered', not 'granted [permission]'. The next sentence — 'that he does not come back, we cannot sufficiently wonder at' — only makes sense if Wilhelm had ordered the mathematician to return and is now surprised he hasn't; 'granted him this' instead implies Wilhelm permitted him to stay away, which would make the following expression of surprise incoherent. At: “notwithstanding that he gave us to understand [the same] in writing, and that we graciously granted him this, he has non”.

**Repaired.** No Dreyer extract exists for this letter (no page reference); the fix rests entirely on internal evidence — the German the transcribed original's own word 'befohlen' and the logical coherence of the surrounding sentence, which only makes sense as a command to return, not a grant of leave to stay away. No text error claims were present to require Dreyer verification. Grade B: sound but uncollated against the edition of record.

documents.incipit: MIN gandske wenlig helsen nu oc altidt forsendt med Wor Herre. Magnifice d:ne rector, oc …

text.original:
MAGNIFICO DOMINO RECTORI, HEDERLIG OC HØGLERDT MAND, DOCTOR ANDERS CHRISTENSØN, MEDICINAe PROFESSORI VDI KIØBENHAFFNS VNIUERSITET, MIN SYNDERLIG GODE WEN, GANDSKE WENLIGEN TILSCHREFFUIT.

MIN gandske wenlig helsen nu oc altidt forsendt med Wor Herre. Magnifice d:ne rector, oc kiere doctorAndres, synderlig gode wen. Nest min wenlig tacksigelse for alt beuist gode, huilcket ieg aff formuen wil findis willig at forskylde, er min gandske wenlig bøn til eder, at i will wel giøre, oc lade vocire oc fordre for eder, oc andre flere aff eders collegis, hederlige oc høglerde professoribus, eders collegam, hederlig oc høglerdt mand doctor Nielß Crage, oc der till medt ocsaa m. Nielß Colding, om hand er nogen stedts at finde der vdi byen, oc lade dennom i min fogits, wed naffn Christen Judes neruerelse, huilcken ieg der paa fuldmact giffuit haffuer, effter som hand paa mine wegne eskendis worder, bestaa oc bekiende, alt hues de wide sig i sandhed at haffue tildraget den tidt, min tiener Rasmus Persøn, som nu er vdi Gunsøgaard, haffde vdsendt vdi forgangne sommer to mend aff Roschild til mig, borgemester Christen Skyt, oc en anden, wed naffn Peder Swerdtfeger, effterdi de war da her tilstede hoß mig, at de derfor enten samptligen, eller huer i seer for sig, widne och offentlich vdi alle eders neruerelse bekiende oc bestaa saa widt som de wide, at denne handell anrørendis er, oc kunde medt en gode conscientz for Gud oc dennom sielff wide oc bestaa at were i sandhed tilgangen, oc ydermere for øffuerigheden, der som behoff giøris, bekiender.

Oc er her till lougligen steffnt oc kaldit for:ne Rasmus Persen, ocsaasaa at tage forbemelte mend medt sig, om de haffuer noget heri at sige, som i kunde forfare aff den steffning oc kaldsbreff, min fogitt haffuer ladet leßt for hannom, paa huilcken hand oc sielff paaskreffuit haffuer. Oc møder ocsaa der hoß mine kaldtsmend, som haffuer her offuer werit, oc wille bestaa det i eders paahør, enten Rasmus møder sielff, heller oc hans fuldmectige medt de andre to, eller oc icke. Er der for min gandske wenlige bøn til eder, at i wille well giøre, oc lade mig widerfaris hervdj hues billigt oc ret er, ac landzens skick oc brug medbringer. Oc at ieg kand faa alltingst nu strax beskreffuit, oc vnder vniuersitetens segel bekrefftigit. Forseendis mig till eder oc de andre eders collegis, at i hervdi giørendis worder, saa at ieg icke skal haffue mig der vdoffuer at beklage, men tacke eder for eders wmage oc gode wilge vdi alle maade, huilcken ieg oc saa altidt will findis, saa widt mig mugligt kand were, at forskylle gandske godtwillig oc tilgnegt.

Oc will hermedt nu oc altidt haffue eder Gud almectigste befalendis.
Datum Vraniburg den 21. junij anno 1591.
Tyghe Brahe
Egen hand.
text.english:
**To the Magnificent Lord Rector, the honourable and most learned man, Doctor Anders Christensen, Professor of Medicine in the University of Copenhagen, my especially good friend — written in all friendliness.**

My wholly friendly greeting, now and always, conveyed with Our Lord. Magnificent Lord Rector, and dear Doctor Anders, especially good friend. Next after my friendly thanks for all the kindness shown [me] — which I will be found willing to requite according to my means — my wholly friendly request to you is that you would be so good as to summon and call before you, and before several others of your colleagues, the honourable and most learned professors, your colleague, the honourable and most learned man Doctor Niels Krag, and besides him also Master Niels Colding, if he is anywhere to be found there in the town, and to let them, in the presence of my bailiff, by name Christen Jude — to whom I have given full authority [in the matter], according as he is called upon on my behalf — affirm and acknowledge all that they know in truth to have taken place at the time when my servant Rasmus Persøn, who is now at Gunsøgaard, had sent out last summer two men from Roskilde to me, burgomaster Christen Skyt, and another, by name Peder Sverdfeger, inasmuch as they were then present here with me; that they therefore, either jointly or each one separately for himself, witness and publicly, in the presence of you all, acknowledge and affirm so far as they know what concerns this affair, and [what] they can with a good conscience before God and to themselves know and affirm to have truly come to pass, and further acknowledge it before the authorities, where need be.

And the aforesaid Rasmus Persen has herewith been lawfully summoned and cited, [and] also to take the aforementioned men with him, if they have anything to say herein, as you may learn from the summons and writ of citation which my bailiff has had read out to him, [and] upon which he has himself also endorsed [his name]. And [there] appear also there my summoners [witnesses to the citation], who have been over here, and will affirm it in your hearing — whether Rasmus appears himself, or else his attorney with the other two, or not [at all]. Therefore my wholly friendly request to you is that you would be so good as to let me obtain herein what is fair and right, and as the custom and usage of the land brings with it. And that I may get the whole [matter] now at once set down in writing, and confirmed under the University's seal. Trusting to you and the others, your colleagues, that you will act herein in such a way that I shall not have cause to complain of it, but to thank you for your trouble and good will in every way — which I too shall always be found, so far as may be possible for me, to requite, wholly willingly and devotedly.

And herewith I will, now and always, commend you to God Almighty.
Given at Uraniborg, the 21st of June, in the year 1591.
Tyge Brahe
[In] his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** *Doctor Anders Christensen* (Andreas Christiernus / Christierni, 1551–1606), professor of medicine at the University of Copenhagen and, in 1591, its **Rector** (hence *Magnifico Domino Rectori*). The letter is addressed to him in that office, asking the consistory (university court) to take sworn testimony.
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe**, writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven. The subscription *Egen hand* ("[in] his own hand") marks the original as an autograph — consistent with witness A being the *Originalbrev*.
- **Document type.** A private letter of legal business, not a chancery register copy: Tycho asks the rector and his colleagues to receive and minute sworn witness-statements *under vniuersitetens segel* ("under the University's seal"). The matter is a lawsuit between Tycho and his former servant.
- **The Latin editorial regest** (Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* XIV, p. 70, no. 87) identifies the parties: the suit is between Tycho and **Erasmus Petri e vico Gundsömagle** (= Rasmus Pedersen / *Rasmus Persøn* of the village of Gundsømagle), and the witnesses sought are *doctor Nicolaus Kragius* and *magister Nicolaus Koldingus*. This confirms the persons named in the Danish body.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Doctor Nielß Crage* = **Niels Krag** (Nicolaus Cragius, c. 1550–1602), humanist, historian and professor at Copenhagen; here a *collega* of the rector.
 - *m. Nielß Colding* = **Master Niels Colding** (Nicolaus Koldingus); the prefix *m.* = *Magister* (academic Master, this chapter's convention).
 - *min fogit … Christen Jude* = **Christen Jude**, Tycho's *foged* (bailiff/steward) on Hven, given *fuldmagt* (power of attorney) to act on his behalf; the variant *Judes* (gen.) of the working transcription matches Dreyer (*Iudes*).
 - *min tiener Rasmus Persøn … nu … vdi Gunsøgaard* = **Rasmus Pedersen**, Tycho's former *tiener* (servant/retainer), now at **Gundsømagle** (a village NW of Roskilde, Zealand); the adverse party.
 - *borgemester Christen Skyt* = **Christen Skyt**, *borgemester* (burgomaster) of **Roskilde**; a witness.
 - *Peder Swerdtfeger* = **Peder Sverdfeger** ("Sword-cutler," likely an occupational by-name, not relabelled); the second Roskilde witness.
- **Code-switches (Latin within Danish), preserved by this chapter's convention** The address-rubric is Latin (*MAGNIFICO DOMINO RECTORI … MEDICINAe PROFESSORI …*); the body switches into Latin for the academic and legal vocabulary it has no native term for: *vocire* (← *vocare*, "to summon/call"), *collegis / collegam* ("colleagues / colleague"), *professoribus* ("professors"), *conscientz* (← *conscientia*, "conscience"), and the closing *Datum* ("Given"). These are kept in the Source block and rendered in the Translation.
- **Reading note (working transcription vs. Dreyer).** Where the working transcription reads *oc fordre* ("and demand/cite"), the Dreyer digitised text layer (p. 70, l. 28) reads *oc farcire* — an evident misreading of a Latin-form verb (*citare*?) in the same summoning series as *vocire*. The sense ("summon and cite") is unaffected; the cleaner working reading *fordre* is followed and Dreyer is recorded. Dreyer's line 39 likewise reads *saa widt forn de wide* where the working text reads *saa widt som de wide* ("so far as they know"); the working reading is adopted, the *forn/som* divergence being an digitised text layer artifact of the long-s.
- **Orthography (chancery Danish, c. 1591).** *gandske wenlig(en)* = *ganske venlig(en)* ("wholly friendly"); *helsen* = *hilsen* ("greeting"); *beuist gode* = *bevist gode* ("kindness shown"); *forskylde / forskylle* = *forskylde* ("requite, deserve in return"); *eskendis worder* = "is called upon / required"; *bestaa oc bekiende* = "affirm and acknowledge"; *lougligen steffnt oc kaldit* = *lovligen stævnet og kaldt* ("lawfully summoned and cited"); *kaldsbreff* = "writ of citation"; *kaldtsmend* = "summoners" (here the citation-witnesses); *fuldmectige* = "attorney / proxy"; *billigt oc ret* = "fair and right"; *landzens skick oc brug* = "the custom and usage of the land"; *for:ne / forme / forbemelte* = *fornævnte / forbemeldte* ("aforesaid / aforementioned," standard chancery abbreviations); *tilgnegt* = *tilgnegen / tilgiven* ("devoted").
- **Negation check.** One negation in the body: *eller oc icke* ("or not [at all]," closing the threefold alternative of how Rasmus may respond to the citation — in person, by proxy, or not at all). It is reproduced once; the polite formula *icke skal haffue mig der vdoffuer at beklage* ("[that] I shall not have cause to complain of it") contains a second *icke*, also reproduced. No conditional in the letter inverts a command; the legal force is a private party's *bøn* (request) to the university court, not an order.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datum Vraniburg den 21. junij anno 1591* = "Given at **Uraniborg**, 21 June 1591" (O.S.; Denmark kept Old Style until 1700). The dateline agrees with the catalogue label (*1591. 21. juni. Uraniborg*) and with the Dreyer regest (*1591, 21. junii*) — **no date discrepancy.**
- **Correction.** Corrected the English translation's place-name: Tycho's tenant Rasmus Persøn is said to reside "vdi Gunsøgaard" (Dreyer, TBOO XIV p.56), not at Gundsømagle as previously rendered.

documents.incipit: HIS sane litteris, quas nunc ad te mitto, perillustris ac eruditissime vir, brevitatem …

text.original:
NOBILITATE PERILLUSTRI ET ERUDITIONE PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO. D. TYCHONI BRAHE DANO, DOMINO DE KNUDSTRUP, ET ARCIS URANIBURG IN INSULA HELLESPONTI DANICI HUÆNA FUNDATORI.

HIS sane litteris, quas nunc ad te mitto, perillustris ac eruditissime vir, brevitatem sum secutus: et quamvis in Epistola illa, quam cum eo opere, quo te merito, grati animi meæque erga te observantiæ declarandæ causa, nuncupavi, communitam dedi, quamque brevi ad te sum transmissurus, pluribus egerim: tamen ne negligentiæ nomine me accusares, tibi indicandum duxi, me hactenus a Patavina poli investigatione ac Martis affixorumque syderum meridiana altitudine investiganda, quam tantopere cum GELLIO tuo, vel potius, nostro, observare cupiebas, supersedisse: cum, quod eiusmodi observationibus nec opportunum loci situm, nec commodam ad ea exploranda occasionem, ut ingenue GELLIUS ipse testabitur, invenire potui, tum etiam quod diversorum negotiorum cumulo varijsque molestijs, quas mors carissimæ Matris gravissimas auxit, plurimum toto illo æstivo tempore, quo Venetijs et Patavij hæreo, sum circumventus. Sextantem interim tuæ inventionis, et tui gratia, et meæ exercitationis causa, fabrefieri feci, eumque cœlo exactissime ad singula minuta, dum unâ cum dicto GELLIO easdem nonnullarum fixarum distantias, quales ex tuis observationibus in Fixarum Catalogo tu ipse antea notasti, deprehendi, respondere comperi. Eundem Bononiam mecum exportabo, ibique Quadrantem maiorem ad altitudines observandas elaborare faciam; et plures tui causa observationes perficere conabor. Radium etiam Astrologicum iustæ magnitudinis construi faciam; in cuius oblongi extremitate cylindrus sit apponendus, ubi scilicet in aliorum radijs oculus applicatur: in transversarij vero extremitatibus affigendæ erunt duæ pinnulæ cum suis foraminibus, sicut in tuis Instrumentis facere soles, quæ tamen libere circumvolvantur, ut radij per eius rimulas ac iuxta cylindri extremitates transmissi paralleli fiant. Hoc transversarium volo, ut lateraliter tantum moveatur, dividendo ipsum in particulas illas, in quas hasta seu fustis divisa est, pro ratione sinus totius particularum 10000: hoc enim pacto portio transversarij ab hasta secta erit tangens anguli, qui fit ad cylindrum, dum unus observator per pinnulam fixam in hastæ extremitate, alius vero per pinnulam in extremitate transversarij sitam, stellas inspiciunt.

Privilegium tuorum operum, quod anxie petij, ab Illustrissimis Venetis obtineri nequit: id enim responsi a nonnullis nobilibus tuli: Senatum Venetum non solere illorum operum, quæ extra Urbem edantur, concedere privilegia; et si aliqua sub Libris alibi excusis sua legantur, ea honoris tantum, non valoris gratia esse concessa, cum Bibliothecæ Venetæ ex ipsius Senatus gratia id iuris habeant, ut quoscumque libros alibi impressos, non obstantibus quibusvis, nedum ipsius Senatus, privilegijs, Venetijs denuo typis mandare possint. Illud tamen honoris privilegium, ubi opus illud iam typis excusum antea vidissent, ab Illustrissimis Venetis haberi posset; solent enim, quicquid edatur, legere et perscrutari, num scilicet contra Sacrosanctam Ecclesiam, bonos mores, aut Principes Christianos quicquam scriptum sit, priusquam sua illa privilegia impertiantur. Illustrissimi autem Ducis Mantuæ et Ferrariæ, per familiares et amicos, privilegium facile, uti spero, obtinebo. Expecto adhuc magno cum desiderio Librum tuum primum, quem iam sub prœlo esse ex GELLIO intellexi; interim obnixe te rogo, ut si quid in tui gratiam possum, libere mihi committere ne graveris. Vale, perillustris Vir, et Astronomiæ Princeps, quam restaurare, ut hucusque felicissime a te factum, pro communi commodo nunquam intermitte.

Iterum diu feliciterque vale.
Datæ Patavij, Kalendis Augusti 1591.
Perillustri Dominationi tuæ addictissimus
IOAN. ANTONIUS MAGINUS.
text.english:
**To the most illustrious in nobility and most outstanding in erudition, Master Tycho Brahe the Dane, Lord of Knudstrup, and founder of the castle of Uraniborg on the island Hven of the Danish Hellespont.**

In this present letter that I now send you, most illustrious and most learned man, I have aimed at brevity; and although in that letter which I joined to the work I dedicated to you — deservedly, to declare my gratitude and my regard for you — and which I shall shortly send on to you, I treated of more matters, yet, lest you charge me with negligence, I have thought I should inform you that hitherto I have held off from the Paduan investigation of the pole and from investigating the meridian altitude of Mars and of the fixed stars — which you so greatly desired me to observe together with your Gellius, or rather, ours. For both because I could find, for observations of that kind, neither a suitable situation of place nor a convenient opportunity for examining them — as Gellius himself will frankly testify — and also because I have been very greatly hemmed in, throughout all that summer season during which I am stuck at Venice and Padua, by a heap of various affairs and by sundry troubles, which the death of my most dear mother has gravely increased. Meanwhile I have had a sextant of your invention made — both for your sake and for my own practice — and I have found that it answers most exactly to the heavens, to the very minute, since together with the said Gellius I detected the same distances of certain fixed stars as those which you yourself had earlier noted from your observations in the Catalogue of Fixed Stars. I shall carry it with me to Bologna, and there I shall have a larger quadrant fashioned for observing altitudes; and I shall try, for your sake, to carry through more observations. I shall also have a cross-staff (radius astronomicus) of proper size constructed: at the end of its long [shaft] a cylinder is to be fitted, where, that is, in other cross-staffs the eye is applied; and at the ends of the cross-piece two sights (pinnules) with their holes are to be affixed, as you are wont to do on your instruments — sights which, however, turn freely round, so that the rays sent through their slits and along the ends of the cylinder become parallel. This cross-piece I wish to move only sideways, dividing it into those same parts into which the shaft or rod is divided, in proportion to the whole sine of 10,000 parts: for in this way the portion of the cross-piece cut off by the shaft will be the tangent of the angle that is formed at the cylinder, while one observer sights the stars through the fixed sight at the end of the shaft, and the other through the sight set at the end of the cross-piece.

The privilege [copyright] for your works, which I anxiously sought, cannot be obtained from the Most Illustrious Venetians; for this is the answer I had from certain nobles: that the Venetian Senate is not accustomed to grant privileges for those works that are published outside the City; and that if any of its own [privileges] are to be read in books printed elsewhere, these have been granted for the sake of honour only, not of legal force, since the Venetian libraries have, by the grace of the Senate itself, the right to put back into print at Venice whatsoever books printed elsewhere, notwithstanding any privileges whatever — not even the Senate's own. That privilege of honour, however, could be had from the Most Illustrious Venetians once they had first seen the work already printed; for they are accustomed to read and scrutinise whatever is published — to see, that is, whether anything has been written against the Most Holy Church, good morals, or Christian princes — before they bestow those privileges of theirs. But from the Most Illustrious Duke of Mantua and Ferrara I shall easily obtain a privilege, as I hope, through members of his household and friends. I still await with great longing your First Book, which I have understood from Gellius to be already under the press; meanwhile I earnestly beg you not to be reluctant to entrust to me freely whatever I can do for your sake. Farewell, most illustrious Man and Prince of Astronomy — which, as you have hitherto most happily done, never cease to restore for the common good.

Again, fare you well long and happily.
Given at Padua, on the Kalends of August [1 August] 1591.
Most devoted to Your most illustrious Lordship,
Giovanni Antonio Magini.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Ioan. Antonius Maginus* = **Giovanni Antonio Magini** (1555–1617), from 1588 Professor of Mathematics at Bologna (having won the chair over Galileo); astronomer, cartographer, and table-maker, and one of Tycho's principal Italian correspondents. His *Tabulae Primi Mobilis* (Venice, 1604) and *Carteggio* (ed. A. Favaro) carry this exchange.
- **Address.** *Dominus de Knudstrup* — **Lord of Knudstrup**, Tycho's Scanian ancestral seat. *Arcis Uraniburg in insula Hellesponti Danici Huaena fundatori* — "founder of the castle of Uraniborg on the island Hven of the Danish Hellespont"; *Hellespontus Danicus* ("the Danish Hellespont") is the humanist epithet for the Øresund, the strait in which **Hven** lies.
- ***Gellius*** = **Gellius Sascerides** (1562–1612), Tycho's Danish pupil and former Uraniborg assistant, then studying medicine at Padua (matriculated October 1589). He described Tycho's instruments to Magini and supplied star-distances from Tycho's catalogue; he is the channel for much of this letter's technical content. Magini's *"GELLIO tuo, vel potius, nostro"* ("your Gellius, or rather, ours") is a courtesy claiming a share in him.
- ***Epistola … quam cum eo opere … nuncupavi*** — the dedicatory letter Magini attached to a work he dedicated to Tycho. The dedication-context (a work "I dedicated to you") and the *Liber primus* awaited below place this in the run-up to Magini's exchanges around his *Novae coelestium orbium theoricae* (1589) and the later tables.
- **Instruments.** *Sextans tuae inventionis* → **sextant of your invention** (one of Tycho's signature instruments;). *Quadrans maior* → **larger quadrant**. *Radius Astrologicus* (= *radius astronomicus*) → **cross-staff (radius astronomicus)** by this chapter's convention; Magini writes *Astrologicus* but the instrument is the astronomical cross-staff, so the controlled rendering is used and the variant noted here. *Pinnula* → **sight (pinnule)**; *transversarium* → **cross-piece** (the sliding transversal); *hasta seu fustis* → **shaft or rod** (the graduated main staff). *Fixarum Catalogo* → Tycho's **Catalogue of Fixed Stars** (the star catalogue then in progress, ultimately the 1,000-star catalogue).
- **The cross-staff geometry.** Magini describes a tangent-graduated cross-staff: a *cylindrus* (cylinder) at the eye-end of the shaft replaces the usual eyepiece; two freely-rotating pinnules at the ends of the transversal align their slits so the rays "become parallel." The transversal is graduated *"pro ratione sinus totius particularum 10000"* — **in proportion to the whole sine [radius] of 10,000 parts**, i.e. the *sinus totus* (the radius of the trigonometric circle) is set at 10,000, the standard table-value; so the segment of the transversal "cut off by the shaft" reads directly as the **tangent of the observed angle** at the cylinder. The construction (a tangent scale read by two observers) is rendered literally; no step is supplied beyond the Latin.
- **The Venetian *privilegium* passage.** *Privilegium* → **privilege (copyright)**: the printing-monopoly grant. The reported answer has three linked clauses, each preserved with its negation: (1) the Senate *non solet* — **is not accustomed** — to grant privileges for works published outside Venice; (2) any Venetian privileges appearing in books printed elsewhere are *"honoris tantum, non valoris gratia"* — **for honour only, not for legal force**; (3) Venetian libraries may reprint any foreign-printed book at Venice *"non obstantibus quibusvis, nedum ipsius Senatus, privilegijs"* — **notwithstanding any privileges whatever, not even the Senate's own** (*nedum* = "let alone / not even," intensifying, not excepting). Four explicit negations in the source (*nequit, non solere, non valoris, non obstantibus … nedum*) are reproduced; none added or dropped. The "privilege of honour" is obtainable only *after* the work is printed and has passed Venetian censorship (against *Sacrosancta Ecclesia, boni mores, Principes Christiani*).
- ***Librum tuum primum … sub proelo*** → **"your First Book … under the press"**: Tycho's *Epistolarum astronomicarum liber primus* (Uraniborg, 1596), then in preparation/printing — Magini awaits it.
- ***Astronomiae Princeps … restaurare*** → **"Prince of Astronomy … to restore"**: a salute to Tycho's *instauratio astronomiae* programme (, *restoration/renewal of astronomy*); "never cease to restore [it] for the common good."
- **Calendar / dating crux (named).** The dateline reads *"Datae Patavij, Kalendis Augusti 1591"* = **Padua, the Kalends of August 1591 = 1 August 1591**. Magini, in Catholic Italy, writes **New Style**. The edition label ("1591. 22. januar n.s. Padua") flatly contradicts the source's own dateline by more than six months; by this chapter's convention the header leads with the as-written date (1 August 1591) and appends the catalogue date, and the conversion is **not** silently performed. The "22 January" label is almost certainly a catalogue/data error (a 22-Jan letter of the Magini exchange may have been conflated): the body's internal markers — the *summer season* ("toto illo aestivo tempore") at Venice/Padua, the still-recent death of his mother, and Tycho's *Liber primus* only now reported "under the press" — are consistent with **August**, not January. The discrepancy is recorded, not reconciled.
- **Edition note.** The source edition field names *Tabulae Primi Mobilis* (Venice, 1604), where Magini later quoted the Tycho correspondence; the letter's primary printed witness is, however, Tycho's *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica* (fol. H), whence Favaro re-edited it in the *Carteggio*. No manuscript witness is recorded in the source.
