documents.abstract: Announces the discovery of a quick method for extracting square roots of large numbers after years of effort, and previews the result for Tycho before wider publication.
documents.incipit: DIU multumque plurimis ab hinc annis cogitavi (Nobilissime ac doctissime vir) ut viam …

text.original:
NOBILITATE PERILLUSTRI ET ERUDITIONE PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO TYCHONI BRAHE DANO DOMINO DE KNUDSTRUP, ET ARCIS URANIBURG IN INSULA HELLESPONTI DANICI HUÆNA FUNDATORI.
IO. ANTONIVS MAGINVS PATAVINUS MATHEMATICVS
S. P. D.

DIU multumque plurimis ab hinc annis cogitavi (Nobilissime ac doctissime vir) ut viam invenirem expeditam, ac facilem, qua cuiuscunque numeri quamvis magni quadrata radix colligi ex tempore posset. Opus sane arduum, et perquam difficile, in quo quantum insudarim, nemo plane credet, nisi qui ipse aliquando periculum fecit, et saepe quidem a proposito rei difficultas me deterruit. Verum enim vero res tandem ita mihi faeliciter successit, ut plus, quam optarem, invenerim: nam quid in hoc genere calculi praestiterim, tu primum doctissime Brahe, deinde reliqui omnes Matheseos cultores, ad quorum manus haec pervenerint, probe perspicient. Nolo autem hîc in laudandis meis inventis nimis audax studiosis videri, ne momus quispiam propriae laudis parum modestum praeconem me esse cavilletur. Caeterum qualecunque hoc sit opus, tibi, gloriosissimi nominis viro, ac nostrae aetatis Astronomo eminentissimo, grati animi et observantiae erga te singularis caussâ dicare volui, idque maximis de causis. Primum enim tu ipse es, cui maxime debeo, quod amicitiae tuae fores tam amanter ac humaniter mihi aperuisti, atque mihi plus honoris tribuisti, quam eruditio (si qua est) tenuis mea, ac perexigua postulabat, cum mihi tuum secundum librum de recentioribus mundi Phaenomenis per Danum quendam studiosum misisti, simulque per eundem, quid de illis sentirem, quaesivisti; nec non etiam quod meae Epistolae humanissime respondisti, multa mecum de rebus Astronomicis disserendo. Deinde tu unus es, cui hanc meam Tetragonicam tabulam acceptam fore maxime confido, propterea quod ipsa faelicissime uti poteris ad eliciendos inaequalitatum motuum planetarum angulos, et promptiori quidem compendio, quam per Tangentium, et Secantium tabulas. Tandem quia tu ille es praestantissimus Astronomiae instaurator, cui plurimum debet nostra aetas, et debebunt posteri omnes, quando quidem non ego solum, sed omnes fere sincerae mentis viri de tuis Astronomicis fundamentis spem eam conceperunt, ut a te solo Astronomiae restitutionem avide expectent. Etenim tu tales miro artificio, ac invento caelestium sphaerarum confinxisti hypotyposes, quales probe sufficere posse ad tuenda phaenomena, et apparentias coelitus animadversas, ac ad definienda coelestium luminum loca ad quaevis tempora, non ambigendum est. Hortor itaque te, obtestorque, exiguo hoc munusculo tibi oblato, ut, quod faeliciter exorsus es, et multo jam tempore in hoc doctrinae genere moliris, tandem absolvas: namque nullum alium rectius et faelicius id praestare posse quam te, qui ingenio es acerrimo natus ad Astronomiae collapsae illustrationem, recte ac sincere judico, idque sperant omnes. Etenim si tuum laboriosissimum ac praestantissimum Theatrum absolutum quamprimum nobis communicabis, iis profecto, qui olim motuum correctionem tentarunt, et qui nunc pertentant, omnem eripies gloriam, atque in posterum tentaturis omnem praeripies occasionem, et materiam.

Scio quidem post tuorum laborum editionem mea scripta correctionem desideratura, sed tantum abest, ut haec me perturbent, ut potius desiderem quamprimum tuas speculationes publici juris fieri: nam confestim Ephemerides meas corrigam, quarum secunda editio avide expectatur, vel, si opus erit, de novo alias pertexam. Illud etiam per hanc epistolam tibi significare liceat, me Patavii, et Bononiae poli investigationem, ac Martis, eorumque affixorum siderum meridianas altitudines, quas tantopere me observare optabas, hactenus praetermisisse, neque ob id tamen negligentiae nomine a te accusari velim, cum hoc praestandi mihi a variis negociorum fluctibus, qui me oppresserunt, erepta sit facultas, accedente etiam loci incommoditate, praesertim Patavii, de quo tibi idem iste testari poterit. Sextantem illum Astronomicum, quem ex tuo invento et in tui gratiam Patavii fabrefieri curavi, exactissime coelo respondere ad singula minuta recte percepi, quoniam easdem distantias adunguem nonnullarum fixarum, quas in tuo catalogo ex tuis observationibus notasti, deprehendi. Atque hunc jam Bononiam mecum exportavi, ubi observationes plurimas in tui commodum perficere tentabo. Quinetiam et hoc te latere nolo, Nobilissimum ac doctissimum virum Paulum Bonfilium patritium Bononiensem, tuique studiosissimum, fabrefieri curasse propriis expensis Quadrantem ex ligno, et metallo decempedalem, qui non tam minuta, quam minutorum partes in observationibus exhibebit. Idem Nobilissimus vir Sextantem quoque ejusdem magnitudinis habere studet, quibus Instrumentis in summa turri, quam in suâ domo habet, observationes coelestes in tui gratiam perficere commodius valeamus, de quibus omnibus suis loco et tempore certior fies. Hîc finem epistolae huic meae imponam, te enixe rogans, ut, si quid possum, tuo jure me utare. Vale vir praeclarissime, Astronomorumque decus, atque Astronomiam perficere tuis lucubrationibus et vigiliis perge, et Spartam, quam accepisti (ut ajunt) orna.

Iterumque diu, et faeliciter vale.
Bononiae Kalendis Februarii. M. D. XCII.
text.english:
**To the man of most illustrious nobility and most outstanding erudition, Tycho Brahe the Dane, Lord of Knudstrup and founder of the castle of Uraniborg on the Danish island of Hven.**
**Giovanni Antonio Magini of Padua, mathematician, sends heartiest greeting.**

Long and hard, for very many years past, have I pondered (most noble and most learned sir) how I might find a ready and easy method by which the square root of any number, however large, could be obtained on the spot. A task indeed arduous, and exceedingly difficult, in which no one will at all believe how much I sweated, unless he be one who has himself at some time made the trial; and often, indeed, the difficulty of the matter deterred me from my purpose. But in truth the thing has at last so happily succeeded for me that I have found out more than I could have wished: for what I have accomplished in this kind of calculation, you first, most learned Brahe, and then all the rest of the cultivators of mathematics into whose hands these things shall come, will rightly perceive. Yet I do not wish here, in praising my own inventions, to seem too bold to scholars, lest some Momus carp that I am too immodest a herald of my own praise. But whatever this work may be, I wished to dedicate it to you — a man of most glorious name, and the most eminent astronomer of our age — out of a grateful spirit and of my singular regard toward you, and that for the greatest reasons. For first, you yourself are the one to whom I owe it most, that you opened the doors of your friendship to me so lovingly and courteously, and granted me more honour than my slender and very scant erudition (if there be any) deserved, when you sent me your second book on the more recent Phenomena of the world by a certain Danish scholar, and at the same time, through the same man, inquired what I thought of them; and likewise that you most courteously answered my letter, discoursing with me at length on astronomical matters. Next, you are the one man to whom I am most confident this Tetragonic table of mine will be welcome, because you will be able to use it most happily for eliciting the angles of the inequalities of the planets' motions, and indeed by a readier short-cut than by the tables of Tangents and Secants. Last, because you are that most outstanding restorer of astronomy, to whom our age owes most, and to whom all posterity will owe most — since indeed not I alone, but almost all men of sincere mind have conceived this hope from your astronomical foundations, that from you alone they eagerly await the restoration of astronomy. For you have, with wonderful skill and invention, fashioned such hypotyposes of the celestial spheres as — it is not to be doubted — can well suffice to save the phenomena and the appearances observed in the heavens, and to define the places of the celestial luminaries for any times whatever. I urge you therefore, and entreat you, by this little gift offered to you, that what you have happily begun, and have now for a long time been labouring at in this kind of learning, you may at last complete: for that no other can perform it more rightly and more happily than you — you who were born with a most keen genius for the illustration of fallen astronomy — I judge rightly and sincerely, and so all men hope. For if you will share with us, as soon as possible, your most laborious and most outstanding Theatre once completed, you will surely snatch away all glory from those who once attempted the correction of the motions, and who now keep attempting it, and you will forestall every occasion and matter from those who shall attempt it hereafter.

I know indeed that, after the publication of your works, my own writings will stand in need of correction; but so far is this from troubling me that I rather desire your speculations to be made public as soon as possible: for I shall at once correct my Ephemerides, of which a second edition is eagerly awaited, or, if need be, weave others anew. This too let me be allowed to make known to you by this letter: that I have hitherto neglected, at Padua and at Bologna, the investigation of the pole, and the meridian altitudes of Mars and of the fixed stars near them, which you so greatly wished me to observe; nor on that account, however, would I be accused by you under the name of negligence, since the power of performing this has been wrested from me by the various surges of business that have overwhelmed me, with the inconvenience of the place added besides, especially at Padua — to which this same man will be able to testify to you. That Astronomical sextant which, after your invention and for your sake, I had made at Padua, I have rightly perceived to answer the heavens most exactly to each single minute, since I found the same distances, to a hair's breadth, of several of the fixed stars which you have noted in your catalogue from your observations. And this I have now carried with me to Bologna, where I shall attempt to complete very many observations for your benefit. Moreover, this too I would not have hidden from you: that the most noble and most learned man Paolo Bonfilio, a patrician of Bologna and most devoted to you, has had made at his own expense a Quadrant of wood and metal, ten feet in size, which will exhibit in observations not so much the minutes as the parts of minutes. The same most noble man is eager to have also a Sextant of the same magnitude, so that with these Instruments, in the top of a tower which he has in his house, we may be the better able to complete celestial observations for your sake; about all of which you shall be informed in their place and time. Here I shall put an end to this letter of mine, earnestly asking you that, if I can do anything, you use me by your right. Farewell, most distinguished man and ornament of astronomers; and go on to perfect astronomy by your lucubrations and your vigils, and adorn the Sparta which you have received (as they say).

And again, long and happily, farewell.
At Bologna, on the Kalends of February [1 February]. 1592.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Io. Antonius Maginus Patavinus* = **Giovanni Antonio Magini** (1555–1617), professor of mathematics at Bologna from 1588 (the chair Galileo also sought), astronomer, cartographer, and author of widely-used *Ephemerides*. He styles himself *Patavinus* ("of Padua") by origin, though he writes from Bologna. The address-superscription gives Tycho's full titulature: *Dominus de Knudstrup* (**Lord of Knudstrup**, his ancestral seat in Scania) and founder of **Uraniborg** on **Hven**.
- ***insula Hellesponti Danici Huaena*** — "the island of Hven in the Danish Hellespont": a humanist conceit for the **Øresund** (the Sound), styled the "Danish Hellespont." Kept as the figure it is.
- **Greeting.** *S. P. D.* = *salutem plurimam dicit*, "sends heartiest greeting".
- **The dedication.** The letter is the **dedicatory epistle** prefixed to Magini's square-root work — *hanc meam Tetragonicam tabulam*, rendered "this Tetragonic table of mine" — i.e. his *Tabula tetragonica*, a table for extracting square roots, published Venice 1592. Magini commends it to Tycho as a computing aid "for eliciting the angles of the inequalities of the planets' motions … by a readier short-cut than by the tables of Tangents and Secants." This places the letter in the orbit of Tycho's own **prosthaphaeretic** computing interests, though that term does not appear in the source and is not imported here.
- ***tuum secundum librum de recentioribus mundi Phaenomenis*** — "your second book on the more recent Phenomena of the world": Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis liber secundus* (Uraniborg, 1588), sent to Magini, with Tycho's request for Magini's opinion, *per Danum quendam studiosum* ("by a certain Danish scholar" — unnamed here).
- ***Momus*** — in Greek mythology the god of mockery and fault-finding; "lest some Momus carp" = lest some captious critic. Kept as the proper name.
- **Astronomy — technical terms**: *Astronomiae instaurator / restitutio / illustrationem … collapsae* — Tycho as the **restorer** of fallen astronomy, the *restitutio astronomiae* programme, rendered "restoration / restorer of astronomy"; *hypotyposes caelestium sphaerarum* — "hypotyposes of the celestial spheres," i.e. his world-model (the term *hypotyposis*, an outline/representation, is kept); *tuenda phaenomena … apparentias* — "to save the phenomena and the appearances" (the standard *salvare apparentias* idiom); *inaequalitatum motuum planetarum angulos* — "the angles of the inequalities of the planets' motions"; *meridianas altitudines* — "**meridian altitudes**"; *poli investigationem* — "the investigation of the pole" (latitude determination); *catalogus … fixarum* — Tycho's star **catalogue**.
- ***Theatrum*** — "Theatre": Magini's term for the great projected work Tycho is labouring at (his *Theatrum astronomicum* / the grand instauration), capitalised as in the source; rendered literally "Theatre" and flagged, since it is Magini's metaphor for Tycho's magnum opus rather than a fixed title.
- **Instruments**: *Sextans Astronomicus* — "**Astronomical sextant**," built *ex tuo invento* ("after your invention") at Padua; *Quadrans … decempedalis ex ligno et metallo* — a **quadrant** "ten feet in size, of wood and metal," resolving "not so much the minutes as the parts of minutes." *ad singula minuta* / *minutorum partes* — arc-minutes and fractions of arc-minutes.
- **Paolo Bonfioli.** *Paulus Bonfilius patritius Bononiensis* = **Paolo Bonfioli**, a Bolognese patrician and astronomy enthusiast ("most devoted to you"), who funded the large quadrant and sought a matching sextant, with a tower-top observing platform in his house. (Spelling of the surname normalised in the apparatus; the Latin form *Bonfilius* is kept in the Source and translation.)
- ***Ephemerides … secunda editio*** — Magini's *Ephemerides coelestium motuum*; he undertakes to recompute them once Tycho's results appear. *de novo alias pertexam* — "weave others anew" (the weaving metaphor kept).
- ***Spartam, quam accepisti (ut ajunt) orna*** — "adorn the Sparta which you have received (as they say)": the proverb *Σπάρταν ἔλαχες, ταύταν κόσμει* ("Sparta is your portion; do it credit"), via Erasmus, *Adagia* (ii.5.1) — "make the most of the lot assigned to you." Magini's *ut ajunt* ("as they say") flags it as the proverb it is; kept and glossed.
- ***adunguem*** — *ad unguem*, "to a hair's breadth" (literally "to the fingernail," the sculptor's idiom for exactitude).
- **Calendar.** *Bononiae Kalendis Februarii M.D.XCII* = "At **Bologna**, on the **Kalends of February** (1 February), 1592." Magini, a Catholic in Bologna, wrote **New Style** (Gregorian), as the edition label marks ("n.s."); the dateline and the catalogued date agree on 1 February 1592. The Roman-calendar idiom *Kalendis Februarii* is rendered with the idiom and glossed to the civil date by this chapter's convention No in-letter date discrepancy.
- **Edition note.** The edition's edition field names the *Astronomiae instaurata mechanica*; this dedicatory epistle to Magini's *Tabula tetragonica* is also printed among the *Epistolae* in Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VII. Both are recorded; no MS witness is listed.
- **Correction.** Corrected 'spectationes' (observations) to 'speculationes' (speculations/theoretical works) in the Latin per Dreyer, TBOO V p.128, l.14, and updated the corresponding English clause, which had shifted Magini's request from Tycho's theoretical system to mere observational data.
- **Correction.** Corrected the run-together 'DANICIHUAeNA' to the two words 'DANICI HUAeNA' in the dedication heading's Latin per Dreyer, TBOO V p.127, l.4 (no change to the English).
- **Correction.** Corrected the invented surname 'Bonfioli' to 'Bonfilio' in the English, matching the Latin 'Bonfilium' already present and confirmed at Dreyer, TBOO V p.128, l.30 (no change to the Latin).

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter (address heading, all three main paragraphs, the sextant/quadrant/Bonfilio passage, closing) against Dreyer TBOO V pp.126-129 read as page images. Two text error found in the transcribed original against Dreyer's print (a glued heading word, and 'spectationes' silently substituted for Dreyer's 'speculationes' — a real word-level corruption with mild semantic consequence) plus one proper-name mistranslation (Bonfilium rendered 'Bonfioli' rather than 'Bonfilio'). Per the grading rule, any text error caps the grade at C regardless of individual severity; this letter was self-graded A, which the collation does not support.

**3 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). the transcribed original glues 'DANICI' and 'HUAeNA' into a single word; Dreyer prints them as two words. The English sense (island of Hven) survives, but the Latin transcription is corrupted. Dreyer prints: *IN INSULA HELLESPONTI DANICI HUAeNA FUNDATORI (p.127 line 4 — two separate words)*.
- **text error** (medium). the transcribed original substitutes 'spectationes' (viewings/observations) for Dreyer's actual word 'speculationes' (theoretical works/speculations) — a genuine word-level corruption that shifts what Magini is asking Tycho to publish, from his theoretical astronomical system to mere observational data. Dreyer prints: *ut potius defiderem quamprimum tuas fpeculationes publici juris fieri (p.128 line 14 — 'speculationes', not 'spectationes')*.
- **mistranslation** (low). Dreyer's and the transcribed original's Latin both read 'Bonfilium' (from 'Bonfilius'), which Italianizes as 'Bonfilio' (i.e. 'Bonfiglio'); the translation instead invents the surname 'Bonfioli', not supported by the Latin. At: “the most noble and most learned man Paolo Bonfioli”.

**Repaired.** Collated all three defects directly against the Dreyer page images (TBOO V pp.126-129): p.128 l.14 confirms 'fpeculationes', p.127 l.4 confirms the two separate words 'DANICI HUAeNA', and p.128 l.30 confirms 'Paulum Bonfilium'. All three are genuine, now corrected at the appropriate layer (Latin, or English, or both per defect type). No remaining crux.

text.original:
DEM DURCHLEUCHTIGEN, HOCHGEBORNEN FÜRSTEN VND
HERRN WILHELMEN LANDTGRAFFEN ZU HESSEN, GRAFFEN ZU CATZENELNBOGEN, DIETZ,
ZIEGENHAIN VND NIDDA, MEINEM GNEDIGEN HERRN.

Durchleuchtiger Hochgeborner Furst:. Gnediger Herr. Nebst meiner alzeit
bereitwilliger diensterbietung hab ich nicht vnterlassen konnen Ewrer F. G. bey
gegenwertiger, auff die anstehende Franckfurter Messe furgefallener botschafft
zuzuschreiben.

Erstlich was die Elendtsthiere (von welcher Zuuerschaffung ich
meinen müglichen vleiß zugesagt) belangt, hab ich sie an etlichen orten in
Norwegen in bestellung. Aber dweill die Segellation noch
nicht von wegen des winters angehet, kan ich so baldt keinen bescheidt darauff
bekomen. Alßbaldt mir aber eine der mehr solicher Thiere zugestalt werden, dem
ich auffs füriahr erwarte, will ichs Ew. F. G. wissen lassen: damit sie durch
Ewer F. G. eigen abgefertigten Bothen (wofehrne mirselber keine gelegenheit
fürfelt dasselb zuuerrichten) der die Steige vnd wege wisst, mügen von hierab
geholet werden.

Ich hab an Ewer F. G. Mathematicum Rothmannum, in omnem
euentum, wan er bey Ew. F. G. were
widerumb ankomen, beyuerwartes Schreiben gerichtet. Da er sich aber noch nicht
hette widereingestalt, alsdan kan Ew. F. G. den brieff durch einen andern
erbrechen vnd verlesen lassen, vnd den einhalt darauß vermerken. Das fürnehmest
in dem selben Schreiben ist: Wan Rothmannus
die nehest in fine Decembris
geschehene Eclipsin ☾æ, durch Ew. F. G. Instrumenta per omnia sua momenta et alia
Requisita gantz vleissig denotirt hette,
das mir dieselbige Obseruationes mochten mitgetheilt werden.
Dan wie woll es alhie zur selbigen Zeit gar nicht klar gewesen ist, das man die
berürte Eclipsin hette obseruiren konnen, so hab ich doch den motum ☾æ durch
vielfaltige Obseruationes so
offt vnd lange inquirirt vnd dem nachgeforscht, das ich mich
versehe, derselbig foll meinen numeris in einer iusten concordantz, zu
aller Zeit eintreffen: vnd das ich also per
collationem obseruationis istic factæ, cum numeratione e proprijs
Tabulis in motu ☾æ die
Differentiam
Meridianorum iust gnug drauß schliessen müge. Im fall aber
Rothmannus zu der Zeit nicht were bey Ew. F. G. zur
stelle gewesen, gedencke ich woll, es werde Ew. F. G. Automatopæus, oder jmandt anders, dieß, so es
sonst alda klar gewesen ist, nicht versäumbt haben, das es mir alsdan gleichwoll
mochte mitgetheilt werden: Vnd so noch andere Eclipses für handen, die in verschiedenen
iahren seind vleissig obseruirt worden, es sey kurtz oder
langk verlitten, werrs all eins, mochte ich derer denotation,
wie vnd von welchen stehrnen sie genomen sein, auch woll gehrne theilhafftig
werden, vmb fürberürter vrsach willen.

Es wirdt ohn Zweiffell der Mesthlinus solicher obberürten obseruation etliche im
fürrahte haben, per altitudines stellarum
vel quacunque alia ratione sedulo
deprehensas. Da derwegen Ew. F. G. die gnedige versehung
zuthun wolte vnbeschwert sein, ihn hierumb anlangen zu lassen, würde er Ewer F.
G. dieselbige nicht versagen, damit sie mir alsdan auch konten zukomen. Dan ich
bin selber nicht mit ihm bekandt. Ich begere nur die nudas obseruationes, eben wie sie abgemerckt
seindt, vnd will woll selbft darnach die tempora hierauß nach meinen eigen ratiocinijs extricirn. Da auch derselb
Mesthlinus ♄num
circa annos 76. 77. vnd 78 darzu auch ♂tem anno 76 vnd 78 in situ acronychio ethliche
mahll vleissig denotirt hette, wolte ich gehrne, das mir
soliche obseruationes
gleichfals zustünden, auff das ich sie mit den meinigen (welche ich circa eadem tempora, iedoch nicht
so viell und volkomlich, als ich gehrne wolte, bekomen) zu collationirn hette. Ich habe sonst: derer Obseruationum circa Solis oppositum, ein gut
theill im fürrahte, ferme per totum
Eccentrici ambitum: gleichwoll ab er wolte ich gehrn vmb
sonderlicher vrsache willen, circa dictos
annos in hisce duobus Planetis ihre Apparentias acronychas
examinirt,vnd mit den andern, die ich für mich gebracht, conferirt haben. Er mag sie denotirt haben, wie er
will, siue intermediante Radio per
distantias a certis Fixis, siue per lineas rectas iuxta fili
extensionem, modo illi vsitato decussatim facta
animaduersione: so will ich doch eben woll drauß, so viell
als müglich ist, mich zurichten wissen, wan mir nur die Nomina stellarum, et ipsa obseruationis
ratio angezeigt wirdt.

Ich hab auch in Italiam vnd Hispaniam, so woll als auch in Poloniam geschrieben, das ich etliche
Eclipses Lunares præteritorum
annorum (die da irgends accurate celitus genomen sein) bekomen, vnd auß
diesen, auch den iehnigen, die ich auß Teutschland erlangen kan, Meridianorum Differentias,
rechter, dan bisher geschehen ist, erforschen, vnd also die Geographiam (dweill sie der
Astronomey, wie Ewer F.
G. woll bewust ist, nicht geringe handtreichung thut) in dem fall, souiel
müglich ist, restituiren mochte.

Ewer F. G. wolte ich auch gar dienstlich gebetten haben, das sie
ihrem Automatopæo oder Vhrmacher befehl geben
wolte, das, wan er irgendts einen iungen ledigen Gesellen wüste, der mit den
Horologijs vnd Automatis konte vleissig
vmbgehen, vnd auff meine Instrumenta
Astronomica warten, er verschaffe, das derselbig mit dem
ersten sich herin zu mir verfügte. So wolte ich ihn alhie zu solichem thun
gebrauchen, vnd so gut lohn geben, als er anderßw o bekomen konte. Dan mein
Goldtschmidt, welcher alhie auffem lande bey mir gewohnet, auff meine Instrumenta gewartet, dern selbst
mit eigener handt viell gemacht, vnd mir viell iahr hierin vleissig vnd
getreulich gedient hat, ist mir (leider) für kurtzer Zeit abgestorben, das ich
darumb an stat desselbigen einen andern geschickten Gesellen bedarff, welcher
hie zu lande nicht woll zu bekomen seind. Versehe mich, Ew. F. G. Automatopæus werde hierin das beste thun.

Mich verlangt, Ewer F. G. Obseruationes stellarum fixarum zu bekomen, vnd dieselbige mit den meinigen zu conferiren. Dan ich glaube nicht anders, dan Rothmannus soll je nach der handt damit
fertig sein. Was meinen ersten Tomum belangt, darin ich hieruon vielfaltig tractir, wirdt
Ew. F. G. denselben mit Gottes Hülff, in diesem zukunfftigen Sommer zusehen
kriegen, dan er mit etlichen andern sachen in Truck baldt verfertigt ist.

Ich hab Ew. F. G. Mathematico auch geschrieben von 18
Minuten, die in Obseruationibus
Cometæ anni 80mi mihi communicatis,
allenthalben mangeln, dan so offt der Comet per Meridianum gangen ist, das gleich 18
Minuten alda zu Cassell zu weinig genomen seind, da meine Obseruationes aber eodem tempore factæ, alzeit
totidem Minuta plus
haben. Woher ich erachte, es sey solicher defect durch einen
Quadrantem vitio Perpendiculi, tot
Scrupulis non rite directi, commissirt worden. Ich hab
hieuon mit Rothmanno, da
er hir war, selber geredt, vnd ihm dasselb per collationem vestrarum atque mearum Obseruationum
demonstrirt: der sich dan darob verwundert vnd keine eigentliche vrsach darzu
gewust hat. Hat ab er globt, so baldt er wider bey Ew. F. G. gen Cassell ankeme, diesen grundtlicher nachzuforschen.
Dan er sey damahls, da dieser Comet ist obseruirt worden, in Ew. F. G. Dienste nicht gewesen. Da es dan durch
den Automatopæum oder einen
andern versehen were, wolte ich gehrn einigen bericht haben, woran sich dieser
mangell zugetragen hette, ehe ich diese Obseruationes in descriptione istius Cometæ in brauch
stelle. Das aber in den meinigen Obseruationibus meridianis, in eodem factis keine Irrung
sey, weisen des Thaddaei
gleichfals zu Prag genommene Altitudines gnugksamb auß, die
mit den meinigen, habita saltem ratione
diuersitatis Horizontum, zimblich woll vbereinstimmen.
Ich will Ew. F. G. aber mit solichen vnd andern dießmahll nicht lenger bemühen
vnd auffhalten, sonder dieselbe, nehest erwartung ihrer gnedigen widerantwort
vnd bericht bey gegenwertiger botschafft, wan die von der Messe widerankompt,
hiemit in Gottes almechtigen gnadenreichen schirm zu langetwiriger
leibsgesondtheit vnd friedlicher Landtsregirung dienstvleissig befohlen
haben.

Dat. Vraniburg den Februarii Anno 1592.

E. F. G.
Alzeit dienstewilliger
TYCHO BRAHE
manu
propria.

Weitergebe ich Ewre F. G. dienstlich zuuerstehen, das ich an Ew. F. G. Sohn
Landgraff Moritz
geschrieben hab, vnd seine F. G. dienstlich gebetten, das sie wolte
unbeschwert sein, mir ein Carmen in
commendationem Operum meorum Astronomicorum zu componirn, dweill ich gnugksamb berichtet bin, das seine
F. G. ein gute Venam
poëticam haben soll, vnd darzu lust trage. Versehe mich
darumb, es werde seine F. G. sich verdemutigen, ein solichs Carmen auff die eine seidt an
dem ersten bogen (da der Titul meorum
Tomorum, die ich
itzunder in Truck zu uerfertigen vnterhanden hab, mit dem Diplomate Cæsareo verzeichnet
ist, von welchem ich ihrer F. G. Exemplaria zugeschickt hab) mit eigener handt
anzuschreiben. Welchs mir sehr angenehm sein soll vnd semer F. G., wie ich
mich versehe, nicht vnrühmlich, darzu ad promotionem horum studiorum gereichen wirdt.
text.english:
**To the Most Illustrious, High-born Prince and Lord Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda, my gracious Lord.**

Most Illustrious, High-born Prince, gracious Lord. Together with my ever-ready offer of service, I have not been able to refrain from writing to Your Princely Grace by the present messenger, who has come up for the impending Frankfurt Fair.

First, as concerns the elk [Elendtsthiere], for the procuring of which I promised my utmost diligence: I have them on order in several places in Norway. But since sailing has not yet begun, on account of the winter, I cannot so soon obtain any [definite] word about it. As soon, however, as one or more of such animals shall be made over to me — which I expect for the spring — I shall let Your Princely Grace know, so that they may be fetched away from here by Your Princely Grace's own dispatched messenger (in the event that no opportunity falls to me myself to accomplish the same), one who knows the paths and the ways.

I have addressed to Your Princely Grace's Mathematician Rothmann, *for every event* [in omnem eventum], in case he should have arrived back with Your Princely Grace, a letter enclosed herewith. But should he not yet have returned and installed himself [there], then Your Princely Grace can have the letter opened and read out by another, and take note of its contents therefrom. The chief matter in that same letter is: that if Rothmann should have noted down most diligently, by Your Princely Grace's *instruments* [Instrumenta], the eclipse of the ☽ Moon that lately occurred *at the end of December* [in fine Decembris], *in all its moments and other requisites* [per omnia sua momenta et alia Requisita], those *observations* [Observationes] might be communicated to me. For although it was here at that same time not at all clear [enough] that one could have observed the said eclipse, yet I have so often and so long inquired into the *motion of the* ☽ *Moon* [motum ☾ae] by manifold *observations*, and tracked it, that I am confident it will agree at all times with my *numbers* [numeris] in a just concordance; and that thus, *by a collation of the observation made there with the computation from my own Tables in the Moon's motion* [per collationem observationis istic factae, cum numeratione e propriis Tabulis in motu ☾ae], I may infer from it accurately enough the *difference of meridians* [Differentiam Meridianorum]. But in case Rothmann should not have been on the spot with Your Princely Grace at that time, I rather suppose that Your Princely Grace's *clockmaker* [Automatopaeus], or someone else, will not have neglected this, supposing it was otherwise clear there, so that it might nevertheless be communicated to me. And if there are still other *eclipses* on hand that have been diligently observed in various years — be it long ago or lately elapsed, it is all one — I would also gladly be made a sharer of their notation, [namely] how and from which stars they were taken, for the aforesaid reason.

Without doubt Maestlin [Mesthlinus] will have several of the above-mentioned [kind of] observation in store, *carefully obtained by altitudes of the stars or by whatever other method* [per altitudines stellarum vel quacunque alia ratione sedulo deprehensas]. If, therefore, Your Princely Grace would be willing, without trouble, to make the gracious provision of having him approached on this matter, he would not refuse them to Your Princely Grace, so that they might then come to me too. For I am not myself acquainted with him. I desire only the *bare observations* [nudas observationes], just as they were marked down, and I shall well know thereafter how to *extract* [extricirn] the *times* [tempora] from them by my own *reasonings* [ratiociniis]. If, too, that same Maestlin should have diligently noted down ♄ Saturn [Saturnum] about the years [15]76, 77, and 78, and likewise ♂ Mars [Martem] in the years [15]76 and 78, *in the acronychal position* [in situ acronychio], several times, I would gladly have such observations fall to me as well, so that I might *collate* [collationirn] them with my own (which I obtained about the same times, yet not so many and so complete as I would gladly have). I have otherwise a good part of the *observations about the Sun's opposition* [Observationum circa Solis oppositum] in store, *almost throughout the whole circuit of the eccentric* [ferme per totum Eccentrici ambitum]; nevertheless, for a particular reason, I would gladly have *examined* their *acronychal appearances* [Apparentias acronychas] in these two planets about the said years, and *compared* [conferirt] them with the others that I have brought forward for myself. He may have noted them down however he will — *whether by the intervening cross-staff, by distances from certain fixed [stars], or by straight lines along the extension of a thread, by observation made crosswise in that customary manner* [sive intermediante Radio per distantias a certis Fixis, sive per lineas rectas iuxta fili extensionem, modo illi usitato decussatim facta animadversione] — yet I shall all the same know how to set myself right from them, as far as is possible, provided only that the *names of the stars and the very method of observation* [Nomina stellarum, et ipsa observationis ratio] are indicated to me.

I have also written into *Italy and Spain* [Italiam vnd Hispaniam], as well as into *Poland* [Poloniam], that I may obtain certain *lunar eclipses of past years* [Eclipses Lunares praeteritorum annorum] (those, that is, that were somewhere *accurately taken from the heavens* [accurate caelitus genomen]), and that from these — as also from those I can procure out of Germany — I may investigate the *differences of meridians* [Meridianorum Differentias] more correctly than has hitherto been done, and thus *restore* [restituiren] geography in that respect, so far as is possible (since geography, as Your Princely Grace well knows, lends astronomy no small assistance).

I would also most dutifully have asked Your Princely Grace to give command to your *clockmaker* [Automatopaeo] or watchmaker, that if he should know anywhere a young, unmarried journeyman who could deal diligently with *clocks and automata* [Horologiis vnd Automatis] and attend to my *astronomical instruments* [Instrumenta Astronomica], he should arrange that the same betake himself in here to me at the first [opportunity]. So would I employ him here for such work, and give as good a wage as he could get elsewhere. For my goldsmith — who dwelt here with me in the country, attended to my *instruments*, made many of them with his own hand, and served me herein diligently and faithfully for many years — has (alas) died on me a short while ago, so that I therefore need another skilled journeyman in his stead, of whom there are scarcely any to be had here in this country. I trust Your Princely Grace's clockmaker will do his best in this.

I long to obtain Your Princely Grace's *observations of the fixed stars* [Observationes stellarum fixarum] and to compare them with my own. For I believe nothing other than that Rothmann must by now be finished with them. As concerns my *first volume* [ersten Tomum], in which I treat of this matter at length, Your Princely Grace will get to see it, with God's help, in this coming summer, for it, together with several other things, is soon to be completed in print.

I have also written to Your Princely Grace's Mathematician concerning *18 minutes* that are everywhere lacking *in the observations of the comet of the year [15]80 communicated to me* [in Observationibus Cometae anni 80mi mihi communicatis]; for as often as the comet passed *across the meridian* [per Meridianum], just 18 minutes were taken there at Kassel too few, whereas my observations *made at the same time* [eodem tempore factae] always have just so many minutes more. Whence I reckon that such a defect was *committed by a quadrant, through a fault of the plumb-line, not rightly set by so many scruples* [durch einen Quadrantem vitio Perpendiculi, tot Scrupulis non rite directi, commissirt]. I spoke of this myself with Rothmann, when he was here, and demonstrated the same to him *by a collation of your observations and mine* [per collationem vestrarum atque mearum Observationum]; whereat he marvelled, and knew no proper cause for it. But he promised, as soon as he should arrive back with Your Princely Grace at Kassel, to investigate this more thoroughly. For he was not, at the time when this comet was observed, in Your Princely Grace's service. If, then, it was attended to by the clockmaker or by another, I would gladly have some report as to whereon this deficiency arose, before I put these observations to use *in the description of that comet* [in descriptione istius Cometae]. But that in my own *meridian observations* [Observationibus meridianis], made in the same [period], there is no error, the *altitudes* [Altitudines] taken likewise at Prague by Thaddaeus sufficiently show, which agree tolerably well with mine, *at least when account is taken of the diversity of horizons* [habita saltem ratione diuersitatis Horizontum]. I will not, however, trouble and detain Your Princely Grace any longer this time with such matters and others, but, awaiting Your gracious reply and report by the present messenger when he comes back from the Fair, herewith commend the same most diligently into the all-powerful, grace-rich protection of God, unto long bodily health and peaceful governance of the land.

Given at Uraniborg, in February, the year 1592.
Your Princely Grace's
ever willing-in-service
TYCHO BRAHE
with his own hand.

*[Postscript.]* Further I dutifully give Your Grace to understand that I have written to Your Grace's son, Landgrave Maurice, and have dutifully asked his Grace to be willing, without demur, to compose for me a Poem in commendation of my astronomical Works, since I am sufficiently informed that his Grace possesses a good poetic vein, and takes delight in it. I trust, therefore, that his Grace will condescend to inscribe such a Poem, with his own hand, upon the one side of the first leaf — where the title of my Volumes, which I now have in hand to prepare for the press, stands set down together with the Imperial Diploma, of which I have sent his Grace copies. This will be very welcome to me, and, as I judge, not without honour to his Grace, and will moreover serve to the advancement of these studies.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** **Tycho Brahe**, writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven, to **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), the astronomer-prince whose Kassel observatory was Tycho's chief institutional peer and rival. The full titulature in the address — Count of *Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda* — is the standard Hessian style and is preserved. (Wilhelm died on 25 August 1592, a few months after this letter.)
- **Document type / register.** A learned-court letter in chancery German, switching freely into Latin for every technical noun and verb (*Observationes, in omnem eventum, per omnia sua momenta, motum ☾ae, Differentiam Meridianorum, Apparentias acronychas, restituiren, conferirt*, etc.). The Latin code-switches are retained in the translation in [square brackets] after the English rendering, by this chapter's convention; technical terms follow the editorial glossary–5.2.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Rothmannus* = **Christoph Rothmann**, Wilhelm IV's mathematician; he had visited Tycho at Hven in 1590 and (as the letter notes) had by 1592 effectively left Kassel service. Tycho is unsure whether Rothmann has returned, hence the contingency instructions.
 - *Mesthlinus* = **Michael Maestlin** (1550–1631), the Tübingen astronomer (later Kepler's teacher). Tycho stresses *"I am not myself acquainted with him"* (*ich bin selber nicht mit ihm bekandt*) — a hedge preserved exactly.
 - *Thaddaeus* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius, 1525–1600), the Prague imperial physician-astronomer, whose Prague altitudes of the comet Tycho cites to vindicate his own meridian observations.
 - *Automatopaeus* (Greek-derived Latin, "automaton-/clock-maker") = the Landgrave's **clockmaker**, the celebrated Jost Bürgi (not named in the letter); rendered "clockmaker," with the term flagged. The parallel German gloss *oder Vhrmacher* ("or watchmaker") confirms the sense.
 - *Goldtschmidt* — Tycho's resident **goldsmith / instrument-maker** at Uraniborg, recently deceased; not named here.
- **Astronomy — technical notes.**
 - *Eclipsin ☾ae … in fine Decembris* — the **lunar eclipse** of late December 1591; cloud at Hven prevented Tycho observing it, hence his appeal for the Kassel timing as a check on his lunar tables and for deriving the **difference of meridians** (longitude difference Hven–Kassel). The glyph ☾ is kept in the source block and named "Moon" in the translation by this chapter's convention; *☾ae* is the Latin genitive *Lunae* abbreviated on the glyph.
 - *in situ acronychio / Apparentias acronychas* — **acronychal position / appearances**: a planet observed at opposition to the Sun (rising at sunset). Kept in Latin with the English; *acronychal* retained as the period technical term.
 - *circa Solis oppositum … per totum Eccentrici ambitum* — Tycho's program of **solar-opposition** observations of the superior planets distributed **around the whole circuit of the eccentric** (orb), the method of determining a planet's orbital elements. *Eccentric* / *opposition* per glossary.
 - ♄ (year markers 76/77/78) = **Saturn**; ♂ (76/78) = **Mars**; named in English, glyphs kept in source. *♄num / ♂tem* = the Latin accusatives *Saturnum / Martem* abbreviated on the glyph.
 - *Radio … per lineas rectas iuxta fili extensionem … decussatim* — the **cross-staff** (*radius astronomicus*, glossary) and alternative thread-/sighting methods of taking angular distances; rendered descriptively.
 - *Cometae anni 80mi* — the **great comet of 1580**, observed at both Kassel and Hven; the **18-minute** systematic discrepancy in the Kassel meridian transits is the crux Tycho attributes *vitio Perpendiculi* — a **fault of the [quadrant's] plumb-line** mis-set by "so many scruples" (*Scrupuli* = arc-minutes here). This is the clock-vs-instrument dispute documented in Dreyer (*Tycho Brahe*, on the Kassel observations) and Thoren (*Lord of Uraniborg*: "eighteen minutes in their timings of the comet of 1580").
 - *ersten Tomum* — Tycho's **first volume**, i.e. the *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* (Vol. I of his projected great work, which would carry the comet and fixed-star material); "soon to be completed in print" is the author's own optimistic forecast (it did not in fact appear until 1602, posthumously) — preserved as written, not corrected.
- **Greek-derived term.** *Automatopaeus* (ἀυτοματοποιός, "maker of self-moving things") — the court clockmaker; flagged rather than silently Englished, with the term shown.
- **Calendar / dateline — flagged crux.** The subscription reads ***"Dat. Vraniburg den Februarii Anno 1592"*** — **the day-of-month is omitted in the source text** (a blank or lost numeral between *den* and *Februarii*). The edition label supplies **"22 februar"**; the identifier encodes …0220…. I have therefore led the header with the **as-written** (incomplete) dateline — "[—] February 1592" — and appended "(catalogued 22 February 1592)," by this chapter's convention: the catalogued 22 February is **not** substantiated by the source's own dateline and is recorded here, not asserted in the header. The date is **Old Style** (Denmark kept Julian until 1700; Hesse-Kassel likewise Julian in this period). The companion Magini letter adjacent in the edition (1 Feb 1592 *n.s.*, Bologna) is unrelated.
- **Formulae (chancery German,).** Address *Mein gnediger Herr* → "my gracious Lord"; *Ew. F. G. (Ewer Fürstlichen Gnaden)* → "Your Princely Grace"; subscription *Alzeit dienstewilliger* → "ever willing-in-service"; *manu propria* → "with his own hand." *Franckfurter Messe* = the **Frankfurt Book Fair**, the channel by which Tycho's messenger travelled and by which the reply is to come back.

- **§1 Dreyer collation:** the German original leaves the day blank, but Dreyer's facing Latin (*Opera Omnia* VI, p. 298) dates it *20. Februarii*, and Wilhelm's reply (VI, p. 300) quotes *"ewer Schreiben sub dato Uraniburg, den 20. Februarij."* The day is therefore **20 February** (not the catalogue's 22); supplied editorially as **[20.]** in the Source and fixed in the header and translation.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript, restored from Dreyer VI, pp. 298–299 (dropped by the working transcription). Dreyer prints this Feb-1592 letter only in Latin (no German facing for the postscript), so the Latin is the source form. "C. E." = Celsitudo Eius (His Highness, sc. Maurice); "C. T." = Celsitudo Tua (Wilhelm).
- **What the recovered text is.** The postscript to Tycho's letter of 20 February 1592 to Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel — not a separate enclosure but the letter's own closing paragraph, written directly after the signature, which the defective transcription had previously truncated at "TYCHO BRAHE manu propria."
- **Landgrave Maurice ('Landgraff Moritz').** Wilhelm IV's son and heir; he succeeded his father later in 1592 (Wilhelm died that summer/autumn) and became known to posterity as Moritz der Gelehrte ("the Learned"), a patron and practitioner of poetry and music in his own right — matching Tycho's flattering claim that he possessed "ein gute Venam poëticam."
- **The volume this concerns.** Corpus evidence (Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, Cambridge 2007, discussing the dedication leaf) confirms Tycho's *Epistolarum astronomicarum liber primus* (Uraniborg, 1596) was in fact dedicated to Landgrave Maurice. This 1592 postscript shows Tycho cultivating that dedication four years in advance, inviting Maurice to autograph a commendatory poem onto the title-leaf of the very 'Tomorum' he was then preparing for the press, alongside the printed Imperial Diploma (Rudolf II's printing privilege).
- **Errors corrected in the prior English of this passage.** (1) "I shall humbly entreat" wrongly casts as future what the German states as already done — 'gebetten' is past tense: Tycho reports he has *already* asked Maurice, in the letter to him he mentions sending. (2) "I have long enough understood" mistranslates 'gnugksamb berichtet' ("sufficiently informed," not "for a long time"). (3) "three copies" of the Imperial Diploma is invented — the German gives only 'Exemplaria' (copies), no number. (4) The closing sentence "Given as above in the letter" has no counterpart anywhere in the German and has been removed as a fabrication. (5) "upon the other part of the first page" mistranslates 'auff die eine seidt' ("on the one side," not "the other").
- **Crux.** 'ihrer F. G.' — the pronoun governing whom Tycho sent the title-leaf/Diploma copies to — differs from the 'Ew./Eure F. G.' used for the addressee Wilhelm throughout the rest of the letter. Read here as continuing to refer to Maurice in the third person (parallel to 'seine F. G.' earlier in the same sentence), i.e. the copies went to Maurice, not to Wilhelm; but an ENHG scribal variant of 'seiner' cannot be wholly excluded.
- **Correction.** Removed a fabricated day-number ('the 20th') from the dateline; the source gives only 'den Februarii Anno 1592', with no day stated.

**1 defect found:**
- **fabrication** (**high**). The German dateline carries no day-number at all ('den Februarii', not 'den 20. Februarii') — the English inserts a specific '20th' with no counterpart in the transcribed original. This is exactly the invented-day-number failure mode this audit was briefed to watch for; the '20' appears to have been pulled from the catalogue metadata (date field / identifier) rather than from the letter's own text. At: “Given at Uraniborg, the 20th of February, the year 1592.”.

**Repaired.** No Dreyer page images were available for this letter (no page reference), so the fix rests entirely on the letter's own internal evidence, which is conclusive on this point: the German dateline as given in the transcribed original literally has no day-number between 'den' and 'Februarii'. Only the fabricated '20th' was removed; nothing else in the letter was checked or touched, since no edition-of-record collation was possible.

documents.incipit: AMIROR eruditissime et dilecte mi ROTHMANNE, te, ex quo hinc discessisti, nihil prorsus …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET ERVDITISSIMO VIRO, D. CHRISTOPHORO ROTHMANNO ILLVSTRISSIMI PRINCIPIS
WILHELMI, LANDTGRAUIJ HASSIÆ, ETC. MATHEMATICO EXIMIO, AMICO SUO
PLURIMUM DILECTO. S. D.

AMIROR eruditissime et dilecte mi ROTHMANNE,
te, ex quo hinc discessisti, nihil prorsus ad me literarum dedisse, elapso ferme
iam sesquialtero<sup></sup> Anno. Neque enim existimo te tam inhumaniter a me vel exceptum, vel
dimissum fuisse, quin paucula verba recordationis ergo, vicissim scribendo
impertiri, aut saltem per alios me salutare, deque tuis rebus commonefacere
æquum fuisset. Scripsit semel atque iterum ad me Illustrissimus tuus Princeps,
atque vbi tam diu morareris miratus est. Verum cum ego ignorarem, quibus in locis<sup></sup> degeres, scripsi hac de re fratri tuo IOHANNI ROTHMANNO, qui te valetudiniarium in patria hærere
tandem significavit. At quoniam existimem<sup></sup> te interea ad Principem tuum reuersum esse, intermittere nolui quo minus
te his compellarem. Rogo autem, vt Eclipsin Lunæ vltimam, si modo illîc<sup></sup> accurate obseruata sit<sup></sup>, mecum, quo ad totum Obseruationis processum, communices. Apud nos tunc
temporis non erat serenum, saltem Lunam biduo, et ante et post, cum esset circa
90. ab Horizonte Eclipticæ gradum, sedulo obseruauimus, id enim solum<sup></sup> concedebatur. Et si quas alias Eclipses vel Cassellis, aut etiam a MESTLINO vel alijs diligenter annotatas, conquirere licebit, fac
vt earum nudas saltem Obseruationes descriptas, pro Meridianorum diuersitatibus
hinc inde rimandis conciliandisque obtineam. Expeto etiam Acronychas Saturni
circa Annum 76. 77. et 78. et Martis 76. et 78.<sup></sup> considerationes, quas proculdubio a MESTLINO per literas impetrabis, dummodo is talibus attenderit.
De 18. illis Minutis (quæ, cum hîc esses, monstraui in Altitudinibus meridianis
Cometæ Anni 1580. illic<sup></sup> obseruatis vbique deficere) cupio a te certior fieri, prout etiam
pollicitus es, quâ occasione idipsum contigerit. Velim insuper, vt mihi exponas
rationem eam facilime contexendi Canones Sinuum, quæ a IVSTO BYRGIO vestro dicitur excogitata. Neque enim satis
assequor, an in recessu habeat id quod primâ fronte
pollicetur; Rogoque, tum de his, tum alijs, deque tuo rerum statu, mihi per hunc ipsum<sup></sup> hominem Bibliopolam nostratem e Nundinis Francofurdianis ad nos redeuntem,
affatim rescribas.

Vale.
TYCHO BRAHE.<sup></sup>
text.english:
**To the most renowned and most learned man, Master Christoph Rothmann, distinguished mathematician of the Most Illustrious Prince Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, etc., his much-beloved friend — heartiest greeting.**

I marvel, my most learned and beloved Rothmann, that since you departed from here you have sent me no letter at all, now that nearly a year and a half has slipped by. For I do not think that you were either so inhumanely received or dismissed by me that it would not have been fair, by way of remembrance, to share in turn a few words by writing, or at least to greet me through others and to keep me informed about your affairs. Your Most Illustrious Prince has written to me once and again, and has wondered where you were tarrying so long. But since I did not know in what places you were dwelling, I wrote about this matter to your brother Johannes Rothmann, who at length signified that you were stuck in your homeland in poor health. Yet since I suppose that you have meanwhile returned to your Prince, I was unwilling to refrain from addressing you with these [lines]. I ask, then, that you share with me — as to the whole course of the observation — the last eclipse of the Moon, if only it was accurately observed there. With us at that time the sky was not clear; we did at least diligently observe the Moon for two days, both before and after, when it was about the 90th degree of the ecliptic from the horizon, for that alone was granted [us]. And if it shall be possible to gather any other eclipses, whether [observed] at Kassel, or also carefully recorded by Maestlin or others, see to it that I obtain at least the bare observations of them written out, for sounding out and reconciling on this side and that the differences of meridians. I seek also the acronychal observations of Saturn around the years [15]76, [15]77, and [15]78, and of Mars [in] [15]76 and [15]78 — considerations which you will doubtless obtain from Maestlin by letter, provided he has attended to such things. About those 18 minutes (which, when you were here, I showed to be everywhere deficient in the meridian altitudes of the comet of the year 1580 observed there) I desire to be more certainly informed by you, as indeed you promised, [namely] by what occasion this very thing came about. I should like, furthermore, that you set out for me that method of most easily constructing canons of sines which is said to have been devised by your Justus Byrgius. For I do not sufficiently grasp whether it holds in reserve what it promises at first sight; and I ask that, both about these matters and about others, and about the state of your affairs, you write back to me fully by this very man, our bookseller, returning to us from the Frankfurt Fair.

Farewell.
TYCHO BRAHE.

Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** **Tycho Brahe**, writing from Uraniborg on Hven, to **Christoph Rothmann** (*Christophorus Rothmannus*, c. 1550–after 1600), mathematician to Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel. Rothmann had visited Hven in 1590; the letter opens by reproaching him for a year and a half of silence since that departure. The letter is one of the set Tycho himself printed in the 1596 *Epistolae astronomicae* (Liber I), which is the edition of record.
- **Persons named.** *IOHANNI ROTHMANNO* = **Johannes Rothmann**, Christoph's brother. *MESTLINO* = **Michael Maestlin** (Maestlin, 1550–1631), then professor at Tübingen, Kepler's teacher; Tycho seeks his planetary and cometary observations through Rothmann. *IVSTO BYRGIO vestro* = **Jost (Justus) Bürgi** (Byrgius, 1552–1632), the Landgrave's clockmaker and instrument-maker at Kassel; "your Justus Byrgius" marks him as a member of the Kassel circle.
- **Place.** *Cassellis* = at **Kassel** (the Hessen court observatory); *Nundinae Francofurdianae* = the **Frankfurt Fair** (book fair), via which the carrier bookseller travels.
- **Astronomy — technical.** *Eclipsin Lunae* = the (last) **lunar eclipse**; *Eclipses* = **eclipses**; *Meridianorum diuersitates … conciliandae* = the **differences of meridians** (longitude differences between observing sites) to be reconciled — the rationale for collecting others' eclipse timings. *circa 90. ab Horizonte Eclipticae gradum* — "about the 90th degree of the ecliptic from the horizon," i.e. the point of the ecliptic culminating / highest above the horizon; rendered literally and not smoothed, as the phrasing is compressed. *Acronychas … considerationes* = **acronychal** observations (a body observed at acronychal rising, i.e. rising at sunset, in opposition to the Sun) of **Saturn** and **Mars** for the stated years. *Altitudines meridianae Cometae Anni 1580* = the **meridian altitudes** of the **comet of 1580**.
- **The "18 minutes" crux of substance (not of reading).** *De 18. illis Minutis … vbique deficere* — Tycho reports that the meridian altitudes of the 1580 comet observed "there" (at Kassel) were found to be deficient everywhere by 18 arc-minutes, a systematic error he had demonstrated to Rothmann in person, and about whose *cause* (*quâ occasione*) he now asks. The number, the systematic sense ("everywhere deficient"), and the open question of cause are preserved exactly; Tycho's own request to be "more certainly informed" is a genuine hedge and is kept.
- **Canones Sinuum / Bürgi's method.** *rationem … contexendi Canones Sinuum, quae a IVSTO BYRGIO … dicitur excogitata* = "the method of constructing **canons of sines** said to have been devised by Justus Byrgius." This is the Kassel computational method (Bürgi's *Kunstweg* / sine-table technique), connected to the additive–subtractive **prosthaphaeresis** technique then current at Kassel; "canons of sines" is kept literal per the editorial glossary, and *prosthaphaeresis* is not introduced into the translation because Tycho does not use the word here. Tycho's skepticism is hedged — *Neque enim satis assequor, an in recessu habeat id quod primâ fronte pollicetur* ("I do not sufficiently grasp whether it holds in reserve what it promises at first sight") — and the hedge is preserved, not sharpened into a verdict.
- **Editorial sigla.** The superscript **A** markers scattered through the text (*sesquialtero*<sup>A</sup>, *locis*<sup>A</sup>, *existimem*<sup>A</sup>, *illîc*<sup>A</sup>, *sit*<sup>A</sup>, *solum*<sup>A</sup>, *78.*<sup>A</sup>, *illic*<sup>A</sup>, *ipsum*<sup>A</sup>, and after the signature) are footnote/variant-reading anchors carried over from the printed edition's apparatus, not part of the letter's own text. They are reproduced in the Source block as printed and ignored in the translation. The underlying readings adopted are the unmarked text as printed; no variant affects the sense of the translation.
- **Orthography.** Edition spelling retained in the Source block: consonantal *u* for *v* and *j* for final *i* (*Landtgrauij*, *alijs*, *literarum*); *vbi*, *vt*, *vltimam* with *v* for initial *u*; *hîc / illîc / quâ / primâ* with the edition's circumflexes; *AMIROR* is the edition's printed form of *admiror* ("I marvel"), so read and translated.
- **Salutation / subscription.** *S. D.* = *salutem dicit*, "(sends) heartiest greeting". *Vale* = "Farewell."
- **Calendar.** The letter bears no dateline in the printed text supplied; the catalogue assigns **20 February 1592, Uraniborg**, which (Denmark being on the Julian calendar until 1700) is **Old Style**. The header follows the catalogued date because the source text carries no internal dateline to lead with; this is flagged here rather than asserted as in-text.

documents.incipit: DURCHLEUCHTIGER/ Hochgeborner Fürst. Ewer F. G. seyndt meine Dienste nach allem vermügen …
documents.editorial_note: **Text recovered.** The postscript or enclosure, missing from the first transcription, has been restored from the text of record and translated. The Source and English columns below are now complete.

text.original:
DEM DURCHLEUCHTIGEN / HOCHGEBORNEN FÜRSTEN VND HERRN/ HERRN MAVRITZ, GEBORN LANDTGRAUEN ZU HESSEN/ GRAUEN ZU CATZENELNBOGEN/ DIETZ/ ZIEGENHAIN VND NIDDA: MEINEM GNEDIGEN HERRN.

DURCHLEUCHTIGER/ Hochgeborner Fürst. Ewer F. G. seyndt meine Dienste nach allem vermügen jederzeit zuvor an bereit. Gnediger Herr. Wiewol ich mit Ew. F. G. weiter nicht bekant bin/ dan da ich Ew. F. G. Herrn Vater/ vor etlichen jaren zu Cassel besuchte/ zu welcher zeit Ew. F. G. noch gar jung war/ So hab ich doch gleichwol sieder der zeit von andern vielmals verstanden/ daß Ew. F. G. mit fürtrefflichen Fürstlichen Tugenden/ auch nicht mit geringer gelehrtheit soll begabt seyn. Vnd hat mir Ew. F. G. Herrn Vaters Mathematicus ROTHMANNVS alhie gesagt/ daß Ew. F. G. mein Name so sehr vnbekandt nicht sey: Viellicht auß den Schreiben/ die ich zu etlichen maln an Ew. F. G. Herrn Vater/ von Astronomischen Sachen dienstlich gegeben hab. Auß welchen vnd andern Vrsachen ich nicht habe vnderlassen wollen/ Ew. F. G. mit diesem meinem geringen/ jedoch diensterbietigem Schreiben zu besuchen/ In hoffnung/ Ew. F. G. werde es im besten auffnemen. Wan mir dan beyde von gedachtem Mathematico vnd andern/ die da gute Wissenschafft darumb haben/ glaubwürdiger Bericht gethan ist/ daß Ew. F. G. ohn dem/ daß sie in Hebraica, Græca, et Latina lingua wol erfahren vnd geübet sey/ vnd andere Artes liberales in pretio halte/ ein excellente gute venam Poëticam, vnd grosse Lust zu solchem Poëtico studio haben solte: So hab ich mich vnderstehen dürffen/ Ew. F. G. dienstlich anzulangen/ daß sie wolte vnbescheret seyn/ per otium ein Carmen commendatorium in Opera mea Astronomica,quæ præ manibus edenda habe zu componiren, vnd mir bey dieser Botschafft/ da die von der Franckfurter Messe widerumb zu rücke zeucht/ gnedich mitzutheilen. Ich versehe mich/ es werde Ew. F. G. solches keines weges inhonorificum seyn/ dan ich bin willens/ dasselbige gestracks auff das andre Blat in meinem primo Tomo (worvon ich drey Exemplaria des ersten Bogens hiebeygelegt habe) drucken zu lassen. Da derowegen Ew. F. G. sich wolte verdemüthigen/ dasselbige Carmen auff die eine Seite/ die da leer ist/ nechst für dem Diplomate Cæsareo, mit eigener Hand selber zu schreiben/ vnd mir also eines darvon widerumb zuzuschicken/ daß ich es darnacher baldt nechstfolgendt einem andern (welches ich a Serenissimo Rege Scotiæ, der auch ein trefflich guter Poët ist/ in gleicher massen täglich gewertig bin/ vnd auff der ersten Seit/ nechst dem Effigie, dieweyl er ein König/ vnd mit vnserm Königlichen Stamme beschwägert ist/ stehen wirdt) möchte imprimiren lassen: Erzeigte Ew. F. G. in dem nicht allein jren Sonderlichen gnedigen Willen gegen mich/ sondern auch ein wolgeneigt liebtragendes Gemüt gegen die herrliche Astronomische Kunst vnd andere hohe Studia, Vnd were es Ew. F. G. ohn das/ von wegen jres Hochgeliebten Herrn Vaters/ der zu dieser Kunst viel Jar her einen grossen Lust vnd gefallen getragen/ vnd hoch darein erfahren ist/ nicht vnrühmlich. Dan je vnd allezeit von Anfang der Welt/ sölche fürtreffliche Kunst/ von hohen mit reichem Verstande erleuchteten Potentaten, Keysern/ Königen vnd Fürsten/ wie auch insonderheit von Ew. F. G. Herrn Vater/ wie gesagt ist/ in grosser Liebe vnd Würde gehalten/ auch nicht ohn gebürliche Vnkosten befördert vnd gehandthabt seyndt. Ich zweiffel nicht/ Ew. F. G. werde gleichsfalls darüber zu halten geneigt seyn/ vnd jr Fürstlich Gemüt in solchen wissendtwürdigen Himlischen vnd hohen Sachen/ bißweylen von den Irdischen (die man doch tractiren muß) erhaben/ je lenger je mehr delectiren vnd acuiren, vnd daher gnediglich gewogen seyn/ meiner obangeregten Bitt bey sich stat sinden zu lassen. So baldt etliche von meinen Tomis durchauß verfertigt seyndt/ wil ich nicht alleine Ew. F. G. Herrn Vater/ dieweyl seine F. G. einen besondern wolgefallen darzu tregt/ vnd dasselb gnedigst von mir begert hat/ sondern auch Ew. F. G. etliche Exemplaria davon communiciren. Vnd wo ich Ew. F. G. nach meinem geringen vermügen sonst dienen kan/ erbiete ich mich williger dan willig/ vnd soll Ew. F. G. in dem jederzeit vber mich zu gebieten haben.

Wil Ew. F. G. in deß Allerhöchsten gnadenreichen Schirm/ zu langwirigem Wolstande/ hiemit dienstlich vnd getrewlich befohlen haben.
Datum Vraniburg, den 20. Februarij, Anno 1592.
Ewer F. G.
Dienstwilliger
TYCHO BRAHE.

INFRA HAS LITERAS TYCHO HOC SEQUENS IPSEMET SUBSCRIPSERAT
EPIGRAMMA.INCLYTE MAVRITI, sublimibus annue cœptis

    Si vacat, atque alio non tua cura vocat:

Nec pigeat nostros venâ illustrare labores

    Mellifluâ, tibi quam fautor Apollo dedit.

Non indigna tuo, nec ages aliena Parente,

    Qui Iura egregie callet amatque Poli:

Nec tibi dedecorum, quia Principis enthea, soli

    Haud obstricta Solo mens agat, alta volet.

Adde quod vna nouem Musas, quas diligis, inter

    Vrania est, primo conspicienda loco;

Hanc igitur modico si ornâris Carmine, fiet

Cum fratre et reliquo plus tibi amica choro.

    Ipse quoque (vt magnis liceat componere parua)

Si mea quid valeat Musula, gratus ero.
text.english:
**To the Most Illustrious, High-born Prince and Lord, Lord Moritz, born Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain and Nidda: my gracious Lord.**

Most Illustrious, High-born Prince. My services, to the full extent of my ability, are at all times beforehand ready for Your Princely Grace. Gracious Lord. Although I am not further acquainted with Your Princely Grace than from the time when, some years ago, I visited Your Princely Grace's Lord Father at Kassel — at which time Your Princely Grace was still quite young — I have nonetheless since that time understood many times from others that Your Princely Grace is said to be endowed with excellent princely virtues, and also with no slight learning. And Your Princely Grace's Lord Father's mathematician *Rothmann* has told me here that my name is not so very unknown to Your Princely Grace: perhaps from the letters which I have at various times rendered, in matters astronomical, to Your Princely Grace's Lord Father. For these and other reasons I have not wished to omit to visit Your Princely Grace with this my humble yet dutifully-tendered letter, in the hope that Your Princely Grace will take it in the best part. Since, then, credible report has been made to me, both by the said mathematician and by others who have good knowledge thereof, that Your Princely Grace — besides being well-versed and practised *in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin tongue* [*in Hebraica, Graeca, et Latina lingua*], and holding the other *liberal arts* in esteem — is said to have an excellent good *poetic vein* [*venam Poëticam*] and a great delight in such *poetic study* [*Poëtico studio*]: I have therefore made bold to approach Your Princely Grace dutifully [with the request] that you would be willing, at your leisure [*per otium*], to compose *a commendatory poem upon my astronomical works which I have in hand to publish* [*ein Carmen commendatorium in Opera mea Astronomica, quae prae manibus edenda habe*], and graciously to convey it to me by this messenger, when he travels back again from the Frankfurt fair. I am persuaded that this will in no way be *dishonourable* [*inhonorificum*] to Your Princely Grace, for I am minded to have the same printed straightway on the second leaf in my *first volume* [*primo Tomo*] (of which I have enclosed herewith three *copies* [*Exemplaria*] of the first sheet). If, therefore, Your Princely Grace would condescend to write that same poem, with your own hand yourself, upon the one side which is blank, next before the *Imperial Diploma* [*Diploma Caesareo*], and so to send me one of them back again, so that I might thereafter have it printed shortly next following another [poem] (which I am likewise daily expecting *from the Most Serene King of Scotland* [*a Serenissimo Rege Scotiae*], who is also a remarkably good poet, and which will stand on the first side, next to the *portrait* [*Effigie*], inasmuch as he is a King and is allied by marriage with our Royal line): Your Princely Grace would thereby show not only your particular gracious good-will toward me, but also a well-disposed, affectionate spirit toward the glorious astronomical art and other high *studies* [*Studia*]; and it would, besides, not be inglorious for Your Princely Grace, on account of your dearly-beloved Lord Father, who for many years has borne a great delight and pleasure in this art, and is highly skilled in it. For ever and always, from the beginning of the world, such an excellent art has been held in great love and worth by exalted potentates, emperors, kings and princes illumined with rich understanding — as also in particular by Your Princely Grace's Lord Father, as has been said — and has been furthered and maintained not without due expense. I do not doubt that Your Princely Grace will likewise be inclined to uphold it, and — your princely spirit at times raised up, in such heavenly and high matters worthy of knowing, above earthly ones (which yet one must handle) — will the longer the more take delight and be quickened therein [*delectiren vnd acuiren*], and hence be graciously disposed to let my above-mentioned request find a place with you. As soon as some of my *volumes* [*Tomis*] are quite finished, I will impart several *copies* [*Exemplaria*] of them not only to Your Princely Grace's Lord Father — since His Princely Grace bears a particular pleasure in it, and has most graciously desired the same of me — but also to Your Princely Grace. And wherever else I can serve Your Princely Grace according to my humble ability, I offer myself more willing than willing, and Your Princely Grace shall in that matter at all times have me at your command.

Herewith I would dutifully and faithfully commend Your Princely Grace to the gracious protection of the Most High, for long-enduring well-being.
Given at Uraniborg, the 20th of February, in the year 1592.
Your Princely Grace's
Devoted servant,
TYCHO BRAHE.

**Below this letter Tycho had himself appended, in his own hand, the following epigram.**

**EPIGRAM.**

Illustrious Maurice, grant your favour to lofty undertakings,
    if you have leisure, and your care is not called elsewhere:

Nor let it weary you to give lustre to our labours with that
    honey-flowing vein which your patron Apollo gave you.

You will do nothing unworthy of your Father, nor foreign to him,
    who excellently knows and loves the laws of the Pole [the heavens]:

Nor is it any disgrace to you that a Prince's god-filled mind, not
    bound to the earth alone, should act, and would fly aloft.

Add to this, that among the nine Muses whom you cherish,
    Urania alone is to be regarded first;

If, then, you adorn her with even a modest song, she will become,
    together with her brother [Apollo] and the rest of the choir, the more your friend.

I too — if small things may be set beside great — shall be
    grateful, should my own little Muse be worth anything.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** Tycho Brahe, writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven. At this date (1592) Tycho was assembling his *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri*, the first volume of which he printed at his own Uraniborg press.
- **Recipient.** *Mauritz, geborn Landtgrave zu Hessen* = **Moritz "the Learned," Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1572–1632), then nineteen; he succeeded his father Wilhelm IV in August 1592, six months after this letter. The opening confirms the relationship: Tycho is "not further acquainted" with Moritz than from a visit to **Moritz's Lord Father, Wilhelm IV**, years earlier (Tycho's 1575 Kassel visit), when Moritz "was still quite young." Throughout, *Ew. F. G. Herrn Vater* ("Your Princely Grace's Lord Father") is **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), Tycho's princely correspondent and fellow-observer, here spoken of as living.
- ***Rothmannus*** — **Christoph Rothmann**, Wilhelm IV's court mathematician at Kassel, who had visited Tycho on Hven in 1590 and could vouch for Tycho's name to the young Moritz.
- **Titulature.** The address gives Moritz's full style: *Landtgrave zu Hessen, Grave zu Catzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain vnd Nidda* — "Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain and Nidda," the standard Hessian comital titles, preserved by this chapter's convention/. *Ew. F. G.* = *Euer Fürstliche Gnade(n)*, "Your Princely Grace," kept throughout.
- **The request — the central matter.** Tycho asks Moritz to compose, in his own hand, a *Carmen commendatorium* (commendatory poem) to be printed in the front-matter of the *primo Tomo* of his astronomical works — specifically on the blank verso (*die eine Seite, die da leer ist*) next before the *Diploma Caesareum* (the **Imperial privilege/diploma** Tycho had obtained). A companion poem from *a Serenissimo Rege Scotiae* — **James VI of Scotland** (later James I of England), whom Tycho had hosted on Hven in 1590 — was to stand on the recto next to the *Effigies* (Tycho's engraved **portrait**), James being given precedence as a crowned king "allied by marriage with our Royal line" (James had married Anne of Denmark in 1589). Adam Mosley (*Bearing the Heavens*, 2007) treats exactly this letter, reading the offer as a status-exchange in which Tycho dangles proximity to an Imperial privilege and a royal poem to secure the patron's contribution.
- **Latin code-switching.** This is genuine chancery German, but Tycho switches into Latin for nearly every technical or bibliographic noun: *in Hebraica, Graeca, et Latina lingua*; *Artes liberales*; *venam Poëticam*; *Poëtico studio*; *per otium* ("at leisure"); *Carmen commendatorium in Opera mea Astronomica, quae prae manibus edenda habe* ("a commendatory poem upon my astronomical works, which I have in hand to publish"); *inhonorificum*; *primo Tomo*; *Exemplaria*; *Diplomate Caesareo*; *a Serenissimo Rege Scotiae*; *Effigie*; *Studia*; *delectiren vnd acuiren* (Latin verbs *delectare/acuere* given German chancery infinitives — "take delight and be quickened/sharpened"); *Tomis*; *communiciren*; *imprimiren*. All are kept in the source and shown bracketed in the translation by this chapter's convention
- **Litotes / negation (tracked).** The letter's courtesy runs on understatement; the negations are reproduced one-for-one and not flattened: *weiter nicht bekant bin* ("not further acquainted"); *nicht mit geringer gelehrtheit* ("with no slight learning"); *mein Name so sehr vnbekandt nicht sey* ("my name is not so very unknown"); *nicht habe vnderlassen wollen* ("have not wished to omit"); *keines weges inhonorificum* ("in no way dishonourable"); *nicht allein … sondern auch* ("not only … but also"); *nicht vnrühmlich* ("not inglorious"); *nicht ohn gebürliche Vnkosten* ("not without due expense"); *Ich zweiffel nicht* ("I do not doubt"). Nine negations in the body, nine in the rendering.
- ***williger dan willig*** — "more willing than willing," a chancery flourish of self-abasement; kept literal.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datum Vraniburg, den 20. Februarij, Anno 1592* = "Given at Uraniborg, 20 February 1592." Denmark used the **Julian calendar (Old Style)** in 1592; the date is O.S. and matches the edition label (*1592. 20. februar. Uraniborg*) — no in-letter discrepancy.
- **Edition note.** The text-of-record is Tycho's own *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Uraniborg, 1596) — the very volume the letter is soliciting verses *for* — corresponding to Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VI. No manuscript witness is recorded in the edition.
- **What it is.** An autograph Latin epigram — not part of the dictated/scribal letter body — that Tycho appended in his own hand beneath a German-language letter to the young Landgrave Moritz of Hesse-Kassel, six months before Moritz succeeded his father Wilhelm IV as Landgrave (Wilhelm IV died August 1592). The scribal heading identifying it as autograph is itself part of the recovered text.
- **Occasion.** Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel was Tycho's most important astronomical correspondent and patron among the German princes; Tycho later dedicated the *Epistolae astronomicae* (1596) to Moritz in his late father's memory [Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens* (2007)]. This epigram shows Tycho already cultivating the son directly as the succession approached, urging him to try his own hand at astronomical verse.
- **Content.** The epigram flatters Moritz's poetic gift ("that honey-flowing vein which your patron Apollo gave you") and urges him to write in honour of Urania, Muse of astronomy — framing this as consonant with his father's own devotion to "the laws of the heavens" and as no derogation from princely dignity for a mind naturally inclined to fly high.
- **Crux.** Lines 7–8 ("Nec tibi dedecorum, quia Principis enthea, soli / Haud obstricta Solo mens agat, alta volet") turn on a compressed, possibly punning contrast between *soli* ("alone") and *Solo* ("the ground/earth" — perhaps also evoking *Sol*, the sun) that resists fully certain resolution; the translation given follows the most natural sense but the exact syntactic binding is not certain.
- **Closing self-deprecation.** Tycho signs off comparing his own poetic effort to Moritz's with an inverted Virgilian modesty tag ("si parva componere magnis licet", here "magnis...parva"), a conventional humanist topos.
