documents.abstract: Sends the first printed gathering of his forthcoming works with its contents table, and asks Scultetus to show it to local booksellers and negotiate terms for copies.
documents.incipit: EN! habes mi SCULTETE, operum nostrorum, diu a te atque alijs desideratum , primum …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO DOCTISSIMOQUE VIRO M. BARTHOLOMÆO SCULTETO, GORLICENSI, RERUM MATHEMATICARUM PERITISSIMO, VETERI SUO AMICO PLURIMUM COLENDO. S.

EN! habes mi SCULTETE, operum nostrorum, diu a te atque alijs desideratum , primum Quaternionem, inscriptionem quatuor subsequentium tomorum eorumque contenta breviter complectentem. Hinc cætera ratiocinare. Addidi MYLIJ vestri succinctum Epigramma, sed in plerisque a me immutatum, eo quod prius illud nimis affectuosum atque insolens quibusdam videri posset; nec tali me dignor honore. Agas vero illi gratias pro suo candido et benevolo erga me meaque studia amore. Si mihi scripserit, ego par pari referre, et amicitiam cum isto inposterum colere, non tergiversabor. Monstra quoque vestratibus Bibliopolis hanc operum nostrorum inscriptionem, et, an aliquot exemplaria iusto pretio obtinere satagant, exquire, quidque pro singulis Alphabetis aut quaternionibus numerandum sit, cum illis transige, posteaque me, et de pretio et de exemplarium numero, quæ habere velint, certiorem effice. Continebit quodlibet horum voluminum, quæ quatuor omnino erunt, circiter sesquina Alphabeta, in charta quam regalem vocant, suntque plurimis Schematis atque Tabulis hinc inde conferta. Tuum itaque erit, nostris desiderijs morem gerere, negotium hoc fideliter, ac si tuum esset (quod et tibi confido) agere, meque per primam oblatam occasionem de singulis commonefacere. Vale, et præstantissimum illum MYLIUM meo nomine diligenter saluta. Iamque ambo feliciter vivite, bibite, valete. Propino vobis hoc die ☉, quo et hîc et isthic alibique potare solent fere omnes (rem scilicet Bacho sacram gratamque facientes) unum alterumque cantharulum, eiusdem Liæi liquore usque ad exuberantiam refertum, idque haustu etiam Bachico, licet non Philosophico, multo minus Theologico, quamvis dies Christianis sacer esse deberet: Ebibo autem pro vestra salute, quod et magnus BARTHOLINUS, nunc mihi domesticus, proxime assidens, lubenter satisfecit. Non crediderim illum artem hanc apud vos didicisse, cum in Patria eius Seelandia rudes ipsius non sint. Vestrum est, nobis iugiter et gurguliter par pari referre, etiam adhibita Musica, quemadmodum nos non sine buccinarum, tibiarum, fidium clangore et suavi concentu, hæc pocula vobis vovimus. Iterum atque iterum vivite, bibite, valete, literasque has ad MONAVIUM Vratislaviam destinate.

Datæ Uraniburgi d. 12. Martij Anno 1592.
TYCHO BRAHE, manu propria.
text.english:
**To the most distinguished and most learned man, Master Bartholomaeus Scultetus of Görlitz, most skilled in mathematical matters, his old friend to be greatly honoured — greeting.**

Look! you have here, my Scultetus, the first gathering [Quaternion] of our works — long desired by you and by others — which sets out the title of the four volumes that follow and briefly comprehends their contents. From this reckon the rest. I have added the terse epigram of your Mylius, but in most places altered by me, because that earlier version might seem to some too effusive and out of the ordinary; nor do I deem myself worthy of such an honour. Do, however, render him thanks for his frank and kindly affection toward me and my studies. If he writes to me, I shall not shrink from returning like for like and cultivating a friendship with him hereafter. Show this title of our works also to your booksellers there, and find out whether they are eager to obtain a number of copies at a fair price; and settle with them what is to be paid for each Alphabet or gathering, and afterward make me the more certain both as to the price and as to the number of copies they wish to have. Each of these volumes — which will be four in all — will contain about one and a half Alphabets [sheets], on what they call royal paper, and they are crammed throughout with very many diagrams and tables. It will therefore be your part to humour our wishes, to conduct this business faithfully, as if it were your own (which I also trust to you), and to keep me apprised of each point at the first occasion offered. Farewell, and diligently greet in my name that most excellent Mylius. And now, both of you, live happily, drink, and be well. I drink your health on this day of the Sun [☉, Sunday] — on which, both here and there and elsewhere, nearly all are wont to drink (performing, that is, a thing sacred and pleasing to Bacchus) — one cup and another, brimful to overflowing with the liquor of the same Lyaeus, and that too with a Bacchic draught, though not a Philosophical one, much less a Theological, even though the day ought to be holy to Christians: but I drink it down for your health, which the great Bartholinus too, now of my household, sitting close beside me, has gladly performed. I would not believe that he learned this art among you, since in his homeland Zealand they are not unschooled in it themselves. It is yours to return like for like to us, continuously and throat-deep, with music brought in too — just as we, not without the blare and sweet concord of trumpets, pipes, and strings, have pledged these cups to you. Again and again, live, drink, and be well; and send this letter on to Monavius at Breslau.

Given at Uraniborg, the 12th day of March, in the year 1592.
TYCHO BRAHE, by his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *M. Bartholomaeus Scultetus, Gorlicensis* = **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (Bartholomäus Schultz, 1540–1614), mathematician, cartographer, and astronomer of **Görlitz** (Latin *Gorlicium*, in Upper Lusatia), where he served as mayor; a long-standing correspondent and friend of Tycho's. The title *M.* (*Magister*) is the academic "Master".
- **Occasion.** The "first *Quaternion*" (*primum Quaternionem*) is the printed specimen gathering — the title-leaf-cum-prospectus announcing Tycho's projected four-volume *opera*: the great programme that would issue (in part) as the *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata*. Tycho is using Scultetus as his book-trade agent in Görlitz/Lusatia to gauge demand among the booksellers and to set a per-gathering price.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Mylius vester* — **(Caspar) Mylius**, a Görlitz man in Scultetus's circle, author of a laudatory *epigramma* on Tycho's works which Tycho says he has toned down. Identification of the praenomen is not secured by the letter; "Mylius" is kept as written.
 - *magnus Bartholinus, nunc mihi domesticus* — "the great Bartholinus, now of my household": a member of the Danish **Bartholin** family then resident with Tycho on Hven, said to be from **Zealand** (*Seelandia*). **Crux flagged:** the famous Caspar Bartholin the Elder (1585–1629) was a child of seven in 1592 and cannot be meant; the person here is an older Bartholin (the epithet *magnus*, "the great/elder," and *artem hanc* — the drinking — are jocular). The precise individual is not determined from the text and is left un-asserted.
 - *Monavius, Vratislaviam* — **Jacob Monau** (Jacobus Monavius, 1546–1603), humanist of **Breslau** (Latin *Vratislavia*, modern Wrocław), another of Tycho's correspondents; Tycho asks Scultetus to forward the letter (and presumably the prospectus) on to him. *Vratislaviam* is the accusative of destination, "to Breslau."
- **Bibliographical / book-trade terms.**
 - *Alphabeta* — an "Alphabet" is the bibliographer's unit of 23 gathering-signatures (A–Z, excluding J, U, W); *circiter sesquina Alphabeta* = "about one and a half Alphabets," i.e. roughly 34–35 sheets per volume. Rendered "Alphabet(s)," glossed.
 - *quaternio* — strictly a quire of four folded sheets (a *quaternion*); here used both for that codicological unit and, in the opening, for the specimen prospectus-gathering. Kept as "gathering [Quaternion]."
 - *charta quam regalem vocant* — "what they call royal paper" (*charta regalis*, a large-format premium paper); Tycho's own hedging phrase *quam … vocant* preserved.
 - *Schematis atque Tabulis* — "diagrams and tables," the figures of the astronomical text.
- **Symbol.** *hoc die ☉* — the glyph **☉** is the symbol of the **Sun**; *dies Solis* = **Sunday**. Per this chapter's convention the glyph is kept in the source block and named in English ("this day of the Sun [Sunday]"). Tycho's wit turns on its being the Lord's Day, on which he nonetheless drinks a "Bacchic, not Philosophical, much less Theological" draught.
- **Classical allusions (kept as metaphor).** *Bacho … Bachico* — **Bacchus**, god of wine; *eiusdem Liaei liquore* — *Lyaeus* ("the Loosener," *Lyaios*) is a cult-epithet of Bacchus, here "the liquor of the same Lyaeus," i.e. wine. *par pari referre* — the proverbial "to return like for like." *iugiter et gurguliter* — a jingling pair, "continuously and throat-deep" (*gurguliter*, from *gurgulio*, the gullet, is a mock-coinage matching *iugiter*); the playful rhyme is signalled rather than smoothed.
- **Epistolary formulae.** Opening *S.* = *salutem* ("greeting"); the triple sign-off *vivite, bibite, valete* ("live, drink, and be well") and *Vale* ("Farewell") by this chapter's convention; subscription *manu propria* = "by his own hand."
- **Calendar / place.** *Datae Uraniburgi d. 12. Martij Anno 1592* = "Given at **Uraniborg** [on Hven], the 12th day of March, year 1592" — Old Style (Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). The catalogue *label* date (1592.12. marts. Uraniborg) agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy. The edition of record is the *Singularia historico-literaria Lusatica* (the Lusatian literary-historical miscellany in which the letter was printed); no manuscript witness is recorded in the edition.

documents.abstract: Requests a measure of *smerle* clay from Hven for her father Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg, and asks for a further supply of burnt antimony.
documents.incipit: Sophia.

text.original:
TYGE BRAHE FICK BREFF NOGETT SMERLLE ANRØRENDIS VT SEQUITUR.

Sophia.

WOR gunst thilfornn. Wider, att høgborne første och herre, her Wllrich, herre och første thill Meckelborg, Vor kierre herre fader, haffuer weed hanns schriffuellse aff Oß werritt begierrenndis, att Wi naadigst wille Hanns f: Naade forschaffe enn prøffue aff thennd jord, som kallis smerle, som glasbrenndere allthiid leyer, och nu nyligenn paa Huenn schulle verre funndenn, thi bede Wi ether och begierre, attj Oß wille vnnde och schiche enn ottinng fuld aff for:ne smerlle, huilched Wi sidenn Hanns Kierlighet wille thillsennde. Sammeledis giffue Wi ether och naadigst att wide, att Wi iche synnderligtt mere haffue aff thennd brennd antimonium, som i Oß senniste gaffue och thillschichede, bedenndis ether ther forre och begierre, attj Oß enndnu nogett aff for:ne brenntt antimonium ville giffue, huorudinnden i giør Oß enn synderlig thienniste och vellgefallenn.

Befallendis etc.
Actum Frederichsborg thennd 14. martij a:o 92.
text.english:
**Tyge Brahe received a letter concerning some smerle, as follows:**

Sophie.

Our favour beforehand. Know that the high-born prince and lord, Lord Ulrich, lord and prince of Mecklenburg, our dear lord father, has by his letter requested of us that we would graciously procure for His Princely Grace a sample of that earth which is called *smerle* [a clay], which glassmakers always use, and which is now lately said to have been found on Hven. We therefore ask and desire of you that you would grant and send to us a *ottingr* full [a one-eighth measure] of the aforesaid *smerle*, which we will then send on to His Lordship. Likewise we also graciously give you to know that we have nothing much left of that burnt antimony which you last gave and sent to us, asking and desiring of you therefore that you would give us yet some [more] of the aforesaid burnt antimony, wherein you do us a singular service and pleasure.

Commending [you] etc.
Done at Frederiksborg, the 14th of March, year [15]92.

documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer.** **Sophie of Mecklenburg** (1557–1631), queen of Denmark, consort of Frederik II (d. 1588) and by 1592 queen dowager during the minority of her son Christian IV. She shared Tycho's interest in chemistry/alchemy and natural philosophy and visited Uraniborg; here she addresses him as a supplier of materials. The plain signature *Sophia* (without the *Wij … etc.* formula of a reigning king's letter) is the dowager-queen register.
- **Document type.** A chancery-register entry (*Dronning Sophies tegnelser*). The **Latin rubric** *"…NOGETT SMERLLE ANRØRENDIS **ut sequitur**"* ("concerning some smerle, **as follows**") heads the Danish body — a code-switch preserved by this chapter's convention
- **Person named.** *her Wllrich, herre och første thill Meckelborg, Vor kierre herre fader* = **Ulrich III, Duke of Mecklenburg-Güstrow** (1527–1603), Sophie's father; "His Princely Grace" (*Hanns f: Naade* = *Hans fyrstelige Naade*) and "His Lordship" (*Hanns Kierlighet* = *Hans Kærlighed*, the chancery courtesy-title "His Affection/Lordship") both refer to him.
- **Place.** *Frederichsborg* = **Frederiksborg** Castle (Hillerød, Zealand), a royal residence.
- ***smerle*** — kept untranslated, glossed "[a clay]." The text defines it as *thennd jord, som kallis smerle, som glasbrenndere allthiid leyer* = "the earth called *smerle*, which glassmakers always use." This is the clay/earth used by glassmakers (Danish *smærgel/smerle*; the same Germanic root as English *smear*, and cognate with the abrasive *Schmergel*/emery family). The note that it had *"now lately been found on Hven"* ties the request to Tycho's own island. Not modernised, since the precise mineral is not certain from the word alone.
- ***glasbrenndere*** = "glass-burners," i.e. **glassmakers / glass-blowers** (literally those who fire/melt glass).
- ***enn ottinng fuld*** — "a *ottingr* full," i.e. an **ottingr**-measure full. The *otting* (literally "an eighth") was an Old Danish measure of capacity (one-eighth of a larger unit, e.g. of a *tønde*/barrel); rendered "a one-eighth measure" with the term flagged, as the exact volume intended is not specified in the letter.
- ***brennd / brenntt antimonium*** = "**burnt antimony**" (*antimonium calcinatum* / *crocus metallorum*), the calcined antimony preparation of period chemistry/medicine and metallurgy. The Latin technical noun *antimonium* is embedded in the Danish (a code-switch typical of the chancery's chemical vocabulary), and Sophie reports she has nearly used up the previous batch Tycho supplied — evidence of an ongoing material exchange between the queen and Uraniborg's laboratory.
- **Orthography (chancery Danish, c. 1592).** *WOR gunst thilfornn* = *Vor gunst tilforn* ("Our favour beforehand," the royal address-formula, this chapter's convention); *Wider* = *Vider* ("Know ye"); *haffuer … begierrenndis werritt* = *har … begærende været* ("has been requesting"); *attj* = *at I* ("that you"); *vnnde* = *unde* ("grant"); *schiche* = *skikke* ("send, dispatch"); *for:ne* = *fornævnte* ("aforesaid," the standard chancery abbreviation); *huilched* = *hvilket* ("which"); *sidenn* = *siden* ("then, afterwards"); *Sammeledis* = *Sammeledes* ("likewise"); *iche synnderligtt mere* = *ikke synderligt mere* ("not much more / nothing much left"); *senniste* = *seneste* ("last, most recently"); *huorudinnden* = *hvorudinden* ("wherein"); *synderlig thienniste och vellgefallenn* = *synderlig tjeneste og velbehag* ("singular service and pleasure"); *Befallendis* = *Befalendes* ("commending [you to God]," the abbreviated closing formula).
- **Negation count.** The body contains a single negation — *iche synnderligtt mere* ("not much more"), reporting that the queen's stock of burnt antimony is nearly exhausted. Both clauses of the letter are positive requests; no command or condition is reversed.
- **Calendar / place.** *Actum Frederichsborg thennd 14. martij a:o 92* = "Done at **Frederiksborg**, the 14th of March, [15]92" (O.S.); *Actum* "Done/Given" kept by this chapter's convention The dateline (14 March 1592) agrees with the catalogue label; no discrepancy.

documents.abstract: Responds to Blotius's letter, acknowledging that their Swiss acquaintance of more than twenty-two years earlier had entirely slipped from memory, and welcomes renewed contact.
documents.incipit: REDDITAe sunt mihi his ipsis diebus tuae literae unâ cum Hagecianis, eximia quadam …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET ERUDITISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO HUGONI BLOTIO, I. V. DOCTORI ET CÆSAREAe MAIESTATIS BIBLIOTHECAe, QUAe VIENNAe IN AUSTRIA EST, PRÆFECTO, AMICO SUO PLURIMUM DILECTO.
VIENNAe AUSTRIAe POST DOMUM PROVINCIALEM.

REDDITAe sunt mihi his ipsis diebus tuae literae unâ cum Hagecianis, eximia quadam humanitate et erga me benevolentia affatim refertae. Asseris inter nos olim in Helvetiae oris notitiam aliquam contractam fuisse. Quae sane ut id, quod res est, affirmem, mihi iam penitus memoriâ exciderat. Idque cum ob ea, quae ex temporum et locorum longinquitate ipsemet adducis obstacula, tum quod diversissimis et quamplurimis, ex eo tempore (quod sane ad minimum viginti duos annos excedit) occupationibus et distractionibus implicitus, eorum omnium, cum quibus in Germania atque alibi inter peregrinandum familiaritatem aliquam contraxi, recordationem animo comprehendere, nisi forte per literas subinde renovaretur, haud sustinuerim. Videor tamen mihi cum quodam Iuvene Belga, ingenioso atque ad discendum alacri, Basileae (uti opinor) non Argentinae (prout tu vis) dum pauculis mensibus illic subsisto, consuetudinem aliquando inijsse; succurritque, iam me ibidem per otium puerilia quaedam Instrumenta Mathematica (cum alia in promptu non essent) tractasse et harum rerum cupidis eorum usum ostendisse, ac si quae superessent, illis non gravatim dono concessisse. Fieri itaque facile poterit, quod tu ipsus Belga fueris, cum quo inter alios de his iucunde egi. Pergratum vero mihi accidit, quod hanc, quae nobis tunc aliquantulum intercessit, cognitionem, utut tot iam interlapsis annis ferme obliteratam, per literas in mentem revocare non intermiseris. Ego hanc in posterum memoriâ solidius firmare et sartam tectam conservare haud negligam. Nobilem etiam et rerum usu eximie valentem virum GERARDUM RANZOVIUM, HENRICI filium, amicum meum fratris loco dilectum et non ita dudum affinitate coniunctum, tuo nomine salutare atque de notitia inter nos olim contracta commonefacere, prout expetis, non tergiversabor. Quin et Magnificentissimo Amplissimoque viro Domino HENRICO RANZOVIO Produci Holsatiae prima quaque oblata occasione scribens (quod et saepius mutuo facere solemus, cum et ille ijsdem, quibus invigilo, studijs impense afficiatur) vel ipsas tuas literas vel earum descriptum adiungam, ut filio mittens, tui recordationem, tam apud ipsum quam caeteros Holsatiae conspicuae nobllitatis viros, tibi quondam in adolescentia notos, sic promptius in memoriam revocem. Quod et apud ipsum GERARDUM, si illi prius quam Parenti eius scripserim, praestabo. Atque is rectius reliquos suos, de quibus loqueris, consangvineos novit, eosque tui memores reddet. Sunt enim, tum is tum etiam alij Holsatiae Nobilitatis eximij viri, praesertim ex ijs, qui exteras nationes perlustrando variorum hominum mores et actiones experti sunt, ab humanitatis officijs nequaquam alieni, ut non dubitem, ijs hanc vestrae conversationis memorationem acceptam futuram.

Scribis in Bibliotheca Imperatoria, cui Viennae praees, reservari ultra 90000 librorum volumina. Si itaque liceret et tibi nonnunquam otium suppeteret, optarem mihi Authorum illorum nomina, unâ cum librorum singulorum inscriptione, praesertim quo ad Philosophica, Mathematica, Astronomica, Medica et Chymica atque similia opera attinet. Idem quoque in Illustriss. Archiducis Austriae MAXIMILIANI atque aliorum, si quos nosti, Illustrium virorum Bibliothecis fieri averem; modo id bona eorum pace admittatur. Sin minus, nolo tibi periculum vel offensas mea de causa creari.

Quia vero Arcis Uraniburgicae, quam in hac Insula praecedentibus annis extrui curavi, mentionem facis, eius aliqualem repraesentationem tibi in adiuncta charta mitto. Licet ab eo tempore, quo haec ita in eum modum excisa sunt, nonnulla, praesertim quo ad vallum circundans et aedificia in eius quatuor angulis extantia, immutata et ampliora reddita sint, et Instrumenta Astronomica plura, tam in Arcis turriculis quam potissimum in Cryptis quibusdam ad collem extra huius moenia, e solidis lapidibus constructis, quae septenas diversi generis ingentes et affabre elaboratas ad Astronomiae negotium rite exequendum inservientes distinctim complectuntur Machinas, hincinde disposita existunt, adeo ut iam coniunctis ijs, quae in Arce servantur, mihi 28 ad minimum in promptu sint Astronomicae Restitutioni opportuna Organa, solertia, labore, sumptibus inaestimabilia. Quin et, ut aliquatenus etiamnum cognoscas, quid praeteritis annis his intermediantibus executus sim, quidque in re Astronomica redintegranda moliar, en habes Operum nostrorum, brevi, favente Coelestium Opifice, in lucem publicam evulgandorum quaternionem primum, eorundem Inscriptionem atque contenta brevibus exponentem. Addidi autem consulto terna eiusdem quaternionis exempla, ut si qui forte fuerint inter vestrates Bibliopolas aut etiam in vicinia, qui horum voluminum aliquot exemplaria iusto pretio obtinere cupiant, illis hanc librorum inscriptionem communicare atque cum ijs de numero Exemplarium, quae adipisci satagunt, deque pretio transigere, eo commodius queas. Quod et te meo nomine haud gravatim facturum confido. Erunt quatuor Tomi, quorum quilibet semiquinque circiter adimplebit Alphabeta, in hac Regali (quam vocant) uti vides, papyro. Suntque plurimis schematibus, numeris et Instrumentorum picturis hincinde referti. Tute igitur, qui Augustae illi Caesareae Maiestatis Bibliothecae negotijs praees, et rem librariam optime calles, facile aestimabis, quantis sumptibus haec in propria meâ, eâdem de caussa constructa Typographia, excudi curârim et quali pretio cum indemnitate nostrorum laborum atque impensarum venire merito queant. Quae omnia tuae prudentiae dispicienda, dijudicanda, exequendaque relinquo. Praestiteris mihi hac ratione rem imprimis gratam et Reipublicae literariae, cuius tu commodum gnaviter et honorifice procuras, haud, ut spero, inutilem, nec tibi ipsi indecoram aut sterilem. Ego enim ad vicissim tibi gratificandum et de te bene merendum promptus inveniar. Carmina, quae altera habet pagina, non semper illic locum invenient, sed ubi digniora quaedam a Principibus et illustrioribus viris, quae expecto, adeptus fuero, illa honoris caussa hanc primi Tomi pagellam occupabunt; caeteris in reliquos Tomos, prout cuiuslibet Autoris requirit status et existimatio, iuxta frontispicia debito loco digestis. Si Poëta es (uti procul dubio es) et te nostram Uraniam aut effigiem (cuius ideam praeter illam, quae quaternioni impressa est, aliam cupro subtilius expressam hîc adiunxi) succincto aliquo Epigrammate ornare, idemque apud alios, si quos nosti, in Austria argutos et acutos Poëtas, tua operâ impetrari, desiderarem. Vale. Plura enim non addam, ne nimium excrescat Epistola; tu prima quaque oblata occasione rescribendo saepiusque (quod et ego non intermittam) scribendo, amicitiam veterem renovare, augere, stabilireque ne supersede. Literas, si Pragam ad praestantissimum virum D. THADDÆUM HAGGÆCIUM miseris, is, cum mihi saepius scribere soleat, et tuas huc tuto diriget.

Iamque iterum atque iterum vale.
Datae Uraniburgi 20. Martij Anno 92.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the most distinguished and most learned man, Master Hugo Blotius, Doctor of both Laws and Prefect of the Library of His Imperial Majesty which is at Vienna in Austria, his much-beloved friend.**
**At Vienna in Austria, beyond the Provincial House.**

Your letter was delivered to me these very days, together with the ones from Hagecius, abundantly filled with a certain singular kindness and goodwill toward me. You assert that an acquaintance was once struck up between us on the shores of Switzerland. Which — that I may affirm the matter as it stands — had by now slipped entirely from my memory. And that both on account of those obstacles which you yourself adduce from the remoteness of times and places, and because, entangled since that time (which assuredly exceeds at least twenty-two years) in the most various and very many occupations and distractions, I have hardly been able to hold in mind the recollection of all those with whom, while travelling, I struck up any familiarity in Germany and elsewhere — unless perhaps it were now and again renewed by letters. Yet it seems to me that I did once enter into an acquaintance with a certain Belgian youth, ingenious and eager to learn, at Basel (as I suppose), not at Strasbourg (as you would have it), during the few months I stayed there; and it comes back to me that there too, in my leisure, I handled certain childish Mathematical Instruments (since others were not at hand), and showed those eager for such things their use, and, if any were left over, freely granted them to those men as a gift. It could therefore easily be that you were that very Belgian with whom, among others, I dealt pleasantly on these matters. It has indeed been most welcome to me that you have not failed to call back to mind by letter this acquaintance, which then passed somewhat between us, even though now, with so many years intervening, it is all but obliterated. For my part I shall not neglect henceforth to fix it more firmly in memory and to keep it whole and sound. Nor shall I shrink — as you request — from greeting in your name the noble man, eminently versed in affairs, **Gerhard Rantzau**, son of Henrik, my friend dear to me in a brother's place and not long ago joined to me by marriage-alliance, and from reminding him of the acquaintance once struck up between us. Indeed, writing at the first occasion offered to the most magnificent and most ample man, Master **Henrik Rantzau**, Governor [Produx] of Holstein (which we are often wont to do for one another, since he too is keenly devoted to the same studies on which I keep watch), I shall enclose either your letter itself or a copy of it, so that, sending it to the son, I may thus the more readily call your memory to mind, both with him and with the other men of conspicuous nobility of Holstein, known to you once in your youth. This I shall also do with Gerhard himself, if I write to him before his Parent. And he knows better than I those other kinsmen of his, of whom you speak, and will make them mindful of you. For both he and likewise other eminent men of the Holstein nobility — especially among those who, by surveying foreign nations, have gained experience of the manners and doings of various men — are by no means estranged from the offices of courtesy, so that I do not doubt this commemoration of your sometime intercourse will be acceptable to them.

You write that in the Imperial Library, over which you preside at Vienna, more than 90,000 volumes of books are kept. If therefore it were permitted, and leisure now and then were available to you, I could wish to have for myself the names of those Authors, together with the title of each book, especially as concerns Philosophical, Mathematical, Astronomical, Medical, and Chemical works, and the like. The same I should also be eager to have done in the libraries of the most illustrious Archduke of Austria **Maximilian** and of others, if you know any, of illustrious men — provided this be allowed with their good leave. But if not, I do not wish danger or offence to be created for you on my account.

But since you make mention of the castle of Uraniborg, which in past years I had built on this island, I send you some representation of it on the enclosed sheet. Granted that, since the time when these things were so engraved in that fashion, certain features — especially as concerns the surrounding rampart and the buildings standing at its four corners — have been altered and made more ample, and several Astronomical Instruments, disposed here and there both in the little towers of the castle and chiefly in certain crypts toward a hill outside its walls, built of solid stone, which severally comprise seven huge Machines of different kinds, skilfully wrought, serving for the due carrying-out of the business of Astronomy — so much so that now, joining to them those that are kept in the castle, I have at least 28 instruments ready to hand, fit for the Restoration of Astronomy, beyond price in skill, labour, and expense. Indeed, that you may also even now somewhat learn what I have accomplished in these intervening past years, and what I am attempting in the renewal of the science of Astronomy — behold, you have here the first quaternion of our Works, shortly, by the favour of the Maker of the heavenly bodies, to be published abroad, setting forth in brief the Title and contents of the same. I have, moreover, deliberately added three copies of that same quaternion, so that, if there should perchance be any among the booksellers of your parts, or even in the neighbourhood, who desire to obtain some copies of these volumes at a fair price, you may the more conveniently communicate to them this title of the books, and transact with them about the number of Copies they are anxious to procure, and about the price. And this I trust you will do in my name without reluctance. There will be four Volumes, each of which will fill about four-and-a-half [semiquinque] alphabets, in this so-called Royal paper, as you see. And they are stuffed here and there with very many diagrams, figures, and pictures of Instruments. You therefore, who preside over the affairs of that august Library of His Imperial Majesty, and are most expert in the book-trade, will easily reckon at what great expense I have had these printed in my own Printing-house, built for that same purpose, and at what price they may deservedly be sold, with indemnity for our labours and outlays. All of which I leave to your prudence to consider, judge, and carry out. By this means you will render me a thing especially welcome, and one not, as I hope, useless to the Republic of Letters, whose advantage you diligently and honourably procure, nor unbecoming or unfruitful to yourself. For I shall be found ready in turn to gratify you and to deserve well of you. The verses which the other page holds will not always find a place there, but when I shall have obtained certain worthier ones from Princes and more illustrious men, which I am expecting, those will, for honour's sake, occupy this little page of the first Volume; the rest being arranged in their due place in the remaining Volumes, according as each Author's standing and esteem requires, next to the frontispieces. If you are a Poet (as you doubtless are), I could wish that you adorn our Urania, or the portrait (an idea of which, besides the one impressed on the quaternion, I have here added, more finely rendered in copper), with some terse Epigram, and that the same be obtained through your effort from others — if you know any in Austria — clever and acute Poets. Farewell. For I shall add no more, lest the Letter swell too much; do not you forbear, by writing back at the first occasion offered and by writing often (which I too shall not neglect), to renew, augment, and stabilise our old friendship. As for letters, if you send them to Prague to that most excellent man Master **Thaddaeus Hagecius**, he — since he is wont to write to me often — will safely direct yours hither too.

And now again and again, farewell.
Given at Uraniborg, 20 March, in the year [15]92.
TYCHO BRAHE,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** Tycho Brahe, writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven. The subscription *manu propria* ("with his own hand") and the autograph signature mark this as a personally signed letter.
- **Recipient.** *Hugo Blotius* = **Hugo Blotius** (Hugo Blotz, 1533–1608), the Dutch humanist who from 1575 was the first formally-appointed custodian (Prefect) of the Imperial Court Library in Vienna. *I. V. Doctori* = *Iuris Utriusque Doctori*, "Doctor of both Laws" (civil and canon). The two had been acquainted in their student days at Basel, where Blotius was involved with Tycho in instrument-/quadrant-making — which is exactly the episode the letter half-remembers (Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*; Christianson, *On Tycho's Island*; Thoren, *Lord of Uraniborg*).
- **Address line.** *VIENNAe AUSTRIAe POST DOMUM PROVINCIALEM* — "At Vienna in Austria, beyond [behind] the Provincial House (Landhaus)," i.e. the postal/topographical direction of Blotius's residence relative to the Lower-Austrian Estates' building. Rendered literally; "Provincial House" = the Landhaus.
- ***notitia in Helvetiae oris*** — the disputed first meeting "on the shores of Switzerland." Tycho's recollection is explicitly **hedged**: he says it had "slipped entirely from my memory," that he *seems* to himself (*videor mihi*) to have met a Belgian youth, and corrects the place — *Basileae (uti opinor) non Argentinae (prout tu vis)*, "at **Basel** (as I suppose), not at **Strasbourg** (as you would have it)." *Argentina* = Strasbourg (Argentoratum). The disagreement between the two men over the place is preserved, not adjudicated; Tycho's qualifiers (*uti opinor*, *Fieri facile poterit*) are kept.
- ***viginti duos annos*** — "at least twenty-two years." Tycho's own reckoning of the interval; counting back from 1592 places the meeting c. 1570, consistent with his second peregrination through Basel.
- ***puerilia quaedam Instrumenta Mathematica*** — "certain childish [i.e. elementary, rudimentary] Mathematical Instruments." *Puerilia* is self-deprecating ("childish/boyish"), not a claim about the instruments' owners; kept literal. *Instrumenta / Organa* both rendered **instrument(s)** by this chapter's convention
- **Persons named.**
 - *GERARDUM RANZOVIUM, HENRICI filium* = **Gerhard (Gert) Rantzau** (1558–1627), son of Heinrich; later himself Governor of Holstein. *affinitate coniunctum* ("joined by marriage-alliance") flags a recent kinship tie; rendered "joined to me by marriage-alliance."
 - *HENRICO RANZOVIO Produci Holsatiae* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598/9), royal Governor (*Statthalter*) of the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein, the great bibliophile, astrologer, and patron — a frequent correspondent of Tycho. *Produx* (here in the ablative *Produci*) is a learned Latinism for the office of *dux/governor*; rendered "Governor [Produx]," the Latin term flagged because it is non-standard.
 - *Illustriss. Archiducis Austriae MAXIMILIANI* = **Archduke Maximilian III of Austria** (1558–1618, "the Deutschmeister"), Habsburg prince and book-collector.
 - *D. THADDAeUM HAGGAeCIUM* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius, 1525–1600), the imperial physician and astronomer at Prague, Tycho's principal correspondent-relay in the Empire; the letter routes return mail through him. The "Hagecianis [literae]" of the opening line are letters that arrived from Hagecius in the same packet.
- **Astronomy / instruments.** *Astronomicae Restitutioni opportuna Organa* = "instruments fit for the **Restoration of Astronomy**" — *restitutio astronomiae*, Tycho's programmatic phrase, kept as "Restoration of Astronomy"; likewise *in re Astronomica redintegranda* = "in the renewal of the science of Astronomy." The count *28 ad minimum … Organa* and the *septenas … Machinas* (the seven great machines housed in the stone *Cryptae* — the underground vaults of **Stjerneborg**, "toward a hill outside [Uraniborg's] walls") are reproduced as written.
- **The engraving and the printed prospectus.** *aliqualem repraesentationem … in adiuncta charta* — Tycho encloses a printed view of Uraniborg, noting it is now partly out of date. *Operum nostrorum … quaternionem primum* = "the first quaternion of our Works" — a printed sample gathering (one *quaternio* = a four-sheet gathering) advertising the planned four-volume edition; *terna … exempla* = three copies sent for circulation to booksellers. *Regali … papyro* = "Royal paper" (a large paper format), *quam vocant* "so-called" flagged as Tycho's own gloss. *semiquinque … Alphabeta*: each volume "fills about four-and-a-half *alphabets*," an *alphabetum* being a printer's count of gatherings signed through the 23-letter signature sequence; *semiquinque* ("four-and-a-half," lit. "five-minus-a-half") rendered literally and glossed. *propria meâ … Typographia* = Tycho's own printing-house on Hven.
- ***Carmina … nostram Uraniam aut effigiem … Epigrammate*** — Tycho solicits a complimentary **epigram** (verse) from Blotius for the frontispiece, to honour his **Urania** (the figure/Muse, here standing for the work and the press's emblem) or his portrait, of which a finer copper engraving is also enclosed. The request for verse is kept as a request for verse, by the audit's rule.
- ***Reipublicae literariae*** — the **Republic of Letters**, the international scholarly commonwealth; rendered with the standing English term.
- **Epistolary formulae.** Heading *…AMICO SUO PLURIMUM DILECTO* = "his much-beloved friend." *Vale … Iamque iterum atque iterum vale* = "Farewell … And now again and again, farewell." *manu propria* = "with his own hand."
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Datae Uraniburgi 20. Martij Anno 92* = "Given at Uraniborg, 20 March, year [15]92" — **Old Style** (Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700; this chapter's convention). The edition *label* ("1592. 20. marts. Uraniborg") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy. The N.S. equivalent would be 30 March 1592, but the letter is not so marked and the date is left as written.

- **§1 Dreyer collation:** Dreyer (*Opera Omnia* VII, p. 329) reads *ultra 90000 librorum volumina* — **90,000** volumes of the Imperial Library, corroborated by Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, p. 184. The working transcription's *9000* had dropped a digit; corrected in the Source block and translation.

documents.incipit: QUI fiat, nobilissime et excellentissime D. PETRE IUNI, quod ad meas bis vel ter ad te …

text.original:
PETRO IUNIOTYCHO BRAHE.

QUI fiat, nobilissime et excellentissime D. PETRE IUNI, quod ad meas bis vel ter ad te datas, plane surdus et mutus videare, equidem ne suspicari quidem, nedum scire liquet. Si enim aliquanto locorum intervallo, Oceani interfluxu disiungamur, attamen cum satis frequens hincinde fiat navigatio, quam et affinitatis inter haec duo regna necessitudo crebriorem oportunioremque reddit, nihil hinc suppetit ad excusandum subsidij. Gravibus quidem et multiplicibus in Aula et Repub. distraheris negotijs. Verum haec tot tantaque esse nequeunt, quin semel arrepto calamo TYCHONI Dano, amico nequaquam fucato atque in horas mutabili, vel paucissimis respondere concederetur. TYCHONEM autem dico, ne, si forte idem tibi accidat, quod illa apud OVIDIUM de suo amatore conqueritur, ipsum quoque nomen sui oblivioni dedisse metuens, ut sic eius verba invertam: Forsitan et quis fit TYCHO vel unde roges, ut sic tibi mei memoriam nonnihil, ut apparet, obliteratam in animum revocem. De quibus autem ad te iam aliquoties scripsi, haec ferme erant: ut BUCHANANI vitam sponte dudum promissam describi, transmittique curare non gravarere: inprimis vero, ut privilegium a Serenissimo Rege vestro tua authoritate atque intercessione mihi procurares: quo caveretur, ne ullum meorum operum hîc impressorum in ipsius Maiestatis regno venderetur, aut absque mea permissione divenderetur. Misique (ni fallor) diplomatis Caesariani, eodem nomine quoad fines Romani Imperij clementer concessi, apographum, quod et nunc facio, si forte alterum non est redditum: non tam ut hinc conspicias, quo tenore conficiendum sit (ipsemet enim pro ea, qua vales, prudentia et eloquendi eximia facultate facile verba invenies, quibus res haec peragatur exorneturque) quam ut huius exemplo promptius Regi vestro persuadeatur, ne in hoc quod peto benevole etiam concedendo difficilem se praebeat: cum et apud eos, quibus de facie ignotus sum, talia minimo negotio impetrârim. IACOBUS enim CURTIUS, Imperij Vicecancellarius, vir praecipuae in Aula Caesariana authoritatis et in literis politioribus, adeoque ipsa Mathesi excellenter versatus, hoc Caesaris privilegium mihi sponte propria procuravit, conscripsit, suisque sumptibus conducto tabellario transmisit, ut ex Literarum ipsius unâ additarum exemplari, quod hîc simul habes, videre licet. Te igitur mihi, quem (modo recordari vacat) ex aliquantulo in hac insula Uraniburgica congressu cognitum habes, hac in parte non defuturum confido. Si in Icona nostram libris edendis praefigendam, acuto et succincto aliquo epigrammate luseris, rem utrique, uti spero, nostrum non inhonorificam praestiteris. Idem petij a magnifico D. Cancellario IOHANNE METELLANO, cuius in poësi argutum ingenium vel paucula illa carmina ostendunt, quae ianuae conclavis vestri Regis, cum hîc unâ adesset, utut inter circumbibendum et colloquendum, obiter quidem, sed non sine nervoso acumine, discedensque mnemosyni loco scripsit, quae etiamnum illic spectantur. Mirifice placet carmen, quod serenissima Maiestas Regia HENRICO GYLD[ENSTIERN], Praefecto Bahusensi, affini meo dilecto, inter transeundum, elogij gratia exaravit. Et vivida in hoc ad Poësin cernitur affectio, ingenijque acumen pari solertia coniunctum. Si non nimium audax censerer, submisse optarem, ab ipsius Maiestate et mihi aliquid de ipsius melliflua et Parnassiaca vena clementer impertiri. Quod ut mihi meisque lucubrationibus honorabile, sic etiam ipsius Maiestati apud eruditos et cordatos censores non indecorum reputabitur. Tua intercessione atque suasu votis meis hac in parte non gravatim (prout confido) satisfiet: hacque ratione me tibi adhuc devinctiorem reddideris. Rogâram in alteris, ut ministrum aliquem, natione Scotum, qui hortulanum ageret, unumque, si fieri posset, aucupem mihi honeste hîc sustentandum mittere satageres, quod et nunc ut praestes † petoque, quamprimum libera et commoda huc concedatur navigatio, eiusmodi hominem unum vel alterum e vestratibus nanciscar. Quin et sic desiderijs meis belle subveneris. Quod si quid in hac nostra patria fuerit, in quo vicissim tibi gratificari per me concedatur, tuum erit ne rogare quidem, sed verbulo solum, quicquid in votis habueris, indicare. Experiere me in exequendo alacrem et promptum.

Vale.
Datae Uraniburgi 20 Martij A. 1592.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To Master Peter Young, Tycho Brahe.**

How it comes about, most noble and most excellent Master Peter Young, that to my letters sent to you two or three times you seem quite deaf and dumb, I cannot even guess, let alone clearly know. For although we are separated by a certain distance of place, with the Ocean flowing between, yet, since voyaging back and forth is frequent enough — and the bond of kinship between these two kingdoms makes it the more frequent and the more convenient — no support for an excuse is to be had from this quarter. You are, to be sure, pulled this way and that by grave and manifold affairs at Court and in the commonwealth. But these cannot be so many and so great that, the pen once snatched up, you should not be allowed to answer Tycho the Dane — a friend by no means feigned, or changeable by the hour — in however few words. And I say "Tycho," lest, if perchance the same should befall you that she in Ovid complains of regarding her lover, I have to fear that you have consigned to oblivion even his very name; so that I may thus invert his words: "Perhaps you may ask too who Tycho is, or whence" — that I may in this way call back into your mind my memory, somewhat blotted out, as it appears. Now the matters about which I have already written to you several times were roughly these: that you would not find it burdensome to see to it that the Life of Buchanan, long since freely promised, be transcribed and sent across; but above all, that by your authority and intercession you would procure me a privilege from your Most Serene King, whereby it should be provided that none of my works printed here be sold within His Majesty's kingdom, or vended without my permission. And I sent (unless I am mistaken) a copy of the Imperial diploma graciously granted on the same account so far as the bounds of the Roman Empire extend — which I do now also, in case the other one has perchance not been delivered: not so much that you may discern from it in what terms the thing is to be drawn up (for you yourself, with that prudence in which you are strong and your outstanding faculty of expression, will easily find words by which this matter may be carried through and adorned), as that, by this example, your King may the more readily be persuaded not to show himself difficult about graciously granting what I ask — since even among those to whom I am unknown by face I have obtained such things with the least trouble. For Jacob Kurtz, Vice-Chancellor of the Empire, a man of foremost authority at the Imperial Court and excellently versed in the more polished letters, and indeed in mathematics itself, procured this privilege of the Emperor for me of his own accord, drew it up, and at his own expense sent it across by a hired courier — as may be seen from the copy of his own letter added herewith, which you have here at the same time. I am confident, therefore, that in this matter you will not fail me — you who (if only there be leisure to recall it) came to know me from a brief meeting on this island of Uraniborg. If you should play with some sharp and pithy epigram to be prefixed to my Icon [portrait], to be set before the books I am bringing out, you would, as I hope, render a service not without honour to us both. The same I have asked of the magnificent Master Chancellor John Maitland, whose keen wit in poetry even those few verses show that he wrote at the door of your King's chamber, when he was here in company — in passing, to be sure, amid the drinking-round and the conversing, yet not without sinewy acuteness — and, as he departed, wrote by way of a memento, which are still to be seen there. Wonderfully pleasing is the poem that His Most Serene Royal Majesty, in passing, composed by way of an elogium for Henrik Gyld[enstierne], Governor of Bohus, my beloved kinsman. And in him a lively bent toward Poetry is discerned, and a keenness of wit joined with equal skill. Were I not to be judged too bold, I would humbly wish that to me too something of His Majesty's mellifluous and Parnassian vein might graciously be imparted. And as this would be honourable to me and to my labours, so too it will be reckoned not unbecoming to His Majesty in the eyes of learned and judicious critics. By your intercession and persuasion my wishes in this matter will (as I trust) be satisfied without reluctance; and in this way you will have bound me to you still more closely. I had asked in another [letter] that you would take pains to send me some servant, Scottish by nation, who might act as a gardener, and one — if it could be done — to act as a fowler, to be maintained here honourably; and that you do this now also I ask †, so that, as soon as free and convenient voyaging hither is open, I may get hold of one or two men of this kind from among your countrymen. Thus indeed you would handsomely come to the aid of my desires. But if there be anything in this our homeland in which it may in turn be granted me to gratify you, it will be yours not even to ask, but only with a little word to indicate whatever you may have in your wishes. You will find me brisk and ready in carrying it out.

Farewell.
Given at Uraniborg, 20 March, the year 1592.
Tycho Brahe.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** *Petrus Iunius* = **Peter Young** (1544–1628), Scottish humanist, tutor (with George Buchanan) to **James VI of Scotland**, and royal almoner; the Scottish envoy who visited Uraniborg in August 1586 (presenting Tycho with a portrait of Buchanan) and who returned in the king's company in spring 1590 (Dreyer, *Tycho Brahe*; *On Tycho's Island*). The "brief meeting on this island" Tycho recalls is the 1586 visit.
- **Heading.** The transcription runs the rubric together as *"PETRO IUNIOTYCHO BRAHE"* — i.e. **"To Peter Young, Tycho Brahe"** (the missing space between *IUNIO* and *TYCHO* is a transcription artefact, not a word; restored in translation).
- ***BUCHANANI vitam*** — the **Life of George Buchanan** (1506–1582), the celebrated Scottish humanist and James VI's preceptor: his autobiographical *Vita ab ipso scripta*. Tycho asks Young to have a copy transcribed and shipped.
- ***privilegium … a Serenissimo Rege vestro*** — a **printing/sales privilege** from James VI protecting Tycho's self-printed books within Scotland, modelled on the Imperial privilege Tycho already held (see next note). *"ne ullum meorum operum … venderetur, aut … divenderetur"*: two coordinated negative purpose-clauses — that none of his works be **sold**, nor **vended** (resold/retailed) without his permission; both negations preserved.
- ***diploma Caesarianum … IACOBUS CURTIUS, Imperij Vicecancellarius*** — the **Imperial privilege** granted "as far as the bounds of the Roman Empire extend," procured for Tycho by **Jacob Kurtz von Senftenau** (Jakob Kurz/Curtius, d. 1594), **Vice-Chancellor of the [Holy Roman] Empire**, here praised as learned in letters and in mathematics. Tycho encloses a copy (*apographum*) of both the diploma and Kurtz's covering letter as a template for the Scottish request.
- ***Icona nostram … epigrammate*** — Tycho's **engraved portrait (*Icon*)** intended to be prefixed to his printed works; he invites Young to compose a short epigram for it. (Tycho did circulate such engraved portraits; cf. the *Icones* sheets in Nielsen's bibliography.)
- ***IOHANNES METELLANUS*** = **John Maitland of Thirlestane** (c. 1537–1595), **Lord Chancellor of Scotland**, who accompanied James VI; Tycho recalls verses Maitland inscribed at the door of the king's chamber during the 1590 visit. *Metellanus* is the latinised form of Maitland.
- ***HENRICO GYLD[ENSTIERN], Praefecto Bahusensi*** — **Henrik Gyldenstierne**, governor (*lensmand / praefectus*) of **Bohus** (Bohuslän), described by Tycho as his "beloved kinsman" (*affinis*). The source abbreviates the surname *GYLD.*; expanded in brackets, following the editorial expansion. James VI is said to have composed a complimentary poem (*elogium*) for him in passing.
- ***serenissima Maiestas Regia … melliflua et Parnassiaca vena*** — **James VI** as poet; Tycho, praising the king's "mellifluous and Parnassian vein," angles (hedged: *si non nimium audax censerer … submisse optarem*) for a royal poem of his own. The hedge — "were I not to be judged too bold, I would humbly wish" — is kept; not sharpened into a request.
- **Ovid allusion.** *"quod illa apud OVIDIUM de suo amatore conqueritur … ut sic eius verba invertam: Forsitan et quis fit TYCHO vel unde roges"* — Tycho **inverts** a line of Ovid (the abandoned-heroine voice of the *Heroides*; the model is the type "perhaps you ask who I am, or whence"), turning a lover's lament that the beloved has forgotten her very name into a witty reproach that Young may have forgotten *Tycho's* name. The transcription's *"quis fit"* is read as *quis sit* ("who … may be"); the printed *fit* is kept in the Source block and the reading flagged. The wordplay is preserved, not flattened. **[Crux: Ovidian source line not pinpointed here; treated as an echo of the *Heroides* incipit-type, not a verified single verse.]**
- ***affinitatis inter haec duo regna necessitudo*** — "the bond of kinship between these two kingdoms": alludes to the dynastic tie between Denmark and Scotland following James VI's 1589 marriage to **Anne of Denmark** (Frederik II's daughter), which underlay James's 1590 visit.
- ***hortulanum … aucupem*** — a **gardener** and a **fowler (bird-catcher)**, Scottish servants Tycho had earlier asked Young to recruit for Uraniborg; he renews the request.
- **Editorial mark †.** A **dagger appears in the transcription** after *"quod et nunc ut praestes"* (*"…ut praestes † petoque…"*), marking an editorial crux/uncertain reading at this point in the source apparatus. It is reproduced verbatim in the Source block; the surrounding syntax (*"…ut praestes … petoque, quamprimum … nanciscar"*) is itself somewhat strained, and the translation follows the sense ("that you do this now also I ask, so that … I may get hold of …") while flagging the marked spot. **[Crux: the † reading.]**
- **Calendar / dateline.** The letter's own dateline reads only ***"Datae Uraniburgi Martij A. 1592"*** — **"Given at Uraniborg, March 1592"**, with **no day stated**. The catalogue/edition assigns **20 March 1592** (O.S.), which is **not substantiated by the dateline text**; by the audit's rule the header leads with the as-written month and appends the catalogued day. Denmark was on the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar. A companion letter to Hagecius two days later is dated 22 March 1592, consistent with a 20 March dating but not proving it from this text. **[Crux: in-letter dateline gives month only; "20 March" is editorial.]**
- **Correction.** Restored the day-number '20' to the closing dateline ('Datae Uraniburgi 20 Martij A. 1592'), dropped from our transcription; Dreyer, TBOO VII p.332, confirmed by page image.

documents.abstract: Sends the first printed gathering of the *Progymnasmata* with six extra copies for distribution, explaining that Curtius persuaded him to publish a forerunner volume of his planned astronomical restoration.
documents.incipit: QUAMVIS non ita dudum sit, quod tibi scripserim, optime et amantissime mi THADDÆE, tamen …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD THADDÆUM HAGECIUM.

QUAMVIS non ita dudum sit, quod tibi scripserim, optime et amantissime mi THADDÆE, tamen et has superaddere non gravabor; amicorum enim est sæpius se invicem, si coram non licet, saltem literis invisere. Ut vero aliquatenus cognoscas, id quod superioribus indicavi, me hortatu et suasu magnifici Domini CURTII potissimum impulsum, Astronomiæ instaurationem, quam in opus integrum et peculiare reservare constitueram, nunc Progymnasmatis quibusdam Prodromi loco in publicum emittere, en habes operum meorum, quæ typis brevi, Deo volente, absolventur, quaternionem primum, eorum contenta sua inscriptione indicantem, ex qua cætera facile ratiocinabere; hincque colliges me idipsum, quod tunc literis pollicitus sum, nunc moliri. Addidi autem eiusdem quaternionis sena exempla, ut suppeterent, quæ hincinde ad Bibliopolas tum vestrates, tum etiam in Austria, Hungaria atque Polonia degentes mitteres, si forte aliqui illic essent, qui exemplaria nonnulla horum tomorum iusto pretio obtinere sategerint. Erunt autem quatuor, et quilibet eorum iustæ magnitudinis, ad semiquinque videlicet Alphabeta in hac Regali sic dicta (uti vides) papyro excrescens, suntque plurimis schematibus et tabulis hincinde referti. Ubi a te certior factus fuero, num aliquot exemplaria cupiant, deque numero et pretio, mittam hac instante æstate, favente Numine, quotquot expetierint, præsertim quantum duos priores tomos attinet. Expecto indies Privilegium regis Hispaniarum, Cæsareano subiungendum, quod ubi nactus fuero, publicationem non diutius differam.

Carmina, quæ hîc vides, in secunda pagina, non semper id spacij replebunt, sed ubi a serenissimo Scotorum Rege et illustrissimo Principe Landgravio iuniore MAURITIO, qui ambo eximia pollent vena poëtica, quædam in operum horum commendationem concinnata, prout confido, accepero, epigrammata illa hanc paginam honoris caussa occupabunt. Secundo autem tomo genere et autoritate nobilium virorum carmina pariter præfigam. Ubi scio quæ prædictus magnificus CURTIUS in gratiam communium studiorum concinnare non degravetur (nam ut Oratorem agit eloquentem et eximium, sic a Poësi quoque illum non abhorrere existimârim) ea Producis Holsatiæ Domini HENRICI RANZOVIJ versibus iam antea obtentis (quod et is hisce studijs non parce afficiatur) præponam, reliquis clarorum et doctorum virorum lusibus metricis in frontispicia duorum postremorum tomorum reservatis. Scripsi autem ipsemet proximis diebus serenissimo Scotorum Regi IACOBO Sexto et ipsius Cancellario IOANNI METELLO hac de re carmine elegiaco, tum quoque Epigramma quoddam literis ad illustrissimum Principem MAURITIUM Landgravium iuniorem hoc nomine datis subiunxi, quorum carminum descriptum hîc addidi, si forte talibus delectaris, et si plures nosti Principes, poëseos gnaros et horum studiorum amantes, indica eorum nomina unâ cum titulis, nam et ad eos pariter carminibus scribam, carminaque in Astronomiæ commendationem, uti spero, ab ipsis impetrabo. Conducibile enim et decorum sentio, hæc studia a viris Principibus atque in fastigio humanarum dignitatum collocatis commendari atque ornari, ut eo facilius alacriusque plures ad hæc per se ob sublimitatem difficultatemque, quodque minus lucrosa sint, alias abhorrentes, ad eorum culturam invitentur. Scis enim tritum illud: Principibus placuisse viris non ultima laus est, licet ego Philosophice et penitius rem introspiciendo aliter censuerim. Nolo te nunc pluribus obtundere, nec enim dubito, quin tam his quam alijs nostris desiderijs, quantum in te est, sis sponte profuturus. Ego ad tibi pariter gratificandum offero omnem operam et studium, adeoque me ipsum totum. Vale, et magnisicentissimum Dominum CURTIUM meis verbis honorifice saluta.

Iamque iterum bene vale.
Dat. 22 Martij Anno 92.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, pp. 333–334; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Intellexi ex Domini Doctoris SAGERI Lubecensis literis, nuper ad me datis, RHETICI Bibliothecam tibi fuisse in testamento deputatam. Quod si sic est, rogo, ut quicquid ad rem Astronomicam facit, sive id a præceptore suo COPERNICO, sive suapte industria habuerit, meis limitibus descriptum mature communicare velis. Et si eclipsin Lunae ultimo in fine præcedentis anni contingentem, caelitus illic denotastis, vel ullas alias, sive a te ipso sive aliunde conquisitas, in promptu habes vel nancisci poteris observationes, me quoque earum compotem per primam occasionem effice, quo Meridianorum discrepantiam hinc certius quam alias, adhibitis nostris vel observationibus vel numeris, rimari concedatur.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Thaddaeus Hagecius.**

Although it is not so very long since I wrote to you, my excellent and most loving Thaddaeus, yet I shall not begrudge adding these lines too; for it is the way of friends to visit one another the more often — if not in person, then at least by letter. But that you may to some degree learn what I intimated in earlier [letters] — that I, impelled chiefly by the exhortation and persuasion of the magnificent Master Curtius, am now bringing out before the public, in the guise of a Forerunner, in certain *Progymnasmata*, the restoration of astronomy which I had resolved to reserve for a complete and separate work — here you have the first quaternion of my works (which, God willing, will shortly be finished at the press), indicating its contents by its own title, from which you will easily reckon the rest; and from this you will gather that I am now setting in motion the very thing which I then promised you by letter. I have added, moreover, six copies of the same quaternion, so that there might be a supply for you to send out here and there to the booksellers — both those among you and those residing in Austria, Hungary, and Poland — if perchance there should be any there who would take pains to obtain some copies of these volumes at a fair price. They will be four [in number], and each of them of a just size, growing namely to four and a half [*sic*] alphabets [of sheets] in this so-called Royal paper (as you see); and they are filled throughout with very many diagrams and tables. As soon as I am made more certain by you whether they desire any copies, and about the number and the price, I shall send — this coming summer, the Deity favouring — as many as they shall have requested, especially as concerns the two earlier volumes. I am awaiting daily the Privilege of the King of the Spains, to be joined to the Imperial one; and as soon as I have obtained it, I shall no longer defer the publication.

The verses which you see here, on the second page, will not always fill that space; but as soon as I have received — from the most serene King of the Scots and from the most illustrious Prince, the younger Landgrave Maurice (both of whom are strong in an exceptional poetic vein) — certain pieces composed in commendation of these works, as I trust [I shall], those epigrams will occupy this page for honour's sake. To the second volume, likewise, I shall prefix verses [matching it] in kind and in the authority of noble men. When I know what the aforesaid magnificent Curtius will not think it beneath him to compose for the sake of our common studies (for as he plays the eloquent and excellent Orator, so I should judge that he does not shrink from Poetry either), these I shall set before the verses of the Governor of Holstein, Master Henrik Rantzau, already obtained before now (since he too is not sparingly affected by these studies) — the remaining metrical sports of famous and learned men being reserved for the frontispieces of the two last volumes. I myself, moreover, have in these last days written to the most serene King of the Scots, James the Sixth, and to his Chancellor John Maitland [Metellus], on this matter in an elegiac poem; and then too I appended a certain Epigram to a letter given to the most illustrious Prince Maurice, the younger Landgrave, in this name [i.e. on this same account]; of which poems I have added a transcript here, in case you happen to take delight in such things. And if you know more Princes, skilled in poetry and lovers of these studies, signify their names together with their titles, for I shall write to them likewise in verse, and I shall obtain from them, as I hope, poems in commendation of astronomy. For I judge it both profitable and fitting that these studies should be commended and adorned by men who are Princes and set on the summit of human dignities, so that the more easily and the more eagerly many — who otherwise shrink from these things on account of their loftiness and difficulty, and because they are less lucrative — may be invited to their cultivation. For you know that well-worn line: *"To have pleased leading men is not the least praise"* — although I, looking into the matter philosophically and more deeply, should judge otherwise. I do not wish to weary you now with more, for I do not doubt that, in these as in our other desires, so far as in you lies, you will of your own accord be of service. I for my part, to do you a like kindness, offer all my labour and zeal, and indeed my whole self. Farewell, and greet the most magnificent Master Curtius honourably in my words.

And now once more, fare you well.
Given 22 March, the year [15]92.


*[Postscript:]* I have understood, from the letter of Doctor Sager of Lübeck lately sent to me, that Rheticus's library was bequeathed to you by [his] testament. If that is so, I ask that you be willing in good time to communicate to me, described within my bounds, whatever bears upon astronomical matters — whether he had it from his teacher Copernicus or by his own industry. And if you noted from the heavens there the eclipse of the Moon occurring at the very end of last year, or have to hand, or can procure, any other observations — whether obtained by yourself or from elsewhere — make me too a sharer of them at the first opportunity, so that the discrepancy of meridians may from this be more surely investigated than otherwise, with our observations or numbers applied.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / place.** Tycho Brahe, writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven (not stated in the dateline, which gives only day, month, and year; the place is supplied from the correspondence context and is bracketed in the header accordingly). The witness is the **draft** (Danish *Kladde*) in Tycho's own papers, ÖNB cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.57.
- **Recipient.** *Thaddaeus Hagecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayck, 1525–1600), the Prague physician-astronomer, imperial court physician, and Tycho's principal Bohemian correspondent and broker at the Imperial court; here serving as Tycho's distribution agent for the *Progymnasmata* among Central-European booksellers and as a conduit to potential princely patrons.
- ***magnificus Dominus Curtius*** — **Jakob Kurz von Senftenau** (Iacobus Curtius a Senftenau, d. 1594), Imperial *Reichsvizekanzler* (vice-chancellor). He had urged Tycho to issue the work; Tycho both names him as the prompter of the early publication and hopes for commendatory verses from him ("as he plays the eloquent Orator, so [he] does not shrink from Poetry"). Tycho closes by asking Hagecius to greet him.
- ***Astronomiae instaurationem … Progymnasmatis … Prodromi loco*** — the **restoration of astronomy** (Tycho's *astronomia instaurata* programme, per glossary) which he had meant to reserve for a single complete work, but now issues piecemeal as *Progymnasmata* (preliminary "exercises") "in the place of a **Forerunner** (*Prodromus*)." The work meant is the *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata*, eventually completed posthumously (Prague, 1602). *Progymnasmata* and *Prodromus* are kept as period titles/terms.
- ***quaternionem … sena exempla*** — a **quaternion** is a gathering of four sheets (eight leaves); Tycho sends the first printed gathering as a specimen, plus *sena exempla* = **six copies** of it, for Hagecius to circulate to booksellers in Austria, Hungary, and Poland.
- ***semiquinque … Alphabeta … in hac Regali … papyro*** — a bibliographical measure: each of the four volumes will run to *"four and a half alphabets"* (*semiquinque Alphabeta*) of sheets, on **"Royal" paper** (*papyrus Regalis*, a large sheet-format). An "alphabet" = the signature-run A–Z (commonly 23 sheets), so "four and a half alphabets" indicates the projected bulk. **Lexical note:** *semiquinque* is an unusual coinage; rendered literally "four and a half" (= *quinque* less a half), and flagged with *[sic]* rather than smoothed.
- ***Privilegium regis Hispaniarum, Caesareano subiungendum*** — Tycho awaits a printing **privilege** from the **King of Spain** (*rex Hispaniarum*, Philip II), to be added to the **Imperial** privilege already in hand, before publishing. *regis Hispaniarum* (genitive plural "of the Spains") reflects the standard early-modern style of the Spanish crown's composite realms; rendered "King of the Spains."
- ***serenissimus Scotorum Rex … IACOBUS Sextus*** — **James VI of Scotland** (later James I of England), who had visited Hven in March 1590 and was a practising Latin poet ("strong in an exceptional poetic vein"). Tycho hopes for, and has solicited by an elegiac poem, a commendatory epigram from him.
- ***Cancellarius IOANNES METELLUS*** — **John Maitland of Thirlestane** (c. 1543–1595), Lord Chancellor of Scotland, who accompanied James VI on the Hven visit; *Metellus* is the latinised by-name. Identification confirmed against Norlind, *Tycho Brahe* (1970), who notes the king came "in the company of his chancellor Maitland (Metellus)."
- ***illustrissimus Princeps Landgravius iunior MAURITIUS*** — **Moritz "the Learned," the younger Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1572–1632), son of Wilhelm IV; himself a poet. (To him Tycho would dedicate the *Epistolae astronomicae* of 1596.)
- ***Produx Holsatiae Dominus HENRICUS RANZOVIUS*** — **Henrik Rantzau** (Heinrich Rantzau, 1526–1598), royal *Statthalter* (governor; here Latin *Produx*, lit. "Produce/Governor") of the Danish duchy of **Holstein**, humanist patron and astrology enthusiast, whose commendatory verses Tycho already holds. *Produx* is an unusual title-form; rendered "Governor."
- ***lusibus metricis*** — "metrical sports / playful pieces," the humanist term for occasional verse; rendered "metrical sports" to preserve the deprecatory register Tycho intends.
- **Allusion (proverb).** *"Principibus placuisse viris non ultima laus est"* = **Horace,** *Epistles* **I.17.35** — "To have pleased leading men is not the least praise." Tycho quotes it as a *tritum illud* ("that well-worn line") and then immediately distances himself from it: *"although I, looking into the matter philosophically and more deeply, should judge otherwise."* The hedge is preserved, not flattened — Tycho endorses princely patronage as expedient for promoting astronomy while reserving a higher philosophical valuation.
- **Epistolary formulae.** Heading without an explicit *S.* salutation (a working draft); closes *Vale … Iamque iterum bene vale* = "Farewell … And now once more, fare you well" (glossary). *meis verbis … saluta* = "greet [him] in my words / on my behalf."
- **Calendar.** *Dat. 22 Martij Anno 92* = "Given 22 March, the year [15]92" — Old Style (Denmark on the Julian calendar). The edition label ("1592. 22. marts.") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy. No day-name or place in the dateline; the year is given as "92" and expanded to 1592 in brackets-by-context (the century is unambiguous from the correspondence).

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript, restored from Dreyer VII, pp. 333–334 (dropped by the working transcription); the report (via Sager of Lübeck) that Rheticus's library was bequeathed to Hájek, with Tycho's request for any Copernicus/Rheticus astronomical material.
