text.original:
CLARISS. ET NOBILISSIMO VIRO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, WENÆ INSULÆ DOMINO REGIS DANIÆ CONSILIARIO ET MATHEMATICO DOCTISSIMO, AMICO SUO.

APOLOGIAM tuam Clariss. D. TYCHO, ut accepi, obiter percurri, nam prolixitas tua et meæ occupationes accuratius legere non permiserunt, et primo eius argumento, quod aliquo modo munieras, statim respondi hoc Naturæ motu, quo Sublunaria maximi circuli tramitem tenere possunt, exposito, idque veritatis caussa, ne pluribus hac de re opus esset; in reliquis tum nec nostra quicquam infirmare, nec tua magis confirmare visus es: responsum D. FULLERO nostro datum est, qui in una navium erat, quæ ad Regem nostrum tum in Dania profectæ sunt; sed illis, audito Regis inde discessu ex medio itinere redeuntibus, redditum est, nec remittendum putavi, nisi Mathematicis tuis, quæ pervertere dicebamur, similiter excussis. Verum tot nos ab eo tempore obruerunt negocia et profectiones, ut vestrates hîc vix semel atque iterum convenire licuerit, nec ante hyemem tua relegere potuerim, nonnihil otij tum nactus, quod breve fuit, et controversia de veneficarum nugis sæpe interruptum, hæc Elenctica meditatus sum, et scripsi non in te solum, quem amicitiæ causa lenius tractavi, sed illos quoque, qui meo tempore hunc errorem in Germania publicarunt, contra quos theses quasdam, tredecim aut pluribus abhinc annis scriptas, inter chartas reperi; deerant tantum ipsorum observata, quæ ex Germania expectaveram, ex quibus plenius redarguendi erant: Interea literæ tuæ cum observatione cuiusdam obscurioris Phænomeni sub superioris veris finem ad me perlatæ sunt, ex quibus intellexi responsum ad tua et expeti et expectari abs te, itaque ne te diutius remorarer, nostra in hanc antilogicam ad te formam statim redegi et eo die absolvi, quo Eclipsin ☉lis superiori anno conspexeram, et paucis post diebus hoc exemplum rescribi curavi, ut ad te mitti potuerat cum legato vestro, qui tum hîc erat; sed me ad biduum tantum absente prius discesserat, quam speraveram, et redeunti mihi nulla alia opportunitas ad te scribendi vel mittendi restabat, ante autumnalem navigationem: Interea dum in hac vicinia cum ægris versor, unde ad quamcunque oblatam occasionem redire facile poteram, præter opinionem in Angliam vocor longissimo itinere, nec prius domum redire concessum fuit, nec inde iterum discedere ante summam hyemem licuerat. Expectanda enim erat gravissimi circa hepar Apostematis suppuratio et expurgatio in amicissimo quodam nobili: post Martini festum et prope circa solstitium hybernum reversus, hoc scriptum nostrum in Museo reperi ac ad te missum non fuisse ægerrime tuli: atque hinc bona fide factum est, quod superiori anno nostra non acceperis: sat cito nunc, si, quod opto, illam miram opinionem tibi poterit excutere: quod ni fecerit, omni ratione destitutam relinquet, scio: at absque ratione nec sentiendum nec loquendum Philosopho; cede igitur et veritatem amplectere, nec conare amplius nova sydera cœlo addere: cur enim tranquillum Æthera turbares? Si consenseris, tua iuncta opera hanc veritatem plene decidi posse mihi persuadeo: sunt enim mihi perfectæ demonstrationes, quibus remotiones Cometarum, quocunque ferantur modo, certo definiri possunt, nec ulla opinor observata tibi desunt: σὺν δύ' ἐρχομένω: conferamus operas: nihil apud me erit, quod tibi non lubenter communicabitur: tu vicissim id agito: Valde cupio illius ROTHMANNI videre, quibus volatili admodum sagacitate ad ♄num usque has fumositates insequitur: si communicaveris, tuo committetur iudicio, quam vere ille tam alte sapiat, alioqui paradoxon a vobis ex proposito defendi videri poterit. Observata quæ hactenus videre contigit, pro principijs demonstrationis remotionum haberi nequeunt: tantum ad apparentem in longitudinem et latitudinem motum faciunt: talia expeto ubi azimutha non variantur et quæ diversis regionibus accepta sunt. Canon mirificus a generoso quodam consangvineo nostro hîc construitur, cui otij et ingenij ad tantum opus satis est: cum perfectus fuerit, tibi communicabitur: Sed de tuis nihil adhuc resciscere potuimus: fac, quæ in chymicis singularia habeas, intellegamus. Scire nostrum nihil est, nisi alij sciant nos scire: De ☉ et ☾ in ☿ reductione aut physicorum tinctura, si quid experientia constat, rescribe, non oberit fortasse nostra collatio: Si quid contra nos amplius cogitas, paucis agito et maiori calami modestia, et si ita libet, publico iudicio nostra subijciamus, ne etiam antilogijs nostris amicitia et consuetudo scribendi intercidat. Si quid hîc expetis, mihi significa: non deero ut potero. Vale quam felicissime D. TYCHO et hoc cerotum ad restinguendam illam in cœlo phlogosin abs te accensam ab amico antagonista medico missum benigne accipito et usurpato.

Datæ Edinburgi 27 Martij 92.
Tuus IOAN. CRAIGIUS Scotus.
text.english:
**To the most distinguished and most noble man, Master Tycho Brahe, lord of the island of Hven, councillor to the King of Denmark and most learned mathematician, his friend.**

Your *Apologia*, most distinguished Master Tycho, I have run through cursorily, as I received it — for your prolixity and my own occupations did not allow me to read it more carefully — and to its first argument, which you had in some manner fortified, I at once replied, having set out this motion of Nature whereby things sublunary can keep to the track of a great circle; and that for truth's sake, lest there should be need of more words on this matter. In the rest you did not then seem either to weaken our position at all, or to confirm your own the more. My answer was given to our Master Fuller, who was on one of the ships that set out at that time for our King, [then] in Denmark; but when those [ships], hearing of the King's departure from there, turned back from the middle of their journey, it was returned [to me]; nor did I think it should be sent back unless your mathematical [arguments], which we were said to be subverting, were likewise sifted through in the same way. But from that time so many affairs and journeys have overwhelmed me that I was scarcely able to meet your countrymen here once or twice, nor was I able to re-read your [piece] before winter; having then got some little leisure — which was short, and often interrupted by the controversy over the trifles of the witches — I meditated these refutations [Elenctica], and wrote not against you alone, whom for friendship's sake I have handled more gently, but also against those who in my time published this error in Germany, against whom I found among my papers certain theses, written thirteen or more years ago; only their observations were lacking, which I had awaited from Germany, [and] from which they were to have been refuted more fully. Meanwhile your letter, with the observation of some rather obscure phenomenon, was brought to me toward the end of last spring, from which I understood that a reply to your [arguments] was both sought and awaited by you; and so, that I might not delay you longer, I at once reduced our [piece] into this disputational form for you and finished it on that very day on which the previous year I had observed an eclipse of the Sun [☉]; and a few days afterward I had this copy written out afresh, so that it could have been sent to you with your envoy, who was then here. But while I was absent only two days, he had departed sooner than I had hoped; and on my return no other opportunity remained for me to write or to send to you before the autumn sailing. Meanwhile, while I was busy in this neighbourhood with the sick — whence I could easily return at whatever occasion should offer — I was, beyond expectation, summoned into England on a very long journey, nor was I permitted to return home sooner, nor had I been allowed to depart thence again before deep winter. For there was to be awaited the suppuration and clearing-out of a most grievous abscess about the liver in a certain very dear nobleman. Having returned after the feast of [Saint] Martin and nearly about the winter solstice, I found this writing of ours in my study, and bore it most grievously that it had not been sent to you; and from this it came about in good faith that you did not receive our [piece] last year. [It comes] soon enough now, if — as I hope — it can shake that strange opinion out of you; and if it does not do so, it will leave it [the opinion] bereft of all reason, I know. But the philosopher must neither think nor speak without reason; yield therefore and embrace the truth, and try no longer to add new stars to the heaven — for why would you disturb the tranquil Aether? If you agree, I am persuaded that, with your effort joined [to mine], this truth can be settled in full; for I have perfect demonstrations by which the distances of comets, in whatever way they may be carried, can be determined with certainty, nor, I think, do you lack any observations: *two going together* [σὺν δύ' ἐρχομένω]. Let us pool our labours: there will be nothing of mine that will not gladly be shared with you; do you in turn do the same. I very much desire to see those [observations] of that Rothmann, by which with a quite volatile shrewdness he pursues these vapours right up to Saturn [♄]: if you communicate them, it will be left to your judgement how truly he is so deeply wise, otherwise it may seem that a paradox is being deliberately defended by you [pl.]. The observations that it has so far befallen me to see cannot be taken as principles for a demonstration of distances: they bear only on the apparent motion in longitude and latitude. Such [observations] I seek where the azimuths are not varied and which are taken in different regions. A marvellous table [Canon] is being constructed here by a certain noble kinsman of ours, who has leisure and talent enough for so great a work: when it is finished, it will be communicated to you. But of yours we have so far been able to learn nothing: see that we understand what singular things you have in chemical matters. Our knowing is nothing, unless others know that we know. Concerning the reduction of the Sun [☉] and Moon [☾] into Mercury [☿], or the tincture of the natural philosophers [physici], if anything is established by experience, write back; our comparing [of notes] will perhaps do no harm. If you think anything further against us, do it in few words and with greater restraint of the pen; and, if it so please [you], let us submit our [pieces] to public judgement, lest by our disputations our friendship and our habit of writing should also lapse. If you seek anything here, signify it to me: I shall not fail [you], as far as I can. Fare you most happily, Master Tycho, and receive kindly and make use of this cerate [cerotum], sent by a friend who is your antagonist [and] a physician, to quench that flame [phlogosis] in the heaven kindled by you.

Given at Edinburgh, 27 March [15]92.
Yours, John Craig, Scot.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Ioannes Craigius Scotus* = **John Craig** (d. 1620), Scottish physician and mathematician, educated at Frankfurt an der Oder (where he taught logic and mathematics) and later first physician to James VI of Scotland. An Aristotelian, he held that comets are **sublunary** and disputed Tycho's celestial cometology; this letter belongs to the Craig–Brahe comet controversy. Tycho replied with his forty-page *Apologia (Apologetica Responsio) … ad Craigum Scotum de Cometis* (preserved in *Opera Omnia* IV).
- **Recipient address.** *Wenae insulae domino … regis Daniae consiliario et mathematico* = "lord of the island of **Hven**, councillor to the King of Denmark, and mathematician." *Wena* = Hven (the island granted to Tycho in 1576).
- ***Apologiam tuam*** — "your *Apologia*": Tycho's defence of his cometary doctrine, sent earlier to Craig and here being answered. Craig confesses to having read it only *obiter* ("cursorily"), pleading Tycho's *prolixitas*.
- ***Naturae motu, quo Sublunaria maximi circuli tramitem tenere possunt*** — "the motion of Nature whereby things sublunary can keep to the track of a great circle": Craig's physical mechanism for making comets (held to be sublunary, i.e. below the Moon) appear to follow a great-circle path — the crux of his anti-Tychonic argument.
- **Master Fuller.** *D. Fullero nostro* — a "Fuller" attached to a Scottish embassy/fleet to Denmark; not securely identified here. Rendered "Master Fuller" (*D.* = *Dominus*,); identity flagged.
- ***controversia de veneficarum nugis*** — "the controversy over the trifles of the witches": the North Berwick witch-trials (1590–91), in which Craig (a royal physician at James VI's court) was caught up; *nugis* ("trifles") marks his dismissive view. Kept literal.
- ***Elenctica*** — "refutations / things refutative" (from Greek *elenktikós*, "of refutation"); Craig's title-word for his polemical tract against Tycho. Retained and glossed.
- ***Eclipsin ☉lis*** — "an eclipse of the Sun." The symbol ☉ with the Latin genitive ending *-lis* (= *Solis*) is kept in the Source block and named "Sun" in translation. The solar eclipse Craig dates his completion by is that observed "the previous year."
- ***nova sydera coelo addere … tranquillum Aethera turbares*** — "to add new stars to the heaven … disturb the tranquil Aether": Craig's reproach that Tycho's celestial comets (and his 1572 nova) violate the immutability of the heavens. *sydera* = *sidera*. Kept as the author's rhetoric, not endorsed.
- **Greek.** *σὺν δύ' ἐρχομένω* — "two going together," a quotation of Homer, *Iliad* 10.224 (*σύν τε δύ' ἐρχομένω καί τε πρὸ ὃ τοῦ ἐνόησεν*, "when two go together, one perceives before the other"), proverbial for collaboration; transliterated *syn dy' erchoménō* and glossed. Craig's appeal to pool labours with Tycho.
- ***remotiones Cometarum*** — "the distances of comets" (their *remoteness*); *remotio* in this technical sense = the comet's distance/parallax determination. *azimutha non variantur* = "the azimuths are not varied," i.e. simultaneous observations from differing regions for a parallax baseline.
- **Rothmann.** *illius Rothmanni* = **Christoph Rothmann**, the Hesse-Kassel mathematician; *ad ♄num usque … fumositates insequitur* = "pursues these vapours right up to Saturn [♄]," mocking Rothmann's (and Tycho's) placing of cometary "vapours" as high as the sphere of Saturn. The glyph ♄ (with Latin accusative *-num* = *Saturnum*) is kept in the Source block and named "Saturn".
- ***Canon mirificus … a generoso quodam consangvineo*** — "a marvellous *table* being constructed by a certain noble kinsman": *Canon* in the mathematical sense of a computational table. The "kinsman" is very probably **John Napier** of Merchiston (Craig's known associate, to whom Craig is traditionally said to have carried news of Tycho's prosthaphaeretic methods); "marvellous table" anticipates the language of Napier's later *Mirifici logarithmorum canonis descriptio* (1614). The identification is inferential and is flagged here, not asserted in the translation. *consangvineus* = *consanguineus*.
- **Alchemy.** *De ☉ et ☾ in ☿ reductione aut physicorum tinctura* = "concerning the reduction of the Sun [☉=gold] and Moon [☾=silver] into Mercury [☿], or the tincture of the natural philosophers." The metal/planet symbols are kept in the Source block and named in translation; in this alchemical register ☉/☾/☿ also denote gold/silver/quicksilver — the double sense is intrinsic and is noted rather than resolved. *physici* = the natural philosophers (alchemical adepts), rendered "natural philosophers" not "physicians."
- ***Scire nostrum nihil est, nisi alij sciant nos scire*** — "Our knowing is nothing, unless others know that we know": a sententia (a well-worn tag, ultimately after Persius, *Sat.* 1.27, *scire tuum nihil est nisi te scire hoc sciat alter*); kept as an epigram.
- ***cerotum … ad restinguendam illam in coelo phlogosin*** — "this cerate [a medicinal wax salve], to quench that *flame* [φλόγωσις, *phlogosis*, "inflammation/conflagration"] in the heaven kindled by you": Craig's closing conceit, the physician-antagonist sending a salve to "treat" the celestial fire (the comet/nova) that Tycho had "kindled" in the sky. *cerotum* and the Graecism *phlogosin* are kept and glossed; the joke (medical cure for an astronomical "inflammation") is preserved, not flattened.
- **Calendar & place (dateline crux).** *Datae **Edinburgi** 27 Martij 92* = "Given at **Edinburgh**, 27 March [15]92" (O.S.; Scotland kept the Julian calendar and, in 1592, still began the civil year on 25 March — but here "92" plainly = 1592, the controversy's known date). **The edition label field reads "Uraniborg," which the letter's own dateline contradicts: Craig writes from Edinburgh.** The header therefore leads with the as-written place/date and notes the catalogued value; "Uraniborg" most likely records the addressee's location (place of receipt) rather than the place of writing, and is not adopted. No date is silently converted.

text.original:
DEM VESTEN/ VNSERM LIEBEN BESONDERN / TYCHONI BRAHE, HERRN ZU KNUDSTRUP.
WILHELM VON GOTTES GNADEN/ LANDTGRAUE ZU HESSEN/ GRAUE ZU CATZENELNBOGEN/ ETC.

VNSERN gnedigen Gruß zuvor/ Vester lieber Besonder. Wir haben ewer Schreiben de dato Vraniburg, den 20. Februarij, wol empfangen vnd gelesen. So viel nu erstlich die von vns begerete Elendsthier belangt/ thun wir vns der angewendten mühe vnd bestellung/ so ihr deßhalben gethan/ gegen euch in Gnaden bedancken/ Vnd mögen euch hiermit nicht verhalten/ daß wir vor dreyen Monaten vier Elende auß Schweden bekommen/ deroselben vns aber albereit drey gestorben/ daß wir also von denselben nur eine junge Kuhe/ vnd dan sonst noch einen Elendsochsen/ so wir vor zweyen Jaren auß Schweden bekommen/ haben. Die Vrsach aber/ daß sie also weg sterben/ halten wirs dafür/ daß es dahero komme/ weyl der liebe Gott vorm Jar so ein statliche Mast bescheret/ daß auch die Eycheln sehr dicke auff einander gelegen/ vnd faul worden seyn/ daß sie derselben etwan zu viel gessen haben mögen/ daß inen endtlich die feulung im Leibe gemacht/ vnd daran sterben müssen/ Inmassen vns dan ein gute anzahl Reher/ deßgleichen 19. Gembse/ so wir vorm Jar aussem Landt zu Beyern bringen/ vnd gleicher gestalt in vnserm Thiergarten zur Zapffenburg thun lassen/ auch kurtz auff einander gestorben seyn. Woferne jr vns nu zu dem noch vbrigen Elendsochsen/ ein par starcker Elendskuhe von zweyen oder dreyen Jaren bey gegenwertigem herausser schicken kundtet/ geschehe vns daran zu gantz angenemen gefallen/ Wollen es auch vmb euch in Gnaden widerumb zubeschulden vnuergessen seyn/ dan sonderlich der eine Elendsochse/ den wir nu baldt zwey Jar gehabt/ sich gerne paren wolte/ vnd sich in der brunst gantz vnfletig erzeigen thut.

Was dan die jüngst im verschienen Decembri geschehene Eclipsin Lunæ vnd deroselben Obseruation betrifft/ ist es an dem/ daß wir dieselbige in abwesen vnsers Mathematici ROTHMANNI (der sich dan seiner noch jmmerwehrenden Schwachheit halben bey vns nicht wider eingestellt) nicht obseruiret haben/ Sondern/ inmassen wie jr dan in beyliegendt zu sehen/ wie sie von vnserm Mathematico, den wir newlicher Tage auff vnsere Vniuersitet Marpurg bestellet haben/ auffgerissen worden.

Sonst mögen wir euch nicht verhalten/ daß die Römische Keyserliche Maiestet vor etlichen Tagen an vns allergnedigst geschrieben/ vnd begeret/ daß wir jrer Keyserlichen Maiestet vnsern Vhrmacher Iosten Byrgi mit dem Globo, den er hiebevor gemacht/ vnd darauff die Motus Planetarum eingebracht hat/ zuschicken wolten. Welches wir dan jrer Keyserlichen Maiestet nicht verwegern mögen/ vnd seyndt demnach gemeynt/ gedachten vnsern Vhrmachern erstes Tages zu jrer Keyserlichen Maiestet abzufertigen/ doch daß er sich förderlich widerumb bey vns einstellen solle/ wie wir vns dan versehen/ er auff künfftigen Michaelis widerumb bey vns seyn werde.

Vnd ob er euch wol den begerten Goldtschmidts gesellen/ so mit den Automatis vnd Horologijs etlicher massen vmbzugehen wisse/ gerne zuweisen wolte/ so ist doch deroselbigen jetziger zeit keiner allhier anzutreffen/ Es soll sich aber er vnser Vhrmacher auff seiner reyse nach einem solchen Goldtschmidts gesellen vmhoren/ vnd da er denselbigen antreffen wirdt/ alßdan mit jm handlen vnd euch zuweisen.

Was dan vnser Sohn Landtgraff MORITZ an euch schreiben thut/ vnd in Commendationem ewers Operis Astronomici gemacht/ daß habt jr hierneben zu empfangen/ vnd begeren gnediglich/ wan solch Opus gar versertigt/ jr wollet vns desselbigen ein Exemplar zuschicken.

Wolten wir euch hinwider gnediglich diß nicht verhalten. Vnd seyndt euch mit gnedigem Willen wol geneigt.

Datumin vnser Stadt vnd VestungCassel/ am 2. Aprilis, Anno 1592.
WILHELM, LANDGRAFF ZU HESSEN.
text.english:
**To the Steadfast, Our trusty and well-beloved, Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup.**
**Wilhelm, by the grace of God, Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, etc.**

Our gracious greeting beforehand. Trusty and well-beloved. We have duly received and read your letter dated Uraniborg, the 20th of February. Now, so far as first concerns the elk that we requested of you, we thank you graciously for the pains and procurement that you have undertaken on that account; and we may not conceal from you herewith that three months ago we obtained four elk out of Sweden, of which, however, three have already died on us, so that of those we have only one young cow, and then otherwise one elk-ox besides, which we obtained out of Sweden two years ago. As for the cause that they die off thus, we hold it to be this: that, because the dear God last year sent so plentiful a mast that the acorns lay very thickly upon one another and turned rotten, they may perhaps have eaten too much of them, which finally bred the rot in their bodies, and they must die of it — even as a good number of roe-deer of ours, likewise 19 chamois, which we brought last year out of the land of Bavaria and had placed in the same manner in our game-park at Zapfenburg, have also died off in quick succession. If now, alongside the elk-ox still remaining to us, you could send us out a pair of strong elk-cows of two or three years' age by the present [bearer], it would be done us as a quite welcome pleasure; and we will be unforgetful to requite it graciously toward you in turn — for in particular the one elk-ox, which we have now had for nearly two years, would gladly mate, and in the rut shows itself altogether unruly.

Now as for the eclipse of the Moon that lately occurred this past December, and the observation of it: the case is that we did not observe it ourselves, in the absence of our mathematician Rothmann (who, on account of his still-continuing infirmity, has not yet presented himself again with us), but, just as you may see in the enclosure, [it has been recorded] as it was sketched out by our mathematician whom we have these recent days appointed to our University of Marburg.

Furthermore, we may not conceal from you that the Roman Imperial Majesty some days ago wrote to us most graciously and desired that we should send to His Imperial Majesty our clockmaker Jost Bürgi, together with the globe that he made some while ago and upon which he has brought in the motions of the planets [motus planetarum]. This we may not refuse His Imperial Majesty, and we are accordingly minded to dispatch our said clockmaker to His Imperial Majesty at the first day [i.e. without delay], yet on condition that he is to present himself again with us promptly, as we expect that he will be back with us again by next Michaelmas.

And although he [Bürgi] would gladly have assigned to you the goldsmith's journeyman you requested, one who knows in some measure how to handle automata and clocks [automata et horologia], yet none such is at present to be found here; but our clockmaker shall, on his journey, make inquiry after such a goldsmith's journeyman, and, when he meets with one, shall then treat with him and assign him to you.

Then, as to what our son, Landgrave Moritz, writes to you, and has composed in commendation of your astronomical work [in commendationem operis astronomici], that you have to receive herewith; and we graciously desire that, when such work is quite completed, you will send us a copy of it.

This we would graciously not conceal from you in return. And we are well disposed toward you with gracious goodwill.

Given in our city and fortress of Kassel, on the 2nd of April, in the year 1592.
Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse.

documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer.** *Wilhelm von Gottes Gnaden, Landgraue zu Hessen* = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), "Wilhelm the Wise," the astronomer-prince of Kassel and Tycho's chief correspondent among the German rulers; this is among his last letters to Tycho (he died in August 1592). The titulature is given in full and the princely *Wir/euch* register preserved.
- **Recipient address.** *Dem Vesten, vnserm lieben Besondern, Tychoni Brahe, Herrn zu Knudstrup* — "To the Steadfast, Our trusty and well-beloved, Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup." *Vest(er)* ("steadfast, firm") is the standard chancery honorific for a nobleman; *vnser lieber Besonder(er)* is the fixed princely address-formula rendered by this chapter's convention ("Our trusty and well-beloved"). *Herr zu Knudstrup* names Tycho's Scanian family seat.
- **Tycho's incoming letter.** *ewer Schreiben de dato Vraniburg, den 20. Februarij* — Tycho's letter "dated Uraniborg, the 20th of February" [1592, O.S.], here acknowledged. *de dato* is a Latin chancery tag left in place.
- **The elk (***Elende / Elendsthier / Elendsochse / Elendskuhe***).** Early New High German *Elen(d)* = the **elk / European moose** (*Alces alces*); *Elendsthier* "elk-beast," *Elendsochse* "elk-ox (bull)," *Elendskuhe* "elk-cow." The two princes traded live elk for their game-parks; Wilhelm here reports a die-off and asks Tycho to procure more from Sweden via the bearer. *Mast* = the autumn fall of acorns/beech-mast on which the animals fed; the Landgrave attributes the deaths to rotten acorns. *Reher* = roe-deer; *Gembse* = chamois; *Beyern* = Bavaria. *Zapffenburg* = the Landgrave's game-park at **Zapfenburg** (near Spangenberg, Hesse). *brunst* = the rut; *vnfletig* here = "unruly, uncleanly/violent" (in rutting behaviour). The animal-husbandry register is kept plain, not modernised.
- **The lunar eclipse.** *die jüngst im verschienen Decembri geschehene Eclipsin Lunae* = "the eclipse of the Moon that lately occurred this past December" — the **lunar eclipse of 9/19 December 1591**. *Eclipsin Lunae*, *Obseruation*, *Mathematici*, *obseruiret*, *auffgerissen* ("sketched/drawn out," of the observation diagram) — the technical nouns code-switch into Latin within the German, by this chapter's convention. *beyliegendt* = the enclosure (the observation sent with the letter).
- **Christoph Rothmann.** *vnsers Mathematici Rothmanni* = **Christoph Rothmann**, the Kassel court mathematician and Tycho's correspondent, here reported absent through his *jmmerwehrende Schwachheit* ("still-continuing infirmity"); he had left Kassel and did not return to court service. His unnamed successor is *vnser Mathematicus, den wir … auff vnsere Vniuersitet Marpurg bestellet haben* — newly appointed to the **University of Marburg** (the Hessian university).
- **The Emperor and Jost Bürgi.** *die Römische Keyserliche Maiestet* = **Emperor Rudolf II** (Holy Roman Emperor, r. 1576–1612), styled "the Roman Imperial Majesty." *vnser Vhrmacher Iosten Byrgi* = **Jost Bürgi** (1552–1632), the Kassel court clockmaker and instrument-maker (and independent inventor of logarithms/prosthaphaeresis-style computation). The *Globus … darauff die Motus Planetarum eingebracht* is Bürgi's celebrated mechanized **planetary globe** (a clockwork-driven globe showing the *motus planetarum*, "motions of the planets"). *Michaelis* = **Michaelmas** (29 September), the term by which Bürgi is expected back. — *erstes Tages* rendered "at the first day," i.e. without delay.
- **Goldsmith's journeyman; automata and clocks.** *Goldtschmidts gesellen … so mit den Automatis vnd Horologijs etlicher massen vmbzugehen wisse* — a journeyman goldsmith able "in some measure to handle automata and clocks" (*automata et horologia*), whom Tycho had requested for his own Uraniborg workshop; the Latin technical nouns are kept and glossed.
- **Landgrave Moritz's commendatory poem.** *vnser Sohn Landtgraff Moritz … in Commendationem ewers Operis Astronomici gemacht* = **Moritz, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1572–1632, "Moritz the Learned"), Wilhelm's son and successor, who has written verses *in commendationem operis astronomici* ("in commendation of [Tycho's] astronomical work"). The *Opus Astronomicum* whose completed copy Wilhelm asks for is most plausibly the volume Tycho was then assembling — the *Epistolae astronomicae* / *Progymnasmata* programme — but the letter does not name the title; the referent is left as written, not specified. The clause *daß habt jr hierneben zu empfangen* indicates the poem was enclosed.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datum in vnser Stadt vnd Vestung Cassel, am 2. Aprilis, Anno 1592* = "Given in our city and fortress of **Kassel**, on the 2nd of April, the year 1592" (**O.S.**; Hesse-Kassel, a Lutheran territory, kept the Julian calendar). The header date (2 April 1592) is the dateline as written and agrees with the catalogue label. *Datum* (the chancery dating-verb) rendered "Given."
- **Edition note.** This letter is printed in Tycho's own *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Uraniborg, 1596; reprinted in Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VI). No manuscript witness is recorded in the edition (witnesses:[]).
- **Source typography.** The printed run-together forms *Datumin*, *VestungCassel* (missing word-spaces at line breaks in the source) are reproduced verbatim in the Source block and silently word-spaced in the translation.

DEM VESTEN/ VNSERM LIEBEN BESONDERN/ TYCHONI BRAHE, HERRN ZU KNUDSTRUP.
MORITZ VON GOTTES GNADEN/ LANDTGRAUE ZU HESSEN/ GRAUE ZU CATZENELNBOGEN/ ETC.

VNSERN gnedigen Gruß zuvor/ Vester lieber Besonder. Wir haben ewer Schreiben de dato Vraniburg, den 20. Februarij, an vns gethan/ empfangen/ gelesen/ vnd darauß nach der lenge was jr an vns begeret verstanden. Daß wir nu für einen solchen hohen vnd fürtreffligen Poëten gerümbt/ vnd euch vnsere Poëtica so hoch commendiret worden/ daran geschicht vns zwar zu viel/ dan wir wissen solche statliche Commendation,vnd wie jr vns auch zutrawet/ im a Werck nicht zu erweisen/ Ohn ist es aber nicht/ daß wir vns in vnsern angehenden Studijs in Poësi etwas exerciret, doch aber solch Exercitium durch andere vns mehr angelegene Sachen/ numehr eine geraume zeit nicht gebrauchet.

Nichts desto weniger aber haben wir ewerm gesinnen nach ein Carmen commendatorium, so gut wir es machen können/ vor ewere Opera Astronomica, so jr in Druck außgehen lassen wollet/ verfertiget/ vnd dasselbige auff die Seite vor dem Diplomate Cæsareo, da jr es hin begeret/ mit eigen Handen geschrieben. Da euch nu vnser Carmen commendatorium annemlich sein würde/ geschehe vns daran ein gnediges gefallen.

Wolten wir euch hinwider gnediglich nicht verhalten/ Vnd seyndt euch mit gnedigem willen wolgeneigt.

DatumCassel/ am 2. Aprilis, Anno 1592.
MORITZ LANDTGRAFF ZU HESSEN.

MAVRITIVS HASSIÆ LANDTGRAVIVS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE, NOBILEM
ET CLARISSIMVM VIRVM.

VRANIE superat reliqvas divina Sorores,

    Dicitur et sacri gloria prima Chori.

Hanc coluere Patres Prisci, Regesqve potentes,

    Qui propius Mentis vi tetigere DEOS.

Hanc optat sapiens studiorum figere metam,

    Vt famæ celebris præmia digna ferat.

Qvanto etenim Terras celsus supereminet Æther;

    Jllius est tanto notio lavde prior.

Ipsa docet Cæli motus, Cælumqve tueri

    Vultibus erectis nos jubet ipse DEVS.

Ne ventura malis timeamus fata, sed Astris

    Præmoniti, ad Superûm confugiamus opem.

Nec quæramus humi pastum, sed lavde vehatur,

    Qvi struxit Cæli tale Creator Opus.

Ergo tuis lætus meritis studijsqve fovere

    Perge DEAM tantam; Munera larga dabit.

Qvandoqvidem dudum miratur, pervia cuncta

    Esse tuis Fabricis quæ latuere prius.

Hinc tibi scrutanti Leges sublimis Olympi,

    Inter honoratum præparat Astra locum.
text.english:
**To the Honourable, Our trusty and well-beloved, Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup.**
**Moritz, by the grace of God, Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, etc.**

Our gracious greeting beforehand, Our trusty and well-beloved. We have received your letter sent to us, dated Uraniborg the 20th of February, [and] read it, and from it understood at length what it is you desire of us. That we should now be extolled as so lofty and excellent a poet, and that our poetry should be so highly commended to you — in this indeed too much is done to us, for we know we cannot make good such a stately commendation, [nor live up to] the trust you place in us, in the [a] work; yet it is not untrue that in our early studies we did exercise ourselves somewhat in poetry — though for a good while now we have not employed that exercise, on account of other matters more pressing upon us.

Nonetheless, in accordance with your request, we have made ready a commendatory poem [Carmen commendatorium], as well as we were able to make it, for your astronomical works [Opera Astronomica] which you intend to bring out in print; and we have written that same [poem] in our own hand, on the page before the Imperial privilege [Diplomate Caesareo], where you desired it [to be]. Should our commendatory poem now be acceptable to you, we should take a gracious pleasure in it.

This we would not, in turn, graciously withhold from you; and we are well-disposed toward you with gracious goodwill.

Given at Kassel, the 2nd of April, in the year 1592.
Moritz, Landgrave of Hesse.

**MORITZ, LANDGRAVE OF HESSE, TO TYCHO BRAHE, A NOBLE AND MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN.**

Divine Urania surpasses the rest of her Sisters,
    and is called the foremost glory of the sacred Choir.

Her the Fathers of old cultivated, and mighty Kings,
    who by the power of mind touched the gods more nearly.

Her the wise man chooses to set as the goal of his studies,
    that he may bear away the worthy rewards of famed renown.

For by as much as the lofty Ether rises above the Earth,
    by so much does the knowledge of it stand first in praise.

She herself teaches the motions of the heavens, and God himself
    bids us look upon heaven with faces raised.

Let us not fear the fates that evils bring, but, forewarned
    by the Stars, let us take refuge in the help of those above.

Nor let us seek our fodder on the ground, but let him be borne up by praise
    who, as Creator, built so great a Work as the heavens.

Therefore, rejoicing in your merits, go on cherishing
    with your studies so great a Goddess; she will grant bountiful gifts —

seeing that she has long marvelled that all things which before lay hidden
    have become open to your instruments.

Hence, for you as you search out the laws of lofty Olympus,
    she prepares an honoured place among the Stars.

documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer.** **Moritz "the Learned," Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1572–1632), who had succeeded his father **Wilhelm IV** on the latter's death (25 August 1592 — so Moritz writes here still as the young heir, in his nineteenth year, though already styling himself *Landgraf*; his father was alive at the date of writing). A polymath, composer, and Latinist, Moritz inherited his father's astronomical patronage and the Kassel observatory circle (Rothmann, Bürgi). The full chancery titulature — *Landgraf zu Hessen, Graf zu Katzenelnbogen* — and the princely first-person plural (*Wir / euch / unser*) are preserved by this chapter's convention
- **Recipient address.** *Dem Vesten* = "To the Honourable/Steadfast" (the conventional honorific for a nobleman below princely rank); *unserm lieben Besondern* = "Our trusty and well-beloved"; *Herrn zu Knudstrup* = "Lord of **Knudstrup**" (the Brahe family seat in Scania).
- **Occasion.** Tycho's *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (printed at Uraniborg; Liber I appeared 1596), the very volume that prints this exchange. Tycho had written on 20 February 1592 (cited *de dato Uraniburg, den 20. Februarij*) requesting that Moritz contribute a commendatory poem to be placed before the work, next to the imperial privilege. The letter is Moritz's reply enclosing/announcing the poem.
- **Latin code-switches** (kept in the source, italicised on first use): *de dato* "dated"; *Poëta / Poëtica / Poësi* "poet / poetry / poetry"; *Commendation / commendiret / Carmen commendatorium* "commendation / commended / commendatory poem"; *Exercitium* "exercise (practice)"; *Opera Astronomica* "astronomical works"; *Diplomate Caesareo* "the **imperial privilege**" — i.e. the printing *privilegium* / *Privileg* granted by the Holy Roman Emperor (here Rudolf II), conventionally printed at the front of a book; *ut*-style chancery diction. The mixing of Latin technical/legal nouns into a German princely body is the expected Kassel-court register.
- **Orthography (chancery German, c. 1592).** *ewer / ewerm* = *euer / euerm* "your"; *jr* = *ihr* "you (pl./formal)"; *gethan* = *getan*; *darauß* = *daraus*; *gerümbt* = *gerühmt* "extolled"; *statliche* = *stattliche* "stately, splendid"; *zutrawet* = *zutraut* "entrust/credit"; *numehr* = *nunmehr* "now, by now"; *außgehen* = *ausgehen* "bring/go out"; *außgehen lassen* "have published"; *annemlich* = *annehmlich* "acceptable"; *seyndt* = *seind/sind* "are." The *v/u* convention (*Vnsern, vns, vnser*) and *ß / -tz* spellings are period-standard.
- **Textual crux — *"im a Werck"*.** The source reads *"… wie jr vns auch zutrawet/ im a Werck nicht zu erweisen …"*. The stray lower-case *a* between *im* and *Werck* corresponds to no German word in context; it is almost certainly an editorial/printer's reference-mark (a marginal-note or sidenote signal of the kind the 1596 *Epistolae* uses) that has been pulled inline in the working transcription, the intended reading being *im Werck* = "in [the/its] working-out, in deed/in practice" (i.e. Moritz cannot in *practice* live up to the praise). The printed *a* is retained verbatim in the source block and bracketed *[a]* / *[the]* in the translation rather than silently deleted; the sense-reading *im Werck* "in deed/in practice" is adopted but flagged. (Cf. the parallel printer's-mark interruption.)
- **Spacing artefacts of the transcription.** *"Commendation,vnd"* (missing space after the comma) and *"DatumCassel"* (run-together *Datum Cassel*) are reproduced as in the working transcription; both are typesetting/transcription spacing slips, not substantive. *Datum Cassel* = the dating formula "Given at **Kassel**."
- **Negations.** Three are present and all reproduced: (1) *im [a] Werck **nicht** zu erweisen* "**not** able to make good in practice"; (2) *Ohn ist es aber **nicht**, daß …* — the period idiom *es ist nicht ohne, daß* = "it is not untrue / not without foundation that," i.e. an affirmative concession ("yet it is true that …"), here rendered "yet it is not untrue that"; (3) *Wolten wir euch hinwider gnediglich **nicht** verhalten* "this we would **not** graciously withhold from you in turn" (the standard chancery closing affirming the favourable communication). The double-negative idiom in (2) is the only point where a literal word-count could mislead an English reader; it is rendered as the affirmative concession the German idiom carries, and flagged here.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datum Cassel, am 2. Aprilis, Anno 1592* = "Given at **Kassel**, 2 April 1592." Hesse-Kassel kept the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar at this date (Protestant Germany did not adopt the Gregorian reform until 1700), so [O.S.]; this agrees with the catalogue label (*1592. 2. april. Kassel*). No in-letter date discrepancy. The cited incoming date *den 20. Februarij* (of Tycho's letter from Uraniborg) is likewise O.S.
- **The enclosed carmen commendatorium.** This is the Latin dedicatory poem itself that Landgrave Moritz of Hesse-Kassel promises in the already-published body of the letter ("we have written that same poem in our own hand, on the page before the Imperial privilege...") — composed by Moritz personally to be printed before Rudolf II's imperial privilege (Diplomate Caesareo) in Tycho's forthcoming Opera Astronomica, i.e. the *Astronomiae Instauratae Mechanica* (Wandsbek, 1598). Letter and enclosure belong to the well-documented Hven-Kassel correspondence — Wilhelm IV, then his son and successor Moritz, corresponding with Tycho and his court astronomer Christoph Rothmann — which Mosley's *Bearing the Heavens* identifies as the single most-studied portion of Tycho's surviving correspondence.
- **Content of the poem.** Fourteen lines of elegiac couplets celebrating Urania, muse of astronomy, as chief among the Muses and the pursuit of "ancient Fathers and mighty kings," closing with direct praise of Tycho: Urania "has long marvelled" that his "Fabricis" (instruments/constructions — Tycho's own term, as in the *Mechanica*'s subject matter) have made accessible what before lay hidden, and the poem promises him "an honoured place among the Stars" for searching out "the laws of lofty Olympus."
- **Duplication in the recovered segment.** The recovered text repeats the full heading ("MAVRITIVS HASSIAE LANDTGRAVIVS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE...") and the entire fourteen-line poem twice, verbatim. This reads as a duplication artifact of the recovery process rather than a feature of the original enclosure — the letter's own published German prose refers to "ein Carmen commendatorium" in the singular, with no hint that two copies were sent. Translated once here per house rule against padding; the duplication should be checked against the underlying manuscript/print exemplar (the Rothmann-Kassel correspondence materials are held at the Hessian State Archive, Marburg, and the Kassel university library) before being treated as meaningful.
- **Register.** Rendered as close, line-for-line English prose, preserving the couplet breaks of the Latin elegiacs rather than attempting an English metrical equivalent.

documents.incipit: QUAS ad me 13. Novembris dedisti literas, quod humanitatem et eruditionem nulla sui parte …

text.original:
AMPLISSIMO NOBILISSIMOQUE VIRO, VIRTUTE ET ERUDITIONE PRÆSTANTISSIMO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE DOMINO DE KNUDSTRUP ET VRANIENBURG, AMICO SUO CARISSIMO. GENEROSE VIR.

QUAS ad me 13. Novembris dedisti literas, quod humanitatem et eruditionem nulla sui parte non spirarent, præcipue vero quod tui nominis inscriptionem præ se ferrent, mihi certe, ut decuit, acceptissimæ fuerunt. Cum enim in Danica mea peregrinatione nihil tam admirabile excellentis ingenij tui raris dotibus, nihil tam gratum quam sanciendæ tecum amicitiæ occasio contigerit, nec minorem in conservanda constantiam, quam in contrahenda amicitia benignitatem tuam ex amicissimis literis perspiciam, ni et tuam merito humanitatem amplectar et meam in scribendo negligentiam, tum crebrioribus literis tum alijs quibuscunque, quæ mearum virium sunt officijs, sarciam, ingratus prorsus et tanti viri amicitia indignus merito censear. Literis etiam tuis adiunctam effigiem, oris tui dignitatem et temperatam benignitate gravitatem, laudabili sculptoris industria, ad vivum referentem, quod ea oculos imagine pascat, cuius assidua recordatione animus iucundissime afficitur, pretiosissimis quibusque muneribus, quæ tibi fortuna affatim suppetit, præstantiorem certe existimavi. Et quos ad illius (ut ais) ornatum versus a me poscis, hos quidem addidi, non quod, quæ tui nominis fama abunde commendetur, alio quovis ornamento mea sententia indigeat, sed ut quæ virtutum et doctrinæ tuæ per universum orbem diffusa gloria effigiem tuam in omnibus literatorum omnium bibliothecis sublimem constituet, meo etiam nomini locum aliquem tuo merito ibidem inveniat. Ijs itaque utere, non quidem ut digni sunt, sed ut nostra amicitia et tuo iudicio dignum videbitur. Ego pariter, quæ a te Domino PETRO IUNIO mandata sunt, nisi hactenus ab eo effecta sunt, quamprimum illius conveniendi occasio sese obtulerit, ea qua decet fide et diligentia præstabo: quodque de hortulano et aucupe ad me scribis, effectum brevi curabo. Porro IOANNEM CRAIGIUM medicum Edinburgensem, quem mihi tam diligenter ac studiose commendas, ob probitatem et eruditionem antea quidem mihi semper charum, nunc tua causa multo chariorem censeo ac dum vivam censebo: qui cum veritatis eruendæ studio ac fortassis ut te ipso interprete scriptorum tuorum subtilitatem sibi non prius intellectam facilius assequeretur, silentibus imo vero cum admiratione tua inventa approbantibus alijs omnibus Europæ doctissimis mathematicis, Axiomata quædam tua impugnare ausus sit, quamvis nonnullis odium potius quam benevolentiam audacia meruisse videri possit, quæ tamen eximia nullisque perturbationibus obnoxia tua virtus est, sola victoria contentus et devicti hostis magnitudine tuam gloriam illustrari recte iudicans CRAIGIUM sollicite adeo atque accurate commendas, et commodis atque honoribus auctum cupis, ut egregiam de te bene merendi occasionem in eo viro iuvando mihi oblatam perspiciam. Itaque ubi mea vel opera vel ope rem suam vel dignitatem promoveri posse existimaverit, eam certe diligentiam atque alacritatem adhibebo, ut tuam commendationem meritum pondus apud me consecutam et res ipsa et illius literæ ad te abunde testentur. Et si alia qualibet in re tibi ijsve, quos tuorum in numero habes, consilio auxilio gratia vel auctoritate hîc usui esse possum, ita quæso vel negotia vel homines mihi commendes, ut beneficium tum demum contulisse te credas, cum meam operam expetieris. Interim ne te cœlestibus et divino tuo ingenio dignis curis distentum frustra morer, hoc solum a te petam, ut amicitiam nostram (quod humanitas et constantia tua satis spondent) inviolatam a temporis et longe dissitorum locorum iniuria tueri ac paria a me perpetuo expectare velis.

Vale.
Datæ Lethnitoniæ die XVI Maij Anno 1592.
Mag. Tuæ
addictissimus
[IOHANNES METELLANUS.]
text.english:
**To the most worthy and most noble man, most excellent in virtue and learning, Master Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup and Uraniborg, his most dear friend. Noble Sir.**

The letter you sent me on 13 November was assuredly most welcome to me, as was fitting — because it breathed forth humanity and learning in its every part, but above all because it bore the inscription of your name. For since in my journey in Denmark nothing so wonderful befell me as the rare gifts of your excellent genius, and nothing so gratifying as the opportunity of sealing a friendship with you; and since I perceive from your most friendly letter that your kindness is no less in keeping faith than it was in forming our friendship — unless I duly embrace your humanity in return and make good my negligence in writing, both by more frequent letters and by all other services that lie within my power, I should deservedly be reckoned wholly ungrateful and unworthy of the friendship of so great a man. The likeness, too, attached to your letter — rendering to the life, by the praiseworthy industry of the engraver, the dignity of your countenance and a gravity tempered with kindness — I judged assuredly more excellent than any of the most precious gifts that fortune supplies you in abundance, in that it feeds the eyes with that image whose constant remembrance affects the mind most pleasantly. And the verses which you ask of me for its adornment (as you say), these indeed I have added — not because, in my opinion, what is abundantly commended by the fame of your name stands in need of any other ornament, but so that, just as the glory of your virtues and learning, spread through the whole world, will set your likeness on high in the libraries of all the learned everywhere, my name too may by your merit find some place there as well. Use them, therefore — not indeed as they deserve, but as shall seem worthy of our friendship and of your judgement. I likewise, as to the matters entrusted by you to Master Peter Young, unless they have hitherto been carried out by him, will, as soon as an occasion of meeting him presents itself, perform them with the faith and diligence that is fitting; and as to what you write to me about the gardener and the fowler, I will see it accomplished shortly. Furthermore, as to John Craig, physician of Edinburgh, whom you so carefully and earnestly commend to me — dear to me always before, indeed, on account of his honesty and learning, I now reckon him, and while I live shall reckon him, much dearer for your sake. Since, in his zeal for uncovering the truth, and perhaps that with you yourself as expositor he might more easily attain the subtlety of your writings not previously understood by him, he dared to attack certain of your axioms — while all the other most learned mathematicians of Europe were silent, nay rather approved your discoveries with admiration — although to some his boldness may seem to have earned hatred rather than goodwill: yet such is your virtue, surpassing and subject to no perturbations, that, content with victory alone and rightly judging that your glory is set off by the greatness of the enemy overcome, you commend Craig so solicitously and so carefully, and desire him advanced in advantages and honours, that I perceive an outstanding opportunity offered me of deserving well of you in helping that man. And so, wherever he shall judge that his fortune or his standing can be furthered by my work or my aid, I will assuredly apply such diligence and zeal that both the thing itself and his letters to you may abundantly attest that your commendation has obtained its deserved weight with me. And if in any other matter whatsoever I can be of use here, by counsel, aid, favour, or authority, to you or to those whom you count among your own, then, I beg, commend your affairs or your men to me in such a way that you may believe you have only then conferred a kindness when you have sought out my service. Meanwhile, lest I detain you in vain when you are engrossed in cares worthy of the heavens and of your divine genius, this alone I shall ask of you: that you be willing to keep our friendship (as your humanity and constancy sufficiently pledge) inviolate against the injury of time and of places far apart, and to expect the like from me perpetually.

Farewell.
Given at Lethington, the 16th day of May, in the year 1592.
Most devoted to Your Worship,
[John Maitland.]

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Iohannes Metellanus* = **John Maitland of Thirlestane** (c. 1537–1595), Lord Chancellor of Scotland under James VI from 1587. *Metellanus* is the standard Latinised form of the surname Maitland. The signature stands in **[square brackets] in the source** — an editorial supply by Dreyer, the name not being in the copy-text witness; preserved as such here.
- **Recipient styling.** *Domino de Knudstrup et Vranienburg* = "Lord of **Knudstrup** and **Uraniborg**" — Tycho's ancestral seat in Scania and his observatory-residence on Hven, treated together as his territorial designation.
- **Place.** *Lethnitonia* = **Lethington**, Maitland's estate in East Lothian (the house, later renamed Lennoxlove, near Haddington). Header gives "Lethington" per the dateline.
- **Occasion / "my journey in Denmark."** Maitland had been in Denmark in 1589–90 as a principal of the embassy attending **James VI's** marriage to **Anne of Denmark**; the Scottish party (which also included Peter Young and others) visited Tycho on Hven, the meeting to which *Danica mea peregrinatione* refers.
- ***Petro Iunio*** = **Peter Young** (Sir Peter Young of Seaton, 1544–1628), James VI's former tutor and a royal diplomat, the Scottish intermediary through whom Tycho's "matters" (*mandata*) were being handled; Latinised *Iunius*.
- ***Ioannes Craigius medicus Edinburgensis*** = **John Craig** (d. 1620), Edinburgh physician and mathematician who had ventured to dispute certain of Tycho's *Axiomata* (his cosmological/observational tenets), the controversy Tycho recounts in his own letters of c. 1589–90; named in the apparatus by this chapter's convention
- ***effigiem … sculptoris industria, ad vivum referentem*** — the engraved **portrait** Tycho had enclosed (Tycho circulated engraved likenesses of himself), and for which Maitland here supplies commendatory **verses** (*versus … ad illius ornatum*). The verses themselves are not transcribed within this letter.
- ***hortulano et aucupe*** — "the **gardener** and the **fowler**" (*auceps*, a bird-catcher / keeper of fowl): two servants or specialists Tycho had asked Maitland to procure or arrange for; the specific arrangement is not elaborated.
- ***Axiomata … impugnare ausus sit*** — "he dared to attack certain of your *axioms*": *Axiomata* kept as a technical term for Tycho's stated principles/tenets. The passage trades on the topos that an opponent's stature magnifies the victor's glory (*devicti hostis magnitudine tuam gloriam illustrari*).
- **No Greek, no astronomical/astrological symbols** occur in this letter.
- **Calendar.** *die XVI Maij Anno 1592* = "the 16th day of May, 1592." Scotland was on the **Julian calendar (Old Style)** in 1592 (it did not adopt the Gregorian reform until 1600/1752); dated O.S. accordingly. The catalogue *label* ("1592. 16. maj. Lethington") agrees with the dateline — no discrepancy. The opening reference to Tycho's letter "*13. Novembris*" (13 November, presumably 1591) is the letter being answered, not the date of this one.

documents.abstract: Asks why the promised Norwegian elk have not been delivered, noting his April courier went unanswered and that his existing Swedish elk have all died.
documents.incipit: VNSERN gnedigen Gruß zuvor/ Vester lieber Besonder. Ihr wisset euch zweiffels frey zu …

text.original:
DEM VESTEN/ VNSERM LIEBEN BESONDERN/ TYCHONI BRAHE, HERRN ZU KNUDSTRUP.
WILHELM VON GOTTES GNADEN/ LANDTGRAUE ZU HESSEN/ GRAUE ZU CATZENELNBOGEN/ ETC.

VNSERN gnedigen Gruß zuvor/ Vester lieber Besonder. Ihr wisset euch zweiffels frey zu erinnern/ welcher gestalt jr vns hiebevor etlicher Elende halber gute vertröstung gethan/ Darauff wir auch nicht vnderlassen/ vnderm dato, den 2. Aprilis, einen eigenen Botten mit einem Schreiben an euch haltendt/ abzufertigen/ daß/ wo solche Elende bey euch ankommen weren/ er vns dieselbige anhero bringen solte. Wir haben aber sider dem das geringste nicht vernommen/ ob solcher Botte bey euch ankommen/ oder aber ob er lebendig oder todt sey/ oder wie es sonst vmb jnen stehe/ daß vns biß noch von euch keine Antwort zukommên ist. Wie aber deme/ weil vns die Elende/ so vorm Jar auß Schweden bekommen/ alle gestorben/ vnd wir nur einen Elendtochsen/ so vns vor zweyen Jaren auß Schweden zukommen/ haben/ derselbe dan sehr schön vnd fein zahm ist/ vnd diß Jar albereit ein fein Gehörn von anderthalben Schuhe hoch geschoben hat/ vnd jm niergendt woran mangelt/ alß daß er kein Weibichen hat/ damit er sich paren möchte. Alß begeren wir gnediglich/ woferne euch solche vertröstete Elendsthier/ vnd sonderlich ein Weibichen zukommen were/ jr wollet vns dieselbige auff vnsern kosten so baldt vberschicken. Daran thut jr vns zu angenemen gefallen. Vnd seyndt wir es vmb euch hinwider in allen Gnaden/ damit wir euch ohne das gewogen/ zu erkennen geneigt.

Datum in vnser Stadt vnd Vestung Cassel/ am 30. Iulij, Anno 1592.
WILHELM LANDTGRAFF ZU HESSEN.
text.english:
**To the steadfast, our trusty and well-beloved, Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup.**
**Wilhelm, by the grace of God, Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, etc.**

Our gracious greeting beforehand, our trusty and well-beloved. You doubtless know to call to mind in what manner you gave us, some time ago, a good promise touching certain elk; whereupon we also did not fail, under the date of 2 April, to despatch a courier of our own to you, carrying a letter, [to the effect] that, if such elk had come into your hands, he was to bring the same to us here. But since then we have heard not the least thing — whether that courier reached you, or indeed whether he be alive or dead, or how it otherwise stands with him — so that up to now no answer has come to us from you. But however that may be: since the elk we obtained a year ago out of Sweden have all died, and we have only one elk-bull, which came to us out of Sweden two years ago — the same being indeed very handsome and finely tame, and having already this year put forth a fine antler a foot and a half high, and which lacks nothing anywhere, save that it has no female with which to mate — therefore we graciously desire that, in case such promised elk-beasts, and especially a female, should have come into your hands, you would send the same over to us at our cost as soon as may be. Therein you do us an acceptable pleasure. And we are inclined, for our part, to acknowledge it to you again in all graciousness, in which we are besides well-disposed toward you.

Given in our city and fortress of Kassel, on 30 July, Anno 1592.
WILHELM, LANDGRAVE OF HESSE.

documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer.** *Wilhelm von Gottes Gnaden, Landtgraue zu Hessen* = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), the "astronomer-prince," Tycho's foremost princely correspondent and the patron of the Kassel observatory (with Christoph Rothmann and the instrument-maker Jost Bürgi). This is one of his last letters: he died on 25 August 1592, less than a month after this dateline.
- **Recipient titulature.** *Herrn zu Knudstrup* = "Lord of Knudstrup," Tycho's ancestral seat (Knutstorp) in Scania; the full princely address-formula and titulature are preserved by this chapter's convention
- **Honorifics / formulae.** *Dem Vesten* = "to the steadfast" (an honorific epithet, *vest/fest* "firm, steadfast," for a nobleman below comital rank); *Vnsern gnedigen Gruß zuvor* = "Our gracious greeting beforehand"; *Vester lieber Besonder* = "our trusty and well-beloved" (the standard princely address to a favoured subordinate, this chapter's convention). The princely first-person plural (*Wir / euch*) is kept throughout.
- ***Catzenelnbogen*** = the County of **Katzenelnbogen**, a hereditary Hessian comital title; kept in the period spelling.
- **Subject: *Elend / Elende / Elendtochsen / Elendsthier*.** The pivotal term. *Elend(t)* here is **elk** (European elk / moose, *Alces alces*) — early-modern German *Elen(d)tier*, not the modern homograph *Elend* "misery." Rendered "elk" throughout. Specifically: *Elende* (plural) = "elk"; *Elendtochsen* = "elk-bull" (*Ochse* "ox/bull," here the male animal); *Elendsthier* = "elk-beast(s)"; *Weibichen* (dimin. of *Weib*) = "female (cow)." The exchange concerns living elk shipped from Sweden via Tycho (well-placed to procure Scandinavian game) to stock the Landgrave's menagerie at Kassel — Wilhelm's one surviving bull lacks a mate.
- ***Schuhe*** (in *anderthalben Schuhe hoch*) = "feet," the linear measure (singular *Schuh* ≈ 0.28–0.29 m in Hessian usage); *anderthalben* = "one and a half." The antler is described as "a foot and a half high"; the measure-word is kept as "foot/feet," not converted.
- **Negation count.** The letter carries the legally/factually load-bearing negations: *nicht vnderlassen* ("did not fail" — i.e. did despatch the courier, a double-negative affirmation, preserved as such); *das geringste nicht vernommen* ("heard not the least thing"); *keine Antwort* ("no answer"); *niergendt woran mangelt, alß daß* ("lacks nothing anywhere, save that"). Each is reproduced one-for-one; none added or dropped.
- ***vertröstung … vertröstete*** = "promise / promised" (*Vertröstung* "assurance, undertaking"); rendered as a promise/undertaking, not a modern "consolation."
- **Orthography (chancery German, 1592).** *jr/jm/jnen* = *ihr/ihm/ihnen*; *vns/vnserm/vnser* = *uns/unserm/unser*; *sider dem* = *seitdem* ("since then"); *vorm Jar* = *vor dem Jahr* / "the year before"; *albereit* = *bereit(s)* ("already"); *paren* = *paaren* ("to pair, mate"); *woferne* = "in case, if"; *vberschicken* = "send over"; *zukommên* prints with a tilde for the nasal (*zukommen*). The virgule (/) is the printed sentence-comma of the 1596 edition and is left in the source block.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datum … am 30. Iulij, Anno 1592* = "Given … on 30 July, 1592," **Old Style** (Hesse-Kassel, a Lutheran state, kept the Julian calendar in 1592). *Datum* "Given" rendered by this chapter's convention The in-letter back-reference *den 2. Aprilis* (the April courier) is likewise O.S. The edition **label** ("1592. 30. juli. Kassel") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy.
- **Edition.** Printed by Tycho himself in the *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Uraniborg, 1596), Liber I — the volume gathering the Hesse-Kassel correspondence; reprinted in Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VI. No manuscript witness is recorded in the edition.
- **Correction.** Restored the distinction between the letter's two elk shipments: 'vorm Jar' now reads 'a year ago' (not 'the year before last', which duplicated the letter's separate later phrase 'vor zweyen Jaren', 'two years ago').

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (medium). 'vorm Jar' (a year ago / last year) is rendered as 'the year before last', which collapses onto the letter's separate, distinctly-phrased 'vor zweyen Jaren' (two years ago) used one clause later for the surviving elk-bull; the original draws a clear one-year-ago vs. two-years-ago distinction between two different elk shipments that the translation blurs. At: “since the elk we obtained the year before last out of Sweden have all died”.

This cannot be verified against the edition of record and is flagged accordingly; the fix is limited to what is demonstrable from the letter's own internal evidence, by the audit's rule for a defect with no supplied extract.

documents.abstract: Lists errata in the controversy copy sent to Brahe and announces he will make his full reply, undeterred by Brahe's disciples or teachers.
documents.incipit: CLARISSIME D. TYCHO, in altero antilogiæ nostræ exemplarium, quæ ab eodem amanuensi …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO ET CLARISSIMO VIRO D. TYCHONI BRAHE HVENÆ INSULÆ DOMINO, MATHEMATICO LONGE PRÆSTANTISSIMO.

CLARISSIME D. TYCHO, in altero antilogiæ nostræ exemplarium, quæ ab eodem amanuensi descripta sunt, quorum primum ad te missum fuit, hæc errata reperiuntur: εδειξαι pro δεῖξαι. Ubi SCULTETI fit mentio, exprobas pro exprobras. Et cum artificium vestrum examinatur, ex his pro in his, ut in Cœlestibus: quæ si in tuo occurrant, vel similia, peto corrigas. Pro reliquis responsurus sum, nec discipulos tuos veriturus, imo ne præceptores tuos. Veritas et honestas mihi sufficient ad defensionem contra quoscunque. Et tamen, ut percurri obiter primum Tomum tuum, quamvis in multis a te dissentiam, cœpi potius tuam industriam et eximias virtutes admirari, quam illarum iniuriarum, quæ nec te nec me digna fuere, recordari. Clementissimus Deus cœptis tuis benigne faveat et ad optatum exitum perducat.

Datæ 5 Augusti Edinburgi.
IOAN. CRAIGIUS
Doctor Medicus.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most renowned man, Master Tycho Brahe, lord of the island of Hven, by far the most outstanding mathematician.**

Most renowned Master Tycho, in the second of the copies of our controversy [*antilogia*] — which were written out by the same amanuensis, the first of which was sent to you — the following errata are found: *εδειξαι* [*edeixai*] for *δεῖξαι* [*deîxai*]. Where mention is made of SCULTETUS, *exprobas* [you reproach] for *exprobras* [you reproach]. And where your method is examined, *ex his* [from these] for *in his* [in these], as in [the passage on] the Heavens: should these, or the like, occur in your [copy], I ask that you correct them. As for the rest, I shall make my reply, and I shall not stand in awe of your disciples — nay, not even of your teachers. Truth and honesty will suffice me for a defence against any whomsoever. And yet, having run through your first Tome cursorily, although I dissent from you in many things, I have begun rather to admire your industry and your exceptional merits than to call to mind those injuries which were worthy neither of you nor of me. May God most merciful graciously favour your undertakings and bring them to the wished-for end.

Given 5 August, at Edinburgh.
JOHN CRAIG,
Doctor of Medicine.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Ioan. Craigius, Doctor Medicus* = **John Craig** (d. 1620), the Scots Aristotelian physician then practising in Edinburgh; earlier professor of mathematics and logic at Frankfurt an der Oder, later royal physician to James VI, fellow of the London Royal College of Physicians (1604) and incorporated M.D. at Oxford (1605). Despite his court contacts, he was *not yet* a royal physician at the time of this exchange, and he never visited Denmark (Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*; *Tycho Brahe and Prague*, "The Dynamic of a Dispute," p. 75).
- **Recipient titulature.** *Hvenae insulae domino* — "lord of the island of **Hven**," Tycho's fief (granted by Frederik II in 1576); the seat of Uraniborg. *Mathematico longe praestantissimo* — the high astronomical compliment, kept formal.
- ***antilogia*** (Greek *ἀντιλογία*, "contradiction, controversy, debate-in-utramque-partem") — here the **controversy / point-by-point exchange** between Craig and Tycho. The substance was their epistolary dispute (1589–94) over Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (1588) on the **comet of 1577**: Craig, on Aristotelian grounds, rejected Tycho's parallax demonstration that the comet was a supralunary (aethereal) rather than a meteorological body, and objected to Tycho's fluid-heaven world-system that dispensed with solid celestial spheres. The term is left as **controversy** in the running text with the Greek-derived word flagged.
- ***amanuensis*** — a copyist/scribe; two fair copies of the controversy were made by the same hand, the first sent to Tycho, the second (the one Craig is now collating) retained by Craig, who lists the scribal *errata* by which the two diverge so that Tycho may bring his copy into agreement.
- **The errata list (a copy-collation, not a substantive argument).** Three scribal slips are corrected:
 - **Greek:** *εδειξαι* **for** *δεῖξαι*. The transmitted source prints the erroneous form **εδειξαι** (no accents) and the correct form **δεῖξαι** with circumflex; reproduced as printed by this chapter's convention *δεῖξαι* is the aorist active infinitive of *δείκνυμι*, "to show / to demonstrate / to prove" — the technical sense here (to *demonstrate* the comet's parallax). The faulty *εδειξαι* would be a malformed augmented form; the point is purely orthographic/scribal, so both forms are transliterated and glossed rather than emended into one.
 - *exprobas* **for** *exprobras* — at the mention of **Scultetus**. The intended word is *exprobras*, "you reproach / you cast in [his] teeth" (2nd person sing. of *exprobrare*); *exprobas* is the copyist's haplography (dropped *-r-*). Both forms carry the same sense ("you reproach"), so the English cannot show the difference; the **Latin pair is kept** to preserve the correction Craig is actually making.
 - *ex his* **for** *in his* — "from these" mistakenly written where "in these" is meant, "where your method is examined... as in [the passage on] the Heavens" (*ut in Coelestibus*). Again a one-preposition scribal slip; the Latin pair is retained.
- ***Sculteti*** (gen.) = **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (Bartholomew Schultz, 1540–1614), the Görlitz astronomer-mathematician and Tycho correspondent whose observations of the 1577 comet figured in Tycho's analysis in *De mundi* — hence a passage in the controversy where Tycho is said to "reproach" Scultetus.
- ***primum Tomum tuum*** — "your first Tome." The referent is the printed comet-volume Tycho had circulated (the 1588 *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis*, the second part of Tycho's larger *Progymnasmata* programme). Craig's "first Tome" is taken at face value as the volume he had received; whether it designates that volume's ordinal place in Tycho's scheme is not decided by the letter and is **not** silently reconciled here.
- ***nec discipulos tuos veriturus, imo ne praeceptores tuos*** — "I shall not stand in awe of your disciples — nay, not even of your teachers." The combative register (Craig promising a substantive *responsio* and disdaining intimidation) is preserved; *imo ne... quidem* force ("nay, not even") rendered without softening.
- **Negation check.** The letter contains two negations in the defiance sentence — *nec... veriturus* and *ne praeceptores* — and one in the concessive *quamvis in multis a te dissentiam* ("although I dissent from you in many things"); all three are reproduced, none added or dropped. The closing *quae nec te nec me digna fuere* carries a double *nec* ("worthy neither of you nor of me"), both retained.
- **Source-text artifact.** The working transcription (harvested CSV) carries a stray > immediately before *quam illarum iniuriarum*; this is a markup/extraction artifact, not a feature of the Dreyer text or the MS, and is omitted from the Source block. It does not affect the reading: *admirari... quam... recordari* ("admire... rather than... call to mind") is a straightforward *potius... quam* comparison.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datae 5 Augusti Edinburgi* = "Given 5 August, at **Edinburgh**." No year is given in the dateline; the year **1592** comes from the edition label and the Vienna MS context, not from the letter's own subscription — so it is **not** asserted in the header's date-as-written portion beyond what the document attests. Scotland under James VI used the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar, so the date is O.S. (catalogued "1592. 5. august. Edinburgh").

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter against TBOO VII pp.337-338 (read 336-339 to confirm boundaries: p.336-337 top belongs to a preceding Metellanus letter, p.339 opens a following Tycho-to-Metellanus letter). Latin matches the transcribed original exactly, word for word (long-s/ligature typography aside). Every proper name (Sculteti, Craig, Edinburgh), the errata list (Greek edeixai/deixai, exprobas/exprobras, ex his/in his), the date (5 August), and the closing sentiment are all rendered faithfully in the English. No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found.
