documents.incipit: PERPAUCIS abhinc mensibus, Nobilissime et amplissime vir, literas tuas, quibus nostris …

text.original:
MAGNIFICO ET AMPLISSIMO VIRO, EXΙΜΙΑ TAM GENERIS QUAM DOCTRINÆ NOBILITATE INPRIMIS CONSPICUO, DOMINO IOHANNI MÆTELANO, SERENISS. SCOTORUM REGIS CANCELLARIO, AMICO SUO PLURIMUM HONORANDO

PERPAUCIS abhinc mensibus, Nobilissime et amplissime vir, literas tuas, quibus nostris superiore hyeme ad te datis respondes, iam pridem accepi. Quæ quod genuinum non modo raræ, quæ in te est, eruditionis specimen, inprimisque Romani sermonis nitorem, sed iucundissimam humanitatis fragrantiam affatim redolerent, gratissimæ mihi fuerunt. Ex quo itaque tuæ illæ ad me perlatæ essent, avide semper desiderabam, ut certo aliquo fretus internuntio ijs nonnihil responderem. Sed cum eorum, per quos meas ad te transmittere in animo haberem, præter meam opinionem navigatio iam tandem præpeditur, indeque accideret ut responsio ad tuas in hoc usque tempus dilata sit, idcirco minime intermittendum duxi, quin cum mercatoribus, qui hinc ad vos appellunt, ante ingruentem brumam paucis rescriberetur, qualemcumque gratæ mentis et memoriæ significationem apud te testatam relinquerem, meque vicissim tui amantem declararem. Agnosco equidem non exigua benevolentiæ erga me tuæ extare indicia, præsertim dum eruditis et argutis tuis versibus effigiem, unâ cum Urania nostra (ut superiora tua in me officia tacitus præteream) eleganter ornare non degravatus sis. Quo sane nomine gratias tibi ago, agamque perpetuo maximas. Unicum tamen est, quod in his non tam desidero quam liberius et iusto abundantius dictum sentiam, in quo etiam nimium Poëtarum indulsisse licentiæ videris, idque nimirum per terna illa verba, quibus tria ultima concluseris Epigrammata. Quæ cum saltem Creatori immenso et ineffabili Creaturis nequaquam competant, ea cuipiam conditæ naturæ asscribere, quocunque dicendi tropo excusentur, inconveniens, imo piaculum censuerim. Quare si loco horum quippiam aliud substitueris, quod fragilis humanæ conditionis metas non transcendat, rectius meo iudicio feceris, mihique rem magis gratam præstiteris. En quanta hîc utar erga te audacia et parrhisia, quam ingenuus candor ille tuus nostraque amicitia non difficulter (uti spero) excusabunt. Habeo insuper gratias, quod D. IOHANNEM CRAIGUM Medicum vestratem, vel ob meam commendationem cariorem habueris atque ad optima quæque promovere receperis, utut is nuper arrogans quoddam contra nostra Placita Scriptum tertio demum ab Apologiæ illi transmissæ anno parturierit, quod affectato et insolenti nomine Capnuraniæ restinctionem (proh Dædaleum inauditarum hactenus vocum fabricatorem) appellare non erubuit. In quo se omnia quæ in libro nostro secundo de Novis Æthereis Phænomenis atque Apologia ipsi hoc nomine destinata continentur, refutare atque infirmare inverecunda præsumptione iactavit, cum tamen ne minimum quidem eorum, apud eos, qui rem ipsam penitius introspicientes, usu eandem debite exercere didicerunt, nec præiudicio cæco impediuntur, vel semel vacillare faciat. Longe igitur consultius fecisset enervis iste Cometarum (qui revera cœlestes sunt, nec flagrantes in aëre fumositates, ut ille in suum nimium credens, ac si in hunc baptizatus fuisset, ARISTOTELEM, commentus est) restinctor, si proprium opinionum suarum incendium et æstuantem animi ardorem ac inflammatos affectuum motus extinguere didicisset. Veritatis, quam tuemur, invictam arcem et firma huius propugnacula, obtusis hisce, quibus eam invadere conatur, argumentorum telis, non magis lædet aut expugnabit, quam si æneum et insuperabilem HERCULIS clypeum plumbea confodere sarissa præsumpserit. Nostra enim ille aut parum minusque recte intelligit, aut ob præoccupatas opiniones intelligere nolit, aut ea distrahit, depravat, invertit, male accommodat. Imo cavillatur et calumniatur fere ubique effreni quadam petulantia, adeo ut ne quidem a scommatis, dicterijs, nænijs, superciliosis oblocutionibus alijsque id generis inflati et impotentis animi pomposis ineptijs sibi temperet, deque ijs, quæ nunquam viderit aut fundamentaliter hauserit, nedum ut usu diuturno sibi familiaria reddiderit, iudicium immaturum et præposterum futili potius quam subtili acumine interponere non vereatur. Hem egregiam a CRAIGO vestrate pro tot annorum in hac palæstra veritatis inquirendæ stabiliendæque causa exantlatis laboribus, proque perassiduis vigilijs, studijs indefessis, sumptibus inæstimabilibus, reporto gratiam. Certe si non maiorem a cæteris Europæ eruditis Mathematicis consequutus fuero, aut ego frustra tot tantaque egerim (dummodo nihil aliud quam hominum gratitudinem et non potius solam veritatem, quæ sibiipsi sufficiens meritum est, spectarem) aut illi valde ingrati reputabuntur. At nemo est ex omnibus Italiæ, Galliæ, Angliæ, Germaniæ, Bohemiæ et Poloniæ Mathematicis, qui, quantum ego sciam, nostra non libere et libenter approbet, ijsque (utut Peripateticorum in Scholis usitata dogmata in quibusdam convellant) grata mentis significatione subscribat. Solus hic vester præ omnibus alijs sibi sapiens veritatem, quam in lucem ex inveteratis opinionum et errorum tenebris producere elaboramus, offuscare, ut sic, quemadmodum iste ex devastato Dianæ templo, nomen sibi quoddam comparet, anticipata quadam philautia et præsumptione non indecens reputavit; quasi is solus penitius rem introspiciat, quam cæteri omnes, et cornicum oculos configere valeat. Verum eiusmodi cothurnis et sophisticis contradictionibus, veritati a nobis assertæ frustra obstrepentibus, nihil in posterum nostra Urania respondere dignabitur, ne bonas horas altioribus solidioribusque tribuendas usqueadeo inutiliter collocet. Abblandiatur et placeat is sibi inque suo cerebello triumphet, quantum allubescit. Veritas certissimis et infallibilibus observationibus (quamvis et has dentata sua strigili rodere et turgido ac temerario ausu improbare nefas haud existimarit, utut tales et his merito conferendas assequi et imitari vix sustineat) fundata et certis demonstrationibus Geometricis (quas ille non minus, sive per inscitiam sive affectati iudicij temeritatem, malitiose sugillat) in apertum deducta imbelles non moratur oppugnantis insultus. Ne autem quis suspicetur, me, quod causæ diffidam, responsionem aversari, mittam Capnuranicas ipsius commentationes, vel potius commenta, ad præstantes quosdam in Germania Mathematicos, observationibus cœlestibus accurate instituendis assuetos et in hac materia solide versatos (cæteris enim parum ista intelligentibus, fucatis, quibus scatet, sophismatis, facile imposuerit CRAIGIUS vester ille) qui controversiam hanc exquisita scientia et diuturno usu, decernere nôrunt, et singulis ad æquam trutinam expensis, citra affectus et præiudicium ullum, iustam ferent censuram. Forte etiam prodibit suo tempore amicorum vel discipulorum meorum aliquis, qui hanc controversiam dirimere et ad invalidos Craigicarum obiectionum ictus retorquendos otium sibi sumat. Sicque tandem infringat solido propria delusus ab arte. In me equidem non amplius inveniet Antagonistam. Præstat enim Tomis nostris Progymnasmatum Astronomicorum (quos nunc præ manibus habeo) absolvendis operam locare, quam talibus affectatis obmurmurationibus retundendis inutiliter occupari. Quorum non solum primus (qui de Nova Stella ubertim agit) CRAIGI circa hanc quoque ignorantiam et crassa errata abunde patefaciet, sed et reliqui duo de quinque Cometis ex professo tractantes, eosque omnes cœlestes, citra omne dubium, fuisse apertissime demonstrantes, quam perperam et frustra CRAIGUS hic nostris assertionibus refragetur, cuivis luce Meridiana clarius ob oculos ponent. Hinc, si volet, suæ evidentissimæ hallucinationis, ignorantiæ et ineptitudinis redargutionem depromat, atque demum melius perspectis ijs, quibus seducitur, deviationibus, in veritatis semitam (modo id fieri queat) revertatur.

Quæ licet ita se habeant, et CRAIGUS in ultimo suo scripto non solum veritatis, sed et modestiæ limites multifariam transilierit, parumque ob benevolentiam in illo amando, Regique et tibi eum commendando, non gravatim a me præstitam, grati vicissim animi retulerit: tamen tantum abest ut ipsi ob id male cupiam, quin longe potius etiamnunc, imo multo plus quam antea tibi commendatum velim, quo tua auctoritate et intercessione illius res familiaris augeatur et subsidia ipsi studiorum Mathematicorum plenius rectiusque instituendorum largius suppeditentur, ut id quod aliquot iam annis theorice contemplatus est, per ipsam exercitationem in usu explorare, veritatemque latentem ipsa Praxi eruere commodius valeat. Quæcunque enim per Experientiam in Pragmatiam ratam transferri debeant, longe maiores requirunt impensas et studiorum nervos, quam quæ otiosa quadam speculatione animo concipiuntur. Quæ cum forte huic CRAIGO non ita abunde (prout res ipsa postulat) suppetant, adeo ut ne quidem ea quæ olim in Germania Instrumenta (quæ satis paratu vilia fuisse non dubito) se habuisse iactat, nunc ad manus illi sint, ideo de rebus ipsis opinione quadam propria vel auctoritate aliorum falsam persuasionem audentius fovet et abortivum ingenij factum excludit. Rebus itaque iuvandus, quo rerum medullas promptius capiat, nec inanibus saltem verborum corticibus se, alias nudum, oppalliet. Atque hæc de illo satis aut forte ad te alijs distentum nimia. Ego nihilominus ut hæc omnia benevole accipias et quod iusto plus Craigicis hisce, mihi sane parum, tibi (quemadmodum existimo) longe minus gratis mecum motis controversijs, in tuum sinum, suadente id amicitia nostra, deponendis immorer, teque gravioribus Reipub. administrandæ munijs intente occupatum diutius, quam par est, detineam, in potiorem partem pro tuo candore interpreteris, te etiam atque etiam rogatum habeo. Vale, et amicitiam nostram per literas continuare non intermitte. Ego vicissim nec locorum nec temporum iniuria vincar, quo minus tui memoriam firmiter animo retinere, et data occasione Epistolis ad te scribendis (cum aliter non detur) in mentem revocare, studiose enitar.

Iterum quam felicissime vale.
Datæ Uraniburgi 19. Augusti Anno 1592.
Magnif. tuæ studiosiss.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the magnificent and most eminent man, conspicuous above all for the exceptional nobility both of his birth and of his learning, Master John Maitland, Chancellor to the Most Serene King of the Scots, his friend to be most highly honoured.**

A very few months ago, most noble and eminent man, I received — though it was already some while back — your letter, in which you reply to the one I sent you last winter. And because it breathed forth in abundance not only a genuine specimen of the rare erudition that is in you, and above all the polish of the Roman tongue, but also the most delightful fragrance of humanity, it was most welcome to me. And so, from the moment your letter was brought to me, I always eagerly longed to reply to it somewhat, relying on some sure messenger. But since the sailing of those by whom I had it in mind to send my [letter] to you is now at last impeded, contrary to my expectation, and from this it came about that my reply to yours was put off until this very time, I therefore judged it by no means to be neglected that, with the merchants who put in here on their way to you, a few words at least should be written back before the onset of winter, so that I might leave with you some attestation, of whatever kind, of a grateful mind and memory, and declare myself in turn one who loves you. I acknowledge indeed that there exist no small tokens of your goodwill toward me, especially in that you did not think it beneath you elegantly to adorn, with your learned and witty verses, my portrait, together with our Urania (to pass over in silence your earlier services to me). For which, to be sure, I give you thanks, and shall give the greatest thanks for ever. Yet there is one thing in them which I do not so much miss as feel to have been said too freely and more lavishly than is right, and in which too you seem to have indulged the licence of the poets to excess — namely, by those three words with which you concluded the last three epigrams. Since these can in no way belong to creatures, but only to the immense and ineffable Creator, I should reckon it unfitting — nay, a sin to be expiated — to ascribe them to any created nature, by whatever figure of speech they be excused. Wherefore if in place of these you substitute something else, which does not overstep the bounds of frail human condition, you will, in my judgement, act more rightly, and render me a more agreeable service. See how great a boldness and frankness [parrhisia] I here employ toward you, which that ingenuous candour of yours and our friendship will (as I hope) not find it hard to excuse. I owe you thanks besides, that you have held Master John Craig, a physician of your country, the dearer even on account of my commendation, and have undertaken to advance him to all the best things — although he has lately, in the third year after the Apology was sent to him, brought forth a certain arrogant writing against our tenets, which he did not blush to call, by an affected and insolent name, the *Extinguishing of Capnurania* (alas, what a Daedalus, a fabricator of words unheard-of until now!). In which, with shameless presumption, he has boasted that he refutes and overthrows all that is contained in our second book *On the New Aethereal Phenomena* and in the Apology destined for him under this title — though he does not make even the least of those things waver so much as once, in the eyes of those who, peering more deeply into the matter itself, have learned to ply it duly by practice, and are not hampered by blind prejudice. Far more advisedly, then, would that feeble extinguisher of comets (which are in truth heavenly, and not blazing exhalations in the air, as he, trusting too much in his own Aristotle — as if he had been baptised into him — has imagined) have done, had he learned to extinguish the fire of his own opinions, and the seething heat of his mind, and the inflamed motions of his passions. The unconquered citadel of the truth which we defend, and its firm bulwarks, he will no more wound or storm with those blunt weapons of argument by which he tries to assail it, than if he should presume to pierce the bronze and insuperable shield of Hercules with a leaden pike. For our matters he either understands little and less than rightly, or, on account of his preoccupied opinions, refuses to understand, or else he distorts, corrupts, inverts, and misapplies them. Indeed he quibbles and slanders almost everywhere with a certain unbridled insolence, so that he does not even restrain himself from gibes, sarcasms, doggerel, supercilious revilings, and other pompous follies of that kind, [the marks] of a puffed-up and impotent mind; and concerning things he has never seen nor drawn in at their foundations — let alone made familiar to himself by long practice — he is not afraid to interpose a judgement immature and preposterous, with an acumen futile rather than subtle. Ha! a fine thanks I get from your countryman Craig for the labours drained over so many years in this wrestling-school of seeking out and establishing the truth, and for unremitting vigils, untiring studies, and inestimable expense! Surely, if I shall not have obtained a greater thanks from the rest of Europe's learned mathematicians, either I shall have done so many and so great things in vain (provided I were to look to nothing other than men's gratitude, and not rather to truth alone, which is a sufficient reward to itself), or they will be reckoned greatly ungrateful. But there is no one among all the mathematicians of Italy, France, England, Germany, Bohemia, and Poland who, so far as I know, does not freely and gladly approve our matters, and (however much in certain points they overturn the dogmas usual in the Peripatetics' schools) subscribe to them with a token of a grateful mind. This countryman of yours alone, wise in his own eyes above all others, has thought it not unbecoming — out of a certain anticipated self-love [philautia] and presumption — to becloud the truth which we labour to bring into the light out of the inveterate darkness of opinions and errors, so that thus, just as that man [did] from the devastated temple of Diana, he might procure for himself some name; as though he alone peered more deeply into the matter than all the rest, and were able to peck out the eyes of crows. But to contradictions of this sort — tragic bombast and sophistical, clamouring in vain against the truth we have asserted — our Urania will henceforth deign to make no reply, lest she so uselessly spend good hours that ought to be given to higher and more solid things. Let him flatter himself and please himself and triumph in his little brain as much as he likes. The truth, founded upon most certain and infallible observations (although he has not thought it impious to gnaw even these with his toothed scraper and to condemn them with swollen and rash daring, however much he could scarcely manage to attain and imitate such [observations], or others worthily to be compared with these), and brought into the open by sure geometrical demonstrations (which he no less maliciously belittles, whether through ignorance or the rashness of an affected judgement), does not heed the unwarlike assaults of its attacker. But lest anyone suspect that I shun a reply because I distrust my cause, I shall send his Capnuranic disquisitions — or rather fabrications — to certain distinguished mathematicians in Germany, accustomed to setting up celestial observations accurately and solidly versed in this subject matter (for upon others who understand these things but little, that Craig of yours might easily impose with the painted sophisms in which he abounds), men who know how to decide this controversy by exquisite knowledge and long practice, and who, weighing each point in a fair balance, apart from any passion and prejudice, will pass a just verdict. Perhaps too there will come forth in his own time some one of my friends or pupils who will take it upon himself, at leisure, to settle this controversy and to turn back the invalid blows of Craig's objections. And so at last let him, deluded by his own art, be broken against the solid [truth]. In me, indeed, he will find an antagonist no longer. For it is better to bestow my pains on finishing our volumes of the *Astronomical Preliminaries* (which I now have in hand) than to be uselessly occupied in beating back such affected mutterings. Of these volumes, not only will the first (which treats copiously of the New Star) abundantly lay open Craig's ignorance and gross errors in this matter too, but the remaining two — treating expressly of the five comets, and most plainly demonstrating that all of them, beyond all doubt, were heavenly — will set before anyone's eyes, more clearly than the noonday light, how wrongly and vainly Craig here opposes our assertions. Hence let him, if he will, draw out the refutation of his most evident hallucination, ignorance, and ineptitude; and at length, having better discerned the deviations by which he is led astray, let him return into the path of truth (if only it can be done).

Though things stand thus, and Craig in his last writing has in many ways overleapt the bounds not only of truth but also of modesty, and has shown a grateful mind but little in return for the goodwill — bestowed by me not grudgingly — in befriending him and commending him to the King and to you: yet so far am I from wishing him ill on that account, that I would rather far more even now — nay, much more than before — have him commended to you, so that by your authority and intercession his household estate may be increased, and the means of pursuing mathematical studies more fully and rightly may be more liberally supplied to him, so that what he has now for some years contemplated in theory he may the more conveniently test in use through practice itself, and bring out the hidden truth by Practice itself. For whatever things must be carried over from Experience into established Practice require far greater expense and sinews of study than those that are conceived in the mind by a certain idle speculation. And since these things perhaps are not so abundantly at this Craig's command (as the matter itself requires) — so much so that not even those Instruments which he boasts of having once had in Germany (instruments which I do not doubt were cheap enough to procure) are now at his hand — he therefore the more boldly fosters a false persuasion about the matters themselves, whether from some opinion of his own or by the authority of others, and shuts out the miscarried product of his talent. He must therefore be helped with resources, so that he may more readily grasp the marrow of things, and not, being otherwise naked, cloak himself merely with the empty husks of words. And this about him is enough — or perhaps too much for you, distracted by other matters. I nonetheless beg you, again and again, to take all this kindly, and to interpret in the better part, according to your candour, the fact that I dwell more than is right on these Craigic controversies — stirred up against me, indeed, to my small profit and (as I think) far less to your liking — controversies to be laid into your bosom at the prompting of our friendship; and that I detain you, intently occupied with the weightier offices of administering the commonwealth, longer than is fitting. Farewell, and do not cease to continue our friendship by letters. I in turn shall not be overcome by the injury of places or of times, but shall strive zealously to keep your memory firmly in mind, and, when occasion is given, to recall it by writing letters to you (since otherwise it is not granted).

Again, may you fare most happily.
Given at Uraniborg, 19 August, the year 1592.
Most devoted to Your Magnificence,
Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Iohannes Maetelanus* = **John Maitland of Thirlestane** (c. 1543–1595), Lord Chancellor of Scotland under James VI from 1587, and a Latin poet of some accomplishment. He had visited (or been associated with) Tycho's circle during the 1590 royal connections between Scotland and Denmark (James VI's marriage to Anne of Denmark; the Scottish party's contact with Hven). Maitland had written commendatory verses on a portrait of Tycho and on "our Urania" (see below).
- **Subject of dispute.** *D. Iohannes Craigus, Medicus vestratem* = **John Craig** (d. 1620), Scottish physician and Aristotelian (later physician to James VI), an Edinburgh-trained Paduan graduate who maintained — against Tycho — the Aristotelian doctrine that comets are sublunary atmospheric exhalations, not celestial bodies. The exchange ran 1588–1592: Tycho sent Craig his second book *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (the *Novis Aethereis Phaenomenis* named here) and an *Apologia* (1589, never printed); Craig replied in March 1592, in manuscript, with the polemic Tycho here mocks.
- ***Capnuraniae restinctio*** — Craig's manuscript tract, fully *Capnuraniae restinctio, seu cometarum in aethera sublimationis refutatio* ("The Extinguishing of Capnurania, or a refutation of the raising-up of comets into the aether"). *Capnurania* is Craig's coinage from Greek *kapnós* (καπνός, "smoke") + *Urania*, i.e. "smoky-Urania" — a jeer that Tycho's celestial astronomy is built on (cometary) smoke. Tycho calls Craig a *Daedalum … vocum fabricatorem*, "a Daedalus, a fabricator of words," mocking the neologism. Rendered "the *Extinguishing of Capnurania*"; the wordplay is flagged, not flattened.
- **Greek loan-words in the Latin.** *parrhisia* (παρρησία, "frank speech, candour") — kept and glossed "frankness [parrhisia]." *philautia* (φιλαυτία, "self-love") — kept and glossed "self-love [philautia]." Both are common in humanist Latin; no Greek script appears in the body.
- ***ex devastato Dianae templo … nomen sibi … comparet*** — "from the devastated temple of Diana … procure for himself some name." A pointed allusion to **Herostratus**, who burned the Temple of Artemis (Diana) at Ephesus in 356 BC precisely to make his name immortal. Tycho casts Craig as a man seeking fame by an act of destruction. Kept as allusion and identified here.
- ***cornicum oculos configere*** — "to peck out the eyes of crows," a proverbial phrase (cf. Cicero, *Pro Murena* 25) for outwitting the most cunning; ironic here. Kept as idiom.
- ***aeneum … Herculis clypeum plumbea … sarissa*** — "the bronze shield of Hercules [pierced] with a leaden pike"; a *sarissa* is the long Macedonian pike. The futility-image is kept literal.
- ***cothurnis*** — the *cothurnus* is the high boot of tragic actors; metonymic for inflated, tragic-style bombast. Rendered "tragic bombast."
- ***dentata sua strigili rodere*** — "gnaw with his toothed scraper"; a *strigilis* is the bather's scraper. The metaphor of corrosive carping is kept literal.
- **Astronomy / the works named.** *libro nostro secundo de Novis Aethereis Phaenomenis* = Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (Uraniborg, 1588), the second book of his planned trilogy, arguing the comet of 1577 was supralunary. *Tomis nostris Progymnasmatum Astronomicorum* = the *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* (the "Astronomical Preliminaries"; *Progymnasmata* lit. "preliminary exercises," kept by sense as *Astronomical Preliminaries*), whose **first** volume "treats copiously of the New Star" (the 1572 nova, *De nova stella*) and whose projected further volumes were to treat the **five comets**. The translation preserves Tycho's claim that all five comets *citra omne dubium … coelestes … fuisse* ("were, beyond all doubt, heavenly") as his own assertion, with the hedge *citra omne dubium* kept as written.
- ***Apologiae illi transmissae anno … tertio*** — "in the third year after the Apology was sent to him." Tycho dates Craig's polemic to the third year after the (1589) *Apologia* was transmitted, i.e. 1591/92; the manuscript reached Tycho in spring 1592 (so Norlind, after Dreyer VII). Reported, not silently reconciled with the catalogue year.
- ***Urania nostra*** — "our Urania," the Muse of astronomy, figuring both Tycho's science and (in the portrait passage) the personified frontispiece-figure of his published astronomy; Maitland's commendatory verses had honoured her. Kept as "Urania."
- **Theological scruple.** The *terna illa verba* ("those three words") with which Maitland's last three epigrams closed are not quoted in the letter; Tycho objects that they ascribe to a creature (*conditae naturae*) what belongs only to the *Creator immenso et ineffabili* — a *piaculum* ("a sin to be expiated"). The specific words are a **crux**: the source does not name them, so the exact phrasing Tycho found impious cannot be recovered from this text alone.
- **Negations checked.** The clauses of praise-with-reservation were translated counting the negations: *non … desidero quam … sentiam* ("I do not so much miss … as feel"); *non degravatus sis* ("you did not think it beneath you"); *non erubuit* ("he did not blush"); *ne minimum quidem … vel semel vacillare faciat* ("he does not make even the least … waver so much as once"); *non amplius inveniet Antagonistam* ("he will find an antagonist no longer"); *tantum abest ut … male cupiam, quin … commendatum velim* ("so far am I from wishing him ill … that I would rather … have him commended") — the *tantum abest ut … quin* construction is reproduced with its full reversing force, not flattened.
- **Dateline / calendar.** *Datae Uraniburgi 19. Augusti Anno 1592* = "Given at **Uraniborg** (on Hven), 19 August 1592." Denmark used the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar in 1592, so the date is O.S.; this agrees with the edition label (*1592. 19. august. Uraniborg*). No internal date discrepancy.
- **Edition / witness.** Edition of record: *Tychonis Brahei et ad eum doctorum virorum epistolae ab anno 1588* (= Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VII, pp. 334 ff.). MS witness as given in the source header: A = Vienna, ÖNB, cod. Vindob. lat. 9737f.

text.original:
ILLVSTRISSIMO PRINCIPI AC DOMINO, DOMINO WILHELMO, LANDTGRAVIO HASSIÆ, COMITI IN CATZENELLEBOGEN, DIETZ, ZIGENHAIN ET NIDDA: PRINCIPI AC DOMINO CLEMENTISSIMO. S. D.

LITERAS Celsit. tuæ, Illustrissime Princeps, circa Aprilis auspicia per proprium Tabellarium ad me destinatas iuxta proxime sequentis Mensis initia recte accepi. In quibus Alces quasdam Noruegicas C. T. antea a me promissas, ad se e vestigio transmitti desiderat. Accidit autem, vt ijsdem pene diebus Consanguinei mei Nobilissimi viri AXILLI GVLDENSTERN Regij in Noruegia Vicarij literæ vna ad me perlatæ sint, quibus conquerebatur se Nauclerum, qui bestias istas incolumes et illæsas huc transferre in se recipere vellet, offendere illic neminem. Idcirco in animo se habere scribebat, possentne terrestri huc itinere perduci, periculum fieri curare. Scripsi nihilominus eidem AXILLO semel atque iterum, iamque antea mihi factas pollicitationes illi in memoriam reuocaui. Verum is neque terrenis locis, conuallibus vndique inuijs, et confragosis rupibus armentis illis transitum difficiliorem reddentibus, tuto et certo adduci posse respondebat. Et licet id fieri concederetur: neutiquam tamen negotium hoc ob æstiuum Solis ardorem, et antequam Caniculares præterijssent feruores (quos id genus animantium in peregrinis a natiuo solo terris, primo ingressu haud facile sustinet) optatos habiturum successus sperabat. Qua de re se quamprimum profectione in Daniam tum temporis institutâ plenius hîc mecum communicaturum recepit. Atque hinc contigit, vt dum indies vel ipsius Proregis ad nos aduentum auide expectarem, vel animalium istorum copiam nobis interea fieri posse confiderem, C. T. Tabellarium diutius hîc apud me detinere necesse habuerim, donec certi aliquid hâc de re mihi constaret. Nec enim sine Alcibus illis ad T. C. remittendum duxi, præsertim cum is indicârit, sibi iniunctum fuisse, vt non absque his rediret. Sed quamuis prædictus hic AXILLVS expectatione nostra serius, vtpote circa Mensis huius ingressum, huc aduentârit; Peropportune tamen accidit, vt ad idem fere tempus, quo alter T. C. nuntius, posteriores literas de eadem re me commonefacientes asportârit, AXILLVS e Noruegia huc primum appelleret, meque in hac Insula mox inuiseret. Confestim itaque cum ipso de Alcibus dudum promissis, sedulo egi. Verum is difficultates non paucas, quo minus terrâ mariue integra huc valetudine perduci queant, obijciebat, curque hactenus eas mittere non licuerit, causas edidit. At ego instabam, recentiorem illum C. T. nuncium, qui iampridem accedebat, quemadmodum Feræ eiusmodi e longinquis adduci debeant, satis callere: siquidem prius e Suecia aliquot tales T. C. indemnes attulerit. Protinus itaque duobus Nobilibus, quibus Arcem et Prouinciam, cui in Noruegia præest, se absente commiserat, per literas mandauit, vt quinque Alces, quas hinc inde in mei gratiam conquisierat, atque in varijs locis alendas (donec inde commode huc transferri possent) disposuerat, eidem nuncio vna cum alimentis cæterisque rebus necessarijs diligenter et sine mora procurarent. Is proinde acceptis hisce literis, vna cum libero a me commeatu in Noruegiam iter accelerat, vt obtentis ibi quinis hisce Alcibus, ijsdemque in nauem impositis, recta Bremam traijciat, atque hinc terrestri passu desiderata iam diu animalia ad T. C. qua poterit, cura et sedulitate perducat. Quod si singula sana et viuida istic sistere concessum fuerit, non dubito, quin T. C. petitioni, adeoque diutinæ expectationi, iam tandem, quantum in nobis erat, satisfecerimus. Retulit autem Consanguineus ille meus, cum hîc præsto esset, vnam inter istas quas habet Alces satis grandæuam, eandemque masculam esse: reliquas vero quatuor iuniores partim masculas, partim fæmellas. At quotquot et qualescunque fuerint, vt C. T. has boni consulere, atque moram hanc, qua tota pene æstate responsio hæc dilata sit, ob antedictas causas excusatam habere dignetur, demisse etiam atque etiam rogo: nec Tabellario primum amandato, quod tam diu hîc hæserit, succensere velit. Si qua alia in re T. C. in hisce oris mea qualicunque opella, quod eidem gratum acceptumque fuerit, quippiam præstari queat, inueniet me vbique et in omnibus quam promptissimum. De Astronomicis nostris exercitijs nunc nihil dicam. Quid in his moliar T. C. alias data occasione intelliget. Id saltem addam, me non libenter ex hoc vltimo T. C. Grammatophoro percepisse, ROTHMANNVM necdum redijsse, Tuæque Celsitud. Instrumenta Astronomica interea a Cœlestium considerationibus prorsus feriari. Ideoque quam maxime optarem, vt C. T. alium quendam harum rerum peritum, in ipsius locum substitui curet, qui inchoatam telam rite pertexat, et Obseruationibus sedulo continuandis deinceps inuigilet. Sed meum non est T. C. quippiam præscribere, præsertim cum naturali quadam propensitate et singulari fauore ad hæc studia amplianda et promouenda, non sine præclara laude, feratur. DEVS T. C. ad omne bonum opus exequendum, quam diutissime conseruet incolumem.

Iamque T. C. quam felicissime valeat.

Datæ Vraniburgi, 20. Septemb. Anno 1592.

Celsit. T. Addictiss.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the Most Illustrious Prince and Lord, Lord Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, Count in Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda: a most gracious Prince and Lord. Greeting.**

Your Highness's letter, Most Illustrious Prince, dispatched to me by your own courier about the beginning of April, I duly received toward the beginning of the next month. In it Your Highness desires that certain Norwegian elk [Alces], earlier promised to you by me, be conveyed to you forthwith. But it happened that on almost those same days a letter from my most noble kinsman, Master Axel Gyldenstierne, the King's Governor in Norway, was brought to me together with it, in which he complained that he could find no skipper there who would undertake to bring those beasts here unharmed and unhurt. He therefore wrote that he had it in mind to make trial of whether they could be brought here by an overland route. None the less I wrote to that same Axel once and again, and recalled to his memory the promises that had earlier been made to me. But he replied that they could not safely and surely be brought, since the land places too — valleys impassable on every side, and rugged crags — made the passage harder for those herds. And even were it granted that this be done, he still did not hope that the business would have the wished-for success on account of the summer heat of the Sun and before the dog-day fervours had passed (which a creature of that kind, in lands foreign to its native soil, does not easily endure at its first arrival). On this matter he undertook that, on the journey into Denmark which he had then arranged for the time, he would communicate with me here more fully. And hence it came about that, while day by day I was eagerly awaiting either the Viceroy's own arrival to us, or trusting that in the meantime a supply of those animals might be procured for us, I was obliged to detain Your Highness's courier here with me longer, until something certain about this matter should be settled for me. For I did not think it right to send him back to Your Highness without those elk, especially since he indicated that it had been enjoined upon him that he should not return without them. But although the aforesaid Axel arrived here later than we expected — namely about the beginning of this month — yet it fell out very opportunely that at almost the same time at which Your Highness's other messenger brought a further letter reminding me of the same matter, Axel first put in here from Norway and soon visited me on this Island. Forthwith, therefore, I dealt diligently with him about the elk long since promised. But he raised not a few difficulties as to their being brought here by land or sea in sound condition, and set forth the reasons why hitherto it had not been possible to send them. Yet I pressed him, [arguing] that that more recent messenger of Your Highness, who had now for some time been arriving, was well enough skilled in how wild beasts of that kind ought to be brought from afar — seeing that he had earlier brought some such [beasts] from Sweden to Your Highness unharmed. So at once he gave order by letter to the two noblemen to whom, in his absence, he had committed the castle and the province over which he presides in Norway, that they should diligently and without delay furnish to that same messenger, together with fodder and the other necessary things, five elk which he had sought out here and there for my sake and had distributed in various places to be fed (until they could conveniently be brought hither from there). He accordingly, having received these letters, together with a free safe-conduct from me, hastens his journey into Norway, so that, once these five elk have been obtained there and put aboard ship, he may cross straight to Bremen, and thence by land bring the animals so long desired to Your Highness with what care and diligence he can. And if it be granted that he set them down there each one sound and lively, I do not doubt that we shall now at last, so far as in us lay, have satisfied Your Highness's request, and indeed your long expectation. That kinsman of mine, moreover, reported, when he was present here, that one among those elk which he has is of fair age and is a male; but the other four, being younger, are partly males, partly females. But however many and of whatever kind they prove to be, I most humbly beg, again and again, that Your Highness may deign to take these in good part, and to hold this delay — by which this reply has been put off almost the whole summer — excused for the aforesaid reasons; nor be angry at the courier first sent off, that he has lingered here so long. If in any other matter, on these shores, anything can be rendered to Your Highness by my poor service of whatever sort, that may be welcome and acceptable to you, you will find me everywhere and in all things most ready. Of our astronomical exercises I shall now say nothing. What I am setting in hand in these matters Your Highness shall learn on another occasion as opportunity is given. This much only I shall add: that I have learned, not gladly, from this last letter-bearer of Your Highness, that Rothmann has not yet returned, and that Your Highness's astronomical instruments meanwhile lie wholly idle from the observation of the heavens. And therefore I could most greatly wish that Your Highness would see to it that some other man skilled in these matters be put in his place, who may duly finish the web once begun, and may henceforth keep watch over the observations to be diligently continued. But it is not for me to prescribe anything to Your Highness, especially since by a certain natural inclination and singular favour you are borne toward the enlarging and advancing of these studies, not without distinguished praise. May GOD preserve Your Highness unharmed, for the carrying out of every good work, as long as may be.

And now may Your Highness fare most happily.

Given at Uraniborg, 20 September, in the year 1592.

Most devoted to Your Highness,
TYCHO BRAHE.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** Addressed to **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), the astronomer-prince of Kassel, Tycho's chief princely scientific correspondent. The full titulature — *Comiti in Catzenellebogen, Dietz, Zigenhain et Nidda* = Count in Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda — is the standard Hessian style, preserved by this chapter's convention Wilhelm died on 25 August 1592 (N.S.), shortly before this letter was written (20 September O.S.); Tycho on Hven would not yet have known of his death.
- **Sender / place.** **Tycho Brahe** at **Uraniborg** on Hven (*Vraniburgi*, this chapter's convention).
- **Axel Gyldenstierne** (*Axillus / Axillo Guldenstern*, here in the genitive/dative; d. 1603) — Danish nobleman, **royal governor (statholder) of Norway** 1588–1601. Tycho calls him *Consanguineus meus* ("my kinsman") — the Brahe and Gyldenstierne families were connected by marriage. The terms *Regius in Noruegia Vicarius*, *Prorex* ("Viceroy"), and the phrase *Arcem et Prouinciam, cui in Noruegia praeest* ("the castle and province over which he presides in Norway") all denote this governorship (his seat was Akershus, Oslo).
- ***Alces*** — **elk** (European elk / moose, *Alces alces*). The letter is the principal document of Wilhelm IV's standing request, fulfilled through Tycho, for live Norwegian elk; the famous (later) story of one of Tycho's own elk dying after drinking beer and falling down stairs at Landskrona belongs to a separate, later episode and is **not** in this letter — not imported here.
- ***Caniculares … feruores*** — "the dog-day fervours," the *dies caniculares*, the hottest part of summer associated with the heliacal rising of the Dog Star (Sirius/Canicula); rendered idiomatically with the dog-day sense kept.
- ***Christophorus Rothmannus*** (*ROTHMANNVM*) — **Christoph Rothmann**, Wilhelm IV's mathematician at Kassel, who had left Kassel in 1590 (travelling to visit Tycho on Hven) and had not resumed his post. Tycho's remark that the Kassel *Instrumenta Astronomica … a Coelestium considerationibus prorsus feriari* ("the astronomical instruments lie wholly idle from the observation of the heavens") urges the Landgrave to appoint a successor observer — a request whose timing is poignant, the Landgrave being already dead.
- ***inchoatam telam rite pertexat*** — "duly finish the web once begun": a weaving metaphor (Penelope's *tela*) for completing the unfinished programme of Kassel observations; kept as metaphor.
- **Astronomy.** *Astronomica nostra exercitia* = "our astronomical exercises"; *Instrumenta Astronomica* = "astronomical instruments"; *Coelestium considerationibus* = "the observation of the heavens." No technical terms beyond these general ones occur — this is a logistical letter about livestock, not an observational report.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S. D.* = *salutem dicit*, "sends greeting"; *Celsit. tuae / C. T. / T. C.* = *Celsitudo tua*, "Your Highness"; *valeat … quam felicissime* = "may [Your Highness] fare most happily"; *Celsit. T. Addictiss.* = *Celsitudini Tuae addictissimus*, "Most devoted to Your Highness."
- ***Tabellarius / nuntius / Grammatophorus*** — three words for the messenger/letter-carrier: *Tabellarius* ("courier"), *nuntius* ("messenger"), and the Greek-derived *Grammatophorus* (γραμματοφόρος, "letter-bearer"); the variation is the author's, preserved by varying the English.
- ***libero … commeatu*** — "a free safe-conduct" (a *commeatus*, pass/permit for travel), here issued by Tycho to the messenger; rendered "safe-conduct."
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Datae Vraniburgi, 20. Septemb. Anno 1592* = "Given at Uraniborg, 20 September 1592" — **Old Style** (Denmark used the Julian calendar until 1700; this chapter's convention). The catalogue label ("1592. 20. september. Uraniborg") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy. Note that Wilhelm IV's death (25 August 1592) is reckoned **New Style** in Imperial/Hessian usage; the two styles are not reconciled here, only flagged.
- **Source-text note (editorial sigla stripped).** The working transcription carries scattered superscript-*A* markers (apparatus/variant sigla from the harvested edition — e.g. *promissas^A*, *literae^A*, *scribebat^A*) and several run-together word-joins (e.g. *DOMINOA CLEMENTISSIMO*, *S. D.ALITERAS*). These are not part of the letter text; they have been removed and the affected words restored to their plain forms in the Source block above, and the salutation/body and the subscription split onto their own lines. No lexical reading was altered. The edition of record is the **1596 *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri*** (the volume Tycho printed at Uraniborg; reprinted in Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VI), per the source's edition field. No MS witness is recorded for this letter in the edition.

documents.incipit: ILLVSTRISSIME et Generosissime Princeps: Plurimâ equidem T. C. me læticiâ affecit, dum …

text.original:
ILLVSTRISSIMO PRINCIPI AC DOMINO, DOMINO MAVRITIO, LANDTGRAVIO HASSIÆ, COMITI IN CATZENELLEBOGEN, DIETZ, ZIGENHAIN ET NIDDA: PRINCIPI AC DOMINO CLEMENTISSIMO. S. D.

ILLVSTRISSIME et Generosissime Princeps: Plurimâ equidem T. C. me læticiâ affecit, dum non modo Literis suis clementer nostris respondere: Sed et Carmen commendatitium in Opera, quæ molimur, Astronomica, scite et eleganter concinnare, proprijsque digitis circa frontispicia chartæ transmissæ consignare, non dedignata sit. Pro qua etiam clementi erga me, meaque studia affectione gratias T. C. demisse ago, quas possum, maximas. Exhibebunt utique versus illi clarissimum T. C. erga tam sublimes Artes et me etiam favoris et benevolentiæ Τεκμήριον, Posteritati in auspicijs meorum Operum Astronomicorum iugi memoria consecrandum: mihi vero devotæ erga T. C. observantiæ μνημοσὺνον nulla oblivione interiturum suppeditabit. Cur autem non antea T. C. hoc nomine rescripserim, et quare Tabellarium hunc tam diu hîc detinuerim, caussas in Literis ad Illustrissimum T. C. Dominum Parentem datis, luculenter exposui. Quin et antea idem per Præstantis. et Eruditis. Virum Doctorem NICOLAVM THEOPHILVM, nunc in Academia Hafniensi Iuris Professorem, olim T. C. Parenti in Cancelliæ negotijs operam nauantem, indicare animus erat: Quo etiam nomine ad ipsum perscripseram. Verum intellexi postea, ob aduersam valetudinem iter eius, quod in HASSIAM adornârat, præpeditum fuisse. Præter voluntatem igitur meam accidit, quod adeo tarde tam Illustrissimi Parentis, quam T. C. Literis nunc respondeatur. Quam moram ut C. T. clementi animo in potiorem partem accipiat, atque excusatam habere velit, etiam atque etiam submisse rogo. Nec ulterius T. C. impolitis hisce meis literulis, alijs forte intentam, gravabo. Verum C. T. Deo Opt. Maximo, quam plurimum commendatam cupio. Is C. T. vitam et actiones in vestigia Paternarum virtutum dirigat, et ad Reipub. emolumentum feliciter disponat.

Vale.

Datæ Vraniburgj, 21. Septemb. Anno 1592.

Celsit. T. Addictis.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the Most Illustrious Prince and Lord, Lord Moritz, Landgrave of Hesse, Count in Catzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda: a Most Clement Prince and Lord. [He] sends greeting.**

Most Illustrious and Most Noble Prince: Your Highness has indeed filled me with the greatest joy, in that you have not disdained not only graciously to reply to my letters, but also skilfully and elegantly to compose a commendatory poem upon the astronomical works which we are undertaking, and to sign it with your own hand about the title-page of the sheet sent [to me]. For this clement regard toward me and toward my studies I humbly render Your Highness the greatest thanks I can. Those verses will assuredly furnish, to posterity, a token [Τεκμήριον] — to be consecrated in lasting remembrance at the very outset of my astronomical works — of Your Highness's most illustrious favour and goodwill toward such lofty arts and toward me as well; and to me, in truth, they will supply a memorial [μνημοσὺνον] of my devoted respect toward Your Highness, one that shall perish by no forgetting. But why I did not write back to Your Highness on this account before now, and why I have kept this courier here so long, I have set forth clearly in the letter given to Your Highness's Most Illustrious Lord Father. Indeed, before this, it had been my mind to make the same known through the most excellent and most learned man, Doctor Nicolaus Theophilus — now Professor of Law in the University of Copenhagen, formerly busying himself in chancery affairs for Your Highness's Father — and on that account I had written to him as well. But I learned afterward that, owing to ill health, his journey, which he had arranged into Hesse, had been hindered. It has therefore happened against my will that a reply is being made only now, and so tardily, both to the Most Illustrious Father's and to Your Highness's letters. That Your Highness may take this delay, with a clement mind, in the better part, and be willing to hold it excused, I most submissively beg again and again. Nor shall I burden Your Highness any further with these unpolished little letters of mine, your attention being perhaps bent on other things. But I desire that Your Highness be most fully commended to God, Best and Greatest. May He direct Your Highness's life and deeds into the footsteps of your Father's virtues, and dispose them happily for the good of the commonwealth.

Farewell.

Given at Uraniborg, 21 September, the year 1592.

Devoted to Your Highness,
TYCHO BRAHE.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe**, writing from Uraniborg on Hven. The letter was later printed by Tycho himself in his *Epistolarum astronomicarum liber primus* (Uraniborg, 1596), the volume that is the edition of record here; Dreyer reprints it in *Opera Omnia* VI.
- **Recipient.** *Mauritio, Landtgravio Hassiae* = **Moritz "the Learned," Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1572–1632), who had succeeded his father **Wilhelm IV** on the latter's death on 25 August 1592. The salutation's territorial style — *Comiti in Catzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain et Nidda* — is the standard Hessian comital titulature; place-names kept in their period form with modern spellings given (Katzenelnbogen, Diez, Ziegenhain, Nidda).
- **"Dominum Parentem" / "Paternarum virtutum."** The letter twice invokes Moritz's *father*. This is the diplomatic crux of the dating (see **Calendar / crux** below): Tycho writes *as though Wilhelm IV were still living* — he says he had set out his reasons "in the letter given to Your Highness's Most Illustrious Lord Father," and closes praying that Moritz follow "the footsteps of your Father's virtues."
- ***Carmen commendatitium … proprijsque digitis … consignare.*** Moritz had written a **commendatory poem** for Tycho's projected astronomical works and signed it in his own hand about the title-page (*frontispicia*) of the sheet sent to Tycho. *Carmen commendatitium* rendered "commendatory poem"; *frontispicia* = the title-page / frontispiece region of the sheet.
- ***Opera … Astronomica, quae molimur.*** "the astronomical works which we are undertaking" — Tycho's planned publications (the *instauratio astronomiae* programme); *Opera* kept as "works," not narrowed to a single title.
- **Greek.** *Τεκμήριον* (*tekmḗrion*) = "a sure token, proof, attestation"; rendered **"a token"** (of favour). *μνημοσὺνον* (printed thus; classical *μνημόσυνον*, *mnēmósynon*) = "a memorial, remembrance, keepsake"; rendered **"a memorial."** Both Greek nouns are transcribed in the source block as printed and glossed here by this chapter's convention The accentuation *μνημοσὺνον* (grave on the antepenult-area) is the 1596 print's own; not normalised.
- ***Nicolaus Theophilus, nunc in Academia Hafniensi Iuris Professorem, olim T. C. Parenti in Cancelliae negotijs operam nauantem.*** The Latinised **Nicolaus Theophilus**, then **Professor of Law at the University of Copenhagen** and formerly active in the chancery service of Moritz's father (Wilhelm IV). Tycho had meant to route his reply through him, but Theophilus's planned journey into Hesse was stopped by ill health. *Crux (identity):* the precise Danish/vernacular form of "Nicolaus Theophilus" is not securely established from the present text alone; the man is identified only by office and prior service and is so left, rather than asserting a vernacular name the source does not give. *Cancelliae* is the print's spelling for *Cancellariae* ("chancery"); *operam nauantem* = *navantem*, "devoting effort, busying himself."
- ***Tabellarium hunc … detinuerim.*** *Tabellarius* = **courier / letter-carrier**; Tycho apologises for having detained Moritz's courier so long at Hven.
- **Negation / sense check.** *non modo … respondere, sed et … concinnare … non dedignata sit* = "you have **not** disdained **not only** to reply … **but also** to compose …" — the two negatives belong to distinct clauses (*non modo* "not only" + *non dedignata sit* "did not disdain"); the net force is affirmative courtesy ("you graciously deigned to do both"), and is so rendered, with no negation added or dropped. *nulla oblivione interiturum* = "destined to perish **by no** forgetting," i.e. that will never be forgotten — the single litotes is preserved as the emphatic positive it is, not flattened to a bare "lasting."
- **Honorifics.** *S. D.* = *salutem dicit*, "sends greeting". *T. C.* / *C. T.* = *Tua Celsitudo* / *Celsitudo Tua*, "Your Highness," used interchangeably through the letter; rendered uniformly "Your Highness." *Celsit. T. Addictis.* (subscription) = *Celsitudini Tuae Addictissimus*, "Most devoted to Your Highness." *Deo Opt. Maximo* = "to God, Best and Greatest."
- **Orthography (Neo-Latin print, 1596).** *laeticiâ* for *laetitiâ*; *caussas* for *causas*; *proprijsque, negotijs, alijs, auspicijs* with consonantal *-ij-*; *adornârat* = *adornaverat* (contracted); *Reipub.* = *Reipublicae*; *Vraniburgj / Datae* for *Uraniburgi / Datae*. *e*-caudata printed as *HASSIAe / LANDTGRAVIO HASSIAe* retained.
- **Textual note (extraction artifact).** The working transcription carries a stray capital **"A"** interpolated at numerous word-boundaries (e.g. *LANDTGRAVIO**A** HASSIAe*, *DOMINO**A** CLEMENTISSIMO*, *Exhibebunt**A** … illi**A***, *Τεκμήριον**A***, *μνημοσὺνον**A***, *Virum**A***, *nauantem**A***, *nunc**A***, *cupio**A***, *BRAHE.**A***). These are not letters of the source: they fall at points carrying no Latin sense and recur mechanically. They are read as an digitised text layer/encoding artifact (most likely Dreyer's apparatus reference-marks or a footnote-anchor glyph mis-decoded as "A") and have been **removed** from the Source block to give the readable Latin; the decision is logged here by this chapter's convention rather than reproducing the noise as printed. None affects the sense of any clause.
- **Calendar / crux.** Dateline *Datae Vraniburgj, 21. Septemb. Anno 1592* — **21 September 1592 (O.S.)**; Denmark and Hesse were both still on the Julian calendar. The catalogue *label* gives the same date, so no header/label conflict. **The substantive crux is the addressee-vs-content tension:** Wilhelm IV had died on **25 August 1592 (O.S.)**, four weeks *before* this dateline, yet Tycho addresses the new Landgrave Moritz while speaking of Wilhelm as a living "Lord Father" to whom he had written and whose footsteps he prays Moritz will follow. The likeliest reading is that news of Wilhelm's death had not yet reached Hven by 21 September — Tycho already knew Moritz as a correspondent (the commendatory poem) but not yet that he had succeeded — and that the salutation to "Landgrave Moritz" reflects Moritz's standing as the verse's author rather than knowledge of the succession. This is flagged, not resolved; the date is reproduced exactly as written and is **not** "corrected."

documents.incipit: QUAMVIS mi amantissime Domine D. THADDÆE, nihil a te literarum tota hac elapsa aestate …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO, VARIOQUE DOCTRINARUM GENERE ERUDITISSIMO EXCELLENTISSIMOQUE VIRO, DOMINO THADDÆO HAGGECIO AB HAYCK, PHILOSOPHIAe ET MEDICINAe DOCTORI EXIMIO, AMICO SUO IN PRIMIS COLENDO.

QUAMVIS mi amantissime Domine D. THADDÆE, nihil a te literarum tota hac elapsa aestate acceperim, te tamen incolumi, Deo vitam tibi feliciter prorogante, adhuc esse valetudine spero et ex animo exopto. Ego diutinam hanc literarum intermissionem nequaquam inde accidisse reor, quod vel tu praeter solitum tam diu a scribendo plane cessaveris aut ad meas, quas interea ad te destinâram, nihil omnino responderis; sed (uti alias contigit) ob Tabellariorum perfidiam et incuriam, si quas ad me (prout nihil ambigo) dederis, intercidisse, aut in tanta, quibus disiungimur, locorum intercapedine alicubi interceptas fuisse suspicor; praesertim cum in proximis meis, quas te accepisse non dubito, tuam de quibusdam illic contentis responsionem quam primum ad me perferendam, unâque iudicium de libro nostro ad te ablegato, mihi per opportunitatem communicandum, serio desiderârim. Quorum tamen neutrum tanto temporis intervallo praestitum fuisse antedictis causis ascribendum censeo. Rogo itaque peramanter ut idonea oblata commoditate, tum de praecipuis superiorum ad te literarum momentis, me certiorem reddere, tum etiam de primo nostrorum Progymnasmatum Tomo tibi transmisso censuram tuam interponere mihique impertire velis. Quem iam dudum integrum ad te misissem, nisi varijs exacto hoc semestri negotijs praepeditus fuissem, quo minus hunc typographico labore ad colophonem, uti constitueram, perducere potuerim. Quam primum autem eundem absolvere licuerit (id quod instante nunc hyeme, Deo conatus nostros feliciter adiuvante, futurum confido) mox omnibus numeris absolutum istuc transportari curabo.

Sed quas iam, praestantissime vir, bullatas naenias ad te adduco? En CRAIGI istius scriptum admodum insolens ac scopticum, quo se omnia, quae in libro nostro secundo de Aethereis sunt Phaenomenis, atque Apologia illi hoc nomine destinata, refutare atque infirmare perfricta fronte iactârit; cum tamen ne minimum quidem eorum apud eos, qui non caeco praeiudicio, sed solidis rationibus haec metiuntur, vacillare faciat. Usqueadeo vir ille Aristotelis de Cometarum generatione fumositatibus, suisque praeiudicatis opinionibus occaecatus est, ut non modo nostra penitus improbare, invertere, distrahere, male accommodare, et scommatis, oblocutionibus, dicterijs, fallacibus cothurnis et sophisticis elenchis turgido ac temerario quodam ausu passim excipere non vereatur: sed etiam ipsi veritati certissimis Observationibus et invictis Demonstrationibus assertae vim et fucum facere, suisque ut obtemperet pomposis sophismatis, invitam eam cogere non erubescat. Hem egregiam ab hoc CRAIGO pro tot non modo assiduis in hac palaestra Astronomica exantlatis laboribus, sed quod tam studiose ipsum Regi Scotorum, cum hîc mecum praesto esset, et Cancellario (ut ex ipsius ad me data Epistola, cuius descriptum unâ ad te mitto, plenius cognosces) tum coram tum per literas iterum atque iterum commendârim, gratiam nunc reporto. At ingratus, qui bene merita non reddit, ingratior, qui dissimulat aut negat; sed omnium ingratissimus, qui beneficium maleficio recompensat. Verum de hoc novo Prometheo et vanissimo Capnuranicae restinctionis compilatore satis.

A te autem, mi exoptatissime THADDÆE, in primis desidero, ut scriptum hoc magnifico Domino CURTIO, siquando per alias graviores quibus vacat occupationes tantum temporis concedatur, legendum exhibeas, ut inde liquido perspiciat Peripateticum hunc Athletam non propterea tam fastuoso et pertinaci subinde certamine manus mecum conserere, quasi hoc pacto veritatem plenius inveniri, stabiliri aut illustrari omnibus nervis contenderet; sed ut inventam potius calumnijs et cavillis labefactare, et suarum opinionum ac errorum laqueis irretitam in pristinas ignorantiae tenebras reducere queat. Peto insuper ut Capnuranicas hasce subtilitates vel futilitates verius cum ijs, quae in Tomo nostro secundo et Apologia de hoc negotio Cometico pertractata sint, conferre non degravere. Et quae in hasce Scoticas affanias et captiosas argutias animadvertenda censueris, ea in charta denotare et ad me quam primum transmittere velis oro. Interea autem antilogiam istam sarctam tectam apud vos conservari, nec ad alios propalari cupio, mihique, ut ita fiat, omnino persuadeo. Ego, si tantum mihi per alias, quibus operam impendo, lucubrationes otij suppetat, has arrogantes et insulsas strophas ac calumnias facile retundam, vel alijs forte potius affatim discutiendas et diluendas relinquam. Tu, si quid ad me (id quod magnopere a te expeto) antequam navigatio ob frigoris inclementiam interclusa fuerit, rescripseris, id commode Rostochium ad D. D. BRUCÆUM vel Lubecam ad D. D. IOHANNEM SAGERUM communem nostrum amicum dirigere poteris. Inde postea ad me per occasionem tuto et certo facile perferetur.

Vale.
Datae Uraniburgi 28. Septembris Anno 1592.
Quaeso ut salutes meo nomine magnificum Dominum CURTIUM quam officiosissime.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and, in every various kind of learning, most erudite and most excellent man, Master Thaddaeus Hagecius of Hájek, distinguished Doctor of Philosophy and of Medicine, his friend above all to be honoured.**

Although, my most loving lord Master Thaddaeus, I have received no letter from you throughout this whole summer now past, I nevertheless hope, and from my heart wish, that you are still safe and in good health, God prospering your life happily. I in no way reckon that this long interruption in our correspondence has come about because either you, contrary to your custom, have for so long altogether ceased from writing, or have given no reply at all to the letters of mine that I had meanwhile sent to you; rather (as has happened on other occasions) I suspect that, through the faithlessness and carelessness of the couriers, any [letters] you may have given to be carried to me (as I do not at all doubt you did) have been lost, or have been intercepted somewhere in so great a distance of places as separates us — especially since in my most recent [letter], which I do not doubt you received, I earnestly desired that your reply concerning certain matters contained therein be conveyed to me as soon as possible, and together with it your judgement of our book dispatched to you, to be communicated to me as opportunity allowed. Yet neither of these, I judge, having been rendered in so great an interval of time, is to be ascribed to the causes aforesaid. I therefore most lovingly ask that, when a suitable occasion offers, you would both make me more certain about the chief points of the earlier letter to you, and also lend and impart to me your assessment of the first volume of our *Progymnasmata* transmitted to you. This [volume] I would long since have sent to you complete, had I not been hindered by various pieces of business in the course of this past half-year, so that I could not, as I had resolved, bring it through the labour of the press to its colophon. But as soon as I am permitted to complete it (which, with winter now pressing on, and God prospering our efforts happily, I am confident will be) I shall at once see to it that it be conveyed thither, finished in every particular.

But what bullae-sealed dirges [bullatas naenias] do I now bring to you, most excellent man? Behold the writing of that fellow Craig, exceedingly insolent and scoffing, in which with brazen brow he has boasted that he refutes and overturns everything that is in our second book on the Ethereal Phenomena and in the Apology directed to him under this same head; whereas in fact he makes not the least of these things waver in the eyes of those who measure these matters not by blind prejudice but by solid reasonings. So far has that man been blinded by Aristotle's smoke-fumes about the generation of comets, and by his own preconceived opinions, that he does not fear not only to disapprove utterly, to invert, to distort, to misapply our [arguments], and everywhere to carp at them with gibes, contradictions, taunts, fallacious buskins [cothurni], and sophistical refutations [elenchi], with a certain swollen and reckless audacity; but he does not even blush to do violence and false colouring to the truth itself — established by the most certain observations and unconquerable demonstrations — and to drive it, unwilling, into compliance with his own pompous sophisms. Ha — a fine return I now reap from this Craig, in exchange for so many labours not only unceasingly drained dry in this astronomical wrestling-school, but also for having so zealously commended him, again and again, both in person and by letter, to the King of the Scots himself (when he was here present with me) and to the Chancellor — as you will learn more fully from his own letter sent to me, a copy of which I send to you along [with this]. But ungrateful is he who does not repay good deserts; more ungrateful, he who dissembles or denies them; but most ungrateful of all, he who repays a kindness with an injury. But enough about this new Prometheus and most empty compiler of a *Capnuranic* extinction.

From you, however, my most longed-for Thaddaeus, I desire above all that you exhibit this writing to be read by the magnificent Master Curtius — whenever, amid the other weightier occupations he is engaged in, so much time may be granted — so that from it he may clearly perceive that this Peripatetic Athlete does not for this reason engage hand to hand with me in so haughty and obstinate a contest, time and again, as though by this means he were striving with all his sinews that truth be more fully found out, established, or illustrated; but rather that he may undermine truth once found, by calumnies and cavils, and, having ensnared it in the toils of his own opinions and errors, lead it back into the former darkness of ignorance. I ask, moreover, that you not think it too burdensome to compare these *Capnuranic* subtleties — or futilities, more truly — with the matters treated in our second volume and Apology concerning this cometary business. And whatever you may judge worth remarking upon in these Scottish ravings and captious quibbles, I beg that you would set down on paper and transmit to me as soon as possible. Meanwhile, however, I desire that that counter-argument [antilogia] of his be kept whole and under cover among you, and not divulged to others; and I altogether persuade myself that it will be so done. I, if only I have leisure enough amid the other lucubrations on which I expend my effort, shall easily beat back these arrogant and insipid tricks and calumnies — or rather, perhaps, shall leave them to others to be amply dispelled and dissolved. You, if you write back anything to me (which I greatly request of you) before the sailing-passage be closed off through the inclemency of the cold, will be able conveniently to direct it to Rostock to Master Doctor Brucaeus, or to Lübeck to Master Doctor Johannes Sagerus, our common friend. From there it will afterwards easily be brought to me, safely and surely, as occasion offers.

Farewell.
Given at Uraniborg, 28 September, the year 1592.
I pray that you would greet the magnificent Master Curtius in my name as dutifully as possible.
Yours, Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** *Tycho Brahe*, at Uraniborg on Hven, to **Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayck** = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (1525–1600), Bohemian physician, astronomer, and imperial court physician at Prague; Tycho's chief scientific correspondent in the Empire and the man who had supplied him manuscript material used in the *Progymnasmata*. The standing salutation register ("most loving lord," "most longed-for Thaddaeus") matches their long friendship.
- ***Progymnasmatum … primo Tomo*** — the first volume of Tycho's *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata* (the "Preliminary Exercises," on the nova of 1572). The work was printed slowly at Uraniborg and not published until 1602/1603; here in 1592 the volume is still incomplete — Tycho says he could not "bring it through the labour of the press to its colophon" (*typographico labore ad colophonem … perducere*). *colophon* kept as the printer's-term it is.
- ***libro nostro secundo de Aethereis … Phaenomenis*** — the second book of Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (1588), on the comet of 1577. *Apologia illi hoc nomine destinata* — the apologia (defence) Tycho addressed to Craig "under this same head," i.e. answering Craig's objections to that book.
- **The Craig polemic.** *Craigus / Craigi istius* = **John Craig** (d. 1620), Scottish physician (later physician to James VI/I), an Aristotelian who disputed Tycho's claim that the comet of 1577 lay in the supralunary (ethereal) region rather than being a sublunary exhalation. The two had exchanged sharp letters (Craig's of 9 July 1589 survives in this same correspondence). Tycho calls him a "Peripatetic Athlete" (*Peripateticum Athletam* — a follower of Aristotle's Peripatetic school, cast as a brawler in the "astronomical wrestling-school," *palaestra Astronomica*) and "this new Prometheus."
- ***bullatas naenias*** — literally "bubble-/bulla-dirges": rendered "bullae-sealed dirges." *naeniae* are funeral-dirges, hence worthless droning; *bullatae* puns on *bulla* (a sealed document / an empty bubble), so the phrase doubly belittles Craig's tract as a pompously sealed yet hollow lament. The double sense is flagged rather than collapsed to one reading.
- ***Capnuranicae restinctionis … Capnuranicas … subtilitates*** — *Capnuranica* is from Greek καπνός (*kapnós*, "smoke") + οὐρανός (*ouranós*, "heaven/sky"): "smoke-in-the-heaven," Tycho's mocking coinage (or echo of Craig's own title) for Craig's Aristotelian doctrine that the comet was a smoky exhalation. *restinctio* = "extinction / quenching" (of the cometary fire/fumes). Kept transliterated and glossed; *Capnuranic* italicised as a retained technical coinage. **Crux flagged** (see Confidence).
- ***Aristotelis … Cometarum generatione fumositatibus*** — "Aristotle's smoke-fumes about the generation of comets": the Aristotelian theory (Meteorologica) that comets are dry terrestrial exhalations ignited in the upper air — the very doctrine Tycho's parallax measurements overturned.
- ***fallacibus cothurnis et sophisticis elenchis*** — "fallacious buskins and sophistical refutations." *cothurnus* (the tragic actor's high boot) = bombast/inflated style; *elenchi sophistici* alludes to Aristotle's *Sophistici Elenchi* (fallacious refutations) — Tycho turns the Aristotelian's own logical apparatus against him. Both kept as the rhetorical/technical terms they are.
- ***Domino CURTIO / magnificum Dominum CURTIUM*** — **Jacob Kurtz von Senftenau** (Jacobus Curtius, d. 1594), imperial Vice-Chancellor at the court of Rudolf II in Prague, a learned patron of astronomy; Tycho wants Curtius to read Craig's tract and see its bad faith. The closing postscript renews the greeting to him.
- ***Regi Scotorum … et Cancellario*** — the **King of the Scots** = James VI (later James I of England), whom Tycho had hosted on Hven in 1590; and his **Chancellor** (John Maitland of Thirlestane). Tycho stresses he had repeatedly recommended Craig to both.
- ***D. D. BRUCAeUM*** — **Heinrich Brucaeus** (1530–1593), professor of medicine and mathematics at Rostock; a forwarding address. *D. D.* = *Domino Doctori*, "Master Doctor." ***D. D. IOHANNEM SAGERUM*** — **Johannes Sager** (Sagerus), a Lübeck contact and "our common friend," a second forwarding node. The two are given as the reliable mail-relay before the sea-passage closes for winter (*antequam navigatio ob frigoris inclementiam interclusa fuerit*).
- ***antilogiam istam sarctam tectam … conservari*** — "that counter-argument of his be kept whole and under cover": *antilogia* = a counter-/contrary-argument; *sarcta tecta* is the legal-administrative formula "in good repair, intact," here "whole and under cover." Tycho asks that Craig's tract be held privately, not circulated.
- ***Scoticas affanias*** — "Scottish ravings": *affaniae* = idle nonsense, twaddle (Craig being Scottish).
- ***novo Prometheo*** — "this new Prometheus": an ironic flourish — Craig as a would-be fire-bringer who in fact only deals in smoke (tying back to the *Capnuranica* / "extinction" jibe).
- **Editorial note on the source.** The verbatim block reproduces the printed forms as given, including *responionem* (for *responsionem*), the *æ*-ligature spellings rendered *Ae* (THADDAeO, AHaycк→ab Hayck, HAGGECIO, CRAIGO etc.), and *j* for consonantal *i* (*varijs, negotijs, sophismatis*); these are not normalised in the Source block.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Datas Uraniburgi 28. Septembris Anno 1592* — 28 September 1592, **Old Style** (Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). No in-letter date discrepancy; the catalogue label agrees with the dateline (place "Uraniborg"). No conversion made.
- **Correction.** Latin corrected against Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia VII, pages 342 and 343: "responionem" corrected to "responsionem"; the closing "Datas" corrected to "Datae". The English translation already read correctly at both sites and required no change.

text.original:
PETRO IUNIO TYCHO BRAHE. S.

QUAMVIS, nobilissime et amplissime vir, ultimis meis de neglecta ad priores aliquot responsione familiari quadam libertate tecum expostulantibus, nihil adhuc rescripseris: tamen et has illis aggregare non supersedebo, utut diutinam hanc tuam sive oblivionem sive spontaneam forte scribendi intermissionem vix (amicitia nostra sic exigente) excusatam habeam. Eroque ob id nunc brevior: praesertim cum superiora tibi adhuc satis in praesenti esse memoria (in quibus etiamnum tuam operam obnixe desidero) mihi persuadeam. Neque enim meas tibi non relatas diffido: ex quo a magnifico D. IO. METELLANO, Cancellario vestro, responsum acceperim, cui eodem tempore literas tuis simul coniunctas destinâram. Cum vero in superioribus praeter alia ut a Serenissimo Rege carmen quoddam in mearum lucubrationum Astronomicarum commendationem impetrares, peramanter te rogassem: et nunc ad ipsius Maiestatem ipsemet hac de causa elegiacam hanc qualemcunque epistolam exarârim (quam tibi ipsius Maiestati meo nomine submisse offerendam unâ mitto) idcirco etiamnum a te idipsum quibus possum precibus rogo, ut tua intercessione, eaque, qua apud ipsam Maiestatem polles, authoritate et consilij grata (quod et mereris) acceptatione, quo id clementissimi beneficij mihi impertiatur, quantum in te est, elaborare non degraveris. De privilegio ab ipsius Maiestate obtinendo, cuius apud te antea satis superque mentionem feci, nunc nihil superaddam. Haec igitur singula, et si quae praeterea sunt, alias significata, tuae erga me benevolentiae et amicitiae nostrae fidelitati fideliter etiam exequenda committo.

Vale.
Datae Uraniburgi 1 Oct. A. 1592.
Tuae Magnificentiae studiosissimus
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To Peter Young. Tycho Brahe sends greeting.**

Although, most noble and worthy sir, you have as yet sent no reply to my last letter, in which with a certain familiar freedom I remonstrated with you over your neglect to answer some earlier ones, I shall nonetheless not refrain from adding these too to those — even though I can scarcely hold this long silence of yours, be it forgetfulness or perhaps a deliberate intermission of writing, to be excused (our friendship requiring as much). And for that reason I shall now be the briefer, especially since I persuade myself that those earlier matters are still sufficiently present to your memory (in which matters I still earnestly desire your good offices). For indeed I do not distrust that my [letters] have [in fact] reached you: seeing that I have received an answer from the worshipful Master Jo. Maitland, your Chancellor, to whom at the same time I had addressed a letter joined together with yours. But since in those earlier letters I had, among other things, very affectionately asked you to obtain from the Most Serene King some poem in commendation of my astronomical labours, and since now, for this very reason, I have myself drawn up this elegiac epistle, such as it is, to His Majesty in person (which I send herewith, to be humbly presented to His Majesty in my name by you), I therefore ask the very same thing of you yet again, with what entreaties I can: that by your intercession — and by that authority in which you are strong with His Majesty, and by his gracious acceptance of the counsel (as indeed you deserve) — you will not think it a burden to labour, so far as in you lies, to the end that this most clement favour be bestowed on me. Of the privilege to be obtained from His Majesty, of which I have already made mention to you more than enough, I shall now add nothing further. These several matters, then, and any others besides that have been indicated elsewhere, I commit to be faithfully carried out by your goodwill toward me and by the fidelity of our friendship.

Farewell.
Given at Uraniborg, 1 October, the year 1592.
Most devoted to Your Magnificence,
Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender & recipient / address line.** *PETRO IUNIO · TYCHO BRAHE. S.* — the source prints the two elements run together (*PETRO IUNIOTYCHO*); read as *Petro Iunio. Tycho Brahe S[alutem].* = "To Peter Young, Tycho Brahe (sends) greeting". **Peter Young** (*Petrus Iunius*, 1544–1628), Scottish humanist, royal tutor (*paedagogus*) to the young James VI and one of the King's most trusted advisers and book-agents; he had visited Hven and was Tycho's standing channel to the Scottish court.
- **Recipient's honorific.** *nobilissime et amplissime vir* → "most noble and worthy sir"; the subscription *Tuae Magnificentiae studiosissimus* → "Most devoted to Your Magnificence" (the *Magnificentia* register carried over from's *studiosiss.* formula).
- ***IO. METELLANO, Cancellario vestro*** — **John Maitland of Thirlestane** (c. 1543–1595), Lord Chancellor of Scotland; *Metellanus* is the latinised form of *Maitland*. *vestro* ("your," plural) = the Chancellor of your [Scottish] realm. Tycho elsewhere corresponded with Maitland directly (letter of 16 May 1592, Lethington).
- ***Serenissimo Rege / ipsius Maiestas*** — **James VI of Scotland** (1566–1625; later James I of England), Young's pupil and sovereign, who had visited Uraniborg in 1590. Not named in the letter; identified here on first occurrence. The *carmen … in commendationem* is the commendatory poem Tycho sought from the King for his astronomical publications.
- ***elegiacam hanc qualemcunque epistolam exarârim*** — "I have drawn up this elegiac epistle, such as it is": Tycho's own verse-letter to James VI, composed in elegiac couplets, enclosed for Young to present. *qualemcunque* ("such as it is") is Tycho's self-deprecating hedge, preserved. (*exarârim* = syncopated *exaraverim*; *destinâram* = *destinaveram*.)
- ***lucubrationes Astronomicae*** → "astronomical labours / lucubrations" (literally night-work by lamplight); here Tycho's published astronomical writings, for which the royal commendation is sought.
- ***De privilegio ab ipsius Maiestate obtinendo*** → "the privilege to be obtained from His Majesty": a printing/publishing privilege (the standard early-modern grant of exclusive right against piracy), which Tycho wished the King to grant; he declines to repeat the particulars here.
- **Latin idiom / syntax.** *meas tibi non relatas diffido* carries a double negative whose force is "I do not distrust that my [letters] have been delivered to you" — i.e. Tycho is confident they arrived; the two negations (*non … diffido*) are reproduced as a litotes of confidence, not collapsed. *non supersedebo* → "I shall not refrain"; *non degraveris* → "you will not think it a burden"; each negation is rendered one-for-one.
- **Dateline.** *Datae Uraniburgi 1 Oct. A. 1592* = "Given at **Uraniborg** (on Hven), 1 October, the year 1592" (O.S.; Denmark kept Old Style). The dateline date agrees with the catalogue label (1592. 1. oktober. Uraniborg); no discrepancy.
- **MS witness.** A = Oxford, Bodleian Library, Smith 77 (an *Afskrift* / copy). Edition of record per the edition: *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia* (Dreyer VII).
- **Correction.** Latin heading 'IUNIOTYCHO' corrected to 'IUNIO TYCHO' (missing space) per Dreyer, TBOO VII p.344.
