text.original:
NOBILISSIMO CLARISSIMOQUE VIRO D. TYCHONI BRAHE, MATHEMATICO EXIMIO, DOMINO ET AMICO PLURIMUM OBSERVANDO. S. P.

EGI cum MYLIANDRO de Typographico ministro, verum in præsentia de nullo ipsi constat. Mathematicarum disciplinarum studiosi pauci hodie, plerique enim Theologiæ studio vacant. Certum et præsens viaticum inquiram diligentius. De CRAIGO miror, nec scio quomodo paralaxin refellere queat, qua moti veteres ARISTOTELIS interpretes viam lacteam in cœlo statuerunt. Velim mihi proximis literis indicari rationes quibus eam evertere conatur, nisi forte observationem culpet. Nam vidi nonnullorum scripta, qui hunc eundem Cometam infra Lunam statuant. Ego certe parallaxi aut nulla aut exigua et minore quam in Luna in hoc Cometa concessa, non video quomodo suam sententiam tueri queat. Si editus est, dabitur aliquando copia legendi. Si autem non est editus, iudico illum hæc scripsisse, ut magis excitet ingenij tui acumen, et cogites quæ contra dici possint. Homo est eruditus, ut ex DUNCANO intellexi, maiorem modestiam in eo requirerem, si cavillando et detorquendo tua infringere conatur. Attamen non pæniteat commendasse, decet enim bonum virum iuvare plurimos, obesse nemini. Futuram eclipsim, si conspicietur, accuratius observabo: Globum tuum vel Sphæram armillarem satis affabre confectam vidi, verum parum meis oculis aptam, qui iam incipiunt obtusiores fieri. Non satis autem intelligo cur Terræ polos detorseris a polis mundi et Zodiaci.

Bene vale.
Rostochij Va Novembris A.° Domini 1592.
HENRICUS BRUCÆUS
plane tuus.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most renowned man, Master Tycho Brahe, distinguished mathematician, his lord and friend much to be respected — heartiest greeting.**

I have dealt with Myliander concerning a printer's assistant, but at present he knows of none. Few today are students of the mathematical disciplines, for most give themselves over to the study of theology. I shall inquire more diligently after a sure and ready means of support [for him]. About Craig I wonder, and I do not see how he can refute the parallax by which the ancient interpreters of Aristotle were moved to place the Milky Way in the heaven. I should like to have set out for me, in your next letter, the grounds by which he attempts to overturn it — unless perhaps he finds fault with the observation [itself]. For I have seen the writings of certain men who place this very same comet below the Moon. For my part, certainly, once a parallax either nil or slight, and less than that in the Moon, is granted in this comet, I do not see how he can maintain his opinion. If it has been published, the chance to read it will be given at some time. But if it has not been published, I judge that he wrote these things rather to rouse the keenness of your intellect, and that you might consider what can be said against [them]. He is a learned man, as I have understood from Duncan; I should require greater modesty in him, if it is by quibbling and twisting that he attempts to undermine your [arguments]. Yet let it not be regretted that I commended him, for it befits a good man to help very many and to harm no one. The coming eclipse, if it shall be visible, I shall observe more accurately. Your globe, or the armillary sphere, I have seen, made skilfully enough — but little suited to my eyes, which are now beginning to grow duller. I do not, however, sufficiently understand why you have turned the poles of the Earth aside from the poles of the world and of the Zodiac.

Fare you well.
At Rostock, the 5th of November, in the Year of the Lord 1592.
Henricus Brucaeus,
wholly yours.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Brucaeus* = **Heinrich Brucaeus** (Hendrik van den Broeke, c. 1530/31–1593), born at Alost (Aalst) in Flanders, professor of medicine and of mathematics at the University of Rostock, and an established astronomical correspondent of Tycho's. Writing late in life (he died the following year), he refers to his failing eyesight.
- **Recipient / place.** Tycho is at this date at **Uraniborg** on Hven; Brucaeus writes from **Rostock** (*Rostochium*; this chapter's convention).
- ***Myliander*** — a Rostock contact (most plausibly connected to the local book trade / university milieu) through whom Brucaeus sought to recruit a compositor for Tycho's private press on Hven. **Identification crux:** the name is not securely fixed here; not resolved beyond the printing-recruitment context the letter itself supplies.
- ***Typographicus minister*** — rendered "printer's assistant" (a journeyman compositor / press-hand for Tycho's Uraniborg printing office); *viaticum* "means of support / provision" — i.e. the wages or maintenance that would secure such a man. Latin technical-of-trade nouns kept in sense by this chapter's convention
- **The Craig controversy (the core of the letter).** *Craigo* = **John Craig** (Craigius, d. 1620), the Scottish physician (later physician to James VI/I) who disputed Tycho's doctrine that comets are supralunary. Tycho had sent Craig an "apology" defending his comet book; Craig in turn composed a refutation (the *Capnuraniae restinctio*, against Tycho's "smoke-in-heaven"), upholding the Aristotelian doctrine that comets are sublunary exhalations. Brucaeus's whole technical paragraph is his reaction to Craig's argument. Brucaeus does not know whether Craig's piece is yet *editus* ("published") — at the time of writing it apparently was not — and hedges that, if unpublished, it may be a private provocation to sharpen Tycho's wits; the hedge is preserved, not resolved.
- ***paralaxin / parallaxi*** — **parallax**; spelled *paralaxin* (acc.) once and *parallaxi* (abl.) once in the source, both retained as printed. Brucaeus's argument: Aristotle's ancient interpreters placed the **Milky Way** (*via lactea*) in the heaven (i.e. as a celestial, not sublunary, phenomenon) precisely on a parallax argument; he cannot see how Craig overturns parallax. The decisive clause — *parallaxi aut nulla aut exigua et minore quam in Luna … concessa* ("a parallax either nil or slight, and less than that in the Moon, being granted") — is the standard Tychonic test: a comet showing no measurable parallax, or one smaller than the Moon's, must lie beyond the Moon.
- ***observationem culpet*** — "he finds fault with the observation": Brucaeus's alternative supposition that Craig attacks not the inference but Tycho's observational data; rendered without sharpening.
- ***Cometam infra Lunam statuant*** — "place this very same comet below the Moon," i.e. as sublunary. *hunc eundem Cometam* ("this very same comet") implies a specific comet under discussion; the letter does not name it, so it is left unspecified rather than identified.
- ***Duncano*** — **Duncan**, a Scot (the period form *Duncanus*) cited as Brucaeus's informant on Craig's learning; not further identified here.
- ***cavillando et detorquendo … infringere*** — "by quibbling and twisting … to undermine"; the contemptuous pair is kept. *tua* ("your [arguments / positions]") is supplied in brackets as the understood object.
- **Instruments.** *Globum tuum vel Sphaeram armillarem* — "your globe, or the armillary sphere" (this chapter's convention: *globus* → globe, *armillae/sphaera armillaris* → armillary sphere). Brucaeus has seen one of Tycho's instruments but finds it hard on his ageing eyes.
- ***Futuram eclipsim … accuratius observabo*** — "the coming eclipse … I shall observe more accurately" (*eclipsis* → eclipse,); the specific eclipse is not named in the letter.
- **The terrestrial-poles question.** *cur Terrae polos detorseris a polis mundi et Zodiaci* — "why you have turned the poles of the Earth aside from the poles of the world and of the Zodiac." This records Brucaeus's puzzlement at a feature of Tycho's cosmological/diagrammatic model (the poles of the terrestrial axis displaced from the poles of the celestial sphere *mundi* and from the ecliptic poles *Zodiaci*). *polos mundi* rendered "poles of the world" (the celestial poles). The exact construction Brucaeus is reacting to is not elaborated in the letter and is not reconstructed here.
- **Salutation / subscription.** *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam* ("heartiest greeting,"); *Bene vale* → "Fare you well"; *plane tuus* → "wholly yours."
- **Dateline.** *Rostochij Va Novembris A.° Domini 1592* = "At Rostock, the 5th of November, in the Year of the Lord 1592." *Va* is the ordinal *quinta* (5th); the as-written date agrees with the catalogue label ("1592. 5. november. Rostock"). **Old Style:** Rostock (Mecklenburg, Lutheran) and Denmark both kept the Julian calendar in 1592; the date is O.S.

documents.incipit: Thill Thyge Brahe.

text.original:
RASMUS PEDERSSEN I KUNSØEMAGLE FICH BREFF THILL THYGE BRAHE OM SIN EGEN SAG ANRØRENDIS.

Thill Thyge Brahe.

WOR gunst thilforn. Wiidt effthersom Raßmus Pedersen vdj Gunßøemagle vnderdanigst haffuer ladet giffue Oß thill kiende, huorledis handt aff thig vdj attschillige maade delis, thilthallis och paa thet yderste forfølges: for:ne hans gaardt, som handt aff thig nogen thiidt forleden høygt och diurtt fest haffuer, hannum att were formeent och forbøden, saa handt jcke sicker och vden stoer fare thør komme ther jndt, hans broder och thieniste karll och aff thig att were vlouffforuunden fengßligen ahntastet och endnu holdis vdj fengsell, och endog handt jcke gierne wille were vdj saadan mangfoldige och vendige klamer och thrette met thig, meden møget mere thill nogen rolig ende, saa fremt hannum nogen liidelige och billige middell och willckor aff thig egien motte wederfares, bode for thend store jndfestning hand thig for for:ne gardt giffuet haffuer, som och for huiß bygning hand ther paa haffuer bekostet och ahnuendt, saa handt theroffuer icke schulle slet och aldelis forderffuis och ødeleggis, vnderdanigst begierendis, att saadane hans arme och elendige wilckor aff saadane languarendis klamer, thrette och forfølging motte ahnsehes och betenkes, och Wij naadigst wille vnde och giffue hannum Wortt beschermelße breff thill aldt rette att motte beschyttes och beschermis. Tha bede Wij thig och wille, attu saadane hans elendighet och yderste forderff selff fører thig thill sindt och gemøte och wedt thin conscientz betrachter och offuer ueyer, och ther udinden star thig selff thill rette, och huiß christeligt, billigt och louligt ehr emodt hannum forethager och begynder, paa thet Wij theraff jcke schulle foraarsagis effther hans vnderdanigst begiering att vnde och giffue hannum, som en Wore och kronens vndersotte och thend thig aldene aff Wor kiere herre fader sallig och hoglofflig ehukomelße ad gratiam forleent ehr, for:ne Wortt beschermelße breff thill ald rette att handhaffuis och forsuaris. Wij ehre och naadigst vdj thend endelig meening och forsett att wille lade Wore obne befalling vdj samme sag vdghae thill Oß elsk:e Lauge Beck, Wor mandt, thiener och landtzdomer her vdj Wortt landt Sielandt, att handt met andre flere Wore ther thill forordnede gode mendt samme sag met thet allerførste schulle thagge for thennum och endeligen kiende och døme ether emellum vdj alle huiß jrringer och thrette, ether emellum ehr eller were kandt, och aff andre Wore godemendt jcke thilforn om kiendt och dømpt ehr, paa thet jngen aff anten siider schulle haffue thennum att beklage at schee emodt rette och forkortt. Ther som thu nu est thilsindtz att wille haffue eller naffn giffue nogen godemendt, som paa thin siide kunde were vdj samme befalling, thu tha strax met thet allerførste thig therom emodt Oss elsk:e Wor thilforordnede regierings raadt ehrklerer och naffn giffuer, huem thu paa thin siide est begierendis, dog thennum, som boe her vdj landet och ehre vparthiesche vdj samme sag, paa thet samme Wor befalling met thet allerførderligst kunde vdschriffuis och fuldgiøris, och met for:ne languarende och vendige klamer och thrette en gang for alle motte komme thill ende. Ther met scheer Wor wilge, thj thag her aldelis jngen forsømmelße fore.

Befallendis etc.
Schreffuit Haffniae 17. nouembris a:o 1592.
text.english:
**Rasmus Pedersen in Gundsømagle received a letter to Tyge Brahe touching his own cause.**

To Tyge Brahe.

Our favour beforehand. Know that, inasmuch as Rasmus Pedersen of Gundsømagle has most humbly given us to understand how he is by you, in sundry ways, sued, charged, and to the uttermost prosecuted: that his aforesaid farm, which he some while ago took of you on lease at a high and dear [rent], has been refused and forbidden him, so that he dares not come into it safely and without great danger; that his brother and serving-man have, without [their having] been lawfully convicted, been seized and imprisoned by you and are still held in prison; and although he would by no means wish to be in such manifold and perverse wrangling and dispute with you, but rather [to come] to some peaceable end — provided that some tolerable and equitable terms and conditions might be granted him by you again, both for the great entry-fine which he has given you for the aforesaid farm, and also for whatever building he has there laid out and expended upon it, so that he should not thereby be utterly and altogether ruined and undone — most humbly desiring that such poor and wretched conditions of his, [arising] from such long-lasting wrangling, dispute, and prosecution, might be regarded and considered, and that we would graciously grant and give him our letter of protection, that he might be protected and defended in all that is right. We therefore ask you and will that you yourself take such wretchedness and uttermost ruin of his to mind and heart, and weigh and consider it by your conscience, and therein hold yourself to what is right, and undertake and set in hand against him whatsoever is Christian, equitable, and lawful; to the end that we be not thereby caused — in accordance with his most humble request — to grant and give him, as one of our and the crown's subjects, and one who was granted to you alone by our dear lord father, of blessed and most laudable memory, *ad gratiam* [as a favour], the aforesaid our letter of protection, that he be maintained and defended in all that is right. We are also graciously of this final mind and intent, to have our open command in this matter go forth to our beloved Lauge Beck, our man, servant, and provincial judge here in our land of Zealand, that he, together with several other good men of ours appointed thereto, shall at the very first take this matter before them and finally hear and judge between you in all such errors and disputes as are or may be between you, and have not heretofore been heard and adjudged by other good men of ours, to the end that neither of either side should have cause to complain of being [dealt with] contrary to right and shortchanged. If you are now minded to wish to have, or to name, any good men who on your side might be in this same commission, then you shall at once, at the very first, declare yourself thereupon and name to our beloved appointed council of regency whom you desire on your side — yet [only] such as dwell here in the land and are impartial in this matter — to the end that this our command may with all speed be written out and effected, and that with the aforesaid long-lasting and perverse wrangling and dispute an end may at last be made once and for all. Therein is done our will; therefore take herein no neglect at all.

Commanding [you to God], etc.
Written at Copenhagen, 17 November, in the year 1592.

documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer.** **Christian IV of Denmark** (b. 1577, r. 1588–1648); in 1592 still a minor of fifteen, the kingdom governed by a council of regency (*regeringsråd*) — hence the letter's reference to "our beloved appointed council of regency" as the body Tycho is to address, and the deferral to "our dear lord father, of blessed memory," **Frederik II** (d. 1588), who had granted Tycho the prebend and its lands. The royal "we" is the formal crown voice, not a personal pronouncement by the boy-king.
- **Recipient / beneficiary.** *Thyge Brahe* = **Tycho Brahe**, here addressed not as astronomer but as landlord. *Rasmus Pedersen* (Raßmus Pedersen) of **Gunderslevmagle** (*Gunßøemagle / Kunsøemagle*, a village in southern Zealand) is one of Tycho's tenant farmers, the petitioner whose complaint the letter conveys. The document is a *missive* to Tycho prompted by — and embodying — Rasmus Pedersen's suit (the rubric: "Rasmus Pedersen … received a letter to Tyge Brahe touching his own cause").
- **Document type.** A chancery draft/concept of an open letter or missive (*koncept*), preserved among the *uindførte koncepter* (drafts not entered in the registers) of the Danish Chancery Archive. The opening rubric and the closing *Befallendis etc.* / *Schreffuit Haffniae* are Latin–Danish chancery formulae; the body is Danish. *ad gratiam* ("as a favour / out of grace") is the one Latin phrase embedded in the body — kept and glossed.
- **Lauge Beck.** **Lauge (Lave) Beck** (1568–1607), of Førslev, *landsdommer* (provincial judge) of Zealand; here designated by the king as the commissioner who, with other appointed *gode mænd* ("good men," i.e. noble arbiters/assessors), is to convene a final adjudication of the long-running dispute between Tycho and his tenant. This is an early instance of the crown intervening in Tycho's seigneurial conduct toward the peasantry of his fiefs — the kind of friction with tenants and the regency that contributed to the deterioration of his position in Denmark.
- **Legal substance (rendered with care).** The petition alleges three grievances against Tycho as landlord: (1) Rasmus Pedersen is barred from the farm he leased at a high rent ("dares not come into it safely and without great danger"); (2) his brother and serving-man were *imprisoned without lawful conviction* (*vlouffforuunden … fengßligen ahntastet* = "seized in custody without [their] being lawfully convicted") and are still held; (3) he stands to be "utterly ruined," having paid a large *indfæstning* (entry-fine, *jndfestning*) and spent on buildings. The king does **not** command Tycho to release or restore; the operative instruction is conditional and admonitory — Tycho is to weigh the case by his conscience and *of his own accord* do "whatsoever is Christian, equitable, and lawful," **so that** the king be not driven (*jcke schulle foraarsagis*) to issue the requested letter of protection. The threat of the protection-letter, and of a binding arbitration under Lauge Beck, is the lever; the act demanded of Tycho is left to him.
- **Negation count (verified).** The Danish body carries the following negations, all reproduced and none added: *jcke sicker … thør komme* ("dares not … safely"); *vlouffforuunden* (the privative "un-lawfully-convicted"); *jcke gierne wille were* ("would by no means wish to be"); *icke schulle … forderffuis* ("should not be ruined"); *Wij theraff jcke schulle foraarsagis* ("that we be not caused"); *aff andre … jcke thilforn om kiendt och dømpt ehr* ("have not heretofore been adjudged"); *jngen aff anten siider* ("neither of either side"); and the closing *thag her aldelis jngen forsømmelße fore* ("take herein no neglect at all"). The conditional *saa fremt … motte wederfares* ("provided that … might be granted") governs the tenant's willingness to settle and is kept as a proviso, not flattened into an assertion.
- **Orthography (chancery Danish, c. 1592).** *WOR gunst thilforn* = *Vor gunst tilforn* ("Our favour beforehand," the royal address-formula, this chapter's convention); *Wiidt* = imperative *vid* ("know"); *effthersom* = *eftersom* ("inasmuch as"); *delis, thilthallis, forfølges* = passives *deles, tiltales, forfølges* ("is sued, charged, prosecuted"); *fest* = *fæst* ("took on lease"); *formeent* = *forment* ("refused, denied"); *jndfestning* = *indfæstning* (the lease entry-fine); *huiß* = relative *hvis* here = "whatever / what(soever)"; *gemøte* = *gemyt* ("heart, disposition"); *conscientz* = "conscience"; *for:ne* = *fornævnte* ("aforesaid," standard chancery abbreviation); *Oß elsk:e / Oss elsk:e* = *Os elskelige* ("our beloved," courtesy epithet); *obne befalling* = *åbne befaling* ("open command"); *vparthiesche* = *upartiske* ("impartial"); *vendige klamer* = *vrange/vendte klammeri* here "perverse [or turned-about] wrangling"; *allerførderligst* = *allerførderligst/allerforderligst* ("with all speed"); *Befallendis* = *befalendes* (the closing "commending [you to God]"). *vnderdanigst* ("most humbly") recurs three times, marking the tenant's, not Tycho's, posture.
- **Calendar / place.** *Schreffuit Haffniae 17. nouembris a:o 1592* = "Written at **Copenhagen** (*Hafnia*), 17 November, year 1592" (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). The dateline and the edition label (Copenhagen) agree; no date discrepancy.
- **Correction.** English corrected from the real but wrong Zealand village 'Gunderslevmagle' to 'Gundsømagle', matching the source ('Kunsøemagle'/'Gunsøemagle') and Dreyer's own editorial Latin summary ('vico Gundsömagle'), per Dreyer, Opera Omnia XIV pp.63, 65.

Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO XIV pp.63-64 read as page images (letter runs from the drop-cap 'W' on p.63 through 'Befallendis etc. Schreffuit Haffniæ 17. nouembris a:o 1592' on p.64). Collated the whole letter clause by clause — the farm dispute, the imprisoned brother and servant, the entry-fine and building costs, the referral to Lauge Beck and the regency council, the closing formula and date — all render accurately. The one defect found is a place-name misidentification (Gunsøemagle/Gundsömagle misrendered as the unrelated village Gunderslevmagle), verified against both the letter's own Danish text and Dreyer's independent Latin case-summary on the same page, and corroborated externally (Tycho's 1579 Roskilde-canon fiefdom over Gundsømagle/Gundsøgård). Downgraded from published grade Probable to C because a wrong toponym in a legal/land dispute is exactly the kind of fact a scholar or cataloguer would carry forward uncorrected.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (medium). The village is named 'Kunsøemagle'/'Gunsøemagle' in the letter and 'Gundsömagle' in Dreyer's own editorial Latin summary of the same case — all three point to Gundsømagle, the Sømme-herred village near Roskilde that Tycho held in fee as a Roskilde canon from 1579 (confirmed independently: Roskilde-historie.dk / Trap Danmark on Gundsømagle sogn). The published English instead names a different, real Zealand village, 'Gunderslevmagle' (near Skælskør/Næstved), misidentifying the location of Tycho's disputed tenant farm and the imprisoned brother — a specific factual error a scholar citing this document would carry forward. At: “Rasmus Pedersen in Gunderslevmagle received a letter to Tyge Brahe touching his own cause.... how he is by you... one ”.

Dreyer's own editorial Latin item-summaries for this and the companion letter (items 96, 98) independently and consistently identify the village as Gundsømagle, corroborating the source's own spellings. Only the English was corrected; the Latin needed no change. No other part of the letter was touched.

documents.abstract: Explains his long silence by recounting months of serious illness: recurring stomach pain followed by jaundice and a continuous fever lasting through the summer.
documents.incipit: NOBILISS. vir, Domine et amice observande. Uno die mensis Febr. huius anni redditae …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE DANO, URANIEBURGI DOMINO ETC D. ET AMICO SUO OBSERVANDO. S.

NOBILISS. vir, Domine et amice observande. Uno die mensis Febr. huius anni redditae fuerunt mihi plures literae tuae, atque hae diversis temporibus scriptae; quas cum perlegissem, nostro quoque D. CURTIO legendas dedi. Ab eo ipso die totum hoc tempus huc usque valetudine adversa transegi, initio quidem interpollatim recurrebat ingens et intolerabilis dolor ventriculi flatulentus. Postea cum diebus pluribus durasset, iterumque intermisisset aliquando dies 14, aliquando 20, tandem post gravissimum insultum erupit in Ictericiam, quae post dies aliquot febrem continuam protulit. Haec Ictericiae coniuncta me afflixit per menses tres, nimirum August. Sept. et Octob. Salutis spes fuit exigua, sive quis naturam et cursum utriusque morbi, sive corpus subiectum considerasset. Medici certe male ominari consueverunt ei aegroto, quando Icterus excipit febrem. Iam vero praeter ea accessit aetas senilis annorum 66. Quid igitur de recuperanda sanitate sperare potui? Interea non exhorrui mortem: imo libentissime deposuissem hoc corpusculum, si divinae voluntati placuisset. Sum enim iam pertaesus huius aerumnosae vitae, video etiam patriae nostrae magnas impendere calamitates, quarum utinam non essem spectator. Etsi autem sola Dei bonitate ex morbo difficili liberatus sum: tamen, mi TYCHO, vires mei corpusculi ita labefactatae sunt, ut eas nunquam redituras facile intelligam. Ac futuras eas subinde languidiores, varia symptomata, quibus creberrime impetor, praenunciant. Nam et Catharri graves, et pristinus dolor ventriculi, et arenulae, et alij dolores varij, quasi agmine facto in me irruunt, mirifice affligunt et divexant. Addo, me propemodum attingere limites Tympanitis. Sed, ut dixi, ista non expavesco, ut qui sciam Dei consilio et voluntate omnia fieri. Deo me totum commendo, eundemque oro, facere velit, ut reliquum vitae ei soli vivam in timore, expectans cum alacritate diem discessus mei. Itaque iam omnibus alijs studijs, maiori ex parte, nuncium mitto, uni illi studio intentus, ut bene mori addiscam.

Literas, inquam, illas tuas, quas D. CURTIO me dedisse legendas dixi, morbo illo diuturno impeditus, nondum recipere potui. Hodie, qui est dies ultimus Novembris novo stylo, cum hasce postremas tuas scriptas 28 Septembris a tabellario Magdeburgensi cum scripto illo acerbo sane tui istius fastuosi, praefracti, mordacis et malesani antagonistae accepissem, una et altera pagina perlecta, et obiter perlustrato eo scripto, altero mox die, et epistolam tuam et scriptum illud legenda dedi D. CURTIO, et profecto fuerunt ei admodum grata, quod de te iam diu ne verbum quidem. Postera die, quae fuit 2 Decembris, ad ipsum redeo, ut eius sententiam de scripto illo audirem (nam tabellarius Magdeburgensis discessum parabat, quem noluissem vacuum meis literis redire illuc). Is primum iubet te salvere plurimum, tibique significare scriptum illud tui Scoti non inniti ullis firmis rationibus. Omnem doctrinam parallaxium suis quibusdam phantasmatibus prorsus tollere velle, hostile, non amicum scriptum esse. Itaque censere, omnino abs te refutandum esse. Dixit etiam se illud scriptum accuratius perlecturum esse. Ego quoque, dum modo firmiori sim futurus valetudine, diligenter illud perlegam, deque eo plenius cum D. CURTIO conferam. Haec dum scribo, subijt in mentem Scotus ille, subtilis doctor dictus, quod de eo referant scriptores, fuisse a discipulis confossum stylis pugillaribus. Ego, tuum hunc antagonistam Scotum, quod admirandam et praeclaram Astronomicae doctrinae partem de parallaxibus, suis sophismatis penitus evertere cupiat, ab omnibus studiosis Astronomiae, Baculis Iacobaeis, Gnomonibus et Circinis multo iustius illo subigendum et confodiendum esse censerem. Hoc tu solus, cui nec facultas nec voluntas deest, calamo felicissime praestare poteris. B.V. Datae Pragae die 2. Decemb. novo stylo, Anno D. 1592.

Privilegium Caesareum emendatum, hodie mihi a D. CURTIO traditum, tibi mitto.

THAD.
text.english:
**To the most noble Master Tycho Brahe the Dane, lord of Uraniborg etc., his master and friend to be esteemed — greeting.**

Most noble sir, my master and friend to be esteemed. On a single day in the month of February of this year several letters of yours were delivered to me, these written at various times; and when I had read them through, I gave them also to our Master Curtius to read. From that very day I have passed all this time up to now in ill health: at the outset, to be sure, a huge and intolerable flatulent pain of the stomach kept recurring intermittently. Afterwards, when it had lasted for several days, and had again let up — sometimes for 14 days, sometimes for 20 — at last, after a most grievous attack, it broke out into jaundice [Ictericia], which after some days brought on a continuous fever. This [fever], joined with the jaundice, afflicted me for three months, namely August, September, and October. The hope of recovery was slight, whether one considered the nature and course of either malady, or the body that was its subject. Physicians, certainly, are accustomed to forebode ill for that patient in whom jaundice follows upon a fever. And now, besides these, there has come on the old age of 66 years. What, then, could I hope concerning the recovery of health? Meanwhile I have not shuddered at death: nay, I would most gladly have laid down this poor body, had it pleased the divine will. For I am now thoroughly weary of this wretched life; I see too that great calamities hang over our homeland — of which would that I were not a spectator. But although by the goodness of God alone I have been freed from a hard sickness, yet, my Tycho, the strength of my poor body has been so shaken that I readily understand it will never return. And that it will be from time to time the more feeble, various symptoms, by which I am very frequently assailed, foretell. For grievous catarrhs, and the old pain of the stomach, and gravel [arenulae], and various other pains rush upon me as though in a marshalled column, afflict me wondrously, and torment me. I add that I am all but reaching the borders of tympanites [dropsy of the belly]. But, as I have said, I do not take fright at these things, as one who knows that all things come to pass by God's counsel and will. I commend my whole self to God, and beseech him that he will be willing to grant that I may live the remainder of my life for him alone, in [his] fear, awaiting with eagerness the day of my departure. And so now, for the greater part, I send word of dismissal to all other studies, intent upon that one study alone: to learn well how to die.

Those letters of yours, I say, which I told you I had given to Master Curtius to read, I have not yet been able to recover, hindered by that long sickness. Today, which is the last day of November by the new style, when I had received this latest letter of yours, written on 28 September, from the Magdeburg courier — together with that truly bitter screed of that haughty, headstrong, biting, and ill-minded antagonist of yours — and had read through one page and another, and looked over that screed in passing, then on the very next day I gave both your letter and that screed to Master Curtius to read; and they were assuredly most welcome to him, since for a long time now [there had been] not even a word about you. On the following day, which was 2 December, I return to him, that I might hear his opinion of that screed (for the Magdeburg courier was making ready to depart, and I should not have wished him to return thither empty of my letters). He first bids you a hearty good-day, and [bids me] signify to you that that writing of your Scot rests upon no firm reasonings; that to wish to overthrow the whole doctrine of parallaxes utterly by certain phantasms of his own is the writing of an enemy, not a friend; and so he judges that it must by all means be refuted by you. He said too that he would read that writing through more carefully. I also, provided I shall be in firmer health, will read it through diligently, and will confer about it more fully with Master Curtius. While I write this, there has come into my mind that famous Scotus, called the Subtle Doctor — what the writers report of him, that he was stabbed through by his pupils with writing-styluses [stylis pugillaribus]. As for me, I should judge that this Scot, your antagonist — because he desires to overthrow utterly, by his sophisms, that admirable and excellent part of astronomical doctrine concerning parallaxes — ought far more justly than that other one to be subdued and stabbed through by all the students of Astronomy, with cross-staffs [Baculi Iacobaei], gnomons, and compasses [Circini]. This you alone, in whom neither the ability nor the will is wanting, will be able to accomplish most happily with your pen. Fare you well. Given at Prague, 2 December by the new style, in the year of the Lord 1592.

The amended Imperial privilege, handed to me today by Master Curtius, I send to you.

THAD.

- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus Hagecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayck, 1525–1600), the Bohemian court physician, astronomer, and alchemist at Prague — Emperor Rudolf II's *protomedicus*. Tycho's long-standing scientific ally and his chief conduit to the Imperial court; the observer of the 1572 nova whose *Dialexis* (1574) Tycho read closely. It was Hagecius who, after this correspondence, helped open the way to Tycho's reception by Rudolf II in 1599.
- ***D. CURTIUS*** — **Jacobus Curtius** (Jakob Kurz von Senftenau, *d.* 1594), Imperial Aulic vice-chancellor (*Reichsvizekanzler*) under Rudolf II and an accomplished mathematician-patron in Prague. He acts here as a learned referee of Tycho's dispute and as the channel for the *Privilegium Caesareum* (the Imperial printing privilege Tycho was seeking).
- **The "Scot" / "Scotus."** *tui Scoti … tuum hunc antagonistam Scotum* = "your Scot … this Scot, your antagonist." The antagonist is **John Craig** (Johannes Craig / Craigius), the Scottish physician and Aristotelian who disputed Tycho's denial of the celestial spheres and, in particular, attacked Tycho's parallax-based proof that the comets and the 1572 nova lay beyond the Moon. Hagecius exploits a sustained **pun on "Scotus"**: the antagonist is literally *the Scot* (Craig), but the name also summons **Johannes Duns Scotus**, the *doctor subtilis*. Hagecius recalls the (apocryphal) tale that Duns Scotus was stabbed to death by his pupils with their *styli* (writing-styluses), and turns it into a learned witticism: Craig deserves, even more justly, to be "stabbed through" by astronomers — not with styluses but with the instruments of the science he assails. The wordplay is preserved, not flattened.
- ***scriptum illud acerbo … antagonistae*** — "that bitter screed … of [your] antagonist": Craig's polemical writing against Tycho, which Tycho had forwarded with his own letter of 28 September. Curtius's verdict — that it "rests upon no firm reasonings" and "must by all means be refuted" — is reported, not endorsed by Hagecius as his own settled judgement (he reserves his fuller reading for when his health allows); the hedge is kept.
- **Astronomy.** *doctrina parallaxium / de parallaxibus* → **the doctrine of parallaxes / concerning parallaxes** — the crux of the whole exchange: parallax measurement was Tycho's instrument for placing comets and the nova in the supralunary heavens, and Craig's *phantasmata* ("phantasms," i.e. baseless fancies) sought to dissolve it.
- **Instruments.** *Baculis Iacobaeis* = **cross-staffs** (*radius astronomicus* / Jacob's staff; this chapter's convention); *Gnomonibus* = **gnomons**; *Circinis* = **compasses** (a pair of compasses / dividers — here the draughtsman's-and-observer's instrument, not a magnetic compass). The trio names the working tools of the practical astronomer, weaponised in the conceit.
- **Medicine.** *dolor ventriculi flatulentus* → flatulent pain of the stomach; *Ictericia / Icterus* → **jaundice**; *febris continua* → **continuous (continual) fever**; *Catharri* → **catarrhs**; *arenulae* → **gravel** (renal/urinary grit — period term, kept); *Tympanitis* → **tympanites** (drum-tight tympanitic dropsy of the abdomen; cf. *hydrops*, this chapter's convention) — "I am all but reaching the borders of tympanites," i.e. approaching that fatal condition. The clinical sequence (recurrent gastric pain → jaundice supervening on fever → bad prognosis) is rendered without modernising the nosology.
- ***bene mori addiscam*** — "to learn well how to die" (the *ars moriendi* topos); the rhetorical pivot of the opening section, kept as the *sententia* it is.
- ***patriae nostrae magnas impendere calamitates*** — "great calamities hang over our homeland": Hagecius's foreboding for Bohemia (the gathering religious-political tensions of the 1590s); reported as his apprehension, not as fact.
- **Closing formulae.** *S.* = *Salutem* ("greeting," this chapter's convention); *B.V.* = *Bene Vale* ("Fare you well"); *Datae Pragae* = "Given at Prague"; *THAD.* = the writer's abbreviated signature (Thaddaeus).
- **Privilegium Caesareum.** "The amended Imperial privilege" — the corrected/renewed Imperial printing privilege for Tycho's works, transmitted via Curtius; a concrete fruit of Hagecius's court brokerage.
- **Calendar / dating crux (flagged, not resolved).** The letter is **New Style** throughout (Hagecius, in Catholic Imperial Prague, writes Gregorian; Tycho on Hven and his Magdeburg courier were on the Julian Old Style — Tycho's enclosed letter is dated *28 September*, presumably O.S.). Hagecius's own narrative carries an **internal inconsistency**: he writes *"Hodie, qui est dies ultimus Novembris novo stylo"* ("Today, which is the last day of November, n.s.") = 30 November; says he gave the documents to Curtius *"altero mox die"* (the very next day); then *"Postera die, quae fuit 2 Decembris, ad ipsum redeo"* ("On the following day, which was 2 December, I return to him"); and dates the letter *"die 2. Decemb. novo stylo."* From 30 November, "the next day" is 1 December and "the following day" 2 December — so the two intermediate steps span 30 Nov → 1 Dec → 2 Dec, which is internally coherent only if *"altero mox die"* and *"Postera die"* denote the **same** following day described twice (30 Nov + 2 = 2 Dec leaves a one-day gap if read as three distinct consecutive days). Per this chapter's convention the dateline is reproduced as written and the discrepancy is recorded, not reconciled: the header date follows the source's own subscription, **2 December 1592 N.S.**, matching the catalogue label; the narrative day-count is flagged here. **A second minor discrepancy:** Hagecius gives his age as *"annorum 66,"* though a 1525 birth-year makes him 67 in late 1592 — reproduced as written, not corrected.

documents.abstract: Reports to Moritz that the Norwegian elk repeatedly promised to his late father Wilhelm could not be delivered alive despite repeated efforts.
documents.incipit: DVRCHLEUCHTIGER/ Hochgeborner/ Gnediger Fürst vnd Herr/ Nechst erbietung meiner …

text.original:
DEM DURCHLEUCHTIGEN/ HOCHGEBORNEN FÜRSTEN VND HERRN/ HERRN MORITZEN, LANDTGRAFFEN ZU HESSEN/ GRAFFEN ZU CATZENELNBOGEN/ DIETZ/ ZIEGENHAIN VND NIDDA: MEINEM GNEDIGEN HERRN.

DVRCHLEUCHTIGER/ Hochgeborner/ Gnediger Fürst vnd Herr/ Nechst erbietung meiner vntherthenigen willigen Dienste/ sol Ew. F. G. ich vnterthenigklich nicht vorhalten/ Wie dan ohne das sonder zweiffel E. F. G. gnedige wissenschafft haben werden/ Welcher gestalt der auch Durchleuchtiger Hochgeborner Fürst vnd Herr/ Her WILHELM, Landtgraff zu Hessen/ Graff zu Catzenelnbogen/ Dietz/ Ziegenhain vnd Nidda/ Hochloblicher gedachtnus/ zu vnterschiedlichen mahlen vnter anderen/ etlicher Ellende halben aus Norwegen seiner F. G. zum besten zu bestellen ghar fleissigk an mich geschrieben. Ob ich nuhn wol mir zum höchsten angelegen sein lassen/ Das seiner F. G. ich darinne meinen vnterthenigen geflissenen Willen im Werck bezeigen mochte/ auch etliche deroselbigen Thiere zu wege gebracht; So habe ich doch das Glück nicht haben mügen/ das dieselbigen lebendich an seine F. G. angebracht wurden. Als er aber endtlich Zeigern dieses an mich gnedichlich abgefertigt/ mit befellich/ er solte nitt zu rücke kommen/ ehe er deroselben Thiere mit sich brächte/ hab ich denselbigen Botten von hinnen ab in Norwegen abgefertiget/ vnd allen müglichen fleiss angewendet/ das mihr fünff sülcher Ellende geschafft würden/ Wie mir von Kuniglicher Majett. in Norwegen Stadthalteren/ meinem Blutsverwanten AXEL GVLDENSTERN zugesagt vnd gehalten ist worden. Von denselbigen fünffen/ die er da wol zu passe bekommen/ Hat er mir Zwei/ ein Weiblein vnd ein Menlein lebendig alhie angebracht. In mittelst aber ist alhie die trawrige Zeittunge von Hochgemelter Ihrer F. G. tödtlichen Abgang aus dieser Welt erschollen. Darob ich nit allein (weil er mir alzeit in Gnaden gewogen gewesen) sondern auch alle fromme Hertzen hohes vnd nidriges standes/ billich ein betrüptes mitleiden gehabt. Vnd were zwar wol zu wünschen gewesen/ da es dem Allerhöchsten also gefallen/ das sein F. G. noch ein lange zeitt der Cristlichen Kirchen/ auch sönst dem gantzen Vatterlandt Teutscher Nation zum trost vnd besten/ leben hette mügen. Wan aber seiner Gödtlichen Allmacht in dero weisen gericht nit zu greiffen/ so muß man auch hierinne sich desselbigen vnwandelbaren willen gehorsamlich vntergeben. Der getrewe Gott wolle seine Rutte/ vnd woluerdiente straffe von vns gnedichlich abwenden/ vnd hohe Hâupter vnd Fürsten/ so noch vbrich vnd lebendig geblieben/ erhalten/ Damit seine Kirche vnd Glidtmassen bei denselbigen dürch gnedige Göttliche hülffe/ Rhat/ Trost/ Schütz vnd Schirm haben mügen. Weil dan Gnediger Fürst vnd Herr/ ich es billich dafür halte/ das Hochgemeltes Ew. F. G. löblichen Herrn Vattern befellich zu folge/ Dennoch diese Thiere/ so vbrig/ vnd lebendig geblieben/ an bestimpten Ordt/ vnd an statt seiner löblichen F. G. itzo E. F. G. zugefertiget werden/ Also thue deroselbigen ich sie hiemit bei dero eignen Botten vnthertenigk vbersenden/ Mit vntertheniger Bitt/ E. F. G. wolle sölches nit anders als aus vnterthenigen geneigten willen gescheen/ gnedichlich vermercken/ Nicht weiniger auch/ als dero Hochlöbliger Herr Vatter gethon/ mihr in Gnaden gewogen sein. Könte ich zu alter zeitt vnd gelegenheit E. F. G. hinwiederumb vnthertenige dienste/ worinne es sein wolle/ erzeigen/ solten dieselbigen meinen geneigten vnd getrewen willen in Werck gnedichligk zu erspüren haben/ die ich hiemit im gnedigen schutz des Allerhöchsten bei guter Seel vnd Leibes Gesundtheidt/ vnd angehender heilsamer Regierung (zu welcher Ew. F. G. ich auch hiemit von Gott dem Allmechtigen Glück vnd Segen wünsche) lange Zeitt zu erhalten getrewligk vnd vnterthenigk thu befhelen.

Datum Vraniburgk auff Huen/ den 22. Decembris, Anno 1592.
Ewer F. G.
Dienstwilliger
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the Most Serene, High-born Prince and Lord, Lord Moritz, Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda: my gracious Lord.**

Most Serene, High-born, Gracious Prince and Lord: next after the tender of my humble, willing service, I should not humbly withhold from Your Princely Grace — as indeed Your Princely Grace will without doubt otherwise have gracious knowledge — in what manner the likewise Most Serene, High-born Prince and Lord, Lord Wilhelm, Landgrave of Hesse, Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda, of most laudable memory, did at sundry times among other matters write to me very diligently, that I should procure for his Princely Grace's benefit certain elk [Ellende] out of Norway. Now although I let it be of the highest concern to me that I might show his Princely Grace my humble, sedulous goodwill in this matter in deed, and also brought several of those animals to pass, yet I could not have the good fortune that the same were delivered alive to his Princely Grace. But when he at length graciously dispatched to me the bearer of this [letter], with command that he should not come back before he brought those animals with him, I dispatched that same messenger from here onward into Norway, and applied all possible diligence that five such elk be procured for me — as was promised to me, and kept, by His Royal Majesty's Governor in Norway, my blood-kinsman Axel Gyldenstern. Of those same five, which he there obtained in good condition, he has delivered to me here two alive, a female and a male. In the meantime, however, the sorrowful tidings have rung out here of the aforesaid His Princely Grace's mortal departure out of this world. Whereat not only I (since he was always graciously well-disposed toward me), but also all godly hearts of high and low estate, have justly had a grieved compassion. And it were indeed greatly to be wished — had it so pleased the Most High — that his Princely Grace might have lived yet a long time, to the comfort and benefit of the Christian Church, and likewise of the whole fatherland of the German nation. But since His Divine Omnipotence in its wise judgment is not to be grasped, so must one in this too submit obediently to that same unalterable will. May the faithful God graciously turn away His rod, and well-deserved punishment, from us, and preserve the high heads and princes who yet remain over and living, so that His Church and her members may have through them — by gracious divine help — counsel, comfort, protection, and shelter. Since then, Gracious Prince and Lord, I justly hold it fitting that, in accordance with the aforesaid command of Your Princely Grace's laudable Lord Father, these animals which have remained over and alive be nonetheless now consigned to the appointed place, and, in the stead of his laudable Princely Grace, to Your Princely Grace, accordingly I herewith humbly send them to the same by Your own messenger; with humble request that Your Princely Grace would graciously take note that this is done from none other than a humble, well-affected will, [and] would no less than your most laudable Lord Father did be graciously well-disposed toward me. Could I at any time and occasion show Your Princely Grace humble service in return, in whatever it might be, the same should graciously find my well-affected and faithful will [made good] in deed; [and] I herewith faithfully and humbly commend Your Princely Grace [to God], to be preserved a long time in the gracious protection of the Most High, in good health of soul and body, and in a wholesome government now begun (to which I herewith likewise wish Your Princely Grace fortune and blessing from God the Almighty).

Given at Uraniborg on Hven, the 22nd of December, in the year 1592.
Your Princely Grace's
ready in service,
Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** Tycho Brahe, writing from Uraniborg, his observatory-house on Hven.
- **Recipient.** ***Moritz, Landtgraff zu Hessen*** = **Moritz ("the Learned"), Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1572–1632), who had just succeeded his father. The full titulature *Graff zu Catzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain vnd Nidda* (Count of Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain, and Nidda) is the standing Hesse-Kassel style and is preserved by this chapter's convention; *Katzenelnbogen* is left in its period spelling *Catzenelnbogen* in the source.
- ***Her WILHELM, … Hochloblicher gedachtnus*** = **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1532–1592), Moritz's father and Tycho's long-standing scientific correspondent. The phrase *Hochloblicher gedachtnus* ("of most laudable memory") marks him as recently deceased: Wilhelm died **25 August 1592 (O.S.)**, which the letter reports as the "sorrowful tidings" that arrived while the elk were being procured. Thus the gift, originally requested by the father, is here redirected to the son.
- ***AXEL GVLDENSTERN*** = **Axel Gyldenstierne** (1542–1603), Royal Governor (*Stadthalter / statholder*) of Norway 1588–1601, here named as Tycho's *Blutsverwanter* ("blood-kinsman" — the Brahe and Gyldenstierne families were related by marriage and blood among the Danish high nobility). He supplied the elk from Norway.
- ***Kuniglicher Majett.*** = "His Royal Majesty" — **Christian IV of Denmark-Norway** (a minor until 1596; Gyldenstierne governed Norway in the crown's name).
- **Subject term: *Ellende* / *Ellende* (sg./pl.).** Early New High German *Ell(en)d* = the **elk** (European elk / moose, *Alces alces*; modern German *Elch*), a prized Scandinavian game animal sought by German princes for their menageries and parks. Rendered "elk" throughout; "those animals" (*deroselbigen / dieselbigen Thiere*) refers to the same. The letter records that of five elk obtained in Norway, **two** reached Hven alive — *ein Weiblein vnd ein Menlein*, "a female and a male" (i.e. a cow and a bull elk).
- **Negation check.** The two load-bearing negatives are reproduced exactly: *sol … ich vnterthenigklich **nicht** vorhalten* ("I should **not** withhold" — a litotes of disclosure, i.e. "I make known"), and the courier's commission *er solte **nitt** zu rücke kommen/ ehe er … brächte* ("he was **not** to come back before he brought [them]"). No negation has been added or dropped. The litotes is kept literal ("should not withhold") rather than smoothed to "I hereby report."
- **Chancery register.** The whole letter is in the deferential subject's register to a prince: *Ew./E. F. G.* = *Euer/Eure Fürstliche Gnaden*, "Your Princely Grace"; *vntherthenig(lich)* "humble / humbly"; *gnedichlich* "graciously." Spelling is Tycho's own Saxon-inflected chancery German as set by his Uraniborg/printed *Epistolae*: *v/u* for *u/v* (*vnd*, *vntherthenig*), *-tz/-ck*, doubled vowels (*Hâupter*, *Zeittunge*), *mügen* for *mögen*, *dürch*, *sülcher*. The circumflex in *Hâupter* is reproduced as printed.
- **Edition of record.** Printed by Tycho himself in *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Uraniborg/Wandsbek, 1596), the volume from which the edition's text descends; in Dreyer's *Opera Omnia* the Hesse-Kassel correspondence is in vol. VI. No manuscript witness is recorded in the edition.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *den 22. Decembris, Anno 1592* — given in the running civil style, no Roman-calendar idiom. Denmark used the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar in 1592 (and until 1700); the date is therefore O.S. Hesse-Kassel (Protestant) was likewise still Old Style at this date. No in-letter date discrepancy; the catalogue label ("1592. 22. december") agrees with the dateline.
- **Place.** *Vraniburgk auff Huen* = **Uraniborg on Hven** (the island in the Øresund granted to Tycho by Frederik II in 1576).

Compared the published English line-by-line against the German the transcribed original: the address/titles of Landgrave Moritz, the account of Wilhelm's repeated requests for elk from Norway, the dispatch of the bearer with orders not to return without the animals, the arithmetic (5 elk procured via Axel Gyldenstern, 2 delivered alive here, one female one male), the news of Wilhelm's death and the conventional condolence/submission language, the decision to forward the two surviving animals to Moritz via his own messenger in his late father's stead, and the closing date (22 December 1592) and signature all have full, accurate counterparts. No invented facts, no dropped clauses, no flipped subjects/antecedents found.

documents.abstract: Reports Galileo's new mathematics chair at Padua, Maginus's Tabula Tetragonica under Tycho's patronage, and a Venetian plan to dispatch a mathematician to Egypt on Tycho's behalf.
documents.incipit: ... MAGINVS per totam ferme æstatem hîc PATAVII et VENETIIS moratus est. Quâ de caussâ, …

text.original:
... MAGINVS per totam ferme æstatem hîc PATAVII et VENETIIS moratus est. Quâ de caussâ, non satis constat.

Interea GALLILÆVS de GALLILÆIS FLORENTINVS Professionem Mathematicam hîc adeptus est, qui suarum lectionum septimo Decembris initium fecit. Exordium erat splendidum in magnâ auditorum frequentiâ. A Dno. PINELLO is liberaliter commendatur, quem, si posset, perlibenter in Dni. TYCHONIS amicitiam insinuaret. Tu, qui animum TYCHONIS novisti, poteris, quod ex re erit, in hisce disponere. MAGINVS êdidit nuper librum, cui Titulum fecit [Tabula Tetragonica] sub TYCHONIS patrocinio. Exemplar mihi ad te mittendum dedit, quod primâ occasione transmittam. Retulit etiam, Illustrissimos VENETOS in consilio rogatorum deliberasse, ut aliquis Matheseως peritus stipendio 300. Coronatorum in ÆGYPTVM ablegaretur, qui pro TYCHONE isthic observaret. Tantæ enim hîc TYCHO certe est celebritatis, quantæ nemo eorum, qui nunc vivunt.

Datæ Patavii 28. Decembris Anni 1592.
text.english:
... Maginus stayed here, at Padua and at Venice, for almost the whole summer. For what reason, it is not sufficiently clear.

Meanwhile Galileo de' Galilei of Florence has obtained the Chair of Mathematics here, who made the beginning of his lectures on the seventh of December. The opening was splendid, before a great throng of hearers. He is generously recommended by Master Pinelli, who, if he could, would most gladly insinuate him into the friendship of Master Tycho. You, who have come to know Tycho's disposition, will be able to arrange matters in this affair as shall be fitting. Maginus has lately published a book, to which he gave the title [*Tabula Tetragonica*], under Tycho's patronage. He gave me a copy to be sent on to you, which I shall forward at the first opportunity. He reported, too, that the Most Illustrious Venetians had deliberated in the Council of the *rogati* that some man skilled in mathematics [Matheseōs] should be dispatched to Egypt at a salary of 300 *coronati*, to observe there on Tycho's behalf. For so great, assuredly, is Tycho's renown here as belongs to none of those who are now living.

Given at Padua, the 28th of December, the year 1592.

Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent / addressee.** Both are unidentified in the catalogue: an *Unknown doctor of medicine* writing from Padua to an *Unknown Danish student* who is in personal contact with Tycho ("you, who have come to know Tycho's disposition"). The writer is evidently a member of the Paduan academic-medical orbit reporting Italian astronomical news northward; the addressee functions as an intermediary to Tycho. No firmer identification is asserted.
- **Fragment.** The leading ellipsis ("...") is in the source: this is an excerpt, the closing portion of a longer letter; only the final movement and dateline survive in the edition. Translated as the partial text it is.
- ***Maginus*** = **Giovanni Antonio Magini** (1555–1617), professor of mathematics at Bologna and a correspondent of Tycho's. The *librum cui Titulum fecit Tabula Tetragonica* is Magini's *Tabula tetragonica* (Venice, 1592), a table of squares for computation; that it appeared *sub Tychonis patrocinio* ("under Tycho's patronage") is confirmed by the surrounding scholarship.
- ***Galileo de' Galilei of Florence*** = **Galileo Galilei** (1564–1642). He took up the chair of mathematics at the University of Padua in late 1592; the letter's notice that he *initium fecit septimo Decembris* ("made the beginning [of his lectures] on the seventh of December") is a near-contemporary witness to the start of his Paduan inaugural — here said to have drawn *magna auditorum frequentia* ("a great throng of hearers").
- ***Pinellus*** = **Gian Vincenzo Pinelli** (1535–1601), the Paduan humanist whose library and circle were the hub of Veneto learning; he is reported as eager to bring Galileo into Tycho's friendship. *insinuaret* ("would insinuate / introduce") kept in its period sense of effecting an introduction, not pejorative.
- **Greek.** *Matheseως* — the Greek genitive *Mathéseōs* ("of mathematics / of the science"), the Greek ending **-εως** grafted onto the Greek stem within an otherwise Latin sentence (*aliquis Matheseōs peritus* = "someone skilled in mathematics"). Transcribed as printed and rendered; the code-switch is flagged, not silently Latinised to *Matheseos*.
- ***consilio rogatorum*** — the Venetian **Council (Consiglio) of the *Rogati***, i.e. the Senate (the *Pregadi*); the senators were the *rogati* ("those summoned/invited"). Rendered "the Council of the *rogati*" with the technical Venetian term kept.
- ***Coronatorum*** — *coronati*, the gold *scudo/corona* coin; "300 *coronati*" kept as the named coin, not converted.
- ***in Aegyptum ablegaretur … qui pro Tychone isthic observaret*** — "should be dispatched to Egypt … to observe there on Tycho's behalf." The notice of a proposed Venetian-funded astronomical mission to Egypt observing *pro Tychone* is the letter's testimony to Tycho's Italian celebrity (*Tantae … celebritatis, quantae nemo eorum qui nunc vivunt* — "of such renown as belongs to none now living").
- **Reading note.** The working transcription reads *isthic* ("here/there"); the Dreyer *Opera Omnia* page image (vol. VI) prints *istinc* ("from there / thence," idiomatically "there"). Both yield "observe there"; the translation follows the sense common to both. The bracketed *[Tabula Tetragonica]* reproduces the editor's square brackets in the source.
- **Edition of record.** The source's edition field names the *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica*; the letter is, however, an epistola printed in Dreyer's *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia* (the *Epistolae* volumes), and the matching page image is in vol. VI. The field is reported as given and the actual printed locus noted; no MS witness is recorded in the edition.
- **Calendar / place crux.** Dateline: *Datae Patavii 28. Decembris Anni 1592* = "Given at **Padua**, 28 December 1592." The catalogue label reads "1592. 28. december n.s. **Bologna**." **The dateline says Padua, not Bologna**; the header therefore leads with Padua and notes the catalogued place. The *n.s.* of the label is consistent with a writer in the Veneto (Catholic territory, on the Gregorian calendar since 1582); the date is preserved as written and tagged **New Style** — not converted. The 7 December lecture-date is likewise N.S. as written.

documents.abstract: Asks Rantzau to assist with forwarding perspective drawings sent by his former architect, now supervising construction of Varberg castle in Halland.
documents.incipit: QUAMVIS perpaucis abhinc diebus, nobilissime et amantissime Domine RANZOVI, ultimis tuis …

text.original:
HENRICO RANZOVIO PRODUCI CIMBRICO S. D. TYCHO BRAHE.

QUAMVIS perpaucis abhinc diebus, nobilissime et amantissime Domine RANZOVI, ultimis tuis ad me datis literis nonnihil responderim: facit tamen diutina illa, quæ nobis intercedit, amicitia, tum negotium etiam quoddam postmodum interveniens, ut te alijs insuper compellare nihil addubitem; ex quo illam hanc quoque operam superioribus officijs erga me suis non invite aggregaturam, id vero, quicquid est, tua auctoritate et adiumento promptissime ac ocijssime istic expeditum iri mihi persuadeam. Commodum autem accidit, ut meus olim architectus, quem in quibusdam Astronomicis et Geometricis, dum mecum esset, instruxeram, alias suopte ingenio ad delineationes artis perspectivæ proclivem, ad me imagines quasdam calamo repræsentatas, quas frontispicio et calci meorum librorum hîc excudendorum adiungere constitui, huc ex Hallandia (ubi iam apud fratrem meum Varbergi arcis structuræ, Regis mandato, præest) transmiserit. Quas nunc ad te, mi RANZOVI, mitto, amice rogans, velis tua autoritate et iussu efficere, ut Hamburgi vel Lubecæ ab excellenti quodam artifice quam optime incidantur, mihique prima quaque occasione, quod intra sex vel septem hebdomadas fieri quam maxime cuperem, sartæ tectæ remittantur. Quicquid cœlatori pro labore pendendum sit, certior a te factus lubens solvam. Da quæso operam, ut meis hac in parte votis prompte et mature satisfiat. Præstiteris hoc nomine non solum mihi rem admodum gratam, sed et tibi ipsi studijsque communibus operam (uti spero) dignam et utilem elocaveris. Ego si qua in re tibi vicissim pro his alijsque affatim erga me exhibitis benevolentiæ officijs inservire queam, faxo ne studium et voluntatem de te pariter, quocunque modo possum, bene merendi in me unquam desideres.

Vale.
Uraniburgi 9. Ianuarij An. 93.
text.english:
**To Heinrich Rantzau, Governor of the Cimbrian land — Tycho Brahe sends greeting.**

Although but a very few days ago, most noble and most loving Master Rantzau, I made some reply to the last letter you sent me, yet that long-standing friendship which subsists between us — and also a certain piece of business which has since come up — makes me not at all hesitate to approach you with further matters besides; whence I persuade myself that you will not unwillingly add this present service too to your earlier kindnesses towards me, and that this matter, whatever it amounts to, will be dispatched there most promptly and most speedily by your authority and assistance. Now it has fallen out conveniently that my former architect — whom, while he was with me, I had instructed in certain matters of astronomy and geometry, being besides by his own native talent inclined to the drawings of the perspective art — has transmitted to me from Halland (where he now superintends, by the King's command, the building works of Varberg castle in the service of my brother) certain images rendered with the pen, which I have determined to attach to the frontispiece and the tail-piece of my books that are to be printed here. These I now send to you, my Rantzau, asking as a friend that you would by your authority and command bring it about that they be engraved at Hamburg or Lübeck, as excellently as possible, by some outstanding craftsman, and be sent back to me safe and sound at the very first opportunity — which I should most exceedingly wish to be done within six or seven weeks. Whatever is to be paid to the engraver for his labour, once informed of it by you I will gladly discharge. Take pains, I beg, that my wishes in this matter be satisfied promptly and in good time. By so doing you will not only have rendered me a most welcome service, but will also (as I hope) have bestowed upon yourself and upon our common studies a labour worthy and useful. As for myself, if in any matter I can in turn be of service to you in return for these and the other offices of goodwill abundantly shown towards me, I will see to it that you never find wanting in me the zeal and the will to deserve well of you likewise, in whatever way I can.

Farewell.
At Uraniborg, 9 January, the year [15]93.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe**, writing from **Uraniborg** on the island of Hven.
- **Correspondent.** *Henricus Ranzovius* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (also Henrik Rantzau, 1526–1598), royal *Statthalter* (governor) of the duchies of Schleswig-Holstein for the Danish crown, humanist, astrological enthusiast, patron and bibliophile, and one of Tycho's most active intermediaries to the German printing and engraving trade. The two corresponded frequently, and Rantzau repeatedly used his standing in the Hamburg–Lübeck region to arrange technical and printing services for Tycho.
- ***Produci Cimbrico*** — "Governor of the Cimbrian land": *Cimbria* is the humanist name for the Cimbrian (Jutland) peninsula / the duchies of Schleswig-Holstein, so the title styles Rantzau as the (vice-regal) ruler of that land. *Produx* here renders his governorship in elevated humanist diction; "Governor" is given, with the honorific weight noted rather than inflated to a literal "Duke."
- ***meus olim architectus*** — "my former architect": the draughtsman-architect Tycho had earlier employed and trained at Hven, now (1593) directing, by royal command, the building works at **Varberg** castle in **Halland** in the service of Tycho's brother. *apud fratrem meum* = "in the service of my brother" — Tycho's brother **Steen Brahe**, then lensmand (fief-holder/governor) of Varberg. The architect is most plausibly identified with **Hans van Steenwinckel the Elder**, who worked at both Hven and Varberg, though the letter does not name him; the identification is left unstated here.
- ***delineationes artis perspectivae*** — "the drawings of the perspective art": the architect's skill in perspective draughtsmanship, which Tycho exploits for the engraved plates.
- ***imagines … calamo repraesentatas*** — "images rendered with the pen": pen-drawn designs (the artwork) to be cut by an engraver.
- ***frontispicio et calci meorum librorum*** — "the frontispiece and the tail-piece of my books": the engravings are destined as the opening and closing plates of the books Tycho was preparing to print at his own Uraniborg/Hven press (*hîc excudendorum*, "to be printed here"). This places the letter among the documents of Tycho's self-publishing programme of the 1590s.
- ***incidantur … coelatori*** — *incido* "to engrave / cut (in metal)" and *coelator/caelator* "engraver, chaser": the technical vocabulary of copperplate engraving, to be executed by a master craftsman at **Hamburg** or **Lübeck**.
- ***sartae tectae*** — the legal-idiomatic phrase *sarta tecta* ("kept in good repair," lit. "patched and roofed"), here used figuratively of the plates being returned "safe and sound / in good order."
- **Internal dating reference.** *perpaucis abhinc diebus … nonnihil responderim* — Tycho notes he had answered Rantzau's previous letter "a very few days ago"; this is a chronological pointer to a slightly earlier letter, not a dating discrepancy.
- **Calendar / place.** *Uraniburgi 9. Ianuarij An. 93* = "At Uraniborg, 9 January [15]93" — **Old Style** (Julian; Denmark retained O.S. until 1700). The dateline as written agrees with the catalogue label (1593, 9 January, Uraniborg); no discrepancy.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S. D.* = *salutem dicit*, "sends greeting"; *Vale* = "Farewell."

documents.abstract: Thanks Kurz for securing the Imperial privilege for his astronomical works and recalls Kurz's earlier expressions of goodwill and favour toward the mathematical arts.
documents.incipit: MAGNIFICE et generosissime Domine CURTI, amice summopere colende, non sine grata mente et …

text.original:
MAGNIFICO AMPLISSIMOQUE VIRO, NOBILITATE GENERIS, PRUDENTIA ATQUE ERUDITIONE ADMODUM CONSPICUO DOMINO IACOBO CURTIO A SENFFTENAV, CÆSAREAe MAIESTATIS CONSILIARIO ATQUE IMPERIJ PROCANCELLARIO DIGNISSIMO, AMICO SUO IN PRIMIS HONORANDO. S.

MAGNIFICE et generosissime Domine CURTI, amice summopere colende, non sine grata mente et memoria vetera tua in me praestita officia etiamnum recolo et amplector, dum tua, qua plurimum vales apud augustissimam Caesaream Maiestatem, auctoritate et consilio, amplissimum , huius Maiestatis Privilegium meis Operibus Astronomicis praefigendum mihi antea clementer impertiri procuraveris, atque gravissimam tuam de his artibus censuram ac propensissimam de ijs bene merendi voluntatem, literis tuis insignem quoque candoris et benevolentiae erga me tuae significationem ostendentibus affatim declarâris. Quibus pristinis in me exhibitis promeritis non parvum insuper cumulum iam nuper aggregaveris, dum recognitum hoc et quibusdam auctum Caesareae Maiestatis Diploma, quo omni ex parte laborum ac impensarum mearum indemnitati caveretur, gratiosissime mihi concedi et transmitti effeceris. Qua de causa et sincerum tuum erga me et haec sublimia studia (quibus ipsemet etiam non modice afficeris, adeo ut si Reipub. administrandae cura his altioribus coelestium siderum contemplationibus non invideret, facile in his utilissimum quid e divite praestantis tui ingenij penu depromeres) amorem luculentius perspiciam, et me rursum debendae gratitudinis nomine tibi in posterum arctius devinciri agnoscam. Tibi itaque, amplifice et praestantissime vir, pro tantis totiesque in me elocatis officijs gratias ago ingentes et immortales, meque tibi vicissim recipio, si quam re unquam grati erga te animi declarare indicia concedatur, perpetuo fore quam promptissimum. Caeterum ex Domini D. THADDÆI literis unâ allatis, insolens illud mei Antagonistae scriptum ad tuas pervenisse manus cognovi. Quem quidem virum in Mathematicis apprime versatum esse non diffiteor. Verumtamen Aristotelicis Disciplinis, quibus ab ineunte aetate (prout plerisque in illa regione usu venire solet) imbutus, usqueadeo serviliter se mancipavit, ut quae ab his vel latum ungvem dissentiant, quantumvis veriora et aliter invictis Apodixibus demonstrata agnoscere et fateri aut nolit aut nequeat. Proinde ex contentioso et arroganti hoc scripto satis perspicere potes, te nimis de eo candide antea sensisse, dum eiusmodi contradictiones ita pro summa animi tui ingenuitate excusaveris, ac si id ille eiusque similes vellent, ut simulate obiectiones quasdam speciosas proponendo pleniorem et exactiorem harum rerum doctrinam publici commodi et posterorum gratia extorquerent. Illum enim rem serio agere et pro ARISTOTELE suo tanquam pro aris et focis pugnare, hinc non obscure animadvertes. Rogo itaque T. M. ut antagonisticam hanc compilationem, utut pretiosissimis suis otijs indignam, diligentius introspicere, mecumque unâ de hac gravissimum suum communicare iudicium non dedignetur. Quamvis autem insulsae eius argutiae confestim a me non immerito essent redarguendae, malo tamen Progymnasmatis Astronomicis, quibus nunc incumbo, in lucem edendis operam locare, quam id generis cavillationes inanes et sophisticas refellendo temporis iacturam facere. Ubi vero primus noster, qui de Nova Stella ubertim tractat Tomus, unâ cum subsequentibus Cometarum libris, in publicum exierit, tum demum candidi et cordati aestimatores non difficulter discernent, quam perperam et inique CRAIGUS his nostris, a Philosophia Peripateticorum dissentientibus placitis tantopere adversetur. Prodibit forte suo etiam tempore discipulorum meorum aliquis, qui eius invalidas obiectiones facile diluat. Misi autem unâ cum his ipsis Domino THADDÆO primum horum (de quibus dixi) Progymnasmatum nostrorum librum, tibi simul exhibendum, ut si quando a gravioribus Reipub. administrandae munijs nonnihil superesset temporis, eum evolvere atque solertissimam tuam de eodem censuram literis aperire non degravarere. Quod ut facias, maiorem in modum te rogatum habeo. Sequentem Tomum, qui trium superiorum Planetarum Phaenomena emendate expediet, mecum aliquantisper reservo, cum ut unam adhuc ultra res, quas in promptu habeo, acronychiam in Saturno animadversionem, ob tarditatem motus eius, qua lente peripheriam sui Eccentrici emetitur, nanciscar, tum praesertim, ut Martem, quando Soli primam decuriam Virginis obtinenti iuxta Perigaeum sui Eccentrici hoc anno opponetur, sedulo observare liceat. Incidit enim tunc diversitas utriusque calculi Alphonsini et Copernicei, quae maxima pene in eius motu contingere potest, adeo ut haec trientem fere unius signi attingat. Quare restitutio nostra in huius Sideris apparentijs tunc maxime probabitur. Apparebit autem tunc Mars solito maior, ita ut ab imperitis pro insueto aliquo sidere reputabitur. Sed ne te Politicis rebus ob illustre quod sustines officium indesinenter occupatum, meis his literis nimium interpellem, pluribus supersedeo. Vale et amicitiam nostram semel per literas incoatam, ijsdem, siquidem aliter fieri nequit, conservare et stabilire non gravere. Quod et vicissim a me expectabis.

Iterum quam felicissime vale.
Datae Uraniburgi 19. Aprilis Anno 1593.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the magnificent and most ample man, most conspicuous in nobility of family, in prudence, and in erudition, Master Jacob Kurz von Senftenau, most worthy Councillor of His Imperial Majesty and Vice-Chancellor of the Empire, his friend to be honoured above all — greeting.**

Magnificent and most noble Master Kurz, friend to be cherished in the highest degree: not without a grateful mind and memory do I even now recall and embrace the services you of old rendered me — when, by that authority and counsel of yours, in which you have great weight with His most august Imperial Majesty, you formerly took care that the most ample Privilege of His Majesty, to be set at the front of my astronomical Works, should be graciously bestowed upon me; and when, by letters of yours that displayed also a notable token of your candour and goodwill toward me, you abundantly declared your most weighty judgement of these arts and your most ready disposition to deserve well of them. To these former merits shown toward me you have lately added no small further heap, when you most graciously brought it about that this Diploma of His Imperial Majesty — revised and augmented in certain particulars, by which provision was made on every side for the indemnity of my labours and expenses — should be granted and transmitted to me. For which reason I more clearly perceive both your sincere love toward me and toward these lofty studies (by which you yourself too are not slightly affected, so that, were the care of administering the Commonwealth not to begrudge you these higher contemplations of the heavenly stars, you would readily draw forth from the rich storehouse of your excellent genius something most useful in them); and I acknowledge that I am once again, by the name of the gratitude I owe, more closely bound to you for the future. To you, therefore, most ample and most excellent man, for services so great and so often laid out upon me, I give immense and undying thanks, and I in turn pledge myself to you, [promising] that — if ever it be granted me to declare by some deed the tokens of a mind grateful toward you — I shall perpetually be most ready [to do so]. For the rest, from the letter of Master Doctor Thaddaeus brought along [with yours], I have learned that that insolent writing of my Antagonist has come into your hands. The man I do not deny to be exceedingly well versed in mathematics. Nevertheless he has so slavishly made himself a bondman to the Aristotelian disciplines — in which he was steeped from his earliest years (as is wont to happen with most people in that region) — that whatever dissents from them by even a finger's breadth, however truer it be and otherwise demonstrated by invincible proofs [Apodixes], he either will not or cannot acknowledge and confess. Accordingly, from this contentious and arrogant writing you can see well enough that you earlier judged of him too charitably, when out of the great ingenuousness of your mind you so excused contradictions of this sort, as though he and his like wished, by feigningly putting forward certain specious objections, to extort a fuller and more exact doctrine of these matters for the public good and for the sake of posterity. For that he is acting in earnest, and fighting for his Aristotle as if for altar and hearth, you will here not obscurely observe. I therefore ask Your Magnificence not to disdain to look into this antagonistic compilation more diligently — unworthy as it is of your most precious leisure-hours — and to share with me your most weighty judgement upon it. But although his insipid quibbles ought rightly to be refuted by me without delay, I prefer nevertheless to bestow my labour on bringing into the light the *Astronomical Progymnasmata* on which I am now engaged, rather than to waste time in confuting cavils of that kind, empty and sophistical. But once our first Volume — which treats copiously of the New Star — together with the ensuing books on the Comets, has gone forth into public, then at last candid and judicious appraisers will not find it hard to discern how wrongly and unfairly **Craig** so greatly opposes these doctrines of ours, which dissent from the Philosophy of the Peripatetics. Perhaps in due time some one of my pupils too will come forth, who may easily dissolve his feeble objections. I have sent, however, along with this very [letter], to Master Thaddaeus the first book of these *Progymnasmata* of ours (of which I have spoken), to be shown to you as well, so that, if ever a little time should remain over from the weightier duties of administering the Commonwealth, you would not find it burdensome to unroll it and to disclose by letter your most skilful judgement of it. That you may do so, I have asked you most especially. The next Volume, which will treat correctly the Phenomena of the three superior Planets, I reserve with me for some while — both that I may obtain one further observation, beyond the matters I have ready to hand, namely an acronychal [rising] in Saturn, on account of the slowness of its motion, by which it measures out the circumference of its eccentric so slowly; and especially that I may be permitted diligently to observe Mars when this year it will be in opposition to the Sun, which then holds the first decan of Virgo, near the perigee of its eccentric. For there falls then the divergence of the two computations, the Alphonsine and the Copernican, which can occur in its [Mars's] motion well-nigh at its greatest, so that this [divergence] reaches almost a third of one sign. Wherefore our restoration [of astronomy] will then be most amply proved in the appearances of this Star. Mars will then appear larger than usual, so that by the unskilled it will be reckoned some unaccustomed star. But lest, with these letters of mine, I interrupt you too much — you who, on account of the illustrious office you bear, are ceaselessly occupied with political affairs — I forbear to say more. Farewell, and do not find it burdensome to preserve and make firm the friendship between us, once begun through letters, by those same [letters], since indeed it cannot be done otherwise. Which you shall in turn expect from me.

Again, most happily, farewell.
Given at Uraniborg, 19 April, the year 1593.
TYCHO BRAHE.
