text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD THADDÆUM HAGECIUM.

PLURIMUM sane gavisus sum, optime mi THADDÆE, quod ex literis tuis, his ipsis diebus mihi redditis, perceperim te adhuc mediocriter bona, pro hac ætate, frui valetudine. Verebar enim ne gravissimi illi morbi, quos te diu multumque infestasse, ultimis significasti, sæviores adhuc redditi, te nimis valetudinarium lecto detinerent, vel forte humanitus tibi quid interea accidisset, præsertim ex quo meis literis præcedente anno per civem quendam Gorlicensem ad te datis nihil tanto tempore responderis. Itaque valde etiam nunc addubito, an has recte acceperis, siquidem nullam mentionem in his literis facias, vel de contentis earum vel de Tomo nostro primo Progymnasmatum Astronomicorum, quem unâ Magnifico Domino IACOBO CURTIO et tibi inspiciendum dijudicandumque misi. Imo iam bis tibi eiusdem libri exemplar communicari curavi, posterius tamen locupletius auctum et in quo pauca admodum desiderarentur, quo minus publici iuris fierent. Mirari autem satis nequeo, quod in nullis literis interea ad me datis huius rei mentionem facias, quare ad aliorum manus pervenisse hos libros et alibi detineri suspicor. Id equidem invite ferrem. Quod Astronomica studia in hoc senio apud te conticescant, quodque Chymica ob vanitatem neglexeris, recte fieri censeo, his enim nimium indulgere, est, ut plurimum, oleum et operam perdere, illis penitius tractandis valetudinis in hac ingravescente ætate afflictio non sustinet; optime igitur feceris, si supramundanis, ut te etiam facere dicis, contemplandis et valetudini curandæ solummodo intentus fueris. Privilegium Cæsareum ultimum illud et quadam in parte locupletatum Doct. SAGERUS Lubecensis iam dudum ad me misit, pro quo etiam in ultimis literis et Ampliss. D. CURTIO et tibi gratias obnixe egi, quod et nunc facio.

Cometam quendam in Iulio et Augusto superioris anni illuxisse certum quidem est ex multorum relatione, at nos eum hîc Uraniburgi, utut diligentius forte quam alij cœlestibus attendentes, non conspeximus, tum quod rarissima ijs temporibus hîc fuerit serenitas, tum quia versus Septentrionem, si quando cœlum per intervalla sudum esset, chasmata crebra viserentur, quæ Cometam istic versantem per se, uti audio, admodum tenuem existentem, facile visui subduxerunt. Invigilavimus ijsdem mensibus omni serena nocte (quæ tamen uti dictum est crebra non fuit) Martis potissimum stellæ ad acronychium situm tendentis observationibus, ut discrimen calculi Alphonsini et Copernicei, quod in ipsa oppositione 9 gradus (maiori quam unquam alias intervallo) excessit, cœlitus dirimere liceret, utque hanc acronychiam Martis observationem cæteris per plurimos antecedentes annos habitis coniungerem. Deprehensus autem est Mars (ut et hoc obiter hîc indicem) quando Soli e diametro opponebatur, numeros COPERNICI 4½ gradibus excedere, Alphonsinos vero integris quinis gradibus antevertere, quæ differentia maior quam alias in ♂, cum pernox est, obveniens propter vicinitatem Perigæi eccentrici (ut communiter loquar) contigit, illic enim error in vero Apogæi loco, qui apud COPERNICUM quinos gradus attingit, admodum fœcundus existit, ut de eccentricitate, quam is suis hypothesibus patrocinari volens nimium coarctavit, ut de alijs quæ huc requiruntur nunc non dicam. Interim vero (ut ad rem redeam) dum Martis observationi, quoties noctes defæcatæ id permiserunt, gnaviter insistentes, Cometam illum, de quo iam rumor increbuerat, uspiam videre nequivimus, utut data opera illam cœli plagam circa finem Augusti crebrius inspicientes, quemadmodum et alij, qui in vicina Haffnia aliquas noctes huic inspiciendo vigiles traduxerunt, voto suo frustrati sunt. Perscriptum nihilominus ad me est, quod studiosus quidam Danus CHRISTIERNUS IOHANNIS RIPENSIS nomine, qui antequam in Germaniam concessisset, aliquot annis in exercitijs Astronomicis hîc mihi inservierat, confecto uno vel altero ad imitationem meorum instrumentulo, eius observationi, qua licuit accuratione, incubuisse, neque tamen aliquid certi nisi bis, ob exilitatem Cometæ et serenitatis penuriam denotasse. Quicquid tamen id fuerit, is brevi e Cimbria Patria sua (nuper enim in Daniam reversus est) huc ad me veniens secum adferet. Tunc si viderim operæ pretium esse, observationes istas examinabo atque an Parallaxes inde scrutari liceat, tentabo, ut vel sic, id quod nobis invitis neglectum est, quodammodo resarciam, atque hunc Cometam quinis illis maxima diligentia a me Cœlitus denotatis atque secundo Tomo Progymnasmatum Astronomicorum descriptis adiungam, mutuando mei quondam discipuli observationes atque eas loco mearum usurpando.

Quæ cl. ille PEUCERUS tibi de hac Crinitâ per literas significavit, nihil ferme ad rem faciunt, nullas enim habet observationes, quæ locum eius apparentem prodant, nedum quæ Parallaxibus enodandis sufficiant, imo ne quidem diem rectum annotat, quo illum viderit, neque ista invicem congruunt, quod ab initio dicat, se saltem bis eum vidisse in Asterismo Ursæ maioris et postea circa finem subiungat, quod a Capellæ et Hædorum sidere non procul constiterit; hi enim duo asterismi ultra duodecimam cœli partem inter se distant. Qualis igitur quæso hæc fuerit observatio etiam ex solo visu petita? Ista igitur otiosa et mentione indigna uti fuere, ita etiam nunc sint, relinquamus.

Gaudeo et præstantissimo illi D. CURTIO communi amico nostro congratulor, quod Sextantis instrumentum ex officina Lantgraviana adeptus sit, quo siderum intercapedines infallibiliter rimari possit. Est procul dubio ad imitationem cuiusdam ex meis factum, quo per unicum observatorem distantiæ mensurantur, licet nonnihil maiori negotio quam alijs Sextantibus, qui duos requirunt collimatores, quod si sic est, habet rimulas iuxta centrum prioribus pinnacidijs parallelas et divisionem per puncta transversalia nobis usitatam, tunc quoque fulcrum, cuius beneficio in omnem planitiem versus quascunque stellas commode dirigi queat: atqui hæc VITICHIUS Lantgravio apud me visa præordinavit. Verum ipsemet Princeps loco cochleæ, qua ego in laxando vel coarctando instrumenti angulo utor (quam VITICHIUS indicare neglexerat) catenulam rotulis inhærentem addidit. Poterit D. CURTIUS periculum fieri curare, an intermediante hoc suo novitio Sextante eædem prorsus quarundam fixarum remotiones deprehendantur, quales pag. 30 et sequenti in eo fragmento Epistolarum Astronomicarum ad Lantgravium scriptarum, quod iam dudum tecum communicavi, nostris Sextantibus cœlitus designatæ, exponuntur; eas enim scio exactas esse, quibus si Curtiani Sextantis inventa ad amussim corresponderint, non potest non eius perfecte elaboratus esse, cum omne verum suo vero consonum sit. Exoptarem autem, ut Quadrantem quoque iustæ magnitudinis et e solido metallo constantem pariter divisum et pinnacidijs instructum in promptu haberet, quo per altitudines meridianas Solis et stellarum declinationes unâ cum Poli sublimitate exquisite scrutari commodum foret, quamvis et hoc eodem Sextante intra sublimitatem sexaginta graduum ad æquilibrium Horizontis sit dispositum atque in plano meridiani directo id ipsum præstare non admodum sit invium, qua de re eum admonere potes.

Gratum insuper mihi est, quod Globum magnum sexpedalem in diametro construi curet, prospiciat autem diligenter ne in rotunditate eius undiquaque procuranda plus quam existimaret difficultatis lateat, præsertim ut ea in materiâ ligneâ utut varie composita, mutationi tamen auræ suaque ipsius natura instabilitati obnoxia, diuturna et constans sit. Consultius itaque duxerim, ut Globum istum ad rotunditatem accuratam, quoad fieri potest, deductum, permittat primum unius ad minimum æstatis calorem et hiemis frigus, varia ijs intercedente auræ mutatione, experiri, donec ad consistentiam aliquam deducatur, tumque denuo globositatem eius examinet, atque ubi opus fuerit, emendari curet, postmodum, ubi sensibiliter nihil remittere et variationem nullam suscipere animadverterit, laminis orichalcicis lævigatis et subtiliter adunatis superinduci faciat, et tunc demum in rotunditatem exquisitam omni ex parte redigi, politaque superficie subdivisionibus graduum in singula minuta per puncta transversalia commoditatem præbente elaborari provideat, alias enim stellas nostras, quas circiter octingentas cap. 2 prioris Tomi in ipso minuto adeoque nonnunquam semisse unius diligentissime quo ad longum et latum cœlitus derivatas recensuimus, vix eâ quâ opus fuerit subtilitate et correspondentia Globo insigniverit. Haud ignota loquor, nam et is noster orichalcicus Globus, qui sex pedes in diametro adæquat, aliquot annorum laboriosam difficultatem obiecit, antequam ad omnimodam perfectionem perductus sit, ut de sumptibus nihil dicam, qui si numerati sigillatim essent, forte mille Ioachimicorum expensam æquarent aut superarent.

Quod tam amice atque honorifice sæpedictus D. CURTIUS me ad comitia Imperialia, quæ proxime Ratisbonæ celebrabuntur, invitat, est cur illi officiose gratias agam, et si res meæ multipliciaque, quibus occupor, negotia id ferrent, eius benevolæ petitioni equidem non [renuntiarem]. Verum cum mihi in hac insula, utut non admodum magna, maximis tamen occupationibus distento, vix tantum supersit otij et temporis, ut in vicinas Daniæ oras ad consanguineos et amicos vel etiam propriorum negotiorum causa nonnunquam excurrere liceat, si itaque tam longinquum in Germaniam iter cum iactura et dispendio rerum, quas hîc tracto et urgeo, suscipere nequeam, habebit me D. CURTIUS pro congenita sibi humanitate et iudicij dexteritate, uti spero, sufficienter excusatum. Scripsissem vero ipsemet nunc illi, si tantum superesset opportunitatis, et nuncius in vicinam Germaniam properans abitum non adeo festinaret. Quod vero nunc hac in parte prætermissum fuerit, alias oblata commodiore occasione affatim compensare non supersedebo. Resaluta itaque meo nomine Excellentissimum D. CURTIUM tui uti video meique amantissimum.

Iamque uterque vestrum bene valete.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Thaddaeus Hagecius.**

I was indeed very glad, my excellent Thaddaeus, that from your letter — delivered to me these very days — I gathered that you still enjoy moderately good health, for your age. For I had feared that those most grievous illnesses, which (as you signified in your last) had long and sorely afflicted you, had grown still fiercer and were keeping you confined to your bed, too much an invalid, or that perhaps in the meantime some human accident had befallen you — especially since, to my letter sent to you last year by a certain citizen of Görlitz, you made no reply in so long a time. And so even now I am much in doubt whether you received that letter rightly, since in this present one you make no mention either of its contents or of our first volume of the *Astronomical Preliminaries* [*Progymnasmata Astronomica*], which I sent for the Magnificent Master Jacob Curtius and yourself together to inspect and judge. Indeed I have now twice had a copy of that same book conveyed to you — the later one, however, more richly enlarged, and in which very few things were lacking that would keep it from being made public. But I cannot wonder enough that in none of the letters sent to me in the interim do you make mention of this matter; wherefore I suspect that these books have come into other men's hands and are being detained elsewhere. That I should indeed take amiss. That astronomical studies should fall silent with you in this old age, and that you have neglected the chemical [studies] for their vanity, I judge to be rightly done; for to indulge too much in these is, for the most part, to waste oil and labour, while the affliction of your health in this advancing age does not permit the deeper handling of those [astronomical] matters; you will do best, therefore, if you are intent solely upon contemplating supramundane things — as you say you also do — and upon caring for your health. That last Imperial privilege, enlarged in a certain part, Doctor Sagerus of Lübeck sent to me some while ago; for which, in my last letter, I rendered earnest thanks both to the most worthy Master Curtius and to you, as I do now also.

That a certain comet shone forth in July and August of last year is indeed certain from the report of many; but we did not catch sight of it here at Uraniborg — though attending to the heavens perhaps more diligently than others — both because the clear weather was exceedingly rare here in those times, and because toward the North, whenever the sky was at intervals cloudless, frequent chasms [aurorae] were seen, which easily withdrew from view the comet lingering there — being of itself, as I hear, very faint. Throughout those same months, on every clear night (which, as I said, were not frequent), we kept watch chiefly on observations of the star Mars as it was tending toward its acronychal position, that we might settle from the sky itself the discrepancy of the Alfonsine and the Copernican calculation — which at the very opposition exceeded 9 degrees (a greater interval than ever before) — and that I might join this acronychal observation of Mars to the rest taken over very many preceding years. Mars was found (let me note this too here in passing), when it stood diametrically opposite the Sun, to exceed the numbers of Copernicus by 4½ degrees, but to outrun the Alfonsine ones by full five degrees; which difference, greater than at other times in Mars when it is visible all night long, came about on account of the nearness of the eccentric perigee (to speak in the common way), for there the error in the true place of the apogee, which in Copernicus amounts to five degrees, proves very fertile [of error] — to say nothing now of the eccentricity, which he, wishing to support his own hypotheses, contracted too much, nor of the other things that are required here. Meanwhile, however (to return to the matter), while we were diligently pressing on with the observation of Mars whenever clear nights allowed it, we were nowhere able to see that comet, of which the rumour had now grown, although we deliberately inspected that quarter of the sky rather often around the end of August; just as others too, who passed several nights watchful in nearby Copenhagen to inspect it, were frustrated of their wish. Nonetheless it has been written to me that a certain Danish student, Christen Hansen of Ribe by name, who before he withdrew into Germany had for some years served me here in astronomical exercises, having made one or another little instrument in imitation of mine, applied himself to the observation of it with what accuracy he could — yet noted nothing certain except twice, on account of the faintness of the comet and the scarcity of clear weather. Whatever it may have been, he will shortly bring it with him, coming here to me from his fatherland Cimbria [Jutland] (for he has lately returned to Denmark). Then, if I see it to be worth the trouble, I shall examine those observations and shall try whether parallaxes may be investigated from them, so that in this way I may in some measure repair what was, against our will, neglected, and join this comet to those five [comets] noted by me from the sky itself with the greatest diligence and described in the second volume of the *Astronomical Preliminaries* — borrowing the observations of my one-time pupil and using them in place of my own.

What that distinguished Peucer signified to you by letter about this hairy [star / comet] contributes almost nothing to the matter, for he has no observations that would yield its apparent place, far less such as would suffice for unravelling parallaxes; indeed he does not even note the right day on which he saw it, nor do those [statements] agree among themselves, since at the beginning he says he saw it at least twice in the asterism of the Great Bear, and afterward, near the end, he adds that it stood not far from the star of the She-Goat and the Kids; for these two asterisms are more than a twelfth part of the heaven apart from each other. Of what sort, then, I ask, can this observation have been, sought even from mere sight alone? Therefore, as those things were idle and unworthy of mention, so let them now be too; let us leave them.

I also rejoice and congratulate that most excellent Master Curtius, our common friend, that he has obtained a sextant instrument from the Landgrave's workshop, by which he may infallibly probe the intervals of the stars. It is without doubt made in imitation of one of mine, by which distances are measured by a single observer — albeit with somewhat greater trouble than other sextants, which require two sighters. If it is so, it has little slits beside the centre, parallel to the forward sights, and the division by transversal points that we use; then too a support, by whose aid it may be conveniently directed in every plane toward any stars whatever: and indeed these features Wittich devised beforehand, having seen [them] with me, for the Landgrave. But the Prince himself, in place of the screw which I use in loosening or tightening the angle of the instrument (which Wittich had neglected to point out), added a little chain attached to small wheels. Master Curtius will be able to have a trial made, whether by means of this novel sextant of his exactly the same distances of certain fixed stars are found as those set out on page 30 and the following, in that fragment of the *Astronomical Letters* written to the Landgrave (which I shared with you some while ago), designated by our sextants from the sky itself; for I know those to be exact, and if the findings of the Curtian sextant correspond to them to the line, then it cannot but be that his is perfectly wrought, since every truth is consonant with its own truth. But I could wish that he also had at hand a quadrant of just size and made of solid metal, likewise divided and furnished with sights, by which it would be convenient to investigate exactly, through the meridian altitudes of the Sun and stars, the declinations together with the elevation of the Pole — although this too may be done with the same sextant, when it is set to the balance of the horizon within an elevation of sixty degrees, and to do that very thing in the direct plane of the meridian is not very impracticable; about which matter you can advise him.

It is moreover pleasing to me that he is having a great globe, six feet in diameter, built; but let him diligently take care lest in procuring its roundness on every side there lie more difficulty than he would suppose — especially that it be lasting and constant, [being made] in wooden material which, however variously put together, is yet liable to the change of the air and by its own nature to instability. I should therefore have judged it more advisable that, having brought that globe to an accurate roundness so far as can be done, he should first let it experience the heat of at least one summer and the cold of [one] winter, with the varied change of air coming between them, until it is brought to some settled state; and then examine its globosity afresh, and where there is need have it corrected; thereafter, when he perceives that it sensibly slackens nothing and takes on no variation, let him have it overlaid with sheets of brass, smoothed and finely joined, and only then provide that it be reduced on every part to an exquisite roundness, and that its surface, once polished, be worked with subdivisions of the degrees into single minutes by transversal points, affording convenience; for otherwise he will scarcely mark out upon the globe, with the fineness and correspondence that will be needed, our stars — which, about eight hundred, we have catalogued in chapter 2 of the first volume, derived from the sky itself most diligently as to length and breadth, to the very minute and so sometimes to the half of one. I do not speak of things unknown [to me], for that brass globe of ours too, which equals six feet in diameter, set before [me] a laborious difficulty of several years before it was brought to perfection of every kind — to say nothing of the costs, which, were they to be reckoned item by item, would perhaps equal or surpass the outlay of a thousand joachimsthalers.

That the oft-named Master Curtius so kindly and honourably invites me to the Imperial Diet, which will shortly be held at Regensburg, is reason for me dutifully to render him thanks; and if my affairs and the manifold business with which I am occupied allowed it, I would indeed not [decline] his kind request. But since to me on this island — though not very large, yet [I being] stretched by the greatest occupations — there scarcely remains so much leisure and time that I may sometimes make an excursion to the neighbouring shores of Denmark to my kinsmen and friends, or even for the sake of my own affairs; if, then, I cannot undertake so long a journey into Germany with the loss and expense of the matters which I here handle and press forward, Master Curtius will hold me, by the humanity innate in him and the dexterity of his judgement, as I hope, sufficiently excused. I would indeed have written to him myself now, if only there were so much opportunity left, and the messenger hastening into nearby Germany were not hurrying his departure so much. But what has now been left undone in this respect, I shall not forbear amply to make up another time, when a more convenient occasion is offered. Return the greeting, therefore, in my name to the Most Excellent Master Curtius, most loving — as I see — of both you and me.

And now fare you both well.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus Hagecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayek, 1525–1600), the Bohemian court physician, astronomer and alchemist at Prague, and a central figure in the European network that disputed the parallax of the 1572 nova; Tycho's long-standing correspondent and his principal channel to the imperial court of Rudolf II. The letter survives only as Tycho's own draft (*Kladde*) in the Vienna codex.
- **Date.** The source carries no internal dateline; the catalogue assigns it to **1594** (identifier …15940000001), consistent with the internal content — Mars's opposition observed at Uraniborg and the "comet of last year, July–August," i.e. the comet of **1593** (C/1593 O1). Header dated "1594 [O.S.]" on that catalogue basis, with the year **not** asserted from any dateline the text itself supplies; the absence of a written dateline is itself noted here. Denmark was on the Julian calendar (O.S.) throughout.
- **Place.** *Uraniburgi* — **Uraniborg**, Tycho's observatory on the island of Hven; the catalogue place-label "Uraniborg" matches the internal *hîc Uraniburgi* ("here at Uraniborg").
- **Persons named.**
 - *IACOBUS / D. CURTIUS* = **Jakob Kurz von Senftenau** (Jacobus Curtius, d. 1594), imperial vice-chancellor under Rudolf II, an amateur of astronomy who had commissioned a sextant from the Hessen workshop and a six-foot globe; Tycho's dedicatee-in-prospect and patron at court. The recurring "common friend."
 - *cl. ille PEUCERUS* = **Caspar Peucer** (1525–1602), Melanchthon's son-in-law, physician and astronomer; here cited (and dismissed) for unreliable naked-eye notes on the 1593 comet.
 - *Doct. SAGERUS Lubecensis* = **Doctor Sagerus of Lübeck** (Caspar/Kaspar Sager), the intermediary who forwarded the renewed imperial printing privilege; identification by name and city as given.
 - *VITICHIUS* = **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586) of Wrocław, the mathematician whose instrument designs Tycho says were realised at Kassel; Tycho repeatedly claimed (as here) that the Hessen sextant derived from his own instruments by way of Wittich's intermediary visit — a sensitive priority point in the Brahe–Wittich–Kassel triangle.
 - *CHRISTIERNUS IOHANNIS RIPENSIS* = **Christen Hansen (Christiernus Iohannis) of Ribe**, a former Danish assistant of Tycho's who attempted to observe the 1593 comet; "of Ribe" = the Jutland cathedral town. (*e Cimbria Patria sua* names **Jutland/Cimbria** as his homeland.)
- **Places.**
 - *Gorlicensem* — a citizen **of Görlitz** (Lusatia), the courier of the previous year's lost-or-delayed letter.
 - *Haffnia* — **Copenhagen**.
 - *officina Lantgraviana* / *Lantgravio* — the **Landgrave's workshop** and **Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (d. 1592); the Kassel observatory's instrument shop.
 - *Ratisbonae* — **Regensburg**, site of the forthcoming Imperial Diet (*comitia Imperialia*; the Diet of 1594).
 - *Cimbria* — **Jutland** (the Cimbrian peninsula).
- **Works.** *Progymnasmata Astronomica* (Tomus primus / secundus) = Tycho's *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata* — rendered **"Astronomical Preliminaries"**; vol. 1 (the nova/refraction/solar theory) was in circulating proof, vol. 2 was to treat the comets. *fragmentum Epistolarum Astronomicarum ad Lantgravium* = the printed gathering of the *Epistolae Astronomicae* (Liber I, the Hessen correspondence) Tycho had already shared with Hagecius; "page 30 and the following" cites that fragment.
- **Astronomy — technical terms**.
 - *acronychium situm / acronychiam … observationem* — **acronychal** position/observation, i.e. Mars at opposition, rising as the Sun sets; kept as the technical term.
 - *oppositio* → **opposition**; *Soli e diametro opponebatur* → "stood diametrically opposite the Sun" (the same configuration).
 - *calculus Alphonsinus / Copernicus* → the **Alfonsine** and **Copernican** computation/tables; Tycho reports the sky falling 4½° from Copernicus and 5° from the Alfonsine numbers — *the figures are reproduced exactly as written* (9°, 4½°, 5°), with no silent reconciliation of the "9 degrees" total against the two component errors.
 - *Perigaei eccentrici / vero Apogaei loco / eccentricitate* → **eccentric perigee / true place of the apogee / eccentricity**; *hypothesibus* → hypotheses. Tycho's epistemic hedge *(ut communiter loquar)* "to speak in the common way" is preserved.
 - *Parallaxes* → **parallaxes** — the distance-test for whether the comet was sub- or supralunar.
 - *chasmata crebra* → "frequent chasms": **aurorae / auroral rifts** ("chasmata" is the period term for auroral phenomena toward the North); glossed [aurorae] rather than silently modernised.
 - *Crinita* → "the hairy [star]," a standard Latin epithet for a comet (*stella crinita*); kept as the image and glossed.
 - *Asterismus Ursae maioris* → "the asterism of the **Great Bear**"; *Capellae et Haedorum sidere* → "the star of the **She-Goat and the Kids**" (Capella and the Haedi, in Auriga). *duodecima coeli pars* → "a twelfth part of the heaven" (= 30°), left as written.
 - *Poli sublimitas* → "the **elevation of the Pole**" (polar altitude = latitude); *altitudines meridianas … declinationes* → **meridian altitudes … declinations**.
- **Instruments**.
 - *Sextans / Sextantibus* → **sextant(s)**; *Quadrans* → **quadrant**; *Globus … orichalcicus / sexpedalis* → a six-foot **globe** sheathed in *orichalcum* (**brass / latten**).
 - *pinnacidia / pinnula* → **sights / pinnule**; *collimatores* → "sighters" (the two observers a two-man sextant needs); *rimulae* → "little slits" (sighting slits); *divisio per puncta transversalia* → **transversal-point division** (Tycho's diagonal-dot scale subdivision).
 - *cochlea* → "screw"; *catenula rotulis inhaerens* → "a little chain attached to small wheels" (the Landgrave's chain-and-pulley fine-adjustment substituted for Tycho's screw); *fulcrum* → "support" (the instrument's mount/stand).
 - *ad amussim* → "to the line" (exactly, by rule); *ad aequilibrium Horizontis* → "to the balance of the horizon" (levelled).
- **Symbol.** **♂** (in *maior … in ♂*) = **Mars**; the glyph is retained in the Source block and named "Mars" in the translation. Mars is elsewhere written out (*Martis*) in the same passage.
- **Money.** *mille Ioachimicorum* → "a thousand **joachimsthalers**" (*Joachimsthaler* / thaler, the Bohemian Joachimsthal silver coin); kept as the period unit.
- **Chemistry / programme.** *Chymica ob vanitatem neglexeris* → "you have neglected the **chemical** [studies] for their vanity"; *supramundanis … contemplandis* → "contemplating **supramundane** things" (matters above the world — devotional/theological, as opposed to alchemy). *oleum et operam perdere* → "to waste oil and labour," the proverbial tag, kept as idiom.
- **Editorial insertion in the source.** *eius benevolae petitioni equidem non [renuntiarem]* — the bracketed verb **[renuntiarem]** ("[I would] not decline/renounce") is an editorial supply in the source (the draft left it incomplete); the brackets are reproduced as printed and carried into the translation as **"[decline]."** The negation *non* + the supplied verb yields "I would not decline," i.e. Tycho would accept were he free — the one negation in the clause is preserved.
- **Epistolary formulae**. Salutation header *AD THADDAeUM HAGECIUM* kept as title-line. Closing *Iamque uterque vestrum bene valete* → "And now fare you both well" (plural, addressed to Hagecius and Curtius jointly — *uterque vestrum*); *Resaluta … meo nomine* → "Return the greeting in my name." No *S./S.P.D.* opening appears (it is a draft).

text.original:
NOBILI AC GENEROSO DOMINO,
DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHÆ. MAGNIFICE ET
GENEROSE DOMINE.

GRATA mihi inprimis erat illa mei mentio,
quam in literis a te ad Clarissimum Dominum IUNIUM Serenissimi Regis
consiliarium et iam apud vos legatum missis perlegeram. Nam licet mihi probe
conscius essem, minime  me concernere, quæ de me scripseras, tamen laudari a tali viro, in quo
tot generis, tot fortunæ et eruditionis ornamenta sunt, nemini non acceptum vel
gratum esse potest, et nisi aliqua literarum significatione id agnovissem,
fuissem profecto ingratissimus. Spondeo itaque Magnifice Domine, me tuo merito
et tui amantissimum et posthac studiosissimum futurum et officijs, quibus
possim, curaturum, ut vere id de me possis iudicare. Unum hoc peto, ut si quæ
offensionum causæ adversus fratrem meum supersint, illas mihi velis pro tua
humanitate condonare. Nam licet in ea qua frater opinione sim, supra cœlum Lunæ
nihil corruptioni obnoxium gigni posse, tamen te virum tantum, tot annorum
experientia confirmatum, tot Mathematicis organis instructum aliter sentire,
alijsque viris magnis tuam sententiam probasse, nisi multa essent, quæ tecum
facerent, nunquam mihi persuadebo. Sed in hoc
doctiorum sit iudicium. Rem ipsam mitto, scripti fraterni genus non probo.
Acerbius enim, quam par erat, adversus virum tantum se gessit, quem pro
admirabili eruditione colere debuerat. Sed in philosophicis concertationibus a
prima ætate versatus usu acrimoniam disputandi sibi comparavit. Scriptum illud
nunquam exijt, et scio me apud fratrem posse ut perpetuo supprimatur, vel si
malis cum honorifica tui nominis et eruditionis mentione, et omni felle purgatum
exeat; immo ut cum HORATIO loquar, sive
flammis mandare velis, sive mari Adriano, utrumvis pro tuo arbitrio expectabis.
Interea me tui amantissimum et in eo nulli concedentem in futurum pro tuo
amplectere. Deus optimus maximus in omnibus rebus tuis gerendis semper adsit,
semper te et tua gubernet precor.

Vale.

Tui semper observantissimus
THO.
CRAGIUS

Expectant nostri omnes tuum de felicissima et auspicatissima principis nostri
genesi iudicium.
text.english:
**To the noble and well-born lord, the Lord Tycho Brahe. Magnificent and well-born Lord.**

Especially welcome to me was that mention of myself which I read through in the letter sent by you to the most distinguished Master Young, councillor of the Most Serene King and now legate among you. For although I was well aware in my own conscience that what you had written about me concerned me but little, yet to be praised by such a man — in whom there are so many ornaments of birth, of fortune, and of learning — cannot but be acceptable or pleasing to anyone; and had I not acknowledged it by some token of a letter, I should truly have been most ungrateful. I pledge therefore, Magnificent Lord, that by your desert I shall both be most devoted to you and hereafter most zealous [for you], and shall see to it, by such services as I can, that you may judge this of me truly. This one thing I ask: that, if any grounds of offence against my brother yet remain, you would be willing of your kindness to forgive me [them]. For although I am of the same opinion as my brother — that above the heaven of the Moon nothing subject to corruption can be brought forth — yet that you, so great a man, confirmed by the experience of so many years, equipped with so many mathematical instruments, should think otherwise, and that you should have proved your view to other great men, I shall never persuade myself [of this], unless there were many things that made on your side. But on this point let the judgement be the more learned men's. The matter itself I set aside; the manner of my brother's writing I do not approve. For he bore himself more sharply than was fitting against so great a man, whom for his admirable learning he ought to have honoured. But, engaged from his earliest years in philosophical contests, he has by habit acquired for himself a keenness in disputing. That writing has never come out, and I know that I have it in my power with my brother that it be suppressed for ever — or, if you should prefer, that it come out with honourable mention of your name and learning, and purged of all gall; nay, to speak with Horace, whether you would wish to consign it to the flames or to the Adriatic sea, you shall await either one as you please. Meanwhile embrace me, as your own, as most devoted to you and yielding to none in this in time to come. May God, Best and Greatest, ever be at hand in the conduct of all your affairs; ever, I pray, may He govern you and yours.

Farewell.
Ever most observant of you,
Thomas Craig. All our people await your judgement upon the most happy and most auspicious nativity of our prince.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Tho. Cragius, Doctor Medicus* = **Thomas Craig** (Cragius), the Scotsman writing to excuse his brother. The signature gives "Doctor of Medicine"; the family is the Craig family of Edinburgh. The letter is the conciliatory counterpart to the bitter cometary dispute (1589–1594) between Tycho and the writer's brother.
- ***frater meus*** — "my brother": **John Craig** (d. 1620), the Edinburgh physician and Aristotelian who, between 1589 and 1594, conducted a sharp epistolary controversy with Tycho, disputing Tycho's supralunary (superlunary) placement of the comet of 1577. Tycho circulated copies of the Craig exchange to correspondents such as Brucaeus and Hagecius. This letter is Thomas Craig's distancing of himself from the *manner* (not entirely the matter) of his brother's polemic.
- ***Dominum IUNIUM … Serenissimi Regis consiliarium et iam apud vos legatum*** — "Master Young … councillor of the Most Serene King and now legate among you." *Iunius* is the Latinised form of the Scots surname **Young**: **Peter Young** (Petrus Junius, 1544–1628), the royal tutor and councillor of **James VI** of Scotland, who served as the king's ambassador (legate) to Denmark in 1594. *iam apud vos legatum* ("now legate among you [pl.]") locates Young in Denmark at the time of writing — the channel through which Tycho's favourable mention of Thomas Craig reached him. *Serenissimi Regis* = James VI of Scotland (the "Most Serene King").
- **Astronomical doctrine.** *supra coelum Lunae nihil corruptioni obnoxium gigni posse* = "that above the heaven of the Moon nothing subject to corruption can be brought forth" — the Aristotelian doctrine of the incorruptible heavens, the very position from which John Craig denied that the 1577 comet could be a supralunary (celestial) body. Thomas Craig states he *shares* his brother's Aristotelian opinion, while declining to set his own judgement against Tycho's instrument-based demonstration.
- ***tot Mathematicis organis instructum*** = "equipped with so many mathematical instruments" (*organa* → **instruments**, this chapter's convention): a deferential nod to Tycho's observational apparatus at Uraniborg as the ground of his authority.
- **Allusion (Horace).** *ut cum Horatio loquar, sive flammis mandare velis, sive mari Adriano* = "to speak with Horace, whether you would wish to consign [it] to the flames or to the Adriatic sea." An echo of Horace, *Odes* I.16 (and the topos of *Ars Poetica* on suppressing one's writings): Thomas Craig offers Tycho absolute discretion over the unpublished tract — burn it, drown it, or let it appear emended. The metaphor is kept, not flattened.
- ***Rem ipsam mitto*** — "the matter itself I set aside / I let go": *mitto* here in the rhetorical sense "I pass over, I waive," i.e. Craig does not contest the substance of the dispute, only the tone. Rendered "I set aside" to preserve the deliberate reservation (he does not concede the substance).
- **Dating.** The edition label is *"1594. empty"* — i.e. assigned to the year 1594 with **no day or month** in the source. The letter carries **no dateline and no place** in the transcription: the subscription ends at the signature. The header therefore gives "[s.l.], 1594" (year only, no place stated) rather than asserting a day the source does not substantiate. The year is consistent with Peter Young's 1594 Danish embassy and with the close of the Tycho–Craig controversy; it is editorial (Dreyer's), not from an internal dateline. O.S. is assumed (Scotland and Denmark both kept the Julian calendar in 1594), but the letter states no style.
- **Honorifics.** *Magnifice et Generose Domine* → "Magnificent and well-born Lord"; *S.* (implied salutation idiom) and the closing *Vale* → "Farewell"; *Tui semper observantissimus* → "Ever most observant of you".
- **Negation check.** The source carries the conciliatory negations exactly: *minime me concernere* ("concerned me but little"), *nunquam mihi persuadebo* ("I shall never persuade myself"), *scripti fraterni genus non probo* ("the manner … I do not approve"), *Scriptum illud nunquam exijt* ("that writing has never come out"). All four are reproduced; none added or dropped. The double construction *nunquam mihi persuadebo … nisi multa essent, quae tecum facerent* is rendered with its conditional intact ("I shall never persuade myself … unless there were many things that made on your side"), preserving Craig's guarded acknowledgement that Tycho must have strong grounds.
- **Names the occasion: the young Prince's nativity.** The recovered closing sentence asks Tycho for his astrological judgement on 'the most happy and most auspicious nativity of our prince' — i.e. a horoscope for the newborn heir of Scotland.
- **Cross-reference to the companion letter.** The same request is pursued in far greater detail in John Craig's letter of 22 April [1594] (brahe-t_15940422001), which reports the birth of 'a most longed-for infant Prince' — Prince Henry Frederick, Duke of Rothesay, born to James VI and Anne of Denmark at Stirling Castle on 19 February 1594 (Old Style) — and supplies the birth-time and latitude Tycho would need to cast the nativity. Read together, the two Craig letters (brothers, both signing 'Doctor Medicus') show the Scottish circle soliciting Tycho's genethliacal judgement on the new heir in tandem.
- **Correction.** Latin and English: the title 'Doctor Medicus' / 'Doctor of Medicine' removed from Thomas Craig's signature — Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 365 closes the signature at 'THO. CRAGIUS.' with no title; the title belongs to the preceding, separate letter of his brother John Craig ('IOAN. CRAIGIUS, Doctor Medicus.', p.364) and had contaminated this letter's signature in error.

text.original:
PRIUILEGIUM TYCHONI BRAHÆ CONCESSUM COLDINGÆ VII MARTIJ ANNO 1594.

VNIUERSIS et singulis tenore præsentium notum facimus: Cum generosus ac fidelis nobis dilectus Tycho Brahæ de Knudtstrup ex antiqua et præclara huius regni nostri nobili Brahorum familia originem ducens post varios diuturnosque in studio Astronomico, cui inde ab ineunte ætate fuit addictissimus, exantlatos labores fructus eorundem nonnullos haud asspernendos, nunc in communem reipublicæ literariæ vtilitatem in publicum edere decreuerit: Astronomicæ videlicet instaurationis progymnasmata quædam luculenta, integro quod adornat operi præmittenda, ac vereri se nobis demisse ostenderit ne idem opus, postquam publicatum fuerit, alij temere non exiguo ipsius detrimento æmulentur, et propterea nobis quam humilime supplicauerit, vt pro solita nostra clementia indemnem ipsum præstemus. Visum est nobis pro fauore nostro erga eum singulari hoc illi diplomate nostro regio prouidere, quo serio ac seuere mandamus cautumque esse volumus, ne qui omnino in regnis ducatibus atque prouincijs nostris cuiuscunque status aut conditionis existant ullos libros ab ipso Tychone Brahæ siue proprijs siue alienis typis editos, præsertim eos, qui rem Philosophicam atque Astronomicam concernunt, vel recudere vel alibi impressos aut recusos adducere vel uenundare, siue totaliter siue partialiter, sine ipsius hæredumue eius consensu, publice uel occulte præsumant, sub pæna decem marcarum auri puri pro dimidia fisco nostro regio, reliqua uero parte ipsi Tychoni Brahæ siue eius hæredibus (præter librorum omnium amissionem, quos ipsis uel per se uel suos sibi vendicare, inque potestatem suam redigere fas esto) nulla sperata remissione applicandarum. In cuius rei ac voluntatis nostræ fidem et testimonium hoc diploma regio nostro sigillo munitum, manu propria subscripsimus ac a regni nostri senatoribus nunc præsentibus subscribendum mandauimus.

Actum in regia nostra Coldingæ.
text.english:
**A privilege granted to Tycho Brahe at Kolding, 7 March in the year 1594.**

To each and all we make known by the tenor of these presents: Whereas the well-born Tycho Brahe of Knudstrup, faithful and beloved of us, who draws his origin from the ancient and illustrious noble family of the Brahes of this our realm, after various and long-continued labours exhausted in the study of astronomy — to which from his earliest years he has been most devoted — has now resolved to publish, for the common benefit of the republic of letters, certain not-to-be-despised fruits of those same labours: namely certain brilliant *preliminary exercises* [progymnasmata] of the *restoration of astronomy* [astronomicae instaurationis], to be set before the whole work that he is preparing; and whereas he has humbly shown us that he fears lest, after that work has been published, others should rashly emulate [it] to his no slight detriment, and has therefore most humbly besought us that, of our accustomed clemency, we keep him from harm: it has seemed good to us, in our singular favour toward him, to provide for him by this our royal diploma, whereby we earnestly and strictly command, and will it to be enacted, that none whatsoever within our kingdoms, duchies, and provinces, of whatever estate or condition they be, shall presume — publicly or covertly — either to reprint any books published by Tycho Brahe himself, whether from his own presses or from others', and especially those that concern philosophical and astronomical matters, or to bring in [copies] printed or reprinted elsewhere, or to put [them] up for sale, whether wholly or in part, without the consent of him or of his heirs; under penalty of ten marks of pure gold — one half to be applied to our royal treasury, the other half to Tycho Brahe himself or to his heirs (besides the forfeiture of all the books, which they, whether by themselves or through their own [agents], shall be entitled to claim for themselves and to bring into their own power) — with no remission to be hoped for. In faith and testimony of which matter and of our will, we have subscribed this diploma, fortified with our royal seal, with our own hand, and have commanded it to be subscribed by the senators of our realm now present.

Done at our royal [residence of] Kolding.

documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer / document type.** A royal printing **privilege** (*privilegium* / *diploma regium*) issued in the name of **Christian IV of Denmark** (r. 1588–1648), then in his minority under the regency council; the edition names "Christian 4." as sender. It is a one-party legal instrument (a grant), not an epistolary exchange — hence the "recipient" is properly the realm at large, with Tycho Brahe as the beneficiary; the header records this. The text is cast throughout in the royal "we" (*facimus, mandamus, subscripsimus*).
- **Beneficiary.** *Tycho Brahae de Knudtstrup* = **Tycho Brahe of Knudstrup** (the family seat in Scania), here styled *generosus ac fidelis nobis dilectus* ("well-born, faithful and beloved of us"), the standard chancery honorific for a noble subject.
- **The work protected.** *Astronomicae instaurationis progymnasmata* = the **Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata** ("preliminary exercises [toward] the restoration of astronomy"), Tycho's great work on the new star of 1572 and on solar/lunar theory, then in press at Uraniborg and not completed until after his death (1602). *progymnasmata* (Greek προγυμνάσματα, "preliminary exercises/drills") is Tycho's own title-word, kept and glossed. *instauratio (astronomiae)* → "restoration (of astronomy)" by this chapter's convention — Tycho's programmatic term; the genitive here (*instaurationis*) modifies the *progymnasmata*. *integro... operi praemittenda* — "to be set before the whole work," i.e. these exercises form the opening volume of a larger projected corpus.
- ***siue proprijs siue alienis typis editos*** — "published whether from his own presses or from others'." A pointed clause: Tycho ran his **own press** at Uraniborg (*proprijs typis*), and the privilege covers both his self-printed books and any printed for him elsewhere.
- **The penalty clause.** *sub paena decem marcarum auri puri* = "under penalty of ten marks of pure gold," split *pro dimidia... reliqua uero parte* (half to the royal *fiscus* / treasury, half to Tycho or his heirs) — the conventional fine-sharing formula. *praeter librorum omnium amissionem... quos... sibi vendicare... fas esto* = "besides the forfeiture of all the [offending] books, which [the heirs] shall be entitled (*fas esto*) to claim and seize." The parenthesis is a grant of right to Tycho's side, not a further penalty; rendered as such.
- **Negations (checked).** The operative prohibition carries the structure *ne qui... ullos libros... vel recudere vel... adducere vel uenundare... sine... consensu... praesumant* — one governing negation (*ne... praesumant*, "that none presume"), with *sine ipsius... consensu* ("without his consent") as the condition. Three negation-bearing elements total (*ne qui*, *ullos*, *sine consensu*); all three reproduced, none added. The force is: no one may do any of the three acts (reprint / import / sell) without consent. *nulla sperata remissione* ("with no remission to be hoped for") closes the clause and is preserved.
- **Reading note (transcription vs. Dreyer page image).** The working transcription reads *supplicauerit* (3rd-sg., agreeing with Tycho as subject of the *Cum...* clause); the Dreyer digitised text layer shows *supplicauere*, but Dreyer's printed text is heavily mangled by long-s/ligature digitised text layer errors in this passage (e.g. *Typhone* for *Tychone*, *Angulari* for *singulari*, *exibant* for *existant*, *recuses* for *recusos*). The singular *supplicauerit* is grammatically required by the surrounding singular verbs (*decreuerit... ostenderit*) and is followed here; the variant is noted, not silently corrected.
- **Place / dateline.** The date and place stand only in the **rubric heading**: *COLDINGAe VII MARTIJ ANNO 1594* = "at **Kolding** [*Coldingae*], 7 March in the year 1594" (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The body's closing *Actum in regia nostra Coldingae* ("Done at our royal [seat at] Kolding") repeats the place without a date. The edition label ("1594. 7. marts. Kolding") agrees with the rubric; no discrepancy. Kolding (Koldinghus) was a principal royal residence in Jutland. The line *Ex Archivo Regni Daniae: Latina 1586–99, fol. 289 f.* in the Dreyer page image is the editor's source-note, not part of the document.
- ***reipublicae literariae*** = "the republic of letters," the humanist commonwealth of learning; kept as the period idiom.

text.original:
GENERIS NOBILITATE, OMNI
DOCTRINARUM ET VIRTUTUM EXCELLENTIA PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO D. TYCHONI BRAHE, HWÆNE
INSULÆ, DOMINO ILLUSTR. REGIS DANIÆ CONSILIARIO, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO
HONORANDO.

EXTINCTA nunc prope Nobiliss. D. TYCHO tuarum de me literarum
memoria, quæ in huiusmodi rebus admodum labilis esse solet, et de humanitate tua
ea concepta opinione, ut apud ipsum quoque offensiones deferbuisse existimem, ad
amicitiam redeundum videtur. Quod hoc tempore vir præstantissimus Dominus
IUNIUS, qui nunc legatum ad vos agit,
diligenter egit, qui ut utrique nostrum plurimum favet, ita animorum
coniunctionem, quæ inter nos fuit, minime dissolvi cupit, neque ego fore
speravi, ut tantum laxaretur. Si ulla mea disputatione id evenire posse,
suspicatus fuissem, vel mihi indixissem silentium vel dissentientem, quia aliter
non ratio passa est, non disserentem habuisses amicum, cum hoc amicitia nostra
non ferre videatur. Quod ad scriptum nostrum attinet, defensionem eius nolo
agere, hoc tantum profiteri libet, scriptori nec voluntatem nec propositum
fuisse tui vel minimum commovendi. Tacuissem libenter, et ita res meæ suadebant,
nam Mathematica vix unquam cum ullo commodo tractavi, sed silere non passus es,
assentire non potui, nisi assentari voluissem; si absque argumento sententiam
dixissem, non acquievisses; candide et sincere tecum agi petijsti, gratam tibi
fore nostram operam pollicitus es. Occurrebant in Apologia tua, quæ stomachum
cuivis commovere potuissent, ut imperitiæ, ignorantiæ, mancipati iudicij et
similium insimulari, absque causa absque ulla offensione data. Itaque voluntatem
tuam meis rebus cœpi præferre, et illa qualicunque disquisitione tibi
gratificari libuit. Amicitia me dirigente pro veritate et Uraniæ tuæ dignitate
quædam attuli, quæ eo acceptiora fore credideram, quo magis pro his facerent,
quia has Deas tanto studio et industria colis, ut nemo hoc nostro sæculo pari,
superioribus nemo magis; ut nostra defensione offensum te iri, ne suspicatus
fuerim, præsertim si absque contumelia id agerem, a qua certe ita cavi, ut ab
igne, neque enim Philosophum eiusmodi contentionem decere existimavi, neque ullo modo nostræ convenire amicitiæ. Nonnulla certe res ipsa
a me expresserat, quæ in quæstionem tantum directa, in offensionem non erant
rapienda. Si tua perverti, distraxi, male accommodavi et cætera, quæ nunc et
excidere et si hærerent non repetenda sunt, loca modo
designes. Quæ feci inscius, non invitus mutabo. Brevitati equidem studui, quæ
copiose et pluribus locis a te allata sunt, ne prolixitas tædium pareret,
contraxi, sensu tuo religiose observato, in nudam argumenti speciem redegi, ubi
dissentiendum fuit, partim serio, partim etiam per iocum ostendi; idque
doctissimorum et optimorum, in simili negocio, exemplo, ut inde offensum te iri
nequaquam crediderim, præsertim cum nihil iniuriose fieret, aut alioqui
cogitatum sit. Tua quoque me nemo magis admiratus est semper, illorumque iusta
æstimatio nunquam passa est amorem tui minui, tantum abest, ut ijs quicquam
voluerim detractum, quin potius indefessum tuum et vix imitabile in cœlum
studium in cœlum semper, ubicunque licuit, tulerim; neque enim si in re una
dissentimus, eaque non tanti ponderis, in cæteris similiter, sed ubi ex apodicto
agis, me tuis subscribentem inprimis habes. Ac in illa re, quæ a me hactenus
allata sunt, tuo subijcio iudicio, tuo etiam permitto arbitrio, salva veritate,
quam scio te salvam velle, mutes, expungas, cancelles quæ libet; privatim tecum
egi, nec nostra ad alios referenda fuere, qui parum illa vel faciebant, vel
sapiebant; mihi uno verbo si constitisset, molestius te nostra capere, quæ in
gratiam tuam fuere scripta, in eandem quoque abolita fuissent. Grati animi
officia a me requiris, nec alia a me unquam profecta sunt, eaque ex amore magis
quam debito, nisi communi nomine deberi possint, quod in commune Reipub.
literariæ incrementum a te immensa præstita sint, quo nomine patiar et me
teneri. Quod ad factam mei mentionem apud Regem et ad D. Cancellarium
attinet, in eo quoque benevolentiam tuam agnosco et amplector, sed nec petij nec
opus fuit: Serenissimum Regem ipse et omnes
mei, quamvis aulam  non sectemur, clementissimum semper experti sumus, quem Deus optimus max. conservet. D. Cancellarius, antequam ulla inter vos esset notitia, meis rebus
favit plurimum, et aliqua sangvinis ratio est, nec mea illi familiæ officia
unquam defuere. Ab illo vero tempore vix alloqui eum contigit, semel fortasse in
casu cuiusdam ægri. Sed ista valeant, et quæcunque alia, ex quibus amicitia
nostra turbari possit, ipse hoc accepto documento, ei, ut potero, studebo, nec
dubito quin et tu alienior non sis futurus. Si controversi  quicquam inter nos contigerit, me facile silentem habebis, a te etiam
atque etiam peto, ut absque iniuriosis vocibus id fiat; his non inquiritur sed
supprimitur veritas. Illa inter nos regula sanciatur, ut nudis solum rationibus
agatur, extra rem nihil proferatur. Sic disserere integra amicitia licebit.
Cupivit doctissimus vir D. Legatus, ut secum te
inviserem, non patiuntur id amici. Si venissem, gratusne fuissem hospes? Interea
his literis revisere te volui, et amicitiam nostram redintegrare. Tu amicum, qui
veram profitetur amicitiam, pristino more et amore complectere. Accepistis natum
nobis esse infantem Principem exoptatissimum, R. matrem vultu et corporis lineamentis refert, redivivum diceres
beatæ memoriæ illustriss. FRIDERICUM
Regem, in lucem cœpit contendere hora tertia post Μ. N. diei 19. Februarij, in
eam venit media ad quartam. Arx Sterlini eiusdem cum hac nostra urbe fere
latitudinis est, vix uno aut altero scrupulo in Boream declinat, Uraniam, si
placet, consule. Salutat P. T. frater
meus natu maior; ad te hoc tempore scripsisset, nisi Serenissimæ
Reginæ negotia impedijssent;
putat sibi maiores gratias esse redditas, quam illud epigramma meritum est;
gratum tamen ipsi fuit, sua tibi accepta esse, et paratus est, quibus poterit
officijs, tibi gratificari.

Vale præstantissime D. et clementissimus Deus tibi
vitam et vires suppeditet, ut illi admirando operi, quod præ manibus habes,
optatum finem possis imponere.

Datæ Edinburgi 22. Aprilis.

Tui observantiss.
IOAN.
CRAIGIUS,
Doctor Medicus.

Salutem precor doctissimis et præstantissimis viris Domm. D. D. CRAIGIJS.
text.english:
**To the man most pre-eminent in nobility of birth and in every excellence of learning and virtue, Master Tycho Brahe of the island of Hven, councillor to the Most Illustrious King of Denmark, his lord and friend to be honoured.**

Now that the memory of your letters concerning me is nearly extinguished, most noble Master Tycho — a memory that in matters of this kind is wont to be quite fleeting — and having formed of your kindness the opinion that with you too the offences have cooled, it seems a return must be made to friendship. This at the present time the most pre-eminent man Master Junius, who is now acting as envoy to you, has diligently brought about; for as he greatly favours us both, so he by no means wishes the union of minds that there was between us to be dissolved — nor did I hope that it would be so far loosened. Had I suspected that it could come about through any disputation of mine, I should either have imposed silence upon myself, or — since reason did not allow otherwise — you would have had a friend who dissented but did not dispute, since this our friendship seems not to bear. As regards my writing, I do not wish to mount a defence of it; I am content only to declare this much: that the writer had neither the will nor the intent of provoking you even in the least. I would gladly have kept silent, and so my own affairs counselled me, for I have scarcely ever handled mathematics with any profit; but you did not suffer me to be silent, and I could not assent unless I had wished to play the flatterer; had I pronounced an opinion without an argument, you would not have been satisfied; you asked that you be dealt with candidly and sincerely, [and] you promised that my service would be welcome to you. There occurred in your *Apologia* things that could have stirred anyone's gall — such as being charged with inexperience, ignorance, a judgement enslaved, and the like, without cause, without any offence given. And so I began to set your wish before my own affairs, and it pleased me to gratify you with that examination, such as it was. With friendship guiding me, on behalf of the truth and of the dignity of your Urania I brought forward certain things, which I had believed would be the more acceptable the more they made for these [Goddesses], because you cultivate these Goddesses with such zeal and industry that no one in this our age does so equally, and no one in earlier ages more; so that I never suspected you would be offended by my defence, especially if I carried it out without insult — from which indeed I guarded myself as from fire, for I judged that a contention of this kind neither befitted a philosopher nor was in any way suited to our friendship. Certain things, to be sure, the subject-matter itself had wrung from me, which, being aimed only at the inquiry, were not to be snatched up into offence. If I have distorted, pulled apart, ill-adapted your [statements] and the rest — which now both escape me and, even if they stuck [in mind], are not to be rehearsed — only point out the passages. What I did unknowingly I shall change, and not unwillingly. I did indeed aim at brevity: the things adduced by you copiously and in many places I drew together, lest prolixity breed tedium; with your sense scrupulously preserved, I reduced [them] to the bare appearance of the argument; where I had to dissent, I showed it partly in earnest, partly even in jest — and that after the example of the most learned and the best men in a like business — so that I could in no way have believed you would be offended thereby, especially since nothing was done injuriously, nor was so intended in any case. No one, too, has ever admired your [achievements] more than I, and a just esteem of them has never allowed my love of you to be lessened — so far am I from having wished anything detracted from them, that rather I have always, wherever I was permitted, borne your tireless and scarcely imitable zeal toward heaven up to heaven; for if we dissent in one matter, and that one of no great weight, it does not follow that [we do so] likewise in the rest — but where you proceed from demonstration, you have me subscribing to your views among the very first. And in that matter, the things which have hitherto been brought forward by me I submit to your judgement, I commit also to your discretion: with the truth kept safe — which I know you wish kept safe — change, strike out, cancel what you please. I dealt with you privately, and my writings were not to be carried to others, who either set little store by them or had little understanding of them; had it been established to me in a single word that you took my writings amiss — which were written for your sake — for that same sake they would also have been abolished. You ask of me the offices of a grateful mind; nor have any others ever proceeded from me, and these out of love rather than out of debt — unless they can be owed under the common title, since immense things have been furnished by you toward the common increase of the Republic of Letters, under which title I shall suffer myself too to be bound. As regards the mention made of me before the King and to Master the Chancellor, in that too I acknowledge and embrace your goodwill, but I neither asked it nor was there need: I myself and all my [house], though we do not attend the court, have always found the Most Serene King most clement — whom may God, Best and Greatest, preserve. Master the Chancellor, before there was any acquaintance between you, greatly favoured my affairs, and there is some tie of blood, nor have my services to that family ever been wanting. But since that time it has scarcely befallen me to speak with him — once perhaps, in the case of a certain sick man. But let these matters rest, and whatever others there may be from which our friendship could be disturbed; I myself, having received this lesson, will attend to it as I shall be able, and I do not doubt that you too will not be the more estranged. If anything contentious should arise between us, you will easily have me silent; [and] I beg of you again and again that it be done without injurious words: by these the truth is not investigated but suppressed. Let this rule be sanctioned between us, that we proceed by bare reasons alone, and that nothing be brought forward beside the matter [in hand]. Thus it will be permitted to dispute with friendship whole. The most learned man Master the Envoy wished that I should visit you together with him; my friends do not allow it. Had I come, should I have been a welcome guest? Meanwhile by this letter I have wished to revisit you, and to make our friendship whole again. Do you embrace, in your former manner and love, a friend who professes a true friendship. You [pl.] have received word that a most longed-for infant Prince has been born to us; he recalls his royal mother in countenance and in the lineaments of his body — you would call him King Frederick, of illustrious blessed memory, brought to life again. He began to strive into the light at the third hour after Μ. N. [midnight] on the 19th day of February; into it he came at half past three. The Castle of Stirling is of nearly the same latitude as this our city, scarcely by one scruple or two does it incline to the North — consult Urania, if you please. My elder brother greets you most warmly; he would have written to you at this time, had the affairs of the Most Serene Queen not hindered him; he thinks greater thanks have been rendered to him than that epigram deserved; yet it was pleasing to him that his [verses] were acceptable to you, and he is ready, by whatever offices he can, to gratify you.

Farewell, most pre-eminent Master, and may God most clement supply you with life and strength, that upon that admirable work which you have in hand you may be able to impose the wished-for end.
Given at Edinburgh, 22 April.
Most observant of you,
John Craig,
Doctor of Medicine. I wish greeting to the most learned and most excellent men, the Lord Doctors Craig.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Ioan. Craigius, Doctor Medicus* = **John Craig** (Joannes Craig, d. 1620), Scottish physician and mathematician, trained at Frankfurt(-Oder) and physician at Edinburgh, later physician to James VI/I. He is the fourth of Tycho's four acrimonious antagonists (with Ursus, Wittich, and Rothmann). This letter (Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VII, 362.2–364.18) is Craig's **complete capitulation** in the cometary dispute that had run since Craig's first reply to Tycho's 1588 *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (letter of May 1589), through Craig's combative *Capnuraniae restinctio* of 1592 (his refutation of comets being raised into the aether) to this conciliatory peace overture; a parallel letter from his brother on his behalf followed the same year (TBOO VII, 364.20–365.16).
- ***Hwaenae insulae … Regis Daniae consiliario*** — "of the island of **Hven** … councillor to the King of Denmark": the address gives Tycho's seat (Uraniborg on Hven) and his royal office under Frederik II / Christian IV.
- ***Dominus Iunius … legatum ad vos agit*** / ***D. Legatus*** — "Master Junius … is acting as envoy to you" / "Master the Envoy": **Peter Young** (latinised *Iunius*), the Scots ambassador (royal tutor and diplomat) then on embassy to Denmark; Tycho had earlier commended Craig to him (letters of 1590 and 1593). Craig's wish to accompany the envoy on a visit to Hven was blocked by his friends.
- ***Apologia tua*** — **Tycho's *Apologia***: the polemical reply (within the cometary controversy) in which, Craig complains, he had been charged with "inexperience, ignorance, a judgement enslaved." Translated as the work-title *Apologia*; *italicised* on first use.
- ***scriptum nostrum*** — "my writing": Craig's own contribution to the dispute (his *Capnuraniae restinctio* and attendant critiques); rendered neutrally as "writing" since Craig declines to defend or re-title it here.
- ***Uraniae … has Deas … Uraniam consule*** — "your Urania … these Goddesses … consult Urania": *Urania* is the Muse of astronomy, here a figure for Tycho's astronomical work (and for astronomy/astrology generally). The closing *Uraniam, si placet, consule* ("consult Urania, if you please") is a playful invitation to Tycho to cast or check the new prince's nativity from the data given; "Urania" kept, per the edition's *Uraniae* convention.
- ***ex apodicto agis*** — "where you proceed from demonstration": *apodicto* (from Greek *ἀπόδειξις*, apodictic/demonstrative proof) — Craig concedes Tycho's conclusions wherever they rest on demonstration, dissenting only on the one disputed (and, he says, minor) point. Latinised Greek technical term; kept and glossed.
- ***Reipub. literariae*** — "the Republic of Letters" (*Respublica literaria*), the early-modern commonwealth of scholars; expanded from the abbreviation.
- **The King and the Chancellor.** *apud Regem … ad D. Cancellarium* — the **King** is **James VI of Scotland** (later James I of England), styled *Serenissimus Rex*; the **Chancellor** is **John Maitland of Thirlestane**, Lord Chancellor of Scotland, to whom Tycho had also written about Craig (1591–92) and with whom Craig claims a tie of blood (*aliqua sangvinis ratio*). *Serenissimae Reginae* = **Anne of Denmark**, James's queen (and sister of Christian IV).
- ***frater meus natu maior*** — "my elder brother": **Thomas Craig** (of Riccarton, c. 1538–1608), the jurist and Neo-Latin poet, author of the *epigram* (verses) sent to Tycho that this passage acknowledges; he sent his own letter to Tycho the same year.
- **The royal birth.** *infantem Principem exoptatissimum … FRIDERICUM Regem … diei 19. Februarij* — the "most longed-for infant Prince" is **Henry Frederick, Prince of Wales** (b. 19 February 1593/94 O.S. at Stirling Castle, d. 1612), James VI's heir, said here to resemble his late grandfather **King Frederik II of Denmark** ("Frederick … brought to life again"), the dedicatee's former patron. *Accepistis* is **second-person plural** ("you [pl.] have received word") — Craig addresses the news to Tycho and his circle. **Date note:** the birth-date *19 February* is given inside the letter; the letter's own dateline is *22 April*. Both are **Old Style** (Scotland and Denmark kept the Julian calendar); reproduced as written, not converted. (The civil year in Scotland began 25 March, so 19 February 1594 in modern reckoning fell in the legal year 1593 — not stated in the source and not interpolated here.)
- **Birth-time crux — *hora tertia post Μ. N. … media ad quartam*.** The Greek abbreviation **Μ. N.** is read as **midnight** — most plausibly *Μεσονύκτιον* (Greek "midnight") or a Greek-lettered abbreviation of Latin *Media Nox* — giving "began to strive into the light at the third hour after midnight … came [fully] into it at half past three [a.m.]." *Media ad quartam* = "the middle toward the fourth [hour]" = **3:30**. The expansion of **Μ. N.** is editorial: the Greek glyphs are kept verbatim in the Source block, the bracketed gloss **[midnight]** marks the reading, and the precise resolution is *flagged, not asserted* — this is the named crux. (Craig gives the time precisely so that Tycho can cast the prince's geniture, hence the immediately following latitude of Stirling and the "consult Urania" invitation.)
- ***Arx Sterlini … latitudinis … uno aut altero scrupulo … in Boream*** — "the Castle of **Stirling** … of [nearly the same] latitude … by one scruple or two … to the North": *scrupulus* here = a **minute of arc** (1/60 of a degree); Craig tells Tycho that Stirling lies almost on Edinburgh's parallel, scarcely a minute or two further north — geodetic data supplied for the horoscope.
- **Dateline.** *Datae Edinburgi 22. Aprilis* = "Given at **Edinburgh**, 22 April" (O.S.); the year is not written in the source dateline but is securely **1594** from the edition (TBOO VII) and from the contemporaneous royal birth (19 Feb. 1593/94), hence bracketed in the header.
- **Subscription.** *Tui observantiss.* = "Most observant of you" (a courtesy superlative parallel to the *E. Tuae studiosiss.* of the formula list,); *Doctor Medicus* = "Doctor of Medicine."
- **A crux, not a clean continuation.** The recovered line is a standard epistolary salutation formula ('Salutem precor...' — 'I wish greeting to...') addressed, in the dative plural, to 'the Lord Doctors Craig' (Domini Doctores Craigii) — i.e. both brothers collectively, John and Thomas Craig. A letter signed by John Craig alone closing by greeting 'the Doctors Craig' in the plural, apparently including himself, does not read as a natural authorial sign-off.
- **Likely explanation, left unresolved.** This has the shape of an *opening* salutation, not a closing one — plausibly the superscription of an adjoining letter (perhaps from Tycho, or a third party, to both Craig brothers jointly) that has been run on to the end of John Craig's letter in the source transcription. Flagged here rather than resolved; per instructions, no web search was made to chase it further.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the entire letter clause-by-clause against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.362-364, including the salutation heading, every proper name (Junius the legate, the unnamed Chancellor, King Frederick, Stirling Castle, Craig's elder brother, the closing address to the 'Domini Craigii'), the birth-hour detail for the infant Prince (third hour after midnight on 19 February, delivered at half past three), and the date and signature (22 April, John Craig, Doctor of Medicine). Latin the transcribed original matches Dreyer's print exactly throughout, word for word — no text error. No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found; the English renders the letter's argument (Craig's defence of his critical Apologia commentary, the peace overture, the royal-birth news) faithfully. Note for the record: this letter's the published grade was the translator's own C, but full page-image collation against Dreyer found no defect to support that grade.

text.original:
TILL THYGE BRAHE, EN WED NAFFN CHRISTOFFER PEPELER ANRØRENDIS.

Christianus 4.

WOR gunst tilforne. Wiid, effter som Nelle Christoffer Pepelers hustru wnderdanigstt till Oß haffuer supplicerit och tilkiende giffuett, huorledis effter att hendis hoßbunde, for:ne Christoffer Pepeler, haffuer werritt thin fougitt oc du derfore vdj nogenn sager, som hannom och thig skall haffue for samme hans thieniste emellom werritt, ladett hans godtz vdj Wor kiøpstedt Bergenn wdj Wortt riige Norge arestêre oc beslaa, oc sidenn effter din forthrøstning oc for:ne hans hustruis schriffuelße oc begiering haffuer sig begiffuit till Wor kiøpstedt Helsingøer, saa hand thin thiener ther sammestedtz paa thine wegne for for:ne sag haffuer satt nøyachtig borgenn, huilckett thu wanseett dog skall hannom ther effter ladett fenckligenn thage oc hensette paa Hueen, effter som hendis indlagde supplication ydermere formelder oc wduiiser, tha bede Wij thig oc Wille, att naar thu her met besøgis, thu tha therudinden retter thig selff och bethencker oc till sinde fører, medt huad rett oc billighet sligt skee kand, attu baade haffuer thagett borgenn af hannom oc sidenn hannom fenckligenn lader anholde, attu therfore om thet sig saaledis befindis, lader hannom egienn løß och sidenn medt rettenn hannom tillthaler, anseendis huad vdj sig selff christeligt oc rett er, saa Wij for widere thes klagemaall oc offuerlob maa bliffue forschonett.

Actum Hafniæ 8. junii a:o 94.
text.english:
**Concerning Tyge Brahe, touching one Christoffer Pepeler by name.**

Christian IV.

Our favour beforehand. Know that, inasmuch as Nelle, the wife of Christoffer Pepeler, has most humbly petitioned Us and made known how — after her husband, the aforesaid Christoffer Pepeler, had been your bailiff, and you therefore, in certain matters which are said to have arisen between him and you over that same service of his, had caused his goods to be arrested and seized in Our market-town of Bergen in Our realm of Norway, and [how] he then, upon your assurance and upon the aforesaid letter and request of his wife, had betaken himself to Our market-town of Helsingør, so that he there in the same place, on your behalf, posted sufficient bail to your servant for the aforesaid matter — [how], notwithstanding this, you are nonetheless said to have had him thereupon taken prisoner and confined on Hven, as her enclosed petition further sets forth and shows: We therefore ask you and will that, when you are visited [with this letter], you then in this matter govern yourself and consider and call to mind with what right and equity such a thing can be done — that you have both taken bail of him and then have him held prisoner — [and] that therefore, if it be found to be so, you set him free again and then proceed against him at law, having regard to what is in itself Christian and right, so that We may be spared further complaint and importunity in the matter.

Done at Copenhagen, 8 June in the year [15]94.

documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer.** **Christian IV of Denmark** (r. 1588–1648), then in his minority (the regency council governed until his 1596 coronation); royal letters in these years issue in his name. *Christianus 4.* is the Latin register-form of the subscription. Tycho was at this date still in possession of Hven, six years from his 1597 departure.
- **Recipient / subject.** **Tyge Brahe** (Tycho), addressed as the recipient; **Christoffer Pepeler**, formerly Tycho's *fougitt* (bailiff/steward), is the subject of the complaint; **Nelle** ("Nelle Christoffer Pepelers hustru"), Pepeler's wife, is the petitioner. None is further identified among the works consulted beyond this letter.
- **Document type.** A chancery-register entry (Jyske Tegnelser). The heading is a **Latin–Danish rubric** in the register's hand: *"TILL THYGE BRAHE … ANRØRENDIS"* ("Concerning Tyge Brahe … touching …") — the standard register caption, preserved by this chapter's convention The subscription *Christianus 4.* is likewise the Latin chancery register-form.
- **Legal structure (the load-bearing logic).** The body is one long chancery period reporting the wife's allegation and issuing the royal directive. Its skeleton is: *because* Pepeler (Tycho's ex-bailiff) had his goods seized in Bergen over service disputes; *and* on Tycho's own assurance came to Helsingør and posted sufficient bail through Tycho's servant; *yet* was nonetheless imprisoned on Hven — the king directs Tycho to weigh "with what right and equity" he could both take bail *and* then imprison the man, and, **conditionally**, *"om thet sig saaledis befindis"* ("if it be found to be so"), to release him and instead proceed against him *medt rettenn* ("at law"). The release order is thus **conditional on the facts proving out**, not absolute; this conditional mood (*om … befindis*) is preserved and not sharpened into an unconditional command.
- **Negations.** The Danish body contains **no explicit negative particle** (*icke/jcke*). The only negation-adjacent forms are the concessive *wanseett dog* ("notwithstanding … nonetheless") and *forschonett* ("spared"); neither is a logical "not." The translation introduces none.
- **Reportative subjunctive (hedge).** The constructions *skall haffue … werritt* and *skall … ladett* ("is said to have been," "is said to have had") mark the whole account as the wife's allegation reported to the king, not as findings the king asserts as proven. Rendered "are said to have," consistent with the conditional release order; not flattened to plain assertion.
- **Orthography (chancery Danish, c. 1594).** *WOR gunst tilforne* = *Vor gunst tilforn* ("Our favour beforehand," the royal address-formula, this chapter's convention); *Wiid* = *Vid* ("know"); *effter som* = "inasmuch as"; *hoßbunde* = *husbonde* ("husband"); *for:ne* = *fornævnte* ("aforesaid," the standard chancery abbreviation); *fougitt* = *foged* ("bailiff, steward"); *godtz* = *gods* ("goods, property"); *arestêre oc beslaa* = "arrest and seize/attach"; *forthrøstning* = *fortrøstning* ("assurance, guarantee"); *schriffuelße* = *skrivelse* ("letter, written communication"); *satt nøyachtig borgenn* = "posted sufficient bail/surety" (*borgen* = bail, surety); *huilckett … wanseett* = *hvilket … uanset* ("notwithstanding which"); *fenckligenn thage oc hensette* = "take prisoner and confine"; *formelder oc wduiiser* = *formelder og udviser* ("states and shows"); *besøgis* = "is visited [with this letter]," i.e. served/reached by it; *retter thig selff* = "govern/conduct yourself"; *till sinde fører* = "call to mind"; *billighet* = "equity, fairness"; *om thet sig saaledis befindis* = "if it be found to be so"; *løß* = *løs* ("free, loose"); *medt rettenn … tillthaler* = "proceed against / sue at law"; *klagemaall oc offuerlob* = "complaint and importunity (vexation)"; *forschonett* = *forskånet* ("spared").
