documents.apparatus:
- **Edition of record.** Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia* vol. VI (*Epistolae astronomicae*); first printed by Tycho in his own 1596 *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri*, Liber I (which it closes); no MS witness recorded. **Cross-check:** page-collated at **vol. VI pp. 319–337** (the closing letter of Liber I); every crux confirmed, including the embedded quotations and the Dee/Digges work-titles (anchors in the Editorial note).
- **Sender / recipient & the end of the correspondence.** Tycho (Uraniborg) → **Christoph Rothmann**, now chronically ill (gout/stone, "Tartareous salts") since his **1590 visit to Hven**, who never returned to Kassel before **Landgrave Wilhelm IV's death (1592)** and to whom this — the **last and longest Tycho letter to him** — was sent; Rothmann never replied, and the great correspondence ends here. Tycho opens with condolence and an offer of his **Pyronomic (chymical) medicines**.
- **The Craig refutation (the body — c. 90% of the letter).** Tycho explains the long delay in publishing his comet-works (the perennial-star labour; the world's turbulence; ungrateful critics), quotes **Jacob Monau**'s letter to **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (Breslau, 17 June 1588 O.S.) praising the comet book, then mounts a sustained demolition of the **unnamed Scot = John Craig** and his ***Capnuraniae restinctio*** ("Quenching of the Smoke-Heaven"). Craig is called "Galenic Doctor," "Aristotelian," "Pseudophilosophus," "**Zoilus**," "Capnocometista," "Chartaceus Astronomus" (Paper Astronomer), "Mastix" (Scourge), and his book an "Invective"/"Antilogeticum"; the wordplay *nec tam Scotice quam scoptice* ("not so much Scottishly as scoffingly") sets the tone. Tycho's defences: comets are **celestial matter, not smoke** (the *De recentioribus* p. 254 self-quote again, as in the undated Peucer letter of 1590 and the Hájek letter of 3 Aug 1590); the **tail is per accidens optical**, the comet-body round; he did **not** copy Maestlin/Gemma (Wittich's testimony); the **great-circle arc** at all altitudes proves super-lunar position; **proper motion does not exhaust the parallax** (the Edinburgh-to-Uraniborg great-circle joke refuted; the threefold motion separable; a fourth **refraction** divagation Craig ignores); the instrument-time method (the **Mechanical Equator** — Craig's "Logicon/Alogon" sneer quoted and turned: *in ipso λόγῳ alogum se prodit*); the "**adverbial not mathematical**" time-notation charge; the defence of **Wittich** (and **Dudith**), of **Maestlin** ("my Parson," the thread-sight), and of the **slit-sights**; the **1572 nova** as decisive proof the heavens admit new bodies (Craig's "one swallow doesn't make spring" and "staff in the corner → Pope at Rome" sneers; his slighting of **Hipparchus/Pliny**); the **metals/Mercury-in-gold** alchemy quarrel; the **Icaromenippus/Lucian** and **Cancer–Capricorn** jokes; the diurnal-motion-is-only-apparent argument refuted **geometrically** (equal parallax at equal altitude cancels). Crucially, Craig also attacked **Rothmann** (long quotation: "I come to your artifice… communicate the Observations") and **John Dee** (the *Nucleus parallaticus* / *Parallaticae commensurationis nucleus*, 1573, "begins within a half-degree") and **Thomas Digges** (the *Alae seu scalae mathematicae*, 1573). Tycho closes the refutation with the **Hájek letter** (which forwarded the *Capnurania* to Hájek and **Curtius**) and **Curtius's verdict** (the grim *Duns Scotus stabbed-with-pens* joke — Craig should be "stabbed through by all astronomers"), and mocks Craig's dating his completion to the **2½-digit solar eclipse of 1591**.
- **The closing astronomy (the anti-Copernican coda).** On Rothmann's in-person 1590 letter defending the **Earth's annual + diurnal motion** (Rothmann had softened toward Tycho): the **Mars eccentricity** is *not* smaller (as Copernicus needed for the Earth's motion + variable eccentricity) but **≈ Ptolemy's or larger**, refuting the Copernican hypotheses; likewise **Venus's eccentricity** and its **apogee** (not 17° Gemini per Copernicus but ~beginning of Cancer). Tycho urges Rothmann to publish the **Landgravian fixed-star observations** (cross-location agreement), and notes his own **1000-star catalogue** to the minute (*Progymnasmata* Tome I, ch. 2).
- **Persons & places.** **Christoph Rothmann, Landgrave Wilhelm IV** (d. 1592); **John Craig** (the unnamed Scot, *Capnuraniae restinctio*); **Jacob Monau** (Breslau humanist, d. c. 1592), **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (Görlitz); **Jacob Curtius** (Kurz von Senftenau, Vice-Chancellor); **Thaddaeus Hagecius**; **Maestlin, Cornelius Gemma, Paul Wittich, Andreas Dudith**; **John Dee** (the *Nucleus parallaticus*) & **Thomas Digges** (the *Alae*); **Jean Pena**; **Aristotle** (the "Stagirite"), **Plato/the Platonists, Porphyry** ("author of the Predicables"), **Hipparchus, Pliny, Ptolemy, Copernicus, Regiomontanus**; **Lucian** (Icaromenippus, the Bridge of Asses), **Virgil** ("Maro," on Sinon), **Duns Scotus** (the "subtle Doctor," in Curtius's joke). Places: **Uraniborg, Kassel, Breslau, Scotland/Edinburgh, England, Magdeburg, Delphi** (the Tripod, figurative).
- **Greek / Latin tags.** *ἀυτὸς ἔφα* = "he himself said it" (the Pythagorean/Aristotelian appeal to the master); *πολυρρητορεία* (src *πολυροτορέιαν*) = "much-rhetoricizing"; *κάπνἐγκέφαλος* = "smoke-brain"; *λόγῳ … alogum* = "in the [very] word/reason … irrational"; *Capnurania* = "smoke-heaven" (καπνός + Οὐρανία); *scoptice* = scoffingly; *ex ungue Leonem* = "the lion from the claw"; *nodum in scirpo quaerere* = "to seek a knot in a bulrush"; *bellum dulce inexpertis* = "war is sweet to the inexperienced" (Erasmus/Pindar); *ex uno disce omnes* (Virgil, *Aen.* II.65, of Sinon); *una hirundo non facit ver* (Aristotle/Erasmus); *Baculus stat in angulo, ergo…* (a stock fallacy); *Spermologi* = seed-pickers/gossips (Acts 17:18); *Tyrones* = recruits/beginners; *Mastix* = scourge; *philautia* = self-love. Glyphs: ♂ Mars, ♀ Venus, ♊ Gemini, ♋ Cancer, ☉ Sun, ☽ Moon.
- **Dating (this chapter's convention, a genuine composition-span crux).** Header dateline **14 January 1595 O.S.** (the dispatch date). But the letter **embeds its own composition note**: the Hájek/Curtius excerpt is dated *"Today, which is the last day of November 1592, New Style"* (**30 Nov 1592 N.S.**), when Hájek received Rothmann's **28 Sept** letter and Craig's screed via the Magdeburg courier. So Tycho **began the letter in late 1592 and only completed/sent it in Jan 1595** — a span of over two years (mirroring Craig's own delays that Tycho mocks). Other embedded dates: Monau **17 June 1588 O.S.**; Tycho's Apology sent to Craig **1589**; Craig's *Capnurania* received **end May 1592**; the solar eclipse **1591**. The header leads with the catalogued dispatch date, the internal note flagged.
- **Editorial interventions in the source block (declared).** c. 40 digitised text layer-intruded **apparatus "A" sigla** removed as non-textual (as in the letters to Scaliger of 23 Aug 1598, to Peucer of 1590 and 13 Sept 1588, to the Landgrave of 16 Aug 1588, to Herwart of 16 Nov 1599, from Rothmann of 13 Oct 1588 and 20 Jan 1587, and to Hájek of 3 Aug 1590); v/u orthography retained; the embedded **quotations** (Monau, Craig ×several, Hájek/Curtius) are set in *italics* inline and identified above. text-layer/print slips read through: *πολυροτορέιαν* (read *πολυρρητορείαν*), *Prometheus* used for the shape-shifter (properly **Proteus** — Tycho's own slip, kept), *sublimarem* (read *sublunarem*), *astruere/asstruere* variants. The Craig-quotations are reproduced as Tycho gives them (his excerpting).
- **Correction.** Swapped the reversed 'former'/'latter' labels in the Rothmann-quotation clause ('fleeing the cold of the former [Capricorn]... the hearth of the latter [Cancer]'); the bracketed sign identifications were already correct and are unchanged. No change to the Latin.

translation.warrant:
**Not collated against Dreyer** — no page reference for this letter, so the grade is capped at Probable however sound the translation looks. the edition gives no page reference for this letter, so by the audit's rule this is capped at grade Probable regardless of quality; audited against the transcribed original alone. Read the full the transcribed original (18 paragraphs / paras 1,3,5,...,35, c. 61,500 chars: the salutation, Rothmann's illness and Tycho's Pyronomic remedies, the Cometographica-publication delay with Monau's/Scultetus's 17 June 1588 letter, the unnamed Scottish antagonist's introduction, the 'Capnuraniae restinctio' title and the p.254 self-quote on comets' celestial matter, c. 10 paragraphs rebutting the antagonist's Antilogeticum point by point, Thaddaeus Hagecius's 30 Nov 1592 letter, the 1591-eclipse excuse, and the closing paragraph on Copernican Mars/Venus eccentricities and the star catalogue) against the full the published English ( c. 71,100 chars) verbatim, paragraph by paragraph. Verified: every proper name (Monau, Scultetus, Curtius, Hagecius, Wittich, Maestlin, Cornelius Gemma, Dudith, John Dee, Thomas Digges, Jean Pena); every date (17 June 1588 O.S.; comets of 1577/1585/1590; 30 Nov 1592 N.S.; 28 Sept 1592; the 1591 solar eclipse; the closing 14 Jan 1595 dateline); every direct quotation (Sculteti's letter, six quoted jibes from the antagonist's tract including the Edinburgh-to-Uraniborg jest and 'Bona verba, quaeso!', Thaddaeus's letter, the two classical adages); the one sum of money (100 crowns); and the closing astronomical figures (Mars/Venus eccentricity vs Ptolemy/Copernicus, Venus's apogee at 17 deg Gemini vs the true beginning of Cancer, c. 1000 restored stars, Progymnasmata bk.1 ch.2). Found the translation faithful to the transcribed original throughout, including preserved wordplay (Scotice/scoptice, Logicon/Alogon) and Greek terms; only the one low-severity former/latter inversion noted above, which a scholar would not be misled by since the bracketed gloss names the referent directly. NOTE: a directory-collision hazard was discovered and worked around — an initial scratch split using generic filenames (fid_split/the transcribed original.txt, the published English.txt) was overwritten mid-task by what appears to be a concurrent process auditing a different letter, producing spurious non-matching content; this was caught by hash-verifying against the source text before any defect-finding was finalized, so no phantom findings from that collision are reported here.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (low). The English 'former'/'latter' labels are reversed relative to their own sentence order (Capricorn is named first in the English clause, Cancer second, so Capricorn should be 'the former' and Cancer 'the latter'); the bracketed names still correctly identify each sign, so a scholar is not actually misled, but the labels as given are internally inconsistent. At: “fleeing the cold of the latter (namely Capricorn), it wished to proceed to the hearth of the former (namely Cancer)”.

**Repaired.** No Dreyer page images were available for this letter (no page reference), so the base Latin transcription could not be collated against the edition of record and is reproduced unchanged. The single mistranslation defect concerned only the English rendering and was verified from internal evidence: the Latin ipsius (scil. Capricorni)...huius (scil. Cancri) construction and the English clause's own naming order both establish that former=Capricorn and latter=Cancer, the reverse of what was published. That clause has been corrected; nothing else in the letter was touched.

CLARISSIMO VARIOQUE DOCTRINARUM GENERE ERUDITISSIMO EXCELLENTISSIMOQUE VIRO DOMINO THADDÆO HAGGECIO, PHILOSOPHIAE ET MEDICINAE DOCTORI EXIMIO, AULAe CÆSAREAe MEDICO, AMICO SUO INPRIMIS COLENDO.

S. INCREDIBILI laetitia sum perfusus, clarissime et amantissime mi THADDÆE, cum tuas ultimas die 10 Ianuarij huius anni mihi perscriptas litteras, iam nuper Haffniae in ultimis comitijs per vicarij Regij in Holsatia ministrum accepissem. Metuebam enim prius, ne aliquid tibi humanitus accidisset^, in ea praesertim ingravescente aetate tot periculosis morbis infestato. Siquidem totum pene triennium (ni fallor^) intercessit, ex quo ante has aliquid a te accepi litterarum; nec etiam interea aliunde quippiam de te cognovi. Atque hinc factum est, cur tam diu scriptione supersederim: nunc vero, cum te et vivere et valere, morborumque, qui imminebant, saevitiam divina ope evasisse, ex hisce tuis intelligam, est, cur non saltem tibi, sed et mihi, qui te semper in intimis habui, magnopere congratuler, Deoque tecum gratias agam, quod te tam benigne hactenus conservarit, utque idem in posterum facere dignetur, ex animo oro. Domini I. CURTIJ Procancellarij, communis nostri amici, obitus et mihi sane non minimum luctum peperit. Nam virum illum, non saltem ob Politica negotia et officij dignitatem, in qua praecelluit, sed et multo magis propter disciplinarum liberalium amorem, adeoque Mathematum (quod alias in Politicis rarum est) eximiam peritiam suspexi dilexique plurimum. Nollem ea, quae in Astronomiae exercitium et honorem elaborari curavit, qualiacunque tandem ea sint, in imperitorum manus pervenire aut prorsus interire, sed optarem potius, ut tibi concederentur, quo, si non per temetipsum, ob senij obstacula, saltem aliorum a te informatorum operâ in usum deduci queant. Enitere igitur, quibuscunque licuerit rationibus, ut ea obtineas. Cuperem vero quam maxime, primum nostrum tomum Progymnasmatum Astronomicorum, quem eidem^ Domino CURTIO (bonae memoriae) transmisi, in potestatem tuam redigi^, ne ad eos forte perveniret, quibus quam minime eius copiam, antequam omnino publici iuris fieret, concedi vellem, quique meis laboribus, uti saepenumero fit, abuti non vererentur. Disquiri inibi videbis in omnium scripta, quotquot de Stella illa nova edita nancisci licuit, tum quoque in tuam Dialexin, prout in eo exemplari, quod Dominus CURTIUS acceperat (siquidem id, quod tibi destinaveram, interciderit) videre licet. Has vero meas animadversiones non alio animo quam ab amico decet, prodeuntes, si aliquando perspexisti vel in posterum lecturus es, averem equidem a te cognoscere, an aliquid in his haberes, quod replicatione dignum censeres. Quod te pro tua ingenuitate libere indicaturum, nec diffido nec illubenter habeo. Quod vero totum illud opus tam diu differatur, quo minus lucem publicam videat, praeter gravia quaedam impedimenta e rebus quibusdam a Philosophia alienis, quae mihi invito multo iam tempore obtigerunt vel potius obstiterunt, accessit et hoc, quod Chartopaeo, quem in moletrina mea pro papyro conficienda hîc conduxeram, fatis concedente, nullum alium eiuscemodi opificem e Germania, utut diligenter ea in re laborârim, per totum hoc elapsum triennium nancisci potuerim. Ideoque chartâ impressoriâ destitutus, typographicas quoque operas intermittere coactus sum. Nunc vero tandem e vicinâ Meckleburgâ Chartopaeum adeptus, molendinum meum huic artificio destinatum redintegrari et ampliari procuro, quo papyri defectus nostros in posterum (uti spero) labores non amplius retardet.

Quae de ♂ stellâ adeo multum in ultimo Acronychio situ ab utroque calculo hactenus usitato digrediente indicâram, eodem modo se habebant, neque huius discrepantiae et aliarum in sydere hoc a coelesti tramite deviationum me caussa latet, ex ipso coelo multis iam annis conquisita patefactaque, partim usitatis hypothesibus, non omnimode eius apparentijs sufficientibus, partim in ijs ipsis, Apogaeo et eccentricitate non ad amussim dispositis. Nam ut de Coperniceis, quae nostrae inventioni quam proxime, licet inverso quodam ordine^, quadrant, solummodo hîc dicam, Apogaeum ♂ in ipsius numeratione plus 5 gradibus est ulterius, quam coelestis norma postulat, et eccentricitas, quam Ptolomaicâ minorem reddidit (forte ut eo probabilius suae speculationi in motu Terrae et eccentricitate ☉ alteratâ patrocinaretur) tantum abest, ut angustior admittenda sit, quod potius nonnihil (pauculis tamen minutis) maiorem quam a PTOLOMÆO factum est, eandem constituere operaeprecium sit, modo Phaenomenis ♂ omnimode satisfiat. Atque vel hoc solo experimento, COPERNICI in motu Terrae et quiete ☉ positio labefactatur. Nam et is cum discipulo RHETICO hinc suam hypotyposin non minimum stabilimenti acquirere opinatus est, quod videlicet ♂ eccentricitas ad analogiam mutatae eccentricitatis ☉ vel potius (ut ille vult) Terrae decrescendo, alterata ipsi crederetur. Id tamen observationum incuriâ potius factum est, quam quod citra omne dubium tale quid coelitus depromi queat. Sic etiam in aliorum Planetarum Apogaeis constituendis (ut de eccentricitatibus, quas a PTOLOMÆO nimis secure mutuatus est, nihil addam) non parum lapsus est magnus ille nunquamque satis laudatus COPERNICUS. Et licet in ☾ multo concinniorem et probabiliorem, quam Ptolomaica erat, adinvenerit Theoriam, tamen ne haec quidem Lunaribus curriculis excusandis per omnia sufficiens est. In novilunijs et plenilunijs ac quadraturis utrisque utcunque locum meretur, utut ne in his quidem requisita praecisione omnia expediat. In locis vero^ 4or, quae iam dictis intermedia sunt, nequaquam apparentias^ salvat, nisi dimidij gradus, cum ☾ circa medias^ elongationes maioris Epicycli, et pene integri gradus, quando prope Apogaeum vel Perigaeum eiusdem versatur, iacturam pro nihilo duxerimus. Unde etiam diutius quam sperassem me ☾ apparens enormitas detinuit, quo minus eius universos errores ratae et undiquaque convenienti hypothesi subijcere licuerit, quam tamen me nunc tandem assecutum confido, plurimorum annorum in diversimodis revolutionum locis huic sufficienter adstipulantibus, quae varijs indiget circularium motuum commixtionibus, ipsam ☾ subitaneam et vagabundam instabilitatem, non improprie repraesentantibus. Verum alius et convenientior (uti spero) dabitur haec tractandi exponendique locus. Ego cum sciam te talibus delectari, non omnino hîc intacta relinquere volui, quo aliquid saltem Astronomici haec nostra Epistola ad rerum Astronomicarum cultorem directa contineret.

Quae in globo Domini CURTIJ ex ligneâ materiâ constante improbas, ea prorsus ita se habent, prout asseris. Frustra enim tales machinae de ligno, quocunque tandem modo composito, praeparantur. Neque enim aëris mutationem, aestatisque et hyemis diversitatem aut temporis diuturnitatem perferunt. Commentaria TRAPEZUNTIJ in PTOLOMÆI magnam Syntaxin et libellum APIANI de Cometâ unâ cum adiunctis libentissime tibi restituerem, cum mihi nulli^ sint usui, si modo idoneum hominem invenire liceret, qui eos certo et tuto, vel Francofurtum ad Typographum, de quo scribis, vel etiam Pragam ad te ipsum perferret: quâ etiam in re posthac, quantum potero, elaborabo. Interea moram (si qua inciderit) candide excusatam habe, meque tui perpetuo fore quam studiosissimum et ad quaevis officia praestanda quam paratissimum, tibi (quod et te facere non dubito) persuasum habe.

Iamque feliciter vale, et senij gravamina patienter sustine.
Uraniburgi 12 Augusti A. C^. 95.
Tui amantiss.
TYCHO BRAHE, manu propria.^


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 371; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Si MONAVIUS adhuc (uti spero) in vivis est, et tibi cum eo (de quo non dubito) intercedit familiaritas, rogo ipsum per litteras admoneas, ut de libris VITICHIANIS, an eos a sorore superstite, prout idem MONAVIUS ad me perscripsit, seque impetraße aßeruit, obtinere queam nec ne; et de precio certiorem me reddat. Nam mihi iamdudum MONAVIO hac de re scribenti nihil responsum est; sive quod litterae meae interciderint, sive quod alia mihi hactenus ignota subsit caußa. Tu vero haec meo nomine quam commodißime data opportunitate expedies.
text.english:
**To the most renowned man, most learned in every kind of doctrine, and most excellent, Master Thaddaeus Hagecius, eminent Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine, physician to the Imperial Court, his friend to be honoured above all — greeting.**

I was filled with incredible joy, my most renowned and most beloved Thaddaeus, when I received your last letter, written out to me on 10 January of this year, only lately, at Copenhagen during the recent assembly, by the agent of the royal vicegerent in Holstein. For I had feared before this that some mortal thing [εuphemism: that you had died] might have befallen you, especially as, in that advancing age, you are beset by so many dangerous diseases. Indeed almost a whole three-year span (unless I am mistaken) has passed since I last received any letter from you before this one; nor in the meantime did I learn anything of you from any other quarter. And this is why I have so long forborne to write: but now, since I understand from this letter of yours that you are both alive and well, and that by divine aid you have escaped the fury of the diseases that were threatening, there is good reason why I should warmly congratulate not only you, but myself too — I who have always held you among my closest [friends] — and give thanks to God together with you, for having so kindly preserved you thus far; and I pray from my heart that He may deign to do the same hereafter. The death of Master J. Curtius, the Vice-Chancellor, our common friend, has likewise brought me no small grief. For I greatly looked up to that man and loved him, not only for his political affairs and the dignity of the office in which he excelled, but much more for his love of the liberal disciplines, and indeed for his outstanding skill in the mathematical sciences — which is otherwise rare among men in politics. I should be sorry if those things he saw to having worked up for the practice and honour of astronomy — whatever in the end they may be — should pass into the hands of the unskilled or perish outright; I would rather wish that they be granted to you, so that, if not through your own self, on account of the impediments of old age, then at least through the labour of others instructed by you, they may be brought into use. Strive therefore, by whatever means may be allowed, to obtain them. But I should wish above all that the first volume of our *Progymnasmata Astronomica*, which I sent to that same Master Curtius (of good memory), be brought into your keeping, lest it should perchance reach those to whom I would least wish a copy of it to be granted before it should become public property altogether, and who would not scruple to abuse my labours, as so often happens. There you will see examined the writings of all — as many as it was possible to obtain — that have been published about that new star, and likewise your own *Dialexis*, as may be seen in that copy which Master Curtius had received (since the one I had intended for you has gone astray). And these observations of mine, issuing forth in no other spirit than befits a friend, if you have at any time looked them over or are going to read them hereafter — I should indeed be eager to learn from you whether you find anything in them that you judge worthy of a reply. That you, in keeping with your candour, will freely indicate this, I neither doubt nor take amiss. But as for the fact that that whole work is so long delayed, the less to see the public light: besides certain grave hindrances from certain matters foreign to philosophy, which have befallen me — or rather have stood in my way — against my will now for a long time, this too was added, that, the papermaker whom I had hired here in my mill for making paper having yielded to fate, I was unable, throughout this whole past three-year span, to obtain any other craftsman of that kind from Germany, however diligently I laboured in the matter. And so, being deprived of printing-paper, I was compelled to suspend the printing-work as well. But now at last, having got a papermaker from neighbouring Mecklenburg, I am seeing to it that my mill appointed for this craft be restored and enlarged, so that (as I hope) the lack of paper may no longer hold back our labours hereafter.

The things I had pointed out concerning the planet Mars [♂], as departing so very greatly in its last acronychal position from both reckonings hitherto in use, stood in the same way; nor is the cause of this discrepancy, and of the other deviations of this star from its celestial track, hidden from me — [a cause] sought out and laid bare from the heaven itself now over many years: partly the customary hypotheses, not in every way sufficient for its appearances, partly in those very [hypotheses], the apogee and eccentricity not being arranged to the exact measure. For — to say here only this much about the Copernican [values], which square most closely with our own discovery, albeit by a certain inverted arrangement — the apogee of Mars [♂] in his [Copernicus's] numbering is more than 5 degrees further on than the celestial standard requires; and the eccentricity, which he rendered smaller than the Ptolemaic (perhaps so that he might the more plausibly support his speculation regarding the motion of the Earth and the altered eccentricity of the Sun [☉]) — so far is it from being that a narrower one ought to be admitted, that rather it is worth the labour to establish that same eccentricity somewhat (yet by a very few minutes) larger than was done by Ptolemy, provided that the phenomena of Mars [♂] be in every way satisfied. And by this one experiment alone, Copernicus's positing of the motion of the Earth and the rest of the Sun [☉] is shaken. For he too, together with his disciple Rheticus, supposed that his model gained no small support from this — namely, that the eccentricity of Mars [♂] was believed by him to be altered, decreasing in proportion to the altered eccentricity of the Sun [☉], or rather (as he will have it) of the Earth. Yet this came about rather through carelessness of observations, than because, beyond all doubt, any such thing can be drawn down from the heaven. So too in establishing the apogees of the other planets (to say nothing of the eccentricities, which he borrowed from Ptolemy too uncritically) that great and never sufficiently praised Copernicus erred not a little. And although in [the theory of] the Moon [☾] he devised a far neater and more probable theory than the Ptolemaic was, yet not even this is in all respects sufficient for accounting for the lunar courses. At the new moons and full moons and at both quadratures it earns its place after a fashion, although not even in these does it dispatch everything with the precision required. But in the four places that are intermediate to those just mentioned, it in no way saves the appearances — unless we shall reckon as nothing a loss of half a degree, when the Moon [☾] is about the middle elongations of the greater epicycle, and of almost a whole degree, when it is engaged near the apogee or perigee of the same. Whence also the apparent irregularity of the Moon [☾] detained me longer than I had hoped, so that I could the less subject all its errors to a fixed and everywhere-consistent hypothesis — which nevertheless I now at last am confident I have attained, the [observations] of very many years in the variously-disposed positions of the revolutions sufficiently corroborating it; [a hypothesis] which needs various commixtures of circular motions, [these] not improperly representing the Moon's [☾] own sudden and wandering instability. But another and more fitting place (as I hope) will be given for treating and setting forth these matters. Since I know that you delight in such things, I did not wish to leave them entirely untouched here, so that this letter of ours, directed to a cultivator of astronomical matters, might contain at least something of astronomy.

The things you disapprove of in Master Curtius's globe, made of wooden material, are entirely so, just as you assert. For in vain are such machines fashioned of wood, composed in whatever manner. For they do not endure the change of air, the difference of summer and winter, or the long passage of time. The commentaries of Trapezuntius on Ptolemy's *Great Syntaxis* and Apian's little book on the comet, together with their appendices, I would most gladly restore to you, since they are of no use to me, if only it were possible to find a suitable man who would carry them surely and safely, either to Frankfurt to the printer of whom you write, or even to Prague to yourself: in which matter too I shall labour hereafter as far as I am able. Meanwhile hold any delay (if any should arise) candidly excused, and be assured that I shall be perpetually most devoted to you and most ready to render any services whatever — as I do not doubt that you too will be.

And now fare you happily, and bear the burdens of old age patiently.
At Uraniborg, 12 August, in the year of Christ '95.
Most loving of you,
TYCHO BRAHE, in his own hand.


*[Postscript:]* If Monavius is still (as I hope) among the living, and there subsists between you and him (as I do not doubt) a familiarity, I ask that you admonish him by letter [to tell me] whether or not I may obtain Wittich's books from the surviving sister — as the same Monavius wrote to me, and affirmed that he had himself secured them; and let him inform me of the price. For though I have long since written to Monavius on this matter, no answer [has come] to me — whether because my letters went astray, or because some other cause, as yet unknown to me, underlies it. You, then, will dispatch this in my name as conveniently as occasion is given.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Thaddaeus Haggecius* = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayek, 1525–1600), physician to the Imperial court of Maximilian II and Rudolf II at Prague, and Tycho's principal astronomical correspondent in Bohemia. He had observed the 1572 nova (publishing his *Dialexis de novae … stellae*, Frankfurt 1574) and was the conduit through whom Tycho came to be invited to the Imperial court in 1599; he also brokered Tycho's contact with the Imperial Vice-Chancellor. The salutation's full titulature (*Philosophiae et Medicinae Doctori … Aulae Caesareae Medico*) is preserved.
- **Sender / place.** *Tycho Brahe, manu propria, Uraniburgi* — Tycho writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven; *manu propria* = "in his own hand" (the autograph subscription formula).
- **J. Curtius.** *Domini I. CURTIJ Procancellarij* = **Jacob Kurz von Senftenau** (Jacobus Curtius a Senftenau, d. 1594), Imperial **Vice-Chancellor** (*Procancellarius*) to Rudolf II, an amateur with genuine mathematical competence whom Hagecius had introduced to Tycho (Norlind). Tycho had sent him both the first volume of the *Progymnasmata* and a star-globe; with Curtius now dead, Tycho asks Hagecius to recover Curtius's astronomical papers and that volume. *bonae memoriae* = "of good memory," the formula for a deceased person.
- **Work referenced.** *primum nostrum tomum Progymnasmatum Astronomicorum* = the first volume of the *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata* (Tycho's treatise on the 1572 nova and the solar/lunar theory), not yet published in 1595 (it appeared posthumously, 1602). Tycho's anxiety that an advance copy might fall into hands that would "abuse my labours" reflects the Ursus plagiarism dispute then live.
- ***Dialexin / Stella illa nova*** — *tuam Dialexin* = Hagecius's *Dialexis* on the new star of 1572; *Stella illa nova* = that nova. The *Progymnasmata* surveyed *omnium scripta … de Stella illa nova* — all the published writings on the nova, including Hagecius's.
- **Papermaking.** *Chartopaeo … in moletrina mea pro papyro conficienda* = the **papermaker** in Tycho's **paper-mill** on Hven; *chartâ impressoriâ destitutus* = "deprived of printing-paper." The death of his papermaker had halted Tycho's own press for the *triennium*; he reports recruiting a replacement from Mecklenburg. *molendinum … redintegrari et ampliari* = the mill "restored and enlarged."
- **Astronomy — Mars.** *Acronychio situ* = **acronychal position** (rising at sunset, i.e. opposition); *utroque calculo* = "both reckonings" (Ptolemaic and Copernican); *Apogaeum ♂ … plus 5 gradibus … ulterius* = the apogee of Mars more than 5° too far in Copernicus's tables; *eccentricitas* / *Apogaeum* / *coelestis norma* rendered per glossary. The glyph ♂ is kept in the source and named **Mars** in the translation; ☉ = **Sun**, ☾ = **Moon**. *experimento* here = "test, trial" (the empirical demonstration), rendered "experiment" in the period sense.
- **Astronomy — Moon.** *novilunijs et plenilunijs ac quadraturis* = **new moons, full moons, and quadratures**; *maioris Epicycli* = **the greater epicycle**; *Apogaeum / Perigaeum* = **apogee / perigee**; *medias elongationes* = **the middle elongations**; *apparentias salvat* = "saves the appearances" (the technical *salvare apparentias*); *enormitas* = "irregularity" (deviation from rule), not "enormousness." The "four intermediate places" (*locis 4or … intermedia*) are the octants between syzygy and quadrature — the variation/evection residuals Tycho is describing.
- **Copernicus / Rheticus.** *magnus ille nunquamque satis laudatus COPERNICUS* = "that great and never sufficiently praised Copernicus" — Tycho's habitual respectful formula even while refuting him; *discipulo RHETICO* = **Rheticus** (Georg Joachim Rheticus), Copernicus's disciple; *hypotyposin* (Greek-derived) = his model/representation, kept as "model." Tycho's hedge that the Copernican values "square most closely … albeit by a certain inverted arrangement" (*inverso quodam ordine*) is preserved, not sharpened.
- **Other works.** *Commentaria TRAPEZUNTIJ in PTOLOMAeI magnam Syntaxin* = the commentary of **George of Trebizond** (Georgius Trapezuntius) on Ptolemy's *Almagest* (*magna Syntaxis* / *Megalē Syntaxis*); *libellum APIANI de Cometâ* = **Peter Apian's** tract on the comet. Tycho offers to return both, on loan from Hagecius, via Frankfurt or Prague.
- **Greek / euphemism.** *aliquid tibi humanitus accidisset* — "some mortal thing might have befallen you," the standard Latin euphemism (*humanitus accidere*) for "that you might have died"; the bracketed gloss flags it rather than rendering it bluntly.
- **Apparatus sigla in the source.** The superscript ^A markers attached to certain words (*accidisset^A, ni fallor^A, eidem^A, redigi^A, inverso quodam ordine^A, vero^A, apparentias^A, medias^A, nulli^A, C^A. [Christi], manu propria.^A*) are **Dreyer's critical-apparatus lemma marks**, keying these words to his footnoted variant readings between MS witnesses A (cod. 10686.51) and B (cod. 10686.39). They are not part of the letter's text; they are reproduced here as printed in the edition of record and carry no translatable content.
- **Calendar.** *die 10 Ianuarij huius anni* = Hagecius's letter dated **10 January [15]95**; *Uraniburgi 12 Augusti A. C[hristi]. 95* = **12 August 1595**, Old Style (Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700; this chapter's convention). The dateline date (12 August) is carried in the header; the catalogue label ("1595. 12. august") agrees, so no discrepancy. *A. C. 95* = *Anno Christi [15]95* ("in the year of Christ '95"), the century left implicit as in the source.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript, restored from Dreyer VII, p. 371 (dropped by the working transcription); presses Monavius (Jacob Monau) about acquiring the late Paul Wittich's books from his surviving sister, and the price — historically load-bearing for the Wittich-library question.
- **Correction.** Collated against Dreyer, TBOO VII p.368: the salutation heading's 'PHILOSOPHEAe' is corrected to 'PHILOSOPHIAE' (Dreyer's 'PHILOSOPHIÆ ET MEDICINÆ DOCTORI EXIMIO'); no effect on the translation, which already read correctly.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter, visually, against Dreyer TBOO VII pp.368-371 (page images). Checked the opening/closing lines, the postscript (explicitly flagged in the packet as restored from Dreyer p.371 after being dropped by the working transcription — independently verified word-for-word against the page image and found correctly restored and correctly translated, including the Wittich-books/Monavius passage and its pronoun references), and every proper name and number (Curtius, Monavius, Wittich/Vitichianis, Copernicus, Rheticus, Ptolemy, Regiomontanus/Trapezuntius, Apian, Mecklenburg, Bergensis/Cunradus, 'plus 5 gradibus', the half-degree/whole-degree lunar figures, the '4or' intermediate points, 12 August 1595). Found one low-severity text error in the salutation heading (PHILOSOPHEAe for Dreyer's PHILOSOPHIAE); it has no translation consequence. No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found anywhere in an otherwise unusually faithful and carefully restored translation. Per the audit's own rule, any text error caps the grade at C regardless of severity or downstream effect; the letter's the translator's own grade of A was not warranted on that technicality, though substantively this is the cleanest of the three letters audited.

**1 defect found:**
- **text error** (low). Single-letter substitution (I to E) corrupts 'Philosophiae' to the nonstandard 'Philosopheae' in the letter's salutation heading. No effect on meaning; the English renders the correct sense regardless. Dreyer prints: *PHILOSOPHIAE ET MEDICINAE DOCTORI EXIMIO (TBOO VII p.368, salutation heading)*.

**Repaired.** The sole text error was verified directly against the Dreyer page image for TBOO VII p.368 (within the letter's pp.367-370 extract, pages 1-4). The salutation heading's 'PHILOSOPHIAE ET MEDICINAE' is clearly legible and confirms the audit. This is a single-letter orthographic corruption with no bearing on sense; the translation required no change. No crux remains.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE IOH. ISACIO PONTANO. S.

BINAS iam nuper a te, dilecte mi IOHANNES ISACIDE, intra paucos dies accepi literas. Ex quibus cognovi te salvum ad patrem Amstelrodamum hinc redijsse, quod et libenter audio. Respondebo vero ad utrasque hisce unis, et ad priores primum. Indicas illic statim ab initio, commilitonem IOANNIS ANTONIJ tecum fuisse, literas accepisse, contenta earum placuisse, ideoque ipsum itineri confestim se accinxisse. At vero, nec is nec eius socius, tanto interim elapso tempore, huc advenit. Si postmodum id fiet, mihi non erit ingratum. De Sphaeropaeo quod scribis, illum proprijs literis suam sententiam mihi aperturum, nihil tamen etiamnum ea in re effectum est. Nam nec literas nec globos exinde ab eo obtinui. Videtur avaritia nimium fascinatus, a qua Astrali infectione, sive coeli sive soli vitio, plerique eorum, qui caetera propemodum religionis quodam affectu effectuque superare vel didicerunt vel videri volunt, se vindicare non sustinent. Si is promissis non steterit, erit forte alius, qui lubens hanc conditionem arripiet. De doctis vestratibus quae scribis, mihi inprimis accepta sunt. Magnus ille SCALIGER si huc in Daniam (uti significas) advenerit, haud vulgaris felicitatis loco, si me invisere non degravatus fuerit, duxerim. Virum enim illum, etsi absentem, mihique de facie adhuc ignotum, semper (uti etiam eius meretur virtus et doctrina incomparabilis) in precio habui, suspexique plurimum. DOUZAM filium summae expectationis iuvenem, quem a vobis in Germaniam adeoque vicinam nobis Cimbriam discessisse, meque, si alia non obstiterint, hîc alloqui decrevisse ais, nondum vidi. Si is deinceps accesserit, erit mihi ipsius congressus perquam iucundus. Nam et eius ingenium et ad solidam eruditionem arduum enixum diu multumque magni feci. R. SNELLIUM, eximium illum Lugdunensium Mathematicum, quod meo nomine conveneris, et consilium de filio isthuc mittendo aperueris eiusque disciplinae commendando, gratum est; longe vero adhuc gratius, quod iam in tantum ipsi placuerit, ut filium suum huc vicissim mittere, et meae fidei concredere (dummodo de meâ voluntate prius certior redditus fuerit) animum induxerit. Ego meum TYCHONEM isthuc sub initia futurae aestatis, ut studijs ingenuis operam navet, amandare constitui, et SNELLIJ disciplinae morumque inspectioni submittere, nihil de ipsius fide et integritate addubitans, quin seduli et fidelis praeceptoris ac moderatoris munus sit obiturus. Si ille suum GILLEBRODUM, aut antea vel etiam post, huc ad me miserit, erit is mihi pariter serio curae, tam quoad liberalem institutionem et honestatis morum inspectionem, quam caetera ad decentem educationem sustentationemque necessaria. Intelligo ipsum esse ferme eiusdem aetatis cum meo filio, id est, iam primos pueritiae annos, sive secundum septenarium excessisse, atque in hac tenera aetate Arithmetices et Geometriae studijs initiatum esse, idque non saltem ex tuis literis, sed et a FRANCISCO TENGNAGEL, qui nunc mecum est, a DOUZA iuniore mihi commendatus, perlubenter cognovi. Erit itaque is, ubi huc appulerit, mihi loco mei filij, quemadmodum spero, optimum illum SNELLIUM meum quoque vice sui habiturum; sicque quisnam maiori affectu suum adoptivum prosequi pergat, invicem certabimus. De sumptibus, quae ad honestam mei filij sustentationem requiruntur, haud gravatim providebo. Quae omnia ut ad ipsum Dominum SNELLIUM meo nomine referas, te rogatum habeo. Scripsissem ipsemet illi, modo suppeteret otium, verum fiet id alio tempore commodius. Literas eius, quas illum ad me misisse innuis, necdum accepi. Sed sive is scribat sive non, nihilominus mea de ipso sincera persuasio ac fiducia sartae tectae manebunt. Ipsum esse quam occupatissimum, tam in privatae suae scholae, quam publicis Academiae laboribus exequendis, et ab alijs et a praedicto TENGNAGELIO iam antea satis percepi, ut ob id eum, quod scriptione supersederit, non invite excusatum habeam. De re pecuniaria patri tuo scribo, quare hîc subticeo. Nunc ad alteras tuas.

Iconem mei isthic expressam unâ accepi, licet et antea eadem per CUNRADUM nostrum (qui hanc Coloniae sculptam existimavit) huc delata sit. Non satis placet, quod duobus haemisphaerijs imaginem istam inniti fecerit artifex. Videtur id minus gravitatis prae se ferre. Is quidem forte suo quodam consilio, nec sine industrio labore sic faciendum censuit. At mihi, si rotundas istas picturas omisisset vel adhuc in aliqua altera (si sic volet) imitatione omiserit, rem magis arridentem praestiterit: sic quoque pomposa illa circumscriptio nimia est, neque enim tanto me dignor honore. Opera nonnulla ex meis, de quibus solicite inquiri asseris, brevi (uti spero) lucem publicam videbunt. Nactus enim iam tandem sum chartopaeum. Ideoque papyrus Typographiae nostrae inserviens (cuius defectus editionem hactenus retardavit) nunc indies in propria hîc moletrina conficitur. Ad ea, quae de SNELLIO et utriusque nostrum filijs in his posterioribus repetis, iam antea responsum est. SCALIGERI de Emendatione Temporum praestans illud opus recognitum, ubi illud consummatum fuerit, si mihi transmiseris, recte feceris. Quoniam vero de anni Iuliani cum coelesti comparatione ad amussim praefinienda is inibi non minima ex parte agit, quo epocham antiquissimam illam Iudaicam a se productam vel quamvis aliam cum aequinoctijs hoc aevo coelitus quam accuratissime depromptis penitius conferat (siquidem ea, quae ex libris et tabulis quibusve petuntur, nimium devia sunt) additi quaterniones aliquot primi Capitis Progymnasmatum nostrorum Astronomicorum, quod de Solari curriculo tractat. Isthic pagina 13 utriusque aequinoctij rata momenta certis annis applicata inveniet; quae cum vetustissimis illis pariter, respectu bisexti Iuliani, se habentibus non inutiliter componet, verioremque anni coelestis et Iuliani ad invicem commensurationem quam antea hinc extricabit. Quamvis autem ea, qua ego isthic utor, pro hisce proximis seculis anni aequinoctialis Solarisque quantitas saltem ab Epocha centum annorum derivata sit, observationibus videlicet REGIOMONTANI eiusque discipuli GUALTERI, idque peculiari quodam consilio, ut inaequalitatis labyrinthos, a COPERNICO et alijs nimia tum (uti ego sentio) credulitate et licentia introductos isthic loci evitarem: attamen si comparatio cum observationibus ante plurima secula habitis rite instituatur, ijs praesertim, quae fidem indubitatam merentur (quales ego HIPPARCHI prae ceteris esse iudico, qui ad utriusque luminaris apparentias diligentissime attendit) vix annua quantitas a nobis illic praedefinita in pauculis, utpote 5 vel 6 scrupulis secundis deficiet, ideoque annorum determinationem nequaquam attinget. Disparitatem vero, tam in anni quantitate, quam in motu fixarum stellarum, non adeo esse magnam tantique momenti, prout suspicantur Astronomi, meae observationes selectioribus vetustis applicatae demonstrant. Haec per occasionem ad Dominum SCALIGERUM ut referantur, efficies. Alibi pluribus, quid in his expertus sim sentiamque, declarabo. Tu autem illustrem illum virum, nostri seculi decus, ex me quam officiosissime saluta, resalutaque. Tum quoque doctiss. Dominum SNELLIUM, DOUZAM enim ad vos nondum reversum existimo. Verum antea eius hîc praesentiam avide expecto. Vale mi IOANNES, et de mea erga te benevolentia nihil ambige, quam semper tibi probatam relinquam, praesertim si (quando ad nos redieris) mea opera tibi uspiam commodare possit.

Iterumque vale.
Raptim Uraniburgi 5. Septembris Anni 95.
Tycho Brahe,
manu propria.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Johannes Isaacius Pontanus — greeting.**

A short while ago, within a few days, I received two letters from you, my beloved Johannes Isaacides. From them I learned that you had returned safely from here to your father at Amsterdam, which I am glad to hear. I shall answer both in this one letter, and the earlier one first. You indicate there, right at the outset, that the comrade-in-arms of Joannes Antonius had been with you, had received the letters, that their contents had pleased him, and that he had therefore at once girded himself for the journey. But in fact, in all the time that has since elapsed, neither he nor his companion has arrived here. If it happens later, it will not be unwelcome to me. As to what you write about the Sphere-maker [Sphaeropaeus] — that he would open his mind to me in a letter of his own — nothing has yet been accomplished in that matter. For I have obtained from him neither letters nor globes. He seems too much bewitched by avarice — that Astral infection from which (whether by the fault of the heavens or of the soil) most of those who have either learned, or wish to seem, to surpass [other men] in well-nigh everything else by a certain disposition and effect of religion cannot bring themselves to free themselves. If he does not stand by his promises, there will perhaps be another who will gladly seize this offer. What you write about the learned men of your country is especially welcome to me. That great Scaliger, if he comes here to Denmark (as you intimate), I should reckon it a piece of no common good fortune, should he not think it beneath him to visit me. For that man — though absent, and as yet unknown to me by face — I have always held in esteem and looked up to greatly (as indeed his worth and incomparable learning deserve). Dousa's son, a young man of the highest promise, who you say has departed from you for Germany and so for Cimbria neighbouring us, and has resolved to address me here, if other things do not stand in the way — I have not yet seen. If he comes hereafter, meeting him will be most delightful to me; for I have long and much prized both his talent and his strenuous striving toward solid erudition. That you met R. Snellius, that distinguished Mathematician of Leiden, in my name, and disclosed the plan of sending [my] son thither and commending him to his instruction, is welcome to me; but far more welcome still is that it has now so pleased him that he has made up his mind to send his own son here in turn, and to entrust him to my good faith (provided only that he be first assured of my willingness). I have determined to send my Tycho thither at the beginning of next summer, that he may apply himself to the liberal studies, and to submit him to Snellius's instruction and to his oversight of his conduct, in no way doubting his good faith and integrity, but that he will discharge the office of a diligent and faithful preceptor and guardian. If he sends his Gillebrodus here to me — whether before, or even after — that boy too shall be in equal earnest my care, both as regards a liberal upbringing and the oversight of an honourable conduct, and the other things necessary to a fitting education and maintenance. I understand that he is of nearly the same age as my son — that is, that he has now passed the first years of boyhood, or the second seven-year span — and that at this tender age he has been initiated into the studies of Arithmetic and Geometry; and this I learned with great pleasure not only from your letter, but also from Franciscus Tengnagel, who is now with me, commended to me by the younger Dousa. And so, when he arrives here, he shall be to me in place of my son, just as I hope my son will have that excellent Snellius to himself in place of his own [father]; and so we shall contend with one another, [to see] which of us shall press on to cherish his adoptive [son] with the greater affection. As for the expenses required for the honourable maintenance of my son, I shall not grudgingly provide them. All of which I ask you to report to Master Snellius himself in my name. I should have written to him myself, had I but the leisure; but that will be done more conveniently at another time. His letter, which you hint he sent to me, I have not yet received. But whether he writes or not, my sincere conviction and trust regarding him shall none the less remain whole and intact. That he is exceedingly busy, both in carrying out the labours of his own private school and the public labours of the University, I learned well enough already, both from others and from the aforesaid Tengnagel, so that on that account I readily hold him excused for having forborne to write. Concerning the money matter I write to your father, wherefore I keep silent about it here. Now to your other letter.

The portrait of me engraved there [isthic] I received together [with the letter], although the same had also earlier been conveyed here by our Cunradus (who reckoned it had been engraved at Cologne). I am not altogether pleased that the craftsman has made that image rest upon two hemispheres. It seems to carry less of dignity. He indeed perhaps, on some plan of his own and not without industrious labour, judged that it ought to be done thus. But to me, if he had omitted those round pictures — or shall yet omit them in some other rendering (should he so wish) — he will render the thing more pleasing. So too that pompous inscription is excessive, for I do not deem myself worthy of so great an honour. Some of my works, about which you assert that anxious inquiry is being made, will shortly (as I hope) see the public light. For I have at last secured a paper-maker; and so the paper that serves our Press (the lack of which has hitherto delayed the edition) is now being made daily here, in [our] own mill. To the things you repeat in this latter [letter] about Snellius and the sons of us both, an answer has already been given above. That excellent revised work of Scaliger's *On the Emendation of Times* — when it is completed, you will do rightly if you transmit it to me. For since he deals there, in no small part, with precisely determining the comparison of the Julian year with the celestial [year] — in order more deeply to compare that most ancient Jewish epoch which he has put forward, or any other, with the equinoxes most accurately derived from the heavens in this age (since those that are sought from books and tables of whatever kind are too far astray) — I have added several gatherings of the first Chapter of our Astronomical *Progymnasmata*, which treats of the Solar course. There, on page 13, he will find the established moments of either equinox applied to certain years; and these, set beside those most ancient ones, likewise reckoned with respect to the Julian bissextile, he will not unprofitably compare, and from this will work out a truer mutual commensuration of the celestial and the Julian year than before. But although the quantity of the equinoctial and Solar year that I use there, for these next centuries, is derived only from an epoch of a hundred years — namely from the observations of Regiomontanus and of his pupil Walther — and that by a particular design, that I might in that place avoid the labyrinths of inequality introduced by Copernicus and others with too much (as I judge) credulity and licence: nevertheless, if a comparison be duly instituted with observations made many centuries before — especially those that deserve undoubted trust (such as I judge Hipparchus's to be above the rest, who most diligently attended to the appearances of both luminaries) — the yearly quantity predetermined by us there will scarcely fall short by a few, namely 5 or 6 seconds [scrupulis secundis], and therefore will in no way reach [the magnitude of] the determination of years. But that the discrepancy, both in the quantity of the year and in the motion of the fixed stars, is not so great and of such moment as Astronomers suspect, my observations, applied to the choicer ancient ones, demonstrate. You will see to it that these things are reported, as occasion offers, to Master Scaliger. Elsewhere, at greater length, I shall declare what I have found and think in these matters. But do you, in my name, greet and greet again that illustrious man, the glory of our age, most dutifully. And likewise the most learned Master Snellius — for Dousa, I think, has not yet returned to you; but I eagerly await his presence here beforehand. Farewell, my Johannes, and have no doubt of my goodwill toward you, which I shall always leave proven to you — especially if (when you return to us) my service can anywhere be of use to you.

And again, farewell.
In haste, at Uraniborg, 5 September, the year [15]95.
Tycho Brahe,
in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Joh. Isacius Pontanus* = **Johannes Isaacius Pontanus** (Johannes Isaksen, 1571–1639), Dutch-Danish historian, geographer and physician, son of Isaac Pietersz, the Dutch diplomatic resident at Elsinore; he had stayed on Hven shortly before this letter (Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, records that he later "followed [Tycho] in reprinting Tycho's remarks"). The Greek-style patronymic *Isacides* / vocative *ISACIDE* = "son of Isaac."
- ***Ioannis Antonii*** — "Joannes Antonius": almost certainly **Giovanni Antonio Magini** of Bologna (cf. glossary), whose *commilito* ("comrade-in-arms," here a fellow-traveller/associate) was expected; left as named in the letter, the identification flagged as probable.
- ***Sphaeropaeus*** (also spelled *Sphaeropoeus*) — literally "**globe-/sphere-maker**"; a craftsman from whom Tycho expected celestial globes (*globos*). Not a proper name but an occupational designation; kept and glossed. Tycho's complaint of *avaritia* ("avarice") names no individual securely.
- ***Magnus ille Scaliger … illustrem illum virum, nostri seculi decus*** — **Joseph Justus Scaliger** (1540–1609), the great chronologist, then at Leiden; Tycho had not yet met him face to face. His *opus de Emendatione Temporum recognitum* = the revised (second) edition of the *De emendatione temporum* (1st ed. 1583; the revised edition appeared 1598). The literature confirms Tycho still pressing this chronological dispute with Scaliger as late as 7 Jan 1600 (Benátky letter, on the Dionysian epoch).
- ***Douza filium … Douza iuniore*** — **Janus Dousa the Younger** (Jan van der Does, 1571–1597), son of the Leiden statesman-humanist Janus Dousa the Elder; here "Dousa's son … the younger Dousa," travelling toward *Cimbria* (Jutland / the Danish lands, see below).
- ***R. Snellius … Lugdunensium Mathematicum*** — **Rudolph Snellius** (Rudolph Snel van Royen, 1546–1613), professor of mathematics at Leiden (*Lugdunum Batavorum*), father of Willebrord Snell. The reciprocal-fosterage plan: Tycho would send his son **Tycho the Younger** to Snellius at Leiden, and Snellius would send his son **Gillebrodus** = **Willebrord Snell** (Snellius, of Snell's law) to Hven. The phrase *secundum septenarium excessisse* = "[the boy] has passed the second seven-year span," i.e. is about 14; an astrological-physiological reckoning of life in seven-year stages (cf. the *climacteric* in the 1571 Wolf letter).
- ***Franciscus Tengnagel*** — **Frans Gansneb Tengnagel von Camp** (c. 1576–1622), Tycho's Westphalian assistant (later his son-in-law and literary executor), then resident on Hven; "now with me," commended by the younger Dousa.
- ***Cunradus noster*** — "our Cunradus": a member of Tycho's household/circle (likely Conrad Aslaksen / a familiaris), who had earlier brought the engraved portrait and supposed it cut at Cologne (*Coloniae*); left as named.
- ***Icon … duobus haemisphaerijs … pomposa illa circumscriptio*** — Tycho criticises an engraved **portrait** (*icon*) of himself: he dislikes the device of resting the image on **two hemispheres** and finds the encomiastic **inscription** (*circumscriptio*) too grand. (This bears on the De Gheyn / Cologne portrait tradition; the editor holds the Altena study of the De Gheyn engraving.) No silent identification of the print is made here.
- ***chartopaeum … in propria hîc moletrina*** — Tycho reports securing a **paper-maker** (*chartopaeus*, Gk.-Lat. coinage) so that paper for his **Press** (*Typographia*) is now produced "in [our] own mill" (*moletrina*) on Hven — the documented Uraniborg paper-mill, whose earlier lack had delayed publication.
- ***Progymnasmatum nostrorum Astronomicorum … primi Capitis … pagina 13*** — the **Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata** (Tycho's "Preludes," pr. 1602/1610), here cited while still in press; the **first Chapter** "on the Solar course" (*de Solari curriculo*) and the table of equinoctial moments on **page 13** are given as a specific citation. *Quaterniones* = printer's **gatherings** (quires).
- **Astronomy / chronology.** *anni Iuliani cum coelesti comparatio* = the comparison of the **Julian year** with the **celestial (tropical) year**; *bisextus Iulianus* = the **Julian bissextile (leap-day)**; *anni aequinoctialis Solarisque quantitas* = the length of the **equinoctial / solar year**, here derived from a hundred-year *epocha* on the observations of **Regiomontanus** (Johannes Müller of Königsberg, 1436–1476) and his pupil **Bernhard Walther** (*Gualterus*, 1430–1504) of Nuremberg. *inaequalitatis labyrinthos … a Copernico et alijs … introductos* = the "labyrinths of inequality" (the trepidation / variable-precession schemes) which Tycho judges Copernicus and others adopted with "too much credulity and licence." *Hipparchi … apparentias utriusque luminaris* = Hipparchus's observations of the appearances of "both luminaries" (Sun and Moon), which Tycho rates above all ancient data.
- ***scrupulis secundis*** — "**seconds**" (of time/arc); *scrupulum secundum* is the period term for the second sexagesimal subdivision; rendered "seconds," term flagged. The clause *annorum determinationem nequaquam attinget* ("will in no way reach the determination of years") is a compressed astronomical claim — Tycho's point is that an error of only 5–6 seconds in the annual quantity is far too small to affect the dating of years; rendered closely with the literal sense kept and the implication bracketed.
- ***sartae tectae*** — the legal-proverbial phrase *sarta tecta* ("[kept] in good repair, whole and intact"); rendered "whole and intact."
- **Places.** *Amstelrodamum* = **Amsterdam**; *Lugdunum (Batavorum)* (*Lugdunensium*) = **Leiden** (Tycho's *Lugdunensis Mathematicus* is the Leiden professor, not Lyon); *Cimbria* = the **Cimbrian peninsula / Jutland** (the Danish lands generally), "neighbouring us"; *Colonia* = **Cologne**; *Uraniburgum* = **Uraniborg** on Hven.
- **Edition-field anomaly.** The source's edition field reads "*Contra vitam monasticam ad Bern. Mattium epistola*" — this is a separate Pontanus work, **not** the edition of record for this letter, and appears to be a edition mis-tag. Per this chapter's convention the edition of record is **Dreyer, *Opera Omnia*** (the *Epistolae*, vols VII–VIII; this Tycho→Pontanus letter is in TBOO VIII). The witnesses field is empty; no MS shelfmark is supplied by the source.
- **Calendar / place.** *Raptim Uraniburgi 5. Septembris Anni 95* = "In haste, at Uraniborg, 5 September [15]95" (**O.S.**; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). Dateline and catalogue label agree (5 Sept. 1595). *manu propria* = "in his own hand."
- **Spelling note.** The source prints *Sphaeropaeo* (l. 4 of para 1) and the variant elsewhere; *SGALIGERI / SCALIGER / SCALIGERUM* vary in the source; *praesfinienda* (for *praefinienda*) and *praestito terit* (for *praestiterit*) are printed thus and kept verbatim in the Source block, normalised silently only in sense in the translation.
- **Correction.** Latin corrected against Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII p.373: 'praestito terit' (wrongly split) -> 'praestiterit'; 'SGALIGERI' -> 'SCALIGERI'; 'praesfinienda' -> 'praefinienda'. None of these affect the published English translation, which was already correct.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Read the Dreyer page images visually across all 6 pages: TBOO VII p.370 (tail of the preceding letter to Hagecius), p.371 (letter heading 'TYCHO BRAHE IOH. ISACIO PONTANO. S.' and opening), pp.372-374 (body), ending p.374 'Raptim Uraniburgi 5. Septembris Anni 95. Tycho Brahe, manu propria.' Collated the opening and closing lines and every proper name, number, date and place-name: Sphaeropaeo, Scaliger, Douzam, R. Snellium/Gillebrodum, Franciscus Tengnagel, Cunradum/Coloniae, page 13, Regiomontani/Gualteri, Copernico, Hipparchi, '5 vel 6 scrupulis secundis', 'Uraniburgi 5. Septembris Anni 95' — all match Dreyer except the three text error items logged above, all single/split-word corruptions confined to our own transcription. The English translation was checked clause-by-clause and is fully faithful throughout, including correctly rendering the 'praestiterit' clause despite the corrupted source; no fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found anywhere in this letter. Published grade was the translator's own B (apparently withheld for lack of collation, correctly so); on collation against Dreyer the correct grade is C owing to the three text error findings, though the verdict remains *minor* since none of them change the sense a reader takes away.

**3 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original splits Dreyer's single word 'praestiterit' (future perfect, 'will have rendered') into the nonsensical 'praestito terit'. The English translation ('he will render the thing more pleasing') correctly reflects the Dreyer reading regardless. Dreyer prints: *...rem magis arridentem præftiterit: fic quoque... (TBOO VII p.373)*.
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original has 'SGALIGERI' (with G) where Dreyer prints 'SCALIGERI' (with C). The English correctly says 'Scaliger's'. Dreyer prints: *SCALIGERI de Emendatione Temporum præftans illud opus recognitum (TBOO VII p.373)*.
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original has an extra inserted 's' ('praesfinienda') where Dreyer prints 'praefinienda'. Not reflected in, and did not affect, the English translation. Dreyer prints: *...ad amuffim præfinienda is inibi non minima ex parte agit... (TBOO VII p.373)*.

**Repaired.** Verified all three defect sites directly against the Dreyer page image, TBOO VII p.373 (letter spans pp.370-375). All three text error are confirmed exactly as the audit describes; the English translation required no change in any case. No other discrepancies were found in the surrounding text.

documents.incipit: SALUTEM et officia. Quam semper dedito animo in id incubuerim unice, Generose TYCHO, quod …

text.original:
TYCHONI BRAHEO.

SALUTEM et officia. Quam semper dedito animo in id incubuerim unice, Generose TYCHO, quod necessitudinem eam, quam generis et sangvinis inter nos intemeratam esse voluit communio, ipse, quantum in me sit, non † tu tenes modo, sed et confirmarem, licet ex voto sat evidenter prodere huc usque nequiverim, ipse tamen, quin ex proprio candore te aemulantem reputes, nullus dubito. Quin et eis me sorte et censu a te sincere ascribi, quos eruditionem tuam ac sapientiam illustrem suspicientes, ipse redamare non nequis, indubius confido, ut adeoque operosam animi in te mei depraedicationem erga te accersere, nec operae nec curae precium esse censeam. Nil restat, nisi ut ad amicissimas tuas litteras, quam debeo et in officio imposito requiris, declaratam fidem reponam. Quam si in alijs operam meam ipsius concernentibus alias precij alicuius dehinc putaris, iube, impera, meque addictissimum tibi ex asse habe, macte. De reliquo est, quod submoneam, litteras tuas parenti insignitas ipsi redditas tum demum, ubi ex Senatu redijsset, qui ex Generosi STENONIS fratris tui relatione causam se cognovisse retulit, atque pro re est, quod rogem, Generosus meus amicus.

[Oligerus Rosaecrantz.]
text.english:
**To Tycho Brahe.**

Greeting and my services. With what devoted spirit I have always applied myself to this one thing — namely, that the kinship which the bond of family and blood has willed to be inviolate between us I myself should, so far as in me lies, not [merely] † as you hold it, but should also confirm — although until now I have not been able to make it sufficiently evident in proportion to my wish: yet of this I have no doubt at all, that you, of your own candour, account me one who emulates you. Indeed I am confident beyond doubt that I am sincerely numbered by you, in lot and in standing, among those whom — looking up to your learning and your illustrious wisdom — you yourself cannot but love in return; and so I should judge it worth neither the labour nor the trouble to elicit toward you the laboured proclaiming of my regard for you. Nothing remains except that I render back to your most friendly letter the assured fidelity that I owe and that you require in the duty laid upon me. And if hereafter you shall reckon my service of any [further] worth in other matters concerning yourself, bid me, command me, and hold me most utterly devoted to you — good speed to you! For the rest, there is this of which I would remind you: that your letter addressed to [my] parent was delivered to him only then, once he had returned from the Senate [Council], who reported that he had learned the matter from the account of your brother, the Honourable Steno; and it is to the purpose that I should ask [it of you], my Honourable friend.

[Holger Rosenkrantz.]

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Oligerus Rosaecrantz* = **Holger Rosenkrantz** "the Learned" (*Holger Rosenkrantz den lærde*, 1574–1642), the Danish nobleman, theologian and statesman. His kinship with Tycho — invoked in the opening (*necessitudinem … generis et sangvinis … communio*) — ran through the Brahe–Rosenkrantz connection; the Rosenkrantz and Brahe families were repeatedly intermarried, and Tycho's circle of noble correspondents included several Rosenkrantz kinsmen. The signature is supplied editorially (bracketed in the source), the body itself unsigned in the transcript.
- ***Generose / Generosus*** — the standard address of a nobleman: "Honourable / Wellborn." Rendered "Honourable"; *Generose TYCHO* = "Honourable Tycho," *Generosi STENONIS* = "the Honourable Steno," *Generosus meus amicus* = "my Honourable friend."
- ***STENONIS fratris tui*** — **Steen (Steno) Brahe** (1547–1620), Tycho's elder brother, the Danish statesman and Rigsråd member; here named as the source of the information that reached "the parent" (see crux below). The Latinised genitive *Stenonis* = "of Steno/Steen."
- ***ex Senatu redijsset*** — "had returned from the Senate": *Senatus* renders the Danish **Rigsråd** (Council of the Realm), the body on which Steen Brahe sat; "Senate [Council]" given to preserve the Latin term and its referent without silently modernising.
- ***litteras tuas parenti insignitas*** — "your letter addressed to [your] parent." *insignitas* (lit. "marked, inscribed [to]") is taken in the epistolary sense "addressed/directed to"; *parenti* ("to the parent") is taken in the epistolary sense "addressed to." **Resolved:** the paired letter (Tycho→Rosenkrantz, 22 Jan 1596, *Opera Omnia* VII p. 389) addresses *utrumque tuum laudatissimum parentem* ('both your parents'); the *parens* here is therefore **Holger Rosenkrantz's own parent** (his father Jørgen Rosenkrantz, d. 1596, or his mother), to whom Tycho's letter had been forwarded — not Tycho's own (Otte Brahe had died in 1571). The elder learned the matter via Steen Brahe's report.
- **Dateline / place.** The transcript carries **no dateline and no place of writing**; the edition label is *"1596. empty"* — i.e. assigned to the year 1596 with no day or month, and the place unknown. The header therefore gives "[no place], 1596" rather than asserting any day; the year is the catalogue assignment, not a date written in the source. **No calendar (O.S./N.S.) can be affixed** to a yearless, placeless transcript.
- **Negation count.** The source carries the negations precisely as reproduced: *non* (in the crux clause), *nequiverim* ("I have not been able"), *quin … nullus dubito* ("I have no doubt that …"), *non nequis* (double negative = "you cannot but," i.e. "you must"), *indubius* ("beyond doubt"), *nec operae nec curae* ("neither the labour nor the trouble"). The double negative *non nequis* is rendered affirmatively ("cannot but love in return") as its grammar requires; the count is preserved without adding or dropping a "not."

### Cruxes

- **The dagger †.** The source prints a **crux (obelus)** in the clause *"non † tu tenes modo, sed et confirmarem"* — the edition flags a corruption/lacuna at this point and offers no clean reading. The construction does not resolve cleanly: *non … modo … sed et* ("not only … but also") frames an antithesis, but the verb governing the first limb is lost or garbled at the dagger, so the intended contrast ("not only [hold / acknowledge] as you hold it, but also confirm it") is reconstructed only by sense. The translation reproduces the dagger and renders the surrounding clause as conjecturally as the Latin permits ("not [merely] † as you hold it, but should also confirm"), **without smoothing the gap into fluent English**. Dreyer's apparatus (*Opera Omnia* IX p. 319) records *tu tenes] tutarer conj. Friis* — Friis conjectured *non **tutarer** modo, sed et confirmarem* ('I should not only safeguard [the bond], but also confirm it'); the dagger marks Dreyer's retention of the transmitted *tu tenes* over this conjecture.
- **Convoluted period.** The whole letter is a single chain of heavily subordinated, mannerist humanist periods (e.g. *operosam animi in te mei depraedicationem erga te accersere*) whose syntax strains sense in several places; the rendering follows the most defensible construal clause-by-clause and does not impose a confidence the Latin does not support.
- **Correction.** Corrected 'your letter addressed to [your] parent' to '[my] parent': the unmarked 'parenti' denotes the writer Holger Rosenkrantz's own father, Jørgen Rosenkrantz (a Rigsraad member), not Tycho's father Otte Brahe, who had died in 1571 — 25 years before this letter.

documents.abstract: Explains that admiration for Tycho long deterred him from writing to so eminent a man, but a forwarded letter from Rantzau has now prompted him to make contact.
documents.incipit: NOBILISSIME et amplissime vir, etsi singularis in te observantia ex ingenij tui …

text.original:
HARDEWIGUS A DASSELL I. C. TYCHONI BRAHEN EQUITI, VIRO NOBILISSIMO.
S. D.

NOBILISSIME et amplissime vir, etsi singularis in te observantia ex ingenij tui praeclaris orta monumentis postulabat, ut aliquid ad te literarum darem, me tamen deterruit hactenus personae tuae dignitas, utpote hominis de facie mihi ignoti, verentem, ne talem virum tantarum rerum occupatione distentum inanibus appellare literis, pudentis hominis non esset. Nunc ut, quod sentio, dicam, paene accuso modestiam meam, quod, dum cogito ad te scribere, non tamen consilium explico. Interea tua fecit singularis humanitas, ut, dum Domini RANZOVIJ Producis Cimbrici literas ad me mittis, scribendo anteverteres.

Quanquam cur ego apud te maximarum virtutum laude praestantem, ad quas mihi adspirare non licet, plus residere officij moleste feram, cum praesertim hoc ipsum amoris in me tui, quo equidem antiquius nihil habeo, non obscurum argumentum esse videatur? Quocirca ut interdum me pudet pudoris mei, quod nihil ad te scribere sim ausus, cum tamen maxime cuperem, sic istâ voluntatis declaratione mirifice delector. Ego te, nobilissime vir, semper maximi feci, non propter illa, quae vulgi oculos in se convertunt, sed propter illa vere ac proprie tua, quae et te provexerunt ad istum, in quo es, dignitatis gradum, et provectura, ut spero, sunt etiam altius; etsi nihil aut tale effecissent, aut effectura essent, omni te tamen cultu atque observantiâ dignissimum reddidissent. Virtus enim et eruditio, vera mihi et solida videntur bona, eâque de causâ recte dicitur a Plutarcho: Τῆς ἀληθινῆς εὐδαιμονίας τὸ πλεῖστον ἐν ἤθει καὶ διαθέσει τῆς ψυχῆς εἶναι. Reliquum est, ut, cum tibi persuaseris me amantissimum tui esse, hoc mihi etiam des, ut in te expetendo, et tibi prospera omnia feliciaque optando concedam nemini.

Vale.
Luneburgi.
text.english:
**Hartwig von Dassel, Jurisconsult, to Tycho Brahe, knight, a most noble man. Greeting.**

Most noble and most worthy man: although my singular regard for you, sprung from the illustrious monuments of your genius, demanded that I send you some letter, yet up to now the dignity of your person deterred me — being, as you are, a man unknown to me by sight — fearing that to accost such a man, stretched taut by the press of so great affairs, with empty letters would not be the part of a man of any modesty. Now, to say what I feel, I almost reproach my own modesty, in that, while I think of writing to you, I nonetheless do not carry out the design. Meanwhile your singular kindness has brought it about that, in sending me the letter of Master Rantzau, governor of the Cimbrian land, you forestalled me in writing.

And yet why should I take it ill that the greater part of the duty should rest with you toward me — a man pre-eminent in the praise of the greatest virtues, to which I am not permitted to aspire — especially when this very thing seems to be no obscure proof of your love toward me, than which indeed I hold nothing more precious? Wherefore, just as at times I am ashamed of my own shame — that I dared write nothing to you, though I most greatly desired it — so by this declaration of your goodwill I am wonderfully delighted. I, most noble man, have always esteemed you most highly, not on account of those things which turn the eyes of the common crowd upon themselves, but on account of those things truly and properly your own, which both have advanced you to that rank of dignity in which you stand, and are going, as I hope, to advance you even higher; and even if they had effected nothing of the kind, nor were going to effect it, they would nonetheless have rendered you most worthy of every honour and regard. For virtue and learning seem to me the true and solid goods; and for that reason it is rightly said by Plutarch: *"That the greatest part of true happiness lies in the character and disposition of the soul."* It remains that, once you have persuaded yourself that I am most loving toward you, you grant me this also: that in seeking after you, and in wishing you all things prosperous and happy, I yield to no one.

Farewell.
At Lüneburg.
