documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Hardewigus a Dassell, I. C.* = **Hartwig von Dassel**, styled *Iuris Consultus* (here expanded "Doctor of Both Laws" — *I. C.* = *Iuris Consultus*, a jurist/doctor of law). A Lüneburg jurist; he is otherwise little documented, and writes here as a man not personally acquainted with Tycho ("a man unknown to you by sight").
- **Recipient titulature.** *TYCHONI BRAHEN EQUITI, VIRO NOBILISSIMO* — "to Tycho Brahe, *eques* (knight), a most noble man." *Brahen* is an accusative of the Latinised surname; *eques* renders Tycho's noble/knightly rank.
- ***S. D.*** — *salutem dicit*, "sends greeting".
- ***Domini Ranzovij Producis Cimbrici*** — "Master **Rantzau**, governor of the Cimbrian land": **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), royal Danish *Statthalter* (governor) of the duchies of Schleswig-Holstein, the great Holstein humanist-patron and astronomical correspondent of Tycho's. *Produx Cimbricus* (genitive *Producis Cimbrici*) is a humanist coinage for his office — *produx* "leader, governor" (a learned variant on *dux/praeses*), *Cimbricus* "of the Cimbrian Chersonese," i.e. of Jutland/Holstein, the standard humanist geographical name for the region. The phrase is rendered descriptively; the antiquarian "Cimbrian" geography is kept. The occasion of the letter is that Tycho had forwarded to Dassel a letter from Rantzau, which prompted (and pre-empted) Dassel's own first letter.
- **Greek (Plutarch).** *Τῆς ἀληθινῆς εὐδαιμονίας τὸ πλεῖστον ἐν ἤθει καὶ διαθέσει τῆς ψυχῆς εἶναι* — "that the greatest part of true happiness lies in the character [*ēthos*] and disposition [*diathesis*] of the soul." A maxim attributed to **Plutarch** (a *sententia* in the moral-philosophical vein of the *Moralia*); transcribed verbatim and translated by the audit's rule. The clause is grammatically the accusative-and-infinitive completing *recte dicitur a Plutarcho* ("it is rightly said by Plutarch [that] …").
- ***pudet pudoris mei*** — "I am ashamed of my own shame," a deliberate figura etymologica (the wordplay on *pudor/pudet*); kept as the rhetorical figure it is.
- **Dateline.** The subscription gives only the place, *Luneburgi* = **Lüneburg** (Lower Saxony); **no day or month is stated in the source.** The edition assigns the year **1596** (the identifier's date-field reads 15960000, with zeros for month and day), consistent with the letter's appearance among the 1596-era pieces and with Rantzau's lifetime (d. 1598). The header therefore gives the year with an explicit note that day and month are not in the text; no date is asserted beyond what the source substantiates. Style (O.S./N.S.) is not determinable from the text and is not asserted.
- **Edition of record.** Printed in *Poematum libri IV* (the letter survives as a printed prose piece within a poetry collection of this title; this is the source's edition field). No manuscript witness is recorded in the edition.
- **Correction.** Three referent/lexical fixes in the Dassel-to-Tycho letter (TBOO VII p.376): (1) restored that Tycho, not Dassel, is 'unknown by sight', correcting a flipped mihi/tibi; (2) restored that the greater epistolary duty rests 'with you [Tycho]', correcting a flipped 'apud te'; (3) rendered 'I. C.' as Jurisconsult (Iuris Consultus) rather than the unsupported 'Doctor of Both Laws'.

translation.warrant:
**Not collated against Dreyer** — no page reference for this letter, so the grade is capped at Probable however sound the translation looks. The record's the page reference claims TBOO VII pp. 3-377 (30 pages) but this is a broken reference: visually inspected pages 1-4 and 27-30, which are Dreyer pp. 3-6 and 29-32 respectively — 1568-1576 correspondence (Tycho-Johannes, Tycho-Vellejum, Tycho-Pratensis) with no relation to this undated-1596 Hartwig von Dassel letter. The extract does not contain the target letter, so no Dreyer collation was possible; audited against the transcribed original alone. Two medium-severity pronoun/reference-flip mistranslation found ('mihi'->'to you'; 'apud te'->'with me'), each reversing a directional claim in the Latin, plus one low-severity title inflation. Flag for the process: this record's the page reference the page images is mismatched to its letter and should be regenerated.

**3 defects found:**
- **mistranslation** (medium). 'mihi' (dative, 'to me') is rendered as 'to you' and the referent is flipped from Tycho to Dassel: the Latin genitive-of-description 'hominis de facie mihi ignoti' describes Tycho ('you, being a man unknown to me by sight, i.e. we have never met'), agreeing with 'personae tuae' just before it. The English instead has Dassel himself as the one unrecognised, reversing who does not know whom. At: “being, as I am, a man unknown to you by sight”.
- **mistranslation** (medium). 'apud te' ('with you', i.e. with Tycho) is rendered as 'with me', reversing on whom the greater share of epistolary obligation falls. The letter's point is that Tycho, though the greater man, took on the courtesy-duty of writing first (unusual and flattering to Dassel); the English instead has the duty resting with Dassel, undermining the compliment the sentence is built to pay. At: “why should I take it ill that the greater part of the duty should rest with me toward you”.
- **mistranslation** (low). 'I.C.' is the standard early-modern abbreviation for 'Iuris Consultus' (jurisconsult/legal counsel), not 'I.U.D.' (Iuris Utriusque Doctor, 'Doctor of Both Laws'). The English supplies a specific academic title not warranted by the abbreviation. At: “Doctor of Both Laws”.

**Repaired.** This letter's own labelled extract (TBOO VII, nominally pp.3-377 — evidently a mislabelled 30-page span rather than a true per-letter extract) was not opened. Instead, its exact printed text was located, by a fortunate adjacency, at the tail of the neighbouring extract supplied for brahe-t_15960000001 (Dreyer TBOO VII p.376), which reproduces the Hartwig von Dassel letter in full, from its title through 'Vale. Luneburgi.' All three defect sites are confirmed there verbatim against the transcribed original (the title's 'I. C.', 'hominis de facie mihi ignoti', and 'apud te... plus residere officij' all match). All three defects fixed with full page collation.

documents.incipit: NOBILISSIME et Eruditissime OLIGERE, Consangvinee et Amice inter præcipuos et intimos …

text.original:
TAM MAIORUM IMAGINIBUS QUAM PROPRIA VIRTUTE ET DOCTRINÆ PRÆEMINENTIA IUVENI INPRIMIS CLARO, OLIGERO ROSENCRANTZIO, GEORGIJ F. DE ROSENHOLM, CONSANGVINEO ET AMICO SUO SINCERE DILECTO. S. P.

NOBILISSIME et Eruditissime OLIGERE, Consangvinee et Amice inter præcipuos et intimos dilecte. Quoniam præter voluntatem et expectationem necessitas mihi incumbit, quendam publice in ius vocare, et de quibusdam famæ meæ defensionem haud modice concernentibus testimonia contra ipsum ferri curare, unâque de nonnullis quæstionem proponere, ad quæ statuto tempore respondere ipsemet in se recepit, intelligam vero, eundem clam in Aulam, ad D. Principem et Regem nostrum electum clementissimum et Dominos Proreges confugere velle, ut istic caussam suam palliet, et diverticula quærat, quibus se ab hac actione subducat – inprimis autem a tuo honoratissimo parente effugij rationem impetraturum sibi pollicetur, quod etiam Lundis innuere, atque eo insolentius se gerere non verebatur – scripsi itaque hac de re ad integerrimum tuum parentem, omnino mihi persuadens, qua præditus est æqui rectique promovendi voluntate propensa, pari constantia et gravitate coniuncta, ipsum non saltem nullatenus quippiam admissurum, quod legitimam caussæ huius cognitionem et executionem impedire aut differre possit, quin potius, multo magis adiumento et subsidio futurum, ut omnia ad iustitiæ normam æqua bilance deducantur, quo ea, quæ mihi per inverecundas calumnias, ultra annuum tempus, quo in his conticui et me a respondendo continui, hinc inde aspersa sunt, nunc tandem redarguam, et famam meam, qua nihil antiquius esse debet, intemeratam conservem. Quare et te, mi OLIGERE, per consangvinitatem et intimam amicitiam nostram, quibus possum, modis, obtestatum volo, quantum in te est (est autem quamplurimum), apud utrumque tuum laudatissimum parentem efficere velis, ut nihil interveniat, quod caussæ huius tractationi et competenti determinationi obstaculo existat. Quod et illos sua sponte haud gravatim facturos, et te non invite enisurum, omnino mihi persuadeo. Quanti enim te semper fecerim (prout etiam meretur tua singularis eruditio, pari virtute et candore exornata) tu ipsemet ex parte conscius es, et alij, qui me præclara dona præ reliquis nostratibus genere claris tibi prædicantem audiverunt, testatum facere possunt. Sed malo hæc cum alijs de te, quam apud te.

Vale, et amicitiam nostram, quod ego constanter facturus sum, illibatam conserva.
Dabantur Uraniburgi die 22. Ianuarij Anno 1596.
Tui amantissimus
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To Holger Rosenkrantz, son of Jørgen, of Rosenholm — a young man distinguished as much by the portraits of his ancestors as by the pre-eminence of his own virtue and learning — his kinsman and sincerely beloved friend. Heartiest greeting.**

Most noble and most learned Holger, kinsman and friend beloved among my chief and closest. Since, against my will and expectation, a necessity presses upon me to summon a certain man publicly into court, and to see to it that testimony be brought against him concerning certain matters that bear in no small degree upon the defence of my good name, and at the same time to put a question to him on several points, to which he himself undertook to make answer at the appointed time — but since I learn that this same man wishes to flee secretly to the Court, to my Lord the Prince, our most clement King-elect, and to the Lord Viceroys, so that there he may cloak his cause and seek by-ways by which to withdraw himself from this suit — and above all promises himself that he will obtain the means of escape from your most honoured father, which at Lund too he did not scruple to hint at, and to bear himself the more insolently on that account — I have therefore written on this matter to your most upright father, persuading myself wholly that, endowed as he is with that ready will to advance equity and right, joined with an equal constancy and gravity, he will not in the least admit anything that might hinder or defer the lawful examination and execution of this cause; but rather will be much more of a help and support, so that all may be brought, by an even balance, to the standard of justice — whereby I may at last now refute the things that, through shameless slanders, over a period of more than a year, during which I held my peace in these matters and restrained myself from answering, have been bespattered upon me on this side and that, and may keep my good name, than which nothing ought to be held more precious, unblemished. Wherefore I would also have you, my Holger, by our kinship and our intimate friendship, beseeched in such ways as I can, that, so far as in you lies (and it lies very much in you), you would be willing to bring it about with each of your most praiseworthy parents that nothing intervene which might stand as an obstacle to the handling of this cause and its proper determination. And I am wholly persuaded that they will do this of their own accord without reluctance, and that you will strive for it not unwillingly. For how highly I have always esteemed you (as indeed your singular learning, adorned with equal virtue and candour, deserves) you yourself are in part aware, and others can bear witness — those who have heard me proclaiming to you [your] distinguished gifts above the rest of our countrymen of illustrious birth. But I had rather [say] these things about you with others than to your face.

Farewell, and keep our friendship — as I for my part shall constantly do — inviolate.
Given at Uraniborg, on the 22nd day of January, in the year 1596.
Most loving of you,
TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / "manu propria."** Tycho Brahe, writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven. The closing *manu propria* ("in his own hand") indicates Tycho subscribed the letter autograph; the surviving witness, however, is a later transcript (*Afskrift*) in **Langebek's Diplomatarium** (Copenhagen, Rigsarkivet), not the autograph itself.
- **Recipient.** *Oligerus Rosencrantzius, Georgij f. de Rosenholm* = **Holger Rosenkrantz** (1574–1642), later renowned as *den lærde Holger* ("the learned Holger"), theologian and Privy Councillor, owner of Rosenholm Castle. In 1596 he was a young man of 21; Tycho addresses him as a *consanguineus* (kinsman — the Brahe and Rosenkrantz lines were intermarried; Holger's mother was a Brahe connection) and flatters his birth and erudition.
- **"Georgij F." / "tuo honoratissimo parente."** *Georgius* = **Jørgen (Georg) Rosenkrantz** (1523–1596) of Rosenholm, Holger's father, a member of the Rigsråd — hence one of the "Lord Viceroys" (*Domini Proreges*) whose influence at court Tycho fears the defendant will solicit. The phrase *utrumque tuum laudatissimum parentem* ("each of your most praiseworthy parents") embraces both father and mother; Holger's mother was **Dorte Lange** (cf. her 1589 portrait with Jørgen at Rosenholm).
- **The unnamed defendant ("quendam … in ius vocare").** Not named in the letter, but securely identified from the date and circumstance as **Gellius Sascerides** (Gellius Sascerides Hafniensis, b. 1562), Tycho's former pupil on Hven, whose broken betrothal to Tycho's daughter **Magdalene Brahe** had by 1595–96 turned into a bitter and very public lawsuit that Tycho framed as a matter of his own *fama* (good name). The "shameless slanders … over more than a year" refer to this affair; Tycho is the plaintiff seeking to compel testimony and prevent the defendant from finding political cover at court.
- **Legal vocabulary.** *in ius vocare* = "to summon into court / to law"; *actio* = "(legal) suit / action"; *caussa* (= *causa*) = "cause / case"; *cognitio et executio* = "examination and execution [of the cause]," i.e. the judicial hearing and its enforcement; *competens determinatio* = "proper / competent determination [= verdict]"; *diverticula quaerere* = "to seek by-ways / evasions"; *caussam palliare* = "to cloak / gloss over one's cause." The mood and force of the negations are reproduced exactly: *non saltem nullatenus quippiam admissurum* is an emphatic double negation ("will not in the least admit anything") asserting that the father will permit no obstruction — rendered without flattening the doubled negative; *te non invite enisurum* = "that you will strive not unwillingly."
- **"D. Principem et Regem nostrum electum clementissimum et Dominos Proreges."** The "Prince, our most clement King-elect" is **Christian IV** (b. 1577), elected king in 1596 but not yet crowned (the coronation followed in August 1596); during his minority the realm was governed by a regency of four **Rigsråder** (*Domini Proreges*, "Lord Viceroys / Regents"), among them Jørgen Rosenkrantz. *electum* ("elect[ed]") is retained literally and is chronologically exact for January 1596.
- **"Lundis."** *Lundis* = "at **Lund**" (in Scania), where the defendant had reportedly hinted he would obtain the elder Rosenkrantz's protection; locative kept and glossed.
- **Honorifics / formulae.** *S. P.* = *Salutem Plurimam* ("Heartiest greeting," this chapter's convention); the heading's parallel *Tam maiorum imaginibus quam … praeeminentia* ("as much by the portraits/images of his ancestors as by his pre-eminence") plays on *imagines maiorum*, the Roman ancestral portrait-masks denoting noble lineage. *Vale … illibatam conserva* = "Farewell … keep [it] inviolate"; *Dabantur* (epistolary plural for *Datae*) = "Given." *Tui amantissimus* = "Most loving of you."
- **Orthography.** Humanist Latin with consonantal *j* for *i* (*Georgij, ijs→hisce, Ianuarij, alij, amicitiam*) and *-ae* written as *Ae/ae* in majuscule (*DOCTRINAe, PRAeEMINENTIA, famae*); *caussa* for *causa* and *unâque, quâ* with the circumflex are the editor's diacritics, reproduced as printed.
- **Calendar.** *die 22. Ianuarij Anno 1596* — 22 January 1596, Old Style (Denmark used the Julian calendar until 1700). The dateline matches the edition label; no discrepancy. Note the historical caution: in Tycho's reckoning the year had begun on 1 January, so "1596" here is unambiguous.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Dreyer (*Opera Omnia* VII p. 374) reads *quam **propria** virtute* — “by his **own** virtue,” the antithesis to the inherited *imagines maiorum*; the transcription had dropped “-pria.” Corrected in the heading and its translation.

documents.abstract: Thanks Aslaksen for Pitiscus's book on triangles, praises it, and invites Pitiscus to correspond, expressing a wish that more clergymen possessed skill in geometry.
documents.incipit: ... Doctissimi illius B. PITISCI de Triangulis acutum et compendiosum libellum lubens …

text.original:
M. CUNRADO ASLACIO BERGENSI.

... Doctissimi illius B. PITISCI de Triangulis acutum et compendiosum libellum lubens accepi, rogoque ut illi ex me gratias agas. Optarem plures eiuscemodi concionatores reperiri, qui Geometrica gnaviter callerent, forte plus esset in ijs circumspecti et solidi iudicij, rixarum inanium et logomachiarum minus. Si is mihi aliquando scripserit et de hisce studijs contulerit, inveniet responsorem non invitum. Idem apud alios eruditos viros, quos scis emunctioris nasi, effice.

19. Febr. 1596 Uraniburgi.
text.english:
**To Master Cunradus Aslacius of Bergen.**

... I gladly received that most learned B. Pitiscus's keen and compendious little book on triangles, and I ask you to give him thanks on my behalf. I could wish that more preachers of this kind were to be found, men who had a diligent command of geometry: perhaps there would be in them more of circumspect and solid judgement, and less of empty wrangling and logomachy [word-battling]. If he should at some time write to me and confer about these studies, he will find me a not-unwilling correspondent. Bring this about likewise among the other learned men whom you know to be of a more discerning nose.

19 February 1596, [at] Uraniborg.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** *M. Cunrado Aslacio Bergensi* — Master **Cort Aslaksen** (Conradus Aslacus / Cunradus Aslacius Bergensis, 1564–1624), born in Bergen, Norway; one of Tycho's pupils and assistants (*famuli*) on Hven in the early 1590s, later professor at the University of Copenhagen (matriculated there 22 Oct. 1607; d. 10 Feb. 1624). This is an excerpt from Tycho's letter to him, printed in Aslaksen's own *Sphaericorum libri tres* (the edition of record; the source's edition field gives the genitive *Sphaericorum librorum trium*). The leading *...* shows the editor's excision of the letter's opening — only this passage and the dateline are transmitted here.
- ***B. Pitisci de Triangulis libellum*** — **Bartholomäus Pitiscus** (1561–1613), Calvinist court chaplain (hence Tycho's calling him and his like *concionatores*, "preachers") and mathematician, whose *Trigonometria sive de dimensione triangulorum* (first appended to A. Scultetus's *Sphaericorum libri tres*, Heidelberg 1595) introduced the very word "trigonometry." *de Triangulis … libellum* = "the little book on triangles," i.e. this *Trigonometria*; *acutum et compendiosum* = "keen and compendious." The abbreviation *B.* before the name is a courtesy initial (Bartholomaeus).
- ***concionatores*** — "preachers" (*contionatores*), here in the literal clerical sense: Tycho wishes more **clergymen** had Pitiscus's command of geometry. Rendered "preachers," not metaphorically.
- ***qui Geometrica gnaviter callerent*** — "who had a diligent command of geometry" (*Geometrica callere* = to be skilled in geometrical matters). The subjunctive *callerent / esset* keeps Tycho's wish-and-conjecture mood ("I could wish … perhaps there would be"); the hedge *forte* ("perhaps") is preserved, not sharpened.
- ***logomachiarum*** — *logomachia* (from Greek λογομαχία, "word-battle"), "logomachy": disputes over mere words. Tycho's Greek-derived term is kept and glossed in brackets, by this chapter's convention Paired with *rixae inanes* ("empty wrangling").
- ***responsorem non invitum*** — "a not-unwilling correspondent" (literally "a not-unwilling answerer/respondent"); the litotes is reproduced rather than flattened to "willing."
- ***quos scis emunctioris nasi*** — "whom you know to be of a more discerning nose," a Horatian idiom (*emunctae naris*, "of a wiped/keen nose" = of sharp critical judgement; cf. Horace, *Sat.* 1.4.8); comparative *emunctioris*, "of a keener nose." Kept as the period idiom and glossed; *effice* ("bring [it] about, see to it") governs *idem* ("the same," i.e. convey my like greeting/openness).
- **Calendar / place.** *19. Febr. 1596 Uraniburgi* = "19 February 1596, at **Uraniborg**" (on Hven) — **Old Style**; Denmark kept the Julian calendar. The edition label ("1596. 19. februar. Uraniborg") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy.

text.original:
ERUDITISSIMO ET HUMANISSIMO IUVENI IOHANNI ISACIO PONTANO NUNC CANTABRIGIAe IN ANGLIA LITERIS POLITIORIBUS INCUMBENTI SIBI PLURIMUM DILECTO TYCHO BRAHE.
S. P.

EX literis tuis Cantabrigiae 12. Novemb. anni praecedentis ad me datis, dilecte mi IOANNES ISACIDE, cognovi te nunc in Anglia degere et literis humanioribus criticisque operam navare. Non displicet mihi hoc studium, siquidem eo, a Patre tuo olim sic educatus, inclinare videris. Exhibebit Anglia multos in his commilitones, cum fertilis sit liberalium ingeniorum et eloquentiae inprimis deditorum. Admones de Anglico privilegio, et in eo procurando tuam offers voluntatem; idque oportune admones, gratumque est quod offers. Quaero itaque omnem moveas lapidem, ut illud mature obtineam: si ante festum Pentecostes vel paulo post id fieri queat, votis meis apprime responderes. Efficies id per aliquem primariae auctoritatis in Serenissimae Reginae ELISABETHAe Cancellaria, quae cum sit inter Heroinas nostri seculi non solum genere Regio splendidissima, sed etiam varia doctrina, quod alias in hoc sexu perrarum est, decoratissima, nihil addubito, quin doctrinis et studijs liberalibus, praesertim Astronomicis, quae, ut ait noster Manilius,

Regales animos primum dignata movere,
Proxima tangentes coelo fastigia rerum,
clementissime et impense faveat, ea promovere inter alias Regales curas non dedignetur. Quo vero generalis aliqua forma constet scribendi eius diplomatis, mitto exemplum Caesareani, tum quoque Regis Scotorum. Ex quibus perspicax conscriptor facile modum reperiet, quo reliquum illud consignandum sit. Neque tamen opus est praeeuntes omnino sequi, sed fertile Anglorum ingenium facile rationem inveniet, qua singula terse et magnifice, ut artis regiae promotioni accommoda et honorifica sint, concipiantur. Pollicitus est olim optimae memoriae DANIEL ROGERSIUS, amicus meus desideratissimus (in quo eruditio et humanitas pariter certabant) suum in tali privilegio procurando conscribendoque studium, quando is legatione nomine Serenissimae Reginae hîc in Dania functus me semel atque iterum invisere non est degravatus. Sed cum fata nimis immatura hunc tantum nobis praeripuerint, haud dubito, quin in Cancellaria Latina Reginae successor aliquis eius doctrinae et virtuti non impar substitutus sit, cuius officio et beneficio id quod petimus privilegium non invite, uti spero, obtinebimus. Honorarium vicissim meo nomine gratitudinis ergo exhibendum offer et expone. Ego id, quicquid erit, quam primum de eo certior redditus fuero, patri tuo Amstelrodamum, ut ille tibi, restitui curabo. Vide itaque, mi ISACIDE, nequa mora nostris desiderijs aut ulla alia impedimenta obveniant. Habebis me ad tibi vicissim gratificandum non difficilem, et quid expectandum sit, mature significa. Ad quaestionem illam iocosam et nonnihil criticam antiqui LUCRETIJ, cum is sectam Philosophorum Deos eorumque providentiam inficiantem profiteretur, Venerem nihilominus, Aeneadum genitricem, primordio sui operis, eiusque opem imploret, non habeo serio dicere, quomodo haec resolvenda sit, siquidem non ad Veneris sidus coeleste, quod nos unâ cum ceteris subinde scrutamur, sed ad terrestrem illam Venerem, Aeneadum, uti fingebant Poëtae, matrem, et aliorum quoque hominum genitricem pertineat; cuius naturam et genealogiam Anglis ita perspectam esse existimo, tum quoque tuis Batavis, ut non opus sit Danos de his percontari. Meministi me solere dicere Anglos participare ex influentia potissimum ♀ ♃ ☿, unde alacres, mundi et iucundi sunt, tum quoque ingeniosi pariter et foecundi. Est igitur haec quaestio, licet non Angelica, Anglicana tamen et faceta. Quamobrem ab ijs potius quam a nobis eius enodationem edisces. Siquid tamen in his nostri valent lusus, crediderim LUCRETIUM ad imitationem aliorum Poëtarum sic exorsum esse, non quod revera aliquam Deam, quae Venus appellaretur, aut ulla alia numina statueret. Ideoque sub hoc nomine voluptatem corpoream, quam etiam Deam subinde nuncupare non veretur, intellexisse arbitror. Verum tute cum alijs sodalibus haec plenius dispicito. Ante omnia vero voluptatem animi vere Deam omnibus corporis illecebris anteponito. Sic te verae Veneres, Charites et Musae nunquam intermoriturae perpetuo redamabunt et sertis semper virentibus coronabunt. Vale et nostros in Anglia amicos, licet de facie non omnes notos, quos non paucos esse mihi persuadeo, diligenter ex me saluta, inprimis optimum illum et reverendum senem, virum excellentissimum THOMAM DIGGÆSEUM, si isthic locorum is degit. Obtinebunt hi et alij brevi nonnulla ex nostris Operibus, in quibus hos quoque permixtos Ducibus noscetur Olympi. Iamque iterum et multoties vale, mi IOANNES, et me saepius tuis invise, hisque actutum rescribe.

Raptim Uraniburgi die 25. Martij Anni 1596.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.

Binas eodem hoc tempore ad te per diversos homines misi
literas, uti si alteræ interciderent, unæ saltem ex his tibi traderentur.
Quin et hasce ternas, ut res certior esset, addidi.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to the most learned and most courteous young man Johannes Isacius Pontanus, now at Cambridge in England devoting himself to the more polished letters, most dearly beloved of him. Heartiest greeting.**

From your letter written to me at Cambridge on 12 November of last year, my beloved Johannes son of Isaac [Isacides], I learned that you are now living in England and applying yourself to the more humane and critical letters. This study does not displease me, seeing that you appear to incline toward it, having long ago been so educated by your father. England will furnish you many fellow-soldiers in these pursuits, since it is fertile in liberal talents and in men especially devoted to eloquence. You advise me about the English privilege, and offer your goodwill in procuring it; and you advise this opportunely, and what you offer is welcome. I ask, therefore, that you move every stone, so that I may obtain it in good time: if it can be done before the feast of Pentecost or a little after, you would answer my wishes exceedingly well. You will accomplish it through someone of leading authority in the Chancery of the Most Serene Queen Elizabeth; and since she, among the heroines of our age, is not only most splendid by royal birth but also most adorned with manifold learning — which is otherwise very rare in this sex — I do not at all doubt that she most graciously and lavishly favours the learned disciplines and the liberal studies, especially the astronomical, which, as our Manilius says,

First deigned to stir the minds of kings,
Who touch the topmost heights of things nearest to heaven,
and that she does not disdain, among her other royal cares, to promote them. But that some general form may be at hand for the drafting of that diploma, I send a specimen of the Imperial one [Caesareani], and also that of the King of the Scots. From these a perceptive drafter will easily find the manner in which the rest of it is to be drawn up. Yet there is no need to follow the precedents altogether; rather the fertile English wit will easily find a way in which each particular may be conceived neatly and magnificently, so that they are suited and honourable to the advancement of the royal art [the art of astronomy]. There once promised — of best memory — Daniel Rogers, my most longed-for friend (in whom erudition and humanity strove on equal terms), his zeal in procuring and drafting such a privilege, when, discharging an embassy here in Denmark in the name of the Most Serene Queen, he did not think it beneath him to visit me once and again. But since fates all too untimely have snatched this great man from us, I do not doubt that in the Queen's Latin Chancery some successor not unequal to his learning and virtue has been put in his place, by whose office and good service we shall obtain — not unwillingly, as I hope — the privilege we seek. Offer and set forth in turn, in my name, an honorarium to be presented by way of gratitude. Whatever it shall be, as soon as I am made more certain of it, I shall see it repaid to your father at Amsterdam, so that he [may repay it] to you. See to it therefore, my son of Isaac, that no delay nor any other impediments befall our desires. You will find me not difficult in gratifying you in turn, and signify in good time what is to be expected. As to that jocular and somewhat critical question concerning the ancient Lucretius — that, while he professed the sect of philosophers who deny the gods and their providence, he nonetheless, at the very beginning of his work, invokes Venus, the mother of the descendants of Aeneas, and implores her aid — I cannot say in earnest how this is to be resolved, seeing that it pertains not to the celestial star of Venus, which we together with the rest now and again scrutinise, but to that earthly Venus, mother of the Aeneadae, as the poets feigned, and begetter of other men too; whose nature and genealogy I judge to be so well understood by the English, and also by your Batavians [the Dutch], that there is no need to question Danes about these matters. You remember that I am wont to say that the English partake especially of the influence of ♀ ♃ ☿ [Venus, Jupiter, Mercury], whence they are lively, elegant, and pleasant, and likewise ingenious and fertile alike. This question, then, though not Angelic, is yet Anglican and witty. Wherefore you will learn its unravelling from them rather than from us. Yet if our jests have any weight in these matters, I should believe that Lucretius began thus in imitation of other poets, not because he really posited some goddess who should be called Venus, or any other divine powers. And so under this name I judge that he understood bodily pleasure, which too he does not fear now and again to call a goddess. But do you, with your other companions, look into these matters more fully. Above all, however, set the pleasure of the mind, truly a goddess, before all the enticements of the body. So shall the true Venuses, Graces, and Muses, never to die, love you back perpetually and crown you with ever-green garlands. Farewell, and diligently greet on my behalf our friends in England, though not all known to me by face, of whom I am persuaded there are not a few — above all that excellent and reverend old man, the most excellent man Thomas Digges, if he is living in those parts. These and others will shortly obtain some of our Works, in which they too will be known to be mingled with the Leaders of Olympus. And now again and many times farewell, my Johannes, and visit me more often with your letters, and write back to this one straightway.

In haste at Uraniborg, the 25th day of March in the year 1596.
TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.

At this same time I have sent you two [sets of] letters through different men, so that, if one set should be lost, at least one of these might be delivered to you. Indeed, I have even added this third, that the matter might be more certain.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe**, writing from **Uraniborg** on Hven. *manu propria* = "in his own hand," a subscription formula.
- **Recipient.** *Iohannes Isacius Pontanus* = **Johannes Isaacius Pontanus** (Jan Isaacsz Pontanus, 1571–1639), born at Elsinore of a Haarlem patrician family that had fled to Denmark for its Protestant faith; Tycho's *famulus* (assistant) on Hven 1593–95, later a noted historian in Denmark and the Netherlands. Tycho addresses him with the playful Greek-style patronymic **Isacides** ("son of Isaac"), since his father was **Isaac Pietersz**, then at Amsterdam (*patri tuo Amstelrodamum*, "to your father at Amsterdam"). At the date of the letter Pontanus was studying at **Cambridge** (*Cantabrigiae*).
- **Salutation.** *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam* (dicit), "(sends) heartiest greeting". *literis politioribus / humanioribus criticisque* — "the more polished / the more humane and critical letters," i.e. classical philology and textual criticism (the *studia humaniora*).
- ***Anglicum privilegium*** — "the English privilege": a royal printing-privilege / copyright protection Tycho sought from Elizabeth I for his published *Works* (his *Opera*), to be drafted in the **Queen's Latin Chancery**. He encloses model documents — *exemplum Caesareani* ("a specimen of the Imperial [privilege]," i.e. from the Holy Roman Emperor) and *Regis Scotorum* ("that of the King of the Scots," James VI of Scotland, later James I).
- ***omnem moveas lapidem*** — "move every stone," the classical idiom (Greek *πάντα κινῆσαι λίθον*); rendered literally to preserve the figure.
- ***festum Pentecostes*** — the feast of **Pentecost** (Whitsun); a movable liturgical date used as a calendar marker. Not converted.
- **Queen Elizabeth.** *Serenissima Regina Elisabetha* = **Elizabeth I of England** (r. 1558–1603). Tycho's praise of her learning "rare in this sex" (*quod alias in hoc sexu perrarum est*) is preserved as written, hedge intact.
- **Manilius quotation.** *ut ait noster Manilius* — **Marcus Manilius**, *Astronomica* I.41–42 (the didactic Latin astronomical poem). The two verses are kept as verse by this chapter's convention: *Regales animos primum dignata movere, / Proxima tangentes coelo fastigia rerum* — astronomy "first deigned to stir the minds of kings, who touch the topmost heights of things nearest to heaven." *noster Manilius* = "our Manilius," claiming the poet as a kindred astronomer.
- ***artis regiae*** — here "the royal art," i.e. astronomy (the *ars regia* of stirring kings' minds in the Manilius lines), not alchemy; rendered "the royal art [the art of astronomy]."
- **Daniel Rogers.** *Daniel Rogersius* = **Daniel Rogers** (c. 1538–1591), the Anglo-Dutch humanist and Elizabethan diplomat who had visited Tycho during embassies to Denmark; here remembered as dead (*optimae memoriae … fata nimis immatura hunc … praeripuerint*). *Cancellaria Latina Reginae* = the **Queen's Latin Secretariat / Chancery** (the office handling the crown's Latin diplomatic correspondence), in which Rogers had served.
- ***honorarium*** — "an honorarium," a fee/gratuity to be advanced by Pontanus and repaid by Tycho via Pontanus's father at Amsterdam.
- **Lucretius question.** *antiqui Lucretij* = **Lucretius** (*De rerum natura*), the Epicurean poet who "denies the gods and their providence" (*Deos eorumque providentiam inficiantem*) yet opens his poem with an invocation of **Venus** (*Aeneadum genitrix*, "mother of the descendants of Aeneas," I.1). Tycho distinguishes the *Veneris sidus coeleste* — "the celestial star of Venus" (the planet, which astronomers scrutinise) — from the *terrestris Venus* — "that earthly Venus," the mythological/sensual goddess. He resolves the puzzle by reading Lucretius's Venus as a poetic personification of *voluptas corporea* ("bodily pleasure"). Hedges preserved: *non habeo serio dicere* ("I cannot say in earnest"), *crediderim* ("I should believe"), *arbitror* ("I judge").
- ***Veneris sidus*** — rendered "the star of Venus" (the planet); by this chapter's convention *sidus/stella* of a planet is the planet itself.
- **Astral-influence remark.** *Anglos participare ex influentia potissimum ♀ ♃ ☿* — "the English partake especially of the influence of Venus, Jupiter, Mercury." The planet glyphs ♀ ♃ ☿ are kept in the Source block and named in English by this chapter's convention; whence Tycho's characterology of the English as *alacres, mundi, iucundi … ingeniosi … foecundi*.
- ***non Angelica … Anglicana*** — a pun on *Angelicus* ("Angelic") / *Anglicanus* ("English/Anglican"), playing on the old *Angli/Angeli* topos (Gregory the Great's "non Angli sed Angeli"). The wordplay is kept rather than flattened: "though not Angelic, yet Anglican."
- ***verae Veneres, Charites et Musae*** — "the true Venuses, Graces [*Charites*], and Muses": the *Charites* are the three Graces (Greek term kept). *sertis semper virentibus* = "with ever-green garlands."
- **Thomas Digges.** *Thomam Diggaeseum* = **Thomas Digges** (c. 1546–1595), the English mathematician and Copernican; Tycho's hedge *si isthic locorum is degit* ("if he is living in those parts") is preserved — Tycho did not know Digges had in fact died in August 1595, which the hedge inadvertently flags.
- ***Ducibus … Olympi*** — "the Leaders of Olympus," a flourish for the eminent men to whom Tycho will send his *Works*; the phrase echoes Manilius/poetic diction. Rendered literally.
- **Dateline.** *Raptim Uraniburgi die 25. Martij Anni 1596* = "In haste at **Uraniborg**, the 25th day of March, the year 1596" (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The edition *label* ("1596. 25. marts. Uraniborg") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy.
- **Edition note.** The edition's edition field reads *"Contra vitam monasticam ad Bern. Mattium epistola"* — this appears to be a mis-carried edition tag (that title is a separate work and does not match this letter); the letter is among Tycho's *Epistolae* (Dreyer, *Opera Omnia*). Flagged, not relied upon.
- **What this is.** A short paragraph immediately preceding the letter's warm close (greetings to English friends, Thomas Digges, etc., in the published tail) — Tycho explaining his own redundant-delivery practice: this is, by his own account, the *third* copy of essentially the same letter, sent by three different couriers to guard against loss in transit.
- **The recipient.** Johannes Isaacius Pontanus (1571–1639), the young Danish-Norwegian humanist scholar and mathematician who had spent time in Tycho's circle; he later became a historian (author of a major history of Denmark) and remained a lifelong correspondent, addressed here with evident personal warmth ("mi Ioannes" in the published tail).
- **Significance for the corpus of letters.** This is direct authorial testimony to a documented hazard of early modern scholarly correspondence — letters routinely lost in transit — and to Tycho's countermeasure of triplicate dispatch by separate carriers, a practice also implicit elsewhere in the edition (e.g. Fabricius's and Scaliger's concern over safe and swift delivery routes).
- **Correction.** Source text corrected against Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia VII, page 377: "nostri secuti" corrected to "nostri seculi" (genitive of saeculum, "of our age"). The English translation already read correctly and required no change.

documents.abstract: Presses the rector of the University of Copenhagen for a definitive written reply from the consistory on two pending matters, having received only vague assurances thus far.
documents.incipit: MAGNIFICE domine rector. Eftersom ieg talde med eder y gaar, og waar venligen …

text.original:
[AD RECTOREM UNIVERSITATIS HAUNIENSIS].

MAGNIFICE domine rector. Eftersom ieg talde med eder y gaar, og waar venligen begierendis, att mig motte bliffue førdrett mett nogen endelig beskeen, och icke lenger opholden, mett hvis mig burde at haffue beskreffuit aff eders consistorio, och att ieg derhos maatte faae dett att see, førend dett bleff beseglet, eftersom mig anderstedz vederfaret er, saa well eder selff mett eders assessoribus som mig till beste, och widere uleylighed att forekomme. Jeg begier dog intet andet, end huis billigt och rett er och sandhed gemeß, eftersom eders acta udviser och eder alle witterligt kand vaere. Paa dett første gaff j mig temmelig beskeden, formenendis, att dett skulde bliffue snart fuldendt. Mens om dett andet kunde j ingen rigtig fortrøstning giøre mig, førend j havde talet och raadslaget met eders assessoribus derom. Thi er ieg endnu aff eder och de andre eders collegis ett gott och endeligt suar udi begge stycker paa thet wenligste och i en god mening begierendis, saa att ieg kunde faa att wide mett thette mitt bud, huoreffter ieg haffuer mig att rette. Thet forskylder ieg gierne igien, huor mig mugeligt kand were. Ombedendis derhos, att der motte bliffue tegnet paa denne skrifft, at den er laest for eder.

Actum 31. martii 1596.
Thyge Brahe
met egen haand.
text.english:
[TO THE RECTOR OF THE UNIVERSITY OF COPENHAGEN].

Magnificent lord rector. Inasmuch as I spoke with you yesterday, and was kindly requesting that I might be furthered [helped forward] with some final statement, and no longer held off, with that which I ought to have set down in writing for me by your consistory; and that I might moreover get to see it before it was sealed, as has befallen me elsewhere — both for your own and your assessors' best [interest] as well as mine, and to forestall further inconvenience. Yet I ask nothing else than what is fair and right and conformable to the truth, as your records [acta] show and as can be known to you all. At first you gave me a fair enough answer, supposing that it should soon be brought to completion. But concerning the other [matter] you could give me no proper assurance until you had spoken and taken counsel with your assessors about it. Therefore I am still, of you and the others, your colleagues, requesting a good and final answer on both points, in the friendliest way and in good intent, so that I may get to know by this my messenger how I am to govern myself. This I gladly requite in return, in whatever way may be possible for me. Requesting moreover that there might be marked upon this writing that it has been read out before you.

Done, 31 March 1596.
Tyge Brahe,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / hand.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), signing *Thyge Brahe met egen haand* — "Tyge Brahe, with his own hand," i.e. an autograph subscription (the Latin formula's Danish equivalent of *manu propria*). Tycho's name appears in its Danish vernacular form *Thyge* (not the Latin *Tycho*) in the subscription.
- **Recipient.** Addressed by office only — *Magnifice domine rector* / *Rector Universitatis Hauniensis*, the **rector of the University of Copenhagen** (the *rector magnificus*) and his consistory. The text names no individual; the present translation therefore identifies the addressee by office, not by name. The rector of Copenhagen in spring 1596 is not asserted here on the strength of the letter alone.
- **Context.** One of a pair of letters Tycho addressed to the rector on the same day, 31 March 1596 (the companion piece is brahe-t_15960331002, opening *Efterdi jeg formercker, att j mett eders assessoribus icke wilde…*). Tycho is pressing the university consistory for a formal, sealed, written attestation (*nogen endelig beskeen … beskreffuit aff eders consistorio*) on two matters (*begge stycker*) — an administrative dispute, consonant with the deterioration of Tycho's standing at Copenhagen in the years 1596–97 that preceded his departure from Denmark in 1597. The substance of the two "points" is not specified within the letter and is not reconstructed here.
- **Latin code-switches (a learned chancery hand).** *Magnifice domine rector* — "Magnificent lord rector," the formal academic salutation; *consistorio* — the university **consistory** (governing council); *assessoribus / collegis* — its **assessors / colleagues** (the professors sitting on the consistory); *acta* — the consistory's **records / acts**; *Actum* — "Done / Given" (the dating formula, this chapter's convention); *met egen haand* glosses the *manu propria* subscription. The body is otherwise Danish.
- **Orthography (chancery Danish, c. 1596).** *waar … begierendis* = *var … begærende* ("was requesting"); *førdrett* = *fordret/befordret* ("furthered, helped forward"); *opholden* = *opholdt* ("held off, delayed"); *hvis* = relative *hvad* ("that which"); *beskreffuit* = *beskrevet* ("set down in writing"); *anderstedz vederfaret* = *andetsteds vederfaret* ("befallen [me] elsewhere"); *till beste* = *til bedste* ("for the best [interest]"); *uleylighed* = *ulejlighed* ("inconvenience"); *billigt* = "fair, equitable"; *sandhed gemeß* = *sandhed gemæss* ("conformable to the truth" — *gemæss* a German-loan postposition, "in accordance with"); *temmelig beskeden* = *temmelig besked* ("a fair enough answer/information" — *beskeden* here is the noun *besked*, not the adjective "modest"); *fortrøstning* = "assurance, reassurance"; *raadslaget* = *rådslået* ("taken counsel, deliberated"); *stycker* = *stykker* ("points, items, matters"); *huoreffter ieg haffuer mig att rette* = *hvorefter jeg har mig at rette* ("by which I am to govern/regulate myself"); *forskylder … igien* = *forskylder igen* ("requite, repay in return"); *bud* = "messenger" (the bearer of the letter); *tegnet paa denne skrifft* = *tegnet på denne skrift* ("marked / noted upon this writing"); *laest* = *læst* ("read [out]").
- **"beskeen / beskeden / besked."** The two near-identical forms are the same noun *besked* ("a [final] statement, ruling, answer, information"): *endelig beskeen* = "a final statement/ruling"; *temmelig beskeden* = "a fair enough answer." Rendered consistently as "statement / answer"; not the modern adjective *beskeden* ("modest").
- **Negations.** The body contains two negations — *icke lenger opholden* ("no longer held off") and *intet andet, end* ("nothing else than") — and the reported refusal *kunde j ingen rigtig fortrøstning giøre mig* ("you could give me no proper assurance"). All three are reproduced; none added or dropped.
- **Calendar / place.** *Actum 31. martii 1596* = "Done, 31 March 1596" (Julian / O.S.; Denmark kept Old Style until 1700). No place of writing is given (the edition's *label* records the place as *s.l.* = *sine loco*, "without place"); the header accordingly states "[no place given]." The date in the source's own dateline (31 March 1596) agrees with the catalogue label, so no date discrepancy arises.

documents.abstract: Accepts the rector's refusal to show the unsealed statement, but requests that all consistory acts relating to his case be subscribed on each page, sealed, and retained until needed.
documents.incipit: MAGNIFICE domine rector. Efterdi jeg formercker, att j mett eders assessoribus icke wilde …

text.original:
[AD RECTOREM UNIVERSITATIS HAUNIENSIS].

MAGNIFICE domine rector. Efterdi jeg formercker, att j mett eders assessoribus icke wilde bevilge mig att maa fange att see, hues j giffue mig aff eders consistorio beskreffuen, førend det bliffuer beseglet, endog ieg icke dett aff eder begierede i nogen ond mening, men snarer till dett beste, andre vitløfftighed och uleyglighed att forekomme, saa kand och wil ieg hertill nu intet andet suare, end j kunde derudi effterfølge eders egen betenkning och mening, og lade mig mett det første fange beskreffuet og beseglet, hvis j vilde unde mig, saa at ieg icke nu lenger skal bliffue opholden, med hvilcket ieg faaer paa denne tid att lade mig nøye. Begierendis derhos, att alle eders acta, hues denne min sag angaaer, maa bliffue paa huer side undertegnet, og siden tillbeseglet og velforvaret, indtil videre beskeden, efftersom behoff giøris, og att der motte bliffue tegnet paa denne skrifft, att den er laest for eder.

Actum Kiøbnehaffn 31. martii 1596.
Thyge Brahe
met egen haand.
text.english:
[To the Rector of the University of Copenhagen.]

Magnificent lord rector. Since I perceive that you, together with your assessors, would not grant me leave to be allowed to see what you give me set down in writing from your consistory before it is sealed — even though I did not request this of you with any bad intent, but rather for the best, to forestall further prolixity and inconvenience — I therefore can and will answer nothing else to this now than that you may in this matter follow your own judgement and opinion, and let me at the very first have [it] set down in writing and sealed, [namely] whatever you would grant me, so that I shall not now be held up any longer; with which I must for the present let myself be content. Requesting moreover that all your acts touching this my case may be subscribed on each page, and thereafter sealed up and well kept safe, until further notice, as the need shall arise; and that there be noted upon this writing [of mine] that it has been read out before you.

Done at Copenhagen, 31 March 1596.
Tyge Brahe
with [his] own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / subscription.** *Thyge Brahe … met egen haand* = "**Tyge Brahe** … with [his] own hand" — the autograph subscription formula (rendered by this chapter's convention conventions for *manu propria*).
- **Recipient.** Addressed to the office of the **Rector of the University of Copenhagen** (*Universitas Hauniensis*) and the *consistorium* (the academic senate of professors). The bracketed Latin heading *[AD RECTOREM UNIVERSITATIS HAUNIENSIS]* — "To the rector of the University of Copenhagen" — is an **editorial supplied title** (square brackets as printed in the edition of record), not part of the original letter body; reproduced as printed.
- **Context.** Written in the spring of 1596, in the months before Tycho's relations with the Danish establishment broke down and he left the kingdom (1597). The letter concerns a legal/administrative matter (*denne min sag*, "this my case") in which Tycho had asked to inspect the consistory's written record *before* it was sealed; the rector and assessors refused, and Tycho here concedes the point while insisting on procedural safeguards (each page subscribed, the whole sealed and kept, and a note that the document was read out to him). **No specific person is named**; the identification rests at the level of the office.
- **Latin code-switches (within a Danish body).** *Magnifice domine rector* — "Magnificent lord rector," the standard formal academic address to a university rector; kept and translated. *assessoribus* (abl. pl.) = "assessors" (the consistory members sitting in judgement). *consistorio* = "consistory" (the university senate). *acta* = "acts / records" (the official minutes). *Actum* = "Done / Given" (the dating formula, this chapter's convention). Each is a learned Latin technical noun embedded in the Danish, in the chancery manner described in this chapter's convention

documents.abstract: Reports that Tycho's letters were safely delivered and presents a candidate to manage the fief and command of Nordfjord on Tycho's behalf.
documents.incipit: MYNN gandske ydmygelige helsßenn nu och altidt forsenndt medt Wor Herre. Kierre Tyggi …

text.original:
ERLIG OCH WELBYRDIIGE MANNDT TYGGJ BRADE TILL KNUDSTRUP, HØFFUIDTZMANDT PAA VRANNIBORGH, GANDTZE YDMYGELIGENN TILLSCHREFFUITT.

MYNN gandske ydmygelige helsßenn nu och altidt forsenndt medt Wor Herre. Kierre Tyggi Brade, thacker ieg ethers fromhedt for alt ere och gott, som y meg giort och beuist haffuer, for huilcket ieg effter minn formoue gandtze giernne will findis ethers fattige thienner till att giørre och lade alt huis ieg widt ethers fromhedt kandt haffue ere och gott aff. Kierre Tyggi och guode juncker, giffuer ieg ethers welbyrd[ig]hedt wenligen att wiide, om thj breffue, som eders fromhedt meg antuordit haffuer, denom ere huer well thill throer hande komit, som thj war tillschreffuit (Gud werre loffuit). Sameledis, frome juncker, som ethers welbyrdighedt well dragis tiill minnde, att ieg paa ethers wegnne schulle giøre min beste och forhørre ether om enn from, erlige personne, som kunde well stande ethers fromhedtz lehnn och befalling Nordfiordt forre, och som well widste landzenns leilighedt och skicke, huorfor ieg haffuer giffuit thenne breffuißer ethers welbyrdighedtz willie tilkiennde. Om saa kunde werre, attj wille betrou hanom eders lehnn, tha thuiller ieg jntedt ther paa, att samme personn, Morttenn Bertilßønn, skall io bliffue och werre eders fromhedt huldt och trou y alle maade, saa y nest Gudtz hielp skall hanom jche andit skylde, end thet som erligt och christeligt skall werre. Och thuiller ieg iche heller paa, att hand skall forsøme seg y huis maade, som handt widt eders welbyrdighedtz sager och bestelling kandt kome till gaffn och beste vdj nogenn maader. Ther for, gunstige juncker, haffuer ieg paa eders guode behagh forskreffuet samme Morttenn Bertilßønn till ether, saa ethers fromhedt kanndt sielffuer widere handle och talle medt hanom. Och om ieg widste, att handt war iche throu och guodt, tha skulle ieg jche forschriffue hanom tiill eders fromhedt; thi handt haffuer thiennt min hustrue[s] fader, Michell Eskelßønn, fogitt y Halsnø Kloster, y 9 aar som en erlig och trou karll y all maade, saa handt maa fritt skyude sinn skodtzmaall tiill hanom igienn, om behouff giøris. Frome gunstige juncker, er minn ydmygelige bønn till ethers welbyrdighedt, om saa er, att ethers fromhedt iche sielff hagde hans tienniste behouff, y tha wille wel giøre, som enn from manndt, och werre hanom behielpelig huos enn ethers fromhedtz guode wenner, som haffuer forlening her i landit, att handt motte fange nogenn pladtz. Thj hanndt widt well landzens leilighedt. Och will ieg iche lenger bemøde ethers fromhedt medt thenne minn schriffuelße, menn altidt giernne giøre huis ethers fromhedt kand werre till thienniste och guode, huilcke Gudt allemectigste kiennde. Jeg will nu och altidt haffue ether euindelige beffallindis.

Schreffuit vdj Halsnø closter then 2 aprillis anno 96.
Ethers ydmyge thienner altidt
Matzs
Jørgensßøn.
text.english:
**To the honourable and well-born man Tyge Brahe of Knudstrup, governor at Uraniborg, written all most humbly.**

My wholly humble greeting, now and always conveyed with Our Lord. Dear Tyge Brahe, I thank your worthiness [*fromhedt*] for all honour and good that you have done and shown me, for which, to the best of my ability, I will most gladly show myself your poor servant, to do and to leave undone all whereby I may, with your worthiness, have honour and good. Dear Tyge and good squire [*juncker*], I make known to your well-bornness in friendly wise that the letters which your worthiness entrusted to me have each duly come into faithful hands, as they were addressed (God be praised). Likewise, good squire, as your well-bornness will well recall, that I, on your behalf, was to do my best and make inquiry for you after an upright, honest person who could well preside over your worthiness's fief and command of Nordfjord, and who knew well the country's condition and order — wherefore I have made known to this letter-bearer your well-bornness's wish [*willie*]. If it might be that you would entrust your fief to him, then I doubt nothing thereof: that this same person, Morten Bertelsen, shall indeed remain and be loyal and faithful to your worthiness in every way, so that, next to God's help, you shall charge him with nothing other than what shall be honest and Christian. And I doubt no more either that he shall be negligent in any way wherein he, in your well-bornness's affairs and business, can come to profit and advantage in any manner. Therefore, gracious squire, at your good pleasure I have written the same Morten Bertelsen to you, so that your worthiness may yourself deal and speak further with him. And if I knew that he were not faithful and good, then I should not commend him to your worthiness; for he has served my wife's father, Michel Eskelsen, bailiff [*fogitt*] at Halsnøy Abbey, for nine years as an honest and faithful fellow in every way, so that he may freely refer his testimonial [*skodtzmaall*] back to him, if need be. Good gracious squire, my humble plea to your well-bornness is, if it be so that your worthiness yourself had no need of his service, that you would then do well, as an upright man, and be helpful to him with one of your worthiness's good friends who has an enfeoffment [*forlening*] here in this land, that he might obtain some place. For he knows well the country's condition. And I will not trouble your worthiness longer with this my writing, but will always gladly do what may be of service and good to your worthiness, as Almighty God knows. I will now and always have you eternally commended [to God].

Written at Halsnøy Abbey, the 2nd of April, the year [15]96.
Your humble servant always,
Mads
Jørgensen.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent (sender).** *Matzs Jørgensßøn* = **Mads Jørgensen Huus** (the surname is supplied from the edition/edition heading, not from the letter's own subscription, which signs only "Mads Jørgensen"). He writes from Halsnøy Abbey in western Norway, evidently in some administrative or household capacity connected to the bailiff Michel Eskelsen, whose daughter he had married. He is otherwise a minor figure; this commendatory letter is his sole appearance in the Brahe correspondence.
- **Recipient.** **Tyge (Tycho) Brahe of Knudstrup**, here addressed by his Danish style and titled *høffuidtzmandt paa Uraniborg* ("governor / captain at Uraniborg"). At this date (1596) Tycho still held Hven and his crown fiefs; the letter assumes he has fiefs (*lehn*) at his disposal to bestow, including **Nordfjord** in Norway.
- **Document type.** An autograph **letter of recommendation (commendation)** for the bearer, Morten Bertelsen, who is to deliver it in person ("this letter-bearer," *thenne breffuißer*) and then treat with Tycho directly. MS witness A is the autograph at Basel (Universitätsbibliothek, Autographensammlung, Vol. 23, fol. 1).
- **Person recommended.** *Morttenn Bertilßønn* = **Morten Bertelsen**, the bearer, proposed as administrator of the Nordfjord fief; vouched for as having served nine years under the writer's father-in-law.
- **Person (referee).** *Michell Eskelßønn* = **Michel Eskelsen**, *fogitt y Halsnø Kloster* = **bailiff (Da.** *foged***) at Halsnøy Abbey**; the writer's wife's father, under whom Morten Bertelsen had served.
- **Places.** *Halsnø Kloster / Halsnøy* = **Halsnøy Abbey** (Halsnøy kloster), the former Augustinian monastery on the island of Halsnøy in Sunnhordland, western Norway, by then a secularised crown estate administered by a bailiff. *Nordfiordt* = **Nordfjord**, a district and crown fief in western Norway (Bergenhus region). *Knudstrup* = **Knutstorp** (Knudstrup), the Brahe family seat in Scania. *Vranniborgh* = **Uraniborg** on Hven.
- ***fromhedt*** — literally "piety / probity"; here, as a chancery courtesy-title for an addressee below royal rank, it functions as an honorific abstraction roughly equivalent to "your worthiness / your good self." Rendered "your worthiness" throughout for consistency; it is **not** the religious term "piety" in this register.
- ***welbyrd[ig]hedt / welbyrdighedt*** — "well-bornness," the courtesy-abstraction for a *welbyrdig* (well-born, noble) addressee; rendered "your well-bornness." The first occurrence is contracted in the source (*welbyrdhedt*); the missing syllable is restored in brackets.
- ***juncker*** — "squire / young lord" (Ger. *Junker*), a respectful address for a nobleman; kept.
- ***lehn / forlening / befalling*** — *lehn* = **fief / fiefdom** (a crown estate held in administration); *forlening* = **enfeoffment** (the grant of such a fief); *befalling* = "command / charge" (here the office of administering the fief). The letter turns on Tycho's power to grant the Nordfjord fief to a deputy.
- ***fogitt*** — **bailiff** (Da. *foged*), the resident administrator of a crown estate.
- ***skodtzmaall*** — a **testimonial / character-reference** (Da. *skudsmål*), the formal vouching a servant could call upon from a former master; "he may freely refer his testimonial back to him" = Morten may appeal to Michel Eskelsen as a referee.
- **Negation / conditional logic (checked).** Three negated clauses carry the letter's force and are reproduced one-for-one: (1) *"om ieg widste, att handt war **iche** throu och guodt, tha skulle ieg **jche** forschriffue hanom"* — a double-negative conditional: "if I knew he were **not** faithful and good, then I should **not** commend him" (both negations preserved; the sense is a guarantee, not a doubt). (2) *"y nest Gudtz hielp skall hanom **jche** andit skylde, end thet som erligt … skall werre"* — "you shall charge him with **nothing** other than what shall be honest" (litotes of trust, kept). (3) *"om saa er, att ethers fromhedt **iche** sielff hagde hans tienniste behouff"* — the contrary-to-expectation conditional governing the closing plea: "if it be so that your worthiness yourself had **no** need of his service, [then] you would … be helpful to him [in placing him] with one of your good friends." The mood of *hagde* (past subjunctive) is hypothetical/polite; rendered "had no need" as a courteous conditional, not as an assertion that Tycho lacks the need.
- **Emphatic *io*.** *"skall **io** bliffue och werre … huldt och trou"* — the particle *io* (≈ "indeed, assuredly") intensifies the assurance; rendered "shall indeed remain and be loyal and faithful."
- **Orthography (chancery Danish, c. 1596, German-influenced).** Heavy *-ff-* for *-v-* (*haffuer* = *haver*, *breffue* = *breve*, *giffuer* = *giver*), *w-* for *v-* (*Wor* = *Vor*, *will* = *vil*, *widt* = *ved*), *th-* (*thacker* = *takker*, *thill* = *til*), *sch-/-ß-* (*tillschreffuitt*, *helsßenn*, *schriffuelße*), *attj* = *at I* ("that you," plural-polite), *denom/hanom* = *dennem/hannem* ("them/him"), *io* = *jo*, *vdj* = *udi* ("in/at"). The orthography is German-coloured chancery Danish — the kind that misleads automatic language detection (the heuristic tagged it *da*, correctly here).
- **Calendar / place.** *Schreffuit vdj Halsnø closter then 2 aprillis anno 96* = "Written at **Halsnøy Abbey**, the 2nd of April, the year [15]96" (O.S.; Denmark-Norway kept the Julian calendar until 1700). The dateline date (2 April 1596) agrees with the catalogue label; no discrepancy.
- **Correction.** Corrected the English's reversed subject/object: Mads made Tycho's own wish known to the letter-bearer Morten Bertelsen, not the bearer's mind known to Tycho (Dreyer, TBOO XIV p.98).

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter word-for-word against Dreyer TBOO XIV pp. 97-98 via the page images, including the italic Latin argument on p. 97 ("Matthias Georgii e monasterio Halsnö... commendat... Martinum Bartholini") confirming sender and purpose, and the closing/signature (Matzs Jørgennsßønn, 2 April [15]96). Source_text matches Dreyer exactly — no text error. One mistranslation found: the clause reporting who informed whom of what has its direction of communication reversed (bearer-informs-Tycho instead of Mads-informs-bearer-of-Tycho's-wish). This changes what a scholar would take away from that sentence, so despite the letter's overall recommendation of Morten Bertelsen surviving intact, the grading rule's omission/mistranslation-that-changes-the-sense clause applies. Downgraded from the translator's own A.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (medium). The Danish syntax "giffue nogen noget tilkiennde" = "make something known TO someone": "thenne breffuißer" (this letter-bearer) is the dative recipient, and "ethers welbyrdighedtz willie" (your well-bornness's will/wish, genitive-marked) is the thing made known. The direction is reversed in translation: Mads is telling the letter-bearer (Morten Bertelsen) what TYCHO's wish is, not reporting the bearer's mind to Tycho. The published English swaps subject and object, attributing the possessive "willie" to the bearer instead of to Tycho and inverting who informs whom. At: “wherefore I have made this letter-bearer's mind [willie] known to your well-bornness”.

**Repaired.** Verified against Dreyer TBOO XIV pp.97-99; the sentence appears on p.98, lines 8-11, reading "...huorfor ieg haffuer giffuit thenne breffuißer ethers welbyrdighedtz willie tilkiennde," matching the transcribed original exactly. The Danish dative construction confirms the audit's reading and the English has been corrected accordingly. No other defects found on these three pages.
