documents.abstract: Argues that it falls to the new chancellor to support astronomy and the liberal disciplines, citing Manilius on the art's glory for kingdoms and kings.
documents.incipit: CUM ad dignitatem præcipuam in hoc regno Daniæ evectus sis, magnifice domine cancellarie, …

text.original:
MAGNIFICO ET NOBILISSIMO VIRO, DIGNITATE, PRUDENTIA ET DOCTRINA INPRIMIS CONSPICUO, DOMINO CHRISTIANO FRISIO DE BORREBY, SERENISSIMI REGIS NOSTRI CANCELLARIO ET A CONSILIJS INTIMO, AMICO SUO HONORANDO.

CUM ad dignitatem præcipuam in hoc regno Daniæ evectus sis, magnifice domine cancellarie, amice honorande, eqvidem ex te ipso absqve ullo monitore intelligere potes, quæ decus regni concernunt, tuarum esse partium hortatu et consilijs promovere. Qvod in disciplinarum liberalium liberali etiam sustentatione et conservatione non minima ex parte consistere pro tua prudentia non ignoras, præsertim cum ipsemet doctrinis humanioribus præclare imbutus sis. Astronomia autem inter omnes scientias locum principem merito obtinens, in qvantum et regnis et regibus gloriosa semper exstiterit, multæ rationes multaqve exempla attestantur, ut ob id a Manilio poeta, Augusto imperatori scribente, hoc elogio deprædicetur, qvod

Regales animos primum dignata movere est
Proxima tangentes cælo fastigia rerum.

Hanc igitur tam sublimem artem ex decreto et clementi voluntate Friderici IIdi, laudatissimæ memoriæ regis in hac insula Huenna summis viribus excolere adeoqve redintegrare jamdudum agressus sum, ingentibus ausis et laboribus, neqve sumptibus mediocribus, omnes nervos eo intendens, ut in honorem patriæ illa illustrior et absolutior quam uspiam antea prodiret. Qva in re quid hactenus non saltem qvoad instrumentorum idoneorum, qvalia forte alibi nullo ævo extiterunt, et ædificiorum huc spectantium exstructione, sed et in observationibus qvam plurimis, nulla fere serenitate omissa, coelitus deducendis atque ex his restituendis astrorum motibus effecerimus, judicent alij, qvotqvot Evropa habet vel vnqvam habitura est horum intelligentes et cupidos. Qvos confido non illubenter concessuros me omnes stellas fixas, visui commode patentes, tanta subtilitate et certitudine restituisse, qvanta a nullis veterum aut recentiorum effectum est, res sane ardua multisqve seculis frustra desiderata, sed et solis lunæque curricula in normam cælo ad amussim consonam a nobis esse redacta, omnium ætatum subsecuturæ experientur animadversiones. Qvin et in reliqvis planetis (qva in parte adhuc sedulo laboramus, circuituum tarditate in nonnullis cunctationem exigente) id ipsum exeqvi indies magnis conatibus enitimur; hypothesi jam antea scienter excogitata, quæ antecedentium omnium astronomorum speculationes, fatentibus id hujus seculi artificibus præcipuis, eludit. Constituerat vero dictus rex serenissimus, artis hujus regiæ culturam in hac insula perpetuare et fundatione liberali ejus ad posteros conservationi prospicere. Verum nimis immature (proh dolor) nobis ereptus, id ante supremum diem exeqvi non potuit. Retuli itaqve de eo statim post ipsius obitum ad regni senatum, attestans etiam serenissimam reginam et quosdam e senatoribus conscios, qvi illud ex rege, cum in vivis esset, inaudivissent. Qvare et universus senatus mox non inuite, literis in membrana exaratis (qvarum hic exemplar adjunxi) regium illud propositum confirmavit, et se, cum princeps administrationi rerum admoveretur, omni conatu et svasu elaboraturum, ut is artis hujus perpetuationi in hac insula clementer et liberaliter provideret, addixit. Qvin et tunc feudum qvoddam in Norvagia mihi concessum est, et alias meæ indemnitati, qvantum ea tempora patiebantur, consultum, spe facta, qvod in posterum omnia ex voto uberius evenirent. Præter omnem nihilominus meam expectationem accidit, quod statim ac serenissimus noster rex coronatus est, feudo illo citra ullam (uti confido) meam culpam privatus sim, adeo ut potissima portio eorum, qvæ astronomicæ restaurationis subsidia spectabant, mihi subtracta sit, non mediocri meo incommodo. Rem enim familiarem (omnia qvæ tum e regijs feudis tum bonis hæreditarijs acquirere licuit, in hoc opus expendendo) hactenus potius imminuatam quam auctam, nimis vere expertus sum, cum alijs hujus regni nobilibus, meis coæqualibus, contra evenerit, qvi et propria conservarunt et insuper e regijs rem fecerunt. Accedit et hoc, qvod his primordijs, ab artis hujus sustentatione adeo aversis, dubius reddar, qvid de ejus in hoc regno promotione et conservatione in posterum sperandum sit; anne illius exercitatio prorsus deserenda veniat, an vero alia ejus continuandæ media sint qværenda, qvorum hoc fortassis patriæ nostræ minus honorificum, illud certe exteri ægerrime paterentur, qvi vndeqvaque quotannis ad me datis literis serio hortantur, ut inchoatam telam pertexere non omittam, sed confectam orbi aliqvando communicem, qvod non mediocris copia literarum ex Italia, Gallia, Germania, Bohemia, Anglia et Scotia alijsqve regionibus profecta et apud me reservata ostendet. Qvin et ipsemet, qvi potiorem in his ætatis partem consumpsi, tot annorum exantlatos labores, tot vigilatas noctes tantosqve erogatos sumptus incassum factos reddi admodum invite ferrem. Qvin potius ne id fieret utqve expectationi regum qvorundam, principum atqve præstantissimorum hinc inde virorum satisfaciam, nec multis spem conceptam laudabilem illaudabiliter frustremur, omnino rationes ineundæ, quibus id, quod semel bene inchoatum est, totqve annis continuatum, aliqvando in publicam orbis utilitatem absolvatur, ubicunqve tandem locorum et qvibuscunqve medijs id commode exseqvi liceat. Qvæ cum ita se habeant et necessario nobis facienda sint, in tuum sinum deponenda, tibiqve hisce literis aliqvatenus ea exponenda duximus, qvo autoritate atqve prudentia, qva vales, huic incommodo subvenire et mature obviare velis, qvod etiam te libere et lubenter facturum mihi persvadeo siqvidem non difficulter prævideas, qvam honorifica huic regno artis tam sublimis conservatio existat, qvamqve minus apud alias nationes decorum eidem foret, si ejus instaurationem tam diu tantoqve molimine hic factitatam, cujus fama plurimas Europæ regiones jam penetravit, aut negligi aut aliorsum transferri necessum fuerit. Ut vero aliqvatenus perspicias, qvænam in hoc regno ad astronomiæ redintegrationem indefesso studio hactenus molitus sim, habes hic primum tomum epistolarum astronomicarum e nostris, qvi suo loco brevem instrumentorum a me ejus artis gratia elaboratorum descriptionem, vna cum ædificijs huc pertinentibus exhibet, adjunctis in fine qvorundam ex ijsdem organis jconibus, qvibus introspectis, utcunqve tibi constabit, arbitror, me non obiter, sed summis viribus imo etiam supra ipsas vires tanta perfecisse. Qvod etiam tibi ipsi, si aliqvando mihi in hac insula adesse haud gravatus fueris, opinione verius æstimabitur. Oblatus qvidem est idem liber una cum jconibus serenissimo regi meo nomine submisse, anteqvam Hafnia ultimo discederet, sed cum tunc in itineris Cimbrici præcinctu esset, neqve ad ea serio attendere, neqve de ijs, qvæ proponebantur, qvidpiam certi statuere ipsius majestati commodum erat. Rogo itaqve officiose, magnifice domine cancellarie, ut patriæ saltem causa hoc tam arduum negotium tibi cordi esse sinas, et de ijs, quæ artis adeo eximiæ apud nos conservationem et propagationem concernunt, serio cogites, regiqve nostro serenissimo opportunum in his des consilium. Hoc autem tempore nihil aliud expeto, qvam ut feudum in Norvagia mihi ademptum clementer restituatur, si non diutius, saltem in diem calend. maij, qvo feudorum apud nos commutatio fieri soleat, ut præfectus meus tunc mihi rationes reddituum (qvos alias nullos toto hoc anno inde accepi) reddere qveat. Interea serenissimus rex et secum et ex prudentissimi senatus consilio deliberatius statuat, qvid in posterum circa hæc fieri velit, cujus ego regiæ voluntati, in qvamcunqve partem res vergat, lubens acqviescam. Porro te etiam obnixe rogatum habeo, ut per hunc meum ministrum nonnulla mihi de antedictis rescribere, tuamqve sententiam aperire ne recusare velis, qvo mature, qvid facto opus sit, mecum statuere qveam. Exspectabit istic, donec id tibi per alias occupationes opportunum fuerit. Ego vicissim de te pro virili bene mereri, tuoqve honori et nomini officiose studere non intermittam. Vale, atqve hanc in scribendo prolixitatem, re ita exigente, candide et benevole accipe.

Iterum cum tota familia felix et incolumis vale, annumqve hunc ut auspicato ingrediaris absolvasqve, opto.
Dabantur Uraniburgo pridie calendarum januarij anni 1597.
text.english:
**To the magnificent and most noble man, conspicuous above all for rank, prudence, and learning, Master Christian Friis of Borreby, Chancellor and Privy Councillor of our most serene King, his friend to be honoured.**

Since you have been raised to a foremost dignity in this kingdom of Denmark, magnificent lord chancellor, honoured friend, you can of course understand from your own self, without any prompter, that it falls to your part to advance by your exhortation and counsel those things which concern the honour of the realm. And in your prudence you are not unaware that this consists, in no small part, in the liberal maintenance and preservation of the liberal disciplines — especially since you yourself are excellently steeped in the more humane studies. Now astronomy, deservedly holding the chief place among all the sciences, how glorious it has always proved both to kingdoms and to kings, many reasons and many examples attest; so that on this account it is celebrated by the poet Manilius, writing to the emperor Augustus, with this encomium — that

It first deigned to move royal minds,
those that touch the summits of affairs nearest to the sky.

This art, then, so sublime, I long ago undertook, by the decree and gracious will of Frederick II, king of most laudable memory, to cultivate and indeed to renew on this island of Hven with my utmost strength — with vast ventures and labours, and with no moderate expense, straining every sinew to this end, that for the honour of my homeland it might come forth more illustrious and more complete than anywhere before. As to what I have accomplished therein hitherto — not only in the construction of suitable instruments (such as perhaps existed in no age elsewhere) and of the buildings pertaining to this work, but also in very many observations to be drawn down from the heavens, scarcely any clear sky being let slip, and in the restoration of the motions of the stars from these — let others judge, as many as Europe has, or ever will have, who understand and desire these matters. I am confident they will not unwillingly grant that I have restored all the fixed stars conveniently open to the sight with such precision and certainty as has been achieved by none of the ancients or moderns — an arduous matter indeed, and longed for in vain through many ages — and that the courses of the Sun and Moon too have been reduced by us to a rule exactly consonant with the heavens, as the observations of every age to follow will find. Moreover, in the remaining planets (in which part we still diligently labour, the slowness of the circuits in some of them demanding delay) we strive to carry out the very same thing day by day with great efforts; with a hypothesis already devised with full knowledge beforehand, which — as the foremost practitioners of this age confess — eludes the speculations of all preceding astronomers. Now the said most serene king had resolved to perpetuate the cultivation of this royal art on this island and, by a liberal endowment, to provide for its preservation to posterity. But, snatched from us all too untimely (alas!), he could not carry this out before his last day. I therefore reported the matter, immediately after his death, to the council of the realm, calling to witness also the most serene queen and certain of the councillors who were privy to it, who had heard it from the king while he was still living. Wherefore the whole council too, not unwillingly, soon confirmed that royal intention by letters engrossed on parchment (a copy of which I have here attached), and pledged that, when the prince should be brought to the administration of affairs, it would labour with every effort and persuasion that he should graciously and liberally provide for the perpetuation of this art on this island. And at that time, too, a certain fief in Norway was granted to me, and otherwise provision was made for my indemnity, so far as those times allowed, the hope being given that in future all things would turn out more abundantly according to my wish. Nevertheless, contrary to all my expectation it happened that, as soon as our most serene king was crowned, I was deprived of that fief through no fault of mine (as I trust), so that the most important portion of those things which served as supports for the restoration of astronomy has been withdrawn from me, to my no slight disadvantage. For I have learned all too truly that my estate (in spending upon this work everything that I was able to acquire both from the royal fiefs and from my hereditary goods) has hitherto been diminished rather than increased — whereas the contrary has befallen other nobles of this realm, my equals, who have both preserved their own and, besides, made their fortune from the king's. There is added this also: that from these first beginnings, so averse to the maintenance of this art, I am rendered doubtful what is to be hoped, in future, concerning its promotion and preservation in this kingdom — whether the practice of it must be abandoned altogether, or whether other means of continuing it must be sought; of which the former would perhaps be less honourable to our homeland, while the latter foreigners would certainly bear most grievously, who from every quarter, year by year, in letters sent to me earnestly exhort me not to leave off weaving to its end the web I have begun, but to share it, when finished, with the world at last — as a no slight store of letters, dispatched from Italy, France, Germany, Bohemia, England, and Scotland and other regions and kept by me, will show. And I myself, too, who have spent the better part of my life on these things, should very unwillingly bear that the labours endured through so many years, so many wakeful nights, and so great expenditures laid out, should be rendered made-in-vain. Rather, that this should not happen, and that I may satisfy the expectation of certain kings, princes, and most excellent men here and there, nor frustrate without praise the laudable hope conceived by many, means must by all means be entered upon whereby that which has once been well begun, and continued through so many years, may at last be brought to completion for the public benefit of the world — wherever in the end, and by whatever means, it may conveniently be carried out. Since these things are so, and must of necessity be done by us, I have judged that they should be laid in your bosom, and to some extent set out to you in this letter, that by the authority and prudence in which you are strong you may be willing to come to the aid of this difficulty and to forestall it in good time — which I persuade myself you will also do freely and gladly, since you may without difficulty foresee how honourable to this kingdom is the preservation of so sublime an art, and how less than seemly it would be for it in the eyes of other nations, if the renewal of it, so long and with such great effort wrought here — whose fame has already penetrated very many regions of Europe — should have to be either neglected or transferred elsewhere. But that you may to some extent perceive what I have hitherto, with untiring zeal, set in motion in this kingdom toward the renewal of astronomy, you have here the first volume of astronomical letters from among ours, which in its place presents a brief description of the instruments wrought by me for the sake of that art, together with the buildings pertaining hereto, with the figures of certain of those same instruments appended at the end; on inspecting which, I think it will be in some measure evident to you that I have accomplished such great things not in passing, but with my utmost strength — nay, even beyond those very strengths. Which will also be more truly estimated by you yourself, if you should at some time not be loath to be present with me on this island. The same book, together with the figures, was indeed offered submissively in my name to the most serene king, before he last departed from Copenhagen; but since he was then on the eve of the Cimbrian journey, it was convenient for his majesty neither to attend seriously to these matters, nor to settle anything certain concerning the things that were proposed. I therefore dutifully ask, magnificent lord chancellor, that for the homeland's sake at least you may let this so arduous business be at heart to you, and that you may seriously consider those things which concern the preservation and propagation of so excellent an art among us, and may give our most serene king timely counsel in these matters. At this time, however, I seek nothing else than that the fief taken from me in Norway be graciously restored — if not for longer, at least until the first of May, the day on which the changing of fiefs is customarily done among us — so that my steward may then be able to render me the accounts of the revenues (of which I have otherwise received none from there in this whole year). Meanwhile let the most serene king, both with himself and from the counsel of his most prudent council, determine more deliberately what he would wish to be done about these matters in future; in whose royal will, to whichever side the matter incline, I shall gladly acquiesce. Further, I also hold you earnestly asked that, through this my servant, you not be unwilling to write back to me something about the aforesaid matters and to disclose your opinion, so that I may in good time determine with you what needs to be done. He will wait there until it shall be convenient for you, amid your other occupations. I, in turn, shall not cease to deserve well of you to the best of my ability, and dutifully to study your honour and name. Farewell, and take this prolixity in writing — the matter so demanding — candidly and kindly.

Again, fare you well, happy and unharmed, together with your whole household; and I wish that you may both enter upon and complete this year under good auspices.
Given at Uraniborg, the day before the Kalends of January [31 December], of the year 1597.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** Tycho Brahe to **Christian Friis of Borreby** (Christian Friis til Borreby, 1556–1616), appointed Chancellor of the Realm (*kongens kansler* / *Danmarks Riges kansler*) by the young Christian IV soon after the king's coronation (29 August 1596), succeeding the late Niels Kaas. Corpus background: *On Tycho's Island* (Manderup Parsberg "held authority as royal chancellor but was about to hand it to Christian Friis of Borreby"); Dreyer, *Tycho Brahe* ("He had appointed Christian Friis of Borreby, Chancellor …"). The letter is Tycho's formal appeal to the new chancellor over the loss of his Norwegian fief and the imperilled royal support for his work — a key document of the crisis that ended in his 1597 departure from Denmark.
- **Place / date.** *Dabantur Uraniburgo pridie calendarum januarij anni 1597* = "Given at **Uraniborg** [on Hven], the day before the Kalends of January, of the year 1597." The day before the Kalends of January is **31 December**; reckoned to the *coming* year's Kalends it is the last day of **1596** (Old Style — Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). The header therefore reads **31 December 1596 [O.S.]**; the edition identifier agrees (15961231). The Roman idiom is kept and glossed by this chapter's convention
- **Manilius verse.** *Regales animos primum dignata movere est / Proxima tangentes caelo fastigia rerum* — Manilius, *Astronomica* I.41–42 (the proem, on how the heavenly art first stirred the minds of kings, who hold the summits of affairs nearest the sky). Tycho ascribes it to "Manilius … writing to the emperor Augustus" (the *Astronomica* was composed under Augustus/Tiberius). Kept as verse by this chapter's convention
- **The enclosed book.** *primum tomum epistolarum astronomicarum e nostris … adjunctis in fine qvorundam ex ijsdem organis jconibus* = "the first volume of astronomical letters from among ours … with figures (*icones*) of certain of the instruments appended at the end" — Tycho's own *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Liber I, Uraniborg 1596), whose appended *icones* depict his instruments. *organis* rendered "instruments" and *icones* "figures" per glossary.
- **Astronomical claims.** *redintegrare / restituendis astrorum motibus / astronomicae restaurationis / instaurationem* — Tycho's *instauratio astronomiae* programme: rendered "renew / restore the motions of the stars / restoration of astronomy / renewal" per glossary. *omnes stellas fixas … restituisse* = the fixed-star catalogue; *solis lunaeque curricula in normam … redacta* = the solar and lunar theories reduced to a rule consonant with observation. *hypothesi jam antea scienter excogitata, quae antecedentium omnium astronomorum speculationes … eludit* = the Tychonic world-system ("a hypothesis … which eludes the speculations of all preceding astronomers"). The author's hedges are preserved: the fixed stars are restored *visui commode patentes* ("conveniently open to the sight"), the planets are still in progress (*adhuc sedulo laboramus*), and the chancellor's good will is hoped (*uti confido*, "as I trust"; *mihi persvadeo*, "I persuade myself"), not asserted.
- **The fief and the politics.** *feudum qvoddam in Norvagia* = the Norwegian fief (Nordfjord) granted under Frederik II; *coronatus est … feudo illo … privatus sim* = Tycho's deprivation of it upon Christian IV's coronation (1596). *literis in membrana exaratis* = the council's confirmatory letters "engrossed on parchment." *itineris Cimbrici* = "the Cimbrian journey," i.e. the king's progress through Jutland/the Cimbrian peninsula (the *Cimbri* being the classicising name for the Jutes). *calend. maij* = "the Kalends of May" = **1 May**, the customary fief-transfer term; kept and glossed.
- **Negations / conditional force (checked).** The conditional appeal *si non diutius, saltem in diem calend. maij* is rendered exactly: "if not for longer, at least until the first of May" — a minimum request, not a renunciation. *citra ullam … meam culpam* = "through no fault of mine"; *non mediocri meo incommodo* / *neqve sumptibus mediocribus* = litotes ("no slight … / no moderate …"), preserved. The double-negative *nec multis spem conceptam laudabilem illaudabiliter frustremur* ("nor frustrate without praise the laudable hope …") is reproduced with both negatives intact.
- **Honorifics / formulae.** *Magnifico … domino … amico suo honorando* / *magnifice domine cancellarie, amice honorande* — the magnate-and-councillor register, rendered "magnificent lord chancellor, honoured friend" (cf. glossary). *Vale … Iterum … vale* = "Farewell … Again, fare you well". *Dabantur* = "Given" (the issuing formula). *proh dolor* = "alas!" kept as an interjection.
- **Editorial note.** Source spellings are as transcribed in the Dreyer base (*qv-* for *qu-*, *-ij* for *-ii*, *Evropa*, *Huenna*, *jconibus*); reproduced verbatim in the Source block, normalised silently only in the translation. No competing reading affects the sense; "[15]97 → 31 Dec 1596" is the only interpretive point, handled in the calendar note above.

documents.abstract: Corrects the claim that he left Denmark merely because of revenue losses, arguing that all his revenues were withdrawn and that his emigration had deeper causes.
documents.incipit: VIDETUR Cassolius in ultimis ad me discessus mei ex Dania cavsas non satis ponderasse, …

text.original:
CAVSAe DEMIGRATIONIS D:NI TYCHONIS BRAHE EX PATRIA DANIA BREVITER AB IPSO AD PASCOLIUM MULÆUM EXPOSITAe.

VIDETUR Cassolius in ultimis ad me discessus mei ex Dania cavsas non satis ponderasse, forte qvod illi minus essent perspectae, dum ait non nisi aliqvam proventuum jacturam me fecisse, idqve etiam aliis mei ordinis evenisse, et talium solere miram esse vicissitudinem, qvod a te et Bagone illo accepisse se insinuat. Atqve si haec a te prolata sunt, aut meae e patria migrationis occasiones non penitus te cognovisse [?credo], aut eas patriae et nostratium cavsa politice et cavte subtices et dissimulas. Sunt qvidem ab aliis nobilibus reditus qvidam subtracti, qvi eos in privatum commodum vertebant, at a me omnes, adeo ut ne qvidem a praebenda mea Roschildensi vindicanda sibi, qvod alias insolitum est, abstinuerit cancellarius, qvi potius ea, qvae tracto, studia, juxta senatusconsulti rationem promovere debuisset. Ego vero, uti multis constat, non saltem eos, qvos a rege habui, sed et qvoscunqve de bonis haereditariis acqvirere licuit, sumptus in astronomicae artis instavrationem, qvo sic etiam patriae honori studerem, impendi. Verum tolerabilis fuisset haec utut gravis jactura, si non disertis verbis ad me scripsisset cancellarius, regi non esse integrum in astronomicorum instrumentorum conservationem qvicqvam impendere. Sicqve omnium senatorum literae aliud spondentes, exavtoratae, quas statim ab obitu laudat. mem. regis Friderici nostri in membrana exaratas, et singulorum manibus et sigillis munitas concesserunt, me vivente et vidente totus ille apparatus astronomicus, qvem ex clementi voluntate nunqvam satis lavdati regis istic institueram, interire debuerit, ne dum ut ad posteros in perpetuum regni honorem, juxta decretum tam dicti regis, qvam regni senatorum continuaret in perpetuum. Qvin nec in propriis qvidem aedibus Hafniae, propriis etiam sumptibus haec exercitia tractare licuit, interdicente id, sub nomine hujus, qvi nunc est, regis, licet tum in Germania absentis, aulae magistro, isqve per urbis praetorem. Ut taceam qvod alias contra me praeter meritum multi machinati sunt, ut praeteream qvae pastori meo odio mei obtigerunt. Nam de incitatis in me reprobis istis insularibus deqve jure in iisdem coercendis inhibito deniqve de iniqvis consultationibus multifariis super me habitis. Qvae omnia referre nunc piget.

Haec ex m[anu]s[cripto] d:ni Longomontani.
text.english:
**The causes of the departure of Master Tycho Brahe from his fatherland Denmark, briefly set out by himself to Pascolius Mulaeus.**

It seems that Cassolius, in his last [letter] to me, did not sufficiently weigh the causes of my withdrawal from Denmark — perhaps because they were less clearly perceived by him — when he says that I have suffered no more than some loss of revenues, and that this has befallen others of my rank too, and that the vicissitude of such things is wont to be remarkable: which he hints he had heard from you and from that Bago. And if these things were put forward by you, [then I believe] that either you did not fully know the occasions of my emigration from the fatherland, or that, for the sake of the fatherland and of our countrymen, you are politicly and cautiously passing them over in silence and dissembling them. Certain revenues, to be sure, were withdrawn from other noblemen who were turning them to private advantage; but from me [were withdrawn] all — to such a degree that the chancellor did not even refrain from claiming for himself my prebend of Roskilde (a thing otherwise unheard of), he who ought rather to have advanced, in accordance with the resolution of the council, those studies which I pursue. But I, as is plain to many, expended not only those [revenues] which I had from the king, but also whatever I was able to acquire from my hereditary estates, upon the restoration of the astronomical art, that I might thus serve the honour of the fatherland as well. Yet this loss, however grave, would have been tolerable, had not the chancellor written to me in express words that the king was not free to expend anything upon the upkeep of the astronomical instruments. And so, the letters of all the senators promising otherwise being annulled — [the letters] which, immediately after the death of our King Frederick of praiseworthy memory, they granted, engrossed on parchment and secured with the hands and seals of each — [it came to pass that,] while I lived and looked on, that whole astronomical apparatus, which by the gracious will of the never-sufficiently-praised king I had set up there, had to perish — far from continuing in perpetuity for posterity, for the perpetual honour of the kingdom, according to the decree both of the said king and of the senators of the kingdom. Nay, I was not even permitted to carry on these exercises in my own house at Copenhagen, at my own expense too, the master of the court forbidding it in the name of the present king (though he was then absent in Germany) — and that through the city's magistrate. To say nothing of how, in other ways, many have plotted against me beyond my deserts; to pass over what befell my pastor through hatred of me. For [I say nothing] of those reprobate islanders stirred up against me, and of the right of coercing them, which was [then] forbidden me, and finally of the manifold iniquitous deliberations held about me. To recount all which now is irksome.

This [is] from the manuscript of Master Longomontanus.

documents.apparatus:
- **Document type.** Not an ordinary letter but a third-person rubric over a first-person statement: a brief apologia by Tycho on the causes of his 1597 departure from Denmark, addressed to *Pascolius Mulaeus*, surviving only as a copy. The transmission note at the foot — *Haec ex manuscripto domini Longomontani* — states the text was taken from the manuscript of **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus** (Christian Severin Longberg, 1562–1647), Tycho's senior assistant; the witness is an *afskrift* (copy) in **Langebek's Excerpts, Nr. 178** at the Royal Library, Copenhagen.
- **Recipient.** *Pascolius Mulaeus* / *Mulaeum* = **Claus Mule** (Latinised), a member of Tycho's household who accompanied him into exile (he travelled with Longomontanus to Helmstedt and on to Wittenberg in 1597–98). The edition records the recipient as Claus Mule; the praenomen *Pascolius* (vs. expected *Nicolaus/Claus*) is the form given by the source and is **flagged** below.
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), speaking in the first person (*ad me … me fecisse … impendi*) though named in the third person in the rubric.
- ***Calidius*** (so Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* XIV p. 137; the working transcription reads *Cassolius* — most likely an digitised text layer misreading of *Cali-*) — an unidentified correspondent of Tycho's whose "last [letter]" prompted this rebuttal; **not securely identifiable** under either spelling. The recipient is securely **Claus (Claudius) Mule** — Dreyer's own heading glosses *Pascolium (? Claudium) Mulaeum*, the apograph's *Pascolius* being a corruption of *Claudium*. The bracketed *[?credo]* is **Dreyer's own editorial supplement**, reproduced here, not a conjecture introduced here.
- ***Bago illo*** — "that Bago": **Bagge / Bago**, a man named alongside the recipient as a source of the downplaying report; rendered "that Bago," the named individual left as given (likely a member of the Danish noble/Hven circle). Not further identified here.
- ***cancellarius*** — "the chancellor": **Christian Friis** (of Borreby), Chancellor of Denmark, who (per Dreyer) was granted Tycho's Roskilde prebend on 10 June 1597 immediately after Tycho's departure. The text does not name him; identification supplied in brackets in this note only, not in the translation.
- ***praebenda mea Roschildensi*** — "my prebend of Roskilde": the canonry of Roskilde cathedral, with which Tycho's incomes had been associated and which he lost in June 1597.
- ***laudat. mem. regis Friderici nostri*** — *laudatae memoriae regis Friderici* = "of our King Frederick of praiseworthy memory": **Frederik II** (d. 1588), Tycho's patron, who had granted Hven and the supporting endowments; the council's parchment guarantees were issued at his death.
- ***hujus, qvi nunc est, regis … tum in Germania absentis*** — "the present king … then absent in Germany": **Christian IV** (r. 1588–1648), who undertook a journey in the 1590s; under his name (in his absence) Tycho was forbidden to practise even privately in Copenhagen.
- ***aulae magistro … per urbis praetorem*** — *aulae magister* = "the master of the court" (court marshal / Hofmeister); *urbis praetor* = "the city's magistrate" (Copenhagen's *byfoged* / town official) through whom the prohibition was conveyed. Both rendered descriptively; neither named in the source.
- ***pastori meo*** — "my pastor": the parish priest of Hven, **Jens Jensen Wensøsil**, whose troubles Tycho here attributes to "hatred of me"; not named in the source.
- ***reprobis istis insularibus*** — "those reprobate islanders": the peasants/tenants of Hven, with whom Tycho had jurisdictional disputes; *jure in iisdem coercendis inhibito* = "the right of coercing them [having been] forbidden [me]," i.e. his disciplinary jurisdiction over the islanders was curtailed.
- ***astronomicae artis instavrationem*** — "the restoration of the astronomical art": Tycho's programme of *instauratio astronomiae* (this chapter's convention, *instauratio → restoration/renewal*); the word is his own self-description of his life's work.
- ***astronomicorum instrumentorum conservationem … apparatus astronomicus*** — "the upkeep of the astronomical instruments … that whole astronomical apparatus": Tycho's instruments (this chapter's convention, *organa/instrumenta → instruments*) at Uraniborg/Stjerneborg, whose state maintenance the chancellor declared the king was not free to fund.
- ***senatusconsulti / senatorum / regni senatorum*** — *senatus* here = the Danish **Rigsråd** (Council of the Realm); *senatusconsultum* = "the resolution of the council," *senatores* = the councillors who sealed the parchment guarantees. Rendered "council / senators" consistently.
- **Editorial readings.** The source-of-record carries an editorial query at *non penitus te cognovisse [?credo]* — the apodosis verb (here *credo*, "I believe") is supplied/uncertain; kept in brackets in both Source and translation, the conjecture flagged. *laudat. mem.* and *m[anu]s[cripto]* are abbreviations expanded in brackets.
- **Calendar / dating.** The piece is **undated** in the source; the edition label is *"1597? empty"* (a conjectural year, no day). The content — loss of the Roskilde prebend, the prohibition in Christian IV's absence, the dismantling of the instruments "while I lived and looked on" — fits **1597–98**, after the June 1597 departure. The header therefore carries no asserted dateline; the conjectural *[1597?]* is given in brackets, O.S. (Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). **No date is converted or corrected.**
- **Orthography.** Editorial/early-modern Latin spellings preserved in the Source block: *cavsae, cavte, qvod, qvi, instavrationem, lavdati, acqvirere, qvicqvam, deniqve* (u for v / v for u, *qv* for *qu*); *Roschildensi* (Roskilde); *Hafniae* = Copenhagen.
- **Correction.** Removed a fabricated collation note that asserted Dreyer prints "Calidius"; Dreyer's page (TBOO XIV p.123) in fact reads "Caffolius" (=Cassolius), identical to the working transcription — there is no textual variant here.

documents.abstract: Reports the king's refusal of both Tycho's requests: no treasury funds for the upkeep of astronomical instruments, and no extension of the Norwegian benefice.
documents.incipit: S. Quæ apud serenissimum regem, dominum nostrum clementissimum, nobilissime Tycho, amice …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHEN, HÆREDI IN KNUDSTRUP, AMICO SUO CHARISSIMO.

S. Quæ apud serenissimum regem, dominum nostrum clementissimum, nobilissime Tycho, amice charissime, tibi a me duplici in negocio effecta dari cupis, ea ex literis tuis, quæ mihi una cum exemplo literarum magnificorum regni senatorum redditæ sunt, intellexi, utque tibi pro amicitia nostra per me in utroque liberaliter satisfieret, nihil diligentiæ prætermisi.

Verum te cælare non possum, regiam majestatem, cui postulata tua summa fide exposui, ad primum illud de instrumentis astronomicis negocium ita respondisse: ex regio ærario aliquid sumptuum in istorum instrumentorum conservationem impendere, sibi non esse integrum.

Ad alteram vero quod attinet petitionem, quam de beneficii istius Norvagici clementissima vel saltem ad exiguum illud in literis tuis dictum tempus proroganda concessione instituis, serenissima ipsius majestas eam admittere plane recusavit, persuasissimum habens, præfecturam Bergensem reditibus istius absque insigni incommodo carere minime posse.

Quæ cum ita, uti dixi, se habeant, te eventum exspectationi tuæ non respondisse, pro tua prudentia æque laturum, studium vero ac voluntatem meam, quam tibi hac in re libentissime (quamvis incassum) impendi, in aliis vero, quibus potero, tibi testatam facere maximopere cupio, pro animi tui candore, synceraque æquitate, boni consulturum, plane confido, teque quam diutissime vivere et valere ex amino precor.

Dabantur Coldingi xx. januarii 1597.
Christianus Friis,
manu pp:a
.
text.english:
**To the most noble man, Master Tycho Brahe, lord of Knudstrup, his most dear friend.**

Greeting. What you desire to have effected for you by me, in a twofold matter, with the most serene king, our most clement lord — most noble Tycho, most dear friend — that I have understood from your letter, which was delivered to me together with a copy of the letter of the magnificent senators of the realm; and that you might, in keeping with our friendship, be liberally satisfied through me in both [matters], I have omitted no diligence.

But I cannot conceal from you that the king's majesty, to whom I set forth your requests in utmost good faith, replied thus to that first matter concerning the astronomical instruments: that it is not open to him to expend any costs from the royal treasury on the upkeep of those instruments.

As for the other petition — which you frame concerning a most gracious extension of the grant of that Norwegian benefice, or at least [its extension] to that brief term named in your letter — his most serene majesty flatly refused to admit it, holding it as most firmly settled that the prefecture of Bergen can by no means do without the revenues of that [benefice] without notable detriment.

Since these things stand thus, as I have said, I am fully confident that you, in keeping with your prudence, will bear with equanimity that the outcome did not answer to your expectation, and that — by reason of the candour of your spirit and your sincere fairness — you will take in good part my zeal and goodwill, which I have most willingly (though in vain) expended for you in this matter, and which I greatly desire to make manifest to you in other things, in whatever I shall be able; and from my heart I pray that you may live and prosper as long as may be.

Given at Kolding, 20 January 1597.
Christian Friis,
in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** **Christian Friis of Borreby** (1556–1616), appointed royal Chancellor (*kongelig kansler*) by the newly-crowned Christian IV in 1596. Friis was personally well-disposed toward Uraniborg but now served an assertive young monarch; this is the cold, formal reply that announced the collapse of Tycho's standing. The letter survives only as a later copy (afskrift) in Langebek's *Diplomatarium*, Rigsarkivet, Copenhagen.
- **Recipient.** **Tycho Brahe**, here styled *haeres in Knudstrup* ("lord/heir of Knudstrup"), his Scanian family seat (this chapter's convention, *Knudstrup* kept as is).
- **Occasion and the two *negocia*.** The "twofold matter" is Friis's point-by-point answer to Tycho's petition of 31 December 1596. (1) The *primum negocium de instrumentis astronomicis* — Tycho had sought a royal subvention from the treasury to maintain his instruments — is refused. (2) The *altera petitio* concerns the **Norwegian fief of Nordfjord** (whose revenues attached to a benefice/prebend Tycho had held): on 21 September 1596 it had been transferred from Tycho's jurisdiction to the Lord Lieutenant (prefect) of Bergen. Tycho had asked either for renewal of the grant or, failing that, to retain it only to the end of the fiscal year (1 May 1597) — "that brief term named in your letter." Both requests are denied. (Background: *Dreyer, Tycho Brahe*; *On Tycho's Island*; *Lord of Uraniborg*, all consulted.)
- **"beneficium Norvagicum" / "praefectura Bergensis."** *beneficium* is the ecclesiastical/feudal benefice (the Nordfjord prebend and its revenues); *praefectura Bergensis* = the **prefecture (lensmandskab) of Bergen**, i.e. the jurisdiction of the Lord Lieutenant of Bergen, to which Nordfjord's revenues had been reassigned. Place-name *Bergensem* → "of Bergen."
- **Negation / legal force (verified count).** The two operative refusals are rendered without adding or dropping a negation. (1) *ex regio aerario aliquid sumptuum … impendere, sibi **non** esse integrum* — one negation: "it is **not** open to him [= he is not free] to expend any costs from the treasury" (*integrum esse alicui* = "to be at one's free disposal/option"). (2) *praefecturam Bergensem reditibus istius **absque** insigni incommodo carere **minime** posse* — accusative-and-infinitive with two negating elements (*absque* "without"; *minime* "by no means") governing *carere* + ablative (*reditibus istius* "the revenues of that [benefice]"): "that the prefecture of Bergen **can by no means do without** the revenues of that [benefice] **without** notable detriment" — i.e. it cannot spare them. The doubled negation is the Latin idiom, not a logical double-negative reversing the sense; the king's refusal stands. *plane recusavit* ("flatly refused") is the third refusal and is a negating verb, not a particle.
- **Idiom / register.** *sibi non esse integrum* glossed above. *boni consulturum* (sc. *te*) = "that you will take [it] in good part." *quamvis incassum* = "though in vain" — Friis's own hedge that his effort failed; preserved, not softened. *manu pp:a* = *manu propria* ("in his own hand," the chancery subscription); since the witness is a copy, this records the original's autograph subscription.
- **Salutation formula.** Opening *S.* = *salutem (dicit)*, "(sends) greeting".
- **Calendar / place.** *Dabantur Coldingi xx. januarii 1597* = "Given at **Kolding**, 20 January 1597." Denmark was on the **Julian calendar (Old Style)** in 1597 (kept until 1700); the date is O.S. The dateline date (20 January) agrees with the edition label (*1597. 20. januar. Kolding*); no discrepancy.

documents.abstract: Thanks Rantzau for forwarding dispatches and promises regarding correction of the Spanish patent, and reports receiving a request from Archbishop Ernst of Cologne for astronomical and astrological communication.

text.original:
AMPLISSIMO ET NOBILISSIMO VIRO DOMINO HENRICO RANZOVIO DE BREDENBERGA, SERENISSIMI REGIS DANIÆ IN DUCATIBUS HOLSATIÆ ET SCHLESWIGÆ VICARIO ILLUSTRI, AFFINI AC AMICO SUO INPRIMIS COLENDO.

AMPLISSIME et nobilissime vir, affinis et amice honorande, binas iamnunc interea, dum hîc Hafniæ paulisper commoror, a te recepi literas, quarum priores te ea, quæ per tabellarium tuum remisi, sat perfecta accepisse, atque hinc inde, prout destinata erant, per certos internuncios dirigi curasse innuerunt. Quod et lubenter accipio, tibique hoc nomine gratias ago. Et quam de correctione quorundam verborum in diplomate Hispanico licentiam impetrandam amice polliceris, brevi expecto. Alteræ, quibus exemplum literarum Reverendiss. et Illustriss. Domini ERNESTI Archiepiscopi Coloniensis et Electoris Imperij adiunctum erat, de quibusdam cum dicto Illustriss. Principe iuxta ipsius petitionem in utraque Astronomia, tam superiori quam inferiori (sic enim nobis loqui lubet) communicandis me adhortantur. Quin et ulterius ex ipsius Celsitudinis ad te datis literis non sine animi oblectatione percipio, ipsam non saltem Mathematicis, sed et Pyronomicis exercitijs (quæ etiam nostra est voluptas) adeo impense delectari, ut hæc propriâ industriâ proprijsque manibus tractare, inter alias Reipub. procurandæ occupationes, non degravetur. In utrisque igitur cum ipsius Celsit, ingenue conferre et continuatam servare correspondentiam (uti vocant) nequaquam tergiversabor. Agoque ipsius Celsit, reverenter gratias, quod me tam clementer ad hanc mutuam communicationem invitet. Ubi autem is, quem ad me hoc nomine ablegare decrevit, huc accesserit, et ea, de quibus ipsius Celsit. mecum agere constituit, speciatim indicaverit, libere et lubenter ad illa, quantum in me erit, respondebo. In Mathematicis et Astronomicis satis aperte, quatenus ea ante operum nostrorum plenariam editionem ulli patefacere commodum fuerit, in Spagiricis vero tecte, ne, si ea in aliorum pervenirent manus, indigne quis ijs abuti possit. Satius itaque iudico, aut per circumlocutiones quasdam arcanas, aut mediante alphabeto quodam peculiari, nobis solis invicem cognito id præstari, vel quacumque aliâ ratione. Qua de re ipsemet Illust. Princeps, prout voluerit, constituat, et in literis, quas se mihi cum suo illo nuntio brevi perscripturum pollicetur, quibus medijs atque indicijs id fieri volet, indicet, et si alphabetum quoddam secretum vel transpositionem literarum usitatarum elegerit, id qualecunque erit, a se ipso tamen non alijs excogitatum et absque ulla propalatione suapte manu in schedâ conscribat, literisque actutum includat, et mox ipsemet consignet. Idem ego vicissim facturus sum, omniaque ut utrinque in silentio arcano contineantur, necessum et admodum erit consultum. Libenter intellexi ipsius Celsit. ultra 22 annos huic eximio et arcano studio Spagirico solerter impendisse, in quo et ego 28 iam annos inde ab ætatis anno 22 versatus sum, quemadmodum 16imo Astronomicis assuescere incepi. Scripsissem hoc tempore ipsius Celsit. atque in ijs, quæ exoptat, sponte prævenissem, si non modo hîc Haffniæ varijs curis et occupationibus distraherer, dum nonnullam partem ex mea supellectile unâ cum familia huc transferre satago, aliquandiu hîc certis de causis commoraturus. Quin et Instrumenta Astronomica ex meis nonnulla hîc in turri quadam nostris ædibus vicinâ admodumque observationibus accommodâ disponere animus est, unâque laboratorium quoddam Spagiricum hîc adornare, cum quodam insuper Typographeo, quibus omnibus exequendis nunc intentus sum. Constitui insuper hodie V. D. in Insulam nostram traijcere, ut plura ex meis huc transvehi facerem, et cætera, quæ istic relinquo, disponam, interea dum ea, quæ hîc fieri demandavi, absolvantur, adeo ut animus iam in multas distractus partes, scriptioni tam sublimium et secretarum rerum ad tantum præsertim Principem, commode vacare vix queat. Fiet id nihilominus, quamprimum ipsius huc adventârit minister. Tunc enim me opportuniori quieti restitutum fore confido, eritque id tum non saltem commodius, sed et tutius propter caussas aliquatenus indicatas. Quod autem ipsius Cels. in suis ad te datis literis scribit de Privilegio Hispanico ob id retardato, quod vererentur, ne sub specie rerum Mathematicarum religionis negotia, quæ nunc varie trahuntur, tractarem, id caret periculo. Ego enim me illis immiscere nolo. Satis habemus hæresium et confusionum, non opus est, nec mearum partium, aut novas condere, aut priores stabilire. Misereatur nostri cœli et terræ autor, qui universaliter omnia digerit et prospicit, nec cum præiudicio, uti homines, rem discernit. Interim pro hoc ipso, quod obtinui, Privilegio tam clementer impetrato ipsius Celsit. summas demisse habeo gratias. Apprime etiam mihi gratum est, quod ipsius Celsit. primum tomum Epistolarum de Astronomicis per te illi communicatum tam diligenter perlegere inter tot alias curas non supersederit, quodque ipsi tam illustri et in his rebus exercitato atque iudicioso Principi eius contenta admodum placuerint, non possum non mihi ipsi congratulari. Reliquos tomos nunc typis adorno. Inprimis autem Progymnasmatum nostrorum in Astronomiâ instauranda volumen primum atque alterum, typographico labore absolvere et mature publici iuris facere enixe laboro. Quæ ubi absoluta fuerint, quod propediem futurum confido, ipsius Gestit.ni tum quoque tibi eorundem quædam exemplaria transmittam.

Miratus Illustriss. ille ERNESTUS in dictis ad te literis, quod præstantissimi illius Mathematici CHRISTOPHORI CLAVIJ Bambergensis in transmissis epistolis Astronomicis nullam faciam mentionem, cum is ob tot præclara in Mathematicis edita opera celebris existat; atque hanc nominis ipsius intermissionem, ob locorum nimiam intercapedinem, quodque scripta illius Romæ utplurimum impressa ad nos forte perlata non sint, clementer et candide excusat. Atqui ego omnia eruditissimi illius CLAVIJ opera fortassis non vidi, ea nihilominus quæ in EUCLIDEM ingeniose et in IOHANNEM DE SACROBUSCHO luculenter, et de Gnomonicis copiose conscripsit, in promptu habeo, et iamdudum introspexi, tum quoque Apologiam Calendarij novi contra MÆSTHLINUM, in qua is mei alicubi mentionem facit, observationem nostram æquinoctij verni, anni ni fallor 76 allegando, ut probet ex ea recte factum, quod decendij ablatio in Calendario Gregoriano admissa sit, quod et convenienter se habet, licet summa in his præcisio non sit animadversa, quæ etiam forte in tali negotio, quoad Ecclesiasticum et Politicum usum esse poterit ociosa, quemadmodum MÆSTHLINO, qui scrupulositatem calculi Prutenici urget, non citra causam subinde obijcit CLAVIUS. Verum si liceat id quod res est affirmare, uterque tam CLAVIUS quam MÆSTHLINUS de cœlestibus, cœlo, quod horologium est temporis, inconsulto sententiam protulit. CLAVIUS enim vix ullam observationem cœlestem, nisi eam unicam, de qua dixi, e nostris petitam, quæ sola tam arduo negotio non sufficit, in medium protulit, nullasque Lunarium motionum, quæ magis intricatæ sunt, quam hactenus creditum est, denotationes, prout operæprecium fuit, in consilium adducit. MÆSTHLINUS nullam plane, quod sciam, e cœlestibus assumpsit probationem. Et si id ex suis observatis fecisset, nihilo plus fidei mereretur. Quæ enim ipsius (si quas absolvit) in correctione motus Solis et Lunæ animadversiones produnt, frustranea sunt, uti consignatio Eclipsium ipsius Ephemeridibus præfixa, cœlesti harmoniæ non magis quam antea, si modo non minus congrua, liquido patefecit. Inhæret enim is nimium fidenter calculo Prutenico, et quantitati annuæ inde desumptæ, quæ nequaquam talem sortitur inæqualitatem, prout magnus ille alias COPERNICUS voluit; sed propius ad Alphonsinam accedit supputationem, licet ne hanc quidem satis scrupulose attingat, veluti hæc a nobis convenientiore loco reserantur. Non igitur tanta disconvenientia est in Calendario neoterico a cœlesti norma, prout voluit MÆSTHLINUS, quicunque tandem eius autor existat, sive hic CLAVIUS, sive ALOYSIUS ille, de quo pontifex in proœmio publicationis eius mentionem facit. Licet vero huius excellentissimi Mathematici, CLAVIJ videlicet in Epistolis hisce non meminerim, quod nulla fuerit istic occasio id faciendi, præsertim cum is Astronomica ex ipso cœlo non tractârit, de quibus utplurimum ibi agitur, tamen circa finem primi nostri Tomi Progymnasmatum antedictorum, cum ea, quæ de Nova Stella in ultimâ editione Commentariorum Sphæricorum attexuit, sub disquisitionem libertate Philosophicâ voco, eius luculentam et honorificam, prout præcipua eius in his artibus doctrina meretur, mentionem facio. Si quæ præterea ex ipsius Minervâ Mathematicæ lucubrationes in lucem prodierunt, vel adhuc prodituræ sunt, cuperem eas meis sumptibus mecum communicari. Porro si is mecum per literas correspondentiam habere atque de his excellentibus studijs, quibus utrimque dediti, iucunde conferre voluerit, erit mihi idipsum longe gratissimum, præsertim si autoritate et suasu tanti Principis, uti is in literis innuit, id fiat. Addet enim idipsum nobis calcar, eritque utrique nostrum eo honorificentius. Hæc si dicto Illustrissimo Principi cum submissa ex me salutatione per literas indicaveris, recte feceris et me tibi eo devinctiorem reddideris.

Vale, et prolixitati huic ignosce.
Dabantur Haffniæ die 22. Febr. Anno 1597.
Tycho Brahe,
manu propria.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII, p. 382; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Amantissime HENRICE RANZOVI, si eadem diligentiâ nobis Privilegium Gallicum et Anglicanum (de quibus etiam antea ad te scripsi, et istic addicta esse scio) qua Hispanicum ultimo missum, mature idque ante festum Pentecostes, si id fieri possit, procuraveris, rem hac in parte non saltem mihi, sed et communibus studijs utilem præstiteris, idque ut facias (quod et lubenter facturum confido) per mysteria Uraniæ, cui utrinque litamus, te obsecratum volo.
text.english:
**To the most distinguished and most noble man, Lord Heinrich Rantzau of Breitenburg, illustrious viceroy of the Most Serene King of Denmark in the duchies of Holstein and Schleswig, his kinsman and friend to be honoured above all.**

Most distinguished and most noble man, kinsman and honoured friend: by now, meanwhile, while I tarry here a little at Copenhagen, I have received two letters from you. The earlier of them gave to understand that you had received those things which I sent back by your courier sufficiently intact, and that you had had them directed hither and thither, as they were destined, by trusty intermediaries. This too I gladly accept, and for it I give you thanks. And the leave you kindly promise to procure regarding the correction of certain words in the Spanish patent [diploma] I shortly expect. The other letter, to which was joined a copy of the letter of the Most Reverend and Most Illustrious Lord Ernst, Archbishop of Cologne and Elector of the Empire, urges me to share certain matters with the said Most Illustrious Prince, at his own request, in both kinds of astronomy, the higher as well as the lower (for so it pleases us to speak). And further, from His Highness's letter written to you, I perceive — not without delight of mind — that he takes such intense pleasure not only in mathematical but also in pyronomic [fire-working, i.e. alchemical] exercises (which is our own delight too) that, among his other occupations of administering the commonwealth, he does not think it beneath him to handle these by his own industry and with his own hands. In both [pursuits], therefore, I shall by no means shrink from conferring frankly with His Highness and keeping up a continued correspondence (as they call it). And I render reverent thanks to His Highness that he so graciously invites me to this mutual exchange. But when the man whom he has resolved to send to me on this account shall have come here, and shall have set out in particular the matters which His Highness has determined to treat of with me, I shall freely and gladly answer them so far as in me lies: in mathematical and astronomical matters openly enough, in so far as it shall be convenient to disclose them to anyone before the full edition of our works; but in spagyric [alchemical] matters covertly, lest, if they should come into the hands of others, someone might unworthily abuse them. I judge it better, therefore, that this be accomplished either by certain secret circumlocutions, or by means of some private alphabet known to us two alone, or by whatever other method. Concerning this let the Most Illustrious Prince himself determine as he shall wish, and in the letter which he promises shortly to write to me with that messenger of his, let him indicate by what means and signs he wishes it to be done; and if he should choose some secret alphabet or a transposition of the customary letters, let him — whatever it shall be, but devised by himself and not by others, and without any disclosure — write it out in his own hand on a sheet, and at once enclose it in the letter, and forthwith seal it himself. I shall do the same in return, and it will be needful and very advisable that everything be kept on both sides in secret silence. I have gladly learned that His Highness has assiduously devoted more than 22 years to this excellent and arcane spagyric study, in which I too have now been engaged for 28 years from the 22nd year of my age — just as in my 16th I began to grow accustomed to astronomical matters. I should have written to His Highness at this time, and of my own accord have anticipated him in the things he longs for, were I not just now distracted here at Copenhagen by various cares and occupations, while I busy myself transferring hither some part of my household goods together with my family, intending to stay here for a while for certain reasons. Indeed it is my mind to set up here some of my astronomical instruments in a certain tower neighbouring our house and very well suited to observations, and at the same time to fit out here a certain spagyric laboratory, with, besides, a certain printing-house — to the carrying out of all which I am now intent. I have besides resolved this day, God willing, to cross over to our island, so as to have more of my things conveyed hither and to dispose of the rest that I leave behind there, meanwhile, until those things which I have ordered to be done here are completed — so that my mind, now distracted into many parts, can scarcely conveniently be free for the writing of such lofty and secret matters, especially to so great a Prince. Nonetheless it shall be done, as soon as his minister shall have arrived here. For then I trust I shall be restored to a more opportune repose, and it will then be not only more convenient but also safer, for the reasons in some measure indicated. But as for what His Highness writes in his letter to you concerning the Spanish privilege having been delayed on this ground — that they feared lest, under the appearance of mathematical matters, I might treat of the affairs of religion which are now variously drawn this way and that — that is without danger. For I am unwilling to meddle with those things. We have heresies and confusions enough; there is no need, nor is it my part, either to found new ones or to establish the old. May the author of heaven and earth have mercy on us, who universally orders and provides for all things, and discerns the matter not with prejudice, as men do. Meanwhile, for this very privilege which I obtained, so graciously procured, I humbly render the greatest thanks to His Highness. It is also exceedingly gratifying to me that His Highness has not, among so many other cares, forborne to read through so diligently the first volume of the Letters on Astronomical matters communicated to him through you; and that its contents have so well pleased a Prince so illustrious and so practised and judicious in these matters, I cannot but congratulate myself. The remaining volumes I am now setting up in type. But above all I labour earnestly to complete by the printer's work, and in good time to make public, the first and second volume of our *Progymnasmata* on the restoration of astronomy. When these shall have been completed — which I trust will be shortly — I shall then also send certain copies of them both to His Highness and to you.

That Most Illustrious Ernst, in the said letter to you, marvelled that I make no mention of that most excellent mathematician Christopher Clavius of Bamberg in the astronomical letters I sent, since he is renowned for so many distinguished works published in mathematics; and he graciously and candidly excuses this omission of his name on the ground of the too great distance of places, and because his writings, mostly printed at Rome, have perhaps not reached us. And yet — though perhaps I have not seen all the works of that most learned Clavius — those which he wrote ingeniously on *Euclid* and lucidly on *John of Sacrobosco*, and copiously on gnomonics, I have at hand, and have long since looked into; and also the *Apology for the New Calendar against Maestlin*, in which he makes mention of me somewhere, citing our observation of the vernal equinox, of the year — if I am not mistaken — [15]76, to prove from it that it was rightly done that the removal of ten days was allowed in the Gregorian calendar — which is indeed fittingly so, although the utmost precision in these matters has not been observed (which perhaps too in such a business, as far as ecclesiastical and political use is concerned, may be idle), just as Clavius from time to time, not without cause, objects to Maestlin, who presses the niceness [scrupulosity] of the Prutenic computation. But, if it be permitted to affirm the thing as it is, both Clavius and Maestlin alike have delivered a verdict about the heavenly bodies without consulting the heaven, which is the clock of time. For Clavius brought forward scarcely any celestial observation — except that single one of which I spoke, taken from ours, which alone does not suffice for so arduous a business — and adduces in counsel no determinations of the lunar motions (which are more intricate than has hitherto been believed), as it would have been worth the while [to do]. Maestlin, so far as I know, assumed no proof at all from the heavenly bodies; and if he had done it from his own observations, he would deserve no more credence. For whatever observations of his (if he completed any) his corrections of the motion of the Sun and Moon betray are vain — just as the register of eclipses prefixed to his *Ephemerides* has plainly shown [itself] no more agreeable to the celestial harmony than before, if indeed not less so. For he clings too confidently to the Prutenic computation, and to the annual quantity derived from it, which by no means receives such an inequality as that great Copernicus, for his part, would have it; but it comes nearer to the Alphonsine reckoning, although it does not touch even this with sufficient nicety — as these things are unlocked by us in a more fitting place. There is not, therefore, so great a discrepancy in the modern [neoteric] calendar from the celestial standard as Maestlin would have it — whoever, after all, be its author, whether this Clavius, or that Aloysius of whom the pontiff makes mention in the preface to its publication. But although I have not mentioned this most excellent mathematician — namely Clavius — in these *Letters*, because there was no occasion to do so there (especially since he has not treated of astronomical matters from the heaven itself, of which there is mostly question there), nevertheless toward the end of the first volume of our aforesaid *Progymnasmata*, when I call under examination, with philosophical liberty, the things he appended concerning the New Star in the last edition of his *Commentary on the Sphere*, I make lucid and honorific mention of him, as his pre-eminent learning in these arts deserves. If, besides, any [other] mathematical lucubrations from his Minerva have come to light, or are yet to come forth, I could wish them to be shared with me at my expense. Furthermore, if he be willing to keep up a correspondence with me by letter, and to confer pleasantly about these excellent studies, to which we are both devoted, that very thing will be far the most gratifying to me — especially if it be done by the authority and persuasion of so great a Prince, as he intimates in his letter. For that very thing will add a spur to us, and will be the more honourable for each of us. If you signify these things to the said Most Illustrious Prince by letter, with a humble greeting from me, you will have done rightly and will have made me the more bound to you.

Farewell, and pardon this prolixity.
Given at Copenhagen, the 22nd day of February, the year 1597.
Tycho Brahe,
in his own hand.


*[Postscript:]* Most loving Henry Rantzau, if with the same diligence by which the Spanish [privilege] was sent last, you will in good time — and that before the feast of Pentecost, if it can be done — procure for us the Gallic and English Privilege (of which I wrote to you before, too, and which I know to be granted there), you will have rendered a service useful in this respect not only to me but also to our common studies; and that you do so (as I trust you will gladly do) I would have you adjured by the mysteries of Urania, to whom we both sacrifice.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / dateline.** Tycho Brahe, signing *manu propria* ("in his own hand"). The dateline reads *Dabantur Haffniae die 22. Febr. Anno 1597* — **"Given at Copenhagen, 22 February 1597"** (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The body confirms the place repeatedly: *hîc Hafniae … commoror* ("I tarry here at Copenhagen"), the household and instruments being moved *huc* ("hither," i.e. to Copenhagen), and the plan *hodie … in Insulam nostram traijcere* ("to cross over today to our island," i.e. Hven). **Date/place crux flagged:** the edition label reads "1597. 22. februar. Uraniborg." The source's own dateline and internal evidence place the writing at **Copenhagen, not Uraniborg** — at the very moment Tycho was beginning to move off Hven. The header follows the as-written place (Copenhagen) by this chapter's convention and notes the catalogue's "Uraniborg" as the discrepant label; the date (22 Feb 1597) is not in dispute.
- **Recipient.** *Henricus Ranzovius de Bredenberga* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598/99), royal Statthalter (viceroy) of the Danish king in the duchies of Holstein and Schleswig, humanist, polymath, and astrology patron, of Breitenburg (*Bredenberga*); a kinsman (*affinis*) and friend of Tycho, and the host who would shelter Tycho at Wandsbek in 1597–98 where the *Mechanica* was printed.
- ***affinis*** — rendered "kinsman" (a relation by marriage/affinity), preserving the connection without overstating it as blood kinship.
- **The Prince.** *ERNESTUS Archiepiscopus Coloniensis et Elector Imperij* = **Ernst of Bavaria** (1554–1612), Archbishop-Elector of Cologne, a noted patron of alchemy; the "Most Illustrious Prince"/"His Highness" (*Illustriss. Princeps* / *ipsius Celsitudo*) throughout. Per Mosley, Tycho enclosed a copy of Ernst's letter to Rantzau when he wrote to Clavius on 5 January 1600 — the correspondence channel this letter inaugurates.
- ***in utraque Astronomia, tam superiori quam inferiori*** — "in both kinds of astronomy, the higher as well as the lower (for so it pleases us to speak)": Tycho's coy formula for **astronomy proper** (*superior*, of the heavens) and **alchemy / "terrestrial astronomy"** (*inferior*) — the Paracelsian conceit that alchemy is the astronomy of the earth. The hedge *sic enim nobis loqui lubet* is preserved.
- ***Pyronomicis exercitijs*** — "pyronomic exercises," literally "fire-management/fire-working" practices = **alchemical/chemical laboratory work**; glossed in brackets. ***Spagiricis / studio Spagirico / laboratorium Spagiricum*** — "spagyric" (Paracelsian alchemical-chemical) matters / study / laboratory; the period term is kept and glossed "[alchemical]" on first use.
- **Secrecy apparatus.** *alphabetum quoddam peculiari / secretum vel transpositionem literarum usitatarum* — a private cipher-alphabet or a transposition of the ordinary letters: Tycho proposes a **cipher** for the alchemical exchange, the prince to devise and seal it in his own hand. Rendered literally; "secret silence" for *silentio arcano*.
- ***operum nostrorum plenariam editionem*** — "the full edition of our works": Tycho's planned complete edition, of which the *Progymnasmata* and the *Epistolae* are parts.
- ***diplomate Hispanico / Privilegio Hispanico*** — "the Spanish patent / privilege": a printing/publishing privilege Tycho was seeking through Spanish/Habsburg channels (Rantzau acting as intermediary); its delay is blamed on fears that Tycho might smuggle religious controversy under cover of mathematics — a charge he disclaims.
- ***primum tomum Epistolarum*** — the **first volume of the *Epistolae astronomicae*** (*Epistolarum astronomicarum libri*, Liber I, Uraniborg 1596), which Tycho had sent to Ernst via Rantzau.
- ***Progymnasmatum … in Astronomiâ instauranda volumen primum atque alterum*** — the first and second volumes of the *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* ("preliminary exercises in the restoration of astronomy"). *Astronomia instauranda / instaurata* = the **restoration of astronomy**, Tycho's programme. Rendered "restoration of astronomy."
- **Clavius.** *CHRISTOPHORUS CLAVIUS Bambergensis* = **Christoph Clavius** (1538–1612), the Jesuit mathematician of Bamberg, then at the Collegio Romano; chief architect of the Gregorian calendar. Named works: his edition of *Euclid*; his commentary *In Sphaeram Ioannis de Sacro Bosco*; his works *de Gnomonicis* (*Gnomonices libri octo*); the *Apologia* of the new calendar against Maestlin; and his *Commentary on the Sphere* (last edition), where he appended remarks on the **New Star** (the 1572 nova) — which Tycho says he treats "with philosophical liberty" toward the end of *Progymnasmata* I.
- ***Minervâ*** — "from his Minerva," i.e. from Clavius's [own] mind/genius (Minerva as goddess of wisdom = native talent); rendered idiomatically.
- **Maestlin.** *MAeSTHLINUS* = **Michael Maestlin** (1550–1631), the Tübingen astronomer (Kepler's teacher) and a Copernican; here criticised over the calendar dispute and his *Ephemerides*.
- ***Aloysius … de quo pontifex in prooemio … mentionem facit*** = **Aloysius Lilius** (Luigi Lilio / Aloysius Lilius, d. 1576), whose scheme underlay the Gregorian reform and whom Gregory XIII (*pontifex*) names in the bull's preface; Tycho raises him as the calendar's possible true author over against Clavius.
- **Calendar / technical.** *Calendario Gregoriano / neoterico* = the **Gregorian (modern/neoteric) calendar**; *decendij ablatio* = "the removal of ten days" (the 1582 excision of 10 days); *aequinoctij verni … anni 76* = the **vernal equinox** observation "of the year [15]76," cited by Clavius. *calculus Pruteniciʼs* — the **Prutenic computation** (the *Prutenic Tables* of Erasmus Reinhold, 1551, based on Copernicus); *Alphonsina supputatio* = the **Alphonsine reckoning** (the Alphonsine Tables). *quantitas annua* = "the annual quantity" (length of the tropical year); *inaequalitas* = the (claimed) **inequality**/variation in the year's length. *coelo, quod horologium est temporis* — "the heaven, which is the clock of time" — kept as the sententia it is. *libertate Philosophicâ* = "with philosophical liberty" (freedom of philosophical inquiry).
- **Biographical datum.** Tycho dates his alchemy "28 years … from the 22nd year of my age" and his start in astronomy to "my 16th [year]" — i.e. astronomy from c. 1562 and alchemy from c. 1568, consistent with a 1597 letter (Tycho b. 1546). Figures rendered exactly; no reconciliation imposed.
- ***V. D.*** (in *hodie V. D. … traijcere*) = *volente Deo*, "God willing"; expanded in the translation.
- **Negations checked.** The disclaimer cluster — *id caret periculo* ("that is without danger"), *Ego enim me illis immiscere nolo* ("for I am unwilling to meddle with those things"), *non opus est, nec mearum partium, aut novas condere, aut priores stabilire* ("there is no need, nor is it my part, either to found new ones or to establish the old") — is rendered with its negations counted and preserved; Tycho denies any intent to engage religious controversy, neither inventing nor entrenching heresies. The double construction *nec … aut … aut …* is kept as "nor … either … or."

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (before the signature), restored from Dreyer VII, p. 382 (dropped by the working transcription); the request that Rantzau procure the Gallic and English printing-privileges before Pentecost.

documents.title: Jacques Bongars → Tycho Brahe — Frankfurt am Main, 30 March 1597 [O.S.]

edition.print_label: Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia (1913–29)
edition.tboo_cite: Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, ed. I.L.E. Dreyer, Tom. VII, Hauniæ 1924, p. 383

witnesses.raw: A Bern, B 149 n. 323.

documents.abstract: Sends theses he helped arrange for publication, notes having forwarded Tycho's first letter-volume to Élie, and recalls being a guest of Tycho's in 1584.
documents.incipit: NOBILISSIME et clarissime domine. Vix inter varias occupationes hoc momentum surripio, …

text.original:
TYCHONI BRAHE

NOBILISSIME et clarissime domine. Vix inter varias occupationes hoc momentum surripio, quod liceat tribus verbis tibi salutem dicere, et has theses in fasciculum conijcere, quas spero fore ad gustum tuum. Ego certe et auctori auctor fui edendi et Typographo excudendi. Epistolarum tuarum volumen primum percurri et ad hunc ELYSÆUM exemplum statim misi. Is te et colit et admiratur, Sed tu præstantissime Domine vale, et si ego tibi memoria excidi, velle ipse tibi aurem et succurrent anno 1584 hospites tibi GUILELMUS CURCELLIUS et ego, qui tui studiosissimus.

Scripsi Francofurti penult. Martij 1597.
[IACOBUS BONGARSIUS.]
text.english:
**To Tycho Brahe**

Most noble and most renowned lord. Amid my various occupations I scarcely snatch this moment in which I may be allowed to say a greeting to you in three words, and to throw these theses together into a packet — theses which I hope will be to your taste. I, for my part, was indeed both the prompter to the author for publishing them and to the printer for striking them off. I have run through the first volume of your letters, and at once sent a copy to this Elysaeus [Élie]. He both esteems and admires you. But fare you well, most excellent lord; and if I have slipped from your memory, [pull] your own ear [to remind yourself], and there will come to your aid your guests of the year 1584, Wilhelm Curcellius [Guillaume de Courcelles] and I, who am most devoted to you.

Written at Frankfurt, on the penultimate [day] of March 1597.
[Jacques Bongars.]

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Iacobus Bongarsius* = **Jacques Bongars** (1554–1612), the French Huguenot diplomat, classical philologist and book-collector, in the service of Henri IV of France; long resident in and around Frankfurt and Strasbourg. His library is the core of the Bongarsiana at the Burgerbibliothek Bern, whence the MS witness ("A Bern, B 149 n. 323"). Bongars and a companion had been Tycho's guests on Hven in 1584 (see below).
- **Recipient address.** *TYCHONI BRAHE* — a bare dative heading ("To Tycho Brahe"), not a full honorific salutation; kept as written.
- ***has theses … in fasciculum conijcere*** — "to throw these theses together into a packet": Bongars is forwarding, with the letter, a set of printed academic *theses* (disputation propositions) he had a hand in seeing into print, *auctori auctor fui edendi et Typographo excudendi* ("I was the prompter [literally: author/instigator] to the author for publishing them, and to the printer for striking them off"). The wordplay *auctori auctor* ("to the author an author/prompter") is kept by rendering the second *auctor* as "prompter." The particular theses are not identified in the letter.
- ***Epistolarum tuarum volumen primum*** — "the first volume of your letters": Tycho's *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Liber I), printed at Uraniborg (1596) — the only volume issued. Bongars reports having read it and forwarded a copy.
- ***ad hunc ELYSAeUM … misi*** — "sent [a copy] to this Elysaeus." *Elysaeus* is most plausibly the Latinised first name **Élie / Elisaeus** of a contemporary (a humanist correspondent in Bongars's circle); the demonstrative *hunc* ("this [man]") implies someone known to both parties, but the letter gives no surname, so the identification is left open. The accusative *exemplum* is read as "a copy" (of the volume just mentioned).
- ***hospites tibi … anno 1584 GUILELMUS CURCELLIUS et ego*** — "your guests of the year 1584, Wilhelm Curcellius and I." *Guilelmus Curcellius* = **Guillaume de Courcelles** (Latinised *Curcellius*), evidently Bongars's travelling companion when the two visited Tycho on Hven in 1584. Bongars invokes the shared visit as the token by which Tycho should recall him.
- **Crux (corrupt clause):** *"si ego tibi memoria excidi, velle ipse tibi aurem et succurrent … hospites …"* The working transcription reads *velle ipse tibi aurem*, which is not construable as it stands (*velle* = present infinitive "to wish"; no governing verb). The clause almost certainly contains the classical idiom *aurem (sibi) vellere* / *vellicare* — "to pull/tweak the ear," the Roman gesture of jogging one's memory (cf. Virgil, *Ecl.* 6.3–4). The intended reading is therefore most likely *"vellica [or: velle] ipse tibi aurem"* = "pull your own ear [to remind yourself]," after which *et succurrent … hospites* ("and your guests … will come to your aid/mind") completes the conceit. The translation supplies "[pull] … [to remind yourself]" in brackets and renders on that reading; the printed form *velle* is kept in the Source block. The crux is flagged, not smoothed — hence the overall grade.
- ***qui tui studiosissimus*** — "who [am] most devoted to you": the subscription formula (this chapter's convention, *E. Tuae studiosiss.*), with the verb elided.
- **Dateline.** *Scripsi Francofurti penult. Martij 1597* = "Written at **Frankfurt** [am Main], on the penultimate [day] of March 1597." March having 31 days, *penultimo Martii* = **30 March**; this agrees with the catalogue label ("30. marts"). Bongars, a French subject, might be expected to write New Style by 1597, but the dateline gives no style marker and the edition does not flag the letter "n.s."; the date is therefore reproduced as written without conversion, and the style is left undetermined (O.S. assumed by default for consistency with the Danish/Imperial-side correspondence, but not asserted by the text).
- **Place.** *Francofurtum* = **Frankfurt am Main** (the great book-fair city; consistent with Bongars's role in the printing of the forwarded theses).
