documents.title: Tycho Brahe → Heinrich Rantzau — Copenhagen, 31 March 1597 [O.S.]

edition.print_label: Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia (1913–29)
edition.tboo_cite: Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, ed. I.L.E. Dreyer, Tom. VII, Hauniæ 1924, p. 383

witnesses.raw: A Wien, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, cod. Vindob. lat. 9737f.

documents.abstract: Notes that several letters, some for Rantzau's eyes only, have gone unanswered, and urges a reply, assuring him the matter discussed is being actively pursued.
documents.incipit: NONNULLAS dedi literas ad te ante aliquot septimanas, Nobilissime ac amplissime Domine …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO ET AMPLISSIMO VIRO, VIRTUTE ET ERUDITIONE INPRIMIS CONSPICUO DOMINO HENRICO RANTZOVIO DE BREDENBERGA, PRÆSIDI SEGEBERGENSI ET PRODUCI HOLSATIÆ ET DITMARSIÆ, AMICO ET AFFINI SUO PLURIMUM COLENDO.
S.

NONNULLAS dedi literas ad te ante aliquot septimanas, Nobilissime ac amplissime Domine HENRICE RANZOVI, affinis et amice honorande, inter quas quædam erant tibi aperte tradendæ, quædam vero secreto, ut seorsim solus eas legeres. Confido eas te accepisse, verum responsum ad illas usque huc nondum accepi ullum, quod per hunc tabellarium avide expeto expectoque, si forte aliqua ratione id neglectum est. Vale, et rem de qua tibi scripsi serio agi persuasum habe.

Iterumque vale.
Dabantur Hafniæ 31. Martij Anno 97.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most worthy man, eminent above all for virtue and erudition, Master Heinrich Rantzau of Breitenburg, Governor of Segeberg and Lord-Lieutenant of Holstein and Dithmarschen, his kinsman and friend much to be honoured — greeting.**

I sent you several letters some weeks ago, most noble and most worthy Master Heinrich Rantzau, my honoured kinsman and friend, among which some were to be delivered to you openly, but some in secret, so that you alone might read them apart. I am confident that you received them, yet up to now I have received no reply at all to them — which I eagerly seek and await by this courier, in case by some chance it has been neglected. Farewell, and be assured that the matter about which I wrote to you is being pursued in earnest.

And again, farewell.
Given at Copenhagen, 31 March, the year [15]97.
TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** *Henricus Rantzovius de Bredenberga* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (Henrik Rantzau, 1526–1598), the great Holstein humanist, statesman, and bibliophile; royal governor (*Statthalter*) of the Danish king in the duchies. He was a long-standing patron, correspondent, and connection of Tycho's, and is here addressed as *affinis* — "kinsman / connection by marriage" (the Brahe and Rantzau families were allied; *affinis* denotes relationship by marriage rather than blood). *de Bredenberga* = of **Breitenburg**, his castle and seat on the Stör in Holstein.
- **Titulature.** *PRAeSIDI SEGEBERGENSI* = "Governor of **Segeberg**" (Rantzau's administrative seat at Segeberg in Holstein). *PRODUCI HOLSATIAe ET DITMARSIAe* — *produci* is the dative of *produx*, a rare/post-classical title here equivalent to provincial governor or lord-lieutenant; rendered "Lord-Lieutenant of **Holstein and Dithmarschen**." The form is unusual and is flagged rather than normalised to the more common *prorex* or *praeses*.
- **Address spelling.** The superscription has *RANTZOVIO*; the body has *RANZOVI* (vocative, without the medial *t*). Both spellings of the name are reproduced as printed; no emendation is adopted.
- ***aperte … secreto*** — "openly … in secret": the earlier batch of letters contained both an open portion and a confidential portion meant for Rantzau alone (*seorsim solus*). The "matter" (*rem*) pursued *serio* ("in earnest") is not named in this note — the substance lies in those prior letters, not here.
- ***tabellarium*** — "courier / letter-carrier"; Tycho asks for a reply to be returned by the same bearer of the present note.
- **Salutation / subscription.** *S.* = *salutem* ("greeting," this chapter's convention). *Vale … Iterumque vale* = "Farewell … And again, farewell". *manu propria* = "in his own hand," the autograph subscription formula.
- **Calendar / place.** *Dabantur Hafniae 31. Martij Anno 97* = "Given at **Copenhagen** [*Hafnia*], 31 March, the year [15]97" (O.S. — Denmark kept the Julian calendar). The dateline agrees with the catalogue label; *Anno 97* is the abbreviated year, expanded to [15]97. *Dabantur* ("were given," epistolary plural/imperfect) rendered "Given."
- **Context (1597).** The letter belongs to the months just before Tycho's departure from Denmark: he left Hven in 1597 and quit the kingdom that year, his royal support withdrawn after Frederik II's death. The unanswered "secret" letters and the matter "pursued in earnest" likely touch his deteriorating position and search for new patronage, for which Rantzau was a natural intermediary — but the note itself does not specify this, and the inference is not pressed into the translation.

documents.title: Tycho Brahe → [open testimonial, for Christian Severini Longomontanus] — Copenhagen, 1 June 1597 [O.S.]

edition.print_label: Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia (1913–29)
edition.tboo_cite: Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, ed. I.L.E. Dreyer, Tom. VII, Hauniæ 1924, p. 384

witnesses.raw: A København, Rigsarkivet, Langebeks Diplomatarium. Afskrift

documents.abstract: Certifies that Longomontanus served faithfully for nearly eight years in astronomical work, conducted himself virtuously, and is released at his own request with a commendation to all.
documents.incipit: EGO TYCHO BRAHE OTTONIDES hæreditarius de Knudstrup, et Arcis Uraniburgi in insula Daniæ …

text.original:
TESTIMONIUM DOMINO LONGOMONTANO A TYCHONE DATUM.

EGO TYCHO BRAHE OTTONIDES hæreditarius de Knudstrup, et Arcis Uraniburgi in insula Daniæ Venusia Fundator et Præses, tenore præsentium testor, quod harum exhibitor CHRISTIANUS SEVERINI F. Lymvicus, mihi in Astronomicis exercitijs per octennium ferme fideliter navaverit operam, et in cæteris præterea se gesserit, uti virtutis et bonarum literarum amantem decere posset. Nunc vero cum a me missionem peteret, non invite dimittendum censui, suoque arbitrio relinquendum. Commendatum igitur volo omnibus cuiusque ordinis et status, ut illum sua humanitate et beneficentia complectantur. In cuius rei fidem sigillum meum apposui et manu mea propria subscripsi.

Actum Hafniæ Calendis Iunij Anno 1597.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**A testimonial given to Master Longomontanus by Tycho.**

I, Tycho Brahe, son of Otte, hereditary lord of Knudstrup, and founder and director of the castle of Uraniborg on the Danish island of Venusia [Hven], by the tenor of these presents bear witness that the bearer of this [letter], Christian son of Søren [Severinus], of Longberg [Lymvicus], has for nearly eight years faithfully devoted his labour to me in astronomical pursuits, and has moreover conducted himself in all other respects as might befit a lover of virtue and of good letters. But now, since he sought his discharge from me, I judged that he was not to be let go unwillingly, and that he should be left to his own choice. I wish him therefore commended to all of whatever order and station, that they may embrace him with their kindness and beneficence. In faith whereof I have affixed my seal and have signed with my own hand.

Done at Copenhagen, on the Kalends of June [1 June], in the year 1597.
TYCHO BRAHE,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Document type.** Not a letter in the ordinary sense but an open **testimonial / letter of recommendation** (*testimonium*) — hence no named addressee in the edition (recipient: empty); it is directed *omnibus cuiusque ordinis et status*, "to all of whatever order and station." Surviving only as a copy (*Afskrift*) in Langebek's Diplomatarium at the Danish National Archives (Rigsarkivet).
- **Issuer.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), here styling himself in full: *Ottonides* ("son of Otte" — see this chapter's convention, *Otto / Ottonides* = Otte Brahe, Tycho's father), *haereditarius de Knudstrup* ("hereditary lord of Knudstrup," the family seat in Scania), and *Arcis Uraniburgi … Fundator et Praeses* ("founder and director of the castle of Uraniborg"). Written at Copenhagen in June 1597, in the final months before Tycho left Denmark — Uraniborg's operations were by then winding down.
- **Subject / bearer.** *Christianus Severini F. Lymvicus* = **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus** (1562–1647), later the leading Tychonic astronomer of the next generation and professor at Copenhagen, author of the *Astronomia Danica* (1622). The Latin gives his patronymic literally: *Severini F[ilius]* = "son of Søren (Severinus)." *Lymvicus* is the Latin toponym from **Longberg / Lomborg** in Jutland (whence the humanist surname *Longomontanus*, "of the long mountain"); rendered "of Longberg" with the printed form flagged. The testimonial documents his service "for nearly eight years" (*per octennium ferme*) — he had joined Tycho on Hven c. 1589.
- **Place.** *Hafniae* = **Copenhagen**.
- ***missionem peteret*** — "sought his discharge / leave to depart" (*missio* = an honourable release from service), not "a mission." Translated as "his discharge."
- ***harum exhibitor*** — "the bearer of this [letter]" (lit. "the exhibitor of these [presents]"), the standard formula by which a testimonial identifies the person carrying it.

- **Calendar / dateline.** *Actum Hafniae Calendis Iunij Anno 1597* = "Done at Copenhagen, on the Kalends of June (1 June), 1597" (O.S. — Denmark kept the Julian calendar). documents.incipit: NOBILIS, generose et magnifice Domine. Gratulor non tam Magnificentiæ vestræ, quam …

text.original:
DAVID CHYTRÆUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

NOBILIS, generose et magnifice Domine. Gratulor non tam Magnificentiæ vestræ, quam Academiæ et urbi Rosarum, de incolumi in hanc urbem adventu vestro, quam vere Generosæ Nobilitatis vestræ sapientia, virtus, doctrina et in Rempublicam literariam merita et Nominis vestri claritas, splendor ac gloria, excellenti virtute ac bene meritis parta, deinceps illustriorem et clariorem efficiet. Quod igitur CICERO alicubi in Orationibus exclamat: O terram illam beatam, quæ hunc virum exceperit! patriam ingratam, si eiecerit, miseram, si amiserit! idem ego ijsdem verbis nunc usurpo, et Deum æternum, suæ sapientiæ et virtutis radios, ingenij et virtutis Heroicæ dona in mentes præstantium virorum effundentem, precor, ut Μ. V. incolumem et florentem perpetuo servet, et migrationem in hanc urbem clementer gubernet, ut paulo post eos, qui talem virum dimiserunt, erroris sui pœniteat, et quem retinere omnibus viribus non studuerunt, retrahere tandem ad se omni contentione enitantur. His coram Μ. V. ad nos advenienti gratulaturus eram, si accurrere ad M.V. per Arthritidem, quæ me totum possedit, licuisset. Nunc, quæ proficisci a mea tenuitate possunt officiola, reverenter defero, et pro eruditissimis ad me literis et volumine epistolarum, mecum superioribus mensibus communicato, reverenter gratias ago.

Bene et feliciter Μ. V. in æternum valeat.
Postridie Viti, Anno 1597.
Μ. V. reverenter colens
DAVID CHYTRÆUS.
text.english:
**DAVID CHYTRAEUS TO TYCHO BRAHE.**

Noble, well-born and magnificent Master. I offer my congratulations not so much to Your Magnificence as to the University and the city of the Roses [Rostock], upon your safe arrival in this city — [an arrival] which the wisdom, virtue, and learning of your truly well-born Nobility, and your deserts toward the republic of letters, and the renown, splendour, and glory of your name, won by [your] excellent virtue and good deserts, will hereafter render the more illustrious and the more famous. That, therefore, which CICERO somewhere cries out in his Orations — "O blessed [is] that land which shall have received this man! [O] ungrateful the homeland, if it cast him out; wretched, if it lose him!" — I now take up in the very same words; and I pray the eternal God, who pours out the rays of His wisdom and virtue, the gifts of genius and of heroic virtue, into the minds of outstanding men, that He may keep Your Magnificence safe and flourishing for ever, and graciously govern your removal into this city, so that a little later those who let such a man go may repent of their error, and may at last strive with all their effort to draw back to themselves the man whom they did not endeavour to keep with all their might. I would have offered Your Magnificence these [congratulations] in person, as you arrived among us, had it been permitted me to hasten to Your Magnificence — [hindered] by the arthritis [gout] which has wholly possessed me. Now I reverently tender such small services as can proceed from my slenderness [of means], and I reverently give thanks for your most learned letter to me and for the volume of letters shared with me in the past months.

May Your Magnificence fare well and happily for ever.
The day after [the feast of] St. Vitus, the year 1597.
Reverently honouring Your Magnificence,
DAVID CHYTRAEUS.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *David Chytraeus* = **David Chytraeus** (Kochhafe, 1530–1600), the eminent Lutheran theologian and historian, professor at the **University of Rostock** and one of its dominant figures; a Melanchthonian, author of the *Chronicon Saxoniae*. He had been in correspondence with Tycho and is recorded by Dreyer as having written this friendly note on 16 June 1597 regretting that his health prevented him from paying his respects in person.
- **Occasion.** The letter congratulates Tycho on his arrival at **Rostock** in June 1597, at the outset of his self-imposed exile from Denmark. The barbed passage about "those who let such a man go" / refused "to keep [him] with all their might" alludes, by transparent implication, to the Danish authorities whose withdrawal of support drove Tycho abroad; Chytraeus predicts they will come to regret it. The hedge is the author's own — he speaks of *those who let such a man go* without naming them — and is preserved rather than sharpened into a direct accusation against the Danish crown.
- ***urbs Rosarum*** — "the city of the Roses," a learned epithet for **Rostock** (playing on *Rostochium* / the rose in the city arms); rendered "the city of the Roses [Rostock]." *Academia* here = the **University of Rostock**.
- **Μ. V.** — the abbreviation throughout (printed with a Greek capital mu, *Μ*, for Latin *M*) = *Magnificentia Vestra*, **"Your Magnificence"** — the standard honorific for a person of Tycho's rank; the Greek-letter mu is a compositor's substitution for the Latin majuscule and carries no separate sense. Rendered consistently "Your Magnificence."
- **Cicero allusion.** *O terram illam beatam … miseram, si amiserit!* — Chytraeus quotes (acknowledging it as Cicero, *in Orationibus*) the apostrophe from Cicero, *De lege agraria* (Second Oration) II.xxxv.95, on Capua, here redeployed to Tycho and Denmark. The quotation is kept as a quotation and set off accordingly.
- ***Arthritis*** — period term for **gout / arthritic joint-disease** ("which has wholly possessed me"); glossed "the arthritis [gout]." Not silently modernised.
- ***officiola*** — diminutive of *officia*, "small [dutiful] services / little kindnesses"; the self-deprecating diminutive (paired with *mea tenuitate*, "my slenderness [of means/ability]") is preserved.
- ***volumine epistolarum … superioribus mensibus communicato*** — "the volume of letters shared with me in the past months." Almost certainly Tycho's *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Liber I, Uraniborg 1596), which he was then circulating to learned correspondents; identification likely but not stated in the letter, so left as the text gives it.
- **Negations.** Two negations occur and are reproduced as exactly two: (1) *non tam … quam* — the idiomatic "not so much … as" correlative (no true denial, a comparative emphasis), and (2) *quem retinere omnibus viribus non studuerunt* — "the man whom they did **not** endeavour to keep with all their might." Neither is dropped or added.
- **Dateline.** *Postridie Viti, Anno 1597* = "the day after [the feast of] St. **Vitus**." St. Vitus's day is **15 June**, so *postridie Viti* = **16 June 1597** (O.S.; Denmark and Lutheran Germany were still on the Julian calendar). This agrees with the edition label ("1597. 16. juni") and with Dreyer's dating; no discrepancy. The place is not named in the dateline but is **Rostock**, established by the body (*in hanc urbem … urbi Rosarum*) and by Dreyer — hence supplied in brackets in the header.

documents.incipit: ILLUSTRISSIME princeps, domine clementissime. Binas Celsit. Tuæ per civem quendam …

text.original:
ILLUSTRISSIMO PRINCIPI AC DOMINO, DOMINO MAURITIO, HASSIÆ ETC. LANDTGRAVIO, COMITI IN CATZENELNPOGEN, DIETZ, ZIGENHAIN et NIDDA ETC., DOMINO CLEMENTISSIMO.

ILLUSTRISSIME princeps, domine clementissime. Binas Celsit. Tuæ per civem quendam Cassellanum literas mihi clementer missas, calendis ipsis junij accepi. Cum autem tunc in procinctu essem itineris Germanici, quemadmodum etiam sequenti statim die Haffnia discessi, meque huc Rostochium contuli (ubi etiamnum paulisper, donec res meæ navigio adventarint, subsisto) nulla dabatur commoditas ijsdem respondendi et longe minus ea, quæ Germanico idiomate exaratis continebantur, exequendi. Jn negotio Erici Langij, amici et affinis mei dilecti, quod T. C. tam clementem sedulam dederit operam, ut, quo in statu res eius versentur, quantoque ære alieno laboret, nobis innotesceret, est cur C. T. submisse gratias plurimas habeam. Verum incommode, et præter opinionem accidit, quod hac æstate comitia regni (uti quotannis fieri solet) celebrata non sint, in quibus maxima pars nobilitatis Danicæ convenire assolet, cum quorum aliquibus, præsertim ijs, qui Erico consanguinitatis vel affinitatis iure coniuncti essent, de debitis eius exolvendis (si qua ratione id obtinere possem) fideliter agere animus erat. Quin etsi comitia illa more solito successissent, nimis tamen sero is, qui T. C. literas, una cum debitorum Erici rationibus attulit, isthuc accesserat. Neque enim ultra quatuordecim dies post ascensionis festum procerum et nobilium regni in urbe illa congressus prorogari solent. Extra vero id tempus, illi, qui Erico aut sanguine, aut alia ratione coniuncti sunt, ita dispersi hinc inde habitant, ut eorum voluntates experiri, et simul cum illis de hoc negotio agere minime oportunum sit. Accessit et hoc, quod mihi, qui hac de re cæteros solicitare constitueram, iam tum e patria in Germaniam discedendum erat, adornato inde a paschatis festo itinere, ut ne propria quidem omni ex parte satis exequi, nedum aliena curare licuerit. Quare T:am C:m, quod in Erici rebus ob prædicta impedimenta nihil tunc temporis præstari potuerit, clementer excusatum habituram confido, et ut creditores eius adhuc aliquandiu, donec melior detur ratio atque occasio illis satisfaciendi, cum ipso contenti esse velint, sua authoritate et clementia effecturam.

Meæ autem in Germaniam transmigrationis rationes nimis longum foret T. C. hic exponere. Neque etiam tempus et calamus id nunc patiuntur. Id saltem brevibus indicabo, quod, cum intellexissem eos qui nunc fatis apud nos præsunt politicis, minus Uraniæ nostræ arduis laboribus favere, et eorum sufficientem sustentationem suis clancularijs consilijs avertere, nec ijs quæ a Friderico secundo laudatissimæ memoriæ circa hæc (approbantibus id post ipsius obitum omnibus regni senatoribus, literis confirmantibus) decreta erant, satis acquiescere, neque regem nostrum serenissimum alias optima indole et natura præditum ita de his, uti decuit, admonere voluisse: existimavi, mature talibus difficultatibus subveniendum, ne omnia, quæ tot iam annis in astronomiæ instaurationem magno conamine, nec parvis sumptibus molitus sum, interirent. Quare huc in Germaniam sponte secessi, ut alias commoditates ea ipsa continuandi absolvendique quærerem, quo omnia in utilitatem reip. literariæ ad posteritatem sarcta tecta transmitti possent. Qua in parte si T. C. nostris desiderijs consilio auxilioque subvenire non degravata fuerit, præstiterit rem, non saltem mihi, sed toti astronomico studio, quod parens tuus laudatissimæ memoriæ tanto amore prosequutus est, quo etiam ipsemet non modicum afficeris, percommodam, et cum eorum, qui nunc supersunt, tum etiam posterorum, grata memoria laudeque celebrandam. Et si T. C. hac de re quidpiam clementer ad me scribere, literasque illas ad producem Holsatiæ dominum Henricum Ranzovium dirigere voluerit, ille eas facile isthuc, ubicunque locorum me versari noverit, perferri curabit. Porro icones instrumentorum meorum, quas transmiseram T:æ C:ni, esse redditas lubens cognovi, et pro opere canonis triangulorum (cuius quidem antea quaterna exemplaria coëmeram) vicissim mihi donato gratias submisse ago. Interim vero non possum ex literis T. C. aut aliunde percipere, utrum liber epistolarum astronomicarum, quem T:æ C:i, quod paternas mecum communicatas literas contineret, dedicandum censui (quem etiam ob id non ingratum futurum, mihi persuadebam) ad C:nis Tuæ manus pervenerit, nec ne. Quod si exemplar a me transmissum intercidit, dabo operam, ut aliud per occasionem oblatam eidem substituatur: nisi forte e nundinis Francofurtensibus ultimis, ubi aliquot eiusdem libri exemplaria prostabant, eius copia facta sit. Sed desino T:m C:m pluribus nunc detinere, cum et ipsemet in hoc peregrino loco inter alia plurima negotia atque interpellationes vix hæc ipsa scribendi otium nactus sim. Vbi maiori tranquillitati, favore numinis, restitutus fuero, plura etiam et accuratiora dare non intermittam. Interea hæc festinanti calamo, et, citra commoditatem effusa T. C. clementer accipiat, ac diu feliciterque valeat.

Dabantur Rostochio die 17. junij anni 1597.
Tuæ Cels, addictiss.
Tycho Brahe
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the Most Illustrious Prince and Lord, Lord Moritz, Landgrave of Hesse etc., Count in Katzenelnbogen, Dietz, Ziegenhain and Nidda etc., his most gracious Lord.**

Most Illustrious Prince, most gracious Lord. The two letters of Your Highness, graciously sent to me by a certain citizen of Kassel, I received on the very Kalends of June [1 June]. But since I was then on the point of setting out on a journey into Germany — as indeed I departed from Copenhagen the very next day, and betook myself here to Rostock (where I am still tarrying a little while, until my effects arrive by ship) — there was no opportunity of replying to them, and far less of carrying out the things that were contained in those written in the German tongue. In the matter of Erik Lange, my beloved friend and kinsman by marriage, that Your Highness has given such gracious and diligent effort, that there might be made known to us in what state his affairs stand and with how great a debt he labours, there is reason why I should most humbly render Your Highness very many thanks. But it has fallen out inconveniently, and beyond expectation, that this summer the Diet of the realm (as is wont to be held each year) has not been held — at which the greatest part of the Danish nobility is accustomed to assemble; with some of whom, especially those who were joined to Erik by right of consanguinity or affinity, it was my intention to deal faithfully concerning the discharge of his debts (if by any means I could obtain it). Indeed, even had that Diet proceeded in the wonted manner, yet too late had he arrived there who brought Your Highness's letters together with the accounts of Erik's debts. For the gatherings of the grandees and nobles of the realm in that city are not wont to be prolonged beyond fourteen days after the feast of the Ascension. But outside that time, those who are joined to Erik either by blood or by some other tie dwell so scattered here and there that to sound out their wills, and at the same time to treat with them of this business, is by no means convenient. This too was added, that I myself — who had resolved to solicit the rest in this matter — had even then to depart out of my homeland into Germany, the journey having been prepared from the feast of Easter onward, so that I was not even permitted to attend to my own affairs adequately in every part, much less to see to another's. Wherefore I trust that Your Highness will graciously hold me excused that nothing could be accomplished at that time in Erik's affairs on account of the aforesaid hindrances; and that, by your authority and clemency, you will bring it about that his creditors may be willing to rest content with him yet a little while longer, until a better means and occasion of satisfying them be given.

But the reasons for my migration into Germany it would be too long to set forth here to Your Highness. Nor indeed do the time and the pen now permit it. This at least I shall indicate in brief: that, when I had understood that those who now preside over political destinies among us favoured but little the arduous labours of our Urania, and were diverting their adequate maintenance by their clandestine counsels, and were not sufficiently abiding by those things which had been decreed concerning these matters by Frederick II, of most praiseworthy memory (with all the senators of the realm approving it after his death, and confirming it by letters), nor had been willing duly to admonish, as was fitting, our most serene King — who is otherwise endowed with an excellent disposition and nature — about these things: I judged that such difficulties must be met betimes, lest all those things should perish which now for so many years I have laboured at, with great effort and at no small expense, towards the restoration of astronomy. Wherefore I have withdrawn hither into Germany of my own accord, that I might seek other facilities for continuing and completing those very labours, whereby everything might be transmitted, whole and entire, to posterity for the benefit of the republic of letters. In which part, if Your Highness will not be too burdened to assist our desires with counsel and aid, you will have rendered a service most opportune — not to me alone, but to the whole study of astronomy, which your father of most praiseworthy memory pursued with so great a love, and by which you yourself too are affected in no small degree — and one to be celebrated with the grateful remembrance and praise both of those who now survive and also of those to come. And if Your Highness will graciously be willing to write anything to me on this matter, and to direct those letters to the governor [*producem*] of Holstein, Lord Heinrich Rantzau, he will readily see to it that they are carried thither, wherever in the world he may know me to be staying. Further, I was glad to learn that the engravings of my instruments, which I had sent to Your Highness, were duly delivered; and for the work of the canon of triangles given me in return (of which I had indeed earlier bought four copies), I humbly render thanks. In the meantime, however, I cannot perceive from Your Highness's letters or from elsewhere whether the book of astronomical letters — which I judged should be dedicated to Your Highness, because it contained your father's letters shared with me (and which for that reason too I persuaded myself would not be unwelcome) — has come into Your Highness's hands or not. But if the copy sent by me has gone astray, I shall take care that another be substituted for it as occasion offers: unless perhaps a supply of it was had from the last Frankfurt fair, where several copies of the same book were on sale. But I cease now to detain Your Highness with more, since I myself too, in this foreign place, amid very many other affairs and interruptions, have scarcely found leisure to write these very lines. When I shall have been restored to greater tranquillity, by the favour of the deity, I shall not fail to send still more and more accurate things. In the meantime, may Your Highness graciously receive these things, poured out with a hurrying pen and without due care, and may you fare well long and happily.

Given at Rostock, on the 17th day of June in the year 1597.
Most devoted to Your Highness,
Tycho Brahe,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / context.** Tycho Brahe, writing from **Rostock** in the first weeks of his self-imposed exile from Denmark. Having lost the favour of the regency government following Frederick II's death (1588) and the accession of the young Christian IV, Tycho had abandoned Hven in spring 1597, sailing from Copenhagen early in June; the letter is written during his stopover at Rostock while awaiting his effects by ship. He would go on to Wandsbek (the guest of Heinrich Rantzau), then to Prague.
- **Recipient.** *Mauritius, Hassiae Landtgravius* = **Moritz "the Learned," Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel** (1572–1632), who had succeeded his father **Wilhelm IV** in 1592. The full address-style enumerates the subsidiary Hessian comital titles: *Catzenelnpogen* = **Katzenelnbogen**, *Dietz* = **Diez**, *Zigenhain* = **Ziegenhain**, *Nidda*.
- ***Erici Langij, amici et affinis mei dilecti*** — **Erik Lange** (1553–1613), Danish nobleman and alchemist, betrothed to Tycho's sister **Sophie Brahe** in 1590 (in Danish law a binding tie — hence *affinis*, "kinsman by marriage"). Ruined by his pursuit of *chrysopoeia*, Lange had fled his creditors and was then on the Continent in Moritz's orbit; Moritz had written to Tycho reporting on the state of Lange's debts, which Tycho here acknowledges and to which he replies that the failure of the annual Danish *comitia* (Diet) had frustrated his plan to lobby Lange's noble kinsmen for repayment.
- ***producem Holsatiae dominum Henricum Ranzovium*** — **Heinrich Rantzau** (Henricus Ranzovius, 1526–1598), the great Holstein humanist, royal *Statthalter* (governor; *produx/produx* here = lieutenant-governor) of the Danish duchies. Tycho names him as the relay-point for return correspondence; Rantzau was his host at Wandsbek shortly after.
- ***liber epistolarum astronomicarum … dedicandum censui*** — Tycho's *Epistolarum astronomicarum liber primus* (Uraniborg, 1596), the printed correspondence with Wilhelm IV and Christoph Rothmann, which Tycho **dedicated to Moritz precisely because it contained his late father's letters** ("paternas mecum communicatas literas"). The literature confirms the dedication-to-Moritz and its rationale (Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*; the dedication leaf (:)4r). Tycho is here anxiously inquiring whether the presentation copy reached Moritz, offering a replacement, and noting copies were on sale at the most recent **Frankfurt book fair** (*nundinae Francofurtenses*).
- ***icones instrumentorum meorum*** — "the engravings of my instruments": Tycho had sent Moritz a set of the instrument plates (the *icones*, later gathered in the *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica*, 1598). *Icones* rendered "engravings/figures" per the instrument register.
- ***opere canonis triangulorum*** — "the work of the canon of triangles," i.e. a printed table of trigonometric functions (*canon triangulorum* = a canon/table for the solution of triangles), sent to Tycho by Moritz in return; Tycho notes he had already bought four copies. *canon* kept and glossed.
- **Astronomy.** *astronomiae instaurationem* = "the **restoration of astronomy**" — Tycho's programmatic phrase (*instauratio astronomiae*), rendered by this chapter's convention *Uraniae nostrae … arduis laboribus* = "the arduous labours of our **Urania**" (the Muse of astronomy, standing metonymically for Tycho's astronomical enterprise at Uraniborg).
- **Negation note (legal/political force).** The long central sentence carries a chain of complaints against the regency, governed by *cum intellexissem* and strung on a *minus … nec … neque* structure; the three negative limbs are reproduced exactly: (1) they *favoured but little* (*minus … favere*) Tycho's work and were *diverting* (*avertere*) its funding; (2) they were *not sufficiently abiding* (*nec … satis acquiescere*) by Frederick II's decrees; (3) they *had not been willing to admonish* (*neque … admonere voluisse*) the young King. No negation has been added or dropped. The conditional *si T. C. … non degravata fuerit* ("if Your Highness will **not** be too burdened") is a single litotes-style negative — a courteous request, not a prohibition — and is rendered as such. *clancularijs consilijs* = "by their clandestine/secret counsels," kept at full pejorative force (no softening to "private").
- ***sarcta tecta*** — a fixed legal-administrative idiom ("in good repair, whole and entire," lit. of buildings kept *sarta tecta*, "patched and roofed"); rendered "whole and entire."
- **Calendar.** *calendis ipsis junij* = "on the very **Kalends of June**" (= 1 June); Roman-calendar idiom kept and glossed by this chapter's convention. The dateline *Dabantur Rostochio die 17. junij anni 1597* = "Given at Rostock, 17 June 1597" agrees with the catalogue label; **O.S.** (Denmark and the Lutheran German principalities were still on the Julian calendar in 1597). *post ascensionis festum* / *a paschatis festo* — movable feasts (Ascension; Easter), kept as named feasts, not converted to civil dates.
- **Subscription.** *Tuae Cels. addictiss.* = "Most devoted to Your Highness" (*Celsitudini Tuae addictissimus*, by this chapter's convention); *manu propria* = "with his own hand" (the original is an autograph letter, per the MS witness).

documents.abstract: Recounts twenty-two years of astronomical work on Hven at Frederick II's encouragement and justifies his departure, having had no opportunity for a royal audience beforehand.
documents.incipit: STUORMECTIGE hoyeborne allernaadigste herre. Nest min villige och troff thienistis …

text.original:
STUORMECTIGE hoyeborne allernaadigste herre. Nest min villige och troff thienistis vnderdanige formelding E: M: giffuer ieg paa det vnderdanigste thilkende, at som ieg ingen leylighedt haffde att komme E: K: M: thil orde, førend ieg affdrog, och ey viste, om dett kunde vere E: K: M: angenem eller icke, saa foraarsagis ieg nu E: K: M: paa dett korteste schrifftligen att lade vide, huis ieg ellers mundtligen haffde y sinde vnderdanigst att berette. Daa, effthersom ieg aff vngdommen haffuer haffdt sønderlig thilgeneyenhedt den löfflig astronomische konst grundelig att lære och forstaa och siden att bringe rett paa fode, och der offuer haffde achtit thilforn att bliffue vdi Tysklandt bequemmeligen dett att vdrette, saa haffuer E: K: M: herre fader, hoyeloufflige ihukommelse, der Hans Mayt: saadant fornam, naadigste begerit och bevegitt mig till ditt samme paa Huæn att anstille och giøre. Huilchett ieg och paa anden och tyffvende aar medt alsomstørste fliidt, vmage och bekaastning efftherkommit haffuer formeenendis mig nochsom dermedt haffue bevist, att ieg dett helst haffde villet giordt min egenn herre och koning och fæderne landt thil ære aff yderste formue. Och haffde E: K: M: herre fader naadigste for gott anseedt och loffuit, att huis ieg der anrettit thil samme konst schulle medt en fundatz nødtorffteligen forsørgis och perpetueris, med flere guode wilkaar, som mig bleff naadigste thilsagdt. Huilchet E: K: M: frue moder, min naadigste droning, vden tuiffvell endnu dragis thil minde, och thilforn hoes Dannemarchis raadt haffuer ladit thilkende giffue, saa ieg derfor haffuer bekommit det hele Dannemarchis riges raadz obne pergmentz breff, som mig saadant haffuer confirmerit och viidere derudom fortrøstitt. Huorudoffuer ieg siden haffuer giordt en vsigelige stuoer vmage och bekaastning ydermere end thilforn forhaabendis, att naar E: K: M: kom thil regimentztidt, schulde da haffue en naadigste behag dertill, och lade mig och mine nyde dett gott att.

Men nu haffuer dett sig anderledis tildragitt en ieg haffde troffuit, huorudom ieg vil nu vformeldit lade videre omstendt. E: K: M: er vden tuiffvel bevist, att ieg er affschildt med huis ieg schulde haffue thil samme konstis vnderholding, och mig bleffuen opschreffuit, att E: K: M: war icke til sindz saadant att ville holde ved macht, foruden møgitt andit, som vformodendis er thilkommit, och (som ieg achter) vden min schyld och brøde er hendit. Och efftherdi ieg endelig aff den naade, som Gud giffuer, faaer att fuldkomme huis ieg engang medt saa stuoer alvorlighedt och y lang tidt fortagitt och dreffuit haffuer, huilchet och mange nationer vitterligt er, och stuorligen adtraader, och icke sielff haffuer y formue dett nochsom att bekaaste; thi ieg alrede er kommen saa thil achters, der ieg endskønt haffde de forrige forlæninger, att ieg alligvel nøddis thil att affhende alt mitt fæderne guodtz. Forseer ieg mig till, att E: K: M: naadigste anseer saadan min nødtorfftighedt och icke tager denne min vdreyße thil nogen vnaade, efftherdi att ieg aff diße och flere aarsager saa hoyeligen trengdis att søge anden middel och raadt, att dett som well er begyndt kand bliffue thilbørligen fuldkommit, och ieg mitt guode naffn och rycte y fremmede land kand vidt macht holde. Dog er ieg icke y den mening vddragen, att ieg aldelis ville forlade mitt fæderne land, mens ickon att vere vde om hielp och bistandt hoes andre herrer och potentater, om saa mugligt kunde vere, paa dett ieg icke schulde were E: K: M: eller rigett formøgitt thil besuering. Dersom dett kunde bliffue mig forgyntt, att ieg y Dannemarck maa min forthagne arbeytt forfølge, vil ieg dett icke forsige; thi ieg endnu som thilforn alsomhelst E: K: M for nogen andre potentater, och mitt egen fæderne rige thil ære och loufflig effthersagn, alt huis ieg aff yderste formue kunde vdrette, saa fremt dett kunde skee med lidelig vilkaar och vden min skade. Huis och icke, vil ieg dog, huor dett er forseet, att ieg anderstedz skal bliffue, stedtze vere E: K: M: med all loufflig effthersagn och vnderdanighedt aff min ringe formue villig. Settendis dett vnderdanigst til E: K: M: guode bethenckende, att ieg ingenlunde aff nogen lettferdighedt (helst paa denne alder, ieg er offuer halfftridiesintyffue aar, och icke med ringe huesgesindt beladen, huilche ieg med stuoer vgeleyenhedt nødis att giøre fremmede) drager aff mitt fæderne land og fra min guode slecht och venner, och kandt dett som endnu er paa Huæn aff mig giordt, nochsom vdviße, att icke thilforn haffde werit min acht och mening saaledes att ville drage derfra. Forhaabis derfore vnderdanigste, naar E: K: M: dette medt sine omstendighedt rett betrackter, att E: K: M: werer och bliffuer min naadigste herre och konningh, och mig och mine medt al kongelig gunst och naade tilbevogenn. Jeg wil althid findis E: K: M: vnderdanig, throff och villig aff min yderste formue, huor Gud almegtigste mig min leylighedt haffuer forsiunit. Denn samme guode Gudt, som raader for all wertzlige regimente, vnde E: K: M: vdi sin kongelige regieringh lycke, velsignelße, guode raad och anßlagh.
text.english:
Most Mighty, high-born, most gracious Lord. After the humble tender of my willing and faithful service, I make known to Your Majesty most humbly that, since I had no opportunity to speak with Your Royal Majesty before I departed, and did not know whether it might be agreeable to Your Royal Majesty or not, I am therefore now moved to let Your Royal Majesty know in writing, as briefly as may be, what otherwise I had it in mind humbly to report by word of mouth. Now then, inasmuch as from my youth I have had a singular inclination thoroughly to learn and understand the laudable art of astronomy and afterwards to set it rightly upon its feet, and had on that account formerly intended to settle in Germany so as conveniently to accomplish it, Your Royal Majesty's lord father, of high and laudable memory, when His Majesty perceived this, most graciously desired and moved me to set about and do that same thing on Hven. Which thing I have also, in the two-and-twentieth year [now], carried out with the very greatest diligence, labour, and expense, presuming that I have thereby sufficiently shown that I would most gladly have done it to the honour of my own lord and king and of [my] fatherland, [and] to the utmost of my ability. And Your Royal Majesty's lord father had most graciously seen fit and promised that whatever I there set up for that art should, by a foundation [*fundatz*], be sufficiently provided for and perpetuated, together with several other good conditions which were most graciously assured to me. Which Your Royal Majesty's lady mother, my most gracious Queen, without doubt still calls to mind, and beforehand had it made known to the Council of Denmark, so that I therefore obtained the whole Council of the realm of Denmark's open parchment letter, which confirmed such [provision] to me and further gave me assurance thereof. Wherefore I have since taken upon myself an unspeakably great labour and expense, yet more than before, in the hope that, when Your Royal Majesty should come to the time of [your own] rule, Your Majesty would then have a most gracious pleasure therein, and would let me and mine enjoy the good of it.

But now it has fallen out otherwise than I had believed, the particulars whereof I will for the present leave further unmentioned. Your Royal Majesty is without doubt aware that I have been deprived of what I should have had for the maintenance of that same art, and [that] it was put to me in writing [*opschreffuit*] that Your Royal Majesty was not minded to wish to uphold such [provision] in force — besides much else that has come about unlooked-for, and (as I judge) has befallen without my fault or offence. And inasmuch as I must in the end, by the grace that God gives, complete what I have once undertaken and pursued with such great earnestness and over a long time — a thing which is also known to many nations, and greatly desired [by them] — and do not myself have it in [my] means sufficiently to defray it; for I am already come so far behind [in means] — even though I had the former fiefs — that I am nevertheless constrained to dispose of all my patrimonial estate: I trust that Your Royal Majesty will most graciously regard such my necessity, and will not take this my journeying-out [*vdreyße*] into any disfavour, since for these and several causes I was so highly pressed to seek other means and counsel, so that what is well begun may be duly completed, and I may keep my good name and repute abroad in full force. Yet I have not journeyed out with the intent that I would altogether forsake my fatherland, but only to be abroad [seeking] help and assistance from other lords and potentates, if so it might be possible, to the end that I should not be too much of a burden to Your Royal Majesty or to the realm. If it could be granted me that in Denmark I may pursue my undertaken work, I will not refuse it; for I, now as before, [would] most willingly [serve] Your Royal Majesty before any other potentates, and to the honour and laudable repute of my own fatherland's realm [do] all that I could accomplish to the utmost of my ability — provided it could be done on tolerable conditions and without my hurt. And if not, yet — wherever it is provided that I shall remain elsewhere — I will at all times be willing [to serve] Your Royal Majesty with all laudable repute and humility, according to my slender ability. Submitting it most humbly to Your Royal Majesty's good consideration, that I do by no means out of any levity (least of all at this [my] age — I am over fifty years old, and burdened with no small household [*huesgesindt*], which with great inconvenience I am constrained to make strangers [abroad]) depart from my fatherland and from my good kindred and friends; and that what is even yet on Hven, made by me, may sufficiently show that it had not formerly been my purpose and intent thus to wish to depart from there. I most humbly hope, therefore, that when Your Royal Majesty rightly considers this with all its circumstances, Your Royal Majesty will be and remain my most gracious Lord and King, and [will be] favourably disposed toward me and mine with all royal grace and favour. I will at all times be found humble, faithful, and willing toward Your Royal Majesty to the utmost of my ability, wherever God Almighty shall have provided me my occasion. May the same good God, who governs all worldly rule, grant Your Royal Majesty in your royal governance good fortune, blessing, good counsel, and good resolve.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601) to **Christian IV of Denmark** (r. 1588–1648), then aged 20 and reigning in his own right since the regency ended in 1596. This is Tycho's apologia written shortly after he had quit Hven and Copenhagen in the spring of 1597 — among the most consequential letters in his correspondence, justifying his departure from Denmark while leaving the door open to a return.
- **Place.** No place is named in the dateline as transmitted; the body's deictic *"paa Huaen … aff mig giordt"* ("on Hven … made by me") treats Hven as remote. Tycho had withdrawn to Copenhagen (and soon Rostock); the witnesses are later copies (*Afskrift*), and Dreyer prints no place-line. The header therefore gives **[n.p.]**.
- **Document type / witnesses.** Two later manuscript copies: **A** = KB, *Langebeks Ekscerpter* no. 178; **B** = Rigsarkivet, *Langebeks Diplomatarium* — both eighteenth-century transcripts (Langebek), not the original. Shelfmarks reproduced as given.
- **Calendar.** No explicit dateline survives in the transcribed text; the edition label is *"1597. 10. juli"* (10 July 1597), Old Style (Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). As the body furnishes no internal date, the header follows the catalogue label and is marked **[O.S.]**; no in-letter date discrepancy arises (none is stated).
- **Chancery-Danish orthography (c. 1597).** *E: K: M:* = *Eders Kongelige Majestæt* ("Your Royal Majesty"); *E: M:* = *Eders Majestæt*. *Nest … formelding* = *Næst … formælding* ("after the tendering [of service]"). *troff* = *tro* ("faithful"); *affdrog* = *afdrog* ("departed"); *löfflig / loufflig* = *lovlig* ("laudable, lawful"); *thilgeneyenhedt* = *tilgenegenhed* ("inclination"); *bequemmeligen* = *bekvemmeligen* ("conveniently"); *anstille* = *anstille* ("set about, arrange"); *forlaeninger* = *forleninger* ("fiefs, enfeoffments"); *affhende* = *afhænde* ("dispose of, alienate"); *forgyntt* = *forundt* ("granted, vouchsafed"); *forsige* = *forsige* ("refuse, decline"); *tilbevogenn* = *tilbevågen* ("favourably disposed"); *anßlagh* = *anslag* ("resolve, design"). Long-*ß* and *w/v/u* variation are chancery features.
- ***fundatz*** — a **foundation** (endowment/charter), the Latin-derived chancery term for the endowed establishment Frederik II had promised would perpetually maintain the Uraniborg programme; kept as a technical term, glossed.
- ***E: K: M: herre fader*** = **Frederik II** (r. 1559–88), who granted Tycho the fief of Hven in 1576. ***frue moder, min naadigste droning*** = the Queen Dowager **Sophie of Mecklenburg** (1557–1631), Christian IV's mother. ***Dannemarchis riges raadz obne pergmentz breff*** = the **open letter (charter) of the Council of the Realm**, on parchment, confirming the endowment.
- ***paa anden och tyffvende aar*** — "in the two-and-twentieth year": Tycho counts from the 1576 grant, making 1597 roughly the twenty-second year of his work on Hven. Rendered as written; no silent arithmetic adjustment.
- ***regimentztidt*** — "the time of [Christian's] rule" (i.e. his majority/personal reign); Tycho had hoped the young king's accession to full power would secure the endowment.
- **Age statement / numeral.** *"ieg er offuer halfftridiesintyffue aar"* — *halfftridiesintyffue* = *halvtredsindstyve*, the Old Danish vigesimal numeral for **fifty** (*halvtredje sinde tyve* = "[the] half-third times twenty" = 2½ × 20 = 50), the source of modern Danish *halvtreds* "50." So *"offuer halfftridiesintyffue aar"* = **"over fifty years [old]."** Tycho, born 14 December 1546, was 50 in July 1597 — internally consistent. The translation reads **"over fifty."** The trap to avoid is reading the *halv-* element as "half of [the next ten]" to yield 55; that is wrong here — the figure is 50. *(Numeral flagged for the vigesimal false-friend; the reading itself is secure.)*
- ***huesgesindt*** = *husgesinde* ("household, household retinue/servants"); *"icke med ringe huesgesindt beladen"* = "burdened with no small household," whom Tycho would have to uproot and "make strangers" (resettle abroad).
- ***affschildt med huis ieg schulde haffue*** = "deprived of [*afskilt med* = parted/separated from] what I should have had" — i.e. the revenues/fiefs withdrawn. ***opschreffuit*** = *opskrevet* ("put to [me] in writing / notified in writing").
- **Negation audit.** Six negations carry the letter's legal and rhetorical force and are reproduced exactly: (1) *"angenem eller **icke**"* = "agreeable … or not"; (2) *"E: K: M: war **icke** til sindz … att ville holde ved macht"* = "was **not** minded to wish to uphold [it]"; (3) *"**icke** sielff haffuer y formue"* = "do **not** myself have the means"; (4) *"**icke** tager denne min vdreyße thil nogen vnaade"* = "will **not** take this my departure into any disfavour"; (5) *"er ieg **icke** y den mening vddragen, att ieg aldelis ville forlade mitt faederne land"* = "I have **not** journeyed out with the intent that I would altogether forsake my fatherland"; (6) *"paa dett ieg **icke** schulde were … formøgitt thil besuering"* = "that I should **not** be too much of a burden"; plus *"vil ieg dett **icke** forsige"* = "I will **not** refuse it," and *"att **icke** thilforn haffde werit min acht … saaledes att ville drage derfra"* = "that it had **not** formerly been my intent thus to depart from there." The conditional *"Dersom dett kunde bliffue mig forgyntt … vil ieg dett icke forsige"* is genuinely concessive (a real offer to stay if the conditions are met); rendered as such, not sharpened into a demand.
- ***vformeldit lade videre omstendt*** — "leave the further particulars unmentioned": *uformeldt* ("unmentioned, unreported"); *omstendt* = *omstænder/omstændigheder* ("circumstances, particulars"). Tycho pointedly declines to detail his grievances.
- **No Greek, no astronomical symbols, no verse** occur in this letter; the only technical term is *fundatz* (above).

text.original:
COPIA LITERARUM MISSARUM AD DUCEM VLDARICUM.

DURCHLEUCHTIGER hochgebornner furste. E:F:G:sein meine vntherthenighe, bereidtwillige dienste allzeit bevor. Gnediger herr, demnach E:F:G:in allen gnadenn mir vnd meinen studis zugethon zusein, ich hiebevornn gnuchsam vernohmenn, welches auch vnter andern E:F:G:do mit gnedichlich beweisen, das E:F:G: mich fur etzlichen Jahren ihn meiner behausung auff der insell Huenna gnedichlich zu besuchenn, vnnd meinne daselbst angerichtete sachen zu besehenn gewirdiget, daafür ich nochmals E:F:G:mit vnterthenigkeitt danchen thue.

So kan E:F:G:zu vermelden jch nit vnterlasen, welcher gestalt ich gewiser hochwichtiger vrsachen halben, die viell anders beschaffen, als vieleicht in gemein davonn magk geredet werden, deren vmbstende jch doch alhie will vorbey gehen, dieweill es in die fedder allis nicht woll zu bringen ist, aus meinenn lieben vatterlandt Dennemarck mich begeben, vnd doch aus sonderlichen bedencken bißanhero nicht hab weitters ziehen wollen alls in E:F:G: stadt Rostogk, welche gleich auf der grendze zwischen Deutschlandt vndt Dennemarcke belegen, zweiffuell auch nicht, wen E:F:G: die vmbstende an gerechter vrsachen, so mich zu solchem genotdrenget, daß jch in diesem meinen hohen alter, vndt mit nicht geringen haußgesinde, beladen, alles auf der jnsell Huenna, so ich mit vielfeltiger vnd fast vngleublicher muhe vnd bekostung vber die zwandzigk jhar angerechtet vnd ins werck gebracht hab, verlassen, mich vnd de meinen mit groser vngelegenheit frembd machen musßen, grundtlich erfahren werden. Es werden E:F:G:zu herdzen annehmen, vnd darüber ein gnediges mitleiden haben, das der woll angefangen vndt fast vollendte trefflich arbeit, welche sich vielle hohes standes, vnd andere vorneme gelaertte leutte, hin und wieder schier inn gantze Europa seher woll gefallen lasßen, vnd ein groses verlangen darnach gehabt, vndt noch haben, das diese hochnudzbare arbeit, welche ihnn viellhundert jaren niemandtz mit sulcher muhe vndt fleis, jedoch mir ohne ruhm zu reden, sich vnterstehen wollenn, ann den tagk gebracht, vnd zu gemeinen nutz publicirt werden möchten, so plötzlich vnnd vnuermutlich vnterlasen, vnd fast zu nicht soll gemacht werden. Dahero zwar meinen gnedigsten kunig vnd lieben vatterlandt, welchem sulches furnemblich zu ehren vnd löblicher nachsag angestellet war, bey frembden nationen vielleicht nictt woll wirt außgeleget, das solche löbliche werck nictt itzo so woll als bey könnig Friderichs, hochlöblicher gedechtnuß, zeitten, wie auch ihm nachfolgenden interregno, solte gebürlicher weis erhalten vnd bestettiget werden, welches mir warlich vonn hertzen wehe thutt, das sulches meinen gnedigsten herren vnd kunigh vnd vielgeliepten vatterlandt von meinent wegen nach geredet sein solthe, vnd hette giernne geheim, das keine notwendigkeit dieses verursacht, wie ich dan auch lange zeit mitt groser gedult alles ertragen, vnd beserung jedoch vergeblich gehoffet. Wo vonn zwar viell zu berichten were, wen ichs nicht dafur achten thette, daß es beser sey alles noch zur zeit in stillheit pleiben zu lasßen, vnd dieweill ichs vor mein person nictt hab endern können, muß ichs es auch Got vnd der zeit alßo befehellen. Derwegen ich mich zu E:F:G:in vnterthenigkeit versehe, E: F: G: werden darob, daß ich allhie jn E:F:G:statt mit sampt meinen haußgesinde ein zeit langk, biß die gelegenheit sich anders erreuget verhalte, kein vngnedigen mißgefallen tragen, sondern mit Dero F: gnaden vnd gunst wie hiebeuor gnediglich gegen mich bewogen sein vnd bleiben. Bitte darneben dienstliches fleisses, es wollen E:F:G:mir mit gutten ratt gnedichlich erscheinen, wie etwa diesße hochlöbliche astronomische sachen, die ich in so viel jaren mit vnglauplicher mue vnd vnkosten getreiben vnd vorgesetzt hab, ferner befordert mugen werden. Das im fhall es ie in Dennemarck über hoffnung hernacher nit meher gescheen solte, das sölche löbliche kunst alda gehandthabt vnd befurdert, dennoch anderswo im römischen reich demselben zu ehrenn durch notturfftige mittell vnd ersprießliche furschub erhalten vndt ad posteros continuirt werden möge. Daran E:F:G:nict alleinne mir vnd den meinen eine gnedige gutthat betzeigen wirt, sondern es werden auch E:F:G:das E:F:G:die hochlöbliche vhralte kunst alßo befördert, bey mennichliche vnd sonderlich bey den nachkommen grosen rühm, lob vnd ehr erlangen. Vnd ich soll es auch in meinen publicandis operibus mit aller danckbarkeit erkennen, vnd löblich zu preisen nict vntterlasßen. Thue hiemis E:F:G:zu langwiriger gesondtheit vnd freidsammer regerung dem gnedigen schudz des Allmechtigsten, mit sampt E: F: G: viellgeliepten gemallin, getrewlich befehellen.

Dattum Rostogk, den 29. jullij a:o 1597.
text.english:
**Copy of the letter sent to Duke Ulrich.**

Most Serene, high-born Prince. May my humble, ready services ever be commended to Your Princely Grace beforehand. Gracious lord: inasmuch as I have heretofore amply learned that Your Princely Grace is graciously devoted to me and to my studies — which Your Princely Grace also, among other things, graciously showed therein, that some years ago Your Princely Grace deigned graciously to visit me in my dwelling on the island of Hven, and to view the works I had set up there — for which I once more render thanks to Your Princely Grace with all humility.

So I cannot forbear to relate to Your Princely Grace in what manner I have, on certain weighty causes — which are constituted quite otherwise than perhaps may be commonly spoken of, the particulars whereof I will nevertheless here pass over, since it is not all well to be committed to the pen — betaken myself away from my dear fatherland Denmark; and yet, out of particular considerations, have until now not wished to remove any further than into Your Princely Grace's city of Rostock, which lies just upon the border between Germany and Denmark. Nor do I doubt that Your Princely Grace will thoroughly come to understand the particulars of the just causes that have driven me to this — namely, that I, burdened in this my advanced age, and with no small household, have had to abandon everything on the island of Hven (which over more than twenty years I set up and brought into being with manifold and almost incredible toil and expense), and to make myself and mine, with great inconvenience, strangers [abroad]. Your Princely Grace will take it to heart, and have a gracious compassion thereupon, that the well-begun and nearly completed excellent work — in which many of high estate, and other eminent learned men, here and there well-nigh throughout all Europe, have taken great pleasure, and have had, and still have, a great longing — that this most useful work, which in many hundreds of years no one would venture upon with such toil and diligence (yet I speak it without boasting), brought to light and published for the common good, is so suddenly and unexpectedly to be left off and almost brought to naught. Whence, to be sure, it may perhaps not be well construed among foreign nations of my most gracious king and dear fatherland — to whose honour and laudable repute this was chiefly undertaken — that such a laudable work should not now be maintained and confirmed in fitting wise, as it was in the times of King Frederick, of most laudable memory, and likewise in the interregnum that followed him; which truly grieves me from the heart, that such a thing should be said reproachfully of my most gracious lord and king and much-beloved fatherland on my account; and I would gladly have kept secret that no necessity caused this, even as I have also for a long time borne everything with great patience, and yet hoped for amendment in vain. Whereof, to be sure, there were much to report, did I not deem it better that for the present all should be left to rest in silence; and since for my own person I have not been able to change it, I must commit it likewise to God and to time. Therefore I trust myself to Your Princely Grace in all humility, that Your Princely Grace will bear no ungracious displeasure that I tarry here in Your Princely Grace's city, together with my household, for a time, until the occasion show itself otherwise, but will, with your princely favour and grace, be and remain graciously disposed toward me as heretofore. I beg besides, with dutiful diligence, that Your Princely Grace will graciously favour me with good counsel as to how these most laudable astronomical matters, which I have pursued and prosecuted over so many years with incredible labour and cost, may be further advanced — so that, in case beyond hope it should hereafter no longer come to pass in Denmark that such a laudable art be there practised and furthered, it may nevertheless elsewhere in the Roman Empire, to the honour of that same [art], be preserved by needful support and profitable furtherance, and continued unto posterity [ad posteros]. Wherein Your Princely Grace will show a gracious benefaction not to me and mine alone, but Your Princely Grace will also, by thus furthering the most laudable, most ancient art, attain great renown, praise, and honour with everyone and especially with those who come after. And I too shall acknowledge it with all thankfulness in my works to be published, nor fail to praise it laudably. Herewith I faithfully commend Your Princely Grace, together with Your Princely Grace's much-beloved consort, to the gracious protection of the Almighty, unto long-lasting health and a peaceful reign.

Given at Rostock, the 29th of July, in the year 1597.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / document type.** The text is **Tycho Brahe's own retained copy** of a letter he sent, headed by the Latin rubric *COPIA LITERARUM MISSARUM AD DUCEM VLDARICUM* ("Copy of the letter sent to Duke Ulrich"); the code-switch into Latin for the archival rubric over a German body is preserved. The witness is a later copy in Langebek's Diplomatarium (Copenhagen, Rigsarkivet). No autograph original is cited.
- **Recipient.** *Duke Ulrich* = **Ulrich III of Mecklenburg** (Ulrich von Mecklenburg-Güstrow, 1527–1603), the senior reigning Duke of Mecklenburg, sovereign of the Baltic region of which **Rostock** was the chief city. The letter recalls that the Duke had years earlier honoured Tycho with a visit to **Hven** (Uraniborg). Tycho, who had departed Copenhagen for Rostock on 2 June 1597, here petitions the Duke for protection and patronage during his exile.
- **Context.** Written at the outset of Tycho's voluntary exile from Denmark. Frustrated under the new regime following King Frederik II's death (1588) and the minority/interregnum before Christian IV's effective majority, Tycho had abandoned Hven. The letter is at once a courtesy, an apologia (he insists his fatherland and king should not be reproached on his account), and a request for counsel on continuing his astronomical work — anticipating that it may have to be carried on **elsewhere in the Roman Empire** rather than in Denmark.
- **Honorific abbreviations.** *E:F:G:* = *Euer Fürstliche Gnaden*, "Your Princely Grace" — the standard address to a reigning duke; rendered consistently, the repeated honorific not abbreviated away. *Dero F: gnaden* = *Dero Fürstliche Gnaden*, "your princely grace/favour." *Durchleuchtiger hochgebornner Fürst* = "Most Serene, high-born Prince."
- **Latin code-switches within the German.** *studis* (= *studiis*, "studies"); *interregno* ("the interregnum," the period after Frederik II's death); *publicat … werden* and *publicandis operibus* ("published … / in my works to be published" — Latin *publicare*, Tycho's term for issuing his work to the public); *ad posteros continuirt* ("continued unto posterity [ad posteros]"). These macaronic Latin nouns/verbs in a German matrix are a chancery-letter feature; the Latin is kept and glossed.
- **Persons / places named.** *König Friderich(s) hochlöblicher gedechtnuß* = **King Frederik II of Denmark** (r. 1559–88), "of most laudable memory" (i.e. deceased), Tycho's patron who granted him Hven in 1576. *meinen gnedigsten Kunig* ("my most gracious king") = the reigning **Christian IV** (king from 1588, crowned 1596), unnamed. *Insell Huenna* = the island of **Hven**, site of Uraniborg. *Dennemarck* = Denmark; *Rostogk* = **Rostock**; *römisches Reich* = the **Holy Roman Empire** ("the Roman Empire"). *Deutschlandt* = Germany.
- ***die hochlöbliche, vhralte Kunst*** — "the most laudable, most ancient art," i.e. astronomy; *astronomische Sachen* = "astronomical matters." Tycho's instauration programme is in view ("the well-begun and nearly completed excellent work").
- **Negations (verified count).** The conditional clause beginning *Das im fhall es ie in Dennemarck über hoffnung hernacher nit meher gescheen solte, das sölche löbliche kunst alda gehandthabt vnd befurdert …* carries two negating elements — *nit meher* ("no longer") governing the whole protasis — translated "in case beyond hope it should hereafter no longer come to pass in Denmark that such a laudable art be there practised and furthered." The apodosis (*dennoch anderswo … erhalten … continuirt werden möge*) is positive: "it may nevertheless elsewhere … be preserved … and continued." The "not" attaches to the Danish-continuation clause only, not to the Empire clause; logic and count preserved. The earlier *hette giernne geheim, das keine notwendigkeit dieses verursacht* ("I would gladly have kept secret that no necessity caused this") likewise reproduces the single internal negation *keine* without addition.
- **Hedges preserved.** *die viell anders beschaffen, als vieleicht in gemein davonn magk geredet werden* ("which are constituted quite otherwise than perhaps may be commonly spoken of") and *vielleicht nictt woll wirt außgeleget* ("may perhaps not be well construed") keep Tycho's own *vieleicht*/*vielleicht* ("perhaps"); not sharpened.
- **Calendar.** *Datum Rostogk, den 29. jullij a:o 1597* = "Given at Rostock, the 29th of July, in the year 1597." Denmark and Mecklenburg both kept the **Julian calendar (Old Style)** in 1597; the date is O.S. The dateline agrees with the catalogue label (*1597. 29. juli. Rostock*); no discrepancy.
- **Orthography (Early New High German, c. 1597).** *vntherthenighe* = *untertänige* ("humble"); *behausung* = *Behausung* ("dwelling"); *gewirdiget* = *gewürdigt* ("deigned"); *bekostung* = *Bekostung* ("expense"); *haußgesinde* = *Hausgesinde* ("household servants/family"); *frembd machen* ("to make [oneself] a stranger/an exile"); *genotdrenget* = *genötdrängt/genötigt* ("constrained, driven"); *nach geredet* = *nachgeredet* ("said reproachfully, defamed"); *fhall* = *Fall* ("case"); *furschub* = *Fürschub* ("furtherance, support"); *gemallin* = *Gemahlin* ("consort, wife").
- **Correction.** Restored three literal German spellings to match Dreyer, TBOO XIV p.112: 'publicirt' (was 'publicat'), 'mittell' (was 'mitteil'), and the closing dateline 'Dattum' (was 'Datum'). None affects sense; the English required no changes.

text.original:
IACOBUS BORDINGUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

S.

REDDITÆ mihi sunt literæ tuæ, Vir Nobilissime, quibus significas, te patrium solum vertere coactum, et nunc Rostochij subsistere, quod etiam ex alijs iam pridem intellexeram. Doleo profecto non modo vices tuas, sed ingens quoque illud rerum Astronomicarum dispendium, quod ob hasce rerum tuarum inexpectatas conturbationes eventurum, unâ prævideo. Sed quid facias? cum hæc nulla tua culpa aut merito acciderint, nullumque in eo studio laborem, quantumvis gravem aut molestum, detrectâris, omnibus æquis censoribus facile excusatus eris. Verum de his aliquando coram plura. De Illustrissimi Principis mei in te clementi favore nihil est quod dubites. Literas tuas C. E. reverenter obtuli, ac curabo, ut non tantum ad illas responsum, sed etiam commendatorias ad Sereniss. Daniæ Regem intra biduum vel triduum accipias. Nunc enim tantum otij mihi non fuit, ut confici potuerint, nec etiam iusto diutius illos detinere volui, qui tuas attulerint. Quod reliquum est, officia mea tibi defero promptissima.

Vale.
Gustrovij die 2. Augusti Anno 1597.
T. studiosissimus
IACOBUS BORDINGUS.
text.english:
**Jacob Bording to Tycho Brahe.**

Greeting.

Your letter has been delivered to me, most noble Sir, in which you make known that you have been forced to leave your native soil and now reside at Rostock — a thing I had also long since learned from others. I grieve, indeed, not only over your own fortunes, but also over that immense loss to astronomical affairs which, together [with them], I foresee will come to pass on account of these unexpected disturbances of your circumstances. But what are you to do? Since these things have befallen through no fault or deserving of yours, and since you have shirked no labour in that pursuit, however heavy or troublesome, you will easily be excused in the eyes of all fair-minded judges. But of these matters, more at some time face to face. As to my Most Illustrious Prince's gracious favour towards you, there is nothing for you to doubt. I have reverently presented your letter to His Princely Grace [C. E.], and I shall see to it that within two or three days you receive not only a reply to it, but also a letter of recommendation to the Most Serene King of Denmark. For just now I had not so much leisure that they could be completed, nor did I wish to detain longer than was right those who brought your [letter]. For the rest, I tender you my most ready services.

Farewell.
At Güstrow, the 2nd day of August, the year 1597.
Most devoted to you,
Jacob Bording.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Iacobus Bordingus* = **Jacob Bording** (the Younger), physician (*Leibarzt*) at the Mecklenburg ducal court at Güstrow. He is the son of the better-known **Jacob Bording the Elder** (1511–1560), the Antwerp-born professor of medicine at Copenhagen and royal physician to Christian III of Denmark; the family thus had standing connections at the Danish court, which is precisely the leverage this letter exploits — Bording undertakes to procure a ducal letter of recommendation addressed to the Danish king on Tycho's behalf.
- **Recipient / situation.** **Tycho Brahe**, by August 1597 had left Hven and Denmark after the breakdown of his relations with the young **Christian IV** and the new royal council, and was lodging at **Rostock** (*Rostochij subsistere*) before moving on toward the Imperial court. *patrium solum vertere coactum* — "forced to leave [literally: to turn from] your native soil"; *solum vertere* is the classical legal idiom for going into exile, and Bording's diplomatic choice of it (rather than a blunter word) is preserved.
- ***Illustrissimi Principis mei*** — "my Most Illustrious Prince": Bording's master, the **Duke of Mecklenburg** resident at Güstrow, i.e. **Ulrich III** (1527–1603). Named only by title in the letter; the identification is supplied here.
- **C. E.** — the abbreviated honorific *Celsitudini Eius* / *Celsitudo Eius*, "His Highness / His Princely Grace," to whom Bording presented Tycho's letter. Expanded in the translation as "His Princely Grace [C. E.]," the abbreviation flagged rather than silently filled (cf. this chapter's convention, *Celsitudo* → "Highness"). The reading is secure in sense but the exact case-form behind the two letters is editorial.
- ***commendatorias*** (sc. *literas*) — "a letter of recommendation / commendatory letter," the ducal letter to the Danish king that is the practical object of the whole note.
- ***Sereniss. Daniae Regem*** — "the Most Serene King of Denmark," i.e. **Christian IV** (r. 1588–1648; assumed personal rule 1596). Title only; identified here.
- ***ingens illud rerum Astronomicarum dispendium*** — "that immense loss to astronomical affairs": Bording's foreboding that Tycho's exile will damage the science itself (*dispendium* = loss, detriment), not merely Tycho's personal fortune.
- **Salutation / subscription.** *S.* = *salutem* (dicit), "greeting". *Vale* = "Farewell." *T. studiosissimus* = *Tui studiosissimus*, "Most devoted to you" (the addressee being a private nobleman, not an "Excellency," the form is the plain *Tui* rather than *Excellentiae Tuae*; rendered "Most devoted to you" accordingly).
- **Calendar / place.** *Gustrovij die 2. Augusti Anno 1597* = "At **Güstrow**, the 2nd day of August, the year 1597" (O.S.; Mecklenburg, a Lutheran territory, still kept the Julian calendar in 1597). The dateline agrees exactly with the edition label (*1597. 2. august. Güstrow*); no date discrepancy. *biduum vel triduum* = "two or three days" (the Latin idiom for a span of two / three days), kept as the natural English.
- **Text witness.** The surviving authority is a later transcript (*Afskrift*) in **Langebek's Diplomatarium** (Copenhagen, Rigsarkivet), not an autograph; ordinary copyist orthography (*-ij* for *-ii*, *otij*, *alijs*; the printed *â/û* circumflexes mark ablatives/contractions). No reading affects the sense.

text.original:
DEM EDLEN VNND EHRENUESTEN VNNSERM LIEBEN BESONDERN TYCHONI BRAHE ZU [KNUDSTRUP], JETZO ZU ROSTOCK

VONN Gottes gnaden Vlrich, hertzogk zue Meckelburgk. Vnnsern gunstigen gruß vnd geneigten willen zuuor. Erenuester, lieber besonder, Wir haben ewer sc[h]reiben empfangen, vnnd darauß vngerne vermercket, das sich eine sulche Veranderung, alß jhr Vnnß darin zuerkennen geben, mit euch zugetragen, vnd Wir wol erachten können, das euch allerhande vngelegenheidt vnd beschwerung darauß entstehet, so tragen Wir zwar mit euch eine gnediges mitleiden, vnnd als Wir dan nitt allein selbst zuerinnern wißen, was Wir vor etlichen Jahren vor schöne instrumenta astronomica auff der jnsula Huen bey euch gesehen, sondern auch sonsten zum theil auß ewern in druck außgegeuen vnd Vns mitgetheilten operibus, zum theil aber auß anderer leutte bericht erfahren, wo hin jhr ferner ewer arbeitt gerichtet gehabt, so were dennoch wol zu wunschen, das jhr in der selben continuation an voriger ewer stelle hettet bleiben lasßen, vnd des wolangefangen werck zu glucklich endtschafft außfhuren mugen, wie Wir auch den euch derowegen bey verwantes kurtzes schreiben an die kön: w: zu Dennemarcken, Vnsern freundtlichen hertzvielgeliebten herrn son, mittheilen wollen, diesen einhalt ihr auß der abschriefst zuersehen, vnd Wir nun zu eweren bedencken stehen, ob eß euch dienstlich sein mochte, das jhr eß vbergeben lasßet oder nicht. Sonsten können Wir gar wolleiden, das ihr euch ewer gelegenheidt nach alda in Vnser stadt Rostogk auffhaltet biß zu andern ewer besßer beqvemlichheidt, dan Wir kein vrsachen wisßen, warumb Wir solches zu wiedern sein lasßen, welcher gestalt aber die von euch nun lange zeit hero getrieben astronomische sachen ferner dieser orter oder sonsten in Deutschlandt dergestaldt, wie es von euch nun edtlicher iher hero damit gehalten werden, möchten vergesetzt vnd nach notturft befordert werden konnen, darauf werdet jhr ohne zweiffel selbst wolgedacht haben. Sonsten musen woll bekennen, das eine grosßes dazu gehordt, vnnd in eines jeden vermugen nicht ist solche sachen außzufuhren, vnd das derowegen dieselben groser potentaten patrocinij vnnd befurderung wol bedurffen. Dieweil euch aber die gelegenheidt in Teudtschlandt beser bekendt, also das sie euch anzuteutten von notten, sintemal ihr selbst viele jahr darin zugebracht, so wertet ihr auch selbst zum besten wiesen, wes euch zu thun sein wil. Haben euch zue gnedigsten antwort nicht verhalten wollen, vnd Wir sein mit gnaden wolgewogen.

Datum Gustrow, den 4. augustij anno 1597.
Vlrich h: z: Meckelburgk.
text.english:
**To the noble and honourable, our trusty and well-beloved Tycho Brahe of [Knudstrup], now at Rostock.**

Ulrich, by the grace of God Duke of Mecklenburg. Our gracious greeting and favourable goodwill beforehand. Honourable, [our] well-beloved, We have received your letter, and from it noted with displeasure that such a change as you give Us to understand therein has befallen you; and We can well judge that all manner of inconvenience and hardship arises for you from it. We do indeed bear you a gracious compassion; and inasmuch as We not only know of Our own recollection what fine astronomical instruments [*instrumenta astronomica*] We saw with you some years ago on the island of Hven, but have also learned, partly from your works [*opera*] put out in print and communicated to Us, partly from other people's report, whither you had further directed your work, it were nonetheless much to be wished that you had let yourself remain in the continuation of the same in your former place, and might have carried the well-begun work through to a happy conclusion — as We, accordingly, are also minded to communicate to you herewith by an enclosed short letter to His Royal Dignity of Denmark, Our friendly and heartily-beloved lord [and] son, the content of which you are to see from the copy; and We now leave it to your consideration whether it might be of service to you that you have it delivered, or not. For the rest, We can very well suffer that you, as your circumstances require, lodge there in Our city of Rostock until [you find] another, better convenience for yourself, for We know no reason why We should let this be opposed; but in what manner the astronomical matters carried on by you now this long while past might further, in these parts or otherwise in Germany, be set forth and promoted according to need, in the way they have now for several years been conducted by you — on that you will doubtless yourself have well reflected. For the rest, We must indeed confess that a great deal is required thereto, and that it is not within everyone's power to carry such matters through, and that they therefore have good need of the patronage and furtherance of great potentates. But since the circumstances [or opportunities] in Germany are better known to you — so that to point them out to you [is] needful, ‹seeing› that you yourself have spent many years therein — you will also yourself best know what is for you to do. We have not wished to withhold from you [this] as a most gracious answer, and We are graciously well-disposed [towards you].

Given at Güstrow, the 4th of August, year 1597.
Ulrich, Duke of Mecklenburg.
