documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Ulrich III, Duke of Mecklenburg[-Güstrow]** (1527–1603), reigning from Güstrow. He was the father of **Sophie of Mecklenburg**, queen of Denmark (wife of Frederik II), and hence the maternal grandfather of **Christian IV**; this kinship governs the letter's diplomatic offer (see below). The edition's heuristic tags the letter *de* — correct here: this is genuine chancery German, not German-orthography Danish.
- **Recipient address.** *"…TYCHONI BRAHE ZU [KNUDSTRUP], JETZO ZU ROSTOCK"* — "Tycho Brahe of [Knudstrup], now at Rostock." **[KNUDSTRUP]** is bracketed in the source as printed by Dreyer (the place is supplied editorially / partly illegible in the apograph). Knudstrup (Knutstorp, Skåne) was the Brahe family seat. The letter dates from the months after Tycho's self-imposed departure from Denmark (spring 1597) and his stay at Rostock before moving on toward Imperial patronage; "the change that has befallen you" is his loss of the Hven establishment.
- **Recipient as instrument-maker's patron and witness.** *"schöne instrumenta astronomica auff der jnsula Huen"* — Ulrich recalls having himself seen Tycho's fine **astronomical instruments** on Hven; *operibus … in druck außgegeuen vnd Vns mitgetheilten* = "your works put out in print and communicated to Us," i.e. presentation copies (the *Mechanica*, the *Epistolae*, the *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* in progress). Latin technical nouns code-switched into the German body (*instrumenta astronomica, opera/operibus, continuation, patrocinij*) are preserved by this chapter's convention; *instrumenta* rendered "instruments" by this chapter's convention
- **"die kön: w: zu Dennemarcken … Vnsern … herrn son."** *kön: w:* = *königliche Würde*, "His/Her Royal Dignity"; the king is **Christian IV** (r. 1588–1648). Ulrich calls him *"Vnsern freundtlichen hertzvielgeliebten herrn son"* — literally "our friendly, heartily-beloved lord [and] son." In strict relationship Christian IV was Ulrich's **grandson through his daughter** (Sophie); Dreyer's heading to the immediately following letter (no. 128, the enclosed letter itself) glosses it *"ad Christianum IV regem, nepotem ex filia"* ("to King Christian IV, his grandson through [his] daughter"), and in that letter Ulrich writes of *"den grosvaterlichen verwantnus"* ("the grandfatherly kinship"). "Son" is therefore the loose princely-courtesy register, not a literal filiation; rendered "lord [and] son" with the bracketed *[and]* marking the editorial reading of the asyndeton, and the true relationship recorded here rather than substituted into the text.
- **The enclosed intercession.** Ulrich offers Tycho an enclosed *"kurtzes schreiben"* of intercession to the Danish crown (the *abschriefst* / copy Tycho is given), leaving it to Tycho's discretion *"ob eß euch dienstlich sein mochte, das jhr eß vbergeben lasßet oder nicht"* = "whether it might be of service to you that you have it delivered, or not." The disjunction *oder nicht* is preserved.
- **Negations / conditional force (checked, by the audit's rule).** Six negations in the body, all reproduced: *nitt allein … sondern auch* ("not only … but also," correlative); *kein vrsachen … warumb Wir solches zu wiedern sein lasßen* ("no reason why We should let this be opposed"); *in eines jeden vermugen nicht ist* ("it is not within everyone's power"); *oder nicht* (above); *nicht verhalten wollen* ("have not wished to withhold"). The closing *"Haben euch … nicht verhalten wollen"* is the standard chancery litotes ("we did not wish to keep [this answer] from you"), kept literal.
- ***bey verwantes … schreiben*** — *verwantes* here = *verwandt(es)* in the chancery sense "enclosed / appended," not "related (by kin)"; rendered "an enclosed … letter."
- **Place / calendar.** *Güstrow* — the Mecklenburg-Güstrow residence town. *Datum Güstrow, den 4. augustij anno 1597* — 4 August 1597, **Old Style** (Mecklenburg, like Denmark, kept the Julian calendar; the dateline year 1597 matches the catalogue label). The working transcription gives *anno 1597*; the Dreyer page image abbreviates *anno 97* — no substantive difference.
- **Textual crux (governs the grade).** *"Dieweil euch aber die gelegenheidt in Teudtschlandt beser bekendt, also das sie euch anzuteutten von notten, sintemal ihr selbst viele jahr darin zugebracht."* As transmitted (and as printed by Dreyer from the Langebek **apograph**), the clause reads literally "so that to point them out to you [is] needful, seeing that you yourself have spent many years therein" — but the *sintemal* ("seeing that / since") clause supplies a reason for the **opposite** sense ("there is **no** need to point them out to you, since you have spent many years there"). The expected *nicht* (*… euch anzuteutten **nicht** von nöten*) is **absent** from the source; the witness is a later copy (*Afskrift / apographum*), so a copyist's omission of *nicht* is the most economical explanation. **By this chapter's convention the missing negation is not silently supplied:** the translation renders the words as they stand and brackets nothing into the negative; the intended meaning ("no need to point them out") is recorded here only. The ‹seeing› in angle brackets marks *sintemal* rendered as the subordinator.

documents.incipit: DURCHLEUCHTIGSTER, grosmechtiger könig. E: K: M: seindt Vnsere freundtliche willige …

text.original:
ANN DEN KÖNIG ZU DENNEMARCK.

DURCHLEUCHTIGSTER, grosmechtiger könig. E: K: M: seindt Vnsere freundtliche willige dienste, vnd was Wir den grosvaterlichen verwantnus nach jederzeitt mehr liebs vnnd gutts vermagen zuvor. Freundtlicher hertzviellgeliebter sohnn, Vns hatt der ehrnuester Vnser lieber besonder Tycho Brahe vnderthenig zuerkennen gegeben, welcher masen er aus hochwichtigen vrsagen, welche Vns doch allerdinge nicht bekant, mit groser seiner vngelegenheitt vndt beschwerung sich aus E: K: M: königreiche Dennemarcken, seinen lieben vatterlande, begeben, vnd sich eine zeittlangk in Vnser stadt Rostogk niederlasen musen, mitt ferner vndertheniger fleisiger bitte, Wir wolthen Vns daselbige nitt zu wieder, zondern viellmer jhnn zu gnaden Vns befolen sein lasen. Wann Wir nun aber bey Vns leichtlich abnehmen konnen, das durch solche seine verenderung, die von jhme nicht alleinn woll angefangene, sondern auch bereitts so viel jahre hero getriebene vnd befurderte löbliche astronomische sachen, dermasen nicht vollends continuiret werden könen, wie ers jhme woll furgenommen, vnd Wir aber solches vor Vnsere persohn, weill Wir es dafur achten, das auch dardurch E: K: M: königreiche ann dem grosen ruhm vndt nahmen, so es bisshero solcher herlichen kunst halben gehabt, ettwas abgehen muchte nicht gernne schehen; alß haben Wir dem nach E: K: W: hier ann freundtlicher gutter wollmeinung erjneren wollen, mitt gandske freundtlicher bitte, E: K: W: wolte nicht geschehen lasen, das gedachtes werck so plötzlich in ein abnehmen kommen, sondern vielmher dero in Gott ruhenden herren vatters, lobsehliger vndt christmilder gedechtnus, vndt aller reichs ratte beschlus ferner nachsetzen, vndt gedacten Tychonem Brahe alls einem furtreffentlichen vndt ihn der astronomia der masen erfaren vndt wolluerdienten mann, daß seines gleichen nictt leichtlich zu finden, do sonsten E: K: W: keinne erhebliche vrsachen hetten, worumb es nicht geschehen köntte, ann voriger ordt gnedigst restituiren. Welchs dann ohne zweiffell E: K: W: und dero gandzen königereich zu mher ruhm vnd ehrenn, wie es auch zu dem ende von ihm angefangen, vnd biß dahero mit groser muhe vndt arbeitt so weitt getrieben, das es keiner ihm baldt nachthun wirt, gereichen wurde. Wir geschweigen, das ermeltes Tychonis studium in astronomia auch fast in allen landen also bekandt vndt berhumet ist, das es pilligk gutter befurderung woll wirdigk, vndt weill Wir ihme dann auch sonsten mit gnaden vnd aller gutter wollgewogen, so bitten Wir dahero vmb so viellmher gandz freundtlich E: K: W: wolle diese Vnsere commendationn vndt intercession nicht anders als ihm besten vermercken vndt auffnehmen. Vnd Wir seindt E:K:W: jederzeit zu aller angenehmen freundtlichen willfahrung vndt grossvatterlichen dienst ertzeigung geneigt vnd gandz willigk.

Datum Gustruoe den 4. augusti anno 97.
Vonn Gottis gnaden Vlrich hertzog
zu Meckelnburgk, furst zu Wenden,
graffe zu Schwerin,
der lande Rostogk
vnd Stargard herr.
text.english:
**To the King of Denmark.**

Most Serene, mighty King. Our friendly, willing service to Your Royal Majesty beforehand, and whatever more of love and good we are at all times able [to render], in keeping with our grandfatherly kinship. Friendly, heartily well-beloved son: the honourable man, Our trusty and well-beloved Tycho Brahe, has humbly made known to Us how, for weighty reasons — which, however, are not at all known to Us — he has, with great inconvenience and hardship to himself, departed from Your Royal Majesty's kingdom of Denmark, his dear fatherland, and has had to settle himself for a time in Our city of Rostock; with the further humble, earnest petition that We would not take this amiss of him, but rather hold him commended to Us in [Our] grace. Now since We can readily judge for Ourselves that, by such a removal of his, the praiseworthy astronomical works — which he has not only well begun, but has now for so many years pursued and advanced — cannot be brought to full completion in the way he had well purposed; and since, for Our own part, We should not gladly see this happen, because We hold it that thereby Your Royal Majesty's kingdom might lose something of the great renown and name which it has hitherto had on account of that splendid art: therefore We have wished herein to remind Your Royal Worship in friendly, good intent, with quite friendly petition, that Your Royal Worship would not let it come to pass that the said work should so suddenly fall into decline, but rather should further give effect to the resolve of your lord father — of laudable and Christian-gracious memory, now resting in God — and of the whole Council of the Realm, and most graciously restore the said Tycho Brahe — as an excellent man, so experienced and so well-deserving in astronomy that his like is not easily to be found — to his former place, provided Your Royal Worship have not otherwise weighty reasons why it might not be done. This would then, without doubt, redound to the greater renown and honour of Your Royal Worship and of your whole kingdom — even as it was begun by him to that end, and has hitherto, with great toil and labour, been carried so far that none will soon match him in it. We say nothing of the fact that the said Tycho's pursuit of astronomy is so well known and renowned in well-nigh all lands that it is rightly well worthy of good furtherance; and since We are besides graciously and in all good will disposed towards him, We therefore beg all the more, quite in friendship, that Your Royal Worship would mark and receive this Our commendation and intercession in no other way than for the best. And We are at all times inclined and quite willing to show Your Royal Worship every agreeable, friendly compliance and grandfatherly rendering of service.

Given at Güstrow, the 4th of August in the year [15]97.
By the grace of God, Ulrich, Duke of Mecklenburg, Prince of [the] Wends, Count of Schwerin, Lord of the lands of Rostock and Stargard.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Ulrich III, Duke of Mecklenburg[-Güstrow]** (1527–1603), reigning from Güstrow. He was the maternal grandfather of the recipient: his daughter **Sophie of Mecklenburg** was the queen consort of Frederik II and the mother of Christian IV. Hence the repeated *grosvaterlich / grossvatterlich* ("grandfatherly") register and the address of the King as *sohnn* ("son," i.e. grandson) throughout — the literal kinship governs the letter's tone.
- **Recipient.** **Christian IV of Denmark** (r. 1588–1648; assumed personal rule 1596). The *herren vatter … in Gott ruhenden* whose resolve Ulrich invokes is his late father **Frederik II** (d. 1588), who had granted Tycho the island of Hven in 1576.
- **Subject.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), who had left Denmark in spring 1597 and settled for a time at **Rostock** (the Mecklenburg city, named in the text as *Vnser stadt Rostogk*). This is the intercessory cover-letter Ulrich enclosed when forwarding to his grandson a petition from Tycho, requesting that the King restore Tycho to his "former place" (Hven and his Danish appointments). It matches the companion piece in the edition, Tycho → Duke Ulrich, Rostock, 29 July 1597 (brahe-t_15970729001), which Ulrich is here answering and relaying.
- **Document type.** A surviving copy (*Afskrift*) in Langebek's Diplomatarium; the heading *ANN DEN KÖNIG ZU DENNEMARCK* ("To the King of Denmark") is the chancery docket, not part of the salutation.
- **Honorific abbreviations.** *E: K: M:* = *Eurer Königlichen Majestät* ("Your Royal Majesty"); *E: K: W:* = *Eurer Königlichen Würde(n)* ("Your Royal Worship/Dignity"). The letter switches register from the higher *Majestät* in the opening address to the slightly more familiar *Würde* in the body; the distinction is preserved in the translation ("Your Royal Majesty" vs. "Your Royal Worship") rather than levelled.
- **Chancery formulae.** *Vnser lieber besonder* (= *unser lieber besonder[er]*) = "Our trusty and well-beloved" (the princely address-formula for a favoured subject/client). *commendationn vndt intercession* — the two Latin technical nouns *commendatio* and *intercessio* are code-switched into the German, the standard diplomatic terms for a letter of recommendation/formal plea on another's behalf; kept and rendered "commendation and intercession."
- **Orthography (Early New High German chancery, c. 1597).** *seindt* = *sind*; *vnd/vndt/vnnd* = *und*; *Wir/Vns/Vnser* (majuscule) = the princely first-person; *jhnn/jhme/ihm* = *ihn/ihm*; *zondern* = *sondern*; *gandske / gandz / gandzen* = *ganz(e)* ("quite, whole"); *muchte / köntte* = *möchte / könnte* (subjunctive); *vrsagen* = *Ursachen* ("reasons"); *schehen / geschehen* = "happen / come to pass"; *abnehmen* (noun) = "decline, falling-off"; *restituiren* = restore (Latinate); *furtreffentlich* = *vortrefflich* ("excellent"); *wolluerdient* = *wohlverdient* ("well-deserving"); *berhumet* = *berühmt* ("renowned"); *pilligk / wirdigk / willigk* = *billig / würdig / willig*.
- **Negation check.** The two double-negative courtesy constructions are rendered with their full logic preserved, not simplified: (1) *Wir wolthen Vns daselbige nitt zu wieder … lasen* = "We would not take this amiss" (Tycho's plea that the Duke not resent his settling at Rostock); (2) the petition that the King *wolte nicht geschehen lasen, das gedachtes werck so plötzlich in ein abnehmen kommen* = "would not let it come to pass that the said work should so suddenly fall into decline." The conditional escape-clause *do sonsten E: K: W: keinne erhebliche vrsachen hetten, worumb es nicht geschehen köntte* is a deliberately deferential double negative — "provided Your Royal Worship have not otherwise weighty reasons why it might not be done" — leaving the King's discretion intact; its mood and polarity are reproduced exactly.
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Datum Gustruoe … den 4. augusti anno 97* = "Given at **Güstrow** [the Mecklenburg ducal seat], the 4th of August in the year [15]97" (O.S.; Denmark and Mecklenburg both still on the Julian calendar). The edition *label* date (1597. 4. august. Güstrow) agrees with the dateline; no header/label discrepancy. **The intrusive "35" between "Gustruoe" and "den 4. augusti"** is unexplained in the source text — almost certainly a register/folio number or copyist's marginal numeral absorbed into the line of the Langebek *Afskrift*, not a calendar element. It is reproduced verbatim in the Source block and bracketed "[35,]" in the translation rather than silently dropped or "corrected" into the date; this is the one flagged crux.
- **Titulature.** The subscription styles Ulrich *furst zu Wenden, graffe zu Schwerin, der lande Rostogk vnd Stargard herr* — "Prince of [the] Wends, Count of Schwerin, Lord of the lands of Rostock and Stargard," the standard secondary titles of the Mecklenburg dukes; rendered in full per this chapter's princely-titulature rule.
- **Correction.** Removed a stray "35" from the closing dateline: Dreyer's printed text reads simply "Datum Guftrue den 4. augufti anno 97" (TBOO XIV p.114); the digit was Dreyer's own marginal line-count, wrongly absorbed into the transcription and then into the translation as a bracketed "[35,]".

documents.incipit: Literæ tuæ eruditissimæ pariter ac humanissimæ, cognate optime, amoris eximij erga me …

text.original:
MAGNIFICO ET AMPLISSIMO VIRO, NOBILITATE GENERIS ET ERUDITIONIS ADMODUM CONSPICUO D:NO ERICO SPARRE, SER:MI SVECIÆ REGIS CANCELLARIO AC CONSILIARIO PRUDENTISSIMO, LIBERO BARONI IN N., COGNATO ATQVE AMICO SUO INPRIMIS HONORANDO.
S. P. D.

Literæ tuæ eruditissimæ pariter ac humanissimæ, cognate optime, amoris eximij erga me testes, ijs ipsis diebus, quibus Haffnia relicta in Germaniam migrandum erat mihi, redditæ sunt. Verum enimvero, tunc rebus meis ad abitum adornandis ita distrahebar, tum quoque amicis ob abitum invisentibus præpediebar, ut, licet nihil magis mihi in votis fuerit, attamen temporis iniquitas omnem scribendi occasionem præriperet. Postquam vero huc Rostochium appuli, atque hic certis de caussis, quemadmodum et antea Haffniæ per integrum anni quadrantem substiti (præsertim, quo nostratibus, si pænitere ipsos admissi erroris posset, deliberatius rem expendendi tempus concederem, neve nimis præpropere ardua, quæ tracto, studia alio transtulisse viderer), ne hic quidem aptior scribendi facultas, contra quam opinabar, oblata fuit, cum nullum iter ad confinia utriusque regni parantem nancisci liceret. Accessit et hoc, quod nescio quis rumor, utrum te inde in Sueciam interiorem vel Poloniam ad s:m vestrum regem te recepisses, incertum me redderet. Cumque eo nomine celeberrimum virum d. Davidem Chytræum, huius academiæ antesignanum, honorifica, prout virtus merebatur, nominis tui mentione compellassem, siquidem eum crebro de rebus regnorum illorum a multis edoceri scirem, et inter te ac ipsum alias commutari literas inaudivissem, attamen dubium, quod animo conceperam, eximere non potuit. Jtaque scribendi officium adhuc paulo diutius differendum censui, donec, ubinam locorum morareris, certo mihi innotesceret. Cum vero ne sic quidem profecerim, et longiores in hac urbe moras nectere, nec mihi commodum, nec etiam ob ingravescentem indies pestem consultum sit, propediem ad magnificum dominum Henricum Ranzovium, affinem et amicum meum singularem, perbenigne ab eodem invitatus, me conferre statui, isthic moraturus, donec rebus meis ulterius ex divino provisu prospexero. Quocirca aliquid ante meum hinc abitum literarum ad te omnino dandum ratus sum, ea spe fretus posse id ad communem utrique necessarium Gabrielem Sparre directum, ubicunque tandem locorum hæreres, commodum tibi transmitti.

Desiderium tui cognoscendi et compellandi, non saltem ob sanguinis coniunctionem, sed etiam ob suspiciendam virtutem ac eruditionem tuam pari rerum usu auctam me quoque iampridem incesserat, ut hoc votum explendi copiam sive in Dania sive alibi fata hactenus invidisse admodum moleste feram. Nunc vero cum magis magisque disiungamur et mihi patrium solum vertere ac alias in exteris regionibus commoditates quærere necessum fuerit, omnem spem alloquij tui mihi ereptam video et quam maxime doleo. Caussæ vero, quæ me huc adegerunt, tot tantæque fuerunt, ut calamo eas exprimere vix valeam, neque etiamnum tutum arbitrer. Qui magni viri haberi cupiunt, licet graviter nonnunquam impingant, tamen nec errores agnoscere volunt, nec in ijs redargui. Satis equidem mature hanc mutationem prævidi, nihilque prius habui, quam ut eam quovis pacto præcaverem et averterem, literis idcirco ad s:mi regis nostri cancellarium datis (quarum hic exemplum adiunxi), sed successu prorsus irrito. Nihil enim impetrare licuit, imo inter alia responsum, regi nostro quidquam sumptuum in jnstrumentorum meorum astronomiæ conservationem impendere integrum non esse. An vero ex regis ipsius voluntate vel alterius privato affectu idque eo prætextu promanaverit, non dixerim. Nec verbis eventus defuit. Nam non tantum feudo illo Norvagico, cuius in literis fit mentio, confestim post coronationem regiam peractam adempto contenti non fuerunt ij, qui fatis reipublicæ in Dania nunc præsunt; sed et reliqua omnia ab optimo rege Frederico l. m. in artis vere regiæ sustentationem deputata subtraxerunt, et simul senatorum regni literas, artis eius liberalem conservationem perpetuamque spondentes non respexerunt; licet quidam adeoque præcipuus eorum has una subsignarit et subscripserit; quin etiam canonicatum Roskyldensem (quem solum habui residuum) dictus cancellarius sibi acquirere ac in proprium commodum vertere non dubitavit. Tantum abest, ut artis adeo præclaræ et patriæ nostræ forte non inhonorificæ continuationem et perpetuationem pro virili (uti decuit) promovere voluerit. Scripsit autem non ita pridem illustrissimus dux Uldaricus, s:mi regis nostri avus, ad ipsum regem atque artis huius in integrum istinc restitutionem diligenter suasit. Quibus literis et meas addideram, etiamnum operam meam s:mo regi nostro et patriæ in perficienda isthic astronomiæ instauratione, quam tam diu tantisque conatibus molitus sum, per eas submisse offerens, modo id commodum exequi liceat et indemnitati meæ consulatur. Sin vero nihil his effectum fuerit, quod priora ac inconsulta quorundam consilia emendet (uti sperare vix licet, idque non tam ob ipsius s:mi regis nostri animum per se satis generosum et integrum, quam eorum, qui nunc soli quidvis pro arbitrio moderari volunt, aversam voluntatem), mox ad jmperatoriam ma:tem aliosque viciniores reges ac præcipuos Germaniæ principes scribere decrevi, et quid clementis eorum circa artis tam sublimis ulteriorem sustentationem voluntatis ac arbitrij sit, experiri. Vtrum videlicet quidpiam sumptuum ad hoc subministrare velint, quo ea in publicum reipublicæ literariæ emolumentum perfectior quam unquam antea, prodeat, atque orbi communicetur. Quo etiam nomine potentissimum vestrum regem Sigismundum submisse sollicitare proposui, si (uti spem concepi) ipsius m:tas, ut est erga ingenuas artes, cum et his ipsamet imbuta sit, benificentissima, hanc etiam curam et laudem cæteris addendam, suaque regia munificentia dignam censeat. Posset forte aliqua ex jnsulis Prussiæ vicinis commoditatem huic negotio præbere, vel id quocunque alio modo fieri, prout ipsius m:ti visum foret. Qua in re tuum prudens cum auxilio consilium, mi amicissime cognate, obnixe peto et expecto, an videlicet hoc studium astronomicum ipsius ma:ti offerendum, et an idem cum magno quoque cancellario communicandum putes; et utrum specifice jnsula Dalan prope Rigam, vel Bornhovium, aut jnsula Werden prope Dantiscum, similesve loci nominandi nec ne, vel quavis alia ratione quidpiam, quod utile foret, tentandum. Jdque eo audentius a te peto, quod in literis tuis, singulari benevolentia refertis, tale quid sponte offerre videris, dum officia mihi et studia tua, hoc præsertim tempore perbenigne ac amice addicis. Ego, si nihil aliud de me polliceri possum, hoc certe sponsum volo, me ex eorum numero, qui virtutes tuas et eruditionem maximi faciunt et colunt, si non primas tenentem, saltem nemini concedentem fore, et ipso ad minimum animo tua erga me officia pro virili compensaturum.

Vale mi charissime cognate et me (quod te facturum nihil ambigo) redamare perge.
Datæ Rostochij pridie eius diei, qua inde discedere constitui, 7:a nimirum septembris stylo veteri anni etc. 1597.
Tui studiosiss.
Tycho Brahe
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the magnificent and most worthy man, by nobility of birth and of learning altogether distinguished, Master Erik Sparre, Chancellor and most prudent Councillor to the Most Serene King of Sweden, free baron in N., his kinsman and friend especially to be honoured. [Tycho Brahe] sends heartiest greeting.**

Your letter, most learned and likewise most kind, best of kinsmen, a witness of your singular love towards me, was delivered to me in those very days on which, Copenhagen left behind, I was to remove into Germany. But in truth I was then so distracted with setting my affairs in order for departure, and likewise so hindered by friends calling on me on account of that departure, that — although nothing was more in my prayers [than to write] — the unkindness of the time nevertheless snatched away every opportunity of writing. And after I had put in here at Rostock, and for certain reasons stopped here (as also earlier at Copenhagen) for a whole quarter of a year — chiefly that I might grant my countrymen a more deliberate time for weighing the matter, in case they could come to repent of the wrong committed, and that I might not seem to have transferred elsewhere too headlong the arduous studies I am engaged in — not even here was a fitter chance of writing offered to me, contrary to my expectation, since I could find no one preparing a journey to the borders of either kingdom. To this was added that some rumour or other left me uncertain whether you had withdrawn from there into the interior of Sweden or into Poland to your Most Serene King. And although on that account I had addressed that most celebrated man Master David Chytraeus, the foremost figure of this university, with honourable mention of your name (as your worth deserved) — since I knew him to be often informed by many about the affairs of those kingdoms, and had heard that letters were on other occasions exchanged between you and him — yet he could not remove the doubt I had conceived in my mind. And so I judged that the duty of writing must be put off a little longer still, until it should become certainly known to me in what place you were staying. But since I have made no progress even so, and since to weave longer delays in this city is neither convenient for me nor, on account of the plague growing heavier by the day, advisable, I have resolved very shortly to betake myself to the magnificent Master Henrik Rantzau, my kinsman by marriage and my especial friend, most kindly invited by him, intending to stay there until, by divine providence, I shall have provided further for my affairs. On which account I have thought I must by all means give you some letter before my departure hence, relying on this hope, that it may conveniently be transmitted to you, directed to Gabriel Sparre, the kinsman necessary to us both, wherever in the end you may be lodged.

A longing to know you and to address you had long since come upon me too — not merely on account of the bond of blood, but also on account of your virtue, to be looked up to, and your learning, augmented by a matching experience of affairs — so that I bear it most grievously that the fates have hitherto begrudged me the chance of fulfilling this wish, whether in Denmark or elsewhere. But now, when we are parted more and more, and when it has been necessary for me to turn from my native soil and seek other conveniences in foreign regions, I see every hope of conversing with you snatched away from me, and I grieve at it as much as may be. The causes, indeed, that have driven me hither were so many and so great that I can scarcely express them with the pen, nor do I even now judge it safe. Those who desire to be held great men, though they sometimes strike grievously against [the truth], yet are unwilling either to acknowledge their errors or to be refuted in them. Early enough, to be sure, did I foresee this change, and I held nothing more important than to guard against and avert it by any means whatsoever — letters being therefore sent to the Chancellor of our Most Serene King (of which I have appended a copy here) — but with an outcome entirely vain. For nothing could be obtained; nay, among other things [came] the reply that it was not open to our King to expend any costs upon the maintenance of my instruments of astronomy. But whether this issued from the King's own will, or from another's private feeling and under that pretext, I would not say. Nor was the deed wanting to the words. For not only were those who now preside over the destinies of the commonwealth in Denmark not content with that Norwegian fief — of which mention is made in the letters — being taken away immediately after the royal coronation had been carried through; but they also withdrew all the rest that had been assigned by that best of kings, Frederick of blessed memory, for the support of the truly royal art, and at the same time gave no regard to the letters of the senators of the realm, pledging the generous and perpetual maintenance of that art — although a certain one, and indeed the chief of them, had countersigned and subscribed these together [with the others]; nay more, the said Chancellor did not hesitate to acquire for himself the canonry of Roskilde (the only thing I had left remaining) and to turn it to his own profit. So far was he from being willing to promote with his whole strength (as was fitting) the continuation and perpetuation of an art so illustrious and perhaps not without honour to our fatherland. Not long ago, however, the Most Illustrious Duke Ulrich, grandfather of our Most Serene King, wrote to the King himself and diligently urged the full restoration of this art there. To which letter I had also added my own, even now through them submissively offering my service to our Most Serene King and to the fatherland in completing there the restoration of astronomy, which I have laboured at so long and with such great efforts — provided only it may be allowed to carry it out conveniently and that my own indemnity be cared for. But if nothing shall be effected by these [letters] to mend the earlier and ill-considered counsels of certain persons (as one may scarcely hope, and that not so much on account of the disposition of our Most Serene King himself, of itself sufficiently generous and upright, as on account of the averse will of those who now alone wish to manage everything at their own pleasure), I have resolved presently to write to His Imperial Majesty and to other nearer kings and to the chief princes of Germany, and to learn what their gracious will and pleasure may be concerning the further support of so sublime an art — namely, whether they are willing to furnish any costs towards this, that it may come forth more perfect than ever before for the public benefit of the republic of letters, and be communicated to the world. On which account, too, I have proposed humbly to solicit your most powerful King Sigismund — if (as I have conceived hope) His Majesty, being most beneficent towards the liberal arts, since he is himself imbued with them too, should judge that this care and praise also is to be added to the rest, and worthy of his royal munificence. Perhaps some one of the islands neighbouring Prussia might afford a convenient place for this business, or it might be done in whatever other way, as should seem good to His Majesty. In which matter I earnestly seek and await your prudent counsel together with your help, my most friendly kinsman — namely, whether you think this astronomical pursuit is to be offered to His Majesty, and whether the same is to be communicated also with the Grand Chancellor; and whether specifically the island of Dalan near Riga, or Bornholm [Bornhovium], or the island of Werden near Danzig, or similar places are to be named or not, or whether by some other plan something should be attempted that would be useful. And this I ask of you the more boldly because in your letter, filled with singular goodwill, you seem to offer such a thing of your own accord, when you most kindly and amicably pledge your services and devotion to me, especially at this time. As for me, if I can promise nothing else of myself, this at least I would have pledged: that of the number of those who esteem and cherish your virtues and learning most highly I shall be, if not holding the first place, at any rate yielding to none; and that, in mind at the very least, I shall requite with all my strength your services towards me.

Farewell, my dearest kinsman, and continue to love me in return (which I do not at all doubt you will do).
Given at Rostock, on the day before that on which I have determined to depart hence — namely on the 7th of September, Old Style, in the year, etc., 1597.
Most devoted to you,
Tycho Brahe
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), writing from Rostock during his self-imposed exile, three months after leaving Hven (he had departed Copenhagen for Rostock in mid-1597 and would move to Henrik Rantzau's castle at Wandsbek that October). The letter is a candid appeal to a Swedish kinsman for help in finding a new royal patron after the loss of his Danish support.
- **Recipient.** *Ericus Sparre* = **Erik Sparre** (1550–1600), the learned Swedish High Chancellor and royalist statesman, partisan of King Sigismund III against the regent Duke Karl (later Charles IX). He had passed through Denmark in March 1597 fleeing Duke Karl, heading for Sigismund's court; he was executed in the Linköping Bloodbath of 1600. *liber baro in N.* — "free baron in N." — the place-name is abbreviated to a bare initial in the address (left as "N." in both source and translation).
- **Address / salutation.** *S. P. D.* = *salutem plurimam dicit*, "sends heartiest greeting"; the sender's name is implicit in the formula and supplied in brackets.
- ***cognatus*** — "kinsman." Tycho repeatedly addresses Sparre as *cognate* (the Brahe and Sparre families were related); kept consistently as "kinsman."
- **David Chytraeus** — *Davidem Chytraeum, huius academiae antesignanum* = David Chytraeus (1530–1600), the eminent Lutheran theologian and historian, leading figure ("standard-bearer," *antesignanus*) of the University of Rostock, where Tycho was then residing.
- **Henrik Rantzau** — *Henricum Ranzovium, affinem et amicum meum singularem* = **Henrik Rantzau** (Heinrich Rantzau, 1526–1598), Statthalter of the Danish king in Holstein, humanist and astrologer, Tycho's friend and kinsman by marriage (*affinis*), who invited Tycho to his Wandsbek castle near Hamburg.
- **Gabriel Sparre** — a kinsman common to both correspondents (*communem utrique necessarium*), proposed as the intermediary for forwarding the letter; the Latin *necessarium* here in the legal/familial sense "close relation/connection," rendered "kinsman."
- **The "letters to the Chancellor of our King" and the appended copy.** *literis … ad s:mi regis nostri cancellarium datis (quarum hic exemplum adiunxi)* — Tycho had petitioned **Christian IV**'s chancellor and enclosed a copy with this letter. *s:mi regis nostri* (Most Serene King "of ours") = the **Danish** king, Christian IV, throughout; *s:m vestrum regem* / *vestrum regem Sigismundum* (King "of yours") = **Sigismund III** of Sweden and Poland. The possessives carefully distinguish Tycho's sovereign from Sparre's.
- ***cancellarius* / *dictus cancellarius*** — the Danish chancellor is **Christian Friis** (of Borreby, 1556–1616), royal chancellor under Christian IV; by an executive order of June 1597 Tycho's **Roskilde canonry** was transferred from Tycho to Friis. *canonicatum Roskyldensem (quem solum habui residuum)* = "the canonry of Roskilde (the only thing I had left remaining)" — the prebend of the Three Holy Kings (the Magi) in Roskilde Cathedral, which Tycho had held until 1597.
- ***feudo illo Norvagico … confestim post coronationem regiam peractam adempto*** — "that Norwegian fief … taken away immediately after the royal coronation had been carried through": Tycho's Norwegian fief of Nordfjord, withdrawn after Christian IV's coronation (29 August 1596). *cuius in literis fit mentio* — "of which mention is made in the [appended] letters."
- ***optimo rege Frederico l. m.*** — "that best of kings, Frederick, of blessed memory": **Frederik II** (r. 1559–88), Tycho's original patron; *l. m.* = *laudatae* (or *piae*) *memoriae*, "of blessed/praiseworthy memory."
- ***senatorum regni literas … licet quidam adeoque praecipuus eorum has una subsignarit*** — the council of the realm (Rigsråd) had pledged perpetual maintenance of Tycho's work in a signed letter; Tycho notes pointedly that one of the signatories — "and indeed the chief of them" (*praecipuus eorum*, i.e. the chancellor himself) — was among those now reneging. The barbed clause is kept intact.
- **Duke Ulrich** — *illustrissimus dux Uldaricus, s:mi regis nostri avus* = **Ulrich III, Duke of Mecklenburg-Güstrow** (1527–1603), maternal grandfather (*avus*) of Christian IV (through Queen Sophie of Mecklenburg). He had written to the Danish king urging the full restoration (*in integrum … restitutio*) of Tycho's astronomical establishment.
- **Astronomy / Tycho's programme.** *astronomiae instaurationem … perficienda* = "completing … the restoration of astronomy" (*instauratio* = Tycho's *astronomia instaurata* programme, this chapter's convention); *artis vere regiae* / *artis tam sublimis* = "the truly royal art" / "so sublime an art" — astronomy. *jnstrumentorum meorum astronomiae conservatio* = "the maintenance of my instruments of astronomy" (his Uraniborg instruments, this chapter's convention).
- **Proposed sites for a new observatory.** *jnsula Dalan prope Rigam* — an island "Dalan" near Riga (probably **Dalen / Dole (Dalholm)**, an island in the Daugava near Riga; identification not certain — see crux); *Bornhovium* — most plausibly **Bornholm** (the Danish/Baltic island), though the form is unusual; *jnsula Werden prope Dantiscum* — the island of **Werder near Danzig** (Gdańsk). All are weighed as possible locations under Sigismund's Baltic dominions. *ex jnsulis Prussiae vicinis* = "some one of the islands neighbouring Prussia."
- ***imperatoriam ma:tem*** — "His Imperial Majesty": the Holy Roman Emperor **Rudolf II**, to whom Tycho would in the event turn, becoming Imperial Mathematician in 1599.
- ***magno … cancellario*** — "the Grand Chancellor": the Polish-Lithuanian Grand Chancellor (under Sigismund as King of Poland), distinct from the Swedish chancellor Sparre himself.
- **Orthography.** The transcription preserves the edition's *j* for consonantal/final *i* (*ijs, eximij, amicissimo* → *ijs, jnstrumentorum, jnsula, Jtaque, Jdque*), the *v/u* conventions, and the abbreviations *s:mi / ser:mi* (*serenissimi*), *ma:tem / m:tas / m:ti* (*maiestatem* etc.), *d:no* (*domino*), *l. m.* (*laudatae memoriae*); these are expanded in the apparatus, not in the source block.
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Datae Rostochij … 7:a nimirum septembris stylo veteri anni etc. 1597* = "Given at Rostock … on the 7th of September, **Old Style**, in the year, etc., 1597." Tycho explicitly flags the style (*stylo veteri*, O.S.) himself — characteristic of a Lutheran writing to a correspondent in the orbit of Catholic (New-Style) Poland. The as-written date (7 September 1597 O.S.) agrees with the catalogue label; no discrepancy. The N.S. equivalent would be 17 September 1597, but by this chapter's convention it is not silently substituted. Tycho dates the letter "the day before that on which I have determined to depart" (*pridie eius diei, qua inde discedere constitui*) — i.e. he planned to leave Rostock on 8 September O.S.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD HENRICUM RANZOVIUM.

S. P.

LITERÆ tuæ, Nobilissime et Amantissime Domine RANZOVI, amice et affinis honorande, per Præfectum tuum CHRISTIANUM mihi redditæ sunt, cum quo loca a te peramice oblata collustravi, et pro benevolo hoc erga me affectu gratias officiose ago quas possum maximas, pro virili oblatâ occasione relaturus. Placeret quidem utraque conditio, et præ cæteris ea, quæ Segebergæ monstrata est; verumenimvero, cum nonnihil remotiores sic simus ab urbe quâdam amplâ, nec ego otiosam libenter vitam traducerem, sed libros quosdam e meis prælo ferme absolutos omnino perficere vellem, ad quod Typographia requireretur, et Artifices, qui figuras sculpere nossent, tum quoque qui Instrumentum unum vel alterum pro Observationibus cœlitus obtinendis (modo nullum ex ijs quæ Haffniæ reposui, mature inde recepero) pararent. Si itaque prope Lubecam vel Hamburgum aliquod prædium mihi ad tempus, donec rebus meis commodius prospectum fuerit, concedere posses, feceris rem inprimis exoptatam. Constitui vero Deo volente, cras Bramstedium usque circa vesperam venire, quia tam cito negotia mea expedire non possum, præsertim in quibusdam scribendis, ut circa meridiem tibi adsim. Si interim Bredenbergam iveris, subsequar confestim, ita ut die Lunæ annuente numine ibi ulterius de omnibus consilium tecum capiam, et desiderium hoc visendæ Arcis eius amplissimæ, inprimisque splendidæ bibliothecæ tuæ, quod me iampridem incessit, nunc tandem expleam. Interea Mæ. Tæ. omnia fausta precor, eamque quam diutissime incolumem ex animo voveo.

Datæ Segebergæ 17. Septembris Anni 97.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Henrik Rantzau.**

Heartiest greeting.

Your letter, most noble and most loving Master Rantzau, my friend and kinsman to be honoured, was delivered to me by your steward Christian, with whom I inspected the places you had so amicably offered; and for this kindly disposition towards me I dutifully give you the greatest thanks I can, intending to repay the offered occasion to the best of my power. Both arrangements would indeed please me, and above the rest the one that was shown [me] at Segeberg; but in truth, since we should thus be somewhat too far removed from some large town — and since I would not willingly pass an idle life, but should wish to bring quite to completion certain of my books, all but finished at the press, for which a printing-house would be required, and craftsmen who knew how to engrave figures, and likewise [someone] who might prepare one or another instrument for obtaining observations from the heavens (provided I recover in good time none of those which I have stored at Copenhagen) — if therefore you could grant me for a time some estate near Lübeck or Hamburg, until my affairs have been more conveniently provided for, you would do a thing especially longed-for. But I have resolved, God willing, to come tomorrow as far as Bramstedt about evening — since I cannot dispatch my business so quickly, especially in [the matter of] certain things to be written — so as to be with you about midday. If in the meantime you have gone to Breitenburg, I shall follow at once, so that on Monday, with the divine favour assenting, I may there take further counsel with you about everything, and may now at last fulfil this longing to see that most spacious castle of yours, and above all your splendid library, which has long since seized me. Meanwhile I pray every good fortune for Your Lordship, and from my heart I vow [you] safe and sound as long as possible.

Given at Segeberg, 17 September, the year [15]97.
TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** Tycho Brahe, writing during his departure from Denmark. He left Hven in spring 1597 and, after a stay at Rostock, moved westward through Holstein; by 17 September 1597 he and his *familia* had reached Segeberg Fortress, the seat of the king's governor of Schleswig-Holstein, finding the governor away at Bramstedt (so "On Tycho's Island," confirming the situation behind this letter). The "books all but finished at the press" point to the works then in progress (the *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* and *Epistolae*); the instruments "stored at Copenhagen" (*Haffniae reposui*) are those of his dismantled Hven establishment.
- **Recipient.** *Henricus Ranzovius* = **Henrik Rantzau / Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), the Danish crown's *Statthalter* (royal governor) of Schleswig-Holstein, a major humanist patron, author, and bibliophile; his castle of **Breitenburg** held one of the most celebrated private libraries of the age. He died the following year (1598). Addressed as *affinis* ("kinsman"): the Brahe and Rantzau families were connected by marriage.
- ***Praefectum tuum Christianum*** — "your steward/bailiff Christian": Rantzau's *praefectus* (estate official) who carried the letter and guided Tycho over the offered properties; rendered "steward." First name only is given; not further identified here.
- **Places.** *Segeberga* = **Segeberg** (Bad Segeberg, Holstein), the fortress where Tycho was lodged and from which the letter is dated. *Bramstedium* = **Bramstedt** (Bad Bramstedt), where Rantzau then was. *Bredenberga* = **Breitenburg**, Rantzau's principal seat with the great library (the *Arx amplissima … splendida bibliotheca* of the next clause); the Latinised place-name *Bredenberga* reflects the Low-German form *Bredenberg*. *Lubeca* = **Lübeck**; *Hamburgum* = **Hamburg**; *Haffnia* = **Copenhagen**.
- **Technical terms.** *praelo … absolutos / Typographia* — "[books] finished at the press / a printing-house": Tycho's need to carry his own typographic and engraving capacity with him into exile. *figuras sculpere* = "to engrave figures" (the diagrams/illustrations of his astronomical books). *Instrumentum … pro Observationibus coelitus obtinendis* = "an instrument for obtaining observations from the heavens" — *instrumentum* per glossary ("instrument"); *observationes* kept as "observations." No planetary or zodiac symbols occur in this letter.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam* (*dicit*), "heartiest greeting". *Mae. Tae.* = *Maiestati Tuae* / *Magnificentiae Tuae* — see crux below. *manu propria* = "in his own hand" (an autograph subscription).
- **Reading crux — *Mae. Tae.*** The abbreviation *Mae. Tae.* (expanded by Dreyer) is rendered "Your Lordship." It most plausibly stands for *Magnificentiae Tuae* ("Your Magnificence"), the courtesy due a high noble and governor; it is **not** *Maiestati Tuae* ("Your Majesty"), which would be reserved for a sovereign and would not suit a letter to Rantzau. The expansion is editorial; the precise courtesy-title behind the contraction is not certain from the abbreviation alone, and is flagged rather than silently fixed.
- **Calendar.** *Datae Segebergae 17. Septembris Anni 97* = "Given at Segeberg, 17 September, the year [15]97" (**Old Style** — Denmark and the Lutheran territories kept the Julian calendar). The dateline date (17 September) agrees with the catalogue label ("1597. 17. september. Segeberg"); no discrepancy. *die Lunae* = "on Monday" — left as the weekday named, not converted to a civil date.

Collated all place names (Segeberga/Segeberg, Bramstedium/Bramstedt, Bredenbergam/Breitenburg, Lubecam/Lübeck, Hamburgum/Hamburg, Haffniae/Copenhagen) and the steward's name (Christianum/Christian) against the page image; the transcribed original matches Dreyer word-for-word. No fabrication, omission, or material mistranslation; one interpretive rendering ('Arcis eius' as 'that castle of yours' rather than literal 'its castle') is defensible in context (Breitenburg was just named) and not counted as a defect.

text.original:
OS ELSCHELIGE ERLIGE OG VELBIURDIG MAND TYGE BRAHE TIL KNUDSTRUP, VOR MAND OG TIENER.

CHRISTIAN den 4., med Guds naade Danmarkes, Norges, Wendis og Gottis konning. Vor gunst tilforn. Vid, at thin skriffvelße, som du Os tilschreffvet haffver sub dato Rostoch den 10. dag julij sidst forleden, er Os nu i thenne uge underdanigst tilstillet, udi hvilken iblant andet opregnes, først at du ingen leilighed havde at tale med Os, førend du drogst her af riget, ey heller du vidste, om sligt var Os angenehm eller icke, derfor haffde du Os underdanigst skrifftlig villid lade forstaa, og at Os uden tuiffl er bevist, at du est af med huis du til den astronomische konstes underholdning her til dags haver været med benaadet, ogsaa at [Vi] samme kunst icke ville holde ved magt, sampt andet meere, som wformodendes sig tildraget og uthen thin skyld og brøde thig er hendet og vederfaret, som du meener. Thernest at thu icke hafver sielff then formue, at du samme konst kand med thin bekostning fuldkomme; og om thu endskiønt haffde thine forrige forlenninger, tha estu dog saa kommen til achters, at du nødes til at afhende thit godtz. Och effterthi thu af forberørdte aarsage est trengt til at søge paa andre stæder, hos fremmede potentater og herrer, hielp, middel og raad thend astronomische kunst at forfremme oc thit naffn hos udlændische ved macht at holde, tha beder thu, at Vi saadan thin reyße icke vilde tage til nogen wnaade, besynderligen forthi thu icke end aldeeles vilt forlade thit fæderneland. Vijdere formelder thu, at thersom thet kand bliffve thig forgyndt, at thu her uthi rijget maa thit foretagne arbeyd forfølge, tha vilde thu thet icke forsijge, men Os og thit fæderne rijge then ære gierne for nogen anden forunde, om thet kand schee med lijdelige vilkor oc uden thin skade, efftersom thin vijdløfftig skriffvelße derom vijdere indholder. Tha ville Vi thig therpaa naadigst icke forholde, først hvad anlanger, at thu icke haffver hafft leilighed at tale med Os, førend du drogst her af riget, oc thig var vbewist, om sligt kunde være Os angenehm eller ey, saa vedstu thig vel at erindre, at du udi nogle uger laae udi Vor kiøbsted Kiøbenhaffn, førend du drogst af rijget, oc icke allene icke forloff af Os begierede, at thu maatte af rijget bort-reijße, som thig haffde burd at giøre, men aldrig engang thalede med Os, undertagendes then ene gang, the Huensche bønder og thu varst for Os udi rette, oc thig bleff paalagt oc befalet at møde for Os paa slottet. Oc enddog thu icke blues thin undschyldning her om at giøre, saaleedes som thu varst Vor jeffnlijge, tha ville Vi dog vdi thenne Vor skriffvelße thig lade vijde, at Vi sligt forstaae, ocsaa at Vi effter thenne dag ville anderleedes være af thig respecteret, saafrembt thu i Os skalt befinde en naadig herre oc konning. Angaaende attu icke tuiffler, at Os er bevist thig at være opschreffvet noget, som thu varst med forlænet, og dog formelder sligt at være scheed uden thin skyld og brøde, saa vedst thu thig sielff at erindre, huad klagemaal Vore fattige undersaatter oc bønder paa Huæn imod thig hafft hafver. Huorledis thu med kircken ther sammesteds handlet haffver, hvis indkomst og tiender thu udi mange aar til dig haffver annammet, oc ingen forordnet til kircke-verge, men ladet den bygfeldig staa, wdi lijge maade taget jorden fra p[ræ]stegaarden, husene enpart aftaget, oc præsten, som ther udi boe skulde og jorden bruge, sig og sin hustru til ophold, hannem haffver thu giffvet nogle β om ugen, och spißet hannem hos thine arbeyds folk, saa ther paa nogle faa aars tid haver været mange praester, og dog icke haffver bekommet kald af meenigheden effter ordinantzen, ey heller ere dømbte derfra, som thet sig burde. Uthi huad maade daabens ord ere i langsommelig thiid udeladt, imod disße rigers vedtagne brug, med thit vidschab, sligt er huer mand ald for vitterligt. Hvilket forberørte med andet meere, som sig paa thet forberørte lille og ringe land tildraget haver oc Os en god rum tijd, førend thet er kommen offentlig for hver mand, til denne dag haffver været bevist, haver aarsag givet, Vore og kronens bønder andre at forlæne, som thennem ved low, ret og landsens vedtagne brug holde ville. Hvad belanger, at thu ikke est saa formuendes, attu kanst af dit eget fuldkomme den foretagne astronomische konst, om thu skiønt solte thit fæderne-gods oc haffde enda thine forlæninger, men er draget af riget fremmede potentater om hielp at besøge, og icke i then meening, at thu thit fæderneland plat vilde forlade, og beder underdanigst, at Vi slig thin reyße icke ville tage til wnaade, saa bæres stor tvifl, at du de penninge, som du haver bekommet for thit soldte godtz, hafver anlagt paa the astronomische instrumenter, effterthi ther sijges, at thu i mange tusind thal haffver thennem til herrer og førster at vdlaane, thine børn til bæste oc icke riget til nogen ære eller konsten til forfremmelße. Ocsaa er Os aldeeles ukiært at forfare, at du hos andre herrer og førster uthi the maader hielp søger, lijgesom Wi oc riget ware saa wformuendes, at Vi sligt ikke af sted kunde komme, mindre thu med qvinde og børn skulle uddrage og slig penninge hos andre bettle. Thog effterthi thet nu giord er, tha nødes Vi sligt at lade skee, og icke Os i nogen maade anmode, enten thu drager af landet eller bliver derudj. Sidst, efftersom thu underdanigst formelder, at dersom thet thig maa forloffves, thit forretagne arbeid her i riget at fuldende, tha vilde du det ikke forsige, oc at thet skee maatte uden thin skade, faa ville Vi thig herpaa naadigst hafve svaret: at saafremt thu thiene vil for en mathematico og giøre thet, hand bør at giøre, tha skaltu først underdanig tilbiude thin tieniste og therom bede som en tienere bør at giøre, og icke med slig fortagdte ord (at thu thet icke vilt forsijge) fremføre thin meening. Naar thet skeer, tha ville Vi Os siden therpaa tilbørligen vide at erklære. Och efftersom thin skriffvelße thilmed noget seltzom er stijlet, oc icke uden stor wforstand oc dristighed, ligesom Vi thig meere schulde giøre regnschab, huorfor og af huad aarsag Vi paa Vort og kronens godtz giorde forandring, og Vi therhos Os erindrer, hvorleedes thu adschillige snach om Vor kiære her fader haffver iblant thine e[pistolæ] ladet udgaae Hans Kierlighed saavelsom thig self til forvid og forkleinering, tha ville Vi thet med thette Vort breff forbødet haffve, attu samme thit breff, som thu Os nu haffver tilschreffvet, icke lader udgaae paa prent, saa frembt thet skeer, thu icke af Os therfor vilt tiltales og straffes, som thet sig bør. Befalendes thig Gud.

Skreffvet paa Vort slot Kiøbenhaffn thend 8. octobr: a:o 1597. Vnder Vort signet.
Christian.
text.english:
**To our beloved, honourable and well-born man Tyge Brahe of Knudstrup, our man and servant.**

Christian the Fourth, by the grace of God King of Denmark, Norway, the Wends and the Goths. Our favour beforehand. Know that your letter, which you wrote to us under date of Rostock, the 10th day of July last past, has now this week been most humbly delivered to us; in which, among other things, the following are set out: first, that you had no opportunity to speak with us before you departed from this realm, nor did you know whether such [a departure] was agreeable to us or not, and that you therefore had wished most humbly to make [it] known to us in writing; and that it is doubtless made known to us that you are deprived of that wherewith you have hitherto been graced for the maintenance of the astronomical art, and also that [we] would not keep up that same art, together with more besides, which (as you maintain) has befallen and come upon you unlooked-for and without your fault and offence. Next, that you do not yourself have the means to complete that same art at your own expense; and that even though you still had your former enfeoffments, you have nonetheless fallen so far into arrears that you are compelled to dispose of your estate. And since, for the aforesaid reason, you are constrained to seek in other places, from foreign potentates and lords, help, means and counsel to advance the astronomical art and to keep up your name among foreigners, you therefore ask that we would not take such a journey of yours in any ill grace, especially because you will not yet altogether forsake your fatherland. Further you state that, should it be granted you that you may here within the realm pursue your undertaken work, you would not refuse it, but would gladly grant to us and your native realm that honour before any other, if it can be done on tolerable terms and without harm to you, as your prolix letter further sets out concerning this.

Therefore we will most graciously not withhold from you our answer thereon. First, as concerns [the claim] that you had no opportunity to speak with us before you departed from this realm, and that it was unknown to you whether such [a departure] could be agreeable to us or not: you well know how to recall that you lay for some weeks in our market-town of Copenhagen before you departed from the realm, and not only did you not request leave of us that you might travel away out of the realm — as you ought to have done — but you never once spoke with us, save that one time when the Hven peasants and you stood before us at law, and you were enjoined and commanded to appear before us at the castle. And although you are not ashamed to make your excuse on this matter, as if you were our equal, yet we will nonetheless in this our letter let you know that we understand such [conduct], and also that after this day we will be otherwise respected by you, if so be that you are to find in us a gracious lord and king. As regards [the point] that you do not doubt it is made known to us that something has been entered against you concerning that wherewith you were enfeoffed, and yet you state that such [a thing] has happened without your fault and offence: you yourself know how to recall what complaint our poor subjects and peasants on Hven have had against you. [Namely] how you have dealt with the church in that same place, whose income and tithes you have for many years taken to yourself, and have appointed no one as churchwarden, but let it stand in disrepair; likewise [how you] took the land away from the parsonage, demolished part of the buildings, and [as for] the priest, who was to dwell therein and use the land for the support of himself and his wife — to him you have given a few shillings [β] a week, and fed him among your workfolk, so that within the space of a few years there have been many priests there, and yet [they] have not received a call from the congregation according to the ordinance, nor have [they] been [duly] dismissed therefrom, as ought [to have been done]. In what manner the words of baptism have for a long time been left out, contrary to the accepted usage of these realms, with your knowledge — such [a thing] is all too well known to every man. Which aforesaid [matters], together with more besides, that have come to pass on the aforesaid small and mean land, and have been made known to us a good long while before it came openly before every man, to this day — [these] have given cause [for us] to enfeoff others, our and the crown's peasants, who will maintain them by law, justice and the accepted usage of the land.

As concerns [the claim] that you are not so well provided that you can of your own [resources] complete the undertaken astronomical art, even if you sold your patrimonial estate and still had your enfeoffments, but [that you] have departed from the realm to seek out foreign potentates for help, and not with the intent that you would utterly forsake your fatherland, and [that you] humbly ask that we would not take such a journey of yours in ill grace: great doubt is borne [as to whether] you have laid out the money you have received for your sold estate upon the astronomical instruments, since it is said that you have them out on loan to lords and princes in many thousands [of dalers], for the benefit of your children and not for any honour to the realm or for the advancement of the art. Also it is altogether displeasing to us to learn that you seek help from other lords and princes in those ways, as if we and the realm were so unprovided that we could not bring such [a thing] to pass — much less that you, with wife and children, should travel away and beg such money from others. Yet since it is now done, we are obliged to let such [a thing] happen, and not to importune us in any way [as to] whether you depart from the country or remain therein. Last, since you most humbly state that, if it be permitted you to complete your undertaken work here in the realm, you would not refuse it, and that it might be done without harm to you, we will most graciously have answered you hereon: that if you will serve as a mathematician and do that which he ought to do, then you shall first humbly offer your service and request it thereon, as a servant ought to do, and not put forward your meaning with such veiled words (that you "would not refuse it"). When that is done, we will thereafter know how to declare ourselves fittingly thereon. And since your letter is moreover couched in a somewhat strange [manner], and not without great want of understanding and boldness — as though we should render you the more account of why and for what reason we made a change upon our and the crown's estate — and since we therewith recall how you have, among your letters [epistolae], let go forth divers gossip about our dear lord father, to His Love's reproach and disparagement as well as your own: we will therefore by this our letter have forbidden [it], that you do not let that same letter, which you have now written to us, go forth in print; and if that happens, [know] that you will be arraigned and punished by us therefor, as is fitting. Commending you to God.

Written at our castle of Copenhagen, the 8th of October, in the year 1597. Under our signet.
Christian.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. documents.apparatus:
- **Issuer.** **Christian IV of Denmark** (r. 1588–1648), then aged 20 and newly in personal rule after the regency that followed Frederik II's death (1588). This is the famous letter in which the young king repudiates Tycho's appeal, itemises the Hven tenants' and church grievances against him, and refuses to recall the patronage — the document that effectively confirmed Tycho's self-exile.
- **Recipient.** **Tycho Brahe (Tyge Brahe) of Knudstrup** (1546–1601), styled *Vor mand og tiener* ("our man and servant") — the feudal-vassal formula, deliberately deflating the standing Tycho had claimed.
- **Occasion / the cited letter.** Tycho's own appeal, written *sub dato Rostoch den 10. dag julij sidst forleden* = "under date of Rostock, 10 July last past" — i.e. from Rostock, where Tycho had gone after leaving Hven in spring 1597. This is an **in-letter date** (the date of the document being answered), not the date of this letter; reproduced as written, not reconciled, by this chapter's convention
- **Structure.** The king's reply tracks Tycho's appeal point by point: he first **summarises** Tycho's four heads (no chance to speak; loss of endowment; lack of private means; the request not to be held in disgrace, and the conditional offer to stay), then **answers** each in turn. The translation preserves this summary-then-rebuttal structure and the heavy chancery subordination.
- **Editorial insertion *[Vi]*.** The source as transcribed reads *…ogsaa at [Vi] samme kunst icke ville holde ved magt* — the bracketed *[Vi]* ("we") is the edition's supplied subject; kept in brackets in both Source and Translation. The clause reports Tycho's grievance that the crown would not maintain the astronomical establishment.
- **Negation check (load-bearing).** Several clauses turn on stacked negations and are rendered with the exact count of the source:
 - *icke allene icke forloff af Os begierede … men aldrig engang thalede med Os* = "not only did you **not** request leave of us … but you **never** once spoke with us" — a double-negative emphatic ("not only not … but never"), reproduced as three negations, not collapsed.
 - *thu icke blues thin undschyldning her om at giøre* = "you are **not** ashamed to make your excuse on this matter" (i.e. you are shameless enough to excuse yourself) — a single negation; the sense is reproachful, the negation kept.
 - *icke ville holde ved magt / ikke ville tage til nogen wnaade* — the requests that the king would **not** keep up the art / would **not** take the journey in ill grace are Tycho's reported pleas; the king's own refusal is voiced separately. Kept distinct so the negations are not transferred between speakers.
 - *icke … forsijge* ("would **not** refuse [it]") — Tycho's conditional offer to stay, which the king mocks as *fortagdte ord* ("veiled / disguised words"); the negation is central to the king's complaint and is preserved verbatim, including in the parenthetical quotation.
- **Conditional / mood (flagged).** The closing prohibition is a conditional with chancery legal force: *tha ville Vi thet … forbødet haffve, attu … icke lader udgaae paa prent, saa frembt thet skeer, thu icke af Os therfor vilt tiltales og straffes* — literally "we will have forbidden [it], that you do **not** let [the letter] go forth in print; if so be it happens, [that] you will **not** be arraigned and punished by us therefor." The Danish is elliptical: the *saa frembt thet skeer* ("if it happens") clause, with its own *icke*, is best read as an **apodosis of consequence** — *if you do print it, you will (not escape being) arraigned and punished* — i.e. the *icke* governs an implied "[think] not [that you will escape]". The transcription's literal "you will not be arraigned" would invert the threat; the king is plainly threatening punishment (cf. *som thet sig bør*, "as is fitting"). The translation renders the evident legal force ("[know] that you will be arraigned and punished") while this note records the elliptical construction and the syntactic crux. **This is the principal crux of the letter** — see the confidence grade.
- **The peasants' suit.** *the Huensche bønder og thu varst for Os udi rette* = "the Hven peasants and you stood before us at law" — the 1590s litigation between Tycho and his Hven tenants over labour-services and the parsonage, heard before the king. Corroborated by the king's itemised rebuttal (Christianson, *On Tycho's Island* / *Lord of Uraniborg*: Tycho took the church's incomes and tithes without maintaining it, removed glebe land from the parsonage, etc.).
- **β (the shilling sign).** *nogle β om ugen* — the glyph **β** is the early-modern Danish abbreviation for *skilling* (shilling); rendered "a few shillings [β]," the symbol kept in the Source block by the audit's rule. The complaint is that Tycho paid the resident priest a pittance and boarded him among the labourers.
- **Church / liturgical charge.** *daabens ord ere … udeladt* = "the words of baptism have … been left out," *imod disße rigers vedtagne brug* "contrary to the accepted usage of these realms" — the grave accusation that the baptismal formula was omitted (a Reformation-confessional offence), *med thit vidschab* "with your knowledge." *effter ordinantzen* = "according to the [Church] Ordinance" (the 1539/1542 Danish *Kirkeordinans*); *kald af meenigheden* "a call from the congregation."
- ***mange tusind thal*** — "many thousands [of dalers / in tale]"; *thal* (= *tal*, "tale/count, reckoning") is here the money-of-account; "[of dalers]" supplied in brackets as the implied unit. The charge is that Tycho lent out large sums to princes for his children's benefit rather than spending on the realm's honour.
- **The late king and the *Epistolae*.** *adschillige snach om Vor kiaere her fader … iblant thine e[pistolae] ladet udgaae* = "let divers gossip about our dear lord father go forth among your letters [epistolae]" — a reference to Tycho's *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Uraniborg, 1596), the published correspondence in which passages touched the late **Frederik II**; *Hans Kierlighed* ("His Love") is the chancery honorific for the deceased king. The prohibition on printing the present letter follows directly from this grievance.
- **Latin code-switches.** *sub dato* ("under date of"); *en mathematico* (Latin ablative *mathematico*, "[as] a mathematician," used inside the Danish syntax); *e[pistolae]* (abbreviated in the source, expanded in brackets). Preserved by this chapter's convention
- **Orthography (chancery Danish, c. 1597).** *Vor gunst tilforn* = the royal address-formula ("Our favour beforehand,"); *Vid* = *vid* ("know!"); *thin/thig/thu* = *din/dig/du*; *huis* = *hvis* (here relative "that which"); *est af med* = "are deprived of / done with"; *forlenninger/forlaeninger* = *forleninger* ("enfeoffments, fiefs"); *til achters* = *til agters* ("into arrears, behindhand"); *afhende thit godtz* = "dispose of your estate/goods"; *wnaade* = *unåde* ("disgrace, ill grace"); *forsijge* = *forsige* ("refuse, decline"); *lijdelige vilkor* = "tolerable terms"; *vijdløfftig* = *vidtløftig* ("prolix, long-winded"); *vbewist/bevist* = *ubevidst/bevidst* ("unknown / known"); *jeffnlijge* = *jævnlige* ("equal, peer"); *bygfeldig* = "in disrepair, dilapidated"; *p[rae]stegaarden* = *præstegården* ("the parsonage," with the *prae-* abbreviation expanded in brackets); *enpart* = "in part"; *fortagdte* = *fordægte/fortagne* ("veiled, dissembling"); *seltzom* = *sælsom* ("strange, odd"); *wforstand* = *uforstand* ("want of understanding"); *forkleinering* = "disparagement, belittling"; *Befalendes thig Gud* = "Commending you to God."
- **Calendar / place.** *Skreffvet paa Vort slot Kiøbenhaffn thend 8. octobr. a:o 1597* = "Written at our castle of Copenhagen, the 8th of October 1597" (O.S.; Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). The dateline and the edition label (8 October 1597, Copenhagen) **agree**; no date discrepancy in the header. The only date inside the letter belonging to a different document is Tycho's *10 July* appeal from Rostock (above).

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO XIV pp.120-124 read as page images. Letter no.134 (Christian IV to Tycho, 8 Oct 1597) runs pp.121-123; checked neighbouring pp.120 and 124 and confirmed they belong to the preceding and following letters, not this one. Collated the full Danish text sentence-by-sentence against the printed page images (not digitised text layer): opening/closing formulas, the Rostock/10 July date, the Copenhagen sojourn and Hven-peasants lawsuit, the Hven church/parsonage/priest complaints, the 'nogle β om ugen' (weekly shillings) detail, the 'mange tusind thal' (many thousand dalers) loan accusation, the baptism-formula clause, the printing prohibition and threat of prosecution, and the Copenhagen castle/8 October 1597 dateline and signature. All proper names (Rostock, Copenhagen, Hven), the one specific date, and all financial/quantity phrases in the English match Dreyer's printed Danish with no addition, omission, or flipped sense. Published grade was C (the translator's own, by the audit's rule, unverified); independent collation finds no defect and upgrades to A.
