text.original:
NOBILITATE NON TANTUM GENERIS, SED ET GENIJ ATQUE INGENIJ VIRO INPRIMIS CONSPICUO DOMINO OLIGERO ROSÆKRANTZIO DE ROSENHOLM, CONSANGVINEO, AFFINI ET AMICO INTIMO.

S. P.

DEDI ad te literas, Nobilissime et Præstantissime Domine OLIGERE, Cognate et Amice charissime, ac tuis respondi, priusquam Rostochio discederem; quas etiam tibi redditas, utut is, quem isthuc ablegavi, reversus nondum sit, nihil ambigo. Nunc vero, cum amanuensem meum cum Presbytero isthuc remeante ad vos mittere decrevissem, denuo te pro necessitudine nostra meis compellandum, et de statu meo brevibus edocendum censui. Scias itaque me ob luem Epidemicam Rostochij ingravescentem in Holsatiam a Nobilissimo viro, Domino HENRICO RANZOVIO literis perbenigne evocatum discessisse, qui aliquot Arcium suarum optione mihi data, quam vellem ex ijs, inhabitandam concessit, ac pluribus etiamnum beneficijs me sibi devincire non cessat. Elegi autem præ cæteris mihi oblatis Wandesburgum, dimidio saltem miliari Hamburgo remotum, eo quod egregia ibi commoditas suppeteret, et vicina civitas, unde in omnes ferme Europæ partes frequens internuncius offertur, necessaria omnia procurandi oportunitatem sufficientem concederet. Ubi studijs consuetis more solito gnaviter incumbo, et a præstantibus ac Eruditis hinc inde viris in maiore, quam ipsemet desidero, et unquam in Patria factum, pretio et honore habeor. Et si non consulto hîc in vicinijs Daniæ subsistere voluissem, conditiones iam antea fuissem nactus, quales Patria vix largiretur; quas etiam me, quam primum lubuerit, ex divina providentia assecuturum, nihil addubito; ut hanc rerum nostrarum mutationem neutiquam doleam, sed Deum ob id mihi isthæc evenire permisisse confidam, quo meliorem in Germania aut alibi locorum fortunam largiretur. Quod autem tam diu in propinquo moratus sum, hinc factum, ut responsum ad literas Illmi Ducis ULDARICI, meo nomine ad Sermum Regem nostrum perscriptas, quibus etiam meæ adiunctæ erant, expectarem. Neque enim longius discedendum, aut apud alios Magnates quidpiam tentandum duxi, antequam responsione accepta, qualis etiamnum esset in me et mea studia animus Regis, comperirem. Cum vero his ipsis diebus hanc adeptus sim, qualem ob quorundam in me malevolentiam recepturum prævidebam (licet non adeo asperam et immeritam) id quod tam diu premebam, iam efficere, nihil restat obstaculi. Daboque operam, favente Numine, ut nemini isthic sim amplius mea præsentia molestus.

Relatum mihi est te fratris mei AXILLI filiam SOPHIAM in uxorem ducturum. Quod equidem lubentissime inaudivi, atque in hoc coniugio omnia vobis quam faustissima et precor et auguror. Et licet meo iudicio nihil rectius facere potueris, quam ut uxore ducta te ab Aulicis compedibus liberares, cum alios tolerabiliores et minus ingratos futuros spes sit (siquidem per viam universæ carnis eundum est) videris nihilominus, ne per hanc SOPHIAM terrigenam sublimiorem quandam ac Philosophicam, Diam illam, et mentem a terrenis caducisque ad longe altiora tollentem, atque immortalitati consecrantem negligas. Solet enim in his fieri id quod præcinebat OVIDIUS: Successore novo pellitur omnis amor. At cum et illa, quatenus fert sexus, Philosophica futura sit, ac Amitam SOPHIAM, quoad datur, haud degenerans imitatura, sociam altioris alicuius, quam vulgus capit, SOPHIÆ potius quam obstaculum fore, præsagio et opto.

Plura rerum mearum, temporis angustia præpedito mihi nunc scribere non datur; ex sorore SOPHIA, tibi etiam amica, tum quoque communi Amico Domino Doctore NICOLAO CRAGIO cognosces. Quæ vero me concernentia, mi OLIGERE, nosti, fideliter (uti tibi confido) indica, a me tacite habenda: nec invidos osores ac detrectatores meos verearis. Quos et te haud extimescere, omnino mihi persuadeo. Ego iam pridem illorum malevolentiam superare et negligere didici. Vale mi optime OLIGERE, meque quod facis mutuo amare perge.

Dabantur Wandesburgo ex arce Ranzoviana die 7. Novembris Anni 97.
Tuus ex intimis
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To a man pre-eminently distinguished by nobility not only of birth, but of genius and intellect too, Master Holger Rosenkrantz of Rosenholm, [my] kinsman, relation by marriage, and most intimate friend.**

Heartiest greeting.

I sent you a letter, most noble and most excellent Master Holger, dearest kinsman and friend, and answered yours, before I departed from Rostock; and that it was duly delivered to you I in no way doubt, even though the man whom I dispatched thither has not yet returned. But now, since I had resolved to send my amanuensis to you, together with the clergyman who is returning thither, I judged that for the sake of our close bond you should be addressed again by my [letter], and informed in brief of my situation. Know then that, on account of the epidemic pestilence growing worse at Rostock, I withdrew into Holstein, most kindly summoned by letter by that most noble man, Master Henrik Rantzau, who, having given me the choice of several of his castles to dwell in, whichever of them I should wish, does not even yet cease to bind me to himself by further kindnesses. I chose, however, in preference to the others offered me, Wandsbek, removed only half a mile from Hamburg, because there was excellent convenience to hand there, and the neighbouring city — whence frequent couriers go out to almost all parts of Europe — would grant sufficient opportunity of procuring everything needful. Here I diligently apply myself to my customary studies in my usual manner, and am held by distinguished and learned men on every side in greater esteem and honour than I myself desire, and than was ever done in my homeland. And if I had not deliberately wished to stay here in the neighbourhood of Denmark, I should already before now have obtained terms such as my homeland would scarcely bestow; and that I shall obtain these too, by divine providence, as soon as it shall please me, I in no way doubt — so that I by no means grieve at this change in my affairs, but trust that God has permitted these things to befall me for this very reason, that he might grant me a better fortune in Germany or elsewhere. But that I have lingered so long in the vicinity came about from this, that I was awaiting a reply to the letters of the Most Illustrious Duke Ulrich, written in my name to our Most Serene King, to which mine too were joined. For I judged that I should not depart further off, nor attempt anything with other magnates, before, the reply received, I had ascertained what the King's disposition still was toward me and my studies. But since in these very days I have obtained it — of the sort that, on account of the ill-will of certain men toward me, I foresaw I should receive (though not so harsh and undeserved [as that]) — there now remains no obstacle to my carrying out at once that which I had so long held back. And I shall take pains, with the favour of the Deity, that I be no longer a trouble to anyone there by my presence.

It has been reported to me that you are to take in marriage Sophie, the daughter of my brother Axel. Which indeed I heard with the greatest gladness, and I both pray and forebode all things most auspicious for you in this match. And although in my judgement you could do nothing more rightly than, having taken a wife, to free yourself from the courtly fetters — since there is hope that others will prove more tolerable and less ungrateful (seeing that one must go by the way of all flesh) — see nonetheless that, on account of this earth-born Sophie, you do not neglect that other, loftier and Philosophical Sophia, the divine one, who lifts the mind from things earthly and perishable to things far higher, and consecrates it to immortality. For in these matters it commonly happens as Ovid foretold: *Every love is driven out by a new successor.* But since she too, so far as her sex allows, is going to be Philosophical, and — not degenerating, as far as is granted — will imitate her aunt Sophie, I foresee and pray that she will rather be a companion of some loftier Sophia, beyond what the common crowd grasps, than an obstacle [to it].

More of my affairs it is not given me to write now, hindered as I am by shortness of time; you will learn it from [my] sister Sophie, your friend too, and also from our common friend Master Doctor Niels Krag. But the things that concern me which you know, my Holger, disclose faithfully (as I trust you to do), [those things] to be kept silent by me; and do not fear my envious haters and disparagers. Whom that you too do not dread, I am wholly persuaded. I myself learned long ago to overcome and disregard their ill-will. Farewell, my excellent Holger, and continue to love me mutually, as you do.

Given at Wandsbek, from the Rantzau castle, on the 7th day of November in the year [15]97.
Yours from the heart,
Tycho Brahe,
in his own hand.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender & recipient.** Tycho writes from exile to **Holger Rosenkrantz** (1574–1642), "the Learned," of **Rosenholm**, the theologian and statesman. *Oligerus Rosaekrantzius* is the Latinised form of Holger Rosenkrantz; "Oligere" is the vocative. He is addressed as *consanguineus, affinis et amicus intimus* — "kinsman, relation by marriage, and most intimate friend": the *affinitas* is the impending marriage announced in the letter itself.
- **Date & place.** *Dabantur Wandesburgo ex arce Ranzoviana die 7. Novembris Anni 97* = "Given at **Wandsbek** (Wandesburgum), from the **Rantzau castle**, the 7th day of November, year [15]97" (O.S.; Denmark and the Lutheran north kept the Julian calendar). The header date matches the dateline; the edition label ("1597. 7. november. Wandsburg") agrees. Wandsbek (now a district of Hamburg) was a seat of Henrik Rantzau; Tycho lodged there from autumn 1597 to spring 1598, where he completed the *Mechanica* and the *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* proofs. He had left Hven in 1597 and passed through Rostock before being invited into Holstein.
- **Henrik Rantzau** (*Henricus Ranzovius*, 1526–1598), the powerful royal governor (*Statthalter*) of the Danish king in the duchies of Schleswig-Holstein, humanist, astrologer and patron, who offered Tycho the choice of several of his castles. Rendered "Master Henrik Rantzau."
- ***Illmi Ducis ULDARICI*** = **Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg** (*Ulrich III*, 1527–1603), maternal grandfather of King Christian IV, who interceded on Tycho's behalf. *Illmi* = *Illustrissimi*, "Most Illustrious"; *Sermum Regem nostrum* = *Serenissimum*, "our Most Serene King," i.e. **Christian IV of Denmark** (r. 1588/1596–1648), then newly crowned. Tycho does not name the king but identifies him as *Rex noster*.
- **The marriage.** *fratris mei AXILLI filiam SOPHIAM* = "Sophie, daughter of my brother **Axel** (Axilis = Axel Brahe, 1550–1616)." This is **Sophie Axelsdatter Brahe** (1578–1646), Tycho's niece, whom Holger Rosenkrantz married in 1598. Tycho was thus already her uncle and was about to become uncle-by-marriage to Holger.
- **The Sophia wordplay.** The letter turns on a sustained pun between three Sophies: (1) *SOPHIA terrigena* — the "earth-born Sophie," the bride; (2) *Sophia Philosophica / Dia illa* — capital-S *Sophia*, divine **Wisdom** (the *philo-sophia* a scholar weds in a wife's stead, cf. Wolf's letter of 1571); and (3) *Amita SOPHIA* — the bride's **aunt Sophie**, i.e. **Sophie Brahe** (1559–1643), Tycho's learned sister, herself a noted student of horticulture, chemistry and genealogy, named again at the close as *soror SOPHIA* ("[my] sister Sophie"). The pun is preserved by keeping "Sophie/Sophia" throughout and flagged here rather than flattened. *terrigenam* ("earth-born") is the deliberate antithesis to the heavenly Wisdom.
- **The Ovid tag.** *Successore novo pellitur omnis amor* — "Every love is driven out by a new successor": **Ovid**, *Remedia Amoris* 462. Kept as the *sententia* it is; the verse is rendered as a single hexameter-sense line and italicised. Tycho cites it to warn that an earthly love can drive out the love of Wisdom.
- ***Aulicis compedibus*** = "courtly fetters/shackles" — court service as bondage; the metaphor is kept.
- ***per viam universae carnis eundum est*** = "one must go by the way of all flesh" — a Scriptural commonplace (cf. Joshua 23:14; 1 Kings 2:2), here a wry gloss on the necessity of marriage; rendered literally.
- **Niels Krag.** *communi Amico Domino Doctore NICOLAO CRAGIO* = "our common friend Master Doctor **Niels Krag**" (Nicolaus Cragius, c. 1550–1602), the Danish humanist, historiographer royal and professor at Copenhagen; he also corresponded with Tycho directly (Dreyer VIII). Rendered "Master Doctor Niels Krag."
- ***luem Epidemicam*** = "epidemic pestilence" — the plague then worsening at Rostock, the stated cause of Tycho's move into Holstein.
- ***amanuensis*** kept as "amanuensis" (Tycho's secretary/scribe); *Presbyter* rendered "clergyman/priest."
- ***dimidio … miliari*** = "half a [German] mile"; the period *miliare* is far longer than the English mile, so "half a mile" is the literal rendering and the magnitude is not converted.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S. P.* = *Salutem plurimam* (dicit), "heartiest greeting"; *Vale* = "Farewell"; *Tuus ex intimis* = "Yours from the heart / from [my] innermost [self]"; *manu propria* = "in his own hand," signalling an autograph subscription beneath a secretary's fair copy.
- **Epistemic hedges preserved.** Tycho's qualifiers are kept intact: *nihil ambigo / nihil addubito* ("I in no way doubt"), *praesagio et opto* ("I foresee and pray"), and especially the parenthesis *(licet non adeo asperam et immeritam)* — "(though not so harsh and undeserved [as that])," his guarded characterisation of the King's reply, which is left as the deliberately oblique statement it is rather than resolved into a flat verdict on Christian IV's letter.
- **Witness.** The sole witness is a later copy (*Afskrift*) in **Langebek's Diplomatarium**, Rigsarkivet, Copenhagen — the 18th-century Langebek transcripts of the Rosenholm family archive of Tycho's letters to Holger (the originals having since been largely lost), so the text descends through a copy, not an autograph.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter (Tycho to Holger Rosenkrantz, 7 Nov 1597) against Dreyer TBOO VIII pp.8-10 page images. Every proper name (Rantzau, Wandsbek, Hamburg, Axel, Sophie, Niels Krag, Ulrich), number/date (7 November 97), and the closing 'manu propria' subscription match Dreyer exactly. Considered whether 'dimidio saltem miliari' ('at least/only half a mile') is mistranslated as 'only half a mile', but 'saltem' is genuinely ambiguous between a minimum-threshold and a restrictive ('merely') sense in this context, so declined to record it as a defect rather than manufacture a weak objection. No fabrication, omission, or hedge loss found.

text.original:
NOBILITATE NON TANTUM GENERIS, SED ET GENIJ ATQUE INGENIJ VIRO IN PRIMIS CONSPICUO DOMINO OLIGERO ROSÆKRANTZIO DE ROSENHOLM, CONSANGVINEO, AFFINI ET AMICO INTEGERRIMO.

S. P.

CORDATISSIME mi OLIGERE, cognate desideratissime et affinis exoptatissime. Postquam priores hisce .......................... viserint tandem an non potius sui ipsius, et patriæ, cuius honori studere merito debuissent, maiore incommodo quam meo ................ nostræ satis arguunt compositoris malevolum animum pari præiudicio et avaritiæ nefanda labe infectum:

Proh superi quid non mortalia pectora cogis
Sacra sitis Rosei fontis, præbendaque sacra!

Dolendum certe est, imo supra modum dolendum, iuvenem hunc Regem, alias suapte natura virtutis capacem et generoso animo præditum, talibus glaucomatistis ita occæcari et in devia deduci, ut id, quod verum rectumque sit et Regno ac sibi forsan maiore duratione honorificum, quam multa alia, quæ inutiliter fiunt et profunduntur, perspicere et sentire nequeat, utpote alienis oculis et auribus tam videns quam audiens. Veniet forsan tempus quando et oculatior, magisque auritus (experientia et usu rerum sic suadente) reddetur. At quantum ad me meaque tamdiu exantlata studia nimis sero. Præveniam potius, et mihi ............. favente divina providentia, dum adhuc tempus superest ........... iamque alea iacta est, numeratæ tesseræ re......Bene sit Regi precor, utut mihi præter culpam et iniuriam non faventi. Bene sit vobis omnibus .............. præsertim integrioribus. Bene sit universæ Daniæ ex animo opto.

.............. Deo tra.......... fortuna, sequamur. Iamque vale mi amantissime OLIGERE, et quæ hîc desiderantur, in prioribus atque postscriptis lege, TYCHONEMque ex asse tuum sincere redamare, quod et sponte facturus es, nunquam desiste.

Iterumque et sæpius vale.
Dabantur subito Wandesburgo prope Hamburgum, die 16. Novembris Anni 97.
Tuus intimus et extimus
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.

POSTSCRIPTA.AMANTISSIME OLIGERE, si res tuæ
ullo modo ita ferrent, nihil magis in votis haberem, quam ut peractis Regijs
Nuptijs velles Bredenbergam venire et
mihi isthic indicato prius tempore, idque per certum et fidelem internuncium,
obviam ire: partim invisendi optimi illius Senis RANZOVIJ communis nostri Affinis et Amici
integerrimi gratia, partim ut bibliothecam eius, qua vix ampliorem et
splendidiorem Germania habet, lustres, sive
isthic fuerit Produx, sive non; est enim mihi semper liberum, nec dubito quin et
tibi, quem pariter is (prout tua meretur virtus) ex animo diligit; partim etiam,
ut nos invicem adhuc semel (dum modo sæpius non liceat) compellemus, antequam
longius disiungamur; quod non saltem sanguinis ratio et amicitiæ vinculum, sed
et nova inter nos affinitas exposcit. Neque enim ignoras, me
post Patrem esse e sponsæ agnatione proximum adeoque primum, ideoque non
negligendum aut prætereundum; veluti in cæteris vix admisisti. Atque hæ erunt
tibi sufficientes caussæ, imo unica earum, quod isthuc impetrata vel non
impetrata venia eas. Et si de me tacere, idque tibi soli secretum reservare,
cautius duxeris, libenter id concedam. Mihi enim perinde est, sive quis mea de
caussa palam sive clam agat; modo id quod æquum est et res postulat, agat.
Indica saltem actutum, quid a te in his præstari possit, ut et ego de meis
interea rebus sic eo commodius disponam. Exemplum nuperarum (de quibus in
prioribus dictum) literarum nunc non addo. Habebis id alias aut ubi
convenerimus, si etiamnum in Cancellaria vestra tectum habetur; uti solent ea,
quæ lucem oderunt. De tua enim voluntate nihil addubito. Cum
ante mensem circiter Observationes meas Astronomicas invitante Serenitate hîc
Wandesburgi renovarem, atque in
libro, quo priores Uraniburgi circa
æquinoctium vernum desinentes denotâram, has posteriores subiungere voluissem,
ut earundem tanto tempore præter solitum interruptarum occasio mihi et alijs in posterum memoria non excideret (quod tamen vix
futurum) exposui primum isthic prosa discessus mei ex Insula Venusia, adeoque tota Dania, rationes brevibus
comprehensas, moxque dictante genio incidit Carmen elegiacum, quod unâ isthic
adscripsi. Cuius hîc te participem reddo, cum sciam te Poëticis delectari, atque
ex Pegaseis fontibus canoras hausisse lymphas. Si itaque et tu pariter
responderis, non quidem consolandi gratia (cum scias me nihil in his asperi, sed
potius omnia ex usu putare), verum ut Uraniæ e Dania vestra in alia magisque gratiosa et commoda
loca mecum migranti Propempticum concinnes, nobisque utrinque sic congratuleris,
rem tam illi quam mihi non saltem iocundam sed et acceptam præstiteris. Neque
authoris nomen prodere opus erit: uti et mea apud te secreta haberi, et nemini
quidpiam inde communicari velim. Tradas potius Vulcano, ubi legeris. Sufficit in
memoria habere qua vales, cum et antea hæc ita se habere, satis superque
memineris. Iamque pluries vale. Dabantur ut supra in literis.

T. B.

ALTERA POSTSCRIPTA MINORIS MOMENTI.CUM Præfectum illum, quem discedens Venusiæ
nostræ præfeci, DAVIDEM PETRI nomine, apud me
suspectum reddiderit Parochus ille prior in Insula, interea dum hîc mecum egit,
nescio an odio aliquo privato an rei veritate, et inter alia narrârit, eum, cum
Patri tuo optim. mem. inserviret, aliquot centenis eum defraudasse, rogo velis
mihi scheda aliqua obiter indicare, quid de huius Præfecti fide vel secus
exploratum habeas. Nescio enim quantum Parocho isti fidendum sit, cum quia
alteri infensus erat, tum quod me sibi omnino optime cupientem, supra quam credi
posset, ante abitum despexerit, adeoque ut contumelias et calumnias, nulla de
caussa in os mihi dicere non erubuerit, quas tamen patienter ferens, ex alto
derisi, hominemque tanquam sui non compotem, addito viatico et munere, dimisi.
Quod te scire volui, ne in mei gratiam quidpiam de eo amplius sis sollicitus.
Plura ab ESCHILLO BILLE nostro
intelliges, qui acta habet in literas relata et testificata. Datum ut in
prioribus.

T. B.
text.english:
**To a man conspicuous in the first rank not only by the nobility of his lineage, but also by that of his spirit and his talent, Master Holger Rosenkrantz of Rosenholm, my kinsman, relation by marriage, and most upright friend.**

Heartiest greeting.

Most sensible Holger, my most longed-for kinsman and most desired relation, after my earlier [letters?] with these …………………… [they?] shall at last have seen whether [it is] not rather to the greater detriment of themselves and of the homeland — to whose honour they ought by rights to have devoted themselves — than to mine …………… our [affairs?] sufficiently prove the ill-willed disposition of the contriver, infected alike with prejudice and with the abominable taint of avarice:

Alas, ye gods above, to what do you not drive mortal hearts —
the accursed thirst of the Rosy fount, and the sacred prebends to be bestowed!

It is to be lamented, indeed lamented beyond measure, that this young King — otherwise of his own nature capable of virtue and endowed with a generous spirit — is so blinded by such purblind men [glaucomatistae] and led into byways, that he cannot perceive and feel that which is true and right, and perhaps more honourable to the Kingdom and to himself, in lasting longer, than the many other things that are done and poured out to no purpose — being, as it were, one who both sees with others' eyes and hears with others' ears. There will come a time perhaps when he too will be made more clear-sighted and more hearing (experience and the practice of affairs thus counselling). But as far as concerns me and my studies, so long laboured through, [it will be] too late. I will rather forestall [it], and, with divine providence favouring me ………… while time still remains …………, and now the die is cast, the dice counted [are?] thrown ……… May it go well with the King, I pray — even though he is, beyond any fault or wrong on my part, not favourable to me. May it go well with you all …………… especially with the more upright. May it go well with all Denmark, I wish from my heart.

…………… to God …………… fortune, let us follow. And now farewell, my most beloved Holger, and what is wanting here, read in my earlier [letters] and in the postscripts; and never cease to return Tycho's love sincerely, as wholly your own — which indeed you will do of your own accord.

And again and yet again, farewell.
Given in haste at Wandsbek near Hamburg, on the 16th day of November in the year [15]97.
Your intimate, and your outermost,
TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.

**POSTSCRIPT.**

Most beloved Holger, if your affairs would in any way allow it, I should wish for nothing more than that, the Royal Wedding once concluded, you would be willing to come to Breitenburg, and there — the time having first been indicated to me, and that through a sure and faithful go-between — to meet me: partly for the sake of visiting that excellent old man Rantzau, our common kinsman and a most upright friend; partly so that you might survey his library, than which Germany scarcely has an ampler or more splendid one, whether the Statthalter be there at the time or not — for access is always free to me, nor do I doubt that it is to you as well, whom he likewise loves from the heart, as your worth deserves; and partly also, that we might address one another once more, if oftener is not allowed, before we are separated by a greater distance — which not only the tie of blood and the bond of friendship, but also the new kinship between us, demands. Nor indeed are you unaware that, after her father, I am the nearest — indeed the first — of the bride's kin, and therefore not to be neglected or passed over, as in other matters you have scarcely allowed me to be. And these will be sufficient reasons for you — nay, even any one of them alone — that you should go there, whether leave be obtained or not. And if you should judge it more prudent to say nothing of me, and to keep that a secret to yourself alone, I will gladly grant it. For it is all the same to me, whether anyone acts openly or secretly on my account, provided he does what is fair and what the matter requires. Only let me know at once what can be accomplished by you in these matters, so that I too may in the meantime so arrange my own affairs the more conveniently.

I do not now add a copy of the recent letters, of which I spoke in my earlier ones. You shall have it another time, or when we meet, if it is even now kept hidden in your Chancery, as things that hate the light are wont to be. For of your goodwill I do not doubt at all.

When, about a month ago, [the fair] weather inviting me, I resumed my astronomical observations here at Wandsbek, and wished to append these later ones in the book in which I had recorded the earlier ones, ending around Uraniborg at the vernal equinox — so that the occasion of their being interrupted for so long a time, beyond what was usual, might not in future slip from my memory or others' (though that is scarcely likely to happen) — I set out there first, in prose, the reasons, briefly comprised, for my departure from the Island of Hven, and indeed from the whole of Denmark; and presently, my genius dictating, there fell out an elegiac poem, which I appended there together with it. Of this I now make you a partaker, since I know you delight in poetic things, and have drawn tuneful waters from the Pegasean springs. If, then, you too should reply in kind — not, indeed, for the sake of consoling me, since you know that I think there is nothing harsh in these things, but rather that all works to my advantage — but so as to compose a Propempticon for Urania, migrating with me from your Denmark into other, more gracious and convenient places, and so to congratulate us both, you will render a thing not merely pleasant but also welcome, to her as much as to me. Nor will it be necessary to disclose the author's name: just as I wish my own [verses] to be kept secret with you, and nothing of them to be communicated to anyone. Rather, once you have read it, you should hand it over to Vulcan. It is enough to keep alive in practice that gift in which you excel, since you remember well enough, and more than enough, that this has always been so. And now, farewell many times over. Given as above in the letter.

T. B.

**A SECOND POSTSCRIPT, OF LESSER MOMENT.**

Since that Bailiff whom, on departing, I set over our Hven — David Petri by name — has been made suspect to me by that former Parish Priest of the Island, while he was lately dealing with me here (I know not whether from some private hatred, or from the truth of the matter), and related, among other things, that he, while in service to your father of blessed memory, had defrauded him of some hundreds, I ask that you be willing to indicate to me, in passing, on some note, what you have ascertained about this Bailiff's honesty or otherwise. For I do not know how far that Parish Priest is to be trusted, both because he was ill-disposed toward the other, and because, before his departure, he scorned me — who wished him extremely well — beyond what could be believed, so much so that he did not blush to utter insults and slanders to my face for no cause; which, however, bearing patiently, I laughed off loftily, and dismissed the man, as one not in possession of himself, with travel-money and a gift added. This I wished you to know, lest for my sake you should be further troubled about him. You will learn more from our Eskild Bille, who has the proceedings set down in writing and attested. Given as in the earlier letters.

T. B.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / context.** Tycho Brahe, writing from **Wandsbek (Wandsburg)**, the castle near Hamburg held by his patron Heinrich Rantzau, where Tycho lodged in the autumn of 1597 after his departure from Denmark and Hven (he left in the spring/summer of 1597). The letter's bitterness toward "the young King" and his counsellors belongs to this moment of grievance over the loss of his royal support.
- **Recipient.** *Oligerus Rosaekrantzius de Rosenholm* = **Holger Rosenkrantz** "the Learned" (1574–1642), the Danish nobleman of Rosenholm, theologian and humanist, Tycho's kinsman and relation by marriage (*consanguineus, affinis*). The address-superscription's word-play on *generis / genij / ingenij* (lineage / spirit / talent) is kept in the rendering.
- **Place.** *Wandesburgo prope Hamburgum* = **Wandsbek**, then a Holstein estate of Heinrich Rantzau, now a district of Hamburg. (A companion letter to Rosenkrantz of **7 November 1597** is dated *"Wandesburgo ex arce Ranzoviana"* — "from the Rantzovian castle" — fixing the residence.)
- **"The young King."** *iuvenem hunc Regem* = **Christian IV of Denmark** (b. 1577), who had assumed personal rule in August 1596 (aged 19); Tycho blames not the King himself but the counsellors who, he says, blind him.
- **Verse (the centre of the letter).** Tycho adapts **Virgil, *Aeneid* III.56–57**: *"Quid non mortalia pectora cogis, / auri sacra fames!"* ("To what do you not drive mortal hearts, accursed thirst for gold!"). Tycho keeps the first line nearly verbatim (*Proh superi quid non mortalia pectora cogis*) and rewrites the second as a pun: *"Sacra sitis **Rosei** fontis, praebendaque sacra!"* — "the accursed thirst of the **Rosy** fount, and the sacred **prebends**." *Rosei fontis* ("of the rosy/Rosen fount") puns on the name **Rosenkrantz / Rosenholm** and/or on the courtier faction; *praebenda* are ecclesiastical/court **prebends** (stipendiary benefices). The line is kept as verse. *Sacra* is used antithetically — "accursed" (the Virgilian *sacra* = "execrable") in the first sense, "sacred/holy" (the benefices) in the second; the bitter irony is in the source and is preserved, not smoothed.
- ***glaucomatistae*** — "purblind men," literally those afflicted with *glaucoma* (clouded sight): a coinage of contempt for the King's counsellors, picked up by the following "sees with others' eyes, hears with others' ears." Kept as metaphor.
- ***compositor*** — *compositoris malevolum animum* = "the ill-willed disposition of the contriver/intriguer." Here *compositor* is the schemer who "composed" the situation against Tycho, not a typesetter; the referent (a specific hostile counsellor) is left unnamed in the text and so is not supplied here.
- ***alea iacta est*** — "the die is cast" (the Caesarian/Suetonian tag); followed by *numeratae tesserae re……* "the dice counted … [thrown?]." The verb after *re* is lost in the lacuna; **[thrown]** is offered conjecturally in square brackets (e.g. *reiectae* / *reiacta*) and flagged — the source breaks off.
- ***Tuus intimus et extimus*** — "Your intimate, and your outermost": a paradoxical sign-off (innermost in affection, outermost — i.e. furthest off / on the periphery — in place or fortune), rendered literally and left as the pointed flourish it is.
- ***ex asse tuum*** — "wholly your own" (*ex asse* = "to the whole, entirely," the Roman inheritance idiom).
- **Lacunae (textual crux — the governing limitation).** The sole witness is a later **afskrift (copy) in Langebek's Diplomatarium** at the Rigsarkivet; it is **damaged/illegible in many places**, marked here by runs of dots exactly as transmitted. The lacunae fall in load-bearing positions — the opening conditional period (*Postquam priores hisce … viserint … nostrae satis arguunt*), the *Praeveniam … alea iacta est* sentence, and the closing *Deo tra…… fortuna, sequamur* clause — so the connective logic of several sentences is genuinely uncertain. No lacuna has been filled in the translation beyond the single bracketed conjecture **[thrown]** and bracketed clarifying subjects (**[letters?]**, **[affairs?]**, **[they?]**) flagged with question marks; nothing is silently restored.
- **Negations.** The source carries three load-bearing negatives, all preserved: *an **non** potius sui ipsius … incommodo* ("whether **not** rather to [their own] detriment"); *mihi praeter culpam et iniuriam **non** faventi* ("**not** favourable to me, beyond any fault or wrong [on my part]"); and *nunquam desiste* ("**never** cease"). None added, none dropped.
- **Calendar.** *die 16. Novembris Anni 97* = **16 November 1597**, Old Style (Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). The dateline matches the catalogue label; no discrepancy. *Dabantur* ("Given/Issued") kept.
- **What the recovered text is.** Both postscripts to Tycho's 16 November 1597 letter to Holger ("Oliger") Rosenkrantz — the main POSTSCRIPTA and the shorter ALTERA POSTSCRIPTA — were entirely absent from the prior transcription; only the letter's final valediction survived as the published tail.
- **Addressee and the new kinship.** Holger Rosenkrantz "the Learned" (1574–1642), later a leading Danish statesman and theologian, is here anticipating marriage into Tycho's own family: Thoren records that "in the late 1590s, Holger married a daughter of... Axel Brahe (Tycho's brother)" [Thoren, *Lord of Uraniborg*], and Christianson identifies her as Tycho's niece Sophie Axelsdatter Brahe, who with Holger "maintained a learned household" at Rosenholm comparable to Uraniborg [Christianson, *On Tycho's Island*]. This dates and explains the letter's talk of a "nova inter nos affinitas" (new kinship) and Tycho's claim to be, after the bride's father, her nearest kinsman.
- **The Royal Wedding.** "Peractis Regijs Nuptijs" refers to the wedding of King Christian IV to Anna Catherine of Brandenburg, held at Haderslevhus in November 1597 — the very event this letter, dated 16 November 1597, anticipates. Christianson records that Heinrich Rantzau himself was travelling to attend the same wedding, and that Tycho corresponded with him about it at just this time [Christianson, *On Tycho's Island*].
- **Rantzau and Breitenburg.** "Bredenberga" is Rantzau's seat of Breitenburg, whose library Tycho calls the ampler and more splendid than any other in Germany — consistent with Lohmeier's account of the Breitenburg library (c. 6,300 volumes by 1590). Tycho was resident at Rantzau's Wandsbek castle when writing.
- **A lost occasional poem.** Tycho reports composing, about a month earlier (i.e. October 1597), a prose account of his reasons for leaving Hven and Denmark plus an accompanying elegiac Latin poem, entered into his observing log to mark the resumption of his astronomical observations at Wandsbek after the interruption since leaving Hven in March 1597. He asks Holger, in strict confidence — "hand it over to Vulcan" (burn it) once read — to compose a companion *Propempticon* (a classical send-off/farewell-poem genre) for "Urania" migrating with him from Denmark. This is a new, previously unpublished data point on Tycho's own poetic self-fashioning of the 1597 departure.
- **David Petri and Eskild Bille.** The second postscript concerns David Petri, i.e. David Pedersen, independently confirmed as "Tycho Brahe's bailiff on Hven 1597-1601" left in charge of Uraniborg and Stjerneborg on Tycho's 1597 departure [Christianson, *On Tycho's Island*, Biographical Directory s.v. "Pedersen, David"]. Hven's former parish priest had accused David of once defrauding Holger's late father while in his service; Tycho, distrusting the priest (whom he says he dismissed with severance pay despite the priest's insults), asks Holger's independent judgment and names "Eschillus Bille" — Eskild (Eske) Bille — as holding the documented record; a letter from Eske Bille to Tycho is independently attested in Zeeberg's edition of the Sophie Brahe/Urania Titani correspondence register.

text.original:
NOBILISS. ET EXCELLENTISS. DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, DOMINO IN KNUDSTRUP ET EQUITI DANO, DOMINO ET AMICO MEO SUMMA OBSERVANTIA COLENDO.

NOBILISSIME et Excellentissime Domine TYCHO, cum post abitum tabellarij summopere tunc festinantis observationes in ♃ ad 20 Nov. diem habitas calculo subijcere vellem, inveni me errasse in assignatione distantiae ♃ ab Aldeb. quae revera tunc erat 8° 51', non vero 9°51', quod ex festinatione factum esse scias. Distantia vero ♃ et Hu. Orio. vera fuit 19°8', ut post diligenti consideratione sextantis inveni. Verum sextans quo utor (ut et in literis indicavi) mihi nequaquam satisfacit, maxime propter vulgarem divisionem, eamque minus ratam. Sic ergo se habent.

20 Nov. H. 12 P. M.

Dist. ♃ et Aldeborae	8°	51'
Dist. ♃ et Hu. dext. Orion.	19	8
Altit. Merid. ♃	57	54½ vel 55'
Altit. Aldeb.	52	0
Altit. Aequat.	36	22	Ergo se recte positio instr. quadr. tunc habuit.
Decl. ♃	21	33 fere B.
Asc. R.	70	13

Asc. hanc ex asc. R. Aldeb. et ex asc. R. Hu. dex. Orion. inquisivi viceversa. Asc. R. Hu. Orio. ex loco longit. et latit. iuxta tuum Canonem constitui videlicet hoc tempore 83 Gr. 23' fere.

Longitudo ♃	11	39	♊
Latitudo ♃	0	42½	Merid.

Fuit ergo medio motu ☉ iuxta tuam restitutionem oppositus die 22 Nov. Hor. 2½ circiter P. M. iuxta verum motum ☉ opponebatur die 23 Nov. Hor. 9 A. M.

Si Ephemerides STADIJ se recte habent, calculus parum deviat. Sed tuum de his iudicium peto, et quae calculi utriusque sit differentia.

♂ quoque hisce diebus aliquoties diligenter considerabo, quod tamen ut in posterum subtilius et expeditius fiat, T. Ex. observationum mearum in literis propositarum dilucida resolutione haud dubie efficiet. Et hanc designationem Tabellario in vicina urbe adhuc commoranti transmisi, ut literis meis eam insereret. Vale.

De altitudine ☾ capienda dubium.

Cum ☾ limbus uno quasi minuto extans per rimulam capitur, observatio certa esse non potest; nam centrum ☾ haberi nequit. Nam circa unum latus pinnacidij per unam rimulam conspicitur limbi extremitas, per alteram rimam conspicitur maior portio ☾. Relinquitur igitur, incertam esse altitudinem, cum nec medium Lunae (ut in stellis) habeatur, nec etiam revera sciri possit, an portio unius vel 2 minut. vel plus minusve de corpore Lunari conspiciatur, et proinde ignoretur, an semidiameter ☾ uno vel duobus minutis minor sit addenda vel subtrahenda. Hoc dubium in accipienda ☾ altitudine certa me valde torquet. Cupio igitur certi quid in hoc negotio ex T. E. cognoscere.

Vale.
23 Nov. 97.
T. Exc.
observ.
D. FABRICIUS.

N. B. Quomodo etiam minimarum stellarum centrum per rimulas
sext. vel quadr. haberi possit, valde miror (cum illarum diameter vix 1
minut.). Aut enim rimulas valde amplas esse oportet, et sic incertus per
rimulam talem laxam vel amplam prospectus esse videtur, aut si rimulæ
mediocres, non videbitur. Quomodo igitur agendum sit, magnopere scire cupio,
et quæ rimularum pro minimis stellis laxitas vel amplitudo maxima esse
debeat in instru. 4 pedum, cognoscere valde desidero.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most excellent lord Tycho Brahe, lord of Knudstrup and Danish knight, my lord and friend to be honoured with the deepest respect.**

Most noble and most excellent lord Tycho, when, after the departure of the courier — who was then in the greatest haste — I wished to subject to calculation the observations made on Jupiter [♃] for the day of 20 November, I found that I had erred in the assignment of the distance of Jupiter [♃] from Aldebaran, which in truth was then 8° 51', and not 9° 51' — which, you should know, came about through the haste. But the true distance of Jupiter [♃] and the shoulder of Orion [Hu. Orio.] was 19° 8', as I afterwards found upon careful examination of the sextant. The sextant I use, however (as I also indicated in my letter), by no means satisfies me, chiefly on account of its common [scale] division, and that one less exact. So, then, they stand as follows.

20 November, 12 hours after noon [12 P.M.].

Distance of Jupiter [♃] and Aldebaran	8°	51'
Distance of Jupiter [♃] and the right shoulder of Orion	19	8
Meridian altitude of Jupiter [♃]	57	54½ or 55'
Altitude of Aldebaran	52	0
Altitude of the equator	36	22	Therefore the setting of the quadrant instrument was then correct.
Declination of Jupiter [♃]	21	33 nearly, North.
Right ascension	70	13

This right ascension I sought out from the right ascension of Aldebaran and from the right ascension of the right shoulder of Orion, [and] conversely. The right ascension of the shoulder of Orion I established from its place in longitude and latitude according to your Canon, namely at this time 83 degrees 23' nearly.

Longitude of Jupiter [♃]	11	39	Gemini [♊]
Latitude of Jupiter [♃]	0	42½	South [Merid.]

It [Jupiter] was therefore, by the mean motion of the Sun [☉] according to your restoration, in opposition on the day of 22 November, at about hour 2½ after noon [P.M.]; by the true motion of the Sun [☉] it was in opposition on the day of 23 November, at hour 9 before noon [A.M.].

If Stadius's Ephemerides are correct, the calculation deviates but little. But I ask your judgement on these matters, and what the difference of the two calculations may be.

Mars [♂], too, I shall examine carefully several times in these days; yet that this may be done more subtly and more expeditiously hereafter, Your Excellency will doubtless bring about by a clear resolution of my observations set out in my letter. And I have sent this notation to the courier, who is still staying in the neighbouring town, so that he might insert it among my letters. Farewell.

A doubt concerning the taking of the Moon's [☾] altitude.

When the limb of the Moon [☾], standing out by as it were one minute, is captured through the little slit, the observation cannot be certain; for the centre of the Moon [☾] cannot be obtained. For around one side of the sight [pinnule], through one little slit the edge of the limb is seen, [and] through the other slit a greater portion of the Moon [☾] is seen. It remains, therefore, that the altitude is uncertain, since neither is the middle of the Moon obtained (as with the stars), nor indeed can it truly be known whether a portion of one or 2 minutes, or more or less, of the lunar body is seen, and accordingly it is not known whether the semidiameter of the Moon [☾], smaller by one or two minutes, is to be added or subtracted. This doubt in taking a certain altitude of the Moon [☾] greatly torments me. I desire, therefore, to learn something certain in this matter from Your Excellency.

Farewell.
23 November [15]97.
Your Excellency's
observer,
D. Fabricius.

**N.B.** How, too, the centre of even the smallest stars can be obtained through the slits of a sextant or quadrant, I greatly wonder (since their diameter is scarcely 1 minute). For either the slits must be very wide — and then the sighting through such a loose or wide slit seems uncertain — or, if the slits are of middling [width], nothing will be seen [at all]. How, therefore, one is to proceed, I very much desire to know; and what the greatest looseness or width of the slits ought to be for the smallest stars, in an instrument of 4 feet, I very much desire to learn.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *D. Fabricius* = **David Fabricius** (1564–1617), Frisian Lutheran pastor (then at Resterhave / Ostfriesland) and observational astronomer; discoverer of the variable star Mira Ceti (1596). He had opened a correspondence with Tycho and would visit him at Wandsbek in 1598; here he is in the deferential posture of a provincial observer submitting raw data to Tycho for adjudication. The subscription *observ[ator]* ("observer") marks the role he claims toward Tycho. This letter survives as an autograph inserted between leaves 153 and 154 of GKS 316 fol. (the *Thesaurus Observationum*), the leaf-block (150–157) of Fabricius's own observations Tycho appended to his 1597 observations.
- **Recipient titulature.** *Dominus in Knudstrup et Eques Danus* = "lord of **Knudstrup** and Danish knight" — Tycho's ancestral seat in Scania and his noble rank; titulature kept in full by this chapter's convention
- **Astronomical objects / abbreviations.**
 - *Aldeb. / Aldeborae* = **Aldebaran** (α Tauri).
 - *Hu. Orio. / Hu. dext. Orion.* = *Humerus dexter Orionis*, **the right shoulder of Orion** (the bright star at Orion's right shoulder, conventionally α Orionis / Betelgeuse). Expanded in the translation; the manuscript's contracted form is kept in the Source block.
 - The planet/luminary glyphs are named in English by this chapter's convention with the glyph retained in the Source block: ♃ = **Jupiter**, ☉ = **Sun**, ☾ = **Moon**, ♂ = **Mars**, ♊ = **Gemini**.
- **Technical terms (editorial glossary,–5.2).** *distantia* → distance (angular separation); *sextans* → **sextant** (Tycho's *sextans astronomicus*); *altitudo meridiana* → **meridian altitude**; *altitudo aequatoris* ("altitude of the equator") → the altitude of the celestial equator, i.e. the co-latitude check by which Fabricius confirms the quadrant's setting; *declinatio* → **declination**; *ascensio recta* (*Asc. R.*) → **right ascension**; *longitudo / latitudo* → **(celestial) longitude / latitude**; *semidiameter* → **semidiameter**; *pinnacidium* → **sight (pinnule)**; *quadrans* → **quadrant**. The instrument-noun *instr. quadr.* is expanded as "the quadrant instrument."
- ***vulgaris divisio*** — "the common [scale] division": Fabricius complains his sextant has only an ordinary (undivided-into-transversals) graduation, "and that one less exact" (*eamque minus ratam*). The bracketed "[scale]" marks an editorial insertion clarifying *divisio*.
- ***tuum Canonem*** — "your **Canon**": Tycho's canon/table of fixed-star places (his star catalogue), against which Fabricius reduces the shoulder of Orion to 83°23' right ascension. Rendered "Canon," not modernised.
- ***iuxta tuam restitutionem*** — "according to your **restoration**": Tycho's restored solar theory / tables (*restitutio* by this chapter's convention, Tycho's programme of *astronomia instaurata*). The mean-motion opposition (22 Nov.) and true-motion opposition (23 Nov.) of Jupiter to the Sun are reckoned from it.
- ***Ephemerides Stadij*** — the **Ephemerides of Johannes Stadius** (1527–1579), the widely used Copernican-based ephemerides; *Stadij* is the genitive of *Stadius*. Name kept.
- **Symbols / numerals.** *B.* after the declination value (*21 33 fere B.*) is read as **Borealis / Boreal = North** (the declination is north); rendered "North." This reading is consistent with *Merid.* beside the latitude (see next). **Flagged:** *B.* is an abbreviation; "North" is the supported expansion in context (a +21° declination in Gemini), but the single letter is not spelled out in the source.
- ***Merid.*** (beside *Latitudo ♃ 0 42½*) — abbreviation, here taken as **Meridiana** = northern (boreal) ecliptic latitude, i.e. the latitude lies to the north; rendered "[North]" in brackets. **Crux flagged:** *Merid.* could in principle abbreviate *Meridionalis* (southern); the bracketed "North" follows the boreal sense paired with the boreal declination, but the abbreviation alone does not decide the hemisphere — recorded, not silently resolved. (See Confidence.)
- **Calendar.** The dateline *23 Nov. 97* (O.S.; Denmark and the Lutheran German lands kept the Julian calendar) **agrees with the edition label** *1597. 23. november*; no discrepancy. The internal dates (20 Nov. observation; 22/23 Nov. computed oppositions) are reproduced exactly as written and are **not** converted. The time-notation *P. M.* / *A. M.* is the period's "post/ante meridiem" reckoning from noon (so *H. 12 P. M.* = 12 hours after noon = midnight ending 20 Nov.); rendered "after noon / before noon" with the Latin retained in brackets, not silently modernised to clock time.
- **Negations.** The Moon-altitude paragraph turns on a chain of negated clauses (*non potest … nequit … nec … nec … ignoretur*); all four negations are reproduced one-for-one, and the disjunction *addenda vel subtrahenda* ("to be added or subtracted") is kept as a genuine either/or — Fabricius's point is precisely that he cannot tell which.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *Vale* → "Farewell" (×3); subscription *T. Exc. observ. D. Fabricius* → "Your Excellency's observer, D. Fabricius."
- **What this is.** A further note, headed "N.B.", added after Fabricius's signature and dateline (23 November 1597) — a true postscript in substance if not in name, continuing the instrument-sighting question already under way in the published tail (the difficulty of centring the Moon's disc in a pinhole sight, "per rimulam").
- **The correspondent.** David Fabricius (1564–1617), the East Frisian pastor-astronomer later famous for discovering the variability of Mira Ceti; an independent observer whom Kepler rated the finest observational astronomer in Europe after Tycho's death, and who briefly joined Tycho's household staff at Wandsbek in 1598 and again at Prague in 1601 [Christianson, *On Tycho's Island* (Cambridge, 2000)].
- **Where this letter physically sits.** This exact letter of 23 November 1597 is not merely epistolary — it survives bound into Tycho's own manuscript observation volume, inserted between folios 153 and 154, immediately after a note in Tycho's hand that his 1597 observations were "somewhat poor" and needed supplementing with Fabricius's own (folios 150–157, all in Fabricius's hand).
- **Technical vocabulary.** "Rimula" (little slit/crack) is the standard term for the narrow aperture-sight fitted to Tycho's sextants and quadrants; Mosley's index glosses the type as "slit-sights" (pp. 55–56, 105–106) [Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens* (Cambridge, 2007)] — confirming the rendering used here.
- **Crux.** The passage poses a genuine, unresolved technical dilemma in Fabricius's own words (wide slit = imprecise sighting; narrow slit = invisible star) rather than a corrupt reading; nothing in the Latin itself is in doubt, but the abbreviations "sext.", "quadr.", and "instru. 4 pedum" are silently expanded in translation only, not in the source.
- **Correction.** 'Latitude of Jupiter 0°42½′ North [Merid.]' corrected to 'South [Merid.]' — 'Merid.' abbreviates Meridionalis (South), as confirmed by Dreyer TBOO VIII p.13, where the same letter uses 'B.' (Borealis) for North two lines above in Jupiter's declination.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (**high**). "Merid." abbreviates Meridionalis (South), not North; the same letter uses "B." (Borealis) for North two lines earlier when giving Jupiter's declination, so "Merid." here is the parallel abbreviation for the opposite direction. The English silently glosses it as "North", flipping Jupiter's ecliptic latitude to the wrong hemisphere in a letter whose entire content is precise numerical astronomical data. **Repaired.** Collated against the Dreyer page images for this letter (TBOO VIII pp.13-15, all 3 pages read). P.13 clearly shows 'Decl. 4 21 33 fere B.' (Declination, North) followed a few lines later by 'Latitudo 4 0 42½ Merid.' (Latitude, South) — the letter's own internal contrast between 'B.' and 'Merid.' confirms the audit's identification. No other cruces found on the three pages.

text.original:
VIRO NOBILISSIMO ET AMPLISSIMO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, DANO, MATHEMATICORUM PRINCIPI AD MANUS.

CUM te, Vir amplissime, Mathematicorum omnium non huius tantum ætatis, sed totius ævi Monarcham constituerit incomparabilis doctrina iudicijque præstantia, iniquum fecero, si opusculo de proportione cœlorum nuper in lucem dato (sub titulo: Prodromus dissertationum cosmographicarum) ullam gloriam, tuo iudicio et commendatione neglecta, aucuper. Quæ me causa movit, ut ignotus ex hoc obscuro Germaniæ angulo literas ad te mitterem, oratum per illum ingentem Veritatis amorem, quem in te quoque inesse fama tuæ magnitudinis prædicat: ut, quid tibi de isthoc videatur negocio, ea synceritate et humanitate, quæ in te prædicatur, explices, brevibusque literis significes. O me felicem, si quod MÆSTLINO, idem et TYCHONI videbitur: quibus ego duobus propugnatoribus non dubitabo totius orbis iam excitatas insectationes forti animo sustinere. Sin autem id consecutus fuero, ut quæ insunt infirma, inepta, et puerilia, qualia mihi per ætatem multa exciderunt, censura volueris notare: an ego non rursum huiusmodi reprehensionem totius mundi, si esset, assensui præferam? Exemplaria non dubito, quin antea habeas: quare facile patior, ut difficultas transmittendi per tantum intervallum a mittendo me avocet. Tuorum autem operum ad nos nihil perfertur: quæque de te sciebam, ex MÆSTLINO didiceram. Dabis igitur veniam, si quibus in locis tui nominis mentionem faciens, iniuriam tibi tuæque hypothesi faciam. Plura dicturum quæsiturumque reverentia me retinet. Aperi luctanti voci viam, scriptis ad me paucissimis: efficies enim, ut tibi demonstrem, quanto sim discendi, quam laudis cupidior.

Vale, Vir Nobilissime, meaque tibi studia commendata habe.
Idibus Decemb. An. 1597.
Nobilitatis et Magnitudinis
Tuæ Reverent.
M. IOHANNES KEPLERUS,
Illustrium Styriæ Procerum in Gymnasio
Græcensi Mathematicus.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most eminent lord Tycho Brahe, the Dane, Prince of Mathematicians — into his own hands.**

Since, most eminent Sir, incomparable learning and outstanding judgement have established you as the Monarch of all mathematicians not only of this age but of the whole of time, I shall act unjustly if, in the little work on the proportion of the heavens lately brought to light (under the title *Prodromus dissertationum cosmographicarum* [Forerunner of Cosmographical Dissertations]), I were to angle for any glory while neglecting your judgement and commendation. This is the cause that has moved me, unknown as I am, to send a letter to you from this obscure corner of Germany — begging you, by that immense love of Truth which fame, [speaking] of your greatness, proclaims to dwell in you also, to set out what your view of this matter may be, with that sincerity and kindness which is proclaimed in you, and to make it known to me in a brief letter. O happy me, if what seems good to Maestlin shall seem the same to Tycho too! For with these two as my champions I shall not hesitate to bear with a stout heart the attacks already roused against me from the whole world. But if instead I shall obtain this — that you should be willing to mark with your censure whatever is weak, inept, and childish in it (and many such things, owing to my [youthful] age, have slipped from me) — shall I not once again prefer a reproof of this kind, to the assent of the whole world, were it [mine]? I do not doubt that you already have copies; and so I readily allow the difficulty of conveyance across so great a distance to call me away from sending one. But none of your own works reaches us: whatever I knew about you, I had learned from Maestlin. You will therefore grant me pardon if, in certain places where I make mention of your name, I do you and your hypothesis an injury. Reverence holds me back from saying and asking more. Open a way for my struggling voice by writing me but a very few lines: for you will bring it about that I may show you how much keener I am to learn than to be praised.

Farewell, most noble Sir, and hold my endeavours commended to you.
On the Ides of December [13 December], the year 1597.
Of Your Nobility and Greatness
the reverent
Master Johannes Kepler,
Mathematician of the Illustrious Estates of Styria in the Gymnasium of Graz.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / direction of the letter.** Despite the edition identifier (brahe-t_…), this is **Johannes Kepler → Tycho Brahe**, Kepler's celebrated *first* letter to Tycho — his approach as a then-unknown 25-year-old district mathematician in Graz to the reigning observational authority. (The edition's archival logic files the whole correspondence under Brahe.)
- **Correspondent addressed.** *Tychoni Brahe, Dano, Mathematicorum Principi* — **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), styled "Prince of Mathematicians." *Ad manus* ("into his own hands") is the address-direction on the cover.
- **Sender's self-styling.** *M. Iohannes Keplerus, Illustrium Styriae Procerum in Gymnasio Graecensi Mathematicus* = **Master Johannes Kepler, Mathematician of the Illustrious Estates of Styria at the Graz Gymnasium** (the Protestant *Stiftsschule* / *Landschaftsschule* in **Graz**, where Kepler held the post of provincial mathematician 1594–1600). *M.* = *Magister* (academic Master, this chapter's convention). The place of writing (Graz) is supplied to the header from this subscription; the dateline itself names only the date.
- ***opusculo … sub titulo: Prodromus dissertationum cosmographicarum*** — the *Mysterium Cosmographicum* (Tübingen, 1596/97), whose full title opens *Prodromus dissertationum cosmographicarum, continens mysterium cosmographicum…* Kepler's "little work on the proportion of the heavens" (*de proportione coelorum*) is his polyhedral-nesting account of the planetary spacing. The title is kept in Latin and glossed.
- ***Maestlino*** = **Michael Maestlin** (Maestlinus, 1550–1631), Kepler's astronomy teacher at Tübingen and his Copernican mentor, who oversaw the printing of the *Mysterium*. Named twice; spelling normalised to "Maestlin" in the translation.
- ***tuae hypothesi*** — **"your hypothesis,"** i.e. Tycho's world-system (the geo-heliocentric arrangement); *hypothesis* in the period sense of a cosmological model/arrangement, not a tentative conjecture. Kepler — an open Copernican — pre-apologises for places in the *Mysterium* where his treatment may slight Tycho's model. Rendered "hypothesis" and the model-sense noted (cf. this chapter's convention *orbis/sphaera*).
- ***Mathematicorum … Monarcham … Principi*** — the doubled superlative styling ("Monarch of all mathematicians of the whole of time"; "Prince of Mathematicians"). Kept at full courtesy-register; this is captatio benevolentiae, not a settled title.
- ***totius orbis iam excitatas insectationes*** — "the attacks already roused against me from the whole world": the controversy Kepler anticipated (and met) over the *Mysterium*'s Copernican and a-priori argument. *propugnatoribus* "champions / defenders" — Maestlin and Tycho cast as Kepler's two backers.
- ***qualia mihi per aetatem multa exciderunt*** — "many such things, owing to my age, have slipped from me": Kepler's own hedge of youth/inexperience. Preserved as a hedge, not sharpened into a claim of error.
- ***Exemplaria non dubito, quin antea habeas*** — "I do not doubt that you already have copies": Kepler presumes Tycho has obtained the book, and so excuses himself (citing *difficultas transmittendi per tantum intervallum*, the difficulty of conveyance over so great a distance) from sending one. He was mistaken — Tycho had not yet seen it — which colours Tycho's reply.
- ***Aperi luctanti voci viam*** — "Open a way for my struggling/labouring voice": *luctanti* of a voice straining (with diffidence/reverence) to be heard; rendered "struggling," the strain kept.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *Vale* → "Farewell"; *meaque tibi studia commendata habe* → "and hold my endeavours commended to you"; the subscription *Nobilitatis et Magnitudinis Tuae Reverent[issimus]* → "Of Your Nobility and Greatness the [most] reverent" (the abbreviation *Reverent.* expanded to a superlative subscription-formula; the bracketed *-issimus* is editorial).
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Idibus Decemb. An. 1597* = **"on the Ides of December (13 December), the year 1597,"** rendered with the Roman idiom and glossed to the civil date by this chapter's convention. **Style:** dated by Kepler, a Lutheran in Inner-Austrian Habsburg territory; Styria/Graz had adopted the **Gregorian (New Style)** calendar (introduced in the Inner-Austrian lands 1583), so this "13 December" is very probably **N.S.**, whereas Tycho on Hven still reckoned **O.S.** The header is tagged [O.S.] to match this chapter's default Tycho-side convention and the edition, **but the likely N.S. origin of the dateline is flagged here, not silently converted** (the O.S. equivalent would be 3 December 1597). This is the named calendar crux.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. All 3 pages read as page images (Dreyer VIII pp. 14-16). Confirmed the transcribed original is a verbatim match of Dreyer's printed Latin for Kepler's first letter to Tycho. Checked every name (Maestlino, Tychoni), the title 'Prodromus dissertationum cosmographicarum', and the date 'Idibus Decemb. An. 1597' (Ides of December = 13th). No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, hedge-loss, or text error found. Published self-grade was B; upgraded to A on full collation since no defects survive scrutiny.

text.original:
GENEROSO TYCHONI
BRAHEO, MATHEMATICO PRINCIPI, COGNATO ET AFFINI
DESIDERATISSIMO.

GENEROSE mi TYCHO, cognate affinis desideratissime, amicorum intime. Iam
inde quo literæ tuæ desideratissimæ pridie Non. Decembris reddebantur, medijs
his turbis nuptialibus, laboriosissimis districtus præpedimentis distineor, ne
quod valde exoptâram, responsum usque huc festinare licuerit. In præsens vero,
ubi liberior aliquanto adspirat aura, rarissimam hanc felicitatem, qua cum
amicis ingenuæ mentis tuto communicare conceditur, flagrantissime cupitam,
adlubentius eo excipio, quo rariores eius census, multivarios inter, ut nosti
ingenia, habeam et æstimem. Utut autem facile sciam nil præter spem, haud multa
præter voluntatem, exuli iam pridem tibi, modo libero, accidisse, doleo nihilo
etiamdum minus, non tui equidem, sed mei ipsius, sed patriæ immerentis, sed
bonorum in patria omnium, quibus integrior mens et animus, caussa, quos paucorum
quorundam livor, alia obtentui sumpta caussa, suo desiderio, sua gloria, suo
privavit amore et gaudio; alias equidem, ut nihil est certe, quod, natura sic
imperante, in rebus caducis apparere solentius
autumem dissimilium inter se haud interrupta unquam contentione et pugna, quam
non abstrusis modo, sensusque latentibus Naturæ laboribus familiarem, sed et
concitatis destinati humanarum rerum dispensatoris Mentis facinoribus pene
domesticam indies ostentari suspicimus, ita et nihil est, cur eundem hunc Naturæ
morem demirarer, si vel maxime hoc ex circo etiam Musæ iunctim omnes recentibus
æmulationibus proscriptæ exularent, tecumque castra moventes, se in universum
hinc, ubi nihil prisci et integri moris, subducerent; magis est vel tandem
experiendo discere, perversam eiuscemodi, non utique alias insolentem, scena hac
tripudiantis invidentiæ, caute suspectare inconstantiam, prudenterque provisis, quæ tempus commonet, subductas sui rationes non stolidis
ac evanidis, ast solidis et ævo dignis firmare munimentis, ne alienis quam
proprijs innixi mage virtutibus, ad aleatorios quosvis fortunæ iactus * cernimus
nutare, quin et concidere penitus eveniat. Tu vero nobis, tu inquam TYCHO generose facem hîc prætulisti, tu
tuo nobis præluxisti exemplo, tu veræ virtutis ipsi sibi ex asse undique
sufficientis, vestigia posuisti, quibus insistere, quis ad hanc metam adspirans
non adniteretur? Ipse ego certe (qui licet illustri huic consessui accersiri non
merear, in spem tamen secundam aut tertiam saltem acciri indies adnitor) multa
nec levia in me malevolentiæ indicia, utut premantur, erumpere sentisco, ast σὺν
δαίμονι ἐσϑλῷ quod spero incassum, nec enim ad hosce ventus ego mea distendi
vela, neque enim importuoso isti me commiserim vado. Sed de me coram ipse
præsens, ne adfectu et præcipitantia, quorum caussas procul habeo, imprudens
nimis in literas intutas, relatrices, rationum mearum secreta conijcere videar,
quæ non aliter constant, quam si nulli, nisi alteri mihi reddantur. Ad diem
itaque anni adproperantis quintum decimum, favente Numine, aliud vitæ meæ
facturus initium, tædiosissimo huic renunciaturus ergastulo, rogationi tuæ
amicissimæ vel non rogatus sponte adsentiri iam pridem est animus, nec vero ad
ullius unquam æmulationes et odia me in his, quæ recta sunt, comparaturus sum
unquam. Et vero quid mage dedeceret, te, quem non affinitate modo, sed et
sanguine, sed et necessitudinis vinculis omnibus peculiari sorte, iure primum
æstimo, colo et observo, te inquam post tot benevolentissimi animi in immerentem
indicia, insalutatum præterire? Age ergo, num circa dictum tempus sat commodus
tibi meus videatur accessus, litera per hunc tabellarium
adsignifices una aut altera; faxo ego hîc interim, ne, quod in me desideres,
præter vires forte, siet quidquam; alia præsenti adloquio reservanda, quo et si
quæ nova sunt, quæ referre interest, relata velim, nisi quod hoc unicum in
præsens referre intersit, communem nostrum CRAGIUM in Poloniam brevi
ablegandum, ad 1. Ianuarij litteris huc esse
advocatum, quem, itinere per Holsatiam
sumpto, te invisurum nullus dubito, cui et quo me adiungere queam, modo non
festinantior abierit, enixe studebo. Ego vero si non studio me continerem, finem
vix habiturum esset hoc meum per litteras adloquium, ut et potiora, imo vero,
quod ego sentio potissima, Epistolij tui capita commodiori opportunitati lubens
reservem. Ludant interea meæ Musæ, qua valent, ad hæc; aperte equidem, ast suo
sub velo. Interea te præpotenti rerum nostrarum gubernatori, Trinuno Numini, cum
universa tua familia, consilijs et actionibus, commendo. Vale felicissime.

Te nulli secundus integerrimo colens animo

OLIGERUS
ROSÆCRANTZ.
Perscribebam

Haderslebiæ XVI Decemb.
CIↃ CI
IIIC.

Salutari te suo nomine officiosissime voluit IACOBUS ULFELDIUS, quem te
sincere etiam maioribus renitentibus amare et suspicere scias.
text.english:
**To the noble Tycho Brahe, prince of mathematicians, kinsman and most longed-for relative by marriage.**

My noble Tycho, most longed-for kinsman and relative, most intimate of friends. Ever since your most-longed-for letter was delivered on the day before the Nones of December [4 December], I have been held fast, hemmed in by these wedding tumults and their most laborious encumbrances, so that I have not been able to hasten until now the reply I had so greatly desired. But at present, when a somewhat freer breeze breathes upon me, I take up the more gladly this rarest happiness — so ardently desired, the happiness of being permitted to share safely with friends of a free and honest mind — the more so since I hold and prize its returns as the rarer, amid temperaments as varied as you know them to be. But although I readily know that nothing beyond [your] hope, and not much beyond [your] wish, has befallen you — long since an exile, now a free man — I grieve nonetheless not at all the less, not on your account indeed, but on my own, but on that of an undeserving fatherland, but on that of all good men in the fatherland, men of a sounder mind and spirit; for the spite of certain few, taking up some other cause for a pretext, has robbed [the fatherland] of its desire for [you], of its glory in [you], of its love and joy in [you]. For the rest, indeed — just as there is surely nothing which, nature so ordaining, I would judge to appear more habitually in transient things than the never-once-interrupted strife and contention of unlike things among themselves, a strife we see displayed daily not only as familiar to the hidden, sense-eluding labours of Nature, but as almost domestic in the violent doings of the appointed Mind that dispenses human affairs — so too there is no reason why I should marvel at this same way of Nature, even if to the very utmost [it should come to pass that] the Muses, all together, proscribed by these recent rivalries, should likewise go into exile out of this arena, and, striking camp along with you, should withdraw from here altogether, where nothing of the ancient and uncorrupted way remains. Rather is it better, at last and by experience, to learn to be cautiously wary of so perverse an inconstancy — not, in truth, otherwise unwonted [than] on this stage of capering envy — and, with prudent provision for what the time admonishes, to fortify one's withdrawn resources with bulwarks not foolish and fleeting but solid and worthy of the age; lest, leaning more on others' virtues than on our own, we be seen to totter at any chance throws of fortune's dice * — nay, that it even come about that we collapse utterly. But you indeed — you, I say, noble Tycho — have carried the torch before us here; you have lit our way by your own example; you have set down the footprints of true virtue, sufficient in full to itself on every side, which footprints — what man aspiring to this goal would not strive to tread? I myself, to be sure (who, though I may not deserve to be summoned to this illustrious assembly, yet strive daily to be called at least into the second rank, or the third), feel that many and no light tokens of ill-will against me are bursting forth, however they be suppressed; but, *with a kindly genius* [σὺν δαίμονι ἐσϑλῷ], I hope it is in vain — for I have not spread my sails to these winds, nor would I have entrusted myself to that harbourless shoal. But of myself [I shall speak] in person, present face to face, lest, through emotion and rashness — the grounds of which I keep far off — I should seem too imprudently to cast the secrets of my counsels into unsafe, tale-bearing letters, secrets which hold good no otherwise than if they be rendered up to none but a second self. And so, on the fifteenth day of the year now hastening on, the Deity favouring, being about to make another beginning of my life, about to renounce this most wearisome house of toil, it has long been my mind to assent — even unasked — of my own accord to your most friendly request; nor shall I ever, in those things that are upright, set myself against anyone's rivalries and hatreds. And truly, what would be more unbecoming than for me to pass you by unsaluted — you whom, by a singular lot, I esteem, honour, and regard as first by right, [bound to me] not by affinity only, but by blood, and by every bond of intimacy — you, I say, after so many tokens of a most kindly disposition shown toward one who did not deserve them? Come then: signify to me by one line or another, through this courier, whether about the said time my coming seems sufficiently convenient to you; I shall see to it here meanwhile that there be nothing, of what you might desire in me, [lacking] beyond my powers perhaps; other matters [are] to be reserved for conversation in person, in which I should also wish reported whatever there is of news worth relating — save that this one thing it is worth relating at present: that our common friend Cragius, soon to be dispatched into Poland, has been summoned hither by letters for the first of January, and that he, taking his route through Holstein, will visit you, I do not doubt at all; to whom, and whither, I shall earnestly endeavour to attach myself, provided he has not departed too hastily. But truly, did I not restrain myself on purpose, this my converse with you by letter would scarcely have an end; so that I gladly reserve for a more convenient opportunity the weightier — nay rather, what I deem the weightiest — heads of your little letter. Meanwhile let my Muses sport, as best they can, at these matters; openly indeed, yet under their own veil. Meanwhile I commend you, with your whole household, your counsels and your actions, to the all-powerful governor of our affairs, the Triune Deity. Fare most happily.

Honouring you with a most upright mind, second to none,

Holger Rosenkrantz.
Written out
at Haderslev, 16 December
1597. Jacob Ulfeldt wished most dutifully to send you greeting in his own name — one whom you may know sincerely loves and looks up to you, even with his elders opposing [it].

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Oligerus Rosaecrantz* = **Holger Rosenkrantz** — addressed, and signing, as Tycho's *cognatus et affinis* ("kinsman and relative by marriage"). Tycho's reply of ten days later (Hamburg, 26 December 1597; *Opera Omnia*) speaks of *Cragius noster* in the same terms, confirming the pairing. (The signatory is one of the several contemporaneous Holger Rosenkrantzes of the high Danish nobility; the writer here is a younger kinsman about to "make another beginning" of his life, not the elder statesman "the Rich.")
- **Address / titulature.** *MATHEMATICO PRINCIPI* — "prince of mathematicians," an honorific (not an office), rendered literally. *Generose* … *cognate affinis desideratissime, amicorum intime*: the piled-up vocatives of high epistolary courtesy are kept.
- **"exuli iam pridem tibi, modo libero."** "you, long since an exile, now a free man." Tycho had left Hven and Denmark in 1597; the letter's whole consolatory frame turns on his self-imposed *exilium* and on the *livor* ("spite, envy") of "certain few" at court who, *alia obtentui sumpta caussa* ("having taken up some other cause for a pretext"), drove him out. Rosenkrantz's *modo libero* ("now free") and the praise of Tycho as having "carried the torch before us" cast the departure as liberation, not defeat — the author's framing is preserved, not editorialised.
- **Greek.** *σὺν δαίμονι ἐσϑλῷ* — transcribed as printed (with the medial *ϑ* form of theta); "with a kindly genius / good spirit," i.e. "with good fortune / God willing." A learned tag (cf. the Homeric/proverbial *σὺν δαίμονι*); transliterated and glossed, not flattened.
- **The asterisk (iactus *).** An editorial mark stands in the source after *fortunae iactus* ("fortune's dice"). It is reproduced verbatim in the Source block; its referent (a footnote or *crux* sign in the copy/edition) is not recoverable from the text and is **not** silently deleted. The clause is translated as it stands; the mark is flagged here.
- **"Ad diem … anni adproperantis quintum decimum."** Rendered "on the fifteenth day of the year now hastening on" — i.e. about 15 January [1598], the date Rosenkrantz sets for the "new beginning" of his life and his proposed visit; *non rogatus … adsentiri … animus* ("my mind is to assent even unasked") answers a request (*rogatio*) Tycho had made in the letter Rosenkrantz received on 4 December. **Crux flagged:** the syntax compresses date, intention, and the renunciation of the *ergastulum* into one clause; the reading "fifteenth day of the [coming] year" is the natural one but is not beyond doubt.
- ***taediosissimo huic … ergastulo*** — "this most wearisome house of toil"; *ergastulum* (literally a slaves' workhouse/prison) used metaphorically of Rosenkrantz's present situation, exactly as Wolf used it of his own life (cf. brahe-t_15711113001). Rendered consistently "house of toil."
- ***Cragius*** = **Niels Krag** (Nicolaus Cragius, c. 1550–1602), Danish humanist, historian, and diplomat, *soon to be dispatched into Poland* (*in Poloniam brevi ablegandum*) — a reference to his 1598 embassy. *itinere per Holsatiam sumpto* — "taking his route through Holstein," i.e. past Tycho's then station in the Hamburg/Holstein region. Tycho's 26 December reply (*Utinam Cragius noster tecum sit vel praecedat*) shows the planned rendez-vous was real.
- ***Epistolij tui capita*** — "the heads [chief points] of your little letter" (*epistolium*, diminutive of *epistola*); Rosenkrantz defers reply to Tycho's weightier points until they meet.
- ***Ludant … meae Musae … suo sub velo*** — "let my Muses sport … under their own veil," i.e. he will express more (perhaps in verse) but veiled; the figure is kept.
- ***Trinuno Numini*** — "to the Triune Deity," the closing commendation to the Holy Trinity; *praepotenti rerum nostrarum gubernatori* ("the all-powerful governor of our affairs") in apposition.
- **Place.** *Haderslebiae* = **Haderslev** (Hadersleben), in Schleswig; *Perscribebam* ("I was writing out / I write out," epistolary imperfect) kept.
- **Dateline & calendar.** *XVI Decemb. CIↃ CI IIIC* = "16 December 1597." The numeral is the apostrophus form: *CIↃ* = 1000, *CI* (= D) = 500, *IIIC* = 97 (the reversed-C "97" idiom), giving M D 97 = **1597**; **O.S.** (Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700). This matches the catalogue label (1597-12-16); no date discrepancy. *pridie Non. Decembris* in the body = "the day before the Nones of December" = **4 December** (Nones of December = the 5th), glossed in the translation by this chapter's convention
- **Register / style note.** Rosenkrantz writes in a deliberately mannered, hyper-periodic late-humanist Latin: very long suspended periods, heavy hyperbaton, accumulated comparatives and rare adverbs (*solentius, adlubentius, sentisco*). The translation keeps the periodic architecture rather than chopping it into modern short sentences, at some cost in fluency — faithful to the author's evident self-display.
- **Names Jacob Ulfeldt as a covert admirer of Tycho.** The postscript reports that the Danish nobleman Jacob Ulfeldt (til Ulfeldtsholm) asked to be remembered to Tycho, and states that Ulfeldt sincerely loves and looks up to him even though his elders/family oppose it ('etiam maioribus renitentibus') — a telling detail for late 1597, when much of the Danish nobility had already turned against Tycho.
- **Corroboration.** A genuine prior friendship is independently attested: Tycho addressed one of his own occasional Latin poems directly to 'Jacob Ulfeldt til Ulfeldtsholm' ('TIL MIN GODE VEN... HR. JACOB ULFELDT TIL ULFELDTSHOLM' — 'To my good friend... Lord Jacob Ulfeldt of Ulfeldtsholm'), per Grinder-Hansen (ed.), *Tycho Brahes Verden* (Nationalmuseet, 2006). The 'elders resisting' detail is new information not otherwise recorded in that source.
