documents.abstract: Explains that his departure from Denmark was prompted by pressing reasons and not intended as a slight to the King, who may have been misled by ill-wishers.
documents.incipit: DURCHLEUCHTIGER hochgeborner furst, gnedigster herr. Nachdem jch auß hochwichtigen vnd …

text.original:
COPIA DESS BRIEFS, SO AN DEM HERRN ADMINISTRATORN ICH INN DER EIL ZU BRAMBSTADT GEGEBEN HABE.

DURCHLEUCHTIGER hochgeborner furst, gnedigster herr. Nachdem jch auß hochwichtigen vnd nodtwendigen vrsachen, so in die feder nicht alle woll zubringen, mich auß meinem lieben vaterlandt Dennemarck begeben musßen, vnndt hernacher bin innenworden, das die kön. maytt: zu Dennemarcken etc., mein gnedigster herr vndt könig, solche meine außreise, vielleicht durch etzliche meiner mißgönner angebenn, also ausgenommen, alß wen das jhr kön: maytt: zu verdruß geschehen sey. Welches ich mit aller warheidt sagen kan, daß keines weges meine meinung gewesen, sondern hette gern alda geblieben, vnndt meinem gnedigstem herrn vndt könig vndt lieben vaterlandt, hernacher wie zuuor, alles zu ehren vndt rumblicher nachsage gethan, was in meinem geringen vermögen sein köntte, wan solches mit guther ruhe vnd gelegenheidt, vndt ohne meinen schaden vnnd verlierung der zeit, hette geschehen mugen.

Vnd kan ein jeder leichtlich ermessen, daß ich in diesen meinem hohen alter, nun jch über die funfftzig jahr bin, mit fraw vndt seks kinder vnd anderem meinem haußgesinde beladen, mich nicht leichtferttiger weiß, vndt ohne hochdringenden vrsachen hab endtfrembdett. Dieweil es aber also vielleicht auß Gottes vorhengnuß hatt geschehen mußen, will ich mich auch mit diesem meinem zustandt gerne genugen lasßen, vnd anderßwo versuchen, was gluch der liebe Gott bescheren will, dan jch darumb keinen verlangen trage, nunmehr vor mein person in Dennemarck zu sein vndt gerestituirt zu werden, vnd wan das schon geschehen solte, so ist es mir doch sehr vngelegen, auf der jnsull Huen lenger zuwohnen vnd stets zu bleiben, wouon jch ahn einem andern ortt meine vrsachen vorzeichnet habe. Wolte deßwegen vnterthenigst E:F:G: gebetten haben, dieselben sich vnschwer erzeigen wollen, ahn jhr kön: maytt:, seinen vielgeliebten herrn sohn, ein schreiben von meinetwegen zuthun, daß jhr kön. maytt: mir hirin nichts zu vngnaden aufnehmen wolle, sondern mein gnedigster herr vndt könig sein vndt bleibenn; jch wil doch anderßwo, wo dan Gott mir meine gelegenheidt vorsehen hat, jhr königl. maytt: getrew erfunden werden, auch deroselbigen vnd meinem vielgeliebtenn vaterlandt zu ehren thun alles was mir immer muglich, welches vielleicht anderswo eben sowoll, wo nicht mehr, vndt viel beqvemer vnd ruhelicher als in Dennemarck geschehen kan. Wofern aber jhr kön. maytt: mit deroselben hochweisen reichs räthen noch des sins wurden, das dieselben die astronomische studia in Dennemarck vndt auf der jnsull Huen zu Vraniburgk, auß gnedigstem willen vnd begehren des hochlöblicher gedechtnuß königs Friderich zu dem brauch von mir gebauet vnd aufgerichtett, durch ersprießliche mittel, deroselben vnd dem reich zu ehren vnd hochgemeltem löblichen könig Friderich zur gedechtnuß, ferner vnterhalten wollen, wil ich gerne meinen außersten fleiß ahnwenden, das solches, wo schon nicht durch mich selbst, doch durch einen von den meinen (so ich datzu vnterwiesen hab, vnd ferner vnterweisen wil) ins werck gestellet werde, vnd das vielleicht, nicht mit geringerm fleiß, als wen ich selbst da were; will auch nechst denvier vberauss grossen vnd etzlichen anderen astronomischen jnstrumenten, die ich da gelasßen hab, noch mehr, nachdem es von nötten, da hinstellen lasßen, vnd alles ordiniren vnd vorschreiben, wie es mit den observationibus vnd dero gebrauch gehalten soll werden, auff das, was einmahl da so wohl angefangen vnd gecontinuirt ist, köntte stets bey macht erhaltten werden, jhr königl: mayttz:, meinem gnedigsten herrn vnd könig, vndt dem reiche zu ehren, auf das nicht anderswo solte gesaget werden, daß solche lobliche sachen gar zerstöret vnd zu nicht gemacht sein. Es wolle aber daneben jhr kön: maytt: mit notturfftichlicher vnterhaltung, dasselbe mit canonicien vndt geistlichen lehen, nach einhalt der algemeinen reichs räthe brieff in interregno gnedigst vorsehen, vnd mit einer bequemen fundation perpetuiren. Von diesem vnd was hier vndter zuuorstehen gelanget ahn E:F:G: mein vnterthenige bitte, dieselben j: kön: maytt: zu Dennemarck, meinem gnedigsten herrn vnd könig, dieses erinnern vnd vortragen lasßen wollen, wofern aber es j: kön: may: nicht gefiele, die astronomische sachen auf der insul weiter zu erhalten, daß alsdan mit sr. may: gnedigsten vnndt guten willen, jch die alda noch vberige jnstrumenta, vndt was mir sonsten zugehörig, möchte lasßen wecknehmen vnd anderswo zu nutz bringen. Daneben auch, wofern es j: maytt: nicht zu widern were, das jch einige compensation wieder vor alle meine grosse muhe vnd bekostung, die ich alda über die 20 jar ertragen hab, vnd vielmehr dazu außgelegt, als von hochlöblichen könig Friderich vnd denn reichs rath mir erstreckt vnd gegonnet worden, erlangen möchte. Welches in jhr kön: maytt: gnedigsten willen vndt wolgefallen jch vnterthenigst heimbstelle. Wnndt thue E:F:G: ich mich in vntherthenigkeit vorsehen, dieselbigen hierahn kein misßgefallen tragen werden, das E:F:G: ich hiemit vntertheniglich vnndt guther meinung ersuche, E:F:G: hinwiederumb mit aller vnterthenigkeit nach meinem geringen vormugen zudienen, wil ich stets williger dan willig gefunden werden. Thue E:F:G: sambt dero vielgeliebten gemahlin, jungen herrn vndt freulein in den gnaden schütz des Almechtigen getreulich zu gluchlicher vnd langwerender regierung entpfehlen.

Datum Bramstadt den 22. decembris anno 1597.
text.english:
**Copy of the letter that I gave in haste to the Lord Administrator at Bramstedt.**

Most Serene, high-born Prince, most gracious Lord. Whereas for weighty and pressing reasons — which cannot all well be set down with the pen — I have had to remove myself from my dear fatherland Denmark, and have afterwards become aware that the Royal Majesty of Denmark, etc., my most gracious lord and king, has taken this departure of mine — informed of it, perhaps, by certain of those who begrudge me — in such a way as if it had been done to His Royal Majesty's displeasure. Which I can say with all truth was in no way my intention; rather I would gladly have remained there, and would have done for my most gracious lord and king and my dear fatherland, afterwards as before, everything to [their] honour and praiseworthy renown that might lie within my slender means, had this been able to come about with good peace and opportunity, and without harm to myself and loss of time.

And anyone can readily judge that I, in this my advanced age — now that I am past fifty years, burdened with a wife and six children and the rest of my household — have not estranged myself in any frivolous manner, nor without most urgent reasons. But since it has thus had to come about, perhaps by God's providence, I will gladly let myself be content with this my condition, and try elsewhere what fortune the dear God will grant; for I bear no desire on that account to be in Denmark any longer for my own person and to be restored [to my place]; and even should that come to pass, it is nonetheless very inconvenient for me to dwell any longer on the island of Hven and to remain there always — concerning which I have recorded my reasons in another place. I would therefore most humbly have entreated Your Princely Grace that you might be pleased to show yourself not unwilling to write a letter on my behalf to His Royal Majesty, your most beloved lord son, [asking] that His Royal Majesty would not take anything herein to my disgrace, but be and remain my most gracious lord and king; for I will nonetheless, elsewhere — wherever God has provided my opportunity — be found faithful to His Royal Majesty, and will do for the honour of the same and of my most beloved fatherland everything that may ever be possible to me, which perhaps can be done elsewhere just as well, if not more, and far more conveniently and peaceably than in Denmark. But if His Royal Majesty, with his most wise Councillors of the Realm, should still be of the mind that they wish to maintain further — by fruitful means, to the honour of the same and of the realm, and to the memory of the aforesaid praiseworthy King Frederik — the astronomical studies in Denmark and on the island of Hven at Uraniborg, built and set up by me for that use out of the most gracious will and desire of King Frederik of laudable memory: then I will gladly apply my utmost diligence that this be put into effect — if not by myself, then by one of my own people (whom I have instructed for it, and will instruct further) — and that, perhaps, with no less diligence than if I myself were there. I will also, besides the four exceedingly large and certain other astronomical instruments which I have left there, have yet more set up there as need requires, and will arrange and prescribe everything as to how the matter of the observations and their use is to be conducted, so that what has once been so well begun and continued there might always be kept in force, to the honour of His Royal Majesty, my most gracious lord and king, and of the realm — so that it not be said elsewhere that such praiseworthy things have been utterly destroyed and brought to nothing. But may His Royal Majesty besides this, with sufficient maintenance, most graciously provide for it with canonries and ecclesiastical benefices, according to the tenor of the letter of the general Councillors of the Realm in the interregnum, and perpetuate it with a suitable endowment. Concerning this, and what is to be understood thereunder, my humble request goes to Your Princely Grace that you would be pleased to have His Royal Majesty of Denmark, my most gracious lord and king, reminded of this and have it laid before him; but if it should not please His Royal Majesty to maintain the astronomical concerns on the island any longer, that then, with His Majesty's most gracious and good will, I might have the instruments still remaining there, and whatever else belongs to me, taken away and brought to use elsewhere. And besides, that — if it were not repugnant to His Majesty — I might obtain some compensation in return for all my great labour and expense, which I have borne there for over twenty years, and have laid out far more thereto than was extended and granted to me by the laudable King Frederik and the Council of the Realm. Which I most humbly leave to His Royal Majesty's most gracious will and pleasure. And I assure myself in humility of Your Princely Grace that you will bear no displeasure herein, [seeing] that I herewith humbly and in good meaning entreat Your Princely Grace; [and] to serve Your Princely Grace in return with all humility according to my slender ability, I will ever be found more ready than willing. I commit Your Princely Grace, together with your most beloved consort, young lords and ladies, faithfully to the gracious protection of the Almighty, unto a happy and long-enduring reign.

Given at Bramstedt, the 22nd of December, in the year 1597.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe**, writing in December 1597 from Bramstedt (Bad Bramstedt, in Holstein), some months into his self-imposed departure from Denmark. He had left Hven in spring 1597 and Copenhagen that summer, moving via Rostock to Heinrich Rantzau's estate at Wandsbek; the meeting with the margrave at Bramstedt was arranged by Rantzau. The "another place" where he says he has recorded his reasons (*ahn einem andern ortt … vrsachen vorzeichnet*) is his contemporaneous elegy *Elegia ad Daniam* and his other appeals.
- **Recipient.** *Der Herr Administrator* / *Durchleuchtiger hochgeborner Fürst* = **Joachim Friedrich** (1546–1608), Margrave of Brandenburg, then **Administrator of the Archbishopric of Magdeburg** (the Protestant prince-administrator's title, hence "Administrator"). He had been in Denmark in late 1597 for the marriage of his daughter; on the return journey he met Tycho at Bramstedt on 22 December 1597. In January 1598, weeks after this letter, he succeeded his father as **Elector of Brandenburg**. The header's *Herr Administrator* and the body's *Durchleuchtiger Fürst* are the same person.
- **"your most beloved lord son" (*seinen vielgeliebten herrn sohn*).** The "Royal Majesty of Denmark" is **Christian IV** (r. 1588–1648); Tycho addresses Joachim Friedrich as a kinsman able to intercede with the young king. The relationship is courtly/diplomatic, not literally paternal: Christian IV's queen would later be Joachim Friedrich's granddaughter, but in 1597 the deference reflects the older prince's standing. The phrase is rendered literally and the relationship clarified here rather than smoothed.
- **"past fifty years … wife and six children" (*über die funfftzig jahr … fraw vndt seks kinder*).** Tycho was born December 1546, so genuinely just past fifty. *Fraw* = his common-law wife Kirsten Jørgensdatter. The number of children (*seks*) is as written; six are named in the household at this date.
- ***König Friderich*** — **Frederik II of Denmark** (r. 1559–88), who in 1576 granted Tycho the island of Hven and underwrote Uraniborg; repeatedly invoked here ("of laudable / praiseworthy memory") as the founder whose legacy the establishment embodies.
- **Instruments.** *die vier vberauss grossen … astronomischen jnstrumenten* = "the four exceedingly large astronomical instruments" left behind at Uraniborg/Stjerneborg (per glossary, *organa* → instruments; here *Instrumenten / Instrumenta*). *observationibus* (Latin ablative, code-switched) = "observations". *gecontinuirt, gerestituirt, perpetuiren, fundation, compensation, canonicien, in interregno, ordiniren, vorschreiben* are the letter's Latinate chancery vocabulary, kept in register.
- ***canonicien vndt geistlichen lehen … in interregno*** — "canonries and ecclesiastical benefices … in the interregnum": Tycho proposes that the establishment be endowed from church prebends, citing a letter of the Councillors of the Realm issued during the interregnum (the regency between Frederik II's death in 1588 and Christian IV's majority in 1596). Rendered literally; *Lehen* here = ecclesiastical livings/prebends.
- **Negation / legal force.** The pivotal clauses each turn on a single negation, reproduced one-for-one: (1) *keines weges meine meinung gewesen* — "in no way my intention" (the departure was **not** meant as an affront); (2) *daß jhr kön. maytt: mir hirin **nichts** zu vngnaden aufnehmen wolle* — the king should take **nothing** herein to Tycho's disgrace; (3) the two conditional *wofern aber … nicht gefiele / nicht zu widern were* clauses governing the fallback requests (removal of the instruments; compensation) — translated as conditionals ("but if it should not please …"; "if it were not repugnant …") without strengthening or weakening their hypothetical mood.
- **Hedges preserved.** *vielleicht durch etzliche meiner mißgönner* ("perhaps by certain of those who begrudge me"); *vielleicht auß Gottes vorhengnuß* ("perhaps by God's providence"); *welches vielleicht anderswo eben sowoll, wo nicht mehr* ("which perhaps … just as well, if not more") — each *vielleicht* / conditional kept as a hedge, none sharpened to assertion.
- **Orthography (Early New High German chancery, c. 1597).** *jch / vnd / vnndt = ich / und*; *vrsachen = Ursachen*; *außreise = Ausreise*; *gluch / gluchlicher = Glück / glücklicher*; *funfftzig = fünfzig*; *seks = sechs*; *müsßen, lasßen, außgelegt* with *ß* for *ss*; *könig. maytt: / kön: maytt: = königliche Majestät*; *E:F:G: = Euer Fürstliche Gnaden* ("Your Princely Grace"); *j: kön: may: = Ihre königliche Majestät*; *sr. may: = Seiner Majestät*. *Brambstadt / Bramstadt* = **Bramstedt** (Bad Bramstedt, Holstein). *Vraniburgk = Uraniborg*; *Huen = Hven*.
- **Honorifics.** *Vnsern gnedigen Gruß* is absent (the letter opens directly with the princely address); the closing commendation *in den gnaden schütz des Almechtigen … entpfehlen* ("commit … to the gracious protection of the Almighty") is the standard chancery valediction, translated in full rather than dropped.
- **Calendar / place.** *Datum Bramstadt den 22. decembris anno 1597* = "Given at Bramstedt, 22 December 1597." **Old Style**: Tycho and the Holstein/Danish sphere kept the Julian calendar in 1597 (Denmark until 1700). The edition's catalogue label (22 December 1597, Bramstedt) agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy. The header opening (*… ICH INN DER EIL ZU BRAMBSTADT GEGEBEN HABE*, "which I gave in haste at Bramstedt") is an archival rubric on the file copy (Langebek's Diplomatarium), not part of the letter proper; preserved by this chapter's convention

documents.incipit: NOBILISSIME OLIGERE, cognate et affinis charissime, redditæ mihi quidem sunt literæ tuæ …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO ET ERUDITIONE NON VULGARI PRÆEMINENTISSIMO VIRO D. OLIGERO ROSENKRANTZIO DOMINO HÆREDITARIO IN ROSENHOLM, COGNATO, AFFINI ET AMICO MEO INTEGERRIMO.
S.

NOBILISSIME OLIGERE, cognate et affinis charissime, redditæ mihi quidem sunt literæ tuæ postremæ, eruditæ illæ et amoris ac constantiæ erga me plenissimæ. Sed aberam tunc Wandesburgo in oppidulo quodam sex miliaribus inde distante, quod Brambsted vocatur, ut cum Domino Produce isthic mihi obvio de quibusdam loquerer. Reperi autem ibidem Illustm Dominum Administratorem et ipsius Illmam coniugem, qui me singulari favore clementer complexi sunt. Domum autem reversus pridie Natalitiorum hasce tuas accepi, quas una e filiabus meis reddidit, nuntij, qui eas apportarat, nulla facta mentione, cum ea, ubi is esset, ignoraret. At cum postmodum statim ad currum conscenderem huc Hamburgum cum meis iturus, ut festos dies hîc transigeremus, mihi indicabatur, nuntium tuum adhuc adesse; non quidem retrospicere licuit, sed data scheda, quæ illum suo officio perfunctum testaretur, redire eum permisi, cogitans hîc cum Nobilibus Danis, qui D. Administratorem domum deduxerunt, tuis respondere velle, quod etiam sufficienter præstarem, nisi illi hodie præter opinionem, incidente quadam ingrata necessitate, abitum festinassent, cum alias me unâ cum BALTHASARE ALFELDIO Wandesburgi invisere constituissent. Cogor igitur premere ea, quæ latius ad te scribere animum induxeram, illa in adventum tuum ad me Wandesburgum, quem tam amice polliceris, procrastinaturus. Ego itaque te desideratissime OLIGERE isthic, volente Numine, præstolabor, et avidissime cum alacritate excipiam. Utinam CRAGIUS noster tecum sit vel præcedat; tunc inter nos coram sermones miscebimus de ijs, quæ nunc scribere importunitas vetat, quæque per se calamus non satis tuta sustinet. Fac igitur mature stes promissis, de quo etiam nihil addubito, utque queas nobis salvus adesse.

Vale.
Dabantur Hamburgo, postridie Natalitiorum Anno 97.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 18; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Resaluta meo nomine quam officiosissime D. IACOBUM ULFELDIUM, de cuius fide et constanti in me amore satis certus sum; neque enim levitatibus et nugis est obnoxius. Scripsissem illi, nisi temporis penuria præpedirer. Saluta etiam BROCKENHUSIUM illum, qui se meum vocat discipulum; eius literis respondere iam non suppetit otium; habeat itaque me excusatum.
text.english:
**To the most noble man, pre-eminent in no common learning, Master Holger Rosenkrantz, hereditary lord of Rosenholm, my kinsman, kinsman-by-marriage, and most upright friend — greeting.**

Most noble Holger, dearest kinsman and kinsman-by-marriage, your latest letter has indeed been delivered to me — that learned letter, brimful of your love and constancy towards me. But I was at that time away from Wandsbek, in a certain little town some six miles distant from there, called Bramstedt, in order to confer about certain matters with the Lord Provost [Produx], who met me there. And I found in that same place the Most Illustrious Lord Administrator and his Most Illustrious consort, who graciously embraced me with singular favour. But having returned home on the eve of Christmas [pridie Natalitiorum], I received this letter of yours, which one of my daughters delivered, no mention being made of the messenger who had brought it — since she did not know where he was. Yet when soon afterwards I was at once mounting the carriage to go here to Hamburg with my household, that we might pass the festal days here, it was reported to me that your messenger was still at hand; I could not, to be sure, look back [to deal with it then], but, giving him a note that should attest he had discharged his duty, I let him return — intending here to wish to answer your letter together with the Danish noblemen who had escorted the Lord Administrator home, which I should indeed do sufficiently, had they not today, beyond expectation, an unwelcome necessity having intervened, hastened their departure — whereas otherwise they had resolved to visit me, along with Balthasar Alefeldt, at Wandsbek. I am therefore compelled to suppress those things which I had set my mind to write to you at greater length, putting them off until your coming to me at Wandsbek, which you so amiably promise. And so, most longed-for Holger, I shall await you there, God willing, and shall receive you most eagerly and with alacrity. Would that our Cragius were with you, or came ahead; then between ourselves, face to face, we shall exchange conversations about those matters which importunity now forbids to write, and which of itself the pen cannot bear safely enough. See to it, then, that you stand by your promises in good time — of which I have no doubt at all — and that you may be able, safe and sound, to be present with us.

Farewell.
Given at Hamburg, the day after Christmas [postridie Natalitiorum], the year [15]97.
Yours, TYCHO BRAHE,
with my own hand.


*[Postscript:]* Greet again on my behalf, most dutifully, Master Jacob Ulfeldt, of whose faith and constant love towards me I am sufficiently sure; for he is not given to levities and trifles. I should have written to him, were I not hindered by want of time. Greet too that Brockenhus who calls himself my disciple; there is now no leisure to spare to answer his letter; let him therefore hold me excused.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe**, here in his post-Hven exile: having left Denmark in 1597, he was residing at the castle of **Wandsbek** (*Wandesburgum*), near Hamburg, as guest of Heinrich Rantzau. The letter is signed *manu propria* ("with my own hand").
- **Recipient.** *Oligerus Rosenkrantzius, dominus haereditarius in Rosenholm* = **Holger Rosenkrantz** "the Learned" (1574–1642), the young Danish nobleman and theologian of **Rosenholm** (Jutland). Tycho addresses him as *cognatus et affinis* — kinsman and kinsman-by-marriage — and a sequel letter of 22 January 1598 (also from Wandsbek) continues the same exchange about Rosenkrantz's promised visit.
- ***cognato, affini*** — *cognatus* = a blood-relative/kinsman; *affinis* = a relative by marriage. Both retained distinctly rather than collapsed into "relative," since the pairing is a deliberate courtesy formula.
- ***Domino Produce*** — *Produx* (acc./abl. *Producem/Produce*) is an unusual title; rendered "the Lord Provost [Produx]" with the Latin flagged. It denotes a local official (the *Propst*/provost of Bramstedt or a comparable administrative head) whom Tycho met at Bramstedt; the exact office is not specified in the text. **Flagged**, not silently resolved.
- ***Illustm Dominum Administratorem … ipsius Illmam coniugem*** — *Illustm* and *Illmam* are abbreviations for *Illustrissimum* / *Illustrissimam* (expanded in the translation as "Most Illustrious"). The **Administrator** is the Lutheran Administrator of the Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen, **Johann Adolf of Holstein-Gottorp** (Administrator of Bremen 1585–96 and of Lübeck, then Duke of Holstein-Gottorp from 1590), here with his consort — the regional prince in whose orbit Tycho was then moving. (Identification from the regional and chronological context; the text gives the office, not the name.)
- ***Brambsted*** = **Bad Bramstedt** in Holstein, north of Hamburg; *Wandesburgo* = **Wandsbek**, now a district of Hamburg. *sex miliaribus* = "six miles" (German miles, hence a substantial distance).
- ***Balthasar Alfeldio*** = **Balthasar (von) Alefeldt** (Ahlefeldt), of the Holstein noble family; named as one of the company who had meant to visit Tycho at Wandsbek.
- ***Cragius noster*** = **Niels Krag** (Nicolaus Cragius, c. 1550–1602), the Danish humanist, historian, and diplomat; "our Cragius" marks him as a mutual friend. The 22 January 1598 sequel reports that Cragius would pass straight on to Lübeck rather than come to Wandsbek as hoped.
- ***quae … calamus non satis tuta sustinet*** — "matters which … the pen cannot bear safely enough": Tycho's discretion about confidential matters (his standing with the Danish crown and his exile) is preserved as written, not paraphrased into a definite topic. The reticence is itself the point.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S.* = *salutem (dicit)*, "(sends) greeting"; *Vale* = "Farewell"; *manu propria* = "with my own hand."
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Dabantur Hamburgo, postridie Natalitiorum Anno 97* = "Given at Hamburg, **the day after Christmas**, the year [15]97" (O.S.; Denmark and the Lutheran north kept the Julian calendar). *postridie Natalitiorum* = the day after the Nativity = **26 December**, which agrees with the catalogue label (*1597. 26. december*). **No in-letter date discrepancy:** the body's *pridie Natalitiorum* ("the eve of Christmas," 24 December) is the date Tycho *received* Rosenkrantz's letter at Wandsbek, a distinct earlier event from the *postridie Natalitiorum* (26 December) dateline of writing at Hamburg; the two are consistent with the narrated sequence (return home 24 Dec → set out for Hamburg → write 26 Dec). The *Anno 97* is given as written, not expanded to 1597 except in brackets.
- **Witness.** A = Copenhagen, Rigsarkivet, **Langebeks Diplomatarium**, a later copy (*Afskrift*), per the source's witness field; the autograph is not the surviving witness.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (greetings to Jacob Ulfeldt + Brockenhus), restored from Dreyer VIII, p. 18 (dropped after "manu propria").

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VIII pp.17-19 read as page images. Letter ("NOBILISSIMO ET ERUDITIONE NON VULGARI...") runs from bottom of p.17 through p.18, including the postscript greeting Iacobus Ulfeldius and Brockenhusius, which our transcribed original already marks as restored from Dreyer p.18 (dropped by the working transcription) — verified the restored text matches Dreyer verbatim. All proper names (Wandesburgo/Brambsted, Balthasar Alfeldio, Cragius), the two paired date-formulae (pridie/postridie Natalitiorum) and the year (Anno 97) match. English translation is faithful throughout, including the postscript. Published grade was B (uncollated default); full Dreyer collation with zero defects earns A.

documents.abstract: Relays that Scaliger has incorporated Tycho's vernal and autumnal observations into his own work and suggests Holland would suit Tycho better than Germany.
documents.incipit: .....SCALIGER observationes utrasque (quæ munificentiæ tuæ sunt) vernalem aio et …

text.original:
IOHANNES ISACIUS PONTANUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

.....SCALIGER observationes utrasque (quæ munificentiæ tuæ sunt) vernalem aio et autumnalem, suis inseruit, et videbis propediem. De secessu vero in Germaniam itidem intellexerat, et dolere se fatetur, si eiusmodi rerum conturbaretur commoditas, quarum iam fructus redundaret ad Europam universam. Placet quidem ei Germania; sed nescit, an mores undiquaque gentis ad illam facilitatem humanitatemque apti, quæ debebatur, apti tibi. Optaret, si Dania omnino deserendi staret animus, Bataviam potius inviseres, amicam studijs, benignam....; et denique te tuasque virtutes et honorabit, et fere dixerat, adorabit. Esset certe in omnem eventum hæc ora propinquior Daniæ, et ille hîc Ordinum sensus, ut omnes gratias non modo retinendas, verum etiam acquirendas sciant.
text.english:
**Johannes Isaksen Pontanus to Tycho Brahe.**

..... Scaliger has inserted both observations (which are [a token] of your generosity) — the vernal, I say, and the autumnal — among his own, and you will see [them] very soon. About your withdrawal into Germany he had likewise understood, and he confesses that he grieves [to think] that an opportunity for affairs of this kind should be disturbed, the fruit of which would now overflow to the whole of Europe. Germany pleases him, to be sure; but he does not know whether the manners of a nation [that are] everywhere suited to that easy graciousness and humanity which was owed [to you] are suited to you. He would wish — if your mind were set on abandoning Denmark altogether — that you would rather visit Batavia [Holland], friendly to studies, kindly....; and, in fine, he both will honour you and your virtues and, he had almost said, will adore [them]. This shore would certainly, in any event, be nearer to Denmark; and such here is the disposition of the States, that they know all favours are not only to be retained but even to be gained [for you].

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** *Iohannes Isacius Pontanus* = **Johannes Isaksen Pontanus** (1571–1639), Danish-Dutch humanist, physician and historian (later royal historiographer of Denmark and professor at Harderwijk); in the later 1590s he was in the Netherlands and moved in the Leiden learned circle, which placed him to relay Scaliger's words to Tycho. The letter survives only as a later **copy** (*Afskrift*) in the Langebek collection (Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Langebek 178), which accounts for the truncated openings (the leading and internal ellipses are in the transmitted text).
- **Recipient / occasion.** Addressed to **Tycho Brahe** in 1598, the year he left Denmark for good; the letter speaks of his contemplated *secessus* ("withdrawal") and of "abandoning Denmark altogether," and relays counsel on where to settle — squarely the 1597–98 self-exile context.
- ***Scaliger*** — **Joseph Justus Scaliger** (1540–1609), the foremost philologist of the age, then professor at the University of Leiden (from 1593). Pontanus reports Scaliger's reaction at second hand; the epistemic frame is Pontanus's ("he confesses," "he would wish," "he had understood"), and is preserved as reported speech rather than asserted as Tycho-fact.
- ***observationes utrasque … vernalem … et autumnalem*** — "both observations … the vernal and the autumnal": evidently a pair of Tycho's observations (most naturally of an **equinox** — the vernal and the autumnal — though the noun *aequinoctium* is not in the text and is therefore **not** supplied in the translation). Scaliger, whose chronological work *De emendatione temporum* (1583; 2nd ed. 1598) turned on exactly such equinox data, has "inserted [them] among his own." Rendered "observations" per glossary; the unstated object (equinoxes vs. other phenomena) is flagged, not decided.
- ***quae munificentiae tuae sunt*** — literally "which are of your munificence," i.e. which are [a gift / token] of your generosity (Tycho had supplied the observations); rendered with a bracketed *[a token]* since the predicate noun is elided in the Latin.
- ***aio*** — "I say" (Pontanus's own parenthetical emphatic, not Scaliger's); kept as the writer's interjection.
- ***secessu … in Germaniam*** — "withdrawal into Germany": Tycho's mooted plan to settle in the Empire. *Secessus* here = a retiring/withdrawal (to live elsewhere), not a literal secession.
- ***Bataviam … amicam studijs, benignam*** — "Batavia, friendly to studies, kindly": **Batavia** = Holland / the (northern) Netherlands, the humanist name for the Dutch provinces; Scaliger (himself settled at Leiden) urges Tycho toward the Dutch Republic instead of Germany. Rendered "Batavia [Holland]" on first occurrence.
- ***Ordinum sensus*** — "the disposition of the **States**": *Ordines* = the **States** (the States-General of the United Provinces, or the States of Holland), the governing assembly; *sensus* their inclination/mind. The sentence reports the States' favourable attitude toward attracting Tycho.
- **Textual cruxes.** (1) ***an mores undiquaque gentis … apti tibi*** — the clause is grammatically strained in the transmitted copy: *apti* ("suited") stands **twice** (once before the relative clause, once after *debebatur*), one of which is a copyist's dittography in this *Afskrift*. The sense is "[he does not know] whether the manners of the nation everywhere are suited to you [as fitted to] that graciousness and humanity which was owed [to you]." The doubled *apti* is preserved verbatim in the Source block and the redundancy flagged here rather than silently emended. (2) The internal "....." after *benignam* marks a lacuna/omission in the transmitted text, not an editorial cut here.
- **Date / calendar.** The source carries **no dateline**; the edition catalogues it as **"1598. empty"** (i.e. year only, no day/month). The header therefore gives the year as catalogued and flags that the source text substantiates no finer date. Denmark was on the **Julian calendar (O.S.)** in 1598; absent a dateline, no style is asserted by the source itself, and no conversion is made.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Read Dreyer TBOO VIII p.20 page image in full. Collated the Scaliger-inserted-observations sentence, the withdrawal-into-Germany/grief clause, the convoluted 'mores...apti...apti tibi' sentence, the Batavia-invitation clause (with its genuine ellipsis gap preserved, not filled), the 'fere dixerat, adorabit' hyperbole, and the closing States/Ordinum sentence against the transcribed original and the published English; the transcribed original matches Dreyer's fragment verbatim and every clause of the translation is faithful, including correctly bracketed interpretive supplements ([a token], [for you]) for genuinely compressed or elliptical Latin. No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, hedge-loss, or text-error found; the translator's own grade Possible does not survive this collation.

documents.abstract: Thanks Hagecius for arranging to send a defamatory pamphlet and declines to reply to its author, deeming him unworthy of refutation.
documents.incipit: Post scripta ad D. D. Thaddaeum Hagecium

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD THADDÆUM HAGECIUM.

Post scripta ad D. D. Thaddaeum Hagecium

IN alteris tuis, optime mi THADDÆE, facis mentionem istius calumniatoris Ditmarsici, quodque eius scriptum maledicum in Daniam ad me mitti, antequam in Moraviam abires, procuraveris, mihi significas, quo maturius id obtinerem, pro qua tua in me benevolentia gratias habeo. Famosum istum libellum non quidem inde accepi, nescio, an eo pervenerit, literae enim solae absque libro mihi redditae sunt hîc Wandesburgi, e Dania transmissae; attamen ante paucos dies istum a quodam studioso Helmstadiensi mihi missum accepi. Extimas tu quidem, me ad omnia percommode responsurum, quod etiam mihi foret quam facilimum. Verum ego cum tam impudente conviciatore, qui omnes verecundiae limites transilijt, et totus calumnijs et mendacijs scatet, verba commutare mihi probrosum duco, neque enim dignus est, ut in scriptis meis nominetur, nedum refutetur. Erit forte alius, qui pro me tum quoque ROTHMANNO, bonae mem. id faciet, eiusque effrenem maledicentiam retundet. Ego vero eum non verbis sed verberibus dignum censeo, et iuxta leges puniendum, quod contra Imperij constitutiones, tam famosum, impudens et meris nugis, mendacijs et malitijs refertum scriptum in publicum edere non sit veritus, et nihilominus Caesaris Mathematicum in frontispicio se profitetur, nec tamen Typographi nomen subiungere audet, uti fit in famosis libellis. Constitui itaque, modo cum bona Caesaris venia, uti spero, id fieri queat, istum pessimum blateronem in ius vocari curare, et publice plagij iniuriarum et mendaciorum accusatum et convictum legibus coerceri et puniri, tum quoque Typographum, qui tam scurrilia impressit citra ordinationes Imperij, mulctari, totumque illud scriptum uti meretur irritum reddi, auctorem vero, unâ cum Typographo, quem tu facile nosti, istic re et corpore in arresto detineri, donec res iure decisa sit. Interim ad praecipuas Germaniae Academias tam Pontificias quam alias scriptum istud mittam, et earum censuram, adiuncta mea declaratione, exquiram, quae omnia postea in ius proponam. Quid Helmstadiensis Academia de hoc iudicet, ex ijs, quae studiosus ille unâ cum libro transmisso ad me perscripsit, videre est, quae est eiusmodi: »Rerum novarum hic nihil est, nisi verum et ferum istum Ursum non hominem (cuius librum hîc quidem non venalem, sed a magno quodam viro acceptum, vobis mitto) pro suo ingenio in vos debacchatum esse, qui, quod vobis gratulamur, sui ipsius ore suam prodidit inscitiam, et innata verborum virulentia ac canina calumniandi rabie vestram probe ultus est iniuriam, utque doctissimus noster CASELIUS, caeteraque Professorum cohors attestatur, quod impuro suo scripto de doctorum virorum coetu plane se exemit, nec dignus est, ut Caesaris amplius vocetur Mathematicus, nedum ut sit. Sed nae ego desipio, qui γλαῦκας εἰς Ἀθήνας. Introspiciatis! Brunsvicensem Cancellarium Pragae fuisse, vere ad vos delatum est, URSUMque exemplar sui operis illi obtulisse, quo pravi ingenij scurrili specimine statuit hîc professionem ambire atque impetrare. Sed ut Cancellarij humanitatis erat, oblatum librum non renuere, ita sapientiae, tam impurum scriptum plane improbare et irridere, quod etiam ab Illmo nostro (uti ab aulico mihi coniunctissimo certo comperi) prorsus damnatum est, adeo ut eius indignitas muneris alicuius illi apud nos deferendi Illustrissimo cogitationem plane ademit. Nos illius torsa in se tela laetamur, vestramque virtutem a tali gregario milite invictam, ut novum quiddam non miramur, qui, si vos isthic agere intellexisset, haud dubie ut in alijs omnibus discessum e Dania exilij convitio calumniose perstrinxisset. Sed huius monstri calumnias nunquam melius quam silentio retundetis, non enim dignus est ira Caesaris.« Haec ille, et postea in postscriptis quibusdam de DUNCANO LIDDELIO Scoto Professore isthic agente, quem meas sibi publice arrogasse Hypotheses, quas tamen a me, cum in Dania semel atque iterum mihi adesset, didicerat, fama percrebuit, ideoque scire avebam, an res ita se haberet, nec ne, sic proloquitur: »Maxima diligentia inquisivi de vestris hypothesibus, an DUNCANUS eas sibi arrogaret, nec potui intelligere ex ijs, qui quotidie cum illo conversantur, eum nunquam ausum fuisse eas appellare suas hypotheses, quod etiam in publicis eius praelectionibus nunquam audivi. Scit bene se obtinere non posse, ut fides ei adhibeatur, sed aliquoties dixit de suo conterraneo CRAIGO, licet saltem privatim apud suos familiares, quem suum vocat Praeceptorem, quod vos aliquando scripsistis quaedam contra illum, in quibus illum mancipium ARISTOTELIS appellatis, quod eum male habet. Ille, cum Rostochij privatim doceret, vestras Hypotheses Tychonianas appellavit, nec pro suis venditavit, qui satis est conscius a nemine esse excogitatas, antequam vos eas invenissetis, quia in Dania eas a vobis intellexerat, diu antequam URSI istius Ditmarsici plagiarij vestri Fundamentum Astronomicum (si dijs placet) evulgatum est, ubi iste perfrictae frontis URSUS hanc inventionem, quam tamen non satis capere videtur, sibi attribuere non erubescit, quam procul dubio apud vos habuit, cum ante multos annos Nobiliss. viro ERICO LANGIO serviens, Uraniburgi cum dicto ERICO per multos dies mansisset. De hoc URSO, cum DUNCANUS maledicum in vos scriptum vidisset, licet vobis ob suum conterraneum et praeceptorem CRAIGUM non valde faveret, sic dixit: Se satis mirari non posse istius URSI impudentem audaciam, et quod nulla honestas, nulla modestia, nullum virtutis vestigium in eo reperiatur, quod omnes etiam docti coguntur fateri, et aiunt: ipsum evacuasse omnis impudentiae poculum, ipsumque valde, uti et meritus est, execrantur, neque potest honestus animus cordati cuiusvis viri aliud in posterum sentire de isto impudenti URSO, quam ipsum omnes verecundiae limites supra modum excessisse, neque dignum, ut in consortio honestorum virorum amplius versetur.«

Haec nimirum est Helmstadiensium Professorum de URSO isto Ditmarsico sententia, cui plures etiam Academiae non difficulter adstipulabantur, et quotquot sunt Hamburgi viri docti, ad quos infamis iste liber pervenit, non meliori Elogio auctorem ornant. Haec vero ob id tibi paulo prolixius refero, dilectissime THADDÆE, quod sciam tibi etiam tam inverecundum et scelestum facinus displicere, rogoque ut rationem ineas, mihique tuum consilium aperias, quomodo is absque Caesaris offensa de iure castigandus sit, neque enim ad tot tantaque convitia atque calumnias salvo honore meo prorsus silere decet, cum non saltem me, sed et domum meam honestissimam, de qua fama hactenus verita est aliquid improbi loqui aut sentire, scurrilibus mendacijs et infamationibus proscindere non erubescat, multaque alia, quae piget referre, singula tamen suo tempore, in ipsum, prout meretur, retorquenda; sed haec aliquantisper dissimulanda censeo, donec in altero negotio, quod longe maioris est momenti, ex voto, uti confido, omnia transacta fuerint. Ista alia suam bene invenient occasionem, praesertim ubi Caesar, cum rectius noverit et clam apud Ducem Brunsvicensem Professionem in Academia Helmstadiensi ambivisse, aut repulsam passum esse resciverit. Nec etiam ea, quae in eodem scripto circa calcem habet, admodum honorifice de Caesare, cuius se iactat Mathematicum, prolata videntur, ubi suam penuriam, sibique nihil dari, et nescio quae alia in Reges et Principes scommata seu potius convitia exaggerat. Os enim ex eo abundat quo cor repletum est. Velim itaque, mi THADDÆE, ut in hoc quoque negotio tuum mihi significes cum consilio iudicium, et quomodo Eruditi atque honesti viri istic tam in aula quam urbe scriptum illud aestiment, et an Caesari tale quid innotuerit, atque utrum placeat vel displiceat, tum quoque ut de Typographo, quae scire opus est, cognoscas. Feceris mihi hac etiam in parte rem imprimis acceptam, et nihil addubito, quin tuo hîc non sis defuturus officio, cum sciam te non minus aegre ferre ea, quae in me evomuntur, maledicta verba, quam si eiuscemodi quid tibi ipsi contingeret, velut et ego in te semper pari affectus sum animo. Vale.

Haec Mathematum quidam Professor Wittebergensis, M. MELCHIOR IŒSTELIUS scripsit ad CHRISTIANUM SEVERINI LONGOMONTANUM, meum antea Studiosum, qui sic habet:

De RAYMARI nuperrime in te impudentia et debacchatione per librum quendam suum recens, ut intelligo, editum sparsa, idem IŒSTELIUS literis suis ultimis ad me missis haec subiungit:

»Pervenit ante paucos dies ad manus meas libellus quidam RAIMARI, in quo toto non tam sophistice quam scurriliter in Generosum Dominum TYCHONEM invehitur. Etsi autem certum est, neminem sanum aut cordatum hoc probaturum, Generosum item equum non curare latratum canum, tamen minime dubito, quin saltem coquus Domini TYCHONIS futilitatem et virulentiam ipsius retundet.«
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Thaddaeus Hagecius.**

Postscript to Master Doctor Thaddaeus Hagecius

In your second letter, my excellent Thaddaeus, you make mention of that Dithmarschen slanderer, and you inform me that, before you departed for Moravia, you arranged for his scurrilous writing to be sent to me in Denmark, so that I might obtain it the sooner — for which goodwill of yours toward me I render thanks. That defamatory little book I did not, indeed, receive from there; I do not know whether it [ever] arrived there, for it was the letters alone, without the book, that were delivered to me here at Wandsbek, forwarded from Denmark; nevertheless, a few days ago I received that [book], sent to me by a certain student at Helmstedt. You reckon, to be sure, that I shall reply to everything quite handily, which would indeed be most easy for me. But I judge it shameful to bandy words with so impudent a reviler, who has overleapt all the bounds of decency and teems wholly with slanders and lies; for he is not worthy to be named in my writings, far less refuted. There will perhaps be someone else who will do this on behalf of myself and also of Rothmann, of good memory, and will blunt his unbridled scurrility. I, for my part, judge him worthy not of words but of whippings, and to be punished according to the laws, in that, against the constitutions of the Empire, he has not feared to publish a writing so defamatory, so impudent, and stuffed with mere trifles, lies, and malice — and nonetheless professes himself His Imperial Majesty's Mathematician on the title-page, yet does not dare to append the printer's name, as is done in defamatory pamphlets. I have therefore resolved — provided it can be done, as I hope, with His Imperial Majesty's good leave — to see that this vilest babbler be summoned to law, and, publicly accused and convicted of plagiarism, of injuries, and of lies, be restrained and punished by the laws; and likewise that the printer, who printed such scurrilous matter contrary to the ordinances of the Empire, be fined; and that that whole writing be, as it deserves, declared void; and that the author, together with the printer — whom you readily know — be there detained in arrest, in goods and in person, until the matter has been decided at law. Meanwhile I shall send that writing to the principal universities of Germany, both the Catholic ones and the others, and shall seek out their censure, with my own declaration appended — all of which I shall afterward lay before the court. What the University of Helmstedt judges of this may be seen from what that student wrote out to me along with the book he forwarded, which is of this sort: »There is no news here, except that that true and savage Bear [Ursus], no man, (whose book — not, indeed, on sale here, but received from a certain great man — I send you) has, after his fashion, raved against you; who, as we congratulate you, has by his own mouth betrayed his own ignorance, and by his inborn virulence of words and his canine madness for slandering has well avenged your wrong; and, as our most learned Caselius and the rest of the company of Professors attest, by his foul writing he has plainly removed himself from the company of learned men, and is not worthy any longer to be called His Imperial Majesty's Mathematician, far less to be one. But truly I am playing the fool, [carrying] owls to Athens [γλαῦκας εἰς Ἀθήνας]. Look closely! That the Chancellor of Brunswick was at Prague has been truly reported to you, and that Ursus offered him a copy of his work, by which scurrilous specimen of his crooked wit he resolved to seek and obtain a professorship here. But as it was a mark of the Chancellor's courtesy not to refuse the offered book, so it was a mark of his wisdom plainly to disapprove and deride so foul a writing — which was also wholly condemned by our Most Illustrious [Lord] (as I have learned for certain from a courtier most closely bound to me), to such a degree that its unworthiness plainly took from the Most Illustrious [Lord] the thought of conferring any office on him among us. We rejoice at his weapons turned back upon himself, and that your virtue is unconquered by such a common soldier — so that we do not wonder at it as anything new; for he, had he understood that you were active there, would doubtless, as in all other things, have slanderously carped at your departure from Denmark with the reproach of exile. But you will never blunt this monster's slanders better than by silence; for he is not worthy of His Imperial Majesty's anger.« Thus he; and afterward, in certain postscripts, concerning Duncan Liddel, the Scottish Professor active there — of whom a report had spread that he had publicly claimed as his own my Hypotheses, which yet he had learned from me when he was with me in Denmark once and again, and so I was eager to know whether the matter was so, or not — he speaks thus: »With the greatest diligence I inquired about your hypotheses, whether Duncan claimed them as his own, and I could not gather, from those who converse with him daily, that he had ever dared to call them his hypotheses; which I have never heard in his public lectures either. He well knows that he cannot bring it about that credence be given him; but he said several times of his fellow-countryman Craig — though only privately, among his intimates — whom he calls his Preceptor, that you once wrote certain things against him, in which you call him a bond-slave of Aristotle, which galls him. He, when he was teaching privately at Rostock, called your Hypotheses 'Tychonic,' and did not peddle them as his own, being well enough aware that they were devised by no one before you discovered them, because he had learned them from you in Denmark, long before that Dithmarschen plagiarist Ursus's *Astronomical Foundation* (if it please the gods) was published abroad — wherein that brazen-browed Ursus does not blush to attribute to himself this invention, which, however, he does not seem sufficiently to grasp, [and] which without doubt he got from you, when, serving years ago the most noble Erik Lange, he had stayed with the said Erik at Uraniborg for many days. Of this Ursus, when Duncan had seen the scurrilous writing against you, although he did not much favour you on account of his fellow-countryman and preceptor Craig, he spoke thus: that he could not sufficiently marvel at the impudent audacity of that Ursus, and that no honesty, no modesty, no trace of virtue is found in him — which even all the learned are compelled to admit, and they say: that he has drained the whole cup of impudence, and they greatly execrate him, as indeed he has deserved; nor can the honest mind of any sensible man henceforth feel otherwise about that impudent Ursus than that he has beyond measure exceeded all the bounds of decency, and is not worthy to consort any longer in the company of honest men.«

This, then, is the verdict of the Helmstedt Professors about that Dithmarschen Ursus — to which several other universities also assented without difficulty; and however many learned men there are at Hamburg, to whom that infamous book has come, they adorn its author with no better eulogy. But I report these things to you at somewhat greater length, most beloved Thaddaeus, for this reason: because I know that so shameless and wicked a deed displeases you also; and I ask that you devise a plan and disclose your counsel to me, [as to] how he may lawfully be chastised without offence to His Imperial Majesty — for it does not befit my honour to keep wholly silent at so many and so great revilings and slanders, since he does not blush to rend with scurrilous lies and defamations not only me but also my most honourable house, of which rumour has hitherto feared to speak or think anything dishonourable, and many other things which it irks me to relate — each of them, however, in its own time, to be turned back upon him as he deserves; but I judge that these things should be dissembled for a while, until in the other affair, which is by far of greater moment, everything shall have been transacted according to [my] wish, as I trust. Those other matters will well find their own occasion, especially once His Imperial Majesty — when he comes to know more correctly, and learns that [Ursus] secretly sought a professorship at the University of Helmstedt with the Duke of Brunswick, or suffered a rebuff — [shall be informed of it]. Nor, too, do the things he has near the end of the same writing seem to be uttered very honourably about His Imperial Majesty, whose Mathematician he boasts himself to be, where he magnifies his own want, and that nothing is given him, and I know not what other gibes — or rather revilings — against Kings and Princes. For the mouth overflows from that with which the heart is filled. I should wish, therefore, my Thaddaeus, that in this matter too you signify to me your judgement together with your counsel, and how learned and honest men there, both at court and in the city, esteem that writing, and whether anything of the kind has come to His Imperial Majesty's notice, and whether it pleases or displeases [him]; and likewise that you find out, concerning the printer, what it is needful to know. You will have done me, in this part also, a thing especially welcome; and I do not doubt at all that you will not fail in your good office here, since I know that you bear the abusive words spewed out against me no less hard than if something of the kind befell you yourself — just as I too have always been disposed toward you with an equal feeling. Farewell.

These things a certain Professor of Mathematics at Wittenberg, Master Melchior Jöstel, wrote to Christian Sørensen Longomontanus, formerly my student, which run thus:

Concerning Reimarus's impudence and raving lately spread abroad against you through a certain book of his, recently, as I understand, published, the same Jöstel adds these things in his last letter sent to me:

»A few days ago a certain little book of Reimarus's came into my hands, in the whole of which he inveighs against the Noble Master Tycho not so much sophistically as scurrilously. But although it is certain that no sane or sensible person will approve this, [and] that a noble horse likewise heeds not the barking of dogs, yet I do not doubt in the least that Master Tycho's cook, at any rate, will blunt his futility and virulence.«

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** Tycho Brahe to **Thaddaeus Hagecius** (Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku, 1525–1600), the Bohemian court physician and astronomer in Prague, Tycho's long-time friend and his principal channel to the imperial court of Rudolf II. The letter is an *appendix* (*"Post scripta"* / postscript) to a fuller letter, gathering the documentary evidence Tycho wished Hagecius to use against Ursus.
- **Date / place.** The edition label is *s.l.* ("no place [given]"); no dateline survives in the transcript. The body locates Tycho *hîc Wandesburgi* — "here at **Wandsbek**" (Wandesburgum, now a district of Hamburg, where Tycho lived 1597–98 after leaving Denmark) — and the events (receipt of Ursus's *De astronomicis hypothesibus* of 1597, Tycho's plans to prosecute) fix it to **1598 (O.S.)**, the year given in the source header and the identifier. The header therefore carries the bracketed place and the year; the apparatus notes that neither a day nor month is in the text. No date is silently asserted beyond the year the source supplies.
- **"istius calumniatoris Ditmarsici" / "URSUS"** — **Nicolaus Reimarus Ursus** (Reimers Bär, d. 1600), of **Dithmarschen** (*Ditmarsicus*), then Imperial Mathematician at Prague. His *De astronomicis hypothesibus … tractatus* (Prague 1597) attacked Tycho and claimed the geo-heliocentric world-system; Tycho regarded it as plagiarism of his own system, learned during Ursus's 1584 visit to Uraniborg in the service of Erik Lange. The pun on his name — *Ursus* = "Bear" — is exploited in the Helmstedt letter (*"verum et ferum istum Ursum non hominem"*, "that true and savage Bear, no man"); kept and glossed.
- **"ROTHMANNO, bonae mem."** — **Christoph Rothmann**, the Hesse-Kassel mathematician; *bonae memoriae*, "of good [i.e. blessed] memory," indicates Tycho here believed Rothmann dead (his date of death is in fact uncertain). Ursus's tract had also attacked Rothmann.
- **"Caesar / Caesaris Mathematicum"** — *Caesar* throughout = **Emperor Rudolf II**; *Caesaris Mathematicus* = "the Emperor's Mathematician," the imperial post Ursus held and styled himself by on his title-page (*in frontispicio*). Rendered "His Imperial Majesty / His Imperial Majesty's Mathematician."
- **"contra Imperij constitutiones … citra ordinationes Imperij"** — the imperial press laws (the Reichspolizeiordnung provisions against unsigned defamatory libels); the absence of the printer's name is precisely the statutory offence Tycho points to.
- **Helmstedt letter (the inset quotation).** Sent to Tycho by an unnamed *studiosus Helmstadiensis* (a student at the **University of Helmstedt**, the Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel university). **"CASELIUS"** = **Johannes Caselius** (1533–1613), the eminent Helmstedt humanist. *"Brunsvicensem Cancellarium"* = the Chancellor of Brunswick(-Wolfenbüttel); *"Illmo nostro … Illustrissimo"* = "our Most Illustrious [Lord]," i.e. the reigning Duke (Heinrich Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel), at whose university Ursus had reportedly angled for a chair.
- **Greek.** *γλαῦκας εἰς Ἀθήνας* — "owls to Athens," the proverb (cf. Aristophanes, *Birds* 301; the owl being Athena's bird and Athens' civic emblem) for redundant effort, our "coals to Newcastle." Transcribed verbatim (with the printed final-sigma forms) in the Source block and translated with the proverb flagged, by this chapter's convention
- **"DUNCANO LIDDELIO Scoto" / "CRAIGO"** — **Duncan Liddel** (1561–1613), the Scottish physician-astronomer then professor at Helmstedt, reported (the report is here being checked and *not* confirmed) to have claimed Tycho's planetary hypotheses; he is reported rather to have taught them honestly as *Hypotheses Tychonianae* ("Tychonic hypotheses") while teaching privately at **Rostock**. **"CRAIGO" / CRAIGUS** = **John Craig** (d. 1620), Liddel's Scottish fellow-countryman and (so Liddel called him) *Praeceptor*, "preceptor," with whom Tycho had a separate dispute; *"mancipium Aristotelis"* = "a bond-slave of Aristotle," Tycho's reported jibe at Craig.
- **"ERICO LANGIO"** — **Erik Lange** (1553–1613), the Danish nobleman, alchemist, and Tycho's friend (later brother-in-law's circle); Ursus had been in his service and so came to Uraniborg.
- **"Fundamentum Astronomicum (si dijs placet)"** — Ursus's work is named ironically; *Fundamentum Astronomicum* is in fact the title of an *earlier* Ursus work (Strasbourg 1588). The parenthetical *si dijs placet*, "if it please the gods," is a sarcastic period idiom (≈ "if you please / God help us"); kept and glossed, the irony preserved rather than smoothed.
- **"plagij" / "plagiarij"** — *plagium*, the legal offence of man-stealing/literary theft; *plagiarius*, "plagiarist." Rendered "plagiarism / plagiarist"; this is among the earliest technical legal uses in the Tycho dossier.
- **Closing inset.** **M. Melchior Jöstel** (1559–1611), Master (*Magister*) and professor of mathematics at **Wittenberg**, wrote to **Christian Sørensen Longomontanus** (Christen Sørensen, 1562–1647), Tycho's senior assistant ("formerly my student"); *"RAYMARI / RAIMARI"* is again Ursus (Reimarus). The sentence *"Generosum … equum non curare latratum canum"* ("a noble horse heeds not the barking of dogs") is a proverb, kept as such. The closing jest — that even **Master Tycho's cook** could refute Ursus — is an insult-by-belittlement (Ursus is so feeble that the lowliest of Tycho's household would suffice); rendered straight.
- **Scriptural allusion.** *"Os enim ex eo abundat quo cor repletum est"* — "For the mouth overflows from that with which the heart is filled," a paraphrase of Matthew 12:34 / Luke 6:45 (*ex abundantia cordis os loquitur*); rendered as the proverb-allusion it is.
- **Negation check.** The legal-force clauses were counted: *"non sit veritus"* ("has not feared," i.e. did dare), *"nec … audet"* ("does not dare"), *"non … nominetur, nedum refutetur"* ("not to be named, far less refuted"), *"non verbis sed verberibus"* ("not of words but of whippings"), *"non … prorsus silere decet"* ("it does not befit … to keep wholly silent"), *"non erubescit"* ("does not blush"), *"nunquam … nedum"*, and the closing *"non … defuturus officio"* ("will not fail in your office"). Each negation is reproduced one-for-one; none added or dropped.
- **Correction.** Latin corrected against Dreyer, TBOO VIII pp.57-59 (page images): rejoined the place-name 'Uraniburgi' and the following word 'cum', which the working transcription had fused across a page-break catchword into 'Uraniburgicum' (p.57-58); and restored the dropped phrase 'et debacchatione' ("and raving") describing Ursus/Reimarus's pamphlet, with the English updated to match (p.59).

- **text error** (low). Dreyer's text splits across a page break with a printer's catchword ('cum' previewed at the foot of p.57, then repeated as the first word of p.58). The transcribed original glued the place-name 'Uraniburgi' to the stray catchword, producing the non-word 'Uraniburgicum'. Dreyer prints: *De RAYMARI nuperrime in te impudentia et debacchatione per librum quendam suum recens... editum sparsa (p.59, line 3-4)*.

documents.abstract: Addresses Rudolf II invoking the Imperial tradition of astronomical patronage and solicits the Emperor's clement reception of his petition.
documents.incipit: AUGUSTISSIME Imperator RUDOLPHE Secunde. Cum de tuae Imperatoriae Maiestatis erga …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD IMPERATOREM RUDOLPHUM SECUNDUM.

AUGUSTISSIME Imperator RUDOLPHE Secunde. Cum de tuae Imperatoriae Maiestatis erga liberalia studia, praesertim in his principaliora, Mathematica et Astronomica, clementi favore, diu multumque inaudiverim, ipsaque tua Caesarea Maiestas non tantum potentissimorum et laudatissimorum maiorum suorum ALPHONSI Regis Arragonum etc. MATTHIAe HUNNIADIS, HENRICI illius secundi ob indefessam rerum coelestium contemplationem Astronomi dicti, CAROLI quinti, FERDINANDI ac Augustissimi Parentis MAXIMILIANI secundi aliorumque, studijs his impense addictorum, quos numerare longum foret, celebratissimo exemplo, sed et sua ipsiusmet vere Heroica et Caesarea inclinatione, quantum Regnorum ac Reip. gubernatio ferunt, ijsdem his laudabiliter vacet exercitijs: omnino mihi polliceor, Caesaream tuam Maiestatem clementi animo accepturam, me viarum intercapedine alijsque difficultatibus, quo minus Caesaream tuam Maiestatem ipse cito adeo, ac praeoptarim alias, accedere liceat, praepeditum, hasce literas arduum licet negotium concernentes summisse exhibere non vereri ipsi. Cuius meae fidentiae caussam hanc primam habeo et praecipuam Imperatoriae tuae Maiestatis clementissimum erga me eaque, quae multis abhinc annis tracto studia, favorem, iampridem mihi vel ex solo eo singulari diplomate perspectum, quod Caesarea tua Maiestas tanquam in epistola ad me directo sermone clementer mihi impertiri, non sine harum artium praeclaro elogio, dignata est. Caesarea itaque tua Maiestas praesentibus hisce clementer scire dignetur, me, evidentibus ijsque haud levibus de caussis mutato Patrio solo, in Germaniam tuae Caesareae Maiestati subditam cum Astronomica mea supellectile, adeoque tota familia, nuper concessisse, ut est rerum humanarum omnium quaedam subinde vicissitudo. Ubi, favente coelestium Opifice, Astronomicos meos labores per 21 Annos in patria mea dulcissima Dania exantlatos continuare ac ad propositum scopum dirigere et absolvere decrevi, impetrata primum hîc alicubi et constituta rebus coelestibus sat commoda, constanti et inviolabili sede, unde fundamentalis earundem tractatio aeviternum ad posteros etiam in Imperij ipsius decus (uti confido) non contemnendum transmitti possit. Quocirca ad tuam Imperatoriam Maiestatem omnium primo mihi concedendum, eiusque clementissimam voluntatem quam humillime explorandam censui, an non illustre hoc Astronomicum negotium solide et solenniter institutum in aliqua suarum ditionum porro continuare atque ad optatum finem, Dei beneficio, perducere daretur. Sunt mihi ad hoc Opus in promptu Instrumenta varia, eaque maxima et affabre elaborata, qualia et quanta vix uspiam invenire datur. Sunt plurimorum annorum exactissimae Observationes veterum inventis non cedentes. Sunt multa alia huc conducentia, et non pauca, imo praecipua iam confecta. Ut vero Caesarea tua Maiestas specimen aliquod eorum habeat, mitto cum filio meo Organorum, quae hactenus in usu habui, quotquot tam cito exscindi curare licuit, delineationem, apposita earundem succincta explicatione. Offero quoque humiliter Canonicam Affixarum Stellarum expositionem, quotquot in nostro climate utcunque visuntur, numero millenarum, quas omnes intra Annos 20 praeteritos summa et indefessa diligentia meis Organis coelitus quam scrupulosissime demensus sum, cum sine harum, potissimum Zodiaco vicinarum, exacta verificatione Planetarum viae et motiones ad amussim non percipiantur. Qua etiam in parte (quoad errantia videlicet sidera) quid hactenus praestiterimus, quidque in posterum superaddendum restet, prior ille, de quo dixi, liber suo loco pandit. Plura meorum de Astronomia Operum tua Caesarea Maiestas, cui me meaque studia omnia humiliter offero et commendata cupio, brevi, aspirante Universitatis authore, obtinebit. Interea hasce primitias alijs gravioribus viam sternentes non aversetur. De caetero Caesarea tua Maiestas per Dominum Procancellarium Imperij aut aliquem e suis Consiliarijs intimis, referente Domino Doctore THADDÆO HAGGECIO, clementer intelligat, qui a filio meo praesente singula uberius cognoscat. Utque Caesarea tua Maiestas, hoc intermediante, sibi humillime meo nomine proposita clementer excipiat, et responsum, quandocunque eidem commodum fuerit, impertiri dignetur, qua possum submissione precor.

Deus Coelestium et Terrestrium author tuam Caesaream Maiestatem felici Imperij et Regnorum gubernatione quam diutissime florentem et incolumem tueatur.

Datae Wandelburgo ex Arce Ranzoviana prope Hamburgum sita, die 2 Ianuarij Anni 1598.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO EMPEROR RUDOLF THE SECOND.**

Most August Emperor Rudolf the Second. Since I have for a long while and much heard tell of Your Imperial Majesty's clement favour toward the liberal studies — and, foremost among these, toward the mathematical and astronomical [studies] — and [since] Your Imperial Majesty Himself, not only by the most celebrated example of His most powerful and most praised ancestors — Alfonso, King of Aragon, etc., Matthias Hunyadi, that Henry the Second who for his unwearied contemplation of the things of the heavens was called the Astronomer, Charles the Fifth, Ferdinand, and that most August Parent Maximilian the Second, and others, who were earnestly devoted to these studies, whom it would be long to number — but also by His own truly heroic and imperial inclination, devotes Himself in laudable fashion to these same pursuits, so far as the government of His kingdoms and of the commonwealth allow: I altogether promise myself that Your Imperial Majesty will receive with clement spirit [the fact] that I, hindered by the long stretch of the roads and by other difficulties from being able to approach Your Imperial Majesty as soon as, and as I should otherwise have most preferred, do not fear to present humbly this letter, though it concerns an arduous matter. The first and chief cause of this confidence of mine I hold to be Your Imperial Majesty's most clement favour toward me and toward those studies which I have pursued for many years now — long since made plain to me even from that single, extraordinary diploma which Your Imperial Majesty deigned clemently to grant me, addressing me as it were in a letter in direct speech, and not without splendid praise of these arts. May Your Imperial Majesty therefore deign clemently to know by these present [letters] that I, for evident and by no means slight causes, having changed my native soil, have lately withdrawn into Germany, subject to Your Imperial Majesty, with my astronomical equipment and indeed with my whole household — as there is from time to time a certain vicissitude in all human affairs. There, the Maker of the heavenly things favouring [me], I have resolved to continue the astronomical labours which I toiled through over 21 years in my most sweet homeland Denmark, and to direct them to their proposed goal and bring them to completion — once there has first been obtained and established somewhere here a settled and inviolable seat, sufficiently suited to the heavenly matters, whence the fundamental treatment of those same [matters] may be transmitted to posterity for all time, and (as I trust) to no contemptible adornment of the Empire itself. Wherefore I judged that I must first of all be granted access to Your Imperial Majesty, and most humbly explore His most clement will [as to] whether it might not be granted [me] to continue this illustrious astronomical undertaking — solidly and solemnly established — onward in some one of His dominions, and to bring it, by God's beneficence, to the wished-for end. I have ready to hand for this Work instruments various, and those very great and skilfully wrought, such, and so great, as one is scarcely granted to find anywhere. There are most exact observations of very many years, not yielding to the discoveries of the ancients. There are many other things conducing hereto, and not a few — indeed the chief ones — already completed. But that Your Imperial Majesty may have some specimen of these, I send with my son a delineation of the instruments which I have hitherto had in use — as many as could be engraved so quickly — with a concise explanation of the same appended. I also humbly offer a canonical exposition of the fixed stars — as many as are in any way seen in our clime, to the number of a thousand — all of which, within the 20 years past, I have measured out from the heavens by my instruments, with the utmost and unwearied diligence, as scrupulously as could be; since without an exact verification of these — especially of those near the zodiac — the courses and motions of the planets are not perceived to the line. In which part too (with respect, that is, to the wandering stars) what I have so far accomplished, and what remains to be superadded hereafter, that former book of which I spoke sets forth in its place. More of my works on astronomy Your Imperial Majesty — to whom I humbly offer myself and all my studies, and wish them commended — shall shortly obtain, the Author of the Universe favouring [it]. Meanwhile let Him not turn away from these first-fruits, which pave the way for others weightier. For the rest, may Your Imperial Majesty be clemently informed through the Lord Vice-Chancellor of the Empire, or some one of His privy councillors — Lord Doctor Thaddaeus Hagecius reporting [the matter] — who may learn each particular more fully from my son, [who is] present. And I pray, with what submission I can, that Your Imperial Majesty, through this intermediary, may clemently take up the [matters] most humbly proposed in my name, and deign to grant a response whenever it shall be convenient to Him.

May God, the Author of the heavenly and the earthly things, keep Your Imperial Majesty, by a fortunate government of the Empire and the kingdoms, flourishing and unharmed for the very longest time.

Given at Wandsbek, from the Castle of Rantzau situated near Hamburg, on the 2nd day of January, in the year 1598.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), then in self-imposed exile from Denmark; **Rudolf II** (1552–1612), Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1576–1612), residing at Prague — to whose service Tycho was angling. This is Tycho's formal overture to imperial patronage, carried by his eldest son. It is the prose counterpart of the dedication of the *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica* (dated 31 December 1597 at Wandsbek), and the *delineation of the instruments* it announces is the engraved instrument-catalogue of that very work.
- **Place.** *Wandesburgo ex Arce Ranzoviana prope Hamburgum* = **Wandsbek** (now part of Hamburg), at the castle of **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), the Danish royal governor (*Statthalter*) of Holstein and humanist patron, who hosted Tycho in 1597–98. Tycho had left Hven in 1597 ("changed my native soil").
- **The son.** *cum filio meo … a filio meo praesente* — "with my son … from my son, present": **Tycho Brahe the Younger** (b. 1581), here acting as his father's envoy to court (though the diplomatic mission to Prague is more usually associated with Tycho's assistant Franz Tengnagel; the letter names only *filius meus*). Rendered literally as "my son," not resolved to a named agent.
- **The ancestors named.** A roll of imperial/royal patrons of astronomy: ***Alphonsus Rex Arragonum*** = **Alfonso X of Castile** (1221–1284), patron of the Alfonsine Tables — Tycho's "etc." and "of Aragon" loosely subsume the Iberian crowns (Alfonso X was King of Castile and León; the slip is the source's, kept). ***Matthias Hunniades*** = **Matthias Corvinus (Hunyadi)**, King of Hungary (1443–1490), patron of Regiomontanus. ***Henricus ille secundus … Astronomi dicti*** = a **Henry "the Astronomer"**; the epithet was applied to several Henries (e.g., Henry III of Castile "el Doliente" is sometimes confused; medieval tradition styled an Emperor/king "Henry the Astronomer") — Tycho's exact referent is not securely fixed and is left as the text gives it (**crux**, see below). ***Carolus quintus*** = **Charles V** (1500–1558); ***Ferdinandus*** = **Ferdinand I** (1503–1564); ***Maximilianus secundus*** = **Maximilian II** (1527–1576), Rudolf's father (*Augustissimus Parens*).
- **Instruments / observations.** *Organa* / *Instrumenta* → **instruments**; *Organorum … delineatio* = "a delineation [drawn representation/engraving] of the instruments" — the plates of the *Mechanica*. *Canonica Affixarum Stellarum expositio … numero millenarum* = a **canonical exposition of the fixed stars, to the number of a thousand** — Tycho's **1,000-star catalogue** (*Stellarum inerrantium restitutio*), measured *meis Organis coelitus* ("from the heavens by my instruments"). *ad amussim* = "to the line / exactly" (a builder's-rule idiom), here rendered "to the line."
- ***prior ille … liber*** — "that former book of which I spoke": i.e. the instrument-volume (*Mechanica*) just mentioned, which in its place treats the planets (*errantia sidera*, "the wandering stars").
- ***primitias … alijs gravioribus viam sternentes*** — "these first-fruits, which pave the way for others weightier": the *Mechanica* + star-catalogue as forerunners of Tycho's larger projected works (the planetary theory / *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata*).
- **Court officials.** *Dominus Procancellarius Imperij* = the **Imperial Vice-Chancellor**; *Consiliarij intimi* = **privy councillors**. ***Thaddaeus Haggecius*** = **Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku** (Thaddaeus Hagecius, 1525–1600), Bohemian physician-astronomer and imperial counsellor at Prague, Tycho's long-standing correspondent and his key intermediary at Rudolf's court.
- ***singulari diplomate … in epistola ad me directo sermone*** — "that single, extraordinary diploma … addressing me as it were in a letter in direct speech": an earlier personal mark of imperial favour shown to Tycho; rendered without sharpening the simile (*tanquam … directo sermone*).
- ***aspirante Universitatis authore*** / ***Deus Coelestium et Terrestrium author*** — "the Author of the Universe favouring [it]" / "God, the Author of the heavenly and the earthly things": Tycho's pious framing; *aspirante* = "breathing favour upon," the standard *Deo aspirante* hedge, kept as a conditional ("favouring").
- **Calendar.** *die 2 Ianuarij Anni 1598* = **2 January 1598**. Denmark and the Empire's Protestant correspondents used the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar; the dateline is taken at face value as **O.S.** The catalogue label ("1598. 2. januar. Wandsburg") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy. No style marker (*n.s.*) is present.
- **Hedges preserved.** *(uti confido)* "as I trust"; *favente coelestium Opifice* / *Dei beneficio* / *aspirante … authore* — Tycho's success-conditions are kept as conditionals, not flattened into assertions; *vix uspiam invenire datur* "one is scarcely granted to find anywhere" (not "nowhere"); *non contemnendum* "no contemptible" (litotes kept).
- **Correction.** Restored 'Wandelburgo' (Dreyer, TBOO VIII p.20) for the one-letter departure 'Wandesburgo' in our transcription of the closing dateline; the English 'Wandsbek' was unaffected.
