documents.abstract: Asks Rosenkrantz for the name, address, and preferred language of an Austrian baron introduced by Erik Lange, in order to solicit testimony about the plagiarist Ursus.
documents.incipit: NOBILISSIME Domine OLIGERE, Consangvinee et Affinis desideratissime et præ multis …

text.original:
OLIGERO ROSÆKRANTZIO, VIRO CORDATO ET MIHI AMICO, CONSANGVINEO ET AFFINI CHARISSIMO.

NOBILISSIME Domine OLIGERE, Consangvinee et Affinis desideratissime et præ multis dilecte. Incidit aliquid hodie post tuum a me discessum, quod in scheda memoriali tibi tradita annotatum non recordor: nempe quod sit nomen Baronis illius Austriaci, qui uxorem in Cimbria duxit. Illud enim mihi memoriâ excidit. Cuperem etiam scire, ubinam habitet, et quomodo intitulandus sit, iuxta morem vobis consuetum; quo illi scribam convenientius de putidissimo et mendacissimo isto Plagiario, cuius hîc facta est mentio; atque eorum, quæ ipsi de eo constant, cum mecum ab ERICO LANGIO adductus esset, indicationem efflagitem. Admoneas etiam, an Latinæ linguæ sit peritus, nec ne; quo sciam, an Germanice vel Latine illi scribendum sit, aut etiam Danice, si hoc callet idioma. Vale, et literas Regi destinatas, ad non Regias oblique respondentes per hunc nuncium remitte, quantum otium tibi permiserit, critizatas, atque glossis marginalibus auctas: quod etiam ut in prioribus facias, quibus hæ nonnulla respondent, rogo; nec te id effecturum diffido, quoniam sic in te recepisti.

Iamque ulterius et perpetuo quam felicissime vale, mi exoptatissime et desideratissime OLIGERE.
Raptim Wandesburgi die 14. Februarij Anni 98.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To Holger Rosenkrantz, a man of sense and my friend, a kinsman and connexion by marriage most dear.**

Most noble Master Holger, kinsman and connexion most longed-for and beloved before many. Something occurred to me today, after your departure from me, which I do not recall having noted down in the memorandum-slip handed over to you: namely, what is the name of that Austrian baron who took a wife in Holstein [Cimbria]. For it has slipped my memory. I should also like to know where he lives, and how he is to be styled, according to the custom usual among you [of the nobility]; so that I may write to him more fittingly about that most rotten and most lying Plagiarist, of whom mention was made here; and so that I may earnestly request a statement of those things which are established to him concerning the man, since he had been brought to me by Erik Lange. Advise me too whether he is skilled in the Latin tongue or not; so that I may know whether I am to write to him in German or in Latin, or even in Danish, if he is versed in this language. Farewell; and the letters destined for the King, which obliquely answer the not-royal ones, send back by this messenger — so far as your leisure shall allow you — once they have been subjected to critical judgement [critizatas] and enlarged with marginal glosses: which I ask that you do also in the case of the earlier ones, to which these in some part correspond; nor do I doubt that you will accomplish it, since you have so taken it upon yourself.

And now further and forever, fare you most happily, my most wished-for and most longed-for Holger.
In haste, at Wandsbek, on the 14th day of February of the year [15]98.
Yours, TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe**, writing from exile after leaving Denmark in 1597. By February 1598 he was lodged at **Wandsbek** (see below), the residence of Heinrich Rantzau near Hamburg, where he completed the *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica* and the *Epistolarum astronomicarum liber* later that year.
- **Recipient.** *Oligerus Rosaekrantzius* = **Holger Rosenkrantz** ("the Learned," 1574–1642), Danish nobleman, theologian and scholar, related to Tycho by blood and marriage (*consanguineus et affinis*). The address renders him *vir cordatus* — "a man of sense / good judgement"; cf. the same epithet applied to Rosenkrantz elsewhere in the correspondence.
- ***Cimbria*** — the humanist Latin name for the **Cimbrian peninsula**, i.e. Jutland/Holstein (the Cimbric Chersonese); rendered "Holstein [Cimbria]" since the Austrian baron's marriage "in Cimbria" places it in that region. The exact district is not specified by the text and is not narrowed here.
- ***Plagiarius*** ("Plagiarist") — Tycho's habitual term of abuse for **Nicolaus Reimers Bär** (Latin *Ursus*, 1551–1600), the Imperial Mathematician at Prague whom Tycho accused of having stolen and published his geo-heliocentric world-system (in Ursus's *Fundamentum astronomicum*, 1588). The intensifiers *putidissimus et mendacissimus* ("most rotten and most lying") are kept at full superlative force. **Identification flagged:** Ursus is not named in this letter; the equation rests on Tycho's consistent usage of *Plagiarius* for him in 1597–98 and on the context (a man Tycho means to denounce by letter). The text itself leaves the "Plagiarist" unnamed.
- ***Ericus Langius*** = **Erik Lange** (1553–1613), Danish nobleman and alchemist, Tycho's friend and the betrothed of Tycho's sister Sophie Brahe; here named as the person who had earlier brought the Austrian baron into Tycho's company (*cum mecum … adductus esset*).
- ***scheda memorialis*** — "a memorandum-slip" / aide-mémoire that Tycho had given Rosenkrantz on his departure; this letter supplies a point he had forgotten to include.
- ***iuxta morem vobis consuetum*** — "according to the custom usual among you": *vobis* is read as the second-person plural of the noble/courtly class to which Rosenkrantz belongs (the proper styling and titulature of a baron). Rendered "among you [of the nobility]," the bracketed gloss marking the interpretive expansion.
- ***literas Regi destinatas, ad non Regias oblique respondentes*** — "the letters destined for the King, which obliquely answer the not-royal ones." A compressed and deliberately oblique phrase: letters meant for the King (almost certainly **Christian IV of Denmark**) that reply indirectly to other, *non*-royal letters. **Crux flagged:** the referent of *non Regias* (the "not-royal" letters being answered) is not specified in the text and is left literal rather than resolved; *oblique* ("obliquely, indirectly") is Tycho's own hedge and is preserved, not sharpened into a definite construction.
- ***critizatas*** — a Greek-derived coinage (from κριτής / κρίνειν, "to judge, sift") meaning "critically examined, subjected to critical judgement"; here, that Rosenkrantz go over the letters with a critic's eye before returning them. Kept as a flagged technical neologism and glossed rather than smoothed to a single English verb. Paired with *glossis marginalibus auctas*, "enlarged with marginal glosses" (annotations in the margin).
- ***manu propria*** — "in his own hand": Tycho's autograph subscription. The sole MS witness, however, is a later copy (*afskrift*) in **Langebek's Diplomatarium**, so the surviving text is a transcript, not the autograph itself.
- **Dateline & place.** *Raptim Wandesburgi die 14. Februarij Anni 98* = "In haste, at **Wandsbek** [Wandesburgum, the Rantzau castle near Hamburg, now in Hamburg], on the 14th day of February of the year [15]98" (O.S.; Denmark and the North-German Protestant correspondents kept the Julian calendar). *Raptim* ("in haste") preserved. The header date follows the dateline and agrees with the catalogue label (14 February 1598).

documents.abstract: Sends her servant Johann Müller to study mathematics and spagyric preparation of medicaments under Tycho, requesting compliance with the terms previously promised.
documents.incipit: VANN Gottes gnadenn Katharina, geborne vndt vermehlte marggreffin, auch churfurstin zue …

text.original:
DEM ERNUESTEN VNNSERM BESONDERN LIEBEN TYCHO BRAHEN VFF KNUDTTSTRUP VNNDT WRANENNBURGK.

VANN Gottes gnadenn Katharina, geborne vndt vermehlte marggreffin, auch churfurstin zue Brandenburgk, jnn Preusen hertzogin. Wnsern gnedigenn grues zuuorn. Ernuester besonder lieber, Wir thuen euch auff eur begehrn hiermitt Vnserm diener vndt lieben getrewenn Johann Mullern zu dem ende vbersendenn, das ehr ein zeittlang mitt euch conuersiren, vnnd sich in mathematico studio aldar exerciren muegte. Begehrn demnach an euch hiermitt ganntz gnedigst, jhr wollett euch nichtt allein jnn dem kegenn jhnen willfehrigk erweisenn, sonndern auch in spagiricis medicamentorum præparationibus, vnnd was jhr sonnstenn auss erfahrung in pyronomicis habtt, jhnen guettwillig vnterrichtenn, vnndt euch inn diesem allenn dermassen erzeigen, wie vff eurre Vnns durch jhnen, Vnnsernn diener, gethene zuesage erbietenn, zu euch Vnser vngezweifeltes gnedigstes vertrawenn gerichtett. Das wollenn Wir jnn allenn gnadenn, darmitt Wir euch sonnds woll gewogenn, hinwieder mitt danck zu erkennen vnuorgessenn halltenn. Vnnd ob Wir jhn woll gherne nebenn eurem sohne ettwass ehe wieder abgeferttiget haben wollten, so seindt doch Vnnserm freundtlichenn hertzlieben herrn gemahl bißhero andere wichtiche sachenn vorgefallenn, das man darzue fueglich nichtt ehe kommenn konnenn. Werdet der wegenn euren sohn, der es zwartt wie auch gedachter Johann Muller an vleissigsten vnndterthenigstenn sollicitiren nicht manglen lassen, im besten enttschuldigett haltenn. Wir seindt der vnzweifeligen zuversichtt, es werden bey der könn: wd:, Vnnserm freunthlichen hertzvielgeliebten herrn vettern vnnd sohne, die euch mittgetheilte intercession schrifftenn ohne frucht nicht abgehen, sonndernn dardurch eure sachenn wiederumb zu selbst wunschendenn gueten standt gelangenn, wie Wir euch denn gnediglich wunschenn, vnnd mochtens euch gnediger meinunge nicht verhaltenn, deme Wir mitt gnadenn gneigtt.

Datum Cöln an der Sprew, denn 14. februarij anno 98
Katarina korforsten, m: h:
text.english:
**To the Right Honourable, Our particular dear Tycho Brahe of Knudstrup and Uraniborg.**

By the grace of God, Katharina, born and married Margravine, also Electress of Brandenburg, Duchess in Prussia. Our gracious greeting beforehand. Right Honourable, particular dear [friend], We herewith send you, at your request, Our servant and dear faithful Johann Müller, to the end that he may for a time converse with you and there train himself in the study of mathematics. We therefore desire of you herewith, most graciously, that you will show yourself compliant toward him not only in this, but also instruct him willingly in the spagyric preparations of medicaments, and in whatever else you have from experience in the pyronomic [arts]; and that you will conduct yourself in all this in such a manner as the promise made to Us through him, Our servant, on your behalf gives undertaking — toward you Our undoubted most gracious trust being directed. This We shall, in all the grace wherewith We are indeed well disposed toward you, in turn acknowledge with thanks and hold unforgotten. And although We should indeed gladly have had him dispatched back, together with your son, somewhat sooner, yet other weighty matters have hitherto befallen Our friendly, heartily dear lord and husband, such that one could not fittingly come to it sooner. You will therefore hold your son excused in the best [sense] — who indeed, like the said Johann Müller, will not let it be wanting in most diligent, most humble solicitation. We are of the undoubted confidence that, with the Royal Majesty, Our friendly, most heartily beloved lord cousin and son, the letters of intercession imparted to you will not go off without fruit, but that thereby your affairs will again attain the good standing you yourself wish for — as We do graciously wish you; and We would not, of gracious intent, withhold this from you, to whom We are inclined with grace.

Given at Cölln an der Spree, the 14th of February, year [15]98.
Katharina, Electress, with my own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Katharina of Brandenburg-Küstrin** (1549–1602), Electress of Brandenburg, wife of the Elector **Johann Georg of Brandenburg** (r. 1571–98 — the *"freundtlichen hertzlieben herrn gemahl"*, "friendly heartily dear lord and husband," named below). She titles herself "born and married Margravine, also Electress of Brandenburg, Duchess in Prussia" — the standard Hohenzollern intitulatio (the Elector of Brandenburg held the Duchy of Prussia in fief).
- **Recipient.** **Tycho Brahe**, addressed "of Knudstrup and Uraniborg" (*VFF KNUDTTSTRUP VNNDT WRANENNBURGK*) — his ancestral seat at Knudstrup in Scania and his observatory-castle on Hven. By the dateline (14 Feb. 1598) Tycho had in fact already left Hven (he departed for the Continent in 1597); the address preserves his styled titles, not his current residence.
- **Johann Müller.** Katharina's *diener* (servant/court attendant), sent to study with Tycho. Not securely identified beyond the letter; not to be conflated with the astronomer Johannes Müller (Regiomontanus, †1476). The literature shows Tycho, in a related letter (Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VIII), agreeing to receive "the boy" the Illustrious Lady had decided to send, "and a spagyric laborator [worker] too" — consistent with Müller's training brief here.
- **"eurem sohne" / "euren sohn"** — Tycho's son (the text does not name which; Tycho's sons Tycho the younger and Jørgen were of an age to act as suitors at court). He is at the Brandenburg court soliciting Tycho's affairs alongside Müller.
- **"der könn: wd:" = *der königlichen Würde*** ("the Royal Majesty / royal dignity"), named "Our friendly, most heartily beloved lord cousin and son." This points to **Christian IV of Denmark** (r. 1588–1648), to whom intercession on Tycho's behalf would be sought; the *vetter und sohn* register reflects the dynastic kinship between the Hohenzollern and Oldenburg houses. *Identification flagged:* the source gives only the abbreviated style, not a name; "Christian IV" is the most natural referent but is supplied editorially.
- ***intercession schrifftenn*** — "letters of intercession," i.e. recommendatory letters interceding on Tycho's behalf (regarding his loss of the Hven living and royal favour). Kept as "letters of intercession."
- **Technical / Latin code-switch.** The chancery German switches into Latin for the learned matter: *mathematico studio* = "the study of mathematics"; *spagiricis medicamentorum praeparationibus* = "spagyric preparations of medicaments" (Paracelsian chemical pharmacy — *spagyric* kept as a period term, not modernised to "chemical"); *in pyronomicis* = "in pyronomics," the art of the regulated fire/furnace (assaying and distillation by controlled heat) — rendered "in the pyronomic [arts]," the bracketed noun supplied. *conuersiren, exerciren, sollicitiren, intercession* are Latinate chancery verbs, rendered to match the learned register.
- **Negations (verified count, 5).** *nichtt allein … sonndern auch* = "not only … but also"; *nichtt ehe kommenn konnenn* = "could not come to it sooner"; *nicht manglen lassen* = "will not let it be wanting"; *ohne frucht nicht abgehen* = "will not go off without fruit"; *nicht verhaltenn* = "would not withhold." All five negations are reproduced; none added or dropped. The double construction *ohne frucht nicht abgehen* ("not go off without fruit") is a litotes affirming success, kept as the period idiom.
- **Orthography (chancery German, c. 1598).** *VANN/VANN Gottes gnadenn* = *von Gottes Gnaden* ("by the grace of God"); *Wnsern/Vnsern* = *unsern*; *grues zuuorn* = *Gruß zuvor* ("greeting beforehand," the address-formula, this chapter's convention); *thuen* = *tun*; *muegte* = *möchte*; *willfehrigk* = *willfährig* ("compliant"); *guettwillig* = *gutwillig*; *vnuorgessenn* = *unvergessen*; *abgeferttiget* = *abgefertigt* ("dispatched"); *fueglich* = *füglich* ("fittingly"); *vleissigsten vnndterthenigstenn* = *fleißigsten untertänigsten* ("most diligent, most humble"); *vettern* = *Vetter* ("cousin/kinsman"). The princely *Wir/euch* register and full titulature are preserved.
- **Subscription.** *Katarina korforsten, m: h:* — "Katharina, Electress" (*Kurfürstin*, the spelling phonetic/Low-German-influenced), with *m: h:* = *mit (eigener) Hand* / *manu propria*, "with my own hand." Rendered "with my own hand."
- **Place / calendar.** *Cöln an der Sprew* = **Cölln an der Spree**, the twin town of Berlin and seat of the Brandenburg court (the *Cöllnisches Schloss*); not Cologne on the Rhine. *14. februarij anno 98* = 14 February 1598; Brandenburg and Denmark were both on the Julian calendar (O.S.) in 1598. The dateline as written governs the header; the edition label ("1598. 14. februar. Cölln an der Spree") agrees.

Dreyer TBOO XIV pp.134-136 read as page images; Katharina's letter (Dreyer's item 144) entirely on p.135. the transcribed original matches Dreyer's printed German verbatim throughout. Collated translation clause-by-clause: the sending of Johann Müller for instruction in mathematics, spagyric and pyronomic arts, the apology for the delay, the intercession for Tycho with the King, and the closing all render faithfully. Names and date (14 February [15]98) correct. No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found.

documents.abstract: Rebukes Vedel for adopting a judge's tone and for failing to keep a promised journey, addressing also some matters concerning Lange and English letters.
documents.incipit: NUPER cum OLIGERUS ROSENKRANTZ consanguineus Affinis et Amicus meus dilectus hîc me per …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD ANDREAM SEVERINI VELLEIUM.

NUPER cum OLIGERUS ROSENKRANTZ consanguineus Affinis et Amicus meus dilectus hîc me per duas invisisset hebdomadas, redditæ mihi sunt unâ cum CHRISTIERNI LANGIJ tuæ literæ, ad quas tunc respondendi commoditas non dabatur. Videntur hæ ultimæ tuæ, licet lenire et excusare quædam in prioribus laborent, a primis tamen illis motu proprio ad me datis [non] longe abesse, et privilegijs scatere iudicis, quæ tamen tibi lubens condono, siquidem non aliter vis. Obijcis ab initio post ea, quæ de LANGIO et Anglicis literis habes (ad quæ postea respondebo) quod iter tuum iuxta promissum non præstitum arguam. Et quid ni? cum sponte promiseris, nec præstiteris? Valetudinem tuam, rem domesticam et anni tempus tunc æque noras atque postea. Miraris igitur me ita singula tua verba et iota notare. Atqui scis me semper Geometrice loqui, cum serio loquor. Quod et in alijs, præsertim Amicis, quibus bene fido, et requiro et observo. Quorsum enim verba, nisi rebus consona? Hoc ego idem sentio atque illudere et negligere. Neque perinde esse, ac candide, aperte et libere agere, uti tu vis. Immo quiddam his repugnans.

Quod aliquo loco non sis inter reliquos Pharisæos et Gnathones, equidem tibi congratulor, nec hanc felicitatem invideo. At quod non talia antea affectâris, quodque adhuc ijs, si liceret, te participem non redderes, haud dixerim. Si autem me hîc fallis, est cur tibi hanc animi celsitudinem et constantiam magis adhuc congratulor. Et si nunc ex Politicis non pendes, veluti antea, cordatius forsan agis. Eorum fructus sunt præ foribus. Cudentur Machiavellistarum doli et technæ in ipsorum, uti meriti sunt, capita. Quod et hactenus iustus iudex exequi solitus est. Quod prandio alicuius interfueris, nihil ad me. Neque ob id ea de re mentionem feci, quia hoc morarer, sed quoniam tu occasionem dabas de ERICO LANGIO et me quædam addendo, quæ tamen neuter nostrum curat. Si talibus, qui astutam vapido servant sub pectore vulpem, fidis, te ipsum decipis. Qui et quales eiusmodi sint, fere omnes in Dania norunt, atque in posterum plus forte noscent. O patria, o mores. Omnia nunc ruere in peius fata ipsa docebant. Si tibi deinceps vixeris, uti scribis, rectissime feceris. Nam uti nunc agitur scena Mundana, si unquam antea, locum meretur illud NASONIS »nimium prælustria vita«, et »bene qui latuit, bene vixit«. Quod mihi iam tandem congratularis mutationem hanc et sortem aliam, rectius facis, quam cum prius eandem indoleres, tanquam invidens mihi hanc felicitatem. Sic enim ego infirmas accipio querelas. Et, si sufficienter delictum illud expiare volueris, tacita quædam psalmodia Uraniæ nostræ omnibusque nobis Propempticum concinna, quodque ea e Cimmerijs, non dico Cimbricis, tenebris, quibus diu multumque offuscabatur, sese tandem Superum dono et provisu vindicârit, atque in apertam et gratam Universæ Europæ lucem universalior reddita asseruerit, congratulare; nobis autem, quod tot Machiavellismis, iniurijs, odijs, invidijs, malevolentijs, calumnijs et detrectationibus atque contemptibus superatis tranquilliori auræ restituti simus. Hisce igitur si Carmine aliquo, uti Poëta es, applauseris, apposite feceris et in gratiam cum Urania nobisque omnibus redieris.

Rogas deinceps, ut desinam minuta quæque in literis tuis non recte intellecta exaggerare. Te scripsisse, quod tu cum familia mei essetis amici in Dania despecti, me statim accepisse, vos a me despectos. Atqui tua non tam clare sonabant verba, pro ut nunc ea explicas. Aiebas enim: Vale,salutatus a tuis amicis in Dania despectis. Non addidisti, te aut tuis. Ideoque tuam sententiam prima fronte non satis assecutus sum. Ingerebat hoc dubium, quod scirem, mihi in Dania a calumniatoribus imputari, quod in despectum patriæ, Regis, consangvineorum et amicorum inde discesserim. Et sane OLIGERUS ROSENKRANTZIUS, cui hæc tua verba legenda dedi, non aliter capere potuit, quam ac si tale quid insinuares. Obscurius enim quam decuit, scripta sunt. Nec ego plane asserui, te quidpiam in me loqui. Ideoque addidi: »si recte tuam mentem percipio« aut simile quid. Et quod tu infers, me excepisse, quasi vos me despiceretis, scilicet tu et tui, id non saltem est minutula quæque exaggerare, sed et sensum meum quasi data opera plane pervertere: cum de te et tuis, quos semper dilexi atque etiamnum diligo, nihil sinistri suspicer, sed in genere de meis in Dania malevolis locutus sim, a quibus despicior, eosque vicissim ex alto rideo et despicio, si quando præ altioribus curis eorum (quod tamen rarissime facio) meminisse lubet. Tuos casus, tuaque infortunia magna ex parte scio, et horum authores non ignoro. Habemus enim hîc mutuo participationem quandam, licet mihi nihil mali inde evenerit, sed longe plus boni etiam invitis authoribus. At nihil tibi hîc exprobro, condolui semper, et amovere ista studui et cum quorundam ex meis offensione, et plus pro te laboravi, quam conscius es, aut facile crediturus. Norunt id utriusque nostrum, non saltem Amici, sed et inimici, tum quoque neutrales.

Quod neque tu neque ego moriemur inulti, omnino mihi persuadeo. Nam iustus est Deus, etiam tacentibus et patienter sustinentibus, et quæ immerito pertulerunt hominibus, illi vindicta danda est, oc hand vil rette det nod, om † Thule nogen sdoon end aldrig leffde eller haffde leffuet: Non tamen Planetarum revolutiones præficiendæ sunt ei, qui libere et sine tempore, in tempore tamen satque tempestive agit.

Demum de victualibus mentionem facis, quod primum et præcipuum esse [de]buit. De his enim nunc maxime agitur in tanta hîc annonæ caritate, quanta vix unquam fuit, et familiæ meæ propria, quæ quartum attingit septenarium, præter eos, qui indies invisunt. At tu videris hîc aurem claudere, paa dansche at være schulørit, oc icke gide høret oc mercket ret. Nam quid pro quo infers. Satis scio, etiam absque tuo iuramento (saa sandt hielpe mig Gud) (an hoc Theologicum est?) quod si præsens ipse fuissem, non potuissem ista expedire aliter sine rerum dispendio: scilicet postquam hyems intervenisset, portus conclusi essent, nec terrestre iter commodum foret. At antea, dum primas istas tuas scribebas, nulla eiusmodi erant obstacula, aut si qua erant, quare adeo categorice promisisti? quare tot tantaque præstanda enumerasti? Sororem etiam meam in auxilium vocans, a qua ne verbum intellexi, licet ter eidem scripserim. Crediderim vos omnes excellenter iudicare. At si quid vobis Scanicæ, id est veræ et fidei tenacis, restat mentis, en nulla nunc adsunt subterfugia, quin recte facere liceat, modo libeat. Ego nullum in me officium ingratum esse sinam. Et si adhuc accesseris unâ cum LANGIO aut etiam solus sine ipso, idque ante Paschatis festum (modo fieri queat) inprimis erit id mihi acceptum et eo plenius priora diluentur errata.

Vale cum uxore a me salutata, totaque domo.
Dabantur Wandesburgi die 18. Februarij Anni 1598.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Anders Sørensen Vedel.**

Lately, when Oluf Rosenkrantz — my kinsman, relation-by-marriage, and beloved friend — had visited me here for two weeks, your letters were delivered to me together with that of Christen Lange, [letters] to which there was then no convenient occasion of replying. These latest letters of yours, though they labour to soften and excuse certain things in the earlier ones, nonetheless seem [not] to be far removed from those first ones sent to me of your own accord, and to teem with a judge's prerogatives — which, however, I gladly pardon you, since you will have it no otherwise. At the outset, after the matters you raise concerning Lange and the English letters (to which I shall reply later), you object that I charge you with not having made your journey according to your promise. And why not [charge you with it]? — since you promised of your own accord, and did not perform it. Your health, your household affairs, and the season of the year you knew then just as well as afterwards. You wonder, then, that I so mark each of your words and every jot. But you know that I always speak geometrically, when I speak in earnest; which in others too, and especially in friends whom I trust well, I both require and observe. For to what end are words, unless they answer to facts? This I hold to be one and the same thing as to mock and to be negligent — and not at all the same as to deal candidly, openly, and freely, as you would have it; rather, [it is] something contrary to these.

That you are in some place not among the rest of the Pharisees and Gnathos, I do indeed congratulate you, nor do I envy you this good fortune. But that you did not before aspire to such things, and that even now you would not, if it were allowed, make yourself a partaker in them — that I would not say. If, however, you are here deceiving me, there is the more reason why I should congratulate you on this loftiness and constancy of mind. And if you now do not hang upon Politics, as before, you act perhaps more shrewdly. Their fruits are at the door. The wiles and devices of the Machiavellians will be hammered down upon their own heads, as they have deserved — which a just judge has hitherto been wont to carry out. That you were present at someone's dinner is nothing to me. Nor did I make mention of that matter on that account, as though I were troubled by it, but because you gave occasion [for it] by adding certain things about Erik Lange and me — things which, however, neither of us cares about. If you trust such men, who keep a cunning fox hidden beneath a stale breast, you deceive your own self. Who and what sort such men are, almost all in Denmark know, and hereafter will perhaps know more. O fatherland, O manners! That all things now rush headlong to the worse, the very fates were teaching. If henceforth you live for yourself, as you write, you will have done most rightly. For as the worldly stage is now played, if ever before, that saying of Naso [Ovid] deserves its place — »[shun] a life too brightly conspicuous«, and »he who has lain well hidden, has lived well«. That you now at last congratulate me on this change and altered lot, you do more rightly than when you earlier grieved over the same, as though begrudging me this good fortune. For thus do I take feeble complaints. And, if you should wish sufficiently to expiate that fault, compose some silent psalmody, a Send-off-song [Propempticon], for our Urania and for us all; and congratulate [her] that she has at last, by the gift and provision of those above, claimed herself out of those Cimmerian — I do not say Cimbric — shadows, by which she was long and greatly darkened, and, made more universal, has set herself free into the open and welcome light of all Europe; and [congratulate] us, that, so many Machiavellisms, injuries, hatreds, envies, ill-wills, calumnies, and disparagements and contempts being overcome, we have been restored to a calmer air. If, therefore, you applaud these things with some Poem, since you are a Poet, you will have done it fittingly, and will have returned into favour with Urania and with us all.

You ask, next, that I cease to magnify each small thing in your letters not rightly understood. [You say] that you wrote that you, with your family, my friends, were despised in Denmark, [and] that I straightway took it that you were despised by me. But your words did not sound so clearly as you now explain them. For you said: »Farewell, greeted by your friends despised in Denmark.« You did not add »by you« or »by yours«. And so at first sight I did not sufficiently grasp your meaning. This doubt was thrust [upon me] because I knew it to be imputed to me by slanderers in Denmark that I had departed thence in contempt of my fatherland, my King, my kinsmen and my friends. And indeed Oluf Rosenkrantz, to whom I gave these words of yours to read, could take them no otherwise than as if you were insinuating something of the sort. For they were written more obscurely than was fitting. Nor did I plainly assert that you were saying anything against me; and so I added: »if I rightly perceive your meaning« or something similar. And as for what you infer — that I took it as though you despised me, namely you and yours — that is not merely to magnify each little thing, but even, as if of set purpose, plainly to pervert my sense: since concerning you and yours, whom I have always loved and even now love, I suspect nothing sinister, but spoke in general of those ill-willed toward me in Denmark, by whom I am despised, and whom I in turn laugh at and despise from on high, whenever (which, however, I very rarely do) it pleases me, in the midst of higher cares, to remember them. Your misfortunes and your reverses I know for the most part, and I am not ignorant of their authors. For we here have a certain shared portion of them in common, though no harm has come to me from that quarter, but far more good, even against the will of their authors. But I reproach you with nothing here; I have always condoled with you, and have striven to remove those troubles even at the cost of giving offence to certain of my own people, and I have laboured more for you than you are aware of, or would readily believe. This both [our] Friends and [our] enemies — and the neutrals too — know, of us both.

That neither you nor I shall die unavenged, I am wholly persuaded. For God is just, even toward those who keep silent and patiently endure; and to men [for those things] which they have undeservedly suffered, vengeance must be rendered by Him — and he will set that wrong to rights, even if † Thule nobody at all… now never lived or had lived: yet the revolutions of the Planets are not to be set in command over Him who acts freely and outside time, yet in time, and timely enough.

At last you make mention of provisions, which ought to have been the first and chief thing. For of these is now most of all the question, in such dearth of grain here as has scarcely ever been; and [provisions] proper to my household, which reaches the fourth seven [i.e. some twenty-eight persons], besides those who visit daily. But you seem here to close your ear — in Danish, to be hard of hearing, and not to care to hear and mark rightly. For you draw a *quid pro quo*. I know well enough, even without your oath (»so truly help me God« — is this Theological?), that if I myself had been present, I could not have despatched those matters otherwise without loss of goods: namely, after winter had set in, the harbours were closed, nor was a journey by land convenient. But before — while you were writing those first letters of yours — there were no obstacles of the kind; or if there were any, why did you promise so categorically? why did you enumerate so many and so great things to be performed? Calling even my sister to your aid — from whom I have not understood a word, though I have written to her three times. I would believe that you all judge excellently. But if there remains to you any Scanian, that is, true and faithful-keeping, mind, behold, no evasions now present themselves but that it may be possible to do rightly, only let it please [you]. I will let no service done me be ungrateful. And if you should still come, together with Lange, or even alone without him — and that before the feast of Easter (provided it can be done) — that will be especially acceptable to me, and the earlier errors will thereby be the more fully washed away.

Farewell, with your wife greeted by me, and your whole household.
Given at Wandsbek, the 18th day of February, in the year 1598.
Your TYCHO BRAHE,
with his own hand.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Andreas Severini Vellejus* = **Anders Sørensen Vedel** (1542–1616), Danish historian, royal historiographer, ballad-collector and clergyman of Ribe; a long-standing friend (and, by this date, a strained one) of Tycho's. The edition's person register fixes this identification.
- **Sender / place / date.** Tycho writes from **Wandsbek** (Lat. *Wandesburgum*), the estate near Hamburg where, in self-imposed exile after leaving Hven and Denmark (1597), he stayed with Heinrich Rantzau and saw the *Astronomiae Instauratae Mechanica* and the *Epistolarum* volume through the press. Dateline *die 18. Februarij Anni 1598* (O.S.; Denmark and the German Protestant correspondents kept Old Style). The catalogue label agrees (*1598. 18. februar. Wandsburg*).
- **Persons named.** *Oligerus Rosenkrantz* = **Oluf (Holger) Rosenkrantz**, Tycho's kinsman and relation by marriage (*consanguineus Affinis*). *Christiernus Langius* = **Christen Lange**. *Ericus Langius* = **Erik Lange** (1553–1613), the alchemist nobleman, betrothed to Tycho's sister Sophie Brahe — hence the "sister" (*soror mea*) called to Vedel's aid near the letter's end.
- **Latin language note.** The letter is **Neo-Latin throughout**, with four short **Danish** interpolations (see below); the heuristic tag la is correct here. Spelling is Dreyer's edition: consonantal *j* in *-ijs* (*privilegijs, odijs, Cimmerijs*), *Geometrice, Machiavellistae*.
- **CRUX — the editorial [non].** *a primis tamen illis … [non] longe abesse* — the [non] is **Dreyer's bracketed editorial insertion**, not in the witness as transmitted; it is kept bracketed in the Source block and rendered bracketed ("**[not]** … far removed") in the translation by the audit's rule (no editorial word inserted unbracketed). With the *[non]*, Tycho says Vedel's softer "last letters" are *not* far from the offensive "first" ones — i.e. still objectionable, consistent with the reproachful continuation ("teem with a judge's prerogatives"). **Without** the *[non]* the clause would reverse to "do seem far removed [= an improvement]," which the following sentences contradict. The negation is therefore load-bearing; the sense follows the bracketed reading but the bracket is preserved and the dependence flagged. Likewise *[de]buit* later in the source is Dreyer's bracketed expansion of *debuit*.
- **Geometrice loqui** — "to speak geometrically," i.e. with exact, demonstrative precision (each word answering to fact "like a geometric proof"); a characteristic Tychonic self-description, not a technical-astronomy term — left as the plain idiom.
- **Pharisaeos et Gnathones** — "Pharisees and Gnathos": hypocrites (Scriptural) and parasitic flatterers (Gnatho, the toady of Terence's *Eunuchus*); kept as types.
- **astutam vapido servant sub pectore vulpem** — "keep a cunning fox hidden beneath a stale/sour breast": a near-quotation of Persius, *Satires* 5.117 (*astutam vapido servas sub pectore vulpem*); kept as the borrowed image.
- **Ovid (NASONIS).** Both tags are from **Ovid, *Tristia* III.4** (Ovid = P. Ovidius **Naso**): *»nimium praelustria vita«* compresses *Tristia* III.4.4–6 (*vive sine invidia … nimium … praelustria vita[s]* — "shun a life too brightly conspicuous"); *»bene qui latuit, bene vixit«* = *Tristia* III.4.25 verbatim ("he who has lain well hidden has lived well"). Tycho quotes them as a paired sententia; kept as quotation, the elliptical *vita* of the first tag flagged (the verb is suppressed — "shun" is supplied in brackets-sense and noted here rather than smoothed).
- **Propempticum / Urania.** *Propempticum* (Greek *προπεμπτικόν*) = a **send-off / bon-voyage poem**; Tycho asks the poet Vedel to write Urania (the Muse of astronomy = Tycho's restored astronomy, *astronomia instaurata*) a farewell ode on her departure from Denmark. *psalmodia* = "psalmody," a (silent) song of praise.
- **Cimmerijs, non dico Cimbricis, tenebris** — a **bilingual/learned pun**: the *Cimmerian* darkness of Homer/Ovid (proverbial deep gloom) set against *Cimbric* (= **Danish/Jutish**, from the Cimbri of Jutland). Tycho says astronomy escaped "Cimmerian — I do not say Cimbric [= Danish] — shadows": a barbed gibe at Denmark, made deniable by the near-homophone. Kept and glossed, the wordplay flagged rather than flattened.
- **DANISH interpolation 1 (dagger-marked CRUX).** *oc hand vil rette det nod, om † Thule nogen sdoon end aldrig leffde eller haffde leffuet*. The opening is clear early-modern Danish: *oc hand vil rette det nød* = "and He will set that distress/wrong to rights." The remainder is **corrupt or obscure in the witness**: *Thule* (the classical name for the far North = Denmark/Scandinavia) + *nogen* ("anyone/nobody") + *sdoon* (an unintelligible form — possibly a copyist's garble) + *end* + *aldrig leffde eller haffde leffuet* ("…never lived or had lived"). The **†** marks the editor's locus of corruption. A coherent surface sense cannot be recovered without conjecture; rendered word-for-word and explicitly flagged ("† Thule nobody at all… now never lived or had lived"), **not** smoothed into fluent English. This is the letter's principal crux.
- **DANISH interpolation 2.** *paa dansche at vaere schulørit, oc icke gide høret oc mercket ret* = "in Danish, [namely] to be hard of hearing [*skørørt/skuløret* 'thick of ear'], and not to care to hear and mark rightly." Tycho code-switches into Danish to characterise Vedel's wilful deafness; the *quid pro quo* immediately following keeps the legal/rhetorical idiom.
- **DANISH interpolation 3 (oath).** *saa sandt hielpe mig Gud* = "so truly [may] God help me" — a standard Danish oath-formula; Tycho parenthetically and sarcastically queries whether such swearing is *Theologicum* (becoming of a clergyman like Vedel). Kept in Danish in the Source, glossed in translation.
- **quartum attingit septenarium** — "reaches the fourth seven," i.e. his household numbers in the **fourth group of seven** (toward 28 persons); rendered literally with the sense bracketed, not silently converted to a round figure.
- **Scanicae … mentis** — "a Scanian mind," i.e. of **Scania** (Skåne), the southern-Swedish province then Danish and the Brahe family's home country; Tycho glosses it himself as "true and faithful-keeping," punning on regional character. Kept and glossed.
- **annonae caritate** — "dearth of grain/provisions"; *annona* = the grain-supply/market price (cf. the same idiom in the 1571 Wolf letter). The 1597–98 northern dearth is the real-world referent.
- **Negation audit.** The source's negations were counted and reproduced one-for-one, with particular care at the bracketed *[non] longe abesse* (see CRUX), at *Non addidisti, te aut tuis* ("You did **not** add 'by you' or 'by yours'"), at *nihil sinistri suspicer* / *nihil tibi exprobro*, and at the closing *Non tamen Planetarum revolutiones praeficiendae sunt* ("the revolutions of the Planets are **not** to be set in command"). No negation was added or dropped.
- **Planetarum revolutiones … qui libere et sine tempore, in tempore tamen … agit** — *revolutio* here in its astrological/astronomical sense (planetary cycles,/5.3) but turned theological: the planetary cycles must not be made to govern God, "who acts freely and outside time, yet in time, and timely enough." Kept literal.
- **Calendar.** Single date, internally consistent: *18. Februarij Anni 1598* (O.S.). No in-letter date discrepancy; label and dateline agree.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VIII pp.25-28 read as page images (Read pages=1-4; images small enough not to need further splitting). The letter itself runs only pp.25(bottom)-27(top) - extract p.4 (TBOO p.28) is the start of a different letter (Monavius to Tycho) and was excluded from collation. Collated the full letter text - opening (NUPER cum OLIGERUS ROSENKRANTZ...), the Ovid tag (NASONIS 'nimium praelustria vita'/'bene qui latuit, bene vixit'), every proper name (Oligerus Rosenkrantz, Christiernus Langius, Ericus Langius), the embedded Danish clauses (paa dansche at vaere schulørit; saa sandt hielpe mig Gud; oc hand vil rette det nod...), and the closing date (Wandesburgi die 18. Februarij Anni 1598) - against the Dreyer images word for word. No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found; no divergence between the transcribed original and Dreyer's print (one trivial dagger/asterisk footnote-marker variant before 'Thule' is orthographic apparatus, not text, and is not counted as a defect).

text.original:
IACOBUS MONAVIUS AD TYCHONEM
BRAHE.S.BONA quidem fide, sed paulo tardius mihi redditus est et in manus
meas pervenit fasciculus ille, quem circa finem anni superioris ad me misisti,
Nobilissime et præstantissime Domine TYCHO, magnamque debeo gratiam Viro optimo
et amico integerrimo Domino VINCENTIO
MOLLERO, quod in eo curando voluit tibique mihique gratificari.
Vix autem possum exprimere verbis, quam grata mihi fuerit Epistola tua, tam
amice scripta, et quam accepta ea, quæ unâ cum literis tuis ad me pervenire
voluisti. Cæterum quod tam serum responsum mitto, non tantum fit eam ob causam,
de qua dixi, sed etiam propter invaletudinem meam, quam totis fere tribus
mensibus sensi prorsusA incommodum, et quæ me velut ineptum fecitA ad omnes res agendas. Nondum quidem ab ea sum prorsusA liberatus. Sed tamen per Dei gratiam, habere cœpi melius, et sentio vires
tum animi tum corporis non parum firmiores, quam fuerunt. Deus Opt. Max. si
volet, poterit hoc robur augere, idque tantum cupio fieri ad gloriam sancti
nominis ipsius, et ad animæ meæ, quæ mihi est cura in his terris præcipua,
salutem. Quod attinet ad famam obitus mei isthuc ad te perlatam, unde tibi data
occasio faciendi mentionem nominis mei in Epistolis tuis, facile potuit hic
error committi in aula Cæsaris, ubi fratrem habui unicum Medicum Imperatorium,
Virum, quem ab alijs, quam a me prædicari malo, qui [ante] annos decem obijt Pragæ. Quia autem
hic error tibi expressitA tam honorificas et amicas voces de me, ut inde, quanti memoriam nominis
mei post obitum meum facturus fueris, æstimare liceat:
agnosco me plurimum debere tuis erga me amori et animo, quem utA mihi conserves, donec vixero, obnixe rogo; ego vicissim, donec in hoc
corpore sangvis erit, te vicissim amare observare et colere...prædicare et
laudare non desinam. Frater ille meus charissimus, cuius modo feci mentionem,
erat rerum Mathematicarum et amantissimus et intelligentissimus, ac propterea
tui quoque unice observans et studiosus: ac illum sæpe hoc egisse [scio] ut amicitiam tuam consequeretur, a qua cura etiam non abstinuisset, si
Deus ei longiora vitæ spatia concessisset. Nunc in alia Schola philosophatur,
coram Deum cernens, et cœlos opera manuum eius contemplans......amori erga
fratrem, si memoriam illius hoc loco tibi volui commendare. Cæterum quod ad
discessum tuum e patria, et præsertim ex Uranoburgo attinet: primum de eo certior factus sum, ex literis
communis amici Domini DAVIDIS.....postea enim plenius
edoctus de omnibus illis circumstantijs a CHRISTIANO SEVERINO
LONGOMONTANO, qui circa finem anni superioris ad nos
venit.......et quem per aliquot dies apud nos retinuimus, et hospitem
gratissimum habuimus; atque utinam tunc venissent ad me literæ tuæ, cum adhuc
apud nos hæreret. Erat enim de te valde sollicitus et hac inprimis de causa.Ego quidem de ijs quid dicam? Cum essem aliquando Magdeburgi, vidi super domo quadam aureis
literis inscriptum saxo, quod erat supra fores, hunc ineptum
sensu, sed reipsa nimis verum versum: Est erit atque fuit
Vndanck in fine laborum. Hic versiculus mihi subinde venit in
mentem, quando de te rebusque tuis cogitavi. Sed et hoc mihi incidit, quod si
mundus hic non sit dignus istis Atlanticis bonis et donis nostri TYCHONIS? Etiam
hoc cogitavi, quod si hæc Τύχη, quæ Domino TYCHONI contigit, nunciet instare
finem mundi? Utut sit, adhuc valde dubito, tuamne vicem [an patriæ potius tuæ], imo totius Reipublicæ Christianæ magis dolere debeam. Legi diligenter,
quæ ad me misisti, et pro ijs communicatis magnas tibi gratias ago, neque est,
ut putes, ea ventura in manus aliorum. Miratus sum Regem nihil voluisse conferre
in hæc studia, Regibus et eorum subsidijs atque [adiumento] dignissima, qui tamen nuper tantos sumptus fecitA in coronationis festo. Aliud fuit iudicium ALFONSI: imo aliud etiam ipsius patris
FRIDERICI. Nolo de his plura; in
quibus tamen hoc etiam addo, me idem facere, quod tu facis, hoc est discernere
Actorem a Poëta fabulaeA. Facis tu etiam hoc præclare, quod tanto animo (nimirum cœlo et astris
digno) hæc quæ tibi contigerunt, fers, nec propterea cogitas aliquid omittere in
laudabili cursu abs te.....et olim instituto, et per tot annos servato, sed quod
cogitas ad metam usque illum.....Da hic Deus ut perficias quod cœpisti. LAZARUS
....... vir magnanimus frequenter in ore solitus fuit habere versum istum: Esse aliquid si velle tenes, et posse tenebis. Tibi vero
datum est et velle et posse. Amplissimi viri D. HENRICI RANZOVIJ maior nunc erit
gloria, et fiet ipsius nomen illustre clarius, postquam Musis tuis hospitium conditA. Erit enim vicina urbs Hamburga,
tibi satis oportuna ad absolvenda ea, quorum editio fuit cœpta in Huenna. De consilijs tuis, quæ apud ........ meum
deponis, diligenter cogitavi, et spero ea sic geri posse, ut [non] plane careat successu, verum opus erit tempore: cum nunc omnia, quæ
aguntur in aula Cæsarea, tantum ....... Martem in hoc gravissimo Reipublicæ
christianæ periculo, quod hoc anno non sine causa (Deus omnia avertat) metuitur.
Agam interea, quantum nunc agi potest per amicos, ut quasi via quædam sternatur,
ad ea, quæ sunt deinceps ..... cura et opera tractanda; faciam te quoque
certiorem de rebus omnibus, quæ argumentum facere ad ea, quæ sane tui animi,
consilij et instituti.... Si viveret adhuc Dominus IACOBUS CURTIUS, quantopere ostenderet
sibi esse cordi et curæ res tuas et negotium publicum! Sed tamen spero, non
defuturos aliter etiam in aula amicos, de quibus alio tempore, si Deus volet,
rebus magis exploratis te monebo. Pro transmisso libro Epistolarum, qui mihi a
te est amplissimum munus, magnas ago gratias, et peto magnopere, cum reliqua
tua, quæ iam cœpta sunt, ad finem perducta fuerint, ut ijs etiam ....... meam
ornare non recuses. Dabitur opera, ne te huius ...... et beneficij iure et
merito pœniteat.Literas tuas ad IOHANNEM
ROTHMANNUM, quem cognovi nunc vitam agere in
Republica Erfurdensi, per certos homines curaboA, si quidA aliud a me postulas fieri, semper tibi parata erit pro viribus fida mea
opera. Ex CHRISTIANO tuo hoc etiam libenter cognovi: Te nimirum natum esse
eodem et anno et mense, quo ego sum in lucem editus, valde etiam delectatus sum,
inter...quæ nunc mecum communicasti, lectione carminum tuorum ad ........ quæ
non legi sine varijs animi perturbationibus. Multa enim de multis, tum tuis tum
ijs quæ sunt similia, cogitaviA. GeramA tibi morem in eo quod petis, et curabo, ne aliquis te non indignus
........ de rebus tuis, quæ te digna sint. Tu vicissim, si non est molestum,
exorna meum Symbolum aliquo Epigrammate. Quale sit Symbolum meum, cognosces ex
nostro VINCENTIO MOLLERO, qui, si
voles, dabit tibi legendum Libellum quendam nostrum, quem de eodem Symbolo
curavi ..... publice edi. Equidem miseram ad te exemplum, quod doleo perijsse.
Si postuletis aliud, non invitus communicabo. Interim habe tibi hanc
inscriptionem ..... mei.Salutat te reverenter amanter et officiose optimus senex Doctor
HERMANNUS noster, cui vix credas
quam grata fuerit salus et abs te dicta, et nomine præstantissimi senisA...Si non est molestum, rogo ut meis etiam verbis reverenter et
officiose salutes Illustrem Dominum HENRICUM
RANZOVIUM, qui suam erga me benevolentiam semel et iterum mihi
declaravit. Tu eam, si placet, augebis et confirmabis. Et
quoniam HEMMINGIJ
vestriA facta est mentio, tuque de eo nunc liberius scribere potes, rogo te per
amicitiam nostram, dic mihi in aures meas, an fidem mereatur hæc inclusa
pagella, quæ ante aliquot annos fuit circumlata.Deus scit me istud quærere nec malo animo, nec ad malam fidem
...... enim amo et colo istum optimum et optime meritum senem, quem aliquis cum
potest amare et colere, sed tantum cœpi mihi constare historiam rei gestæ, de
qua mihi et alijs semper iure integrum iudicium. Bene et feliciter vale, vir
præstantissime et Nobilissime, mihique conserva tuam ...... benevolentiam, cuius
fundamenta prima, eaque tunc valde tenuia ...... sunt ante multos annos .....
cum ex tuis peregrinationibus reversus per aliquot septimanas viveres in domo et
mensa hospitis tunc mei M. LAURENTIJ DANI. Ego te amare et
observare, et meam tibi fidem quocunque potero genere ........... nunquam

text.english:
**Jakob Monau to Tycho Brahe. Greeting.**

In good faith indeed, but a little too late, was that packet delivered to me and came into my hands which you sent me toward the end of last year, most noble and most excellent Master Tycho; and I owe great thanks to that best of men and most upright friend Master Vincent Moller, in that, in seeing to its delivery, he was willing to do a kindness both to you and to me. I can scarcely express in words how welcome your letter was to me, written in so friendly a way, and how acceptable were those things which you wished to reach me together with your letter. As for my sending so late a reply, it comes about not only for the reason I have mentioned, but also because of my ill-health, which for nearly three whole months I felt to be wholly[A] troublesome, and which made[A] me, as it were, unfit for transacting any business. I am indeed not yet wholly[A] freed of it. Yet nevertheless, by the grace of God, I have begun to be better, and I feel the powers both of mind and of body not a little stronger than they were. God, Best and Greatest, if he will, can increase this strength; and I desire it to come about only for the glory of his holy name, and for the salvation of my soul, which is my chief care in these lands. As for the report of my death carried to you there — whence you were given occasion to make mention of my name in your letters — this error could easily be committed at the Emperor's court, where I had an only brother, an Imperial Physician, a man whom I would rather have praised by others than by me, who[A] died at Prague ten years ago. But because this error drew[A] from you such honourable and friendly words about me, that from them one may estimate how greatly you would have honoured the memory of my name after my death: I acknowledge that I owe very much to your love and goodwill toward me, which I earnestly beg that[A] you keep for me as long as I shall live; and I in turn, so long as there is blood in this body, shall not cease to love, esteem, and honour you in turn … to proclaim and to praise you. That dearest brother of mine, of whom I have just made mention, was both a most devoted and a most understanding student of mathematical matters, and on that account uniquely respectful of you too and devoted to you; and [I know][A] that he often did this, that he might gain your friendship — from which care he would not have refrained, had God granted him a longer span of life. Now he philosophizes in another School, beholding God face to face, and contemplating the heavens, the work of his hands …… [out of] love toward my brother, [it is] if I have wished in this place to commend his memory to you. For the rest, as touching your departure from your homeland, and especially from Uraniborg: I was first made more certain of it by a letter from our common friend Master David …… for afterward I was more fully informed of all those circumstances by Christian Sørensen Longomontanus, who came to us toward the end of last year ……, and whom we kept with us for some days and held a most welcome guest; and would that your letter had come to me then, while he was still tarrying with us. For he was very anxious about you, and chiefly on this account. As for me, what indeed should I say of these things? When I was once at Magdeburg, I saw inscribed in golden letters on a stone, on a certain house, which was above the door, this verse — silly in its sense, but in fact only too true: It is, it will be, and it has been — Ingratitude at the end of labours [Vndanck in fine laborum]. This little verse comes to my mind again and again, whenever I have thought about you and your affairs. And this too occurred to me: what if this world is not worthy of those Atlantean goods and gifts of our Tycho? This too I thought: what if this Chance [Τύχη], which has befallen Master Tycho, announces that the end of the world is at hand? However it be, I am still very much in doubt whether I ought to grieve more for your lot [or rather for your homeland's][A] — nay, for that of the whole Christian Commonwealth. I have diligently read what you sent me, and I give you great thanks for sharing them; nor is it as you might think — that they will come into the hands of others. I marvelled that the King was willing to confer nothing upon these studies, most worthy of kings and of their subsidies and [help][A], who yet lately made[A] such great expenditures at the festival of his coronation. Other was the judgment of Alfonso; nay, other too was that of his own father Frederick. I will say no more of these matters; on which, however, I add this also, that I do the same as you do — that is, to distinguish the Actor from the Poet of the play[A]. You too do this admirably, in that with so great a spirit (worthy indeed of heaven and the stars) you bear these things that have befallen you, nor on that account do you think to leave off anything in that laudable course [begun] by you …… and once instituted and kept for so many years; but you think [to pursue] it right to the goal …… God grant here that you complete what you have begun. Lazarus ……, a great-spirited man, was wont frequently to have on his lips that verse: If you hold to willing, you hold something; and you will hold to being able [Esse aliquid si velle tenes, et posse tenebis]. But to you it is given both to will and to be able. The glory of that most distinguished man Master Heinrich Rantzau will now be the greater, and his illustrious name will become more renowned, now that he founds[A] a lodging for your Muses. For the neighbouring city of Hamburg will be opportune enough for you, for completing those things whose publication was begun on Hven. About your designs, which you deposit with my …… [friend], I have thought diligently, and I hope they can be so managed that they will [not][A] altogether lack success — but there will be need of time: since now all things that are transacted at the Imperial court [look] only to[wards] …… Mars, in this most grave peril of the Christian Commonwealth, which this year, not without cause (God avert all this!), is feared. Meanwhile I shall do what can now be done through friends, so that a way may, as it were, be paved for those things which are next …… to be handled by care and effort; I shall also make you more certain about all matters which make an argument toward those things which are truly [matters] of your own spirit, counsel, and purpose ……[A]. If Master Jacobus Curtius were still living, how greatly he would show that your affairs and the public business were dear and a care to him! But still I hope that friends at court will not be lacking in other ways too, about whom, at another time, if God will, I shall advise you once the matters have been more fully explored. For the book of Letters sent to me, which is from you a most ample gift, I give great thanks, and I greatly ask that, when your remaining works, which are now begun, have been brought to an end, you not refuse to adorn with them my …… [name] also. Pains will be taken that you may not, by right and deservedly, repent of this …… and kindness. Your letters to Johann Rothmann, whom I have learned now leads his life in the Republic of Erfurt, I will[A] see to through trusty men; if[A] you ask anything else of me to be done, my faithful service will always be ready for you to the best of my powers. From your Christian I also gladly learned this — namely, that you were born in the same year and the same month in which I was brought into the light; I was also greatly delighted, among …… the things you have now shared with me, by the reading of your poems to …… which I did not read without various perturbations of mind. For I thought[A] much about many things, both yours and those that are like them. I will gratify[A] you in what you ask, and I will see to it that no one unworthy of you …… about your affairs which are worthy of you. You in turn, if it is not troublesome, embellish my Symbolum with some Epigram. What my Symbolum is, you will learn from our Vincent Moller, who, if you wish, will give you to read a certain little book of ours, which concerning that same Symbolum I had …… published. I had indeed sent you a copy, which I grieve has perished. If you should ask for another, I will not unwillingly share it. Meanwhile, keep for yourself this inscription …… of mine. Our most excellent old man Doctor Hermann greets you reverently, lovingly, and dutifully, to whom you would scarcely believe how welcome was the greeting spoken by you, and in the name of that most excellent old man[A] …… If it is not troublesome, I ask that in my words too you reverently and dutifully greet the Illustrious Master Heinrich Rantzau, who has declared his goodwill toward me once and again. You, if it please, will increase and confirm it. And since mention has been made of your[A] Hemmingius, and you can now write more freely about him, I ask you, by our friendship, tell me in my own ears whether this enclosed little page deserves credence, which some years ago was circulated. God knows that I ask this neither out of ill-will, nor toward bad faith …… for I love and revere that best of men, who has so well deserved — an old man whom one ought to love and revere when one can; but only so that the history of the matter, of which I and others always [had] a free judgment by right, might begin to be clear to me. Fare well and happily, most excellent and most noble man, and keep for me your …… goodwill, whose first foundations — and those then very slight …… — were [laid] many years ago …… when, returned from your travels, you were living for some weeks in the house and at the table of my then host, Master Lauritz Dan. I shall never cease to love and esteem you, and to [pledge] my faith to you by every kind of means I can ……

At Wrocław,[A] 7 March, at the time of an eclipse of the Sun, 1598.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Iacobus Monavius* = **Jakob Monau** (1546–1603), the Wrocław (Breslau) humanist, poet, and Calvinist patron of letters, celebrated for his personal device (*symbolum*) "*Pietas contenta lucratur*," around which he gathered a famous album of contributed epigrams from European scholars — hence his request below that Tycho contribute one. Letter from Tycho's exile period: after losing Hven and royal support, Tycho had left Denmark (mid-1597) and was in 1598 a guest of Heinrich Rantzau in Holstein, working toward Hamburg-area publication.
- **Dateline / calendar.** *Vratislaviae VII. Martij … 1598* = "At **Wrocław** (Breslau, *Vratislavia*), 7 March 1598." The edition labels this **n.s.** (New Style); Monau, in Habsburg Silesia, used the Gregorian calendar. Header carries the as-written date with [N.S.]. *"tempore eclipseos Solis"* ("at the time of a solar eclipse") is an astronomical timestamp, not a separate date: a partial solar eclipse fell on **7 March 1598 N.S.** — the dateline is internally consistent and is not converted here, by this chapter's convention
- **MS witness / state of the text.** The sole witness is a later transcript (*Afskrift*) in **Langebek's Diplomatarium** (Copenhagen, Rigsarkivet). The copy is defective: Dreyer's printed text is riddled with lacunae (each..... marks lost or illegible words) and with superscript **A** markers keying his textual notes — chiefly editorial restorations of damaged words. Bracketed words in the source ([ante], [scio], [non], [an patriae potius tuae], [adiumento]) are **Dreyer's conjectural restorations**, reproduced as such; the superscript A's and the..... lacunae are preserved verbatim in the Source block and carried as Secure-marks and ellipses in the translation rather than silently smoothed. The translation's own bracketed words supply English syntax across the lacunae and are flagged as editorial.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Vincentio Mollero* = **Vincent(ius) Moller** of Hamburg, the intermediary forwarding the packet (corroborated by Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens*, citing TBOO VIII 30.20–22).
 - *frater … unicus Medicus Imperatorius … obijt Pragae* — Monau's brother **Peter Monau (Petrus Monavius, 1551–1588)**, personal physician to Emperor Rudolf II, who died at Prague; "ten years ago" fits a 1598 letter. The false rumour of *Jakob's* death (which Tycho had repeated in his published *Epistolae*) arose by confusion with the brother's real death.
 - *David* — *"common friend Master David,"* unidentified here (name stands without further specification in the defective copy); not over-identified.
 - *Christiano Severino Longomontano* / *Christiano tuo* = **Christian Sørensen Longomontanus** (1562–1647), Tycho's chief assistant, who had visited Monau late in 1597.
 - *Henrici Ranzovij* / *Henricum Ranzovium* = **Heinrich Rantzau** (1526–1598), royal Statthalter (viceroy) in Holstein, who gave Tycho hospitality and a base near Hamburg in his exile (corroborated by *On Tycho's Island*).
 - *Iacobus Curtius* = **Jacob Kurz von Senftenau (Jacobus Curtius)**, Imperial vice-chancellor and a patron of the sciences (d. 1594); Monau wishes him still alive to advance Tycho's cause at court.
 - *Iohannem Rothmannum* = **Johann Rothmann**, then resident in Erfurt (the *Republica Erfurdensis*); recipient of a letter Monau will forward. (Distinct from Tycho's earlier correspondent Christoph Rothmann of Kassel.)
 - *Hermannus noster* — the "old Doctor Hermann," a Wrocław associate of Monau's, not securely identifiable from the damaged text; left unidentified.
 - *Hemmingij vestri* — almost certainly **Niels Hemmingsen (Nicolaus Hemmingius, 1513–1600)**, the Danish theologian (*"your Hemmingius"* — i.e. the Dane); the *"enclosed little page … circulated some years ago"* concerns a contested report about him that Monau asks Tycho to authenticate. Identification is probable but rests partly on the damaged context; flagged.
 - *M. Laurentij Dani* = **Master Lauritz (Laurentius) Dan**, Monau's former host with whom the young Tycho lodged for some weeks on returning from his travels.
- **The King / Alfonso / Frederick.** *Regem … nihil voluisse conferre … qui tamen nuper tantos sumptus fecit in coronationis festo* — **Christian IV of Denmark** (crowned 1596, hence *"coronation festival"*) withdrew support; *iudicium Alfonsi* invokes **Alfonso X "the Wise" of Castile**, the royal patron of the Alfonsine Tables, as the model of a king who funded astronomy; *ipsius patris Friderici* = **Frederik II**, Tycho's late patron. The contrast (lavish coronation vs. nothing for science) is Monau's, kept unsoftened.
- **Greek.** *Τύχη* — "Chance / Fortune"; a pun on Tycho's name, exactly as in the Wolf letter's *εὐτυχέστατε Τυχών*. *"haec Τύχη, quae Domino TYCHONI contigit"* = "this Chance [Τύχη] which has befallen Master Tycho" — wordplay on Τύχη / Tycho preserved (transcribed + glossed), not flattened.
- **The Magdeburg verse (German tag).** *"Est erit atque fuit — Vndanck in fine laborum"*: a macaronic Latin-German house-inscription, "It is, it will be, and it has been — **ingratitude at the end of labours**." *Vndanck* (German *Undank*, "ingratitude / thanklessness") is kept in the Source-block spelling and glossed; the line is kept as the verse Monau quotes, applied as bitter comment on the world's treatment of Tycho.
- **The two maxims, kept as verse.**
 - *"Esse aliquid si velle tenes, et posse tenebis"* — "If you hold to willing, you hold something; and you will hold to being able," attributed to **"Lazarus … a great-spirited man."** The name is immediately followed by a lacuna; **probably Lazarus von Schwendi** (1522–1583, Imperial general and statesman), but the loss prevents certainty — left as "Lazarus …" and flagged, not asserted.
 - The Atlas image (*"istis Atlanticis bonis et donis"*, "those Atlantean goods and gifts") casts Tycho as an Atlas bearing the heavens; kept as metaphor.
- **Technical / programmatic terms.** *Symbolum* — Monau's personal **device/emblem** (the kernel of his epigram album); kept untranslated and italicised on first use, per the keep-rule for fixed humanist terms. *libro Epistolarum* = Tycho's printed *Epistolarum astronomicarum libri* (Uraniborg, 1596), the "book of Letters" Tycho had gifted. *"ea, quorum editio fuit coepta in Huenna"* = the works whose printing had begun on **Hven** (Uraniborg) and which Tycho hoped to finish near Hamburg. *"discernere Actorem a Poëta fabulae"* — the Stoic-theatrical commonplace of distinguishing the **Actor** (who merely plays the assigned part) from the **Poet/Author of the play** (who assigns it): God writes the drama, man acts his role; kept literal.
- **Epistolary formulae.** Opening *S.* = *salutem [dicit]*, "greeting". *coram Deum cernens* of the dead brother — "beholding God face to face." Closing *Bene et feliciter vale* = "Fare well and happily".
- **Negation check.** The two operative negations are reproduced exactly: (1) the King *"nihil voluisse conferre"* — *"was willing to confer **nothing**,"* and (2) Dreyer's restored *"ut [non] plane careat successu"* — *"that they will **not** altogether lack success"* (i.e. that the designs may yet partly succeed). The [non] is editorial (bracketed in both Source and translation); without it the clause would assert the opposite, so the bracket is load-bearing and is flagged as Dreyer's restoration, not silently absorbed.

text.original:
DEM GESTRENGEN, EDLEN VND ERNVESTEN HERREN TYCHO BRAHEN ITZO ZU WANDESBECK, MEINEM BESONDERN GUNSTIGEN LIEBEN HERREN VNDT FORDERER.

GENEROSE et Magnifice D. TYCHO, omni cum observantia colende mihi Domine. Negotium commissum apud D. IOANNEM BŒKELIUM, quomodo confecerim, a M.V. ex scheda inserta apparebit. Duci OTTONI Brunsvicensium et Luneburgensium de sententia Μ.V. diligenter scripsi. C. ipsius omnino acquiescit et..quod M. Vestræ commodum futurum est. De accessu Reginæ in hanc civitatem nihil ad me perfertur, sicut et ex filio nihil tale accipio. Verum is, quæ alias publice et notorie sparguntur, confirmat. M.V. et mihi quoque ubi vacaverit a negotijs, ...dabo operam, ut illam invisam. Reliqua committo prudentiæ Μ.V. Quæ ut cum suis optime valeat, toto pectore opto. Datæ raptim Hamburgæ XI. Martij An. 1598.

Μ.V. omni cum observantia
qui colo
VITUS WINSHEMIUS.
text.english:
**To the stern, noble, and honourable Lord Tycho Brahe, now at Wandsbek, my especially gracious, dear lord and patron.**

Noble and Magnificent Master Tycho, my lord to be honoured with all respect. How I have carried out the business entrusted [to me] with Master Johann Bokel will appear to Your Magnificence from the slip [of paper] enclosed. I have written diligently to the Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg, [Otto], concerning Your Magnificence's view. His Highness [C(elsitudo)] entirely concurs, and ⟨…⟩ what will be to Your Magnificence's advantage. Concerning the Queen's arrival in this city nothing is reported to me, just as I get nothing of the sort from [my] son either; he does, however, confirm the things that are otherwise being put about publicly and notoriously. When it shall be free of business [time permitting] both for Your Magnificence and for me as well, ⟨…⟩ I shall take pains to visit her. The rest I commit to Your Magnificence's prudence. That you, with yours, may fare most excellently, I wish with my whole heart. Given in haste at Hamburg, 11 March, the year 1598.

Your Magnificence's, with all respect,
[he] who honours [you],
Vitus Winshemius.

documents.apparatus:
- **Correspondent.** *Vitus Winshemius* = **Vitus Winshemius (Veit Oertel/Ortel von Windsheim)**, the younger — here a Hamburg agent/intermediary of Tycho's during his Wandsbek exile; he acted as Tycho's local man of affairs in the city (the Latin epistolary register and the *D. Doctor* address in Tycho's reply imply a learned physician/lawyer of the Hamburg circle). Tycho's reply survives, dated **28 March 1598, Wandsbek** (identifier brahe-t_15980328001), opening *"Excellentissime Domine Doctor Vinshemi…"*. The name is shared with the better-known Wittenberg Greek scholar Veit Oertel von Windsheim (1501–1570), who is too early to be this writer.
- **Recipient / place.** **Tycho Brahe**, then resident at **Wandsbek** (*Wandesbeck / Wandsburg*), the estate of Heinrich Rantzau just outside Hamburg, where Tycho lived in 1597–98 after leaving Denmark and where he completed and printed the *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica* (1598). The letter is sent from **Hamburg** (*Hamburgae*) into Wandsbek.
- ***D. Ioannem Boekelium*** = **Johann Bökel (Johannes Bokelius, 1535–1605)**, the leading Hamburg physician of the day, professor and city physician (*Stadtphysicus*). Some "business" (*negotium*) of Tycho's had been transacted through him; the details were sent on a separate enclosed slip (*scheda inserta*), now lost.
- ***Duci Ottoni Brunsvicensium et Luneburgensium*** = the **Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, Otto** — i.e. of the house of Braunschweig-Lüneburg. (Tycho's circle of ducal dedicatees of the *Mechanica* included Duke Otto II of Braunschweig-Lüneburg, 1528–1603, recipient of a presentation copy; the identification of this *Otto* with that duke is plausible but not made explicit in the letter, so the given name is bracketed in the translation.)
- ***Regina*** — "the Queen": in the Hamburg–Danish context of 1598 most naturally **Sophie of Mecklenburg, queen dowager of Denmark** (Tycho's sometime visitor), but the letter does not name her; the rumour of a royal "arrival in this city" is reported only as hearsay (*publice et notorie sparguntur*) and the writer keeps it expressly unconfirmed. Identification left open per the source's own reserve.
- ***ex filio*** — "from [my] son": Winshemius's own son, evidently a source of city news; unnamed.
- **Abbreviations.** *M.V. / Μ.V.* = *Magnificentia Vestra*, "Your Magnificence" (the standard honorific answering the address *Magnifice D. Tycho*). The source alternates the Latin majuscule *M.V.* with a **Greek capital Mu (Μ.V.)** — a scribal/typographic variation in Langebek's copy, here reproduced as printed (source block) and rendered uniformly "Your Magnificence." *C.* (in *C. ipsius … acquiescit*) is expanded as *C(elsitudo)*, "His Highness" (i.e. the Duke just named); the expansion is editorial and so the rendering is supplied with the bracketed source letter.
- **Lacunae in the witness.** The copy-text carries two breaks, reproduced verbatim in the source block: (1) *"et..quod M. Vestrae commodum futurum est"* — a short gap after *et*, here marked ⟨…⟩; the syntax around the gap is incomplete and the exact connective sense ("and [will do] what will be to Your Magnificence's advantage") is reconstructed, not secure; (2) *"…dabo operam, ut illam invisam"* — a gap before *dabo*, also marked ⟨…⟩. Both are gaps in Langebek's *Afskrift*, not editorial cuts; they are flagged, not smoothed.
- ***scheda inserta*** — "the enclosed slip [of paper]" (a separate sheet sent with the letter), now not preserved with the text.
- **Honorific / closing formulae.** Address *Gestrengen, edlen vnd ernvesten Herren* — the German chancery courtesy stack "stern (i.e. authoritative), noble, and honourable lord," kept in register; *Forderer* = "patron, promoter." Subscription *"Μ.V. omni cum observantia qui colo"* = "Your Magnificence's, with all respect, [he] who honours [you]" — the relative *qui colo* left slightly elliptical in the Latin and rendered with a bracketed antecedent.
- **Calendar / dateline.** *Datae raptim Hamburgae XI. Martij An. 1598* = "Given in haste at Hamburg, 11 March, the year 1598" (**Old Style**: Denmark and the north-German Lutheran cities kept the Julian calendar in 1598). The dateline agrees with the catalogue label (*1598. 11. marts. Hamborg*); no discrepancy. *raptim* ("in haste") kept.
