documents.incipit: DIU multumque in votis habui, Illustris Domine IOSEPHE SCALIGER, cum adhuc in Dania …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD IOSEPHUM SCALIGERUM.

S. P.

DIU multumque in votis habui, Illustris Domine IOSEPHE SCALIGER, cum adhuc in Dania Patria mea morarer, ut tecum per litteras amicitiam contraherem, præsertim cum a plerisque isthinc ad nos venientibus tuum in me, licet de facie tibi ignotum, candorem et benevolentiam aliquoties perceperim, sed semper aliquid intervenit obstaculi, quominus id efficere commodum fuerit. Nunc autem, cum hunc Nobilem et doctum adolescentem FRANCISCUM TEGNAGLIUM mihi domesticum et meæ e Dania migrationis comitem in Bataviam ablegarem, non intermittendum duxi, quin aliquid saltem ad te litterarum darem, utut iam essem occupatissimus. Ad quod me etiam non minimum invitavit excellentissimum et laboriosissimum illud opus tuum redintegratum de Temporum Emendatione, quod his ipsis diebus primum accepi, atque quantum per negotia licuit, perlustravi. Nec possum satis mirari exactam tuam in eo concinnando diligentiam, pari iudicio atque eruditione coniunctam. Debet tibi sane vel pro hoc solo labore (ut cæteros illos præclarissimos a te exantlatos præteream) omnis posteritas immensas gratias, quod temporum epochas et rationes tam sedulo et subtiliter extricare volueris. Nec curandum si qui (uti fit) inveniantur ingrati Zoili, quales et hactenus nonnullos habuisti, qui e contradictionibus famam venari satagunt, sed ex alto despiciendum. Memini, me cum ad quendam eorum mihi Heidelberga scribentem litteras responsi loco darem, de te ipsum (siquidem is occasionem præbuerat) discrete admonuisse, ut te tuaque suspiceret potius quam vellicaret, atque a talibus contradictionibus abstineret, vel ad minimum ut modestius et maiori verecundia rem ageret. Quid hoc pacto apud ipsum profecerim, ignoro. Nam postea inter nos altum silentium.

Reperi in hoc novo tuo volumine, dum illud evolverem, te alicubi circa finem facere mentionem mearum observationum, quas circa utrumque Æquinoctium in Dania habui, easque cum Hipparcheis conferre, ut anni Alphonsini a te nunc assumpti magnitudinem probares. Ago autem tibi officiose gratias, quod tam honorifice et candide mei et mearum inventionum isthic memineris, et cuperem, ut hæc ipsa uberius adhuc expenderes, conferendo nimirum HIPPARCHI omnes observationes, sed prius limitatas, ut sibi invicem, quoad fieri poterit, correspondeant, aut seligendo eas quæ exactiores videbuntur; hac tamen adhibita cautione, ut is annus Iulianus retro numeratus eandem cum nostro, qui adhibetur, habeat respectu bissexti rationem, ita ut vel ambo sint bissextiles vel pariter hinc removeantur. Ideoque nostra Tabella utriusque Æquinoctij, quam e primo capite Progymnasmatum Astronomicorum assumpsisti, eos annos continue exhibet, qui ab uno in alterum bissextilem includuntur. Pluribus enim opus non erat, licet multos præterea in promptu habeam pariter sibi invicem correspondentes. Optandum sane foret, ut veteres parem in his præstitissent accurationem, quod tamen ab ijs factum non esse, propriæ eorum annotationes, ut tu quoque non iniuria arguis, produnt; utique magis indubiam Anni Cœlestis rationem, quoad minima momenta, nunc obtineremus, præsertim si a pluribus Artificibus per aliquot interlapsa secula res nunquam hians aut claudicans comprobata esset. Quin et utrobique medium Æquinoctium capiendum, ut intricatio ea, quæ ex Apogæi et Eccentricitatis mutatione provenit, præcaveatur. Conducit etiam ALBATEGNIJ Aratensis intermedias Observationes in consilium adhibere. Quibus omnibus rite expensis et adhibita in singulis cautela, quod parallaxin ☉ inter observandum Æquinoctia forte neglexerint, atque his etiam Æquatoris inclinationem non satis scrupulose applicârint, dummodo ex altitudine ☉ meridiana in utroque solstitio Poli sublimitatem rimati sunt, existimârim de Alphonsina Anni quantitate nonnihil adhuc decessurum, ita ut vix 49 minuta ultra integras horas explere possit, nedum ea in 6 H. excederet. Si itaque omnes quas habes observationes Hipparcheas tam in æquinoctio vernali quam autumnali in Tabella discrete expositas (annotando ubique qualis iste annus fuerit respectu bissexti Iuliani) mecum communicaveris, dabo operam, ut hæc cum nostris ulterius collata exactum quid non tantum anno Civili, sed et Astronomico præfiniendo suppeditent. Et si plures in promptu tibi sunt vetustissimæ Æquinoctiorum Observationes, diligentiam aliquam redolentes, eas etiam pari modo impertiaris, quæso. Tum quoque de Epocha antiquissima illa Iudaica, quando Æquinoctium die 21. Aprilis sex horis a Meridie extitisse creditur, si quid indubitati habes, unde id probari queat, et ad quem meridianum referendum sit, atque quomodo hic annus ad bissextum sese habuerit, quantumque ab hisce temporibus citra omnem ambiguitatem distiterit, expone et plenius de his omnibus, quæ a te collecta, mecum per litteras agere non degravare. Erit id mihi longe gratissimum. Quicquid vicissim mea opella præstari queat, quod tibi acceptum sit, habebis me semper ex voto. Fieri autem potest, ut nonnulla horum in hoc libro tuo elucidaveris, quæ adhuc explorata non habeo. Nam mihi accurate eum relegere plurimæ occupationes nondum permiserunt. Porro referet dictus adolescens quædam ad te meo nomine secreto, de quibus tuum iudicium et consilium cognoscere averem. Is etiam plura, cum mearum rerum sit conscius, de ijs aperiet. Quare ut ipsum benigne audias, tibique commendatum habeas, etiam atque etiam rogo.

Vale vir tam doctrina quam genere revera illustris.
Dabantur subito Wandesburgo ex Arce Ranzoviana, quæ est prope Hamburgum, die 14. Martij Anni 1598.
Illustris tuæ Magnis. studiosiss.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Joseph Scaliger.**

Heartiest greeting.

Long and earnestly, Illustrious Master Joseph Scaliger, did I wish — while I still abode in Denmark, my homeland — to enter into friendship with you by letter, especially since from very many who came to us from those parts I had several times perceived your goodwill and kindly favour towards me, unknown to you though I was by face; but always some obstacle intervened, so that there was no convenient opportunity to bring it about. Now, however, since I was dispatching this noble and learned young man Frans Tengnagel — a member of my household and the companion of my removal from Denmark — into Holland, I thought I ought not to let the chance slip without at least sending you some lines, occupied as I now am to the utmost. To this I was no little invited, too, by that most excellent and most laborious work of yours, now reissued, *On the Emendation of Times* [*de Temporum Emendatione*], which I received for the first time these very days, and have, so far as my affairs allowed, looked through. Nor can I sufficiently marvel at your exact diligence in composing it, joined with equal judgement and erudition. For this labour alone (to pass over those other most distinguished ones you have toiled through) all posterity surely owes you immense thanks, in that you were willing to disentangle the epochs and reckonings of times so painstakingly and so subtly. Nor need one be troubled if some ungrateful Zoili are found (as happens), such as you have had not a few hitherto, who busy themselves hunting fame out of contradictions; rather, they are to be looked down upon from on high. I recall that, when I was sending a letter by way of reply to a certain one of them who was writing to me from Heidelberg, I discreetly admonished him about you yourself (since indeed he had given the occasion) — that he should look up to you and your works rather than carp at them, and abstain from such contradictions, or at the very least conduct the matter with more modesty and greater deference. What I accomplished with him in this way, I do not know. For afterwards there was deep silence between us.

I found, in this new volume of yours, as I was unrolling it, that somewhere near the end you make mention of my observations, which I made about both equinoxes in Denmark, and that you compare them with those of Hipparchus, in order to test the magnitude of the Alphonsine year now assumed by you. I render you dutiful thanks that you remember me and my discoveries there so honourably and candidly; and I could wish that you would weigh these very matters yet more fully — by comparing, namely, all the observations of Hipparchus, but first delimited, so that they may correspond to one another so far as can be, or by selecting those which shall seem the more exact; with this caution, however, applied: that the Julian year, reckoned backward, should have the same relation, with respect to the bissextile [leap day], as ours which is in use — so that either both are bissextile or both are alike removed from it [the leap day]. And therefore our Table of both equinoxes, which you took from the first chapter of the *Astronomical Exercises* [*Progymnasmata Astronomica*], exhibits continuously those years which are comprised from one bissextile to the next. For more were not needed, though I have besides many ready to hand likewise corresponding to one another. It were assuredly to be wished that the ancients had shown a like accuracy in these matters; that they did not, however, their own annotations betray, as you too not without justice argue — assuredly we should now obtain a more indubitable reckoning of the celestial year, down to the least moments, especially if, by several practitioners through several intervening centuries, the matter had been verified never gaping nor limping. Moreover, on both sides the mean equinox is to be taken, so that the entanglement which arises from the change of the apogee and of the eccentricity may be guarded against. It is profitable also to bring al-Battānī of al-Raqqa's [Albategnius Aratensis'] intermediate observations into the deliberation. All these things having been duly weighed, and caution applied in each — [namely] that they perhaps neglected the parallax of the Sun [☉] while observing the equinoxes, and that to these too they did not apply the inclination of the equator scrupulously enough, provided they searched out the elevation of the pole from the meridian altitude of the Sun [☉] at each solstice — I should reckon that something will yet have to be deducted from the Alphonsine quantity of the year, so that it can scarcely fill out 49 minutes beyond the whole hours, far less exceed those by 6 hours. If, therefore, you communicate to me all the observations of Hipparchus that you have, both at the vernal and the autumnal equinox, set out distinctly in a Table (noting everywhere what sort of year that one was with respect to the Julian bissextile), I shall take pains that these, further collated with ours, may furnish something exact for fixing in advance not only the Civil but also the Astronomical year. And if you have ready to hand several most ancient observations of the equinoxes that savour of some diligence, impart those too in like manner, I beg. Then also, concerning that most ancient Jewish epoch, when the equinox is believed to have occurred on the 21st day of April, six hours from the meridian [i.e. past noon] — if you have anything indubitable whereby it can be proved, and to which meridian it is to be referred, and how this year stood with respect to the bissextile, and how far it was distant from these times without any ambiguity — set it forth; and do not think it a burden to treat with me by letter more fully of all these things gathered by you. That will be by far most welcome to me. Whatever in return my poor effort can render that may be acceptable to you, you shall always have me at your wish. It may be, however, that you have elucidated some of these matters in this book of yours which I have not yet investigated. For my very many occupations have not yet allowed me to read it through carefully. Further, the said young man will report certain things to you in my name in confidence, on which I should be eager to learn your judgement and counsel. He too will disclose more about them, since he is privy to my affairs. Wherefore I ask again and again that you give him kindly hearing and hold him commended to you.

Farewell, a man truly illustrious as much by learning as by birth.
Given in haste at Wandsbek, from the Rantzau Castle, which is near Hamburg, on the 14th day of March of the year 1598.
Most devoted to Your Illustrious Magnificence,
TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** Tycho Brahe, writing from exile: having left Denmark in 1597, he had wintered (autumn 1597 – spring 1598) at **Wandsbek**, the castle of Heinrich Rantzau near Hamburg, where he printed the *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica* and the star-catalogue. The subscription *manu propria* ("in his own hand") attests autograph signature of the (clerk-copied) letter.
- **Recipient.** *Iosephus Scaliger* = **Joseph Justus Scaliger** (1540–1609), the foremost chronological scholar of the age, then professor at Leiden. His *Opus novum de emendatione temporum* founded modern technical chronology.
- ***opus … redintegratum de Temporum Emendatione*** — Scaliger's *Opus novum de emendatione temporum*; *redintegratum* ("reissued / restored anew") signals the **second, revised edition** (Frankfurt 1598; first edition Paris 1583), which Tycho says he had just received. Tycho owned a copy of the 1583 edition (now Prague UL, *Ex Bibliotheca Tychoniana* no. 41).
- **Francis(cus) Tegnaglius** = **Frans Gansneb genaamd Tengnagel** (1576–1622), Dutch-born nobleman, Tycho's assistant ("of my household") and travelling companion in the move from Denmark; later married Tycho's daughter Elisabeth. Here sent as Tycho's confidential envoy *in Bataviam* — to **Holland / the Low Countries** (*Batavia*, the humanist name for the Dutch provinces), i.e. toward Leiden.
- ***Zoili*** — "Zoili" (from Zoilus, the proverbial carping critic of Homer): captious detractors; Tycho's standing term for hostile critics, kept as the classical plural with note.
- **The Heidelberg critic.** *quendam eorum … Heidelberga scribentem* — an unnamed correspondent who had attacked Scaliger; Tycho recalls counselling him to defer to Scaliger. The identity is not stated in the letter and is left unidentified here (not silently supplied).
- **Chronology / astronomy of the year-length.**
 - *anni Alphonsini … magnitudinem* — the **Alphonsine** value of the tropical year (365 d 5 h 49 m 16 s in the Alfonsine Tables), which Scaliger had adopted; Tycho argues from his own equinox observations that it is still slightly too long.
 - *vix 49 minuta ultra integras horas … nedum … in 6 H. excederet* — Tycho's estimate that the excess over the 365 whole days is barely **49 minutes beyond the [5] whole hours**, and certainly does not reach a full 6 hours (i.e. the Julian 365¼-day value is too long). "[5]" is not in the text; "integras horas" ("the whole hours") is rendered literally and the implied figure flagged, not inserted.
 - *Progymnasmatum Astronomicorum* — Tycho's *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* (the "Preliminary Exercises for the Restored Astronomy," pr. 1602/1610); its first chapter carried his equinox table, which Scaliger had used.
 - *respectu bissexti* — "with respect to the bissextile," i.e. whether a backward-reckoned Julian year is or is not a leap year; the caution is that compared years must be in the same leap-cycle phase. *bissextus*/*bissextilis* rendered "bissextile [leap day]/leap year."
 - *medium Aequinoctium* — the **mean equinox** (as opposed to apparent), to be used on both sides so as to avoid the *intricatio* arising from the secular change of the **apogee** (*apogaeum*) and **eccentricity** (*eccentricitas*) — glossary.
 - *Albategnij Aratensis* = **al-Battānī of al-Raqqa** (Latin *Albategnius*; *Aratensis* = of al-Raqqa, ancient Aracta/Callinicum, c. 858–929), whose 9th–10th-c. equinox observations Tycho recommends as the key intermediate data between antiquity and his own.
 - *parallaxin ☉ … Aequatoris inclinationem … Poli sublimitatem … altitudine ☉ meridiana … solstitio* — solar **parallax**; the inclination of the equator (obliquity); the **elevation of the pole** (latitude); the **meridian altitude** of the Sun at each **solstice** — all glossary. The Sun-glyph ☉ is kept in the Source block and named "the Sun" in translation by this chapter's convention
- **The Jewish epoch crux.** *de Epocha antiquissima illa Iudaica, quando Aequinoctium die 21. Aprilis sex horis a Meridie extitisse creditur* — Tycho asks Scaliger about a very ancient Jewish chronological epoch at which the (vernal) equinox was reputedly on **21 April, six hours past noon**. The clause *sex horis a Meridie* is rendered "six hours from the meridian," glossed "past noon"; this is a chronological datum Scaliger treated, queried by Tycho, not a date in the letter's own reckoning.
- **Calendar of the dateline.** *die 14. Martij Anni 1598* — **14 March 1598, Old Style**, consistent with the edition label ("1598. 14. marts. Wandsburg"); Tycho, writing as a Dane in Lutheran territory, used the **Julian** calendar (Denmark and Hamburg/Holstein had not adopted the Gregorian reform). No conversion is made. The recipient Scaliger, in Leiden, was in a New-Style jurisdiction — a style-gap Tycho does not here remark on, but which is the very subject of the 1600 sequel letter (where Tycho cites Scaliger's claim that the Dionysian Christian epoch is two years short). Recorded, not reconciled.
- ***Wandesburgo ex Arce Ranzoviana … prope Hamburgum*** = **Wandsbek, from the Rantzau Castle, near Hamburg** (the residence of Heinrich Rantzau, Stattholder of Holstein and Tycho's host).
- **Formulae.** *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam* → "Heartiest greeting"; *Vale* → "Farewell"; *Illustris tuae Magnis[itudini] studiosiss[imus]* → "Most devoted to Your Illustrious Magnificence"; *manu propria* → "in his own hand."

documents.incipit: DILECTE CHRISTIANE, scripsit ad me ante paucos dies IACOBUS MONAVIUS Vratislaviensis, …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD CHRISTIANUM LONGOMONTANUM.

DILECTE CHRISTIANE, scripsit ad me ante paucos dies IACOBUS MONAVIUS Vratislaviensis, Amicus meus integerrimus, te sub finem anni præteriti Vratislaviam venisse, et discessus mei causas e Dania per omnes circumstantias sibi retulisse, tum quoque te admodum de me solicitum fuisse, atque hac inprimis de causa inde abijsse Lipsiam. Quod sane mihi auditu pergratum fuit, dum te ita animatum agnosco. Ego tibi vicissim ex animo bene favere atque ad meliora quæque promovere non intermittam. Indicavit insuper ibidem MONAVIUS, quod te ad sororem WITICHIJ B. M. deduci curaverit, ubi omnes illius libros perlustraveris. Rogo itaque ut de ijs, qui et quales fuerint, præsertim manuscripti, et an eos vendere velit, qualique pretio, mihi significes. Vidisti proculdubio plagiarij mei impuri illius URSI maledicentissimum scriptum, in quo præter alia innumera convitia meo et meorum honori non parcit. Ego quidem refutatione illum indignum censeo, cum omnes modestiæ limites imo honestatis longe transcenderit; efficiam tamen ut non impune ferat. Cum vero tibi de plagio ipsius tum quoque omnibus circumstantijs procul dubio ex aliorum, qui tunc adfuerunt, relatu innotuerit, rogo in charta designare velis, quidnam hac de re a tuis apud me commilitonibus inaudivisti. Ego quidem nonnulla adhuc recordor, sed poterant aliqua tanto temporis intervallo, et inter tot alias curas mihi facile excidisse; tum quoque quid alij in Academijs, ubi interea fuisti, de hoc maledico scripto sentiant. Verum ut tecum plenius non tantum de hoc negotio, quod ex alto despicio, sed et de alijs quibusdam longe maioris momenti loqui queam, antequam ad ulteriora hinc peregrinationem suscipiam, atque plus forte disiungamur, cuperem quam maxime, ut meis sumptibus actutum huc Wandesburgum, dimidio saltem milliari Hamburgo remotum, te conferres, quo de necessarijs quibusdam tecum præsens agere queam. Neque enim omnia chartis committere commodum est. Si viaticum tibi ad manus non est, mutuo ab aliquo pete, vel oppignora quid, a me, qualecunque tandem sit, bona fide redimendum, aut aliquis pro te spondeat. Faxo ut illi sit indemne. Non est quod verearis, ne te hîc ultra voluntatem detineam, nam ipsemet non constitui hîc diu manere. Est nunc apud me IOHANNES MOLLERUS Electoris Brandenburgici Mathematicus, qui Hvenæ in coronatione (ut scis) nobis aderat. Is negotijs præest Astronomicis et studiosis meis, quos hîc non minus quam antea Uraniburgi haud paucos sustento. Vide iam, mi CHRISTIERNE, ne fallas exspectationem meam, sed quam primum te hîc sistas. Invenies me vicissim gratum, ut huius pro me suscepti itineris te neutiquam pœniteat. Sume tecum exemplar Ephemeridum novarum N. EVERHARDI e novis (ut iactitat) Tabulis supputatarum, quod illas in aliqua Academia facile nancisceris, et si quid aliud nosti, quod meis desiderijs conveniat. Hamburgi hic liber venalis non est. Mihi nihil præter solum eius libri titulum in catalogo hucusque videre licuit.

Vale, et confestim, prout tibi confido, ad nos advola.
Raptim Wandesburgi die 24. Martij Anni 1598.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO CHRISTIAN LONGOMONTANUS.**

Beloved Christian, a few days ago Jacob Monau of Breslau, my most upright friend, wrote to me that towards the end of last year you had come to Breslau and recounted to him, in all its particulars, the causes of my departure from Denmark; and that you too had been greatly anxious on my account, and had gone off from there to Leipzig chiefly for this reason. This indeed was most welcome for me to hear, since I recognize you to be so disposed. I in turn shall not cease to wish you well from my heart and to advance you to all that is better. Monau also reported, in the same place, that he had had you conducted to the sister of Wittich, of blessed memory, where you went through all his books. I ask you therefore to let me know about these — which and of what kind they were, the manuscripts especially, and whether she is willing to sell them, and at what price. You have doubtless seen the most slanderous writing of that impure plagiarist of mine, Ursus, in which, besides countless other abuses, he does not spare my honour and that of my own people. I for my part judge him unworthy of a refutation, since he has far overstepped all bounds of modesty — indeed of decency; yet I shall see to it that he does not get off unpunished. But since his plagiarism, and likewise all the circumstances, have doubtless become known to you from the report of others who were then present, I ask you to be willing to set down on paper what you have heard about this matter from those fellow-students of yours who were with me. I myself still recall a number of things, but some could easily have slipped from me over so great an interval of time and amid so many other cares; and also [I ask] what others in the universities, where you have been in the meantime, think about this slanderous writing. But so that I may speak with you more fully not only of this business — which I look down upon from on high — but also of certain others of far greater moment, before I undertake my journey onward from here, and before perhaps we are more parted, I should very much wish that, at my expense, you would betake yourself at once here to Wandsbek, distant from Hamburg by but half a [German] mile, so that I may treat with you in person about certain necessary matters. For it is not convenient to commit everything to paper. If you have no travel-money at hand, borrow it from someone, or pawn something — to be redeemed by me in good faith, whatever it may finally be — or let someone go surety for you. I shall see to it that he is held harmless. There is no cause for you to fear that I shall detain you here beyond your wish, for I myself have not resolved to stay here long. There is now with me Johannes Müller, mathematician to the Elector of Brandenburg, who (as you know) was present with us at Hven at the coronation. He is in charge of the astronomical work and of my students, of whom I maintain here not a few, no less than before at Uraniborg. See now, my Christian, that you do not disappoint my expectation, but present yourself here as soon as possible. You will find me grateful in return, so that you shall by no means regret this journey undertaken for my sake. Bring with you a copy of the new ephemerides of N. Eberhart, computed from new Tables (as he boasts), for you will easily come by them in some university; and anything else you know of that suits my wishes. Here at Hamburg this book is not for sale. Up to now I have been able to see nothing of it but the bare title of the book in a catalogue.

Farewell, and at once — as I trust you — fly to us.
In haste, at Wandsbek, the 24th day of March, the year 1598.
TYCHO BRAHE,
in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe**, writing from his temporary exile residence at Wandsbek castle, near Hamburg, in the year after he had left Hven (1597). His programme of *instauratio astronomiae* continued there with a reduced household.
- **Recipient.** *Christianus Longomontanus* = **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus** (1562–1647), Tycho's most senior and longest-serving assistant, later professor of astronomy at Copenhagen. He had left Tycho's service in 1597 and was travelling through the German universities; the literature consulted (Christianson, *On Tycho's Island*) confirms he took his M.A. at Rostock in spring 1598 and then made this short summer visit to Wandsbek "to discuss the Ursus affair." Tycho addresses him familiarly as *Dilecte Christiane* and, in the close, *mi Christierne* (the Danish vocative form) — both rendered "Christian" to keep the single referent clear.
- ***Iacobus Monavius Vratislaviensis*** = **Jacob Monau (Monavius)** of **Breslau** (*Vratislavia* = Breslau / Wrocław), 1546–1603, humanist and Tycho's correspondent. Per the literature consulted (*On Tycho's Island*), it was Monau who introduced Longomontanus to Wittich's sister and her late brother's library at Wrocław.
- ***soror Witichij B. M.*** — the sister of **Paul Wittich** (c. 1546–1586), the Wrocław mathematician whose visit to Hven in 1580 left a lasting imprint on Tycho's instruments and trigonometric methods (and whose later relations with Tycho turned into a priority dispute). *B. M.* = *beatae memoriae*, "of blessed memory" (Wittich was by then dead); rendered as such. Tycho's request that Longomontanus inventory the books — *especially the manuscripts* — and ascertain a sale price is the documented attempt to acquire Wittich's library.
- ***plagiarius … Ursus*** = **Nicolaus Reimers Bär**, called **Ursus** ("the Bear"), c. 1551–1600, Imperial Mathematician, whom Tycho accused of stealing his geo-heliocentric world-system during a 1584 visit to Hven. The *maledicentissimum scriptum* is Ursus's *De astronomicis hypothesibus* (Prague, 1597), whose scurrilous attack on Tycho prompted the long *Apologia* / *Astronomical Letters* counter-campaign (and, eventually, Kepler's *Apologia Tychonis contra Ursum*). *plagiarij mei … illius Ursi* — "that plagiarist of mine, Ursus": *mei* marks Ursus as the one who plagiarized *Tycho*, not a possessive of fondness; rendered "that … plagiarist of mine."
- ***efficiam tamen ut non impune ferat*** — "yet I shall see to it that he does not get off unpunished." A double construction (*non … impune*) carrying a single negation of impunity; reproduced exactly (one "not"). Tycho first says Ursus is beneath refutation, then immediately reverses to promise retaliation — the tension is the author's, preserved.
- ***commilitones*** — literally "fellow-soldiers"; here the metaphor for Tycho's resident assistants/students at Hven who witnessed the Ursus visit. Rendered "fellow-students of yours who were with me."
- ***Wandesburgum … dimidio saltem milliari Hamburgo remotum*** — **Wandsbek**, "distant from Hamburg by but half a [German] mile." The unit is the German *Meile* (≈ 7.5 km), far larger than the English mile; "[German]" is bracketed as an editorial clarification not in the source. *saltem* here = "at [most] only / merely" — Tycho stresses the *shortness* of the trip, not a minimum; rendered "but half a mile."
- ***viaticum … oppignora … spondeat … Faxo ut illi sit indemne*** — a chain of finance offers: borrow, pawn (Tycho to redeem in good faith), or have a guarantor; *Faxo* (archaic future of *facio*) "I shall see to it" that the guarantor "is held harmless" (*indemnis*). The pronoun *illi* refers to the surety (*aliquis*), not the lender; rendered "that he is held harmless."
- ***Iohannes Mollerus, Electoris Brandenburgici Mathematicus*** = **Johannes Müller**, mathematician to the **Elector of Brandenburg**, present at Hven at "the coronation" (Christian IV's coronation, 1596, which Tycho's circle attended). He now superintends Tycho's astronomical work and students at Wandsbek.
- ***Hvena / Uraniburgum*** = the island of **Hven** and **Uraniborg**, Tycho's former observatory; he notes he still keeps "not a few" students at Wandsbek, "no less than before at Uraniborg."
- ***Ephemerides novae N. Everhardi … e novis (ut iactitat) Tabulis supputatae*** = the new **ephemerides of N. Eberhart** (Nicolaus Everhardus / Eberhart), "computed from new Tables (as he boasts)." *ut iactitat* "as he boasts/brags" is Tycho's skeptical aside about the author's own claim for his Tables — the hedge is preserved, not smoothed into neutral report. Tycho has seen only the title in a sale catalogue, the book being unavailable at Hamburg.
- ***Sacris Uraniae*** sign-off not present here; instead the close is the urgent *ad nos advola* ("fly to us"), a hyperbolic imperative kept as such.
- ***manu propria*** — "in his own hand": the subscription marks the letter as autograph (though witness A is a later copy in Langebek's *Diplomatarium*).
- **Calendar / place.** *Raptim Wandesburgi die 24. Martij Anni 1598* = "In haste, at Wandsbek, 24 March 1598." Denmark and the Lutheran north were still on the **Julian calendar (Old Style)** in 1598; the date is O.S. and matches the edition label. No in-letter date discrepancy.

documents.abstract: Asks Winshemius to press Bökel to deliver books already paid for by Holger Rosenkrantz, threatening legal action if Bökel refuses to honour his promises.
documents.incipit: EXCELLENTISSIME Domine Doctor VINSHEMI, Amice honorande. Accepi nudius tertius ab OLIGERO …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD VITUM VINSHEMIUM.

EXCELLENTISSIME Domine Doctor VINSHEMI, Amice honorande. Accepi nudius tertius ab OLIGERO nostro literas, in quibus facit circa calcem mentionem librorum, qui adhuc apud Dominum D. BŒKELIUM residui sunt, quos omnino obtinere desiderat, et æquum sane est, ut, ex quo pecuniam totam is receperit, libros omnes tradat, aut se ita apud OLIGERUM purget, ut sit contentus. Ego consanguineo meo et affini amicoque intimo deesse non possum, quin procurem id, quod a me requirit. Si sponte BŒKELIUS hoc præstare noluerit, cogor iure rem agere, utut id libenter non facerem. Rogo itaque peramanter tam OLIGERI quam meo nomine, velis adhuc semel apud ipsum urgere, ut stet promissis. Excusationes, quas ultimo adduxit, vix accipiet OLIGERUS, nam ille aliter ad me rettulit ea de re, imo VESALIJ Anatomiam mihi dono dedit, licet ego id recusarim, nisi alium ex meis libris æquivalentem eius loco habere vellet. Nec valor eius est maior sex vel septem Ioachimicorum, etiamsi de novo ematur. Fac itaque, mi Domine Doctor VINSHEMI, ut OLIGERI expectationi satisfiat, et schedas, quas hac de re ultimo accepisti, remitte. Scripturus enim sum hisce diebus OLIGERO et negotium hoc expositurus.

Vale, et si quæ nova scis, indica.
Raptim Wandesburgi die 28. Martij Anni 98.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Vitus Winshemius.**

Most excellent Master Doctor Winshemius, my honoured friend. Two days ago I received a letter from our friend Oligerus [Holger], in which, towards the close, he makes mention of the books that still remain with Master Doctor Bökel — which he very much desires to obtain; and it is indeed only fair that, seeing he [Bökel] has received the whole sum of money, he should hand over all the books, or else so clear himself with Oligerus that he be satisfied. I cannot fail my kinsman and relative and most intimate friend, but must see to what he asks of me. If Bökel should be unwilling to do this of his own accord, I am compelled to pursue the matter at law, however little I should do so willingly. I therefore ask you most affectionately, in Oligerus's name as in my own, that you would be willing to press him once more to stand by his promises. The excuses he last brought forward Oligerus will scarcely accept, for he reported the matter to me otherwise — indeed he made me a gift of Vesalius's Anatomy, though I declined it, unless he would take in its place another, equivalent book of mine. Nor is its value greater than six or seven joachimsthalers, even if it be bought new. See to it, then, my Master Doctor Winshemius, that Oligerus's expectation be satisfied, and send back the papers which you last received on this matter. For I am about to write to Oligerus in these next days and set this business out [to him].

Farewell, and if you know any news, let me know.
In haste, at Wandsbek, on the 28th day of March, the year [15]98.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / place.** **Tycho Brahe**, writing in his self-imposed exile after leaving Denmark; *Wandesburgi* = **Wandsbek** (now part of Hamburg), where he stayed at the castle of Heinrich Rantzau from 1597 into 1598. *Raptim* ("in haste") is the standard hurried-subscription flourish.
- **Recipient.** *Vitus Vinshemius* = **Vitus Winshemius** (Veit Oertel von Windsheim) — here the **younger** of that name (the elder humanist Veit Oertel, 1501–1570, was long dead), professor of medicine at Wittenberg, acting as Holger Rosenkrantz's intermediary in the dispute with Bökel.
- ***Oligerus noster*** = **Holger Rosenkrantz** (1574–1642), "the Learned," the Danish nobleman and scholar, then a young man on his peregrinatio. Tycho calls him *consanguineus meus et affinis amicusque intimus* — "my kinsman and relative and most intimate friend"; the Brahe and Rosenkrantz families were indeed connected by blood and marriage. This chapter's neighbouring letters confirm the identification (a 7 March 1599 letter is headed *Oligerus Rosenkrantz ad Tychonem Brahe*).
- ***D. Boekelius*** = **Johann Bökel** (Johannes Bocatius / Boccatius, 1535–1605), the prominent Hamburg town physician and medical writer. The *œ*-ligature spelling *BOeKELIUM / BOeKELIUS* of the copy is preserved in the Source block.
- ***Vesalij Anatomia*** — Andreas **Vesalius**'s *De humani corporis fabrica* (or an *Epitome* of it); referred to generically as "Vesalius's Anatomy." Bökel had pressed the volume on Tycho as a gift, which Tycho declined except as an even exchange.
- ***Ioachimicorum*** — **joachimsthalers** (*Joachimsthaler*, the silver coin struck at Joachimsthal, ancestor of the "thaler/dollar"); "six or seven joachimsthalers" gives the book's market value. Kept as the period coin-name and glossed.
- ***schedas*** — "papers / slips," the documents (notes, accounts, or correspondence) bearing on the dispute that Winshemius had been sent and is asked to return; rendered "papers."
- ***cogor iure rem agere*** — "I am compelled to pursue the matter at law": *iure agere* is the legal idiom for bringing a formal/judicial action. Tycho's hedge *utut id libenter non facerem* ("however little I should do so willingly") is preserved, not sharpened into a bare threat.
- ***nudius tertius*** — the classical idiom "two days ago" (literally "now the third day [counting inclusively]"); rendered "two days ago."
- **Calendar.** No Roman-calendar idiom in the dateline: *die 28. Martij Anni 98* = 28 March 1598. Denmark and Tycho used the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar; marked [O.S.]. The header date matches the source dateline; the edition *label* ("1598. 28. marts. Wandsburg") agrees — no discrepancy.
- **Witness.** Survives only in a later transcript (*Afskrift*) in **Langebek's Diplomatarium**, Rigsarkivet, Copenhagen; spellings (the *œ*-ligatures, the all-capitals proper names) follow that copy as printed by Dreyer.

documents.incipit: CLARISSIME et Excellentissime Domine Doctor BORDINGE, Cancellarie dignissime et Amice …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD IACOBUM BORDINGUM.

S. P.

CLARISSIME et Excellentissime Domine Doctor BORDINGE, Cancellarie dignissime et Amice honorande. Cum hic Mechanicus senex M. PETRUS IACHENOW denuo isthuc a me rediret, non omittendum duxi, quin ad Illustrissimum Principem ULDARICUM, Dominum meum Clementissimum, aliquid literarum submisse darem, siquidem eius Celnis Clementissimam erga me voluntatem indies magis magisque experiar. Rogoque ut ipsius Celni easdem meo nomine submisse offeras atque in meliorem partem interpreteris, si quid liberius, re sic urgente, indicavi, idque in silentio secreto prematur, cum ex eâ, quam erga Illustrissimum illum et optimum Principem, tum quoque te, gero fiduciâ, sinceroque animo proficiscantur. Poterunt hæc forte nimis audacter prolata censeri, siquidem veritas plærumque odiosa sit; attamen si rei molem et eorum, quæ mihi immerito contigerunt, cumulum spectemus, vix supremis labris attigisse, quæ dicenda forent, videbor. Verum ego hæc omnia Deo committo. Veritas temporis filia aliquando forte prodet, quid æque aut inique factum sit. Illmo Duci necdum quidpiam responsum esse, etiamnum intelligo. Quod et præsagiebam. Quale responsum ad meas receperim, ex ijs utcunque intellexisti, quas Lubecâ tibi perscripsi, cum inde Instrumenta mea et supellectilem librariam huc transferri curarem. Quare

Sat Patriæ nostrisque datum, nunc Teuthona tellus
Excipit, et Patriam largitur maximus Orbis.

Curo quædam ex meis Operibus hîc labore Typographico compleri, quæ, ubi absoluta fuerint, vobiscum communicabo. In re pecuniariâ me isthic concernente satis actum est. Recepi literas fideiussorias et priores restitui.

Novarum rerum nihil peculiare est, nisi quod res composita dicatur inter Pontificem et Ferrariæ Ducem. Batavos se absentare et tractationem de pace aversari, neque enim hostibus satis fidunt tam sæpe circumventi. Novam Reginam in Anglia electam frementibus Scotis narrant. Nihil tamen adhuc certi constat. Vobis proculdubio isthic his plura et certiora innotuerunt. Rex noster Sermus fuit apud Dominum RANZOVIUM Bredenbergæ præcedente hebdomadâ ab eo isthic magnifice et splendide exceptus et mox inde Haderslebiam recepit. Plura nunc non vacat. Sum enim occupatissimus. Tu vero mi amantissime Domine BORDINGE quam felicissime vale, meque solitâ benevolentiâ (quemadmodum et ego tui amorem non deponam unquam) constanter prosequere.

Raptim Wandesburgo die 29. Martij Anni 1598.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO JAKOB BORDING.**

Heartiest greeting.

Most renowned and most excellent Master Doctor Bording, most worthy Chancellor and honoured Friend. Since the old craftsman here, Master Petrus Jachenow, was returning thither from me once again, I thought it not to be neglected that I should submissively address some lines to the Most Illustrious Prince Ulrich, my Most Clement Lord — seeing that day by day I experience more and more His Highness's most clement goodwill toward me. And I ask that you submissively present them to His Highness in my name, and interpret them in the better sense, if I have indicated anything rather freely, the matter being so pressing; and that it be kept in close silence — since they proceed from the trust which I bear toward that Most Illustrious and best Prince, and toward you as well, and from a sincere heart. These things may perhaps be reckoned to have been uttered too boldly, since the truth is for the most part odious; yet if we consider the weight of the matter and the heap of the things that have undeservedly befallen me, I shall be seen scarcely to have touched, with the tips of my lips, what would need to be said. But I commit all this to God. Truth, the daughter of time, will perhaps one day bring forth what has been done justly or unjustly. That nothing has yet been answered to the Most Illustrious Duke, I understand even now. Which I also foresaw. What sort of answer I received to my own [letters], you have learned in some fashion from those [letters] which I wrote out to you from Lübeck, when I was arranging for my instruments and my library furnishings to be transferred hither from there. Wherefore —

Enough has been given to my homeland and to my own; now the German land
Receives me, and the widest world bestows a homeland.

I am having certain of my works completed here by the labour of the press, which, when they have been finished, I shall share with you. In the money matter concerning me thither, enough has been done. I have received the letters of guaranty and have returned the earlier ones.

Of new things there is nothing particular, except that the affair is said to be settled between the Pope and the Duke of Ferrara. [They report] that the Dutch are absenting themselves and turning away from the negotiation for peace, for, so often circumvented, they do not sufficiently trust their enemies. They tell of a new Queen elected in England, with the Scots seething. Yet nothing certain is as yet established. Doubtless more, and more certain, things have come to your knowledge there. Our Most Serene King was with Master Rantzau at Bredenberg in the preceding week, magnificently and splendidly received by him there, and soon thereafter withdrew to Hadersleben. There is no leisure now for more, for I am most busy. But do you, my most beloved Master Bording, fare most happily, and continue to follow me steadfastly with your accustomed benevolence (just as I, too, shall never lay aside my love of you).

In haste, from Wandsbek, on the 29th day of March, the year 1598.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / context.** Tycho Brahe, writing from **Wandsbek** (*Wandesburgo*), the castle of Heinrich Rantzau near Hamburg where Tycho lodged in 1597–98 after leaving Denmark; the *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica* was completed here, and this letter (*"I am having certain of my works completed here by the labour of the press"*) belongs to that printing campaign. The letter is a covering note: it accompanies a now-lost submissive letter to Duke Ulrich that Tycho asks Bording to deliver and gloss favourably.
- **Recipient.** *Iacobus Bordingus* = **Jakob Bording** (the younger), at this date **chancellor of (the Duke of) Mecklenburg** (so Dreyer, *Tycho Brahe*, p. 246); a learned correspondent and Tycho's intermediary at the Güstrow/Mecklenburg court. Salutation *Cancellarie dignissime* ("most worthy Chancellor") confirms the office.
- ***Illustrissimus Princeps Ulldaricus / Illmo Duci*** = **Ulrich, Duke of Mecklenburg(-Güstrow)** (1527–1603), to whom Tycho was appealing in his exile; *Dominus meus Clementissimus* ("my Most Clement Lord") is the courtesy register, with *eius Celnis* / *ipsius Celni* = *eius Celsitudinis* / *ipsius Celsitudini* ("His Highness," abbreviated), rendered "His Highness" by this chapter's convention
- ***M. Petrus Iachenow*** — *"the old craftsman"* (*Mechanicus senex*) **Petrus Jachenow**, a workman/messenger shuttling between Tycho and the Mecklenburg court; *M.* = *Magister*, "Master."
- ***Dominus Ranzovius … Bredenbergae*** = **Heinrich Rantzau** (Henrik Rantzau, 1526–1598), royal governor (Statthalter) of the Danish duchies and Tycho's Wandsbek host, at his seat **Bredenberg** (Breitenburg, Holstein). *Rex noster Sermus* = *Rex noster Serenissimus*, "our Most Serene King" — **Christian IV of Denmark**.
- ***Haderslebia*** = **Haderslev** (Hadersleben), in the duchy of Schleswig.
- ***Lubeca*** = **Lübeck**, Tycho's prior staging-point; *Instrumenta mea et supellectilem librariam* = "my instruments and my library furnishings" — the documented Lübeck→Wandsbek transfer of Tycho's apparatus and books. *Instrumenta* rendered "instruments" by this chapter's convention
- **Verse couplet.** *Sat Patriae nostrisque datum …* is kept as verse by this chapter's convention It is a Tychonic adaptation of the Virgilian/Lucanic *patriae … datum* topos (cf. *Aeneid* / the *sat patriae* tag); the sense: having given enough to Denmark, Tycho now takes Germany — and the wide world — as his homeland. *maximus Orbis* rendered "the widest world" (superlative kept; "world" not "orb," since here it is the terrestrial world, not an astronomical *orbis/sphaera*).
- ***Veritas temporis filia*** — "Truth, the daughter of time" (*veritas filia temporis*), the proverbial *sententia*; kept as the maxim it is.
- ***literas fideiussorias*** — "letters of guaranty / suretyship" (bonds of guarantee); *priores restitui* = "I returned the earlier ones." A financial-settlement detail (*In re pecuniariâ … satis actum est*), left in its own legal-commercial register.
- **News items (all hedged by Tycho — preserved, not sharpened).** (1) *res composita … inter Pontificem et Ferrariae Ducem* — the settlement between the **Pope (Clement VIII)** and the **Duke of Ferrara**, i.e. the Devolution of Ferrara to the Papal States (1597–98); Tycho reports it as *dicatur*, "is said to be." (2) *Batavos … tractationem de pace aversari* — the Dutch (States) shunning peace negotiations (the run-up to the Franco-Spanish Peace of Vervins, May 1598); given with the explanatory hedge *neque enim hostibus satis fidunt* ("for they do not sufficiently trust their enemies"). (3) *Novam Reginam in Anglia electam frementibus Scotis* — a *report* (*narrant*) of "a new Queen elected in England, with the Scots seething." This is unfounded rumour: Elizabeth I reigned until 1603. Tycho immediately flags it — *Nihil tamen adhuc certi constat* ("yet nothing certain is as yet established") — and the translation preserves the rumour-frame ("They tell of …") and the explicit hedge rather than resolving or "correcting" it.
- **Greek / symbols.** None in this letter.
- **MS / textual note.** The sole witness is the Vienna draft (*Kladde*), cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.24; readings follow Dreyer's edited text. Abbreviations in the source expanded silently only where unambiguous (*Sermus* = *Serenissimus*, *Illmo* = *Illustrissimo*, *Celnis/Celni* = *Celsitudinis/Celsitudini*); flagged here rather than altered in the Source block.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 29. Martij Anni 1598*, from Wandsbek (Holstein). Denmark and the German Protestant territories were still on the **Julian calendar (Old Style)** in 1598; the date is O.S. and is not converted. The catalogue label ("1598. 29. marts. Wandsburg") agrees with the dateline; no discrepancy.

GEORGIJ F. ROSENCRANTZIO DANO, DOMINO HÆREDITARIO IN ROSENHOLM, ET INTER NOBILES DOCTO, INTERQUE
DOCTOS NOBILI, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO IN AeVITERNUM COLENDO ΕΙΣ XEIPE.TICHONI
BRAHE NON MINUS APERIENDAS ET LEGENDAS.ΕΥ ΠΡΑΤΤΕΙΝ.BINAS tuas literas, illas LubecaA, has Hamburgo ad me
datas, quam blande exosculatus fuerim, Generose ROSENKRANTZI, animus meus tibi
multis acceptis beneficijs devinctus a multisque perspectus annis tanquam in
speculo et tabula apud te loqui potest, lingua non potest. Tute enim nosti, quam
impense te amem, colam, quantique faciam, ut quoties literas tuas video,
frigidam toties mihi suffundi, et ad cursum amicitiae protensiorem me instigari a
te persuadear. Quod cum intelligere te ex literis tuis intelligam, non est, quod
pluribus tibi fidem faciam. At vero quantumvis dulcis mihi utraque tua fuit
Epistola, amariores tamen aliquanto fueruntA, quod simul in illis de plagio Liddeliano in illustrem Astronomum
TYCHONEM BRAHE, consangvineum et affinem tuum, virum multiplici scientia
admirandum, narrabas. Quod magis animum percellebat, quia ipse Dominus TYCHO
suis idem ad me literis testatum reddiderat. Querebatur tecum de singulari tum
impudentia, tum ingratitudine DUNCANI
LIDDELIJ Scoti, qui nunc in Inclyta Iulia Matheseos Professorem
agit, quod is non tantum literis ad suos privatim datis, sed et ex publica
praelectionum suarum cathedra Tychonianarum Hypotheseon se primum esse inventorem sitA gloriatus. Querela illa certior fuit, quod multis bonorum virorum
testimonijs et literis videbam TYCHONI fidem eius rei factam luculenter, et
gravior, quod is nonA solus, sed et cum alijs duobus Plagiarijs tantum facinus in TYCHONEM
ausus fuisset. Indignabar mecum et ridebam tamen cum
Phavorino cornices illas, homines in alienis plumis tripudiantes, ridiculos,
quod ambitiose ad maiora aspirarent, odiosos, quod ea consequerenturA apud quosdam, miserabiles, quod tandem apud omnes laude turpiter
exciderent. Solent enim subventanea (quod aiunt)
parere, qui laudem ex fuco virtutis, non ex virtute, concipiunt. Hac spe
potuissem ego et meum et tuum animum tranquillum reddere, nisi insuper adiectum
fuisset, quod propius me tangit et pungit acrius. Legi enim LIDDELIJ illius verba, quod is in
testimonium Plagij sui (cuius tamen TYCHONEM praepostere insimulare vult) me
testem invocet et adducat. Sic enim scribit: »Primas meas
theorias iuxta triplicem hypothesin satis imperfectas, quas ante septennium
Rostochij proposui, TYCHO a Doctore
CRAMERO Pastore nunc
Stetinensi accepit.« Sic
ait. TYCHO BRAHE ergo inventa sua hausit ex meo libro, ex LIDDELIJ praelectionibus, qui harum
hypothesium inventor est, qui primus deduxit, qui primus explicuit, si Dijs
placet, atque in eius rei testimonium fide dignum, egone a LIDDELIO asciscor? Obstupui, ingenue
fateor, ubi haec lego, me in falsum rei testimonium dicendum vocari, et abusu mei
nominis (quod hucusque sincerum Dei beneficio servare studui) rem tam a vero
alienam ceu pallio involvi et incrustari. Mi Domine ROSENKRANTZI, tute ipsemet nosti,
cum tot annos unâ viximus, quo DUNCANUM hunc loco semper habuerim, quam honeste de illo tibi
fuerim locutus, quod is fores Scholae Mathematicae et aliarum
quarundam Philosophiae partium mihi adolescenti aperuisset; quod autem nunc
obloqui illi cogar, id vellem ne fuisset unquam opus. Sed meministi mecum illud
PERICLIS Atheniensis, cum amicus eum
rogaret, ut pro se causaque eius falsum deieraretA, δεῖ με συμπράττειν τοῖς φίλοις ἀλλὰ μέχρι τοῦ βωμοῦ, et quod Philosophus
noster: ἀμφοῖν ὄντοιν φίλοιν ὅσιον προτιμᾶν τὴν ἀλήϑειαν. Non possum enim contra
veritatem, nisi quis simul meA adulatore et amico uti velit, quod a pia mente duco esse alienum. Ego de
illo Magistro meo non potuissem tantam in me sperare iniuriam, qua me nunc
affecit, quem nihil eius conscium ad falsum rei testimonium allegavit.
Falsimonium committit (quod in foro crimen falsi appellant) qui annulo
signatorio alieno suas periculi et doli plenas clam domino obsignat literas;
nonne illum idem patrare credas, qui alienis alienorum nominum subscriptionibus
in testimonium sine testimonio vocatis sua falsa confirmat? Praeposterum est te
vera loqui, cum ne quidem loquaris, affirmare ea, quae num affirmes nescias. Ita
mecum agit LIDDELIUS, ut testis
sim, testis nunquam auditus, ut affirmem, ignorem, vera loquar, cum ne quidem
loquar. Indignum, insanum. Quia vero tantopere is meummetA hac de re testimonium flagitare videtur, ago verum hoc meum testimonium,
contra illud suum, non meum. Tibi et TYCHONI de hoc plagio Lidelliano vera
petenti, quantum mihi quidem constat, deponam, idque tam perspicue, ut si tu
paulo superiorum annorum ἀνάμνησιν tecum per otium renoves, omnia puncta tua mihi ultro sis adiecturus. Docuit DUNCANUS LIDDELIUS Scotus in Academia Rostochiana Mathemata, quando ego
auditor fui anno 88 et sequenti, inter caetera explicando etiam motum secundum
iuxta triplicem hypothesin, primam Alphonsinorum, secundam COPERNICI, et aliam tertiam novam.
De hac tertia nova agitur, cuius sit auctoris? Me oportet reddere testimonium?
Egone respondeam? Respondeat ipse DUNCANUS, idque ex scriptis Commentarijs, quae ego adhuc hodie
mecum servo bona fide, qua et servant alij multi, tunc adolescentes, nunc viri,
qui tum temporis eadem eiusdem usi sunt institutione privata, inter quos est
quoque, ut unum nominem, communis noster amicusA M. IOACHIMUS PRÆTORIUSA, Collega in hoc templo et Gymnasio mihi honorandus. In
quibus commentarijs (tu oculatus mihi testis es, vidisti, legisti) DUNCANUS novam illam Diatyposin

quinque planetarum motus salvantur? etc. Sic tum temporis docuit, sic
dixit, sic dictitavit, sic didicimus, sic audivimus, sic scripsimus, sic
credidimus. At, inquis, nunc aliter Helmstadij dicit, aliter docet? Id vero ego capere non possum,
quo modo, si DUNCANUS unus sit et
esse velit, Rostochij hanc hypothesin sibi
derogare, Helmstadij vero eandem arrogare
per tam breve locorum temporisque intervallum queat? Nisi cum Horizonte animum
linguamque mutarit, quod ego vix concesserim. Credo ego
potius DUNCANO LIDDELIO
Rostochiensi Studioso contra DUNCANUM
LIDDELIUM Professorem Helmstadianum. Dicit forte prae modestiaA et verecundia se illa vice TYCHONI inventionem ascripsisse? Ergone hac

Et qui novit viri ingenium, neque hoc admittet. Quid multis? Barbari dicere
solebant, prout iacet litera; ita hîc quoque dicendum et pronunciandum iamA est, ex dictatis Rostochianis unius LIDDELIJ tertiam hypothesin, quam et nova placita solebat
appellare, non DUNCANI sed
TYCHONIS esse; propria confessio, inquiunt Iurisperiti, est fortissima probatio.
Satis superque haec tibi, mihi et alijs sufficere possent, nisi, quia sic sermo
coeptus est, unum et alterum adhuc verbum ex ijsdem liberet adijcere. Dici non
potest, quam praeclare tumA temporis in ipsa tractatione istius hypotheseos, quoties occasio dabatur,
de TYCHONE Scotus senserit, et omnibus veteribus praetulerit, et cum
Illustrissimo Landgravio Hassiae b. m.
coniunxerit. Sic enim in eiusdem commentarijs tit. de longit. et latit. in Sphaeram BRUCÆI legitur. »An vero stellae fixae suas

verum Landgravius et TYCHO BRAHE
ex crebris observationibus invenerunt stellas fixas latitudines suas ad
mutationem obliquitatis Zodiaci variasse.« Et de latitudine ☾ ait: »Quod antea a
nemine ante TYCHONEM observatum est, latitudo Lunae maxima
mutata est, et hodie est 5° 15'.« Item de eccentricitate
Solis tit. de motu Solis inquit: »in quibus omnibus Artifices hoc
seculo, ut sunt Illustrissimus Princeps Landgravius et TYCHO BRAHE, multa invenerunt, quae
observationibus COPERNICI non satis consentiunt.« Sic ille. Quis
hîc, quaeso, per febrim potuisset suspicari, LIDDELIUM tanti artificis, quem sic ipse commendaret,
praeceptorem esse, et illum huius discipulum, uti nunc iactitare audet? Ni
seipsum Scotus tantumA artificem, aut artificibus illis artificiosiorem et superiorem
constituisset, talis non constituereturA. Sed tu, Domine ROSENKRANTZI, pro ἀγχινοίᾳ tua, qua polles, me etiam tacente,
aliud argumentum certitudinis pro TYCHONE, ut opinor, colliges, quando audisA, quod observata, quae COPERNICO non satis consentiunt, TYCHONI ascribat, ut sic tecum

invenire et statuere vult, is ut longe prius observata τῶν φαινομένων Syderalium
nova acquisierit, necesse habet; quare? quia hypotheses novae, non praesuppositis
novorum φαινομένων fundamentis, anilia sunt τερετίσματα, quandoquidem
hypothesium sit salvare motus observatos; quod si ergo LIDDELIUS Scotus in obscuro latens et
instrumentis destitutus nulla φαινόμενα nova primus observavit, quid eum principioA impulit, ut ab hypothesi Coperniana (quam mordicus tueri solebat)
desiliret, et de novaA cogitare inciperet? Mirum enim, si se observata a TYCHONE primo accepisse largiri posset. Sic me iudice haudA leve argumentum duxeris ad evincendum DUNCANI Plagium. Taceo, quod in ipsa tractatione huius novae
hypotheseos, talem se praestiterit LIDDELIUS, ut multis indicijs sit colligere, eum auctorem et
inventorem non esse. Qui enim ipse inventorA et auspex est in scientia apodictica certae alicuius hypotheseos, quam
alios docet, illum dedecet fluctuare aut aliquid eius in medio suspensum
relinquere. Sic enim DUNCANUS, ubi
generaliter Tychonianum typum depinxit: »An primus motus, quo
omnia ab ortu in occasum feruntur, ob Terrae motum an coeli extimi rectius
dicatur, in medio hîc relinquimus; probabilius forte videbitur, si extimo
coelo ascribatur.« Audis, quam non usurpet sibi arbitrium
statuendi, decidendi, sed aliunde quasi afflatum exspectet, quid hîc sentiendum
sit, quid non sit, quem procul dubio tum temporis nondum ex TYCHONE hauserat.
Fortius est, quod ibidem paulo post ansam praebet sentiendi et disputandi contra
hanc Hypothesin, cum inquit: »COPERNICI hypothesin absurdam
plerisque videri, hanc vero (Tychonianam subintelligens) principijs
Geometriae nihil repugnareA, licet nonnulla videatur physica absurda ponere.«
Intelligebat autem orbes aethereos ex ARISTOTELIS sententia, quod paulo
post usu ex disputatione Physicae Aristoteleae cum eodem habita didici. Proposuit
enim idem ibidem Disputationes physicas, in quarum nona, cum ad libros priores
de coelo venisset, intrepide orbes reales defendere volebat, quos cum exercitij ergo opponendo Tychoniana observata refellerem, excanduit
homo tantum in modum, ut etiam hanc datam hypothesin plane repudiaret et
damnaret, immemor fortasse τῆς μεταβάσεως τοῦ γένους. Unde acerbitati istius ego
cedens, surrexi tum temporis, atque Scholis istius valedixi, ut meministi me tibiA saepius narrasse, et plurimi adhuc in vivis sunt, qui et spectatores et
auditores eius fabulae fuerunt. Quae ideo repeto, non ut de re ipsa (quam inter
puerilia nostra pono) agam, sed ut evincam LIDDELIUM semper hypothesin illam sic tractasse, sic contra
disputasse, ut alterius, non suum inventum esse clarissime dederit cuivis
contestatum. Rigidius enim pro illa pugnasset, si proprium figmentum (ex quo
immortaliter se victurum esse sperasset) fuisset. Talis, ut audis, ROSENKRANTZI, fuit Scotus in Schola illa Astronomica
Rostochij, quoties collecto grege illi
docenti assedimus; sed est tamen quod dissimulare nequeo, quod et alij mei tum
temporis commilitones (quos nominare possumA) norunt. Quando M. DUNCANUS
haud obscure colligeret, magno applausu excipi TYCHONIS novam, eamque tam
concinnam hypothesin, tumA laudis, ut opinor, immatura aviditate flagrans (ut erat natura
gloriosior) uni et alteri suorum auditorum (coetu dimisso) insusurrare solebat,
se habere literas propria TYCHONIS manu exaratas, in quibus TYCHO illi hanc
hypothesin adscribat, his inter caetera verbis: »Rem acu
tetigisti«. Verum nunquam tamen plene literas eas mihi quidem
visendas legendasveA
volebat aperire, nescio cur, etiam cum multis rogaretur. Quia
autem integras legere non licuit, multi mecum potius credebant publicis
commentarijs DUNCANI, quam eiusdem
clancularijs et subreptitijs susurris. Exemplar istarum, quas iactat, literarum
Helmstadij descriptum mihique
communicatum nunc legi, sed lectis illis merito exclamo: Quid est ollas et
cucurbitas lippire, si hoc non sit? Seipsum amare et sapere vix Iovi conceditur.
Perstringit enim amor sui oculos, ut quid album a nigro distet, discerni non
queat. Sed ego illud prolixius hîc agere non teneor. Epistola ubi in lucem
fuerit protracta, pro se loquetur.Habes, domine ROSENKRANTZI, quid mihi ex Liddelianis commentarijs constet, de
inventione novae seu Tychonianae hypotheseos. Quod etsi fere praeterire potuissem,
tamen ne tuae petitioni deesse voluisse viderer, nolui omittere. At vero plus mea
interest, an verum dicat Scotus,
quod propositas a se ante Septennium Theorias a me acceperit TYCHO, ut affirmare
non erubescit.Narrabo autem brevibus, ut se res habet, atque non minus tibi quam
mihi notum, ut quasi te tibi narrantem me audias,
modo recorderis. Cum Anno 91, a. d. 14 Calend. Iunij e palaestra Academica
Rostochiana avocati essemus ab Illustri tuo Domino Parente, GEORGIO, Prorege Daniae b. m. et substitissemus Hafniae aliquamdiu, indultum est utrique, ut ad
Insulam Huenam (qua Urania TYCHONIS tum
temporis pedem fixerat) excurreremusA, quod Dominus parens tuus intelligebat, nos quoque singulari Astronomiae
amore accendi et magni Dnum TYCHONEM ex illa arte facere.
Hac occasione ego, ut cum artifice de arte conferre possem, coepi recentius
ὑπομνήματα, quae tam a DUNCANO,
quam Dno
BRUCÆO, illo magnae famae viro, et alijs
praeceptoribus meis imbibissem, ruminare. Et quia partim navi eundum erat, ad
facundum itineris comitem commentaria, quae uno grandi volumine complicata
habebam, et adhuc habeo, ut nosti, adhibere coepi. In quo volumine inter alia
etiam LIDDELIJ dictata
continebantur. Ita κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς librum ad Insulam Tychonianam mei, non illius
causa transtuli. Ubi illuc ventum est, post multa, ut fit, familiares et eruditae
collationes de rebus varijs (quia tota insula erat cornu copiae rerum visu et
auditu mirabilium) itemque de arte Astronomica inciderunt et, nescio qua
occasione, de BRUCÆO, de LIDDELIO et alijs in hac scientia tumA temporis in Academia Rosarum claris. Sensi autem statim non levibus ex
signis, TYCHONEM sinistre sentire de LIDDELIO, quod is ea, quae ex privato cum TYCHONE colloquio,
quando ante ibi fuisset, furtim subduxisset, alijs in Academia iniussus
propalasset. Ego excusavi virum, quod is non sibi illa nova placita arrogasset,
sed nominatim sub Tychoniano titulo et honore proposuisset. Quod cum difficulter
sibi pateretur persuaderi Dominus TYCHO, oportune incidebat, me subito
interventu fidem facere posse libro meo, quem manu propria ex
ore ipsius excepissem. Sic ecce producitur liber, ostendo locum unum et alterum,
ubi hoc fiebat, ut supra annotavi. Quo viso acquievit plane Vir Nobilis, et de
istis commentarijs inter nos nihil quicquam amplius actum, nihil cogitatum,
nihil somniatum est ab illo toto tempore usque in hodiernum diem. Septimus nunc
agitur annus ab illo tempore, quo Uraniburgi ego et tu fuimus. Ante illud tempus nec ego nec
literae meae, nec manus nec nomen in Daniam,
quod ego sciverim, ad TYCHONEM unquam venerunt. Quis enim ego, adolescens tum
temporis, quis, inquam, eram aetate, ingenio, fama, ut cum tanto viro et genere
et fama Nobilissimo atque ab ipso Magistro nostro saepe proclamato huius saeculi
artifice, qui cum Landgravio solus
esset in Astronomia artifex, literis amicitiam contraxissem, aut mea ad illum
mittere potuissem? Post illud tempus, quo et secunda vice, interlapso triennio,
in Daniam redijmus, ego nullas de rebus
Astronomicis vel ad TYCHONEM vel alium quenquam dedi aut dare potui literas. Meministi enim professionis meae Witebergensis
Herculeas molestias, et studiorum genus longe sanctius, quam ut de illisA rebus mihi in Theologico studio semper παρέργοις ne per suspirium
cogitare, nedum ad Artificem aliquid conferre quiverim. Effricta igitur fronte
mentitur (da verbo veniam) qui dicit TYCHONEM unquam Theorias Liddelianas a me
accepisse. Dictum puta. In testimonium veritatis vocoA conscientiam meam, quae mihi mille testes est, et teA, Dn. OLIGERE, qui
probe adhuc annales istius διατριβῆς nostrae Academiae, in qua
iuncti unis aedibus, una mensa, uno lecto, diu noctuque, domi foris fuimus, ni
fallor, remetiris. Iniuria igitur Scoti estA, eaque in me iniuriosissima, quod me nunquam auditum hoc modo in
testimonium sui falsimonij invocat, tantum ut me invisum et suspectum bonis
viris, quos contra insurgit, reddat; malitia, quod alios abusu mei nominis
decepit; impudentia, quod me ignorantem et nihil tale cogitantem in suos
praescriptos cogit gyros, ut mea lingua, non quod mea mens verum esse concepit,
loquatur, sed quod ille finxit, vel absens effutiat. Nonne os meum quovis
mancipio hoc pacto esset servilius? Satis pro imperio. Unde vero scit, TYCHONEM
theorias has a me accepisse? Ego non dixi nec potui dicere, ille non vidit nec
potuit videre, neque ullus alius. Si audivisse se dixerit, reddam cum THALETE Milesio responsum, qui aiebat verum a falso
tantum abesse, quam oculi distant ab auribus, sentiens eos plerumque mentiri,
qui audita non visa referunt. Aut quid si dicam, quod dicat se audivisse, quae
nunquam audivit? Si per divinationem sit assecutus, dicat an ex sortibus, an
augurijs, an ex asterismis, an somnijs. Sed ex his procul dubio, nisi forte
compertum sit, ex graculorum garritu, εἶπε καὶ ἁ Γραῖα τἀλαϑέα κοσκινόμαντις, dicebat ille apud THEOCRITUM.Habes, Nobilissime Domine ROSENCRANTZI, non ex ingratitudine in praeceptorem olim meum (quae
enim haec gratitudo in gratiam praeceptoris commentiri?) sed ex
candore et veritate, qua amicitia nostra fundatur, redditum verum testimonium
contra effictum illud, non meum de plagio, ut vocas, Liddeliano. Tu hoc exemplo
edoctus recordare tui usitati symboli Νῆφε καὶ μέμνησο ἀπιστεῖν: tum alias, tum
si alij in posterum de me similibus mendaciorum floccis tuas aures opplere tentarintA, reserva alteram mihi liberam, quod cum feceris, et veritas et amicitia
