documents.abstract: Acknowledges Kepler's letter and praises the *Prodromus Dissertationum Cosmographicarum*, admiring its wit and the ingenious speculation binding planetary distances to the regular solids.
documents.incipit: ERUDITISSIME et praestantissime Vir, Literae tuae e Styria Id. Dec. superioris anni ad me …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO Μ. IOHANNI KEPLERO ILLUSTRIUM STYRIAe PROVINCIALIUM IN GYMNASIO GRÆCENSI MATHEMATICO EXIMIO, AMICO SUO PLURIMUM DILECTO. GRETZ IN STIRIEN.

ERUDITISSIME et praestantissime Vir, Literae tuae e Styria Id. Dec. superioris anni ad me datae circa initia Martij per Tabellarium Helmstadio venientem mihi redditae sunt, quae praeter doctrinam et humanitatem singularem erga me, licet tibi de facie ignotum et longe dissitum, testantur benevolentiam, quo etiam nomine tibi gratias habeo. Librum tuum, quem Prodromum vocas Dissertationum Cosmographicarum, iam ante videram, et quantum aliae occupationes ferebant, perlegeram. Placet is sane non mediocriter, et ingenij tui acumen sagaxque studium non obscure hinc elucent, ut de stylo terso ac rotundo nihil dicam. Ingeniosa certe et succincta est speculatio, Planetarum distantias et circuitus symmetrijs regularium corporum, uti facis, adstringere, et plurima in his satis consentire videntur, non obstante quod proportiones Coperniceae per omnia in minimis quibusque haud ubique adstipulentur, cum eae ab ipsis etiam apparentijs nonnihil deflectant. Quare laudo hanc tuam in excogitandis perquirendisque talibus diligentiam. An vero per omnia ijs acquiescendum sit, non ita facile dixerim. Si veriores Eccentricitatum utrarumque in singulis Planetis commensurationes, quales plurimis annis conquisitas in promptu habeo, adhibeantur, poterint accuratiorem in his trutinam exhibere. Verum mihi in complendis et edendis meis operibus Astronomicis, quae in Dania quodammodo imperfecta reliqueram, occupatissimo non suppetit nunc otium, ea accuratiore lima inter se conferendi. Fiet hoc forte alias. Id autem te scire velim, Eccentricitates ipsas utriusque illius, ut sic nunc loquar, Eccentrici, quas COPERNICUS paulo aliter excusavit, non habere eas adinvicem proportiones, ut una sit alterius tertia pars; veluti ex PTOLEMÆO deduxit. Neuter vero eorum demonstratum reliquit. Sed haec aliam inter se habent rationem et in singulis variant. Neque enim tres acronychiae observationes, utut inter se in Eccentrico (quod praestat) remotae, sufficiunt ad trium superiorum Planetarum Apogaea (quae etiam non paucis gradibus tam ALPHONSI quam COPERNICI placita coelitus eludunt) et Eccentricitates ambas ad amussim extricandas; sed per totum orbis circuitum in plurimis locis haec experiunda veniunt, veluti a nobis quoque factum est, adeo ut etiam tardigradi illius Saturni circuitum expectaverimus. Nam eundem Soli in ♎ oppositum ante annos 29. Augustae Vindelicorum diligenter observavi, quemadmodum et nunc; uti etiam in intermedijs Acronychijs dispositionibus, quotquot habere licuit, in toto Boreali semicirculo nullis omnino praetermissis, quemadmodum etiam in reliquis duobus Planetis, quorum circuitus minori clauditur tempore. Habeo enim in promptu 35 annorum Observationes coelestes, inde ab adolescentia factas, quarum 25 posteriores magna accuratione pollent: quas omnes non vulgaris thesauri loco conservo, et hinc Astronomiae restaurationem molior. Ut vero de Marte aliquid exempli loco addam, cum is maximam ingerat varietatem, atque inter Coelum et Tabulas discrepantiam caeteris evidentiorem, scias tantum abesse, ut eius Eccentricitas sit minor reddita (prout voluit COPERNICUS, quo suae imaginationi circa quietem Solis fidem faceret) ut potius nunc aliquanto maior sit, quam ea, quae a PTOLEMÆO prodita est, licet discrimine non magni momenti, Apogaeo eius quinque gradibus COPERNICI terminos anticipante. Quin et orbis annuus iuxta COPERNICUM aut Epicyclus secundum PTOLEMÆUM non videtur eiusdem semper magnitudinis, quoad ipsum Eccentricum collatione facta; sed alterationem introducit in omnibus tribus superioribus sensibilem, adeo ut angulus differentiae in ♂ ad Gradum unum Minuta 45. excrescat. Quomodo haec cum tua speculatione concilianda sint, tute videris. Veneris Eccentricitas multo minor est, quam statuit vel PTOLEMÆUS vel COPERNICUS, et Apogaeum eius non est in orbe sidereo fixum, uti hic voluit, sed initia ♋ nunc attigit; nec tamen solari (quod in medio sexti gradus haeret) uti volunt Alphonsini, plane unitum. Haec et similia, quorum plura suo tempore habebis, tuae alias industriae excogitationi applicata eam, an undequaque rite constet, probabunt. Ego omnem orbium realitatem, quomodocunque tandem assumantur, coelo eliminandam censeo. Quod me omnes Cometae, inde a nova stella conspecti, qui nullius orbis leges totaliter secuti sunt, quidam vero contrarium quid prae se ferebant, indubitanter edocuerunt (ut de refractionibus frustra multiplicatis ex orbium solidorum copia nihil superaddam). Nec poterit Terra annuo cieri motu, ut de librationibus otiosis (neque enim talis est aequinoctiorum praecessio, ut opinabatur COPERNICUS) taceam: utut diurnus plausibiliter ob minorem gyrum illi attribui queat, modo tam gravi et opaco corpori is competeret, quieti potius, quam motui accommodo. Quare ut tollantur Epicycli, vix alia commodiore ratione Hypotheses ordinari queunt, quam ut circa Solem mobilem sint centra circuituum quinque Planetarum quiescente Terra, et circa hanc revolutis luminaribus et tota octava (uti vocant) Sphaera, eam etiam in meditullio respiciente. Cuius abscessus iuxta COPERNICUM in immensum pene abit, eiusque positionem vel hoc solo absurdo infringit. Nec etiam tua cogitata hîc ullam cum caeteris Symmetriam (prout simul fieri debuit) admittunt. Oportet autem in re bene proportionata nihil dari inproportionatum, alias tota Symmetria confunditur, et suspecta evadit: praesertim in hoc loco, ubi tam magnum atque evidens ingeritur obstaculum. Haec et alia, quae singula commemorare nunc non vacat, me circa tuam inventionem alias solertissimam, optime KEPLERE, dubium reddunt. Interim non possum non conatus tuos, tam eximios et raros magnifacere. Hortorque ut ulterius his animum intendas, desque operam, ut simile quid nostris hypothesibus, quas ubi non incompertas esse liber ille ostendit, applicare possis, cum pene omnia ijs pariter conveniant. Neque ob id opus est, ut orbium statuatur compages solida. Sufficit circuitus et remotiones siderum inter se talem concinnitatem atque harmoniam observare. Nec praetereunda est octava Sphaera, quin in hoc choro proportionabiliter locum aliquem obtineat. Nullum enim est dubium in universo omnia certa harmonia et proportione ad invicem divinitus relata et ordinata esse, ita ut tam numeris quam figuris succincte comprehendantur, veluti a Pythagoreis et Platonicis iamdudum aliquatenus praevisum est. His itaque ulterius ingenij nervos applica, et si omnimodam consonantiam, quae nulla ex parte claudicet, et in qua nihil etiam desideretur, adinveneris, eris mihi magnus Apollo. Quantum ego tuis hac in re arduis conatibus subvenire potero, me neutiquam habebis difficilem, praesertim si me nunc in Germania degentem et e patria huc cum tota familia, ne tantus ille periret Thesaurus Astronomicus, tot annis, laboribus et sumptibus comparatus, profectum aliquando inviseris et mecum coram de eiuscemodi sublimibus rebus iucunde et grate contuleris. Vale. Dabantur Wandesburgi in arce Ranzoviana semisse tantummodo milliaris Hamburgo remota, quam nunc inhabito, et translatis huc e Dania machinis meis Astronomicis totaque suppellectile libraria rebus coelestibus non minus quam antea invigilo, et Divina gratia otio fruor Philosophico.

D. 1. April. stylo veteri Anno 1598.
TYCHO BRAHE.
manu propria.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, pp. 46–48; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
POSTSCRIPTA. NESCIO quo casu acciderit, ut idem Tabellarius, qui mihi tuas Helmstadio attulit, famosum quoque et nefarium scriptum cuiusdam feri Ursi potius quam veri hominis, inde mihi simul tuis alligatum adportârit. Huius cum impudentes calumnias et infanda mendacia atque convicia, quibus supra modum et citra omnem verecundiam scatet, obiter percurrerem, reperi etiam ibi tuum quoddam Epistolium, quo se ornare et sua flagitia tegere nititur. Quod cum perlegissem, miratus sum te eum tanti facere. Sed errorem excusavi, quod non nisi auditu et scripto isto, quod Fundamentum vocat Astronomicum, hoc faceres. In quo fere nihil habet quod suum est. Omnia potius aliis surrepta et praerepta, prout facere consuevit. Et plagium quod ego ipsi imputo in meis Hypothesibus, non saltem error crassus, quem in delineatione Martij orbis commisit, sed et multa alia, quae suo tempore pandam, evincunt. Estque etiamnum apud me fasciculus quidam eorum, quae quando Nobili cuidam Dano meo affini inserviens anno 84 cum eodem Uraniburgi adesset, clam descripsit. In quibus non dissimilia egit. Ego sane hanc Hypothesium rationem iam longe antea excogitatam, nec eam libro de Cometa Anni 77 inseruissem, nisi tales Plagiarios, quibus haec apud me innotuerat, veritus fuissem. Quare et hoc miror, quod eius voces Hypothesin, cum et in libro tuo et literis hisce eam mihi (nec immerito) attribuas. Interim etiam magna eius praedicas Elogia, utinam non Hyperbolen! In titulo vocas eum Mathematicum nobilissimum (qualis sit Mathematicus, non dixerim, Nobilitas eius, si genus spectes, est ex rusticis Dithmarsis, qui eum etiam fastidiunt). Ais deinde Illustrissimam eius gloriam ipsum tibi notum fecisse, qua Mathematicos huius aevi tantum praecedat unus, quantum Phoebeius orbis minuta sidera. Plura addidisses, si tempus ferret. At quam competenter etiam ulteriora excusas, quod Mathematicorum non sit garrulitas. Nescio an tale quid tunc apud te tacite senseris, genio sic suggerente. Praeterea quod omnes Docti magni ipsum faciant, eum praeceptorem appellas, hypotheses meas illi tribuis. Et tandem concludis, ut sideribus (quorum permodicam habet notitiam) et scientiae, quam sibi hinc inde (si qua est) corradit et suffuratur, tanquam decus Germaniae valeat. Talia de ignoto inconsiderate scripsisse videris: quae ego quidem nullatenus moror. Imo mallem vera esse, vel aliquem eiuscemodi dari, cui tanta in Astronomicis et Mathematicis competerent Elogia. Ego non ultimus essem, qui eius celebraret gloriam. Non tamen supra PTOLEMÆUM aut COPERNICUM, aliosque eximios viros, qualis in Germania MÆSTHLINUS nunc est, efferrem, nisi dignum fore satis perspectum haberem. Sed sint haec qualiacunque velint, id equidem non arridet, quod tua sic in libro isto contra me maledico abutatur Epistola, ut hac quasi se purgare, atque quantus sit, quamque multum ipsi tribuendum (si Dijs placet) probare velit, se ipsum ita nimium extollendo et sibimet placendo atque aliis tacite detrahendo. At quoniam in iuventute ea per ignorantiam scripsisti, nec forte existimâras eum unquam literas illas publicaturum, nedum ut iis in aliorum despectum et contumeliam unquam abusurus foret, idcirco est, cur haec placidius feram. Cuperem nihilominus ut primo quoque tempore apud me declaratum relinqueres, an tibi gratum sit quod sic fecerit, et quid de scripto isto virulento sentias, tum quoque alii Eruditi, ad quorum manus illud pervenit. Neque enim dubito, isthuc perlatum, siquidem Pragae excusum sit, suppresso tamen Typographi nomine, uti fit in famosis libellis. Plura de his non addo. Nec enim digna sunt, ut multis revocentur. Tuum est haec ipsa obiter subiuncta candide interpretari et schedam hanc Vulcano tradere. Iamque iterum et saepius Vale. Datum ut supra in literis. T. B.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and excellent man, Master Johannes Kepler, distinguished mathematician of the Illustrious Estates of Styria in the Gymnasium of Graz, his very dearly beloved friend. Graz in Styria.**

Most learned and excellent Sir, your letter, sent to me from Styria on the Ides of December [13 December] of last year, was delivered to me about the beginning of March by a courier coming from Helmstedt; and besides your learning and singular courtesy towards me — though I am unknown to you by face and far distant — it bears witness to your goodwill, on which account too I give you thanks. Your book, which you call the *Forerunner of Cosmographical Dissertations* [*Prodromus Dissertationum Cosmographicarum*], I had already seen before, and, so far as my other occupations allowed, had read through. It pleases me, indeed, not moderately, and the keenness of your wit and your sagacious zeal shine forth from it not obscurely — to say nothing of its polished and well-rounded style. It is certainly an ingenious and compact speculation to bind the distances and circuits of the planets to the symmetries of the regular solids, as you do; and very many things in this seem to agree well enough, notwithstanding that the Copernican proportions do not everywhere lend their support in each and every smallest detail, since they themselves depart somewhat even from the appearances. For which reason I praise this diligence of yours in devising and investigating such matters. But whether one ought to rest content in them in every respect, I would not so readily say. If the truer measurements of both eccentricities in each of the planets — such as I have ready to hand, gathered over very many years — be applied, they will be able to display a more accurate balance in these things. But, being most fully occupied in completing and publishing my astronomical works, which I had left in some manner unfinished in Denmark, I have now no leisure to spare for comparing these things with one another by that more accurate file. This will perhaps be done at another time. This, however, I would have you know: that the eccentricities of each of those (so let me now put it) eccentrics — which Copernicus accounted for somewhat otherwise — do not have those proportions to one another such that the one is a third part of the other, as he deduced from Ptolemy. Yet neither of the two left it demonstrated. But these things have another ratio among themselves and vary in each [planet]. For three acronychal observations, however far apart from one another in the eccentric (which is preferable), do not suffice for unravelling exactly the apogees of the three superior planets (which also, by no few degrees, elude in the heavens the doctrines of both Alfonso and Copernicus) and both eccentricities; but throughout the whole circuit of the orb, in very many places, these things must be tried by experience, as has been done by us too, so much so that we waited even for the circuit of that slow-moving Saturn. For I diligently observed that same planet in opposition to the Sun in ♎ Libra 29 years ago at Augsburg, just as now too; as also in the intermediate acronychal dispositions, as many as it was permitted to have, in the whole northern semicircle, with absolutely none passed over — just as in the remaining two planets, whose circuit is closed in a lesser time. For I have ready to hand the celestial observations of 35 years, made ever since my youth, of which the later 25 are strong in great accuracy: all of which I keep in the place of no common treasure, and from these I am labouring at the restoration of astronomy. But, to add something about Mars by way of example, since it brings on the greatest variety, and a discrepancy between the heaven and the tables more evident than the rest — you should know that so far is its eccentricity from being rendered smaller (as Copernicus wished, in order to give credit to his imagining concerning the rest of the Sun) that it is rather now somewhat greater than that which was reported by Ptolemy, though by a difference of no great moment, its apogee anticipating the bounds of Copernicus by five degrees. Indeed, the annual orb according to Copernicus, or the epicycle according to Ptolemy, does not appear to be always of the same magnitude, when a comparison is made with the eccentric itself; but it introduces in all three superior planets an alteration that is perceptible, so much so that the angle of difference in ♂ Mars grows to one degree and 45 minutes. How these things are to be reconciled with your speculation, you yourself will see. The eccentricity of Venus is much smaller than either Ptolemy or Copernicus laid down, and its apogee is not fixed in the starry orb, as he wished, but has now reached the beginning of ♋ Cancer; nor yet is it plainly united to the solar [apogee] (which sticks in the middle of the sixth degree), as the Alfonsines would have it. These and similar things, of which you shall have more in their own time, applied to the devising of your otherwise [admirable] industry, will prove whether it holds good in every respect. I, for my part, judge that the whole reality of the orbs, however in the end they be assumed, is to be eliminated from the heaven. Of which all the comets seen since the new star — which followed totally the laws of no orb, while some indeed bore something contrary — have taught me beyond doubt (to add nothing further about the refractions vainly multiplied out of the abundance of solid orbs). Nor will the Earth be able to be moved by an annual motion — to say nothing of idle librations (for the precession of the equinoxes is not such a thing as Copernicus supposed): although the diurnal [motion] might plausibly be attributed to it on account of its lesser turning, provided it suited so heavy and opaque a body, which is fitter for rest than for motion. Wherefore, in order that the epicycles may be removed, the hypotheses can scarcely be arranged by any more convenient method than that the centres of the circuits of the five planets be about the moveable Sun, the Earth being at rest, and that about this [Earth] the luminaries and the whole eighth (as they call it) sphere be revolved, the latter also regarding it [the Earth] in its very midst. Whose remoteness, according to Copernicus, goes off almost into the immeasurable, and he breaks down his own position by this absurdity alone. Nor, moreover, do your conceptions here admit any symmetry with the rest (as ought to have been the case at the same time). But it is fitting that in a thing well proportioned nothing disproportionate be granted, otherwise the whole symmetry is confounded and turns out suspect: especially in this place, where so great and evident an obstacle is brought in. These and other things, which it is not now free to recount one by one, render me doubtful, most excellent Kepler, concerning your invention, otherwise most skilful. Meanwhile I cannot but make much of your efforts, so distinguished and rare. And I urge you to bend your mind further to these things, and to take pains that you may apply something similar to our hypotheses — which, as that book shows them not to be unknown [to you], since almost everything agrees equally with them. Nor on that account is there need for a solid framework of orbs to be laid down. It suffices to observe such a fitness and harmony of the circuits and distances of the stars among themselves. Nor is the eighth sphere to be passed over without its obtaining some place proportionably in this choir. For there is no doubt that in the universe all things are divinely related and ordered to one another by a certain harmony and proportion, in such a way that they are concisely comprehended as much by numbers as by figures, as was already in some measure foreseen long ago by the Pythagoreans and Platonists. To these things, therefore, apply the sinews of your wit yet further; and if you should discover a consonance of every kind, which limps in no part, and in which nothing whatever is wanting, you shall be to me a great Apollo. As far as I shall be able to assist your arduous efforts in this matter, you will by no means find me difficult — especially if you should one day visit me, now dwelling in Germany, having set out hither from my homeland with my whole household, lest that great Astronomical Treasure, gathered over so many years with such labours and expense, should perish; and if you should confer with me face to face about sublime matters of this kind, pleasantly and gratefully. Farewell. Given at Wandsbek in the Rantzau castle, only half a mile distant from Hamburg, which I now inhabit; and, my astronomical instruments and the whole furniture of my library having been brought hither from Denmark, I keep watch over celestial matters no less than before, and by divine grace enjoy philosophical leisure.

The 1st of April, Old Style, the year 1598.
TYCHO BRAHE.
With his own hand.


*[Postscript:]* POSTSCRIPT. I know not by what chance it came about that the same courier who brought me your letters from Helmstedt carried hither at the same time, tied up with yours, a notorious and wicked writing of a certain man — a "wild Bear" [Ursus] rather than a true man. As I ran cursorily through his shameless calumnies and unspeakable lies and abuse, with which beyond measure and past all shame it teems, I found there too a certain little letter of yours, with which he tries to adorn himself and to cloak his villainies. When I had read it through, I marvelled that you make so much of him. But I excused the error, [judging] that you did this only on hearsay and on that writing of his which he calls Fundamentum Astronomicum. In it he has hardly anything that is his own; all rather filched and snatched from others, as he is wont to do. And the plagiarism which I impute to him in [the matter of] my Hypotheses — not only the gross error which he committed in the delineation of Mars's orb, but also many other things, which I shall disclose in their own time — prove [it]. And there is still with me a certain bundle of the things which, while he was in the service of a certain Danish nobleman, my kinsman, and was present with him at Uraniborg in the year [15]84, he secretly copied out; in which he acted not unlike [this]. I, in truth, had devised this scheme of the Hypotheses long before, and would have inserted it in the book on the Comet of [15]77, had I not feared such Plagiarists, to whom these things had become known with me. Wherefore I marvel at this too, that you should call it a Hypothesis of his, since both in your book and in this letter you attribute it (and not undeservedly) to me. Meanwhile you also proclaim great Eulogies of him — would they were not Hyperbole! In the title you call him a most noble Mathematician (what kind of Mathematician he is, I would not say; his Nobility, if you look to his lineage, is from the Dithmarsh peasants, who even disdain him). You say next that his most illustrious glory made him known to you, by which he alone so far precedes the Mathematicians of this age as the Phoebean orb [the Sun] the tiny stars. You would have added more, had time allowed. But how fittingly you also excuse the rest, [saying] that garrulity belongs not to Mathematicians! I know not whether you then felt some such thing tacitly within you, your genius so suggesting. Besides, [saying] that all the great Learned make much of him, you call him a teacher, and ascribe my hypotheses to him. And at last you conclude that he may avail, as it were the glory of Germany, for the stars (of which he has very slight knowledge) and for the science which he scrapes together and pilfers for himself here and there (if there be any). Such things you seem to have written inconsiderately about one unknown [to you]: which I, for my part, in no way regard. Nay, I would rather they were true, or that there were someone of such a kind to whom so great Eulogies in Astronomy and Mathematics were due. I should not be the last to celebrate his glory. Yet I would not exalt him above Ptolemy or Copernicus, and the other excellent men — such as Maestlin now is in Germany — unless I held it sufficiently clear that he would be worthy. But be these things whatever they will, this indeed does not please me: that your Letter is so abused in that book of his against me, the slanderer, that by it he wishes, as it were, to purge himself and to prove how great he is, and how much (so please the gods) is to be ascribed to him — by thus too much extolling himself and pleasing himself and tacitly disparaging others. But since you wrote those things in your youth, through ignorance, nor perhaps had supposed that he would ever publish those letters, much less that he would ever abuse them to the contempt and contumely of others, that is why I bear these things more calmly. Nonetheless I should wish that, at the first opportunity, you would leave it declared to me whether it is pleasing to you that he has done so, and what you think of that virulent writing — and likewise the other Learned into whose hands it has come. For I doubt not that it has been carried thither, since it was printed at Prague, the Printer's name being suppressed, however, as is done in libellous tracts. I add no more about these things; for they are not worth being recalled at length. It is for you to interpret candidly these very things subjoined in passing, and to hand this sheet over to Vulcan [the fire]. And now again and often, Farewell. Given as above in the letter. T. B.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender / recipient.** **Tycho Brahe** (1546–1601), then in self-imposed exile from Denmark; **Johannes Kepler** (1571–1630), at this date *Landschaftsmathematiker* (mathematician to the Estates) and teacher at the Protestant *Stiftsschule* / Gymnasium at Graz in Styria. This is Tycho's celebrated first substantive reply to the young Kepler — his answer to the *Mysterium Cosmographicum* — and the opening of the correspondence that would bring Kepler to Prague in 1600.
- ***Μ.*** before *Iohanni* — the abbreviation *M.* = *Magister* (academic "Master"), here written with a Greek capital Mu (Μ) in the source; rendered "Master". Reproduced as printed in the Source block.
- **Place.** *Wandesburgum, arx Ranzoviana* = **Wandsbek** (now in Hamburg), the castle of the Rantzau (Rantzow) family — Tycho's host Heinrich Rantzau's seat — where Tycho resided 1597–98 between leaving Hven and removing to Prague. *semisse … milliaris* = "half a [German] mile" from Hamburg.
- **Place of address.** *Gretz in Stirien* = **Graz in Styria** (German address-line on the cover), repeating the Latin *Gymnasium Graecense … Styriae*.
- ***Prodromum … Dissertationum Cosmographicarum*** — the full title of Kepler's 1596 book, the *Mysterium Cosmographicum* (*Prodromus Dissertationum Cosmographicarum, continens Mysterium Cosmographicum*); its thesis nests the planetary orbs within the five Platonic regular solids — Tycho's *symmetriae regularium corporum*.
- **Dating of the incoming letter.** *Literae tuae … Id. Dec. superioris anni* = Kepler's letter of **13 December [1597]** (Ides of December), delivered "about the beginning of March" via a courier from **Helmstedt** (*Helmstadium*); Roman-calendar idiom kept and glossed by this chapter's convention
- **Astronomy — technical.** *acronychiae observationes / Acronychae dispositiones* = **acronychal observations** (observations of a planet at opposition, rising at sunset); *Eccentricitates utriusque … Eccentrici* = the two **eccentricities** of the (bisected) eccentric — Tycho denies the Ptolemaic-Copernican simple bisection (one eccentricity = a third of the other / equant-bisection); *Apogaea trium superiorum Planetarum* = the **apogees** of the three superior planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars); *orbis annuus … aut Epicyclus* = the Copernican **annual orb** vs. the Ptolemaic **epicycle**; *octava Sphaera* = the **eighth sphere** (of the fixed stars); *aequinoctiorum praecessio* = the **precession of the equinoxes**. Glossary renderings kept consistent.
- **The Mars datum.** *angulus differentiae in ♂ ad Gradum unum Minuta 45. excrescat* — the discrepancy reaches **1° 45′**; *Apogaeo eius quinque gradibus COPERNICI terminos anticipante* — Mars's apogee runs 5° ahead of Copernicus's value. This is the very Mars-anomaly that Tycho here flags and would later set Kepler to work on. Tycho's claim that Mars's eccentricity is *greater* than Ptolemy's (against Copernicus, who shrank it *quo suae imaginationi circa quietem Solis fidem faceret*, "to give credit to his imagining concerning the rest of the Sun") is reproduced as his own argued position, not endorsed.
- **The Tychonic system.** *circa Solem mobilem … centra circuituum quinque Planetarum quiescente Terra* — Tycho's geo-heliocentric **hypotheses**: the five planets circle the moveable Sun, while Sun, Moon and the eighth sphere circle the resting Earth. *omnem orbium realitatem … coelo eliminandam* — his abolition of the **solid orbs**, argued from the cometary evidence "since the new star" (the 1572 *nova* and the comet of 1577 onward).
- **Symbols.** ♎ = **Libra**, ♋ = **Cancer**, ♂ = **Mars**; glyphs kept in the Source block and named in English by this chapter's convention
- ***eris mihi magnus Apollo*** — "you shall be to me a great Apollo," a proverbial classical compliment (cf. Virgil, *Ecl.* 3.104) = "you will be my oracle / supreme authority"; kept as the figure it is.
- ***Thesaurus Astronomicus*** — "the Astronomical Treasure," Tycho's term (cf. *non vulgaris thesauri loco conservo*) for his 35-year observational archive — the asset he uprooted his household to preserve. The phrase is rendered literally.
- ***restitutio / Astronomiae restaurationem*** — *hinc Astronomiae restaurationem molior*, "from these I am labouring at the **restoration of astronomy**," Tycho's *astronomia instaurata* programme.
- **Hedges preserved.** Tycho's epistemic qualifiers are kept un-sharpened: *non ita facile dixerim* ("I would not so readily say"); *forte alias* ("perhaps at another time"); *ut sic nunc loquar* ("so let me now put it"); *non magni momenti* ("of no great moment"); *plausibiliter … modo … competeret* (the conditional concession on the diurnal motion). The praise–doubt structure (*laudo … An vero … dubium reddunt … non possum non … magnifacere*) is mirrored, not flattened to one valence.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *D. 1. April. stylo veteri Anno 1598* = **1 April 1598, expressly Old Style (Julian)** — Tycho marks the style himself, anticipating his Catholic-Imperial correspondent's New Style; the catalogue label (1 April 1598, Wandsbek) agrees, so no header reconciliation is needed. *manu propria* = "with his own hand."

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** The substantial POSTSCRIPTA — Tycho's reaction to the enclosed Ursus Fundamentum Astronomicon, the 1584 Uraniborg-copying plagiarism charge, and the rebuke of Kepler for over-praising Ursus "decus Germaniae" — restored from Dreyer VIII, pp. 46–48 (dropped after "manu propria").
- **Correction.** Postscript, l.2-3: 'feri Ursi' (Dreyer, TBOO VIII p.46) restored for the corrupted 'seri Ursi', recovering the 'feri...veri' (wild Bear/true man) pun on Ursus's name; English 'late Bear' corrected to 'wild Bear'. l. following: 'Fundamentum Astronomicum' (Dreyer, TBOO VIII p.47), the real title of Ursus's 1588 tract, restored for the corrupted 'Fundamentum Astronomicon'; English title order corrected to match.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. All 6 Dreyer pages read as page images (TBOO VIII pp.44-49) and collated the full letter and its postscript (explicitly flagged in the transcribed original as 'restored from Dreyer... dropped by the working transcription') against the transcribed original and the published English. Checked every proper name (Copernicus, Ptolemy, Alfonso/Alphonsi, Maestlin, Ursus), number (29 years ago at Augsburg, 35 years of observations of which 25 later ones, apogee anticipates Copernicus by 5 degrees, angle of difference 1 degree 45 minutes, service to a Danish nobleman in [15]84, the [15]77 comet book), place (Graz/Gretz in Styria, Wandsbek, Hamburg, Silesia/Styria/Innsbruck as the Emperor's alternate refuges are NOT in this letter - none found misapplied), and the closing formula (1 April 1598 Old Style, half a mile from Hamburg). The main letter body (pp.44-46) is a fully faithful, thorough translation with no fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss. In the postscript, found two low-severity text error where our transcribed original's Latin departs from Dreyer's print (feri->seri; Astronomicum->Astronomicon); the English translation itself faithfully renders whatever the (corrupted) source said, and neither error changes the letter's overall sense (Ursus's plagiarism accusation and self-serving letter remain intact).

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). Source Latin reads 'seri' (serus, late) where Dreyer's page image clearly prints 'feri' (ferus, wild); the correct reading makes an antithetical pun 'feri...veri' (wild Bear vs. true man) on Ursus's name, which the corrupted 'seri' loses. The English is a faithful rendering of the corrupted source, so the fault is upstream in our Latin. Dreyer prints: *famofum quoque et nefarium fcriptum cuiufdam feri Urfi potius quam veri hominis (TBOO VIII p.46, Postscripta, l.2-3)*.
- **text error** (low). Source Latin has the substantive form 'Astronomicon' where Dreyer prints the adjective 'Astronomicum' agreeing with 'Fundamentum'; the real title of Ursus's 1588 tract is 'Fundamentum Astronomicum', not 'Astronomicon'. Translation is faithful to the (corrupted) source, so the fault is upstream in our Latin. Dreyer prints: *fcripto ifto, quod Fundamentum vocat Aftronomicum (TBOO VIII p.47, l.2-3)*.

**Repaired.** Both defects verified directly against the Dreyer page images (TBOO VIII pp.46-47, within the letter's own extract, read pages 1-4) at the precise lines cited by the audit; the printed long-s/f forms and line breaks match the audit's citations exactly, and the 'feri Ursi...veri hominis' reading is independently supported by grammatical parallelism (genitive adjective-noun pairs) and by the fact that Ursus was still alive in 1598, so 'seri' (late, i.e. deceased) could not be correct. No crux remains in either defect.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD ANDREAM SEVERINI VELLEIUM.

S. P.

CLARISSIME et eruditissime Domine Magister ANDREA, veteri amicitia mihi iunctissime. Scripsi ad te ante aliquot hebdomadas per tabellarium quendam Ripensem, qui semel atque iterum hîc fuit, et inter alia de victualibus isthic in meum usum conquirendis denuo admonui. Nec dubito eas te recepisse litteras, utut altum agens silentium nihil interea responderis. Quod tamen te facturum existimabam, si non prius, saltem circa hoc tempus, cum boum mercatores inde Hamburgum frequentes veniunt. Rogo itaque ut id, quod omissum est, emendes, atque de victualibus procurandis quae spes sit, indices. Scripsi denuo ea de re ANDREAe SEVERINI, civi isthic primario, qui suam mihi hoc in negotio dudum addixit operam. Spero ipsum suo officio non defuturum. Tu tamen nihilominus, quantum in te est, fac ut desiderijs meis respondeat eventus, nec tot pollicitationes nimium frustra. Adhortare etiam amicos et consanguineos meos per occasionem, si quos faventes et fidos inveneris, ut mihi iam extero, et amplam hîc in summa annonae caritate alenti familiam id praestent officij, quod sibi vellent, si eorum talis esset conditio. A sorore MARGARETA, quam mihi non defuturam putabas, ne verbum quidem accepi, licet bis illi scripserim, vix tertio facturus. Scio quidem victualium exportationem severe isthic prohibitam esse; attamen non me indigenam Regni Nobilem, sed mercatores hoc edictum concernere crediderim, nisi forte odio mei id fiat. Quod quomodo in Patria promeritus sim, ignoro. Id tamen scio, me isthic ultra tonnam auri insumpsisse, ut eius honori studerem; et quod plus est, prorsusque irreparabile, viginti unum Annos de potissima aetatis parte isthic non satis commode contrivisse. Quod quam maxime doleo. Nec mihi haec temporis et aetatis iactura evenisset, nisi ab optimo et laudatiss. mem. Rege FRIDERICO ita persuasus fuissem, cui et Patriae id concedendum ratus sum. Neque enim ullo modo persentiscere tunc potui, me nihil aliud quam invidiam, odium, calumnias et fraudulentas persecutiones inde reportaturum, unâ cum rei familiaris non exigua iactura. Sed ita est, uti nuper ad me clarissimus ille IACOBUS MONAVIUS Vratislavia perscripsit, inter alia hunc Kluppelhardum addens: »Est, erit atque fuit Vndanck in fine laborum«. Imo is et altius ea quae mihi in patria evenerunt, si non nimis hyperbolice exaggerans, in haec verba prorumpit: »Sed et hoc mihi incidit: Quid si mundus hic non sit dignus istis Atlanticis bonis et donis nostri TYCHONIS. Etiam hoc cogitavi: quid si haec Τύχη, quae Domino TYCHONI contigit, nunciet instare finem mundi? Utut sit, adhuc valde dubito, tuamne vicem an Patriae potius tuae, imo totius Reip. Christianae magis dolere debeam«. Moxque addit: »Miratus sum Regem nihil voluisse conferre in haec studia Regibus et eorum subsidijs atque adiumento dignissima, qui tamen nuper tantos sumptus fecit in coronationis festo. Aliud fuit iudicium ALPHONSI, imo aliud etiam ipsius patris FRIDERICI«. Haec et similia non saltem ille sed et multi alij viri in Germania atque alibi cordatiores et mihi et sibi invicem de me meisque rebus saepius scribunt. Ego vero invite fero quod Regi meo serenissimo et toti Patriae imputentur ea, quae paucorum machinata est perversitas, ab unico et veteri meo osore, quem tute nosti, de quo etiam ex Anglia mihi relatum est, praestantibus viris ibi innotuisse eum has turbas ex inveterata contra me invidia subdole et Machiavellice solum movisse, idque per alios, cum ipsemet par non esset, proficiscens. Quod et multis Germanis, nescio quibus indicijs innotuit; adeo ut vel sic (si non satis ante) famosus evadat. Ego semper Regem et Patriam, omnes in ea probos et integros viros excusare soleo. De caeteris taceo, et dissimulo ad tempus. Omnia successive et per intervalla suam sortiuntur maturationem et fructuum edunt specimen, ut quivis ea quae sevit, metat. Sed valeant ista unâ cum istis.

Tu vero mi amantissime Domine Magister ANDREA me, prout antea constituisti, hîc invise, ut semel adhuc, siquidem saepius non liceat, nos invicem intueamur et colloquamur, antequam disiungamur longius. Hyems nunc non obstat. Est inter Pascha et Pentecosten iucundissimum Anni tempus et profectionibus imprimis aptum. Valetudo si qua tibi est remissior, motu corporis inter peregrinandum et aëris mutatione recuperatur potius quam infringitur, cum quies illi minus conveniat. Nihil igitur aliud obstare poterit, quin post paucas hebdomadas hîc adsis, quam cura domestica et parsimonia; domui satis uxor providebit. Et maior est in amoris constantia parsimonia Amicum veterem negligere quam aliquam pecuniulae partem, quae resarciri potest, atque alias interdum profluit? Dedi etiam literas eodem tempore ad CHRISTIERNUM LANGIUM quo ad te, cuius filius etiamnum mecum est, et ne quidem ab illo quidpiam responsi accepi. Adest iam tempus ad quod usque filium eius in meam familiam me recepturum addixi. Vellem itaque ut Parens se, quid in posterum de eo agi velit, resolveret. Est quidem is satis modestus, et quantum ego scio, honeste se gerens, attamen hisce sublimioribus, quae ego tracto studijs, minus idoneus. Nescio an alijs. Neque ea quibus ego incumbo, ipsi in posterum multum usui esse poterunt. Oportet enim in ijs excellere, si quid hinc emolumenti sperandum. Effice igitur ut Parens mihi mature de sua voluntate scribat. Alterum quoque LANGIUM IOHANNEM per literas suadente OLIGERO ROSENKRANTZIO nostro sollicitavi, qui etiam nihil rescripsit. Miror vestram taciturnitatem, cum ego multo forte pluribus onustus occupationibus responsione non supersedeam, undecunque tandem ad me perferantur literae, quod creberrime fit ex varijs Europae locis, sed nihil novi est me a meis in Patria negligi, apud exteros non item.

Vale et si potes audesque, veni, nihilque metue, res enim caret periculo. Stans tegor in solido, ventus strepat, ignis et unda. Saluta ex me uxorem tuam unâ cum alijs amicis Ripensibus.

Dabantur Wandesburgi die 10. Aprilis Anno 98.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Anders Sørensen Vedel.**

Heartiest greeting.

Most distinguished and most learned Master Anders, joined to me most closely by an old friendship. I wrote to you some weeks ago by a certain courier of Ribe, who has been here once and again, and among other things reminded you once more about the provisions to be procured there for my use. Nor do I doubt that you received that letter, even though, keeping a deep silence, you have meanwhile sent no reply — which yet I thought you would do, if not sooner, at least about this time, when the cattle-merchants come in numbers from there to Hamburg. I ask you therefore to make good what has been omitted, and to indicate what hope there is of provisions being procured. I have written again on this matter to Anders Sørensen, a leading citizen there, who long ago pledged me his service in this business. I hope he will not fail in his duty. You none the less, so far as in you lies, see to it that the outcome answers to my wishes, and that so many promises [come] not too much to nothing. Exhort too my friends and kinsmen, as occasion offers — if you find any well-disposed and faithful — that to me, now an exile, and here maintaining a large household amid the utmost dearth of provisions, they may render that good office which they would wish [done] for themselves, were their own condition such. From my sister Margrete, who you thought would not fail me, I have not had so much as a word, though I have written to her twice, and shall scarcely do so a third time. I know indeed that the export of provisions is there strictly forbidden; yet I should think that this edict concerns not me, a native nobleman of the Realm, but the merchants — unless perhaps it is done out of hatred of me. How I have deserved [this] in [my] Fatherland, I do not know. This, however, I do know: that I spent there above a barrel of gold to study its honour; and, what is more, and altogether beyond repair, that I wore away there one-and-twenty years of the best part of [my] life, none too comfortably. Which I grieve over as deeply as can be. Nor would this loss of time and of [my] prime have befallen me, had I not been so persuaded by the most excellent King Frederick, of most praiseworthy memory, to whom and to the Fatherland I judged that it should be granted. For in no way could I then have foreseen that I should carry off thence nothing other than envy, hatred, slanders, and fraudulent persecutions, together with no small loss to my estate. But so it is, as that most distinguished Jacob Monau lately wrote to me at length from Breslau, adding among other things this blunt German saying [Kluppelhard]: »*Ingratitude* [*Vndanck*] is, will be, and was at the end of [one's] labours.« Nay, he breaks out — going deeper into the things that have befallen me in my homeland, if [he is] not exaggerating too hyperbolically — into these words: »But this too has occurred to me: What if this world be not worthy of those Atlantean goods and gifts of our Tycho? This too I have pondered: what if this *Týchē* [Fortune] that has befallen Master Tycho announces that the end of the world is at hand? However that be, I am still much in doubt whether I ought rather to grieve over your case, or over that of your Fatherland — nay, of the whole Christian commonwealth.« And presently he adds: »I have wondered that the King was unwilling to bestow anything upon these studies — most worthy of kings and of their support and aid — who nevertheless lately made such great outlays at the coronation feast. Other was the judgement of Alfonso — nay, other too [the judgement] of his own father Frederick.« These and like things not only he, but many other men of sounder sense in Germany and elsewhere, write often, both to me and to one another, about me and my affairs. But I bear it unwillingly that there are charged to my most serene King and to the whole Fatherland those things which the perversity of a few has contrived — by a single old hater of mine, whom you yourself know; of whom it has also been reported to me from England that it became known to eminent men there that he alone stirred up these troubles, out of an inveterate envy against me, by stealth and in Machiavellian fashion, and that, going about it through others (since he himself was not equal [to it]), [he did so]. Which has become known to many Germans too, by I know not what indications — so that even thus (if not enough before) he turns out infamous. I am always wont to excuse the King and the Fatherland, and all upright and honest men in it. Of the rest I keep silent, and dissemble for a time. All things, successively and at intervals, attain their ripening and yield a showing of their fruits, so that each man reaps what he has sown. But let these matters fare well, along with those [men].

But you, my most beloved Master Anders, visit me here, as you earlier resolved, that — once more at least, if it may not be oftener — we may look upon each other and converse together before we are parted further apart. Winter is now no hindrance. Between Easter and Pentecost is the most delightful time of the year, and especially apt for journeys. If your health is at all the weaker, it is restored rather than impaired by the body's motion in travelling and by the change of air, since rest suits it less well. Nothing else, therefore, will be able to stand in the way of your being here after a few weeks, save household care and thrift; your wife will provide for the house well enough. And is it the greater thrift, in the constancy of love, to neglect an old friend than [to spend] some little portion of money, which can be made good, and which besides flows away from time to time anyhow? I also gave a letter, at the same time as [the one] to you, to Christiern Lange, whose son is even now with me, and from him I have not had any reply at all. The time is now at hand up to which I pledged that I would receive his son into my household. I should wish, therefore, that the father would resolve what he wishes done about him hereafter. He is indeed modest enough, and, so far as I know, behaves honestly, yet [is] less suited to these loftier studies which I treat. I do not know whether [he is suited] to others. Nor will the things on which I am bent be able to be of much use to him hereafter. For one must excel in them, if any profit is to be hoped for from this. See to it, therefore, that the father writes to me in good time about his will [in the matter]. I have also solicited by letter the other Lange, Johan — at the urging of our Holger Rosenkrantz — who likewise has written nothing back. I marvel at your [pl.] silence, since I, burdened perhaps with far more occupations, do not put off a reply, from wherever at length the letters are brought to me — which happens very frequently, from various places of Europe; but it is nothing new that I am neglected by my own people in the Fatherland, [though] not so among foreigners.

Farewell, and if you can and dare, come, and fear nothing — for the matter is without danger. Standing, I am sheltered on firm ground; let the wind bluster, [and] fire and wave. Greet for me your wife, together with the other friends of Ribe.

Given at Wandsbek, on the 10th day of April, in the year [15]98.
Yours, Tycho Brahe,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** Tycho Brahe, writing from **Wandsbek** (Lat. *Wandesburgum*, then in Holstein, now part of Hamburg), where he stayed 1597–98 with Heinrich Rantzau after leaving Denmark in voluntary exile (June 1597). The letter is suffused with the bitterness of that exile.
- **Recipient.** *Andreas Severini Velleius* = **Anders Sørensen Vedel** (1542–1616), the Danish royal historiographer and ballad-editor, resident at **Ribe** (Lat. *Ripa*; *tabellarius Ripensis* = "courier of Ribe"; *amici Ripenses* = "friends of Ribe"); an old friend of Tycho's. Salutation/subscription formulae translated by this chapter's convention (*S. P.* = *salutem plurimam* → "Heartiest greeting"; *Vale* → "Farewell"; *manu propria* → "with his own hand").
- **Anders Sørensen, leading citizen of Ribe.** A second, distinct *Andreas Severini* — *civis primarius* of Ribe acting as Tycho's purchasing agent — not the recipient (who is also *Andreas Severini*); the doubling of the patronymic is in the source and is kept.
- **Sister Margrete.** *soror Margareta* = **Margrete Brahe**, Tycho's sister.
- ***ultra tonnam auri*** — "above a barrel of gold," Danish *en tønde guld*, a proverbial vast sum (≈ 100,000 rixdollars); rendered literally and glossed.
- ***viginti unum Annos … isthic … contrivisse*** — "one-and-twenty years … wore away there": Tycho counts from c. 1576 (the grant of Hven) to his 1597 departure.
- **King Frederick.** *Rex Fridericus, laudatiss. mem.* = **Frederik II** (r. 1559–88), "of most praiseworthy memory," who granted Tycho Hven; contrasted implicitly with the young **Christian IV** (crowned 1596), under whom Tycho's support lapsed.
- **Jacob Monau.** *Iacobus Monavius* = **Jacob Monau** (Monawius, 1546–1603), the Breslau (*Vratislavia* = **Wrocław/Breslau**) humanist and patron, a correspondent of Tycho's. The passages in guillemets (»…«) are Tycho's verbatim quotation of Monau's letter to him.
- ***Kluppelhardum*** — a Latinised accusative of a German coinage (cf. *Klüppel/Knüppel* "cudgel" + *hart* "hard"), i.e. a "blunt / rough-hewn German saying." Tycho's own nonce-word; rendered "this blunt German saying" with the original bracketed, the word flagged rather than smoothed. **Crux:** the exact register (jocular vs. coarse) is not certain.
- ***Vndanck in fine laborum*** — Monau's macaronic proverb embedding the German *Undank* ("ingratitude") in a Latin frame: "Ingratitude is, will be, and was at the end of [one's] labours" — a variant of the German *Undank ist der Welt Lohn* ("ingratitude is the world's reward"). The German word *Vndanck* is kept in the source block and bracketed in the translation per the code-switch policy.
- **Greek.** *Τύχη* — *Týchē*, "Fortune / [bad] luck"; Monau puns on Tycho's name (*Tycho* ↔ *týchē*), echoing the established wordplay (cf. Wolf 1571, *εὐτυχέστατε Τυχών*). Transliterated and glossed, the pun flagged not flattened. *Atlanticis bonis et donis* = "Atlantean goods and gifts," i.e. burdens/gifts worthy of Atlas (the Titan who bears the heavens) — apt for an astronomer.
- ***Alphonsi*** — **Alfonso X of Castile** ("the Wise," r. 1252–84), patron of the Alfonsine Tables, the archetype of the astronomy-funding prince; Monau contrasts his liberality (and Frederik II's) with the present king's.
- ***coronationis festo*** — the coronation feast of **Christian IV** (crowned 29 August 1596), on which the crown spent lavishly while withdrawing Tycho's support.
- **The "single old hater."** *unicus et vetus osor … quem tute nosti … Machiavellice* — Tycho's unnamed enemy at court, whom Vedel is presumed to know; not identified in the text and left unidentified here. The "report from England" of his exposure is given as Tycho relays it (hearsay), and the hedges are preserved.
- ***Christiernus Langius / Iohannes Langius*** — **Christiern (Christian) Lange** and **Johan Lange**, Danish noblemen; Christiern's son was then a pupil in Tycho's household. *Oligerus Rosenkrantzius* = **Holger Rosenkrantz** (here "our Holger," a mutual friend; likely Holger Rosenkrantz "the Learned," 1574–1642, though the elder Holger Rosenkrantz is also possible — identification left open).
- ***vestram taciturnitatem*** — "your [plural] silence": Tycho widens the reproach from Vedel alone to the whole circle of unresponsive Danish correspondents.
- ***Stans tegor in solido, ventus strepat, ignis et unda.*** — a self-standing **sententia / motto**, roughly hexametric in cadence: "Standing, I am sheltered on firm ground; let the wind bluster, [and] fire and wave." Kept as a maxim; *strepat* read as a jussive/concessive subjunctive ("let it rage"), with *ignis et unda* governed by it in parallel. A defiant Stoic emblem of constancy in exile.
- **Calendar / place.** *Dabantur Wandesburgi die 10. Aprilis Anno 98* = "Given at **Wandsbek**, the 10th day of April, [15]98" (**O.S.** — Tycho, a Dane in Holstein, still reckoning Old Style). The edition label ("1598. 10. april. Wandsburg") agrees with the dateline; **no date discrepancy.** (A neighbouring letter in the source CSV, Tycho → Maestlin, is dated 21 April 1598 from the same place — a different letter, not a variant of this one.)
- **Allusion.** *quivis ea quae sevit, metat* — "each man reaps what he has sown" (Galatians 6:7), woven into Tycho's threat-tinged forecast that wrongs will bear fruit in time; the Scriptural register is kept.
- **Correction.** English: fixed a wrong-antecedent mistranslation in Jacob Monau's embedded remark — 'ipsius patris Friderici' refers to the young King Christian IV's own father, Frederick II, not (as the bracketed '[your]' falsely implied) to Tycho's own father Otte Brahe.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter visually against TBOO VIII pp.48-50 (Dreyer page images, not digitised text layer). Latin the transcribed original matches Dreyer verbatim throughout, including proper names (MONAVIUS/Vratislavia, MARGARETA, LANGIUM, ROSENKRANTZIO), the sum ('ultra tonnam auri'), the count ('viginti unum Annos'), and the closing date/signature ('Wandesburgi die 10. Aprilis Anno 98 / Tuus Tycho Brahe manu propria'), all confirmed on the page images with no text error. One mistranslated pronoun-antecedent found in the Monau quotation, downgrading from the translator's own B.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (**high**). This is Monau's embedded quote about the young King (Christian IV); 'ipsius' is reflexive to 'Regem' (the King), so 'ipsius patris Friderici' means the King's own father, Frederick II — not Tycho's father. The bracketed '[your]' fabricates a false genealogical claim (Tycho's actual father was Otte Brahe), a wrong-antecedent error of the exact type this process is known to produce. At: “Other was the judgement of Alfonso — nay, other too [the judgement] of [your] father Frederick himself.”.

**Repaired.** Verified against the Dreyer page image TBOO VIII p.49, which prints 'Aliud fuit iudicium ALPHONSI, imo aliud etiam ipfius patris FRIDERICI«' verbatim as in the transcribed original, so no Latin change was needed. The surrounding context on the same page (Monau's complaint that 'the King' declined to fund Tycho's studies despite lavish coronation spending) confirms 'ipsius' refers back to 'Regem', not to Tycho. Only the English mistranslation required correction; the remainder of the letter was not re-collated beyond the single defect site per the prime rule.

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO DOMINO M. MICHAELI MÆSTLINO, MATHEMATICARUM ARTIUM INSIGNITER PERITO, EARUNDEMQUE IN INCLYTA ACADEMIA TUBINGENSI PROFESSORI CELEBERRIMO, MIHI PLURIMUM DILECTO. TÜBINGEN.

S.

ANNUS iam agitur decimus, eruditissime et præstantissime MÆSTLINE, ex quo quidam e meis domesticis, qui aliquandiu mihi in rebus Astronomicis inservierat, exemplum tuarum literarum Tubingâ ad se datarum in Daniam mihi transmisit, quibus pollicebaris, te librum nostrum de Cometa anni 77 tibi ab eodem communicatum diligenter perlecturum, tuamque de eius contentis sententiam conscripturum, atque mecum de eis per literas collaturum, quas te Marpurgum ad eundem mittere decrevisse, ad me postea procurandas innuisti. At ego toto interlapsis annis, neque hac de re aut quapiam alia, negocium Astronomicum, quo utrinque afficimur, concernente, ne verbulum quidem a te accepi, sive scripto, sive aliorum indicatione, qui isthinc venientes me Uraniburgi, dum adhuc in Patria degerem, inviserunt. Existimassem equidem te ob communia nobis studia scriptione aliqua saltem tot interlabentibus annis non supersessurum, præsertim cum id facturum sponte in te receperis. Ne vero ego ob id tecum per literas, siquidem aliter non liceat, familiaritatem contrahendi omnem occasionem respuisse videar, quod ab humanitate et exercitijs, quibus delectamur, sublimioribus alienum foret: en nunc prævenio, et ad scribendum respondendumque ultro te invito: data nimirum hac commodiore, qua nunc fruor, oportunitate, quam antea in Dania, ex quo in arce quadam Ranzoviana, dimidio saltem miliari Hamburgo remota, nunc habitem, unde in varia, non saltem Germaniæ, sed totius pene Europæ loca creber et commodus datur nuncius. Si itaque quid habes, de quo mecum in rebus Astronomicis, sive Cometicum illud negocium, sive quidvis aliud concernat, conferre libuerit, invenies me pro meo modulo, et quantum hactenus in ijs assequi licuit, ad respondendum non difficilem.

Allatum mihi nuper est eruditum quoddam scriptum Mathematici excellentis JOANNIS KEPLERI e Styria, in quo revolutiones Planetarum secundum formam Coperniceam ad 5 regularia corpora harmonice redigere ingeniosa sane speculatione conatur, qua etiam de re nuper ad me perscripsit, egoque illi, quantum præ occupationum mole licuit, meam vicissim de talibus aperui sententiam. Video autem te in eodem libro de Hypothesi a nobis ante annos complures adinventa nonnulla quasi dubitanter adferre, cum promiscue eam etiam alijs tribuas, plagiarijs forte meis nimium auscultans, tum quoque plura de eadem inferens, quæ si consideratius expendisses, et sententiam nostram atque omnes occasiones huius Hypotheseos constituendæ undiquaque perspectas habuisses, hæsitationibus eiuscemodi forte supersedisses. Atqui ego, si tibi quid in hac inventione scrupuli restet, id amovere atque penitius rem omnem explanare paratus sum, quod etiam res ipsa docebit, ubi Planetarum motus ad eam normam a nobis adeo accurate expansos cognoveris, ut nihil sit, quod sensus amplius requirant, utut tu in eodem libello de Astronomiæ correctione non saltem dubitare, sed et animum abijcere videaris, licet antea aliter spem feceris. Si ab anteriore per corpora ista regularia dimensione facta, ea restituenda erit, potius quam ex accuratis observationibus a posteriori sumptis, veluti insinuas, utique nimis diu, si non prorsus in perpetuum frustra expectabimus, antequam tale quid a quoquam præstari poterit. Cum enim istorum regularium corporum dimensionis explicatio, si omni ex parte admittenda foret, observationibus antecedentibus niti et comprobari debeat, nec etiam particularia quæque præter generaliora illa, utcunque se habentia, hinc ea qua opus est præcisione derivari possunt, quod te non latere arbitror. Neque etiam adhuc satis extricatæ sunt Planetarum biformes inæqualitates, quas duplici eccentrico vel circello excusant. Ignoratur enim iusta harum proportio, ut de Apogæis non dicam longe aliter se habentibus, quam fert non saltem Alphonsina, sed et Copernicea ratiocinatio. Quin et annua illa diversitatis evidens insinuatio necdum satis comperta est, ita ut undiquaque suis numeris absolute constet, ut ob id e Coperniceis proportionibus circulorum hæc ea, qua requiritur, subtilitate rimari invium sit; qua etiam de re eruditissimum KEPLERUM per literas admonui, et in Marte, ubi hæ differentiæ magis sunt sensibiles, exemplum indicavi. Verum de his et similibus nimis prolixum foret hîc singula exequi.

Ubi opera mea Astronomica lucem publicam viderint, quod nunc magnis viribus nec minoribus quam antea in Patria urgeo, perspicies, uti spero, rem Astronomicam aliter quam putatur redintegrari posse, et me non contemnendam in ea locasse operam; quare de his plura nunc non addo. Aliud quiddam est, etsi minoris momenti, quod tamen ad negocium hoc omnimode exequendum non parum conducit, pro ea videlicet, quam meridianorum ingerit in rotundo Terræ globo alteratio, diversitate necdum satis accurate explorata, de quo tecum agere averem. Si itaque aliquot Eclipses, præsertim Lunares, isthic exquisita diligentia præteritis annis observatas habes (de quo non dubito) earum momenta per observationum etiam circumstantias mecum mature communices velim, quo collatione facta cum 20 aut pluribus Lunæ deliquijs a me non paucis iam transactis annis diligenter consideratis conferri queant. Existimo me aliqua inter ea, quæ ego denotavi, inventurum, quæ etiam a te isthic observata sunt, atque hinc meridianorum intercapedo, aut ad minimum ductus alicuius meridiani per certa quædam Germaniæ loca pervestigari poterit, præsupposito nimirum quodam cognito ad rationem eam, quam PTOLEMÆUS et COPERNICUS assumserunt. Hoc si mihi præstiteris officij, rem non saltem gratam, sed etiam Astronomiæ promotioni non inutilem effeceris. Idem quoque apud alios, quotquot novi cœlestibus apparentijs fideliter attendere, qui sane perpauci (quod dolendum est) existunt, experior, ut certi quid in his, quoad licuerit, statuatur. Ad ultima duo luminarium deliquia, quæ in Februario proxime elapso contigerunt, te sedulo attendisse non dubito; quare eorum etiam momenta et phases isthic animadversas indica. Lunæ Eclipsis, quæ 11. eius mensis die contigit, hîc ubi polus elevatur 53° 35½', principium habuit, quando superior Lunæ limbus attollebatur supra horizontem 24° fere. Hinc tempus provenit, adhibito viso loco Lunæ iuxta nostram restitutionem et refractionum impedimento sublato, H. 4. 14' post mediam noctem antecedentem. Finis deliquij infra horizontem evenit. Visa autem est Luna ferme tota offuscari, minima eius portiuncula ab umbra Terræ libera existente. Solis eclipsatio, quæ 25. die accidit, hîc, quantum inter recurrentes nubes animadvertere licuit, initium habuit H. 9. 52' A.M. per Armillas Æquatorias 6 pedum in diametro (nam Instrumenta mea Astronomica huc in Germaniam e Dania, ut conscius sis, transtuli) temporis momenta denotando. Medium eius, uti neque finem, ob crassiusculas et continuas nubes intervenientes conspicere non dabatur. Conveniunt hæc tempora in utraque Eclipsi satis præcise cum nostro redintegrato calculo, ex 18 Lunaribus et 6 Solaribus prius subtiliter denotatis eclipsationibus depromto, ut de alijs hincinde sæpenumero expensis amborum luminarium motionibus huc etiam conducentibus nihil addam. Quantitas corporis Solaris Lunæ interventu offuscati debuit iuxta mea ratiocinia esse digit. 10¾ in hoc horizonte, idque a superiori parte, cum calculus Coperniceus et phasin et momenta huius obscurationis aliter exhibeat, uti et in Lunari Eclipsi tam is quam Alphonsinus nimium cis et ultra exorbitârunt. An deliquij Solaris magnitudinem nostris numeris recte attigerimus, iudicent illi, qui eius medium sereniore aura usi conspexerunt. Id vero sciendum est, Lunam in novilunijs eclipticis non apparere ea magnitudine, qua alias in plenilunijs, utut in eadem fuerit a Terra remotione, sed quasi pro quinta parte eam certis de causis alibi reserandis constringere; unde fit ut Luna nunquam totum Solem prorsus obtegere queat, etiamsi centraliter quoad visum interponatur, lumine Solari eam aliquali adhuc vestigio ambiente, quod et in hoc ultimo deliquio animadvertere poterant illi, quibus maxima offuscatio patuit. Oportuit enim tunc Solem de Lunari corpore utrinque plus includere, idque corniculatim, quam linea per diametrum ducta exigebat, utut Lunæ diameter tunc fuerit iuxta nostrum etiam calculum 34¾', apparere autem apud Solem non potuit maior quam 28', quam limitationem a nemine antea animadversam cognovi, sed in aliquot Solis observationibus, cum tam a superiore quam inferiore parte tegeretur, sic me docuit experientia. Tuum erit, excell. MÆSTLINE, quid in his et similibus compertum habeas, mihi etiam aperire, atque in posterum iucundam inter nos de rebus Astronomicis collationem, quam et ego non invite admittam, exercere. De Eclipsium autem, potissimum Lunarium, a te subtiliter animadversis momentis me, quam primum fieri queat, certiorem redde, ut correctionem longitudinum, de qua dixi, quam brevi in quadam tabella adornare constitui, tam hinc, quam ex alijs quibusdam aliunde conquisitis indicijs eo promtius expediam. Iam vale, v. cl. et de rebus Astronomicis laudabiliter merite, in quibus etiam expoliendis et locupletandis ut in posterum perseveres, te adhortor. Ubi rescripseris, effice, ut literæ quocunque tandem viarum ductu, sive per Norimbergam, sive aliquam aliam celebrem Germaniæ urbem Hamburgum perferantur, in hospitium isthic meum, quod est apud HERM. REUTTER sub signo coronæ aureæ, sicque eas me certo obtenturum non ambigo.

Iamque iterum et sæpius vale.
Dabantur Wandesburgo die 21 Apr. 1598.
TYCHO BRAHE, manu propria.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 55; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Cum intellexissem Tabellarium toto hoc die Hamburgi moraturum, curavi exemplum literarum KEPLERI ad me unâ cum meo responso describi, hisque adiungi, quo de earum etiam contentis certior fieres: ubi plura huc facientia invenies.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and excellent man, Master Michael Maestlin, signally skilled in the Mathematical Arts, and most celebrated Professor of the same in the renowned Academy of Tübingen, by me most beloved. Tübingen.**

Greeting.

It is now the tenth year, most learned and excellent Maestlin, since **one of my household — who for some while had served me in Astronomical matters — sent me into Denmark a copy of your letter, written from Tübingen to him**, in which you promised that you would diligently read through **our book on the Comet of the year [15]77** (communicated to you by him), and write your opinion of its contents, and confer with me by letter about them — which you had resolved to send to Marburg, to that same man, to be afterward procured to me. But **in all the intervening years I have received not even a little word from you** — on this or any other matter concerning the Astronomical business by which we are both affected — whether by writing or by the report of others who, coming thence, visited me at Uraniborg while I still dwelt in my fatherland. I should indeed have thought that you, on account of our common studies, would not have refrained from at least some writing in so many passing years — especially since you had of your own accord undertaken to do it. But lest I should seem, on that account, to have spurned every occasion of contracting a familiarity with you by letter (which would be alien to humanity, and to the loftier exercises in which we delight) — behold, **I now anticipate [you], and of my own accord invite you to write and reply**: this more convenient opportunity being now given me than before in Denmark, since I now dwell **in a certain Rantzau castle, but half a mile distant from Hamburg**, whence a frequent and convenient messenger is given to various places, not only of Germany, but of almost all Europe. If, then, you have anything you would confer with me about in Astronomical matters — whether the Cometary business or anything else — you will find me, to my small measure (and so far as I have hitherto been able to attain in them), not difficult in replying.

**There was lately brought to me a certain erudite writing of the excellent Mathematician Johannes Kepler, from Styria, in which, by an ingenious speculation indeed, he attempts to reduce the revolutions of the Planets (according to the Copernican form) harmonically to the 5 regular [Platonic] solids** — about which matter he lately wrote me, and I in turn opened to him my view of such things, so far as the mass of [my] occupations allowed. But I see that **in the same book** [Kepler's *Mysterium*, with Maestlin's notes] **you bring forth some things, as if doubtfully, about the Hypothesis I invented several years ago — since you promiscuously attribute it also to others** (perhaps too much hearkening to my plagiarists), **and infer more about it** which, had you weighed it more considerately, and had a thorough view of my opinion and of all the occasions of establishing this Hypothesis, you would perhaps have abstained from such hesitations. But I, if any scruple remains with you in this invention, am ready to remove it, and to explain the whole matter more deeply — as the thing itself will also teach, when you have learned the Planets' motions, expanded by me so accurately to that norm that there is nothing the senses can further require — though you, in that same booklet, seem **not only to doubt about the correction of Astronomy, but even to cast away [your] courage**, although before you gave hope otherwise. **If [Astronomy] is to be restored from the prior dimension made through those regular solids, rather than from accurate observations taken *a posteriori* (as you insinuate), we shall assuredly wait too long — if not utterly in vain forever — before any such thing can be furnished by anyone.** For since the explication of those regular solids' dimension — if it were to be admitted in every part — must rest on, and be proved by, antecedent observations; nor can the particulars (beyond those more general things, however they stand) be derived hence with the precision that is needed — which I think does not escape you. Nor, moreover, are the **biform inequalities of the Planets** yet sufficiently extricated, which they excuse by a double eccentric or epicyclet; for the just proportion of these is unknown — to say nothing of **the Apogees standing far otherwise than not only the Alphonsine, but the Copernican reckoning bears**. Nay, that evident insinuation of an annual diversity is not yet sufficiently ascertained, so as to agree absolutely, in all its numbers, on every side — so that to search this out, from the Copernican proportions of circles, with the subtlety required, is impassable; **of which matter too I have admonished the most learned Kepler by letter, and have indicated an example in Mars, where these differences are more perceptible.** But of these and the like, it would be too prolix to pursue each here.

When my Astronomical works shall have seen the public light — which I now urge with great forces, no less than before in my fatherland — you will perceive, as I hope, that the Astronomical business can be restored otherwise than is thought, and that I have placed in it no contemptible labour; wherefore of these I add no more now. **There is another matter, though of less moment, which yet conduces not a little to fully carrying out this business: namely, that diversity — not yet accurately enough explored — which the alteration of meridians introduces on the round globe of the Earth** [longitude], about which I should wish to deal with you. If, then, **you have several Eclipses, especially Lunar, observed there with exquisite diligence in past years** (which I do not doubt), I would have you communicate their moments to me in good time, with the circumstances too of the observations — so that, a comparison being made, they can be compared with the **20 or more lunar eclipses I have diligently considered now over not a few past years**. I think I shall find among those I have noted some which were also observed by you there; and thence **the interval of meridians — or at least the draw of some meridian through certain places of Germany — can be investigated**, presupposing, of course, something known, according to the reckoning which Ptolemy and Copernicus assumed. If you render me this service, you will do a thing not only welcome, but also not useless to the promotion of Astronomy. The same I seek too from others, as many as I know to attend faithfully to the celestial appearances — who are indeed very few (which is to be lamented) — that something certain may be established in these, so far as may be. **To the last two eclipses of the luminaries, which happened in the February just past [1598], I do not doubt you attended diligently**; wherefore indicate the moments and phases of these observed there too. **The Lunar Eclipse which happened on the 11th of that month — here, where the pole is elevated 53° 35½′ [Wandsbek] — had its beginning when the Moon's upper limb was raised about 24° above the horizon. Hence the time comes out — using the Moon's seen place by our restitution, and the impediment of refractions removed — 4h 14′ after the preceding midnight.** The end of the eclipse occurred below the horizon. The Moon was seen almost wholly obscured, the smallest little portion of it being free from the Earth's shadow. **The Solar eclipse which fell on the 25th — here, as far as could be noted among recurring clouds — had its beginning at 9h 52′ A.M., by the Equatorial Armillae of 6 feet in diameter (for I have transferred my Astronomical Instruments hither into Germany from Denmark, that you may be aware), noting the moments of time.** Its middle — as also its end — could not be seen, on account of the rather thick and continuous intervening clouds. **These times, in both Eclipses, agree precisely enough with my restored calculation, drawn from 18 Lunar and 6 Solar eclipses previously subtly noted** (to say nothing of the other motions of both luminaries, often weighed here and there, also conducing hither). The quantity of the Solar body obscured by the Moon's intervention ought, by my reckonings, to have been **10¾ digits in this horizon, and that from the upper part** — whereas the Copernican calculation shows both the phase and the moments of this obscuration otherwise, as also in the Lunar Eclipse both it and the Alphonsine deviated too much, this side and beyond. Whether I have rightly attained the magnitude of the Solar eclipse by my numbers, let those judge who beheld its middle, enjoying clearer air.

But this must be known: **that the Moon, in ecliptic new-moons [conjunctions], does not appear of that magnitude which it has otherwise in full-moons — even though it be at the same distance from the Earth — but constricts it, as it were by a fifth part, for certain causes to be disclosed elsewhere; whence it comes about that the Moon can never wholly cover the whole Sun, even if it be centrally interposed to the sight, the Solar light still surrounding it with some trace** — which those to whom the maximum obscuration was visible could note even in this last eclipse. For the Sun then had to include more of the Lunar body on both sides — and that horn-wise [*corniculatim*] — than the line drawn through the diameter demanded; for although the Moon's diameter then was, by my calculation too, 34¾′, yet **it could not appear, at the Sun, greater than 28′** — which limitation I have found noticed by no one before, but experience taught me so, in several observations of the Sun, when it was covered both from the upper and from the lower part. It will be for you, excellent Maestlin, to open to me too what you have ascertained in these and the like, and henceforth to exercise that pleasant collation between us about Astronomical matters, which I too will not unwillingly admit. But of the moments of the Eclipses — especially Lunar — subtly noted by you, make me more certain as soon as can be, that I may the more readily expedite the correction of longitudes of which I spoke (which I have resolved shortly to set forth in a certain little table), both from these and from certain other indications gathered elsewhere. Now farewell, most renowned man, and laudably deserving of Astronomical matters — in the polishing and enriching of which I exhort you also to persevere hereafter. When you have replied, see that the letters be carried to **Hamburg**, by whatever route at last — whether through **Nuremberg** or some other famous German city — to my lodging there, which is **at Herman Reutter's, under the sign of the Golden Crown**; and so I do not doubt I shall certainly obtain them.

And now again, and oftener, farewell.
Given at Wandsbek, the 21st day of April, 1598.
**Tycho Brahe**, in his own hand.


*[Postscript:]* Since I had understood that the courier would tarry the whole of this day at Hamburg, I have had a copy made of Kepler's letter to me, together with my reply, and joined to these — that you might be made the more certain of their contents too: where you will find more things bearing on this matter.
