documents.title: Tycho Brahe → Christoffer Valkendorf — Wandsbek [near Hamburg], 28 May 1598 [O.S.]

edition.print_label: Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia (1913–29)
edition.tboo_cite: Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, ed. I.L.E. Dreyer, Tom. XIV, Hauniæ 1929, p. 139

witnesses.raw: A København, Rigsarkivet, Privatarkiver, Kristoffer Valkendorff. Original letter

documents.abstract: Thanks Valkendorf for the support he gives Tycho's bailiff on Hven in managing disobedient peasants and settling their claims.
documents.incipit: MIN gandsche vennlig hillsen nu och allthiid forsendt medt Vor Herre. Kierre her …

text.original:
ERLIG OCH WELLBYRDIG MAND CHRISTOFFER WALLCKENDROP THILL GLOERUP, DANMARKIS RIGES HOFFMESTER OCH RAAD, MIN SYNDERLIGE GODE WENN, GANDSCHE WENLIGENN THILLSCHREFFUITT

MIN gandsche vennlig hillsen nu och allthiid forsendt medt Vor Herre. Kierre her hoffmester, sønderlige gode ven, nest min vennlig thacksiigellse for allt beviist gode, hvillcket igen att forskyllde ieg vill findes aff formuen villig. Giffuendiß eder derhoes gandske wennligen thillkiende, att epthersom min fougidt, ieg haffuer betroidt att haffue opsyn paa Hvæn, haffuer nogle gange schreffuitt mig thill, att hand bekommer allthiid god biistand och raad hoes eder, naar hand haffuer nogit att giffue fore, som angaar bønderne derpaa landit, och att i allthiid svarer hannom vell, och hiellper hannom formedellst eders authoritheet och myndighedt derudi thill rette, saa vill ieg haffue eder paa dett wennligste bethackit for denne eders gode villge imod mig, alligevell att ieg icke nu sellff der er thillstede. Dersom mand rett wiste, hordan mottvillige och vlydige bønder der er paa samme lille landt, och hvad ieg haffuer liid aff dennom all denn stundt ieg bode der, och alligevell haffdt gedullt medt dennom, och giort dennom thill gode wiidere end de forskylldede, da skulle mandt kandtskee mene anderlediß derom, end thill diß skeed er. Kierre her hoffmester, epthersom eder witterligt er, att ieg bleff aff medt Nordtfiords forlening vdi Norge om Michaelisthiide strax epther krøningen, saa formener ieg, att mig burde att haffue hvis rente och indtkomst der gick aff y dett hallffue aar thillforn, horudaff ieg dog thill diß en føye thing haffuer bekommit, alligevell att ieg nogle gange haffuer schreffuitt did op derudom. Wille derfore haffue eder paa dett wennligste ombedit, att i ville vell giørre och medtdeele mig eders gode schriffuellse thill slotzherren paa Bergenhues, att hand ville forskaffe dett saa, att ieg eller min fulldtmegthige maatte medt dett første thill gode rede bekomme hvis mig der rester och bøer att haffue medt rette. Kierre her hoffmester, forthencker mig icke, att ieg bemøder eder hermedt, ieg forseer mig endnu allt gott thill eder och throer eder saa vell, att i baade vdi denne och andre maader bethencker leyligheden och verrer mig thill dett beste behiellpelig vdi allt dett, som billigt och rett er, och eder mueligt kand verre att giørre; [y] hvis maade ieg kan giørre nogit vdigen, som i kan haffue ære och gott aff, vill ieg stedtze [findes] medt all thacknemmelighedt ganndsche [villig och] redebon derthill. Och vill icke nu lenger ophollde eder, mens nu och allthiid haffue eder Gud allmegthigste befalidt.

Datum Wandeßbeck widt Hamborg denn 28 dag maij aar 1598.
Tyghe Brahe.
Egen hand.
text.english:
**To the honourable and well-born man Christoffer Valkendorf of Glorup, Lord High Steward and Councillor of the Realm of Denmark, my especial good friend, [this] most amicably written.**

My most friendly greeting, now and always, conveyed with [the blessing of] Our Lord. Dear Lord Steward, especial good friend — next [after] my friendly thanks for all the kindness shown me, which to repay in turn I shall be found willing according to my means. Giving you herewith most amicably to know that, since my bailiff, whom I have entrusted with the oversight on Hven, has several times written to me that he always receives good assistance and counsel from you whenever he has anything to bring forward that concerns the peasants there on the land [the island], and that you always answer him well, and by your authority and power help him to his right in the matter — so I would most amicably thank you for this your good will toward me, even though I am not now myself present there. If one rightly knew how wilful and disobedient the peasants are on that same little land, and what I have suffered from them the whole while I dwelt there — and yet had borne with them, and done them good further than they deserved — then one would perhaps think otherwise about it than has hitherto been the case. Dear Lord Steward, since it is known to you that I was deprived of the Nordfjord fief in Norway about Michaelmas-time, just after the coronation, I therefore consider that I ought to have whatever rent and income accrued from it in the half-year before — of which, however, I have to this day received [but] a trifling thing, although I have several times written up there about it. I would therefore most amicably have asked you to be so good as to grant me your good letter to the castellan of Bergenhus, that he would so arrange it that I, or my attorney, might at the first [opportunity] receive in good order whatever remains [owing] to me there and ought by right to be mine. Dear Lord Steward, think no ill of me that I trouble you herewith; I still expect all good of you, and trust you so well that, both in this and in other ways, you will consider the circumstance and be helpful to me for the best in all that is fair and right, and that may be possible for you to do. In whatever way I can do anything in return from which you may have honour and good, I will always [be found], with all gratitude, wholly [willing and] ready thereto. And I will not now detain you any longer, but, now and always, [will have] commended you to God Almighty.

Given at Wandsbek near Hamburg, the 28th day of May, the year 1598.
Tyge Brahe.
[His] own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Christoffer Valkendorf til Glorup** (1525–1601), **Rigshofmester** (Lord High Steward of Denmark) and member of the *Rigsraad* (Council of the Realm) — the senior crown officer Tycho also approached (jointly with Chancellor Christian Friis) in the intercession letters of early 1598 (cf. brahe-t_15980125001). The MS is the **original letter** in Valkendorf's own private archive at the Rigsarkivet. *Tycho addresses him in warm terms* (*min synderlige gode ven*) — notable, since Valkendorf had earlier been counted among Tycho's adversaries at court; here he is the helpful patron of Tycho's Hven bailiff.
- **Setting.** Written from **Wandsbek** (the Rantzau estate near Hamburg) in May 1598, during Tycho's post-Hven exile, the year he printed the *Mechanica* and the *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* there. Tycho has left Hven (1597) but **still holds the island and its tenants in absentia**, his *foged* (bailiff) managing it.
- **Two requests.**
 1. **Thanks for backing the bailiff.** Valkendorf has repeatedly given the Hven bailiff "good assistance and counsel" in disputes with the island's *bønder* (peasant tenants); Tycho thanks him and vents about the tenants' *mootvillige och ulydige* ("wilful and disobedient") conduct during his own residence — a candid grievance over the long-running friction between Tycho and the Hven peasantry (the corvée and tenancy disputes that dog his lordship of the island).
 2. **The Nordfjord arrears.** Tycho had been **stripped of the Nordfjord fief (*forlening*) in Norway about Michaelmas (29 Sept) 1596, "just after the coronation"** — i.e. just after Christian IV's coronation (29 August 1596), one of the deprivations that marked the new reign's withdrawal of favour. He claims the **rent and income for the preceding half-year**, of which he has had only "a trifling thing," and asks Valkendorf for a letter to the **castellan of Bergenhus** (the royal *slotsherre* at Bergen) so that he or his attorney may collect the arrears.
- **Persons & places named.** Christoffer Valkendorf; Tycho's (unnamed) Hven bailiff; the peasants of **Hven**; the **castellan of Bergenhus**; the **Nordfjord** fief; *krøningen* = the **coronation of Christian IV** (1596).
- **Register / orthography.** Chancery Early Modern Danish in Tycho's own warm-but-deferential register; period spellings (*hillsen, wennligen, fougidt, forlening, schriffuellse*), German-influenced *sch-/w-/-ck* (note this orthography elsewhere causes mis-tagging of Danish letters as German — this chapter's convention). Subscription *Egen hand* ("[his] own hand"), the Danish equivalent of *manu propria*.
- **Editorial brackets.** The square brackets in the source — *[y]*, *[findes]*, *[villig och]* — are the **edition's restorations** of small gaps/abrasions in the original, supplying obvious words; they do not affect the sense and are reproduced as printed.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *28 dag maij aar 1598* at Wandsbek; **Old Style (Julian)**, as Denmark and Tycho kept it. The edition label agrees (1598. 28. maj) — no discrepancy.

Collated the full Danish letter — the Hven bailiff/peasants passage, the Nordfjord fief and Michaelmas/coronation reference, the Bergenhus castellan request, and the bracketed damaged-manuscript supplements ([y], [villig och]) — word-for-word against the printed page. documents.title: Thaddaeus Hagecius → Tycho Brahe — Prague, 30 May 1598 [N.S.]

edition.print_label: Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia (1913–29)
edition.tboo_cite: Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, ed. I.L.E. Dreyer, Tom. VIII, Hauniæ 1925, p. 68

witnesses.raw: A København, Rigsarkivet, Langebeks diplomatarium. Afskrift

documents.abstract: Urges Tycho to come to Prague without delay, reporting that Vice-Chancellor Coraduz has commended him favourably to the Emperor.
documents.incipit: NOBILISSIME Domine TYCHO et amice observande, scripsi tibi propemodum ante mensem …

text.original:
THADDÆUS HAGECIUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

NOBILISSIME Domine TYCHO et amice observande, scripsi tibi propemodum ante mensem integrum, et cum hucusque nihil rescripseris, nisi forte tardiusculæ ad te pervenerunt meæ, te ipsum exspectabam, exspectoque etiamnum. Dominus Procancellarius CORADUCIUS diebus hisce me allocutus est, et dixit te iam Cæsari de meliori nota commendasse, modo ipse venias, et te Cæsari præsentes; in hoc solo cardo rei vertitur.

Aliud, quod scribam, non habeo, nisi ut quamprimum ad nos advoles.

B. V.
Pragæ penult. Maij novo Stylo 1598.
T. THAD.
text.english:
**Thaddaeus Hagecius to Tycho Brahe.**

Most noble Master Tycho and esteemed friend, I wrote to you almost a full month ago, and since up to now you have written nothing back — unless perhaps my letters reached you somewhat late — I was awaiting your own self, and await you even now. Master Vice-Chancellor Coraduz addressed me in these days, and said that he had already commended you to the Emperor in the most favourable terms, provided only you come yourself and present yourself to the Emperor: on this alone the hinge of the matter turns.

I have nothing else to write, except that you fly to us as soon as possible.

Fare well.
Prague, the penultimate [day] of May, New Style, 1598.
Yours, Thaddaeus.

documents.incipit: CLARISSIME et praestantissime vir, quas in Decembri superioris anni ante semestre Basileâ …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO DOCTORI IO. IACOBO GRYNÆO, APUD BASILIENSES VERBI MINISTRO ET IN INCLYTA ILLA ACADEMIA PROFESSORI CELEBERRIMO, AMICO SUO HONORANDO. BASEL.

CLARISSIME et praestantissime vir, quas in Decembri superioris anni ante semestre Basileâ ad me dedisti literas, recte quidem accepi, quibus tamen rescribendi nulla sese obtulit interea commoditas, antequam idem, qui tuas reddidit tabellarius, e Dania reversus, et ad vos denuo pergens, hac transiret, quare moram hanc candide accipias rogo. Non possum non ingentes tibi agere gratias, optime GRYNÆE, quod de me, utut longa viarum intercapedine dissito, tibique de facie ignoto, adeo benevole et sincere sentires, et ea quae mihi ob quorundam in Patria livorem et malevolentiam, crassâ veri ignorantiâ, sive per imprudentiam, sive datâ operâ, non dixerim, coniunctam ab inexpectato, et aliter quam forte promeritus eram, evenerunt, tibi adeo cordi esse sinas, ut huic rerum nostrarum conturbationi condoleas, meque consoleris et confirmes. Debemus equidem omnes prae caeteris Regionibus, plurimum Patriae, quae nos edidit, excepit et fovit. At quid faciendum, si haec gratitudinem nostram respuat, neque bene merita agnoscat, imo pro his quaevis incommoda et damna machinetur otiumque et commoditatem virtuti rebusque bonis operam navandi interturbet atque praeripiat? Et quis quaeso Patriae suae mores atque iudicia subinde perversa in hac mundanae scenae confusione et irregularitate unquam corriget? praesertim hoc saeculo, quando omnia videntur in peius ruere. Ferenda igitur sunt forti et constanti animo, quae caveri et emendari nequeunt, et de verâ illa ac Coelesti potius Patriâ omnis turbulentiae et enormitatis experte, serio cogitandum eoque anhelandum. Interim vero dum in hoc terrestri versamur exilio, eas quae nobis obveniunt graviores interdum adversitates, quam ijs sustinendis pares simus, siquidem avertere non datur, loci mutatione declinare atque evitare licitum existimo; ideoque et ego a gravioribus iniurijs, quas non paucas a quibusdam nostratium, qui nunc fatis Reipublicae ferme soli praeesse volunt, pertuli, totque fluctibus et tempestatibus in Germaniam discedendo, auxiliante Coelesti Numine, me vindicavi: sperans tranquilliorem et tutiorem me hîc inventurum portum. Quam arduae vero caussae me eo impulerint, verbis eloqui non facile datur, nec satis consultum arbitror, si quis ea, quae in Insula illa Hellesponti Danici, quam inhabitavi, molitus sum tot praeterlapsis annis, quaeque abiens isthic effecta reliqui, conspexerit expenderitque, non obscure vel hinc colliget gravissima fuisse illa, quae me haec omnia posthabere et Patrium solum deserere totamque familiam in Germaniam transferre adegerunt. Habet praesens tabellarius secum librum quendam hîc per otium hybernum excusum, quem meo permissu Nepoti ex fratre OTTHONI BRAHE, qui cum suo praeceptore in vestra laudatissima Academia aliquandiu antea versatus est, filius meus natu maior dono mittit; hunc si tantum tibi a gravioribus officij tui curis superest otij, ut quaedam in eo perlustrare vacet, mandavi tabellario, ut dum isthic moratur, tibi inspiciendi copiam faciat; cognosces hinc utcunque, veluti opinor, praesertim ex ijs, quae appendicis loco de structuris addidi, et quae infra Insulae topographiam consignata sunt, mihi antea non fuisse in animo talia unâ cum tota Patria totque in ea sanguine iunctis et amicis derelinquere. Adiuncta sunt eidem libro quaedam carmina manu scripta, quae hanc mutationem aliquatenus attingunt, quod si ea etiam percurrere commodum fuerit, erit tibi id liberum. Sed desino de his plura.

Ego hanc sortem, quae mihi contigit, lubens et fortiter, Divinâ favente clementiâ, feram, nec quidpiam inde movebor aut cursum a virtutis tramite remittam, quamvis mihi unâ cum meis extra Natale solum in peregrinis oris reliquum vitae, prout Deo visum fuerit, transigendum sit, nec enim Patriam hisce terreni globi angustis limitibus metior. Sed perinde esse duco, ubi quis in huius terrae superficie degat, modo bene et commode degat, nec contra conscientiam quidpiam agere aut admittere cogatur. Domino HENRICO RANZOVIO, affini et amico meo honorando, literas tuas praelegi curavi, illique ex te salutem dixi; is vicissim te peramanter resalutat, gratumque illi fuit, quod tam honorifice de illo scripseris et senseris. ANTHONIUM RANZOVIUM nondum convenire licuit, neque mihi constat, ubi is moretur; cum dabitur occasio, huic etiam tuo nomine salutem nunciari curabo. Plura nunc ob occupationum molem addere non vacat. Haec itaque qualiacunque subito effusa boni consulas, et amicitiam inter nos semel per literas contractam hac etiam ratione, siquidem aliter non liceat, conservare non desinas. Deus te cum tota domo incolumem conservet et a malis tueatur.

Dabantur Wandesburgo die 7. Iunij Anni 98.
Tuae excell. studiosiss.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and excellent man, Doctor Johann Jacob Grynaeus, minister of the Word among the people of Basel and most celebrated professor in that renowned Academy, his honoured friend. Basel.**

Most renowned and excellent man: the letter you sent me from Basel half a year ago, in December of last year, I did indeed duly receive — but no convenient means of writing back offered itself in the meantime, until the same carrier who delivered yours, returning from Denmark and proceeding again to you, passed this way; wherefore I beg you take this delay in good part. I cannot but give you the greatest thanks, excellent Grynaeus, that — of me, though sundered by a long stretch of road and unknown to you by face — you should think so benevolently and sincerely, and should let those things which befell me, **through the envy and malevolence of certain men in my fatherland** (out of gross ignorance of the truth, whether through imprudence or by design I will not say — combined, unlooked-for, and otherwise than perhaps I had deserved), so touch your heart, that you grieve with me at this disturbance of my affairs, and console and strengthen me. We all owe, beyond other regions, most to the **fatherland that brought us forth, received and cherished us**. But what is to be done, **if it spurns our gratitude, and does not acknowledge good deserts — nay, contrives against them all manner of harms and losses, and disturbs and snatches away the leisure and convenience for devoting one's labour to virtue and good things?** And who, pray, will ever correct the manners and the often perverse judgements of his fatherland, in this confusion and irregularity of the worldly stage — especially in this age, when all things seem to rush to the worse? The things, then, that cannot be guarded against and amended must be borne with a brave and constant mind; and we must think seriously of, and pant after, that **true and Heavenly fatherland**, free of all turbulence and enormity. But meanwhile, while we dwell in this earthly exile, the graver adversities that sometimes come upon us — heavier than we are equal to bearing — if we are not granted to avert them, **I hold it licit to decline and avoid by a change of place**. And so I too, from the graver injuries (not few) which I suffered from certain of my countrymen — **who now wish to preside almost alone over the fortunes of the Commonwealth** — and from so many waves and tempests, by departing into Germany, with Heaven's aid, vindicated myself, **hoping to find here a calmer and safer harbour**. By what hard causes I was driven thither it is not easy to express in words; yet I think it not ill-advised [to say that] **whoever shall have beheld and weighed what I wrought, over so many past years, on that Island of the Danish Hellespont which I inhabited, and what I left finished there on departing**, will gather even hence, not obscurely, that those things were most grievous which forced me to set all this behind me, to desert my native soil, and to transfer my whole family into Germany. The present carrier has with him **a certain book, printed here over the winter's leisure**, which, with my permission, my elder son sends as a gift to **my brother's son, Otto Brahe** — who for some time previously studied, with his tutor, in your most praised Academy. If you have so much leisure left over from the graver cares of your office that you may scan some things in it, I have charged the carrier, while he stays there, to give you the chance of inspecting it. You will recognise hence in some measure, as I think — **especially from what I added by way of appendix, concerning the structures, and what is set down below as the topography of the Island** — that it was not formerly in my mind to abandon such things, together with my whole fatherland and so many bound to me there by blood and friendship. There are also **joined to the same book certain poems in manuscript, which touch this change [of fortune] in some degree**; if it be convenient to run through these too, that is free to you. But I cease to say more of these matters.

This lot which has befallen me I will bear gladly and bravely, by Divine clemency favouring, nor will I be moved by it at all, nor slacken my course from the path of virtue, although I, together with mine, must pass the remainder of my life outside my native soil, on foreign shores, as it shall seem good to God; **for I do not measure my fatherland by these narrow limits of the terrestrial globe.** But I judge it all one where a man lives on the surface of this earth, provided he live well and conveniently, and be not compelled to do or admit anything against conscience. I had your letter read aloud to **Lord Heinrich Rantzau**, my honoured relation and friend, and gave him your greeting from you; he in turn most lovingly returns your greeting, and it was welcome to him that you wrote and thought so honourably of him. **Anton Rantzau** I have not yet been able to meet, nor do I know where he stays; when occasion is given, I will see that a greeting be announced to him too in your name. More I have no leisure to add now, on account of the mass of occupations. So take in good part these things, of whatever quality, suddenly poured out; and do not cease to preserve, by this means too (if it may not be otherwise), the friendship once contracted between us by letter. May God preserve you, with your whole house, unharmed, and guard you from evils.

Given at Wandsbek, the 7th of June, the year [15]98.
Most zealous of your excellency,
**Tycho Brahe**, in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Johann Jacob Grynaeus** (1540–1617), the Basel Reformed theologian, *antistes* and professor — an admirer who had written to console Tycho (a stranger by face) over his troubles. The exchange is courteous and warm; this is Tycho's reply.
- **Significance — Tycho's *apologia* for leaving Denmark (one of the central documents of the self-exile).** The letter is Tycho's reasoned, dignified justification for abandoning Hven:
 - The **meditation on *Patria***: we owe most to the fatherland that bore us, *but* "if it spurns our gratitude … contrives all manner of harms … snatches away the leisure for virtue" — who can correct a fatherland's perverse judgements? One must bear what cannot be amended and long for the **"true and Heavenly fatherland."**
 - The doctrine of licit departure: when adversities exceed our strength and cannot be averted, **"I hold it licit to decline them by a change of place"** — hence Tycho's withdrawal "from the graver injuries I suffered from certain of my countrymen, who now wish to preside almost alone over the fortunes of the Commonwealth" (a pointed allusion to the regency faction under Christian IV's minority — Christoffer Valkendorf and the council).
 - The cosmopolitan close: **"I do not measure my fatherland by these narrow limits of the terrestrial globe"** — it matters not where on earth one lives, provided one live well and not against conscience.
- **Hven named — "the Island of the Danish Hellespont."** *Insula illa Hellesponti Danici, quam inhabitavi* = **Hven**, in the Øresund (the "Danish Hellespont," the Sound). Tycho invokes "what I wrought there over so many years, and what I left finished on departing" as silent proof that he never meant to abandon it.
- **The enclosed book = the *Astronomiae Instauratae Mechanica*** (Wandsbek 1598) — *librum quendam hîc per otium hybernum excusum*, "a book printed here over the winter's leisure," whose self-description clinches the identification: it contains an **appendix "concerning the structures"** (the descriptions of **Uraniborg and Stjerneborg**) and **"the topography of the Island"** (the Hven map) — exactly the *Mechanica*'s closing matter. Tycho's **elder son** sends a **gift copy** to **Otto Brahe** (Tycho's brother's son, formerly a student at Basel), routed via **Grynaeus**. *(A documented Mechanica gift-distribution event — see cross-references below.)*
- **The manuscript poems.** *Carmina manu scripta … quae hanc mutationem … attingunt* — handwritten poems "touching this change of fortune," i.e. Tycho's **elegiac verses on his departure from Denmark** (the *Elegia* addressed to Dania / Urania that circulated with the exile), sent loose with the book.
- **The Rantzaus.** **Heinrich Rantzau** (*Henricus Ranzovius*, 1526–1598), the great Holstein statesman-humanist and Tycho's host-patron (Wandsbek was his estate), to whom Tycho read Grynaeus's letter aloud — Rantzau returns warm greetings. **Anton Rantzau**, a kinsman, not yet met.
- **Persons & places named.** Johann Jacob Grynaeus; **Otto Brahe** (nephew, at Basel); Tycho's **elder son** (unnamed; Tycho Brahe the Younger); **Heinrich Rantzau**; **Anton Rantzau**; the unnamed Danish regency faction. Places: **Wandsbek**, **Basel**, **Hven** ("Island of the Danish Hellespont"), Denmark, Germany.
- **Cross-references.** A documented **Mechanica distribution event** — the gift copy (Tycho the Younger → Otto Brahe, via Grynaeus, Basel, June 1598) belongs to the documented distribution history of the *Mechanica*; the apologia itself belongs with the Hven-surrender / self-exile thread.
- **Calendar.** Holstein was **Old Style** in 1598; no *stylo* marker; dateline **7 June 1598** read **Old Style** (per the catalogue label). Header left unqualified to match.
- **Correction.** Latin corrected against Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia VIII, page 70: "aliquando" corrected to "aliquandiu"; the English clause describing Otto Brahe's time at Basel, which had followed the corrupted reading, corrected from "once before studied" to "for some time previously studied".

text.original:
GEORGIUS ROLLENHAGIUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

S.

ETSI nihil erat, Nobilissime et Doctissime TYCHO, quod ad te praecipue nunc scriberem, tamen cum forte accederet me Tabellarius Lipsicus, volui te hisce salutare, et quae meus affinis ad me de URSO et de exspectatione tui scribit, tecum communicare. Is affinis meus arte quidem est gemmarum scalptor ingeniosus, sed officio apparitor Caesaris, estque hoc eius, quod mitto, chirographum, ut si nota tibi iam tamen sint, intelligas ibi quoque innotuisse; sin ignota, deliberes, quid ad eam exspectationem tibi sit faciendum. Quod bene vertat ad salutem tuam et Uranies Deus Opt. Max., cum Illmo D. Brunsvicensi de negotio tuo locutus sum. Ille quidem praeclare de te sentit, sed Regni et Regis desertionem causatur. Et quamvis causas declararem tuas, et Regem ab alijs regi dicerem, tamen mansit in sententia, ideo quod a suis Nobilibus se deseri, et coram camera accusari molestissime fert. Coniunx existimabat exspectandam esse occasionem, qua coram Regem ipsum convenires: sic omnia facile te impetraturum. Princeps in vinculis habet PETRUM HAGEN L. L. Salderiorum advocatum. Ipsos quoque fratres Salderios Lemgaviae sub Comite Lipiensi nuper coepit, propediem eosdem in Lycaoniam suam attracturus. Habent enim Leones Leonina ingenia. Deus, in cuius manu est cor Principis, dirigat illud ad clementiam et iustitiam. Saluto generosum senem Maecenatem meum D. HENRICUM RANZOVIUM, eique facilem, viridem, et laetam senectutem precor. Pestis grassatur passim in vicinia, praesertim Halberstadij, et ad nos eius semina quaedam allata sunt. Deus avertat ulteriora.

Vale.
Datae die 18. Iunij Anno 98.

EXEMPLUM LITERARUM GERMANICARUM QUÆ LATINIS
HISCE INCLUSÆ ERANT.

MEIN gandtzwillig dienst jedertzeit beuor. Insunder
gunstiger her Swager, das es Euch, samt Euhren lieben Hausfrauwen
wolginge, frisch vnd gesundt wehrt, solde mir lieb sein. Ick danck Godt
den Almechtigen vor liebes gesundheit, der erhalte uns ferner nac seinem
willen, amen.

Nachdem mir der Her Swager vor diesem
von des VRSI halben gescriben, hab ich
ein weinig nachfrag gehabt allhie bei Ihr May. Camerdiener, ob
derselbige VRSUS im vngnaden wehre bey
Ihr May. saa hab ich den bericht bekommen, das ehr woll nicht im
vngnaden sei, alleine das ehr sich vor viell ausßgeben vndt itzundt
nicht sich befindet, vnd in astrologia das geringest nicht vorstehet
etc. Es hatt sich also begeben, das ehr von Ihr May. ist probiert
worden, mit des Fürsten von Siebenbürgen seiner natiuitet, darinne er
wider den anfangk, noch ende gewust, dadurch ehr in
vorachtung vnd vorlachung kommen, vnd dieweil ehr das ziell vnd die
warheit nicht gesetzt, vnd sein judicium falsch, will itzundt dagegen
scriben, vnd vorachtet vnd scalliert die Astrologiam aus das Höegste
auss, es sein lauter lügen vnd bedrug darin, da ehr sie doch von ersten
gelobt vnd dardurch zu Ihr May. gekommen. Die ander vrsach ist das wi
man ihm gefragt worumb ehr den sich zu hoff angegeben darfür, vnd Ihr.
May. Herrn Brüdters Höegstseliger gedechnusß Ihr Thema gemacht (welch
sich recht befunden) vnd itzundt dar wider sei, hat er nichts wissen
zubeantworden. Man hat aber ehrfaren, das ehr solchs nicht selbst
gemacht, sondern auss des ELIÆ
PREUSENS seinen Büchern genommen, vnd sich dardurch also
herfür gethan etc. So hab ich auch vornommen, das TICHO BRAHE alhier
ahn vnsern hoff wirdt kommen, vnd Ihr. May. grosse vorlangen nach ihm
haben, vnd werden ihm ein Sloß ihngeben drey meil wegs von Prag, dar
ehr seinen residentz soll haben, ein seer lustiger Ort, Brandeiss genant.
Deß von DIEFFENBACHS Söne sein alhier zu Prag, die werden nach
Strasburg geschicht zu studiern, vnd wen der Her Swager will schrieben
an die örter, dar ehr meint, will ichs woll behendigen, vnd habe gutte
gelegenheitt darzu. Sonsten aus diesmal nicht mehr.

Den Godt beuohlen
samt Euhren lieben Hausfrauwen vnd kinder, vnd von
mihr vnd meinen Hausfrauwen gegrüst.

Datum Prag den lesten May stylo
nouo 98 Anno.

E. D. W . Swager vnd
Discipulus
CASPAR
LEHMAN
Röm. Kay. Maytt Hartschir.
text.english:
**Georg Rollenhagen to Tycho Brahe.**

Greeting.

Although there was nothing, most noble and most learned Tycho, that I should especially write to you now, yet, since the Leipzig courier happened to come to me, I wished to greet you with these [lines], and to share with you what my kinsman writes to me about Ursus and about the expectation of you. This kinsman of mine is, by art, indeed an ingenious engraver of gems, but, by office, an apparitor [usher] of the Emperor; and this which I send is his own handwriting, so that — if these things are nonetheless already known to you — you may understand that they have become known there too; but if [they are] unknown, you may deliberate what you ought to do in regard to that expectation. May God Best and Greatest turn it well to your welfare and Urania's: I have spoken with the Most Illustrious Lord of Brunswick about your business. He indeed thinks excellently of you, but pleads [as an objection] the desertion of the Kingdom and the King. And although I declared your reasons, and said that the King is ruled by others, he yet remained in [his] opinion — for the reason that he most grievously resents being deserted by his own nobles, and accused before the [imperial] chamber. His consort thought that the occasion must be awaited on which you might meet the King himself in person: thus you would easily obtain everything. The Prince holds in chains Peter Hagen, advocate-at-law of the Salderns. The Saldern brothers themselves, too, he lately seized at Lemgo, under the Count of Lippe — [intending] shortly to drag the same into his own Lycaonia. For Lions have leonine natures. May God, in whose hand is the heart of the Prince, direct it to clemency and justice. I salute the generous old man, my Maecenas, Master Heinrich Rantzau, and pray him an easy, green, and glad old age. Plague rages here and there in the vicinity, especially at Halberstadt, and certain seeds of it have been brought to us. May God avert worse.

Farewell.
Given the 18th day of June, in the year [15]98.

**Copy of a German letter, which was enclosed within this Latin one.**

My wholly willing service, always beforehand. Especially favouring Lord brother-in-law: that it should go well with you, together with your dear wife, that you be fresh and healthy, would be dear to me. I thank God the Almighty for my own dear health; may He preserve us further according to His will, amen.

Since my Lord brother-in-law wrote to me before this concerning Ursus, I have made a little inquiry here with His Majesty's chamber-servant, whether the same Ursus were in disfavour with His Majesty; and I have received word that he is indeed not in disfavour, only that he gave himself out for much [more than he is], and now does not find himself equal to it, and understands the least thing in astrology not at all, etc. It has thus come about that he was put to the test by His Majesty with the nativity of the Prince of Transylvania, in which he knew neither the beginning nor the end, whereby he has fallen into contempt and mockery; and since he did not set down the mark and the truth, and his judgment was false, he now wishes to write against it [astrology], and disdains and reviles Astrology to the very utmost, [saying] that there is nothing in it but sheer lies and deceit — though he indeed praised it at first, and thereby came to His Majesty. The other reason is that, when he was asked why he had put himself forward at court on this account, and had cast the horoscope [Thema] of His Majesty's late brother of most blessed memory (which was found to be correct), and is now against it, he had nothing he knew how to answer. But it has been found out that he did not make this himself, but took it out of the books of Elias Preuss, and thereby made himself prominent, etc.

I have also learned that Tycho Brahe is to come here to our court, and that His Majesty has a great longing for him, and that they will give him a castle three miles' way from Prague, where he is to have his residence — a very pleasant place, called Brandeis. The sons of [Herr] von Dieffenbach are here at Prague; they are to be sent to Strasbourg to study; and if my Lord brother-in-law wishes to write to the places he has in mind, I will gladly deliver it, having good occasion for it. Otherwise, for this time, no more.

Herewith commended to God, together with your dear wife and children, and greeted from me and my wife.

Given at Prague, the last of May, new style, in the year [15]98.

Your Lordship's willing [servant,] brother-in-law and disciple, Caspar Lehman, halberdier of the Roman Imperial Majesty.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Georg Rollenhagen** (1542–1609) of **Magdeburg** (the place not in the dateline but established by the later instrument-transport letter brahe-t_16000619001); Tycho's agent and friend.
- **The Ursus intelligence.** Rollenhagen forwards news, in the hand (*chirographum*) of **his kinsman** — "by art an ingenious gem-engraver, by office an Imperial **apparitor** [court usher]" — about **Ursus** (Nicolai Reimers Bär, Tycho's rival, then Imperial Mathematician) and about the **expectation of Tycho** at the imperial court; Tycho is to weigh how to act. (This is two years before the Ursus suppression of brahe-t_16000727001.)
- **The Duke of Brunswick.** *Illmus D. Brunsvicensis* = **Heinrich Julius, Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel** (1564–1613), often at the imperial court. He esteems Tycho but objects to his "**desertion of the Kingdom and the King**" (of Denmark) — the recurrent reproach of Tycho's self-exile; Rollenhagen pleaded that "the [Danish] King is ruled by others." The Duke's *consort* advised that Tycho should wait to meet the Danish king in person.
- **The Saldern affair.** *Petrus Hagen, L[egum] L[icentiatus], Salderiorum advocatus* — Peter Hagen, legal advocate of the **von Saldern** family, imprisoned by the Duke; the **Saldern brothers** seized at **Lemgo** (under the **Count of Lippe**) — a contemporary noble feud. *in Lycaoniam suam attractare* / *Leones Leonina ingenia* — a play on the Duke's wolfish/leonine harshness (*Lycaon* the wolf-king; "lions have leonine natures"). The whole sentence is wordplay on the Duke's reputation for ruthlessness toward refractory nobles.
- ***Maecenas meus … Henricus Ranzovius*** = **Heinrich Rantzau**, the aged patron, wished "an easy, green, and glad old age." *Pestis … Halberstadij* — plague at **Halberstadt**, spreading.
- **Calendar.** *die 18. Iunij Anno 98* = **18 June 1598**; Magdeburg (Lutheran) = **Old Style**. Header agrees with the label.
- **What it is.** A German newsletter from Prague, dated "the last of May, new style, [15]98," enclosed as an *exemplum literarum Germanicarum* inside Georg Rollenhagen's Latin letter to Tycho of 18 June 1598 O.S. Rollenhagen — the Magdeburg schoolmaster-poet and regular Tycho/Rantzau correspondent (attested repeatedly in Oestmann's *Rantzau und die Astrologie* and Zeeberg's Rantzau studies) — evidently forwarded it to Tycho as court intelligence.
- **The writer, identified.** Signed "Caspar Lehman, Röm. Kay. Mayt. Hartschier" [halberdier/guardsman of the Roman Imperial Majesty] — this is almost certainly Caspar Lehmann (d. 1622), Rudolf II's imperial gem- and glass-cutter at Prague, later renowned as the founder of German glass engraving. Christianson, *On Tycho's Island* (Cambridge, 2000), independently records that "an imperial astrologer and gem artist, Caspar Lehmann, acted as Tycho's informer" and "sent the welcome news that Ursus had displayed his own dishonesty and lack of skill to the emperor and was no longer in favor" (n.56) — almost word for word the content recovered here, strongly suggesting this letter is, or directly feeds, that very report.
- **Ursus's disgrace.** Nicolaus Reimers Ursus — Tycho's rival, then Rudolf II's Imperial Mathematician — is reported to have been tested by the emperor with the nativity of the Prince of Transylvania and to have failed conspicuously, his earlier (correct) horoscope of the Emperor's late brother exposed as lifted from the books of one "Elias Preuss" — not identified in the works consulted, and to be distinguished from Tycho's own former Uraniborg assistant Elias Olai Cimber (Elias Olsen Morsing).
- **Tycho's move to Prague, anticipated over a year early.** Already by May 1598 — a full year before Tycho actually reached Bohemia and settled at Benátky in August 1599 — Prague court gossip had it that Tycho "will come here to our court" and would be given a castle three miles from Prague called "Brandeis" [Brandýs nad Labem]. Dreyer records that Rudolf later did offer Tycho a choice among Lyssa, Brandeis and Benátky, of which Tycho chose Benátky; this letter shows the plan, and the specific castle, already circulating as rumor well before the event.
- Crux: "Elias Preusens," "von Dieffenbach," and the unnamed deceased "Herr Bruder" of the Emperor (whose nativity Ursus reportedly cast correctly — most likely Archduke Ernst of Austria, d. 1595, but not independently confirmed here) are not resolved in the works consulted. The closing abbreviation "E. D. W." before "Swager vndt Discipulus" is of uncertain expansion; rendered loosely as "Your Lordship's willing [servant]."
- **Correction.** Latin corrected from 'attractare' to 'attracturus' per Dreyer, TBOO VIII p.72.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter (Latin body + the enclosed German letter from Caspar Lehman, both in full) against Dreyer TBOO VIII pp. 72-73, read as page images (the letter opens and closes entirely within these two pages). Checked every proper name (Petrus Hagen, the Saldern brothers, Heinrich Rantzau, Elias Preuss, Tycho Brahe, the von Dieffenbach sons, Caspar Lehman), place (Lemgo, Halberstadt, Brandeis/Brandeiss, Prague, Strasbourg), and date (18 June / last of May new style, 1598). Found one text error (the transcribed original 'attractare' vs Dreyer's 'attracturus') which does not itself corrupt the sense conveyed in the English. No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found. Per the grading rule any text error caps the grade at C even though this one is low-severity and the translation's sense is unaffected; verdict is *minor*, not *serious*.

**1 defect found:**
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original prints the infinitive 'attractare' where Dreyer prints the future participle 'attracturus'. A genuine word-form departure from Dreyer, not a spelling convention. It does not corrupt the translation itself: the published English ('[intending] shortly to drag') actually renders the sense of Dreyer's real 'attracturus' correctly, better than it would render the transcribed original's 'attractare'. Dreyer prints: *propediem eofdem in Lycaoniam fuam attracturus (p.72)*.

**Repaired.** Collated the single defect against the Dreyer page image (TBOO VIII p.72), which clearly reads 'propediem eosdem in Lycaoniam suam attracturus'. The published English already matched Dreyer's sense, so only the Latin required correction. No uncertainty remains in this letter.

text.original:
TAM DOCTRINA EXIMIA QUAM PROSAPIA CLARA VIRO INSIGNITER DECORATO DOMINO OLIGERO ROSENKRANTZIO DE ROSENHOLM, CONSANGVINEO, AFFINI ET AMICO INTIMO.
S. P.

QUAe nuper tibi destinavi, exoptatissime mi OLIGERE consangvinee et affinis carissime, per CLAUDIUM MULÆUM, quem ante Comitia istuc misi, te omnia nunc accepisse non dubito. Succurrit post MULÆI abitum in libro de Astronomia Mechanica pagina quae est G. 3. in qua Domini IACOBI CURTIJ, circa quadrantis cuiusdam subdivisionem, inventio exhibetur, in ipso titulo ante hoc nomen: CURTIO omissam esse literam I. vel potius IAC. unde praenomen eius indicaretur, et postea in infima eiusdem tituli linea impressum est: GENEROSE ADINVENTA pro INGENIOSE ADINVENTA; quod nescio an in eo, quod misi, exemplari emendatum sit; sin minus, cuperem id adhuc abs te calamo, quod facile fit in tam densa papyro, corrigi, ne Zoili et hîc habeant quo abutantur. Quid de literis Berlinensibus actum sit, ex te cognoscere aveo. Si quid in Comitijs illis, quod mea interest scire, tibi innotuit, hoc quidquid est, mature etiam, antequam MULÆUS (modo fieri potest) reversus fuerit, significa. Fuit ante triduum hîc apud me IACOBUS ROSENKRANTZIUS noster, in Belgium hinc cogitans; is graves et difficiles in hisce Comitijs controversias motum iri referebat; et inter alia PEPLERI istius caussam recognoscendam decidendamque existimavit. At quo iure id fieri queat, ignoro, cum citationis forma mihi etiam non sit praesentata, nec quidpiam a Praefecto meo de ea innotuerit, ut existimem, eam ne quidem Uraniburgi lectam esse, aut si id factum, non debito tempore aut modo; sed sit hoc quidquid velit; si ius et fas locum inveniunt, nihil periculi, sin secus, nihil novi. Existimo, imo expertus sum, quod si ego in Dania quidpiam proponerem, quod aeque verum sit atque ea, quae Geometrice demonstrantur, posse nihilominus ea ipsa apud quosdam, qui iustitiae praeesse volunt, falsitatis insimulari. Quid igitur faciendum, ubi ius et veritas ob privatos affectus atque personae odium locum non merentur? Aiebat insuper dictus noster Consangvineus, se exemplum literarum, quas Sermo Regi nostro, cum Rostochij essem, scripsi, unâ cum responso ad easdem, cum Fioniam transiret, apud Nobiles quosdam reperisse, et si recte memini, CANUTUM RUD hîc nominavit, quem a CAROLO BRUSCHIO talia accepisse opinabatur. Quod si sic est, optarem, eos, qui horum facti sunt participes, ea, quae mihi rescripta sunt, rectius quam litera ipsa praetendit, explanata habere, quae incautis et inscijs plausibilis forte videri queat, cum tamen longe aliter res se habeat, et mihi foret quam facilimum, uti ipsemet scis, omnia isthic obiecta replicare et contrario modo demonstrare, sed obstant ea, quae prius dixi, et authoritas eorum, qui haec vafre consarcinarunt, veritati nunc praevalet. Opus igitur est patientia, et tandem bona caussa triumphat, si non in Dania, saltem alibi: O utinam in nos illud Virgilianum non propediem quadraret. Excessere omnes adytis arisque relictis Dij, quibus imperium hoc steterat. Item illud paulo antea: Fuimus Troes, fuit Ilium et ingens gloria Danorum. Solet enim regnum divinitus puniendum sanis destitui consilijs, et in partes quorundam vafritia discindi, atque sub veri bonique praetextu contraria tecte agere. Solent etiam omnia praecedere, qualia non pauca isthic audiuntur, si modo, quae narrantur, veritati congruunt. Cum quaesivissem a praenominato ROSENKRANTZIO de halece characterizato in Norvegia reperto, nihil quidem certi de eo referre potuit, attamen aliud piscium genus, quod latini aculeatum, nostrates Hornfisk vocant, adhuc longe mirabilioribus notatum characteribus nuper prope insulam Tossingam, seu potius parvulam illi adiacentem, repertum esse, certissime affirmavit; quarum figurarum, si tibi hac de re quid constat, efformationem mecum communicari vellem. Scripsit mihi postea CRAMERUS tuus, et carmen quoddam literis inclusit. Misit etiam BRASCHIUS Poëta Rostochiensis Heroicum in mei gratiam concinnatum, sed neutrum satis placet; habes tamen hîc utrumque, Cramerianum ipsius manu scriptum, unâ cum literis, prout accepi; neque enim describendi otium suppetit; quod tamen, cum exemplum eius non habeam, mihi remitti velim. Habeo praeterea alia eiusmodi, inter quae est quoddam ex orientali Frisia admodum prolixum; et cuduntur hinc inde adhuc plura in memoriam rei apud nos bene gestae. Expectat autem Germania avide tuum pro vicina sua responsum. Expecto et ego commentaria illa, quae scis, quibus mea per oportunitatem intertexam; ubi vero tua absoluta fuerint, ea cum KRAGIO nostro tacite communica, ut et is ex rei transactae historia, quam pro maiori parte novit, suam quoque interponat sententiam. Exemplum earum, quas THADDÆUS HAGGÆCIUS ante aliquot hebdomadas Praga mihi scripsit, Domino Doctori NICOLAO KRAGIO iam antea misi, qui procul dubio te eius reddidit participem. Sed et hisce diebus breves quasdam ab eodem THADDÆO denuo accepi, quarum hîc habes descriptum; paucioribus rem expedit, siquidem dubitavit an hîc essem, an vero iter Pragam versus suscepissem; vides eos serio meum adventum expetere et expectare, atque ipsi Caesari me concernentia iam innotuisse. Tu et KRAGIUS consulite in medium, et aliorum quoque, quibus res meae serio et sincere cordi sunt, sententiam tacite expiscemini. Ego nihil certi concludere possum, antequam TEGNAGLIUS et MULÆUS ad me reversi fuerint. Fuit hesterna die apud me Dominus Doctor VITUS WINSHEMIUS a comitibus Oldenburgensibus, ubi dissidij cuiusdam inter eos componendi caussa adfuerat, iam primum reversus; is inter alia de Doctore BŒKELIO rettulit, ipsum urgere pecuniam sibi pro libris, quos accepisti, promissam; a te vero sibi perscriptum aiebat, ne pecuniam illam eidem BŒKELIO traderet, antequam omnes libros residuos depromeret, quod ipsum praestare aut nolle aut non posse intelligo, et praetendere tres vel quatuor saltem restare, eosque non magni momenti, quique in ipsius non sint potestate. Quaesivit igitur WINSHEMIUS a me, quid illi hac in re faciendum existimarem; suasi, ut tuae voluntati morem gereret et secum pecuniam reservaret, donec alter per omnia tuis desiderijs et suae pollicitationi satisfecisset. At ille excipiebat, sibi brevi Berlinum et in Misniam eundum, BŒKELIUM vero tam diu pecunia carere nolle, imo stomachabundum dixisse, quod mallet libros suos recipere, quam diutius pecuniam istam expectare. Statuimus itaque, ut Dominus Doctor VITUS in sua absentia pecuniam a te missam alteri fidedigno viro ex amicis suis Hamburgi traderet, et si interea responsum a te reciperet (nam se tibi hac de re scripsisse innuebat) filius ipsius, qui isthic remanet, literas tuas aperiret, atque secundum earum contenta negotium hoc exequeretur. Tuum itaque est mature, quid in his fieri vis, significare; si tuo loco essem, aut restituerem illi libros, siquidem sic vult, aut concederem illi pecuniam iam antea addictam, utut pauculos illos libros procurare nolit aut forte nequeat, quo possis ab ipso liberari; est enim paulo morosior, et insuper (quod tamen cum multis commune habet) γυναικοκρατούμενος, Imperatrice eius nimis importuna existente. Cuius rei MULÆUS documentum dabit; ego nihilominus, quidquid hac in re fieri velis, quantum in me est, effectum dabo. Currum, quem promisisti ante Pascha, Pentecostes etiam festi, imo et IOHANNIS BAPTISTAe tempora, frustratus est, et licet Cimber sis, privilegioque gentis gaudeas, tamen te praeter caeterorum morem quidpiam Schanicae constantiae habere, praesertim cum per coniugium in Schanum quodammodo transplanteris, existimarem potius, ideoque per incuriam quandam eorum, quibus hoc negotium mandasti, neglectum esse. Sed sit quidquid velit, nolim tibi hac in parte uti etiam nulla alia gravis esse; saltem scire desidero, quid expectandum sit vel secus, ne frustra alium confieri procurem. De aedibus etiam meis Haffniensibus quid fieri possit vel non, a te certior reddi aveo. Iamque cum utraque tua SOPHIA, addita insuper tertia illa quae et URANIA appellatur, quam felicissime vale; saluta fratrem AXILLUM et alios, si quos mei isthic tangat memoria. Deus vos omnes tueatur a malo.

Dabantur Wandesburgo die 23. Iunij Anni 98.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the man signally adorned as much by eminent learning as by illustrious lineage, Lord Holger Rosenkrantz of Rosenholm, my kinsman, relation, and intimate friend.**
Heartiest greeting.

What I lately destined to you, my most longed-for Holger, kinsman and dearest relation, through **Claus Mule** — whom I sent thither before the Diet — I do not doubt you have now received all. It came to me, after Mule's departure, that **in the book on Mechanical Astronomy [the *Mechanica*], on the page which is G.3, where the invention of Lord Jacob Curtius about the subdivision of a certain quadrant is shown — in the title itself, before this name "Curtio," the letter "I" (or rather "IAC.") is omitted, by which his praenomen would be indicated; and later, in the lowest line of the same title, "GENEROSE ADINVENTA" was printed for "INGENIOSE ADINVENTA."** Whether it is corrected in the copy I sent, I do not know; if not, I should wish it yet to be corrected by you with the pen (which is easy in such dense paper), lest the Zoiluses have here too something to abuse. What was done about the **Berlin letters**, I long to learn from you. If anything in that **Diet** which concerns me to know has become known to you, signify it — whatever it be — in good time, even before Mule returns (if it can be done).

Three days ago **Jacob Rosenkrantz**, our [kinsman], was here with me, thinking [to go] hence into the Low Countries; he reported that grave and difficult controversies would be stirred in this Diet, and among other things judged that **the case of that "Pepler"** would be reviewed and decided. But by what right this can be done, I do not know, since the form of citation was not even presented to me, nor has anything of it become known from my Praefect [the Hven governor] — so that I think it was not even read at Uraniborg, or, if it was, not at the due time or in the due manner. But be this what it will: if right and divine law find place, no danger; if otherwise, nothing new. **I think — nay, I have experienced — that if I should propose anything in Denmark as true as the things that are demonstrated Geometrically, those very things could nonetheless be accused of falsehood [*falsitatis insimulari*] by certain men who wish to preside over justice. What, then, is to be done, when right and truth, on account of private passions and hatred of a person, do not merit a place?**

Our said kinsman said besides that, passing through **Funen**, he found among certain Nobles **a copy of the letters I wrote to our Most Serene King [Christian IV] while I was at Rostock, together with the answer to them**; and, if I remember rightly, he named here **Knud Rud**, who he thought had received such things from **Carl Brusch**. If it is so, I should wish that those who are made partakers of these have the things written back to me **explained more rightly than the letter itself pretends** — which might perhaps seem plausible to the incautious and ignorant, though the matter stands far otherwise; and it would be most easy for me (as you yourself know) to rebut all the objections there and demonstrate the contrary — but the things I said before obstruct [me], and the authority of those who craftily patched these together now prevails over truth. **Patience, then, is needed; and at last the good cause triumphs — if not in Denmark, at least elsewhere.** O would that the Virgilian [line] did not soon fit us: *"All the gods, by whom this empire had stood, have departed, the sanctuaries and altars left"*; likewise that, a little before: *"We have been Trojans; Ilium has been, and the vast glory of the Danes."* For a kingdom that is to be punished by Heaven is wont to be **deprived of sound counsels, and torn into factions by certain men's craft, and, under the pretext of truth and good, to do contrary things covertly**. And all such things are wont to precede [a fall] — not a few of which are heard there, if only what is narrated agrees with the truth.

When I had asked the aforesaid Rosenkrantz about **the "characterized" herring found in Norway** [a herring marked with figures], he could indeed report nothing certain of it; yet he most certainly affirmed that **another kind of fish — which the Latins call *aculeatum*, our people *Hornfisk* [garfish] — marked with far more wonderful characters, was lately found near the island of Tåsinge** (or rather a little [island] adjacent to it); the formation of which figures, if anything is established to you on this matter, I should wish communicated to me. Your **Cramer** afterward wrote me, and enclosed a certain poem in the letter; **Brasch too, the Rostock Poet, sent a Heroic [poem] composed in my honour** — but neither pleases enough. You have both here, however: Cramer's in his own hand, with the letter, as I received it (for I have no leisure to copy it) — which, however, since I have no copy of it, I should wish returned to me. I have besides others of the kind, among which is **a very prolix one from East Frisia**; and more are being struck, here and there, in memory of the matter well done among us. **Germany eagerly awaits your response on behalf of its neighbour [Denmark].** I too await **those commentaries you know of**, in which I may by occasion interweave my own; and when yours are finished, **share them quietly with our Krag [Niels Krag]**, that he too may interpose his opinion, from the history of the transacted matter which he for the greater part knows. A copy of those which **Thaddaeus Hagecius** wrote me from Prague some weeks ago I sent already to Lord Doctor **Nicolaus Krag**, who doubtless made you partaker of it. But these days too I have again received some brief [letters] from the same Thaddaeus, of which you have here the copy; he expedites the matter in fewer words, since he doubted whether I was here, or had set out on the journey toward Prague. **You see they seriously seek and await my arrival, and that things concerning me have already become known to the Emperor himself.** Do you and Krag consult together, and quietly fish out the opinion of others too, to whom my affairs are seriously and sincerely at heart. I can conclude nothing certain before **Tengnagel and Mule** have returned to me.

Yesterday Lord Doctor **Veit Winsheim** was with me, just returned from the Counts of Oldenburg (where he had been to settle a certain dissension among them); he reported, among other things, about Doctor **Bökel** — that he presses for the money promised him for the books you received; but that you had written him not to give Bökel that money before he produced all the remaining books, which I understand he either will not or cannot do, alleging that only three or four remain, of no great moment, and not in his power. Winsheim therefore asked me what I thought he should do in this; I advised that he comply with your will and keep the money by him, until [Bökel] had in all things satisfied your wishes and his own promise. But he objected that he must soon go to Berlin and into Meissen, and that Bökel would not lack the money so long — nay, said stomachfully that he would rather take back his books than wait longer for that money. So we resolved that, in his absence, Lord Doctor Vitus would give the money sent by you to another trustworthy man of his friends at Hamburg; and if meanwhile an answer came from you (for he hinted he had written you of this), his son who remains there would open your letter and execute this business according to its contents. It is for you, then, to signify in good time what you wish done in these. If I were in your place, I would either restore him the books (if he so wishes), or grant him the money already assigned — even though he will not, or perhaps cannot, procure those few books — that you may be freed from him; for he is a bit morose, and besides (which yet he has in common with many) **ruled by his wife [γυναικοκρατούμενος], his Empress being too importunate** — of which Mule will give proof. I nonetheless will give effect, so far as in me lies, to whatever you wish done in this.

The **wagon** which you promised before Easter, then Whitsun, nay and the time of St. John the Baptist [24 June], has disappointed [me]; and though you are a Cimbrian [Jutlander], and enjoy your nation's privilege [of slowness], I should rather think you have something of **Scanian constancy** beyond the custom of the rest — especially since by marriage you are somewhat transplanted into a Scanian — and that therefore it was neglected through some carelessness of those to whom you entrusted this business. But be it what it will: I should not wish to be burdensome to you in this — as in no other thing; I only desire to know what is to be expected, or not, lest I procure another to be made in vain. About my **Copenhagen house**, too, what can be done or not, I long to be made more certain by you. And now, with both your **Sophias** — adding besides that third one which is also called **Urania** — fare most happily. Greet brother **Axel**, and others, if my memory touch any there. May God guard you all from evil.

Given at Wandsbek, the 23rd day of June, the year [15]98.
Yours, **Tycho Brahe.**

Climax: a **dark Virgilian prophecy of Denmark's fall**, quoting *Aeneid* 2 — *"All the gods … have departed"* and *"We have been Trojans … and the vast glory of the Danes"* — a kingdom "to be punished by Heaven" losing sound counsel.

(A datum for the prodigy/portent interest of the age.)
 - **The Prague prospect (June 1598).** Already developing: **Hagecius** writes from Prague (forwarded via **Niels Krag**); "they seriously seek and await my arrival, and things concerning me are already known to the Emperor." Tycho awaits **Tengnagel and Mule** before deciding.

text.original:
COPIA LITERARUM SERENISS: ELECTORIS COLONIENSIS AD DOMINUM HENRICUM RANZOUIUM.

ERNESTUS electus et confirmatus archiep[i]scopus Coloniensis, sacri Romani imperij per Italiam archicancellarius et princeps elector, episcopus Leodiensis, palatinus Rheny, utriusque Bauariæ dux. Clementi salutatione Nostra premissa. Nobilissime singulariter dilecte mihi et illis studijs, in quibus tam preclaram Braheus operam posuit, nihil est nunc gratius et literis a te missis nihil acceptius, et tua etiam commendatione nihil grauius, et ipso Braheo, ut mores et doctrina viri merentur, nihil fuit neque erit commendatius. Vidi, quæ misit sublimibus de illis specimina, mire placuerunt et reliquorum magnam sitim in animo meo excitauerunt. Perge, Ranzoui præstantissime, affinem illum, te dignum, Daniæ totique Germaniæ gloriosum, fouere. Ego, quod potero, et ipsius causa, et quia uideo tibi, quem, ut æquum est, facio maximi, rem curæ esse, diligenter eum, ut feci, cæs: ma:ti commendare pergam, et non committam, ut meam in se beneuolentiam ulla ex parte sentiat claudier. Ex eodem Francisco Tengnaglio hæc eadem copiosius intelliges.

Vale.
Leody xxv junij 1598.
Ernestus mpp.
text.english:
**Copy of the letter of the Most Serene Elector of Cologne to Master Heinrich Rantzau.**

Ernst, elected and confirmed Archbishop of Cologne, Arch-Chancellor of the Holy Roman Empire throughout Italy and Prince-Elector, Bishop of Liège, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of both Bavarias. Our clement greeting premised. Most noble, singularly beloved: to me, and to those studies in which Brahe has placed such distinguished effort, nothing is now more pleasing, and than the letters sent by you nothing more acceptable, and than your recommendation also nothing weightier; and than Brahe himself — as the man's character and learning deserve — nothing was, nor will be, more commended [to me]. I have seen the specimens which he sent concerning those lofty matters; they pleased me marvellously, and excited in my mind a great thirst for the rest. Continue, most excellent Rantzau, to cherish that kinsman of yours — worthy of you, and glorious to Denmark and to all Germany. I, for what I shall be able, both for his sake and because I see that the matter is a care to you (whom, as is just, I esteem most highly), will continue diligently — as I have done — to commend him to His Imperial Majesty, and will not allow him to feel my benevolence toward him to be in any part curtailed. From the same Frans Tengnagel you will understand these same things more copiously.

Farewell.
Liège, the 25th of June, 1598.
Ernst, with his own hand.

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO NOBIS SINGULARITER DILECTO TYCHONI BRAHE, DOMINO DE KNUDSTRUP.

ERNESTUS electus et confirmatus archiepiscopus Coloniensis, sacri Romani imperij per Italiam archicancellarius et princeps elector, episcopus Leodiensis, palatinus Rheny, dux utriusque Bauarie. Clementi Nostra salutatione premissa. Nobilissime singulariter dilecte, quas mihi iuuenis ille notus a te literas dedit et quæ de rebus tuis addidit, singulari lætitia legi et audiui. Munus vero litterarium librorum tuorum, quos ut a te rerum istarum peritissimo profectos et de cœlestibus illis corporibus tractantes, quorum vel solus aspectus idiotarum oculos pascit, cognitio uero et meum et omnium peritorum animos honestiore uoluptate moratur, mihi supra modum fuit acceptum. Gratias pro ijs tibi ago et quod factum a me hactenus non indiligenter, pergam sedulo te tuaque cæs: mti: commendare. Declaraui hunc animi mei sensum latori literarum tuarum et harum relatori. Ex eo intelliges, quæ de omnibus, quæ scire cupiebas, illum feci certiorem. Vale et tibi persuade et tua et studiorum caussa me quiduis conaturum.

Leody xxv iunij 1598.
Ernestus, mpp.
text.english:
**To the most noble, singularly beloved by us, Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup.**

Ernst, elected and confirmed Archbishop of Cologne, Arch-Chancellor of the Holy Roman Empire throughout Italy and Prince-Elector, Bishop of Liège, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of both Bavarias. Our clement greeting premised. Most noble, singularly beloved: the letters which that known youth gave me from you, and the things he added about your affairs, I read and heard with singular gladness. But the literary gift of your books — which, as proceeding from you, most skilled in those matters, and as treating of those celestial bodies whose very sight alone feeds the eyes of the unlearned, but whose knowledge engages both my mind and the minds of all the skilled with a more honourable pleasure — was beyond measure acceptable to me. I give you thanks for them; and, as has been done by me hitherto not undiligently, I will continue diligently to commend you and your affairs to His Imperial Majesty. I have declared this sentiment of my mind to the bearer of your letters and the reporter of these [present ones]. From him you will understand the things whereof I have made him more certain, concerning all that you desired to know. Farewell; and persuade yourself that, both for your sake and for the sake of [your] studies, I will attempt anything.

Liège, the 25th of June, 1598.
Ernst, with his own hand.

documents.incipit: ALLERGNEDIGSTER herr vnd vetter. E: Röm: Kay: Maytt: kann jch in vnterthenigen vertrawen …

text.original:
AN DIE RÖMISKE KAY: MAYTT:.

ALLERGNEDIGSTER herr vnd vetter. E: Röm: Kay: Maytt: kann jch in vnterthenigen vertrawen nicht verhalten, wie das mir der ansehenliche vnd hochberumbte Tycho Brahe gehorsamblich zuerkennen geben, wie daß ehr auß etlichen hochwichtigen vrsachen sein vaterlandt das königreich Dennemarck zuuerlassen, vnd sich mit allen seinen jnstrumentis mathematicis vnter E: Kay: Maytt: allergnedigste protection in dem Teutschlandt niderzuthun, gentzlichen endschlossen sey. Vnd wie woll sein doctrina vnd berumbter löblicher nahme dermasßen jn vnd ausser Teutschlandt nicht allein, sondern auch E: Kay: Maytt: zuuorderst gnedigst woll bekandt, so hat ehr doch auß dem hohen vertrawen, so ehr propter conformia studia zu mir gesetzt, ahn mich gehorsamblich begert, sein personn vnd löbliche intention E: Kay: Maytt: vnterthenigst zu recommendiren. Weil mir dan vorhin wolbewust, dass E: Kay: Maytt: summus fautor vnnd protector aller gelehrter leut, vnndt insonderheit vnter andern dem mathematico studio geneigt sein, so hab jch desto eher diese stoltzigkeit auf mich genommen, dem ehrlichen vnd berumbten man in seinem begeren zuwilfahrenn. Belanget der halben ahn E: Kay: Maytt: mein vnterthenigste bitt, sie wollen jhnen Tycho Brahe sambt seinen studijs in jhren kayserlichen schutz vnnd promotion auf- vnd annehmen, auch sich auf seine weitere vorschleg vnd gehorsamblich begeren dermassen allergnedigst resoluiren, damit ehr Tycho Brahe sehenn vnnd spuhrenn möge, das seine löbliche, hochberumbtte vnd indefessi labores ein gnedigsten mæcenatem bekommen haben. Solche ertzeigte gnadt will nit allein jch, sondern tota Germanica patria wirdt gleichsfalß gegen E: Kay: Maytt: gehorsambst zuuerdienen alletzeit geflisßen sein. Weil auch seine merita dermassen geschaffen, alßo das ehr billich pater astronomorum et unicus hujus laudatissimæ scientiæ restaurator mag genendt werden, so halt jch weitere recommendation vor vnnöttig, sondern das jch vielmehr E: Kay: Maytt: vnterthenigst deßhalben zu congratuliren schuldig mich erkenne, weil derhalben mit meinen weitern schreiben E: Kay: Maytt: nit auffhalten, sondern thue mich derselben zu kayserlichen hulden vnnd gnaden vnterthenigst beuehlenn.

Luttich d. 26. iunij 98.
E: Kay: Maytt: gehorsamer churfurst vnnd vetter
Ernst, ertzbischoff zu Cöllen.
text.english:
**To the Roman Imperial Majesty.**

Most gracious lord and cousin. I cannot, in humble confidence, withhold from Your Roman Imperial Majesty how the distinguished and highly renowned Tycho Brahe has obediently made known to me that he, for several highly weighty reasons, is wholly resolved to leave his fatherland the Kingdom of Denmark, and to settle in Germany, with all his mathematical instruments, under Your Imperial Majesty's most gracious protection. And although his learning and renowned, laudable name are well known not only within and beyond Germany, but also, and above all, most graciously to Your Imperial Majesty, he has nonetheless — out of the high trust he has placed in me on account of our kindred studies — obediently desired of me that I commend his person and laudable intention most humbly to Your Imperial Majesty. Since, then, it was well known to me beforehand that Your Imperial Majesty is the supreme patron and protector of all learned men, and especially inclined, among other [studies], to the mathematical study, I have the more readily taken this boldness upon myself, to comply with the honest and renowned man in his request. There pertains, therefore, to Your Imperial Majesty my most humble petition: that you would take up and receive Tycho Brahe, together with his studies, into your imperial protection and advancement, and would resolve so most graciously upon his further proposals and obedient request, that he, Tycho Brahe, may see and feel that his laudable, most renowned and indefatigable labours have obtained a most gracious Maecenas. Such shown grace not I alone, but the whole German fatherland, will likewise be ever zealous to deserve, most obediently, toward Your Imperial Majesty. And since his merits are of such a kind that he may rightly be called the father of astronomers and the sole restorer of this most praiseworthy science, I hold further recommendation needless; rather I acknowledge myself bound, much more, to congratulate Your Imperial Majesty most humbly on that account. Wherefore I will not detain Your Imperial Majesty with further writing of mine, but commend myself most humbly to the same's imperial favour and graces.

Liège, the 26th of June [15]98.
Your Imperial Majesty's obedient Elector and cousin,
Ernst, Archbishop of Cologne.

- **Direction & significance.** This is the actual **letter of recommendation** by which the Elector-Archbishop of Cologne commended Tycho to **Emperor Rudolf II** — the document Tycho refers to, and circulated copies of, across his patronage-seeking correspondence of 1598 (*Quae Coloniensis mea de causa Imperatori scripsit* in brahe-t_15980905001; cf. brahe-t_16000420001). It is a key instrument in Tycho's transition from exile to imperial service.
- **Sender.** **Ernst of Bavaria** (1554–1612), **Elector-Archbishop of Cologne** and Prince-Bishop of Liège (hence writing from **Liège / Lüttich**), brother of Duke Wilhelm V of Bavaria — a leading Catholic prince and himself a patron of mathematics and astrology. He addresses the Emperor as *Herr und Vetter* ("lord and cousin"), the conventional form among Imperial princes.
- **Recipient.** **Emperor Rudolf II** (*Römische Kaiserliche Majestät*).
- **The macaronic register.** The letter is chancery German studded with **Latin technical and rhetorical phrases**, preserved verbatim and rendered in place: *instrumenta mathematica* ("mathematical instruments"), *propter conformia studia* ("on account of kindred studies"), *summus fautor* ("supreme patron"), *indefessi labores* ("indefatigable labours"), *Maecenas* (the type of the patron), *tota Germanica patria* ("the whole German fatherland"), and — the rhetorical climax — **pater astronomorum et unicus huius laudatissimae scientiae restaurator**, "the father of astronomers and the sole **restorer** of this most praiseworthy science." The *restaurator/restitutio* language is Tycho's own programme-term (*astronomia instaurata*,), here deployed by his advocate.
- **Place.** *Lüttich* = **Liège**, seat of Ernst's prince-bishopric.
- **Epistolary formulae & abbreviations.** *E: Röm: Kay: Maytt:* = *Eure Römische Kaiserliche Majestät* ("Your Roman Imperial Majesty," declined throughout); subscription *gehorsamer Churfürst und Vetter* → "obedient Elector and cousin."
- **Calendar.** Dateline *d. 26. Iunij 98* at Liège; the edition marks **n.s. (New Style)** — correct, the Catholic Rhineland and prince-bishoprics having adopted the Gregorian calendar. Reproduced as written; the year is given in the source as "98."
- **Witness note.** Survives as an **afskrift (copy)** in Langebek's Diplomatarium at the Copenhagen Rigsarkiv — fittingly, since Tycho himself kept and distributed copies of it.

text.original:
AN BARUITIUM, JHRER KAY: MAYTT: GEHEYMEN SECRETARIUM.

Ernst etc.

WAS Wir jhrer kay: maytt: wegen des weitberuhmbten Tychonis Brahe vnterthenig zuschreiben, das hastu ab dem einschluss zu[v]ernehmen. Jst darauf Vnser gnedigst gesinnen an dich, wan du vernehmen wurdest, das solche schreiben jhrer kay: maytt: vberantworttet werdenn, das du pro uiribus daran vnd darob seyst, damit dieser ehrlicher man balt bescheidt auf seine æquissimas prætensiones haben möge, dann diese zeugnuss Wir ihme geben können, das ehr unicus restaurator hujus laudatissimæ scientiæ, vnd das Vnser patria Germanica jhme selbst nit allein congratuliren, sondern apertis ulnis et brachijs zu empfahen geflissen sein soll. Vndt weil sein personn vnd studia dermassen per uniuersum orbem beruhmbt, auch vnter andern dem gewesenen vicecansellario Kurzio gar woll bekandt gewest, so achten Wir vor vnnöttig, dir sein personn weiter zu recommendiren. Allein haben Wir dir auch zu erkennen geben wollen, das Wir jhme Tychoni Brahen, tum propter conformia studia tum propter eius insignia erga artem mathematicam merita, mit sondern gnaden zugethan sein, alsso das Wir Vnß zu dir gnedigst versehen, du werdest jhnen auch von vnserntwegen bey j: kay: maytt: gehorsamblich zurecommendiren nit vnterlassenn, vnndt Wir bleiben dir mit gnaden gewogen.

Luttich den 26. iunij 98.
Ernst, ertzbischoff zu Cöllenn.
text.english:
**To Barvitius, His Imperial Majesty's secret secretary.**

Ernst, etc.

What we are humbly writing to His Imperial Majesty concerning the far-famed Tycho Brahe, that you will gather from the enclosure. Thereupon it is our most gracious desire of you that, when you perceive that such writings are delivered to His Imperial Majesty, you be, *to the best of your powers* [*pro viribus*], at it and over it, so that this honourable man may soon have a decision upon his *most equitable claims* [*aequissimas praetensiones*]; for this testimony we are able to give him: that he is the *sole restorer of this most praiseworthy science* [*unicus restaurator huius laudatissimae scientiae*], and that our *German fatherland* [*patria Germanica*] should not only congratulate itself on him, but should be zealous to receive him *with open arms and embrace* [*apertis ulnis et brachiis*]. And since his person and *studies* are so renowned *throughout the whole world* [*per universum orbem*] — and were, among others, very well known to the late vice-chancellor Kurz [Curtius] — we deem it unnecessary to recommend his person further to you. Only, we wished also to make known to you that we are devoted to him, Tycho Brahe, with especial grace — *both on account of [our] conformable studies and on account of his signal merits toward the mathematical art* [*tum propter conformia studia tum propter eius insignia erga artem mathematicam merita*] — so that we most graciously trust in you that you, on our behalf also, will not fail obediently to recommend him to His Imperial Majesty; and we remain graciously inclined toward you.

Liège, the 26th of June, [15]98.
Ernst, Archbishop of Cologne.

documents.incipit: CLARISSIME vir ac frater in Domino dilecte, CLAUDIUS MULERUS tuus domesticus tradidit …

text.original:
NOBILITATE, SAPIENTIA, PIETATE ET VIRTUTE PRAESTANTISSIMO VIRO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, DOMINO PATRONO ET AMICO VETERI SUMMA OBSERVANTIA COLENDO.

CLARISSIME vir ac frater in Domino dilecte, CLAUDIUS MULERUS tuus domesticus tradidit mihi literas tuas humanissime scriptas, ex quibus intelligo te memorem esse veteris nostræ consuetudinis atque amicitiæ, id quod mihi pergratum et periucundum fuit. Rogo Deum optim. max. ut te quam diutissime sanum et incolumem cum tota familiâ conservet. Etsi autem per valetudinem non licet prolixius scribere, tamen animus meus, donec vixero, tibi adhærebit sincerus. Quod autem salutes me nomine MONAVIJ præstantissimi viri HERMANNI et DANIELIS BUCRETIJ, est mihi pergratum, precorque illis vicissim et animi et corporis constantem valetudinem, et rogo te clarissime vir, ut in tuis ad eos literis vicissim salutem dicas meo nomine. Porro quod MONAVIUS petat copiam quarundam literarum PHILIPPI ad me scriptarum, non possum ipsius voto satisfacere. Nam et ipsæ li[teræ] perierunt et fuerunt scriptæ de privatis negotijs et politicis non publicandis etc. Quare rogo, ut boni consulas, quod non possim in hac re tuæ petitioni satisfacere, alias promptissimus ad omnia præstanda, quæ tibi intellexero fore grata. Vale vir clarissime cum familia tua et domesticis omnibus. Deus te conservet, amen.

Roschildiæ 27. Iunij Anno 1598.
NICOLAUS HEMMINGIUS,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the man most excellent in nobility, wisdom, piety, and virtue, Master Tycho Brahe, his lord, patron, and old friend, to be honoured with the utmost respect.**

Most distinguished man and brother beloved in the Lord, Claude Muler, your domestic, delivered to me your most kindly-written letter, from which I understand that you are mindful of our old acquaintance and friendship — which was most pleasing and most delightful to me. I pray God Best and Greatest to preserve you, sound and unharmed, as long as possible, with your whole household. And although, by reason of [my] health, I am not permitted to write at greater length, yet my mind, as long as I shall live, will cleave to you, sincere. But that you greet me in the name of Monau, [and] of the most excellent men Hermann and Daniel Bucretius, is most pleasing to me; and I pray for them in turn constant health of mind and body, and I ask you, most distinguished man, that in your letters to them you, in turn, say a greeting in my name. Further, as to Monau's seeking a copy of certain letters of Philip [Melanchthon] written to me — I cannot satisfy his wish. For both the letters themselves have perished, and they were written about private and political matters, not to be published, etc. Wherefore I ask that you take it in good part that I cannot, in this matter, satisfy your request — being otherwise most ready to perform everything which I shall understand will be pleasing to you. Farewell, most distinguished man, with your family and all your household. May God preserve you, amen.

Roskilde, 27 June, in the year 1598.
Niels Hemmingsen,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Niels Hemmingsen** (Nicolaus Hemmingius, 1513–1600), the most eminent Danish Lutheran theologian of his age and a pupil of **Melanchthon**; by 1598 very old (he died 1600) and living in retirement at **Roskilde** (he had been removed from his Copenhagen chair in 1579 on a charge of Calvinist leanings). He addresses Tycho as *frater in Domino dilecte* ("brother beloved in the Lord") and "old friend."
- **Bearer.** *Claudius Mulerus, tuus domesticus* = **Claude Muler** (Mulerius), a French member of Tycho's household, who carried the letter (he reappears as the would-be courier in brahe-t_16000919001).
- **The Melanchthon letters.** *Monavius* = **Jacob Monau** (Monavius, 1546–1603), the Breslau (Wrocław) humanist — which explains the **Wrocław** provenance of the witness. Monau had asked, through Tycho, for copies of certain **letters of Philip Melanchthon** (*Philippi*) to Hemmingsen; Hemmingsen declines: they have perished, and concerned *private and political matters not to be published*. (Hemmingsen does **not** sharpen or apologise beyond this; the refusal is preserved as written.)
- ***Hermann and Daniel Bucretius*** — two further men whom Tycho had greeted on Monau's behalf; **flagged**: read as a pair (likely brothers) sharing the surname *Bucretius*, but not securely re-identified; rendered "Hermann and Daniel Bucretius."
- **Calendar.** *Roschildiae 27. Iunij 1598* = **27 June 1598**; Denmark (Roskilde) = **Julian / Old Style**. Header agrees with the label.
