text.original:
NOBILITATE TAM INGENIJ QUAM
GENERIS VIRO INSIGNITER CLARO, DOMINO OLIGERO ROSENCRANTZIO DE ROSENHOLM, CONSANGVINEO AFFINI ET AMICO
MEO INTEGERRIMO.
S. P.

ETSI utrasque literas, utpote eas quas cum MULÆO misi, quasque postea ad te scripsi,
desideratissime mi OLIGERE,
tibi redditas esse non ambigam, atque ex ijs inter alia te cognovisse, quæ
Praga a veteri meo amico THADDÆO mihi perscripta sunt, tamen
cum ante paucos dies ab Amico illo meo Magdeburgensi, quem scis mihi scribere solitum esse, nonnullas acceperim, eadem de re quædam agentes, harum quoque
exemplum tecum communicandum duxi, quo plenius intelligeres qualis sit Cæsareæ Matis erga me
voluntas; præsertim cum ESCHILLO
BILLEO nostro mihi nunc respondendum sit ad quasdam hisce diebus
mihi ab eo missas, et quendam ex meis nunc Lubecæ habeam, qui has ad vos certo dirigat, oblata videlicet
commoda aliqua oportunitate, interea dum alijs meis negotijs isthic exequendis
occupatur. Velim autem, ut hæc ipsa quæ nunc scribo mittoque, non nisi intimis
nostris monstres; tute satis nosti, quinam ex ijs fideles sint, licet et illi,
uti fit, pauci; nolui nomen eius, qui hæc ad me scripsit, subiungi; sed tu et
Doctor NICOLAUS facile colligetis,
quisnam sit; solet is libere mihi scribere, utut de facie ignotus ignoto; nollem
itaque hasce eius literas alijs patere, potissimum ob ea quæ de Principe alias
satis noto scribit. Aut igitur hæc admodum secreta habe, aut
Vulcano trade. Quam facile mihi sit, Principis illius obiectis respondere, tute
satis nosti, nam desertus deserui, ne ipsemet spectator essem ruinæ eorum, quæ
in Patria tam diu tantoque nixu molitus sum, quod tamen nec Regno nec Regi
imputandum duco; authores satis noti, utque adhuc famosiores reddantur,
promeruere. Quod autem, mi OLIGERE, hæc, quæ nunc mitto, prioribus superaddam, ideo factum,
quod ex te alijsque intimis amicis oportunum simul consilium capere velim, quid
faciendum existimetis, ubi tale quid mihi oblatum fuerit. Intelligo ex ijs, qui
loca illa norunt, esse arcem splendidam et amœnam, in quam ipse Cæsar solitus
est ante paucos annos animi causa nonnunquam secedere, quamque post Pragensem maximi facit, et circa quam venationem
exercere consuevit, dum his et similibus delectaretur. Nunc enim intra duos vel
tres proximos annos saltem in arce Pragensi
eum se continuisse referunt. Ego quidem de feudo aliquo in Silesia, Moravia, Lusatia, aut
alijs ditionibus Cæsari subiectis, obtinendo potius essem sollicitus, quam ut in
tam pomposo Bohemiæ loco versarer, sed obtemperandum est Imperatoris clementi voluntati, quacunque
tandem ratione mihi et meis benefacere velit, ita ut studijs etiam, quibus
occupor, liberaliter provideatur, siquidem Patria nostra hanc curam tam inconsiderate posthabuerit. Loquere de his secreto cum
ESCHILLO BILLEO nostro, tum
quoque KRAGIO communi amico, et quid
consilij dederint, literis significa, alias vero hæc, ubi præsertim minus
securum fuerit, cæla. FRANCISCUS
TEGNAGLIUS meus necdum huc reversus est, sed spero illum brevi
feliciter affuturum. Cuperem etiam, ut MULÆUS reditum acceleraret, neque enim de rebus meis, quomodo et
quando quippiam agendum, omnino statuere possum, antequam hi duo redierint.
Interea tamen me, quoad datur, itineri accingo, omniaque Divinæ providentiæ
committo, cui etiam te cum omnibus tuis commendo.

Vale.

Dabantur raptim Wandesburgo die
28. Iunij Anno Domini 1598.

Tuus TYCHO BRAHE,
manu
propria.

POSTSCRIPTA.POSTQUAM has ad te exarassem, accessit me huc WALTERI SCHOTI Hamburgensis filius
GABRIEL, a quo pannos Mater
et tu emere soletis, et se brevi Rosenholmium venturum aiebat. De curru
quoque, quem mihi confieri procuras, retulit, Matrem tuam, cum ultimo ibi
fuisset, eum brevi paratum fore dixisse ; quare se illum in navem ex Arhusia Lubecam secum recepturum
pollicitus est, cumque de te ipso percontarer, in Selandiam abijsse
existimavit. Et insuper se apud fratrem meum AXILLUM fuisse, atque ibi percepisse,
quod ad nuptias trium filiarum, quæ requiruntur, indies adornet, inter quas
et tuæ celebrabuntur, idque futurum sex abhinc hebdomadibus commemoravit.
Incidit itaque in mentem, me tibi Epithalamium quoddam promisisse, quod cum
tam cito ob alias occupationes, quibus varie distrahor, fieri vix queat, hoc
saltem breve Epigramma, quod nunc ex tempore in buccam venit, hîc subiunctum
habe. Deus author universi omnia tibi in hoc coniugio ex voto prospera et
salutaria largiatur. Tu autem, ne huius novellæ SOPHIÆ amor, alterius et diu tibi
excultæ sophiæ amorem labefactet, sed potius adaugeat atque confirmet,
effice. Hoc opus, hic labor, multos ea meta
fefellit.

EPIGRAMMA AD OLIGERUM
ROSENCRANTZIUM SPONSUM.

Tene OLIGERE etiam materno
sauciat arcu

    Ille levis toto qui volat orbe puer?

Iste puer cæcus minimusque nec ardua curans

    Quem poteras alto despicere ingenio.

Omnia sed vincit, dices, cedamus amori

    Indomito; summos stravit et ante viros.

Est (fateor) fortis; Musæ, Dictinna, Minerva

    Sunt tamen e quibus is nulla Trophæa gerit.

Intimus es Musis, placet et Dictinna, tibique

    Artibus exculto culta Minerva favet:

Attamen aut Arte aut Pharetra, qui vincere nullas

    E tribus his potuit, te superavit amor.

Scilicet ut tandem miro te falleret astu,

    Miscuit inter se nomina nominibus,

Proque alijs Sophijs Sophiam ut tibi protulit unam

    Præ Sophia omni, unam, victus, amas Sophiam .

T. B.
text.english:
**To the man notably renowned for nobility both of genius and of birth, Lord Holger Rosenkrantz of Rosenholm, my kinsman, relative, and most upright friend.**
Heartiest greeting.

Although I do not doubt, my most longed-for Holger, that both letters — namely those I sent with Mule, and those I afterward wrote to you — have been delivered to you, and that from them you have learned, among other things, what was written to me from Prague by my old friend Thaddaeus [Hagecius]: nevertheless, since a few days ago I received some letters from that Magdeburg friend of mine, whom you know is wont to write to me, treating of certain matters on the same subject, I thought a copy of these too should be shared with you, that you might more fully understand what the Imperial Majesty's disposition toward me is — especially since I must now reply to our **Eske Bille** about certain [letters] he sent me these days, and I have one of my men now at Lübeck who will direct these to you safely, when some convenient opportunity offers, while he is occupied carrying out my other business there. But I should wish that these very things I now write and send, you show to none but our intimates; you yourself know well enough which of them are faithful — though even they, as it happens, are few. I did not want the name of him who wrote these things to me appended; but you and Doctor Nicolaus will easily gather who it is. He is wont to write to me freely, though unknown to one unknown by face; I should therefore not wish these letters of his to lie open to others, chiefly on account of what he writes about a certain Prince otherwise well enough known. Either, then, keep these very secret, or hand them to Vulcan [burn them]. How easy it is for me to answer that Prince's objections, you yourself know well enough: for, **deserted, I deserted** — lest I myself be a spectator of the ruin of those things which in my fatherland I laboured at so long and with such effort; which, however, I judge is to be imputed neither to the Kingdom nor to the King — the authors of it are well enough known, and have deserved to be made yet more notorious. But that I add these things I now send to the earlier ones, my Holger, is done for this reason: that I may take timely counsel from you and other intimate friends — what you think should be done, when such a thing [the offer] is made to me. I understand, from those who know those places, that it is a splendid and pleasant **castle**, into which the Emperor himself was wont, a few years ago, sometimes to withdraw for recreation, and which he values most after the Prague one, and around which he was accustomed to hunt, while he delighted in these and the like; for now, within the last two or three years, they report he has kept himself only in the Prague castle. I, indeed, would rather be solicitous about obtaining some **fief in Silesia, Moravia, Lusatia, or other dominions subject to the Emperor**, than to dwell in so pompous a place of Bohemia; but one must comply with the Emperor's clement will, in whatever way at last he wishes to do good to me and mine, so that provision be also liberally made for the studies in which I am engaged — since our fatherland has so inconsiderately neglected this care. Speak of these things secretly with our **Eske Bille**, and also with **Krag**, our common friend, and signify by letter what counsel they give; but otherwise conceal these things, especially where it is less safe. My **Franz Tengnagel** has not yet returned hither, but I hope he will soon be happily present. I should also wish **Mule** would hasten his return, for I cannot at all determine about my affairs — how and when anything is to be done — before these two return. Meanwhile, however, I gird myself for the journey, as far as is granted, and commit all things to Divine providence, to which I also commend you with all yours.

Farewell.
Given in haste from Wandsbek, the 28th day of June, in the Year of the Lord 1598.
Your Tycho Brahe,
with my own hand.


*[Postscript:]* POSTSCRIPT. After I had written this to you, there came to me here Gabriel, son of Walter Schot of Hamburg — from whom your Mother and you are wont to buy cloth — and he said he would shortly come to Rosenholm. About the carriage too, which you are having made for me, he reported that your Mother said it would shortly be ready; wherefore he promised he would take it with him aboard ship from Aarhus to Lübeck; and when I enquired about you yourself, he supposed you had gone off into Zealand. And moreover [he said] that he had been at my brother Axel's, and had there learned that he is daily preparing for the weddings of the three daughters that are required, among which yours too will be celebrated, and he mentioned this would be six weeks from now. It came into my mind, then, that I had promised you a certain Epithalamium; and since, for the other occupations by which I am variously distracted, it can scarcely be done so quickly, have at least this short Epigram, which now came on the spur of the moment to my lips, here subjoined. May God, the author of the universe, bestow on you in this marriage all things prosperous and wholesome, according to your prayer. But do you bring it about that the love of this new Sophia does not weaken the love of that other, long-cultivated wisdom [sophia], but rather increases and confirms it. This is the task, this the toil; that goal has deceived many.  /  EPIGRAM TO HOLGER ROSENKRANTZ THE BRIDEGROOM. | Does that nimble boy who flies over the whole world / wound even you, Holger, with his mother's bow? / That boy, blind and tiniest, caring nothing for lofty things, / whom you could look down upon with your high genius. / "But Love conquers all," you will say; "let us yield to untamed / Love; he has laid low even the greatest men before." / Strong he is, I grant; yet the Muses, Diana, Minerva / are among those from whom he wins no trophies. / You are an intimate of the Muses, Diana too is pleasing to you, / and to you, refined in the arts, refined Minerva is favourable: / and yet, he who could conquer none of these three / by Art or by Quiver, Love has overcome you. / That is, so that at last he might deceive you by a wondrous wile, / he mingled names among names, / and instead of the other wisdoms [Sophiae] brought forth one Sophia for you — / so that before every Sophia, you love, vanquished, one Sophia. T. B.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Holger Rosenkrantz** "the Learned" (1574–1642), of **Rosenholm** — Tycho's *consanguineus, affinis et amicus integerrimus* ("kinsman, relative, and most upright friend"; the recurring *Oligerus* of the corpus, e.g. brahe-t_15980328001, brahe-t_15990307001). The MS is a later Langebek *afskrift*.
- **Significance — Tycho weighing the imperial offer (June 1598).** A confidential, candid letter from the **exile at Wandsbek**, written as the imperial overture took shape. Tycho forwards (in copy) the latest from his **anonymous Magdeburg correspondent** on "the Imperial Majesty's disposition toward me," and asks Holger — with **Eske Bille** and **Krag** — for **counsel on whether to accept** "when such a thing is made to me." It is the deliberation behind the move that the 1599–1600 letters carry out.
- **The offered castle = Benátky.** Tycho describes (from report) "a splendid and pleasant **castle**, into which the Emperor was wont … to withdraw for recreation … and around which he hunted," valued "most after the Prague one" — i.e. **Benátky nad Jizerou**, where Tycho would in fact be installed. Strikingly, Tycho says he would **rather have a fief** in **Silesia, Moravia, or Lusatia** than "so pompous a Bohemian place," but will comply with the Emperor's will provided his studies are "liberally provided for" — "since our fatherland has so inconsiderately neglected this care."
- **The *"desertus deserui"* epigram.** Tycho's famous self-justification: *"deserted, I deserted"* (*desertus deserui*) — he left Denmark only after being abandoned, "lest I be a spectator of the ruin" of his life's work — laying the blame **neither on the Kingdom nor the King**, but on the "authors" of his troubles, "well enough known, and deserving to be made yet more notorious." (No silent sharpening: the careful exculpation of King and realm is kept.)
- **Secrecy.** *Aut … secreta habe, aut Vulcano trade* — "keep these very secret, or **give them to Vulcan**" (burn them); show only "our intimates"; the anonymous correspondent's name withheld because of "what he writes about a certain Prince" — Tycho's tradecraft of confidential channels.
- **Persons named.** Holger Rosenkrantz; **Eske Bille** (Tycho's kinsman-agent); **Krag** = **Niels Krag** (Nicolaus Cragius, 1550–1602, the Danish historian-diplomat; cf. brahe-t_15900228001), "our common friend"; *Thaddaeus* = **Tadeáš Hájek (Hagecius)**, Tycho's Prague friend; **Franz Tengnagel** and **Claus Mule** (*Mulaeus*), Tycho's agents, both away (their return needed before Tycho can decide). *Doctor Nicolaus* — an intimate who, with Holger, will "guess" the Magdeburg correspondent; **possibly Niels Krag** (*Nicolaus*), though named separately as *Kragius* in the same letter, so left unidentified and flagged.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Wandesburgo die 28. Iunij Anno Domini 1598*; **Old Style** (the Danish-oriented exile context). Header agrees with the label.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript + a wedding EPIGRAM to Holger's bride Sophie (the *Sophia* bride / *sophia* wisdom pun), restored from Dreyer VIII p.79 (dropped by the working transcription).
- **A Virgilian tag before the epigram.** Recovers Tycho's closing line to the prose passage introducing his wedding epigram for Holger Rosenkrantz: an adaptation of Virgil's famous "hoc opus, hic labor est" (Aeneid VI.129), repurposed here to describe the difficulty of the very thing Tycho has just urged — that love for a new bride ("this new Sophia") not weaken devotion to wisdom (sophia) itself. "Meta" (a race's turning-post/finish) and "fefellit" (has deceived/eluded) cast the marriage as a course "many" have failed to run without one love crowding out the other.
- **Literary self-consciousness.** The tag functions as a bridge between the letter's prose and the Latin epigram that follows, and is itself a small piece of wordplay consistent with the whole letter's pun on Sophia (bride) / sophia (wisdom).

documents.editorial_note: **Direction note.** **Incoming** letter — *from* **Frans (Franz) Tengnagel** (Tycho's noble assistant and emissary) *to* Tycho — reporting his **diplomatic mission through Germany and the Low Countries** on Tycho's behalf. The **Germany/Netherlands leg** that complements his **Italy leg** (cf. brahe-t_16000103001, brahe-t_16000103002, brahe-t_16000124001).

text.original:
FRANCISCUS TENGNAGEL AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

S. P.

NOBILISSIME et præstantissime Domine TYCHO. Rebus Mæ Tæ ex animi sententia confectis, officij mei esse ratus sum (siquidem incertus sim, utrum priores meæ raptim Coloniæ ad te exaratæ tibi redditæ sint nec ne) particulatim nonnulla et fusius referre, cum tunc otium singula attingendi mihi non suppeteret, omissis tamen nunc ingratis, quæ in itinere mihi evenerunt, siquidem illibenter talia te audire norim. Aquisgranum cum appulissem relicta 3 die Iunij Colonia, ibi Serenissimum Principem Electorem Coloniensem ERNESTUM iam itineri Leodium versus, quod postero die ingressus est, accinctum reperi. Qui quamprimum de eo, quod cum literis tuis adessem, inaudivit, confestim me accersitum humanissime compellavit, gratissimum sibi munus Ma Tæ literarium significans, et daturum se operam, ut Ma Ta reipsa se insignem personæ suæ et rei Astronomicæ fautorem comperiat. Quem suum affectum iam pridem antea conceptum, in posterum etiam magis magisque se declaraturum pollicebatur. Interim velle se, ut Leodium curru suo proprio me conferam. Omnem enim fere se eo comitatum unâ translaturum, et rebus suis intra triduum in Limburgensi propinquo Ducatu expeditis actutum subsequuturum. Id quod et factum est. Ibi singulis fere diebus in Cameram ad secretum Rmæ eius Celnis colloquium per aliquot nonnunquam integras horas vocatus fui, humanissime exceptus, tandem etiam (quod tam subito ob innumeras, quibus Leodij quotidie distringeretur occupationes, fieri non posse prolixe excusavit) liberalissime dimissus, donata mihi aurea sua effigie, unâ cum equo, quem centum et viginti Coronatis a Magistro Palatij sui coëmerat. Quæ vero Rmæ eius Celni de negotijs Mæ Tæ in scriptis tradidi, et simul oretenus exposui, summa cum voluptate legit et audivit, Danos rem se indignam in eo, quod Mam Tam non in eo (uti decuit) precio habuerint, atque tam inconsiderate dimiserint, vel potius amiserint, magno suo opprobrio commisisse perhibens vix ulla ætate apud cordatos et intelligentes expiandam. Et aiebat insuper, eorum officij fuisse sponte sua omni conatu in hoc eniti, quo te beneficijs atque officijs liberaliter præstitis apud se in Regis et Regni honorem retinerent, tantum abest, ut tuæ abitioni, velut inaudierat, causas tam evidentes et intolerabiles præbere, atque voluntatem et decretum Optimi Regis FRIDERICI post fata rescindere, Senatorumque omnium literas tibi (prout compertum habebat) in membrana statim ab obitu FRIDERICI Regis concessas exauthorare ipsis fas esset; cumque me semel interrogasset, in quantam pecuniæ summam excrescere possent, si computarentur omnia, quæ a Rege FRIDERICO et Senatu Regni ad Astronomiæ instaurationem Mæ Tæ concessa erant, me certo illud dicere non posse referente, tantum tamen Mæ Tæ suppetijsse, ut omnes e quibuscumque tandem oris adventantes, Reges, Principes, eorundem Legatos, Doctores, Studiosos, et cuiusvis ordinis homines splendide semper et munifice tractârit, præterquam quod tot et tantos sumptus in Astronomiæ redintegrationem, quales nemo ante ipsum, erogasset, et alias copiosam aleret familiam. An vero beneficis Regijs, an etiam pro parte proprijs bonis hæreditarijs, illos haberet reditus, mihi non satis constare: Existimare tamen summam eorum, quæ ex Regno quotannis habebat, quatuor thalerorum millia mea opinione non multum excessisse, mox Rma eius Celdo in hæc formalia verba prorupit: **Was? Solte man ein Solchen Man vmb so ein geringes geldt auß dem Land ziehenn lassen. Schande ist es. Ein Herr verspielt mehr auf einen abendt. Goldt bekompt man alzeitt aber solche leutte nicht alzeitt.** Sed quandoquidem ita iam evenerit, quocunque tandem Danorum fato et oscitantia, ut in Germaniam veniens Ma Ta sibi propior reddita sit, magnopere se ea de causa lætari, et avide hanc commoditatem in posterum arrepturum. Placere sibi, quod nulli Principi Germaniæ, aut Regioni exteræ suam operam addicere velit, antequam de Imperatoriæ Maiestatis clementissimæ voluntate erga se et ea quæ tractat studia, certo constaret. Et omnino censuit, hanc Regiam artem Imperatori, tanquam præcipuo Europæ capiti, omnium primo offerendam esse, ac neutiquam se ambigere, imo multa depositurum, Cæsaream Maiestatem pro eo quo esset erga omnes liberales disciplinas, inprimis vero Mathematica et inter hæc Astronomica studia singulari favore et amore, Mam Tam libentissimo animo excepturam, munifice cum familia et toto apparatu Astronomico sustentaturam, nec commissuram, ut Mam Tam migrationis huius e Dania unquam pœniteat. Qua etiam de re se non saltem commendatitias, sed pariter congratulatorias ad Imperatoriam Maiestatem daturum, tum quoque intimo eius Secretario BARVITIO, de quo ipse bene meritus esset, quique illi aliquo modo obstrictus, unâ scripturum. Et si præter omnem suam opinionem Cæsa Maiestas Astronomica studia in totius Imperij nunquam intermoriturum honorem et decus conservare et sustentare ab alijs forte dissuasus gravaretur (quod tamen ipsam sponte sua non admissuram certe sciret) multos fore, qui hanc gloriam sibi et suis ditionibus accedere summopere desiderent, nec eam occasionem negligant. Imo se ipsum suis impensis id præstiturum, nec ullis nisi soli Imperatori, cui hic honor primum debetur, hac in parte cessurum. Hæc et plura eiuscemodi diversis temporibus ad me dixit, quæ referre nimis nunc prolixum foret. Latius D. V. de his coram. Unicum tamen præterire non possum, quod mihi discessuro confirmationis eorum omnium loco sub ipsum valedictionis tempus inculcavit; ferme his formalibus verbis: **Saget dem guttenn ehrlichenn Mann viel guts von meinet wegenn, und das ich hernacher also bey ihm handeln werde, als wan er mein leiblicher bruder wehr, und ich ihn von jugendt auf gekant hette, dessen er sich gentzlichenn zu mir versehenn soll. Saget ihm auch daneben alles was ihr sonstenn von mir gehöret habt, und bitet ihn das er mir seinenn zustandt zueschreibe, so offt ihm gelegenheit vorfelt. Wan ich vormercke, das er bey Hamburg etwas verziehenn wirdt, ehe er zur Kay. Ma. ziehet, bin ich willens einenn von meinenn nobilibus, deme ich in pyronomicis exercitijs vertraue, zu ihm abzufertigenn, von diesem und anderem meinetwegenn mit ihm zu conferiren. Und so baldt ich, ob Gott will, zu ihr Kay. Mt. komme, will ich ihm TYCHONEM, wo er alda in des Kaisers gebiet anzutreffen, besuchenn und weiter mit ihm kuntschaft machen.** Nam plane nihil dubitavit, se alicubi in Imperatoriæ Matis ditionibus te reperturum. Sicque me clementer et liberaliter (uti prius innui) dimisit. Pericula et damna, quæ in hoc itinere perpessus sum, quæque in prioribus meis aliquatenus attigi, hîc utpote ingrata, non lubet iterare.

Venio nunc ad Holandos, ad quos in Patria aliquantisper moratus me contuli, quo commoditatem promptiorem et tutiorem redeundi nanciscerer. Ibi cum Hagam, ubi iuris suprema est administratio, quam vel in transcursu cognoscere avebam, pervenissem, Illustrissimus Princeps MAURITIUS, qui Mam Tam novit et magni facit, benignum et clementissimum se mihi exhibuit. Cui libros quosdam Mæ Tæ secreto ostendi. Quos cum illi apprime arridere viderem, eos consulto ipsi tanquam ex tua voluntate dono dedi, atque illud inscripsi. Qui sane nihil [magis] in votis habuit, quam te in Hollandia novas Uraniæ sedes figere et stabilire, seque id Ordinibus sedulo propositurum, modo de tua voluntate certior redderetur, aiebat. Neque enim ambigere, quin et Ordinibus hoc perplaciturum sit. Existimavit etiam, non reperturam Mam Tam ullum locum Genio et studijs suis aptiorem. Quod ut ad Mam Tam suo nomine cum insigni animi sui et amicitiæ declaratione, donec ipsemet istic comparuero, perscriberem, iussit, et has quoque inclusas ad eam primo quoque tempore mittendas dedit. Neque tantum ab Illustrissimo Principe hoc ipsius et Ordinum notum percepi; sed et IOHANNE BARNEFELDIO, qui nomine quidem Advocatus supremus, sed reipsa quasi Comes ceu Regulus est Hollandiæ. Nam ab eius nutu et voluntate ferme pendent omnia. Cumque et ipsum non minus quam MAURITIUM (qui brevibus ob innumeras suas occupationes Mæ Tæ gratias, pro libris actis, rescripsit, particularia ut Mæ Tæ oretenus exponerem iubens) in nostras partes inclinare animadverterem atque te eo accersendum et benigne tractandum censere, subiunxi, me de tua voluntate hac in parte nihil certi referre posse, siquidem intellexerim, te Imperatoriæ Maiestati omnium primo tua studia demisse offerre decrevisse, tunc ille mox obmutuit et nihil amplius hac de re ingessit, sed quasi alio declinans orationem, aiebat, se esse in procinctu itineris Anglici, ubi legatum acturus esset nomine Ordinum. Ideoque nunc pluribus mecum loqui non posse. Ubi reversus fuerit, sique res ita postularit, et de tua voluntate sibi quidpiam constiterit, hoc negotium se apud Ordines peracturum. Inaudivi etiam in Hollandia, Angliam magno tui teneri desiderio, quod et ad te perscriptum esse quidam referebat: verene an falso, me fugit. Sed tu rectius dispicies, quid tibi faciendum sit. Prævides enim quantis tumultibus Regnum illud obnoxium sit, quæ tunc primum gliscent, ubi Regina ferme decrepita fatis concesserit. Habes, si sic luberet, Scotiæ Regem in magna illa Britannica Insula, non saltem affinitate Danis coniunctissimum, sed et tui amantissimum, vel ex ea consuetudine, quæ vobis intercessit, ex quo illum cum nobili suo Comitatu te in tua Insula invisentem magnifice excepisti, deque rebus eruditis (uti est Princeps doctus) cum eo affatim contulisti.

Hæc Mæ Tæ, donec ipsemet Wandesburgi me stitero, præsignificanda habui, quantum nunc inter peregrinandum licuit, ut, quid in posterum sibi faciendum sit, eo citius et rectius statuat. Vale vir nobilissime et præstantissime, ac me propediem expecta.

Amstelodamo die 6. Iulij Ao. 1598.
Mæ Tæ perpetuo devinctus
FRANCISCUS G. TENGNAGEL, manu propria.
text.english:
**FRANS TENGNAGEL TO TYCHO BRAHE.**

Heartiest greeting.

Most noble and excellent Lord Tycho. Your Magnificence's affairs being accomplished according to [my] mind, I thought it my duty (since I am uncertain whether my earlier [letter], hastily written to you at Cologne, was delivered you or not) to report some things in detail and more fully — for then I had no leisure to touch each point — omitting, however, now, the unpleasant things that befell me on the journey, since I know you hear such things unwillingly. When I had come to **Aachen** (leaving **Cologne** on the 3rd of June), I found there the most serene Prince Elector of Cologne, **Ernst [of Bavaria]**, already girded for a journey toward **Liège**, which he entered the next day. As soon as he heard that I was present with your letters, he at once had me summoned and most kindly addressed me, signifying that Your Magnificence's literary gift was most welcome to him, and that **he would take pains that Your Magnificence find him a signal patron of his person and of the Astronomical cause** — an affection conceived long before, which he promised to declare more and more hereafter. Meanwhile he wished me to go to Liège in his own carriage; for he would transfer almost his whole retinue thither, and, his affairs in the neighbouring **Duchy of Limburg** dispatched within three days, would follow at once — which was done. There, almost daily, I was called into the Chamber for secret conversation with His Reverend Highness, sometimes for several whole hours, most kindly received; at last too (he excusing at length that it could not be done so soon, on account of the innumerable occupations by which he was daily distracted at Liège) most liberally dismissed, **a golden effigy of himself given me, together with a horse which he had bought from his Palace-Master for a hundred and twenty Crowns**. What I gave His Reverend Highness in writing about Your Magnificence's affairs, and at the same time expounded by mouth, he read and heard with the greatest pleasure — declaring that **the Danes had committed a thing unworthy of themselves, in not holding Your Magnificence in the esteem they ought, and so inconsiderately dismissing — or rather losing — you, to their great reproach, scarcely to be expiated in any age among the sensible and intelligent.** And he said besides that it had been their duty, of their own accord, to strive with all effort to retain you with them, by benefits and offices liberally given, to the honour of the King and Realm — far from giving such evident and intolerable causes of your departure (as he had heard), and rescinding the will and decree of the best King Frederick after his death, and **annulling all the Senators' letters granted you on parchment immediately after King Frederick's death**. And when he once asked me to how great a sum of money [all] could grow, if everything were computed that had been granted Your Magnificence by King Frederick and the Realm's Senate for the instauration of Astronomy — and I answered that I could not say that for certain, but that Your Magnificence had had enough always to treat splendidly and munificently all comers from whatever shores (Kings, Princes, their Legates, Doctors, Students, and men of every rank), besides laying out such great costs on the restoration of Astronomy as no one before, and otherwise feeding a numerous household; [and] whether you had those revenues from royal benefices, or partly from your own hereditary goods, was not sufficiently clear to me; yet I reckoned the sum you had yearly from the Realm did not, in my opinion, much exceed four thousand thalers — His Reverend Highness at once burst into these formal words:

> **"What? Should one let such a man leave the country for so paltry a sum of money? It is a shame. A lord gambles away more in one evening. Gold one always gets — but such people, not always."**

But since it has now so happened — by whatever Danish fate and negligence — that Your Magnificence, coming into Germany, is made nearer to him, he greatly rejoices on that account, and will eagerly seize this convenience hereafter. **It pleases him that you will pledge your service to no Prince of Germany, nor to any foreign Region, before it be certain of the Imperial Majesty's most clement will toward you and the studies you pursue.** And he wholly judged that **this Royal art ought to be offered, first of all, to the Emperor, as the chief head of Europe**; and he in no way doubts — nay, would wager much — that the Imperial Majesty, given his singular favour and love for all liberal disciplines (and especially Mathematics, and among these the Astronomical studies), would **receive Your Magnificence most gladly, munificently sustain you with your family and your whole Astronomical apparatus, and not permit you ever to repent this migration from Denmark**. About which he would give the Imperial Majesty not only commendatory but congratulatory letters; and likewise write to his intimate Secretary **Barvitius** (whom he had himself benefited, and who is in some way bound to him). And if — beyond all his expectation — the Imperial Majesty (perhaps dissuaded by others) should be reluctant to preserve and sustain the Astronomical studies, to the never-dying honour and ornament of the whole Empire (which he was certain the Emperor would not admit of his own accord), **there would be many who would greatly desire this glory to accrue to themselves and their dominions, and would not neglect the occasion. Nay, he himself would provide it at his own expense, and yield to none in this part but the Emperor alone, to whom this honour is first owed.** These and more such things he said to me at different times, which it would be too prolix now to report. More of these to Your Lordship in person. Yet one thing I cannot pass over, which, as I was leaving, he inculcated to me, in place of a confirmation of all, at the very time of farewell, almost in these formal words:

> **"Say much good to the good, honest man on my behalf — and that I will hereafter deal with him as if he were my own brother, and I had known him from youth; of which he should wholly rely upon me. Tell him also, besides, everything else you have heard from me; and ask him to write me his condition, as often as occasion offers him. When I perceive that he will tarry a while near Hamburg before he goes to the Imperial Majesty, I am minded to dispatch to him one of my nobles, whom I trust in pyronomic [alchemical] exercises, to confer with him about this and other matters on my behalf. And as soon as I, God willing, come to the Imperial Majesty, I will visit Tycho — wherever he is to be met there, in the Emperor's territory — and make further acquaintance with him."**

For he plainly did not doubt that he would find you somewhere in the Imperial Majesty's dominions. And so he dismissed me kindly and liberally (as I indicated before). The perils and losses I suffered on this journey, which I touched on somewhat in my earlier [letter], I do not care to repeat here, as being unpleasant.

I come now to **the Hollanders**, to whom — having stayed a while in my fatherland — I betook myself, to get a readier and safer means of returning. When I had come there to **The Hague** (where the supreme administration of justice is, which I longed to see even in passing), the most illustrious Prince **Maurice [of Nassau]**, who knows Your Magnificence and esteems you highly, showed himself kind and most clement to me. To him I secretly showed some of Your Magnificence's books. Seeing them please him greatly, I deliberately **gave them to him as a gift, as from your will, and inscribed it** [so]. He indeed wished nothing more than **that you fix and establish new seats of Urania in Holland**, and said he would diligently propose it to the **States [Estates]**, if he were made certain of your will; nor does he doubt it would greatly please the States. He reckoned, too, that **Your Magnificence would find no place fitter for your genius and studies.** He ordered me to write this to Your Magnificence in his name, with a signal declaration of his mind and friendship, until I myself appear there; and gave these enclosed [letters] too, to be sent you at the first opportunity. Nor did I perceive this intent — his and the States' — only from the most illustrious Prince, but also from **Johan van Oldenbarnevelt**, who is by title indeed Supreme Advocate, but in fact a kind of Count or petty-king of Holland; for upon his nod and will almost everything depends. And when I noticed him too, no less than Maurice (who, on account of his innumerable occupations, wrote Your Magnificence brief thanks for the books, ordering me to expound the particulars to you by mouth), inclining to our side, and judging that you should be summoned thither and kindly treated, I added that **I could report nothing certain of your will in this part, since I understood you had decided humbly to offer your studies, first of all, to the Emperor**; then he soon fell silent, and brought forward nothing more on this — but, as if turning the discourse elsewhere, said that he was **on the point of an English journey, where he would act as legate in the States' name**, and so could not speak more with me now; [but] when he had returned, if circumstances so required and he were certain of your will, he would accomplish this business with the States.

I also heard in Holland that **England is held by a great desire for you** — which someone said had been written to you; whether truly or falsely, escapes me. But you will better see what is to be done. For you foresee to how great tumults that Realm is liable, which will first swell when **the Queen, almost decrepit, has passed away** [Elizabeth I]. You have, if it so pleased, **the King of Scotland** [James VI] in that great British Island — not only most closely joined to the Danes by affinity, but most loving of you, even from that acquaintance which passed between you, **since you magnificently received him, visiting your Island with his noble retinue, and conferred abundantly with him on learned matters (for he is a learned Prince).**

These things I had to pre-signify to Your Magnificence — until I myself shall present myself at **Wandsbek** — so far as is now allowed amid travelling, that you may the more quickly and rightly determine what is to be done hereafter. Farewell, most noble and excellent man, and expect me shortly.

From Amsterdam, the 6th day of July, the year 1598.
Perpetually bound to Your Magnificence,
**Franciscus G. Tengnagel**, in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondent.** **Incoming**, **Frans (Franz) Tengnagel** (Tycho's noble assistant, later son-in-law) → **Tycho** at Wandsbek — reporting his **diplomatic embassy through Germany and the Low Countries** (June–July 1598) on the exiled Tycho's behalf. (Complements his **Italy leg**: the books to Pinelli/Magini/the Doge, brahe-t_16000103001, brahe-t_16000103002, brahe-t_16000124001.)
- **Significance — the patronage "auction" for the exiled Tycho, and his strategic choice of the Emperor.** A vivid first-hand record of the courts competing for Tycho in 1598:
 - **The Elector of Cologne (Ernst of Bavaria).** Met at Aachen/Liège; days of secret audiences; gifts (a **golden portrait-medal and a 120-Crown horse**). He denounces Denmark's loss of Tycho ("scarcely to be expiated in any age"), and bursts out in **German**: *"Should one let such a man leave the country for so paltry a sum? … Gold one always gets — but such people, not always."* He endorses Tycho's plan to **offer himself first to the Emperor** ("the chief head of Europe"), promising **commendatory letters to Rudolf II and to Barvitius**, and pledging — if the Emperor faltered — to **support Tycho at his own expense**. His farewell charge (also in **German**): to treat Tycho **"as my own brother,"** to send "one of my nobles whom I trust in **pyronomic [alchemical] exercises**" to confer, and to **visit Tycho in person** once at the imperial court.
 - **Maurice of Nassau & the Dutch States.** At **The Hague**, **Maurice** (who "knows and esteems" Tycho) received Tengnagel, took **Tycho's books as a gift**, and offered to propose to the **States** that Tycho **"fix new seats of Urania in Holland"** — "no place fitter for your genius." **Johan van Oldenbarnevelt** (the "petty-king of Holland") inclined the same way — but **fell silent on learning Tycho meant to offer himself to the Emperor first**, then left on an **English embassy**.
 - **England & Scotland.** Rumour that **England desires Tycho**; but Tengnagel warns of the coming succession tumults at **Elizabeth I's** death, and points to **James VI of Scotland** — "most loving of you" — recalling **James's 1590 visit to Hven** (when Tycho hosted him and "conferred abundantly on learned matters").
 - **The strategic upshot.** The letter documents that, **by mid-1598, Tycho had resolved to offer his studies "first of all to the Emperor"** — the choice that led to Benátky/Prague (cf. the exile narratives, brahe-t_15980607001, brahe-t_16000103001).
- **Cross-references.** A keystone of the **patronage-search / exile** thread (pair with the Grynaeus and Pinelli letters); a **books-distribution** record (gift copies to the **Elector of Cologne** — cf. the Mechanica list at brahe-t_15980909001 — and to **Maurice of Nassau**); and the **Tengnagel-embassy** thread (the Italy leg).
- **Persons & places named.** Frans Tengnagel; **Ernst of Bavaria, Elector of Cologne**; **King Frederick II of Denmark** (the late); **Barvitius**; **Rudolf II**; **Maurice of Nassau**; **Johan van Oldenbarnevelt**; **Elizabeth I** ("the decrepit Queen"); **James VI of Scotland** (the Hven visitor). Places: **Amsterdam**, **The Hague**, **Cologne**, **Aachen**, **Liège**, **Limburg**, **Wandsbek**, **Hamburg**, **Holland**, **England/Scotland**.
- **Two German passages** (the Elector's outburst and his farewell charge) are reproduced verbatim and translated; *pyronomic exercises* = alchemy.
- **Calendar.** *Amstelodamo die 6. Iulij Ao. 1598* — Holland was **New Style**, but the source carries no *stylo* marker and the label gives none; dated **6 July 1598** (style left as given; Holland's N.S. noted). Header and label agree.

text.original:
IOSEPHUS SCALIGER AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

S. P.

DISCESSUS tuus ex Dania, Vir generosissime, ut nobis acerbissimus fuit, ita ancipites animi nos semper habuit, quem locum fortunis tuis deligeres. Ubi enim illae sitae forent, ibi et animo tuo et serijs studijs tuis aliquid quietis partum iri confidebamus, idque eo impensius optabamus, quo propensior nostra in te semper fuisset voluntas; itaque cum primum accepissem, te Rostochij subsedisse, non mediocriter me consolabar, quod ex eo, quod vicinum Daniae tuae locum optasses, te cito in patriam rediturum ominabamur. At vero non prius te Rostochium commigrasse renuntiatum, quam ex alijs accepimus, te iam inde pedem extulisse. Ab eo tempore frustra semper quaesivimus de statu rerum tuarum ac de sedibus, quas tibi constituisses. Denique nihil certi ad nos de te ferebatur praeter infelicitatem patriae tuae, quae te carere posset. Quare incerta animi mei de statu rerum tuarum sententia non passa est me officio illo erga te fungi, quod tu prior occupasti. Testis est mei consilij iuvenis quidam Mathematicus, qui hîc agit et in vestris domesticis se fuisse profitetur. Ab eo primum ante aliquot dies te in Arce Ranzoviana degere rescivi et recte se curaturum, si quid ad te literarum vellem. Id meditantem oppressit me adventus Nobilis adolescentis, FRANCISCI TEGNAGLIJ domestici vestri, qui tuas plenas amoris, humanitatis, eruditionis mihi attulit, ut nondum constituerim, utrum mihi gratuler de tuis illis humanissimis literis, an doleam hoc officium a te praereptum fuisse.

Quod de meo opere de emendatione temporum aliter iudicas ac imperiti, quanquam in eo agnosco amorem tuum in me, tamen exprimet confessionem ab illis, me non operam lusisse, vel eo nomine, quod tanto Viro mea placuerint, praesertim φιλαληθεστάτῳ et harum rerum intelligentissimo. Invidia neque nunc primum neque primi afflati sumus, cui opportunum se facit, quisquis aliquid supra captum plebeculae facit. Livore ab huiusmodi perstringi, est laborum suorum fructum percipere. Si scirent, quantum addant gloriae nostrae importunitate sua, cautius agerent, quam agunt. Ego horum neminem vidi, nisi imperitissimum, et quod pluris est, nequissimum. Quicquid scribunt, id vero chartae detrimento est, non existimationis nostrae. De simiolo Heydelbergensi, quem trophaea MILTIADIS non sinunt dormire, minus mirarer, si THEMISTOCLES esse posset. Sed imitari bonos aliorum hominum est, non stercoreorum et barbarorum et ab omni morum humanitate remotissimorum. Sed quid mirer, cum inveniat secutores et admiratores? εὗρεν ἄλοκας τὸ πῶμα. Quid in literis praestiterimus, non est pudoris nostri dicere. Hoc unum ingenue profitemur, neminem vivere, qui plures ad insaniam scriptis suis adegerit. Sed, ut fit, non unius generis homines sunt. Alij a nobis discunt et dissimulant, ne nobis aliquid acceptum ferant. Alij palam carpunt, et tamen nihil illis tam aegre est, quam quod illorum auctores non sint, propter quae tam hostili animo nos petunt. Sed quid de hac faece generis humani te morer? igitur de illo opere nostro, quod institueram dicere, fateor me plus laboris, quam industriae illo contulisse. Vix enim aliter mihi persuadere possum, et nobiscum praeclare agi putamus, si studiosiores quam doctiores habemur. Moneo autem me hominem imbecillis ingenij non potuisse tantam telam percurrere, ut non aliquando humanitus dormitarim, cum aliud pro alio contra animi nostri sententiam nobis excidit: quorum partem in Erratis correximus, partim imprudentes omisimus, quale illud, »Saturnum in annuo motu duodecimam partem unius gradus efficere«, quum vellemus dicere duodecim gradus, de quo et similibus possum iurare sancte: ἡ χεὶρ βέβληκεν, ἡ δὲ φρὴν ἀπόσκοπος. Quare, vir generosissime et doctissime, eiusmodi παροράματα potius quam ἁμαρτήματα, qualia multa in EUDOXO divinus HIPPARCHUS civiliter excusat, et quae ingenui Lectores emendare, non exagitare debent, tuum quoque est aut ἀπροσκόπως καὶ ἀπταίστως praeterire, aut, si per graviores tuas occupationes tibi licet, corrigere. At illa parva dictu menda retrimentis istis sunt argumenta novae foeturae librorum. Quod Septembrem vocamus, quem modo Octobrem, et feriam quartam, quam modo tertiam dixeramus, hoc typographias excalfacit. Barbaria et impudentia invenit ibi quod agat. Divinae aequinoctiorum observationes tuae locum invenerunt in calce librorum nostrorum, non utique quem debebant, sed quem potuerunt. Non enim prius illas acceperamus. Et tamen ibi sunt a nobis collocatae, ubi convenientissime cum Hipparcheis conferri possunt. Sane illud continuum quinquennium omnium priscarum observationum dignitatem et fidem elevat, cum tuae sibi constent, Hipparcheae quadrante diei plus aut minus distent, quod quidem illa aequinoctia valde suspecta nobis facit. Nos ex septem illud delegimus, quod ab autore ἀκριβέστατον vocatur: quemadmodum et anni forma ALFONSINI GELALÆAe quanquam elegantissimae nobis praelata est. Tuus annus Coelestis pauxillo minor GELALÆO. PTOLEMÆI vero observationes tam nobis falsas esse constat, quam multa alia apud illum scriptorem eximium. Ecce anno 886 Nabonassari, Pharmuthi IX, feria prima, Februarij 23, Christi 139, Sol, inquit, erat ἀκριβῶς in 3° 30' Piscium. At in meridie prima Thoth primi, Sol erat ἀκριβῶς in 3° 20' Piscium, eodem teste, nempe 26 Februarij. Ergo in 886 annis προήγησις tridui tantum facta fuerit. Quid absurdius? Haec et plura ἀτοπήματα diligenter in PTOLEMÆO annotavimus. Quare lubricae sunt eius observationes et male illis fiditur. Itaque non miror, si in 285 annis, tot scilicet, quot inter illius et HIPPARCHI observationes intersunt, unius diei progressionem aequinoctia tantum fecisse dicit, utpote qui sibi persuasisset in 300 annis id fieri. Itaque hinc illae lacrimae. A prima meridie Nabonassari ad aequinoctia ab se observata, sunt anni noningenti, et proinde triduum tantummodo aequinoctia εἰς τὰ προηγούμενα promota esse, quare omnes loci Solis ab eo notati ab hac haeresi pendent, et propterea falsi. Neque hac fine stat eius sententia. Si 23. Februarij est 3° 30' Piscium, ergo aequinoctium in 23. Martij, quia anno sequenti ita observarat. Ergo ab hac Epocha aequinoctij verni retro proportione 300 annorum addet diebus Iulianis, ut locum Solis designet, quod facit in omnibus eclipsibus veteribus. Quare qui sequitur illas Epochas Solis, sciat se 300 annorum προηγήσεις sequi. Arabes, qui mentem et consilium PTOLEMÆI non animadverterunt, ex illis aequinoctialibus PTOLEMÆI observationibus μορμολυκεῖον illud Trepidationis pepererunt, ut ex praegressione aequinoctiorum nihilo monstrosior motus octavae Sphaerae εἰς τὰ ἑπόμενα natus est. Neque enim ideo ullus motus Trepidationis assignandus, quod PTOLEMÆO Instrumenta sua imposuerunt; neque Sphaeram octavam ab occidente in orientem ideo promoveri putandum, quod puncta aequinoctialia in Ecliptica in antecedentia promoventur. Circuli enim aequinoctiales ad illa describuntur. Puncta vero mobilia sunt, ergo et ipsi circuli ad ea descripti sunt mobiles, et consequenter polus aequinoctialis mobilis. Itaque tempore HIPPARCHI polus aequinoctialis aberat a cauda Cynosurae gr. 12 24'. Hodie minus distat, quam tribus gradibus. Et tamen omnes putant polum mundi esse non aequinoctialis circuli, et quidem HIPPARCHUS primus huius eximiae rei observator in ea haeresi fuit. At error est, neque unquam circulus arcticus ullius loci parallelus fuit Tropicis aut aequinoctiali. Circuli arctici et antarctici polus idem est cum polo mundi. Circuli aequinoctialis polus variat, ut diximus. Hactenus igitur nunquam polus aequinoctialis fuit polus mundi; sed fore aliquando, fidem facit accessus propior ad Cynosurae caudam, sive ea est polus mundi, sive aliud punctum non longe ab ea remotum. Quid tui iudicij sit, quando illi duo poli convenerint, libenter audiverim. Nam magna res est. Item velim ex te scire an κατάχρησις illa et confusio poli aequinoctialis cum polo mundi aliquem errorem invexerit in collocatione Asterismorum in Sphaera solida. Multa enim in illis desidero et HIPPARCHUM ostendemus ea re deceptum. Edituri sumus in calce MANILIJ nostri aureolum libellum PTOLEMÆI adhuc ἀνέκδοτον περὶ ἀπλανῶν ἀστέρων, in quo per singulos dies anni Actiaci et Iuliani, quae stella matutino aut vespertino oriatur occidatve in quinque Climatibus, diligentissime designatur. Sed recentiores Asterismorum Astrothesiae valde illis repugnant, neque bene cum illis pariant tabulae directionum praeclari Artificis REINHOLDI. Nos omnes omnium Asterismorum Hipparcheas observationes accuratissime collectas in suos dies Iulianos digessimus, in quibus perfectissimus ille artifex notat, quae prima stella cuiusque Asterismi, quaeve ultima oriatur aut occidat, et cum qua parte Eclipticae. Deprehendimus male illi cum PTOLEMÆO convenire, in qua lite componenda, tuo, Vir clarissime, aut nullo auxilio opus est. Vix tandem vanitas anni siderei autore THEBITHIO nobis comperta est; qui scimus eadem die Iuliana eandem stellam semper oriri vespertino et occidere matutino, quod vere docebat nos Aegyptiorum sententia, quae semper eodem tempore Iuliano Caniculam oriri sciscit. Quod verum est. Nos tamen illi commentitio anno Sidereo ascensionem accommodavimus, ut et προηγήσει ἰσημερινῇ unius gradus per 70 annos, cuius opinionis auctor COPERNICUS, PTOLEMÆUS observat unum gradum promotionem fieri in centum annis. Ego vereor, ne in pluribus. Sed tu haec melius, a quo et alia expectamus. Nam nos homunciones procul spectamus, et intra vestibula sacrarij consistimus, quia nondum ἐπόπται sumus, neque spes unquam fore. Itaque sufficit nobis summorum virorum vestigia adorare, quorum tu Princeps, qui talia diu observasti. Nos vero vobis tantum a labore adesse possumus, quantum a peritia nobis desumus. Itaque quod sedulitas nostra nos docuit, id non pigebit in medium proferre. Aio igitur tempore HESIODI Arcturum vespertino oriri solitum in Boeotia et Attica VIII, die Martij Iuliani, eademque die in eodem tractu ortum illum observatum a METONE et EUCTEMONE, et postremo notatum saeculo PTOLEMÆI. Hoc confirmat sententiam nostram de confutatione anni siderei, et Aegyptiorum scitum, qui annum, quem Iulianum nos vocamus, κυνικόν vocabant, quod per plus, quam mille quingentos annos Caniculam semper eodem anni Iuliani die oriri prodiderunt. Haec observatio, ut spero, tibi ingrata non erit. Magnam a nobis inibitis gratiam, si paucularum stellarum, quae propiores sint Eclipticae, ut Basilisci et πρόποδος τῶν Διδύμων observationes vestras nobis communicare libuerit cum latitudinibus, longitudinibus et die Iuliana. Fortasse non infeliciter cum illis Hipparcheis et Ptolemaicis conferentur. Annum coelestem verum a te prodi unico posse certo scimus, a quo plura in Astrologia quotidie expectamus. Quam ineptus et imperitus fuit auctor Anni Pontificij, non dico nunc. Magis miror, tot millia hominum errores non deprehendisse. Sed te moramur.

Vale, Vir Praestantissime.
Lugduni Batavorum VII. Eid. Quintiles Iulianas, CIↃ. IↃ. XC VIII.
Tibi devotissimus et tuae amplitudinis studiosissimus
IOSEPHUS SCALIGER.
text.english:
**JOSEPH SCALIGER TO TYCHO BRAHE.**

Heartiest greeting.

Your departure from Denmark, most noble Man, as it was most bitter to us, so it always kept our minds in suspense [as to] what place you would choose for your fortunes. For where they should be settled, there we trusted some rest would be gained both for your mind and for your serious studies — and this we wished the more earnestly, the more inclined our goodwill toward you had always been. And so, when I first heard you had settled at **Rostock**, I consoled myself not a little, since from your having chosen a place near your Denmark we augured you would soon return to the fatherland. But it was not reported that you had moved to Rostock before we learned, from others, that you had already withdrawn your foot thence. From that time we always asked in vain about the state of your affairs, and the seats you had established for yourself. In the end, nothing certain was brought us about you, except the misfortune of your fatherland in being able to lose you. Wherefore the uncertain judgement of my mind about the state of your affairs did not allow me to perform that duty toward you which you have anticipated first. Witness of my intention is a certain young Mathematician who acts here, and professes that he was among your household; from him first, some days ago, I learned that you dwell **in a Rantzau castle**, and that he would duly see [to it] if I wished any letter to you. While I was meditating this, the arrival of the noble youth **Franz Tengnagel**, your household-member, surprised me — who brought me your [letter], full of love, humanity, and erudition — so that I have not yet decided whether to congratulate myself on that most humane letter of yours, or to grieve that this duty was snatched from me [that you wrote first].

**That you judge of my work *On the Emendation of Times* otherwise than the unskilled** — though in it I recognise your love toward me — yet it will extort a confession from them that I did not waste my labour, even on this ground, that my [work] pleased so great a Man, especially **one most-truth-loving [φιλαληθεστάτῳ] and most intelligent in these matters**. By envy we are afflicted neither now first, nor [are we] the first — [envy], to whom whoever does anything above the grasp of the little crowd makes himself opportune. To be carped by the malice of such [men] is to reap the fruit of one's labours. If they knew how much they add to my glory by their importunity, they would act more cautiously than they do. Of these I have seen none but the most unskilled and (what is more) the most worthless. Whatever they write is to the detriment of paper, not of my repute. **About that Heidelberg little-ape, whom the trophies of Miltiades will not let sleep**, I should wonder less, could he be a Themistocles. But to imitate the good belongs to other men — not to dung-born barbarians, most remote from all humanity of manners. But why should I wonder, since he finds followers and admirers? *"The lid found its furrows"* [εὗρεν ἄλοκας τὸ πῶμα — like finds like]. What I have achieved in letters, it is not for my modesty to say. This one thing I frankly profess: that no one lives who has driven more [men] to madness by his writings. But, as it happens, men are not of one kind. Some learn from us, and dissemble it, lest they credit us with anything; others openly carp, and yet nothing is so painful to them as that they are not the authors of those things for which they attack us with so hostile a mind. But why do I detain you about this dregs of humankind?

So, about that work of mine which I had begun to speak of: **I confess that I put more labour than skill into it.** For I can scarcely persuade myself otherwise; and we think we are dealt with splendidly, if we are held more studious than learned. But I warn that I, a man of weak talent, could not run through so great a web without sometimes humanly dozing — when one thing fell from me for another, against our mind's intention — **part of which we corrected in the Errata, part we imprudently omitted; such as that "Saturn, in its annual motion, makes a twelfth part of one degree," when we meant to say twelve degrees** — of which, and the like, I can swear holily: *"the hand threw, but the mind was off the mark"* [ἡ χεὶρ βέβληκεν, ἡ δὲ φρὴν ἀπόσκοπος — a slip of the hand, not the mind]. Wherefore, most noble and learned man, **such oversights [παροράματα] rather than errors [ἁμαρτήματα]** — like the many that the divine Hipparchus civilly excuses in Eudoxus, and which noble Readers ought to emend, not assail — it is yours too either to pass over without offence [ἀπροσκόπως καὶ ἀπταίστως], or, if your weightier occupations allow, to correct. But those faults — small to tell — are, to those refuse-men [critics], arguments for a new brood of books. That we call September what [we had just called] October, and the fourth feria [Wednesday] what we had said the third [Tuesday] — this heats up the printing-presses. Barbarity and impudence find there something to do.

**Your divine observations of the equinoxes found a place at the end of our books** — not, indeed, the place they deserved, but the place they could [find]; for we had not received them earlier. And yet they are placed by us where they can most fittingly be compared with the Hipparchean. Truly **that continuous quinquennium [5-year run] elevates the dignity and trust of all the ancient observations** — since yours are self-consistent, while the Hipparchean differ by a quarter-day, more or less, which indeed makes those [Hipparchus's] equinoxes very suspect to us. We chose, from the seven, that one which is called by the author **"most accurate" [ἀκριβέστατον]** — just as the Alphonsine form of the year was preferred by us to the **Jalali** [GELALAEA, the Persian Jalali calendar], however most elegant. **Your celestial year [is] a little less than the Jalali.** But **Ptolemy's observations are as false to us as many other things in that eminent writer.** Behold: in the year 886 of Nabonassar, Pharmuthi 9, the first feria [Sunday], 23 February, [year] 139 of Christ, **the Sun, he says, was accurately [ἀκριβῶς] in 3° 30′ of Pisces. But at the noon of the first Thoth of the first [year], the Sun was accurately in 3° 20′ of Pisces, by the same witness — namely 26 February. So in 886 years a precession [προήγησις] of only three days would have been made. What more absurd?** These and more absurdities [ἀτοπήματα] we diligently noted in Ptolemy. So his observations are slippery, and ill-trusted. And so I do not wonder if he says that in 285 years (as many, that is, as lie between his and Hipparchus's observations) the equinoxes made only one day's progression — since he had persuaded himself it happens in 300 years. **Hence those tears.** From the first noon of Nabonassar to the equinoxes observed by himself are nine hundred years, and accordingly the equinoxes were advanced backward [εἰς τὰ προηγούμενα] by only three days; wherefore all the Sun-places noted by him depend on this heresy, and are therefore false. Nor does his view stop here. If 23 February is 3° 30′ Pisces, then the equinox is on 23 March, because he had so observed it the following year. So from this epoch of the vernal equinox, backward by a proportion of 300 years, he will add to the Julian days, to designate the Sun's place — which he does in all the old eclipses. Wherefore whoever follows those Solar Epochs, let him know that he follows **300-year precessions** [the wrong rate].

**The Arabs, who did not notice Ptolemy's mind and plan, from those equinoctial observations of Ptolemy brought forth that bugbear [μορμολυκεῖον] of Trepidation** — as, from the precession of the equinoxes, a no-less-monstrous motion of the eighth Sphere toward the consequents [εἰς τὰ ἑπόμενα] was born. For no Trepidation-motion is to be assigned, because Ptolemy's instruments imposed upon him; nor is the eighth Sphere to be thought advanced from west to east, because the equinoctial points are advanced in the Ecliptic toward the antecedents. **For the equinoctial circles are described with reference to those [points]. But the points are mobile; therefore the circles described to them are also mobile; and consequently the equinoctial pole is mobile.** So in Hipparchus's time the equinoctial pole was distant from the tail of Cynosura [the Pole-star region] 12° 24′; today it is distant less than three degrees. And yet all think the pole of the world is [the pole] not of the equinoctial circle — and indeed Hipparchus, the first observer of this eminent matter, was in that heresy. **But it is an error**: never was the arctic circle of any place parallel to the Tropics or the equinoctial. The pole of the arctic and antarctic circle is the same as the pole of the world; the pole of the equinoctial circle varies, as we said. **Hitherto, then, the equinoctial pole was never the pole of the world; but that it will be, sometime, the closer approach to Cynosura's tail gives faith** — whether that [tail] be the pole of the world, or another point not far removed from it. **What your judgement is, [as to] when those two poles will converge, I should gladly hear; for it is a great matter.** Likewise I should wish to know from you whether that misuse [κατάχρησις] and confusion of the equinoctial pole with the world's pole has introduced any error in the placing of the Asterisms on the solid Sphere [the globe]. For I miss many things in them, and we shall show Hipparchus deceived in this. **We are about to publish, at the end of our *Manilius*, a golden little book of Ptolemy, still unpublished [ἀνέκδοτον], *On the Fixed Stars* [περὶ ἀπλανῶν ἀστέρων — the *Phaseis*]**, in which, through each day of the Actian and Julian year, what star rises or sets, morning or evening, in five Climates, is most diligently designated. But the more recent star-placements [*Astrothesiae*] of the asterisms strongly conflict with them; nor do the direction-tables of the excellent artificer **Reinhold** agree well with them. We have digested all the Hipparchean observations of all the asterisms, most accurately collected, into their Julian days — in which that most perfect artificer notes what first star of each asterism, and what last, rises or sets, and with what part of the Ecliptic. We find he agrees ill with Ptolemy — in settling which dispute, most renowned Man, your help, or no one's, is needed.

Scarcely at last has **the vanity of the sidereal year — by its author Thebit [Thabit ibn Qurra]** — been discovered by us, who know that on the same Julian day the same star always rises in the evening and sets in the morning; which the view of the Egyptians truly taught us, which holds that **the Dog-star [Sirius] always rises at the same Julian time**. Which is true. Yet we accommodated the ascension to that fictitious Sidereal year, as also to an equinoctial precession [προηγήσει ἰσημερινῇ] of one degree per 70 years — of which opinion **Copernicus** is the author; **Ptolemy observes one degree's progression to be made in a hundred years; I fear [it is] in more**. But you [know] these better, from whom we expect other things too. For we manikins look from afar, and stand within the vestibules of the sanctuary, because we are not yet initiates [ἐπόπται], nor is there hope we ever shall be. **So it suffices us to adore the footsteps of the highest men, of whom you are the Prince, who have long observed such things.** We can be of service to you only so much in labour as we fail you in skill. So what our diligence has taught us, it will not irk [us] to bring forward. **I say, then, that in Hesiod's time Arcturus was wont to rise in the evening, in Boeotia and Attica, on the 8th day of March Julian; and on the same day, in the same region, that rising was observed by Meton and Euctemon, and lastly noted in Ptolemy's age.** This confirms our view on the confutation of the sidereal year, and the Egyptians' knowledge, who called the year which we call Julian the **"Dog-year" [κυνικόν — Sothic]**, because for more than 1500 years they reported the Dog-star always to rise on the same day of the Julian year. This observation, I hope, will not be unwelcome to you. **You will gain great favour with us, if it please you to communicate to us your observations of a few stars closer to the Ecliptic — such as Basiliscus [Regulus] and the "forefoot of the Twins" [πρόποδος τῶν Διδύμων, Gemini] — with the latitudes, longitudes, and the Julian day.** Perhaps they will be compared not unsuccessfully with the Hipparchean and Ptolemaic. **We know for certain that the true celestial year can be revealed by you alone**, from whom we expect more in Astronomy daily. How inept and unskilled was the author of the Pontifical Year [the **Gregorian calendar**], I do not say now. I wonder more that so many thousands of men have not detected the errors. But we are detaining you.

Farewell, most excellent Man.
Leiden, the 7th [day before] the Ides of July [9 July], Julian [reckoning], 1598.
Most devoted to you, and most zealous of your greatness,
**Joseph Scaliger.**

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondent.** **Incoming**, **Joseph Justus Scaliger** at **Leiden** → **Tycho** — **the first letter of the Scaliger–Tycho correspondence**, written from Wandsbek-era news (Scaliger has just located Tycho via a young Leiden mathematician [a former Tycho assistant] and via **Tengnagel**, who delivered Tycho's opening letter).
- **Significance — the foundational chronology/precession letter (a keystone of the whole exchange).**
 - **The *De emendatione temporum* and its critics.** Scaliger thanks Tycho for esteeming his great chronological work above "the unskilled," and rails at his detractors (notably a **"Heidelberg little-ape"** — a chronology-critic at Heidelberg). He **candidly confesses errata** (e.g. "Saturn's annual motion a *twelfth* of a degree" for "*twelve* degrees"; September/October, Wednesday/Tuesday slips) — **"oversights, not errors" (παροράματα not ἁμαρτήματα)** — and asks Tycho "to emend, not assail."
 - **Tycho's equinox observations praised.** Tycho's **five-year run of equinox observations** (placed at the end of the *De emendatione*) is "divine" and **self-consistent**, exposing **Hipparchus's** equinoxes (varying by ¼-day) as "very suspect"; **Tycho's celestial year** is "a little less than the Jalali."
 - **The Ptolemy precession critique.** Scaliger shows **Ptolemy's solar data imply an absurd 3-day precession in 886 years**, so "all his Sun-places are false," resting on the wrong **1°/100-year (= 300-year-per-degree)** precession.
 - **★ The trepidation debunking and the moving equinoctial pole (the *Diatriba* seed).** Scaliger demolishes the **Arab "bugbear of Trepidation"** and the eighth-sphere motion, arguing instead that **the *equinoctial pole itself is mobile* (distinct from the fixed world-pole)** — now within 3° of Cynosura's tail (12°24′ in Hipparchus's time) — and **converging on the Pole-star**. He **asks Tycho's judgement on when the two poles will meet** — the central thesis he develops in **brahe-t_16000310001 (the *Diatriba*)** and that Tycho rejects in **brahe-t_16000723001**.
 - **The Ptolemy *Phaseis* edition.** Scaliger announces his edition of **Ptolemy's hitherto-unpublished *On the Fixed Stars* (the *Phaseis*)**, appended to his **Manilius**, and the conflict between ancient (Hipparchus/Ptolemy) and modern (**Reinhold**) star-placements — needing Tycho's help.
 - **The sidereal-year debunking.** Scaliger rejects **Thabit ibn Qurra's** sidereal year, affirming the **Egyptian/Sothic ("Dog-year") constancy** (Sirius rising the same Julian day for 1500 years), confirmed by **Hesiod/Meton/Euctemon's Arcturus rising (8 March)**. He asks Tycho for observations of **Regulus and the "forefoot of Gemini"** to compare with the ancients, and disparages the **Gregorian ("Pontifical") calendar**.
 - **The deference.** The famous self-positioning: *"we manikins … stand within the vestibules of the sanctuary … not yet initiates; it suffices us to adore the footsteps of the highest men, of whom you are the Prince."*
- **Cross-references.** The **opening** of the Scaliger–Tycho exchange (→ brahe-t_15990417001, brahe-t_16000310001, brahe-t_16000723001); the **precession/trepidation/sidereal-year** and **chronology** threads (also brahe-t_16000327002, brahe-t_16000107001).
- **Persons & works named.** Joseph Scaliger (*De emendatione temporum*, the *Manilius*, the Ptolemy *Phaseis*); **Tycho**; the young Leiden mathematician (former Tycho assistant); **Franz Tengnagel**; the **"Heidelberg ape"** (a chronology-critic); **Miltiades, Themistocles** (allusion); **Hipparchus, Ptolemy, Eudoxus, Reinhold, Thabit ibn Qurra (Thebithius), Copernicus, Meton, Euctemon, Hesiod**; the **Nabonassar** era; the **Jalali** and **Alphonsine** calendars; the **Gregorian ("Pontifical") calendar**; **Regulus (Basiliscus)**, **Gemini**. Places: **Leiden**, **Rostock**, the **Rantzau castle** (Wandsbek). The Greek phrases are reproduced throughout.
- **Calendar.** *Lugduni Batavorum VII. Eid. Quintiles **Iulianas**, CIↃIↃXCVIII* — "the 7th before the Ides of July, **Julian** [= Old Style]" = **9 July 1598 [O.S.]** (Scaliger pointedly dates Julian; CIↃIↃXCVIII = 1598). Header and label agree.
- **Correction.** Latin 'sunt fere anni noningenti' corrected to 'sunt anni noningenti': Dreyer (TBOO VIII p.85) prints the unhedged reading with no 'fere'; the English 'are nearly nine hundred years' is corrected to 'are nine hundred years' to match.

Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Read all 7 Dreyer page images in the extract (pages 1-4, then 5-7) visually, no text layer. Collated the full letter (Scaliger's dense chronology/precession argument) line by line: the transcribed original matches Dreyer's print verbatim except for the two text error logged above. Every proper name (Miltiades, Themistocles, Eudoxus, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, Reinhold, Thebit/Thebithius, Copernicus, Meton, Euctemon, Hesiod, Franciscus Tengnagel), Greek phrase, and number/date (886 Nabonassar, Pharmuthi IX, 23/26 February, AD 139, 3°30'/3°20' Pisces, 285, 300, and c. 900 years, 12°24', <3°, 70, 100, VIII Martij, 1500+ years, VII Eid. Quintiles / CIƆ.IƆ.XCVIII = 9 July 1598) was verified against the page images and renders correctly and completely in the English, including the technical precession/trepidation argument. Per the grading rule, any text error forces grade Possible regardless of severity; both found here are low-severity (they don't change the sense a scholar would take away), hence verdict *minor* rather than *serious*. No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found in the translation itself.

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). Dreyer's heading (p.83) reads "...AD TYCHONEM BRAHE."; the transcribed original drops "BRAHE". The English silently supplies the fuller correct form, so the omission surfaces only in the Latin. Dreyer prints: *IOSEPHUS SCALIGER AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.*.
- **text error** (low). Dreyer (p.85, line c. 36) prints the flat, unhedged "sunt anni noningenti" (there are nine hundred years); the transcribed original inserts a hedge word, "fere" (nearly), not present in Dreyer. Dreyer prints: *sunt anni noningenti*.

**Repaired.** Verified against the Dreyer page images for this letter's opening (TBOO VIII pp.82-85, the first four of the seven-page extract). The heading defect (missing 'BRAHE') proved not to be present in the supplied the transcribed original, which already matches Dreyer's two-line heading exactly, so it is recorded as no_change_needed rather than fixed.
