documents.abstract: Reports conversations about the causes of Tycho's departure from Denmark, defending the fatherland against those who condemn it for losing him.
documents.incipit: S. eruditissime d:ne magister Johannes, amice rara fide mihi perspecte. Multi, ex quo …
documents.editorial_note: **Direction note.** A third party's letter, not Tycho's correspondence: a hostile letter from Johannes Stygge to Hans Aalborg, the Copenhagen bookseller, preserved among the Tycho papers in Langebek's diplomatarium. It gives the view of the Danish party hostile to Tycho; its claims are the writer's.

text.original:
ERUDITISSIMO NEC NON PERSPICATISSIMO VIRO DOMINO M. JOHANNI ALBURGIACO, BIBLIOPOLAe HAFFNIENSI PRIMARIO, AMICO MEO PERANTIQUO, DENTUR.

S. eruditissime d:ne magister Johannes, amice rara fide mihi perspecte. Multi, ex quo patriam reliqui, de Tychonis Brahe e Dania discessu nescio quae garrire ausi eius causas a me sciscitati sunt, quibus ea, quae patriae nostrae honorifica erant, retuli, licet quibusdam, quibus Tycho iste cum nova sua necdum visa aut explorata mathesi pro oraculo habetur, satisfacere nec valui nec potui, putantibus, me in gratiam patriae ista excogitare. Multa enim illi, qui Tychonis partibus nimium student (qui sane non pauci sunt, etiam inter viros illustres), cum in patriam tum praecipue in eos, qui rebus isthic nunc praesunt, minus honorifica pronunciant. Quae quam sint falsa, te minime latere arbitror. Sunt qui Daniam utroque orbatam oculo (et quod ipsa non videat, et quod artium lumine destituta conspici ab aliis nequeat) caecam nunc redditam nimis insolenter dicere praesumant. Nonnulli novam barbariem ex qua exulavere Musae, vocitant, alii Machiavellismum, alii invidiam, alii subdolam vafriciem, nonnulli avaritiam; quidam etiam quorundam inscitiam et ruditatem praetendunt nobisque exprobrant (quod scilicet instar galli Aesopici inter margaritam et hordei granum discernere nequeamus). Et quomodo, quaeso, ego solus tot praestantium virorum praejudicia refellere sustineam? Cum omnes fere Tychonem tanti faciant, quasi non sit alius in Dania nobilis, qui melius literas didicerit quam ille, sicque nos alios pro ciphris habent; thi naar een kommer først for ordet at staae tilig op, maae han siden sove saalaenge som han vil, ut vulgatum fert dicterium. Quare nihil optabilius ducerem, quam extare aliquod scriptum publicum, quo Tycho, quam parum possit et quam inutilis nobis fuerit, ignorantibus patefaciat, sicque patria nostra a calumniis insciorum et Tychoni nimis faventium liberari poterit. Fieri enim posset, ut quae nunc oretenus saltem inter doctos et praestantes viros narrantur et hinc inde per literas ab iis sparguntur, fidem apud incautos inveniant et fortassis etiam aliquando scriptis eorum publicis immisceantur; patriam itaque nostram ab his vaniloquis liberare, quantum in me est, percuperem. Relatione autem quorundam Hamburgensium, cum nuper in convivio simul essemus, non sine magno gaudio intellexi, penes te esse librum quendam, quem rarissimae doctrinae caesaris mathematicus contra insolentem hunc Tychonem in publicum Praga emisit, at cum apud bibliopolas hic de eodem mox avide conquisivissem, responderunt, illum Francofurti non extare, sed existimarunt, bibliopolam praecipuum Hafniensem illum undecunque tandem adeptum esse, uti eos te notare non dubitavi. Aderat etiam alius quidam, qui quosdam ex professoribus Hafniensibus eum librum pro eximio valdeque grato dono a te accepisse referebat, quodque iis adeo scriptum hoc placeat, ut in sinu gaudeant atque sibi congratulentur, quod aliquis tam egregius vir se Tychoni opposuerit atque illum suis coloribus merito depinxerit. Nam et ego arbitror, sic eos, qui discessus ejus causas e Dania dedisse insimulantur, a suspicione liberari posse atque exteris rectius constare, quam nulla vel perexigua fuerit jactura, quod Tychonem hunc patria nostra amiserit et retinere noluerit. Est quidem adhuc Tycho ille in arce Ranzoviana quadam non longe hinc remota, sed rarissime civitatem ingreditur. Et cum accedit, tot curribus et equis tamque pompose venit, ac si plus quam nobilis esset. Titillat enim ipsum, quod e variis Germaniae locis, uti audis, veniant multi clari et praestantes viri, qui ipsum invisunt et magni faciunt, et quod primarii quique in urbe ipsum in nimio honore habeant. Ideoque suos conterraneos non amplius agnoscit vixque Danus haberi vult, adeo ut cum proprio suo consobrino Jodoco Hogio, qui aliquandiu hic fuit, ne semel loqui voluerit, et ille, cum accedere eum videret, tam splendide et insolenter se gerere non est ausus; multo minus ego, quem ne aspicere quidem dignatur, cum in curru sublimi per plateas sex equis, sequente uno et altero, vehitur, circumcurrente magna hominum caterva, qui eum, ac si princeps esset, videre gestiunt. Intellexi quoque, quod, quando templum diebus his solennibus ingreditur, quod tamen raro facit, tunc sternunt in ipsius sella, quam ipsi deputarunt in praecipuo quodam templi loco, ante ipsum sericum pannum et pulvinaria conferunt, ligesom hand var meer end andre got folk. Et magnum etiam honorem ipsius conjugi et filiabus tribuunt, saa det var nok, de vare grevinder, saa statzlig holdes de. Interim ego lateo et cum magnificentia nihil habeo commercii. Sed ad rem revertar. Quoniam igitur mihi multum subsidii in mea peregrinatione ex hoc libro, si eum mecum habuero et aliis monstrare potuero, ad refutandas aliorum objectiones manare posse confido, te per amicitiam nostram etiam atque etiam obtestor, velis mihi tria aut quatuor exemplaria de eodem concedere honoris eorum tuendi gratia, qui Tychonis abitum clam procurasse referuntur, utque inde habeam plura argumenta, quibus nostrates defendam. Feceris mihi sic rem longe gratissimam et tibi aliisque, uti spero, non inhonorificam. Nam cum doctissimis illis in academia Hafniensi scriptum illud summopere, ut etiam meretur, arrideat et illi rectius de Tychone, quem etiam melius norunt, judicare possunt quam caeteri, praesertim inaestimabilis ille mathematicus d:ns d. Thomas Finchius nunc, ut audio, rector magnificus (qui nequaquam opus habuit, cum in insula ista Tychonis inutilia instrumenta vidit, a nasutulo illo et cornuto adhuc institui, quomodo vocarentur qualemcunque haberent usum, uti mihi, antequam e patria discederem, relatum est), cuius unius judicium (praesertim cum et ille semigermanus sit et propterea apud Germanos plus fidei merebitur) pluris faciendum quis dubitat, quam mille aliorum sciolorum, qui in Tychonis instrumenta et scripta tam bene inquirere non norunt? Nec dubito, quin famosissimus ille vir et non saltem in Dania, sed etiam plurimis aliis in regionibus notus, doctor Petrus Severini, cum et iste Tychonem intus et in cute plus satis norit, suam acutissimam censuram de eodem argutissimo scripto protulerit, modo eam aperire pro singulari et abstrusa sua prudentia aliisque communicare non dedignatus fuerit. Et quia in tanti viri mentionem hic incido, narrabo quippiam, quae ex Anglis quibusdam studiosis Hamburgum, cum primum huc venissem, transeuntibus audivi, quod non parum aegre ferebam. Erant illi in eodem mecum diversorio, cumque Danum me esse cognovissent (quod tamen inter quosvis doctos, cum ob Tychonis abitum tam male audiant Dani, dissimulare soleo), quaesiverunt a me, an illustrem illum et celeberrimum virum Tychonem Brahe nossem, quod tamen plane abnegare non potui, dicens vidisse quidem in Dania eum, et, licet nobilis, obscurum tamen alias ibi eum esse nec ita celebrem, ut illi putant. Dicebant, se audivisse, illum nunc in Germania esse, vellent eum multorum nomine, praecipue cuiusdam, si recte memini, Johannis Deen, salutare. Ego respondi, me, ubi esset, ignorare nec multum curare (nam alias statim concurrissent, quod et postea ab aliis edocti fecerunt). Mox subjunxit quidam eorum Ruffus: Nescis tu Danus ea, quae nos in Anglia scimus? Severinus, regis medicus, diutino et clandestino eius odio (ob medicamenta eius Theophrastica, quae is tam egregie parare novit et olim regi Friderico et nobilibus postea aliis quoque gratis dare solitus est) laboravit, quia putavit, suae sic aliquid decedere existimationi. Hunc igitur apud nos dicunt multa subdole in Tychonem machinatum esse, ut tandem is talia indigne ferens discederet. Mox ego respondi: quomodo ille doctor hoc facere posset, cum non sit nobilis? Tycho est ex clara et magna familia in Dania, nec habent apud nos tantam autoritatem ut apud vos doctores, et quare non fecit id antea, si potuit, quam nunc? Tunc ille excepit: etiamsi doctor is non est nobilis, tamen habet alios quosdam nobiles et quidem praecipuos, qui apud regem multa possunt, qui doctori huic valde auscultant; per eos potuit tanquam per tertiam et quartam manum efficere, quod per semet ipsum non dabatur. Ego inutili[!]: doctor ille seorsim et solitarie vivit, sua tantum curat, nec se rebus politicis immiscet, estque Tychonis, uti existimo, propter communia studia amicus. At ille: hi, qui ita latent et nolunt videri id, quod agunt, agere, sed per alios clam agunt, a talibus maxime cavendum, praesertim si habent Italica ingenia et honores atque divitias supra sortem affectant; se scire aliquot tales in Anglia, etiam humili genere natos, sed ut plurimum illis male cadere solere. Tum ego stomachabundus sic conclusi, quod ista, quae de doctore illo Dano narrant, sunt somnia et merae suspiciones, nec unquam quid tale in Dania audivi; quomodo ergo vos, Angli qui estis, sciretis? Et mox discessi, indignum illum reputans, cum quo amplius verba commutarem, veritus, ne a verbis ad verbera res deveniret, visus enim mihi superbe nimis Danis ob hunc Tychonem insultare, quasi non essent in Dania alii boni viri illo longe praestantiores et doctiores. Sed valeant ista (nolo enim omnia, quae de his audivi, scio sentioque, scribere, nec admodum etiam tutum videtur), fac saltem, ut exemplaria libri expetiti aliquot quocunque tandem pretio certo obtineam. Pecunias, quas expetis, cognatus meus Claudius Dyre tibi solvet, et libros ad me, ubicunque fuero (neque enim hic diu morari Hamburgi constitui), perferri curabit. Rogoque, ut simul mihi tuam quoque censuram de eodem libro scribere non degraveris et me in omnibus voti facere compotem. Si quid sit, in quo tibi vicissem gratificare potero, alacrem me eius habebis executorem. Ante omnia vero cave, ne quis ex amicis Tychonis (si quos forte adhuc ibi habeat) resciscat, me illa exemplaria a te accepisse.

His vale cum conjuge tua lectissima, quae ut plures tibi procreet haeredes, vide.
Hamburgo 10. die julii anni 1598.
Johannes Stygge, mea manu.
text.english:
**To the most erudite and most perspicacious man, Master Johannes Alburgiacus [Hans Aalborg], chief Bookseller at Copenhagen, my very old friend — to be given.**

Greeting, most erudite Master Johannes, friend of rare fidelity, well known to me. Many, since I left the fatherland, daring to chatter I-know-not-what about **Tycho Brahe's departure from Denmark**, have asked me its causes; to whom I reported what was honourable to our fatherland — though I could not satisfy some, for whom that Tycho, **with his new mathematics, not yet seen or explored, is held as an oracle**, [and who] think I devise these things to favour the fatherland. For those who too much favour Tycho's side (and they are indeed not few, even among illustrious men) pronounce many less-honourable things, both against the fatherland and especially against those who now preside over affairs there. How false these are, I think you well know. There are some who too insolently presume to say that **Denmark is now made blind, deprived of both eyes** (both that it itself does not see, and that, destitute of the light of the arts, it cannot be seen by others). Some call it a **new barbarism, from which the Muses are exiled**; others, **Machiavellism**; others, **envy**; others, sly cunning; some, **avarice**; some even allege the ignorance and rudeness of certain men, and reproach us — that, forsooth, like Aesop's cock, **we cannot discern between a pearl and a barley-grain**. And how, pray, should I alone sustain the refuting of so many distinguished men's prejudices? — since almost all make so much of Tycho, as if there were no other noble in Denmark who learned letters better than he, and so hold us others for ciphers; *for "when a man once gets the name of an early riser, he may afterward sleep as long as he likes,"* as the common saying has it [Danish]. Wherefore I should think nothing more desirable than that **there exist some public writing by which Tycho may lay open to the ignorant how little he can do, and how useless he was to us** — and so our fatherland may be freed from the calumnies of the ignorant and of those too favourable to Tycho. For it could happen that what is now told only by mouth among learned and distinguished men, and scattered here and there by them in letters, may find credit among the incautious, and perhaps even sometime be mingled into their public writings; and so I should much wish, as far as in me lies, to free our fatherland from these vain-talkers.

Now, by the report of certain Hamburgers, when we were lately together at a banquet, I learned, not without great joy, that **you have a certain book which the Emperor's mathematician of rarest learning [Ursus] published at Prague against this insolent Tycho**; but when I eagerly sought it here among the booksellers, they answered that it is not to be had at **Frankfurt**, but reckoned that the chief Copenhagen bookseller had got it from somewhere — and I did not doubt they meant you. There was present too another, who reported that **certain of the Copenhagen professors had received that book from you as an excellent and very welcome gift, and that this writing so pleases them that they rejoice in their bosom and congratulate themselves that some so distinguished a man has opposed Tycho and rightly painted him in his [true] colours.** For I too judge that thus those who are accused of having given the causes of his departure from Denmark can be freed from suspicion, and it can be better established to foreigners how no loss, or a very slight one, [resulted] from our fatherland's having lost this Tycho, and being unwilling to retain him. That Tycho is indeed still in a certain **Rantzau castle, not far distant hence, but very rarely enters the city; and when he comes, he comes with so many carriages and horses, and so pompously, as if he were more than noble.** For it tickles him that, from various places of Germany (as you hear), many famous and distinguished men come to visit him and esteem him highly, and that the chief men in the city hold him in excessive honour. And so **he no longer acknowledges his compatriots, and scarcely wishes to be held a Dane** — so much that **with his own cousin Jost Høg [Jodocus Hogius], who was here a while, he would not speak even once**; and that man, when he saw [Tycho] approach, did not dare bear himself so splendidly and insolently — much less I, whom he does not even deign to look at, when **in a lofty carriage he is drawn through the streets by six horses, with one or two [more] following, a great crowd of people running about, eager to see him as if he were a prince.** I learned too that, when he enters the church on solemn days (which, however, he rarely does), they then spread, in his seat (which they assigned him in a chief place of the church), before him a silk cloth, and bring cushions — *"as if he were more than other good folk"* [Danish]. And they pay great honour, too, to his wife and daughters — *"so that it was enough [as if] they were countesses, so grandly are they held"* [Danish]. Meanwhile I lie hidden, and have no commerce with [his] magnificence. But let me return to the matter.

Since, then, I am confident that much help can flow to me, in my travels, from this book — if I have it with me and can show it to others — toward refuting others' objections, I beseech you again and again, by our friendship, **be willing to grant me three or four copies of it**, for the sake of guarding the honour of those who are reported to have secretly procured Tycho's departure, and that I may have thence more arguments by which to defend our countrymen. You will do me a most welcome thing, and one not dishonourable to you and others, as I hope. For since that writing pleases those most learned men in the Copenhagen academy greatly (as it deserves), and they can judge of Tycho — whom they also know better — more rightly than the rest: **especially that inestimable mathematician, Lord Dr. Thomas Fincke**, now (as I hear) Rector Magnificus — who by no means needed, when he saw Tycho's useless instruments on that island, **to be taught by that sharp-nosed, horned fellow [Tycho]** what they were called, or what use (such as it was) they had, as was told me before I left the fatherland — whose single judgement (especially as he too is half-German, and on that account will merit more credit among the Germans), who doubts is to be valued more than a thousand other sciolists, who do not know how to inquire so well into Tycho's instruments and writings? Nor do I doubt that that most famous man, known not only in Denmark but in very many other regions too, **Doctor Petrus Severinus [Peder Sørensen]** — since he too knows Tycho inside and out, more than enough — has given his most acute censure of the same most subtle writing, if only he has not disdained, in his singular and abstruse prudence, to open it and share it with others.

And since I here fall upon mention of so great a man [Severinus], I will narrate something I heard from **certain English students passing through Hamburg, when I had first come hither** — which I bore not a little ill. They were in the same inn with me; and when they had learned that I was a Dane (which, however, I am wont to dissemble among learned men, since the Danes are so ill-spoken-of on account of Tycho's departure), they asked me whether I knew that illustrious and most celebrated man Tycho Brahe — which I could not plainly deny, saying that I had indeed seen him in Denmark, and that, though noble, he is otherwise obscure there, and not so celebrated as they think. They said they had heard he is now in Germany, [and] **wished to greet him in the name of many — especially of one, if I remember rightly, Johannes Deen**. I answered that I do not know where he is, nor much care (for otherwise they would have run to him at once — which, taught afterward by others, they did). Soon one of them, **a red-haired one [Ruffus]**, added: *"Do not you, a Dane, know what we in England know? **Severinus, the king's physician**, laboured under his [Tycho's] long and secret hatred — on account of his **Theophrastic [Paracelsian] medicines**, which he knows so excellently to prepare, and used of old to give freely to King Frederick, and afterward to other nobles too — because he [Tycho] thought that something thus detracted from his [own] reputation. **This man [Severinus], therefore, they say among us, contrived many things slyly against Tycho, so that at last he, bearing such things unworthily, departed.**"* Soon I answered: how could that doctor do this, since he is not noble? Tycho is of an illustrious and great family in Denmark, nor have doctors with us such authority as with you; and why did he not do it before, if he could, rather than now? Then [the Englishman] rejoined: even though that doctor is not noble, yet he has certain other nobles — and indeed chief ones, who can do much with the king, [and] who hearken greatly to this doctor; **through them, as through a third and fourth hand, he could effect what was not granted [him] through himself.** I [replied]: that doctor lives apart and solitarily, cares only for his own [affairs], nor mixes himself in political matters, and is, as I think, Tycho's friend, on account of their common studies. But he: **those who thus hide, and do not wish to seem to do what they do, but act secretly through others — such are most to be guarded against, especially if they have Italian wits, and affect honours and riches above their lot**; he knew some such in England, even of humble birth, but for the most part it is wont to fall out ill for them. Then I, stomachfully, thus concluded: that **these things they tell about that Danish doctor are dreams and mere suspicions, and I never heard any such thing in Denmark; how, then, should you, who are English, know it?** And I soon departed, reckoning him unworthy that I should exchange more words with him, fearing lest the matter come from words to blows — for he seemed to me too proudly to insult the Danes over this Tycho, as if there were not in Denmark other good men far more distinguished and learned than he. But let these things be (for I do not wish to write all that I have heard, know, and feel about them — nor does it even seem altogether safe); only see to it that I certainly get some copies of the desired book, at whatever price. The money you ask, my kinsman **Claus Dyre [Claudius Dyre]** will pay you, and will see the books carried to me, wherever I am (for I have resolved not to stay long here at Hamburg). And I ask that you would not find it a burden to write me at the same time your own censure of the same book, and make me get my wish in all things. If there be anything wherein I can gratify you in turn, you will have me an eager performer of it. But **above all, beware lest any of Tycho's friends (if perchance he have any still there) learn that I got those copies from you.**

Farewell herewith, with your most choice wife — and see that she bears you more heirs.
From Hamburg, the 10th day of July, the year 1598.
**Johannes Stygge**, in my own hand.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondents (third-party, anti-Tycho).** **Johannes Stygge** (a disaffected Dane abroad) → **Hans Aalborg** (*M. Johannes Alburgiacus*, the chief Copenhagen bookseller). **Not Tycho's own correspondence**, but a hostile letter preserved in the Tycho dossier (Langebek's diplomatarium). Its value is precisely as a **hostile-witness document** — the **anti-Tycho Danish faction's narrative**, the mirror-image of Tycho's own apologias.
- **Significance — the "other side" of the exile.**
 - **The anti-Tycho resentment.** Stygge is stung that Tycho's partisans (even "illustrious men") brand Denmark — for losing Tycho — as **"blind," a "new barbarism," "Machiavellism," "envy," "avarice,"** unable "to discern a pearl from a barley-grain." He longs for **a public writing exposing "how little Tycho can do and how useless he was."**
 - **The Ursus book sought as ammunition.** He begs Aalborg for **3–4 copies of "the book the Emperor's mathematician [Ursus] published at Prague against Tycho"** — reportedly given by Aalborg as a welcome gift to **Copenhagen professors** who "rejoice that someone has painted Tycho in his true colours." A striking record of **Ursus's *De astronomicis hypothesibus* circulating as anti-Tycho propaganda in Copenhagen**.
 - **The hostile portrait of Tycho at Wandsbek.** Tycho riding through Hamburg in a **six-horse carriage "as if a prince,"** honoured by visitors and city notables, **snubbing his cousin Jost Høg**, no longer "wishing to be held a Dane," his **church seat draped with silk** (*"as if more than other good folk"*) and his **wife and daughters treated "as if countesses"** (Danish phrases). The envious counter-image to Tycho's self-presentation.
 - **The Danish critics named.** **Thomas Fincke** (the mathematician, then Rector of Copenhagen) and **Petrus Severinus (Peder Sørensen)**, the royal Paracelsian physician — cited as learned men who "know Tycho better" and judge him low. Tycho is sneered at as **"that sharp-nosed, horned fellow"** (*nasutulo et cornuto* — possibly a jibe at his prosthetic metal nose).
 - **The John Dee reference.** **English students at Hamburg wished to greet Tycho "in the name of … John Dee [Johannes Deen]"** — a documented **Dee–Tycho contact line** (relevant to the John Dee research thread). ⚑ Flagged for the Dee project.
 - **The Petrus-Severinus conspiracy theory.** The English students' tale: that **Severinus, the king's Paracelsian physician, out of secret jealousy, engineered Tycho's downfall "through nobles, as through a third and fourth hand"** — and the warning against men "with Italian wits who affect honours above their lot." Stygge (here, oddly, defending the doctor) dismisses it as "dreams and mere suspicions." A revealing trace of contemporary **conspiracy narratives about Tycho's fall** (and of the Tycho–Severinus Paracelsian rivalry).
 - **The secrecy.** Stygge's closing plea — *"beware lest any of Tycho's friends learn I got these copies from you"* — underscores the covert, factional character of the anti-Tycho campaign.
- **Cross-references.** The **anti-Tycho / exile** counter-narrative (mirror to brahe-t_16000103001, brahe-t_15980607001, brahe-t_15980706001); the **Ursus** book's reception in Copenhagen (the Ursus thread); the **John Dee** contact (→ the Dee research project); and the **Petrus Severinus / Paracelsian** angle.
- **Persons & places named.** Johannes Stygge; **Hans Aalborg** (Copenhagen bookseller); **Tycho Brahe** (the target); **Ursus** ("the Emperor's mathematician," unnamed); **Thomas Fincke**; **Petrus Severinus**; **Jost Høg** (Tycho's cousin); **King Frederick II**; **John Dee**; **Claus Dyre** (Stygge's kinsman); the English students ("Ruffus"). Places: **Hamburg**, **Copenhagen**, **Wandsbek** (the Rantzau castle), **Frankfurt**, **Hven** ("that island"), **England**.
- **Notable phrases.** The Danish proverb *"naar een kommer først for ordet at staae tilig op…"* ("get the name of an early riser, sleep as long as you like"); the Danish gibes *"ligesom hand var meer end andre got folk"* and *"de vare grevinder."* A corrupt word *Ego inutili[!]* (rendered "I [replied]") is editorially flagged in the source.
- **Calendar.** *Hamburgo 10. die julii anni 1598* (Hamburg O.S.; no *stylo* marker; label gives no N.S.) → **10 July 1598 [Old Style]**.
- **Correction.** The English translation's bracketed identification of the letter's 'Johannis Deen' as the English mathematician John Dee has been removed as unwarranted; Dreyer (TBOO XIV, p.144) prints the bare Latin name with no gloss or apparatus support for that identification, and no external scholarship was found to confirm it. The name is now left untranslated and unidentified.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. All 6 Dreyer pages read as page images (TBOO XIV pp.141-146); letter 152 runs pp.142-145 within the extract. Collated the address heading, opening ("S. eruditissime d:ne magister Johannes..."), the Rantzau-castle/church-honours passage, the Fincke/Severinus passage, the English-students-at-the-inn anecdote (including the Severinus/Tycho mutual-hatred sentence, whose 'eius'/'suae' pronouns were checked against Latin grammar and found correctly resolved to Tycho in the English, not flipped), and the closing ("Hamburgo 10. die iulii anni 1598") against the page images. All matched Dreyer's print exactly (including the source's own '[!]' crux at 'Ego inutili[!]', which Dreyer also prints, so not a fresh error) except the one identification flagged above, which is an unsupported gloss rather than a source or Dreyer divergence.

**1 defect found:**
- **fabrication** (medium). The English asserts, via the bracketed equivalence '[Johannes Deen]', that this bare Latin name is the historical John Dee, the English mathematician/astrologer/magus. Neither the source text, nor Dreyer's printed page, nor Dreyer's apparatus (checked) supports this identification; a web check of the tekstnet.dk edition and general search likewise turned up no scholarly identification of this figure as John Dee. The letter gives no other identifying detail (occupation, title, place) beyond the bare name being one among several English well-wishers. Presenting this as a settled identity is an invented fact with no counterpart in the source, and it is the kind of claim (a documented Tycho-John Dee contact in 1598 Hamburg) a scholar could wrongly go on to cite. At: “wished to greet him in the name of many — especially of one, if I remember rightly, John Dee [Johannes Deen]”.

**Repaired.** Verified TBOO XIV p.144 (line c. 24) directly from the Dreyer page image: the printed text reads 'quidam, fi recte memini, Johannis Deen, falutare' with no footnote or marginal gloss naming John Dee. The audit's claim is confirmed; the fabricated identification has been struck and no replacement guess substituted, per the prime rule. No other part of the letter was touched.

documents.abstract: Reports receiving Holger's delayed letter, notes the Brandenburg electoral letters were not presented to the King, and alludes to collusion between the two Chancellors.
documents.incipit: QUAS ante discessum tuum ex ultimis Comitijs Hafniensibus deproperasti, desideratissime …

text.original:
TAM ANTIQUAe PROSAPIAe QUAM PROPRIA VIRTUTE INPRIMIS NOBILI ET ERUDITIONE SIMUL SOLIDA CLARO VIRO DOMINO OLIGERO ROSÆKRANTZIO DE ROSENHOLM, CONSANGVINEO, AFFINI ET AMICO INTEGERRIMO.

S. P.

QUAS ante discessum tuum ex ultimis Comitijs Hafniensibus deproperasti, desideratissime mi OLIGERE, Consangvinee, Affinis, et (quod plus reputo) Amice integerrime, his ipsis diebus ob moras, quas isthic nectebat MULIUS, pridie accepi. Erantque utut festinanter scriptae, et ad singula, quae expectabam, propter otij penuriam non respondentes, admodum gratae. Quod literae Electoris et Electorissae Brandenburgensis Regi et Reginae oblatae non sint, parum moror. Neque enim ob [id] eas misi, quod magnopere cuperem, ut exhiberentur. Ideoque (uti scis) liberum id tibi reliqui. Scio eas scatere [politic[is]mis et aulicismis], uti fit apud tales homines. Allene det var anderledes lovet; naar jeg seer til, da colluderer de begge [Canceler] med hverandre, for den eene ravn piller ikke øyet ud paa den anden: quamvis alterum magis integrum et sincerum duxerim, quam vestrum istum NICOLAI MACHIAVELLI Neophitum, qui adhuc quotidie discit a suo [praeceptore contiguo]. Nec tamen id quod tu insinuas, inde inferri posse, si traditae fuissent literae, existimarim. Nam conditio mea nullatenus isthic defletur. Et cur hoc, cum ego ipse hanc praetulerim et etiamnum praeferam priori? Neque commutarem, om man endskiønt vilde give mig Penge til, som naar man bytter. Nec ullis modis reditum captavi per literas illas, utut tam vestratibus quam mihi invisum, plus tamen forte mihi quam illis. Ideoque sollicite excepi apud Principem hunc urgentem, ne tale quid verbo scriptove moveret. Neque eae, quas Bramstedij illi obtuli, quarum exemplar (ni fallor) habes, tale quid prae se ferunt. Recompensationem solummodo expensarum moderate requirebam, suo forte tempore validius. Videbo, quomodo literae illae suis restituantur autoribus, modo id citra offensam per aliqualem excusationem fieri queat, vel (si mavis) praetextum. Quod autem Regi libros destinatos non tradideris, nec tuum nec aliorum probo consilium. Maluissem enim certis de causis mature exhibitos, quam retentos. Neque tamen suspicor, te tenacitate quadam, et amore mei atque librorum eos pro te ipso servare voluisse, ne forte aemuli nostri et malevoli ad se [dono Regis] reciperent. An [Regi] placituri sint nec ne, susque deque fero. Nec sane ob id illi communicandos censeo, quod sic ipsius gratiam aucupari cupiam; cum sat sciam, ne quidem gratiori munere aliquo aut quovis officio ob eos, quibus magis auscultat, id impetrari posse (quod et cordate fero) vel literae meae Rostochio scriptae cum suo responso (necdum uti pollicebaris, critizatae) satis superque testatum relinquunt. Nec si[c] intempestive [supplex] fio, cum nihil petam, nihil deprecer, nihil supplicem, sed potius labores meos quos [ille] cum suis aspernatus est, me Caesari nunc dedicare, aliumque atque adeo summum Imperij caput pro studiorum meorum Maecenate quaerere, posthabitis invidentibus et detrectantibus [Danis] ostendo ostentoque, ut hoc potius (si quid foret insimulandum) culpae imputari posset, quam quod nimis me demitterem. Tu itaque, mi OLIGERE, omnino libros [Regi] trade in manus, sive [volenti] sive [repugnanti], aut si id tibi commodum non fuerit, fac ut per aliquem alium meorum, aut etiam [RAMELIUM] id fiat; ita tamen, ut per quoscunque sive temet ipsum vel alios Regi porrigantur, tibi, siquidem Rex (uti scio) talibus [imo nullis (quod dolendum)] libris delectatur, cedant. Invenies facile rationem. Quod et antea, cum mecum hîc esses, praemonui. Sin [Rex] ipsemet (quod [miraculi] loco duxerim) eos retinere voluerit, aut etiam praeter omnem nostram praevisionem et amolitionem in aliorum, quorum quam minime vellemus, potestatem devenerint, id ferendum erit. Habeant, quod tacite suspiciant atque admirentur, quodque capere aut imitari non possint, palam vero contra conscientiam (uti solent) rodant, extenuent, invertant et cavillentur. Id populus curat scilicet. Faxo autem, si res ita ceciderit, ut tu nova, etiam picta et ornata obtineas exemplaria, quibus hanc iacturam leves, praefixis etiam carminibus, sed in te directis, qualia nuper, dum Duci IOHANNI ADOLPHO hos libros dono mitterem, praeposueram, quorum tenorem in adiuncta scheda habes. Liber de Stellis erat in charta, non membrana scriptus. Et hunc Duci ULDARICO Megapolitano non concessi, cum alterum nuper antepositis etiam suis carminibus dono mitterem. Quanti utrunque fecerit, quam comiter et benigne TENGNAGLIUM meum exceperit, quam gratus erga me fuerit, atque in posterum esse velit, et quam clementi denique favore me prosequatur Sermus Elector Coloniensis, ex ijs, quae ad CRAGIUM nostrum scripsi, cognosces, et aliquatenus etiam ex adiunctis literarum exemplis, quae cum CRAGIO quoque communices, praesertim quae antea non habet, velim, ut et ille nostra tibi. Quae enim alteri vestrum scribo mittoque, utrique scribo et mitto pauculis differentibus. Exemplum scripti istius famosi apud CRAGIUM videbis, quale mihi Helmstadio missum est. Addidit quidam ex meis studiosis annotationes marginales, ubi praecipue fit mei honorifica mentio, ne diu tam memorabilia locum quaerenda forent. Egregius sane liber, qui a Professoribus Hafniensibus tanto applausu, licet tacito murmure inter eos susurrato excipiatur. Gaudent monstris monstrosa ingenia et prava pravis. Ostendet tibi dictus noster communis secreto literas quasdam a [IOANNE STUGGIO] IOANNI Omnivendae, vel potius Ardelioni ex composito scriptas adinstar Beinenkorf, ut ille et ij, quibus hoc scurrile scriptum magni et grati muneris instar congratulatus est, sibi sic assensum et laudem praeberi frustra laetentur; aut si fucum capiunt, sciant alios scire, quam parum veri bonique illi sciant vel sapiant, quamque insulsi invidi et malevoli sint censores, quodque nos eos clam se titillantes et conridentes palam pungamus et rideamus, imo ex alto despiciamus. Librum autem hunc, qui mea Elogia depraedicat et ebuccinat, mihi per hunc ipsum nuncium remitti volo. Nullum enim aliud habeo exemplar. Ubi plura nactus fuero, vobis et alijs communicabo. Eroque adhuc facilior, quam institor iste vester librorum. Nam gratis dabo et aperte faciam, quod is subdole et tecte. Ephemerides istae novae ex novis (si Dijs placet) Tabulis supputatae ne quidem apud Germanos fidem merentur, quam autor in Praefatione venditat, nedum apud [vos Danos], qui terrena potius quam Coelestia curatis. Heu tam aversus Equos vestris Sol iungit ab oris. In Septentrione enim semper habitavit barbaries. Et verendum, ut ne nunc quidem satis extirpata sit, aut postliminio redeat, contemptis ingenuis et humanioribus literis unâ cum virtutis integritate. Quod Cognatus meus [LINDENOVIUS], ea quae ipsemet non invite, antequam disiungeremur, promisit, nunc concedere tergiversetur, licet tunc aeque erat in Politicis prudens atque nunc, non miror. Cimber enim est, cur non Cimbrizet et nippizet? Quamvis (ut dicam quod res est) parum curem, sive communicet, sive non. Potioribus enim intentus sum, quam ut talibus Mundanae scenae frivolis nugis immorer. Volebam saltem memoriae et rei bene gestae causa hanc historiolam penes me habere, att man kunde laese den som et Eventyr om Afftenen. Scripsit is ad me, et quod in diversis locis haereret haec confabulatio, non mitti excusavit. Tum quoque de Comoedia, quae isthic a personato Anglo introducta est, quodque ferme in Tragoediam versa fuerit, indicavit. Kan skee den [gammele] pater conscriptus lader ikke af, furijs sic impellentibus, etiam in defunctum saevire, førend han staar op igien og giør Jertegn. Mones, et quidem recte, ut circumspecte in quibusdam agam. Quod et facio, faciamque. Imo plus taceo, dissimuloque in tantis iniuris, tamque falsis obiectionibus, quam forte opus esset. Sed serviendum est tempori et loco. Quod differtur, non aufertur. Sunt Regibus, fateor, longae manus. At Philosophis et veritatem tuentibus adhuc longiores et fortiores. Nam ipsorum Imperia et Iurisdictiones etiam ultra fata mortalium se extendunt. Caetera momentanea et caduca sunt. Tandem bona causa triumphat. Reges et Dominos habere debent, qui se non habent, et non concupiscunt, quae Reges Dominique concupiscunt. Illi semper metuant, ne fractus labatur axis, et pavidos feriant ruinae. Rex est, qui metuit nihil. Hoc Regnum sibi quisque dat. Sed de his satis.

Aedes meas Hafniacas pro duobus millibus non vendam. Constiterunt mihi, antequam ultimo ibi essem, et quaedam in ijs complevissem, ultra 3000 Ioachimorum. Tunc vero vix intra millenos in eas ulterius erogavi. Satis est constans structura, quae alijs in Civitate lapideis domibus duratione sua non cedet. Nec fundus ille paludosus, quem tanta arte emendavi, ponderosiorem sustinuit. Si vendi iusto precio nequiverint, date saltem operam, mei Amici, ut inquilinum fidelem pro ijs ad Michaëlis festum obtineam, qui id quod aequum erit, inde solvat. Causa PEPLERI etiam invitis (uti existimo) ijs, qui eam promovere satagebant, male illi cessit, et prout revera meritus erat, imo mitius. Si Amstelredami mansisset, neque [HUITFELDIO] auscultasset, sed apud me in Norvegia rursus habitandi veniam unâ cum culpa deprecatus fuisset, siquidem me ad condonandum non futurum difficilem ISAACUS PETRI iam antea illi indicarat, forte rectius sibi consuluisset. Sed confisus meis adversarijs nunc praedominantibus (apud quos ego, etiamsi Geometrice demonstrarem, nihil veri iustique obtineo) maluit hanc Camarinam movere, et maiora subire pericula maioresque miserias. Cum BŒKELIO per MULÆUM uti voluisti, agam, ubi fuerit, nunc enim peregre abest. Quid obtinuero, ex adiuncto responso videbis. Pecuniam totam iam antea tradiderat illi WINSHEMIUS, me inscio, nec tamen, postquam rescivi, multum dissentiente. Erat enim is valde importunus, praesertim vero uxor; et minabantur, at de vilde slaae Skade og Interesse paa. Et nescio, quae alia crocitabant. Quid igitur faceremus? Litem forensem ob id movere tibi forte ingratum fuisset, nec nobis volupe. Et habet is inter iudices sibi addictos, ut vix aliquid obtinuissemus. Nam et hîc iudicia sunt personalia, non realia, ferme ut apud vos, licet paulo minus ob processum Iuris Civilis in cognoscendis causis et non praeiudicandis magis aequum et legitimum. Dabo operam, quantum in me est, ut eos, quos adhuc desideras, nanciscaris. Quod si obtinere nequivero, transeant cum caeteris. Satis habes librorum. Unica SOPHIA omni praevalebit Philosophiae, etiam Platonicae et veriori, nedum Aristotelicae et fucatae, atque in Logimachijs verborum fundatae. Ignosces, quod de Praeceptore tuo id quod res est, dicam. Nam et ipsi Itali, qui alias ei admodum mancipati sunt, illum hoc (uti scis) elogio depraedicare non sunt veriti:

Doctorem calamo ingratus, Dominumque veneno
Perdidit, igne Patrum dogmata, nos tenebris.

Non tamen reprehendenda duxerim, quae in ipso laudabilia et recte constituta sunt, qualia te Lynceis oculis discernere posse non ambigo. Praestabit tamen (uti opinor) vivae illi palpabili et tractabili SOPHIAe operam dare, quae pro libris liberos dabit, pro facundia faecunditatem, ut pulchra faciet te prole parentem. Quod ante revolutionem Phoebi annuam faxit Deus. Cecini tibi breve et fortuito incidens Epigramma loco Epithalamij; quod nescio an acceperis, siquidem nullam in literis eius facis mentionem, nisi serius forte nactus sis, quam eas scriberes. In omnem itaque eventum denuo reliquis, quae mitto, cum alias sit breve, addidi. Restituas mihi velim carmen CRAMERI tui, quod cum caeteris in hoc genere coacervare lubet. Multa enim hinc inde talia ab Eruditis in mei gratiam cuduntur, ut suo tempore videbis. Plura nunc non addo. Ubi tu plura rescripseris et currum promissum, quem indies expeto expectoque, ne iter meum retardetur, miseris, ulterius respondebo. Vide saltem, ne quidpiam eorum silentio praetereas, de quibus antea movi, quaeque memoriae causa denotata habes. Iamque felix et incolumis cum tua costa vale, et matrem tuam officiose ex me saluta. Hancque non neglige, atque non detento hoc Nuncio actutum rescribe. Iterumque vale. Dabantur Wandesburgo die 10. Augusti Anni 1598.

BŒKELIUS hisce diebus domi non fuit, ut responsum eius tibi mittere nunc possem. Quam primum is redierit, omnem hac in re movebo lapidem, ut desiderijs tuis satisfiat.

Tuus TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the man as noble in his most ancient lineage as in his own virtue, and renowned withal for solid learning, Master Holger Rosenkrantz of Rosenholm — my kinsman, kinsman-by-marriage, and most upright friend.**

Heartiest greeting.

The letter which you dashed off before your departure from the last Diet at Copenhagen, my most longed-for Holger — kinsman, kinsman-by-marriage, and (what I value more) most upright friend — I received only yesterday, in these very days, owing to the delays that Mule was contriving there. And, however hastily written, and not answering — for want of leisure — each of the points I was awaiting, it was most welcome. That the letters of the Elector and Electress of Brandenburg were not presented to the King and Queen, troubles me little. For I did not send them because I greatly desired that they be displayed; and so (as you know) I left that to your discretion. I know they teem with political and courtly turns, as happens with such men. *Only, it was promised otherwise; when I look into the matter, the two Chancellors collude with one another, for the one raven does not peck out the other's eye:* though I should reckon the one of them more upright and sincere than that Niccolò-Machiavelli novice of yours, who still daily learns from his neighbouring preceptor. Yet I do not think that what you hint at could be inferred from it, had the letters been delivered. For my condition is by no means bewailed there. And why should it be, since I myself have preferred, and still prefer, this present state to my former one? Nor would I exchange it — *even if one were to throw in money besides, as when one strikes a bargain.* Nor did I in any way angle for a return through those letters — though such a return is hateful both to your countrymen and to me, yet perhaps more to me than to them. And so I anxiously took care, with this Prince who was pressing the matter, that he should raise no such thing by word or in writing. Nor do the letters which I presented to him at Bramstedt — of which (unless I am mistaken) you have a copy — carry any such intent. I was only moderately requesting compensation for my expenses — more forcefully, perhaps, in its own good time. I shall see how those letters may be restored to their authors, provided it can be done without offence, by some excuse — or (if you prefer) pretext.

But that you did not deliver the books intended for the King, I approve neither your counsel nor that of the others. For, for certain reasons, I should have preferred them presented in good time rather than held back. Yet I do not suspect that you wished, out of some tenacity and love of me and of the books, to keep them for yourself, lest perhaps our rivals and ill-wishers should receive them to themselves as the King's gift. Whether they will please the King or not, I take with complete indifference. Nor indeed do I judge that they should be imparted to him because I would thus be eager to court his favour; since I know well enough that not even by some more pleasing gift, nor by any service, could that be obtained — on account of those to whom he gives more ear (which I bear with equanimity) — as my letters written from Rostock, together with their reply (not yet "critiqued," as you were promising), leave more than sufficiently attested. Nor do I thus unseasonably turn suppliant, since I ask nothing, beg off nothing, entreat nothing, but rather I show — and make a show — that I now dedicate to the Emperor my labours, which he with his counsellors spurned; and that, the envious and disparaging Danes set aside, I seek another, indeed the supreme head of the Empire, as the Maecenas of my studies — so that this (if anything were to be charged against me) might rather be imputed as a fault than that I should abase myself too far.

You therefore, my Holger, by all means deliver the books into the King's hands, whether he will it or resist; or, if that is not convenient for you, see that it be done through some other of my people, or even through Ramel — yet so that, by whomsoever they are handed to the King, whether yourself or others, they fall to you, since the King (as I know) takes delight in such books — nay, in no books at all, which is to be lamented. You will easily find a way; as I forewarned you before, too, when you were here with me. But if the King himself should wish to keep them (which I should count a kind of miracle), or even if, beyond all our foresight and contriving, they should come into the power of others into whose hands we should least wish, that must be borne. Let them have something to look up to and marvel at in secret — something they can neither grasp nor imitate — but openly, against their conscience (as is their wont), gnaw at, belittle, pervert, and carp at. The common people care for that, forsooth. But I shall see to it, should the matter so fall out, that you obtain new copies — illustrated and ornamented, too — by which you may relieve this loss, with verses also prefixed, but addressed to you, such as I had lately prefixed when I sent these books as a gift to Duke Johann Adolf; the tenor of which you have in the enclosed slip. The book of the Stars was written on paper, not on vellum; and this one I did not grant to Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg, when I lately sent him the other book as a gift, with its own verses likewise prefixed. How highly he valued both; how courteously and kindly he received my Tengnagel; how grateful he was toward me, and wishes to be hereafter; and finally with how clement a favour the Most Serene Elector of Cologne attends me — you will learn from what I have written to our Krag, and to some extent also from the enclosed copies of letters, which I would have you share with Krag too, especially those he does not already have, just as he shares mine with you. For what I write and send to either of you, I write and send to both, with a few small differences.

At Krag's you will see the copy of that infamous writing, such as was sent to me from Helmstedt. One of my students added marginal notes, especially where honourable mention is made of me, lest such memorable passages should have long to be sought out. A fine book indeed — received by the Copenhagen professors with such applause, though with a muffled murmur whispered among themselves! Monstrous wits delight in monsters, and crooked wits in crooked things. Our said common friend will show you in secret certain letters written by Johann Stuggius to one "John Sell-all" — or rather to some busybody — composed by arrangement, in the manner of a *Bienenkorb* [beehive-lampoon], so that he, and those to whom he presented this scurrilous writing as though a great and welcome gift, may vainly rejoice that assent and praise are thus offered them; or, if they perceive the trick, let them know that others know how little of truth and goodness they know or savour, and what tasteless, envious, and ill-willed critics they are, and that we, while they tickle and laugh among themselves in secret, openly prick and laugh at them — nay, look down on them from on high. But this book, which proclaims and trumpets my praises, I wish sent back to me by this same messenger; for I have no other copy. When I have got more, I will share them with you and others; and I shall be even more obliging than that book-peddler of yours, for I shall give freely and do openly what he does slyly and covertly.

Those new Ephemerides, reckoned from new Tables (if it please the gods!), do not earn even among the Germans the credit that the author vaunts in his Preface — still less among you Danes, who care for earthly things rather than heavenly. *Alas, so turned away from your shores does the Sun yoke his horses!* For in the North barbarism has always dwelt; and it is to be feared that even now it is not sufficiently rooted out, or may return by right of postliminy, with liberal and humane letters despised together with the integrity of virtue. That my kinsman Lindenov now shuffles over granting what he himself, not unwillingly, promised before we parted — though he was then just as prudent in political matters as now — I do not wonder. For he is a Cimbrian: why should he not play the Cimbrian, and haggle? Though (to say the truth) I care little whether he imparts it or not, for I am bent on weightier matters than to linger over such frivolous trifles of the worldly stage. I only wished, for memory's sake and the record of a thing well managed, to keep this little history by me — *that one might read it like a fairy-tale of an evening.* He wrote to me, and excused that the account was not sent, since this story was held up in various places. He also reported about the comedy that was put on there by a masked Englishman, and how it nearly turned into a tragedy. *Perhaps the old "conscript father" does not cease — the furies so driving him — to rage even against the dead, before he rises up again and works portents.* You advise me — and indeed rightly — that I should proceed circumspectly in certain matters — which indeed I do and shall do. Nay, I keep silent and dissemble, amid such great injuries and such false accusations, more than perhaps is needful. But one must serve the time and the place. What is deferred is not taken away. Kings have long hands, I confess; but philosophers and the guardians of truth have longer and stronger still. For their dominions and jurisdictions extend even beyond the destinies of mortals, while the rest is momentary and perishable. In the end the good cause triumphs. Those who do not possess themselves must have kings and lords — and they do not covet what kings and lords covet. Let *those* ever fear lest the broken axle-tree slip and the ruins strike them in their terror; *he is a king who fears nothing — this kingdom each man gives to himself.* But enough of these matters.

My house at Copenhagen I will not sell for two thousand. It cost me, before I was last there and had finished certain things in it, over 3,000 joachimsthalers; and then I spent scarcely a further thousand or so upon it. It is a sound enough structure, which in durability will not yield to the other stone houses in the city; nor has that marshy ground, which I improved with such art, borne any heavier building. If they cannot be sold at a fair price, at least take pains, my friends, that I may obtain a trustworthy tenant for them by Michaelmas, who will pay from it what is fair. The case of Pepler turned out badly for him — even against the will (as I think) of those who were busy promoting it — and as he had truly deserved, nay, more mildly. Had he stayed at Amsterdam and not listened to Huitfeldt, but rather begged leave to dwell with me again in Norway, together with pardon for his fault — since Isaac Petersen had already told him that I would not be hard to forgive — he would perhaps have counselled himself better. But, trusting in my adversaries now in the ascendant (with whom I obtain nothing of truth or justice, even were I to demonstrate it geometrically), he chose to stir up this Camarina, and to undergo greater dangers and greater miseries. As for your wish to make use of Boekel through Mule, I will deal with him when he is back, for he is now abroad; what I shall have obtained, you will see from the enclosed reply. Winsheim had already handed over the whole sum to him, without my knowledge — yet, after I learned of it, not much against my will; for he was very importunate, and especially his wife, and they threatened *that they would impose damages and interest,* and I know not what else they croaked. What, then, were we to do? To start a lawsuit over it would perhaps have been disagreeable to you, and no pleasure to us; and he has among the judges men devoted to him, so that we should scarcely have obtained anything. For here too the courts are personal, not impartial, much as with you — though somewhat less so, on account of the procedure of the Civil Law, which is more equitable and lawful in trying cases and not prejudging them. I will take pains, so far as in me lies, that you obtain those you still want; but if I cannot obtain them, let them pass with the rest. You have books enough. A single Sophia will outweigh all philosophy — even the Platonic and truer sort, still more the Aristotelian and counterfeit kind, founded on word-battles. You will forgive me for saying of your Preceptor what is the truth; for even the Italians themselves, otherwise quite enslaved to him, have not feared to extol him (as you know) with this epigram:

*The ingrate destroyed his Teacher with the pen, his Lord with poison, the Fathers' doctrines with fire, and us with darkness.*

Yet I would not have those things blamed which in him are praiseworthy and rightly established — such as I do not doubt you can discern with lynx eyes. Still it will be better (as I think) to devote your effort to that living, palpable, and tractable Sophia, who will give you children for books, fecundity for eloquence, so that she will make you, fair one, a parent with offspring — which may God bring to pass before Phoebus's yearly revolution. I sang you a short epigram, struck off by chance, in place of an epithalamium; whether you received it I do not know, since you make no mention of it in your letter — unless you got it later than you wrote them. And so, against every contingency, I have added it again to the rest of what I send, since it is short anyway. I should like you to return to me the poem of your Cramer, which it pleases me to heap up with the others of this kind; for many such are coined here and there by the learned in my honour, as you will see in due time. I add no more now. When you have written back further, and have sent the promised carriage — which I daily desire and await, lest my journey be delayed — I will answer at greater length. Only see that you pass over in silence none of those matters I raised before, and which you have noted down for memory's sake. And now, happy and unharmed, fare well with your rib, and dutifully greet your mother on my behalf; do not neglect her, and, without detaining this messenger, write back at once. Again, farewell. Given at Wandsbek, the 10th day of August, the year 1598.

Boekel has not been at home these days, so that I cannot now send you his reply. As soon as he has returned, I will move every stone in this matter, so that your wishes may be satisfied.

Yours, Tycho Brahe.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Edition of record.** Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia* vol. VIII (*Epistolae*). MS witness: A = Copenhagen, Rigsarkivet, Langebeks Diplomatarium (an *Afskrift* / later copy, not Tycho's autograph). Square brackets in the source block reproduce the editor's conjectural readings/insertions (e.g. *[id], [Canceler], [praeceptore contiguo], [volenti], [repugnanti], [gammele]*); they are kept as printed by this chapter's convention
- **Date / place.** Dateline *Dabantur Wandesburgo die 10. Augusti Anni 1598* — agrees with the catalogue label. **Wandsbek** (then *Wandesburg*, the Rantzau estate just east of Hamburg) was Tycho's residence from late 1597 through summer 1598, between his departure from Denmark and his move toward the imperial court. Tycho kept the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar.
- **Recipient.** **Holger Rosenkrantz of Rosenholm** (1574–1642), later called "the Learned" — Danish nobleman, theologian, and Tycho's kinsman. The triple address *consanguineus, affinis, amicus* ("kinsman, kinsman-by-marriage, friend") is literal: the Rosenkrantz and Brahe houses were repeatedly intermarried.
- **The book-gifts — the central thread.** "These books" are Tycho's two 1598 presentation pieces, dispatched to princely patrons during the Wandsbek campaign for new patronage: the printed **_Astronomiae instauratae mechanica_ (Wandsbek, 1598)** and the **manuscript star-catalogue** (the *"Liber de Stellis,"* the 1000-star catalogue, here noted as *"written on paper, not on vellum"* — grander recipients received the de-luxe vellum copy). **Duke Johann Adolf of Holstein-Gottorp** received *both*; **Duke Ulrich III of Mecklenburg** received *only* the other (the *Mechanica*), *not* the star-book. This dovetails exactly with **brahe-t_15980816001** (16 Aug 1598), where Duke Ulrich, having received Tycho's gift and seen the Hven instruments, recommends Tycho to Rudolf II. The verses Tycho "prefixed" are the dedicatory poems; he promises Holger fresh illustrated copies with verses re-addressed to him.
- **Persons named.**
 - **Mule (*Mulius* / *Mulaeus*)** — a Danish intermediary/agent handling Tycho's correspondence and the "Boekel" business; not securely identified here.
 - **The Elector and Electress of Brandenburg / the King and Queen** — Christian IV of Denmark and his new queen **Anne Catherine of Brandenburg** (married Nov 1597), daughter of Elector **Joachim Friedrich of Brandenburg**; hence the Brandenburg-court letters addressed to the Danish royal pair (the bride's family). *Identification of the King and Queen as Christian IV and Anne Catherine is secure from the dynastic logic; treat as MEDIUM-HIGH.*
 - **The "two Chancellors" / the "Machiavelli novice" with his "neighbouring preceptor"** — the Danish chancery leadership, satirised: the senior figure (the *praeceptor*) and his junior pupil (*Neophitus*). The Danish Rigskansler at this date was **Arild Huitfeldt** and the Kansler **Christian Friis** (to Kragelund); Tycho does not name them, and the pairing is left **unidentified** in the translation rather than forced. *Crux — see Confidence.*
 - **Niels Krag (*Cragius*)** — Danish humanist, historian and diplomat, Tycho's correspondent and the shared conduit ("our said common friend") for the circulating documents.
 - **Frans Gansneb Tengnagel (*Tengnaglius*)** — Tycho's assistant (later son-in-law), here received "courteously and kindly" by the Elector of Cologne.
 - **The Most Serene Elector of Cologne** — **Ernst of Bavaria**, Archbishop-Elector of Cologne; Tycho courts his favour during the patronage search.
 - **Johann Stuggius (*Ioannes Stuggius*)** — author of the anti-Tycho satirical letters circulating from the Copenhagen academic milieu; cf. the hostile "Stygius" letter **brahe-t_15980710001**. *"John Sell-all" (Ioannes Omnivenda)* and *"the busybody" (Ardelio)* are derisive nicknames for the recipients/peddlers of the lampoon, not real names.
 - **Lindenov (*Lindenovius*)** — Tycho's kinsman, reneging on a promise; mocked as a *Cimber* (Jutlander) who would *"Cimbrize and haggle."*
 - **Pepler (*Pepleri*)** — a former associate/servant of Tycho's whose lawsuit went badly; he had once dwelt with Tycho in Norway (Tycho's fief), had moved to Amsterdam, and (against the advice relayed through **Isaac Petersen**) "listened to **Huitfeldt**" rather than seeking Tycho's pardon.
 - **Henrik Ramel (*Ramelius*)** — German-born Danish statesman, an alternative deliverer of the books to the King.
 - **Boekel (*Boekelius*), Winsheim (*Winshemius*)** — parties to a money matter Holger had asked Tycho to pursue; Winsheim had paid over the disputed sum; Boekel was abroad.
 - **Cramer (*Crameri*)** — a poet in Holger's circle whose verse Tycho wishes returned for his collection of complimentary poems.
- **The "Ephemerides … from new Tables."** A recently-published set of ephemerides, disparaged by Tycho as over-praised in its own preface; the author is unnamed and **not securely identified** (a contemporary ephemeris-maker, e.g. of the Magini/Origanus type). Left general in the translation.
- **Code-switches into Danish.** The letter repeatedly drops from Latin into Early Modern Danish for sardonic, proverbial, or confidential asides — a hallmark of Tycho's intimate correspondence. The italicised English passages render: *"Only, it was promised otherwise … the one raven does not peck out the other's eye"*; *"even if one were to throw in money besides, as when one barters"*; *"that they would impose damages and interest"* (*slaae Skade og Interesse paa*, a legal threat); *"that one might read it like a fairy-tale of an evening"* (*et Eventyr om Afftenen*); and *"before he rises up again and works portents"* (*førend han staar op igien og giør Jertegn*). All are translated, never dropped.
- **Classical and Scriptural allusion.**
 - *"the one raven does not peck out the other's eye"* — the Latin proverb *cornix cornici numquam confodit oculum* (here in Danish), of those who shield one another.
 - *"stir up this Camarina"* — the Greek proverb *Καμάριναν κινεῖν* ("to move Camarina," a marsh best left undisturbed; cf. Virgil, *Aen.* 3.701), i.e. to invite trouble.
 - *"Kings have long hands"* — Ovid, *Heroides* 17.166 (*an nescis longas regibus esse manus*).
 - The closing sententiae are **Senecan**: *"he is a king who fears nothing — this kingdom each man gives to himself"* = Seneca, *Thyestes* 388–390 (*rex est qui metuit nihil … hoc regnum sibi quisque dat*); *"lest the broken axle-tree slip and the ruins strike them"* echoes Horace, *Odes* 3.3.7–8 (*si fractus illabatur orbis, impavidum ferient ruinae*).
 - The verse couplet on **Aristotle** (*"The ingrate destroyed his Teacher with the pen…"*) is a circulating Italian anti-Aristotelian epigram: Aristotle charged with ruining Plato (his *Doctor*) by his pen, Alexander (his *Dominus*) by poison, the Church Fathers' doctrines by fire, and posterity by darkness. Tycho cites it to needle Holger's Aristotelianism — *"your Preceptor."*
- **The *Sophia* pun.** *"Unica SOPHIA … vivae illi palpabili et tractabili SOPHIAe"* and *"cum tua costa"* ("with your rib," Gen. 2:21–22 for *wife*) turn on a double sense: **Sophia = Wisdom** and a bride named **Sophie**. Tycho urges Holger to prefer the *living* Sophia — marriage and children (*pro libris liberos*, "children for books") — to bookish philosophy, and reports having sent a short **epigram in place of an epithalamium (wedding-song)**. The wife is most plausibly **Sophie Brahe** (daughter of Axel Brahe), whom Holger Rosenkrantz married in this period; *identification MEDIUM — left as the text's pun rather than asserted.*
- **Self-positioning.** The letter is a key document of Tycho's **post-Denmark patronage turn**: he insists he is no suppliant (*"I ask nothing … I dedicate my labours to the Emperor"*), seeks "the supreme head of the Empire" (Rudolf II) as his *Maecenas*, and frames the rupture with Denmark so that any fault lies with the *"envious and disparaging Danes,"* not with himself. The Copenhagen house he refuses to undersell (>3,000 dalers spent; seeking a tenant by Michaelmas) shows him still managing Danish property in absentia.
- **Correction.** Restored 'Mones, et quidem' (dropped from the published Latin) before 'recte, ut circumspecte in quibusdam agam', per TBOO VIII p.90; the English '[The messenger advised me]' was a fabricated supplement filling the resulting gap and is replaced with 'You advise me', matching Dreyer's 2nd-person 'Mones' addressed to Rosenkrantz.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VIII pp.87-93 read as page images. Checked opening/closing lines and every proper name, date, sum of money, and place-name: Rosenkrantz/Rosenholm salutation, 10 August 1598 date and Wandsbek dateline, money figures (2000 / 3000 / c. 1000 Joachimsthalers) all match; place-names Bramstedt, Rostock, Helmstedt, Copenhagen, Mecklenburg, Cologne, Amsterdam, and Norway all confirmed verbatim including the unusual 'apud me in Norvegia' and 'ISAACUS PETRI', which the translation renders correctly. Found one genuine text-fidelity defect: our transcribed original omits 'Mones, et quidem' present in Dreyer p.90, and the English's bracketed supplement for that gap assigns the advice to 'the messenger' rather than to the letter's recipient, whom Dreyer's actual verb addresses in the second person. Also flagged a minor low-confidence mistranslation (not entered as a defect due to uncertainty about the idiom 'fucum capiunt') and a low-severity gender-attachment slip in 'pulchra... te... parentem' (English attaches 'fair one' to the male addressee, which is grammatically impossible for 'pulchra'; correct referent is Sophia or the offspring) — omitted from the defects list as sub-threshold given the text error already determines the grade.

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (**high**). Our published the transcribed original silently drops the two words 'Mones, et quidem' ('You advise, and indeed') that Dreyer prints, leaving the sentence without its verb or subject. Dreyer prints: *...førend han staar op igien og giør Jertegn. Mones, et quidem recte, ut circumspecte in quibusdam agam. (TBOO VIII p.90, col. 2, ~l.33-36)*.
- **fabrication** (medium). The bracketed supplement invents 'the messenger' as the advice-giver; Dreyer's restorable verb 'Mones' shows the advice came from the letter's addressee (Rosenkrantz) himself, not a messenger — a wrong actor, not a neutral fill-in. At: “[The messenger advised me] rightly, that I should proceed circumspectly in certain matters.”.

**Repaired.** Collated directly against the Dreyer page image, TBOO VIII p.90, which reads '...førend han staar op igien og giør Jertegn. Mones, et quidem recte, ut circumspecte in quibusdam agam. Quod et facio, faciamque.' — confirming both the text error (dropped 'Mones, et quidem') and the fabrication (the invented 'messenger' as advice-giver, where Dreyer's 'Mones' is unambiguously 2nd-person singular, addressed to Rosenkrantz). No crux remains; both defects fully resolved against the edition of record.

text.original:
COPIA LITERARUM ILLUSTRISSIMI PRINCIPIS, DOMINI VDALRICI DUCIS MEGAPOLENSIS AD IMPERATOREM.

ALLERDURCHLEUCHTIGSTER, großmechtigster und unuberwindtlichster römischer kayser. E: Kay: Majtt: ßeindt meine allerunterthenigste gehorßamste bereitwillige dienste jederzeit zuvor. Allergnedigster herr, E: Rom: Kay: Maj:tt gebe ich hiemit allerunterthenigst zuerkennenn, daß gegenwertiger der ehrnveste Tycho Brahe mit seinem gantzen haußweßen auß seinem vaterlandt, dem königreich Dennemarcken, gezogen, nicht aber darumb alß ob er da nicht woll hette bleiben mugenn, oder auch in einiger ungnade bey der Kön: Maj:stt daßelbst ßein ßolte, sondernn alleinn aus denn urßachen, nachdem er vermercket undt vernommenn, daß die astronomische sachen, die er inn ßo viel iahren mit großer mühe undt unkost alda angerichtet undt getribenn, wie vor beschehen, wieder ßein verhoffenn nicht geachtet noch befürdert werden mögen, darumb er sich selbst willig inn Teutschlandt weitere und beßere gelegenheit dazu zu suchen begebenn. Unndt ob ich woll derowegenn, alß er sich inn meiner stadt Rostock aufgehaltenn, an die Kön: M: zu Dennemarcken, meinen freundtlichen hertzvielgeliebten herrn sohn, ein freundtlich unndt fleißigs erinnerunges schreibenn gethan, dieße astronomische sachen dero königreich zu ehren zu restituiren unndt zu unterhaltenn, weil aber darauff nun einn ganzes iahr verfloßenn, unnd ich nicht spühren könnenn, daß er revocirt werde, unndt gleichwoll solche herrliche kunst, an sich selbst werth, daß sie unterhalten unndt promoviret werde unnd großer potentatenn patrocinii woll bedarff, unnd schade, das dieß so weit numehr gebrachte werch inn ein abnehmenn kommen solte, dan ich bekennenn muß, das mir dergleichenn instrumenta mathematica, alß ich bey ihm auff der insull Huen im königreich Dennemarcken gesehenn, an andern örtern niemalß vorkommenn: Alß habe ich nebenst andern vor guth angesehenn, nachdem es im reich Dennemarcken nicht mehr geschehenn kann, das sie irgendt im Teutschlandt gebürlichen unterhalten unnd foviret würde, wie dießelbige vonn alters hero allezeit von vielen königen unndt potentaten nach außweißung der löblichen exempel, so E: Kay: Maj:stt auß den historien, mehr dann gnugsamb bekandt, lieb unndt in würdenn gehaltenn worden, unndt weil dann E: Kay: Maj:st, alß daß oberhaubt deß heiligenn römischenn reichs, ein ßonderliche zuneigung zu offtberürter kunst tragen, so habe ich demnach nicht unterlaßen können, E: Röm: Kay: Maj:st ermelten Tychonem Brahen mit derselbigenn weitberümbtenn kunst allerunterthenigst zu recommendiren, unndt bitte E: Röm: Kay: Maj:st darauff unterthenigstes höchstes fleißes, sie wolle es nicht anderß dann gnedigst vermerckenn, unndt sich mehrgedachtes Tychonis Brahen unndt seines herrlichen studii allergnedigst annehmenn unndt ihm alle kayserliche guthe befurderung widerfahrenn lassenn. Daß binn ich umb E: Kay: Maj:st (ßo ich damit göttlicher almacht zu aller glücksehligen wolfart, derselbenn aber mich auch zu fernern kayserlichen gnaden, allerunterthenigst unnd getreulich befehle) jederzeit unterthenigst unnd gehorsambst zuverdienen willig unnd geflissenn.

Datum Gustrow den 16. augusti anno 1598.
E: Röm: Kay: Maj:ts unterthenigster unnd gehorsamer furst
Ulrich
herzog zu Meckelnburgk.
text.english:
**Copy of the letter of the Most Illustrious Prince, Lord Ulrich, Duke of Mecklenburg, to the Emperor.**

Most serene, most mighty, and most invincible Roman Emperor. To Your Imperial Majesty [be] my most humble, most obedient, and ready services at all times, beforehand. Most gracious Lord: I herewith most humbly give Your Roman Imperial Majesty to know that the present honourable Tycho Brahe has departed, with his whole household, from his fatherland, the kingdom of Denmark — not, however, as though he could not well have remained there, or should be in any disgrace with the Royal Majesty there, but solely for the reasons that, after he had noted and learned that the astronomical matters which he had over so many years set up and pursued there, with great labour and expense, could — contrary to his hope — no longer be valued nor furthered as before, he therefore willingly betook himself into Germany to seek further and better opportunity for it. And although I therefore, while he stayed in my city of Rostock, sent to the Royal Majesty of Denmark, my dear and heartily-beloved Lord son, a friendly and earnest letter of reminder, that he restore and maintain these astronomical matters to the honour of his kingdom — yet, since a whole year has now elapsed thereupon, and I have not been able to perceive that he is recalled; and since such a splendid art is in itself worthy that it be maintained and promoted, and has good need of the patronage of great potentates; and [since it would be] a pity that this work, now brought so far, should fall into decline — for I must confess that the like mathematical instruments, such as I saw with him on the island of Hven in the kingdom of Denmark, have never come before me in any other place — therefore I, together with others, have deemed it good that, since it can no longer happen in the realm of Denmark, it be fittingly maintained and fostered somewhere in Germany; as the same [art] has from of old always been held dear and in honour by many kings and potentates, according to the showing of the praiseworthy examples more than sufficiently known to Your Imperial Majesty from the histories. And since Your Imperial Majesty, as the head of the Holy Roman Empire, bears a special inclination toward the oft-mentioned art, I could not therefore omit most humbly to recommend the said Tycho Brahe, with that same far-famed art, to Your Roman Imperial Majesty; and I ask Your Roman Imperial Majesty thereupon, with most humble and utmost diligence, that you would take it in no other than the most gracious way, and most graciously take up the oft-mentioned Tycho Brahe and his splendid study, and let all imperial good furtherance befall him. For which I am, toward Your Imperial Majesty (whom I herewith most humbly and faithfully commend to divine omnipotence for all blessed welfare, and myself to your further imperial graces), at all times most humbly and obediently willing and zealous to deserve well.

Given at Güstrow, the 16th of August, the year 1598.
Your Roman Imperial Majesty's most humble and obedient prince,
Ulrich,
Duke of Mecklenburg.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Significance — the imperial commendation itself.** This is the **copy (*Copia literarum*) of Duke Ulrich III's letter recommending Tycho to Emperor Rudolf II** — the *"splendid letter of commendation to the Roman Imperial Majesty"* that **Tycho thanks Ulrich for in brahe-t_15980914002** (14 September 1598). Written from **Güstrow, 16 August 1598**, during Tycho's stay at Rostock, it is a cornerstone document of the campaign that brought Tycho to the imperial court (cf. the later imperial-establishment letters: brahe-t_16000106001, brahe-t_16000324001).
- **Sender.** **Ulrich III, Duke of Mecklenburg-Güstrow** (1527–1603). He addresses **Christian IV of Denmark** as *"meinen freundtlichen hertzvielgeliebten Herrn Sohn"* ("my dear, heartily-beloved Lord son") — a **courtesy kinship-term**: Christian IV was in fact Ulrich's **grandson** (Ulrich's daughter Sophie of Mecklenburg married Frederik II; Christian IV was their son). The dynastic-courtesy force is kept literal with this note, by the audit's rule (no silent "correction").
- **The argument Ulrich makes to the Emperor.**
 1. **Tycho left Denmark neither in disgrace nor for inability to stay**, but solely because his astronomical work "could no longer be valued nor furthered as before" — the diplomatic framing of the rupture (consonant with Tycho's own account, e.g. brahe-t_16000323001).
 2. Ulrich had **reminded Christian IV** (during Tycho's Rostock stay) to "restore and maintain" the work "to the honour of his kingdom" — but a year passed with no recall.
 3. **First-hand testimony:** "the like mathematical instruments, such as I saw with him **on the island of Hven**, have never come before me in any other place" — Ulrich had **personally visited Tycho on Hven** and seen the instruments. A valuable independent witness to the Uraniborg installation.
 4. The appeal to Rudolf II as *"head of the Holy Roman Empire,"* himself inclined to the art, with the *exempla* of kings and potentates who patronised astronomy "from the histories" — and the request that the Emperor **take Tycho and his study under imperial patronage and furtherance**.
- **Persons named.** Ulrich III of Mecklenburg (sender); **Rudolf II** (addressee); **Christian IV** of Denmark (*"Herr Sohn"* = grandson); Tycho Brahe; the island of **Hven**; Tycho's stay at **Rostock**.
- **Register / formulae.** High imperial-petition German (*Allerdurchlauchtigster … unüberwindlichster römischer Kaiser*; *E: Kay: Maj:tt* = *Euer Kaiserliche Majestät*). Latin terms embedded (*restituiren, promoviret, patrocinii, recommendiren, instrumenta mathematica*) by this chapter's convention The heading *Copia literarum* marks this as the archival copy in Langebek's *Diplomatarium*.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Güstrow den 16. Augusti anno 1598*; Lutheran Mecklenburg kept the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar. Header agrees with the label.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO XIV pp.144-147 read as page images; the Ulrich-to-Rudolf II letter (no. 153, 1598, 16 aug.) runs from p.145 ('COPIA LITERARUM ILLUSTRISSIMI PRINCIPIS...') through p.146 ('...Ulrich herzog zu Meckelnburgk.'); pp.144 and 147 hold unrelated neighbouring letters and were not needed. Collated the full German text word for word against Dreyer: matches the transcribed original exactly, including the sum-free recommendation, the reference to the Hven instruments, and the date (16. augusti anno 1598, Güstrow). Checked the published English against this verified text clause by clause: no fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found.
