text.original:
TAM NATALIUM SPLENDORE QUAM PROPRIA VIRTUTE, PRÆEMINENTI DOCTRINA VIRO INPRIMIS CLARO OLIGERO ROSÆKRANTZIO DE ROSENHOLM, CONSANGUINEO, AFFINI ET AMICO DESIDERATISSIMO.

S. P.

CUM ante biduum per Studiosum Danum, qui se ea loca, ubi in Cimbria habitas, transiturum pollicitus est, quaedam ad te deproperassem, accidit ut heri sero eas, quas Hafniae antepenultimo Augusti ad me dederas, acceperim. Quare statim misso Hamburgum cursore meo, an Studiosus ille adhuc ibi haereret, inquiri iussi. Quem cum hodie primum ante meridiem isthinc discessurum rescivissem, has responsionis loco iterum festinanter exaro. Si alias ad me ante mensem circiter dedisti literas, quam eae erant, quibus ultimo rescriptum est, scias me illas non recepisse. Scribis nunc te scire, me currum promissum accepisse. At unde hoc? Hafnia enim tuae datae sunt, et meus, qui paulo ante apud te erat, amanuensis, indicabat eum ne Lubecam quidem nedum huc allatum esse. Quod et literae meae insinuabant. Rectius itaque scias, me eum non accepisse. Et nihil fere est, quod nunc adeo iter meum remoretur, atque hoc ipsum. Si Lubecam venisset, actutum me certiorem reddidisset de eo IOACHIMUS BUCH, aliquoties hoc nomine a me per literas admonitus. Si vis, ut eum obtineam, fac ut id quam citissime fiat. Caeteroquin Hamburgi alium coëmere necesse habeo. Scio tamen per te non stetisse, quod res haec tam lente procedat. Et gratias habeo pro hoc erga me officio maximas, relaturus per opportunitatem. De libris, cur non oblati sint, prolixe disseris. At eiusmodi argumenta apud me pondus non inveniunt, imo ne sexcenta his graviora, utpote qui adversariorum et calumniatorum perversas oblocutiones non ita ponderem, ut tu vel alij isthic sub alis eorum depressi, sed flocci faciam. Libertati enim me asserui, quam tuebor. Cum hîc esses, aliter sentiebas et sponte in te recepisti, quod libros [Regios] in manus tradere velles, imo et quaedam alia inculcare de rescriptis ad me [Cancellarij] literis, ipso forte [Rege] inscio. Tunc omnia placebant, adeo ut [Regi] quaedam scribenda relegeris et approbaveris; quae tamen nunc volens omisi, ne, postquam semel inclemens responsum ad Rostochio scriptas accepissem, ulterius supplex insimuler. At quorsum nunc vetus illa et avita constantia! An postquam in Daniam redijsti, Coelum ruit! o pavidae mentes! Miseret sane me Patriae quondam meae, quod nemo ferme in ea sit (uti audio) qui verum iustumque ingenue profiteri audeat, imo ne quidem de his mussitare. Quo haec vergant, tandem exitus monstrabit. Sed utinam non nimis sero tunc sapiatis atque animum resumatis! Non putarim, te Carminis illius, quod Astronomiae nostrae mechanicae praefixum est, paenitere atque ob id libros ipsummet exhibere tergiversari. Neque enim tibi incommodare poterit, quod communiter usu receptum est, nempe in Zoilos malevolos et inscios talia libris attexere; et ipsemet, cum praesens esses, sciebas, quomodo per alios (si qui oblatrarant) excusares. Quicquid id est, cum mei non sit moris, ea, quae semel deliberato constituta sunt, retractare, stat etiamnum, ut et ante, sententia, libros illos [Regi] ipsi in manus esse tradendos, quocunque tandem vultu eos accipiat, et quomodocunque a mei malevolis et osoribus id vertetur aut pervertetur. Altiora tracto, quam ut tam humiles censuras suscipiam. Optarem tamen id per te ipsum fieri, ea saltem de causa, ut tibi, non alijs, cederent libri illi, quemadmodum inter nos ventilatum est. Sin vero id fieri nequeat, offerat eos Affinis meus OLAUS ROSENSPAR, qui et literas meas tradidit, infrugiferas et perverse exceptas; ut sint libri hi quasi earum Corollarium et taciti testes, me non ignorare, quam parvam habeat proportionem [Dania] ad totam Terrae superficiem; utpote quae apice minimi digiti in Globo Terrestri bicubitali tota tegi possit. Et quid de immenso Coelo sentiendum, quod animo volvimus, quod mente comprehendimus et superamus? O humiles curae! Nihil peius me habet, quam quod non carmina quaedam ijsdem libris praenotarim, quae meos pungerent calumniatores, ad similitudinem eorum, quae alijs quibusdam Exemplaribus Viris Principibus transmissis praeposui. Nam, ut scias, Electori Coloniensi, Principi Uraniae MAURITIO, Duci Megapolitano ULDARICO Avo Regis, et Duci ADOLPHO Holsatiae, Affini eius (ut de SCALIGERO non dicam intelligentiore horum aestimatore) libri hi additis ijsdem, quos tibi praescriptos misi, versibus, communicati sunt. Num et illi hinc statuent, me sibi supplicem fieri? Num inde quis ratiocinabitur, me paenitudine duci, quod Caesari eos dedicarim, cui tamen necdum oblati sunt, cum ipsemet hoc efficere constituerim? quasi non moris sit, libros uni Regi vel Principi dedicatos alijs etiam dono dare. Neque sane unquam mihi in mentem venit, quidpiam operum meorum, etiamsi in Dania mansissem, [Regi] nuncupare, cum sciam eum ἄμουσον esse et literas aversari, imo forte nec cuiquam alij, cum librorum dedicatio adeo usitata illiberale quid et mendicitatem quandam prae se ferat, nisi id ad pares fiat, atque eorum, quae isthic tractantur, gnaros. Nam quod Landtgravio primum Epistolarum Tomum inscripsi, ut Patris memoriam et diutinam mecum amicitiam recolerem, id factum est, utque plus fidei illae Epistolae mererentur, quod nihil in ijs esset supposititium. Nec ego quidpiam inde reportavi, ne quidem gratiarum actionem, quamvis bis vel ter idem Princeps mihi postea scripserit. Quod tamen neutiquam curo, cum ad tam vilia non respiciam. Sed de his plus satis, et forte nimium. Tute facile, quid tibi faciendum sit, in his et alijs statues. Si nolit ROSENSPARRIUS, offerat RAMELIUS. Scurrilem istum librum, quem te remittere ais, non recepi. Fac ut eum mature obtineam. Constitui enim famosum ipsum scriptorem Pragae cum Caesaris venia secundum Ius tractari curare; nec aliud Exemplar in promptu est, unde accusationum capita depromam. Nec si esset, ulterius relegere vacat, aut annotationes marginales, pro ut ibi factum, assignari facere.

Apud BŒKELIUM iterum agam in tua causa quod potero. Vix tamen praeter verba quidpiam impetrabo. Quid tandem factum hîc fuerit, postmodum significabo. Si Sophiam praevalere Philosophiae non censes, senties. Utra autem Philosophia praeferenda, Platonicane an Aristotelica, tecum non disputo. Inexhausti sunt naturae abyssi. Inde veritatem petamus, non ex argutis disceptationibus, quibus ea saepius amittitur quam recuperatur. An versus et Epigrammata, quae misi, acceperis, non innuis, et iam etiam altum silentium de responsione Daniae ad Germaniam, et de Commentarijs in literas, quas scis, sponte pollicitis et pluribus eiusmodi. Existimarim illud Horatianum etiam apud te locum inventurum, quamvis in aliam sententiam detortum: Coelum non animum mutat, qui trans mare currit. Sed plura non addo. Neque enim plura vacat. Instat meridies, abitum parat Nuncius, animus est impatiens. Tu itaque cum utraque tua SOPHIA quam optime vale. Et, si lubet, actutum rescribe, missis Lubecam literis, quae me postea, sive hîc adsim sive non, facile invenient. Saluta etiam matrem tuam ex me officiose, et CRAGIUM nostrum, si forte apud te est, de quo tamen ambigo. Nam cum Iutus Iuto quidpiam spoponderit, idem reputo, ac si augur auguri.

Iterum quam felicissime valete.
Raptim Wandesburgo 9. Septembris Anno 1598.
Tuus ex asse TYCHO BRAHE, manu propria.
text.english:
**To the man pre-eminent as much by the splendour of his birth as by his own virtue, by his eminent learning especially renowned, Holger Rosenkrantz of Rosenholm, my most longed-for kinsman, relation, and friend.**

Heartiest greeting.

When, two days ago, I had hurried off certain things to you by a Danish Student who promised he would pass through the places where you dwell in Jutland, it happened that late yesterday I received your letter sent me at Copenhagen on the antepenultimate of August. So at once, sending my courier to Hamburg, I ordered inquiry whether that Student still lingered there. And having learned that he would leave only today, before noon, I again hastily scratch these in answer. If you sent me another letter about a month ago, besides that to which I last replied, know I did not receive it. You now write that you know I received the promised **wagon**. But whence this? For yours were sent from Copenhagen, and my amanuensis (who a little before was with you) reported it had not even been brought to Lübeck, much less hither — as my letters also intimated. Know therefore, more rightly, that I have *not* received it. And there is almost nothing now that so delays my journey as this very thing. If it had come to Lübeck, **Joachim Buch** would at once have informed me, [he being] several times admonished by my letters by this name. If you wish me to obtain it, see it done as quickly as possible; otherwise I must buy another at Hamburg. I know, however, it has not stood by you that this matter proceeds so slowly; and I give the greatest thanks for this service toward me, to be repaid when occasion offers.

**About the books — why they have not been presented — you discourse at length.** But arguments of that kind find no weight with me — no, nor six hundred weightier than these — inasmuch as I do not so weigh the perverse cavils of adversaries and calumniators, as you, or others there, depressed under their wings, [do], but count them not worth a straw. **For I have asserted myself to liberty, which I will defend.** When you were here, you thought otherwise, and of your own accord undertook that you would **deliver the [royal] books into [the King's] hands**, nay, and inculcate certain other things about the **[Chancellor's] letters** written back to me, the [King] himself perhaps unaware. Then all pleased [you], so much that you re-read and approved some things to be written to the [King]; which, however, I now willingly omitted, lest — after I had once received an unkind reply to those written from Rostock — I be further charged as a suppliant. But to what end now that old, ancestral constancy! Did Heaven fall after you returned to Denmark? O timid minds! **I truly pity my former fatherland, that there is almost no one in it (as I hear) who dares ingenuously to profess what is true and just — nay, not even to mutter of these things.** Whither these things tend, the outcome will at last show. But would that you may not then grow wise too late, and resume your courage! I should not think that **you repent of that Poem which is prefixed to our *Astronomia Mechanica*** [the *Mechanica*], and on that account shirk presenting the books yourself. For it cannot incommode you — [it being] commonly received by usage to attach such things in books against malevolent and ignorant **Zoiluses**; and you yourself, when present, knew how to excuse it through others (if any barked). Whatever it is — since it is not my custom to retract what is once deliberately decided — **the verdict stands, as before: that those books are to be delivered into the [King's] own hands**, with whatever face he at last receive them, and however it be twisted or perverted by my malevolent haters. I handle higher things than to take up such humble censures. Yet I should wish it done through you yourself, at least for this cause: that those books should fall to you, not to others, as was discussed between us. But if it cannot be done, **let my kinsman Oluf Rosensparre present them — he who also delivered my letters, fruitless and perversely received — so that these books may be, as it were, a Corollary to them, and silent witnesses that I am not ignorant how small a proportion [Denmark] has to the whole surface of the Earth: which could be wholly covered by the tip of the little finger on a two-cubit Terrestrial Globe.** And what is to be thought of the immense Heaven — which we revolve in mind, which we comprehend and surpass? O humble cares! Nothing troubles me worse than that I did not prefix to these same books certain poems to sting my calumniators, after the likeness of those I set before certain other copies sent to Princely Men.

For, that you may know: **to the Elector of Cologne, to the Prince of Urania, Moritz [of Hesse], to Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg, the King's grandfather, and to Duke Adolf of Holstein, his kinsman — not to speak of Scaliger, a more intelligent appraiser of these — these books were communicated, with the same verses added which I sent prescribed to you.** Will they too conclude from this that I make myself a suppliant to them? Will anyone reason thence that I am led by repentance that I dedicated them to the Emperor — to whom, however, they are not yet offered, since I resolved to do this myself? As if it were not the custom to give books dedicated to one King or Prince to others also as a gift. Nor indeed did it ever come into my mind to dedicate any of my works — even had I remained in Denmark — to the [King], since I know him to be **unmusical [ἄμουσος] and to shun letters** — nay perhaps not to anyone, since the dedication of books, so common, carries something illiberal and a kind of beggary about it, unless it be made to equals, and to those knowing the matters there handled. For that I inscribed the first volume of the *Letters* to the **Landgrave** [Wilhelm IV] — to recall the Father's memory and his long friendship with me — was done that those Letters might merit more credence, [there being] nothing supposititious in them; nor did I get anything thence, not even thanks, though that Prince [Moritz] wrote me afterward twice or thrice. Which yet I in no way care for, since I look not to such cheap things. But of these, more than enough — and perhaps too much. You will easily decide, in these and other matters, what is to be done by you. If **Rosensparre** be unwilling, let **Ramel** present [them].

That **scurrilous book** [of Ursus] which you say you are returning, I have not received. See that I get it in good time; for **I have resolved to have the infamous writer himself dealt with at Prague, by law, with the Emperor's leave**, and no other copy is at hand from which to draw the heads of accusation. Nor, if there were, is there leisure to re-read it further, or to have marginal annotations assigned, as was done there. With **Bökel** I will again do in your cause what I can; yet I shall scarcely obtain anything beyond words. What is at last done here, I will signify afterward. If you do not judge that **Wisdom [Sophia] prevails over Philosophy, you will feel it**. But which Philosophy is to be preferred — Platonic or Aristotelian — I do not dispute with you. Inexhaustible are the abysses of nature. Thence let us seek truth, not from subtle disputations, by which it is more often lost than recovered. Whether you received the verses and Epigrams I sent, you do not indicate; and now too there is deep silence about "Denmark's response to Germany," and about the Commentaries on the letters you know of, voluntarily promised, and more of the kind. I should think that Horatian [line] will find a place even with you, though twisted to another sense: **"He changes his sky, not his mind, who runs across the sea."** But I add no more, for there is no leisure for more. Noon presses, the Messenger prepares to leave, my mind is impatient. So fare you most well, with both your **Sophias**. And, if you like, write back at once, sending the letters to Lübeck, which afterward — whether I am here or not — will easily find me. Greet too your mother dutifully from me, and our **Krag** [Niels Krag], if perchance he is with you (of which, however, I am doubtful). For when a Jutlander has promised a Jutlander anything, I reckon it the same as if [it were] augur to augur.

Again, fare most happily.
In haste from Wandsbek, 9 September 1598.
Yours to the last farthing,
**Tycho Brahe**, in his own hand.

Tycho refuses to retract: **"the verdict stands … the books are to be delivered into the King's own hands, with whatever face he receive them."** He'd prefer Holger to present them (so the gift reverts to Holger); failing that, his kinsman **Oluf Rosensparre**, or else **Henrik Ramel**. He frames the gift as "silent witnesses" of his cosmic perspective — Denmark being coverable "by the tip of the little finger on a two-cubit globe."

documents.incipit: an den herren Tycho Brahen, waß d. Veidt Winßheimb bey d. Johan Böyklen wegen der bücher …

text.original:
BERICHT.

an den herren Tycho Brahen, waß d. Veidt Winßheimb bey d. Johan Böyklen wegen der bücher deß herren Tychoen beuehlicht nach außgerichtet. Eß hat d. Winßheimb alßbaldt nach empfangenem schreiben, darjnnen von dem herren Tychoen dieser sachen gemeldet würdt, sich zu d. Böyklen in der perohn begeben vndt jhnen zu hauße gesucht. Do ehr jhn aber nicht gefunden, darumb ehr d. Böykel hernacher zu d. Winßheimben in seine behaußung sich vorfüget, do jhn der d. Winßheimb deßhalben, wie eß der her Tycho in seinem schreiben angedeutet, angesprochen, worauff d. Böykel diesen bericht vndt antwort vngefehrlichen von sich gegeben, daß ehr Oligero Roßenkrantz auff seine bitte doctoris Pieremanni sehligen bucher auß guttem willen zukommen laßen vor 150 thaler, vnndt wehre solcher kauff vberhaubt vndt in einer summen geschehen; ehr hette auch, wie ehr domalß wehre wegkfehrig geweßen, dem Nicolao Mulaeo solche bücher alle vberantwortet vndt jhm dieselbe außleßen laßen, vndt wehre Rosenkrantz midt denen vndt daß ehr jhm angetzeiget, wie ehr seinem sohne etliche von dießen büchern nach Helmstedt midtgegeben, wohl zufrieden geweßen, wie ehr dan deßen wegen an Rosenkrantz forderlichst selbst schreiben vndt hirjnnen notturftiglich erjnnern wolte. Er hette auch den Wesalium hernacher geschigket, vnangesehen daß Olgar Rosenkrantz solch buch nicht begehrret geweßen, bestehet also entlichen darauff, daß ehr von diesen büchern nichts mehr bey sich habe, vndt solche derhalben nicht von sich geben konne. Welcheß d. Winßheimb, wie es an jhn gelanget, dem herren Tychoen Brahen vnangetzeiget nicht laßen sollen, wubeneben doch d. Böykell anderß mehr zu seiner endtschuldigung angetzogen, welcheß alleß hirmidt anzuhengen von vnnöten erachtet.

De libris residuis a Bochelio extorquendis die decimo septembris adfui vna cum m. Christiano Longomontano et ex mandato d:nj Tychonis ei contenta literarum Holligeri illud negotium concernentium praelegi, cupiens vt in eadem singula nobis praesentibus se resolueret. Quibus praelectis e vestigio respondit Buchelius, verum quidem fuisse se vendidisse Holligero libros catalogo inscriptos, et liberum ad bibliothecam perlustrandam Holligero aut eius interniuncio fuisse accessum, seque (quod iure iurando per animae salutem aliquoties affirmauit) nihil plane interea e bibliotheca illa clanculum distraxisse, neque aliud responsum extorquere potuimus, etiamsi aliquoties coram institimus aequum iustumque esse, vt catalogo librorum Holligero venditorum omnino satisfieret. De libris Tomae Aquinatis similiter affirmavit aliquot quidem eiusdem reliquia bibliothecae olim interfuisse, sed quo pacto ijdem aut inde distincti aut surrepti se nesciuisse. Deinde manuscriptum librum physicum cum vrgeremus non ut describendum sed ut descriptum Holligero primo fuisse devenditum, ita subiecit, filium suum eundem Brunsuigam secum assumpsisse, eo autem reverso curaret unum aut describi aut eundem librum mitti, tandem cum adhuc vlterius flagitaremus, vt id quod aequum et iustum esset, praestaret, et se atque alios a pluribus liberaret molestijs, respondit, se, si Holligerus libros acceptos restitueret, pecuniam eidem renumeraturum, atque ita nobis acquiescendum fuit, re non vt voluimus confecta. Haec contestamur singuli propria manu subscripta.

Christianus Longomontanus
Claudius Mulenus
propria manu.
text.english:
**REPORT.**

To Lord Tycho Brahe: what Doctor Veit Winsheim, as commissioned, has accomplished with Doctor Johann Böckel concerning the books in Lord Tycho's matter. Doctor Winsheim, immediately upon receiving the letter in which this matter is mentioned by Lord Tycho, betook himself to Doctor Böckel in person and sought him at [his] house; but, not finding him, Doctor Böckel afterward presented himself at Doctor Winsheim's dwelling, where Doctor Winsheim addressed him on the matter, as Lord Tycho had indicated in his letter. Whereupon Doctor Böckel gave this report and answer, in substance: that he had, at his request, out of good will let **Holger Rosenkrantz** have the books of the late Doctor **Pieremann** for 150 thalers, and that such purchase had been made wholesale and in one [lump] sum; he had also — being then about to travel away — handed over all such books to **Nicolaus Mule** [Claus Mule] and let him pick them out; and Rosenkrantz had been well content with those, and [content] that he [Böckel] had told him how he had given his son some of these books to take to **Helmstedt**, as he would write to Rosenkrantz himself about this without delay and duly remind [him] of it. He had also afterward sent the **Vesalius**, notwithstanding that Holger Rosenkrantz had not asked for that book; he insists, then, finally, that he has nothing more of these books with him, and therefore cannot hand them over. Which Doctor Winsheim ought not to leave unreported to Lord Tycho Brahe, as it reached him — though Doctor Böckel adduced still other things for his excuse, all of which it is deemed needless to append here.

Concerning the residual books to be recovered from Böckel, on the tenth day of September I was present, together with Master Christian Longomontanus, and by Lord Tycho's mandate I read out to him [Böckel] the contents of Holger's letter touching that business, desiring that he resolve himself on each point, in our presence. These read out, Böckel answered on the spot that it was indeed true he had sold to Holger the books listed in the catalogue, and that free access to survey the library had been [granted] to Holger or his intermediary; and that he (which he several times affirmed by oath, upon his soul's salvation) had plainly purloined nothing secretly from that library in the meantime; nor could we extort any other answer, even though we several times insisted to his face that it was fair and just that the catalogue of books sold to Holger be entirely satisfied. Concerning the books of **Thomas Aquinas**, he likewise affirmed that some remnants of the same had once been among the library, but how the same were either separated thence or filched, he knew not. Then, when we pressed that the **manuscript physics book** had first been sold to Holger not as one to be copied but as [one already] copied, he replied thus: that his son had taken the same with him to **Brunswick**, but on his return he would see to it that one [copy] either be made, or the same book be sent. At last, when we demanded yet further that he perform what was fair and just, and free himself and others from much trouble, he answered that, if Holger would restore the books received, he would repay him the money; and so we had to acquiesce, the matter not concluded as we wished. These things we attest, each subscribed with [his] own hand.

Christian Longomontanus
Claus Mule,
with [our] own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Senders / form.** A two-part **report and sworn testimony** addressed to Tycho, signed by **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus** (*Christianus Longomontanus*) and **Claus Mule** (*Claudius Mulenus / Nicolaus Mulaeus*), two members of Tycho's *familia* (cf. brahe-t_16000919001, where "Claude Muler" and Longomontanus act as Tycho's couriers). The first part is a **German *Bericht*** of Doctor Winsheim's dealings; the second a **Latin first-person attestation** by Mule (with Longomontanus present) of their own confrontation with Böckel on 10 September. The MS is in the Rigsarkivet's *Genealogisk-heraldisk Selskab* papers.
- **Significance — the Böckel-books affair (continuation of the Winshemius/Rosenkrantz thread).** This directly continues the dispute of **brahe-t_15980328001** (Tycho→Vitus Winshemius), where Tycho, on behalf of his kinsman **Holger Rosenkrantz**, pressed **Johann Böckel** to hand over the books still owed. The matter: Böckel had sold Holger the library of the late **Doctor Pieremann** (for **150 thalers**, wholesale); Holger claims books are missing from the catalogue.
- **Böckel's defence (as reported).**
 1. The sale was *en bloc* for 150 thalers; he had handed **all** the books to **Claus Mule** to sort, and Rosenkrantz was content (including with Böckel's son having taken some to **Helmstedt**).
 2. He had even sent the **Vesalius** (the *De humani corporis fabrica*; cf. brahe-t_15980328001) though Holger had not asked for it.
 3. Under the formal questioning of 10 September (Mule reading out Holger's letter), Böckel **swore "upon his soul's salvation"** that he had **secretly purloined nothing** from the library.
 4. On the **Thomas Aquinas** volumes: some "remnants" had once been in the library, but how they were separated or filched, he did not know.
 5. On the **manuscript physics book** (which Holger says was sold to him *as already copied*, not to be copied): Böckel's **son had taken it to Brunswick**, and on his return Böckel would have a copy made or send the book.
 6. Final offer: if Holger **returns the books received, Böckel will repay the money** — so the agents "had to acquiesce, the matter not concluded as we wished."
- **Persons named.** **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus**; **Claus Mule** (= Nicolaus Mulaeus); *Doctor Veit Winsheim* = **Vitus Winshemius** (the younger), Wittenberg medical professor and Holger's intermediary (cf. brahe-t_15980328001); *Doctor Johann Böckel* = **Johann Bökel** (Bocatius/Boccatius, 1535–1605), Hamburg town physician; *Oligerus / Holger* = **Holger Rosenkrantz** "the Learned," Tycho's kinsman; *Doctor Pieremann* (the late owner of the library); Böckel's son (to **Helmstedt** / **Brunswick**); **Vesalius** and **Thomas Aquinas** (the books in dispute).
- **Textual / language flags.** The German header *"wegen der bücher deß herren Tychoen"* reads "concerning the books in Lord Tycho's matter" — Tycho acting **on Holger's behalf** (the books are Holger's; Tycho is the commissioning principal), per the thread; rendered to keep that sense, with the ambiguity noted. Latin *requia* (for *reliquiae*, "remnants/remains") and *nobus* (for *nobis*) are the copy's slips, read by sense. Chancery-report syntax in both languages is dense; the negations (Böckel "purloined nothing") are kept exact.
- **Calendar.** Dated *die decimo septembris / 10 September* 1598; **Old Style** (Lutheran north-German/Danish context). No place in the dateline (edition *s.l.*); header marked "[no place stated]."
- **Correction.** Latin: 'nobus' corrected to 'nobis', and 'requia' corrected to 'reliquia', per Dreyer, Opera Omnia XIV, p.147 (translation unaffected in both cases — already correctly rendered).

text.original:
NATALIUM SPLENDORE AeQUE AC PROPRIA VIRTUTE AC ERUDITIONE INPRIMIS CONSFPICIO VIRO DOMINO OLIGERO ROSÆKRANTZIO DE ROSENHOLM, CONSANGUINEO, AFFINI ET AMICO INTEGERRIMO.

VIX octiduum elapsum est, Nobilissime et Charissime OLIGERE, ex quo per Studiosum quendam NICOLAUM ALBINUM nomine ad te de rerum mearum statu perscripsi, nunc vero, cum nihil addubitem, quin eae literae perlatae sint, tamen cum inopinata se haec occasio offerret per Nobilissimum Virum FRANCISCUM RANZOVIUM, qui iam e Belgio redux rursus iter isthuc parabat, denuo ad te perscribendum ratus sum, quo de curru, quem me accepisse innueras, te denuo admonerem, ut eum actutum huc procurares, quippe qui maxima ex parte iter meum remoraretur. Lubecam enim eum necdum allatum certo mihi constat. Caeteroquin non intermisisset IOACHIMUS BUCK (pro ut semel atque iterum ab ipso expetij) quin te per literas ilico de eo fecisset certiorem. Rogo itaque etiam atque etiam, ne longiores hac in re morae nectantur, sed ut sequenti ad summum hebdomada huc ad me perferatur (Uden saa er, att I vilde holde Jytske Louff, det er at beholde hvad mand loffuer, saa at en anden faar intet deraff. Da maatte man endda i det mindste lade en vide det, saa man skulle ikke vente det thill forgieffues); nam diutius praestolari non possum. Sed quamvis tum iter ingressus fuero, tamen non ambigo, quin is nihilo serius ad me perveniat, pro ut, antequam discessero, disponam.

Plura iam non vacat, cum de caeteris in prioribus satis superque tuis responsum existimem.

Vale mi OLIGERE quam diutissime cum matre tua et coniuge SOPHIA a me meisque diligenter salutatus.
Raptim Hamburgi die 14. Septembris Anno 1598.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the man conspicuous especially by splendour of birth, as also by his own virtue and erudition, Master Holger Rosenkrantz of Rosenholm, kinsman, relative by marriage, and most upright friend.**

Scarcely a week [and a day] has elapsed, most noble and dearest Holger, since I wrote to you — through a certain student named Nicolaus Albinus — about the state of my affairs; but now, although I doubt not at all that those letters have been delivered, yet, since this unexpected occasion offered itself through the most noble man Frans Rantzau — who, now returned from Belgium, was again preparing the journey thither — I have judged that I should write to you again, to remind you once more about the wagon which you had hinted you had received, that you procure it hither at once, since it for the most part delays my journey. For I am certain it has not yet been brought to Lübeck. Otherwise Joachim Buck would not have failed (as I sought of him once and again) to make you certain of it at once by letter. I ask, therefore, again and again, that no longer delays be woven in this matter, but that it be conveyed hither to me by next week at the latest *(Unless it be that you wish to keep Jutish Law — that is, to keep what one has promised, so that another gets nothing of it. In that case one might, at the very least, let a man know it, so that he should not wait for it in vain)*; for I cannot wait any longer. But although I shall by then have set out on my journey, yet I do not doubt that it will reach me none the later, as I shall arrange before I depart.

There is no more leisure now, since I reckon that enough and more than enough has been answered, about the rest, in [reply to] your earlier [letters].

Farewell, my Holger, as long as possible, [you] being diligently greeted by me and mine, together with your mother and your wife Sophia.
Hastily, at Hamburg, the 14th of September, in the year 1598.
Your Tycho Brahe,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Holger Rosenkrantz** "the Learned" (1574–1642), Tycho's *consanguineus, affinis et amicus* (kinsman, relative by marriage, and friend); cf. the Cramer/Liddel letters (brahe-t_15980331001, …0524001). His wife **Sophia** = **Sophie Axelsdatter Brahe**; his mother is also greeted.
- **Occasion.** A homely, impatient note about a **wagon (*currus*)** that Rosenkrantz was to procure and forward to Tycho at Hamburg — it is holding up Tycho's onward **journey** (south, toward the Empire, in his 1597–98 exile). Tycho is sure it has not yet reached **Lübeck**, since **Joachim Buck** (his Lübeck contact) would otherwise have written. Couriers: **Nicolaus Albinus** (a student, the earlier letter) and **Frans Rantzau** (*Franciscus Ranzovius*, back from Belgium/the Low Countries and travelling that way again).
- **⚠ Danish code-switch (kept and translated).** Mid-sentence, Tycho drops from Latin into **Danish** for a proverbial joke: *"Uden saa er, att I vilde holde Jytske Louff, det er at beholde hvad mand loffuer, saa at en anden faar intet deraff. Da maatte man endda i det mindste lade en vide det, saa man skulle ikke vente det till forgieves"* — "Unless it be that you wish to keep **Jutish Law** — that is, to keep what one promises, so that another gets nothing of it; [then] one might at least let a man know it, so that he should not wait for it in vain." The phrase *holde jysk lov* ("keep Jutland law") is a Danish proverbial pun: to keep for oneself what one has promised to another. Preserved verbatim in the Source block and rendered in italics (by this chapter's convention); a deliberate bilingual joke between kinsmen, **not smoothed away**.
- **⚠ Dateline.** *Raptim Hamburgi die 14* — the dateline gives only "**the 14th**," **without month or year**. The edition (identifier …0914… / label "14. september") supplies **14 September 1598**; the internal "scarcely a week has elapsed since…" and the Hamburg exile context are consistent. Header dates **14 September 1598**, the month/year flagged as editorially supplied. Hamburg (Lutheran) = **Old Style**.
- **Correction.** Two restorations against Dreyer (TBOO VIII pp.113-114): removed an unsupported 'tuto ad te' from the opening paragraph (with a matching trim to the translation), and restored the full closing dateline 'die 14. Septembris Anno 1598.', replacing the translation's bracketed guess '[of September]'.

documents.incipit: DURCHLEUCHTIGER hochgeborner fürst, E.F.G. seindt meine vnterthenige bereitwillige …

text.original:
DEM DURCHLEUCHTIGEN HOCHGEBORNEN FURSTEN VND HERRN, HERRN VLRICHEN HERTZOGEN ZU MECKELNBURGK, FÜRSTEN ZU WENDEN, GRAFENN ZU SCHWERIN, DER LANDE ROSTOCK VND STARGAARD HERRN, MEINEM GNEDIGEN FÜRSTEN VND HERRN.

DURCHLEUCHTIGER hochgeborner fürst, E.F.G. seindt meine vnterthenige bereitwillige dienste iedertzeit bestes fleißes zuuor. Gnediger furst vnnd herr. Daß E.F.G. mir auff mein junsthin verschinnes monnats julij gegebenes schreibenn dero gnedige antwordt nicht allein vbersendet vnnd ihr mein propositum vnnd furnehmen wollgefallenn lassen, sondern auch so ein herrlich commendationschreiben ahnn die röm. kay. maytt. gnedig communiciret vnnd wiederfahren lassen, darahn haben E.F.G. mir eine besondere gnadt vnnd wolthat bewiesenn, vnnd thue deßhalbenn gegen E.F.G. mich inn aller vnterthenigkeit vnnd zum höchstenn darfur nicht alleine bedanckenn, sondernn erkenne mich auch schuldig, daßelbe vmb E.F.G. nach eusserstem meinem vermugenn iederzeit hinwider inn vntherthenigkeit zuerkennenn.

Dieweil dan auch ab E.F.G. gnedig ahn mich beschehenen schreibenn ich vermercket, daß E.F.G. jhr mein vberschicktes buch de mechanica astronomia lieb vnndt angenehm sein vnnd in dero furstliche bibliotheck aufhebenn vnd stadt findenn lassen, so ist mir solchs zuuemehmenn gantz erfreulichen gewesen, vndt thue E. F. G. daß ander vonn meiner restitutio affixarum stellarum, welches jch auch höchstgedachter röm. kay. maytt. vnterthenigst dediciret, vnterthenig vberschickenn, worahn jch vber die zwanzig jahrlang nebens andern astronomischen sachen mit hochem fleiß [gearbeit] vnndt zugebracht, also das (ohne ruhm zu [melden) in] dieser zeit nie keiner solchen fleiß vnd [muhe hat an] gewendet, dan diese ... minuto vnnd (wo es von ... [du]rch meine große vnnd ... uiret vnnd nachgerech-... astronomi nur den sechsten theill eines gradus verzeichnet vnnd doch bißweilenn vber einen gantzenn gefeilet habenn, bin aber nicht willens, daßelbe so balt, alweiln es mich viell muhe vnnd vnkost gestandenn, inn druck alß publiciren zulassen, sondern es nur manu scriptum, wie dieses, jhrer kay. maytt. zuofferiren.

Langet derhalbenn ahn E.F.G. mein vntertheniges fleißiges bitten, E.F.G. wollen solches nichtweniger alß das vorige von mir gnedig auf- vnndt ahnnehmen vnnd inn dero bibliotecam zum gedechtnuß verwahrenn vnnd aufhebenn lassenn, auch iederzeit mein gnediger furst vnnd her, wie bißhero geschehen, sein vnd bleibenn. Jn solchem gegen E.F.G. mein danckbares gemuedt zuerzeigenn, soll vnnd will jch mich iederzeit vngespart meiner geringfuegigen dienstenn eußersten vermugens vnterthenig erfinden lassenn. Thue hiemit E.F.G. sambt dero hertzvielgeliebten gemahlin inn den schutz vnndt schirm Gottes deß allmechtigen zu langer bestendiger [ge]sundtheit vnnd fürstlicher wolfart getreulich befehlen.

Datum Wandeßburg denn 14. septembris annj 1598.
E:F:G: vnterthen[iger vnd] di[enstwilliger
Tycho] Brahe
mitt eigner handtt
text.english:
**To the most serene, high-born Prince and Lord, Lord Ulrich, Duke of Mecklenburg, Prince of the Wends, Count of Schwerin, Lord of the lands of Rostock and Stargard, my gracious Prince and Lord.**

Most serene, high-born Prince — to Your Princely Grace [be] my humble, ready services at all times, with best diligence, beforehand. Gracious Prince and Lord. That Your Princely Grace not only sent me your gracious answer to the letter I gave last, in the past month of July, and were pleased with my purpose and undertaking, but also so graciously communicated and bestowed such a splendid letter of commendation to the Roman Imperial Majesty — therein Your Princely Grace has shown me a special grace and benefit; and I therefore not only thank Your Princely Grace for it, in all humility and most highly, but also acknowledge myself bound to requite the same toward Your Princely Grace, to the utmost of my ability, at all times, in humility.

And since, too, from Your Princely Grace's gracious letter to me I have noted that Your Princely Grace finds my book *de mechanica astronomia*, which I sent, dear and agreeable, and lets it be kept and given a place in your princely library — this has been quite a joy for me to learn; and I humbly send Your Princely Grace the other [work], of my *restitution of the fixed stars*, which I have likewise most humbly dedicated to the aforesaid Roman Imperial Majesty, [and] on which, above twenty years long, alongside other astronomical matters, I have with high diligence [laboured] and spent [my time] — so that (without [boasting] to say it) in this age no one has expended such diligence and [labour]; for these [positions are reckoned] to the minute, and (where it … through my great and … [measured] and recalculated …) whereas [earlier] astronomers noted only the sixth part of a degree, and yet have sometimes erred by a whole one. But I am not willing to let the same be published in print so soon — since it has cost me much labour and expense — but only to offer it in manuscript, like this one, to His Imperial Majesty.

There comes therefore to Your Princely Grace my humble, diligent request, that Your Princely Grace would, no less than the former [book], graciously receive and accept this from me, and let it be kept and preserved in your library as a memorial, and also be and remain at all times my gracious Prince and Lord, as has hitherto been the case. In showing my grateful heart toward Your Princely Grace herein, I shall and will at all times let myself be found humble, and unsparing of my poor services, to the utmost of my ability. I herewith faithfully commend Your Princely Grace, together with your heartily-beloved consort, to the protection and shelter of God Almighty, for long, constant health and princely welfare.

Given at Wandsbek, the 14th of September, the year 1598.
Your Princely Grace's humble and service-willing
[Tycho] Brahe,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Ulrich III, Duke of Mecklenburg-Güstrow** (1527–1603), full titulature reproduced (as in brahe-t_15880815001, brahe-t_16010415003, brahe-t_16010604001). The MS is the **original letter**, explicitly **in poor condition** (*i dårlig stand*) — hence the lacunae below.
- **Significance — a double-book presentation (census-relevant).** This letter documents Tycho's **presentation of two of his Wandsbek-press works to the ducal library at Güstrow**, in the exile year 1598:
 1. *mein vberschicktes buch **de mechanica astronomia*** = the **_Astronomiae Instauratae Mechanica_** (Wandsbek 1598), already received and *"given a place in [Ulrich's] princely library."*
 2. *daß ander vonn meiner **restitutio affixarum stellarum*** = the **"restitution of the fixed stars"** — i.e. the **fixed-star catalogue** (the work of the *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata*), here sent as the *second* gift, *"likewise dedicated to the Roman Imperial Majesty."*
 This is a **documented presentation/ownership event for a 1598 Wandsbek *Mechanica*** (Duke Ulrich III's copy, into the Güstrow *Fürstliche Bibliothek*) — directly relevant to the Mecklenburg strand of the *Mechanica*'s documented distribution history.
- **The star-catalogue and Tycho's accuracy claim.** Tycho stresses he is **not yet willing to print** the star-restitution (it "cost much labour and expense") but offers it *manu scriptum* ("in manuscript, like this one") to **Rudolf II** — the famous practice of presenting the **manuscript star catalogue** to the Emperor rather than publishing. His accuracy boast: his positions are reckoned **"to the minute,"** whereas earlier astronomers recorded only **"the sixth part of a degree" (≈ 10 arc-minutes)** and "sometimes erred by a whole degree." (Twenty-plus years of labour — the Hven programme.)
- **Damaged passage (flagged; this chapter's convention).** The witness is physically damaged; the precision-boast sentence is **partly lost**: *"dan diese … minuto vnnd (wo es von … [du]rch meine große vnnd … uiret vnnd nachgerech-… astronomi nur den sechsten theill eines gradus verzeichnet …"*. The bracketed words ([gearbeit], [melden) in], [muhe hat an], [du]rch, [ge]sundtheit, and the subscription [iger vnd] di[enstwilliger, Tycho]) are the **edition's restorations** of legible-by-context gaps; the ellipses (…) mark **irrecoverable lacunae**, left unfilled in the translation ("[measured]" supplied tentatively in brackets where sense demands a verb). The general sense (minute-precision vs. earlier astronomers' coarser figures) is secure; the exact wording of the broken clause is not.
- **Persons / things named.** Duke Ulrich III; **Rudolf II** (*röm. kay. Maytt.*); the **Mechanica** and the **fixed-star catalogue**; Ulrich's *hertzvielgeliebte Gemahlin* ("heartily-beloved consort") — **Anna of Pomerania-Wolgast**, Ulrich's second wife (cautiously, not asserted from the text). The July 1598 letter Tycho refers to, and Ulrich's commendation to the Emperor, belong to Tycho's exile-period campaign to secure imperial patronage (cf. the intercession letters of 1598).
- **Register / formulae.** Deferential chancery German, subject's first person (*E.F.G.* = *Euer Fürstliche Gnaden*); subscription *mit eigner Hand* (= *manu propria*); the Latin technical titles (*de mechanica astronomia*, *restitutio affixarum stellarum*, *manu scriptum*) embedded in the German by this chapter's convention
- **Calendar / date crux.** Dateline *14. Septembris anni 1598* at Wandsbek; **Old Style**. The edition label ("10 september") disagrees with the dateline and the identifier (15980914002, the 14th); the **label is in error**, rejected in favour of the source's own date, by this chapter's convention

documents.incipit: HAC ipsa hora domum rediens a quodam Holsato Nobili in vicinia habitante, reperi hîc tuas …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO TAM NATALIUM SPLENDORE QUAM PROPRIA VIRTUTE VIRO DOMINO OLIGERO ROSÆKRANTZIO DE ROSENHOLM, CONSANGUINEO, AFFINI ET AMICO SUO DESIDERATISSIMO.

S. P.

HAC ipsa hora domum rediens a quodam Holsato Nobili in vicinia habitante, reperi hîc tuas literas, Charissime Domine OLIGERE, et nunc primum ex ijs certior redditus sum, currum diu promissum Lubecam venisse, a Factore autem meo eundem Oldesloviam, pro ut mandaram, translatum percepi, unde crastina die, volente Deo, eundem huc adferri curabo. Mora autem nimia, quæ intercessit, undecunque tandem orta, et tot frustra ea de re a me perscriptæ literas tam in Daniam quam Lubecam, effecerunt, ut ante triduum alium mihi præter eum, quem de novo confieri curavi, Hamburgi compararem pretio 50 Ioachimicorum. Ago nihilominus tibi gratias pro tua in me benevola voluntate quam maximas, quod me hoc donare volueris, relaturus per opportunitatem. Et licet illum necdum viderim, spero nihilominus eiusmodi esse, ut usui meo inservire queat. Si quid desideratur, Hamburgi facile supplebitur. Moram illam plus quam Iuticam, si navi cum lignis combustioni idoneis Lubecam transmissa meo naulo, pro ut iam dudum pollicitus es, redimere volueris, et familiæ meæ muliebri, quam discedens hîc relinquo, pro arcendo hîc frigore ita mature prospicere, id quicquid est, promptius expiabis. Non possum ex hisce tuis, quæ 7. Augusti Hafnia datæ sunt, colligere, te omnes meas accepisse. Adeo parce rescribis, nec singula a me mota attingis. Quin et semel atque iterum ad te scripsi, ex quo in Cimbriam te redijsse coniectabar. Cuperem, ut ad singulas prompte responderes, nec verborum aut characterum ita tenax esses, ut nunc uxorius alijs forte quam antea distrahare negocijs. Si quid scripseris, mitte saltem hîc Wandesburgum, sive per Lubecam, sive alia via, licet fieri possit, ut tunc hîc præsto non sim. Constitui enim, favente Divina Clementia, post non adeo multos dies iter propositum ingredi; præsertim cum iam currus et cætera (tuæ tamen literæ me facile invenient) requisita sufficienter in promptu sint.

Redijt ante quatriduum D. D. VITUS VINSHEMIUS Witteberga, ubi diu abfuerat, et attulit secum fasciculum quendam libellorum de LUTHERI historia cum duabus ad te Epistolis, quas nunc ad te dirigo. Aderant 9 exemplaria eiusdem libelli, quorum octo tibi simul mitto, nonum mihi reservo, ut per otium videam, quæ contineat, et an dissona sint ab ijs, quæ me olim, cum Lipsiæ studerem (ab alio authore, cuius nomen nunc non succurrit, profecta) legisse memini. Variant enim in talibus scriptores, prout affectibus indulgent.

De cæteris, quæ hæ ultimæ tuæ continent, nihil addo. Nec enim moror, qualia apud vos fiant connubia; et de eo, quem tangis, iam diu antea scivi, quantum fidentium ei vel secus, ut non opus sit ex hac novitia affinitate me cautiorem reddi. Invaletudinem alterius non miror; imo potius miror, eum valere posse, qui alios multis modis invalentes reddidit. Viderit, ne ea citius illi eveniant, quam putat, quæ iam antea prædixi prædicoque. Sunt, qui ex me audiverunt. Quid BŒKELIUS responderit in tuo negocio de libris non præstitis, ex adiuncta scheda vides. Misi ad eum CLAUDIUM MULIUM cum M. CHRISTIERNO SEVERINI, qui diu mihi fuit domesticus. Nihil ab eo ferme reportamus præter morosa verba. Si rem vis iure decidi, fiat id per alios. Mihi ob iter instans id non est commodum. Sed suaderem potius, ut id omitteres, et ad Doctorem VITUM VINSHEMIUM, qui tui studiosus haberi vult, serio scriberes, ut is (siquidem pecuniam alteri, priusquam volebas, tradidit) efficeret et urgeret, ut quæ tibi revera debentur, obtineas. Miniteris etiam aliquantulum, te actionem contra eum moturum iuridicam, si per se id, quod æquum est, non fecerit. Sic VINSHEMIUS metuens, quod is huic actioni misceri debeat (uti est per se meticulosus) eo validius omnem movebit lapidem, ut tibi tua, quæ emisti, nisi quatenus quædam eorum pro lubitu remittere voles, cedant. Consultissimum iudicarem, ut, siquidem BŒKELIUS sponte obtulerit resolutionem pecuniarum, modo libros reciperet, eos illi prima oportunitate remitteres. Satis enim alias et habes et habere poteris librorum talium. Ego in hoc negocio quod potui feci. Quod autem expectationi utriusque nostrum non respondeat eventus, non est, quod mihi imputes, sed potius BŒKELIJ tenacitati, ne quid dicam amplius. Vix possum in proprijs rebus obtinere, ut Hamburgenses id, quod ius æquumque postulat, libera voluntate efficiant. Tanta est istorum hominum sordities et avaritia insatiabilis, a quibus tamen me post exiguum tempus liberatum iri spero.

Tu autem mi optime OLIGERE, diu cum nupera coniuge mea nepte a me diligenter salutata ac omnibus tuis quam felicissime vale; et si vacat (debet autem vacare) brevi rescribe.

Raptim Wandesburgo 25. Septembris 1598.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the most noble man — as much by the splendour of his birth as by his own virtue — Lord Holger Rosenkrantz of Rosenholm, his most longed-for kinsman, relation-by-marriage, and friend.**

Heartiest greeting.

This very hour, returning home from a certain Holstein nobleman dwelling in the neighbourhood, I found your letter here, dearest Lord Holger; and now first from it I have been informed that **the long-promised wagon has come to Lübeck** — and I gather from my factor that it has been moved on to Oldesloe, as I had ordered, whence tomorrow, God willing, I will have it brought here. But the excessive delay that intervened — from wherever it at last arose — and the many letters I wrote in vain about it, both into Denmark and to Lübeck, made me, three days ago, **buy another at Hamburg for 50 joachimsthalers**, besides the one I had had newly built. Nonetheless I give you the greatest thanks for your benevolent goodwill toward me, in that you wished to make me this gift, to be repaid when occasion offers. And although I have not yet seen it, I hope it is of such a kind as can serve my use; if anything is wanting, it will easily be supplied at Hamburg. **That more-than-Jutish delay you will the more readily atone for, whatever it amounts to, if you will redeem it by sending a ship with firewood fit for burning to Lübeck at my freight (as you long ago promised), and provide thus early for my womenfolk — whom I leave here on departing — against the cold here.** I cannot gather from this letter of yours (dated at Copenhagen 7 August) that you received all of mine: so sparingly do you write back, nor do you touch on the several points I raised. Indeed I have written to you once and again, since I guessed you had returned to Jutland. I could wish you would answer each point promptly, and not be so chary of words or characters — now that, being a married man [*uxorius*], you are perhaps distracted by other business than before. If you write anything, send it at least here to **Wandsbek**, whether by Lübeck or another way — though it may happen that I am then not at hand here. For I have resolved, by Divine Clemency favouring, to set out within not very many days on the journey I have proposed — especially since the wagon and the other requisites are now sufficiently ready (your letters, however, will easily find me).

Four days ago **Dr. Veit Winsheim** returned from **Wittenberg**, where he had long been absent, and brought with him a certain bundle of pamphlets **on the history of Luther**, with two letters to you, which I now forward to you. There were 9 copies of the same booklet, of which I send you eight together; the ninth I reserve for myself, to see at leisure what it contains, and whether it differs from what I remember reading long ago, when I studied at **Leipzig** (from another author, whose name does not now come to me). For writers vary in such matters, according as they indulge their feelings.

Of the rest your last letter contains, I add nothing. For I do not concern myself with what marriages are made among you; and as for the man you touch on, I knew long before how far he is to be trusted or not, so that there is no need for me to be made more cautious by this new relationship-by-marriage. The other's ill-health I do not wonder at; nay rather I wonder that he can be well, who has made others unwell in many ways. Let him see to it that the things I foretold before, and foretell [still], do not befall him sooner than he thinks. There are those who have heard it from me. **What Bökel replied in your affair, about the books not delivered, you see from the enclosed sheet.** I sent to him **Claus Mule together with Master Christen Sørensen [Longomontanus]**, who was long a member of my household. We bring back from him almost nothing but morose words. If you wish the matter decided at law, let it be done through others; for me, on account of the imminent journey, it is not convenient. But I should rather advise that you drop it, and **write seriously to Dr. Veit Winsheim** (who wishes to be held a friend of yours), that he — since he handed the money to the other party before you wished — should bring it about and press that you obtain what is truly owed you. Threaten even a little that you will move a legal action against him, if he does not of himself do what is fair. So Winsheim, fearing he must be mixed up in this action (being by nature timorous), will the more strongly move every stone, that your goods, which you bought, may fall to you — except so far as you may willingly remit some of them. I should judge it most prudent that, **if Bökel of his own accord has offered a refund of the money provided he take back the books, you return them to him at the first opportunity** — for you have, and can have, enough other such books elsewhere. In this business I have done what I could. That the outcome does not answer the expectation of us both is not for you to impute to me, but rather to Bökel's tenacity — to say no more. I can scarcely obtain, even in my own affairs, that the **men of Hamburg** do of their free will what right and equity demand: so great is the sordidness and insatiable avarice of those men — from whom, however, I hope to be freed after a short time.

But you, my excellent Holger — long, with your recent wife, my niece, diligently greeted by me — and with all yours, farewell most happily; and if you have leisure (and you ought to have leisure), write back soon.

In haste from Wandsbek, 25 September 1598.
Yours, **Tycho Brahe**, in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Holger Rosenkrantz** "the Learned" of Rosenholm (1574–1642), Tycho's kinsman and (now) relation-by-marriage — he had **recently married Sophie Brahe, daughter of Tycho's brother Steen Brahe, i.e. Tycho's niece** (the closing "your recent wife, my niece" fixes this; cf. the sister-vs-niece distinction maintained across the corpus). Tycho twits him as *uxorius* — a distracted newlywed.
- **Setting — Wandsbek, on the eve of departure (autumn 1598).** Written from **Wandsbek (Wandesburgum)**, the Holstein estate of Heinrich Rantzau where Tycho lodged after leaving Hven — *the very place and season the* Mechanica *was being printed and finished* (cf. the documented production history of the *Mechanica*). Tycho is about to set out on "the proposed journey" (toward Dresden/Wittenberg, ultimately the Emperor), and is putting his household in order: he leaves his **womenfolk** wintering at Wandsbek and asks Holger to redeem a long delay by **shipping firewood to Lübeck at Tycho's freight** against the cold.
- **The wagon.** A *currus* (travelling-wagon/carriage) Holger had promised arrived late at Lübeck → Oldesloe; the delay made Tycho **buy another at Hamburg for 50 joachimsthalers** (plus one newly built). He thanks Holger for the gift all the same.
- **Winsheim's Luther pamphlets.** **Dr. Veit Winsheim** (*Vitus Vinshemius*, the Wittenberg academic; cf. the "Winshemius's son-in-law" note at brahe-t_15990507001) returned from Wittenberg with a bundle of **booklets on the history of Luther** and two letters for Holger; Tycho forwards 8 of 9 copies, keeping one to compare against a different account he had read as a student at **Leipzig**. His aside — *writers vary "according as they indulge their feelings"* — is a characteristic note on partisan historiography.
- **The veiled enemy.** A cryptic passage on an unnamed man "who has made others unwell in many ways," whose illness Tycho does not pity and to whom he repeats a standing **dark prediction** ("there are those who have heard it from me"). Left unidentified per the no-fabrication rule.
- **The Bökel book-debt affair.** **Johann Bökel / Boeckel** (the Hamburg physician) had not delivered books in a transaction of Holger's. Tycho sent his men **Claus Mule (*Claudius Mulius*) and Master Christen Sørensen — Longomontanus** (*M. Christierno Severini*, "long a member of my household") — to Bökel, getting "morose words." Tycho's advice: drop the suit, instead press **Winsheim** (who paid the money out prematurely) with a threat of legal action; and if Bökel offers a refund for the returned books, accept. A vivid complaint about **Hamburg mercantile "sordidness and insatiable avarice."**
- **Persons named.** Holger Rosenkrantz; **Sophie Brahe** (his wife, Tycho's niece, unnamed but identified); **Veit Winsheim** (*Vitus Vinshemius*); **Johann Bökel** (*Boeckelius*, Hamburg); **Claus Mule** (*Claudius Mulius*); **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus** (*M. Christiernus Severini*); the unnamed veiled enemy. Places: **Wandsbek**, **Lübeck**, **Oldesloe**, **Hamburg**, **Wittenberg**, **Leipzig**, **Copenhagen**, **Jutland (Cimbria)**, Denmark.
- **Notable phrase.** *Moram illam plus quam Iuticam* — "that **more-than-Jutish delay**," a proverbial jab at proverbial slowness (Tycho had just guessed Holger "returned to *Cimbria*," Jutland); kept idiomatically and glossed.
- **Calendar.** Holstein/Denmark were **Old Style** in 1598; the letter carries no *stylo* marker, so the dateline **25 September 1598** is read **Old Style** (per the catalogue label, which gives no N.S. flag); header left unqualified to match.

documents.incipit: NOBILIS et Magnifice Domine Patrone colende! Ὅσσον ἔαρ χειμῶνος, ὅσον μᾶλον Βραβύλοιο …

text.original:
DAVID CHYTRÆUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

S. P.

NOBILIS et Magnifice Domine Patrone colende! Ὅσσον ἔαρ χειμῶνος, ὅσον μᾶλον Βραβύλοιο ἅδιον, tanto mihi gratior et dulcior tua Epistola multis alijs eodem tempore allatis fuit, quam a summo et laudatissimo Mathematum artifice, ac vere (ut Summus et Clarissimus ille Princeps ad Cæsaream Mtem de te testatur) patre Astronomorum huius Seculi et unico huius laudatissimæ scientiæ instauratore scriptam, singulari mihi et liberis meis honori et ornamento esse iudico. Periucunda etiam, adeo benigna et humanissima voluntatis tuæ significatio hac in parte fuit, quod exiguum et tenue observantiæ erga te huius Academiæ officium, tibi Rostochium ingresso exhibitum, quod sine scelere prætermitti non poterat, mentione literarum tuarum non indignum esse censes, tibique non ingratum nec iniucundum accidisse; τούς τε ἀγαμοὺς καὶ ἀντὶ μικρῶν οἴδασθαι χάριν ostendis. Ad Eruditos vero et Claros viros scribens, cum amicorum omnia communia sint, maxime duxi communes amicorum amicos esse oportere. Ideoque de amici præstantissimi Viri statu præsenti, cuius cognoscendi desiderio teneri illos non dubitabam, significandum existimavi, præsertim cum eruditissimæ illius et sublimi ingenio tuo accurate elaboratæ epistolæ (ad quendam Midam his studijs iniquiorem) exemplum ideo te mihi coram dedisse intelligerem, ut cum pluribus etiam alijs amicis communicarem. Quare non solum IACOBO MONAVIO, verum PAULO SCHEDIO MELISSO, etiam Poëtarum nostræ ætatis Principi, et IOHANNI POSTHIO, utriusque Artis Apollineæ antistiti, et ABRAHAMO ORTELIO Geographo, quem proximus Mensis Iunius Terris eripuit, et aliquot alijs minus celebribus impertivi legendam; qui animo et voce grata officium meum vicissim prædicarunt. Nobilissimo autem Heroi HENRICO RANZOVIO, sapientia et virtute præstanti, de hac munificentia gratulor, quod cæteris laudibus amplissimis hanc quoque addidit, ut ATLANTI Herculeis laboribus axem stellis ardentibus aptum sustinenti hospitium ex Patria discedenti præberet, cuius memoriam URANIA ad omnem posteritatem grata recolet et diuturnius quam ullæ Pyramides aut Obelisci propagatam celebrabit. Quæ URANIA

Regales animos primum dignata movere,
Proxima tangentes Cœlo fastigia rerum,
nunc etiam invictissimi Imperatoris RUDOLPHI animum flectit, ut patrem Astronomorum huius seculi et unicum laudatissimæ huius scientiæ instauratorem, in patria Centauris quibusdam ac Midis fastiditum, ad se invitet et Regiam hanc ac cœlestem sapientiam Cæsareo suo Patrocinio et sumptu excoli et in sublimi illa arce ætheream artem conservari et longe lateque in suo Imperio spargi cupiat, sicut primi CÆSARIS IULIJ, confusam eo tempore Anni Romani rationem restituere molientis, animum movit, ut SOSIGENEM Mathematicum in Ægypti regno minus honorifice a quibusdam habitum, Romam ad se traduceret, ut sublimem illam ac Cœlestem siderum doctrinam in sublimi summi Imperatoris terrarum theatro, maiori cum sua gloria et Reip. fructu propagaret. Proficiscere igitur Deo duce et auspice CHRISTO, quo te Augustissimus Imperator et tua τύχη vocat et viri Excellentissimi ac optimi D. D. THADDÆI HAGGÆCIJ, studiorum tuorum socij, et amici coniunctissimi, cum quo annis abhinc triginta Viennæ mihi etiam necessitudo intercessit, consuetudine et familiaritate iucundissima, et Reipublicæ profutura, felix fruere; et opera, tot annorum vigilijs et curis elaborata, feliciter pertexe. Nec prolixiore Epistola nunc te ad iter accinctum remorari volo, sed Deum ardentibus votis precor, ut te incolumem ac florentem optimis studijs servet et cursum huius viæ et vitæ totius, ad Dei gloriam et Reipublicæ salutem gubernet. Poëmata in tui gratiam scripta ad Daniam, et Germaniæ de tali hospite lætantis, et BRASCHIJ nostri RUDOLPHO Cæsari et tibi de tuo adventu gratulantis, inprimis vero Epigramma, quod restitutioni Siderum, Duci ULRICO inscriptæ, præmisisti, summa cum voluptate legi ac coniunctim ea typis descripta extare et in eruditorum manibus versari, toto pectore opto.

Bene et feliciter vale.
Rhodopoli Nonis Octobris Anno 1598.
Mtiam . reverenter colens
DAVID CHYTRÆUS.
text.english:
**DAVID CHYTRAEUS TO TYCHO BRAHE.**

Heartiest greeting.

Noble and Magnificent Lord, Patron to be revered! *"As much as spring [is sweeter] than winter, as much as the apple [is] sweeter than the sloe"* — by so much was your Letter more pleasing and sweeter to me than the many others brought at the same time; which, written **by the highest and most praised craftsman of the Mathematical arts, and truly (as that Highest and most renowned Prince testifies of you to the Imperial Majesty) the father of the Astronomers of this age and the sole restorer of this most praised science**, I judge to be a singular honour and ornament to me and my children. Very pleasant, too — so kind and most humane — was the signification of your goodwill in this respect: that you judge the slight and thin act of respect toward you of this University [Rostock], shown to you on your entering Rostock (which could not without crime be omitted), not unworthy of mention in your letter, and [say it] befell you not unwelcome nor unpleasant; you show [the saying] that *"the good know how to be grateful even for small things."* But writing to learned and renowned men — since all things of friends are common — I have especially thought that friends' friends ought to be shared; and therefore I judged I should signify [to them] the present state of my most excellent friend, with the desire of knowing which I did not doubt they were held — especially since I understood you had given me, in person, a copy of that most learned letter, accurately elaborated by your sublime genius (**to a certain Midas, rather hostile to these studies**), for this very reason: that I might share it with several other friends. Wherefore I imparted it to be read not only to **Jacob Monau**, but to **Paul Schede Melissus**, the Prince of the Poets of our age, and to **Johann Posthius**, master of both Apollonian arts [poetry and medicine], and to **Abraham Ortelius the Geographer — whom this past June snatched from the earth** — and to some others less famous, who with grateful mind and voice in turn proclaimed my service. And to the most noble Hero **Henrik Rantzau**, excelling in wisdom and virtue, I give congratulation on this munificence: that to his other most ample praises he added this too, that he gave hospitality, to you departing from your fatherland — **an Atlas sustaining, by Herculean labours, the axis fitted with burning stars** — whose memory Urania, grateful, will cherish to all posterity, and will celebrate, propagated longer than any Pyramids or Obelisks. Which Urania —

*who first deigned to move royal minds,*
*[those] touching the summits of things nearest to Heaven* —

now also bends the mind of the most invincible Emperor **Rudolf**, that he invites to himself the father of the Astronomers of this age and the sole restorer of this most praised science — **disdained in [his] fatherland by certain Centaurs and Midases** — and desires that this royal and celestial wisdom be cultivated by his imperial patronage and expense, the ethereal art preserved in that lofty citadel, and spread far and wide through his Empire: **just as Urania moved the mind of the first Caesar, Julius** — striving to restore the then-confused reckoning of the Roman Year — **that he brought over to himself at Rome Sosigenes the Mathematician** (held less honourably by some in the kingdom of Egypt), that he might propagate that sublime and celestial doctrine of the stars in the lofty theatre of the highest Emperor of the lands, with greater glory to himself and fruit to the Commonwealth. **Set out, therefore, with God as leader and Christ as guide, whither the most august Emperor and your Tyche [Fortune] call you**; and enjoy happily — to the Commonwealth's profit — the most pleasant company and familiarity of the most excellent and best man Lord Doctor **Thaddaeus Hagecius**, the companion of your studies and most closely-joined friend (with whom, thirty years ago at Vienna, a bond also passed for me); and happily weave to the end the works elaborated by the vigils and cares of so many years. Nor will I now delay you, girded for the journey, with a longer letter, but pray God with ardent vows that he keep you safe and flourishing in your best studies, and govern the course of this journey and of your whole life, to God's glory and the Commonwealth's salvation. The poems written in your honour for Denmark, and [those] of Germany rejoicing over such a guest, and [those] of our **Brasch** congratulating Rudolf Caesar and you on your coming — but especially the **Epigram which you prefixed to the restitution of the Stars, inscribed to Duke Ulrich** — I read with the greatest pleasure; and I desire with my whole heart that they be set forth in print together, and circulate in the hands of the learned.

Fare well and happily.
At Rostock, on the Nones of October [7 October], the year 1598.
Reverently revering Your Magnificence,
David Chytraeus.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **David Chytraeus** (1530–1600), the great Rostock theologian and historian — Tycho's friend, and author of the *annual history / Saxonia* into which Tycho wished his migration-narrative inserted (cf. brahe-t_16010415002, brahe-t_16000920002, brahe-t_16000916002). This is one of **Chytraeus's last letters to Tycho** (he died in 1600). The MSS are copies at Prague and in Langebek's *Diplomatarium*.
- **Significance — a humanist congratulation on the imperial call (autumn 1598).** Written as Tycho is "girded for the journey" to Bohemia. It is a showpiece of learned encomium, with two load-bearing points:
 1. **The testimonial quoted.** Chytraeus twice calls Tycho **"the father of the Astronomers of this age and the sole restorer of this most praised science,"** explicitly *"as that Highest and most renowned Prince testifies of you to the Imperial Majesty"* — i.e. quoting **Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg's commendation of Tycho to Rudolf II** (the letter translated at brahe-t_15980816001). A direct cross-reference confirming how Ulrich's praise circulated.
 2. **The Sosigenes/Julius Caesar parallel (the centrepiece).** Just as **Julius Caesar**, reforming the confused Roman calendar, **brought Sosigenes the Alexandrian mathematician** (slighted in Egypt) to Rome, so **Rudolf II** now invites Tycho — "disdained in his fatherland by certain Centaurs and Midases" — to cultivate astronomy under imperial patronage. The flattering analogy (Tycho: Rudolf:: Sosigenes: Caesar) places Tycho's transplantation in the grandest historical frame.
- **The "anti-Midas" letter and its circulation.** Chytraeus reports sharing a polemical letter of Tycho's *"to a certain Midas, rather hostile to these studies"* (a Danish/learned detractor — "Midas" with ass's ears, the type of the philistine) with a roster of the learned: **Jacob Monau; Paul Schede Melissus** ("Prince of the Poets"); **Johann Posthius** (poet-physician, "master of both Apollonian arts"); and **Abraham Ortelius the geographer — "snatched from the earth this past June" (Ortelius d. 28 June 1598)**, a precise dating. He also praises **Henrik Rantzau** for hosting "an Atlas sustaining the starry axis" (Tycho at Wandsbek).
- **Greek and verse.**
 - *Ὅσσον ἔαρ χειμῶνος, ὅσον μᾶλον Βραβύλοιο ἅδιον* — **Theocritus, *Idylls* V.92–93** ("as spring is sweeter than winter, the apple than the sloe"); kept verbatim, translated.
 - *τούς τε ἀγαμοὺς … χάριν* — a Greek maxim, "the good know how to be grateful even for small things" (the *ἀγαμούς*/*ἀγαθούς* reading uncertain; rendered by sense, flagged).
 - *τύχη* — **"Tyche/Fortune," a pun on Tycho's name** ("whither the Emperor and your *Tyche* call you").
 - The hexameter couplet *"Regales animos primum dignata movere…"* (Urania moving royal minds) is kept as verse.
- **The Duke-Ulrich epigram.** Chytraeus singles out the **epigram Tycho prefixed to the "restitution of the Stars," inscribed to Duke Ulrich** (cf. brahe-t_15980914002, the star-catalogue presented to Ulrich) — and **Brasch's** congratulatory poems to Rudolf and Tycho — wishing them all printed together.
- **Persons named.** David Chytraeus (sender); **Duke Ulrich** (the "Prince" who testified); **Jacob Monau**, **Paul Melissus**, **Johann Posthius**, **Abraham Ortelius** (d. June 1598); **Henrik Rantzau**; **Rudolf II**; **Sosigenes** and **Julius Caesar**; **Tadeáš Hájek (Hagecius)**; **Martin Brasch**.
- **Calendar / place.** *Rhodopoli Nonis Octobris Anno 1598* — *Rhodopolis* ("City of Roses") = the learned name for **Rostock**; *Nones of October* = **7 October**. Lutheran Rostock kept the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar. Header agrees with the label.

text.original:
SERENISSIMO PRINCIPI AC DOMINO D. FERDINANDO DE MEDICES, MAGNO DUCI HETRURIÆ, FLORENTIÆ, SENARUM, PISARUM, DOMINO MEO CLEMENTISSIMO.

SERENISSIME et Illustrissime Princeps, Domine Clementissime. Cum hîc Adolescens genere Nobilis et liberalibus disciplinis præclare imbutus, qui mihi per aliquot Annos fuit domesticus, in Italiam nunc cogitet, sitque Tuæ Serenitati ab Amplissimo et Nobilissimo Domino HENRICO RANZOVIO Produce Cimbrico Affini meo honorando, diligenter commendatus, non intermittendum duxi, quin et ego, licet Serenitati Tuæ ignotus, idem submisse præstarem, præsertim ex quo eius mores, integritas et docile ingenium mihi ex diutina consuetudine quam optime perspecta sint. Quocirca Serenitatem Tuam submisse rogatam habeo, ut eum vel meo etiam nomine, sibi de meliori (ut aiunt) nota commendatum habeat. Tradidi illi duos libros, simul ut commodius veherentur colligatos, Serenitati Tuæ ex me submisse offerendos: Quorum contenta Tituli et Præfationes expedient: Quos ut clementissimo vultu suscipere, meque suo favore et benevolentia complecti non dedignetur, qua possum submissione oro. Plura de me meisque studijs, atque ad Cæsaream Maiestatem e Dania Patria mea migratione ab eodem harum exhibitore (si cognoscere non degravetur) clementissime percipiet. Quocirca Serenitatem Tuam gravissimis Reipub. gubernandæ negocijs occupatam ulterius remorari desino. Deus Optimus maximus eam quam diutissime conservet florentem et incolumem.

Dabantur Dresdæ Misniæ die 8 Novembris Anni 1598.
Serenitati Tuæ
Submisse addictiss.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria scripsi.
text.english:
**To the Most Serene Prince and Lord, Lord Ferdinando de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, of Florence, of Siena, of Pisa, my most clement Lord.**

Most Serene and Most Illustrious Prince, most clement Lord. Since here a youth — noble by birth and excellently imbued with the liberal disciplines, who was my domestic for some years — now thinks of [going] into Italy, and has been diligently commended to Your Serenity by the most ample and most noble Master Heinrich Rantzau, Cimbrian Viceroy, my honoured kinsman, I judged it ought not to be omitted that I too — though unknown to Your Serenity — should humbly do the same, especially since his character, integrity, and docile talent have been most thoroughly known to me from long acquaintance. Wherefore I have humbly asked Your Serenity to hold him commended, in my name also, "with the better mark" (as they say). I have handed him two books — bound together, that they might be the more conveniently carried — to be humbly offered to Your Serenity from me, the contents of which the titles and prefaces will make plain; which [books] I beg, with what submission I can, that you not disdain to receive with most clement countenance, and to embrace me with your favour and benevolence. More about me and my studies, and about my migration from Denmark, my homeland, to the Imperial Majesty, you will most clemently learn from the same bearer of this letter (if you do not find it burdensome to learn it). Wherefore I cease to delay Your Serenity, occupied with the most weighty affairs of governing the commonwealth, any further. May God Best and Greatest preserve Your Serenity, flourishing and unharmed, as long as possible.

Given at Dresden in Meissen, the 8th day of November, in the year 1598.
Most humbly devoted to Your Serenity,
Tycho Brahe,
I wrote with my own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Ferdinando I de' Medici** (1549–1609), **Grand Duke of Tuscany** (Florence, Siena, Pisa). A letter of recommendation and book-gift. The witness's provenance is notable: the autograph descended into the **Galileo / Accademia del Cimento papers** at the Biblioteca Nazionale in Florence (Gal. 286).
- **The young man recommended.** "A youth, noble by birth … my domestic for some years," now going to **Italy**, already commended by **Heinrich Rantzau** (the Holstein humanist and Danish *Statholder*, here *Produx Cimbricus* = "Cimbrian Viceroy/Pro-duke," i.e. royal governor of the Cimbrian/Jutland–Holstein lands; Tycho's *affinis*). *Identification flagged*: most plausibly **Frans Tengnagel** (who travelled to Italy in this period and returned by early 1600 — cf. brahe-t_16000308002/…0309002), though Tycho does not name him.
- **The book-gift.** *duos libros … colligatos* = **two of Tycho's printed works**, bound together for carriage, offered to the Grand Duke (their contents to be known from the *titles and prefaces*) — almost certainly the recently issued *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica* (1598) and/or *Epistolae astronomicae* (1596) / *Progymnasmata*. *Identification flagged* (the two are not titled).
- ***de meliori nota*** — "with the better mark," i.e. in the most favourable terms (the same idiom as in brahe-t_15980530001).
- **Calendar.** *Dresdae Misniae die 8 Novembris 1598* = **8 November 1598**, **Dresden in Meissen** (Lutheran Saxony) = **Old Style**. Header agrees with the label. (Tycho was wintering in Saxony — Dresden/Wittenberg — before his move to Bohemia.)

text.original:
IOH. GEORG GŒDELMANN AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

MAGNIFICE Domine TYCHO. Gunstiger Herr, vnndt vornehmer freundt, Ich habe alhier zu Prag mit freudenn vernommen, daß Ihr, Gottlob, frisch vnndt gesundt zu Dreßdenn ankommen, vnndt weil Ihr daneben zu wissen begeret, ob Ihr euch zu der Kay. Maytt. begebenn, oder euch in der nehe, wegen der eingefallenen sterbens leufft, derowegen die Kay. Maytt. von Prag hinweg getzogenn, aufhaltenn sollet, so kann ich euch darauf nicht bergenn, daß obwoll die Kay. Maytt. ein großes verlangenn (alß die in Astronomischen Sachen, gleich wie ihr Großvater CAROLUS V hoch auch erfahrenn) nach dem Herrn, alß nach dem vornemsten Mathematico totius Mundi, dessen Nomen auch vnsterblichen sein wirdt, hatt, auch den Herrn nit weit vonn sich habenn will, dieweil aber ihr Maytt. wegen der vergifften Seuchenn, welche fast alle örter im Königreich Böheim inficiret, bey sich noch nicht entschlossen, wo sie Ihr Hofflager anstellenn wollenn, alß wirdt der Herr biß auff Ihr Maytt. endtliche weitere anordnung, zu Dreßden, oder Wittemberg, mitlerweil sich auffhaltenn. Thue hiemit vnß Göttlicher Almacht beuehlenn.

Geben Prag, 12. Novembris. Anno 98.
Deß Herrn dienstvilliger
JOHAN GEORG GÖDELMAN. D.
text.english:
**Johann Georg Gödelmann to Tycho Brahe.**

Magnificent Master Tycho, favourable Sir and distinguished friend. I have learned here at Prague, with joy, that you have, praise God, arrived fresh and well at Dresden. And since you besides desire to know whether you should betake yourself to His Imperial Majesty, or hold yourself in the vicinity — on account of the outbreak of mortality [plague], for the sake of which His Imperial Majesty has withdrawn from Prague — I cannot, thereupon, conceal from you that, although His Imperial Majesty has a great longing (being, just like his grandfather Charles V, also highly versed in astronomical matters) for you, as for the foremost Mathematician *of the whole world*, whose *name* too will be immortal, and does not wish to have you far from himself: nevertheless, since His Majesty — on account of the venomous pestilence which has infected almost all places in the Kingdom of Bohemia — has not yet resolved with himself where he will set up his court-residence [*Hoflager*], the Sir [you] should, until His Majesty's final further arrangement, meanwhile stay at Dresden or Wittenberg. I herewith commend us to God's Almighty [protection].

Given at Prague, the 12th of November, in the year [15]98.
Your service-ready,
Johann Georg Gödelmann, D[octor].

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Johann Georg Gödelmann** (1559–1611), jurist, Saxon privy councillor and diplomat (and author of a celebrated treatise on witchcraft); here writing from Prague as a court-contact, advising Tycho on the timing of his approach to the Emperor.
- **Occasion.** Tycho, having reached **Dresden** on his way south in the autumn of 1598, asked whether to proceed to the Emperor or wait. Gödelmann reports that **plague** (*sterbens leufft* / *vergiffte Seuche*) had driven **Rudolf II** from Prague and left the court without a fixed seat; he advises Tycho to **stay at Dresden or Wittenberg** until the Emperor settles his *Hoflager* (court-residence). (Tycho did winter at Wittenberg — cf. brahe-t_15990110001, …0111001, dated there Jan. 1599 — before reaching Bohemia in 1599.)
- ***ihr Großvater Carolus V*** — "his grandfather Charles V": genealogically **correct**, not a slip — Rudolf II's mother was **Maria of Austria**, daughter of Emperor **Charles V**, so Charles was Rudolf's maternal grandfather. Gödelmann flatters the Emperor's astronomical bent as inherited.
- **Code-switching (kept and italicised).** Latin technical/honorific nouns embedded in the German: *Mathematico totius Mundi* ("Mathematician of the whole world"), *Nomen* ("name"), *inficiret* ("infected"). Rendered into English but flagged as the writer's own Latin within the German. Princely titulature (*Kay. Maytt.*, *Ihr Hofflager*) preserved.
- **Calendar.** *Geben Prag, 12. Novembris. Anno 98* = **12 November 1598**; Prague (imperial) = **New Style**. Header agrees with the label.
- **Correction.** Two single-word transcription corrections against Dreyer, TBOO VIII p.118: 'uber'→'aber' and 'sic'→'sie'. Neither affected the published English, which already carried the correct sense.

Our published German the transcribed original reads 'uber' where Dreyer prints 'aber' (the adversative conjunction 'however/nevertheless'); a genuine word substitution against the edition of record. The English translation happens to render the correct sense ('nevertheless, since His Majesty...'), so the corruption did not propagate, but the transcribed original itself departs from Dreyer.
