text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET EXCELLENTISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO IOHANNI ANTONIO MAGINO MATHEMATUM IN CELEBRI BONONIENSIUM GYMNASIO PROFESSORI EXIMIO ET AMICO SUO INPRIMIS DILECTO.

Clarissime et Excellentissime Vir.

CUM plures iam elapsi sint anni, atque uti existimo ad minimum quinque, ex quo quidam inter meos domesticos studiosos eruditum tuum librum quem Tabulam Tetragonicam vocas, mihique dedicasti, Hafnia e nundinis Francofurtensibus istuc per bibliopolam nostratem allatum, Uraniburgum secum attulerit, idque uno vel altero anno postquam a te evulgatus esset (neque enim ullum a teipso accepi exemplar, sive nullum miseris, sive quod prae nimia viarum intercapedine interciderit) ego vero postquam illud exemplum, quod studiosus meus asportavit, inspexissem et diligentius perlustrassem, mihi admodum placuit, utut nonnulla in eo sint, in quibus tibiipsi forte non satis pro hac prima conceptione satisfeceris, nec in magna numerorum copia processus sit sufficienter expeditus, praeterquam quod id de quo eius usum pro me praecipue infers, circa aequationum nimirum angulos in Planetis facilius, quam per Tangentium et Secantium Tabulas inde colligendos, mihi qua ratione id fieri posset, necdum perspectum, siquidem angulos illos per solas numerorum προσθαφαιρέσεις, nempe additionem et subtractionem absque omni multiplicatione aut divisione minimo negocio investigare liceat; quam πραγματείαν non saltem in omni genere triangulorum sphaericorum, sed et planorum magno Astronomici calculi compendio locum mereri nobis constat; laude nihilominus dignissimum censui et etiamnum censeo hunc tuum laborem in componenda illa tabula cum suo usu, qui sane late patet et multiplex esse potest. Quod autem non antea tibi de his rescripserim, factum est, quod diu a teipso expectarem exemplar aliquod mihi destinatum, quod alicubi in itinere haerere putavi, ut rescribendo gratus vicissim esse possem, partim quod certum et fidelem internuncium non repererim, qui tibi tuto quippiam a me perferret.

Quae vero et tuo et aliorum nomine in epistola illic praefixa rogas, videlicet ut Astronomiae instaurationem, quam diu multumque molior, mature absolvam et publici iuris faciam, id equidem ut secundum tua et multorum vota praestarem, nihil magis ipsemet in votis habui: sed obstiterunt hactenus quaedam, partim proprie ad artem redintegrandam stabiliendamque facientia, partim ex huius inferioris et terrestris mundi tumultuaria scena prodeuntia, et politicis fatis obnoxia.

Prius illud tarditas circuituum superiorum Planetarum, praesertim ♄i causatur, quo minus sufficientes acronychias observationes per totum circuli ambitum citius adipisci concederetur; neque enim tres sufficiunt ad eorum Apogaea et Eccentricitates explicandas, uti imitatione PTOLEMÆI et COPERNICI hactenus frustra creditum est, inaequalitate adhuc alia, quam eorum ferunt hypotheses, coincidente, et Eccentricitate illa, quae Aequanti tribuitur, non retinente eandem ad alteram proportionem, quam illi assumunt et pro cognito praesupponunt potius quam demonstrant; aliter enim ea se habet et in singulis variat. Taceo nunc, quantum difficultatis ingerant, quantumque temporis requirant reliqui duo inferiores Planetae, inprimis vero vagabundus et varijs ambagibus implicitus ☿, rarissimeque apparens, cum alias circa horizontem, ubi hi duo observandi ut plurimum veniunt, pauca admodum concedatur aëris satis pura serenitas, ob vapores istic obvolantes, decliviore etiam Sphaera aliquid obstaculi suggerente. Quin et ☾, utut singulis mensibus recurrat, non parum suis anfractuosis et pluribus, quam hactenus creditum est, inaequalitatibus obnoxia nos torsit, donec non ex tribus solummodo Eclipsibus haud sufficientibus, uti antecessores, eius motiones scrutaremur, sed sexies ternis aut pluribus eosdem eruere, ut alia praetereantur, necesse habuerimus.

Alterum obstaculum, quod politicum dixi, quodque per se ingratum, meam intentionem studiumque in hac arte redintegranda alias indefessum multifariam exagitavit turbavitque inde a defuncto laudatissimae memoriae Rege Danorum FRIDERICO Domino et fautore meo clementissimo, qui me meaque studia, quoad vixit, clementer et benigne iuvit et promovit: in interregno octennali frigidius ijs, quae requirebantur, prospectis, donec tandem creato hoc novo Rege adolescente, qui, sive ob aetatem iuniorem, sive dissuadentibus, aut minus adhortantibus dynastis, utut alias heroico sit animo et ingenio acri praeditus, ac iudicio pro hac aetate plus quam credi posset valens, huius sublimis scientiae in suo regno promotioni attendere non duxit operaepretium, sed per Cancellarium literis a me, quod subsecuturum esset, discrete praemonitum, mihi responderi permiserit, sibi non esse integrum in Astronomici exercitij Instrumentorumque eo pertinentium sustentationem quippiam impendere, subtractis etiam successive, statim ac coronatus est, sumptibus ab optimo Parente et Regni consiliarijs mihi concessis et eo deputatis, non curantibus ijs qui Regi sunt ab intimis, Senatus Consultum mox ab obitu FRIDERICI Regis mihi in membrana impertitum, et a Primario eorum qui nunc Curiae Magister est, suapte manu subscriptum et sigillo munitum, sic quod alias insolitum est, exauthorari fecit. Unde factum est, supervenientibus etiam alijs molestationibus, ut priusquam Astronomiae, cuius tam diu tamque impense reaedificationem in Patria molitus sum, ruinam ibidem indecoram hisce oculis spectarem, multo potius maluerim ipsam Patriam cum omnibus in ea consanguineis et amicis derelinquere atque in Germaniam me cum Coniuge et liberis totaque mea familia, assumpto mecum ingenti illo apparatu Astronomico, concedere, quod ante sesquialterum annum, si forte adhuc inscius es, praesenti et forti animo a me factum est. Substiti tamen interea cum meis iuxta fines Daniae et Germaniae in arce quadam Ranzoviana prope Hamburgum sita, quo nostratibus rem rectius dispicienda Patriae, cui multum debemus, adhuc studens, satis temporis relinquerem, atque eo forem excusabilior, si alio me prorsus converterem. Verum cum id nihilominus incassum fieret, et Augustissimus Romanorum Imperator RUDOLPHUS resciscens me e Dania emigrasse atque ad Holsatiae australiorem oram habitare, me pro ea qua est erga Mathematicas artes, quas ipsemet etiam laudabiliter exercet, Clementissimo favore praeditus, ad se in Bohemiam evocari mandavit, spe facta quod non frustra venturus essem. Sum itaque iam nunc in itinere, et hic Dresdae aliquantisper cunctor, donec missis in aulam Caesaris literis edocear, ubi et quando eius Maiestas adeunda sit, hoc praesertim tempore, cum ob luem epidemicam passim istic grassantem turbata sint omnia, et Caesar Praga in alium salubriorem locum, ubi solitarie agit, discesserit. Responsum est Caesarem accessum meum libenter intellexisse; sed cum ipsemet in Bohemia vix locum inveniat, ubi a periculo contagij increbrescentis tutus sit, suadere et cupere, ut aliquamdiu hîc aut alibi in vicinia me contineam, donec remiserint istic morbi populariter grassantes; interea velle se de commoda et opportuna sede cogitare atque prospicere, ubi me meaque collocet. Huic clementissimo Caesaris responso, uti par est, acquiescens, constitui, volente supremo Numine, in vicinam aliquam superioris Saxoniae vel Misniae Academiam hisce diebus me conferre, ut aliqua in Progymnasmatis meis alijsque operibus typographico labore necdum plane ob eas, quae mihi in Patria evenerunt, conturbationes absoluta, ibi compleri procurem, donec pacatiore et saniore in Bohemia restituta degendi commoditate a Caesare eo accedere iubear. Quod tibi indicandum duxi, optime MAGINE, ut de statu mearum rerum conscius esses, utque simul ex iam commemoratis aliquatenus intelligeres, quae et quanta Astronomiae, quam intendo, instaurationem remorata sint. Plura et particulariora exhibitor harum FRANCISCUS TIGNAGLIUS nomine tibi seorsim aperiet. Est ille adolescens genere nobilis, natione Germanus, qui mihi usque in tertium annum fuit domesticus, meaeque e Dania migrationis comes, estque artibus liberalibus egregie imbutus, et Mathematicis etiam, interea dum mecum fuit, operam non contemnendam navavit, observationibus simul assuefactus et numerorum tractationi, alias per se apprime ingeniosus et disciplinis quibusvis capessendis idoneus, moribus insuper integris et virtute praeditus, ideoque ob tam praeclaras animi dotes mihi semper carissimus fuit, et filij loco habitus. Hunc igitur de meliori, uti dicunt, nota tibi commendatum habeas, te etiam atque etiam rogo, quicquid in illum contuleris officij et beneficii, eum insuper apud Illustres et praestantes istic viros commendatione tua promovendo, id totum non tam ipsi quam mihi te praestitisse scias, inveniesque me ad compensandum perpetuo pro virili quam paratissimum. Tradidi illi librum quendam tibi ex me donandum, qui duos in se commodioris vectionis causa complectitur: prior Mechanicam Astronomiae artem, prout a nobis in usu hactenus fuit, exhibet: posterior stellas fixas millenas accuratissime restitutas labore diutino atque ingenti, impendioque haud mediocri. Hoc habe librarium vicissim munus pro libro mihi prius inscripto, donec plura ex meis quae desideras chalcographico labore penitus absoluta fuerint. Sunt illi quaedam etiam alia ad manus, quatenus in hac mea peregrinatione in promptu erant, quae simul monstrabit, et de pluribus me meaque studia concernentibus te edocebit. Spero me ubi commodius et durabilius ocium in Germania adeptus fuero, tuis et aliorum votis in Astronomiae illustratione et locupletatione consumanda uberius satisfacturum.

Inserui priori libro circa calcem epistolas tuas ad me datas, cum spacium pro ijs et Curtianis vacaret, idque certis de causis, praesertim ut alios ad haec studia amanda excolendaque excitarem: et licet te inconsulto hoc fecerim, tamen haud ingratum fore confido, siquidem tibi, ut existimo, id non sit inhonorificum. Observationes quas polliceris in altera Epistola, si quas interea peregistis, obtinere averem. Sin vero id hactenus neglectum est, ut in posterum sedulo resarciatur et praestetur, rogo; cedet id in artis nostrae, veluti spero, emolumentum, eritque et tibi et alijs, qui hoc factitarint, laudabile. Instrumenta si conficere libuerit, liber is formam et rationem luculenter suppeditabit.

Plura nunc non addo, forsan in iam exaratis epistolae metas excessi, quod tamen libenter amicitiae nostrae et studiorum communium causa admisi, locis etiam quibus disiungimur crebras interlocutiones non admittentibus, ideoque, ubi fieri potest, non abbreviandis. Sique plura hîc forte omissa scire desideras, is, quem tibi nunc enixe commendavi adolescens, cum rerum mearum haud sit ignarus, plura expediet, atque votis tuis hac in parte, uti mihi polliceor, satisfaciet. Eum itaque iterum atque iterum tibi acceptum habe, et ad meliora quaeque, quantum in te est, istic iuva et promove, quo aliquando, favente Numine, ad me reversus, tuam in se benevolentiam merito praedicare possit, idque erit mihi longe gratissimum.

Vale.
Dabantur Dresdae Misniae, ubi est aula Electorum Saxoniae, Novembris 28 stilo veteri. Anno etc. 1598.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, pp. 124–125; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Si tres Eclipses huius anni istic a te vel quopiam alio observatae sunt, fac me eius denotationis participem pro meridianorum differentia hinc elicienda. Meis instrumentis sic designatae sunt, ut momenta observata et ad medium earundem reducta, ita se habuerint. A° 1598. Feb. d. 20. Eclipsis [Lunae] medium 17h 58' P.M. Vandesburgi prope Hamburgum, defecerunt II digiti de [Luna]. Martij d. 6. Eclipsis ☉is medium 11h 5' A.. N. Uraniburgi in Dania. Magnitudo Eclipsationis ibidem apparuit a parte superiori intra 9 et 10 digitos. Augusti d. 16. Eclipsis [Lunae] medium 7h 42' P.M. Vandesburgi. Haec omnia tempora recte consentiunt cum nostra restitutione. Quantum vero a calculo tam Alphonsino quam Coperniceo discrepent, tute vide. Longitudinem Vandesburgi praesuppono 33° 35'. Uraniburgi 36° 45' atque eandem proxime Venetiarum.

Referet etiam idem adolescens quædam ad te meo nomine secreto, in
quibus si mihi tu operam tuam præstiteris, aut per alium istic hominem idoneum,
rem longe acceptissimam præstiteris, et ubi de tua voluntate mihi per eundem
innotuerit, pluribus instruam, quomodo res peragenda erit, et formam præscribam.
Habeo certas causas cur potius in Italia quam Germania id fieri averem. Multum
mea interest, ut hoc perficiatur, quod et levi negocio exequi licebit; impensas
lubens solvam inveniarque vicissim gratus. Habet exhibitor harum quædam secum
eius negocij documenta, quæ tibi clam monstrare et exponere poterit.

Tuæ Excellentiæ
Studiosissimus
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu
propria scripsi.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and excellent man, Lord Giovanni Antonio Magini, eminent Professor of Mathematics in the celebrated Gymnasium of Bologna, and his especially beloved friend.**

Most renowned and excellent Man.

Since several years have now elapsed — at the least five, as I reckon — from when one of my household students brought to Uraniborg **your erudite book, which you call the *Tabula Tetragonica*, and dedicated to me** (carried from Copenhagen, from the Frankfurt fair, thither by a bookseller of ours), and that one or two years after it had been published by you — for I received no copy from you yourself, whether you sent none, or whether it perished through the over-great stretch of the roads — I, when I had inspected and more diligently perused that copy which my student carried off, found it much to my liking; although there are some things in it in which you perhaps did not fully satisfy yourself, for this first conception, and the process is not sufficiently expedited in a great supply of numbers. Besides, that for which you chiefly infer its use for me — namely, the deriving thence of the angles of the equations in the Planets more easily than through Tables of Tangents and Secants — I have not yet seen by what method that could be done, **since those angles may be investigated, with least trouble, by the sole prosthaphaereses [προσθαφαιρέσεις] of numbers — namely addition and subtraction, without any multiplication or division**; which method [πραγματεία] we are sure merits a place, not only in every kind of spherical triangles, but of plane ones too, with great compendium of astronomical calculation. Nonetheless I judged, and still judge, this labour of yours, in composing that table, with its use (which is indeed broadly open and can be manifold), most worthy of praise. That I did not write back to you about these before, came about because I long expected from you yourself some copy destined for me (which I thought stuck somewhere on the road), that I might be grateful in return by writing back; partly because I did not find a sure and faithful messenger to carry anything from me to you safely.

**As to what you ask, both in your own name and others', in the epistle prefixed there — namely, that I mature and make public the restoration of Astronomy which I long and much labour at — I myself wished nothing more than to perform this, according to your wishes and those of many; but certain things have hitherto stood in the way** — partly things properly making to the restoring and establishing of the art, partly things proceeding from the tumultuous scene of this lower and earthly world, and subject to political fates.

The first [obstacle] is caused by **the slowness of the circuits of the superior Planets, especially Saturn [♄]**, whereby less leave is granted of getting sufficient acronychal [opposition] observations through the whole compass of the circle sooner; **for three do not suffice to explicate their Apogees and Eccentricities** (as has hitherto been vainly believed, in imitation of Ptolemy and Copernicus) — another inequality, than their hypotheses bear, coinciding, and that Eccentricity which is assigned to the Equant not retaining the same proportion to the other, which they assume and presuppose as known, rather than demonstrate; for it is otherwise, and varies in each [case]. I am silent now how much difficulty they introduce, and how much time they require, the remaining two inferior Planets — especially **the wandering Mercury [☿], implicated in various windings, and most rarely appearing** — since otherwise, around the horizon (where these two for the most part come to be observed), very little sufficiently pure clear air is granted, on account of the vapours flying about there, the more declining Sphere also offering some obstacle. Nay, **the Moon [☾] too, though it recurs each month, has tortured us not a little by its tortuous inequalities — more than has hitherto been believed — until we had to investigate its motions not from only three insufficient Eclipses (like our predecessors), but to draw the same out from six-times-three [18] or more** (to pass over other things).

**The other obstacle, which I called political, and which is in itself ungrateful, variously agitated and disturbed my intention and study in restoring this art (otherwise untiring) ever since the death of the King of the Danes, Frederick, of most praised memory, my most clement Lord and patron** — who, while he lived, clemently and benignly helped and promoted me and my studies. **In the eight-year interregnum [regency], the things that were required were more coldly provided** — until at last, this new King, a youth, being created [crowned], who (whether on account of his younger age, or with dynasts dissuading or less encouraging — though otherwise he be of heroic mind, and endowed with a sharp wit, and strong in judgement, for this age, more than could be believed) **did not think it worthwhile to attend to the promotion of this sublime science in his realm**; but, through the Chancellor (I having discreetly forewarned by letter what would follow), permitted me to be answered **that it was not in his power to spend anything on the maintenance of the Astronomical exercise and of the instruments pertaining to it** — the costs granted me, and assigned thereto, by the best Parent [Frederick] and the Realm's councillors being also successively withdrawn, as soon as he was crowned (those who are the King's intimates not caring); and **the Senate-decree given me on parchment immediately after King Frederick's death — subscribed in the hand of the chief of them (who is now Court-Master), and secured with a seal — he caused to be annulled** (a thing otherwise unusual). Whence it came about — other molestations supervening too — that, **before I should behold with these eyes the unseemly ruin, in that same place, of the Astronomy whose rebuilding I had so long and so intensely laboured at in my fatherland, I much preferred to abandon the fatherland itself, with all my blood-kin and friends in it, and to withdraw into Germany with my wife and children and whole household, taking that huge Astronomical apparatus with me** — which (if perhaps you are still unaware) was done by me a year and a half ago, with present and brave mind. Yet I stopped meanwhile, with my [household], **near the borders of Denmark and Germany, in a certain Rantzau castle situated near Hamburg**, to leave my countrymen, while still studying the fatherland's matter (to which I owe much), time enough to consider it more rightly, and to be the more excusable if I should turn entirely elsewhere. But since this nonetheless came to nothing, and **the most august Roman Emperor Rudolf, learning that I had emigrated from Denmark and dwelt on Holstein's southern shore, endowed (as he is) with most clement favour toward the Mathematical arts (which he himself too laudably practises), commanded me to be called to him into Bohemia**, with hope given that I should not come in vain. So **I am now on the journey, and linger a while here at Dresden**, until — letters being sent to the Emperor's court — I am informed where and when His Majesty is to be approached; especially at this time, when on account of the epidemic plague raging there everywhere all things are disturbed, and the Emperor has withdrawn from Prague into another, healthier place, where he lives solitarily. The answer was that the Emperor gladly heard of my coming; but since he himself scarcely finds a place in Bohemia where he is safe from the danger of the increasing contagion, [he] advises and wishes that I keep myself a while here, or elsewhere in the neighbourhood, until the diseases raging popularly there abate; meanwhile he will think of, and provide, a convenient and opportune seat where to place me and my [things]. Acquiescing, as is fitting, in this most clement response of the Emperor's, I have resolved, the supreme Godhead willing, **to betake myself these days to some nearby Academy of upper Saxony or Meissen, that I may there have certain things in my *Progymnasmata* and other works — not yet quite finished in the printing-labour, on account of the disturbances that befell me in the fatherland — completed**, until I am ordered by the Emperor to go thither, when a more peaceful and healthful convenience of living is restored in Bohemia. Which I judged should be indicated to you, excellent Magini, that you might be aware of the state of my affairs, and at the same time understand somewhat, from what has now been recounted, what and how great [things] have delayed the restoration of Astronomy which I intend. **More, and more particular [things], the bearer of these, Franz Tengnagel by name, will open to you separately.** He is a youth noble by birth, German by nation, who was my household-member up to the third year, and the companion of my migration from Denmark; and he is excellently imbued with the liberal arts, and in Mathematics too (while he was with me) bestowed no contemptible labour — habituated at once to observations and to the handling of numbers — otherwise of himself most ingenious, and apt for grasping any disciplines, endowed besides with integral morals and virtue; and so, for such distinguished gifts of mind, he was always most dear to me, and held in a son's place. **Him, then, hold commended to you "from the better mark," as they say**; I ask you again and again [that], whatever of office and benefit you confer on him — promoting him besides, by your commendation, among the Illustrious and distinguished men there — you would know you have rendered all that not so much to him as to me; and you will find me most ready perpetually, to my power, to repay it. **I have given him a certain book, to be presented to you from me, which comprises two [works] in itself for easier carriage: the first exhibits the Mechanical art of Astronomy, as it has hitherto been in use with us [the *Mechanica*]; the second, the thousand fixed stars, most accurately restored by long and huge labour, and no mediocre expense [the star-catalogue].** Have this gift of books in turn, for the book formerly dedicated to me [the *Tabula Tetragonica*], until more of mine, which you desire, shall be quite finished by the engraving-labour. He has some other things too at hand, so far as they were ready in this peregrination of mine, which he will at the same time show, and will instruct you about more things concerning me and my studies. I hope, when I have got more convenient and durable leisure in Germany, to satisfy your wishes and others' more fully, in consummating the illustration and enrichment of Astronomy.

**I inserted, near the end of the first book, your letters sent to me** — when space was free for them and for the Curtius [letters] — and that for certain reasons, especially to excite others to love and cultivate these studies; and although I did this without consulting you, yet I trust it will not be unwelcome, since (as I think) it is not dishonourable to you. The observations you promise in the second Epistle, if you have done any meanwhile, I should wish to obtain. But if it has hitherto been neglected, I ask that it be diligently made up and performed in future; it will turn to the profit of our art (as I hope), and will be praiseworthy both to you and to others who do it. If you wish to make instruments, that book [the *Mechanica*] will clearly supply the form and method.

I add no more now; perhaps in what is already written I have exceeded the bounds of a letter — which, however, I have gladly admitted for the sake of our friendship and common studies, the places too by which we are separated not admitting frequent conversations, and so [the letters] not to be abbreviated where it can be otherwise. And if you should wish to know more things perhaps here omitted, the youth whom I have now earnestly commended to you, since he is not ignorant of my affairs, will expedite more, and will satisfy your wishes in this part (as I promise myself). So have him welcome again and again, and help and promote him there, to all the better things, so far as in you lies — that one day, God favouring, returned to me, he may deservedly proclaim your benevolence toward him; and that will be far the most welcome to me.

Farewell.
Given at Dresden in Meissen, where is the court of the Electors of Saxony, the 28th of November, Old Style, the year etc. 1598.


*[Postscript:]* If three Eclipses of this year have been observed there by you or by anyone else, make me partaker of that record, for the difference of meridians to be elicited thence. By my instruments they were noted thus, so that the moments observed and reduced to the middle of the same stood as follows. In the year 1598: Feb. 20, Eclipse [of the Moon], middle 17h 58′ P.M., at Wandsbek near Hamburg; 2 digits of [the Moon] were wanting. March 6, Eclipse of the Sun ☉, middle 11h 5′ A.M., New Style, at Uraniborg in Denmark; the magnitude of the eclipse there appeared, from the upper part, between 9 and 10 digits. August 16, Eclipse [of the Moon], middle 7h 42′ P.M., at Wandsbek. All these times agree rightly with our restitution. But how much they differ from the calculation, both Alphonsine and Copernican, see for yourself. The longitude of Wandsbek I presuppose at 33° 35′; of Uraniborg 36° 45′; and that of Venice nearly the same.

The same young man will also relate to you certain things in my name, secretly, in which — if you should lend me your aid, or through some other suitable man there [in Italy] should render me a service — you will do me a thing most welcome by far; and once his willingness has become known to me through the same [messenger], I shall instruct you more fully how the matter is to be carried through, and shall prescribe the form of it. I have certain reasons why I should wish this to be done in Italy rather than in Germany. It matters much to me that this be accomplished, which can also be carried out without great trouble; I will gladly pay the expenses, and shall in turn be found grateful. The bearer of this letter has with him certain documents of that business, which he will be able to show and explain to you privately.

To Your Excellency,
Most devotedly,
TYCHO BRAHE,
I have written with my own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Giovanni Antonio Magini** at **Bologna** — this is the **first** Tycho-to-Magini letter (cf. the later brahe-t_16010220001, brahe-t_16000103002, brahe-t_16010124001).
- **Significance — the foundational Magini letter: the *Tabula Tetragonica*/prosthaphaeresis, the fullest exile narrative, the scientific obstacles, and the *Mechanica* gift.**
 - **The *Tabula Tetragonica* and prosthaphaeresis.** Tycho acknowledges Magini's **table of squares (*Tabula Tetragonica*, 1592), dedicated to him** (received late, second-hand), and judges its labour praiseworthy — but counters that the planetary-equation angles "for which you chiefly recommend it" are better got by **prosthaphaereses (addition/subtraction, no multiplication/division)** — the trigonometric product-to-sum method, "in every kind of spherical and plane triangles." (Cf. Herwart's own prosthaphaeresis, brahe-t_15990917001.)
 - **The scientific obstacles to publishing.** A candid statement of why the *Progymnasmata* is delayed: **Saturn's slow orbit** (three oppositions don't fix the apogee/eccentricity — Ptolemy/Copernicus "vainly believed"; the equant-eccentricity proportion "varies"); **Mercury's elusiveness**; and **the Moon's complex inequalities, needing "eighteen or more eclipses," not three**.
 - **★ The fullest exile narrative.** One of Tycho's most complete: **Frederick II's** patronage; the **eight-year regency's** cold neglect; **Christian IV's** refusal "that it was not in his power to spend anything," via the **Chancellor**; the **withdrawn revenues** and the **annulled parchment Senate-decree** (signed by "the chief, now Court-Master"); the choice to **leave the fatherland with wife, children, and the "huge astronomical apparatus" "a year and a half ago"**; the **Wandsbek** wait; the **imperial call** from Rudolf II; and the **Dresden interim** during the Bohemian plague (the Emperor "living solitarily," advising Tycho to wait nearby).
 - **The Saxony-academy plan.** Tycho means to go to a **upper-Saxony/Meissen academy** to finish the *Progymnasmata* printing (interrupted by the Danish troubles) — the **Wittenberg** stay that followed.
 - **★ The *Mechanica* + star-catalogue gift.** Tycho sends Magini, via **Tengnagel**, **a bound volume of two works — the *Mechanica* + the 1000-star catalogue** — "in return for" the *Tabula Tetragonica*. *(A documented Mechanica/catalogue distribution event.)* And he notes he has **printed Magini's letters in his *Epistolae*** (with the Curtius letters), "without consulting you … to excite others."
 - **The Tengnagel commendation.** A warm character-portrait of **Franz Tengnagel** — "noble by birth, German, my household-member, companion of my migration … held in a son's place" — commended to Magini and the Bolognese/Roman learned.
- **Cross-references.** The **Magini** correspondence's opening (→ brahe-t_16010220001, brahe-t_16000103002, brahe-t_16010124001); the **exile-narrative** thread (brahe-t_16000103001, brahe-t_16000103002); the **Mechanica/catalogue distribution** layer; the **prosthaphaeresis** thread (brahe-t_15990917001); the **Tengnagel-embassy** thread.
- **Persons & works named.** Magini (the *Tabula Tetragonica*); **King Frederick II** & **Christian IV**; the Danish **Chancellor** and **Court-Master**; **Rudolf II**; **Franz Tengnagel**; **Ptolemy, Copernicus**; the *Mechanica*, the star-catalogue, the *Progymnasmata*, the *Epistolae*. Places: **Dresden** (Saxon Electors' court), **Uraniborg/Denmark**, **Copenhagen**, **Frankfurt**, **Hamburg** (the Rantzau castle), **Bohemia/Prague**. Glyphs ♄ ☿ ☾ reproduced; Greek προσθαφαιρέσεις / πραγματεία reproduced.
- **Calendar.** *Dresdae Misniae … Novembris 28 **stilo veteri** Anno etc. 1598* → **28 November 1598 [Old Style]** (Tycho explicitly marks Old Style at Saxon Dresden); header and label agree.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Scientific postscript (three 1598 eclipses + the Wandsbek/Uraniborg/Venice longitudes), restored from Dreyer VIII pp.124–125 (dropped by the working transcription).
- **What it is.** The concealed core of a letter Tycho sent from Dresden (28 November 1598) to Giovanni Antonio Magini in Bologna — the surviving published text is only the purely astronomical tail (eclipse timings and longitudes). This recovered passage is the confidential errand referred to only obliquely elsewhere in the letter.
- **The messenger.** "The same young man" ("idem adolescens") is almost certainly Tycho's son-in-law and secretary Franz Tengnagel, who in November 1598 travelled to Italy as Tycho's emissary, meeting Magini in Bologna and being made a Knight of San Marco by the Doge of Venice [Christianson, *On Tycho's Island* (2000)].
- **What the secret was.** Dreyer records precisely this errand: Tycho wanted an Italian scholar to write a eulogy of him — a request Magini could not fulfil himself but two years later recommended to Bernardino Baldi, then compiling a collection of *Lives* of the mathematicians [Dreyer, *Tycho Brahe* (1890)]. Tycho in fact never appears in Baldi's completed *Lives* or *History* [Thoren, *The Lord of Uraniborg* (1990)].
- **Why Italy, not Germany.** Tycho gives a practical reason of reputational strategy — he wanted the panegyrist to be Italian rather than German, presumably to extend his fame into the humanist literary culture Baldi represented, beyond the German-speaking scholarly world where he was already well known.
- **The documents.** The "certain documents" Tengnagel carried and could show Magini "privately" were presumably materials to brief a prospective biographer — a self-fashioning dossier consistent with Tycho's documented eagerness to control his own public image during the Dresden exile.
- **Correction.** Address heading: corrected 'BONONIENSEM' to 'BONONIENSIUM' per Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia* VIII, p.120 (a corrupted accusative-singular reading restored to the printed genitive plural). No change to the English translation, which was already correct.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Read all 8 Dreyer page-images (TBOO VIII pp.119-126) and collated the full letter to Magini line by line against the published English and the transcribed original, including the disputed postscript. The postscript (eclipse data: Feb 20 17h58' PM Wandsbek 2 digits, Mar 6 11h5' AM Uraniborg 9-10 digits, Aug 16 7h42' PM Wandsbek; longitudes Wandsbek 33 deg 35', Uraniborg 36 deg 45'; plus the secret-business paragraph to be conveyed via Tengnagel) is printed on TBOO VIII pp.124-125 exactly as our transcribed original and the published English give it — the earlier hand-restoration from Dreyer is verified correct, no fabrication. Every other proper name (Frederick, Rudolf, the Chancellor/Curiae Magister, Ptolemy, Copernicus, Franciscus Tignaglius/Tengnagel), number (5 years, 8-year interregnum, 1.5 years, sexies ternis=18), date (28 November 1598 stilo veteri, Dresden), and sum checked correctly against the page images. One text error found in the dedicatory heading (Bononiensem vs Dreyer's Bononiensium) forces grade Possible under the grading rule even though it does not change what a scholar would take from the letter's content; verdict recorded as *minor* reflecting that low materiality.

**1 defect found:**
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original's address heading reads the grammatically anomalous 'BONONIENSEM' (accusative singular, does not agree with ablative 'gymnasio'); Dreyer's printed text has 'BONONIENSIUM' (genitive plural, 'of the Bolognese') — a corrupted word relative to the edition of record. Does not affect the sense of the English translation, which renders the phrase correctly either way. Dreyer prints: *MATHEMATUM IN CELEBRI BONONIENSIUM GYMNASIO PROFESSORI EXIMIO (TBOO VIII, p.120)*.

**Repaired.** Verified against the Dreyer page image, TBOO VIII p.120 (address heading of the Magini letter), read directly from the extract PDF. The heading clearly prints 'MATHEMATUM IN CELEBRI BONONIENSIUM GYMNASIO PROFESSORI EXIMIO' with genitive plural BONONIENSIUM. This is the letter's only defect and it is now resolved; no crux remains.

text.original:
POSTSCRIPTA THADDÆI HAGECIJ AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

CUM hasce ad te literas obsignassem, daturus eas tuo tabellario, misi adhuc meum puerum hodie, qui est 1. Decembr. cum hacce schedula ad D. CORRADUCIUM, quam ad te mitto, ex qua intelliges voluntatem Cæsaris. Est sigillum Dni CORRADUCIJ et manus. Multum gavisus sum, me tandem ante hunc meum abitum hoc responsum et resolutionem Cæsaris accepisse. Hisce quod addam amplius non est necesse.

EXEMPLUM LITERARUM DOMINI D. THADEI AD AMPLISSIMUM PROCANCELLARIUM IMPERIJ
RUDOLPHUM
CORRADUCIUM.Magce D. et Patrone observandiss. Hucusque noster Dominus
TYCHO omnia egit ex consilio tuæ Magtiæ et voluntate clementi Cæsaris. Venit cum
uxore, liberis et familia ac 12 equis longo et difficili
itinere, sumptibus magnis, Dresdam usque. Et nulli alij Principi, nulli nationi
suam operam voluit devovere nisi uni Cæsari. Rogat igitur, et ego intercedo,
efficere velit, ut responsum a Cæsare accipiat et negotia sua dirigere
stabilireque possit, ac ne ita dubius cum magno suarum rerum dispendio hæreat.
Literas meas ad BARVITIUM reverenter peto
prima occasione mitti curet, eumque etiam sua schedula
commonefaciat, ut Cæsari negotium proponat, et ultimam resolutionem Dresdam
mitti curet. Non pœnitebit, scio, Domine, huius operæ, et futurus est D. TYCHO,
ubi de facie aliquando innotuerit, longe gratissimus.

B. v.
Ex ædibus nostris 1. Decembris Anno 1598.T. M. promptus ad officia
THADEUS

RUDOLPHUS CORRADUCIUS AD THADDÆUM HAGECIUM.Quæ D. BARVITIUS iussu Cæsaris de Dno TYCHONE
nostro ad me rescripsit, hæc sunt: »De TYCHONIS adventu Cæsar perlibenter intellexit; ut Dresdæ
vel Pragæ vel alibi in vicinia tantisper, donec aula certo in loco recolligatur,
subsistat, cupit; ubi deinde ille commode et opportune collocari possit, benigne cogitat.« Hactenus Dnus
BARVITIUS, quæ Magtiæ tuæ
ad hasce suas significanda duxi. Interim rogo, ut Dnum
TYCHONEM meis verbis quam officiosissime salutet meamque operam eidem
polliceatur meque, quod ei ob ingentes meas occupationes non scribo,
diligentissime excuset.

RUDOLPHUS
CORRADUCIUS,
manu propria.
text.english:
**Postscript of Thaddaeus Hagecius to Tycho Brahe.**

When I had sealed these letters to you, intending to give them to your courier, I have today — which is 1 December — sent my boy besides, with this note to Master Coraduz, which I send on to you, from which you will understand the will of the Emperor. It bears Master Coraduz's seal and hand. I have rejoiced greatly that at last, before this my departure, I have received this reply and resolution of the Emperor. To these things there is no need that I add anything more.

**Copy of a letter of Master Thaddeus Hagecius to the Most Ample Vice-Chancellor of the Empire, Rudolph Corraducius.**

Magnificent Lord and most honoured Patron. Thus far our Lord Tycho has done everything on the counsel and advice of Your Magnificence and by the gracious will of the Emperor. He has come, with his wife, children and household, and twelve horses, by a long and difficult journey and at great expense, as far as Dresden. And to no other Prince, to no [other] nation, has he wished to devote his service, but to the Emperor alone. He asks, therefore — and I intercede [on his behalf] — that you be pleased to bring it about that he receive an answer from the Emperor, and be able to direct and settle his affairs, and not be left hanging thus in doubt, to the great detriment of his estate. I respectfully beg that you see to it that my letter to Barvitius be sent at the first opportunity, and that you also remind him by your own note to lay the matter before the Emperor, and see to it that the final resolution be sent to Dresden. You will not repent, I know, my Lord, of this labour, and Master Tycho, once he has become known to you face to face, will prove exceedingly grateful.

Farewell. From our house, 1 December, in the year 1598. Ready to serve Your Magnificence, Thaddeus.

**Rudolph Corraducius to Thaddeus Hagecius.**

What Master Barvitius, by the Emperor's order, has written back to me concerning our Lord Tycho, is this: 'Of Tycho's arrival the Emperor has learned with the greatest pleasure; he wishes him to remain for a time at Dresden, or Prague, or elsewhere nearby, until the court is gathered again in some fixed place; where he may then be conveniently and suitably settled, he graciously has in mind.' Thus far Master Barvitius — which words I have thought it right to make known to Your Magnificence in this [letter] of mine. Meanwhile I ask that you greet Master Tycho most dutifully in my words, and promise him my service, and most diligently excuse me for not writing to him myself, on account of my immense preoccupations.

Rudolph Corraducius, with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Thaddaeus Hagecius** (Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku, 1525–1600), imperial physician at Prague, astronomer, and Tycho's long-standing friend and chief broker at the Rudolfine court; the principal channel by which Tycho's reception into imperial service was negotiated.
- ***D. Corraducius*** = **Rudolf Coraduz** (Coraduz / Coraduz), Imperial Vice-Chancellor (*Reichsvizekanzler*; *Procancellarius* in the companion letter brahe-t_15980530001). The enclosed note conveyed "the will of the Emperor" — **Rudolf II**'s favourable resolution on Tycho's appointment — under Coraduz's seal and hand.
- **Document type.** A *postscriptum* — a postscript written after the main letter had been sealed, hence its separate transmission.
- **⚠ Date.** The body fixes the day explicitly: *hodie, qui est 1. Decembr.* = **1 December 1598**; the identifier (…12 01…) agrees. The edition catalogues the piece under **1 November**; the one-month discrepancy is reproduced, not reconciled — the header follows the as-written **1 December**. New Style (Prague, imperial Catholic).
- **What the recovered text is.** The postscript already published for this letter (Hagecius to Tycho, 1 December 1598) tells Tycho he is forwarding a note from "D. Coraducius" bearing on "the will of the Emperor," but breaks off before quoting it. The recovered segment is that enclosure in full: fair copies of two letters — (1) Hagecius's own appeal to the imperial Vice-Chancellor on Tycho's behalf, and (2) the Vice-Chancellor's reply, itself quoting the Emperor's secretary verbatim.
- **The three courtiers named are Tycho's patronage brokers at Rudolf II's court in the winter of 1598–99**: Thaddaeus Hagecius (Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku), the Emperor's physician and Tycho's chief broker in Prague; Rudolph Corraducius (Rudolf von Coraduz), Vice-Chancellor of the Empire; and Johannes Barvitius, Rudolf II's confidential secretary and closest adviser — Christianson (*On Tycho's Island*, and *Measure of the Heavens*) names all three as the inner circle Hagecius mobilised to secure Tycho's imperial appointment.
- **Concrete biographical detail not in the letter proper.** Hagecius's covering letter to Corraducius specifies that Tycho arrived at Dresden "with his wife, children and household, and twelve horses" (*cum uxore, liberis et familia ac 12 equis*), by a long and costly journey — a precise snapshot of the size and expense of the 1597–98 exodus from Denmark that the published tail does not give.
- **This is the actual textual source of "the will of the Emperor" referenced in the already-published tail.** Corraducius quotes Barvitius's report of Rudolf II's own instruction (set off with guillemets in the source): the Emperor is glad of Tycho's arrival and wants him to wait at Dresden, Prague, or nearby until the peripatetic imperial court settles in one place, at which point he will be suitably provided for — the direct documentary basis for the extended limbo Tycho experienced before his Benátky/Prague settlement.
- **Hagecius stresses Tycho's exclusive loyalty to the Emperor** ("nulli alij Principi, nulli nationi suam operam voluit devovere nisi uni Cæsari") — a rhetorical move consistent with the delicate diplomatic position Tycho was in, having left Denmark and needing to be seen as uncompromisingly committed to Habsburg service rather than shopping his services elsewhere.

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO ET ERUDITISSIMO VIRO DOMINO OLIGERO ROSENKRANTZIO DE ROSENHOLM, CONSANGUINEO, AFFINI ET AMICO INTIMO, MIHIQUE CHARISSIMO.

S. P.

CHARISSIME OLIGERE, Amice, Consangvinee et Affinis integerrime, de statu mearum rerum cognoscendo te esse sollicitum, id sic suadente eo, quo me prosequeris amore, et ego vicissim te, non dubito. Sic itaque brevibus habe: Wandesburgo statim a Michaëlis festo discedens Pragam versus ad Caesarem iturus, Magdeburgi primum per octiduum ob Ducem Brunsvicensem, tum quoque ERICUM LANGIUM substiti, postea Dresdae per mensem integrum, quo responsum a Caesare, an illis temporibus, cum Praga abesset ob luem Epidemicam, accedendus et compellandus foret, expectarem; quale vero tandem receperim, ex altera pagina cognosces. Caetera exemplum literarum ad KRAGIUM nostrum, quod adiunxi (neque enim nunc vacat eadem ad te repetere) edocebit. Ingressurus est hac ipsa hora filius meus TYCHO cum quibusdam comitibus iter Wandesburgum, ut familiam meam muliebrem huc meis curribus adducat; constitui enim, favente Deo, hîc Wittebergae hyemare, aut saltem tam diu manere, donec denuo a Caesare in Bohemiam vocer. Plura non addo, quia pluribus otium deest. Tu vero, mi OLIGERE, copiosius rescribe, et de singulis, quae scire mea interesse nosti, affatim instrue, meque saepius, interea dum hîc sum, tuis literis invise. Invenies me ad par pari referendum minime segnem. Habebis brevi plura carmina ad Caesarem de me, tum quoque ad me a varijs Poëtis concinnata, quae nunc describere non licuit. Tu interim, ut Dania Germaniae respondeat, effice, pro ut in te sponte recepisti, si modo Iutorum sit pollicitis aliquando stare. Si ego Schanus tale quid addixissem, certe fidem meam dudum redemissem, utut fuerim non minus quam tu occupatissimus. Sed si adhuc promissis steteris, erit veniae locus. Cum HUNNIO hîc necdum familiaritatem contraxi, pridie enim primum huc veni, sed fiet id facile in posterum, uti etiam cum reliquis huius Academiae Eruditis. POLYCARPUM decumbentem, cum Dresdae essem, bis invisi, humanissime ab illo exceptus; is te salutari voluit. Salutem etiam tibi dicit Hospes meus Dnus Doctor IOHANNES IESSENIUS, qui mihi in Philippaeis olim aedibus commodam habitationem pro me et meis lubenter et benevole concessit. Vale, et brevi plura a me expecta. Sed da operam, ut praevenias. Saluta coniugem SOPHIAM Neptem meam, utque alteri SOPHIAe praevaleat, indulge.

Dabantur properanter Wittebergae die 5. Decembris Anni 1598.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 126; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
POSTSCRIPTA. IMPURUM istud et calumnijs scatens Dithmarsi istius scriptum, quod tibi inspiciendum misi, necdum recepi, utut in literis ultimis, quas, cum Wandesburgi essem, accepi, indicaveris te illud mihi remisisse; fac igitur, ut mature habeam, neque enim eo carere possum propter illa, quae in margine adscripta erant, ut inde dem occasionem alteri cuipiam ista maledicta in suum authorem retorquendi; sed luet is brevi quae meritus est. Retulit de eo ad me Doct. IOHANNES GŒDELMANNUS, Consiliarius Saxonicus et CHYTRÆI Gener, quem proculdubio nosti, quod URSUS iste plane contemptus sit et despectui habitus ab omnibus cordatis viris et ijs, qui in aula sunt Caesaris, postquam tam insulsum et temerarium scriptum publicavit, esseque ab ipso Caesare neglectum et vili pensum.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most learned man, Lord Holger Rosenkrantz of Rosenholm, kinsman by blood, kinsman by marriage, and most intimate friend, and most dear to me.**

Heartiest greeting.

Dearest Holger — friend, kinsman by blood, and most upright kinsman by marriage — that you are anxious to learn the state of my affairs, the love with which you attend me (and I you in turn) so persuading, I do not doubt. So have it thus, in brief: leaving Wandsbek right after the feast of Michael, to go toward Prague to the Emperor, I halted first at Magdeburg for eight days, on account of the Duke of Brunswick, and also of Erik Lange; afterward at Dresden for a whole month, there to await a reply from the Emperor — whether at that time, since he was away from Prague because of the epidemic plague, he was to be approached and addressed. What [reply] I finally received, you will learn from the other page. The rest, the copy of the letter to our Krag, which I have appended (for there is no time now to repeat the same to you), will teach you. This very hour my son Tycho is to set out on the journey to Wandsbek, with some companions, to bring my womenfolk hither with my wagons; for I have resolved, God favouring, to winter here at Wittenberg, or at least to remain so long until I am called again by the Emperor into Bohemia. I add no more, because for more there is no leisure. But do you, my Holger, write back more fully, and instruct me amply on the particulars which you know it concerns me to know, and visit me the more often with your letters while I am here. You will find me by no means slow to render like for like. You will shortly have several poems to the Emperor about me, and also to me, composed by various Poets, which I could not now transcribe. You, meanwhile, see to it that Denmark answers Germany [in correspondence], as you spontaneously undertook — if only it be in Jutlanders to stand by their promises sometime. Had I, a Scanian, pledged such a thing, I should certainly have redeemed my word long ago, however much I have been no less busy than you. But if you will yet have kept your promises, there will be room for pardon. With Hunnius I have not yet struck up acquaintance here, for I came hither only yesterday; but it will easily happen hereafter, as also with the rest of the learned of this Academy. Polycarp, lying ill, I visited twice while I was at Dresden, and was most kindly received by him; he wished to be remembered to you. Greeting to you, too, is sent by my host, Lord Doctor Johannes Jessenius, who has freely and kindly granted me convenient lodging, for myself and mine, in the house that was once Philip's. Farewell, and shortly expect more from me — but take pains to forestall me. Greet your wife Sophie, my niece, and indulge her, that she may outdo the other Sophie.

Given hastily at Wittenberg, the 5th day of December, in the year 1598.
Your Tycho Brahe.


*[Postscript:]* POSTSCRIPT. That impure writing of the Dithmarsian, teeming with calumnies, which I sent you to inspect, I have not yet received back — although in your last letter, which I received while I was at Wandsbek, you indicated that you had sent it back to me; see to it, then, that I have it in good time, for I cannot do without it on account of those things which were noted in the margin, that I may thence give occasion to some other man of turning those slanders back upon their author; but he shall shortly pay what he has deserved. Doctor Johann Gödelmann, Saxon Councillor and Chytraeus's son-in-law — whom you doubtless know — reported to me concerning him, that this Ursus is plainly despised and held in contempt by all sensible men, and by those who are at the Emperor's court, after he published so insipid and rash a writing, and that he is neglected and lightly esteemed by the Emperor himself.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender & moment.** **Tycho Brahe** at **Wittenberg**, December 1598, having just arrived ("only yesterday") — a chatty progress-report to his closest Danish kinsman during the slow approach to imperial service. It pairs with brahe-t_15980905001 (Wandsbek, Sept 1598) as the two main Tycho→Holger letters of the migration.
- **Recipient.** **Holger Rosenkrantz "the Learned"** of **Rosenholm** — *consanguineus, affinis et amicus intimus* (kinsman by blood and marriage; cf. brahe-t_15980905001).
- **The itinerary.** From **Wandsbek**, just after **Michaelmas (29 Sept)**, toward Prague; halted a week at **Magdeburg** (on account of the **Duke of Brunswick** and **Erik Lange**), then a whole month at **Dresden**, awaiting the Emperor's word on whether to approach him (Rudolf II being absent from Prague *ob luem epidemicam* — because of the **plague**). Tycho now resolves to **winter at Wittenberg** until summoned into Bohemia; his son is being sent back to Wandsbek to fetch the **womenfolk** and wagons.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Dux Brunsvicensis* = the **Duke of Brunswick** (Heinrich Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel).
 - *Ericus Langius* = **Erik Lange** (d. 1613), Danish nobleman and alchemist, Tycho's friend and prospective brother-in-law (betrothed to Tycho's sister Sophie Brahe) — chronically in debt and abroad.
 - *Kragius noster* = **Niels Krag (Nicolaus Cragius)** (c. 1550–1602), Danish humanist, historian and diplomat — recipient of a parallel letter Tycho encloses in copy.
 - *filius meus Tycho* = **Tycho Brahe the Younger**, sent to fetch the household.
 - *Hunnius* = **Aegidius Hunnius** (1550–1603), the leading Wittenberg Lutheran theologian, not yet met.
 - *Polycarpus* = **Polycarp Leyser (Leiser)** the Elder (1552–1610), Saxon court preacher, visited (ill) at Dresden.
 - *Dnus Doctor Iohannes Iessenius* = **Johannes Jessenius**, Tycho's **host** at Wittenberg, who lodged him *in Philippaeis aedibus* — "in the house that was once Philip's," i.e. **Melanchthon's former house** (*Philippus* = Philipp Melanchthon) — a resonant detail (cf. Jessenius across the 1600 letters).
 - *coniunx Sophia, neptis mea* = **Sophie Brahe**, Holger's **wife** and Tycho's **niece**; *altera Sophia* = the **other Sophie** — Tycho's learned **sister Sophie Brahe** (the wordplay: may the niece "outdo" the aunt).
- **The Scanian/Jutlander jest.** *si modo Iutorum sit pollicitis … stare … Si ego Schanus …* — Tycho teases Holger (a Jutland landowner) about Jutlanders keeping promises, contrasting himself as a **Scanian** (*Schanus*, of Skåne); rendered straight as the friendly regional jab it is.
- **Witness note.** Survives as an **afskrift (copy)** in Langebek's Diplomatarium, Copenhagen.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam*; *Dabantur properanter* → "Given hastily"; *Vale* → "Farewell"; *ad par pari referendum* → "to render like for like."
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 5. Decembris Anni 1598* at Wittenberg; no style marker. Lutheran Saxony was on the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar; reproduced, not converted.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (the unreturned Ursus book + Gödelmann's report that Ursus is despised at court), restored from Dreyer VIII p.126 (dropped by the working transcription).
- **Correction.** English corrected from 'a week' to 'eight days', matching 'per octiduum' (Latin and Dreyer agree; only the translation was at fault), per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII p.125.

documents.editorial_note: **Note.** The counterpart to **Niels Krag's reply of 4 December 1599 (brahe-t_15991204001)**: Tycho's fullest account of the **1598 journey** (Wandsbek → Magdeburg → Dresden → Wittenberg), the imperial-summons mechanism, and the **Wittenberg lodging in Melanchthon's house**.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD NICOLAUM KRAGIUM.

S. P.

CUM Dresdæ adhuc essem, ante paucos dies literas tuas accepi, Præstantissime et Amantissime Domine Doctor NICOLAE KRAGIE, quæ Haffnia datæ erant Calendis Octobris huius anni. Indicas autem ab initio te meas non accepisse, quas HOLGERUS ROSENKRANTZIUS noster in tua absentia secum in Cimbriam recepit; miror itaque eum tanto tempore illas retinuisse. Existimaverat quidem ille, te esse invisurum sese Rosenholmij, uti ei forte pollicitus eras, at ego illi scripseram, quod frustra te exspectaret, æque enim rarum esse Iutum Iuto vera dicere et fidem facere, atque augurem auguri, neque sane in hoc augurio falsus sum meo ipsius incommodo, siquidem plæraque erant in illo, quem tibi inscripseram, fasciculo, quæ te mature scire avebam; spero tamen te id iam accepisse et eius contenta omnia percepisse, quare ut de ijs, ubi præsertim opus est, mihi mature respondeas, rogo; atque simul indices, quid de literis illis actum sit, quas IOHANNES STYGIUS in Daniam ad quendam mea de caussa se scripsisse rettulit, et quomodo intellectæ acceptæque. Quæ de Praefecto meo Huennensi in hisce ultimis attingis, parum moror, is non saltem erga me infidelis deprehenditur, atque iniquas reddere rationes suæ villicationis, sed insuper nihil ferme eorum exequitur, quæ aliquoties ei per literas mando, non sine rerum mearum gravi dispendio, adeo ut aliqua adhuc ex instrumentis meis et reliqua supellectile isthic in Insula, aut etiam Haffniæ residua sint, quæ necdum Lubecæ accipere potuerim, utut aliquoties hac de re scripserim et MULÆUS, cum præsens esset, illi singula oretenus exposuit; taceo quod nullos pisces ex tot meis piscinis tanti constantibus, sive salitos sive exsiccatos, uti volui, nancisci queam, sed is illis in suum et suorum commodum saltem utitur, vel potius abutitur. Verum quid de eo faciendum sit, ESCILLUS BILLEUS dispiciat et statuat, cui supremam inspectionem rerum mearum concredidi. Quod autem ais esse quosdam, qui Insulam meam a me petitam volunt, peiore mea futura conditione, equidem non intelligo, quid hæc verba sibi velint, nimis enim obscura sunt, et in varium sensum trahi possunt. Cum tota Dania mihi nimis coarctata censeatur, quî quæso insulula tam angusta tamque illucrifera me remorabitur, his pauciora et longe maiora affectantem sperantemque? Sed vertat se meus osor et invidus in quascunque volet partes, quicunque tandem is sit, non multum de me triumphabit, sed potius infringet dentem solido, propria delusus ab Arte. Atqui ego de Insula illa non sum magnopere sollicitus, neque etiam quodpiam emolumentum inde habeo, sed potius plus damni, neque tamen ullo iure eam mihi adimere possunt, salvis Regis FRIDERICI Literis, neque etiam sine Senatorum omnium iudicio et consensu id facere licet, si modo non quidvis licet citra ius et fas; oportet etiam me legitime citari. Sed restituant mihi solummodo meas impensas aut dimidiam saltem earum partem, quas in illam expendi ultra summam quam a Rege FRIDERICO et Senatoribus Regni accepi, aut decernant, om det er billigt att jeg skulle liide saadan Skade thill forgeffvis. Sed de his alias agemus, quando status mearum rerum fuerit in tutioribus et inexpugnabilibus terminis, quod brevi me assecuturum, favente summo Numine, confido. Erit forte aliquis potentior, qui mei patrocinium in se recipiet, atque a tot iniurijs et damnis, quot in Dania passus sum, vindicabit.

Quia vero de rebus meis certior fieri desideras, sic habe: Paulo post Michaëlis festum Wandesburgo Pragam versus ad Cæsarem iter suscepi, comitante me etiam familia mea muliebri Magdeburgum usque, deinde reversa. Substiti autem Magdeburgi per octiduum in gratiam ERICI LANGIJ nostri, qui mihi per quinque dies illic aderat, postea Dresdam profectus, ubi certo illic comperissem, Cæsarem relicta Praga ob morbos Epidemicos, in tutiorem locum septem miliaribus inde distantem se recepisse, nec quempiam admittere, nisi paucissimos quosdam quotidianos ministros, Aulam dissipatam esse, Cancellariam remotam, Consilia et Iudicia omnia silere, in summa Iustitium esse et actiones cunctas ob contagium populare conturbatas, consultius duxi scriptis Pragam ad THADDÆUM nostrum literis, an in tali rerum statu ulterius procedendum sit, expiscari, atque interea Dresdæ responsum præstolari. THADDÆUS acceptis meis in hanc sententiam literis, eas Domino Procancellario Imperij RUDOLPHO CORRADUCIO, qui Pragæ remanserat, actutum legendas exhibuit, is vero descriptum earum confestim Cæsari misit, petens a BARVICIO, ut de Cæsaris voluntate quamprimum fieri possit, quidpiam certi rescribat cumque hoc aliquamdiu protraheretur, uti sunt lenta, quæ apud Magnates expedire oporteat, præsertim eo tempore, quando Literæ Praga allatæ ob infectionis metum, non nisi post aliquot dierum intervallum legebantur. Hinc evenit, ut usque in quartam hebdomadam Dresdæ responsum exspectare necesse habuerim, THADDÆO interea moræ etiam plusquam ego ipsemet impatiente, semel atque iterum responsum urgente, et cum BARVICIO hac de re quasi expostulante, illique IACOBUM CURTIUM Prædecessorem, quod ille multo citius me concernentia præstitisset, exprobrante, et tandem etiam ad Dominum CORRADUCIUM, qui Pragæ adhuc erat, hac de re schedam scribente. Accidit autem, ut eo ipso die BARVICIJ Secretarij Literæ ad CORRADUCIUM pervenirent, quibus Cæsaris resolutio continebatur, quam CORRADUCIUS actutum Schedæ THADDÆI propria manu subscripsit, eamque sigillo suo munitam THADDÆO demisit, ut me de voluntate Cæsaris inde certiorem efficeret. Quæ autem erant eorum, de quibus dixi, formalia verba, ex adiuncta charta percipies. Ego itaque accepto hoc Clementissimo Cæsaris responso, me illi lubenter acquiescere rescripsi; nam et antea THADDÆO per literas significaram, me in superiori Saxonia potius quam Dresdæ mansurum, donec morbi illi populariter in Bohemia grassantes remiserint, et Cæsari commodius fuerit me eo vocare; neque enim periculo caruit cum meo iuvenili comitatu illas oras passim peste et dysenteria infectas tunc intrare. Recepi itaque me cum meis huc Wittebergam, ubi D. V. hyemare constitui, nisi prius a Cæsare, sopita istic lue Epidemica accersitus fuero, eritque mihi hîc oportunum in operibus meis necdum Hamburgi ob Typographorum imperitiam et paucitatem plane absoluta Typis complere. Habito hîc in ædibus, quæ olim erant optimæ recordationis viri PHILIPPI MELANCHTONIS, nunc CASPARIS PEUCERI, inquilino earum modo exciente Domino Doctore IOHANNE IESSENIO Philosopho et Medico eximio, qui me perlubenter, imo non sine gaudio ad se recepit, et potissimam ædium partem pro me meaque familia, quam diu lubuerit, inhabitandam benigne concessit. Adest commoditas pro observationibus continuandis, suntque mihi ad manus hîc quædam ex meis Instrumentis, quæ in Bohemiam mecum sumere constitui. Est etiam locus pro laboratorio Pyronomico, in quo nonnulla, interea dum hîc sum, parare animus est, præter ea, quæ prius Wandesburgi confecta in promtu habeo. Cæsar enim talibus impense delectatur, eaque proprijs manibus versat, non minus quam Mathematica, quæ probe intelligit et alijs præfert. Ideoque aiunt, ipsum magno mei desiderio teneri, adeo ut in locum, quo nunc secessit, Podebra dictum, me ad se accersere, ut quotidie istic illi adessem, voluerit, iam præparato pro me et meis amplo hospitio, sed increbrescente pestis vehementia in illa vicinia, ita ut aliquot bruta animantia inficerentur, de mutatione loci cogitavit, ita ut aut in Sileciam, aut Styriam aut etiam versus Insbrug se recipere cuperet, relicta Bohemia, modo id tutum foret, et ab indigena Nobilitate permissum. Atque hinc etiam factum, ut responsum de me aliquandiu retardaretur quodque eiuscemodi quale in charta vides acceperim. Adfuit mihi Dresdæ doctor IOHANNES GŒDELMANNUS Consiliarius Saxonicus, CHYTRÆI gener, ijs ipsis diebus, quando Dresda mihi abeundum fuit, is inter alia mihi dixit, se Pragæ, unde nuper advenerat, a fidedignis audivisse, Cæsarem in tantum meum expetivisse adventum, ut hæc verba pronunciarit: »Si solummodo illum virum hîc mecum haberem, cum quo de rebus Mathematicis et Astronomicis, tum quoque Pyronomicis iucunde conferre possim, atque eius opera perlustrare, non caperet me tantum temporis tædium, veluti nunc sit, dum Praga absum. Sed quid faciam, si illum confestim huc vocavero, et mihi ipsi sit alio discedendum, non bene consulo illi et eius comitatui, hoc præsertim periculoso tempore. Præstat itaque id in commodiorem et oportuniorem commoditatem differre, interim de illo convenienti loco constituendo dispiciam.« Atque alia eiuscemodi, quæ nunc prætereo, ut spem magnam conceperim, Cæsarem non ita aversurum me meaque studia, quemadmodum in Dania factum est. Curo autem per filium meum TYCHONEM, addito uno vel altero comite, familiam meam muliebrem huc Wandesburgo evocari, missis meis curribus, qui eam cum supellectile necessaria advehant; eo enim regredi, nisi forte pro disponendis residuis rebus, ijsque alio mittendis, non est animus. Sat Boreæ datum, utinam non nimium, sed tribuendum erat aliquid patriæ, quam diu id fieri potuit.

FRANCISCUS meus TEGNAGLIUS cum ego Dresda huc concederem, in Italiam abijt, illic aliquantulum mansurus linguæ discendæ causa; eum Principi Venetorum, Duci Parmensi, et magno Duci Hetruriæ atque Florentiæ per Literas commendavi, missis ad singulos eorum ijs, quos Regi nostro offerre volui, Libris, quod tamen an factum sit, ignoro. Itidem feci apud MAGINUM Mathematicum. Quin et Elector Coloniensis illum in mei gratiam, et a me rogatus, ijsdem Italiæ Principibus, excepto Veneto, Italicis Literis, quarum hîc exemplum habes, commendavit, ut sperem res eius bono loco istic futuras. Cum mihi scripseris, quod Rostochio ad D. CHRISTOPHORUM STURTIUM I. C. directis literis facile efficies, singulis duabus, uti scis, septimanis huc inde veniente auriga, de omnibus, quæ me meaque negotia concernere nosti, luculenter commonefacias velim, idque solito sæpius, cum nunc maior, interea dum hîc sum, concedatur oportunitas, nisi mare apud vos congelatur. Carmina in mei gratiam ab eximijs Poëtis ad Cæsarem congratulationis caussa concinnata, tum quoque ad me brevi videbis, otium ea describendi in hac festinatione non supererat, mitto tamen exemplum CHYTRÆI Rostochiensis, quod nuper Dresdæ accepi, siquidem illud in promptu erat, isthic ob POLICARPUM sic volentem ex autographo immutatum. Sed ille ob festinum meum inde discessum illud necdum accepit, est alias vir humanissimus, satisque Politicus, meque, dum ibi essem, honorifice excepit. Sum etiam benigne habitus a Duce Administratore, qui me ad se invitavit, posteaque ad iuniores Principes, donata deinde eleganti torque aurea cum sua Effigie; quin et alibi a Principibus Germaniæ clementer acceptus fui, qui, ut eos in reditu inviserem, rogarunt, spe etiam tacite facta, quod si Cæsar mihi benefacere velit, eos etiam suo officio non defuturos. Quomodo Coloniensis me meaque Cæsari commendavit, vel potius illi mea de caussa congratulatus sit, et quid in mei gratiam ad eundem Cæsarem Dux ULDARICUS Avus maternus Regis Daniæ scripserit, exempla earum literarum, quas ROSENKRANTZIO, aut etiam tibi, si recte memini, communicavi, edocebunt. Dedit etiam ad me Princeps MAURITIUS humanissimas literas, in quibus non pro autoritate Principum agit, sed me pro amico bono habet et sic nuncupat. Ex literis TEGNAGLIJ Amsterodamo de ijs, quæ in legatione eius evenerunt, antequam Wandesburgum ad me rediret, perscriptis, hæc et plura cognosces, ubi eas describere vacabit, tibique mittere. Sed desino plura, cum charta vix plura ferat.

Tu itaque, mi optime KRAGIE, cum coniuge a me salutata, liberisque vestris felicissime vale.
Dabantur Wittebergæ die 5. Decembris Anno 1598.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO NIELS KRAG.**

Heartiest greeting.

While I was still at **Dresden**, a few days ago I received your letter, most excellent and most loving Lord Doctor Niels Krag, which had been sent from Copenhagen on the Kalends of October [1 October] of this year. You indicate at the outset that you did not receive mine, which our **Holger Rosenkrantz** took with him into Jutland in your absence; I wonder, then, that he kept them so long. He had thought, indeed, that you would visit him at Rosenholm (as perhaps you had promised him); but I had written him that he would wait for you in vain, for it is as rare for a Jutlander to tell a Jutlander truth and keep faith as for augur to augur — nor, indeed, was I wrong in this augury, to my own inconvenience, since most things were in that bundle addressed to you which I longed for you to know in good time. Yet I hope you have now received it, and perceived all its contents; wherefore I ask that you answer me in good time about them, especially where there is need; and at the same time **indicate what was done with those letters which Johannes Stygius reported he had written to someone in Denmark on my account, and how they were understood and received**. What you touch on, in your last, about my **Praefect of Hven** [the island-governor], I care little for: he is found not only unfaithful toward me, and to render unfair accounts of his stewardship, but moreover executes almost none of the things I order him several times by letter — not without grave loss of my affairs — so that some of my instruments and remaining furniture are still on the Island, or even at Copenhagen, which I have not yet been able to receive at Lübeck, though I have written several times of this, and **Mule**, when present, explained each thing to him by mouth. I say nothing of the fact that I can get no fish from so many of my fishponds (costing so much), whether salted or dried, as I wished — but he uses them, or rather abuses them, only for his own and his people's benefit. But what is to be done about him, let **Eske Bille** look to and decide, to whom I have entrusted the supreme oversight of my affairs. As to what you say — that there are some who wish my Island taken from me, my condition to be worse — I do not understand what these words mean, for they are too obscure, and can be drawn into various senses. Since all Denmark is reckoned too cramped for me, how, pray, will so narrow and unprofitable a little island detain me, who aspire and hope for fewer and far greater things? But let my hater and enviar turn himself whatever way he will — whoever he be at last — he will not much triumph over me, but rather **break his tooth on the solid, deluded by his own Art**. And indeed I am not greatly solicitous about that Island, nor do I have any profit from it, but rather more loss; nor yet can they take it from me by any right, **King Frederick's letters being valid**, nor is it allowed to be done without the judgement and consent of all the Senators — unless, indeed, anything be allowed beyond right and divine law; I must also be lawfully cited. But let them only restore me my expenses, or at least half of them, which I spent on it beyond the sum I received from King Frederick and the Realm's Senators — or let them decree **whether it is fair that I should suffer such loss in vain** [Danish]. But of these we shall treat another time, when the state of my affairs is in safer and impregnable terms — which I trust I shall shortly attain, the supreme Godhead favouring. There will perhaps be some more powerful one, who will take my patronage upon himself, and vindicate me from so many injuries and losses as I have suffered in Denmark.

But since you desire to be more certainly informed of my affairs, take it thus: **A little after Michaelmas [29 Sept] I undertook the journey from Wandsbek toward Prague, to the Emperor — my womenfolk accompanying me as far as Magdeburg, then returning**. I halted at Magdeburg for eight days, for the sake of our **Erik Lange**, who was with me there for five days; afterward I set out for **Dresden**, where, when I had learned for certain that **the Emperor, having left Prague on account of the epidemic diseases, had withdrawn into a safer place seven miles distant thence, and admitted no one but a very few daily servants; that the Court was dispersed, the Chancellery removed, all Councils and Courts silent — in sum, that there was a suspension of justice [*iustitium*], and all transactions thrown into confusion by the popular contagion** — I judged it more advisable, by letters sent to Prague to our **Thaddaeus [Hagecius]**, to fish out whether in such a state of affairs I should proceed further, and meanwhile to await the answer at Dresden. Thaddaeus, having received my letters to this effect, at once showed them to the Imperial Vice-Chancellor **Rudolf Coraduz**, who had remained at Prague, to read; he sent a copy of them straightway to the Emperor, asking **Barvitius** to write back something certain about the Emperor's will as soon as could be. And since this dragged on a while (as the things are slow that must be expedited with Magnates, especially at that time, when letters brought from Prague were not read, for fear of infection, until after an interval of several days), it came about that I had to await the answer at Dresden into the fourth week — Thaddaeus meanwhile even more impatient of the delay than I myself, urging the answer again and again, and as it were expostulating with Barvitius about it, and reproaching him with **Jacob Curtius**, his predecessor (who would have done the things concerning me much sooner), and at last writing a note about this to Lord Coraduz, who was still at Prague. It happened, however, that on that very day Secretary Barvitius's letter reached Coraduz, in which was contained the Emperor's resolution — which Coraduz straightway subscribed in his own hand to Thaddaeus's note, and, secured with his seal, sent down to Thaddaeus, to inform me thence of the Emperor's will. And what were the formal words of those [resolutions] of which I spoke, you will perceive from the adjoined paper.

I, then, having received this most clement response of the Emperor's, wrote back that I gladly acquiesce in it; for I had earlier signified to Thaddaeus by letter that I would stay in upper Saxony, rather than at Dresden, until those diseases raging popularly in Bohemia should abate, and it should be more convenient for the Emperor to call me thither; for it was not without danger then to enter, with my youthful retinue, those regions infected everywhere with plague and dysentery. **So I withdrew with my [household] hither to Wittenberg, where I have resolved, God willing, to winter** — unless I am first summoned by the Emperor, the epidemic plague there laid to rest; and it will be convenient for me here to complete in print my works not yet quite finished at Hamburg (on account of the unskillfulness and scarcity of the Printers). **I dwell here in the house which was once that of the man of best remembrance, Philip Melanchthon — now Caspar Peucer's — its tenant, Lord Doctor Johannes Jessenius, an eminent Philosopher and Physician, having just vacated it; who received me most gladly, nay not without joy, and kindly granted the chief part of the house for me and my family to inhabit as long as I please.** There is convenience here for continuing observations, and I have at hand here certain of my Instruments which I resolved to take with me into Bohemia. There is also a place for a **Pyronomic [alchemical] laboratory**, in which I intend to prepare some things while I am here, besides those previously made at Wandsbek which I have at hand. For **the Emperor is greatly delighted by such things, and handles them with his own hands, no less than the Mathematical [arts], which he well understands and prefers to others. And so they say he is held by a great desire for me** — so much that he wished to summon me to the place to which he has now retired (called **Poděbrady**), that I might be with him there daily, an ample lodging being already prepared for me and mine; but, the plague's vehemence increasing in that neighbourhood (so that some brute animals were infected), he thought of changing his place — so as to wish to withdraw either into Silesia, or Styria, or even toward Innsbruck, leaving Bohemia, provided it were safe, and permitted by the native Nobility. And hence too it came about that the answer about me was delayed a while, and that I received such a one as you see in the paper. There was with me at Dresden Doctor **Johann Gödelmann**, a Saxon councillor, **Chytraeus's son-in-law**, on those very days when I had to leave Dresden; he told me, among other things, that he had heard at Prague (whence he had lately come), from trustworthy [men], that the Emperor so desired my arrival that he pronounced these words: *"If only I had that man here with me, with whom I could pleasantly confer about Mathematical and Astronomical matters, and Pyronomic ones too, and peruse his works, so great a tedium of time would not seize me, as it now does, while I am away from Prague. But what shall I do, if I summon him here at once, and I myself must depart elsewhere? I do not consult well for him and his retinue, especially at this dangerous time. It is better, therefore, to defer it to a more convenient and opportune occasion; meanwhile I will look into establishing a fit place for him."* And other such things, which I now pass over — so that I have conceived a great hope that the Emperor will not so turn away me and my studies, as was done in Denmark. I am arranging, through my son **Tycho** (with one or two companions added), that my womenfolk be summoned hither from Wandsbek, my wagons being sent to bring them with the necessary furniture; for I have no mind to return thither, except perhaps to arrange the remaining things and send them elsewhere. **Enough has been given to Boreas [the North] — would it were not too much; but something had to be granted to the fatherland, as long as it could be done.**

My **Franz Tengnagel**, when I came hither from Dresden, went off into **Italy**, to stay there a while for the sake of learning the language; **I commended him by letter to the Prince of Venice [the Doge], the Duke of Parma, and the Grand Duke of Tuscany and Florence — sending to each of them the Books which I wished to offer our King** — though whether it has been done, I know not. Likewise I did with **Magini** the Mathematician. Nay, and **the Elector of Cologne**, for my sake and at my request, commended him to the same Princes of Italy (except the Venetian) by Italian letters — a copy of which you have here — so that I hope his affairs there will be in good place. Since you have written me that you can easily effect [delivery] by letters directed to Rostock, to Dr. **Christoph Sturtz**, jurist — a wagon coming hither and thither (as you know) every two weeks — I would have you inform me clearly about all the things you know to concern me and my affairs, and that more often than usual, since a greater opportunity is now granted while I am here, unless the sea freezes with you. The poems composed in my honour, by distinguished Poets, to the Emperor for congratulation's sake — and also to me — you will see shortly; the leisure for copying them out in this haste was not left over; yet I send a specimen of **Chytraeus the Rostocker's**, which I lately received at Dresden (since it was ready), there altered from the autograph at **Polycarpus's** wish. But he [Chytraeus] has not yet received it, on account of my hasty departure thence; he is otherwise a most humane man, and sufficiently Politic, and received me honourably while I was there. I was also kindly entertained by the **Duke Administrator** [of Saxony], who invited me to him, and afterward by the younger Princes, an elegant gold chain with his Effigy being then given me; nay, and elsewhere I was clemently received by the **Princes of Germany**, who asked that I visit them on my return, with a tacit hope too given that, if the Emperor should wish to benefit me, they too would not fail their office. How the Cologne [Elector] commended me and mine to the Emperor — or rather congratulated him on my account — and what **Duke Ulrich, the maternal grandfather of the King of Denmark**, wrote to the same Emperor for my sake, the copies of those letters (which I communicated to Rosenkrantz, or also to you, if I remember rightly) will teach. **Prince Maurice [of Nassau]** also gave me most humane letters, in which he does not act by the authority of Princes, but holds me for a good friend, and so names me. From Tengnagel's letters written from Amsterdam, about the things that happened in his legation before he returned to me at Wandsbek, you will learn these and more, when there is leisure to copy them and send them to you. But I cease [to add] more, since the paper scarcely bears more.

So fare you, my excellent Krag, most happily — with your wife, greeted by me, and your children.
Given at Wittenberg, the 5th of December, the year 1598.
