documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Niels Krag (Nicolaus Cragius)**, the Danish royal historian — the counterpart to **Krag's reply of 4 Dec 1599 (brahe-t_15991204001)**. Written from **Wittenberg**, where Tycho wintered 1598–99 before the move to Bohemia.
- **Significance — the fullest account of the 1598 journey, the imperial-summons mechanism, and the Wittenberg sojourn.**
 - **The journey narrative.** **A little after Michaelmas 1598, Tycho left Wandsbek for Prague**, the women returning from **Magdeburg** (where he stayed 8 days for **Erik Lange**); then **Dresden**, where he learned the Emperor had fled the **Bohemian plague** (the Court dispersed, a *iustitium*). The **summons mechanism** is vividly documented: **Hagecius → Coraduz → Barvitius → the Emperor**, with the answer delayed four weeks (plague-quarantined letters), Hagecius "more impatient than Tycho," reproaching Barvitius with **Jacob Curtius** (his predecessor).
 - **★ The Wittenberg lodging.** Tycho **wintered in Wittenberg, in "the house once Philip Melanchthon's, now Caspar Peucer's," vacated by Johannes Jessenius** — with room for **observations** and a **Pyronomic (alchemical) laboratory**. (Cf. the Vedel letter, brahe-t_15981230001, from the same Wittenberg winter.)
 - **★ Rudolf II's eagerness (the Gödelmann quote).** Via **Johann Gödelmann** (Chytraeus's son-in-law), Tycho relays the Emperor's own reported words — *"If only I had that man here, with whom I could confer on Mathematical, Astronomical, and Pyronomic matters …"* — a vivid window on Rudolf's **alchemical and astronomical eagerness** and the reason for the delayed call (the Emperor at **Poděbrady**, contemplating flight to Silesia/Styria/Innsbruck).
 - **The defiant Hven stance.** Tycho dismisses rumours of the **island being taken from him** ("all Denmark is too cramped … how will so narrow an island detain me?"); insists it cannot be taken without **King Frederick's letters, the Senators' consent, and a lawful citation** — or else his expenses repaid (the Danish tag *"whether it is fair that I should suffer such loss in vain"*). The faithless **Hven Praefect** (withholding instruments and fish) is left to **Eske Bille**.
 - **The patronage embassy.** **Tengnagel went to Italy** with Tycho's **gift books** for the **Doge of Venice, the Duke of Parma, the Grand Duke of Tuscany, and Magini** — plus the **Elector of Cologne's** Italian letters of commendation. Tycho recalls the **German princes' receptions** (a **gold chain from the Saxon Duke Administrator**), the commendations of **Cologne** and **Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg** (Christian IV's grandfather) to the Emperor, and **Maurice of Nassau's** friendly letters. (Cf. Tengnagel's own report, brahe-t_15980706001.)
 - **The Stygius cross-reference.** Tycho asks Krag **"what was done with the letters Johannes Stygius reported writing to someone in Denmark on my account"** — a direct reference to the **anti-Tycho letter brahe-t_15980710001**; Tycho was aware of the hostile letter-writing.
 - **"Enough given to Boreas."** A poignant line on his self-exile: *"Sat Boreae datum, utinam non nimium; but something had to be given to the fatherland, as long as it could be done."*
- **Cross-references.** The counterpart to **brahe-t_15991204001 (Krag, 4 December 1599)**; the **exile/journey** thread; the **Wittenberg winter** (brahe-t_15981230001); the **Tengnagel patronage-embassy** (brahe-t_15980706001); the **anti-Tycho Stygius letter** (brahe-t_15980710001); the **Mechanica/books distribution** layer.
- **Persons & places named.** Niels Krag; **Holger Rosenkrantz**; **Johannes Stygius**; the **Hven Praefect** (unnamed); **Claus Mule**; **Eske Bille**; **King Frederick II**; **Erik Lange**; **Thaddaeus Hagecius**; **Rudolf Coraduz**; **Barvitius**; **Jacob Curtius**; **Rudolf II**; **Philip Melanchthon**, **Caspar Peucer**, **Johannes Jessenius** (the Wittenberg house); **Johann Gödelmann** (Chytraeus's son-in-law); **David Chytraeus** & **Polycarpus** (the poem); the **Saxon Duke Administrator**; **Franz Tengnagel**; the **Doge of Venice, Duke of Parma, Grand Duke of Tuscany, Magini, Elector of Cologne, Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg, Maurice of Nassau**; **Christoph Sturtz** (the Rostock relay); **Christian IV**. Places: **Wittenberg**, **Dresden**, **Magdeburg**, **Wandsbek**, **Prague**, **Poděbrady**, **Hven**, **Copenhagen**, **Lübeck**, **Italy**, **Amsterdam**.
- **Calendar.** *Wittebergae die 5. Decembris Anno 1598* (Saxon Wittenberg, Old Style; no *stylo* marker) → **5 December 1598 [O.S.]**; header and label agree.

documents.abstract: Recounts the journey from Wandsbek toward Prague, halted at Dresden when plague in Bohemia worsened and the Emperor withdrew, having been summoned through Coraduz and Hagecius.

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET DOCTISSIMO VIRO M. ANDREAe WELLEIO, CANONICO RIPENSI, AMICO SUO ........ ET DILECTO.
S. P.

CUM hic Tabellarius sponte se mihi [of]ferret, qui in Cimbriam ire et Ripas transire constituit, non intermittendum duxi, amantissime Domine Magister ANDREA, quin aliquid saltem literarum ad te darem. Fecissemque idipsum, antequam Wandesburgo discessi, si negotiorum mole et internuncij penuriâ non fuissem praepeditus. De statu autem mearum rerum sic habe. Cum statim a Michaëlis festo inde abijssem Pragam versus cogitans, a Caesare per Dominum CORRADUCIUM Imperij Procancellarium, intermediante etiam D. THADDÆO HAGGECIO, aliquoties eo accitus, accidit ut cum Dresdam venissem, certo intelligerem, omnia Pragae ob luem Epidemicam isthic uti et alibi in Bohemia ingravescentem, conturbata esse, Caesarem inde discessisse, atque in tutiorem locum se recepisse, consiliarios autem hinc inde dispersos, aulamque totam dissipatam ideoque consilia et iudicia publica feriari et iustitium esse. Quare illic paulisper subsistens, misi proprium Tabellarium cum literis, me Dresdam advenisse indicantibus, et quid in tali rerum statu faciendum sit sciscitantibus. Quarum exemplo a CORRADUCIO Caesari, ubi tunc degebat, transmisso, responsum postea est a Domino BARVITIO, supremo Secretario et Caesari ab intimis consiliis, Caesaream Matem perlibenter de meo adventu intellexisse, utque Dresdae vel alibi in vicinia subsistam, donec aula recolligatur, cupere; interea de loco, ubi commode collocari possim, benigne cogitare. Quo responso accepto (cui etiam lubens acquievi, cum periculosum alias foret Bohemiam ingredi) me huc Wittebergam cum meis recepi. Ubi Deo volente hybernare constitui, vel saltem donec a Caesare avocer, quem scio mihi et meis rebus clementer ac serio favere, idque maiore studio et desiderio quam ...nia factum est, spero etiam constant ... Interim vero dum hîc dego, nonnulla quae in operibus meis nondum Typograph[ico] labore absoluta sunt, complere animus est, unâ cum ijs quae Caesari speciatim destinavi. Habito autem hîc Wittebergae in aedibus, quae olim erant optimae recordationis PHILIPPI MELANCHTONIS, nunc PEUCERI, inquilino earum me excipiente Domino Doctore IOHANNE IESSENIO Philosophiae et Medicinae Doctore. Qui ut est vir syncerus et humanus, meique amantissimus, plusquam dimidiam aedium partem pro me et mea familia inhabitandam benigne concessit, ita ut mediocri hîc fruar oportunitate, donec res meae providentia divina uberiorem commoditatem sortitae fuerint. Curo autem nunc adduci Wandesburgo familiam meam muliebrem proprijs curribus, per filium Tychonem, pro qua ......... donec amplior volente Numine a Caesare nobis omnibus concessus fuerit. Cuius in arbitrium totus mi... clauditur orbis. Haec brevibus significare volui ob veterem inter nos necessitudinem, ne rerum nostrarum inscius esses, aut me tui immemorem suspicareris. Forte tamen similia aut his plura a Mag. CHRISTIERNO SEVERINO LONGOMONTANO, meo aliquande domestico, qui etiam me Magdeburgum comitatus est et Gynaecaeum meum idem Wandesburgum reduxit, intellexisti. Relatum enim mihi est eum Ripis nuper fuisse, et meas isthuc ad eum perlatas esse literas, quas illi, quam primum huc veni, destinavi. Scripsi nunc et alteras eidem, sive isthic sive alibi sit, tradendas. Quod si per alios expeditum non fuerit, a te fieri cuperem, ubicunque eum morari nosti. Vale cum tota domo, salutata a me tua coniuge peramanter.

Per hunc vero Tabellarium ........tius, cum non raro Witebergam [lite]ras mittendi detur occasio, rescribe. Iterumque vale et Praesidi arcis vestrae de me salutem nuntia unâ cum aliis amicis, si quos forte apud vos habeo residuos. Precor vobis omnibus Annum hunc instantem auspicatum et salubrem.

Iamque tertium et pluries vale.
Dabantur Witebergae die penultima Anni 1598.
TYCHO BRAHE

De terræmotu, qui has Germaniæ oras duabus
vicibus conquassavit, die 16. Decembris inter 6 et 7 matutinam, tam hîc quam
Magdeburgi et et Lipsiæ atque
in alijs hinc inde locis, te inaudivisse opinor. Si quid tale apud vos vel alibi
in Dania experti sitis, indica. Existimo
enim a Septentrione vel Occasu tremorem illum venisse. Qui tamen in hoc tractu
divina clementia nihil damni intulit.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and most learned man, Master Anders Vedel, Canon of Ribe, his friend ........ and beloved.**
Heartiest greeting.

Since this courier offered himself to me of his own accord — one who has resolved to go into Cimbria [Jutland] and pass through Ribe — I thought I should not omit, most loving Lord Master Anders, to give you at least some letter. And I would have done this very thing before I departed from Wandsbek, had I not been hindered by the mass of business and the scarcity of a messenger. But of the state of my affairs, take it thus. When, immediately after Michaelmas, I had set out thence, intending [to go] toward **Prague** — being several times summoned thither by the Emperor through Lord **Coraduz**, Vice-Chancellor of the Empire, with Doctor **Thaddaeus Hagecius** also mediating — it happened that, when I had come to **Dresden**, I learned for certain that everything at Prague was thrown into confusion on account of the **epidemic plague** growing worse there and elsewhere in Bohemia; that the Emperor had departed thence and withdrawn to a safer place; and that the councillors were scattered here and there, and the whole court dispersed, and therefore the public councils and courts on holiday, and there being a cessation of business. Wherefore, staying there a while, I sent my own courier with a letter indicating that I had come to Dresden, and inquiring what should be done in such a state of affairs. A copy of which, transmitted by Coraduz to the Emperor where he then was, was answered afterward by Lord **Barvitius**, the chief Secretary and [one] of the Emperor's intimate councils: that the Imperial Majesty had learned of my coming most gladly, and desired that I stay at Dresden, or elsewhere in the neighbourhood, until the court reassembles, meanwhile kindly considering a place where I might conveniently be settled. Which answer received (in which I gladly acquiesced, since it would otherwise be dangerous to enter Bohemia), I withdrew hither to **Wittenberg** with my [household]. Where, God willing, I have resolved to winter — or at least until I am summoned by the Emperor, whom I know favours me and my affairs clemently and seriously, and that with greater zeal and longing than [……], I hope also constant[ly ……]. But meanwhile, while I dwell here, it is my mind to complete some things in my works not yet finished by typographic labour, together with those I have specially destined for the Emperor. And I dwell here at Wittenberg **in the house which was once [the house] of Philip Melanchthon, of best memory — now [of] Peucer** — its tenant receiving me, Lord Doctor **Johann Jessenius**, Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine. Who, as he is a sincere and humane man, and most loving of me, kindly granted more than half the house for me and my household to dwell in, so that I enjoy here a moderate convenience, until my affairs, by divine providence, obtain a more abundant accommodation. But I am now having my **womenfolk** brought from Wandsbek in my own carriages, through my son Tycho, for [whom ……], until a larger [dwelling], God willing, be granted us all by the Emperor — in whose decision my whole world is enclosed. These things I wished to signify briefly, on account of the old bond between us, lest you be ignorant of my affairs, or suspect me forgetful of you. Yet perhaps you have learned similar, or more, from Master **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus**, formerly my servant, who also accompanied me to Magdeburg, and brought my womenfolk back to Wandsbek. For it has been reported to me that he was lately at Ribe, and that my letters were brought thither to him, which I sent him as soon as I came hither; I have now written another to the same, to be delivered whether he be there or elsewhere. And if it be not dispatched through others, I should wish it done by you, wherever you know him to be staying. Farewell, with your whole house, your wife being most lovingly greeted by me.

But by this courier ……, since opportunity of sending letters to Wittenberg is given not rarely, write back. And again farewell; and announce a greeting from me to the **Governor of your castle**, together with the other friends, if I happen to have any remaining among you. I pray for you all that this coming Year be auspicious and salubrious.

And now a third time, and many times, farewell.
Given at Wittenberg, the penultimate day of the year 1598.
TYCHO BRAHE

Of the earthquake which shook these shores of Germany twice, on the 16th of December between 6 and 7 in the morning, both here and at Magdeburg and Leipzig and in various other places, I suppose you have heard. If you have experienced anything of the kind among yourselves, or elsewhere in Denmark, tell me. For I judge that tremor to have come from the North or the West. Which, however, by divine clemency, brought no damage in this region.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Anders Sørensen Vedel** (*Andreas Severini Vellejus*, 1542–1616), the Danish historian and **Canon of Ribe** — Tycho's old friend (the addressee also of brahe-t_15710518001, 1571). The MS is a **Langebek excerpt-copy**, which accounts for the lacunae.
- **Significance — the 1598 Wittenberg winter (a key biographical letter).** Tycho narrates the **interrupted journey to Prague**:
 - Summoned to the imperial court "immediately after **Michaelmas** [29 Sept 1598]" through **Coraduz** (Vice-Chancellor) with **Tadeáš Hájek (Hagecius)** mediating, he got as far as **Dresden**, where he learned the **plague** had thrown Prague into confusion — the **Emperor withdrawn** to safety, the **court dispersed**, public business suspended (*iustitium*).
 - From Dresden he wrote ahead; **Barvitius** (the chief imperial secretary) answered that **Rudolf II** welcomed his coming but wished him to wait "at Dresden or nearby until the court reassembles," meanwhile pondering where to settle him.
 - So Tycho **wintered at Wittenberg** — *"in the house once Philip Melanchthon's, now Peucer's,"* whose tenant, **Johann Jessenius**, gave him **more than half the house** for his household. (A celebrated detail: Tycho lodged in **Melanchthon's former Wittenberg house** — now **Caspar Peucer's**, Melanchthon's son-in-law — as Jessenius's guest; cf. brahe-t_15981231001, the same-period Longomontanus letter.)
 - He is completing unfinished printed works and those "specially destined for the Emperor," and having his **womenfolk (*gynaeceum*)** brought from Wandsbek by his son Tycho, awaiting "a larger dwelling … in whose [the Emperor's] decision my whole world is enclosed."
- **Longomontanus at Ribe.** Tycho notes that **Longomontanus** — "formerly my servant, who accompanied me to Magdeburg and brought my womenfolk back to Wandsbek" — was lately **at Ribe**, and asks Vedel to forward an enclosed letter to him (cf. brahe-t_15981231001, brahe-t_15990111001).
- **Persons named.** Anders Sørensen Vedel; **Coraduz** (Vice-Chancellor); **Tadeáš Hájek (Hagecius)**; **Barvitius** (chief secretary); **Philip Melanchthon** (the late owner of the house); **Caspar Peucer** (its present owner); **Johann Jessenius** (Tycho's host); **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus**; Tycho's son (Tycho the Younger); **Rudolf II**; the **Governor of [Ribe] castle** and Vedel's wife (greeted).
- **Textual flags (the witness is a Langebek excerpt).** Several **lacunae/corruptions** are preserved with ellipses and bracketed editorial supplements: the address-line gap (*amico suo ……*); *"si … non fusilem praepedita"* (read as "had I not been hindered"); *"maiore studio … quam …nia … spero etiam constant …"*; *"pro qua ………"*; *"totus mi… clauditur orbis"*; *"Per hunc … ……tius … rescribe."* None obscures the overall sense; left marked, not conjectured.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die penultima Anni 1598* = **30 December 1598**; Wittenberg/Saxony kept the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar. The edition label ("1598. 30. december. Wittenberg") agrees.
- **What this is.** An added paragraph of news preceding the letter's closing courier-and-greetings section (which is what the published tail actually preserves) — Tycho reporting a recent German earthquake to Anders Sørensen Vedel and asking whether it was felt in Denmark too. Written from Wittenberg, where Tycho was then encamped in transit from Wandsbek toward Prague.
- **Crux — "inaudivisse."** The verb is *inaudio*, a later/Neo-Latin near-synonym of *audio* ("to hear, hear tell of"), not a privative ("not to hear"); so "te inaudivisse opinor" reads "I suppose you will have heard [of it]" rather than its surface-tempting negative. Rendered accordingly, but flagged since the *in-* prefix invites misreading.
- **Source note.** The source text has a doubled conjunction, "tam hîc quam Magdeburgi et et Lipsiæ" — reproduced here verbatim and untouched per the house rule; almost certainly a transcription duplication rather than an authorial repetition, but not corrected.
- **Context.** The letter is one of several from this period showing Tycho relaying naturalia (comets, earthquakes) to his correspondents as a matter of course alongside astronomical and personal business; no other source consulted specifically corroborates a 16 December 1598 earthquake at Wittenberg/Magdeburg/Leipzig, so the event itself is reported here only on Tycho's own authority.
- **Correction.** Latin corrected from 'non fusilem praepedita' to 'non fuissem praepeditus' per Dreyer, TBOO VIII p.131. (A second flagged instance, the doubled 'et et' at the pp.132–133 page-break, was checked against Dreyer and found to be genuinely doubled in the edition of record; left unchanged.)

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD CHRISTIANUM LONGOMONTANUM.

S.

QUAS Wandesburgo ad me dedisti literas, eruditissime et amantissime M. CHRISTIERNE, eas hîc Wittebergæ accepi penultimo die huius anni. Refers ab initio in ijs de incuria Typographi Hamburgensis, qua quaternionem ibi relictum non saltem non emendatiorem edidit, sed adhuc magis quam antea corrupit, ut et in priori negligens fuit; sed quid faciendum cum talibus hominibus, qui nec fidem servant, nec quæ profitentur, satis callent? Constitui igitur duos illos quaterniones de motu Lunæ hîc, volente Deo, terse et emendate imprimi curare, ubi et reliquos quatuor Lunam concernentes, quos nunc sub prælo habeo. Ne igitur sis de priori iactura solicitus, et ferendum est, quod averti non potest. Quod vero excusas moram tuam aliquantulam isthic Wandesburgi, apud familiam meam muliebrem, tantum abest ut hoc ægre feram, quin potius tibi gratias habeam, quod id mihi et illis officij præstare volueris, ut non saltem Magdeburgo eos isthuc deduxeris, sed et aliquamdiu cum illis manseris, ne nimis solitariæ essent, donec ANDREAS minister reverteretur. Quoniam vero existimo te res tuas domi ordinasse, ut in Germaniam denuo cogites, aut nunc forte eo reversus sis, cuperem ut me de statu rerum tuarum certiorem redderes. Intellexisti ex ijs, quas ad te dedi, quam primum huc veni, me Wittebergæ hibernare, volente Numine, constituisse, et quæ sint causæ cur sic faciam. Si igitur res tuæ ullo modo id ferrent, ut me accedere posses, feceris mihi rem apprime gratam, nec tibi ipsi infrugiferam. Cum enim et antea a te intellexerim, et hæ tuæ literæ non obscure insinuent, quod in Academiam aliquam exteram ascendere cupias, ubi secundum conditiones atque ætatem honeste vivere possis, poterit id sane aliquantisper non incommode fieri, donec divina providentia res meæ quietum et certum locum in portu exoptato et firmo, concedente uti spero Cæsare, obtinuerint. Tunc melius tibi et tuis commodis prospicere non omittam, interim etiam de liberali sustentatione meis sumptibus tibi providebo, nec quicquam tibi deesse patiar, quod oportuna vivendi ratio exigat. Atque ubi præsens fueris (neque enim de tua erga me voluntate aut obsequio quidquam dubito) plenius de ijs, quæ tibi usui esse poterint, inter nos agemus. Gratum mihi inprimis est, quod de Apologia Antagonistæ mei Scotici refutanda serio cogites, vellem id mature fieri, ut Tomum illum de Cometa anni 77. sic concludere possim, atque interea dum hîc sum, typis absolvere, unâ cum alijs meis operibus antea inceptis, necdum prorsus ad Colophonem deductis. Tu vero mi dilectiss. Domine CHRISTIANE, te in his quam primum resolve; ego tibi et tuis commodis, quantum in me est, nullatenus sum defuturus, sed omni benevolentia et ad meliora semper promovendi amore et animi propensitate prosequar, idque re ipsa potius quam verbis, quam primum se occasio obtulerit, ostendam.

Vale.
Dabantur Witebergæ ex ædibus ...... (ubi nunc cum Domino D. IESSENIO ... conversor) ultimo die anni completi.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO CHRISTEN LONGOMONTANUS.**

Greeting.

The letter you sent me from Wandsbek, most learned and most loving Master Christen, I received here at Wittenberg on the penultimate day of this year. You report, at the beginning of it, on the carelessness of the Hamburg printer, by which the gathering left there he not only did not bring out more correct, but corrupted even more than before — as he was negligent in the former one too. But what is to be done with such men, who neither keep faith, nor are skilled enough in what they profess? I have therefore resolved to have those two gatherings on the motion of the Moon printed here, God willing, cleanly and correctly — where [I have] also the remaining four concerning the Moon, which I now have under the press. So do not be anxious about the former loss; and what cannot be averted must be borne. But that you excuse your somewhat long stay there at Wandsbek, with my womenfolk — so far am I from taking this ill that I rather give you thanks, that you were willing to render this service to me and to them: in that you not only conducted them thither from Magdeburg, but also stayed with them a while, lest they be too solitary, until Andreas the servant returned. And since I judge that you have set your affairs in order at home, so as to think of [coming to] Germany again — or perhaps have now returned thither — I should wish you to inform me of the state of your affairs. You understood, from those [letters] I sent you as soon as I came hither, that I had resolved to winter at Wittenberg, God willing, and what the reasons are why I do so. If, therefore, your affairs would in any way allow that you could come to me, you will have done me a thing exceedingly welcome, and not unfruitful for yourself. For since I have understood before from you, and these your letters not obscurely hint, that you desire to advance to some foreign Academy [university], where, according to your circumstances and age, you may live honourably — this can indeed be done conveniently enough for a while, until, by divine providence, my affairs obtain a quiet and certain place in the wished-for and firm harbour, the Emperor granting it, as I hope. Then I shall not omit to provide better for you and your interests; and meanwhile I shall provide for your liberal maintenance at my own expense, nor shall I let anything be wanting to you that a fitting manner of life requires. And when you are present (for I doubt nothing of your goodwill or compliance toward me) we shall treat more fully between us of the things that may be of use to you. It is especially welcome to me that you are seriously thinking of refuting the *Apologia* of my Scottish antagonist; I should wish it done in good time, so that I may thus conclude that Tome on the Comet of the year [15]77, and meanwhile, while I am here, finish it in print, together with my other works begun earlier, not yet quite brought to the colophon. But do you, my most beloved Lord Christen, resolve yourself in these matters as soon as possible; I, for my part, will in no way fail you and your interests, so far as in me lies, but will pursue you with all benevolence, and with a love and inclination of mind ever to promote you to better things — and this I will show by the deed itself rather than by words, as soon as occasion offers.

Farewell.
Given at Wittenberg, from the house …… (where I now dwell with Lord Doctor Jessenius …) on the last day of the completed year.
TYCHO BRAHE,
with my own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus** (Christian Severin, 1562–1647), Tycho's senior assistant and the most gifted of his *familia* — here addressed *M. Christierne / Domine Christiane*, "Master Christen." After years at Hven he had left Tycho's service to settle his affairs in Denmark; this letter presses him to rejoin Tycho in Germany. (One of a close sequence of Tycho→Longomontanus letters from the Wittenberg winter; cf. brahe-t_15990111001, two weeks later.)
- **The Hamburg printer and the lunar theory (printing history).** Longomontanus had reported the **incompetence of the Hamburg printer**, who botched a *quaternio* (gathering) of the **lunar-theory** text — corrupting it further instead of correcting it. Tycho resolves to reprint **those two gatherings *de motu Lunae*** at **Wittenberg**, where he already has "the remaining four concerning the Moon … under the press." This is the printing of the **lunar theory** for the *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata* (the great work then dragging toward completion); "do not be anxious about the former loss — what cannot be averted must be borne."
- **Longomontanus's service to Tycho's household.** Tycho warmly thanks him for escorting his **womenfolk** (*familia muliebris* — wife Kirsten and the daughters) **from Magdeburg to Wandsbek** and staying with them "lest they be too solitary, until **Andreas** the servant returned" — a humane domestic glimpse of the exile years.
- **The offer of patronage.** Tycho, wintering at Wittenberg and awaiting (as he hopes) a settled "harbour" under the **Emperor**, urges Longomontanus to come to him: he may meanwhile "advance to some foreign **Academy**" suited to his age and station, while Tycho **maintains him liberally at his own expense** and promises to "provide better" once his own affairs are secure. The "wished-for and firm harbour … the Emperor granting it" anticipates the move to Bohemia.
- **The Craig controversy (cometary polemic).** *Apologia Antagonistae mei Scotici* = the **Apologia of John Craig** (*Joannes Craigius*), the Scottish mathematician who had disputed claims in Tycho's *"Tome on the Comet of 1577"* — i.e. the second volume of the *Progymnasmata*-complex, **_De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis_** (on the comet of 1577). Tycho is delighted that **Longomontanus will write the refutation**, so that he can **conclude and print that Tome** while at Wittenberg, "together with my other works … not yet brought to the colophon." (The Craig exchange runs through the 1589–90 correspondence, e.g. brahe-t_15900125001.)
- **Lodging with Jessenius.** *cum Domino D. Jessenio … conversor* — Tycho records that at Wittenberg he is **living with Johannes Jessenius** (the anatomist), the same friend who recurs in brahe-t_16000327002 and brahe-t_16001008001.
- **Persons named.** Longomontanus; the Hamburg printer (unnamed); Tycho's womenfolk; **Andreas** the servant; **John Craig** (the "Scottish antagonist"); **Johannes Jessenius**; the **Emperor** (Rudolf II).
- **Lacunae (flagged).** The dateline is defective in the witness (a Langebek *afskrift*): the **house-name is lost** (*ex aedibus ……*) and there is a gap in the parenthesis (*cum Domino D. Jessenio … conversor*); marked with ellipses, not conjectured.
- **Calendar / date.** *ultimo die anni completi* = **the last day of the completed year = 31 December 1598**; received by Tycho *penultimo die huius anni* (30 December). Wittenberg/Saxony kept the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar. The edition label gives only the place ("Wittenberg") with **no date**; the date is supplied from the dateline and identifier (15981231001) — noted.

text.original:
GENIO, INGENIO, GENERE VIRO EXIMIE DECORATO ET CONSPICUO OLIGERO ROSENKRANTZIO, AMICO CONSANGVINEO, AFFINI INTEGERRIMO. ROSENHOLM.

S. P.

SCRIPSI tibi, desideratiss. mi OLIGERE, quamprimum huc Witebergam veni, et de statu rerum mearum te certiorem reddidi, quas literas te accepisse existimo, ideoque ijs indicata repetere nolo. Cum vero commodum sese obtulisset hic Tabellarius, qui se etiam Arhusiam venturum aiebat, non intermittendum duxi, quin aliquas saltem denuo ad te darem. Cupio autem per eundem ex te cognoscere, quomodo vivas et valeas, et quid rerum agas, tum quoque, si quid mea interest scire, ut fideliter et amice significes. Ego hîc volente Numine hybernabo, cum Bohemiam nunc ingredi lues Epidemica illic magis magisque invalescens non sinat, Cæsare ipso vix ibi locum satis huius contagij convenientem inveniente, ut ob id eum inde excedere animum induxisse nonnulli referant. Familia mea muliebris necdum advenit, pro qua adducenda misi TYCHONEM filium cum equis et curribus meis. Quam primum advenerit, quod intra paucos dies futurum existimo, equos in nundinis Lipsensibus distrahere constitui, ne mihi sint, interea dum hîc subsisto, oneri. Facile, uti spero, alios instante vere recepturus. Interea Typographicum laborem urgeo, ut compleantur Libri mei, in Dania non absoluti, nec etiam prorsus Wandesburgi. Paro adhuc alios pro Cæsare, quantum otium hoc ferre poterit.

Cæterum hoc insuper incidit, quod antea exciderat, ut te interrogarem de duobus illis libris Regi vestro offerendis, an id factum sit, necne. Si exhibiti sunt, cupio scire, per quem, et quomodo excepti, et a quo postea accepti, cum is, uti constat, talibus non afficiatur, quæ tamen omnia parum moror, veluti etiam nullam inde gratiam aut affectavi aut speravi, uti neque antea ex tot non sine meo damno meritis ullam promereri potui, quod pariter ex alto negligo. Sin vero hi libri adhuc penes te sunt, cuperem eos bene ab iniuria aëris et pluviarum munitos (quod per lineum cera imbutum facile præstatur) per hunc Tabellarium mihi remitti, quo in quibusdam eos recognoscere et locupletare queam, præsertim quoad stellarum restitutionem, et addito deinde tertio quodam eiusdem formæ et magnitudinis, quem etiam Cæsari dedico; omnes enim tres, præfixo singulis peculiari Epigrammate, Regi in Comitijs proximæ æstatis exhiberi, Deo volente, procurabo, sive per te sive per alium quempiam ex meis, si tibi id non fuerit commodum. Adiungentur, uti spero, quædam alia ex meis operibus, hisce maiora, ut videant vestrates, si quos ea cura tangat, me isthic non fuisse otiosum, nec tempus inutiliter collocasse, nostrosque labores non ob id negligi aut interire, quod quidam ex ijs eos pessundare conati sint. Habeo etiam alias rationes, cur sic fieri velim, nec censuris contrarijs, undecunque petitis, afficior.

Cum Dresdæ essem, adfuit mihi IVARDUS FRISIUS, fratrem Regis comitatus; is forte tibi nonnulla de me rettulit, aut alijs. Vellem eum satis attentum fuisse, ut adhuc plura referre potuisset, non tam tibi quam ijs. Si memoriam, vel potius facundiam eius inaudivisti, indicatione pande, et quomodo illa intellecta acceptaque fuerint. Scis quid velim, de pluribus etiam, uti et prius rogavi, me (cum tam certus adsit internuntius) commonefacias; Exemplaria omnium librorum meorum, tam alibi quam hîc absolutorum, brevi, favente Deo, obtinebis, ut duorum illorum, quos habuisti, iactura cum fœnore resarciatur. Salutavi nuper ex te, quamvis non rogatus, Doctorem HUNNIUM, cum simul in arce, unâ cum alijs Professoribus, a Præside invitati essemus. Is te vicissim resalutat. Quin et alii hîc Professores, qui te norunt et plurimi faciunt, salutem tibi dicunt. Inter quos etiam est Hospes meus Dominus D. IOHANNES IESSENIUS. Vale cum Coniuge tua, mea Nepte, quam felicissime, et instantem annum, feliciter inchoatum, quam prosperrime etiam absolvite, multosque insuper alios. Et his proximis det Deus, ut vobis ludat ROSENKRANTZIUS [in] aula Parvulus. Saluta Matrem, coniugem, et amicos meos, si quos absentia mei adhuc memores esse admittit.

Dabantur properanter Witeberga, pridie novi Anni 1599.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the man eminently adorned and conspicuous in character, talent, and birth, Holger Rosenkrantz, [my] most upright friend, kinsman, [and] relative. [At] Rosenholm.**

Heartiest greeting.

I wrote to you, my most longed-for Holger, as soon as I came hither to Wittenberg, and informed you of the state of my affairs — which letter I think you have received, and so I will not repeat what was indicated in it. But since this courier offered himself conveniently, who said he would also come to **Aarhus**, I thought I should not omit to give you at least some [letter] again. I desire, by the same [courier], to learn from you how you live and fare, and what you are doing; and also, if there be anything it concerns me to know, that you faithfully and amicably signify it. I will here, God willing, winter, since the **epidemic plague** — growing ever stronger there — does not now allow me to enter Bohemia, the Emperor himself scarcely finding there a place sufficiently free of this contagion (so that some report he has resolved to depart thence). My **womenfolk** have not yet arrived, for whose bringing I sent my son Tycho with my horses and carriages; as soon as they arrive, which I think will be within a few days, I have resolved to sell the horses at the **Leipzig fair**, lest they be a burden to me while I stay here — hoping easily to get others in the coming spring. Meanwhile I press the typographic labour, that my books may be completed (not finished in Denmark, nor quite at Wandsbek); and I am still preparing others for the Emperor, as far as this leisure will allow.

For the rest, this moreover occurs to me, which had earlier slipped [my mind]: that I should ask you about **those two books to be offered to your King** — whether it was done or not. If they were presented, I desire to know by whom, and how received, and by whom afterward taken — since he, as is well known, is not affected by such things; all which, however, I little regard, just as I neither sought nor hoped for any favour thence (as neither before could I earn any from so many merits, not without my loss) — which I likewise disregard from on high. But if these books are still with you, I should wish them — well protected from the injury of air and rains (which is easily done with linen soaked in wax) — sent back to me by this courier, so that I may revise and enrich them in certain [respects], **especially as regards the restitution of the stars**; and then, **a third of the same form and size being added — which I also dedicate to the Emperor** — for all three, a special **Epigram** prefixed to each, I will, God willing, have **presented to the King at the Diet of next summer**, whether through you or through some other of mine, if it be not convenient for you. There will be added, as I hope, certain other of my works, greater than these, that your countrymen — if any be touched by that care — may see that I have not been idle abroad, nor spent my time uselessly, and that our labours are not neglected or perishing because **some of them tried to ruin them**. I have also other reasons why I wish it so done; nor am I moved by contrary censures, sought from wherever.

When I was at **Dresden**, **Ivar Friis** was with me, accompanying the King's brother; he perhaps reported some things about me to you, or to others. I could wish he had been attentive enough to report yet more — not so much to you as to those [others]. If you have heard of his memory — or rather his eloquence — disclose it by some indication, and how those things were understood and received. You know what I wish; about more things too, as I asked before, remind me (since so sure a messenger is at hand). You will soon, God favouring, obtain copies of all my books, finished both elsewhere and here, so that the loss of those two you had may be repaid with interest. I lately greeted **Doctor Hunnius** on your behalf, though unasked, when we were together invited to the castle, with other Professors, by the Governor; he greets you back. Nay, other Professors here too, who know you and esteem you greatly, send you greeting — among whom is also my host, Lord Doctor **Johann Jessenius**. Farewell, with your wife, my niece, most happily; and complete the coming year, happily begun, as prosperously as may be, and many others besides. And in these next [years] may God grant that **a little Rosenkrantz may play for you in the hall**. Greet your mother, wife, and my friends, if my absence allows any to be still mindful of me.

Given in haste from Wittenberg, the day before the new year 1599.
Your Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient & date.** **Holger Rosenkrantz** at **Rosenholm**, addressed with the alliterative flourish *Genio, Ingenio, Genere* ("in character, talent, and birth"). Dated *pridie novi Anni 1599* = **31 December 1598** — one of the three same-day Wittenberg letters (with brahe-t_15981231001 to Longomontanus and brahe-t_15981230001 to Vedel, 30 Dec). The MS is a later Langebek *afskrift*.
- **The Wittenberg winter.** Tycho confirms he is **wintering at Wittenberg** because the **plague** bars Bohemia (even the Emperor "scarcely finding a place free of contagion," reportedly about to leave); his **womenfolk** are being brought by his son Tycho with horses and carriages (to be sold at the **Leipzig fair**); he presses the **printing** of his unfinished books and prepares "others for the Emperor."
- **Significance — the two books the Danish King kept, and the three-book Diet plan (cross-ref to brahe-t_15990920001).** Tycho asks whether **the two books offered to King Christian IV** were ever presented, and how received — noting drily that the King "is not affected by such things," and that he himself "neither sought nor hoped for any favour." (This is the same pair of books that, per **Henrik Ramel's letter to Sophie Brahe**, brahe-t_15990920001, **the King retained "because your dear brother had given them" though he cared little for them**.) If the books are **still with Holger**, Tycho wants them **sent back** (wrapped in wax-soaked linen against the weather) so he can **revise and enrich them — "especially as to the restitution of the stars" — add a third of the same format dedicated to the Emperor**, prefix a **special epigram** to each, and have **all three presented to the King at next summer's Diet**, alongside greater works — "that your countrymen … may see that I have not been idle abroad … and that our labours do not perish because some tried to ruin them" (a pointed allusion to his Danish detractors).
- **Persons & news.** *Ivardus Frisius* = **Ivar Friis**, who at **Dresden** had accompanied **the Danish King's brother** and may have reported on Tycho; *Doctor Hunnius* = **Aegidius Hunnius** (1550–1603), the Wittenberg theologian, greeted at a castle dinner given by the Governor; **Johann Jessenius**, Tycho's host at Wittenberg (cf. brahe-t_15981230001, brahe-t_15981231001). The closing wish — *"may a little Rosenkrantz play for you in the hall"* — hopes for a son for Holger and his wife (**Tycho's niece**, Sophie Brahe, Axel Brahe's daughter).
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Witeberga, pridie novi Anni 1599* = **31 December 1598**; Wittenberg/Saxony kept the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar. (The edition label "1598. 31. december" agrees.)

documents.incipit: VIR Illris. Gratissimæ fuerunt mihi literæ Dominationis Tuæ, tum quod præcipuum erga me …

text.original:
FERDINANDUS MAGNUS ETRURIÆ DUX AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

VIR Illris. Gratissimæ fuerunt mihi literæ Dominationis Tuæ, tum quod præcipuum erga me præseferant amorem atque benevolentiam, tum etiam quod per eas occasionem oblatam video mutuæ voluntatis meæ aliquo erga eius Dm officij genere declarandæ. Nam licet ipsa mihi de facie, ut eius quoque testantur literæ, ignota fuerit, ea tamen, quæ de ipsius nomine ac virtute circunferuntur, Dm Tm non minus mihi claram quam notam reddere potuerunt. Sed quando ipsa fama ad id non sufficeret, hanc tamen ex ijs duobus voluminibus quæ ad me misit, et in quibus vera hominis species innotescit, abunde consequi potuissem. Cuius quidem muneris pro eo ac debeo Di Tæ gratias ago. Illud enim propter subiectæ rei et novi operis rationem charissimum mihi fuit, et si quid otij dabitur aliquando, utar etiam ad illud opus visendum, alicuius in ea re versato legentis opera. Et si illud commode fieri poterit, ut reliqua Dis T. opera, qualiacunque hactenus in lucem prodierunt aut in posterum prodibunt, ad me transmittantur, pro certo habeat in loco me non exigui muneris habiturum. Quod vero ad illum adolescentem attinet, quem mihi maxime commendavit, dabo operam, quemadmodum etiam hactenus factum est, ut et ipse intelligat, quanti ponderis apud me fuerit Dis Tæ commendatio, et ipsa quoque cognoscat posse se ac debere non in hac solummodo re, sed in quacunque alia, quæ videri possit ad eius Dis existimationem et commodum pertinere, omnia a me semper officia polliceri. Quod reliquum est, Deum opt. max. præcor ut Dm Tm diutius servet incolumem, quo de præclarissimis artibus ac literarum studijs benemereri longius possit.

Datum .......
text.english:
**Ferdinand, Grand Duke of Tuscany, to Tycho Brahe.**

Illustrious Man. Your Lordship's letters were most pleasing to me — both because they bear before [me] a special love and benevolence toward me, and also because through them I see an occasion offered for declaring my mutual goodwill toward your Lordship by some kind of office. For although you have been unknown to me by face — as your letters too attest — yet those things which are circulated about your name and virtue have been able to render your Lordship to me no less illustrious than known. But even if fame itself did not suffice for that, I could nonetheless have abundantly attained it from those two volumes which you sent me, and in which the true likeness of the man becomes known. For which gift, indeed, I give your Lordship thanks, as I ought. For it was most dear to me, on account of the nature of the subject-matter and of the new work; and if any leisure shall ever be given, I will also use, for viewing that work, the help of some reader versed in that matter. And if it can conveniently be done that the rest of your Lordship's works — whatever have hitherto come into the light, or shall come forth hereafter — be transmitted to me, let him hold for certain that I shall reckon it in the place of no small gift. But as concerns that young man whom he most strongly commended to me, I will give effort — as also has been done hitherto — both that he himself may understand how much weight your Lordship's recommendation had with me, and that your Lordship too may know that you can and ought to promise yourself all good offices from me always — not in this matter only, but in any other which may seem to pertain to your Lordship's estimation and advantage. For what remains, I pray God Best and Greatest to preserve your Lordship long unharmed, that you may be able the longer to deserve well of the most excellent arts and the studies of letters.

Given …….

documents.apparatus:
- **The Grand Duke's reply.** This is **Ferdinando I de' Medici**'s gracious answer to Tycho's recommendation-and-book-gift of 1598 (brahe-t_15981108001). He thanks Tycho for the **two volumes** sent ("in which the true likeness of the man becomes known"), asks that **the rest of Tycho's works**, past and future, be sent too, and confirms his patronage of **the young man** Tycho had recommended. The witness survives in the **Medici archive** at Florence (Archivio Mediceo, vol. 65).
- ***duo volumina*** = the two of Tycho's printed works given in 1598 (see brahe-t_15981108001 apparatus); *ille adolescens, quem mihi commendavit* = the recommended youth (probably Tengnagel — *identification flagged* there).
- **Chancery third person.** The Grand Duke writes of Tycho in the third person throughout (*Dominatio Tua* / *eius Dominatio* — "your Lordship" / "his Lordship"), the formula of princely letters; rendered accordingly.
- **⚠ Date.** The source breaks off at *Datum …….* — **the dateline is lost** in the witness. The edition assigns the year **1599** (identifier …0000…, label "1599, empty"); the day and month are **not recoverable** and are not invented. Florence (Tuscany, Catholic) used New Style, but no date survives to mark.

- **§1 Dreyer collation:** located at *Opera Omnia* VIII, **p. 156** (witness *E codice Florentino Archivii publici Medicei vol. 65*); Dreyer's index pointer "VIII 154" is an index error. The lost dateline (*Datum......*) is reproduced by Dreyer — genuinely lost in the edition of record, not a transcription gap. **Open reading:** Dreyer prints *praescieras* (2nd-sg.) where the working transcription has *praeseferant* (3rd-pl.); the translation follows *praeseferant* — flagged for review.

documents.incipit: MEIN freundlichenn grueß mit wunschung alles guthen zuuor, ehrnuester vnndt achtbar, …

text.original:
DEM EHRNUESTENN VNND ACHTBARNN ANDREASS MEYERN, FURSTLICHEN MECKELBURGISCHENN RENTMEISTERN VND RATH, MEINEM JNSONDERS GUNSTIGEN VNNDT GUTENN FREUNDT. WISMAR.

MEIN freundlichenn grueß mit wunschung alles guthen zuuor, ehrnuester vnndt achtbar, gunstiger herr renttmeister, besonder guter freundt. Jch kann euch freundtlich nicht bergenn, welchergestalt mir meine elteste tochter anhero zugeschriebenn vnnd zuuernemen gegebenn, daß sie ahnn euch schreibenn vnnd vonn denn baldt betagtenn zinßenn ein zwey hundert taller auffnehmenn lassenn wolte, zweiffell derowegenn nicht, denn das solches beschehenn sein werde, vnnd jhr dargegenn gedachter meiner tochter handtschrifft zuhandenn empfangenn habenn, welche eben souill gelttenn alß wann jchs selbst gethan hette, sollenn auch hernechst wider geburlich gekurtzet werdenn. Jch habe vor etzlichenn wochenn einen eigenen bottenn inn Dennemarckenn abgeferttiget, der meinung, daß mir etzlich geldt von meinen doselbst noch außstehendenn haubtsummen vbersendet werdenn solte. Dieweil es aber itzo vielleicht der winter oder anders was verhindert, kann jch nicht wißenn, wie balt jch dasselbe geldt vberkommenn könne, vnndt jch gleichwoll itziger zeit inn diesenn frembdenn örternn geldes wolbenöttiget, sintemalln jch mich mit denn meinen inn die zwölff personnen starck vnndt souil pferde inn die funff wochen zu Dreßdenn aufgehaltenn, zugeschweigen was mir sonsten auf dem wege gekostet, worvber mein zehrgeldt, welchs jch zur Pragischen reise mitgenommen, aussgangenn, alß ist derowegenn ahn euch mein freundliches bittenn, jhr wollenn mir die freundtschafft beweisenn, vnndt noch zwey hundert thaller mit diesenn wittembergischen fuhrmann Dauidt gegenn vberantworttung meiner quitantz, welche jch ihme zu handen zugestellet, vberschickenn, vnndt jhme dieselbenn, wenn ehr vonn Rostock wider zu ruck auf Gustrow kumpt, empfangenn lassenn, daß ihr es mitlerzeit alda bestellen wollet.

Die victualienn, welche jch vonn euch empfangenn, belangend, bitte jch mir vnschwer zuerke[nnen] zugebenn, was sie kostenn, sollenn in den zinßen nichtweniger auch abgezogenn vnnd gerechnet werdenn. Jnn diesenn erzeiget ihr mir ahnitzo einen sonderlichenn angenehmen dienst, vnndt jch bin es vmb euch mit wunschung eines glucksehligenn neuwen jahrs jedertzeit hinwider zubeschuldenn geflissenn vnnd bereitwillig, vnndt thue euch göttlicher almacht befehlenn.

Datum Wittemberg denn 9. januarij a:o 99.
Eur a[ller]f[r]w[ndlichster]
Tycho Brahe
eigenhd.
text.english:
**To the honourable and worshipful Andreas Meier, princely Mecklenburg rent-master and councillor, my especially favourable and good friend. Wismar.**

My friendly greeting, with the wish of all good, beforehand. Honourable and worshipful, favourable Lord rent-master, especial good friend: I cannot, in friendship, conceal from you in what manner my eldest daughter has written to me here, and given me to understand, that she meant to write to you and have a couple of hundred thalers taken up from the soon-falling-due interest. I do not doubt, therefore, that this will have been done, and that you have received in return my said daughter's bond to hand — which is worth just as much as if I had given it myself — and these [thalers] shall hereafter be duly deducted [from the account]. Some weeks ago I dispatched a special messenger into Denmark, in the expectation that some money should be sent me from my principal sums still outstanding there. But since now perhaps the winter, or something else, hinders it, I cannot know how soon I may obtain that money; and I am withal, at this time, in these foreign parts, in good need of money — seeing that I have stayed some five weeks at Dresden with my people, some twelve persons strong and as many horses, not to mention what it otherwise cost me on the road, whereby my travel-money, which I took along for the Prague journey, has run out. So my friendly request to you, therefore, is that you would show me the kindness and send me another two hundred thalers by this Wittenberg carter David, against delivery of my receipt (which I have handed to him); and have the same paid to him when he comes back from Rostock to Güstrow — so that you would meanwhile have it made ready there.

As for the victuals which I received from you, I ask you to let me know, without difficulty, what they cost; they shall, no less, be likewise deducted and reckoned against the interest. In this you now render me an especially welcome service; and I am, with the wish of a happy New Year, at all times zealous and ready to deserve it of you in return. And I commend you to divine omnipotence.

Given at Wittenberg, the 9th of January, in the year '99.
Your most friendly,
Tycho Brahe
in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender & moment.** **Tycho Brahe** at **Wittenberg**, January 1599 — mid-migration, between his departure from Denmark (1597) and his establishment in Bohemia (1599). The letter is the **earliest** of the Tycho↔Meier series and the **financial backstory** to the later debt crisis: it shows the *normal* working of the relationship — Tycho drawing cash advances against the interest on capital he had lent the Mecklenburg house, through its rent-master, while travelling.
- **Recipient.** **Andreas Meier**, *fürstlich-mecklenburgischer Rentmeister und Rat* at **Wismar** — here in routine, cordial dealings, two years before the acrimony of 1601 (brahe-t_16010527001, brahe-t_16010718001).
- **The transaction.**
 - Tycho's **eldest daughter** had arranged to draw ** c. 200 thalers** against the *bald betagte Zinsen* ("soon-falling-due interest"), giving Meier her own **bond (*Handschrift*)** — which Tycho ratifies as binding as his own.
 - Tycho asks for **a further 200 thalers** by the **Wittenberg carter David**, against a receipt, payable when David returns from Rostock to **Güstrow** — his travel-funds (*Zehrgeld*) for the Prague journey having run out after a **five-week stay at Dresden** with a party of "twelve persons and as many horses."
 - He had sent a messenger to **Denmark** to draw on capital still outstanding there, but feared winter would delay it.
 - The **victuals (*Victualien*)** Meier had supplied are to be costed and set against the interest.
- **Persons named.**
 - *meine älteste Tochter* = Tycho's **eldest daughter** (Magdalene Brahe), acting on his account.
 - *der wittenbergische Fuhrmann David* = the **Wittenberg carter David**, the courier/cash-bearer.
- **Places.** *Wittemberg* (place of issue); *Wismar* (Meier's seat); *Dresden* (the five-week stop); *Rostock*, *Güstrow* (the Mecklenburg payment-points); *Dänemark* (outstanding capital); the *Pragische Reise* (the Prague journey ahead).
- **Formulae & abbreviations.** Burgher-courteous register; subscription *Eur allerfreundlichster* ("Your most friendly") + *eigenhändig* ("in his own hand," autograph). *Datum* → "Given."
- **Calendar.** Dateline *den 9. Januarij a:o 99* at Wittenberg; no style marker. Lutheran Saxony kept the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar in 1599; reproduced as written, not converted. (The year is given as "99.")
- **Correction.** Restored the approximative hedge of the German 'in die zwölf... in die fünf Wochen' ('some twelve... some five weeks'), confirmed idiomatic (not exact) by Dreyer's print (TBOO XIV p.149); the translation had previously stated both as precise counts.

documents.title: Tycho Brahe → [Andreas Meyer, Mecklenburg rent-master] — Wittenberg, 10 January 1599 [O.S.]

edition.print_label: Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia (1913–29)
edition.tboo_cite: Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, ed. I.L.E. Dreyer, Tom. XIV, Hauniæ 1929, p. 150, no. 158

witnesses.raw: A Schwerin, Landeshauptarchiv Schwerin, Renterei-Akten. Originalbrev

documents.abstract: A formal quittance acknowledging receipt of two hundred reichsthaler in advance interest from rent-master Andreas Meyer, signed and sealed at Wittenberg.
documents.incipit: JCH Tycho Brahe, erbgesessenn zu Knudtstrup im reiche Dennemarckenn vnnd kön: maytt: alda …

text.original:
JCH Tycho Brahe, erbgesessenn zu Knudtstrup im reiche Dennemarckenn vnnd kön: maytt: alda ambtman auf Vraniburgk, vrkunde vnd bekenne hiemit inn crafft dieses, daß jch vonn dem ehrnuesten vnnd achtbarnn Andreaß Meyernn, furstlichenn meckelburgischenn junger herrschafft verordenten rentmeister, zwey hundert reichsthaller zinße, so erst auf schieristkommendenn monnat aprilis dieses neun vnndt neuntzigstenn jahrs betaget sein wurden, heut dato auff rechnung entpfangenn habe. Thue derowegenn gedachtenn herrnn rentmeister solcher woll entpfangenenn zwey hundert thaller, alß werenn dieselbigenn auf obberurtenn termin erleget vnnd betzalet gentzlichenn wie es zu rechte am krefftigstenn vnnd bestendigstenn geschehenn solle, quitirenn vnnd loßsagenn. Zu mehrer vrkundt hab jch diese quitanz mit eig[enen handt] vnterschriben vnnd mein angeborn pitzschafft hierauff gedruckt.

Actum Wittemberg denn zehenden tag januarij anno 99.
Tycho Brahe
eigenhd.

(l.s.)
text.english:
I, Tycho Brahe, hereditary lord at Knudstrup in the kingdom of Denmark, and His Royal Majesty's bailiff [*Amtmann*] there at Uraniborg, attest and acknowledge hereby, by force of this [document], that I have today, on account, received from the honourable and respectable Andreas Meyer — appointed rent-master of the princely Mecklenburg junior lordship — two hundred reichsthaler of interest, which were to fall due only in the next coming month of April of this ninety-ninth year. I therefore acquit and release the said Master rent-master of these two hundred well-received thaler, as though the same had been fully discharged and paid at the aforementioned term — as may, in law, be done in the most effective and binding manner. In further attestation I have signed this quittance with my own hand, and pressed my hereditary seal hereupon.

Done at Wittenberg, the tenth day of January, in the year [15]99.
Tycho Brahe,
in his own hand.

(Place of the seal.)

documents.title: Tycho Brahe → Christen Sørensen Longomontanus — Wittenberg, 11 January 1599 [O.S.]

edition.print_label: Dänische Bibliothek (Copenhagen 1738–47)

documents.abstract: Urges Longomontanus to travel to Wittenberg, offers travel funds, and proposes either the Imperial Mathematician post at Prague or an academic position at Wittenberg.
documents.incipit: CHARISSIME M. CHRISTIERNE, bis tibi scripsi, postquam huc Witebergam veni, quas literas …
documents.editorial_note: **Text recovered.** 14 words missing from inside this letter — dropped by a defective transcription of the source — have been restored from the text of record and translated into place.

text.original:
TYCHO
BRAHE AD CHRISTIANUM LONGOMONTANUM.

S.

CHARISSIME M. CHRISTIERNE, bis tibi
scripsi, postquam huc Witebergam veni,
quas literas accepisse te utrasque reor, vel saltem alteras. Cuperem, ut ad me
huc accederes, antequam denuo Pragam versus
iter suscipiam. Fiet id cum tuo emolumento. Si viatico cares, suppeditabit tibi
hic auriga, ego illi restituam. Intellexi ex tuis, antequam Wandesbecho
abires, mihi scriptis, conditionem in aliqua Academia te optare hîc in
Germania, s[ignifica mihi an]
Pragæ isti, qui se Cæsaris Mathematicum iactat,
succedere velis (brevi enim ille se subducet, si modo iam factum non
sit) sin tibi non placuerit, effi
ciam
ut ....... eo vocetur, nec is ab [hoc] munere suscipiendo abhorret; [tunc]
operam dabo, ut tu hîc Witebergæ in eius locum substituare .......re, cum præsente
plura ad ........ quavis alia ratione expete ....... commodis, quantum in me
est, studebo.

Vale.

Raptim Witebergæ inter
plurimas occupationes die 11. Ian. Anno 99.

TYCHO BRAHE,
manu
propria.

Habes hîc literas a BRASCHIO
Poëta, Dresda mihi missas et fortuito
resignatas.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Christen Longomontanus.**

Greeting.

Dearest Master Christen, I have written to you twice since I came here to Wittenberg — both which letters I think you have received, or at least one of them. I could wish that you would come to me here, before I undertake the journey toward Prague again. It will be done to your profit. If you lack travel-money, the carrier here will supply it to you; I will repay him. I understood from your [letter] written to me before you departed from Wandsbek that you desire a position in some Academy here in Germany. [Signify to me whether] you wish to succeed that fellow at Prague who boasts himself the Emperor's Mathematician (for he will shortly withdraw himself, if it has not already been done); but if it should not please you, I will bring it about that […] be summoned thither — and he does not shrink from undertaking [this] office; [then] I will give my effort that you be substituted here at Wittenberg in his place […], since, with you present, [I could say] more things to […]. By whatever other means seek […]; for your advantages, as much as is in me, I will strive.

Farewell.
Hastily, at Wittenberg, amid very many occupations, the 11th day of January, in the year [15]99.
Tycho Brahe,
in his own hand.

*[Postscript:]* POSTSCRIPT. Here you have letters from Braschius the Poet, sent to me from Dresden, and opened by accident.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus** (Christian Severin "Longomontanus," 1562–1647), Tycho's longest-serving and ablest Danish assistant, later professor at Copenhagen and author of the *Astronomia Danica* (1622). At the start of 1599 he had recently left Tycho's service (after the Wandsbek period) and was seeking an academic post in Germany; Tycho here tries to draw him back before departing for Prague.
- **"That fellow at Prague who boasts himself the Emperor's Mathematician"** = **Nicolai Reimers Bär (Ursus)**, the Imperial Mathematician and Tycho's plagiarism-adversary (see brahe-t_16000727001). Tycho — confident that Ursus "will shortly withdraw himself" (Ursus left Prague in 1599 and died in 1600) — dangles the imperial mathematicianship before Longomontanus, with a fallback scheme to install Longomontanus at Wittenberg instead.
- ***viaticum*** — travel-money; *auriga* — the carter/driver who would advance it.
- **⚠ Textual lacunae.** The witness (a Langebek transcript) is **damaged**, with several gaps marked by the editor's *.......* (and one bracketed restoration, *s[ignifica mihi an]*). The lost passages name (a) the substitute Tycho would have "summoned" to Prague in Longomontanus's stead, and (b) the precise Wittenberg arrangement; these are **not reconstructed** here. Gaps are rendered "[…]"; the bracketed editorial restoration is kept as printed.
- **Calendar.** *Witebergae … die 11. Ian. Anno 99* = **11 January 1599**, Wittenberg (Lutheran Saxony) = **Old Style**. Header agrees with the label. (Written two days after the Mecklenburg quittance brahe-t_15990110001, also from Wittenberg.)
- **A postscript recovered entire.** This letter's existing English translation currently ends flatly at the signature, with no postscript at all; the gap restores the opening of one, enclosing a letter (or letters — Latin "literas" is grammatically plural but idiomatically often covers a single letter) from "Braschius the Poet," sent from Dresden, which Tycho says he had opened by accident.
- **Identifying Braschius.** An independent letter from Nicolaus Braschius to Tycho Brahe, dated 8 August 1600, Rostock, is on record (Basel, Universitätsbibliothek, G I 23; brahe-t_16000808001 in this corpus) — confirming Braschius as a real, otherwise-attested correspondent active in Tycho's circle in this period, evidently a poet with Saxon/Dresden connections.
- **The courier detail.** "Fortuito resignatas" (opened by chance) is a small courtesy-note: Tycho is explaining, to Longomontanus, why an enclosure addressed elsewhere arrives already unsealed.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Read TBOO VIII p.136 (Dreyer, 'Tycho Brahe ad Christianum Longomontanum') as a page image; letter entire on this page. The Latin is genuinely damaged in the original (Dreyer himself prints '.......' lacunae and bracketed conjectural supplements '[hoc]', '[tunc]', 's[ignifica mihi an]'); our transcribed original reproduces every lacuna, bracket and conjectural word in the same positions as Dreyer, letter for letter. The English translation handles every gap correctly with matching bracketed/ellipsis markers and does not smuggle in invented content to fill the damaged spans; the intact clauses (travel money, the succession to the 'Caesaris Mathematicum' at Prague, the postscript about Braschius' letter from Dresden) are all rendered accurately. Despite the letter's the translator's own grade Possible (presumably a caution flag for the heavy lacunae), collation found no fabrication, omission, or mistranslation — the damaged passages are honestly marked as such in both source and translation, which is the correct practice, not a defect.

documents.abstract: Transmits the Emperor's command summoning Tycho immediately to Prague and expresses personal eagerness to meet him in person.
documents.incipit: ILLUSTRIS ac Clarissime eques et Domine obserme. Sacra Caesarea Maiestas Dominus noster …

text.original:
DEM EDLEN VNNDT GESTRENGEN RITTER HERRN TYCHO BRAHE ZU KNUDSTORP MEYNEM SONDERS GUNSTIGEN VND VIELGELIEBTEN HERRENN.
TRESEN ODER WITTENBERGK.

ILLUSTRIS ac Clarissime eques et Domine obserme. Sacra Caesarea Maiestas Dominus noster Clementissimus mandavit mihi, ut Illustrem Dominationem tuam statim huc vocem, cui hisce meis humillime obsequi et debui et volui. Curet itaque Dominatio Tua Illustris quam diligentissime, ut quam primum poterit, se ad iter accingat, sicque coram Caesare hîc Pragae statuat, ut is hac in parte in Dominatione tua illustri, vel etiam me ipso, ne minimum quidem defuisse animadvertat. Porro de hac Illustris D. T. personae Augusta evocatione non tam D. T. Illri gratulor, quam mihi ipsi. Mirum in modum gaudeo, utpote qui hac occasione, te tantum ac talem virum et praeter generis nobilitatem, omni virtutum et literarum genere exornatum atque excultum coram videre tuisque doctissimis sermonibus quandoque frui potero. Vale quam optime et diutissime, Vir Nobilissime, omnemque adhibe diligentiam, ut nobis salvus atque incolumis huc advenias.

Datae Pragae die 27. Ianuarij Anno 1599, quem tibi cum multis alijs felicissimum a Deo ter Optimo Maximo precor.
Illustri atque Clariss. D. T. deditissimus
RUDOLPHIUS CORADUCIUS,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the noble and stern [valiant] knight, Master Tycho Brahe of Knudstrup, my especially favourable and dearly-beloved Lord. At Dresden or Wittenberg.**

Illustrious and most distinguished knight and most observed Lord. His Sacred Imperial Majesty, our most clement Lord, has commanded me to call Your Illustrious Lordship hither at once; which [command], by these my [letters], I both ought and wished most humbly to obey. Let Your Illustrious Lordship therefore see to it, as diligently as possible, that, as soon as you can, you gird yourself for the journey, and so present yourself before the Emperor here at Prague, that he may perceive that in this matter nothing at all — not even the least — has been wanting, whether on Your Illustrious Lordship's part or on my own. Furthermore, on this august summoning of Your Illustrious Lordship's person, I congratulate not so much Your Illustrious Lordship as myself. I rejoice in a marvellous manner, inasmuch as on this occasion I shall be able to see in person — and sometime to enjoy the most learned discourses of — you, so great and such a man, who, besides nobility of birth, are adorned and cultivated with every kind of virtues and of letters. Fare most well and most long, most noble Man, and apply all diligence to come hither to us safe and unharmed.

Given at Prague, the 27th day of January, in the year 1599 — which [year] I pray, from God thrice Best and Greatest, may be most happy for you, together with many others [to come].
Most devoted to Your Illustrious and most distinguished Lordship,
Rudolf Coraduz,
with his own hand.
