documents.abstract: Laments the moral corruption and religious disorder of the age, citing Virgil on irreversible decline, before the text breaks off; little substantive content beyond this preserved.
documents.incipit: QUOTIESCUNQUE ad statum præsentium temporum, qui est miserrimus, Nobilissime et magnifice …
documents.editorial_note:
**Text recovered.** The letter's recovered passages — dropped by a defective transcription of the source and absent until now — has been restored from the text of record and translated. The Source and English columns below are now complete.

**Direction note.** **Incoming** letter — *from* the jurist-poet **Hartwig von Dassel (Hardewigus Dasselius)**, a kinsman/friend of Heinrich Rantzau, *to* Tycho. A humanist **consolatio**: a jeremiad on the age, and a **eulogy for Heinrich Rantzau** — Tycho's Wandsbek host — who died **1 January 1599**. Survives in Dassel's own printed *Poemata + Epistolae* (no manuscript witness).

text.original:
HARDEWIGUS A DASSELL I. C.
TYCHONI BRAHEN VIRO NOBILISS. EQUITI ET MATHEMATICO EXCELLENTISS.
S.
D.

QUOTIESCUNQUE ad statum præsentium temporum, qui est miserrimus, Nobilissime et
magnifice vir, amice colende, oculos animumque converto (converto autem omnes
fere dies noctesque) toties mihi in mentem venit, quod Poëta
his versibus canit:

Sic omnia fatis

In peius ruere, et retro sublapsa referri,

Non aliter, quam qui adverso vix flumine lembum

Remigijs subigit, si brachia forte remisit,

Atque illum in præceps prono rapit alveus amni.

Neque enim ulla unquam extitêre tempora hisce nostris turbulentiora, quibus omnia
mundi regna τὴν ἐσχάτην πτῶσιν minitantur, in quibus tanta undique tamque
effrenis morum corruptela, tot et tantæ mortalium in diversa studia commotiones,
tot tantæque rerum perturbationes, quibus oportune componendis unus solus aut
occupatus fuerit aut suffecerit, in quibus simul religio et verus Dei cultus
τινί μηδὲν ποιεῖσθαι προτιμότερον, et publica et privata ita undique in
turbulentiam convoluta iacuerint. Quamquam enim retroacta tempora suas secum
molestias quasdam et turbationes semper attulerint, nec bellis civilibus ne
quidem atrocissimis in toto caruerint, tamen de hoc constat apertissime, nulla
unquam eiusmodi fuisse, quibus hæc omnia simul mala, tanquam uno edita partu,
unâ effusa phialâ, confluxerint, ut nec immerito sola præ cæteris omnibus
anteactis seculis summe deplorata et calamitosa dici queant. Quæ enim fuêre
(dicat mihi quispiam, qui collatas singulorum
temporum historias cognovit) unquam secula, cum his ex
virtutum et vitiorum præposteris exacte extremitatibus conferenda? in quibus sic
omnia sursum deorsumque sacra et profana sibi invicem confusa extiterint et
perplexa? in quibus sic omnia vitia et turpitudines ad summum pervenerint
fastigium, in quo sine rubore etiam et propemodum cum aliqua laudis vindicatione
steterint? virtus, honestas, devolutæ ad imum ubi pessundatæ et proculcatæ
iacuerint? in quibus maior solutioris et petulantis vitæ impunitas et licentia,
maiores passim in nationum et regnorum statibus intestini motus ac seditiones?
Adeo per præceps totus uno veluti coniurato impetu in dedecus et omnium vitiorum
barathrum, in mutuum excidium et perniciem grassatur et ruit mundus. Miserrimus
est profecto miseræ et omni ope destitutæ Germaniæ nostræ status. Non externus hostis hanc populatur, non
aliena fraus diripit, sed suis ipsa viribus ruit, ad seipsam evertendam callida
est et dolos struit. Quid obsecro existimandum, externos populos, Italos puto,
Gallos, Hispanos, loqui de nobis? Quid literæ et scripta testabuntur? Durum est
et asperum dictu, sed dicendum tamen. Nobilium in nobiles, civium in cives, imo
fratrum, adfinium, cognatorum, propinquorum in suos commemorabitur impius et
nefarius furoris atque avaritiæ et invidiæ impetus, insidiæ, circumventio,
inductio, fallaciæ. Non tantum mali in summa calamitate esse potest, quantum in hac ignominia et dedecore. Quæ autem hæc est rabies? Nihil
curare aliquem, quid liberis, uxori, consanguineis, affinibus suis fiat? an
nobiscum extingui delerique cupimus omnia? Et illæ Neronianæ et Caianæ sententiæ
in animo et voces in ore sunt: »Me mortuo terra absumatur
ignibus;« vel magis etiam tristes:

»ignes, ruinæ populum premant,

turpisque egestas, sæva cum luctu fames.«

O gentis et nationis laudatissimæ ingens probrum! Mirantur interim multi, quonam
malo Genio, quove fato nostro, illa morum corruptela totque discordiæ et
dissidia tam in ordine politice, quam in ecclesiastico passim nata sint, et
indies magis magisque augeantur, non abs re quidem id mirantur, et dolent etiam
ob rei, quæ tam multa secum mala invehat, et pietati iustitiæque interitum
minetur, diuturnitatem et magnitudinem. Verum si admiratores illi et animorum
nostrorum pravitatem vitæque labem, de quibus paulo ante dictum, ac gravissima,
quibus ea tota scatet ac sordet, vulnera sibi ob oculos ponant, et, quod
proximum est, in tot et tantis, quibus laboramus morbis, nullam fere sanitatis
speciem et spem reliquam esse considerent, non amplius mirabuntur; sed dolebunt
nihilominus, quod de morbis nostris curandis nullo modo nec cogitemus nec
laboremus. Vitia hæc sunt, ut uno verbo dicam, et
scelera, bellorum et calamitatum sons et caput; quibus nisi exstirpatis,
nullus miseriarum finis sperandus videtur. Non prosequar
omnia, quia et infinita sunt, et alibi ab alijs explicata satis, sed maiori
quidem illorum, qui sapienter ea disseruerunt et nos ad meliora erudierunt,
laude, quam nostrâ, qui nec ullis præceptis moniti sapere, nec ullis malis
affecti resipiscere possumus, utilitate.

Et quid pluribus commemorandis tempus teram, cum, si avaritiam et ambitionem,
teterrimas animorum pestes, unam dissensionum et calamitatum in toto Romano
imperio causam esse dixero, complexus omnia videar? Hic unus malus Genius est,
qui nos tamdiu vexat, hoc ipsum est illud factum, quod et privatis rebus
detrimentum et publicis exitium affert. Hæ duæ inquam sunt pestes, quæ pietati et
iustitiæ, quæ Germaniæ nostræ, quæ Ecclesiæ
extremam, si quæ possint, perniciem machinantur, quæque ἀταξίαν et confusionem
adhuc, proh dolor, regnantem in Ecclesiam invexerunt? Hæc enim cum erat
pauperior et Apostoli ceterique Pastores auro et argento carebant, virtutibus
omnibus circumfluebant. Episcopi erant docti, modesti, prudentes, sobrij,
laboriosi, vigilantes et tanquam lumina universo populo prælucebant. Singuli vero
e populo tantâ charitate alij alios complectebantur, ut nemo, quod
possideret, suum esse diceret, sed omnia essent communia. Erantque concordes et perdurantes
in doctrina Apostolorum, laudantes Deum
eique pro omnibus gratias agentes. Fides vero tanta erat, ut
nec minis nec ullis cruciatibus a confessione Christianâ deterreri possent. Verum
ubi liberalitate et zelo Principum interdum inconsiderato, eadem Ecclesia
in opes et potentiam crevit, ex eo paulatim eius virtus (ut ait D. HIERONYMUS)
decrevit, quoad in eum statum et præcipitium delaberetur, quo in præsentiâ
redacta est, ut difficillimum sit iudicatu, utri sint deteriores, Pastores an
populus; quos inter se concertare dicas, utri alteros ambitione et avaritiâ
vincant. Certe priscos pietatis ac tum fundandæ et ædificandæ autores, Deum,
Prophetas, CHRISTUM, Apostolos et alios pios Doctores, tum eiusdem confirmandæ
adiutores, ut Imperatores, Reges, Principes, piasque Respubl. et populos si
consulunt et audiunt, longe aliam viam inibunt, longe aliam rationem sequentur.
Sed (ut non minus vere quam festive dicitur) famelicus venter auribus caret;
vesana illa habendi et dominandi fames nihil audit, donec plene satiata fuerit,
si plene tamen unquam satiari potest, quæ contra, quo plura absorbuit, eo plura
appetere, et gazas gazis, regnaque regnis cumulare et solet et gaudet.

Sed mitto iam illorum hominum sordes et perfidiam, et ad ea accedo, quorum
cognitione equidem valde consternatus sum, neque enim sine sensu doloris nuper
ex literis tuis accepi, Nobilissimum Virum D. HENRICUM RANZOVIUM, Regis Daniæ Producem Cimbricum, affinem nostrum, ipsis Calendis Ianuarij beato fine e
mortalium consuetudine exemptum esse, quo sane nuncio non
potui non magnopere commoveri, præsertim tam repentinâ morte. Erat enim mihi
ob singularem prudentiam, eximias virtutes, animique et corporis præstantissimas
dotes, adeo charus, ut nulla vis rerum aut temporum præscriberet modum in eo
amando, suspiciendo et observando. Sed quia divinam in rebus humanis voluntatem
dominari non ignoramus, non forti modo, sed æquo etiam animo, quod mutare non
possumus, ferre debemus; hoc nostrum incommodum gravissimamque iacturam eo
ferimus animo, quo debemus. Tantum vero abest, ut illius vicem doleamus, ut etiam
ipsius causâ gaudendum esse intelligamus. Etenim cui magis propitium et placatum
Deum fuisse, cuive facilius aditum ad æternam et beatam illam vitam patuisse
censendum est, quam ei, qui (ut ipse quoque de eo sentis) et integerrime semper
ac castissime vixerit et ex hac vitâ pie sancteque discesserit? Profecto illius
obitum dolere invidentis esset potius quam amantis. Quare tuum erit, cum is tam
præclare vitæ suæ cursum confecerit, hac cogitatione desiderium, quo ex illo
afficeris, lenire. Quod facilius etiam assequêre, si literis sacris aliquid tui
studij et temporis impertieris, ex quibus id, quod ipse expertus confirmare
possum, præter suavissimum quendam animi fructum ac voluptatem, quam percipies,
omnia quæ evenire homini possunt incommoda, non tolerabilia solum, sed ad
salutem etiam animorum vim habere maxime intelliges. Sed hæc
hactenus. Fuit sane Generosus Dominus HENRICUS
RANZOVIUS, qui nunc rebus humanis exemptus est, vir et ore et
more imaginem honesti referens, opum honorumque contemptor, recti pervicax, ut
animâ, ita ore liber eoque gratus bonis, gravis improbis, Doctorum et
Literatorum, sed bonorum amans, illis ignavâ operâ non ferebat; eruditionem
gravem seriamque, a qua in publicum boni mores, bona valetudo manarent,
complectebatur, illa acuminis irriti ludicra et difficilimas nugas aversabatur.
Iam pietate et animi robore supra vulgi captum ingeniumque. Sed non ille ad
huius seculi gustum, seculi improbi, maligni, ingrati, quo vitijs malisque
artibus non modo impunitas, sed apud plerosque etiam honos, innocentiam atque
virtutem vix usquam sine periculo aperte colueris. CHRISTIANO tertio Regi
Daniæ a puero charus, neque id
immerito. Nam et ipsi RANZOVIO una
illa post Deum cura, habere clementissimum Regem eumque florentissimum videre.
Erat ille familiâ inter Holsatos nobili natus, sed postea ob egregias virtutes,
eruditionem haud vulgarem, trium Regum Daniæ, CHRISTIANI III ,
FRIDERICI II et CHRISTIANI IV in Ducatibus Sleswigæ, Holsatiæ
et Ditmarsiæ, summâ cum dignitate Vicarius perpetuus. Primos annos bonis
artibus, cæteram ætatem Reipubl. dedit, ubi maturior illa et rebus gerendis
simulac regendis genesis ætas accessit, tum
Legationibus obire, laborare, vigilare, negotijs publicijs
intentus sua negligere, bonos omnes passim ad communem pacem adhortari,
prudentibus animum addere, imprudentibus mala imminentia exponere. Tu autem
felix, RANZOVI, confecto innocenter cursu tuo, iam hac servitute liber vivis et
vivis cum Deo, beatus [in] æternum. Sed ad laudes D. RANZOVIJ
non addam plura.

Quod vero, nobilissime vir, tu quoque in extrema epistolæ tuæ parte mortem
RANZOVIJ non fictis lamentis prosequeris, facis tu quidem, quod non te solum,
sed omnes literatos facere decet. Quod autem et eius sapientiam, doctrinam,
virtutem et humanitatem pleno ore prædicas, in eo animi tui candorem et agnosco
et magnopere laudo, cumque te laudum eius tam studiosum esse animadvertissem,
non dubitavi, quin grata tibi lectio futura esset eorum, quibus tumulum eius
ornavi, epigrammatum; quare adscribenda ea censui, tua vicissim, si qua
scripseris, expectans. Tu, nobilissime vir, hanc confidentiam compellationis
meæ, et, quæ tanquam garriens commiseratione maligni huius seculi motus ad te
perscripsi, in bonam partem accipies, beneque valebis.

Luneburg, 28. Ianuarij
Anno [1599].
text.english:
**Hartwig von Dassel, Jurisconsult, to Tycho Brahe, most noble Knight and most excellent Mathematician. Greeting.**

As often as I turn my eyes and mind to the state of present times — which is most wretched — most noble and magnificent man, friend to be revered (and I turn them thither almost every day and night), so often there comes into my mind what the Poet sings in these verses:

> *"Thus all things by the fates rush to the worse, and, slipping back, are carried backward — no otherwise than one who scarce, against the stream, drives his skiff with the oars: if perchance he has slackened his arms, the channel snatches him headlong down the sloping current."* [Virgil, Georgics 1.199–203]

For never have there existed times more turbulent than ours, in which all the kingdoms of the world threaten the uttermost fall [τὴν ἐσχάτην πτῶσιν]; in which there is so great and so unbridled a corruption of morals on every side, so many and so great commotions of mortals into divergent pursuits, so many and so great disturbances of affairs that to set them right in due season one man alone would scarcely find occupation enough, or be sufficient for the task; in which likewise religion and the true worship of God were things to which nothing, in anyone's eyes, was held preferable, and public and private affairs alike lay everywhere rolled up into turbulence. For although bygone times always brought with them certain troubles and disturbances of their own, nor were they ever wholly free even of the most atrocious civil wars, yet of this it is most plainly established, that there was never any age of such a kind into which all these evils together — as if brought forth in one birth, poured out from a single vial — flowed together, so that not undeservedly may these times alone, beyond all the foregoing ages, be called supremely deplored and calamitous. For what ages ever were — let anyone tell me who has compared the histories of each several time — that could be matched against these, by the exact extremities to which virtues and vices, turned upside down, have come? In which sacred and profane things thus lay confounded and entangled together, the one with the other, from top to bottom? In which all vices and baseness thus arrived at their utmost height, standing there without a blush, and almost claiming some vindication of praise? In which virtue and honesty lay rolled down to the very bottom, cast down and trampled underfoot? In which there was greater impunity and licence for a looser and more wanton life, and everywhere greater intestine commotions and seditions in the condition of nations and kingdoms? So utterly, by one as it were conspiring onset, does the whole world rush and fall headlong into disgrace and the pit of all vices, into mutual destruction and ruin. Most wretched, indeed, is the state of our wretched Germany, destitute of all help. No foreign enemy lays her waste, no alien fraud plunders her — she falls by her own forces, is cunning for her own overturning, and weaves snares against herself. What, I ask, must we suppose foreign peoples — the Italians, I imagine, the French, the Spanish — say of us? What will letters and writings attest? It is hard and bitter to say, yet it must be said. There will be recounted the impious and nefarious onset of fury, avarice, and envy — of nobles against nobles, citizens against citizens, nay of brothers, kinsfolk, relations, neighbours against their own — the ambushes, the circumvention, the seduction, the deceits. There cannot be as much evil in the utmost calamity as there is in this ignominy and disgrace. But what madness is this? That no one cares what becomes of his children, his wife, his blood-kin, his relations? Or do we wish that, with us, everything should be extinguished and blotted out? And those Neronian and Caligulan sentences are in the mind, and on the tongue: "When I am dead, let the earth be consumed by fires" — or, even sadder:

> *"Let fires, ruins press the people down, and base want, with savage hunger and grief."*

O the vast reproach of a most praised people and nation! Many meanwhile marvel by what evil genius, or by what fate of ours, that corruption of morals, and so many discords and dissensions born everywhere, alike in the political order and in the ecclesiastical, have arisen, and day by day grow ever greater; and not without reason do they marvel at it, and grieve also at the long duration and the greatness of a thing that brings with it so many evils, and threatens the ruin of piety and justice. But if those who marvel would set before their eyes the depravity of our minds and the taint of our life — of which a little before I spoke — and the most grievous wounds with which that life wholly teems and is befouled, and, which comes next, would consider that in so many and so great diseases as we labour under scarcely any appearance or hope of health remains, they will marvel no longer; but they will grieve nonetheless, that we in no way either think about or labour at the curing of our diseases. These, to say it in one word, are the vices and crimes that are the source and head of wars and calamities; unless these are rooted out, no end of our miseries seems to be hoped for. I will not pursue all of this, since it is both endless and has been sufficiently set forth elsewhere by others — to the greater credit indeed of those who have discussed it wisely and instructed us toward better things, than to any profit of ours, who can neither be made wise by any precepts we are warned with, nor be brought to our senses by any evils that afflict us.

And why should I waste time recounting more, since, if I shall have said that avarice and ambition — the foulest plagues of minds — are the one cause of the dissensions and calamities in the whole Roman Empire, I shall seem to have embraced all? This is that one evil genius which so long vexes us; this same thing it is that brings both loss to private affairs and ruin to public. These two, I say, are the plagues which contrive the uttermost ruin, if they can, of piety and justice, of our Germany, of the Church — and which have brought into the Church that disorder [ἀταξίαν] and confusion that still, alas, reign? For when the Church was poorer, and the Apostles and the other Pastors lacked gold and silver, they overflowed with all virtues. The bishops were learned, modest, prudent, sober, industrious, watchful, and shone before the whole people like lights. And among the people, each embraced the others with such charity that no one called what he possessed his own, but all things were held in common. And they were of one mind and persevered in the teaching of the Apostles, praising God and giving him thanks for all things. And their faith was so great that they could be deterred, neither by threats nor by any torments, from the confession of Christ. But when, by the liberality and (sometimes inconsiderate) zeal of Princes, that same Church grew into wealth and power, from that its virtue (as Saint Jerome says) gradually decreased, until it slipped down into that state and precipice to which it is now reduced, so that it is most difficult to judge which are the worse, the Pastors or the people — you would say they vie with one another as to which shall outdo the other in ambition and avarice. Surely, if they would consult and give ear to the ancient founders of piety — God, the Prophets, Christ, the Apostles, and other pious Doctors — and then to those who helped confirm the same, such as Emperors, Kings, Princes, and pious Commonwealths and peoples, they would enter upon a far different path, and follow a far different plan. But (as is said no less truly than wittily) a hungry belly has no ears; that mad hunger for having and for ruling hears nothing, until it be fully sated — if indeed it can ever be fully sated — which, on the contrary, the more it has swallowed, the more it craves, and is wont, and delights, to heap up treasure upon treasure, and kingdom upon kingdom.

But I now dismiss the sordidness and perfidy of those men, and come to the things by the knowledge of which I am greatly dismayed; for not without a sense of grief did I lately learn from your letter, that the most noble man Lord Heinrich Rantzau, the King of Denmark's Pro-duke of the Cimbric [land] [Statthalter of Holstein], our kinsman, was on the very Kalends of January [1 January] taken, by a blessed end, from the company of mortals — by which news indeed I could not but be greatly moved, especially by so sudden a death. For he was so dear to me, for his singular prudence, his eminent virtues, the most excellent gifts of his mind and body, that no force of circumstances or times prescribed a measure to my loving, looking up to, and observing him. But since we are not ignorant that the divine will rules in human affairs, we ought to bear, not with a brave only but with an even mind, what we cannot change; this our misfortune and most grievous loss we bear with the mind we ought to. But so far is it from our duty to grieve his lot, that we understand we must even rejoice on his own account. For to whom should God be reckoned to have been more propitious and appeased, or to whom should an entrance to that eternal and blessed life be judged to have lain more open, than to him who (as you too think of him) both ever lived most uprightly and most chastely, and departed from this life piously and holily? Surely to grieve his death would be the part of one who envies him, rather than one who loves him. Wherefore it will be your part, since he has so gloriously finished the course of his life, to soften with this thought the longing with which you are affected on his account. Which comfort you will the more easily attain, if you impart some of your study and time to the sacred letters [Scripture], from which — a thing I can myself confirm from experience — besides a certain most sweet fruit and pleasure of mind which you will perceive, you will come especially to understand that all the misfortunes that can befall a man have the power not only to be borne, but even to work toward the health of our souls. But enough of this. He was indeed, the noble Lord Heinrich Rantzau, now taken from human affairs, a man bearing the image of honour both in face and in manner; a contemner of wealth and honours; stubborn for the right; free of soul as of speech, and thereby pleasing to the good, weighty to the wicked; a lover of Doctors and Men of Letters — but of the good ones, whom he never served with idle effort; he embraced grave and serious erudition, from which good morals and good health might flow forth to the public, and turned away from the playthings of idle cleverness and most difficult trifles. Moreover, in piety and strength of mind he was above the common grasp and wit of the crowd. But he was not suited to the taste of this age — a wicked, malicious, thankless age, in which for vices and evil arts there is not only impunity, but among most men even honour, while innocence and virtue you could scarcely cultivate openly anywhere without danger. Dear from boyhood to Christian III, King of Denmark — and not undeservedly; for to Rantzau himself, too, this was, after God, his one care: to have a most merciful King, and to see him most flourishing. He was born of a family noble among the Holsatians, but afterward, for his outstanding virtues and no common erudition, perpetual Vicar [Statthalter], with the highest dignity, of three Kings of Denmark — Christian III, Frederick II, and Christian IV — in the Duchies of Schleswig, Holstein, and Dithmarschen. His first years he gave to the good arts, the rest of his age to the Commonwealth; and when that riper age for conducting and governing affairs together had come upon him, then he gave himself to undertaking embassies, to labouring, to watching; intent upon public business, he neglected his own; he exhorted all good men everywhere to common peace, gave heart to the prudent, and set forth to the imprudent the evils that threatened. But you, fortunate Rantzau, your course innocently finished, now live free of this servitude, and live with God, blessed for eternity. But to the praises of Lord Rantzau I will add no more.

But that you too, most noble man, in the last part of your letter, follow Rantzau's death with no feigned laments — in this you do indeed what becomes not you alone, but all the lettered. And that you proclaim, with full mouth, his wisdom, learning, virtue, and humanity — in that I both recognise and greatly praise the candour of your mind; and since I had noticed you so zealous of his praises, I did not doubt that the reading would be welcome to you of the epigrams with which I adorned his tomb; wherefore I judged they should be appended — expecting yours in turn, if you have written any. You, most noble man, will take in good part this confidence of my addressing you, and the things which — as it were chattering, from compassion at the commotions of this malign age — I have written out to you; and you will fare well.

Lüneburg, the 28th of January, the year [1599].

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondent.** **Incoming**, **Hartwig von Dassel (Hardewigus Dasselius)** — jurist (*Iuris utriusque Consultus*) and Neo-Latin poet, a kinsman/friend of Heinrich Rantzau — **to Tycho**. Survives in **Dassel's own printed *Poemata* + *Epistolae***.
- **Significance — the death of Heinrich Rantzau (Tycho's host) and a humanist age-lament.**
 - **★ The death of Heinrich Rantzau (1 January 1599).** The letter's documentary core: **Tycho had announced, in a letter to Dassel, the death of Heinrich Rantzau — the great Holstein humanist-statesman, *Statthalter (Royal Vicar)* of Schleswig-Holstein under three Danish kings (Christian III, Frederick II, Christian IV), and Tycho's host at Wandsbek** — who died on the Kalends of January 1599. This confirms Tycho's closeness to Rantzau (his Wandsbek patron; cf. the Wandsbek letters and brahe-t_15980607001) and his participation in the Rantzau memorial.
 - **The Rantzau eulogy.** A full humanist portrait: "contemner of wealth and honours … free of soul and speech … lover of [good] Doctors and Men of Letters … grave and serious erudition," dear to Christian III from boyhood, perpetual Statthalter — "now living with God, blessed for eternity."
 - **The age-lament.** An elaborate **jeremiad on the corruption of the age**: the world "rushing to the worse" (the Virgilian *Georgics* boat-against-the-current); **Germany "falling by her own forces"** (nobles against nobles, kin against kin); **avarice and ambition "the one cause of the dissensions and calamities in the whole Roman Empire"**; and the **decline of the Church from apostolic poverty/virtue to wealth/corruption** (citing **Jerome**), with the tags "a hungry belly has no ears" and the Neronian "*Me mortuo terra absumatur ignibus*."
 - **The tomb-epigram exchange.** Dassel encloses **his epigrams for Rantzau's tomb** and **expects Tycho's in return** — a record of Tycho composing memorial verse for his patron (cf. Tycho's own poetic interests, brahe-t_16010414001).
- **Cross-references.** The **Heinrich Rantzau / Wandsbek** thread (Tycho's host-patron; the Wandsbek letters); the **literary-memorial** network.
- **Persons & works named.** Hartwig von Dassel; **Tycho**; **Heinrich Rantzau** (the deceased Statthalter); **Christian III, Frederick II, Christian IV** of Denmark; **Jerome**; **Virgil** (*Georgics*); **Nero, Caligula** (the tyrant-sayings). Places: **Lüneburg**, Germany, **Schleswig/Holstein/Dithmarschen** (Rantzau's Statthalterate).
- **Quotations.** The opening verses = **Virgil, *Georgics* I.199–203** (the skiff against the current). The "*ignes, ruinae populum premant*" couplet is a tragic-verse tag (Senecan in tone). The Greek phrases (τὴν ἐσχάτην πτῶσιν "the uttermost fall"; ἀταξίαν "disorder") are reproduced. The text as printed elides some clauses (Dreyer's source); the translation follows the printed text faithfully.
- **Calendar.** *Luneburg, 28. Ianuarij Anno [1599]* — year supplied editorially; Lüneburg (Old Style); → **28 January 1599 [O.S.]** (label and identifier agree).
- **Scope of the gap.** Roughly two-thirds of Hartwig von Dassel's 28 January 1599 letter to Tycho Brahe was missing from the prior translation, which carried only the opening address, the Virgil epigraph, and disconnected fragments joined by ellipses. The recovered Latin restores the entire moralising excursus on the corruption of the age (the letter's longest single stretch) and roughly half of the eulogy for Heinrich Rantzau; the closing paragraph about the enclosed epitaph-epigrams was already complete and is unchanged here.
- **Sender.** Hardewigus/Hartwig von Dassel signs as "I.C." (Iuris Consultus — Doctor of both Laws), writing from Lüneburg. He does not turn up in our absorbed Tycho reference layers (Christianson, Dreyer, Thoren, Mosley) under this name, so he reads as a minor, lettered correspondent in Tycho's wider humanist network rather than a familiar figure of the household (*familia*).
- **The occasion.** The letter is an obituary letter for Heinrich Rantzau (1526–1599), Tycho's patron, kinsman, and host at Wandsbek — his dates and Wandsbek residence are independently confirmed [Christianson et al., *Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science*, giving "Heinrich of Rantzau (1526-1599)"]. Von Dassel reports his death "on the very Kalends of January" (1 January 1599) and frames it inside a long jeremiad on the corruption of the age, invoking Virgil (*Georgics* 1.199-203) and St Jerome on the Church's decline from apostolic poverty into wealth and ambition, before turning to Rantzau's career as thrice-appointed Statthalter of Schleswig-Holstein-Dithmarschen under Christian III, Frederick II, and Christian IV — matching Norlind's identification of Rantzau as "Statthalter in Schleswig-Holstein."
- **Rantzau's epitaph epigrams.** The closing paragraph (already sound in the prior translation) shows von Dassel enclosing his own Latin epigrams composed for Rantzau's tomb, inviting Tycho to answer with epigrams of his own — a concrete data point for the corpus of Rantzau memorial verse produced within weeks of his death.
- **Cruxes to flag.** (1) The embedded Greek tag "τινί μηδὲν ποιεῖσθαι προτιμότερον" in the first restored paragraph is elliptical — it lacks the expected object of comparison ("preferable to what") — and has been translated by inferred sense rather than settled philology; a genuine, unresolved crux. (2) "illis ignavâ operâ non ferebat" (of Rantzau's support for good scholars) is compressed idiom, rendered here by sense as "whom he never served with idle effort," i.e. he supported them diligently rather than passively.
- **Correction.** The salutation header is corrected from 'Doctor of Both Laws' to 'Jurisconsult': Dreyer (TBOO VIII p.137) prints 'HARDEWIGUS A DASSELL I. C.' — I.C. abbreviates Iuris Consultus, not Iuris Utriusque Doctor (I.U.D.). A fabricated editorial bracket claiming an 'apparatus' crux note for the Greek tag τινὶ μηδὲν ποιεἶσθαι προτιμότερον has been removed; Dreyer (TBOO VIII p.137) prints the Greek with no such apparatus.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VIII pp.133-142 read as page images; pp.133-136 proved to belong to three other letters, so the actual Dassel letter was located and collated on pp.137-141 (confirmed by the running headers 'HARDEW. DASSELIUS AD TYCHONEM 28 IAN. 1599'). Checked the Virgil tag (Georgics 1.199-203, correctly identified in the English), both Greek phrases (ὰταξίαν and the one above), the Neronian/Caligulan tags and the two embedded verse quotations, Rantzau's death on the Kalends (1st) of January 1599, his title, the three kings named (Christian III, Frederick II, Christian IV) and three duchies (Schleswig, Holstein, Dithmarschen), the Jerome citation, and the closing dateline 'Luneburg, 28 Ianuarij Anno [1599]' — all agree exactly between Dreyer, the transcribed original and the English, sentence for sentence, across this long philosophical letter. Two low-severity defects found, both editorial/paratextual rather than substantive: an over-specified honorific, and a bracketed reference to a nonexistent apparatus.

**2 defects found:**
- **mistranslation** (low). 'I.C.' is the standard early-modern abbreviation for 'Iuris Consultus' (jurisconsult/legal counsellor), not 'Iuris Utriusque Doctor' (which would be abbreviated I.U.D. and means 'Doctor of Both Laws'); the header over-specifies Dassel's degree. At: “Hartwig von Dassel, Doctor of Both Laws, to Tycho Brahe, most noble Knight and most excellent Mathematician.”.
- **fabrication** (low). The bracket invents a pointer to 'the crux noted in the apparatus'; no apparatus criticus exists anywhere in this document or accompanies the source text — the note promises documentation that was never supplied. At: “[a Greek tag whose comparandum is missing — see the crux noted in the apparatus]”.

**Repaired.** Both defects were verified directly against Dreyer's page images, TBOO VIII p.137 (the letter's opening page). The heading 'I. C.' is legible and unambiguous. The Greek tag τινὶ μηδὲν ποιεἶσθαι προτιμότερον is likewise legible and confirmed to stand alone with no footnote or apparatus marker on the page. No text error was flagged for this letter and none was found; the Latin is left untouched. Nothing remains uncertain for the two audited defects.

documents.abstract: Explains the ten-month delay receiving Tycho's reply via Maestlin, acknowledges most excerpted words in his Ursus letters as his own, but sees no proven crime in their publication.
documents.incipit: CUM intellexissem ex MÆSTLINI literis, quas ad me dedit superiori Augusto, respondisse te …
documents.editorial_note: **Direction note.** **Incoming** letter — *from* **Johannes Kepler** *to* Tycho — Kepler's **apologia for his earlier flattering letter to Ursus**, which Ursus had printed in his defamatory *De astronomicis hypothesibus* (1597) and weaponised against Tycho. Place not given (**Graz**, where Kepler then was); dated only to **February 1599** (the edition gives no day). The text as the edition transmits it ends without valediction or date.

text.original:
IOANNES KEPLER AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

CUM intellexissem ex MÆSTLINI literis, quas ad me dedit superiori Augusto, respondisse te ad epistolium meum, eiusque responsionis exemplar apud MÆSTLINUM esse, proxima occasione apud illum institi, ut id exemplar ad me mitteret, quando literæ tuæ mihi non redderentur. Sic casu et diligentia tua factum, ut quamvis pereuntibus tuis literis, tamen quod me scire velles, post decimum mensem intellexerim. Hæc initio te certiorem reddidi, quia in illa querela tua, me Christe, quam iustissima! postulas, ut primo quoque tempore meam tibi sententiam aperiam, ne ex hac decimestri mora maior tibi de me suspicio culpæ suboriretur. Quantum igitur attinet meas ad URSUM literas, ex ijs, quæ excerpsisti verbis, pleraque mea agnosco. Ex eo fit, ut quamvis ad aliqua, de quibus dubito, pene cohorrescam, nullum tamen negare possim. In hac itaque parte nullum adhuc URSI crimen est, quod liqueat. Utrum autem integram epistolam publicaverit, maior apud me dubitatio: quæ facile discuteretur, si mihi exemplar typi esset. Nam in ijsdem literis desiderium meum tuorum operum legendorum expressi, eaque in re operam URSI expetij. Quantam autem per Deum immortalem! et quammultiplicem mihi facit iniuriam ferus homo! Ambiebam eius amicitiam missa epistola. Si petitionem meam admisit, fidem eius desidero: sin sprevit, tamen inhumanus est. Sermones amicorum, literæ magis, privatæ esse debent; has ille publicavit, nec me consuluit, nec facturum, nec factum nunciavit, nec exemplar misit. Quibus est curæ æquitas, nec in hostem quidem tale quid audent. Remisisset mihi, quod veteres aiebant, nuncium, aut abolevisset schedam, si non placuit amicus. Quamquam si literis eius ad me altero tandem anno scriptis, si iudicio eius de me, fides haberi potest, et placuit conditio, et amicitiam colere instituerat. Sed hæc levia sunt: illa maior improbitas, iure utique vindicanda, si cui in foro aut spes aut oblectatio: quod id quod γεωμετροῦντι dictum ego volebam, ipse sibi maledicenti, quod scribis, applicat. Acerbissimum omnium, quod quem intelligebat ex meis literis a me maximi fieri, illis ipsis meis literis, quantum potuit, dehonestavit. Sic nimirum ipsi me de laudato inimico suo placuit ulcisci. Sed neque satis mirari possum consilium hominis, dum consilium meum illius hyperbolicæ laudationis ventilo. Quid? Tantine facit ista mea præconia? At cuius hominis? Si vir esset, contemneret, si prudens, non ventilaret. Quærebam obscurus ego laudatorem clarum vixdum nati inventi, mendicabam ab ipso stipem, ecce stipem ipse mendico extorsit. Præceptorem dixi: næ parvam laudi accessionem facit ex adulatione discipuli. Quærat eorum præconia, qui se præceptores ipsius ferunt. Quod si mihi partes iudicis tradit (nec apertius id potuisset, quam sic ostentata mea epistola) sciat iam mihi alios quam discipulo mores competere. Toleratur in discipulo utcunque adulatio, si ex opinione præceptoris et amore profecta ad finem discendi dirigatur: in iudice adulatio flagitium est. Quæ sic scribenda duxi, ut quamvis præstat securitatis causa honoratissimum quemque virum irasci minime, tamen, si non aliter honori tuo consuli posset, haberes arbitrium publicatæ calumniæ publice obviam eundi. Sed missum tandem ipsum faciamus. Nec enim, quam ipse male, sed quam ego bene fecerim, quæritur. Et sunt quidem in illa mea epistola pleraque, quæ defendi, aliqua, quæ excusari, aliqua quæ pessima suspicione liberari debent.

Ordiamur ab eo quod gravissimum est: quod nempe crimini mihi das, contra quam senserim, in os ipsi locutum. Quod dum agis, ita loqueris, ut mihi absolutissimum de alijs iudicium tribuere videaris. Quam ego suspicionem, si a me, quod perquam facile est, removero, magna parte purgationis me defunctum esse putabo. Etenim qui vir sit URSUS, iam non disputare placet, certe quo tempore epistolam illam scripsi, et imbecilliori eram iudicio et non parum ipsi iam diu tribueram. Venit Grætium Doctor quispiam ex Italia reversus Librum eius mihi exhibens, quem triduo concesso raptim percurrerem. In eo salutatos schematismis reperio præcipuos huius temporis Mathematicos, reperio magnificam in præfatione provocationem ad simile quid audendum, ad Astronomiam e fundamentis extruendam, reperio compendia quædam aurea, quæ Tubingæ a MÆSTLINO celebrari memineram, reperio doctrinam sinuum, doctrinam triangulorum, vulgaria quidem, sed nova mihi omnia, ut videat, quo remige famam verberet. Nam pleraque postea in EUCLIDE et REGIOMONTANO reperi, quæ tum ipsi tribuebam. Neque metuas, ut quæ iam dixi, bene cum invento meo stare queant. Dicat ipse pro me MÆSTLINUS, quam tenuibus principijs institerim initio, qui profecto, si tam ieiunum me secundo dimisisset, quam primo dimiserat, nunquam tam exquisitam mihi commendationem (qua tamen, dum vixero, inferior ero) impertivisset. Itaque hac ego specie doctrinæ de URSO in præclaram opinionem erectus, incidi postea in quosdam ex nobilitate Styriaca Mathematum amantes, quibus, quod esset necessaria subinde mora in aula Cæsaris, URSI notitia erat. Illi hominis prædicare ingenium, inventa, hortari me, ut anniterer in eius familiaritatem pervenire, polliceri suam operam. Sed DIOGENEM quempiam mihi describebant aliqui, cui nisi aut lubeat, aut cum improbitate aliqua extorqueri nihil possit. His ego de causis inventa paulo post speculatione mea, cum non esset mihi vicinior Mathematicus, ad quem commodius scriberem, ad scribendum impulsus, formam ipsam partim ad hominis naturam, quæ ferebatur, partim ad eas, quas tum forte fortuito legebam, efficacissimæ brevitatis epistolas dissoluto in pompam animo ex recenti inventionis meæ amore accommodavi securus de hoc eventu. Quomodo si quid mihi excidit paulo maius, quam de ipso senseram, in gratiam laudatorum ipsius et mei ipsius amore, totum id iuvenilis temeritatis est, nec aliter excuso, dummodo sceleris suspicionem aboleam. Ex ijs, quæ dixi, vides primum me bona conscientia Gloriam ipsi tribuisse, qua videbatur regnare in aula Cæsaris et apud Mathematicos, quos in libello suo alloquebatur, illustrissimam autem cur dixerim, causam non reperio, nisi quod Illustres nostri eam prædicant, et Illustrissimus prædicare videtur, dum eum in Aula habet, et quod pomposum ingenium facile muscam conspicatur, ex qua faciat Elephantum. Eodem refero et id, quod, cum constaret de aliquibus, dixi (si modo dixi) ab omnibus doctis ipsum magnifieri. Certe enim MÆSTLINUM et TYCHONEM inter doctos habebam, quos sciebam non admodum præclare de ipso sentire. Quod autem etiam plura in hunc modum declamaturus fuissem, si tempus tulisset, id non memini me polliceri. Imo illa de garrulitate aliena a Mathematicis protestatio non facta est ad excusanda etiam plura huiusmodi, sed potius ad corrigenda priora. Quod si vero mea sunt omnia et singula ista verba, quod Mathematicos huius ævi tantum præcedat unus quantum Phœbeius orbis minuta sidera: me Christe magnam iniuriam multis præclarissimis viris, atque adeo meæ ipsius conscientiæ imprudens feci. Illud verissime dicere possum, nunquam me ullo modo serio, per lusum, publice, privatim, in os, aurem, ex animo volentem et prudentem hoc dixisse, quod REGIOMONTANO, COPERNICO, RHETICO, REINHOLDO, TYCHONI, MÆSTLINO, cæteris unus URSUS præferendus sit. Nunquam sensi, nunquam præsenti animo scripsi, nunquam tam flagitiosam adulationem probavi. Quod si verba mea genuina tale quid sonant, quod nescio, casus in culpa est, meaque festinatio, et quod quid scripserim, non relegi. Poëticum, ut vides, totum id est, et ex Poëta desumptum, et poëtico spiritu dictum: quod non tantum iam nolo, sed et tum, cum scripsi, nolebam, aliorsum rapi volebam, aliam repræsentari, quod antecellat vulgus, vulgus, inquam, Mathematicorum, quod et credebam, et citra præcipuam gloriam fieri potest. Non protestarer tanta asseveratione contra manifesta verba (si modo talia sunt) nisi in ipsa illa epistola documentum maximum extaret meæ innocentiæ, quo de supra. Nam etsi quibus verbis TYCHONIS mentionem fecerim, nescio, fecisse tamen scio: et eiusmodi mentionem quidem, atque ex eiusmodi opinione profectam, quæ merito URSUM pungat, si eum tam feliciter titillant hæc sui ipsius elogia. Sed caute, ut video, posthac scribendum erit. Adeo nunquam non salutare quippiam URSI in aurem insusurrando præcipiunt. Cætera, quæ allegas, levia sunt. Præceptorem dixi, quia ex eius libro aliqua hauseram utilia; Nobilissimum vero, quia in his provincijs Austriacorum nobilitati datur Eruditio et Munus aulicum; Hypotheses vero eius feci, in quibus aliquid mutavit; nam si bene memini, Terram et ipse voluit, et in Martis circulo discrepat, sive, ut dicis, errat. Nam etsi ex MÆSTLINO de hac te inter et ipsum controversia olim inaudiveram, tamen cum et MAGINUS in Italia et RŒSLINUS in Alsatia singuli pro se simile quippiam ex hypothesibus COPERNICI derivassent, existimavi idem et URSO excogitata proclive fuisse. Denique quod finis principio respondet, nihil mirum, nec ulla in voto improbitas, ut valeat sideribus et scientiæ. Id equidem studeat, maledictis omissis et vana ostentatione. Decus autem Germaniæ mihi quilibet est, cui tantum tribuo, quantum illi tribuebam, quia nempe Mathemata verum decus sunt unius Germaniæ. Hæc adeo prolixe, cum ut dolorem meum testarer iusta querela, tum ut appareret, arbitrari me non omnino nihil ad meam existimationem pertinere, quid tu de me sentias.
text.english:
**JOHANNES KEPLER TO TYCHO BRAHE.**

When I had understood, from Maestlin's letter (which he sent me last August), that **you had replied to my little letter, and that a copy of your reply was with Maestlin** — since your letter was not delivered to me — I pressed him at the next occasion to send me that copy. So it came about, by chance and by your diligence, that **though your letter perished, yet what you wished me to know I understood after the tenth month**. This I made known to you at the outset, because, **in that complaint of yours — by Christ, how most just! — you demand that I open my view to you at the first opportunity, lest from this ten-month delay a greater suspicion of fault toward me should arise in you.** As far, then, as concerns **my letters to Ursus**: from the words you excerpted, I recognise most as mine. Hence it is that, although at some, of which I am in doubt, I almost shudder, yet I can deny none. **In this part, then, there is as yet no crime of Ursus that is clear.** But whether he published the whole letter, [there is] greater doubt with me — which would easily be resolved, had I a printed copy. For in those letters I expressed my desire to read your works, and in that matter sought Ursus's help. **But how great — by the immortal God! — and how manifold an injury the savage man does me!** I sought his friendship by sending the letter. If he admitted my petition, I miss his good faith; if he spurned it, he is yet inhuman. The conversations of friends — more, their letters — ought to be private; these he published, neither consulted me, nor announced he would do it, nor that he had, nor sent a copy. Those who have a care for fairness do not dare such a thing even against an enemy. He would have sent the message back to me (as the ancients said), or destroyed the sheet, if the friend did not please him — although, if his letters to me, written at last the next year, if his judgement of me, can be trusted, both the condition pleased [him] and he had begun to cultivate friendship. But these are light matters. **That [is] the greater wickedness, by all means justly to be avenged (if any has in the court either hope or delight): that what I meant to be said "to one doing geometry" [γεωμετροῦντι], he applies to himself, reviling [you], as you write.** Bitterest of all: that **the one whom he understood from my letters to be most highly esteemed by me [you], he, by those very letters of mine, dishonoured as much as he could.** So, forsooth, it pleased him to avenge himself on me regarding his praised enemy. But neither can I sufficiently marvel at the man's plan, while I ventilate my own plan of that hyperbolic praise. What? Does he value those proclamations of mine so highly? But [praise] of what man? If he were a [true] man, he would despise it; if prudent, he would not ventilate it. I, obscure, sought a famous praiser of my scarcely-born invention; I begged a coin from him; behold, the beggar himself has extorted a coin. I called him "preceptor": truly he makes small addition to his praise from a disciple's adulation. Let him seek the proclamations of those who bear themselves as his preceptors. But **if he hands me the part of a judge (and he could not [do it] more openly than by thus displaying my letter), let him know that other manners now befit me than [those of] a disciple. Adulation is tolerated, somehow, in a disciple, if, proceeding from esteem and love of the preceptor, it be directed to the end of learning; in a judge, adulation is a crime.** These things I thought should thus be written, so that — although for safety's sake it is best that every most-honoured man be least angry — yet, **if your honour could not otherwise be provided for, you might have the choice of going publicly against the published calumny.** But let us at last dismiss the man himself. For the question is not how badly *he* acted, but how well *I* acted. And there are indeed, in that letter of mine, most things which ought to be defended, some which [ought] to be excused, some which [ought] to be freed from the worst suspicion.

**Let us begin from what is gravest: namely, that you charge me with the crime of having spoken to his face against what I felt.** In doing which, you so speak as to seem to attribute to me an absolute judgement about others. Which suspicion, if I remove it from myself (which is very easy), I shall think myself discharged of a great part of the purgation. For what kind of man Ursus is, I do not now choose to dispute; certainly, at the time I wrote that letter, **I was both of weaker judgement, and had long attributed not a little to him.** A certain Doctor, returned from Italy, came to Graz, showing me his book — which, three days being granted, I hastily ran through. In it I find **the chief Mathematicians of this time greeted with diagrams; I find in the preface a magnificent provocation to dare something similar, to build Astronomy from its foundations; I find certain golden compendia which I remembered being celebrated at Tübingen by Maestlin; I find the doctrine of sines, the doctrine of triangles — common, indeed, but all new to me — so that he might see by what oar he beats [the way to] fame.** For most of what I then attributed to him I afterward found in **Euclid and Regiomontanus**. And do not fear that what I have just said can [not] stand well with my own invention: let **Maestlin** himself say for me on how slender principles I stood at the beginning — who indeed, had he dismissed me as meagrely the second time as he had the first, would never have imparted to me so exquisite a commendation (to which, however, while I live, I shall be inferior). And so I, raised by this appearance of learning into a splendid opinion of Ursus, **fell in afterward with certain of the Styrian nobility, lovers of Mathematics, who, because of their necessary occasional stay at the Emperor's court, had acquaintance with Ursus.** They proclaimed the man's genius and inventions, urged me to strive to enter his familiarity, promised their help. But some described to me **a kind of Diogenes, from whom nothing could be got unless he pleased, or [it were] extorted with some improbity.** For these causes, a little after my invention by my own speculation — since there was no nearer Mathematician to whom I could more conveniently write — impelled to write, **I accommodated the very form [of the letter] partly to the man's reported nature, partly to those letters of most efficacious brevity which I then happened by chance to be reading — my mind dissolved into pomp from the recent love of my invention — secure about this outcome.** So that, if anything fell from me a little greater than I felt about him, in favour of his praisers and from love of myself, it is all of youthful temerity, and I excuse it no otherwise — provided I abolish the suspicion of crime.

From what I have said, you see, first, that **I attributed to him, with good conscience, the Glory by which he seemed to reign at the Emperor's court and among the Mathematicians whom he addressed in his booklet**; but why I said "most illustrious," I find no cause, except that **our Illustrious [nobles] proclaim it, and the Most Illustrious [Emperor] seems to proclaim it, while he keeps him at Court — and that a pompous genius easily spots a fly, of which to make an Elephant.** To the same I refer that which (when it was established about some) I said — *if* I said it — that he is magnified by all the learned. For certainly I held Maestlin and Tycho among the learned, whom I knew not to think very splendidly of him. But that I would have declaimed even more in this manner, had time allowed, I do not remember promising. Nay, that protestation about garrulity, alien to Mathematicians, was not made to excuse even more of this kind, but rather to correct the earlier. **But if all and each of those words are mine — that one [Ursus] precedes the Mathematicians of this age as much as the Phoebean orb [precedes] the tiny stars — then, by Christ, I imprudently did great injury to many most distinguished men, and even to my own conscience.** This I can say most truly: **that never, in any way — seriously, in jest, publicly, privately, to the face, to the ear, from the heart, willing and prudent — did I say that one Ursus is to be preferred to Regiomontanus, Copernicus, Rheticus, Reinhold, Tycho, Maestlin, [and] the rest.** Never did I feel it, never with present mind did I write it, never did I approve so shameful an adulation. But if my genuine words sound such a thing (which I do not know), the fault is chance's, and my haste, and that I did not re-read what I had written. **It is all Poetic, as you see, and taken from a Poet, and said with a poetic spirit** — which not only now do I not want, but even then, when I wrote it, I did not want; I wanted it carried elsewhere, another [sense] represented: that he surpasses the vulgar — the vulgar, I say, of Mathematicians — which I both believed, and can happen short of [his having] chief glory. I would not protest with such asseveration against manifest words (if such they are), did there not exist, in that very letter, the greatest document of my innocence, whereof above. For **though in what words I made mention of you I do not know, yet I know I did make mention — and such a mention, indeed, and proceeding from such an opinion, as deservedly stings Ursus, if these self-praises so happily tickle him.** But cautiously, I see, must I write hereafter — so [much] do they teach [me], by ever whispering something "salutary" into Ursus's ear. The rest you allege are light: **I called [him] "preceptor," because from his book I had drawn some useful things; "most noble," because in these Austrian provinces erudition and a court office are given to the nobility; I made [them] his hypotheses, in which he changed something** — for, if I remember well, he too wanted the Earth [mobile], and differs in the circle of Mars, or, as you say, errs. For although I had once heard from Maestlin of this controversy between you and him, yet since **both Magini in Italy and Röslin in Alsace had, each for himself, derived something similar from the hypotheses of Copernicus, I reckoned that the same had been easy for Ursus too to devise.** Finally, that the end answers the beginning, [is] no wonder, nor any wickedness in the wish — that he flourish by the stars and by science. Let him indeed study that, with maledictions and vain ostentation omitted. And "Ornament of Germany" — to me, anyone is [that] to whom I attribute as much as I attributed to him, because **Mathematics is the true ornament of Germany alone.** These things [I write] so prolixly, both that I might testify my grief by a just complaint, and that it might appear that I reckon it **not at all nothing to my reputation, what you think of me.**

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondents.** **Incoming**, **Johannes Kepler → Tycho**, from **Graz**, **February 1599**. **Kepler's *apologia* for his 1595 letter to Ursus** — which Ursus had printed in his *De astronomicis hypothesibus* (1597), using Kepler's extravagant praise as an endorsement against Tycho. Tycho had written Kepler a stinging complaint (which never arrived; Kepler got a copy via **Maestlin** ten months later); this is the reply.
- **Significance — a keystone of the Tycho–Kepler–Ursus triangle, and a revealing self-portrait.** One of the most psychologically important letters in the history of science: the young, obscure Kepler, who had **flattered Ursus to win patronage** ("one Ursus precedes the mathematicians of this age as much as the sun's orb the tiny stars"; "preceptor," "ornament of Germany"), now must **explain himself to the man he most needed to keep — Tycho**.
 - **Ursus's betrayal.** Kepler is outraged that Ursus **published a private letter** without consent or a copy, **applied Kepler's praise to himself while reviling Tycho**, and "dishonoured the one [Kepler] esteemed most [Tycho] with Kepler's own words." He invites Tycho, if needed, to **go publicly against the published calumny**.
 - **The self-defence (the heart).** Kepler dismantles the charge of "speaking against what he felt": at the time he was **"of weaker judgement,"** dazzled by Ursus's book (read in three days, found "new" things he later traced to **Euclid and Regiomontanus**), urged on by **Styrian nobles** who knew Ursus at court, and warned Ursus was **"a kind of Diogenes"** yielding nothing unless flattered. He confesses the letter's **"pomp"** was **"all Poetic … taken from a Poet, said with poetic spirit,"** the excess of **"youthful temerity"** and "love of my [new] invention" — *not* a sincere ranking. He swears he **never truly preferred Ursus to Regiomontanus, Copernicus, Rheticus, Reinhold, Tycho, or Maestlin**.
 - **The defence of the substance.** He explains each phrase: "preceptor" (he learned useful things from the book), "most noble" (Austrian custom gives office to nobility), "most illustrious" (the Emperor keeps Ursus at court); and notes that he **"made them Ursus's hypotheses, in which he changed something"** — observing, tellingly, that **Magini (Italy) and Röslin (Alsace) had each independently derived similar geo-heliocentric schemes from Copernicus**, so he thought Ursus could too. The crucial point of innocence: in the very same letter **he had also honoured Tycho** "from such an opinion as deservedly stings Ursus."
 - **The relationship preserved.** The closing is the key: Kepler writes "so prolixly" because **"I reckon it not at all nothing to my reputation what you think of me"** — the anxious deference that, despite the awkwardness, kept the door open to the **collaboration sealed in 1600** (cf. brahe-t_16000828001, brahe-t_16001017001).
- **Cross-references.** The **Tycho–Kepler–Ursus** keystone: pair with Kepler's *analysis* of Ursus's plagiarism (brahe-t_16000911001), the Ursus legal endgame (brahe-t_16000926003), and the employment letters (brahe-t_16000828001, brahe-t_16001017001).
- **Persons named.** Johannes Kepler; **Tycho**; **Ursus (Nicolaus Reimers Bär)**; **Michael Maestlin** (the intermediary, Kepler's teacher); **Regiomontanus, Copernicus, Rheticus, Reinhold, Tycho, Maestlin** (the truly great, whom Kepler would not rank below Ursus); **Euclid, Regiomontanus** (sources of Ursus's "novelties"); **Magini, Helisaeus Röslin** (independent geo-heliocentric derivers); **Diogenes** (the character-type for Ursus); **Rudolf II** (Ursus at court). Greek *γεωμετροῦντι* ("to one doing geometry") reproduced.
- **Date/place & completeness.** Place omitted (**Graz**); dated **February 1599** (identifier 15990200001, label "1599-02"; no day). **The source as supplied ends mid-discourse, without valediction, date, or signature** — the famous Apologia-letter is longer; the text as transmitted appears **partial**. Flagged for a completeness check against the full text.

documents.abstract: Reports the imperial summons to Prague via Coraduz, explains delay due to deep snow and horses sold at Leipzig, and plans to depart within fourteen days.
documents.incipit: EXOPTATE accidit, excellentissime et amantissime Domine Doctor THADDÆE, amice honorande, …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET EXCELLENTISSIMO VIRO DOMINO DOCTORI THADDÆO HAGGECIO AB HAYCK, INCLYTI REGNI BOIEMIAe ARCHIATRO ORDINARIO, AMICO SUO VETERI ET HONORANDO.

S. D.

EXOPTATE accidit, excellentissime et amantissime Domine Doctor THADDÆE, amice honorande, quod heri magnifici et amplissimi Domini CORADUCIJ, Procancellarij Imperialis, literas humaniss. Pragam ex mandato Sae Imperatoriae Maiestatis, Domini nostri clementissimi, me evocantes accepi. Et parerem sane actutum huic augustae et clementissimae evocationi absque ulla mora, statimque iter ingrederer, si viarum transitus ubique ferme nivibus altis repletus id pateretur et equi idonei in promptu essent; nam meos, uti ultimis indicavi, nuper Lipsiae distrahi feci. Omnem tamen curam impendam, ut intra paucos dies pro uno vel altero curru alij coëmantur, aut si id commode fieri nequeat, conducantur, resque meas ita disponam, ut post 14 ab hinc dies iter, favente divino Numine, ad vos suscipere queam. Spero enim itinerum nimias nunc difficultates tum minus obfuturae; et interea expecto nuncium, quem, statim ac huc veni, in Daniam misi, ut inde mihi novum adferret viaticum, consumpto priore in itinere Dresdensi atque hîc, quemadmodum me prius tibi per literas significasse memini. Sin vero is ob hyemis duritiem et perseverantiam mariumque congelationem istic moram traxerit, ut ante dictum tempus adesse nequeat, dabo nihilominus operam, ut aliunde viaticum acquiram, ne ea de causa iter ulterius procrastinetur, sed assumptis mecum paucis comitibus et ministris, reliquos unâ cum familia mea muliebri hîc relinquam, donec ad vos excurrens de Caesaris clementissima voluntate certior factus fuero. Et, si intellexero vias per partem aliquam Slesiae commodiores, quam per Misniam (ut multi existimant) futuras, illac cursum dirigam, quanquam nonnihil longiore ambagine, ut sperem, me intra quatuor abhinc hebdomadas vel circiter, conatibus nostris favente divina ope, Pragae vobis adfuturum.

Cuperem autem quam maxime te ibi praesentem tunc reperire, ut tuo frui possim alloquio, et abs te consilium, sicubi opus fuerit captare, cum ego tanquam peregrinus locorum et hominum ignarus sim. Vellem etiam me in aliqua civitate, quam transire oporteat, tuis literis obvijs praemoneri, in quodnam Pragae hospitium, quod a lue tutum sit et mihi commodum, me conferre possim. Mallem id publicum non esse, ut tranquillus degam et propria etiam quadra, si id magis expediat, vivam. Per Slesiam autem, uti opinor, transituro, quoniam (veluti intelligo) primum Brandusium Pragae proximum occurrit, optarim me istac tuas, quae me de hospitio et alijs necessarijs instruant, invenire literas.

Oportune vero accidit, ut hodie sese offerret quidam auriga Olomucensis, VALENTINUS MULLER nomine, alias vacuo curru Pragam, unde hisce diebus venit, rediturus. Qui cistam quandam cum meis grandiusculis unâ cum alijs thecis secum advehit, in quibus est instrumentum quoddam cocleis disiungi et componi aptum atque tam distantijs quam altitudinibus siderum accurate rimandis serviens, et praeterea nonnulla alia huic exercitio deputata facile portatilia. Pepigi cum dicto auriga pro decem Ioachimicis, dimidium illi hîc solvi, reliquos 5 taleros eum a te accepturum promisi. Rogo itaque, ut recepta in tuas aedes hac cista, velis fidem meam redimere et pecuniam hanc aurigae meo nomine numerare, quam primum volente Numine advenero, tibi cum alijs mea de causa forte alias expositis nummis restituendam. Cuperem illo instrumento non saltem elevationem poli, interea dum ibi sum, accurate denotare, sed et observationi Planetarum, ♄ni praesertim tunc acronychij, diligenter attendere, cum sit iuxta limites maximae latitudinis boreae, quo in loco ante 29 annos me eundem Augustae Vindelicorum observasse memini, licet instrumentis tum non adeo exquisitis instructus, ut nunc integra eius peracta sit revolutio, quam in alijs quoque ipsius, quotquot interea habere licuit, acronychijs sitibus diligenter examinavi, uti et in reliquis duobus superioribus Planetis, quo Apogaea et Eccentricitates eorundem exactius, quam hactenus praestitum est, praefiniri possint, quod et satis praecise me assecutum nihil dubito. Sed de his et similibus plurimisque alijs coram Deo dante plenius agemus.

Scripsi etiam magnifico et amplissimo D. CORADUCIO de occasionibus, cur meus accessus aliquantulum differatur, ut morulam hanc pro suo candore eo promptius excusatam habeat, cui etiam tanquam fautori et promotori apud Caesaream Maiestatem benignissimo et habeo et perpetuo me debere agnosco gratias relaturus, si vires meae ulla ratione id unquam sustinuerint. Vale mi charissime THADDÆE, utque te sanum et prosperum Pragae inveniam, tuaque desideratissima frui possim consuetudine, faxit Deus. Dabantur Vitembergae die 26. Feb. stylo novo Anno etc. 99.

Tui amantissimus TYCHO BRAHE.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, pp. 146–147; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Saluta meo nomine quam officiosissime Dominum BARVICIUM.  /  POSTSCRIPTA. INDICARAM tibi antea me quaedam hic Witebergae typis complere in meis operibus decrevisse, praesertim ea, quae in Progymnasmatum torno primo tecum communicato desiderantur. Cumque papyrus idonea ac priori similis hic vel Lipsiae non praestaret, egi cum Chartopaeis in vicinia habitantibus, ut eiuscemodi chartam in copia mihi pararent, at illi negligentiores negotium nimium procrastinarunt, ut ob id eam, quam Wandesburgi residuam habui in Dania propria mea moletrina confectam, nuper huc advehi curârim. Sed quoniam mihi nunc Pragam ex clementissima Caesareae Maiestatis voluntate eundum est et iter maturandum, cogor ista omnia insecta relinquere, donec inchoatam telam pertexendi commodior detur occasio. Apposui quaedam carmina partim ab insigni huius Academiae Poëta et Professore TAUBMANO mihi, cum Dresdae essem, missa, partim a BRASCHIO eximio pariter Academiae Rostochiensis Poëta, interea dum hic sum, mihi impertita, si forte tibi ea legere vacarit; videntur in eo genere Horatianae odae arguta et erudita. Addidi etiam Domini Doctoris DAVIDIS CHYTRÆI literas, quae etiam Dresdae mihi redditae sunt, si quidem in ijs tui faciat mentionem; poteris illas usque in meum adventum reservare.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and most excellent man, Lord Doctor Thaddaeus Hagecius of Hájek, ordinary Chief-Physician [Archiater] of the renowned Kingdom of Bohemia, his old and honoured friend.**

Greeting.

As longed-for [*exoptate*] it happened, most excellent and most loving Lord Doctor Thaddaeus, friend to be honoured, that yesterday I received the most courteous letter of the magnificent and most ample Lord **Coraduz, Imperial Vice-Chancellor, summoning me to Prague by the mandate of the Sacred Imperial Majesty**, our most clement Lord. And I would indeed obey this august and most clement summons at once, without any delay, and would immediately set out, if the passage of the roads — almost everywhere filled with deep snows — allowed it, and if suitable horses were at hand; for mine, as I indicated in my last [letter], I lately had **sold at Leipzig**. Yet I will spend all care that within a few days others be bought for one or two wagons, or, if that cannot conveniently be done, hired; and I will so arrange my affairs that **after 14 days from now** I may, God favouring, undertake the journey to you. For I hope the now-excessive difficulties of the roads will then be less of a hindrance; and meanwhile I await the messenger whom, as soon as I came hither, I sent into Denmark to bring me **fresh travel-money [*viaticum*]** — the former being spent on the Dresden journey and here, as I remember I signified to you before. But if he, on account of the harshness and persistence of winter and **the freezing of the seas**, has drawn out his delay there, so that he cannot be present before the said time, I will nonetheless take pains to get travel-money from elsewhere, lest the journey be further put off; but, **taking a few companions and servants with me, I will leave the rest, together with my womenfolk, here**, until — running over to you — I am made more certain of the Emperor's most clement will. And if I understand that the roads through some part of **Silesia** will be more convenient than through **Meissen** (as many think), I will direct my course that way, although by a somewhat longer roundabout — so that I hope, **within four weeks from now or thereabouts**, by divine help favouring our endeavours, to be present with you at Prague.

But I should most greatly wish to find you present there then, that I may enjoy your conversation and take counsel from you wherever there be need, since I, as a stranger, am ignorant of the places and the men. I should also wish to be forewarned, by your letters meeting me in some city I must pass through, **into what lodging at Prague — safe from the plague and convenient for me — I may betake myself.** I should prefer it not be a public one, that I may live tranquilly, and even at my own table [*propria quadra*], if that be more expedient. But to me passing through Silesia, as I think — since (as I understand) **Brandeis**, nearest to Prague, first occurs — I should wish to find there your letters instructing me about the lodging and other necessaries.

But it happened opportunely that today a certain wagoner of **Olomouc, Valentin Müller by name**, offered himself, otherwise about to return with an empty wagon to Prague, whence he came these days. He carries with him **a certain chest with my larger [things], together with other cases, in which is a certain instrument, fit to be taken apart and assembled by screws, serving for accurately searching out both the distances and the altitudes of the stars**, and besides some other things assigned to this exercise [of observation], easily portable. I agreed with the said wagoner for **ten joachimsthalers**, paid him half here, [and] promised that he would receive the remaining 5 thalers from you. I ask therefore that, this chest received into your house, you would redeem my pledge and pay this money to the wagoner in my name — to be restored to you, as soon as, God willing, I arrive, with other monies perhaps otherwise laid out on my account. I should wish, with that instrument, not only to note the elevation of the pole accurately while I am there, but also to attend diligently to the observation of the Planets — **especially of Saturn [♄], then acronychal [at opposition], since it is near the limits of maximum northern latitude**; in which place I remember to have observed the same **29 years ago at Augsburg**, though then furnished with instruments not so exquisite — so that **now its complete revolution has been accomplished**, which I have also diligently examined in its other acronychal positions, as many as I could obtain meanwhile, as too in the remaining two superior Planets [Jupiter and Mars], **so that the Apogees and Eccentricities of the same may be defined more exactly than has hitherto been done** — which I doubt not I have attained precisely enough. But of these and similar things, and very many others, we will treat more fully in person, God granting.

I have also written to the magnificent and most ample Lord Coraduz about the reasons why my coming is somewhat deferred, that he may the more readily hold this little delay excused, according to his candour — to whom also, as my most kindly patron and promoter with the Imperial Majesty, I both give and acknowledge that I perpetually owe thanks, to be repaid if my powers ever in any way sustain it. Farewell, my dearest Thaddaeus; and may God grant that I find you healthy and prosperous at Prague, and may enjoy your most longed-for company. Given at Wittenberg, the 26th of February, New Style, the year etc. [15]99.

Most loving of you, **Tycho Brahe**.


*[Postscript:]* Greet Lord Barwitz in my name as dutifully as may be.  /  POSTSCRIPT. I had indicated to you before that I had resolved to complete certain things here at Wittenberg in print, among my works — especially those which are wanting in the first volume of the Progymnasmata communicated to you. And since suitable paper, like the former, was not to be had here or at Leipzig, I dealt with the paper-makers dwelling in the neighbourhood, that they should prepare me such paper in quantity; but they, the more negligent, too much procrastinated the business, so that on that account I lately had brought hither that [paper] which I had left over at Wandsbek, made in Denmark at my own mill. But since I must now go to Prague by the most clement will of the Imperial Majesty, and must hasten the journey, I am compelled to leave all these things unfinished, until a more convenient occasion be given of weaving to the end the web I have begun. I have appended some poems — partly sent to me, when I was at Dresden, by Taubmann, the distinguished Poet and Professor of this Academy; partly bestowed on me, while I am here, by Braschius, likewise an eminent Poet of the Academy of Rostock — if perhaps you have leisure to read them; in that kind they seem witty and learned, like Horatian odes. I have also added the letter of Lord Doctor David Chytraeus, which was likewise delivered to me at Dresden, inasmuch as he makes mention of you in it; you may keep them until my arrival.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Thaddaeus Hagecius ab Hayck** (Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku, 1525–1600), imperial-Bohemian *Archiater* (chief physician), astronomer, and Tycho's oldest and most trusted Bohemian friend and broker at the imperial court (cf. brahe-t_15990321001 and the long Hagecius series). He died later in 1599; this is among the last of their letters.
- **Significance — the eve of the journey to Prague (the imperial call answered).** Written from **Wittenberg** the day after Tycho received **Coraduz's letter of summons** (by Rudolf II's mandate) to **Prague**. The letter is the logistical heart of the move that would make Tycho Imperial Mathematician:
 - **Roads & horses:** deep snow everywhere; Tycho had **sold his horses at Leipzig** (his last letter), must buy or hire wagon-teams; reckons ** c. 14 days** to set out, ** c. 4 weeks** to reach Prague.
 - **Money:** awaiting a **messenger sent to Denmark for fresh *viaticum*** (the earlier spent on the Dresden leg); the **seas frozen** may delay him, so Tycho will raise funds elsewhere rather than wait.
 - **Household:** he will take **a few companions and servants**, **leaving the rest with his womenfolk at Wittenberg** until the Emperor's will is confirmed in person.
 - **Route:** **Silesia (via Brandeis/Brandýs)** vs. **Meissen** — Silesia longer but better; asks Hagecius to send letters ahead to a transit city.
 - **Lodging:** begs Hagecius to secure a **private, plague-free lodging** at Prague (not a public inn), where he can keep his **own table**.
- **The instrument shipment & the Saturn observation (the astronomical core).** A wagoner of **Olomouc, Valentin Müller**, returning empty to Prague, carries ahead a **chest with a screw-jointed portable instrument** for measuring **stellar distances and altitudes** — for **10 joachimsthalers**, half paid, half to be paid by Hagecius on receipt. Tycho means to use it at once to fix the **pole-elevation** at Prague and, above all, to observe **Saturn at opposition (*acronychus*) near its maximum northern latitude** — *the same configuration he had observed 29 years before at Augsburg* (**c. 1570**, with cruder instruments). Saturn's c. 29-year period means **one full revolution has now elapsed**, letting him refine the **apogees and eccentricities of the three superior planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars)** — a vivid glimpse of the continuity of Tycho's planetary program from his youth to the imperial years.
- **Coraduz.** **Rudolf von Coraduz (Korad/Coraduz)**, Imperial Vice-Chancellor (*Procancellarius*), Tycho's chief patron-broker at court; Tycho writes him separately to excuse the delay.
- **Notable readings.** *exoptate* (opening) is written in the source as the Greek-lettered flourish **ΕΧΟΡΤΑΤΕ / EXΟΡΤΑΤΕ** = Latin *exoptate*, "as longed-for/desired" — rendered accordingly (minor orthographic flag, sense secure). *propria quadra* — "[at] my own table/fare" (Juvenalian idiom for self-catering). *acronychus/-ij* — **acronychal**, i.e. rising at sunset = at opposition (glossary term). *grandiuscula* — "my larger [things]" (the bulkier instruments/effects).
- **Persons & places named.** Thaddaeus Hagecius; **Coraduz** (Vice-Chancellor); **Rudolf II** (*Caesar*); **Valentin Müller** of Olomouc (wagoner). Places: **Wittenberg** (whence written), **Leipzig**, **Dresden**, **Silesia**, **Meissen**, **Brandeis (Brandýs)**, **Prague**, **Augsburg** (the 1570 observation).
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Vitembergae die 26. Feb. **stylo novo** Anno … 99* — Tycho dates it **explicitly New Style** (anticipating the imperial reckoning, though Saxony itself was still Old Style) → **26 February 1599 [N.S.]**. Header and label agree.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing greeting (Barwitz) + postscript (the Progymnasmata paper-failure, Wandsbek-mill paper, Taubmann/Braschius odes, the Chytraeus letter), restored from Dreyer VIII pp.146–147 (dropped by the working transcription).
- **Correction.** Restored the dropped numeral "5" in "reliquos 5 taleros" (Dreyer, TBOO VIII, p.146); the English "remaining thalers" is now "remaining 5 thalers" to match.

Collated the full Latin word-for-word against the transcribed original and found one departure: Dreyer prints 'reliquos 5 taleros' where our transcribed original and the translation both read 'reliquos taleros', dropping the numeral.
