text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET EXCELLENTISSIMO VIRO DOMINO VITO WINSHEMIO, I. V. DOCTORI EXIMIO, ET DECANO HAMBURGENSI, AMICO SUO HONORANDO.
HAMBURGK.

S. P.

CLARISSIME et Præstantissime Vir, Amice honorande. Accepi binas a T. Ex. literas, postquam huc Wittebergam veni, quibus iam antea respondissem, si per negotia licuisset, et tabellarius oportune in promptu fuisset, quo nunc se offerente, non intermittendum duxi, quin aliqua saltem, utut et nunc occupatissimus, ad te darem. Ago autem T. Ex. gratias, quod amicitiæ nostræ memor, me suis invisere non sit degravata, et peto, ut tarditatem in rescribendo prorsus candore excusatam habere velit. Existimo Ex. Tuam ex filio meo TYCHONE, cum istic esset, adducturus huc Matrem cum sororibus, intellexisse, in quo statu res meæ essent, et qua de causa huc Wittebergam me recepissem, monstrato Magnifici Domini CORADUCIJ Procancellarij Imperialis rescripto, quod, dum Dresdæ essem, nactus sum. Præterita vero septimana mihi denuo allatæ sunt Amplissimi illius CORADUCIJ literæ, me ex clementissima Imperatoriæ Maiestatis Voluntate hinc Pragam benignissime evocantes, quarum exemplum addidi. Accingo itaque me nunc itineri, ut, quam primum fieri possit, me istic Cæsareæ Maiestati subiectissime sistam, relicturus interea hîc Gynæceum meum, donec, quomodo Cæsarea Maiestas erga me meaque studia animata sit, coram intellexero. Deus Opt. Max. faxit, ut omnia prosperos habeant successus. Cæterum Dominum OLIGERUM ROSENKRANTZIUM nostrum de hac Augusta (ut et CORADUCIUS eam in literis appellat) evocatione, certiorem per Tuam Ex. reddi, misso illi hoc exemplo, aut eius descripto averem, idque ut quam primum certus in illas oras datur nuncius expediat, peramanter rogo. Plura nunc non vacat. Te itaque protectioni Divinæ commendatum habeo.

Datæ Wittebergæ die 2. Martij Anni 99.
Tuæ Excell. studiosiss.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the most distinguished and most excellent man, Master Veit Winsheim, distinguished Doctor of Both Laws and Dean at Hamburg, his friend to be honoured. Hamburg.**

Hearty greeting.

Most distinguished and most excellent man, friend to be honoured. I received two letters from Your Excellency after I came here to Wittenberg, to which I would already have replied, had business allowed and a courier been opportunely at hand; one now offering itself, I judged I should not omit to send you at least something — however most occupied I am even now. And I give Your Excellency thanks that, mindful of our friendship, you did not find it burdensome to visit me with your [letters]; and I ask that you be willing to hold my tardiness in replying excused with all candour. I think Your Excellency understood, from my son Tycho — when he was there, [intending] to bring hither [his] Mother with [his] sisters — in what state my affairs were, and for what cause I had betaken myself here to Wittenberg, the rescript of the Magnificent Master Coraduz, Imperial Vice-Chancellor, having been shown [him], which I obtained while I was at Dresden. But this past week the letters of that most ample Coraduz were brought to me again, most kindly summoning me from here to Prague, by the most clement will of the Imperial Majesty — a copy of which I have added. I therefore now gird myself for the journey, that, as soon as possible, I may present myself most submissively there to the Imperial Majesty, leaving meanwhile here my women's household, until I have understood in person how the Imperial Majesty is disposed toward me and my studies. May God Best and Greatest grant that all [things] have prosperous outcomes. For the rest, I would be eager that our Master Holger Rosenkrantz be made more certain, through Your Excellency, about this august summons (as Coraduz too calls it in his letters) — this copy, or a transcript of it, being sent to him; and I most lovingly ask that you despatch it as soon as a sure messenger into those regions is given. There is no more leisure now. I therefore hold you commended to the Divine protection.

Given at Wittenberg, the 2nd of March, in the year [15]99.
Most zealous of Your Excellency,
Tycho Brahe.

text.original:
OLIGERUS ROSENKRANTZ AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

[IGNES spirant, noctesque diesque meditantur,] sed in proprias fauces regurgitandos.

[Si meo non certe affectu ullo temerato,] sed gravissimis quam plurimis argumentis confirmato, et meditationibus, mihi crede, satis multis et constantibus maturo [consilio parere volueris], quod spero, [suaserim primum omnium, litteris regi destinatis insulam Huennam quasi gratias pro regia liberalitate] (prudenter et placide submonitis submonendis) [agens rursum deferas], ut tamen quo [tua tibi cadant instrumenta], prudenter ͻ: Politice submoneas. Alterum vero est, ne [expensarum invisam et odiosam restitutionem] vel saltem velle [exigere videaris], nedum vel [exigas vel exagites]. Vis, sufficientes dicam rationes et mearum meditationem momenta. [Dicam, sed ne quæso mihi succenseas, bono] tibique optime [cupienti animo hæc dico]. Primum, si feceris, ante omnia, [magnanimitatem tuam] ostenderis. Dein [te omnimodo liberum ab omni iurisdictione Regis vindicaris], quod vel unicum quantum siet, ipse perpende, quod tamen nisi hoc modo fieri nequit. Adhæc [si retineas, videas ne te tanquam en Lensmand, ut bona tibi a Rege concredita inhabites, iure quodam suo cogere præsumat]. Et ut omnia uno: [quamdiu insulam eam retinueris, tanquam subditus cuivis vocationi parere,] quibus certe magnas [tibi parare possunt] incommoditates et difficultates, insuper [citatus, ipse, seu præsens comparere], quod tibi valde foret difficile et prorsus impossibile, [aut quod ais pronunciatum perferre cogereris]. Et vero quid non [ipse] magna tua cum laude et præter multorum existimationem [eam deferre malles], cum [possint ipsi, ubi velint, etiam quodam iure eam præcipere, pretendentes] quippe [litteras tibi a Rege concessas] (quæ quidem [ad vitam eam] tibi [appropriat insulam]) sub [conditione] Astronomiæ [hic in Dania excolendæ conceptas] esse. Tu ipse [ingenia eorum nosti]; nihil certe intermiserint, ut interim [immensum istud discrimen inter alium aliquem nobilem Regis subditum et te] (in quo non postrema [bonitatis causæ tuæ] ratio vertitur) vel alto silentio [dissimulent] vel [malitiose elevent]. Ad alterum cogites velim, quam nec natura nec eius imitatores quid frustra committant, [iure vero quidpiam tentare] frustraneum simul ac periculosum, ubi et quod me tacente ipse satis intelligis, [quam inconstantes sint principum animi,] simul ac [quam non corvus unus alteri, quod dicitur, oculos eruat], tecum attentissime pro tua prudentia perpendas velim. Bono hæc animo dico, fidem testor et candorem; nec dicerem nisi bono. Nec quidpiam video, licet videre nunquam non laborem, quod [rebus tuis ulla ratione adversari queat et institutum tuum tandem turbare queat], præter [hæc duo]. Sed hæc Deo et tuæ prudentiæ.
text.english:
**HOLGER ROSENKRANTZ TO TYCHO BRAHE.**

[They breathe fire, and brood on it night and day,] but [it is] to be spewed back down their own throats.

[If — by an affection on my part certainly not warped by any (bias),] but confirmed by very many most weighty arguments and (believe me) by reflections sufficiently many and constant — [you will be willing to heed] mature [counsel], as I hope, [I would advise, first of all, that — by a letter addressed to the King — you surrender back the island of Hven, as it were rendering thanks for the royal liberality] (the things to be intimated having been prudently and calmly intimated), [acting so that you hand it back again]; yet so that you prudently — that is (ͻ:), **politically** — give notice in such a way [that your instruments may fall to you], (i.e. that you keep your instruments). The second [point] is this: that you not [seem] even to wish [to demand] the [hateful and odious restitution of your expenses], much less [demand it or stir it up]. You wish me to state sufficient reasons, and the weight of my reflections. [I will state them — but please do not be angry with me; with a good] heart, and [wishing you the very best, I say these things]. First, if you do it, you will above all have displayed [your magnanimity]. Next, [you will free yourself wholly from all jurisdiction of the King] — which, even as a single thing, weigh for yourself how great it is — a thing which, however, cannot be done except in this way. Besides, [if you retain it, see to it lest he presume to compel you, by some right of his own, as a *Lensmand* [fief-holder], to reside upon the goods entrusted to you by the King]. And to put it all in one: [as long as you retain that island, [you would be bound], as a subject, to obey any summons] — by which they can certainly contrive great inconveniences and difficulties [for you] — and moreover, [if cited, to appear yourself, in person], which would be very hard for you and altogether impossible, [or you would be forced to suffer the sentence pronounced, of which you speak]. And indeed, why would you not yourself rather, [with great praise to yourself and beyond many men's expectation, surrender it], since [they themselves can, when they will, seize it even by a certain right, alleging] indeed [that the letters granted you by the King] (which do indeed [appropriate that island to you] [for life]) were drawn up under the [condition] [of Astronomy being cultivated here in Denmark]. You yourself [know their dispositions]; they will assuredly have left nothing undone, so that meanwhile they either [conceal] in deep silence, or [maliciously belittle], that [immense difference between you and some other noble subject of the King] (wherein turns not the least part of [the goodness of your cause]). As to the second [point], I would have you consider how neither Nature nor her imitators undertake anything in vain — whereas [to attempt anything by law] is at once futile and perilous; where also — what, though I be silent, you well enough understand yourself — [how inconstant are the minds of princes,] and likewise [how, as the saying goes, one crow does not peck out another's eyes], I would have you weigh most attentively with yourself, according to your prudence. I say these things with a good heart; I call my good faith and candour to witness; nor would I say them but for good. Nor do I see anything — though I never cease labouring to see — that could in any way oppose your affairs and at last disturb your undertaking, save [these two things]. But these [I leave] to God and to your prudence.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Holger Rosenkrantz** "the Learned" (1574–1642), the Danish nobleman and scholar, Tycho's *consanguineus* (kinsman) and intimate friend; the edition and the neighbouring correspondence confirm the heading *Oligerus Rosenkrantz ad Tychonem Brahe* (cf. brahe-t_15980328001 apparatus, which already cites "a 7 March 1599 letter" of this title). Writing from Denmark, hence **Old Style**.
- **Significance — political counsel on surrendering Hven.** A candid, confidential letter of advice at the crux of Tycho's break with Denmark. Holger urges two things: **(1)** that Tycho **formally surrender the island of Hven back to the King by letter, framed as thanks for the royal liberality** — *prudenter, ϲ: Politice* ("prudently — that is, politically") — while quietly securing that **he keep his instruments**; and **(2)** that Tycho **not demand reimbursement of his expenses** (the great sums sunk into Uraniborg/Stjerneborg), which would be "hateful and odious."
- **The reasoning.** Holger's case: voluntary surrender (a) shows **magnanimity**; (b) **frees Tycho wholly from the King's jurisdiction** — whereas while he holds Hven he remains, *tanquam en Lensmand* ("as a *Lensmand*," a royal fief-holder), a **subject liable to any summons**, who could be cited to **appear in person** (impossible for the now-absent Tycho) or made to **suffer a pronounced sentence**. He warns that the crown party can in any case **reclaim Hven "by a certain right,"** since the royal letters granting Tycho the island *for life* were issued **on condition that astronomy be cultivated in Denmark** — a condition Tycho's departure had voided. He counsels against any recourse to **law** (*iure quidpiam tentare* — "futile and perilous"), citing the **inconstancy of princes** and the proverb that the great close ranks against an outsider.
- **Code-switch & abbreviation.**
 - *en Lensmand* — **Danish** embedded in the Latin: "a *Lensmand*," holder of a royal *len* (fief). Kept and glossed.
 - *ͻ:* (reversed-C colon) — the early-modern siglum for *id est* / *scilicet*, "that is"; it glosses *prudenter* as *Politice* ("politically"). Rendered "that is (ϲ:)".
- **Proverbs / allusions.** *noctesque diesque meditantur* echoes the Virgilian/Ennian epic cadence (cf. *noctes atque dies*); *corvus … alteri … oculos [non] eruat* = the classical *cornix cornici oculos non effodit*, "one crow does not peck out another crow's eyes" — i.e. men of the same order protect one another against an outsider; *bonum animum*/*candorem testor* are the friendship-formulae of frank counsel.
- **Textual crux — the square brackets (flagged, not resolved; this chapter's convention).** The source presents the body in **alternating bracketed and un-bracketed stretches**, with the bracketed portions carrying the politically sensitive content (the King, his jurisdiction, the surrender of Hven, the reclaim-by-right) and the un-bracketed words supplying connective tissue (*sed … quod spero … ut tamen … Vis … Primum …*). The bracketing is the **edition's**. **Resolved by collation against Dreyer, *Opera Omnia* VIII (pp. 148, 162–163) + the vol. IX critical apparatus (p. 309):** the brackets are the edition's **editorial restorations and conjectures of a single defective witness** — the Langebek *Diplomatarium afskrift* (the apparatus reads *regurgitandos conj. Friis] regurgitandas cod.*, i.e. Friis emending the one codex by conjecture) — **not** the decipherment of an enciphered letter. The bracketed spans and their boundaries match the edition of record exactly. The brackets are reproduced as-is in the source block; the translation renders the full text continuously, marking the bracketed spans.
- **Persons named.** Holger Rosenkrantz (sender); **Tycho Brahe** (recipient); the **King** (Christian IV) and his noble *subditi* — the crown party — unnamed individually; the island of **Hven**.
- **Calendar.** Dated 7 March 1599; **Old Style**, per the Danish sender. No place in the dateline; "[Denmark]" supplied in the header as the evident origin, flagged by brackets.

documents.abstract: Reports John Craig's disparagement of Tycho as arrogant, his grievance over Tycho's complaint to the King of Scotland, and his dismissal of Tycho's published letters against him.
documents.incipit: Reverende domine, amice pl. observande.

text.original:
REVERENDO ET CLARISSIMO VIRO D:NO MAGISTRO JONAe JACOBO VENUSINO, AMICO ET PATRONO PLURIMUM OBSERVANDO. HAFNIAM.

Reverende domine, amice pl. observande.

CUM post longam peregrinationem superiori aestate patriam et amicos reviserem, multi viri docti, qvis Germaniae, Daniae, et vicinorum regnorum status esset, diligenter ex me qvaesiverunt, inter qvos Johannes Cragius magni apud nostrates nominis astronomus, qvia magnam aetatis partem in Germania consumpserat, qvi nunc ibidem in mathesi excellerent vehementer scire avebat. Cum ego cum multis aliis Tychonem Brahe etiam nominassem, statim ille: fastuosus homo ille, qvi multa profert, sed pavca probat, qvia mecum aliqvando in lite qvadam philosophica minus pro arbitrio certasset, gravissimam de me ad Scotiae regem qverelam detulit, et non ita pridem, inqvit, ab ipso epistolas nonnullas aeditas ajunt, in qvibus me sine nomine acriter perstrinxit, sed nullam inde lavdem reportabit. Proinde isto fumi venditore relicto, dic, ait, anne alios in Dania nosti astronomos insignes. Ego honorificam tui, ut debui, mentionem feci, et post varios de humanitate tua sermones magnetis tui memini. Is qvia se multa de hoc lapide scire existimabat, amicitiam contrahere, et qvicqvid singulare in mathesi experientia didicisset, tecum communicare desiderabat. Certior a me de naturae tuae bonitate et exqvisita eruditione factus, literas meis inclusas ad te misit; qvod serius venerint, effecit turbulentus Svediae status, qvo ego praecipiti avtumno delatus fui. Qvaeso nunc boni consule; adiunctae sunt etiam aliae ad Tychonem, si possis efficere, ut ad ipsum perferantur, cures rogo. Sin minus, ad me remitte; aperire, si placet, poteris meo periculo; hanc mihi potestatem dedit Cragius. Si cras ad me rescripseris, avt ipse ad te veniam avt Svediae meumque statum ad te perscribam, jam avriga properabat. Navigandi Gedanum occasionem hic expectare cogor.

Vale cum toto coetu tuo.
Helsingora xx martii Mdic. T. r. a.
Patricius Gordonius
text.english:
**To the reverend and most distinguished man, Master Jon Jacobsen Venusinus, friend and patron much to be observed. To Copenhagen.**

Reverend lord, friend much to be observed.

When, after a long peregrination, last summer I revisited my homeland and [my] friends, many learned men diligently asked of me what was the state of Germany, of Denmark, and of the neighbouring kingdoms; among whom John Craig — an astronomer of great name among our [countrymen], because he had spent a great part of his life in Germany — was vehemently eager to know who now excelled there in mathematics. When I had named, among many others, Tycho Brahe also, at once he [said]: "That arrogant man, who puts forth much but proves little — because he once contended with me, in a certain philosophical dispute, less to [his own] liking, he brought a most grave complaint about me to the King of Scotland; and not long ago, they say, some letters were published by him, in which he sharply censured me without [naming my] name — but he will carry off no praise thereby. Accordingly, leaving that smoke-seller aside," he says, "tell [me], do you know other notable astronomers in Denmark?" I made honourable mention of you, as I ought; and, after various discourses about your kindness, I made mention of your magnet [loadstone]. He, because he thought he knew much about this stone, desired to contract a friendship, and to share with you whatever singular [thing] he had learned in mathematics by experience. Made more certain by me of the goodness of your nature and your exquisite erudition, he sent letters, enclosed in mine, to you; that they have come rather late, the turbulent state of Sweden brought about, whither I was carried in the headlong autumn. I pray [you], now take [it] in good part. There are also adjoined other [letters], to Tycho — if you can bring it about that they be conveyed to him, see to it, I pray. But if not, send [them] back to me; you can open [them], if you please, at my risk — Craig gave me this power. If tomorrow you write back to me, either I myself will come to you, or I will write out to you [the affairs] of Sweden and my own state — [but] now the carter was hastening. I am compelled to await here the occasion of sailing to Danzig.

Farewell, with your whole company.
Elsinore, the 20th of March, 1599. Most devoted to Your Reverence,
Patrick Gordon.

documents.apparatus:
- **A document of the Tycho–Craig controversy.** The Scottish traveller **Patrick Gordon** reports to **Jon Jacobsen Venusinus** a conversation with **John Craig** (*Johannes Cragius*, d. 1620), the Scottish physician-astronomer (later physician to **James VI/I**), Tycho's antagonist in the long **dispute over comets** (Craig held comets to be sublunary/optical; Tycho refuted him). Hearing Tycho named, Craig burst out that he is "**that arrogant man, who puts forth much but proves little**," a "**smoke-seller**" (*fumi venditor* — charlatan); complains that, after their "philosophical dispute," **Tycho had lodged a grave complaint against him with the King of Scotland**, and had "**published letters censuring me anonymously**" — the anti-Craig matter in Tycho's *Epistolae astronomicae* (1596). A rare outside witness to how bitterly Craig resented Tycho. (*de me … detulit*: read with Tycho as subject — Tycho complained to James VI *about Craig* — per the historical record; the reported speaker is Craig.)
- **Recipient.** **Jon Jacobsen Venusinus** (Jon Jakobsen Venusin, d. 1608), Danish polymath, royal historiographer and professor at Copenhagen, with a known interest in the **magnet** (*magnes* — loadstone); Gordon reports that Craig, hearing of Venusinus's magnetic studies, wishes to correspond. The letter forwards **Craig's letters to Venusinus** and, enclosed, **further letters for Tycho** — so the piece enters the Tychonic correspondence as a transmittal.
- **Persons & places.** *nostrates* = "our countrymen" (Scots); *Scotiae rex* = **James VI of Scotland**; *Gedanum* = **Danzig (Gdańsk)**; the "turbulent state of Sweden" and Gordon's autumn passage allude to the **Swedish succession crisis** (Charles vs Sigismund). *T. r. a.* = *Tuae Reverentiae addictissimus* ("most devoted to Your Reverence").
- **Calendar.** *Helsingora xx martii Mdic* — *Mdic* = **M D IC** = 1000 + 500 + 99 (subtractive *IC* = 99) = **1599**; **Elsinore (Helsingør)**, Denmark = **Old Style**. **20 March 1599.** Header agrees with the label.
- **Correction.** In Craig's reported speech, corrected 'less to [my] liking' to 'less to [his own] liking': the Latin's unstated possessive on 'pro arbitrio' is reflexive to the dispute's subject (Tycho), not to Craig, per the sentence's grammar and Dreyer's printed text (TBOO XIV p.151).

(=1599) and the dedication 'Ex apographo in Bibliotheca Regia Hauniensi: Ny kgl. Saml. 8vo Nr. 271, Side 67 f.' Checked every name (Johannes Cragius, Jon Jacobsen Venusinus, Patricius Gordonius), place (Helsingora/Elsinore, Gedanum/Danzig), and the date. One mistranslation found: the bracketed '[my]' possessive on 'pro arbitrio' misattributes whose satisfaction is at stake, reversing the sense of who came off worse in the Tycho-Craig dispute — a real interpretive point about the anecdote's balance, not a stylistic quibble. Everything else in the letter is faithful.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (medium). The subject of 'certasset' throughout this clause is 'ille' (Tycho), so the unstated possessor of 'pro arbitrio' defaults reflexively to Tycho, not to the first-person narrator Craig — i.e. the dispute went less to TYCHO's own liking (he came off worse), which is what supplies the causal motive for 'he [Tycho] brought a grave complaint about me to the King of Scotland' in the next clause. The English's bracketed '[my]' reassigns the dissatisfaction to Craig, reversing who was bested in the exchange — turning Craig's implicit boast about worsting Tycho into an ambiguous statement about his own disappointment, and breaking the causal logic of why Tycho then complained to the king. At: “he once contended with me, in a certain philosophical dispute, less to [my] liking”.

**Repaired.** Collated against Dreyer TBOO XIV pp.150-152 (in full); the clause is confirmed verbatim on p.151. The correction itself turns on standard Latin reflexive-possession grammar (unmarked possessives default to the clause's grammatical subject), which the page confirms textually; the interpretation is not contested elsewhere in the sentence, since it alone restores the causal 'because...he complained' logic. Single defect fixed.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD CHRISTIANUM LONGOMONTANUM.

S.

SCRIPSI tibi eruditissime et mihi plurimum dilecte M. CHRISTIANE bis, postquam huc Wittebergam veni, et semel a te literas accepi sub initium huius anni Ripis datas, ubi et priores meas tibi redditas ex tuis percepi, alteras postmodum Rostochium misi, quas te, quamprimum per hyemis asperitatem eo navigare licuit, ibi reperisse existimo. Ad tuas vero nunc brevibus, cum antea non sit oblata occasio, respondebo. Gratissimam rem praestas, quod in refutatione Capnuraniae Scoticae diligentem operam loces. Sunt saltem speciosa et pomposa eius omnia, ac veritati fucum faciunt. Invenies in libro nostro secundo de Cometa anni 77. suo loco, praesertim ubi in NOLTIJ placita disquiro, quantum in devia ab observatis detrudatur Cometes, si 5 proxime graduum parallaxin admisisset. Subsidium, quod expetis ab alijs Cometis, evidentius rem ostendentibus, satis firmum suppetit Cometa anni 80, qui et in meridiano et in 90 gradu iuxta horizontem non aliam declinationem mutavit, quam postulavit eius alteratio diurna, ex meridianis altitudinibus successive explorata, habita tamen refractionis in decliviori situ insinuatione, ut de alijs nunc nihil addam. Verum has confirmationes a pluribus Cometis petitas postea subiungere licebit, indicatione aliqua prius facta in Antapologia tua, qua introspecta, ulterius quid sentiam scies, quod mallem praesenti oretenus, quam absenti per literas indicare. De bruto Dithmarsico non ob id scripsi, quod a te redargutionem calumniarum eius expeterem, neque enim dignus est; sed saltem ut denotares obiter in charta aliqua, quae a nostris domesticis de plagio eius inaudivisti, quemadmodum fecit M. CHRISTIANUS IOHANNIS Ripensis, alterum expediet D. D. IOHANNES ROTHMANNUS, uti manes fratris defuncti postulant. Constitueram hîc edere sex illos quaterniones, qui in ☾ desiderantur, atque sic Tomum primum Progymnasmatum absolvere, ut in hisce Francofurdianis nundinis venalis extare possit, et iam inchoatus erat labor ille Typographicus, postquam papyrum meam impressoriam Wandesburgo acceperam. Verum dum Eclipsi ☾ die ultimo Ianuarij diligenter hîc per mea instrumenta attendo, deprehendi eius initium per ⅖ unius horae quam proxime calculum praevertere, ideoque a proposito destiti, donec huic deviationi provisum fuerit. Scis enim me exactam requirere concordantiam, quoad fieri possit. Nec satis mirari possum, quî fiat, quod Eclipsis anni 81, in Ianuario etiam facta et prope Apogaeum, tam belle nostris numeris conveniat, haec autem pariter iuxta Apogaeum et eodem anni tempore ita discrepet. Suspicor igitur aliquam adhuc inaequalitatem Anomaliae Lunae subesse, quae post aliquot annos peracta Eclipsium ad similia ferme loca restitutione praesertim iuxta Apogaeum et Perigaeum evidentius pateat, qua de re tecum, qui omnes nostras Eclipses diligenter examinasti, atque ipsarum varietates perspectas habes, conferre averem, ut eo citius huic obstaculo succurratur, quod facile fieri posse existimo. Sum in alijs rebus occupatissimus, ut satis huic disquisitioni vacare nequeam. Si igitur me accesseris cum auriga Wittebergensi, ubi isthuc reversus fuerit, rem mihi apprime gratam nec tibi inutilem praestiteris.

Sum denuo evocatus Pragam ex Clementissimo Caesaris mandato, per literas amplissimi Domini Procancellarij CORADUCIJ, ut ex adiuncto exemplari vides; et paro nunc omnia ad iter, quod tamen ante Pascha ingredi non licebit ob aquarum nimiam copiam, postquam nives subito dissolutae sunt, vias difficillimas et periculosas reddentem. Si adfueris et me comitari libuerit, dabo operam, ut tuis rebus rectius consulatur, quam uspiam alibi, sin vero hîc manere aut redire isthuc mavis, erit et hoc tibi liberum. Ego tuis commodis quocunque modo, quantumque in me est, sedulo studebo. Non patiar, ullum erga te officium desiderari.

Vale et literas has nemini ostende.
Dabantur Wittebergae die 21. Martij 1599.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO CHRISTEN LONGOMONTANUS.**

Greeting.

I have written to you twice, most learned and most beloved Master Christen, since I came hither to Wittenberg, and once received a letter from you, sent from Ribe at the beginning of this year — wherein I also perceived from yours that my earlier ones had been delivered to you; the others I afterward sent to Rostock, which I think you found there as soon as it was possible to sail thither through the harshness of winter. But to yours I will now reply briefly, since no occasion was offered before. You do a most welcome thing, in placing diligent effort on the **refutation of the Scottish *Capnurania***. All his things are at least specious and pompous, and put a [false] colour on the truth. You will find, in our second book on the Comet of [15]77, in its place — especially where I examine **Noltius's** opinions — how far the Comet would be thrust into deviations from the observations, had it admitted a parallax of nearly 5 degrees. The support you seek from other Comets, more evidently showing the matter, is firmly enough supplied by the **Comet of [15]80**, which, both on the meridian and at the 90th degree along the horizon, changed no other declination than its diurnal alteration required (explored successively from the meridian altitudes, the influence of **refraction** in the more inclined position being however taken into account) — to say nothing now of the others. But these confirmations sought from several Comets may be appended afterward, some indication being first made in your ***Antapologia***; which once examined, you will further know what I think — which I should prefer to indicate to you present, by word of mouth, than to you absent, by letter. Concerning **the Dithmarsic brute** I did not write that I might seek from you a refutation of his calumnies — for he is not worthy of it — but only that you might note down in passing, on some paper, what you have heard from our household about his **plagiarism**, as **Master Christian Jensen of Ribe** did; the other [part] Lord Doctor **Johannes Rothmann** will expedite, as the shade of his deceased brother demands. I had resolved to publish here those **six quaternions that are wanting in [the theory of] the Moon**, and so to complete the **first Tome of the *Progymnasmata***, that it might be on sale at this Frankfurt fair; and that typographic labour was already begun, after I had received my printing-paper from Wandsbek. But while I diligently attend here, with my instruments, to the **Eclipse of the Moon on the last day of January**, I found that its beginning **anticipated the calculation by very nearly ⅖ of one hour** — and therefore I desisted from my purpose, until this deviation be provided for. For you know I require exact concordance, so far as can be done. Nor can I sufficiently wonder how it comes about that the eclipse of [15]81 — also in January and near the **Apogee** — agrees so beautifully with our numbers, while this one, likewise near the Apogee and at the same season, so discrepates. I suspect, therefore, that **some inequality of the Moon's Anomaly still underlies it**, which after some years — by the return of eclipses to nearly the same places, especially near Apogee and Perigee — may appear more evidently; about which I should wish to confer with you, who have diligently examined all our eclipses and have their varieties thoroughly known, that this obstacle may the sooner be remedied (which I think can easily be done). I am most occupied with other matters, so that I cannot be sufficiently free for this disquisition. If, therefore, you come to me with the **Wittenberg coachman**, when he has returned thither, you will do me a thing exceedingly welcome, and not unprofitable to you.

I am again summoned to **Prague** by the Emperor's most clement mandate, through a letter of the most ample Lord Vice-Chancellor **Coraduz** — as you see from the enclosed copy; and I now prepare everything for the journey, which, however, it will not be permitted to begin before Easter, on account of the excessive abundance of waters (after the snows were suddenly thawed), rendering the roads most difficult and dangerous. If you are present and it please you to accompany me, I will take pains that your affairs be better provided for than anywhere else; but if you prefer to stay here, or to return thither, this too will be free to you. I will assiduously strive for your interests, in whatever way, and as far as in me lies; I will not allow any service toward you to be wanting.

Farewell, and **show this letter to no one**.
Given at Wittenberg, 21 March 1599.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus**, then in Denmark (at Ribe), Tycho's senior assistant (cf. brahe-t_15981231001, brahe-t_15990111001). Written from the **Wittenberg winter** of 1598–99. The MS is a later Langebek *afskrift*.
- **The Craig refutation — *"Capnurania Scotica."*** Tycho welcomes Longomontanus's work on **refuting "the Scottish *Capnurania*"** — Tycho's mocking coinage (Greek *kapnos* "smoke" + *Urania*) for **John Craig's** cometary doctrine that comets are **terrestrial smoke/vapour**: "all his things are specious and pompous, and put a false colour on the truth." (The commission of brahe-t_15981231001; *Antapologia* = Longomontanus's counter-defence against Craig's *Apologia*.) Tycho points him to his **second book on the comet of 1577** (the *De mundi … recentioribus phaenomenis*) — esp. against **Noltius** — and to the **comet of 1580** as decisive evidence (its declination changed only by diurnal parallax, refraction accounted for), arguing comets show **no large (≈5°) parallax** and so are **celestial, not sublunary**.
- **The Ursus plagiarism dispute ("the Dithmarsic brute").** *brutum Dithmarsicum* = **Nicolaus Reimers Bär ("Ursus")** of Dithmarschen, who had **plagiarised Tycho's geo-heliocentric system** and attacked him (in *De hypothesibus astronomicis*, 1597). Tycho — holding him "not worthy" of formal refutation — asks Longomontanus only to **note down what the household heard of his plagiarism**, as **Master Christian Jensen of Ribe** had; "the other part **Doctor Johannes Rothmann** will expedite, as the shade of his deceased brother demands" — apparently **Johannes Rothmann vindicating the memory of his late brother** (most plausibly **Christoph Rothmann**, the Hesse-Kassel mathematician, whose work Ursus had also touched; identification flagged, not asserted).
- **The lunar-theory crux (technical; this chapter's convention).** Tycho had begun printing the **six quaternions of the lunar theory** to finish the **first Tome of the *Progymnasmata*** for the **Frankfurt fair** — but **halted** when the **lunar eclipse of 31 January [1599]** began **≈ ⅖ hour (24 min) before his calculation**. He marvels that the eclipse of **1581** (also January, near **apogee**) fitted his numbers "beautifully," while this one (likewise near apogee, same season) "discrepates," and **suspects an unaccounted inequality of the Moon's anomaly** — to be tested by eclipses returning near **apogee/perigee** — wanting Longomontanus (who knows all his eclipses) to help. A first-rate document of Tycho's still-unfinished lunar theory.
- **The Prague summons.** Tycho is **again summoned to Prague** by **Coraduz's** letter (enclosed in copy), preparing the journey — not before **Easter**, the thaw-flooded roads being "most difficult and dangerous." He offers Longomontanus to accompany him (with better provision than anywhere else) or to stay/return, as he prefers.
- **Glyphs/terms.** ☾ = **Moon**; *parallaxis* → **parallax**; *refractio* → **refraction**; *declinatio* → **declination**; *Apogaeum/Perigaeum* → **apogee/perigee**; *Anomalia* → **anomaly**; *inaequalitas* → **inequality**.
- **Persons named.** Longomontanus; **John Craig** (the *Capnurania*); **Noltius**; **Nicolaus Reimers Bär (Ursus)** ("the Dithmarsic brute"); **Christian Jensen of Ribe**; **Johannes Rothmann** (and his late brother — Christoph Rothmann?); **Coraduz** (Vice-Chancellor); **Rudolf II**.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Wittebergae die 21. Martij 1599*; Wittenberg/Saxony kept the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar. Header agrees with the label.
- Correction. Latin corrected 'detrudetur' to the subjunctive 'detrudatur' (Dreyer VIII p.149); English unaffected.

Collated opening/closing lines and every proper name (Noltius, Antapologia, M. Christianus Iohannis Ripensis, Johannes Rothmannus, Coraducius), date (21 Martij 1599, Eclipse 'die ultimo Ianuarij', years 77/80/81), and figure (the ⅕-hour discrepancy) against Dreyer; translation is accurate throughout. One text error found in the transcribed original (see above); per the grading rule any text error caps the grade at C even though its severity is low and the translation itself is unaffected.

Dreyer prints the present subjunctive 'detrudatur' (required inside the indirect question governed by 'disquiro'); our transcribed original has the indicative-looking 'detrudetur'. A single-letter corruption of the verb's mood. The English translation is unaffected — it happens to render the counterfactual sense correctly regardless. Dreyer prints: *quantum in devia ab obfervatis detrudatur Cometes, fi 5 proxime graduum parallaxin admififfet (TBOO VIII p.149)*.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD IOSEPHUM SCALIGERUM.

S. P.

ILLUSTRIS et Magnifice Vir, Amice inprimis honorande. Redditæ mihi sunt tuæ literæ unâ cum libris mihi dono missis serius quam expectassemus, et ego, quod multis distentus fuerim negotijs atque alias varie praepeditus, nec in promptu esset, qui meas certo referret, tardius etiam quam decuisset, quamque ipse maluissem, rescribo, quod mihi a tua ingenua humanitate condonari cupio. Pro utroque autem libro mihi tam benigne concesso proque tuo non modico labore in excerpendis ijs, quæ apud HIPPARCHUM, et nonnunquam etiam PTOLOMÆUM in hoc negotio de Fixis Sideribus præcipua erant, ijsdemque propria manu in mei gratiam tanta diligentia conscriptis, non possum tibi promeritas satisque dignas agere gratias, nedum referre, neque enim video qua ratione hoc tuum tam eximium in me beneficium compensare valeam, animum tamen gratum, et tui honoris studiosissimum semper me servaturum tibi persuadeas, et si quæ ex mea tenuitate in hisce, quibus utrinque afficimur, studijs proficisci poterint, ea non invite tecum vicissim communicabo. Fateris ipsemet, Vir Excellentissime, multa esse in his, quæ circa Fixas tam ab HIPPARCHO quam PTOLOMÆO consignata sunt, quæ suis numeris rite non constent, nec sibi ipsis consentiant, et sane res ita se habet; ego enim paucissima in ijs reperio, quæ convenienter ad Cœli normam digesta sint, deviatione satis manifesta prorsusque intolerabili plurimis in locis sese prodente, sive id Observationum incuria (quas tamen sic nimis crassas fuisse oportuisset) sive transcriptorum negligentia aut quacunque alia de causa id commissum fuisse existimemus. Si loca Fixarum a me summa diligentia præteritis aliquot annis explorata, pro quibus ipsum Cœlum etiamnum testatur, retro ad tempora PTOLEMAEI et HIPPARCHI, per motum interea ijs competentem, numeraverimus, atque hinc Declinationes, Culminationes, Ortus et Occasus quoscunque ad eadem quibus illi usi sunt Climata deduxerimus, certe rarissime cum eorum annotatis consentire depræhendentur: Et licet nonnunquam concordantia aliqua inveniatur, tamen ea ἐν πλάτει tantum et nimis lato modo sumta est; nullatenus enim admitti poterit stellas irregulariter et diversimode interea motas fuisse, cum omnes uniformem et regularem in uno eodemque Orbe observent progressionem, quod invariata earundem ad invicem distantia et dispositio indubitate ostendit, quæ vel hinc liquet, quod omnes Fixæ, quæ ab HIPPARCHO et PTOLOMÆO in uno lineæ rectæ ductu existere proditæ sunt, etiamnum eundem prorsus tramitem conservent, prout a nobis sedulo disquisitum est. Miror itaque a tam Excellentibus Artificibus non satis accuratam in his præstitam esse diligentiam, cum res sit magni momenti, nec Planetarum motiones certo explorari queant, nisi prius ad amussim præfinita sint Fixarum loca, quod etiam me in ijs, quæ PTOLOMÆUS circa Erraticarum apparentias tradidit, non parum reddit ancipitem quoad exactam illam, quam desidero, rationem. Attamen loca inerrantium stellarum, quæ ex Abaco HIPPARCHI suo Almagesto inseruit, non videntur tantam enormitatem præ se ferre, atque hæc est, quam liber transmissus in plerisque exhibet.

Verum his nunc omissis, quæ limitare, atque quatenus fieri potest in concinniorem rationem redigere, suo forte tempore elaborabimus, aliud est quod nunc potius desiderarem, de quo etiam, si recte memini, prius te rogavi, ut nimirum Æquinoctiorum omnium ab HIPPARCHO observatorum rationes designatas obtineam, ita ut Annis Iulianis retro subactis rite applicentur, et simul quomodo Annus ille respectu bissexti se habuerit, indicetur: Cuperem vero ipsa HIPPARCHI verba, quatenus illa eiuscemodi observationes concernunt, nihil enim horum in libris mihi impertitis invenire licuit; tum quoque si quas alias in his vetustissimas in promptu habes cœlitus deductas animadversiones. Australes Asterismos nobis Europæis hactenus incognitos convenienti diligentia observatos necdum vidi, repræsentarunt quidem circa Polum Austrinum stellas quasdam nobis incompertas Globorum in vestra Batavia confectores; sed nimis ieiuna et parca est ista designatio, crediderim multo plures isthic apparere. Si plenior et accuratior earundem descriptio penes te est, eamque mecum communicare non degravatus fueris, rem admodum acceptam præstiteris. ALBATEGNIUM quoque fidelius quam antea castigatum, si tua opera aliquando obtinuerimus, non parum commodi hisce studijs inde accedet. Utinam Arabicum Exemplum obtinere posses; neque enim dubito quin, cum linguæ illius, uti et plurimarum aliarum usque ad miraculum, apprime gnarus sis, hac in parte plurimum sis huic studio profuturus.

Porro ut rerum mearum statum aliquatenus perspectum habeas, scias me, postquam e loco prioris meæ habitationis discesseram, in Bohemiam ex Cæsareæ Maiestatis clementissima voluntate cogitans, Dresdam Misniæ ubi pervenissem, omniaque in Bohemia ob luem Epidemicam isthic passim grassantem conturbata esse cognovissem, substitisse ibi paulisper, donec mihi ex Aula Cæsarea præscriptum erat, ipsius Maiestatem clementissime cupere, ut alicubi in vicinia me continerem, donec malum illud Epidemicum remitteret. Ideoque huc Wittebergam propter Academiæ celebritatem me aliquantisper recepi. Evocatus autem sum nuper denuo Pragam, ex clementissimo Cæsaris mandato, per literas Amplissimi Domini RUDOLPHI CORADUCIJ Procancellarij Imperialis. Et quamprimum quædam in libris nonnullis, quos Cæsareæ Maiestati humilime offerre decrevi, plane absolvero (quod brevi me effecturum spero) denuo iter Pragense ingredi, atque Cæsareæ Maiestatis benignissimæ voluntati debita subiectione morem gerere in animum induxi. Deus Optimus Maximus successus prosperos et exoptatos largiri dignetur. Ubi vero portum aliquem quietum pro meis studijs, sive isthic sive alibi invenero, plenius te de rebus nostris edocebo, atque de ijs, quæ studia hæc, quibus iucunde utrinque afficimur, concernunt, uberius tecum conferre non intermittam. Interim hæc, ob plurimas occupationes pro præsenti mittendi ad vos literas occasione deproperata, boni consule, inque cœpto erga me favore et amore persiste.

Vale Vir Illustris et Excellentissime, seculi nostri decus.
Dabantur subito Wittebergæ die 17 Aprilis Anni 99, st. vet.
Illustri Magnif. tuæ addictiss.
TYCHO BRAHE, manu propria.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO JOSEPH SCALIGER.**

Heartiest greeting.

Illustrious and magnificent Man, friend especially to be honoured. Your letter, together with the books sent me as a gift, was delivered to me later than we had expected; and I — both because I have been distracted by many affairs and otherwise variously hindered, and because there was not at hand one who could surely carry mine — write back later too than was fitting, and than I myself should have preferred; which I wish to be pardoned me by your noble humanity. For both books so kindly granted me, and for your no small labour **in excerpting what was chief in Hipparchus, and sometimes also in Ptolemy, in this business of the Fixed Stars — and these written out in your own hand, for my sake, with such diligence** — I cannot give you the thanks deserved and worthy, much less repay them; nor do I see by what means I might requite this so signal benefit of yours toward me. Yet persuade yourself that I shall always keep a grateful mind, most zealous of your honour; and if anything can proceed from my slenderness in these studies, with which we are both affected, I will not unwillingly share it with you in turn. You yourself confess, most excellent Man, **that there are many things in what was recorded about the Fixed [stars] by both Hipparchus and Ptolemy which do not duly tally with their own numbers, nor agree with themselves** — and indeed the matter is so; for I find very few in them digested fitly to the norm of the Sky, **a deviation manifest enough and altogether intolerable betraying itself in very many places** — whether we judge it committed by carelessness of the Observations (which must then have been far too gross), or by the negligence of transcribers, or from any other cause. **If we count the positions of the Fixed [stars], explored by me these past years with the utmost diligence (for which the Sky itself still testifies), back to the times of Ptolemy and Hipparchus, by the motion [precession] belonging to them meanwhile**, and thence derive declinations, culminations, risings and settings whatsoever for the same Climes they used, they will certainly very rarely be found to agree with their notations. And although some concordance is sometimes found, yet it is taken only **broadly [ἐν πλάτει]** and in too loose a manner. **For it can in no way be admitted that the stars moved irregularly and diversely in the interim, since all keep a uniform and regular progression in one and the same Orb** — which their unchanged mutual distance and disposition undoubtedly shows; and this is clear even from this, that **all the Fixed [stars] which were reported by Hipparchus and Ptolemy to lie in one straight line still keep the very same track**, as has been carefully investigated by us. I wonder, then, that by such Excellent Artificers a diligence not accurate enough was shown in these things — since the matter is of great moment, and **the motions of the Planets cannot be surely explored unless the positions of the Fixed [stars] are first precisely predetermined** — which also makes me not a little doubtful, in what Ptolemy transmitted about the appearances of the Wandering [stars], as to that exact reckoning which I desire. Yet the positions of the fixed stars which **[Ptolemy] inserted into his Almagest from the Abacus [table] of Hipparchus** do not seem to bear so great an enormity as this which the book transmitted [by you] exhibits in most places.

But, these things now set aside — which to limit, and so far as can be done reduce to a neater reckoning, we shall perhaps work out in their time — there is **another thing I would rather now desire, about which (if I recall rightly) I asked you before: namely that I may obtain the reckonings of all the Equinoxes observed by Hipparchus, set down so that they may be rightly applied with the Julian years reduced backward, and at the same time that it be indicated how that year stood with respect to the bissextile [leap year].** I should wish indeed Hipparchus's own words, so far as they concern such observations — for I could find none of these in the books imparted to me — and also any other most ancient celestial observations of this kind you have at hand. **The Southern Asterisms, hitherto unknown to us Europeans, observed with fitting diligence, I have not yet seen**: the makers of Globes in your Holland [Batavia] did indeed represent, around the South Pole, certain stars unknown to us; but that designation is too meagre and sparse — I should believe that many more appear there. If a fuller and more accurate description of them is with you, and you would not find it a burden to share it with me, you will do a most welcome thing. **Al-Battani [Albategnius] too, more faithfully corrected than before, if we should one day obtain it by your labour, will bring no small advantage to these studies. Would that you could obtain an Arabic copy**; for I do not doubt that, since you are excellently skilled in that tongue (as in very many others, to a miracle), you will in this part greatly profit this study.

Further, that you may have my situation somewhat clear: know that I — after I had departed from the place of my former dwelling, intending [to go] into Bohemia by the Imperial Majesty's most clement will — when I had reached **Dresden in Meissen**, and had learned that everything in Bohemia was thrown into confusion by the epidemic plague raging there far and wide, **halted there a while**, until it was prescribed me from the Imperial Court that His Majesty most clemently wished me to keep myself somewhere in the neighbourhood until that epidemic evil should abate. And therefore **I withdrew hither to Wittenberg for a while, on account of the Academy's renown.** But I have lately been summoned again to Prague, by the Emperor's most clement mandate, **through a letter of the most ample Lord Rudolf Coraduz, Imperial Vice-Chancellor**. And as soon as I shall have quite finished certain things in **some books which I have resolved humbly to offer the Imperial Majesty** (which I hope to do shortly), I have resolved to set out again on the Prague journey, and to comply with the Imperial Majesty's most kindly will with due submission. May God, Best and Greatest, deign to grant prosperous and longed-for success. And when I find some quiet port for my studies, whether there or elsewhere, I will instruct you more fully of my affairs, and will not cease to confer more amply with you about what concerns these studies, with which we are both pleasantly affected. Meanwhile take in good part these [lines], hurried for the present by the occasion of sending a letter to you, amid very many occupations; and persist in the favour and love toward me you have begun.

Farewell, illustrious and most excellent Man, the ornament of our age.
Given hastily at Wittenberg, the 17th day of April, the year [15]99, Old Style.
Most devoted to your illustrious Magnificence,
**Tycho Brahe**, in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Joseph Justus Scaliger** at Leiden — the chronologist and philologist. This is the **earlier** of the two Scaliger letters in the literature consulted (cf. the July-1600 precession letter, brahe-t_16000723001 / 16000623001).
- **Significance — Tycho's critique of the ancient star catalogues (a major statement of his fixed-star programme).**
 - **The Hipparchus/Ptolemy catalogues are corrupt.** Tycho agrees with Scaliger that much in Hipparchus's and Ptolemy's fixed-star data "does not tally with its own numbers nor agree with itself," with "intolerable deviation" — from gross observation, transcribers' negligence, or other cause.
 - **The precession test.** Tycho's method: take **his own carefully-determined star positions and reckon them back, by precession, to Ptolemy's and Hipparchus's epochs** — they "very rarely agree." The stars cannot have moved irregularly, since **their mutual distances are invariant and collinear stars stay collinear** — a clean statement of the rigidity of the stellar sphere under uniform precession.
 - **Why it matters.** "**The motions of the Planets cannot be surely explored unless the positions of the Fixed [stars] are first precisely predetermined**" — the methodological core of Tycho's whole enterprise (and the ground of his doubt about Ptolemy's planetary data).
 - **A textual observation.** The star-positions Ptolemy drew **from Hipparchus's "Abacus" into the Almagest** seem less corrupt than the (more enormous) figures in the book Scaliger sent.
 - **Three requests to Scaliger:** *(1)* **Hipparchus's own equinox observations**, set to reduce against Julian years (with leap-year status) — for chronology/precession; *(2)* a **fuller catalogue of the new Southern asterisms** — Tycho has seen only the "meagre" southern stars on the **Dutch globe-makers'** globes (the Keyser–Houtman southern constellations via the Dutch globes; cf. the globe-maker / Blaeu-at-Uraniborg thread, the letter to Tobias Fischer of 16 May 1600, brahe-t_16000516002) and believes "many more appear there"; *(3)* **a better-corrected al-Battani (Albategnius), ideally an Arabic copy** — praising Scaliger's "miraculous" command of Arabic and other tongues.
- **Biographical status report (spring 1599).** Tycho's itinerary after leaving Hven/Germany: **→ Dresden** (halted by the **Bohemian plague**) **→ Wittenberg** ("for the Academy's renown") — now **summoned again to Prague by Coraduz's letter**, to set out once he finishes **the books he means to offer the Emperor** (the *Mechanica* / *Progymnasmata* presentation set). A precise fix on the pre-Benátky interim.
- **Persons & works named.** Joseph Justus Scaliger; **Hipparchus**, **Ptolemy** (the *Almagest*, Hipparchus's *Abacus*); **al-Battani (Albategnius)**; **Rudolf Coraduz** (Vice-Chancellor); **Rudolf II**; the **Dutch globe-makers**. Places: **Wittenberg**, **Dresden/Meissen**, **Bohemia/Prague**, **Holland (Batavia)**.
- **Calendar.** *die 17 Aprilis Anni 99, **st. vet.*** → **17 April 1599 [Old Style]** (Tycho explicitly marks Old Style at Wittenberg/Saxony); header and label agree.

text.original:
IACOBUS BONGARSIUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

NOBILISSIME ET AMPLISSIME DOMINE.

TRES iam septimanæ abierunt, ex quo redditæ mihi sunt illæ, quas ad me dedisti IX Martij. Sed neque eas accepi, quas memoras datas sub finem superioris anni, neque FRANCISCUM TENGNAGLIUM vidi, quem a te, tanto viro, commendatum omnibus fuisse officijs proferebas. Non gravaberis itaque repetere et quæ illis litteris erant explicata, et quæ huius fidei commiseras. Me certe, magno tuo merito, habebis ad omnia, quæ quidem sunt meæ potestatis, semper paratissimum. Nec addo plura; sed mandata tua exspecto cupide. Tuas vero tute poteris committere bibliopolæ, qui CLAUDIJ MARINI WECHELIANI officinæ præest Pragæ.

Francofurti 1. Maij 1599.
text.english:
**Jacques Bongars to Tycho Brahe.**

Most noble and most ample Master.

Three weeks have now passed since those letters were delivered to me which you sent me on 9 March. But I have neither received those which you mention as sent toward the end of last year, nor have I seen Frans Tengnagel, whom you declared to have been commended — by you, so great a man — with every good office [i.e. recommended to receive every courtesy]. You will not, therefore, find it burdensome to repeat both what was set out in those letters, and what you had entrusted to his good faith. Me certainly, by your great merit, you shall always have most ready for everything that is indeed within my power. Nor do I add more; but I eagerly await your instructions. Your own [letters] you can safely entrust to the bookseller who is in charge, at Prague, of the office of Claude de Marne the Wechelian.

Frankfurt, 1 May 1599.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Jacques Bongars** (Jacobus Bongarsius, 1554–1612), French humanist, philologist, and diplomat in Imperial service; a learned correspondent and book-conduit for Tycho. The letter survives in his papers at Bern (the Bongars collection, source of the *Codices Bongarsiani*).
- ***Franciscus Tengnaglius*** = **Frans Gansneb genaamd Tengnagel van de Camp** (c. 1576–1622), Tycho's noble assistant, later (1604) his son-in-law; here being recommended to Bongars but not yet arrived.
- ***Claudij Marini Wecheliani officina*** = the printing-and-bookselling house of **Claude de Marne** (with Jean Aubry, the heirs of **Andreas Wechel**) — the great Frankfurt scholarly firm; Bongars names its agent **at Prague** as the safe relay for letters to him.
- **Near-duplicate.** This letter recurs almost verbatim a year later as **brahe-t_16000501001** (Frankfurt, 1 May 1600, to Tycho at Benátky) — evidently Bongars re-sent the same unanswered text; the two share the *Tengnagel* and *Wechel-agent* matter with only minor verbal variants (*sunt*/*erunt*, *proferebas*/*prosecutus*).
- **Calendar.** **Frankfurt am Main**, a predominantly Protestant Imperial city, kept the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar until 1700; the date is taken as O.S. (the edition gives no *n.s.* tag). *Flagged* as a mild assumption, since the writer is a Catholic-service Frenchman; nothing in the letter turns on the style.

documents.abstract: Acknowledges Rosenkrantz's letter on the vernal equinox and relays Vice-Chancellor Coraduz’s messages conveying the Emperor’s favour and the summons to Prague.
documents.incipit: QUAS circa æquinoctium vernum huius anni ad me e Rosenholmiano tuo dedisti literas, …

text.original:
VIRTUTE, ERUDITIONE ET GENERE VIRO INPRIMIS CLARO, DOMINO OLIGERO ROSÆKRANTZIO A ROSENHOLMIO, AMICO INTEGERRIMO, CONSANGVINEO FIDELISSIMO, AFFINI AMANTISSIMO, AD PROPRIAS MANUS.

S. P.

QUAS circa æquinoctium vernum huius anni ad me e Rosenholmiano tuo dedisti literas, OLIGERE desideratissime, ante paucos dies hîc accepi. Excusas ab initio tarditatem in rescribendo, et quod meæ præpostere ac sero ad te perlatæ sint; alterum hoc ferendum est ob viarum intercapedinem et Tabellariorum incuriam, prius amicitia nostra facile in meliorem partem interpretatur. Percipio ex hisce, quod descriptum verborum Domini CORADUCIJ, Procancellarij Imperialis, quibus me, cum Dresdæ essem, de clementissima Cæsaris voluntate certiorem reddidit, legeris, idque tibi placuisse. Scripsit vero idem CORADUCIUS circa finem Ianuarij huius anni alteras ad me, quibus ex Clementissimo ipsius Cæsareæ Maiestatis mandato me Pragam benigne evocat, quarum exemplar misi ad D. D. VITUM WINSHEMIUM, communem nostrum amicum, oblata nimirum occasione per Tabellarium Hamburgum subito euntem, quo is illud ad te dirigeret, quod et se, nacta confestim oportunitate, fecisse; paulo post mihi rescripsit, ut te illud nunc accepisse existimem, vel saltem dum in Scania esses, simile extractum apud sororem SOPHIAM vidisse, ut ob id reiteratione non sit opus. Coactus autem sum iter hoc Pragense diutius procrastinare, quam vellem, partim ob itinerum impedimenta, per aquarum illuviem post nivem subito resolutam præter solitum incidentia, partim quod Libri Cæsari destinati tam cito ac cuperem plane absolvi nequierint, superveniente etiam Filiæ natu maioris gravi invalitudine, alijsque nonnullis obstaculis concurrentibus, quæ volens prætereo. Fuit interim Pragæ D. D. THOMAS FRANTZIUS, WINSHEMIJ Gener, quem nosti; is huc reversus, multa de Clementissima Cæsareæ Maiestatis erga me voluntate, et quam benigne quamque honorifico loco me habere constituerit, prout a Domino Procancellatio CORADUCIO sibi, ut ea mihi indicaret, iniunctum aiebat, retulit: quæ tamen hîc sigillatim attingere nolo, verum ubi ipsemet illic præsens expertus fuero, quo in statu res meæ futuræ sint, te plenius de singulis edocebo. Profectus est dictus FRANTZIUS ante paucas hebdomadas hinc Hamburgum, ut inde ad comites in Orientali Frisia, quorum causas in aula Cæsaris agit, se conferret, cumque ante abitum eius semel atque iterum familiarius invicem conversaremur, tuique subinde honorifica facta esset mentio, aiebat se te quoque invisurum, prout ab illo petieras, si modo res eius id ullatenus tolerarent. Ego vero, ut id faceret, ipsum adhortabar. Quod si præstiterit, plura ab illo percipies, quam calamus nunc sustinet.

Cæterum quæ de Insulula ista, quæ tanti mihi constitit, scribis et mones, tanquam ex candido et mihi bene cupienti animo profecta, candide et sincere accipio. Argumenta, quæ adducis, satis probabilia sunt, et licet apud me irrefragabilem Geometricamque demonstrandi vim non mereantur, siquidem tam hæc quam plura eiusmodi replicare et validiora ijsdem opponere non sit difficile, tamen tuis et aliorum hac in parte consilijs non prorsus resistendum censeo; aliquantulum saltem temporis ad deliberandum, quid hac in re faciendum vel omittendum sit, mihi concedi cupio, ne nimis præcipitanter quid agat. Neque enim certi quid mecum statuere potero, antequam Pragæ Cæsaris Clementissimam de meis rebus voluntatem omnimode perspectam habuero; tunc demum satis erit temporis de his atque alijs quidpiam concludere, nec sane consultum videtur prius sponte Insulam restituere: imo si retinerem, donec illi, prout in cæteris (quæ plus emolumenti attulerunt) factum est, quocunque tandem prætextu mihi eam adimant, forte plus commodi quam incommodi hinc sum habiturus. Quid si aliquando mihi obijcerent, quod non fuissent eam recepturi, nisi sponte restituissem, volenti nullam fieri iniuriam, et pleraque alia, quibus lubens supersedeo? Minas certe eorum, quantæcunque sint, non reformido, fretus causæ bonitate; viderint ipsi; spero quod Deus me aliquando a tantis iniurijs vindicabit, cuius præsidio dum nitor, fortuna omnis superanda ferendo est. Plura et particulariora nunc nec vacat nec lubet. Accingo me, quantum possum, ad iter Pragense, relicturus Dresdæ Gynæceum, donec in Bohemiam excurrero. Tu vero, mi exoptatissime OLIGERE, unâ cum Coniuge tua et Nepte mea, resalutata a me peramanter tam matre tua quam illa, felicissime vale. Salutem ex te dixi Viris hîc Eruditis, quorum familiari notitia prius usus es, quod et antea feci, sæpe enim tuam memoriam iucunde recolimus, illi vero te vicissim resalutant, et optima quæque tibi et tuis precantur.

Iterum vale.
Dabantur Wittebergæ die 7. Maij Anni 1599.
Tuus absens ut præsens
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, pp. 155–156; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Libros, quos expetis, per hunc Tabellarium mittere nec commodum nec consultum visum est; habebis eos alias; vel da operam, ut exemplaria Regi oblata, quæ ille sine dubio respuebat, a RAMELIO accipias, qua de re ad sororem SOPHIAM antea perscripsi. Nunc saltem adiungo quædam Carmina Poëtarum duorum, quos nosti, et quorum venam probare solitus es.
text.english:
**To the man especially renowned in virtue, erudition, and birth, Lord Holger Rosenkrantz of Rosenholm, [my] most upright friend, most faithful kinsman, most loving relative — to his own hands.**

Heartiest greeting.

The letter you sent me about the vernal equinox of this year, from your Rosenholm, most longed-for Holger, I received here a few days ago. You excuse, at the outset, your tardiness in replying, and that mine reached you out of order and late; the latter must be borne, for the distance of the roads and the carelessness of couriers; the former our friendship easily interprets in the better part. I perceive from this that you have read the **copy of the words of Lord Coraduz, the Imperial Vice-Chancellor**, by which he informed me, when I was at Dresden, of the Emperor's most clement will — and that it pleased you. But the same Coraduz wrote me another [letter], about the end of January this year, by which, **by the Imperial Majesty's most clement mandate, he kindly summons me to Prague**; a copy of which I sent to Lord Doctor **Vitus Winshemius**, our common friend (an occasion offered by a courier suddenly going to Hamburg), that he might direct it to you — which he wrote back, a little after, that he had done at the first opportunity; so that I think you have now received it, or at least, while you were in **Scania**, saw a similar extract with [my] sister **Sophie** — so there is no need to repeat it. But I was compelled to put off this Prague journey longer than I would: partly for the **hindrances of the roads** (beyond the usual, from the flood of waters after the snow suddenly thawed); partly because the **Books destined for the Emperor** could not be quite finished as soon as I wished; my **elder Daughter's grave illness** also supervening, and some other obstacles concurring, which I willingly pass over. Meanwhile Lord Doctor **Thomas Frantzius, Winshemius's son-in-law, whom you know**, was at Prague; returned hither, he reported much of the Imperial Majesty's most clement will toward me, and how kindly and in how honourable a place he has resolved to hold me — as, he said, had been enjoined on him by Vice-Chancellor Coraduz, that he should tell me — which, however, I will not touch on here in detail; but when I myself, present there, have learned in what state my affairs will be, I will more fully inform you of the particulars. The said Frantzius set out a few weeks ago hence to Hamburg, to go thence to the **Counts in East Frisia, whose causes he agitates at the Emperor's court**; and since, before his departure, we conversed familiarly together once and again, and honourable mention was made of you, he said he would visit you too, as you had asked of him, if his affairs would in any way allow it — and I exhorted him to do it. If he does, you will learn more from him than the pen now sustains.

For the rest: what you write and advise about **that little island, which cost me so much**, I accept candidly and sincerely, as proceeding from a candid mind that wishes me well. The arguments you adduce are probable enough; and although with me they do not merit an irrefragable, geometric force of proof — since both these and more of the kind it is not hard to rejoin, and to oppose stronger ones — yet I think your counsels and others' in this part are not entirely to be resisted: **I desire that at least a little time be granted me to deliberate what should be done or omitted in this matter, lest one act too precipitately. For I cannot determine anything certain before, at Prague, I have thoroughly perceived the Emperor's most clement will about my affairs;** then at last there will be time enough to conclude something about these and other things — **nor does it seem advisable to surrender the Island voluntarily before [that]**. Nay, if I should keep it until they take it from me by whatever pretext at last (as was done with the other [holdings], which brought more profit), **perhaps I shall have more advantage than disadvantage from it**. What if they should sometime object that they would not have taken it back, had I not surrendered it of my own will — that "no injury is done to one willing" — and many other [things], which I gladly forbear? Their threats certainly, however great, I do not dread, relying on the goodness of my cause; let them see to it. I hope God will one day vindicate me from such great injuries; relying on whose protection, **"every fortune must be overcome by enduring."** More and more particular things — now there is neither leisure nor inclination. I gird myself, as much as I can, for the Prague journey, about to leave the **womenfolk at Dresden** until I have run over into Bohemia. But do you, my most longed-for Holger — together with your wife and my niece — fare most happily; both your mother and she being most lovingly greeted by me. I have given a greeting from you to the learned men here, with whose familiar acquaintance you formerly enjoyed (as I did before), for we often pleasantly recall your memory; and they in turn greet you back, and pray every best thing for you and yours.

Again, farewell.
Given at Wittenberg, the 7th day of May, the year 1599.
Yours, absent as present,
Tycho Brahe, with my own hand.


*[Postscript:]* To send the books you ask for by this courier has seemed neither convenient nor advisable; you shall have them another time; or take pains that you receive, from Ramel, the copies offered to the King — which he without doubt spurned — about which matter I wrote before to [my] sister Sophie. For now I at least add certain Poems of two Poets, whom you know, and whose vein you are wont to approve.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Holger Rosenkrantz** of Rosenholm, Tycho's *consanguineus et affinis*. Written from the **Wittenberg winter/spring of 1599**, as Tycho prepared for Bohemia. The MS is a later Langebek *afskrift*.
- **The imperial summons (chain of evidence).** Tycho recounts how **Coraduz** (Vice-Chancellor) had informed him of the Emperor's will at **Dresden**, then (about end of January 1599) sent a second letter **summoning him to Prague** — a copy of which Tycho forwarded via **Winshemius** to Holger (and which Holger's wife/Tycho's sister Sophie also had in extract). The **Prague journey was delayed** by thaw-flooded roads, the unfinished **books for the Emperor**, and his **elder daughter's grave illness** (Magdalene; cf. brahe-t_15990925001).
- **Thomas Franz — the jurist/East-Frisia agent (key for the "Doctor Franz" identity).** *D. D. **Thomas Frantzius**, Winshemii Gener* = **Thomas Franz, Winshemius's son-in-law**, a jurist who **"agitates the causes of the Counts in East Frisia at the Emperor's court"** — i.e. the **"Doctor Franz, the jurist, now Chancellor of the Count of Emden"** of brahe-t_16000918001 and the *Frantzius Iurisconsultus* courier of brahe-t_16001008001. He had relayed Coraduz's favourable account of Tycho's prospects. **His first name is Thomas** — so he is **not** the *Wolfgang* Franz addressed in brahe-t_16000327002 (a distinct person; see the corrected note there).
- **Significance — Tycho's reply on the surrender of Hven (the central matter; cross-ref to brahe-t_15990307001).** Holger had **advised Tycho to surrender Hven voluntarily** (his counsel survives as brahe-t_15990307001, the bracketed/enciphered letter). Tycho here **answers that advice**: he takes it "candidly," grants the arguments "probable" (though not of "geometric" force, and answerable), and will **not resist the counsel outright** — but **insists on time, and will not surrender "that little island, which cost me so much," voluntarily before he has secured the Emperor's will at Prague.** Indeed, he reasons it **better to let them take Hven "by whatever pretext"** (as with his other Danish holdings) than to yield it freely — lest they later say "no injury is done to one willing." He **fears no threats**, "relying on the goodness of my cause," closing with the Virgilian tag ***"fortuna omnis superanda ferendo est"*** ("every fortune must be overcome by enduring," *Aeneid* V.710). A first-rate document of Tycho's stance on the Hven question.
- **Persons named.** Holger Rosenkrantz (and his wife **Sophie Brahe**, "my niece," and his mother); **Coraduz**; **Vitus Winshemius**; **Thomas Franz** (the jurist/East-Frisia agent); **Sophie Brahe** (Tycho's sister); Tycho's **elder daughter** (Magdalene); the Counts of **East Frisia**; **Rudolf II**.
- **Classical tag (kept/identified).** *fortuna omnis superanda ferendo est* — **Virgil, *Aeneid* V.710**.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Wittebergae die 7. Maij Anni 1599*; Wittenberg/Saxony kept the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar. Header agrees with the label.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (the books withheld via the courier; Ramel; the appended poems), restored from Dreyer VIII pp.155–156 (dropped by the working transcription).

documents.incipit: CUM hac ipsa hora, Vir nobilissime et Mathematicorum omnium facile Princeps, ex urbe …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO DOCTISSIMOQUE VIRO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, DOMINO A KNUDSTRUP, MATHEMATICORUM OMNIUM FACILE PRINCIPI, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO SINGULARI OBSERVANTIA COLENDO.

CUM hac ipsa hora, Vir nobilissime et Mathematicorum omnium facile Princeps, ex urbe Imperatoris literas acceperim, quibus certior factus sum te eo venisse a Caesarea Maiestate vocatum, et plane confidam Maiestatem suam pro singulari favore, quo Matheseos artem prosequitur, ut inde aliorsum te conferas, aegre laturam et vix atque adeo ne vix quidem esse passuram, omnino decrevi his literis de adventu isto tuo tibi et mihi gratulari. Quod si aliqua in re studia tua pro exilibus viribus meis iuvare possem, haberes me paratissimum. Mallem equidem hoc saltem primo alloquio, animi mei propensam in te voluntatem aliqua ratione potius declarare, quam quidquam a te petere, sed cum inpraesentiarum nihil istiusmodi occurrat, hoc tibi significandum duxi. Ex traditione antiquissimi Authoris Poëtae Romani, qui eo ipso tempore vixit et floruit, accepi anno ante CHRISTUM quarto inchoante, summi miraculi instar habitum fuisse passim ab omnibus, quod stella Veneris seu Lucifer, cum pro ratione motus sui, ipsissimo illo tempore, ante Solis ortum lucere debuisset, nuspiam in coelo visa fuerit, atque non apparente Lucifero dies illuxerit. Rationem esse ego conijcio, quod iam dicta Veneris stella tum temporis a stella Mercurij Eclipsin fuerit passa, nec enim video, quanam alia de caussa haec res prodigij loco posteritati tradita fuisset, Romae praesertim, ubi tum temporis quales quales saltem astronomi non defuerunt. Adhibui itaque calculum Prutenicum, et reperi, quod currente anno ante CHRISTUM quarto, die septima Ianuarij circa Solis ortum stella Mercurij subierit stellam Veneris, sed ex eodem calculo reperi quoque simul unâ, quod eadem Mercurij stella 2° 44' latitudine tum Borealior Venere fuerit. Quare despondissem animum nisi ex Epistolis tuis Astronomicis, et quae de Cometis scripsisti, animadvertissem, te latitudines praesertim ♀ et ☿ longe aliter observasse, quam calculus exhibeat. Rem itaque hanc omnino ad te deferendam esse duxi, cuius de ea iudicium audire percuperem, ut quod merito cuiusvis alterius sit praeferendum. Ad hanc meam petitionem accedit etiam alia. Soleo identidem Eclipses luminarium, quae ante CHRISTUM retro vel circa tempora CHRISTI, iuxta traditiones Authorum, contigerunt, ex tabulis Prutenicis supputare, et ea quoque, quae PTOLEMÆUS in magna Syntaxi hac de re tradit, conferre (quae quidem utplurimum calculo Prutenico consentire videntur). Attamen calculus iste non videtur satis exacte Eclipses exhibere. Intellexi quidem ex praefatis Epistolis tuis Astronomicis te ex nova restauratione cursus ☉ et ☾ Eclipses luminarium huius nostri seculi, longe aliter et exactius deprehendere, quam ullae tabulae hactenus exhibuerint. Utrum vero accuratissimae istae tuae observationes recentes eo rem deducant, ut etiam tempus et quantitatem illarum Eclipsium, quae circa tempora CHRISTI et ante illam aetatem retro contigerunt, exactius definire queas, id inquam, spero quidem, nescio tamen et non sine ratione addubitare mihi videor, cum veteres utique observationes desideres. Ideoque etiam atque etiam te rogo, ut hac quoque in re iudicium et prudentiam tuam mihi impertiri non dedigneris; summe enim desiderarem defectus luminarium vetustissimos quosque calculo (quoad eius fieri potest) praecisius assequi, et quanam ratione id fieri queat, rescire. Quodsi ullo genere officiorum studiorumque meorum hoc beneficium tuum in me collatum exaequare potero, semper ero promptissimus.

Vale feliciter, et has literas meas boni consule.
Datae Monachij 23. Iulij Anno 1599.
Dominationis Tuae Nobilissimae studiosissimus
IOAN. GEORGIUS HERUART ab Hohenburg,
Serenissimo utriusque Bavariae Duci a consilijs intimis, Praeses Schuabae et Statuum provincialium Cancellarius, manu propria.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most learned man, Lord Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup, easily the Prince of all Mathematicians, his Lord and friend to be cultivated with singular respect.**

Since at this very hour, most noble Man and easily Prince of all Mathematicians, I have received a letter from the Emperor's city, by which I am informed that you have come thither, summoned by the Imperial Majesty — and I fully trust that His Majesty, for the singular favour with which he pursues the art of Mathematics, will be loath that you betake yourself elsewhere thence, and will scarcely (nay, not even scarcely) suffer it — I have altogether resolved by this letter to congratulate you and myself on that coming of yours. And if in any matter I could aid your studies, according to my slender powers, you would have me most ready. I should indeed prefer, in this first address at least, to declare in some way my mind's inclined goodwill toward you, rather than to ask anything of you; but since at present nothing of that kind occurs [to me], I thought this should be signified to you. **From the tradition of a most ancient Author, a Roman Poet who lived and flourished at that very time, I have learned that, at the beginning of the fourth year before Christ, it was held everywhere by all as a supreme miracle that the star of Venus, or Lucifer [the Morning Star] — when, by the reckoning of its motion, it ought at that very time to have shone before the Sun's rising — was nowhere seen in the sky, and, Lucifer not appearing, the day dawned.** I conjecture the reason to be that the said star of Venus at that time **suffered an Eclipse by the star of Mercury** — for I see no other cause why this thing would have been handed down to posterity in place of a prodigy, especially at Rome, where at that time astronomers of some sort at least were not lacking. I therefore applied the **Prutenic calculation**, and found that, in the course of the fourth year before Christ, on the **7th of January about sunrise, Mercury passed beneath Venus** — but from the same calculation I also found, at the same time, that Mercury was then more northern than Venus by **2° 44′ of latitude**. Wherefore I should have despaired, had I not noticed, from your **Astronomical Letters** and what you have written about the **Comets**, that you have observed the latitudes especially of **Venus and Mercury** far otherwise than the calculation exhibits. I have therefore thought this matter should by all means be referred to you, whose judgement about it I greatly desire to hear, as one to be deservedly preferred to anyone else's.

To this request of mine another is also added. I am wont, again and again, to compute from the **Prutenic tables** the eclipses of the luminaries that occurred before Christ, back [in time], or around the times of Christ, according to the traditions of Authors; and to compare also what **Ptolemy** hands down on this matter in the **Great Syntaxis** [Almagest] (which indeed for the most part seem to agree with the Prutenic calculation). Yet that calculation does not seem to exhibit the eclipses exactly enough. I have understood from your aforesaid Astronomical Letters that you, from the **new restoration of the course of the Sun and Moon**, detect the eclipses of the luminaries of this our age far otherwise and more exactly than any tables have hitherto exhibited. But whether those most accurate recent observations of yours bring the matter to this — that you can also more exactly define the **time and magnitude of those eclipses which occurred around the times of Christ, and before that age back [in time]** — that, I say, I indeed hope, yet I know not, and not without reason I seem to myself to doubt, since you must in any case lack ancient observations. And therefore I ask you again and again that in this matter too you would not disdain to impart to me your judgement and prudence; for I should most greatly desire to attain more precisely by calculation each of the most ancient eclipses of the luminaries (so far as it can be done), and to learn by what method this can be done. And if by any kind of services and studies of mine I shall be able to match this benefit conferred by you upon me, I shall always be most ready.

Fare happily, and take this letter of mine in good part.
Given at Munich, 23 July, the year 1599.
Most devoted to Your Most Noble Lordship,
Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg,
privy councillor to the Most Serene Duke of both Bavarias, President at [Burghausen in] Swabia and Chancellor of the provincial Estates, with my own hand.
