documents.apparatus:
- **Sender — and the opening of the Tycho–Herwart correspondence.** **Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg** (1553–1622), the Bavarian chancellor and polymath (his titles given in the subscription: **privy councillor to the Duke of Bavaria**, *Präsident* at **Burghausen** (*Schwaben*), and *Kanzler* of the provincial Estates). This **23 July 1599** letter is the **first of the long Tycho–Herwart correspondence** on **ancient eclipses and chronology** (the other Herwart letters in the edition are all 1600: brahe-t_16000403001, brahe-t_16000504003, etc.). Survives in two witnesses — Herwart's own Munich **draft (Kladde)** and a Copenhagen copy in **Resen's *Inscriptiones Hafnienses*** (1668).
- **Significance — the two requests (chronology & ancient eclipses; this chapter's convention).**
 1. **The "invisible Morning Star" of 4 BC.** Herwart reports, from "a most ancient Roman Poet who lived at that very time," that **at the start of the fourth year before Christ** the **Morning Star (Venus/Lucifer)**, which by computation should have shone before sunrise, **was nowhere seen** — held as "a supreme miracle." His hypothesis: **Venus was occulted ("eclipsed") by Mercury.** By the **Prutenic tables** he finds Mercury "passed beneath Venus" on **7 January (4 BC) at sunrise**, but with Mercury **2° 44′ more northern in latitude** — so no true occultation by the tables; he appeals to Tycho's *Astronomical Letters* and cometary work, which show **Venus/Mercury latitudes** differing "far otherwise than the calculation," and asks Tycho's verdict. (The Roman poet is unnamed; left unidentified per the no-fabrication rule.)
 2. **Dating ancient eclipses.** Herwart routinely computes from the **Prutenic tables** the eclipses "around the times of Christ, and before," comparing **Ptolemy's *Almagest*** — but finds the calculation imprecise. He asks whether Tycho's **new restoration of the Sun's and Moon's courses** can fix the **time and magnitude of the most ancient eclipses** more exactly — doubting it, since Tycho "must lack ancient observations," but eager for his method. This is the chronological-astronomy programme (dating sacred and classical history by eclipse) that drives the whole Herwart exchange.
- **Technical terms (kept;).** *calculus Prutenicus* → the **Prutenic Tables**; *magna Syntaxis* → the **Almagest** (*Great Syntaxis*); *Lucifer* → the **Morning Star** (Venus); *defectus / Eclipsis luminarium* → **eclipse of the luminaries**; ♀ = **Venus**, ☿ = **Mercury**, ☉ = **Sun**, ☾ = **Moon** (glyphs kept in source).
- **Editorial sigla.** The transcription carries scattered superscript **"A"** marks — the **edition's witness-sigla** flagging readings of witness **A** (the Munich Kladde) against **B** (the Resen copy); they are apparatus markers, not text, and are disregarded in the translation (and noted here).
- **Persons named.** Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg (sender); **Rudolf II** (the Emperor); **Ptolemy**; the unnamed ancient Roman poet; the Duke of Bavaria (in the titulature).
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Monachij 23. Iulij Anno 1599*; Catholic Bavaria kept the **Gregorian (New Style)** calendar; marked [N.S.]. (The 4 BC date is Herwart's chronological reckoning, reproduced as he gives it.)
- Correction. Latin signature corrected 'HERWAUART' to 'HERUART' (Dreyer VIII p.158); English unaffected.

documents.abstract: Reports Emperor Rudolf II's generous reception at Prague, his lodging in the Curtius house, and his preference to seek a more secluded residence outside the city.
documents.incipit: INVENI peculiari Dei providentia et dono Caesarem hunc RUDOLPHUM Secundum mei et eorum, …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD CHRISTIANUM LONGOMONTANUM.

INVENI peculiari Dei providentia et dono Caesarem hunc RUDOLPHUM Secundum mei et eorum, quae tracto, studiorum clementi favore amantissimum, qui satis liberaliter mihi et meis hanc ob rem prospicere non est tergiversatus, veluti alias, Deo volente, ipsius Caesareae Maiestatis erga me benignissimam voluntatem, ubi adfueris, intelliges. Introductus quidem sum, statim ac Pragam veneram, etiam antequam audientiam apud Caesaream Maiestatem habueram, in aedes Curtianas splendide et magnifice exstructas. Verum cum praeviderem, me isthic in urbe, ob aulam tam amplam et hominum omnis generis maximam copiam, otio philosophico vix perfrui posse, exoptavi potius extra illam seorsim habitare. Quo intellecto ipsius Caesarea Maiestas postmodum tres eximias arces, unius vel etiam dimidij diei itinere Praga distantes, per quendam nobilem virum, mihi ut eo deduceret adiunctum, monstrari curavit, ut ex ijs eam, quae meae intentioni commodior videretur, eligerem. Quarum una est Brandisium (ubi haec scribo) verum quia caeteris nonnihil declivior, et propriae Caesaris delectationi, praesertim ubi venationibus indulget, destinata, hîc habitare non visum opportunum. Reliquae duae appellantur Lyssa et Benachia, ambae etiam splendidissimae et iucundissimae arces. Inter quas Benachiam (quae Venetiae Bohemorum ob amoenitatem interpretatur) praetuli, quo unâ cum omnibus meis hodie vel cras, quod Deus fortunatum velit, introducturus est hic Capitaneus Brandeisensis, ex Caesaris mandato ea de causa heri Pragam ad me evocatus. Est locus editus, ut undique libere pateat Horizon, Aedificia splendida et commoda; prope est parva civitas ad fluviolum Eifer in Albim excurrentem sita, ipsique Arci quasi contigua. Distat Praga 5 miliaribus, via existente plana, ut iter saltem sit 6 horarum. Hîc favente divina clementia, cum meis habitare constitui, donec de feudo, quod Caesarea Maiestas mihi pro me et mea familia posterisque clementissime addixit, alicubi per occasionem prospectum fuerit. Interim domum etiam opportunam Pragae ipsius Caesarea Maiestas mihi clementer concedere vult, quam, quoties eo excurrero, cum meis inhabitem, ut commodius degere et propria quadra vivere possimus, etc.

Datae festinanter in transcursu Brandisio, dum Benachiam petimus, die 20. Aug. stylo novo An. 1599.
Tuus TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Christian Longomontanus.**

I have found, by God's special providence and gift, this Emperor Rudolf the Second most loving toward me and toward the studies I pursue, with clement favour; who, liberally enough, has not been reluctant to provide for me and mine on this account — as you will otherwise understand, God willing, when you are present, of His Imperial Majesty's most benign will toward me. I was indeed received, as soon as I had come to Prague — even before I had had audience with His Imperial Majesty — into the Curtius house, splendidly and magnificently built. But since I foresaw that there, in the city, on account of so great a court and the very large throng of men of every kind, I could scarcely enjoy philosophical leisure, I chose rather to dwell apart, outside it. This understood, His Imperial Majesty thereupon had three excellent castles — distant from Prague a day's, or even half a day's, journey — shown to me, through a certain nobleman assigned to conduct me thither, so that from them I might choose the one that should seem more convenient to my purpose. Of these, one is Brandeis (where I write this); but because it is somewhat more low-lying than the rest, and set apart for the Emperor's own pleasure — especially when he indulges in hunting — it did not seem opportune to dwell here. The remaining two are called Lysá and Benátky, both likewise most splendid and most delightful castles. Among these I have preferred Benátky (which, for its pleasantness, is rendered "the Venice of the Bohemians"), whither, together with all my people, today or tomorrow — may God grant it fortunate — this Captain of Brandeis is to install [me], having been called out to me from Prague yesterday, by the Emperor's command, for this very cause. It is an elevated place, so that the Horizon lies freely open on every side; the buildings splendid and convenient; nearby is a small town set on the little river Iser, which runs out into the Elbe, and as it were contiguous to the castle itself. It is distant from Prague five [German] miles, the road being level, so that the journey is but six hours. Here, by divine clemency's favour, I have resolved to dwell with my people, until provision shall somewhere be made, as occasion allows, concerning the fief which His Imperial Majesty most graciously assigned to me, for myself and my family and posterity. Meanwhile His Imperial Majesty also wishes graciously to grant me a convenient house at Prague itself, which, as often as I run thither, I may inhabit with my people, so that we may live more conveniently and keep our own table, etc.

Given hastily, in passage from Brandeis, while we make for Benátky, the 20th of August, New Style, in the year 1599.
Your Tycho Brahe,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender, recipient & moment.** **Tycho Brahe** to his chief assistant **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus** (1562–1647), written *in transit* from Brandeis to Benátky on **20 August 1599** — Tycho's own eyewitness account of **how he came to settle at Benátky nad Jizerou**, the establishment where Kepler would join him months later. Longomontanus, then briefly returned to Denmark, is being told where to rejoin his master ("when you are present").
- **The narrative.** On reaching Prague, Tycho was first lodged in the **Curtius house** (*aedes Curtianae* — the Prague palace associated with the late imperial vice-chancellor Jacob Curtius von Senftenau), even before his audience with the Emperor; but, wanting *otium philosophicum* away from the crowded court, he asked to live outside the city. Rudolf II then had **three castles** shown him — **Brandeis** (Brandýs nad Labem, rejected as low-lying and reserved for the Emperor's hunting), **Lysá** (Lyssa), and **Benátky** (Benachia) — and Tycho chose Benátky.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Caesar Rudolphus Secundus / Caesarea Maiestas* = **Emperor Rudolf II**, throughout the gracious patron.
 - *Capitaneus Brandeisensis* = the **Captain (governor) of Brandeis**, commanded to install Tycho at Benátky (the same office whose holder's Prague wedding figures in brahe-t_16000515002).
 - *quidam nobilis vir* = an unnamed nobleman assigned as Tycho's guide.
- **Places & topography (valued for the Benátky description).** *Benachia … Venetiae Bohemorum* — Benátky "the **Venice of the Bohemians**," a folk-etymology of the name (Czech *Benátky* ≈ "Venice"). Tycho prizes its **elevation and free horizon** (*locus editus, ut undique libere pateat Horizon*) — the prime requirement for an observatory. *fluviolus Eifer* = the river **Iser / Jizera**, "running out into the **Elbe** (*Albis*)"; the small town adjoins the castle. Distance from Prague: **5 German miles ≈ a 6-hour journey**.
- **Terms of the grant.** *feudum … pro me et mea familia posterisque* = a hereditary **fief** promised by the Emperor for Tycho and his descendants (the long-sought secure endowment, never finally settled); plus a **house at Prague** for his visits, so that he and his household may "keep their own table" (*propria quadra vivere*).
- **Edition note.** The edition cites this letter to the collection *Tychonis Brahei et ad eum doctorum virorum epistolae ab anno 1588*; it is also printed in Dreyer's *Opera Omnia* (vol. VIII). The surviving witness is an **afskrift (copy)** in Langebek's Diplomatarium, Copenhagen.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *Datae festinanter* → "Given hastily"; *manu propria* → "with his own hand."
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 20. Aug. stylo novo An. 1599* — explicitly **New Style**, Tycho already dating Gregorian in the Emperor's lands. Reproduced, not converted.
- **Correction.** Latin: 'Brundisio' corrected to 'Brandisio', and 'militaribus' corrected to 'miliaribus', per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 159.

Langebek. 179...]'. Collated the full Latin word-for-word against Dreyer. Found two the transcribed original corruptions relative to Dreyer's print (Brundisio/Brandisio; militaribus/miliaribus); the first is a genuine place-name substitution (Brindisi, Italy vs. Brandeis, Bohemia) serious enough to mislead a reader relying on the transcribed original alone, even though the published English translation itself renders both correctly (Brandeis, five miles) and is not at fault. All other names, numbers, and the closing date/place ('die 20. Aug. stylo novo An. 1599') match exactly. Self-graded A; our collation finds source-text corruption warranting C despite a sound translation.

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (medium). The transcribed original reads 'Brundisio' (evoking Brundisium/Brindisi in Italy) where Dreyer prints 'Brandisio', matching the place-name 'Brandisium' (Brandeis) used earlier in this same letter; a real, potentially misleading place-name corruption in our source. The English correctly says 'Brandeis' regardless, so the translation itself is unaffected. Dreyer prints: *Datae festinanter in transcursu Brandisio, dum Benachiam petimus*.
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original has 'militaribus' (an inserted 't', suggesting 'military') where Dreyer has 'miliaribus' (miles) - a corrupted word; the English correctly reads 'five miles' regardless. Dreyer prints: *Distat Praga 5 miliaribus, via existente plana*.

**Repaired.** Verified both defects by direct visual inspection of the Dreyer TBOO VIII pages containing this letter (pp.158-159 within the supplied 30-page extract). Both corrections are unambiguous in the page image; the 'miliaribus' spelling was cross-checked against a second, clearer occurrence of the same word later on p.159. Neither correction affects the English translation, which was already faithful to Dreyer's readings. No other divergence from Dreyer was found in the letter text itself.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD IOH. G. HERWARTUM AB HOHENBURG.

S.

SIC est, Vir Nobilis et magnifice Amice, licet de facie mihi ignote, plurimi tamen ob præclaras ingenij tui dotes semper faciende, quod a Sacra Cæsarea Maiestate Pragam clementissime vocatus ab ipsius Cæsarea Maiestate in ipsius clientem clementissime sim acceptus, et liberaliter prout ferunt hæc tempora mihi et meis studijs ab ipsius Cæsarea Maiestate provisum. Concessus etiam est benignissime habitationi meæ locus hic in arce Benachia 5 miliaribus Pragâ distante, ubi commodius et tranquillius quam in urbe, consuetis meis exercitijs Astronomicis et Spagyricis vacare licebit, et opus Astronomicum, quod diu multumque molior, favente Cœlestium Opifice in ipsius Cæsareæ Maiestatis et Imperij honorem (siquidem ob quorundam inscitiam et invidiam in patria mea id fieri nequiverit) absolvere et consecrare, qua etiam de caussa totum meum apparatum Astronomicum et supellectilem omnem, quam Magdeburgi reliqui, huc transferri curo.

Cæterum ut ad . T. eruditas quæstiones pro virili respondeam, sic habeat. Veneris stellam anno ante CHRISTUM 4 inchoante cœlitus non conspectam, magni miraculi loco ducerem, si res ea indubie constaret: sit fides apud Autorem, qui cum Poëta fuerit, Privilegio forsitan Poëtico usus est, cum ne quidem Historici, qui magis veraces haberi volunt, et certe esse debebant, in cœlestibus ostentis recte indicandis, experientiæ consona semper proferant, adeo ut interdum Chasmata quædam et ignitas aëris inflammationes, varias formas sæpe exhibentes, pro Cometis habeant, quos tamen ipso in Cœlo locum obtinere, illicque cursum suum absolvere, e septem, quos intra 22 Annos conspexi, ratis observationibus demonstrative comprobavi. Concedatur vero ♀ris stellam tunc miraculose delituisse: ☿ij tamen interventu id fieri potuisse, ut sic Eclipsin passa sit, verisimile non videtur, neque enim ☿ij stella in cœlo tantæ apparet magnitudinis, ut ♀ris stellam, quæ multo maior conspicitur, abscondere possit. Adde quod ☿ij stella luminosa sit, nec opaco corpore prædita ut ☾, ideoque si quando centraliter ♀ri et visui nostro interponeretur, lumen suum illius lumini potius coniungeret, sicque illud augeret magis quam imminueret. Taceo quod ob motus celeritatem diu sub ♀ris stella ☿ consistere nequeat, nisi in easdem partes æquarentur ambarum motus, quod rarissime evenit. Præterea cum ipsemet ex calculo Prutenico adinveneris, stellam ☿ij tunc fuisse 2¾ G. ♀re borealiorem, satis partiliter et exacte pro Eclipsatione non iungebatur. Licet enim in latitudine non saltem horum duorum Planetarum, quos inferiores vocant, sed et cæterorum magna diversitas in cœlo ab utrisque tabulis deprehendatur, tamen adeo enormiter ☿ij stellam quoad latitudinem exorbitare non animadverti. Observavi quidem ♀rm, cum esset circa medietatem ♓ium iuxta Perigæum Epicycli (ut communiter loquuntur) latitudinem Boream assequi posse partium 9 Min. 50, tribus gradibus plus quam fert Alphonsinorum calculus, licet is Coperniceum unico circiter excedat, ita ut in 10um G. completum excrescere possit eius ab Ecliptica in Boream digressio; idque bis denotavi, utpote anno 1587 et 1595 interiecto (uti requiritur) octennio, quibus etiam temporibus ♀rem intra triduum et quatriduum tam vespertinam quam eoam meis instrumentis observavi et commutationem illius (uti vocat COPERNICUS) hinc promptius restitui. Sic etiam in ☿io et tribus superioribus Planetis non modicam adinveni in eorum latitudinibus (veluti innui) a cœlesti norma exorbitationem, adeo ut ne quidem in tribus illis, ubi simplicior ratio est, limites maximarum latitudinum rite prædefiniti sint a PTOLEMÆO, cuius placitis nimis secure æquievit COPERNICUS, nec nodi intersectionum circuituum Planetarum cum Ecliptica ita se habent, respectu Apogæorum, uti ex PTOLEMÆO assumpsit idem COPERNICUS. Et si ea quæ de his tradidit PTOLEMÆUS, ipsius ævo cœlo consona erant, oportebit nodos hosce simulque limites maximæ latitudinis longe alium sensibiliter per se habere motum, quam is est, qui ab Apogæorum mutatione procedit, differentia nunc intercedente multorum graduum. Quin et in ipsa ☾ non minima conspicitur in latitudine varietas atque a traditione antecessorum diversitas. In novilunijs siquidem et plenilunijs latitudinem maximam obtinere potest 4 partium et 58', quæ Ptolemaicum limitem intra 2' attingit. At in □tis eandem tertia gradus parte iuxta limitem boream et austrinum adauget, et quod magis mirum est, nodorum insuper motum exhibet inæqualem singulis mensibus hinc inde reciprocantem, idque sensibili intervallo, quod gradum 1 35' attingit. Ex modo dictis itaque (de quibus tamen alias latius et particularius volente Deo agam) satis liquet, quod . T. latitudinis Planetarum calculum e tabulis consuetis erutum, non citra rem suspectum habeat; nihilominus circa ea tempora, quando in ☿ij latitudine e tabulis Prutenicis supputatio est instituta, usque adeo magnum insinuari potuisse errorem vix crediderim, quod PTOLEMÆI temporibus, quibus ille astrorum observationibus invigilavit, decies magis quam nunc sumus propiora fuerint. Et canones Prutenici illo ævo Ptolemaicis quam proxime subscribunt. At si in observatis PTOLEMÆI error aliquis subrepsit, quod non raro factum haud sine causa suspicor, frustra super hoc fundamentum ædificamus; quare circumspecte admodum, nec nisi limitatione competenti adhibita eius placitis utendum.

De Eclipsibus, quæ scribis, ita se habent quod Prutenicæ tabulæ ijs, quæ PTOLEMÆI ætate contigerunt, quam proxime consentiant, nec tamen singulis satis præcise adaptatæ sint; constat enim COPERNICUM ad Ptolemaicas Eclipses, quatenus in nonnullis fieri potuit, tanquam Epochas suos numeros applicuisse. In omnibus tamen accuratam amussim invenire non sustinuit, ob aliam quandam inæqualitatis lunaris nec a PTOLEMÆO nec ipso animadversam implicationem. Neque enim tres Eclipses prout illi factitarunt, sufficiunt ad primam inæqualitatem ☾æ enucleandam, ut de altera adhuc intricatiore hîc nihil dicam; sed pluribus in diversis Eccentrici seu maioris Epicycli locis opus est ijsdemque accuratissime denotatis. Ut vero hæc aliquatenus in uno saltem exemplo dispicias, mitto deliquij ☾æ in principio huius anni pragmatiam, tam in triangulari demonstratione ex hypothesi nostra, quam numeris correspondentibus ab eximio Mathematico Wittebergensi M. IOSTELIO, dum ibi aliquamdiu ob luem in Bohemia grassantem et alijs de causis subsisterem, me concedente factitatam et typis excusam. Ubi vero meæ tabulæ, favente divina ope, de motu luminarium (quas cæteris Planetis præmittere animus est) sub auspicijs Romani Imperatoris RUDOLPHI Secundi in lucem prodierint, testabitur experientia, eas non saltem nostro seculo adamussim quadrare, sed et vetustissimis illis Eclipsibus sufficienter congruere, quatenus veterum observata ipsissimis Cœli apparentijs præcise consona fuêre. Et quid quæso vel in ☾a vel cæteris Planetis ab omni vitio immune præstare poterant, cum stellas fixas minus fideliter correctas adhibuerint, quemadmodum mille affixarum stellarum accuratissima restitutio in ipso minuto adeoque nonnunquam eius semisse a me præteritis aliquot annis exantlata et nuper Cæsareæ Maiestati in membrana manuscripta subiectissime exhibita, abunde testari poterit, collatione cum consuetis abacis instituta. Obtuli etiam eidem Cæsareæ Maiestati in alio libro manuscripto Solis et Lunæ restitutionem ad singulos dies duorum proximorum annorum, apposita simul discrepantia utriusque calculi Alphonsini et Copernicei, quæ subinde non exigua est. Quin et in tertio quodam eiusdem formæ et magnitudinis libro Mechanicam Astronomiæ partem Instrumenta mea, quæ hactenus elaboravi repræsentantem, eumque typis, postquam Dania excessi, impressum, ipsius Cæsaris Maiestati pariter humillime dedicavi. De hoc ultimo misissem nunc tria exemplaria, duo pro illustrissimis Ducibus Bavariæ GUILHELMO seniore ac patre et MAXIMILIANO filio regente, tertium pro te ipso, sed nullum iam ad manus habeo quod coloribus rite illuminatum (uti vocant) existit. Verum id Pragæ modo fieri procuro, quo peracto, quod modo dixi præstabo: et forte plura etiam mittam, quæcunque tam cito describi curare potero. Interim pauculis verbis indicare non degraveris, an dicti Illustrissimi Principes vestri talibus afficiantur. Valeat T. M. quam felicissime et diutissime, meque literis suis, uti benevole incepit, eruditis sæpius invisere, atque amicitiam semel ijs, cum aliter vix liceat, inchoatam ijsdem continuare et conservare pergat; inveniet me ad idem præstandum quam paratissimum, ut nunquam sic se certasse priorem pœniteat, omniaque ei studia mea et quæcunque a me proficisci possunt officia, lubens polliceor atque offero. Cæterum quod non prius rescripserim, varijs occupationibus, quibus Pragæ præpediebar, et migrationi in hanc arcem nuperæ imputet, et candide excusatum habeat. Volui istam tarditatem in rescribendo ea, quam vides, prolixitate compensare, quæ ut accepta sit rogo.

Iamque iterum et sæpius T. M. quam optime valeat.
Dabantur ex arce Cæsareæ Benachia die 31. Augusti Anno 1599.
. T. studiosissimus
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO JOH. G. HERWART VON HOHENBURG.**

Greeting.

So it is, noble and magnificent Friend — though unknown to me by face, yet always to be highly valued for the eminent gifts of your genius — that, **clemently called to Prague by the Sacred Imperial Majesty, I have been most clemently received as His client, and liberally (as these times allow) provided for, with my studies, by His Imperial Majesty. A place for my dwelling has also most kindly been granted here, in Benátky castle, 5 miles distant from Prague, where I shall be free — more conveniently and tranquilly than in the city — to pursue my accustomed Astronomical and Spagyric [alchemical] exercises**, and to complete and consecrate the Astronomical work I have long and much laboured at, to the honour of His Imperial Majesty and the Empire (since, through certain men's ignorance and envy, it could not be done in my fatherland) — for which cause too I am having my whole Astronomical apparatus, and all the furnishings I left at Magdeburg, transferred hither.

But, to answer Your Magnificence's erudite questions to my power: thus hold it. **That the star of Venus was not seen in the heaven at the beginning of the 4th year before Christ, I would count in the place of a great miracle, if the thing were undoubtedly established.** Let the credit rest with the Author, who, since he was a Poet, perhaps used a Poetic licence — since not even the Historians (who wish to be held more truthful, and certainly ought to be) always report, in correctly indicating celestial portents, things consonant with experience; so that sometimes they take certain **chasmata** [sky-cleavings] and fiery inflammations of the air (often showing various forms) for **Comets** — which, however, hold a place in the heaven itself, and there complete their course, as I have demonstratively proved, by reliable observations, of the seven I beheld within 22 years. But grant that the star of Venus [♀] then miraculously hid itself: **that it could have happened by the intervention of Mercury [☿] — that it thus suffered an eclipse — does not seem likely**; for Mercury's star does not appear in the heaven of such magnitude as to be able to hide Venus's star, which is seen much larger. Add that **Mercury's star is luminous, and not endowed with an opaque body like the Moon [☾]**; and so, if it were ever centrally interposed between Venus and our sight, it would rather join its light to that light, and so augment it more than diminish it. I am silent that, on account of the speed of its motion, **Mercury cannot long abide under Venus's star, unless both their motions were equalised in the same direction, which most rarely happens**. Besides, since you yourself found, from the Prutenic calculation, that **Mercury's star was then 2¾° more northern than Venus**, it was not partilely and exactly enough joined for an eclipse. For although a great diversity of latitude is detected in the heaven, from both tables — not only of these two Planets, which they call the lower, but of the rest too — yet I have not noticed Mercury's star to deviate so enormously as to latitude.

I have indeed **observed Venus, when it was about the middle of Pisces [♓], near the Perigee of the Epicycle (as they commonly speak), able to reach a Northern latitude of 9° 50′ — three degrees more than the Alphonsine calculation gives** (though that exceeds the Copernican by about one), so that its digression from the Ecliptic into the North can grow to a full 10°; and this I noted twice, namely in the years **1587 and 1595, with the eight-year interval interposed (as is required)** — at which times too I observed Venus, both evening and morning, within three and four days, with my instruments, and thence more readily restored its "commutation" (as Copernicus calls it). So too **in Mercury and the three superior Planets I found no small deviation in their latitudes from the celestial norm** (as you hint) — so that not even in those three (where the reckoning is simpler) are the **limits of the maximum latitudes rightly predefined by Ptolemy** (whose tenets Copernicus too securely accepted); nor do the **nodes of the intersections of the planets' circuits with the Ecliptic stand, with respect to the Apogees, as Copernicus assumed from Ptolemy**. And if what Ptolemy transmitted of these was consonant with the heaven in his age, **these nodes, and the limits of maximum latitude, must have a far different, perceptible motion of their own than that which proceeds from the change of the Apogees** — a difference of many degrees now intervening. **Nay, in the Moon itself no small variety of latitude is seen, and a diversity from the predecessors' tradition. For in new and full moons the maximum latitude can be 4° 58′, which reaches the Ptolemaic limit within 2′; but in the quadratures [□] it augments the same by a third of a degree, on the north and south limit; and — what is more wonderful — it shows besides the motion of the nodes unequal, reciprocating back and forth each month, and that by a perceptible interval, which reaches 1° 35′.** From what has just been said, then (of which, however, I will treat more fully and particularly elsewhere, God willing), it is clear enough that Your Magnificence not without cause holds suspect the planet-latitude calculation drawn from the usual tables. Nonetheless, around those times when the computation in Mercury's latitude was made from the Prutenic tables, I should scarcely believe that so great an error could have crept in — because **Ptolemy's times, when he watched the star-observations, were ten times nearer [to his epoch] than we now are**; and the Prutenic canons subscribe most closely to the Ptolemaic for that age. But if some error crept into Ptolemy's observations (which I suspect, not without cause, has not rarely happened), we build upon this foundation in vain; wherefore his tenets are to be used very circumspectly, and only with a competent limitation applied.

Concerning the **Eclipses** of which you write, it is thus: that the **Prutenic tables agree most closely with those which happened in Ptolemy's age, yet are not precisely adapted to each**; for it is established that **Copernicus applied his numbers to the Ptolemaic Eclipses (so far as could be done in some) as Epochs**. Yet in all he could not attain an accurate exactness, on account of **a certain other implication of the lunar inequality, noticed by neither Ptolemy nor himself**. For **three eclipses, as they practised, do not suffice to work out the Moon's first inequality** — to say nothing here of the second, yet more intricate one; but more are needed, in different places of the Eccentric or greater Epicycle, and those most accurately noted. That you may consider this somewhat, in at least one example, **I send the practical working [*pragmatia*] of the lunar eclipse at the beginning of this year** — both in the triangular demonstration from our hypothesis, and in the corresponding numbers, worked out (with my leave) and printed by **the eminent Wittenberg Mathematician M. Jöstel**, while I tarried there a while, on account of the plague raging in Bohemia and other causes. But when **my tables of the motion of the luminaries (which I purpose to publish before the other Planets) shall, by divine help, come to light under the auspices of the Roman Emperor Rudolf II**, experience will testify that they fit not only our age exactly, but also sufficiently agree with those most ancient Eclipses — so far as the ancients' observations were precisely consonant with the very appearances of the heaven. And what, pray, could they furnish, in the Moon or the other Planets, immune from all fault, **when they used the fixed stars less faithfully corrected** — as **the most accurate restitution of a thousand fixed stars, [done] to the very minute, and sometimes to its half, drawn out by me over the past years, and lately most submissively exhibited to the Imperial Majesty in a manuscript on parchment**, will abundantly testify, by a comparison set up with the usual tables. **I also offered the same Imperial Majesty, in another manuscript book, the restitution of the Sun and Moon for each day of the next two years, with the discrepancy of both calculations — the Alphonsine and the Copernican — set down at once (which is sometimes not small). Nay, and in a third book of the same form and size — the Mechanical part of Astronomy, representing my Instruments which I have hitherto elaborated, and printed after I left Denmark — I likewise most humbly dedicated to His Imperial Majesty.** Of this last I would have sent now **three copies — two for the most illustrious Dukes of Bavaria, William the elder and father, and Maximilian the son, [now] reigning; the third for yourself — but I have none at hand now that is properly illuminated with colours (as they call it)**. But I am now having this done at Prague; which finished, I will do what I just said, and perhaps send even more — whatever I can have copied so quickly. Meanwhile do not find it a burden to indicate, in a few words, whether your said most illustrious Princes are affected by such things. May Your Magnificence fare most happily and most long, and continue often to visit me with your erudite letters, as you have benevolently begun, and to continue and preserve the friendship once begun by them (since otherwise it can scarcely be); you will find me most ready to do the same, so that you may never repent of having thus striven first; and I gladly promise and offer you all my zeal and whatever services can proceed from me. For the rest, that I did not write back sooner, impute it to the various occupations by which I was hindered at Prague, and to my recent migration into this castle, and hold it candidly excused. I wished to compensate that tardiness in writing back by the prolixity you see — which I beg may be welcome.

And now again, and oftener, may Your Magnificence fare most well.
Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 31st day of August, the year 1599.
Most zealous of Your Magnificence,
**Tycho Brahe.**

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondent.** **Tycho → Hans Georg Herwart von Hohenburg** (Munich) — **the letter Herwart answers in brahe-t_15990917001 (17 September 1599)**, where he cites "your letter from Benátky on the last day of last month." Read the two as a pair.
- **Significance — Tycho's reply on the Venus-star and his planetary/lunar discoveries (a major scientific letter).**
 - **The Benátky establishment.** Tycho confirms his clemently-granted seat at **Benátky, "5 miles from Prague,"** for his "Astronomical and Spagyric [alchemical] exercises," with his apparatus being moved from **Magdeburg**.
 - **The Venus-star debunked (physical refutation).** Against **Herwart's theory that a reported non-appearance of Venus "at the beginning of 4 BC" was a Mercury-occultation** (cf. brahe-t_15990917001; the chronology question Scaliger also attacked, brahe-t_16000310001), Tycho marshals **physical arguments**: the "Author" was a *poet* (poetic licence); **Mercury is far too small to hide the much larger Venus; Mercury is luminous, not opaque like the Moon, so it would *add* light, not eclipse it; Mercury moves too fast to stay under Venus; and it was 2¾° off in latitude** (Herwart's own Prutenic figure) — far from a partile conjunction. A model of Tychonic empirical reasoning. *(He also defends, in passing, the supra-lunar place of comets — "seven in 22 years.")*
 - **Planetary-latitude discoveries.** Tycho reports observing **Venus reach 9° 50′–10° N latitude (3° beyond the Alphonsine, c. 1° beyond the Copernican), noted twice (1587 & 1595, the required 8-year interval)**; and deviations of **Mercury and the three superior planets** from Ptolemy/Copernicus — concluding that the **maximum-latitude limits and the nodes have an independent motion**, not derivable from the apogees, differing now "by many degrees."
 - **The lunar discoveries (the core, celebrated in Herwart's reply of 17 September 1599).** **Max lunar latitude 4° 58′ at syzygy (within 2′ of Ptolemy's limit), but +⅓° at the quadratures; and — "more wonderful" — the nodes' motion is unequal, reciprocating monthly by up to 1° 35′.** This is Tycho's **variation of the inclination and libration of the nodes** (cf. the same to Scaliger, brahe-t_16000723001).
 - **On eclipses and tables.** The Prutenic tables fit Ptolemy-era eclipses (Copernicus used them as epochs) but not precisely — for **"three eclipses do not suffice to work out the Moon's first inequality," still less the second**; more, in varied epicycle positions, are needed. Tycho sends **the worked lunar eclipse of early 1599** (triangular demonstration + numbers **printed by Melchior Jöstel at Wittenberg**, where Tycho waited out the Bohemian plague), and promises his **luminary tables "under the auspices of Rudolf II"** (the future Rudolphine work) — superior because the ancients "used the fixed stars less faithfully corrected."
 - **The three books offered to Rudolf II** (a precise inventory): (1) **the 1000-fixed-star restitution "to the minute, sometimes the half," on parchment**; (2) **a Sun–Moon restitution for each day of the next two years, with Alphonsine/Copernican discrepancies**; (3) **the *Mechanica*** (printed since leaving Denmark). And a **Mechanica gift plan**: three coloured/illuminated copies — for **Duke William V of Bavaria ("the elder, father") and Duke Maximilian I ("the son, reigning") and Herwart** — to follow once illuminated at Prague. *(A datable Mechanica distribution arrangement.)*
- **Cross-references.** Pair with **brahe-t_15990917001 (Herwart's reply, 17 September 1599)**; the **lunar-theory** thread (brahe-t_16000723001); the **Venus-star/chronology** thread (brahe-t_16000310001); and the **Mechanica-distribution** layer (the Bavarian-duke copies).
- **Persons & places named.** Herwart von Hohenburg; **Rudolf II**; the unnamed Roman-poet "Author" (the Venus-star source); **Ptolemy, Copernicus**; the **Alphonsine** and **Prutenic** tables; **Melchior Jöstel** (Wittenberg); **Duke William V** & **Duke Maximilian I of Bavaria**. Places: **Benátky**, **Prague**, **Magdeburg**, **Wittenberg**. Glyphs ♀ ☿ ☾ ♓ □ reproduced.
- **Place/calendar.** Dateline *ex arce Caesareae Benachia die 31. Augusti Anno 1599* → **Benátky, 31 August 1599 [N.S.]**; the **catalogue label's "Wittenberg" is a location error** (contradicted by the dateline — Tycho had moved to Benátky by late August 1599; cf. brahe-t_15990922001), flagged for review of the catalogue date. text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD OLIGERUM ROSENCRANTZIUM.

S. P,

AD eas, quas antequam Witeberga discederem, pauculis interiectis septimanis, a te accepi literas, Exoptatissime mi OLIGERE, tunc responsum misi, speroque id tibi iam pridem redditum. Abij autem inde cum meis omnibus circa Solstitium Aestivum, neque enim diutius isthic haerere ausus fui, utut viatico, quod e Dania expectabam, non satis instructus. Scripsit enim aliquoties ad me THADDÆUS noster, Caesarem pene singulis diebus de me, an advenissem, percontatum esse. Nec tamen prius licuit profectionem instituere, partim quod tertius ille liber, qui luminarium restitutos motus exhibet, Imperatori destinatus, antea absolvi nequiverit, partim quod filia mea natu maior, quae periculose ibi decubuit, paulo ante id temporis primum convaluerit. In itinere autem Dresdam a nobili et Magnifico viro Domino IOHANNE [LOe]SERO, quem procul dubio nosti, Bretziae in Arce eius humaniter invitati et laute tractati sumus. Cumque biduo post Dresdam venissemus, relicto illic apud civem quendam primarium mihi notum, Virum integrum et officiosum, Gynaeceo meo, ipsemet Pragam, cum filijs et reliquo comitatu me contuli. Ubi statim ac advenissem, a multis praecipuis Viris perhumaniter et honorifice exceptus sum, inprimis vero a Magnifico Domino IOHANNE BARVICIO Imperij supremo Secretario, Caesareae Maiestati a Consilijs intimis, qui unus pene omnia agit apud Caesarem. Is in horto quodam, non multum ab Arce remoto (siquidem non longe a Caesare abesse audet) tam nomine Imperatoriae Maitis quam Consiliariorum et proprio, de adventu meo humanissimis verbis mihi congratulatus est, admotumque acceptum esse Caesari meum accessum referebat, eiusque erga me etiam, necdum visum, clementem animum depraedicabat. Cumque libros tres, Caesari humillime offerendos, unâque Literas Electoris Coloniensis et Ducis Magnopolitani commendatitias monstrassem, se de ijs Caesarem percontaturum aiebat, ignorare enim, e cuius manu illa accipere velit; responsumque dedit sequenti die, Caesaream Maiestatem a nemine alio quam me ipso ea velle suscipere, brevique in Arcem ad se me vocaturum. Ostendi etiam Domino BARVICIO quasdam literas, ab Illustrissimo Duce OTTONE, Harburgi prope Hamburgum habitante, ad Illustrem et Generosum Dominum RUMPHIUM Curiae Caesareae Magistrum, praecipuaeque post Caesarem isthic authoritatis virum, mea de caussa scriptas. Suasit Dominus BARVICIUS, ut ipsemet eas illi intra diem unum vel alterum (quod alias per filium TYCHONEM fieri volebam) offerrem. Captata itaque commoditate, in Arcem curru vectus, ad eundem Dnum RUMPHIUM mox introductus sum, qui etiam benignissime me excepit, et perhumaniter affatus est. Inter alia vero aiebat, se multa relatione Praestantium virorum prius de me inaudivisse; gaudere autem, quod nunc praesentem videat; sed non posse se et alios satis mirari, quod Rex me e Dania dimittere voluerit, idque eius iuvenili aetati, quod Marti potius quam Arti operam daret, tribuendum censuit; at ego e contra Regem excusavi, quamque virtute et ingenio polleat, extuli. Mox ille subiunxit: oportet igitur eos, qui ab illo secundi, et autoritate isthic praevalent, aut bonarum Artium rudes, aut malevolos et invidos esse, cum Regis et Patriae honori non rectius consulant; ad quae verba ego non multa respondi, id saltem subijciens, me non dubitare, si Regi omnia de me rite proposita fuissent, ac ab ijs, quos intime habet, illi commendata, ipsum non minus, quam Pater antea, Laudatissimae memoriae FRIDERICUS, Astronomica mea excercitia in suo Regno conservaturum; sed forte peculiari Dei providentia sic factum esse, ut ea, quae in Astronomicis diu multumque molitus sum, nunc alio, atque ad ipsum Imperatorem, Imperij caput, transferenda sint. Haec et similia cum dicto Domino RUMPHIO (qui elegantissime Latine loquitur) verba commutans, literas praenominati Principis illi tradidi, isque, discedentem aliquantulum deducens, meas res sibi curae futuras, seque eas apud Caesarem promoturum, pollicitus est. Insinuavit autem quidam ex Amicis postea, id quod Dominus BARVICIUS adeo ursit, ut in Arcem ascendens ipsemet literas Domino RUMPHIO inscriptas ei in manus exhiberem, id propterea factum, quod Caesar e conclavi suo, quod e regione est, me hac occasione antea videre vellet, quam ad se vocaret. Quamprimum vero ex Arce descenderem, mox obviam factus Dnus BARVICIUS in aedes quasdam splendidas et magnificas (quas prior Imperij Cancellarius, Dominus IACOBUS CURTIUS laudatae memoriae Italica architectura exstruxerat, et horto pulcherrimo cinxerat expensis maioribus quam 20 Ioachymicorum) iussu Caesaris introduxit singulaque in ijs monstravit, subiungens, Caesaream Maiestatem eas mihi a vidua procurare velle, si placerent, in ijs a Domino CURTIO turriculam, quam cernerem, ob id exstructam, ut observationibus coelestibus inserviret, et esse eas aedes Arci atque habitationi Caesaris vicinas, ut promptior sit accessus. Verum cum is ex taciturnitate mea, et quod dicerem, turriculam eam vix uni ex meis instrumentis sufficere, nedum pluribus, colligeret animum meum non admodum eo inclinari, ulterius inferebat: Si forte Pragae habitare mihi non luberet, concessurum facile Imperatorem Arcem quampiam ex suis, unius vel dimidij diei itinere ab urbe distantem, ubi pacatius agerem, extra invidiam aliorum positus. Id cum magis mihi arridere animadverteret, praesertim cum dicerem, me, ut otio fruerer Philosophico, non nimium ab alijs interpellatus, ob id maluisse in Dania insulam eam inhabitare, subiunxit, se Caesari id relaturum, et iam intellexisse, eius animum in has alteras partes inclinare; Caesarem etiam de salario annuo mihi clementer impertiendo constituisse; de quo ubi audientiam, uti vocant (quod intra duos vel tres dies futurum existimavit) nactus essem, plenius mecum agendum. Elapsis mox pauculis diebus, Caesar me in Arcem ad se accersi iubet: constitutum vero fuit antea in Senatu, ut aulae magister Dns RUMPHIUS me ad Caesarem solemniter introduceret, quod hoc esset magis honorificum; at Caesar id tunc temporis renuit, sive quod quidam ex ministris RUMPHIJ ijs diebus peste infectus et in civitatem delatus obijsset, sive quod ipsius Maiestas cum me solo, nemine praesente, loqui maluerit, quod et factum est; nam cum ad ianuam conclavis, in quo Caesar esset, me duxisset Dns BARVICIUS, se non ingredi, nisi a Caesare vocatum, insinuans, extra remansit. Ingressusque solus ego ad Caesar. Matem, quam solam etiam mensae cuidam in superiori conclavis parte dorso innitentem conspexi, nemine alias in toto conclavi praesente, et ne quidem puero famulante, exhibitaque debita reverentia, Caesar me statim nutu capitis propius ad se vocavit; cum accessissem, clementer manum mihi porrigebat; moxque paululum recedens, oratiunculam habui Latino sermone, qua, ex ipsius Caesar. Matis clementissimo mandato, per literas sui Cancellarij CORADUCIJ me vocatum nunc comparere, quod et prius, si res meae id ullo modo ferre potuissent, fecissem, dixi, utque hanc moram clementissime excusatam habere dignaretur, et me atque ea, quae diu multumque tractavi, studia Caesareo favore prosequi ac sibi commendata esse velit. Quo etiam nomine literas a Serenissimo Coloniensi Electore et Illustrissimo Duce Megapolitano scriptas, ipsi humillime porrigerem, moxque literas illas eius Maiestati in manus tradidi, quas et clementer accepit meque praesente aperuit. Verum ijs in mensam repositis, et nondum lectis, statim ipsius Caesarea Maiestas copiosiore etiam sermone, quam ego eam alloquebar, mihi clementissime respondit; et inter alia gratum sibi esse meum accessum, atque me cum meis studijs sibi curae futurum promisit, ac inter loquendum blanditer quasi arrisit, ut favorem eximium ipso vultu ostenderet. Verum omnia, quae referebat, verba capere non potui, tam submisse ipsa natura loquitur. Deinde ego, pro hac clementissima animi sui indicatione humillime gratias agens, de libris tribus, quos ipsius Maiestati subiectissime dedicatos in promptu haberem, mentionem feci; quos cum se lubenter a me accepturam clementissime responderet, ego mox eos a filio TYCHONE, qui in exteriori conclavi expectans secum habuit, ad me recipiens, denuoque ingressus, Caesareae Matem, quae adhuc mensae astabat, in manus exhibui; quae postquam eos clementissime accepisset, atque prope se in mensa reposuisset, ego rursus brevi narratione, quid singuli eorum continerent, summatim indicavi; rursusque ipsius Caesarea Maiestas sermone satis luculento excepit, atque eos gratos sibi futuros benignissime indicavit. Sicque praestito honore discessi; et BARVICIUM ante ianuam adhuc praestolantem reperi, qui statim audito signo ad Caesarem introvocatus, me, ut, antequam rediret, non descenderem, rogavit, statimque reversus dixit, Caesarem automatum illud, quod in curru haberem (hoc enim, cum in Arcem curru veherer, per fenestram conspexerat) sibi monstrari cupere, illud itaque per filium e curru mox allatum, BARVICIO tradidi, atque eius usum Caesari ostendendum monstravi. Quod cum fecisset, atque ad me reversus esset, aiebat, Caesarem dixisse, se unum vel alterum eiuscemodi habere, quorum tamen nullum tam magnum esset, neque penitus ea ratione factum, posse aliquem e suis Astronomis sibi ad huius imitationem quoddam conficere, sed nolle me eo privari; et addebat insuper BARVICIUS, Caesarem singulari Clementia et gratia erga me affectum esse, brevique negotio ad consiliarios relato, velle mecum de salario annuatim numerando atque habitatione idonea transigi curare. Interim iuberent, Gynaeceum meum, quod Dresdae me reliquisse intellexerat, Pragam ad me advehi faciam, ipsius Caesaream Maiestatem nobis omnibus ita prospecturam, ut ad commode vivendum nihil sit defuturum. Quare sequenti mox die filium TYCHONEM unâ cum CLAUDIO MULÆO, pro adducendo Gynaeceo Dresdam misi, quod post octiduum Pragam advenit. Intera de salario mecum per eundem Dominum BARVICIUM et sequentibus etiam aliquot diebus, per intervalla, actum est, siquidem is sit occupatissimus, et nonnulli e Senatoribus Imperatoriae voluntati non satis cito, uti fit, auscultent, lenteque omnia in illa aula ob negotiorum magnitudinem et copiam procedant. Cupiente vero BARVICIO ex Caesaris mandato, ut familiam meam, quanta sit, et eorum, qui ad Artis sustentationem requirerentur, summam consignarem, atque magnitudinem horum omnium in taxa, uti aiunt, deducerem, primum quidem lubens feci; at alterum Caesareae Matis Clementissimae voluntati et libero arbitrio humillime commisi. Quae paucis post diebus 3000 aureorum in certa quadam pecunia mihi benignissime deputavit, et insuper quaedam alia accidentaria ...... pro oeconomia et alijs rebus, quae 1000, si computentur, excedunt. Haec Senatus consulto peracta sunt, quibusdam id facile approbantibus, at pluribus, uti fieri solet, nonnihil reluctantibus, quod nemo ex illis, qui pluribus annis Caesari inservijssent, tantum haberent salarium. Vicit tamen Caesaris ........ci ut sic fieret ursit, cumque per praedictum Dominum BARVICIUM mihi hoc significari curasset, iussit insuper dici, si haec mihi non sufficerent, et in posterum quidpiam desiderarem, nec sibi esse accurtatam manum, nec mihi obturatum os, quod his ipsis verbis ad me idem retulit BARVICIUS. Quin et feudum secundum constitutionem Imperij haereditarium, ut liberis et familiae meae post me consuleretur, Clementissime nec invite addixit, quam primum aliquod in suis ditionibus vel Imperio vacarit, quod mihi et meis commodum esset. Qua etiam de re literas, quas vocant promissivas, brevi accepturus. Et quoniam me Pragae aedes Curtianas non admodum cupere (habui enim meas rationes, cum quod viduam, quae eas adhuc inhabitat, mea de caussa emigrare nolim, tum quod nimijs visitationibus, in tanta praesertim civitate, prope Arcem obnoxius essem) intellexit Caesar, promisit nihilominus clementissime aliam in urbe habitationem mihi oportunam, quam, ubi eo accederem, sive vocatus, sive sponte, cum meis commode incolere possem, et propria quadra vivere minoreque sumptu; forte tamen Curtianam illam suo tempore accipiam, ubi vidua sponte emigrarit, quae nunc, uti audio, novas affectat nuptias, more iuvencularum viduarum. Iussit insuper Caesar, praeterquam quod Salarium meum ab eo tempore, quo ab ipsius Caesarea Mate vocatus sum Pragam, etiamsi multo interiecto tempore non advenerim, incipere deberet, ut mihi 2000 florenorum statim honorarij loco pro introitu darentur, quos et accepi. Dixit quoque inter alia aliquando ad me BARVICIUS [si] foret, ut ante decennium huc ad Caesarem advenissem, [cum] omnia erant meliora et promptiora, nec ita difficultatibus obnoxia, uti nunc ob bellum in Hungaria, tunc Caesarem potuisse multo faciliorem et liberaliorem se erga me praebere; cumque hoc semel atque iterum insinuaret, ego quidem respondi, nihil adhuc periculi esse: Caesarem Turca fere semper superiorem fuisse, et Deum in posterum suum Christianismum protecturum. Verum tacite mecum cogitavi, neminem me ipso magis dolere, quod non ante decennium statim ab obitu laudatissimae memoriae FRIDERICI Regis Patria excesserim, atque huc me contulerim, quod et tunc fecissem, nisi literae a toto Senatu ....... magno meo incommodo, maximoque rei familiaris dispendio, me ....... de his alias agemus, non iustum sit, ut aliqua mihi fiat pro tantis expensis compensatio. Quibus transactis, per Capitaneum quendam Caesareum, eius Mate sic iubente, in Arces prope Pragam dispositas deductus sum, ut ex ijs eligerem aliquam, quae mihi et meis studijs commodior foret. Nomi........ et aliae; sed quoniam ut ex ijs una cum civitatibus propinquis p.........arat, et tertiam in edito positam, Caesar .........enter accederet, qui quondam Bohemici Aulae Magistri fuerat, et Caesar secundum iuris ten.........ata, dissuasit Dominus BARVICIUS earum perlustrationem. Eae vero, quas v........um unius vel etiam dimidij diei profectione Praga absunt, quarum prima dicitur Brandeiss, estque potissima Caesaris Arx in vicinia sita, utpote tribus saltem miliaribus Praga distans, in quam se delectationis gratia interdum se ....... venationes habet circumquaque praecipuas. Altera Lyssa dicta est, etiam .......da, 4 milliaribus ab urbe remota. Tertia Benachia appellatur, qua ....... sub initium huius anni a .......ruvij cuiusdam senio confecti et defuncti .......nis, producentis quindecim .....................int, illi enim, non satis concordes, haereditatem alias inter se dividere nequiverunt, sed sponte Caesari haec bona vendiderunt. Perlustratis itaque his tribus, deducente Capitaneo, Arcibus, et in singulis benigne et honorifice exceptus, praetuli Benachiam, 6 horarum itinere (est enim via plana) Praga semotam, quae ob loci amoenitatem et fluviolum Isaram circumlabentem atque in Albim postea se exonerantem, Bohemorum vernacula lingua sonat, ac si diceres Venetiae Bohemorum, estque in edito et aprico loco sita, iucundissimo prospectu, adiacente parva quadam civitate, in qua religio, quam Evangelicam vocant, praevalet, plurimis tamen ex Picardis, qui Calvinisticae (quam Sectatores orthodoxam nuncupant) appropinquant, in eadem degentibus. Cum Caesar intellexisset, me hanc Arcem prae ceteris eligere, mox per praedictum Capitaneum, qui Brandusijs praeest, me huc introduci curavit, ubi nunc cum familia, commode et pacate, quod Deo acceptum fero, solus habito, nemine obstrepente aut interturbante, sed dicto Capitaneo ex voluntate Caesaris omnia officia mihi lubenter exhibente. Qua etiam de caussa intra unam vel aliam septimanam Brandusio huc accurrit, ut mihi in ijs, quae requiruntur, praesto sit. Mandavit etiam Caesar eidem Capitaneo, ut omnia necessaria pro observatorio, meis instrumentis omnibus rite disponendis idoneo, actutum procuret, quo iuxta meam ordinationem omnia ante hyemem apposite exaedificentur, tum quoque ut laboratorium, ea qua voluero ratione, mihi oportuno loco confici curet, et omnia, quae alias a Mechanicis fieri velim, solvat. Si haec mihi in Patria evenissent, quantis sumptibus pepercissem, pro quibus nunc mihi nulla restat gratia, sed potius ingrata omnia [nihil feci]sse benigne. Obtulit insuper Caesarea Maiestas sponte sua, se novum Uraniburgum Arcem in suo territorio suisque sumptibus aedificaturum, quod Danico illi non cederet, sed multis parasangis excederet. Delectatur enim ipsius Caesarea Matas summopere non saltem Divina illa Astronomia Mathematicisque studijs, sed et architectonicis structuris, quae e Geometria et Perspectiva fluunt. Cumque ipsius Maiestas Libros sibi a me humillime oblatos (de quibus antea memini) diligenter perlegisset, adeo ut in multam noctem primis diebus, referente id BARVICIO, ijs occuparetur (neque enim tam abiecti apud ipsum erant, quemadmodum in vestris oris) a me multa de eorum contentis per eundem BARVICIUM sciscitatus est, et placuit illi valde structura Uraniburgi in primo tomo designata. Sed cum laboratorium in ea tam cito reperire non posset, id sibi indicari voluit. Placuerunt caetera omnia, ita ut Dominus BARVICIUS eos Caesari acceptissimos esse mihi retulerit.

Ex iam recensitis, Amantissime OLIGERE, rerum mearum statum, qualis nunc sit, intellexisti. Agoque Deo propitio gratias, quod sic mihi et meis prospexerit, ut ex adversitatibus illis, quas in Patria diu multumque passus sum, eluctari potuerim, et mihi et meis rectius consulere. Speroque in posterum, eodem Divino Numine favente, adhuc prosperiora. Caeterum de honoribus et dignitatibus Politicis mihi oblatis, imo antequam Pragam venirem, cum adhuc Witebergae essem, deputatis (prout forte ex Domino Doctore FRANTZIO, Domini Doctoris VITI WINSHEMIJ genero, aut oretenus; aiebat enim te, in Orientalem Frisiam abiturus, invisere velle; aut per literas intellexisti, quemadmodum is ex Domino CORRADUCIO Procancellario haec, cum Pragae esset, se accepisse aiebat, ut mihi referret, quo promptius accederem) nihil nunc addere volo. Suaserunt Pragae amici quidam, ut talia susciperem, quae tamen semper ex alto despexi. At si facturus sum, propter vestrates, qui me tam insolenter contemptui habuerunt, facturus sum; quod et THADDÆO nostro urgenti dixi; verum is sic subiunxit: Non tantum propter tuos Danos id admittes, sed etiam propter nostros Bohemos, adeoque in ipsa aula aliqui tam obtuso et rustico ingenio, et non minus quam vestrates ignorent discernere inter aurum et orichalcum, attamen aliqui inveniuntur, qui rectius iudicent, quique, licet aeque atque tu honores Politicos, respectu virtutis et doctrinae eximiae, parvi ducant, ob vulgarium tamen iudiciorum captum, quo commodius in mundo vivatur, ita faciendum existimant. Qui, quamvis pauci reperiantur, tamen prae caeteris iudicio valent, tuique sunt amantissimi, quos partim hactenus pro primo hoc congressu nosti, partim in posterum plenius tibi innotescent. In hunc modum ille. Verum de his postmodum dispiciam, si non ea prorsus despiciam; neque enim in ijs quid consulto et discrete fieri potest ante Magci Domini CORRADUC1J Procancellarij reditum e Roma, ubi Legatum Caesaris nomine apud P. M. agit, qui circa Michaëlis festum expectatur. Neque etiam volo, ut prius quid in talibus concludatur; est is mihi admodum favens, licet de facie ignoti adhuc simus, Mathematicarum quoque rerum, ut dicitur, amantissimus, hac in re antecessoris CURTIJ aemulus.

Habes nunc, charissime mi OLIGERE, historiolam mearum rerum, ex quo e Germania in Bohemiam cum meis migravi; de ijs, quae antea facta sunt, meoque e Dania discessu probe omnia nosti, ut ea repetere non sit opus, quae meminisse animus horrens iterare refugit. Et certe videor historiolam potius quam literas conscripsisse, dum calamo lapso teque fusius alloquor, quo [de] rebus meis plenius edoceare. Quam tamen prolixitatem tibi non ingratam fore, cum alias literas humaniores, adeoque ingentia librorum volumina, non, ut alij, qui Nobiles haberi volunt, fastidias, mihi persuadeo. De libris vero tibi promissis (ut tandem aliquid subiungam) sic habe. Non immemor sum pacti, nec difficilis ad servandum; sed cum exemplaria omnia de Mechanica Astronomia, quotquot coloribus exornata, sive uti vocant illuminata, ................................. Pragae suis coloribus imbui, quod ubi factum fuerit, obtinebis non saltem hunc primum tomum, sed et alterum de affixarum restitutione, tum quoque tertium de luminarium a me correcto motu, quem tamen ultimum denuo e prima conceptione describi curare oportet, cum nullum mihi ad manus mundum sit exemplar, postquam illud, quod Witebergae exaratum est, Caesi Mati unâ cum reliquis obtulerim. Ne sis itaque huius morae impatiens, mi OLIGERE, habebis et haec et alia ex meis, favente Numine, quam primum fieri poterit, nec sine foenore. Interim relinque sorori nostrae SOPHIAe eos, quos Regi destinaram (hos enim repudiatos et RAMELIO donatos ipsam consequi posse intellexi) quod etiam non displicet, malo etenim sic fieri, quam ut in invidorum et in osorum manus pervenirent.

Superest, ut calamum sistam, nisi hoc unicum superaddere luberet. Insulae Huennae, quam istic inhabitavi, resignationem voluntariam, quam suasisti (de qua etiam me, cum huc venirem, plenius rescripturum .......ui) nullatenus approbare animus est, dissuadentibus etiam ijs, qui Politicis non perfunctorie imbuti sunt, imo quibusdam id mihi vitio datum iri, tanquam prae contumaci insolentia, postquam ad Caesareas partes transivi, hoc facerem, quasi Danos meos, et quae isthic haberem, praefracto animo negligerem. Si vero insulam ij, qui ........ praesunt, mihi auferre voluerint, ob id quod ad Caesarem me contulerim, ipsius Caesaream Maitem aut operam daturam, ut Rex Daniae nihil damni mihi sua de caussa inferre patiatur, aut id, quicquid erit, alia ratione compensaturam. Obiectent vestrates, quicquid velint, facilis erit responsio, si modo iustitiae et veritati sit locus; sin minus, transeat id cum caeteris, et iustus iudex omnia decernat. Iamque cum coniuge tua, Nepte mea dilecta, quam felicissime vale, integerrime OLIGERE, salutata unâ cum hac Matre tua Nobilissima et honestissima ac simul alijs amicis, si qui in Cimbria vestra mei memores adhuc supersint, quos aliquos saltem adhuc restare crediderim. Iterumque et saepius quam optime vale, meque de tuis rebus luculenter etiam prima quaque occasione certiorem effice.

Dabantur ex Arce Caesarea Benachia die 9. Septembris Stylo novo, Anni Domini 1599.
Totus Tuus
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
