documents.incipit: MIN gantske wenlig hilsen nu och altidt forsendt med Wor Herre. Kiere Mette Mulis, …

text.original:
ERLIG VELBYRDIG QVINDE, METTE HANS MULIS, BOENDE PAA NISLEFFGAARD, MIN TILFORLADENDE SYNDERLIGE GODE VEN, DETTE VENLIGEN TILHÆNDE.

MIN gantske wenlig hilsen nu och altidt forsendt med Wor Herre. Kiere Mette Mulis, tilforladendis synderlige gode wen. Nest min gantske wenlig och store taksigelse for alt megit beuist gode, huilckit at forskylde ieg stedse wil findis aff min yderste formue gantske willig och redebon till vdi alle de maader, ieg nogen tid kand giøre nogit, som eder til aere och tieniste kand were. Och skal j ochsaa haffue saa megen stor aere och tak for eders gode skriffuelse, forn ieg bekom fran eder, der wii ware till Witenberig, det war mig saa megit kiert, at ieg fick eders breff, och kunde forfare, horledis eder och eders kiere mand med eders liide. Och skulde ieg wel for lang tid siden haffue skreffuet eder til udigen, mens ieg haffuer siden slet ingen wisse budt kunde fangit till eder; derfore kunde ieg icke lade, at ieg jo nu skulde skriffue eder till udigen, effterdi at mig stedis nu saa wisse budt ind udi Danmarck med eders kiere søn Clauß Mule och min broder Tyge, hwilcke min kiere fader haffuer sendt did ind i landet till hans slecht och gode wenner, hans aerende att bestille. Kiere Mette, anlangendis woris leylighedt her i fremmede land, saa maae j gantske wenligen wide, att baade min kiere fader, moder, och wii sydskende liider, Gud were loffuit, alle well. Gud allermechtigste vnde os altidt de samme tidende fra eder och alle eders att høre och spørge, dett er os gantske kiert att fornemme. Och er min kiere fader om St. Hans dags tiide med min kiere moder och os alle dragen fran Wittenberig och op till Prag till den romske keyserlig mayestat effter hans mayestats naadigst begiering, och er hand der well bleffuen antagen och naadigst forsynit, saa att hand lader sig well nøye. Och haffuer keyserlig mayestat vndt hanum ett aff sine slotte, liggendis i lante Bemen 5 mile fran Prag, att boe paa, huilckit hans mayestat lod hannum iblant tre aff sine slotte selff vduelle. Och haffuer hans mayestat naadigst foraerit min kiere fader tho tusend gylden, och loffuit hannum til aarlig pension tre tusend gylden først att begynde med. Saa att hans mayestat er min kiere fader med all keyserlig gunst och naade well beuogen. Wor Herre giffue widere lycke och benedidelse. Kiere Mette, dette kunde ieg icke lade att giffue eder vdi en god mening tilkiende, helst effterdi ieg weed, att j er woris gode wen och gierne seer, att det gaaer os wel, for huilcken eders gode willie j skal were paa det allerhøyeste betacket och wii aff woris ringe formue vdigien forskylde wil. Disligeste, kiere Mette, maa j ochsaa wenligen wide, att min kiere fader loffuet och tilsagde eders kiere søn Claus Mule, att dett første Gud vil, hand kommer fran Danmarck til os vdigien, da will hand forskaffe hannum med en første vdi Italien paa sin bekostning och gierne forhielpe hannum til det beste, huor hannum mueligt kand were, baade for eders och hans egen skyld. Og vdi alle de maader min kiere moder och wii syskend kand giøre nøget, som eder eller hanum eller nogen aff eders til willige och tieniste kand were, wille wii det aff woris yderste formue hiertens gierne giøre, huilcket och i alle maade baade aff eder och hanum wel forskyldt er. Kiere Mette, wil ieg icke nu lenger opholde eder med denne min widtløfftige schriffuelse, thii ieg tencker well, att eders søn Claus Mule schriffuer eder all widere beskening til om min kiere faders och woris leylighedt, och ochsaa eders svoger doctor Niels Krag, thii min fader haffuer selff schreffuit hanum widtløfftelig nock til der vd om. Och will ieg her med nu och altidt haffue eder den euige alsommechtigste gode Gudt, med all langvarendis sundhed, lycke och benedidelse, med alt huis eder kiert er, til siel och liff befalit. Och lader min kiere fader, moder, syskende och ieg hilse eders kiere mand och eder med alle eders kiere børn, med mange m. maal m. gode netter.

Datum paa det keyserlig slot Benatica den 25. septembris stilo novo, anno d:ni 1599.
Magdalene Brahe
med min egen handt.
text.english:
**To the honourable, well-born woman Mette, [wife of] Hans Mule, dwelling at Nislevgård, my trusted especial good friend, [this] amicably to hand.**

My quite friendly greeting, now and always, conveyed with [the blessing of] Our Lord. Dear Mette Mule, trusted especial good friend. Next [after] my quite friendly and great thanks for all the much kindness shown, which to repay I shall always be found — to my utmost ability — quite willing and ready, in every way I can ever do anything that may be to your honour and service. And you shall also have so much great honour and thanks for your good letter, which I received from you when we were at **Wittenberg**; it was so dear to me that I got your letter, and could learn how you and your dear husband, with yours, fare. And I should well, long ago, have written to you again, but I have since been able to get no sure messenger to you at all; therefore I could not forbear writing to you again now, since so sure a messenger is now available to me [going] into Denmark — with **your dear son Claus Mule and my brother Tyge**, whom my dear father has sent there into the country, to his kin and good friends, to attend to his business. Dear Mette, concerning our circumstances here in a foreign land, you may quite amicably know that **both my dear father, mother, and we siblings fare, God be praised, all well**. May God Almighty grant us always to hear the same tidings from you and all yours; it is quite dear to us to perceive [them]. And my dear father, about **St. John's Day** [24 June], with my dear mother and us all, **moved from Wittenberg up to Prague**, to the Roman Imperial Majesty, at His Majesty's gracious request; and he has there been well received and graciously provided for, so that he is well content. And the Imperial Majesty has **granted him one of his castles, lying in the land of Bohemia, 5 miles from Prague, to dwell in — which His Majesty let him himself choose from among three of his castles**. And His Majesty has graciously **presented my dear father with two thousand gulden, and promised him as annual pension three thousand gulden to begin with** — so that His Majesty is well disposed toward my dear father with all imperial favour and grace. May Our Lord give further fortune and blessing. Dear Mette, this I could not forbear to give you to know, in good intent, especially since I know you are our good friend and gladly see that it goes well with us — for which good will you shall be most highly thanked, and we will repay it according to our humble ability. Likewise, dear Mette, you may also amicably know that **my dear father promised and assured your dear son Claus Mule that, the first [moment] God wills it — [when] he comes back from Denmark to us — he will provide for him with a prince in Italy at his own expense, and gladly help him to the best** he can, both for your sake and his own. And in every way my dear mother and we siblings can do anything to the willing service of you, or him, or any of yours, we will do it most heartily, to our utmost ability — which is also in every way well deserved both by you and by him. Dear Mette, I will not now detain you longer with this lengthy letter of mine, for I think your son Claus Mule writes you all further news of my dear father's and our circumstances, and also **your brother-in-law Doctor Niels Krag**, for my father has himself written to him fully enough about it. And herewith I will, now and always, commend you to the eternal, almighty good God, with all long-lasting health, fortune, and blessing, with all that is dear to you, in soul and body. And my dear father, mother, siblings, and I bid greet your dear husband and you, with all your dear children, with many a thousand-thousand-thousand good nights.

Given at the imperial castle Benátky, the 25th of September, New Style, in the year of the Lord 1599.
Magdalene Brahe,
with my own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender — Magdalene Brahe.** **Magdalene Brahe** (b. 1574), **Tycho's eldest daughter**, writing **in her own hand** from Benátky. A rare and valuable autograph letter from within Tycho's *familia* (and one of few surviving in a daughter's voice).
- **Recipient.** **Mette [Kotte], wife of Hans Mule, of Nislevgård** — the **mother of Claus Mule** (Claudius Mulenus / Nicolaus Mulaeus), Tycho's household-member and agent (cf. brahe-t_15980910001, brahe-t_16000919001), and (per this letter) **kinswoman of Niels Krag**.
- **Significance — a prime source for Tycho's imperial settlement.** Written just three months after the move, the letter states the **terms of Rudolf II's patronage** with unusual concreteness:
 - The family **moved from Wittenberg to Prague "about St. John's Day [24 June 1599]"** at the Emperor's request, and Tycho "is well content."
 - The Emperor **granted Tycho one of his castles in Bohemia, 5 miles from Prague — which Tycho was let choose from among three** (i.e. **Benátky**, chosen over two others).
 - The Emperor **gave Tycho 2,000 gulden outright and promised an annual pension of 3,000 gulden "to begin with."**
 This is one of the **earliest and most direct testimonies to the famous 3,000-gulden imperial salary** and the choice of Benátky — the more authoritative for coming from inside the household.
- **The Claus Mule / Italy promise.** Magdalene relays that **Tycho promised to send Mette's son Claus Mule to a prince in Italy at his own expense**, once Claus returns from Denmark — a glimpse of Tycho's patronage of his servants (cf. the parallel Italian plans for his own son, brahe-t_16000504001).
- **Persons named.** **Magdalene Brahe** (sender); **Mette [Kotte]** and her husband **Hans Mule** of Nislevgård; **Claus Mule** (their son, co-courier with Tyge to Denmark); **Tyge** (Tycho the Younger, Magdalene's brother); **Tycho Brahe** ("my dear father"); **Kirsten Jørgensdatter** ("my dear mother," unnamed); **Niels Krag** (*Doctor Niels Krag*, Mette's *svoger* — kinsman/brother-in-law; cf. brahe-t_15980628001, brahe-t_16010311001); **Rudolf II**.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Benatica den 25. Septembris stilo novo, anno d:ni 1599*; explicitly **New Style** (imperial). Header agrees with the label.
- **Correction.** English corrected from 'your kinsman Doctor Niels Krag' to 'your brother-in-law Doctor Niels Krag', restoring the precise sense of Danish 'svoger' (Dreyer, TBOO XIV p.153).

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD DANIELEM CRAMERUM.

S.

RESCRIPSI tibi, clarissime et eruditissime Domine Doctor CRAMERE, paulo antequam Witeberga discederem, quas te accepisse reor. De meis autem rebus, postquam inde abiens in Bohemiam ex clementissimo mandato et evocatione augustissimi Imperatoris me contulerim, quia nimis longum foret hîc sigillatim omnia enarrare, iussi describi exemplum nuperarum ad OLIGERUM ROSÆKRANTZIUM nostrum a me datarum, quae historiolam quandam eorum, quae mihi hîc evenerunt, continent, cuius te facio participem. Inde per circumstantias omnia hauries; cum enim tam arcta sit inter OLIGERUM et te amicitia, is, quod descriptum suarum literarum tibi communicem (secretum tamen habendum, nec nisi secretis amicis ostendendum) minime aegre laturus est. Quare de meis negotijs nihil hîc addo, solummodo Deo immortali gratias ago. Agasque tu et omnes pij probique mecum, quod omnia bene et ex voto successerint.

Caeterum est aliud te non minima ex parte concernens, quod te non caelandum duxi. Cum Witebergae essem, accesserat eo Danus quidam studiosus mihi familiariter notus, BARTOLDUS IVARI MULÆUS dictus, qui cum Barone quodam Svetico STENONE BIELCHE meo consanguineo accesserat, cumque per aliquot dies ibi mecum conversarentur, accidit, ut STENO ille DUNCANI Scoti mentionem faceret, ambo enim illi Helmstadij studiorum caussa, unde etiam venerant, aliquamdiu fuere. Ego mox subijciens plagium eius in me eidem Baroni, praesente BARTHOLDO illo, aperui, cumque miraretur et quasi subhaesitaret, produxi tuas litteras ad OLIGERUM ROSÆKRANTZIUM prolixe ea de re scriptas ijsque legendas dedi. Nescio vero quî factum sit, quod, dum in alterum diem eas secum servaret Danicus ille studiosus, sibiipsi exemplum inde tacite exaravit, quod, cum Helmstadium venisset, Scotulo isti monstravit. Quomodo autem is acceperit, ex ipsius BARTOLDI literis, quas ante paucos dies nactus sum, verbotenus referam. »Deinde quoad Doctoris CRAMERI literas, eas DUNCANO exhibui, reticens tamen unde perceperim. Ibi homo coepit impietatem miselli asini (sic enim criminabatur) adeo culpare, ut eundem ingratissimum erga praeceptorem cuculum vocitaret, simulque se Magnif. tuae excusans, meque ad ordinem lectionum, quem hisce adiunxi, remittens, ubi honestissimam vestri mentionem fecisse gloriabatur«. Haec ille. Quae vero insinuat de ordine praelectionum impresso unâque transmisso, e quibus isthic verbis DUNCANUS se purgare praesumit, ea sub titulo Philosophicarum praelectionum sic habent: »DUNCANUS LIDDELIUS Scotus D. publice proponit doctrinam sinuum et triangulorum, qua absoluta, theorias Planetarum, secundum hypothesin PTOLEMÆI et COPERNICI et illam mundani systematis hypothesin, quam describit TYCHO BRAHE lib. 2 de aethereis Phaenomenis.« Ista iste, egregia sane et honestissima de me mentio, imo vulpeculae potius dolus; cum enim sibi conscius sit, se meas hypotheses sibi apud alios clam venditasse, et sic plagium commisisse, cum publice non audeat idem facere, neque meas esse fateri vult, ne contradicat ijs, quae prius commentus est, ideoque generaliter et astute loquendo, dicit saltem eas hypotheses, quas ego libro illo secundo describo; potest enim aliquis etiam ab alio inventa describere, nec ob id sua esse. Eadem vafritie usus est in thematibus quibusdam anno 95 Helmstadij editis, ubi inter Parerga Mathematica (sic enim vocat et recte, nam vere Parerga tractat, et de re inperspecta nugatur) propositione secunda sic habet: »Cum tres discrepantes hypotheses sint, quibus apparentiae coelestes solvuntur et explicantur, quarum una est PTOLEMÆI, altera COPERNICI, tertia est illa, cuius meminit TYCHO BRAHE lib. de Cometa anni 77, dubitatur, an aliqua ex his omnibus diversa dari possit, deinde quaenam harum apparentijs magis congruat.« Vide quam sibi similis et hîc et istic, idque ob eandem, quam dixi, caussam; o! astutule et nasutule Scotule. At non satis recordatur, uti oportebat mendacem memorem esse. In intimatione, quam Decanus Facultatis Medicae in Academia Iulia FRANCISCUS PARCOVIUS, sub quo LIDDELIUS in Doctorem promovit, ... haec verba, se conscio et forte etiam praescribente, inserta esse, publiceque edita et affixa, quae postquam LIDDELIJ mentionem, utinam tam veram quam pomposam, fecisset, sic proloquitur: »Quod enim ad Mathesin attinet, non solum in veterum hypothesi bene versatus est, sed et recentiorem laboriosam et operosam COPERNICI hypothesin optime novit«, in qua quicquid consecutus sum, ipsi debere me ingenue fateor. Quin et aliam novam hypothesin, quam publice et privatim docuit, licet alterius nomine usurpetur, adinvenit, cuius rei multi eius discipuli clarissimum ei dant testimonium. Sed addo descriptum totius intimationis; misissem impressum exemplar, sed cum unicum saltem habeam, eo carere nequeo. Annon ibi satis aperte proditur DUNCANUM mea inventa sibi arrogare? Neque enim excusare se potest, quod se inscio haec a suo promotore ascripta sint; vel si sic, cur non inficiatus est atque se invito factum protestatus? cur se sic alienis plumis ornari cornicula ista passa est? Sed dispiciemus suo tempore Deo volente de his latius. Interea huius pusilli Scoti arrogantiam et insolentiam ex alto despiciemus. Si in viros cordatos et eruditos atque ipso longe meliores scurriliter debacchari et mea de caussa eos misellos asinos ingratissimosque cuculos vocitare, quod veritatem quaesiti non subticeant, perrexerit, efficiam ut publice plagij accusatus et convictus secundum ius luat, id est infamis fiat, nec amplius irritet crabrones. Tu interim pro te, quae vera et iusta nosti, meditare atque consigna, et si lubuerit, in uno vel altero quaternione in publicum ede, tui meique defensionis gratia, ut habeat iste biliosus Scotulus, quod ipsum mordeat atque remordeat, si possit, donec illi occludatur os. Si Doctor NICOLAUS CRAGIUS, in Dania Historicus, quem nosti, velit aperte fateri, quae hac de re novit, quod eum etiam libenter facturum spero, non longa erit disputatio, an LIDDELIUS istas hypotheses a me didicerit, an vero ego ab illo. Assidebat enim mensae in arce olim Uraniburgica idem Doctor, cum hasce hypotheses LIDDELIO, cui nunquam tale quid antea, ne per somnium quidem, in mentem venerat, aperui. Quin et ipsi Doctori NICOLAO, ob sinceram inter nos amicitiam, iam diu antea designationem earundem hypothesium in patenti charta, prout a me sedulo expetierat, concesseram, uti ipsemet non invite fatebitur, et quod omnium maxime rem arguit, ipsae Liddelianae ad me datae literae ipsiusque manu scriptae, fraudem et plagium eius testabuntur. de istulo nunc satis. Tu quid tui sit officij, facile absque me monitore nosti.

Carmina quaedam in mei gratiam a varijs conscripta addam, si ea denuo exarare tempus permiserit, sin minus, habebis alias. Interea tu etiam aliqua ulterius pro tua arguta vena meditare, et Caesaris in me atque atque ea quae tracto studia clementissimam benignitatem collauda.

Vale atque brevi rescribe.
Dabantur ex arce Caesarea Benachia sive Venetijs Bohemorum Anno 99 die 26. Septembris stylo renovato.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 187; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Alter plagiarius et Mastiges meus impurissima fera Ditmarsica ante paucas hebdomadas Praga se subduxit, deserta uxore, quam nuper duxerat, uti perhibent, meretricula, sive quod male sibi conscius esset, et poenas secundum leges metueret, quas etiam vix effugiet, sive quod alibi latitando nova ruminetur mendacia novasque calumnias, pro stabiliendis prioribus, uti fieri solet, sicque decuplo pluribus opus erit, sed obstruetur et illi, Deo volente, os, ita ut mallet facta infecta esse.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO DANIEL CRAMER.**

Greeting.

I wrote back to you, most renowned and learned Lord Doctor Cramer, a little before I left Wittenberg, which I suppose you received. But of my affairs — after, departing thence, I betook myself into Bohemia by the most clement mandate and summons of the most august Emperor — since it would be too long to narrate everything severally here, **I have had a copy made of my recent [letter] to our Holger Rosenkrantz, which contains a certain little history of what has befallen me here**, of which I make you partaker. Thence you will draw everything through its circumstances; for since the friendship between Holger and you is so close, he will by no means take it ill that I share a copy of his letter with you (yet to be held secret, and shown to none but secret friends). Wherefore of my affairs I add nothing here, only I give thanks to immortal God. And do you, and all the pious and upright, give thanks with me, that all has succeeded well and according to my prayer.

But there is another thing, concerning you in no small part, which I judged should not be hidden from you. When I was at Wittenberg, there had come thither a certain Danish student familiarly known to me, called **Bartold Ivari Mule**, who had come with a certain Swedish Baron, **Sten Bielke, my kinsman**; and when they conversed with me there for some days, it happened that Sten made mention of **Duncan the Scot** — for both of them had been a while at **Helmstedt** for study's sake, whence too they had come. I, soon adding [the matter], opened to that Baron, in Bartold's presence, **[Duncan's] plagiarism against me**; and when he wondered and as it were hesitated, I produced **your letter to Holger Rosenkrantz, written at length on this matter**, and gave it them to read. But I know not how it came about that, while that Danish student kept it overnight, he **silently made a copy for himself**, which, when he came to Helmstedt, **he showed to that little Scot**. How [Duncan] received it, I will report word for word from Bartold's own letter, which I got a few days ago: *"Then as for Doctor Cramer's letter, I showed it to Duncan, concealing, however, whence I got it. There the man began so to blame the impiety of the 'wretched little ass' (for so he slandered [Cramer]) that he called him 'a most ungrateful cuckoo toward his preceptor'; and at the same time, excusing himself to Your Magnificence, and referring me to the order of lectures which I append, where he boasted he had made most honourable mention of you."* So far he.

What he intimates about the **printed lecture-order**, sent along — by which words Duncan presumes to clear himself — runs thus, under the title of Philosophical lectures: *"**Duncan Liddel** the Scot, D[octor], publicly proposes the doctrine of sines and triangles; which finished, the theories of the Planets, according to the hypothesis of **Ptolemy** and **Copernicus**, and **that hypothesis of the world-system which Tycho Brahe describes in book 2 of the aethereal Phenomena**."* This [is] his — a fine and most honourable mention of me, forsooth; nay, rather a little fox's trick. For since he is conscious that **he secretly peddled my hypotheses to others as his own, and so committed plagiarism**, [and] since he dares not do the same publicly, nor will he admit they are mine (lest he contradict what he earlier fabricated), therefore, speaking generally and cunningly, he says only "those hypotheses which I describe in that second book" — for one can also describe another's inventions, without their being on that account his own. He used the same craft in certain theses published at Helmstedt in [15]95, where among "**Mathematical Parerga**" (so he calls them, and rightly, for he truly handles by-works, and trifles about a matter not grasped), in the second proposition he has: *"Since there are three discrepant hypotheses by which the celestial appearances are solved and explained — one of Ptolemy, another of Copernicus, the third that which Tycho Brahe mentions in his book on the Comet of '77 — it is doubted whether any other, different from all these, can be given; and then which of these agrees more with the appearances."* See how like himself both here and there, and for the same cause I have said; O cunning and sharp-nosed little Scot! But he does not remember enough that **a liar ought to have a good memory**. In **the announcement which Franz Parcovius, Dean of the Medical Faculty in the Academia Julia [Helmstedt], under whom Liddel was promoted to Doctor**, [posted] — these words, with [Liddel's] knowledge, and perhaps even at his dictation, were inserted, and publicly published and posted; which, after making mention of Liddel (would it were as true as it is pompous), speaks thus: *"For as to Mathematics, he is not only well versed in the ancients' hypothesis, but knows excellently the more recent, laborious, and elaborate hypothesis of Copernicus"* — in which "whatever I have attained, I frankly confess I owe to him. Moreover **he discovered another new hypothesis, which he taught publicly and privately, though it is usurped under another's name; of which thing many of his disciples give him the clearest testimony.**" But I add a copy of the whole announcement; I would have sent the printed copy, but since I have only one, I cannot do without it. **Is it not there openly betrayed that Duncan arrogates my inventions to himself?** For he cannot excuse himself that these things were ascribed by his promoter without his knowledge; or, if so, why did he not deny it, and protest it was done against his will? Why did that little crow let itself be so adorned with others' feathers? But we shall look into these things more amply in time, God willing. Meanwhile we shall look down from on high upon this little Scot's arrogance and insolence. If he goes on scurrilously raving against sensible and learned men far better than himself, and on my account calling them "wretched asses" and "most ungrateful cuckoos" — because they do not keep silent the truth they are asked — **I will bring it about that, publicly accused and convicted of plagiarism, he pay according to the law — that is, become infamous** — and no longer provoke the hornets. You, meanwhile, meditate and set down for yourself what you know to be true and just; and if you please, **publish it, in a quaternion or two, in defence of yourself and me**, that this bilious little Scot may have something to bite and bite back at, if he can — until his mouth is shut.

**If Doctor Nicolaus Cragius [Niels Krag], the Historian in Denmark, whom you know, will openly confess what he knows of this matter — which I hope he will gladly do — there will be no long dispute whether Liddel learned those hypotheses from me, or I from him.** For that same Doctor was sitting at table, in the once-Uraniborg castle, **when I opened these hypotheses to Liddel — to whom never anything of the sort had before come into mind, not even in a dream.** Moreover, to Doctor Niels himself, for the sincere friendship between us, I had long before granted **a designation of these same hypotheses on an open sheet, as he had diligently sought from me** — as he himself will not unwillingly confess; and, what most of all proves the matter, **Liddel's own letters to me, written in his own hand, will testify to his fraud and plagiarism.** Of the little fellow, enough now. You easily know your own duty without my prompting.

Some poems written for me by various [hands] I will add, if time permit me to copy them out anew; if not, you shall have them another time. Meanwhile do you too meditate something further, by your sharp vein, and praise the Emperor's most clement kindness toward me and the studies I pursue.

Farewell, and write back shortly.
Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, or the Venice of the Bohemians, the year [15]99, the 26th day of September, by the renewed [New] style.


*[Postscript:]* My other plagiarist and tormentor [Mastiges], that most impure Dithmarsian beast [Ursus], a few weeks ago withdrew himself from Prague, having deserted the wife — a little harlot, as they report — whom he had lately married: whether because he was ill-conscious to himself, and feared the penalties according to the laws (which he will scarcely escape), or because, lurking elsewhere, he is ruminating new lies and new calumnies to prop up the former ones (as is wont to happen), and so ten times more will be needed — but his mouth too will be stopped, God willing, so that he would rather his deeds were undone.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Daniel Cramer** (1568–1637), the Pomeranian theologian-poet and Tycho's polemical ally (cf. brahe-t_16000401001), here enlisted against Liddel as later against Craig/Ursus.
- **Significance — the Duncan Liddel plagiarism dossier (the corpus's fullest statement of that dispute).** This letter assembles Tycho's whole case against **Duncan Liddel (1561–1613)**, the Scottish mathematician-physician at **Helmstedt (Academia Julia)**, for **claiming the Tychonic geo-heliocentric world-system as his own**. (It fixes the "Duncan" of brahe-t_16000401001 — with Niels Krag's testimony — as **Duncan Liddel**.) The evidence Tycho marshals:
 - **The Bartold Mule episode.** At Wittenberg, the Danish student **Bartold Ivari Mule**, travelling with **Sten Bielke** (a Swedish baron, Tycho's kinsman), heard Tycho's charge and read **Cramer's letter to Holger Rosenkrantz**; he secretly copied it and showed it to Liddel at Helmstedt — whose contemptuous reaction (calling Cramer "a wretched ass," "an ungrateful cuckoo") Tycho quotes from Mule's letter.
 - **Liddel's evasive "honourable mention."** His **printed lecture-catalogue** ("the planetary theories according to Ptolemy, Copernicus, and **that hypothesis which Tycho Brahe describes in book 2 of the aethereal Phenomena**") and his **1595 Helmstedt theses ("Mathematical Parerga," prop. 2)** both name Tycho's system only *generally* — a "fox's trick," Tycho says, to avoid admitting he had peddled it as his own.
 - **The damning promotion-notice.** The doctoral announcement by Dean **Franz Parcovius**, "with Liddel's knowledge and perhaps dictation," claims **Liddel "discovered another new hypothesis … though it is usurped under another's name"** — i.e. publicly crediting Liddel with the Tychonic system. Tycho: "Is it not openly betrayed that Duncan arrogates my inventions?"
 - **The witnesses.** **Niels Krag (Nicolaus Cragius)**, the Danish royal historian, **sat at Tycho's Uraniborg table when Tycho revealed the hypotheses to Liddel** — "to whom never had such a thing come into mind, not even in a dream"; Tycho had also given Krag **a diagram of the system on an open sheet**. And **Liddel's own letters** will prove the plagiarism. (Krag's verbatim testimony is quoted in brahe-t_16000401001.)
 - **The threat and the commission.** Tycho threatens to have Liddel **"publicly accused and convicted of plagiarism … become infamous"**; he asks Cramer to **publish a defence (a quaternion or two)**.
- **Cross-references.** The master document of the **Duncan Liddel priority dispute** — pair with brahe-t_16000401001 (the Niels Krag testimony) and route alongside the parallel **Ursus** dispute (brahe-t_16000911001 etc.). "Book 2 of the aethereal Phenomena" / "book on the Comet of '77" = Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (1588), where the geo-heliocentric system was first published.
- **Persons & places named.** Daniel Cramer; **Holger Rosenkrantz** (the shared letter); **Bartold Ivari Mule**; **Sten Bielke**; **Duncan Liddel**; **Franz Parcovius** (Helmstedt medical dean); **Niels Krag (Nicolaus Cragius)**; **Ptolemy, Copernicus**; **Rudolf II**. Places: **Benátky** ("Venice of the Bohemians"), **Wittenberg**, **Helmstedt** (Academia Julia), **Hven/Uraniborg**, Denmark.
- **Place/calendar.** Source dateline *ex arce Caesarea Benachia sive Venetijs Bohemorum … die 26. Septembris **stylo renovato*** → **Benátky, 26 September 1599 [N.S.]**. The **catalogue label's "Wittenberg" is a location error** (contradicted by the dateline); led with the source and flagged for review of the catalogue date.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript reporting Ursus had fled Prague, restored from Dreyer VIII p.187 (appended to the Tycho→Cramer letter of 16/26 Sept 1599; dropped by the working transcription).
- **Correction.** Postscript closing idiom corrected from 'facta insecta esse' to 'facta infecta esse' per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p.187 (the classical tag 'facta infecta' = deeds made undone); the English translation was already correct and required no change.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the whole letter, including the postscript marked 'restored from Dreyer', visually against Dreyer TBOO VIII pp. 184-187, read within the supplied 183-188 extract (p.183 is the tail of a prior Tycho-to-Longomontanus letter, p.188 the continuation of the next Tycho-to-Scaliger letter, both checked to confirm the boundary). Verified the whole Bartold Ivari Mule / Sten Bielke / Duncan Liddel plagiarism narrative word for word, including the two embedded quotations (Bartold's letter, and Duncan's 1595 Helmstedt 'Parerga Mathematica' theses) and the Franciscus Parcovius encomium, plus the names Niels Krag/Cragius, Franciscus Parcovius, Helmstedt/Helmstadium — all match Dreyer exactly. Gave particular scrutiny to the embedded first-person clause on p.186, 'in qua quicquid consecutus sum, ipsi debere me ingenue fateor', since an abrupt person-shift there is exactly the shape of the process's known pronoun-flip defect (a self-boast turned into a claim about Tycho): the transcribed original matches Dreyer verbatim at this point, and the English preserves the same ambiguous person-shift already present in the Latin (Parcovius's encomium itself lurches from third person to an embedded first-person avowal and back) rather than introducing a new inversion — so this is not counted as a translator-introduced defect. Confirmed the restored postscript (the Ursus/'Mastiges' paragraph) is genuinely present on Dreyer p.187 and correctly reinstated. One text error found, in the postscript's closing words ('insecta' for Dreyer's 'infecta'); does not affect the English, which already carries the correct sense. No fabrication, omission, or sense-changing mistranslation found.

**1 defect found:**
- **text error** (low). Our source Latin misprints the classical idiom 'facta infecta' (deeds made undone — from the Roman-comedy tag 'quod factum infectum fieri nequit') as the nonsensical 'facta insecta'; Dreyer p.187 reads 'infecta'. The published English already renders the correct sense ('his deeds were undone'), so the translation itself is not at fault — only our stored the transcribed original is corrupted. Dreyer prints: *ita ut mallet facta infecta eße*.

**Repaired.** Verified the single text error against the Dreyer page image (TBOO VIII p.187, postscript, lines 8-10), read visually in the extract PDF. The plate clearly shows 'facta infecta eße', confirming the audit's claim. Only the Latin postscript was touched; nothing else in the letter was altered.

text.original:
DEN ERENUESTEN, ACHTBARN VND WOLWEISEN HERRNN N. N., BURGERMAISTERN VND RATHMANNEN DER LÖBLICHENN STADTT HAMBURG, MEINEN JNSONDERN GUNSTIGENN HERRN VND GUTTEN FREUNDEN.

ERENUESTE, achtbare, wolweise, erbare, jnsondere gunstige herrnn vnnd gutte freund, denselbenn sein mein gantz geflissene jederzeitt willige dienst möglichem vleiß nach zuuor. Vnnd kan E.E. vnnd W.W. freindtlicher meinung zuuerstehenn gebenn jch nit vnterlassenn, das, nachdem ich ein gantzes jar nahe bey ewer hoch- vnd weitberumpten stadtt Hamburg auf dem Rantzouischenn hauß Wandesbeck, wie E.E. vnd W.W. bewust, gewonet, von jhrer röm: kay: mt:, vnserem allergnedigstenn herrn zum andernmal an den kaiserlichenn hoff von Wittenberg ab jch bin allergnedigst erfordert wordenn, vnnd, als jch alda meiner gelegenheitt nach gehorsamlich compariret, allen kaiserlichenn gnedigenn willenn vnd bewogenheitt vntertäniglichenn gespuret vnnd mit allermildesten prouision allergnedigst versorget wordenn. Als aber jhre röm: kay: mt: vernommenn, das jch noch etzliche von meinenn astronomischenn instrumenten, die so groß wehrenn, das man sy nit auf der axs furenn könne, jm königreich Dennemarck, meinem liebenn vaterlandt, nebenn etzlichenn andern sachen hinderlassenn hett, jst jhr. röm: kay: mt: allergnedigst gesonnenn vnnd mir thun befehlenn, solches alles nebenn dem, so jch noch zu Magdenburg, alher jn jhr königreich Behmen fur dem winter furderlichst zuebringenn. Zue besserem fortgang aber dessenn hatt jhr. röm: kay: mt: ein schraibenn an E.E. vnd W.W., sowol an einen erbarn rath der stadt Magdenburg, mir allergnedigst hieuon zuestellen vnd an dieselbigen abgehenn lassenn, welches an E.E. vnd W.W., beynebenn jch denselbigenn thue zueschickenn, nit zweifelnde, E.E. vnd W.W. werdenn hierin jhr röm: kay: mt: gehorsamlichenn wilfahrenn vnd mit schiff, sowol anderer gelegenheit, wie es dan meine leutte anzeigenn werdenn, wan die sachenn auß Dennemarck alda ankommenn, zu prouidiren vnd furderlichenn sein, damit, ehe die Elb zufreuret, alles mag wol verwahret hierauf, so weitt als sy schifreich ist, gebracht werdenn. Hieran geschiet vnd thuenn E.E. vnd W.W. zuforderst jhr. röm: kay: mt:, vnserm allergnedigstenn herren, ein allergnedigstes sonders vnd angenehms wolgefallenn, auch mir vnd dem astronomischen werck, so jch vorhabe, gutte promotion, welche jch bey jhr. kay: mt: wil zuruhmenn wissenn, vnnd vmb E.E. vnd W.W., welche jch hiemit Gott jnn seinenn schutz vnd schirm befohlenn habenn wil, hinwiderumb nach meinem vermögenn altzeit geflissenn sein zuuerdienen.

Datiret auf dem kayserlichenn schloß Bennatka, am 29 tag septembris stylo nouo, anno 1599.
Ewer E.E. vnd W.W. altzait freindtwilliger
Tycho Brahe
mitt eigen handtt.
text.english:
**To the honourable, worshipful, and right-wise Lords N. N., Burgomasters and Councillors of the praiseworthy city of Hamburg, my especially favourable Lords and good friends.**

Honourable, worshipful, right-wise, worthy, especially favourable Lords and good friends: to the same [be] my wholly assiduous, ever-willing service, according to my utmost diligence, beforehand. And I cannot omit to give Your Honours and Wisdoms amicably to understand that, after I had dwelt a whole year near your high- and far-famed city of Hamburg, at the Rantzau house of Wandsbek — as Your Honours and Wisdoms know — I was, for the second time, most graciously summoned by His Roman Imperial Majesty, our most gracious Lord, to the imperial court, away from Wittenberg; and when I had there obediently presented myself, according to my circumstances, I humbly met with every imperial gracious good will and favour, and was most graciously provided for with a most bountiful provision [stipend]. But when His Roman Imperial Majesty learned that I had left behind, in the kingdom of Denmark, my dear fatherland, some of my astronomical instruments — which were so large that they could not be carried upon the axle [by wagon] — together with certain other things, His Roman Imperial Majesty is most graciously minded, and commands me, to bring all this, together with what I [have] still at Magdeburg, hither into his kingdom of Bohemia, with all dispatch before the winter. And for the better furtherance of this, His Roman Imperial Majesty has most graciously had a letter [addressed] to Your Honours and Wisdoms, as well as to the worthy Council of the city of Magdeburg, delivered to me hereupon, and dispatched to the same; which [letter] to Your Honours and Wisdoms I herewith send on to you — not doubting that Your Honours and Wisdoms will herein obediently comply with His Roman Imperial Majesty, and will furnish ship as well as other means (as my people will then indicate, when the things from Denmark arrive there), and be furthering [the matter], so that, before the Elbe freezes over, everything may be brought up [the river] hither, well secured, as far as it is navigable. In this Your Honours and Wisdoms do, first and foremost, a most gracious, special, and welcome pleasure to His Roman Imperial Majesty, our most gracious Lord; and also, to me and to the astronomical work which I have in hand, a good furtherance — which I shall know how to commend before His Imperial Majesty; and toward Your Honours and Wisdoms — whom I herewith will have commended to God's protection and shelter — I will in return, according to my ability, be ever assiduous to deserve well.

Dated at the imperial castle of Benátky, the 29th day of September, New Style, in the year 1599.
Your Honours' and Wisdoms' ever friend-willing
Tycho Brahe,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipients.** The **Burgomasters and Council (Senate) of the city of Hamburg** — addressed collectively (*N. N.* = *nomina nominanda*, the clerk's placeholder for the individual names), in the high civic register *E.E. vnd W.W.* (*Ehrenveste und Wohlweise*, "Your Honours and Wisdoms"). The MS survives in the **Hamburg Staatsarchiv** among the *Transito- und Porto-franco* (transit / toll-exemption) papers — the apt file for a freight-passage request.
- **The matter — moving Tycho's instruments to Bohemia.** A **logistics letter of the first importance for the material history of Tycho's instruments.** Having dwelt a year at **Wandsbek** (the Rantzau house near Hamburg) and then been summoned a *second time* by **Rudolf II** to the imperial court (from Wittenberg), and provided with a generous stipend, Tycho now executes the Emperor's command to bring to **Bohemia, before winter,** the great **astronomical instruments left in Denmark** — "so large that they could not be carried on the axle [by wagon]" — together with other goods still lying at **Magdeburg**. He forwards the **imperial letters** that Rudolf had addressed to the Hamburg and Magdeburg councils, asking Hamburg to provide **ship and other means** to carry everything **up the Elbe, as far as it is navigable, before the river freezes**.
- **The attached inventory slip (witness note) — what actually arrived.** The MS bears the endorsement *Lectum in senatu 21. April a:o 1600* ("read in the senate, 21 April 1600") and an attached slip listing the goods *"Van Tychone Braden"* that **reached Hamburg on 22 April 1600**: *10 kasten [crates/baskets], 1 kiste [chest], ein halbe Tonne [half-barrel], ein Achtendel [eighth-barrel], 14 Tonnen "karzen", 2 große Eisen [large irons], 4 eiserne Kachelöfen [iron tiled-stoves], 3 bleierne Kessel [lead kettles/cauldrons], 1 Blasebalg [bellows], 1 kleines Feldbett [small field-bed], 1 großes "tweklafftiges" Eisen mit einem runden Bauche* [one large two-fathom iron with a round belly]. The lead cauldrons, bellows and iron stoves point to Tycho's **alchemical/metallurgical apparatus** as well as the instruments; the *"großes zweiklaftiges Eisen mit rundem Bauche"* is plausibly a major instrument component or its iron mounting. This is direct documentary evidence of the **April 1600 transit of Tycho's effects through Hamburg** toward Prague.
- **Dating crux (this chapter's convention — flagged, resolved by the source).** The letter's own dateline reads **"am 29 tag septembris stylo novo, anno 1599"** — **29 September 1599, New Style** — and the edition identifier (15990929001) agrees. The edition's label field, however, reads *"1599. 27. januar n.s. Benatky"*; this **January date is a catalogue error** and is rejected in favour of the as-written dateline, by this chapter's convention (lead with the source's own date). The "before the winter / before the Elbe freezes" urgency fits a **late-September** letter, not a January one. The seven-month gap to the senate's reading (*lectum 21 April 1600*) reflects the slow assembling and shipment of the goods from Denmark and Magdeburg: the covering letter and imperial mandates were presented when the freight at last came up the Elbe in spring 1600. (That the goods could not in fact be moved "before the winter" of 1599/1600, but only in April 1600, is consistent with — not contradicted by — the September dateline.)
- **Persons/places named.** Rudolf II (*röm. kay. Mt.*); the councils of **Hamburg** and **Magdeburg**; **Wandsbek** (the Rantzau house); **Wittenberg**; **Magdeburg**; the kingdoms of **Denmark** and **Bohemia**; the **Elbe**.
- **Register / formulae.** Subscription *mit eigen Hand* (= *manu propria*); the autograph attestation. Imperial-style honorifics (*allergnedigst, allermildeste Provision*) throughout.
- **Correction.** Corrected the German: "schüutz" restored to Dreyer's "schutz" (TBOO XIV p.154).

text.original:
MAGNIFICO ET NOBILISSIMO VIRO, D. TYCHONI BRAHE, DOMINO IN KNUDSTORP, MATHEMATICO PRÆSTANTISSIMO, DOMINO AC AMICO S. HONORANDO.
S.

magnifice et nobilissime vir, domine ac amice honorande. Literas tuas Venetijs Bohemorum 28 septemb. datas summa cum voluptate perlegi, cum quod de tua valetudine, tum et quo in loco T. M. subsistat, me certiorem fecerint. Literæ s. cæs. m:tis, domini nostri clementiss., quarum mentionem T. M. facit, senatui nostro non sunt exhibitæ, forsitan incuria tuorum neglectæ; quamprimum autem allatæ et in senatu lectæ fuerint, ex ijsque intellexero, quid tua causa s. cæs. m:tas fieri velit, lubens, quantum in me erit, negotium promouebo. Simonem a Petkum, ut de singulis, quæ tua scire interest, te certiorem reddat, admonui, qui copiose se rescripturum recepit. Ferramenta Wandesburgi relicta quod attinet, existimo de ijs nihil certi statui posse, antequam Bredo Ranzouius ad tuas responderit. His paucis T. M. æterni Dei tutelæ commendo, qui eandem diutiss: incolumem conseruet.

Dabantur Hamburgj 8 octob. a:o 1599.
Mag:æ T. studiosiss:
Vinc. Moller L.
text.english:
**To the magnificent and most noble man, Master Tycho Brahe, Lord in Knudstrup, most outstanding Mathematician, his lord and friend to be honoured. Greeting.**
Greeting.

Magnificent and most noble man, lord and friend to be honoured. Your letter, dated at the Venice of the Bohemians [Benátky] on 28 September, I read through with the greatest pleasure, since it made me more certain both about your health and in what place Your Magnificence is residing. The letters of His Sacred Imperial Majesty, our most clement lord, of which Your Magnificence makes mention, have not been presented to our Senate — perhaps neglected through the carelessness of your people; but as soon as they have been brought and read in the Senate, and I have understood from them what His Sacred Imperial Majesty wishes done on your behalf, I will gladly, as much as shall be in me, promote the business. I have admonished Simon von Petkum to make you more certain about the particulars which it concerns you to know, and he has undertaken to write back to you copiously. As regards the ironwork [the iron instruments/tools] left at Wandsbek, I judge that nothing certain can be settled about them before Breide Rantzau has replied to your [letter]. With these few [words] I commend Your Magnificence to the protection of the eternal God, who may preserve you safe as long as possible.

Given at Hamburg, 8 October, in the year 1599.
Most devoted to Your Magnificence,
Vincent Moller, L[icentiate].

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Vincent Moller** (the Elder, 1527–1599/1600), a Hamburg patrician and Senate figure (the *L.* after his name = *Licentiatus* in law); Tycho's local contact during and after his stay near Hamburg. He acts here as Tycho's intermediary with the **Hamburg Senate** over imperial letters concerning Tycho's affairs.
- ***Venetijs Bohemorum*** — "at the Venice of the Bohemians," a learned by-name for **Benátky nad Jizerou** (Czech *Benátky* = "Venice"), Tycho's residence from 1599; rendered with the gloss. Tycho's incoming letter was dated there 28 September.
- ***Literae s. caes. m:tis*** = letters of **His Sacred Imperial Majesty** (Rudolf II) on Tycho's behalf, which had not reached the Hamburg Senate. *Simon a Petkum* = **Simon von Petkum** (Peckius), a diplomat/agent who would write Tycho the particulars. *Bredo Ranzouius* = **Breide Rantzau** (1556–1618), the Holstein noble (governor of the Rantzau lands) under whom the *Wandsbek* matter fell.
- ***Ferramenta Wandesburgi relicta*** — "the ironwork left at **Wandsbek**": Tycho's heavy **iron instruments/fittings** left behind at Wandsbek (where he had lodged 1597–98 at Heinrich Rantzau's castle) when he moved on; their fate awaited Breide Rantzau's reply. (*Ferramenta* = iron tools/instruments; rendered with the gloss.)
- **⚠ Date.** The dateline reads *Hamburgj 8 octob. a:o 1599* = **8 October 1599**; the identifier (…10 08…) agrees. The edition catalogues it under **8 September** — the one-month discrepancy is reproduced, not reconciled; the header follows the as-written **8 October**. Hamburg (Lutheran) = **Old Style**.

text.original:
ERLLIIG OCH WELBYRDIG MAND TTYGE BRAHE TTILL KNUDSTRUP, MYNN ALLERKIERISTE BRODER, GANSKE HULLELIGEN OCH WENLIGENN THILLSKREUIT.

MYNN allerkieristhe broder, Gudtt allmectigsthe were nu och alltidtt hos eder och beuare eder nadelig och well fraa alltt dett, som eder kann were skadeligtt till liff eller siell, och Gud wnde migh altid att spørge, att dett maa gaa eder løkelig och well i alle maade, dett will iegh troligen ønske aff Gudtt. M. a. k. broder, giffuer iegh eder ganske wenligen advide, att iegh er nu paa reyssen medtt min Ttaghe, och fulde iegh hanem først till Hadersløff, och der iegh kom did, daa war Gertt och Ttalle affdragen hen ttill en aff deris garde, heder Lindvid, ny mille fra Harsløff, hor hand lader byghe; saa skreff di mig ttill, at jegh wille medtt Ttage kome did ttill dem och saa følgis med dem till Briedenburch, som er paa vij mille ner Hamburigh, saa ville Gertt forhøre om selskaff, som Ttage kune kome i følge medt ttill Brunsvigh och sa ud ttil Bassell, som ieg vil haa ham henn. Saa drogh jeg daa ttill denem ttill dett Lindvid, och war der i ttho eller ttre dage, och fulle denem saa hid ttill Briedenburgh och har werid her i 6 daghe, och giør di migh altt dett gode di kan, sa ieg er komen ttill rett gode wener her, som giør mig altt gott, Gudtt were louitt, och blir jeg her enu ttill paa mandagh, for da drager Gertt ttill Kill pa en ricksdagh, och systher drager ttill Harsløff igen, for di wentter kongenn did strax mod s. Mortens dagh, for der skall da were en richsdag ttill Flensburgh, hor kongen will were paa dentid. Saa actter jeg met Guds hielp att drage herfraa med Ttage ttill Wandersbeck wid Hamborig, och der were en 3 eler 4 dage och forhøre om gott selskaff, som Ttage kan komme i følge med ttill Brunsuigh, Gud giue ttill løcke.

Titans skriuer Mikell hade werid paa Hadersløff och mentt att fundet mig der for en 3 uger sinn, och der ieg ike da war der, drog han till Horssens, och fik mor fru Anne breuene till mig, och hun sene dem ouer till Køffuenhaffn, och der di kom did, war jeg aff dragen, saa sene jeg it bud fra Koling och ouer till Køffuenhaffn efftter same breff, och dett bud kom nu hid ttill mig ttill Briedenburg i andags gardtt, och fick iegh med dett bud eders søns Ttygis skriffuelsse, hor aff iegh formerker, att hand er i Køffuenhaffn nu och haffuer breff ttil mig fraa eder, huilkett hand ike kune nu sene mig, men ville sielff anttvorde mig dett, om jegh kom ttil Køuenhaffn ingen enn 3 ugher; ellers will hand faa dochter Nils Krag breuene, nar hand drager henn; och sener hand mig tthu breffue, itt till min broder Knud, och itt ttill min systher Margrette, huilke jeg strax will sende denem; och skriuer dochter Nils mig nogitt till om eders lieglighet, hor aff jeg formerker, att i lider nu rett well, Gud were loffuitt, och haffuer faid itt hus aff kiesserenn, och mer end 4000 gyllen ttill arlligh penge aff kiesseren; och brød jeg min systher Margrettis breff op och wille och der aff forfare, hor eder lide, di jeg har lenge lengtist efftther bud fra eder, sin i er komen ttill Pragh; saa er dett mig i sanhedtt saa rett hierttelig kiertt, att jegh forfarer, att dett gaer eder saa well, Gud were loffuitt, att i har funditt en plads, som i kan haa rolighedtt, och folk kann skøn paa eder, och holle aff eders handell, och giøre eder gott.

Jegh hade ttillforn hørtt nogitt aff dette, di dett bleff dochter Nils skreuit till aff Ttyskland, doch huem jegh sagde dett for, ville ike ttro dett, saa jeg wiste dett doch ike wist, førend jeg kom till Gertt Ranszuo; hand sagde mig, ad dett war vist, och ad hand hade selff nyligen skreuitt eder till, och kan i ike ttro, hor kiertt dett er bade ham och Ttalle, ad det gar eder well, y sandhed, jeg kan merkett, att det er dem bade rett kiertt; i hor det er gan til met det snak, der var sagd for eder, daa har det wertt en misforstand, dy har hatt derom, di Ttale er jer och rett god, des wid jegh wist; ieg har formerktt bade aff dem och aff Gerttis søster, at fru Kiersten, hans moder, er eder saa god och forttryder sa hartt, huad di har giortt jer i Danmark, och adtt hun ttaker eder for hinis kintt Lisebett, y har hiolpidtt, der ttal hun saa megitt om; saa har jegh nu derfor skreffuitt hinde ttill och ttakett hine saa for altt det gode, hun har beuist eder, och er ier wen sa god, och derhos lader hine wide, huad ttinder jegh har nu sportt om eder, och ad eders søn er i Køffuenhaffn efftter di instrumenter, som enu war ttilbaghe. Jegh hauer i disse daghe laditt Gertt, sett dett breff, som i hade skreuitt kongen til och huad suar i fik derpaa, jegh har selff lest dett for ham och ttyd ham meningen derpaa, sa Ttalle hørdett, di forstod dem well derpaa; saa lod jeg ham och se det lile breff, som kiesserens canzeller hade skreuitt eder till.

Jegh var y sist i ttall medtt Mercurius i Skane paa Lanskrune; daa spore hand migh om eder, daa sagde ieg, att jegh hobtist, adtt dett gik eder well, och lod ham saa lesse den same lile copii, som den romiske canzeler hade skreuitt; daa sagde hand, det war gott, och war ham kertt, ad det gik jer well; och litt der efftter sagde han mig nogen tiner om kiesseren, som mig ike behagitt; daa suarid jeg, det kune bli gott eligvell, i hade andre go vener der i haffuidtt; sa sad hand atter litt, saa kom hand med end it snak och sagde, tto aff di, som war eders beste vener der aff kiesserens rad, di war affsaatt; daa mente ieg dett kun endaa bli gott; dett ser jeg gierne, sagde handtt. Dett war saa smok snak, vi hade, och jegh forstod det saa well. Min bror Jørgen war och der, han spore mig sa flitig om eder och ønskett saa, att altting kune gaa well for eder der wde.

Nu ttenker jeg well, ad di nu i Køffuenhaffn ttill dene heredagh for besken att wide om eders hanell. M. a. k. broder, nu att skriffue nogitt om Titan, saa har hand hafft en febris i 3 uger, doch hobis jeg met Guds hielp, att dett er nu gott igen med ham. Dett synis som denn Hanns Ernst will ike gaa rett om medtt ham; Erich har lertt ham consten, och der war giortt hanell melem dem, adtt huem di skulle lere consten, der skull di bade were om, och bade were lige guode y huad penge di for derfore; nu hade di forskreuen nogenn folk, som di skall haa penge aff, nu wille Hans Ernst enne haa di penghe; och har hand och skreuit kiesseren till och ttilbøditt ham consten, och wille ike lade Erich wide der aff; doch Erich hobis hand will kome ham for; ieg ttenker, att Erich will sielff ttill kiesserenn; och wid jeg wist, att Erich har consten wist, och hade handtt ttilbøditt wor konge denn, men hand ville ingen suar skriffue der paa, men war kun spodsch der offuer, och hade Hans Ernst och skreuitt kongenn ttill siden och begertt, at han ville lade Erich bekome suar, hor aff jegh sener eder enn copii, di jeg lod selff anttvore kongen dett breff med sekreteren, men handtt wille inted suare der till, for di har nu giortt ham her altt huad di kune; nu er di ttillfris medtt ham, och lader som di wid intid aff huad di ttilforn har giortt, di Erich hade erindrid kongen nogit derom i sin suplicatz. Nu Gud almectigsthe hielpe well och giøre dett engang bedre for os. Jeg hade skreuitt Erich ttill, ad han ville møde mig istes vid Harsløff, om han war her nogenstes i egnen, sa kune hand da ike møde mig der; nu har ieg skreuitt ham ttill, om han vile kome hid ttil mig eler til Hamburig eller ttil Lüneburg eller hor han will, daa will jeg møde ham och ttalle med ham, før jegh drar her aff egnen, och har jeg latt itt bud løffuid ud ttill ham her fraa och wentter dett igen om en 3 eler 4 dage; dersom hand will møde migh her ittstes, da vill jeg bie ham, ellers vill jeg met Guds hielp følge Ttage till Brunsuigh, saa er det kun en dags reysse ttill dett Kelbna. Dersom hand holler hus, sa vill jeg drage did till ham, di jegh ma enelig ttalle med ham, men jeg er saa ner ham, med Guds hielp, och wide hor det er met hans hanell. Gud giffue wos løcke och radtt, ad wij motte och faa nogen godtt lieglighedtt engangh.

M. a. k. broder, nu om min Ttage, saa acter jeg att lade ham drage till Bassell och bli der itt aar; dochter Nils har skreuitt met ham till den docter Greneus der, Sten Bille har och skreuitt enn dochter till, er den andens broder, att di vell forhielpe Ttage till dett beste. Erich har skreuitt mig ttill, att ham syntist, att det wor best, att Ttage bleff till Hiedellbierg først itt aar och lerde sprogitt, att hand ike skulle først lere dett sleme suisisch sprog ttill Bassell, men ieg will enu se dett ann, før ieg slutter dett, hor han skall were, di han kan vell och lere god ttysk til Bassel; blir det ike forsnartt forkoltt att feris, da skall hand drage ttill Bassell, di den haffhanell, der er ttill Hiedelbierg, hauer ike migh; nar han nu komer did, som hand først skal vere, sa skall hand strax skriffue eder ttill; saa ttror jeg eder saa vell, att i skriuer for ham ttil di lerde paa det sted, att di vill fordre ham till dett besthe. Gud almectigste beuare ham well, i hor hand komer, och senne ham well hiem till mig ighenn.

M. a. k. broder, jeg ttenker min moder har vell nu faid eders skriuelsse, der blir hun gladtt vid, di hun war nu saa omhygelig for jer, sin i war dragen till kiesseren. Jeg sener jer itt breff, Henrich Romell skreff mig ttill om di bøgher. Jeg drager till Fusing til min søster fra Harsløff, nar jeg komer did igen, di hun har begert det aff migh; hinis søner er nu dragen y gardenn. Jeg skriuer nu dette breff her och sener dett ttill Køffuenhaffn, och hobis, att dett komer der førend eders Ttyche drager derfraa; hade jeg nu bekomid huis i har skreuitt mig till, dett hade jegh gierne seett, men jeg skal skriff efftter dett. M. a. k. broder, saa wid jegh nu intet syneligtt mer att skriffue eder ttill, men i skall altid finde mig for eders hulle systher, der altid gierne will giøre huis jeg wid eder kiertt er, och hobis wi finis well engang, Gud giue wy maa findis glade och helbredtt. Och will nu och altid haffue eder Gud allmectigste beffallidtt, bade till siell och liff, med all løcke och welfartt. Lader Giertt och Ttalle och min Ttaghe helsse eder medtt manghe m. guode netther; giører well och siger Kirsten och eders børn och alle eders guode wener (huilke ocssa ere mine) manghe m. guode netter paa minne wegnne.

Datum Briedenburgh denn 24. october 1599.
Sophia Brahe Ottis datter.
text.english:
**To the honest and well-born man Tyge Brahe of Knudstrup, my dearest brother, quite lovingly and friendlily written.**

My dearest brother, may God Almighty be with you now and always, and keep you graciously and well from all that can be harmful to you, in body or soul; and may God grant me always to hear that it may go happily and well with you in every way — that I faithfully wish from God. My dear kind brother, I give you quite friendlily to know **that I am now on the journey with my Tage**; and I first accompanied him to **Haderslev**; and when I came there, **Gert and Talle [Rantzau] had moved off to one of their estates, called Lindewedel** [Lindved], nine miles from Haderslev, where he is building; so they wrote me that I should come with Tage there to them, and then accompany them to **Breitenburg, which is within 7 miles of Hamburg** — [where] Gert would inquire about a company [a travelling party] that Tage could join, to go to **Brunswick and so out to Basel, where I want him**. So I then went to them, to Lindewedel, and was there two or three days, and accompanied them hither to Breitenburg, and have been here 6 days; and they do me all the good they can, so that I have come to right good friends here, who do me all good, God be praised. And I shall stay here yet until Monday, for then Gert goes to **Kiel** for a Diet, and sister goes back to Haderslev — for they expect the King there soon, toward **St. Martin's day [11 Nov]**, for there shall then be a Diet at **Flensburg**, where the King will be at that time. So I intend, with God's help, to go hence with Tage to **Wandsbek by Hamburg**, and be there 3 or 4 days, and inquire about good company that Tage can join to Brunswick. God grant good luck.

**Titan's** secretary **Mikell** had been at Haderslev, and thought to have found me there about 3 weeks ago; and since I was not there then, he went to **Horsens**, and **mother Lady Anne** got the letters to me, and she sent them over to **Copenhagen**; and when they came there, I had departed; so I sent a messenger from **Kolding** over to Copenhagen for the same letters, and that messenger now came hither to me at Breitenburg the day before yesterday; and I got, with that messenger, **your son Tyge's letter**, from which I perceive that he is in Copenhagen now, and has a letter for me from you — which he could not now send me, but would deliver it to me himself, if I came to Copenhagen within 3 weeks; otherwise he will give **Doctor Niels Krag** the letters when he travels [thither]. And he sends me two letters, one to my brother **Knud**, and one to my sister **Margrette**, which I will send them at once. And Doctor Niels writes me something about your situation, from which I perceive that **you now fare right well, God be praised, and have got a house from the Emperor, and more than 4000 gulden in yearly money from the Emperor**; and I broke open my sister Margrette's letter, and would also learn from it how you fare, for I have long longed for word from you since you came to Prague. So it is truly so heartily dear to me, that I learn it goes so well with you (God be praised), **that you have found a place where you can have peace, and people can appreciate you and value your work [*handel*], and do you good.**

I had heard something of this before, for it was written to Doctor Niels from Germany — though whomever I told it to would not believe it, so I did not know it for certain, until I came to **Gert Rantzau**; he told me that it was certain, and that he had himself lately written to you, and you cannot believe how dear it is, both to him and to Talle, that it goes well with you. Truly, I can tell it is right dear to them both. However it went with that talk that was said about you, then it has been a misunderstanding they have had about it, for **Talle is right good to you too, that I know for certain**; I have perceived, both from them and from Gert's sister, that **Lady Kirsten, his mother, is so good to you, and regrets so hard what they did to you in Denmark**, and that she thanks you for her child **Lisbeth**, whom you have helped — she talks so much about it. So I have now therefore written her, and thanked her for all the good she has shown you, and [she] is so good a friend to you; and besides, [I] let her know what tidings I have now learned about you, and that your son is in Copenhagen for the instruments that were still left behind. I have in these days **let Gert see the letter you had written the King, and what answer you got on it** — I read it myself for him, and explained the meaning of it to him, so that Talle heard it; for they understood it well. So I let him also see **the little letter the Emperor's Chancellor had written you**.

I was lately in conversation with **"Mercurius" in Skåne, at Landskrona**; then he asked me about you, then I said that I hoped it went well with you, and let him read **the same little copy that the Roman Chancellor [Coraduz] had written**; then he said it was good, and dear to him, that it went well with you. And a little after, **he told me some things about the Emperor that did not please me**; then I answered, it could be good nonetheless, [for] you had other good friends you had there. So he sat again a little; then he came with another remark, and said: **two of those who were your best friends there, of the Emperor's council, they were dismissed** [from office]; then I thought it could still be good. "That I see gladly," he said. It was such pretty talk we had, and I understood it so well. **My brother Jørgen** was also there; he asked me so diligently about you, and wished so much that everything could go well for you out there.

Now I do think that they are now in Copenhagen, for this Diet, for word [seeking news] about your situation. My dear kind brother, now to write something about **Titan**: **he has had a fever for 3 weeks, though I hope, with God's help, that it is now well again with him.** It seems as if that **Hans Ernst** will not deal rightly with him [Erik]: **Erik has taught him the [alchemical] art [*consten*]**, and there was a deal made between them, that whomever they should teach the art, they should both be in on it, and both share equally in whatever money they got for it. Now they had engaged some people [investors], from whom they should get money; now Hans Ernst alone wanted to have those moneys; and he has also written the Emperor, and offered him the art, and would not let Erik know of it — though Erik hopes he will get ahead of him; I think **Erik will himself [go] to the Emperor**. And I know for certain that **Erik has the art for certain**, and he had offered our King it, but he [the King] would write no answer on it, but was only mocking about it; and Hans Ernst had also written the King since, and asked that he would let Erik get an answer — of which I send you a copy; for I myself had the King delivered the letter by the secretary, but he would answer nothing to it, for they have now done to him [Erik] here all that they could. Now they are content with him, and act as if they know nothing of what they did before — for Erik had reminded the King somewhat of it in his supplication. Now may God Almighty help well, and make it once better for us. I had written Erik that he should meet me lately near Haderslev, if he were anywhere in the region — so he could not meet me there [then]; now I have written him whether he will come hither to me, or to Hamburg, or to Lüneburg, or wherever he will, [and] then I will meet him and talk with him, before I leave the region; and I have sent a messenger out to him from here, and expect it back in 3 or 4 days. If he will meet me here lately, then I will wait for him; otherwise I will, with God's help, accompany Tage to Brunswick — so it is but a day's journey to that **Kelbra** [?]. **If he keeps house [is settled somewhere], then I will go thither to him, for I must absolutely talk with him**; but I am so near him, with God's help, [I shall] also [learn] how it is with his affairs. God give us luck and counsel, that we might also get some good opportunity once.

My dear kind brother, now about my **Tage**: I intend to let him **go to Basel and stay there a year**; **Doctor Niels [Krag] has written, with him, to that Doctor Grynaeus there; Sten Bille has also written to a doctor [there], [who] is the other's brother**, that they will help Tage to the best. **Erik has written me that it seemed to him best that Tage stay at Heidelberg first a year and learn the language, that he should not first learn that bad Swiss tongue at Basel** — but I will yet consider it, before I decide where he shall be, for he can well also learn good German at Basel; if it does not get too soon too cold to travel, then he shall go to Basel, for the … [*haffhanell* — unclear] that is at Heidelberg does not [please] me. When he now comes where he shall first be, then he shall write you at once; so I trust you so well that **you will write for him to the learned at that place, that they will advance him to the best**. God Almighty keep him well, wherever he comes, and send him well home to me again.

My dear kind brother, I think **my mother [Beate Bille]** has now got your letter; she will be glad of it, for she was so anxious for you since you went to the Emperor. I send you a letter; **Henrik Ramel** wrote me about the books. I go to **Fusingø** to my sister from Haderslev, when I come there again, for she has asked it of me; her sons have now gone into the estate. I write this letter here now, and send it to Copenhagen, and hope that it comes there before your Tyge leaves thence. Had I now got what you have written me, I would gladly have seen it — but I shall write for it. My dear kind brother, so I now know nothing notable more to write you; but you shall always find me your loyal sister, who always gladly will do what I know is dear to you; and [I] hope we meet well once — God grant we may meet glad and in health. And [I] will now and always have you commended to God Almighty, both to soul and body, with all luck and welfare. Gert and Talle and my Tage greet you with many good-nights; do well, and say to **Kirsten** and your children and all your good friends (who are also mine) many good-nights on my behalf.

Given [at] Breitenburg, the 24th of October 1599.
**Sophia Brahe, Otte's daughter.**

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondent.** **Incoming**, **Sophie Brahe (Sophia Brahe Ottesdatter, 1559–1643)** — Tycho's younger sister, the astronomer- and chemist-noblewoman, betrothed to the alchemist **Erik Lange** — **to Tycho**. An original autograph (Basel).
- **Significance — a centerpiece of the Sophie Brahe / Erik Lange story, and a warm family chronicle.**
 - **Escorting her son to Basel.** Sophie is travelling with her son **Tage Thott** (by her first husband Otte Thott), bound for study at **Basel** via **Brunswick**, hosted by **Gert Rantzau, his wife "Talle," and his mother Lady Kirsten Rantzau** at **Breitenburg**. She asks Tycho to write recommendations; **Niels Krag and Sten Bille have written to the Grynaeus brothers at Basel** (cf. Tycho's own Grynaeus letter and the nephew Otto Brahe at Basel, brahe-t_15980607001). **Erik Lange's advice**: send Tage to **Heidelberg** first (to avoid "that bad Swiss tongue").
 - **Joy at Tycho's imperial fortune.** Sophie has heard (via **Niels Krag**, her sister **Margrette's** letter, and Tycho's son **Tyge** in Copenhagen) that Tycho **"has got a house from the Emperor, and more than 4000 gulden a year"** — "so heartily dear to me … that you have found a place where people appreciate you." She has shown the sympathetic Rantzaus **Tycho's letter to King Christian IV, the unkind royal reply, and Coraduz's letter**.
 - **The Erik Lange alchemy saga (the emotional core).** A vivid, intimate report on **Erik Lange** — Sophie's beloved, the ruined alchemist: his partner **Hans Ernst** is **cheating him over "the art" [*consten* = alchemy]** and the investors' money, secretly offering it to the Emperor; **Erik "has the art for certain,"** offered it to the **Danish King (who only mocked it)**, and may go to the Emperor himself. Sophie is **desperate to meet Erik** (Hamburg, Lüneburg, or wherever) before leaving — "I must absolutely talk with him." (Cf. Tycho's own query after Erik Lange, brahe-t_16000000002.)
 - **Court intelligence.** A coded conversation with **"Mercurius"** at **Landskrona** (a Danish court figure, codename) reveals **two of Tycho's friends on the imperial council "were dismissed"**; her brother **Jørgen Brahe** present. The family network — mother **Beate Bille**, siblings **Knud, Margrette**, the Fusingø sister, **Henrik Ramel** (about books) — threads throughout.
- **Cross-references.** A keystone of the **Sophie Brahe / Erik Lange** thread (pair with brahe-t_16000000002, where Tycho asks Petkum after Erik Lange and reports Sophie at Wandsbek) and the **Brahe-family** network; the **Basel/Grynaeus** student connection (brahe-t_15980607001).
- **Persons & places named.** **Sophie Brahe**; **Tycho**; **Tage Thott** (her son); **Gert Rantzau** & wife "**Talle**" & mother **Lady Kirsten Rantzau**; **Mikell** (courier); **Lady Anne** (a kinswoman — unidentified, flagged); **Tyge** (Tycho the Younger); **Niels Krag**; **Knud Brahe**, **Margrette Brahe** (siblings); **"Mercurius"** (Landskrona court figure — codename, flagged); **Jørgen Brahe**; **Erik Lange**; **Hans Ernst**; **Rudolf II**, **Christian IV**; the **Grynaeus** brothers (Basel); **Sten Bille**; **Beate Bille** (mother); **Henrik Ramel**; **"Titan"** (a person with a fever — unidentified, flagged). Places: **Breitenburg**, **Haderslev**, **Lindewedel**, **Kiel**, **Flensburg**, **Wandsbek/Hamburg**, **Brunswick**, **Basel**, **Heidelberg**, **Copenhagen**, **Kolding**, **Horsens**, **Landskrona**, **Lüneburg**, **Fusingø**.
- **Date.** Source dateline *denn 24. october 1599* (identifier 15991024001 agrees) → **24 October 1599 [O.S.]**; the **catalogue label's "24 September" is an error** (contradicted by the dateline and identifier), flagged for review of the catalogue date.
- **Reading flags.** **"Titan"** — a person Sophie reports ill with fever, distinct from Tage and Erik (possibly a nickname for a family member or an alchemy associate; unidentified). **"Mercurius"** — a coded designation for a Danish-court figure. **"Lady Anne"** — an unnamed kinswoman. **"haffhanell"** (the Heidelberg objection) — uncertain word. None affect the overall sense.
- **Correction.** Two mistranslations corrected against Dreyer (TBOO XIV p.158): 'Titan writes that Mikell had been...' is corrected to 'Titan's secretary Mikell had been...' ('Titans skriuer Mikell' is a noun phrase naming Mikell as Titan's secretary, not a report-by-letter from Titan); and 'her kinswoman Lisbeth' is corrected to 'her child Lisbeth' ('kintt' = archaic Danish for 'child').

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO XIV pp.156-160 read as page images and collated the transcribed original word-for-word against pp.157-159, which carry the full letter (no.166, Sophie Brahe to Tycho, 24 Oct 1599): opening and closing lines, every proper name (Gert/Talle Rantzau, Lindved, Mikell, Tyge, Niels Krag, Knud, Margrette, Kirsten, Lisebett, Jørgen, Beate Bille, Henrik Ramel, Erik, Hans Ernst, Sten Bille, Grynaeus), every number (9 miles to Lindved, 7 miles Breitenburg-Hamburg, 2-3 days, 6 days, three separate '3 weeks', 4000 gulden, 'two of the Emperor's councillors'), every date (24 Oct 1599, St Martin's day, dispatch date), and every place-name (Haderslev, Lindved, Breitenburg, Kiel, Flensburg, Wandsbek, Horsens, Copenhagen, Kolding, Landskrona i Skåne, Heidelberg, Basel, Fusingø). Our Danish matches Dreyer's print throughout — no text error. Found one high-severity mistranslation that misidentifies Mikell's relationship to the code-named 'Titan' (almost certainly Erik Lange) and invents an act of writing absent from the source, plus one lower-confidence mistranslation of the archaic word for 'child' as 'kinswoman'. The first defect changes what a scholar reconstructing Sophie Brahe's/Erik Lange's correspondence network would take away, so the letter cannot stand at its the translator's own grade Secure.

**2 defects found:**
- **mistranslation** (**high**). 'Titans skriuer' is a noun phrase ('Titan's secretary/scribe'), with 'Mikell' in apposition naming him — Mikell is the subject of 'hade werid' (had been), i.e. Titan's (Erik Lange's) secretary who went to Haderslev looking for Sophie. The English instead makes 'Titan' the subject of an invented verb 'writes', turning a plain narrative clause into a false report-by-letter and dropping the master-secretary relationship between Titan/Erik Lange and Mikell. At: “Titan writes that Mikell had been at Haderslev, and thought to have found me there about 3 weeks ago”.
- **mistranslation** (low). 'Kind' is the archaic Danish word for 'child' (cognate with English 'kin' / German 'Kind'), not 'kinswoman'; Lady Kirsten more likely thanks Tycho for having helped her child Lisbeth than an unspecified female relative. Lower confidence than the Titan/Mikell finding since 'kinswoman' is not indefensible, but the more probable reading is 'child'. At: “she thanks you for her kinswoman Lisbeth, whom you have helped”.

**Repaired.** Both defects were verified directly against Dreyer's page images, TBOO XIV pp.156-159 (the full letter). Both source phrases match the transcribed original exactly as printed by Dreyer on p.158, confirming no text error and that both defects are matters of translation. The Mikell/secretary reading is grammatically unambiguous. The 'kintt'/'child' reading is the more probable sense per the audit's own note (archaic Danish, cognate with 'kin'/'Kind') and is adopted, though 'kinswoman' was not indefensible — flagged low severity in the source audit and treated accordingly.

text.original:
ERLIG OCH WELBIURDIGH MAND, THIGE BRAHE THILL KNUDTZTORP, MIN KIERE BRODER, GANDSKE BRODERLIGEN THILSCHREFFUIDT.

MYNN gandsche wennligh hilßenn nu och alltiid forßennd met Gud Kere Tyge och kere broder, nest mynn wennligh tacßielße for allt beuist gode, huilchit ieg aff formuenn steze wyll findis goduylig at forschyle. Kere broder, ieg haffuer fornumit wdaff dyn schriffuelße, att dynn leylighed er nu bleffuenn god, saa att du haffuer nu bekomit hoss keysseren gode wylkar, huilchit mig wdj sandhed møgitt kert er att høre; och som du wdj dinn schriffuelße est begerendis, att der som dig bliffuer giortt nogenn forhynndring paa dine jnstrumenter, att ieg daa will hielpe til, saa møgitt mugligtt war, at dig jngenn forhyndringh der paa matte sche, saa forsser ieg mig, att dig well jngen forhindringh der paa scher; men der som dett schede, will ieg giøre saa møgit derwdj som mig mugligtt ehr; och wdj huess made ieg wid digh att tienne, schall du altiid fynnde mig wiligh. Och wyll nu och altiid haffue digh Gud alme[ct]iste beffalendis met allt huiss digh kertt er.

DatumKøbenhaffnn denn 25 October 99.
Axel Brahe
egen hann.
text.english:
**Honourable and well-born man, Tyge Brahe to Knudstrup, my dear brother, written to in all brotherliness.**

My quite friendly greeting, now and always foresent with God, dear Tyge and dear brother; next, my friendly thanks for all the good [you have] shown, which I, of my ability, shall ever be found well-willing to requite. Dear brother, I have understood from your writing that your situation has now become good, so that you have now obtained good terms with the Emperor — which in truth is very dear to me to hear. And as, in your writing, you are requesting that, should any hindrance be done to you upon your instruments, I would then help, as much as may be possible, that no hindrance befall you thereon — so I trust that no hindrance does befall you thereon; but should it so happen, I will do as much therein as is possible to me; and in whatever way I know to serve you, you shall always find me willing. And [I] will, now and always, have you commended to God Almighty, with all that is dear to you.

Given at Copenhagen, the 25th of October, [15]99.
Axel Brahe,
[his] own hand.
