documents.apparatus:
- **Edition of record.** Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia* vol. VIII (*Epistolae*). The edition's source_edition ("*Tychonis Brahei et ad eum doctorum virorum epistolae ab anno 1588*") is the later printed collection. MS witnesses: **A** = Copenhagen, Rigsarkivet, Langebeks diplomatarium (copy); **B** = Copenhagen, Det Kongelige Bibliotek, copy in an exemplar of P. J. Resen, *Inscriptiones Hafnienses* (1668). **Cross-check:** page-collated at **vol. VIII pp. 209–217** (Dreyer internal pp. 195–204), from cod. Vindob. lat. 10702; every numeral confirmed against the edition of record (anchors in the Editorial note).
- **Sender / recipient.** Tycho (at **Girsitz**, an Imperial castle c. 3 [German] miles from Prague, his plague-refuge from Benátky). **Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg** (1553–1622), Bavarian **Chancellor**, polymath and book-collector (and Kepler's correspondent). This is the **companion to Tycho's reply of 28 August 1600** (to Herwart's Jan–May 1600 series); here the friendship is "by fame, face unknown."
- **Strand 1 — exile, transport, plague.** Tycho's **eldest son** (Tycho the Younger) sent to Denmark for the **remaining instruments**; the Emperor's letters to the **Magdeburg magistrate** to ship instruments + library + goods down the **Elbe** to Bohemia; Magdeburg's evasion, the second Imperial letter via **Barvitius**, and the Elbe too low from drought. The **plague** nearing Benátky drove his household to Girsitz; **Rudolf II's** "paternal" favour (salary via the Captain of **Brandeis**; leave to remove to Vienna, declined). On **Denmark**: "one's homeland is where one lives well"; he sends a packet documenting his emigration's causes, points to his *Epistolae* "p. 198," and encloses **poems** by sympathetic poets (more expected from **Scaliger** and **Paul Melissus**), the last two **epigrams** approved by the Emperor for the marble doors of the new **Observatory and Laboratory**.
- **Strand 2 — the technical argument (obliquity / precession / year / eccentricity).**
 - **Venus not eclipsed by Mercury**: not in every conjunction is Mercury below Venus (sometimes above), per both Tycho's and Copernicus's hypotheses.
 - **Ancient imprecision** ("rough Minerva"): the fixed-star places good only to c. 10′ (sometimes ½°), betrayed by constant star-*distances* not matching their numbers.
 - **Obliquity essentially constant.** Applying Tycho's measured **maximum obliquity 23° 31½′** to the declinations of **Timochares/Hipparchus/Ptolemy** reproduces present latitudes — so the obliquity was not really changed, only the ancients imprecise (within ⅓°). Worked examples: **Castor & Pollux** (latitude 18–19′ off); **Altair** (*Vultur volans*, decl. 5⅚° N → lat. 29° 40′, Ptolemy's table ⅓° high); **Mars** (apogee now 23½° Leo, 5° before Copernicus; N-lat 4° 35′ vs Ptolemy 4⅓°); **Saturn** (N-lat 2° 49½′ vs Ptolemy 3° 6′) and **Jupiter** (1° 39½′ vs 2° 5′, "25′ wanting") — proving the **nodes/latitude-limits do not follow the apogee motion** (contra the received view; Copernicus too credulous of Ptolemy).
 - **Obliquity history**: al-Battānī ( c. 700 yr ago, +4½′), al-Zarqālī/Arzachel (*Asrael*, +2½′), Prophatius (Jacob ben Makhir, ~within ½′, 300 yr ago); Aristarchus→Ptolemy constant at 23° 51⅓′; the moderns (Peurbach/Regiomontanus/Werner/Copernicus) c. 4′ low from **uncorrected winter solar refraction (8–9′)**; Regiomontanus & **Walther**'s Nuremberg zenith-distances confirm Tycho's value within ½′.
 - **Precession uniform**: Hipparchus→al-Battānī (1006 yr) 14° 15′; al-Battānī→now (705 yr) exactly 10°; ⇒ **1°/70½ yr = 51″/yr** (Ptolemy's 1°/100 yr merely estimative).
 - **Year-length**: 365ᵈ **5ʰ c. 49ᵐ** (Regiomontanus/Walther + Tycho), not Copernicus's longer value — Copernicus's vernal equinox now off **14½ h** (→ 1 day 3 h per century).
 - **Solar eccentricity**: Ptolemy/Hipparchus 2½ⁿ (ecc-radius = 60) → al-Battānī/Azrael 2° 5′ → Tycho **2° 9′**. The ancients sought a "**Pythagorean harmony**"; "whoever delivers values consonant with the appearances will be my great Apollo." Closes with the *Aeneid* tag *hoc opus, hic labor est* and the theological coda that **God founded all things harmonically** (man the **microcosm**, μικροκόσμῳ).
- **Strand 3 — publication, prosthaphaeresis priority, books.** Tables of the luminaries to be printed first, but "no bare numbers without observations and demonstrations"; the rest reserved for the "**Theatre of Astronomy**." The **Hamburg printer** who corrupted the *Progymnasmata* lunar gatherings; the failed Wittenberg printing; the Imperial summons. **The prosthaphaeresis story** (a key priority document): Tycho took it up c. 20 yr ago from **Rheticus's** *Dialogus* (triangle tables to sextant-degrees), with **Werner's** *De motu octavae sphaerae* giving a handle; **Paul Wittich** (Breslau) worked on it during his **4-month 1580 Uraniborg visit**; Wittich then went to **Landgrave Wilhelm IV**, exposing Tycho's instruments and divulging the "triangle mysteries" to the clockmaker **Jost Bürgi**; whence a "**scurrilous sycophant**" (unnamed — **Nicolaus Reimers Ursus**) got them and published them "maimed" at **Strasbourg** (in his *Fundamentum astronomicum*, 1588); **Clavius** then inserted them (miscrediting Ursus) in his *Astrolabium*; **Jacob Curtius** tried to extend them to plane triangles; Tycho with **Melchior Jöstel** (Wittenberg) completed the spherical + plane reduction "by prosthaphaereses alone." Finally (bracketed passages) the **book exchange**: the *Mechanica* copies still with a Prague illuminator; **50 books** selected from the Munich princes' library catalogue (incl. **Hebrew** books) + **6** from the Frankfurt fair catalogue; and the request, via the Bavarian princes' authority (Tycho's name concealed), for **Cyprian Leovitius's** manuscripts (Ephemerides, directions tables, a genethliacal-astrology work) held by the **Fuggers** at Augsburg — with the recollection of Tycho's youthful **Augsburg** years and the **21-foot great quadrant** in **Paul Hainzel's** garden (c. 1569).
- **Persons & places.** **Rudolf II**; **Johann Anton Barvitius** (imperial secretary); the **Captain of Brandeis**; **Joseph Scaliger**, **Paul Melissus** (Schede, the poet); **Timochares, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus**; **al-Battānī** (*Albategnius*), **al-Zarqālī/Arzachel** (*Asrael Hispanus*), **Jacob ben Makhir** (*Prophatius Iudaeus*); **Peurbach, Regiomontanus, Bernhard Walther, Johann Werner, Copernicus**; **Rheticus, Paul Wittich, Jost Bürgi, Nicolaus Reimers Ursus** (the unnamed sycophant), **Christophorus Clavius, Jacob Curtius (Kurz von Senftenau), Melchior Jöstel**; **Cyprian Leovitius**, the **Fuggers**, **Paul Hainzel**; **Alfonso X** ("old Alfonso"). Places: **Magdeburg, the Elbe, Benátky, Girsitz, Prague, Vienna, Dresden, Wittenberg, Strasbourg, Augsburg, Munich, Nuremberg**.
- **Glyphs / Greek / tags.** ♀ Venus, ☿ Mercury, ☾ Moon, ☉ Sun, ♂ Mars, ♄ Saturn, ♃ Jupiter, ♋ Cancer, ♌ Leo, ♎ Libra, ♐ Sagittarius, ♊ Gemini; **□** = *quadraturis* (quadratures). *μικροκόσμῳ* = microcosm. *crassa Minerva* = "with rough Minerva" (crudely, Horace/Cicero). *Differ, habent parvae commoda magna morae* — Ovid, *Fasti* III.394 (≈ "small delays have great advantages"). *hoc opus, hic labor est* — Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.129. *Lynceo oculatiores* — "more keen-sighted than Lynceus." *erit mihi magnus Apollo* — Virgil, *Ecl.* III.104. *Vultur volans* = Aquila/Altair. *Heliconis fontibus / venas acuere* — poetic inspiration.
- **Calendar.** Dateline **16 November 1599 New Style** (*stylo renovato*) — as an Imperial-territory letter in Catholic Bohemia, Tycho here writes N.S. (contrast his Danish O.S. datelines, e.g. the Landgrave letter of 16 Aug 1588). Matches the catalogue label.
- **Editorial interventions in the source block (declared).** (1) c. 55 digitised text layer-intruded **apparatus "A" sigla** removed as non-textual (as in the letters to Scaliger of 23 Aug 1598, to Peucer of 1590, and to the Landgrave of 16 Aug 1588). (2) The source's **square brackets** around the three late passages (book-list; Augsburg/Fugger recollection; closing) are **retained as printed** — Dreyer's/witness-level brackets (the bracket even cuts mid-sentence at "*inter alia] intellexisse*"), flagged here, not introduced by me. (3) The editorial *[qui]* (Dreyer's supplement in "PTOLEMAeUM [qui] 460 ab eodem abfuit") is kept in brackets. Spelling *Erathostenis*/*Eratosthenem*, *Witebergâ*/*Wittebergae*, *Noribergae* left as printed.
- **Correction.** Two word-level transcription corruptions restored against Dreyer (TBOO VIII): 'expeditioni' -> 'expectationi' (p.193), with the corresponding English clause corrected from 'your dispatch' to 'your expectation'; and 'antenus' -> 'anterius' (p.196, no effect on the English).

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. All 14 Dreyer pages read as page images (TBOO VIII pp.191-204: the tail of I.A. Maginus's letter, the full Tycho-to-Herwart letter, and the head of Tycho's letter to Kepler). Collated the opening and closing lines, every named person (Barvitius, the Fuggers, Cyprian Leovitius, Paul Hentzelius/Hainzel, Scaliger, Melissus, Wittich, Landgrave Wilhelm, Jost Buergi, Clavius, Jacob Curtius, Joestelius, Rheticus, Werner, al-Battani, Azrael, Prophatius, Aristarchus, Eratosthenes, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, Timochares, Peurbach, Regiomontanus, Walther, Copernicus), every place-name (Girsitz, Benatky, Prague, the Elbe, Magdeburg, Bohemia, Wittenberg, Breslau, Strasbourg, Munich, Augsburg, Bavaria, Nuremberg, Denmark, Uraniborg), the date (16 November 1599 N.S.), and the dense run of astronomical numbers (obliquity/latitude/precession figures for Castor-Pollux, Aquila, Mars, Saturn, Jupiter, plus every historical interval from Aristarchus to al-Battani) against the page images. Two source-text words diverge from Dreyer's print: 'expeditioni' for his 'expectationi' (p.193, which also skews the English at that clause) and 'antenus' for his 'anterius' (p.196, no translation effect). No fabrication, omission, or hedge-loss found; the translation is otherwise a complete, careful, literal rendering including all bracketed passages.

**3 defects found:**
- **text error** (medium). The transcribed original reads 'expeditioni' (dispatch/errand); Dreyer's page prints 'expectationi' (expectation) - a genuine word-level corruption in the transcription, not a variant spelling. Dreyer prints: *quod tuae expectationi non prius morem gesserim (TBOO VIII, p.193)*.
- **mistranslation** (medium). Because it follows the corrupted the transcribed original, the English renders 'your dispatch' where Dreyer's actual word 'expectationi' requires 'your expectation' - Tycho is apologising for disappointing Herwart's expectation, not for failing to act on a dispatched errand. At: “that I have not sooner complied with your dispatch”.
- **text error** (low). 'antenus' is not a Latin word; Dreyer prints 'anterius' ('earlier'), which also matches the word's correct use elsewhere in this same letter. No effect on the English, which already renders the sense correctly as '3½° earlier'. Dreyer prints: *3½ anterius distare in antecedentia P. 65½ (TBOO VIII, p.196)*.

**Repaired.** All three defects were verified against the Dreyer page images (TBOO VIII pp.193 and 196, read visually, not via the digitised text layer). P.193 confirms 'expectationi' where our transcribed original had 'expeditioni', which also required correcting the English clause 'your dispatch' to 'your expectation'. P.196 confirms 'anterius' where our transcribed original had the non-word 'antenus'; the existing English already rendered the correct sense ('earlier') and needed no change. No other text was touched.

documents.abstract: Brief maternal letter expressing gladness that Tycho has found settled circumstances, reporting her own good health, and commending him and his household to God.
documents.incipit: KIERRE Thiige och kierre sønn, Gud allmegthiste werre nu och allthid huoß dig och alle …

text.original:
ERLLIIG OCH VELBYERDIG MAND THYGGE BRAHE THILL VRANIBORIGH, MINN KIERRE SØNN, GANDSCHE VENLIGEN THILL SKREFFUENN.

KIERRE Thiige och kierre sønn, Gud allmegthiste werre nu och allthid huoß dig och alle dine och beuarre dig naadeligen och vell fra alltt dett, som vntt er. Kierre sønn, haffuer jeg dig paa thet allervenligste bethackitt for din guode skriffuelße, som du skriffuer mig thill, kierre sønn, och villtt wide, huor jeg nu er thill passe, saa er dett ennnu, Gud verre loffuett, gott mett mig. Kierre sønn, saa er ditt breff mig møgitt kiertt att hørre, att du, Gud verre loffuett, er nu kommen thill roulighed, och huis ditt breff er annlangindis, er mig møgitt kiertt, att dig och dine lider alltt vell, Gud verre loffuett; thj Gud vill ingen haffue forgett, som hannom frøckther. Och som din sønn haffuer ochsaa berett for migh, att din leilighed gaar dig løckelig och vell annd, Gud verre loffuet, saa vill jeg, kierre sønn, icke lenger ophollde dig mett denne minn korthe skrifuellße. Du skalltt alle miine dauge finde mig for din hulle maader och will her mett haffue dig Gud allmegthiste beffallendis, dig och alle dine, mett alltt løcke och vellfardt.

Aff Billisgaardt then 26 nouembris anno 99.
Beatte Bille
text.english:
**Honourable and well-born man, Tyge Brahe to Uraniborg, my dear son, written to in all friendliness.**

Dear Tyge and dear son, may God Almighty be now and always with you and all yours, and keep you graciously and well from all that is evil. Dear son, I have most kindly thanked you for your good writing, which you write to me; dear son, and [you] would know how I now fare — so it is still, God be praised, well with me. Dear son, so is your letter very dear to me to hear: that you have, God be praised, now come to peace [a settled rest]; and as concerns your letter, it is very dear to me that you and yours are all faring well, God be praised — for God will have none forgotten who fear Him. And as your son has also reported to me, that your situation goes happily and well for you, God be praised — so I will, dear son, not detain you longer with this my short writing. You shall, all my days, find me [to be] your devoted mother; and [I] will herewith have you commended to God Almighty — you and all yours — with all fortune and welfare.

From Billesgård, the 26th of November, in the year [15]99.
Beate Bille.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender — Tycho's mother.** **Beate Bille** (1526–1605), widow of **Otte Brahe** and mother of Tycho; writing from **Billesgård** (her estate in Skåne). A tender maternal letter: she rejoices that Tycho has "come to peace" (*kommen til rolighed*) and that, as his son had also told her, his "situation goes happily and well" — i.e. she has heard of his secure new position under the Emperor. She signs herself *din hulde moder*, "your devoted mother."
- **The grandson as messenger.** *din søn* ("your son") who "reported to me" that Tycho's affairs prosper = one of Tycho's sons (most likely **Tycho the Younger**, then travelling between Bohemia and Denmark; cf. brahe-t_16000329003, …0414002), evidently the bearer of news to his grandmother.
- **Orthography.** Late-16th-c. Danish: *erlliig* (ærlig), *velbyerdig* (velbyrdig), *thill skreffuenn* (tilskrevet), *allmegthiste* (almægtigste), *beuarre* (bevare), *skriffuelße* (skrivelse), *thill passe* (til pas, faring/in health), *roulighed* (rolighed, peace/quiet), *annlangindis* (anlangendes, concerning), *frøckther* (frygter, fears), *leilighed* (situation), *løckelig* (lykkelig), *hulle maader* = *hulde moder* (devoted mother), *beffallendis* (befalende, commending). Reading-verified as **Danish**.
- **Calendar.** *Billisgaardt then 26 nouembris anno 99* = **26 November 1599**; Denmark (Skåne) kept the **Julian / Old Style** calendar. Header agrees with the label.

documents.incipit: KIERE Thygge och min kiere morßøfterßenn, Gudt vere althidt huoß thig medt sin helig andt …

text.original:
ERLLIG OCH WELBYURDICH MANDT THYGGE BRADE TILL KNUDSTRUP, HØFFUITZMANDT PAA BENACSIA, MIN KIERRE NESTSSØSCHINDT BARN OCH SYNDERLIG GODE WEN, GANTZ WENLIG THILLSCHREFFUITT.

KIERE Thygge och min kiere morßøfterßenn, Gudt vere althidt huoß thig medt sin helig andt och beuare thig medt altt, huis thig kiert er, fra alltt ont. Jegh thacker thig gandske vennligen och gierne for aaltt beuist erre och gott, huilcket att forschyllde ieg vill althidt findis villige y huis mader meg mouligt er. Kiere Thygge, ieg haffuer stackit sidenn bekomit thinn schriffuelße, och theraff formerker thinn leglighedts gode thillstandt ther vde i thendt landtz egn, huilcken er mig som Gudt ßaa kiertt att høre, som du vaarst min egenn sønn heler broder. Och vill ønsche aff Gudt allermegtigste, att thet maa bliffue jo lenger jou beder. Sammelethis, kiere morßøsterßen, som samme thin schriffuelße ochsaa formelder om dj pendinge, ieg thig skylldig er, atu thenom thill thenne omslag maate bekomme, saa schall Gudt vide, att ieg helder end giernne (som och billichtt vaar) ville samme thinn begiering eptherkomme, thersom thet vaar mig mouligt. Menn nu kandt ieg thenom saa hastig och snnart jcke thill vege bringe, aff thend aarßage jegh nu vdj thenne thillkomindis vgge schall giffue kong. maytt. 6000 daller paa min sallige broder Peders vegnne, och thersom thet icke hafde verit, skulle du for:ne thinne pendinge giernne haffue bekommit, och beder thig ther for, kiere Thygge och kiere mor[sø]sterßøn, paa thet vennligst, du ville haffue gedultt medt for:ne pendinge thill nu jull førstkomindis ett aar, schall Eske Billde thenom paa thine vegnne, vden alldt vider forhalling heller vndschylding, bekomme. Dog renten er aarligen och endnu thette aar ochsaa bettalidt. Och ther som ieg i nogen mader kandt thienne thig igenn, skaltu i[n]genn thuill haffue paa, ieg giør jou giernne som ieg och pligthig er. Nytt att schriffue theg thill, er her inthet synderligt. Thij huadt vdj Thydschland sig thilldrager, vedst thu beder endt vij j diße lande; thij penninge haffuer affthackidt alle vore pentzionierer, som vj schulle haffue kundschaff aff, saa vell som och ander, vij sider saa secker och frij som en fougell vnder garnedt. Hertug Kaarell aff Suerig thiranißer grußammb, haffuer nu faaedt aldt Findlandt indt och ombragt och ladit rete alle dij adell ther y landit. Jeg frygter Erick Spaare och hanns paartie ville snart følge epther, huilckett Gudt aff vennde.

Kongen aff Pollenn ßende 8 schibbe met 800 mand her igenom sundit, schulle indthage Elsborige, paa huilcke johan Gyldenstiern vaar admierall. Hoffuidtschibbit, som admierall vaar paa, bleff vnder Halldlandtz side medt mieste paartenn skiøtt, huilkedt vij nu lader opthage och bierge oss thill beste, thet andit schibb, nest admierallen, bleff och med thop och thagell; the ander ere kommen thillbage hidt thill Kiøbenhaffuen, ville gierne bliffue her vdj vintherlege (thij the thør icke løbe hiemmb, hertug Kaarell er thenom for i vegenn met 12 schibe); the haffuer huercken att bide eler brydde; erre beuilgidt at maa bliffue her i byen paa nogen thidlang att there for thierris pendinge, huilcket erre saare faa; the haffuer soldt och selger endnu dagelig aff thierris krudt och laadt for pendinge thill vnderholding, doch thet vill icke naa lanngt. Thet er vell snucket verheffthig folck, men the haffuer icke thet, the kunde schyulle thennom vdj.

Jacop Sieffelltt haffuer Gudt kaldit nu for xiiij dage forledenn, epther hand haffde giortt thuende sin døthers brøllup med Niels Schrammb och Hans Lindernou thill Gaffuenøe. Huis andit nytt her er, som icke synderligt haffuer paa sig, thet ved thin sønn thig vell adt berete; thij vill ieg nu icke lennger forhinder thig met thenne min schriffuelße, men vill beffale dig met huiß thig kiertt er thendt gode Gud udj volldt.

Ex Kiøbenhaffuen thendt 3 decembris a:o 99.
Axell Gyldenstern
med egen hand.
text.english:
**To the honourable and well-born man Tyge Brahe of Knudstrup, captain at Benátky, my dear first cousin and especial good friend, [this] most amicably written.**

Dear Tyge, and my dear cousin [mother's-sister's-son], may God ever be with you with his Holy Spirit, and preserve you, with all that is dear to you, from all evil. I thank you quite amicably and gladly for all the honour and good shown me, which to repay I will always be found willing in whatever way is possible for me. Dear Tyge, I have a short while ago received your letter, and from it note the good state of your circumstances there in that region — which is as dear to me to hear (God knows) as if you were my own son or brother; and I will wish from God Almighty that it may grow the better the longer. Likewise, dear cousin, as your same letter also makes mention of the **money I owe you**, that you might receive it at this *Umschlag* — God knows I would more than gladly (as was also fair) comply with that request of yours, if it were possible for me. But now I cannot bring it to hand so quickly and soon, for the reason that I, in this coming week, must give the Royal Majesty **6,000 dalers on behalf of my late brother Peder**; and had it not been for that, you should gladly have received your aforesaid money. And I ask you therefore, dear Tyge and dear cousin, most amicably, that you would have patience with the said money until **next Christmas a year hence**, [and] **Eske Bille** shall receive it on your behalf, without all further delay or excuse — though the **interest** is paid yearly, and this year too. And if I can serve you in any way in return, you shall have no doubt [of it]; I do it gladly, as I am also bound. As for news to write you, there is nothing special here; for what passes in **Germany** you know better than we in these lands — for money has dismissed all our pensioners [informants], from whom we should have intelligence, as well as others: **we sit as secure and free as a bird under the net**. **Duke Charles of Sweden** tyrannizes cruelly: he has now taken all **Finland**, and put to death and executed all the nobility there in the land. I fear **Erik Sparre** and his party will soon follow — which God avert.

The **King of Poland** sent **8 ships with 800 men** here through the Sound, [meaning] to take **Älvsborg**, on which **Johan Gyldenstierne** was admiral. The flagship, on which the admiral was, was for the most part shot up off the **Halland** side — which we now have salvaged and recovered for our benefit; the second ship, next the admiral's, [was taken] too, with top and tackle [and all]. The others have come back here to **Copenhagen**, [and] would gladly stay here in winter quarters (for they dare not run home — **Duke Charles is in their way with 12 ships**); they have neither [bread to] bite nor [aught to] brew; they are permitted to stay in the city for some time, [living] on their money, which is very little; they have sold, and still daily sell, of their powder and shot for money for their keep — but it will not reach far. They are indeed neat, valiant folk, but they have not that wherein they might shelter themselves.

**Jacob Sehested** God has now called [hence] a fortnight ago, after he had made the weddings of two of his daughters — with **Niels Skram** and **Hans Lindenov of Gavnø**. Whatever other news there is here, which is nothing special, your son will well know to report to you; therefore I will not now hinder you longer with this my letter, but will commend you, with all that is dear to you, into the good God's keeping.

From Copenhagen, the 3rd of December, the year [15]99.
Axel Gyldenstierne,
with my own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender & kinship.** **Axel Gyldenstierne** (1542–1603), Danish Rigsraad councillor and Statholder of Norway (1588–1601) — Tycho's **maternal cousin**, addressed as *min kiere morsøstersøn* ("my dear mother's-sister's-son") and, in the address, *næstsøskendebarn* (first cousin): their mothers were Bille sisters. He addresses Tycho as *"captain at Benátky"* (the imperial castle). The MS is the **original letter**.
- **Significance — a Danish kinsman's news-letter (December 1599).** Two strands:
 1. **A private debt.** Axel **owes Tycho money** (which Tycho's letter had asked to receive at the *Umschlag*); he cannot pay now, since "in this coming week" he must give the **King 6,000 dalers on behalf of his late brother Peder**, and begs delay **until next Christmas a year hence**, when **Eske Bille** will collect on Tycho's behalf — "though the interest is paid yearly." (Tycho's web of Danish loans, like the Mecklenburg one.)
 2. **Scandinavian war-news.** A vivid bulletin of the **Polish–Swedish war** and the **Swedish succession crisis**:
 - **Duke Charles of Sweden** (later Charles IX) "tyrannizes cruelly," having taken **Finland** and executed its nobility (the 1599 reduction of Finland / Åbo executions); Axel fears **Erik Sparre** (the Swedish statesman) "will soon follow" — as indeed he did, in the **Linköping Bloodbath** (1600).
 - The **King of Poland** (Sigismund III Vasa) sent **8 ships, 800 men** through the **Sound** to take **Älvsborg**, under admiral **Johan Gyldenstierne**; the flagship was **shot to pieces off Halland** (and salvaged by the Danes), a second ship taken, the rest **stranded at Copenhagen** — unable to sail home (Duke Charles blocking with 12 ships), destitute, **selling their powder and shot** to live: "neat, valiant folk, but they have not that wherein they might shelter themselves." A striking eyewitness of the stranded Polish squadron.
 3. **Family news.** The death of **Jacob Sehested** (a fortnight earlier), after marrying two daughters to **Niels Skram** and **Hans Lindenov of Gavnø**.
- **Persons named.** Axel Gyldenstierne (sender); his late brother **Peder Gyldenstierne**; **Eske Bille** (to collect Tycho's money); **Duke Charles of Sweden**; **Erik Sparre**; **King Sigismund III of Poland**; **Johan Gyldenstierne** (the Polish-service admiral); **Jacob Sehested** and his daughters' husbands **Niels Skram** and **Hans Lindenov**; Tycho's son (Tycho the Younger, "your son … will report").
- **Idiom (kept and glossed).** *"vi sidder så sikker og fri som en fugl under garnet"* — "we sit as secure and free as **a bird under the net**" (i.e. heedless of imminent danger); *"hverken at bide eller brygge"* — "neither [bread] to bite nor [aught] to brew" (utterly without provisions).
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Ex Kiøbenhaffuen thendt 3 decembris a:o 99*; **Old Style** (Denmark). Header agrees with the label.
- **Place-name.** *Benacsia* = **Benátky**; *Elsborige* = **Älvsborg** (the Swedish fortress at the Göta mouth); *Halland*, *Sundet* (the **Sound**).

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Read TBOO XIV pp.168-170 in full; the Gyldenstierne letter runs pp.168-169 (signed and dated 3 Dec. [15]99), p.170 is the following letter (Michael Vibe) included as buffer. No defects found.

documents.editorial_note: **Direction note.** **Incoming** letter — *from* **Niels Krag (Nicolaus Cragius)**, the Danish royal historian and Tycho's loyal friend, *to* Tycho. **This is the source of the verbatim Duncan-Liddel testimony** that Tycho quoted as "Krag's letter of 4 December" in **brahe-t_16000401001 (to Daniel Cramer, 1 April 1600)** and the Duncan dossier **brahe-t_15990926001 (to Cramer, 26 September 1599)** — see Apparatus.

text.original:
MAGNIFICO DOMINO, VIRTUTE, ERUDITIONE ET GENERE NOBILISSIMO, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE URANIBURGICAe BENACHIAe IN BOHEMIA PRÆSIDI, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO OBSERVANDO.
S. P. D.

MAGNIFICE Domine TYCHO, Domine et amice observande. Verum est quod reversus ex Legatione Anglica binas tuas literas domi repererim, sed quomodo ijs respondere potuerim per tabellarium Witebergensem, mihi non constat. Nam in literis tuis est, te ad festum Pentecostes iturum vocatu Caesaris Pragam. Ego autem, post Dominicam Trinitatis huc appuli; itaque non est quod suspiceris hoc literarum officium intermissum aliquo metu potentiorum, quibus iam pluribus indicijs innotuit mea in amicitia sinceritas et constantia, quam ut novam aliquam offensam mihi pariat. Neque mihi de moribus Anglorum aliquid adhaesit eorum diuturniore convictu et usu, sed tam longe ab ijs vitijs absum, quam te vellem longe abesse a perstringendo et mordendo per iocum et ludum innoxios et fidos tuos amicos: in quorum numero ita me ponas, ut qui nihil unquam passus sim studio et observantiae decedere, etsi fortean non usquequaque tibi officio meo satisfecerim. Res tuas, mi Domine TYCHO, cognovi abunde ex literis tum mihi tum ad ROSÆCRANTIUM datis, magnoque mihi gaudio est eo loco esse, ut tibi tuisque bene sit, parta quiete et invento Maecenate, qui tam munifice tuis studijs et honorifice consultum voluerit. Nec est quisquam eorum, quos tu magnifacis, qui tuae fortunae lingua animoque plus faveat, quam ego, invidiae eo nomine haud expers. Cogor enim aliquando propugnare huius rei veritatem contra eos, qui tuis laudibus nulla unquam a te affecti iniuria obtrectant et tua merita perperam aestimando infra istam fortunam deijciunt. Ac metuebam ab aliquibus male, cum intellexissem huc TYCHONIDEM tuum cum MULÆNO nostro missos ad expetenda instrumenta residua: sed Dei provisu omnes conticuere, nec quisquam contra mutire ausus. Iuvi ego ipsos, quantum in me fuit et res sinebat, auctorque fui, ne literas tuas exhiberent ijs, a quibus sincere auxilium sperari non poterat. Nam aliquando venere quaedam in oblivionem, quae nos ipsos praestat quoque tacita habere, quam dubiam operam aliorum periclitari. Vergit enim quorundam aetas ad extrema, et tamen in sordibus rerum caducarum cogitationes omnes defigimus parum aut nihil de aeternis illis solliciti. Neque dormientes neque vigilantes somniamus aut meditamur aliud quam pecuniam, cui gloriam, honorem et quidquid laudabile est, postponimus. Addimus aliquid de humana severitate (non dicam crudelitate) cuius tristia recens visa in duobus nobilibus et tribus plebeis alijsque exempla. Merito igitur habent quod laetentur, quibus aut favor aulicus hîc affulget, aut res suas ita pararunt, ut migrandi taedium non expavescant.

Mihi, Deo sit gloria, nihil adversi admodum adhuc contigit. Cancellario probantur, quae a me hac legatione gesta sunt omnia, qui vidit, ad fidem et industriam me nihil reliquum fecisse, sed alijs non item, nescio qua de causa. MULÆNUM nostrum quod provehere ad Medicen promittis, facis ut tua virtute et humanitate dignum, nec puto te habuisse vel habiturum unquam, qui te sinceriore animo colat et observet. Verum metuo valde, ne longior apud nos mora ab Italica profectione per hanc hiemem retinuerit. Sed profecto faciendum ita fuit, nec poterunt citius tua negotia expedire. Causas ipsi tibi reddant, quas veras esse non dubitaveris. Quia vero id iter non successit, alia ratione forte tibi fuerit consilium eius iuvandi invenire. Si animus est, ut illum a te dimissurus unquam omni modo, fiat bona cum gratia et aetati mature consulatur. Omnino, si tibi eum non gratum et obsequentem esse voluissemus, alia fuisset ratione prospectum, et prospicietur, Deo propitio, si eum missum feceris. Sin tibi et tuis placet, habebis eum. Cum voluptate audio TEGNALIO tantum beneficij et honoris a te et per te praestari, optoque, ut deinceps sit, qualem tu esse cupis. TYPOTIUS amicus meus unde habuerit, quod me impulsore patriam deserueris, conijcere non possum. Quicunque hoc comminisci ausus est, nec te novit nec intelligit, quid doloris apportet a fidelissimi amici convictu et mutuo adspectu tanta locum intercapedine disiungi. Sed Dominus TYPOTIUS, si recte memini, ipse a me audivit deplorari abitum tuum, tum patriae, tum mea causa, nedum meo sensu hoc factum credere possit, cui eam suspicionem animo exemptam cupio. De libro publicato, quod ad te scripserat ESCHYLUS BILLEUS, nihil mihi exaudire contigit, nec operae pretium te facturum existimo, si tale aliquod procuderes, qui melius horas tuas collocare potes, et verum est quod addis, multos absque tua voluntate eo te labore exonerare. Quaere a TYCHONIDE, quid filius Magistri IOHANNIS MICHAELIJ in mensa patris narravit. Miraberis, sat scio, iuxta atque nos dolemus. Quid mihi etiam in Anglia et Belgio exprobratum, piget referre. Quod de DUNCANO me scribere vis, fateor, quod res est, me non libenter doctorum controversijs velle immisceri, aut ijs nomen meum inseri. Ac fortean in maiore gloria Hypotheseos istius inventio erit, si simpliciter edito sub tuo nomine scripto illustraveris et explicaveris, quam si contentionibus obscuraveris, quod quidem factum non ignoro in Progymnasmatibus, hoc ipso consilio, ne quis eam sibi deinceps vendicaret; sed vellem hoc peculiari scripto fieri, non ita prolixo, sed quod in scholis proponi posset. Tum vix futurum amplius puto, ut quisquam tuae amplius laudi decerpat. DUNKANUS certe quicquid tandem privatim egerit, publice nunquam eam sibi adrogabit, qui ne per somnium quidem de ea cogitavit, antequam ex te hoc tanquam mysterium cognosceret. Quod simul ac patefecisses, memini a te dictum, plus ei communicatum, quam frater fratri edisserere fortean vellet. Atque reperi in paucis hisce diebus inter schedas meas chartam, qua mihi petenti eam signasti, sive ante DUNKANI adventum, sive quo tempore apud te fuit, incertus sum. Sed mi Domine TYCHO, patere te hoc ab amico moneri, ut polemica omnia seponas, et per quae coepisti, vestigia incedas. Nunquam aliquis magnus contentionibus fuit. Semper aliqui sunt, qui iniquae parti etiam favent, nec quicquam tam solide unquam refutatur, quin adversarius inveniat, quod probabiliter oppugnet, et iudicia hominum ex verbis capiuntur, quia res istae subtiles a paucis intelliguntur. Ac ne per alios quidem hoc fieri vellem, nam ijs etiam respondebitur, ac per eorum latus in te tela dirigentur. Inimici et invidi habebunt ex scommatibus, quod rideant et gaudeant, sicuti iam factum in scurrili quodam scripto URSI novisti. Itaque cum CHRISTIANUS tuus ad te redeat, cuius tibi magnus usus esse poterit, pertexe eam telam quam feliciter orsus es, et cude nobis novum coelum denascente natura, et fatiscente industria hominum. Hac via ad immortalitatem homines grassantur.

De honoribus publicis quod est in litteris Rosaekrantianis, et feudo Imperij, mea sententia est, quod prius te vellem in possessionem feudi venire, antequam honores illos ambires, aut oblatos acceptares, alias fortean titulus tibi pro re sufficiet, et imputabitur honor pro beneficio reali. Simul ac vero consecutus es feudum promissum, tunc nollem te honores illos aspernari. Liberis tuis ita melius consultum erit, quorum TYCHO tuus ea est aetate, ut e re foret exteros iam visere, et cupit hoc ipse magnopere. Non dubium, quin ille ingenij bonitate et mansuetudine amicos multos sibi parare possit, sed auctoritas et existimatio ex literis et peregrinatione quaerenda ipsi est. De reliquis etiam non dubito te sollicitum esse, non solum ut haereditatem, sed etiam ut nobilitatem et integra omnia status politici relinquas. Haec ita accipe ut profecta ab eo animo, qui tibi tuisque sincere bene vult. Si praesens essem, plura de his; nam per calamum non ita licet omnia, neque fieri potest, ut quae meditata nobis sunt, veniant in mentem universa, cum pennam movemus. CRAGIUS tuus antiquum obtinet, ita et tu ne desinas TYCHO esse, qui fuisti.

De statu rerum nostrarum pleraque referre TYCHONIDES poterit. Publice nobis pax adhuc est, sed privatim multi male contenti. Variae sunt offensiones multorum de hoc statu rerum, et pauci sunt, qui non male ominantur. Amicitia Anglica ex tenui apta est. Cum CAROLO Sueco neque satis convenit, quia per absentiam Regis naves eius ingressae mare, quod iuris Danici. Apprehenderunt Lubecenses et alios. Adornantur Legati eo mittendi ab reditu PETRI FRANCISCI, quia viam paraturus modo in Sueciam est. Nos arces et oppida in Norvegia et Scania, Hallandia, Blekingia ad fines munimus et reparamus quantum possumus, sed a pecunia non satis instructi sumus. Rex Poloniae misit classem suam cum milite per fretum Oritanum, quae naufragium passa est, nec in Sueciam appulit. CAROLUS iam potitur fere toto regno, postquam hac aestate Finlandiam domuit, et partes illas Livoniae vicinas. De nobilibus captivis in Suecia, qui sunt praecipui ERICUS SPARRE, GUSTAVUS BANNER, ERICUS BANNER, TUROV BIELCKE et GEORGIUS POSE, constans fama supplicium sumendum. Miserunt huc ad Regem petentes eius intercessionem. Exigua spes Polono superest recuperandi regni hereditarij. Non obscurum, quid CAROLUS moliatur, etsi aliud prae se ferat.

De matre tua TYCHONIDES referre poterit, quae vidit et audivit. Amita valde infirma est, et oculi caligaverunt. Quid vero soror agat, et ubi iam sit, ex eius litteris accipies. Faxit aeternus pater, ut sperato tandem coniugio cum gaudio potiatur. Nos ea audivimus de rebus Domini LANGIJ, quae erigunt animos ad expectationem melioris fortunae. De morte IACOBI SEEFELD puto ab alijs ad te perscriptum. Vix duabus vel tribus septimanis a nuptijs duarum filiarum, quae uno die celebratae, in fine comitiorum insperato diem suum clausit. Serenissimus Rex modo in Iutia est, dicitur tamen CHRISTI natalia Haffniae celebrare velle. Utinam te per idem tempus videre tunc possemus. Posses tu gaudia nostra multis modis augere, sed spero nos te brevi visuros. Nec enim committes, quin ad nos aliquando excurras saltem exiguo comitatu, si non omnes adducas. Desiderio isto valde flagro, quod tu ut expleres, tuo cum bono forte fuerit. Iam si tibi prolixitate satisfeci, gaudeo. Si molestiam et taedium ingessi, ipse in causa es, qui ita requisivisti. Utut sit, rogo omnia pro candore tuo boni consulas, et quod occupatus haec sine cura exaraverim. Vale cum coniuge et liberis felicissime, quibus omnibus ita cupio, ut mihi ipsi bene esse velim. Salutat te uxor mea et frater eius LAURENTIUS et parentes. Item MICHAEL Chirurgus, alijque amici nonnulli, nominatim GABRIEL SPARRE et PETRUS BRAHE.

Iterum vale.
Dabantur Haffniae pridie Nonas Decembres anno 1599.
T. T.
NIC. CRAGIUS.
text.english:
**To the magnificent Lord, most noble in virtue, erudition, and birth, Lord Tycho Brahe, Governor of the Uraniborg of Benátky in Bohemia, his Lord and friend to be observed.**
Heartiest greeting.

Magnificent Lord Tycho, Lord and friend to be observed. It is true that, returned from the **English Legation**, I found your two letters at home; but how I could have answered them by the Wittenberg courier, I do not see. For in your letters it stands that you would go to Prague at the feast of **Pentecost**, by the Emperor's summons; but I arrived here after **Trinity Sunday**. So there is no [cause] that you should suspect this duty of letters was omitted from any fear of the more powerful — to whom my sincerity and constancy in friendship is now known by many signs, [too much] for it to breed me some new offence. Nor did anything of the English manners cleave to me from a longer association and use of them; but I am as far from those vices as I should wish you far from **carping and biting, through jest and play, your innocent and faithful friends** — among whose number place me thus: as one who never let study and observance fail, even if perhaps I have not in all things satisfied you with my service. Your affairs, my Lord Tycho, I learned abundantly from the letters given both to me and to **Rosenkrantz**; and it is great joy to me that you are in such a place that it may be well with you and yours, **peace gained and a Maecenas found, who so munificently and honourably wished your studies provided for**. Nor is there any of those you esteem who favours your fortune, with tongue and mind, more than I — not free, on that account, of envy. For I am sometimes forced to **defend the truth of this against those who detract from your praises** (never harmed by you in any injury), and, wrongly estimating your merits, cast them below that fortune. And I feared ill from some, when I had understood that your **Tychonides [Tycho the Younger], with our Mule, were sent here to seek the remaining instruments**; but by God's providence all kept silent, and none dared mutter against [it]. I myself helped them, as far as was in me and the matter allowed, and was the author [of advice] that they not show your letters to those from whom sincere help could not be hoped. For sometimes certain things have come into oblivion which it is better for us too to keep silent, than to hazard the doubtful aid of others. For the age of some men inclines to its extremity; and yet we fix all our thoughts in the filth of perishable things, little or not at all anxious about those eternal ones. Neither sleeping nor waking do we dream or meditate anything but money, to which we postpone glory, honour, and whatever is praiseworthy. We add something of human severity (I will not say cruelty), of which **sad examples were lately seen in two nobles and three commoners and others**. Rightly, then, have they cause to rejoice for whom either court favour shines here, or who have so prepared their affairs that they do not dread the tedium of migrating.

To me, glory be to God, nothing very adverse has yet befallen. By the Chancellor all that I did in this legation is approved — who saw that I left nothing wanting in fidelity and industry; but not so by others, for I know not what cause. That you promise to advance **our Mule to Medicine**, you do as worthy of your virtue and humanity; nor do I think you have had, or will ever have, one who cultivates and observes you with a sincerer mind. But I much fear that a longer stay with us has held [him] back from the Italian journey through this winter. But assuredly it had to be done so, nor could they expedite your affairs sooner. Let them render you the causes themselves, which you will not doubt are true. Since, however, that journey has not succeeded, perhaps by another method you will find counsel for helping him. If [your] mind is ever, in any way, to dismiss him from you, let it be done with good grace, and his age provided for maturely. Altogether, had we not wished him to be agreeable and obedient to you, it would have been provided otherwise — and will be provided (God favouring), if you dismiss him. But if he pleases you and yours, you will have him. With pleasure I hear so much benefit and honour rendered to **Tengnagel** by you and through you, and I wish that hereafter he may be such as you wish. Whence my friend **Typotius** got [the notion] that you deserted the fatherland at my instigation, I cannot guess. Whoever dared invent this neither knows you, nor understands what grief it brings to be sundered, by so great an interval of place, from the company and mutual sight of a most faithful friend. But Lord Typotius, if I remember rightly, himself heard from me **your departure lamented, both for the fatherland's sake and for mine** — much less, then, could he believe this done by my [will] — from whom I wish that suspicion removed from his mind. About the published book of which **Eske Bille [Eschylus Billeus]** had written you, I happened to hear nothing; nor do I think you would do worthwhile to forge any such [reply], you who can better place your hours; and it is true, as you add, that **many would relieve you of that labour without your will**. Ask **Tychonides what the son of Master Johannes Michaelius narrated at his father's table**. You will wonder, I know well, even as we grieve. What was reproached to me, too, in England and Belgium [Holland], it irks me to report.

**As to what you wish me to write about Duncan: I confess (as is the case) that I do not gladly wish to be mixed into the controversies of the learned, nor my name inserted in them. And perhaps the invention of that Hypothesis will be in greater glory if you simply illustrate and explain it, in a writing published under your name, than if you obscure it with contentions** — which indeed I know was done in the *Progymnasmata*, with this very plan, lest anyone afterward claim it for himself; but I should wish this done in a special writing, not so prolix, but such as could be proposed in the schools. Then I think it will scarcely happen further that anyone plucks at your praise. ***Duncan certainly, whatever he may at last have done privately, will never publicly arrogate it [the Hypothesis] to himself — he who did not even in a dream think of it, before he learned this from you as a mystery. Which, as soon as you had revealed [it], I remember was said by you, [that] more was communicated to him than a brother would perhaps wish to expound to a brother. And I have found, in these few days, among my papers, a sheet on which, at my request, you marked it for me — whether before Duncan's arrival, or at the time he was with you, I am uncertain.*** But my Lord Tycho, **suffer yourself to be advised this by a friend: set aside all polemics, and walk in the footsteps by which you began**. No one was ever great by contentions. There are always some who favour even the unjust side; nor is anything ever so solidly refuted but that the adversary finds something to attack plausibly; and men's judgements are taken from words, because those subtle matters are understood by few. Nor would I wish this done even through others, for they too will be answered, and through their flank weapons will be aimed at you. **Enemies and the envious will have, from the gibes, something to laugh and rejoice at — as you have now seen done in a certain scurrilous writing of Ursus.** And so, when your **Christianus [Longomontanus]** returns to you — who can be of great use to you — **weave on that web which you have happily begun, and forge us a new heaven, [while] nature is reborn and men's industry grows weary. By this way men advance to immortality.**

As to the public honours that are in Rosenkrantz's letters, and the **fief of the Empire**: my opinion is that I should wish you first to come into possession of the fief, before you sought those honours, or accepted them offered — otherwise perhaps the title will suffice you for the substance, and the honour will be imputed for a real benefit. But as soon as you have obtained the promised fief, then I should not wish you to spurn those honours. Your children will thus be the better provided for — of whom **your Tycho [the Younger] is of that age that it would be to the purpose now to visit foreign [lands], and he himself greatly desires this**. No doubt he can, by his good nature and gentleness, gain himself many friends; but authority and reputation are to be sought by him from letters and from travel. About the rest, too, I do not doubt you are solicitous — not only to leave an inheritance, but also nobility, and all things of political status, intact. Take these as proceeding from a mind that sincerely wishes well to you and yours. Were I present, [I would say] more of these; for by the pen not everything is so allowed, nor can it happen that what we have meditated all comes to mind, when we move the pen. **Your Cragius holds his old [self]; so do you too not cease to be the Tycho you were.**

Of the state of our affairs, Tychonides will be able to report most. Publicly we have peace still, but privately many are ill-content. Various are the offences of many about this state of affairs, and few there are who do not ill-omen. **The English friendship hangs by a thin [thread].** With **Charles the Swede** it agrees not enough, because in the King's absence his ships entered the sea of Danish right [the Sound], [and] seized Lübeckers and others. Legates are being prepared to be sent thither, on the return of **Peter Francis**, who is now to prepare the way into Sweden. We fortify and repair the castles and towns in **Norway and Skåne, Halland, Blekinge**, at the borders, as much as we can, but we are not sufficiently supplied with money. **The King of Poland sent his fleet, with soldiers, through the Øresund strait, which suffered shipwreck, and did not reach Sweden.** Charles now possesses almost the whole realm, after he subdued **Finland** this summer, and those parts of **Livonia** nearby. Of the **captive nobles in Sweden** — the chief of whom are **Erik Sparre, Gustav Banér, Erik Banér, Ture Bielke, and Georg Posse** — the constant report is that punishment will be taken [they will be executed]. They have sent hither to the King, seeking his intercession. Little hope remains to the Pole of recovering his hereditary realm. It is not obscure what Charles contrives, though he pretends otherwise.

Of your **mother**, Tychonides will be able to report what he saw and heard. [Your] **aunt is very infirm, and her eyes have dimmed [gone blind]**. But what your **sister [Sophie]** does, and where she now is, you will learn from her own letters. **May the eternal Father grant that she at last enjoy, with joy, the hoped-for marriage. We have heard such things of Lord Lange's [Erik Lange's] affairs as raise [our] spirits to the expectation of a better fortune.** Of the death of **Jacob Seefeld**, I think it has been written you by others: scarcely two or three weeks from the wedding of [his] two daughters (celebrated on one day), at the end of the Diet, he unexpectedly closed his day. **The Most Serene King is now in Jutland, but is said to wish to celebrate Christ's nativity at Copenhagen.** Would that we could see you at the same time then! You could augment our joys in many ways; but I hope we shall see you soon. For you will not fail to run over to us sometime, at least with a small retinue, if you do not bring all. With that desire I greatly burn — which, for you to fulfil, may perhaps be to your good. Now, if I have satisfied you by [my] prolixity, I rejoice; if I have brought trouble and tedium, you yourself are the cause, who so required [it]. However it be, I ask that you take all in good part, per your candour, and that, [being] busy, I have scratched these without care. Farewell most happily, with wife and children, to all of whom I wish [well] as I would wish well to myself. **My wife greets you, and her brother Laurentius, and [her] parents; likewise Michael the Surgeon, and some other friends — by name, Gabriel Sparre and Peter Brahe.**

Again, farewell.
Given at Copenhagen, the day before the Nones of December, the year 1599.
Yours wholly,
**Nic. Cragius.**

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondent.** **Incoming**, **Niels Krag (Nicolaus Cragius, c. 1550–1602)** — the Danish royal historian and diplomat (just back from the **English legation**), Tycho's steadfast friend — **to Tycho**.
- **Significance — the source of the Duncan-Liddel testimony, Krag's counsel, and a Baltic bulletin (a keystone letter).**
 - **★ The Duncan-Liddel testimony (origin).** The passage *"Duncan certainly … did not even in a dream think of [the Hypothesis] before he learned this from you as a mystery … and I have found, among my papers, a sheet on which you marked it for me"* **is the original of the verbatim testimony Tycho quoted** as "Krag's letter of 4 December last year" in **brahe-t_16000401001 (to Daniel Cramer, 1 April 1600)** and the **Duncan dossier brahe-t_15990926001 (to Cramer, 26 September 1599)**. Krag declines to enter the public controversy but **affirms, for the record, that Duncan Liddel learned the Tychonic world-system from Tycho** — and counsels Tycho to publish the system plainly under his own name "in a special writing … such as could be proposed in the schools."
 - **The counsel against polemic (memorable).** Krag's wise exhortation: *"Set aside all polemics … No one was ever great by contentions"*; enemies "will have, from the gibes, something to laugh at, as in **Ursus's scurrilous writing**." Instead, with **Longomontanus** returned, *"weave on that web you have happily begun, and **forge us a new heaven** … By this way men advance to immortality."*
 - **The imperial honours/fief advice.** Krag counsels Tycho to **secure the promised imperial fief *before* seeking the offered honours** (lest "the title suffice for the substance"); and notes **Tycho the Younger** is of an age to travel for "authority and reputation."
 - **The Mule/Medici and Tengnagel matters.** Tycho's wish to **place Claus Mule with the Medici** (delayed by winter); the honours rendered **Tengnagel**; and the denial (re **Jacobus Typotius**) that Krag "instigated" Tycho's departure — *"I lamented your departure, for the fatherland's sake and mine."*
 - **The Danish/Baltic bulletin.** Danish discontent and the **thin English friendship**; tension with **Charles of Sweden** (his ships in the Sound seizing Lübeckers); the **Polish fleet wrecked in the Øresund**; Charles's conquest of **Finland and Livonia**; and the **captive Swedish nobles — Erik Sparre, Gustav Banér, Erik Banér, Ture Bielke, Georg Posse — awaiting execution** (the **Linköping Bloodbath** prisoners; cf. brahe-t_16000919002, where Bacmeister reports the executions of March 1600). The **sad domestic executions** ("two nobles and three commoners") in Denmark.
 - **Family news.** Tycho's **mother (Beate Bille)** and **aunt** (blind); and — poignantly — **the hope for Sophie Brahe's long-deferred marriage to Erik Lange**, "Lord Lange's affairs" now raising "expectation of a better fortune" (cf. Sophie's own letter, brahe-t_15991024001, and brahe-t_16000000002). The death of **Jacob Seefeld**.
- **Cross-references.** The **Duncan-Liddel** keystone (origin of the testimony in brahe-t_16000401001 and brahe-t_15990926001); the **Ursus** thread; the **Sophie Brahe / Erik Lange** thread (brahe-t_15991024001, brahe-t_16000000002); the **Linköping prisoners** (brahe-t_16000919002); the **Mule/Medici** and **imperial-honours/fief** threads.
- **Persons & places named.** Niels Krag; **Tycho**; **Holger Rosenkrantz**; **Tycho the Younger** (*Tychonides*); **Claus Mule** (the Medici post); **Franz Tengnagel**; **Jacobus Typotius**; **Eske Bille**; **Johannes Michaelius** & son; **Duncan Liddel**; **Longomontanus** (*Christianus*); **Ursus**; **Charles IX of Sweden**; **Peter Francis** (legate); **Sigismund III of Poland**; the Linköping prisoners (**Erik Sparre, Gustav Banér, Erik Banér, Ture Bielke, Georg Posse**); **Christian IV**; **Beate Bille** (mother), the **aunt**, **Sophie Brahe** & **Erik Lange**; **Jacob Seefeld**; Krag's **wife**, her brother **Laurentius**, **Michael the Surgeon**, **Gabriel Sparre**, **Peter Brahe**. Places: **Copenhagen**, **Benátky**, **Norway/Skåne/Halland/Blekinge**, the **Øresund**, **Sweden/Finland/Livonia**, England, Jutland.
- **Calendar.** *Haffniae pridie Nonas Decembres anno 1599* — "the day before the Nones of December" = **4 December 1599 [O.S.]** (Denmark Old Style; the date Tycho cites as "*pridie Nonarum Decembris*"). Header, identifier, and label agree.
- **Correction.** 'ad Medicen' ('to Medicine') was mistranslated as 'to the Medici [court]', inventing a Florentine-Medici connection with no support in Dreyer's text (TBOO VIII p.212); corrected to reflect that the passage concerns Mulaenus's Italian medical studies.

documents.incipit: MYNN ganndsche ydmygh och wennlig helsenn nu och altid forsenndtt med Gud vor herre. …

text.original:
ERLICH OCH WELBYRDIGH MANNDTT THYGE BRAHE THILL KNUDTTSTRUP, HØFFUIDTZMANND OFFUER WRANIEBORGH OCH PAA DETT KEYSERLIGE SLOTT BENACHIA, MYNN GUNSTIG OCH SØNNDERLIG GODE WENN GANNDSCHE WENNLIGEN.

MYNN ganndsche ydmygh och wennlig helsenn nu och altid forsenndtt med Gud vor herre. Kierre Thyge Brahe, bethacher jeg Ethers Welb. gandsche storligenn for møgitt beuist gode och wenschaff, som j mig och mine giortt och beuist haffuer, huilkett igien att forschylde jeg gierne vill finndis redebonn och willigh.

Ethers Welb. schriffuelse haffuer jeg entpfanget, huorudaff jeg erfarer, att j och hues ether kiertt er lider well, Gud vere loffuett. Saa haffuer jeg epther ethers schriffuelse hiulpett ethers kierre sønn thill rette, och forschaffed hannom her en skude, som schall føre ethers instrumenter her fran Huenn och thill Lubech. Jeg haffde først fragtett itt schiff der thill med offuerlob paa; samme schipper beuilgett selff att reyse thill Huenn att besee instrumenterne, beretted att verre wmueligtt att faa y nogett stortt schiff for deris storhedts schyld, huorfor jeg endelig motte fragte en aabenn skude, som før er rørtt, med ethers sønns beuilninngh. Nyett aff denne landtz ende haffuer andre ethers wenner well schreffuitt ether thill om. Jeg ønscher Ethers Welb. med alle dj ether kiertt er altidtt att lide vell, dett schall verre mig ganndsche kiertt att høre. Och j hues maade jeg aff min ringe formuffue kand thiene Ethers Fromhed thill gode, skall j altid finnde mig willigh. Will hermed haffue Ethers Welb. med hues ether kiertt er Gud almectigste euindelig befalenndis. :

Aff Kiøbenhaffnn den 5 decembris a:o 99.
E:W: w: t:
Michell Vibe
egen handt.
text.english:
**Honourable and well-born man Tyge Brahe to Knudstrup, Captain over Uraniborg and at the Imperial castle Benátky [Benachia], my favourable and especial good friend — [written] quite friendlily.**

My quite humble and friendly greeting, now and always foresent with God our Lord. Dear Tyge Brahe, I thank Your Well-born[ness] quite greatly for the much-shown good and friendship which you have done and shown to me and mine — which to requite in turn I will gladly be found ready and willing.

I have received Your Well-born[ness]'s writing, from which I learn that you, and what is dear to you, fare well, God be praised. So, according to your writing, I have helped your dear son to rights, and procured him here a boat [*skude*], which shall carry your instruments from here, from Hven, to Lübeck. I had first chartered a ship for it, with an upper deck; the same skipper himself agreed to travel to Hven to inspect the instruments, [but] reported it to be impossible to get [them] into any large ship, on account of their size; wherefore I finally had to charter an open boat, as before mentioned, with your son's approval. News from this end of the land your other friends have surely written to you about. I wish Your Well-born[ness], with all that is dear to you, ever to fare well — that shall be quite dear to me to hear. And in whatever way I, of my slight means, can serve Your Piety for good, you shall always find me willing. Herewith [I] will have Your Well-born[ness], with what is dear to you, eternally commended to God Almighty.

From Copenhagen, the 5th of December, in the year [15]99.
Your Well-born[ness]'s willing servant,
Michel Vibe,
[his] own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Mikkel Vibe** (Michel Vibe, 1561–1624), Copenhagen merchant (later burgomaster); here a practical agent for Tycho in Denmark.
- **The Hven → Lübeck shipment.** A key document in the **removal of Tycho's instruments from Hven**: at Tycho's instruction, Vibe helped **Tycho's son** charter a boat (*skude*) to carry the instruments **from Hven to Lübeck**. He first hired a **decked ship** (*med overløb*) whose skipper went to Hven to inspect them, but found it **impossible to fit them into any large ship "on account of their size,"** so an **open boat** was chartered, with the son's approval. (The Baltic leg — Hven → Lübeck — complementary to the later Elbe leg, Hamburg/Magdeburg → Leitmeritz → Prague: cf. brahe-t_16000619001, …1009001.)
- **Titulature.** The address still styles Tycho *Høvedsmand over Uraniborg* ("Captain/governor over Uraniborg") **and** "at the Imperial castle **Benátky** [*Benachia*]" — registering his new Bohemian seat alongside the old Danish title.
- **Orthography.** Late-16th-c. Danish: *erlich* (ærlig), *welbyrdigh* (velbyrdig), *høffuidtzmannd* (høvedsmand), *helsenn* (hilsen), *skude* (small boat), *offuerlob* (overløb, deck), *skipper*, *forschylde* (forskylde, requite), *Fromhed* (Piety, an honorific). *E:W: w: t:* = *Eders Velbyrdigheds villige tjener* ("Your Well-born[ness]'s willing servant"). Reading-verified as **Danish**.
- **Calendar.** *Kiøbenhaffnn den 5 decembris a:o 99* = **5 December 1599**; Denmark = **Old Style**. Header agrees with the label.

No fabrication, omission, or mistranslation found.
