text.original:
ERUDITISSIMO ET
PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO DOMINO IOANNI
KEPLERO, MATHEMATICO EXIMIO, NUNC IN STIRIA VEL AUSTRIA
DEGENTI, AMICO SUO IMPRIMIS DILECTO.

EXOPTATISSIMAS et eruditissimas tuas
literas, Vir Doctissime, et ob eximias ingenij tui dotes, licet de facie mihi
necdum cognite, plurimum tamen dilecte, accepi præcedenti æstate Wittebergæ, paulo antequam inde discederem, cum
in procinctu essem itineris Bohemici. Ideoque tum ijs respondendi nulla dabatur
opportunitas, uti neque postea usque in hoc tempus ob rerum mearum
vicissitudinem et novum earundem in locis peregrinis apparatum. Nactus autem iam
aliquantulum otij unâ cum mittendi ad te meas commoditate, non diutius
rescriptione supersedendum arbitratus sum. Quæ ab initio de maleferiato isto
URSO tui purgandi causa
prolixe commemoras, non equidem tot verbis et tam
exquisita declaratione indiguissent, cum ipsemet alias te satis excusatum
habeam, nihilque tibi imputem, quod is literas tuas, et eas quidem, uti nunc ex
te percipio, mutilatas et depravatas, sui ornandi causa (nam sic forte opus
habuit) isti quod evulgavit scurrili et maledico scripto, te inscio et invito,
inseruerit. De Hypothesibus meis ab illo præreptis et pro suis venditatis, non
tanta esset quæstio, nisi in isto inverecundo et figmentis atque calumnijs
scatente libro honorem et existimationem meam, imo patriam, prosapiam, domum
honestissimam, impudentissimis et scelestissimis mendacijs, scurrili et vesano
calamo arrodere et, quantum in ipso est, defamare, atque talia in publicum typis
spargere non erubuisset, cum tamen ipsemet fateatur in præfatione, me bene esse
de illo meritum, et adest mihi carmen quoddam ipsius, licet insulsa (uti solet)
vena effutitum, propriaque eius manu scriptum, quo mihi gratias agit, quod non
saltem per plusculos dies, cum aliquando Uraniburgi apud me esset, cibo et potu illum largiter aluerim,
sed et insuper discedenti pecunias dederim. En qualem pro his atque alijs refert
gratiam! Occasionem sumpsit horum convitiorum, quod in primo nostro Tomo
Epistolarum Astronomicarum extet CHRISTOPHORI ROTHMANNI Mathematici Landgraviani Epistola, in qua
URSUM istum impurum vocat
nebulonem, qualis enim esset, in aula sui
Principis, ipsa experientia iam edoctus, tum quoque relatione
aliorum ex ijs locis, ubi antea vixerat. Ego vero in alia quadam ad dictum
ROTHMANNUM Epistola, id
saltem mimetice refero et simul insinuo, quo dolo quædam ex meis clanculum
subtraxerat, quorum nonnulla recepi, quæ etiamnum ipsius manu (quam negare non
potest) exarata penes me sunt, et sane si mihi otium a gravioribus studijs tunc
superfuisset, Epistolas illas, dum typis nostris excudebantur, quoad singula
contenta revidendi, non passus fuissem, librum illum a me editum istius efferi
et putidi URSI nomine
conspurcari, non quod eiuscemodi adiuncto epitheto indignus censeri possit, aut
ulla illi, secundum hominum consueta iudicia loquendo, sic fieret iniuria, prout
non saltem ROTHMANNUS, sed
etiam multi alij, qui eum satis novere, perspectum habent. Verum quia non
libenter in meis scriptis ullius vitam et mores, qualescunque sint, perstringo,
unde etiam in Epistola Magnifici Domini IACOBI
CURTIJ optimæ memoriæ postea Wandesburgi a me Libro de Mechanica Astronomia subiuncta, nomen
istius omisi, utut dictus Dominus IACOBUS
CURTIUS eum diserte appellaret et plagiarium meum insuper
intitularet. Sed accidit, ut dum studiosis quibusdam ex meis hunc laborem
corrigendi operas typographicas in isto Epistolarum libro concredidissem, atque
illis originalia, prout manuscripta erant, tradidissem, illi nihil immutandum
duxerint, neque me magis serijs distentum interpellare ausi sint, ideoque omnia,
prout autographa habebant, imprimi permiserint,
sicque incuria quadam factum est, quod ipsius nomen cum epithetis appositis
isthic retentum sit. An vero hæc sufficiens et iusta satis sit causa, tam supra
omnem modum vesana malitia, in me et meos, adeoque patriam ipsam debacchandi,
brevi dispiciemus. Potuisset equidem de iniuria, si qua foret sibi illata,
conqueri, atque hanc licitis medijs amoliri, non autem ex effræni vindictæ
cupiditate, tam impotenti animo furere, omniaque longe deteriora reddere. Neque
tamen est cur existimes, quod in istum nugatorem sim
commotior, quam meæ conditiones admittant, ut tu (candido tamen animo) infers,
non enim Cæsaris ira (uti quidam etiam
ad me perscripsit) dignum arbitror. At quoniam contra ius et fas, contraque
laudatissimas Imperij Constitutiones me scripto plus quam famoso præter omnem
veritatem et meritum meum dehonestare perfricta fronte conatus est, iure cum
ipso agi curabo, atque secundum leges reprimi et castigari. Subduxit is se
Praga in Silesiam paulo post meum isthuc accessum, sed nuper, uti
rescivi, tacite redijt, forte quod ibi me non amplius esse intellexerat, at quam
longæ mihi sint manus, etiamsi præsto non sim, brevi in Aresto detentus, et
postea in iudicium protractus sentiet. Quoniam vero intelligo ex tuis, te
spurcas et scurriles istas chartas non vidisse, mitto exemplar, ut et de tua
Epistola isthic promptius dispicias, ac cætera, qualia sint, æstimes. Videbis
utique quam insana, maledica, conviciosa et fœtida sit compilatio, quamque suum
authorem apprime redoleat; impudentiores calumnias nunquam forte legisti.
Abhorrent ab ijs aures omnium cordatorum et proborum.

Verum de isto effero URSO Dithmarsico plus satis, neque enim tot a te vel me prolatis
verbis dignus est, et si ipsum intus et in cute (ut aiunt) nosses (non iam
loquor de Scabie Gallica, qua ob vitæ impuritatem scatet) idem mecum testareris,
imo iamdudum testatus fuisses. Unicum saltem addam, Hypotheses nostras asserendi
causa, licet hoc minimum sit, et longe plura validioraque in promptu habeam
argumenta. Hypotheses illas anno 1584 a me primum excogitatas, quas iste sibi
arrogare non veretur, ipsius revera inventum esse, quis crediderit, qui eum
ullis observationibus cœlestibus, unde novæ Hypotheses extruendæ, nunquam
assuefactum fuisse novit? Imo si unius Planetæ, præsertim e tribus superioribus
apparentem locum per hanc neotericam suppositionem, secundum omnes
particularitates demonstrare nequierit (uti vix poterit) cui quæso intelligenti,
suum esse inventum, fidem faciet? Sed non ille saltem, verum et alij, dum ego
mea premo atque in lucem edere cunctor, hanc excogitationem sibi attribuere ausi
sunt. Inter quos est Scotus quidam, DUNCANUS nomine, Helmstadij Medicinæ et Mathematum Professor, qui cum hanc
rationem a me in Dania accepisset, eam
primum Rostochij privatim suis discipulis
dictavit, nec meam esse inficiatus est, sed
Tychonicam ultro appellavit, quod in propinquo essem et me, si aliter faceret,
id facile resciscere posse vereretur. Clam tamen ijs, quibus maxime fidebat
discipulis, in aurem susurrabat, se quidem honoris causa eam hypothesin mihi
ascribere, ut plus gratiæ et authoritatis habere possit apud auditores suos,
revera tamen suam ipsius esse, quod et postea Helmstadij remotior a me factus, audentius et inverecundius
commisit, partim in publicis suis prælectionibus, partim intimationibus
quibusdam. Sed ista fraus et impostura cum ab alijs, tum præsertim Domino
Doctore DANIELE CRAMERO apud
Stetinenses Verbi ministro, Viro
singulariter erudito, qui Scoti istius Rostochij olim auditor erat inter præcipuos unus, detecta est,
et suo forte tempore plenius detegetur. Si otium superfuerit, curabo exemplum
literarum eius ad Nobilissimum Virum OLIGERUM ROSÆKRANTZIUM meum consanguineum, cuius Pædagogum
dictus CRAMERUS tum agebat, hac de
re in Daniam post meum discessum
scriptarum, hisce apponi. Sic quoque RŒSLINUS, licet magis astute et caute, mea pro suis venditare
præsumpsit, ita tamen, ut mihi hanc speculationem non derogarit, sed se eam,
postquam similia adinvenisset, in libro meo de Cometa anni 77ti reperisse fateatur. Egregius sane sucus, si fidem mereri posset,
nam liber ille meus, cuius meminit, per 9 annos antea impressus erat et plurimis
de hac a me introducta cœlestium revolutionum dispositione iam innotuerat. At si
nihil aliud, id saltem et quam maxime fraudem prodit, quod dum hanc Hypothesin,
ut suus fieret partus, in nonnullis aliter formare conatus sit, eamque, si Dijs
placet, emendare, in enormes absurditates impegerit, ipsam symmetriam ac
proportionem Revolutionum interturbando, atque ab ipsis apparentijs alienissimam
statuendo; ut inde satis liqueat, eum non saltem has hypotheses nequaquam
intelligere, nedum ut earum author sit, sed ne quidem ullas alias, imo
Astronomiæ penetralia necdum introspexisse.

MAGINUM
Italum nunquam existimarim tale quid affectasse. Quod si fecit, literis propria
manu ad me datis, quibus se illam Hypothesin ex libro nostro secundo de Æthereis
Phænomenis primum perspexisse, sibique apprime placere,
modo Martis orbis Solarem transire posset (putavit enim ex vulgata sententia
reales esse in cœlo orbes) fassus est, contraria admisit. A MAGINO vero, si qui alij huius
speculationis conscij sunt, hac occasione habuerunt, inter quos etiam est
FRANCISCUS PATRITIUS, qui
eius mentionem in erudito alias de nova Philosophia Volumine facit, is quidem
meam esse expresse asserit, sed eam ita pervertit, et per ignorantiam male
accomodat, et contra mea ipsius postulata et assumpta eam coinquinat et
insectatur, ut plurima isthic ex ipsius relatione apposita pro meis non
agnoscam, quod etiam publice protestabor. Sed de
Hypothesi hac vel alia non multum alterabimur, quæstio est: quis eam rationem
invenire possit, tam in quantitatibus et motionibus continuis, quam discretis,
ut phænomena cœlestia per omnia fatentur.

Hoc opus, hic labor est, et sic spectemur agendo.

Porro siquidem ab initio innuisti, te a MÆSTLINO primum tibi a me inscriptas accepisse, qui etiam, quas
ad illum dederam, tecum communicavit, miror ipsum nec illis neque alijs, quas
prius, imo ante aliquot annos miseram, quippiam tanto tempore respondere
voluisse. An hoc sit viri ingenui et Mathematicis disciplinis solerter imbuti,
tute æstima. Non est alias mihi moris, ignotos literis prævenire, sed utplurimum
ab illis præveniri soleo, nedum ut ad meas tanto temporum tractu responsionem
nullam recipiam. Sed imposterum ei, quem plurimi semper feci, uti scripta mea in
publicum edita testari poterint, meis ingratis, uti video, literis non ero
molestus. Placent tibi quæ ad illum et te de re Astronomica scripsi. Atqui ea se
sic omnino habere, certo exploratum habeo, multoque plura et his maiora adhuc
abstrusa esse, quæ antecessorum, tam veterum quam recentiorum, diligentiam
eluserunt.

Suades, imo multis rationibus, quas ego non improbo, persuadere
conaris, ut Observationes meas cœlestes publici iuris faciam, quod quidem suo
tempore præstare non detrectabo, cum his, quæ tu affatim adducis, tum alijs de
causis. Verum tam cito id efficere, antequam pleraque ex ijs, quæ a me in
Astronomicis instaurata sunt, atque selectoribus ex ijsdem observationibus
fundata, in lucem prodierint, non consultum duco, nam præter alia, hoc ipsum,
quod tu de hypothesibus meis mihi præreptis et de CYPRIANI Ephemeridibus, alijs
quoad partem attributis et depravatis, refers, terret atque dissuadet.
Obtinebitis tamen aliquando, favente cœlesti Numine, ea, quæ a me plurimis annis
in cœlestibus denotata sunt, non quidem tam manca et mutila, ne dicam incerta,
prout ea sunt, quæ pauculis chartis mandavit WERNERUS, vel potius IOHANNES SCHŒNERUS (nam WERNERI observata nulla vidi, tu, si
quæ habes, communica) a REGIOMONTANO et GUALTHERO relicta, sed exacta sibique constantia atque in tanta
simul copia, ut vix magno quodam volumine constringi queant. Adiungam præter
librum Epistolarum, de quo supra, Mechanica nostra, huc spectantia, quæ
instrumenta, quibus ultra 20 annos usus sum, complectuntur, si commode tibi
Praga adferri poterint. Ex Epistolis
præter alia prius insinuata perspicies, an eæ tam parvi momenti atque inutiles
sint, veluti præ animi impotentia occæcatus ille censor vult, et an laudatissimæ
memoriæ Landgravio WILHELMO quidpiam derogent (veluti idem impudenter, ut Filio eius
me invisum redderet, commentus est). Ex Mechanicis colliges, quanto molimine
Astronomiæ redintegrationem aggressus sim, quantaque in his usus diligentia,
quantisque impensis. Invenies etiam ibidem circa posteriorem partem
consignationem eorum, quæ hactenus in hoc genere studiorum exanthlavi, quæque
inposterum, aspirante cœlestium Opifice, pertexenda restant, tum quoque literas
illas laudatæ memoriæ Domini IACOBI
CURTIJ et MAGINI, quarum antea mentionem feci. Misissem illuminatum (uti
vocant) exemplar, quo promptius omnia discerneres, sed nunc non suppetit.

De libro tuo, uti is cum suo authore meretur, semper, ex quo mihi introspectus est, honorifice sensi, nec te aut alios,
quocunque modo de hisce sublimibus et a vulgi captu remotis disciplinis præclare
merentes, et veritatis nucleum serio affectantes laude sua privavi aut privabo
unquam, quin potius extuli, et in posterum extollam. Hoc præcipuum est, quod in
tuo ingenioso illo scripto cum plerisque tamen alijs errore communi admittis,
non probo, te realitatem quandam orbibus cœlestibus inesse statuere, quo sic
promptius Coperniceis
imaginationibus viam struas, eisque facilius subscribas. Motiones cœlestes
Symmetriam quandam observare, et rationes subesse, cur circa hæc vel alia centra
a terris vel Sole dispariter remota convolvantur, non negarim, sed harmonia et
dispositionum analogia ex posteriori, ubi motus et motuum occasiones ad amussim
constiterint, non autem ex priori, uti et tu et MÆSTLINUS voluistis, petenda erit;
quin et hîc difficillime invenienda. Quam operam si quis superaddiderit, illum
antiquum PYTHAGORAM, qui harmoniam
concinnam cœlestibus, imo toti mundo inesse præsentiebat, superare dixerim. Et
licet circulares in cœlo motiones nonnunquam angulares quasdam et varias
figuras, atque ut plurimum oblongas composito suo motu efficere, curiose singula
trutinanti, videri possint: fit tamen id per accidens et abhorret ratio ab hac
suppositione. Oportet enim omnino ex circularibus componi astrorum circuitus,
alias perpetuo uniformiter et æquabiliter in se non revertentur et perennitatem
frustrabunt, præterquam quod minus simplices, magisque anomalæ erant, nec etiam
doctrinæ et usui accommodæ. De ☿ non est cur doleas, eius stellam a me
non esse observatam, aut quod idem cum COPERNICO in eius Phænomenis ostendendis prætendere velim. Licet
enim a Solis radijs rarissime digrediatur et inclinatior apud nos in Dania sit sphæra, quam Frueburgi in Prussia, ubi
vixit COPERNICUS, pluresque
mare circa Insulam habitationis nostræ
emiserit vapores, quam Vistula: plurimis
tamen vicibus, imo pene singulis annis, dum in Uraniburgo nostro sideribus invigilarem, tam Eous quam
vespertinus, accurate a nobis cœlitus denotatus: ut neque huius astri, utut rarissime pateat et multis anfractibus sit obnoxium,
nos fugere possit semita, nequaquam ab aliorum dubijs animadversionibus, uti
coactus est facere COPERNICUS, mutuanda. De ♀ quantum hactenus pervestigare
licuit, certum est, eius Apogæum non multum a Solari antrorsum removeri, aliter
quam sensit COPERNICUS, nec
eidem tamen plane uniri, ut ALBATEGNIJ imitatione volunt Alphonsinæ. In Eccentricitate tamen eius non est par ratio, nam
eam multo minorem Solari deprehendi. An mutabilis sit,
nondum dixerim, sed non magnopere id probabit vel improbabit tua per se
ingeniosa ratiocinia.

E stella Polari vel quavis alia subtiliter eruere, an orbis annuus
Terræ a COPERNICO
excogitatus, si is esset, octavæ sphæræ stellis aliquantulam insinuet
Parallaxin, iam ante sæpius et diligenter experiri tentavi: verum nihil
eiuscemodi, diligenti facta animadversione, hactenus comperi. Nam stellam
polarem, quocunque anni tempore supra vel infra polum præcise observatam,
adhibita eiusdem ab illo remotione vera (quæ hoc anno est 2° 51' 1O'', et
cum 6° 13' 26'' ♈ et ♎ Meridianum supra et infra Polum
transit) eandem in dimidio scrupulo, imo intra quartam vel sextam eius partem
(subtiliora visus non discernit) præbuisse poli sublimitatem animadverti, quod
et CHRISTOPHORO ROTHMANNO,
qui Coperniceæ Speculationi indulgens aliquid discriminis hîc subesse opinatus
est, iamdudum indicavi, ut hinc nihil pro COPERNICO tuo (cuius concinnam et
ingeniosam speculationem alias admirari et deprædicare soleo) tuendo, residuum
sit solatij. Petas aliunde, si dabitur.

Sed de his atque alijs plenius tecum iucunde et perlubenter agam,
pluraque ex meis communicabo, si me, uti polliceris, aliquando inviseris, quod
tibi iam minus molestum erit quam antea, cum in Bohemia non admodum a vobis remota, nunc sedes Uraniæ novas
fixerim, atque in arce Cæsariana Benachia
quinque milliaribus Praga remota habitem. Nam
me a Cæsarea Maiestate, huc e
Germania clementissime vocatum, et
benignissime ac liberaliter receptum esse, te ab alijs iam antea cognovisse (ex
quo dimidium iam annum hîc subsistam) existimo. Nolim tamen ut fortunæ asperitas
te nos accedere compellat, sed potius arbitrium proprium et erga communia studia
amor et affectio. Quicquid tamen id erit, invenies me non fortunæ, qualiscunque
illa sit, sed tuum amicum, qui etiam in adversa sorte suo consilio et auxilio
tibi nequaquam sit defuturus, sed potius te ad optima quæque promoturus. Et si
mature accesseris, eas forte rationes inveniemus, quibus tibi et tuis inposterum
rectius quam antea consultum erit. Vale. Quando rescripseris, literas ad Dominum
Doctorem BLOTIUM, Viennam, qui Cæsaris Bibliothecæ isthic præest, mitte: is eas facile
Pragam, unde me mox invenient, procurabit.

Iterum quam felicissime vale.

Dabantur Benachiæ sive Venetijs
Bohemorum die 9 Decembris Stylo renovato 1599.

Tui Amantissimus
TYCHO
BRAHE,
manu propria scripsi.

POSTSCRIPTA.SI se occasio commoda obtulerit, rogo ut MÆSTLINUM meo nomine moneas de Eclipsibus ab illo observatis,
cum meis conferendis, ob Meridianorum differentiam eruendam. Dum enim relego
exemplum literarum ad MÆSTLINUM,
video me isthic mentionem fecisse Eclipsis Solis, quæ die 25 Februarij Anni 99  contigit, ubi nescio qua incuria digiti Ecliptici denotantur 10¾: forte
quod per aliquem ex studiosis meis, calculum nimis festinanter exequentem, sic
perperam reperti. Cum verior ratio ex meis Tabulis, prout ipsemet postea
disquisivi, præbeat digitos 9½, qua etiam quantitate Sol deficere a quodam ex
meis Uraniburgi isthic (ut 4 residuorum
instrumentorum, quæ præ magnitudine efferri tam cito nequibant, curam haberet)
relicto studioso deprehensus est, et tempora alias per armillam Æquatoriam 18
pedum in Diametro, a principio usque ad finem (fuit enim toto isthic tempore
serenum) meæ restitutioni apprime congruentia cœlitus denotata sunt, quæ erant
eiuscemodi, ut deliquium inciperet isthic H. 10 M. 10, finem haberet H. 12 M.
19, ideoque medium existeret H. 11 M. 12. Hæc ad MÆSTLINUM, quando illi scripseris,
referre poteris, ipsumque rogare atque efficere, ut ab ipso Eclipses tam Lunares
quam Solares, quotquot hactenus observavit, per te, siquidem ille mihi
rescribere nolit, obtineam.

Reperi inter chartas meas exemplum literarum CRAMERI, de quo prius memini, iamdudum
nescio in quos usus descriptum, quod hisce addo, et simul exemplum Epistolæ
cuiusdam M. IOHANNIS
CHRISTIERNI Dani, nunc Lugduni Batavorum studiorum causa
degentis, qui mihi erat domesticus, cum liber noster de Cometa anni 77
Uraniburgi imprimeretur, et paulo
post quam URSUS iste apud me
fuerat, accessit, ideoque quam fraudulenter egerat, ex cæteris meis studiosis
cognitum habuit. Addidi etiam testimonium Scribæ Nobilissimi Viri ERICI LANGIJ, cui URSUS tunc inservijt, qui etiam præsto
erat, cum iste suum herum comitatus mecum fuit. Quam testificationem ipsemet
ERICUS postea Magdeburgi in præsentia publici Notarij
confirmavit, et quæcunque alias URSUS in famoso isto scripto habet, quatenus sibi ea de re
quippiam constabat, falsissima esse testatus est, erecto de duodecim eiuscemodi
punctis, quæ illi proponebantur, e libro illo famoso excerptis, publico, uti
vocant, Instrumento, quod alias videbis; hinc cætera æstimabis.

T. B.

Ne vacaret sequens Paginæ facies,
ascribi feci tria Epigrammata ex ijs, quæ a me, postquam Benachiam veni, lusa sunt. Plura carmina a varijs,
postquam e Dania in Germaniam migravi, concinnata, cum Domino Doctore
BLOTIO veteri amicitia mihi
iuncto communicavi, ipsumque ut te eorundem participem redderet, rogavi, quæ si
acceperis, plura inde percipies, et si qui sunt apud vos Poëtæ arguti, uti
procul dubio sunt, fac ut numerum adaugeant.
text.english:
**To the most learned and excellent man, Master Johannes Kepler, distinguished mathematician, now living in Styria or Austria, his especially beloved friend.**

Your most longed-for and most learned letter, most learned Sir — and, for the surpassing gifts of your talent, most dear to me, though not yet known to me by face — I received last summer at Wittenberg, a little before I departed thence, when I was on the point of the Bohemian journey. And so no opportunity was then given of answering it, nor afterwards until this time, on account of the vicissitude of my affairs and the new setting-up of them in foreign places. But having now gained a little leisure, together with the convenience of sending a letter to you, I judged that I should put off writing back no longer. What at the outset you recount at length, to clear yourself concerning that mischievous Ursus, did not indeed need so many words and so elaborate an explanation, since I otherwise hold you sufficiently excused, and impute nothing to you in that he inserted your letter — and that too, as I now learn from you, mutilated and corrupted — for the sake of adorning himself (for so perhaps he had need) into that scurrilous and slanderous writing which he published, without your knowledge and against your will. Concerning my Hypotheses snatched away by him and vended as his own, there would not be so great a question, had he not, in that shameless book teeming with fabrications and calumnies, blushed not to gnaw — with a scurrilous and frenzied pen, and, so far as in him lies, to defame — my honour and reputation, nay, my fatherland, my lineage, my most honourable house, with the most impudent and wicked lies, and to scatter such things abroad in print; even though he himself confesses in the preface that I had deserved well of him, and I have a certain poem of his — though poured out (as is his way) from a tasteless vein, and written in his own hand — in which he thanks me that, when he was once at Uraniborg with me, I not only fed him generously with food and drink for several days, but also gave him money on his departure. See what thanks he returns for these and other kindnesses! He took occasion for these abuses from the fact that in the first volume of our *Astronomical Letters* there stands a letter of Christoph Rothmann, the Landgrave's mathematician, in which he calls that impure Ursus a scoundrel — for what sort of man he was, Rothmann had been taught by experience itself at his Prince's court, and also by the report of others from the places where Ursus had formerly lived. I, however, in a certain other letter to the said Rothmann, merely report it by way of mimicry, and at the same time hint by what guile he had secretly filched certain things of mine — some of which I recovered, and which are still in my keeping, written in his own hand (which he cannot deny). And indeed, had I then had leisure to spare from weightier studies to review those Letters, as to each particular content, while they were being printed at our press, I should not have suffered the book published by me to be defiled with the name of that savage and rank Ursus — not that he could be reckoned unworthy of such an attached epithet, or that any wrong would thus be done him, speaking by men's customary judgments (as not only Rothmann, but also many others who know him well, are aware). But because I do not willingly, in my writings, censure anyone's life and morals, whatever they be — whence also, in the letter of the Magnificent Lord Jacob Curtius of best memory, afterwards appended by me at Wandsbek to the book on the Mechanics of Astronomy, I omitted his name, although the said Lord Jacob Curtius expressly named him and moreover entitled him my plagiarist. But it happened that, when I had entrusted to certain of my students the labour of correcting the printer's proofs in that book of Letters, and had handed them the originals as they were in manuscript, they thought nothing should be changed, nor dared to interrupt me while I was taken up with more serious matters, and so allowed everything to be printed as they had it in the autographs; and thus by a certain carelessness it came about that his name, with the appended epithets, was retained there. But whether this be a sufficient and just enough cause for raging with such measureless mad malice against me and mine — and indeed against my fatherland itself — we shall shortly see. He could have complained of the wrong, if any had been done him, and removed it by lawful means; not raged with so ungoverned a mind, out of an unbridled lust for revenge, and made everything far worse. Yet there is no reason for you to suppose that I am more stirred against that trifler than my condition allows — as you infer (with candid mind, however) — for I do not judge him worthy of the Emperor's wrath (as someone also wrote to me). But since, against right and divine law, and against the most praiseworthy Constitutions of the Empire, he has with brazen face attempted to dishonour me by a more-than-libellous writing, beyond all truth and my desert, I will see to it that he be proceeded against at law, and repressed and chastised according to the laws. He withdrew from Prague into Silesia a little after my arrival there, but lately, as I learned, he returned secretly — perhaps because he understood that I was no longer there; but how long my hands are, even if I be not at hand, he will shortly feel: detained under arrest, and afterwards dragged into court. And since I understand from your letter that you have not seen those filthy and scurrilous papers, I send a copy, that you may both more readily make out your own letter there, and judge the rest, of what kind they are. You will assuredly see how insane, slanderous, abusive, and fetid the compilation is, and how thoroughly it reeks of its author; more impudent calumnies you have perhaps never read. The ears of all sensible and upright men shrink from them.

But enough, and more than enough, of that savage Ditmarsh Ursus; for he is not worthy of so many words uttered by you or me; and if you knew him "inside and under the skin" (as they say) — I do not now speak of the French scab, with which he teems on account of the impurity of his life — you would testify the same with me, nay, would long since have testified it. Let me add just one thing for the sake of asserting our Hypotheses, though this be the least of it, and I have far more and stronger arguments at hand. Who would believe that those Hypotheses, first devised by me in the year 1584, which he does not fear to arrogate to himself, are really his invention — knowing that he was never practised in any celestial observations, from which new Hypotheses are to be built up? Nay, if he cannot demonstrate, according to all particulars, the apparent place of even one planet — especially of the three superior — by this newfangled supposition (as he scarcely will be able), to what intelligent man, I ask, will he prove that the invention is his own? But not he alone — others too, while I keep my own work back and delay to bring it to light, have dared to attribute this device to themselves. Among whom is a certain Scot, Duncan by name, Professor of Medicine and of the Mathematics at Helmstedt, who, having received this method from me in Denmark, first dictated it privately to his students at Rostock, and did not deny it was mine, but of his own accord called it "Tychonic" — because I was nearby, and he feared that, if he did otherwise, I could easily find it out. Yet secretly, to those students he most trusted, he whispered in the ear that he ascribed that hypothesis to me only for honour's sake, that he might have more favour and authority with his hearers, but that it was really his own; which afterwards, having become more remote from me at Helmstedt, he did more boldly and shamelessly, partly in his public lectures, partly in certain printed notices. But this fraud and imposture has been detected — both by others and especially by Doctor Daniel Cramer, minister of the Word among the people of Stettin, a singularly learned man, who was once one of the chief auditors of that Scot at Rostock; and in its own time it will perhaps be more fully exposed. If leisure remains, I will see to it that a copy of his letter — written about this matter to the most noble Holger Rosenkrantz, my kinsman (whose tutor the said Cramer then was), and sent into Denmark after my departure — be appended to these. So too Roeslin, though more cunningly and cautiously, presumed to vend my [hypotheses] as his own — yet in such a way that he did not deprive me of this speculation, but confesses that he found it, after he had himself devised similar things, in my book on the Comet of the year [15]77. A fine bit of juice indeed, if it could earn belief — for that book of mine which he mentions had been printed nine years before, and the arrangement of the celestial revolutions introduced by me had already become known to very many. But if nothing else, this above all betrays the fraud: that while he tried to form this Hypothesis somewhat differently, so that it might become his own offspring, and to "emend" it (if it please the gods), he ran into enormous absurdities — disturbing the very symmetry and proportion of the Revolutions, and setting it up most alien to the appearances themselves; so that it is thence sufficiently clear that he not only by no means understands these hypotheses (let alone is their author), but not even any others — nay, has not yet looked into the inner sanctum of Astronomy.

I should never have thought that the Italian Magini affected any such thing. But if he did, he admitted the contrary in a letter given to me in his own hand, in which he confessed that he had first perceived that Hypothesis from our second book on the Aetherial Phenomena, and that it greatly pleased him — provided the orb of Mars could cross the Solar [orb] (for he thought, on the common opinion, that the orbs in heaven are real). And from Magini, if any others are privy to this speculation, they had it on this occasion — among whom too is Francesco Patrizi, who makes mention of it in his otherwise learned volume on the New Philosophy. He indeed expressly asserts it to be mine, but so perverts it, and through ignorance misapplies it, and against my own postulates and assumptions defiles and worries it, that I do not acknowledge as mine very many things there set down on his report — which I shall also publicly protest. But about this Hypothesis or another we shall not be much exercised; the question is: who can find that method — both in continuous quantities and motions, and in discrete ones — such that the celestial phenomena answer to it in every respect.

*This is the work, this the toil — and so let us be judged by our doing.*

Further, since at the outset you hinted that you first received from Maestlin those [letters] addressed by me to you, who also shared with you those I had sent to him, I marvel that he was willing to answer nothing in so long a time — neither to those nor to others which I had sent earlier, indeed some years ago. Whether this be [the act] of an honest man, skilfully imbued with the mathematical disciplines, judge for yourself. It is not otherwise my custom to anticipate strangers with letters, but for the most part I am wont to be anticipated by them — let alone that I should receive no reply to mine over so long a stretch of time. But henceforth I will not trouble with my letters — ungratefully received, as I see — him whom I have always esteemed most highly, as my published writings can testify. You are pleased with what I wrote to him and to you on astronomical matters. And indeed I hold it for certain that these things are altogether so, and that many more and greater than these still lie hidden, which eluded the diligence of our predecessors, both ancient and modern.

You urge — nay, with many reasons, which I do not disapprove, you try to persuade — that I make my celestial Observations public, which in its own time I will not refuse to do, both for the reasons you abundantly adduce and for others. But to do it so soon, before most of what has been restored by me in astronomy, and founded on the choicer of those observations, has come to light, I do not think advisable; for, besides other things, this very fact which you report — about my hypotheses snatched from me, and about Cyprian's Ephemerides, in part attributed to others and corrupted — frightens and dissuades me. Yet you shall obtain at length, by the favour of the heavenly Deity, what I have noted in the heavens over very many years — not indeed so defective and mutilated, not to say uncertain, as are those which Werner (or rather Johannes Schöner) committed to a few pages — left by Regiomontanus and Walther (for I have seen no observations of Werner; you, if you have any, share them) — but exact and self-consistent, and at the same time in such abundance that they could scarcely be confined in one great volume. Besides the book of Letters, of which above, I will add our *Mechanics*, pertinent here, which comprise the instruments I have used for over 20 years, if they can conveniently be brought to you from Prague. From the Letters, besides other things hinted before, you will perceive whether they are of such small moment and useless, as that censor — blinded by impotence of mind — would have it, and whether they derogate anything from the Landgrave Wilhelm of most praiseworthy memory (as the same man impudently fabricated, to render me hateful to his Son). From the *Mechanics* you will gather with how great an effort I undertook the renewal of astronomy, and with how great diligence and how great expense I employed in these things. You will also find there, toward the latter part, a record of what I have hitherto drained off in this kind of studies, and what remains hereafter to be woven through, with the Maker of the heavens favouring; and likewise those letters of the Lord Jacob Curtius of praised memory and of Magini, which I mentioned before. I would have sent an "illuminated" (as they call it) copy, that you might more readily discern everything, but it is not now to hand.

Of your book, as it deserves along with its author, I have always thought honourably, ever since I looked into it; nor have I ever deprived — nor will I ever deprive — you or others who in any way deserve nobly of these sublime disciplines, remote from the grasp of the crowd, and who seriously aim at the kernel of truth, of their due praise; but rather I have exalted them, and shall exalt them hereafter. This is the chief thing which, in that ingenious writing of yours — though you admit it with most others by a common error — I do not approve: that you lay down a certain reality to be in the celestial orbs, so as the more readily to build a way to the Copernican imaginations and the more easily to subscribe to them. That the celestial motions observe a certain symmetry, and that there are reasons underlying why they revolve about these or other centres differently distant from the earth or the Sun, I would not deny; but the harmony and the analogy of the arrangements is to be sought *a posteriori*, once the motions and the occasions of the motions have been exactly established — not *a priori*, as both you and Maestlin wished; nay, even so it is most difficult to find. And if anyone should add this labour, I should say that he surpasses the ancient Pythagoras, who divined that a fitting harmony was present in the heavens — nay, in the whole world. And although the circular motions in heaven can sometimes seem, to one who weighs each thing curiously, to produce by their composite motion certain angular and various figures, and for the most part oblong ones, yet this happens *per accidens*, and reason shrinks from this supposition. For the circuits of the stars must be composed entirely of circular [motions]; otherwise they will not perpetually return uniformly and equably upon themselves, and will frustrate perpetuity — besides that they would be less simple and more anomalous, and not suited to doctrine and use either. Concerning Mercury, there is no reason for you to grieve that its star has not been observed by me, or that I would pretend the same as Copernicus in displaying its Phenomena. For although it very rarely departs from the Sun's rays, and the sphere is more inclined with us in Denmark than at Frauenburg in Prussia, where Copernicus lived, and the sea around the island of our dwelling sends up more vapours than the Vistula, yet on very many occasions — nay, almost every year, while I kept watch over the stars at our Uraniborg — it was accurately noted by us in the heavens, both as morning and as evening star; so that the path of this star, however rarely it lie open and however subject to many windings, cannot escape us — by no means to be borrowed from the doubtful observations of others, as Copernicus was forced to do. Concerning Venus, so far as it has been possible to investigate hitherto, it is certain that its apogee is not much moved forward from the Solar one — otherwise than Copernicus thought — yet not entirely united with it, as the Alphonsine [Tables], in imitation of Albategnius, would have it. In its eccentricity, however, the ratio is not equal, for I found it much less than the Solar. Whether it is mutable, I would not yet say; but your reasonings, ingenious in themselves, will not greatly prove or disprove it. To find out subtly, from the Pole-star or any other, whether the annual orb of the Earth devised by Copernicus, if it existed, would insinuate some little parallax into the stars of the eighth sphere, I have before now often and diligently tried to test; but, careful observation being made, I have hitherto found nothing of the kind. For I have observed that the Pole-star — observed precisely above or below the pole at any time of year, with its true distance from the pole applied (which this year is 2° 51' 10'', and it crosses the meridian above and below the pole at 6° 13' 26'' of Aries and Libra) — gave the same elevation of the pole within half a minute [scruple], nay, within a quarter or sixth part of it (finer things the sight does not discern); which I long ago indicated to Christoph Rothmann too, who, indulging the Copernican speculation, supposed that some discrepancy lay hidden here — so that hence there is no consolation left for defending your Copernicus (whose elegant and ingenious speculation I am otherwise wont to admire and extol). Seek it elsewhere, if it shall be given.

But of these and other things I will deal with you more fully, pleasantly and most gladly, and will share more of my own, if you, as you promise, shall some time visit me — which will now be less troublesome to you than before, since I have now fixed Urania's new seat in Bohemia, not very far removed from you, and dwell in the imperial castle Benátky, five miles distant from Prague. For that I was most graciously called hither from Germany by the Imperial Majesty, and most kindly and liberally received, I think you have already learned from others (since I have now stayed here half a year). Yet I should not wish that the harshness of fortune compel you to come to us, but rather your own choice and your love and affection toward our common studies. Whatever it shall be, you will find me not fortune's friend — whatever that be — but yours, who even in adverse lot will by no means fail you with his counsel and aid, but rather will promote you to all that is best. And if you come in good time, we shall perhaps find ways by which it will be better provided for you and yours hereafter than before. Farewell. When you write back, send your letters to Doctor Blotius at Vienna, who is in charge of the Emperor's Library there; he will easily forward them to Prague, whence they will soon reach me.

Again, fare most happily.
Given at Benátky, or the Venice of the Bohemians, the 9th day of December, New Style, 1599.
Your most loving
Tycho Brahe;
I wrote [this] with my own hand.


*[Postscript:]* POSTSCRIPT. If a convenient occasion offer itself, I ask that you remind Maestlin in my name about the Eclipses observed by him, to be compared with mine, for deriving the difference of meridians. For while I re-read the copy of my letter to Maestlin, I see that I made mention there of the Solar Eclipse which fell on the 25th of February of the year [15]99, where, by some carelessness or other, the eclipse-digits are noted as 10¾ — perhaps because they were thus wrongly found by one of my students, who carried out the calculation too hastily. Whereas the truer reckoning from my Tables (as I myself afterwards investigated) yields 9½ digits — which is also the quantity by which the Sun was found to be deficient by one of my [men], a student left at Uraniborg (so that he might have charge of the four remaining instruments, which, on account of their size, could not be carried away so quickly); and the times, observed from the heaven by means of the Equatorial armilla 18 feet in Diameter, from beginning to end (for it was clear there the whole time), agreed exactly with my restitution, and were of this kind: that the eclipse began there at 10h 10m, had its end at 12h 19m, and so the middle fell at 11h 12m. These things you may report to Maestlin, when you write to him, and ask and bring it about that I may obtain from him — through you, if he be unwilling to write back to me — the Eclipses, both Lunar and Solar, as many as he has hitherto observed. I have found among my papers a copy of Cramer's letter, of which I made mention before, transcribed long ago for I know not what use, which I add to these; and at the same time a copy of a letter of a certain Master Johannes Christiernus, a Dane, now living at Leiden for the sake of his studies, who was a member of my household when our book on the Comet of the year [15]77 was being printed at Uraniborg, and who arrived a little after that Ursus had been with me, and therefore learned from my other students how fraudulently he had acted. I have added also the testimony of the secretary of the most noble Erik Lange, whom Ursus then served, and who was likewise at hand when that man, attending his master, was with me. This testification Erik himself afterwards confirmed at Magdeburg in the presence of a public Notary, and testified that whatever else Ursus has in that libellous writing — so far as anything of the matter was known to him — was utterly false, a public Instrument (as they call it) having been drawn up concerning twelve such points laid before him, excerpted from that libellous book, which you will see elsewhere; from this you will judge the rest. T. B.  /  That the next page's surface might not be empty, I had three Epigrams inscribed there, from those composed by me after I came to Benátky. More poems, fashioned by various hands after I migrated from Denmark into Germany, I shared with Doctor Blotius, joined to me in old friendship, and asked him to make you a sharer of them too; if you receive them, you will gather more therefrom, and if there are any keen Poets among you (as without doubt there are), see that they increase the number.

documents.apparatus:
- **Edition of record.** Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia* vol. VIII (*Epistolae*). MS witness: A = Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, cod. Vindob. lat. 10702 (the Tycho–Kepler correspondence codex).
- **Date / place.** Dateline *"die 9 Decembris Stylo renovato 1599"* — explicitly **New Style** (Gregorian), from *"Benachia sive Venetijs Bohemorum"* — **Benátky nad Jizerou**, the imperial castle c. 5 (German) miles from Prague, glossed with the pun *"the Venice of the Bohemians"* (*Benátky* is the Czech word for Venice). The catalogue label confirms n.s.
- **Historic significance.** This is **Tycho's substantive reply to Kepler's first approach** and the letter in which Tycho *invites Kepler to Benátky* — the contact that brought Kepler into Tycho's household in 1600, gave him access to the Mars observations, and led (after Tycho's death in Oct 1601) to Kepler's elliptical-orbit discovery and the *Rudolphine Tables*. One of the cornerstone documents of the Scientific Revolution. It belongs with the rest of the Tycho–Kepler arc in this corpus (Kepler's Ursus-apologia 15990200001; the 1600 quarrel pair 16000408001 / 16000000001; the employment letters 16000828001 / 16001017001; Herwart's quote of Kepler-on-Ursus 16000911001).
- **The Ursus affair.** **Ursus** = **Nicolaus Reimers Bär** (*Raimarus Ursus Dithmarsus*, "the Ditmarsh Bear"), imperial mathematician at Prague, who had published a geo-heliocentric world-system as his own (*Fundamentum astronomicum*, 1588) and savagely attacked Tycho — incorporating a mutilated copy of **Kepler's flattering 1595 letter** — in *De astronomicis hypothesibus* (1597). Kepler's long apology (for the unauthorised use of his letter) is what Tycho here graciously waves aside. Tycho recounts: Ursus's own preface admits Tycho "deserved well of him"; Tycho holds a thank-you poem in Ursus's own hand for hospitality and money at Uraniborg; Ursus took offence at **Rothmann's** letter (printed in Tycho's *Epistolae astronomicae*, 1596) calling him a *nebulo* ("scoundrel"), and at Tycho's own report of Ursus's theft of papers. Tycho disclaims responsibility for the printed epithets (left in "by a certain carelessness" of his student proof-correctors), and announces a **libel suit under the Imperial Constitutions** — Ursus had fled to Silesia and returned secretly ("how long my hands are … he will feel, under arrest and dragged into court"). *(Ursus in fact died in August 1600, before judgment.)*
- **The priority dispute over the Tychonic system.** Tycho dates his invention of the hypotheses to **1584** and rebuts four rival claimants/transmitters:
 - **Ursus** — denied competence (no observational basis).
 - **Duncan Liddel** (*"a certain Scot, Duncan"*), Professor of Medicine and Mathematics at **Helmstedt**: got the method from Tycho in Denmark, taught it at **Rostock** as "Tychonic" (out of fear), but privately claimed it as his own, and at Helmstedt did so openly in lectures and printed *intimationes*. The fraud "detected especially by **Doctor Daniel Cramer**, minister at Stettin," once Liddel's chief auditor at Rostock and then tutor (*Paedagogus*) to **Holger Rosenkrantz**, who wrote about it to Rosenkrantz after Tycho left Denmark. — This is the same Liddel plagiarism dossier as **brahe-t_15990926001**, **brahe-t_15991204001** (Krag's testimony-origin), and **brahe-t_16000324002** (where Tycho presses Krag as eyewitness).
 - **Helisaeus Roeslin** — claimed to have found the system in Tycho's *De cometa* (1577) only *after* independently devising similar ideas; Tycho notes the book was printed nine years before and that Roeslin's attempted "emendation" wrecked the symmetry of the revolutions.
 - **Giovanni Antonio Magini** of Bologna — exculpated: Magini admitted in an autograph letter that he first saw the hypothesis in Tycho's *De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis* (the "second book on the Aetherial Phenomena"), objecting only that the orb of Mars would have to cross the Solar orb (Magini holding the **real-orbs** view). **Francesco Patrizi** got it via Magini and mentioned it in his *Nova de universis philosophia* (1591), attributing it to Tycho but garbling it against Tycho's own postulates — which Tycho says he will publicly disown.
- **The methodological core (historically poignant).** Against Kepler's *Mysterium Cosmographicum* (1596), Tycho objects to two things: (1) Kepler's positing of **real (solid) celestial orbs** as a bridge to Copernicanism — Tycho's comet work had abolished solid spheres; (2) Kepler's **a priori** harmonic method — Tycho insists the harmony of the heavens be sought *a posteriori*, "once the motions and their occasions are exactly established," and would rank one who succeeds above **Pythagoras**. Crucially, Tycho here **defends strictly circular motion** ("the circuits of the stars must be composed entirely of circulars … reason shrinks from" oblong/angular composite figures) — the very assumption Kepler would overturn, with Tycho's own data, in deriving the elliptical orbit of Mars.
- **The anti-Copernican parallax argument.** Tycho rehearses his decisive empirical objection to the heliocentric system: repeated precise observations of the **Pole-star** (its true polar distance "this year 2° 51' 10''," meridian transits at 6° 13' 26'' of **Aries** and **Libra**) show **no annual stellar parallax** — the pole-altitude constant to within a half-, quarter-, or sixth-minute (the limit of the eye). He had reported this to **Rothmann**, who had expected a discrepancy. Hence "no consolation remains for defending your Copernicus" (whose ingenuity Tycho nonetheless praises). Also: observational claims on **Mercury** (☿ — observed at Uraniborg "almost every year," not borrowed as Copernicus had to) and **Venus** (♀ — apogee not much advanced beyond the Solar, eccentricity much less than the Solar). *(Planetary/zodiac glyphs are kept in the source block and named in English by this chapter's convention: ☿ = Mercury, ♀ = Venus, ♈ = Aries, ♎ = Libra.)*
- **What Tycho promises to send.** A copy of Ursus's libel (so Kepler can see his own mutilated letter); the *Epistolae astronomicae* (with the Curtius and Magini letters, and the vindication of Landgrave **Wilhelm IV** against Ursus's slander aimed at turning Wilhelm's son **Moritz** against Tycho); and the *Astronomiae instauratae mechanica* (the instruments "used for over 20 years," and the closing record of work done and to do) — *"if they can conveniently be brought from Prague."* He cites the meagre observational remains of **Werner / Schöner / Regiomontanus / Walther** as the foil to his own exact and abundant store.
- **Other persons & references.** **Michael Maestlin** (Kepler's Tübingen teacher and the conduit for Tycho's earlier letters), reproached for never replying; **Cyprian** = **Cyprian Leovitius** (Cyprianus Leovicius), whose *Ephemerides* Kepler had reported as misattributed/corrupted — cited by Tycho as a further reason to delay publishing; **Hugo Blotius (*Blotius*)**, imperial librarian at **Vienna**, named as the forwarding address for Kepler's reply.
- **Latin tags & allusions.** *"Hoc opus, hic labor est"* — **Virgil**, *Aeneid* 6.129 (of the hard return from the underworld); joined to *"spectemur agendo"* ("let us be judged by our deeds," cf. **Ovid**, *Metamorphoses* 13.120). *"intus et in cute"* — **Persius**, *Satires* 3.30 ("inside and under the skin," = through and through). *"Scabies Gallica"* — the "French scab" (syphilis), a period slur. *Astronomiae penetralia* — "the inner sanctum of astronomy." *exanthlavi* (Greek-derived, *ἐξαντλέω*) — "I have drained off / accomplished [with toil]."

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing POSTSCRIPTA (the Maestlin eclipse-comparison reminder; the 25 Feb 1599 solar eclipse — 9½ digits via the 18-ft equatorial armilla, begin 10h10/end 12h19/mid 11h12; the enclosed Cramer + Johannes-Christiernus letters + Erik Lange's notarial testimony against the 12 points of Ursus's libel; the 3 Benátky epigrams via Blotius), restored from Dreyer VIII pp.210–211.
- **Why a student stayed behind at Uraniborg.** Recovers the reason a lone student was left at Uraniborg after Tycho's 1597 departure from Denmark: to have charge of four large instruments too bulky to be carried away quickly — direct evidence that the removal of Tycho's instrument-park from Hven was piecemeal and constrained by the sheer size of some pieces.
- **Fits the letter's own later reference** to instruments "pertinent here" (the *Mechanica*) being "conveniently brought to you from Prague," situating this abandoned rump of equipment within the broader 1597–99 dispersal/relocation of Tycho's observational apparatus.
- No new named person; "a student" (studiosus) remains unnamed in this passage, as in the existing translation.
- **Correction.** Restored the day-number "25" dropped from the postscript's Latin eclipse-date clause ("quæ die 25 Februarij Anni 99 contigit", TBOO VIII p.210, line 12) and the fraction "¾" dropped from the English rendering of the erroneous eclipse-magnitude figure ("digiti Ecliptici denotantur 10¾", TBOO VIII p.210, line 13), both per Dreyer's printed text.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Read the full Dreyer extract (TBOO VIII, the letter proper on pp.203-211) as page images-4, 5-8, and 9-11, plus targeted re-reads of pp.208-209 to check the Mercury/Venus planetary glyphs. Collated the opening and closing formulas and every proper name, date, sum, and place-name across the c. 2600-word body and postscript: Wittenberg, Bohemia, Rothmann, Jacob Curtius, Wandsbek, Prague/Silesia, 1584, Duncan/Helmstedt/Rostock, Daniel Cramer/Stettin, Holger Rosenkrantz, Roeslin, the 77 comet book (9 years), Magini, Francesco Patrizi, Maestlin, Cyprian, Werner/Schoner/Regiomontanus/Walther, 20 years, Pythagoras, Mercury/Venus apogee-eccentricity passage, the pole-star figures (2 51' 10'', 6 13' 26''), Benatky (five miles from Prague, half a year), Blotius/Vienna, and the full postscript apparatus (Cramer's letter, Johannes Christiernus/Leiden, Erik Lange's secretary, Magdeburg notarization, twelve points, three epigrams). All of this matches Dreyer and the English renders it faithfully with no fabrication, omission, pronoun-flip, or hedge-loss found. Two isolated numeric slips surfaced in the eclipse-postscript: our house Latin drops the day-number '25', and the English drops the fraction '3/4' from the reported eclipse-digit count. Per the grading rule, the text error alone caps this at grade Possible even though neither defect touches the letter's substantive content (the Ursus dispute, hypothesis priority, or the Kepler relationship).

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). our own the transcribed original has silently dropped the day-number '25' from the eclipse date; Dreyer prints it plainly. The English translation happens to supply '25th' correctly, but not from our own the transcribed original as published — the house Latin itself is defective. Dreyer prints: *"quæ die 25 Februarij Anni 99 contigit" (TBOO VIII p.210, line 12)*.
- **mistranslation** (medium). The English silently drops the fraction '¾', reporting the erroneously-calculated eclipse magnitude as a flat 10 digits instead of 10¾ digits — a real alteration of the numeral Tycho is in the process of correcting (against the true 9½ digits given two sentences later). At: “"the eclipse-digits are noted as 10"”.

**Repaired.** Verified both defects directly against the Dreyer page image for TBOO VIII p.210, which plainly prints "quæ die 25 Februarij Anni 99 contigit" and "digiti Ecliptici denotantur 10¾". Both readings are unambiguous in the page image and match the audit's claims exactly. No other page of the extract was needed since both defects sit in the same postscript passage on p.210. Nothing else in the letter was touched.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD HUGONEM BLOTIUM.

S.

CHARISSIME et præstantissime vir, amice plurimi semper mihi faciende. Cum forte per literas communis amici nostri Domini Doctoris HELLERI aut etiam aliunde intellexeris, me nunc in Bohemia degere, et occasiones, cur huc venerim, simul ad te, ut existimo, relatæ sint, nolo nunc pluribus ijs recensendis immorari. Id saltem te rogo, ut veteris inter nos amicitiæ Basileæ, uti scis, contractæ, et postea cum in Dania adhuc subsisterem, continuatæ memor, eorum etiam, quæ cum apud Nostrates hærerem, pollicitus es, recorderis, nimirum ut catalogum librorum in inclyta istic Cæsareana Bibliotheca, præsertim quod ad Philosophicos et Mathematicos attinet, mecum communices. Id si etiamnum in hac ob loci maiorem commoditatem præstiteris, rem equidem acceptissimam feceris. Literas hisce adiunctas cum libris quibusdam excellenti in Styria Mathematico IOHANNI CÖPLERO destinatis ad eum, ubicunque isthic vel alibi in vicinia moretur, rogo, ut per certum internuncium dirigere non degraveris. Habitavit antea in urbe Græcia, nescio an etiamnum ibi sit, intellexi enim eorum res turbatas esse. Si quod ab ipso responsum acceperis, Pragam ad dictum Doctorem HELLERUM mitte, mox me inveniet. Vale. Dabantur properanter ex arce Cæsareana Girsitza, ubi nunc aliquantisper ago, donec lues Epidemica Bennachiæ, ubi alias ex clementissima Cæsaris voluntate habito, prorsus remiserit.

Iamque iterum et sæpius vale.
14. die Decembris Anno 1599.
Tui amantiss.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria scripsi.

Intellexi vitriolum Ungaricum et
terebinthinam etiam Ungaricam, tum
quoque tartarum ex vino Ungarico cadis
adhærentem isthic in mediocri esse precio, quæ
tamen singula hîc care veneunt. Si itaque, quanti singulorum ex his libra isthic, præsertim si in
aliqua copia prostent, et simul quo precio libra Croci vestratis emi queat,
mature indicaveris, rem gratam sic præstiteris. Sique ex ijs pro assignato
precio placuerint, mittam pro qua emantur pecunia. Vellem ex tribus materijs
primo nominatis multum habere, utpote de singulis centenarium ad
minimum.

Adiunxi carmina quædam a varijs Poëtis, postquam e Dania in Germaniam transmigravi, in mei gratiam concinnata, quæ per
otium legere poteris posteaque cum Dom. IO. KEPLERO communicare, atque ipsi cum fasciculo illi
destinato mittere. Si qui apud vos arguta vena præditi sunt Poëtæ, uti esse
non dubito, fac numerum adaugeant. Memini enim te aliquando e Vienna vestra satis acuta et sonora in Daniam mihi misisse Epigrammata.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Hugo Blotius.**

Greeting.

Dearest and most excellent man, friend ever to be most highly esteemed by me. Since you have perhaps learned — through the letters of our common friend Master Doctor Heller, or also from elsewhere — that I now dwell in Bohemia, and since the occasions for which I came hither have, as I suppose, at the same time been reported to you, I do not now wish to linger in recounting them at greater length. This only I ask of you: that, mindful of the old friendship contracted between us at Basel (as you know), and afterward continued while I still resided in Denmark, you remember also those things which you promised while I was staying among our [people] — namely, that you would share with me the catalogue of the books in the renowned Imperial Library there [at Vienna], especially as regards the Philosophical and the Mathematical [ones]. If you would perform this even now — on account of the greater convenience of [my present] location — you would do me a most acceptable thing indeed. The letters adjoined to these, with certain books destined for the excellent Mathematician in Styria, **Johann Kepler**, I ask that you not find it burdensome to direct to him — wherever he may be staying there, or elsewhere in the vicinity — through a sure intermediary. He dwelt formerly in the city of Graz; I know not whether he is even now there, for I have understood that their affairs have been disturbed. If you receive any answer from him, send it to Prague, to the said Doctor Heller; it will soon find me. Farewell. Given hastily from the Imperial castle of Girsitz, where I now stay for a little while, until the epidemic plague at Benátky — where otherwise, by the most clement will of the Emperor, I dwell — has entirely abated.

And now again, and often, farewell.
The 14th day of December, in the year 1599.
Most loving of you,
Tycho Brahe,
I wrote with my own hand.

I have learned that Hungarian vitriol, and Hungarian turpentine too, and likewise the tartar that clings to the casks of Hungarian wine, are to be had there at a moderate price, though each of these sells dear here. If, then, you would let me know in good time what a pound of each of these costs there — especially if they are available in any quantity — and at the same time at what price a pound of your [region's] saffron may be bought, you will thereby do me a welcome service. And if, at the price stated, they suit me, I will send money with which they may be bought. I should like to have a good quantity of the three materials named first, that is, at least a hundredweight of each.

I have enclosed certain poems by various poets, composed in my honour since I removed from Denmark into Germany, which you may read at your leisure and afterward share with Master Johannes Kepler, sending them to him along with that bundle intended for him. If there are among you poets gifted with a witty vein — as I do not doubt there are — see that they add to the number. For I recall that you once sent me, from your Vienna, epigrams sharp and sonorous enough, into Denmark.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Hugo Blotius** (Hugo Blotz, 1533/4–1608), the **Imperial Court Librarian** at Vienna (the *Hofbibliothek*), a Netherlandish humanist; Tycho's friend from their **Basel** days (1568–70) and during Tycho's Danish years. The witness is, fittingly, in **Blotius's papers at the Vienna Nationalbibliothek** (cod. Vindob. lat. 9737).
- **The two requests.** (1) Tycho asks Blotius to make good an old promise: to send him the **catalogue of the Imperial Library's holdings, especially in Philosophy and Mathematics** — now the more useful since Tycho is close by in Bohemia. (2) **Of high significance for the Tycho–Kepler relationship:** Tycho asks Blotius to forward an **enclosed letter and certain books to "Johann Kepler [*Iohanni Cöplero*], the excellent Mathematician in Styria,"** wherever he may be — Tycho noting that Kepler "dwelt formerly in **the city of Graz** [*urbs Graecia* = Graz/Graecium]," but that he hears "their affairs have been disturbed." This refers to the **Counter-Reformation expulsion of Protestants from Inner Austria/Graz** (1598–1600), which was about to drive Kepler out — and which helped bring him to Tycho at Benátky in **February 1600**. The letter thus documents Tycho's outreach to Kepler **two months before** their first meeting.
- ***Doctor Helleri / Hellerum*** = "Doctor Heller," a common friend at Prague serving as Tycho's forwarding address. *Identification flagged*: not securely fixed (a Prague-based Heller).
- **Place.** *arce Caesareana Girsitza* = the Imperial manor of **Girsitz / Jiřice** (near Benátky), where Tycho had temporarily withdrawn while the *lues epidemica* (plague) at **Benátky** abated. (The edition label gives only "Girsitz"; the body supplies the date.)
- **Calendar.** *14. die Decembris … 1599* = **14 December 1599**; Bohemia (imperial) = **New Style** (no *n.s.* tag in the edition, but the imperial location fixes it). Header so marked.
- **Subject matter.** This is Tycho's own request, appended to a letter otherwise devoted to his temporary quarters at Girsitz during the Benátky plague, for raw materials used in his chemical/spagyric work: Hungarian vitriol (a sulphate salt, a staple of Paracelsian pharmacy and of Tycho's own medicinal preparations), Hungarian turpentine, cask-tartar from Hungarian wine (cream of tartar, likewise a spagyric staple), and saffron (*crocus*) — he asks Blotius to price each by the pound and offers to send money once quantities and prices are confirmed, wanting "at least a hundredweight" of the first three.
- **Addressee.** Hugo Blotius (1533–1608), the Dutch-born prefect of the Imperial Library in Vienna and a long-standing correspondent of Tycho's since their student days together at Basel (Thoren, *Lord of Uraniborg*) — Vienna is the natural market for goods arriving from Hungary, which explains why Tycho asks Blotius rather than a Prague contact.
- **Kepler cross-reference.** Tycho refers to "Master Johannes Kepler" by name and asks Blotius to pass on a bundle of commemorative poems to him — at this date (14 December 1599 N.S.) Kepler had not yet arrived in Prague (he would not meet Tycho in person until early 1600), so this is a trace of the pre-meeting correspondence network through which the two astronomers were already circulating material before their historic collaboration began.
- **Literary networking.** Tycho mentions poems written in his honour by "various poets" since his move from Denmark into the Empire, and explicitly solicits more from poets in Blotius's Viennese circle, recalling that Blotius had once sent him "sharp and sonorous" epigrams from Vienna — evidence of Tycho actively cultivating a corpus of Latin encomiastic verse around his own person and exile, material that (via Kepler) may have been intended for a future printed collection.
- **Crux: *Croci vestratis*.** "Your [region's] saffron" is translated as ordinary saffron (*Crocus sativus*, a valuable spice/dye/medicinal ingredient), consistent with its being priced alongside vitriol, turpentine and tartar by the pound; the same Latin word could in principle denote an alchemical "crocus" preparation (e.g. crocus martis, an iron-oxide medicinal powder), but the absence of any qualifying noun (*Martis*, *Veneris*, etc.) and the plain commodity-pricing context both favour the literal spice/dye reading.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VIII pp.214-217 read as page images (Read pages=1-4). Collated the full Latin letter (opening, the Kepler/Koppler request, the Girsitz/Benatky place-names, the vitriol-turpentine-tartar postscript with its prices and hundredweight quantity, and the closing poems paragraph) word-for-word against the printed page. Text matches the transcribed original exactly (allowing long-s normalization). Every proper name (Heller, Cöplero/Kepler, Girsitza, Bennachiae) and number (14 December 1599, centenarium/hundredweight) in the English has a clean counterpart in both the transcribed original and Dreyer. No fabrication, omission, mistranslation, hedge-loss, or text-error found.

documents.editorial_note:
**Text recovered.** The letter's recovered passages — dropped by a defective transcription of the source and absent until now — has been restored from the text of record and translated. The Source and English columns below are now complete.

**Direction note.** **Incoming** letter — *from* the Bremen astrologer **Ludolf Riddershusen** *to* Tycho. A technical **astrological consultation** (seven questions on primary directions and house systems).

text.original:
DEM
WOLLEDLEN GESTRENGEN VNDT HOCHGELARTEN HERRN TICHONI BRAHE,
ERBGESESSEN ZU KNUDTSTRUP, ITZIGER ZEIT ABER AHM
KEYSERLICHEN HOFE ZU PRAGE, MEINEM GROSSGUNSTIGEN HERRNN VNDT
PRÆCEPTORI.
PRAGE.

S. P.

GENEROSE ac Magnifice Heros, fautor et Mœcenas summa
observantia colendissime, post humilem promptorum meorum officiorum oblationem
Generositati Vestræ pro universis et singulis ex singulari heroica erga me
immeritum innata affectione in me collatis beneficijs denuo et imprimis ago et
habeo gratias quas possum maximas. Deinde Generositatem Vestram celare nequeo,
quod iam elapso anno nullas scripserim literas. Causa fuit non modo domesticarum
mearum curarum in hac mea solitudine intollerabilis moles, verum etiam rumor
circa præterita Bacchanalia hîc et Hamburgi
de discessu Generositatis Vestræ ex hac lachrymarum valle sparsus, quo auditu
ita eram perterrefactus, ut iam de studio Astrologico, cui hactenus summopere
incubui, ob defectum Tabularum ab alijs editarum actum esse arbitrarer. Tandem
vero iam ante aliquot dies ex literis lætabundis Domini DAVID. FABRICIJ, Generositatem Vestram
cum tota inclita familia
Pragam salvam et incolumem pervenisse, Illustrissimumque,
potentissimum atque invictissimum Imperatorem, Dominum nostrum Clementissimum,
Generositati Vestræ clementissime favere, laus Deo, cognovi, quapropter etiam
cum illius, tum vero Generositatis Vestræ, literis motu impulsus, hasce meas
Fabricianis adiungere volui.

Quandoquidem igitur Generositas Vestra iam antea in suis
Resolutionibus mihi benigne communicatis, circa quæstionem de modo dirigendi
indicavit: Non esse modum dirigendi exactiorem, quam is, qui a REGIOMONTANO traditus est, totidem vero
gradus Meridianum transeuntes, quot quemlibet alias positionis Circulum, sed
numerandos potius in Meridiano, quia illic directe permeant, quodque in
obliquissima Sphæra tunc unâ dirigendi ratio locum habeat; utut domorum
distributio Regiomontana istis administrari nequeat. Et hanc ob caussam Generos.
Vestra potius approbet CAMPANI divisionem,
quæ totum Cœlum ubique respicit et universalis existit. Cui tamen Generos.
Vestra æqualem per Eclipticam, ob planetarum iuxta hanc incessum, partitionem
applicare soleat, imitatione veterum Astrologorum; verum alia atque alia in hac
et illa ordinatione considerando, prout vel ratione totius Cœli vel solius
Zodiaci, requiratur animadversio. Hæc, inquam, etsi satis luculenter indicata
sint, nihilominus Generositatem Vestram reverenter et obnixe rogatam velim, ut
Generositas Vestra mihi unum atque alterum breve schema
operationis et demonstrationis communicari dignetur.

Haberem insuper nonnulla alia non aspernanda, videlicet an directio
iuxta gradus Zodiaci eiusque Polum etiam possit inducere effectus, sicut illa,
quæ respectu Poli Æquatoris fit, et an tunc eodem modo mensuratio annorum sit
instituenda iuxta motum ☉lis in Radice Genituræ,
sicut alias, an vero diversa hîc mensuratio sit ordinanda.

Deinde quoniam in directione Ascendentis omnium Astrologorum
unanimi consensu observari hactenus solitæ sint ascensiones obliquæ sub
elevatione Poli cuiusque Regionis, in qua quis natus est, an etiam Generositas
Vestra censeat, quod si quis per aliquot multos annos in longinqua aliqua
regione multum a loco seu regione nativitatis distante moretur, an nihilominus
directio Ascendentis ex ascensionibus obliquis, quas Tabula Directionum sub
elevatione Poli regionis nativitatis demonstrat, facienda sit; an vero ex
Ascensionibus obliquis sub elevatione Poli istius loci, sub quo quis degit, ut
exempli gratia natus est aliquis sub elevatione Poli 51 gradus, postea patria
egressus in alia regione, sub elevatione Poli 54 graduum sita, per totos
triginta et plures annos commoratus est et adhuc moratur, an eius Ascendentis
directio sit instituenda ex Tabula 51, an vero 54 graduum elevationis, et quæ
sit ratio, quare locus nativitatis, quoad directionis effectum, magis hominem et
corpus nati afficiat, quam locus commorationis,
in quo vitam degit? cum tamen fere singulis annis in effectibus Eclipsium, pro
diversitate meridianorum et locorum, citius aut tardius sequatur effectus.

Tertio, quia ex Diario ELIÆ OLAI
Cimbri Octogenariam divisionem Thematum ☌, ☍, et
□ ☉lis et ☾æ,
tanquam experientia et rationibus suffultam, ab illo comprobari intellexi,
percuperem brevibus cognoscere illas ipsas rationes Octogenariæ divisionis, et
quo experimento res inventa fuerit.

Quarto, quia experientia docet, non tantum Directiones maleficorum
malos inducere effectus, sed et transitus ♄ni et
♂tis, sive id fiat corpore, sive radijs
infœlicibus, per præcipua Genituræ loca, præsertim Ascendens interdum mala
operari, interdum vero non; quæritur, an ex caussis Astrologicis possit haberi
et dari certitudo aliqua, qua præsciri possit, quando
transitus illi ♄ni et ♂tis
nocituri sint, nec ne; an alia caussa sit quam convenientia Directionis et
progressus, quod transitus isti interdum operentur super Ascendens, interdum
vero non?

Quinto. An malorum planetarum effectus directione inducti per bonos
planetas omnino tolli vel impediri possint, et qua potissimum ratione aut re
malorum operationes impediantur?

Sexto. Qui aspectus sive Directio malorum pro morte naturali quam
pernitiosissimus sit observatus, et quæ constitutio malorum vel Directio pro
morte violenta omnium pessima sit observata per experientiam.

Septimo. Videri quoque multos infaustas et violentas Genituras
habentes fœlicem tamen vitam agere et naturali morte occumbere, et econtrario
plurimos optimam genesin vel saltem exiguam violentæ mortis significationem
habentes violenter interire. Quæritur, unde hæc operationum sive effectuum
diversitas, Astrologice loquendo, oriatur.

Harum itaque quæstionum Resolutiones, nisi Generositati Vestræ
admodum essem molestus, mihi aliquando etiam communicari submisse peterem. Quia
etiam in Astrologicis absque restitutione motus ☾næ
nihil solerter efficere possum, maiorem in modum similiter rogarem, ut Generos.
Vestra mihi significet, anne eiusdem Restitutio publici iuris reddita sit, ut
eandem mihi comparare possem. Et quia Generos. Vestra sibi nonnullas certas
Observationes in Genethliacis communicari expetijt, hasce ut ratas et satis
compertas adiungere velim, plures indies colligam. In Meteorologicis non nisi
vulgare habeo.

Demum Generositatem Vestram iterum atque iterum reverenter et
obnixe rogitans, ne me immeritum favore et benevolentia ex innata heroica erga
me affectione prosequi deserat, et diuturnum illud silentium mihi benigne
ignoscat.

Deus Opt. Max. Generos. Vestram cum
tota inclita familia salvam et incolumem ut conservet, tueatur atque defendat,
ex animo precor.

Datum Bremæ 16 Xbris Anno 99.

Generosi
Vestræ
Addictissimus
LUDOLPHUS RlDDERS[HUSIUS].

Anno 1512 die 22 Iunij inter horam 17 et 18 P. M. Consul
Dominus DANIEL a BUREN, qui Anno 62 partes
Doct. ALB. HARDENBERGIJ sive
CALVINI contra reliquos consules
defendebat et exinde toti Civitati maximas turbas excitavit, natus est Bremæ.
Hic Anno 39 in Senatorium ordinem et postea Anno 47 in Consulem electus, in
principio vero Anni 92 ob decrepitam ætatem officio Consulatus abdicans, Anno 93
circa 28 Iunij morbo correptus, die 10 Iulij post horam quintam matutinam placide
obdormivit.

Anno 1565 die 24 Novembris inter horam 10 et 11
pomeridianam nata est prædicto Domino Consuli filia MARGARETHA a BUHREN, sed
Anno 94 die ♃is 16 Maij pleuresi grassante correpta moriebatur 23 Maij.

Anno 1539 die 22 Iulij circa horam quintam matutinam natus est
Bremæ Dominus THEODORICUS a REDEN qui Anno 76

Anno 97 die prima Iunij mane morbo correptus pillulas ab affine proprio, Doct.
IOH. BAPTISTA SERVETIO, Medico,

Anno 1551 die 10 9bris hora 17 post M. Bremæ natus est WICHMANNUS MIDDELSTORP. Anno 75 die 16 Feb. in

festum Paschalis in ædibus Consulis LUDERI a
BELMERS pie defuncti, ex alto in navem cadebat, et nisi navis

Anno 1566 die 21° Iulij hora 7 P. M. natus est Bremæ
HILDEMANNUS DEDDEKEN, qui Anno 90 post festum
Penthecostes in mare a pyratis globo transiectus est.

TIBBEKE, uxor ALEXANDRI
BIKKERS, quæ Anno 96 die 26 Feb. pleuresi grassante correpta,

Anno 1566 die ☾æ 24 Iunij inter horam 1 et 2 noctis P. M. natus
est Domino IOHANNI SCHULTEN, Senatori huius
Civitatis, filius FRANSZ. Hic filiolus Anno 71 die ☿ij 20 Iunij hora quinta
pomeridiana a muliere quadem, ipsum transiente, ex alto ponte orientali in fossam
Civitatis trudebatur, sed a Patre citra omnem spem salvatus, qui cum ipso fere
perijsset. Patre postea mortuo, Anno 86 in autumno Amsterodami ob dissipationem
bonorum cum scortis et Anno 90 primo 9bris a Magistratu, Matre idipsum petente,
eandem ob causam secunda vice in carcerem coniectus est. Elapso anno in
Italiam profectus est, utrum adhuc
superstes sit nec ne, ambiguitur.

Ego L. R. Anno 1551
die 15 Septembris post horam 12 noctis sequentis Bremæ sum natus, in pueritia mihi
infinita contigere inconvenientia. Anno 73 die 14 Martij nocte sequente Brunswigæ
ardentissima febre et Anno 78 die 3 9bris singulari genere morborum et angina
iterum corripiebar. Anno 73 13 Maij uxorem duxi. Anno 1578 16. Feb. inter horam 6
et 7 vespertinam natus est mihi filius GREGORIUS, et hic ab ineunte ætate usque in annum 95 vario genere

firmiori valetudine, laus Deo, utitur. Anno 82 15 Iulij paulo post horam 12 noctis

Et quia non dubito, quin Generositas Vestra loca planetarum ad
natalem meum et filiorum meorum restituta habeat, ut igitur eo magis periculum
certitudinis artis facere possem, etiam atque etiam reverenter et obnixe rogo,
ut Generos. Vestra eorundem Restitutiones benigne mihi communicari dignetur.
Etsi vero Generos. Vestræ pro hisce et omnibus alijs in me immeritum collatis
beneficijs quicquam compensare non videam, nihilominus qui Generosi Vestræ
cordi sunt, me ad omne officium quam paratissimum devinctum habebunt.
