text.english:
**[German address] To the right-noble, stern, and highly-learned Lord Tycho Brahe, hereditary [lord] at Knudstrup, but at this time at the Imperial Court at Prague, my greatly-favouring Lord and Preceptor. At Prague.**

Heartiest greeting.

Noble and magnificent Hero, my patron and Maecenas, most to be revered with the utmost respect: after the humble offering of my ready services, I again and above all give and render Your Generosity the greatest thanks I can, for each and all the benefits conferred on me, undeserving, out of [your] singular heroic and inborn affection. Next, I cannot conceal from Your Generosity that for this past year I have written no letters. The cause was not only the intolerable mass of my domestic cares in this my solitude, but also a rumour, spread about last Carnival here and at Hamburg, of Your Generosity's departure from this vale of tears — at the hearing of which I was so terrified that I thought it was now all over with the Astrological study, on which I have hitherto most earnestly bent myself, for want of the Tables published by others. But at last, some days ago, from a joyful letter of Lord David Fabricius, I learned (praise God) that Your Generosity, with your whole renowned family, has reached Prague safe and sound, and that the most illustrious, most powerful, and most invincible Emperor, our most clement Lord, most clemently favours You; wherefore, moved both by his letters and by Your Generosity's, I wished to join these mine to Fabricius's.

Since, then, Your Generosity formerly indicated in your "Resolutions" [answers] kindly shared with me, on the question of the method of directing [primary directions]: that there is no more exact method of directing than that handed down by Regiomontanus — [counting] as many degrees crossing the Meridian as [cross] any other circle of position, but rather to be counted on the Meridian, since there they pass directly; and that in the most oblique Sphere the directing-method then holds at once, although the Regiomontanus distribution of houses cannot be administered there; and that for this reason Your Generosity rather approves Campanus's division, which regards the whole Heaven everywhere and is universal — to which, however, Your Generosity is wont to apply an equal partition through the Ecliptic (because of the planets' procession along it), in imitation of the ancient Astrologers, considering different things in this and that arrangement, as the consideration is required either by reason of the whole Heaven or of the Zodiac alone: these things, I say, though indicated clearly enough, I would nonetheless reverently and earnestly ask Your Generosity that you deign to share with me one or two brief schemes of the operation and demonstration.

I should besides have some other things, not to be despised — namely whether direction by the degrees of the Zodiac and its Pole can also induce effects, like that which is done with respect to the Pole of the Equator; and whether then the measurement of years is to be instituted in the same way, by the motion of the Sun [☉] in the Radix of the nativity, as otherwise — or whether a different measurement is to be ordered here.

Then, since in directing the Ascendant, by the unanimous consent of all Astrologers, the oblique ascensions under the Pole-elevation of the Region in which one was born have hitherto been observed: whether Your Generosity also judges that, if someone tarries for many years in some far region much distant from the place of his nativity, the direction of the Ascendant should nonetheless be made from the oblique ascensions which the Table of Directions shows under the Pole-elevation of the birth-region — or rather from the oblique ascensions under the Pole-elevation of the place where he lives? For example: one is born under a Pole-elevation of 51 degrees; afterward, having left his fatherland, he has dwelt, and still dwells, for thirty whole years and more in another region situated under a Pole-elevation of 54 degrees — is his Ascendant-direction to be instituted from the Table of 51, or of 54 degrees of elevation? And what is the reason why the place of nativity, as to the effect of direction, affects the man and the body of the native more than the place of habitation in which he passes his life? — since yet, almost every year, in the effects of Eclipses, the effect follows sooner or later according to the diversity of meridians and places.

Third: since from the Diary of Elias Olai the Cimbrian I understood the Octogenary [eighty-fold] division of charts — by the conjunction [☌], opposition [☍], and square [□] of the Sun [☉] and Moon [☾] — to be approved by him as supported by experience and reasons, I should much like to learn briefly those very reasons of the Octogenary division, and by what experiment the thing was found.

Fourth: since experience teaches that not only the Directions of the malefics induce bad effects, but also the transits of Saturn [♄] and Mars [♂] — whether by body or by unhappy rays — through the chief places of the nativity, especially the Ascendant, sometimes work ill, sometimes not: it is asked whether, from Astrological causes, any certainty can be had by which it may be foreknown when those transits of Saturn and Mars will be harmful, or not; and whether there is any other cause than the agreement of the Direction and the progression, that those transits sometimes operate upon the Ascendant, sometimes not.

Fifth: whether the effects of the malefic planets, induced by direction, can be wholly removed or hindered by the benefic planets — and by what means above all the operations of the malefics are hindered.

Sixth: which aspect or Direction of the malefics has been observed most pernicious for natural death; and which constitution of the malefics, or Direction, has been observed by experience worst of all for a violent death.

Seventh: it is seen also that many having unlucky and violent nativities nevertheless lead a happy life and die a natural death, and contrariwise that very many having the best genesis — or at least a slight signification of violent death — perish violently. It is asked whence this diversity of operations or effects arises, astrologically speaking.

The Resolutions of these questions, then, unless I were quite troublesome to Your Generosity, I would humbly ask to be shared with me sometime. And since in Astrological matters I can do nothing skilfully without the restitution of the motion of the Moon [☾], I would likewise greatly ask that Your Generosity signify to me whether the Restitution of the same has been made public, that I might procure it. And since Your Generosity desired that certain reliable Observations in genitures be shared, I would add these as proven and well-ascertained, and will collect more day by day. In Meteorological [matters] I have nothing but the common sort.

Lastly, again and again reverently and earnestly entreating Your Generosity not to cease pursuing me, undeserving, with favour and benevolence out of [your] inborn heroic affection, and kindly to pardon me that long silence.

I pray from my heart that God, Best and Greatest, may keep, guard, and defend Your Generosity, with your whole renowned family, safe and sound.

Given at Bremen, 16 December, the year [15]99.
Your Generosity's most devoted,
**Ludolf Riddershus[en].**

*[Here follows, appended in the same letter, Riddershusen's dossier of dated Bremen births and deaths, offered as astrological test-cases:]*

In the year 1512, on the 22nd of June, between the 17th and 18th hour P.M., was born at Bremen Consul Lord Daniel von Büren — who in the year [15]62 defended the party of Doctor Albert Hardenberg, or of Calvin, against the rest of the consuls, and thereby stirred up the greatest disturbances for the whole City. He was elected in the year [15]39 into the Senatorial order, and afterward in the year [15]47 [elected] Consul; but at the beginning of the year [15]92, resigning the office of the Consulate on account of decrepit age, in the year [15]93, about the 28th of June, seized with sickness, on the 10th of July, after the fifth hour of the morning, he fell peacefully asleep.

In the year 1565, on the 24th of November, between the 10th and 11th hour in the afternoon, was born to the aforesaid Lord Consul a daughter, Margaretha von Büren; but in the year [15]94, on Thursday [♃], the 16th of May, seized by a raging pleurisy, she died on the 23rd of May.

In the year 1539, on the 22nd of July, about the fifth hour of the morning, was born at Bremen Lord Theodoricus von Reden, who in the year [15]76, in autumn, was elected into the Senatorial order; he was a man of great stature and corpulent, and had two wives, with whom he received very great inheritances. This man, in the year [15]97, on the first of June, in the morning, seized with sickness, and taking pills from his own kinsman, Doctor Johann Baptista Servetius, physician, straightway in the Doctor's arms exchanged life for death.

In the year 1551, on the 10th of November, at the 17th hour after noon, was born at Bremen Wichmann Middelstorp. In the year [15]75, on the 16th of February, he collapsed dangerously to the ground, and was compelled to employ the executioner, by name Dionysius, to treat him; in the year [15]86, about the feast of Easter, in the house of Consul Luder von Belmers — [the latter] having piously died — he fell from a height into a ship, and had the ship not been there, he must needs have perished in the Weser. At length, at the beginning of the year [15]92, seized with various kinds of sicknesses, and on the 11th of June again dangerously laid low upon the ground, and so detained by sickness until the year [15]93, on the 8th of October, in the night following, he fell peacefully asleep, though many remedies had been applied in vain.

In the year 1558, on the 25th of August, after the twelfth hour of noon, was born at Frankfurt an der Oder Meimarus von Borken, Secretary of this City, since his parent, Doctor Johann von Borken, was of the patrician stock of our City. This man, in the year [15]83, on Wednesday [☿] in the evening after the feast of the Annunciation of Mary, at Bederkesa, the castle of this City, broke his leg. In the year [15]87, after the feast of Bartholomew the Apostle, he lay sick unto death of a hot [feverish] disease. In the year [15]91, on the 4th of August, from an excessive over-indulgence in wine the day before, spitting blood from his mouth, he died in a frenzy.

In the year 1566, on the 21st of July, at the 7th hour P.M., was born at Bremen Hildemann Deddeken, who in the year [15]90, after the feast of Pentecost, was shot through with a [musket-]ball by pirates at sea.

In the year 1552, on the 7th of February, about the sixth hour in the afternoon, was born at Bremen Lord Gerhard Gerken, a distinguished Musician, no ordinary friend of mine, but an enemy of Astrology. In the year [15]81 he was taken on as Secretary of the City, and in the year [15]93, on the 3rd of July, elected Senator. In the year [15]91, on the Tuesday after Quasimodogeniti [the Sunday after Easter], and again on the fourth of August, he lay dangerously ill; afterward, in the year [15]94, on the 28th of November, again seized [with illness] for some months, and restored to health beyond hope. At length, in the year [15]96, after the feast of Pentecost, seized anew and detained by a long sickness, on the day of St Michael the Archangel, between the 10th and 11th hour before noon, in my presence, he peacefully passed away, though aids had been applied in vain by two Doctors of Medicine of the City. It is a wonder that he did not attain to a decrepit age, since he had the Moon [☾] in conjunction with Jupiter [♃] in its own house, in the eleventh [house], free from the malefics, and the Ascendant unafflicted.

This good man's wife, Brigitta Gröninges, was born at Bremen in the year 1559, on the 11th of May, Thursday [♃] before the feast of Pentecost, between the 7th and 8th hour in the morning; but in the year [15]98, the plague raging, fleeing betimes from the City into a garden, on the 6th of August, in the garden, she was seized by the plague; on the 12th of the same [month], between the 1st and 2nd hour of the night following, she fell peacefully asleep — nor were remedies lacking to her. And this honest matron had the Moon in Cancer [♋] ascending, in Trine to Jupiter [♃], [Jupiter] being in Pisces [♓].

In the year 1555, on the 24th of March, between the 2nd and 3rd hour in the afternoon, was born at Bremen Tibbeke, wife of Alexander Bikkers, who in the year [15]96, on the 26th of February, seized by a raging pleurisy, lost a dear daughter, and was herself restored to health. But afterward, in the same year, on the 4th of September, from grief for her dead daughter, she was reduced to insanity, and most wretchedly detained [in that state] until the feast of Easter of the year [15]97, at which she returned to health. But truly in the year [15]98, about the 10th of September, seized again by the plague, on the 15th of the same [month], at the 2nd hour of the night following, she died.

In the year 1566, on Monday [☾], the 24th of June, between the 1st and 2nd hour of the night, P.M., was born to Lord Johann Schulten, Senator of this City, a son, Fransz. This little son, in the year [15]71, on Wednesday [☿] the 20th of June, at the fifth hour in the afternoon, was pushed by a certain woman, passing by him, from the high eastern bridge into the City moat, but was saved by his Father beyond all hope — who himself very nearly perished along with him. His father having afterward died, in the year [15]86, in autumn, at Amsterdam, on account of squandering his goods with harlots, and in the year [15]90, on the first of November, by the Magistrate — his Mother herself requesting it — for the same cause he was, a second time, cast into prison. The year having elapsed, he set out for Italy; whether he is still living or not is uncertain.

*[Postscript:]* I, L. R., was born at Bremen in the year 1551, on the 15th of September, after the twelfth hour of the night following; in my boyhood endless misfortunes befell me. In the year [15]73, on the 14th of March in the night following, at Brunswick I was seized with a most burning fever, and in the year [15]78, on the 3rd of November, again with a singular kind of diseases and with quinsy. In the year [15]73, on the 13th of May, I took a wife. In the year 1578, on 16 February, between the 6th and 7th hour of the evening, my son Gregorius was born to me, and he, from his earliest age until the year [15]95, was afflicted with various kinds of diseases. In the year 1579, on the 26th of December, between the 3rd and 4th hour of the night following, my second son Hieronimus was born to me, who enjoys (praise God) better and firmer health. In the year [15]82, on the 15th of July, a little after the 12th hour of the night following, my third son Christianus was born to me. He, in the year [15]83 about the feast of [St] James, and in the year [15]84, on 3 April, lay sick unto death, but afterwards likewise enjoys good health. And since I do not doubt that Your Generosity has the places of the planets restored for my own nativity and my sons', that I might therefore the more make a test of the art's certainty, I again and again reverently and earnestly ask that Your Generosity deign kindly to share with me the Restitutions of the same. And although I do not see that I can repay Your Generosity anything for these and all the other benefits conferred on me, undeserving, nevertheless those who are dear to Your Generosity will find me bound and most ready for every service. The notations of the days are taken from the Julian Calendar.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondent.** **Incoming**, **Ludolf Riddershusen (Riddershusius)** — a Bremen astrological student/practitioner who treats Tycho as his "Preceptor" — **to Tycho** at Prague.
- **Significance — Tycho as astrological authority, and a death-rumour.**
 - **The "Tycho is dead" rumour.** A notable biographical datum: **a rumour of Tycho's death circulated at Bremen and Hamburg around Carnival 1599** ("his departure from this vale of tears"), terrifying Riddershusen — corrected only "some days ago" by **David Fabricius's** letter reporting Tycho safe at Prague and favoured by the Emperor. (Fabricius is the link — cf. his recruitment in brahe-t_15990922001.)
 - **A genuine astrological consultation (seven questions).** The body is a window on **Tycho's reputation as an astrological authority** and on late-Renaissance technical astrology. Riddershusen first recapitulates Tycho's earlier "Resolutions" on **primary directions** — endorsing the **Regiomontanus** method of directing but preferring the **Campanus house-division** (as "universal"), with an **equal ecliptic partition** "in imitation of the ancient astrologers" — then poses seven questions: (1) a worked scheme of the directing operation; (2) zodiacal-pole vs equatorial-pole direction and the time-measure; (3) **the relocation problem** — whether to direct the Ascendant from the **birthplace** latitude (51°) or the **place of long residence** (54°), and *why* birthplace dominates; (4) the predictability of harmful **Saturn/Mars transits**; (5) whether **benefics can cancel malefic directions**; (6) the worst configurations for natural vs **violent death**; (7) why charts and outcomes so often diverge.
 - **The "Octogenary division" and Elias Olai.** Riddershusen cites the **"Diary of Elias Olai the Cimbrian" (Elias Olsen Morsing**, Tycho's former Hven assistant and diarist) for an **"Octogenary [80-fold] division"** of charts by Sun–Moon conjunction/opposition/square — and asks its rationale. *(A trace of Tycho's Hven astrological/meteorological diary tradition.)*
 - **The lunar tables.** Riddershusen says he "can do nothing in astrology **without the restitution of the Moon's motion**" and asks whether Tycho's lunar **Restitution is yet published** — echoing the same demand from Magini (brahe-t_16010220001) and the lunar work referenced to Scaliger (brahe-t_16000723001).
- **Cross-references.** The Sun/Moon/Saturn/Mars and aspect glyphs (☉ ☾ ♄ ♂ ☌ ☍ □) are reproduced as transcribed. Notes the **death-rumour** and the **Elias Olsen Morsing octogenary-division** datum.
- **Persons & places named.** Ludolf Riddershusen; **David Fabricius** (the bearer of the good news); **Regiomontanus**, **Campanus** (house systems); **Elias Olai / Elias Olsen Morsing** (the "Cimbrian," Tycho's diarist); **Rudolf II**. Places: **Bremen**, **Hamburg**, **Prague**, **Knudstrup**.
- **Calendar.** *Bremae 16 Xbris [Decembris] Anno 99* → **16 December 1599 [Old Style]** (Bremen reckoning; no *stylo* marker; label gives no N.S.). Header read Old Style.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing genealogical postscript (Riddershusen's own + his three sons' nativities, with a request to compute their restitutions; "ex Calendario Iuliano"), restored from Dreyer VIII p.221 (dropped by the working transcription).
- **What was recovered.** The lost interior passage is Riddershusen's own appended dossier of eleven dated Bremen birth-and-death notices (consuls, a secretary, a musician-senator, and their wives/children), several carrying explicit astrological configurations (Moon–Jupiter aspects, Ascendant condition). It sits between the signed close of the main letter ("Ludolphus Riddershusius") and the already-published autobiographical postscript beginning "Ego L. R. Anno 1551..." — i.e. it is Riddershusen practising exactly what he asks Tycho for earlier in the same letter: "certain reliable Observations in genitures," supplied as raw test-data for the astrological questions posed above.
- **Elias Olai Cimber, identified.** The "Diario Eliæ Olai Cimbri" cited for the "Octogenary division" (question three, already-published portion) is almost certainly Elias Olsen Morsing's *Diarium astrologicum et meteorologicum anni 1586* — the first book printed at Tycho's own Uraniborg press, by Tycho's own assistant ("Elias Olai Cimber, discipulus Tychonis," per the Opera Omnia index of correspondents). Riddershusen is thus citing back to Tycho a work by a member of Tycho's own household.
- **Two fabricated dates corrected.** The previously published partial translation supplied "the 15th of September" (for Riddershusen's own 1551 birth) and "15 July" (for his son Christianus's 1582 birth). The complete source text given for this retranslation has no day-number in either place ("Anno 1551 die Septembris"; "Anno 82 Iulij"). Both are corrected here to reflect the actual source, with the gap marked; the origin of the earlier "15"s is unexplained and should be checked against the manuscript or a critical edition before being reused.
- **Bremen persons.** Daniel von Büren, Theodoricus von Reden, Wichmann Middelstorp, Meimarus von Borken, Hildemann Deddeken, Gerhard Gerken and their households are purely local Bremen civic figures (consuls, senators, a City secretary) not otherwise identified in the works consulted (Christianson, Dreyer, Thoren); confirming them would require Bremen municipal/archival sources outside our current holdings.
- Crux: "in lla" in the Gerken entry, read here as "in the eleventh [house]" (i.e. undecima domo), but the abbreviation is not certain.
- Crux: "Mirum, quidni ad decrepitam pervenerit ætatem" (Gerken entry) is rhetorically ambiguous; rendered as ironic — Gerken in fact died at about forty-four despite the favourable Moon-Jupiter configuration Riddershusen describes, which is presumably the point being made.
- **Correction.** Collated against Dreyer, TBOO VIII pp.215-222. Restored two dropped day-numbers silently missing from the source text: 'die 15 Septembris' (Riddershusen's own birth, p.221) and 'Anno 82 15 Iulij' (birth of his son Christianus, p.221), both translated into the English, removing the 'day not given in the source' hedges. Also corrected three cosmetic corruptions against Dreyer's text with no effect on the English: the German address heading 'HERNNTICHONI' to 'HERRN TICHONI' (p.216), 'locum' to the plural 'loca' (p.221), and 'comæ pensare' to the single word 'compensare' (p.221).

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Dreyer TBOO VIII pp.215-222 read as page images in three passes (1-4, 5-8, and a close re-read of p.218 and p.221) and collated the full letter plus its appended Bremen-births/deaths dossier line by line against the transcribed original and the published English. Every name, date, and number in the biographical dossier (Daniel von Büren, Margaretha von Büren, Theodoricus von Reden, Wichmann Middelstorp, Meimarus von Borken, Hildemann Deddeken, Gerhard Gerken, Brigitta Gröninges, Tibbeke/Alexander Bikkers, Johann Schulten/Fransz) checked out exactly against Dreyer, and the astrological-questions section (Regiomontanus/Campanus, the 51/54-degree example, the Octogenary conjunction/opposition/square of Sun and Moon, Saturn/Mars transits) also checked out — the translation of the substantive content is faithful, with no fabrication, omission, or mistranslation found. However, our transcribed original itself departs from Dreyer in five places, all in the autobiographical closing section on p.221: two dropped day-numbers ('15' before Septembris and before Iulij) that silently remove dates Dreyer actually gives (the translator honestly flagged these as 'day not given in the source' rather than inventing them, but the information loss is real and traces to our transcribed original, not the translator), plus three minor corruptions (a glued/transposed address heading, 'locum' for Dreyer's 'loca', and 'comæ pensare' for Dreyer's 'compensare'). Per the grading rule, any text error caps the grade at C regardless of the translation's own fidelity.

**5 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original glues and transposes the two words 'HERRN TICHONI' into 'HERNNTICHONI'; Dreyer prints them as two clean words. Cosmetic — English correctly renders 'Lord Tycho Brahe' regardless. Dreyer prints: *HERRN TICHONI BRAHE (p.216, address heading)*.
- **text error** (medium). Dreyer gives the day as '15 Septembris'; our transcribed original has silently dropped the '15'. The English translator noticed the gap and flagged it honestly ('day not given in the source') rather than fabricating, but the published sentence still omits a date Dreyer actually prints. Dreyer prints: *Ego L. R. Anno 1551 die 15 Septembris post horam 12 noctis sequentis Bremæ sum natus (p.221, line 1)*.
- **text error** (medium). Same fault pattern as the previous entry: Dreyer reads 'Anno 82 15 Iulij' (15 July); our transcribed original drops the '15'. Again honestly flagged in translation rather than fabricated, but the date is genuinely recoverable from Dreyer and is missing from our text. Dreyer prints: *Anno 82 15 Iulij paulo post horam 12 noctis sequentis natus est mihi filius tertius CHRISTIANUS (p.221, line 10)*.
- **text error** (low). Dreyer has plural 'loca' (agreeing with the participle 'restituta'); our transcribed original has singular 'locum', a minor grammatical corruption. Does not affect the English rendering, which is correct either way. Dreyer prints: *quin Generositas Vestra loca planetarum ad natalem meum et filiorum meorum restituta habeat (p.221, line 14-15)*.
- **text error** (low). Dreyer's single word 'compensare' (to repay) is split/garbled into 'comæ pensare' in our transcribed original. The translator correctly inferred the intended sense ('repay') despite the corruption, so the English is unaffected, but the transcribed original itself departs from Dreyer. Dreyer prints: *quicquam compensare non videam (p.221, line 18)*.

**Repaired.** All five defects were verified directly against page images of Dreyer, TBOO VIII pp.215-222 (the full extract for this letter). Both date defects and the 'loca'/'compensare' corruptions appear on p.221 exactly as the audit's dreyer field states; the address-heading defect is confirmed on p.216. No defect was rejected — the audit's claims all match the printed edition. Nothing outside these five defect sites was touched.

documents.abstract: Congratulates Tycho on his imperial patronage and describes Jacob Kindler, a Silesian alchemist at Zittau practising a Paracelsian art of transmuting metals into stones.
documents.incipit: LITERIS tuis, Magnifice et Generose Do[mine] TYCHO, instructus, in cognitionem ex CHYTRÆO …

text.original:
MAGNIFICO ET GENEROSO TYCHONI BRAHÆ, DOMINO IN KNUSTORPH ET HUENA, DOMINO ET FAUTORI SUO, OMNI OFFICIJ GENERE COLENDO.

LITERIS tuis, Magnifice et Generose Do[mine] TYCHO, instructus, in cognitionem ex CHYTRÆO et alijs præsentis tui status et conditionis veni, de quo me certiorem factum esse summopere gaudeo. Gratulor etiam tibi de tanto Mœcenate, opere et studio tuo digno, quo non solum tibi prospectum, sed toti posteritati plurimum inserviri intelligo. Chymicus Silesius, quo de antea ad te perscripsi, Sittæ in Silesia degit, vocaturque IACOBUS KINDLER, olim ibidem vel in vicinia scholæ Cantor. Artificium, quod illum celebrem facit, describitur in lib. Vexationum PARACELSI sub titulo Hæc est ars, cursumque sphæræ Saturninæ vocant, quo omnes planetæ terrestres, mediante Saturno et uno minerali adiecto, exiguo negocio in lapides vertuntur, qui deinceps nulla vi ignis aut vulcano quantumvis torvo, postliminium perveniunt, ↄ: in metalla redeunt. Huius revolutionis spectator ipse fui atque dirigere scio, sed finem, quem author ibidem promittit, assequi ignoro. Literas tuas FRANCISCO SCHRODERO Sundensi inscriptas, quotquot ad me pervenerunt, summa fidelitate isthic misi, nec non ad responsionem illum adhortatus sum, ac suam taciturnitatem illi exprobravi, ad quod mihi nuper respondit, tibi quoque suis literis Witebergam delatis responsum esse. Sero forte, quod tuus discessus illinc prævenerit illud, aut quicquid intervenerit.

Nova, quæ hîc habemus, ex adiuncto scripto cognosces. Alias forma Academiæ et Reipub. eadem est, quam reliquisti; discursum Suecicum tibi quoque misissem, sed nulla hîc exemplaria, ut qui Stockholmiæ impressus est, prostant.

Vale, nec non qui tibi curæ sunt, et me inter tuos familiares retineto.
Data Rostochij 19. Decembris anni 1599.
T. Magnif. studiosiss.
Christopho. Henniochus,
Medicus.
text.english:
**To the magnificent and generous Tycho Brahe, lord in Knudstrup and Hven, his lord and patron, to be honoured with every kind of office.**

Instructed by your letter, magnificent and generous Master Tycho, I came into knowledge of your present status and condition — from Chytraeus and from others — about which I greatly rejoice to have been made more certain. I also congratulate you on so great a Maecenas [patron], worthy of your work and study, by which I understand that not only have you been provided for, but the whole of posterity is greatly served. The Silesian chemist, about whom I wrote to you before, lives at Zittau [Sitta] in Silesia, and is called **Jacob Kindler**, formerly Cantor of the school there or in the vicinity. The art which makes him famous is described in the *Book of Vexations* of Paracelsus, under the heading "This is the art," and they call it the *course of the Saturnine sphere*, by which all the terrestrial planets [the metals], by means of Saturn [lead] and one mineral added, are with little trouble turned into stones — which thereafter, by no force of fire, or by however grim a Vulcan, "come back from exile," that is, return into metals. Of this revolution I was myself a spectator, and I know how to direct it; but the end which the author there promises, I know not how to attain. Your letters inscribed to Franz Schröder of Stralsund, as many as reached me, I sent thither with the utmost fidelity, and also exhorted him to a reply, and reproached him with his silence; to which he lately answered me that an answer had also been [given] to you, by his letters carried to Wittenberg — late, perhaps, because your departure thence forestalled it, or [because] something intervened.

The news which we have here, you will learn from the enclosed writing. Otherwise the form of the Academy and the commonwealth is the same as you left it; I would also have sent you the Swedish discourse, but there are no copies here — being one that was printed at Stockholm, [where such things] are on sale.

Farewell — and likewise those who are a care to you — and keep me among your familiars.
Given at Rostock, 19 December, in the year 1599.
Most zealous of Your Magnificence,
Christoph Henniochus,
Physician.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Christoph Henniochus** (*Medicus*, a physician) — the alchemical correspondent of brahe-t_16000329003 (Tycho's reply, 29 March 1600). This letter (19 Dec 1599) is the one Tycho there acknowledges as "brought by my son at the beginning of this year," and it is here that Henniochus **identifies the Silesian alchemist** Tycho asked after.
- **The alchemist identified.** *Chymicus Silesius … Sittae in Silesia degit, vocaturque Iacobus Kindler, olim … scholae Cantor* — the man is **Jacob Kindler**, living at **Zittau** (*Sitta*; in Upper Lusatia, near Silesia), a former school **Cantor**. His "art" is the **[pseudo-]Paracelsian *Liber Vexationum*** process called the *cursus sphaerae Saturninae* ("course of the Saturnine sphere"): the **metals** (*planetae terrestres* — the seven "planets" = the seven metals of alchemy) are, "by means of **Saturn** [= lead] and one added mineral," turned into "stones" and then back into metals (*postliminium* = "[returning] from exile," a Roman-law term for restored status). Henniochus witnessed the operation and can run it, but cannot reach the *finis* (the promised goal). The symbol **ↄ:** = *id est* ("that is"). Reinforces the Tychonic alchemy thread (cf. brahe-t_15860301001, …16000329003).
- ***Maecenas*** = Tycho's new imperial patron (Rudolf II); Henniochus had learned of Tycho's new footing "from **Chytraeus** and others" (David Chytraeus of Rostock, then in his last year). *Franciscus Schröderus Sundensis* = **Franz Schröder of Stralsund**, the delinquent correspondent of brahe-t_16000329003. *discursus Suecicus* = a "Swedish discourse" (a political pamphlet on the Swedish succession war) printed at **Stockholm**.
- **⚠ Place of writing.** The dateline reads *Data Rostochij* = **Rostock**; the edition catalogues the letter under **Wittenberg**. The internal references are mixed — Henniochus forwarded Tycho's letters via **Wittenberg** and reports that "the form of the Academy … is the same as you left it" (Tycho had wintered at Wittenberg in 1599) — which may be why the catalogue says Wittenberg; but the **as-written dateline (Rostock)** governs the header, with the discrepancy flagged. Either way the place is **Lutheran = Old Style**.
- **Calendar.** *19. Decembris anni 1599* = **19 December 1599, Old Style**. Header agrees with the label's date (the place differs, as noted).

text.original:
MAGNIFICO ET NOBILISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO GEORGIO HERWARTO AB HOHENBURGK, SERENISSIMO UTRIUSQUE BAVARIÆ DUCI A CONSILIJS INTIMIS, PRÆSIDI SCHWABÆ ET STATUUM PROVINCIALIUM CANCELLARIO, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO INPRIMIS HONORANDO. MÜNCHEN.

S. P.

POSTQUAM priores, circa medium Novembris ad te, Vir Nobilissime et Præstantissime, directas, et paulisper, donec in Aulam eas mittendi atque inde ad te procurandi suppeteret commoditas, mecum retentas, tandem cum adiunctis chartis emisissem, accidit, ut aliæ tuæ eodem ferme tempore, cum meæ illæ prolixiores scriptæ, mihi redderentur, idque primum paulo ante solstitium hybernum instantibus ferijs Natalitijs, quæ licet breviusculæ fuerint, plurimum tamen mihi acceptæ, cum quod te in amicitia nostra sic, donec aliter liceat, continuanda, perseverantem nec scribendi occasionem ullam intermittentem ostenderent; tum quia te patienter moram meam in rescribendo ferre (siquidem nulla in ijs usus esses, quod non immerito facere licuisset, expostulatione) inde colligerem, utut caussæ huius tarditatis tibi necdum perspectæ erant, quas te nunc acceptis meis cognovisse atque ratas habuisse mihi polliceor.

Accessit et hoc, quod literæ illæ tuæ steriles non fuerint, sed triplices in Sole Cassellis factas tribus diversis, attamen continuis annis sedulas observationes easdemque Geometrice et per numeros pro eruendo inde Apogæo et Eccentricitate Solari expensas, fœcundo partu secum adferrent. Fuit equidem id mihi admodum gratum, cum animadversiones illas prius non viderim. Neque enim a laudatissimæ memoriæ GULIELMO Principe Landtgravio aut etiam eius Mathematico CHRISTOPHORO ROTHMANNO mihi antea (quod omissum miror) communicatæ erant, alias Epistolarum Tomo primo, qui literas ijsdem annis inter nos commutatas habet, eas unâ cum competente disquisitione et cum nostris inventis collatione inseruissem, ut ob id probe a te factum, quod vel ex hac omissione coniecturam non fallacem conceperis, eas prius ad manus meas non pervenisse; eoque rectius et acceptius mihi nunc impertiris.

Multum autem me torsit, quod prima introspectione animadverterim, Apogæum quidem Solis cum nostro utcunque congruere. Nam dimidij gradus differentia discerni in tam subtili Pragmateia difficulter potest. Nec etiam sensibiliter quid officit, siquidem iuxta ipsum Apogæum non nisi unico minuto longitudinem Solis variet, in cæteris locis adhuc minus. Verum ubi Eccentricitatem trifariam investigatam et ubique quasi in ipsis secundis sibi constantem conspexissem, a nostro nihilominus deficere quasi 6 minutis de 60 partibus semidiametri Eccentrici, mirum in modum, quid sub his scrupulis lateret scrupuli, hæsitavi. Cum enim revisis meis Observationibus, quas circa eosdem dies in Uraniburgo nostro Danico habueram, et supputato simul loco Solis e nostro restituto calculo, quæ Eccentricitatem præsupponit part. 2 m. 9 ad minimum, viderem longitudinem ☉ ubique intra unicum minutum illi congruere, quam observata Cassellana tribuerunt, nec possibile esset, ex ijsdem datis tam prope consentientibus, adhibito non fallaci demonstrationis processu, qualem tuum quoque esse cognovi, tam diversimodam nihilominus prodire Eccentricitatem, quid taciti sese insinuasset obstaculi, non ita facile ab initio patuit. Nam et alia ab ea, qua tu usus, ratione, per prostaphæreses nimirum, repetito tuo pro maiori parte calculo; visus est is recte se habere. Nec poterat refractionis insinuatio quæ in primo exemplo, ubi ☉ 27 proxime gradibus 2 min. in ultimo, Sole tertium ♒ gradum transeunte, et 19 saltem gradibus elevato eandem 5 minutorum ingerebat (ut de intermedio, in quo hæc diversitas minus sensibilis erat, nihil addam) nostram intentionem turbare; siquidem loca ☉ in Ecliptica cum nostris numeris adeo prope consentientia, ROTHMANNUM non saltem Parallaxes Solis sed et refractiones, de quo aliquoties a me (uti ex Epistolis a te citatis liquet) admonitus erat, solerter præcavisse, satis probarunt. Neque etiam, quod Eclipticæ obliquatio maxima dimidio scrupulo minor in calculo transmisso assumpta sit, quam a nobis præsupposita, tam evidentem in Eccentricitate hac discrepantiam parere potuit, sicuti neglecta temporis æquatio insensibilem variationem suggerere. Circumspecte itaque omnia (uti tunc mihi videbar) in tuis demonstrationibus et superstructis numeris trutinando, et meas quoque rationes, quæ ab Æquinoctijs et medietate ♉ atque ♌ in Eccentricitate atque Apogæo ☉ eruendis paulo adhuc maiore tam compendio quam certitudine procedunt, denuo sub calculi incudem revocando, nihilque in ijs aberratum esse comprobando, abieci, tanquam mihi ipsi non satisfaciens, hanc aliquantisper disquisitionem; qua tamen peractis sacris Natalitijs denuo in manus resumpta et toto tuo calculo a principio usque in finem (quod antea circa extrema neglectum erat, ex quo cætera tam belle constarent) tandem inventum est, in quo latuerit huius discrepantiæ nodus. Cum enim circa ipsum calculi exitum, quando ex radice quadrata, quæ in omnibus tribus exemplis sibi ferme similis est, atque in numerum 3591 quam proxime conspirat, perventum est, ut inde Eccentricitatis quantitas eliceretur, depræhendimus, quod per incuriam aliquam, quod facile inter gravissimas tuas occupationes alias fieri potuit, aut si a quopiam alio hæc Pragmateia instituta est (neque enim cuius sit indicasti) numerus ille in Tabulam sinuum intromissus quantitatem Eccentricitatis perperam monstrarit, ideoque iusto minorem, cum proportionaliter saltem, prout 60 loco totius radij acciperentur, eruenda foret, sicque eadem quam proxime mecum prodibit Eccentricitatis determinatio; quæ etiam in pauculis scrupulis secundis, nullius pene momenti, nostram excedat potius, quam quod 6 minutis ab ea deficiat. Imo si observationes in Sole a nobis Anno 1583 diligenter factitatas in consilium adhibuerimus, eadem cum transmissa inquisitione prodibit Eccentricitas. Nam et nos eandem tunc adinvenimus part. 3592, qualium radius est sive sinus totus 100000, sive part. 2 m. 9⅓, qualium idem 60, Apogæo etiam tunc in part. 5¾ ♋ reposito; et eodem per septennium usque in Annum 1590, qui medius est trium ex tuis, per additionem 9 minutorum, prout requirit Apogæi mutatio a PTOLEMÆO eousque facta (nam quæ in libro modo misso Apogæi notatur progressio aliquanto tardior est, eo quod ex observatione REGIOMONTANI ante 100 Annos facta peculiari consilio saltem derivata sit, uti et Anni quantitas iusto paulo minor assumpta, nec tamen in utrisque his tanta est discrepantia, ut fert COPERNICI ratiocinatio) in ipso scrupulo (quod mirum est) cum Landtgraviano Anni 1590 Apogæo consentiens. Ut vero promptius et plenius percipias, qua methodo et quibus dedomenis nos et Apogæum et Eccentricitatem ☉ verificaverimus, atque unde hæc minutula differentia in nostra numeratione inter quæsita Anni 1583 et aliorum quorundam postea subsequentium irrepserit, en habes Progymnasmatum nostrorum de Astronomia instaurata Tomum primum, quatenus rerum nostrarum variæ conturbationes et vicissitudines eum hactenus typis complere permiserunt. Quali Titulo in publicum brevi, favente cœlesti Numine, emittendus, et quæ in eodem superaddenda restant, prima circumposita charta manifestat. Illic cap. statim primo hæc Solaris curriculi restitutionem concernentia affatim expediunt. Quæ de ☾ appendicis loco eidem subnectenda, suo tempore videbis. Secundum caput restitutionem affixarum Stellarum accuratissimam usque in octavum centenarium inde ab ipso fundamento extruit, tandemque canonice recenset. Quibus postea eas, quæ desiderantur, usque ad integrum millenarium supplevi. Reliqua voluminis pars de supra modum miraculosa Anni 1572 Stella luculenter tractat. Invenies alias in hoc opere nonnulla ex ijs, quæ prius inter nos ventilata sunt, plenius disquisita, et non pauca alia, quæ tuo (uti spero) arridebunt ingenio. Consule hunc boni, tibique soli reserva, donec eundem auctiorem et plane absolutum obtineas, unâ cum alijs quibusdam ex meis in hoc genere studiorum laboribus. Sphalmata Typographica, quæ nonnulla inter revidendum comperi, tute, qui rem ipsam probe capis, facile restitues. Vide quid pepererint ternæ ternorum etiam Annorum Solis observationes mihi a te benevole missæ. Si plures in alijs etiam Astris sive Cassellis sive alibi sedulo factas procuraveris, neque illæ sine fœnore redibunt. Intellexi WERNERUM quasdam a se habitas animadversiones cœlestes in publicum êdidisse, quæ si præter eas, quas de aëris mutatione vidi, aliquid circa Phænomena Astrorum cœlitus denotata habent, et tibi de eo libro quidpiam constat, cuperem exemplar mihi aliquantisper concedi.

Pluribus te nunc morari nolo; sed expecto brevi tam ad priores meas, quam hasce responsionem. Id saltem superaddam, inventionem Apogæi et Eccentricitatis ex Observatis Anni 1583 a me, prout in libro, quem nunc mitto, expositam, mihi magis placere alterâ, quam deinceps ex subsequentibus Annis adhibui; siquidem æquationis temporis ratio isthic applicata, postea vero omissa. Sicque Apogæum et Eccentricitas e Landtgravianis observatis petita rectius convenient cum nostrâ illâ priori (uti dixi) annotatione, licet differentia, quæ alias intercidit, nullius pene sit æstimationis. Quam tamen discrepantiunculam observationes ☉ hîc in Bohemiâ, favente Numine, continuandæ facile diriment; siquidem Æquator 6 ferme gradibus hîc altior quam in Daniâ ad quadragesimum Gradum extet, et ob id nulla Solis refractio, quæ sensibus obvia sit, iuxta ipsa Æquinoctia (prout in Daniâ sit) sese insinuet.

Vale itaque quam optime, et Anni huius instantis iubilæi, ac plurium aliorum curricula felici animi et corporis rerumque externarum statu transige.

Dabantur Girtzitzæ, unde cras, volente Deo, Benaticam reverti constitui, pridie Calend. Ianuar. Anni Domini 1600.
Tuæ Magæ addictissimus
TYCHO BRAHE manu propria scripsi.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 226; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Apposui calculum Apogæi et Eccentricitatis Solis, in tribus transmissis exemplis per prostaphæreses nobis usitatas reiteratum, qui a tuo vix differt, exceptâ Eccentricitatis, prout in literis monui, emendatione. Adiunxi quoque Odam quandam non invenustam, mihi hisce diebus e Pomeraniâ missam, ut eam caeteris tibi communicatis carminibus annectere queas.
text.english:
**To the magnificent and most noble man, Lord Georg Herwart von Hohenburg, Privy Councillor to the most serene Duke of both Bavarias, President of Swabia, and Chancellor of the Provincial Estates, his Lord and friend especially to be honoured. Munich.**

Heartiest greeting.

After I had at last sent off — with the appended papers — my earlier [letter], directed to you about the middle of November (and kept by me a little while, until the convenience of sending it to the Court, and procuring it thence to you, should be at hand), it happened that **another letter of yours was delivered me at almost the same time as that more prolix one of mine was written** — and that first a little before the winter solstice, with the Christmas holidays at hand. Though it was rather brief, yet it was most welcome to me, both because it showed you persevering in our friendship (thus to be continued, until it may be otherwise), and missing no occasion of writing; and because I gathered thence that you patiently bear my delay in replying — since you used in it no expostulation, which you might not undeservedly have done — although the causes of this tardiness were not yet clear to you; which I trust you have now, on receiving mine, recognised and held excused.

This was added too, **that your letter was not sterile, but brought with it, in a fertile birth, three diligent observations of the Sun made at Kassel in three different but continuous years, and the same worked out geometrically and by numbers, for deriving thence the solar Apogee and Eccentricity.** This was indeed very welcome to me, since I had not seen those observations before. For they had not previously been communicated to me by the Landgrave **Wilhelm**, of most praised memory, nor by his Mathematician **Christoph Rothmann** (which I wonder was omitted); otherwise I should have inserted them in the **first Volume of the Epistles** (which has the letters exchanged between us in those very years), together with a competent disquisition and a comparison with my own findings. So that it was rightly done by you, that even from this omission you formed a not-false conjecture that they had not reached my hands before; and you the more rightly and acceptably impart them to me now.

**But it much tortured me that, at first inspection, I noticed the Sun's Apogee indeed somehow to agree with mine** — for a half-degree's difference can with difficulty be discerned in so subtle a practical computation [*Pragmateia*]; nor does it perceptibly hurt anything, since at the Apogee itself it varies the Sun's longitude by but one minute, in the other places still less. **But when I beheld the Eccentricity — investigated three ways, and everywhere constant to itself almost in the very seconds — nonetheless falling short of mine by about 6 minutes of the 60 parts of the Eccentric's semidiameter, I hesitated wondrously, [as to] what scruple lurked beneath these scruples.** For when, my own Observations revised (which I had made about the same days at our Danish Uraniborg), and the Sun's place at once computed from our restored calculation (which presupposes an Eccentricity of 2° 9′ at the least), I saw the Sun's longitude everywhere agreeing within a single minute with what the Kassel observations gave — and it was not possible, **from the same data so closely agreeing, using a non-fallacious process of demonstration (such as I found yours too to be), for nonetheless so differing an Eccentricity to come out** — what silent obstacle had insinuated itself was not so easily clear at first. For by a method other than yours (namely, by **prosthaphaereses**), repeating your calculation for the most part, it seemed to stand correctly. Nor could the insinuation of **refraction** disturb my intention — which in the first example, where the Sun [was near 27°], in the last (the Sun passing the third degree of **Aquarius [♒]**, and elevated only 19°), introduced the same [of] 5 minutes (to say nothing of the intermediate, in which this diversity was less perceptible) — since the Sun's places in the Ecliptic, agreeing so closely with my numbers, sufficiently proved that **Rothmann had skilfully forestalled not only the Sun's Parallaxes but also the refractions** (about which he had several times been admonished by me, as is clear from the Epistles you cited). Nor could the fact that the maximum obliquity of the Ecliptic was assumed half a scruple less in the transmitted calculation than was presupposed by me produce so evident a discrepancy in this Eccentricity — any more than the neglected equation of time could suggest more than an insensible variation. So, weighing all things circumspectly (as I then thought) in your demonstrations and the numbers built upon them, and recalling my own reckonings too (which proceed — for deriving the Sun's Eccentricity and Apogee from the Equinoxes and the middle of **Taurus [♉] and Leo [♌]** — with even a little more compendium and certainty) to the anvil of calculation, and proving that nothing had been erred in them, **I threw this disquisition aside for a while, as not satisfying myself**. Yet, when the sacred Christmas-days were over, taking it again in hand and [going through] your whole calculation from the beginning to the end (which before had been neglected about the extremes, since the rest agreed so nicely), **at last it was found wherein the knot of this discrepancy lurked.** For around the very exit of the calculation — when, from the square root (which in all three examples is almost similar to itself, and conspires most closely to the number **3591**), it was reached, so that thence the quantity of the Eccentricity might be elicited — we detected that, **by some carelessness (which could easily otherwise happen amid your gravest occupations, or if this computation was instituted by some other — for you did not indicate whose it is), that number, introduced into the Table of sines, wrongly showed the quantity of the Eccentricity, and so [made it] less than just, since it ought to be derived proportionally** (taking 60 for the whole radius); **and so the same determination of the Eccentricity comes out most closely with mine** — exceeding mine, indeed, by a few seconds of almost no moment, rather than falling short of it by 6 minutes. Nay, if the **solar observations diligently made by me in the year 1583** be brought into counsel, the same Eccentricity comes out as the transmitted inquiry. For I too then found it **3592 parts** (of which the radius, or total sine, is 100000) — or **2° 9⅓′** (of which the same is 60) — the **Apogee then placed at 5¾° Cancer [♋]**; and the same, through seven years to the year **1590** (which is the middle of your three), by adding **9 minutes** (as the Apogee's change from Ptolemy down to then requires — for the Apogee-progression noted in the book just sent is somewhat slower, since it was derived by a special method from an observation of **Regiomontanus** made 100 years before, as also the year-quantity was assumed a little less than just; yet in both these the discrepancy is not so great as Copernicus's reckoning bears) — agreeing **in the very minute (which is wonderful) with the Landgrave's 1590 Apogee.**

But that you may the more readily and fully perceive **by what method and from what data I have verified the Sun's Apogee and Eccentricity**, and whence this minute difference in my numeration crept in between the result of 1583 and certain others subsequently following — **behold, you have [here] the first Volume of our *Progymnasmata* of Restored Astronomy**, so far as the various disturbances and vicissitudes of my affairs have hitherto permitted me to complete it in print. With what Title it is shortly to be published (Heaven favouring), and what remains to be added in it, the first appended sheet makes manifest. **There, in the very first chapter, these things concerning the restitution of the Solar course are amply dispatched.** What is to be subjoined about the **Moon** by way of appendix, you will see in time. **The second chapter builds the most accurate restitution of the fixed Stars, up to the eighth hundred, from the very foundation, and at last reviews them canonically; to which I afterward supplied those that are wanting, up to the full thousand. The remaining part of the volume treats clearly of the supremely miraculous Star of the year 1572** [the supernova]. You will find, besides, in this work some of the things formerly ventilated between us more fully investigated, and not a few others which will (as I hope) please your genius. Take it in good part, and reserve it to yourself alone, until you obtain the same augmented and quite completed, together with some others of my labours in this kind of study. The typographical errors (of which I found some while revising), you, who grasp the matter itself well, will easily correct. **See what those three solar observations of three years, benevolently sent me by you, have produced!** If you procure more, diligently made — in other Stars too, whether at Kassel or elsewhere — these too will not return without interest. I understand that **Werner** has published some celestial observations of his own; if, besides those on the change of weather which I have seen, they have anything concerning the Phenomena of the Stars noted from the heaven, and you know anything of that book, I should wish a copy granted me for a while.

I do not wish to delay you longer now; but I expect shortly a reply both to my earlier [letter] and to this. This only will I add: that **the invention of the Apogee and Eccentricity from the observations of the year 1583 (as set forth in the book I now send) pleases me more than the other which I afterward used from the subsequent years** — since the reckoning of the equation of time was applied there, but afterward omitted; and so the Apogee and Eccentricity sought from the Landgrave's observations will agree more rightly with that prior annotation of mine (as I said), though the difference, which otherwise intervenes, is of almost no estimation. This little discrepancy, however, the **observations of the Sun to be continued here in Bohemia (Heaven favouring) will easily resolve — since the Equator stands here almost 6 degrees higher than in Denmark, toward the fortieth degree, and on that account no Sun-refraction, perceptible to the senses, insinuates itself near the very Equinoxes (as it does in Denmark).**

Fare, then, most well, and pass the course of this coming Jubilee Year, and of many others, in a happy state of mind and body and outward affairs.

Given at Girsitz — whence tomorrow, God willing, I have resolved to return to Benátky — on the day before the Kalends of January, in the year of the Lord 1600.
Most devoted to Your Magnificence,
**Tycho Brahe**, written in my own hand.


*[Postscript:]* I have appended the calculation of the Sun's Apogee and Eccentricity, repeated through the prosthaphaereses used by us in the three transmitted examples, which scarcely differs from yours — save for the correction of the Eccentricity, as I noted in the letter. I have also added a certain Ode, not without charm, sent to me from Pomerania these last days, that you may annex it to the other poems shared with you.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Hans Georg Herwart von Hohenburg** (Munich) — addressed with his full Bavarian titles (Privy Councillor, President of Swabia, Estates' Chancellor). The third Tycho↔Herwart letter in the literature consulted (cf. brahe-t_15990831001 and brahe-t_15990917001; and the later brahe-t_16000911001).
- **Significance — a forensic analysis of the Kassel solar observations, and the sending of the *Progymnasmata*.**
 - **The Kassel solar data.** Herwart had sent **three diligent solar observations made at Kassel in three successive years** (the **Landgrave Wilhelm IV / Christoph Rothmann** observatory), reduced for the **solar Apogee and Eccentricity** — never before seen by Tycho (who would else have printed them in his *Epistolae* vol. I).
 - **The error hunt (a model of Tychonic forensic computation).** Tycho found the **Apogee agreeing** (a half-degree being negligible) but the **Eccentricity short of his own by c. 6′ of 60** — yet the underlying solar longitudes agreed "within one minute." After excluding **refraction** (Rothmann had guarded against parallax *and* refraction, on Tycho's earlier urging), **obliquity**, and the **equation of time**, he **set the puzzle aside over Christmas**, then **traced the discrepancy to a computational slip**: a square-root value (~**3591**) **fed into the sine-table without the proper proportional scaling (radius = 60 vs 100000)** — once corrected, the Kassel Eccentricity **matches his own**. His own values: **Eccentricity 2° 9⅓′ (= 3592 of 100000), Apogee 5¾° Cancer in 1583**, advancing ** c. 9′ over 7 years to 1590**, "agreeing in the very minute with the Landgrave's 1590 Apogee." (He notes the *Progymnasmata*'s slower apogee-progression derives from a **Regiomontanus** observation a century back.)
 - **The *Progymnasmata* vol. I sent (a contents-inventory).** Tycho sends Herwart the **first volume of the *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata*** as far as printed: **ch. 1** the solar restitution; an appendix on the **Moon**; **ch. 2** the **fixed-star catalogue (built to 800, supplied to a full 1000)**; the rest on the **Star of 1572 (the supernova)**. To be kept private until the completed copy. *(A datable Progymnasmata presentation to Herwart.)*
 - **The Bohemia advantage.** Tycho notes solar observations are *better* in Bohemia: the **Equator c. 6° higher than in Denmark, so no sensible refraction near the equinoxes** — promising to resolve the residual discrepancy.
 - **Werner.** Tycho asks for a copy of **Werner's** published celestial observations, if they bear on star-phenomena (not just weather).
- **Cross-references.** Pair with the other Herwart letters (brahe-t_15990831001, brahe-t_15990917001, brahe-t_16000911001); the **Kassel / Wilhelm IV / Rothmann** observational thread; and the **Progymnasmata printing/distribution** thread (brahe-t_16000107001, brahe-t_15990922001).
- **Persons & places named.** Herwart von Hohenburg; **Landgrave Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel** (the late); **Christoph Rothmann**; **Ptolemy, Regiomontanus, Copernicus**; **Werner** (a published observer); the **Star of 1572**. Places: **Girsitz (Jiřice)**, **Benátky**, **Kassel**, **Uraniborg/Denmark**, **Munich**. Glyphs ☉ ☾ ♒ ♉ ♌ ♋ reproduced.
- **Calendar.** *Girtzitzae … pridie Calend. Ianuar. Anni Domini 1600* — "the day before the Kalends of January" = **31 December 1599 [N.S.]** (identifier 15991231001, label "31 december n.s."; the "Anni Domini 1600" reflects the imminent new year). Header and label agree.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (the appended solar apogee/eccentricity calculation + a Pomeranian Ode), restored from Dreyer VIII p.226 (dropped by the working transcription).

documents.abstract: Acknowledges a letter brought by Kepler on his arrival with Baron Hoffmann, and mentions failed earlier correspondence sent from Wandsbek to Jutland.
documents.incipit: MIN gandske wenlig hilsen nu och altid forsend met Vor Herre. Welbørdig her Seyffert …

text.original:
[TYCHO BRAHE AD SIGFRIDUM RINDSCHAT].

MIN gandske wenlig hilsen nu och altid forsend met Vor Herre. Welbørdig her Seyffert Rindtschadt, gunstige gode wen, nest min wenlig tacksigellße for allt beuist gode, huilket igien att forskylde ieg stedze will findis aff formuen willig, y hues maade ieg kand giøre nogit, som eder till aere och gode kan werre. Giffuendis eder derhos gandske wenligen tillkiende, att eders gode och vellmeente skriffuelße er mig for en 10 eller 12 vger siden tillhende kommen met m. Johanne Keplero, som fuldis hid y dette kongerige Behemen met den welbørdige fryherre, her Johan Friderick Hoffman, eders slecht och byr och min gunstige gode wenn, och war samme eders skriffuelße mig megit kierkommen, saa well som forbeneunte m. Kepler, thi ieg haffde y langthiidt adtraad att wille wijde, hor y war och horledis det gick eder, haffde och, der ieg bode paa Wandeßbechk wed Hamburgk paa itt aars thiid att giørre, førend røm. key. may., voris allernaadigst herre, lodt naadiste kallde mig hid till sig, skreffuit itt breff till eder och sendt det ind vdi Jüdland, y den ein, som ieg haffde meent, atty bode, mens ieg fick beskeen ygien, att y war dragen derfran hen y eder faederne landtt.

Angaendis forbemelte m. Keplero, war hans ankombst mig ochsaa saare angenehm, thi ieg haffuer vdj lang thiidt holdit megit aff hannom for hans herlige ingenium och skickelligheet skyldt y die mathematische och astronomische konster, som y wijde mig ocsaa att haffue y sønderlighedt løst till, och der hand war kommen till Prag, sende strax derepther forbeneunte her Jehann Friderich Hoffmann hannom hid till mig, och bleff hand saa her hos mig met samme her Hoffmans gode wille och samtøcke ved 2 maaneder. Siden drog handt till her Hoffman vdi Prag ygien och var der hos hannom vdj 2 eller 3 wger, epther hans beger, och der hans welbørdighed war saa dragen hen y itt baadt, for hans sundhedt skyld, lod hand mester Keplerum komme hidt till mig igien, paa det ieg, som tillforn, ydremere kunde conuersere met hannom y die astron[om]ische konster, intill hand kunde bekomme god gelegenhed att drage tillbage vdjgien y Stiermarck, och haffde hand achtedt sig adsteedt did hen y en aff disse dage met første leylighed, som hand kunde bekomme fra Prag.

Mens midlertiidt er hidkommen till mig aff Danmarck en herremand aff fornemme adell och Rossenkrantz slecht, der y landit børdig, som er och min nehr slecht och bør. Handt er tillsinds att drage ind vdi Østerich, der underdanigst att praesentere sin tienist høyborne erßhertzog Mathias, och siden att lade bruge och forsøye sig y den wngerische krig, och achter hand sig nest Gudz hielp vdj morgen herfran och hen till Pilsen, hor røm. key. may. endnu er, der att forsøye, om handt kand forhuerue en forschrifft till høybemelte ershertzog Matias, att hans først: naade wille thage hannom vdi tieniste, och att hand wille lade hannom werre sig met all gunst och naade befallid. Saa haffuer ieg tallt met samme Rossenkrantz, att hand wille tage mester Keplerum paa wognen met sig till Wien y Østerich och staa hans tering, huilket hand och godwilligen haffuer loffuid att wille giørre for min skyld; haffuer ieg och raad och offuertallt mester Kepler, att hand sin reysse wille forholle till samme herremand kommer hid ygien fra Pilsen, huilket ieg haabis att kunde skee inden 14 dage y det seeniste, saa att hand da kandt følgis med hanom lettelligen och foruden all bekaastning intill Wien. Och endog dette søntis mester Kepler att wille falle for langt, thi hand yller hiem ygien for hues hand haffuer att giøre for herrene y Stirmarkid och for sin høstruff skyld, saa haffuer hand dog omsier herudj beuilliget och eptherfølt mit raad, eptherdi hand formerkte, att ieg mente det gott och troligen met hannom, som han och stedtze herepther skall befinde hos mig, epthersom ieg och mercker hannom att werre wertt affholdid och promouerit till det beste. Kierre herr Syberet, dette kunde ieg icke lade att giffue eder paa denne tiid tillkiende, om m. Keplero, som y kommenderit till mig, paa det y kunde wijde aarsagen, horfor hand bliffuer saa lenge wde, och haffue hannom wndskyldit, baade hos die andre herrer vdj Styrmarket och hos eder selff, och wdj ligge maade lade giffue hans høftruff, naar eder stedis boedt, dette tillkiende. Jeg skriffuer nu icke ydermere suar paa eders skriffuelße till mig for tidsendz korthedt skyld, menß achter det nest Gudz hielp att giørre met m. Kepler, naar hand drager did y landit ygien, thi hand haffuer set sig forre paa weyen att besøge eder, saa achter ieg att suare eder nochsom till alle puncter, som eders breff indholder och enda ydermere. Medlertid beder ieg eder gandske gierne, att y will haffue mig vndskyldid och ochsesaa handle det, saa att det bliffuer icke tagid m. Kepler till mødstøcke, att [hand] bliffuer saa lenge vde. Ydermere aarsag dertill skall y, nest Gudz hielp, faa att wiide y min anden skriffuelße, naar hand ankommer. Och will hermed nu och alltid haffue eder Gud allmechtugste befalid, giører vell och siger eders kierre høstruff, fru Magdalene Munck, mange gode netter paa min och min kierre høstruff och børns weyne.

Daterit paa det keyserlige slot Bennatickden.
text.english:
**[TYCHO BRAHE TO SIGFRID RINDSCHAT].**

My quite friendly greeting, now and always, conveyed by Our Lord. Well-born Sir Seyfried Rindschadt, favourable good friend: after my friendly thanks for all the kindness shown me — which to requite I shall always be found willing according to my means, in whatever way I can do anything that may be to your honour and good. Giving you herewith, quite kindly, to know that **your good and well-meant letter came to my hands some 10 or 12 weeks ago, with Master Johannes Kepler**, who came hither into this Kingdom of Bohemia with the well-born baron, **Sir Johann Friderich Hoffmann** — your kinsman and townsman, and my favourable good friend — and that same letter of yours was very welcome to me, as was the aforesaid Master Kepler; for I had long desired to know where you were and how it fared with you. I had also — when I dwelt at **Wandsbek near Hamburg** for about a year, before the Roman Imperial Majesty, our most gracious lord, graciously had me called hither to him — **written a letter to you and sent it into Jutland**, to the place where I had thought you dwelt; but I received word back that you had moved away thence into your fatherland.

Concerning the aforesaid **Master Kepler**, his arrival was likewise very agreeable to me; **for I have long thought much of him, for the sake of his splendid genius and aptitude in the mathematical and astronomical arts** — in which, as you know, I too have particular delight. And when he had come to Prague, the aforesaid Sir Johann Friderich Hoffmann straightway sent him hither to me; and so **he stayed here with me, with the said Sir Hoffmann's good will and consent, about 2 months**. Then he went back to Sir Hoffmann in Prague, and was there with him 2 or 3 weeks at his request; and when his lordship had gone off to a [healing] bath for his health's sake, he let Master Kepler come hither to me again, **so that I, as before, might further converse with him in the astronomical arts**, until he could get good opportunity to travel back again into **Styria**; and he had intended to set off thither one of these days, with the first occasion he could get from Prague.

But meanwhile there has come to me from Denmark **a gentleman of distinguished nobility and of the Rosenkrantz family**, born there in the country, who is also my near kinsman and relative. He is minded to travel into **Austria**, there most humbly to present his service to the high-born **Archduke Matthias**, and then to let himself be employed and try himself in **the Hungarian war**; and he intends, with God's help, tomorrow [to go] from here on to **Pilsen**, where the Roman Imperial Majesty still is, there to try whether he can obtain a letter of recommendation to the said Archduke Matthias, that his princely Grace would take him into service and let him be commended to him with all favour and grace. So **I have spoken with this same Rosenkrantz, that he would take Master Kepler on his wagon with him to Vienna in Austria and bear his expenses — which he has willingly promised to do for my sake**; and I have also advised and prevailed upon Master Kepler to hold off his journey until this same gentleman comes here again from Pilsen — which I hope can happen within 14 days at the latest — **so that he may then travel with him easily, and without any cost, as far as Vienna**. And although this seemed to Master Kepler that it would fall out too long [a delay] — for he hastens home again, on account of what he has to do for the lords in Styria, and for his wife's sake — yet he has at last consented herein and followed my advice, since he perceived **that I meant it well and faithfully toward him** (as he shall also always find with me hereafter), seeing that I judge him worthy to be esteemed and advanced to the best.

Dear Sir Syfried, this I could not omit to make known to you at this time, concerning Master Kepler whom you commended to me, so that you might know **the reason why he stays away so long, and may have him excused — both with the other lords in Styria and with you yourself** — and likewise let his wife know this, when you get a messenger. I do not now write a fuller reply to your letter, for shortness of time, but intend, God willing, to do it through Master Kepler when he travels thither into the country again — for he has resolved to visit you on the way — so that I intend to answer you sufficiently on all the points your letter contains, and even more besides. Meanwhile I beg you quite gladly that you will hold me excused, and also handle it so that **it not be held against Master Kepler that he stays away so long**. Further reason for it you shall, God willing, get to know in my next letter, when he arrives. And herewith I will now and always have you commended to God Almighty. Fare well, and bid your dear wife, **Lady Magdalene Munck**, many good-nights on behalf of me and my dear wife and children.

Dated at the imperial castle of Benátky.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Sigfrid / Seyfried Rindscha[d]t** (the address varies: *Seyffert Rindtschadt*, *herr Syberet*, *Sigfrid*) — Kepler's patron-connection in **Styria/Graz**, a kinsman and "townsman" of the baron **Hoffmann**; his wife is **Lady Magdalene Munck** (a Danish-sounding name, suggesting a Dano-Styrian link that explains Tycho's writing him in Danish). Not further identified here.
- **Significance — the *warm* face of the Tycho–Kepler crisis (companion to the bitter Jessenius letter).** This Danish draft was written **from Benátky in the very same weeks as the angry letter to Jessenius (brahe-t_16000408001, 8 April 1600)** — and shows the opposite register entirely. To Kepler's patron, Tycho:
 - **praises Kepler's "splendid genius (*herlige ingenium*) and aptitude in the mathematical and astronomical arts,"** saying his arrival was "very agreeable";
 - narrates Kepler's stay matter-of-factly (≈2 months with Tycho → 2–3 weeks back with Hoffmann in Prague → returned to Tycho while Hoffmann took a cure);
 - **arranges and funds Kepler's return to Styria** — persuading a visiting **Rosenkrantz kinsman** (bound for Archduke Matthias's service in the Hungarian war, via Pilsen and Vienna) to carry Kepler **on his wagon to Vienna at no cost**, and persuading Kepler to wait c. 14 days for him;
 - asks the patron to **excuse Kepler's long absence** to "the other lords in Styria" and to Kepler's wife, insisting **"I meant it well and faithfully toward him … I judge him worthy to be esteemed and advanced to the best."**
 The juxtaposition is the heart of the document: even while venting fury to the mediator, Tycho protects Kepler's standing with his employers and pays his way home. *(The reconciliation that followed, and Kepler's eventual succession, are prefigured here far more than in the Jessenius letter.)*
- **Biographical details.** Confirms Kepler **travelled to Bohemia with Hoffmann**; the **two-month first residence** at Benátky; the shuttling to Prague and back; and Tycho's own earlier **year at Wandsbek near Hamburg** before the imperial call, during which he had tried (in vain) to reach Rindschat by a letter sent into Jutland.
- **The unnamed Rosenkrantz.** "A gentleman … of the Rosenkrantz family … my near kinsman," bound for **Archduke Matthias** and the **Hungarian (Turkish) war** — not individually identified; left as given.
- **Persons named.** Sigfrid/Seyfried Rindschat; **Johannes Kepler**; **Johann Friderich Hoffmann** (baron, Kepler's host); **Archduke Matthias**; **Rudolf II** (at Pilsen); the unnamed **Rosenkrantz** kinsman; **Lady Magdalene Munck** (Rindschat's wife); Kepler's wife (Barbara, unnamed). Places: **Benátky**, **Prague**, **Wandsbek**/Hamburg, **Jutland**, **Styria**, **Austria/Vienna**, **Pilsen**.
- **Date.** Undated in the draft ("Dated at the imperial castle of Benátky," no day); identifier 16000000001 and label "Benatky" carry only the year. **Internal evidence** — "10–12 weeks since your letter came with Kepler," Kepler now about to leave for Styria, the Rosenkrantz departing "tomorrow" for Pilsen — ties it **to the same spring-1600 weeks as the 8 April 1600 Jessenius letter**; dated here **[Benátky, c. April 1600]** without inventing a precise day.
- **Language note.** Tycho's **Early Modern Danish** chancery hand, read securely; spelling is heavily phonetic (*ingenium*, *conuersere*, *promouerit* are his own Latinisms in the Danish). The witness is a **draft (Kladde)** in the Basel autograph collection.
- **Correction.** Source text corrected against Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia XIV, page 205: "Vor Horre" corrected to "Vor Herre" (the standard Danish greeting-formula "Our Lord"). The English translation already read correctly and required no change.
