text.original:
[TYCHO BRAHE AD SIMONEM DE PETKUM]

MEIN freundtlichen grues mit wunschung alles gutts zuuor, erbar vnd furnemer Symon von Petkum, inbesonders gutter freundt. Eur schreiben hab ich, zu Hamburgk den 12 februarij diesen jhars datirt, bekommen, vnd daneben die beide von magistro Dauide Fabricio vnnd herrn Ritherhausen zu Brehmen. Was nun anlanget die brieffe an mir hero zu bestellen, gilt es mir gleich, ob ihr sie gehn Leipzig vnd von dannen auff Dressden an mein wirt, oder auch auff Nurrenbergk vnd von dannen hieher, oder auff Prag ahn herrn doctor Heller, auff die kleine zeitte wonhafftig, dirigirt, so werde ich sie wohl bekommen, so ferne ihr nicht gelegenheit habt, von dannen dieselbige brieffue an mir directe zu schicken.

Der her burgmeister Vincentius Mullerus schreibt, das jhre key. may. ahn die herrn von Hamburgk gethanes schreiben jhnen noch nicht geliebert sey, aber wen das gescheen vnd er daraus vernummen, was jhr may. von meinetwegen allergnedigst begerren thutt, will ehr, so vill ihme ihmmer meuglig, helffen die sache promouiren, worfur ich mich gegen ihme thu bedancken, vnd hab ihme selbst weitern bescheidt dauon zugeschrieben, welchen brieff ihr ihme von meinetwegen könnet vberantwortten. Das dieselbige literae caesareae noch nicht alda den herrn sein vberliebert, kan ich gedencken, das die vhrsache sey, das mein factor zu Lübeck, Jochum Boch, den selbigen brieff bej sich behelt, bis er die jnstrumenten neben dem andern gutt gehn Hamburgek schicke, vnd wan das mitlerweill nicht gescheen ist, so wirt ehr es halt thun, wovon ich ime auch geschrieben hab, welchen brieff ihr alßbalt könnet zu ihm schicken. Vnd so balt die instrumenten vnd das ander gutt, so ich zu Lubch hab, gehn Hamburg ist ankommen, so bitt ich freundtlich ihr wollet bei den herren alda soliciterern, das sie wollen die furordnung thun, das man kuntte schiffe dazu bekommen, das es alles sambt was ihr alda habt, so vhnverkaufft ist, köntte ihr key. may. zum gnedigsten gefalln hirauff in Bohemen gefurt werden, vnd so die herren wollen ein von ihren eygenen diener dabey haben, der auff köntte sehen, das alle ding richtig zuginge, wehre es mir sehr angenem, vnd so sie mülstein oder andern wahren, welche alhie leichter alß da bey euch zu bekommen, wieder hin ab füren zu lassen gesint, auff das die schiff nicht ledich zu hauß kemen, köntte derselbige auch darauf auffsehn haben, vnd ich woltte auch gehrn meuglichen fleiß anwenden, das solchs mit dem ehesten vnd mit vortheill ausgericht werde.

Vnd wie wohl ihr meinet, das nutzlich kuntte sein, das ihr may. noch ein schreibent ließ an den erbarn rath alda der sachen wegen abgehen, so achte ich es vhnvonnötten, dieweill das vorrige schreibent noch verhanden oder villeigt nun schon vberliebert. Ich vorsiehe mich, das die hern von Hamburgk werden sich wohl wissen gehorsamblich nach jhr key. may. ehrsten schreiben wissen zu richten, das es keines mehreren bedarff, vnd das sie keineswegens thun werden wie die Magdaeburger, ahn welchen jhr key. may. zuo mahl von meinetwegen geschrieben, vnd sie gleichwohl subterfugia gefunden vnd die schuere belegerung, so sie vor ein halbhundert jahr gelitten, praesendirt, das sie solchs nicht thun köntten. Welchs jhr may. hart hatt verdrossen, vnd sie den kop darvber schuttelt, vnd zu vhnwillen auffgenohmen. Die rehtte wahren auch gahr spötsch darüber, das sie durfften jhr may. so ein ringes abslagen, vnd hat einer von ihnen, welcher teglich mehr alß andere zu jhr may. zutritt hat, diesse formalia verba darzu gesagt: Wir hetten gemeint, die von Magdeburgk wehren hoffleutte, nuhn vormercken wihr, daß sie bauren sein, es kan wohl die zeit kommen, das sie jhre may. wiederumb bedarffen, alsdan kan mahn wohl ein bessere vnd mehr glaublich enthschuldung vnd praetext finden, alß sie itzunder thun, das sie also repulsam bekommen. Haec ille, audientibus quibusdam allijs, tum quoque meo sollicitatore, dixit, vnd hat alßbalt jhr may. gnedigst befolen, das ein ander brieff wurde geschrieben ad reuerendum capittulum vnd die ehrwerdige dumbherrn zu Magdaeburgk, daß sie solchs jhr may. zum gnedichsten gefallen thun wolten, welchs sie auch sich darzu gantz gehorsamlich erbotten. Vnd ich thu den brieff itzunder zu jhnen verschicken, mallet jam renatus Magdaeburgensis se id officij Caesari non denegasse et nunc libenter, si liceret, obtemperaret, sed sero sapiunt Phryges, Caesar etiam non uult amplius, ut per ipsos id fiat et potius opera reuerendi capituli uti dictum. Wan etzliche brieffue von hern Josepho Scaligero oder sunst auß Niederlant ankommen, oder bescheit von dem ephemeridum compilatore, so last mihr dieselbige mit ehester gelegenheit bekommen, vnd sendet diesen beigelegten brieff ahn magistrum Dauidem Fabricium nebenst dem andern ahn herrn Ritterhusium zu Brehmen; wehn derselbe den ahn Fabricium bekommet, so wirt er in wohl alßbalt gehen Resterhaffuen vorschaffuen. Ich vormercke auß des heern Dauidis Fabrici schreibend das so ehr einige gutte gelegenheit alhie köntte bekomen, das er nicht vhngneigt wehre allhie zu sein, worauff ich im gutten bescheit geschrieben, wolte gehrn, das ehr eigentlich den brieff köntte bekommen, dan so es ihm also gefellig wehr, köntte ehr mit seiner frauwen vnd kinder vnd nöttichstem gerette hir mit schiffen von Hamburgk her auffkommen; vnd was er dazu fur nöttwendig viaticum bedarff, köntt ihr ihm von meinetwegen vorstrecken, vnd so ihr keins von meinem gehlt habt, damit es wider kan erlegt werden, so will ich es euch zu danck lassen wiederumb mit den leutten, so von Hamburgk hjerauff kommen, zustellen, vnd geburlich interesse davon geben, das ihr ohne schaden sollt sein.

Das ihr meiner lieben schwester, fraw Sophia Brahe, habt einen von meinen kutschwogen sambt deme, was dazu gehörig, nach ihren begehr folgen lassen, daran habt ihr recht gethan, vnd ich trage darahn kein missgefallen, es kumbt vmb so ein gering ding nicht zuischen ihr und mihr, ich wolte ihr alß meiner hertzlieben schwester viel ein grösserß zugefallen geschehen lassen.

Was ihr von meinem übrigen gutt könnet alsbalt zu gelte machen, das thutt, aber daß positiff vnd die kleine geschutz von kupfer, eeissen oder waß sönsten metallisch ankombt, das schicket hierauff nebenst dem, so von Lybch geschicket wirt, darvnter auch thunnen, vnd stellt es alles, es sei was es wolle, auff ein klar register, dass ich richtigen bescheid davon wisse. Schreibt mihr auch zu, wie lang mein schwester ist alda zu Wandesbech gewessen, vnd wo sie hingezogen, dan ich kan nicht glauben, das sie noch alda sey, sönsten hette ich ihr wohl geschrieben. Last mihr auch wissen, ob Erich Lange ist zu Hamburgk gewesen, vnd wie es mit seinen sachen stehet, vnd woh er itzunder sein wohnung hat; wan ehr alda in die nahent ist, vnd mihr etwas schreiben will, so könt ihr mihr dasselbe zuschicken.

Was ahnlanget, das die frau stathalterin euch geschrieben hat von den 5000 thallern, wan sie dieselbige solten gewertigk sein, so ist es an dehm, das mein gutter freundt vnd blutsvörwanter ihn Dennemark, Eske Bilde, solte von meinetwegen dasselbige gelt in vorgangen vmbslag erleget haben, vnd meinen brieff wieder gefodert, aber er hat nicht zeittlich genug bescheit davon krigen können, sondern hatt sich erbotten zu nechstkumbstigen vmbslag alles richtig zu machen, vnd ich vormeine, das ehr die 300 thaller zum interesse schon erlegt hat.

Von wegen meiner vhnkostung, so ich ahm gebau vnd eissenwerch zum Wandesbech gethan, vorsihe ich mich, das die frau stathalterinn mihr nicht lenger aufhalten wirt, vnd meinen schaden nicht begehren. Vnd dieweill sie jhren sohn Bredo Wandesbech hatt abgehandelt, kan sie woll es selbst am besten richtig machen; will sie auch nicht die trallien vnd eeissenwerch, vnd waß ich sonst da hab machen lassen, behallten, vnd zahlen das, so zuvohr nicht davon bezalt ist worden, so könt jhr es alles wiederumb wegknehmen, vnd alles das eeisien wegenlassen vnd mit dem andern gutt hierauffschicken. Es sein auch noch etzliche schlosser, welche ich alda hab machen lassen, vnd zwo kachellofen, nebenst anders, so ihr wohl wirt können erfaren. Vorsihe ich mich, das ihr in diesen vnd allen anderen werdet von meinetwegen thun was billig vnd recht sein kan, dasselbige vmb euch vnd den eurigen wiederumb zu vorschulden will ich stetz geflissen sein. Vnd thu vnß hiemit semtlichen in schutz des Allmechtigen befehlen.

Was ihr von meinetwegen zu böttenlohn errleget oder sönsten, das das gutt mit brettern vnd mätten wohl vorwart werde, oder in andern wegen beköstiget, sol euch zu danch wiederumb bezallt werden.
text.english:
**[TYCHO BRAHE TO SIMON VON PETKUM]**

My friendly greeting, with wishing of all good, first — honourable and distinguished Simon von Petkum, especially good friend. **Your letter, dated at Hamburg the 12th of February this year, I have received, and with it the two from Master David Fabricius and Mr. Ridderhusen at Bremen.** Now as concerns the forwarding of letters to me here: it is all one to me whether you direct them **via Leipzig and thence to Dresden, to my host; or via Nuremberg and thence hither; or to Prague, to Dr. Heller, dwelling on the Lesser Town [Kleine Seite]** — so [that] I shall well get them — unless you have a chance to send the same to me directly from there.

**Burgomaster Vincent Möller** writes that the Imperial Majesty's letter to the lords of Hamburg has not yet been delivered to them; but when that has happened, and he has learned from it what His Majesty most graciously desires on my behalf, he will help promote the matter as much as ever he can; for which I thank him, and have written him further instruction myself, which letter you can deliver to him on my behalf. That the imperial letter is not yet delivered to the lords there, I think the cause is that **my factor at Lübeck, Jochum Boch [Joachim Buch], keeps that letter by him until he sends the instruments, with the other goods, to Hamburg**; and if that has not meanwhile happened, he will do it — about which I have also written him, which letter you can send him at once. And as soon as the instruments and the other goods I have at Lübeck have arrived at Hamburg, I ask you kindly to **solicit the lords there to arrange that ships could be got for it, so that all of it — together with whatever you have there unsold — could be brought up here to Bohemia, to the Imperial Majesty's most gracious pleasure**; and if the lords will have one of their own servants along, who could see that everything goes properly, it would be very agreeable to me; and if they are minded to ship **millstones or other wares (easier got here than there with you) back down, so the ships do not come home empty**, the same [man] could oversee that too, and I would gladly apply all possible diligence that it be done quickly and with advantage.

And although you think it might be useful for His Majesty to let another letter go to the honourable Council there about the matter, I deem it unnecessary, since the previous letter is still on hand, or perhaps already delivered. **I expect the lords of Hamburg will know how to comply obediently with His Majesty's first letter, so that no more is needed — and that they will by no means do as the Magdeburgers**: to whom His Majesty wrote twice on my behalf, and they nonetheless found subterfuges and **pleaded the harsh siege they suffered a half-hundred years ago, [as excuse] that they could not do such.** Which His Majesty took grievously ill, and shook his head over it, and took as displeasure. The councillors too were quite mocking that [the Magdeburgers] dared refuse His Majesty so trifling a thing; and **one of them — who has daily more access to His Majesty than others — said these formal words to it: "We had thought those of Magdeburg were courtiers; now we perceive they are peasants. The time may well come when they need His Majesty again; then one can well find a better and more credible excuse and pretext than they do now — so that they get a rebuff."** *This he said, certain others hearing, and my solicitor too*; and His Majesty at once most graciously ordered **another letter be written to the reverend Chapter and the venerable canons at Magdeburg, that they would do such to His Majesty's most gracious pleasure** — which they also quite obediently offered to do. And I now send the letter to them. *The Magdeburger, as it were reborn, would now wish that he had not denied that service to the Emperor, and would now gladly obey if it were permitted — but **too late are the Phrygians wise** [sero sapiunt Phryges]; the Emperor too no longer wishes it be done through them, but rather that the service of the reverend Chapter be used, as said.*

When any letters from Mr. **Joseph Scaliger**, or otherwise from the Low Countries, arrive, or word from the **ephemerides-compiler**, let me get the same at the earliest occasion; and **send this enclosed letter to Master David Fabricius, along with the other to Mr. Ridderhusen at Bremen**; when the latter gets the one to Fabricius, he will soon convey it to **Resterhafe** [Fabricius's Frisian parish]. **I perceive from Mr. David Fabricius's letter that, if he could get some good situation here, he would not be disinclined to be here**; whereupon I have written him a good answer, [and] would gladly that he actually got the letter — for if it so pleased him, **he could come up here, with his wife and children and most necessary gear, by ship from Hamburg**; and what necessary travel-money he needs for it, you could advance him on my behalf; and if you have none of my money to repay it with, I will gladly have it conveyed back to you with the people who come up here from Hamburg, and give due interest on it, so that you shall be without loss.

That you let my dear sister, **Lady Sophia Brahe**, have one of my coach-wagons, with what belongs to it, at her request — in that you did right, and I bear no displeasure at it: it does not come to such a trifle between her and me; **I would let a much greater favour befall her, as my heartily-dear sister.**

What of my remaining goods you can quickly turn to money, do that; but **the positive [organ], and the small cannon of copper, iron, or whatever else is metallic, ship up here**, along with what is sent from Lübeck — barrels among them — and **put it all, whatever it be, on a clear register, so that I know proper account of it.** Write me also **how long my sister was there at Wandsbek, and whither she has moved** — for I cannot believe she is still there, else I would have written her. Let me also know **whether Erik Lange was at Hamburg, and how his affairs stand, and where he now has his dwelling**; if he is near there, and will write me something, you could send it to me.

As concerns the **Statthalterin [Governess]** writing you about the **5000 thaler** — whether she should expect them: the matter is that my good friend and blood-relation in Denmark, **Eske Bille**, should have paid that money on my behalf at the past **settlement-term [omslag]**, and demanded my bond back; but he could not get word of it in time, but offered to make all right at the next settlement — and I suppose he has already paid the **300 thaler interest**.

As for my expenses on building and ironwork at Wandsbek, I expect the Statthalterin will not hold me up longer, nor desire my loss. And since **she has bargained Wandsbek [back] from her son Breide [Rantzau]**, she can best make it right herself; [but] if she will not keep **the grilles and ironwork, and what else I had made there**, and pay what was not paid for before, then you could take it all away again, **and remove all the iron and ship it up here** with the other goods. There are also **several locks I had made there, and two tiled stoves**, besides other things, which you will well be able to learn. I expect you will, in this and all else, do on my behalf what is fair and right; the same, toward you and yours, I will always be diligent to requite. And herewith I commend us all to the protection of the Almighty.

What you advance on my behalf for messenger-fees, or otherwise — that the goods be well protected with boards and mats, or in other ways provisioned — shall be repaid you with thanks.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondent.** Tycho's **reply to Simon von Petkum** (his Hamburg/Wandsbek agent), answering **brahe-t_16000212001 (12 February 1600)** point by point. A **draft (Kladde)**, breaking off unsigned.
- **Significance — Tycho's northern logistics and the great Magdeburg anecdote.**
 - **Forwarding routes.** Letters via **Leipzig→Dresden, Nuremberg, or Prague (Dr. Heller, on the Lesser Town)**.
 - **The instrument-ship.** Via **Vincent Möller** (Hamburg burgomaster) and **Jochum Boch (Joachim Buch)** at Lübeck (who holds the imperial letter until the Lübeck goods reach Hamburg); the plan to bring **all the instruments and unsold goods up to Bohemia by ship**, with a Hamburg overseer, the ships returning with **millstones**.
 - **The Magdeburg anecdote (a vivid court scene).** **Magdeburg twice refused** the Emperor's request to ship Tycho's stored goods, **pleading "the harsh siege they suffered a half-hundred years ago"** (the 1550–51 Siege of Magdeburg) — Rudolf II "shook his head" in displeasure; and **a councillor's jibe**: *"We had thought those of Magdeburg were courtiers; now we perceive they are peasants … the time may come when they need His Majesty again."* The Emperor redirected the order **to the Magdeburg cathedral Chapter** (cf. brahe-t_16000405001); Tycho caps it with the Latin tag ***"sero sapiunt Phryges"*** ("too late the Phrygians grow wise") — the now-willing Magdeburgers are too late.
 - **David Fabricius's recruitment.** Tycho **invites Fabricius to come to Prague "with wife and children" by ship from Hamburg**, with travel-money advanced by Petkum — the next step from the death-rumour aftermath (cf. brahe-t_16000212001, brahe-t_15991216001). Routed via **Ridderhusen at Bremen → Resterhafe** (Fabricius's parish).
 - **Sophie Brahe & Erik Lange.** Tycho approves the coach-wagon given his **sister Sophie Brahe** ("a much greater favour I would let befall her"); asks where she has gone from Wandsbek; and inquires after **Erik Lange** — the alchemist nobleman (Sophie's betrothed/husband, ruined by alchemy and living in exile-debt) — "how his affairs stand, where he now dwells."
 - **The remaining goods.** A striking inventory to ship: **"the positive [organ]" (a chamber pipe-organ), the small cannon (of copper/iron), barrels, grilles, locks, two tiled stoves, and ironwork** from Wandsbek — all to be put "on a clear register." A rare glimpse of Tycho's household furnishings.
 - **Finances.** The **5000-thaler bond** to be redeemed by **Eske Bille** at the next *omslag* (cf. brahe-t_15991029001), the **300-thaler interest** likely already paid; the **Wandsbek building costs** and the **Statthalterin / Breide Rantzau** estate matter (cf. brahe-t_16000212001).
- **Cross-references.** Pairs with **brahe-t_16000212001 (Petkum's letter, 12 February 1600)**; the **Magdeburg-transport** thread (brahe-t_16000405001, brahe-t_16000103002); the **Fabricius-recruitment** thread (brahe-t_15990922001, brahe-t_15991216001); and **Sophie Brahe / Erik Lange**.
- **Persons & places named.** Simon von Petkum; **David Fabricius**; **Ludolf Ridderhusen** (Bremen); **Dr. Heller** (Prague); **Vincent Möller** (Hamburg); **Jochum Boch / Joachim Buch** (Lübeck); the **Magdeburg Chapter/canons** & the unnamed imperial councillor; **Rudolf II**; **Joseph Scaliger**; the **ephemerides-compiler**; **Sophie Brahe** (sister); **Erik Lange**; the **Statthalterin** & **Breide Rantzau**; **Eske Bille**. Places: **Benátky**, **Hamburg**, **Lübeck**, **Magdeburg**, **Leipzig**, **Dresden**, **Nuremberg**, **Prague**, **Bremen**, **Resterhafe**, **Wandsbek**.
- **Latin tags.** *Haec ille … dixit* ("this he said"); *mallet iam renatus Magdeburgensis …* ("the Magdeburger, as it were reborn, would now claim …"); ***sero sapiunt Phryges*** (proverb: "too late the Trojans grow wise"). Rendered in italics with translation.
- **Date/place.** Undated **draft**; replies to Petkum's **12 Feb 1600** letter and discusses Sophie Brahe still at/leaving Wandsbek → dated **[Benátky, c. February/March 1600]** (identifier 16000000002, label "Benatky"). Flagged.

**1 defect found:**
- **mistranslation** (medium). 'mallet... non denegasse' (would prefer/wish that he had NOT refused) is a counterfactual wish about the past, implying the Magdeburger DID refuse and now regrets it — which is exactly what the following idiom 'sero sapiunt Phryges' (the Phrygians grow wise too late) comments on. The English instead has him 'now claim that he did not deny' the service, turning an admission-with-regret into a present-tense denial of fact — the opposite posture toward his own past conduct. At: “The Magdeburger, as it were reborn, would now claim that he did not deny that service to the Emperor, and would now glad”.

**Repaired.** Verified against the Dreyer page image, TBOO XIV p.197 (letter spans pp.195-199; pages 195-198 examined). The Latin 'mallet... non denegasse... et nunc libenter, si liceret, obtemperaret, sed sero sapiunt Phryges' is grammatically a regretful counterfactual wish (perfect infinitive under 'mallet'), consistent with the following proverb about too-late wisdom; the published English had converted this into a present-tense denial, which the fix corrects. The Latin itself is left untouched as instructed for a mistranslation defect.

text.original:
AD SAC:Æ CÆS:Æ MAIESTA:IS D:NI NOSTRI CLEMENTIS:I MANUS PROPRIAS HUMILLIMA SUPPLICATIO TYCHONIS BRAHE.

ALLERDURCHLAUCHTIGSTER, großmechtigster römischer kayser auch zu Hungern vndt Beheimb königh, allergnedigster herr. Auff Ewer Kay: May: allergnedigstenn vnd zu vnterschiedtlichen mahlen ergangenen befehlich kan ich gleichwohl meine besoldung, so mir nue lenger alß ain jahr restiret, biß dato noch nicht bekommenn, welchs mihr sehr beschwerlich vorfelt vnndt nit wohll mueglichen lenger außzuestehen. Bitte darumb Ewer Kay: May: ich allervnterthenigst, die geruhen allergnedigft zuuerordnen, daß mihr baide die restirende vndt kunfftige besoldung auß Ewer Key: May: herschafften alhie ihn Behemen (wo es dan Ewer Kay: May: allergnedigst gefallig) geraichet, vndt alle quatember richtig gemacht werden möge, auff das ich die guette zeit mit vergeblichen sollicitationibus nebenst großen schaden vndt bekummernußenn (wie bißhero leider geschen) nit lenger zuebringe.

Waß andere mangel betreffendt ihn den sachen, so von Ewer Kay: May: allergnedigst mir von anbegin vndt hernacher bewilliget sindt, aber noch nicht wiederfahren, hab ich dem herrn Baruitio ain kurz verzaichnuß davon vberliefert Ewer Kay: May: meinet wegen vnterthenigst vorzuetragen, vndt bin der genzlichen hoffnung, daß ich auff diß alles mit dem ehesten ein allergnedigste resolution bekommen werde, auff daß ich ainmahl aigentlich wißen möchte, wie ich alhie darahn wehre, vndt ob ich ainige faste vndt bestendige gelegenheit erlangen köntte, mein vorhabendes hohes studium vndt astronomisches wergk Ewer Röm: Kay: May: vnd dem reich zue sondern ruhm, nutz vnd ehren alhie vnterthenigst zuuohlzihen, oder vonnötten wehre andere bequemigkait darzue zue suchen. Ewer Röm: Kay: May: ihn allen vnterthenigstem gehorsamb zue dienen ich mich iederzeit ganz schuldig erkenne. Ewer Röm: Kay: May: allervnterthenigster gehorsambster diener

Tycho Brahe

text.english:
**To the own hands of His Sacred Imperial Majesty, our most clement Lord: the most humble supplication of Tycho Brahe.**

Most serene, most mighty Roman Emperor, and King of Hungary and Bohemia, most gracious lord. Notwithstanding Your Imperial Majesty's most gracious command, issued at various times, I still cannot, to this date, obtain my salary, which has now been in arrears for more than a year — which falls very grievous to me, and is not well possible to endure longer. I therefore most humbly beg Your Imperial Majesty that you would most graciously deign to ordain that both the arrears and the future salary be furnished me out of Your Imperial Majesty's lordships here in Bohemia (where it then most graciously pleases Your Imperial Majesty), and be duly settled every quarter [*Quatember*], so that I may no longer spend the good time with vain *solicitations*, alongside great damage and troubles (as has hitherto, alas, happened).

As concerns other deficiencies in the matters which were most graciously granted me by Your Imperial Majesty from the beginning and afterward, but have not yet been fulfilled, I have delivered to Master Barvitius a short schedule thereof, to be submitted most humbly to Your Imperial Majesty on my behalf; and I have the entire hope that I shall, on all this, with the soonest, obtain a most gracious resolution — so that I might at last actually know how I stand here, and whether I could attain some firm and lasting situation to carry out here, most humbly, my intended high study and astronomical work, to Your Roman Imperial Majesty's and the realm's special renown, profit, and honour — or whether it were needful to seek other convenience for it. I at all times acknowledge myself entirely bound to serve Your Roman Imperial Majesty in all most humble obedience. Your Roman Imperial Majesty's most humble, most obedient servant,

Tycho Brahe,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Document type.** A formal **petition (*Supplicatio*)** addressed "to the own hands" of **Emperor Rudolf II** — the Latin superscription *Ad Sacrae Caesareae Maiestatis … manus proprias humillima supplicatio Tychonis Brahe*. The witness survives in the imperial **Familienakten** at the Vienna Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv.
- **The unpaid salary.** The core grievance of Tycho's Bohemian years: his **imperial salary, "more than a year in arrears,"** despite repeated imperial orders. He asks that arrears and future salary be paid **from the imperial domains in Bohemia** and settled **every quarter** (*alle Quatember* — the quarterly Ember-tide terms), to spare him the "vain *solicitations*, great damage, and troubles" of chasing the treasury. A candid testimony to the chronic dysfunction of the Rudolfine fisc.
- **Other unfulfilled promises.** Tycho refers to a *Verzeichnis* (schedule/list) of further unmet promises which he has given to **Barvitius** (Johann Barvitius, the privy secretary; cf. brahe-t_15980626002, …16000507001) to lay before the Emperor; he hopes for a "**resolution**" so he may know "how he stands," and whether he can pursue his "high study and astronomical work" there — "**or whether it were needful to seek other convenience**" (a veiled threat to look elsewhere).
- ***sollicitationibus*** / ***Quatember*** — Latin/technical terms kept and rendered (solicitations; the quarterly terms). *manu pp.* = *manu propria*.
- **Calendar / date.** The petition is **undated** in the source (edition: "Benatky," year **1600**, identifier …0000…). Internal content (the year-plus arrears; the Barvitius schedule) fits **1600**, during the Benátky residence. Bohemia (imperial) = **New Style**; no day/month survives.

text.original:
ILLUSTRISSIMO ET CLARISSIMO VIRO DOMINO VINCENTIO PINELLIO PATRICIO PATAVINO DOMINO ET AMICO SUO OBSERVANDISSIMO.
ILLUSTRIS ET MAGNIFICE VIR.
S.

CUM superiore Anno Italiam peragrasset Nobilis et Eruditus adolescens FRANCISCUS TENGNAGLIUS, qui aliquamdiu antea tam in Daniâ quam Germaniâ meus domesticus fuit, et Dresdâ a me in Italiam profectus inter alia, ut Patavium transiens te officiose meo nomine salutaret, atque de statu mearum rerum edoceret, in mandatis habuit. Reversus autem nuper ad me, cum ab ipso percontarer, an te allocutus esset, respondit se, quam primum Patavium permeasset, saltem biduum ibi mansisse: interim te conveniendi nullam datam fuisse commoditatem. Reiecit itaque illud in reditum suum, donec ulteriore Italiâ perlustrata in Germaniam ipsi revertendum foret. At cum rursus Urbem vestram accederet, et quod antea omissum erat, præstare satageret, te ibi non invenit; sed in villam tuam animi caussâ secessisse Mathematicus vester GALILÆUS DE GALILÆIS referebat. Re itaque hac præter utriusque nostrûm expectationem infectâ is ad me (uti dictum) redijt. Ex quo vero Excellentissimo Domino MAGINO ad suas, quas idem mihi attulit, respondendum nunc foret literas, te quoque non prætereundum censui, ut quod antea per præsentem TENGNAGLIUM nostrum fieri non poterat, nunc literis (siquidem aliter non licet) compensetur.

Existimo te ab alijs iam antea utcunque percepisse, quomodo Patrium solum verterim, atque in Germaniam ultro concesserim, derelicto Uraniburgo nostro Danico totoque eius apparatu Astronomico mecum ad exteros translato; siquidem quorundam invidiâ et malevolentiâ factum sit, ut omnes reditus ad sustentationem Divinæ illius scientiæ Astronomicæ a nunquam satis laudatæ memoriæ Rege FRIDERICO deputati, statim ac novitius hîc Rex coronatus atque rerum administrationi adhibitus esset, subtracti fuerint, et simul a Cancellario pariter novitio, quem per literas diligenter admonueram, ut hoc sublime studium iuxta intentionem antecedentis Regis et Senatusconsulti, Patriæ saltem honoris caussâ isthic conservari et perpetuari posse, a Rege hocce obtineret, et simul discrete præmonui de ijs, quæ subsequerentur, si id non fieret, mihi rescriptum sit, Regi non esse integrum quicquam in Instrumentorum meorum huic exercitio inservientium sustentationem de suo conferre. Secessi itaque primum Haffniam, quæ Regni metropolis est, trium vel 4 horarum saltem itinere maritimo ab Insulâ illâ Uraniburgicâ distantem. Ubi cum in ædibus amplis iuxta vallum a me ipso exædificatis studia mea proprijs sumptibus continuare in animum induxissem, eâque de caussâ nonnulla ex Instrumentis meis ibi commode disposuissem, a Curiæ Magistro nomine Iunioris Regis, licet tunc in Germaniâ absentis, id efficere prohibitus sum. Quare cum has præclaras Artes isthic adeo neglectas, imo exosas animadverterem, ut neque publicis neque privatis impensis ijs invigilandi otium atque commoditas concederetur, malui universam Patriam plurimosque in eâ sanguine iunctos et Amicos inibi omnes derelinquere, quam laborum Uraniæ nostræ frustrationem atque interitum spectare. Substiti tamen in transmarino Ducatu Megapolitano per Anni quadrantem et postea in vicinâ Cimbris Holsatiâ integrum Annum, ut nostratibus, Patriæ adhuc studens, rem rectius deliberandi satis relinquerem temporis. Quod cum incassum fieri viderem, et interea ab Augustissimo et Potentissimo Imperatore RUDOLPHO Secundo, Domino nostro Clementissimo, inde in Bohemiam evocarer, rebus meis, quam primum fieri potuit, in Germaniâ compositis et translatis Magdæburgum ad Albim situm Instrumentis unâ cum reliquâ supellectile domesticâ Dresdam veni, ubi, postquam de Epidemicis morbis in Bohemiâ populariter grassantibus, quodque Cæsar ob ea pericula Pragâ relictâ in Arcem quandam seorsim se recepisset, intellexissem, et simul a Magco Domino CORRADUCIO, Imperij Procancellario, per literas de Cæs. Matis Clementissimâ voluntate admonerer, ut nimirum paulisper in viciniâ me continerem, donec malum illud in Bohemiâ remitteret, atque Aula Cæsa recolligeretur, expectavi aliquandiu in propinquâ Saxoniâ, quoad iterum ex mandato Cæsaris a prædicto Domino CORRADUCIO Pragam per literas vocarer, quo superiore æstate cum totâ familiâ adveniens, a Cæsa Mate mox benignissime receptus sum, atque annuo salario satis liberali, quo Astronomiæ studio et rei domesticæ consuleretur, provisum, concessaque Arx quædam Cæsareana Benachia, quam ob loci eximiam amœnitatem et fluvium Isaram circumcurrentem indigenæ Venetias Bohemorum nuncupant, quæ quinque saltem milliaribus Germanicis sive sex horarum itinere Pragâ metropoli removetur. Hanc tribus alijs pariter oblatis, quod locus sit tranquillus et iocundus, ac simul admodum êditus, adeoque Observationibus cœlestibus commodior, prætuli: ubi etiam convenientia pro meis Instrumentis ordine et sigillatim disponendis ædificia mandato et sumptu Cæsaris confestim structa sunt, in quæ in Bohemiam mecum allata Organa, prout usus requirit, collocata sunt. Reliqua ex Germaniâ, quam primum hyems desierit, huc pariter advecta, ibidem usui adaptabuntur, ut sic, Cœlestium favente Opifice, Uraniæ nostræ, quam Patria repudiavit, fundamina hîc reponantur, atque in Cæsæ Matis totiusque Imperij honorem Astronomiæ redintegratio continuetur, atque quam primum fieri possit, compleatur. Quod post Divini Numinis providentiam huic optimo Imperatori omnium liberalium Artium, inprimisque Mathematicarum Mæcenati benignissimo acceptum est ferendum. Namque is Clementi manu nobis hæc otia fecit.

Hæc te, Clarissime Domine PINELLE, scire volui, si forte antea non satis innotuerunt, ut rerum nostrarum vicissitudo et in Bohemiâ a Cæsare benignissime restitutum hospitium te non lateret. Libros autem, quos Cæsæ Mati dedicatos, cum primum adveni, humillime obtuli, quoad duos priores, te vidisse autumo. Nam et Sermo Principi atque Senatui Veneto a prænominato Iuvene meâ caussâ reverenter exhibiti sunt, qui etiam eum Equitis aurati honore decorârunt. Si vero nondum eos tibi inspicere contigit, ab Illustri et Clarissimo viro IOHANNE FRANCISCO SAGGREDO id facile (uti opinor) impetrabis. Tertius erat de restitutis motibus Solis et Lunæ eorundemque cum consuetis calculis comparatione, quem alias (uti spero) videbis.

Porro ut per occasionem, quæ nunc ob Aulæ Cæsareæ propinquitatem promptior quam antea occurret, me Eruditis tuis literis invisere, atque quod hisce meis incomptis prævenerint, candide accipere non degraveris, quæso. Vale, salutato a me peramanter ob conformia studia Præstantissimo isthic Mathematum Professore GALILÆO DE GALILÆIS; qui si mihi (uti constituerat) per dictam occasionem scripsisset, me in respondendo non invenisset difficilem. Poterit tamen id alio fortassis tempore præstari. Iamque iterum vale, vir illustris et celeberrime, atque Annum hunc Iubilæum pluresque alios subsequentes quam felicissime transige.

Dabantur ex Arce Cæsareanâ Benaticâ 3 die Ianuarij Anno 1600.
text.english:
**To the most illustrious and renowned man, Lord Vincenzo Pinelli, patrician of Padua, his most esteemed Lord and friend.**
Illustrious and magnificent Man.
Greeting.

When last year the noble and learned youth **Franz Tengnagel** — who for some time before had been a member of my household, both in Denmark and in Germany — travelled through Italy, having set out from Dresden to Italy by me, he had it among his charges that, passing through **Padua**, he should dutifully greet you in my name, and inform you of the state of my affairs. But lately returned to me, when I asked him whether he had spoken with you, he answered that, as soon as he had reached Padua, he stayed there but two days, [and] meanwhile no opportunity of meeting you was given. He therefore put it off to his return, until, the rest of Italy traversed, he should have to come back into Germany. But when he again approached your City, and busied himself to do what had before been omitted, he did not find you there; but **your Mathematician, Galileo Galilei [Galilaeus de Galilaeis], reported that you had retired to your country villa for relaxation**. And so, this matter failing beyond the expectation of us both, he returned to me (as I said). But since I must now answer the letter of the most excellent **Lord Magini**, which he brought me, I judged you too not to be passed over — that what before could not be done through our Tengnagel in person, may now be compensated by letter (since otherwise it is not allowed).

I think you have already in some way perceived from others **how I turned from my native soil, and withdrew of my own accord into Germany, abandoning our Danish Uraniborg and bringing all its Astronomical apparatus with me abroad** — since by certain men's envy and malevolence it came about that **all the revenues assigned, for the support of that divine science of Astronomy, by King Frederick of never-sufficiently-praised memory, were withdrawn as soon as the new King here was crowned and applied to the administration of affairs**. And likewise by the also-new **Chancellor**, whom I had diligently admonished by letter to obtain from this King that this sublime study might — according to the intention of the preceding King and the Senate-decree, at least for the honour of the fatherland — be preserved and perpetuated there (and I discreetly forewarned of what would follow, if it were not done) — it was written back to me **that it was not in the King's power to contribute anything of his own to the support of my instruments serving this exercise**. I therefore first withdrew to **Copenhagen**, the realm's metropolis, distant only a three- or four-hours' sea-journey from that Island of Uraniborg. There, when I had resolved to continue my studies at my own expense in a large house I had myself built by the rampart, and for that cause had conveniently arranged some of my instruments there, **I was prohibited from doing so by the Court-Master, in the name of the Younger King** (though he was then absent in Germany). Wherefore, seeing these excellent Arts so neglected there — nay, hated — that neither by public nor by private means was leisure and convenience granted to watch over them, **I preferred to abandon my whole fatherland, and all the many there joined to me by blood, and my friends, rather than to behold the frustration and destruction of our Urania's labours.** I halted, however, in the transmarine **Duchy of Mecklenburg** for a quarter of a year, and afterward in neighbouring **Holstein** (near the Cimbrians) a whole year — that, still studying the fatherland's [good], I might leave my countrymen enough time to deliberate the matter more rightly. When I saw this done in vain, and was meanwhile **summoned thence into Bohemia by the most august and most powerful Emperor Rudolf II**, my most clement Lord — my affairs in Germany composed and removed as soon as could be (my Instruments, with the rest of my household goods, [left] at Magdeburg on the Elbe) — I came to **Dresden**; where, after I had learned of the epidemic diseases raging popularly in Bohemia, and that the Emperor, on account of those perils, had left Prague and retired apart into a certain Castle — and was at the same time admonished by letter from the magnificent **Lord Coraduz, Imperial Vice-Chancellor**, of the Imperial Majesty's most clement wish, namely that I keep myself a while in the neighbourhood until that evil in Bohemia should abate and the Imperial Court reassemble — I waited a while in nearby Saxony, until I was again, by the Emperor's mandate, called to Prague by the said Lord Coraduz. Arriving thither last summer with my whole family, I was soon most kindly received by the Imperial Majesty, and provided with **a sufficiently liberal annual salary**, by which the study of Astronomy and the household might be cared for; and there was granted me **a certain imperial Castle, Benátky** — which, for the place's exceeding loveliness and the river **Iser [Jizera]** running around it, the natives call **the Venice of the Bohemians** — distant from the metropolis Prague only five German miles, or a six-hours' journey. This I preferred to three others likewise offered, because the place is quiet and pleasant, and at the same time quite high, and so more convenient for celestial Observations; where also **buildings fit for arranging my Instruments in order and severally were at once erected, by the Emperor's order and expense**, into which the apparatus brought with me into Bohemia has been placed, as use requires. The rest, from Germany, as soon as winter ends, brought hither likewise, will there be fitted for use — so that thus, the heavenly Maker favouring, **the foundations of our Urania, which the fatherland repudiated, may be re-laid here, and the restoration of Astronomy be continued, for the honour of the Imperial Majesty and of the whole Empire, and completed as soon as may be**. Which, after the providence of the Divine Godhead, is to be set to the account of this best Emperor, the most kindly Maecenas of all the liberal Arts, and especially of the Mathematical. For **with clement hand He has made us this leisure** [*nobis haec otia fecit*].

These things, most renowned Lord Pinelli, I wished you to know — if perhaps they were not before sufficiently known — that the vicissitude of my affairs, and the lodging most kindly restored to me in Bohemia by the Emperor, might not be hidden from you. As for **the books which, dedicated to the Imperial Majesty, I most humbly offered when I first arrived** — as to the two earlier ones, I suppose you have seen them. For [they] were reverently presented, on my behalf, by the aforesaid Youth, to the Prince [Doge] and Senate of Venice — **who also honoured him with the dignity of a Golden Knight** [*eques auratus*]. But if it has not yet befallen you to inspect them, you will easily obtain it (as I think) from the illustrious and renowned man **Giovanni Francesco Sagredo**. The third was on the restored motions of the Sun and Moon, and their comparison with the customary calculations [the *Progymnasmata*], which you will see elsewhere (as I hope).

Further, I beg that — by the occasion which now, because of the nearness of the Imperial Court, will occur more readily than before — you would not find it a burden to visit me with your learned letters, and to take candidly that these rough ones of mine have forestalled [you]. Farewell; and **greet for me, most lovingly, for our conformable studies, the most excellent Professor of Mathematics there, Galileo Galilei [Galilaeo de Galilaeis]; who, if he had written to me (as he had resolved) through the said occasion, would not have found me difficult in replying. Yet this can perhaps be done at another time.** And again farewell, illustrious and most celebrated man, and pass this Jubilee Year, and many others following, most happily.

Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 3rd day of January, the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Gian Vincenzo Pinelli** (1535–1601), the great Paduan humanist, polymath, and book-/manuscript-collector, whose library was the hub of Padua's learned world (Galileo frequented it).
- **Significance — Tycho's fullest *apologia*/autobiography of the Hven departure, and the Galileo connection.**
 - **The exile narrative (the corpus's most complete).** A detailed account of leaving Denmark: **King Frederick II's astronomy revenues withdrawn as soon as the "new King" (Christian IV) took power**; the "new Chancellor" replying that **"it was not in the King's power to contribute anything"**; Tycho's retreat to **Copenhagen** (the rampart house) and the **Court-Master's prohibition** "in the name of the Younger King"; the choice to abandon the fatherland; the **quarter-year in Mecklenburg + year in Holstein** "to leave my countrymen time to deliberate"; the **imperial summons via Coraduz**; the **Dresden/Saxony wait** during the Bohemian plague; and the **grant of Benátky** ("the Venice of the Bohemians," on the **Jizera/Iser**, 5 German miles from Prague), chosen over three others, with imperial-funded instrument-housings — "the foundations of our Urania, which the fatherland repudiated, re-laid here." Closes with the Virgilian echo ***nobis haec otia fecit*** (Ecl. 1.6) applied to Rudolf II.
 - **The Galileo connection (rare and notable).** Twice: **Galileo ("the most excellent Professor of Mathematics there")** reported Pinelli's absence to Tengnagel; and Tycho asks Pinelli to **"greet Galileo most lovingly, for our conformable studies,"** adding that **Galileo "had resolved to write to me" and "would not have found me difficult in replying."** One of the very few documented Tycho–Galileo contact points — and a record of Galileo's *intended* (never realised) letter to Tycho.
 - **The Venice book-presentation and Tengnagel's knighthood.** Tycho's **books dedicated to the Emperor** (the *Mechanica* etc.) were **presented to the Doge and Senate of Venice** by **Tengnagel**, whom Venice **honoured as a *Golden Knight* (eques auratus)**; copies obtainable from **Sagredo**. The "third book" is the *Progymnasmata* ("the restored motions of Sun and Moon").
 - **The Magini link.** Written alongside Tycho's reply to **Magini** (cf. brahe-t_16010220001), both carried in the same Italian exchange.
- **Persons & places named.** Vincenzo Pinelli; **Franz Tengnagel** (now *eques auratus* of Venice); **Galileo Galilei**; **Giovanni Antonio Magini**; **Giovanni Francesco Sagredo**; **King Frederick II** & **Christian IV** of Denmark; the Danish **Chancellor** and **Court-Master** (unnamed); **Rudolf II**; **Coraduz**; the **Doge and Senate of Venice**. Places: **Benátky** ("Venice of the Bohemians," on the **Jizera**), **Prague**, **Padua**, **Venice**, **Copenhagen**, **Hven/Uraniborg**, **Mecklenburg**, **Holstein**, **Magdeburg**, **Dresden**, **Saxony**.
- **Cross-references.** A **keystone of the self-exile thread** (cf. brahe-t_15980607001 to Grynaeus) and **the principal Tycho–Galileo document**; route through the Galileo/Padua and exile-narrative threads.
- **Calendar.** *3 die Ianuarij Anno 1600* at Benátky (imperial reckoning) → **3 January 1600 [N.S.]** (identifier 16000103001 agrees; label gives only "Benatky").

text.original:
EXCELLENTISSIMO ET ERUDITISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO IOHANNI ANTONIO MAGINO, MATHEMATUM IN ILLUSTRI BONONIENSIUM GYMNASIO PROFESSORI, AMICO SUO PLURIMUM DILECTO.

REVERSUS ad me FRANCISCUS TENGNAGLIUS noster tuas attulit, Excellentissime et Eruditissime plurimumque mihi dilecte Domine D. MAGINE, meis quidem respondentes, sed tamen de singulis, de quibus tecum agebam, non sufficienter agentes, quod occupationibus tuis lubens tribuo. Gratum vero mihi in primis est, quod ijs quae ille proponebat assentitus sis, atque in illis tuam operam sive per temetipsum sive per alios in Italiâ Eruditione pollentes effectui daturum benevole pollicitus.

Existimo te a dicto TENGNAGLIO summa rerum huc pertinentium fastigia hausisse. Adiunxi hisce brevem discursum de occasionibus mei e Daniâ discessus, ut eo promptius negocium concipi possit, et quasdam alias literas huc pertinentes. Coetera ipsius relatio ac Carmina tradita, quae nunc prioribus addo, supplebunt. Da itaque operam, optime MAGINE, ut mature res omnis conficiatur, mihique primae conceptiones intra duos menses (si ullo modo fieri possit) huc in Bohemiam mittantur, quo quae necessaria duxero, mutem, addam vel adaugeam, cum nemini melius quam mihi ipsi mea perspecta sint, moxque vobis revisa et locupletata remittam. Placet vero admodum illa ratio, de quâ TENGNAGLIUS admonuit, ut potius Panaegyricum quid sit quam per Dialogos. Sic enim res omnis concinnius comprehendi poterit et maiori authoritate: ita tamen, ut a generalioribus ad particularia descendendo primum universae Artis Astronomicae ortus, incrementa, promotiones, augmenta et variae mutationes ac peregrinationes recenseantur; quae omnia ab alijs scriptoribus, qui hoc argumentum tractârunt, facile cum delectu quodam hauriri poterunt. Et si alij defuerint, IOHANNES STADIUS in ijs, quae Tabulis Bergensibus abs se dictis subiunxit, occasionem suppeditabunt: quae tamen in quibusdam, ubi liberius excurrit, castiganda erunt, uti erat vir ille in dicendo facilior quam verior. Utinam in calculo Astronomico, qui fucum (uti historica) non patitur, idem non commisisset. Quâ in re non immerito a te redarguitur. Sed parcamus iam manibus defuncti. Est aliquid prodire tenus, si non datur ultra.

Deinde postquam narratum est, quomodo e Graeciâ in Italiam et Hispaniam, postmodum vero ad Germanos et deinde in Daniam versus Septentrionem migrârit Astronomia; quo cum ulterius ob Arctoum frigus nimiamque sphaerae inclinationem progredi commode non posset, neque etiam diu ibi subsistere, tandem in Germaniam reversa est, adeoque in ipsam Bohemiam, Germaniae quasi cor et meditullium, ubi apud Augustissimum Imperatorem RUDOLPHUM II clemens et benignum hospitium nacta est, ut demum verificaretur, quod olim MANILIUS ad AUGUSTUM Caesarem protulit: *[Regales animos primum dignata movere, / Proxima tangentes Coelo fastigia rerum.]*

Hinc sumptâ occasione poterit postea digressio quaedam fieri ad me et ea, quae mihi in Daniâ evenerunt, tanquam relatione eorum, qui ex Germaniâ et Bohemiâ in Italiam proficiscuntur, comperta. Decet tamen in his modum aliquem servare et modeste ac moderate omnia agere, ita ut Patriae nostrae et Regi plurimisque in ijs praeclarâ et antiquâ Nobilitate viris integris et cordatis, quibus partim inscijs partim invitis ea evenerunt, quae discessui meo ansam praebuerunt, parcatur, utque illi sint excusabiles. Perstringendi vero solummodo pro merito Cancellarius modernus et Aulae magister, qui cum Patriae honorem ex officio promovere debuissent, eum potius ob avaritiam et sorditiem pari invidiâ, malignitate et odio coniunctam (cum ipsi liberalibus scientijs vel nihil vel admodum parum tincti essent) impediverunt et exterminârunt. Nomina eorum invenies in ijs, quae de caussis discessus mei Latine exarata nunc mitto. Nec interest, si illi expresse nominentur in scripto illo, tanquam nomina eorum hac occasione aliunde in Italiâ relata fuerint, cum alias obscuri sint, digni tamen, ut ex tali facinore famosi evadant, quemadmodum ille, qui Dianae templum Ephesijs incendio absumpsit, cuius tamen nomen hoc pacto deletum est. Atque in hunc vel similem modum possunt ea, quae Uraniae nostrae et mihi contigerunt, amplificari.

Inaudivi te Ephemerides tuas magnâ equidem diligentiâ supputatas (utut quidam Francofurti ad Oderam, êditis nuper quibusdam alijs ab anno 1595 incipientibus et ultra tuas decennio prolongatis, minutula quaedam, quae momentum non habent, in ijs carpere praesumpserit) auxisse ad minimum integro decennio. Exemplar non vidi: neque enim fuit in Catalogo Nundinarum Francofurtensium proxime antecedentium. Cuperem itaque ex te habere, ut videam, an aliqua inibi praeter priorem diligentiam exantlaveris. Neque enim dubito, tua in hoc genere (cum numerorum tractatione atque compendijs praepolleas) emuncta et solida esse, quantum fert fundamentum illud cui superstructa. Coeterum quae de Tabulis meis in motu Luminarium restituto expetis, ut ijs, donec reliquorum Planetarum numeratio ipsi Coelo consona subsequatur, in commodum Reip. literariae uti possis, libenter tecum communicarem, si ea quae non tam typis excusa quam manuscripta in his parata habeo, nunc ad manus essent. Nam ut de rerum mearum vicissitudine, quam a praenominato TENGNAGLIO intellexisti, nihil hîc repetam (piget enim istorum recordari, nedum ea memorare) scias me praecipuam partem suppellectilis meae interea, dum huc in Bohemiam a Caesarea Maiestate Clementissime evocatus transeo, Magdaeburgi ad Albim quasi in medio Germaniae reliquisse, donec de ipsius Maiestatis Clementissimâ voluntate certior redderer; inter quam non saltem Instrumenta quaedam ex meis, plura quam huc attuli, sed et maxima pars Operum meorum tam impressorum quam manuscriptorum conservatur. Et licet Caesarea Maiestas ante complures hebdomadas Magdaeburgensibus clementer scripserit atque mandârit, ut omnes res meas ibi reservatas huc in Bohemiam intermediante Albi adduci procurent, tamen interveniente hyeme, quae fluminis congelationem atque impedimenta varia facile suggerere potuit, id usque in instans vernum tempus procrastinare necessum habuerunt. Unde fit, ut tuis votis hac in parte, etiamsi quam maxime vellem, nunc subvenire nequeam, sed spero Progymnasmatum nostrorum Astronomiae instauratae primum Tomum brevi, favente Coelesti Numine, in publicum êditum iri: moxque exemplar tibi impertiar. Isthic capite primo, quae in calculo curriculi utriusque Luminaris desideras, sufficienter invenies. Interim hanc incidentem morulam patienter habe. In reliquis Planetis adhuc strenue laboro. Res enim est maioris difficultatis, pluribusque anfractibus obnoxia, quam hactenus creditum. Quid in his atque alijs ad negocium Astronomicum facientibus hucusque aspirante ipso Coeli authore perfecerim, liber is, quem TENGNAGLIUS tibi ex me dono dedit, de Mechanicâ Astronomiae parte circa finem edocebit. Quem unâ cum altero de affixarum maiore labore quam aestimatione restitutis locis te accepisse gaudeo; velimque ut tibi soli reserves, vel saltem ne indignis et ingratis communices.

Observationes, quas per nova Instrumenta ad imitationem quorundam ex meis fabrefacta te in Italiâ fieri effecturum iam dudum pollicitus es (de quibus etiam antea per literas inculcavi) necdum conspicere licuit. Averem sane tale quidpiam isthic diligenter effici, ex quo minor Sphaerae apud vos quam hîc inclinatio maiorem largiatur commoditatem stellas praesertim Australiores rite examinandi. Nec desunt vobis ingenia ad quidvis apta, modo in talibus instruantur et adhibeantur. Neque dubito quin ditiores, qui hac sublimi cognitione afficiuntur, sumptus non invite sint subministraturi. Quod et illis erit honorificum. Quae vero in his praecipue facienda atque eligenda sint, ut Mechanice omnia ad amussim et utiliter conficiantur, liber, de quo dixi, quemque habes, ansam praebebit. Omnem itaque move lapidem, ut non sub tecto et tuguriolis (uti nunc communiter fit) sed sub dio atque ipso Coelo Astronomiam (velut par est) veterum imitatione exerceamus, et sic spectemur agendo.

Vale, et Annum hunc Iubilaeum, multosque alios in Artis huius nunquam satis laudatae promulgationem feliciter exige.

Dabantur ex Arce Caesareanâ Benaticâ 3 Ian. 1600.
Excellentiae tuae studiosissimus
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the most excellent and most learned man, Lord Giovanni Antonio Magini, Professor of Mathematics in the illustrious Gymnasium of Bologna, his most beloved friend.**

**Franz Tengnagel**, our [man], returning to me, brought your [letters], most excellent and learned and most beloved Lord Magini — answering mine, yet not sufficiently treating the several points I was raising with you, which I gladly attribute to your occupations. It is most welcome to me that you assented to what he proposed, and benevolently promised to give effect to it, whether by yourself or through others in Italy excelling in Erudition.

I think you have drawn from the said Tengnagel the chief heads of the matters pertaining hither. **I have adjoined to these a brief discourse on the occasions of my departure from Denmark**, that the business may be the more readily conceived, and certain other relevant letters. The rest his report, and the **Verses** handed over (which I now add to the earlier), will supply. Take pains, then, excellent Magini, that the whole thing be finished in good time, and that **the first conceptions be sent me here into Bohemia within two months** (if it can by any means be done), so that I may change, add, or augment what I judge necessary — since my affairs are better known to no one than to me myself — and I will soon send them back to you, approved and enriched.

**I much approve that plan of which Tengnagel advised: that it be rather a Panegyric than [done] through Dialogues.** For so the whole matter can be more elegantly comprehended, and with greater authority — yet so that, descending from the more general to the particular, **first the origin, increments, promotions, augments, and various changes and migrations of the whole Astronomical Art be recounted** — all of which can easily be gathered, with some selection, from other writers who have treated this argument. And if others fail, **Johannes Stadius**, in what he subjoined to his *Tabulae Bergenses*, will supply occasion — though in some places, where he runs too freely, [they] must be corrected, for that man was readier than truer in speaking. Would that, in astronomical calculation — which (unlike history) suffers no false colouring — he had not committed the same! In which matter he is not undeservedly refuted by you. But let us now spare the shade [*manes*] of the dead. **"It is something to advance thus far, if it is not given to go beyond"** [Horace].

Then, after it is narrated **how Astronomy migrated from Greece into Italy and Spain, afterward to the Germans, and then into Denmark, toward the North** — whither, since it could not conveniently proceed further (on account of the Arctic cold and the excessive inclination of the sphere), nor stay there long, **it at last returned into Germany, and indeed into Bohemia itself, the heart and midmost, as it were, of Germany, where it found a clement and kindly lodging with the most august Emperor Rudolf II** — so that at last there be verified what **Manilius** once uttered to **Augustus Caesar**: *“[Astronomy,] first deigning to stir the minds of kings, and those reaching the topmost summits of affairs that border on Heaven.”* [the couplet — Manilius, *Astronomica* I.7–8 — is blank in the working transcription but printed by Dreyer; supplied editorially: *Regales animos primum dignata movere, / Proxima tangentes Coelo fastigia rerum.*]

Hence, occasion being taken, **a digression can afterward be made to me, and what befell me in Denmark — as if learned by the report of those who travel from Germany and Bohemia into Italy.** Yet it befits to keep some measure in these, and do all modestly and moderately, **so that our fatherland, and the King, and the many men of distinguished and ancient Nobility, upright and sensible — by whom (partly unknowing, partly unwilling) those things happened that gave occasion to my departure — be spared, and be excusable.** **Only to be censured, for their desert, are the modern Chancellor and the Court-Master** — who, when they ought by their office to have promoted the fatherland's honour, **rather, out of avarice and sordidness joined with equal envy, malignity, and hatred (since they were either not at all, or very little, tinged with the liberal sciences), impeded and exterminated it.** Their names you will find in what I now send, written in Latin, about the causes of my departure. Nor does it matter if they be expressly named in that writing — as if their names were on this occasion reported from elsewhere in Italy — since they are otherwise obscure, yet worthy that, from such a deed, they become infamous: **like the man who consumed the temple of Diana of the Ephesians by fire, whose name was nonetheless [by decree] deleted** [Herostratus]. And in this or a like manner, what befell our Urania and me can be amplified.

I have heard that you have augmented **your Ephemerides** — calculated indeed with great diligence (although a certain man at **Frankfurt-on-Oder**, having lately published certain others, beginning from the year 1595 and prolonged a decade beyond yours, presumed to carp at certain trifles in them that have no moment) — by at least a whole decade. I have not seen the copy; for it was not in the Catalogue of the most recent Frankfurt Fair. I should therefore wish to have it from you, to see whether you have drawn out anything therein beyond your former diligence. For I do not doubt that your [work] in this kind is refined and solid (since you excel in the handling of numbers and in compendia), so far as the foundation on which it is built allows. As for what you seek concerning **my Tables of the restored motion of the Luminaries** — that you may use them, for the advantage of the literary Commonwealth, until the numeration of the remaining Planets, consonant with heaven itself, follow — I would gladly share them with you, if what I have prepared in these (not so much printed as in manuscript) were now at hand. For (not to repeat here the vicissitude of my affairs, which you learned from the aforesaid Tengnagel — for it pains me to recall such things, much less narrate them), know that **I left the chief part of my stuff, meanwhile as I crossed hither into Bohemia, called most clemently by the Imperial Majesty, at Magdeburg on the Elbe, as it were in the middle of Germany**, until I should be made more certain of His Majesty's most clement will — among which are kept not only some of my Instruments (more than I brought here), but also **the greatest part of my Works, both printed and manuscript**. And although the Imperial Majesty several weeks ago clemently wrote and ordered the Magdeburgers to see all my things kept there brought hither into Bohemia by way of the Elbe, yet, winter intervening (which could easily bring the river's freezing and various impediments), they had to postpone it to the coming spring. Whence it comes that I cannot now succour your wishes in this part, however much I would. But **I hope the first Volume of our *Progymnasmata* of restored Astronomy will shortly, Heaven favouring, be published; and I will soon impart a copy to you. There, in the first chapter, you will sufficiently find what you desire in the calculation of the course of both Luminaries.** Meanwhile bear this incidental little delay patiently. On the remaining Planets I still strenuously labour; for the matter is of greater difficulty, and liable to more convolutions, than has hitherto been believed. What I have so far accomplished in these and other things conducing to the Astronomical business — the heavenly Author himself aspiring [it] — **the book which Tengnagel gave you as a gift from me, on the Mechanical part of Astronomy [the *Mechanica*], will teach near its end.** Which, together with the other, on the positions of the fixed stars restored with greater labour than esteem, I rejoice that you received; and I should wish you to keep them to yourself alone, or at least not share them with the unworthy and ungrateful.

The observations which you long ago promised you would have made in Italy, by new Instruments fashioned in imitation of certain of mine (of which I urged you before too by letter), I have not yet been able to behold. I should indeed long for some such thing to be diligently done there — **whence the smaller inclination of the Sphere with you than here would grant greater convenience for rightly examining the stars, especially the more southern.** Nor do you lack talents apt for anything, if only they be instructed and applied in such; nor do I doubt that the richer, who are taken with this sublime knowledge, will not unwillingly supply the costs — which will be honourable to them too. What is chiefly to be done and chosen in these, that all may be made mechanically exact and useful, the book of which I spoke, which you have, will give occasion. **Move every stone, then, that we may exercise Astronomy not under roof and little huts (as is now commonly done), but under the open sky and the very Heaven (as is fitting), in imitation of the ancients — and so be regarded in the doing.**

Farewell, and spend this Jubilee Year, and many others, happily in the promulgation of this never-sufficiently-praised Art.

Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, 3 January 1600.
Most zealous of Your Excellency,
**Tycho Brahe.**

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Giovanni Antonio Magini** (1555–1617), professor of mathematics at **Bologna** (cf. his letter, brahe-t_16010220001). The letter survives in **Magini's printed *Tabulae Primi Mobilis***.
- **Significance — the Italian parallel to the Brasch commission: a panegyric history of astronomy, and the naming of Tycho's enemies.**
 - **The panegyric-history project (cf. brahe-t_16010414001 to Brasch).** Tycho asks **Magini to arrange a Latin *panegyric* (not dialogues)** on the history of astronomy — the **origin and migrations of the Art**, culminating in **Rudolf II and Tycho** — sending Tycho the draft within two months for revision. He supplies a "brief discourse on the occasions of my departure from Denmark," relevant letters, and **verses**. *(Tycho is orchestrating his own literary monument in parallel across Germany [Brasch] and Italy [Magini].)*
 - **The *translatio astronomiae*.** Greece → Italy/Spain → the Germans → Denmark ("toward the North"); there it could go no further "for the Arctic cold and the excessive inclination of the sphere," so it **returned to Germany — to Bohemia, "the heart of Germany," to Rudolf II** — fulfilling a (here-omitted) line of **Manilius to Augustus**.
 - **Naming the villains (the Herostratus device).** A pointed contrast to the Pinelli/Grynaeus letters: Tycho insists his **fatherland, King, and the upright nobility be spared and excused** — but that **"the modern Chancellor and the Court-Master"** (his enemies, "very little tinged with the liberal sciences," who "out of avarice and sordidness … impeded and exterminated" Danish astronomy) be **expressly named and made infamous**, "like the man who burned the temple of Diana at Ephesus" (**Herostratus**). Their names are in the enclosed Latin account of his departure. *(A rare, explicit demand to immortalise his persecutors by infamy.)*
 - **Stadius.** Recommends (with correction) **Johannes Stadius's** *Tabulae Bergenses* notes as a source — "readier than truer," rightly refuted by Magini; "let us spare the shade of the dead" (*Est aliquid prodire tenus*, Horace).
 - **Ephemerides & tables.** Magini has **augmented his Ephemerides by a decade**; the rival "at Frankfurt-on-Oder" (the ephemerides from 1595 = **David Origanus**) carped at trifles. Tycho cannot yet share his own **luminary tables** (manuscript, stuck with the bulk of his **works and instruments at Magdeburg** awaiting the Elbe thaw), but promises the **first volume of the *Progymnasmata*** soon (its ch. 1 = the luminary calculations).
 - **The *Mechanica* gift to Magini.** Confirms **Tengnagel gave Magini the *Mechanica* ("on the Mechanical part of Astronomy") and the fixed-star book** ("restored with greater labour than esteem") — to be kept private. *(A *Mechanica* distribution event.)*
 - **The southern-observation appeal & the open-sky credo.** Tycho urges Magini to build Tycho-style instruments and observe in Italy, **exploiting Italy's lower latitude for the southern stars** (cf. the Egypt plan, brahe-t_16000124001), funded by wealthy enthusiasts — and ends with his manifesto: **"exercise Astronomy not under roof and little huts … but under the open sky, in imitation of the ancients, and so be regarded in the doing."**
- **Cross-references.** Pair with **brahe-t_16010414001** (the Brasch History-of-Astronomy) as the **twin literary-monument commissions**; with **brahe-t_16010220001** (Magini's letter) and **brahe-t_16000103001** (Pinelli, same day, same Italian burst); the southern-observation thread (brahe-t_16000124001); and the **Magdeburg-storage** and **Mechanica-distribution** threads.
- **Persons & works named.** Magini; **Franz Tengnagel**; **Johannes Stadius** (*Tabulae Bergenses*); **Manilius / Augustus**; **Rudolf II**; the **modern [Danish] Chancellor and Court-Master** (Tycho's enemies, named only in the enclosure); **Herostratus** (the unnamed Ephesus arsonist); **David Origanus** (the Frankfurt-on-Oder ephemerides rival, unnamed); the *Progymnasmata*, the *Mechanica*. Places: **Benátky**, **Bologna**, **Magdeburg/Elbe**, Greece/Italy/Spain/Germany/Denmark (the *translatio*).
- **Text note (RESOLVED §1 collation).** The Manilius couplet "to Augustus" is blank after *protulit:* in the working transcription, but **Dreyer prints it** (*Opera Omnia* VIII p. 244): *Regales animos primum dignata movere, / Proxima tangentes Coelo fastigia rerum* (= *Astronomica* I.7–8). Supplied editorially in the Source and translation by this chapter's convention (the edition of record), in [square brackets].
- **Calendar.** *3 Ian. 1600* at Benátky (imperial reckoning) → **3 January 1600 [N.S.]**; header and label agree. (Same day as the Pinelli letter, brahe-t_16000103001.)
- **Correction.** Latin corrected against Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII p.229: 'BONONIENSEM' -> 'BONONIENSIUM' (case agreement, 'Gymnasium of the Bolognese'); 'reas visa' (a wrongly split word) -> 'revisa' (reviewed). Neither correction affects the published English translation.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Read the Dreyer page images visually (not the digitised text layer) across all 6 pages: TBOO VIII pp.228 (tail of prior letter), 229-232 (the Magini letter proper). Collated the opening and closing lines and every proper name, number, date and place-name: Tengnaglius, Magino, Rudolphus II, Manilius/Augustum (the couplet 'Regales animos primum dignata movere / Proxima tangentes Coelo fastigia rerum', which our transcribed original left as an editorially-supplied blank, is confirmed printed by Dreyer verbatim as supplied), Stadius/Tabulis Bergensibus, Francofurti ad Oderam, 1595/decennio, Magdeburgi ad Albim, Dabantur ex Arce Caesareana Benatica 3 Ian. 1600 — all match Dreyer except the two text error items logged above, both single/split-word corruptions confined to our own transcription. The English translation itself was checked clause-by-clause against the transcribed original and is faithful throughout: no fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found. Grade is downgraded from the translator's own A to C solely because of the two text error findings (per the grading rule); the verdict is *minor* because neither error changes the sense conveyed to a reader.

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original prints the wrong case ending (BONONIENSEM, accusative singular) where Dreyer prints BONONIENSIUM (genitive plural, correctly agreeing with 'Gymnasio Bononiensium' = Gymnasium of the Bolognese). The English rendering ('Gymnasium of Bologna') is unaffected either way. Dreyer prints: *MATHEMATUM IN ILLUSTRI BONONIENSIUM GYMNASIO PROFESSORI (TBOO VIII p.229)*.
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original splits Dreyer's single word 'revisa' (reviewed) into the nonsensical two words 'reas visa'. The English ('approved and enriched') is a reasonable rendering of the correct Dreyer reading regardless. Dreyer prints: *...moxque vobis revisa et locupletata remittam. (TBOO VIII p.229)*.

**Repaired.** Verified both defect sites directly against the Dreyer page image, TBOO VIII p.229 (letter spans pp.228-233). Both text error are confirmed exactly as the audit describes; the English translation was already correct in both places and required no change. No other discrepancies were found in the surrounding text.

text.original:
GENEROSO ATQUE MAGNIFICO VIRO, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, IN KNUDTSTRUPP ET URANIBURG, ET DOMINO SUO, FAUTORI AC PROMOTORI SUMME HONORANDO.

Salutem plurimam D.

PRÆTER omnem spem et expectationem meam accidit, Generose Domine TYCHO, fautor ac promotor honorandissime, ut hîc diutius moras trahere cogar. Nihilominus tamen ex voto et animi sententia mihi hactenus omnia successerunt, et uti spero amodo etiam successura esse. Tuas a Consobrino tuo CLAUDIO BILLEO cum Idea sive typo Structuræ novæ Benachiensis 8 Idus Ianuarij sartas tectasque accepi, quibus properante hinc Posta confestim rescribo. Ideam adhuc hodie Magnifico Domino BARVITIO, Cæsareæ Maiestati humilime ad exhibendum, offeram, cæteraque sedulo et diligenter, quæ in memoriale assignata reperi, exequar. Cæsarea Maiestas cum quotidie tui ad D. BARVITIUM fecisset mentionem, deque te Cæsareo favore valde sollicita esset, quinam valeres, quidnam rerum ageres, an nihil ei transmitteres, Dominus BARVITIUS, me quidem inscio, tua Progymnasmata Astronomiæ ad ipsius Maiestatem detulit. Dominus BARVITIUS ad me aiebat: »Ich muste nur Ihrer Röm. Kay. Mts. etwas weisenn von dem Herrn TYCHONE, damit von Ihr Kay. Mts. ich nit so offters gefraget werde, weil ich dan sobaldt nichts darauf zu andtwortenn weis, und zue fridenn bleibe.«. Quæ ipsius Cæsarea Maiestas actutum aperuit et per integrum diem vultu hilari et clementissimo, imo paterno erga te quem gerit animo, clementissime perlustravit, uti coram plenius id tibi aperiam; per festinationem enim Postæ commode hoc fieri nunc nequit. Annuatim a Cæsarea Maiestate clementissime ex ferarum genere tres tibi sunt deputatæ, et aliquot Züber (uti in Bohemia vocant) piscium, de qua re ex mandato ipsius Cæs. Maiestatis a Domino BARVITIO ad Dominum Capitaneum Brandeisensem iam scriptum est, nec non de Prædio, ut aliquod eligat, et per primam occasionem, quid ille sentiat, Dominum BARVITIUM certiorem faciat, quas literas mecum dante Deo afferam. Pecunias antea promissas post diuturnam moram etiam nunc obtinui. Magnificus Dominus CORRADUCIUS te officiose et peramanter resalutat omniaque felicia precatur; dicta salute et congratulatione ad me dicebat: »Pro congratulatione hac quam mihi nuncias, et salute quam nomine Domini TYCHONIS BRAHE dicis, gratias tibi ago maximas; vicissim eum, cui mea studia offero, peramice salutabis. Ego illum virum tanto amore prosequor, itaque ipsi faveo, licet de facie mihi ignotus sit, ut nîl supra, non modo ob insignem ac præclaram quam prositetur artem Astronomicam, sed et ob generis splendorem, dan er eines tapfferenn Geschlechts und Herkommens, auch vornehmer Man, dessen gleichenn izo in toto terrarum Orbe nit zu findenn, utinam ut quam primum copia mihi eum videndi et cum ipso loquendi se offerat; sed id brevi fore puto.« Dominus TYPOTIUS ante biduum huc Pilsnam Lipsiâ appulit, qui etiam te salva impertit salute.

Iamque diutissime ac felicissime cum tota Domo vale viveque annos Platonicos.
Dabantur calamo celeri Pilsnæ ipso die quo mihi tuæ cum modella sunt redditæ, Anno assertæ salutis 1600.
Tæ Mæ addictiss.
DANIEL FELS,
manu propria.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 233; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Quod meæ superioribus diebus tardius quam debebant tibi sint redditæ, culpa mihi non est danda, sed id vel Postæ, per quam rescripseram actutum, vel Domino Doctori HELLERO, ad quem meas direxeram, imputandum. Cum viaticum mihi desit, nec hîc mutuo accipere possum nummos, scripsi D. HELLERO, ut per Postam 8 Ioachimicos mihi, bonâ ac fide et gratia a te restituendos, transmittere velit. Iterum vale measque festinationi ignosce, meque incolumem tu incolumis expecta. Progymnasmata tua Astron. a Cæs. Maiestate nondum recepi, quotidie adhuc ipsius Cæs. Maiestas ea perlustrat.
text.english:
**To the generous and magnificent man, Lord Tycho Brahe, in Knudstrup and Uraniborg, and his Lord, patron and promoter most highly to be honoured.**

Heartiest greeting.

Beyond all my hope and expectation it has fallen out, generous Lord Tycho, most honoured patron and promoter, that I am compelled to draw out my stay here longer. Nevertheless all things have so far succeeded for me according to my wish and mind's intent, and, as I hope, will succeed henceforth too. Your [letter], with the design or model of the new Benátky structure, I received safe and sound from your cousin Claus Bille on the 6th of January, to which — as the post hastens from here — I reply at once. The design I shall today offer to the Magnificent Lord Barvitius, to be humbly laid before the Imperial Majesty, and I shall carefully and diligently carry out the rest which I found set down in the memorandum. Since the Imperial Majesty daily made mention of you to Lord Barvitius, and was very solicitous about you, with imperial favour — how you fared, what you were doing, whether you were sending him nothing — Lord Barvitius, without my knowledge indeed, brought your *Progymnasmata of Astronomy* to His Majesty. Lord Barvitius said to me: *"I simply had to show His Roman Imperial Majesty something of Lord Tycho, so that I should not be asked by His Imperial Majesty so often — since I then know of nothing to answer thereto at once — and may be left in peace."* Which [book] His Imperial Majesty at once opened, and for a whole day, with a cheerful and most clement countenance — indeed with the paternal disposition he bears toward you — most graciously perused; as I shall more fully disclose to you in person, for through the haste of the post this cannot now be conveniently done. Annually there have been most graciously assigned to you by the Imperial Majesty three [head] of the wild-game kind, and several *Züber* (as they call them in Bohemia) of fish — concerning which, by the Imperial Majesty's mandate, Lord Barvitius has already written to the Lord Captain of Brandeis; and also concerning an estate, that you may choose one, and at the first opportunity inform Lord Barvitius what you think of it — which letters, God granting, I shall bring with me. The money promised before, after a long delay, I have now likewise obtained. The Magnificent Lord Coraduz returns your greeting dutifully and most lovingly, and prays every happiness for you; the greeting and congratulation delivered, he said to me: *"For this congratulation which you bring me, and the greeting you say in the name of Lord Tycho Brahe, I give you the greatest thanks; in turn you will greet most amicably him to whom I offer my devotion. I pursue that man with such great love, and so favour him — although he is unknown to me by face — that nothing could be beyond it: not only for the distinguished and illustrious astronomical art which he professes, but also for the splendour of his lineage, for he is of a valiant family and descent, and a distinguished man besides, whose like is not now to be found in all the world. Would that the chance of seeing him and speaking with him might offer itself as soon as may be — but that, I think, will be soon."* Lord Typotius arrived here at Pilsen from Leipzig two days ago, who also bestows on you a safe greeting.

And now, most long and most happily, fare and live, with all your House, the Platonic years.
Given with swift pen at Pilsen, on the very day on which your [letter], with the model, was delivered to me, in the year of asserted salvation 1600.
Most devoted to Your Magnificence,
Daniel Fels,
with his own hand.


*[Postscript:]* That my [earlier letters] were delivered to you these last days later than they ought to have been, the blame is not to be laid on me, but is to be imputed either to the Post, by which I had at once written back, or to Lord Doctor Heller, to whom I had directed mine. Since I lack travel-money, and cannot here borrow coin, I have written to Doctor Heller to be willing to send me by the Post 8 Joachimsthalers — to be repaid by you in good faith and favour. Again farewell, and pardon my haste, and, sound yourself, await me sound. Your *Progymnasmata of Astronomy* I have not yet received back from the Imperial Majesty: the Imperial Majesty still peruses it daily.
