documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Daniel Fels**, Tycho's *familiaris* and **on-the-spot agent at the imperial court** (then at Pilsen), who managed Tycho's court business and carried letters (cf. brahe-t_16000306002, where Tycho calls him "my familiar Daniel Fels, who has stayed for some while at Pilsen with you").
- **Significance — Tycho's court-business at Pilsen, January 1600.** A detailed dispatch on the negotiations that secured Tycho's imperial establishment:
 - **The Benátky building plans.** Fels has received from Tycho's cousin **Claus Bille** (*Claudius Billeus*, *consobrinus*) Tycho's letter with the *"design or model of the new Benátky structure"* (Tycho's projected observatory/works at Benátky), to be laid before the Emperor via Barvitius, plus a *memoriale* (memorandum) of further requests.
 - **The Progymnasmata before the Emperor.** *Dominus Barvitius* = **Johann Anton Barvitius**, Rudolf II's Latin secretary, who — pressed daily by the Emperor for news of Tycho — had on his own initiative laid Tycho's **_Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata_** before His Majesty, who "for a whole day … most graciously perused" it "with the paternal disposition he bears toward you."
 - **The court provisions & estate.** The Emperor has granted Tycho an **annual allowance of three head of game and several *Züber* (tubs) of fish** (the German measure, glossed by Fels), arranged through the **Captain of Brandeis (Brandýs nad Labem)**, the royal estate near Benátky; and Tycho is invited to **choose an estate (*praedium*)**. The previously promised **money** has at last been paid.
 - **The Coraduz greeting.** **Coraduz** (Vice-Chancellor; cf. brahe-t_16000324001) returns Tycho's greeting with an effusive testimonial.
- **German code-switches (kept and flagged; this chapter's convention).** Two passages of **direct speech break from Latin into German**:
 - *Barvitius:* "*Ich muste nur Ihrer Röm. Kay. Mts. etwas weisen von dem Herrn Tychone, damit … ich nit so offters gefraget werde … und zufrieden bleibe.*" ("I simply had to show His Imperial Majesty something of Lord Tycho, so as not to be asked so often … and be left in peace.")
 - *Coraduz* (macaronic, mid-sentence): "*…sed et ob generis splendorem, **dan er eines tapferen Geschlechts und Herkommens, auch vornehmer Mann, dessen gleichen jetzt in toto terrarum orbe nicht zu finden**…*" ("…but also for the splendour of his lineage, **for he is of a valiant family and descent, and a distinguished man besides, whose like is not now to be found in the whole world**…"). The Latin↔German switch within Coraduz's own quoted words is preserved.
- **Persons named.** Daniel Fels; **Claus Bille** (Tycho's cousin); **Johann Anton Barvitius** (imperial secretary); **Rudolf Coraduz** (Vice-Chancellor); the **Captain of Brandeis**; *Dominus Typotius* = **Jacobus Typotius** (Jacques Typoets, 1540–1601), the imperial historiographer, just arrived from Leipzig.
- **Flourishes / dating.** *vive annos Platonicos* = "live the **Platonic years**" (the Great Year — a hyperbolic long-life wish). *8 Idus Ianuarij* = the **6th of January** (the Roman-calendar idiom, glossed); the dateline repeats "the very day your letter … was delivered." *Anno assertae salutis 1600* = "in the year of asserted salvation 1600"; **New Style** (imperial). Header agrees with label.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (the delivery-delay apology, the request to Dr Heller for 8 Joachimsthalers, "the Emperor still peruses the Progymnasmata daily"), restored from Dreyer VIII p.233 (dropped by the working transcription).

documents.incipit: ACCESSUM meum in Bohemiam, quod a Caesâ Mate hîc Clementissime receptus sim, tibi iam …

text.original:
S. CLARISSIME ET ERUDITISSIME DOMINE BARTHOLOMÆE SCULTETE VETERI AMICITIA MIHI IUNCTISSIME.

ACCESSUM meum in Bohemiam, quod a Caesâ Mate hîc Clementissime receptus sim, tibi iam antea innotuisse, ex Domino Doctore SCHWALMIO communi nostro amico, paulo postquam Pragam adveneram, percepi. Rediens enim ille ex Silesiâ attulit schedam quandam memorialem tuâ manu exaratam, in qua Progymnasmatum meorum tomum primum tecum communicari rogabas: ac responsum ad meas, quas idem tibi tradidit, nullum reportavit, uti neque ad illas, quas Wittebergâ ad te dedi, rescribere voluisti, traditâ saltem tabellario chartulâ, quae probaret, eum meas exhibuisse. Quî vero fiat, quod in respondendo tam difficilis sis, equidem ignoro. Si curae tam publicae quam privatae impedimento sunt, scias me non minoribus distineri, et tamen haud intermittere, quin amicis scribam. Sed si in posterum hanc desidiam emendâris, erit veniae locus.

Progymnasmata desiderata mittere necdum potui, quia primus quaternio nondum impressus est, uti neque Conclusio; et deficiunt alias in primo capite sex quaterniones de motu ☾ae, quos Hamburgi quidem typis imprimi mandavi; sed in absentiâ meâ adeo depravate id factum est, ut eos recudere oporteat. Postquam vero in Bohemiam concessi, nihil eiuscemodi hucusque praestare licuit, partim ob pestem Pragae aliquamdiu grassantem, quodque isthic typographias numeris et figuris Astronomicis aptas non habeant, partim quod propriam meam Magdaeburgi unâ cum quibusdam ex meis Instrumentis atque supellectile domesticâ, interea dum ego in Bohemiam tendo, relictam ante hyemem me obtenturum frustra crediderim. Mandârat siquidem Caesa Matas per literas Magistratui eius loci, ut res meas omnes isthic conservatas mature huc in Bohemiam per Albim transvehi procuraret. Verum dum isthic moras nectunt, et nescio quae subterfugia quaerunt, superveniens hyemis asperitas id ante ver instans fieri posse vetuit. Sicque tam illud opus, quam alia a me inchoata et necdum typis plane consummata absolvere, postquam huc veni, non est concessum. Interim tamen in hac Arce Caesaris Benaticâ structurae pro Instrumentis meis Astronomicis ordine et sigillatim disponendis iussu eius Matis confectae sunt, in quarum aliquas ea, quae mecum attuli, iam disposita sunt, donec coetera, quibus relicta sunt convenientia loca, advenerint. Laboratorium etiam Spagyricum pro Pyronomicis meis exercitijs, quibus unâ delector, paratum est; satisque commode in hac Arce, quam tribus alijs pariter oblatis praetuli, cum meis habito; et de necessarijs a Caesâ Mate mihi liberaliter, quantum haec ferunt difficilia tempora, provisum. Absum autem hîc a vestro Gorlitzio vix plus itinere duorum dierum, aestivo praesertim tempore, ut facilior et crebrior (modo sic volueris) literarum inter nos commutatio fieri possit. Et si me aliquando hîc invisere tibi grave non fuerit, advenies non tam exoptatissimus hospes, quam Amicus antiquus nunquam antiquandus, sed perpetuo mihi futurus charissimus.

Quoniam vero intellexi Gorlitzij apud vos esse excultas Typographias, quae stylorum formâ et varietate praepolleant, simulque moletrinas papyro conficiendae idoneas ibi reperiri, cuperem a te resciscere, quali precio quaternio impressus in formâ papyri maiusculâ, quam Regalem vocant, ecudatur, idque in quarto, ita ut munda et nitida sit papyrus, typi vero partim ex cursivâ maiusculâ, partim minori et antiquâ mediocri, incidentibus nonnunquam quibusdam tabulis et figuris Geometricis, ita ut Exemplaria sint 1500, et quot quaterniones singulis hebdomadibus absolvi queant, quidque correctori idoneo numerandum. Ut vero mentem meam circa haec rectius percipias, apposui unum vel alterum quaternionem, formam papyri atque impressionis rationem ostendentem. Coetera per temetipsum facile capies atque dispones. Da itaque operam, amantissime SCULTETE, ut votis meis hac in parte respondeat eventus, idque mature resciscam, quo Exemplaria unâ cum pecuniâ necessariâ, quam tuae fidei committam, isthuc tempestive transmittere queam. Quae illuc primo quoque tempore labore typographico compleri averem, haec ferme sunt. In volumine primo Progymnasmatum instaurationis Astronomicae dimidium circiter Alphabetum hinc inde desideratur; ideoque quam citissime fieri queat, convenientibus locis supplendum. In libro illo de Cometâ Anni 77, quem dudum a me obtinuisti, subiunxi postea Apologetica quaedam scripta, quae Hamburgi quidem impressa sunt; sed refutatio cuiusdam Eruditi in Scotiâ viri, qui contra eiusdem libri praecipua contenta nonnulla inferre praesumpsit, necdum addita, quae forte quaterniones 16 adimplere poterit. Praeterea librum secundum Epistolarum Astronomicarum e nostris, quem paulo antequam Daniâ excessi, typis proprijs excudi inchoâram. Sed solummodo absoluto dimidio Alphabeto mihi inde in Germaniam emigrandum erat, sicque opera illa ob varias intercidentes irrequietudines intermissa est. Restant duo circiter Alphabeta plus minus typis pertexenda, idque totum minori illâ antiquâ, qualem primus Epistolarum tomus iam antea editus (quem proculdubio habes) exhibet.

Hos inquam libros iam antea typis nostris inceptos isthic apud vos ad Colophonem opere Typographico quam celerrime diduci posse, ut hoc Anno Iubilaeo publici iuris fierent, plurimum exoptarem. Fac igitur me de singulis huc pertinentibus per primam quamque occasionem (siquidem proprijs typis id nunc fieri nequeat) certiorem, et cum typographis vestris atque papyri confectoribus, prout aequum fuerit, transige, et quid ad minimum exigant, significa. Non poterunt mihi facile in hoc utroque negocio imponere, cum ipsemet utrumque, tam quoad typographicas impensas, quam papyri praeparationem in Insulâ olim Uraniburgicâ diu multumque proprijs sumptibus exercere curârim. Confido autem, sic persuadente veteri inter nos necessitudine, te desiderijs meis hac in parte non defuturum. Feceris sic non saltem mihi rem gratam et amicitiâ nostrâ haud indignam, sed et Divinae illius Astronomiae cultoribus inprimis acceptam nec (uti spero) inutilem. Cumque tu non postremum inter eos locum obtineas, te sponte tuâ rem omnem promoturum, nihil addubito. Sicque eo citius et promptius Exemplaria Operum meorum, quae requiris, nanciscêre.

Vale et actutum rescribe, meque de singulis diligenter admone. Opto tibi cum omnibus tuis hunc praesentem Annum Iubilaeum multosque alios instantes auspicatos et salutares. Iterumque vale. Dabantur ex Arce Benaticâ 5 milliaribus Pragâ versus Borrhapelioten remotâ Anno Epochae Christianae Dionysiacae 1600, quem tamen duobus Annis deficere IOSEPHUS SCALIGER in renovato Opere de Emendatione temporum (uti prius unico) contendit, Ianuarij die 7° stylo renovato. Tu, si potes (uti forte potes, siquidem in similibus diligenter versatus) hanc litem dirime.
text.english:
**Greeting. Most renowned and most learned Lord Bartholomäus Scultetus, most closely joined to me by old friendship.**

That I had come into Bohemia, and was here most clemently received by the Imperial Majesty, had — I perceived, a little after I reached Prague — already become known to you, through **Doctor Schwalm, our common friend**. For he, returning from Silesia, brought a certain memorial-note written in your hand, in which you asked that the first volume of my *Progymnasmata* be shared with you; but he brought back no answer to mine, which he had delivered to you — just as you were unwilling to write back to those I sent you from Wittenberg, [or] at least to give the courier a slip proving that he had presented mine. **Why it comes about that you are so difficult in replying, I do not know.** If public and private cares are a hindrance, know that I am held by no smaller ones, and yet do not fail to write to my friends. But if hereafter you mend this slackness, there will be room for pardon.

**The *Progymnasmata* you desire I have not yet been able to send, because the first quaternion is not yet printed, nor the Conclusion; and there are also wanting, in the first chapter, six quaternions on the motion of the Moon [☾], which I had ordered printed at Hamburg — but in my absence it was done so corruptly that they must be reprinted.** After I withdrew into Bohemia, I have hitherto been able to do nothing of the kind — partly on account of the plague raging some while at Prague, and because there they have no printing-houses fit for astronomical numerals and figures; partly because I had vainly believed I should obtain, before winter, my own [press], left at **Magdeburg** together with some of my Instruments and household goods while I made for Bohemia. For the Imperial Majesty had by letter ordered the Magistrate of that place to see all my things kept there transported in good time hither into Bohemia by the Elbe; but while they weave delays there, and seek I know not what subterfuges, the oncoming harshness of winter forbade it could be done before the coming spring. And so neither that work, nor others begun by me and not yet quite finished in print, has it been granted me to complete since I came hither.

**Meanwhile, however, in this imperial Castle of Benátky, structures have been made, by His Majesty's order, for arranging my Astronomical Instruments in order and severally**; in some of which what I brought with me is already placed, until the rest — for which fit places are left — shall arrive. **A Spagyric [alchemical] Laboratory, too, for my Pyronomic exercises, in which I likewise delight, has been prepared**; and I dwell comfortably enough, with my [household], in this Castle — which I preferred to three others likewise offered; and I have been liberally provided by the Imperial Majesty with necessaries, so far as these difficult times allow. **I am here scarcely more than a two-days' journey from your Görlitz** (especially in summer-time), so that an easier and more frequent exchange of letters between us can be made (if only you so wish). And if it be not a burden to you to visit me here sometime, you will come not so much a most longed-for guest as an old Friend, never to grow old [to me], but to be forever most dear.

But since I have learned that at Görlitz, with you, there are **excellent printing-houses, pre-eminent in the form and variety of their types, and likewise paper-mills fit for making paper**: I should wish to learn from you **at what price a quaternion is printed in the larger paper-format which they call Royal — and that in quarto — so that the paper be clean and bright, the types partly of the larger cursive, partly of the smaller and middling antique, with certain Geometric tables and figures sometimes falling in; so that there be 1500 copies; and how many quaternions can be finished each week; and what is to be paid a fit corrector.** That you may the more rightly grasp my mind about these, I have appended one or two quaternions, showing the paper-format and the manner of printing. The rest you will easily take in and arrange by yourself. Take care, then, most loving Scultetus, that the outcome answer my wishes in this part, and that I learn it in good time, that I may seasonably send thither the copies, together with the necessary money, which I will commit to your trust.

What I should wish to have completed there, at the first opportunity, by the printer's labour, are about these: **In the first volume of the *Progymnasmata* of the Astronomical Restoration, about half an alphabet [of gatherings] is wanting here and there**, and so is to be supplied, in fit places, as quickly as can be. **In that book on the Comet of the year [15]77** — which you obtained from me long ago — I afterward subjoined certain Apologetic writings, which were indeed printed at Hamburg; **but the refutation of a certain Erudite man in Scotland, who presumed to bring some things against the chief contents of that book, is not yet added — which may perhaps fill 16 quaternions.** Besides, **the second volume of our Astronomical Letters**, which a little before I left Denmark I had begun to print with my own types — but, only half an alphabet finished, I had to emigrate thence into Germany, and so that work was interrupted by various intervening unrests. There remain about two alphabets, more or less, to be woven out in type, and that whole [in] the smaller antique [type], such as the first volume of the Letters, already published (which you doubtless have), exhibits.

These books, I say — already begun in our types — **I should most greatly wish could be drawn out there with you, by the printer's work, to the Colophon as swiftly as possible, that they might be made public in this Jubilee Year** [1600]. Make me, then, informed of every particular pertaining hither, by the first occasion (since it cannot now be done with my own types); and transact with your printers and papermakers, as shall be fair, and signify what they demand at the least. They will not easily be able to impose on me in either business, since I myself took care to practise both — as much the printing costs as the preparation of paper — long and much, at my own expense, on the once-Uraniborgian Island. And I trust — the old bond between us so persuading — that you will not fail my wishes in this part. So you will do a thing not only welcome to me, and not unworthy of our friendship, but especially acceptable, and (as I hope) not useless, to the cultivators of that divine Astronomy. And since you hold no last place among them, I in no way doubt that you will of your own accord promote the whole matter. And so the more quickly and readily will you obtain the copies of my Works which you require.

Farewell, and write back at once, and admonish me diligently of every particular. I wish you, with all yours, this present **Jubilee Year**, and many others to come, auspicious and wholesome. And again farewell. Given from the Castle of Benátky, **5 miles from Prague toward the north-east [Borrhapeliotes]**, in the year of the Christian Dionysian Era 1600 — which, however, **Joseph Scaliger, in his renewed work *On the Emendation of Times*, contends to be deficient by two years (as before by one)** — the 7th day of January, by the renewed [New] style. You, if you can (as perhaps you can, being diligently versed in such things), settle this dispute.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (1540–1614), the Görlitz mathematician, cartographer, and burgomaster — Tycho's old friend (cf. the chronology-jest at brahe-t_16000327002, where he appears with the chronologers).
- **Significance — Tycho's publication program and the bid to print at Görlitz (a key bibliographical document).**
 - **The state of the *Progymnasmata*.** Vol. I still lacks **its first quaternion, the Conclusion, and six quaternions on the lunar motion** — the latter **printed corruptly at Hamburg in Tycho's absence and needing reprinting** (cf. brahe-t_15990922001). "About half an alphabet of gatherings" is wanting throughout.
 - **The Görlitz printing proposal.** Tycho asks Scultetus to price, at the **Görlitz presses and paper-mills**, a quaternion in **"Royal" large paper, quarto, 1500 copies**, with mixed type (large cursive + smaller antique) and **geometrical figures** — enclosing **sample quaternions**. He notes he cannot be cheated, having **run both press and papermaking himself at Uraniborg**.
 - **Three works to finish:** (1) the ***Progymnasmata* vol. I**; (2) the **Comet-of-1577 book**, to which must still be added **the refutation of "a certain Erudite man in Scotland" — i.e. John Craig** (the comet dispute; c. 16 quaternions); (3) the ***Astronomical Letters* vol. II**, begun on Tycho's own press in Denmark (only half an alphabet done), c. 2 alphabets remaining — all to be "made public in this **Jubilee Year** 1600."
 - **The Benátky establishment.** **Purpose-built housings for the instruments** by imperial order (some already installed); **a Spagyric (alchemical) laboratory for Tycho's "Pyronomic exercises"** — a vivid record of Tycho's chemistry continuing at Benátky; the castle chosen over three others; c. 2 days from Görlitz.
 - **The Magdeburg-press delay** (cf. brahe-t_16000405001, brahe-t_16000124001): his own press and goods stuck at Magdeburg, the city "weaving delays," winter blocking the Elbe.
 - **The Scaliger chronology dispute.** The dateline again raises **Scaliger's *De emendatione temporum*** claim that the era is "deficient by two years (as before by one)" — and challenges the chronologist Scultetus to "settle this dispute." (Same controversy as brahe-t_16000327002.)
- **Persons & places named.** Bartholomäus Scultetus; **Dr. Schwalm** (common friend); **John Craig** ("a certain Erudite man in Scotland"); **Joseph Scaliger** (*De emendatione temporum*); **Rudolf II**. Places: **Benátky** ("5 miles NE of Prague"), **Prague**, **Görlitz**, **Hamburg**, **Magdeburg**, the **Elbe**, **Silesia**, **Wittenberg**, **Uraniborg**.
- **Notable terms.** *Spagyricum laboratorium / Pyronomica exercitia* — alchemical/chemical (fire-based) work. *Borrhapeliotes* — the **north-east** (Greek wind-name; Benátky lies NE of Prague). *Alphabetum* — a printer's run of gatherings (A–Z); "half an alphabet" ≈ 11–12 gatherings.
- **Calendar.** *Ianuarij die 7° **stylo renovato*** → **7 January 1600 [N.S.]** (identifier 16000107001 agrees; the label carries only "Benatky"). The "Christian Dionysian Era" formula and the Scaliger two-year jest are Tycho's chronological flourish.
- **Correction.** Latin: 'exaratum' corrected to 'exaratam' (TBOO VIII p.234), restoring grammatical agreement with the feminine accusative 'schedam'.

documents.incipit: PAUCIS diebus ex quo Pragam veneram, Excellentissime et amantissime Domine MONAVI, …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET EXCELLENTISSIMO VIRO DOMINO IACOBO MONAVIO, PATRITIO VRATISLAVIENSI, ILLUSTRISSIMI DUCIS SILESIAe CONSILIARIO DIGNISSIMO, AMICO SUO INPRIMIS HONORANDO.

S. P.

PAUCIS diebus ex quo Pragam veneram, Excellentissime et amantissime Domine MONAVI, schedam quandam a te e vestra Silesia mihi asportavit Dominus D. SCHWALMIUS, si recte memini: quae nihil aliud quam de Carmine quodam Domini TOBIAe FISCHERI Poëtae vestratis, quâ occasione id in eum modum concinnatum sit, continebat. Grata mihi fuit tua chartula ipsiusque Carmen, in quo paucula verba mutata sunt iuxta censuram criticam, prout in adiunctis pagellis videre est, quibus etiam nonnulla alia, praeter ea, quae prius habes, adscripta sunt. Velim, ut tam haec quam priora cum eodem communices. Scripsissem ipsemet iam illi, si literas eius ad me humanissimas tam cito invenire potuissem. Nescio enim, ubi illas cum quibusdam alijs, interea dum res meae huc Pragâ transferuntur, reposuerim. Quando eas reperire dabitur, rescriptionem non ulterius intermittam. Interim ipsum meo nomine officiose saluta, et pro benevolo suo erga me animo gratias age.

Scripsi tibi aliquoties antea de libris Witichianis a sorore haerede coëmendis. Quod si iam tua operâ praestari possit, ut iusto precio eos obtinere queam, praesertim quoad Exemplaria quae habuit tria COPERNICI a se marginalibus quibusdam illustrata de Revolutionibus Coelestibus, et quae de Triangulis conscripserat, atque de Hypothesibus Coelestibus si quae inveniuntur, feceris mihi rem apprime gratam. Precium indicatum confestim solvam. Relatum quoque ad me est, quendam apud vos ante aliquot Annos fuisse Astronomiae peritum, qui observationes nonnullas Coelestes suo tempore perfecerat; quas filium ipsius adhuc conservare aiunt. Habitat autem is (si rite audita recordor) in plateâ quam vocant die Stockgasse, nomen eius excidit; tu (opinor) facile id conijcies atque inquires, rogoque peramanter, ut ab ipso impetrare velis earundem observationum, quot et qualescunque fuerint, descriptum mihi concedi. Inveniar vicissim erga illum gratus. Indica insuper, ubi rescripseris (quod te mature facturum confido) an aliqua apud vos sit Typographia, quae tales stylos habeat, qualibus liber primus Epistolarum Astronomicarum e nostris, quem existimo te habere, excusus est. Constitui enim alterum Tomum, in quo 12 primi quaterniones, antequam res meae in Daniâ conturbarentur, absoluti sunt, complere, in eâdem formâ papyri et characteris, quâ prior confectus est. Et transige simul cum Typographo idoneo, quid pro quolibet quaternione, ita ut Exemplaria imprimantur 1500, illi numerandum sit. Et simul papyri valerem indica, quidque correctori gnaro in singulas septimanas dandum. Si intellexero, omnia isthic rite succedere posse, mittam unâ cum Exemplari ad mundum scripto pecuniam, pro quâ papyrus coëmatur, et coetera persolvantur. Ignoscas vero mihi, mi MONAVI, quod te alias occupatissimum meis negotijs sic molestem. Ego quidvis vicissim tuâ caussâ faciam, quâcunque in re mea opera tibi unquam usui esse poterit.

Vale.
Dabantur ex Arce Caesareanâ Benaticâ, ubi nunc cum meis habito, die 10 Ianuarij stylo renovato Anni 1600.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and most excellent man, Lord Jacob Monau, patrician of Breslau, most worthy Councillor of the Most Illustrious Duke of Silesia, his friend especially to be honoured.**

Heartiest greeting.

A few days after I had come to Prague, most excellent and most loving Lord Monau, a certain note from you, from your Silesia, was brought to me by Lord Doctor Schwalm, if I remember rightly — which contained nothing other than [matter] about a certain Poem of Lord Tobias Fischer, a poet of your parts, on what occasion it had been composed in that fashion. Your note was welcome to me, and his Poem, in which a few little words have been changed according to critical judgement, as may be seen in the appended leaves, to which some other things, besides those you already have, have also been added. I should wish you to share both these and the earlier [pieces] with the same [poet]. I would have written to him myself already, could I have found his most courteous letters to me so quickly; for I know not where I have put them, with certain others, while my things are being moved hither [to and from] Prague. When it shall be granted me to find them, I will delay a reply no further. Meanwhile greet him dutifully in my name, and give thanks for his benevolent disposition toward me.

I have written to you several times before about the **Wittich books**, to be bought from the sister-heir. And if it can now be brought about by your effort that I may obtain them at a just price — especially as regards the **three Copies he had of Copernicus, *On the Celestial Revolutions*, annotated by himself with certain marginal notes**, and **what he had written *On Triangles***, and ***On the Celestial Hypotheses***, if any are found — you will have done me a thing exceedingly welcome. The price named, I will pay at once. It has also been reported to me that there was among you, some years ago, a man skilled in Astronomy, who had made some celestial observations in his time, which they say his son still keeps. He lives (if I rightly recall what I heard) in the street they call *die Stockgasse*; his name escapes me. You, I think, will easily guess and inquire it; and I most lovingly ask that you would obtain from him that a copy of those observations — however many, and of whatever kind, they were — be granted to me; I will in turn be found grateful toward him. Indicate moreover, when you reply (which I trust you will do in good time), whether there is any printing-house among you that has such types as those by which the first book of our *Astronomical Letters* — which I think you have — was printed. For I have resolved to complete the **second Tome**, of which the first 12 gatherings were finished before my affairs in Denmark were thrown into confusion, in the same form of paper and type as the former was made. And settle at the same time with a suitable Printer what is to be paid him for each gathering, such that **1,500 copies** be printed; and at the same time indicate the cost of paper, and what is to be given weekly to a skilled corrector. If I understand that everything can proceed properly there, I will send, together with a fair copy, the money with which paper may be bought and the rest paid. But forgive me, my Monau, that I trouble you — otherwise most occupied — thus with my business; I will in turn do anything for your sake, in whatever matter my effort may ever be of use to you.

Farewell.
Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, where I now dwell with my household, the 10th day of January, in the renewed [New] style, of the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Jacob Monau (Jacobus Monavius)** (1546–1603), Breslau humanist, *patricius Vratislaviensis* (patrician of **Breslau / Wrocław**) and **Councillor of the Duke of Silesia** — a noted literary patron and Tycho's Silesian agent (cf. brahe-t_16010322001, where Monau is proposed as a letter-relay). *Vratislaviensis* = of **Breslau/Wrocław** (not Bratislava).
- **The Tobias Fischer poem.** A commendatory *Carmen* by **Tobias Fischer**, a Silesian poet, sent via *Dominus D. Schwalmius* (Doctor Schwalm); Tycho returns it lightly emended "according to critical judgement," with additions, for Monau to pass back to the poet — the routine traffic of the friends'-verse collection.
- **The Wittich books (the historically significant request).** Tycho repeats a standing request that Monau buy for him, "from the sister-heir," the library of the late **Paul Wittich** (the Breslau mathematician, d. 1586, who had visited Tycho at Hven in 1580 and exchanged computational methods — *prosthaphaeresis*; cf. the Tycho–Hagecius correspondence, e.g. brahe-t_15820923001). He names specifically:
 - the **three copies of Copernicus's *De revolutionibus orbium coelestium* annotated in Wittich's own hand** (*marginalibus … a se illustrata*);
 - Wittich's writings ***On Triangles*** (*de Triangulis* — trigonometry); and
 - ***On the Celestial Hypotheses*** (*de Hypothesibus Coelestibus*), "if any are found."
 **The Wittich-annotated volumes.** These are the **Wittich-annotated Copernicus copies** central to the modern "Wittich-not-Tycho marginalia" question — surviving exemplars include the Apianus–Wittich volume at the University of Chicago and a Copernicus at Prague; marginalia of this group were later misattributed to Tycho. This letter is Tycho's own documented attempt to acquire them.
- **The Breslau astronomer's observations.** Tycho also seeks, via Monau, a copy of the celestial **observations of an unnamed deceased Breslau astronomer**, kept by his son, who lives "in the street called *die Stockgasse*" — Tycho's habitual hunt for predecessors' observational records. (Name not recovered — flagged.)
- **Printing the second Tome of the *Epistolae* in Silesia (printing history).** Tycho asks whether a Breslau press has type matching the **first book of his *Astronomical Letters*** (*Epistolarum astronomicarum liber primus*, Uraniborg 1596), so as to **complete the second Tome** — of which the first **12 gatherings** were printed "before my affairs in Denmark were thrown into confusion" — in matching paper and type. Concrete figures: a press-run of **1,500 copies**, with per-gathering printer's fee, paper cost, and weekly pay for a skilled corrector all to be negotiated. A valuable datum for the production economics of Tycho's books.
- **Persons named.** Jacob Monau; *Schwalmius* (Doctor Schwalm, the courier); **Tobias Fischer** (the poet); **Paul Wittich** (the late mathematician); the unnamed Breslau astronomer and his son.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 10 Ianuarij stylo renovato Anni 1600* — *stylo renovato* = the **renewed (New/Gregorian) style**; imperial usage. Header agrees with the label.
- **Correction.** Latin corrected: 'PATRITO' to 'PATRITIO' in the salutation, and 'molestam' to 'molestem' (subjunctive), per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII pp.236, 237.

documents.abstract: Thanks his uncle Tycho for years of kindness, excuses tardy correspondence by preparations for a study-tour that began 13 December, and promises more regular letters.
documents.incipit: DE tuo mei amore, quo indeusque a teneris annis large sum usus, tuisqve beneficiis, …

text.original:
GENEROSO VEREQVE NOBILI VIRO DN. TYCHONI BRAHE DE KNUDSTRUP, AVUNCULO MEO CARISSIMO.

DE tuo mei amore, quo indeusque a teneris annis large sum usus, tuisqve beneficiis, qvibus me semper complexus es, avuncule carissime, gratias, ut par est, ago qvam maximas, polliceorqve, si mea unqvam extare possunt officiola, in te constabunt promptissima paratissimaqve. Ne avtem mirere, avuncule carissime, qvod pavlo tardior in literis hactenus fui, siqvidem variis ego rebus cogitationibusqve, de instituenda præsertim peregrinatione, varie sum occupatus, qvibus tamen, avxiliante omnipotenti Deo, decimus tertius dies mensis decembris proxime absoluti anni, felicem expectatumqve finem imposuit; fore itaqve spero, ut diligentius post hac, qvoties per occasionem licuerit, literis tecum de meis rebus agam, certo enim certius mecum statuo, te de mea salute æqve solicitum atqve de genuini nati. Verum ut cognoscas, ubinam gentium ubiqve terrarum nunc vivam, scito, me cum comite mei itineris studiorumqve Nicolao Mathiæ Bachendorphio ad nominatum diem (cum tamen recta Basilæam decrevissem) Heidelbergam pervenisse, ubi propter urentis frigoris vehementiam usqve ad vernas nundinas proxime instantes Francofurdinas anchoram figere visum fuit, factumqve est integris, lavs Deo, omnibus. In itinere avtem meo comitata me est mater mea svavissima, soror tua perqvam dilecta, Brunsvigam usqve, ubi post pavcos dies obvium habuit Ericum Lange, qvi cum ipsa, ut puto, in Cimbriam iter fecit. Plura nec tempus nec tabellarii festinatio in præsentiarum scribere permittit. Velis ergo per pavca hæc boni consulere, alias enim majora dabo.

Vale.
Heidelberga 18 cal. feb. a:o 1600.
Tacho Tot O. f.
mea manu.
text.english:
**To the generous and truly noble man, Master Tycho Brahe of Knudstrup, my dearest [maternal] uncle.**

For your love toward me — which I have enjoyed largely from my tender years up to this point — and for your benefits, with which you have always embraced me, dearest uncle, I give, as is fitting, the greatest thanks, and promise that, if my poor little services can ever be of any account, they will stand toward you most ready and most prepared. But do not wonder, dearest uncle, that I have hitherto been somewhat tardy in [my] letters, since I have been variously occupied with various matters and deliberations — especially about the undertaking of a journey [study-tour]; to which, however, with omnipotent God's help, the thirteenth day of the month of December of the just-completed year put a happy and hoped-for end. So I hope that hereafter I shall the more diligently, as often as occasion allows, treat with you by letter about my affairs; for I hold it more certain than certain that you are as anxious about my welfare as about that of a son of your own begetting. But that you may know in what nation, in what part of the world, I now live: know that I, with the companion of my journey and studies, Niels Mathiesen Bachendorph, arrived on the said day at Heidelberg (although I had decided [to go] straight to Basel), where, on account of the violence of the burning cold, it seemed good to cast anchor until the next coming Frankfurt spring fair; and it was done with all of us whole [in health], praise God. On my journey my sweetest mother — your most beloved sister — accompanied me as far as Brunswick, where, after a few days, she met Erik Lange, with whom, as I think, she made the journey into Cimbria [Holstein]. More, neither the time nor the courier's haste permits [me] to write at present. Be willing, therefore, to take these few [words] in good part; for otherwise I will give greater [ones].

Farewell.
Heidelberg, the 18th [day] before the Kalends of February [15 January], in the year 1600.
Tage Thott, son of Otte,
by my [own] hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender — Tycho's nephew.** **Tage Ottesen Thott** (1580–1658), the Danish nobleman, son of **Otte Thott** and of **Sophie Brahe** — Tycho's astronomer-sister. He addresses Tycho as *avunculus carissimus* ("dearest maternal uncle"), and his mother as "**your most beloved sister**" — fixing the family triangle. He signs *Tacho Tot O[ttonis] f[ilius]*, "Tage Thott, son of Otte."
- **The study-tour.** Tage, with his tutor-companion **Niels Mathiesen Bachendorph**, on a *peregrinatio academica*; he had meant to go "straight to Basel" but, the cold being fierce, wintered at **Heidelberg** until the **Frankfurt spring fair**.
- **Sophie Brahe and Erik Lange — a notable family datum.** *mater mea … soror tua … comitata me … Brunsvigam usque, ubi … obvium habuit Ericum Lange, qui cum ipsa … in Cimbriam iter fecit* — Tycho's sister **Sophie Brahe** accompanied her son as far as **Brunswick**, where she met **Erik Lange** (the alchemist, her long-betrothed and later husband), with whom she travelled "into **Cimbria**" (the Jutland/Holstein peninsula). A direct contemporary witness to the famous Sophie Brahe–Erik Lange union (Lange's debts had kept them apart for years).
- **Calendar.** *Heidelberga 18 cal. feb. a:o 1600* = *ante diem XVIII Kalendas Februarii* = **15 January 1600**; Heidelberg (Calvinist Palatinate) kept the **Julian / Old Style** calendar. The internal "thirteenth day of December of the just-completed year" is the O.S. date on which his travel-plans were settled. Header agrees with the label (15 January).

documents.incipit: EXCELLENTISSIME et eruditissime Domine M. MARTINE BOCHAZI, amice honorande, ex literis …
documents.editorial_note: **Text recovered.** 11 words missing from inside this letter — dropped by a defective transcription of the source — have been restored from the text of record and translated into place.

text.original:
TYCHO
BRAHE AD MARTINUM
BOCHAZIUM.

S.

EXCELLENTISSIME et eruditissime Domine M. MARTINE BOCHAZI, amice honorande, ex
literis tuis ultimo ad me datis non obscure percepi tuum in me studium et
singularem benevolentiam, cum quod M. NICOLAUM, Conterraneum meum,
tam humaniter nuper exceperis, atque negocia a CLAUDIO BILLEO consobrino in Gallijs meo nomine expedienda tuo
quoque consilio promovere volueris, tum etiam quod exemplaria aliquot Carminum
tibi concreditorum mihi ad mundum describi procures, in quibus recte coniectatus
es, quod Epigramma quoddam TUTO pro TYCHO perperam haberet. Debet enim illud,
uti apposite restituisti, sic ultimo claudi:Ære RUDOLPHE tuo, TYCHO labore
tuo.

Et si quæ alia eiuscemodi invenisti sphalmata scriptoris, bene feceris, si
emendaveris. Quoniam vero beneficium unum alterum alliciat, et videam te
nostratibus favere, præsertim si mea commendatione fulti te accesserint, non
potui prætermittere, quin iuvenem Danum, qui ante triduum cum filio meo natu maiore (quem in Daniam pro auferendis isthic residuis
instrumentis, et Lubecam primum, deinde
Hamburgum, quod et
factum est, tranvehendis miseram) huc Witebergâ, ubi aliquandiu studuerat, comitatus est, [literis]
hisce [ad] te pro[mo]verem, siquidem is se tibi insinuari exoptârit meque hoc
nomine rogârit; intellexerat enim inter nos familiaritatem non vulgarem esse,
meque tibi, uti par est, plurimum tribuere, quare non potui non ipsius
desiderijs annuere. Ut vero paucis cognoscas, quis et qualis is sit, sic habe.
Oriundus est ex ea parte Daniæ, quam
Cimbricam alij vocant Chersonesum, nostrates Iutiam dicunt, in civitate isthic primaria Ripensi, quæ cathedralem habet ecclesiam et capitulum
Canonicorum celebre atque opimum, ubi etiam parens illius, honesta alias familia
natus, præcipuum gerit officium et Superintendentem agit, loco veterum
Episcoporum, vir apprime eruditus et antiqua consuetudine mihi notus, qui M.
PETRUS HEGELUNDUS appellatur.
Filius autem hic, IOHANNES nomine,
aliquamdiu in Academia Haffniensi
diligentem literis operam navavit, posteaque Witebergæ studia liberalia non minori sedulitate continuavit,
atque in ijs pro sua ætate egregium et laudabilem fecit profectum, estque
insuper honestis et compositis moribus præditus, ut spes non dubia sit, eum ad
præclaram aliquam frugem Dei beneficio perventurum.
Quocirca, mi optime BOCHAZI, ut
tibi hunc iuvenem Danum de meliori (uti aiunt) nota
commendatum habeas, utque eius conatus iuves, ipsumque ad optima quæque tuo
consilio promoveas, te etiam atque etiam rogatum habeo. Feceris sic mihi rem
apprime gratam et pluribus nominibus me, tui alias amantissimum, devinxeris.
Cuperet is aliquantisper Pragæ subsistere, ut
inchoatam studiorum suorum telam in vestro Collegio pertexere queat, atque mores
isthic hominum addiscere, sicque successive sibi viam sternere et commoditatem
parare ulterius peregrinandi et forte Italiam
perlustrandi. Da itaque operam, amantissime Domine BOCHAZI, ut isthic apud vos oportune,
et si locus commodus esset, in vestro Collegio, ibi potius degat, ut non nimium
de sua pecunia, quâ ad ulterius peregrinandum opus habet, illi consumendum sit,
sed frugaliter, ita tamen, ut necessaria non desint, vivere ac studijs
humanioribus simul vacare possit. Qua de re ille ipsemet suam plenius tibi
expositurus sententiam, atque ego, ubi vobis, favente Numine, adfuero, quod
statim atque Cæsarea Maiestas
Pragam redierit, futurum spero, ulterius
tecum tam de his quam alijs collocuturus sum. Interim effice, ut hanc nostram
intercessionem apud te pondus habuisse, qua etiam de re nihil addubito,
resciscam, et Exemplaria Carminum, quotquot transscripta habes, mitte, meque tui
studiosissimum redamare perge.

Vale.

Dabantur properanter ex arce Venetiensi 17 Ian. A. 1600.

POSTSCRIPTA.ADVENIT cum filio inde a littore Balthico quidam alius e conterraneis nostris
M. CHRISTIERNUS
LONGOMONTANUS nomine, a me huc vocatus: siquidem is iam
antea, dum in Daniâ morarer, mihi in
Insulâ nostrâ Uraniburgicâ per
octennium fuerat domesticus, et in Exercitijs Astronomicis operam diligentem
nobis præstiterat. Turbatis autem isthic Uraniæ sacris, quorundam inscitiâ
et malevolentiâ, ille, ruinas tantas me spectare nolente, sed inde cum totâ
familiâ in Germaniam me recipiente,
pariter abijt, et cum bonâ nostrâ veniâ primum in Prussiam navigavit. Postea perlustratâ Poloniâ per Silesiam et reliquam Meridionaliorem Germaniæ partem Rostochium venit; ubi cum percepisset, me in Arce Ranzovianâ prope Hamburgum aliquantisper consedisse, me ultro
accessit, et aliquanto tempore isthic mecum moratus, cum interea a Cæsâ Mate
Pragam evocarer, atque paulo post iter in
has oras susciperem, is me Magdæburgum comitatus est. Cumque Gynæceum meum, quod
eousque tunc mecum habueram, Wandesburgum remitterem, donec ego Pragam excurrendo (quod tamen tunc lues populariter in
Bohemiâ grassans impedijt)
Cæsæ Matis
Clementissimam voluntatem perciperem, eum
Gynæceo adiunxi, ut illud tutius reduceret, cum ipsius
diu mihi perspecta esset fides et erga me studium. Ubi vero is hoc recte
executus esset, in Cimbriam Patriam
suam nonnihil exspatiatus est, posteaque Rostochium reversus, ibi eventum rerum mearum in Bohemiâ præstolatus est. Nunc vero cum filio,
accersitus (uti dixi) denuo apud me comparuit. Et licet eius in studijs
Astronomicis operâ hîc Benachiæ
ulterius uti constitueram, tamen cum necdum omnia hîc rite disposita habeam,
et alias numerosa mihi sit familia, expectemque indies
Mathematicum quendam Electoris Brandeburgensis cum suâ coniuge, pro quo Cæsar scripsit, ut domus hæc mihi
deputata vix plures commode capiat, ipse etiam prædictus M. CHRISTIERNUS
Pragæ degere, atque isthic, quæ in
Astronomicis illi facienda significâro, sedulo exequi non aversetur: placuit
itaque mihi et hæc ratio, ut meis sumptibus ibi, donec illi aliter
prospexero, vivat, et pro me, quæ in hoc genere studiorum continuanda
præfinivero, elaboret. Quocirca rursus ad tuum unâ cum consilio auxilium rem
hanc defero, omniaque tuæ prudentiæ et fidei committo, ipsumque, qui mihi
semper charus et acceptus fuit, tibi quam diligentissime commendo, rogans te
per amicitiam nostram, velis de commoditate aliquâ oportunâ, tam quoad
habitationem quam victum, ipsi prospicere, sive id in collegio vestro, sive
alibi in propinquo competenter fieri queat, meque per eundem intra unum vel
alterum diem cum curru meo huc revertentem de singulis commonefacere.
Præstiteris sic rem inprimis gratam, et quovis officio, quantum per me
licet, vicissim compensandam.

Vale.

Datum ut prius.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO MARTIN BACHAZEK.**

Greeting.

Most excellent and most learned Lord Master Martin Bachazek, friend to be honoured: from your last letter to me I perceived, not obscurely, your devotion to me and singular goodwill — both that you lately received so kindly Master **Nicolaus**, my fellow-countryman, and that you were willing to further, with your counsel too, the business to be expedited in France in my name by my cousin **Claus Bille**; and also that you procure for me some fair copies of the **Poems** entrusted to you, in which you rightly conjectured that a certain Epigram wrongly had "TUTO" for "TYCHO." For it ought, as you aptly restored it, to close thus at the end:

*"By your money, Rudolf; by your labour, Tycho."*

And if you have found any other such slips of the scribe, you will do well to correct them. But since one kindness allures another, and I see that you favour my countrymen — especially if, supported by my commendation, they come to you — I could not omit to recommend to you, by this letter, a **young Dane** who, three days ago, accompanied hither (from Wittenberg, where he had studied a while) my **elder son** — whom I had sent into Denmark to bring away the instruments remaining there, and to convey them first to Lübeck, then to Hamburg, which was done. For he greatly desired to be introduced to you, and asked me on this account, having understood that there is no common familiarity between us, and that I esteem you highly, as is fitting; wherefore I could not but grant his wishes. That you may know in few [words] who and what he is, take it thus: he is sprung from that part of Denmark which others call the **Cimbric Chersonese**, [and] our countrymen call **Jutland** — in the chief city there, **Ribe**, which has a cathedral church and a famous and rich chapter of Canons, where also his **father** holds the chief office and acts as **Superintendent**, in place of the old Bishops — a man exceedingly learned, and known to me by old acquaintance, who is called **Master Peter Hegelund**. This son, **John** by name, devoted diligent effort to letters a while in the **University of Copenhagen**, and afterward continued his liberal studies at **Wittenberg** with no less assiduity, making in them, for his age, an excellent and praiseworthy progress; and he is moreover of honourable and composed manners, so that there is no doubtful hope that he will, by God's grace, attain to some illustrious fruit. Wherefore, my excellent Bachazek, I ask you again and again to hold this young Dane commended to you "of the better mark" (as they say), and to aid his endeavours, and promote him to every best thing by your counsel. You will thus do me a thing exceedingly welcome, and bind me — otherwise most loving of you — on many counts. He would wish to stay a while at Prague, that he may weave to its end the web of his studies, begun, in your **College**, and learn the manners of the people there, and so successively pave a way for himself and prepare the means of travelling further, and perhaps of traversing Italy. Give heed therefore, most loving Lord Bachazek, that he may rather dwell there with you conveniently, and — if a convenient place be [open] — in your College, so that he need not spend too much of his money (which he needs for travelling further), but may live frugally, yet so that necessaries be not lacking, and at the same time be free for the humaner studies. About which he himself will set out his view to you more fully; and I, when I am present with you (God favouring) — which I hope will be as soon as the Imperial Majesty has returned to Prague — shall speak with you further, both of these and other matters. Meanwhile bring it about that I may learn that this our intercession has had weight with you (of which I doubt nothing); and send the copies of the Poems, as many as you have transcribed; and continue to love me back, most devoted to you.

Farewell.
Given in haste from the Venetian castle, 17 January, the year 1600.


*[Postscript:]* POSTSCRIPT. There has arrived, with my son, from the Baltic shore, another of my countrymen, Master Christian Longomontanus by name, summoned hither by me: for he had already before, while I dwelt in Denmark, been a member of my household on our island of Uraniborg for eight years, and had rendered me diligent service in the Astronomical Exercises. But when the rites of Urania were there disturbed, through the ignorance and malevolence of certain men, he — I being unwilling to look on so great ruins, but withdrawing thence with my whole household into Germany — departed likewise, and with our good leave first sailed into Prussia. Afterwards, having traversed Poland, he came through Silesia and the rest of the more southerly part of Germany to Rostock; where, when he had learned that I had meanwhile settled for a while at the Rantzau castle near Hamburg, he came to me of his own accord, and having stayed there with me some time — since meanwhile I was summoned to Prague by the Imperial Majesty, and a little after undertook the journey into these regions — he accompanied me to Magdeburg. And when I was sending back my Gynaeceum [the household women], which until then I had kept with me, to Wandsbek, until I should ascertain the most clement will of the Imperial Majesty by an excursion to Prague (which excursion, however, was then hindered by a plague raging widely through Bohemia), I joined him to the Gynaeceum, that he might more safely conduct it back, since his fidelity and devotion toward me had long been clear to me. And when he had rightly carried this out, he travelled somewhat into the Cimbric land, his fatherland, and afterwards, having returned to Rostock, there awaited the outcome of my affairs in Bohemia. But now, with my son, summoned (as I said) anew, he has appeared before me again. And although I had resolved to make further use of his work in the Astronomical studies here at Benátky, yet — since I do not yet have all things duly arranged here, and have besides a numerous household, and a certain Mathematician of the Elector of Brandenburg with his wife is daily expected (for whom the Emperor has written), so that this house assigned to me can scarcely conveniently hold more — and since the aforesaid Master Christian himself does not refuse to live at Prague and diligently to carry out thence the things I shall signify for him to do in Astronomical matters: this plan therefore pleased me too, that he should live there at my expense, until I provide otherwise for him, and labour on my behalf at what I shall prescribe to be continued in this kind of studies. Wherefore I again refer this matter to your aid together with your counsel, and commit all things to your prudence and fidelity, and most diligently commend to you the man — who has always been dear and acceptable to me — asking you by our friendship that you be willing to provide for him some fitting convenience, both as to lodging and as to victuals, whether this can be suitably done in your College or elsewhere nearby; and to apprise me of each particular through the same man, who within a day or two will return hither with my carriage. You will thus do a thing especially welcome, to be repaid in turn by any service, so far as lies in my power. Farewell. Given as before.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Martin Bachazek** (Martin Bacháček z Nauměřic, 1539/41–1612), mathematician and **Rector of the Charles University (Carolinum / Collegium) at Prague** — Tycho's Prague academic contact. The MS is in Basel.
- **Significance — a student-recommendation, and the famous "Rudolf/Tycho" distich.** Two parts:
 1. **Thanks & the epigram correction.** Tycho thanks Bachazek for receiving "Master **Nicolaus**, my fellow-countryman" (a Dane of Tycho's circle — probably **Claus Mule**/Nicolaus Mulaeus), for furthering his cousin **Claus Bille's** business in France, and for fair-copying **commendatory Poems**. Bachazek had spotted a scribal error — **"TUTO" for "TYCHO"** — and rightly restored the closing pentameter, which Tycho quotes: ***"Aere Rudolphe tuo, Tycho labore tuo"*** — "By your money, Rudolf; by your labour, Tycho" — the neat epigram of the imperial patronage (Rudolf's purse, Tycho's toil), kept in Latin and translated.
 2. **The recommendation of Johannes Hegelund.** Tycho commends a **young Dane** who had accompanied his **elder son** (Tycho the Younger, back from the Denmark instrument-errand) from Wittenberg: **John Hegelund**, son of **Peter Hegelund** (Peder Jensen Hegelund, 1542–1614, **Superintendent of Ribe** — the Lutheran successor of the old bishops — "known to me by old acquaintance"), of **Ribe** in **Jutland** (the *Cimbrica Chersonesus*). Having studied at **Copenhagen** and **Wittenberg**, he wishes to continue at the **Prague Collegium**, then perhaps travel to Italy; Tycho asks Bachazek to lodge him in the College so he may live frugally, and promises to speak more once back at Prague.
- **Persons named.** Martin Bachazek; **Claus Mule** (*M. Nicolaus*, probable); **Claus Bille** (Tycho's cousin); **Peter Hegelund** (Superintendent of Ribe) and his son **John Hegelund**; **Rudolf II** (in the distich); Tycho's elder son (Tycho the Younger).
- **Place-name pun.** *ex arce Venetiensi* — "from the **Venetian** castle": **Benátky nad Jizerou** (whose Czech name *Benátky* means "Venice") is here Latinised as *Venetia* — a learned pun for Benátky, not the Italian Venice. Rendered "the castle of Benátky," with the pun noted.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *17 Ian. A. 1600*; **New Style** (imperial). Header agrees with the label.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Large closing POSTSCRIPTA — Longomontanus's movements (8 yrs at Uraniborg; Prussia/Poland/Silesia→Rostock→the Rantzau castle near Hamburg→Magdeburg; the Gynaeceum returned to Wandsbek; arriving with Tycho's son) + the request to lodge him at the Prague College, restored from Dreyer VIII pp.239–240 (dropped by the working transcription).
- **Plague delayed Tycho's own trip to Prague.** Recovers the reason Tycho did not himself go to ascertain the Emperor's will in person, but instead sent Longomontanus back with the Gynaeceum to Wandsbek: an outbreak of plague then "raging widely" through Bohemia made the excursion inadvisable.
- **Corroborates the plague chronology elsewhere in the edition.** Dovetails with the 3 August 1600 Rosenkrantz letter's own account of "the plague, with the Emperor's Court dispersed for almost a whole year" — the two letters describe the same episode from different points in its course, sharpening the timeline of Tycho's 1599 movements between Wandsbek, Magdeburg and Prague.
- **Correction.** "Given in haste from the castle of Benátky" corrected to "Given in haste from the Venetian castle," restoring Tycho's pun on arx Venetiensis (Dreyer, TBOO VIII, p.239); the Latin "concreditorum" (p.238) was already correct and required no change.

documents.incipit: NOBILISSIME et Magnifice vir, Domine et amice honorande: Accepi hac ipsâ horâ literas a …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD ANONYMUM.

S.

NOBILISSIME et Magnifice vir, Domine et amice honorande: Accepi hac ipsâ horâ literas a meo domestico DANIELE FELS, qui isthic apud vos in Aulâ moratur, quibus iussu tuae Magae scribit, Caesaream Matem Clementissime cupere, ut per primam oportunitatem iudicium meum de hoc Anno, praesertim quoad morbos Epidemicos, brevibus et succincte comprehensum eius Mati per primam oportunitatem transmittam. Etsi vero Astrologis praedictionibus indulgere non soleam, quod eam certitudinem non spondeant, quam requiro, et quam Astronomia, quae motiones siderum solummodo scrutatur, admittit (quam etiam ob id potius excolo) et praeter haec generales illae Mundi influentiae non saltem a superioribus Astris, sed et inferioribus caussis atque Elementari Naturâ dependeant (quod et antea Tuae Magae me innuisse memini) adeo ut qui has citra omnem hallucinationem rite praeviderint, vel nulli vel admodum pauci hactenus extiterint, qui vero particulares et individua concernentes rectius vaticinati sint, plures inventi: Attamen quia Sa Caesarea Maiestas, Dominus noster Clementissimus, sic a me fieri vult, cuius mandatis lubens et subiectissime (uti decet) obtempero, quam primum fieri poterit, meas hac de re coniecturas ex Astrologiâ qualicunque petitas paucis consignabo, atque ipsius Mati ad tuam Magam meo nomine humillime exhibendas dirigam, utut libris meis tam manuscriptis quam alijs huc conducentibus, quod Magdaeburgi apud reliquam supellectilem detineantur, etiamnum destituar. Alias iamdudum perfecissem id, quod ex mandato Caesae Matis Tua Maga eo ipso die, quo Clementissime audientiam obtinueram, expetijt; quod quale sit, ipsemet novit.

Porro Magam tuam caelare non possum (quod et alias ad ipsam hodie perscribere in animum induxeram) filium meum natu maiorem, quem cum alio quodam ex familiaribus meis ante sedecim hebdomadas in Daniam pro auferendis residuis isthic Instrumentis ablegâram, nunc primum huc reversum esse, re omni bene expeditâ. Instrumenta enim quatuor, quae ob magnitudinem discedens ibi reliqui, unâ cum quibusdam alijs, primum Lubecam, deinde ad Albis ostia Hamburgum, ubi nunc conservantur, sarcta tecta transferri fecit, contradicente isthic in Patriâ nemine: licet eo ipso tempore, quo Rex Comitia extraordinarie cum toto Regni Senatu et potissimâ Nobilitate celebravit, Haffniam appulerit: sed omnibus potius cordatis ac ingenuis unâ cum consanguineis et Amicis nostris de Caesae Matis Clementissimo erga me favore atque horum studiorum promotione mihi affatim congratulantibus, paucis tantum invidis et malevolis dolorem dissimulantibus ac atque obmutescentibus. Quae pariter indicanda duxi, quo per oportunitatem ipsius Mati a tuâ Magâ Instrumenta mea omnia, tam ea, quae prius evehi curâram, quam quae in Daniâ reliqui, nunc esse in fundo Germanico, atque instante vere, favente Deo, huc per Albim non incommode advehi posse, referri queat.

Coeterum ut dictum DANIELEM sollicitatorem isthic meum, qui iam sex ferme hebdomadibus abest, quamprimum per graviores occupationes licuerit, expedire et huc remittere non degravetur, officiose rogo.

Valeat Maga tua quam felicissime et diutissime.
Raptim Benachiâ die 20 Ianuarij 1600.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO AN ANONYMOUS [PERSON].**

Greeting.

Most noble and magnificent Man, Lord and friend to be honoured: I have received this very hour a letter from my servant Daniel Fels, who stays there with you at the court, in which, by Your Magnificence's order, he writes that the Imperial Majesty most graciously desires that, at the first opportunity, I transmit to His Majesty my judgement about this Year — especially as regards epidemic diseases — comprised briefly and succinctly. Now, although I am not accustomed to indulge in **astrological predictions** — because they do not promise that certainty which I require, and which **Astronomy**, that examines only the motions of the stars, does allow (which for that reason I rather cultivate); and because, besides, those general influences of the World depend not only on the higher Stars, but also on lower causes and on Elementary Nature (which I remember having hinted to Your Magnificence before); so that of those who have rightly foreseen these [general influences] without any delusion there have hitherto been either none, or very few, while of those who have prophesied more rightly concerning particulars and individual matters, more have been found — nevertheless, because the Sacred Imperial Majesty, our most clement Lord, wishes it so done by me, whose commands I willingly and most submissively (as is fitting) obey, as soon as it can be done I shall set down in a few words my conjectures on this matter, drawn from astrology of whatever sort, and shall direct them to be most humbly laid before His Majesty, in my name, through Your Magnificence — even though I am still deprived of my books, both manuscript and others bearing on this, since they are detained at Magdeburg with the rest of my furniture. Otherwise I should long ago have completed that which, by the Imperial Majesty's mandate, Your Magnificence requested on the very day on which I had most graciously obtained an audience; what it is, you yourself know.

Furthermore, I cannot conceal from Your Magnificence (which I had also resolved to write to you fully today, on another matter) that **my elder son** — whom, with another of my household, I had sent into Denmark sixteen weeks ago to bring away the instruments remaining there — has now at last returned hither, every matter well dispatched. For the **four instruments** which, on account of their size, I had left there on departing, together with certain others, he had transferred safe and sound first to Lübeck, then to Hamburg at the mouths of the Elbe, where they are now kept, with no one in the fatherland gainsaying — although he arrived at Copenhagen at the very time when the King was holding an extraordinary Diet with the whole Senate of the Realm and the chief Nobility; rather, all the wise and well-born, together with our kinsmen and friends, congratulated me abundantly on the Imperial Majesty's most clement favour toward me and the promotion of these studies, only a few envious and malevolent ones dissembling their chagrin and falling silent. These things I thought should likewise be indicated, so that, at an opportunity, it may be reported to His Majesty by Your Magnificence that all my instruments — both those I had earlier had carried out, and those I left in Denmark — are now on German soil, and that, with spring approaching, God favouring, they can be conveyed hither up the Elbe without difficulty.

For the rest, I dutifully ask that you would not find it burdensome — as soon as more serious occupations permit — to dispatch and send back hither the said Daniel, my agent there, who has now been away nearly six weeks.

May Your Magnificence fare most happily and most long.
In haste, at Benátky, the 20th of January 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient (unnamed; flagged).** Headed *Ad Anonymum* — an **unnamed senior court official** (*Magnificentia Tua*) at the imperial court, under whom Tycho's agent **Daniel Fels** operated and through whom Tycho's communications reached the Emperor. On the evidence (Fels writes "by your order"; the official conveys Rudolf II's wishes and will lay Tycho's prognostication before him) the most likely identification is **Johann Anton Barvitius**, the imperial secretary who handled exactly this traffic (cf. brahe-t_16000106001), though **Coraduz** (the Vice-Chancellor) is also possible. Not asserted.
- **The imperial request — a prognostication for 1600.** Via Fels, the official relays that **Rudolf II wants Tycho's astrological judgement on the year 1600, especially as to epidemic diseases** (the plague of 1599 was barely past). The request itself is a window onto the Emperor's appetite for astrology.
- **Tycho on astrology vs astronomy (the doctrinally important passage).** Tycho states his reservations plainly: he does **not normally indulge astrological prediction**, because it lacks "that certainty which I require, and which Astronomy — examining only the motions of the stars — does allow" (hence his preference for astronomy); the *general* "influences of the world" depend "not only on the higher Stars but also on lower causes and Elementary Nature"; and so **general** forecasts have almost never been got right "without delusion," whereas forecasts of **particulars** have more often hit the mark. Yet he will obey the Emperor and supply conjectures "drawn from astrology of whatever sort" — hampered, he notes, by his **books being detained at Magdeburg** with his furniture. A characteristic, qualified Tychonic statement on the limits of judicial astrology.
- **The return of the four great instruments from Denmark.** Tycho reports that his **elder son** (Tycho the Younger; cf. brahe-t_16000126001/002), sent to Denmark sixteen weeks earlier, has returned, having moved the **four large instruments** left behind (with other goods) safe **first to Lübeck, then to Hamburg at the Elbe mouth**, "with no one in the fatherland gainsaying" — even though he reached Copenhagen during an **extraordinary Diet** (the King with the whole *Rigsraad* and chief nobility). He stresses the warm reception (kinsmen and the "wise and well-born" congratulating him on the imperial favour), "only a few envious and malevolent ones … falling silent." The official is to report to the Emperor that **all** Tycho's instruments are now on **German soil** and can come up the **Elbe** in spring. (Dovetails with the Hamburg-transit letter, brahe-t_15990929001, and the Jöstel/Wittenberg-college letters, brahe-t_16001008001/16001009001.)
- **Persons named.** **Daniel Fels** (Tycho's court agent/*sollicitator*); the elder son (Tycho the Younger); the **King** (Christian IV) and the Danish Diet; **Rudolf II**.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 20 Ianuarij 1600* at Benátky; **New Style** (imperial). Header agrees with the label.
- **Correction.** Latin: 'ipidemicos' corrected to 'Epidemicos', per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p.240 (translation unaffected — already correctly rendered 'epidemic diseases').

documents.incipit: SERENISSIME et Potentissime Princeps, Domine Clementissime. Quod Serenissima Celsitudo …

text.original:
SERENISSIMO AC POTENTISSIMO PRINCIPI AC DOMINO. DOMINO FERDINANDO, MAGNO HETRURIÆ, FLORENTIÆ, SENORUM AC PISARUM DUCI, DOMINO SUO CLEMENTISSIMO AD MANUS PROPRIAS.

SERENISSIME et Potentissime Princeps, Domine Clementissime. Quod Serenissima Celsitudo Tua mihi, licet de facie ignoto et tam longe dissito, adeo clementer et benevole superiori æstate scribere non dedignata fuerit, humillima et obsequentissima mente eidem gratias ago quas possum maximas. Accepi eas literas, cum primum Pragam sub initia Iulij, a Sa Cæsareâ Maiestate, Domino meo Clementissimo, isthuc e Germania vocatus, et benignissime susceptus advenissem. Quæ sane non parvâ me affecerunt voluptate, quod inde perciperem tantum Principem, inter Europæos paucissimis cedentem, non saltem me immeritum Clementissimo suo favore prosequi, sed et Divinæ illius Astronomiæ (cui plurimis abhinc Annis, arduo et indefesso studio, nec modicis impensis operam navavi) mysterijs solerter et iucunde affici, prout hæc sublimis et Heroica Scientia, inde ab initio Regibus et Principibus, Heroicisque Viris, in sublimi rerum mundanarum fastigio collocatis, semper acceptissima, atque ab ijs in præcipuo honore habita fuit. Quâ etiam de caussâ Augustissimus Imperator RUDOLPHUS II me unâ cum Uraniâ nostrâ, Patriâ, quod ibi debite conservari et perpetuari nequiret, sponte excedentem huc in Bohemiam (uti dictum) ubi nunc in Arce quâdam Cæsareanâ, itinere saltem dimidij diei Pragâ remotâ, eius fundamina et culturam denuo instauro, arcessiri voluit, atque huic Regali Studio, Regaliter quoque et liberaliter prospicere non degravatus est. Libros quos Serenissimæ Tuæ Celsitudini humillime misi, eidem gratos fuisse, mihi plurimum congratulor.

Quoniam vero ex prædictis Serenissimæ Celsitudinis Tuæ literis percepi, illam plura ex meis in re Astronomicâ Operibus Clementissimo animo requirere, nullatenus intermittam, quin per primam quamque oportunitatem, ipsius optimæ voluntati, quâ possum reverentiâ, morem geram; et præstitissem id iam antea quam lubentissime, si supellex mea libraria, quæ Magdæburgi in Germania etiamnum reservatur, huc allata fuisset, quod tamen instanti vere, ubi Albis fluvius hoc hyberno tempore congelatus, denuo erit navigabilis, futurum spero. Sic enim a Cæsareâ Maiestate Magdæburgensibus per literas iniunctum est. Ex quo insuper Serenissima Celsitudo Tua Nobilem et Eruditum Adolescentem, FRANCISCUM TENGNAGLIUM, meum aliquandiu domesticum, qui dictos libros Serenissimæ Tuæ Celsitudini submisse a me obtulit, ex aliquali nostrâ humillimâ commendatione Clementissimo favore non indignum censuit, sed ita sibi acceptum habuit, ut nuper huc ad me reversus Serenissimæ Celsitudinis Tuæ Clementissimam et singularem erga se benignitatem satis deprædicare nequiverit, id equidem tanti beneficij loco reputo, ac si a Tuâ Serenissimâ Celsitudine mihi ipsi præstitum foret. Et quia vel inde Serenissimæ Celsitudinis Tuæ Clementissimum erga me animum haud obscure intelligam, non verebor Serenissimam Tuam Celsitudinem in alio quodam haud dissimili negotio eo audentius demisse compellare, præsertim cum Ipsamet in suis ad me Clementissimis literis benignissima sua officia mihi ultro offerre dignetur. Est autem eiuscemodi.

Cuperem quam maxime non saltem in Italia, ubi minor est quam hîc Sphæræ Mundanæ inclinatio, sed et in Ægypto apud Alexandriam, siquidem ibi adhuc rectior est, nonnulla in Astrorum Observationibus, quæ hîc non ita patent, perficere. Quamobrem filium meum natu maiorem ex me ipso denominatum, adolescentem 18 Annorum, quem inde ab ipsa pueritia ad hæc exercitia assuefeci, adiuncto illi pro comite quodam ex meis studiosis, qui usque in tertium Annum in rebus Astronomicis factitandis fideliter et sedulo mihi inservivit, harumque non vulgarem peritiam sibi interea comparavit, favente Divino Numine, instanti vere, vel quamprimum fieri poterit, ad Smam Tuam Celnem in Hetruriam mittere, tradito illi uno vel altero Instrumento ex meis, quod portatile sit (si modo id commode effici queat) unâ cum instructione, quomodo plura, prout opus fuerit, isthic paranda sint, et quænam ijs cœlitus denotanda. Daboque simul operam, ut is aliquos librorum meorum a S. T. Celne clementissime desideraturum secum adferat. Deinde studiosus ille, relicto in Smæ Tuæ Celnis Aulico servitio (modo S. T. Celni sic placuerit) filio meo, in Ægyptum navigabit, atque ea quæ isthic ulterius observari poterunt, iuxta meam præscriptionem pariter designabit. Qua in re Inclyta Venetiarum Respublica, quando aliquam eo navem ablegat, competentem promotionem (uti etiam spem aliqualem prædicto TENGNAGLIO, hac de re, dum ibi esset, meo nomine solicitanti fecit) potissimum vero Tuæ Serenissimæ Celsitudinis authoritate et intercessione allecta, non est (uti spero) denegatura. Si itaque Sma Celdo Tua filium meum unâ cum adiuncto ipsi comite, per annuum tempus aut circiter in Aula sua apud se retinere, sibique commendatum habere, pro singulari suo et Clementissimo erga me favore, non aversetur, quibus possum precibus demisse oro, ut de sua Clementissima hac in parte voluntate me per literas certiorem reddere non degravetur, aut etiam id Generosissimo et Magnificentissimo suo apud Sam Cæsam Matem Legato, qui Pragæ est, significare. Fecerit sic Serenissima Celsitudo Tua non saltem mihi humillimo suo servitori, ad omnia obsequia pro virili præstanda paratissimo, sed et ipsi Cæsareæ Maiestati, cui hæc studia cordi sunt, rem (uti non dubito) inprimis acceptam et Serenissimæ Tuæ Celsitudini (modo ipsius laudibus aliquid accedere possit) gloriosam et apud omnem posteritatem commendabilem.

Sed desino Serenissimam Tuam Celsitudinem, gravissimis Ditionum suarum rebus gubernandis intentam, ulterius interpellare. Deus Opt. Max. eam quam diutissime sospitem et florentem conservet.

Dabantur ex Arce Cæsareanâ Benaticâ Die 24 Ianuarij An. 1600.
Serenissimæ Celsitudinis Vestræ humillimus servitor
TYCHO BRAHE, manu propria scripsi.
text.english:
**To the most serene and most powerful Prince and Lord, Lord Ferdinando, Grand Duke of Tuscany, Florence, Siena and Pisa, his most clement Lord — into his own hands.**

Most serene and most powerful Prince, most clement Lord. That Your most serene Highness did not disdain to write to me — though unknown by face and so far distant — so clemently and benevolently last summer, I give You, with most humble and obedient mind, the greatest thanks I can. I received that letter when I had first come to Prague, about the beginning of July, called hither from Germany by the Sacred Imperial Majesty, my most clement Lord, and most kindly received. It affected me indeed with no small delight, that I perceived thence so great a Prince — yielding to very few among Europeans — not only to pursue me, undeserving, with His most clement favour, but also to be skilfully and pleasantly taken with the mysteries of that divine **Astronomy** (on which, for very many years now, with arduous and untiring study, and at no modest expense, I have bestowed my labour) — as this sublime and Heroic Science has, from the beginning, always been most acceptable to Kings and Princes and Heroic Men set on the lofty summit of worldly things, and held by them in special honour. For which cause also the most august Emperor **Rudolf II** willed that I be summoned hither into Bohemia — withdrawing of my own accord, together with our **Urania**, from my fatherland, because she could not there be duly preserved and perpetuated — where now, in **a certain imperial Castle, a journey of but half a day distant from Prague** [Benátky], I again restore her foundations and cultivation; and He has not thought it beneath Him to provide for this Royal Study, royally too and liberally. **The books which I most humbly sent to Your most serene Highness, that they were welcome to You, I greatly rejoice.**

But since from Your most serene Highness's said letter I perceived that You, with most clement mind, desire more of my Works in Astronomical matters, I will by no means fail, at the first opportunity, to comply with Your excellent wish, with what reverence I can; and I would have done it most gladly already, **had my library-stock — which is still kept at Magdeburg in Germany — been brought hither**; which, however, I hope will come about this coming spring, when the river **Elbe**, frozen in this winter season, shall again be navigable (for so it has been enjoined upon the Magdeburgers by the Imperial Majesty, by letter). Moreover, since Your most serene Highness judged the noble and learned youth **Franz Tengnagel** — for some while a member of my household, who humbly presented those books to Your most serene Highness from me — not unworthy, on some humble commendation of ours, of Your most clement favour, but held him so acceptable that, lately returned hither to me, he could not sufficiently proclaim Your Highness's most clement and singular kindness toward him: I count this in the place of so great a benefit, as if it had been done to me myself by Your most serene Highness. And because even thence I clearly understand Your Highness's most clement disposition toward me, I will not fear the more boldly and humbly to address Your most serene Highness on another, not dissimilar, business — especially since You Yourself, in Your most clement letter to me, deign of Your own accord to offer me Your most kindly services. It is of this kind.

**I should most greatly wish to perfect certain observations of the stars — which here are not so open [to view] — not only in Italy (where the inclination of the celestial Sphere is less than here), but also in Egypt, at Alexandria, since there it is yet more upright [*rectior*].** Wherefore **my elder son, named after myself, a youth of 18 years, whom from his very boyhood I have habituated to these exercises** — adding to him as companion a certain one of my students, who has faithfully and diligently served me, even into a third year, in carrying out astronomical work, and has meanwhile acquired no common skill in these things — I purpose, God favouring, **this coming spring, or as soon as it can be done, to send to Your most serene Highness into Tuscany**, having given him one or two of my Instruments, such as is portable (if only it can conveniently be made so), together with instruction how more are to be prepared there as need requires, and what is to be marked by them from the heavens. And I will at the same time take care that he bring with him some of my books, which Your Highness will most clemently desire. Then that student — my son being left in Your most serene Highness's court service (if so it please Your Highness) — **will sail to Egypt, and will likewise mark down what can there be further observed, according to my prescription**. In which matter the renowned **Republic of Venice**, when it sends some ship thither, will not (as I hope) refuse competent furtherance — as it gave some hope, too, to the aforesaid Tengnagel, soliciting on this matter in my name while he was there — but above all drawn by Your most serene Highness's authority and intercession. If, then, Your most serene Highness, of Your singular and most clement favour toward me, would not be averse **to keep my son, together with the companion adjoined to him, for a year's time or thereabouts in Your Court with You, and to hold him commended**, I humbly beg, with what prayers I can, that You would not think it a burden to inform me by letter of Your most clement will in this part, or even to signify it to Your most noble and magnificent **Legate at the Imperial court, who is at Prague**. So would Your most serene Highness do a thing — as I do not doubt — especially welcome not only to me, Your most humble servant, most ready to render all obedience to the utmost, but also to the Imperial Majesty Himself, to whom these studies are dear; and glorious to Your most serene Highness (if anything can be added to Your praises), and commendable to all posterity.

But I cease to interrupt Your most serene Highness further, intent on the weightiest affairs of governing Your Dominions. May God, Best and Greatest, preserve You safe and flourishing as long as possible.

Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 24th day of January, the year 1600.
Your most serene Highness's most humble servant,
**Tycho Brahe**, written in my own hand.
