documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany** (Florence, Siena, Pisa) — the same correspondent as brahe-t_16010430001 (30 April 1601). This is the **earlier** of the pair (Jan 1600 vs Apr 1601).
- **Significance — the Alexandria/Egypt observation plan and the bid to place the son at the Medici court (the back-story to the letter of 30 April 1601).**
 - **The low-latitude observation project.** Tycho's striking ambition: to make observations impossible at Bohemian latitude **by sending observers south — to Italy, "where the inclination of the celestial Sphere is less," and above all to Alexandria in Egypt, "where it is yet more upright"** (nearer the *sphaera recta* of the equator, where the southern stars and the zodiac ride higher — the classic site of Ptolemaic astronomy). A rare glimpse of Tycho planning a *southern expedition* to extend his star-work.
 - **The personnel.** His **elder son, Tycho Brahe the Younger ("named after myself," aged 18)**, trained "from boyhood," with **a student-companion** of three years' astronomical service, to carry **one or two portable instruments** plus instructions; the **son to remain in the Medici court**, the **student to sail on to Egypt**.
 - **The Venice connection.** Tycho counts on **the Republic of Venice** to ship the student to Egypt — hope already raised to **Tengnagel** when he solicited there — especially with the Grand Duke's backing.
 - **Tengnagel's Florence embassy.** Confirms **Franz Tengnagel** carried Tycho's **gift books to Ferdinando** and was warmly received — the diplomatic groundwork.
- **Aftermath cross-reference.** The plan did not unfold as designed: by **April 1601 (brahe-t_16010430001)** the son had gone to Italy **with the Persian embassy** instead, was **left at Siena**, and the **Capuchin calumny** had made Rome dangerous — with Tycho then seeking to place him at **Henri IV's** court. Read the letter of 24 January 1600 and that of 30 April 1601 as the **plan and its derailment**.
- **Other details.** Tycho's **library is still stored at Magdeburg**, awaiting the spring thaw of the **Elbe** (the Emperor having ordered the Magdeburgers to release it) — which is why he cannot yet send the Grand Duke more books. He writes from **Benátky**, "half a day from Prague," restoring "Urania's foundations."
- **Persons & places named.** Ferdinando I de' Medici; **Rudolf II**; **Franz Tengnagel** (the book-bearing emissary); **Tycho Brahe the Younger** (the 18-year-old son); the unnamed **student-companion** (3 years' service, bound for Egypt); the **Republic of Venice**; the **Tuscan Legate** at Prague (unnamed). Places: **Benátky**, **Prague**, **Germany/Magdeburg**, the **Elbe**, **Italy/Tuscany**, **Egypt/Alexandria**, **Venice**.
- **Calendar.** *Die 24 Ianuarij An. 1600* at Benátky (imperial reckoning) → **24 January 1600 [N.S.]**; header and label agree.

text.original:
ILLUSTRI ET GENEROSO DOMINO, DOMINO IOHANNI FRIDERICO HOFFMANNO, LIBERO BARONI IN GRUENPUECHEL ET STRECHAW, PRÆFECTO PROVINCIÆ DUCATUS STYRIÆ ET ARCHIDUCATUS AUSTRIÆ MARSCALCHO UBIQUE HÆREDITARIO BURGRAVIO IN STEYER NEC NON SAC. CÆS. MAIESTATIS AULÆ CONSILIARIO ET SERENISSIMI ARCHIDUCIS MAXIMILIANI CUBICULARIO PRIMARIO, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO INPRIMIS HONORANDO.

ILLUSTRIS ET GENEROSE VIR, DOMINE ET AMICE HONORANDISSIME.

MAGNO equidem gaudio affectus sum, cum heri vesperi ex meis Domesticis huc Pragâ revertentibus percepissem Illustr. Generos. Tuam ex Austriâ nuper salvam et incolumem redijsse. Quo nomine non saltem Illustri Generositati Tuæ, sed et mihi ipsi quamplurimum congratulor, siquidem de Generositatis Tuæ erga me et ea, quæ tracto studia Astronomica, sincera et benevola affectione vel ex pauculo, quem superiori æstate invicem habuimus congressu, ita mihi optima quæque polliceor, ut in tanti viri, qui non saltem Genere clarus sit, sed et doctrinis liberalibus insigniter excultus, familiaritatem incidisse, non postremæ felicitatis loco ducam. Cumque nunc Pragam Nobilem et Eruditum adolescentem FRANCISCUM TENGNAGLIUM, mihi domesticum, qui ante paucas hebdomadas ex Italia huc reversus est, unâ cum filio meo natu maiore ex me denominato certis de caussis amandem, non potui intermittere, quin hasce pro felici reditu candido animo Illust. G. T. congratulantes unâ mitterem, atque ijs simul iniungerem, ut Tuam Illust. Generos. captata oportunitate accedentes eam ex me officiosissime salutarent. Pergratum vero est, quod Illustris Dominatio Tua Excellentem Mathematicum Dominum Μ. IOHANNEM KEPLERUM in suo Comitatu huc ad nos in Bohemiam adduxerit, qua etiam in parte non obscure elucet Illust. G. T. erga sublimia illa et a vulgi captu remota Mathematum studia eorumque alumnos singularis et nunquam satis laudatus favor atque benignitas ab omnibus hisce excellentioribus Scientijs addictis merito semper deprædicanda. Intercessit mihi cum illo viro, postquam Daniâ emigravi, nonnulla per Litteras eademque pergrata familiaritas, quæ ex mutua præsentia, quam brevi futuram mihi persuadeo, augeri poterit. Quicquid vero voluptatis et commodi ex hoc nostro congressu promanare poterit, Illustri Dominationi Tuæ præcipua ex parte acceptum ferendum grata mente agnosco. Pluribus Illust. Generos. T. multiplicibus alias pariterque gravissimis occupationibus distentam remorari nolo. Cætera, quæ hîc omitto, ij, quos ablego, si Illust. Domni Tuæ eos admittere commodum fuerit, supplebunt atque ex me referent; quibus ut benignam aurem pro solita sua humanitate præbere non dedignetur, qua possum reverentia, oro et obsecro. Valeat Tua Illust. Generositas quam felicissime et diutissime, huncque noviter inchoatum Annum Iubilæum plurimosque alios insequentes incolumis et florens transigat.

Dabantur ex Arce Cæsariana Benatica die 26 Ianuarij Anni labentis Epochæ Christianæ Dionysiacæ 1600, quam duobus deficere IOSEPHUS SCALIGER probare nititur.
Iterum et sæpius T. Illust. Gen. quam optime valeat, meque et meos sibi commendatos habeat.
Illustri Generositati Tuæ
addictiss.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the illustrious and generous Lord, Lord Johann Friedrich Hoffmann, Free Baron in Grünbüchel and Strechau, Prefect of the Province of the Duchy of Styria, hereditary Marshal everywhere of the Archduchy of Austria, Burgrave in Steyr, and also Aulic Councillor of the Sacred Imperial Majesty and First Chamberlain of the Most Serene Archduke Maximilian, his Lord and friend especially to be honoured.**

Illustrious and generous Man, Lord and most honoured friend.

I was indeed filled with great joy when, yesterday evening, from my servants returning hither from Prague, I learned that Your Illustrious Generosity had lately returned safe and sound from Austria. On which account I congratulate not only Your Illustrious Generosity, but also myself, most heartily; since, concerning Your Generosity's sincere and benevolent affection toward me and the astronomical studies I pursue, I promise myself every best thing — even from the brief meeting we had together last summer — so that I count it no slight happiness to have fallen into the friendship of so great a man, who is not only illustrious by lineage, but also remarkably cultivated in the liberal learnings. And since I am now dispatching to Prague, for certain reasons, the noble and learned young man Franz Tengnagel, of my household — who a few weeks ago returned hither from Italy — together with my elder son, named after me, I could not omit to send along with them these lines congratulating Your Illustrious Generosity, with a candid heart, on your happy return, and at the same time to charge them that, approaching Your Illustrious Generosity at a fitting opportunity, they greet you most dutifully on my behalf. It is very welcome indeed that Your Illustrious Lordship has brought the excellent Mathematician Master Johannes Kepler, in your retinue, hither to us into Bohemia — in which respect, too, there shines forth not obscurely Your Illustrious Generosity's singular and never sufficiently praised favour and kindness toward those sublime mathematical studies, remote from the common grasp, and toward their nurslings — a favour ever deservedly to be proclaimed by all who are devoted to these more excellent Sciences. There has passed between me and that man, since I emigrated from Denmark, a certain and most pleasing familiarity by letters, which will be able to be increased by our mutual presence — which I am persuaded will be soon. And whatever of pleasure and profit may flow from this meeting of ours, I acknowledge, with grateful mind, that it is to be credited in chief part to Your Illustrious Lordship. I do not wish to detain Your Illustrious Generosity, taken up with manifold and likewise most weighty occupations, with more words. The rest, which I omit here, those whom I send will supply — if it be convenient for Your Illustrious Lordship to admit them — and will report on my behalf; to whom that you would not disdain to lend a kindly ear, after your wonted humanity, I beg and beseech with what reverence I can. May Your Illustrious Generosity fare most happily and most long, and pass this newly begun Jubilee Year, and very many others to follow, safe and flourishing.

Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 26th day of January of the passing year of the Christian Dionysian Epoch 1600 — which Joseph Scaliger strives to prove deficient by two [years].
Again and often, may Your Illustrious Generosity fare as well as possible, and hold me and mine commended to you.
Most devoted to Your Illustrious Generosity,
TYCHO BRAHE.

documents.apparatus:
- **Significance — the documentary record of Kepler's arrival to Tycho.** This letter, the **same-day companion of Tycho's first invitation to Kepler** (brahe-t_16000126002, Benátky, 26 January 1600), thanks **Hoffmann for bringing Kepler to Bohemia in his retinue**. The two letters interlock: the *"servants returning hither from Prague yesterday evening"* who reported Hoffmann's return are the same who brought Kepler's letter in the Kepler-invitation; and both letters announce the dispatch of **Franz Tengnagel and Tycho's elder son to Prague** (in whose carriage Tycho invites Kepler to ride back to Benátky). Together they fix the convergence of Tycho and Kepler in the opening weeks of 1600.
- **Recipient.** **Johann Friedrich Hoffmann, Freiherr von Grünbüchel und Strechau** (1555–1608) — *Landeshauptmann* (Prefect) of the **Duchy of Styria**, hereditary Marshal of the Archduchy of Austria, Burgrave in Steyr, **Imperial Aulic Councillor**, and First Chamberlain of **Archduke Maximilian**; a Protestant magnate and patron of learning at whose **Prague house Kepler first lodged**. The full titulature is reproduced.
- **Kepler.** *Excellens Mathematicus M. Johannes Keplerus, Illustrium Styriae Ordinum Mathematicus* = **Johannes Kepler**, then **mathematician to the Estates of Styria** (the post he was losing as the Counter-Reformation drove him from Graz). Tycho records that he and Kepler had a *"most pleasing familiarity by letters since I emigrated from Denmark,"* soon to be increased "by mutual presence" — the prelude to their collaboration. The whole favour of the meeting Tycho credits "in chief part" to Hoffmann.
- **The intermediaries.** *Franciscus Tengnaglius* = **Franz Tengnagel**, "a few weeks ago returned from Italy" (cf. brahe-t_15991104001, brahe-t_16000504001/002); *filius meus natu maior ex me denominatus* = Tycho's **elder son, Tycho Brahe the Younger**. Both are sent to Prague to carry this letter and transact "certain business," and to greet Hoffmann.
- **The summer-1599 meeting.** *ex pauculo … superiori aestate … congressu* — Tycho and Hoffmann had briefly met the previous summer (1599); Tycho builds on that acquaintance.
- **Persons named.** Hoffmann; Johannes Kepler; Franz Tengnagel; Tycho the Younger; Archduke Maximilian (in the titulature); Joseph Scaliger (in the dateline jest).
- **Calendar / chronology jest.** Dateline *die 26 Ianuarij Anni labentis Epochae Christianae Dionysiacae 1600, quam duobus deficere Iosephus Scaliger probare nititur* — "of the passing year of the Christian **Dionysian** Epoch 1600 [the Anno Domini reckoning of Dionysius Exiguus], **which Joseph Scaliger strives to prove deficient by two [years]**." The same **Scaliger chronology jest** Tycho makes in brahe-t_16000327002 (where the year is "really 1602"). **New Style** (imperial). *Annus Jubilaeus* = the **Holy/Jubilee Year 1600**. Header date matches the label.

documents.incipit: REVERSI heri vesperi sero ad me domestici illi mei, quos Pragam miseram, tuas, Eccme et …

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET ERUDITISSIMO VIRO DOMINO Μ. IOHANNI KEPLERO ILLUSTRIUM STYRIÆ ORDINUM MATHEMATICO EXIMIO, AMICO SUO PLURIMI FACIENDO.

REVERSI heri vesperi sero ad me domestici illi mei, quos Pragam miseram, tuas, Eccme et amantissime Domine KEPLERE, ex insperato attulere humanissimas literas, quibus lectis, te Pragæ nunc esse, perlubenter comperi. Invite tamen ex ijsdem colligebam, te necdum meas, quas ultimis Tuis affatim respondentes ante mensem circiter Viennam, ut inde per Dominum Doctorem BLOTIUM tibi, ubicunque invenireris, mitterentur, direxi. Quæ si interea tibi traditæ fuissent, hac reiterata protestatione et excusatione in re ista, quæ tot verba non meretur, supersedisses, atque actutum citra diuturniorem deliberationem et cunctationem huc (siquidem in vicinia es) advolasses. Quod ut etiamnum facias, te etiam atque etiam rogo. Poteris in eodem vehiculo comitari Nobilem et eruditum adolescentem FRANCISCUM TENGNAGLIUM domesticum nostrum, et filium meum TYCHONEM natu maiorem, quos Pragam ob negocia quædam peculiaria, meo nomine isthic expedienda, nunc ablego. Illi enim intra paucos dies, volente Deo, huc revertentur, et locum pro te in curru facile invenient.

De meo isthuc adventu necdum certi quid concludere possum, antequam Cæsaream Maiestatem Dominum nostrum Clementissimum eo reversum esse intellexero. Neque enim quid alias isthic magnopere agam, habeo, nec libenter accedo, nisi a Cæsarea Maiestate clementissime vocer: siquidem id citra temporis, cuius, tanquam thesauri irrecuperabilis, sum parcissimus, aliqualem iacturam, et studiorum, quæ præ manibus habeo, remoram fieri nequeat.

Explorandi etiam hisce noctibus acronychij situs Martis et Iovis, tum quoque Mercurij, quem post occasum Solis discrete apparentem ter proxime elapsis crepusculis observavimus, tum quoque ad Venerem Eoam, quæ etiam nunc interdiu unâ cum Sole, adeoque in ipso Meridiano existens, spectatur, et observationi, prout aliquot quoque annis præteritis a nobis factum, patet, advertendum. Taceo quod Saturnus non longe a □ ☉ mane iuxta Meridianum apparens, pro Parallaxi orbis (uti vocat COPERNICUS) et Latitudine sua (siquidem appropinquet ad limitem maxime Boreum) rimanda, non inconvenientem exhibeat occasionem, donec adventante Aprili plane pernox redditus, Apogæum et Eccentricitatem, unâque ipsam Latitudinem maximam, prout hæc a nobis iam antea explorata sunt, comprobet. Accedit et hoc, quod in proxime futuro plenilunio Luna Eclipsin, licet minutulam, iuxta ipsum occasum paulo ante ortum Solis patietur, cui etiam (ut prioribus sedulo designatis adijci queat, atque restitutio motus Luminarium a nobis prius facta, ulterius examinari) attendendum, modo serenitas oportuna id permiserit.

Vides itaque, mi KEPLERE, quot et quanta exercitia nostra Astronomica ingerant obstacula, nobis tamen haud ingrata (siquidem ijs distineri volupe est) quo minus Pragam tam cito, uti opinatus es, excurrere queam. Tuum itaque erit prævenire, meque hîc mature (uti dictum) invisere. Advenies non tam hospes quam amicus gratissimus, nostrarumque in cœlestibus contemplationum, per ea quæ nunc ad manus habeo, instrumenta spectator et socius acceptissimus. Tunc, volente Numine, coram de pluribus. Vale et Illustrem ac Generosum Dominum Baronem IOHANNEM FRIDERICUM HOFFMANNUM, cui etiam nonnulla congratulationis caussa pro felici reditu scripsi, ex me officiosissime resaluta.

Dabantur properanter ex arce Cæsareana Benatica die 26 Ianuarij 1600.
Tui Amantissimus
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria scripsi.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and most learned man, Master Johannes Kepler, distinguished mathematician to the Illustrious Estates of Styria, his friend much to be esteemed.**

When those servants of mine whom I had sent to Prague returned to me late yesterday evening, they brought, unexpectedly, your most courteous letter, most excellent and most beloved Master Kepler; and on reading it I learned with great pleasure that you are now in Prague. Yet from the same letter I gathered, against my wish, that you had not yet [received] mine — which, fully answering your last, I directed to Vienna about a month ago, so that from there, through Master Doctor Blotius, they might be sent on to you wherever you should be found. Had these meanwhile been delivered to you, you would have spared yourself this repeated protestation and apology in a matter that does not deserve so many words, and would forthwith, without longer deliberation and delay, have flown hither (since you are in the neighbourhood). And that you would do this even now, I ask you again and again. You will be able to travel in the same carriage with the noble and learned young man Franz Tengnagel, a member of my household, and with my elder son Tycho, whom I am now dispatching to Prague on account of certain particular business of mine to be transacted there. For within a few days, God willing, they will return hither, and will readily find a place for you in the carriage.

Concerning my own coming thither, I can as yet conclude nothing for certain, until I have learned that His Imperial Majesty, our Most Clement Lord, has returned there. For I have nothing else of much moment to do there, nor do I willingly go, unless I be most graciously summoned by His Imperial Majesty — seeing that this could not be done without some loss of time (of which, as of an irrecoverable treasure, I am most sparing) and without delay to the studies I have in hand.

[There is] also [reason] to investigate, on these [coming] nights, the acronychal position of Mars and of Jupiter; then too of Mercury, which we observed clearly visible after sunset, in the last three twilights just past; and likewise [we must] attend to Venus as Morning Star, which even now is to be seen by day together with the Sun — and indeed, being on the very meridian, is open to observation, as has also been done by us in several years past. I say nothing of how Saturn — appearing in the morning near the meridian, not far from quadrature with the Sun [□ ☉] — affords a not inconvenient occasion for investigating the parallax of the orb (as Copernicus calls it) and its [own] latitude (since it is approaching the most northerly limit); until, with April coming on, being rendered fully visible all night long, it may confirm its apogee and eccentricity, and together its greatest latitude itself, as these have already before been investigated by us. There is this besides, that at the full moon next to come the Moon will undergo an eclipse — a slight one, to be sure — close to setting [and] a little before sunrise; to which also [we must] attend (so that it may be added to those carefully recorded before, and so that the restoration of the motion of the luminaries, made earlier by us, may be examined further), provided that suitable clear weather permit it.

You see therefore, my dear Kepler, how many and how great are the obstacles our astronomical labours throw in the way — labours not unwelcome to us, however (since to be held fast by them is a pleasure) — to my being able to run over to Prague as soon as you supposed. It will be your part, then, to come first, and to visit me here in good time (as has been said). You will come not so much as a guest as a most welcome friend, and as a most acceptable spectator and partner of our contemplations of the heavens, by means of the instruments I now have at hand. Then, God willing, [we shall speak] face to face of more matters. Farewell; and on my behalf most dutifully return the greeting of the Illustrious and Noble Lord Baron Johann Friedrich Hoffmann, to whom too I have written some words by way of congratulation on his happy return.

Given in haste from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 26th day of January 1600.
Your most loving
TYCHO BRAHE,
I have written [this] with my own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe**, then established at the imperial castle of Benátky nad Jizerou (north-east of Prague), having entered the service of Emperor Rudolf II in 1599. This is the letter that summons the young **Kepler** to join him — one of the most consequential letters in the history of astronomy, written some four weeks before their first meeting (4 February 1600).
- **Recipient.** *M. Iohanni Keplero … Styriae Ordinum Mathematico* = **Johannes Kepler**, then district mathematician (*Landschaftsmathematiker*) to the Protestant Estates of Styria at Graz, recently displaced by the Counter-Reformation expulsion of Protestants and so "in the neighbourhood." *M.* = *Magister* (academic "Master," this chapter's convention).
- **Place.** *arce Caesareana Benatica* = the **Imperial castle of Benátky nad Jizerou** (Latin *Benatecum*; this chapter's convention).
- **Persons named.**
 - *Dominus Doctor Blotius* = **Hugo Blotius (Hugues Blotz)**, imperial librarian (Hofbibliothek) at Vienna, used here as a relay for correspondence.
 - *Franciscus Tengnaglius* = **Franz Gansneb Tengnagel von Camp** (c. 1576–1622), Tycho's noble Westphalian assistant, later his son-in-law and a literary executor of the Tychonic legacy.
 - *filium meum Tychonem natu maiorem* = **Tyge (Tycho) Brahe the Younger**, Tycho's elder son.
 - *Caesarea Maiestas Dominus noster Clementissimus* = **Emperor Rudolf II**, Tycho's imperial patron.
 - *Baro Iohannes Fridericus Hoffmannus* = **Baron Johann Friedrich Hoffmann von Grünbüchel und Strechau**, an imperial councillor and patron of Kepler's, in whose company Kepler had travelled and at whose Prague house he was lodging.
- **Astronomy — observational programme (this is the technical heart of the letter; this chapter's convention).**
 - *acronychij situs Martis et Iovis* = the **acronychal position** of Mars and Jupiter — i.e. their rising at sunset, near opposition to the Sun (the configuration most diagnostic for orbital elements). The Mars-opposition observations of exactly this season are the data Kepler would inherit and exploit. *Acronychal* (Greek *akrónychos*, "at nightfall") is kept as the technical term.
 - *Mercurij … post occasum Solis discrete apparentem* = Mercury seen as a distinct ("discrete") evening object after sunset, at *crepusculis* = the **twilights**.
 - *Venerem Eoam* = **Venus as Morning Star** (*Eous*, "of the dawn / eastern"); the rendering keeps the epithet's force. The daytime/meridian visibility noted is Venus near greatest brilliancy.
 - *□ ☉* = the aspect glyph for **quadrature** (square) with the **Sun**; named in the translation, glyphs kept in the source block.
 - *Parallaxi orbis (uti vocat Copernicus)* = the **parallax of the orb** — Copernicus's own term (*parallaxis orbis*, the great-orbit / annual parallax: the apparent displacement of a superior planet arising from the Earth's annual motion). Tycho cites the Copernican label *without* endorsing Copernican cosmology; the hedge "as Copernicus calls it" is preserved, not flattened into "annual parallax."
 - *Apogaeum et Eccentricitatem … Latitudinem maximam* = **apogee, eccentricity, and greatest latitude** — the orbital elements of Saturn to be confirmed when it becomes *pernox* (visible the whole night long) in April.
 - *plenilunio Luna Eclipsin … minutulam … patietur* = at the coming **full moon** the Moon will suffer a slight **(lunar) eclipse** near setting, just before sunrise. (The lunar eclipse of 9/10 February 1600 N.S. was indeed of small magnitude.)
 - *restitutio motus Luminarium* = the **restoration of the motion of the luminaries** (Sun and Moon) — Tycho's programme term (*restitutio*; this chapter's convention), the renewal of the solar and lunar theories he had already worked out and now wishes to test further.
 - *instrumenta … spectator et socius* = Tycho invites Kepler to be spectator and partner among the **instruments** (*organa/instrumenta*,) he has at Benátky.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *Vale* → "Farewell"; *Tui Amantissimus* → "Your most loving"; *manu propria scripsi* → "I have written [this] with my own hand" (autograph attestation). *Dabantur … Benatica* (epistolary "they were given," i.e. dispatched) rendered "Given … from Benátky."
- **Calendar (this chapter's convention — the chosen pilot crux).** The dateline reads *die 26 Ianuarij 1600*; the edition label marks the letter **n.s. (New Style / Gregorian)**. This is correct and significant: by 1600 Tycho, now in Catholic Imperial service at Benátky, has shifted from the Old-Style (Julian) dating of his Danish and Hessen correspondence to the **New Style** used in Rudolfine lands — the very 10-day Julian/Gregorian gap flagged in §3. The date is **reproduced as written and not converted**; the equivalent Old-Style date would be 16 January 1600, but no conversion is performed in the text. The lunar eclipse mentioned (the next full moon) falls 9/10 February 1600 N.S., consistent with the New-Style dating of the letter.

documents.abstract: Acknowledges Tycho's letter, accepts its excessive praise with humility, and commends the character and bearing of Franz Tengnagel.
documents.incipit: LITTERAS tuas, Vir nobilissime, quibus me tam splendide per egregios iuvenes, …

text.original:
DEM EDLEN VNND GESTRENGEN HERRN TYCHO BRAHAe, HERRN AUF KNUDTSTRUPP VNND VRANIBURGKH, MEINEM SONNDERSLIEBEN HERRN VNNDT GUETTEN FREUNDT.

S.

LITTERAS tuas, Vir nobilissime, quibus me tam splendide per egregios iuvenes, internunctios tuos, salutas, mei amore et commendatione plenas, imo in excultioribus meae tenuitatis nimiam paene laudem continentes, accepi, cum voluptate profecto, dubius tamen, tot inter gratulandi occasiones palmam cui concederem. Ecce autem animi tandem occurrebat sinceritas, omnibus alijs non immerito praeferenda. Caetera, tanquam illius effectus et signa civilitati ac humanitati Tuae adscribens, pari, si non calamo, mentis tamen integritate et studio compensanda.

Quod D. FRANCISCI TENGNAGELIJ, familiaris tui, virtutem ac valorem, quem ipsa facies et mores exprimunt, etiam litterarum tuarum testimonio apud me augere tibi placuerit, nil miror. Est tamen mihi quod gratulor et tibi, qui tantum Adolescentem cognoscendum dederis, gratiam ut referam. Rationem consilij eius de Bohemica hac ora tui procul dubio causa non tam brevi relinquenda plurimum etiam nostro ex interesse approbamus et laetamur, ac ipsi et filio tuo quam valemus et habemus exilitatem in hac aula nostram fideliter et cum libertate offero.

Magistrum KEPLERUM, omni praeconio maiorem, favoreque tuo et patrocinio multis rationibus dignum, tibi iam commendatum amplius nunc non commendo, sed ipsum se spectandum et fruendum potius praemitto, apud te, mihi, ut spero, multarum rerum praeconem et conciliatorem. Intermediatoris tamen quod officium ita amanter et benigne cum gratiarum actione susceperis, ad me pertinet, Domine TYCHO, ac facis in eo, te certe ac humanitate tua, quin nostra, ad te perpetuo amandum et colendum benevolentia haud indignum.

Addo idipsum, nostri gratia quicquid porro accesserit, id omne non tam ad cumulum tuorum in nos meritorum esse referendum, quam alta et grata memoria prosequendum. In specie vero, quae et ipsius KEPLERI ratione conferenda essent aliqua, in occasionem nostri conventus differre cogimur, quem nobis efficiat Deus propediem, ut spero et opto.

Vale ac reliqua ex ipso KEPLERO et tuis.
Pragae 3 Februarij A. D. 1600.
T. D. ex animo
IOHANNES FRIDERICUS HOFFMANN,
L. Baro.
text.english:
**To the noble and gallant Lord Tycho Brahe, lord of Knudstrup and Uraniborg, my especially dear lord and good friend.**

Greeting.

Your letter, most noble man — in which you so splendidly greet me through those excellent young men, your messengers, [a letter] full of love and commendation of me, indeed containing in its more polished phrases almost excessive praise of my slender worth — I received with pleasure, in truth, yet at a loss to which among so many occasions for thankfulness I should award the palm. But behold, the sincerity of your mind presented itself at last, not undeservedly to be preferred to all the rest. The other [qualities], ascribing them as the effects and tokens of that [sincerity] to your courtesy and humanity, are to be repaid with an integrity and zeal of mind equal [to yours], if not of pen.

That it pleased you to enhance with me — by the testimony of your letter too — the virtue and worth of Master Franz Tengnagel, your familiar (which his very face and bearing express), I do not wonder at. Yet I have cause to congratulate, and to render you thanks, who have given me so fine a young man to know. The reasoning of his plan to leave this Bohemian shore — doubtless not so soon, [and] for your sake — we likewise much approve and rejoice at, out of our own interest as well; and to him and to your son I faithfully and freely offer our slender [standing] in this court, so far as we are able and have it.

Master Kepler — greater than all proclamation, and worthy of your favour and patronage on many grounds — already commended to you, I now commend no further, but rather send him on ahead to be beheld and enjoyed in person; with you he will be, as I hope, the herald and reconciler of many matters for me. Yet that you have so lovingly and kindly, and with thanksgiving, taken up the office of intermediary — that, Lord Tycho, falls to me [to acknowledge]; and in it you do a thing assuredly not unworthy of being perpetually loved and revered by me with goodwill — by you and your humanity, nay ours.

I add this very thing: whatever shall further accrue for our sake, all of it is to be set down not so much to the heap of your services toward us, as to be attended with deep and grateful memory. But in particular, certain matters that should be conferred upon by reason of Kepler himself, we are forced to defer to the occasion of our meeting — which may God bring about for us soon, as I hope and wish.

Farewell, and the rest from Kepler himself and from your people.
Prague, the 3rd of February, in the Year of the Lord 1600.
Yours from the heart,
Johann Friedrich Hoffmann,
Free Baron.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & sender.** An **inbound** letter **to** Tycho. **Johann Friedrich Hoffmann von Grünbüchel und Strechau**, *liber baro* (**Free Baron**), imperial councillor and a patron of Kepler's — the same magnate at whose Prague house Kepler lodged and whose greeting Tycho sends in the famous summons-letter (brahe-t_16000126002, where he is *Baro Iohannes Fridericus Hoffmannus*). The mixed presentation (German address-line over a Latin body) is preserved.
- **Occasion.** Dated **3 February 1600** — the day *before* Kepler's first arrival at Benátky (4 February). Hoffmann, who had brought Kepler from Graz to Prague, here **sends Kepler on to Tycho** (*ipsum … praemitto*) and acknowledges Tycho's letter of welcome carried by Tycho's "young messengers." It is thus a hinge document of the Tycho–Kepler meeting, the patron's side of the introduction.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Magister Keplerus* = **Johannes Kepler**, *omni praeconio maior* ("greater than all proclamation"), commended by Hoffmann as a "herald and reconciler of many matters" at Tycho's.
 - *D. Franciscus Tengnagelius, familiaris tuus* = **Franz Gansneb Tengnagel von Camp**, Tycho's noble assistant, whose worth Tycho had praised and whose intended departure from Bohemia (to visit Westphalia — cf. brahe-t_16000306002) is referred to here.
 - *filius tuus* = one of Tycho's sons.
- **Epistolary formulae & titles.** *S.* = *salutem* ("Greeting"); *Vale* → "Farewell"; subscription *T. D. ex animo* = *Tuae Dominationi ex animo* ("Yours from the heart") + *L. Baro* = *liber baro* ("Free Baron"). The German address *meinem sonderslieben Herrn und guten Freund* → "my especially dear lord and good friend."
- **Register.** A studied, almost mannered courtier's Latin — heavy with the humility topos (*meae tenuitatis … exilitatem nostram*, "my slender worth … our slender standing"), antithesis (*si non calamo, mentis tamen integritate*), and deferred clauses. The convolution is preserved rather than smoothed.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Pragae 3 Februarij A. D. 1600*; the edition marks **n.s. (New Style)** — correct for an Imperial-court letter from Prague. Reproduced, not converted.

documents.editorial_note: **Direction note.** **Incoming** letter — *from* Tycho's northern agent **Simon von Petkum** *to* Tycho. Place omitted in the source (*s.l.*); written from the **Wandsbek/Hamburg area** (Sophie Brahe is "here at Wandsbek"). A business + news letter in Petkum's Low-German-inflected hand.

text.original:
DEM GESTRENGEN, EEDLEN VND ERNUESTEN JUNCKHEREN TYCHONJ BRAHE, ERBGESESSEN VFF KNUDTSTORP, ASTRONOMIÆ RESTAURATORJ, DIENSTLEICH ZUHANDEN. PRAGE ODER IN DER JEGENT, NEMLICH ZU GERSITZ. A. 1600.

GOTTES gnade vnd friede zuuor. Gestrenger, edler, ernuester, großgunstiger junckher Tycho, benebenst ehrerbietung meiner gantzwilligen dienste magk ich Ew. Gestre. nicht vorhalten, das ych zwar von hern magistro Dauide Fabricii itzo 2 schreiben verhanden, die er mir gantz hoch vnd tewer per gantz gewiße bodtschafft euch zusendendt begeret hat. So ist warleich in all die zeit keiner (der directe nach Prag wolte) mir furkomen, wowol mir vnter andern auch von hern doctor Vito Winßhemio vortrostung gethan. Habe derentwegen discrete vnd diuise (ich meine vff Leiptzigh vnd dernach vf Dreßdinn zu vbergeben) E. G. dieselbigen lieber zuordenen wollen als lenger dieselbige bej mir zubehalten, nemlich auff Leiptzigh, von dannen an h. Hans Tuchman nach Dreßdenn vnd alsovordt zu E. Gest. henden zukommen. Da dis allso nicht wol vordtginge, so haben Ewre Gestrengheit zubedencken, ob sie euch nicht beßer per Nurenberch durch hern Leonhard Dillher, keiserlichen factoren, müchten zur hand konnen kommen, so geschege die vorwexelung nur and einen vnd nit zu zween orteren, dauon Ewer Gestr. aduis zum nechst.

Was von der schiff für die jnstrumente zu hoffen, das werden Eur G. aus hern Vincentij Mollerj (der its vornjar burgemeister geworden is) seinem schreiben zuuornemen. Mich ducht gudt zu sein, wan keis. mst. ein klein schreiben derowegen an e. erb. radt von Hamhurgk abgehen liße. Das schreiben konte noch wol so bald hervnter kommen, alse die jnstrumente hir mugen anlangen.

Vor acht tagen hab ich briefe von Dauide Fabricio bekommen, darinnen ich sein gantz liebreiches gemut kegen Ew. Gestr. erspure, want ime felschleich (Godt lob) berichtet worden Euw. Gest. obitus. Er thut in seinem schreiben nicht anders alß wen ime sein liebester vatter oder son abgestorben were.

Dieweil er mir nunmer einen seiner schwege[r] vnd freunde Ludolfs Ridderhusen zu Bremen namkundich gemacht hat, habe ich daher nu gelegenheit, ime dieselbige wochentleich, so offt es nodt es, zusenden.

Damit ich inn in sodaner betrubnis nicht lange hielte, habe ich stracks volgendes tages ime vber Bremen geschrieben, vnd der sachen anders berichtet, nemlich das ich noch den 14 nouembris briefe von E. Gestr. vnderzeichnet empfangen hette, er solte es dafür halten, das das nicht wurde war sein, mit Gottes hülffe. Vnd kumpt mir frombt vor, das er der briefe keinen (die ich vor dieser seiner anordening zu waßer bej schyppen zu Norden vnd in die grete wonende gegeben habe) vberkommen hat. Die schiffere haben dennoch mir daßelbige veste gelobet. So kunte ich auch anders keine botten haben, dan an den ordt gelangen keine botten. Ich hoffe dennoch er wirdt sie teslich bekommen haben.

Vber Bremen is henfurt der gewiße pas, weils der Ludolff Ridderhusen es vff sich nimpt, dieselbig vordtzusenden.

Heut habe ich abermal E. Gest. brieff ime bej meinem eingeslag zugesant, das er abermall ewer wolstandes wirdt mügen confirmiret sein.

Jmgleichen auch an hern Josephum Scaligerum geschrieben vnd der Ew. Gest. schreiben darneben einen amsterdamisch botten selber in die handt gegeben vnd in dauon bezallt, jn meinem schreiben mir erbotten Ew. Gestr. gerne zu ubersenden all daßjennige, was mir geschicket wurd.

Was dem conditore nouarum ephemeridum Euerarto zu Bruxell wonende belanget, weis ich nicht woll, ob ich bej im was wurde ausrichten, darumme das die briefe von hinnen durch viendelandt vber Antorff gehen müssen. Vnd müchte man sich der vnkost trosten, so mangellt es mir doch an kundtschafft mit ime. Vnd tesleichen, die warheit zu bekennen, ist es mir gar aus dem sinne kommen. Nu ich aber vormercke, das E. Gest. damit ein will geschieht, so will ichs per tertium vnterlegen. Einer genomet Peter vp Meer, köningkleicher hispanischer radt vnd befellhaber, ist mir familiaris, durch denselbigen meine ich in mein schreiben beizubringen vnd andtwordt zuerhalten, so habe ich einen zu Antorff, genomet Johan tho Westen, bei demseluigen werden diesen brief zwischen Brüßell vnd Hamborch hinc inde eingethan, der soll das bottenloen mir vorlegen.

Des junckher swester Sophia is alhie zu Wandesbeke. Derselbigen habe ich vff ir beger vollgen lassen j kutswagen mit dem was von zugehorigen darbej, war; jtem noch j radt, welches er sunst mangelte. Daßelbige was dafur sollj will sie E. Gestr. gudt thun. Vorhoffe mich gentzleich daranne keinen vndanch begangen haben, das vbrige wagengerede is vast geringe vnd verdorben gut. Sie konte nicht mer dan ein gudt radt (zu den die bej erster kutsen weren) finden odder aussuchen laßen.

Aus Dennemarck habe ich nicht sunderlichs, habe auch zwar mit fleis darnach nicht erkundet. Hertzogh Carl hat numer die gantze swedische cron zu seinem willen. Der polnische kuningk haltet dieser sachen halber itzundt oder wirdts bald in Polen halten; was er vornemen wirdt, gibt zeit. Aus Muscouia zeitung, das kuningk Erich aus Sweden, sonn Gustaus, alda bej den großfürsten woll gehalten wirde. Wan es im an furmügen nicht mangelte, wolte er sich inbillden, auch zur krone Sweden zugehoren. Man vormeint aber, der muscowiter wirde mit hertzogk Carl oder mit Sweden den angestelleten friede nicht brechen. Engelant (wie man sagt) tractiret den friede mit denn hispanischen. Dy hollender slagen alle fridesmiddell aus. Einer der fornembste midt vnter denen von Amsterdam hat an einen guten fründt also geschrieben: Wan vnsern staten vnd regenten gegeben wurde eine gantze große oxßenhaut, darauff zuschreiben alle die conditiones pacis, die inen nur gelustede, vnd man inen alle daßelbige nachgeben wolte, so würden sie dennoch den frieden nicht begern. Sie die hollender haben zuuor ein placat (wie sie es nennen) lassen ausghen, darinne sie cauiere vnd idermennichlich steden, stenden vnd potentaten zu gebieten, sich vnterwinden, zu interdicerende die segelation auis Spanien mit getreide. Vnsere schiffe haben sie etlike in Hollant eingebracht, vnd es gestrigis tages beschedt bej den botten alhie angebracht worden, das eines derselbigen schiffe mit vrteil vnd rechte confiscieret worden sey. Die staten vntersthen sich mer hochheit alse wol menniger hoger potentat nicht thun dorfte.

Magr. Georgius Frobenius mus vff ostern Wandesbech reumen. Die frome stathalterinn hat es iren sone Breden wider abgehandelln, gibt fur, das sie selbest es gebrauchen will. Der vnkostung halber, so Ew Gestr. an gebeuen gethan, folget noch von Keile nen sunderlige erklerung. Will aber vmme das andtwordt bej Frobenio anhalten.

Die stadthaltersche schreibt mir, das ich mich erkleren müge, ob ich nicht weis, wannen her sie der 5000 thaler soll gewertich sein. Jch habe ir geandtwordet, das E. Gestr. das durch Esche Bilde zuuorrichtende angeordnet haben.

Jn eile we[i]s ich E. G. mer nicht zuschreiben, one alleine wunsche euch samptt euw. lieben vieltugentreichen husfrouen vnd tochteren allesamptt, wie auch den sonen, gesundtheit vnd wolfartt. Datum eilentz den 12 februarij a. 1600.

Auch is meine frundtleiche bitte, Ew. Gest. müchten meinen nepotj befolen mir auch zuschreiben vnd seinen progressum vnd zustant zuuormelden. Got gebe, das es ime auch wol ghehe. Ew. Gest. dienstwilliger

Simon von Petkum.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia XIV, p. 188; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Damit das bottenlon Ew. Gest. nicht dobbellt gerechnet werde, gebe ich E. Gest. zuwißen, das ich von hinnen aus vff Leiptßigh, Bremen, Leiden etc. bezale.
text.english:
**To the stern, noble, and honourable Squire Tycho Brahe, hereditary [lord] of Knudstrup, Restorer of Astronomy, to be delivered into [his] hands at his service. At Prague, or in the region, namely at Görlitz. A[nno] 1600.**

God's grace and peace first. Stern, noble, honourable, greatly-favouring Squire Tycho, alongside the offering of my wholly-willing services I cannot withhold from Your Honour that I have on hand 2 letters from **Master David Fabricius**, which he begged me, most earnestly and dearly, to send you by quite sure messenger. But truly, in all this time, none (who wished to go directly to Prague) has come to me — though among others **Dr. Veit Winsheim** too gave me some hope. I have therefore resolved, discreetly and in divided fashion (I mean, to hand them on via Leipzig and then via Dresden), to dispatch them to Your Honour rather than keep them longer with me — namely to **Leipzig**, thence to **Mr. Hans Tuchman** at **Dresden**, and so on into Your Honour's hands. Should this not go well, Your Honour should consider whether they might not better reach you **via Nuremberg, through Mr. Leonhard Dillher, the imperial factor**, so that the trans-shipment happen at one place and not two; of which, Your Honour's advice next.

What is to be hoped of the **ship for the instruments**, Your Honour will learn from the letter of **Mr. Vincent Möller** (who this spring became burgomaster). It seems to me good if the **Imperial Majesty would let a small letter go out, on that account, to the honourable Council of Hamburg**. The letter could well come down here as soon as the instruments may arrive here.

Eight days ago I got letters from David Fabricius, in which I perceive his wholly loving heart toward Your Honour; **for he had been falsely (God be praised) informed of Your Honour's death**. In his letter he behaves no otherwise than as if his dearest father or son had died.

Since he has now made known to me one of his brothers-in-law and friends, **Ludolf Ridderhusen at Bremen**, I now have the opportunity to send to him [Fabricius] the same weekly, as often as is needed.

That I might not hold him long in such grief, I wrote him the very next day via Bremen, and informed him of the matter otherwise — namely that I had received letters signed by Your Honour **as late as 14 November**; he should hold it that it [the death] will not be true, with God's help. And it seems strange to me that he got none of the letters (which, before this arrangement of his, I gave to water-going skippers living at **Norden** and in the **Krummhörn [Grete]**). The skippers nonetheless firmly promised me [delivery]; nor could I have other messengers, for no [land] messengers reach that place. Yet I hope he will have got them by now.

Via Bremen is henceforth the sure route, since Ludolf Ridderhusen takes it upon himself to forward them.

Today I have again sent Your Honour's letter to him [Fabricius] in my enclosure, so that he may again be confirmed of your good state.

Likewise I have written also to **Mr. Joseph Scaliger**, and besides gave Your Honour's letter into an Amsterdam messenger's own hand, and paid him for it; in my letter I offered to forward gladly to Your Honour everything that may be sent to me.

As for **the maker of new ephemerides, Everart, dwelling at Brussels**, I do not well know whether I should accomplish anything with him, because the letters from here must go through enemy-country [the war-zone], via **Antwerp**. And though one might console oneself about the cost, I yet lack acquaintance with him; and likewise, to confess the truth, it had quite slipped my mind. But now that I perceive Your Honour's will is to have it done, I will arrange it through a third party. One named **Peter up Meer, royal Spanish councillor and commander**, is familiar to me; through him I mean to convey my letter and obtain an answer; so I have one at Antwerp named **Johan tho Westen**, by whom these letters between Brussels and Hamburg will be put in, back and forth, [and] who shall advance me the messenger-fee.

The Squire's sister **Sophia is here at Wandsbek**. At her request I let her have 1 coach-wagon, with what belonged to it; item, one more wheel, which was otherwise lacking. What it should cost, she will make good to Your Honour. I hope entirely to have committed no ingratitude in this; the rest of the wagon-gear is very paltry and spoiled goods. She could find, or have sought out, no more than one good wheel (besides those that were with the first coach).

From Denmark I have nothing special, nor indeed have I diligently inquired. **Duke Charles now has the whole Swedish crown to his will.** The Polish King holds, or will soon hold, [a diet] in Poland on account of this matter; what he will undertake, time will tell. News from **Muscovy**, that **King Erik of Sweden, son of Gustav, is well kept there by the Grand Duke** [*see note*]; if he did not lack means, he would fancy himself to belong to the Swedish crown too. But it is thought the Muscovite will not break the arranged peace with Duke Charles or with Sweden. **England** (as they say) negotiates peace with the **Spanish**. The **Dutch** reject all means of peace. One of the foremost among those of **Amsterdam** wrote to a good friend thus: *"If our States and regents were given a whole great ox-hide on which to write all the conditions of peace that pleased them, and all of it were granted them, they would still not want peace."* The Dutch have previously issued a **placard** (as they call it), in which they presume to command and forbid all cities, estates, and potentates … **to interdict the sailing from Spain with grain**. Some of our ships they have brought into Holland; and yesterday news came by the messenger here that one of those ships **has been confiscated by judgement and law**. The States arrogate to themselves more sovereignty than many a high potentate might dare to do.

Master **Georg Frobenius** must vacate **Wandsbek** by Easter. The pious **Governess [Statthalterin]** has bargained it back from her son **Breide [Rantzau]**, pretending she wishes to use it herself. As to the cost which Your Honour laid out on buildings, a special declaration follows yet from **Kiel**; but I will press Frobenius for the answer.

The Governess writes me that I should declare whether I do not know whence she is to expect the **5000 thaler**. I have answered her that Your Honour arranged this to be discharged through **Eske Bille**.

In haste I know nothing more to write to Your Honour, except only [that] I wish you, together with your dear, very virtuous housewife and daughters all, as also the sons, health and welfare. Dated in haste, the 12th of February, A[nno] 1600.

Also it is my friendly request that Your Honour might charge **my nephew** to write to me too, and report his progress and condition. God grant it go well with him too. Your Honour's service-willing,
**Simon von Petkum.**


*[Postscript:]* So that the messenger-fee be not reckoned to Your Honour twice over, I give Your Honour to know that I pay [it] from here onward via Leipzig, Bremen, Leiden, etc.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondent.** **Incoming**, **Simon von Petkum** — Tycho's agent/factor in the Hamburg–Wandsbek region, who managed his northern affairs after the move south — **to Tycho** at Prague. An original autograph (Basel).
- **Significance — Tycho's northern logistics, the death-rumour, and a war bulletin.**
 - **The death-rumour and Fabricius's grief (links to Riddershusen's letter of 16 Dec 1599).** Confirms, from another angle, the **false rumour of Tycho's death** (winter 1599/1600): **David Fabricius**, "falsely informed of Your Honour's death," grieves "as if his dearest father or son had died." Petkum reassures him (citing Tycho's letter of 14 Nov). **Ludolf Ridderhusen of Bremen** — the astrologer-correspondent of **brahe-t_15991216001** — is here identified as **Fabricius's brother-in-law** and the new **Bremen forwarding-hub** for letters to Fabricius. (Both letters — of 16 December 1599 and 12 February 1600 — report the death-rumour and the Fabricius connection — a clean cross-link.)
 - **The forwarding network.** Routes Tycho's correspondence via **Leipzig → Hans Tuchman at Dresden**, or via **Nuremberg → Leonhard Dillher (imperial factor)**; to Fabricius via **Bremen/Ridderhusen** and Frisian **skippers (Norden, the Krummhörn)**; to **Scaliger** via an **Amsterdam messenger**.
 - **The instrument-ship.** News awaited from **Vincent Möller** (newly burgomaster of Hamburg) on the **ship for the instruments**; Petkum suggests **an imperial letter to the Hamburg Council** to speed it (cf. the Magdeburg/Elbe transport thread, brahe-t_16000405001 etc.).
 - **The Brussels ephemerides-maker.** Tycho wants contact with **"Everart," a maker of new ephemerides at Brussels** — difficult, since letters must cross the **Dutch–Spanish war-zone** via Antwerp; Petkum will route via **Peter up Meer** (a Spanish councillor) and **Johan tho Westen** at Antwerp. (Identity of "Everart" not established.)
 - **Sophie Brahe at Wandsbek.** Tycho's **sister Sophie Brahe** is at **Wandsbek**; Petkum gives her a coach-wagon and a wheel.
 - **The war bulletin.** **Charles of Sweden** holds the whole crown; the Polish diet; a (garbled) report of **"King Erik of Sweden, son of Gustav," kept in Muscovy** [historically problematic — see note]; **England–Spain peace talks**; the **Dutch refusing peace** (the memorable **ox-hide** quip) and their **placard embargoing the Spanish grain-trade**, with Hanseatic ships confiscated in Holland. A vivid snapshot of the closing **Eighty Years' War / Baltic** situation, winter 1600.
 - **Wandsbek estate matters.** **Georg Frobenius** must quit Wandsbek by Easter (the **Statthalterin** — Heinrich Rantzau's heirs' line — having "bargained it back" from her son **Breide Rantzau**); a cost-declaration for Tycho's buildings pending from **Kiel**; and the **5000 thaler** to be discharged through **Eske Bille**.
- **Persons & places named.** Simon von Petkum; **David Fabricius**; **Veit Winsheim**; **Hans Tuchman** (Dresden); **Leonhard Dillher** (Nuremberg); **Vincent Möller** (Hamburg burgomaster); **Ludolf Ridderhusen** (Bremen, Fabricius's brother-in-law); **Joseph Scaliger**; **"Everart"** (Brussels ephemerides-maker); **Peter up Meer**; **Johan tho Westen** (Antwerp); **Sophie Brahe** (Tycho's sister); **Charles of Sweden**; **Sigismund III of Poland**; **"King Erik son of Gustav"** (in Muscovy); **Georg Frobenius**; the **Statthalterin** & **Breide Rantzau**; **Eske Bille**. Places: Wandsbek, Hamburg, Prague, Görlitz, Leipzig, Dresden, Nuremberg, Bremen, Norden/Krummhörn, Amsterdam, Brussels, Antwerp, Kiel, Denmark, Sweden, Poland, Muscovy, Holland.
- **Note — the "King Erik" report.** *"King Erik of Sweden, son of Gustav … kept by the Grand Duke [of Muscovy]"* is **historically problematic**: Gustav Vasa's son **Erik XIV** died in 1577. Petkum is relaying a **stale or garbled rumour** (possibly a confusion, a pretender, or old news of the deposed line); rendered exactly as the source has it and flagged, per the no-fabrication / no-silent-correction rule.
- **Calendar.** *den 12 februarij a. 1600* — no *stylo* marker; the Hamburg/Wandsbek region was **Old Style** in 1600; read **12 February 1600 [O.S.]** (label gives no N.S.; place *s.l.*, supplied Wandsbek/Hamburg).

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Second closing postscript after the signature "Simon von Petkum.", restored from Dreyer XIV p.188 (dropped by the working transcription). NB Dreyer prints this German original in vol XIV (the file's "vol VIII" tag points to Tycho's reply).

documents.incipit: SP. Id equidem erat, quod soror mihi intima, mater tua, charissime nepos, ad me die 24 …

text.original:
[TYCHO BRAHE AD TACHONEM THOTT].

SP. Id equidem erat, quod soror mihi intima, mater tua, charissime nepos, ad me die 24 octobris superioris anni, cum Bredenbergæ in Holsatia esset, perscripsit, missis in Daniam ad filium meum Tychonem literis, qui ibi tunc pro auferendis residuis meis jnstrumentis reliquaque supellectile aliquamdiu morabatur et sub initia huius anni, re omni ex voto peracta, huc ad me in Bohemiam reversus est: te nimirum, quamprimum ad quietas sedes in illa tua peregrinatione pervenires, de loco, ubi subsisteres, deque rerum tuarum conditionibus, mihi scripturum, quod te nunc ex matris voluntate atque constantia, a qua te non degeneraturum mihi polliceor, effecisse, perlubenter video. Placet, quod Heidelbergæ ob hyemis asperitatem substiteris, donec vere futuro Basilæam petas. Quamprimum vero de tempore, quo isthuc tibi proficiscendum erit, me edocueris (quod ut mature facias, velim), mittam tibi literas, quibus clarissimo viro d. d. Johanni Jacobo Grynæo te diligenter commendabo. Nec dubito, quin is vel mea de caussa res tuas sibi curæ esse sinat. Est enim is, licet de facie utrinque ignoti simus, mei amantissimus, et bis vel ter, postquam Dania excessi, cultissimas et officij ac humanitatis plenas ad me dedit literas. Quibus etiam respondi, licet ultimæ meæ, quas Vitebergæ nonnihil hærens ad ipsum per tabellarium Danicum Escillum, quem nosti, direxi, mihi ab eodem reportatæ sint, quod ipsum domo abfuisse caussaretur. At si nulla commoditas, antequam Heidelberga abieris, mihi denuo scribendi concessa fuerit, fiat id saltem, ubi Basilæam perveneris; ibique mox dictum illum ecc:mum Grynæum accedens ipsum ex me officiose saluta. Nec dubito, quin, ubi intellexerit, te meum ex sorore nepotem esse mihique charum, te et res tuas ad optima quæque suo consilio (a quo etiam te deflecti nolim) sit promoturus. Ante omnia vero pietati, virtuti et bonis literis strenue operam nava, ut cultior in patriam revertaris, et quam maxime tibi a pravo cave sodalitio, quod multos perdidit; et præceptori tuo recta monenti lubens auschulta. Coetera Deus providebit. Adjunctas ecc:mo illi Paulo Melisso, poetarum nostri seculi antesignano, una cum carminibus, dicta prius ex me salute, porrige, et si quid rescripserit, per oportunitatem mitte. Salutem etiam dic m. Jacobo Christmanno, isthic mathematico et Græcæ linguæ (uti opinor) professorj, simulque indica, Uraniam nostram, quæ me ex Dania huc intra saltus Bohemicos volens comitata est, sub auspiciis et clementissimo favore augustissimi imperatoris Rudolphi secundi hospicium benignum et commodum hic nactam esse; in quo nova suorum sacrorum ponat fundamina, prioribus illis apud Danos non cedentia, nec adeo (uti speramus) fastidita aut lubrica, ut vix repedationem sit subitura. Quod et Pythagoras in suis scite dictis inconsultum duxit. Si res tuæ sic tulerint, ut ante reditum in patriam has etiam oras perlustrare non invium fuerit, me hic invise. Neque enim citra rem fuerit, te aulam cæsaream, quæ Pragæ est, atque horum hominum mores spectare.

Vale cum præceptore tuo, quem etiam salvere iubeo, quam optime.
Dabantur properanter ex arce cæsareana Benatica, quinque milliaribus Praga remota, quam nunc indulto jmperatoris cum meis tranquille inhabito, anno 1600 die 17 februarij stilj renovati.
text.english:
**[TYCHO BRAHE TO TAGE THOTT].**

Heartiest greeting. This indeed was what my most intimate sister, your mother, dearest nephew, wrote to me on the 24th of October of last year, when she was at Bredenberg in Holstein, in a letter sent into Denmark to my son Tycho — who was then staying there a while to bring away my remaining instruments and the rest of my furniture, and at the beginning of this year, every matter accomplished according to my wish, returned hither to me in Bohemia: namely, that you, as soon as you should reach quiet quarters in that peregrination of yours, would write to me about the place where you were lodging, and about the conditions of your affairs — which I see most gladly you have now done, in accordance with your mother's will and constancy, from which I promise myself you will not degenerate. I am pleased that you have halted at Heidelberg on account of the harshness of winter, until in the coming spring you make for Basel. As soon as you inform me of the time when you must set out thither — which I should wish you to do in good time — I will send you a letter by which I will diligently commend you to the most renowned man Lord Doctor Johann Jacob Grynaeus. Nor do I doubt that he, even for my sake, will make your affairs his care. For he, though we are unknown to each other by face, is most loving of me, and two or three times since I left Denmark has sent me most cultivated letters, full of courtesy and humanity; to which I also replied — although my last, which (lingering a while at Wittenberg) I sent him by the Danish courier Eskil, whom you know, was brought back to me by the same, because he pleaded that Grynaeus had been away from home. But if no convenience of writing to me again be granted before you leave Heidelberg, let it at least be done when you reach Basel; and there, approaching that most excellent Grynaeus soon, greet him dutifully on my behalf. Nor do I doubt that, when he understands you are my nephew by my sister and dear to me, he will advance you and your affairs to every best thing by his counsel — from which I should not wish you turned aside. But above all, devote yourself strenuously to piety, virtue, and good letters, that you may return more cultivated to your fatherland; and beware as much as you can of bad company, which has ruined many; and gladly hearken to your tutor when he advises rightly. The rest God will provide. The enclosed [letter], together with the poems, hand to that most excellent **Paul Melissus**, standard-bearer of the poets of our age, having first given a greeting from me; and if he write anything back, send it at an opportunity. Say a greeting also to Master **Jacob Christmann**, the mathematician there and (as I think) professor of the Greek tongue; and at the same time indicate that our **Urania**, who willingly accompanied me from Denmark hither within the Bohemian glades, has, under the auspices and most clement favour of the most august Emperor Rudolf II, found here a kindly and convenient lodging, in which she may lay new foundations of her sacred rites, not inferior to those former ones among the Danes — nor (as we hope) so disdained, or so slippery, that she would scarcely undergo a retreat; which Pythagoras too, in his shrewd sayings, deemed ill-advised. If your affairs so allow that, before your return to the fatherland, it be not out of your way to traverse these regions too, visit me here; for it would not be without profit for you to behold the imperial court, which is at Prague, and the manners of these people.

Farewell, with your tutor — whom I also bid be greeted — as well as may be.
Given in haste from the imperial castle of Benátky, five miles distant from Prague, which I now by the Emperor's indulgence peacefully inhabit with my household; the year 1600, the 17th day of February, of the renewed style.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Tage Ottesen Thott** (1580–1658), Tycho's **nephew** — *"my nephew by my sister."* His own letter to Tycho from Heidelberg, 15 January 1600 (brahe-t_16000115001), survives. He was then on his *peregrinatio academica* (study-tour), wintering at **Heidelberg** with his travelling-companion Niels Mathiesen Bachendorph before going on to **Basel**.
- **His mother = Sophie Brahe.** *Soror mihi intima, mater tua* — Tycho's "most intimate sister," who wrote from **Bredenberg in Holstein** (24 Oct 1599), is **Sophie Brahe** (1559–1643), Tycho's learned astronomer-sister; Tage was her son by her first husband, **Otte Thott** of Eriksholm. The identification is fixed by the companion letter (brahe-t_16000115001), where the mother "met **Erik Lange** at Brunswick and made the journey into Holstein" — Erik Lange being Sophie's second husband (the alchemist).
- **The commendation to Basel.** Tycho promises a letter of recommendation to **Johann Jacob Grynaeus** (1540–1617), the Basel theologian (rector of the university; cf. brahe-t_15941023001), with whom Tycho corresponded though they never met; the Danish courier **Eskil** had carried Tycho's last letter to Grynaeus (returned, Grynaeus being away). Tycho's avuncular counsel: piety, virtue, good letters; beware bad company; heed the tutor.
- **The Heidelberg contacts.**
 - **Paul Melissus** (Schede), "standard-bearer of the poets of our age" — Tage is to deliver an enclosed letter and poems to him (the recurring Melissus thread, cf. brahe-t_16000305001, brahe-t_16000329004).
 - **Jacob Christmann** (1554–1613), Heidelberg orientalist and astronomer. Tycho calls him "professor of the **Greek** tongue (as I think)" — *hedged, and in fact slightly off:* Christmann was professor of **Hebrew**, then the first professor of **Arabic** at Heidelberg. The hedge (*uti opinor*) is preserved, the correction noted here (no silent emendation).
- **The Urania passage (the letter's eloquent heart).** Tycho bids Tage tell Christmann that **"our Urania"** — the Muse of astronomy — "**who willingly accompanied me from Denmark hither within the Bohemian glades**," has under **Rudolf II's** favour found "a kindly and convenient lodging, in which she may lay new foundations of her sacred rites, not inferior to those former ones among the Danes" — and (Tycho hopes) not so "disdained or slippery" that she must again **retreat** (*repedatio*), "which **Pythagoras** too, in his shrewd sayings, deemed ill-advised" (the Pythagorean precept against turning back / retracing one's steps). A poignant figure for the transplantation of his astronomy from Hven to Bohemia.
- **Persons named.** Tage Thott; **Sophie Brahe** (his mother, Tycho's sister); Tycho's son (Tycho the Younger); **Johann Jacob Grynaeus**; the courier **Eskil**; **Paul Melissus**; **Jacob Christmann**; **Rudolf II**; **Pythagoras**.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 17 Februarij stylo renovato anni 1600* — **New Style** (imperial); the note *quinque milliaribus Praga remota* fixes Benátky "five miles from Prague." Header agrees with the label (the recipient's own letter, by contrast, is O.S. Heidelberg — the gap is preserved across the pair).

text.original:
ILLUSTRI ET GENEROSO VIRO, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, ASTRONOMORUM NOSTRI SECULI PRINCIPI, DOMINO ET PATRONO DILECTISSIMO.

S. P. D.

ILLUSTRIS et Generose Domine TYCHO, patrone observandissime, ex litteris, quas proxime per M. CHRISTIANUM misi, Generositati Vestræ innotescere potuit, quo in statu sint res Transylvani, qui ad Generositatem Vestram excurrerat. Petijt is interim aliquoties a me, ut eum apud Generositatem Vestram humiliter excusarem. Idoneum alium nullum possum exquirere, ut ut percuperem. Forsan autem in viciniâ vestrâ aliquis oblatus est.

Benedictus sit Dominus Deus noster, qui iam tandem Angelo percutienti iuga Bohemica ex misericordiâ suâ frenum iniecit. Is clementissime Halcyonia et aërem saluberrimum unâ cum longâ vitâ Generositati Vestræ concedat, ut in emolumentum publicorum studiorum et ad gloriam nominis divini omnia illa, quæ feliciter cœpit, ad exoptatissimum finem perducere possit. Speramus etiam rabiem Theologicam interim ibi nonnihil deferbuisse. Etsi vero nihil scriptione magnopere dignum nunc temporis habebam, tamen D. D. IESSENIUM, communem amicum nostrum, tanquam planetam ab Eclipticâ Witebergensi nunc iterum in latitudinem meridionalem Bohemicam excurrentem, sine aliquibus meis ad Generositatem Vestram pervenire nolui. Commendo Generositatem Vestram cum omnibus eidem addictis divinæ protectioni fideliter.

Witebergæ dominicâ Lætare, non secundum Lilianos, sed secundum Iulianos fastos, licet nunc concurrant in paucis, anno Christi 1600, quem tamen præter IOSEPHUM SCALIGERUM etiam BARTHOLOMEUS SCULTETUS 1601 esse comprobat.
G. V. studiosiss.
WOLFG. FRANZIUS
text.english:
**To the illustrious and generous man, Master Tycho Brahe, prince of the astronomers of our age, lord and most beloved patron.**

Hearty greeting.

Illustrious and generous Master Tycho, most observed patron: from the letters which I lately sent through Master Christian [Longomontanus], it could become known to Your Generosity in what state are the affairs of the Transylvanian who had run off to Your Generosity. He has meanwhile asked me several times to excuse him humbly with Your Generosity. I can seek out no other suitable [man], however much I might wish to. But perhaps in your vicinity someone has presented himself.

Blessed be the Lord our God, who has now at last, out of his mercy, cast a bridle on the Angel smiting the Bohemian regions. May He most clemently grant Halcyon days and most healthful air, together with long life, to Your Generosity, so that — to the profit of public studies and to the glory of the divine name — you may be able to bring all those things which you have happily begun to a most-wished-for end. We hope, too, that the Theological frenzy has meanwhile cooled down somewhat there. And although I had nothing now greatly worth the writing, yet I did not wish Doctor Jessenius, our common friend — like a planet now again running out from the Wittenberg Ecliptic into Bohemian southern latitude — to reach Your Generosity without some lines of mine. I faithfully commend Your Generosity, with all those devoted to you, to the divine protection.

Wittenberg, on Laetare Sunday — not according to the Lilian [Gregorian], but according to the Julian calendar, though they now coincide in but few [points] — in the year of Christ 1600, which, however, besides Joseph Scaliger, Bartholomäus Scultetus too proves to be 1601.
Most zealous of Your Generosity,
Wolfgang Franzius.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Wolfgang Franz(ius)** (1564–1628), theologian at **Wittenberg**; a learned, witty letter from Tycho's Saxon circle.
- **The Transylvanian.** *res Transylvani, qui ad Generositatem Vestram excurrerat* — an unnamed **Transylvanian** who had "run off" to Tycho and whom Franzius cannot replace; he asks Tycho to excuse him. (Background to Tycho's shifting household of assistants.) *M. Christianus* = **Longomontanus**, the earlier courier.
- **The plague lifting.** *Angelo percutienti iuga Bohemica … frenum iniecit* — "[God] has cast a bridle on the **Angel smiting the Bohemian regions**" (the plague-angel; *iuga* = "ridges/yokes," here the lands of Bohemia): the **abatement of the Bohemian plague** of 1599–1600 (cf. the plague at Benátky in brahe-t_15991214001). *Halcyonia* = "halcyon [calm] days." *rabies Theologica* = the "Theological frenzy" (the confessional/dogmatic controversies) — hoped to have cooled.
- **Jessenius as a "planet."** *D. D. Iessenium … tanquam planetam ab Ecliptica Witebergensi … in latitudinem meridionalem Bohemicam excurrentem* — a charming astronomical conceit for **Jan Jessenius** (Jan Jesenský, 1566–1621), the anatomist and Tycho's friend (later author of Tycho's funeral oration), here "running south," like a planet leaving the ecliptic, **from Wittenberg to Bohemia** — and carrying this very letter.
- **⚠ Calendar — and the year-number dispute.** Franzius dates pointedly *dominicâ Laetare … non secundum Lilianos, sed secundum Iulianos fastos* — "on **Laetare Sunday** (the 4th of Lent), by the **Julian**, not the **Lilian** [Gregorian, after Aloysius Lilius] calendar." In 1600 (Julian) Easter fell on 23 March O.S.; **Laetare Sunday = 2 March 1600 O.S.**, matching the identifier. His "they now coincide in but few [points]" is a learned aside on the two calendars. He adds the **century-numbering controversy**: that the year "is 1601" according to **Joseph Scaliger** and **Bartholomäus Scultetus** (the Görlitz mathematician) — i.e. the debate over whether 1600 or 1601 completed the century. All preserved, not "corrected." Wittenberg (Lutheran) = O.S.
