documents.editorial_note: **Direction note.** **Incoming** letter — *from* **Magini** (at **Bologna**) *to* Tycho (then at Benátky — hence the catalogue label "Benatky," which names the *recipient's* seat, not the place of writing). Magini's reply to Tycho's letter of 3 January 1600 (**brahe-t_16000103002**); it **originates the Bernardino Baldi plan** that Tycho approves in **brahe-t_16010124001 (24 January 1601)**.

text.original:
IOHANNES ANTONIUS MAGINUS AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

TUAS ad me literas 3° Ianuarij datas et mihi opera Clarissimi Domini IOANNIS FRANCISCI SAGREDI Patricij Veneti et amicissimi mei redditas accepi die 22 Februarij. Eae mirum in modum, et quantum dici vix potest, gratae fuere; sed ijs respondere statim non potui ob praematurum tabellarij discessum; nactusque otium integrae hebdomadis ad te pluribus quam umquam antea scribendum putavi. Tuum illud praecipuum negotium mihi tanta fiducia mandatum pro eo ac debeo curabo, nihilque praetermittam, quod ad dignitatem tuam pertinere videatur. Res est maximi ponderis, proinde haud negligenter tractanda, sed consideranda accuratissime. Huc usque, ut fatear ingenue, ut etiam tu ipse affirmas, non aliam tibi operam dedi, nisi ut vertendas Latine curarem epistolas illas Germanice scriptas, quae ad octo sunt, quod mihi praestitit Germanus quidam medicinae studiosus, idque in gratiam Transylvani cuiusdam mei auditoris: ubi diu laborassem in inveniendo eius rei interprete, propterea quod nullum familiariter nossem eorum, qui Bononiae sunt e natione Germanica, qui perpauci sunt. Ac certe tum domesticis, tum scholasticis et publicis et privatis negotijs, tum valetudine parum firma impeditus, (cum distillatione laborarim dies complures huiusce hiemis culpa; quae omnium quas umquam meminerim inclementissima huc usque fuit ob nivium incredibilem vim omnia obsidentium, ut vix aliud agere, quam ad ignem pellendo frigori sedere potuerim, libellum aliquem ibi incommode legendo) etsi maxime voluissem, non multum tamen in rebus Dominationis tuae promovere potuissem. Sed deinceps mitescente caelo, spero me non poenitendam operam tibi navaturum. Primum etenim ex omnibus hisce scriptis excerpam brevia aliquot capita et quasi summam conficiam ad facile alios edocendos idoneam, cuius plura exempla ubi fecero, ad varios amicos transmittam.

Assentior tibi de narratione rerum tuarum non in dialogo facienda sed occasione panegyrici. Sed venit mihi tamen in mentem quod rationi nostrae multo sit conducibilius atque aptius. Intelligo BERNARDINUM BALDUM Urbinatem Guastallae Abbatem, qui olim edidit HERONIS opus de machinis se movendis e Graeco a se ipso translatum, multis abhinc annis provinciam suscepisse scribendarum vitarum praestantium Mathematicorum. Hominem quidem de facie non novi, sed tamen scio, cum aliquando Bononia transiret, domum ad me venisse, ut me de facie nosset, ut mihi postea dictum, nam me non invenit. Ex hoc spero, si quid ab eo petam, tamquam a mei studioso, facile impetraturum. Itaque scribere ad eum cogito et cum eo agere, ut vitam tuam diligenter conscribat, et ad me eius historiae exemplum mittat: illud postea cum encomijs tui poëticis coniungere licebit, et qui encomia illa collegerit, idem sibi ab illo eius historiae copiam factam dicere poterit. Sed is tamen prius diligenter de omnibus rebus, quae argumenti eius erunt, edocendus est. Ego quaecumque huc spectantia colligere potero, non praetermittam; sed bimestre spatium pusillum est, quando ij, quorum opera indigemus, suas quoque habent occupationes, quibus distinentur. Hoc mihi in huiusmodi negotio optimum consilium videbatur: quod meum tamen iudicium tuae prudentiae permitto.

Eclipsin Solarem anni 1598 instrumentis mathematicis non observavi, cum hîc prae manibus non haberem idoneum instrumentum. Horologio tamen ex pulvere, quod quadrantes horarum indicabat, accomodato ad horam exortus Solis, percepi eclipsin ipsam tardiorem fuisse hora pene una, quam prodat calculus Prutenicus, et eius magnitudo novem puncta non excessit, quamvis expectaretur hîc maior obscuratio. Hoc idem et Romae et Patavij observatum fuit, scilicet tardiorem fuisse ad integram fere horam et minorem fuisse obscurationem. Exemplar epistolae Illustrissimi Cardinalis SS. QUATTUOR, nepotis felicis memoriae INNOCENTIJ octavi Summi pontificis, in qua mihi de illa eclipsi, prout Romae contingit, historiam narrat, ad te mitto, ut videas, si ex illa quidquam haurire potes, et si tibi bona occasio de illo honorifice loqui patere poterit, mihi gratissimum erit; est enim patronus meus humanissimus, cui maxime debeo ob innumera beneficia in me collata. Nullas praeteritis temporibus feci observationes ob varia impedimenta, cum semper integras epistolas conscripserim apud aliquos Cardinales et Principes, quando scilicet hîc erant a scholis vacationes. Quod tempus maxime huic negotio erat idoneum.

Laboravi non parum, ut perciperem tuam rationem supputandi Lunarem cursum ex quinternione mihi relicto a D. FRANCISCO TENGNALIO, a pag. 113 incipiente. Notandum vero quod haec omnia, quae de revolutionibus etc. usque ad pag. 120, sed non sine magno labore rem tandem assequutus sum, cum nullum extet exemplum dictae computationis, et cum apud me non sint, quae de octavae sphaerae ac de Solis motu exarasti, tamquam praecedentia hunc Lunarem motum. Unde pro habendo Solis motu ex tuis fundamentis confugi ad Ephemeridem tuam motus Solis ad annum 1591 mihi a te olim liberaliter communicatam, notavique in ea Solem attigisse locum Apogaei, nempe gr. 5. 32' ♋ die 17 Iunij, h. 13,44 p. m., hîcque nulla est differentia inter verum motum et medium: excerpsi deinde motum Solis medium ex meis tabulis congruentem dicto temporis momento et inveni quidem ipsum scr. 2' 52'' minorem, dempta prius a loco ☉ tuo aequinoctiorum praecessione, quam gr. 28 17' 42'' tunc te praesupposuisse arbitratus fui. Quocirca mihi videtur his temporibus posse elicere medium Solis motum ex meis tabulis addendo eidem 2' 52'', ut cum tuis radicibus concordet. Posthaec varia ratione supputavi locum ☾ ex tuis tabulis, idque ad diem 9 Ianuarij anni 1587 atque etiam ad 15m et 16m eiusdem, quibus observasti verum ☾ locum per instrumenta, ut recenses pag. 56 tuarum Epistolarum astronomicarum, cuius libri reliquit mihi folium D. GELLIUS tuus a pag. 49 usque ad 56. At veram supputationis ☾ formam secundum tua placita non recte prius cognovi, quam confugissem ad triangulorum operationes, quibus certior factus fui, te aequationes illas exactissime colligere non curasse, facturum postea id meliori occasione, scilicet in tuo Theatro absolutissimo, cum ex angulo maximae 2i epicicli aequationis gr. 7 41' 15'' a te per observationes deprehenso colligatur recta AD a centro Terrae ad centrum primi Circelli par. 98677 qualium DE datur 1100. Sed ex angulo minimae aequationis perigeae elicitur recta AD 101312. Forsan lato modo pro dictis aequationibus definiendis sumpsisti dictam rectam AD tanquam sinum integrum, quod etiam mihi confirmat variatio centri maxima a te posita m. 45' 20'', cum recta AB semidimetiens scilicet parvi circelli ad mundi centrum sit 1320, qui numerus sinus est m. 45' 20'' vel 45' 24''. Experiri volui, quantam efficeret varietatem semidiameter CD parvi Circelli, super quo moveri statuis centrum primi epicicli, et inveni angulum maximae aequationis primi epicicli gr. 7 27' 43'', centro primi epicicli versante in Apogaeo parvi illius Circelli, statuendo scilicet rectam AD particularum 101640 iuxta tuos numeros. Idem angulus maximae aequationis in Perigaeo illiusmet Circelli prodit gr. 7 30' 35''; different, a priore m. 2' 52''. Sed uterque horum angulorum sensibili differentia ab angulo maximae aequationis a te definito gr. 7. 41¼ discrepat, ut suspicer commensurationes orbium Lunarium a te positas aliqua correctione indigere, praesertim quod videam etiam calculum ex tuis tabulis prodeuntem ad unguem tuismet observationibus non congruere, quod in bonam accipias partem velim, tanquam a sincero et ingenuo viro prodiens, qui zelotypia tui honoris laborat. Ab initio variationem orbis non solum subducebam a medio motu ☾ a Sole, vel eidem addebam iuxta tabulam, sed etiam a medio argumento vel anomalia: sed postea ex calculo triangulorum cognovi te aequationem anomaliae ex duplici illa variatione, quam argumentum medium subit, composuisse, quod mihi valde placuit. Suppositio haec tua Lunaris mirum arguit tuum ingenium et praestantiam: sed maxime praecavendum est, ne numeri ex ipsa derivantes ab observationibus vitio tuorum supputatorum discrepent. Non me latet magnum ac permolestum esse laborem in supputandis hisce aequationum tabulis. Ego tamen, cum compendia quaedam mira in computationibus triangulorum possideam a me nuper excogitata, exiguam persentirem molestiam in his tabulis de novo ad 2a scrupula exactissime construendis. Quod libenter tibi significare volui, ut si mea opera posthac indigueris, libere possis uti, praesertim pro reliquis quinque planetis, quorum unamquamque tabulam in decem diebus perfecte absolverem. Quod tibi incredibile videri non debet. Tabulam enim primi mobilis universalem habeo a me ad singula decem minuta (ad instar illius REGIOMONTANI, quae est ad singulos gradus) supputatam, et alias insuper tabulas, quibus calculationes triangulorum sphaericorum per ingressus laterales absolvo. Et in planis triangulis quando anguli inquirendi sunt, eademmet tabula utor artificio quodam a me invento, quod etiam locum habet in triangulo obliquangulo, in quo, datis duobus lateribus cum angulo ab ijs comprehenso, inquirendi veniunt anguli, qua operatione indigemus tantopere in aequationibus planetarum definiendis.

Scias profecto me adeo tui esse studiosum et observantissimum, ut nihil aliud cogitem, quam ut tibi me gratum probem. Quin et hoc te non latere volo, tantopere mihi esse in optatis, ut me adhuc vivo prodeat in lucem correctio caelestium motuum, ut nulli parcendum labori existimem, quo id assequi liceret, etsi nihil ex eo ad gloriam profici putem, sed satis habeam fructum illum, ut scilicet mihi tantum usui sint in exercenda Astrologia iudiciaria vulgo dicta, qua mirum in modum delector.

Ephemeridum mearum unum tantum tomum ab anno 1598 incipientem et in annum 1610 desinentem denuo impressum evulgavi, in quem nihil novi reposui, praeter auctuaria quaedam in Isagogicis, cum compendio directionum secundum viam rationalem, et Quadrante Directorio ad mentem PTOLEMÆI. Exemplar ad te libenter mitterem, si congrua mihi esset occasio; aestate hac proxima alter tomus, viginti feto quentes annos complectens, excudetur; et tunc enixe curabo, ut ad te utriusque tomi Exemplar deferatur.

Vidi nuper quae contra me inutiliter effutivit DAVID ORIGANUS in editione suarum Ephemeridum, et exactissime cognovi illum unum esse ex illis, qui ex insectandis et censurandis alijs gloriam sibi quaerere conantur; sed poenitebit aliquando se de me quicquam protulisse, ubi ostendero ipsum gravius in suis Ephemeridibus a calculo Prutenico aberrasse, quam a me factum sit, praesertim in postremis illis annis, ultra scilicet 1620, cum meas ibi desinentes Ephemerides non habuerit prae oculis, quod maximo argumento erit, et aperte satis demonstrabit, ipsum plurima ex meis desumpsisse. Pro emersionibus et occultationibus Planetarum ac Fixarum mutuavi arcus visionum a PTOLEMÆO definitos, quos parum a vero recedere in fixis puto, sed in Planetis credo cum STADIO esse varios, penes differentiam ipsorum Planetarum a Terra. Si quid notatu dignum ex tuismet observationibus circa hosce arcus habes, illud mihi humanissime communicare ne graveris; quod te subnixe oro ac deprecor: polliceor enim ingenue, quidquid illud erit, a te recepisse testaturum.

Vale, vir praeclarissime, et me, ut soles, ama ac addictissimum habe.
Bononia 4 Martij MDC.
Perillustri Dominationi tuae addictissimus
IO. ANTONIUS MAGINUS, Patavinus.
text.english:
**JOHANNES ANTONIUS MAGINUS TO TYCHO BRAHE.**

Your letter to me, dated the 3rd of January and delivered me by the agency of the most renowned **Lord Giovanni Francesco Sagredo, a Venetian patrician and my dearest friend**, I received on the 22nd of February. It was wonderfully — and beyond what can scarcely be said — welcome; but I could not answer it at once, on account of the courier's premature departure; and, having got the leisure of a whole week, I thought I should write you more [fully] than ever before. **That chief business of yours, committed to me with such trust, I will care for as I ought, and will omit nothing that may seem to pertain to your dignity. It is a matter of the greatest weight, and so to be treated not negligently, but considered most accurately.** Hitherto, to confess frankly (as you yourself also affirm), I have given you no other work than to see those **letters written in German — there are about eight — translated into Latin**; which a certain German student of medicine performed for me, and that for the sake of a certain Transylvanian hearer of mine — after I had long laboured to find a translator for the matter, because I knew familiarly none of those who are at Bologna of the German nation, who are very few. And certainly, hindered both by domestic and by scholastic and public and private business, and by health none too firm (for I have laboured with a catarrh [*distillatio*] for many days, by the fault of this winter — which has hitherto been the most inclement of all I can remember, for the incredible force of the snows besieging everything, so that I could scarcely do anything but sit by the fire driving off the cold, inconveniently reading some little book there) — even had I most wished it, I could not have advanced much in Your Lordship's affairs. But hereafter, the weather growing milder, I hope to do you work not to be regretted. For first I will **excerpt some brief chapters from all these writings, and make, as it were, a summary fit for easily instructing others**; of which, when I have made several copies, I will send them to various friends.

**I agree with you that the narration of your affairs should be made not in dialogue, but on the occasion of a panegyric. But there comes to mind, nonetheless, something much more conducive and apt to our plan. I understand that Bernardino Baldi of Urbino, Abbot of Guastalla — who once published Hero's work *On Self-Moving Machines*, translated by himself from the Greek — undertook, many years ago, the province of writing the Lives of distinguished Mathematicians.** I do not indeed know the man by face; but yet I know that, when he once passed through Bologna, he came to my house, to know me by face (as was told me afterward, for he did not find me). From this I hope that, if I ask anything of him, as of a well-wisher of mine, I shall easily obtain it. **And so I think to write to him, and to deal with him, that he diligently write your Life, and send me a copy of that history; it can afterward be joined with the poetic encomia of you, and whoever shall have collected those encomia can say that the copy of that history was made for him by [Baldi].** But he must first be diligently informed of all the matters which will be his argument. Whatever pertaining hither I can collect, I will not omit; but a two-month space is little, when those whose work we need have their own occupations too, by which they are detained. This seemed to me the best counsel in a business of this kind — which judgement of mine, however, I leave to your prudence.

**The Solar Eclipse of the year 1598 I did not observe with mathematical instruments, since I had not here at hand a suitable instrument.** Yet, by a sand-clock [*horologium ex pulvere*] which marked the quarters of hours, adjusted to the hour of the Sun's rising, **I perceived that the eclipse itself was later by nearly a whole hour than the Prutenic calculation gives, and its magnitude did not exceed nine points [digits], although a greater obscuration was expected here.** This same thing was observed also at Rome and at Padua — namely, that it was later by nearly a whole hour, and the obscuration smaller. **A copy of the letter of the most illustrious Cardinal of the Santi Quattro — nephew of Innocent VIII, the Supreme Pontiff of happy memory — in which he narrates to me the history of that eclipse, as it happened at Rome, I send to you**, that you may see whether you can draw anything from it; and if a good occasion to speak honourably of him may lie open to you, it will be most welcome to me — for he is my most humane patron, to whom I owe much, for innumerable benefits conferred on me. I made no observations in past times, on account of various impediments, since I always **wrote whole letters [stayed?] with certain Cardinals and Princes** — namely, when there were here the vacations from the schools; which time was most fit for this business.

**I laboured not a little to perceive your method of computing the Lunar course, from the quinternion left me by Lord Franz Tengnagel, beginning at p. 113** — and be it noted, all these things which [you wrote] about the revolutions etc., up to p. 120; but not without great labour did I at last attain the matter, since no example of the said computation exists, and since I do not have what you wrote about the eighth sphere and the Sun's motion, as preceding this Lunar motion. Whence, in order to have the Sun's motion from your foundations, **I resorted to your Ephemeris of the Sun's motion for the year 1591, formerly liberally communicated to me by you**; and I noted in it that the Sun reached the place of the Apogee — namely **5° 32′ Cancer [♋], on 17 June, at 13h 44′ p.m.** — and here there is no difference between the true motion and the mean. I then excerpted from my tables the Sun's mean motion agreeing with the said moment of time, and found it indeed **2′ 52″ less**, having first subtracted from your Sun's place the precession of the equinoxes — which I reckoned you then presupposed [to be] **28° 17′ 42″**. Wherefore it seems to me that for these times I can elicit the Sun's mean motion from my tables by adding 2′ 52″ to it, that it may agree with your roots. After this I computed, by various methods, the Moon's place from your tables — and that for the 9th of January 1587, and also for the 15th and 16th of the same, on which you observed the Moon's true place by instruments, as you recount on p. 56 of your *Astronomical Letters*, of which book your **[Gellius Sascerides]** left me a leaf, from p. 49 to 56. **But the true form of the Moon's computation, according to your principles, I did not rightly know before I had resorted to triangle-operations** — by which I was made the more certain that **you did not take care to collect those equations most exactly, [intending] to do that afterward on a better occasion, namely in your most absolute Theatre** [the *Mechanica*/*Progymnasmata*]; since, from the angle of the maximum equation of the second epicycle — **7° 41′ 15″, found by you through observations** — there is collected the straight line **AD**, from the centre of the Earth to the centre of the first little circle, [as] **98677 parts**, of which **DE** is given [as] 1100; but from the angle of the minimum perigeal equation there is elicited the straight line AD [as] **101312**. Perhaps, broadly, for defining the said equations, you took the said straight line AD as the whole sine — which the maximum variation of the centre, posited by you [as] **45′ 20″**, also confirms to me, since the straight line **AB** (the semidiameter, namely, of the small circle to the world's centre) is **1320**, which number is the sine of 45′ 20″ or 45′ 24″. I wished to test how great a variation the semidiameter **CD** of the small circle — on which you posit the centre of the first epicycle to move — would make; and I found the maximum-equation angle of the first epicycle [to be] **7° 27′ 43″**, the centre of the first epicycle being at the Apogee of that small circle (positing, namely, the straight line AD of 101640 parts, according to your numbers); the same maximum-equation angle, at the Perigee of that same circle, comes out [as] **7° 30′ 35″** — differing from the prior by 2′ 52″. **But each of these angles differs, by a sensible difference, from the maximum-equation angle defined by you [as] 7° 41¼′ — so that I suspect that the commensurations of the Lunar orbs posited by you need some correction**, especially since I see that even the calculation coming out of your tables does not agree to the nail with your own observations — which I would have you take in good part, as proceeding from a sincere and ingenuous man, who labours with jealousy [zeal] for your honour. From the beginning I subtracted the orb-variation not only from the Moon's mean motion from the Sun (or added it, according to the table), but also from the mean argument or anomaly; but afterward, from the triangle-calculation, **I learned that you composed the anomaly-equation from that double variation which the mean argument undergoes — which pleased me much. This Lunar supposition of yours wonderfully argues your genius and excellence; but it must most be guarded lest the numbers deriving from it differ from the observations, by the fault of your computers.** It does not escape me that it is a great and most troublesome labour to compute these tables of equations. Yet I, since I possess **certain wonderful compendia in the computations of triangles, lately devised by me**, should feel little trouble in constructing these tables anew, to seconds, most exactly. Which I gladly wished to signify to you, that, if you need my work hereafter, you may freely use it — especially for **the remaining five planets, each table of which I would perfectly complete in ten days**. Which ought not to seem incredible to you. For I have **a universal Table of the primum mobile, computed by me to single ten-minutes** (after the likeness of that of Regiomontanus, which is to single degrees), and besides other tables, by which I complete the calculations of spherical triangles by lateral entries; and in plane triangles, when the angles are to be sought, I use the same table, by a certain artifice invented by me — which also holds place in the oblique triangle, in which, two sides being given with the angle comprehended by them, the angles come to be sought — the operation we so greatly need in defining the equations of the planets.

Know assuredly that I am so zealous and observant of you that I think of nothing else than to prove myself grateful to you. Nay, I would not have this hidden from you: that **it is so much in my wishes that the correction of the celestial motions come to light while I am yet alive**, that I think no labour is to be spared, by which it might be attained — even though I think nothing is profited from it toward glory, but have fruit enough [in] this: namely, that **they be of so much use to me in practising the judicial Astrology, as it is commonly called, in which I wonderfully delight.**

Of my **Ephemerides** I have published anew only one volume, beginning from the year 1598 and ending in the year 1610, into which I put nothing new, except certain augmentations in the Introductory [parts], with a compendium of directions according to the rational way, and a Directory Quadrant after the mind of **Ptolemy**. I would gladly send you a copy, were a fit occasion mine; this coming summer the second volume, comprising the twenty following years, will be printed; and then I will earnestly take care that a copy of both volumes be delivered to you.

I saw lately what **David Origanus** uselessly blurted against me in the edition of his Ephemerides, and I have most exactly recognised that he is one of those who try to seek glory for themselves by attacking and censuring others; but he will someday repent of having put forth anything about me, when I shall show that **he erred more gravely, in his Ephemerides, from the Prutenic calculation, than was done by me** — especially in those last years, beyond 1620, namely, when he did not have my Ephemerides (ending there) before his eyes; which will be the greatest argument, and will clearly enough demonstrate that he took very much from mine. For the emersions and occultations [risings and settings] of the Planets and Fixed [stars], I have borrowed the **vision-arcs defined by Ptolemy**, which I think recede little from the truth in the fixed [stars]; but in the Planets I believe, with **Stadius**, that they are various, according to the difference of the Planets themselves from the Earth. If you have anything worthy of note, from your own observations, about these arcs, do not find it a burden to communicate it to me most humanely — which I earnestly beg and entreat of you; for I frankly promise that I will testify to have received whatever it be from you.

Farewell, most distinguished man, and love me, as you are wont, and hold [me] most devoted.
Bologna, 4 March 1600.
Most devoted to Your most illustrious Lordship,
**Giovanni Antonio Magini, of Padua.**

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondent.** **Incoming**, **Magini** (Bologna) → **Tycho** — the reply to **Tycho's letter of 3 January 1600 (brahe-t_16000103002)**; survives in Magini's printed *Tabulae primi mobilis*.
- **Significance — the origin of the Baldi plan, the 1598 eclipse, and a detailed lunar-theory analysis.**
 - **★ The Bernardino Baldi proposal (origin).** Magini, agreeing that Tycho's *Life* should come "on the occasion of a panegyric, not in dialogue," **proposes commissioning Bernardino Baldi of Urbino (Abbot of Guastalla, translator of Hero's *On Self-Moving Machines*) to write Tycho's biography for his *Lives of the Mathematicians***, then attaching the poetic encomia — with a cover story that the Life supplied the encomia. **This is the proposal Tycho approves in brahe-t_16010124001 (24 January 1601)** — the Italian self-monument scheme. Magini has had **eight German letters translated into Latin** (via a German medical student) toward it; the harsh Bologna winter and his catarrh delayed the rest.
 - **The 1598 solar eclipse.** Magini observed it only crudely (a **sand-clock**, no proper instrument): **nearly an hour later than the Prutenic tables, magnitude c. 9 digits** (as at Rome and Padua). He encloses the **Cardinal of the Santi Quattro's** account (the Cardinal being "nephew of Innocent VIII" and Magini's patron), asking Tycho to speak honourably of him — the thread Tycho takes up in his reply of 24 January 1601.
 - **★ The lunar-theory analysis (the technical core).** Magini works painstakingly through **Tycho's multi-epicycle lunar model** (from the **Tengnagel quinternion**, pp. 113–120; plus a leaf of the *Epistolae* left by **Gellius Sascerides**), reconstructing the solar mean-motion offset (+2′52″; precession 28°17′42″) and the lunar geometry (lines **AD, DE, AB, CD**; the small circle; the first/second epicycle). He finds the **maximum second-epicycle equation 7°41′15″** implied by Tycho's observations, but his own re-derivation gives only **7°27′43″–7°30′35″** — so **"the commensurations of the lunar orbs need some correction,"** the calculation "not agreeing to the nail with your own observations." He praises the model ("wonderfully argues your genius") but warns of **computers' errors**, and **offers to recompute all the planetary equation-tables** (each in ten days) using his own **prosthaphaeretic compendia** and his **10-minute *primum mobile* table** (cf. brahe-t_16010220001).
 - **Astrology, ephemerides, Origanus, heliacal arcs.** Magini wants Tycho's corrected motions chiefly **for judicial astrology, "in which I wonderfully delight"** — not for glory. His **Ephemerides** (1598–1610 reprint + a coming 20-year volume); his promised refutation of **David Origanus** (who "took much from mine"); and the **heliacal vision-arcs** (Ptolemy for the fixed stars; variable for planets, "with Stadius") — all the matters Tycho addresses in his reply of 24 January 1601.
- **Cross-references.** Pairs with **brahe-t_16000103002 (the letter answered)** and **brahe-t_16010124001 (Tycho's reply approving Baldi, 24 January 1601)**; the **Magini** correspondence (brahe-t_16010220001, brahe-t_15981128001); the **lunar-theory** thread (Herwart, brahe-t_15990917001); the **Cardinal SS. Quattro** and **Origanus** threads.
- **Persons & works named.** Magini; **Giovanni Francesco Sagredo**; the **German medical student** & the **Transylvanian hearer**; **Bernardino Baldi** (the *Lives of the Mathematicians*; his Hero translation); the **Cardinal of the Santi Quattro** (nephew of **Innocent VIII**); **Franz Tengnagel** (the quinternion); **Gellius Sascerides** (the *Epistolae* leaf); **David Origanus**; **Johannes Stadius**; **Ptolemy, Regiomontanus**; the *Mechanica*/*Progymnasmata* ("your Theatre"). Places: **Bologna**, **Rome**, **Padua**, **Benátky** (the recipient). Glyphs ☉ ☾ ♋ reproduced.
- **Calendar / place.** Dateline *Bononia 4 Martij MDC* → **Bologna, 4 March 1600 [N.S.]** (Italy New Style). The catalogue **label "Benatky" names the recipient's seat, not the place of writing** (Magini wrote from Bologna) — noted, not a date error.
- **Correction.** 'Intelligo' (Dreyer, TBOO VIII p.251) restored for the corrupted imperative 'Intellige'; Magini is reporting what he has gathered about Baldi, not instructing Tycho. English corrected from 'Understand that' to 'I understand that'.

text.original:
ILLUSTRI ET PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO TYCHONI BRAHE, IMPERATORIS RUDOLPHI II ASTRONOMO, AMICO S. S. IN AULA IMPERATORIS VEL BENATICA 5 MEILEN VON PRAG.

SÆPIUS de te mihi percontanti, BRAHEE nobilissime, nihil certi potuit significari a gentili tuo, qui heic commoratur studiorum gratiâ. Nam sese intellexisse aiebat, fore ut in Galliam te penetrares, nisi res tuæ in aulâ Cæsareâ optatissimum sortirentur exitum. Nunc autem vehementer gaudeo, Uranien tuam repperisse locum speculationi commodissimum, idque beneficio munificentissimi Imperatoris RUDOLPHI II. TAUBMANNUS et BRASCHIUS, Poëtæ laureati, me submonuerant de quibusdam carminibus in Tychen tuam componendis, quæ nunc cum hisce litteris accipies, et cum reliquis amicorum lucubrationibus, si placuerint, coniunges. Antea quoque a DAVIDE CHYTRÆO v. cl. reddita mihi fuerant exempla nonnulla epistolarum inter te et cancellarium Danicum commutatarum, ex quibus statum (vel potius ruinam) rerum tuarum, cum etiamnum in patriâ degeres, plus satis intellexi. Ea CHYTRÆO remisi, ita illo volente.

De exemplari Astronomiæ instauratæ, in quo plurimæ coloribus depictæ machinæ visuntur, magnas tibi et ago et habeo gratias: ut et de fasciculo elegantissimorum carminum unâ coniunctorum, quæ sanê libenter legi: sed tamen vehementer indolui, rem eo pervenisse, ut sponte exilium susciperes: quod nihilominus tibi ex animi sententiâ successit, fruituro meliore commoditate quam ipsâ in patriâ. Nuper fui adsiduus in manuscriptis quibusdam codicibus, ut viderem, nunquid reperirem antiqui de lapide illo Philosophico, ad quem inveniendum tot labores hactenus frustra desudavere. Investigabo etiam, si forte quid ad nos pervenerit a veteribus de rebus Astronomicis. Hoc enim te maximê expetere video. Fasciculo, quem TAUBMANNUS iussu tuo ad me transmiserat, epistola tua non fuit addita. Hanc unicam nuperrimê abs te exaratam a Dano quodam nobili accepi, cui vicissim hanc meam concredidi. Rectê fecisses, si Pragæ mihi quempiam nominasses, cui fasciculum committerem, tibi porro transmittendum. Amicus illic est mihi summus WENCESLAUS LAVINIUS ab OTTENFELDO, medicus excellentissimus, cum quo Lutetiæ familiarissimê vixi; ubi tum simul erat illustris Baro CAROLUS a ZEROTINO Moravus; Norimbergæ autem est CÆSAR CALANDRINUS, vir ornatissimus, quem adhuc vivere arbitror. Hic litteris transmittendis operam nobis suam haudquaquam denegaturus erit.

Scripsi hæc festinabundus, cum Oda quæpiam ZEROTINO Baroni inscripta ad prelum adornanda esset.

Tu bene vale et me ama.
Dat. Haidelbergæ die V. Martij veteris, anno MDC.
P. MELISSUS.

CRAMERUM vellem in Senarijs suis observare
quarto loco Iambum, qui etiam in secundo requiritur necessario. Corriget igitur,
ubicumque spondeus positus est, si vult imitari HORATIUM et SENECAM in Trag.
Produxit syllabam no in Pannoniæ et ge corripuit in Indulge. Et hoc limandum.
text.english:
**To the illustrious and most excellent man Tycho Brahe, astronomer of Emperor Rudolf II, [his] friend, greeting. At the court of the Emperor, or at Benátky, 5 miles from Prague.**

When I have rather often inquired about you, most noble Brahe, nothing certain could be told me by your kinsman who is staying here for the sake of his studies. For he said he had understood that you would press on into France, unless your affairs at the imperial court should obtain a most longed-for outcome. But now I greatly rejoice that your Urania has found a place most convenient for observation, and that by the bounty of the most munificent Emperor Rudolf II. Taubmann and Brasch, laureate Poets, had prompted me about certain poems to be composed upon your Tyche; these you will now receive with this letter, and will join, if they please, with the other lucubrations of [your] friends. Earlier too, by the renowned David Chytraeus, some copies of letters exchanged between you and the Danish chancellor had been delivered to me, from which I understood more than enough the state — or rather the ruin — of your affairs, while you still lived in your homeland. These I returned to Chytraeus, he so wishing.

For the copy of the *Astronomia instaurata*, in which very many engines [instruments] are seen depicted in colours, I both give and owe you great thanks; as also for the bundle of most elegant poems joined with it, which I read very gladly. Yet I grieved deeply that the matter had come to this, that you should of your own will take up exile — which has, none the less, turned out for you according to your heart's wish, you being about to enjoy a better convenience than in your homeland itself. Lately I have been assiduous over certain manuscript codices, to see whether I might find anything of the ancients about that Philosopher's Stone, to find which so many labours have hitherto sweated in vain. I will also investigate whether perhaps anything has come down to us from the ancients on Astronomical matters; for I see you seek this above all. To the bundle which Taubmann had transmitted to me by your order, your letter was not added. This one [letter], very lately written by you, I received from a certain Danish nobleman, to whom in turn I entrusted this of mine. You would have done rightly had you named me someone at Prague to whom I might commit a bundle, to be passed on to you. I have there a great friend, Wenceslaus Lavinius von Ottenfeld, a most excellent physician, with whom I lived on the most familiar terms at Paris — where at that time was likewise the illustrious Baron Karl von Žerotín, the Moravian; while at Nuremberg is Caesar Calandrinus, a most distinguished man, whom I think to be still living. He will by no means deny us his service in forwarding letters.

I have written this in haste, since a certain Ode inscribed to Baron Žerotín had to be made ready for the press.

Fare you well, and love me.
Given at Heidelberg, the 5th day of March, Old [Style], in the year 1600.
P. Melissus.

I could wish that Cramerus, in his Senarii, would observe an Iamb in the fourth place, which is also necessarily required in the second. Let him correct, then, wherever a spondee has been set, if he wishes to imitate Horace and Seneca in [his] Tragedy. He has lengthened the syllable "-no" in "Pannoniae," and shortened "-ge" in "Indulge." And this must be filed smooth.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & sender.** An **inbound** humanist letter **to** Tycho. **Paulus Melissus (Paul Schede Melissus)** (1539–1602), the celebrated German Neo-Latin poet, imperial *poeta laureatus* and **librarian of the Bibliotheca Palatina at Heidelberg** — writing to congratulate Tycho on his settlement under Rudolf II and to send commendatory verse.
- **Recipient.** **Tycho Brahe**, "astronomer of Emperor Rudolf II"; the address carries a German routing-tag — *am Hof des Kaisers oder zu Benátky, 5 Meilen von Prag* ("at the Emperor's court, or at Benátky, 5 miles from Prague").
- **The poems & the verse-economy.**
 - *Taubmannus* = **Friedrich Taubmann** (1565–1613), Wittenberg poet and professor; *Braschius* = **Brasch**, the Rostock poet (cf. brahe-t_15980905001) — both *Poetae laureati* who prompted Melissus to compose verses *in Tychen tuam* ("on your Tyche" — a pun: Greek *Týchē* "Fortune"/the Muse, ≈ Tycho's name), enclosed here for Tycho's collection of friends' poems.
 - *exemplar Astronomiae instauratae … machinae coloribus depictae* = Melissus thanks Tycho for a **colour-illustrated copy of the *Astronomiae Instauratae Mechanica*** (Wandsbek 1598), with its hand-coloured instrument plates — a notable detail on the deluxe presentation copies.
- **Persons named.**
 - *gentilis tuus* = a **kinsman of Tycho's** (one of the Brahe nephews then studying in Germany) at Heidelberg.
 - *David Chytraeus* = **David Chytraeus** (1530–1600), the Rostock theologian-historian, who had shown Melissus copies of Tycho's letters with the **Danish chancellor** documenting "the ruin of your affairs" before the exile.
 - *Wenceslaus Lavinius ab Ottenfeldo* = **Václav Lavín z Ottenfeldu**, Bohemian physician, Melissus's intimate from his **Paris (*Lutetia*)** days, proposed as a Prague relay.
 - *Carolus a Zerotino Moravus* = **Karel starší ze Žerotína** (Karl von Žerotín the Elder, 1564–1636), the Moravian magnate, also known to Melissus from Paris and the dedicatee of an Ode now at press.
 - *Caesar Calandrinus* = **Cesare Calandrini**, at **Nuremberg**, another possible courier.
- **The alchemy/antiquity note.** Melissus offers to search the Palatina's **manuscript codices** for ancient lore on the **Philosopher's Stone** (*lapis Philosophicus*) and on **astronomy** — "for I see you seek this above all," a glance at Tycho's alchemical and source-gathering interests.
- **Place.** *Heidelberga* = Heidelberg; *Lutetia* = Paris; *Norimberga* = Nuremberg.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S. S.* in the address ≈ *salutem [plurimam]*; *bene vale et me ama* → "fare well, and love me"; *Dat.* = *Datum* → "Given."
- **Calendar (this chapter's convention — explicit Old Style).** Dateline *die V. Martij **veteris*** = "5 March, **Old Style**" — the **Calvinist Palatinate kept the Julian calendar**; marked expressly *veteris [styli]*, to be contrasted with Tycho's New-Style Prague datelines. Year *MDC* = 1600. Reproduced, not converted.
- **What this is.** A closing paragraph of technical literary criticism, added just before the letter's actual farewell (which the published tail preserves) — the humanist poet Melissus giving Tycho a metrical critique to pass on (or simply reporting his own editorial work) on verses in *senarii*, the six-foot iambic line used in Latin comedy and tragedy.
- **The sender.** Paulus Melissus (Paul Schede, 1539–1602), the leading German Neo-Latin poet of his generation, court librarian at Heidelberg; his closing lines (in the published tail) mention preparing an ode to Baron Karl von Žerotín for the press at the very moment of writing — i.e., this is a working poet's letter, and the Cramerus critique belongs to that same professional register.
- **The metrical point, unpacked.** In the iambic senarius, feet 2, 4, and 6 traditionally require a true iamb (short-long) rather than a substitutable spondee (long-long); Melissus is telling Cramerus that his fourth foot needs the same strictness already expected of the second, on the model of Horace and Seneca's tragic verse — plus two specific scansion faults (an incorrectly long "-no" in "Pannoniae"; an incorrectly short "-ge" in "Indulge").
- **"Cramerus" — not identified in the works consulted.** No figure of this name surfaced in the Tycho-circle biographical sources searched; he was presumably a minor Neo-Latin poet in Melissus's or Tycho's orbit whose verses (perhaps addressed to Tycho, given the letter's destination) needed polishing before publication. Flagged as an open identification rather than guessed at.
- **Register note.** "Diatribam"/technical-prosody vocabulary aside, this passage is a useful reminder that Tycho's correspondence network extended into pure literary humanism — verse composition and correction as a shared court accomplishment, not merely astronomy.

text.original:
ILLUSTRI ET GENEROSO DOMINO, DOMINO IOHANNI FRIDERICO HOFFMANNO, LIBERO BARONI IN GRUENPUECHEL ET STRECHAU, PRÆFECTO PROVINCIÆ DUCATUS STYRIÆ ET ARCHIDUCATUS AUSTRIÆ, MARSCHALCHO UTROBIQUE HÆREDITARIO, BURGRAVIO IN STEYER NEC NON SAC. CÆS. MAI. AULÆ CONSILIARIO ET SERENISSIMI ARCHIDUCIS MAXIMILIANI CUBICULARI PRIMARIO, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO INPRIMIS HONORANDO.

ILLUSTRIS ET GENEROSE VIR, DOMINE ET AMICE HONORANDISSIME.

QUOD Illris Dn° tua Nobilem et Eruditissimum Adolescentem FRANCISCUM TENGNAGLIUM et filium meum TYCHONEM non solum adeo comiter et benevole exceperit (neque enim Illris Dnis tuæ eximiam humanitatem sibi exhibitam huc reversi satis deprædicare poterant) sed et cultissimis suis literis sincera erga me benevolentiâ refertissimis mihi rescribere non degravata sit, pro eo Illi Dni tuæ gratias ago quas possum maximas: si quâ in re mea opella illi unquam usui esse possit, quam lubentissime pro virili relaturus.

Quæ M. KEPLERUS (cuius ingenium et consuetudo mihi perplacent, ut dignum eum censeam, qui ametur et ad optima quæque promoveatur) oretenus ad me retulit, percepi. Et quantum ad primum attinet, de studioso illo hîc alendo et informando, actutum respondi, me non saltem in hoc, sed longe maioribus Illri Dni tuæ pro meo modulo gratificaturum: alterum satis prævidi confici non posse, prius quam expressum ab Aulâ Cæsareâ decretum in Cameram mitteretur; quod iam conscriptum esse intellexi. At ubi hæreat, me latet. Quia vero a dicto TENGNAGLIO cognovi, quod, cum ante quatriduum Brandeisium concessisset, ut cum Domino Capitaneo quædam meo nomine loqueretur, eumque illic non repertum Pragæ quæsivisset, Illrem quoque Dnnem tuam pauculis alloquutus sit, quodque consilium illud de KEPLERO atque illo alio, cum illud Illi Dni tuæ paucis exponeret, eidem placuerit, deque eo ipsamet mecum ulterius loqui velit, dabo operam, ut quamprimum nonnulla, quæ pro Cæsareâ Mate, Domino nostro Clementissimo, elaboro, confecta fuerint (nam prius hinc abire vix ausim) assumpto mecum M. KEPLERO Pragam excurram, quo apud Illrem Dnnem tuam hac de re, prout ea suaserit, deliberemus et certi aliquid statuamus. Neque enim ipse KEPLERUS Illri Dnone tuâ inconsultâ quicquam concludere voluit. Quod et ego probo, siquidem absque eiusdem consensu et suasu nihil nobis faciendum censeam. Intellexi quidem quodammodo, nonnullas difficultates sese insinuare, quibus tamen (uti spero) ex Illris Dnis tuæ prudenti provisu facile occurremus, ijsque medelam adhibebimus. Quare omnia circa hoc negotium, donec cum Illri Dne tuâ præsentes de eo egerimus, differenda arbitramur.

Quæ de Mechanico illo Artifice ab Illri Dne tuâ accersendo antedictus TENGNAGLIUS pariter mihi exposuit, cognitu grata erant. Si eum Illris Dn° tua, ubi accesserit, ad me (uti constituit) amandârit, efficiam, ut in Instrumentis ad observationes ratas idoneo modo fabricandis componendisque instructior ad ipsam redeat. Excogitavi iam nuper quoddam ad varios usus minimo negocio conducens, quodque simul per longinqua itinera commodum sit portatu: idque eam præsertim ob causam, quam TENGNAGLIUS noster Illri Dni tuæ secreto aperiet. Præbebit et hoc circuli Sextantem, et non saltem Altitudines et Siderum distantias etiam ultra sextam Cœli partem usque in Quadrantem, imo etiam eo ampliores, quoad intercapedines, solerter et satis subtiliter rimabitur, atque insuper longitudines ac latitudines Planetarum per totum Zodiacum minimo labore et absque tædiosâ supputatione; tum quoque ascensiones rectas et declinationes Stellarum non longe ab Æquatore utrinque dissitarum promet. Quin et, quod plus est, earundem a Meridiano Æquatorias distantias pro temporis momento inter observandum perquirendo et subinde examinando suppeditabit: ut de alijs quibusdam minoribus utilitatibus nihil addam. Ubi vero artifex ille advenerit, illi structuram eius proponam, et si confectioni absolvendæ idoneus (uti existimo) fuerit, cum Illri tuâ Dnne id, quicquid est, lubens communicabo, atque succinctum et multiplicem eius usum eidem reserabo. Plura nunc non addo, ne Illrem Dnem tuam nimium remorer. Si quæ hîc desiderantur, a TENGNAGLIO uberius, si vacârit, percipiet.

Valeat itaque Illris Dn° tua quam optime et diutissime.
Dabantur ex Arce Cæsareanâ Benaticâ die 6 Martij A. 1600.
text.english:
**To the illustrious and generous Lord, Lord Johann Friedrich Hoffmann, Free Baron in Grünbüchel and Strechau, Prefect of the Province of the Duchy of Styria and of the Archduchy of Austria, hereditary Marshal of both, Burgrave in Steyr, and also Aulic Councillor of the Sacred Imperial Majesty and First Chamberlain of the Most Serene Archduke Maximilian, his Lord and friend especially to be honoured.**

Illustrious and generous man, Lord and most honoured friend.

That Your Illustrious Lordship received the noble and most learned young man Franz Tengnagel and my son Tycho not only so courteously and kindly (for, returning hither, they could not sufficiently proclaim the remarkable humanity shown them by Your Illustrious Lordship), but also did not find it burdensome to write me back with your most cultivated letter, most full of sincere benevolence toward me — for this I give Your Illustrious Lordship the greatest thanks I can; and if in any matter my poor service can ever be of use to you, I will most gladly repay it to the best of my power.

What Master **Kepler** — **whose genius and company please me greatly, so that I judge him worthy to be loved and promoted to every best thing** — related to me by word of mouth, I have understood. As to the first point, about that **student to be maintained and instructed here**, I answered at once that I would gratify Your Illustrious Lordship not only in this, but in far greater things, according to my measure. The other [point] I sufficiently foresaw could not be accomplished before an express decree from the Imperial Court were sent to the Chamber — which I understand has now been drawn up, but where it sticks, escapes me. And since I learned from the said Tengnagel that, when four days ago he had gone to **Brandeis** to speak with the Lord Captain in my name, and, not finding him there, had sought him at Prague, he also addressed Your Illustrious Lordship in a few words — and that **that plan about Kepler, and about that other [person]**, when he set it out to you in few words, pleased you, and you wish to speak with me further about it yourself — I will take pains that, **as soon as certain things I am elaborating for the Imperial Majesty are finished (for I would scarcely dare to leave hence before), I will, taking Master Kepler with me, run over to Prague**, that we may deliberate with Your Illustrious Lordship about this, as you shall advise, and settle something certain. For Kepler himself was unwilling to conclude anything without consulting Your Illustrious Lordship — which I too approve, since I judge nothing should be done by us without your consent and advice. I have indeed understood, in a way, that **some difficulties insinuate themselves**, which however (I hope) we will easily meet by Your Illustrious Lordship's prudent provision, and apply a remedy to them. Wherefore I think all things concerning this business should be deferred until we treat of it, present, with Your Illustrious Lordship.

What the aforesaid Tengnagel likewise set out to me about **that mechanical craftsman to be summoned by Your Illustrious Lordship** was pleasant to learn. If Your Illustrious Lordship, when he has come, sends him to me (as you have determined), I will see that he returns to you better instructed in fabricating and assembling, in a suitable manner, **instruments for sure observations**. I have lately devised **something serving various uses with minimal trouble, and at the same time convenient to carry on long journeys** — and that especially for the reason which our Tengnagel will secretly disclose to you. This will furnish a **Sextant of the circle**, and will skilfully and subtly enough search out not only **altitudes** and the **distances of stars** even beyond the sixth part of the heaven, up to a Quadrant — nay, even greater than that, as to the intervals — and moreover the **longitudes and latitudes of the planets** through the whole Zodiac, with minimal labour and without tedious computation; and will also yield the **right ascensions and declinations of stars** set not far from the Equator on either side. Nay, and (what is more) it will supply their **equatorial distances from the Meridian** for the moment of observation, by searching out and then examining — to say nothing of certain other smaller utilities. When that craftsman has arrived, I will propose its structure to him; and if he be fit (as I think) to complete the making, I will gladly share it, whatever it is, with Your Illustrious Lordship, and unfold to you its compact and manifold use. I add no more now, lest I detain Your Illustrious Lordship too much. If anything is wanting here, you will learn it more fully from Tengnagel, if you have leisure.

May Your Illustrious Lordship therefore fare as well and as long as possible.
Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 6th day of March, the year 1600.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD ANONYMUM.

NOBILISSIME ET MAGNIFICE VIR, DOMINE ET AMICE HONORANDE.

ETSI tam propriâ notitiâ quam relatu familiaris mei DANIELIS FELS, qui aliquandiu Pilsnae apud vos substitit, satis exploratam habeo molem occupationum Mag. tuae, quae parum illi temporis legendis et scribendis epistolis relinquit: non esse tamen illi ingratas meas literas, tanto confidentius mihi persuadeo, quanto minus, urgentibus rebus, a scribendo abstinere possum.

Mitto ad Mag. tuam Nobilem et egregie doctum Iuvenem FRANCISCUM TENGNAGL, quo de iam antea, cum Pragae essem, cum Maga tua locutus sum, quod nonnulla mihi negotia, quae M. tuae recensebam, apud Reverendissimum et Serenissimum Archiepiscopum et Electorem Coloniensem expediverit. Fuit is primum in Dania meus aliquandiu domesticus, inde meae migrationis comes in Germaniam. Cum Latinam et Gallicam linguam calleret, Italiam etiam adivit, eamque linguam primum in aula Magni Ducis Hetruriae, postea Romae in aula R. Cardinalis a Dietrichstein probe addidicit. Nuper vero inde reversus in animum induxit primo patriam, quae est in extremis Westphaliae finibus, [et] parentes suos invisere, post, ubi huc, favente Numine, redierit, S. Caes. Mti, Domino nostro clementissimo, si Maiestas eius hac ipsum clementiâ dignata fuerit, in ministerijs aulicis, quibuscunque eidem usui esse possit, operam fidelissimam subiectissime offerre. Est in eo, praeter singularem doctrinam studiorumque cum politicorum tum philosophicorum cognitionem, virtutis amor, morum integritas et gratia: quod facile M. tua deprehendet, ubi notitiam eius qualemcumque ceperit. Rogo itaque M. tuam quam officiosissime, uti sibi hunc iuvenem admodum commendatum habeat, consilioque et intercessione suâ ad optima quaeque promoveat. Commisi praeterea illi paucula quaedam de meis negocijs nondum omnino expeditis, quae M. tuae, quando commodum erit, vel in memoriam revocet, vel a me significet. Quae M. tuae ad ea respondere placuerit, huic concredat, si non per ipsum, quem an hac viâ remeaturus sit, incertus sum, tum per antedictum DANIELEM, quem unâ mitto, ad me referenda.

Valeat Ma tua quam diutissime et felicissime.
Dabantur ex Arce Caesareanâ Benaticâ die 6 Martij 1600.
Magae Tuae studiosiss.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to an anonymous [correspondent].**

Most noble and magnificent man, lord and friend to be honoured.

Although, both from my own knowledge and from the report of my familiar Daniel Fels — who has stayed for some while at Pilsen with you — I am well enough acquainted with the mass of Your Magnificence's occupations, which leaves you little time for reading and writing letters, yet that my letters are not unwelcome to you I persuade myself the more confidently, the less, with matters pressing, I can refrain from writing.

I send to Your Magnificence the noble and excellently learned young man Franz Tengnagel, of whom I already spoke before with Your Magnificence, when I was at Prague — [asking] that he might expedite for me certain matters which I laid before Your Magnificence, with the Most Reverend and Most Serene Archbishop and Elector of Cologne. He was first, in Denmark, for some time a member of my household; thereafter the companion of my migration into Germany. Being well versed in the Latin and French tongues, he went also to Italy, and learned that language thoroughly — first at the court of the Grand Duke of Tuscany, afterward at Rome, at the court of the Reverend Cardinal von Dietrichstein. Lately, however, returned thence, he has resolved first to visit his homeland, which lies in the farthest bounds of Westphalia, and his parents; afterward, when he shall have returned hither, God favouring, to offer most submissively his most faithful service to His Imperial Majesty, our most clement Lord — should His Majesty deem him worthy of this clemency — in whatever courtly offices he can be of use. There is in him, besides singular learning and a knowledge of studies both political and philosophical, a love of virtue, integrity of character, and grace — which Your Magnificence will readily perceive, once you have taken any acquaintance of him at all. I therefore ask Your Magnificence most dutifully to hold this young man highly commended, and by your counsel and intercession to advance him to all that is best. I have besides entrusted to him a few small matters concerning my business not yet wholly dispatched, which he may, when convenient, either recall to Your Magnificence's memory or signify on my behalf. Whatever Your Magnificence shall be pleased to answer to these, let him entrust to this man, to be reported back to me — if not through himself (for I am uncertain whether he will return by this route), then through the aforesaid Daniel, whom I send along with him.

May Your Magnificence fare as long and as happily as possible.
Given from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 6th day of March 1600.
Most devoted to Your Magnificence,
Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** at **Benátky nad Jizerou**.
- **Recipient.** **Anonymous** in the source (*ad anonymum*): a **high imperial official resident at Pilsen (Plzeň)**, where Rudolf II's court had withdrawn — addressed throughout as *Magnificentia tua*, "Your Magnificence." His identity is not recoverable from the text; he is Tycho's contact for advancing both Tengnagel's suit and Tycho's own pending business at court.
- **Purpose.** A **letter of recommendation** carrying Franz Tengnagel to the official, doubling as a progress-note on Tycho's affairs.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Franciscus Tengnagl* = **Franz Gansneb Tengnagel von Camp** (c. 1576–1622), Tycho's noble assistant and future son-in-law. The letter is a valuable **biographical notice** of him: first a member of Tycho's household *in Denmark*, then companion of Tycho's **migration into Germany** (1597); skilled in Latin and French; sent to **Italy**, where he perfected Italian, first at the **court of the Grand Duke of Tuscany** (Ferdinando I de' Medici, Florence), then **at Rome in the court of Cardinal von Dietrichstein**; now planning to visit his parents in Westphalia before entering imperial service. His earlier errand to the Archbishop-Elector of Cologne is also noted.
 - *Daniel Fels* = Tycho's *familiaris* stationed at **Pilsen**, his on-the-spot agent and the carrier of the reply.
 - *Reverendissimus et Serenissimus Archiepiscopus et Elector Coloniensis* = **Ernst of Bavaria, Elector-Archbishop of Cologne**, with whom Tengnagel had expedited business of Tycho's.
 - *Magnus Dux Hetruriae* = the **Grand Duke of Tuscany** (**Ferdinando I de' Medici**); *R. Cardinalis a Dietrichstein* = **Cardinal Franz Seraph von Dietrichstein** (created cardinal 1599), at Rome.
 - *S. Caes. Maiestas, Dominus noster clementissimus* = **Emperor Rudolf II**.
- **Places.** *Benatica arx* = Benátky; *Pilsna* = **Plzeň** (the court's seat); *Westphaliae extrema fines* = Tengnagel's Westphalian homeland; *Italia, Roma* = Italy and Rome.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *Valeat … quam diutissime et felicissime* → "fare as long and happily as possible"; *Dabantur* (epistolary) → "Given"; subscription *Magae Tuae studiosiss[imus]* = *Magnificentiae Tuae studiosissimus* → "Most devoted to Your Magnificence." Tycho's honorific oscillates between third person (*illi … M. tuae*) and direct address; the shift is preserved.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 6 Martij 1600*; edition marks **n.s. (New Style)**, consistent with the Benátky/Prague series of spring 1600. Reproduced, not converted.
- **Correction.** Latin: 'subsistit' corrected to 'substitit' per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 256.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD RUDOLPHUM CORRADUCIUM.

ILLUSTRIS ET MAGNIFICE VIR, DOMINE ET AMICE OBSERVANDISSIME.

QUANTUM me sollicitum habuit vagus quidam rumor de adversâ Illris Dnis tuæ valetudine, tanto maiori gaudio sum affectus, postquam eam salvam et incolumem e longinquo et difficili itinere Italico, legatione perfunctam amplissimâ, in Bohemiam reversam accepi. Quo nomine Deo Opt. maximo gratias ago, eumque precor, ut in posterum quoque Dem Tam incolumem ac florentem Reip. et literis reservet. Non dubito, quin iam antea Do Ta ex alijs cognoverit, quomodo Clementissimæ voluntati Sæ Cæsæ Matis, quam per literas mihi, cum adhuc Witebergæ subsisterem, Do Ta, priusquam in Italiam iret, significavit, superiori Iulio (siquidem remoræ quædam inopinatæ id prius non permiserint) subiectissime paruerim, et postquam huc in Bohemiam veni, in Sæ Cæsæ Matis clientelam benignissime sim receptus. Quare huius rei prolixiori commemoratione apud Dem Tam alias occupatissimam supersedeo.

Id potius agam, ut Illrem Dem Tam debitâ cum reverentiâ obnixe rogem, ut in eâ benevolentiâ, quâ me nihil tale antea promeritum sic complexa est, ut Sæ Cæsæ Mati (quod et ultro facturam confido) me commendare meaque studia promovere non sit degravata (quamobrem etiam gratias ago quas possum maximas, et acturus sum, quoad vixero) in eâ, inquam, benevolentiâ in posterum quoque persistat, meque, sicubi fuerit opus, auxilio consilioque adiuvet. Nam licet de Cæsæ Matis, cuius Clementissimum erga me favorem ratis indicijs expertus sum, in me perseveranter fovendo constantiâ, quâ alias Heroice prædita est, nullatenus addubitem, cum tamen ego hîc peregrinus habear, et instituto vitæ, studiorum ratione, non minus quam locorum intervallo ab Aulâ vestra sim remotus: facile prævideo, quam multa incidere possint, quæ ab Illri De Tuâ, prudentiâ, rerum usu, authoritate, dignitate inprimis pollente, longe melius, quam per me ipsum caveri, et, prout res postulârit, emendari queant. Neque enim possum mihi omnino polliceri, tutiorem me hîc fore, quam antea in Daniâ, ab invidorum morsibus, eorumque, qui sinistre de ijs, quæ tracto, studijs loquentur et sentient, oblocutionibus. Etenim si isthic, ubi radices altius et firmius egeram, ac Consanguineorum, qui in præcipuâ dignitate ibidem constituti, non exiguâ manu stipatus et munitus eram, hoc tamen inertiæ et invidiæ virus amoliri non ita dabatur, quin hæc mea studia fastidiret et non ubique obvios plurimorum Annorum labores irritos reddere tentaret, aut (quod potius elegi) me meamque domum universam in peregrinas oras cum magnâ rei, maiori temporis irrecuperabilis iacturâ importunitate suâ migrare faceret: quanto igitur magis huic communi omnium, qui præter vulgarem consuetudinem aliquid arduum exantlare satagunt, fortunæ iam hîc in exteris locis expositus ero, nullâ familiæ avitæ potentiâ fultus, nisi mihi Deus Opt. max. de fidis, candidis, Dominationisque Tuæ similibus Amicis et fautoribus prospexerit, qui, aut quâ dexteritate cavendi, aut quâ lenitate consopiendi, aut quo animo excipiendi sint, si qui erunt eiuscemodi adversarij occulti vel aperti, oportune norint. Quod ut Do Ta tantâ promptitudine faciat, quantum ipsi est ad id faciendum facultatis, atque ut hoc, quod molior, Astronomicum exercitium, huc in honorem Cæsaris et Imperij a Tuâ inter primos Dne translatum, tutari etiam et promovere non desinat, id equidem rogarem illam operosius, nisi mihi de præclarissimâ et spontaneâ eiusdem voluntate iam antea liquido constaret. Quæ brevitatis caussâ hîc omisi, quodque ea calamus non facile sustineret, illa Do Tua, ubi vacaverit, oretenus audiet ab exhibitore harum, Nobili et Erudito Iuvene FRANCISCO TENGNAGEL, meo domestico, nuper ex Italiâ ad me redeunte, quem Illrem Dem Tuam iam antea Romæ proculdubio vidisse existimo. Qui cum Di Tæ, cuius est observantissimus, conditiones suas, et quid maxime optet, exponere cupiat, eius caussâ Dem Tuam etiam atque etiam quam officiosissime rogo, uti pariter et illum suâ benevolentiâ complectatur et ad optima quæque promoveat. Quicquid in ipsum beneficij contulerit, id veluti mihi quoque præstitum perpetuo gratâ mente agnoscam.

Valeat Illris Dno tua quam diutissime et felicissime, et hanc meam in scribendo audaciam ac prolixitatem pro suo candore sincere interpretetur.

Dabantur ex Arce Cæsareâ Benaticâ 8 Martij 1600.
Illri Doi Tuæ deditiss.
TYCHO BRAHE.

Mitto per prædictum TENGNAGLIUM duos libros ex meis unâ cum Globo quodam Cœlesti
ad restitutionem stellarum a me factam accurate elaboratum. Quæ ut Illris Dno Tua hac vice, donec plura in
hoc studiorum genere ad colophonem, volente Numine, diduxero, boni consulat,
reverenter oro.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO RUDOLF CORADUZ.**

Illustrious and magnificent man, Lord and friend most to be respected.

As much as a certain vague rumour of Your Illustrious Lordship's ill health held me anxious, with so much greater joy I was filled when I learned that you — safe and unharmed, having discharged a most ample legation — had returned to Bohemia from the long and difficult Italian journey. On which account I give thanks to God Best and Greatest, and pray him that in future too he preserve Your Lordship unharmed and flourishing, for the Commonwealth and for letters. I do not doubt that Your Lordship has already learned from others how, **last July** (since certain unexpected delays did not permit it earlier), I most submissively obeyed the most clement will of the Sacred Imperial Majesty — which Your Lordship had signified to me by letter, while I still stayed at **Wittenberg**, before you went into Italy — and how, after I came hither into Bohemia, I was most kindly received into the Sacred Imperial Majesty's clientage. Wherefore I refrain from a longer recollection of this before Your Lordship, otherwise most occupied.

I will rather do this: that I earnestly ask Your Illustrious Lordship, with due reverence, that — in that benevolence with which you have so embraced me (who had deserved nothing such before), that you did not find it burdensome to **commend me to the Sacred Imperial Majesty and promote my studies** (which I trust you will also do of your own accord — for which too I give the greatest thanks I can, and will give as long as I live) — in that benevolence, I say, you would also persist hereafter, and assist me with help and counsel wherever there be need. For although I in no way doubt the Imperial Majesty's constancy (with which he is otherwise heroically endowed) in perseveringly fostering me — whose most clement favour I have proved by sure tokens — yet, since **I am held here a stranger**, removed from your Court by my manner of life and pursuit of studies no less than by the interval of place, I easily foresee how many things may occur which can be guarded against, and (as the matter requires) amended, far better by Your Illustrious Lordship — pre-eminent in prudence, experience, authority, and dignity — than by myself. **For I cannot altogether promise myself that I shall be safer here than before in Denmark from the bites of the envious, and the slanders of those who will speak and think ill of the studies I pursue.** For if there — where I had struck roots more deeply and firmly, and was surrounded and fortified by no small band of kinsmen established in chief dignity — yet this **poison of sloth and envy** could not be so removed but that it disdained these my studies, and tried to render void the labours of very many years (not everywhere [easily] met), or (what I rather chose) by its importunity drove me and my whole house to migrate into foreign regions, with great loss of property and greater loss of irrecoverable time: **how much more, then, shall I now be exposed, here in foreign places, to this fortune common to all who strive to accomplish something arduous beyond the common run — supported by no power of an ancestral family — unless God Best and Greatest provide me with faithful, candid friends and patrons, like Your Lordship**, who may opportunely know with what dexterity such adversaries (hidden or open, if any there be) are to be guarded against, or with what gentleness lulled, or with what spirit met. That Your Lordship would do this with as much readiness as you have ability to do it, and would not cease also to protect and promote this **astronomical exercise which I undertake — transferred hither, to the honour of the Emperor and Empire, by Your Lordship among the first** — this indeed I would ask of you more laboriously, did not your most excellent and spontaneous goodwill already clearly stand established to me. What I have omitted here for brevity (and what the pen would not easily sustain), Your Lordship, when at leisure, will hear by word of mouth from the bearer of these — the noble and learned young man **Franz Tengnagel**, my servant, lately returning to me from Italy, whom I think Your Illustrious Lordship doubtless already saw at Rome. Since he desires to set out to Your Lordship (of whom he is most respectful) **his own conditions, and what he most wishes**, for his sake I ask Your Lordship again and again, most dutifully, that you would likewise embrace him with your benevolence and promote him to every best thing. Whatever benefit you confer on him, I will perpetually acknowledge, with grateful mind, as though performed to me too.

May Your Illustrious Lordship fare as long and happily as possible, and interpret sincerely, after your candour, this my audacity and prolixity in writing.

Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, 8 March 1600.
Most devoted to Your Illustrious Lordship,
Tycho Brahe.

I send, through the aforesaid Tengnagel, two of my books, together with a certain Celestial Globe accurately worked up according to the restitution of the stars made by me. Which [gifts], for this time — until, the Divine Will permitting, I shall have brought more matters of this kind of study to their conclusion — I reverently beg Your Illustrious Lordship to take in good part.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Rudolf Coraduz (Coraduz)**, **Vice-Chancellor of the Empire** — one of Tycho's principal court patrons (the *Coraduz/Barvitius* axis; cf. brahe-t_16000324001, where Coraduz gives the "no equal in astronomy" testimonial; brahe-t_16000813001).
- **Significance — a patronage letter, and Tycho's eloquent statement of an exile's vulnerability.**
 - **Thanks & the chain of patronage.** Tycho rejoices at Coraduz's safe return from a great **Italian legation** (after a false rumour of his illness), and recalls that it was **Coraduz who, by letter to Tycho at Wittenberg (before going to Italy), conveyed the Emperor's summons** — which Tycho obeyed "last July," and was "received into the Imperial Majesty's clientage." (This fixes Coraduz as the channel of the imperial call.)
 - **The request — continued protection against detractors.** The heart of the letter is a candid, moving plea. Though he trusts the Emperor's "heroic constancy," Tycho — *"held here a stranger,"* far from the Court "by my manner of life and pursuit of studies no less than by the interval of place" — **fears he will be no safer "from the bites of the envious" than he was in Denmark**. There, "where I had struck roots more deeply … fortified by no small band of kinsmen in chief dignity," the **"poison of sloth and envy"** still disdained his work and drove him into exile "with great loss of property and greater loss of irrecoverable time"; **how much more exposed now, "supported by no power of an ancestral family,"** unless God grant him "faithful patrons like Your Lordship" to guard against, lull, or meet "adversaries hidden or open." A first-rate self-portrait of the imperial exile's precariousness (cf. the same theme in the Ursus letter, brahe-t_16000328001).
 - **Coraduz's role.** Tycho credits him as **among the first to have "transferred hither" the astronomical work "to the honour of the Emperor and Empire."**
- **Tengnagel's suit.** The bearer, **Franz Tengnagel** (lately back from Italy, whom Coraduz had seen at Rome), wishes to lay before Coraduz **his own conditions and wishes** — i.e. to advance his own court career (he would marry Tycho's daughter Elisabeth in 1601); Tycho commends him warmly, "whatever benefit you confer on him, I will acknowledge as done to me."
- **Persons named.** Rudolf Coraduz; **Franz Tengnagel**; **Rudolf II**. The "kinsmen in chief dignity" allude to the Brahe/Bille connection in the Danish Rigsraad.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *8 Martij 1600*; **New Style** (imperial). Header agrees with the label.
- **What this is.** A paragraph preceding the letter's close describing an actual gift-parcel — two of Tycho's own printed books plus a celestial globe embodying his corrected star positions — being carried to the recipient by a named courier, Tengnagel. This is the kind of concrete presentation-copy evidence that anchors the reception history of Tycho's works.
- **Franz (Frans) Tengnagel.** Franciscus Gansneb Tengnagel van Camp (1573–1636), Westphalian nobleman, pupil and assistant in Tycho's household at Prague, engaged at this date to marry Tycho's daughter Elisabeth Brahe (the wedding followed in 1601); later an imperial courtier who managed the Brahe heirs' long dispute over Tycho's observational legacy after his death [Christianson, *On Tycho's Island* (2000); Christianson et al., *Tycho Brahe and Prague* (2002); Dreyer, *Tycho Brahe* (1890)].
- **"Restitution of the stars."** *Restitutio stellarum* is Tycho's own standing technical term for his systematically re-derived, corrected fixed-star catalogue — the basis on which contemporary globe-makers (see also the 1594 Aslakssøn letter) were building improved celestial globes; rendered here as "restitution" to match established English usage in the secondary literature (Gingerich, Thoren, Mosley).
- **The recipient, Rudolf Coraduz.** Rudolf von Coraduz (Corraduc, Corraducius), who became imperial vice-chancellor after the death of Jakob Kurz von Senftenau in 1594, was one of Tycho's closest contacts within Rudolf II's inner circle at Prague alongside Secretary Johannes Barvitius [Christianson, *On Tycho's Island* (2000); Christianson, *Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens* (2020)] — explaining the deferential, gift-bearing tone of this letter, written from Benátky in the first months of Tycho's Bohemian exile.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD ANONYMUM.

NOBILISSIME ET EXCELLENTISSIME VIR, DOMINE ET AMICE OBSERVANDISSIME.

QUOD tam amanter Dno Va, quo tempore Wandesburgi adhuc in Holsatiâ hærebam, humanissimis et pariter doctissimis suis literis me prævenire voluerit, tanto gratius id mihi accidit, quanto Clarissimorum et Præstantissimorum virorum amicitias cæterorum familiaritati semper præferendas duxi. Quod vero prius ijs a me responsum non sit, Dno Va non meæ, quæ nulla ad Amicis par pari referendum esse solet, negligentiæ, sed locorum intervallo, peregrinationibus meis continuis, et quod vix ulla interim ad Sermam eius Celnem scribendi certa occasio hucusque sese obtulerit, tribuet. Quam nunc per Nobilem et Eruditum Iuvenem FRANCISCUM TENGNAGEL nactus, qui apud vos prius erat et nuper ex Italia reversus iter istuc in Patriam parat, et Sermam eius Celnem, si ullo modo ob viarum et prædonum grassantium pericula licuerit, humillime compellare animum induxit, has gratitudinis erga se meæ testes exarare volui, etiam atque etiam rogans, ut Dno Va negocia illa, quæ Sermæ eius Celni dictus TENGNAGLIUS oretenus (si eam submisse accedere contigerit) vel literis expositurus est, authoritate et intercessione suâ promovere non gravetur. Quæ ipsemet (ubi, uti spes est, accesserit) TENGNAGLIUS clare et seorsim insinuare poterit, quo responsum mature nanciscar. Fecerit D. V. mihi hac in parte rem inprimis acceptam, et quibusvis, quæ a me proficisci unquam poterunt, officijs vicissim pro virili compensandam.

Valeat Dno Va quam felicissime.
Dabantur ex Arce Cæsareâ Benaticâ die 8 Martij 1600.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to an unnamed [correspondent].**

Most noble and most excellent man, lord and most observed friend.

That Your Lordship was willing to anticipate me so lovingly — at the time when I was still lingering at Wandsbek in Holstein — with your most kind and equally most learned letter, fell to me the more gratefully, the more I have always reckoned the friendships of the most distinguished and excellent men to be preferred to the familiarity of the rest. But that no answer was earlier given them by me, Your Lordship will ascribe not to my negligence — of which there is wont to be none, since among friends like must be returned for like — but to the interval of places, to my continual travels, and to [the fact] that scarcely any sure occasion of writing to his Most Serene Highness has hitherto, meanwhile, offered itself. Which [occasion] I have now obtained through the noble and learned youth Frans Tengnagel — who was formerly with you, and, lately returned from Italy, prepares the journey thither into [his] homeland, and has resolved most humbly to address his Most Serene Highness, if in any way it be permitted, on account of the dangers of the roads and of marauding robbers. [Therefore] I wished to write these [lines] as witnesses of my gratitude toward you, asking again and again that Your Lordship not find it burdensome to promote — by your authority and intercession — those affairs which the said Tengnagel will set forth to his Most Serene Highness by mouth (if it befall him to approach her humbly), or by letters. Which the same Tengnagel (when, as is hoped, he shall have approached) will be able to insinuate clearly and separately, so that I may obtain a timely answer. Your Lordship will have done me, in this matter, a thing especially acceptable, and to be compensated in turn — to the best of my ability — by whatever offices can ever proceed from me.

May Your Lordship fare most happily.
Given from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 8th day of March, 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient — unnamed.** The companion of brahe-t_16000309002 (written the next day), to the **same Cologne electoral channel**: an unnamed *most noble and excellent* official who had written first to Tycho while he was at **Wandsbek in Holstein** (1597–98), and who can promote Tycho's affairs "with his Most Serene Highness" — i.e. **Elector Ernst of Cologne**. *Identification flagged*: not named (the two anonymous Cologne-court letters may be to the same person or to two different councillors).
- **Tengnagel.** *Franciscus Tengnagel* — "formerly with you," now returned from **Italy** and bound for his **homeland**, will approach the Elector "if the dangers of the roads and of marauding robbers permit," and carry Tycho's business by word or letter (cf. brahe-t_16000309002, the same errand).
- ***par pari referendum*** — "like to be returned for like" (the friendship-reciprocity maxim); *praedonum grassantium pericula* — "the dangers of marauding robbers," a realistic note on travel in the war-disturbed Empire of 1600.
- ***Serma eius Celnis*** = *Serenissima eius Celsitudo*, "his Most Serene Highness" (the Elector). *Dno Va* = *Dominatio Vestra*, "Your Lordship."
- **Calendar.** *ex Arce Caesareâ Benaticâ die 8 Martij 1600* = **8 March 1600**; Bohemia (imperial) = **New Style** (edition-tagged *n.s.*). Header agrees with the label.
