documents.incipit: ETSI sub finem superioris Anni per Magistrum quendam natione Danum, Consobrinum meum, …

text.original:
GENEROSO, MAGNIFICO ET NOBILI VIRO, DOMINO I. BONGARSIO, SERENISSIMI ET POTENTISSIMI GALLIARUM REGIS APUD GERMANIAe PRINCIPES LEGATO DIGNISSIMO, AMICO SUO VETERI ET INPRIMIS HONORANDO.

MAGNIFICE ET NOBILISSIME VIR.

ETSI sub finem superioris Anni per Magistrum quendam natione Danum, Consobrinum meum, CLAUDIUM BILLEUM, in Gallias comitantem et Francofurtum (uti statuerat) transeuntem, ad te literas dederim, ac de quibusdam negocijs commonefecerim, cum tamen hic Nobilis et Eruditus Iuvenis FRANCISCUS TENGNAGLIUS, meus domesticus meaeque e Dania emigrationis Comes, ex Italiâ nuper ad me reversus ad Nundinas Francofurtenses ire cogitet, ut inde in Comitatu mercatorum tutius Patriam suam, quae est in extremae Westphaliae finibus, accedere atque Parentes invisere queat, postmodum, favente Numine, huc reversurus: non intermittendum duxi, quin unâ cum eodem (qui rerum mearum apprime gnarus est, easque plenius ad te referre poterit) denuo scriberem. Nec tamen ea, quae de Privilegio a Sermo et Potentissimo Galliarum Rege impetrando, deque debito Optimae memoriae DANZÆI nobis solvendo tunc temporis rogavi, iterum pluribus inculcare lubet, cum de tuâ erga me voluntate tam in his quam alijs nihil addubitem, et praedictus TENGNAGLIUS haec ipsa oretenus promptius expositurus sit. Id saltem hac vice officiose rogatum cuperem, ut de quâdam aliâ re, quam is secreto tuae fidei ex me committet, quid fieri posse vel secus existimaveris, dispicias, quo is tam de hac quam coeteris, ubi se huc receperit, mihi referre queat. Quem etiam, prout amicitiâ non indignum experieris, ut tuâ benevolentiâ complectaris, quaeso. Plura non addo. Neque etiam calamus omnia tuto sustinet. Sed is instar vivae Epistolae omnia rectius expediet.

Vale.
Dabantur ex Arce Caesareâ Benaticâ die 9 Martij 1600. Mae
Tuae studiosiss.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**To the generous, magnificent, and noble man, Master J. Bongars, most worthy Legate of the Most Serene and Most Powerful King of the Gauls [of France] among the Princes of Germany, his old friend and especially to be honoured.**

Magnificent and most noble man.

Although toward the end of last year I gave you letters — through a certain Master, a Dane by nation, my cousin Claude Bille, who was accompanying [travellers] into France and passing through Frankfurt (as he had determined) — and reminded [you] about certain affairs: yet, since here the noble and learned youth Frans Tengnagel, my domestic and the companion of my emigration from Denmark, lately returned to me from Italy, thinks of going to the Frankfurt fair, so that thence, in the company of merchants, he may the more safely approach his homeland (which is on the borders of farthest Westphalia) and visit his parents — afterward, the Deity favouring, to return hither — I judged it ought not to be omitted to write again, together with the same (who is exceedingly well-versed in my affairs, and will be able to report them to you more fully). Nor, however, does it please me to inculcate again, at greater length, those things which I then asked — about the Privilege to be obtained from the Most Serene and Most Powerful King of the Gauls, and about the debt of [Charles de] Dançay, of best memory, to be paid to us — since I doubt nothing of your goodwill toward me, both in these and in other [matters], and the aforesaid Tengnagel will more readily set forth these very things by mouth. This only I would this time dutifully ask of you: that, concerning a certain other matter, which he will secretly commit to your good faith on my behalf, you consider what can — or cannot — be done, so that he may report to me both about this and about the rest, when he returns hither. And I beg you to embrace him with your benevolence, as you will find him not unworthy of friendship. I add no more — nor indeed does the pen safely bear everything; but he, like a living letter, will more rightly despatch everything.

Farewell.
Given from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 9th day of March, 1600.
Most zealous of Your Magnificence,
Tycho Brahe.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Jacques Bongars** (Bongarsius, 1554–1612), here in his diplomatic office: **Legate of the King of France (Henri IV) to the Princes of Germany** (cf. brahe-t_15990501001, …16000501001, the Frankfurt book-trade letters). An "old friend."
- **The two standing requests.** Tycho recalls (from his year-end letter, carried by his cousin **Claude Bille** [*Claudius Billeus*], a Dane bound for France via Frankfurt) two matters he had asked Bongars to advance: (1) a **printing/sales Privilege to be obtained from the King of France** for his works; and (2) **"the debt of Dançay, of best memory, to be paid to us"** — i.e. a sum connected with the late **Charles de Dançay** (Danzaeus, d. 1589), the long-serving **French ambassador to Denmark** and Tycho's friend and patron. A third, confidential matter Tengnagel will convey orally and "secretly."
- **Tengnagel.** *Franciscus Tengnaglius, meus domesticus meaeque e Dania emigrationis Comes* — Frans Tengnagel, "the companion of my emigration from Denmark," back from Italy and bound (via the Frankfurt fair, in a merchant convoy, for safety) to his home "on the borders of **farthest Westphalia**" — once more the "**living letter**" (*instar vivae Epistolae*; cf. brahe-t_16000308002/…0309002). *calamus omnia tuto [non] sustinet* — "the pen does not safely bear everything," the discretion-topos.
- **Calendar.** *ex Arce Caesareâ Benaticâ die 9 Martij 1600* = **9 March 1600**; Bohemia (imperial) = **New Style** (same day as the Cologne-channel letter brahe-t_16000309002). Header agrees with the label.
- **Correction.** Removed an extraneous 'te' after 'saltem' in the Bongars letter; Dreyer's print (TBOO VIII p.260, l.24) has none.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD ANONYMUM

GENEROSE AC MAGNIFICE VIR, DOMINE ET AMICE INPRIMIS HONORANDE.

CUM hic Nobilis et Eruditus Adolescens FRANCISCUS TENGNAGLIUS, quem tua Ma iam antea novit, nuper ex Italiâ huc in Bohemiam ad me reversus, in Patriam suam Parentum invisendorum gratiâ nunc cogitet, et in itinere aut reditu Sermum Electorem Coloniensem, Dominum nostrum Clementissimum, denuo humillime accedere, nisi nimia viarum pericula id vetent, omninô constituerit: idcirco vacuum meis ad Mam tuam literis venire non sum passus, ex quo Mae tuae erga me humanissima officia gratâ mente etiamnum recolam, et perpetuo eorundem meminerim, paria relaturus, si vires sufficiant, is aut occasio ulla sese exhibeat. Licet vero quae ad Mam tuam perscribam, praeter ea, quae is commodius et tutius oretenus exponet, non habeam, tamen Mam tuam hisce officiosissime salutare volui, utque dictum TENGNAGLIUM sibi quam commendatissimum habeat, et utriusque nostrûm negotia apud Sermum Principem, prout antea quoque perlubenter et benevole praestitit, promovere atque expeditionem maturam impetrare non gravetur. Cumque idem TENGNAGLIUS instar vivae Epistolae futurus sit, et tam me quam se ipsum concernentia Mae tuae plene et secreto indicaturus, ulteriore scriptione supersedeo, ac per eundem, quam primum fieri possit, favente Numine, ad me revertentem responsum expecto. Deus opt. max. Mam tuam Reip. et bonis literis quam diutissime prosperam et incolumem servet.

Dabantur ex Arce Caesareâ Benaticâ, quam nunc unâ cum meis inhabito, die 9 Martij 1600.
Mae Tuae studiosiss.
TYCHO BRAHE.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to an unnamed [correspondent].**

Generous and magnificent man, lord and especially honoured friend.

Since the noble and learned youth Frans Tengnagel — whom Your Magnificence already knew before — lately returned hither to me, into Bohemia, from Italy, and now thinks of [going] into his homeland, for the sake of visiting his parents, and has altogether resolved, on the journey or the return, again most humbly to approach the Most Serene Elector of Cologne, our most clement Lord, unless the excessive dangers of the roads forbid it: I therefore have not suffered [him] to come empty of letters from me to Your Magnificence — seeing that I still recall Your Magnificence's most kind offices toward me with grateful mind, and shall perpetually remember them, intending to render the like, if my strength suffice and he, or any occasion, present itself. But although I have nothing to write to Your Magnificence beyond what he will more conveniently and safely set forth by mouth, yet I wished most dutifully to greet Your Magnificence with these [lines]; and [I ask] that you hold the said Tengnagel most commended to you, and that you not find it burdensome to promote the affairs of us both with the Most Serene Prince — as before, too, you very willingly and benevolently did — and to obtain a speedy dispatch. And since the same Tengnagel will be as a living letter, and will fully and secretly indicate to Your Magnificence the things concerning both me and himself, I refrain from further writing; and, through the same, returning to me as soon as may be (the Deity favouring), I await an answer. May God Best and Greatest preserve Your Magnificence, prosperous and unharmed, for the Commonwealth and for good letters, as long as possible.

Given from the Imperial castle of Benátky, which I now inhabit together with my [household], the 9th day of March, 1600.
Most zealous of Your Magnificence,
Tycho Brahe.

**Text recovered.** The postscript or enclosure, missing from the first transcription, has been restored from the text of record and translated. The Source and English columns below are now complete.

**Direction note.** **Incoming** letter — *from* **Joseph Justus Scaliger** *to* Tycho. **This is the letter Tycho answers in brahe-t_16000723001 / 16000623001 (23 July 1600)** — there cited as "your letter written at Leiden on 10 March." The two should be read as a pair.

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO VIRO TYCHONI BRAHE IOSEPHUS SCALIGER IULIJ CÆSARIS F. S.

QUONAM fato meo accidisse dicam, Vir nobilissime, ut qui amicis meis diligentiam, studium et officium meum omnibus in rebus, omni tempore probare paratus sim, non solum omnibus modis, quibus id præstare possim, destituar, sed omnia penitus adversa mihi experiar? Ecce ex quo literas tuas accepi, quas Witebergâ discedens ad me dedisti, nunquam conquievi, quin de te et tuarum rerum statu solicite quæsiverim. Nam postremæ tuæ, quæ mihi omnem scrupulum eximere debebant, eæ vero incertiorem me tuarum rerum reddiderunt. Nanque ex illis neque quando constiteris neque ubi lares posueris, colligere potui. Nunquam tamen ab eo tempore destiti percontandi de te, præsertim quum quidam te in Silesia esse et ibi sedem fortunarum tuarum statuisse, tam constanter affirmarent, ut soli tua negotia scire et curare viderentur. Quamdiu M. CHRISTIANUS Danus, vir optimus et tui studiosissimus, hîc fuit, aliqua spes relinquebatur aut meas literas ad te tuto dandi, aut tuas eliciendi. Sed ille prius discessit, quam postremas tuas acciperem. Nunc eæ, quas hodie accepi, centum triginta diebus postquam datæ sunt, omnino bearunt me, quod me omni cura de te, quæ me anxium habebat, liberarunt, quum hactenus penderem animo, quo terrarum meas ad te mitterem, qui ubi consisteres nesciebam. Quanquam vero virtus tua et eruditio eximia non sinit te latere, neque tuas res ignorari, tamen tanta est locorum intercapedo, quæ te a nobis dividit, ut quod de Sole necessarium est, eum prius apud Eoas nationes, quam Hesperias oriri, id omnino tibi conveniat, cuius lucem nobis serius sentire continget quam ijs, qui te fruuntur hospite et a te præsente hauriunt, quod nos ipsis, ne quid dissimulem, invidemus.

Quanta vero lætitia istæ postremæ nos pertuderint, uno verbo non dixerim. Hoc unum credas velim, nihil mihi gratius esse potuisse, quam tibi otium contigisse, quod et tuis studijs et dignitati tuæ convenientissimum esset. Hoc enim unum semper spirarunt vota mea. Felicem te, mi TYCHO, qui non solum universam Europam testem eruditionis tuæ, sed etiam Cæsarem fautorem, adiutorem, et, quod cœlum ipsum invidere possit, studiorum socium nactus sis. Patriam, quam natales dederant, deseruisti, ut eam, quam doctrina tua meruit, adipiscereris. Regem suum Danis Natura dedit: uni Dano TYCHONI virtus Imperatorem adoptavit. Ab altero te abesse dolendum erat, nisi maiorem, in quo vota tua conquiescerent, haberes. Te vero, magne amice, per ius amicitiæ nostræ oro, ut me de statu, instituto et ratione rerum tuarum frequentius certiorem facias, ne qua in posterum mihi de te dubitatio relinquatur. Nam quæ videri posset cessatio aut negligentia in officio literarum, ea potius fuerit ignoratio status rerum tuarum.

Multa vero erant, de quibus te convenire per literas vellem, siquidem per properantiam istius liceret, qui mihi tuas reddidit: qui, ut ad tuas statim responderem, a me exegit, et ita in ipso articulo oppressit, ut vix spatium reliquerit his exarandis. Diatribam enim meam de præcessione æquinoctiorum et confutatione motus octavæ sphæræ ad te mittere cogito, in qua et innumera veterum testimonia a nemine hactenus animadversa studiose collegimus, et stellam illam, quam Polarem vocant, ante mille nongentos sexaginta sex annos in eo loco hæsisse, ubi hodie est, quinque luculentis vetustissimorum scriptorum testimonijs demonstramus. Præterea tot ἀτοπήματα et absurditates, quæ ex illa hypothesi motus octavæ sphæræ sequuntur, adducimus, ut nemo sit nisi imperitus aut invidus, qui contra hiscere audeat. Addo etiam, quod hactenus omnes latuit, præcessionem æquinoctiorum a THALETE usque et ANAXIMANDRO ad HIPPARCHUM admissam fuisse, primumque omnium HIPPARCHUM eam reiecisse, inducto sphæræ octavæ motu in consequentia, adeo ut contra fidem oculorum extremam in cauda Cynosuræ sive Polarem, ut vulgus vocat, esse omnium septem, quæ in asterismo illo sunt, australissimam prodiderit, quæ tamen fuit ante illum, et est hodie, eritque semper borealissima omnium. En quo posteritatem perduxit tanti viri autoritas. Nam ab illo usque hactenus vos ita creditis, et non alia re quam quod αὐτός ἔφα, quod in Mathesi nunquam locum habere debet. Nulli hominum generi hodie magis nocuit antiquitatis imperitia quam nationi Astrologorum. Nihil magis mirari mihi succurrit, quam nemini Astrologo de vitio illius hypotheseos suboluisse, neque quot et quanta absurda ex illa propagari necesse sit, si unum excipias COPERNICUM, qui et præcessionem æquinoctiorum et obliquitatem circuli æquinoctialis animadvertit, sed ignoratione rerum vetustarum ad absurdæ hypotheses confugit. Sane regularem et æquabilem Solis maximæ declinationis decrescentiam ab unica anticipatione æquinoctiorum pendere necesse est, quod a nobis optime demonstratum est. Aliter non potest, nisi per falsas hypotheses. Hinc sequitur polum mundi alium esse a polo æquinoctialis, et lineas meridianas moveri, neque in eadem sede semper hærere. Id nos egregie ex veteribus scriptoribus demonstramus. Denique tota disputatio est historia mathematica, prius testimonijs ab ultima memoria petitis collecta, deinde geometrice demonstrata. Ea adhuc in litura est. Quum per occupationes licebit in mundo describere, mittam ad te. Unum totam rem transigit, si stella polaris semper eidem loco hæsit, nullum locum esse pertinaciæ: omnia necessario, quæ dixi, consequi debere, atque adeo nullum esse motum octavæ sphæræ.

Quod de nobili viro GEORGIO HERWARTO ab HOËNBURG scribis, is iam dudum mihi de literis suis ad me notus est. Sed de stella Veneris quod scribit, videndum ne illi falsum aliquod Chronicon imposuerit homini eruditissimo, sed pro illo munere, quod gerit, occupatissimo, ut illi meliores auctores consulere non licuerit. Nam ut taceam absurditatem, quis, amabo, est iste Romanus Poëta sine prænomine et nomine? Anno quarto ante Christum natum hoc accidisse unde habet? Quis veterum hoc prodidit? Nam nullus eorum quidem, qui hodie supersunt, eius meminit, et quidem pauci supersunt, qui meminisse potuerint, OVIDIUS et MANILIUS, et nescio an alius præterea. Nam HORATIUS anno quinto ante primum Dionysiacum Christi obijt. Et PROPERTIUS nihil tale. Denique decepit hominem eruditum aut memoria aut scriptor malæ fidei.

De ALBATEGNIO utinam tibi satisfacere possem. Tantum abest, ut exemplar Arabicum nancisci possim, ut ne Latini quidem copia mihi sit impræsentia. Equidem mihi constat multa apud illum auctorem partim obscure, partim imperite reddita, quæ fidelius et lucidius explicari poterant. Mitto tibi MANILIUM nostrum, quem per otium ut tibi liceat legere, opto. Nam ex eius gemmis poteritis aliquando astrologiæ vestræ emblemata instruere. Nullus scriptorum neque apud Græcos neque apud Latinos tam male acceptus fuit, vel a mendis, vel a traiectionibus, vel ab ignoratione priscæ Astrologiæ.

Tuas literas rectius Augustam Vindelicorum mittere possis ad nobiliss. virum MARCUM VELSERUM, patritium et Reip. Augustanæ Septemvirum. Is Amstelradamum recte curabit eas. Nam profecto via Hamburgensis longinquior est: nisi aliter tibi videtur; hoc enim arbitrij tui facio. Tantum opto, ut literæ tuæ non solum tuto mihi, sed etiam cito reddantur.

Vale unice Astronomiæ vindex.
Lugduni Batavorum VI Eid. Martias, stylo novo CIↃ IↃ C.

Nondum mihi diatribam tuam ad literas nobiliss. GEORGIIJ HERWARTI
nisi obiter legere contigit, quia statim a lectione tuarum literarum me ad
has conscribendas contuli. Nunc sedulo omnia legam. Iterum vale.
text.english:
**To the most noble man Tycho Brahe, Joseph Scaliger, son of Julius Caesar [Scaliger], [sends] greeting.**

By what fate of mine shall I say it happened, most noble Man, that I — who am ready to prove my diligence, zeal, and service to my friends in all things, at all times — am not only deprived of all the means by which I might do it, but experience all things utterly adverse to me? Behold: from the time I received your letter, which you sent me on leaving Wittenberg, I never rested but anxiously inquired about you and the state of your affairs. For your last [letter], which ought to have removed every scruple from me, made me the more uncertain of your affairs; for from it I could gather neither *when* you had settled, nor *where* you had set your household. Yet from that time I never ceased asking about you — especially since some so constantly affirmed that **you were in Silesia and had set the seat of your fortunes there**, that they seemed alone to know and tend your business. As long as **M. Christianus the Dane [Longomontanus]**, an excellent man and most devoted to you, was here, some hope was left of sending my letters to you safely, or of eliciting yours. But he departed before I received your last. Now those [letters], which I received today, **a hundred and thirty days after they were sent**, have wholly blessed me, in that they freed me of all the care about you that held me anxious — since hitherto I hung in mind as to where on earth I should send mine to you, not knowing where you stayed. But although your virtue and eminent erudition do not let you lie hidden, nor your affairs be unknown, yet **so great is the distance of places dividing you from us**, that what is necessary of the Sun — that it rises among the Eastern nations before the Western — is altogether fitting for you: whose light it falls to us to feel later than to those who enjoy you as a host, and drink from you present — which (not to dissemble) we envy them.

With how great joy those last [letters] struck me through, I could not say in one word. This one thing I would have you believe: that nothing could have been more pleasing to me than that **leisure has befallen you, most fitting both for your studies and for your dignity**. For this one thing my prayers always breathed. **Happy you, my Tycho, who have got not only all Europe as witness of your erudition, but also the Emperor as patron, helper, and — what heaven itself might envy — companion of your studies. You deserted the fatherland which your birth had given, to gain the one your learning earned. Nature gave the Danes their King; to one Dane, Tycho, virtue adopted an Emperor.** It would have been to be grieved that you were absent from the one [fatherland], had you not a greater, in which your prayers might rest. But I beg you, great friend, by the right of our friendship, **to inform me more frequently of the state, plan, and method of your affairs**, lest any doubt about you be left me hereafter; for what might seem a cessation or negligence in the duty of letters, has rather been ignorance of the state of your affairs.

Many things there were of which I would meet you by letter, if the haste of the man who delivered yours to me allowed — who exacted of me that I answer yours at once, and so pressed me in the very moment that he scarce left space for scratching these. **For I purpose to send you my *Diatriba* on the precession of the equinoxes and the confutation of the motion of the eighth sphere** — in which I have studiously collected innumerable testimonies of the ancients, hitherto noticed by no one, and **demonstrate, by five clear testimonies of the most ancient writers, that the star they call the Pole-star stuck, 1966 years ago, in the same place where it is today**. Besides, I adduce so many absurdities [ἀτοπήματα] that follow from that hypothesis of the eighth sphere's motion, that no one but the unskilled or the envious would dare to open his mouth against [it]. I add also — what hitherto escaped all — that **the precession of the equinoxes was admitted from Thales and Anaximander down to Hipparchus, and that Hipparchus, first of all, rejected it, introducing the eighth sphere's motion *in consequentia*** — so that, against the evidence of the eyes, he reported the star at the tip of Cynosura's tail (or the Pole-star, as the vulgar call it) to be, of all the seven in that asterism, the most southern — which yet was before him, is today, and will always be the most northern of all. See whither the authority of so great a man led posterity! For from him until now **you [astronomers] so believe — and for no other reason than that "he himself said it" [αὐτός ἔφα], which ought never to have place in Mathematics.** To no class of men today has ignorance of antiquity done more harm than to the nation of the Astrologers. Nothing comes to me to wonder at more than that **no Astrologer got wind of the fault of that hypothesis** — nor how many and how great absurdities must be propagated from it — if you except **Copernicus** alone, who noticed both the precession of the equinoxes and the obliquity of the equinoctial circle, but, from ignorance of ancient things, **fled to absurd hypotheses**. For the regular and even decrease of the Sun's maximum declination must depend on the single anticipation of the equinoxes — which has been most well demonstrated by us. Otherwise it cannot be, except by false hypotheses. **Hence it follows that the pole of the world is other than the pole of the equinoctial, and that the meridian lines move, and do not always stick in the same seat.** This we demonstrate excellently from the ancient writers. In short, the whole disputation is **a mathematical history** — first collected from testimonies sought from remotest memory, then demonstrated geometrically. It is still in draft. When my occupations allow it to be written out clean, I will send it to you. One thing settles the whole matter: **if the Pole-star always stuck in the same place, there is no room for obstinacy; all I have said must necessarily follow — and so there is no motion of the eighth sphere.**

As to what you write of the noble man **Georg Herwart von Hohenburg**, he has long been known to me by his letters to me. But as to what he writes **about the star of Venus, it must be seen lest some false Chronicle imposed on that most learned man** — but, for the office he bears, most busy, so that he could not consult better authors. For — to be silent of the absurdity — who, pray, is **that Roman Poet without praenomen and nomen**? Whence does he have that this happened in the **fourth year before Christ was born**? Which of the ancients reported this? For none indeed of those surviving today mentions it — and few survive who could have mentioned it: **Ovid and Manilius, and I know not whether any other besides**. For **Horace died in the fifth year before the first Dionysian [year] of Christ**; and **Propertius** [says] nothing such. In short, either his memory or a writer of bad faith deceived the learned man.

Of **Al-Battani [Albategnius]**, would that I could satisfy you. So far am I from being able to get an Arabic copy, that I have not even a Latin one to hand at present. For my part I am sure that many things in that author are rendered partly obscurely, partly unskilfully, which could be explained more faithfully and lucidly. **I send you our Manilius**, which I wish you may read at leisure; for from its gems you [astronomers] may sometime furnish the emblems of your astrology. No writer, neither among the Greeks nor among the Latins, was so badly handled — whether by corruptions, or by transpositions, or by ignorance of ancient Astrology.

Your letters you might more rightly send to **Augsburg, to the most noble man Marcus Welser, patrician and Septemvir of the Augsburg Republic**. He will properly forward them to **Amsterdam**. For truly the Hamburg route is longer — unless it seem otherwise to you; for this I leave to your judgement. I only wish that your letters be delivered to me not only safely, but also quickly.

Farewell, singular champion of Astronomy.
Leiden, the 6th day before the Ides of March [10 March], New Style, 1600.

I have not yet had occasion to read your treatise on the letters of the most noble Georg Herwart, except cursorily, since immediately upon reading your letter I betook myself to writing this one. Now I shall read everything carefully. Farewell again.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondent.** **Incoming**, **Joseph Justus Scaliger** (1540–1609, son of Julius Caesar Scaliger) at **Leiden** → **Tycho**. **The letter Tycho answers in brahe-t_16000723001 / 16000623001 (23 July 1600)** — read the two as a pair (Tycho there rejects Scaliger's "moving meridians" and offers his own *solar* theory of precession).
- **Significance — Scaliger's full precession theory and his *Diatriba* against the eighth-sphere motion (a major scientific statement).**
 - **The *Diatriba*.** Scaliger announces his (still-draft) ***Diatriba de praecessione aequinoctiorum*** — "a mathematical history," collecting ancient testimonies and then demonstrating geometrically that **the Pole-star held its place 1966 years ago as today** (by "five clear testimonies"), so that **the "eighth sphere's motion" is a fiction** generating only absurdities (ἀτοπήματα).
 - **The Hipparchus thesis.** His striking historical claim: **precession was accepted "from Thales and Anaximander to Hipparchus," and Hipparchus *first rejected it*,** introducing the eighth-sphere motion *in consequentia* — even misreporting Polaris as the *southernmost* of its asterism against plain sight. Posterity, Scaliger charges, followed merely on **"ipse dixit" (αὐτός ἔφα), which has no place in mathematics.**
 - **Copernicus and the conclusion.** Only **Copernicus** noticed precession and the obliquity-change, "but fled to absurd hypotheses." Scaliger derives the **even decrease of the Sun's maximum declination** from "the single anticipation of the equinoxes," and concludes — the point Tycho will reject — that **"the pole of the world is other than the pole of the equinoctial, and the meridian lines move."**
 - **The Herwart "Venus-star" critique.** On a chronological datum **Herwart von Hohenburg** had circulated about a **"star of Venus" in the 4th year before Christ** (a Star-of-Bethlehem-adjacent chronology question), Scaliger is scathing: it rests on "a false Chronicle" and an unidentifiable **"Roman Poet without praenomen or nomen"**; the only poets who *could* have recorded it are **Ovid and Manilius** (Horace died too early, Propertius is silent). (Cf. the Herwart letter, brahe-t_16000911001.)
 - **Al-Battani & Manilius.** Scaliger cannot supply **al-Battani** (no Arabic *or* Latin copy to hand) but criticises its existing renderings; and **sends Tycho his own edition of Manilius** ("from its gems furnish the emblems of your astrology") — the most corruption-marred of all ancient authors. (Tycho thanks him for it in the reply of 23 July 1600.)
 - **The courier route.** Scaliger advises routing letters **via Marcus Welser at Augsburg → Amsterdam**, rather than the longer Hamburg route.
 - **The encomium.** The famous compliment: *"Nature gave the Danes their King; to one Dane, Tycho, virtue adopted an Emperor"* — and the Sun-rises-in-the-East conceit for the distance between them.
- **Cross-references.** The **other half of the Scaliger precession exchange** (with the reply of 23 July 1600; and the earlier letter of 17 April 1599, where Tycho requested Hipparchus's equinoxes, the southern asterisms, and al-Battani); ties to the **Herwart** thread (Herwart's letter of 11 September 1600) and the chronology disputes (the letters to Wolfgang Franz of 27 March 1600 and to Bartholomäus Scultetus of 7 January 1600).
- **Persons & works named.** Joseph Justus Scaliger; **Longomontanus** (*M. Christianus Danus*); **Georg Herwart von Hohenburg**; **Thales, Anaximander, Hipparchus, Copernicus**; **Ovid, Manilius, Horace, Propertius**; **al-Battani (Albategnius)**; **Marcus Welser** (Augsburg). Places: **Leiden**, **Silesia** (the false rumour of Tycho's seat), **Augsburg**, **Amsterdam**, **Hamburg**.
- **Calendar.** *Lugduni Batavorum VI Eid. Martias, **stylo novo** CIↃIↃC* → **Leiden, 10 March 1600 [N.S.]** (VI Ides of March = 10 March; CIↃIↃC = 1600); header and label agree. Tycho received it "130 days after"? — no: Scaliger received *Tycho's* after 130 days; Tycho received *this* one "six weeks before" his July reply.
- **Greek terms reproduced.** ἀτοπήματα ("absurdities"), αὐτός ἔφα ("he himself said it"), *Eoas/Hesperias* (Eastern/Western).
- **What this is.** A closing paragraph, preceding the letter's actual farewell (given in the published tail), in which Scaliger acknowledges receipt of a piece of Tycho's own writing — a "diatriba" addressed to Georg Herwart — promising a fuller reading once this reply is off his desk.
- **"Diatriba" — a false friend.** In this Neo-Latin usage "diatriba" means a learned discourse, dissertation, or treatise, carrying none of the pejorative "angry tirade" sense the English cognate "diatribe" has since acquired; rendered here as "treatise" to avoid the false friend.
- **Georg Herwart identified.** Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg (1553–1622), Chancellor of Bavaria, a learned correspondent of both Tycho and (later, more famously) Kepler, with whom he corresponded on both scientific and religious matters and whom he patronised [Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens* (Cambridge, 2007); Gingerich, *An Annotated Census of Copernicus' De revolutionibus*; Martens, *Kepler's Philosophy and the New Astronomy*]. The published tail of this same letter separately shows Scaliger discussing ancient astrology's mistreatment by copyists and editors — a topic entirely consistent with a Tycho–Herwart exchange on the correct interpretation of "prisca Astrologia."
- **The sender.** Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), the preeminent classical philologist and chronologist of the age, then at Leiden; his letter as a whole (published tail) discusses postal routes for reaching him via Marcus Welser at Augsburg.

documents.incipit: TARDIUS mihi redditæ sunt literæ tuæ X Ianuarij scriptæ, Magnifice Domine TYCHO, Vir …

text.original:
MAGNIFICO ET NOBILISSIMO VIRO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, UNICO STUDIORUM MATHEMATICORUM HUIUS SECULI RESTAURATORI, CÆSA........ DOMINO ET AMICO SIC ........LENTER OBSERVANDO.

S.

TARDIUS mihi redditæ sunt literæ tuæ X Ianuarij scriptæ, Magnifice Domine TYCHO, Vir præstantissime: tardius etiam ad illas rescribo, partim propter adversam meam valetudinem (conflictor enim cum febri tertiana, quæ me graviter adhuc affligit) partim etiam quia Typographus non potuit citius de voluntate sua respondere, quam esset edoctus ab ijs, cum quibus egit de papyro sive charta. Dici autem non potest, quam gratæ fuerint literæ tuæ, e quibus libentissime cognovi de sede fortunarum, vel potius studiorum, hoc tempore tibi assignata ab Augustissimo Cæsare. Deum precor toto pectore, ut hæc omnia tibi velit esse secundissima, atque tuos laudatissimos conatus provehat ad optatissimum finem in tota Republica Christiana.

Doctor FISCHERUS agit tibi reverenter gratias, quod eum dignaris tua benevolentia, cui sese totum addit et commendat: forte non indignus, quem complectaris, præsertim ubi melius hominem nosse cœperis.

Ad libros Wittichianos quod attinet, scire te volo, eo ipso tempore, quo huc allatæ fuerunt literæ tuæ, sororem PAULI WITTICHIJ iam ætate provectam celebrasse nuptias secundas, quarum hic fuit exitus, ut nova nupta post LX dies moreretur. Filium unicum reliquit hæredem, cui nondum constituti sunt certi tutores: quod ubi factum fuerit, videbo, an et quid cum illis agi possit. Fuisset mihi res facilior, si ipsa Wittichiana vixisset diutius: videbo tamen, quid fieri et impetrari queat. Audio ab ijs, qui superstite adhuc sorore PAULI WITTICHIJ inspexerunt libros Wittichianos: illi aiunt, omnia esse varie confusa et distracta tanquam Sybillæ folia, nec miror. Erat mulier illa prorsus mirifica et suo sensu abundans.

Quod ad alterum illum Mathematicum attinet, qui ante aliquot annos hîc vixit, si non est molestum, hortor te, ut epistolam non magnam scribere velis ad Medicum huius urbis fortissimum et doctissimum Doctorem DANIELEM BUCRETIUM. Ei sunt noti hæredes, quos reliquit ille Mathematicus, et scio eum tui tam amantem et observantem atque studiosum esse, ut moturus sit omnem lapidem, et operam daturus, quantam poterit maximam, ut desiderio tuo satisfiat, quantum fieri omnino poterit.

Quod ad negocium typographicum attinet, egi cum nostro, quem habet hæc civitas, typographo, et ei significavi, quid de ipso scire velis. Is respondet scripto peculiari, quod mitto, et simul curavit fieri probam, ut nominant, typorum suorum. Tu hæc, mi Domine, leges et cogitabis, et quæ sit tua voluntas, nobis significabis. Ego, si quid hac in re facere potero, quod tibi gratum sit, aut usibus tuis serviat, faciam hoc summa voluntate.

Si quid ad me scribere voles, fac per certos homines mittas Pragam ad Dn. SIMONEM LUCK, Registrator vnd Taxator Ihrer Kay. Mt. bey der Hoffcammer. Is quicquid acceperit, bona fide ad me curabit. Pro versibus nunc missis, quos ad priora carmina aggregavi, magnas ago gratias. Si plane perducta est ad finem editio operis illius tui, quod aliquando vidi, sed adhuc mancum et mutilum, cui titulus TYCHONIS BR. Dani Astronomiæ instaurandæ progymnasmata volumen primum Uraniburgi 1592: peto a te magnopere, ut exemplum Bibliothecæ meæ donare velis, sicut etiam fecisti (quo nomine adhuc magnas tibi gratias ago) cum volumen primum Epistolarum Astron. ad me misisti. Mea officia et studia paratissima tibi semper constabunt pro viribus.

Non licet nunc plura propter febrim, quæ licet nonnihil per Dei gratiam remittat; tamen, nondum adhuc receptis viribus pristinis, admodum langueo. Ille me sanabit, qui me percussit, qui idem est vita nostra, et longitudo dierum nostrorum: in quo etiam sumus, vivimus, et movemur. Oro te, vir præstantissime, ut veniam d[are velis] epistolæ sic scriptæ, ut facile agnoscatur author eius f........

Bene et feliciter vale in Domino Deo nostro, a quo tibi ex animo precor omnes felicitates et quæcunque animus tuus potest, iuxta illius divinam voluntatem, optare.
Datæ subito XIIIJ Martij 1600.
T. M. omni studio et observantia unice colens et amans
IACOB MONAW.
text.english:
**To the magnificent and most noble man, Lord Tycho Brahe, sole restorer of the mathematical studies of this age, [Imperial …], his Lord and friend so … to be respected.**

Greeting.

Your letter, written **10 January**, was delivered to me rather late, Magnificent Lord Tycho, most excellent Man; and I reply to it rather late too — partly because of my own ill health (for I struggle with a **tertian fever**, which still grievously afflicts me), partly because the **Printer** could not answer about his willingness sooner than he was informed by those with whom he dealt about paper. But it cannot be told how welcome your letter was, from which I most gladly learned of the **seat of [your] fortunes — or rather of [your] studies — assigned you at this time by the most august Emperor**. I pray God with my whole heart that he would have all these things be most favourable to you, and advance your most praised endeavours to the most desired end, in the whole Christian Commonwealth.

Doctor **Fischer** gives you reverent thanks that you deign [to honour] him with your benevolence, to which he wholly devotes and commends himself — perhaps not unworthy for you to embrace, especially when you have begun to know the man better.

As concerns the **Wittich books**, I would have you know that, at the very time your letter was brought here, **the sister of Paul Wittich — already advanced in age — celebrated a second marriage, of which this was the outcome: that the new bride died after 60 days. She left a single son as heir, for whom certain guardians have not yet been appointed**; which, when it has been done, I will see whether — and what — can be transacted with them. The matter would have been easier for me had the Wittich woman herself lived longer; yet I will see what can be done and obtained. I hear from those who inspected the Wittich books while Paul Wittich's sister was still living: they say **everything is variously confused and scattered, like the Sibyl's leaves** — nor do I wonder; that woman was utterly eccentric and full of her own notions.

As concerns that **other Mathematician**, who lived here some years ago: if it be not troublesome, I urge you to write a not-large letter to the most stalwart and learned physician of this city, **Doctor Daniel Bucretius**. To him are known the heirs that Mathematician left; and I know him to be so loving, respectful, and devoted to you that he will **move every stone**, and give the greatest effort he can, that your desire be satisfied, as far as can at all be done.

As concerns the **typographic business**, I dealt with our printer, whom this city has, and indicated to him what you wish to know about him. He answers in a special writing, which I send, and has also had a **sample (proof), as they call it, made of his types**. You, my Lord, will read and consider these, and signify to us your will. I, if I can do anything in this matter welcome to you or serviceable to your uses, will do it with the greatest goodwill.

If you wish to write anything to me, see that you send it, by sure men, to Prague, to Lord **Simon Luck, Registrar and Assessor of His Imperial Majesty at the Court-Chamber** — whatever he receives, he will faithfully convey to me. For the **verses now sent**, which I have added to the earlier poems, I give great thanks. If the edition of that work of yours — which I once saw, but still incomplete and mutilated, whose title is ***Tychonis Brahe Dani Astronomiae Instaurandae Progymnasmata, Volume One, Uraniborg 1592*** — has been quite brought to completion, I greatly ask that you would **give a copy to my Library**, as you also did (for which I still give you great thanks) when you sent me the **first volume of the *Astronomical Letters***. My services and zeal will always stand most ready for you, according to my powers.

It is not permitted me now [to write] more, because of the fever — which, though by God's grace it somewhat remits, yet, my former strength not yet recovered, I quite languish. He will heal me who struck me, who is the same as our life, and the length of our days; **in whom also we are, and live, and move** [Acts 17:28]. I beg you, most excellent man, that you would [be willing to give] pardon to a letter so written that its author is easily recognized [as …].

Fare well and happily in the Lord our God, from whom I pray you, from my heart, all felicities, and whatever your mind can wish, according to His divine will.
Given hastily, 14 March 1600.
Cultivating and loving Your Magnificence uniquely, with all zeal and respect,
Jacob Monau.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender & occasion.** **Jacob Monau (Monavius)** of **Breslau** — this is his **reply to Tycho's letter of 10 January 1600 (brahe-t_16000110001)**, and the antecedent of the later Monau letters (brahe-t_16000516001 / brahe-t_16000614001). Written while Monau is ill with a **tertian fever**.
- **Significance — the Wittich-library provenance (key detail).** Monau answers Tycho's standing request for **Paul Wittich's books** (incl. the annotated Copernicus copies; cf. brahe-t_16000110001): at the very time Tycho's letter arrived, **Wittich's aged sister-heir had remarried — and died 60 days later**, leaving **a single son as heir for whom guardians were not yet appointed** (the *pupillus/tutores* of brahe-t_16000516001). He reports the books, seen while the sister lived, are *"variously confused and scattered, like the **Sibyl's leaves**"* — "that woman was utterly eccentric." This is the **pivotal document for the dispersal of the Wittich library** (the "now that the difficult sister is dead" of brahe-t_16000516001 refers to exactly this).
- **The other Breslau astronomer & Bucretius.** Monau routes Tycho's request for the **dead Breslau astronomer's** papers (cf. brahe-t_16000110001) through **Daniel Bucretius**, "the most stalwart and learned physician of this city," who knows the heirs and "will move every stone."
- **Printing & books.** Monau forwards the **Breslau printer's** terms and a **type-sample (proof)**; thanks Tycho for **verses** added to the commendatory collection; and **requests for his Library a finished copy of the *Progymnasmata*** (*Astronomiae Instaurandae Progymnasmata*, vol. 1, Uraniborg 1592), having only seen it "incomplete and mutilated" — as Tycho had earlier gifted him the **first volume of the *Epistolae Astronomicae***. (A datum for the distribution of Tycho's books.)
- **The relay.** Letters to Monau to go via **Simon Luck, Registrar and Assessor (*Registrator und Taxator*) of the imperial Court-Chamber (*Hofkammer*)** at Prague (German title kept by this chapter's convention).
- **Scripture.** *in quo … sumus, vivimus, et movemur* — **Acts 17:28** ("in him we live and move and have our being"); *Ille me sanabit qui me percussit* echoes Job 5:18 / Deut. 32:39.
- **Persons named.** Jacob Monau (sender); **Tobias Fischer**; **Paul Wittich** (his sister-heir and her son); **Daniel Bucretius**; the unnamed dead Breslau astronomer; **Simon Luck** (imperial Hofkammer registrar); **Rudolf II**.
- **Textual flags.** The witness has **lacunae in the address** (*Caesa…… Domino et amico sic ……lenter observando*) and in the **closing** (*veniam d[are velis] … author eius f……*), reproduced with brackets/ellipses; they do not affect the body. **Calendar:** dateline *XIIIJ Martij 1600*; Silesia (Breslau) on the **Gregorian (New Style)** by 1600; the edition gives no place (*s.l.*) — "[Breslau]" supplied as Monau's seat. Marked [N.S.].

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO ATQUE EXCELLENTISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO TYCHONI DE BRAHE, EQUITI ET DOMINO IN KNUDSDORP, SOLLERTISSIMO ASTRONOMIÆ INSTAURATORI ASTRONOMORUMQUE NOSTRI SECULI PRIMARIO, IN ARCE CÆSAREA BENATICA IAM AGENTE, DOMINO SUO DEBITÆ OBSERVANTIÆ STUDIJS COLENDO.

S. P. D.

QUANTO me gaudio affecerit litteræ MONAVIJ mei, Vir magnifice atque excellentissime, Domine et amice observare, vix queo dicere. Non enim solum te veniam mihi dare nunciabant, qui ignotus ad tantum virum meas mittere ausus fueram, sed et eas tibi gratas fuisse, meque in amicorum tuorum numerum abs te susceptum esse, ac memoriam mei animo tuo servare, quemadmodum tuis ad ipsum litteris sis attestatus. Gratias itaque tibi ago, quas mente meâ concipere possum maximas, pro tantâ tuâ humanitate tantâque in me benevolentiâ, et tam benignâ tamque amicâ ad amicitiam tui admissione. Amavi equidem te et colui, suspexi, miratusque sum iampridem tacito quodam sensu, qui nunc lubens se promit, magisque aspirat ad tam suavem iucundamque tuæ benevolentiæ auram. Merentur id virtus tua, ingenium, eruditio, experientia, dignitas, maiestas, quibus me velut adamantino vinculo nexuisti, quod nulla vis laxabit aut dissolvet umquam, nulla, crede mihi, obscuratura est oblivio, donec

Lumine ademto animam moribundo corpore fundam.
Quod tibi hîc non scriptum, sed veluti per syngrapham sponsum volo.

Rogavi, opera tua a typographo ut mihi comparares tuo, quæcunque abs te edita, debitoque precio me illa persoluturum dixi. Vidi apud nonnullos quædam, non omnia, quod non ad nos perferantur a Bibliopolis nostris, quo divina huius scientiæ studia precio nunc apud plerosque sint, non male perspicientibus. Ea quantopere desiderem, nequeo scribere. Age ergo, Vir magnifice, domine et amice observande, ut tuâ operâ ab illo ea impetrem, et quamprimum Pragam ad ERNESTUM HEINCIUM, Cameræ Cæsareæ Registratorem et Expeditorem, coniugis meæ fratrem germanum, vel Vratislaviam ad MONAVIUM mitte, nec me, quod callidæ amantes solent, diu desiderio isto torque. Precium, quod volet ille, statim numerabitur. Velim addi Instrumentorum tuorum delineationem, quam nuper mihi ostendit Medicus D. BARTHOLOMÆUS SWALBIUS, intimus meus, qui et versus meos tibi gratos fuisse narrabat, sed a te recoctos ad salivam et gustum tuum, quod gaudeo; tamen me tanto viro placuisse, summæ laudi duco. Verum, pace tuâ, paucis mentem meam explicabo. Sensus meus est, te errores astrorum motusque dissipatos, quales fuere hactenus, singulari arte et mirâ industriâ in ordinem redegisse certiorem, Deumque tibi uni, quem eruditio et virtus in sublime vexerunt, quod antehac paucis particulatim concessit, nunc divite et pleno Cornu plenâque manu, quasi nimis tantarum opum largum profusorem, suggerere, ut quemadmodum Sibylla paucis contingere dicit apud MARONEM, ut ex Orco ad superas revertantur, et ijs tantum,

quos æquus amavit
Iuppiter, aut ardens evexit ad æthera virtus:
ita etiam tu solus repertus sis, cui digne ista contigerint ante omnes, teque merito nunc, quæ tam large accepisti, largâ manu quoque posteris largiri debere. Particulam Cœlitus pro In, vel Sub Cœlo, semper ego de loco cum omnibus autoribus intellexi, et obscuriorem mihi reddere videtur sensum, quam si legatur: astra sub cœli gemino axe. Sed ignosce, per Deum te oro, excellentissime domine, quod tam libere hæc scribo. Tibi enim manum do, tuo iudicio acquiesco, tuæ censuræ subscribo, teque valere et astronomiæ stabulum, Herculeis tuis laboribus, abs te magis magisque expurgari cupio,

Quæque opto, rata sint, faxit rex ætheris alti,
Ingeniumque tibi, vires, vitamque ministret.
Vigore animum nervosque robore impleat.

Vale ergo, Vir excellentissime, domine et amice, perpetuis debitæ observantiæ studijs a me colende.
Dabam Suidnicij Silesiorum XIIX die Martij anno epochæ Christianorum MDC.
Excell. atque dignitatis tuæ observantissimus
TOBIAS FISCHERUS, Philos. et Med. Doctor, manu propria.

Editi sunt a MERCATORE anno 1541 Lovanij
duo globi, Cœlestis et terrenus, quos ego ipse meis manibus nuper reduxi.
Nunciatum autem mihi est, paucis abhinc annis eosdem correctiores editos
esse Coloniæ, et formâ adhuc maiore, nec
in alia loca chartas istas divulgari. Peramanter itaque etiam atque etiam te
oro, num vera hæc sint, et an non a typographis illis comparari, si non per
me, per aliquem excellentis autoritatis virum queant, significa.

D. ERNESTUS HENCIUS affinis
meus singulis hebdomadibus ad me suas potest mittere litteras.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most excellent man, Lord Tycho de Brahe, knight and lord in Knudstrup, most skilful Restorer of Astronomy and chief of the astronomers of our age, now residing in the imperial castle of Benátky, his Lord, to be cultivated with the zeal of due respect.**

Heartiest greeting.

With how great joy the letter of my **Monau** affected me, magnificent and most excellent Man, Lord and friend to be respected, I can scarcely tell. For it announced not only that you grant me pardon — I who, unknown, had dared to send mine to so great a man — but also that they were welcome to you, and that I have been **received by you into the number of your friends**, and that you keep memory of me in your mind, as you attested in your letter to him. I therefore give you the greatest thanks I can conceive, for your so great humanity and benevolence toward me, and for so kindly and friendly an admission to your friendship. I have indeed loved and cultivated, looked up to, and admired you long since with a certain silent feeling, which now gladly puts itself forth, and aspires the more to so sweet and pleasant a breeze of your benevolence. This your virtue, genius, erudition, experience, dignity, majesty deserve — by which you have bound me as with an adamantine chain, which no force will ever loosen or dissolve, nor (believe me) shall any oblivion darken, until

*"When light is taken away, I pour forth my soul from my dying body."*

Which I wish [regarded] by you here not [as merely] written, but as pledged, as it were, by a bond.

I asked that you procure for me from your printer your works — whatever has been published by you — and I said I would pay for them at the due price. I have seen some among certain [people], not all, since they are not brought to us by our booksellers (who perceive well enough at what [low] price the divine studies of this science now stand with most people). How greatly I desire them, I cannot write. Come then, magnificent Man, Lord and friend to be respected, that by your effort I may obtain them from him; and send them as soon as possible to Prague, to **Ernst Heincius**, Registrar and Dispatcher of the Imperial Chamber, my wife's own brother, or to Breslau to **Monau** — and do not, as cunning lovers are wont, torment me long with that longing. The price he wishes will be paid at once. I should wish to be added the **drawing of your Instruments**, which the physician Lord **Bartholomäus Schwalb**, my intimate, lately showed me — who also related that my verses were welcome to you, but **recooked by you to your taste and palate** (which I rejoice at; nevertheless I count it the highest praise to have pleased so great a man). But, with your leave, I will explain my mind in a few words. My opinion is that you have, with singular art and wonderful industry, reduced into surer order the **errors and scattered motions of the stars**, such as they have been hitherto; and that God supplies to you alone — whom erudition and virtue have raised on high — what before he granted to few, and [only] piecemeal, now with a rich and full Horn [of plenty] and full hand, as if [you were] too lavish a dispenser of such great riches: so that, just as the Sibyl says in **Maro** [Virgil] that it befalls few to return from Orcus to the upper world, and to those only

*"whom favouring Jupiter loved, or whose blazing virtue raised to the heavens"* —

so you too alone have been found, to whom these things have worthily befallen before all; and that you deservedly ought now to bestow with liberal hand on posterity what you have so liberally received. The particle ***Coelitus*** ["from heaven"], for *In* or *Sub Coelo* ["in" or "under heaven"], I have always understood, with all authors, of place; and it seems to render the sense more obscure to me than if it be read: *"the stars under the twin axis of heaven."* But forgive me — by God I beseech you, most excellent Lord — that I write these things so freely; for I give you my hand, I acquiesce in your judgement, I subscribe to your censure, and I desire that you fare well, and that the **stable of astronomy** be more and more cleansed by you, by your **Herculean labours**:

*And may the things I wish be ratified — may the King of high heaven grant it,*
*and supply you genius, strength, and life;*
*may he fill your mind with vigour, and your sinews with strength.*

Farewell, then, most excellent Man, Lord and friend, to be cultivated by me with perpetual zeal of due respect.
Given at Schweidnitz [Świdnica] of the Silesians, the 18th day of March, in the year of the Christian epoch 1600.
Most respectful of Your Excellence and dignity,
Tobias Fischer, Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine, with his own hand.

Two globes, a celestial and a terrestrial, were published by Mercator in the year 1541 at Louvain, which I myself recently brought home with my own hands. But I have been informed that a few years ago the same [globes], more corrected, were published at Cologne, and in a still larger format, and that these sheets are not made available anywhere else. I therefore beg you, most affectionately, again and again, to inform me whether this is true, and whether they cannot be procured from those printers — if not through me, then through some man of excellent standing.

Master Ernestus Hencius, my kinsman, can send his letters to me every week.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tobias Fischer**, Silesian poet and physician (*Philosophiae et Medicinae Doctor*), of **Schweidnitz (Świdnica)** — the *"Doctor Fischer"* of the Monau correspondence (brahe-t_16000110001, brahe-t_16000516001, brahe-t_16000614001), whose commendatory poem Tycho had emended. This is his **effusive letter of thanks** on being admitted to Tycho's friendship (which Tycho had signalled in his letter to Monau).
- **Significance — a humanist fan-letter, and a book-request.** Beyond the lavish encomium, two concrete points:
 1. **Request for Tycho's published works.** Fischer asks Tycho to have his **printed works** sent (he has seen "some, not all," the booksellers not stocking such little-valued science), to be delivered to **Ernst Heincius** — Registrar and Dispatcher of the **Imperial Chamber** at Prague, **Fischer's brother-in-law** — or to **Monau** at Breslau; "the price will be paid at once." He also wants the **engraved delineation of Tycho's instruments**, which his intimate, the physician **Bartholomäus Schwalb** (*Swalbius* — the *Schwalmius* courier of brahe-t_16000110001), had shown him. Schwalb reported Fischer's verses "welcome to [Tycho], but **recooked to your taste**" — i.e. Tycho's emendation (cf. brahe-t_16000110001/516001).
 2. **A textual nicety in Tycho's verse.** Fischer, "with your leave," questions the word ***Coelitus*** ("from heaven") in one of Tycho's verses, preferring (for clearer local sense) *"astra sub coeli gemino axe"* ("the stars under the twin axis of heaven") — a courteous scholarly demurral, instantly subordinated to Tycho's judgement.
- **The verse quotations (kept as verse; this chapter's convention).**
 - *"Lumine ademto animam moribundo corpore fundam"* — "when light is taken away, I pour forth my soul from my dying body" (a hexameter, apparently Fischer's own / adapted), pledging undying friendship.
 - ***Virgil, Aeneid* VI.129–130**: *"…quos aequus amavit / Iuppiter, aut ardens evexit ad aethera virtus"* — "whom favouring Jupiter loved, or whose blazing virtue raised to heaven" (the Sibyl, on the few who may return from the underworld) — applied as a figure for Tycho's unique divine gift; the surrounding *Sibylla … apud Maronem … ex Orco ad superas revertantur* paraphrases the same passage (*Aen.* VI.126–129).
 - The closing tricolon (*"Quaeque opto, rata sint…"*) — Fischer's own verse-prayer for Tycho's genius, strength, and life.
 - The *astronomiae stabulum … Herculeis tuis laboribus … expurgari* figure casts Tycho's reform of astronomy as **Hercules cleansing the (Augean) stable**.
- **Persons named.** Tobias Fischer (sender); **Jacob Monau**; **Ernst Heincius** (imperial Chamber registrar, Fischer's brother-in-law); **Bartholomäus Schwalb** (physician). Tycho styled *Astronomiae Instaurator* ("Restorer of Astronomy").
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Suidnicij Silesiorum XIIX [=18] die Martij anno … MDC*; Silesia (Schweidnitz) kept the **Gregorian (New Style)** by 1600; marked [N.S.].
- **What it is.** The recovered opening of a letter from Tobias Fischer, a physician and philosopher writing from Świdnica (Schweidnitz) in Silesia, to Tycho Brahe, dated 18 March 1600 New Style — the surviving published text is only the closing valediction and verses.
- **The globes.** Fischer reports having personally brought home a set of Gerard Mercator's celebrated 1541 Louvain celestial and terrestrial globes, and asks Tycho to confirm a rumour of an improved, larger Cologne reissue of restricted distribution. Adam Mosley's *Bearing the Heavens* quotes this identical passage independently (drawing on the printed Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia) in a discussion of Tycho's own instrument- and globe-collecting around 1600 [Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens* (2007)] — strong independent corroboration of both text and sense.
- **Context.** Mercator produced this globe pair at Louvain within the circle of Gemma Frisius and the other Louvain cosmographers who, a decade later, also shaped John Dee's training — the same intellectual milieu behind Sophia's "Louvain Core Group" concept in Dee studies, though this letter itself carries no Dee connection.
- **Ernestus Hencius.** Fischer names "D. Ernestus Hencius," his kinsman ("affinis meus"), as a weekly courier for correspondence between them; no independent identification of this person has been found among the works consulted — worth flagging as an open prosopographical lead.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter and both trailing postscripts against Dreyer TBOO VIII pp.267-270 (page images, read visually). Page 271 was confirmed to belong to the next letter (Iessenius to Tycho, 14/24 March 1600), so nothing of this letter falls outside the read range. Every name, number and date checked (Monavij, Ernestum Heincium / Ernestus Hencius, Bartholomaeus Swalbius, the Virgil tag 'quos aequus amavit Iuppiter...', Mercatore anno 1541 Lovanij / Coloniae, Dabam Suidnicij XIIX die Martij anno epochae Christianorum MDC) matches Dreyer exactly. No defects found; this independently confirms the pre-existing Secure grade rather than merely accepting it on the translator's say-so.
