documents.incipit: CLARISSIME Domine Doctor IESSENI, amice plurimum semper colende, scripsit quidam …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD IOHANNEM IESSENIUM A IESSEN.

S. P.

CLARISSIME Domine Doctor IESSENI, amice plurimum semper colende, scripsit quidam domesticus noster, quem nuper Pilsnae in Aula habui, in rebus meis solicitantem, se a praecipuo quodam Saae Caesae Matis, Domini nostri Clementissimi, Consiliario subintellexisse, URSUM quendam Dithmarsicum supplicationem iam pridem de me conquerentem Consiliarijs porrexisse, sed ignominiose, acri adhibitâ obiurgatione, reiectam: cumque is, qui haec mihi insinuavit, nihil praeterea de contentis supplicationis istius addiderit, et idem Pilsnâ in Patriam suam, quae ad Westphaliam est, abierit, nec eius reditum intra tres vel quatuor menses expectem, ac nihilominus mea intersit tempestive scire, quid impudens iste de me conqueri ausus fuerit, cum illum nullo pacto, imo ne verbulo quopiam, sive per me sive per alios, toto tempore quo in Bohemiâ sum, laeserim, utut iam antea intolerandas ab ipso perpessus iniurias atque calumnias, quas in isto famoso, quod ante triennium Pragae contra me in publicum edidit scripto (quo putidius et vanius, cordatorum iudicio, hoc seculum vix vidit) conglomerare non erubuit; sed peculiari consilio, tum quoque ob graviorum occupationum distractionem, omnia, ac si ea ignorarem, dissimulavi: et certe, si mihi obviam fieret URSUS iste, eum non nôssem, nec mihi constitit, an is interea Pragae, an vero alibi fuerit, nam de ipso percontari non dignatus sum, ut nisi eius supra modum perfricta frons et scurrilitas, mentiendique inverecundia mihi non alias constarent, mirari satis non possem, quid ille de me, ita taciturno, nullâque molestiâ illum afficiente, querelae loco, apud Amplissimos Dominos Consiliarios adferre possit: Neque enim quidpiam habet, quod veraciter dicat, nisi hoc ipsum obijcere velit, quod taceam, atque ex alto ipsius nugas hactenus despexerim, suo tamen forte tempore in ipsum retorquendas, quamvis per eas non tam meae famae atque existimationi (quae mille eiuscemodi Sycophanticos allatratus non moratur) nocuerit, quam quod suam petulantem dicacitatem et scurrilem naturam, convitijs et maledictis scatentem, toti Mundo omnibusque sincere iudicantibus, suo se iudicio, tanquam sorex, prodens, propalaverit. Licet vero Prudentissimi Domini Consiliarij illius levitatem morum et verborum forte non ignorantes, querelas istas non admiserint, sed ipsum obiurgatum dimiserint: ne tamen aliqua suspicio adhuc latitare possit, ipsum nonnulla, haud iniuria, conquestum fuisse, sed occasiones illi, a me vel meis, ut hoc faceret, datas esse: nosti enim illud nimis in mundo tritum: Calumniare audacter, semper aliquid adhaeret; te per amicitiam nostram, quibus possum precibus, rogo, velis omnem movere lapidem, ut exemplar supplicationis eius adipiscar, vel si id commode fieri nequeat, saltem ut summam eorum, quae continebat, resciscam. Quod si alio modo obtineri non possit, spero te apud Magcum et Nobilissimum Dominum MECKERUM (quem non dubijs inditijs, et etiam te, cum ultimo Pragae simul essemus, idipsum referente, mihi sincere faventem persuasum habeo) id, quicquid est, percepturum. Feceritis sic non saltem ille, sed et tu mihi rem admodum acceptam, atque ut mihi a talibus subdolis et immeritis delationibus inposterum praecavere valeam, haud inutilem, imo fortean etiam necessariam. Sic enim fieri conditiones meae nunc exigunt; sum enim hîc peregrinus, nec Illustrium aut authoritate praecellentium Virorum consanguinitate et necessitudine, ut antea in Patriâ, fultus, quin et praeterea hîc extra Aulam vitam ago umbratilem, ignarus, quid isthic de me in quamcunque partem dicatur, nec alias libenter rebus me immisceo alienis, sed meis solummodo vacans studijs, Spartam, quam nactus sum, pro virili ornare satago, ut in honorem optimi Imperatoris atque Imperij ea, favente supremo Numine, moliri atque exequi queam, quae ad omnem posteritatem utilia et memorabilia futura confido. Sed tu, mi amantissime IESSENI, pro ea quae nobis intercedit familiaritate, omnia satis perspicis, ut ulteriore commemoratione non sit opus, et te nostris hac in parte desiderijs non defuturum omnino mihi polliceor.

Vale et praedictum Magcum Dominum MECKERUM ex me officiosissime saluta.
Dabantur festinanti calamo ex Arce Caesareâ Benaticâ Die 28 Martij Anni 1600.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO JOHANNES JESSENIUS A JESSEN.**

Heartiest greeting.

Most renowned Lord Doctor Jessenius, a friend always much to be cultivated: a certain servant of ours, whom I lately had at the court at **Pilsen**, soliciting in my affairs, has written that he gathered from a certain chief Councillor of the Sacred Imperial Majesty, our most clement Lord, that **a certain Ursus, the Dithmarsian, had some time ago presented to the Councillors a supplication complaining about me — but [that it was] ignominiously rejected, with sharp rebuke applied**. And since he who intimated this to me added nothing further about the contents of that supplication, and the same man has gone from Pilsen into his fatherland, which is in Westphalia (nor do I expect his return within three or four months), while it nonetheless concerns me to know in good time **what that impudent fellow dared to complain of about me** — when I have in no way, nay, not by any little word, whether through myself or through others, injured him the whole time I am in Bohemia (although I had already before suffered intolerable injuries and calumnies from him, which he did not blush to heap up in that **infamous writing he published at Prague against me three years ago** — than which, in the judgement of the wise, this age has scarcely seen anything more putrid and vain) — but, by particular design, and from the distraction of weightier occupations, I dissembled everything, as if I knew nothing of it. And certainly, if that Ursus came to meet me, I would not know him; nor is it established to me whether he was meanwhile at Prague or elsewhere, for I have not deigned to inquire about him — so that, did I not otherwise know his beyond-measure brazen front, his scurrility, and his shameless lying, I could not sufficiently wonder what he could bring as a complaint against me — I so silent, and afflicting him with no annoyance — before the Most Ample Lords Councillors. For he has nothing he may truly say, unless he wishes to object this very thing: that I am silent, and have hitherto **from on high despised his trifles** (to be retorted upon him, perhaps, in their own time) — though by them he has harmed not so much my fame and reputation (which heeds not a thousand such sycophantic barkings) as that he has made manifest, to the whole world and all sincere judges, his own petulant scurrility and scurrilous nature, teeming with insults and curses — betraying himself by his own judgement, **like a shrew-mouse**. But although the most prudent Lords Councillors — perhaps not ignorant of his lightness of manners and words — did not admit those complaints, but dismissed him rebuked: yet, lest some suspicion may still lurk that he complained of some things not without cause, but that occasions were given him, by me or mine, to do it (for you know that saying too trite in the world: ***"Slander boldly — something always sticks"***) — I ask you, by our friendship, with what prayers I can, that **you would move every stone, that I may obtain a copy of his supplication** — or, if that cannot conveniently be done, at least that I may learn the sum of what it contained. And if it cannot be had another way, I hope you will get it, whatever it is, with the Magnificent and most noble Lord **Mecker** (whom, by no doubtful signs — and you too reporting the same, when we were last together at Prague — I hold to be sincerely favourable to me). You will thus do me — not he alone, but you too — a thing very welcome, and not useless (nay, perhaps even necessary), that I may guard myself henceforth against such crafty and undeserved accusations. For so my present conditions require: I am here **a stranger**, not propped (as before in my fatherland) by kinship and the bond of illustrious or pre-eminently authoritative men; and besides, here I live a **shadowy [retired] life outside the Court**, ignorant of what is said there about me in any direction; nor do I otherwise gladly meddle in others' affairs, but, devoting myself only to my studies, **strive to adorn, to the best of my power, the Sparta I have obtained** — that, to the honour of the best Emperor and of the Empire, I may, by the favour of the supreme Power, contrive and accomplish things I trust will be useful and memorable to all posterity. But you, my most loving Jessenius, by the familiarity that passes between us, perceive all this well enough, so that there is no need of further mention; and I altogether promise myself that you will not fail my wishes in this part.

Farewell, and greet the aforesaid Magnificent Lord Mecker from me most dutifully.
Given with hurrying pen from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 28th day of March, the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Johannes Jessenius (Jan Jessenský)**, the anatomist and Tycho's intimate (cf. brahe-t_16000324001, brahe-t_16000327002, brahe-t_16001008001), well placed at the imperial court.
- **Significance — a principal document of the Tycho–Ursus feud.** This letter concerns **Nicolaus Reimers Bär, "Ursus"** (c. 1551–1600), of **Dithmarschen** — the imperial mathematician who had **plagiarised Tycho's geo-heliocentric world-system** and savaged him in print. Tycho has learned (via a servant, from a chief imperial councillor) that **Ursus lodged a supplication/complaint against him with the Councillors, which was *ignominiously rejected with sharp rebuke*** — and asks **Jessenius to obtain a copy of that supplication** (or at least its substance), if necessary through the favourable councillor **Lord Mecker**, "that I may guard myself against such crafty and undeserved accusations." This belongs to the **legal/printed contest of 1597–1600** (Tycho was preparing the *Apologia* against Ursus that became, posthumously, the *Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata* appendix / the suit pursued after Ursus's death in 1600). Cross-links to brahe-t_15990321001 (the "Dithmarsic brute" and the plagiarism brief).
- **The earlier defamatory book.** *"that infamous writing he published at Prague against me three years ago"* = **Ursus's *De astronomicis hypothesibus* (Prague, 1597)** — "than which, in the judgement of the wise, this age has scarcely seen anything more putrid and vain." Tycho stresses he had met all this with **deliberate silence** ("from on high I have despised his trifles"), having "in no way injured him … the whole time I am in Bohemia."
- **Tycho's self-portrait (notable).** A striking statement of his position as **imperial exile**: "I am here **a stranger**, not propped by kinship and the authority of great men as before in my fatherland," living "**a shadowy life outside the Court**," meddling in nothing, "devoting myself only to my studies" — and so the more exposed to undeserved slander, hence the need to know the charge. The closing *"the Sparta I have obtained, I strive to adorn"* (*Spartam quam nactus es, hanc orna* — the classical maxim of doing one's duty in one's appointed station) frames his astronomical work "to the honour of the best Emperor and of the Empire … useful and memorable to all posterity."
- **Proverbs / figures (kept and glossed).** *"Calumniare audacter, semper aliquid adhaeret"* — **"Slander boldly, something always sticks"** (the maxim of calumny's residue); *tanquam sorex … prodens* — "betraying himself **like a shrew-mouse**" (the proverb *sorex suo perit indicio*, the shrew destroyed by its own squeak); *Sycophanticos allatratus* — "sycophantic barkings."
- **Persons named.** Johannes Jessenius; **Nicolaus Reimers Bär (Ursus)**, "the Dithmarsian"; **Lord Mecker** (a favourable imperial councillor); **Rudolf II** and the imperial **Councillors**.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Die 28 Martij Anni 1600*; **New Style** (imperial). Header agrees with the label.
- **Correction.** Latin corrected from 'bonorem' to 'honorem' per Dreyer, TBOO VIII p.282.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD DAVIDEM CHYTRÆUM.

S. P.

REVERENDE et Clarissime vir, Amice inprimis honorande. Literas tuas iuxta initia Novembris superioris Anni Rostochio ad me datas paulo post huius primordia per filium huc revertentem accepi, proque singulari tua, quam isthic affatim declaras, erga me affectione et benevolentiâ gratias habeo plurimas. Respondissem citius et quæ in mei gratiam annuis tuis Historijs inserere decrevisti paulo aliter formata misissem, nî mihi tuæ tardius quam existimabas fuissent redditæ; defectus etiam tabellariorum effecit, ut id prius exequi non licuerit. Remitto autem nunc chartam illam, iuxta quam ea, quæ de Cæsa Mate ob me huc vocatum et benignissime exceptum memorare constituisti, in quibusdam, uti vides, certis de caussis mutata consignavi, omnia tamen tuo arbitrio, an sic vel aliter scribi velis, relinquens; acceptumque mihi est, quod hoc officium in mei gratiam non detrectes, et spero id Cæsæ Mati placiturum. Quia vero relationi de hoc præterito Anno illa immisceri non poterant, haud incongruum duxerim ad huius 16 Centenarij, quem Iubilæum vocant, eadem applicare, sumptâ occasione, quod hoc anno Progymnasmata mea Instaurationis Astronomicæ et nonnulla alia Opera, in Daniâ prius inchoata, sub auspicijs Augustissimi Imperatoris RUDOLPHI Secundi, Domini nostri Clementissimi, eius præsidio et liberalitate fultus, in publicum ediderim; sic enim, Deo conatibus nostris aspirante, me effecturum spero.

Habeo insuper gratias, quod ea, quæ isthic in Orbe Arctoo proximis temporibus gesta sunt, communicaveris. Inaudivi CAROLUM Ducem totâ Sueciâ iam potitum; utinam victoriâ illâ moderate uti vellet, nec nimis in eos, qui illi restiterunt, sævire, et Regni Senatoribus (inter quos est optimus ille ERICUS SPARRÆUS noster) parcere, ut pacatius et firmius eius sit in posterum Regimen, ne exitum infelicem sortiatur effera vindictæ cupiditas. Exemplum habet domesticum in ERICO fratre.

Quid in Dania Patria mea geratur, et an novas res isthic moliantur, qui fatis præsunt publicis, necdum mihi liquet. Optandum, ut pace hac, quâ multis iam Annis gaudent, diu frui possint, nec internis aut externis irrequietudinibus turbentur. Batavos pacis conditiones quascunque suspectas habere et renuere, accepi, adeo ut quidam apud eos Primarius nuper Hamburgum in hunc modum (prout eius formalia verba ad me relata sunt) perscripserit: Si concederetur Statibus Hollandiæ in membrana, quæ æquaret magnitudine bovinum tergus, quascunque ipsimet vellent pacis conditiones, consignare, easdemque ratas se habituros addicerent adversarij, tamen pacificationem omnem aversaturos, cum toties sub tali prætextu delusi sint.

De Ungaricis rebus nihil hîc, relatu dignum, scitur; per hyemem transactam parum a Cæsareanis effectum est. Dicitur Turca maiorem parare exercitum quam unquam antea. Cæsar noster vicissim, quantum potest, se contra ipsum armat, utut Imperij Principes pro maiore parte propter Hispanorum incursiones subsidia denegent et quædam alia agant. WAIUODA pro se recuperatam Transylvaniam feudi loco retinere laborat, cuius Legati admodum insolenter et tumultuarie nuper Pilsnæ se gesserunt, idque Imperator indigne ferens misit quendam ex suis, qui ea de re apud WAIUODAM conquereretur. Dicunt aliquot millia Gallicorum equitum et vicinarum Regionum adventare contra Turcas in gratiam Cæsaris belligeraturi. Quantam stragem ediderint superiori Anno Tartaricæ incursiones in superiori Ungaria et parte aliqua Moraviæ, existimo te iam antea percepisse. Deus tam eorum quam Turcarum furores et Tyrannidem reprimere atque a cervicibus Christianorum avertere dignetur. Ubi plura de rebus, quæ ibi atque in viciniâ gesta sunt, intellexero, te eorum reddere conscium non intermittam.

Cæsar adhuc Pilsnæ abest, ubi ultra semestre proxime elapsum mansit, ob luem Epidemicam, quæ gravissime antecedente anno totam Bohemiam et propinquas regiones infestavit, paulo post Pascha, uti existimant, Pragam rediturus. Deus ipsius Matem nobis quam diutissime florentem atque incolumem conservet. Cui etiam Divino Numini te tuosque commendo. Vale et generum tuum Dominum Doctorem IOHANNEM FREDERUM, cui pro carminibus missis gratias habeo, ex me peramanter saluta; scripsissem ei, si otium suppetijsset.

Dabantur ex Arce Cæsareâ Benaticâ Die 28 Martij Anno 1600 stylo novo.

CIRCA hoc tempus inclaruit apud Augustissimum et
potentissimum Imperatorem RUDOLPHUM eius
nominis secundum in Bohemia et
circumiacenti Germania ac vicinis regnis
TYCHO BRAHE ex illustri et perantiquo stemmate nobilitatis Danicæ oriundus interque fratres suos in regno
illo viros splendidos et dignitate præpollentes natu maximus. Is enim, cum
plurimis retro annis divinæ Astronomiæ a mendis repurgandæ et redintegrandæ
incredibiles labores et sumptus exantlasset, hoc anno sua Astronomicæ
instaurationis Progymnasmata et quædam alia in hoc sublimi studiorum genere sub
auspicijs dicti Imperatoris optimi publici iuris fecit, ut Astronomia quoque
suum sic quoddam inveniret Iubilæum. Occasio autem, quod is e Daniâ Patriâ suâ
primum in Germaniam , deinde Bohemiam præter omnium expectationem migravit, hæc
fuit. Ante annos 24 ex clementissimâ provisione laudatissimæ memoriæ Regis
Danorum FRIDERICI II
TYCHO in insula
Hellesponti Danici
Huænna arcem Uraniburgum pro exercitijs sideralis scientiæ isthic commode
peragendis decore et sumptuose extruxit et in eâ plurima instrumenta Astronomica
adeo magnifice et solide elaborata, ut vix similia orbis alibi viderit, a se
inventa et confecta disposuit (veluti etiam in Historiâ nostrâ Arctoâ suo loco
aliqualem huius Uraniburgi fecimus
mentionem) quæ omnia, quoad vixit dictus Serenissimus Rex, isthic in debito usu liberaliter
conservabantur, quemadmodum etiam post eius luctuosum obitum per totum octennium
in Interregno, spe insuper facta, tam a Clementissimo Rege illo FRIDERICO, quam postmodum Regni eius cunctis
Senatoribus, quod illa omnia in honorem Regni et Regis ibidem competenter
sustentanda et perpetuanda forent. Verum cum non saltem præter ipsius TYCHONIS,
sed et multorum aliorum, tam intra quam extra Regnum illud, opinionem id
postmodum aliter ceciderit, ille, ne tantus apparatus Astronomicus tantique ab
illo per 21 annos ibi exantlati labores paulatim collabascerent tandemque
prorsus interirent, maluit Patriâ dulcissimâ et plurimis de nobilitate primariâ
sanguine iunctis cæterisque amicis charissimis derelictis, sponte unâ cum tota
domesticâ familiâ in peregrina transire potius quam huius tam insperatæ et
dolendæ ruinæ spectator esse, ideoque ante triennium, anno nimirum 1597, circa
solstitium æstivum, assumptâ secum (uti dictum) totâ domo suâ, primum huc
Rostochium enavigavit, ubi per anni quadrantem substitit, quo in hac viciniâ
Danis suis rem rectius dispiciendi, Patriæ adhuc studens, tempus relinqueret.
Quâ etiam de caussâ hinc
ingruente hyeme in Holsatiam, Daniæ pariter conterminam, se recepit, eo per literas
Nobilissimi et optimæ memoriæ Herois, Domini HENRICI RANTZOVIJ, Regij isthic Vicarij, affinis sui, invitatus,
a quo arcem Wandesburgum, urbi Hamburgæ vicinam, cum suis inhabitandam accepit,
ibique annuum tempus moratus est. Neque enim longius
indicatâ de caussâ se, utut conditiones non incommodæ interim oblatæ essent,
conferre voluit. Dum itaque ibi subsistit, ad nunquam satis laudatum Imperatorem
RUDOLPHUM de hoc TYCHONIS e Patriâ
discessu rumor perfertur. Quare ipsius Cæsarea
Maiestas, uti est erga omnes liberales disciplinas, inprimis vero
hoc sublime Astronomiæ studium, quod omnibus ætatibus regales animos, cœlo nata
pectora movit, ut id in precio habuerint, animo favorabili et benignissimo
TYCHONEM, de quo antea inaudierat, eum hisce serio invigilare, multumque
operæprecij locasse, ad se vocatum in Bohemiam cum totâ familiâ traduxit, ipsumque Clementissime
acceptum in arce quadam e suis, quinque miliaribus Pragâ, Regni Metropoli, dissitâ,
Bennaticâ dictâ, ut isthic otio fruens
philosophico inchoatam Astronomicæ restitutionis telam pertexeret, alijsque
ingenuo homine dignis exercitijs vacaret, collocavit, et sumptibus ad tam arduos
labores requisitis liberaliter et benignissime ei prospexit, utut ob belli
Turcici diuturnitatem difficiliora quam
alias tunc forent tempora. Res sane summi Orbis Monarchæ liberalitate et
munificentiâ dignissima, atque ad omnem posteritatem deprædicanda. Quin et de
novo Uraniburgo, quod Danico illi non cederet, se convenienti loco et tempore,
pro TYCHONIS Instrumentis ibi collocandis et rite usurpandis, se provisurum,
atque ipsi et familiæ eius Feudo idoneo, ne alienigenæ redditi in posterum ad
honestam sustentationem necessarijs destituerentur, benignissime provisurum,
Clementissimâ voluntate addixit, quemadmodum hæc et similia ad nos et alios hinc
inde viros præstantes et eruditos non sine omnium voluptate a fide dignis relata
et scripta accepimus. Sic Generosus ille TYCHO BRAHÆUS, Astronomiæ cultorum
nostri seculi antesignanus, cuius sublime ingenium et indefessum in hisce
præcipuis disciplinis, quæ circa siderum motus versantur, illustrandis studium,
quod toti Daniæ singulari ornamento et honori superioribus annis fuerat, eâ
relictâ, in Cæsaris ditiones concessit,
ibique portum quietum suis studijs, non sine Dei peculiari provisu, a
potentissimo Imperatore adeptus est. Faxit author Universi, cuius gloriam cœli
enarrant, et opera manuum ostendit æther, ut in Augustissimi Imperatoris
RUDOLPHI II, qui hoc negocium suo
clementissimo favore et liberalitate promovit, totiusque Imperij Germanici decus
et honorem utilitatemque, quo ad sidera durant, nunquam intermoriturum omnia
vergant et stabiliantur.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO DAVID CHYTRAEUS.**

Heartiest greeting.

Reverend and most renowned man, friend especially to be honoured. Your letter, sent me from Rostock about the beginning of November of last year, I received a little after the beginning of this [year], through my son returning hither; and for your singular affection and benevolence toward me, which you abundantly declare therein, I give very many thanks. I would have replied sooner, and would have sent — formed a little otherwise — those things you resolved to insert in my honour into your **annual Histories**, had yours not reached me later than you thought; the lack of couriers, too, prevented my doing it earlier. But I now return that **sheet**, in which I have set down — in certain places changed, as you see, for sure reasons — those things you resolved to record **about the Imperial Majesty, on account of my being called hither and most kindly received**, leaving all, however, to your judgement, whether you wish it written so or otherwise; and it is welcome to me that you do not decline this service in my honour, and I hope it will please the Imperial Majesty. But since those things could not be inserted into the account of this past Year, I should think it not incongruous to apply the same to [the account of] this 16th-century [year], which they call the **Jubilee** — taking the occasion that **this year I have published the *Progymnasmata* of my Astronomical Restoration, and some other Works begun earlier in Denmark, under the auspices of the most august Emperor Rudolf II**, our most clement Lord, supported by his protection and liberality; for so, God favouring our endeavours, I hope to bring it about.

I have thanks besides, that you have communicated what has lately been done there, in the Northern world. I have heard that **Duke Charles has now gained all Sweden**; would that he would use that victory moderately, not rage too much against those who resisted him, and **spare the Senators of the Realm (among whom is that best man, our Erik Sparre)**, that his rule may be more peaceful and firmer hereafter, lest a savage desire of vengeance meet an unhappy outcome. He has a domestic example in [his] brother **Erik**.

What is happening in Denmark, my fatherland — and whether those who preside over public destinies are contriving new things there — is not yet clear to me. It is to be wished they may long enjoy this peace, which they have had now for many years, and not be disturbed by inner or outer unrests. I have heard that **the Dutch hold suspect and refuse any peace conditions whatever** — so much so that a certain leading man among them lately wrote to Hamburg in this manner (as his exact words were reported to me): **that if it were granted to the States of Holland to set down, on a parchment that would equal an ox-hide in size, whatever conditions of peace they themselves wished — and the adversaries pledged to hold the same ratified — yet they would reject all pacification, since they have so often been deceived under such pretext.**

Of Hungarian affairs nothing worth relating is known here; during the past winter little was accomplished by the imperial [forces]. The **Turk** is said to be preparing a greater army than ever; our Emperor in turn arms himself against him as much as he can, although the Princes of the Empire for the most part **deny subsidies on account of the Spaniards' incursions** and do certain other things. The **Voivode** strives to retain Transylvania, recovered for himself, in the manner of a fief; his envoys lately behaved quite insolently and tumultuously at **Pilsen**, and the Emperor, taking it ill, sent one of his men to complain of the matter to the Voivode. They say some thousands of **French cavalry**, and [those] of neighbouring regions, are coming to wage war against the Turks for the Emperor's sake. How great a slaughter the **Tartar incursions** wrought last year in Upper Hungary and some part of Moravia, I think you have already perceived. May God deign to repress the furies and tyranny both of them and of the Turks, and to turn [them] away from the necks of Christians. When I learn more of what is done there and in the neighbourhood, I will not fail to make you aware of it.

The Emperor is still away at **Pilsen**, where he has stayed beyond the past half-year on account of the **epidemic plague** which last year most grievously infested all Bohemia and the neighbouring regions — about to return to Prague, as they think, a little after Easter. May God preserve His Majesty for us, flourishing and unharmed, as long as possible; to which Divine Power I also commend you and yours. Farewell; and most lovingly greet from me your son-in-law Lord Doctor **Johann Freder**, to whom I give thanks for the poems sent; I would have written to him, had leisure sufficed.

Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 28th day of March, the year 1600, New Style.

About this time there rose to renown, at the court of the most august and most powerful Emperor Rudolph, the second of that name, in Bohemia and the surrounding parts of Germany and the neighbouring kingdoms, Tycho Brahe — sprung from an illustrious and most ancient line of Danish nobility, and, among his brothers, men splendid and pre-eminent in rank within that kingdom, the eldest by birth. For he, having in very many years past expended incredible labours and expense in purging and restoring divine Astronomy from its errors, in this year, under the auspices of the said most excellent Emperor, made public his Progymnasmata of the Restoration of Astronomy and certain other works in this sublime kind of study, so that Astronomy too might thus find, as it were, its own Jubilee.

Now the occasion of his migrating, beyond everyone's expectation, from Denmark his native land, first into Germany and then into Bohemia, was this. Twenty-four years ago, by the most gracious provision of King Frederick the Second of Denmark, of most praised memory, Tycho built handsomely, and at great expense, on the island of Hven in the Danish Sound, the castle of Uraniborg, for the convenient carrying-out there of the exercises of the science of the stars; and in it he set up very many astronomical instruments, wrought so magnificently and solidly that the world has scarcely seen the like elsewhere, invented and made by himself — just as we too, in our Historia Arctoa, have in its proper place made some mention of this Uraniborg. All of this, for as long as the said Most Serene King lived, was there generously maintained in its due use, just as also, after his lamentable death, throughout the whole eight years of the Interregnum, hope was moreover given — [earlier] by that most gracious King Frederick himself, and afterward by all the Senators of his Kingdom — that all these things would be suitably supported and perpetuated there, in honour of the Kingdom and of the King.

But since afterward, contrary to the expectation not only of Tycho himself but of many others, both within and outside that Kingdom, this turned out otherwise, he — lest so great an astronomical apparatus, and labours of such magnitude expended by him there over twenty-one years, should gradually collapse and at last utterly perish — chose rather, having left behind his most beloved native land, very many kinsmen of the foremost nobility joined to him by blood, and his other dearest friends, of his own accord to pass into foreign parts together with his whole household, than to be a spectator of this so unhoped-for and lamentable ruin. And so, three years ago now, namely in the year 1597, about the summer solstice, having taken with him, as has been said, his whole household, he first sailed hence to Rostock, where he remained for a quarter of a year, so as to leave time, in that neighbourhood, for his fellow Danes to look more rightly into the matter — he being still solicitous for his native land.

For that reason too, with winter coming on, he withdrew from there into Holstein, likewise bordering on Denmark, invited thither by letters of the most noble Lord Heinrich Rantzau, hero of most excellent memory, the Royal Viceroy there, his kinsman; from him he received the castle of Wandsbek, near the city of Hamburg, to inhabit with his household, and there he stayed a year's time — for, the reason having already been indicated, he was unwilling to settle any further off, however not inconvenient the terms meanwhile offered to him might have been.

While, then, he was staying there, a report of Tycho's departure from his native land was carried to the never sufficiently praised Emperor Rudolph. Wherefore His Imperial Majesty — being disposed, as he is, toward all the liberal disciplines, but chiefly toward this sublime study of Astronomy, which in every age has moved royal minds and hearts born for heaven to hold it in high esteem — with a favourable and most benign spirit, having heard beforehand of Tycho and that he was earnestly devoted to these pursuits and had achieved much of worth, summoned him to himself and brought him across into Bohemia with his whole household. Having received him most graciously, he settled him in a certain one of his castles, five miles distant from Prague, the capital of the Kingdom, called Benátky, so that there, enjoying philosophical leisure, he might weave to completion the web of the restoration of Astronomy which he had begun, and might have leisure for other pursuits worthy of a man of liberal condition; and he provided for him, liberally and most kindly, the expenses required for labours so arduous — even though, on account of the length of the Turkish war, the times were then more difficult than they would otherwise have been. A thing indeed most worthy of the liberality and munificence of the greatest Monarch of the world, and to be proclaimed to all posterity.

Nay more, [the Emperor] pledged, with most gracious will, that as to a new Uraniborg, which should not yield to the Danish one, he would himself provide, at a fitting place and time, for the placing and proper use there of Tycho's Instruments; and that he would most kindly provide him and his household with a suitable fief, lest, once rendered foreigners, they should in future be left destitute of what is necessary for an honest maintenance — even as we ourselves have received these and similar things, related and set down by trustworthy men, not without delight to us all, [addressed] to us and to other excellent and learned men here and there.

Thus that noble Tycho Brahe, standard-bearer among the votaries of Astronomy in our century — whose sublime genius and untiring zeal for illustrating these foremost disciplines concerned with the motions of the stars had in former years been a singular ornament and honour to all Denmark — having left that land behind, passed over into the Emperor's dominions, and there, not without God's own particular providence, obtained from the most powerful Emperor a quiet harbour for his studies. May the Author of the Universe, whose glory the heavens declare and whose handiwork the sky displays, grant that all things may incline toward, and be established in, the never-dying glory, honour, and profit — for as long as the stars endure — of the most august Emperor Rudolph the Second, who has advanced this business with his most gracious favour and liberality, and of the whole German Empire.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient & occasion.** **David Chytraeus**, the Rostock historian — Tycho's reply to **a Chytraeus letter of "about the beginning of November [1599]"** (a later one than brahe-t_15981007001, the 7 Oct 1598 letter), continuing the **annual-history thread**.
- **The migration-narrative for the *Saxonia* (cross-ref).** Tycho returns the **sheet** on which Chytraeus had drafted his account "about the Imperial Majesty … on account of my being called hither," with Tycho's **emendations "for sure reasons,"** all left to Chytraeus's judgement. Since it could not fit the prior year's account, Tycho proposes applying it to **the *Jubilee* year 1600**, on the occasion that "**this year I have published the *Progymnasmata* of my Astronomical Restoration**" under Rudolf II's auspices. (The same narrative Sturtz and Brasch also pursued; cf. brahe-t_16010415002, brahe-t_16000920002, brahe-t_16000916002. Chytraeus would die in 1600, leaving the work unfinished.)
- **The Scandinavian news.** **Duke Charles of Sweden** "has now gained all Sweden"; Tycho hopes he will be **moderate and spare the Senators — "that best man, our Erik Sparre"** (executed at the Linköping Bloodbath, 1600) — warning by the "domestic example" of Charles's deposed brother **Erik XIV**. (Cf. brahe-t_15991203001, brahe-t_16010418001.)
- **The Dutch "ox-hide parchment" anecdote (a vivid set-piece).** Tycho relays a striking figure of **Dutch distrust of Spanish peace overtures**: a Holland leader wrote that even if the **States of Holland** were allowed to write *their own* peace terms "on a parchment as large as an ox-hide," and the enemy pledged to ratify them, **they would still refuse all pacification — "so often have they been deceived under such pretext."** A memorable contemporary image of the Eighty Years' War deadlock.
- **The Hungarian war.** The **Turk** preparing a great army; the Emperor under-supported (the German princes denying subsidies, citing **Spanish incursions**); the **Voivode** (**Michael the Brave**) seeking Transylvania *as a fief*, his envoys "insolent" at Pilsen; **French cavalry** expected; the **Tartar incursions** into Upper Hungary and Moravia. (Cf. brahe-t_16000926002, brahe-t_16010415002.)
- **Persons named.** David Chytraeus (and his son-in-law **Johann Freder**, *Frederus*); **Charles of Sweden** and his brother **Erik XIV**; **Erik Sparre**; the **Voivode** (Michael the Brave); **Rudolf II**.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Die 28 Martij Anno 1600 stylo novo*; **New Style** (imperial). Header agrees with the label. (Same date as the Ursus letter, brahe-t_16000328001.)
- **What the recovered text is.** A third-person Latin biographical notice of Tycho ("CIRCA hoc tempus inclaruit...") that forms the missing head of the letter catalogued as Tycho Brahe → David Chytraeus, Benátky, 28 March 1600; the published tail ("non intermittam... Vale...") is Tycho's own first-person close. Since the recovered text never shifts into Tycho's own voice, it reads as an enclosure carried within his covering letter rather than as part of the letter proper — and the exact seam between the two is itself unrecovered.
- **Not a private scrap.** The identical incipit ("CIRCA hoc tempus inclaruit apud Augustissimum...") recurs in *Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia* (vol. VIII, among the documents around Tycho's letter to Duke Ferdinand of 18/28 January 1601), confirming this text had an established place in the printed correspondence record and is not merely a manuscript fragment lost to the transcription defect.
- **The "Historia Arctoa" authorship crux.** The aside "as we too, in our Historia Arctoa, have in its proper place made some mention of this Uraniborg" is illuminated by a separate, later Brahe letter on record in the register of Tycho's correspondence, in which Tycho refers explicitly to "Historia Arctoa ab optimo illo CHYTRAEO inde ab Anno millesimo quingentesimo inchoata" — "the Historia Arctoa, begun by that excellent Chytraeus from the year 1500" — almost certainly Chytraeus's own *Chronicon Saxoniae* (Rostock 1590; Leipzig 1593), which Tycho hoped to see extended to a full century by 1600. This makes it likely the "we" of the enclosure speaks in Chytraeus's own authorial voice — i.e. that this is, or closely follows, Chytraeus's own draft chronicle entry on Tycho for the year 1600, which Tycho is here returning (corrected or endorsed) under cover of his letter. FLAGGED AS CRUX: the precise authorship and transmission chain — Chytraeus drafting it and sending it to Tycho for correction, versus Tycho supplying a third-person self-notice (a known contemporary convention) for Chytraeus to copy verbatim — cannot be settled from this fragment alone.
- **Internal chronology checks out exactly.** Uraniborg "twenty-four years ago" (built from 1576, correct for a document of March 1600), "twenty-one years" of labour there (1576–1597), departure "three years ago... 1597" via a quarter-year at Rostock then a year at Rantzau's Wandsbek, and the Danish Interregnum given as "eight years" (Frederick II's death 1588 to Christian IV's 1596 majority) — all match the documented record (Dreyer 1890; Christianson, *On Tycho's Island* / *The Measure of the Heavens*).
- **The Emperor's unfulfilled promises.** The notice records, as of March 1600, Rudolf II's pledge to build Tycho a Bohemian "new Uraniborg" and to grant him and his family a fief so that, as émigrés, they would not be left without honest means of support — a specific, datable undertaking that can be set against what was actually delivered before Tycho's death in October 1601 (Benátky, then a Prague town residence, no purpose-built observatory, and only partial family provision).
- **Heinrich Rantzau** appears as the Royal Viceroy in Holstein and Tycho's kinsman who hosted him at Wandsbek Castle in 1597–98, consistent with Lohmeier (2000) on Rantzau.

documents.abstract: Thanks an anonymous correspondent for congratulations on his imperial appointment and reflects on divine providence in securing a tranquil harbour after difficulties in his homeland.
documents.incipit: REVERENDE et Praestantissime Vir, Amice honorande, quas cum filio meo huc revertente mihi …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD ANONYMUM

S. P.

REVERENDE et Praestantissime Vir, Amice honorande, quas cum filio meo huc revertente mihi rescripsisti literas, circa huius labentis Anni initia accepi, et pro Amicâ atque candidâ congratulatione de conditionibus, quas Deus Opt. Max. apud hunc Augustissimum Imperatorem mihi et meis studijs prospexit, proque benevolo tuo voto, quo precaris, ut omnia inposterum feliciter stabiliantur et adaugeantur, maximas quas possum tibi habeo gratias. Elucet hinc sincerus ille tuus affectus, quo me diu multumque prosecutus es; invenies me pari perpetuo erga te tuosque animo. Et certe sic est, uti scribis, agnosco Divini Numinis singularem providentiam et benignitatem, quâ me a difficultatibus, quibus in Patriâ obnoxius fui, Clementer ereptum in portu tranquilliore hîc locavit. Et sane non possum satis depraedicare huius optimi Imperatoris non saltem Caesareum, sed et Paternum (si sic loqui liceret) erga me animum; qui vel inde perspicitur, quod licet ipsius Matas ob Epidemicos morbos, qui gravissime Bohemiam hoc antecedente Anno afflixerunt, Pragâ abfuerit, et in civitate Pilsna hinc 15 miliaribus distante sese continuerit, durante adhuc infectione illâ, atque in hoc quoque loco, quem inhabitandum mihi concessit, totâque viciniâ saeviente, tamen proprio motu de me et meis sollicita fuerit, adeo ut aliquoties huc, quomodo valeremus, expiscatum miserit, simul Clementissime offerendo, si in quamcunque aliam ipsius Matis Arcem, ubi tutius degere foret, secedere vellem, id mihi licere, liberum etiam relinquendo, si Viennam Austriae me conferre luberet, ubi tempestive de commodâ habitatione caeterisque necessarijs mihi prospicere vellet. Atqui ego, actis humilime gratijs, me hîc potius in statione meâ mansurum et Divinae protectioni ac voluntati omnia commissurum respondi. Agoque eidem Deo misericordi protectori toto pectore gratias, quod me totamque domum meam, in tantis periculis, quibus undique cingebamur, incolumes conservârit, oroque, ut inposterum suâ gratiâ nobis adesse dignetur.

Recte a te factum, quod Historiolam nostrae in Bohemiam migrationis, et eorum, quae postea mihi hîc evenerunt, quam OLIGERO ROSÆKRANTZIO, communi amico, ob eam quae nobis intercedit amicitiam intimam, ut de consanguinitate et affinitate nihil dicam, paulo luculentius retuleram, resignaveris atque perlegeris. Cumque inde statum mearum rerum sufficienter perceperis, in quo etiam Dei benignitate nunc persistit atque inposterum, eodem favente, plenius augeri poterit, non duco operaeprecium quidpiam de eodem hîc repetere. Expecto brevi supellectilem meam et Instrumenta Magdaeburgi relicta, tum quoque ea, quae Hamburgi sunt, quae per meos emissarios e Dania ante hyemem eo transferri curavi; scripsit enim Imperator ad utriusque Civitatis Magistratum, ut in sui gratiam illa omnia huc per Albim advehi faciant: cumque Magdaeburgenses Senatores subterfugia quaedam quaererent, ipsius Matas ad Capitulum eiusdem loci hoc nomine alias dedit literas, quod se lubentissime ipsius Caeae Matis voluntati obtemperaturum promisit; interea structurae pro Instrumentis hîc debito modo disponendis parantur.

Quod M. CHRISTIERNO LONGOMONTANO hortator fuisti, ut me accederet, idque ei persuasisti, pergratum mihi est; dabo operam, ut ipsum huius itineris non poeniteat, liberumque ei relinquam vel hîc apud me vel Pragae esse, quam diu voluerit.

De coeteris, quae scribis, bene inter nos convenit, prout aequum et oportunum fuit. Audio apud vos esse Suecum quendam Astronomicis studijs addictum, nomine ........ qui etiam Observationibus Coelestibus delectatur; si efficere poteris, ut is huc veniat, erit id mihi acceptum et ipsi non inutile; iuvabo eius conatus, quantum potero.

Audio Regnum Suecicum illud, continuis bellis et tumultuationibus iam diu conquassatum, in potestatem CAROLI Ducis venisse. Deus flectat eius cor, ut hac victoriâ et potentiâ moderate utatur, atque ijs, quos pro adversarijs habet, clementer parcat.

Nova, quae ex his oris communicem, vix aliqua, quae momentum habeant, in promptu sunt. Bellum Ungaricum magnâ vi continuatur et in futuram aestatem utrinque apparatum. Dicunt Turcam longe maiori exercitu adfuturum quam unquam antea; noster Imperator, licet a Principibus Imperij maiori ex parte nullas speret suppetias, quantacunque tamen poterit militari manu ei resistere eiusque vires et minas infringere, pro eo quem Deus largitus fuerit successu, constituit; ideoque equites et pedites varijs e locis conscribit, ut iusto exercitu tam atroci hosti obviare queat et suos defendere. Deus Opt. Max. omnia in bonum finem dirigat; cui etiam te tuosque commendo.

Vale.
Dabantur ex Arce Caesarea Benatica Die 29 Martij Anni 1600 stylo novo.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO AN ANONYMOUS [PERSON]**

Heartiest greeting.

Reverend and most excellent Man, friend to be honoured: the letter you wrote me back, with my son returning hither, I received about the beginning of this passing year; and for your friendly and candid **congratulation on the conditions which God Best and Greatest has provided for me and my studies with this most august Emperor**, and for your benevolent wish, by which you pray that all may henceforth be happily established and increased, I give you the greatest thanks I can. Hence shines forth that sincere affection of yours, with which you have long and greatly attended me; you will find me of like perpetual mind toward you and yours. And certainly it is so, as you write: I acknowledge the singular providence and kindness of the Divine Power, which clemently snatched me from the difficulties to which I was liable in my fatherland, and placed me here in a more tranquil harbour. And indeed I cannot sufficiently proclaim this best Emperor's not only imperial, but also **paternal** (if it were permitted so to speak) disposition toward me — seen even from this, that although His Majesty, on account of the **epidemic diseases** which most gravely afflicted Bohemia this past year, was absent from Prague and kept himself in the city of **Pilsen**, 15 miles distant (that infection still lasting, and raging in this place too, which he granted me to inhabit, and in the whole neighbourhood), yet **of his own motion he was solicitous about me and mine, several times sending hither to inquire how we fared** — at the same time most clemently offering that, if I wished to withdraw to any other castle of His Majesty's, where it were safer to live, it should be permitted me, and **leaving it free, too, if I should please, to betake myself to Vienna of Austria**, where he would in time provide me a convenient dwelling and the other necessaries. But I, having most humbly given thanks, answered that **I would rather remain here in my station, and commit everything to Divine protection and will.** And I give thanks, with my whole heart, to the same merciful God my protector, that he preserved me and my whole house unharmed amid such great dangers, by which we were surrounded on all sides; and I pray that he deign henceforth to be present to us by his grace.

Rightly was it done by you, that you **unsealed and read through the little history of our migration into Bohemia**, and of what afterward befell me here, which I had related a little more fully to **Holger Rosenkrantz, our common friend**, on account of the intimate friendship between us (to say nothing of kinship and relationship). And since from it you have sufficiently perceived the state of my affairs — in which, by God's kindness, it now persists, and henceforth can be more fully increased — I think it not worthwhile to repeat any of it here. I expect soon my furniture and the **Instruments left at Magdeburg**, and also those at **Hamburg**, which I had transferred thither from Denmark by my emissaries before winter; for the Emperor wrote to the Magistrate of both cities that, for his sake, they should have all conveyed hither by the **Elbe**; and when the **Magdeburg Senators sought certain subterfuges**, His Majesty on that account gave another letter to the **Chapter** of the same place, which promised it would most gladly comply with the Imperial Majesty's will. Meanwhile structures are being prepared for arranging the Instruments here in due manner.

That you were an exhorter to Master **Christen Longomontanus**, that he should come to me, and persuaded him of it, is most welcome to me; I will take pains that he not regret this journey, and will leave it free to him to be either here with me or at Prague, as long as he wishes.

Concerning the rest you write, it is well agreed between us, as was fair and fitting. I hear that there is among you **a certain Swede devoted to astronomical studies, by name …… , who also delights in celestial observations**; if you can bring it about that he come hither, it will be welcome to me, and not useless to him — I will aid his endeavours as much as I can.

I hear that the Swedish kingdom — long shaken by continual wars and tumults — has come into the power of **Duke Charles**. May God bend his heart, that he use this victory and power moderately, and clemently spare those he holds as adversaries.

News from these parts worth weight is scarcely at hand. The **Hungarian war** is continued with great force, and preparation [is made] on both sides for the coming summer. They say the **Turk** will be present with a far greater army than ever before; our Emperor, though for the most part hoping no aid from the Princes of the Empire, has nonetheless resolved to resist him with whatever military force he can, and to break his strength and threats, according to the success God shall grant; and therefore he levies horse and foot from various places, that with a proper army he may meet so atrocious an enemy and defend his own. May God Best and Greatest direct all to a good end; to whom I also commend you and yours.

Farewell.
Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 29th day of March, the year 1600, New Style.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient (unnamed; flagged).** Headed *Ad Anonymum* — addressed to a **"Reverend and most excellent" friend** (a cleric or learned divine) who: had congratulated Tycho on his imperial conditions; is a **"common friend" of Tycho and Holger Rosenkrantz**, to whom Holger had shown Tycho's migration-narrative; had **urged Longomontanus to come to Tycho**; and lives near "a Swede devoted to astronomy." On the evidence, an unidentified **north-German / Rostock-area reverend** of Tycho's circle (parallel in content to the Chytraeus reply, brahe-t_16000328002, but a distinct person). Not identified — left so per the no-fabrication rule.
- **Significance.** A counterpart of the same-period letters on Tycho's imperial establishment:
 - **The Emperor's "paternal" care.** As in the family letters (brahe-t_16000321004, brahe-t_16000321002) and the Coraduz letter (brahe-t_16000308001), Tycho dwells on Rudolf II's **personal solicitude during the plague** — repeated inquiries after his safety, and the **standing offer to relocate him to any safer castle, or to Vienna** — which Tycho declined to "remain in my station."
 - **The migration-narrative.** The recipient had **read the autobiographical *Historiola* of Tycho's migration into Bohemia** that Tycho sent **Holger Rosenkrantz** (the same narrative Chytraeus and Sturtz also sought; cf. brahe-t_16010415002, brahe-t_16000328002).
 - **The instrument-transport.** The **Magdeburg/Hamburg** saga: the Emperor's letters to both cities to ship the instruments up the **Elbe**; the **Magdeburg Senate's "subterfuges"** answered by the Emperor's further letter to the **Cathedral Chapter** (cf. brahe-t_16000404001, brahe-t_16000321005).
 - **Longomontanus** — the recipient had persuaded him to come to Tycho; Tycho will make him welcome.
 - **Recruiting a Swedish observer.** Tycho asks the recipient to send to him **a Swede skilled in astronomy and observation** (name a **lacuna** in the witness) — a glimpse of Tycho recruiting observational staff for Bohemia.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD ANONYMUM

S. P.

ATTULIT literas tuas, Nobilis et Eruditissime Vir, filius meus natu maior, in principio Ianuarij superioris huc rediens, ex quibus caussas diutini tui silentij et intermissionis literarum, ob absentiam in Livoniâ, cognovi, quare te eo libentius excusatum habeo, nihil interim de tuâ constantiâ et semel incepto erga me amore addubitans; invenies et me eundem TYCHONEM meique semper similem in te redamando. Utinam tu sedes Paternas, quas iure merito affectas, æque feliciter recuperare possis, et tranquillum invenire portum, atque mihi et meis studijs, Divinâ Clementiâ, hîc apud Augustissimum Imperatorem pro his primordijs benignissime provisum est, spero in posterum, eodem Numine favente, adhuc uberiora. Si qua in re apud Magnates hîc in Aula tibi aliquando usui esse potero, non deerit tui honorifica mentio secundum nostram in te propensionem. Filius tuus, ubi accesserit, erit mihi acceptus; optarem et te Patrem, si fieri posset, hîc semel videre.

Occupatio Regni Suetici, quo CAROLUM nunc potiri audio, meâ quoque opinione maiores turbas dabit, modo SIGISMUNDO non defuerint vires. Non minor est virtus, quam quærere, parta tueri. Deus aliquando pacem Regionibus illis, diu tempestate bellorum et aliarum calamitatum conquassatis, largiatur. Ubi occasio huc mittendi tibi data fuerit, non intermittas, quæso, tam de publicis, quæ in istis oris geruntur, quam privatis tuis rebus, scribendi officium.

Vale.
Dabantur ex Arce Cæsarea Benatica Die 29 Martij styl. nov. Anni 1600.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to an unnamed [correspondent].**

Hearty greeting.

My elder-born son brought your letter, noble and most learned man, when he returned hither at the beginning of last January; from which I learned the causes of your long silence and interruption of letters — namely, your absence in Livonia. Wherefore I hold you the more willingly excused, doubting nothing meanwhile of your constancy and of the love once begun toward me; you will find me, too, the same Tycho, and ever like myself, in loving you in return. Would that you might as happily recover the paternal seats which you rightly and deservedly strive for, and find a tranquil harbour, as it has been most kindly provided — by Divine Clemency — for me and my studies, here with the most august Emperor, for these beginnings; I hope, hereafter, the same Deity favouring, [for things] yet more abundant. If in any matter I can sometime be of use to you among the Magnates here at court, an honourable mention of you will not be wanting, in accordance with our inclination toward you. Your son, when he comes, will be welcome to me; I would wish to see you, the father, here too, once, if it could be done.

The occupation of the Kingdom of Sweden, which I hear Charles now holds, will, in my opinion too, give greater disturbances — provided strength has not failed Sigismund. It is no less a virtue to guard what has been gained than to seek it. May God at length grant peace to those regions, long shaken by the tempest of wars and other calamities. When occasion of sending hither is given you, do not, I pray, omit the duty of writing — both about public matters that are done in those parts, and about your private affairs.

Farewell.
Given from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 29th day of March, new style, in the year 1600.

documents.incipit: REDDIDIT mihi literas tuas sub initium huius Anni ad me reversus filius TYCHO; estque …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD CHRISTOPHORUM HENNIOCHUM

S.

REDDIDIT mihi literas tuas sub initium huius Anni ad me reversus filius TYCHO; estque mihi gratum, conditiones meas, quas Divino provisu hîc in Bohemia apud Cæsam Matem adeptus sum, tibi probari. De Chymico illo in Silesia, cuius meministi, qui Metamorphosin istam Paracelsicam in libro vexationum indicatam callet, per Dominum Doctorem THADDÆUM HAGGÆCIUM nuper inde Pragam redeuntem inquiri faciam; et si quid certi ab eo rescivero, te eius reddam participem.

FRANCISCUS SCRÖDERUS Sundensis ne verbulum mihi, sive Wittebergæ sive hîc degenti, respondit, aut si id fecit, interciderunt eius literæ: admoneas eum iterum sui officij, si forte resipiscere voluerit, quamvis non multum intersit, sive scribat sive non.

Recordor te semel mihi scripsisse de Granatis Bohemicis, quod ex ijs Chymicum quoddam artificium elicere nôsti; cuperem igitur ex te scire, quale illud sit; reperiuntur enim hîc Granati in satis magnâ copiâ, et tibi, si volueris, aliquos per oblatam oportunitatem mittam.

Vale.
Dabantur ex Arce Cæsarea Benatica Die 29 Martij stylo renovato Anni 1600.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Christopher Henniochus.**

Greeting.

My son Tycho, returned to me about the beginning of this year, delivered your letter to me; and it is pleasing to me that my circumstances — which by Divine provision I have obtained here in Bohemia with His Imperial Majesty — are approved by you. About that Chemist in Silesia whom you mention, who is skilled in that Paracelsian *Metamorphosis* indicated in the *Book of Vexations*, I will have inquiry made through Master Doctor Thaddaeus Hagecius, lately returning thence to Prague; and if I learn anything certain from him, I will make you a sharer of it.

Franciscus Schröder of Stralsund has not answered me a single little word, whether I was staying at Wittenberg or here; or, if he did, his letter went astray: admonish him again of his duty, if perchance he be willing to come to his senses — although it matters little whether he write or not.

I recall that you once wrote to me about Bohemian Garnets, that you know how to elicit a certain chemical artifice from them; I would therefore wish to know from you what that is. For garnets are found here in fairly great abundance, and I will send you some, if you wish, through an offered opportunity.

Farewell.
Given from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 29th day of March, renewed style [New Style], in the year 1600.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD MARTINUM BRASCHIUM

S.

ACCEPTISSIMÆ mihi fuerunt tuæ literæ, Eruditissime et amantissime Domine Magister MARTINE BRASCHI, quas circa initia huius Anni filius meus e Daniâ rediens inter alias ab Amicis Rostochiensibus profectas attulit: ac pro benevolâ et candidâ congratulatione, quam de successu rerum nostrarum apud Augustissimum Imperatorem RUDOLPHUM Secundum, Dominum nostrum Clementissimum, a principio refers, tibi peramanter gratias habeo.

Probâsti etiam tuum erga me sincerum affectum carmine illo Elegiaco unâ transmisso, ubi Uraniam Imperatorem meâ de caussâ adloquentem eique gratias agentem introducis. Adiungam quidem id cœteris tuis mecum antea communicatis, quæ a multis probantur, sed cum in hoc non ita selectis per omnia utaris verbis, et tali concinnitate, quam requirit hoc genus carminis, ad imitationem venæ Ovidianæ aut aliorum Poëtarum, qui in hac facilitate excelluerunt, adeo ut respectu antecedentium carminum te ipso (liceat enim mihi quod censeo ingenue profiteri) minor videaris: et sint præterea in ipsâ Historicâ relatione, quam pressius sequi voluisti, nonnulla, quæ nimis diffusa, quoad particularia, nec satis decore prolata existimem; idcirco Elegiam hanc superioribus versibus, Heroicis et Lyricis, necdum adiunxi aut alijs monstrare lubuit. Sed si tuâ bonâ veniâ id fieri poterit, uti fieri posse mihi polliceor, quædam prius in eadem recognoscam et paulo aliter mutabo, quædam vero prorsus omittam, prout in cœteris quoque hanc mihi libertatem sumpsi, quæ etiam tibi non displicuit; nemini enim res meæ rectius perspectæ esse poterint quam mihi ipsi. Perplacet alias inventio et ductus carminis, sed bonus interdum dormitat HOMERUS. Vides, quantâ erga te utor libertate et confidentiâ: ubi vero aliquale mihi supererit otium, remittam carmen illud, iuxta meam intentionem paulo aliter formatum; vel saltem loca indicabo, quæ a te ipso alterari vellem. Satius itaque erit, ut interea tibi ipsi hoc reservans, nemini exemplum impertiaris, multo minus ut publici iuris facias.

Excellentissimus ille MELISSUS necdum mihi quidpiam misit, spero tamen ipsum, pro eâ quâ præditus est humanitate et erga me affectione, id officij mihi non denegaturum. Si Cæsæ Mati scriptum aliquod, uti innuis, aliquando humillime dedicare constituisti, de quo meum exquiris consilium, cuperem prius scire, quale id esset, et quâ de re, ac Exemplum, si fieri possit, introspicere, tum demum, an gratum sit futurum, partim ex aliorum, qui ipsius Mati ab intimis sunt, partim meâ ipsius æstimatione, coniecturam faciam, tibique id, quicquid erit, solitâ ingenuitate pandam.

Vale.
Dabantur properanter ex Arce Cæsarea Benatica Die 29 Martij Anno 1600 stylo novo.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO MARTIN BRASCH**

Greeting.

Most welcome to me were your letters, most learned and most loving Lord Master Martin Brasch, which about the beginning of this year my son, returning from Denmark, brought among others sent by [my] friends at Rostock; and for the kindly and candid congratulation which from the first you offer on the success of our affairs with the most august Emperor Rudolf II, our most clement Lord, I give you most affectionate thanks.

You have proved your sincere affection toward me, too, by that Elegiac poem sent along [with the letter], in which you bring on Urania addressing the Emperor on my behalf and rendering him thanks. I will indeed add it to your other [poems] earlier shared with me, which are approved by many; but since in this one you do not throughout use such choice words, and such polish as this kind of poem requires — in imitation of the Ovidian vein, or of the other Poets who have excelled in this fluency — so much so that, set beside your preceding poems, you seem (let me be allowed to declare frankly what I judge) lesser than your own self; and since, besides, there are in the Historical narration itself, which you chose to follow rather closely, some things which I judge too diffuse in their particulars, and not set forth becomingly enough — for that reason I have not yet joined this Elegy to the earlier verses, the Heroic and the Lyric, nor cared to show it to others. But if it may be done with your good leave — as I promise myself it may — I will first revise certain things in it, and alter them a little otherwise, and some I will leave out entirely, just as in the others too I took this liberty for myself, which did not displease you either; for to no one can my own affairs be more rightly known than to myself. Otherwise the invention and the conduct of the poem please me well — but good Homer sometimes nods. You see with how great freedom and confidence I deal with you; and when some leisure is left to me, I will send that poem back, shaped a little otherwise according to my intention, or at least I will mark the passages I should wish you yourself to alter. It will therefore be better that, keeping this to yourself meanwhile, you impart a copy to no one — much less make it public.

That most excellent Melissus has not yet sent me anything; yet I hope that he, by that humanity with which he is endowed and his affection toward me, will not deny me that service. If you have resolved, as you hint, to dedicate some writing at some time, most humbly, to His Imperial Majesty — concerning which you ask my counsel — I should wish first to know what it would be, and on what subject, and, if it could be done, to look over a copy; then at last I shall make a conjecture whether it will be welcome, partly from [the judgement] of others who are among His Majesty's intimates, partly from my own estimation, and will lay it open to you, whatever it be, with my wonted candour.

Farewell.
Given in haste from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 29th day of March, in the year 1600, New Style.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Martin Brasch** (*Martinus Braschius*, 1565–1601), Rostock humanist and *Poeta laureatus* — the same poet named in Paul Melissus's letter to Tycho of 5 March 1600 (brahe-t_16000305001) among those who had prompted verses *in Tychen tuam*. Tycho is on the most familiar terms with the Rostock literary circle (*Amici Rostochienses*), which routed letters to him via his son's return from Denmark "about the beginning of this year."
- **The occasion — a verse-portrait of Tycho's imperial fortune.** Brasch had sent an **Elegiac poem** in which **Urania** (the Muse of astronomy) addresses **Emperor Rudolf II** on Tycho's behalf and thanks him — a poetic celebration of Tycho's new imperial patronage. It was meant to join Tycho's growing collection of friends' commendatory verses (the *Heroic* and *Lyric* pieces already gathered).
- **Tycho as candid literary critic (the heart of the letter).** Unusually, Tycho returns a frank, unflattering critique: the diction is not uniformly *selecta* (choice), the *concinnitas* (polished arrangement) falls short of what elegiac verse demands "in imitation of the Ovidian vein," and the closely-followed *Historica relatio* (the narrative of events) is in places too diffuse and "not becomingly enough set forth" — so that Brasch here seems *te ipso minor*, "lesser than his own self." Tycho therefore withholds the poem from the collection and from other eyes, proposes to **revise it himself** (as he had done, with Brasch's prior consent, to the others — "for to no one can my affairs be more rightly known than to myself"), and counsels Brasch **not to circulate or publish** it meanwhile. The whole is softened by the Horatian tag.
- **Classical tag.** *bonus interdum dormitat Homerus* — **Horace**, *Ars Poetica* 359 (*quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus*, "sometimes even good Homer nods"): the polite formula for a fine poet's lapse. Kept as the idiom and identified.
- **Cross-links & persons named.**
 - *Melissus* = **Paul Melissus (Schede)** (1539–1602), the Heidelberg poet, *Comes Palatinus* and laureate. Tycho notes Melissus "has not yet sent me anything" — i.e. as of 29 March 1600 the verses that Melissus's letter of **5 March 1600** (brahe-t_16000305001) says he was enclosing had not yet reached Benátky. The two letters thus bracket the same in-transit packet of poems.
 - *Rudolf II* (*Augustissimus Imperator Rudolphus Secundus*); Tycho's son (the one returning from Denmark, unnamed here).
- **A possible dedication to the Emperor.** Brasch had hinted (*innuis*) at dedicating some writing to Rudolf II and sought Tycho's advice; Tycho, well placed at court, offers to gauge its likely reception "partly from His Majesty's intimates, partly from my own estimation" before Brasch commits — a glimpse of how dedications to the Emperor were vetted through courtier-intermediaries.
- **Place / calendar.** *Arx Caesarea Benatica* = the imperial castle of **Benátky nad Jizerou**; dateline explicitly *stylo novo* — **New Style**, per Tycho's imperial-service usage. Reproduced, not converted.

text.original:
[TYCHO BRAHE AD JACOBUM BORDINGUM].

Magnifice et excellentissime vir, amice inprimis honorande.

JNTELLEXI ex literis, quas per filium meum, circa initia hujus anni huc ad me revertentem, mihi scripsisti, posteriores meas ad jllustrissimum principem ducem Vldaricum, d:num meum clementissimum, tum quoque simul ad te datas, recte esse redditas, et de conditionibus, quas divino provisu apud sa:am cæs:am ma:tem, dominum nostrum clementissimum, adeptus sum, ipsius jll:mam cel:nem clementer et lubenti animo accepisse, atque tibi etiam hunc rerum mearum statum auditu fuisse perjucundum, quo nomine jll:mæ ejus cel:ni humillime gratias ago, et tibi quoque quam plurimas. Si quid postea mihi rescriptum est, quod futurum innuisti, quandoquidem tunc ob occupationum molem et filii festinum isthinc discessum fieri id nequibat, scias me eas literas non accepisse, uti etiam nullas a d:no Henrico Ramelio, affine et amico meo singulari, qui ad te suas missurum, cum mei in Dania emissarii essent, aiebat.

Cœterum quia tempus iam adest, quo interesse (uti vocant) pro decem millibus joachymicis, quos isthic jll:mis junioribus principibus mutuo dedi, numerandum sit, rogo peramanter, velis efficere, ut summam illam, quæ sexcentos adæquat, actutum obtineam. Et quia difficulter, nec etiam satis tuto in moneta argentea sive thaleris huc adferri poterit, optarem, ut in aureis Vngaricis solverentur, ita ut quilibet Vngaricus loco sesquialterius thaleri numeretur, sicque quadringenti tales aurei sexcentis illis joachymicis æquivalerent; talis enim est hujus monetæ aureæ in Dania valor, ita ut apud vos nihil aut admodum parum esse discriminis existimem. Poterint autem aurei illi commode pyxidi alicui includi et obsignari, sicque aurigæ Wittebergensi, ut eos bene conservet atque m. Jœstelio mathematico isthic professori, quamprimum Wittebergam venerit, tradat; is enim affinem quendam Dresdæ habet, qui postea totum illud ad me facile transmittet. Si Vngarici isthic tam cito in promptu non sint, poterint eorum loco mitti engelotti, quorum quilibet duobus joachymicis cum quadrante æquiparatur. Roseinobiles, uti etiam floreni Rhenani hic parum in usu sunt, ideoque eos nollem. Si nulla alia ratio supererit, istam monetam auream loco joachymicorum mihi debitorum exponendi, spero ill:mum principem ducem Vldaricum, pro ea qua ipsius cel:do erga me est clementissima affectione, facile sua authoritate et consilio effecturum (præsertim si ipsius cel:ni abs te hoc negotium meo nomine humillime expositum commendetur), ut desideriis meis hac in parte subveniatur. Si autem vobis aliqua alia commoditas perspecta esset, qua pecuniam illam in joachymicis jmperialibus hic certo et absque meo damno accipere queam, mihi id perinde erit, lubensque acquiescam. Chirographum interesse illud persolutum testans hisce inclusi, quod tuæ fidei committo. Neque enim dubito te, quem semper expertus sum mei studiosissimum, hanc curam, utut alias sis occupatissimus, non detrectaturum, quo absque diutina dilatione id, quicquid est, pecuniarum hic nancisci queam; sic me adhuc pluribus quam antea officiis, quibuscunque per me licuerit modis, vicissim compensandis, tibi reddideris quam devinctissimum.

Vale.
Dabantur ex arce cæsarea Benatica die ultimo martii stylo novo anni 1600.
text.english:
**[TYCHO BRAHE TO JACOB BORDING].**

Magnificent and most excellent man, friend especially to be honoured.

I have understood, from the letter you wrote me by my son, returning hither to me about the beginning of this year, that my later [letters] to the most illustrious prince Duke Ulrich, my most clement lord, and at the same time to you, were duly delivered; and that, concerning the conditions which by divine provision I have obtained with the Sacred Imperial Majesty, our most clement lord, his most illustrious Highness received [the news] graciously and with willing mind, and that to you too this state of my affairs was most pleasing to hear — on which account I give most humble thanks to his most illustrious Highness, and very many to you also. If anything was afterward written back to me — which you hinted would happen, though it could not then be done, because of the mass of occupations and my son's hasty departure from there — know that I have not received those letters; just as [I have received] none from Lord Henrik Ramel, my kinsman and especial friend, who said he would send his to you when my emissaries were in Denmark.

For the rest: since the time is now at hand when the interest (as they call it) for the **ten thousand joachimsthalers** which I lent there to the most illustrious younger princes is to be paid, I most lovingly ask that you would bring it about that I obtain at once that sum, which amounts to **six hundred** [thalers]. And because it can be brought hither with difficulty, and not safely enough, in silver money or thalers, I should wish that it be paid in **Hungarian gold [ducats]**, such that each Hungarian [ducat] be reckoned in place of **one and a half thalers**, and so **four hundred** such gold pieces would equal those six hundred joachimsthalers — for such is the value of this gold money in Denmark, so that I think there is no difference, or very little, with you. Those gold pieces can conveniently be enclosed in some little box and sealed, and [given] thus to the **Wittenberg coachman**, that he keep them well and hand them to **Master Jöstel**, the mathematician [and] professor there, as soon as he comes to Wittenberg; for he has a certain kinsman at **Dresden**, who will then easily transmit the whole to me. If Hungarian [ducats] are not so quickly to be had there, **engelots** can be sent in their place, each of which is reckoned at two joachimsthalers and a quarter. **Rose-nobles**, like **Rhenish florins**, are little in use here, and therefore I should not want them. If no other way shall remain of laying out that gold money in place of the joachimsthalers owed me, I hope the most illustrious prince Duke Ulrich, by that most clement affection his Highness has toward me, will easily bring it about by his authority and counsel (especially if this business be humbly laid before and commended to his Highness by you in my name) that my wishes in this part be met. But if some other convenience be known to you, by which I may receive that money here in imperial joachimsthalers, surely and without my loss, it will be all the same to me, and I will gladly acquiesce. The receipt testifying that interest paid I have enclosed herewith, which I commit to your good faith. For I do not doubt that you — whom I have always found most devoted to me — will not refuse this care, however otherwise most occupied you be, so that without long delay I may obtain here that money, whatever it is; thus you will have bound me most closely to you, [the obligation] to be repaid in turn by more services than before, in whatever ways I shall be able.

Farewell.
Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the last day of March, New Style, the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Jacob Bording**, a leading man of **Lübeck** and Tycho's agent there (cf. the later Tycho→Bording letter, brahe-t_16010412001). The MS is an autograph **draft (*Kladde*)**.
- **Position in the Mecklenburg debt-thread.** This **31 March 1600** letter is the **earliest of the surviving Bording letters** and an early node of the whole 10,000-thaler affair (cf. brahe-t_16001115002 of 15 Nov 1600; the 1601 letters to Meier and Duke Ulrich). It first reports the **good news of Tycho's imperial conditions** (received gladly by Duke Ulrich and Bording — Tycho's letters had been delivered "by my son" returning early in 1600), then turns to the recurring task: collecting the **600-thaler semi-annual interest** on the **10,000 joachimsthalers** lent to the *"younger princes of Mecklenburg."*
- **The numismatic detail (notable for monetary history).** Tycho specifies *how* he wants the 600 thalers paid, to ease safe transport to Bohemia:
 - **Preferred: Hungarian gold ducats** (*aurei Ungarici*) at **1½ thalers each**, so **400 ducats = 600 joachimsthalers** ("such is their value in Denmark").
 - **Route:** sealed in a little box, given to the **Wittenberg coachman**, handed to **Master Jöstel** (Melchior Jöstel, the Wittenberg mathematician; cf. brahe-t_16001008001), whose **Dresden kinsman** forwards the whole to Tycho.
 - **Fallback: *engelotti* (English "angelots"/angels)** at **2¼ thalers each**; but **rose-nobles** and **Rhenish florins** "are little in use here," so he refuses them.
 - Failing all, **Duke Ulrich's** authority is to be invoked (via Bording), or the money taken "in imperial joachimsthalers" if safer. A receipt (*chirographum*) for the interest is enclosed.
- **Persons named.** Jacob Bording; **Duke Ulrich III of Mecklenburg**; the **"younger princes"** (the late Duke Johann's sons; see brahe-t_16000920002); **Henrik Ramel** (*Henricus Ramelius*, Tycho's *affinis* and friend, a Pomeranian/Danish noble); **Melchior Jöstel**; Tycho's son (Tycho the Younger); **Rudolf II** (the imperial conditions).
- **Coin glossary (kept/glossed;).** *aurei Ungarici* = **Hungarian gold ducats**; *joachymici* = **joachimsthalers** (the Joachimsthal silver thaler); *engelotti* = **angelots / English angels** (gold); *roseinobiles* = **rose-nobles** (English gold); *floreni Rhenani* = **Rhenish florins/gulden**.
