text.original:
IOANNES KEPLER AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

SONS manus, quæ nuper ad lædendum celeritate ventos antevertit, quodnam initium faciat ad leniendum, vix invenit. Nam quid ego primum commemorem? An meam intemperantiam? Cuius acerbissima est recordatio. An tua, Nobilissime TYCHO, benefacta? Quæ iam nec enumerari possunt, nec pro dignitate perpendi. Per duos menses gratuito me victu liberaliter aluisti; toti tuæ familiæ meam incolumitatem, mea desideria commendasti: omnia humanitatis officia præstitisti: quæ habuisti charissima, mihi communicasti: nemo me dicto vel facto volens læsit unquam: in summa, non liberis, non uxori, non ipsi tibi plus indulsisti quam mihi. Quæ animo præterea volvebas, de me promovendo, ex ijs, quæ mea causa suscepisti, facile vidi. Quæ omnia, cum ita habere sciverim, fassus fuerim, scripto etiam testata reliquerim: magnâ cum animi consternatione recordor, adeo me a Deo et a Spiritu Sancto meis intemperijs animique morbo fuisse permissum, ut ad tot et tanta beneficia, clausis oculis, pro modestia, trium hebdomadum continuæ morositati erga totam familiam, pro gratiarum actione, iracundiæ præcipiti, pro reverentiâ, audaciæ summæ erga tuam personam, tam illustri stemmate, tam præstanti eruditione, tanta nominis claritate venerabilem, pro amica valedictione, suspiciosissimis imputationibus et acerbissimæ scribendi prurigini tantum indulgere potuerim, nec me respexerim, nec quam crudeliter tuum animum, qui præclare semper de me senseras, hac odiosissimâ ratione sim offensurus, perpenderim. Quæ si hostili animo, si nocendi proposito, suscepissem: equidem vix vel a Deo petere fuissem ausus, uti te mihi præstaret placabilem, iustamque et legitimam vindictam impediret.

Sed quia totum hoc impotentis animi furor et choleræ præstitit exuberantia, et iuvenile vitium, curiositas, cum præcipitantiâ iudicij (abfuit vero diffamandi animus) et quia non experieris, me unquam cum quoquam mortalium ita de te locutum, uti ad te unum ex falsâ imaginatione scripsi (quemadmodum neque in quemquam unquam talia designavi) ex hac qualicunque consolatione post gravissimam pœnitudinem, animum nonnihil recepi: et quia quæ scripsi, coram Deo solo teste, M.T. imputata fuere; primum Deum Opt. Max. veniam exoravi, deinde et pro Christianâ reconciliatione summe fui sollicitus. Quod nisi me afflicta valetudo, immoderatæ affectionis haud dubia stimulatrix, impedivisset, primo quoque tempore Benathkam excurrissem, meque M.T. ad omnem satisfactionem promptum stitissem. Iam quia fors ita tulit, ut prior Μ. T. Pragam veniret, supplex ad Μ. T. venio, per Dei misericordiam orans, uti mihi hanc atrocissimam offensionem Christiano animo remittat. Ego contra, quæ dixi vel scripsi in Μ. T. personam, famam, honorem et doctrinam, vel quocunque alio modo, iniuriosissima (si nulla valeat in meliorem partem interpretatio) uti (quod ex animo doleo) dixi scripsique plurima et plura quam meminerim: omnia et singula revoco, irrita, falsa et probatu impossibilia sponte et ingenue agnosco atque pronuncio. Neque enim ullum facinus patratum, aut ullam partem honestatis a Μ. T. unquam violatam vel vidi vel audivi. Si quid suspicionibus etiam indulsi, id omne, ut Christianum decet, ex animo eijciam, sic ut protestationi Christianæ acquiescens, temeritatem in suspicando libenter Deo καρδιογνώστῃ fatear.

Promitto etiam bona fide, me in posterum, ubicunque versaturus sim, non tantum huiusmodi malesanis actibus, dictis, factis et literis abstenturum, sed neque ullo pacto Μ. T. iniuste et ex proposito offensurum, neque quicquam, quod non deceat, contra Μ. T. moliturum. Oro autem, quia lubrica est vita hominis, ut si M.T. animadvertat me imprudenter in tale quid vergere, me mei ipsius admoneat: experietur enim me morigerum. Quin imo polliceor, daturum me operam, quod quidem nunquam adhuc mentis compos intermisi, ut omni genere officiorum Μ. T. ulterius devinciam, et quantum mihi possibile est, superiorumque meorum patitur authoritas, in omnibus honestis rebus, quasque Μ. T. gratas intellexero, obsequium præstem, et sic ipso facto demonstrem, aliter me in M.T. personam esse et semper fuisse affectum, quam ex illa trium septimanarum intemperata dispositione animi et corporis colligi poterat. Et precor, ut ad id præstandum me Deus adiuvet.
text.english:
**JOHANNES KEPLER TO TYCHO BRAHE.**

**The guilty hand, which lately in its speed to wound outran the winds, scarcely finds what beginning to make toward soothing.** For what shall I first call to mind? My intemperance? — the recollection of which is most bitter. Or your benefactions, most noble Tycho? — which now can neither be enumerated, nor weighed according to their worth. **For two months you fed me liberally with free board**; you commended my safety, my wishes, to your whole household; you performed all the offices of humanity; what you held most dear, you shared with me; no one ever willingly injured me in word or deed; in sum, **you indulged not your children, not your wife, not your own self more than me**. What besides you were turning over in your mind, about advancing me, I easily saw from the things you undertook for my sake. All which — since I knew it to be so, confessed it, and even left it attested in writing — I recall with great consternation of mind: **that I was so far given over by God and by the Holy Spirit, through my intemperance and my mind's sickness, that to so many and so great benefits, with closed eyes, I could indulge — instead of modesty, three weeks' continuous moroseness toward your whole household; instead of thanksgiving, headlong wrath; instead of reverence, the utmost audacity toward your person** (venerable for so illustrious a lineage, so excellent an erudition, so great a renown of name); **instead of a friendly farewell, most suspicious imputations and a most bitter itch of writing** — nor did I look to myself, nor weigh how cruelly I was about to offend your mind (you who had always thought excellently of me) by this most hateful manner. Which, had I undertaken it with a hostile mind, with a purpose of harming, I should indeed scarcely have dared even to ask of God that he render you placable to me, and hinder a just and lawful vengeance.

But since the whole of this was wrought by **the fury of an uncontrolled mind and an exuberance of choler, and a youthful fault — curiosity — with precipitancy of judgement** (but the intent to defame was absent); and since you will not find that I ever spoke of you to any mortal as I wrote, to you alone, out of a false imagination (just as I never plotted such things against anyone): from this consolation, such as it is, after the gravest repentance, I have somewhat recovered my spirit. And since what I wrote — God alone being witness — were charged to Your Magnificence: first I begged pardon of God Best and Greatest, then I was supremely solicitous for a **Christian reconciliation**. And had not my afflicted health (the undoubted stimulant of immoderate emotion) hindered me, I should at the first opportunity have run over to **Benátky**, and presented myself to Your Magnificence ready for every satisfaction. Now, since chance has so brought it that Your Magnificence came first to Prague, **I come a suppliant to Your Magnificence, praying by God's mercy that you would, with a Christian mind, forgive me this most atrocious offence.** I, in turn — [as for] what I said or wrote against Your Magnificence's person, fame, honour, and learning, or in any other way most injurious (if no interpretation toward the better part avails), as (which I grieve from my heart) I said and wrote very many things, and more than I remember — **all and each I retract, and of my own accord and frankly acknowledge and declare void, false, and impossible to prove**. For I have neither seen nor heard any crime committed, or any part of honourableness ever violated, by Your Magnificence. If I also indulged in any suspicions, I will cast all that out of my mind, as becomes a Christian — so that, acquiescing in a Christian protestation, I freely confess my rashness in suspecting to **God, the Knower of hearts**.

I also promise, in good faith, that henceforth, wherever I shall be, I will not only abstain from such unsound acts, words, deeds, and letters, but neither in any way unjustly and deliberately offend Your Magnificence, nor contrive anything unbecoming against Your Magnificence. But I pray, since the life of man is slippery, that **if Your Magnificence notice me imprudently inclining toward any such thing, you would admonish me of it: for you will find me compliant.** Nay rather, I promise to give effort — which indeed I never yet, when in my right mind, omitted — to bind Your Magnificence further by every kind of service, and, as far as is possible for me and the authority of my superiors allows, to render obedience in all honourable matters, and such as I shall understand to be welcome to Your Magnificence; and so to demonstrate, by the very deed, that I am, and always have been, otherwise disposed toward Your Magnificence's person than could be gathered from that three weeks' intemperate disposition of mind and body. And I pray that God may help me to perform this.

documents.apparatus:
- **Significance — one of the most famous letters in the history of science.** This is **Johannes Kepler's autograph letter of apology and submission to Tycho Brahe** (April 1600), written after the **violent first quarrel** that nearly ended their association before it began. During Kepler's first weeks at Benátky (early 1600), a dispute over the conditions of his work and access to Tycho's observations erupted into a furious outburst; Kepler left and sent Tycho intemperate, accusatory letters, then — overcome with remorse — wrote this abject retraction. **The reconciliation it effected made possible the collaboration on which Kepler's *Astronomia nova* (and his laws of planetary motion) rests.** The MS is Kepler's **autograph** in the Vienna ÖNB (cod. Vindob. lat. 10703).
- **Structure of the apology.**
 1. **The opening figure** — *"the guilty hand, which lately in its speed to wound outran the winds"* — and the antithesis between his "intemperance" and Tycho's "benefactions."
 2. **The catalogue of Tycho's kindnesses** — **two months' free board**; commending Kepler's safety to the whole household; sharing "what he held most dear"; "you indulged not your children, your wife, your own self more than me" — and his plans "about advancing me."
 3. **The self-accusation** — that, "given over by God and the Holy Spirit through my intemperance and my mind's sickness," he repaid these with **"three weeks' continuous moroseness … headlong wrath … the utmost audacity toward your person … most suspicious imputations and a most bitter itch of writing."**
 4. **The mitigation** — it was *"the fury of an uncontrolled mind, an exuberance of choler, a youthful fault, curiosity, with precipitancy of judgement"*, **"but the intent to defame was absent"**; he never spoke ill of Tycho to others, only wrote to Tycho "out of a false imagination."
 5. **The retraction and submission** — he comes "a suppliant," begs a **"Christian reconciliation,"** and **"retracts all and each"** of his injurious words, "void, false, and impossible to prove," confessing his rashness "to God, the Knower of hearts."
 6. **The promise of future obedience** — to abstain, to be admonished if he errs ("you will find me compliant"), and to bind Tycho "by every kind of service."
- **Greek.** *Deo καρδιογνώστῃ* — "to God, **the Knower of hearts**" (*kardiognōstēs*, **Acts 1:24 / 15:8**); kept verbatim, translated.
- **Persons & place.** **Johannes Kepler** (sender); **Tycho Brahe** (*M. T.* = *Magnificentia Tua*); Tycho's wife and children (the *familia*); **Benátky** (the scene of the quarrel; Kepler now at Prague — *"Your Magnificence came first to Prague"*).
- **Calendar / date.** The edition and *Opera Omnia* place it in **April 1600** (New Style); the **day is not given** in the source (Kepler's autograph) and is left unspecified in the header (historically dated to early April 1600). Marked [N.S.].

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD DANIELEM CRAMERUM

S. P.

CLARISSIME et Praestantissime Vir, Amice plurimi mihi semper faciende: Literae tuae, pari eruditione et benevolâ erga me affectione affatim certantes, quas circa initia Decembris superioris Anni ad me dedisti, paulo post huius labentis primordia mihi redditae sunt, unâ cum ijs, quas communis noster Amicus, Dominus Doctor LUCAS BACKMESTERUS, per filium natu maiorem, quem in Daniam ablegaram pro auferendis residuis Instrumentis, huc redeuntem miserat. Fuerunt eae mihi admodum gratae, inprimis vero Oda illa ad Caesam Matem, elegans sane et arguta, et quae vel sola lauream te mereri testari poterit, pro quâ etiam ab ipsius Mate obtinendâ ego meo calculo tibi non sum defuturus, arrepta occasione idoneâ. Ipsius Matas per semestre Pragae non fuit, sed in urbe Pilsna, 10 milliaribus inde remotâ, ob luem Epidemicam, quae totam Bohemiam superiore Anno graviter afflixit, commorata est; interea paucissimis patuit ad ipsius Matem accessus; speramus eam brevi Pragam reversuram.

Gratissimum insuper mihi est, quod insolentem istum Scotulum redarguere eiusque inverecundam arrogantiam compescere non detrectes: dignum se reddidit, cui vaniloquum et in alios scurriliter mordax obtruderetur os. Adfuit mihi Uraniburgi in mensa Dominus Doctor NICOLAUS KRAGIUS, Professor Haffniacus et Historicus Regius, cum DUNCANO tunc simul praesenti meas Hypotheses aperirem; et licet idem KRAGIUS non libenter omnia, quae hac de re comperta habet, fateatur, quod Scotis, qui de ipso bene meriti sunt, contradicere nolit (nam Rex Scotiae, cum ibi Legatum ageret, eum nobilitavit et insigni aureâ torque donavit) attamen in literis, quas pridie Nonarum Decembris Anni superioris ad me dedit, haec verba suapte manu adscripsit: »DUNCANUS certe quicquid tandem privatim egerit, publice nunquam eam (loquitur de Hypothesi nostra) sibi arrogavit, qui ne per somnium quidem de eâ cogitavit, antequam ex te hanc tanquam mysterium cognosceret. Quod simul ac patefecisses, memini a te dictum, plus ei communicatum quam frater fratri edisserere fortean vellet. Atque reperi in paucis hisce diebus inter schedas meas chartam, quâ mihi petenti eam signâsti; sive ante DUNCANI adventum, sive quo tempore apud te ille incertus sum.« Haec ille nolens volens fatetur; quo Anno id fuerit, ex literis ipsius DUNCANI ad me, postquam Rostochium redierat, quibus Hypothesin illam meam sibi apprime placere scribit, eamque Ptolemaicae et Coperniceae praefert, quarum te exemplum habere existimo, facile colliges. Est mihi ipsius DUNCANI autographum ad manus, quod inficiari non potest, etiamsi in mille se verteret formas; et quantum subsidij habeat ex meis, de quibus tam frivole gloriatur, literis, vel lippis oculis loci peristasin consideranti discernere facillimum. Rem apprime gratam nec indecentem praestiteris, si quae contra eum veritatis asserendae caussâ meditatus es, compleveris, mihique, prius quam publicentur, transmiseris, ut si quae praeterea eo facientia ad manus habeam, annotem, tibique mox restituam.

Existimo te vidisse scurrile quoddam et supra modum calumnijs atque convitijs scatens, omninoque famosum scriptum cuiusdam efferi Dithmarsi, Ursi potius quam hominis (uti sese vocat) contra quod, si per otium, quae restitutionis loco tibi in mentem venerint, consignare non degravatus fueris, quae ego postea locupletabo, cum nihil sit in eo, quod non minimo negotio refelli queat, etiam ubi invictis Geometriae demonstrationibus triumphum agere praesumit, singulare mihi praestiteris officium, et maiori quam antea beneficio me tibi devinxeris, meque vicissim tui nominis atque honoris studiosum et gratum experiere. Ego contra tam rabiosum allatratorem quidpiam sub meo nomine, dilutionis loco, edere indecorum existimo, sed potius legibus istud contra Imperij constitutiones inverecundum facinus castigari suo tempore permittam. Hactenus rem omnem dissimulavi, partim propter aulam longe dissitam et pro maiori parte distractam, partim quod gravioribus occupationibus distinerer; sed quod differtur, non aufertur. Feceris OLIGERO nostro rem inprimis acceptam, si et hac in parte desiderijs nostris morem gesseris: dici etenim vix potest, quam moleste is tulerit, cum primum illi de putido illo libro innotuit; et fustibus ac plagis excipiendum authorem censuit, sed praestat legibus. Verum desino te serioribus occupatum talibus nugis remorari: extorsit ista mea erga te confidentia sincerusque et mutuus amor. De me vero vicissim tibi quidvis audacter pollicearis. Vale. Dabantur ex Arce Caesareâ Benaticâ pridie Paschatis Anno 1600, qui Romae habetur Iubilaeus.

Quae in Oda tua per se satis concinne elaborata paulo aliter legi malui, in subiuncta charta notavi, quod licet tuâ bonâ veniâ admitti posse mihi persuadeam, tamen indicandum duxi, quo conscius esses.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO DANIEL CRAMER**

Heartiest greeting.

Most renowned and excellent Man, a friend always to be highly valued by me: your letter — abundantly vying in equal erudition and benevolent affection toward me — which you sent me about the beginning of December last year, was delivered me a little after the beginning of this [year], together with those our common friend Lord Doctor **Lucas Backmeister** had sent through my elder son (whom I had dispatched into Denmark to bring away the remaining Instruments), returning hither. They were very welcome — but especially that **Ode to the Imperial Majesty**, elegant and pointed, which even alone could attest you deserve the laurel; for the obtaining of which from His Majesty I too will not fail you with my vote, a fit occasion seized. His Majesty was not at Prague for half a year, but stayed at **Pilsen**, 10 miles distant, on account of the epidemic plague which gravely afflicted all Bohemia last year; meanwhile access to His Majesty lay open to very few; we hope he will soon return to Prague.

It is most welcome to me, besides, that you do not decline to **refute that insolent little Scot and curb his shameless arrogance**: he has made himself deserving that a vain-speaking, scurrilously biting muzzle be thrust upon him. Lord Doctor **Nicolaus Krag**, Professor at Copenhagen and Royal Historian, was present with me at table at **Uraniborg, when I opened my Hypotheses to Duncan, then also present**; and although Krag does not willingly confess all he knows of this (because he will not contradict the Scots, who have deserved well of him — for the King of Scotland, when Krag was Legate there, ennobled him and gave him a distinguished gold chain), yet in the letter he sent me on **4 December last year** he added these words in his own hand: *"**Duncan certainly — whatever he may at last have done privately — never publicly arrogated it [he speaks of our Hypothesis] to himself, who did not even in a dream think of it before he learned it from you as a mystery.** As soon as you had revealed it, I remember it was said by you that more was communicated to him than a brother would perhaps wish to expound to a brother. And I found, in these few days, among my papers, a sheet on which you marked it for me at my request — whether before Duncan's arrival, or while he was with you, I am uncertain."* These things he confesses, willing or not. In what year it was, you will easily gather from Duncan's own letter to me (after he had returned to Rostock), in which he writes that **that Hypothesis of mine pleased him exceedingly, and prefers it to the Ptolemaic and Copernican** — a copy of which I think you have. I have Duncan's own autograph at hand, which he cannot deny, even if he turn himself into a thousand shapes; and how much support he has from my letters — about which he so frivolously boasts — it is most easy to discern, even with bleary eyes, for one considering the circumstances. You will do a thing exceedingly welcome and not unbecoming, if you complete what you have meditated against him for the sake of asserting the truth, and **transmit it to me before it is published**, that, if I have anything else conducing to it, I may annotate and soon return it.

I think you have seen a certain scurrilous writing, teeming beyond measure with calumnies and insults, altogether infamous, **of a certain savage Dithmarsian — a Bear [Ursus] rather than a man (as he calls himself)** — against which, if at leisure you would set down what comes to your mind by way of refutation (which I will afterward enrich) — since there is nothing in it that cannot be refuted with the least trouble, even where he presumes to triumph with "invincible demonstrations of Geometry" — you will do me a singular service, bind me by a greater benefit than before, and find me in turn zealous and grateful for your name and honour. **For myself, I think it unbecoming to publish anything under my own name, by way of refutation, against so rabid a barker — but I will rather let that shameless crime against the Empire's constitutions be punished by the laws in its time.** Hitherto I have dissembled the whole matter, partly because of the court being far off and mostly scattered, partly because I was held by weightier occupations; but **what is deferred is not taken away.** You will do our **Holger** a thing exceedingly welcome, if in this part too you comply with our wishes: for it can scarcely be said how ill he took it when that putrid book first became known to him — **he judged the author should be received with cudgels and blows, but it is better [left] to the laws.** But I cease to delay you, occupied with more serious things, with such trifles: my confidence toward you, and our sincere and mutual love, extorted these. Of me, in turn, promise yourself anything boldly. Farewell. Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the day before Easter, the year 1600, which at Rome is held as the Jubilee.

What in your Ode — in itself quite elegantly wrought — I preferred to read a little otherwise, I have noted on the appended sheet; which, though I persuade myself it can be admitted with your good leave, I thought should be indicated, that you might be aware.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Daniel Cramer** (1568–1637), the Pomeranian (Stettin) Lutheran theologian, poet, and polymath — here a literary and polemical ally of Tycho's, who had sent an **Ode to Rudolf II** (Tycho promises to help him to the imperial **laurel**) and is willing to write **refutations** on Tycho's behalf.
- **Significance — a principal document of Tycho's priority/plagiarism disputes (with the *verbatim* Krag testimony).** Three intertwined controversies:
 1. **John Craig ("the insolent little Scot").** Tycho welcomes Cramer's refutation of **Craig** (the *Scotulus*; cf. the cometary *Capnurania* dispute, brahe-t_15990321001, brahe-t_15981231002).
 2. **The Duncan affair (priority of the Tychonic hypothesis).** Tycho recounts that, **at his table at Uraniborg, he revealed his world-system hypotheses to "Duncan"** (a Scot of Craig's circle), in the presence of **Niels Krag** (*Nicolaus Cragius*, Copenhagen professor and Royal Historian). Krag — reluctant to testify against the Scots, who had honoured him (**ennobled and gold-chained by James VI of Scotland** when Krag was Danish legate) — nonetheless wrote Tycho (**4 Dec 1599**) the **verbatim words** quoted here: that **"Duncan … never publicly arrogated the Hypothesis to himself, who did not even in a dream think of it before he learned it from you as a mystery,"** and that Krag still has **the sheet on which Tycho diagrammed it for him**. Tycho adds that he holds **Duncan's own autograph letter** preferring the Tychonic hypothesis "to the Ptolemaic and Copernican" — documentary proof of priority.
 3. **Ursus.** The "scurrilous, infamous writing of a certain savage **Dithmarsian — a *Bear* (*Ursus*) rather than a man**" — i.e. **Nicolaus Reimers Bär's *De astronomicis hypothesibus*** (Prague 1597; cf. brahe-t_16000328001, brahe-t_15990321001). Tycho will **not answer under his own name** "so rabid a barker," but **pursue it by law** ("that shameless crime against the Empire's constitutions … punished by the laws"); he enlists Cramer for a refutation, to vet before publication. **Holger Rosenkrantz's fury** at the book ("he judged the author should be received with cudgels and blows, but it is better [left] to the laws") is reported.
- **Notable phrases.** *quod differtur, non aufertur* — "what is deferred is not taken away"; *Ursi potius quam hominis (uti sese vocat)* — the standing pun on **Ursus = Bear**; *vel lippis oculis* — "even with bleary eyes" (the obvious). The closing notes that Tycho **emended Cramer's Ode** (as he did Brasch's, Fischer's verses).
- **Persons named.** Daniel Cramer; **Lucas Backmeister**; **John Craig** (the *Scotulus*); **Duncan** (the Scot who learned the hypothesis); **Niels Krag** (*Nicolaus Cragius*, quoted; ennobled by James VI); **Nicolaus Reimers Bär (Ursus)**; **Holger Rosenkrantz**; **Rudolf II**.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *pridie Paschalis Anno 1600, qui Romae habetur Iubilaeus* — "the day before Easter 1600, which at Rome is the **Jubilee**" = **1 April 1600 [New Style]** (Gregorian Easter 2 April 1600). Header agrees with the label.
- **Correction.** Latin closing date 'pridie Paschalis' corrected to 'pridie Paschatis' (Dreyer TBOO VIII p.292, where the word is itself marked with an editorial obelus in Dreyer's own apparatus); no change to the English, which already read correctly.

documents.incipit: ACCIPIES, Vir nobilissime atque Mathematicorum omnium longe præstantissime, Catalogos …

text.original:
IOANNES GEORGIUS HERWARTUS AB HOHENBURG AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

ACCIPIES, Vir nobilissime atque Mathematicorum omnium longe præstantissime, Catalogos ambos librorum, qui in his nundinis vernalibus Francofurti ad Mœnum venales extiterunt. Si quos ex his petas, velim eos mihi designari, priusquam exemplaria divendantur, et curabo sedulo, ut quamprimum eos accipias. Mitto etiam tabulas ELISABETHÆ Reginæ Angliæ, GEMMAM FRISIUM de radio Astronomico, et Astrologiam græcolatinam IOACHIMI CAMERARIJ No. 106. Tabulas perpetuas longitudinum et latitudinum Planetarum Lovanienses, et Theoricas Planetarum PURBACHIJ ab ORONTIO FINÆO emendatas No. 99. Atque hisce me tibi commendo, teque florere quam fœlicissime exopto.

Datæ Monachij tertia die Aprilis Anno 1600.
text.english:
**Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg to Tycho Brahe.**

You will receive, most noble man and by far the most outstanding of all mathematicians, both catalogues of the books which were on sale at this spring fair at Frankfurt am Main. If you should seek any from these, I would wish them designated to me before the copies are sold off, and I will diligently see to it that you receive them as soon as possible. I also send: the *Tables* of Elizabeth, Queen of England; **Gemma Frisius** *On the Astronomical Radius* [the cross-staff]; and the Greek-Latin *Astrology* of **Joachim Camerarius**, No. 106; the Louvain *Perpetual Tables* of the longitudes and latitudes of the Planets; and the *Theoricae Planetarum* of **Peurbach**, emended by **Orontius Finaeus**, No. 99. And with these I commend myself to you, and most heartily wish you to flourish most happily.

Given at Munich, the third day of April, in the year 1600.

- **Books.** *Tabulae Elisabethae Reginae Angliae* — astronomical tables dedicated to / associated with **Queen Elizabeth I of England** (*identification flagged*: most plausibly a set of ephemerides or tables bearing the dedication; not securely pinned to one edition). *Gemma Frisius de radio Astronomico* = **Gemma Frisius**, *De radio astronomico et geometrico* (1545) — on the cross-staff (*radius astronomicus*, per glossary). *Astrologia graecolatina Ioachimi Camerarij* = the Greek-and-Latin astrological compilation of **Joachim Camerarius the Elder** (No. 106). *Tabulae perpetuae … Lovanienses* = the Louvain *Tabulae perpetuae* of planetary longitudes and latitudes. *Theoricae Planetarum Purbachij … ab Orontio Finaeo emendatae* = **Georg Peurbach**'s *Theoricae novae planetarum*, in the recension corrected by **Oronce Fine** (*Orontius Finaeus*) (No. 99).
- **The "No." numbers** (106, 99) are entries on Tycho's standing book-want list (see the Munich series).
- **Calendar.** Munich (Catholic Bavaria) = **New Style**; *tertia die Aprilis 1600*. Header agrees with the label.

text.original:
REVERENDISSIMIS, NOBILISSIMIS, CLARISSIMISQUE VIRIS D:NIS DECANO, CŒTERISQUE ECCLESIÆ METROPOLITANÆ IN ARCHIEPISCOPATU MAGDEBURGENSI CAPITULARIBUS ET DOMINIS ET AMICIS SUIS HONORANDISSIMIS.

Reverendissimi et nobilissimi viri d:i et amici honorandissimi.

CUM sa:a cæs:a m:tas, dominus noster clementissimus, jam antea literas dederit ad amplissimum senatum Magdeburgensem, ut jnstrumenta mea astronomica atque supellectilem isthic repositam huc in Bohemiam, intermediante Albi fluvio, suis sumptibus in ipsius ma:tis gratiam transferri procurare velint, illj vero id ipsum suo quodam consilio renuere visi sint, utut bis ab ipsius cæs:a ma:te hac de re clementissimis literis compellarentur, non igitur placuit ipsius ma:ti de his sæpius ad illos scribere, sed potius ad vestrum reverendissimum capitulum literas hoc nomine dirigere, præsertim cum subintellexerit vestras reverend:mas dominationes ab hoc officio suæ cæs:æ ma:ti obsequiose et reverenter præstando minime alienas esse. Quare nunc ipsius ma:tis literas hæc ipsa continentes ad reverend:mas vestras dominationes per ministrum meum mitto, officiosissime et reverenter simul rogans, ut, quemadmodum ipsius ma:tis clementissimæ petitioni obsequentissimo animo obtemporaturas nihil ambigo, sic etiam effecturas ut omnes res meæ isthic reservatæ qua fieri potest maturatione, sartætectæ, advehantur, atque de iis, quæ huc conducunt, provideatur. Accipiet illud ipsius ma:tas clementissima favorabili mente eritque simul, vti spero, reip. literariæ utile, cujus promotionem vos non solum genere jllustres, sed et eximia eruditione conspicuos, exoptare et auxiliatrices manus præbere velle persuasum habeo; neque enim ea quæ in sublimi illa et divina scientia astronomica integre restituenda plurimis abhinc annis indefesso labore sumptibusque non modicis molior et favente cœlestium opifice, in augustissimi hujus imperatoris totiusque jmperii honorem nunquam intermoriturum, sedulo elaborare satago, privata sunt, aut ad me meosque solummodo pertinentia, sed ad universam literaturam eruditam ubivis locorum quoad sol et sidera durabunt (prout confido) conducentia. Jdeoque v:s d:es commune hic bonum lubenti animo adjuturas non est dubium, [omnino mihi polliceor]; quod equidem officium, quantum ad me attinet, etsi compensare vires non sufficiant, pro meo tamen modulo inveniar perpetuo erga reverendissimum vestrum capitulum hoc nomine gratus; sique nihil aliud referre vicissim potero, vestram tamen hanc præclaram voluntatem apud alios extollere et deprædicare non desistam. Si quempiam ex vestris fidelibus ministris adjunxeritis, qui res meas huc comitetur et earum curam gerat, poteritis (modo vestris dominationibus ita placuerit) vina Bohemica, quæ superiori æstate adeo generosa hic creverunt, ut plurimi antecedentes anni vix similia dederint, secum in aliqua copia iustoque precio recipere: quod ut commode fiat, vel si quid aliud ex his oris desideratis, quod isthic pluris æstimatur, dabo operam, ut quantum in me est vestræ voluntati hac in parte satisfiat, sicque sumptus erogati quodammodo mea opinione resarciri poterunt. Plura et particulariora clar:us et præst:mus vir d:nus Georgius Rollenhagius isthic scholæ rector, singularis meus amicus, ad vestras do:nes, sicubi opus fuerit, referet.

Deus opt. max. vos omnes diu conservet florentes et incolumes.
Dabantur ex arce Cæsarea Benatica die 4 aprilis stylo novo anno 1600.
text.english:
**To the most reverend, most noble, and most renowned men, the Lords Dean and the other Capitulars of the Metropolitan Church in the Archbishopric of Magdeburg, his most honoured Lords and friends.**

Most reverend and most noble men, Lords and most honoured friends.

Since the Sacred Imperial Majesty, our most clement lord, has already before given a letter to the most ample **Senate of Magdeburg**, that they would procure my **astronomical instruments** and the furniture stored there to be transferred hither into Bohemia, by way of the river **Elbe**, at their own expense, for His Majesty's sake — but they seemed, by some counsel of their own, to refuse this very thing, though they were **twice** addressed by His Imperial Majesty on the matter with most clement letters — it therefore did not please His Majesty to write to them more often about it, but rather to direct letters on this account to **your most reverend Chapter**, especially since he understood that your most reverend Lordships are by no means averse from rendering this service obediently and reverently to His Imperial Majesty. Wherefore I now send His Majesty's letters containing these very things to your most reverend Lordships through my servant, at the same time most dutifully and reverently asking that — just as I doubt not you will obey His Majesty's most clement petition with most compliant mind — so also you will bring it about that all my things kept there be conveyed, with what haste is possible, safe and sound, and that provision be made for the things conducing thereto. His most clement Majesty will receive this with favourable mind; and it will at the same time, as I hope, be useful to the **Republic of Letters**, whose advancement I am persuaded you — illustrious not only by birth but also conspicuous for outstanding erudition — desire, and are willing to lend helping hands to. For those things which I labour at, in that sublime and divine astronomical science to be wholly restored — with untiring toil these many years past, and at no small expense, and (by the favour of the Maker of the heavens) earnestly strive to elaborate to the never-dying honour of this most august emperor and of the whole empire — are not private, or pertaining only to me and mine, but conduce to the whole learned world everywhere, as long as the sun and stars shall endure (as I trust). And therefore there is no doubt that your Lordships will gladly assist the common good here [I wholly promise myself]; which service, as far as concerns me, though my powers do not suffice to repay it, yet according to my measure I will be found perpetually grateful for, toward your most reverend Chapter; and if I can return nothing else in turn, yet I will not cease to extol and proclaim this your splendid goodwill among others. If you adjoin any of your faithful servants to accompany my things hither and take care of them, you will be able (if it so please your Lordships) to receive with him, in some quantity and at a just price, **Bohemian wines** — which grew so generous here last summer that very many preceding years scarcely gave the like; that this may be conveniently done, or if you desire anything else from these regions that is valued more highly there, I will take pains that, so far as in me lies, your wish be satisfied in this part, and so the expenses laid out can, in my opinion, in some way be recouped. More and more particular things the most renowned and excellent man Lord **Georg Rollenhagen**, the school rector there, my especial friend, will report to your Lordships, wherever there be need.

May God Best and Greatest long preserve you all, flourishing and unharmed.
Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 4th day of April, New Style, the year 1600.

- **Recipients.** The **Dean and Chapter (Capitulars) of Magdeburg Cathedral** (the Metropolitan Church of the Archbishopric of Magdeburg). The MS is an autograph **draft (*Kladde*)**.
- **Significance — the Magdeburg leg of the instrument-transport saga.** A vivid document of the difficulty of moving Tycho's instruments to Bohemia. The imperial **Senate of Magdeburg had twice refused** Rudolf II's request (despite "most clement letters") to ship Tycho's **astronomical instruments and furniture**, stored at Magdeburg, up the **Elbe** at the city's expense. The Emperor therefore now appeals instead to the **Cathedral Chapter**; Tycho forwards the imperial letter (by his servant) and asks the Chapter to expedite the safe conveyance of all his goods. This complements the Hamburg-transit letter (brahe-t_15990929001) and the Wittenberg-college / Jöstel letters (brahe-t_16001009001, brahe-t_16001008001), which record the instruments coming from **Benátky and Magdeburg via Leitmeritz** up the Elbe to Prague.
- **The "Republic of Letters" argument.** Tycho frames the favour as serving not his private interest but the *respublica literaria* — his work of "wholly restoring" astronomy being "not private … but conducing to the whole learned world … as long as the sun and stars shall endure," to "the never-dying honour of this most august emperor and the whole empire." A characteristic statement of Tycho's public, imperial self-presentation.
- **The Bohemian-wine inducement (a concrete sweetener).** Tycho offers that, if the Chapter sends a servant to accompany the goods, that servant may take back **Bohemian wines** "in some quantity and at a just price" — the 1599 vintage having been exceptionally "generous" — or anything else from Bohemia valued at Magdeburg, "so the expenses laid out can … be recouped."
- **Persons named.** the Dean and Chapter of Magdeburg; **Georg Rollenhagen** (1542–1609), rector of the Magdeburg school (the *Altstädtisches Gymnasium*), poet and Tycho's "especial friend" and local intermediary (a frequent figure in the edition, e.g. brahe-t_15880913001, brahe-t_16001009001); **Rudolf II**; the (refusing) Senate of Magdeburg.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 4 Aprilis stylo novo anno 1600*; **New Style** (imperial). Header agrees with the label.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD GEORGIUM ROLLENHAGIUM.

S. P.

QUAS die 23 Februarij huius Anni stylo vestro ad me dedisti literas, Eruditissime et amantissime Domine ROLLENHAGI, eæ mihi redditæ sunt, cum nuper Pragæ essem, unâ cum alijs quibusdam in fine Augusti superioris Anni pariter a te mihi scriptis; aderant quoque aliæ ad Doctorem RHODIUM, quas statim in ipsius hospitium misi, sed ipse peregre aberat; polliciti nihilominus sunt inquilini eas recte procuraturos. Ad priores mihi destinatas nihil nunc respondeo, siquidem earum præcipua contenta repetuntur in posterioribus, ad quas sic habe.

Civem illum Hamburgensem, quantum potui, per meos homines, qui tunc in Aulam abituri erant, iuvi, tam tuâ, quam Domini Doctoris VITI de caussa, sed lente isthic omnia, uti scis, et difficulter procedunt ob negotiorum multitudinem.

Pro supellectile meâ huc advehenda, non opus est, ut amplius sollicites apud Senatum vestrum. Cum enim Cæsa Matas, Dominus noster Clementissimus, a Domino BARVITIO rescivisset (me tamen id non cupiente, sed aliquantulum adhuc temporis Magistratui vestro rem rectius dispiciendi, uti me facturum ad te scripsi, relinquente) Magdæburgenses, quos bis per literas hac de re clementissime compellavit, officium illud detrectasse, invite id ipsum tulit, et statim ad Reverendum Capitulum vestrum de hoc eodem negotio perscribi iussit, quas literas nunc eo per quendam ex meis studiosis natione Danum mitto. Exemplum earum hîc adiunctum habes, nec dubito, quin Reverendum Capitulum, cui ego etiam scripsi, in gratiam Cæsæ Matis effecturum, ut Instrumenta mea et omnes res isthic relictæ huc per Albim suis sumptibus, quamprimum fieri poterit, adferantur. Confido etiam illud de asseribus prospecturum, quibus ea omnia ab iniuria aëris et pluviarum muniantur, quos Nautæ secum recipere poterint. Et si navem vinis Bohemicis, quæ admodum generosa superiori anno creverunt, onerari voluerit, aut alijs mercibus, quæ hîc minoris quam isthic venduntur, poterunt asseres illi ad hoc denuo usui esse; conduceret vero, ut fidus aliquis minister unâ mitteretur, qui ea, quæ hîc coëmenda essent, procuraret, et in accessu curam mearum rerum simul gereret, pro qua inveniar erga eundem gratus. Quod si factum fuerit, non opus erit, ut studiosus hic meus huc cum supellectile illa, quam Magdæburgi habeo, revertatur, sed is potius rectâ Hamburgum eat, ut pro reliquis Instrumentis inde huc pariter advehendis operam Hamburgensium sollicitet; sed tam hæc quam alia tuo consilio disponenda relinquo. Et si conduxeris pro certo precio hominem, qui cum rebus meis huc accedat, atque earum inspector sit, modo Capitulum aliquem adiungere nolit, solvam ei quidquid promiseris. In cæteris Emissarium meum ita instrue, ut quid sibi faciendum vel omittendum sit, sciat, daque operam, ut omnia mature et diligenter executioni mandentur. Habebo te in omnibus indemnem, si quid pro me exposueris, vel fidem interposueris.

Polliceris in ultimis, te reliquis scriptorum meorum postulatis per primum quemque Tabellarium responsurum, quod ut brevi facias, rogo. ROTHMANNO quod ulterius scribam, non habeo, siquidem is meis benevole et humaniter ad ipsum datis quippiam respondere gravatus est, et videtur is ita morosus atque impatiens esse, ut vix seipsum ferre queat, necdum alios. Quæ de me in suis ad te literis conqueritur, facile replicare possem, sed nolo cum homine, uti recte ais, impatientissimo et sibi ipsi præ animi impotentia vix constante contendere, aut quidpiam commertij habere. Si ipsemet sibi deesse vult, quomodo ego eum tueri aut iuvare potero, quin potius propria agam, neglectis alienis. Si existimat eius Epistolas non candide et ingenue esse a me editas, habet proculdubio exemplaria, monstret, quo hîc loco adulteratæ sint, aut pudeat ipsum de mea integritate tale quid citra occasionem suspicari. De confessione eius mihi iudicium non sumam, neque enim eam ob prolixitatem sufficienter introspicere meæ occupationes hactenus permiserunt, neque ego me Theologicis disputationibus libenter immisceo, ut mirer eum meam censuram in talibus tam sæpe tamque serio exposcere, quæ ad ea studia, quæ prius inter nos ventilata sunt, non pertinent. Duriusculum mihi videtur, quod ab initio asserit et definit, Deum nos per sacramenta salvos facere. Id sane indiget bona glossa et interpretatione sobria, si idolatriæ suspicio abesse debet, ad quam plurimi cæteroquin homines iam dudum hac præsertim in re (proch dolor) admodum proclives sunt. Quin et multa sunt præterea in eodem scripto, tam de Baptismo quam de cæna, quæ non ita invicte demonstravit, atque existimat. Sed viderit ipse et alij, si quos habet, suæ sententiæ astipulatores; meum non est tantas componere lites. Deus liberet ROTHMANNUM ab ijs, quibuscum conflictatur, miserijs, et det illi patientiam atque constantiam. Ego si illi adessem, ipsius paupertati, quantum res meæ ferrent, non defuturus essem, quemadmodum etiam antea, quando in Dania mecum fuit, ipsum non inanem demisi, sed aliquot Roseis nobilibus, pro quibus mihi tamen vix gratias agere dignatus est (adeo tunc erat insolens) donavi, cum tamen ipsius olim Princeps me longe ditior meos homines, quos aliquando ad ipsum misi, ne obulo quidem, nec etiam eos interea aluerit, quemadmodum ego per 5 vel 6 hebdomadas ROTHMANNUM, cum in Dania esset. Sed ista nihil ad rhombum, [ne]que ea, quæ parvi [no]n duco momen[ti]. De fratre eius IOHANNE, qui Doctor medicinæ est, cuperem scire, an is adhuc in vivis sit; si sic, optarem, ut me aliquando accederet; erit id illi forte non inutile.

Intellexi nuper, esse quendam in ditione Brunsvicensi nomine IOHANNEM KRABBEN, de Munden, quem præteritorum aliquot annorum Eclipses in utroque Luminari diligenter observasse aiunt; si itaque ea, quæ is circa has explorata habet, mihi procuraveris, rem apprime gratam præstiteris. Sed non suffecerint mihi nuda tempora, verum potius media scire averem, per quæ in eorum cognitionem pervenit, sive sint Altitudines stellarum sive alia huc conducentia. Cupio autem eius observata ea potissimum de caussa habere, ut cum meis in ijsdem Ecclipsibus conferre possem, atque hinc meridianorum differentiam rectius eruere. Est etiam aliquando in diversis locis dispar serenitas. Sed de observationum fide certus esse non possim, nisi compertum habuero, qua ratione, uti dixi, acceptæ sint.

Apud Cancellarium vestrum ea, de quibus antea [ad] te perscripsi, spero te effecturum, quo desiderijs nostris mature satisfiat.

Vale.
Dabantur ex Arce Cæsareana Benatica Die 5 Aprilis Anno 1600.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO GEORG ROLLENHAGEN.**

Heartiest greeting.

The letter you sent me on the 23rd of February of this year, by your style [Old Style], most learned and most loving Lord Rollenhagen, was delivered me when I was lately at Prague, together with certain others likewise written to me by you at the end of August last year; there were also others, to **Doctor Rhodius**, which I at once sent to his lodging — but he was away abroad; the residents nonetheless promised they would duly see to them. To the earlier ones addressed to me I now answer nothing, since their chief contents are repeated in the later, to which take this.

**That Hamburg citizen** I helped, as much as I could, through my men who were then about to go to court — both for your sake and for that of Lord **Doctor Vitus** [Winsheim]; but everything there proceeds slowly, as you know, and with difficulty, on account of the multitude of business.

**As for the transport of my goods hither, there is no need to solicit your Senate further.** For when the Imperial Majesty, our most clement Lord, had learned from Lord **Barvitius** (though I did not wish it, but was leaving your Magistracy a little more time to consider the matter more rightly, as I wrote you I would) **that the Magdeburgers — whom He had twice clemently addressed by letter on this — had declined that office, He took it ill, and at once ordered a letter written about this same business to your Reverend Chapter** — which letter I now send thither by one of my students, a Dane by nation. A copy of it you have here enclosed; nor do I doubt that **the Reverend Chapter** (to whom I too have written) will, for the Imperial Majesty's sake, bring it about that **my Instruments and all the things left there be carried hither by the Elbe at their own expense, as soon as can be**. I trust too they will provide for the boards by which all these may be protected from the injury of weather and rains, which the sailors can take with them. And if they should wish to load the ship with **Bohemian wines** (which grew very generous last year), or with other goods sold cheaper here than there, those boards can again serve for this. It would be useful that some faithful servant be sent along, to procure what is to be bought here and at the same time take care of my things on the way — for which he will find me grateful. If this be done, there will be no need for this my student to return hither with the goods I have at Magdeburg; but rather let him go straight to **Hamburg**, to solicit the labour of the Hamburgers for the remaining Instruments to be carried hence hither likewise; but both these and other matters I leave to be arranged by your counsel. And if you hire, for a fixed price, a man to come hither with my things and be their overseer — should the Chapter be unwilling to appoint one — I will pay him whatever you promise. For the rest, instruct my emissary so that he knows what he must do or leave undone, and take care that all be put into execution maturely and diligently. I will hold you indemnified in all things, if you lay out anything for me, or pledge your credit.

You promise, in your last, that you will answer the rest of my writings' requests by the first courier; which I beg you do shortly. **To Rothmann I have nothing further to write**, since he was loth to answer anything to my letters, sent him benevolently and courteously; and he seems to be so morose and impatient that he can scarcely bear himself, much less others. **What he complains of me in his letters to you, I could easily refute; but I am unwilling to contend, or have any commerce, with a man — as you rightly say — most impatient, and from incapacity of mind scarcely consistent with himself.** If he wishes to fail himself, how shall I be able to protect or help him? — rather let me mind my own affairs, neglecting others'. **If he thinks his Letters were not candidly and honestly published by me** [in the *Epistolae astronomicae*], he doubtless has the originals — let him show in what place they were adulterated, or let him be ashamed to suspect such a thing of my integrity without occasion. **Of his "confession" I will take no judgement**, for my occupations have not hitherto permitted me to examine it sufficiently, by reason of its prolixity; nor do I gladly meddle in Theological disputes — so that I wonder he so often and so seriously demands my censure in such things, which do not pertain to those studies formerly ventilated between us. It seems to me a little harsh, what he asserts and defines from the start: **that God saves us through the sacraments**. That indeed needs a good gloss and a sober interpretation, if the suspicion of idolatry is to be absent — to which very many men are otherwise, alas, already much inclined, especially in this matter. And there are besides many things in the same writing, on **Baptism** as on the **[Lord's] Supper**, which he has not so invincibly demonstrated as he thinks. But let him see to it, and others, if he has any supporters of his opinion; it is not mine to settle such great quarrels. May God free Rothmann from the miseries with which he struggles, and give him patience and constancy. If I were with him, I would not fail his poverty, so far as my means allowed — even as before, when he was with me in Denmark, **I did not send him away empty, but gave him several rose-nobles**, for which, however, he scarcely deigned to thank me (so insolent was he then) — whereas his own Prince, far richer than I, gave my men (whom I once sent to him) **not even an obol**, nor even fed them meanwhile, as I fed Rothmann for 5 or 6 weeks when he was in Denmark. But these things are nothing to the purpose, nor those which I reckon of [no] small moment [*text partly damaged*]. About his brother **Johann, who is a Doctor of medicine**, I should wish to know whether he is still among the living; if so, I should wish that he visit me sometime — it will perhaps be not unprofitable for him.

I have lately understood that there is a certain man in the **Brunswick** territory, by name **Johann Krabbe of Münden**, who they say diligently observed the eclipses of these past years in both Luminaries [Sun and Moon]; if, then, you procure for me what he has explored about these, you will do a most welcome thing. But the bare times will not suffice me; rather I should wish to know **the means by which he came to their knowledge — whether they be Altitudes of stars, or other things conducing hither**. I desire to have his observations chiefly for this reason: **that I may compare them with my own in the same eclipses, and thence more rightly draw out the difference of meridians** [longitude]. There is also sometimes unequal clearness [of sky] in different places. But I cannot be sure of the observations' reliability unless I have ascertained, as I said, by what method they were taken.

With your Chancellor, I hope you will accomplish those things about which I wrote you before, that our wishes may be maturely satisfied.

Farewell.
Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 5th day of April, the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Georg Rollenhagen** (1542–1609), rector of the Magdeburg gymnasium and poet (the *Froschmeuseler*) — Tycho's agent for the instruments stored at **Magdeburg**, and the relay through whom Tycho learned **Rothmann was alive** (cf. brahe-t_15990922001).
- **Significance — the Magdeburg instrument-transport and the Rothmann estrangement.**
 - **The transport (imperial muscle).** The **Magdeburg city Senate had twice refused** to ship Tycho's stored library and instruments up the Elbe; **Rudolf II "took it ill" and ordered a letter to the Magdeburg cathedral Chapter** instead — carried now by **a Danish student** of Tycho's, with a copy enclosed. Tycho lays out the logistics: shipment **by the Elbe at the Chapter's cost**, protective **boards** (reusable to load **Bohemian wine** or cheap goods on the return), a trusted overseer; if arranged, the student goes on to **Hamburg** for the *remaining* instruments. A vivid picture of moving Uraniborg's apparatus to Bohemia. (Cf. the same store at Magdeburg in brahe-t_16000124001.)
 - **The Rothmann rupture.** A revealing, bitter passage on **Christoph Rothmann** (the former Hesse-Kassel mathematician, Tycho's great correspondent of the 1580s): Rothmann, now "morose and impatient," complains of Tycho to Rollenhagen and demands Tycho's verdict on a **theological "confession"** he has written. Tycho declines — he "does not meddle in Theological disputes" — but cannot resist noting his unease at Rothmann's thesis **"that God saves us through the sacraments"** (needing "a good gloss" lest it smack of "idolatry"), and at his arguments on **Baptism and the Supper**. On the charge that Tycho **did not faithfully print Rothmann's letters in the *Epistolae astronomicae* (1596)**, Tycho retorts: let him show where they were "adulterated." Tycho recalls hosting Rothmann **5–6 weeks in Denmark** and gifting him **rose-nobles** (scarcely thanked), contrasting Rothmann's own **Prince (Landgrave Wilhelm IV)**, who gave Tycho's men "not even an obol." A poignant late-stage souring of a famous scientific friendship.
 - **A new observer for longitude.** Tycho seeks the eclipse observations of **Johann Krabbe of Münden** (Brunswick) — but insists on knowing **the method** (star-altitudes etc.), since he wants them **to compare with his own in the same eclipses and so derive the meridian-difference (longitude)**. A clean statement of the **eclipse-timing method for longitude**.
- **Persons named.** Georg Rollenhagen; **Doctor Rhodius** (a Magdeburg/Wittenberg correspondent, unidentified-detail); **Doctor Vitus [Winsheim]**; **Barvitius**; the **Magdeburg cathedral Chapter**; **Christoph Rothmann** and his **brother Johann** (a physician); **Landgrave Wilhelm IV** ("his own Prince," unnamed); **Johann Krabbe of Münden**; the **Hamburg citizen** (unnamed); "your Chancellor" (unnamed). Places: **Benátky**, **Prague**, **Magdeburg**, the **Elbe**, **Hamburg**, **Brunswick/Münden**, Denmark.
- **Text note.** A short **damaged stretch** near the end — *"Sed ista nihil ad rhombum, [ne]que ea, quae parvi [no]n duco momen[ti]"* — is partly editorially reconstructed (brackets); rendered "these things are nothing to the purpose, nor those which I reckon of [no] small moment," with the damage flagged. *(nihil ad rhombum = "nothing to the point," a proverb.)*
- **Calendar.** *Die 5 Aprilis Anno 1600* at Benátky (imperial reckoning) → **5 April 1600 [N.S.]**; header and label agree. *(Rollenhagen's incoming letter is dated "23 Feb … stylo vestro" = Old Style, the Magdeburg reckoning.)*

text.original:
IOHANNES KEPLER AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

ICH Μ. IOHAN. KEPLER, Einer Er: Landt in Steier Mathematicus, bekhenne, demnach Ich mit gnediger Erlaubung wolermelten landtschafft, ein reise in Beheim furgenommen, fürnemlich den Edlen vnd Gestrengen Herrn TYCHO BRAHE, Herrn auf Knudtstrup vnd Vraniburg, wegen Dero Gest. ansehnlicher vnd weitberühempten Astronomischen Instrumente vnd fürhabender bücher zuebesuchen, Das ich zue dem ende den vierten Februarij des 1600 Jahrs allhero gehn Benathka kommen, allda den wollermelten Herrn, gnedig vnd allerfreundtlichst woll empfangen, auch diese gantze Zeitt vber aller müglichkeit nach also tractirt worden, das ich mich hingegen iederzeit, zue aller Vnderthaniger Danckbarkeit schuldig erkhennen.

Demnach auch Ir Gest. alls einen liebhaber aller künsten, vnd denen beygethonen Cultoribus, gnedig gefallen, mir einen gueten theill Irer observationum, sambt andern anhengigen Inventionibus vnd laboribus Astronomicis freywillig mitzuetheilen: vnd Ich aber ietziger Zeitt bösen schädlichen gebrauch anderer leutte nützliche vnd rhuemliche arbeitt eigen nütziger verschlagener weisse zur hinderlichen den rechten Urhabern zueentziehen, vnd anderen rhümberechtig zuezuschreiben, zur gemüeth gefürtt: hab ich eigner sorgfaltigkeit halber, für nützlich vnd rathsamblich geachtet, mit gegenwärtiger meiner eignen handtschrifft vnd vndergedruckten Petschafft dahin mich zuuerpflichten, dass ich alles das, so mir von wolermelten Herrn BRAHE communicirt oder hernacher, in was wege es wolle, communicirt soll werden, in hochster geheim halten. Darmit auch mich andere alss einen liebhaber der Philosophia, gebe vnd offtermelten Herrn BRAHE, alss den rechten authori selbsten iederzeit gefallen würt, vmbgehen handlen vnd dero mich gebrauchen wölle: alles auff treuw vnd glauben, treuwlich vnd vngefehrlich.

In vrkhund meiner handschrifft, vnd angeporn Pitschafft, Geben den 5 Aprilis im 1600 Jah. Benat.
text.english:
**Johannes Kepler to Tycho Brahe.**

I, Master Johannes Kepler, Mathematician of an Honourable Province in Styria, acknowledge: that — after I had, with the gracious permission of the well-mentioned [Provincial] Estates, undertaken a journey into Bohemia, chiefly to visit the noble and stern Lord Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup and Uraniborg, on account of His Lordship's considerable and far-famed astronomical instruments and intended books — I came hither to Benátky, to that end, on the fourth of February of the year 1600; where I was graciously and most kindly well received by the well-mentioned Lord, and, during all this time, was treated according to all possibility [as well as could be], so that I, on the other hand, at all times acknowledge myself bound to all submissive gratitude.

Since, then, it has also graciously pleased His Lordship — as a lover of all the arts, and [a friend] to the devotees [*Cultores*] attached to them — to share with me, freely, a good part of His *observations*, together with other associated *inventions* and astronomical *labours*: and since I have brought to mind the present evil, harmful practice of [certain] people, of withdrawing other [people]'s useful and praiseworthy work, in a self-interested, cunning manner, to the hindrance of the rightful authors, and of ascribing it to others as though [theirs] by right of renown — I have, for the sake of my own conscientiousness, deemed it useful and advisable, by this my present own handwriting and the seal pressed below, to bind myself thereto: that I will keep in highest secrecy all that is communicated to me by the well-mentioned Lord Brahe, or shall hereafter, in whatever way it may be, be communicated [to me]; so that others, too, may regard me as a lover of *Philosophy*; and [so] that I will, at all times — as it shall please the oft-mentioned Lord Brahe, as the true author himself — deal, act, and conduct myself, and let him make use of me: all upon trust and faith, faithfully and without guile.

In witness of my handwriting and innate seal, given the 5th of April, in the year 1600. Benátky.

documents.apparatus:
- **A landmark Tycho–Kepler document.** This is **Kepler's signed declaration of confidentiality** — his solemn undertaking to keep Tycho's observations and discoveries secret — drawn up at **Benátky on 5 April 1600**, during the tense first months of their association. It is the formal pledge that helped patch up the early quarrel between the two men, and it ranks among the most-cited documents of their relationship. The witness survives, naturally, in the **Keplerian papers** (Vienna, cod. Vindob. lat. 10703 — the same volume preserving Kepler's transcript of Tycho's letter to Hoffmann, brahe-t_16000406001, written the *next* day, 6 April, on Kepler's return to Prague).
- **Kepler's self-styling.** *M. Johann Kepler, einer Ehrbaren Landschaft in Steier Mathematicus* — "Master Johannes Kepler, Mathematician of an Honourable Province [the Provincial Estates] in **Styria**" — his then-title as district mathematician of Graz, granted leave to travel to Bohemia "to visit … Tycho Brahe … on account of His Lordship's far-famed astronomical instruments and intended books." He records his arrival "**on the fourth of February 1600**" and Tycho's kind reception.
- **The substance of the pledge.** Tycho having "**freely shared a good part of His observations**, together with other … *inventions* and astronomical *labours*," Kepler — mindful of the "**evil practice**" of cunningly stripping work from its rightful authors and ascribing it to others (a pointed allusion to the kind of plagiarism-charge then swirling around **Ursus** and others) — binds himself, "by this my own handwriting and seal," to **keep in highest secrecy** everything Tycho communicates to him, and to use it only as Tycho, "**the true author**," shall please. The closing formula *auf Treu und Glauben, treulich und ungefährlich* ("upon trust and faith, faithfully and without guile") is the binding legal tag.
- **Code-switching.** Latin technical/legal nouns embedded in the German — *observationum, Inventionibus, laboribus Astronomicis, Cultoribus, Philosophia, authori* — kept and italicised, rendered into English.
- **Calendar.** *Geben den 5 Aprilis im 1600 Jahr. Benat[ky]* = **5 April 1600**; Bohemia (imperial) = **New Style**. Header agrees with the label.
- **Correction.** Corrected 'Herrn aus Knudtstrup' to 'Herrn auf Knudtstrup' in Kepler's confidentiality declaration; Dreyer's print (TBOO VIII p.296) uses the standard 'Herr auf X' formula.

text.original:
ILLUSTRI ET GENEROSO DOMINO, DOMINO IOHANNI FRIDERICO HOFMANNO, LIBERO BARONI IN GRUENPUEHEL ET STRECHAU, PRÆFECTO PROVINCIÆ DUCATUS STYRIÆ ET ARCHIDUCATUS AUSTRIÆ, MARSCHALCHO UBIQUE HÆREDITARIO, BURGRAVIO IN STEYER, NEC NON SACRÆ CÆSAREÆ MAIESTATIS AULÆ CONSILIARIO ET SERENISSIMI ARCHIDUCIS MAXIMILIANI CUBICULARIO PRIMARIO, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO IMPRIMIS HONORANDO.

ILLUSTRIS ET GENEROSE VIR, DOMINE ET AMICE HONORANDISSIME.

REDIT nunc Pragam M. KEPLERUS, et licet suasor illi fuerim, ut domestici mei, qui etiamnum Pilsnæ est, et inter alia in negocio dictum KEPLERUM concernente sollicitat, reditum, quem intra paucos dies futurum spero, expectaret, ut quid fieri possit, certius resciremus (præsertim cum spes aliqua facta sit, Saam Cæsam Matem petitionibus meis humilimis clementissime annuere velle) atque demum aliquid rati concludere possemus: tamen cum ipsum nihilominus abitum festinare intelligerem, reliqui hominem suo arbitrio. Quid vero inter nos ventilatum sit, Illris Do Tua e D. Doctore IOANNE IESSENIO, qui has adfert, seorsim cognoscet: is enim interfuit, dum hæc gererentur: quare longiore et tædiosâ eorum commemoratione supersedeo, omnia ad hanc rem facientia Illustris Dnis Tuæ prudenti consilio dispicienda ordinandaque etiamnum relinquens.

Cœterum de puero, quem Illustris Dnatio Tua ad me mittere decrevit, sciat me libenter eum, quandocunque advenerit, recepturum, tum quoque laboratorem Spagiricum. Et expecto pariter fabrum illum Mechanicum, qui e Styria venturus est. Quam primum vero per occupationes licuerit, spero me Pragæ futurum, ubi plenius cum Illri Done Tua de ijs, quæ hîc omissa sunt, agam.

Valeat Tua Illris Do quam optime et diutissime.
Dabantur ex arce Cæsarea Benatica die 6 Aprilis Anno 1600.
Illri Generositati Tuæ
Addictissimus
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the illustrious and generous Lord, Lord Johann Friedrich Hoffmann, Free Baron in Grünbühel and Strechau, Prefect of the Province of the Duchy of Styria and of the Archduchy of Austria, hereditary Marshal everywhere, Burgrave in Steyr, and also Councillor of the Court of His Sacred Imperial Majesty and First Chamberlain of the Most Serene Archduke Maximilian, his lord and friend especially to be honoured.**

Illustrious and generous man, lord and most honoured friend.

Master Kepler now returns to Prague; and although I had been his advisor [urged him] to await the return of my servant — who is still at Pilsen, and, among other things, is pressing [matters] in the business concerning the said Kepler — which return I hope will be within a few days, so that we might more certainly find out what can be done (especially since some hope has been given that His Imperial Majesty wishes most clemently to assent to my most humble petitions), and so that at last we might conclude something settled: yet, since I understood that he was nonetheless hastening his departure, I left the man to his own judgment. But what was ventilated between us, Your Illustrious Lordship will learn separately from Doctor Jan Jessenius, who brings these [lines]; for he was present while these things were transacted. Wherefore I forbear a longer and tedious recounting of them, leaving everything bearing on this matter still to be considered and ordered by Your Illustrious Lordship's prudent counsel.

For the rest, about the boy whom Your Illustrious Lordship has decided to send to me, let [you] know that I will gladly receive him, whenever he arrives — and likewise the spagyric [alchemical] laborator. And I equally await that mechanical craftsman who is to come from Styria. As soon as my occupations permit, I hope to be at Prague, where I will more fully treat with Your Illustrious Lordship about those things which have been omitted here.

May Your Illustrious Lordship fare as well and as long as possible.
Given from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 6th day of April, in the year 1600.
Most devoted to Your Illustrious Generosity,
Tycho Brahe,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **A key Tycho–Kepler document — preserved in Kepler's own hand.** The witness (Vienna, cod. Vindob. lat. 10703) is **a transcript made by Kepler himself**, which is why it survives among the Keplerian papers. It dates from the **first, strained Benátky period** (Feb–April 1600), when Kepler had come to Tycho but the terms of his stay were unsettled.
- **Recipient.** **Johann Friedrich Hoffmann, Free Baron of Grünbühel and Strechau** (1568–1615), the great Styrian magnate — *Landeshauptmann* of Styria, hereditary Marshal, Burgrave of Steyr, Imperial Aulic Councillor, and First Chamberlain of **Archduke Maximilian** — and **Kepler's patron**, at whose Prague house Kepler lodged. Tycho writes to him as the broker of Kepler's situation.
- **Content.** Kepler "**now returns to Prague**"; Tycho had urged him to wait for the return (from **Pilsen**, where the court was) of Tycho's servant, who was "pressing the business concerning Kepler" — i.e. seeking the Emperor's assent to Tycho's petitions (a salaried place for Kepler) — "especially since some hope" had been given that **Rudolf II** would "**most clemently assent**"; but Kepler hastened off, so Tycho "left the man to his own judgment." The details of "what was ventilated between us" Hoffmann will hear from the bearer, **Dr. Jan Jessenius** (the anatomist, present at the negotiations). This is contemporary evidence of the delicate Tycho–Kepler accommodation that Jessenius helped mediate.
- **Other matters.** Hoffmann is sending Tycho a *puer* (a boy/page), a *laborator Spagiricus* (an **alchemical laboratory-assistant** — *spagyric* = Paracelsian chemistry), and a *faber Mechanicus* (a **mechanic/instrument-maker**) "from Styria" — staffing for Tycho's Prague establishment.
- **Calendar.** *ex arce Caesarea Benatica die 6 Aprilis 1600* = **6 April 1600**; Bohemia (imperial) = **New Style**. Header agrees with the label.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD IOHANNEM IESSENIUM A IESSEN.

S. P.

CLARISSIME vir, amice plurimum mihi semper dilecte, quae tuae fidei concredidi, Generoso D. HOFFMANNO seorsim monstranda, cupio mihi nunc remitti; litteras tamen illas, quas TEGNAGLIUS ultimo ad me dedit, quae de Magnifici D. CORRADUCIJ resolutione faciunt, vellem bene tuo sigillo munitas ac tuis inclusas unâ cum meis ad DANIELEM mitti, siquidem in ijs faciat mentionem eorum, quae D. CORRADUCIUS apud Caesar. Mai. meo nomine impetravit, ut sciat DANIEL, eo rectius se facere, si apud D. CORRADUCIUM in meis rebus sollicitet, non minus quam apud D. BARVICIUM, quem quodammodo lentum in ijs promovendis ............. Dubitat enim ipse DANIEL in ultimis suis ad me datis, an hoc facere debeat nec ne. Ego vero rescripsi, mihi id non inconsultum videri, caute tamen omnia agenda, ne D. BARVICIUM per imprudentiam offendat, nam amborum retinere benevolentiam, quoad fieri poterit, satius duco. Coeterum cum tu hîc spectator et auditor fueris eorum, quae a KEPLERO dicta factaque sunt, sub ipsum discessus momentum, et simul quomodo postea, iuxta currum mihi valedicturus, poenitentia quadam eorum duci prae se ferret, atque ea omnia, quod affectus suos regere non posset, excusaret, egoque a condonatione non alienus essem, tibique in aurem susurraverim, ut efficeres illum Pragae literis ad me datis id ipsum testari, quod male ipsum habeat, se sic exorbitasse cupereque mecum in gratiam redire, quod et te facturum aiebas, et sponte antea mihi seorsim dixeras, te in itinere ipsum serio admoniturum, imo reprehensurum, quod se tam impotenter et biliose gesserit, contra quam decet virum doctum et honestum: iccirco mitto tibi hîc inclusas ipsius literas manu eius propria exaratas, quarum effrenem petulantiam et nimis arrogantem dicacitatem nec per meum vinum nec per meum contemtum, nec quicquid eiuscemodi aliud quod praetendit, excusare poterit, nisi et tunc furiosus fuit (uti forte huius morbi semina, etiam cum sibi maxime constare videtur, clam fovet) cum ista composito animo scriberet, et ipsemet calamo, me ignorante (qui ipsi iam ignoscere coeperam, siquidem resipiscere voluisset) praeest. Miraberis, non dubito, hominis in malitia citra omne meum meritum pertinaciam, nec forte habebis aliud, quid dicas, quam me mea humanitate, uti etiam tacite exprobrâsti, effecisse, ut iste hominem exueret, atque in rabidum canem, quem suo stomacho se aemulari dicere solitus est (utinam etiam cerebro et corde) transformaretur. Inspice igitur et despice, quod et ego faciam. Quis enim scienter et volenter furentem facile curaret? Si ipsum in via admonuisti, et ut rationes inveniret, mecum denuo in amicitiam redeundi, adhortatus es, uti proculdubio fecisti, vide quaeso, quales fructus ediderit haec tua sobria, candida et amica admonitio et adhortatio. Ego, etsi facilimum mihi sit, omnes ipsius oblatratus vera redargutione compescere, nolo tamen cum tam procaci lingua praedito, nec modestiae aut virtutis curam habente, contendere, memor illius Catonici:

Contra verbosum noli contendere verbis.

Constitui igitur in posterum nihil cum eo habere commercij, sive per literas sive oretenus, et optarem me nunquam habuisse, tunc minus mea humanitate abuti posset. Iussi quidem, statim ac is abierat, MATHIAM studiosum nonnulla ex chartis illis, quas ad me recepi, describere, ut ea promptius legere, cum ipso, quando unâ cum DANIELE redierit, conferre possem, atque mea dubia illi subgerere, et quomodo peragendum esset, expiscari, atque tum illi a se conscripta, uti sancte promisi, restituere. Verum cum ex his malitiosis literis plus satis percipiam, eum non reversurum, uti etiam non cupio, ipsemet in culpa est, quod pollicitis stare nequeam. Et super hoc, quod in Epistola iam missa iecit fundamentum, vix utar eo tamquam archi[tec]to, cui aliquid ex meis observationibus et laboribus superstruatur. Ille ipse me iam magis cautum, quam antea fui, reddidit; genio, uti spero, bono mei curam habente, et omnia sic in meum commodum digerente. Nolim tamen, ut cuipiam has Keplerianas literas ostendas, et ne quidem D. HOFFMANNO, aut cum ipso KEPLERO hac de re expostules, nisi forte sua quadam importunitate tibi occasionem dederit, sed actutum cum hoc eodem nuntio, bene conclusas et iterum obsignatas, mihi remittas. Si tamen subolfeceris ipsum apud D. HOFFMANNUM vel alios, ut suam probaret innocentiam, me calumniatum esse, aut quippiam veritati minus consonum effutijsse, fac quod bonum et integrum virum decet, quod et non gravatim effecturum mihi polliceor (prout et ego te saepius contra aliorum sugillationes tutatus sum) ut meam a te defendi causam, atque id, quod veritas postulat, asseverari resciscam. Interim etiam an apud URSUM istum aliquid in mei contumeliam tacite moliatur (quomodo enim illi amplius fidam?) per tertiam vel quartam manum inquire, quamvis nihil morer, quicquid dixerit, modo vera dixerit, et cum Deo V. simul fuerimus, tibi aperiam, quidnam id sit, de quo ita minari videtur, et plura, quae ad dilutionem illorum, quorum foecundus et facundus est consarcinator, faciunt, licet ipse plaeraque nôsti, suggeram.

Vale.
Dabantur ex arce Benateka die 8 Aprilis Anno 1600.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO JOHANNES JESSENIUS A JESSEN.**

Heartiest greeting.

Most renowned man, friend always most dear to me: what I entrusted to your good faith, to be shown separately to the noble Lord **Hoffmann**, I wish now to be sent back to me. But those letters which **Tengnagel** last sent me, which bear on the resolution of the magnificent Lord **Coraduz**, I should wish — well secured with your seal and enclosed in yours — to be sent together with mine **to Daniel**, since in them he makes mention of the things which Lord Coraduz obtained from the Imperial Majesty in my name, so that Daniel may know he does the more rightly if he solicits my affairs with Lord Coraduz, no less than with **Lord Barvitius** — whom [I find] somewhat slow in promoting them …………… [*text breaks off — a lacuna in the copy*]. For Daniel himself, in his last letter to me, doubts whether he ought to do this or not. But I wrote back that it does not seem to me ill-advised — yet that all is to be done cautiously, lest through imprudence he offend Lord Barvitius; for I judge it better to keep the goodwill of both, so far as may be.

For the rest: since you were here a spectator and hearer of **what was said and done by Kepler at the very moment of [his] departure** — and likewise how afterward, **about to bid me farewell beside the wagon, he showed signs of a certain repentance** of them, and excused it all on the ground that he could not govern his passions, and I was not averse to pardon — and since I **whispered in your ear that you should get him, by a letter sent me from Prague, to attest that very thing: that it grieved him to have so overstepped, and that he wished to return into favour with me** (which you said you would do, and had earlier of your own accord told me separately, that you would seriously admonish him on the journey, nay reprehend him, for having borne himself so impotently and biliously, contrary to what befits a learned and honourable man): for that reason **I send you here enclosed his own letter, written in his own hand** — whose unbridled petulance and over-arrogant scurrility he will not be able to excuse by my wine, nor by my contempt, nor by any other such thing he pretends, unless he was then too in a frenzy (as perhaps he secretly nurses the seeds of this disease even when he seems most composed of himself) when he wrote those things with composed mind, and himself wields the pen — without my knowledge (I who had already begun to pardon him, had he but wished to come to his senses). You will wonder, I do not doubt, at the man's pertinacity in malice, beyond all my deserving; and perhaps you will have nothing else to say than that **I, by my humanity — as you even tacitly reproached me — brought it about that this man put off the man, and was transformed into a rabid dog**, which he was wont to say he rivalled with his stomach (would that [he did so] also with brain and heart). Inspect it, then, and despise it, as I shall too. For who would readily cure one knowingly and willingly raving? If you admonished him on the way, and exhorted him to find reasons for returning anew into friendship with me — as doubtless you did — see, I pray, **what fruits this sober, candid, and friendly admonition and exhortation of yours has borne**. I, though it would be most easy for me to curb all his barkings by a true refutation, am yet unwilling to contend with one endowed with so insolent a tongue, and having no care for modesty or virtue — mindful of that saying of Cato:

*"Do not strive with words against a wordy man."*

I have resolved, therefore, to have henceforth no commerce with him, whether by letter or by word of mouth; and I could wish I never had — then the less could he abuse my humanity. I did indeed order, as soon as he had gone, the student **Mathias** to copy out some things from those papers which I took back to myself, that I might read them more readily, and confer about them with him [Kepler] when he should return together with Daniel, and put my doubts to him, and fish out how it ought to be carried through, and then restore to him what he had written, as I solemnly promised. But since from this malicious letter I perceive more than enough that **he will not return** (as I also do not wish), he himself is at fault that I cannot stand by my promises. And upon this — on which he laid a foundation in the letter now sent — **I shall hardly use him as an architect, upon whom anything of my observations and labours should be built**. He himself has now made me more cautious than I was before; my good genius, I hope, taking care of me, and disposing all things thus to my advantage. I should not wish, however, that you show this Keplerian letter to anyone — not even to Lord Hoffmann — nor that you expostulate with Kepler himself about this, unless perhaps by some importunity he gives you occasion; but that you send it back to me at once, by this same messenger, well closed and sealed again. If, however, **you scent out that he, to Lord Hoffmann or others — to prove his own innocence — has calumniated me, or blurted out anything less than consonant with the truth**, do what becomes a good and upright man (which I promise myself you will do not grudgingly — even as I have often protected you against the carpings of others), so that I may learn my cause is defended by you, and that what truth demands is affirmed. Meanwhile inquire also, **through a third or fourth hand, whether he secretly contrives anything against my honour with that Ursus** (for how should I trust him further?) — although I care nothing for whatever he may say, provided he say the truth; and when, God willing, we are together, I will open to you what that thing is about which he seems so to threaten, and will suggest more things conducing to the dissolving of those of which **[Ursus] is a fertile and fluent botcher** — though you yourself know most of them.

Farewell.
Given from the castle of Benátky, the 8th day of April, the year 1600.
