documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Johannes Jessenius / Jan Jessenský** (1566–1621), the anatomist and Tycho's friend, who had **mediated between Tycho and Kepler** and was present at the Benátky quarrel. (He is the "Planet" of brahe-t_16000327002; later executed in the 1621 Prague Old-Town-Square execution.) The witness is a Vienna copy.
- **Significance — the great Tycho–Kepler rupture of April 1600 (a primary document).** Kepler had come to Benátky early in 1600; a violent quarrel erupted over his working conditions, his access to the observations, and his keep. This letter, written days after, is **Tycho's raw account to the mediator**:
 - **The quarrel and the wagon-side repentance.** Jessenius "was a spectator and hearer of what Kepler said and did at the very moment of departure," and saw how Kepler, **bidding farewell beside the wagon, showed "a certain repentance,"** excusing himself as unable to "govern his passions." Tycho "was not averse to pardon" and had Jessenius coax a written apology from Prague.
 - **The "malicious letter."** Instead, Kepler sent **an angry letter "in his own hand,"** whose "unbridled petulance" Tycho refuses to excuse "by my wine, nor my contempt" — the very pretexts Kepler had alleged (Tycho's table-wine; Tycho's slighting of him). Tycho, wounded, half-suggests Kepler is subject to fits of "frenzy" (*furor*).
 - **The famous metaphor.** Tycho throws back Kepler's own self-description: that Kepler "put off the man and was transformed into a **rabid dog**, which he was wont to say he rivalled **with his stomach** — would that [also] with brain and heart." (Kepler's own self-portrait as choleric/dog-like, turned against him.)
 - **The resolution to break off** — citing the *Disticha Catonis*: ***"Contra verbosum noli contendere verbis"*** ("Do not strive with words against a wordy man") — and the pointed line **"I shall hardly use him as an architect, on whom anything of my observations and labours should be built."** *(The bitter irony: within weeks they reconciled; Kepler returned, inherited the observations, and built the* Astronomia nova *— and the* Rudolphine Tables *— precisely on them.)*
- **The Ursus fear (the sore point).** Tycho asks Jessenius to inquire "through a third or fourth hand" **whether Kepler secretly colludes with Ursus** against Tycho's honour — a live anxiety, since **Kepler had earlier written a flattering letter to Ursus** (Nicolaus Reimers Bär), who printed it in his defamatory *De astronomicis hypothesibus*. "[Ursus] is a fertile and fluent botcher" (*consarcinator*). (Cf. the Ursus thread, brahe-t_16000401001, brahe-t_16000328001.)
- **The court-business frame (opening).** Tycho's affairs at the imperial court: papers to be returned (shown privately to **Hoffmann**); **Tengnagel's** letters on **Coraduz's** "resolution" (what Coraduz obtained from the Emperor in Tycho's name) to be forwarded **to Daniel**, who should solicit Tycho's business with **both Coraduz and Barvitius** (the latter "somewhat slow"), keeping both men's goodwill. *A lacuna* (…………) interrupts the Barvitius clause in the copy.
- **Persons named.** Johannes Jessenius; **Johannes Kepler** (the quarrel); **Johann Friedrich Hoffmann von Grünbüchel** (imperial councillor, Kepler's Prague host); **Franz Tengnagel** (*Tegnaglius*); **Rudolf von Coraduz** (Vice-Chancellor); **Johann Anton Barvitius** (imperial secretary); **Daniel** (an unidentified court-agent/solicitor of Tycho's at Prague who travels with Kepler — left unidentified, flagged); the student **Mathias** (a *studiosus*/assistant, plausibly Matthias Seiffart — not confirmed, flagged); **Nicolaus Reimers Bär (Ursus)**; **Cato** (the *Disticha Catonis*). Place: **Benátky**.
- **Cross-references.** A keystone for the **Tycho–Kepler convergence** thread and the **Ursus dispute** thread; route alongside the reconciliation that followed (Kepler's return and succession).
- **Calendar.** *die 8 Aprilis Anno 1600* at Benátky (imperial reckoning) → **8 April 1600 [N.S.]**; header and label agree.
- **Correction.** Restored singular translation of 'has Keplerianas literas' ('this Keplerian letter') for consistency with the two earlier renderings of the same epistolary-plural noun in this letter, both referring to the single enclosed Kepler letter (Dreyer, TBOO VIII p.299).

documents.incipit: INTELLEXI, Vir nobilissime atque Mathematicorum omnium facile Princeps, ex Agente rerum …

text.original:
IOANNES GEORGIUS HERWARTUS AB HOHENBURG AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

INTELLEXI, Vir nobilissime atque Mathematicorum omnium facile Princeps, ex Agente rerum Serenissimi Principis mei in aulâ Caesareâ, ALEX. PRENDTL, qui ad negotia sua quaedam propria expedienda hâc transijt, literas illas, quas D. Doctori HELLER ad me dirigendas committis, praeposito seu Magistro supremo equorum dispositorum Pragae consignari. Coeterum novi et expertus sum eorum, quibus cura Postae seu equorum dispositorum incumbit, negligentiam et desidiam, atque adeo oscitantiam quoque miram, ita ut literas aliô dirigendas aliorsum nonnunquam transmittant. Tenet itaque haec res me admodum et forte plus nimio solicitum, ne forte ea, quae ad me mittis, intereant. Quare rogo te etiam atque etiam, ut in posterum, si quid literarum ad me dederis, eas praefato Agenti rerum Principis mei, vel in absentia illius IOANNI MENHARDO S. Caes. M. Consilij aulae Imperialis Secretario Latino, qui aulam Imperatoris sequitur, quorum titulos his subscripsi, consignes; curabunt enim illi sedulo, ut sub coperto, uti vocant, Serenissimi mei Principis tuto ad me transferantur.

Novissime literas tuas pridie huius anni labentis datas unâ cum dono partis primae Progymnasmatum restauratae Astronomiae (id quod gratitudinis ergo commemoro) accepi, nullas autem recentiores. Quod si interea temporis nullas ad me dederis, bene se res habet, et omni solicitudine vaco: si quas vero dederis, timeo, ne alicubi delitescant, et obsecro summopere, ut eas reiterari cures, et vel hac ratione solicitudinem alleves.

Atque hisce tibi officia et studia mea paratissima quaeque polliceor.
Datae Monachij die 11 Apr. A. 1600.
text.english:
**Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg to Tycho Brahe.**

I have understood, most noble man and easily Prince of all mathematicians, from the Agent of my Most Serene Prince's affairs at the Imperial court, **Alexander Prendtl** — who passed this way to expedite certain affairs of his own — that those letters which you entrust to Doctor Heller, to be directed to me, are consigned to the prefect, or supreme Master, of the relay-horses [the post] at Prague. But I know, and have learned by experience, the negligence and sloth — and indeed the wondrous somnolence too — of those to whom the care of the Post, or of the relay-horses, is committed, so that they sometimes send letters that ought to be directed one way off in another direction. And so this matter holds me very anxious — perhaps more than is fitting — lest the things you send me should perchance perish. Wherefore I ask you, again and again, that in future, if you give any letters to me, you consign them to the aforesaid Agent of my Prince's affairs, or, in his absence, to **Johann Menhard**, Latin Secretary of the Aulic Imperial Council of His Imperial Majesty, who follows the Emperor's court (whose titles I have subscribed below); for they will diligently see to it that, "under cover" (as they call it) of my Most Serene Prince, they be safely conveyed to me.

Most recently I received your letter, dated the day before [the beginning of] this passing year, together with the gift of the first part of the *Progymnasmata* of restored Astronomy (which I mention out of gratitude); but none more recent. So if, in the meantime, you have given me none, the matter stands well, and I am free of all anxiety; but if you have given any, I fear lest they be lying hidden somewhere, and I most earnestly beseech that you see to their being repeated, and by this means at least relieve my anxiety.

And with these I promise you my most ready services and zeal.
Given at Munich, the 11th day of April, in the year 1600.

documents.incipit: SERENISSIMI Principis, Magni Ducis Hetruriae, Clementissimas literas ab Illma Domne …

text.original:
ILLUSTRISSIMO ET GENEROSISSIMO VIRO DOMINO COSMO CONCINIO E COMITIBUS PENNAe SERENISSIMI MAGNI DUCIS HETRURIAe APUD SACRAM CÆSAREAM MAIESTATEM ORATORI MAGNIFICENTISSIMO DOMINO OBSERVANDISSIMO.

ILLUSTRISSIME ET HONORANDISSIME DOMINE.

SERENISSIMI Principis, Magni Ducis Hetruriae, Clementissimas literas ab Illma Domne Vestra mihi favorabiliter missas, unâ cum proprijs suis, accepi, et magna inde affectus sum voluptate, cum quod Serma eius Celsitudo meis Clementissime respondere, ijsdemque benignissimo animo annuere non dedignata sit, tum etiam quod Illma Domo Vestra mihi tam benevole scripserit, et Sermi Principis sui voluntatem, ubi Pragae adfuero, plenius mihi exponere haud degravetur. Adveniam itaque, auxiliante Deo, quamprimum nonnulla ad aedificia, quae pro Instrumentis meis Astronomicis hîc debito modo disponendis, nunc parantur, pertinentia, adoravero; et observationes quasdam, quibus per instantes aliquot dies (neque enim alias intra annum eiuscemodi revertuntur) invigilandum, Coelitus deduxero. Spero autem haec, et quaecunque praeterea me remorari poterint, intra 14 ad summum dies expediri posse, ut Illmae Doi Vrae, ab hisce curis liberatus, promptius adesse queam, et quae nomine Sermi Principis sui mihi referenda habet, obsequentissimo animo percipere. Interim ut hanc morulam, pro consueta sua humanitate, candide accipiat, meque sibi commendatum habeat, officiosissime peto.

Deus Opt. Max. Illustrm D. V. diu florentem et incolumem conservet.
Dabantur ex Arce Caesareâ Benaticâ Die 14 Aprilis Anni 1600.
Illustrissae Domni Vae
Reverenter addictissimus
T. B.
text.english:
**To the most illustrious and most generous man, Master Cosimo Concini, of the Counts of Penna, most magnificent Ambassador of the Most Serene Grand Duke of Tuscany with His Sacred Imperial Majesty, most observed Lord.**

Most illustrious and most honoured Lord.

I have received the most clement letter of the Most Serene Prince, the Grand Duke of Tuscany, favourably sent me by Your Illustrious Lordship, together with your own; and I have been affected thereby with great pleasure — both because his Most Serene Highness did not disdain most clemently to answer mine, and to assent to them with most kindly mind, and also because Your Illustrious Lordship wrote to me so benevolently, and does not find it burdensome to set forth to me more fully the will of his Most Serene Prince when I shall be at Prague. I will therefore come, God helping, as soon as I have attended to certain things pertaining to the buildings which are now being prepared for arranging my astronomical instruments here in due manner; and as soon as I have brought down from heaven certain observations which must be watched for over the next several days (for they do not otherwise recur within a year). But I hope these — and whatever else can delay me — can be despatched within at most fourteen days, so that, freed from these cares, I may the more promptly be present to Your Illustrious Lordship, and with most obedient mind receive what he has to report to me in the name of his Most Serene Prince. Meanwhile I most dutifully ask that you take this little delay candidly, according to your accustomed kindness, and hold me commended to you.

May God Best and Greatest preserve Your Illustrious Lordship, flourishing and unharmed, for long.
Given from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 14th day of April, in the year 1600.
Reverently most devoted to Your Illustrious Lordship,
T. B.

documents.title: Tycho Brahe → Raphael Ciaparenius — Benátky, 14 April 1600 [N.S.]

documents.incipit: QUAS iussu Illmi et Magnifmi Oratoris Florentini ad me Excella Vra per certum tabellarium …

text.original:
EXCELLENTISSIMO ET ERUDITISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO RAPHAELI CIAPARENIO, APUD ILLUSTRISSIMUM ORATOREM FLORENTINUM PRAGAe DOMUS PRÆFECTO, DOMINO ET AMICO HONORANDO.

QUAS iussu Illmi et Magnifmi Oratoris Florentini ad me Excella Vra per certum tabellarium direxit literas, modo accepi, atque pro hoc mihi praestito officio plurimas eidem gratias habeo, relaturus, si quid unquam meâ opellâ praestari poterit, quod illi vicissim acceptum esse queat. Praedicavit mihi iam antea TENGNAGLIUS noster, qui ante mensem circiter in Patriam, Parentes suos invisurus, abijt, singularem Exae Vrae humanitatem et erga se benevolentiam, quam filio quoque meo, cum vobis adesset, praestitam, magni beneficij loco duco. Daboque operam, quantum in me est, ne se certasse priorem poeniteat, speroque nos, ubi Pragam advenero, ulterioris notitiae atque amicitiae fundamina coram posituros.

Interim et semper Exa Va quam optime valeat.
Dabantur properanter ex Arce Caesareâ Benaticâ Die 14 Aprilis Anni 1600.
text.english:
**To the most excellent and most learned man, Master Raphael Ciaparenius, house-prefect [major-domo] with the Most Illustrious Florentine Ambassador at Prague, his lord and friend to be honoured.**

The letters which, by command of the Most Illustrious and Magnificent Florentine Ambassador, Your Excellency directed to me by a sure courier, I have just received; and for this office rendered me I give him very many thanks, intending to repay it — if ever anything can be performed by my poor effort that may in turn be acceptable to him. Our Tengnagel — who left about a month ago for his homeland, to visit his parents — had already proclaimed to me Your Excellency's singular kindness and benevolence toward himself; which, shown also to my son when he was with you, I count in the place of a great benefit. And I shall give my effort, as much as is in me, that he may not regret having been the first to enter [this contest of courtesy]; and I hope that, when I come to Prague, we shall lay in person the foundations of further acquaintance and friendship.

Meanwhile, and always, may Your Excellency fare most well.
Given hastily from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 14th day of April, in the year 1600.

DER EDELEN VNDT VIELTHUGENDTSAMEN FRAWEN SUSANNEN HAIECKIN, GEBORNER MÖRLIN ETC. DESS HERRN D. THADDÆJ HAGÆCIJ EHLICHEN HAUSSFRAWEN, MEINER INNSONDERS GONSTIGEN VNDT BESONDERN FREUNDIN.

MEINEN freundtlichen gruß mitt wunschung alles guetten zuuor. Edele vndt vielthugendtsame fraw Susanna, ewer schreiben habe ich empfangen vndt daneben die brieffe, so Dauidt Heidlern, euern schuldenern, angehen, vndt bien willens als baldt gen Lübeck meinem factor aldo, einem vornehmen burger, deß nahmen euch itzunder bekandt, zueschreiben vndt vleissig zuuermahnen, daß er dazue thue alles, was ihm jmmer moglich sein kan, nach laut ewer vollmacht vndt ewern herren vndt euch dasselbe geldt einmahnen, vndt werdtt auß beyliegenden zettel zuesehen haben, mitt was worten ich solches vonn ihm begehren wil; wenn ich denn meinen bescheidt hieraus erlange, soll derselbe euch alsbaldt zuewissen gethan werden. Die fraw wolle aber so wohl thun, vndt mihr jhres herren doctoris Thaddæj zuestandt mitt furfallender gelegenheitt ferner wissen lassen. Der allmechtige guetige Gott verleihe ihm helf vndt beystandt, denselben ich euch auch inn seinen schütz vndt schirm trewlich thue befehlen.

Datum vff dem kayss. schloß Benatky den 17 aprilis anno 1600.

Postscripta.Ferner, lieber Jochum Boch, gebe ich euch gantz freundtlich zuewissen, daß
deß edelen vndt hochgelarten herrn doctoris Thaddæj Hagæcij (mitt welchem ich bey 25 Jahren guete freundtschafft vndt correspondentz gehalten)
haußfraw
Susanna Haieckin etc., mihr diese verschienene tage zugeschrieben, vndt
nachdem gedachter ihr herr vndt haußwirt itziger zeitt leider, beyde vonn
alters wegen (denn er ein mann vonn 76 Jahren) vndt anderer zuefelliger
schwacheitt, sehr vnpaßlich ist, so hat sie vonn seinetwegen begehret,
daß ich jhnen mitt gueten raht vndt hulf erscheinen wolte, das sie konte bey einem
der
alda zue Lubeck sein soll, mitt nahmen Dauidt Heidler, hundert gulden, so
obgedachter jhr herr ihm in bahren gelde geliehen, eingemahnet bekommen. So
habe ich ihr vertrostung gethan, das ihr als meiner alda besonder guetter
freundt vndt factor euer bestes daran thuen wurdet, wenn
ihr die zuegehorige brief vndt beweiß nebenst einer richtigen vollmacht bekomet, so
hatt sie alsbaldt mihr solches alles zuegeschickt, wie ich denn euch
hierneben dasselbe thue vberlieffern, vndt ist Thaddæj vndt mein gantz
vleissige bitt an euch, ihr wollet kein muhe undt vleiß sparen, daß diese
vornehme guete ehrliche leute kondten ohne weittern aufschub zue ihrer
bezahlung kommen; mann saget, daß derselbige Dauidt Heidler soll alda reich gefreyhet,
vndt deß herren stadthaubtmans aldo, eines vonn Brandensteins, tochter
bekommen haben, welches ich doch nicht baldt glaube. Wann ihm aber so wehre,
kundte er, der Heidler, leichtlich ein solche geringe schuldt ablegen, oder
wann das schon nicht ist, funde er doch wohl raht, sein brief wieder
einzulossen vndt solch geldt zuebezahlen. Wo ferne er daßelbige nicht gutwillig thuen
wirdt, werde ich verursacht bey römischer kayss. maiestat, vnsern gnedigsten herrn, zue sollicitiren vmb ein gnedigst schreiben an die herren
burgemeister vndt raht zue Lubeck, das sie obgedachten herrn Thaddæum vndt
seiner lieben haußfrawen zue jhrer bezahlung helffen, vndt ernstlich
dazue thuen, waß sich gehoret, sintemaln ich den frommen, ehrlichen mann Thaddæum als
meinen guetten alten freundt inn seiner jtzigen schwacheitt keinesweges
verlassen wil oder kan, als dann wirdt Heidler nicht allein die hauptsum,
sondern alle intereße vndt schäden, so darauf konnen gerechnet werden,
bezahlen mussen, vndt dafur zue recht stehen, daß er sein zuesage
vndt brief nicht gehalten, wie einem ehrlichen mann wohl anstehet, vor welchen ihr
jhm inn gueter meinung warnen könnet, vndt wann ihr mihr vonn meinen andern
sachen wiederumb zueschreibt, so last mihr auch vonn diesen richtigen
bescheidt wissen.
text.english:
**To the noble and very-virtuous lady Susanne Hájek, née Mörlin, etc., the lawful wife of Master Dr. Thaddaeus Hagecius, my especially favourable and particular [lady-]friend.**

My friendly greeting, with the wishing of all good, beforehand. Noble and very-virtuous lady Susanna, I have received your letter, and therewith the letters concerning David Heidler, your debtor; and I am minded to write at once to Lübeck, to my factor there — a distinguished burgher, whose name is now known to you — and diligently to admonish him to do everything therein that may ever be possible to him, and, according to the tenor of your power-of-attorney, to dun in that money for your lord [husband] and for you. And you will see from the enclosed note with what words I will request such [action] of him. When then I obtain my answer hereupon, the same shall at once be made known to you. But would the lady do so well as to let me know further, with arising opportunity, the condition of her lord Doctor Thaddaeus. May Almighty, kindly God grant him help and assistance — the same [Doctor Thaddaeus] I also faithfully commend, together with you, into His [God's] protection and shelter.

Given at the Imperial castle Benátky, the 17th of April, in the year 1600.

**Postscript.** Further, dear Jochum Boch, I let you know in all friendliness that the wife of the noble and highly learned Lord Doctor Thaddaeus Hagecius (with whom I have kept good friendship and correspondence for some twenty-five years), Susanna Hájek, etc., wrote to me these past days; and since her aforesaid lord and husband is at present, alas, very unwell — both by reason of age (for he is a man of seventy-six years) and of another incidental infirmity — she has on his behalf requested that I would come forward to them with good counsel and help, so that she might get called in, from a certain man said to be there at Lübeck, by name David Heidler, the hundred guilders which her aforesaid lord lent him in ready money. So I have given her assurance that you, as my especial good friend and factor there, would do your best in the matter once you receive the pertinent letters and proofs together with a proper power of attorney; whereupon she at once sent me all of this, which I herewith likewise deliver over to you. And it is Thaddaeus's and my very earnest request to you that you would spare no trouble or diligence, so that these distinguished, good, honest people might come to their payment without further delay.

It is said that this same David Heidler is supposed to have married rich there, and to have gotten the daughter of the lord town-captain there, one of the von Brandensteins — which, however, I do not readily believe. But if it were so, he, Heidler, could easily discharge so small a debt; or if that is not so, he would nonetheless find a way to redeem his bond and pay such money. In so far as he will not do this of his own goodwill, I shall be moved to solicit, with the Roman Imperial Majesty, our most gracious Lord, for a most gracious letter to the lords burgomaster and council of Lübeck, that they help the aforesaid Lord Thaddaeus and his dear wife to their payment, and earnestly see to it as is proper — since I in no wise wish, nor can, abandon the pious, honest man Thaddaeus, my good old friend, in his present infirmity. Then Heidler will have to pay not only the principal sum, but all interest and damage that can be reckoned upon it, and answer in law for not having kept his promise and bond, as befits an honest man — of which you may warn him in good part. And when you write to me again about my other affairs, let me also know the proper answer concerning this.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Susanne Hájek, née Mörlin** (*Susanna Haieckin, geborne Mörlin*), wife of **Dr. Thaddaeus Hagecius (Tadeáš Hájek)**, Tycho's old friend and court-broker at Prague (see brahe-t_15981201001, …0530001, …0329003). A business-courtesy letter.
- **Content.** Tycho will help recover a debt owed Susanne (and her husband) by one **David Heidler**: he will write to his **factor [agent] at Lübeck** — "a distinguished burgher, whose name is now known to you" (deliberately unnamed) — instructing him, under Susanne's **power-of-attorney** (*Vollmacht*), to dun in (*einmahnen*) the money; an enclosed note (*beiliegender Zettel*) gives the form of the request. He asks her, in turn, to keep him informed of **Hagecius's health**.
- **Poignancy.** The closing prayer for help and assistance for Hagecius, whom Tycho "faithfully commends … into [God's] protection and shelter," is touched by the fact that **Hagecius was failing** — he died in **September 1600**, a few months after this letter.
- ***denselben ich euch auch in seinen schutz und schirm treulich tue befehlen*** — **flagged construction**: read as "the same [him, Doctor Thaddaeus] I also faithfully commend, [together] with you (*euch*, dative), into His [God's, *seinen*] protection and shelter." The pronoun-stacking is loose chancery German; the sense (a joint commendation of the ailing Hagecius and his wife to God) is rendered accordingly.
- **Register.** Courteous family/business German; the address to the gentlewoman (*Edle und vieltugendsame Frau*) and the polite third-person *die Frau wolle* ("would the lady …") are preserved. A draft (*Kladde*).
- **Calendar.** *kayss. schloß Benatky den 17 aprilis anno 1600* = from the **Imperial castle of Benátky**, 17 April 1600; Bohemia (imperial) = **New Style**. Header agrees with the label.
- **Language and placement.** The recovered text is Early New High German, the Postscripta to Tycho's German letter of 17 April 1600 N.S. from Benátky to Susanne Hájek, née Mörlin, wife of Thaddaeus Hagecius; the postscript itself is addressed past her, to Tycho's Lübeck factor Jochum Boch. Boch is independently attested elsewhere in Tycho's German correspondence as "mein Factor zu Lübeck, Jochum Boch" (Opera Omnia XIV / Friis, *Breve og Aktstykker*, 1875), confirming the standing relationship this postscript presupposes.
- **Persons.** Thaddaeus Hagecius — Tadeáš Hájek z Hájku (1525–1600), Rudolf II's imperial physician and one of Tycho's closest Prague allies of some twenty-five years' standing (cf. Hockey et al., *Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers*) — is here reported gravely unwell; the letter's "76 Jahren" runs slightly ahead of his actual age (about 74–75 in April 1600), whether Tycho's approximation or Susanna's own report relayed through her. His wife Susanna, née Mörlin, is the addressee of the main letter this postscript closes.
- **The debt and Tycho's leverage.** David Heidler, resident at Lübeck and said to have married a daughter of the local Stadthauptmann "von Brandenstein," owed Hagecius 100 gulden lent in cash. Tycho threatens, failing voluntary payment, to solicit a letter from Rudolf II to the Lübeck Bürgermeister and Rat — a small, concrete instance of Tycho using his imperial standing to press a friend's private debt.
- Crux: neither "David Heidler" nor the Lübeck "von Brandenstein" family is identified beyond this letter in the works consulted (Christianson, Dreyer, Friis, the *Tycho Brahes Breve* register); a firm identification would need Lübeck civic/Stadthauptmann records outside our current holdings.

documents.incipit: MITTO, Vir nobilissime atque Mathematicorum omnium facile princeps, ut libri, quos …

text.original:
IOANNES GEORGIUS HERWARTUS AB HOHENBURG AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

MITTO, Vir nobilissime atque Mathematicorum omnium facile princeps, ut libri, quos petijsti, ad te transferantur, his iuncta

IOANNIS VIRDUNGI tabulas resolutas de supputandis motibus syderum,

Tabulas Prutenicas ERASMI RHEINHOLDI,

COPERNICUM de triangulis et Algorithmum demonstratum No. 76.

Habemus exemplar græce manuscriptum HIPPARCHI Bithyni in ARATI et EUDOXI Phænomena librorum 3, cum Asterismis (uti inscribitur in Codice Florentiæ Ao 1567 impresso. Nec enim Asterismi illi sunt HIPPARCHI, nec forte reliqua) et alterum exemplar Magnæ Syntaxeos CL. PTOLEMÆI, literâ pervetustâ et eleganti conscriptum. Quod si tibi dubiæ lectiones occurrant, lubens admodum et sedulo conferam et ad te perscribam. Nec inpræsentiarum occurrunt iam alia, sed hisce tibi officia mea promptissime offero.

Datæ (18 Apr. circiter) A. 1600.
text.english:
**Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg to Tycho Brahe.**

I send, most noble man and easily prince of all mathematicians — so that the books you sought may be conveyed to you — joined herewith:

the *Resolved Tables* of **Johann Virdung**, on computing the motions of the stars;

the *Prutenic Tables* of **Erasmus Reinhold**;

**Copernicus** *On Triangles*, and the *Algorithm Demonstrated*, No. 76.

We have a Greek manuscript exemplar of **Hipparchus** of Bithynia, *on the Phaenomena of Aratus and Eudoxus*, in 3 books, with the *Asterismi* (as it is inscribed in the codex printed at Florence in the year 1567 — for those *Asterismi* are not Hipparchus's, nor perhaps the rest); and another exemplar of the *Great Syntaxis* of **Claudius Ptolemy**, written in a very ancient and elegant hand. And if doubtful readings should occur to you, I will most gladly and diligently collate them and write them out to you. Nor at present do other [matters] occur; but with these I most readily offer you my services.

Given (about 18 April), in the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg** (see the Munich series), forwarding a further consignment from Tycho's desiderata and offering to collate two important Greek manuscripts in his keeping.
- **Printed books sent.** *Ioannis Virdungi tabulae resolutae* = the *Tabulae resolutae* (for computing planetary motions) of **Johann Virdung of Hassfurt**. *Tabulae Prutenicae Erasmi Rheinholdi* = the **Prutenic Tables** of **Erasmus Reinhold** (1551), the Copernican-based tables. *Copernicus de triangulis* = **Copernicus**, *De lateribus et angulis triangulorum* (the trigonometric tract, Wittenberg 1542), here bound with an *Algorithmus demonstratus* (No. 76).
- **Greek manuscripts offered.** *Hipparchi Bithyni in Arati et Eudoxi Phaenomena libri 3* = **Hipparchus of Nicaea (Bithynia)**, *Commentary on the Phaenomena of Aratus and Eudoxus* — the only surviving work of Hipparchus, in three books, with an appended *Asterismi* (star-list); Herwart notes, shrewdly, that the *Asterismi* "are not Hipparchus's, nor perhaps the rest [of the appended matter]," citing the **Florence 1567** printed edition's own rubric. The second is "another exemplar of the *Great Syntaxis* [the **Almagest**] of **Ptolemy**," in a very old and elegant Greek hand. Herwart offers to collate *dubiae lectiones* (doubtful readings) for Tycho — a scholarly textual-criticism service.
- ***Magna Syntaxis*** = Ptolemy's *Almagest* (Gk *Μεγάλη Σύνταξις*).
- **Calendar.** Munich (Catholic Bavaria) = **New Style**. The dateline is itself **approximate in the source** — *Datae (18 Apr. circiter)* "given about 18 April"; the header therefore carries " c. 18 April 1600," matching the edition's "(18 Apr. circiter)."

documents.abstract: Thanks Winshemius for repeated correspondence and reports having interceded with Lord Barvitius through Tengnagel on behalf of a Hamburg citizen Winshemius had commended.
documents.incipit: EXCELLENTISSIME et Eruditissime Domine Doctor VITE WINSHEMI, Amice honorande: Literae …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD VITUM WINSHEMIUM.

S. P.

EXCELLENTISSIME et Eruditissime Domine Doctor VITE WINSHEMI, Amice honorande: Literae Excellentiae Tuae humanissimae et candidi erga me amoris refertissimae bis vel ter, postquam in Bohemiam concessi, mihi redditae sunt; pro quo constanti et sincero erga me affectu gratias habeo plurimas. Memini etiam me Tuae Excae aliquoties rescripsisse, eamque meas pariter accepisse spero. Quantum vero ad ultimas, quas Exa Tua per Civem illum Hamburgensem, quibus Rollenhagianae adiunctae erant, dederat, commodum accidit, quod cum Pragae essem (ablegaturus TENGNAGLIUM nostrum, cum quodam ex meis domesticis, Pilsnam in Aulam Caesaris) eae mihi redderentur. Nam per emissarios meos negotium illud Civis, cuius caussam mihi commendâsti, Domino BARVITIO, summo Secretario, exponi iussi, eumque, ut petitioni eius non deesse velit, diligenter ex me rogavi: quod et factum est. Nam alter ille hisce diebus huc reversus (TENGNAGLIUS enim in suam Patriam inde profectus est, post aliquot septimanas huc, Deo volente, rediturus) retulit Dominum BARVITIUM in se recepisse negotij illius promotionem, quamprimum Civis iste Pilsnam veniret et caussam illam sibi proponeret; quod tamen necdum factum erat, antequam domesticus ille meus inde discederet, qui per integrum mensem ibi substitit. Miror itaque, ubi interea Civis ille fuit, et an Pragae remanserit, Caesaris isthuc reditum expectaturus, ignoro. Semel enim tantummodo mecum Pragae locutus est; postea hominem non vidi, quamvis volebam, ut denuo me accederet, quo plenius eius causae circumstantias cognoscere possem; quas etiam ut FRANCISCO indicaret, iussi. Si in alijs longe maioribus Tuae Exae in his oris gratificari unquam potero, habebit me semper quam promptissimum et nostrae amicitiae perpetuo memorem.

Quae ad OLIGERUM ROSÆKRANTZIUM communem Amicum proferre volui, ignoro an acceperit, multo enim iam tempore nihil ad me literarum dedit. Faciat igitur T. E. me certiorem, quomodo vivat et valeat, utque subinde mihi scribat, ipsum admoneat.

Vale diu et feliciter.
Dabantur ex Arce Caesarea Benaticâ Die 20 Aprilis stylo recognito Anni 1600.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Vitus Winshemius.**

Heartiest greeting.

Most excellent and most learned Lord Doctor Veit Winsheim, honoured friend: Your Excellency's most courteous letters, brimming with candid love toward me, have been delivered to me two or three times since I withdrew into Bohemia; for which constant and sincere affection toward me I give you many thanks. I recall, too, that I wrote back to Your Excellency several times, and I hope you likewise received mine. As for the last, which Your Excellency had sent through that Hamburg citizen — to which the Rollenhagen letters were attached — it fell out conveniently that they were delivered to me while I was at Prague (about to dispatch our Tengnagel, together with one of my servants, to Pilsen to the Emperor's court). For through my emissaries I had that citizen's business — whose cause you commended to me — laid before Lord Barvitius, the supreme Secretary, and diligently asked him on my behalf to be willing not to fail his petition; and this was done. For that other man [my servant], having returned hither these last days (Tengnagel, that is, set off from there for his homeland, to return hither, God willing, after some weeks), reported that Lord Barvitius had taken upon himself the furtherance of that business as soon as the citizen should come to Pilsen and put his case to him — which, however, had not yet been done before that servant of mine departed thence, who tarried there a whole month. I wonder, therefore, where that citizen was in the meantime; and whether he stayed on at Prague to await the Emperor's return thither, I do not know. For he spoke with me only once, at Prague; afterward I did not see the man, although I wished him to come to me again, so that I might more fully learn the circumstances of his case — which I also ordered him to set out to Franciscus. If ever I shall be able to oblige Your Excellency in other, far greater matters in these regions, you shall ever find me most ready and perpetually mindful of our friendship.

What I wished to convey to our common friend Holger Rosenkrantz, I do not know whether he received, for he has now sent me no letter for a long time. Let Your Excellency therefore inform me how he lives and fares, and remind him to write to me from time to time.

Farewell, long and happily.
Given from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 20th day of April, by the corrected style, of the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** at **Benátky nad Jizerou**.
- **Recipient.** *Vitus Winshemius* = **Veit Ortel von Windsheim (Vitus Winshemius the Younger)** (1542–1608), physician and professor at **Wittenberg** — Tycho's correspondent and intermediary in the Saxon/Wittenberg academic world. Addressed throughout as *Excellentia Tua*, "Your Excellency".
- **Persons named.**
 - *Rollenhagiana[e literae]* = letters of **Georg Rollenhagen** (1542–1609), rector at Magdeburg, enclosed with Winshemius's packet; Rollenhagen's own letter to Tycho of 15 May 1601 survives as brahe-t_16010515001.
 - *Tengnaglius / Franciscus* = **Franz Gansneb Tengnagel von Camp**, Tycho's noble assistant (and future son-in-law), here being sent to the imperial court at Pilsen and then travelling on to his Westphalian homeland.
 - *Dominus Barvitius, summus Secretarius* = **Johann Anton Barvitius (Barwitz)**, imperial secretary to Rudolf II — Tycho's channel for promoting the petition of an unnamed *Civis* (citizen) whose cause Winshemius had commended.
 - *Oligerus Rosaekrantzius* = **Holger Rosenkrantz "the Learned"** (1574–1642), Danish nobleman and theologian, the "common friend" whose silence Tycho remarks.
 - *Civis ille Hamburgensis / Civis* = the unnamed **Hamburg citizen** who carried the post, and the (same or another) **petitioner** whose suit at court Tycho was advancing.
- **Places & events.** *Praga* = Prague; *Pilsna* = **Plzeň**, where Rudolf II's court had withdrawn (cf. brahe-t_16000508001); the petitioner was to follow the Emperor there.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S. P.* = *salutem plurimam* ("heartiest greeting"); *Vale diu et feliciter* → "Farewell, long and happily"; *Dabantur* (epistolary) → "Given."
- **Calendar (this chapter's convention — idiom of note).** Dateline *Die 20 Aprilis **stylo recognito** Anni 1600* — "by the **corrected / reformed style**," i.e. **New Style (Gregorian)**. *Stylo recognito* is one of Tycho's variant labels for the Gregorian reckoning (alongside *stylo novo*) now standard in his Imperial-service correspondence; rendered literally and glossed, not silently converted.
- **Correction.** Latin: 'cum is quodam' corrected to 'cum quodam', and 'reddererentur' corrected to 'redderentur', per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 303.

documents.abstract: Explains his methods for astrological Directions and the distribution of the Heaven, arguing they must be calculated to the Horizon of the native's birthplace rather than current residence.
documents.incipit: CLARISSIME et Eruditissime Vir, Amice mihi plurimum semper faciende. Literæ tuæ paulo …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD LUDOLPHUM RIDDERSHUSIUM.

S. P.

CLARISSIME et Eruditissime Vir, Amice mihi plurimum semper faciende. Literæ tuæ paulo post solstitium hybernum superioris Anni ad me datæ præterlapso nuperrimo huius Æquinoctio mihi primum redditæ sunt, quibus si per omnia nunc ita luculenter respondere, uti desiderares, non concedatur, tribuas id occupationum mearum moli; quæ tamen otium utcunque admittit, brevibus exposita, sic habe.

De Directionum administratione et rationibus, tum quoque distributione Cœli, quæ antea significavi, satis per se clara sunt, nec, etiamsi quam maxime vellem, ea exemplis illustrandi nunc suppetit oportunitas. Possunt vero secundum Eclipticam pariter Directiones fieri, non dissimiliter, iuxta motum ☉lis diurnum, numerandæ, nam et has subinde pondus habere animadverti. Debent autem Directiones institui ad Horizontem eius loci, in quo quis natus est, non autem ubi postea habitat; quia quilibet suum secum portat Cœlum suasque influentias, quocunque iverit. Octogenaria Thematum distributio ad hoc conducit, ut robur efficaciæ Planetarum rectius pateat, siquidem dimidius Angulus Rectus sit inter Meridianum et Horizontem, post horum duorum limites, magni sunt roboris. Significata autem ex duodenaria Divisione potius consueto Astrologorum more petenda.

Transitus ♄ni, quia tardigradus est, utplurimum vim habet, ♂tis autera minus. Tunc vero stimulantur effectus, cum in idem tempus similes profectiones coincidunt; impediuntur vero, si contrariæ; et Directiones, quæ generaliorem habent significationem, hîc etiam augendo vel minuendo plurimum possunt. Si eodem tempore inciderint adversæ et prosperæ Directiones, seipsas fere elidunt, et effectum boni malique imminuunt. Directiones, quæ exitum naturalem vel violentem portendunt, variæ se habent, nec ad certum aliquod genus restringi possunt; et oportet multa alia simul considerare, nec Stoicam necessitatem introducere. Geniturarum influxus fausti vel infelices vario modo mutari et transplantari possunt; ut non nimium ijs sit indulgendum. Omnes autem rationes, quibus hoc efficitur, nimis longum foret enarrare. Neque etiam in omnes homines Astra æqualiter influunt, sed quidam se reddunt eorum viribus magis obnoxios quam alij. Verum Deus, Author Universi, omnia pro suo nutu moderatur. Atque hæc ad quæstiones tuas pro tempore respondisse sufficiat.

Ad tempora et eventus Nativitatum, quas misisti, attendere et in eas disquirere nunc non vacat; imo etiamsi vacaret, non multum temporis talibus curis libenter tribuo, gravioribus et maioris momenti studijs potius addictus. Restitutionem motus ☾ris nunc communicare non possum, nondum enim typis edita est, uti neque in cœteris Planetis desiderijs tuis morem gerere. Conservantur adhuc libri mei et res, pro maiori parte, Magdæburgi; ubi advenerint, et oportunius otium nactus fuero, dabo operam, ut plenius in talibus gratificari queam. Literas adiunctas ad Dominum DAVIDEM FABRICIUM absque omni interposita morâ per certum hominem dirige; eius enim interest, ut eas cito nanciscatur.

Iamque vale, quodque pluribus nunc tecum non agam, candide excusatum habe.
Dabantur ex Arce Cæsareâ Benaticâ, 5 milliaribus Pragâ distante, Die 20 Aprilis Anni 1600, stylo recognito.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO LUDOLF RIDDERSHAUSEN.**

Heartiest greeting.

Most renowned and most learned Man, a friend always to be highly esteemed by me. Your letter, sent to me a little after the winter solstice of last year, was first delivered to me only at the most recent equinox just past; to which, if it be not now granted me to reply so fully in every respect as you would wish, attribute it to the mass of my occupations. Yet what my leisure does, in any case, allow — set out briefly — take thus.

Concerning the management and methods of **Directions**, and also the **distribution of the Heaven**, which I indicated before, [they] are clear enough in themselves, nor — even if I most greatly wished it — is there now opportunity to illustrate them with examples. Directions can indeed equally be made according to the Ecliptic, to be reckoned not differently, by the Sun's diurnal motion — for I have observed that these too sometimes have weight. But Directions ought to be set up to the Horizon of the place in which a person was born, not where he afterward dwells; because each carries his own Heaven with him, and his own influences, wherever he goes. The eight-fold distribution of the Figures serves this end, that the strength of the Planets' efficacy may more rightly appear, since a half right-angle [45°] lies between the Meridian and the Horizon; beyond the bounds of these two, [the planets] are of great strength. But the significations are rather to be sought from the **twelve-fold Division** [the twelve houses], after the customary manner of the Astrologers.

The transit of **Saturn**, because it is slow-moving, has for the most part [great] force; that of **Mars** less. The effects are stimulated when similar **profections** coincide at the same time, but are impeded if contrary; and Directions, which have a more general signification, can here too do much, by increasing or diminishing. If at the same time adverse and prosperous Directions fall together, they almost cancel each other out, and lessen the effect of good and of ill. Directions which portend a natural or a violent death vary, and cannot be restricted to any fixed kind; and one must consider many other things at once, and not introduce **Stoic necessity**. The auspicious or unlucky influxes of **genitures** can be altered and transplanted in various ways, so that they are not to be indulged too far. But to relate all the methods by which this is effected would be too long. Nor do the Stars influence all men equally, but some render themselves more subject to their forces than others. Yet God, the Author of the Universe, governs all things according to his will. And let it suffice to have answered these things to your questions, for the time.

To attend to the times and outcomes of the **Nativities** you sent, and to inquire into them, there is now no leisure; indeed, even were there leisure, I do not willingly give much time to such cares, being rather devoted to weightier studies of greater moment. The **restitution of the Moon's motion** I cannot now share, for it is not yet published in print — nor [can I] gratify your wishes in the other Planets. My books and things are still kept, for the greater part, at Magdeburg; when they shall have arrived, and I have obtained more suitable leisure, I will take pains to gratify [you] more fully in such matters. The enclosed letter to Lord **David Fabricius**, direct without any interposed delay, by a sure man; for it is in his interest to obtain it quickly.

And now farewell; and that I do not deal with you at more length now, hold me candidly excused.
Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, distant 5 miles from Prague, the 20th day of April, the year 1600, in the recognised [New] style.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Ludolf Riddershausen** (*Ludolphus Riddershusius*), a learned correspondent who had submitted **astrological questions and nativities** to Tycho. (No prior letter to/from him in the edition; precise biography to firm up.) His letter, sent "a little after the winter solstice" of 1599, reached Tycho only at the spring equinox of 1600.
- **Significance — Tycho's fullest brief statement on predictive-astrology technique.** A compact exposition of his views (this chapter's convention, *Astrology*), kept on the controlled terms:
 - **Directions** (*Directiones*) and the **distribution / division of the heaven** (house systems). Directions may also be reckoned along the **Ecliptic** by the Sun's diurnal motion; they must be cast to the **Horizon of the birthplace**, "because each carries his own Heaven with him … wherever he goes."
 - **Two house schemes contrasted:** the **eight-fold distribution** (quadrants halved at the 45° half-right-angle between Meridian and Horizon) best shows "the strength of the Planets' efficacy," while the **significations** are sought from the customary **twelve-fold division** (the twelve houses).
 - **Transits & profections:** **Saturn**'s transit (slow) is potent, **Mars**'s less; effects are reinforced when **profections** agree, cancelled when they conflict; concurrent adverse and prosperous **Directions** "almost cancel each other out."
 - **Death-directions** vary and resist fixed rules; "one must consider many things at once, **and not introduce Stoic necessity**."
 - **Free-will caveat (doctrinally important):** the influxes of **genitures** "can be altered and transplanted in various ways … not to be indulged too far"; the Stars do not influence all men equally; and "**God, the Author of the Universe, governs all things according to his will.**" Tycho also distances himself from the practice — he declines to work up Riddershausen's nativities, "being rather devoted to weightier studies" (cf. the same posture in brahe-t_16000120001).
- **Glyphs & terms (kept; this chapter's convention/).** ☉ = **Sun**, ♄ = **Saturn**, ♂ = **Mars**, ☾ = **Moon** (names in English, glyphs retained in the source block). *Directiones*, *profectiones*, *genitura*, *thema* per the controlled list.
- **Textual flag — *Octogenaria*.** *Octogenaria Thematum distributio* literally = an "eighty-fold" distribution, but the context (the **45° half-right-angle**, contrasted with the *duodenaria* twelve-fold division) requires the **eight-fold / octant (octotopos) house system** in which each quadrant is bisected. Rendered **"eight-fold distribution"** by sense; the literal *Octogenaria* is flagged as a probable form/print issue and noted here, not silently emended.
- **Other matter.** The **lunar restitution** is "not yet published in print" (cf. brahe-t_15981231001); Tycho's books are still at **Magdeburg**. He asks Riddershausen to forward an enclosed letter to **David Fabricius** (1564–1617, the Frisian pastor-astronomer, discoverer of Mira Ceti; the recurring "David Fabricius" thread) "without delay."
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Die 20 Aprilis Anni 1600, stylo recognito* — *stylo recognito* = the "**recognised**" (New/Gregorian) style; imperial. The note *5 milliaribus Pragâ distante* fixes Benátky "5 miles from Prague." Header agrees with the label.

text.original:
[TYCHO BRAHE AD VIDUAM HENRICI RANTZOVII].

EDLER vnnd vielthugendsam fraw statthalterin, jnbesonders gunstige gutte freundin. Nechst meines freundtlichen grusses vnd willigen dienstes fermeldung geb ich der frawen gantz freundlich zuwissen, das nachdem ich vernommen, daß mein vertrawtter gutter freunndt vnd blutverwanter in Dennemark, Eske Bilde, nicht zeittlich genung hat zuwissen bekommen von der hauptsumme im land zu Holstein zu bezahlen vnnd meinen brieff wiederumb einzulössen, so hab ich ihm wiederumb davon geschrieben, vnnd alle gelegenheit noch einmahl verstendiget, vnnd danebenst copien von brieffuen darzugehörig geschicht, worauff ehr mir wiederumb zugeschrieben, das er alles auff nechstkumpfftigen vmbslag in diesen lauffenden jahr von meinetwegen will richtigmachen. Bitt darumb gantzfreundtlich, die fraw stathalterin wolt eß alles hierin zum besten auffnehmen, vnnd bei dem herrn Diderich von Dingcklauben handlen, das er wolle zufrieden sein biß auf vorgenante zeit; die zinß aber, welche zu nechstvorgangnen vmbslag sollte ausgelegt werden, vorsihe ich mich sey zu rechter zeitt bezahlt. Ferner wolte ich die fraustathalterin gantz freundtlich gebeten haben, daß sie wolte mit allen den eeissenwerck vnd was anders ich alda zu Wandeßbech vmb mein eigen geldt nöttwendig machen lassen, ein richtig anordnung thun, daß eß mihr möchtte wiederumb erstattet werden, vnd nicht ferner auff dero vielgeliebten sohn Bredo, dem ich davon fleissig geschrieben (vnd er mir dog nichtes geanttuort), schicken, furnemlich dieweill, wie ich vernommen, die fraw willenß ist, gedachtem jhren sohn Wandeßbech abzuhandellen vnd selbst einzuhaben. Jch weß genugk, daß die frauw mein schaden nicht begehret, vnd was zuvor darahn von jhren lieben herrn stathalter, seligen dechtnuß, bezalt ist worden, davon die fraw woll bescheid weiß, kan davon abgeregnit werden, bitt nuhr, daß daß vbrige mihr möchtte bezalht werden, vnd meinem factor zu Hamburgk, Symon von Petkom, zugesthelt, der auch nebenst den herrn zu Hamburgk, smid Jacob Holsten, von allen bescheid weiss zu sagen, vnnd darauff zu quitiren. So fern aber der frawen nicht geliebt die vbrige eisentrallien, vnd waß sonst von eisenwergk da gemacht ist, zu behallten, bitt ich, daß gedachten meinen factor muge vergonnet werden, daß er dasselbige alleß, so fur meinem gehlt ist beköstiget vnd nicht bezalt, muge wiederumb wegknehmen, vnd ein theill davon ihn Hamburgk wiederumb zu gelde machen, daß furnembst aber, so von eissenwergk ist, mihr nebenst denn andern meinen guttern so bald nach ihr röm. kay. may., vnserm gnedigen herrn, schrifftlich an die herrn von Hamburgk begehr, dieselben heraufkommen zu schicken.

Jch vorsihe mich zur frawstathalterin, daß sie mihr diss nicht abslagen wirt, sondern mit dem ehesten, weill eß nun bei anderthalb Jahren gewehrt vnd auffgeschoben ist, ein eigentlichen bescheid hierauff machen. Wohrin ich kan die frawstathalterin oder einigen von jhren kindern nach meinem vermugen wiederumb dienstlich sein, will ich allzeitt gantz guttwillig gefunden werden, vnd thu hiemit die fraw stathalterin sambt allen den ihrigen in schütz vnd schirm deß Allmechtigen treulich befehlen.

Datirt auff dem kayserlichen slotz Benateck in Behemen den 22 thag aprilis stylo nouo anni 1600.
text.english:
**[TYCHO BRAHE TO THE WIDOW OF HENRIK RANTZAU].**

Noble and most virtuous Lady governor's-wife, especially favourable good friend. Next [after] the declaration of my friendly greeting and willing service, I give the Lady quite amicably to know that, after I learned that my trusted good friend and blood-relation in Denmark, Eske Bille, did not get to know in time enough about paying the principal sum in the land of Holstein and redeeming my bond, I have written to him again about it, and explained the whole situation once more, and sent besides copies of the relevant letters; whereupon he has written back to me that he will settle everything on my behalf at the next *Umschlag* in this current year. I therefore ask quite amicably that the Lady governor's-wife would take it all herein for the best, and deal with Lord Diderich von Dincklage, that he would be content until the aforesaid time; but the interest which was to be laid out at the last past *Umschlag*, I assume has been paid at the right time. Further, I would quite amicably have asked the Lady governor's-wife that she would make a proper arrangement concerning all the ironwork, and whatever else I had necessarily made there at Wandsbek with my own money, that it might be reimbursed to me — and not [be deferred] further upon her much-beloved son Breide, to whom I have written diligently about it (and he has yet answered me nothing) — especially since, as I have learned, the Lady intends to buy out Wandsbek from her said son and hold it herself. I know well enough that the Lady does not desire my loss; and what was previously paid toward it by her dear Lord governor of blessed memory, of which the Lady well knows the account, can be reckoned off from it. I ask only that the remainder might be paid to me, and delivered to my factor at Hamburg, Simon von Petkum — who, together with the Hamburg man, the smith Jacob Holst, knows how to give account of everything and to give a receipt thereupon. But insofar as it does not please the Lady to keep the remaining iron lattice-work, and whatever else of ironwork has been made there, I ask that my said factor may be permitted to take it all away again — that which was paid for with my money and not [re]paid — and to turn part of it into money again at Hamburg; the chief part, however, which is of ironwork, [I ask] to be sent up to me, together with my other goods, as soon as His Roman Imperial Majesty, our gracious Lord, requests of the Lords of Hamburg in writing that they be sent up.

I trust the Lady governor's-wife that she will not refuse me this, but will — since it has now dragged on and been postponed for about a year and a half — make a definite decision hereupon as soon as possible. In whatever I can in turn be of service to the Lady governor's-wife, or any of her children, according to my ability, I will at all times be found quite willing; and I herewith faithfully commend the Lady governor's-wife, together with all hers, to the protection and shelter of the Almighty.

Dated at the imperial castle Benátky in Bohemia, the 22nd day of April, New Style, the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Christine von Halle** (d. 1604), **widow of Henrik (Heinrich) Rantzau** (1526–1598), the great Holstein humanist and royal *Statthalter* (lieutenant-governor) of the Duchies — hence Tycho's address *Frau Statthalterin* ("Lady governor's-wife"). The source header reads simply *Ad viduam Henrici Rantzovii* ("to the widow of Henrik Rantzau"); the edition supplies her name. The MS is an autograph **draft (*Kladde*)**.
- **Significance — Tycho's unfinished business at Wandsbek (material history).** Wandsbek, near Hamburg, was the **Rantzau estate** where Tycho lived 1597–98 (printing the *Mechanica* and *Progymnasmata*). Two matters:
 1. **The Mecklenburg principal & the Kiel *Umschlag*.** Tycho's kinsman **Eske Bille** had not learned in time how to pay "the principal sum in Holstein" and redeem Tycho's bond; Tycho has re-instructed him, and Bille will settle "at the next ***Umschlag***" (the **Kiel Umschlag**, the great Holstein payment-fair where debts were cleared) this year. Tycho asks the widow to keep the creditor **Diderich von Dincklage** patient until then.
 2. **The Wandsbek ironwork (notable).** Tycho seeks **reimbursement for all the ironwork** (*Eisenwerk*) and other things he had "necessarily made at Wandsbek with my own money," rather than have it left to the widow's son **Breide (Bredo) Rantzau** (who has not answered) — especially as she intends to **buy Wandsbek back from her son**. Failing reimbursement, his Hamburg **factor Simon von Petkum** (with the **Hamburg smith Jacob Holst**) is to **remove the iron**, sell part at Hamburg, and send the **chief ironwork up the Elbe** with Tycho's other goods (once Rudolf II writes to Hamburg) — a concrete glimpse of the **iron fittings/instrument components** Tycho commissioned during the Wandsbek period.
- **Persons named.** Christine von Halle (the widow); **Henrik Rantzau** (the late *Statthalter*); **Breide Rantzau** (her son); **Eske Bille** (Tycho's kinsman-agent); **Diderich von Dincklage** (creditor/agent); **Simon von Petkum** (Tycho's Hamburg factor; cf. brahe-t_15991008001, brahe-t_16000424001); **Jacob Holst** (Hamburg smith); **Rudolf II**.
- **Terms (kept/glossed; this chapter's convention).** *Umschlag* = the **Kiel payment-fair**; *Eisenwerk / Eisentraillen* = ironwork / **iron lattice-work (grilles/railings)**, kept and glossed (the *Eisentraillen* reading is the edition's; flagged minor).
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Benateck in Behemen den 22 thag Aprilis stylo novo anni 1600*; **New Style** (Prague/imperial). Header agrees with the label.
- **Correction.** Latin heading 'VIDUAMHENRICI' corrected to 'VIDUAM HENRICI' (missing space) per Dreyer, TBOO XIV p.200. A second audited defect (ausgelegt/auffgelegt) was checked against the same page and rejected: Dreyer's page in fact reads 'ausgelegt', matching the existing text, not the 'auffgelegt' the audit claimed.

- **text error** (low). Our published German reads 'ausgelegt' (paid out/disbursed) where Dreyer p.200 reads 'auffgelegt' (levied/imposed/assessed) — a real word substitution, not just spelling. The English ('laid out') follows our source's reading rather than Dreyer's actual sense ('levied'), but the overall point of the sentence — that the interest due was assumed settled on time — is not lost. Dreyer prints: *die zinß aber, welche zu nechftvorgangnen vmbflag folte auffgelegt werden, vorfihe ich mich fey zu rechter zeitt bezahlt.*.

**Repaired.** Verified visually against Dreyer page images, TBOO XIV pp.197-200 (the full extract supplied). The heading-spacing defect is confirmed and fixed. The 'ausgelegt/auffgelegt' defect was investigated directly on p.200 and found unsupported by the actual page image, which reads 'ausgelegt' clearly; this is rejected rather than applied, since applying it would have introduced an unverified change against the edition of record. Nothing else on these pages diverges from the transcribed original.

documents.title: Tycho Brahe → Vincent Moller — Benátky, 24 April 1600 [N.S.]

edition.print_label: Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia (1913–29)
edition.tboo_cite: Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, ed. I.L.E. Dreyer, Tom. XIV, Hauniæ 1929, p. 201, no. 194

witnesses.raw: A Basel, Universitätsbibliothek Basel, Autographensammlung, Vol. 35, Fol. 113. Kladde

documents.abstract: Congratulates Moller on his elevation to the Hamburg consulship and urges him to use his authority to intercede in releasing Tycho's instruments and goods held at Lübeck per the Emperor's wishes.
documents.incipit: MAGNIFICE et excellentissime do:ie Vincenti Mullere, amice honorande, pro nupera …

text.original:
MAGNIFICO ET PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO D:NO VINCENTIO MOLLERO, AMPLISSIMÆ REIPUB. HAMBURGENSIS CONSULI PRUDENTISSIMO ET V. I. LICENTIATO EXIMIO, AMICO SUO HONORANDO.

MAGNIFICE et excellentissime do:ie Vincenti Mullere, amice honorande, pro nupera euectione ad dignitatem consularem in amplissima vestra republica E:æ T. ex animo congratulor, optoque, ut fausta et salutaris sit. Ago vero gratias, quod me humanissimis tuis literis inuisere non degrauatus sis, et negocium apud reliquos dignissimos consules et senatores vrbis vestræ, de quo cæs:a ma:tas, d:nus noster clementissimus, meo nomine perscripsit, promoturum polliceris. Spero autem, literas ipsius m:tis iam ad vos peruenisse, aut cum instrumentis et rebus meis, quæ Lubecæ sunt, breui allatum irj. Quare E:m T:m diligenter et peramice rogatam cupio, ut sua authoritate et intercessione procurare velit, quo per omnia c:æ m:tis clementissimæ voluntatj meæque expectationi satisfiat. De quibus Simon de Petkum te plenius instruet, ejus enim fidej et curæ rem omnem commisj. Scripsi etiam denuo illi de ijs, quæ Wandesburgj meo ære parata sunt et nondum persoluta, ut compensationem urgeat, in quo etiam negocio Præstantia Tua suo consilio et auxilio, præsertim quo ad vestræ vrbis fabrum et cæteros opifices, qui sciunt, quantum exposuerim illisque numerauerim, quam optime mihi subueniet, nec diffido eam, vt id ingenue fateantur, lubenti animo effecturam. Si quid in his oris, quod T. P:æ gratum erit, a me præstari poterit, inueniet me vicissim ad illi gratificandum quam paratissimum.

Valeat P:a T:a cum tota domo sua quam optime et diutissime.
Dabantur properanter ex arce Cæsarea Benatika 24 aprilis stylo nouo anno 1600.
text.english:
**To the magnificent and most excellent man, Master Vincent Moller, most prudent Consul of the most ample Commonwealth of Hamburg, and distinguished Licentiate of Both Laws, his friend to be honoured.**

Magnificent and most excellent Master Vincent Moller, friend to be honoured: I congratulate Your Excellency from my heart on [your] recent elevation to the consular dignity in your most ample commonwealth, and wish that it be auspicious and salutary. And I give thanks that you did not find it burdensome to visit me with your most kind letter, and that you promise to promote — with the rest of the most worthy consuls and senators of your city — the business about which His Imperial Majesty, our most clement lord, wrote in my name. I hope that His Majesty's letters have now reached you, or will shortly be brought, together with my instruments and goods, which are at Lübeck. Wherefore I desire Your Excellency diligently and most amicably asked, that you be willing, by your authority and intercession, to procure that satisfaction be made in all respects to the most clement will of His Imperial Majesty and to my expectation. About which Simon von Petkum will more fully instruct you, for I have committed the whole matter to his good faith and care. I have also written to him again about those things which were prepared at Wandsbek at my expense and not yet paid for, that he urge the compensation; in which business, too, Your Excellency will best aid me by your counsel and help — especially as regards your city's smith and the other craftsmen, who know how much I laid out and paid to them; nor do I doubt that you will, with willing mind, bring it about that they candidly confess it. If anything can be performed by me in these regions which will be pleasing to Your Excellency, you will find me, in turn, most ready to gratify [you].

May Your Excellency fare as well and as long as possible, with your whole house.
Given hastily from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 24th of April, new style, in the year 1600.

documents.title: Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg → Tycho Brahe — Munich, 26 April 1600 [N.S.]

edition.print_label: Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia (1913–29)
edition.tboo_cite: Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, ed. I.L.E. Dreyer, Tom. VIII, Hauniæ 1925, p. 305

documents.abstract: Sends two books by François Viète and reports plans to travel to Augsburg to seek out posthumous manuscript works of Cyprian Leovitius and transmit them to Tycho.
documents.incipit: PERVENERUNT ad manus meas, Vir nobilissime atque Mathematicorum omnium facile princeps, …

text.original:
IOANNES GEORGIUS HERWARTUS AB HOHENBURG AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

PERVENERUNT ad manus meas, Vir nobilissime atque Mathematicorum omnium facile princeps, libelli duo, quos vir doctissimus et in Geometricis plane rarus et insignis, FRANCISCUS VIETA, nuper in lucem prodire voluit. Hos cum non dubitem te perlibenter visurum, neque forte aliunde absque difficultate exemplaria adepturum, his iunctos ad te mitto.

Cogito his diebus, si modo negotia publica et politica, quibus admodum distrahor, id permittunt, Augustam me conferre, atque ibi, si ulla ratione fieri poterit, manuscripta opera posthuma CYPRIANI LEOVITIJ indagare et nancisci, ut ea quoque ad te transmittere possim.

Atque hisce tibi fælicissima quæque ex animo precor et opto.
Datæ Monachij die 26 Apr. A. 1600.
text.english:
**Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg to Tycho Brahe.**

There have come into my hands, most noble man and easily prince of all mathematicians, two little books which that most learned man — plainly rare and distinguished in geometrical matters — **François Viète** lately wished to bring into the light. Since I do not doubt that you will see these most gladly, nor perhaps obtain copies elsewhere without difficulty, I send them to you joined herewith.

I am thinking, these days, if only the public and political affairs by which I am much distracted permit it, of betaking myself to **Augsburg**, and there, if it can be done by any means, of tracking down and obtaining the posthumous manuscript works of **Cyprian Leovitius**, that I may transmit those too to you.

And with these I pray and wish you from my heart every happiness.
Given at Munich, the 26th day of April, in the year 1600.

documents.title: Jacques Bongars → Tycho Brahe — Frankfurt am Main, 1 May 1600 [O.S.]

edition.print_label: Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia (1913–29)

documents.abstract: Reports not receiving Tycho's earlier letters or meeting Tengnagel; asks Tycho to repeat their contents; offers assistance and provides a safe Prague address for future correspondence.
documents.incipit: TRES iam septimanæ abierunt, ex quo redditæ mihi sunt litteræ, quas ad me dedisti IX …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO ET AMPLISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO TICHONI BRAHE, VIRO INCOMPARABILE IN ARCE CÆSAREA BENATICA.

NOBILISSIME ET AMPLISSIME DOMINE.

TRES iam septimanæ abierunt, ex quo redditæ mihi sunt litteræ, quas ad me dedisti IX Martij. Sed neque eas accepi, quas memoras datas sub finem anni superioris, neque FRANCISCUM TENGNAGLIUM vidi, quem a te tanto viro commendatum, omnibus fuissem officijs prosecutus. Non gravaberis itaque repetere, et quæ illis litteris erant explicata, et quæ huius fidei commiseras. Me certe, magno tuo merito, habebis ad omnia, quæ quidem erunt meæ potestatis, semper paratissimum. Nec addo plura: mandata tua expecto cupide. Tuas in posterum ad me tuto poteris committere bibliopolæ ei, qui CLAUDIJ MARNIJ Wecheliani officinæ præest Pragæ.

Vir Nobiliss. Deus te servet incolumem.
Francofurto ipsis Kal. Maijs 1600.
Nominis tui studiosissimus
BONGARSIUS.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most ample man, Master Tycho Brahe, an incomparable man, at the Imperial castle of Benátky.**

Most noble and most ample Master.

Three weeks have now passed since the letters were delivered to me which you sent me on 9 March. But I have neither received those which you mention as sent toward the end of last year, nor have I seen Frans Tengnagel, whom — commended by you, so great a man — I would have pursued with every good office. You will not, therefore, find it burdensome to repeat both what was set out in those letters, and what you had entrusted to his good faith. Me certainly, by your great merit, you shall always have most ready for everything that shall indeed be within my power. Nor do I add more: I eagerly await your instructions. Your own [letters] to me you can, in future, safely entrust to that bookseller who is in charge, at Prague, of the office of Claude de Marne the Wechelian.

Most noble Sir, may God keep you unharmed.
From Frankfurt, on the very Kalends of May, 1600.
Most zealous for your name,
Bongars.

- ***ipsis Kal. Maijs*** = "on the very Kalends of May" = **1 May** (Roman-calendar idiom, glossed).
- **Calendar.** Frankfurt (Protestant-majority Imperial city) = **Julian / Old Style** until 1700; taken as O.S. (no *n.s.* tag in the edition), as in the 1599 instance.

documents.title: Tycho Brahe → Matthias, Archduke of Austria — Benátky [nad Jizerou], 2 May 1600 [N.S.]

edition.print_label: Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia (1913–29)
edition.tboo_cite: Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, ed. I.L.E. Dreyer, Tom. VIII, Hauniæ 1925, p. 307-309

witnesses.raw: A København, Rigsarkivet, Langebeks diplomatarium. Afskrift

documents.abstract: Addresses Archduke Matthias, citing his reputed esteem for mathematics, and recalls tokens of favour shown during the Archduke's earlier passage through Denmark.
documents.incipit: QUOD Serenissimam Celsitudinem Vestram ignotus et peregrinus ego hisce compellare audeo, …

text.original:
SERENISSIMO PRINCIPI ET DOMINO, DOMINO MATTHIÆ, ARCHIDUCI AUSTRIÆ, DUCI BURGUNDIÆ, STYRIÆ, CARINTHIÆ, CARNIOLÆ ET WIRTTENBERGÆ, COMITI TIROLIS, DOMINO SUO CLEMENTISSIMO.
Serenissime et Inclyte Princeps, Domine Clementissime.

QUOD Serenissimam Celsitudinem Vestram ignotus et peregrinus ego hisce compellare audeo, id ut pro sua Heroica et congenita Virtute atque clementia candide et benigne accipere dignetur, humilime oro. Impulit me ad hanc audaciam celeberrima fama de Sermæ Celnis Vestræ benignissimo affectu erga quasvis artes ingenuas, præsertim sublimiores illas, quas Mathematicas per excellentiam vocant. Quemadmodum enim Augustissimus et Potentissimus Imperator RUDOLPHUS, Væ Sæ Cnis Dominus Frater, hæc studia plurimi facit atque illis laudabiliter delectatur, sic et Vm Sm Celnem quadam non minus naturæ quam sanguinis conformitate illa pariter in precio habere a plurimis affirmatur: cuius etiam haud obscura τεκμύρια, cum ante annos plusculos, Daniam Patriam meam transeundo, laudatissimæ memoriæ Regem FRIDERICUM Sa Va Co illic invisisset, ad me perlata sunt, quin et paulo post ab Arcis Cronburgicæ Præside mihi insinuatum Sm Cm Vm in Insulam prioris habitationis meæ Uraniburgicam, Instrumentorum, quæ in usum Astronomicæ instaurationis illic construxeram, visendorum gratiâ transfretare constituisse, quod et factum fuisset, nisi maris irrequietudo et glaciei interveniens importunitas propositum hoc impedivissent. Ex eo tempore cœpi Smam Celenm Vm pro meo modulo suspicere et venerari; optassemque, ut consilium illud in Insulam dictam traijciendi successus ratos consecutum fuisset. Cum autem nunc gravibus de caussis, relicta Patria, uti fert rerum Mundanarum vicissitudo, in ditionem Potentissimi Imperatoris Regnumque Bohemiæ ab eius Cæsa Maiestate huc clementissime accitus, transmigrarim, sicque Smæ Celni Væ vicinior redditus sim, eo etiam nunc promptius et confidentius animum mihi sumo aliquid ad Serenissimam Celnem Vam literarum dandi, ut erga eam debitum meum obsequium vel aliqua saltem ratione humilime declarem, præsertim cum adeo oportuna id efficiendi modo sese obtulerit occasio, per hunc Generosum et in literis ac linguis bene versatum Iuvenem FRIDERICUM ROSENKRANTZIUM, Sympatriotam et Consangvineum meum, ad vestram Smam Celnem proficiscentem. Cumque Scra Cæsa Maitas, Dominus meus clementissimus, sua Augusta apud Vam Serm Celnem commendatione et intercessione (quam ROSENKRANTZIUS secum apportat) eum non dedignata sit, supervacaneum et indecens duco quippiam, quod apud Serm Celnem Vm illi promotioni esse possit, ulterius intempestive repetere aut adiungere, hoc saltem dicam, quicquid clementiæ et benevolentiæ Serenissima Celo Va in illum contulerit, id non saltem illi, sed toti Rosenkrantzianæ familiæ, quæ in inclyto Regno Daniæ antiquissima et splendidissima est, tum quoque mihi, qui eiusdem stemmatis aliqua pars sum, beneficio nunquam memoria obliterando et officiosissima mente deprædicando præstituram. Idque de hoc viro polliceri possum, eum Sermæ Væ Celsni fidelem et obsequentissimum futurum, sive privatim in sua Aula, sive publice in bello Ungarico contra Turcam, eius servitiô et qualicunque operâ (est enim ad utrumque humilime paratus) uti voluerit. Deliquit is quidem humanitus et iuvenili quodam lapsu, quod dolendum est, et ipsummet ita contigisse vehementer et ex animo pœnitet, nec suum hoc delictum celare aut excusare præsumit, unde in Regis sui, cui per sexennium in cubiculo fidelissime inservierat, indignationem tantam incidit, ut stimulantibus invidis et osoribus, nullus fuerit veniæ locus, quicquid tandem pro culpæ condonatione et redemptione ipse et illi sanguine iuncti humilime offerrent; attamen sperat se, divina fretus misericordia et bonitate, alibi extra Patriam, potissimum vero in Sermæ Væ Celnis servitio, hanc deplorandæ sortis adversitatem virtute et integritate sua ita superaturum, atque priora illa, fragilitate quadam humana imprudenter commissa, honeste et fortiter gestis diluiturum atque emendaturum, ut tandem, auxiliante divina clementia et Virorum Principum diligenti intercessione apud Regem suum culpæ remissionem submisse impetrare atque in integrum restitui possit, maximo omnium consangvinitate et affinitate ipsi iunctorum, cuiusmodi sunt Nobilissimi quique in Regno Daniæ, gaudio et applausu. Confidimus autem omnes, quotquot eius sortem ex animo dolemus et ad meliora ipsum restitui exoptamus, apud Sam Celnem Vam occasiones et media inventurum, quibus fortunæ asperitatem mitiget atque sermæ Celnis Væ clementissimo favore atque indultu eam vincere et ad potiora emergere possit. Quod faxit misericors et omnis boni largitor Deus.

Cæterum Sermæ Celni Væ per dictum ROSENKRANTZIUM submisse mitto duos libros, quos Sacræ Cæsæ Maiestati, Domino et Mæcenati meo clementissimo, quam primum Pragam veneram, obtuli, et unâ addo globum quendam cælestem e mea inerrantium stellarum accurata et diutino tempore exantlata restitutione apposite conformatum; quæ a tenuitate mea profecta munuscula, ut Sma Celo Va clementi animo accipere, et me meaque studia sibi commendata habere non dedignetur, qua possum reverentia et submissione oro et obsecro. Valeat Serma Celo Va in Reipubæ stabilimentum quam diutissime et florentissime, et successu contra truculentum Christiani nominis hostem per Dei benignitatem felici in posterum quoque utatur.

Dabantur ex Arce Cæsarea Bennaticka die 2. Maij Anni 1600.
Sereniss. Cels. Vestræ addictiss.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**To the most serene Prince and Lord, Lord Matthias, Archduke of Austria, Duke of Burgundy, Styria, Carinthia, Carniola and Württemberg, Count of Tirol, his most clement Lord.**
Most serene and renowned Prince, most clement Lord.

That I, unknown and a foreigner, dare to address Your most serene Highness by these [lines], I humbly pray You may deign to take candidly and kindly, according to Your heroic and inborn Virtue and clemency. What impelled me to this boldness was the most celebrated report of Your most serene Highness's most kindly disposition toward all liberal arts — especially those loftier ones which by excellence they call **Mathematical**. For just as the most august and most powerful Emperor **Rudolf**, Your most serene Highness's Lord Brother, makes much of these studies and laudably delights in them, so Your most serene Highness too is affirmed by very many to hold them in like esteem, by a conformity no less of nature than of blood — of which no obscure **tokens [τεκμήρια]** were brought to me when, some years ago, passing through Denmark my fatherland, Your Highness visited there the King **Frederick**, of most praised memory; nay, and a little after, it was intimated to me by the Governor of **Kronborg** Castle that Your Highness had resolved to **cross over to my Island of Uraniborg, the seat of my former dwelling, to see the Instruments which I had constructed there for the use of the Restoration of Astronomy** — which would have been done, had not the restlessness of the sea and the intervening trouble of ice hindered this purpose. From that time I began, according to my small measure, to look up to and venerate Your most serene Highness; and I could have wished that that plan of crossing over to the said Island had met with sure success. But since now, for grave causes — my fatherland left behind, as the vicissitude of worldly things brings — I have migrated, most clemently called hither by His Imperial Majesty into the dominion of the most powerful Emperor and the Kingdom of Bohemia, and am thus made a nearer neighbour to Your most serene Highness, the more promptly and confidently do I now take heart to send some letter to Your Highness, that I may humbly declare my due obedience toward You, at least in some fashion — especially since so opportune an occasion of doing it has offered itself, **through this noble Youth, well versed in letters and tongues, Friedrich Rosenkrantz, my compatriot and kinsman, setting out to Your most serene Highness**. And since the Sacred Imperial Majesty, my most clement Lord, has not disdained to favour him with His august commendation and intercession to Your most serene Highness (which Rosenkrantz brings with him), I judge it superfluous and unseemly to repeat or add untimely anything further that might further his advancement with Your Highness; this only will I say: **whatever clemency and benevolence Your most serene Highness shall confer upon him, it will be conferred not only on him, but on the whole Rosenkrantz family** — which in the renowned Kingdom of Denmark is most ancient and most splendid — and also on me, who am some part of the same lineage, by a benefit never to be effaced from memory and to be proclaimed with a most dutiful mind. And this I can promise of this man: that he will be faithful and most obedient to Your most serene Highness — whether privately in Your Court, or publicly in the **Hungarian war against the Turk** — for whatever service and work You may wish to use him (for he is humbly ready for either). **He erred indeed humanly, by a certain youthful lapse**, which is to be regretted, and he vehemently and from his heart repents that it so fell out, nor does he presume to conceal or excuse this his fault; whereby **he fell into so great an indignation of his King — whom for six years he had most faithfully served in the chamber — that, the envious and the haters goading, there was no place for pardon**, whatever he and those bound to him by blood at last humbly offered for the remission and redemption of the fault. Yet he hopes that, relying on divine mercy and goodness, **elsewhere outside his fatherland — but above all in Your most serene Highness's service — he will so overcome this adversity of his lamentable lot by his virtue and integrity, and so dilute and amend those former things (imprudently committed by a certain human frailty) by deeds done honourably and bravely**, that at last, with divine clemency aiding and the diligent intercession of Princely Men, he may humbly obtain remission of the fault from his King and be restored to his full standing — to the greatest joy and applause of all joined to him by kinship and affinity, such as are all the noblest in the Kingdom of Denmark. And we all — as many of us as grieve his lot from the heart and long for him to be restored to better things — trust that he will find with Your Highness occasions and means whereby he may soften the harshness of fortune, and by Your most serene Highness's most clement favour and indulgence overcome it and emerge to better things. Which may the merciful God, the bestower of all good, bring to pass.

For the rest, **I humbly send Your most serene Highness, by the said Rosenkrantz, two books which I offered to the Sacred Imperial Majesty, my Lord and most clement Maecenas, as soon as I had come to Prague; and I add, together with them, a certain celestial Globe, fittingly fashioned from my accurate restitution of the fixed stars, drawn out over a long time.** These little gifts, proceeding from my slenderness, I pray and beseech, with what reverence and submission I can, that Your most serene Highness may not disdain to accept with a clement mind, and to hold me and my studies commended to You. May Your most serene Highness fare well, for the establishment of the Commonwealth, most long and most flourishingly, and enjoy hereafter too, by God's goodness, happy success against the truculent enemy of the Christian name.

Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 2nd day of May, the year 1600.
Your most serene Highness's most devoted,
**Tycho Brahe**, in his own hand.
