text.original:
ILLUSTRISSIMO ET GENEROSISSIMO DOMINO DOMINO COSMO CONCINO E COMITIBUS PENNÆ ETC. SERENISSIMI MAGNI DUCIS HETRURIÆ APUD SACRAM CÆSAREAM MAIESTATEM ORATORI DIGNISSIMO DOMINO OBSERVANDISSIMO.

ILLUSTRISSIME ET GENEROSISSIME DOMINE.

SIQUIDEM ab Illma Dominatione Vestra, cum nuper apud ipsam Pragæ essem, intellexerim negotium de mittendo ad Sermum Magnum Ducem Hetruriæ etc. filio meo, in hoc tantummodo consistere, an is catholicam Romanam Religionem amplectetur, nec ne; neque enim Sermam eius Celsitudnem libenter quempiam in sua Aula habere, qui a dicta Religione alienus sit. Ad hoc equidem, quod respondeam nihil aliud habeo, quam me de eo polliceri posse: Si Sermus Magnus Dux eum in suam Aulam recipere dignatus fuerit, quod se ita gesturus sit, ut neminem offendat, aut scandalizet, sive quoad religionem sive alijs in rebus, quemadmodum Nobilem Iuvenem FRANCISCUM TENGNAGLIUM, qui aliquot annis in mea familia fuit, se ita, dum Sermæ Celsitni eius inserviret, exhibuisse confido, ut nemo isthic habeat, in quo iure de eo conqueri possit. Quod et pariter præstitit, dum in Illmi et Rmi Cardinalis a DIETRICHSTEIN Aula aliquantisper moratus est. Si vero Sermæ ipsius Celsitni hæc de religione quæstio aliquid nihilominus scrupuli moverit, posset filius meus unâ cum altero, quem illi adiuncturus sum, studioso, in ipsius Sermæ Celsitnis Academia, quæ Senis est, inter reliquos Germanos aliquantisper degere, ut studiosum illum nonnunquam in observationibus Astronomicis, iuxta meum præscriptum, isthic peragendis adiuvet; oportet enim ad minimum duos esse, interdum etiam tres, qui eo instrumento utantur, quod ego illis traditurus sum. Confectis autem isthic observationibus præcipuis, navigabit studiosus ille in Ægyptum, et facile ibi alios inveniet, qui instructi in pluribus obtinendis ibi præsto sint; quod propositum ipsius Sernam Celnem, quemadmodum clementissime promisit, benignissime promoturam mihi persuadeo. Interim filius manebit isthic in Italia, donec linguam calluerit, quod intra annui temporis spacium fieri posse existimo, ut tunc reversus Sac. Cæsæ Maiestati Domino meo clementissmo in ipsius Maiestatis Aula aliquandiu humillime serviat.

Hæc ad Illam Dominatem referenda habui, et qua possum reverentia Illam Dominationem Vestram rogatam habeo, ut a Sermo suo Principe resolutionem certam, quid hac in re sperare possim, vel secus, tempestive mihi impetrare non degravetur; ego vicissim omnia mea officiola ipsius Sermæ Celsitni et Vestræ quoque Illmæ Dominationi submisse defero.

Valeat Illma Vestra Dominatio diu et feliciter.
Dabantur ex Arce Cæsarea Benatica, 4 Maij Anni 1600.
Illmæ Dominationi Vestræ addictissimus
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria scripsi.
text.english:
**To the most illustrious and most generous Lord, Lord Cosimo Concini, of the Counts of Penna, etc., most worthy Ambassador of the Most Serene Grand Duke of Tuscany to the Sacred Imperial Majesty, a Lord most to be respected.**

Most illustrious and most generous Lord.

Since I have understood from Your Most Illustrious Lordship, when I was lately with you at Prague, that the business of sending my son to the Most Serene Grand Duke of Tuscany, etc., turns on this alone — whether he will embrace the Catholic Roman Religion, or not (for His Most Serene Highness does not willingly have anyone in his Court who is averse to the said Religion) — to this, indeed, I have nothing else to answer than that I can promise concerning him as follows: that, if the Most Serene Grand Duke shall deign to receive him into his Court, he will so conduct himself as to offend or scandalize no one, whether as to religion or in other matters — just as I trust that the noble young man **Franz Tengnagel**, who was for some years in my household, so conducted himself while he served His Most Serene Highness that no one there has anything for which he could justly complain of him. The like he performed, too, while he stayed a while in the Court of the most illustrious and most reverend Cardinal von Dietrichstein. But if this question of religion should nonetheless raise any scruple for His Most Serene Highness, my son could — together with another student whom I shall attach to him — dwell for a while in His Most Serene Highness's Academy, which is at Siena, among the other Germans, so that he might from time to time assist that student in carrying out there the Astronomical observations, according to my prescription; for there must be at least two, sometimes even three, to use that instrument which I shall hand over to them. And when the principal observations have been completed there, that student will sail to Egypt, and will readily find others there, [already] instructed, ready at hand for the obtaining of more; which design His Most Serene Highness, as he most graciously promised, I am persuaded will most kindly further. Meanwhile my son will remain there in Italy until he has mastered the language, which I think can be done within the space of a year, so that, returning then, he may for some time most humbly serve the Sacred Imperial Majesty, my most clement Lord, in His Majesty's Court.

These things I had to refer to Your Lordship; and with what reverence I can, I ask Your Most Illustrious Lordship not to find it burdensome to obtain for me, in good time, from your Most Serene Prince a sure resolution as to what I may hope in this matter, or otherwise. I, in turn, humbly tender all my poor services to His Most Serene Highness and also to Your Most Illustrious Lordship.

May Your Most Illustrious Lordship fare long and happily.
Given from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 4th of May, in the year 1600.
Your Most Illustrious Lordship's most devoted,
TYCHO BRAHE,
I wrote [this] with my own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Significance & companion letter.** This is the **twin** of Tycho's celebrated letter to **Galileo** (brahe-t_16000504002), written the **same day, from the same place** (Benátky, 4 May 1600 [N.S.]). It is the **business letter to the Tuscan ambassador** that lies behind the Galileo letter's opening: there Tycho recalls meeting, at Prague, "the Ambassador of the Grand Duke of Tuscany … Cosimo Concini," whose praise of Galileo prompted the approach. The two letters together document Tycho's spring-1600 dealings with the Medici court. Survives as a **copy** (*afscrift*) in the Medici archive at Florence.
- **Recipient.** **Cosimo Concini**, *e Comitibus Pennae* (of the Counts of Penna), **ambassador (*Orator*) of the Most Serene Grand Duke of Tuscany** — Ferdinando I de' Medici — at the imperial court. (Not to be confused with the later Concino Concini, maréchal d'Ancre, in France.)
- **The matter — placing Tycho's son at the Medici court.** Concini had told Tycho that the only obstacle to receiving **one of Tycho's sons** into the Grand Duke's service was confessional: the Grand Duke "does not willingly have anyone in his Court averse to the Catholic Roman Religion." Tycho — himself Lutheran — answers diplomatically: he will not promise conversion, but pledges that his son will *give no offence or scandal, in religion or otherwise*. (The son intended for Italy is left unnamed in the letter; the plan concerns one of Tycho's sons, probably **Tycho Brahe the Younger** — named cautiously, not asserted from the text.)
- **The precedent of Tengnagel.** Tycho cites **Franz Tengnagel** (*Franciscus Tengnaglius*) — his assistant, soon his son-in-law — who had served the Grand Duke of Tuscany and stayed at the court of **Cardinal Franz von Dietrichstein** (1570–1636, Bishop of Olomouc, made cardinal 1599) "so that no one could justly complain of him." Tengnagel is the same intermediary whose return from Italy frames the Galileo letter; his Italian sojourn is detailed in brahe-t_16000306002.
- **The fallback plan — Siena and the Egypt expedition (astronomical interest).** Should the religious scruple persist, Tycho proposes lodging his son at the **University/Academy of Siena** "among the other Germans" (the *natio Germanica*), where he would assist a **student-observer** sent by Tycho. Tycho stresses the working requirement — *"at least two, sometimes three"* observers are needed to operate the **instrument** he will provide (this chapter's convention, *organum/instrumentum*). Most striking is the design that, once the principal Siena observations are done, the student *"will sail to Egypt"* to make further observations at southern latitudes and recruit local helpers — a concrete glimpse of Tycho's late ambition to extend his observational programme into the southern sky, which he expected the Grand Duke to fund. The son would meanwhile learn Italian (≈ a year) and then return to serve **Rudolf II** at the imperial court.
- **Persons named.** Cosimo Concini (Tuscan ambassador); the *Serenissimus Magnus Dux Hetruriae* = **Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany**; Tycho's son (unnamed); **Franz Tengnagel**; **Cardinal Franz von Dietrichstein**; *Sacra Caesarea Maiestas* = **Rudolf II**.
- **Place.** *Arx Caesarea Benatica* = the imperial castle of **Benátky nad Jizerou**.
- **Epistolary formulae.** Address in the high diplomatic register (*Illustrissima Dominatio Vestra*, "Your Most Illustrious Lordship"; *Serenissima Celsitudo*, "His Most Serene Highness"); subscription *addictissimus* → "most devoted"; *manu propria scripsi* → "I wrote with my own hand" (autograph attestation, though the surviving witness is a chancery copy). Heavy abbreviation (*Illma, Serma, Celsitni, Rmi*) silently expanded; the source block keeps the contractions.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *4 Maij Anni 1600* at Benátky; the edition marks **N.S. (New Style)** — apt for Tycho's imperial-service dating and for correspondence with Catholic Italy. Reproduced, not converted.

text.original:
ADMODUM MAGNIFICO ET EXCELLENTI VIRO DOMINO GALILÆO DE GALILÆIS, MATHEMATICO EXCELLENTISSIMO, AMICO HONORANDO.

CLARISSIME et excellentissime Vir; cum hisce diebus Pragæ fuissem, atque ibi Serenissimi Principis, Magni Ducis Hetruriæ, Oratorem apud Saram Cæsam Matem, Illustrissimum et Generosissimum Dominum COSMUM CONCINUM e Comitibus Pennæ convenissem, inter alia Illustrissmæ Dominationis eius humanissima mecum colloquia (uti sane est Vir eximia comitate, parique doctrina, præter Generis Illustrissmum splendorem, admirandus, nec unquam satis laudatus) incidit etiam Excellentiæ Tuæ honorifica mentio, ob singularem, qua, in Mathematicis præsertim, plurimos alios antecellis, eruditionem. Cumque a tanto Viro tuas dotes etiam deprædicari audirem, simulavit id prius de Excella Ta animo meo conceptam sententiam, ut non potuerim non has ad ipsam scribere, atque sic amicitiæ nostræ et ulterioris inter nos per literas correspondentiæ fundamina ponere. Quia vero a Nobili Adolescente FRANCISCO TENGNAGLIO meo domestico, ex Italia huc redeunte, percepi Excellam Tuam primum nostrum Tomum Epistolarum Astronomicarum perlustrasse, atque in eo nonnulla reperijsse, de quibus mecum conferre cuperet, ego certe idipsum nullatenus detrecto, sed si quid fuerit, quod Exa Ta in disquisitionem inibi vocare velit, erit id mihi gratissimum, invenietque me ad respondendum pro meo modulo quam paratissimum: Sive de Hypothesi nostra Cœlestium revolutionum, quæ Solem centrum facit circuitionis quinque Planetarum, Terram autem, et eam quiescentem, solummodo amborum Luminarium, atque Octavæ, quam vocant Sphæræ, cui assumptioni apparentias quam optime congruere depræhendi, ut nihilominus tollantur vasti illi Epicycli, quemadmodum apud COPERNICUM, et Terra in centro Universi, quod ille non admisit, immota maneat (sunt etiam particularia quædam in hac nostra inventione, quæ neque iuxta Ptolemaicam neque Coperniceam speculationem tam competenter excusari possunt) sive de Restitutione Fixarum Stellarum, sive de Cometis, quos omnes in ipso Cœlo curricula sua absolvere, contra quam volunt Peripatetici, probo, idque in septem a me diligenter observatis demonstratum relinquo, sive de quacunque tandem alia re, cuius in illo libro mentio fit, mecum disserere Excella Tua volet, faciat id ingenue pro suo arbitrio. Ego vicissim meam sententiam illi aperire, atque de rebus Astronomicis cum ea iucunde conferre non intermittam.

Valeat Excella Tua quam optime.
Dabantur ex Arce Cæsarea Benatica Die 4 Maij Anni 1600.
Excellentiæ Tuæ
studiosissimus
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria scripsi.
text.english:
**To the very magnificent and excellent man, Lord Galileo de' Galilei, most excellent Mathematician, [his] friend to be honoured.**

Most renowned and most excellent Man: when in these days I had been at Prague, and there had met the Ambassador of the Most Serene Prince, the Grand Duke of Tuscany, with the Sacred Imperial Majesty — the Most Illustrious and Most Generous Lord Cosimo Concini, of the Counts of Penna — there fell, among that Most Illustrious Lordship's other most courteous conversations with me (for indeed he is a Man admirable, and never sufficiently praised, for his rare affability and equal learning, besides the most illustrious splendour of his lineage), honourable mention also of Your Excellency, on account of the singular erudition by which, in Mathematics especially, you surpass very many others. And when I heard your gifts thus proclaimed by so great a Man, it confirmed the opinion I had previously conceived in my mind of Your Excellency, so that I could not but write this to you, and so lay the foundations of our friendship and of further correspondence between us by letters. But since I learned from the noble young man Franz Tengnagel, my servant, on his return hither from Italy, that Your Excellency had perused our first Volume of Astronomical Letters, and found in it certain things about which you would wish to confer with me, I for my part by no means decline this; but if there be anything which Your Excellency would wish to call into examination therein, it will be most welcome to me, and you will find me most ready to answer, according to my measure —

whether concerning our **Hypothesis of the celestial revolutions**, which makes the Sun the centre of the circuit of the five Planets, but the Earth — and that at rest — the centre only of the two Luminaries [Sun and Moon] and of the Eighth Sphere, as they call it (an assumption to which I have found the appearances to agree as well as possible, so that nonetheless those vast Epicycles are done away with, as in Copernicus, and yet the Earth remains unmoved in the centre of the Universe, which he did not admit — there are also certain particulars in this our discovery which can be accounted for so satisfactorily neither by the Ptolemaic nor by the Copernican speculation);

or concerning the **Restitution of the Fixed Stars**;

or concerning the **Comets**, all of which I prove to complete their courses in the heaven itself, contrary to what the Peripatetics will have it, and this I leave demonstrated in seven [comets] diligently observed by me;

or, in short, concerning whatever other matter mentioned in that book Your Excellency may wish to discuss with me — let [you] do it frankly, at your own discretion. I, in turn, will not fail to open my opinion to you, and to confer pleasantly with you about Astronomical matters.

May Your Excellency fare as well as possible.
Given from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 4th day of May, in the year 1600.
Your Excellency's most devoted,
TYCHO BRAHE,
I wrote [this] with my own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Significance.** This is **Tycho Brahe's letter to Galileo Galilei** — the principal surviving document of contact between the two, surviving among the **Galilean manuscripts** at the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Florence. Tycho, near the end of his life, opens correspondence with the young Galileo (then professor of mathematics at Padua), prompted by reports of Galileo's gifts and by Galileo's own reading of Tycho's published letters. Galileo never substantively replied during Tycho's lifetime; the letter thus stands as Tycho's outstretched, unreciprocated hand across the generational divide.
- **Sender & recipient.** **Tycho Brahe** at **Benátky**; **Galileo Galilei** (1564–1642), *mathematicus excellentissimus*, then at Padua.
- **The occasion & intermediaries.**
 - *Cosmus Concinus e Comitibus Pennae* = **Cosimo Concini**, of the Counts of Penna — the **Tuscan ambassador** (*Orator*) of Grand Duke Ferdinando I de' Medici at the imperial court — whose praise of Galileo at Prague prompted the letter.
 - *Franciscus Tengnaglius* = **Franz Tengnagel**, Tycho's assistant, *returning from Italy*, who reported that Galileo had read Tycho's letters and wished to raise questions (Tengnagel's Italian sojourn is detailed in brahe-t_16000306002).
 - *primus noster Tomus Epistolarum Astronomicarum* = the **first volume of Tycho's *Epistolae Astronomicae*** (*Epistolarum astronomicarum liber primus*, Uraniborg 1596) — the book Galileo had perused.
- **The Tychonic world-system (the scientific heart; this chapter's convention).** Tycho states his **geo-heliocentric hypothesis** in nuce: the **Sun is the centre of the orbits of the five planets**, while the **Earth, at rest**, is the centre only of the **Sun and Moon** (the two *luminaria*) and of the **eighth (fixed-star) sphere**. He claims (i) the **appearances are saved** as well as possible (*apparentias quam optime congruere* — the *salvare apparentias* criterion,); (ii) the "**vast epicycles**" are eliminated *as in Copernicus*; yet (iii) the **Earth stays immobile at the centre**, which Copernicus denied; and (iv) certain *particularia* of his system fit "neither the Ptolemaic nor the Copernican speculation" — his standing claim to a genuine *tertium quid*.
- **The other offered topics.**
 - *Restitutio Fixarum Stellarum* = the **restoration of the fixed stars** — Tycho's renewed star catalogue (*restitutio*,).
 - *Cometae … in ipso Coelo curricula sua absolvere … contra Peripateticos … in septem a me diligenter observatis* = his proof, **against the Aristotelians (Peripatetics)**, that **comets move in the heavens** (not in the sublunary air), demonstrated from **seven comets** he had observed — the anti-Aristotelian thesis (post-1577) that abolished the solid celestial spheres.
- **Persons named.** Galileo; Cosimo Concini (Tuscan ambassador); Franz Tengnagel; *Copernicus*; the *Peripatetici* (Aristotelians).
- **Place.** *Arx Caesarea Benatica* = the imperial castle of Benátky.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *Valeat … quam optime* → "fare as well as possible"; subscription *Excellentiae Tuae studiosissimus* → "Your Excellency's most devoted"; *manu propria scripsi* → "I wrote with my own hand" (autograph attestation). The honorific *Excellentia Tua* oscillates with third-person *ipsa/illi*; the shifts are preserved.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Die 4 Maij Anni 1600* at Benátky; the edition marks **n.s. (New Style)** — correct for Tycho's imperial-service dating, and apt for a letter to Catholic Italy (already Gregorian). Reproduced, not converted.

text.original:
IOANNES GEORGIUS HERWARTUS AB HOHENBURG AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

LITERAS tuas ex arce Benaticâ 8 die Aprilis ad me datas, Vir nobilissime atque Mathematicorum omnium facile Princeps, singulari cum lætitia accepi; ex ijs enim perlibenter intellexi, nullas earum, quas ad me misisti, id quod unice verebar, vel interijsse vel interceptas esse. Nec est quod moram in respondendo ulla ratione excuses; facilius enim plurima et innumerabilia quoque proponuntur, quam vel ad unicum respondeatur. Mihi potius adeo frequens ista reiteratio literarum vitio vertenda foret, siquidem alia ratione libros, quos videre petieras, pluresve eorum simul unâ ad te transmittere potuissem.

Inprimis vero lætor, mihique congratulor, me totam illam hypothesin Lunæ, posteaquam ea ad apparentias cœlestes penitius a te transformata fuerit, a benignitate et benevolentia tua sperare et expectare debere. Atque adeo interea temporis sigillatim aliqua te rescripturum constituisse, ex quibus sententia tua de Lunæ hypothesi magis elucescat. Verissimum enim esse reor, me præcisius iusto calculum de Luna instituisse. Cæterum id a me propterea deditâ operâ et summo studio ita factum est, ut absque calculi errore mentem tuam de cursu Lunæ plane lubrico et vario assequi possem, tametsi verear me nihilominus subinde errasse. Facies itaque mihi rem gratissimam, si, dato et concesso tibi otio, viam mihi demonstraveris, qua intimius sententiam hac in re tuam assequi valeam. Abunde enim mihi nunc temporis satisfactum erit, si ea, quæ tu ex accuratissimis observationibus tuis hactenus constituisti, calculo venari seu imitari queam.

Libros illos, quos ex Bibliotheca Sermi Principis mei ad te transmisi, curabo, ut Ser. Clementiæ suæ Agens, cum is in aulam Imperatoriam redierit, sub indice et designatione eorum recipiat et mihi remittat. Manuscripta illa, quæ CYPRIANUS LEOVITIUS ἀνέκδοτα reliquit, per intermedias personas petieram et quidem instantissime efflagitaveram, sed frustra et incassum laboravi, oleumque et operam perdidi, ideoque captata occasione me ipse Augustam contuli, et præsens coram ea ab Generoso Domino PHILIPPO EDUARDO FUGGERO Barone etc. petij atque impetravi; ea itaque tibi mittam, quam primum securam aliquam rationem mittendi perquirendo investigare potero. Carmen quoque tibi mittam brevi, quod, uti spero, non displicebit.

Atque hisce me tibi officiosissime commendo.
Datæ Monachij 4 die Maij A. 1600.
text.english:
**Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg to Tycho Brahe.**

Your letter, dispatched to me from the castle of Benátky on the 8th of April, most noble man and easily the Prince of all Mathematicians, I received with singular joy; for from it I learned, most gladly, that none of those [letters] you have sent me — the one thing I feared — had either perished or been intercepted. Nor is there any reason for you to excuse the delay in answering on any account; for very many, and innumerable, things are more easily proposed than a single one is answered. Rather, this so frequent reiteration of letters ought to be charged to my fault, since by some other means I might have transmitted to you the books you had asked to see, or several of them together at once.

But above all I rejoice, and congratulate myself, that I must hope and look for that whole hypothesis of the Moon — after it has been more deeply transformed by you to fit the celestial appearances — from your kindness and benevolence; and, further, that you have resolved meanwhile to write back some matters point by point, from which your view on the Moon's hypothesis may shine out more clearly. For I think it most true that I have set up my calculation of the Moon more precisely than is warranted. Yet I did this of set purpose and with the utmost zeal, in order that, without error of calculation, I might reach your mind regarding the Moon's course — plainly slippery and variable as it is — even though I fear I have nonetheless gone astray here and there. You will therefore do me a most welcome thing if, when leisure is given and granted you, you will show me the way by which I may more intimately attain your opinion in this matter. For it will abundantly satisfy me, at this time, if I can hunt out, or imitate, by calculation, the things which you have hitherto established from your most accurate observations.

As for those books which I sent you from the Library of my Most Serene Prince, I will see to it that His Serene Clemency's Agent, when he returns to the Imperial court, receives them under an inventory and designation, and sends them back to me. Those manuscripts which Cyprian Leovitius left unpublished, I had sought through intermediary persons, and indeed demanded most insistently, but I laboured in vain and to no purpose, and wasted oil and effort; and so, seizing the occasion, I betook myself to Augsburg, and there, present in person, sought and obtained them from the Generous Lord Philipp Eduard Fugger, Baron etc.; these, therefore, I will send you as soon as I can, by inquiry, find out some safe means of sending. A poem, too, I will send you shortly, which, I hope, will not displease.

And with these [words] I commend myself to you most dutifully.
Given at Munich, the 4th day of May, in the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & sender.** An **inbound** scientific letter **to** Tycho. **Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg** (1553–1622), Chancellor of Bavaria, jurist and polymath, a major correspondent of both Tycho and Kepler (Kepler's epoch-making letters on the Mars orbit were addressed in part to Herwart). He writes from **Munich**, replying to Tycho's letter of 8 April from Benátky.
- **Recipient.** **Tycho Brahe**, hailed *Mathematicorum omnium facile Princeps* — "easily the Prince of all Mathematicians."
- **The lunar-theory matter (the scientific core; this chapter's convention).** Herwart awaits Tycho's *hypothesis Lunae* — Tycho's **lunar theory**, with its novel inequalities (the *variation* and the *annual equation*), the most intricate part of his work — "after it has been more deeply **transformed to fit the celestial appearances** (*ad apparentias coelestes*)," i.e. fitted to observation. *ad apparentias [salvandas]* is the period idiom *salvare apparentias*, "to save the appearances", kept in force here. Herwart confesses he has computed the Moon "more precisely than is warranted" (*praecisius iusto*) in trying to reverse-engineer Tycho's reasoning from the data, the Moon's course being "plainly slippery and variable" (*plane lubricus et varius*) — a fair characterisation of the lunar inequalities. He asks Tycho to show him the *via* (method) to **imitate by calculation** what Tycho established from observation — the recurring early-modern tension between *calculus* (theory/computation) and *observationes*.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Serenissimus Princeps meus* = Herwart's sovereign, the **Duke of Bavaria** (Maximilian I, in whose service Herwart was chancellor; the ducal **library** is the *Bibliotheca Serenissimi Principis*), with *Serenae Clementiae suae Agens* = the Duke's **agent** at the Imperial court as the return-channel for the loaned books.
 - *Cyprianus Leovitius* = **Cyprian Leovitius (Cyprián Leovic / Karásek z Lvovic)** (1524–1574), the Bohemian astronomer-astrologer, whose **unpublished manuscripts** (*ἀνέκδοτα*, Greek *anékdota*, "unpublished things") Herwart pursued for Tycho.
 - *Philippus Eduardus Fugger, Baro* = **Philipp Eduard Fugger** (1546–1618), of the Augsburg banking dynasty, bibliophile and collector, from whom Herwart obtained the Leovitius manuscripts in person at **Augsburg**.
- **Allusions.** *oleum et operam perdidi* — the proverbial "I have wasted oil and labour" (after **Plautus**, the lamp-oil of fruitless night-work); the Greek *ἀνέκδοτα* is transcribed and glossed by this chapter's convention
- **Places.** *Monachium* = **Munich**; *Augusta* = **Augsburg**; *arx Benatica* = Benátky.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *officiosissime me commendo* → "I commend myself most dutifully"; *Datae* (epistolary) → "Given."
- **Calendar.** Dateline *4 die Maij A. 1600* at Munich; the edition marks **n.s.** — correct, Catholic Bavaria being on the Gregorian calendar. Reproduced, not converted.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD CHRISTIANUM SECUNDUM, ELECTOREM SAXONIÆ.

ILLUSTRISSIME ET INCLYTE PRINCEPS, DOMINE CLEMENTISSIME.

CUM Illustrissima Celsitudo Vestra me, licet peregrinum et de facie ignotum, suas Ditiones, quas administrat, transeuntem, Clementissimo alloquio dignata sit, et torque aureâ cum suâ effigie donârit atque denuo Torgæ, dum in itinere essem Bohemico, ad se in Arcem invitârit, non possum non hanc Illustrissimæ Celsitudinis Vestræ erga me, nihil eiuscemodi promeritum, benignissimum favorem humilime agnoscere atque recolere. Cumque me imparem fatear ad quippiam, quod tanto Principi vicissim gratum sit, præstandum, id saltem submisse polliceri possum, me semper huius Clementissimæ erga me voluntatis et beneficentiæ, quam apud ipsam expertus sum, quoad vixero, memorem futurum, atque apud alios deprædicaturum. Verum enimvero ne prorsus meo officiolo defuisse videar, licet, uti dictum, longe inferior sim, quam ut remunerationis loco pro benignissimis suis erga me meritis retribuere quid valeam, ne tamen omninô ingratus atque horum immemor videar, ex tenui penu, quæ pro meo modulo possum, depromo atque ad Illustrissimam Vestram Celsitudinem per Dominum Doctorem IESSENIUM, in inclyta Vestræ Celnis Academia Wittebergæ Professorem, meum, dum aliquamdiu isthic morarer, hospitem, me hîc in Bohemiâ proximis diebus invisentem, humilime mitto, nimirum de Inerrantium Stellarum accurata restitutione librum, plurimorum Annorum studio et labore partum, atque unâ Globum Cœlestem, in quo Affixæ Stellæ iuxta hanc ipsam a nobis exantlatam verificationem operâ cuiusdam artificiosi Batavi in Insula prioris meæ habitationis Uraniburgica, Regni Daniæ, Patriæ nostræ, solerter et accurate, quantum hæc fert Mechanicæ Sphæræ magnitudo, repræsentatæ sunt. Oroque Illmam Vram Celnem debitâ submissione et reverentiâ, ut hæc munuscula ab homine Illmæ Vræ Celnis observantissimo profecta non aspernari velit, sed Clementissimo animo suscipere atque me in posterum etiam sibi commendatum habere non dedignari. Pluribus illmam Vram Celnem, gravissimis suarum Ditionum administrandarum curis occupatam, interpellare nolo, neque enim decere arbitror de privatis meis rebus ad Illmam Vram Celnem quippiam perscribere, quas tamen si Illma Vra Celdo aliquatenus cognoscere non degravatur, a prænominato Doctore IESSENIO percipiet, quantâ Clementiâ et benignitate Augustissimus et Potentissimus Imperator RUDOLPHUS, Dominus noster Clementissimus, me subiectissimum suum clientem hîc susceperit, et studia mea, quæ diu multumque molior, Astronomica, præ suspiciendâ et nunquam satis laudatâ ipsius Sacræ Cæsæ Matis erga omnes liberales Artes, inprimis vero Mathematicas, affectione et favore Clementissimo, fovere et promovere dignata est, rem hanc a summo, quod gerit in terris, officio non alienam neque se indignam censendo.

Deus opt. Max. Universi author, ipsius Cæsam Matem in totius Reipæ Christianæ et bonarum literarum tutelam atque propagationem quam diutissime nobis incolumem conservet, cui etiam æviterno Numini Divino Illmam Vestram Cnem unâ cum Illma coniuge et liberis inclytis toto pectore pariter commendo: in quo etiam ut Ia Co Va vivat, valeat et floreat diutissime, optime, prosperrime, ex animo precor.

Dabantur ex Arce Cæsareâ Benaticâ Die 6 Maij stylo novo Anni 1600.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO CHRISTIAN II, ELECTOR OF SAXONY.**

Most illustrious and renowned Prince, most clement Lord.

Since Your Most Illustrious Highness deigned to address me most clemently — though a stranger and unknown by face — as I passed through the Dominions you govern, and presented me with a **gold chain bearing your effigy**, and again, at **Torgau**, while I was on my Bohemian journey, invited me to you in the Castle: I cannot but humbly acknowledge and recall this most kindly favour of Your Most Illustrious Highness toward me, who have deserved nothing of the kind. And although I confess myself unequal to performing anything that might in return be pleasing to so great a Prince, I can at least humbly promise that, as long as I live, I will ever be mindful of this most clement goodwill and beneficence toward me which I have experienced with you, and will proclaim it among others. But truly, lest I should seem to have failed altogether in my little duty — though, as I said, I am far too lowly to be able to repay anything by way of recompense for your most kindly merits toward me — yet, lest I seem wholly ungrateful and forgetful of these things, from my slender store I bring forth what I can, according to my measure, and humbly send to Your Most Illustrious Highness, through Lord Doctor **Jessenius**, professor in Your Highness's renowned Academy at Wittenberg — my host while I stayed there a while, and now, in these next days, visiting me here in Bohemia — namely, a **book on the accurate restitution of the Fixed Stars**, won by the study and labour of very many years; and together with it a **Celestial Globe**, on which the Fixed Stars are represented according to this very verification accomplished by us, by the work of a certain skilled Dutchman, on the island of my former dwelling, **Uraniborg**, of the Kingdom of Denmark, our fatherland — skilfully and accurately, so far as the size of this mechanical sphere allows. And I beg Your Most Illustrious Highness, with due submission and reverence, that you would not disdain these little gifts, proceeding from a man most respectful of Your Most Illustrious Highness, but receive them with most clement mind, and not disdain to hold me also commended to you hereafter. I do not wish to detain Your Most Illustrious Highness, occupied with the weightiest cares of governing your Dominions, with more words; nor do I think it fitting to write anything of my private affairs to Your Most Illustrious Highness — which, however, if Your Most Illustrious Highness does not find it burdensome to know in some measure, you will learn from the aforenamed Doctor Jessenius: with how great clemency and kindness the most august and most powerful **Emperor Rudolf**, our most clement Lord, has here received me, his most submissive client, and has deigned to foster and promote my astronomical studies, on which I have long and greatly laboured, by the admirable and never sufficiently praised most clement affection and favour of His Sacred Imperial Majesty toward all the liberal Arts, but especially the Mathematical — judging this matter not alien to the highest office he holds on earth, nor unworthy of himself.

May God Best and Greatest, author of the Universe, preserve His Imperial Majesty safe for us as long as may be, for the protection and propagation of the whole Christian Commonwealth and of good letters; to which everlasting Divine Power I likewise commend with my whole heart Your Most Illustrious Highness, together with your most illustrious consort and renowned children — in whom [God] I pray from my heart that Your Most Illustrious Highness may live, fare well, and flourish, as long, as well, and as prosperously as possible.

Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 6th day of May, New Style, the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Christian II, Elector of Saxony** (1583–1611), then a young prince (the Electorate under the Administrator's regency at this date; cf. brahe-t_16000324001). Tycho had passed through Electoral Saxony on his way from Wandsbek/Wittenberg to Bohemia.
- **Significance — a presentation letter (gifts of book + globe).** Tycho thanks the Elector for two marks of favour — a **gold chain (*torques aurea*) bearing the Elector's effigy**, and an **invitation to the castle at Torgau** during Tycho's Bohemian journey — and reciprocates with two **gifts**, sent through **Jessenius** (Wittenberg professor and Tycho's recent host, then visiting him in Bohemia):
 1. the **book on the accurate restitution of the Fixed Stars** (the fixed-star catalogue, "won by the study and labour of very many years" — the same work presented to Duke Ulrich, brahe-t_15980914002, and carried to Magini, brahe-t_15991104001); and
 2. a **Celestial Globe** carrying his restored star-positions, **made by "a certain skilled Dutchman" at Uraniborg** on Hven — i.e. one of the celebrated **Tychonic globes** produced in the Uraniborg workshop. A notable material-history datum (logged for census/material cross-reference).
- **The Torgau connection.** The Torgau-castle invitation links to the contemporaneous Saxon-court correspondence: Tycho's letter to **Georg von Wolframsdorf**, the Elector's chamber-junker at Torgau (brahe-t_16000508001), dispatched — like this one — through Jessenius.
- **Rudolf II's patronage.** Tycho refers the Elector to Jessenius for the fuller account of how **Rudolf II** "received me, his most submissive client," and fosters his astronomy "by … favour toward all the liberal Arts, but especially the Mathematical" — the standard framing of the imperial establishment (cf. brahe-t_16000106001, brahe-t_16000324001).
- **Persons named.** Christian II of Saxony; **Johannes Jessenius** (courier/host); the unnamed **Dutch globe-maker** at Uraniborg; **Rudolf II**; the Elector's consort and children.
- **Abbreviations.** Heavy honorific contraction (*Illma Vra Celdo/Celnem* = *Illustrissima Vestra Celsitudo/Celsitudinem*; *Ia Co Va* = *Illustrissima Celsitudo Vestra*; *Caesae Matis* = *Caesareae Maiestatis*) silently expanded; the source block keeps them.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Die 6 Maij stylo novo Anni 1600*; **New Style** (imperial). Header agrees with the label. (Same date-cluster as the Galileo/Concini letters of 4 May 1600.)

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD RUDOLPHUM CORRADUCIUM.

ILLUSTRIS ET GENEROSE VIR, DOMINE OBSERVANDISSIME.

CUM rumor hîc nuper increbuisset, Sacram Cæsam Matem, Dominum nostrum Clementissimum, Pragam sub initia modo elapsæ hebdomadæ redituram, et unâ cum ea vestram Illem Domnem ibi affuturam, mox eo excurrens nihil magis in votis habui quam vestram Illem Domnem coram intueri et officiosissime compellare, prout magno eius rei desiderio diu flagravi. Et licet spe hac nunc frustratus sim, id tamen propediem meliori successu futurum confido. Interim domesticum illum meum, qui prius Pilsnæ fuit, isthuc ad vestram Illem Domnem denuo ablego. Et quoniam FRANCISCUS TENGNAGLIUS noster, qui meo nomine vestram Illem Domnem ibi convenit, mihi, cum in procinctu esset sui isthinc in Patriam abitus, per literas fiduciam fecit de nonnullis, quæ Sacra Cæsa Matas, intercessione Illustris Dominationis vestræ, mihi Clementissime indulsit, quorum tamen necdum, ob alias intervenientes remoras, compos factus sum: idcirco Illem Domem vestram, qua possum reverentia rogatam habeo, velit, quatenus per alias suas gravissimas occupationes licet, ut ea executioni committantur, efficere non degravari, inprimis vero quod Prædium illud hîc in veteri Bennaticka mihi Clementissime ab ipsius Cæsa Mate deputatum (illud enim necdum, licet anni tempus eius culturam urgeat, accepi) si itaque Illris Domo vestra ad Capitaneum Brandeisensem hac de re pauculis scribere atque ei ex Clementissimo Sacræ Cæsæ Matis mandato serio iniungere, ut Prædium mihi hoc absque diuturniore dilatione aut apud alios solicitatione tradat, non dubito, quin is sit obtemperaturus: tum quoque ut vestra Illris Domio de ædificijs his Benaticensibus pro Instrumentis meis parandis, et si quæ sunt alia huc facientia, quatenus fieri debeant vel secus, ut eorum structura diu iam neglecta compleatur, provisionem [com]petentem facere velit. Omnia enim hîc nimis lente et difficulter procedunt, nec habeo commoda loca, in quibus organa mea Astronomica, ubi huc Magdæburgo et Hamburgo adlata fuerint, reponam, quo ab iniuria aëris et pluviarum tuta sint. Sed de his atque alijs, quæ necessitas cogit me ad vestræ Illris Domis opem et promotionem confugere, is, quem nunc denuo mitto, plenius [per] oportunitatem exponet. Nolo itaque Illrem Domem vestram alijs quam plurimis gravissimis Reipub. curis distentam hisce remorari.

Deus Opt. Max. eam quam diutissime feliciter valere et florere faciat.
Datæ ex Arce Benaticka die 6 Maij Anno 1600.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to Rudolf Coraduz.**

Illustrious and generous man, most-to-be-revered lord.

When a rumour lately grew strong here that the Sacred Imperial Majesty, our most Clement Lord, would return to Prague about the beginning of the week just past, and that your Illustrious Lordship would be there together with him, I soon ran thither, having nothing more in my wishes than to behold your Illustrious Lordship in person and address you most dutifully — as I have long burned with great desire for that. And although I am now frustrated of this hope, I trust it will shortly come about with better success. Meanwhile I send that servant of mine, who was earlier at Pilsen, again thither to your Illustrious Lordship. And since our Franz Tengnagel, who waited on your Illustrious Lordship there in my name, gave me assurance by letter — when he was on the point of his departure thence for his homeland — concerning certain things which the Sacred Imperial Majesty, by your Illustrious Lordship's intercession, most clemently granted me (of which, however, I have not yet been made possessor, on account of other intervening delays): I therefore have your Illustrious Lordship asked, with what reverence I can, that — so far as your other most weighty occupations allow — you would not find it a burden to bring it about that these be put into execution. Above all, as regards that **estate** here in old Benátky most clemently assigned to me by the Imperial Majesty (for I have not yet received it, though the season of the year presses for its cultivation): if your Illustrious Lordship would therefore write a few words to the Captain of Brandeis about this matter, and earnestly enjoin him, by the most clement mandate of the Sacred Imperial Majesty, to hand over this estate to me without longer delay or soliciting among others, I doubt not he would obey. Then too, that your Illustrious Lordship would make competent provision concerning these buildings at Benátky for the preparing of my instruments — and whatever else conduces hither, how far they ought to be done or otherwise — so that their construction, now long neglected, may be completed. For everything here proceeds too slowly and with difficulty, nor have I convenient places in which to store my astronomical instruments, when they shall have been brought hither from Magdeburg and Hamburg, so that they be safe from the injury of weather and rains. But of these matters and others, in which necessity compels me to take refuge in your Illustrious Lordship's aid and furtherance, the man whom I now send again will more fully explain at opportunity. I do not wish, therefore, to detain with these [lines] your Illustrious Lordship, stretched as you are by so many most weighty cares of the commonwealth.

May God, best and greatest, make you fare happily and flourish for the longest time.
Given from the castle of Benátky, the 6th of May, in the year 1600.

text.original:
MAGNIFICO ET NOBILISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO IOHANNI BARVITIO, SACRÆ CÆSAREÆ MAIESTATIS SECRETARIO SUPREMO ET A CONSILIJS INTIMIS, DOMINO ET AMICO HONORANDISSIMO.

MAGNIFICE ET NOBILISSIME VIR, DOMINE ET AMICE HONORANDISSIME.

QUONIAM ea, de quibus Maga Va mihi per domesticum meum, quem ultimo Pilsnæ habui, spem fecit, brevi effectum exoptatum habitura, adhuc infecta hæreant, et frustra hac præterlapsa septimana cum Sacra Cæsa Maiestate, Domino nostro Clementissimo, Væ Magæ accessum a multis pariter speratum per aliquot dies Pragæ expectarem, cogor denuo (siquidem res ulteriorem moram vix patiatur, et incertus sim, quam cito Sa Cæsa Matas eo redire decreverit) eundem familiarem ad vos amandare, ut si per alias multiplices occupationes fieri nunc commodius quam antea possit, plenariam aliquam resolutionem obtinere queam, quod Magæ Væ favorabili intercessione me impetraturum confido. Quænam vero illa sint, de quibus adhuc sollicitus detineor, is, quem amando, Væ Magæ rectius et plenius, quando ipsum audire commodum fuerit, exponet, ut non opus sit multis verborum ambagibus, eam alias occupatissimam hisce literis ulterius interpellare. Rogo autem Magam Vam officiose, quemadmodum semper sua benevolentia mihi præsto fuit, sic etiam nunc non deesse velit. Inveniet me semper pro mea tenuitate eius vicissim studiosissimum et observantissimum.

Valeat Maga Va quam diutissime et quam felicissime.
Dabantur ex arce Benaticka die 7 Maij Anni 1600.
text.english:
**To the magnificent and most noble man, Master Johann Barvitius, Supreme Secretary of His Sacred Imperial Majesty and of the privy councils, lord and most honoured friend.**

Magnificent and most noble man, lord and most honoured friend.

Since those things — about which Your Magnificence gave me hope, through my servant, whom I last had with [me] at Pilsen, that they would shortly have the wished-for effect — still stick undone, and since this past week I waited in vain, for some days at Prague, for Your Magnificence's access to His Sacred Imperial Majesty, our most clement Lord (an access equally hoped-for by many): I am compelled again — since indeed the matter scarcely suffers further delay, and I am uncertain how soon His Sacred Imperial Majesty has resolved to return thither — to send the same servant to you, so that, if it can now be done more conveniently than before amid your manifold other occupations, I may obtain some full resolution; which I trust I shall obtain through Your Magnificence's favourable intercession. But what those things are, about which I am still held anxious, he whom I send will set forth to Your Magnificence more rightly and fully, when it shall be convenient to hear him — so that there is no need, by many windings of words, to interrupt you (otherwise most occupied) further with these letters. But I ask Your Magnificence dutifully that, as your benevolence has always been at hand for me, so now too you would not be wanting. You will find me always, for my slenderness, in turn most zealous and most observant of you.

May Your Magnificence fare as long and as happily as possible.
Given from the castle of Benátky, the 7th day of May, in the year 1600.

text.original:
NOBILI ET CLARISSIMO ERUDITISSIMOQUE DOMINO IOHANNI IESSENIO A IESSEN, PHILOSOPHIAe ET MEDICINAe DOCTORI ET PROFESSORI VITEBERGENSI PUBLICO, AMICO SUO SINCERE DILECTO.

S

GLOBUM, quem Illustrissimo Principi tuo destinâram, nunc ad te mitto, amantissime Domine IESSENI, ut tuam rectius redimam isthic fidem (si quid de eo iam ante accessum scripsisti) quam tu propriam apud me, in eo, quod te huc rediturum pollicitus es, licet iam id ignorare ais atque detrectas. Addidi librum de Fixarum restitutione accuratissima viginti Annorum indefesso labore exantlata, eumque in membranam exaratum, tum pariter Electori Saxoniae (cui Celsitudini inclyto unâ scripsi) meo nomine humilime a te adferri cupio, ut habeat eius Celsitudo Canonicam Stellarum expositionem in promptu, si forte aliquando maiorem globum confieri curare velit. Exoptarem autem hunc Abacum stelliferum, cuius similem priora secula (absit invidia dicto) vix viderunt, ipsius Celsitudo sibi soli reservare velit, nec alijs communicare, ne sint, qui nostra inventa sibi arrogent atque ijs abutantur, prout aliquoties mihi in alijs quibusdam contigit. Habes etiam hîc Mechanicae Astronomiae exemplar Magnifico Domino Cancellario Vestro ex me, praemissa officiosa salutatione, porrigendum. Subscripsi saltem nomen meum, tu titulum eius, quem non satis perspectum habeo, superius appone, et librum, si sic lubet, compingi effice, antequam illi exhibeas. Adiunxi insuper literas ad nobilissimum Virum, Dominum GEORGIUM a WOLFRAMSDORF, Cubicularium eiusdem Principis, quas illi tradas velim. Habet praeterea [DANIEL?] secum exemplar pro Illustri Domino Cancellario Bohemico, quod illi exhibere vellet, ubi convenienter ligatum fuerit. Sic satis superque obtines ea, quae tibi redeunti committere in me recepi. Tuum est, si promissi memor esse velis, ea, quae a Domino MECKERO expiscanda tibi concredidi, ad me per literas ante abitum referre, et Procuratorem illum, de quo scis, huc ad me dirigere, ita ut cum DANIELE revertente accedat. Tu vero, mi IESSENI, feliciter domum redi, atque quam optime vale.

Dabantur ex arce Caesarea Benatica die 7 Maij Anno 1600.
text.english:
**To the noble, most renowned and most learned Lord Johannes Jessenius a Jessen, doctor of philosophy and medicine and public professor at Wittenberg, his sincerely beloved friend.**

Greeting.

The globe which I had destined for your Most Illustrious Prince I now send to you, most loving Master Jessenius, that I may there more rightly redeem your pledged word (if you have written anything about it before your arrival) than you keep your own with me in the matter of your having promised to return hither — though now you say you know nothing of it and beg off. I have added a book on the most accurate restoration of the Fixed [Stars], drained out by twenty years' indefatigable labour and inscribed on parchment; and this likewise I desire to be brought in my name, most humbly through you, to the Elector of Saxony (to which renowned Highness I have written at the same time), so that His Highness may have a canonical exposition of the stars ready at hand, should he perhaps some day wish to have a larger globe made. I would wish, however, that His Highness keep this star-table — the like of which past ages (be it said without envy) have scarcely seen — reserved for himself alone, and not share it with others, lest there be those who arrogate my discoveries to themselves and abuse them, as has several times befallen me in certain other matters. You have here also a copy of the *Mechanics of Astronomy* to be presented from me, with a dutiful greeting premised, to your Magnificent Lord Chancellor. I have subscribed only my name; do you add his title above (which I have not sufficiently ascertained), and, if you so please, have the book bound before you present it to him. I have moreover enclosed a letter to the most noble man, Lord Georg von Wolframsdorf, chamberlain of the same Prince, which I would have you deliver to him. Besides this, [Daniel?] has with him a copy for the Illustrious Lord Chancellor of Bohemia, which he is to present to him once it has been suitably bound. Thus you obtain, fully and more than fully, the things I undertook to commit to you on your return. It is your part — if you would be mindful of your promise — to report to me by letter, before your departure, the things I entrusted to you to be drawn out by inquiry from Master Mecker, and to direct hither to me that Procurator of whom you know, so that he may come with Daniel on his return. But do you, my dear Jessenius, return home happily, and fare you as well as may be.

Given from the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 7th day of May, in the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe** at **Benátky nad Jizerou**, the imperial castle assigned to him before the move to Prague.
- **Recipient.** **Johannes Jessenius a Jessen** (Jan Jesenský, 1566–1621), physician and anatomist, *professor publicus* at Wittenberg, returning home to Saxony after a visit; he conducted the famous public anatomy at Prague in June 1600 and remained a friend of both Tycho and Kepler. He is the courier for the whole consignment of gifts and books described here.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Illustrissimus Princeps tuus / Elector Saxoniae / eius Celsitudo* = **the Elector of Saxony**, i.e. **Christian II** (Elector 1591–1611; still a minor under the regency of Duke Friedrich Wilhelm until 1601) — Jessenius's territorial prince, the intended recipient of the celestial globe and star-catalogue.
 - *Georgius a Wolframsdorf, Cubicularius eiusdem Principis* = **Georg von Wolframsdorf**, chamber-junker (here *Cubicularius*, "chamberlain") to the Saxon Elector; the enclosed letter to him is brahe-t_16000508001 (Benátky, 8 May 1600 — dated the day *after* this one).
 - *Magnificus Dominus Cancellarius Vester* = the **Chancellor of [Electoral] Saxony**, recipient of a *Mechanica* (Tycho leaves the title blank, not knowing it exactly).
 - *Illustris Dominus Cancellarius Bohemicus* = the **Chancellor of Bohemia**, i.e. **Zdeněk Vojtěch Popel of Lobkowicz** (Chancellor from 1599), recipient of a further *Mechanica*.
 - *[Daniel?]* and *Daniele revertente* = a servant or assistant named **Daniel** carrying one of the presentation copies; the square brackets and query are the editor's, the name being uncertain in the source.
 - *Dominus Meckerus* = **(Master) Mecker**, otherwise unidentified, charged with explaining some matter to Jessenius; *Procurator ille, de quo scis* = an unnamed agent/proctor whom Tycho wants sent to him.
- **Works mentioned.**
 - *globus / Abacus stellifer / maior globus* = a **celestial globe** and the prospect of a **larger globe** — echoing Tycho's own great Augsburg globe at Uraniborg.
 - *liber de Fixarum restitutione … in membranam exaratus* = the **catalogue of the fixed stars** (Tycho's *restitutio* of the stellar positions, the fruit of "twenty years' labour"), here a presentation copy **written on parchment**; *Canonica Stellarum expositio* = its "canonical exposition of the stars." *restitutio* kept as the programme-term.
 - *Mechanica Astronomiae* = **Astronomiae Instauratae Mechanica** (Wandsbek 1598), Tycho's illustrated account of his instruments, distributed as presentation copies to patrons.
- **Place.** *arx Caesarea Benatica* = the **Imperial castle of Benátky**.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S.* = *salutem* ("Greeting"). *Vale / quam optime vale* → "fare you as well as may be." *Dabantur* (epistolary) → "Given." The opening play on *fides* (Jessenius's broken promise to return vs. Tycho redeeming the pledge over the globe) is preserved, not smoothed.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 7 Maij Anno 1600*; edition marks **n.s.** (New Style), consistent with Tycho's Imperial-service dating and with the companion Wolframsdorf letter of 8 May. Reproduced, not converted.
- **Correction.** Latin: 'restitutione' corrected to 'restitutione accuratissima', and 'explicanda' corrected to 'expiscanda', per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, pp. 316-317. English corrected to match at both points.

Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Read all 4 Dreyer pages as page images (TBOO VIII pp.315-318; the Jessenius letter runs pp.316-317, bracketed by the end of the Corraducius letter and the start of the Barvitius/Wolframsdorf/Brahe items). Collated the full body of the transcribed original and the published English against the printed Latin clause by clause: opening address and greeting, the globe/star-restoration book to the Elector of Saxony, the Abacus stelliferum request for exclusivity, the Mechanica Astronomiae copy for the Chancellor, the enclosed letter to Georg von Wolframsdorf, the bracketed-uncertain '[Daniel?]' courier and the later definite 'Daniele', the Mecker/Procurator instructions, the closing valediction, and the dateline 'die 7 Maij Anno 1600' (matches title '7 May 1600 [N.S.]', consistent with Dreyer's dual heading '27 Apr./7 Mai. 1600'). All proper names (Jessenius, Wolframsdorf, Daniel, Mecker), places (Benatica/Benatky, Wittenberg, Saxony, Bohemia), and the date check out with no invented day-numbers, no fabricated clauses, no silently dropped sentences, and no pronoun or custody-attribution errors. Per the grading rule, any text error caps the grade at C even though both instances are low-severity and do not change the letter's overall sense, hence verdict *minor*.

**2 defects found:**
- **text error** (low). The transcribed original silently drops the superlative adjective 'accuratissima' (most accurate/painstaking) that Dreyer prints modifying 'restitutione', losing Tycho's own emphasis on the exactness of his twenty-year star-catalogue restoration; the English inherits the omission ('the restoration' rather than 'the most accurate restoration'). Dreyer prints: *Addidi librum de Fixarum reftitutione accuratißima viginti Annorum indefeßo labore exantlata, eumque in membranam exaratum (TBOO VIII p.316)*.
- **text error** (low). Dreyer prints 'expiscanda' (things to be found out / drawn out by inquiry from Mecker), but our transcribed original substitutes 'explicanda' (things to be explained by Mecker) — a different gerundive that shifts who does the active work (Jessenius eliciting information vs. Mecker volunteering an explanation). The English follows the erroneous the transcribed original reading. Dreyer prints: *ea, quae a Domino MECKERO expifcanda tibi concredidi (TBOO VIII p.317)*.

**Repaired.** Verified both defects by direct visual inspection of the Dreyer TBOO VIII pp.315-318 page images. 'accuratißima' (p.316) and 'expifcanda' (p.317) are both unambiguous. Both corrections carried into the English per the text error repair rule, since each corrupted Latin word had misled the translation. No other divergence from Dreyer was found in this letter.

text.original:
DEM WOLGEBORNEN HERRN, HERRN EHRENFRIDT VON MINCKWITZ, FREYHERRN ZU MINKWITZBURG AUF HOLESSHAU VND DREHNA, ROM. KAY. MA:T. APPELLATION-RATH, MEINEM IMBESONDERN GUNSTIGEN HERRNN VNND GUETTEN FREUNDT.

WOLGEBORNER, jnbesonder gunstiger herr vnd freundt. Nach wunschung freindtlichenn gruesses, auch erböttung meiner gantz willigenn vnnd geflissenen dienstenn gebe jch dem herrn hiemit freindtlichenn zuuerstehenn, wie das der wolgeborene herr Carolus freyherr von Wartenberg gestrigen tages mich alhie auf dem kaiserlichenn schloß Bennatig besuchet, vnnd vnter anderem vermeldet, das der herr auf die pfingstfeyertage bey jhme zu sein gentzlichen bey sich beschlossenn vnd zugesagt habe. Gelanget demnach an den herrnn mein freindtliches biettenn, derselbige wolle mich gunstchtiglichenn wiessenn lassenn, welchen tag der herr jhm es proponiret habe, damit jch mich vnd die meinigen auf die reise præpariren möge. Vnd nachdem der her auch hatt mir gunstchtiglichenn gehlobet, das er diesen weg ziehen will, vnd mich alhie zu besuchen ..., damit wir mit einander hinziehen, dan ich jhm auch haben zusagen mussen, bey jhme zu sein. Versehe mich gennzlich, dass der herr dis nit abschlagen werde. Jn den sachen, davon ich mit dem herrn vertreulich geredet habe, bitte jch den herrn ganz freindtlichenn, derselbige wolle di mitlerzeit wol erwegenn, vnd wan wir, ob Gott wil, zusammen kommen, mir mit einem gutten rat darin erscheinen, dan ich gentzlich muß darzu thun was sich geburet, ut meum et meorum honorem, pro ut decet, legitime tuear. Welchs jch nach vermögenn vmb den herrn vnnd all den seinigenn zuuerschuldenn jederzeitt gantz willig wiel erfundenn werdenn. Vnd thue hiemit den herrnn jch jn schutz des Almechtigenn treulichenn befehlen.

Gebenn auf dem kayserlichenn schloß Bennatig am 7 tag maij a:o 1600.
Des herrn altzeit dinst- und freindtwilliger
Tycho Brahe
Eign h.
text.english:
**To the well-born Lord, Lord Ehrenfried von Minckwitz, Freiherr zu Minckwitzburg, [lord] of Holešov and Drehna, Roman Imperial Majesty's Appellation-Councillor, my especially favourable lord and good friend.**

Well-born, especially favourable lord and friend. After the wishing of a friendly greeting, and the offering of my quite willing and assiduous services, I give the lord herewith friendlily to understand how the well-born lord Carl, Freiherr von Wartenberg, visited me yesterday here at the Imperial castle Benátky, and, among other things, reported that the lord [you] have fully resolved with himself, and promised, to be with him on the Pentecost holidays. There accordingly reaches the lord my friendly request: that the same would favourably let me know which day the lord [Wartenberg] has proposed it to him [you], so that I may prepare myself and mine for the journey. And since the lord [Wartenberg] has also favourably promised me that he will travel this way and visit me here … so that we may travel on together (for I, too, have had to promise him to be with him), I fully trust that the lord [you] will not decline this. In the matters of which I have spoken confidentially with the lord, I ask the lord quite friendlily that the same would, meanwhile, well consider them, and, when we — God willing — come together, present me with good counsel therein; for I must altogether do what is fitting, *so as lawfully to protect my own and my family's honour, as is proper* [*ut meum et meorum honorem, pro ut decet, legitime tuear*]. Which I will, at all times, be found quite willing to requite, according to my ability, toward the lord and all his. And I herewith faithfully commend the lord into the protection of the Almighty.

Given at the Imperial castle Benátky, the 7th day of May, in the year 1600.
The lord's ever service- and friendship-willing,
Tycho Brahe,
[his] own hand.

text.original:
DEM EDELEN, GESTRENGEN VNDT EHRENUEHSTEN GEORGEN VONN WOLFRAMSDORF, ERBSESSEN VFF VOLLMERSHAIN ETC., FURSTLICHEN SECHSISCHEN CAMMER IUNGKHERN ZUE TORGAW, MEINEM INNSONDERS GUNSTIGEN VNDT GUETEN FREUNDT.

EDLER, Gestrenger, Ehrenuehster Innsonders gönstiger vndt guetter Freundt, Dem Herrn sein meine willige geflissene dienste hier wiederumb nach Vermögen zuuor. Vndt wann es demselben glücklich vndt wohl ergienge, wehre es mihr gantz lieb vndt angenehm zuerfahren. Dess Herrn an mich gethanes schreiben, sub dato Torgaw den 3 Martij, habe ich vonn dem H. Doctore IESSENIO wohl empfangen, durch welchen ich auch den herrn hienwieder mit einen schreiben freundtlich zuersuchen nicht hab vndterlassen können. Belangende meinen vndt der Meinigen Zuestandt alhier inn Konnigreich Behemen, ist derselbige vndter Ihr Kays. May. Vnsers allergnedigsten herrn, gnedigsten schutz vndt Gottlob inn guetten wesen, wie der herr mitt mehren Vmbstanden vonn dem obgedachten herrn Doctore IESSENIO, vnserer beider gueten freundt, vernehmen kan. So ich alhier dem herrn im Kaysserlichen hof oder sonsten etwas dienstlich sein kondte, wil ich allzeitt nach meinen Vermögen willig darzue erfunden werden. Von Newer Zeittung weiss ich nichts sonderlichs zueschreiben; allein das man sagt, das der Türck sich gar starck, vndt noch mehr als zuuor, ruste. Vnser gnedigster Kaysser ist noch nicht vonn Pilsen gen Prag wieder ankommen; Man verhoffet aber, das Ihr Maiestet mit dem ehrsten wieder alda sein werde; vndt seindt die Muscowiterischen gesandten, als mann vermeinet, auch dahien gefodert, alda ihr gentzliche abfertigung zueerlangen. Mann ist auch etzlicher anderer gesandten der deutschen Fürsten alda Vermuthen. Diss habe ich also dem herrn vff sein schreiben wiederumb zuerkennen geben wollen. Vndt thue vns hiermitt sambtlichen dem Allmechtigen Gott inn seinen Vätterlichen Schutz vndt beschirmung trewlich befehlen.

Datum vff dem Kayss. Schloss Benatky den 8 Maij Anno 1600.
D. H.
Allzeitt Dienstwilliger
text.english:
**To the noble, gallant and honourable Georg von Wolframsdorf, hereditary lord of Vollmershain etc., Electoral Saxon chamber-junker at Torgau, my especially favourable and good friend.**

Noble, gallant, honourable, especially favourable and good friend: my willing and assiduous services to the gentleman beforehand, here again, as far as is in my power. And were it to go happily and well with him, it would be wholly dear and agreeable to me to learn it. The gentleman's letter to me, dated Torgau the 3rd of March, I duly received from Doctor Jessenius, through whom I have likewise not failed to address the gentleman in turn in friendly fashion with a letter. Concerning the state of myself and mine here in the Kingdom of Bohemia: the same is, under the most gracious protection of His Imperial Majesty, our most gracious Lord, and God be praised, in good condition — as the gentleman may learn at greater length, with fuller circumstances, from the aforesaid Doctor Jessenius, the good friend of us both. Should I here be able to be of any service to the gentleman at the Imperial court or otherwise, I will at all times be found willing thereto according to my power. Of fresh news I know nothing particular to write; only that it is said the Turk is arming very strongly, and yet more than before. Our most gracious Emperor has not yet returned from Pilsen to Prague; but it is hoped that His Majesty will be there again at the earliest; and the Muscovite envoys, as is supposed, have also been summoned thither to obtain their final dispatch. There is also expectation there of several other envoys of the German princes. This, then, I wished to make known to the gentleman in return upon his letter. And herewith I faithfully commend us all together to Almighty God, into His fatherly protection and shelter.

Given at the Imperial castle of Benátky, the 8th of May, in the year 1600.
[In the gentleman's service]
Ever ready to serve

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Tycho Brahe**, at the Imperial castle of Benátky nad Jizerou (Latin *Benatecum*; this chapter's convention), where he was installed in 1599–1600 as imperial mathematician to Rudolf II before moving to Prague.
- **Recipient.** *Georg von Wolframsdorf, Erbsasse auf Vollmershain, fürstlich-sächsischer Kammerjunker zu Torgau* = **Georg von Wolframsdorf**, hereditary lord of Vollmershain and **chamber-junker (Kammerjunker) to the Elector of Saxony**, resident at Torgau. He recurs as *Cubicularius* of the Saxon Elector in the contemporaneous letter to Jessenius (brahe-t_16000507002), where Tycho encloses a letter "to the noble Lord Georg von Wolframsdorf" — i.e. this very letter, dispatched through Jessenius.
- **Persons named.**
 - *H. Doctor Jessenio* = **Johannes Jessenius a Jessen** (Jan Jesenský, 1566–1621), physician and anatomist, professor at Wittenberg, the mutual friend who carried correspondence between Tycho and the Saxon court and who performed the celebrated public anatomy at Prague in June 1600.
 - *Ihr Kays. May. / unser gnädigster Kaiser* = **Emperor Rudolf II**, Tycho's imperial patron.
- **Places & events (the "news").** *Pilsen* = **Plzeň**, where Rudolf II's court had withdrawn (in part to escape plague at Prague); his awaited return to Prague is reported as imminent. *der Türck … rüstet sich* = the **Ottoman armament** of the Long Turkish War (1593–1606). *die Muscowiterischen Gesandten* = the **Muscovite (Russian) envoys** at the Imperial court awaiting their *Abfertigung* (formal dismissal/dispatch); *gesandten der deutschen Fürsten* = envoys of the German princes.
- **Epistolary formulae.** The chancery opening *Dem Herrn sein meine willige geflissene Dienste … zuvor* ("my willing assiduous services to the gentleman beforehand") is the courteous-equal register (Wolframsdorf is addressed in the third person as *der Herr*, "the gentleman," throughout). The subscription *D. H. — Allzeitt Dienstwilliger* is read as *Des Herrn … allzeit dienstwilliger* ("[the gentleman's] … ever ready to serve"); the signature proper is not written out in this draft-register text.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *den 8 Maij Anno 1600*; the edition marks the letter **n.s. (New Style)**, consistent with Tycho's shift to Gregorian dating in Imperial service. Reproduced as written, not converted. The recipient's letter is dated *Torgaw den 3 Martij* (Saxony being a Lutheran territory still on the Julian calendar in 1600 — Protestant Germany did not adopt the Gregorian reform until 1700); the two datelines therefore sit on opposite sides of the 10-day gap, but no conversion is performed.
- **Correction.** Corrected the non-word 'meme' to 'meine' in the opening salutation; Dreyer's print (TBOO VIII p.317) reads 'meine' clearly.

text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET NOBILISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, DOMINO DE KNUSTRUP ET URANIBURCH, AMICO ET DOMINO SUO PLURIMUM OBSERVANDO. PRAGAM. AM KEISERLICH MAIESTATS HOFFUE ZU ERFRAGEN.

S.

Annus iam agitur, nobiliss. et clariss. d. Tycho, cum ego Rostochij, et tu Wittenbergæ ad tempus subsisteres, nec ullam interea occasionem prætermitterem, quin et absentem te, quia præsentem non licuit, per literas adirem, per literas compellarem. Et postmodum quoque, cum ego aliorsum retraherer, et tu Wittenberga commigrares, non destiti tamen de te anquirere ac percunctari, dum in Germaniam tandem ipsam ascenderem et longam post moram intelligerem Pragam te advenisse atque ibidem aut circa eam ex cæsarea majestatis insigni liberalitate ac longis votis astronomiæ jam magnam partem per te restitutæ et porro restituendæ magnifice et feliciter operarj. Gaudeo idcirco tuo, gaudeo denique publico nomine; adhuc honos honestis artibus ac studijs durat. Tu modo in hac, quam ad immortalitatem tibi stravisti, via, gnaviter et indefesse, dis hominibusque faventibus, progredere. Nec deerunt, qui amplectantur, qui admirentur, quandiu tu modo dignum aliquid cœlo, dignum chartis elaboraveris.

Nepotes tui sub mea aliquandiu disciplina jam sunt, ultraque semestre Herbornæ Nassouiorum studijs incumbunt, quod ex adjuncta quoque epistola pro parte vjdebis. Et utinam aliquando illi patre, te patruo digni reperiantur. Certe quod ipsis inculcem exemplar extra te non quæro. De Dania nihil jamdudum accepimus. Ex patris tamen literis intellexi nuper, valde occupatum fuisse elapsa bruma in instruenda classe regem, et aliquot etiam centenos peritissimos naucleros ab ordinibus Hollandiæ petisse atque impetrasse. Quid ille moliatur, aut quid ipsum coquat, tempus dabit. Te autem, nobilissime Tycho, sæpe per literas compellare pro amicitja veteri et nepotum necessitudine debere nos fateor, et optem, ut de ratione mittendi ad te literas certiores redderemur. Comperires profecto officium nostrum neutiquam claudicaturum. Qui has perferre spopondit, aurifaber et pro parte chymicus est. Eo ego familiariter hic usus sum, quia Piscator aliquatenus affinis est. Et spero officium eius in hisce curandis futurum certius, quam ars fere solet illa, quam tractat.

Hisce valebis, clariss. Tycho, officiose salutatus ab hospite nostro, quem dixi, v. cl. Iohanne Piscatore.
Datum Herbornæ Nassouiorum xi maj CIↃ IↃ C. Tui studiosiss.
Iohannes Jsacius.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and most noble man, Lord Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup and Uraniborg, his much-to-be-revered friend and lord. To Prague. To be inquired after at the Imperial Majesty's court.**

Greeting.

A year is now passing, most noble and renowned Lord Tycho, since I was staying for a time at Rostock, and you at Wittenberg, and I let no occasion pass meanwhile but that I approached you, absent as you were (since to do so in person was not allowed), by letters, and addressed you by letters. And afterward too, when I was drawn off elsewhere, and you removed from Wittenberg, I yet did not cease to inquire and ask after you, until at length I came up into Germany itself, and after a long delay learned that you had arrived at Prague, and there, or near it, by the imperial majesty's distinguished liberality — and to the long-prayed-for [good] of astronomy, already in great part restored by you and further to be restored — were labouring magnificently and happily. I rejoice therefore on your account; I rejoice, in the end, on the public account: honour still endures for honourable arts and studies. Only do you, upon this road which you have paved for yourself toward immortality, press on, diligently and indefatigably, with gods and men favouring. Nor will there be wanting those who embrace, who admire — so long only as you go on elaborating something worthy of heaven, worthy of the written page.

Your nephews are now for some while under my tutelage, and for more than half a year apply themselves to their studies at Herborn in Nassau — as you will also see, in part, from the enclosed letter. And would that they may someday be found worthy of their father, and of you their uncle. Certainly, for a model to instil in them, I seek none beyond yourself. From Denmark we have received nothing for a long time. Yet from their father's letter I learned recently that the King was much occupied last winter in fitting out a fleet, and that he sought and obtained also some hundreds of most skilled skippers from the Estates of Holland. What he is contriving, or what is brewing for him, time will tell. But that we ought often to address you, most noble Tycho, by letter — for the sake of our old friendship and the tie of your nephews — I confess; and I could wish that we be made more certain of the means of sending letters to you. You would surely find our service in no way halting. He who has undertaken to carry these is a goldsmith, and in part a chymist. I have made familiar use of him here, because he is somewhat a kinsman of Piscator; and I hope his service in seeing to these [letters] will prove more reliable than that art he practises is wont to be.

With these you will fare well, renowned Tycho, dutifully greeted by our host, of whom I spoke, the very renowned Johann Piscator.
Given at Herborn in Nassau, 11 May 1600. Most devoted to you,
Johannes Isacius [Pontanus].

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & sender.** An **inbound** letter **to** Tycho. **Johannes Isacius Pontanus** (Jan Isaksz. Pontanus, 1571–1639), the Danish-Dutch historian, geographer and humanist (later royal historiographer of Denmark), then teaching at **Herborn**, where he was **tutor to Tycho's nephews**. The address-line gives the routing in German: *am keiserlich Maiestäts Hofe zu erfragen* — "to be inquired after at the Imperial court" (Tycho's whereabouts being uncertain to correspondents).
- **Recipient.** **Tycho Brahe**, at or near Prague, "labouring magnificently" in the imperial service; Pontanus salutes him as the **restorer of astronomy** (*astronomia … magna parte per te restituta et porro restituenda*) on the "road paved toward immortality" — the *restitutio/instauratio* programme-language again.
- **The nephews & the Herborn colony.** *nepotes tui … sub mea disciplina* = Tycho's **nephews** (sons of his brother **Steen Brahe**), under Pontanus's instruction more than half a year at Herborn — the same student group whose member **Erik Brahe** writes the *epistola adiuncta* ("the enclosed letter") referenced here: brahe-t_16000512001, dated the very next day (12 May 1600). The two letters travelled together.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Iohannes Piscator* = **Johannes Piscator** (1546–1625), the eminent Reformed theologian of the Herborn academy, Pontanus's and the students' **host** (*hospes noster*).
 - *Rex* = **Christian IV of Denmark**, reported (via the boys' father's letter) to have fitted out a **fleet** the previous winter and hired "some hundreds" of skilled **Dutch pilots/skippers** (*naucleri*) from the Estates of Holland.
 - the unnamed **goldsmith-and-chymist courier**, a kinsman of Piscator, carrying this letter — Pontanus's wry hope that his reliability exceed that of his alchemical "art."
- **Places.** *Rostochium* = Rostock; *Wittenberga* = Wittenberg (Tycho's 1598–99 way-station); *Herborna Nassoviorum* = **Herborn in Nassau**.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *S.* = *salutem*; *Tui studiosiss[imus]* → "Most devoted to you." The signature *Iohannes Isacius* is Pontanus's patronymic form (Isaac's son).
- **Calendar.** Dateline *xi maj CIↃ IↃ C* — "11 May **1600**" (the Roman *apostrophus* numeral CIↃIↃC = 1600). No style marker; reproduced as written.

text.original:
NOBILITATE GENERIS ET DOCTRINÆ EXCELLENTIA PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO DOMINO TYCHONJ BRAHÆ, D:O DE KNUDSTRUP, PATRUO SUO CHARISS:

SI prospera fueris valetudine, patrue charissime, est quod gaudeam. Ego adhuc, Dej beneficio, bene valeo. Immortales tibj habeo gratias pro omnibus in me collatis beneficiis, inter quæ vel maximum reputandum, quod et parens charissimus pro sua prudentia et tua autoritate non minimum confirmatus studiis literarum nos instituere nec ullis impensis ad tam honestum propositum perficiendum hactenus parcendum censuerit. Quare si pro corporis et fortunæ bonis ad grates rependendas ipsa natura ducimur, quid ijs debebimus, qui vel opera sua mentes nostras (quæ, quantum cælum terræ, tantum corporibus præstent) humanitatis et doctrinæ donis imbuunt, vel imbuendas pro prudentia ac summo judicio suo effecere? Itaque quod officii mej erit, gratum me semper tibj præbebo, et mihi gratulabor, cuj talis contigit patruus, qui virtute, doctrina summorumque operum excellentia non Daniæ aut Germaniæ modo sed Europæ fere universæ venerabilis et charus est. Hanc animi mej significationem jam dudum est quod tibj, charissime patrue, debebam, sed cum de mansione tua nihil nobis certj constaret, hactenus differre coactus fuj. Nos vero jam ultra semestre Herbornæ vivimus, et ad festum Michaelis, ni fallor, sumus mansurj, nec quicquam adhuc ex Dania certj intelleximus. Nam quotidie tabellarium Æschildum expectamus. Fratrem autem meum Otthonem cum Aslachio jam domi esse censeam; cum enim hac commigraremus, in Anglia sive Scotia commorarj acceperamus. Relatum quoque nobis, Tagonem Tot Heidelberge litteris operam navare et alios quosdam nobiles Danos, quos jam credo Genevam excurrisse. Ex Dania rumor hic fuit, Æschilldum Sefeldium post celebratas filiæ nuptias subjto vita defunctum, et Fridericum Rosenkrantium caussa cecidisse et infamem pronuntiatum. Sed te diutius fortasse qvam par est tali garritu detineo. Jtaque te his, patrue charissime, feliciter Deo optimo maximo commendatum habeo, et amanter peto, ut me cum fratre meo Georgio et patruelj Falchone, qui hic quoque una mecum literis incumbunt, diligere porro atque consilio tuo dirigere non dedigneris.

Datum Herbornæ Nassoviorum 12 maj anno 1600. T. T.
Ericus Brahæ Stennonides
m. pp.
text.english:
**To the man most outstanding in nobility of birth and excellence of learning, Lord Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup, his dearest uncle.**

If you are in prosperous health, dearest uncle, I have cause for joy. I myself, by God's goodness, am still well. I owe you undying thanks for all the benefits conferred upon me — among which even the greatest is to be reckoned this: that my dearest father, confirmed in no small measure by his own prudence and by your authority, has resolved to school us in the study of letters, and has judged that no expense should be spared, thus far, to accomplish so honourable a purpose. Wherefore, if we are led by nature herself to repay thanks for the goods of body and of fortune, what shall we owe to those who either by their own labour imbue our minds — which excel bodies as far as heaven excels earth — with the gifts of humanity and learning, or, by their prudence and highest judgement, brought it about that they should be so imbued? Therefore, in whatever shall be my duty, I will always show myself grateful to you, and will count myself fortunate, to whom such an uncle has fallen — one who, by virtue, learning, and the excellence of his supreme works, is venerable and dear not to Denmark or Germany only, but to nearly all Europe. This declaration of my heart is something I have long owed you, dearest uncle; but since nothing certain was established to us about your dwelling-place, I was hitherto compelled to defer it. We have now been living more than half a year at Herborn, and shall stay, unless I am mistaken, until the feast of Michael; nor have we yet learned anything certain from Denmark. For we await the courier Eskild daily. My brother Otto, however, I should reckon to be now at home with Aslaksen — for when we migrated hither, we had heard they were staying in England or Scotland. It has also been reported to us that Tage Thott is plying his studies at Heidelberg, and certain other noble Danes, who, I now believe, have gone off to Geneva. From Denmark there was this rumour: that Eskild Seefeld, after celebrating his daughter's wedding, suddenly departed this life; and that Frederik Rosenkrantz had lost his case and been pronounced infamous. But perhaps I detain you longer than is fitting with such chatter. And so with these [words], dearest uncle, I hold you happily commended to God, best and greatest; and I lovingly ask that you not disdain to go on cherishing me, together with my brother Georg and my cousin Falk — who here too apply themselves to letters along with me — and to direct me by your counsel.

Given at Herborn in Nassau, the 12th of May, in the year 1600. Wholly yours,
Erik Brahe, son of Steen,
with his own hand.
