text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO JOSEPH SCALIGER.**
Illustrious and noble Man, most honoured Lord and Friend.

Six weeks have elapsed, unless I am mistaken, since at the imperial castle of **Benátky**, where the seat of my dwelling now is, I received Your illustrious Lordship's letter, **written at Leiden on the 6th day before the Ides of March [10 March]** — most full not only of the eminent erudition in which you excel, but also of humanity and benevolence toward me (for which too I most dutifully give thanks). But since I was lately summoned by the Sacred Imperial Majesty, our most clement Lord — after he had lately returned hither, from **Pilsen** (where for three quarters of a year he was absent on account of the plague), to the castle of his accustomed residence — for His Majesty deigned most clemently to speak with me of certain things pertaining to the studies I pursue (as has been done amply, once and again): it happened that, two days ago, a noble and learned young man here, **Nicolaus Suckerback of Meissen**, newly come from Italy, recognised and accosted me as I walked among others at court (a certain Baron pointing me out), and indicated that he was a native of **Holland** and meant to go thither shortly, asking whether I wished to send any letters to friends and acquaintances there; and when I inquired of him whether, above all, he could direct mine to you, he took the office upon himself. I had thought he would stay here long enough for me, when your last letter (of which I spoke) was brought from Benátky, to answer it point by point according to its contents, so far as the din and the courtly interruptions of this city allow; but today, seeking me at my lodging, he signified by his servants that he would depart hence about midday — wherefore, lest he return to you quite empty of anything of mine, I judged these meagre and rather brief lines should be written to you, rather than none. And since your letter is not at hand, I will touch at least on a few things I remember from it.

**Your conceptions about the equinoxes, and about saving the motion of the eighth Sphere otherwise, which you promise, I eagerly await.** That the Pole Star, many ages ago — like all the other fixed stars affixed to the eighth Sphere (as they call it) — stuck in the same place of the heaven, I will readily grant you, provided you confess that its declination and right ascension, and also its longitude, and even somewhat its latitude, were altered, both in this [star] and in the others. And that this very thing came about **not so much by an advance of the eighth Sphere as by the anticipation of the equinoxes** — as that great man **Copernicus** likewise seems to have observed — I agree with you too. But on this the hinge of the matter turns: **how that anticipation is to be understood and carried out.** That it comes about **by a motion of the earth's axis** (as Copernicus speculated) — reciprocal and librating, and not quite coinciding with the annual restitution — **is a vain, nay wholly absurd assumption, and does not satisfy the appearances even of this age, let alone all the rest.** **I hold that the Sun itself effects this variation**, in that in different ages it designates a different and different Ecliptic, and induces different intersections of the same with the Equator, backward, and indeed not quite uniformly — as in its place, God willing, I shall show more fully. For I have detected that **the lowest [planet], the Moon, varies its orbit in not very dissimilar fashion every month**, so that not only is **its greatest latitude changed by a third part of a degree** (as much difference as has hitherto been found in the obliquity of the Ecliptic), but I have also learned that **the nodes and intersections with the Ecliptic — though by a forward, uniform motion — come about nevertheless reciprocally and by an unequal ratio, and with a notable enough difference, which can reach 1¾°** — as the restitution of the lunar course, soon (Heaven favouring) to be published **in our *Progymnasmata***, will more fully disclose. If some reasoning, perhaps different from ours, has become known to you — and has been ascertained from the most ancient histories and from reliable observations — by which these things can conveniently be explained, I should wish it communicated to me. Meanwhile, to say the thing as it is, **I cannot follow what you hinted both in this letter and elsewhere: namely that the Pole of the world is other than the Pole of the equinoctial, and that the meridian lines move.** For that seems less fitting — unless perhaps I do not yet grasp your opinion, which is a little obscure; wherefore I desire to be more amply instructed by you on this matter.

**For the Manilius, restored entire by you and transmitted to me, I give many thanks.** I have scanned it through in successive hours, as leisure allowed; and your industry and perspicacity in vindicating this author from corruptions and polishing him — well proved in very many others too — pleased me in the highest degree.

I would write more, were your letter at hand (which would doubtless supply further matter), if only the restlessness of this place allowed it, and if he who is to bring these did not hasten his departure so hurriedly. Wherefore may Your illustrious Lordship take in good part these things suddenly poured out, and continue to pursue me with your favour, and not fail, when a messenger offers, to visit me with your most cultivated letters, I pray.

Farewell.
Given at Prague of the Bohemians, the 23rd day of **July**, New Style, in the year of the Christian, Dionysian, and common Era 1600.
Of Your illustrious Lordship
the most zealous,
**Tycho Brahe**, written in my own hand.


*[Postscript:]* When I had written this letter to you nearly six weeks ago, that Hollander who was to deliver it to you had departed one or two hours sooner than I had supposed; and so I was obliged to keep it by me until now, until another occasion should offer itself of directing it to you.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD IOSEPHUM SCALIGERUM.
ILLUSTRIS ET GENEROSE VIR DOMINE ET AMICE HONORANDISSIME.

ELAPSAe sunt septimanae, ni fallor, sex, ex quo in arce Caesarea Bennaticha, ubi nunc sedes est habitationis meae, Illustris Dominationis tuae literas acceperim VI Eid. Martias Lugduni Batavorum scriptas, easque non saltem eruditionis eximiae, quâ praepolles, sed et humanitatis et benevolentiae erga me (pro quibus etiam officiosissime gratias habeo) refertissimas. Cum vero nuper a Scra Caesa Mate, Domino nostro Clementissimo, postquam Pilsena, ubi per tres anni quadrantes ob pestem abfuit, in arcem consuetae residentiae huc nuper redijt, evocatus sum, siquidem ipsius Matas de quibusdam ad studia quae tracto pertinentibus clementissime mecum loqui dignabatur (prout semel atque iterum affatim factum est) accidit, quod ante biduum Nobilis et eruditus hic Adolescens NICOLAUS SUCKERBACK de Myssen noviter ex Italia veniens me in aula inter alios ambulantem, Barone quodam indicante, agnosceret et compellaret, seque a Batavia oriundum, atque eo brevi cogitare indicaret, rogans, an quidpiam literarum ad amicos et isthic notos mittere vellem, cumque prae caeteris, an ad te meas dirigere possit, ab eo percontarer, id officij in se recepit. Existimavi autem eum tamdiu hîc mansurum, donec allatis tuis ultimis (de quibus dixi) literis e Bennaticha, ijs secundum singula earundem contenta, quatenus in hac urbe strepitus et interpellationes aulicae ferunt, respondere possem; at is hodie me in hospitio quaerens se circa meridiem hinc abiturum in ijs hominibus significavit, quare ne plane mearum vacuus ad vos rediret, has ieiunas et breviusculas, potius quam nullas ad te exarandas duxi. Quoniam vero literae tuae ad manus non sunt, nonnulla saltem, quae ex ijs recordor, attingam.

Conceptiones tuas de aequinoctijs et motu octavae Sphaerae aliter salvando, quas promittis, avide exspecto. Stellam Polarem ante plurima secula, quemadmodum reliqua omnia octavae Sphaerae (uti vocant) affixa sidera in eodem coeli loco haerere, facile tibi concessero, modo declinationem et ascensionem rectam, tum quoque longitudinem et nonnihil etiam latitudinem, tam in hac quam in alijs alteratas fatearis. Quod autem id ipsum evenerit, non tam octavae Sphaerae promotione quam aequinoctiorum anticipatione, prout magnus ille COPERNICUS pariter animadvertisse videtur, etiam tibi astipulor. Sed in hoc cardo negotij vertitur, quomodo anticipatio illa intelligenda et exsequenda sit. Per motum axis terreni, prout speculatus est COPERNICUS, reciprocum et liberatum annuaeque restitutioni non plane coincidentem, id evenire frustranea, imo prorsus absurda est assumtio nec apparentijs vel hoc seculo, nedum caeteris omnibus satisfacit. Ego ipsum Solem hanc varietatem efficere statuo, dum aliam atque aliam diversis seculis designat Eclipticam, aliasque eiusdem cum Aequatore intersectiones retrorsum et quidem non admodum aequaliter inducit, prout suo loco latius Deo volente ostensurus sum. Nam et infimam Lunam non multum dissimili ratione suam orbitam singulis mensibus variare depraehendi, ita ut non saltem latitudo eius maxima ad tertiam gradus partem (quanta etiam omnino in Eclipticae obliquitate hactenus comperta est differentia) mutetur, sed et nodi et intersectiones cum Ecliptica, licet antrorsum motu aequali, reciproce tamen et inaequali ratione id fieri satisque notabili discrimine, quod grad. 1¾ attingere queat, cognovi, prout lunaris curriculi restitutio propediem, favente Numine, in Progymnasmatis nostris publicanda plenius patefaciet. Si tibi aliqua ratio a nostra forte diversa innotuit, et ex historijs antiquissimis ratisque observationibus comperta est, quâ haec commode explicari queant, vellem eam mecum communicari. Interim ut dicam id quod res est, assequi non possum, id quod tam in his literis, quam alibi innuisti: Polum nimirum mundi alium esse a Polo aequinoctialis et lineas meridianas moveri. Videtur id enim minus convenire, nisi forte tuam sententiam, quae paulo obscurior est, necdum percipiam, quare hac de re uberius a te instrui cupio.

Pro MANILIO in integrum a te restituto mihique transmisso plurimas habeo gratias. Perlustravi eundem successivis horis, prout otium tulit, mihique tua industria et perspicacitas in hoc authore a mendis vindicando et expoliendo, quae etiam in plurimis alijs satis explorata est, summopere placuit.

Plura scriberem, si literae tuae in promptu essent, ulteriorem procul dubio materiam suppeditaturae, modo etiam id ferret huius loci irrequietudo, et is, qui hasce allaturus est, abitum adeo festinanter non acceleraret; quare haec subito effusa Illustris Dominatio tua boni consulat, meque favore suo prosequi pergat, ac per internuncij oportunitatem suis cultissimis literis invisere non intermittat, quaeso.

Vale.
Dabantur Pragae Bohemorum die 23 Iulij stylo novo Anno Epochae Christianae Dionysiacae et vulgatae 1600.
Illustris Dominationis tuae
studiosissimus
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria scripsi.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 330; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Cum has literas ante 6 fere septimanas ad te exarassem, discesserat Batavus ille, qui eas tibi traditurus erat, una vel altera hora citius quam existimassem, ideoque eas huc usque mecum reservare oportuit, donec alia sese offerret occasio eas ad te dirigendi.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO JOSEPH SCALIGER.**
Illustrious and noble Man, most honoured Lord and Friend.

Six weeks have elapsed, unless I am mistaken, since at the imperial castle of **Benátky**, where the seat of my dwelling now is, I received Your illustrious Lordship's letter, **written at Leiden on the 6th day before the Ides of March [10 March]** — most full not only of the eminent erudition in which you excel, but also of humanity and benevolence toward me (for which too I most dutifully give thanks). But since I was lately summoned by the Sacred Imperial Majesty, our most clement Lord — after he had lately returned hither, from **Pilsen** (where for three quarters of a year he was absent on account of the plague), to the castle of his accustomed residence — for His Majesty deigned most clemently to speak with me of certain things pertaining to the studies I pursue (as has been done amply, once and again): it happened that, two days ago, a noble and learned young man here, **Nicolaus Suckerback of Meissen**, newly come from Italy, recognised and accosted me as I walked among others at court (a certain Baron pointing me out), and indicated that he was a native of **Holland** and meant to go thither shortly, asking whether I wished to send any letters to friends and acquaintances there; and when I inquired of him whether, above all, he could direct mine to you, he took the office upon himself. I had thought he would stay here long enough for me, when your last letter (of which I spoke) was brought from Benátky, to answer it point by point according to its contents, so far as the din and the courtly interruptions of this city allow; but today, seeking me at my lodging, he signified, in the presence of those men, that he would depart hence about midday — wherefore, lest he return to you quite empty of anything of mine, I judged these meagre and rather brief lines should be written to you, rather than none. And since your letter is not at hand, I will touch at least on a few things I remember from it.

**Your conceptions about the equinoxes, and about saving the motion of the eighth Sphere otherwise, which you promise, I eagerly await.** That the Pole Star, many ages ago — like all the other fixed stars affixed to the eighth Sphere (as they call it) — stuck in the same place of the heaven, I will readily grant you, provided you confess that its declination and right ascension, and also its longitude, and even somewhat its latitude, were altered, both in this [star] and in the others. And that this very thing came about **not so much by an advance of the eighth Sphere as by the anticipation of the equinoxes** — as that great man **Copernicus** likewise seems to have observed — I agree with you too. But on this the hinge of the matter turns: **how that anticipation is to be understood and carried out.** That it comes about **by a motion of the earth's axis** (as Copernicus speculated) — reciprocal and librating, and not quite coinciding with the annual restitution — **is a vain, nay wholly absurd assumption, and does not satisfy the appearances even of this age, let alone all the rest.** **I hold that the Sun itself effects this variation**, in that in different ages it designates a different and different Ecliptic, and induces different intersections of the same with the Equator, backward, and indeed not quite uniformly — as in its place, God willing, I shall show more fully. For I have detected that **the lowest [planet], the Moon, varies its orbit in not very dissimilar fashion every month**, so that not only is **its greatest latitude changed by a third part of a degree** (as much difference as has hitherto been found in the obliquity of the Ecliptic), but I have also learned that **the nodes and intersections with the Ecliptic — though by a forward, uniform motion — come about nevertheless reciprocally and by an unequal ratio, and with a notable enough difference, which can reach 1¾°** — as the restitution of the lunar course, soon (Heaven favouring) to be published **in our *Progymnasmata***, will more fully disclose. If some reasoning, perhaps different from ours, has become known to you — and has been ascertained from the most ancient histories and from reliable observations — by which these things can conveniently be explained, I should wish it communicated to me. Meanwhile, to say the thing as it is, **I cannot follow what you hinted both in this letter and elsewhere: namely that the Pole of the world is other than the Pole of the equinoctial, and that the meridian lines move.** For that seems less fitting — unless perhaps I do not yet grasp your opinion, which is a little obscure; wherefore I desire to be more amply instructed by you on this matter.

**For the Manilius, restored entire by you and transmitted to me, I give many thanks.** I have scanned it through in successive hours, as leisure allowed; and your industry and perspicacity in vindicating this author from corruptions and polishing him — well proved in very many others too — pleased me in the highest degree.

I would write more, were your letter at hand (which would doubtless supply further matter), if only the restlessness of this place allowed it, and if he who is to bring these did not hasten his departure so hurriedly. Wherefore may Your illustrious Lordship take in good part these things suddenly poured out, and continue to pursue me with your favour, and not fail, when a messenger offers, to visit me with your most cultivated letters, I pray.

Farewell.
Given at Prague of the Bohemians, the 23rd day of July, New Style, in the year of the Christian, Dionysian, and common Era 1600.
Of Your illustrious Lordship
the most zealous,
**Tycho Brahe**, written in my own hand.


*[Postscript:]* When I had written this letter to you nearly six weeks ago, that Hollander who was to deliver it to you had departed one or two hours sooner than I had supposed; and so I was obliged to keep it by me until now, until another occasion should offer itself of directing it to you.

documents.incipit: EDLE viel ehr- und tugentsame insonders gönstige vielgeliebte fraw schwegerin, derselben …

text.original:
[TYCHO BRAHE AD ANONYMAM].

EDLE viel ehr- und tugentsame insonders gönstige vielgeliebte fraw schwegerin, derselben sein vnsere sämptliche freundtwillige dienste vnd alles gutten zuvor. Vnd kan deroselben hiemit freundtlichen nitt pergen, das vns der ochße, so der herr schuager zu vnserer notturfft aingekaufft, vns wohl zu handen kommen. Thuen vns dero darumb gehabten mühe zum höchsten vnd fleißigsten bedancken, wollens auch vff alle vorfallende gelegenheit eußerstes vermögs nach zu verschulden nitt vnterlaßen.

Was nuhn das verhörte gutt betrifft, das der herr schuager vnd fraw schuegerin vns zu gefallen in bestallung haben, deran geschiht vns gleichßfals zum höhesten ahngenehmsten gefallen. Wollen auch gegen gemeldte zait, alsnemblich vmb Bartholomei, daßelbe zu besehen ainen von vns abfertigen, allerdinges hierumb vnd schließlichen beschaid zu macchen.

Für die bieren thuen wir vns gleichßfals zum höchsten bedancken.

Vns hiemit göttlicher almacht getreulich entpfhelendt.

Jn eill, Prag den 26. julii a:o 1600


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia XIV, p. 209; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Der poti ist seines pottenlohns allerdinges entrichtet.
text.english:
**[Tycho Brahe to an unnamed lady.]**

Noble, very honourable and virtuous, especially favourable, dearly-beloved lady sister-in-law: to her be all our friendly-willing services and all good, beforehand. And we cannot herewith, in friendly wise, conceal from her that the ox, which the Herr Schwager [brother-in-law] bought for our need, has come well to our hands. We thank her most highly and diligently for the trouble had therein, and will not fail to requite it, to the utmost of our ability, on every occasion that may arise.

Now, as concerns the property under discussion, which the Herr Schwager and the Frau Schwägerin hold in charge [under arrangement] to oblige us — that too is to us a most agreeable pleasure of the highest sort. And toward the said time — namely, about [the feast of] St Bartholomew — we will dispatch one of our [people] to inspect the same, in order to settle this matter altogether and conclusively.

For the pears we likewise give our highest thanks.

Herewith faithfully commending ourselves to God's Almighty [protection].

In haste, Prague, the 26th of July, in the year 1600.


*[Postscript:]* The messenger has in all respects been paid his messenger's-fee.

documents.apparatus:
- **Document type.** A short **family/domestic letter** (a draft, *Kladde*, in the Basel autograph collection), with no recipient named — the edition titles it *ad anonymam*, "to an unnamed [woman]." The exact referent is not recoverable from this isolated draft; rendered "the property under discussion." *Bestallung* here = arrangement/charge, not "appointment."
- **Register.** Family German in the courteous first-person plural (*wir/uns/unsere*); the cascade of honorifics (*Edle, ehr- und tugendsame, gönstige, vielgeliebte*) is the standard address to a gentlewoman. Preserved.
- **Calendar.** *Prag den 26. julii a:o 1600* = **26 July 1600**; Prague (imperial) = **New Style**. Header agrees with the label.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** One-line closing postscript, restored from Dreyer XIV, p. 209 (dropped after the dateline "Jn eill, Prag den 26. julii a:o 1600").

edition.print_label: Dreyer, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia (1913–29)
edition.tboo_cite: Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, ed. I.L.E. Dreyer, Tom. XIV, Hauniae 1929, p. 209, no. 203

witnesses.raw: A Aerkebiskoppens arkiv i Prag. Kladde

documents.abstract: Reports that the printer of Ursus's unauthorized writing is unknown, promises investigation and punishment, and advises Tycho to press the Lord Court-Marshal, under whose jurisdiction Ursus falls.
documents.incipit: QUIS typographus scriptum hoc cuius exemplar nobis D.V. communicauit et cuius authorem se …

text.original:
NOBILI AC CLARISSIMO AMICO NOSTRO HONORANDO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE.
Nobilis et clarissime Domine.

QUIS typographus scriptum hoc cuius exemplar nobis D.V. communicauit et cuius authorem se Nicolaus Reimarus Vrsus Dietmarsus esse fatetur absque consensu nostro in hac urbe impresserit, scire non possumus. Sed ipsum inuestigari et, si repertus fuerit, ut alijs in exemplum debito modo in eundem animadvertatur et exemplaria, si quae penes eundem sunt, auferantur curabimus. Cum autem praememoratus Vrsus sub jurisdictionem illustrissimi d. mareschalci aulici pertineat, poterit apud ipsum D. V:ra instare ac sollicitare, quo eidem Vrso ex officio isto demandetur, ut et typographum indicet et exemplaria, si quae habet, exhibeat. Nos qua ratione a nobis fieri potest ac debet rem iuvare non intermittemus.

Datum Pragae in nostra archiepiscopali residentia, die 27 julii a:o MDC.
text.english:
**To our noble and most distinguished friend, to be honoured, Master Tycho Brahe.**
Noble and most distinguished Lord.

Which printer printed in this city, without our consent, this writing — a copy of which Your Lordship has communicated to us, and whose author **Nicolaus Reimarus Ursus the Dithmarsian** confesses himself to be — we cannot know. But we shall see to it that he himself be investigated, and, if he be found, that he be punished in due manner, as an example to others, and that the copies, if any are in his keeping, be taken away. But since the aforementioned Ursus pertains to the jurisdiction of the most illustrious Lord Court-Marshal, Your Lordship will be able to press and solicit with him, so that it may be enjoined upon that Ursus, from that office, both to indicate the printer and to produce the copies, if he has any. We, in what manner it can and ought to be done by us, will not fail to aid the matter.

Given at Prague, in our archiepiscopal residence, on the 27th day of July, in the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Zbyněk Berka of Dubá** (Zbyněk Berka z Dubé, 1551–1606), **Archbishop of Prague** (1592–1606) — the *Berka Zbyněk* of the edition.
- **Subject — the Ursus affair.** *Nicolaus Reimarus Ursus Dietmarsus* = **Nicolai Reimers Bär**, called **Ursus**, of Dithmarschen (c. 1551–1600), Imperial Mathematician at Prague and Tycho's bitter adversary, whom Tycho accused of plagiarising his geoheliocentric world-system. The "writing" (*scriptum*) is the **defamatory anti-Tycho tract** (the *Tractatus* / *De astronomicis hypothesibus … defensio*), printed at Prague; Tycho had sent the Archbishop a copy and was pursuing its **suppression**. The Archbishop disclaims knowledge of the printer, promises to investigate and confiscate, and directs Tycho to the secular authority that actually has jurisdiction over Ursus.
- ***mareschalcus aulicus*** = the **Court Marshal** (*Obersthofmarschall*), the imperial-court officer under whose jurisdiction Ursus (as an imperial servant) fell; the Archbishop's ecclesiastical authority could not reach him directly.
- **Witness.** The sole witness is the **draft (Kladde)** in the **Archbishop's Archive at Prague** — i.e. the chancery retained copy, hence the editorial first-person plural (*nos … curabimus*).
- **Calendar.** *die 27 julii MDC* = **27 July 1600**; Prague (imperial / Catholic) = **New Style**. Header agrees with the label.

documents.title: Ottavio Cauriani → Tycho Brahe — Prague, 2 August 1600 [N.S.]

witnesses.raw: A København, Rigsarkivet, Langebeks diplomatarium. Afskrift

documents.abstract: Certifies that Friedrich Rosenkrantz has been promised a place among Archduke Matthias's attendants and is currently serving under Colonel Kollonitsch before Pápa.
documents.incipit: HERR FRIDERICH ROSENKRANTZ hat sich bei Jr. Fürstl. Durchl. Erzherzog MATHIAS zu …

text.original:
OTTAVIO CAURIAN AD TYCHONEM BRAHE.

HERR FRIDERICH ROSENKRANTZ hat sich bei Jr. Fürstl. Durchl. Erzherzog MATHIAS zu Osterreich mit Irer Kay. Mt. Interceßion, ertzeiget vnd eingestelt, vnd alberait von Ir Durchl. zuesag bekhommen, vnnd derselben aufwarter nach seinem begern vnndergestellt vnnd vnnderhaltten zuwerden. Weiln aber Ir Mt. Resolution wegen Irer Durchl. veldtzug etwas spät hinauß geschicht worden, vnnd entzwischen herr SEYFRIDT VON KHOLONITSCH, obrister yber 1000 Pferdt, fortgetzogen, so hat Er mit Irer Durchl. vorwissen vnnd gnedigsten bewilligung, sich vnnder denselben gestelt, vnnd ist ietziger zeit vor Papa.

Das deme also sei, hab Ich OTTAUIO CAURIANI, dem Herrn TYCHONI BRAHE, so mich derwegen alhie zu Praag ersuecht, vnnd hieuon wiffenschafft begert, deß zu zeugnuß mein Handschrifft hierundergestelt.

Datum Praag Stilo nouo den 2. Augusti Anno 1600.
OTTAUIO CAURIAN,
manu propria subscripsi.
text.english:
**Ottavio Cauriani to Tycho Brahe.**

Herr Friedrich Rosenkrantz presented and introduced himself to His Princely Highness Archduke Matthias of Austria, with the intercession of His Imperial Majesty, and has already received from His Highness the promise to be admitted and maintained, according to his desire, as one of His [Highness's] attendants. But since His Majesty's resolution concerning His Highness's campaign was sent out somewhat late, and in the meantime Herr Seyfried von Kollonitsch, colonel over 1000 horse, had moved off, he [Rosenkrantz] — with His Highness's foreknowledge and most gracious consent — placed himself under that same [Kollonitsch], and is at present before Pápa.

That this is so, I, Ottavio Cauriani, have set my signature hereunder, as testimony, for Herr Tycho Brahe — who sought me out here at Prague on that account, and desired knowledge of it.

Given at Prague, New Style, the 2nd of August, in the year 1600.
Ottavio Cauriani,
I have subscribed with my own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Document type.** A signed **attestation / certificate** (*Zeugnis*), furnished at Tycho's request, documenting the whereabouts and military engagement of **Friedrich Rosenkrantz**.
- **Sender.** **Ottavio Cauriani** (Caurian), an Italian secretary/agent at the Imperial court in Prague; he certifies the matter "with his own hand" (the Latin subscription *manu propria subscripsi* closing a German body).
- **Subject.** **Friedrich Rosenkrantz** (1571–1602), the Danish nobleman who, after a notorious scandal in Denmark, entered Imperial military service against the Ottomans. Through the **intercession of Emperor Rudolf II** he was promised a place among the attendants of **Archduke Matthias** (1557–1619, the Emperor's brother and commander on the Hungarian front); but, the formal resolution arriving late and the cavalry of colonel **Seyfried von Kollonitsch** ("over 100 horse") having already marched, he attached himself to Kollonitsch's troop and is now **before Pápa** (the Hungarian fortress, scene of the 1600 siege/mutiny). Tycho — Rosenkrantz's kinsman — evidently sought this certificate to document the young man's honourable service.
- **Register.** Imperial chancery German (*Ihr Fürstl. Durchl.*, *Ihr Kay. Mt.*); titulature preserved. *aufwarter* = attendant/courtier; *obrister yber 100 Pferdt* = colonel commanding 100 horse; *veldtzug* = (military) campaign.
- **Calendar.** *Stilo novo … 2. Augusti 1600* = **2 August 1600, New Style** (explicit; Prague, imperial). Header agrees with the label.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Dreyer (*Opera Omnia* VIII p. 330) reads *obrister yber **1000** Pferdt* — colonel over **1000** horse (the working transcription dropped a zero). Corrected in Source and translation.
- **Correction.** Restored the dropped zero in the troop count 'obrister yber 1000 Pferdt' (the transcribed original had '100 Pferdt'), per Dreyer, TBOO VIII p.330. The published English already correctly read '1000 horse'; only the German the transcribed original required correction.

Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Read Dreyer TBOO VIII p.330 page image in full. Collated the Rosenkrantz/Archduke Matthias presentation, the Kollonitsch troop-strength clause, the placing-himself-under-Kollonitsch clause, the 'before Papa [Pápa]' location, Cauriani's attestation formula, and the Prague/2 August 1600 New Style date against the transcribed original and the published English. One text error found: the transcribed original's '100 Pferdt' departs from Dreyer's '1000 Pferdt' — a genuine order-of-magnitude numeric corruption in the source, though the published translation itself independently carries the correct figure. Everything else in the letter — names, dates, place, formulae — matches exactly; no fabrication, omission, mistranslation, or hedge-loss found.

**1 defect found:**
- **text error** (**high**). The transcribed original prints '100 Pferdt' (a colonel over 100 horse) where Dreyer's page clearly prints '1000 Pferdt' (over 1000 horse) — a dropped zero, an order-of-magnitude discrepancy in a troop count. documents.incipit: EXOPTATISSIMAS tuas diuque desideratas, Amantissime OLIGERE, iam tandem accepi literas, …
documents.editorial_note:
**Text recovered.** 38 words missing from inside this letter — dropped by a defective transcription of the source — have been restored from the text of record and translated into place.

**Date note.** Source dateline reads *die 3. Iunij Anno 1600* = **3 June 1600 [N.S.]** (header follows it). The catalogue label carries an ambiguous double "*3. juni n.s. / 3. august n.s.*" — the **June** reading is correct per the text (and the identifier's 0803 "August" is an error; the internal evidence — Kepler "here a third of a year," Friedrich "came a month ago" — fits early June). text.original:
NOBILISSIMO VIRO, TAM GENERIS
QUAM ERUDITIONIS CLARITATE PRÆEMINENTE, DOMINO OLIGERO ROSÆKRANTZIO DE ROSENHOLM,
AMICO, AFFINI ET CONSANGVINEO LONGE CHARISSIMO.

S. P.

EXOPTATISSIMAS tuas diuque desideratas, Amantissime OLIGERE, iam tandem accepi literas,
quibus ab initio tarditatem in rescribendo excusas, idque ijs rationibus, quæ
apud me, alias de te candide sentientem, facile locum inveniunt. Postea de rerum
mearum conditione, quam Divina Clementia hîc apud Augustissimum Imperatorem RUDOLPHUM
Secundum mihi indulsit, et qualiter ea, ad alios a te relata, ijs
placuerit, tibi vero et intimis amicis inprimis auditu iucundissima fuerit,
multa commemoras, quæ sincerum tuum erga me affectum, de quo etiam antea nunquam
dubitavi, affatim testantur, pro quo constanti erga me amore gratias tibi, e
pectore tui vicissim studiosissimo profectas, ago quam possum maximas. Res meæ
adhuc in eodem statu sunt, quo versabantur, cum ultimas tibi scriberem ; neque
enim ob absentiam Cæsaris, qui etiamnum
Pilsenæ, urbe 15 milliaribus hinc remota,
commoratur, quidpiam, quod momentum haberet, incrementi interea sumere poterant,
quod tamen in posterum futurum spero. Nam Cæsarea
Maiestas de clementissimo erga me favore, quod Deo acceptum fero,
nihil remittit, sed indies eundem adauget; optime etiam mihi cupiunt ditionis
huius Primates quique, adeo ut in Regni indigenam, quo omnibus eorum gaudeam
Privilegijs, me adoptaturos, sponte obtulerint. Sed de his nunc plura non addo,
suo forte tempore uberius eiuscemodi indicaturus.

Discessit heri primum a me FRIDERICUS ROSENKRANTZIUS, tuus Patruelis, meusque
consangvineus, qui ante mensem huc venit; doleo animitus, et quis non doleret
optimi illius iuvenis viri infelicissimum casum, atque
inconstantissimæ fortunæ minus exspectatam calamitatem? Ego non saltem, quod a
te mihi tam accurate commendaretur (licet et hoc plurimum semper apud me
ponderis habere debeat) sed quoque ob sangvinis, quod nobis intercedit,
vinculum, quantum in me erat, et prout ipsemet voluit, eius adversitatibus, si
plane ijs mederi non possem, lenimentum saltem addere diligenter laboravi; quod
ut promptius exequerer, author illi fui, ut Pilsenam, in aulam Cæsaris, se conferret, dedique cum eo literas ad Amplissimum Imperij
Procancellarium Illustrem et Magnificum Dominum CORRADUCIUM, quibus eum rogabam, ut intercessorias a Cæsarea Maiestate ad Serenissimum Archiducem
MATTHIAM Fratrem, qui belli
Ungarici Summæ nunc præest, huic
ROSENKRANTZIO impetrare
vellet, quod et expectatione nostra citius obtentum est, ipsemet Domino
CORRADUCIO (qui mihi plurimum favet, et
quidvis in mei gratiam expedire non detrectat) negotium hoc disponente et
promovente; addidit et ipsemet sponte sua privatim alias ad generosum quendam
Baronem in Aula Archiducis sibi familiariter notum literas, non parum quoque
FRIDERICO profuturas; quin
et ego, ut meum etiam qualemcunque adiungerem calculum, ipsi Serenissimo
Archiduci humilime scripsi, et
Consangvinei nostri desideria apud ipsius Celsitnem pro meo
modulo adiuvare non intentatum reliqui, insinuando pauculis eius in Patria
infortunium; sic enim non saltem mihi, sed et FRIDERICO consultum videbatur, quo
præveniremus alios, qui sugillando malum sforte odiosius exasperarent, et sic rem magis suspectam
redderent. Misi simul ipsius Celini duos libros ex meis,
similes per omnia ijs, qui Regi vestro
oblati sunt; et unâ globum quendam, ex nostra stellarum verificatione, affabre
Alchmariæ in Batavia elaboratum, ut his Munusculis
Principis clementem benevolentiam, qua FRIDERICI nostri votis eo lubentius annueret, promptius captare
liceret. Harum vero omnium, de quibus iam dixi, literarum exempla, et simul
ipsius FRIDERICI relationem,
quam huc Pilsena reversus sua manu
consignavit, pariterque eiusdem ad te Epistolam hîc apposui, ut ex ijs lectis
promptius rei peractæ circumstantias haurire queas. Concipio autem non dubiam
spem, FRIDERICUM nostrum hisce
fultum medijs, propositum suum apud Inclytum Archiducem satis feliciter peracturum, præsertim quoad externa
illa et Politica desideria, quæ in suo relinquo favore; trahit sua quemque
voluptas, interdum necessitas urget ea acceptare, quæ alias minus curanda
forent. Sed unus adhuc intrinsecus latet scrupulus, qui non minimum habet
momenti, et cætera omnia remorari, vel etiam irrita reddere, aut prorsus
præscindere, et a tot huius miseræ vitæ adversitatibus atque molestijs eum plane
vindicare possit. Laborat enim, et quidem gravius, quam ipsemet persentiscere
videtur, pulmonis non leviter vitiati affectibus, adeo ut Asthmaticus evadat,
paulatimque Phthisi contabescat, nisi, Dei gratia, mature idoneis medicamentis
(quæ tantis malis præsenter succurrentia non facile
inveniuntur) valetudinem recuperârit, ad quam adipiscendam ea vitæ ratio, ea
regionis et victus conditio, quam ille nunc affectat, obstare potius quam
conducere, metuendum est. Verum et hac in parte non saltem eum præmonui, sed et
consilio atque medicamentorum auxilio, quatenus nunc in promptu habui, ipsi
præsto fui, rationemque præscripsi, quomodo in posterum plura paranda sint, quæ
huic, cui obnoxius est, valetudinis incommodo, mea sententia, quantum Deus
dederit, succurrant; sicque eum Viennam heri,
uti dixi, tendentem, fausta quæque illi precatus, dimisi, adiuncto ipsi quodam
Magistro, qui IOHANNES KEPLERUS appellatur,
Mathematum egregie perito, qui per anni trientem, e Styria adveniens, hîc mecum fuit, et compositis isthic rebus
suis reverti constituit. Is siquidem, cum Viennam in reditu transire debeat, et hominum ac viarum in hoc
itinere gnarus sit, FRIDERICO
utilis comes esse poterit. Cæterum quemadmodum Epistolam tuam ex re grata et
placente circa rerum nostrarum in melius, divina ope, mutationem , non sine gaudibundo applausu inchoasti, et postea in medio tristia et
turbulenta quædam minusque arridentia de calamitate communis nostri sangvine
iuncti interposuisti, sic tandem in fine Catastrophen lætam et apprime auditu
iucundam superinducis, ut comediam quandam repræsentare videaris. Nam quod
postremo refers (ut priora, de quibus nunc satis
dictum arbitror, relinquam) de charissima tua SOPHIA, mea nepte, Deum ipsam fructu
uteri benedixisse, et tunc partui vicinam fuisse, quam etiam feliciter enixam
FRIDERICUS retulit, hæc
inquam me magna voluptate affecerunt, et auditu gratissima fuere. Deus Opt. Max.
hanc, quam vobis dedit, filiolam sospitem conservare et a periculis tueri, ut,
ætate accrescens, utrique Parenti gaudio sit, pro sua bonitate dignetur. Cui
etiam æviterno et triuno Numini te tuamque coniugem, unâque sobolem fœmellam,
toto pectore commendatum habeo.

Vale.

Dabantur ex arce
Cæsarea Benaticka, die 3. Iunij Anno 1600.

Tuus TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.

Addidi carmina quædam, hisce diebus a PAULO
MELISSO, Poëtarum Germaniæ
antesignano, mihi missa, unâ cum exemplo literarum eius, ut scias, qua occasione
ea consignaret. Et quia Odæ CRAMERI tui iuxta
calcem mentionem facit, apposui et hanc. Si otium descriptionem patietur,
adiungam quoque exemplum literarum Domini IOSEPHI
SCALIGERI, quæ etiam nuperrime mihi redditæ sunt. Hæc ubi
perlegeris, cum Domino Doctore NICOLAO,
communi nostro amico, communices, velim.

S. Dilecte consangvinee, cum post peractam victoriam atque trophæum
receptum des instantiam minus validam, iuxta illud: qui volet ingenio cedere  nullus erit, non habeo aliud, quod respondeam, quam aurum apud
me esse, quod ne HERCULES quidem suo clavo extorserit, nedum ut tam invalidis
argumentis cedat .

Vale et cave, ne imposterum deponas cum ijs, qui rem geometrice
metiuntur.

Datæ ut supra in tuis literis.

T. B.

POSTSCRIPTA.CUM has literas iam antea ad te exarassem, paulo postquam a me
discesserat FRIDERICUS
ROSENKRANTZIUS, elapsis iam mensibus duobus, eas mecum interea
reservavi, donec certa et tuta mittendi occasio suppeteret, quam nunc per M.
CHRISTIERNUM LONGOMONTANUM, qui
aliquot annos mihi fuit domesticus, in Daniam redeuntem (quem, si is tua opera indiguerit, ut tibi ex
me commendatum habeas et ad potiora promoveas, quæso) commode nactus, non
diutius eas unâ cum adiunctis, quarum mentionem faciunt, mecum retinendas duxi.
Versor nunc Pragæ, quo ante mensem a Sacra
Cæsaris Maiestate Domino Nostro
Clementissimo, statim ac Pilsena, ubi per
tres anni quadrantes ob pestem abfuit, in arcem solitæ residentiæ redierat, huc
evocatus; dignabatur enim Eius Maiestas
mecum de peculiaribus quibusdam rebus secreto loqui, et nonnulla pro se
efficienda mihi demandare, tum quoque ex me, quæ in
studiorum meorum promotionem et vivendi commoditatem fieri benignissime dudum
iusserat, an ita succederent, cognoscere, quod et sæpius quam semel per integras
horas solitarie in Ipsius Maiestatis
conclavi factum est, et omnia, quæ humillime desiderare poteram, clementissime
mihi indulta; quia vero ignoro, an Ipsius
Maiestas pluribus mecum loqui et quippiam aliud adhuc ulterius
mandare velit, non audeo hinc discedere, priusquam hac de re satis certus fuero.
Interveniunt Legati magnorum Principum, et nunc est hîc Galliarum Regis (qui me
die crastino ad se invitavit) cum splendidissimo comitatu, et magna est
negotiorum moles, quibus Ipsius Maiestas ad
alia atque alia, quæ incidunt, curas dirigere necesse habeat; quantum vero ex
Magnifico Domino CORRADUCIO Imperij
Procancellario intellexi, cuperet Ipsius
Maiestas, ut habitationem sibi propiorem, ubi pariter studia mea
exsequi possem (in quo etiam nunc laboratur) obtinerem, quali id fiet successu,
alias percipies. Est et aliud quoddam negotium, licet minus gratum, attamen
necessarium, quod me voluntario hîc detinet. Dithmarsus enim iste famosi illius in me scripti Author
lethaliter decumbit, partim morbis gravioribus confectus, partim male de isto
facinore conscius, et pœnas metuens; hunc iam dudum in ius citatum ob atroces
illas iniurias et calumnias, quas nosti, legitime iudicari volebam, sed ob
pestem dissipata Cæsaris Aula, iam pæne per
integrum annum, id antehac fieri non potuit; urgeo itaque nunc iuris processum,
siquidem actio sit personalis et periculum in mora, iamque impetravi a Cæsarea Maiestate, ut deputentur e Consiliarijs
certi Commissarij, qui omnia in causa hac debili cognoscant, atque sententiam definitivam pronuncient; qualis hæc futura sit, tandem
rescisces.

Cum hisce præteritis diebus in Aula Arcis horis antemeridianis
inter Generosos et Nobiles Viros ambularem, monstratus mihi est Baro ille
OCTAVIUS CAURIANUS, ad quem Dominus
CORRADUCIUS pro ROSENKRANTZIO nostro scripserat,
quare, captata commoda occasione, cum eo de ROSENKRANTZIO, ubinam esset (nihil
enim is mihi, ex quo hinc discessit, scripsit) et quo in statu res eius
versarentur, sedulo collocutus sum. Is eum clementissime ab Archiduce MATHIA receptum, quod et antea a Domino
CORRADUCIO cognovi, moxque cum equitibus
quibusdam, prout ipsemet cupiebat, in Ungariam profectum, ibi in exercitu esse Cæsaris nostri aiebat, qui in obsidione Castelli
Papæ nunc occupatur, ubi strenuum illum belli Ducem SCHWARTZENBURGIUM, nuper globo sclopetico
ictum occubuisse inaudivimus, eodem etiam OCTAVIO famam confirmanti. Ut vero de rebus ROSENKRANTZIJ eo plenius instruerer,
præsertim cum dicerem, me hisce diebus in Daniam ad quosdam ex eius consangvineis atque amicis scripturum, hanc schedam, sua manu subscriptam, quam
hîc apposui, mecum communicavit. Ubi plura ipsum concernentia percepero, te
eorum ulterius reddam participem. Vale, et Coniugem tuam, neptem meam
charissimam, ex me quam diligentissime resaluta; constitueram ipsemet quidpiam
ad eam scribere, sed hæ interpellationes aulicæ me ita avocant (nam ex hoc ipso
instanti in arcem ascensurus sum) et M. CHRISTIERNUM, de quo dixi, iam itineri accinctum diutius
remorari nolui, ut propria curare vix queam; fiet id, Deo volente, alias,
meliori concesso otio. Saluta quoque ex me officiose matrem tuam, nobilissimam
et honestissimam fœminam, tum quoque alios amicos, quos scis integros esse et
sinceros, atque in amore nostri perseverantes.

Iterum vale.

Dabantur Pragæ festinanter die 3. Augusti stylo novo Anno
1600.

T. T. B.
text.english:
**To the most noble man, pre-eminent as much in the brightness of his birth as of his erudition, Lord Holger Rosenkrantz of Rosenholm, my friend, relation-by-marriage, and kinsman, by far the dearest.**

Heartiest greeting.

Your most longed-for and long-desired letter, most loving Holger, I have now at last received — in which at the outset you excuse your slowness in writing back, and that by reasons which easily find a place with me, who otherwise think candidly of you. Afterward you recount many things about the condition of my affairs, which Divine Clemency has granted me here with the most august **Emperor Rudolf II** — and how, related by you to others, it pleased them, but was to you and your intimate friends especially most delightful to hear — which abundantly attest your sincere affection toward me (of which I never doubted before too); for which constant love toward me I give you the greatest thanks I can, proceeding from a heart most zealous of you in turn. My affairs are still in the same state in which they were when I last wrote you; for on account of the absence of the Emperor — who still tarries at **Pilsen**, a city 15 miles distant hence — they could meanwhile take no increase of any moment, which however I hope will come hereafter. For the Imperial Majesty remits nothing of his most clement favour toward me (which I count as accepted by God), but daily increases it; the leading men of this realm too wish me very well, so much that **they have of their own accord offered to adopt me as a native of the Kingdom, that I might enjoy all their Privileges**. But of these I now add no more, to indicate such things more amply perhaps in their time.

**Yesterday, at last, Friedrich Rosenkrantz departed from me — your cousin and my kinsman — who came hither a month ago.** I grieve from my heart — and who would not grieve at that excellent young man's most unhappy lot, and the less-expected calamity of most inconstant fortune? I — not only because he was so carefully commended to me by you (though this too must always weigh much with me), but also for the bond of blood between us — laboured diligently, as far as was in me and as he himself wished, to add at least some relief to his adversities, if I could not wholly cure them. That I might do this the more readily, I advised him to betake himself to **Pilsen, to the Emperor's court**, and gave him a letter to the most ample Imperial Vice-Chancellor, the illustrious and magnificent Lord **Coraduz**, asking him to obtain for this Rosenkrantz **letters of intercession from the Imperial Majesty to the most serene Archduke Matthias, the [Emperor's] Brother, who now presides over the supreme command of the Hungarian war** — which was obtained sooner than our expectation, Lord Coraduz himself (who greatly favours me, and does not decline to expedite anything for my sake) disposing and promoting this business. He also of his own accord added privately another letter to a certain noble **Baron** at the Archduke's court, familiarly known to him, likely to profit Friedrich not a little; and I too, that I might add my own vote of whatever kind, **wrote humbly to the most serene Archduke himself**, and left nothing untried to aid our kinsman's wishes with His Highness according to my small measure, intimating in a few words his misfortune in his fatherland — for so it seemed advisable, not only to me but to Friedrich, that we might forestall others, who by carping might perhaps exasperate the evil more odiously, and so render the matter more suspect. **At the same time I sent His Highness two of my books, in all respects like those presented to your King** [Christian IV]; **and together with them a certain globe, made with skill at Alkmaar in Holland, from our verification of the stars** — that by these little gifts I might the more readily catch the Prince's clement benevolence, by which he might the more gladly assent to our Friedrich's wishes. Copies of all these letters of which I have spoken, and at the same time Friedrich's own report, which on returning hither from Pilsen he set down in his own hand, and likewise his letter to you, I have placed here, that from reading them you may the more readily draw the circumstances of the matter done. I conceive no doubtful hope that our Friedrich, supported by these means, will accomplish his purpose with the renowned Archduke happily enough — especially as to those external and Political wishes, which I leave to his favour; **each is drawn by his own pleasure; sometimes necessity urges us to accept what otherwise were less to be cared for.**

But one scruple still lurks within, which is of no small moment, and could delay all the rest — or even render it vain, or cut it off entirely, and quite deliver him from so many adversities and troubles of this wretched life. **For he labours — and more gravely than he himself seems to perceive — under the afflictions of a not lightly damaged lung**, so that he is turning **asthmatic, and gradually wasting with consumption [phthisis]**, unless, by God's grace, he shall in good time recover health by suitable medicines (which, presently relieving such great evils, are not easily found) — for the obtaining of which **the manner of life, and the condition of region and diet which he now affects, are to be feared to hinder rather than help**. But in this part too I not only forewarned him, but was at hand to him with counsel and the help of medicines, so far as I now had them ready, and prescribed a method how more are to be prepared hereafter, which may, in my opinion, so far as God shall grant, relieve this affliction of health to which he is subject. And so, as I said, I sent him off yesterday, making for **Vienna**, praying all auspicious things for him — **there being joined to him a certain Master, called Johannes Kepler, excellently skilled in Mathematics, who, coming from Styria, was here with me for a third of a year [four months], and has resolved to return, his affairs there being settled. Since he must, on his return, pass through Vienna, and is acquainted with the men and the roads on this journey, he can be a useful companion to Friedrich.** For the rest, just as you began your letter with a thing welcome and pleasing — about the change, by divine help, of my affairs for the better — not without joyful applause, and then in the middle interposed certain sad and turbulent and less smiling things about the calamity of our common kinsman, so at last at the end you bring on a glad *catastrophe*, especially delightful to hear, so that you seem to represent a kind of comedy. For what you report last (to leave the earlier things, of which enough is now said): **about your dearest Sophia, my niece — that God blessed her with the fruit of the womb, and that she was then near her delivery; whom Friedrich reported also to have happily given birth** — these things, I say, affected me with great delight, and were most welcome to hear. May God, Best and Greatest, deign of His goodness to preserve this **little daughter** He has given you safe, and guard her from dangers, that, growing in age, she may be a joy to both Parents. To which everlasting and triune Godhead I hold you, and your wife, together with your female offspring, commended with my whole heart.

Farewell.
Given from the imperial castle of Benátky, the 3rd day of June, the year 1600.
Yours, **Tycho Brahe**, in his own hand.


*[Postscript:]* POSTSCRIPTS. I have added certain poems, sent me these days by Paul Melissus, the standard-bearer of the Poets of Germany, together with a copy of his letter, that you may know on what occasion he set them down. And because near the foot he makes mention of the Ode of your Cramer, I have appended this too. If leisure permit the transcribing, I shall add also a copy of the letter of Lord Joseph Scaliger, which has likewise very lately been delivered to me. When you have read these through, I should wish you to share them with Lord Doctor Nicolaus, our common friend.  /  Sir, beloved kinsman, since after the victory won and the trophy taken up you press on with a less valid insistence — according to that saying, "there will be none willing to yield to genius" — I have nothing else to answer than that there is gold with me which not even Hercules could have wrested away with his club, far less that it should yield to such feeble arguments. Farewell, and beware lest hereafter you lay a wager with those who measure the matter geometrically. Given as above in your letter. T. B.  /  When I had already written this letter to you, a little after Friedrich Rosenkrantz had departed from me, two months having now elapsed, I kept it by me meanwhile until a sure and safe occasion of sending should be at hand; which I have now conveniently found through Master Christiernus Longomontanus, who for several years was a member of my household and is returning to Denmark (and whom, should he have need of your help, I beg you to hold commended on my behalf and to advance to better things), and I judged that I should keep it by me no longer, together with the enclosures of which they make mention. I am now at Prague, whither I was summoned a month ago by the Sacred Imperial Majesty, our most clement Lord, as soon as he had returned from Pilsen — where for three quarters of a year he was absent on account of the plague — to the castle of his usual residence; for His Majesty deigned to speak with me in secret about certain particular matters, and to commit to me certain things to be done for him, and likewise to learn from me whether the things he had long since most benignly ordered to be done for the advancement of my studies and the convenience of my living were so succeeding — which was done more often than once, for whole hours, privately, in His Majesty's chamber, and all the things I could most humbly desire were most clemently granted me. But since I do not know whether His Majesty wishes to speak with me at greater length and to command anything further beyond this, I do not dare to depart hence before I am sufficiently certain of this matter. The Legates of great Princes are arriving, and now there is here [the Legate] of the King of France (who has invited me to him tomorrow) with a most splendid retinue, and great is the mass of business to which His Majesty must needs direct his cares, to one thing and another as they fall out. As far as I have understood from the Magnificent Lord Coraduz, the Imperial Vice-Chancellor, His Majesty would wish that I obtain a dwelling nearer to himself, where I might equally pursue my studies (which is even now being worked at); with what success this may be, you will learn another time. There is also a certain other business, less welcome yet necessary, which keeps me here of my own will. For that man of Dithmarschen, the Author of that infamous writing against me, lies mortally ill — partly worn out by graver diseases, partly ill at ease in conscience over that deed, and fearing punishment; him I have long since wished, having been summoned to law for those atrocious injuries and calumnies which you know, to be lawfully judged; but because of the plague, with the Emperor's Court dispersed for almost a whole year, this could not be done before. I therefore now press the legal process, since the action is personal and there is danger in delay; and I have now obtained from the Imperial Majesty that certain Commissioners be deputed from the Councillors, to take cognizance of everything in this difficult case and to pronounce a definitive sentence; what this is to be, you will learn at last. When in these past days I was walking in the Court of the Castle in the morning hours among Gentle and Noble Men, there was pointed out to me that Baron Octavius Caurianus, to whom Lord Coraduz had written on behalf of our Rosenkrantz; wherefore, having caught a convenient occasion, I conversed diligently with him about Rosenkrantz — where he might be (for he had written nothing to me since he departed hence), and in what state his affairs stood. He said that Rosenkrantz had been most clemently received by Archduke Matthias, and had soon set out, with certain horsemen, as he himself wished, into Hungary, and was there in the army of our Emperor, which is now occupied in the siege of the Castle of Pápa — where we have heard that that vigorous commander of the war, Schwarzenburg, was lately struck by a musket-ball and fell, the same Octavius likewise confirming the report. But that I might be the more fully informed about Rosenkrantz's affairs (particularly since I said that these days I would be writing into Denmark to certain of his kinsmen and friends), he shared with me this paper, subscribed in his own hand, which I have placed here. When I have learned more things concerning him, I will make you further partaker of them. Farewell, and greet again most carefully on my behalf your wife, my dearest niece; I had resolved to write something to her myself, but these courtly interruptions so call me away (for from this very moment I am about to go up to the castle), and I was unwilling to detain Master Christiernus, of whom I spoke, already girt for his journey, any longer. For I could scarcely attend to my own affairs meanwhile; that will be done, God willing, another time, when better leisure is granted. Greet also dutifully on my behalf your mother, the most noble and most honourable Lady, and likewise your other friends, whom you know to be upright and sincere, and persevering in love of us. Again, farewell. Given at Prague, in haste, the 3rd day of August, New Style, in the year 1600. T. T. B.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Holger Rosenkrantz** of Rosenholm — Tycho's kinsman (and, via his wife Sophie Brahe, nephew-in-law); cf. brahe-t_15980925001.
- **Significance — a multi-thread letter that resolves the Friedrich-Rosenkrantz / Kepler / globe episode.**
 1. **Imperial favour.** Tycho's standing under **Rudolf II** grows daily (the Emperor at Pilsen); the **Bohemian nobility has offered to adopt Tycho as a native of the realm** with full privileges.
 2. **Friedrich Rosenkrantz — the family side of brahe-t_16000502001.** Holger's cousin **Friedrich Rosenkrantz** (the disgraced kinsman of the Archduke Matthias letter of 2 May 1600) came to Tycho "a month ago" and **left yesterday (2 June) for Vienna**. Tycho recounts the whole effort: sending him to the court at **Pilsen** with a letter to **Coraduz**, who obtained the Emperor's **intercession to Archduke Matthias** (head of the Hungarian war) "sooner than expected," plus a private letter to a court **Baron**; and Tycho's own humble letter to Matthias (the letter of 2 May 1600) — discreetly "intimating his misfortune in his fatherland" to forestall worse rumour.
 3. **The gift to Matthias — the globe "made at Alkmaar."** Confirms and *specifies* the gift announced on 2 May 1600: **two books (matching those given to Christian IV) and "a globe, made with skill at Alkmaar in Holland, from our verification of the stars."** A precise **provenance for the celestial globe** sent to Matthias — *made/finished at **Alkmaar** in Holland from Tycho's star-catalogue* — a notable datum for celestial-globe history (cf. the Dutch globe-makers, brahe-t_15990417001, and the Fischer letter brahe-t_16000516002). Flagged for the globe-history layer.
 4. **Friedrich's fatal illness.** A striking medical passage: Friedrich suffers a **"not lightly damaged lung," turning asthmatic, wasting with consumption (phthisis)** — worse than he realises; Tycho gave counsel, medicines, and a regimen, fearing his chosen "manner of life and diet" will harm him. *(Friedrich died in the Hungarian war in 1602.)*
 5. **Kepler travels with Friedrich — resolving the departure.** Tycho sends, **as Friedrich's travelling companion to Vienna, "a certain Master, Johannes Kepler, excellently skilled in Mathematics, who came from Styria and was here with me a third of a year and now resolves to return."** This is the **execution of the very arrangement of the Danish Rindschat letter (brahe-t_16000000001)** — the Rosenkrantz kinsman taking Kepler to Vienna at no cost — and fixes the **departure to 2 June 1600**. The April-1600 Kepler letters — the angry one of 8 April (brahe-t_16000408001) and the warm Danish one (brahe-t_16000000001) — were the *prelude*; this is the *event*. (Note Kepler's residence is here "a third of a year" ≈ 4 months → arrival ~Feb 1600.)
 6. **Holger's newborn daughter.** The "glad catastrophe": **Sophie Brahe (Tycho's niece, Holger's wife) had given birth to a daughter** — reported by Friedrich; Tycho rejoices and blesses the child.
- **Cross-references.** Binds together **brahe-t_16000000001 (Rindschat)**, **brahe-t_16000502001 (Matthias)**, and this letter as **one episode** (Friedrich Rosenkrantz + Kepler → Vienna, June 1600); refines the Rindschadt letter's date to **~May 1600**; adds the **Alkmaar globe-provenance** to the globe-distribution record.
- **Persons & places named.** Holger Rosenkrantz; **Rudolf II**; **Friedrich Rosenkrantz**; **Coraduz** (Vice-Chancellor); **Archduke Matthias**; the unnamed court **Baron**; **Christian IV** ("your King"); **Johannes Kepler**; **Sophie Brahe** (Holger's wife, Tycho's niece) and the **newborn daughter**. Places: **Benátky**, **Pilsen**, **Vienna**, **Styria**, **Alkmaar** (Holland), Hungary, Denmark.
- **Date (this chapter's convention /).** Source dateline *die 3. Iunij Anno 1600* → **3 June 1600 [N.S.]** (led with, by this chapter's convention). The catalogue label's alternative "3 August" (and the identifier's 0803) is an **error** — contradicted by the text and by the internal chronology (Kepler "here a third of a year"; Friedrich "came a month ago," i.e. ~early May → departed 2 June). Flagged for the label-date audit.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** POSTSCRIPTA (Melissus/Scaliger enclosures for Doctor Nicolaus; the gold/Hercules wager-note) + the entire 24 Jul./3 Aug. 1600 continuation letter (the Emperor's audiences after Pilsen; the French king's legate; the Ursus lawsuit + imperial commissioners; Octavius Caurianus + the Friedrich-Rosenkrantz/Hungary news; Schwarzenburg killed by a musket at the Pápa siege), restored from Dreyer VIII pp.333–335 — the working transcription carried only the 3 June first installment. This vindicates the 0803 identifier as the dispatch date.
- **Rosenkrantz's silence.** Recovers Tycho's aside that Friedrich Rosenkrantz "had written nothing to me since he departed hence" — Tycho was reconstructing the young kinsman's movements from third parties (Coraduz, Octavius Caurianus), not from Rosenkrantz himself.
- **The Denmark channel.** Recovers Tycho's own stated motive for pressing Octavius Caurianus for news: he was about to write into Denmark to Rosenkrantz's own kinsmen and friends, and wanted to be "fully informed" first — a small window onto the informal news-network Tycho used to track a troubled relative abroad.
- **Tycho's excuse for brevity.** Recovers his closing explanation to Holger Rosenkrantz for not writing more (and not writing to Sophia, his niece, himself): overwhelmed by business at the Prague/Benátky court, he "could scarcely attend to my own affairs," deferring fuller correspondence to a future time of "better leisure."
- **Correction.** Translation restored to match Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Opera Omnia* VIII, pp.333-335: (1) p.334 'Baro ille Octavius Caurianus' rendered as 'Baron Octavius Caurianus', correcting the unsupported 'rare fellow' and matching this letter's own earlier rendering of 'Baronem' as 'Baron' (p.331); (2) the abbreviated sign-off 'T. B.' closing the jesting Hercules/gold aside (p.333) restored to the English; (3) the letter's final abbreviated signature 'T. T. B.' (p.335) restored to the English. The Latin the transcribed original required no change in any of the three cases.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Full collation: read all 8 Dreyer page images (TBOO VIII pp.329-336), covering the letter's entirety (Rosenkrantz salutation p.331 through the postscript's final sign-off p.335); adjacent letters sharing those pages (Tycho-Scaliger tail, Ottavio Caurian-to-Tycho, Tycho-Longomontanus, Oswaldus-to-Tycho) were identified and excluded from scope. Checked proper names (Friedrich Rosenkrantz, Corraducius, Archduke Matthias, Octavius Caurianus, Schwarzenburg, Kepler, Longomontanus, Melissus, Cramer, Scaliger, Nicolaus), place names (Pilsen, Alkmaar, Papa, Prague, Benatky, Vienna), numbers (15 miles, a third of a year, three quarters of a year) and both closing dates (3 June / 3 August 1600) against the page images: all confirmed correct except one. Dreyer p.334 confirms the source reads 'Baro ille OCTAVIUS CAURIANUS' (Baron), which the English mistranslates as 'that rare fellow' — the same title is correctly rendered 'Baron' earlier in this same letter, so the error is real and internally inconsistent, not a source ambiguity. Also found: two abbreviated sign-offs ('T. B.' mid-postscript p.333; 'T. T. B.' final p.335) silently dropped from the English. The the translator's own grade Secure is not supported by this collation.

**3 defects found:**
- **mistranslation** (medium). 'Baro' means 'Baron' (a noble title), not 'rare fellow'; the same letter correctly translates 'Baronem' as 'Baron' a few paragraphs earlier (p.331), so this is an inconsistent, confirmed mistranslation that drops Caurianus's rank and substitutes an unsupported descriptor. At: “there was pointed out to me that rare fellow Octavius Caurianus”.
- **omission** (low). The abbreviated authorial sign-off closing the jesting 'Hercules/gold' aside is silently dropped from the English. At: “NONE — English runs straight from "Given as above in your letter." into the next paragraph”.
- **omission** (low). The final abbreviated signature (Tuus Tycho Brahe) at the very end of the letter is silently dropped from the English. At: “NONE — translation ends at "...in the year 1600."”.

**Repaired.** Verified against the Dreyer page images, TBOO VIII pp.333-335 (the closing sections of the Rosenkrantz letter of 3 August 1600 N.S.), read directly from the extract PDF. All three defects are confirmed present as described: the 'Baro'/Baron title on p.334, and the two abbreviated Latin sign-offs on pp.333 and 335 which were already correctly present in the transcribed original but dropped from the translation. All three are now fixed; no crux remains.

documents.abstract: Certifies that Longomontanus served eight years as his astronomical assistant in Denmark, then in Germany and Bohemia, and is now freely dismissed to return home.
documents.incipit: EGO TYCHO BRAHE de Knudstrup, ex Dania oriundus, Sacræ Cæs. Mai. arcem Benaticam in Regno …

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD CHRISTIANUM LONGOMONTANUM.

EGO TYCHO BRAHE de Knudstrup, ex Dania oriundus, Sacræ Cæs. Mai. arcem Benaticam in Regno Bohemiæ inhabitans, testor omnibus, cuiuscunque conditionis et dignitatis sint, hisce meis literis, earundem exhibitorem, eruditissimum et honestissimum virum, Magistrum CHRISTIANUM SEVERINI LONGOMONTANUM, natione Cimbrum, mihi per octennium in Dania, et postea aliquamdiu in Germania et Bohemia fuisse domesticum, atque in exercitijs Astronomicis diligentem et fidelem navasse operam. Nunc vero cum res eius non ferant, ut diutius mecum commaneat, vel accrescente ætate cogitet aliam vitæ rationem inire, ideoque in patriam ad suos reverti: ego conatus eius nullatenus impedire volui, sed eum libere et cum bona gratia dimisi. Quare omnes generosos et nobiles viros, præsertim in Dania mihi sanguine iunctos, et alios quocunque locorum claros et eruditos viros officiose et peramanter rogatos habeo, ut prænominatum Magistrum CHRISTIANUM sibi diligenter commendatum habeant, atque ad optima quæque ipsum promovere non degraventur: invenient me vicissim ad quævis officia rursum in eorum gratiam, quantum per me licuerit, præstanda quam paratissimum.

Dabantur Pragæ in metropoli Bohemiæ die 4 Augusti stilo novo Anno Christi vulgari 1600.
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria.
text.english:
**Tycho Brahe to [/ for] Christian Longomontanus.**

I, Tycho Brahe of Knudstrup, sprung from Denmark, dwelling in His Sacred Imperial Majesty's castle of Benátky in the Kingdom of Bohemia, testify to all — of whatsoever condition and dignity they may be — by these my letters, that the bearer of the same, the most learned and most honourable man, Master Christian Severin Longomontanus, a Cimbrian [Jutlander] by nation, was my domestic [assistant] for eight years in Denmark, and afterward for some while in Germany and Bohemia, and rendered diligent and faithful service in astronomical exercises. But now, since his affairs do not permit that he stay longer with me — or [since], as his years increase, he is minded to enter upon another manner of life, and therefore to return into his homeland to his own people — I have in no way wished to hinder his endeavours, but have dismissed him freely and with good grace. Wherefore I have dutifully and most lovingly entreated all generous and noble men — especially those joined to me by blood in Denmark — and other distinguished and learned men wheresoever, that they hold the aforenamed Master Christian diligently commended to them, and not find it burdensome to promote him to every best [advantage]: they will find me, in turn, most ready to render whatever good offices, again, in their favour, as far as shall be permitted me.

Given at Prague, in the metropolis of Bohemia, the 4th day of August, new style, in the common year of Christ 1600.
Tycho Brahe,
with his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Document type.** An **open letter of recommendation** (a testimonial *to all whom it may concern*), given to **Longomontanus** on his departure from Tycho's service — not a private letter "to" him, despite the edition's *ad Christianum Longomontanum*; the *ad* here means it is the testimonial he carries (he is its *exhibitor*).
- **Subject.** **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus** (Christian Severin, 1562–1647), *natione Cimbrum* (a Jutlander, from Lomborg / *Longomontanum*), Tycho's ablest assistant. Tycho certifies **eight years' service in Denmark** and further service "in Germany and Bohemia," and dismisses him "freely and with good grace" to return home (with advancing years) — the amicable end of the long collaboration Tycho had tried to prolong eighteen months earlier (cf. brahe-t_15990111001, the Wittenberg letter luring him back). Longomontanus would become professor at Copenhagen and write the *Astronomia Danica* (1622).
- ***ad optima quaeque … promovere*** — to promote him "to every best [advantage / post]"; Tycho asks his Danish kinsmen and learned men everywhere to advance him, pledging reciprocal good offices.
- **Calendar.** *Pragae … die 4 Augusti stilo novo … 1600* = **4 August 1600, New Style** (*stilo novo* explicit), *Anno Christi vulgari* ("in the common [civil] year of Christ"). Header agrees with the label.

documents.incipit: NOBILISSIME Domine TYCHO, remunerationem quinque scilicet Ioachimicos, propter diarium …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, DOMINO DE KNUDSTRUP, MATHEMATICO NOSTRO SÆCULO PRAESTANTISSIMO, DOMINO AC FAUTORI SUO UNICE COLENDO.
SALUTEM IN CHRISTO IESU

NOBILISSIME Domine TYCHO, remunerationem quinque scilicet Ioachimicos, propter diarium Solis et Lunæ, in Martio huius anni 1600 nobilitati tuæ transmissum, a M. CHRISTIANO LONGIMONTANO accepi, Quare T. N. ut par est, gratias ago et habeo. Quod in superioribus meis literis, num in oras Bohemicas me vellem conferre nec ne, nihil habetur, causa fuit non mea in scribendo negligentia, vel oblivio, sed quod 14 diebus, antequam N. T. sententia de re illa huc allata esset, istæ meæ literæ fuerunt scriptæ et obsignatæ. Ideoque M. MELCHIOREM IOSTELIUM rogavi, ut tuæ nobilitati, mecum prius deliberandum, scriberet. In tali autem deliberatione reperi, consultius fore, si Witebergæ permanens tuæ N. in rebus astronomicis pro animi mei tenuitate inservirem, singulisque diebus aliquot certas horas, utpote tres vel quatuor, in laborem istum impenderem. Tuæ nobilitati si hoc meum propositum placuerit, certum stipendium ex æquo et bono mihi determinare, et quid expectandum, data aliqua occasione, haud gravatim significare poterit.

Vale.
Dabantur Witebergæ 6 Augusti veteri stylo Anni 1600 Christi.
T. N.
humiliter colens
M . IOHANNES OSWALDUS,
Zeillensis Francus.
text.english:
**To the most noble Master Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup, the most outstanding Mathematician of our age, his lord and patron uniquely to be honoured.**
**Greeting in Christ Jesus.**

Most noble Master Tycho, I have received from Master Christian Longomontanus the remuneration — namely five Joachims [Joachimsthaler] — for the diary [ephemeris] of the Sun and Moon transmitted to Your Nobility in March of this year 1600. Wherefore I give and render thanks to Your Nobility, as is fitting. That in my earlier letter nothing is contained as to whether I would betake myself to the Bohemian regions or not — the cause was not negligence or forgetfulness on my part in writing, but that these my letters were written and sealed fourteen days before Your Nobility's opinion on that matter was brought hither. And therefore I asked Master Melchior Jöstel to write to Your Nobility that [the matter] must first be deliberated with me. But in such deliberation I have found that it would be more advisable if, remaining at Wittenberg, I were to serve Your Nobility in astronomical matters according to the slenderness of my mind, and to spend, each day, some certain hours — say three or four — upon that labour. If this my proposal shall please Your Nobility, you will be able to determine for me a certain stipend, in fairness and goodness, and to signify — when some occasion is given — what is to be expected, [and that] not grudgingly.

Farewell.
Given at Wittenberg, 6 August, old style, in the year of Christ 1600.
Humbly honouring Your Nobility,
Master Johannes Oswaldus,
a Franconian of Zeil.

He acknowledges payment of **five Joachimsthaler** (*Ioachimici* — the silver coins of Joachimsthal), conveyed through **Longomontanus**, for a *diarium Solis et Lunae* (a computed Sun-and-Moon ephemeris/"diary") sent to Tycho in March 1600.
- **The proposal.** Rather than move "to the Bohemian regions," Oswaldus proposes to **remain at Wittenberg** and serve Tycho remotely in astronomical computation, "three or four hours each day," for a fixed **stipend** — and asks Tycho to set the terms. A glimpse of Tycho's distributed network of paid calculators.

(Note: dated two days after Tycho's testimonial for Longomontanus, brahe-t_16000804001, which is N.S. at Prague — the same Longomontanus is the link between the two.)
