text.original:
MAGNIFICO ET PRÆSTANTISSIMO GENEROSISSIMOQUE VIRO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, ASTRONOMO PRINCIPI, MATHEMATICO CÆSAREO, DOMINO ET PATRONO COLENDO. PRAGAe IN BEHMEN.
MAGNIFICE ET ILLUSTRIS DOMINE, PATRONE COLENDE.
S.

QUAM iamdudum mihi dari exoptavi occasionem literis tuis per MULÆUM in Daniam commeantem mihi traditis respondendi, ea iam tandem subito se aperit, neque tamen satis exoptata, cum Dresdam usque saltem se extendat, unde tamen ad te perlatum iri omnia spero. Est autem ita, ut scribis: neque enim mihi ingrata aut odiosa censura tua est, hominis doctissimi et præstantissimi, præsertim in ijs, quæ ad te ipsum spectant. De carmine elegiaco loquor: in quo quædam tum in concinnitate, tum in expositione te desiderare scribis. Scripsi hoc ad te, et fassus sum, cum mitterem: non eum laborem aut limam accessisse, quæ cæteris meis fere solet. Scis enim ardorem illum Poëticum temporum intervallis minus aut magis incendi: et interdum ita lenti sumus, ut iaceant omnia. Placet itaque mihi, ut premas, donec correctum fuerit: quod quidem a te si factum fuerit, gratiam habebo: nam laus, ea certe, quam scriptor sibi vendicat, mea erit, labor tuus. Ne tamen ingenij me iacturam fecisse existumes, plane mihi persuadeo, metu isto te eximet Carmen Epicum de VARADINO: quod ad te circa idem tempus fere, quo tuæ datæ sunt, etiam tum traditum tibi esse oportuisset, misi per quendam ALBERTUM HOVI, hominem militarem, Domino illustri MELCHIORI RHEDERO addictum eique a me commendatum. Cui ut tu quoque me commendares et illud carmen, quod in honorem eius composui ipsique inscripsi, ijsdem literis a te contendi: neque minus iam contendo, si aut literæ illæ tibi non redditæ essent, aut tu petitioni meæ, quod secus esse puto, hactenus non satisfecisses. Quod secus hoc esse putem, inde fit, quod ipse RHEDERUS literis humanissimis benevolentiam suam mihi ostenderit et gratitudinis ac remunerationis spem fecerit. Constitit mihi certe illud carmen non exiguo labore et animi intentione, quam auxit Historiæ exprimendæ cum veritate et tamen cum decoro Poëtico difficultas: quorum primam dum quidam Poëta Silesius secutus est, alterum ita neglexit in eadem historia reddendâ, ut nihil ineptius fieri possit. Scribit idem RHEDERUS se ex consilio doctissimorum quorundam virorum, inter quos te quoque esse existimo, Gorlitzium recudendum misisse illud meum carmen. MELISSUS quin iam tandem tibi satisfecerit, plane mihi persuadeo: dicerem hominem plane a se discessisse, nisi fecerit.

De scripto aliquo Cæsareæ Maiestati dedicando, quod consilium tuum mihi impertis, pro eo atque volebam, est quod multum tibi debeam. Habeo quidem confectum Philosophiæ Panegyricum, quo omnia ea tribus prolixis satis orationibus complexus sum, quæ de Philosophia mihi videntur posse honorifice dici: sed eum neque iam mecum habeo, neque hactenus quisquam, quos quidem tentavi, Bibliopolarum in eum excudendum sumptus voluit conferre (ita enim agitur cum scriptis elegantibus, dum florent et leguntur inelegantia) nisi ipse conferam. Quod si Poëmata mea mihi remittantur a MELISSO, qui mihi in editione procurandâ minime satisfacit, cum forte posset (nolo dicere plura: hoc ipsum, quod dixi, tecum sit) quæ ante tribus dedicavi, nescio, an rectius facerem, si mutato consilio soli Imperatori dedicarem, plusque forte inde præmij te et alijs commendantibus reportarem. Distribui autem nunc quidem in tres partes, quarum primam partem quinque Elegiarum libros continentem inscripsi Regi Scotiæ ante iam in me munifico, alteram Epicorum quatuor libros et Lyricorum unum continentem, ULRICO Principi Megapolitaniæ, tertiam tres Epigrammatum et unum Sylvarum librum complexam WILHELMO Curlandiæ Duci. Utinam vero tam felix sim, ut aliquando lucem videant, quam illis hactenus invideri equidem nonnihil doleo. Sed præ his duabus vijs illa mihi inprimis arrideret: si materia aliqua mihi offerretur, qua Imperatoris ipsius aut maiorum eius laudes prædicarem, idque carmen hîc in Academia publice decantarem, simile futurum Rhederiano illi. Illam vero viam et materiem præ alijs amplecterer, quod existimarem eâ ratione me æque magnam gratiam a Cæsarea Maiestate initurum quam magni operis dedicatione. Ignosces mihi, vir magnifice, quod hæc tam libere apud te loquar, quod eo facio, ut eo rectius mihi consulere possis, quoniam id libenter facis, et ea re undique gratiam colligis omnium. Si igitur potes, aut talem materiam mihi suppedita, aut de reliquis, quid videatur, scribe, aut certe aliud consilium suggere. Omnia enim mea tibi lubens committo.

Eram finem facturus etiam dudum debuissem: sed tristis adhuc clausula supererat de obitu CHYTRÆI. Quem hîc non laudo aut deploro: feci utrumque tum in Epigrammatis istis, tum in Programmate, cuius et ipse, volente ita Senatu Academiæ, autor sum; quorum utrunque ad te mitto. Tu certe amicum non vulgarem et ingenuum studiorum tuorum et ingenij excellentissimi æstimatorem et præconem amisisti: ego patrem et patronum singularem (ita enim me semper habuit ut filium) nos omnes præceptorem communem. O tristem nuncium, quem tibi allaturus sum! Sed nolo te conturbare, et iam tabellarius astans inclamat aurem et concludere iubet. Bene igitur et diutissime vale, vir præstantissime, et diu vive non solum tuis, sed et BRASCHIO, quamvis et ille inter tuos est.

Datæ festinanter Rostochij 8 Augusti Anno 1600.
T. Magnif. et Generos.
reverenter colens
BRASCHIUS.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 339; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
M. CHRISTIANUM amanter saluto, a quo me literis non salutari miror.
text.english:
**To the magnificent, most excellent and most noble man, Lord Tycho Brahe, Prince of Astronomers, Imperial Mathematician, my Lord and Patron to be revered. At Prague in Bohemia.**
Magnificent and illustrious Lord, Patron to be revered.
Greeting.

The occasion I had long wished for, of replying to your letter (delivered to me by **Mule** on his way into Denmark), now at last suddenly opens — yet not quite as wished, since it reaches only as far as **Dresden**, whence, however, I hope all will be carried on to you. It is as you write: for your censure is not unwelcome or hateful to me — the censure of a most learned and excellent man, especially in things that concern you yourself. **I speak of the elegiac poem**, in which you write that you found certain things wanting, both in finish and in exposition. I wrote you this, and confessed it when I sent it: that **it had not received that labour and file [*lima*] which my others usually do**. For you know that the Poetic ardour is kindled less or more by intervals of time; and sometimes we are so sluggish that everything lies idle. It pleases me, then, that you **suppress it until it has been corrected**: which, if it be done by you, I shall be grateful — for the praise that a writer claims for himself will indeed be mine, the labour yours. But lest you think I have suffered a loss of talent, I quite persuade myself that **the Epic Poem on Várad** will free you of that fear — which ought to have been delivered to you about the same time your letter was sent. I sent it by a certain **Albert Hovi**, a military man, attached to the illustrious Lord **Melchior Röder** and commended by me to him. That you too would commend me to him, and that poem which I composed in his honour and inscribed to him, I asked of you in the same letter — and I ask no less now, if either that letter was not delivered to you, or you have not yet (which I think otherwise) satisfied my petition. That I think it otherwise comes from this: that Röder himself, by a most courteous letter, has shown me his benevolence and given hope of gratitude and reward. That poem cost me no small labour and intentness of mind — increased by **the difficulty of rendering History with truth and yet with Poetic decorum**; of which, while a certain **Silesian poet** followed the first, he so neglected the latter, in rendering the same history, that nothing more inept could be made. The same Röder writes that, **on the counsel of certain most learned men — among whom I think you too are — he has sent that poem of mine to Görlitz to be reprinted**. That **Melissus** has at last satisfied you, I quite persuade myself: I should say the man had quite departed from himself, had he not done so.

As to **dedicating some writing to the Imperial Majesty** — the counsel you impart to me, just as I wished — it is something for which I owe you much. I have indeed finished a **Panegyric of Philosophy**, in which, in three sufficiently ample orations, I have embraced all that seems to me capable of being said honourably of Philosophy; but I neither have it now with me, nor has any of the booksellers I have tried been willing to lay out the cost of printing it (for so it goes with elegant writings, while inelegant ones flourish and are read) — unless I lay it out myself. But if my **Poems** are returned to me by **Melissus** (who by no means satisfies me in procuring their edition, though perhaps he could — I will say no more: let what I have said stay with you) — which I formerly dedicated to three [patrons] — I do not know whether I should do better if, changing my plan, **I dedicated them to the Emperor alone**, and perhaps got more reward thence, with you and others recommending me. I have for now divided them into three parts: the first, containing five books of Elegies, I inscribed to **the King of Scotland**, already munificent toward me; the second, containing four books of Epics and one of Lyrics, to **Ulrich, Prince of Mecklenburg**; the third, comprising three books of Epigrams and one of *Sylvae*, to **Wilhelm, Duke of Courland**. But would that I were so fortunate that they might one day see the light — which I grieve not a little that they have hitherto been begrudged! Yet before these two ways, that one above all would smile on me: **if some material were offered me by which I might proclaim the praises of the Emperor himself or of his ancestors, and recite that poem publicly here in the Academy** — it would be like that of Röder's. That way and that matter I would embrace before others, because I should reckon that thereby I would win as great a favour from the Imperial Majesty as by the dedication of a great work. You will forgive me, magnificent man, that I speak these things so freely to you — which I do that you may the more rightly counsel me, since you do it gladly, and in that way gather everyone's goodwill on all sides. If, then, you can, either supply me with such material, or write what seems best concerning the rest, or at any rate suggest some other plan; for I gladly commit all my [affairs] to you.

I was about to make an end — I ought to have done so long since — but a sad conclusion still remained, **concerning the death of Chytraeus**. Whom I here neither praise nor lament: I did both, in those Epigrams and in the Programme [funeral notice], of which I am myself the author, the Academy's Senate so wishing; both of which I send to you. **You certainly have lost an uncommon and noble friend, an appraiser and herald of your studies and of your most excellent genius**; I, a singular father and patron (for he always held me as a son); we all, a common teacher. O the sad news I am to bring you! But I will not disturb you, and now the courier, standing by, dins my ear and bids me conclude. So fare well, and very long, most excellent man, and live long, not only for your own, but for **Brasch** too — though he also is among your own.

Written in haste at Rostock, 8 August, the year 1600.
Of Your Magnificence and Nobility
the reverent servant,
**Braschius**.


*[Postscript:]* I greet Master Christian affectionately, and wonder that I am not greeted by him with a letter.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondents.** **Incoming** letter, **Nicolaus Brasch (Braschius)** — the Rostock Neo-Latin poet — **to Tycho** at Prague. Brasch is the verse-correspondent whose poems Tycho repeatedly emended (cf. brahe-t_16010415001, where Tycho "writes back to Master Brasch," and the Cramer/Backmeister circle). This letter shows the relationship from Brasch's side.
- **Significance — the literary-patronage world around Tycho, and the death of Chytraeus.**
 - **Accepting Tycho's criticism.** Brasch gracefully accepts Tycho's **censure of his elegiac poem** (faults of "finish and exposition"), admitting it lacked his usual "labour and file [*lima*]," and asks Tycho to **suppress it until corrected** — "the praise will be mine, the labour yours."
 - **The *Carmen de Varadino*.** Brasch's **epic on the siege of Várad/Großwardein** (a Long-Turkish-War subject), sent via the soldier **Albert Hovi** to **Melchior Röder**, whom Brasch asks Tycho to cultivate; Röder, on learned men's advice (Tycho included), had it **reprinted at Görlitz**. Brasch's reflection on **"rendering History with truth yet with poetic decorum"** — and his scorn for a **Silesian poet** who botched the latter — is a nice statement of historical-epic poetics.
 - **The dedication question (the letter's practical core).** Responding to **Tycho's advice to dedicate a work to Rudolf II**, Brasch surveys his options: a *Panegyric of Philosophy* (unprinted — no bookseller will fund it); his **Poems** (held up by **Melissus** = Paul Schede Melissus), currently dedicated in three parts to **James VI of Scotland** (Elegies), **Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg** (Epics + Lyrics), and **Wilhelm Kettler, Duke of Courland** (Epigrams + *Sylvae*) — which he muses he might **re-dedicate to the Emperor alone**. But his real wish: a commission to **praise the Emperor or his ancestors in a poem recited publicly in the Academy**, for which he asks Tycho to "supply material."
 - **The death of David Chytraeus.** The "sad conclusion": **David Chytraeus** (1530–1600), the great Rostock theologian-historian, had **died (25 June 1600)**. Brasch wrote the official **Epigrams and Programme** (funeral notice) for the Academy and encloses them. His threefold lament is the emotional heart: **Tycho lost "an uncommon friend, an appraiser and herald of your studies and most excellent genius"**; Brasch a "father and patron"; the university "a common teacher."
- **Persons named.** Nicolaus Brasch; **Tycho** (addressee, "Prince of Astronomers, Imperial Mathematician"); **Claus Mule** (*Mulaeus*, courier); **Albert Hovi** (soldier-bearer); **Melchior Röder** (*Rhederus*, the Várad-poem patron); the unnamed **Silesian poet**; **Paul Schede Melissus**; **James VI of Scotland**; **Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg**; **Wilhelm, Duke of Courland**; **David Chytraeus** (whose death is reported). Places: **Rostock**, **Prague**, **Dresden**, **Görlitz**, **Várad**.
- **Calendar.** Rostock/Mecklenburg was **Old Style** in 1600; no *stylo* marker; dateline **8 August 1600** read **Old Style** (per label). Header left unqualified to match. *(Chytraeus's death "25 June 1600" is the conventionally cited date; the letter does not give it.)*

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing greeting (Brasch's, to "M. Christianus"), restored from Dreyer VIII p.339 (after the signature; dropped by the working transcription).

text.original:
ILLUSTRI, GENEROSO ET MAGNIFICO VIRO, MAIORUM INSIGNIBUS, VERA VIRTUTE ET DOCTRINA MULTIPLICI PRÆLUSTRI DOMINO TYCHONI A BRAHE IN BENATIA ET KNUTHSTORFFP EQUITI DANICO, SERENISSIMÆ MAIESTATIS IMPERATORIÆ ET CONSILIARIO ET DOMINO SUO PERPETUA OBSERVANTIA COLENDO.
AD MANUS GÆ MÆ IPSIUS PROPRIAS.

ILLUSTRIS, Magnifice et Generose Domine TYCHO, omni cum observantia perpetuo mihi colende Domine: Literæ Gæ Mæ Væ scriptæ Pragæ 6a Augusti stylo novo, redditæ mihi sunt 10a Augusti stylo veteri, cum reverterer illo ipso tempore ex Comitijs Iuridicis, habitis apud Dithmarsos, ubi per septimanas tres hæseram, evocatus eo ab Inclyto Rege nostro Daniæ. Ago autem primo omnium serio pectore gratias Deo opt. Max. quod Gen. Mm Vm cum omni familia hactenus sospitem et salvam clementer tutatus fuerit, eundemque precor, ut quam diutissime illam florentem servet.

Cœterum Illustrissimo Principi OTTHONI, Duci Brunsvicensium et Lunæburgensium, ea quæ mihi commisit Ga Μ Va, suo nomine debita cum submissione retuli: is quid ad eam rescribi per me voluerit, ex Cels. eius autographo ad me misso, hisce nostris inserto, intelliget.

De congressu Embdæ indicto subitoque iterum discessu Legatorum Danicorum et Anglicorum, quæ scripseram, hæc ita vere se habent. Verum ex eo ad me relatum est, Anglos in Daniam usque sequutos Regem nostrum, ibique negotium omne probe compositum et sopitum esse. Rex ipse noster hoc tempore in Iutiam cum Regina Coniuge excurrisse fertur ad venationes, cuius quoque adventus momentaneus forte Crempæ in vicinia expectatur. De emissis 50 navibus nihil hîc accepimus, certo quod communicari Gæ Mæ Væ possit.

FREDERICO ROSENCRANZIO fœliciorem iam auram aspirare profecto lætor, et ubi occasionem scribendi nactus fuero, OLIGERUM de præsenti hominis fortuna hilariori certiorem reddam. Domino RUMPIO et Domino CORADUCIO, Viris honoratissimis, G. M. Va officia mea ut submissa, data occasione, deferat, reverenter oro. Gm Mm Vm Dominus VINCENTIUS MÖLLERUS Consul quoque officiose resalutat. Valeat quam optime Ga Ma Va omni cum familia, cui me totum dedo.

Datæ raptim Hamburgæ 13a Augusti Anno 1600.
Gm Mm Vm omni cum observantia
qui colit
VITUS WINSHEMIUS,
m. p.
text.english:
**To the illustrious, generous and magnificent man, pre-eminent in ancestral arms, in true virtue and in manifold learning, Lord Tycho a Brahe at Benátky and Knudstrup, Danish knight, councillor of His Most Serene Imperial Majesty, his lord to be revered with perpetual observance.**
**Into His Generous Magnificence's own hands.**

Illustrious, Magnificent and Generous Lord Tycho, my lord forever to be revered with all observance: Your Generous Magnificence's letter, written at Prague on the 6th of August New Style, was delivered to me on the 10th of August Old Style, just as I was at that very time returning from the juridical assembly held among the Dithmarschers, where I had been detained three weeks, having been summoned thither by our Illustrious King of Denmark. First of all I give serious and heartfelt thanks to God, best and greatest, that he has thus far mercifully kept Your Generous Magnificence safe and sound with all your household; and I pray him to keep it flourishing as long as may be.

For the rest, to the Most Illustrious Prince Otto, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg, I reported in your name, with due submission, the things which Your Generous Magnificence committed to me; what he wished to be written back to it through me, Your Magnificence will learn from his own autograph sent to me and enclosed in this our letter.

Concerning the congress appointed at Emden and the sudden departure once more of the Danish and English legates — what I had written holds thus, truly. But it has since been reported to me that the English followed our King all the way into Denmark, and that there the whole business was duly composed and laid to rest. Our King himself is said at this time to have gone off into Jutland with the Queen his consort for the hunt; his arrival, momentary [and brief], is perhaps expected in the neighbourhood of Crempe. Of the 50 ships sent out we have heard nothing here certain enough to be communicated to Your Generous Magnificence.

That a happier breeze now blows upon Frederik Rosenkrantz I am truly glad; and when I get the occasion to write, I will inform Holger of the man's present, more cheerful fortune. To Lord Rumpf and Lord Coraduz, most honoured men, I reverently beg Your Generous Magnificence to convey my submissive services, as occasion offers. Lord Vincent Möller, the Burgomaster, also dutifully returns Your Generous Magnificence's greeting. May Your Generous Magnificence fare as well as possible with all your household, to whom I give myself wholly.

Given in haste at Hamburg, the 13th of August, in the year 1600.
Your Generous Magnificence's, with all observance,
who reveres [you],
Vitus Winshemius,
with his own hand.

departures_from_tekstnet.basis: The text printed here descends from one harvest of tekstnet's page and was read against Dreyer's page images in July 2026; a second harvest of the same page is kept beside it. Where the two disagree in a word, both readings are listed: Dreyer's page decides, and unless the audit paragraph names the word, that check has not yet been made for it. Ligature, diacritic, case and spacing differences are not listed; the source's ligatures have been adopted.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & sender.** An **inbound** letter **to** Tycho. **Veit Ortel von Windsheim (Vitus Winshemius)** (1542–1608), Wittenberg physician, writing from **Hamburg** — replying to Tycho's letter (Prague, 6 Aug) and continuing the relationship attested in Tycho's own letter to him of 20 April 1600 (brahe-t_16000420001).
- **Recipient.** **Tycho Brahe**, titled *eques Danicus* (Danish knight) and imperial councillor, "at Benátky and Knudstrup." The address-line *ad manus Generosae Magnificentiae ipsius proprias* = "into his Generous Magnificence's own hands."
- **Persons named.**
 - *Otto, Dux Brunsvicensium et Lunaeburgensium* = **Otto, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg**, to whom Winshemius delivered a commission of Tycho's, enclosing the Duke's autograph reply.
 - *Fredericus Rosencranzius* = **Frederik Rosenkrantz** (1571–1602), Danish nobleman (disgraced and exiled from the Danish court after the 1599 scandal with Rigborg Brockenhuus, then in military service abroad), whose fortunes are now improving — distinct from *Oligerus* = **Holger Rosenkrantz "the Learned"** (cf. brahe-t_16000420001).
 - *Dominus Rumpius* = **Wolfgang Rumpf von Wielross**, Rudolf II's chief steward / privy councillor; *Dominus Coraducius* = **Rudolf Coraduz (Coraduz)**, imperial vice-chancellor — two of Tycho's principal court contacts at Prague (the *Coraduz/Barvitius* axis).
 - *Vincentius Möllerus, Consul* = **Vincent Möller**, **Burgomaster (*Consul*) of Hamburg**, who adds his greeting.
 - *Inclytus Rex noster Daniae / Rex … cum Regina coniuge* = **Christian IV of Denmark** and his consort.
- **News & places.** *Comitia Iuridica apud Dithmarsos* = a **juridical assembly in Dithmarschen** (Holstein) where Winshemius had served three weeks at the Danish king's summons; *congressus Embdae* = the abortive **Anglo-Danish conference at Emden**; the English envoys followed Christian IV into Denmark, where the dispute was settled; the King is hunting in **Jutland**; *Crempa* = **Krempe** in Holstein; *50 naves* = an unspecified fleet rumour. (The Anglo-Danish friction of 1600 turned on Sound tolls, fishing, and the Spitsbergen/Greenland question.)
- **Epistolary formulae & abbreviations.** Heavily abbreviated honorifics: *G[enerosa] M[agnificentia] V[estra]* = "Your Generous Magnificence" (declined throughout — *Gae Mae Vae*, *Gm Mm Vm*); *m. p.* = *manu propria* ("with his own hand"); *Datae raptim* → "given in haste"; closing *qui colit* → "who reveres [you]."
- **Calendar (this chapter's convention — explicit double date).** The letter itself records the Julian/Gregorian gap: Tycho's letter was "**written at Prague 6 August *stylo novo*** [New Style], **delivered … 10 August *stylo veteri***" [Old Style] — the 10-day difference between Imperial (Catholic, Gregorian) Prague and Lutheran north Germany. Winshemius's own dateline, *13a Augusti 1600* at Hamburg, is Old Style. Reproduced as written; not converted.

translation.warrant: Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter (the Dithmarschen assembly dating in both styles, the Duke Otto/Cologne report, the Emden congress and English legates, the 50-ships item, Rosenkrantz, Rumpf, Coraduz, Burgomaster Vincent Möller) word-for-word against Dreyer TBOO VIII pp.339-340 as page images. Exact match, including both O.S./N.S. dates and the '50 ships' figure. The one spelling variant found (Dreyer's 'Friderico' vs source's 'Frederico' Rosencranzio) is an ignorable early-modern orthographic variant, not a substantive error. No defects found.

documents.editorial_note: **Note.** The formal letter calling the exiled Kepler to Prague — answered by **Kepler's reply of 17 October 1600 (brahe-t_16001017001)**. Written the *same day* as Tycho's letter to Herwart requesting the Kepler-on-Ursus transcript (cf. brahe-t_16000911001, "your letter … of 28 August").

text.original:
ERUDITISSIMO ET PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO IOHANNI KEPLERO, ORDINUM PROVINCIALIUM STYRIÆ MATHEMATICO EXIMIO, NUNC GRATZIÆ DEGENTI: AMICO SUO INPRIMIS DILECTO. GRÂITZ.

QUOD prioribus tuis ante duos Menses ad me datis, Eruditissime et dilectissime Magister KEPLERE, nihil antea responderim, nulla tui, nulla negotij, de quo inter nos actum, oblivione, sed potius, ut temporis oportunitati, quæ in hac Aula non semper suppetit, me accommodarem, atque eo promptius atque felicius omnia exequerer, factum esse credas. Vix enim aliqua interea commoditas intermissa, sed et ultro aliquoties captata. Quod ut rectius percipias, quæ interea acta sunt, brevibus narrabo. Paulo postquam Cæsarea Maiestas, Pilsena relicta, huc Pragam in arcem solitæ residentiæ reversa esset, me Benatica ad se evocavit, ante hebdomadas plus minus septem. Pauculis autem diebus postquam hîc comparuissem, ad audientiam clementissime vocatus, in conclavi suo de varijs mecum loqui ultra sesquialteram horam dignabatur, et postea eodem die etiam per dimidiam circiter. In primo vero accessu, postquam ipsius Maiestas ea, quæ ex me scire averet, proposuisset, iussit, ut, si quæ forent, quæ in rebus meis non ita succederent, prout ab initio mandârat, et si quæ præterea desiderarem, libere exponerem. Ego submisse actis gratijs, me talia in chartula aliqua denotaturum atque Domino BARVITIO traditurum respondi: quod et placuit, imo, ut hoc facerem, mandavit. Cum autem viderem tam exoptatam cum ipsius Maiestate de rebus necessarijs loquendi mihi ultro benignissime oblatam occasionem, de Te quoque, quæ in animo habebam, proloqui non intermittendum duxi, sed arrepta aliqua ansa, ex ea, quæ de instrumentis meis et siderum observationibus atque Astronomia instauranda, incidebat mentio: me solum tanto oneri, licet plurima iam huc conducentia in promptu habeam, non sufficere, sed collaboratoribus opus habere aiebam, ut citius et plenius res tanta in ipsius Maiestatis atque Imperij honorem et commodum absolveretur. Respondit eius Maiestas, se ut votis meis hac in parte satisfiat provisuram. Ibi cum inter alia adminicula huc facientia de te quoque huc e Styria accersendo et per unum atque alterum annum sustentando, tuo etiam discrete addito nomine insinuassem, ipsius Maiestas mox benignissime annuit, atque ut inter cætera, quæ desiderarem, id quoque chartæ mandatum Domino BARVITIO traderem, iussit, nec ullam hac in re difficultatem movit. Locutus sum postea particularius cum Illustri et Magnifico Domino CORRADUCIO, hac ipsa de re, et conditiones tuas illi sigillatim aperui, atque hoc solum pro tempore rogavi, ut literas a Cæsarea Maiestate impetrare vellet ad Principem tuum et Amplissimum Ordinem Styriacum, quibus rogarentur, ut per biennium in gratiam Cæsareæ Maiestatis hîc mihi præsto adesse tibi liceret, et nihilominus annuo isthic frui stipendio, quod per Cæsaris liberalitatem centum florenis annuatim augeri exoptarem, siquidem omnia hîc cariora sunt, quam in Styria. Is vero se lubentissime negotium hoc prolaturum, atque ut exoptatum eventum sortiatur, curaturum benigne pollicitus est. Id saltem suasit, ut denuo rem inter cætera, quæ requirerem, Cæsari, sive oretenus, sive per literas, subiectissime proponerem, atque ut ad se eius executio devolveretur, impetrarem, tunc suo auxilio et consilio nequaquam nobis defuturum. Interea dum ea, quæ ipsius Maiestati submisse proponere constitui, animo volvo, et calamo concipio, iniunxit ipsius Maiestas mihi peculiare quid, pro se, quam primum fieri possit, efficiendum. Eram adhuc in publico hospitio apud Insigne aurei Gryphei, ubi cum nulla tranquillitas eiuscemodi quid agendi concederetur, conduxi aliam, non longe a Generoso Domino HOFFMANNO, habitationem minus irrequietam, in quam vix migrâram, et res meas utcunque disposueram, cum denuo me in arcem accersit Cæsar, et quærit, an ea parata sint, quæ a me fieri voluit. Ego vero per hospitij incommoditatem et migrationem in alias ædes, me excusavi, et nacto iam meliori otio, omnia quam primum fieri possit, intra duas vel tres hebdomadas effecturum promisi, cui etiam responso ipsius Maiestas clementissime acquievit. Interim vero dum hoc, uti pollicitus sum, ago, quod sane non parum requirit diligentiæ et laboris, non audeo ab ipsius Maiestate audientiam humillime petere, et de ijs, quæ in votis habeo, etiam me ipsum non parum concernentia sollicitare, ne videar propria potius curare quam ea, quæ ipsius Maiestas a me requisivit, suadentibus etiam alijs, ut propria interea differam, quo absolutis et exhibitis ijs, quæ ipsius Maiestas a me desiderat, eo facilius, captata sic benevolentia, id quod exopto, assequar.

Atque hæc præcipua causa est, cur responsionem ad priores tuas hactenus distulerim: nolui enim quippiam ad te scribere, antequam res omnis ex voto peracta esset, et literæ, quibus huc honorifice vocareris, conscriptæ. Interim vero ante paucos dies superveniunt alteræ tuæ, quæ licet prioribus non dissimilia ab initio referant, tamen circa calcem catastrophen quandam insperatam habent, qua priora consilia non saltem tua, sed et mea non parum collabascunt. Intelligo enim inde Salarium Styriacum tibi, uti et alijs quibusdam, renunciatum, et insuper exilium impositum, nisi decreto istic promulgato parueris, ut ob id in Wirtenbergensem Ducatum, Patriam tuam, redire malis. At quia in hac rerum tuarum conturbatione et prioris sententiæ frustratione, non habeo præsentius consilium, quod ex re nata tibi dem, quam ut, postposita omni mora, te huc conferas, sive solus, uti antea, sive etiam advecta simul coniuge, unâ cum supellectile et rebus necessarijs, pro quibus omnibus facile, uti arbitror, viaticum invenies, urgente præsertim sic necessitate instanti. Neque enim tibi deerunt tui Mecænates et fautores; aut si opus fuerit, pecuniam, quæ ad iter requiritur, alicubi interea mutuo sumes: ubi adveneris, tum præsentes rectius et tutius inter nos agemus, et rationes inveniemus, quibus hisce difficultatibus subveniri poterit, atque tibi et tuis rebus convenienter prospici, ne tibi opus sit tam cito in Patriam tuam redire, aut alio declinare. Interim nullam occasionem præterlabi sinam, quin te, non saltem intercedente autoritate Domini CORRADUCIJ et Domini BARVITIJ, sed et apud Sacram Cæsaream Maiestatem propria mea intercessione ad optima quæque promoveam, et rebus tuis fluctuantibus atque afflictis subveniam. Imo si cætera omnia, quod tamen non spero, frustranea fuerint, ego ipsemet tibi non sum defuturus, sed in ipso effectu ostensurus, ea quæ tibi me scripsisse memini, cum adhuc prope Hamburgum hærerem, antequam nos invicem de facie novissemus, apud me adhuc rata esse, et constanter servari. Tu saltem nihil hæsita, sed confidenter, quantocius poteris, advola: tum coram de omnibus, quæ requiruntur, expeditius agemus, et tutius quam per literas: nec diffido, quin, ubi adveneris, viam iam præparatam invenies. Hæc summa sit consilij, quod etiam is, qui te mihi commendavit, maxime probat.

Plura nunc non addo, neque enim ea, quæ in utrisque literis fuse attigisti, cum ad negotij promotionem, sic stantibus rebus, minus conducant, repetere volo: uti neque de Mathematicis, utrobique a te motis, quippiam addere, cum ea sint alterius atque maioris otij. Eclipsis tamen Solaris, cuius in ultimis tuis mentionem facis, et observationem qualemcunque assignas, calculum, e tabulis nostris renovatis, communico, ut tibi in conspectu sit, atque cum tua conceptione conferre queas. Quantitas deliquij hîc 5 digitos vix attigit, ut ob id apud Vos 6 excedere non potuerit: dimidium digitum istic plus de Sole tectum fuisse concessero, ob minorem Lunæ parallaxin; sed vix amplius. Diligenter a nobis antequam Benatica discederemus, observata est hæc Eclipsis: aderat adhuc M. CHRISTIERNUS, qui postea a me libere et liberaliter dimissus in Patriam abijt. Dominus a TZERNEMEL, qui tibi fecit spem aliquam ante quinquennium, hîc Pragæ est a Cæsare citatus, et forte aliquando hîc manebit, uti sunt admodum ..... quod indicandum duxi, ne frustra alibi ab eo opem et promotionem exspectes. Ego Bibliothecam meam et instrumenta, quæ Benachiæ habui, sic suadente Domino BARVITIO, huc transtuli: quantum enim intelligo, cupit Cæsar, ut in propinquo habitem, et iam de loco commodo, qui civitati conterminus est, deliberatur, qua de re, ubi accesseris (neque enim abfuturum dubito) tibi, uti spero, non displicitura cognosces.

Vale.
Dabantur Pragæ, die 28 Augusti 1600.
Tui amantissimus
TYCHO BRAHE, m. pr. scripsi.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, pp. 343–344; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
POST SCRIPTA. FACIS in ultimis literis tuis mentionem Scoti istius Capnuranici, quod in ipsum antapologiam, perlecto præsertim libro nostro secundo de Cometa, mediteris: quare te rem gratam et tuæ promissioni meæque expectationi analogam præstiteris. Addixisti etiam, te, quæ in famoso isto scripto Ursino, Mathematica inveniuntur, refutaturum, quatenus rite non constant, quod etiam te effecturum confido. Imprimis autem averem, ut ea quæ inventioni nostræ circa Hypothesin novam fucato et fraudulenter obijcit, eam nimirum ex COPERNICO vel APOLLONIO Pergæo desumptam adhuc dilucidius et plenius quam antea a te refelli, atque ut eam mihi, uti par est, asserere, prout probabilibus rationibus iam antea fecisti, non molestum duceres. Institui contra illum actionem iuridicam, postquam huc Pragam veni, intelligens mihi aliquandiu hîc commorandum, et periculum esse in mora, ast siquidem graviter decumberet: et impetravi a Cæsarea Maiestate (utut quibusdam, quamdiu poterant, remoram inijcientibus) ut Commissarij quatuor deputarentur, duo Barones et duo Doctores iuris, qui sententiam hac de re pronunciarent. Siquidem is per emissarios meos quæsitus, ea, quæ scripserat, retractare noluit, sed potius ad ius provocavit. Verum accidit, ut eadem hora, qua citatio illi insinuanda fuit, extingueretur; at nihilominus ius meum inchoatum prosecuturus sum, siquidem lis iam quasi contestata erat, et actio non plane personalis, sed etiam realis, ob librum famosum, qui perpetuo loco sui autoris loquitur, ut me et meos a calumnijs, quibus scatet, legitime vindicem, et iam a Cæsare Illustrissimo Domino Archiepiscopo commissum est, ut omnia exemplaria, quæ hîc reperiuntur, conquirat et igni tradi faciat, atque Typographum puniat. Decretum etiam Dominus CORRADUCIUS a Cæsare promulgatum pollicitus, ut per totum Imperium liber iste annulletur, et tanquam famosus et scurrilis irritus reddatur. Ego vero postea totum hunc processum unâ cum Commissariorum sententia et Cæsareæ Maiestatis decreto in publicum edere constitui, libello quodam peculiari, qui ad mediocrem excrescet magnitudinem. Quod et ex consensu clementissimo Cæsaris et approbatione Domini CORRADUCIJ mihi iam perspecta, Deo volente, facturus sum. Atque in altera eius parte ad ea, quæ Mathematica sunt, atque Hypotheses concernunt, responsurus, quare tuas quoque de his conceptiones mature obtinere averem; aut si quam citissime (uti spero) accesseris, poterit id differri in tuum adventum. Vale. Datum ut supra in literis. T. B.
text.english:
**To the most learned and excellent man, Lord Johannes Kepler, eminent Mathematician of the Provincial Estates of Styria, now dwelling at Graz, his especially beloved friend. Graz.**

That to your earlier [letter], sent me two months ago, most learned and most beloved Master Kepler, I made no answer before, believe was done by no forgetfulness of you, nor of the business treated between us, but rather that I might accommodate myself to the opportunity of time (which in this Court is not always at hand), and so the more readily and happily carry everything through. For scarcely any convenience meanwhile was let slip — nay, several times one was even sought out. That you may the more rightly perceive what has meanwhile been done, I will narrate it briefly. **A little after the Imperial Majesty, leaving Pilsen, had returned hither to Prague, to the castle of his usual residence, he summoned me from Benátky to him, about seven weeks ago.** A few days after I had appeared here, called most clemently to audience, **he deigned to speak with me, in his chamber, of various things, for more than an hour and a half — and afterward, the same day, for about half [an hour] more.** At the first approach, after His Majesty had proposed what he wished to know from me, he ordered that, if there were any things in my affairs not succeeding as he had at the beginning commanded, and whatever else I desired, I should freely expound them. I, having submissively given thanks, answered that I would note such things on some paper and give it to **Lord Barvitius**; which pleased him — nay, he commanded that I do it. But when I saw so longed-for an occasion of speaking with His Majesty about necessary matters most kindly offered me of his own accord, **I judged that I should not omit to speak out about You too, what I had in mind**; and, seizing some handle, from the mention that fell of my instruments and star-observations and the restoring of Astronomy, **I said that I alone do not suffice for so great a burden (though I have very much already conducing hither at hand), but have need of collaborators**, that so great a work be completed sooner and fuller, for the Imperial Majesty's and the Empire's honour and advantage. His Majesty replied that he would provide that my wishes in this part be satisfied. There, when among other aids conducing hither **I had insinuated about summoning you too hither from Styria, and supporting you for a year or two — discreetly adding your name** — His Majesty soon most benignly assented, and ordered that I put this too on the paper to Lord Barvitius, among my other desires; and he raised no difficulty in this. **I afterward spoke more particularly with the illustrious and magnificent Lord Coraduz** about this very matter, and opened your conditions to him in detail, and asked only this for the present: that he would obtain letters from the Imperial Majesty **to your Prince and to the most ample Estate of Styria, by which they should be asked that for two years, for the Imperial Majesty's sake, you be allowed to be present here to assist me — and nonetheless to enjoy your annual stipend there, which I should wish augmented, by the Emperor's liberality, by a hundred florins yearly (since all things are dearer here than in Styria)**. He benignly promised that he would most gladly forward this business, and take care that it have the longed-for outcome. He only advised that I again propose the matter, among the other things I sought, to the Emperor (whether orally or by letter) most submissively, and obtain that its execution be devolved to him; that then he would in no way fail us with his help and counsel. Meanwhile, while I turn over in mind, and conceive with the pen, what I have resolved submissively to propose to His Majesty, **His Majesty enjoined on me a particular thing to be done for him as soon as possible.** I was still at the public inn at the Sign of the Golden Griffin, where, since no tranquillity for doing such a thing was allowed, I hired another, less restless lodging, not far from the noble **Lord Hoffmann**; into which I had scarcely moved, and arranged my things as I could, when the Emperor summoned me again to the castle and asked whether the things he wished done by me were ready. I excused myself by the inn's inconvenience and the move into another house, and, having now got better leisure, promised to do everything as soon as possible, within two or three weeks; with which answer too His Majesty most clemently acquiesced. Meanwhile, while I do this (as I promised), which indeed requires no little diligence and labour, I do not dare to beg an audience of His Majesty most humbly, and to solicit about the things I have in [my] wishes (concerning me too not a little), lest I seem to care for my own affairs rather than those the Imperial Majesty required of me — others too advising that I defer my own meanwhile, so that, once the things His Majesty desires of me are completed and shown, I may, the goodwill being thus won, the more easily attain what I long for.

And this is the chief cause why I have hitherto delayed the answer to your earlier [letter]: for **I did not wish to write anything to you before the whole matter was accomplished according to [my] wish, and the letters, by which you should be honourably called hither, were written.** But meanwhile, a few days ago, comes **your second [letter]** — which, though at the start it reports things not unlike the earlier, yet near the foot **has a certain unhoped-for catastrophe, by which the prior plans, not only yours but mine too, no little collapse.** For I understand thence that **the Styrian salary has been renounced to you (as to certain others too), and exile besides imposed, unless you obey the decree promulgated there — so that on that account you would rather return into the Duchy of Württemberg, your fatherland.** But since, in this disturbance of your affairs and frustration of the prior resolution, **I have no more present counsel to give you, from the case as it stands, than that, all delay set aside, you betake yourself hither — whether alone, as before, or even bringing your wife with you, together with household goods and necessaries** — for all which you will easily, as I judge, find travel-money, especially with present necessity so urging. For your Maecenases and patrons will not fail you; or, if need be, you will meanwhile borrow somewhere the money required for the journey. When you have arrived, then, present, we will deal between us more rightly and safely, and will find ways by which these difficulties may be relieved, and provision conveniently made for you and your affairs — so that you need not so soon return to your fatherland, or turn aside elsewhere. Meanwhile **I will let no occasion slip but that I promote you to all the best — not only by the intervening authority of Lord Coraduz and Lord Barvitius, but also by my own intercession with the Sacred Imperial Majesty — and succour your fluctuating and afflicted affairs. Nay, if all else (which yet I do not expect) prove vain, I myself will not fail you, but will show in the very effect that what I remember writing to you — while I still lingered near Hamburg, before we knew each other by face — is still ratified with me, and constantly kept.** Only do you hesitate at nothing, but confidently, as soon as you can, **fly hither**; then, in person, we will deal of all that is required more expeditiously, and more safely, than by letter; nor do I doubt that, when you arrive, you will find the way already prepared. Let this be the sum of [my] counsel — which too he who recommended you to me most approves.

I add no more now; for I do not wish to repeat what you touched on fully in both letters (since, as things stand, they conduce less to the promotion of the business), nor to add anything about the Mathematical matters you raised in both — since these are [for] another and greater leisure. Yet **the Solar eclipse, of which you make mention in your last, and to which you assign some observation: I communicate the calculation, from our renewed tables**, that it may be before your eyes, and you may compare it with your conception. **The magnitude of the eclipse here scarcely reached 5 digits, so that on that account it could not have exceeded 6 with you; I will grant that half a digit more of the Sun was covered there, on account of the smaller lunar parallax — but scarcely more.** This Eclipse was diligently observed by us before we left Benátky; **M. Christiernus [Longomontanus] was still present, who was afterward freely and liberally dismissed by me and went away to his fatherland.** Lord **von Tzernembl**, who gave you some hope five years ago, is here at Prague, summoned by the Emperor, and will perhaps stay here for a time, since they are quite … [*lacuna*] — which I thought should be indicated, lest you vainly expect help and promotion from him elsewhere. **I have transferred my Library and the instruments I had at Benátky hither, on Lord Barvitius's advice; for, so far as I understand, the Emperor desires that I dwell near by, and a convenient place, bordering the city, is now being deliberated** — about which, when you have come (for I do not doubt you will), you will find things not displeasing to you, as I hope.

Farewell.
Given at Prague, the 28th day of August, 1600.
Most loving of you,
**Tycho Brahe**, written in my own hand.


*[Postscript:]* POSTSCRIPTS. You make mention in your last letter that you are meditating an anti-apology against that Capnuranic Scot, especially now that you have read through our second book On the Comet; whereby you will have done a thing welcome to me, and answerable to your promise and to my expectation. You also engaged that you would refute the Mathematical matters found in that infamous writing of Ursus, in so far as they do not duly hold good — which too I am confident you will accomplish. But above all I should wish that the things which he objects, with painted falsehood and fraudulently, against our invention concerning the New Hypothesis — namely that it was taken over from Copernicus or from Apollonius of Perga — be refuted by you yet more clearly and fully than before, and that you would not find it troublesome to claim it for me, as is fitting, just as you have already done before with probable arguments. I have instituted a legal action against him, after I came hither to Prague, understanding that I must stay here for some time, and that there was danger in delay should he lie gravely ill; and I have obtained from the Imperial Majesty (however much certain men, as long as they could, threw in obstruction) that four Commissioners be deputed — two Barons and two Doctors of law — to pronounce sentence in this matter. For when he was sought out by my emissaries, he was unwilling to retract what he had written, but rather appealed to the law. But it came to pass that, at the very hour when the citation was to be served on him, he was extinguished [i.e. died]; yet nonetheless I shall prosecute the suit I have begun, since the litigation was, as it were, already joined, and the action is not wholly personal but also real, on account of the infamous book, which perpetually speaks in place of its author — that I may lawfully vindicate myself and mine from the calumnies with which it teems. And it has now been committed by the Emperor to the most illustrious Lord Archbishop, that he gather up all the copies found here and have them given to the fire, and punish the Printer. Lord Coraduz has also promised a decree to be promulgated by the Emperor, that throughout the whole Empire that book be annulled and rendered void, as infamous and scurrilous. And I have resolved afterward to publish this whole process in public, together with the Commissioners' sentence and the Imperial Majesty's decree, in a certain particular tract, which will grow to a moderate size. This too, by the Emperor's most clement consent and the approbation of Lord Coraduz, now clearly seen by me, I shall, God willing, do. And in the other part of it I shall reply to the things which are Mathematical and concern the Hypotheses; wherefore I should wish to obtain your conceptions about these in good time — or, if you come (as I hope) very speedily, it can be deferred to your arrival. Farewell. Given as above in the letter. T. B.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Johannes Kepler**, at **Graz** ("Mathematician of the Provincial Estates of Styria"). **The formal letter calling Kepler to Prague after his Styrian exile** — the immediate precursor to **Kepler's reply of 17 Oct 1600 (brahe-t_16001017001)** and to his permanent arrival.
- **Significance — the sealing of the Tycho–Kepler collaboration (a keystone document).**
 - **The audiences with Rudolf II.** A vivid first-hand account: c. 7 weeks after the Emperor returned from Pilsen, he summoned Tycho and **conversed with him in his chamber for over 1½ hours (+ ½ hour the same day)** about astronomy and Tycho's affairs, inviting him to **set his wishes on a paper for Barvitius**.
 - **Securing Kepler's appointment.** Seizing the opening, Tycho told the Emperor **"I alone do not suffice for so great a burden … I have need of collaborators,"** and **"discreetly added Kepler's name"** — proposing to **summon Kepler from Styria and support him for a year or two**. The Emperor assented; Tycho then arranged with **Coraduz** for imperial letters to **Kepler's Prince (Württemberg) and the Styrian Estates**, asking that Kepler assist Tycho **two years** while keeping his Styrian stipend, **augmented by 100 florins** ("all is dearer here than in Styria").
 - **The court delays.** The Emperor enjoined a **special task** on Tycho; lodged at the **Golden Griffin inn** (too noisy), Tycho **moved to a quieter lodging near Hoffmann**; he dares not press his own requests until the imperial task is done — hence the delay in answering Kepler.
 - **The "catastrophe."** Kepler's **second letter** brought the blow: **the Styrian salary withdrawn and exile imposed** (the 1600 Counter-Reformation expulsion), pushing Kepler toward Württemberg.
 - **Tycho's warm pledge.** The heart of the letter: Tycho urges Kepler to **"come hither, all delay set aside — alone or with your wife and goods,"** promising patrons, loans, and intercession (Coraduz, Barvitius, the Emperor) — and, most movingly, **"if all else fail, I myself will not fail you,"** recalling the promise he wrote Kepler **"while I still lingered near Hamburg, before we knew each other by face."** *"Fly hither … you will find the way already prepared."*
 - **The July-1600 solar eclipse.** Tycho sends his **eclipse calculation from his "renewed tables,"** noting ** c. 5 digits' magnitude at Prague (≤6 at Graz, +½ digit for smaller lunar parallax)**, observed at Benátky with **Longomontanus** (who has since "been freely and liberally dismissed" home — i.e. left Tycho's service).
 - **Von Tzernembl & the move.** Warns that **Georg Erasmus von Tzernembl** (a Kepler patron of five years before) is now at Prague; and reports the **library/instruments moved from Benátky to Prague**, with a **city-adjacent residence being arranged** (the coming Curtius house).
- **Cross-references.** The **Tycho–Kepler convergence** keystone: read with **brahe-t_16001017001 (Kepler's 17 Oct reply)**; the April-1600 quarrel/reconciliation (brahe-t_16000408001, brahe-t_16000000001, brahe-t_16000803001); and the **same-day Herwart letter** behind the Kepler-on-Ursus transcript (brahe-t_16000911001).
- **Persons & places named.** Johannes Kepler; **Rudolf II**; **Barvitius**; **Coraduz**; **Johann Friedrich Hoffmann**; **Longomontanus** (*M. Christiernus*); **Georg Erasmus von Tzernembl**; the **Prince of Württemberg** and the **Styrian Estates**; "he who recommended you to me" (unnamed — Hoffmann/Herwart). Places: **Prague** (Golden Griffin inn), **Benátky**, **Pilsen**, **Styria/Graz**, **Württemberg**, **Hamburg** (the early promise).
- **Text/calendar notes.** A short **lacuna** after "since they are quite …" (the Tzernembl sentence), flagged. The source's "*die 28 Angusti*" is a misprint for *Augusti* → **28 August 1600 [N.S.]** (identifier/label agree). *catastrophe* = the unexpected reversal (a theatrical term).

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** POST SCRIPTA (Kepler's planned antapologia vs the "Capnuranic Scot" Craig; the request to refute Ursus's maths + defend Tycho's hypothesis vs Copernicus/Apollonius; the 4-Commissioner lawsuit, Ursus dying at the citation-hour, the burn-order + Coraduz's Empire-wide annulment-decree, Tycho's plan to publish the process), restored from Dreyer VIII pp.343–344 (dropped by the working transcription).

Collated the full letter, including the postscript, visually against Dreyer TBOO VIII pp.340-344 (page images, not digitised text layer). Checked opening/closing address, every proper name (Barvitius, Corraducius, Hoffmann, Christiernus, Tzernemel, Ursus, Copernicus, Apollonius Pergaeus), every number (7 weeks, 2 years, 100 florins, 2-3 weeks, 5/6/half-digit eclipse magnitude, 5 years, 4 commissioners = 2 barons + 2 doctors of law), and the closing date (28 August 1600); all match Dreyer exactly and are rendered without loss or invention. No defects found.
