documents.editorial_note: **Direction note.** **Incoming** letter — *from* the Bavarian chancellor **Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg** *to* Tycho — whose body is a **verbatim transcript of Johannes Kepler's letter to Herwart of 30 May 1599** analysing the **Ursus plagiarism dispute**. The two diagrams Kepler drew are not reproduced in the source (marked **[Figure]** below).

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO DOCTISSIMOQUE VIRO DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHE, DOMINO A KNUDSTRUP ET URANIBURGO, MATHEMATICORUM OMNIUM FACILE PRINCIPI, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO SINGULARI OBSERVANTIA COLENDO. PRAGAe.

CUM praeteritis diebus, vir nobilissime atque Mathematicorum omnium facile princeps, Augusta transirem, ipse consignavi Theatrum tuum Mechanicum Generoso viro, D. PHILIPPO EDUARDO FUGGERO. Egit ille tum gratias ingentes, et pollicitus est, se tibi in scriptis quoque gratias acturum. Hac ipsa die domum reversus reperi litteras tuas die 28. Augusti stylo novo Pragae exaratas, quibus inter alia desideras quantocitius ea tibi transmitti, quae M. IOANNES KEPLERUS de hypothesibus tuis antehac ad me scripserit. Est is sane Mathematicus insignis, mihique tam eo nomine, quam et ob candorem suum perquam acceptus: quare nollem eum quavis ratione vel occasione offendere. Sed cum scribas fato iam functum illum, qui sibi hypotheses illas arrogaverat, et non modo pro re nata, verum etiam pro benevolentia tua, qua me complecteris, plane mihi persuasum sit, hanc communicationem amico meo D. KEPLERO non fore ingratam, idcirco morem gerere tibi statui. Scripsit autem is 30. die Maij anno proxime elapso 1599 haec verba:

»Fatetur URSUS, se hypotheses illas suas non a seipso habere nisi, quatenus aliquid differt a TYCHONE. Contendit vicissim TYCHO, quas profiteatur hypotheses (qua parte discrepant a Copernicanis) eas se suo Marte invenisse nec aliquid simile uspiam vidisse. Contra URSUS, et suas et TYCHONIS deductas esse APOLLONIJ PERGÆI iam pridem circa tempora CHRISTI publicatis hypothesibus. Huius sui pronunciati caussam reddit loca aliqua COPERNICI, in quibus partim ipsa hypothesis TYCHONIS expresse ponatur ab ipso COPERNICO, partim vero APOLLONIO PERGÆO ascribatur. Atqui nihil minus ijs locis COPERNICUS dicit quam hoc ipsum quod vult URSUS. Neque enim TYCHONIS hypothesin exprimit (fallitur ex allusione URSUS) nec eam APOLLONIO PERGÆO ascribit. Cum ergo fateatur URSUS 1. se hausisse suam hypothesin aliunde, 2. invenisse expressam in COPERNICO et attributam PERGÆO, 3. eandemque esse quam habet TYCHO: fatetur ergo se descripsisse illam ab aliquo, qui idem dicit quod TYCHO.

Notetur hoc, quod qui suas URSO monstrarit hypotheses (dempto exiguo quod mutatu facile est) is eadem plane ὑποτιθεῖ cum TYCHONE. Quis autem is est? URSUS dicit, COPERNICUM illum esse, et in eo PERGÆUM praetereaque neminem. Nemo itaque est Author Ursinarum praeter aut PERGÆUM, in COPERNICO, aut TYCHONEM. At ego dico, PERGÆUM non esse Authorem Ursinarum, nec COPERNICUM. Ergo solus TYCHO praetereaque nemo fuit URSO commonstrator ad suas hypotheses. Firmamentum caussae in eo est, ut genuinum sensum COPERNICI habeamus. Caetera confessione sua concinnavit URSUS ipse. Ergo lib. 3. cap. 25. Revolutionum, ubi Tychonias URSUS a COPERNICO putat exprimi, largitur quidem COPERNICUS aliquos ex motibus, quos ipse Terrae tribuit, Soli transcribi posse: sed non id largitur de motu annuo, nec de motibus 5 Planetarum capitalibus ibi agit: nec id fert argumentum libri, quod versatur in explicatione solius motus Solaris (sive terrestris) sine respectu motuum caeterarum stellarum. Ad evidentiam rei describam duo schemata mentem COPERNICI explicantia:

[Figura] Haec est hypothesis COPERNICI, circa unum orbem Terrae vel Solis.

[Figura] Haec est mutatio, quam libro 3. cap. 25. etiam possibilem ponit, et in dubio relinquit.

In priore schemate A centrum et mundi et corporis Solaris. B centrum Epicycli, quod salvat eccentricum (COPERNICUS ex epicyclis et magno orbe facit eccentricum, idem esse ipse ait). Et B illud aequaliter per anni spacium circa A circumit. C centrum Epicyclij quod mutationem praestat eccentricitatis. Illud C itidem annuo motu circumit circa B, in partem contrariam. D Terra est, quae intra annos 3434 circa C circumagitur.

In altero schemate F est centrum mundi et motus Terrae H, quae annuo motu adhuc aequaliter circumit. E est centrum corporis Solaris, quod circumit circa G centrum in annis 3434. G est centrum epicycli, qui Solem E fert, praestans apogaeo Solis progressum, nam in annis 17188 secundum COPERNICUM et Prutenicas circa F circumit, sub fixis. Itaque movebitur quidem loco suo Sol duobus motibus, sed tardissime, nec multum. Sunt enim circelli valde angusti ad comparationem eius circuli, in quo, in utroque schemate, Terra currit. At URSUS, seu inscitia, seu stultitia (qui haec neminem intellecturum speravit) putat COPERNICUM de tali motu Solis loqui, qui sit similis motui Terrae annuo Copernicano: quique aliquid in parallaxibus 5 Planetarum inferat. Nam hi duo, soli secundo loco concessi a COPERNICO, in consideratione caeterorum Planetarum negliguntur, sive Terrae sive Soli attribuantur: quamvis postulante id demonstratione exiguum aliquid inferant, quod videtur sentire in observationibus TYCHO. Haec de primo loco.

In reliquis locis ex COPERNICO allegatis lib. 5. c. 3, 35 adhuc multo peiorem causam habet URSUS. COPERNICUS mentionem APOLLONIJ PERGÆI eiusque lemmatij ex PTOLOMÆO transtulit, quod miror non legisse URSUM in PTOLOMÆO. Sententia PERGÆI toto fere genere alia est. Non enim versatur ille in consideratione systematis 5 Planetarum, quorum centrum in corpore Solis sit, ut TYCHO atque COPERNICUS et quidam antiqui: sed solum in eo ut dicat, qualem proportionem habere debeat Epicyclus cuiuslibet Planetae, seorsim ad suum orbem proprium et horum ad motum anomaliae commutationis et motum aequalem periodicum, ut ex tali proportione sequatur Planetae illius statio et regressio. Sic etiam defectus eius hypotheseos in eo fuit, quod PERGÆUS opinatus est, quemlibet Planetam una tantum inaequalitate variari, quae a PTOLOMÆO salvatur per epicyclum, nesciens ipsum etiam epicycli centrum inaequaliter incedere, sive secundum PTOLOMÆUM, in Eccentrico. Hunc allegatorum locorum sensum esse omnes professores dicent. At URSUS aut caecus aut vafer, interpositione parenthetica vocis (mobilis) persuadere vult, PERGÆUM vel pro eo COPERNICUM loqui de communi illo motu omnium 5 Planetarum, propter Solem, centrum illorum, annuo motu circumactum: de quo motu TYCHONIS hypotheses sonant, quique a COPERNICO Terrae tribuitur. Atque hoc est firmamentum causae. Qui haec perpendit, illi iam ultro suspicio oritur ex omnibus circumstantijs. Fatetur se furti philosophici reum, se Magdeburgi sententiam TYCHONIS de mundi habitu publicam fecisse, sed iuxta suam, natam scilicet ex quadam matre, quae nuspiam est, ut modo quaerendo comperimus.«

Hactenus illa, quae M. KEPLERUS ad me scripsit. Ad alia quae scribis, responsum habebis, cum primum mihi fuerit tantum otij, atque hisce tibi officia et studia mea offero promptissime.

Datae Monachij die 11. Sept. Anno 1600.
Nobilissimae T. Dni Addictissimus
IOAN. GEORG. HERWART AB HOHENBURG, manu propria.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most learned man, Lord Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup and Uraniborg, easily the Prince of all Mathematicians, his Lord and friend to be revered with singular respect. At Prague.**

When in past days, most noble man and easily Prince of all Mathematicians, I was passing through **Augsburg**, I myself delivered **your *Theatrum Mechanicum* [the *Mechanica*] to the noble Lord Philipp Eduard Fugger**. He then gave great thanks, and promised that he would thank you in writing too. This very day, returned home, I found your letter written at Prague on the 28th of August, New Style, in which, among other things, you desire that there be transmitted to you as quickly as possible **what Master Johannes Kepler had earlier written to me about your hypotheses**. He is indeed a distinguished Mathematician, and most welcome to me both on that account and for his candour; wherefore I should not wish to offend him by any means or occasion. But since you write that **the one who had arrogated those hypotheses to himself [Ursus] is now dead**, and since I am fully persuaded — both from the case as it stands and from your benevolence, with which you embrace me — that this communication will not be unwelcome to my friend Lord Kepler, I have therefore resolved to comply with you. Now he wrote, on the 30th day of May of the year just past, 1599, these words:

*"**Ursus admits** that he does not have those hypotheses of his from himself, except so far as something differs from Tycho. **Tycho** in turn contends that the hypotheses he professes (in the part where they differ from the Copernican) he found by his own effort [*suo Marte*], and saw nothing similar anywhere. **Ursus**, on the contrary, [contends] that both his and Tycho's are derived from the hypotheses of **Apollonius of Perga**, published long ago around the times of Christ. The cause of this his assertion he gives as certain passages of **Copernicus**, in which partly Tycho's hypothesis itself is expressly set down by Copernicus, partly is ascribed to Apollonius of Perga. But Copernicus says nothing less in those passages than this very thing which Ursus wants. For he neither expresses Tycho's hypothesis (Ursus is deceived by the allusion) nor ascribes it to Apollonius of Perga. Since, then, Ursus admits: (1) that he drew his hypothesis from elsewhere; (2) that he found it expressed in Copernicus and attributed to Perga; (3) that it is the same as Tycho's — **he therefore admits that he copied it from someone who says the same as Tycho.**

Let this be noted: that **whoever showed Ursus his hypotheses (apart from a trifle easily changed) posits [ὑποτιθεῖ] plainly the same as Tycho.** But who is that? Ursus says it is **Copernicus**, and in him **Perga**, and no one else. There is therefore no author of Ursus's [hypotheses] except either Perga (in Copernicus) or Tycho. But I say that **Perga is not the author of Ursus's, nor Copernicus. Therefore Tycho alone, and no one else, was Ursus's informant for his hypotheses.** The foundation of the case lies in this: that we have the genuine sense of Copernicus. The rest Ursus has framed by his own confession. So, in **Book 3, ch. 25 of the *Revolutions***, where Ursus thinks the Tychonic [hypotheses] are expressed by Copernicus: Copernicus does indeed grant that some of the motions which he attributes to the Earth can be transcribed to the Sun — but he does **not** grant this of the annual motion, nor does he there treat the principal motions of the 5 Planets; nor does the book's argument bear it, which is engaged in explaining the solar (or terrestrial) motion alone, without respect to the motions of the other stars. For evidence of the matter I will describe two diagrams explaining Copernicus's mind:

**[Figure]** This is Copernicus's hypothesis, about the single orb of the Earth or Sun.

**[Figure]** This is the alteration which in Book 3, ch. 25 he sets down as also possible, and leaves in doubt.

In the former diagram, **A** [is] the centre both of the world and of the Solar body. **B** [is] the centre of the Epicycle which saves the eccentric (Copernicus makes the eccentric out of epicycles and the great orb, [and] says it is the same thing). And that B circles uniformly about A through the space of a year. **C** [is] the centre of the Epicycle which produces the variation of the eccentricity. That C likewise circles about B by an annual motion, in the contrary direction. **D** is the Earth, which is carried about C within 3434 years.

In the other diagram, **F** is the centre of the world and of the motion of the Earth **H**, which still circles uniformly by an annual motion. **E** is the centre of the Solar body, which circles about the centre **G** in 3434 years. G is the centre of the epicycle which carries the Sun E, producing the progress of the Sun's apogee — for in 17188 years, according to Copernicus and the Prutenic [Tables], it circles about F, beneath the fixed [stars]. So the Sun will indeed be moved from its place by two motions, but most slowly, and not much; for the little circles are very narrow in comparison with the circle in which, in both diagrams, the Earth runs. But **Ursus, whether from ignorance or from folly** (who hoped no one would understand these things), **thinks Copernicus speaks of such a motion of the Sun as is similar to the Copernican annual motion of the Earth, and which would introduce something into the parallaxes of the 5 Planets.** For these two [motions], granted to the Sun [only] in the second place by Copernicus, are neglected in the consideration of the other Planets, whether they be attributed to Earth or to Sun — although, the demonstration requiring it, they introduce some little thing, which Tycho seems to perceive in [his] observations. So much for the first passage.

In the remaining passages alleged from Copernicus, **Book 5, ch. 3 [and] 35**, Ursus has a still much worse case. Copernicus transferred the mention of Apollonius of Perga and his little lemma **from Ptolemy** — which I wonder Ursus did not read in Ptolemy. **Perga's view is of an almost wholly different kind.** For he is not engaged in the consideration of the system of the 5 Planets whose centre is in the Sun's body (as Tycho, and Copernicus, and certain of the ancients), but only in this: to state what proportion the Epicycle of each Planet ought to have, severally, to its own proper orb, and these to the motion of the anomaly of commutation and the equal periodic motion — so that from such proportion the station and regression of that Planet may follow. So too the defect of his hypothesis was this, that **Perga supposed each Planet to be varied by only one inequality** (which by Ptolemy is saved by an epicycle), not knowing that the centre of the epicycle itself also proceeds unequally — that is, according to Ptolemy, on the Eccentric. That this is the sense of the cited passages, all the professors will say. But **Ursus, either blind or crafty, by the parenthetic insertion of the word "(mobile)," wants to persuade** [us] that Perga, or in his place Copernicus, speaks of that common motion of all 5 Planets — on account of the Sun, their centre, carried round by an annual motion — of which motion Tycho's hypotheses speak, and which by Copernicus is attributed to the Earth. **And this is the foundation of the case.** Whoever weighs these things, to him suspicion now arises of its own accord from all the circumstances. **[Ursus] confesses himself guilty of philosophical theft: that at Magdeburg he made public Tycho's view of the structure of the world, but according to his own [version] — born, namely, of a certain "mother" that exists nowhere, as we have just now found by inquiry."**

Thus far what Master Kepler wrote to me. To the other things you write, you shall have an answer as soon as I have so much leisure; and herewith I offer you my services and zeal most readily.

Given at Munich, the 11th day of September, the year 1600.
Most devoted to Your most noble Lordship,
**Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg**, in his own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondents.** **Incoming**, **Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg** (1553–1622) — Bavarian chancellor, learned correspondent of Kepler — **to Tycho**. The body is a **verbatim transcript of Kepler's letter to Herwart of 30 May 1599**, sent at Tycho's request (Tycho's letter of 28 Aug 1600).
- **Significance — Kepler's brief in the Tycho-v-Ursus plagiarism case (a keystone of the dispute).** This document carries, in Kepler's own words, his **logical and technical demolition of Ursus's plagiarism defence**:
 - **The logical core.** Ursus claimed both his and Tycho's world-systems derive from **Apollonius of Perga** (via passages of **Copernicus**). Kepler shows Copernicus neither states Tycho's hypothesis nor ascribes it to Apollonius; therefore, from Ursus's own three admissions, **"Tycho alone, and no one else, was Ursus's informant"** — Ursus copied the geo-heliocentric scheme from someone "who says the same as Tycho," and that someone can only be Tycho. *(The pivot: "the foundation of the case lies in having the genuine sense of Copernicus.")*
 - **The technical refutation.** Kepler reads the cited Copernican passages (***De revolutionibus* III.25; V.3, V.35**) in detail — with **two diagrams** of Copernicus's solar/terrestrial models (centres A–D; F–H; the 3434-year and 17188-year cycles, per the **Prutenic Tables**) — to show Ursus **misreads** Copernicus's minor solar motions as the annual motion affecting planetary parallaxes, and **misreads Apollonius's lemma** (transmitted from **Ptolemy**), which concerns only single-inequality epicycle proportions, not a heliocentric five-planet system. Ursus's case rests on a **dishonest parenthetic insertion of "(mobile)."**
 - **The verdict.** Kepler brands Ursus **"guilty of philosophical theft,"** who published Tycho's world-structure at **Magdeburg** as his own, dressed up as born "of a mother that exists nowhere."
 - **Context.** This is the analysis that underlies **Kepler's *Apologia Tychonis contra Ursum*** (commissioned by Tycho). Its transmission here (Sept 1600), with Tycho noting **Ursus "is now dead"** (Ursus died 1600), marks the dispute's late stage. (Cf. the Ursus thread: brahe-t_16000401001, brahe-t_15990922001, brahe-t_16000408001.)
- **A *Mechanica* distribution event.** Herwart **delivered Tycho's *Mechanica* ("Theatrum Mechanicum") to Philipp Eduard Fugger at Augsburg** — a datable gift-distribution event to register with the Mechanica distribution layer.
- **Persons & works named.** Herwart von Hohenburg; **Johannes Kepler** (the quoted author); **Ursus (Nicolaus Reimers Bär)**; **Tycho**; **Philipp Eduard Fugger**; **Copernicus** (*De revolutionibus*), **Apollonius of Perga**, **Ptolemy**; the **Prutenic Tables**. Places: **Munich**, **Augsburg**, **Prague**, **Magdeburg**.
- **Text note.** The **two diagrams** Kepler drew are not reproduced in the source (marked **[Figure]**); the lettered descriptions (A–D; E–H) are translated as written. The Greek *ὑποτιθεῖ* ("posits/hypothesises") is reproduced.
- **Calendar.** *Monachij die 11. Sept. Anno 1600* (Bavaria = New Style) → **11 September 1600 [N.S.]**; header and label agree. (Tycho's referenced letter is "28. Augusti stylo novo.")
- **Correction.** One Latin interpolation corrected per Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII p.357: the phantom clause 'Ptolomaeo sententia' removed from between 'perfuadere vult,' and 'PERGAeUM', restoring Dreyer's direct construction 'perfuadere vult, PERGÆUM vel pro eo COPERNICUM loqui...'. English corrected to match, removing the translator's own compensating bracket that had papered over the interpolation's awkward logic.

translation.warrant:
Collated against **Dreyer, *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*** (the edition of record), reading the printed page images. Collated the full letter (TBOO VIII pp.353-357, within read extract pp.353-358 — p.358 belongs to the next letter, 'Tycho Brahe ad Martinum Braschium') visually against Dreyer, including the entire embedded Kepler quotation on the Ursus/Tycho/Apollonius of Perga priority dispute. Checked all citations (Revolutionum lib.3 c.25, lib.5 c.3 and 35), the two geometric-diagram captions and their letter-by-letter description (A-D, then E-H), the orbital periods (3434 and 17188 years), the '5 Planetarum' figure, place and person names (Augsburg, Fugger, Munich, Kepler, Ursus, Copernicus). One text error found as detailed above; everything else in this dense technical letter renders Dreyer's text faithfully, including the opening/closing lines and the 11 September 1600 dateline.

**1 defect found:**
- **text error** (medium). The transcribed original inserts a clause ('in Ptolemy's view') that is absent from Dreyer's printed page 357. The published English faithfully translates the corrupted source ('wants to persuade that Ptolemy's view [i.e. Perga's, or Copernicus for him] speaks of...') and even adds its own clarifying bracket to paper over the resulting awkwardness — a sign the interpolation garbles the logic of this central sentence in Kepler's account of the Ursus priority dispute, which in Dreyer simply reads 'wants to persuade [us that] Perga, or in his place Copernicus, speaks of...'. Dreyer prints: *At URSUS aut cæcus aut vafer, interpofitione parenthetica vocis (mobilis) perfuadere vult, PERGÆUM vel pro eo COPERNICUM loqui de communi illo motu omnium 5 Planetarum... [Dreyer TBOO VIII p.357, line 3-4: no 'Ptolomaeo sententia' clause — 'vult,' is followed directly by 'PERGAeUM']*.

**Repaired.** The defect verified directly against Dreyer TBOO VIII p.357 page image (not the digitised text layer): the printed text reads 'perfuadere vult, PERGÆUM vel pro eo COPERNICUM loqui' with no intervening clause, exactly as the audit's Dreyer claim states. No other part of the letter was touched; every changed word is accounted for in outcomes above.

documents.editorial_note: **Note.** Tycho's reply to Brasch's letter of 8 Aug 1600 (brahe-t_16000808001). The recipient is addressed **"Martin Brasch"** (*Martinum Braschium*) — the Rostock poet **Martin Brasch / Martinus Braschius (1550–1601)**; that letter's recorded sender "Nicolaus Braschius" is most likely a **catalogue error** (same correspondent — same poems, Chytraeus, Bacmeister, Rostock context). Flagged. Day of month missing in the source ("*die Septembris*"); **15** supplied from identifier/label and confirmed by the internal "yesterday, the 14th of September by the reformed Calendar."

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD MARTINUM BRASCHIUM

QUAS 8 die Augusti stylo vestro ad me dedisti literas, Eruditissime BRASCHI, eas heri, qui erat 14 Septembris iuxta reformatum Calendarium, per Dn. GODELMANNUM, Legatum Saxonicum hîc agentem, recepi, quibus nunc, ipso etiam sic ob nuncij festinationem admonente, hæc, quantum ferunt aliæ meæ occupationes, properanter rescribo. De Elegiaco tuo Carmine bene est, quod meas etiam qualescunque non respuis notas: incœperam quodam die pomeridianis horis (nam ante meridiem seriora tractanda sunt) nonnulla in eodem mutare atque aliter disponere, quædam etiam omittere, atque nonnullibi alia supplere, idque antequam ex Arce residentiæ meæ Bennaticâ huc Pragam a Sacra Cæsarea Maiestate, Domino nostro Clementiss. quamprimum Pilsenâ redierat, clementissime evocatus, ubi etiamnum usque in tertium Mensem ab eadem retineor, et quantum intelligo, cupit ipsius Maiestas, ut in viciniore magisque oportuno habitem loco. Toto vero illo tempore, dum hîc sum, tot mihi pro ipsius Maiestate et alias quoque peragenda fuêre, ut otium mihi non superfuerit ea vel semel in manus resumendi, nedum plenius recognoscendi, sed fiet id, nacta, uti spero, aptiore et tranquilliore commoditate. Interim vellem, ut carmen illud tacitus tibi reservares, nec cuiquam communicares; sunt enim quædam in eo, quæ minus apposite relata sunt, nec pro Cæsare (ut de me ipso nihil dicam) satis decore aut convenienter, de quibus, ubi ijs denuo vacare licuerit, te ingenue admonebo, vel nostra transmutatio id facile edocebit, neque enim dubito, quin pro tuo candore, prout etiam nunc polliceris, sis æqui bonique laturus. Alterum illud carmen Epicum de VARADINO, cuius meministi, nondum vidi; nec mihi cum Domino MELCHIORE RÖDERO, cuius mentionem facis, ulla hactenus intercessit noticia, neque etiam scio, an hîc sit, quantum relatione aliorum audio, in Ungaria est; quare de eo et ijs, quæ ipsum concernunt, non habeo amplius quod scribam.

MELISSUS tandem expectationem et spem, quam de ipso concepimus, redemit, missis, paulo antequam Benaticâ abirem, ternis ad me diversi generis carminibus, quorum Exemplum addam, si tempus descriptionem tulerit. Verum ut dicam quod res postulat, videtur in hisce segniore vena præditus quam alias, sive quod hæc ingravescens ætas (est enim, uti opinor, plus quam sexagenarius) spiritus Poëticos minus alacres et humiliores producat, sive, quod tu etiam fateris, ardor ille temporum intervallis plus vel minus incendatur, interdumque lentior evadat. Præ cæteris autem, Epigramma illud primum, quod de me lusit, minus vividum nec fatis concinnum apparet, unde hanc mihi sumsi audaciam, ut aliqua in eo alterarem, quamvis ne sic quidem per omnia arrideat, nec scio, an is meas animadversiones tam libenter ferat atque tu; quare Epigramma illud, cum alia in mei gratiam hinc inde concinnata carmina aliquando forte cudentur, omittendum potius duco, quam ut publicatum autori suo minus sit honorificum, aut mea ieiuna immutatio illi ingrata stomachum moveat.

De Poëmatis tuis vel orationibus Philosophicis Imperatori dedicandis, non scio quid consulam, nam licet Cæsarea Matas erga eruditos satis sit beneficax et liberalis, nec respiciat, cui religionis formæ addicti sint, tamen Consiliarij difficiliores sunt et lenti in exequendo, minusque favent ijs, qui catholicam (uti vocant) religionem non profitentur: si quid autem in ipsius Maiestatis honorem conscribere lubuerit, sit hoc potius carmen quoddam grave et nervosum, de rebus ab ipsius Antecessoribus inde a CAROLO V. et denique a se ipso hactenus præclare gestis, ubi etiam per occasionem inter cætera eius Elogia inferre poteris, quod Astronomiæ instaurationem ad instar ALPHONSI illius veteris Castiliæ et Siciliæ Regis nostro ævo benignissime promoveat. Oportet etiam succincta aliquot et arguta Epigrammata subiungere, nam talibus maxime afficitur Cæsar, et brevitate gaudet. Verum hæc tuo potius relinquo arbitrio, qui rectius nosti, quid hîc faciendum vel secus.

DAVIDEM CHYTRÆUM superiore Iunio Fatis concessisse iam antea inaudieram, uti et Maio antecedente nostrum in Dania HEMMINGIUM, ambos profectæ ætatis senes et de Republica literaria bene meritos, quorum animæ sint in benedictione et pace: memoria ad posteros unâ cum monumentis relictis perduret ac fructum faciat. Perlustravi ea, quæ in CHYTRÆI obitum concinnasti, apprimeque placuerunt. Legi etiam scriptulum istud unâ transmissum de ijs, quæ hoc Anno in Arctois oris usque ad Mensem Maium memoratu digna evenerunt, in quo sunt plæraque apud Suecos gesta auditu tristia minusque iucunda. Deus omnia moderetur in bonum! Scripserat ad me superiore Anno præfatus optimæ memoriæ CHYTRÆUS et consignationem quandam miserat de ijs, quæ historiolæ huius Anni, meam e Dania huc in Bohemiam emigrationem concernentia, inserere constituerat, eaque meo arbitrio (aliter si luberet) formanda reliquerat. Ego vero illi rescribens chartam literis imposui, qua id quod expetebat iuxta meam sententiam insinuavi. At cum in eo quod misisti scripto nihil eiuscemodi inveniatur, suspicor literas meas non satis mature ad ipsum pervenisse, aut quod morbo impeditus et postea morte præventus ea exequi nequiverit. Si itaque literæ illæ meæ unâ cum scheda inserta adhuc inter ipsius chartas posthumæ inveniuntur, cuperem ea, quæ illi annotâram, convenienti loco historiolæ huius Anni adhuc immisceri, neque enim dubito, quin quispiam Vestratium eam usque ad Anni finem continuaturus sit, ut sic Historia Arctoa ab optimo illo CHYTRÆO inde ab Anno millesimo quingentesimo inchoata hoc millesimo sexcentesimo compleatur, atque hac ratione integrum contineat centenarium. Poterit vero id quod ego fieri averem, mea opinione rectius subiungi ijs, quæ a CHYTRÆO consignata sunt, tanquam ab ipso, dum adhuc viveret, exarata, ne si aliqua ibi reperirentur vicinis Danis minus grata (uti est veritas plærumque odiosa) nemini inter Vestros Professores adhuc superstites id imputari posset. Placebit (uti opinor) Cæsari, ubi viderit longe etiam remotas Academias sua ob Astronomiæ promotionem deprædicare encomia, nam et ab Illustri ac Magnifico Domino CORRADUCIO, Imperij Procancellario, quam primum antecedente Anno e Legatione Italica et Romana huc reversus esset, quæsivit, an Romæ vel alibi in Italia audivisset, quod me ob Astronomiam redintegrandam huc vocârit, cumque is affirmaret, se tam Romæ quam in alijs locis hoc relatione præstantium Virorum percepisse, id Cæsari admodum placuit, et sibi ipsi vel hoc nomine quasi congratulari visus est, prout ab ipso Domino CORRADUCIO hæc ad me perlata sunt; atque hinc cætera, quæ desidero, æstimare licebit. Nihil tamen Vobis præscribo, sed omnia vestro arbitrio et consulto iudicio facienda [vel o]mittenda relinquo. Referet quoque plura ex me supranominatus Dn. Doctor GÖDELMANNUS, ubi vos, uti constituit, accesserit.

Vale et Clarissimum Virum Dn. D. LUCAM BACKMEISTERUM (cui etiam in ultimis meis literis de memorata re, si recte recordor, nonnulla scripsi) ex me officiose saluta. Si tabellarius tam diu expectârit, denuo illi scribam. Saluta etiam cæteros Amicos meos Rostochienses. Magister CHRISTIERNUS ante 6 septimanas hinc a me discessit in Patriam rediturus atque Vos in transitu allocuturus, quare eum iam istic aut esse aut fuisse existimo. Tu vero, mi BRASCHI, nulla intermissa oportunitate, mihi rescribe, habebis me semper tui studiosissimum.

Iterumque vale.
Dabantur festinanti calamo Pragæ die 15 Septembris Anno 1600.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO MARTIN BRASCH.**

The letter you sent me on the 8th day of August, by your style [Old Style], most learned Brasch, I received yesterday — which was the 14th of September by the reformed Calendar — through **Lord Gödelmann, the Saxon Legate acting here**; to which I now, he too urging it on account of the messenger's haste, hastily write back this, so far as my other occupations allow. About your **Elegiac poem**, it is well that you do not reject even such notes of mine as they are. I had begun, one day in the afternoon hours (for before noon the more serious matters are to be handled), to change and arrange otherwise some things in it, to omit some, and here and there to supply others — and that before I was most clemently **summoned from the castle of my residence at Benátky hither to Prague by the Sacred Imperial Majesty**, our most clement Lord, as soon as He had returned from Pilsen; where I am still kept by Him, now into the third month, and, so far as I understand, **His Majesty desires that I dwell in a nearer and more convenient place**. But in all this time, while I am here, I have had so much to do, both for His Majesty and otherwise, that no leisure has remained to me to take it [the poem] up even once more, much less to revise it more fully — but it shall be done, when (as I hope) a fitter and quieter convenience is got. Meanwhile I should wish you to keep that poem quietly to yourself, and share it with no one; **for there are certain things in it less aptly stated, and not decorous or fitting enough for the Emperor (to say nothing of myself)**, of which, when I may again have leisure for them, I will frankly admonish you — or our revision will easily show it; nor do I doubt that, of your candour (as you even now promise), you will take it in good and equal part. That other **Epic poem on Várad**, which you mention, I have not yet seen; nor have I hitherto had any acquaintance with Lord **Melchior Röder**, of whom you make mention; nor do I even know whether he is here — so far as I hear by others' report, he is in Hungary; wherefore of him, and the things concerning him, I have nothing more to write.

**Melissus** has at last redeemed the expectation and hope we conceived of him, having sent me, a little before I left Benátky, three poems of different kinds — of which I will add a copy, if time allow the transcription. But, to say what the matter requires, **he seems in these endowed with a more sluggish vein than otherwise** — whether because his advancing age (for he is, I think, more than sixty) produces poetic spirits less lively and lower, or, as you too confess, because that ardour is kindled more or less by intervals of time, and sometimes turns slower. Above the rest, **that first epigram, which he composed about me**, appears less vivid and not quite elegant; whence I took this boldness, to alter some things in it — although even so it does not in all points please, nor do I know whether he would bear my emendations as gladly as you. Wherefore that epigram — when other poems composed here and there in my honour are perhaps one day struck off — **I judge had rather be omitted than, published, be less honourable to its author, or my meagre alteration, unwelcome to him, move his stomach**.

About **your Poems or Philosophical orations to be dedicated to the Emperor**, I know not what to advise; for although the Imperial Majesty is beneficent and liberal enough toward the learned, and does not regard to which form of religion they are addicted, yet **the Councillors are more difficult, and slow in executing, and favour less those who do not profess the Catholic (as they call it) religion**. But if you should wish to write something in His Majesty's honour, **let it rather be a certain grave and sinewy poem, about the things gloriously done by his Ancestors from Charles V on, and at last by himself** — where also, among his other Elogia, you may by occasion insert that **he most kindly promotes, in our age, the restoration of Astronomy, after the likeness of that old Alfonso, King of Castile and Sicily** [Alfonso X]. You ought also to subjoin some succinct and witty epigrams, for by such the Emperor is most affected, and **he delights in brevity**. But these I leave rather to your judgement, who know better what is here to be done or not.

That **David Chytraeus** passed away to the Fates last June, I had already heard before; as also, the May preceding, **our Hemmingsen in Denmark** — both old men of advanced age and well-deserving of the literary Commonwealth; **may their souls be in blessing and peace**, [their] memory endure to posterity, together with the monuments they left, and bear fruit. I have looked through what you composed on Chytraeus's death, and it pleased me much. I read also that little writing sent along, about the things worthy of mention that befell this year in the Arctic [northern] regions up to the month of May — in which are very many things done among the **Swedes**, sad and unpleasant to hear. May God moderate all to the good! The aforesaid **Chytraeus**, of best memory, had written me last year, and sent a certain memorandum about what he had resolved to insert in this year's "little history" [*historiola*], concerning **my emigration from Denmark hither into Bohemia**, leaving it to be shaped by my judgement (otherwise, if I pleased). And I, writing back to him, enclosed a paper by which I conveyed what he sought, according to my view. But since in the writing you sent nothing of the kind is found, I suspect either that my letter did not reach him in time, or that, hindered by illness and afterward forestalled by death, he could not carry it out. If, then, that letter of mine, together with the inserted sheet, is still found among his posthumous papers, **I should wish what I had annotated for him to be yet inserted in a fitting place of this year's history**; for I do not doubt that someone of yours will continue it to the year's end, so that **the Arctic History — begun by that excellent Chytraeus from the year 1500 — may be completed in this year 1600, and thus contain a whole century**. But what I should wish done, in my opinion, would be more rightly subjoined to what was recorded by Chytraeus, as though written by him while he yet lived — **lest, if anything there be found less pleasing to the neighbouring Danes (truth being for the most part odious), it could be imputed to none among your Professors still surviving.** It will please the Emperor (as I think) when he sees even far-remote Academies proclaim encomia for his promotion of Astronomy; for the Emperor asked the illustrious **Lord Coraduz, Imperial Vice-Chancellor** — as soon as, last year, he had returned hither from the Italian and Roman Legation — whether he had heard at Rome or elsewhere in Italy **that he [the Emperor] had called me hither to restore Astronomy**; and when [Coraduz] affirmed that he had perceived this, both at Rome and in other places, by the report of distinguished Men, it pleased the Emperor much, and he seemed, even on this account, as it were to congratulate himself — as these things were reported to me by Lord Coraduz himself; and from this you may estimate the rest. Yet I prescribe nothing to you, but leave all to be done or omitted by your judgement and considered opinion. The above-named **Lord Doctor Gödelmann** will also report more from me, when he comes to you, as he has resolved.

Farewell; and greet for me dutifully the renowned man **Lord Doctor Lucas Backmeister** (to whom too, in my last letter, I wrote some things about the said matter, if I remember rightly). If the courier waits so long, I will write him again. Greet also my other **Rostock** friends. **Master Christiernus [Longomontanus]** departed from me hence 6 weeks ago, to return to his fatherland and address you in passing; wherefore I think he is now either there, or has been. But you, my Brasch, with no opportunity let slip, write back to me; you shall have me always most zealous of you.

And again farewell.
Given with hurrying pen at Prague, the 15th day of September, the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient (name flagged).** **Martin Brasch / Martinus Braschius (1550–1601)**, the Rostock professor and Neo-Latin poet — addressed here as *Martinum Braschium*. **brahe-t_16000808001 gives the sender as "Nicolaus Braschius," which is most likely a catalogue error**: the two letters are one exchange (the same elegiac poem, *Carmen de Varadino*, Melissus, Chytraeus, Bacmeister, Rostock circle). Identification corrected toward **Martin**; flagged for correction at brahe-t_16000808001.
- **Significance — Tycho's literary diplomacy and the Chytraeus "Arctic History."** Reply to brahe-t_16000808001:
 - **The verse business.** Tycho is emending Brasch's **elegiac poem** but, summoned from **Benátky to Prague** and "kept into the third month" (the Emperor wanting him "in a nearer, more convenient place" — the coming move to the Curtius house), has no leisure; he warns Brasch to keep it private, as some lines are "not decorous enough for the Emperor." He hasn't seen the *Carmen de Varadino* or met **Melchior Röder** (said to be in Hungary). On **Melissus** (Paul Schede Melissus, now ">sixty," with "a more sluggish vein"), Tycho judges the **epigram Melissus wrote about him** weak, and would rather it be **omitted** than published or awkwardly emended.
 - **Advice on dedicating to Rudolf II.** A revealing political note: the Emperor is liberal "regardless of religion," **but the Councillors favour Catholics and are slow**. Tycho counsels a **grave poem on Habsburg deeds "from Charles V"**, casting Rudolf as **"a new Alfonso [X] of Castile"** for promoting astronomy, capped by **brief, witty epigrams** ("the Emperor delights in brevity").
 - **Two deaths.** **David Chytraeus (June 1600)** and **Niels Hemmingsen (May 1600)** — the great Lutheran scholars — mourned ("may their souls be in blessing and peace"). (Cf. brahe-t_16000808001, brahe-t_16000919002.)
 - **The "Arctic History" plan.** Chytraeus's annual **northern chronicle (*historiola*)**: Tycho had sent Chytraeus a sheet on **his own emigration from Denmark to Bohemia** for insertion, but it didn't make it in before Chytraeus's death; Tycho asks that, if the sheet survives among the papers, it be inserted — **attributed to the dead Chytraeus, to shield surviving professors from Danish displeasure** ("truth being for the most part odious") — so the chronicle, "begun from 1500," reaches "a whole century" in 1600. (Cf. the Sturtz-continuation plan, brahe-t_16000919002.)
 - **The Coraduz/Rome anecdote.** A vivid court vignette: **Rudolf II asked Coraduz, back from the Roman legation, whether Tycho's call "to restore astronomy" was known in Italy** — and was pleased to hear it praised at Rome.
 - **Longomontanus** left for Denmark "6 weeks ago"; greetings to **Lucas Backmeister** (the Elder) and the Rostock circle.
- **Cross-references.** Pair with **brahe-t_16000808001 (Brasch's letter, 8 August 1600)** and the Chytraeus-chronicle thread (brahe-t_16000919002).
- **Persons & places named.** Martin Brasch; **Gödelmann** (Saxon Legate); **Melchior Röder**; **Paul Schede Melissus**; **David Chytraeus**; **Niels Hemmingsen**; **Rudolf II**, **Charles V**, **Alfonso X of Castile**; **Coraduz**; **Lucas Backmeister**; **Longomontanus**. Places: **Prague**, **Benátky**, **Pilsen**, **Rostock**, **Rome/Italy**, **Hungary**, Denmark, Sweden.
- **Date.** Day-number missing in the source ("*die Septembris Anno 1600*"); **15 September 1600 [N.S.]** supplied from identifier/label and confirmed by "yesterday … the 14th of September by the reformed Calendar." Flagged.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** The day is **not** merely label-supplied: Dreyer (*Opera Omnia* VIII p. 360; running-head 5/15 Sept.) prints *15 die Septembris* — also confirmed by the internal “yesterday, the 14th of September.” Restored to header, Source, and translation.

documents.incipit: MAGNIFICE et excellentissime vir, amice inprimis honorande. Scripsj bis T:æ M:æ post …

text.original:
[TYCHO BRAHE AD JACOBUM BORDINGUM].

MAGNIFICE et excellentissime vir, amice inprimis honorande. Scripsj bis T:æ M:æ post initium huius annj de pecunia, quæ isthic mihj loco jnteresse debetur, primo per Claudium Mulæum meum domesticum in Daniam abeuntem vere præterito, postea per quendam magistrum Christiernum Longimontanum, natione Danum, quj etiam aliquamdiu mecum fuit et superiore julio se in patriam recepit. Et sperassem sane, me aliquid inter id temporis responsj recepturum, quod tamen factum non est. Quare cum hic tabellarius Rostochium iturus sit et confecto itinere huc Pragam rediturus, non potuj intermittere quin T:am M:am de hoc ipso negotio denuo commonefacerem. Quare te per amicitiam nostram iam tertium rogatum uolo, ut tuo consilio et authoritate interueniente procurare non degraueris, ut pecunia illa, quæ a juniorum principum quæstore mihi isthic soluenda restat, quamprimum fierj possit, huc mittatur siue in aurea siue etiam in argentea moneta, pro ut antea ratione mittendj insinuauj, et si id prius indicato modo per aurigam Wittebergensem efficj nequierit, offeret se certa et tuta occasio per mag: dn: J. Godelmannum, quj hic legatum illustrissimj administratoris electoratus Saxonicj agit, post quatuordecim dies (utj herj mihj retulit) hinc Rostochium proficiscj cogitantem, quj etiam breuj huc reuertj necesse habet, cumque ipse sit amicus meus singularis, eiusque perspecta fides, ab illo obtinuj, ut hoc officium in adferenda secum illa quæ istic mihi numeranda est pecunia in se recipiat, quare illj optime committj poterit. Et si jnteresse pro toto hoc anno usque ad subsequentis primum diem aprilis aut ad minimum huius dimidij elapsi annj una addatur, esset id mihi gratum, nam et æquum uidetur ut si quidem iam per dimidium annum pecunia illa frustrer, alterius dimidij annj solutionis præueniente termino iste defectus compensetur, præsertim ex quo tam oportuna et indubia ratio id quicquid est pecuniarum huc transuehendj per dictum d: d: Godelmannum sese obtulerit. Quare non dubito, præstantissime d:ne Bordinge, quin mihi hac in parte et interueniente principis tuj (si opus fuerit) autoritate sis operam tuam non denegaturus; ubj ille accesserit, secum meum habebit chyrographum ulterius adhuc quam antea factum de solutione testans. Rogo autem peramanter, ut cum hoc tabellario ad nos reuertente pauculis indicare uelis, quid mihi isthic expectandum sit. Ego T:æ M:æ uicissim gratificandum perpetuo inueniar quam paratissimus.

Vale.
Dabantur Pragæ Bohemorum die 16. septembris stylo correcto anno 1600.
text.english:
**[Tycho Brahe to Jacob Bording.]**

Magnificent and most excellent man, friend especially to be honoured. I have written twice to Your Magnificence since the beginning of this year about the money owed me there in place of interest — first by Claude Mule, my servant, going into Denmark last spring; afterward by a certain Master Christen Longomontanus, a Dane by nation, who was also for some time with me and last July betook himself to his homeland. And I had indeed hoped that I would receive some reply in that interval, which, however, has not happened. Wherefore, since this courier is about to go to Rostock and, his journey done, to return hither to Prague, I could not refrain from reminding Your Magnificence once more of this very business. So I would have you asked, now for the third time, by our friendship, that — with your counsel and authority intervening — you would not find it a burden to procure that that money, which remains to be paid me there by the treasurer of the younger princes, be sent hither as soon as may be, whether in gold or also in silver coin, as I earlier intimated regarding the means of sending. And if it cannot be done beforehand in the manner indicated, by the Wittenberg carter, there will offer itself a sure and safe occasion through Master Lord J. Godelmann — who acts here as legate of the most illustrious Administrator of the Saxon Electorate, and who is minded (as he told me yesterday) to set out hence to Rostock after fourteen days, and who must also return hither shortly; and since he is himself my singular friend, and his fidelity proven, I have obtained from him that he take this office upon himself, in bringing with him that money which is to be paid me there — wherefore it may best be committed to him. And if interest for this whole year, up to the first day of next April, or at the least for this half-year now elapsed, be added in together [with the principal], it would be welcome to me; for it seems but fair that, since I am now cheated of that money for half a year, this shortfall be made good by anticipating the term of the other half-year's payment — especially now that so opportune and undoubted a means of conveying hither whatever money there is has offered itself through the said Lord Doctor Godelmann. Wherefore I do not doubt, most excellent Lord Bording, that you will not deny me your effort in this part — with your prince's authority intervening too, if there be need. When he [the messenger] arrives, he will have with him my bond, attesting the payment, drawn yet further than before. And I ask most lovingly that, by this courier returning to us, you would indicate in a few words what I am to expect there. I, in turn, shall be found most ready to oblige Your Magnificence perpetually.

Farewell.
Given at Prague of the Bohemians, the 16th of September, by the corrected style, in the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender & matter.** **Tycho Brahe** at **Prague** — a third dunning letter over **interest owed him by the Mecklenburg house** (here "the treasurer of the **younger princes**," i.e. the under-age Dukes of Mecklenburg), the same capital whose recovery dominates the 1601 Meier/Duke-Ulrich correspondence. This 1600 letter shows Tycho still trying to get the *interest* remitted, a year before the principal dispute boiled over.
- **Recipient.** **Jacob Bording (Jakob Bording the Younger)**, a councillor/physician in Mecklenburg service, used by Tycho as an intermediary of standing (he can invoke "your prince's authority") to chase the payment.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Claudius Mulaeus* = **Claude Mule (Mulaeus)**, Tycho's servant, an earlier letter-carrier to Denmark.
 - *magister Christiernus Longimontanus* = **Christen Sørensen Longomontanus**, Tycho's chief assistant, who carried the second letter and returned to Denmark in July 1600.
 - *mag. dn. J. Godelmannus* = **Johann Georg Gödelmann (Godelmann)** (1559–1611), jurist and diplomat, here **legate of the Administrator of the Saxon Electorate** at the imperial court, and "my singular friend" — engaged by Tycho as a trusted bearer of the cash on his coming journey to Rostock. (Gödelmann recurs across the late correspondence as a recurring-person to be rendered consistently, this chapter's convention)
 - *illustrissimus Administrator Electoratus Saxonici* = the **Administrator (regent) of Electoral Saxony**, **Friedrich Wilhelm I of Saxe-Weimar**, regent for the minor Elector Christian II.
- **The financial ask.** Payment in **gold or silver coin**; the **Wittenberg carter** as fallback route, Gödelmann as the preferred one; interest to be reckoned **to 1 April next**, or at least for the half-year elapsed, the shortfall offset by anticipating the next term; Tycho's fresh **bond (*chirographum*)** to be handed over on receipt.
- **Place.** *Praga Bohemorum* = Prague; *Rostochium* = Rostock; *Wittenberga* = Wittenberg.
- **Witness note.** A **letter draft** in the Basel autograph collection; hence the bracketed editorial heading.
- **Epistolary formulae & abbreviations.** *T. M.* = *Tua Magnificentia* ("Your Magnificence"); *d. d.* = *Dominus Doctor*; *Vale* → "Farewell"; *Dabantur* (epistolary) → "Given."
- **Calendar (this chapter's convention — idiom).** Dateline *die 16. Septembris **stylo correcto*** = "by the **corrected style**," another of Tycho's labels for **New Style (Gregorian)** (alongside *stylo novo*, *stylo recognito*; cf. brahe-t_16000420001). Reproduced literally and glossed, not converted.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD LUCAM BACMEISTERUM.

S.

CLARISSIME et Præstantissime Vir, Amice inprimis honorande, etsi per M. CHRISTIERNUM nostrum hinc discedentem et in Daniam cogitantem, siquidem Rostochium transire et ibi forte aliquantisper subsistere constituerat, literas ad te dederim, partim de rebus meis, partim de ijs, quæ historiolæ annuæ optimæ memoriæ Domini Doctoris DAVIDIS CHYTRÆI, prout ipsemet, etiam dum in vivis erat, proposuerat, inseri averem, commonefacientes; tamen oblata per hunc tabellarium ad Vos euntem et mox huc revertentem tam commoda oportunitate, non intermittendum duxi, quin denuo aliqua tibi scriberem, nec tamen priora multis repetam, id saltem ijs superaddam, me etiamnum desiderare, ut ea, de quibus prius rogâram, historiolæ annuæ præfati Domini D. CHYTRÆI usque ad huius Anni exitum ab aliquo Vestrorum, uti opinor, professore continuandæ, competenti loco inserantur. Video enim in ijs chartis, quas mihi misit Poëta vester Dn. BRASCHIUS, quæ in solstitio æstivo ob Autoris mox subsequentem obitum, narrationem interrumpunt, id omissum esse. Quare pluribus hac de re ad dictum Dn. BRASCHIUM scripsi, qui tibi meas facile ostendet literas, unde plura et particulariora hauries; neque tamen hîc quippiam urgeo, sed omnia cum vestro stabunt cadentque libero iudicio.

Quantum vero ad res meas attinet, sunt eæ adhuc in eodem statu, quo erant, cum ultimas ad te mitterem. Maneo etiamnum hîc Pragæ cum tota familia ex Cæsaris voluntate hîc retentus, donec de loco habitationis commodiore et propinquiore, ubi exercitijs meis Astronomicis vacare possim, mihi clementissime prospexerit, qua de re etiamnum agitur, nam lente in hac Aula ob negotiorum molem omnia procedunt. Supellex mea unâ cum Instrumentis Astronomicis, quæ Magdeburgi aliquamdiu relicta erant, in ea Albis parte, quæ Dresdam et hunc locum intercedit, iam, uti ante biduum inaudivi, navigio appropinquant, ita ut sperem ea instante septimana hîc in Bohemia adfutura. Quare de loco, ubi disponenda sint (siquidem arx Benatica nimis hinc remota sit, nec admodum oportuna) iam eo maturius deliberamus, et negotium hoc acceleretur.

Non dubito, quin literas adfini tuo Magnifico Dn. BORDINGO inscriptas, quas prædictus M. CHRISTIERNUS secum attulit, expedivisse, et contenta earundem, quantum in te erat, promovisse. Si nihil adhuc in re illa pecuniaria, de qua aiebam, effectum est, nec aliqua isthic suppetit commoditas id tuto exequendi, poterit usque in adventum Dn. D. IOHANNIS GÖDELMANNI (qui se quatuordecim abhinc diebus Rostochium profecturum heri mihi indicavit) deferri, ut per ipsum quam optime fiat. Qua de re etiam ad prænominatum adfinem tuum latius perscripsi, quas literas, si tabellarius hic Gustrowium transiens id non præstiterit, actutum dirigas quæso, atque ut idem tabellarius ratum secum adferat responsum, operam da, quin et tu ipsemet cum eodem mihi rescribas, simulque indices, quid rerum in vicina Dania et Suecia geratur. Narratum est hîc ante paucos dies, incerto tamen rumore, dissidium quoddam subortum inter Regem Daniæ Regnique Nobilitatem, quod tamen irrita fama prolatum spero. Deus avertat a Patria mea intestina mala, quæ plurimum secum damni trahere solent. Turca in Ungaria est cum maximo exercitu, cui nostri Imperatoris vix pro quarta parte par est: pugnet pro nobis armipotens Deus, cui etiam te tuosque omnes commendo et bene valere precor.

Dabantur properanter Pragæ Bohemorum 16 die Septembris stylo novo Anno 1600.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO LUCAS BACKMEISTER.**

Greeting.

Most renowned and most excellent Man, friend especially to be honoured: although, through our Master Christen [Longomontanus] — departing hence and intending [to go] into Denmark, since he had resolved to pass through Rostock and perhaps stay there a while — I gave you a letter, partly about my affairs, partly reminding [you] of those things I desired inserted into the **annual little history of Lord Doctor David Chytraeus**, of best memory (as he himself, while still alive, had proposed): nevertheless, so convenient an opportunity being offered by this courier going to you and soon returning hither, I thought I should not omit to write you something again. Yet I will not repeat the earlier things at length; this only I add to them: that I still desire that the matters about which I asked before be inserted in a fitting place in the aforesaid Lord Chytraeus's annual little history — to be continued, as I think, by some professor of yours, up to the end of this year. For I see, in those sheets your Poet Lord **Brasch** sent me — which break off the narration at the **summer solstice**, on account of the Author's soon-following death — that this is omitted. Wherefore I have written more on this matter to the said Lord Brasch, who will easily show you my letter, whence you will draw more and more particular things; yet I press nothing here, but everything will stand and fall by your free judgement.

As far as concerns my affairs, they are still in the same state as when I sent you my last. I still remain here at Prague, with my whole household, retained here by the Emperor's will, until he most clemently provides me a more convenient and nearer dwelling-place, where I may be free for my astronomical exercises — about which the matter is still in hand, for in this Court all things proceed slowly, on account of the mass of business. My furniture, together with the astronomical instruments which had been left a while at **Magdeburg**, are now (as I heard two days ago) approaching by ship in that part of the **Elbe** which lies between **Dresden** and this place, so that I hope they will be here in Bohemia in the coming week. Wherefore, concerning the place where they are to be set up (since the castle of **Benátky** is too remote from here, and not very convenient) we now deliberate the more maturely, and this business is being hastened.

I do not doubt that you have dispatched the letter addressed to your kinsman the Magnificent Lord **Bording**, which the aforesaid Master Christen brought with him, and have furthered its contents as far as was in you. If nothing has yet been effected in that money-matter of which I spoke, nor is any convenient means at hand there of carrying it out safely, it can be deferred until the arrival of Lord Doctor **Johann Gödelmann** (who indicated to me yesterday that he would set out for Rostock fourteen days hence), that it may best be done through him. About which I have also written more fully to your aforenamed kinsman; which letter, if this courier passing through **Güstrow** does not deliver, please direct at once, and take pains that the same courier bring back a definite reply — nay, that you yourself write back to me with the same, and at the same time indicate what is going on in neighbouring **Denmark and Sweden**. It was reported here a few days ago — by uncertain rumour, however — that some **dissension had arisen between the King of Denmark and the Nobility of the Realm**, which I hope was put about by an empty report. May God avert from my fatherland internal evils, which are wont to bring much damage with them. The **Turk** is in Hungary with a very great army, to which our Emperor's is scarcely equal for a fourth part: may God, mighty in arms, fight for us — to whom I also commend you and all yours, and pray that you fare well.

Given in haste at Prague of the Bohemians, the 16th day of September, New Style, the year 1600.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Lucas Backmeister** (Bacmeister, 1530–1608), **Superintendent of Rostock** and theologian — the kinsman of Jacob Bording who handled the Mecklenburg interest-money (cf. brahe-t_16001115001, brahe-t_16000919001), here also Tycho's contact on the Chytraeus history.
- **The Chytraeus annual-history thread (cross-link to Brasch).** Tycho repeats his wish that his **migration narrative** be inserted into **David Chytraeus's annual history** (the *Saxonia* / *Chronicon*), now "to be continued by some professor of yours up to the end of this year." He notes that the **sheets Brasch sent break off at the summer solstice** — Chytraeus having died then — so the desired matter is omitted; he refers Backmeister to his fuller letter to **Brasch** (the reply to which is brahe-t_16000920002, where Brasch reports the search failed and the Chronicle cannot easily be extended). "Yet I press nothing … everything will stand and fall by your free judgement."
- **Tycho's affairs (autumn 1600).** Still **retained at Prague** with his household by the Emperor's will, awaiting "a more convenient and nearer dwelling." His **furniture and the Magdeburg-stored instruments** are now coming **up the Elbe between Dresden and Bohemia** (expected "in the coming week") — the success of the Magdeburg leg (cf. brahe-t_16000404001) — and he is deliberating where to set them up, "since **Benátky is too remote** and not very convenient" (anticipating the move into the Prague Curtius house).
- **The debt-matter & news.** The **600-thaler interest** business via **Bording**: if not yet done, to await **Gödelmann's** departure for Rostock (in 14 days). Tycho asks for news of **Denmark and Sweden**, mentioning an "uncertain rumour" of **dissension between Christian IV and the Danish nobility** (which he hopes false), and reports the **Turk in Hungary** "with a very great army, to which our Emperor's is scarcely equal for a fourth part."
- **Persons named.** Lucas Backmeister; *M. Christiernus* = **Christen Longomontanus** (departed to Denmark via Rostock; cf. brahe-t_16000920002); **David Chytraeus** (the late historian); **Martin Brasch**; **Jacob Bording**; **Johann Georg Gödelmann**; **Rudolf II**; **Christian IV** and the Danish nobility.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Pragae Bohemorum 16 die Septembris stylo novo Anno 1600*; **New Style** (imperial). Header agrees with the label.

text.original:
TYCHO BRAHE AD MELCHIOREM IŒSTELIUM.

S.

DEDI iterum ad te literas, Eruditissime et amantissime Domine M. MELCHIOR IÖSTELI, ante paucos dies, de ijsdem ferme rebus, quas superioribus attigeram; ultimas autem hasce Domino Doctori FRANCIO, Iure consulto, nunc Comitis Embdensis Cancellario, hinc proficiscenti commisi, qui eas se recte curaturum addixit: interim commodum accidit, quod tuae antepenultimo Augusti Wittebergâ ad me datae intervenirent, quae eorum, de quibus antea memineram, resolutionem, quoad principaliora, continent; ad quam sic respondeo.

Polliceris ab initio te collationem Hypothesium brevi missurum, siquidem iam perfectiorem quam antea elaboratam habeas. Fac igitur, ut mature obtineam, et figuras decenter assigna; addenda est autem explicatio sufficiens, non quidem admodum prolixa, sed etiam non nimium concisa; descendendum etenim nonnunquam ad captum Tyronum. Spero itaque me intra duas vel tres hebdomadas id, quicquid erit, a te habiturum.

Quae de M. OeSTWALDO scribis, non improbo. Maneat isthic, siquidem id malit, et supputet nihilominus pro me, quae per ocij intervalla absolvere poterit, numerabo illi in singulos Anni quadrantes sex Ioachimicos, quod in singulas hebdomadas dimidium ferme Ioachimicum facit. Sed volo, ut etiam singulis Anni quadrantibus mittat, quae absoluta habuerit. Haec ad ipsum ferre poteris. Quamprimum Tabulae Lunares unâ cum ijs, quae huc requiruntur, ad mundum descriptae fuerint, mittam exemplar, ut inde Ephemerides supputet incipientes ab hoc labente 1600, et per sexennium instans continuandae, unâ cum Solari Diario atque aspectibus omniumque differentijs, prout antea fecit, solvam autem illi pro cuiuslibet Anni Ephemeride tres Ioachimicos, prout in ultimis ad te literis scripsi, sed vellem, ut calculum maturaret, quo omnia unâ cum adiungendis satis cito inprimi adque instantes Francofurti Nundinas Vernales mitti possint, in 4to maiori excusa.

Cum Typographo vestro M. ZACHARIA LEHMANO age, ut sex illos quaterniones, vel tres duplicatos, qui desiderantur in Progymnasmatis meis, inprimat, atque papyrum similem illi, quae in libro est, aeque nimirum albam et tenuem eiusdemque magnitudinis, sibi procuret, ita ut 1400 exemplaria de quolibet quaternione inprimat. Existimo, quod Ballam eiuscemodi papyri pro 10 florenis nanciscetur; nam et ego antea eam, quae in libro meo de Cometa Anni 77 est, Francofurti emi pro 8 florenis, Basileae paratam et longo itinere isthuc vectam, sed iam forte alia sunt tempora, omniaque nunc cariora. Quicquid id erit, solvam illi iusto et debito modo, ut indemnis sit: prospiciat saltem de papyro, uti dixi, quae conveniens sit, interea dum exemplum paratur. Mittam postea, quae praefationis loco praefigenda, tum quoque quae in conclusione subiungenda, ut et illa absolvat. Si pecunia mea tam cito e Mechelburgensi Ducatu advenerit, potes inde 25 Ioachimicos tecum retinere pro solutione tam papyri quam laboris Typographici, successive exponenda: verum si id non evenerit, mittam ipsemet cum Domino Doctore GÖDELMANO, qui hîc Legatum agit Saxonicum, pecuniam sufficientem; ille enim post 14 dies constituit hinc Rostochium proficisci, atque in itinere Wittebergam transire; forte etiam exemplum secum adferet, si alia negotia descriptionem non remorata fuerint.

Cognovi insuper ex hisce tuis, quâ de caussâ huc venire nequeas, et libenter tuo acquiesco consilio, neque amplius hac de re quidpiam movebo. Confido tamen, quod etiam isthic habitans operam tuam nonnunquam per otij oportunitatem, in ijs, quae a te fieri desiderâro, non denegaturus sis, inveniar vicissim gratus. Et siquidem medicinae applicâsti animum, et in ea facultate promovere constituisti, det Deus, ut omnia tibi feliciter et ex voto succedant. Memineris autem, medicinam rite praeparatam medicum efficere et pro ipso operari; non verba, sive HIPPOCRATIS, sive GALENI, sive cuiusvis alterius diserti authoris. An vero hoc, quod dixi, isthic assequeris, admodum dubito, optare id potius licet quam sperare. Sed efficies facile quod coeteri, ut mundus habeat, quod vult. Haec si IESSENIO nostro dixeris, partim risum, partim bilem illi movebit scio. Miror, quod ille mihi nihil scribat, nec indicet, quid de libro et Globo illi tradito factum sit.

De Genesi illa, quam nôsti, poteris suo tempore, cum rectius vacârit, dispicere et ad me quidpiam perscribere. Vale et primâ quaque occasione responde; saluta amicos meos Wittebergenses, quos nôsti.

Dabantur festinanter Praga Die 18 Septembris Anno 1600 stylo novo.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 364; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Rogo insuper velis providere de studioso uno vel altero ad haec studia apto, prout in ultimis scripsi.
text.english:
**TYCHO BRAHE TO MELCHIOR JÖSTEL.**

Greeting.

I gave a letter to you again, most learned and most loving Lord Master Melchior Jöstel, a few days ago, about almost the same matters I had touched in earlier ones; this last one I entrusted to **Lord Doctor Franz, the jurisconsult, now Chancellor of the Count of Emden**, setting out hence, who pledged to take good care of it. Meanwhile it conveniently happened that yours, sent me from Wittenberg on the antepenultimate [day] of August, came in — which contain the resolution, as to the principal points, of the things I mentioned before; to which I respond thus.

You promise, at the outset, that you will soon send the **collation of the Hypotheses**, since you now have it elaborated more perfectly than before. Do then [so] that I obtain it in good time, and assign the **figures [diagrams]** becomingly; a sufficient explanation must be added — not very prolix, but also not too concise, **for one must sometimes descend to the grasp of beginners**. I hope, therefore, to have it from you, whatever it is, within two or three weeks.

What you write about **Master Oswald** I do not disapprove. Let him stay there, since he prefers it, and nonetheless compute for me what he can finish through intervals of leisure; I will pay him **six joachimsthalers each quarter-year**, which makes nearly half a joachimsthaler a week. But I wish him also to send, each quarter, what he has finished — you can convey this to him. As soon as the **Lunar Tables**, with what is required here, have been fair-copied, I will send a copy, that he may from it compute **Ephemerides beginning from this passing [year] 1600, to be continued for the coming six years**, together with the **Solar Diary**, the aspects, and all the differences, as he did before; and I will pay him **three joachimsthalers for each year's Ephemeris**, as I wrote in my last — but I should wish him to hasten the calculation, that everything, with the additions, may be printed quickly enough and sent to the coming **Frankfurt spring fair**, printed in larger quarto.

Deal with your printer Master **Zacharias Lehmann**, that he print those **six quaternions (or three doubled) wanting in my *Progymnasmata***, and procure paper like that in the book — equally white and thin, and of the same size — so that he print **1,400 copies of each quaternion**. I estimate he will get a **bale of such paper for 10 florins** (for I earlier bought that in my book on the **Comet of [15]77** at Frankfurt for 8 florins — prepared at Basel and carried thither by a long journey — but now perhaps the times are different, and everything dearer). Whatever it be, I will pay him in a just and due manner, that he be without loss: let him only provide suitable paper, as I said, while the copy is being prepared. I will afterward send what is to be prefixed in place of a preface, and what to append in the conclusion, that he may finish those too. **If my money come so quickly from the Duchy of Mecklenburg**, you can retain **25 joachimsthalers** from it for payment of both paper and printing, to be laid out successively; but if not, I will myself send sufficient money with **Lord Doctor Gödelmann, who here acts as the Saxon Legate** — for he has resolved to set out hence for Rostock after 14 days, passing through Wittenberg on the way, and perhaps he will bring the copy with him, if other business has not delayed the fair-copying.

I have moreover learned from this letter of yours **for what cause you cannot come hither**, and I gladly acquiesce in your decision, nor will I press the matter further. Yet I trust that, even dwelling there, you will not deny your effort sometimes, through the opportunity of leisure, in what I shall wish done by you; I will in turn be found grateful. And since **you have applied your mind to medicine**, and resolved to advance in that faculty, may God grant all succeed for you happily and according to your wish. But remember that **rightly-prepared medicine makes the physician, and works for him — not words, whether of Hippocrates, or Galen, or any other eloquent author**. Whether you will attain this, there [at Wittenberg], I much doubt — one may rather wish it than hope for it; but you will easily do what the rest [do], so that the world may have what it wants. If you say these things to our **Jessenius**, I know it will move him partly to laughter, partly to bile. I wonder that he writes me nothing, nor indicates **what has been done about the book and Globe handed to him**. About that **Geniture** you know of, you can, in your time, when you have better leisure, look into it and write me something. Farewell, and reply at the first opportunity; greet my Wittenberg friends whom you know.

Given hastily at Prague, the 18th day of September, the year 1600, New Style.


*[Postscript:]* I ask, moreover, that you be willing to provide one or another student apt for these studies, as I wrote in my last.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Melchior Jöstel**, Tycho's Wittenberg computational collaborator (cf. brahe-t_16000327001, brahe-t_16001008001, brahe-t_16001118001).
- **Resolves the "Wolfgang Franz" identity (cross-ref to brahe-t_16000327002, brahe-t_16001008001).** Tycho entrusts a letter to *"**Doctor Franz, the jurisconsult, now Chancellor of the Count of Emden**"* (East Frisia). This **confirms that "Doctor Franz" is a jurist** (not the Wittenberg theologian Wolfgang Franz, 1564–1628): the recurring **Franz** courier of Tycho's Wittenberg-orbit correspondence is a **lawyer who became chancellor to Count Enno III of East Frisia at Emden**. The earlier identification of the recipient of brahe-t_16000327002 as "the theologian" should accordingly be **corrected to the jurist**.
- **The planetary-hypotheses collation (technical;).** Jöstel will soon send the **collation of the Hypotheses** (the Tychonic/Copernican/Ptolemaic comparison for the second *Epistolae* book; cf. brahe-t_16001118001), with **diagrams** and a clear explanation pitched "to the grasp of beginners."
- **Master Oswald — the ephemeris-computer (terms settled).** **Oswald** (cf. brahe-t_16000327001, where Tycho had offered to bring him to Prague) will **stay at Wittenberg** and compute on retainer: **6 joachimsthalers per quarter** (≈ ½ thaler/week) for general work, plus **3 joachimsthalers per year's Ephemeris**. Once Tycho's **Lunar Tables** are fair-copied, Oswald is to compute **Ephemerides for 1600 + six years** (with **Solar Diary**, aspects, differences) for the **Frankfurt spring fair**, in larger quarto.
- **The printing of the *Progymnasmata* (cross-ref to brahe-t_16001118001).** Tycho instructs that the **printer Zacharias Lehmann** print the **six wanting quaternions** of the *Progymnasmata* in **1,400 copies**, on paper "white and thin" like the book's (≈ 10 fl./bale — he recalls buying paper for the **comet-of-1577 book** at 8 fl., "prepared at Basel"); prefatory and concluding matter to follow. **Funding:** 25 joachimsthalers from the **Mecklenburg money** if it arrives, else via **Gödelmann** (here "the Saxon Legate," about to travel Prague→Wittenberg→Rostock). A precise record of Tycho's late book-production economics.
- **The witty medicine aside (notable for Tycho's chymical bent).** Since Jöstel turns to **medicine**, Tycho — the Paracelsian alchemist — needles him: *"rightly-prepared medicine makes the physician … not the words of Hippocrates or Galen"* — doubting Jöstel will learn *that* at Wittenberg ("you will easily do what the rest do, so the world may have what it wants"), and predicting it would move **Jessenius** "partly to laughter, partly to bile." A characteristic dig at bookish, non-chymical academic medicine.
- **The book and globe.** Tycho wonders that **Jessenius** has not reported "what has been done about the **book and Globe** handed to him" — i.e. the **fixed-star book + celestial globe sent to Elector Christian II of Saxony** via Jessenius (brahe-t_16000506001). Also asks Jöstel to look into "that **Geniture**" (a horoscope;).
- **Persons named.** Melchior Jöstel; **Doctor Franz** (jurist, Chancellor of the Count of Emden); **Master Oswald**; **Zacharias Lehmann** (the printer); **Johann Georg Gödelmann** ("the Saxon Legate"); **Johannes Jessenius**; **Hippocrates** and **Galen** (the medical authorities).
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Praga Die 18 Septembris Anno 1600 stylo novo*; **New Style** (imperial). Header agrees with the label.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (after the dateline), restored from Dreyer VIII p.364; dropped by the working transcription.
- **Correction.** Restored 'forte' (Dreyer, TBOO VIII p.364) for the one-letter corruption 'sorte' in our transcription; the English ('perhaps') already matched Dreyer's actual reading and required no change.

text.original:
GENEROSO ET NOBILI VIRO D:NO TYCHONI BRAHE, DOMINO HEREDITARIO IN KNUDTSTRUP, AMICO SUO INPRIMIS HONORANDO.
Generose et nobilis vir, amice inprimis honorande.

QUOD ad Generos:tis T: litteras, quas jam ternas accepi, aliquanto serius respondeam, non mea culpa factum est. Nam Claudius Mulæus, cui priores traditas Generos:tas T. scribit, ipsemet mihi non adfuit, nec responsum ullum a me petijt. Alteras m. Christianus Longomannus me absente hic in aula reliquit, id quod Generos:tas T: ex adiecta hisce schedula, manu eius scripta, cognoscet. Quare ut me excusatum habeat, maiorem in modum rogo. Jnterim tamen quam posteriores ad manus meas pervenerunt, sexcentos illos thaleros, qui juniorum principum Megapolensium nomine Generos:ti T: debentur, Rostochium ad d. Lucam Backmeisterum, affinem meum, uti Generos:tas T: voluit, perferendos curavi. Egi quidem diligenter cum quæstore, ut in moneta aurea, quod Generos:tas T: cupit, solutio fieret, sed monetam eam in tanta summa conficere non potuit. Quare ut eo quoque nomine Generos:ti T: excusatus sim, itidem rogo. Chyrographum fidei meæ creditum Generos:ti T: remitto, nam alterum, quod m. Christianus Longomannus d. Backmeistero tradidit, quæstor retinuit. Quod reliquum est Generos:tem T: divini numinis protectioni commendo et officia mea eidem defero promptissima.

Datæ Gustrovij 19. die mensis septemb. stylo veteri anno 1600. Gener: T: studiosiss:
Jacobus Bordingus
text.english:
**To the generous and noble man, Master Tycho Brahe, hereditary lord in Knudstrup, his friend especially to be honoured. Generous and noble man, friend especially to be honoured.**

That I answer Your Generosity's letters — of which I have now received three — somewhat late, has not happened by my fault. For Claude Muler, to whom Your Generosity writes the first were delivered, did not himself present himself to me, nor did he seek any answer from me. The second, Master Christian Longomannus left here at the court in my absence — as Your Generosity will learn from the note attached hereto, written in his hand. Wherefore I ask, in the greater degree, that you hold me excused. Meanwhile, however, as soon as the latter [letters] came to my hands, those six hundred thaler which are owed to Your Generosity in the name of the junior Princes of Mecklenburg, I had conveyed to Rostock, to Master Lucas Backmeister, my kinsman, to be delivered — as Your Generosity wished. I dealt diligently, indeed, with the treasurer, that the payment be made in gold coin, as Your Generosity desires; but he could not make up that coin in so great a sum. Wherefore, that I may be excused to Your Generosity on that score also, I likewise ask. The bond entrusted to my good faith I return to Your Generosity; for the other, which Master Christian Longomannus delivered to Master Backmeister, the treasurer retained. As for what remains, I commend Your Generosity to the protection of the divine Power, and offer the same my most ready services.

Given at Güstrow, the 19th day of the month of September, old style, in the year 1600.
Most devoted to Your Generosity,
Jacob Bording.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Jacob Bording** (Bordingus), an official at the **ducal court of Mecklenburg at Güstrow**; *affinis* (kinsman by marriage) of **Lucas Backmeister** of Rostock.
- **The Mecklenburg debt.** This documents the **600 thaler** owed Tycho "in the name of the junior Princes of Mecklenburg" (*juniorum principum Megapolensium* — *Megapolis* = Mecklenburg) — the principal of which the **200 reichsthaler of interest** in Tycho's quittance (brahe-t_15990110001, to the Mecklenburg rent-master Andreas Meyer) were a part. Bording has had the sum conveyed to **Lucas Backmeister** at Rostock, per Tycho's instruction; he apologises that the *treasurer (quaestor)* could not assemble so large a sum **in gold coin** (*moneta aurea*) as Tycho wished, and returns one of the two **bonds** (*chirographa*).
- **Couriers.** *Claudius Mulaeus* = **Claude Muler** (the household member of brahe-t_15980627001), to whom the first letters were entrusted but who never delivered them; *Christianus Longomannus* = **Longomontanus**, who left the second batch at Güstrow and gave the matching bond to Backmeister.
- ***quaestor*** rendered "treasurer" (the ducal fiscal officer); *chirographum* = a handwritten bond/IOU.
- **Calendar.** *Gustrovij 19. die … septemb. stylo veteri … 1600* = **19 September 1600, Old Style** (*stylo veteri* explicit; Lutheran Mecklenburg kept the Julian calendar). Header agrees with the label.
