text.original:
CLARISSIMO ET EXCELLENTISSIMO VIRO DOMINO IOHANNI ANTONIO MAGINO PATAVINO, RERUM MATHEMATICARUM IN ILLUSTRI BONONIENSEM GYMNASIO PROFESSORI ET AMICO SUO HONORANDO. BONONIAM.

S.

LITERAS tuas humanissimas pariter atque eruditissimas, Clarissime et Excellentissime Domine MAGINE, 4 Martij superioris Anni datas, recte quidem accepi; nulla tamen ad eas rescribendi hucusque sese mihi obtulit certa commoditas, priusquam nunc per filium meum natu maiorem, TYCHONEM nomine, Illustrissimum et Amplissimum Magni Persarum Regis Legatum comitantem. Cumque a primario Legato, natione Anglo, ipsum Bononiam, in itinere suo Romam versus, transiturum, perceperim, non omittendum duxi, quin meis te salutarem, atque ad ultimas tuas nonnulla rescriberem.

Quod negotium illud, tuæ fidei secreto commissum, tam diligenter procurare non degraveris, summas tibi habeo debeoque gratias. Et placet sane ista ratio, quam proponis, de Excellentissimo illo BERNARDINO BALDO Urbinate, Guastallæ Abbate, qui vitas Mathematicorum conscribere proposuit. Ibi enim id, quod molimur, quam commodissime inseri poterit. Cuperem tamen (quod et antea rogavi) primas conceptiones mecum communicari, ut meum etiam aliquale iudicium interponam, ex quo res meæ nemini rectius quam mihi ipsi constare possint. Carmina in mei gratiam concinnata, et ulterius, quam priora erant, aucta, filius monstrabit. Si quid in prioribus mutatum est, potest hinc restitui, et ea quæ ibi desiderantur compleri. Cætera tuæ prudentiæ et benevolæ erga me voluntati committo.

Quod Illustrissimus et Reverendissimus Cardinalis SS. QUATUOR, Vir procul dubio eximiæ et variæ doctrinæ, rerumque Mathematicarum amantissimus, Eclipsin ☉lis Anni 98, qua licuerat diligentia, observârit, perlubenter accepi, grataque est eorum, quæ ipsius Dominatio Illustrissima denotavit, mecum communicata descriptio, licet ob serenitatis raritatem, tam præcise omnia (uti voluerit) designare nequierit. Gaudeo, atque hisce studijs plurimum congratulor, quod Romæ inter Illustrissimos etiam Cardinales reperiantur, qui Divinam Astronomiam (uti vel ex hoc solo liquet) in precio habeant. Hæc Eclipsis Uraniburgi in Dania meis adhuc isthic residuis Instrumentis observata est in mea absentia. Habitabam enim tunc prope Hamburgum, ubi serenitas requisita eius apparentias satis accurate rimandi non affulsit. Quæ vero in dicto Uraniburgo animadversa sunt, in adiuncta charta habes, unâque mei calculi Epilogismum, prout is ex novissima restitutione nostra in motu Luminarium diductus est. Quin et huius Anni Eclipsin ☉larem, quæ 10 die Iulij contigit, simul assignavi, tam quoad observationem quam calculum meum reformatum, ut cum vestris in Italia considerationibus, sive a prænominato Illustrissimo Cardinale, sive te ipso, aut quovis alio habitis, conferri queat. Erues ex hisce quos nunc mitto numeris aliam rationem, eandemque exactiorem, quam prior erat, in curriculo Lunari eiusque Phænomenis præfiniendis.

Non ignoravi, Tabulas illas Lunaris motus, quas a Nobili iuvene FRANCISCO TENGNAGLIO, meo domestico, accepisti, immaturas esse; ideoque eas tunc temporis tibi mittere inconsultum duxi. Præterquam enim quod ob rerum mearum, cum e Dania discederem, conturbationem, ea quæ de ☾â prius conceperam, diligentius examinare nequierim, ij etiam numeri, qui a quodam studiosorum meorum, Typographo cuidam imperito Hamburgi, post meum discessum, commissi sunt, admodum negligenter et depravate imprimebantur, ut omnem istum laborem frustraneum habuerim. Dum vero aliquantisper in Saxonia postmodum subsisto, clementissime id concedente Cæsarea Maiestate (quæ me Pragam vocârat) donec pestis in Bohemia remitteret, Tabulas illas Prostaphæresium Lunarium denuo ad scrupula secunda diligentissime supputari feci; ubi non saltem ille, de quo tu mones, sed et alij errores, negligentia tam supputatoris, quam Typographi prius commissi, satis mihi patuerunt. Sed cum ne sic quidem apparentiæ Lunares hinc derivatæ cœlesti normæ tam præcise congruerant, prout desiderabam, aliam inivi rationem, et nactus melius hîc in Bohemia otium, tam Hypothesin Lunaris motus, quam ei superstructos numeros denuo redintegravi, omniaque huc facientia nunc prælo adorno. Quæ ubi Typis absoluta, et Progymnasmatum Astronomicorum e nostris Tomo primo debito loco inserta fuerint, te eorundem, unâ cum toto libro, qui Solaris quoque motionis normam expedit, et millenas circiter fixas stellas accurate emendat, reddam participem. Interea hanc intervenientem morulam candide accipe. Licet autem Tabulæ illæ priores, Lunam concernentes, non exactæ fuerint, nec mihi ipsi suffecerint, tantam tamen deviationem, quantam tu in supputatione trium exemplorum, quæ in Epistolis Astronomicis reperiuntur, inducere videris, non admittunt, prout repetitio calculi iuxta nostram sententiam hisce adiungenda (modo Legatus, opinione citius, non abierit) te edocebit. Ubi vero librum nostrum Progymnasmatum, cuius memini, nactus fueris, omnia plenius et subtiliori indagine inde percipies. Tabulam illam primi mobilis universaliorem a te ad singula 10 minuta extensam si per occasionem mecum communicaveris, rem gratissimam præstiteris. Ego vicissim nonnulla ex meis, sive prælo absoluta vel secus, data oportunitate, retribuam.

Ephemerides tuas 10 Annorum postremo emissas Francofurto accepi. Nihil in ijs, quod a prioribus differat, te correxisse animadverto, sed solummodo quædam supplementi loco addidisse, mea equidem opinione non inutilia. Facis spem reliquorum 20 Annorum mox subsequentium, quos pariter obtinere averem.

ORIGANUM illum, Francofurtensem ad Oderam Mathematicum et Ephemeridum supputatorem, in hisce tuis ultimo editis necdum, prout meruit, redarguisti, facturus fortassis idipsum in residuo Ephemeridum Tomo. Mihi sane eximia tua diligentia in hac pragmateiâ semper placuit, eamque alijs commendare non desino. Et abhorret animus ab ijs, qui philautia quadam et arrogantia moti aliorum labores vel levissima de causa insectantur, sæpe nodum in scirpo quærentes; sed accidit ijs, nec iniuria, quod Comicus aiebat: dicendo quæ volunt, rursus quæ nollent audiunt. Quod Tabulas primi mobilis præstantiores procul dubio, quam hactenus habuimus, mediteris, probo, utque Opus illud lucem publicam mature videat, exopto.

De Heliacis emersionibus et occultationibus Planetarum et fixarum non est, quod admodum sis sollicitus. Res hæc præcisione rata tractari nequit, eo quod limites illi multifariam varient, non saltem ratione diversæ inclinationis sphæræ, sed prout aëris puritas in quovis Horizonte maior minorve fuerit. Nec est in omnibus stellis fixis primæ aut secundæ magnitudinis, par ratio, uti neque in cæteris: differentia etiam non minima incidit, prout stellæ in parallelo aliquo Horizontis, a loco ubi Sol oritur vel occidit, versus meridiem aut septentrionem, plus minusve distiterint. Et Planetæ, prout visibiles diametros, iuxta ☌ vel ☍ ☉lis occasione variæ remotionis a Terra alterant, nonnihil etiam discriminis pariunt, Latitudine ipsorum, quæ necdum satis comperta est, etiam difficultatem non postremam ingerente, ut ob id hoc negotium, per se etiam non admodum necessarium, vix a quoquam iusta amussi extricari posse autumem. Unde etiam in eo hactenus curiosam operam non locavi. Crepusculorum terminos quoad ☉lem a veteribus Astronomis constitutos, mediocriter bene se habere animadverti. Nam ☉lem iuxta æquinoctia arcum crepusculi efficere part. 17½ quam proxime, iam antea in Dania comperi. An id in Italia et alibi, sub rectiore sphæra consentiat, indecisum relinquo. Ephemerides ☉ huius anni, aut nunc per filium, aut postmodum, si tam cito exemplum describi nequeat, obtinebis. Addidi 4 annorum Ephemerides ☉ interea supputatas; ex his facile plures derivabis. Apogæum eius nunc versatur in P. 5 M. 40 ♋: et Eccentricitas est P. 2 M. 9 qualium semidiameter Eccentrici 60. Longitudinem eius non ab inæquali Æquinoctiorum præcessione, qualem COPERNICUS frustra admisit, derivo, sed ab Æquinoctio simplici, quod proximis sæculis insensibiliter variat, et singulis nunc annis 51'' præcise, qualis etiam est fixarum motus, antevertit. Si vero Æquinoctiorum præcessio e Spica ♍ ad imitationem COPERNICI nunc constituenda foret, esset illa hoc ipso anno part. 28 M. 16 exuperans Copernicæam numerationem sexta Grad. parte, licet prima stella ♈ ab Æquinoctio verno non elongetur ultra Gradus 27 M. 37. Quæ discrepantia hinc originem trahit, quod COPERNICUS intervallum longitudinis Spicæ et primæ ♈ ex PTOLEMÆI abaco, non ipso cœlo (uti oportuit) perperam assumpserit, discrimine incidente M. 39, quod est intolerabile. Verum de his et similibus alias forte copiosius tecum philosophari licebit, ubi Opera mea Astronomica, quorum editionem, quantum in me est, urgeo et accelero, lucem publicam viderint. Plurima inibi invenies ab ijs, quæ hactenus in Astronomicis tradita sunt, non parum discrepantia.

Si quid in elevationibus Poli illic in Italia, cuius exactiorem Geographiam moliris, exploratum habes, aut (quod mallem) longitudinibus locorum rectius limitandis, id, quicquid est, mihi impertiaris velim. Conducerent huc ad longitudinis et Meridianorum differentias apposite determinandas Eclipses Lunares, modo aliquas ibi diligenter præteritis annis cœlitus denotatas in promptu haberemus. Quod si non concedatur, attende diligenter per tua Instrumenta ad illam, quam hic labens annus subministrat, qui etiam in fine, statim a brumali Solstitio, quandam evidentem Solarem exhibebit, pariter apud vos studiose observandam, cuius calculum non minus quam Lunarem e numeris nostris, ijs, quæ prius pollicitus sum, subiungo, ut cum animadversione cœlesti isthic conferri queat, et certitudo numerationis nostræ explorari.

Instrumenta mea omnia, quibus in Dania utebar, numero 28, modo hîc Pragæ, non longe ab Arce, in Cæsaris quadam magnifice extructa domo, disposita sunt. Quod Colophonis loco indicare volui. Neque enim plura nunc scribere temporis penuria patitur. Id saltem peramanter te rogo, ut Filium meum, præsentium exhibitorem, tibi diligenter commendatum habeas, atque ut ea, quæ Bononiæ visu digna sunt, monstrari cures, eumque pariter Romæ tuis amicis et familiaribus commendes. Iamque te, Excellentissime Domine MAGINE, quam optime et diutissime valere cupio.

Dabantur Pragæ Bohæmorum Die 24 Ianuarij Anno 1601.
Excellentiæ tuæ studiosissimus
TYCHO BRAHE, manu propria scripsi.
text.english:
**To the most renowned and most excellent man, Lord Giovanni Antonio Magini of Padua, Professor of the Mathematical sciences in the illustrious Gymnasium of Bologna, and his honoured friend. To Bologna.**

Greeting.

Your most courteous and most learned letter, most renowned and excellent Lord Magini, dated 4 March of last year, I duly received; but no sure means of writing back to it has offered itself to me until now — **by my elder son, Tycho by name, accompanying the most illustrious and ample Legate of the Great King of the Persians**. And since I have learned that, from the chief Legate (**an Englishman by nation**), he will pass through **Bologna** on his journey toward Rome, I judged it not to be omitted that I should greet you by my [letter], and write back somewhat to your last.

**That you have not found it a burden to procure so diligently that business secretly committed to your trust, I owe and give you the greatest thanks. And the plan you propose pleases me well — about that most excellent Bernardino Baldi of Urbino, Abbot of Guastalla, who has proposed to write the *Lives of the Mathematicians*. For there, what we are contriving can be most conveniently inserted.** Yet I should wish (as I asked before) that the first conceptions be communicated to me, that I may interpose some judgement of mine too — since my affairs can be known to no one more rightly than to me myself. The **verses composed in my honour, and further augmented than the earlier were, the son will show**. If anything in the earlier was changed, it can be restored hence, and what is wanting there completed. The rest I commit to your prudence and your benevolent will toward me.

**That the most illustrious and most reverend Cardinal of the Santi Quattro [SS. Quatuor]** — a man, doubtless, of eminent and varied learning, and most loving of Mathematical things — **observed the Solar Eclipse of the year [15]98, with what diligence was possible, I received most gladly**; and the description, communicated to me, of what His most illustrious Lordship noted, is welcome — though, on account of the rarity of clear weather, he could not designate everything so precisely as he wished. I rejoice, and greatly congratulate these studies, **that at Rome, even among the most illustrious Cardinals, are found those who hold divine Astronomy in esteem** (as is clear from this alone). This Eclipse was observed at **Uraniborg in Denmark, with my instruments still remaining there, in my absence** — for I was then dwelling near Hamburg, where the clear weather requisite for searching out its appearances accurately did not shine. What was noted at the said Uraniborg you have in the adjoined paper, together with the epilogue of my calculation, as it is drawn from our newest restitution of the motion of the Luminaries. Nay, **I have at the same time assigned this year's Solar Eclipse, which happens on the 10th of July** [1601], both as to the observation and to my reformed calculation, that it may be compared with your considerations in Italy — whether had by the aforesaid most illustrious Cardinal, or by yourself, or by any other. From these numbers I now send, you will draw another reckoning, and that more exact than the former, in defining the Lunar course and its phenomena.

**I was not ignorant that those Tables of the Lunar motion, which you received from the noble youth Franz Tengnagel, my household-member, were immature**; and so I judged it ill-advised to send them you at that time. For besides that, on account of the disturbance of my affairs when I left Denmark, I could not examine more diligently what I had earlier conceived about the **Moon**, those numbers too, which were committed by one of my students to a certain unskilled Printer at Hamburg after my departure, **were printed very negligently and corruptly, so that I held all that labour frustrated**. But while I afterward stayed a while in Saxony (the Imperial Majesty, who had called me to Prague, most clemently granting it, until the plague in Bohemia should abate), **I had those Tables of the Lunar Prosthaphaereses computed anew, most diligently, to the seconds; where not only the error you warn of, but other errors too — committed before by the negligence as much of the computer as of the Printer — became clear enough to me**. But since, even so, the Lunar appearances derived hence did not agree so precisely with the celestial norm as I desired, I entered upon another method; and, having got better leisure here in Bohemia, **I restored anew both the Hypothesis of the Lunar motion and the numbers built upon it, and am now setting all that conduces hither at the press**. Which, when finished in print, and inserted in the due place of the first Volume of our *Astronomical Progymnasmata*, I will make you partaker of — together with the whole book, which also expedites the norm of the Solar motion, and accurately emends about a thousand fixed stars. Meanwhile take this intervening little delay in good part. But although those earlier Tables, concerning the Moon, were not exact, nor sufficient to me myself, **yet they do not admit so great a deviation as you seem to introduce in the computation of the three examples found in the *Astronomical Letters*** — as the repetition of the calculation, according to my view, to be adjoined to these (provided the Legate has not left sooner than expected), will teach you. But when you have got our book of the *Progymnasmata*, of which I spoke, you will perceive all more fully and by a subtler inquiry. **If, by occasion, you would communicate to me that more universal Table of the *primum mobile*, extended by you to single 10 minutes**, you would do a most welcome thing; I in turn, when occasion is given, will repay some of mine, whether finished at the press or not.

**Your Ephemerides of 10 years, last published, I received from Frankfurt.** I notice that you have corrected nothing in them that differs from the earlier, but only added certain things by way of supplement — not useless, in my opinion. You give hope of the remaining 20 years soon to follow, which I should likewise wish to obtain.

**That Origanus, the Mathematician of Frankfurt-on-Oder and computer of Ephemerides, you have not yet refuted in these last-published [of yours], as he deserved** — perhaps to do the same in the remaining Volume of Ephemerides. To me indeed your eminent diligence in this work has always pleased, and I do not cease to commend it to others. And my mind abhors those who, moved by a certain self-love and arrogance, persecute others' labours for the slightest cause, **often seeking a knot in a bulrush** [a problem where none is]; but it happens to them — and not unjustly — what the Comic [Terence] said: *"by saying what they want, they hear in turn what they would not."* That you meditate Tables of the *primum mobile* more excellent, doubtless, than we have hitherto had, I approve; and I wish that that Work may see the public light in good time.

**About the heliacal emersions and occultations [risings and settings] of the Planets and the fixed [stars], there is no [cause] that you should be very anxious. This matter cannot be treated with sure precision, because those limits vary manifoldly** — not only by reason of the sphere's different inclination, but as the purity of the air, in any given Horizon, is greater or less. Nor is the reckoning equal in all fixed stars of the first or second magnitude, as neither in the rest; a not-small difference too falls in, as the stars in some parallel of the Horizon are more or less distant — toward south or north — from the place where the Sun rises or sets. And the Planets, as they alter their visible diameters near the conjunction [☌] or opposition [☍] of the Sun, by occasion of their varying distance from the Earth, also produce some difference; their **Latitude** (which is not yet sufficiently established) introduces a difficulty not the least; so that I reckon this business — not very necessary in itself either — can scarcely be extricated by anyone with just exactness. Whence I have not hitherto placed curious labour on it. **The limits of the twilights with respect to the Sun, set by the ancient Astronomers, I have found moderately well [established]; for I found before, in Denmark, that the Sun, near the equinoxes, makes a twilight-arc of 17½° most nearly.** Whether this agrees in Italy and elsewhere, under a more upright sphere, I leave undecided. The Ephemeris of the **Sun** for this year you will obtain, either now by the son, or afterward, if a copy cannot be made so quickly; I have added the Ephemerides of the Sun for 4 years, computed meanwhile; from these you will easily derive more. **Its Apogee is now at 5° 40′ of Cancer [♋]; and the Eccentricity is 2° 9′, of which the semidiameter of the Eccentric is 60. Its longitude I derive not from an unequal precession of the equinoxes (such as Copernicus vainly admitted), but from a simple Equinox** — which in the recent centuries varies imperceptibly, and now anticipates precisely **51″ each year, such as is also the motion of the fixed [stars]**. But if the precession of the equinoxes were now to be set from Spica of Virgo [♍], in imitation of Copernicus, it would be, this very year, **28° 16′ — exceeding the Copernican numeration by a sixth of a degree** — although the first star of Aries [♈] is not elongated from the vernal equinox beyond 27° 37′. **Which discrepancy draws its origin from this: that Copernicus wrongly assumed the interval of longitude of Spica and of the first of Aries from Ptolemy's table, not from the sky itself (as he ought) — a difference of 39′ falling in, which is intolerable.** But of these and the like it will perhaps be allowed to philosophise with you more copiously another time, when my Astronomical Works (whose edition I urge and hasten, so far as in me lies) shall have seen the public light. Very many things you will find therein not a little discrepant from what has hitherto been handed down in Astronomical [matters].

If you have anything explored in the elevations of the Pole there in Italy (of which you are preparing a more exact Geography), or (which I should prefer) in the more rightly limiting of the longitudes of places, share with me whatever it be. **Lunar Eclipses would conduce hither, for aptly determining the differences of longitude and of Meridians, had we but some diligently noted there in past years.** And if that be not granted, attend diligently, with your Instruments, to the one that this passing year furnishes — which also at its end, right after the winter Solstice, will exhibit a certain evident Solar one, equally to be studiously observed with you; whose calculation, no less than the Lunar, from our numbers, I subjoin to those I before promised, that it may be compared with the celestial observation there, and the certainty of our numeration explored.

**All my Instruments, which I used in Denmark, 28 in number, are now arranged here at Prague, not far from the Castle, in a certain magnificently-built house of the Emperor's.** Which I wished to indicate by way of a colophon; for the scarcity of time does not allow me to write more now. This only I lovingly ask: that **you hold my Son, the bearer of the present [letter], diligently commended to you, and take care that the things worth seeing at Bologna be shown him, and that you likewise commend him at Rome to your friends and familiars.** And now, most excellent Lord Magini, I wish you to fare most well and most long.

Given at Prague of the Bohemians, the 24th day of January, the year 1601.
Most zealous of Your Excellency,
**Tycho Brahe**, written in my own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Recipient.** **Giovanni Antonio Magini** at **Bologna** (cf. brahe-t_16010220001, brahe-t_16000103002). Carried by **Tycho's son** travelling with the **Persian embassy** (cf. brahe-t_16010430001, brahe-t_16000124001).
- **Significance — the Baldi self-monument, the Roman cardinal's eclipse, the lunar-tables saga, and Tycho's solar/precession theory.**
 - **The Bernardino Baldi insertion (a key self-monument document).** Tycho approves Magini's plan to insert Tycho's biography into **Bernardino Baldi of Urbino's *Lives of the Mathematicians* (*Le vite de' matematici*)** — the *Italian* counterpart to the **Brasch/Magini panegyric-history commissions** (brahe-t_16010414001, brahe-t_16000103002). He wants to vet "the first conceptions" himself (and the **augmented verses**).
 - **The Cardinal's eclipse.** A Roman **Cardinal of the Santi Quattro [Coronati]** observed the **1598 solar eclipse**; Tycho is delighted "even Cardinals esteem divine Astronomy," and sends his own **Uraniborg observation + calculation** of that eclipse, plus the **10 July 1601 solar eclipse**, for Italian comparison.
 - **The lunar-tables saga (candid).** Tycho explains why the **lunar Tables Tengnagel gave Magini were immature**: the disruption of leaving Denmark; **a student's negligent, corrupt Hamburg printing**; a Saxony-interval recomputation "to the seconds" that exposed more errors; and finally a **wholly restored lunar hypothesis** now at press for the ***Progymnasmata*** (with the solar norm + the ** c. 1000-star catalogue**). He insists the old tables don't admit the **large deviation Magini found in the three *Epistolae* examples** (cf. brahe-t_16010220001), and asks for Magini's **10-minute *primum mobile* table**.
 - **Ephemerides & Origanus.** Acknowledges Magini's **10-year Ephemerides** (mere supplements, no corrections); urges Magini to **refute Origanus** (David Origanus of Frankfurt-on-Oder) "as he deserved," with a Terence tag ("by saying what they want, they hear what they would not") and the proverb "**seeking a knot in a bulrush**."
 - **Heliacal risings & twilight.** A careful statement that **heliacal risings/settings cannot be treated with precision** (atmospheric purity, latitude, star magnitude, planetary diameter/latitude); and the datum that **the twilight-arc near the equinoxes is c. 17½°** (the solar depression), found in Denmark.
 - **Solar parameters & precession theory.** Tycho's solar elements: **Apogee 5° 40′ Cancer, Eccentricity 2° 9′ (of 60)**; longitude from a **simple (uniform) equinox precessing 51″/year, *not* Copernicus's variable precession** (cf. the Scaliger debate, brahe-t_16000723001); and a sharp catch that **Copernicus took the Spica–Aries interval from Ptolemy's table, not the sky — a 39′ error "intolerable."**
 - **The 28 instruments at Prague.** The closing colophon: **"All my instruments, 28 in number, are now arranged at Prague … in a magnificently-built house of the Emperor's"** (cf. brahe-t_16001110001, brahe-t_16000926003).
- **Cross-references.** The **self-monument** thread (Baldi ↔ Brasch/Magini panegyric, brahe-t_16010414001, brahe-t_16000103002); the **Magini** correspondence (brahe-t_16010220001); the **son/Persian-embassy** thread (brahe-t_16010430001); the **lunar-/solar-theory** and **Progymnasmata** threads.
- **Persons & works named.** Magini; **Tycho the Younger** (the bearer); the **Persian Legate** (Anthony Sherley, "an Englishman"); **Bernardino Baldi** of Urbino (the *Vite de' matematici*); the **Cardinal of the Santi Quattro**; **Franz Tengnagel**; **David Origanus**; **Copernicus, Ptolemy**; **Terence** ("the Comic"); the *Progymnasmata*. Places: **Prague**, **Bologna**, **Rome**, **Uraniborg/Denmark**, **Hamburg**, **Saxony**, **Frankfurt**. Glyphs ☉ ☾ ☌ ☍ ♋ ♍ ♈ reproduced.
- **Calendar.** *Die 24 Ianuarij Anno 1601* at Prague → **24 January 1601 [N.S.]** (label agrees; the doubled "1601…1601" in the label field is a catalogue artefact).

documents.incipit: CUM magni Persarum Regis amplissima Legatio, quæ hîc aliquandiu apud Sacram Cæsaream …

text.original:
SERENISSIMO ET POTENTISSIMO PRINCIPI AC DOMINO, DOMINO FERDINANDO, MAGNO DUCI ETRURIÆ ETC. DOMINO SUO CLEMENTISSIMO.
SERENISSIME ET POTENTISSIME PRINCEPS, DOMINE CLEMENTISSIME.

CUM magni Persarum Regis amplissima Legatio, quæ hîc aliquandiu apud Sacram Cæsaream Maiestatem, Dominum meum Clementissimum, morata est, nunc in Italiam cogitet, et antequam Romam venerit, Serenissimam Celsitudinem Tuam in Etruria sua salutare, et quæ in mandatis habet, eidem reverenter exponere constituerit, mei officij esse ratus sum, Serenissimam Celsitudinem Tuam de TENGNAGLIO nostro clementissime bene meritam hisce literulis submisse compellare, præsertim cum Legationis eius antesignanum, Illustrissimum Dominum AMMONIUM SCHERLEJ, natione Anglum, filius meus natu maior, TYCHO nomine, comitetur. Est autem ille idem filius, quem antea in Serenissimæ Celsitudinis Vestræ Aula aliquandiu servire exoptâram, nisi obstacula quædam intervenissent, quæ attingere supervacaneum. Tradidissem illi Opera, quæ hactenus in Astronomicis elucubravi, secum adsportanda, prout Serenissima Celsitudo Vestra aliquando clementissimis suis ad me literis expetijt, nisi quædam in singulis ferme adhuc desiderarentur, typographico labore necdum absoluto. Quod ubi effectum, Serenissimæ Celsitudinis Vestræ Clementissimæ voluntati demisse et lubentissime obsecundabo.

Remoram nonnullam, quo minus illa ad Colophonem deducta sint, iniecit migratio mea ex Arce prioris habitationis Bennatica huc Pragam, sic clementissime mandante Cæsarea Maiestate, quo propior ei factus, humillima mea servitia ipsius Maiestati promptius præstare possem, allatis etiam huc omnibus Instrumentis Astronomicis, quibus antea in Dania Patria mea usus sum, quæ numero sunt 28, ijsdemque in domo quadam ampla et magnifice, Italica architectura, non longe ab Arce iuxta Cæsaris hortum extructa, ordine dispositis, donec in locum quendam usui eorum aptiorem, a Cæsarea Maiestate clementissime deputatum, transferantur. Quod et brevius futurum spero. Idque Serenissimæ Celsitudini Vestræ debita submissione (siquidem eam benignissime studijs meis favere compertum habeam) indicandum duxi. Pluribus vero eam gravioribus intentam hac mea interpellatione remorari nec volo nec decet. Quare nunc finem facio, id solummodo addens et humillime rogans, ut Serenissima Celsitudo Vestra prædictum filium meum sibi commendatum habere non dedignetur, Deus Opt. Max. Serenissimam Celsitudinem Vestram Reipublicæ emolumento quam diutissime servet florentem et incolumem.

Praga die 28 Ianuarij Anno 1601.
Serenissimæ Celsitudini Vestræ
submisse addictissimus
TYCHO BRAHE,
manu propria scripsi.
text.english:
**To the Most Serene and Most Powerful Prince and Lord, Lord Ferdinand, Grand Duke of Etruria etc., his most Clement Lord.**
**Most Serene and Most Powerful Prince, most Clement Lord.**

Since the most ample Legation of the great King of the Persians — which has tarried here for some time with the Sacred Imperial Majesty, my most Clement Lord — is now minded [to go] into Italy, and, before it comes to Rome, has resolved to salute Your Most Serene Highness in your Tuscany, and reverently to lay before you what it has in its instructions, I have judged it to be of my duty humbly to address Your Most Serene Highness — who have so most clemently deserved well of our Tengnagel — with this little letter; especially since my elder-born son, Tycho by name, accompanies the leader of that Legation, the Most Illustrious Lord Anthony Sherley, an Englishman by nation. And he is that same son whom I had earlier wished to serve for a while in Your Most Serene Highness's Court, had not certain obstacles intervened, which it is superfluous to touch upon. I would have handed to him the Works which I have hitherto elaborated in Astronomy, to carry with him — as Your Most Serene Highness once requested of me by your most clement letters — were not certain [parts] still wanting in almost each of them, the typographic labour not yet completed. When that is done, I will humbly and most gladly comply with Your Most Serene Highness's most clement will.

Some delay, hindering their being brought to the colophon [i.e. to completion], was thrown in the way by my removal from the Castle of my former dwelling, Benátky, hither to Prague — the Imperial Majesty so most clemently commanding, that, being made nearer to him, I might the more readily render my most humble services to His Majesty; all my Astronomical Instruments, too, which I formerly used in Denmark my homeland, having been brought hither — 28 in number — and these set out in order in a certain ample house, magnificently built in the Italian architecture, not far from the Castle, beside the Emperor's garden, until they be transferred to some place fitter for their use, most clemently assigned by the Imperial Majesty; which I hope will be shortly. And this I have thought to indicate to Your Most Serene Highness with due submission (since I have found you most benignly to favour my studies). But I neither wish, nor is it fitting, to detain you — intent on weightier matters — with this my interpellation. Wherefore I now make an end, adding only this, and most humbly asking, that Your Most Serene Highness would not disdain to hold my aforesaid son commended to you. May God, best and greatest, preserve Your Most Serene Highness, for the benefit of the Commonwealth, flourishing and unharmed for the longest time.

Prague, the 28th of January, in the year 1601.
Your Most Serene Highness's
most submissively devoted,
TYCHO BRAHE,
I wrote [this] with my own hand.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender, recipient & register.** **Tycho Brahe** at **Prague**, in the high princely-petition register, to **Ferdinando I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany** (*Magnus Dux Etruriae*, 1549–1609) — a patron who had earlier sought Tycho's published works. The letter commends Tycho's elder son to the Grand Duke.
- **The Persian-embassy occasion (a remarkable historical node).** The *amplissima Legatio magni Persarum Regis* = the famous **Persian embassy of Shah Abbas I**, which travelled through Europe 1599–1602 seeking an anti-Ottoman alliance, had stayed at Rudolf II's court and was now bound for **Italy and Rome**, via the Tuscan court. Its leader — *antesignanus … Ammonius Scherlej, natione Anglus* — is **Sir Anthony Sherley** (1565–1635?), the English adventurer who co-led the embassy. **Tycho's elder son, Tycho Brahe the Younger,** travelled in this embassy's company toward Florence — the occasion and bearer of this very letter.
- **Persons named.**
 - *Ferdinandus, Magnus Dux Etruriae* = **Ferdinando I de' Medici**.
 - *Ammonius Scherlej* = **Anthony Sherley**, the embassy's English leader.
 - *filius meus natu maior, Tycho* = **Tycho Brahe the Younger**, Tycho's elder son, the *commendatus*; once intended for service at the Medici court (frustrated by unstated "obstacles").
 - *Tengnaglius noster* = **Franz Tengnagel**, of whom the Grand Duke had "deserved well" (during Tengnagel's Italian sojourn at the Tuscan and Roman courts, cf. brahe-t_16000306002).
 - *Sacra Caesarea Maiestas* = **Rudolf II**.
- **The works and the move (valuable material history).** Tycho explains he cannot yet send the **Works he has elaborated in astronomy** (the great unfinished publication programme — the *Progymnasmata* and related volumes) because the **printing is not finished** (*typographico labore necdum absoluto … ad Colophonem*). The delay was caused by his **removal from Benátky to Prague** at the Emperor's command, to be nearer the court. He records that his **28 astronomical instruments**, brought from Denmark, are now **arranged in a large house of Italian architecture beside the Emperor's garden** at Prague, pending transfer to a fitter site — a precise datum on the Prague phase of the Tychonic observatory (the Kurtz/Belvedere arrangement).
- **Place.** *Praga* = Prague; *Bennatica arx* = Benátky; *Etruria* = Tuscany.
- **Edition note.** The edition cites the letter to a printed *Bibliotheca mathematica*; it is also in Dreyer's *Opera Omnia*. No manuscript witness is recorded — the text descends through print.
- **Epistolary formulae.** *Serenissima Celsitudo Vestra* = "Your Most Serene Highness" (declined throughout); subscription *submisse addictissimus* → "most submissively devoted"; *manu propria scripsi* → "I wrote with my own hand."
- **Calendar.** Dateline *die 28 Ianuarij Anno 1601* at Prague; the edition marks **n.s. (New Style)** — apt for Imperial Prague and for the Catholic Italian recipient. Reproduced, not converted.

Collated proper names (Ammonium Scherlej = the English translation resolves this to the historically-attested Anthony Sherley, leader of the Persian legation, consistent with "natione Anglum" — an informed identification, not a fabrication), the instrument count (28), the place-names (Bennatica/Benátky, Praga), and closing date (28 Ianuarij Anno 1601) against Dreyer — exact match. Published English is complete and accurate.

text.original:
NOBILITATE PERILLUSTRI ET ERUDITIONE PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO, D. TYCHONI BRAHE DANO, DOMINO DE KNUDSTRUP, ET ARCIS URANIBURG IN INSULA HELLESPONTI DANICI HUÆNA FUNDATORI.

CUM abs te nihil ad nos allatum sit post eas litteras, quas ad me scriptas D. IOANNI FRANCISCO SAGREDO Patritio Veneto commendasti, ut ad me perferendas curaret, quibus ego et statim respondi diligenter, eiusdem opera usus, ut ad te tuto transmitteretur, suspicari coepi suboffensum esse te, quod ego in tua causa procuranda lentior expectatione et voluntate tua fuissem. Sed, mi TYCHO, illud te reputare cum animo tuo velim, quae non in nostra, sed in aliorum manu sunt sita, ea non tam cito confici posse: his accedit occupatio domestica; solus sum meae familiae moderator, quam in officio continere, cui opportuna ac necessaria providere necesse est, ita, quod tempus aut studijs, aut amicorum negotijs obeundis dicatum fuit, id invito mihi domesticae curae eripiunt. Ac dum quidem studia in scholis publice exercentur, et tum mihi et publice et privatim auditoribus studiosisque meis opera danda est; cum autem illa intermittuntur, ne tum quidem otioso mihi esse licet, ultimis enim elapsis duobus annis a Serenissimo Duce Mantuae sum accersitus, ut per vacationum dies, Principibus suis filijs in Mathematica facultate instruendis vacarem. Neque vero sufficere ille sibi duxit omne istud aestivum tempus atque autumnale, quo solemus a publicis lectionibus feriari; sed et hoc, quod ad Quadragesimam usque ab ineunte fere Ianuario nobis vacuum datur, oportet me ab eodem accersitum, magno meo incommodo, Mantuae commorari. Cum igitur ad Aulam Imperatoriam ab ipso Serenissimo Duce sit destinatus Rerum suarum Procurator, Nobilissimus Comes LÆLIUS ARIVABENUS, percommodum mihi visum est, has ad te litteras ab eo perferendas mittere.

Quod itaque ad praeclarum tuum illud de Restitutionibus coelestium motuum opus spectat, vellem equidem incepisse fructum aliquem ex eo percipere. Solum enim habui cathalogum stellarum inerrantium, qui mihi pro thesauro est, itemque Tabulam illam motus Lunaris; putabamque posse me primo quoque tempore habere a te motum Solis correctum, itemque Motus Lunaris complementum, sed, ut video, frustra putabam. Dubitationes etiam mihi sese obijcientes in hac Lunari tua Tabula, cuius supputationes ad unguem congruere tuis observationibus non perspicio, dilui abs te volebam, docerique praeterea de arcubus visionum, stellarum tum errantium, tum inerrantium in eum usum, de quo ad te perscripsi. Adhaec operam meam ultro obtuli in supputandis aequationum Tabulis, neglectis scrupulis Proportionalibus, Argumenti aequationibus et excessibus, iuxta novas meas inventiones, quae ab ijs omnibus, a quibus perspectae sunt, utilissimae ac nobilissimae iudicantur, cum earum ope omnes supputationum labores facile compendiosiores fiant. Habeo et alias quasdam vias, ad eundem scopum attingendum planiores et compendiosiores, quas non tam cito alijs communicandas esse iustis de causis decrevi. Quae ne tu somnia esse putes, mitto ad te Tabulam tuam Lunarem a me novo modo elaboratam, unâ cum eius usu, quibus compendijs perspectis tu videris, num tum diligentia tum inventione PTOLEMÆUM, COPERNICUM et REINOLDUM etiam post me longe reliquerim. Quid enim mea Prostaphaereseων Planetarum Generali Tabula, quae omnibus Planetis communis est, neque viginti paginas excedit, compendiosius excogitari poterit? an non plurimi libentius et maiori compendio per eam, quam per Ephemerides Planetarum computum subducturi sunt? Neque vero tu mireris, velim, si denuo a me supputatas videris centri variationes in hac tua Tabula, et Anomaliae aequationes; hoc enim, ut nullo fere mihi labori fuit, ita magna cum animi mei voluptate feci, quae quidem Anomaliae aequatio prodit ex additione variationis centri et aequationis secundi Epicicli. Aequationes tamen argumenti, seu maioris Epicicli, cum adhaerente eis excessu denuo supputare nolui, licet cognovissem Apogaeas aequationes omnium minimas, quae in novilunijs et plenilunijs contingunt, colligendas esse, manente Luna in puncto G secundi Epicicli, proxima puncto D, dum centrum Eccentrici occupat punctum B parvi Circelli, atque etiam Aequationes omnium maximas, quae in Quadraturis accidunt, definiendas esse, manente Luna in F, et centro Eccentrici in H, Perigaeo parvi circelli, a quibus postea eliciendus esset excessus per subductionem singularum aequationum Apogaearum a singulis his Perigaei aequationibus. Nolui, inquam, eas de integro elaborare, cum eandem viam laboriosam, ne dicam parum accuratam, praesertim in ♂, ♀ et ☿ amplius ingredi non satis e re nostra iudicarem. Si itaque idoneum me putas, qui in aliorum Planetarum Tabulis, iuxta has meas inventiones, ulli tibi usui esse possim, nihil dubites meam implorare operam, nam hac in re, ut quod res est fatear, multo me habebis promptiorem, quam in altera illa mihi tradita Provincia, cuius magna pars in aliorum manu est, ut absque aliorum opera nihil praestare valeamus, qua in his supputationibus nequaquam egeo. Illud etiam addere volo, meas has rationes promptius et commodius subservituras esse variationibus Eccentricitatum, quam usitatam, nam possumus definire numerum multiplicandum sive numerum mysticum ei adiacentem, ad unum situm, notando differentiam, quae pro altero situ extremo consurgit, ut ex ea haberi possit congruus numerus multiplicandus, vel numerus mysticus ad optatum Eccentricitatis situm. Sed pluribus alias, nunc vale, eruditissime vir, meque amantissimum tui, ac praeter omnes studiosissimum observantissimumque redamare non graveris.

Datae Mantuae, in Aula Ducali, die 20 Februarij, anno 1601.
Perillustri Dominationi tuae addictissimus
IOANNES ANTONIUS MAGINUS, Patavinus.
text.english:
**To the man most illustrious in nobility and most excellent in erudition, Lord Tycho Brahe the Dane, Lord of Knudstrup, and Founder of the castle of Uraniborg on the Island Hven in the Danish Hellespont.**

Since nothing has been brought to us from you after that letter — which, written to me, you commended to **Lord Giovanni Francesco Sagredo, a Venetian patrician**, to see delivered to me, and to which I both at once replied carefully (using his help, that it might be safely transmitted to you) — I began to suspect you were somewhat offended that I had been slower in procuring your business than your expectation and wish. But, my Tycho, I would have you consider with your mind that **what is placed not in our own hand but in others' cannot be accomplished so quickly**. To this is added domestic occupation: I am the sole governor of my household, which it is necessary to keep in order and to provide with what is fitting and needful — so that what time was devoted to studies or to friends' business, the domestic cares snatch from me against my will. And while studies are publicly carried on in the schools, I must then give my labour both publicly and privately to my hearers and students; but when these are interrupted, not even then am I allowed to be at leisure — for these last two years past **I have been summoned by the most serene Duke of Mantua to give my vacation days to instructing his princely sons in the Mathematical faculty**. Nor did he think it enough for himself, all that summer and autumn time when we are wont to take holiday from the public lectures; but also this [period], which is given us free from about the beginning of January up to Lent, I must — summoned by him, to my great inconvenience — spend at Mantua. Since, then, the most serene Duke has appointed to the Imperial Court, as Procurator of his affairs, the most noble **Count Lelio Arrivabene**, it has seemed very convenient to me to send this letter to you, to be carried by him.

As, then, concerns that famous work of yours **on the Restitutions of the celestial motions**, I could indeed wish to have begun to perceive some fruit from it. For I have had only **the catalogue of the fixed stars — which is to me as a treasure — and that Table of the Lunar motion**; and I thought I could, at the first opportunity, have from you **the corrected motion of the Sun, and likewise the complement of the Lunar motion**; but, as I see, I thought in vain. **The doubts, too, presenting themselves to me in this Lunar Table of yours — whose computations I do not perceive to agree to the nail with your observations** — I wished to have resolved by you; and to be taught besides about **the arcs of visions** [arcus visionum] of the stars, both wandering and fixed, for that use of which I wrote to you. Moreover, I have freely offered my labour in computing Tables of equations — the **proportional minutes, the Argument-equations, and the excesses** being set aside — according to my new inventions, which by all who have examined them are judged most useful and most noble, since by their help all the labours of computation easily become more compendious. I have also certain other ways, plainer and more compendious, for reaching the same goal, which for good reasons I have resolved not to communicate to others so quickly. Lest you think these are dreams, **I send you your Lunar Table, elaborated by me in a new way, together with its use** — from which compendia, once examined, you may see whether, in diligence and in invention, **I have left Ptolemy, Copernicus, and Reinhold far behind me as well**. For what could be devised more compendious than my **General Table of the Prosthaphaereses of the Planets**, which is common to all the Planets, and does not exceed twenty pages? Will not very many more gladly, and with greater economy, draw their computation by it than through the Ephemerides of the Planets? Nor would I have you wonder if you see, computed anew by me, **the variations of the centre in this Table of yours, and the equations of the Anomaly**; for this — as it was almost no labour to me — I did with great delight of mind; which Anomaly-equation, indeed, comes out from the addition of the variation of the centre and the equation of the second Epicycle. **The equations of the Argument, however, or of the greater Epicycle, with the excess attaching to them, I was unwilling to compute anew** — although I had recognised that the apogee-equations, the smallest of all, which occur at new and full moons, are to be gathered with the Moon remaining at point **G** of the second Epicycle, next to point **D**, while the centre of the Eccentric occupies point **B** of the small circle; and also that the equations greatest of all, which happen at the Quadratures, are to be defined with the Moon remaining at **F**, and the centre of the Eccentric at **H**, the Perigee of the small circle — from which the excess would afterward have to be drawn out, by subtracting the several apogee-equations from these several perigee-equations. I was unwilling, I say, to work these out entire, since I judged it not enough to our purpose to enter further upon that same laborious — not to say, scarcely accurate — way, especially in **♂ [Mars], ♀ [Venus], and ☿ [Mercury]**. If, then, you think me fit to be of any use to you in the Tables of the other Planets, according to these inventions of mine, do not at all doubt to implore my labour; for in this matter — to confess the thing as it is — you will have me far readier than in that other Province committed to me, a great part of which is in others' hands, so that without others' labour we can accomplish nothing — whereas in these computations I in no way need [them]. This too I will add: that **these methods of mine will serve the variations of the Eccentricities more readily and conveniently than the usual** [method]; for we can define the multiplier-number, or the "mystic number" adjacent to it, for one position, by noting the difference that arises for the other extreme position, so that from it the fitting multiplier-number, or mystic number, for the desired position of the Eccentricity, may be had. But of these things more another time. Now farewell, most learned man, and do not be unwilling to love in return one most loving of you, and beyond all most zealous and observant.

Given at Mantua, in the Ducal Court, the 20th day of February, the year 1601.
Most devoted to Your most illustrious Lordship,
**Giovanni Antonio Magini, of Padua.**

documents.apparatus:
- **Direction & correspondent.** **Incoming**, **Giovanni Antonio Magini (Maginus)** (1555–1617) — professor of mathematics/astronomy at **Bologna** (the man who beat Galileo to that chair), a major ephemerides-maker and table-computer — **to Tycho**. He signs "*Patavinus*" (of/from Padua). The letter survives **in Magini's own printed *Tabulae primi mobilis*** (no manuscript witness recorded).
- **Significance — Tychonic tables in Italian hands, and Magini's computational self-advertisement.**
 - **What Magini has of Tycho's work.** Only the **catalogue of fixed stars** ("a treasure to me") and **a Table of the Lunar motion**; he is still waiting (in vain) for the **corrected Solar motion and the "complement" of the Lunar motion** — a window on how partially Tycho's results had circulated before publication.
 - **A genuine objection.** Magini reports the Lunar Table's **"computations do not agree to the nail with [Tycho's] observations,"** and asks Tycho to resolve the doubts — and to teach him about the **"arcs of visions"** (visibility arcs) of planets and stars.
 - **Magini's methods.** He boasts of **new compendious computation methods** (omitting proportional minutes, argument-equations, excesses), a **"General Table of Planetary Prosthaphaereses"** under 20 pages common to all planets, claiming to have left **Ptolemy, Copernicus, and Reinhold** behind. He encloses **Tycho's own Lunar Table re-worked his way**.
 - **The technical lunar passage** is rendered literally: Magini recomputed the **variations of the centre and the anomaly-equations** of Tycho's multi-epicycle lunar model (the "second epicycle," the "small circle," lettered points **G, D, B, F, H**, apogee-/perigee-equations at syzygies and quadratures, the "excess"), but declined to redo the **argument-equations** as too laborious and "scarcely accurate," especially for **Mars, Venus, Mercury**. The lettered points refer to Tycho's/Magini's lunar diagram (not reproduced here); the geometry is translated as written, without reconstruction.
 - **An offer.** Magini volunteers to help compute the **other planets' tables** by his methods — frankly noting he is freer in pure computation than in "that other Province committed to me … a great part in others' hands" (likely his observational/instrument obligations).
- **The courier network.** Tycho's earlier letter reached Magini via **Giovanni Francesco Sagredo** (the Venetian patrician — later immortalised as an interlocutor in **Galileo's *Dialogue***); this reply travels via **Count Lelio Arrivabene**, the **Duke of Mantua's (Vincenzo I Gonzaga's) agent to the Imperial court**.
- **Persons named.** Giovanni Antonio Magini; **Tycho** (addressee, "Founder of Uraniborg on Hven in the Danish Hellespont"); **Giovanni Francesco Sagredo**; the **Duke of Mantua** (Vincenzo I Gonzaga, unnamed) and his sons; **Count Lelio Arrivabene**; **Ptolemy, Copernicus, Erasmus Reinhold**. Places: **Mantua** (ducal court), **Bologna**/**Padua** (implied), **Venice**, the Imperial court.
- **Calendar / date.** The printed source gives only "*die Februarij, anno 1601*" — **no day-number**; the catalogue label supplies **20 February 1601 [N.S.]** (Italy = New Style). Header gives "[20] February 1601 [N.S.]"; the bracket flags the supplied day. (Mantua was New Style.)

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** The day is **not** merely label-supplied: Dreyer (*Opera Omnia* VIII p. 401; running-head 10/20 Febr.) prints *die 20 Februarij*. Restored to header, Source, and translation; the bracket/“supplied” qualification is withdrawn.
- **Correction.** Fixed a pronoun-flip mistranslation in the closing boast: Magini's Latin reads 'etiam post me longe reliquerim' ('I have left them far behind me too'), confirmed at Dreyer, TBOO VIII p.400, l.37. The published English had rendered this 'even after you', misattributing Magini's self-boast about surpassing Ptolemy, Copernicus, and Reinhold to Tycho instead of to Magini himself.

text.original:
GENEROSO ET MAGNIFICO VIRO, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHEO, MATHEMATICORUM FACILE PRINCIPI, CÆSAREÆ MAIESTATIS ASTRONOMO, PATRONO ET DOMINO COLENDO.
PRAG IN BEHEMEN.
MAGNIFICE ET NOBILISSIME DOMINE, PATRONE COLENDE.

TANDEM sub BACCHI sacra ad nos diu expectatus advenit Magnificus Dominus D. GODELMANNUS. Is mihi de te renunciavit, quod accepisses carmen, quod de Mathematicis exorsus sum, et ad te sub natalem CHRISTI misi. Gratum id mihi fuit. Addidit, si saltem in cursu progrederer, te laborem et artem meam Cæsareæ Maiestati commendaturum. Id quoque gratum. Verum interim mirabar, cum ego permulta mihi a te suppeditari petierim, cur non aut omnia illa, aut quædam, quæ tibi nota sunt, simul per D. GODELMANNUM unâ cum literis tuis ad me miseris. Hæc enim potissima causa erat, cur istud fragmentum vel potius bonam partem ad te miserim, ac significavi simul, me ante progredi non posse, quam responsum a te accepissem. Rogo igitur adhuc etiam atque etiam, vir magnifice et generose, ut certa data occasione literas tuas ad me mittas unâ cum illis, quæ petij, quantum in te est. Tandiu enim adhærescere cogor. Scio, quantum me ames; igitur etiam hîc tibi curæ sim. Plura iam non scribo propter imbecillem plane valetudinem.

Bene et feliciter T. M. valeat.
Datæ Rostochij 8 Martij stylo veteri Anno 1601.
T. Magnif.
reverenter colens
MARTINUS BRASCHIUS.
text.english:
**To the generous and magnificent man, Master Tycho Brahe, easily prince of mathematicians, Astronomer of His Imperial Majesty, patron and lord to be honoured. At Prague in Bohemia. Magnificent and most noble Lord, patron to be honoured.**

At length, about the rites of Bacchus [Shrovetide], the long-awaited Magnificent Master Dr. Gödelmann arrived among us. He reported to me, concerning you, that you had received the poem which I began about the Mathematicians and sent to you about the Nativity of Christ. That was pleasing to me. He added that, if only I would proceed in [my] course, you would commend my labour and art to His Imperial Majesty. That too [was] pleasing. But meanwhile I wondered why — since I had asked that very many things be supplied me by you — you did not send me, at the same time, through Master Gödelmann, together with your letter, either all those things, or some of them, which are known to you. For this was the chief reason why I sent you that fragment, or rather a good part [of the poem], and signified at the same time that I could not proceed before I had received an answer from you. I ask therefore, again and yet again, magnificent and generous man, that, when a sure occasion is given, you send me your letter, together with those things which I asked, as far as is in you. For until then I am compelled to stick fast. I know how much you love me; therefore may I be a care to you in this too. I write no more now, on account of my plainly feeble health.

May Your Magnificence fare well and happily.
Given at Rostock, 8 March, old style, in the year 1601.
Reverently honouring Your Magnificence,
Martin Brasch.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Martin Brasch** (Braschius, 1565–1601), professor of philosophy and poetry at **Rostock**; here pressing Tycho for source-material he had promised, needed to complete a **didactic poem "about the Mathematicians"** (*carmen de Mathematicis*) which Brasch had begun and sent Tycho, in part, "about Christmas." (Brasch died later in 1601; his complaint of *imbecillis valetudo*, "feeble health," is poignant.)
- **Tie to brahe-t_16001116003.** This is the follow-up to Tycho's reply of 16 Nov 1600: Gödelmann (the go-between) had relayed that Tycho received the poem and would commend Brasch to the Emperor "if he proceeded"; Brasch answers that he *cannot* proceed until Tycho sends the promised materials.
- ***D. Godelmannus*** = **Johann Georg Gödelmann** (see brahe-t_15981112001), now Saxon-Electoral Legate, the courier between Prague and Rostock.
- ***sub Bacchi sacra*** — "about the rites of Bacchus": the festival of Bacchus, here the **Shrovetide/Carnival season** (late winter), consistent with an 8 March letter reporting Gödelmann's recent arrival; rendered with the gloss. *Caesareae Maiestatis Astronomo* — the address already styles Tycho "Astronomer of His Imperial Majesty."
- **Calendar.** *Rostochij 8 Martij stylo veteri … 1601* = **8 March 1601, Old Style** (*stylo veteri* explicit; Lutheran Rostock kept the Julian calendar). Header agrees with the label.

documents.abstract: Reports Duke Charles's occupation of almost all Livonia, the Polish Diet's resolution to wage war for three years, and personal losses from these events.
documents.incipit: CUM certa per magnificum Dominum IOANNEM GEORGIUM GODELMANNUM mihi scribendi occasio …

text.original:
MAGNIFICO ET NOBILISSIMO VIRO, D. TICHONI BRAHE, MATHEMATICO S. C. MAIESTATIS EXCELLENTISSIMO, AMICO ET PATRONO PLURIMUM OBSERVANDO.
MAGNIFICE AC NOBILISSIME DOMINE TICHO, AMICE HONORANDE.
S.

CUM certa per magnificum Dominum IOANNEM GEORGIUM GODELMANNUM mihi scribendi occasio daretur, plenius scribendum duxi. Vivo, ut possum, quando iniquitas temporis et fortunæ maiora spectare non sinit. Calamitas belli Carolini oppressit meam patriam. Nam Dux CAROLUS totam fere occupavit Livoniam. Sed qua felicitate, eventus docebit. Novisti illius tyranni dictum: aliena appetendo propria amisit. Rex statusque Poloniæ de bello per triennium magnis sumptibus gerendo in Comitijs convenerunt. Funesta ergo omnia in mea patria sunt. Quanta interim animi virtute et constantia opus sit mihi, facile intelligis, qui et bonis omnibus et maximis sumptibus propterea factis excidi. Spem tamen reliquam in DEI auxilio fixam habeo, fore ut postquam nubila et turbulenta ista tempora transierunt, pax florentissima et quies nobis restituatur. Interim tu me benevolentia et fide prosequaris singulari velim.

Quæ ad D. CHYTRÆUM de tuæ vitæ historia scripsisti, heredes eius mihi tradiderunt, quæ plene meis historicis meditationibus inseram, nec alia tui ornandi argumenta omittam. Nam te virum bonum et vere syncerum cognovi, quæ virtutes profecto pulcherrimam istam artem tuam, in qua præcellis, elegantissime illuminant. Quod vero tardius liber meus historiarum prodit, multa in causa sunt, quia et initium cuiusque rei grave est, et veritatem sequi in omnibus hoc seculo scis quam sit periculosum. Deinde alijs adhuc occupor elaborandis. Mox tamen lucem videbunt, ubi meo genio ita visum fuerit.

Vale interim, vir optime, et magnam salutem tuos domesticos meo nomine imperti.
Datæ Rostochio 10 die Martij A. 1601.
Tui amantiss.
CHRISTOPH. STURCIUS.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 403; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Orationem de SIGIS. AUG. B. M. a me habitam adiungo.
text.english:
**To the magnificent and most noble man, Master Tycho Brahe, most excellent Mathematician of His Imperial Majesty, friend and patron much to be observed. Magnificent and most noble Master Tycho, friend to be honoured. Greeting.**

Since a sure occasion of writing to me was given through the magnificent Master Johann Georg Gödelmann, I judged I should write more fully. I live as I can, since the iniquity of the times and of fortune does not permit [me] to look to greater things. The calamity of the Carolinian war has oppressed my homeland. For Duke Charles has occupied almost all Livonia. But with what good fortune, the outcome will teach. You know that tyrant's saying: "by coveting what is another's, he lost his own." The King and the Estates of Poland have agreed, in the Diet, on waging war for three years at great expense. All things, therefore, are deadly in my homeland. With how great virtue and constancy of mind I meanwhile have need, you easily understand — [I] who have fallen from all my goods, and from the greatest expenses made on that account. Yet I have my remaining hope fixed in God's help, that — after these cloudy and turbulent times have passed — a most flourishing peace and quiet may be restored to us. Meanwhile, I would wish that you pursue me with singular benevolence and faith.

What you wrote to Master Chytraeus about the history of your life, his heirs have handed over to me; which I will fully insert into my historical meditations, nor will I omit other matters for adorning you. For I have known you as a good and truly sincere man — which virtues indeed most elegantly illuminate that most beautiful art of yours, in which you excel. But that my book of histories comes forth rather slowly, there are many causes: both because the beginning of anything is hard, and because you know how dangerous it is, in this age, to follow truth in all things; then, I am still occupied in elaborating other [works]. Soon, however, they will see the light, when it shall so seem [good] to my disposition.

Farewell meanwhile, best man, and impart a great greeting to your household in my name.
Given at Rostock, the 10th day of March, in the year 1601.
Most loving of you,
Christoph Sturtz.


*[Postscript:]* I append the oration delivered by me on Sigismund August, of blessed memory.

documents.incipit: NOBILISSIME et clariss. vir, Domine et amice vetus plurimumque colende. Reddidit mihi …

text.original:
NOBILISSIMO ET CLARISSIMO VIRO, DOMINO TYCHONI BRAHEN HÆREDITARIO IN KNUDTSTRUP INCLYTI REGNI DANIÆ, ASTRONOMO EXCELLENTISSIMO, IN S. CÆSAREÆ MAIESTATIS AULA PRAGENSI, DOMINO ET AMICO SUO VETERI, PLURIMUM COLENDO. PRAGAM.

S. P.

NOBILISSIME et clariss. vir, Domine et amice vetus plurimumque colende. Reddidit mihi literas tuas vir clarissimus D. IOH. GEORGIUS GODELMANNUS, amicus meus singularis, cuius consuetudine iucundissima per dies complures usi sumus familiariter. Huic confectis feliciter negocijs suis Dresdam redituro, ducente ac fortunante Deo, 600 illos thaleros a Quæstore Iuniorum Principum tuo nomine acceptos, et hactenus apud me servatos, numeravi, recepta apocha eius. Commutavi autem thaleros Belgicos, quorum maior copia fuit, in alios imperiales, præter paucos. Aurum, in quod eos commutarem, in hisce locis vix reperitur amplius, cum maioris sit valoris in inferiori et superiori Germania. Alios sexcentos ad instans Pascha tibi debitos Quæstor solvere nunc non potuit, licet compellatus eo nomine a D. D. BORDINGO Cancellario, iam etiam Lubecensium Consule. Excusat enim magnos sumptus et expensas superiori Octobri in funus Ducis SIGISMUNDI AUGUSTI p. m. factas Suerini, quos expendere oportuit iuniores Principes tanquam proximos hæredes. Petit igitur brevis adhuc temporis dilationem sibi concedi, et quamvis haberi pecunia ista potuisset, tamen intellexi grave futurum fuisse D. GODELMANNO eam secum deferre. De summa capitali, quam etiam te repetere scribis, quid responderit, nondum comperi. Inquiram vero diligentius, anne Lubecæ vel Hamburgi mercatores sint, qui Pragæ negotientur, ut per hos pecuniæ Pragam transscribi possint; idem tu inquiras inter Pragenses mercatores. Mea sane officia et studia tibi non deerunt.

Literas ad D. CRAGIUM in Daniam mittendas non vidi. Accepi vero alias tuis adiunctas et cuidam CASPARO AGRICOLÆ, Musico regio, inscriptas, quas soluta glacie et navigatione repetita, quæ asperitate hyemis diu intermissa fuit, Hafniam transmittam. M. BRASCHIO, qui minus recte aliquamdiu valuit, quod iussisti, indicavi. Amisimus iterum nuper virum et Iureconsultum præstantissimum D. HENRICUM CAMERARIUM, qui cum patriæ suæ Brunsuigæ in dissidio cum Principe eius componendo inservijsset, et in itinere non procul Soltquella Marchiæ oppido abesset, subita cordis compressione extinctus est die 11 Februarij. Funus huc advectum 27 eiusdem terræ mandatum est honorifice. Hemiplecticus etiam est D. MARCUS LUSCOVIUS Iuriscoss. vir excellens et nunc facultatis senior. Ita nos visitat Dominus, ut appareat magnas imminere in Academia nostra mutationes.

CAROLUS Sueciæ Dux magna celeritate et successu Livoniam occupat, et quamvis exiguam nuper cladem accepit, tamen ab altera parte Dörptam urbem in finibus Livoniæ et Moscoviæ oportuno loco sitam vi occupavit, ac pleraque iam loca munita tenet, præter Rigam urbem primariam, cuius tamen vicinas arces ita occupat, ut commeatu eos terra marique intercludere possit, nisi auxilia maturius a Rege Poloniæ submittantur. Et hæc omnia hyeme maxima ex parte egit. Habet confœderatum sibi Moscovum, et quod mirum est, Suecia interim tota quiescit, et rerum necessariarum copia abundat. Poloni dicuntur in proximis regni Comitijs tres hostes proclamasse, Suecum, Moscovum et Walachum, et in tres annos magnam pecuniæ summam ad bella hæc Regi promisisse. Eventum reget Deus pro suo beneplacito, non pro hominum arbitrio aut potentia. In his regionibus, Dei beneficio, tranquillitas est, et optimus Princeps noster, Dux ULRICUS, recte adhuc valet. Ego tibi tuisque omnibus valetudinem prosperam diuturnamque opto. Salutant te filij mei IOHANNES et LUCAS, qui Theologiam iam profitetur hîc publice, et sponsus est, reverenter. Ex D. GODELMANNO Pragam aliquando veniente copiosius de statu nostro audies.

Rostochij die 11 Martij Anno 1601.
Nobil. et Excell. T. studiosiss.
LUCAS BACMEISTERUS D.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 405; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
M. CHRISTIANUS LONGICAMPIANUS mathematicus paulo post reditum suum Praga in Daniam traiecit, ubi adhuc vivit, nescio tamen quo in loco. Amo hominem, et optassem nobiscum eum manere potuisse propter studia mathematica, quæ fere iam hîc iacent. Iterum vale.
text.english:
**To the most noble and most renowned man, Lord Tycho Brahe, hereditary [lord] in Knudstrup of the renowned Kingdom of Denmark, most excellent Astronomer, in the Prague court of the Sacred Imperial Majesty, his Lord and old friend, much to be cultivated. To Prague.**

Heartiest greeting.

Most noble and most renowned man, Lord and old friend much to be cultivated. The most renowned man Lord **Johann Georg Gödelmann**, my especial friend — whose most pleasant company I enjoyed familiarly for several days — delivered your letter to me. To him, his business happily concluded, about to return to Dresden (God leading and prospering), I **paid out those 600 thalers received in your name from the Treasurer of the Junior Princes** and hitherto kept with me, taking his receipt. But I exchanged the **Belgian thalers**, of which there was the greater quantity, into **imperial** ones, except a few; for gold, into which I might change them, is scarcely to be found any more in these parts, being of greater value in Lower and Upper Germany. The **other six hundred**, owed you at the coming Easter, the Treasurer could not now pay — although urged on that account by Lord Doctor **Bording, Chancellor, [and] now also Consul [Burgomaster] of the Lübeckers** — for he excuses [it by] the great costs and expenses made last October at **Schwerin for the funeral of Duke Sigismund August, of pious memory**, which the junior Princes, as nearest heirs, had to bear; he asks, therefore, that a delay of yet a short time be granted him. And although that money could have been had, I understood it would have been burdensome for Lord Gödelmann to carry it with him. Concerning the **principal sum**, which you write you are also demanding back, what he answered I have not yet learned; but I will inquire more diligently whether there be at Lübeck or Hamburg merchants who do business at Prague, so that through these the moneys may be **transferred by bill to Prague** — let you inquire the same among the Prague merchants. My services and zeal will surely not be wanting to you.

The letters to be sent to Lord **Cragius** [Krag] in Denmark I did not see. But I received others, enclosed with yours and addressed to a certain **Caspar Agricola, the royal Musician**, which — the ice melted and navigation resumed (long interrupted by the harsh winter) — I will transmit to Copenhagen. To Master **Brasch**, who for a while was less than well, I conveyed what you ordered. We have again lately **lost a most excellent man and Jurisconsult, Lord Henrik Camerarius**, who — having served his fatherland Brunswick in composing its dispute with its Prince, and being on a journey not far from **Salzwedel**, a town of the [Brandenburg] Mark — was carried off by a sudden constriction of the heart on **11 February**; the body, brought hither, was honourably committed to earth on the 27th of the same. Also Lord **Marcus Luscovius**, jurisconsult, an excellent man and now senior of the faculty, is struck with one-sided paralysis. So the Lord visits us, that great changes appear to be imminent in our **University**.

**Charles, Duke of Sweden**, occupies **Livonia** with great speed and success; and although he lately took a slight defeat, on the other side he seized by force the city of **Dorpat [Tartu]**, conveniently set on the border of Livonia and Muscovy, and now holds most fortified places except **Riga** the chief city — whose neighbouring castles, however, he so occupies that he can cut them off from supply by land and sea, unless aid be sent in time by the **King of Poland**; and all this he did, for the most part, in winter. He has the **Muscovite** confederated with him; and — what is wonderful — Sweden meanwhile is wholly at rest, and abounds in necessaries. The **Poles** are said, in the last Diet of the kingdom, to have proclaimed three enemies — the Swede, the Muscovite, and the Wallachian — and to have promised the King a great sum for these wars for three years. God will govern the outcome by his good pleasure, not by men's will or power. In these regions, by God's grace, there is tranquillity, and our best Prince, **Duke Ulrich**, is still well. I wish you and all yours prosperous and lasting health. My sons **John** and **Lucas** — [the latter] who now publicly professes Theology here, and is betrothed — greet you reverently. From Lord Gödelmann, coming to Prague at some time, you will hear more fully of our state.

Rostock, 11 March, the year 1601.
Most devoted to Your Nobility and Excellence,
Lucas Backmeister, Doctor.


*[Postscript:]* Master Christian Longomontanus, the mathematician, a little after his return from Prague crossed over into Denmark, where he still lives — in what place, however, I do not know. I love the man, and I could have wished that he had been able to remain with us, for the sake of mathematical studies, which now lie here almost [abandoned]. Again, farewell.

documents.apparatus:
- **Sender.** **Lucas Backmeister** (Bacmeister, 1530–1608), **Superintendent of Rostock** and theologian (cf. brahe-t_16000916002, brahe-t_16001115001). Reply carried via Gödelmann.
- **The Mecklenburg debt (confirmation).** Backmeister reports the mechanics of the **first 600-thaler interest tranche**: paid to **Gödelmann** (returning to Dresden) against receipt, with the **Belgian thalers exchanged into imperial** ones (gold being scarce locally). The **second 600 (due Easter)** the **Treasurer of the junior Princes** could not pay — though pressed by **Bording** (here styled **"Chancellor, and now also Consul [Burgomaster] of Lübeck"**) — pleading the **funeral expenses for Duke Sigismund August** of Mecklenburg at **Schwerin** last October (which the junior princes, as heirs, bore; cf. the death reported in brahe-t_16000920002). On the **principal**, no answer yet; Backmeister proposes transfer **by bill of exchange** through Lübeck/Hamburg–Prague merchants.
- **Rostock news.** Letters for **Krag** (*Cragius*) and **Caspar Agricola, the royal [Danish] Musician** to be forwarded to Copenhagen once the ice clears; **Brasch** "for a while unwell." Two academic losses: the jurist **Henrik Camerarius** (d. 11 Feb 1601 of a sudden "constriction of the heart" near Salzwedel, after mediating Brunswick's dispute with its Duke; buried 27 Feb), and **Marcus Luscovius**, jurist and faculty-senior, struck with **hemiplegia** — "great changes imminent in our University."
- **The Polish–Swedish war (across the correspondence).** **Charles of Sweden** sweeping through **Livonia** (taking **Dorpat/Tartu**, threatening **Riga**), allied with **Muscovy**; the **Poles** at their Diet declaring three enemies (Swede, Muscovite, Wallachian) and voting three years' war-funds. Dovetails with the news of brahe-t_16010321001 (Henniochus), brahe-t_16000920002 (Brasch), and brahe-t_16010418001 (Rollenhagen). **Duke Ulrich** reported well.
- **Persons named.** Lucas Backmeister (and his sons **John** and **Lucas the Younger**, a theology professor); **Johann Georg Gödelmann**; **Jacob Bording** (Chancellor & Lübeck Consul); the Mecklenburg **Treasurer**; **Duke Sigismund August** of Mecklenburg (d., funeral Oct 1600); **Niels/Krag (*Cragius*)**; **Caspar Agricola** (Danish royal musician); **Martin Brasch**; **Henrik Camerarius** (jurist, d.); **Marcus Luscovius** (jurist); **Charles of Sweden**; **Duke Ulrich III**.
- **Calendar.** Dateline *Rostochij die 11 Martij Anno 1601*; Lutheran Rostock kept the **Julian (Old Style)** calendar. Header agrees with the label.

- **§1 Dreyer collation.** Closing postscript (Longomontanus crossed Prague→Denmark, "adhuc vivit"), restored from Dreyer VIII p.405 (after "Lucas Bacmeisterus D."; dropped by the working transcription).

documents.incipit: OCCASIONE oblata intermittere non debui, quin aliquid literarum ad te, Magnifice Dom. …

text.original:
MAGNIFICO ET GENEROSO DOMINO D. TYCHONI BRAHAe, DOMINO HÆREDITARIO IN KNUSTORPFF ET HEERESWART, CÆSAREAe MAIESTATIS CONSILIARIO DIGNISSIMO, AMICO SUO ET DOMINO SUMMA OBSERVANTIA COLENDO.

S. P.

OCCASIONE oblata intermittere non debui, quin aliquid literarum ad te, Magnifice Dom. TYCHO, darem, et quidem per eundem, quem ipse praesentem aliquoties cupivisti, quo etiam hisce in locis exercitatiorem sphagirum nescimus. Novissimae tuae literae sunt quas misisti per NICOLAUM MAUL quondam domesticum tuum, in quibus etiam quae ad grammatophorum expedienda praecepisti exequutus sum.

Quoad Politicum statum omnia apud nos sunt tranquilla, nihilominus tamen multae gliscunt inter magnos dominos, principes et reges simultates, quae bellorum semina et initia esse solent. Inter CAROLUM Sueciae nunc protectorem et urbem Lubecam quomodo convenit, te non latet, quod negocium nondum est consopitum, licet Lubecenses multum in eo laboraverint. Comitia Polonica nuper Warsoviae, quo et Brandenburgicus Elector, adiunctis in adsistentiam Regis Daniae, nostri principis et nonnullorum aliorum, petitum successionem in Feudum Brutenicum, legatos miserat, celebrabantur, quod denegatum illi esse intelligo, nisi regem Poloniae, Suecia nunc privatum, postliminum regem fieri opitulentur. In dictis etiam Comitijs Poloni hostes suos, ut fertur, declararunt, CAROLUM Sueciae, qui iam dudum bellum in Livonia Polonis intulit, et eousque progressus est in Livonia, ut Polonis ibidem nihil restet praeter Rigam. Et meo quidem iudicio hoc bellum non solum ad CAROLUM pertinere videtur, nisi temeritatis sibi hocipso vitium attrahat. Alter hostis Polonorum dictus est Magnus dux Moscoviae, tertius vero Walachiae Waiwoda. Utrum tot hostibus Poloni simul stare poterint, eventus docebit. In Belgico magnus est apparatus iterum belli praefixi: ALBERTUS dux Austriae exercitum ducet in Hollandiam. Hollandici status non segnius vim eius aversari moliuntur. Aestas futura absque Tragedijs magnis non praeteribit, uti praesens est forma rerum. Rex Portugaliae SEBASTIANUS in conflictu Africano amissus, nunc redivivus, ab Hispano non agnoscitur, a suis vero affectatur, qui exutus regno apud Regem Galliae hospitio fruitur. Proh deum, quanta Metamorphosis ista! EXSECCIUS Comes Angliae et successor Reginae in regno hactenus muscitatus, ante biennium a Regina in Irlandiam cum Classe Nautica missus, ob rem non satis fideliter, ut accusatur, gestam, in Parlamento damnatus, et captivus de vita periclitatur. In Patria tua Regno Daniae cura et expensis Regis nonnulla fortalitia et Castella, ut vocant, exstruuntur, nec non in Gothlandia idem fit. Ungarica a nobis non expectabis, quin potius quid rerum ibi agitur, a te perdiscere cupimus. Haec per occationem ad te pervenire volui.

Vale, ut bene etiam sit tuis.
Datae Rostochij 21 Martij anni 1601.
T. Mag. observantiss.
CHRISTOPHO. HENNIOCHUS Med.


*[Postscript — restored from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VIII, p. 408; dropped by the working transcription. See Apparatus.]*
Dux Brunsuiccensis civitati denuo commeatum intercipit, nec ulla ratione placabilis dicitur, inter quos, missis et datis a Caesarea Maiestate commissarijs, nuper frustra de pace tractatum esse, notum est.
text.english:
**To the magnificent and generous Lord, Lord Tycho Brahe, hereditary Lord in Knudstrup and Heereswart, most worthy Councillor of the Imperial Majesty, his friend and Lord to be honoured with the utmost respect.**

Heartiest greeting.

An occasion being offered, I ought not to omit to send you some bit of a letter, magnificent Lord Tycho — and that by the very man whom you yourself several times wished present, than whom we know no more practised spagyrist in these parts. Your most recent letters are those you sent through Nicolaus Maul, formerly your servant, in which I also carried out what you directed for despatching the letter-carrier.

As to the political situation, with us all is tranquil; nevertheless many enmities are swelling among the great lords, princes, and kings, such as are wont to be the seeds and beginnings of wars. How matters stand between Charles, now Protector of Sweden, and the city of Lübeck does not escape you; that business is not yet laid to rest, though the Lübeckers have laboured much over it. The Polish Diet was lately held at Warsaw, to which the Elector of Brandenburg, too, had sent envoys — with those of the King of Denmark, of our own prince, and of some others, joined in support — to seek the succession to the Prussian fief; which I understand was refused him, unless they help the King of Poland, now deprived of Sweden, to be restored as king by right of return. In that same Diet the Poles also, as is reported, declared their enemies: Charles of Sweden, who long since carried war into Livonia against the Poles, and has advanced so far in Livonia that nothing remains to the Poles there but Riga. And in my judgement this war seems not to concern Charles alone — unless by this very act he draws upon himself the charge of rashness. The second enemy of the Poles was named the Grand Duke of Muscovy, and the third the Voivode of Wallachia. Whether the Poles will be able to stand against so many enemies at once, the outcome will show. In the Low Countries there is again great preparation for an appointed war: Albert, Archduke of Austria, will lead an army into Holland; the Dutch States are contriving no less actively to repel his force. The coming summer will not pass without great tragedies, such as the present shape of things is. The King of Portugal, Sebastian, lost in the African battle, now come back to life, is not acknowledged by the Spaniard, but is favoured by his own people; he, stripped of his kingdom, enjoys hospitality with the King of France. Good God, how great a Metamorphosis is that! Essex, Earl of England and reputed successor of the Queen in the kingdom — hitherto kept quiet — sent two years ago by the Queen into Ireland with a naval fleet, [and] for the affair not faithfully enough conducted (as he is charged), condemned in Parliament, is a captive and in peril of his life. In your fatherland, the kingdom of Denmark, by the King's care and expense certain fortresses and castles (as they call them) are being built, and the same is being done in Gotland. Hungarian news you will not expect from us — rather, we desire to learn from you what is going on there. These things I wished to reach you, as occasion served.

Farewell, and may it be well with your people too.
Given at Rostock, 21 March, the year 1601.
Most respectful of Your Magnificence,
Christophorus Henniochus, physician.


*[Postscript:]* The Duke of Brunswick is again cutting off the city's provisioning, and is said to be by no means appeasable; it is known that, commissioners having lately been sent and appointed by the Imperial Majesty, peace was treated of between them, but in vain.
